Even HaEzer:
[Laws of Procreation and Containing 32 Sections]

When the Holy One, blessed be He, created His world and created man, male and female, it is written: "And God blessed them and said to them, 'Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it,'" and similarly, after the flood, He blessed Noah and his sons as it is written: "And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, 'Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.'" For it is the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, to increase the human species for the settlement of the world, as the prophet said: "He did not create it to be empty; He formed it to be inhabited" [Isaiah 45], and when Israel was exiled to Babylon, the prophet Jeremiah sent them [a message] [Jeremiah 29]: "Take wives and bear sons and daughters," meaning - do not say that since we are in exile, why should we increase offspring? Rather, you are obligated to fulfill the commandment as our God, the Lord, commanded us, and the Lord will do with us as He wills. And it is a positive commandment for every Jewish man to marry a woman and fulfill the commandment of procreation. Therefore, the scripture repeated for Noah after the blessing of "be fruitful and multiply," and commanded him and his sons with the command of the Torah: "And you, be fruitful and multiply; swarm in the earth and multiply therein," and this verse is for the commandment, and the first one is for the blessing [Rashi]. And it is a very great commandment because the existence and settlement of the world depend on it. Therefore, even one who has fulfilled the commandment and whose children have died is obligated to marry a woman and bear children again, as will be explained. The reason is that the commandment is for the sake of "He formed it to be inhabited," and since they died, he has not fulfilled the settlement [Yevamot 62]. Therefore, Hezekiah, when he did not want to marry a woman and bear children because he saw with the Holy Spirit that unworthy sons would come from him, the prophet told him in the name of the Lord that he would die in this world and not live in the world to come, and thus he said to him: "Why are you concerned with the secrets of the Merciful? Do what you are commanded, and what pleases the Holy One, blessed be He, let Him do" [Berachot 10]. And this is what we find that our Sages said that from the day that decrees increased, it would have been proper not to marry wives and not to bear children [end of the chapter "Chezkas Habatim"] – this was an expression of lamentation to increase prayer and supplication, and all the legal authorities did not bring this for the reason we wrote, and so wrote our master the Beit Yosef in his response [Siman 14]. Moreover, there the decrees were to make them abandon the religion as explained there, and even this is only for one who has fulfilled the commandment of procreation [Tosafot]. Our Sages also said [Yevamot 63] that anyone who does not engage in procreation is as if he sheds blood, as it is said: "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed," and it is followed by "And you, be fruitful and multiply." And it is also as if he diminishes the image, as it is said: "For in the image of God He made man," and it is followed by "And you, be fruitful and multiply." And it causes the Divine Presence to depart from Israel, as it is said: "To be a God to you and to your descendants after you" – when your descendants are after you, the Divine Presence rests, but if your descendants are not after you, upon whom will it rest? Upon the trees and stones? In wonderment [Yevamot 64]. And anyone who is without a wife is without joy, without blessing, without goodness, without peace, without Torah, and without a wall. He is not called 'man' at all, as it is said: "He created them male and female and called their name Man," for a man without a woman is half a body. And when he marries a woman, his sins are removed and sealed, as it is said: "He who finds a wife finds goodness and obtains favor from the Lord" [Proverbs 18], because he then distances himself from sinful thoughts and is attached to his home, therefore he obtains favor from the Lord. And the Holy One, blessed be He, called the woman a helper, as it is written: "It is not good for

A woman is not commanded in the mitzvah of procreation, for the obligation of the mitzvah is only placed upon the male. This is because in the blessing of Adam HaRishon it is written, "Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it," and in Noah it is not written "and subdue it"—this comes to teach us that the obligation is placed upon the one whose way it is to subdue the earth, and that is the male and not the female, for it is not her way to go out to war and conquer. Additionally, Hashem said to our forefather Jacob, "I am El Shaddai, be fruitful and multiply," and did not use the plural form "be fruitful and multiply"—from this, we learn that the obligation is only upon him alone. And that which is said to Adam "be fruitful and multiply" in the plural form—this is for a blessing and not a commandment. And concerning Noah, where it is written in the plural form—it is because it refers to Noah and his sons as explicitly stated in the verse, and therefore it is precise in saying, "And you, be fruitful and multiply," meaning the obligation is upon Noah and his sons, as it is written at the beginning of the matter, "And God blessed Noah and his sons," to exclude the women, even though they must necessarily be included in the blessing, for the command to leave the ark was also given to the women as it is written there at the beginning of the section, and everything that came out of the ark was blessed, just as Adam and his wife were blessed, for the first creatures were necessarily included in the blessing because the world was founded from them, and without them it is impossible to be fruitful and multiply. And even if the first woman was commanded to be fruitful and multiply, we do not learn from her for future generations, for at that time it was not possible for man to fulfill the mitzvah without her, and similarly Noah and his sons without their wives since they were alone in their world. But afterwards, even though the obligation is not upon the females, nevertheless, every male will find his mate, for Hashem implanted within them that more than the man wishes to marry, the woman wishes to be married. And we can explain the meaning of the verse as follows: "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it"—meaning: now I command both of you to be fruitful and multiply until you fill the earth with the human species, and then the obligation will be upon the one whose way it is to subdue. And similarly, concerning Noah, He said to them in the blessing, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth," meaning now the obligation is also upon the females until you fill the earth, and afterwards, "And you, be fruitful and multiply"—meaning: only you and not the females. And therefore, with Jacob, when the world was already full, He said to him in the singular form "be fruitful and multiply." Similarly, the prophet Jeremiah, when he sent to the exiled, sent to the males to take wives, because the obligation is only upon them and not upon the females.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 10: "Even though a woman is not commanded to be fruitful and multiply, some say that she should not remain without a husband due to suspicion." This is his concluding statement. And in the Tosefta Yevamot, Chapter 8, it is explained that a woman is permitted to remain without a husband. Likewise, Maimonides wrote in Chapter 21 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations that a woman has the right to never marry or to marry a eunuch. However, in Chapter 15 of the Laws of Marriage, he wrote that it is a rabbinic commandment that a woman should not remain without a husband lest she be suspected, as stated there. Nevertheless, everything depends on the situation, for in a place where suspicion is not relevant, we do not worry about this. Furthermore, according to the law, we certainly do not compel her, but it is a good piece of advice that she should not remain without a husband to distance herself from suspicion.

Some of the great authorities have written that although a woman is not commanded in the mitzvah of procreation (Pru Urvu), she is nevertheless obligated in the mitzvah of "settling the world" (Leshavet Yetzarah). However, there is no basis for these words, as the essence of the mitzvah of procreation is for the purpose of "settling" as mentioned in Section 1. And since women are not commanded in the mitzvah of procreation, it automatically follows that they are not commanded in the mitzvah of "settling the world" either. This is also evident from the words of Rambam that we brought in Section 3 and from all the legal authorities that no obligation is imposed on a woman. A clear proof for this is from what our Sages said: if the man is prevented from having children, and he cannot procreate, the woman cannot force him to divorce her, as mentioned in Section 154. If we were to say that she is commanded in "settling the world," why would she not be able to compel him?

It is true that our Rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote that a woman is also relevant to "settling the world" (Gittin 41b and Bava Batra 13), but their intention is not that women are obligated in "settling the world," but that they are relevant to it. Certainly, this is the case, as they too increase the settlement of the world. The verse "Leshavet Yetzarah" is not a commandment but a narrative that the Holy One, blessed be He, created His world to be inhabited by people, and women are included in this. This is what our Rabbis said regarding a half-slave and half-free woman who cannot marry either a slave or a free man: if we were certain that she would marry a man, we would compel her master to free her to not impede the settlement of the world. But since we are not certain she would marry because she is not commanded, therefore we do not compel the master, as mentioned there. This itself is proof that she is not commanded in anything, for if it were otherwise, how could they write that we are not certain she would marry? Rather, the main point is as we said, that certainly anyone through whom there is an impediment to the settlement of the world, like a master who has a half-slave and half-free person, we strive to see that they can increase the settlement of the world, as mentioned in Yoreh De'ah Section 267, even though no obligation is imposed on them. When it is written there that "Leshavet Yetzarah" is a great mitzvah, it does not mean that it is a mitzvah imposed on that person, for the mitzvah is procreation and on those who are commanded in it. Rather, because the reason for procreation is due to "settling the world" as mentioned, and it is the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, to increase the settlement of His world, therefore the court is obligated to ensure that there is no impediment in this great matter, even for those not commanded in procreation.

It is written in She'iltot of Rav Achai Gaon, Parashat Berachah, and this is his language: "The household of Israel is obligated to marry women and to have children and to engage in procreation, as it is written: 'Take wives and have sons and daughters.' And not only Israel, but even idol worshippers are commanded regarding procreation, as it is written, 'And you, be fruitful and multiply.'" End quote. And in Parashat Noach, he also wrote: "The household of Israel is obligated to marry women and have children and fulfill procreation," etc. End quote. And he didn't write there that idol worshippers are commanded regarding procreation, and the mitzvah of procreation is not among the mitzvot of the children of Noah, as our sages explicitly said [Sanhedrin 59b], and so wrote all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). And it seems to me that even the Gaon did not intend it as a complete obligation, since here he is not dealing with the fulfillment of the mitzvah which he already wrote in Parashat Noach, and therefore he wrote there 'to fulfill procreation,' and here he wrote 'to engage in procreation,' and furthermore – if he intended the fulfillment of the mitzvah, why did he bring a verse from Jeremiah and not verses from the Torah? Rather, his intention was the custom of the world and the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, in settling His world, as he concludes there that even one who has fulfilled procreation should marry a woman capable of bearing children, for this is certainly not a positive commandment of the Torah but to increase the settlement of the world, and in this certainly all humanity is equal. And even though the mitzvah is not imposed on the individual, it is imposed on the entirety of humanity to increase the settlement of the world according to the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, who blessed Adam and Noah and their sons with the blessing of procreation, and afterward warned them by saying, 'And you, be fruitful and multiply,' meaning: this is My will. And for Israel, this mitzvah was established upon each individual Israelite to fulfill this mitzvah as they are commanded in all the mitzvot, but idol worshippers, who are not commanded in all the mitzvot – are also not commanded in this, that the obligation should be on each of them, but upon the entirety of the nation the blessing of the Holy One, blessed be He, was to be fruitful and multiply, and His will, blessed be He, that they engage in settling His world, as I wrote in section 4 regarding women. And therefore he brought the verse from Jeremiah, where the prophet did not warn them about mitzvot, but because their hands weakened in exile, he told them not to weaken in maintaining the world, and to take wives and have sons and daughters, and likewise it is appropriate to say to all humanity [and the commentators on the She'iltot struggled with this, see there]. And so our sages said [Yevamot 62a] the children of Noah are members of procreation, and they did not say they were commanded but rather that they are involved in procreation in maintaining the world, which is the will of the Holy One, blessed be He [and this is the intention of Rashi there]. And this is like the Torah forbade castrating any living being, as I wrote in section 5.

Slaves are not commanded to be fruitful and multiply. However, there are among our Rabbis those who hold that they are commanded [Tosafot Chagigah 2b], and they wrote the reasoning that "be fruitful and multiply" is written for all the children of Noah, including Canaan. End of quote. The explanation of their words is: Although from Sinai onwards, the obligation remained only for Israel, nevertheless, slaves who are obligated in commandments like a woman, the obligation remains on them. And even though a woman is exempt - this is because she is not subject to conquest, and this is like the commandment of circumcision in which a slave is obligated [Mishneh Torah, Hilchot Melachim 12]. And this is what they wrote "even for Canaan" - because it is said about him, "a slave of slaves shall he be to his brothers." And know, there is a great principle in this, that even those who are not obligated to fulfill this commandment, nevertheless, when they fulfill "be fruitful and multiply," they perform a commandment, and a commandment in relation to an obligation is called optional. And the proof for this is from Midrash Tanchuma, Parashat Noach, which writes that a man is commanded to be fruitful and multiply more than a woman - implying that she too has a commandment, but she is not obligated to fulfill it. Therefore, if he had children while he was a gentile, he is no longer commanded to be fruitful and multiply, as will be explained, because in this too he has fulfilled his obligation even though he was not commanded to it as an obligation. [And see Ran at the beginning of the second chapter of Kiddushin, which resolves the question of the people of Shem, and see what is written in Siman 36, paragraph 2].

Even though he has fulfilled the commandment of procreation and has many sons and daughters, if his wife dies or he divorces her, he is forbidden to be without a wife, as it is said: "It is not good for man to be alone." This is a commandment of the sages in order to prevent him from coming to improper thoughts [Rambam, Hilchot Ishut, Chapter 15]. Therefore, even if he knows that he is no longer capable of fathering children, he should still not remain without a wife because of improper thoughts [Nimmukei Yosef]. From the general language of the Talmud and the decisors, it seems that there is no distinction in this matter, and even if he is elderly, he is obligated to marry a wife. 

However, we have seen and heard of great and righteous individuals who, upon the death of their wives in their old age, did not remarry until the day of their death. It is possible to say that since this is not a Torah obligation, and the verse "It is not good for man to be alone" is merely a supporting text for this matter [Beit Shmuel], and the reason is solely due to the concern of improper thoughts, and they know themselves to be far from such thoughts due to their old age and weakness, they therefore exempt themselves from this obligation. Similarly, if one knows that it is difficult for him to engage with a woman, he is certainly exempt, and all the more so if he does not have the means to support her.

And so the sages commanded that if one recognizes in himself that he is still capable of fathering children, he should marry a woman who can bear children, provided his means are sufficient to support them. As our Sages said: "If he married a woman in his youth, he should marry in his old age; if he had children in his youth, he should have children in his old age," as it is stated: "In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not withhold your hand, for you do not know which will prosper, this or that, or whether both alike will be good" (Ecclesiastes 11:6). And so the law is ruled [Yevamot 62b]. However, our Master the Rema wrote that if one fears that marrying a woman who can bear children will lead to quarrels and disputes between the children and his wife, he is permitted to marry a woman who cannot bear children. But it is forbidden to remain without a wife due to this concern. End quote. Because due to the concern of quarrels, one can set aside "in the evening do not withhold your hand," but one must not commit a sin, for there is a concern lest his impulse overpower him [Beit Shmuel]. And in general, regarding marrying a woman who can bear children, the Ramban wrote that according to all opinions, he is not compelled to do so, as it is not a decree but rather a recommendation of proper conduct, and they are not stringent about it [Beit Shmuel]. And so it appears from the words of the Rambam who wrote there: A man should not marry a barren, elderly, or sterile woman, or a minor who cannot bear children unless he has fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation. End quote. And it is explained that if he has fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation, he may even marry a woman who cannot bear children. And later he wrote: Even though a person has fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation, he is still commanded by the words of the Scribes not to desist from procreation as long as he has the strength, as anyone who adds one soul to Israel is considered as if he has built a world. End quote [see there in the Magid Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh]. However, this is a form of beautifying the mitzvah and proper conduct as mentioned, and if there is some impediment, he is not compelled to do so. An 'elderly woman' is referred to as one whom everyone calls 'Mother' as is customary for elderly women, and she does not mind it [Niddah 9b]. And even if she minds, since she has reached the age where all women are called so, she is considered elderly [Tosafot there, and see Rashi Moed Katan 9b, s.v. befanav, where there is difficulty].

Our Rabbis of blessed memory esteemed this commandment (of marriage) so highly and equated it to Torah study, as they said [Megillah 27a]: "One may not sell a Torah scroll except to study Torah or to marry a woman." It appears from the words of the Sheiltot [Parashat Noach] that even for the purpose of obtaining money for wedding expenses, one can sell a Torah scroll, see there. And even if one has already fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation (Pru Urvu), and needs to marry a woman capable of bearing children, such as if he has the means to support them, if he is unable to marry unless he sells the Torah scroll – some say he should marry a woman not capable of bearing children and not sell the Torah scroll, and some say he should sell the Torah scroll and marry a woman capable of bearing children, as the mitzvah "In the evening do not let your hand be idle" also overrides the prohibition of selling a Torah scroll. And if even to marry a woman not capable of bearing children he must sell the Torah scroll, and if he does not sell it he will be forced to remain without a wife – some say he should remain without a wife and not sell the Torah scroll, even though he may come to sinful thoughts, and by selling it he would be saved from sinful thoughts, nevertheless one does not sell a Torah scroll except to perform a mitzvah with the money, and not to save oneself from a sin [Beit Shmuel]. And some say one may sell it, as sinful thoughts are worse than "sitting without a wife" [Chelkat Mechokek]. This matter is a dispute among the Rishonim [Ramban wrote that one may sell, and Nimukei Yosef explicitly wrote that one may not sell], and in the Sheiltot of Rabbi Achai Gaon it is ruled that only if he has not fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation is he permitted to sell a Torah scroll, but if he has fulfilled it – it is forbidden [see there in Parashat Beracha]. Further laws regarding the sale of Torah scrolls and books are explained in Orach Chaim chapter 153 and Yoreh De'ah chapter 270, see there.

Maimonides, of blessed memory, writes: "A woman who permits her husband after marriage to abstain from her conjugal rights – this is allowed. When is this the case? When he already has children and has fulfilled the commandment of 'Be fruitful and multiply.' But if he has not fulfilled this commandment, he is obligated to engage in marital relations at every opportunity until he has children, because it is a positive commandment from the Torah, as it is stated: 'Be fruitful and multiply.' And although at all times, as long as he can procreate, he is under the obligation of 'In the evening do not let your hand rest,' as the [Beit Shmuel] writes, nevertheless, for this reason, he is not obligated to engage in marital relations at every opportunity. The obligation is only that he should not abstain completely, and the obligation of marital relations is because he is obligated to her, as it is written 'and her conjugal rights he shall not diminish.' Therefore, if she forgives it – he is permitted, as the [Birkei Yosef] writes. This is contrary to the opinion of some who say that this applies only if he has another wife, but if he does not have another wife – like in our countries where it is forbidden to marry two wives – her forgiveness is ineffective even after he has fulfilled 'Be fruitful and multiply,' as the [commentator on the Taz] writes. For Maimonides explicitly states that because of the positive commandment from the Torah, he is obligated to engage in marital relations at every opportunity, and not because of the commandment of 'In the evening do not let your hand rest,' which is not from the Torah, and is only for the sake of settling the world, as explained in section 8. And in section 76, this will be further explained with God's help."

And when does the obligation to marry fall upon a person? The sages taught: At eighteen for the wedding canopy. It is explained from the words of the Rambam that this is in the eighteenth year and not upon the completion of the eighteenth year. And even though for all other commandments, one is obligated from the age of thirteen and onward, nevertheless, for this commandment, the obligation does not apply then because one needs to learn, and if he marries he will not be able to learn as much [Helkat Mehokek]. Furthermore, at that age, his physical strength is still weak. And in the Gemara, we find that one of the sages boasted and said: The reason I am better than my colleagues is that I married at sixteen, and if I had married at fourteen, I would have said to the adversary, "An arrow in your eye" [Kiddushin 29b], meaning that the evil inclination would not have overpowered him all his life. Therefore, the poskim wrote that one who marries early performs an exemplary mitzvah. However, the great rabbis of these generations, noting the weakening of natural constitutions, have written that one should not marry at thirteen [Pitchei Teshuvah in the name of Birkei Yosef and Mahari Hasid]. And before thirteen, one should not marry, as it would be considered licentiousness. And even though some wanted to differentiate between when the father marries him off and when he marries on his own, nevertheless, the great later authorities did not agree with this — it is forbidden in any case. There is no need to elaborate on this, as in our times it is almost impossible.

And even though the obligation is when a person is eighteen years old, nevertheless, if he does not marry until he is twenty years old, he has not committed a transgression, for at twenty years old one becomes subject to punishment by the Heavenly Court. But from twenty years and onward, if he does not marry a woman, it is a transgression in his hand, unless he is compelled and it is impossible for him to marry. And so the Sages said [there]: Until twenty years the Holy One, Blessed be He, sits and waits for a person to marry a woman. Once he reaches twenty and has not married, He says: "May his bones swell," and this is measure for measure, for bones are created from the father, and this person who does not engage in procreation and diminishes the bones, therefore his bones should swell [Maharsha]. And we compel him to marry a woman in order to fulfill the commandment of procreation.

However, someone who knows himself that if he marries a woman, he will not be able to study Torah because he will need to toil to provide for his wife and children, and he is twenty years old – he is not obligated to marry a woman if his desire does not overpower him, for one who is engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from another mitzvah [Rambam]. And even though one who is engaged in Torah study should not exempt himself from other mitzvot, nevertheless, the mitzvah of procreation, which is to have a male and female child, he still has time to fulfill, and it is considered a mitzvah that does not pass, as the mitzvah of Torah study takes precedence [in my opinion]. And until when should he engage in Torah study if his desire does not overpower him? Until the time he estimates that he has filled his belly with Torah, provided that he does not completely neglect the mitzvah of procreation [Levush]. And there are those who say that there is truly no fixed limit for this, but the main ruling is as stated. And some say that the limit is up to twenty-four years and no more [Yesh Sh'muel, first chapter of Kiddushin]. And if he can study even after he marries – he is obligated to marry a woman, and then study Torah in purity [there].

The Sages said about Ben Azzai that he did not marry a woman, and when they asked him, he replied: "What can I do, my soul desires Torah?" It is possible for the world to be sustained by others [Yevamot 63b]. Therefore, the Rambam, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch wrote that someone whose soul always desires Torah like Ben Azzai and clings to it all his days and does not marry a woman – he does not bear sin, provided that his inclination does not overpower him. These are their words. And even though it is possible for him to marry a woman and it would not be a burden for him because of sustenance [Beit Shmuel], if he is like Ben Azzai, who is completely unable to separate from the Torah. However, it is obvious that such a level is entirely uncommon, and even in the time of the Sages of the Talmud, there was only one Ben Azzai and no one like him, and the Rif did not mention this at all. And it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud [first chapter of Shabbat] that one interrupts Torah study to make a sukkah and a lulav and all the commandments, and anyone who learns not to do – it would be better for him if he had not been created. And it is taught in the Torat Kohanim: "If you walk in my statutes and keep my commandments and do them" – this refers to one who learns in order to do, not one who learns not to do, for one who learns not to do it would be better for him if he had not been created. And Ben Azzai himself indeed betrothed the daughter of Rabbi Akiva [Ketubot 63a], and according to one explanation in the Gemara [Sotah 4b], he married and separated. It is necessary to say that he was completely unable to separate from the Torah, and it is possible that it was a danger to his life if he separated from Torah [it seems to me].

How much is the mitzvah of procreation, to fulfill the positive commandment of "be fruitful and multiply"? [It is] a son and a daughter, and once one has a male and a female – one has fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation. And we learn this from the creation of the world, where the Holy One, Blessed be He, created a male and a female, and they were Adam and Eve. Provided that the son is not a eunuch and the daughter is not an aylonit (a woman who does not develop female secondary sexual characteristics), as they are not capable of reproducing. For with such individuals, when they die, there is no benefit to the settlement of the world, and the world remains in a state of chaos. As it is written: "He did not create it a waste; He formed it to be inhabited."

If one had a son and a daughter and they died but left behind offspring, then he has fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation (Pru U’rvu), for there is continuity of the world from him. The Rambam wrote: In what case is this true? When the grandchildren are a male and a female and they come from a male and a female, even if the male is the son of his daughter, and the female is the daughter of his son, since they come from his two children, he has fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation. But if he had a son and a daughter and they died, and only one of them left a male and a female, he has not yet fulfilled this mitzvah. This is the end of his words. And Rabbeinu Beit Yosef copied it in Shulchan Aruch, section 6. And even though a male and a female came from him, nevertheless, the Torah required that he himself should father a male and a female. If the intention of the Torah were that only from his progeny there should be a male and a female, it could have exempted him with only a male or only a female, since from each of them could come a male and a female. But certainly, the Torah required every man to father a male and a female, and if they died, there should remain from them a male and a female, even if it changes from female to male and male to female, but in any case, there should remain offspring from each of them. And certainly, if only two males or two females remain, it is not sufficient, for the other gender is missing.

And some say that even if only two males remain, it is sufficient, and even though with two males he does not initially fulfill the mitzvah, nevertheless, because the second male comes from the daughter who exempts him from the mitzvah of procreation, the son certainly stands in place of the daughter. And some say that even if only two daughters remain, he has also fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation, because since he had already fulfilled it and now also there remains offspring from both of them, it is as if both of them exist. However, if initially he had two males and they died, and they left a male and a female, it is not sufficient, because since with two males he did not fulfill the mitzvah of procreation, it is impossible for him to fulfill it with what comes from them, even if they give birth to many. And if he had a son and a daughter, and the daughter died and left a daughter and the son is alive, or the son died and left a son and the daughter is alive, he has certainly fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation. However, if the daughter died and left a son, and his son is alive but has not yet given birth, according to the Rambam, he has not fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation, because he does not now have a male and a female. But according to those who say that having two males is sufficient, this would also be valid.

The general rule is: if a male and a female remain from his male and female, even if they are the third or fourth generation or more, he has fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation, even if the female is from the male and the male is from the female. But if only from one of them remains a male and a female, and even if many males and females remain, since from the other nothing remains, he has not fulfilled the mitzvah. However, if two males or two females remain from them, it depends on the opinions that have been explained. And there are those who want to say that according to all opinions, two males or certainly two females are not sufficient, but this does not seem to be the case according to all the poskim, and the Talmudic discussion also implies as written.

Even if one has a male and female child from a woman he was not married to with chuppah and kiddushin, and even if they are mamzerim (children born from forbidden relationships), nevertheless, he has fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation (Pru Urvu). Even if they were deaf-mutes or mentally incapacitated, they are still considered his offspring and are capable of procreating. However, a son from a maidservant or from a non-Jewish woman, as well as a daughter from them – he has not fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation because they are not considered his descendants. 

There are those who want to say that regarding a mamzer, it is only if it is known that he is a mamzer. But if it is not known, he has not fulfilled the mitzvah because our Sages said that an unknown mamzer will not live long. I do not agree, because in any case: as long as he is alive – he fulfills the mitzvah with him. And if he dies and leaves offspring – he fulfills the mitzvah through his offspring, as stated. And if he dies during his lifetime and leaves no offspring, then even if he is not a mamzer, he has not fulfilled the mitzvah. And to say that he is not fit to leave offspring and consider him like a eunuch does not seem correct at all.

It has already been clarified that with a son who is a eunuch or a daughter who is an aylonit (a woman who does not develop secondary sexual characteristics) – one has not fulfilled the mitzvah (commandment) of "be fruitful and multiply." However, if the son is not a eunuch but marries an aylonit, or the daughter is not an aylonit but marries a eunuch, even though they will not have children, still the father has fulfilled the mitzvah because his offspring are capable of procreation [Chalakat Mechokek]. There are those who question this, arguing that since the world will not be settled through them, he has not fulfilled his obligation. This reasoning is not acceptable at all, for if he himself fathered a eunuch or an aylonit, he has still not fulfilled the mitzvah. But if he fulfilled the mitzvah properly and they erred in their marriages, why should he lose his mitzvah due to their actions? A person does not sin for the actions of others. If we were to say otherwise, then if the son converts to another religion (apostasy), we would also say that he has not fulfilled "be fruitful and multiply," which is not comparable to having children who died, where it is considered that Heaven took them and thus the mitzvah is taken away, but not when the children acted deliberately. [And know, there are those who inquire about a woman who became pregnant through bathing (in a bathhouse) if the father has fulfilled "be fruitful and multiply." However, since this is extremely uncommon, there is no need to elaborate on this.]

If he had children while he was a non-Jew and then converted, he has fulfilled the commandment to be fruitful and multiply. And even though he is considered like a newborn child, nevertheless, since they too are considered children for the purpose of being fruitful and multiplying, even though they were not commanded, still, in general, there is upon them something like an obligation to populate the world, which is God's will in His blessing to man and to Noah, as mentioned in section 5. The primary reason for the commandment to be fruitful and multiply is for the purpose of inhabiting the world, and since he has contributed to inhabiting the world, he is no longer obligated in this commandment. When we said that he has fulfilled the commandment to be fruitful and multiply, it does not mean that he has fulfilled this positive commandment, but rather that he has fulfilled it in a way that the commandment to be fruitful and multiply is no longer incumbent upon him. However, if he had children while he was a slave and then was freed, even if both he and his children were freed, he has not fulfilled the commandment to be fruitful and multiply, because in the case of a slave, the children are not considered related to him, unlike in the case of a non-Jew, where his children are considered related to him.

The Rambam and the Tur wrote that this refers to when the father and the children converted. The commentators wrote that if this were not the case, certainly they do not fulfill for him the mitzvah of procreation (HeM and Beit Yosef). And some say that even if he converted alone, he fulfills the mitzvah of procreation (Beit Shmuel in the name of Mahari"l), and so it is implied from several great Rishonim. And indeed, since he is considered like a newborn, what does it help according to the Rambam and the Tur even if the children converted? Rather, certainly he fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation even beforehand, and therefore in any case, he has fulfilled it. Furthermore, it is explicitly explained in the Talmud (Bekhorot 47b) that on the contrary, when they convert, they have no familial relationship with each other (Gra). And it seems to me that there is no disagreement here, and even the Rambam and the Tur agree that if he converted alone, he is no longer commanded in the mitzvah of procreation, since from the outset they are considered children for the purpose of procreation even if they were not commanded, as we have explained. However, he did not fulfill the positive commandment as we have explained, for certainly at Sinai when Israel was commanded about this mitzvah, it was evident that the commandment was to beget those who come under the wings of the Divine Presence. But if the children also converted, they ruled that he fulfilled this positive commandment. And the reason: even though they are not presently related to him, nevertheless previously they were related to him, and in general, they are considered children for the purpose of procreation, and he engaged in the settlement of the world, and now they have come under the wings of the Divine Presence – thus he has truly fulfilled the mitzvah. But without this, although he is not presently commanded, still the mitzvah was not fulfilled (and this resolves all the difficulties).

Regarding what was explained, that upon reaching twenty years of age, one is compelled to marry a woman, our teacher the Rema wrote that in our times, the custom is not to compel in this matter. Similarly, one who has not fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation and seeks to marry a woman who is not capable of bearing children, such as a barren woman, an elderly woman, or a young girl, whether because he desires her or because of her wealth, even though according to the law he should be protested against, the custom for many generations has been not to be meticulous about matters of marriage. Even if he married a woman and lived with her for ten years without fulfilling the mitzvah of procreation, the custom is not to compel him to divorce her. This applies to other matters of marriage as well, provided she is not forbidden to him. These are the concluding words [of the Rema]. There is no valid reason for this custom, and all the reasons given are rejected [according to the Vilna Gaon]. However, the truth is that we do not have the power to protest, but one who acts on his own should be cautious for his own sake. Some have written that if one delays in order to find a suitable match or for another reason, we do not compel him. Nevertheless, one should not delay for a reason external to himself beyond the age of twenty-four [according to the Rema].

From Torah law, a man can marry many women if he is able to support all of them respectfully, and if they are willing to live a life of hardship, the choice is theirs [Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel]. As it is written, "Seven women will take hold of one man" etc. However, only in the case of a yevama (a widow awaiting levirate marriage), the court is required to give her proper advice not to marry him if they see that it is not good for her [Beit Shmuel]. Nevertheless, the advice of the sages is not to marry more than four women even if he is wealthy and capable of supporting more, so that each one can have her conjugal rights once a month, since the conjugal rights of a Torah scholar are from Sabbath to Sabbath as mentioned in Siman 86.

Indeed, more than eight hundred years ago, in the days of Rabbeinu Gershom Me'or HaGolah, he and the sages of his generation saw the problems and disputes arising from having multiple wives. Therefore, they enacted a severe decree, with all the strictness in the world, that a man should not marry another woman while still married to his wife. This decree spread to most of the Jewish diaspora – in France, the Isle, the valley, Ashkenaz, Russia, Poland, and all regions of Austria. This enactment was so widely accepted that if someone were to break this rule, even in a distant place, he would be considered wicked and a fraud, despised by all, and people would distance themselves from him.

Even though some say that the decree was only until the end of the fifth millennium, nevertheless, the Jews have continued to uphold this beautiful enactment for themselves and their descendants. The government also enforces this rule, and the enactment remains in effect until the coming of the redeemer. Even in countries where this decree did not initially spread, such as in the lands of the Turks and in Africa, most people adopted the practice of not marrying more than one wife.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote that there are places where it became customary not to marry more than one woman, and even if this was not explicitly stated in the marriage contract, it is as if it was agreed upon, unless she forgives him, in which case he is permitted to marry another. However, in places where the enactment of Rabbeinu Gershom spread, her forgiveness does not help. Know that in any city or country where there is doubt whether the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom spread, one must uphold it, as we assume it spread everywhere unless it is known that this place never upheld this enactment. Even in the new world – in America and Australia – this decree is observed because most Jews who came there came from places where the enactment spread.

If someone moves from a place where the decree is observed to a place where it is not, or vice versa, certainly, if he moves from a prohibited place to a permitted place, the prohibition still applies to him, even if he does not intend to return, as the prohibition applies to the person and not the place. This person, who left his place, the prohibition applies to him everywhere. If he moves from a permitted place to a prohibited place and does not intend to return, he automatically falls under the local enactment and is forbidden to marry another woman while still married. However, if he comes to live with his wives from a permitted place to a prohibited place, even if he does not intend to return, he does not need to divorce one of them, as Rabbeinu Gershom did not enact his decree in such a case.

Some say that the prohibition applies only to men and not to women. Therefore, if two Ashkenazi women marry a Sephardi man, there is no prohibition on them. This matter is not clear to me.

And even in a place where it is permitted to marry two women, our Sages said (Yoma 18b): a person should not marry a woman in this country and then go and marry a woman in another country, lest the son born to him in this country marries the daughter born to him in the other country, and thus a brother marries his sister. Rashi comments similarly. The Rambam and the Tur wrote that a prominent person whose name is known and whose offspring are recognized is permitted to do so, as they will not come to such a stumbling block. This is also the ruling of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch at the end of Siman 2. However, some of our Rabbis disagree with this (Raavad and Yam Shel Shlomo, Chapter 4 of Yevamot, Siman 5, and similarly in Tosafot, Yevamot 37b, and it appears to be the opinion of the Rif and the Rosh, see also Beit Shmuel).

Now, even in our times when it is forbidden to marry two women, there is still this concern, for if a man divorces his wife or if she dies and he marries a woman in another country, he may end up marrying his sister. Yet, we have never heard that people are careful about this. There are those who say that in our times, since it is forbidden to marry two women, when a man goes to another country, he takes his children with him (Bach). But this reason is insufficient, for is it not possible that he would leave his children with his divorced wife? It is also a stretch to say that because we are few among the nations, each one is considered famous, as it says in Orach Chaim, Siman 547. For nowadays, in large places, the Jewish population has increased, and there is a significant Jewish population even across the ocean, and many travel there every year.

It seems to me that the reason is different: since nowadays the postal service is swift, running daily across the world, it is almost impossible that a father in another country would not regularly receive letters from the children he left in the previous country. Therefore, the children born to him in the other country would not be unaware of their siblings from the previous country.

If Rabbeinu Gershom decreed even in the case of a mitzvah, such as a yevama who falls to him, or in the case of a postponed mitzvah, such as one who stayed with his wife for ten years and she did not bear children and she does not want to accept a get – there is a dispute among the poskim. Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote explicitly that he did not decree in such a case, and he can marry the yevama, and if ten years pass without her bearing children – he can marry another. Similarly, he did not decree in the case of an arusa, meaning: when he betrothed his fiancée – he can marry another because he can divorce his fiancée, and even if she does not want to accept a get, nevertheless he is not obligated to marry her to be obligated in her sustenance, clothing, and marital relations, and this is not considered two wives. Similarly, even if he did not marry another – we do not force him to marry his fiancée, and he can release her with a get, and if she does not want to accept it – we do not force him to marry her, and he is not obligated to her at all. However, Rabbeinu Rema wrote that there are those who say that Rabbeinu Gershom's decree applies even in the case of a mitzvah, and it is forbidden for him to marry his yevama if he has a wife, but he should perform chalitzah for her. But in the case where ten years have passed and she did not bear children – it seems from his words that they permit him to marry another, as he wrote: "And in a case where the first wife is not eligible for divorce, such as if she became insane or if it is lawful to divorce her and she does not want to accept a get from him – it is permissible to allow him to marry another, and all the more so if she is betrothed and does not want to marry him or be released from him." End quote. And in the case where ten years have passed and she did not bear children, he is obligated by law to divorce her as will be explained in Siman 154, but all the great Acharonim have already written that they do not permit this except with the approval of one hundred rabbis and with the permission of the government. And so Rabbeinu Gershom decreed that if there is a need to permit, one hundred scholars, including many of those sitting on the seat of instruction, must agree on this, and they must be from three countries, even if they are from one kingdom such as Lithuania, Russia, and Zemaitija. And furthermore, they have the custom to be lenient even from one country and from three districts called guberniyas. And it is a tradition from the great ones of the world that in any matter where the sages of that city see fit to permit this man to take a wife in addition to his wife, and he has government permission for this – they will present the matter before the great ones of that generation, and one hundred rabbis will agree to the permission, and he will also deposit the sum of the ketubah that is due to her, as well as any additional ketubah and all her obligations with the Beit Din, and afterward, he will marry another. And not necessarily all of them are rabbis, but distinguished scholars worthy of instruction. And it is impossible to explain in writing to whom it is appropriate to permit marrying a wife in addition to his wife, for not all matters are the same. Certainly, in a case where it is impossible to live with her, such as if she became insane or similar – it is clear that they permit him. Similarly, if she has a prolonged illness that the doctors say she can never be cured from and she does not want to accept a get, and also if ten years have passed and she did not bear children and she does not want to accept a get – certainly, they permit him. However, in other matters, it is impossible to explain, and much depends on the discretion of the sages of the place. Similarly, if she wants to accept a get but asks for more than her ketubah entitlement, if the sages of the place, such as the rabbi and the Beit Din, see that he can bear it because the additional amount is not significant given his situation – it is certain that they do not permit him, and he will add to her according to her desire. However, if she asks for a large sum, and according to the discretion of the Beit Din, his situation will be ruined if he gives her what she asks – then they permit him, and similarly in all such cases.

The great authorities also wrote: If she became mentally incapacitated, he should place the get (divorce document) in the hands of a messenger for delivery, so that the get remains in his possession until she recovers. He is obligated to designate a separate house for her and to guard her from improper behavior, and he is obliged to provide her sustenance [Bach and Beit Shmuel]. According to this, after she recovers, the messenger can deliver this get to her. However, many of the authorities have questioned this, arguing that she should not be permitted to remarry based on this get when she recovers, because anything that one cannot do himself at the present time, he cannot appoint a messenger to do. Since at the time the get was given to the messenger she was not eligible for divorce, he could not appoint a messenger then. We have already explained this matter in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 182, Section 4, see there. And many of the authorities wrote that there is no need to deposit the get at all, and what benefit is there in it? For until she recovers, she is not divorced, and when she recovers, he can write her a new get. And if the concern is that he will not want to give a get then, what is the benefit of depositing it, since he can cancel the get, and then they will compel him to give a get? And if the concern is that she might not be willing to accept it, what benefit is there that it was deposited [Bet Meir]? This is also the custom among us. However, when he is permitted to divorce her for another reason, and she is eligible to receive the get but is not willing, when he is permitted and deposits her ketubah, he should also deposit the get, and whenever she agrees, she can receive the get from the messenger [Noda BiYehuda].

In the count of one hundred rabbis from the three communities, even though it is impossible to ensure that there will be a third from each community, nevertheless, a certain number from each community is required. And even if in another community there will be a larger number – one should not be particular about it.

If a man marries a woman in addition to his wife, we compel him by all means of coercion to divorce one of them. Ideally, efforts should be made for him to divorce the second wife whom he married in violation of the prohibition. However, there is no objection to this, and if the first wife consents to receive a get (bill of divorce), and he wishes to remain with the second wife, we do not prevent him from doing so. And even though there are those who say that after the fifth millennium we do not compel someone who violated Rabbeinu Gershom's decree, nevertheless, we do not conduct ourselves in this manner. As Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote, we have already explained that the decree remains in effect until the coming of the redeemer, and there is no difference between the fifth millennium and the sixth millennium.

One of the great early authorities ruled regarding a man who ascended to the Land of Israel while his wife did not ascend with him and he wishes to marry another woman — he should send her a get (divorce document) through an agent, estimate the time it will reach her, and then marry another woman. Even though it is not certain that she will accept the get, nevertheless the prohibition does not apply to him anymore, for by law she was supposed to ascend to the Land of Israel. And although it is impossible to compel her to do so if she has a valid reason, as will be explained in Siman 75, nevertheless it is clear that in such a case the decree that he should remain without a wife does not apply, especially since in the Land of Israel the regulation did not take effect. And although the prohibition still applies as stated in Section 23, nevertheless it is clear that in such a case, even outside the Land of Israel, efforts would be made on his behalf to permit him [to marry another woman].

If a man's wife has converted to the religion of Ishmael (Islam), some say that he should arrange for a divorce (get) through another person and then marry another woman. And in a place where this is the custom – one should not deviate from it. However, in a place where there is no such custom, our teacher, the Rema, writes that there is no need to arrange a divorce for her, and there is no need to be stringent about this, and it is permitted to marry another woman without divorcing the first one. These are his words. And only in places where the custom is to perform levirate marriage (yibum) is it proper to arrange a divorce for her, lest he die and they come to perform levirate marriage with his wife, and she would be the co-wife of this wicked woman, and it would be like the co-wife of a sotah (a woman suspected of adultery) who is forbidden to the levir.

A woman who causes her husband to stumble in prohibitions, and this is clarified by witnesses, he can divorce her against her will as stated in Siman 115. If she does not want to accept the get (divorce document) – he can have the get given to her through another and marry another woman. This applies to all those whom we compel to accept a get as stated there.

Our Master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 11: "It is good to make a stringent enactment regarding anyone who marries another woman while his first wife is alive." End quote. The explanation of his words is: Even in places where the enactment of Rabbenu Gershom has not spread, it is good to make this enactment because it is a proper enactment. Indeed, we do not find that any of the Tannaim, Amoraim, or Geonim had two wives. On the contrary, we find in Midrash Bereshit [Parsha 17] about Rabbi Yossi, who had a bad wife, yet did not marry another until he divorced the first one. The law concerning someone who has waited ten years without having children will be explained in section 154. It will also be explained there about someone who swore not to marry another and did not have children for ten years, see there.

[One should endeavor to marry an appropriate woman, and if necessary, investigate the family. This section contains 26 paragraphs]

A person must make every effort to marry an appropriate woman and not marry one who has any hint of disqualification. Whether the disqualification pertains to her personally, such as being promiscuous or similar issues, or whether the disqualification is in her family, such as having a family history of bastardy (mamzerut) or if he is a Kohen (priest) and her family has a history of profanation (chalalut). The sages of blessed memory have said: Anyone who marries a woman who has a disqualification, Elijah writes, and the Holy One, blessed be He, seals and says, "Woe to him who disqualifies his offspring and damages his family." In the future, Elijah will bind him, and the Holy One, blessed be He, will metaphorically flog him. The reason Elijah writes and binds is because he was very distressed when Israel violated the covenant between them and God, and he was persecuted for this by the wicked people of his generation. And, as it were, the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself testifies that his offspring are disqualified, as it is said, "The tribes of Yah are a testimony to Israel" – when are they a testimony to Israel? When the tribes are the tribes of Yah, then the Holy One, blessed be He, testifies that they are His. He only rests His Divine Presence upon families in Israel that have no hint of disqualification, as it is said, "At that time, says the Lord, I will be God for all the families of Israel, and they will be My people" – meaning, those who are from the families of the kosher Israelites will be My people. Anyone who marries an inappropriate woman because of her beauty or wealth will have children who are not upstanding, and even the wealth will not endure [Kiddushin 70a]. However, if he marries a kosher woman for the sake of wealth, meaning that if not for her wealth, he would have married someone else, there is no sin in this. On the contrary, it is proper to do so if he is a Torah scholar, for this way he will not need to be overly occupied with worldly matters. And so, upright people have the custom of marrying off their daughters to Torah scholars, giving them a lot of money, and supporting them at their table for several years so that they can study. There is no greater mitzvah than this, and in reward for this, they succeed in their endeavors.

Anyone who wishes to marry a woman who is disqualified, his family members can object to him. If he does not want to listen to them, they should make some public demonstration as a sign that his offspring should not intermingle with theirs. 

If a large sum of money was promised to him for the engagement, and later a situation arises where the bride’s father is unable to fulfill what he had promised, although legally the groom can object, nevertheless it is proper and appropriate that he should not keep his bride in limbo because of this and should not quarrel with them, as such matters do not succeed. On the contrary, when one does not quarrel, God will bless him, and his match will turn out well, because money that a person takes for his wife through force is not righteous money. Anyone who does this is also included among those who marry for money. Rather, whatever his father-in-law and mother-in-law give him, he should accept generously, and then he will succeed. However, those who initially intend to deceive the groom with the dowry and think they are doing a mitzvah – they are not acting properly.

The Sages said [Pesachim 49a]: A person should always try to marry the daughter of a Torah scholar. If he does not find the daughter of a Torah scholar, he should marry the daughter of the great ones of the generation, righteous and upright people [Rashi]. If he does not find the daughter of the great ones of the generation, he should marry the daughter of the heads of the congregations. If he does not find the daughter of the heads of the congregations, he should marry the daughter of the charity collectors. If he does not find the daughter of the charity collectors, he should marry the daughter of the school teachers. Similarly, he should strive to marry his daughter to a Torah scholar and not marry his daughter to an ignoramus who is not careful in mitzvot. 

And the Sages said that it is a mitzvah for a person to marry the daughter of his sister [Yevamot 62b], as it is stated: "And do not hide yourself from your own flesh" (Isaiah 58:7). The same applies to the daughter of his brother [Rambam, Hilchot Ishut 2:15], as it is a mitzvah for a person to bring his relatives close. Some say [Rashi] specifically the daughter of his sister because a person's affection is much greater for his sister than for his brother, and as a result, he cherishes his wife. The first opinion holds as it is stated in the Midrash: When a person marries a woman from among his relatives, the verse applies to him: "Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh" (Genesis 2:23). The idea is that the love of relatives is natural, and a man's love for his wife comes because of their deeds, which is incidental to them. When both types of love come together, the tent will be established properly, and there will be peace in the home. 

It is known that there is no closer relative a person can marry than the daughter of his sister and the daughter of his brother [Magid Mishneh]. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, Kiddushin [Chapter 4], it is stated that the reason the Sages required a person who marries a woman to check four mothers in her family, as will be explained, is that the Sages imposed a fine so that a person will be attached to his tribe and his family.

A man should not marry a woman from a family of lepers or from a family of epileptics. This applies specifically when the family has been established with three instances where their children have come to such conditions, as three times establishes a presumption. And although in matters of danger we are cautious even with two occurrences, as mentioned in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 263 regarding two sons who died due to circumcision and the third should not be circumcised, nevertheless, in establishing a family's presumption, it is not considered established until it occurs three times. According to this, if the woman has two sisters who are lepers or epileptics, it is forbidden to marry her, because sisters establish a presumption in relation to circumcision as mentioned there, and the same applies to this matter.

An ignoramus should not marry a kohenet (a woman of priestly descent), and if they do marry, their union will not be successful; either she or he will die soon or another misfortune will come between them, because it is degrading for the descendants of Aaron to be joined with an ignoramus. However, a Torah scholar who marries a kohenet is considered praiseworthy and commendable – Torah and priesthood in one place. And what is considered an ignoramus in this context? One who disparages the commandments. However, someone who observes the commandments, even if he is not a Torah scholar, is not considered an ignoramus. Therefore, there are those who say that we do not have such ignoramuses nowadays as described by the Sages in Pesachim (Chapter 3) and see there (Chidushei HaRashba).

A young man should not marry an elderly woman, for she cannot bear children, and he will neglect the commandment to be fruitful and multiply [Levush]. And an elderly man should not marry a young girl, for this causes licentiousness, as she will engage in adultery under him. The Torah warns against this: "Do not degrade your daughter to make her a harlot" (Leviticus 19:29), and our Sages said, "This refers to one who marries his daughter to an old man" [Sanhedrin 76b]. However, if she genuinely desires him, it is permitted [Chomat Hanechemet]. It is written in Sefer Chassidim [siman 779] about a virgin who married an old man because she genuinely desired him, and they had children who were Torah scholars. Many such stories are known. However, if her desire is only because he is wealthy, it is inappropriate to do so, for in the end, once she gets accustomed to wealth, she will despise him and seek her own satisfaction.

A man should not marry a woman with the intent to divorce her, and regarding this it is said, "Do not devise harm against your neighbor who dwells trustingly beside you." Therefore, if he informs her beforehand that he is marrying her for a limited time, it is permitted. However, some prohibit even in such a case. Indeed, in our times, there is no practical difference in this, as it is forbidden to divorce against her will due to the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom. Consequently, if she agrees to accept a get (divorce document), even if he does not marry her for a limited time, he can divorce her. And if she does not agree, what benefit is there in marrying her for a limited time? And a man should not marry a woman in two places, as stated in Siman 1, Se'if 24, see there.

The sages said (Kiddushin 76b) that one who marries a woman who is a Kohenet (daughter of a priest) must investigate her family background for four maternal generations, which are eight mothers. This means checking four generations on her father’s side and four on her mother’s side, making a total of eight mothers, each generation comprising the mother and the mother's mother. The investigation follows this order: her mother, her maternal grandmother, her maternal great-grandmother, her paternal grandmother, her paternal great-grandmother, her paternal great-great-grandmother, and so forth.

For a Levite or Israelite woman, one additional generation is added on each side, making it ten mothers (Rambam). Some say that the mother herself is also checked, making it twelve mothers. However, the halacha is established in the Gemara that this extensive checking is only necessary if there is a rumor about the family’s lineage. Otherwise, all families are presumed to be of valid lineage.

The investigation aims to ensure there are no mamzerim (illegitimate children) or other individuals disqualified from the congregation. Thus, this check is necessary even if the groom is not a Kohen. If the groom is a Kohen, the check ensures there are no disqualifications like halalim (descendants of priests who violated marriage restrictions).

If he marries a woman from a priestly family, only four generations need to be checked because Kohanim are more careful about their lineage. For Levites and Israelites, an additional generation is examined. The investigation focuses on the maternal line rather than the paternal because men, when fighting, might challenge each other’s lineage, making any disqualifications known. Women, on the other hand, might keep such issues private, hence the need to check the maternal line.

The groom checks the bride’s family, but the bride does not check the groom’s. This is because, in matters of priesthood, a Kohenet can marry someone disqualified from priestly status. The daughters of Aaron were not specifically warned to marry only those fit for priesthood. Hence, there is no concern about mamzerim or other disqualifications from the congregation.

What constitutes a rumor? The Rambam wrote that it involves the testimony of two witnesses that a mamzer, halal, or slave has mixed into the family. Rashi explained that it could be a mere rumor without full testimony, but two witnesses attest to the suspicion of disqualification. 

One might question the Rambam: if there are witnesses of a mamzer mixing into the family, it’s not just a suspicion, and the family should be prohibited from marrying. Why doesn’t she check the groom’s family? It can be argued that even if a mamzer has mixed into the family, each family member is only a doubtful mamzer, and the Torah only forbids a definite mamzer from marrying an Israelite woman. Even though rabbinically they are forbidden, the check is only for the specific individual, not generations back, because it's only a rabbinic precaution (see Choshen Mishpat 5).

According to Rashi, no checking is needed because it’s only a suspicion. Although if the groom is not a Kohen, his status is like the woman’s, since a Kohen has a Torah-level concern, the rabbis were stringent even with a non-Kohen. However, for women, there is no Torah-level prohibition; thus, they were not stringent about generational checks.

If the suspicion is only about priestly disqualification, like a halal mixing into the family, the groom doesn’t need to check unless he is a Kohen (see Choshen Mishpat 3). Some say even according to Rambam and Rashi, checks are only required for Kohanim, not for Levites or Israelites in any case (Tosafot Yom Tov and Perush haMishnayot). Most authorities did not write this. According to Rashi, adding another generation for Levites and Israelites is only for a Kohen marrying, and all discussed in this paragraph follows Rashi and Rambam’s opinions. (This is Rashi’s intent when he wrote “since the Torah was not stringent... the rabbis also did not...” meaning the Torah permits doubtful mamzerim, resolving Tosafot’s question. See Beit Shmuel 9 and Choshen Mishpat 5 for further details.)

Some of our rabbis ruled that when the investigation is for a Kohen due to concern of disqualification (chalalut), one must check four mothers, which are eight (generations). When the investigation is due to concern of illegitimacy (mamzerut) — whether a Kohen marrying a Kohenet, a Levite, or an Israelite, or whether a Levite or Israelite marrying a Kohenet, a Levite, or an Israelite — one adds another pair in the investigation, as they were more stringent regarding the concern of illegitimacy than the concern of disqualification for the priesthood. Indeed, the woman also needs to investigate his family when the concern is due to illegitimacy or other disqualifications from the congregation. [Meor and Ramban as mentioned by the Magid Mishneh, and similarly the Ran in his name].

Some of our sages have ruled that no examination is required, neither for a Kohen who is marrying, nor for a Levite or Israelite, as a mere rumor is of no consequence. Even if the rumor is substantiated, there is still no need for generational examination. The examination of generations is only necessary for a Kohen who is marrying and is concerned that when the Temple is rebuilt, the families of Kohanim will be scrutinized to ensure there is no hint of disqualification, and those found unfit will be removed from service along with their descendants. Therefore, a Kohen who is concerned about this, when he comes to marry a woman and there is some rumor about her family, if she is from a family of Kohanim, he should examine four generations. If she is a Levite or Israelite, he should add another pair of generations. [This is the opinion of the Pirkei Tefillin, and certainly this is also the conclusion when there is a rumor, and what the Tur wrote about the Pirkei Tefillin requires further investigation; see there in Ketubot 24 and in the Ran].

And behold, according to all the opinions that have been explained, there is no concern regarding families about whom no suspicion has arisen, and anyone who comes to marry from them—whether a Kohen, a Levi, or an Israelite—does not need any investigation. This is also clarified as the opinion of the Rif and the Rosh, who did not write about this matter at all, and it is clear that they hold that even if a suspicion arises, there is no need to be concerned with it, because they hold that the investigation is only for a Kohen for the sake of the Temple service when it will be rebuilt, speedily in our days, and at this time there is no practical relevance to this. However, it is simple to all opinions that when there is a clear suspicion with witnesses, an investigation is necessary according to all opinions. And although according to the opinion in paragraph 6 and according to the Rif and the Rosh there is no need for generational investigation, nevertheless, an investigation into the woman's immediate ancestors is clearly required. But without any suspicion, all families are presumed to be kosher.

Indeed, there are some of our Rabbis who hold that when we said all families are presumed to be of valid lineage, this applies to a family that has a presumption of validity, and then no investigation is necessary. But if one's family is not known, proof of lineage must be brought by producing two witnesses that it is a valid family, and even one witness is not trusted for this, only two witnesses [Rema in Tur]. However, this is a singular opinion, and all the decisors do not hold this way. Yet, regarding a Kohen, many of our Rabbis hold that no Kohen is permitted to marry a woman from a family that is not known to be presumed of valid lineage, as many were concerned about invalidation of priestly status [Ramban, Ra’ah, and Ritva in Shitah Mekubetzet on Ketubot 24, and Ran and Rashba in their commentaries there]. According to these Rabbis, when the Sages said all families are presumed to be of valid lineage, this pertains to congregation invalidations and not to priestly invalidations. Therefore, every Kohen must be careful to only marry a woman from a known family that is presumed to be of valid lineage.

And so it seems to me that the opinion of Rashi [there] and the Rambam [Chapter 13, Law 10] is that although all families are presumed to be of valid lineage, this applies to families. However, if a man comes from a distant place and wants to marry a woman, we do not allow him until it is known who he is and from which family he comes, lest he is a mamzer or has another disqualification. For in the case of a family that is established among Israelites, we maintain it in its presumption of valid lineage. But a man who comes from distant places and we do not know him, he has no presumption [of valid lineage] at all [as above, and this resolves the Tosafot's question there on Rashi, and the Maggid Mishneh’s question in Chapter 20, Law 5, see there and examine it carefully]. And one of the great later authorities wrote that the Rambam holds like the previous opinion and so does Rashi of blessed memory [Beit Shmuel, Section 3], that one whose family's lineage is not known must bring witnesses that his family is of valid lineage. But it seems to me as I wrote that if he has a family, there is no need for any proof at all; proof is only needed for an individual who comes from distant places and we do not know his family. Therefore, in practice, it is clear that one must be careful not to marry a man who is not known to us, and similarly a woman who is not known, because many of our rabbis hold this way even according to our words [and certainly according to the Beit Shmuel and as I wrote]. And know, that indeed all families are presumed to be of valid lineage – this is for the validity of Israelites because they have a presumption of valid lineage, but to consider oneself or another as a Kohen, one must bring proof that his family is established as Kohanim, for regarding priesthood he has no presumption, and this will be explained in Section 3 with God's help, and so it is explained by the Rambam in Chapter 20, see there [and see Beit Shmuel, Section 3, what he wrote, and the Maggid Mishneh wrote there a second resolution, etc., and this requires examination as the Beit Meir wrote].

Our sages said (Kiddushin 71a): When the Holy One, Blessed be He, purifies the tribes, the tribe of Levi is purified first, as it is said, "And He shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver; and He shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the Lord an offering in righteousness" (Malachi 3). This will occur in the future. They also expounded: What does "an offering in righteousness" mean? The Holy One, Blessed be He, showed kindness to Israel by ensuring that a family which became intermixed remains intermixed. This means those families that have had invalids, such as mamzerim, intermixed among them due to their wealth and were not recognized, and many families from Israel clung to them - the Holy One, Blessed be He, will not separate them from Israel, but since they became intermixed, they remain intermixed. Hence, they said that money purifies mamzerim, meaning those mamzerim who were intermixed into Israel due to their wealth and were not recognized. And so wrote the Rambam at the end of his work: In the days of the King Messiah, all Israel will be assigned lineage by his word through the Holy Spirit that will rest upon him, as it is said, "And He shall sit as a refiner and purifier," etc., and the sons of Levi will be purified first. He will say, "This one is a priest of lineage, this one is a Levite of lineage," and he will reject those who are not of lineage to Israel, etc., but he will not assign lineage to Israel except to their tribes, notifying that "this one is from such-and-such a tribe and that one from such-and-such a tribe," but he will not say about those presumed to be of valid lineage that this one is a mamzer or this one is a slave, for the rule is that a family which became intermixed remains intermixed. So wrote the Rambam. It appears from the Rambam writing this about the future and not in the laws of forbidden relationships that this rule does not apply to us now at all. However, our rabbis did not write so, and this is their language: It is clear to us that there is no difference between this world and the days of the Messiah concerning commandments, just as we see that Elijah will not reveal intermixed families even though all will be revealed to him, so too we are not to reveal them and are not permitted to do so (Ran there, and similarly in the name of Rabbi Yonatan HaKohen). Another one of the early authorities wrote that at this time when, over the long days, the invalids have intermixed with the valid ones, etc., and the sages said that any family that became intermixed remains intermixed, thus it is presumed valid since the invalids did not intermingle knowingly, and we do not reveal intermixed families, but we do reveal invalids that did not become intermixed, and we announce them so that the valid ones should be cautious of them. Therefore, a person should only be cautious today of known invalids in his time (ShG in the name of Riaz). And one who knows about invalidity is not permitted to reveal it but should leave it in its presumed validity, and in the future, even though it will be known, it will be valid.
