However, it is possible that it is proper to reveal it to the modest ones so they do not cling to them, even though if they did cling to them unknowingly, there would be no prohibition at all. But since the seed is not prepared for sanctity and purity, as the Holy One, Blessed be He, only rests His presence on families of known lineage in Israel, it is proper to reveal them. And this is what we learn in the Gemara (Kiddushin 71a): There was another family there, but the sages did not want to reveal it, but the sages passed them on to their students (Ran there). All this applies to Israel, but priests and Levites will be necessarily separated from their ranks, and about them, it is said, "And purge them as gold and silver." Therefore, in the case of invalidity of priesthood and Levites, it is permissible to reveal. One should not ask and say: By what permission do they leave the families in their presumed validity, and is there no difference between this world and the days of the Messiah? One should say that by the law, each family member is permitted because it is like a double doubt, as will be explained in the law concerning a doubtful invalid who intermixed with a family. The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote [Chapter 19]: Even though all families are presumed to be of valid lineage and it is permitted to marry from them initially, nevertheless, two families that are always quarreling with each other, or a family that is constantly involved in strife and contention, or a person who always causes disputes with everyone and is extremely brazen-faced – we are concerned about them and it is proper to distance oneself from them, for these are signs of invalid lineage. Likewise, anyone who constantly discredits others, such as by casting aspersions on the lineage of families or individuals and saying about them that they are rebellious – we are concerned that he might be a mamzer (illegitimate child), and if he says they are slaves, we are concerned that he might be a slave, for anyone who discredits others does so with his own defect. Similarly, anyone who has brazenness and cruelty, hates people, and does not perform acts of kindness – we are concerned that he might be a Gibeonite, for the signs of the holy Jewish people are being bashful, merciful, and performers of acts of kindness. End of quote. As for a Kohen (priest) who is somewhat brazen-faced, there is no concern, as it is written, "And your people will contend with the priest" [Hosea 4:4]. Nevertheless, if he always causes disputes, we are concerned about him. The Maharshal wrote [Yam Shel Shlomo, Kiddushin, Chapter 4, Section 4]: I say that if in our times you were to be stringent with families that quarrel with each other – you would leave no family in Israel with a presumption of valid lineage, because, due to our many sins, the generation is unrestrained and has no guidance, and families always quarrel with each other. Therefore, it seems that even someone who habitually discredits families and says they are invalid – we do not suspect him of being the invalid one, because the generation is unrestrained and accustomed to this, and we do not suspect his family, only that he himself is a vinegar son of wine. End of quote. And if the Maharshal said this in his generation – all the more so in these generations.

We hold that silence is akin to admission. Therefore, the sages of blessed memory said [Ketubot 14] that when a person is called by some invalid status and he remains silent, we suspect this to be true. The Rambam similarly wrote: "Anyone who is called a mamzer and remains silent, or a Natin and remains silent, or a Chalal and remains silent, or a servant and remains silent — we suspect him and his family, and we do not marry from them unless we investigate, as we explained." End quote. 

We also do not say that because he was silent, it implies that he is the invalid one and all his family are fit, but rather the concern for the family also exists due to his silence [Beit Shmuel]. However, some of our rabbis hold that, on the contrary, anyone who remains silent, it is a sign of his lineage, for it is honorable for a person to avoid strife. And what the sages said, that when he remains silent we suspect him, is when there has already been a rumor of this invalid status about the family. If it were false, he would not remain silent in such a situation. His silence indicates that he admits to the rumor. On the contrary, his silence proves that he is the invalid one in his family, and due to him, the rumor arose, and the entire family is fit [as explained in the Tur, and similarly by the Chochmat Adam and Taz, see Beit Shmuel]. 

And if you ask, without silence, since the rumor has already arisen, shouldn’t it require investigation? Indeed, in such a case, investigation does not help because he has admitted, and the family does not require investigation [Taz]. And even if we say that investigation helps, there is still a difference if he is called a doubtful mamzer or a doubtful Chalal, and the rumor has also arisen. Without silence, if one of the family members marries, she does not need to be divorced because it is a double doubt, as will be explained. But with silence, she must be divorced without clarification, as this is akin to a ruling that he is invalid [Beit Shmuel]. 

Some of our rabbis also hold that silence means nothing. However, the sages’ concern about silence was when he does not remain silent about another invalid status when called but is silent about this one, which indicates it is true [Rashi].

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote that all this applies to a disqualification that pertains to himself. However, if they want to disqualify his offspring in his presence and he remains silent, this is not considered an admission. Nevertheless, we do need to be somewhat concerned. And even if a rumor had already spread previously, his silence does not further disqualify them, for even if his silence is considered an admission, many authorities hold that his admission does not disqualify his children, except in the case of a firstborn. And when they are established in their fitness, according to all opinions, his admission does not affect them, as will be explained in section 4. Certainly, mere silence does not disqualify his children, and we are not concerned about his silence. Although when he himself is disqualified, his children are automatically disqualified as well, when the disqualification pertains to his children and not to himself, his silence means nothing.

Indeed, regarding the fundamental disqualification through silence, our early sages agreed that all this applied in the times of the Sages of the Talmud, when the courts would attend to someone who insulted his fellow and would punish him appropriately. Therefore, silence was considered as an admission. But now, one who remains silent during a quarrel is praiseworthy, unless they call him not during a quarrel. Therefore, in our times, on the contrary, one who remains silent when someone insults his lineage is a sign that he is a noble and distinguished person. And one who hears insults on other matters and remains silent, it is a sign that he is distinguished, and the distinction of the Babylonians is their silence [Talmud]. Therefore, the Rif and the Rosh omitted all matters of silence.

A family in which there is a doubt about a חלל (a disqualified priestly lineage), any kosher woman who marries a member of that family and becomes widowed is forbidden to marry a priest initially. However, if she does marry a priest, she does not need to divorce him because there are two doubts: perhaps she is not the widow of that חלל, and even if she is, perhaps he is not a חלל. Why is she initially forbidden to marry a priest, given that we have a double doubt which should permit it outright? In truth, they only made an additional stringency regarding lineage matters, just as we require two majorities in cases of promiscuity (as stated in Siman 6), even though generally one majority would suffice [Tosafot Ketubot 14]. This stringency is only initially, but post-factum we follow the Torah law. 

Even if the woman herself does not claim with certainty that her husband was not that חלל, she is still permitted due to the double doubt, as a double doubt does not require a certain claim post-factum [as stated in the Talmud there]. If she claims with certainty that he was not a חלל, it appears she would be permitted to marry a priest initially, similar to the case of two majorities when she claims with certainty. However, there is no proof that a double doubt is as strong as two majorities, as some say that even one majority is better than a double doubt, and even those who consider a double doubt better than a majority certainly agree it is not as strong as two majorities [see Beit Shmuel]. 

Nevertheless, from the Talmudic discussion [there] it is evident that it does not deal with her making a certain claim, and one could say that they did not impose this additional stringency in the case of a certain claim. Some say that this applies even if she does not remain silent, but if she remains silent when told her husband was a חלל, even if she marries a priest, she must divorce him [Beit Shmuel]. It seems to me that here, silence is not considered an admission. For instance, in the case mentioned in section 16, when they tell the family head himself, it is assumed he has heard from family members and knows about their disqualification, so silence is indeed an admission. But this woman, who married a member of the family, how would she know about their disqualification? Her silence is not considered an admission, and in all prohibitions we do not consider silence as admission unless she should have known, as stated in Yoreh De'ah Siman 127, see there.

Many have asked: Why do we consider in a case of a doubtful chalal (a descendant of a priest who is disqualified from priestly service) that has become mixed with others as a situation of a double doubt (safek-safeka)? After all, we have ruled in Siman 110 that every double doubt requires both doubts to be either in the substance of the prohibition or both in the mixture, but if one doubt is in the substance and one in the mixture, it does not qualify as a double doubt. Here, one doubt is in the substance of the prohibition - whether the individual is a chalal or not - and the second doubt is due to the mixture within the entire family. However, this is not a question at all, for it is not comparable to every double doubt. Even without the double doubt, she is permitted by law since we follow the majority of the family, and whoever separates from the majority is assumed to be from the majority, as every man who takes a wife brings her to his home [Yam Shel Shlomo, Siman 43]. There is no concern that perhaps he stayed in his place and she came to him – which would make it a case of a fixed situation and considered as a fifty-fifty doubt – for we only worry about this in cases of promiscuity, not in marriage, as it is customary for a man to seek out a woman. Since she is permitted even without the double doubt, we do not worry about this. According to this, since there is also the permissibility of the majority here, it is obvious that if she asserts with certainty, she is permitted to marry a priest even initially [this appears to me].

Some authorities say that this is not a case of one doubt regarding the individual and one doubt regarding the mixture, for we are not judging the mixture at all here, but rather this widow, whether her husband was a chalal (disqualified priest), and if you say he was, perhaps he is not a chalal. This is similar to two chickens in a house, one kosher and the other possibly trefa (non-kosher), and an egg is found there. It is permitted due to the principle of double doubt (safek sefeka): perhaps the kosher chicken laid the egg, and if you say the questionable one laid it, perhaps it is kosher. It is explained there that this is a case of double doubt, and similarly here. 

However, some have rejected this comparison, arguing it is not similar to the case of the egg, where we judge from where the egg came. But here we do not need to judge the widow unless it was not known who her husband was from the family. But if her husband is known, we need to judge the husband, for when he is forbidden, she is also forbidden through his union with her. When we judge him, one doubt concerns his status—whether he is a chalal or not—and the second doubt arises because he is mixed within the family. 

In my opinion, the primary view is the first one, because certainly if the husband were alive and we were judging him, she would be forbidden due to him. But when the husband is dead and we do not need to judge him, we only judge the widow. Additionally, in matters of presumptions, we judge the matter in doubt and not the cause that led to the doubt. Moreover, fundamentally, this is not similar to one doubt concerning the individual and one doubt concerning the mixture. Some say that the reason why one doubt concerning the individual and one concerning the mixture does not help is that initially, when there was doubt regarding the individual and she was clearly forbidden, the mixture does not help, as it is like a definite prohibition. This is not the case if both doubts arise simultaneously, which is considered like a double doubt. Here, both doubts concerning her husband arise simultaneously. This reasoning is agreed upon by our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Tur Yoreh De'ah, section 57, regarding the case of a possibly injured animal. Even according to the opinion there that even if both doubts arise simultaneously, since they are not equal, it is not considered a double doubt—it is also not comparable here. For if we judge the widow, the two doubts are equal: doubt whether her husband was a chalal, and if you say he was, perhaps he is not a chalal. Why should we initiate the doubt with the husband since we are not judging him, as explained?

Some say that specifically the widow, if she remarried, she does not have to leave because she had a presumption of fitness before she married this person. But if his daughter married, she must leave, because she was born in doubt and does not have a presumption of fitness. And some say there is no difference between her and her daughter, and this is the main opinion, because since there is a double doubt and also a majority as mentioned in paragraph 20, what need is there for a presumption? Furthermore, the presumption of the mother was weakened from the day she married this person. And although a weakened presumption is still a presumption, nevertheless, it is not a strong presumption. Additionally, the presumption of the mother also benefits the daughter, as mentioned in Chapter 6 regarding a woman who behaves promiscuously, see there [see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 14, and examine it thoroughly].

If a definite chalal (a person of flawed priestly status) is mixed into the family, every woman among them is forbidden until it is investigated. If she marries, she must leave him, for there is only one doubt here: perhaps he was the chalal, or perhaps he was not. Even according to what we have said, there is a majority to permit, nevertheless, in matters of lineage we do not permit based on a single majority, and we require a double majority as stated there. However, if she claims with certainty that her husband was not a chalal, it seems that if she marries, she does not have to leave him. This is implied in the Gemara, where in cases of certainty, we are lenient in cases of doubt, especially since there is also a majority here [and this is also indicated by the Gra in section 31, see there].

If a definite mamzer or a questionable mamzer is mixed into the family concerning a kohen – the one who marries from this family has the same ruling as if a definite or questionable chalal is mixed in, for the prohibition of a kohen marrying a mamzeret and a chalalah is one and the same [Rambam]. Concerning an Israelite – the woman who marries one of the family members is certainly permitted, for the wife of a mamzer is not prohibited to an Israelite. Regarding the daughters born from the members of this family – some say that if a questionable mamzer is mixed in, it is permissible for an Israelite to marry her even lechatchila (initially) due to a double doubt, since the prohibition for a kohen to marry is a higher standard established by the kohanim in their lineage as stated in the Gemara there, but we do not find this higher standard for Israelites [Yesh”sh, Ta”z, and B”Sh], for the entire matter is only rabbinic, as from the Torah a questionable mamzer is permitted to an Israelite as stated in Siman 4, and only rabbinically is it forbidden, therefore with a double doubt it is permitted even lechatchila, and this is also implied by the language of the Rambam. However, some say that even for an Israelite the ruling is like that of a kohen and it is forbidden to marry her lechatchila, but if she marries, she need not be divorced [Beit Yosef], for since the kohanim established this higher standard, it remains forbidden initially even for those with community disqualifications [Gra], and this is also implied by the language of the Tur at the end of Siman 7 according to our version. The first opinion holds that there is a printing error in the Tur [B”Sh], and it also seems from the conclusion there that if he married, the child would be a questionable mamzer, and this is certainly the case that even for a kohen there is no concern after the fact as stated. [And to say that it refers to the mixture of a definite mamzer, what does it teach us? This has already been explained in Siman 4].

Some say that this applies specifically when the disqualification is confirmed to have mixed in through witnesses, but if it is merely a rumor without substance – even a Kohen does not need to be concerned. However, when there are witnesses who have mentioned a trace of disqualification on the family due to the rumor, it is possible that according to Rashi, as we explained in section 8, there is a need for concern.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that all this applies specifically to someone who knows of the disqualification, but a family in which a disqualification has been mixed in and is not known to the public, once it has been assimilated – it is assimilated. And one who knows of the disqualification is not permitted to reveal it; rather, he should leave it with the presumption of fitness, for all families that have been assimilated into Israel are fit for the future. Nevertheless, it is proper to reveal it to the modest. And this specifically applies to a family that has been assimilated and mixed in, but as long as it has not been mixed in – disqualifications are revealed and publicized so that the fit can separate from them. And see in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 35, who is believed to testify about families. End of quote. And we have already explained this in Section 11. And it seems to me that this only applies to disqualifications regarding the congregation, but the Kohanim need to be concerned, for they will be joined in the future, and it is possible that the Levites also need to be concerned, as mentioned there.

[Laws of the Priesthood and Its Lineage, containing 22 sections]

It has already been clarified in Siman 2 that all families are presumed to be of valid lineage, and it was explained there in section 12 that according to many Halachic authorities, this presumption applies only regarding the invalidation from the assembly of Israel and not to the priesthood. Therefore, a priest (Kohen) who marries a woman must investigate her family's lineage, as mentioned there. However, according to all authorities, the presumption of priesthood is not the same as the presumption of Israelite lineage. For Israelite lineage, there is a general presumption for everyone, but for priesthood, there is no presumption in general unless it is a definite presumption. Thus, our sages stated: Israelites recognize the mamzerim (those of illegitimate birth) among them, but they do not recognize the chalalim (those disqualified from the priesthood) among them. This is because a mamzer is forbidden to enter the assembly, and everyone avoids marrying him – hence, he is well-known. But a chalal is permitted in the assembly, and his disqualification is only for the priesthood, and there is nothing to publicize his disqualification since he is kosher (fit) as any other Israelite. Additionally, the main service of the priesthood was in the Temple, and the Sanhedrin would always investigate the lineage of the priests, and any priest found with even a trace of disqualification would be excluded from service. Therefore, during the time of the Temple, the definite presumption of priesthood was for those who served in the Temple. Thus, our sages stated [Kiddushin 76]: We do not investigate from the altar and above, nor from the platform in the Temple and above, nor from the Sanhedrin and above, for only priests of distinguished lineage are appointed to the altar, Levites of distinguished lineage to the platform, and Israelites of distinguished lineage to the Sanhedrin.

What is a qualified Kohen? Any individual for whom two witnesses testify that he is a Kohen, the son of a specific Kohen, and this father is the son of another specific Kohen, up to a person who does not require further verification, and he is the Kohen who served on the altar [Rambam]. Therefore, when they ascended from the exile, they required each Kohen to show their genealogy record, and those who could not find their record were distanced from the priesthood, as it is written in Ezra [2], "And from the sons of the priests: the sons of Hovaviah, the sons of Hakkoz, the sons of Barzillai... These sought their record of genealogies but it was not found, and they were disqualified from the priesthood." Similarly, if two witnesses testify that they saw him eating terumah of a biblical nature, he is considered qualified, for we hold that one can ascend from the status of eating biblical terumah to being genealogically qualified. However, from rabbinic terumah, one cannot ascend. Similarly, one does not ascend from the practice of lifting hands (the Priestly Blessing) to being genealogically qualified, nor from being called first to the Torah, nor from receiving terumah at the threshing floor [ibid]. Specifically, it is from eating biblical terumah, which is a sin punishable by death for a non-Kohen who eats it, that if he were not a qualified Kohen, he would not eat it. But lifting hands, which is only a positive commandment for a non-Kohen who ascends, does not elevate one to genealogical qualification. [Therefore, one does not ascend from dividing terumah, even though it is not distributed to a slave without his master, as Rambam writes in chapter 12 of Terumot].

And now, in our times, when we do not have the Temple service due to our sins, nor do we have Terumah by Torah law – therefore, in the future, the Holy One, blessed be He, will purify the Kohanim (priests) as it is written, "And He shall sit as a refiner" etc., as it is written there. Nevertheless, all Kohanim in our times are presumed to be Kohanim for all prohibitions of Kohanim, and they ascend first to the Torah, and they ascend to the platform for the Priestly Blessing, and they eat rabbinic Terumah in places where it is still customary to separate Terumot and Ma'aserot by rabbinic decree, as in the Land of Israel. And throughout the Diaspora in our times, we do not even have rabbinic Terumah.

And since the presumptive status of a Kohen (priest) is more stringent than the presumptive status of an Israelite, therefore, someone who comes in this time and says, "I am a Kohen" – is not believed, for a person is not believed to testify about himself and we do not elevate him to the status of a Kohen. He does not read from the Torah first, does not perform the Priestly Blessing, and is not fed Rabbinically decreed Terumah. However, for prohibitions related to the Kohen's status, he is believed, for a person is believed to impose stringencies upon himself. Therefore, he is forbidden to marry a divorced woman, a zonah (a woman with whom relations are forbidden), or a chalalah (a woman of flawed priestly lineage). He is forbidden to become ritually impure by contact with the dead, and if he marries one of these women or becomes ritually impure, he is flogged if he was forewarned. This is not a dubious warning, even if we say that a dubious warning is not considered a warning, for this is a definite warning, as he is forewarned based on his own statement that he is a Kohen. Additionally, the Rambam ruled that a dubious warning is considered a warning, and a woman who has sexual relations with him, if she is disqualified from marrying a Kohen, she is possibly a chalalah and therefore forbidden to a Kohen.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that there are those who say that a person is trusted to read from the Torah first and to lift his hands in blessing nowadays, when we do not have biblical-level terumah, so we do not worry that he might be elevated to the status of receiving terumah. And so is the custom nowadays in all places where terumah is not practiced in these times, and there is no concern for anything. End quote. They raised a difficulty on him: Isn't lifting the hands (in blessing) a biblical prohibition, as it is written "Thus shall you bless" – you (the Kohanim) and not strangers, and a negative commandment derived from a positive commandment is considered a positive commandment. And it seems to me that by Torah law, every person is trusted regarding his own status, even in matters that have a presumption of prohibition, as it is written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 127, and he should have been trusted even in the case of biblical terumah. However, because being elevated from terumah affects lineage, and in matters of Kohanic lineage, many stringencies were enacted, therefore he is not trusted – not for biblical terumah, and also not for rabbinic terumah due to the elevated status of the Kohanim. Therefore, in the time of the Talmud, when rabbinic terumah was still practiced, he was not trusted in any matter, unlike now when we have no form of terumah and by law he is trusted. Therefore, there is no concern for this. Furthermore, in the case of terumah, he was not trusted because he benefits from the property of others who give him the terumah, unlike in our times [see Beit Shmuel], and there is no concern of lineage issues in him holding himself to be a Kohen. In the future, the truth will be revealed, and therefore there is no concern in this matter.

If he speaks innocently, he is also believed regarding Rabbinic terumah, and the Gemara brings a story [Ketubot 26a] about someone who was speaking innocently and said, "I remember when I was a child and I was riding on my father's shoulders. They took me out of school, removed my shirt, and immersed me so that I could eat terumah in the evening. My friends kept their distance from me so as not to make me impure, and they called me Yochanan the bread eater." Rabbi Judah the Prince elevated him to priesthood based on his own words—but only for Rabbinic terumah and for the priestly blessing (duchening), for the reasons explained. However, he was not elevated for Biblical terumah, so as not to elevate him to [full] genealogical status, as there were many precautions taken regarding lineage, as mentioned. The fact that this priest spoke at length is not essential; he simply recounted events as they occurred, as clarified by the Tur [Beit Yosef]. 

Some say he had to mention being taken out of school, for otherwise, we might suspect he was a priest's slave [Tosafot]. Even though we generally do not worry about slaves, as mentioned in Siman 2, that all families are presumed to be of valid lineage, it is possible here that it was known there were slaves among the priests in that city [Nimukei Yosef, see Beit Shmuel and examine this well]. According to this opinion, he also had to say that his friends kept their distance and that they called him Yochanan the bread eater—all to remove him from the presumption of being a slave that was present among the priests in that city [and similarly, according to the Rambam's intent, there is no need to say he holds we worry about slaves, see Beit Shmuel].

If a single witness testifies that someone is a Kohen (priest), he is believed in order to allow him to eat rabbinically ordained terumah, to be called first to the Torah, and to raise his hands in the priestly blessing. According to the law, he would even be believed regarding biblically ordained terumah because a single witness is trusted in matters of prohibitions, whether to be lenient or stringent, in cases where there is no established prohibition or permissibility, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, siman 127. However, because biblically ordained terumah can elevate one’s status for lineage purposes, and lineage has many stringent requirements, as explained.

Not only that, but even Reuven, who is established as a Kohen, is believed to say about Shimon that he is his son and that he is a Kohen, and this is considered as one witness. And even though a relative is disqualified from all testimony, nevertheless, he is believed with a "Migu" that if he wanted, he could have said he is not a relative and been one witness [Ramban]. According to this, if it is known that he is his father, he is not believed [Hilchot Maaser Sheini 19], because we are concerned that he might be a "Chalal." And even though he has a "Migu" that he could have fed him from his Terumah, nevertheless, to elevate him to the Torah and to perform the priestly blessing, he does not have a "Migu" [it appears to me]. According to the Rambam, even if it is known that he is his father, he is believed due to the "Migu" [there]. And even though the "Migu" is only for Terumah, nevertheless, since he is believed for Terumah, he is believed for all matters of priesthood in our times as one witness, because fundamentally there is no concern about this, for presumably he himself says this, and everyone is believed about themselves as stated in section 5. Therefore, a relative is also believed. Furthermore, for being called to the Torah and for the priestly blessing, one is believed about himself even now as stated in section 5 in the name of our teacher, the Rema. [It appears to me, and what the Beit Shmuel wrote in section 7 to be concerned about a "Mamzer" follows his reasoning in section 2, sub-section 3, where the poskim hold like the Rama, and we have already explained there what appears to me regarding this].

We elevate someone to the status of a priest in our times, even to allow him to eat rabbinically ordained terumah. How so? If it was written in a document, "I, so-and-so the priest, borrowed a maneh from so-and-so," and witnesses signed it, he is thus established as a priest among the priests of this time. And some say that even if there are no witnesses signed on it, it is no less credible than if he were making an offhand statement, which is believed regarding priesthood even to eat rabbinically ordained terumah [see Choshen Mishpat]. And although when he says "I am a priest," we do not consider it as an offhand statement and he is not believed for rabbinically ordained terumah, nevertheless, when he signs himself, we consider it an offhand statement because the signature was not made concerning priesthood [see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 9].

And if the entire contract is in the language of the witnesses who wrote "We are witnesses testifying that so-and-so the Kohen borrowed a maneh from so-and-so" — according to the Rashba, of blessed memory, this is valid even for Biblical-level terumah and for lineage, as this is equivalent to two witnesses testifying that he is a Kohen. And why do we not accept their testimony when it is written "I, so-and-so the Kohen, borrowed a maneh from so-and-so" with witnesses signing on it, except for the priesthood in this current age? Because it can be said that the witnesses only testified about the loan itself and not about the priesthood. According to the Rambam, of blessed memory, even when the contract is in the language of the witnesses — it is not considered full testimony, and it is only valid for the priesthood in this current age, because it can be said that they only came to testify that he is recognized as a Kohen from the Kohanim of this time, and did not come to testify about lineage, as they did not come to testify about his priesthood, but to identify who the borrower is. Therefore, when he is from the Kohanim of this time, it serves as a clear sign to identify who he is. Therefore, even if there were two Yosef ben Shimon in one city, and they wrote as a sign that one of them is a Kohen, which some say since they need to scrutinize and differentiate between them — it is full testimony even for lineage, nonetheless according to the Rambam their testimony only benefits for the priesthood in this current age, because for a sign it is a clear sign. Therefore, it is not similar to what is written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 49, regarding two Yosef ben Shimon, and they wrote about one of them "may he live" that he borrowed — it is a clear sign that he is the borrower, and here it is not a clear sign for lineage, since here too it is a clear sign but we say that even for the priesthood of this current age it is a clear sign. And according to what is written there in Choshen Mishpat, Sa'if 8, according to the conclusion of the great recent authorities — the primary ruling in law follows the Rambam, see there.

One is promoted from the duty of blessing the people (duchening) to the status of priesthood in our times, as well as from being called first to the Torah reading. Therefore, one who sees someone blessing the people or being called first to the Torah reading can testify that he is a Kohen and permit him to eat rabbinically ordained terumah. And even though it was stated in section 5 that one is believed about himself to bless the people and to be called first to the Torah reading, nevertheless, in a place where there is rabbinically ordained terumah, he is not believed, as stated there. And regarding being called first to the Torah reading – it is specifically when it is known that he was called first as a Kohen, because otherwise, there is concern that there was no Kohen in the synagogue, and he was called in place of a Kohen, as stated in Orach Chaim, siman 135.

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote: "If someone comes nowadays and says 'I am a Kohen,' and a single witness testifies that he knows this person's father was a Kohen, we do not elevate him to the priesthood based on this testimony alone, as he may be a chalal (disqualified Kohen), until it is testified that this person himself is a Kohen. However, if his father was established as a Kohen, or if two witnesses testify that this person's father was a Kohen, then he is presumed to follow his father's status." End of quote. 

The explanation of his words is that the enhancement made in matters of priesthood to prevent someone from being believed about himself, and to accept a single witness, applies when the witness testifies about the person himself but not when testifying about his father. The enhancement was made in lineage matters to be wary of a single witness's testimony about the father, lest he married a disqualified woman. However, if two witnesses testify about the father or the father is established as a Kohen, this enhancement was not made. Otherwise, every person from a Kohen family would need to bring proof that they were not born from disqualified Kohanim, which is entirely impractical. 

Moreover, even in matters of stoning and burning (capital punishments), we rely on presumptions. When a man and woman live together as husband and wife and their children are attached to them, we presume the children to be theirs. If the father cohabits with his presumed daughter, he is liable for burning; if the son cohabits with his presumed mother, he is liable for stoning (Kiddushin 76b). All the more so, we rely on presumptions in matters of lineage, and the enhancement was only made concerning a single witness. A single witness in testimony is nothing in all of Torah law except for oaths, the suspected adulteress, and the decapitated calf. 

Some of our rabbis disagree on this and hold that the trust given to a single witness is equivalent to the trust of two witnesses, and even if he testifies about the father, the person is presumed to be a Kohen unless there is a rumor that he is a chalal (disqualified Kohen) (see Maggid Mishneh, Chapter 12). Our Master, Rabbi Yosef Karo (author of the Shulchan Aruch), ruled in Section 6 according to Maimonides and did not bring any other opinion at all (see Beit Yosef, subparagraph 7).

If someone is established as a Kohen through their father, a single witness is not believed to disqualify him, because a single witness is not believed to remove a person from their established status. If a rumor spreads from many people that his father married a divorced woman or a chalutzah (a woman released from levirate marriage) and fathered him, even though they are not testifying formally but just as a widespread rumor, since it comes from many people, we are concerned about the rumor and demote him from the higher status of Kehunah (priesthood), but not from the prohibitions of priesthood. Therefore, if he defiles himself by contact with the dead, he is flogged as before, because the concern about the rumor is to be stringent, not lenient. If afterwards, a single witness comes and testifies that his mother is fit for the priesthood, we restore him to his priesthood status based on the witness's testimony, because in the face of a rumor, a single witness is believed. If subsequently, two witnesses come and testify formally that he is a chalal (disqualified priest), he is demoted from his priesthood status and is permitted to defile himself by contact with the dead and to marry a divorced woman, because the matter is established by the testimony of two witnesses. However, if later another single witness comes and testifies like the first witness that he is fit, the man returns to the prohibitions and privileges of the priesthood, because now there are two witnesses testifying to his fitness, as this last witness joins the first, and two witnesses testify to his disqualification. Throughout the Torah, we have a principle to balance two witnesses against two witnesses and to maintain the status quo. Similarly, we maintain this Kohen in the status of his fathers, and consequently, all the witnesses are nullified since they contradict each other, and the rumor is also nullified because there is no difference between one hundred witnesses and two witnesses, and he remains in his established status. Some say that this applies only to Rabbinic Terumah (priestly dues) and not to Biblical Terumah, because in a case of two against two, we do not say to maintain the status quo in a Biblical matter, even though from the Torah it certainly is so; nevertheless, the Rabbis were stringent in this matter, and its status is like any Rabbinic doubt. Others disagree, saying that since the stringency is only Rabbinic, they were stringent only regarding the prohibition of marrying a divorced woman or performing Temple service, but not regarding Terumah. Regarding the principle explained in section 46 that we do not nullify a rumor, this refers to the rumor about divorce, so that she cannot marry a Kohen. Since she has no loss, she can marry an Israelite, but to remove a person from their established status, we certainly nullify a rumor.

In light of the explanation that even a single witness is trusted regarding the presumption of priesthood (Kehunah), the Sages were lenient in this matter such that even if two individuals come forward and each testifies about the other that he is a Kohen, they are believed, and we do not suspect them of collusion, meaning that they agreed among themselves, "You testify about me, and I will testify about you." It appears to me that this leniency applies only to rabbinically mandated terumah, but not to biblically mandated terumah. This must be the case, for we hold that one can be elevated from the status of being permitted to eat biblically mandated terumah to being considered of proven lineage (yichus), and a single witness is not trusted for matters of lineage.

And similarly, they were lenient with the testimony of a single witness even when he testifies only on signs of priesthood, such as when he testifies about Reuven and says, "I remember when I was a child I saw them immersing Reuven to allow him to eat terumah, or that he immersed himself and ate terumah" — we elevate Reuven to the status of priesthood like all the priests of our time. They were so lenient that even if he testifies about something from his childhood, we believe him. And all of this is for the reason we explained in section 5, that according to the law, there is no concern about this. And why are we not concerned that he might be a slave of a priest? Because we do not suspect the congregation of illegitimacy, as we said in section 6.

Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 3: If one of the Anusim (forced converts) testifies that one of them is established in the priesthood, they elevate him to read from the Torah and do not suspect that his mother might be a gentile. End quote. The explanation of the matters is that in the country of Spain during the expulsion, there remained Jews who secretly observed Judaism while openly appearing as non-Jews. If one of them testifies that the father of this person was a Kohen (priest), we do not worry that, since they intermingled with gentiles, it is likely that his mother was invalid because they also kept themselves from intermarriage with gentiles. And even though, according to Maimonides in section [13] (12), a single witness is not reliable without more, nevertheless, according to those who disagree with him, it is valid as stated there. And even according to Maimonides, it is possible that a single witness is reliable for reading from the Torah [Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel]. Additionally, even if two witnesses testified about his father being a Kohen, it would not be sufficient due to the concern of intermingling that we explained, unless we know that they also were careful about their marriages. [This explains the difficulty raised against the Beit Yosef, but he used the language of the responsum in his usual manner, so examine it carefully.]

A woman who did not wait three months after the death of her husband and married another man, and then gave birth after seven months, and it is not known whose child it is, whether she gave birth after nine months and it is the child of the first husband, or she gave birth after seven months and it is the child of the second husband, and one of them was a Kohen (priest) and the other was an Israelite – this child is considered a doubtful Kohen. Similarly, if a Kohen's child got mixed up with an Israelite's child – each one is considered a doubtful Kohen, and they are treated with both the stringencies of Kohanim and the stringencies of Israelites. When they grow up, they can only marry women who are fit for Kohanim, they do not become impure by contact with the dead, they do not eat even rabbinic terumah, and if they marry women who are invalid for Kohanim, they must divorce them with a get. They do not receive lashes for violating these prohibitions or for becoming impure by the dead because they are doubtful Kohanim and one does not receive lashes for a doubt. If they ate terumah, they do not pay the principal and the fifth as a non-Kohen would. The doubtful Kohen does not need to give his own terumah to a Kohen, rather he sells it and keeps the money, for we do not take money out of someone’s possession due to a doubt. He does not receive a portion in the sacred offerings of the Temple or in the distribution of terumah at the threshing floor, and even in the hides of the sacred offerings he does not receive a portion, because the members of the priestly watch would say to him, 'Bring proof that you are a Kohen.' However, if he brings an offering, he keeps the hide for himself, as we do not take it away from him due to a doubt. Similarly, if a firstborn is born to him, he does not need to give five selaim to a Kohen, and he is exempt from giving the firstborn of his animal, and he redeems a firstborn donkey with a lamb which he keeps for himself. The firstborn of his animal is left to graze until it develops a blemish and then it is eaten with its blemish. He is exempt from giving the priestly gifts of the foreleg, the jaw, and the maw. Even if a Kohen and an Israelite got mixed up, they cannot go to the threshing floor to take terumah on behalf of the one who is definitely a Kohen, because since they are not permitted to eat it, it is not given to them lest they come to eat it [Tosafot Yevamot 99:]. And if they ate terumah, although they do not need to give the principal and the fifth to a Kohen, nonetheless, they need to separate the principal and the fifth so that they may achieve atonement [ibid.], and the payments become terumah and are sold to a Kohen, and when Elijah comes, he will clarify who is the Kohen and who is the Israelite [see Magen Avraham 1:]. It seems to me that if this doubtful Kohen performed service in the Temple – according to the Rambam's view that biblical doubts are treated leniently, the owner of the offering does not need to bring another offering, and if the offering was a sin offering or a guilt offering – he is forbidden to bring another offering since one does not bring a sin offering or a guilt offering voluntarily due to a doubt. According to the Rashba's view that biblical doubts are treated strictly – he is required to bring another offering.

Two priests whose children were mixed up, or a woman who did not wait three months and married another man, and both are priests, and she gave birth to a child who is possibly a seven-month baby of the latter or a nine-month baby of the former – they are definite priests even though their lineage is unclear. However, regarding the impurity of death, where a priest becomes impure for his relatives and not for others – the fathers do not become impure for them, nor do they become impure for the fathers, and they do not observe mourning or bereavement for them, and the same applies to them. They do not inherit from them, as the definite heirs exclude them due to doubt, but if one of them dies – the fathers share the inheritance, as it is considered money in doubt and they share it, as there is no presumption against it. They are exempt from punishment for striking or cursing them, unless both strike or curse both – then they are liable in any case. In the Temple – they serve in both shifts, of this one and that one, as they cannot be prevented from serving. However, they do not receive a portion of the holy things, as the members of the watch exclude them, but if both come together – they receive one portion in any case.

It is written: "And it shall be for him and his descendants after him an everlasting covenant of priesthood" (Numbers 25:13), and our Sages relied on this verse to require that his descendants be traceable after him, such that one knows who his father is. And since this is merely a rabbinic support (asmachta) and not a biblical injunction, therefore they did not decree in matters of marriage – if there arises a doubt whether he is a priest, son of this priest, or son of another priest, as in the case where the children of two priests were mixed up, or when the mother did not wait three months [between marriages] as mentioned. However, in cases of promiscuity, they did decree. Therefore, if ten priests separated, and one of them had relations and a son was born – even though he is definitely a priest – nevertheless, they silence him from the status of priesthood, and he does not perform the priestly service, nor does he eat terumah. This stringency applies only to be stringent, but not to be lenient; hence, if he becomes impure through contact with the dead or marries a divorced woman, he receives forty lashes. Even if the matter involves both promiscuity and marriage, such as if she had relations with one priest and within three months married another priest – since there is an aspect of promiscuity, they silence him from the status of priesthood. And although the majority of relations are presumed to be with the husband – this applies if she engaged in promiscuity while married to her husband, but if she engaged in promiscuity beforehand, it is possible that she was already pregnant, and furthermore, they imposed a higher standard in matters of priestly lineage. The same law applies if she engaged in promiscuity after her husband's death within three months. Some hesitate regarding this due to the principle that we attribute the child to the husband.

Specifically in the case of promiscuity where there is a doubt about who the father is, but if a Kohen had relations with an unmarried woman and a son was born and he acknowledges that the son is his, then the son is considered a Kohen in all respects. We do not worry that perhaps she made herself available to others as well, since he acknowledges that the child is his. This will be further explained in section 4, with God's help. And although it is certain that she had intercourse during her niddah days, nevertheless, the son of a niddah is only considered blemished but not invalid, and this will also be explained there. This is not only when he acknowledges that the child is his, but even if he only acknowledges that he had relations with her and she says that she did not have relations with anyone else. However, if he is not present – even though the child is legitimate as explained there – nevertheless, we silence him from the rights of priesthood.

It has already been explained that for complete priestly lineage to serve in the Temple and to eat Terumah by Torah law, two witnesses are required to testify that he is the son of a verified priest whose lineage has been examined. Similarly, when he marries a woman, it is necessary to examine the lineage of four mothers, as stated in Siman 2, because significant measures were taken regarding priestly lineage. However, a strong presumption also suffices—how is this presumption established? If a verified priest went overseas with his examined wife to another country, and afterward, he and his wife come here with small children clinging to her, there is no need to bring witnesses either for the woman that these are her children since they cling to her, or for the children when he says they are his from this woman, and we do not suspect that he took another woman there and fathered them [Tosafot Kiddushin 79b]. If she died and he came alone or the children are grown and do not cling to her, he must bring witnesses that these are his children from this verified woman, or bring proof that the children are his from the woman who died there. He need not bring proof that they are from the woman who went with him overseas, as we do not suspect that he took another woman there [Tosafot ibid and as understood from Rambam]. If he went alone and came with a woman and children clinging to her, he must bring proof that the woman is of verified lineage from the four mothers, but he need not bring proof regarding the children. If they do not cling to her, he must bring proof that the children are his from this woman. If he comes with two women and the children cling to one, even if she has been verified, he must bring proof that these are her children, as we suspect they might be from the other and cling to this verified one because they were raised together. If he and his children come and he says, "I married a woman, and these are her children," he must bring witnesses that she was of verified lineage and that these are her children. This law also applies to an Israelite of verified lineage regarding sitting on the Sanhedrin, and to a Levite of verified lineage regarding the platform in the Temple [Rambam]. In such presumptions where they cling to her, we rule regarding lineage, as we execute by stoning and burning based on presumptions [Tur], as explained in section 12.

A Kohen who married a divorced woman and claims he is not a Kohen is not believed, and we compel him with all kinds of coercion to divorce her. And it is not only when his father is established as a Kohen that he is not believed to say he was born from a chalalah, but even if his father is not known to us and he himself held himself as a Kohen, he is not believed to retract without proof, for we administer lashes based on his own presumption, as he has made himself considered a Kohen. And although some say that for the matter of lashes we require that he has been established for thirty days, nevertheless regarding the prohibition, it is agreed that he prohibits himself immediately by his own words. Furthermore, it seems that even for lashes, we do not require thirty days, and this is also implied from what is explained in section 4, and such a presumption is considered immediate once he has held himself as a Kohen. There are those who mistakenly say that the Kohanim of our time are not full Kohanim because they do not have genealogical records tracing back to Aaron the Kohen, but God forbid to say so, for by law this is not required at all, as we explained in this section and in section 2. It was merely an additional measure that genealogical examination was performed, and since their family is established as Kohanim, they are complete Kohanim forever and ever.

[Laws concerning who is disqualified from entering the congregation of Israel, containing 62 sections]

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 1 of Ishut, Halacha 7: Before the giving of the Torah, a man would encounter a woman in the marketplace, and if both he and she desired, he would pay her and engage in relations with her by the roadside and then depart. This woman was called a "kedesha" (prostitute). Once the Torah was given, the kedesha was forbidden, as it is stated: "There shall not be a kedesha among the daughters of Israel." Therefore, anyone who engages in relations with a woman for the sake of promiscuity without betrothal is liable to lashes from the Torah because he has engaged with a kedesha. This is the end of his words. This does not pertain to rape or seduction for which the Torah mandates a fine, and where there is an obligation of lashes, there is no monetary obligation. Rambam has already explained this in Chapter 2 of Naarah and in the Book of Commandments [Negative Commandment 55], that rape and seduction are incidental, where he persuaded her with words and she does not fall under the category of kedesha, and he is not liable to lashes for this. A kedesha is someone who prepared herself with her own consent or with her father's consent for anyone who wishes to engage in relations with her. In this case, there is no fine but lashes, and regarding this, it is stated: "Do not degrade your daughter to make her a prostitute," which will be explained, with God's help, in Siman 177. This is also explained in the Sifri, and most of the poskim (halachic authorities) agree with this. Similarly, it must be said regarding what is written, "There shall not be a kadesh among the sons of Israel" – this means that a male should not prepare himself for anyone who wishes to engage in relations with him. However, Onkelos interprets this verse as referring to a male and female slave, and so is the opinion of the SeMaG (Sefer Mitzvot Gadol), Ramban, and Rashba, of blessed memory. Rambam, of blessed memory, holds that the prohibition of a male and female slave is by rabbinic decree as he wrote in Chapter 12 of Issurei Biah [see there in Chapter 15 what the Kesef Mishneh wrote in the name of Rabbi Avraham, the son of Rambam, which requires further investigation, and examine it well].

Additionally, he wrote there in chapter 15 that all those who are liable for negative commandments — whether they are disqualified from the congregation or disqualified from the priesthood — are not liable for lashes unless they betroth and consummate. But if they betroth and do not consummate, or consummate and do not betroth, they are not liable for lashes, except for the High Priest with a widow, as mentioned there. And the language of the Torah proves this, for in all those liable for negative commandments, it is written, "He shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord," and entering the congregation is only through betrothal [as mentioned in the name of R. Abraham]. And proof of this: regarding forbidden relations, it is written, "You shall not approach to uncover nakedness," because betrothal does not take effect with forbidden relations. If the Torah's intention was also in cases of negative commandments without betrothal, it would have written the language of uncovering nakedness, which implies mere consummation. Nonetheless, most of the decisors disagree with him, for it is not written in the language of taking as in betrothal, and "he shall not enter" is the language of consummation. This is also proven from the Talmudic discussions, and even Maimonides himself in the first chapter of "A Maiden" proves that he holds this way [for the answer of the Kesef Mishneh in the name of R. Abraham is problematic as he wrote in section 1].

Forbidden sexual unions are of five types: those punishable by karet, those punishable by death by the court, those punishable by negative commandments, those punishable by positive commandments, and those forbidden by rabbinic decree. The prohibitions regarding sexual relations are detailed in Siman 15.

The cases punishable by negative commandments are: a mamzer with an Israelite, an Israelite woman with a mamzer, an Israelite woman with an Ammonite or Moabite, and an Israelite woman with a man who has damaged reproductive organs. A divorced woman who marries another man is forbidden to return to her first husband, and a yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage) with another man before performing chalitza or yibum.

Regarding the Nethinim (Temple servants), according to Maimonides (Rambam), their prohibition is rabbinic, while others say it is from the Torah. This will be clarified later. An Israelite who has relations with a non-Jewish woman, or a non-Jew who has relations with an Israelite woman, according to Maimonides in Chapter 12 of Issurei Biah, this is a biblical prohibition, as it says, "You shall not intermarry with them." According to the Tur, this only applies to the seven Canaanite nations if they convert. If an Israelite has relations with a non-Jewish woman, it is a halacha from Moses at Sinai that zealots may attack him, as will be detailed in Siman 16. There are other prohibitions in this context as mentioned there.

A slave who has relations with an Israelite woman or an Israelite who has relations with a maidservant, according to Onkelos and several of our sages, are punishable by lashes, as it says, "There shall not be a holy person (prostitute)..." According to Maimonides, this prohibition is rabbinic. An Israelite who has relations with an unmarried Israelite woman for the sake of promiscuity, according to Maimonides, this is a biblical prohibition, as mentioned in Siman 1.

For Kohanim (priests), there are four additional prohibitions: a widow to a High Priest, and a divorced woman, a zonah (a woman who has had certain forbidden relationships), or a chalalah (a woman of disqualified lineage) even to a regular priest, as will be detailed in Siman 6. A chalutzah (a woman who performed chalitza) is forbidden to a priest by rabbinic decree.

The cases punishable by positive commandments are: an Egyptian or Edomite of the first or second generation, whether male or female, and a non-virgin to a High Priest. Regarding Egyptians and Edomites, it is written, "The third generation shall enter the congregation of G-d," implying that the first and second generations are not allowed, which is a positive commandment derived from a negative implication. Similarly, with a non-virgin to a High Priest, it is derived from the commandment "He shall marry a woman in her virginity," implying a virgin and not a non-virgin.

If a man performs levirate marriage (yibum) and either he or one of his brothers has relations with the co-wife (tzarah), they transgress a positive commandment, as Maimonides states in Chapter 1 of Yibum. Also, if a woman whose husband suspected her of adultery and she was secluded (sotah), and then her husband has relations with her, he transgresses a positive commandment. If it is certain that she committed adultery, he transgresses a negative commandment and she is also forbidden to her paramour, as Maimonides states in Chapter 2 of Sotah.

Who is the "mamzer" mentioned in the Torah? It is one born from a forbidden relationship that incurs karet (excision) or capital punishment by the court, with the exception of one born from a niddah (a menstruant woman) – even though it incurs karet – nevertheless, the child is blemished but not a mamzer, even rabbinically. The blemish is only that the family is flawed and brazen, but there is no disqualification even for the priesthood, and if it is a daughter, she is permitted to marry a kohen. However, for other forbidden relations – whether the intercourse was unintentional or intentional, coerced or consensual – the child is a mamzer. Both males and females are forbidden forever, as it says: "Even to the tenth generation shall they not enter," meaning forever – and not specifically the tenth generation. Proof of this is that it also says "tenth generation" regarding Ammonites and Moabites and concludes in the verse "forever." See also in Siman 159 regarding the law of one born from a yevama (widow subject to levirate marriage) who marries an outsider.

Natinim, what are they? The Rambam wrote in Chapter 12 of Hilchot Issurei Biah: "One who converts from the seven nations is not forbidden by Torah law to enter the congregation. It is known that none of them converted except the Gibeonites. Joshua decreed that they should be forbidden to enter the congregation, both males and females. He only forbade them during the time when the Temple stood, etc. They are called 'Natinim' because they were given to the service of the Temple. David came and decreed that they should never enter the congregation, even when there is no Temple, etc. Why did he and his court decree this? Because he saw the audacity and cruelty that was in them when they asked for the seven sons of Saul, the chosen one of God, to hang them, and they killed them and did not have mercy on them." End of quote. According to the Rambam, Natinim are not primarily forbidden by Torah law. This is also the opinion of Rashi and the Me'or. The Rambam also holds that the seven nations, after their conversion, are permitted to enter the congregation, as he ruled according to the first statement of Rava (Yevamot 76b), because the discussion (Yevamot 78b) disagrees with the latter statement of Rava.

However, many of our sages disagree with him and hold that the seven nations are forbidden by Torah law even after conversion. Regarding them, it is stated, "You shall not intermarry with them." The Torah prohibition only applied to those who were present when the Israelites entered the Land of Israel, but their descendants are permitted by Torah law regarding conversion. The scripture did not prohibit them forever, nor did it enumerate their generations. Joshua and David decreed that they be forbidden forever. According to this, the prohibition of the Nethinim by Torah law refers to those nations that converted at the time of the Israelites' entry into the Land, and for future generations, their prohibition is rabbinic from Joshua, David, and their courts. This is the opinion of the Ramban and Rashba, of blessed memory. Some of our sages hold that they are forever forbidden by Torah law, and David decreed their servitude. The reason he decreed more stringently on them than on all other disqualified individuals is because they are a complete nation. In any case, according to all the decisors, they are forbidden, and their prohibition is eternal, whether male or female. Therefore, throughout the Talmud, we mention mamzerim and Nethinim together because they are equal in their prohibition.

Ammonites and Moabites are prohibited, and their prohibition is eternal. The halachic tradition from Moses at Sinai states that only the males are prohibited, but their females are permitted upon conversion. Thus, the tradition conveys: "An Ammonite" but not an Ammonitess; "a Moabite" but not a Moabitess. The Torah prohibited them "because they did not greet you with bread and water," and it is customary for a man to greet, not a woman. Additionally, it is written that they hired Balaam to curse Israel, and it was the males who did this, not the females. However, the primary basis of this ruling is from the Sinai tradition, and therefore we do not derive similarly for "a mamzer" (bastard) but not a mamzeret (female bastard); "an Egyptian" but not an Egyptian woman, since the reasons could be debated. They should have greeted Israel with bread and water—men to men and women to women—and the daughters of Moab led the Israelites to sin through immorality. Nevertheless, this is the tradition that came to Moses from Sinai.

An Egyptian and an Edomite, whether male or female, of the first and second generation, are prohibited from entering the congregation of Israel. However, the third generation is permitted, as it is stated: "Children who are born to them, the third generation shall enter the congregation of the Lord." Since it says "children who are born to them," the generations are counted from them themselves. The one who converts is considered the first generation, their children the second, and the children of their children the third, who are permitted to enter the congregation. Therefore, even though in the context of generations, the individual himself is not counted among the generations, as it was said to Abraham concerning those who went down to Egypt, "the fourth generation shall return here," and Jacob was among those who went down, and the generations are counted from his offspring—Judah, Peretz, Chetzron, and his son Caleb was among those who entered the land—there, the term generation refers to their descendants, as it is written in Joshua (22): "and it shall be said to us and to our generations tomorrow," etc. Similarly, it is written at the end of Job, "and he saw his sons and his sons' sons, four generations." Nevertheless, since it writes "to them," they themselves are also included in the generation. This is also the language of the Talmud in Gittin 88b. An Egyptian woman who was pregnant and converted—her child is considered the second generation. An Egyptian of the second generation who marries a first-generation Egyptian woman, or a first-generation Egyptian who marries a second-generation Egyptian woman—the child is considered the second generation, as we follow the lesser status of the two, as it is written "children who are born to them," implying that the status depends on birth, and there is no birth without a father and a mother. Therefore, we need the third generation to be from both sides. This is the opinion of Maimonides (Rambam), but there are some of our Rabbis who hold that we follow the mother, as the Torah makes it dependent on birth, and the mother is the one who gives birth. Therefore, a first-generation Egyptian who marries a second-generation Egyptian woman—the child is permitted to enter the congregation (Rashi, Ramban, and Tur). This, which will be explained that we follow the defect of the two, applies to two different nations and not to one nation (Beit Shmuel). And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it implies like Maimonides (Gra).

An Ammonite convert who marries an Egyptian convert and they have a male child – the child is considered an Ammonite and is prohibited from entering the congregation forever. If they have a female child, she is considered an Egyptian and is prohibited until the third generation. And an Egyptian convert who marries an Ammonite convert, whether they have a male or female child – the child is considered Egyptian and is prohibited until the third generation. Why don't we say that if the child is male, he should be considered an Ammonite like his mother and be prohibited forever? Because logically – if we follow the mother, he should be entirely permitted, as she is not flawed at all and is considered like an Israelite. However, when she is an Ammonite convert and gives birth to a son – he is considered an Ammonite and is prohibited forever. If she gives birth to a daughter – she is permitted, because the child of a female convert is like her, as will be explained. Some say that the daughter is considered an Egyptian and is not like other female converts, and we follow the more flawed parent [Beit Yosef and Taz]. However, the main opinion is the first one [Choshen Mishpat and the Vilna Gaon]. All other nations, after they convert [in ancient times] – their status is like that of Israelites immediately. The sages of blessed memory said a general principle that among the nations, we follow the male, meaning: the offspring born from two different nations in their state of non-Jewishness – we follow the male, and therefore an Egyptian or Edomite convert who marries an Ammonite female convert and they have a son or daughter – the child is considered Egyptian or Edomite, and once they convert, they will be permitted in the third generation. And an Ammonite convert who marries an Egyptian or Edomite female convert – the child is considered an Ammonite, and if he is male, he is prohibited forever, but if female, she is permitted immediately upon entering the Jewish faith. And when they convert and have children – we follow the more flawed parent in both of them as explained. And one should not say why is this so, since there is a valid marriage and no transgression? However, it is a decree of the Torah, as it is written 'for them' – follow their invalidity [Talmud].

A Kohen or Levi who marries an Israelite woman – the child is a Kohen or Levi. An Israelite who marries a Kohen or Levi woman – the child is an Israelite, as the child follows the father, as it is written, "according to their families, by their fathers' houses." An eligible Israelite who marries an Israelite mamzeret, or an Israelite mamzer who marries an eligible Israelite woman – the kiddushin (marriage) is valid, as kiddushin is effective with those who are liable for a negative commandment, and the child is a mamzer, because where there is kiddushin and a transgression, the child follows the defective parent, even if only the mother is defective, as it is written regarding a mamzer, "even unto the tenth generation shall he not enter into the congregation of the Lord," and the word "he" is superfluous, and we derive that the child follows the parent who is disqualified, even if it is the mother. And from this we learn for other negative commandments. And from where do we know that kiddushin is effective with those liable for a negative commandment? Because it is written, "If a man has two wives, one beloved and the other hated," and is there anyone hated before God? And what does it matter to us if the husband does not love her? Rather, what is hated – that she is hated in her marriage, as they transgressed a commandment, and the scripture says "if he has," using the language of existence. And certainly, with those liable for a positive commandment, kiddushin is effective, but with those liable for karet (excision) and death by the court, kiddushin is not effective, and one who cohabits with one of these liabilities – the child is a mamzer. But from those liable for negative commandments and positive commandments – the child is not a mamzer unless the father is a mamzer or the mother is a mamzeret. And a convert [in ancient times] – is permitted to marry a mamzeret, as it is written regarding a mamzer, "he shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord," and the congregation of converts is not called a congregation, but even though he marries permissibly, nevertheless the child is a mamzer, as the child follows the defective parent. And certainly, a mamzer who marries a convert – the child is a mamzer, and so is the law for a Natin (descendant of the Gibeonites) and a Natina (female descendant of the Gibeonites) and other disqualified persons.

A convert [in ancient times] who marries a Jewish woman or a Jew who marries a convert – the child is legitimate as a full Jew and forbidden to a mamzeret (a female born from certain prohibited relationships). A mamzer marries a mamzeret, and similarly, a mamzer marries a Netinah (a descendant of the Gibeonites), or a Netin marries a mamzeret – and their offspring are mamzerim, for a mamzer and a Netin have the same status. When is this said? When both are definite mamzerim, but if one is a definite and the other a doubtful mamzer – they are forbidden to marry each other. Similarly, doubtful mamzerim are forbidden to marry legitimate Jews, and even if both are doubtful – they are forbidden to marry each other, lest one of them is legitimate and the other is not. Even though, by Torah law, doubtful mamzerim are permitted in all cases, as it is written, "A mamzer shall not enter the assembly of the Lord" and we expound: a definite mamzer shall not enter, but a doubtful mamzer may enter the assembly. And similarly, into a definite assembly a mamzer may not enter, but into a doubtful assembly, he may. Nevertheless, the Rabbis prohibited them due to a higher standard in lineage, and their offspring are rabbinically considered mamzerim. 

What constitutes a doubtful mamzer? For example, if born from a doubtful union, where the father had relations with a woman who was doubtfully betrothed or doubtfully divorced, and she is doubtfully a married woman. Also, a yevama (a widow bound to marry her brother-in-law) who did not wait three months after her husband's death and became pregnant and gave birth after seven months, and it is unclear whether the child is the nine-month offspring of the first husband or the seven-month offspring of the second. This child is legitimate regardless, but if the yavam (the brother-in-law) subsequently had relations with her and she gave birth, the child is a doubtful mamzer, for perhaps the first child was a nine-month offspring of the first husband and the yavam married the wife of his brother who had children, and this is a karet prohibition, making the child a mamzer. A doubtful mamzer is forbidden to a Jewish woman and also to a mamzeret, and he should marry a convert or a freed maidservant, as a freed slave has the status of a convert in all matters. There is also another type of rabbinic mamzer: for example, a woman who heard that her husband died and married another, and her husband was alive, and her first husband had relations with her. Even though she is permitted to him by law and the second marriage is not a marriage at all since she was a married woman, nevertheless, the Rabbis decreed that she must leave both husbands, and the child from the first husband is also a mamzer. However, from incestuous relations, the child is not a mamzer even rabbinically [Yevamot 85], and see what I wrote in Siman 6, Seif 21.

And know that this which has been explained, that a convert who marries a Jewish woman, the offspring is prohibited from marrying a mamzeret – this is the opinion of Rambam and the Tur. And some say that since there is kiddushin (betrothal) and no transgression, the offspring follows the father and is permitted to marry a mamzeret. And even though this is not a fixed rule, for instance, a convert who marries a mamzeret, where there is kiddushin and no transgression, and yet the offspring is a mamzer, it is different there because the Torah increased the cases where the offspring follows the invalid parent, as stated in section 10. But in this case, from where do we derive this? And there is one who says that the reason is that it is no worse than a non-Jew who has relations with a Jewish woman, where the offspring is legitimate, as will be explained, and is prohibited from marrying a mamzeret [Maggid Mishneh]. And this is not a sufficient reason, for a non-Jew who has relations with a married woman, the offspring is legitimate, as will be explained, but if a convert has relations with a married woman, the offspring is a mamzer. Furthermore, Rambam himself ruled that a convert who marries a convertess and they have a son, he is permitted to marry a mamzeret, and so too his son and his son’s son, until the name of conversion is forgotten from him, and afterward he is prohibited from marrying a mamzeret. So what difference is there between marrying a convertess and marrying an Israelite? And it seems to me that the reason is that we see in matters of entering the congregation, the Torah was strict to also follow the mother, such as an Israelite who marries a mamzeret, where the offspring is a mamzer and is prohibited from entering the congregation. All the more so should we be stringent that he should not marry a mamzeret when his mother is an Israelite, for we also follow the mother. And in this case, it is not applicable to say he follows his invalid parent, for he is not invalid and is like a complete Israelite, only he is not called a congregation. Therefore, when his mother is an Israelite, he is called a congregation and is prohibited from marrying a mamzeret. [See Maggid Mishneh, Avodat HaMelech, and Yam Shel Shlomo on Kiddushin, chapter 4, section 6.]

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Kiddushin 66): Anyone who cannot have a valid marriage with him but can have a valid marriage with others – the child is a mamzer. And what is this? One who engages in relations with any of the forbidden relatives in the Torah. And anyone who cannot have a valid marriage with either him or others – the child is like her. And what is this? The child of a maidservant or a gentile woman. For an Israelite who engages in relations with a maidservant or a gentile woman – the child is like her and is not considered an Israelite, but a gentile or a slave. And a gentile or a slave who engages in relations with a Jewish woman, whether she is unmarried or married – the child is legitimate but disqualified from the priesthood. This means that if the child is a female, she is disqualified from marrying a priest, as it is a fortiori from a widow to a High Priest whose daughter is disqualified from the priesthood, certainly in this case. Some of our rabbis are uncertain about this, as the prohibitions of the priesthood are different. Maimonides rules that she is fit for the priesthood, and therefore, in practice, if she marries a priest, she is not removed from him, and the child is a doubtful chalal. And do not wonder why an Israelite who engages in relations with a married woman produces a mamzer, while a gentile or slave does not produce a mamzer. For so the Torah decreed, as it is written, "A man shall not take his father's wife," and it is juxtaposed with "a mamzer shall not enter."
