And it was received by tradition that just as with his father's wife, where marriage cannot take effect with him but can with others, so too with all forbidden relations, excluding a gentile and a slave where marriage cannot take effect at all. And since the child is only considered in relation to her and not him, his relations are not considered at all to be judged with the status of mamzerut for engaging with a married woman.

And from where do we know that the offspring follows her? For it is written regarding a Hebrew slave whose master gives him a Canaanite maidservant, "the woman and her children shall belong to her master" – thus, the offspring is attributed to her. And a slave who cohabits with a Jewish woman – the offspring is like her, as a slave has no lineage. Similarly, with a Samaritan and a Jewish woman or a Jew and a Samaritan woman, as it is written "You shall not intermarry with them; you shall not give your daughter to his son, nor take his daughter for your son, for he will turn your son away from Me," and because it does not say "she will turn," we learn that the Torah means: you shall not give your daughter to his son because the husband of your daughter will turn your son that your daughter bears to him away from Me, but it does not apply to "you shall not take his daughter for your son," because the one born from the Samaritan woman is not called your son but her son, and therefore her son is not subject to this turning away. All the prohibition occurs at the first moment when he discharges his seed from the wings of the Divine Presence, but after the child is born, there is no turning away because he is a complete Samaritan. And this that is written "and if you take of his daughters for your sons and his daughters will stray after their gods and they will lead your sons to stray after their gods" – this applies to the Israelite who marries her.

Therefore, a Kuti or a slave who has relations with a mamzeret (a female mamzer) – the child is a mamzer. And a mamzer who has relations with a Kutit (a female Kuti) – the child is like her, and if he converts – he becomes a full Jew. Similarly, if he has relations with a maidservant – the child is a slave, and if he is freed – he becomes a free man. Therefore, they permitted a mamzer to initially marry a maidservant who has accepted the commandments and immersed for the purpose of slavery, in order to permit his children to be freed and allowed to marry into the Jewish community. However, a mamzeret is forbidden to a slave because the children would still be mamzerim. Some say she is permitted. Therefore, a Kuti who has relations with his mother or sister and fathers a son from her, and then converts – that son is permitted to enter the congregation, because while he was still a Kuti, the status of mamzer does not apply to him. If he does not convert and has relations with a Jewish woman – the child is kosher because he is no worse than other Kutim. An Ammonite convert who marries a mamzeret – we follow the defect of both of them, and the child is an Ammonite mamzer. We have already written that a convert and a freed slave are permitted to marry a mamzeret, but nevertheless, it is forbidden to multiply mamzerim in Israel, as their children will be mamzerim. A maidservant is forbidden to a convert because he is obligated to observe all the commandments, and we only permitted a mamzer to marry her for the sake of the offspring. But a convert should marry a free woman. An Ammonite convert may be permitted to marry a maidservant. And what we wrote that a convert who marries a convert’s daughter – the child is permitted to marry a mamzeret until his status as a convert is forgotten – this is according to Maimonides, and some say the period is ten generations, and from then on it is forbidden, as his status as a convert would have been forgotten, and people would say an Israelite is marrying a mamzeret.

A Samaritan who has relations with a maidservant who immersed for the sake of servitude—the child is like her and is considered a servant, since she is obligated in commandments like a woman, and his status is like that of a Samaritan who has relations with a Jewish woman. Similarly, a servant who immersed for the sake of servitude and has relations with a Samaritan woman—the child is like her. However, a Samaritan who has relations with a Samaritan maidservant before she immersed, or a Samaritan servant who has relations with a free Samaritan woman—the child follows the father, for among the nations the lineage follows the male, as it is written, and as long as they have not immersed, they are considered Samaritans.

A person who is half-slave and half-free who has relations with a married Jewish woman – the child has no remedy, because it contains both elements of mamzerut and legitimacy. Therefore, it is forbidden even with a maidservant, and his children are like him forever, and he may only marry a convert. If the child is a daughter, she may marry a proselyte, and the children are considered mamzerim as explained. Some say he is a complete mamzer and is permitted to marry a maidservant. If the woman is unmarried, the child is legitimate, for even from his half-slavery, the child is like her as stated. It appears to me that according to what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch state in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 267, Seif 62, that a half-slave and half-free, according to the ruling that we compel his master to free him, is no longer considered a slave, and his status is like one who is awaiting a writ of emancipation – that child is definitively a mamzer. I am puzzled by the Tur and Shulchan Aruch for writing this law here, but the Rambam, who wrote this law, is understandable, as he follows his own reasoning in Chapter 4 of the Laws of Injury that as long as he has not been freed, his status is that of a complete slave in half of him, as we have already explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 324, Seif 6. However, for the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, this is difficult. It is possible that they hold that regarding prohibition, he is considered a complete slave in half of him, but not regarding monetary matters, and according to what will be explained that a freed slave before receiving a writ of emancipation is forbidden to a Jewish woman, it is clearly proven that regarding prohibition, he is considered a complete slave.

A slave who was immersed for the sake of servitude is prohibited from marrying a Jewish woman. And a Jew is prohibited from marrying a maidservant—whether she belongs to him or to another. According to Onkelos and several poskim, this is a Torah prohibition derived from "There shall not be a sacred prostitute" (Deuteronomy 23:18). According to the Rambam, it is a rabbinic prohibition, as he wrote. However, after the master has freed him, written him a bill of emancipation, and immersed him [according to the Gra]—he is considered a Jew in all respects except that he is permitted to marry a mamzeret and other individuals who are prohibited to the congregation. If his master renounces ownership of him, he goes free and requires a bill of emancipation, as it is written in Yoreh De'ah. As long as the master has not written him a bill of emancipation, he is not permitted to marry a Jewish woman. If his master gave him tefillin, or if he was called to the Torah as a prayer leader or was married to a Jewish woman—since these actions are not typically done for a slave and are signs that he has been freed—nevertheless, he is not permitted to marry a Jewish woman until he has been written a bill of emancipation. However, in all these cases, if he betrothed a woman, we are stringent and consider it a valid betrothal due to the concern that once he was freed, his master might have granted him a bill of emancipation through another person. Some say that even if his master did not marry him off, but he himself married in the presence of his master, we are stringent regarding the betrothal. All the more so, if he married his maidservant, we are stringent regarding the betrothal, as explained in Yoreh De'ah. The law regarding a woman who is half maidservant and half free and who became betrothed is explained in Siman 44.

According to what has been explained, there are four nations prohibited from entering the assembly of Israel: Egyptian, Edomite, Ammonite, and Moabite. All other nations, when they convert and accept upon themselves all the commandments of the Torah, are considered as Israelites, as it is stated, "The assembly, there shall be one statute for you and for the stranger who sojourns with you." And our sages have said that from the time when Sennacherib came and confused all the nations, these four nations were also nullified, and it is not known where they are – thus all nations are permitted. And these are the words of the Rambam in the end of chapter 12 of the laws of forbidden relations: When Sennacherib, the king of Assyria, came, he confused all the nations and mixed them together, and exiled them from their places. And those Egyptians currently in the land of Egypt are different people, and likewise the Edomites in the field of Edom. And since the four prohibited nations have been mixed with all the nations of the world, who are permitted – everything is permitted, for anyone who separates from them to convert is presumed to have separated from the majority. Therefore, when a convert converts in our times [in places where there is royal permission], whether Edomite, Egyptian, Ammonite, Moabite, Cushite, or any other nation – whether male or female – they are permitted to enter the assembly immediately. These are his words. And the Rosh holds that an Egyptian is also prohibited now because the Egyptians have returned to their place, for the scripture gave them a term as it is written in Ezekiel: "At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians," etc. [see the Gra in subparagraph 18].

One may ask about this: since the permission regarding these four nations is because "whatever separates, separates from the majority," it makes sense when he leaves his home and marries the Israelite woman, but when she comes to his home and he marries her – should we not say that anything fixed is considered as half and half, and thus forbidden to him? One could say that according to Torah law, since all the nations have intermixed with each other and each one is in doubt, they are entirely permitted, and doubts are permitted like the doubtful mamzer we wrote about, and they are only forbidden by rabbinic decree, and therefore they did not worry about this. [And so is written in Sha'ar HaMelech that according to Torah law, they are completely permitted; see Even HaEzer.] And we must say so, because otherwise, regarding a person, it is not applicable to say "whatever separates, separates from the majority," since he returns to his home, and for each and every marital act in his home, it would be considered fixed and like half and half. [See Tosafot Ketubot 15a, s.v. 'Dima' and Nazir 12a.] And that which they separated from the Ammonites in the days of Ezra, as it is written at the end of Nehemiah – this is because in the days of Ezra they were still known, as it is written there "Tobiah the Ammonite" [See Rashi at the end of Yadayim].

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 14: If a woman's husband was overseas and stayed there for more than twelve months, and she gave birth after twelve months, the child is a mamzer (illegitimate), because a child does not remain in its mother's womb for more than twelve months. There is an opinion that says the child is not presumed to be a mamzer, and since it is a dispute, the status is that of a doubtful mamzer. End quote. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote regarding this: But within twelve months, there is no concern, as we say that the child remained in its mother's womb for that long. This is specifically if nothing improper was seen regarding her, but if something improper was seen, we do not say that the child remained in the womb for that long, and we are concerned about it. End quote. The first opinion is that of the Rambam, of blessed memory, and the second opinion is that of the Bahag, as brought by the Rosh in the fourth chapter of Kiddushin, see there.

And behold, this is certainly so: When the husband is present and says that the child is not his, he is believed in every matter, as will be explained, for the father is believed [Bava Metzia]. And if the husband says that he came to her one night, certainly even the Rambam agrees that he is believed in every matter. And even in this, it can be said that they do not disagree, for the Rambam speaks when we did not examine her to see what she says; then, after twelve months, we do not attribute to a far-fetched case that he came one night and no one knew about it. And the Bahag speaks when she says so, that he came to her; then, due to her presumption of propriety and not to disqualify the child, we attribute even to a far-fetched situation. And within twelve months, there is no concern at all; nevertheless, since we find in the Gemara [Yevamot 80:] that they acted to permit within twelve months, it shows that it can indeed be so, and therefore we have no reason to be concerned about this. However, if they saw something improper in her and her presumption of propriety was undermined, we do not attribute even within twelve months, since this too is an uncommon matter, especially since some of our Rabbis ruled not like that in Yevamot [Tosafot Niddah 38.]. And although most decisors rule thus, nevertheless in a place where her presumption of propriety was undermined, certainly we are concerned. And nevertheless, it seems to me that to render the child a doubtful mamzer, we do not need to be concerned when she says that he is legitimate. And from the primary law of our Rabbi the Rema [Responsa Maimonides, Ishut, Siman 25], it is only to forbid her to her husband, but to disqualify the child, from where do we know that she would not be believed? And indeed, regarding the child, there is a double doubt: perhaps he is from her husband, and if you say he is not from her husband, perhaps he is from a non-Jew, and the child is legitimate. And so it seems to me the opinion of the great recent authorities. And what our Rabbi the Rema wrote that we are concerned for it, it means not to consider him definitely his son, but not to render him a doubtful mamzer [see Beit Shmuel, Siman 143]. And it is simple that within ten months and a little more, there is no concern at all even without her statement, for this is a common matter [and similarly in Chamudei Daniel and Beit Shmuel].

Indeed, our master, the Beit Yosef, holds that the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (Ba'al Halachot Gedolot) permits even without her declaration. According to this, the primary view aligns with the Rambam, and we do not rely on a far-fetched possibility that is not common at all. Nevertheless, he was cautious to be stringent, considering him not a definite mamzer to permit him to marry a mamzeret, but rather a doubtful mamzer. Also, it is impossible to make him a definite mamzer, since perhaps he is a Cuthean, as has been written. According to this, in the case of "they saw something disgraceful in her," it is possible to be concerned about the child being a doubtful mamzer if she does not declare that he is kosher, and the words of our master the Rama are straightforward. Nevertheless, in a place where the majority are Cutheans, it seems to me that he is not a doubtful mamzer in such a case, and we follow the majority. Only if the child is a daughter, she is forbidden to a priest, as written in section 13. But for ten months and a bit more, there is no concern at all, since this is common, as has been written.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote: A woman who became pregnant from her husband at the end of Sivan and gave birth at the beginning of Kislev, even though there are only five months between them, we do not suspect that the child was conceived earlier, because the months are determinant, and it is considered a seven-month baby. And even if she miscarried in Tishrei and they heard the fetus crying, we do not suspect that she was pregnant earlier, because it is possible for a fetus to cry at five months, but it is a miscarriage and not viable.

Accordingly, one day at the end of a month when she became pregnant and one day at the beginning of the month when she gave birth are considered two months. And even though it seems from the Rambam in several places (such as in Chapter 1 of Yibum, Chapter 2 of Rotzeach, and Chapter 1 of Avel) that nine full months from day to day are required for a child to be viable, and according to our Rabbi the Rema, seven months and two days are sufficient – nevertheless, one could say that even though in several laws we are stringent to say that a child is only viable with complete months, and sometimes even lenient in matters of Rabbinic law like in mourning and similar cases, nevertheless to remove a child from the status of being his father's and to remove a woman from her fitness – we rely on the main law. Furthermore, it is explicitly stated in the Gemara that even if we say that a woman who gives birth at nine months does not give birth in incomplete months but in full nine months, nevertheless one who gives birth at seven months can give birth in incomplete months. Therefore, if she gives birth at the beginning of a seven-month period, one day at the end of the month and one day at the beginning of the next month suffice. The Rambam is referring to a woman who gives birth at nine months. However, for us, even in nine months in such a case, if she became pregnant one day at the end of the month of Nissan and gave birth at the beginning of Kislev to a viable child – she and the child remain in their fitness even if we say that at nine months she does not give birth in incomplete months, because we say that this child is a seven-month child who was delayed, as in a child born in twelve months as mentioned in section 21. And even if we say that for other laws we do not worry about a child being delayed, nevertheless to maintain the woman and the child in their fitness – everyone agrees to this as it is written there. Therefore, in practice – even though there are some of the great ones who question this law – nevertheless many of the great later authorities have taken the ruling of our Rabbi the Rema as the main one, and it is clear that to maintain the woman and the child in their fitness, we rely on this even if we do not rely on it for other matters. A proof is from the case of the delayed birth mentioned in section 21, and from several other laws that will be explained in this section. Therefore, not only when the mother says she is clean and pure, but even if she died and said nothing – we maintain the son as his father's for all matters. However, regarding what is written that if she miscarried in Tishrei and they heard the child crying, we do not worry that she was pregnant beforehand, and therefore it could be that the child cries at three months and some days – many have disagreed, for indeed this is far from reality. Therefore, if such a case occurs – certainly we must be concerned about the woman's promiscuity, especially if her husband is a Kohen who must be concerned not to profane his seed. Similarly, in the case of an extremely promiscuous woman – we must also be concerned about the child in the previous law, and everything is according to the view of the Beit Din. And know, the great ones have agreed that what our Rabbi the Rema ruled that a child born in five months and two days is fit – this is even if she was a virgin, and even though a woman does not become pregnant from the first intercourse – this is when immediately after approaching her he had full intercourse and withdrew from her, but not as is the custom nowadays where they approach each other before full intercourse, and perhaps he aroused her first and ruptured her hymen without his knowledge, and then he fully cohabited and she became pregnant. Furthermore, this is only according to the majority, and there is a minority who become pregnant from the first intercourse, and therefore it is not possible to remove her and her child from their status of fitness, especially if she asserts with certainty.

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 15 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations, Law 20: If there is a rumor that a woman is an adulteress while married, and everyone is gossiping about her, we do not suspect her children of being mamzerim (illegitimate), for most of her cohabitations are presumed to be with her husband, and it is permitted to marry her daughter ab initio. However, she herself is suspected of being a zonah (prostitute). If she is excessively promiscuous, we also suspect her children. End quote. And in Chapter 17 he wrote: If there is a rumor about a virgin that she is not a virgin, we do not suspect her, and she may marry a High Priest. If she has a reputation in the city of being promiscuous, we do not suspect her. Even if her husband divorced her for transgressing Jewish law or based on witnesses to an inappropriate matter, and he died before giving her a get (divorce document), she is permitted to marry a priest. We do not prohibit a woman in such cases except with clear testimony or her own admission. End quote. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote the first law in this chapter, Section 15, and the second law in Section 16.

And it appears to me that regarding the second ruling, it is a matter of law. That is, from a legal standpoint, one should only prohibit based on clear testimony or a confession from her mouth. For even concerning someone suspected of adultery with a married woman, the Rambam holds that we do not extract anything from him except specifically with witnesses of an inappropriate act and a persistent rumor; without this, she should not be separated even from the one suspected. And for the husband, even in such a case, we do not prohibit her, as the Rambam wrote in the 24th chapter of Hilchot Ishut and the 2nd chapter of Hilchot Sotah. 

And regarding the first ruling – it is not a matter of law but merely good advice for someone who wishes to be cautious and marry a woman who is pure. Therefore, it is said that there is no concern at all regarding her daughter because most relations are with the husband. However, concerning the woman herself, there is reason to be concerned about her being considered a "zonah" (harlot), and it is not proper for a Kohen to marry her, even though from the law it is not prohibited. And even for an Israelite who straightens his ways, it is not proper to marry her, as she might ruin him by being prohibited to him. And when she is exceedingly promiscuous, so that it is possible that most relations were not with her husband, it is proper for someone who considers his ways to distance himself even from her offspring. This is the language of concern, but not from a legal standpoint.

However, the prominent later authorities hold that the law is being taught here. Therefore, some distinguish between the voice (rumor) regarding a single woman – where there is no concern, and here with the voice regarding a married woman – where there is concern [Bach], and they reject his words [Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 151 and Chut HaMeshulash, chapter 6, subparagraph 14]. Essentially, it seems that, on the contrary, we are not more stringent with a married woman than with a single woman so as not to uphold the rumor and cast aspersions on the children, as stated in chapter 22 [see Kiddushin chapter 1]. Some differentiate between one type of rumor and another, where here everyone gossips about her, making it worse than a rumor elsewhere [Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel], but I do not know the boundary for these matters. Furthermore, the Rambam concludes there that a woman is not forbidden except by clear testimony or her own admission, and not by any rumor or gossip. Additionally, it is evident in chapter 24 of Ishut and chapter 2 of Sotah that even the greatest gossip without witnesses of impropriety is nothing, even for the accused, and certainly for others. Therefore, it seems as I have stated. It also appears that the Maggid Mishneh and our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, hold this view. This is why they wrote, "Regarding herself, she is suspected of being a zonah, and a Kohen is concerned for her by Torah law, and an Israelite if he wants to distance from impropriety" – meaning that a Kohen must be more concerned because a zonah is forbidden to him by Torah law, but for an Israelite, she is permitted. However, due to impropriety, if he wants to distance himself so as not to stumble in his relations with her, he should also distance himself. This is what is meant by "if she is extremely promiscuous, there is concern even for the children," meaning it is merely a suspicion. This is what our teacher the Rema concluded: "Nevertheless, she is believed to say about her children that they are kosher" – meaning that from the core law, they should not be forbidden if she says they are kosher, even if she is extremely promiscuous. This is also what is written regarding someone who is not extremely promiscuous: if her husband is a Kohen, there is concern for her children being chalalim – this is also merely a suspicion, just as the Kohen is concerned for her being a zonah, and in retrospect, it is clear that there is nothing to it [Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 174]. What is written about someone who is extremely promiscuous, that there is concern even for her children, means even a suspicion of mamzerut, for certainly, there is a suspicion of mamzerut, but from the law, they should not be forbidden, unlike some who want to forbid by law [there]. What is written: "if she was promiscuous when she was single or betrothed but not promiscuous after marriage, even if she was seen committing adultery once, her children are kosher" – meaning even for mere suspicion, there is no concern, for since she was not promiscuous after marriage, it is clear that the majority of her relations are with her husband, and throughout the entire Torah, we follow the majority. Therefore, a general rule is that the majority of relations are with the husband, and we follow this in all laws of the Torah, even concerning inheritance [Pitchei Teshuva in the name of Chut HaShani], and do not question why we attribute the majority of relations to the husband and not to the betrothed, as will be explained. Certainly, it is because she is always with the husband and permissible, unlike with the betrothed [Beit Shmuel]. Know that one of the great authorities ruled regarding a woman who was living with her husband, and there was a persistent rumor that she committed adultery under him, and she was widowed and married a Kohen – that he must be compelled to divorce her because it is a rumor from before the marriage. There is no basis for these words, for certainly, the Kohen should be concerned but not compelled by law, and this is not related to a rumor before marriage, which only applies to rumors of betrothal and divorce when clear things were said about a betrothal, as the Rambam wrote in chapter 9 of Ishut and will be clarified in chapter 6 with God's help. But in the case of a rumor of adultery, there is no woman who would be forbidden to the world and to her husband, and

A woman whose husband went overseas, and she heard that he had died, and she married another man, and then it became known that her first husband is still alive—the child from the second man is a complete mamzer (illegitimate child) according to Torah law and is permitted to marry a mamzeret (female mamzer). If the first husband returned and had relations with her, even though according to Torah law she is permitted to him, the Sages nevertheless penalized her such that she is forbidden even to the first husband, because they penalized her for not being diligent in verifying that he was still alive. And they penalized her that the child from the first husband is a mamzer according to rabbinic law and is forbidden to marry both a mamzeret and a regular Jewish woman, but is permitted to marry a rabbinic mamzeret similar to himself. According to Maimonides (Rambam), the child from the first husband is not a mamzer unless she has not yet divorced the second husband, but after she divorces the second husband, the child from the first husband is no longer a mamzer. And although the divorce from the second husband is not valid, since the marriage itself was not valid, nevertheless, since this is merely a penalty, the Sages only penalized her as long as her actions are ongoing. But once her actions are nullified by receiving a get (divorce document) from him, the child from the first husband is no longer a mamzer. There are those who disagree with this. The primary opinion follows Maimonides, as we do not find explicitly in the early authorities to the contrary. This is also implied in the Jerusalem Talmud, where it is stated that she needs a get from the second husband to clarify the prohibition regarding the first husband, meaning that they validate the betrothal of the second husband to prohibit her to the first husband. Hence, when she divorces the second husband, his actions are nullified, and his get is not more severe than a full get of the second husband when she married another man after the first husband divorced her and then divorced the second man and returned to the first husband—the child from her is not a mamzer, as the prohibition is only a negative commandment of remarrying a divorced wife who has married another man. Certainly, with such a get, the child from the second man is a mamzer even after the first husband divorced her. The child is a mamzer according to rabbinic law, as the penalty against the second husband remains always, even after the death of the first husband. All this applies when she married another man, but if she committed adultery with another man and then her husband returned, the child from him is not a mamzer, as she is only forbidden to him by a negative commandment like a sota (suspected adulteress), and those subject to negative commandments do not produce mamzerim. The prohibition applies only to marriage because it appears as if she is a married woman, but not to adultery.

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote [there]: A single woman who became pregnant from a licentious relationship, if she is asked, "What is this embryo or this child?", if she says, "He is a legitimate child and I was impregnated by an Israelite," she is believed, and the child is legitimate, even though the majority of the city where she committed adultery are deemed unfit. And if her mother was not investigated until she died, or if she was deaf, mute, or insane, or if she said, "I was impregnated by so-and-so, a mamzer, or by so-and-so, a Natin," even if that person admits it is from him, the child is considered a doubtful mamzer. Just as she had relations with the one who admitted to her, so too she could have had relations with another. This is known as a 'she'tuki', who knows his mother but does not definitely know his father. Similarly, a child found in the market, known as an 'asufi', is a doubtful mamzer, as we do not know his status. End of quote.

Explanation of his words: The woman is believed to declare her child as legitimate but is not believed to declare her child as illegitimate. Many of the early authorities agree with this. The reasoning is that the Torah only granted credibility to the father, as will be explained. To declare the child legitimate, the woman is believed, because she has a presumption of being kosher [Nimukei Yosef, end of chapter 7 of Yevamot], and also because a woman who commits adultery checks herself and commits adultery [Tosafot, Ketubot 13b and there 14a in the name of Rabbi Yehuda, see there], for certainly a woman does not want to disqualify her child, even when her inclination overpowers her to commit adultery, she finds a legitimate partner; we do not say that disqualified people tend more to commit adultery, for even kosher people have no guardian over sexual matters [Jerusalem Talmud, there, chapter 5, halacha 8]. And even though regarding herself, we do not permit her to marry a priest except with two majorities, as written in Siman 6 – this is an enhancement in lineage and because she has the option to marry an Israelite. But regarding the child, so that he does not remain disqualified, we permit him even with a majority of disqualified people if she says she had relations with a legitimate person [Ran]. Based on this, we would say that if the child is a daughter, she should not marry a priest, for she can marry an Israelite [Pri Megadim, there]. However, we do not find this in the poskim (decisors), and we cannot say this to permit partially [it seems to me]. To disqualify, she is not believed, for from the Torah, without her statement, the child is a doubtful mamzer and is permitted by Torah law to marry a daughter of Israel, and only rabbinically prohibited, as stated in section 11, and they believed her rabbinically for permissibility, not to make a definite mamzer and permit him to a mamzeret, even though it is permitted by Torah law, nevertheless, it is not proper to increase mamzerim [Pri Shaul]. Therefore, even with a majority of disqualified people, she is believed to declare the child legitimate but not to disqualify, because this is only rabbinic, and she has two presumptions in her favor – the presumption of her kosher status and the presumption of checking herself before committing adultery. To disqualify, she is not believed, even if the one who committed adultery with her, a mamzer, says the child is his, and even if there is no rumor that she committed adultery with other men, for we say just as she committed adultery with this one, so she did with others, and it follows that the child is a doubtful mamzer, and the one who committed adultery is not considered her husband to be believed as a father. This is not similar to what is written in Siman 3, section 20, where a priest who committed adultery with an unmarried woman and admits that the child is his, we do not suspect her of relations with others, see there, for to declare legitimate we certainly do not suspect and uphold her in her presumption of kosher status, but when she disqualifies herself and her child – what credibility do we have to believe her that she did not commit adultery with others since according to her words she is promiscuous and committed adultery with a mamzer? [And this answers the question of the Chokhmat Shlomo at the end of section 25 and the questions of the Beit Shmuel, subparagraph Mem from Terumah, and pay close attention] [See Tosafot, Gittin, chapter 9].

If a woman claims that a certain kosher man is the father of her child, even though she is believed regarding the child's legitimacy, she is not believed to establish him as the man's son for matters of inheritance and other issues. We do not consider him his son unless the man acknowledges that he is his son. Even if the man is not present, we do not consider the child his son, and certainly, if the man explicitly denies that he is his son and contradicts her, she is not believed to establish him as his son. Furthermore, he is not even required to take an oath to contradict her. Even if she demands child support on behalf of the child, it is not like other monetary claims where the claimant can force the defendant to take an oath. The reason is that if we were to allow this, promiscuous women would claim support from upstanding men of Israel to force them to take an oath. Even if she was exclusively associated with this man, if he does not deny it and she was not suspected of being with other men, we would consider the child his son. However, if he denies it, we do not consider the child his son for any matter. Only for the purpose of prohibiting the child from marrying the man's relatives does the Rambam write that we take her words into consideration, and the child is forbidden to marry the man's relatives. Even if a single witness testifies that the child is his son, he is not believed if the man denies it, and he is not required to take an oath to contradict the witness, as it is not a monetary claim. However, if she demands child support based on the witness's testimony, the man is required to take an oath to contradict the witness, as in any monetary claim.

And what we have said, that we take her words into account to prohibit him from marrying the relatives of this particular man – this applies specifically to an unmarried woman. However, if a married woman had an adulterous affair and claims that the child belongs to another man, even if that man is a mamzer (illegitimate child) – we do not take her words into account at all, because we assume that the majority of her cohabitation was with her husband, and the child is legitimate and permitted to marry the relatives of that particular man she claims. And this is specifically when the husband is present with her; but if the husband is not regularly at home, even if he occasionally comes – certainly we take her words into account to prohibit the child from marrying the relatives of this particular man, even though she is not believed to disqualify the child.

This clarification that a single woman who gave birth and her mother was not examined, the child is a doubtful mamzer – this is specifically when there are mamzerim in the city, even if they are a minority and the majority of the city are fit for her, nevertheless the child is a doubtful mamzer. And why do we not follow the majority? Because perhaps the ruling is that she went to the man and it is considered as stationary (kavua) and it is like half and half. Therefore, if it is known that the man went to her, it seems to me that he is fit, and there is proof for this from what the Tur wrote at the end of section 6, see there. And according to what is written there, even if it is not known who went to whom, he should be considered fit. However, from the Talmudic discussion (Kiddushin 73a) it is clear that in such a case it is a doubtful mamzer, and the Tur only says this in the case of a double majority, see there. But if it is known that they went to her – certainly he is fit. And in a place where there is no mamzer in the city – the child is fit in all aspects, because even if she became pregnant from a Cuthean, the child is fit as written in paragraph 13. And why are we not concerned that she committed adultery with her relatives, from whom the child would be a mamzer? It seems to me because it is not common at all to commit adultery with relatives from whom the child would be a mamzer, and also because since they are known people to us, we assume their fitness. However, when she is suspected with them, there is a concern if it is uncertain that she went to the adulterers. However, the main reason for stationary (kavua) is only a stringency, for in the end, there is a majority for permissibility, and when she went, it is like half and half, and perhaps he went to her, and thus it is a majority for permissibility. And so wrote the Rashba in Kiddushin 73a, see there.

A betrothed woman who became pregnant while still in her father's house, if she says that she conceived from her betrothed, if he admits it—even if he does not explicitly admit it, but does not deny it and says he does not remember, or he is not present—the child is legitimate and considered fully his son to inherit him. Also, regarding levirate marriage, if the betrothed dies, the child exempts his mother from the need for chalitzah (ceremonial release). Since she claims with certainty that the child is from her betrothed, and it is permissible from the betrothed, we maintain her in her presumption of propriety and do not suspect at all that she may have had relations with another. As stated in section 31, to legitimize the child, we do not worry that she may have had relations with another. Even concerning inheritance, the other certain heirs cannot say "bring proof that you are our brother," since we associate the child with the betrothed regarding not being a mamzer (illegitimate), it is impossible to differentiate in any matter, and he is his son in every respect.

Not only that, but even if she was widowed from the betrothed and he was not present, and we did not hear that he admitted it, she is permitted to marry a Kohen (priest). Since the child marries an Israelite woman and shares inheritance with his brothers, therefore regarding herself as well, it is considered as if it was done after the fact, and she is fit to marry a Kohen. Once she is permitted, she remains permitted, contrary to the opinion of some who dispute this.

But if she denies and says that the child is not from him, the child is definitely a mamzer (illegitimate), for even with a married woman the Torah grants the father credibility to declare his son a mamzer, as will be explained, and all the more so with a betrothed woman. However, this credibility only pertains to the child, for the Torah granted the father credibility regarding the child, but he is not believed to establish the woman with the status of a harlot and thereby forbid her to a priest if he dies. Why should he be believed about her more than she is about herself? On the contrary, every person is believed more about themselves. And though initially we should forbid her to a priest because we presume the child to be a mamzer, nonetheless, if after the fact she married a priest, she does not need to leave him, for regarding her the Torah did not grant him credibility. And even though we wrote that it is impossible to differentiate in this matter, that pertains to the issues concerning the child himself. But between the child and her, necessarily we must differentiate after the fact because the father is believed regarding the child. And it is obvious that if the betrothed man is a priest, she is forbidden to him because he himself establishes this status upon himself.

And if the betrothed is present and says that the child is not his, and she is not here – the child is considered a doubtful mamzer (illegitimate child). For although it is true that he is believed that it is not his child, how can we make it a definite mamzer? Perhaps she became pregnant from a Cuthean. And specifically when she is present and contradicts him, and does not say that she became pregnant from a Cuthean, and the Torah believes the father, it remains a definite mamzer. But when she is not present, how can we make it a definite mamzer? Perhaps she would say it is from a Cuthean? And there is one who says that we do not say she became pregnant from a Cuthean, and there is no substance to these words.

And even the case of a married woman whose husband is far away, in a manner that there is no concern to say that he came and she gave birth, in a manner that it is definitely a mamzer, if she says it is from a Cuthean – the child is kosher. And if she says nothing and there are Cutheans in the city – it is a doubtful mamzer. And if she says that it is not from the betrothed, and he is silent – the child is a doubtful mamzer by her words, because in the case of a married woman she is not believed at all to disqualify the child, as will be explained. But in the case of a betrothed woman, since the betrothed is not always with her and she is also rabbinically forbidden to him until the marriage, even though she is not believed to make the child a definite mamzer, still it is a doubtful mamzer.

And if she says the child is a mamzer and the betrothed contradicts her and says the child is his – some say that in this case the law is like with a married woman, and he is believed and her words are nothing, for the Torah believes the father and not the mother. And some say it is not similar to a married woman, and it is a doubtful mamzer. The primary opinion is like the first opinion, for is a betrothed not a father, and the Torah believes him. Certainly, if it is known that the betrothed was with her once and she is not suspected of being with others, the betrothed is believed to consider the child his for all matters. However, even in such a case, when the betrothed is not here and she says it is not from the betrothed – she is believed to make it a doubtful mamzer.

And know that everything explained in the previous three sections applies when she is not suspected by others, meaning the people are not spreading rumors about her that she committed adultery with others. However, if there are rumors that she committed adultery, even if they say she committed adultery also with the betrothed, since they are also spreading rumors about her with others, even if it is known that the betrothed had relations with her in her father's house, the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, is that the child is a doubtful mamzer if we did not hear from her that the child is from the betrothed, and we also did not hear anything from the betrothed. And although in the case of a married woman in such a situation we are not concerned about anything because most relations are with her husband, in the case of a betrothed woman it is not applicable to say this, and we say just as she made herself available to the betrothed, she made herself available to others. And if we asked her and she said that she had relations with the betrothed and the child is from him, the child is kosher. And all the more so if it is known that the betrothed had relations with her and there is no rumor that she committed adultery with others, the child is kosher even without her saying so. There are some of our Rabbis who disagree with the Rambam, and say that even if there is a rumor and a voice that she committed adultery with others, since it is known that the betrothed had relations with her, the child is kosher even without their statements, and this is the main ruling in law. And also the Rambam, of blessed memory, who was stringent in this matter, is only in the case of a rumor that is close to certainty and not just a mere voice [Bach]. And if it is not known that the betrothed had relations with her, and there are no accusations that she committed adultery with the betrothed, but they are accusing and spreading rumors that she committed adultery with others, certainly everyone agrees with the Rambam that in general without her statement and his statement, it is a doubtful mamzer. And if she was suspected of adultery with the betrothed and not with others, and it is not known that he had relations with her, the child is kosher even without their statements [Bach], and according to the Rambam, it is possible to be stringent in this matter [see Bach].

A married woman who claims that her fetus is not from her husband is not believed at all to disqualify the fetus, even if the husband is not present, and even if it is known that she committed adultery. This is because most acts of intercourse are attributed to the husband when he is with her in the usual manner of a husband and wife. The Torah only granted credibility to the father, not to the mother. All the more so, if the child is already born and presumed to be legitimate, the mother is not believed to disqualify him. And regarding a betrothed woman, it has already been clarified.

Maimonides wrote: A father who has been established as such regarding his son and says, "This son of mine is a mamzer" (illegitimate) is believed. However, if the son has children, the father is not believed, as the Torah only gave him credibility regarding his son, as it is stated: "He shall acknowledge the firstborn, the son of the hated" – he shall acknowledge him to others. Just as he is believed to say, "This is my firstborn son," so too he is believed to say, "This son of mine is a mamzer or the son of a divorced woman or the son of a chalutzah." Similarly, if his wife was pregnant, he is believed to say, "This fetus is not mine and is a mamzer," and the child will be a definite mamzer. And afterwards he wrote: If she was pregnant, etc., and the father said, "This is not my child," or if her husband was abroad – the child is presumed to be a mamzer. If she says, "I was impregnated by a non-Jew or a slave," the child is kosher, as the husband cannot contradict her words. This is what he wrote in the first ruling, a definite mamzer, and in the second ruling, a presumed mamzer, implying a doubtful mamzer – in the first ruling, she claims it is from her husband, and since she does not claim it is from a non-Jew and the Torah believes the father, therefore he is a definite mamzer. In the second ruling, she does not claim anything, so the child is a doubtful mamzer. This is also the opinion of the Tur, who disagrees with the Beit Shmuel as stated in Section 37. Similarly, when the husband says the child is a mamzer, knowing she committed adultery with a Jew, the child is a definite mamzer since the Torah believes him. But if he only says the child is not his, he cannot make the child a definite mamzer, as perhaps she was impregnated by a non-Jew. However, this is certainly true – in such a case where most of the city are Jews, and it is known that the adulterers visited her – whatever separates, separates from the majority and the child is a definite mamzer, unless she says she was impregnated by a non-Jew, in which case she is believed. See what I wrote in Section 22. This requires further investigation, as it is possible that since she is promiscuous and committed adultery under her husband, she is not believed to declare the child kosher against the majority, and it is not similar to an unmarried woman stated in Section 30, where she has a presumption of being kosher as stated in Section 31. There is an opinion that the father is only believed to say, "This is not my son," but not to say from whom he is, because once he says it is from someone else, it is not his son, and the Torah did not believe him regarding that. This matter is not clear to me, for certainly, he is not believed to establish the child as the son of another based on his words, but since the Torah believes him to say the child is a mamzer according to most authorities, how can he make the child a mamzer if he is not believed to say she committed adultery with someone from whom the child would be a mamzer? Perhaps she committed adultery with a non-Jew, and thus the Torah says that a man and his wife who had a child, the man is believed to say about the child he has been established as his that it is not his and that it is a mamzer or the son of a divorced woman. This is also explicitly understood from the words of Rabbi Moshe Isserles in Section 29. However, when she claims it is from a non-Jew, and there is a basis to say so as we explained, certainly she is believed, for he cannot contradict her in this. But when she is silent or has died, he is definitely believed.

And the fact that a father is believed regarding his son – this is specifically when the son did not have a presumption of legitimacy based on the father. But if the son had a presumption of legitimacy based on the father – the father is no longer believed regarding him, only based on witnesses. For once the father has established his son’s legitimacy, how can he himself undermine the status he has established? And this is specifically when the father himself established the son's legitimacy, but if others established him as his son – this means nothing [according to the Gra]. Similarly, even if he said about his son that he is a mamzer (illegitimate child), and later provided a good reason for his previous statement – he is believed to retract it, for with a valid excuse, he is believed to retract any statement, as it is written in Yoreh De'ah sections 1, 127, and 185, see there. And know, that the father being believed – this applies specifically to his wife, whether she is married or betrothed, but if it is a single woman who says this is the son of so-and-so and he says she conceived from a mamzer – he is not believed to disqualify the child. And she – even though she is not believed to establish him as the son of that man – nevertheless, she is believed to render the child legitimate as explained.

One who declares himself to be a mamzer (a child born from certain prohibited relationships) is believed to prohibit himself from marrying a Jewish woman, not based on the laws of testimony, but because he has rendered himself prohibited to all Jewish women. However, if he has relations with a daughter of a Kohen, he does not render her prohibited by his act, as he is not believed concerning others. Additionally, he is prohibited from marrying a mamzeret until the matter is clarified through witnesses, as he is not believed to permit himself a prohibition, similar to one who is established as a Kohen who is not believed to say he is not a Kohen in order to marry a divorced woman, as mentioned in Siman 3. However, regarding his children, he is believed, as the Torah has given credibility to a father, as mentioned. And even though he himself has considered them to be legitimate, and how can he now be believed to render them illegitimate? Nevertheless, since he is believed to prohibit himself, it follows that they are also prohibited. But if the children have their own offspring, he is not believed concerning them, as will be explained.

The fact that the Torah gave credibility to a father applies specifically to his children, but not to his grandchildren. Therefore, if his children have offspring, he is not credible even regarding his own children, because it is impossible for him to disqualify his child and validate his grandchild. And since he is not credible regarding them (the grandchildren), it follows that he is also not credible regarding his child. The primary source of this law is learned from "he recognizes" concerning the firstborn, and there it refers to recent offspring who do not yet have children of their own. The Torah did not grant him credibility when there are offspring to his offspring.

Our sages said (Kiddushin 73b) that if four women gave birth in one house — the wife of a Kohen, the wife of a Levite, the wife of an Israelite, and the wife of a mamzer — and no one yet recognizes the newborns, the midwife is trusted to say, "This is the son of the Kohen, this is the Levite, this is the Israelite, and this is the mamzer." This trust is not a matter of law but rather because the sages trusted her, as it is generally not possible to ascertain otherwise (Ran there). Therefore, she is only trusted as long as the mothers themselves have not yet recognized their own children. However, if each woman has taken hold of a child and claims it as her own, the midwife is not trusted to challenge their claims. If there is a dispute between the women, it seems to me that the midwife is not trusted if they do not agree with her, and the status of the children remains uncertain. But if the women have not claimed the children themselves, the midwife is trusted. And although regarding a firstborn, she is only trusted immediately, as we explained in Choshen Mishpat 277:13 — this applies specifically to determining the firstborn, as once the child is out of her sight, they did not rely on her to know and recognize who is the firstborn. However, regarding family lineage, she is trusted as long as the children’s status is not established (Magid Mishneh, Laws of Testimony 15, in the name of Ritva). We have already explained this with G-d’s help in Choshen Mishpat there.

And this that the midwife is believed – when is this said? When she has a presumption of credibility and no one has challenged her. For then, since the offspring have not yet been established and we do not know their lineage, she is believed, even though by strict law we should not believe her, as she is not like a single witness who is believed in a matter where there is no established prohibition or permission as stated in Yoreh De'ah, section 127, for she is a woman and disqualified from testimony [See Beit Shmuel]. But if there is any challenge against her, even from one person, and even if the challenge is from a relative or one disqualified [See there] who says that the midwife is testifying falsely – she is not believed. And even if the challenge comes after she testified in court [ibid. and Maggid Mishneh], and although generally a challenge requires two witnesses, here, since the offspring do not yet have a presumption of legitimacy, even a single challenge is considered a challenge [Gemara]. And although in any case where the Torah believes a single witness, he is like two and one cannot discredit him, it is different here because her credibility is not from the law as mentioned [Ran]. And there is no difference whether the challenge is from legitimacy to disqualification or from disqualification to legitimacy since the offspring do not yet have a presumption [Hilchot Ishut]. All the more so if the mothers themselves contradict her, her words are meaningless as stated.

And what is the status of these offspring when there is a challenge regarding them? The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote that the son is presumed to be legitimate, but he has no lineage. End quote. The explanation of his words, as it appears to me, is: Each of the children is fit to join the congregation, but they do not have priestly or Levitical lineage. The reason is that regarding the son about whom the midwife said he is a mamzer (bastard) and he says he is not a mamzer – certainly, he is believed. Conversely, regarding the son about whom the midwife says he is legitimate and he says he is a mamzer – he is also not believed to establish him as a definite mamzer. Since trust is given to the midwife, although she is not trusted in a challenge, nevertheless, to establish someone as a mamzer based on one witness contradicting her has no basis at all. The status of all the offspring is like a mixture of a mamzer among three legitimate ones. Even if we judge them as fixed and as if it were a fifty-fifty situation, still, from the Torah, they are fit to join the congregation. Therefore, even though the Rabbis prohibited them, in this case where most are legitimate, and even if the mixture is just one-on-one, nevertheless, since there is one who declares him legitimate – either the witness or the midwife – the Rabbis did not decree in this case. However, to establish them as having priestly or Levitical status is certainly not possible, and therefore if there is a Kohen (priest) among them – we impose upon all of them also the stringencies of Kohanim. Regarding the trustworthiness of the midwife, I saw someone who says that when she is a relative to the offspring, she is not trusted. This does not seem correct to me, because since it is a rabbinic ordinance due to the fact that in most instances it cannot be done otherwise, what difference does it make if she is a relative or not.

It has already been explained in section 30 that a "shetuki" is a doubtful mamzer, and similarly, a child found in the marketplace, who is called an "asufi" – he is also a doubtful mamzer, since we do not know his status. It has already been clarified that, according to Torah law, they are fit to enter the congregation, as a doubtful mamzer is permitted by Torah law. However, the Sages prohibited them and instituted a higher standard regarding lineage. This "asufi" is also not a definite mamzer – not only in years of famine, when it is possible that he was abandoned due to the distress of hunger, but even not in years of famine – we do not say he is definitely a mamzer and therefore was abandoned.

And so our Sages said (Kiddushin 73a): According to Torah law, an "asufi" is fit. What is the reason? A married woman attributes the child to her husband and would not abandon him. What about the minority of betrothed women and those whose husbands went overseas and cannot attribute the child to their husbands? Since there are also single women, and there are also cases due to famine, it is a fifty-fifty situation, and the Torah states that only a definite mamzer shall not enter, but a doubtful mamzer may enter. However, the Sages instituted a higher standard regarding lineage.

And do not be troubled – even among betrothed and married women, there is a doubt to permit the child, as perhaps she became pregnant from a Samaritan. Why do we need the cases of single women and due to famine? It can be said that it is necessarily discussing a place where the entire town is Jewish, for if it were a place with both Jews and Samaritans, we would be unsure about the found child, perhaps he is not Jewish and a Samaritan woman abandoned him. Further clarification will follow, God willing.

The sages of blessed memory also stated an important principle regarding a foundling: specifically when there is no proof that the child was abandoned with the intent for it to die—then it is considered a doubtful mamzer. However, if there is proof that the child was not abandoned to die, but rather its mother performed an act indicating that it is a legitimate child and she cared for it as she would for a legitimate child—then it is not considered a foundling and is a legitimate child. The sign that it was not abandoned except due to hunger is significant. And even if the year is not one of famine, nevertheless the poor will not cease from the land, and its parents are hungry, and they abandoned it and made a sign indicating that it is a legitimate child and that they have compassion for it—it is a legitimate child, though it lacks parental lineage.

And what is the proof that the child is legitimate? Whether the proof is in his body, such as being circumcised, or his limbs being straight and properly formed as they do for infants, or if he is anointed with oil, or they have applied kohl to his eyes, or they have placed an amulet on him—all of these are signs on his body that they cared for him as a legitimate child. Similarly, if the proof is in the location where he was abandoned, such as being placed in a location where he would be protected from wild animals and found by people, for example, if he is found in a place where many people frequent, or hanging in a tree in a vessel where animals cannot reach and it is near the city, or found in a synagogue or another well-known place near the city, and certainly if found within the city itself, or found on the sides of the public domain—all these cases do not render him an abandoned child, for these are signs that they took care to protect him and only abandoned him due to hunger, or an unmarried woman gave birth to him and cared for him because he is a legitimate child, and due to shame, she abandoned him in a place where he would be found and cared for and remain alive.

A baby who was found abandoned on the road like an abandoned foundling, and then someone came and said, "He is my son and I abandoned him" — he is believed, and similarly, the mother is believed, even in a place where most of the city are non-Jews. This is because it is clear that if the child were not his, he would not take this child to claim him as his son. Therefore, he or she is believed to consider him as their son in all matters, whether lenient or stringent. And all this applies while the child is still abandoned on the road. However, if he has already been taken from the marketplace and then his father and mother come and say, "He is our son" — they are not believed without witnesses, since the child has already been given the status of an abandoned foundling. It seems to me that we should be concerned about their words to be stringent in all matters, like not allowing his mother to perform Yibbum (levirate marriage) and similar cases, but not to be lenient, like exempting his mother from Yibbum. It is impossible to say that we should not consider their words at all — since by law they are believed, but because he has been given the status of an abandoned foundling, the sages said they are not believed. In years of famine, they are believed even afterward, because we say that due to the famine they abandoned him, wanting others to feed him, and therefore they remained silent until he was taken from the marketplace. And he will not be given the status of an abandoned foundling. Moreover, in years of famine, since many are abandoned, the sages did not want to disqualify them due to the spreading of rumors.

And know that in the Jerusalem Talmud, Kiddushin, Chapter 4 [Halacha 2], it states: As long as a child is abandoned in the market, either his father or his mother can testify about him. Once he is gathered from the market, two witnesses are required, and his father and mother together are considered as two witnesses. This implies that only the father alone or the mother alone are not believed, but both together are believed. All the halachic authorities wrote that they are not believed as stated, and it is possible that our Talmud disagrees with this, as our Talmud explains the reason because he is called by the name "foundling," which clearly implies that even though by law he should be considered valid, nevertheless, because of the appellation "foundling," the sages did not want to validate him. Nevertheless, we wrote that two witnesses are believed, as it is unreasonable to say that two witnesses would not suffice to remove a rumor, and in this regard, we do not find that our Talmud explicitly disagrees. It further states there to differentiate between a child who can move himself from his place and one who cannot move himself, and this too is not halachically relevant, as according to our Talmud, the credibility is only immediate while he is still in the market, and then this distinction does not apply. And in the Jerusalem Talmud itself, it seems that this is rejected [see there in the Mahara Fulda’s commentary, who did not write so, and it seems to me that as I wrote is the main understanding, and contemplate well].

Some of our rabbis have written that the case of an "asufi" (a foundling) being considered a doubtful mamzer (illegitimate child) and permitted by Torah law applies only in a place where there is an equal mixture of kosher (permissible) and non-kosher (forbidden) individuals, or a majority of kosher and a minority of non-kosher. However, in a place where the majority are non-kosher and the minority are kosher, he is considered a definite mamzer because we follow the majority [Rashba]. And even though there is a doubt that perhaps the law is like their opinion and it should be considered as if the situation is equally divided, still there is a majority towards prohibition as stated in section 34. [And what our sages said there, "What do you say etc." – it means even if you wish to be stringent, see there and examine it.]

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote: A foundling found in a city with both non-Jews and Jews—whether the majority are non-Jews or the majority are Jews—there is a doubt whether he is non-Jewish regarding lineage. If he betrothed a woman, she would need a conditional divorce. If the court immersed him for the sake of conversion [in ancient times], or if he immersed after he matured, he is like other foundlings found in Jewish cities. If the majority of the city are non-Jews, it is permitted to feed him non-kosher meat. If the majority are Jews, we return his lost property to him. If it is half and half, there is a mitzvah to sustain him and to clear debris from him on Shabbat, and regarding damages, he is treated as any case of monetary doubt, and the burden of proof is on the claimant. Thus are the words of Maimonides.

And this is the view that even after he has immersed and the majority are non-Jews, he is still considered an abandoned child – due to the concern of doubtful mamzer (illegitimate child). Even though in the case of a "shetuki" (a child whose father is unknown), if his mother says he is kosher (legitimate), she is believed even if the majority are disqualified, nonetheless here, where there is no statement about him and he does not have the presumption of legitimacy, they established a higher standard for lineage even with the majority and are concerned for the possibility of mamzerut, just as they established a higher standard for priestly lineage regarding the woman herself when she says she was defiled by a kosher man, she is not believed even if the majority are kosher, only with a double majority as stated in Siman 6. Similarly, in the lineage of Israel, when there is no statement at all, they were concerned even with the majority, even regarding the child. However, when there are two majorities, he is certainly kosher, as it is no less than there. And if he has signs that he is not an abandoned child and the concern is only a doubtful non-Jew or Israelite, when he immerses, he is completely kosher, and only if she is a female she should not marry a priest even if the majority are Israelites. And it should not be said that the reason of the Rambam for not following the majority is due to the principle of "fixed," for this child has separated from the majority and is not fixed. Therefore, indeed, there are those who disagree with him and hold that with the majority of non-Jews, we follow the majority when he immerses and he is like an Israelite, and only if she is a female she is prohibited to a priest as stated. And according to the Rambam, this is what Rav said at the beginning of Ketubot, "But for lineage, no," and the Raavad explains it as Rashi does there.

And regarding his ruling that only in a case of 50-50 (equal likelihood) we uncover the debris – many disagree with him and hold that in a case of saving a life we do not follow the majority. The Rambam, of blessed memory, follows his reasoning in the second chapter of Shabbat that only when one individual separates from a fixed group do we not follow the majority. But when all separate from a fixed group, and at the time they were moving, one of them separated and debris fell on him – we follow the majority. Here, with the found child, it is assumed that the entire city was moving, and therefore we follow the majority [Beit Shmuel]. Also, regarding his ruling that in a 50-50 case we are commanded to save him – they disagree with him and hold that in a 50-50 case we are not commanded [HaMagid Mishneh, and the words of the Beit Shmuel in section 159 are questionable, as this is according to Shmuel, and we rule according to Rav – refer there and scrutinize].

The general rule regarding a Shetuki and an Asufi is as follows: A Shetuki, when his mother has been examined and she says, "I had relations with a kosher person," she is believed, even if most people available were unfit, when she is single, as stated in Section 31. To disqualify him, she is not believed, as stated there. Even when she says, "I had relations with a kosher person," she is not believed to establish him as her son, and an oath is not required if she contradicts herself, as stated in Section 32. When she has not been examined, he is considered a doubtful mamzer (illegitimate child) if there is a minority of mamzerim in the city, and we do not follow the majority, as stated in Section 34. However, if there are no mamzerim in the city, the child is kosher, and we do not worry about relatives unless she is suspected of relations with them, as stated. An Asufi, in a city that is entirely Jewish, if there are no signs that he was abandoned to die, he is considered a doubtful mamzer. If there are signs, he is completely kosher. Why is his status not like that of a Shetuki, who is a doubtful mamzer? A Shetuki is different because we recognize his mother, who is single, and it is certain that she committed adultery, but we do not know with whom. Therefore, even if there is a minority of mamzerim in the city, he is considered a doubtful mamzer. But this Asufi, if there are signs that he was not abandoned to die, we say he is not from a single mother at all; rather, the father and mother abandoned him due to hunger. And in a city that also has Samaritans, the foundling is considered a doubtful Samaritan, doubtful Jew, unless he is circumcised. Any Shetuki or Asufi who is deemed kosher is permitted to marry any Jewish woman, and we do not worry that the Shetuki might marry his paternal sister, or the Asufi his father or mother, because the majority of the majority are permitted to marry him. Only in the case of a Shetuki, when the mother says she became pregnant from a particular person, even though she is not believed to establish him as his son, as stated, nevertheless, his relatives are forbidden to him based on her words.

And from where do we learn that not everyone is prohibited from marrying any woman? For it is written, "Do not profane your daughter by making her a harlot," and the sages said that if one does this, it results in a father marrying his daughter and a brother marrying his sister. And if the law were that anyone who does not know his father is definitely prohibited from marrying any woman who might be a forbidden relative, we would never come to such a conclusion, and the land would not be filled with immorality. Hence, you learn that we do not prohibit forbidden relationships by maintaining them as close relatives in doubt until it is definitively known that she is a forbidden relative to him. For if you do not say so, all the orphans in the world who do not know their fathers would be prohibited from marrying anywhere, lest they encounter a forbidden relationship. [Rambam]

Some have written that although from the Torah they are permitted to marry anyone they wish, nevertheless, from a Rabbinic perspective, they are forbidden to marry until it is clarified that this woman has no possibility of being a relative [Gra, section 279]. There is evidence for this from the case of one who says to his agent, "Go and betroth a woman for me" and the agent went and died, that he is forbidden to marry any woman in the world because of the concern that the agent might have betrothed a woman on his behalf, and this woman might be her relative, as stated in section 35 [there].

However, this does not appear to be the case from all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), for even though they were concerned about lineage even with a very small minority, here it is like a very minor minority, which has no real substance to be concerned that the woman he wants to marry is the daughter or sister of the adulterer who committed adultery with this person's mother. And in the Gemara, there is this reasoning [Kiddushin 73a: all these cases are set aside there].

Moreover, we see that regarding not disqualifying him, the mother is believed even in the majority of disqualifications because of her presumption of fitness, as stated in section 31. The main reason we explained there is to not disqualify him. Now, if we say that a shetuki (a person whose father is unknown) or an asufi (a foundling) who are fit according to the law, such as when his mother was investigated or the asufi has signs, cannot marry any woman due to potential concerns, you are almost prohibiting him from marrying any woman. Every woman whose father or brother was alive when his mother became pregnant would be suspect of incest, fearing that her father or brother is his father. Similarly, he would be prohibited from marrying any widow or divorcee, fearing she might be his father's or his father's brother's wife. This is not logical at all. 

The case of one who sent an agent to betroth a woman, and he is forbidden to all women, is actually not by law but merely a penalty [Tosafot Nazir 12a] because he sent the agent to betroth a woman in general and not a specific woman. And the proof for this is that we do not prohibit all minor girls whose fathers died from marrying, fearing their father received betrothal for them from this agent. Rather, it is certainly just a penalty, and in the case of this shetuki or asufi who did not sin at all, we would not penalize him.

Furthermore, in the Gemara there, when they wanted to state the reason why the Sages prohibited a shetuki whose mother was not investigated from entering the congregation due to concerns of incest when he marries a woman, they rejected this reason and only distanced him due to the importance of lineage. But when there is no importance of lineage, such as when his mother was investigated, and the asufi has signs, there is no such importance [One should not say that for us, where doubts are forbidden to one another, this objection does not exist as stated in Tosafot, and indeed the poskim wrote the reason of importance, so scrutinize].

All doubts are forbidden to marry one another because they established a higher standard regarding lineage. Therefore, a "sheṭuqi" (a person whose father is unknown) should not marry a "sheṭuqit" (a female "sheṭuqi") or an "asufi" (a foundling), and an "asufi" should not marry a "sheṭuqit" or another "asufi," for perhaps one of them is legitimate and the other is disqualified. If they marry, they should not remain married but must divorce with a get, and the child is considered of doubtful status like their parents. These doubtful cases have no remedy except to marry converts or freed slaves, and the child follows the status of the blemished party. How so? If a "sheṭuqi" or "asufi" marries a convert or a freedwoman, or if a convert or freedman marries a "sheṭuqit" or "asufit," the child is a "sheṭuqi" or "asufi," for in all matters of mamzerut (illegitimacy), even if the marriage was permissible, it does not remove the suspicion of mamzerut because the Torah included many cases under the category of mamzer, as stated in section 10. Definite mamzerim and Nethinim (a group with questionable lineage) are permitted to marry each other, and the child is a mamzer. "Sheṭuqi" and "asufi" are permitted to marry Nethinim, and the child is a doubtful mamzer. Some prohibit these doubtful cases from marrying Nethinim. A Nethin is forbidden to marry a maidservant. However, according to the Rambam, who states that the prohibition of a maidservant is not from Torah law, it may be permitted for a Nethin to marry a maidservant.

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote: "It appears to me that any country [city] that has a maidservant or a Gentile woman who is capable of giving birth, since the foundling found there is possibly a Gentile or possibly a slave, when he marries a convert as we have explained – this is a doubtful case of a married woman (eshet ish), and one who has relations with her is exempt because we do not execute based on doubt. Similarly, it appears to me that a shetuki (one who does not know his father's identity) who marries a woman who is prohibited to him, and she is possibly a married woman, since marriages do not take effect with prohibited relations. And who is the woman who might be prohibited to him? Any woman whose father or brother was present when his mother conceived, and any woman who was divorced or widowed, perhaps she is his father's wife or the wife of his father's brother." End quote. This was cited in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 37. And what was written about the foundling being a doubtful married woman – this is when he marries without immersing himself and without circumcision [Choshen Mishpat], because otherwise, in any case, he is considered a full-fledged Jew.
