And what was written about the shetuki – some say this is referring to a shetuki whose mother was not checked and he is a doubtful mamzer by rabbinic law and married in prohibition [Beit Shmuel], and some say it also refers to when his mother was checked, and he married lawfully [Choshen Mishpat]. And it seems to me that the primary opinion is the first one, as will be explained with God's help.

And some of our Rabbis disagree with the Rambam, for in all capital cases we follow the majority, so why not follow the majority here [Raavad]? The Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not bring this opinion at all, and it seems to me that their reasoning is because we see concerning lineage matters that even though generally we follow the majority, nevertheless, the Sages made a higher standard not to follow the majority. Therefore, how can we stone someone who had relations with this woman based on the majority? And even though from the Torah he is liable to death, nevertheless, in such a case, certainly the Sages have the power not to execute him, since they themselves concerning lineage did not follow the majority, all the more so with a death penalty. Although in the case of a shetuki (a person of questionable lineage), one who had relations with her is liable to death, for even if he is a mamzer and forbidden to marry a daughter of Israel according to the Sages' decree, kiddushin (marriage) is valid with those who are forbidden by a negative commandment, and the Sages did not concern themselves with forbidden relations, for when his mother was examined, they permitted him to marry whomever he wishes. Nevertheless, since this shetuki whose mother was not examined, the Sages did not permit him and he married in prohibition. And since he transgressed their words which said not to follow the majority in this matter, how can we execute the one who had relations with her because of the majority? And according to this, the Rambam refers only to a case where his mother was not examined, and perhaps indeed according to this, no one disagrees with the Rambam, and therefore the Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not bring the dissenting opinion. [And perhaps this is what the Magid Mishneh meant, see there thoroughly and understand well.]

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: "It is forbidden to marry Karaites, as all of them are possibly of illegitimate descent (mamzerim), and we do not accept them if they wish to return [to mainstream Judaism]. However, for forced converts (anusim) who return to the Jewish faith, it appears to me that it is permissible to marry them." End quote. [The reason is because] they marry their women with money or intercourse, and they divorce improperly, deviating from the format established by the sages for divorce documents (gittin). Their wives then remarry while their first husbands are still alive, causing their children to be illegitimate (mamzerim) from married women. The early Gaonim wrote regarding heretics who departed from Jewish ways and are promiscuous: they do not write marriage contracts (ketubot) or divorce documents (gittin) for them, nor do they perform chalitza or yibbum [levirate marriage]. Their children are considered mamzerim, and we cannot accept them into the community of Israel, lest they intermingle and increase the number of mamzerim among the Jews. However, if the parents return and accept upon themselves the burden of commandments like other Jews, they are accepted, since they were born from a holy seed and were born legitimately. They scrutinized their offspring, and anyone with a trace of disqualification was separated. But forced converts (anusim) are presumed to have always maintained the purity of their lineage. However, this too depends on the circumstances and their conduct.

The Rambam writes in Chapter 16 of Laws of Forbidden Relations: A man with crushed testicles or a severed member who marries a Jewish woman and has relations with her is liable to lashes, as it says: "A man with crushed testicles or a severed member shall not enter the assembly of the Lord." However, they are permitted to marry a convert or a freed maidservant. Even a priest who has crushed testicles is allowed to marry a convert or a freed maidservant because he is not in his sanctity, and even a Nethin or one of doubtful status is permitted to him, since a man with crushed testicles is forbidden to enter the assembly, the decree was not applied to the Nethinim or those of doubtful status. But a man with crushed testicles or a severed member is forbidden to marry a definite mamzeret, as she is forbidden by Torah law. End quote.

Here is the translation of the passage:

And behold, what he wrote that lashes are administered specifically in cases of marriage and intercourse is according to his opinion that all transgressors of prohibitions do not receive lashes without marriage and intercourse, as explained in Siman 4, Se’if 2, and many disagree with him as mentioned there [the Rema]. And the distinction made between a mamzeret (a female offspring of a forbidden relationship) being forbidden and a netinah (a descendant of the Gibeonites) being permitted follows his view that the prohibition of the netinim is not from the Torah, as mentioned there in Se’if 5. And the allowance for a priest who is injured in his reproductive organs to marry a convert or a freed slave is because his priestly sanctity has been removed. Since the Torah forbids him from entering the congregation, all the more so he does not retain priestly sanctity. And why be stricter with the prohibition of a mamzeret than with the prohibition of a priest? Because the priestly prohibition does not apply to all Israelites, only to priests, and is less severe than the prohibition of a mamzeret, which applies to all Israelites. And even though in matters of priestly lineage they made additional stringencies more than in Israelites’ lineage, this is with a proper priest they were stricter, but not with one who is disqualified. And the reason they were stricter with the congregation’s disqualification of one injured in his reproductive organs more than with other disqualifications that are permitted with a mamzeret is that disqualifications due to lineage differ from disqualifications due to the defect itself, and his family is considered a full congregation, and this reasoning is found in the Jerusalem Talmud [Chapter 7 of Yevamot]. And some say that even a priest injured in his reproductive organs is forbidden to marry a convert or a freed slave just as he is forbidden to marry a mamzeret, for both are Torah prohibitions, and only a netinah, whose prohibition is not from the Torah, is permitted. And indeed, in the Jerusalem Talmud there, they compare these prohibitions [Ba’al HaMaor Chapter 7 of Yevamot, and he also rules like the conclusion of Rava there (76.) and the question regarding a priest injured in his reproductive organs was not resolved, and Rambam, even though he also rules accordingly, nevertheless the reason he rules this way is because of the discussion there (78.), and in this, we do not find him disagreeing with the latter opinion regarding a priest injured in his reproductive organs, and since according to Rava's latter opinion it is conclusively permitted, he ruled thus as above, and examine this well].

Some say that just as a Kohen (priest) with crushed testicles is permitted to marry a convert or a freed maidservant, so too, a man with crushed testicles is permitted to marry a mamzeret (a woman born from certain prohibited relationships) [Ra'avad, Rashba, and Tur ruled according to Rava's principle and the prohibition of Nethinim (Gibeonites) is from the Torah, and so it appears in the Jerusalem Talmud. Rambam does not concern himself with this, as he holds that this is according to Rava's principle, while the plain reading of our Talmud (Yevamot 78b) is like Rav Kahana. Analyze this carefully].

However, in regard to the Rambam's allowance to marry those with uncertain status, such as a shetuki (a person of uncertain paternity) and an asufi (a foundling), some have questioned this: Since a priest (kohen) is prohibited from marrying a mamzeret (a female mamzer), he should also be prohibited from marrying a shetuki. If she is a mamzeret, he is forbidden to marry her, and if she is fit (not a mamzeret), she is still forbidden to him. They struggled to say that the allowance applies when the uncertainties are not from Israel but from a freed slave or similar cases. However, this reasoning does not hold because it should have been explicitly stated. 

In my opinion, the Rambam's prohibition against marrying a mamzeret is not from the Torah (Biblical law). From the Torah, there is no reason to distinguish between the prohibition of a kohen and the prohibition of the congregation; since a person with crushed testicles is not part of the congregation and a mamzeret is also not part of the congregation, why should they be forbidden to each other? Rather, the sages prohibited a kohen from marrying a mamzeret, as the Rambam explicitly writes: "He is prohibited from marrying a definite mamzeret because she is forbidden by Torah law." This indicates that the prohibition is rabbinic for a definite mamzeret. Therefore, the sages were stringent with certain cases but not with uncertainties like the shetuki and asufi, where the prohibition is rabbinic and they were not stringent in the case of a person with crushed testicles. 

From a rabbinic perspective, they indeed differentiated between those invalidated from the congregation due to family lineage and those invalidated due to bodily defects, but from the Torah, there is no reason to differentiate; ultimately, both are invalidated from the congregation. [Although most commentators seem to follow the Rambam that the prohibition of a mamzeret is from the Torah, I believe the main point is as I wrote, which also resolves the questions of the Beit Shmuel and other difficulties.]

There is doubt whether a man with crushed testicles is permitted to marry a maidservant or not. It seems that according to the authorities who hold that the prohibition is from the Torah, as written in the beginning of section 4, he is forbidden to marry her. According to Maimonides, who holds that the prohibition is rabbinic, he is permitted to marry her. However, it is possible to say that according to the authorities who permit marriage with a mamzeret, he is also permitted to marry a maidservant even though her prohibition is from the Torah, and the matter requires further investigation for the final ruling.

And regarding the matter that the Rambam permitted a Kohen with crushed testicles, some say that he is permitted in all prohibitions of the priesthood, such as marrying a divorced woman, a harlot, and a chalalah [illegitimate priestly offspring], since he has been removed from his sanctity. And although they are forbidden to marry him due to the prohibition of his injury, nevertheless, if they are also freed women who are permitted to him – they are not prohibited to him from the perspective of the priesthood. And some say that he is forbidden in all prohibitions of the priesthood, and only a convert and a freed woman, who are not considered a harlot, are permitted to him, for in the Gemara there are those who permit them to a complete Kohen [Kiddushin 78]. And although we do not hold like that, nevertheless, their primary prohibition is from the verse in Ezekiel that states, "Only virgins of the seed of the house of Israel shall they take as wives," and their prohibition is not similar to all the prohibitions of the priesthood [Beit Shmuel]. And there is a practical difference between the two opinions: according to the first opinion – his status is like a complete non-priest, and he is permitted to become ritually impure to the dead, is forbidden from eating terumah and sacrifices, and does not raise his hands [in the priestly blessing]. According to the second opinion – his status is like a blemished Kohen, and he is forbidden to become ritually impure to the dead, but is permitted to eat terumah and sacrifices. And this is also implied in the Talmud in Bechorot and in the Rambam, Chapter 7 of Biat Hamikdash, where a Kohen with crushed testicles and a severed organ are considered among the blemishes, and it is explained there that a blemished Kohen is permitted to eat from the sacrifices. According to the first opinion, it must be said that there it is referring to a case ordained by Heaven, for the prohibition is only when he became injured by human hands, as will be explained. And that which is written in the Torah 'a man with crushed testicles' among the blemishes and it is explicitly stated there "the bread of his God from the most holy and from the holy he may eat," it must also be said that it is referring to an injury ordained by Heaven, and furthermore, this applies to the testicles as the Rambam writes there in Chapter 8 and is not included in this [Choshen Mishpat and Beit Meir, and it appears to me as I have written].

The terms mentioned in the Torah, 'Petzu'a Dakka' and 'Kerut Shofkha' – their meanings are threefold: 'Petzu'a' refers to a wound caused by a sword or knife, and 'Dakka' means crushed, i.e., it was crushed by something and part of the organ was diminished. 'Kerut Shofkha' means severed, and through the severing, something flows out from it. Our Sages learned that all of these refer to the same area, and the flow is the seed that flows out and is not ejected forcefully like an arrow and does not produce offspring. A male is disqualified by three organs – the member, the testicles, and the ducts where the semen is formed, which are called the cords of the testicles. Once one of these three organs is wounded, crushed, or severed, he is disqualified. Thus said our Sages: injured in any of them, crushed in any of them, severed in any of them. Injured in any of them – whether the member is injured, the testicles are injured, or the cords of the testicles are injured, and the same applies to crushed or severed. However, in the member, there are boundaries – a place where it is invalid and a place where it is not invalid, as we will explain with God's help.

How so? At the head of the organ, there is flesh, and where it joins to the organ, it is elevated and surrounds the organ. This is called the "corona." This surrounding flesh is not in a straight circle, but rather, at the top of the organ, the corona extends towards the body and gradually shortens until near the head of the organ. This flesh is not considered like the rest of the organ, for even if it is entirely cut off and only a thread's width remains on the majority of the corona towards the body, it is valid [Tur]. However, if it is cut towards the body and only a thread's width of the corona remains around the entire circumference of the organ towards the ground, it is invalid [Rashi]. And do not be perplexed—since it was cut above, how can it remain below? The truth is that it does not need to be that the entire thickness of the organ is cut, only the flesh from the corona. Therefore, it is possible that the flesh surrounding the corona is cut above and remains below [It appears to me]. According to this view, everything depends on the thread surrounding the upper part of the corona towards the body. But Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: if the head of the corona is severed and even a thread's width remains around the entire organ, it is valid. Thus, there is no concern even if it is cut close to the body, as long as the thread surrounds the entire organ that is not close to the body [Beit Shmuel]. And some say that it is necessary to surround the whole organ close to the body [there in the name of the Riva], and according to this opinion, it is explicitly stated in the Tosefta Yevamot Chapter 10, see there. And in the Jerusalem Talmud [Chapter 8], there is a dispute about this, and it seems that the halacha is according to Rambam, see there. And in our Talmud there, there are variant readings, and according to the version we have, it is explained according to the first opinion, see there [75b]. And know, that although regarding circumcision the corona is considered from the very head of the organ as proven in Yoreh De'ah Siman 264, nevertheless, regarding a severed member, there is no concern except for one thread alone, for in this matter one can still father children [and this resolves all the ambiguities raised by later authorities, see Taz, Bach, and Drisha u’Perisha]. According to what has been explained, if it is cut below the corona, even entirely, it is valid. But if the corona is cut according to the opinions explained, or it is cut above the corona, it is invalid, as Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch wrote, see there.

If the gland (gid) is cut above the corona at an angle like a quill, slanted as if cutting the tip of a quill (to write) – it is kosher, because air does not penetrate the gland and the semen cooks properly [Rashi]. This is because the entire corona remains intact, even though the flesh has been scraped off until the tube of the semen is exposed and the corona remains intact [Bach]. 

However, if it is cut like a gutter, where the interior of the gland is removed and only the walls on both sides remain with a hollow in the middle like a pipe – according to Rashi and the Rosh, it is invalid because air enters the walls and cools the gland, preventing the semen from cooking properly [ibid]. According to the Rambam, it is kosher, since the thickness of the gland has not been reduced, it touches the sides of the womb, warms up, and shoots out like an arrow. Even when shaped like a quill, although it does not touch the sides of the womb and does not warm up as much, nevertheless, because the upper part touches the sides of the womb and air does not penetrate it, it shoots like an arrow [this seems correct to me].

Even according to Rashi and the Rosh, if it is made like a gutter and the flesh is cut from all sides and the walls of the gutter are removed, making it like a quill – it is kosher [Gemara]. According to the Rambam, if it was neither a gutter nor a quill and it was cut and made into a gutter – it is kosher [Beit Yosef].

If the urethra is perforated – if it is perforated below the glans, even if it is a complete perforation from one side to the other, it is valid, for even if it were completely severed there, it would still be valid, as mentioned. However, if the glans itself or above the glans is perforated, it is invalid because the semen drips through the perforation and does not shoot like an arrow and does not lead to conception. Therefore, the measure of the perforation is if the semen can exit through it. If the perforation is sealed, it is valid, as this is a defect that can be remedied, and one can apply a treatment to seal the perforation. Even after it is sealed, it must be tested. This means observing when he experiences a seminal emission to see if the sealing is disrupted and the semen exits through the perforation – if so, it is invalid, but if the seal is strong enough that the rush of semen does not disrupt it, it is valid. 

Some say that if the perforation is large enough that it is known that semen exits through it and it is sealed, there is no need to check if the seal will be disrupted. However, if the perforation is very small and sealed in any amount and it is not noticeable, it should be seen if it is large enough that when this man experiences a seminal emission, the pressure of the gathered semen expands the perforation – if so, it is invalid. Similarly, if it is sealed through a treatment applied to it, we do not worry about the disruption of the seal even with a small perforation. However, if it seals on its own, certainly, we must be cautious in every case. 

It seems to me that we should rely on the words of doctors when they say that the perforation is sealed and will not open, for we even rely on them in cases of prohibitions that carry the penalty of karet (excision). All this applies to the glans itself, but if it is perforated above the glans and then sealed, we no longer worry about the disruption of the seal, because the semen does not exert pressure in collecting except at the exit perforation. Some say that above the glans, sealing does not help, but this does not seem to be the opinion of most of the decisors, and it also does not seem to be implied by the Talmud.

The disqualification of a puncture is when it reaches the cavity of the organ, similar to the punctures that make an animal or bird treif (unfit for consumption), where we require either a puncture that goes from side to side or reaches the cavity of the organ. If it does not reach the cavity, it is nothing. But when it reaches the cavity, the puncture interferes with the path of the seed within the cavity, causing it to leak from the puncture and preventing procreation. Some say that this disqualification up to the cavity applies only to the glans itself, but if there is a puncture above the glans, it is not disqualified unless the puncture goes from side to side. For in the case of the name [i.e., the glans], even if it is as narrow as a reed, it is fit, all the more so if it is punctured up to the cavity [Ba'er Hetev]. And some say that even in the case of the name, it is disqualified if it is punctured up to the cavity [Bach], and in practice, one should be stringent in this matter [Ba'er Hetev]. See what we will explain later regarding the opinion of the Rambam of blessed memory. [And the necessity of Ba'er Hetev from Tosafot in Avodah Zarah: it can be refuted, see there and examine well.]

It is stated in the Talmud [there]: If there is a perforation below the corona that corresponds to above the corona, it is invalid. Rashi explained: "Below the corona" means at the end of the member towards the ground, and the perforation goes diagonally and exits opposite to above the corona towards the body. End quote. Some of our Rabbis explained that you can find this even if it does not go diagonally, but as explained in paragraph 5, the circumference of the corona does not form a straight circle, but on the upper part of the member, the corona extends toward the body, and on the lower part, it shortens until near the head of the member. According to this, it is possible that the perforation is even, but on the upper part of the member, it is below the corona, and on the lower part, it is above the corona [Tosafot]. There is no practical difference in the law between the two explanations. The general rule is that since the perforation goes through from one side to the other, even if on one side it is below the corona, since on the other side it is above the corona, it is invalid because the semen passes through there. Some are even stricter and say that even if the perforation does not go through but is only on the upper part of the member until the cavity and below the corona, but since opposite the lower part of the member it is above the corona, it is invalid [Mordechai]. This is an excessive stringency and there is no valid reason to invalidate this, and we do not hold by this opinion [Beit Shmuel]. Rambam wrote: If there is a perforation below the corona in such a way that opposite it is above within the corona, it is invalid, as any part of the corona is essential. End quote. This is also written in the Shulchan Aruch, following his view that the entire circumference of the corona is necessary [there]. It appears that above the corona, Rambam also agrees with all the authorities that it is invalid, and all this is according to what all the great authorities have understood from his words.

But it appears to me from the words of the Rambam, of blessed memory, that above the glans, a puncture does not invalidate at all. As he wrote regarding a case where the glans was cut, when the glans or above the glans was severed, it is invalid. However, in the case of a puncture, he only mentioned the glans itself and not above the glans. Additionally, in the previous law mentioned in the Gemara, where they said "above the glans," it was explained to mean within the glans itself. Therefore, it is clear that he holds that a puncture above the glans does not invalidate at all.

And the reason is logical since the invalidity of a puncture is due to the fact that the semen drips through there. It is understood that when the semen moves with its heat like an arrow shot, it does not sense in the middle of its path, which is in its full strength, the puncture at its side to go through there. Rather, when it reaches near its end, which is in the glans and needs to exit, it will exit through the puncture if it encounters it there, as we wrote a similar reasoning regarding a blockage in Section 10 at its end.

There is also tangible evidence from several incidents brought in the responses of the great Acharonim where it happened to young boys who played with each other, they tied a string around the organ above the glans, and the boy did not feel it, and the organ swelled until the doctors cut the string and found a puncture in the organ. Afterwards, they married women and had children, and testified about themselves that their semen shoots like an arrow and flows in its usual manner like every man. The great authorities did not find a reason to validate them by law, but according to our words, this is not invalid at all.

In all the words of our earlier rabbis, I did not find explicitly that they say the opposite of this. In the previously mentioned law, one could say that the invalidity is not because of the puncture above the glans, but because it starts below the glans and goes up to above the glans, it necessarily passes through the glans itself. What we wrote in Section 10 regarding the blockage applies here regarding the main puncture as well.

In the Gemara there, a remedy is mentioned for closing a hole: to take a barley grain and scratch around the hole so that blood comes out and coagulates around the hole, thereby healing it. Then, take a large ant and place its head there so that it bites and its head sticks there. We then sever its head, and as long as it remains attached, the flesh heals and connects. The poskim did not bring this remedy because we are not proficient in all the remedies mentioned in the Talmud, and also because not every hole or flesh is the same.

However, the Gemara there states: "This applies to a small hole, but a large one will peel." In other words, after it heals, it peels away and is undone [Rashi]. The Sheiltot in Parashat Tetzaveh explains that this applies to a small hole, but for an adult, since he has set his mind on marital relations, it will not close. This is also written in Ba'al Halachot Gedolot. According to this, it is puzzling—if for an adult it does not work, why did none of the poskim mention this? And since they wrote that closing the hole works in general terms, it implies that closing the hole works for everyone.

It seems to me that the distinction of small and large in the Gemara does not refer to the person but to the hole. Meaning, such a closure works only for a small hole, but not for a large one, which requires a better closure. Since the poskim did not write the remedy, they also did not need to write this distinction. It is possible that even according to the Sheiltot, only a simple closure does not work for a large hole, but a better closure would be effective even for an adult. Therefore, it is possible that all the poskim would interpret it this way. Practically, it seems that it depends on the understanding of expert doctors, as I have written.

There are two ducts in the male organ, one for the emission of semen and one for the emission of urine, and between them is a thin membrane as thin as a garlic peel [Bechorot 44b]. If the passage through which the semen travels becomes blocked and the semen travels through the passage of the urine, the Sages have disqualified him. And even though this is not considered to be wounded, crushed, or severed, nonetheless, the Sages have determined that the semen does not develop properly when it travels through the incorrect passage and he cannot father children. Some of our Rabbis hold that if there is a perforation, he is fit to enter the congregation but will not be able to father children. Similarly, if the passage for the semen is blocked, he is fit to enter the congregation [see Beit Shmuel at the end of section 9], as they believe that a perforation is not included in the category of a severed duct. However, this does not seem to be the opinion of the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, and the main point is puzzling: if so, why is this mentioned in the Gemara at all? According to their view, it is merely a case of infertility. They answer that the mention of these perforations in the Gemara is to teach that if he was with his wife and she gave birth, the child is a mamzer (illegitimate), for it is impossible for him to father a child and she must have committed adultery. The main proof for this opinion comes from the Sifrei, which states that a wounded testicle can heal but a severed duct cannot. In the case of a perforation, it can be healed through sealing. However, this is not conclusive, as its proper interpretation is that a wounded testicle can heal on its own and a severed duct cannot heal on its own, but if sealed properly, it can be rendered fit. And even if we do not interpret it this way, what is the connection? Does the qualification or disqualification depend on this? The Sifrei itself concludes that this is based on medical knowledge, so even though a severed duct cannot heal, a perforation can. Additionally, the proper interpretation is that a wounded testicle can fully heal as it sometimes does, but a severed duct cannot fully return to its original state, though the perforation can be sealed or treated until it is fit.

Maimonides wrote: If the testicles or one of them are severed, or one of them is injured, or one of them is crushed, or it is missing, or it is punctured – it is invalid. End quote. This is specifically when there is a perforating puncture. Some of our Rabbis permit if one testicle (the left) is severed and the right one remains intact, and also if the severed one was whole before it was removed. However, if it was injured and then removed – it is invalid, and they have support from the Jerusalem Talmud. Most of the decisors agree with Maimonides, and they dismiss the Jerusalem Talmud, explaining that it refers to a case by Heaven's hand which is valid, as will be explained. Rabbi Moshe Isserles wrote that this is the main opinion, and I have seen those who are lenient according to the last opinion, but it is better to be strict on a Torah prohibition according to the stringent opinions, which are the majority. End quote. Nevertheless, there are some great authorities who rely on this opinion if it is said that as a man in his strength he can still father children, and also shows no signs of being a eunuch. Their proof for this opinion is strong from the fact that we see many people from whom doctors remove one testicle, yet they still father children, and Heaven forbid to say that all their wives are promiscuous and attributing the children to their husbands. However, according to Maimonides, who will explain that due to illness it is like Heaven's hand, this is no proof, for in any case they are valid, and this will be clarified further with God's help.

If the cords of the testicles are severed, or one of them, or they are crushed or injured – it is invalid. According to those who are lenient regarding the left testicle, the same applies if the cord of the left testicle is missing. And if one of the cords of the testicles is perforated leading to the urinary tract, and thus he urinates from the urinary tract and from the seminal tract – it is valid.

The Sages have said that the reason the Torah disqualified all these invalid individuals from entering the congregation is only when the condition was caused by human action. However, if it happened by the hand of Heaven, it is valid. And what is considered by the hand of Heaven? The Rambam wrote, and this is his language: Any invalidity that we mentioned in this context, when it is not by the hand of Heaven, such as if a person or a dog cut it, or a thorn struck it, and similar things. But if someone was born with crushed testicles or with a severed member, or was born without testicles, or became ill due to his body causing these organs to be nullified, or was born with boils that melted them or severed them, he is valid to enter the congregation, for all these are by the hand of Heaven. 

And some of our Rabbis hold that it is not called by the hand of Heaven unless it is caused by thunder or hail or from his mother's womb, but if it is due to illness, it is considered by human action and invalid. And the Rosh wrote that this appears in the Jerusalem Talmud. And many rule like the Rambam [Bayit Chadash], and in the Jerusalem Talmud, the Rambam explains that there is a dispute whether illness is considered by the hand of Heaven or by human action, and he ruled according to the opinion that it is by the hand of Heaven, and many of the great later authorities agreed to rule like the Rambam. Moreover, even if the testicles were damaged due to illness and the doctor cut them, it is considered by the hand of Heaven, because since they were already damaged or ceased their function, it is as if they are not present, and the cutting is of no consequence [see Pri Tevuah]. And this is the practical halacha even though some are uncertain about this – nevertheless, the practice is significant. However, there is doubt if someone had a stone in his testicle and the doctors cut one or both testicles if this is considered by the hand of Heaven, and it is close to say that this is considered by human action, because the testicles themselves were not damaged, and this seems to be the main opinion. However, if they cut the left testicle, one can rely on the previous opinion that with the left one, even by human action, it is valid. And some are lenient to say that according to that opinion, even if the right one was cut, it is valid, for that opinion holds that as long as one whole and healthy testicle remains, it is valid [Yam Shel Shlomo]. 

And it is uncertain according to the law if one can rely on this opinion – it is a great leniency, and nevertheless, if such a case occurred, it is difficult to force him to divorce his wife.

In all the definite disqualifications that have been explained, if he married a woman and she bore children – they are considered mamzerim (illegitimate children), for he cannot father children [Beit Shmuel, section 3]. However, some say that if his testicles were punctured – they are doubtful mamzerim. According to several authorities, there is no cure for one whose reproductive organ has been severed, and even where there is a cure, we do not assume he has been healed unless it is known that he has been healed [ibid.]. Nevertheless, it seems to me that if the woman is known to be modest and God-fearing – we assume that he has been healed. Additionally, even for one whose reproductive organ has been severed, as stated in section 15, it is possible that he may be healed through medical treatments, see there, and the matter depends on the judgment of the local sages.

In all these cases of disqualification, if there is a doubt whether he is disqualified or not, such as when it is impossible to determine if he is a eunuch or not, and similar situations – it appears that he is permitted to enter the congregation. Just as we derive regarding a mamzer (bastard) that only a definite mamzer is prohibited from entering, but a doubtful mamzer may enter, similarly, we should derive this for a eunuch. The proof for this is that in the Gemara, they learned that a eunuch is due to human action from the case of a mamzer (Yevamot 70a), and although the Sages prohibited even a doubtful mamzer, nevertheless, we do not find that they prohibited a eunuch due to doubt. This is because the disqualification of family lineage is not similar to the disqualification of the body, as stated in paragraph 2. Furthermore, in this case, it is more favorable than a mamzer because we can establish a presumption that he was not born a eunuch. And if there is a doubt that he might be a eunuch from birth, in any case, he is fit, because if he is from birth – it is by Heaven's action and he is fit, and if this is not from birth – we establish him based on the presumption. However, one should consult with doctors and experts, and then if it remains a doubt for all of them, it is indeed considered a doubt. Otherwise, a doubt due to lack of knowledge is not considered a doubt, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 110, in the rules of double doubt, see there.

It is written: "And anything crushed, broken, torn, or cut, you shall not offer to the Lord, nor shall you do this in your land." The tradition teaches that anything in your land—you shall not do. This means that the Torah prohibited castration not only for sacrificial purposes but for any species found in the land that is not offered on the altar. The Torah warns against castrating them. It is impossible to say that this prohibition applies only in the Land of Israel, for it is a personal obligation and not dependent on the land. Any personal obligation applies both in the Land of Israel and outside of it. Since the Torah prohibited castrating any species of animals, it is certainly prohibited to castrate a human being. Thus, our sages said [Shabbat 110b]: From where do we derive that castration in a human is forbidden? The verse states, "nor shall you do this in your land"—do not do it to yourselves. The interpretation is to read it with a different vowelization, meaning you yourselves shall not do this. The reason for this prohibition is that, as we explained in Siman 1, even one who is not commanded to be fruitful and multiply, it is still the will of God that all creations should be fruitful and multiply. Anyone who damages reproductive organs, whether of a human, an animal, a beast, or a bird, transgresses a prohibition. This is because they are disrupting the intention of the Holy One, Blessed be He, in creating the world, which was created to be inhabited.

Therefore, it is forbidden to destroy reproductive organs, whether in humans, animals, wild beasts, or birds, whether impure or pure, whether in the Land of Israel or outside of it. Similarly, in all types of creatures in the world, it is forbidden to destroy reproductive organs, except for harmful creatures that it is a mitzvah to kill. It is forbidden to castrate a dog. And anyone who castrates is liable to receive lashes according to the Torah everywhere, even if one castrates after another has already castrated, he is still liable to lashes. How so? For example, if one person cuts the organ, and another comes and cuts the testicles or removes them, and another comes and cuts the spermatic cords, or one comes and crushes the organ, and another comes and detaches it, and another comes and cuts it—all are liable to lashes. And even if the last one did not complete the castration, but only castrated, whether in humans, animals, wild beasts, or birds. And our sages expounded: if one is liable for cutting, is it not all the more so for detaching? Detaching means completely detaching from the sac, and cutting means that they are still in the sac and somewhat attached. But this includes one who detaches after cutting, who is liable. Similarly, one who is born a eunuch is also forbidden to destroy his reproductive organs. This applies to both men and women, as well as to animals, wild beasts, and birds, whether male or female—it is forbidden to destroy their reproductive organs. However, lashes are only administered for males and not for females, as just as males are commanded in the positive commandment of procreation and not females, so too regarding castration, males are more stringent than females. And so the sages taught in the Torat Kohanim: from where do we derive that females are also included in the prohibition of castration? The verse states "for their corruption is in them." And since they are not included in the prohibition of "you shall not do," therefore they are not subject to lashes, but the prohibition is the same. And some imply from their words that the prohibition for females is only rabbinic, and this seems to be the language of the Rambam. And in Tosafot Makkot, it seems that there is lashes also for females. This requires further investigation.

Not only is it forbidden to engage in actions involving the reproductive organs, but even to drink a cup of "roots" (a potion) that causes sterility through this drink is forbidden. For it is written, "for their corruption is in them"—anything that corrupts the reproductive organs is prohibited by the Torah. Therefore, giving a cup of "roots" to a person or to other living beings to sterilize them is forbidden, even if one drinks it for medicinal purposes, since it causes sterility. And even though an unintended consequence is generally permitted, since this is an inevitable result (a "psik reisha"), it is forbidden. One should endeavor to find a medicine that will not cause sterility, unless this medicine is necessary for saving a life and there is no alternative treatment, just as it is permissible for a doctor to surgically remove the testicles for medicinal purposes if no other option exists. In all of this, there is no difference whether one has fulfilled the commandment of procreation or not.

It is taught in the Tosefta of Yevamot [Chapter 1]: A man is not permitted to drink a cup of roots that would make him sterile, but a woman is permitted to drink a cup of roots so that she will not conceive. And it is also explained in the Gemara that for medicinal purposes, a woman is permitted to drink a cup of roots [there], and so wrote the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch that a woman is permitted to drink a cup of roots to prevent conception. From their language, it implies that even not for medicinal purposes, it is permitted for her to do so. However, some of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) hold that it is only permitted for medicinal purposes or due to the pain of childbirth – such as if she always has difficulty giving birth – and not otherwise [Bach and Shach]. And this also seems to be the primary ruling, and the poskim did not need to mention this because it is certainly forbidden to alter the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, in any other manner. Similarly, it is prohibited to give a male animal a cup of roots. However, if it is necessary for medicinal purposes and done by a non-Jew, it might be permitted [see Pri Toar]. Know that drinking a cup of roots is not related to the prohibition of "No one with crushed testicles or severed member shall enter the assembly of the Lord" (Deuteronomy 23:2), contrary to what some wish to argue on this matter. [And what the Pri Toar wrote from Rashi on Sotah 26, see there in the words of Rashi at the beginning of the passage and examine thoroughly.]

Here is the translation of the passage:

"If someone binds a person and sets a dog or other animals upon him until they make him a eunuch, or if they place him in water or snow until his reproductive organs are destroyed – he does not receive lashes unless he castrates with his own hand, as long as he does not physically touch the reproductive organs, he does not receive lashes. However, he is deserving of rabbinic lashes. 

It is permissible to tie the wattle of a rooster, even though it will not mate because of it, as this is not considered castration. Rather, the rooster is saddened by the loss of its adornment and does not mate due to its sadness. Therefore, there is no prohibition in this, and similarly in all such cases, since nothing is done to the reproductive organs. 

Additionally, it is permissible to tie the female so that a male cannot mate with her, but if a male has already mounted her, it is prohibited to drive him away, whether it is a pure or impure animal, and similarly with a wild animal or a bird. Moreover, there is the prohibition of causing suffering to animals in this matter."

Just as on Shabbat, instructing a non-Jew to perform work is rabbinically prohibited, so too with all prohibitions of the Torah. Any task that a Jew is forbidden to do, he is also forbidden to instruct a non-Jew to do on his behalf. Therefore, it is forbidden to tell a non-Jew to castrate one's animal, beast, or bird, and even if it belongs to another Jew, it is forbidden. However, selling one's animal to a non-Jew who will castrate it is permitted according to most authorities, as the descendants of Noah are not commanded concerning castration, just as it is permissible to sell an animal to a non-Jew who will eat it without ritual slaughter. Nonetheless, there are authorities who hold that the descendants of Noah are also commanded concerning castration, as Rabbi Chidka stated in Sanhedrin 56. In practice, the main ruling follows the opinion of the majority of authorities, and this is also the view of the Rambam in Chapter 9 of the Laws of Kings. Nevertheless, there are those who are stringent regarding this opinion.

And even according to this opinion, if this non-Jew who buys it does not castrate it himself, but gives it to another non-Jew to castrate—it is permissible, for according to this opinion, the prohibition is due to "Do not place a stumbling block before the blind," and since he himself is not doing it but rather gives it to another non-Jew, it is considered a step removed, and we are not commanded to prevent a step removed. And even if the second non-Jew is his agent—there is no agency for a non-Jew, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 182, contrary to the opinion of some who say that there is agency from non-Jew to non-Jew, see there. And according to the first opinion, it is permitted to give a non-Jew an animal for a share of the profit as well, even though he will certainly castrate it, and we do not say that he is doing it for the sake of the Jew, because since he has a share, he is doing it for his own sake and not for the sake of the Jew; it is no different than on Shabbat, where it is permitted in such a case even though the Jew benefits from it.

If a non-Jew takes the animal of a Jew without the Jew's knowledge and castrates it, it is permitted. But if the Jew engages in some trickery so that the non-Jew will take it and castrate it, he is penalized by not being allowed to use it, because the prohibition is evident to everyone. He must sell it to another Jew. He can even sell it to his adult son, as they were not so stringent in this matter. However, selling it to his minor son, the Rambam forbids, as this is considered as though he is keeping it for himself, while the Tur permits it. There is no prohibition of benefit, because since the Torah forbids it for the altar, it implies it is permitted for ordinary use. Even if he did not engage in trickery but the non-Jew knows him and intended to benefit him, he also should not use it and should sell it to another as mentioned. If the Jew transgressed and castrated, or told the non-Jew to castrate, there are opinions that it becomes a complete prohibition and it is forbidden to eat from it. This does not seem to be the case from the Talmud, and also the poskim who are stringent about "it and its offspring" not eating the second one only apply it for that day as mentioned in Yoreh De'ah 16, and even this is merely a stringency and most poskim do not hold this way. (And what is mentioned by the Beit Shmuel in Siman 99 is not relevant here, as there it increases the permissibility over the prohibition and turns a prohibition into a permission).

There is a doubt whether it is permissible to indirectly cause castration, for since it is written regarding castration, "You shall not do," and in every place where it says "You shall not do," it is the direct action that is forbidden, but indirect causation is permitted [Shabbat 120b]. Or it might be that just as indirect causation is forbidden on Shabbat because a person is anxious about their property [ibid.] and will come to do it directly, so too it is with castration. And know that there is only a prohibition of castration and not because of causing pain to living creatures, for all the needs of a person do not fall under the prohibition of causing pain to living creatures. Therefore, if something is needed for healing or for another necessary matter, there is no prohibition of causing pain to living creatures. Therefore, it is permissible to pluck feathers from live geese, but nevertheless, people refrain from doing so because it is cruel and it is not proper for the descendants of Abraham to act in such a manner, and one who does so acknowledges his own negative traits.

Three women are forbidden to all priests: a divorced woman, a harlot, and a profaned woman, as it is written: "They shall not take a harlot or a profaned woman, neither shall they take a woman divorced from her husband." In addition to these, the High Priest is also forbidden to marry a widow and is only permitted to marry a virgin, as it is stated: "And the High Priest among his brethren... he shall take a wife in her virginity. A widow, or a divorced woman, or a harlot, or a profaned woman, these he shall not take; but he shall take a virgin of his own people to wife, and he shall not profane his seed among his people, for I am the Lord who sanctifies him."

This applies equally to a High Priest anointed with the anointing oil, or one who wears the multiple garments but was not anointed with the anointing oil from the time it was hidden away in the days of Josiah and onward. It also applies to a priest who serves, as well as to a High Priest who was appointed and then removed from his position, such as if the High Priest became impure on Yom Kippur and another was appointed in his place, and then the first one returns to his service and the second one steps down.

It appears to me that when the second priest is removed from his position and it is said to him that he is being dismissed from his priesthood, his status reverts to that of an ordinary priest, as a High Priest is appointed by word and dismissed by word. Similarly, a priest anointed for war is commanded to marry a virgin and is forbidden to marry a widow.

Any Kohen who transgresses with one of the women prohibited to Kohanim – he renders her disqualified and she becomes disqualified from the moment he engages in intercourse with her, even if he does not complete the act. If he completes the act and a child is born – the child is disqualified; if it is a male, he is not a Kohen at all, and if it is a female, she is forbidden to marry a Kohen. Know that although the prohibition "he shall not desecrate" is written only regarding the High Priest, nonetheless, we have learned this also applies to a regular Kohen (Kiddushin 77a), and we derive it from the fact that the Torah reiterates the prohibitions regarding the High Priest, which is superfluous, and it is a fortiori from a regular Kohen. The Torah did not need to write this except to add the prohibition of a widow to the High Priest, but to teach us that just as there, his offspring are disqualified, so too here, his offspring are disqualified. And from where do we derive that she herself becomes disqualified through his intercourse? From the fact that it is written "he shall not desecrate" and not "he shall not desecrate his offspring," which implies two desecrations – one for her and one for his offspring.

According to the Rambam, one is only liable for lashes if he betroths and has intercourse, but if he betroths without intercourse or has intercourse illicitly without betrothal, he is not liable for lashes, as it is stated "they shall not take" – implying it must be in the manner of taking (i.e., betrothal). Without intercourse, it is obvious he is not liable for lashes because he has not rendered her profane. Except for a High Priest with a widow – he is liable for lashes even with intercourse without betrothal, since he has rendered her profane with his intercourse and thereby forbidden her to a priest. This is unlike a divorcee, a zonah, or a chalalah, who are already profane to the priesthood before his intercourse, hence he has not rendered her profane with his intercourse, and therefore he is not liable for lashes without betrothal. He follows his reasoning, as we wrote at the beginning of section 4, that for all negative commandments one is only liable with betrothal and intercourse. Many disagree with him on this, arguing that for all cases, if he has intercourse without betrothal, he is liable for lashes just as a High Priest with a widow. And some say that a High Priest is liable for all cases if he has intercourse without betrothal, but not an ordinary priest. For what we learn about rendering profane for an ordinary priest from a High Priest is regarding his offspring being profane, but not to be liable for lashes for the prohibition of "he shall not profane" <small>[Hilchot Ishut 17]</small>. However, most of our Rabbis agree that for all cases one is liable for lashes for the prohibition of "he shall not profane," but if he betrothed and did not have intercourse – according to all the authorities, there are no lashes, since "taking" is only due to rendering profane <small>[ibid]</small>.

The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote: If a High Priest betroths a widow and has relations with her, he receives two lashes: one for "He shall not take a widow" and one for "He shall not desecrate." This is the end of his words. And in the Gemara, it is explained that when he completes the act of intercourse, he receives three lashes—also for "He shall not desecrate his offspring." However, the Rambam, of blessed memory, held that this is not according to the conclusion, for how can one receive two lashes for one prohibition? And the desecration of his offspring only applies when a child is born, according to the Maggid Mishneh. All the poskim agree that for all those disqualified from the priesthood, the law is the same: if he betroths and has relations, he receives two or three lashes upon completing the intercourse; and for intercourse without betrothal, he receives one lash for "He shall not desecrate his offspring," but for her desecration, he does not receive lashes, for she is already desecrated and stands as such, as I have written. And some say that for other priesthood disqualifications, he does not receive lashes for intercourse alone if he did not complete the act, according to the Raavad, and this seems logical, as seen in Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, Prohibition 125. And a priest who has relations with a gentile woman or a maidservant receives lashes for her being a harlot, and betrothal does not apply to them, for betrothal does not take effect with them. And if he has relations with a convert or a freed maidservant without betrothal, he does not receive lashes according to the Rambam, but according to those who disagree with him, he receives lashes for her being a harlot. However, some say that although they are forbidden to a priest as a harlot, nevertheless, their status is not entirely like that of a harlot, as written in section 5, paragraph 6, see there, and I believe that this is the opinion of the Raavad in chapter 18, halacha 3. And know that there is no distinction in these prohibitions between him and her, and in any case where he receives lashes, she also receives lashes, whether in priesthood prohibitions or community disqualifications, as there is no difference between a man and a woman, except in the case of a designated maidservant, where the Torah decreed that she receives lashes and he is liable to bring a sacrifice even if intentional. And similarly, with a gentile woman and a maidservant, lashes do not apply to them, and only he receives lashes, as I have written.

It is well known that one prohibition does not take effect upon another prohibition, unless the two prohibitions come simultaneously. Or even if the second prohibition comes afterward and is more severe than the first. Or even if it is not more severe but it is an inclusive prohibition, where the latter prohibition includes more items that are not forbidden by the first prohibition. Or an additional prohibition, where the second prohibition adds a prohibition on the item that was not included in the first prohibition, and this can occur in two ways: either the prohibition is added to the item itself, such as a divorced woman who becomes a chalalah (a woman of disqualified status), who was initially prohibited to a kohen but permitted to consume terumah if she is the daughter of a kohen, but when the prohibition of chalalah is added, she becomes prohibited from consuming terumah; or the prohibition is added regarding others, such as a widow who becomes divorced, who was initially prohibited to a Kohen Gadol (high priest), and when the prohibition of divorce is added, she becomes prohibited to a regular kohen as well. Therefore, a woman who was first a widow, then becomes divorced, then becomes a chalalah, and then a zonah (a woman who had prohibited relations), and afterward a Kohen Gadol has relations with her, he receives four sets of lashes. Similarly, a regular kohen who has relations with a divorced woman who then becomes a chalalah and afterward a zonah receives three sets of lashes, provided that the prohibitions occurred in this order, where each prohibition adds something, as we explained. But if the order is changed, such as if she was first a zonah and then divorced, he does not receive lashes for the divorce, as there is no additional prohibition, and likewise in all similar cases. 

And know that what we said, that a zonah on a chalalah is considered an additional prohibition, even though no additional prohibition is added, since even as a chalalah she is prohibited from terumah, nonetheless, this is called an additional prohibition because the title of zonah is more severe as she is prohibited to an Israelite, such as if a man's wife committed adultery willingly, she becomes forbidden to her husband. Therefore, even though this zonah is not prohibited to an Israelite, the title of zonah is still more severe than chalalah because there is a zonah who is also prohibited to an Israelite. And it seems to me that this is not truly an additional prohibition but rather a more severe prohibition. However, a widow who was widowed from several men only receives one set of lashes, and we do not say that she should receive multiple sets of lashes because she is the widow of Reuven, the widow of Shimon, and the widow of Levi, for in the end, she only has the status of a widow, and it is one entity and one prohibition, and there is neither an inclusive nor an additional prohibition. But if the Kohen Gadol has relations with two widows, even if they are from the same man, he receives two sets of lashes, as they are separate entities, and there is no distinction between a widow from marriage and a widow from betrothal.

The woman who has performed chalitzah is forbidden to marry a kohen by rabbinic decree because she is similar to a divorcee, and if a kohen marries her, he is punished with lashes of rebellion, and the child born from her is considered a challal by rabbinic decree. If he marries a woman who is in doubt whether she performed chalitzah, we do not require him to divorce her since this prohibition is rabbinic. She is permitted, and her child is legitimate because the sages did not decree on a doubtful case of chalitzah. It is impossible to say that his offspring would be disqualified, because if so, we would force him to divorce her to prevent an increase of disqualified offspring in Israel. The Tur wrote in Siman 7 that she and her child are doubtful challalim, and Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote likewise, which is perplexing. Some wanted to differentiate between promiscuity and marriage, stating that only in promiscuity are they doubtful challalim (Beit Chadash), but this is not logical (Maggid Mishneh). Furthermore, in Yoreh De'ah Siman 373, it is evident from the Tur himself that he agrees with the Rambam, as he wrote there that the child born from a doubtful chalutzah is considered a complete kohen. Therefore, the main ruling follows what I have written, and an error fell into the Tur's books (where it was written 'safek chalalah' and the printer mistakenly changed it to 'chalutzah').

But in the case of a doubtful divorcée, a doubtful zonah and chalalah, or a doubtful widow to a High Priest, the Rambam ruled that we administer rabbinic lashes and compel him to divorce her, and the children are doubtful chalalim and are given the stringencies of both kohanim and Israelites. It appears to me that according to the Rambam, who holds that a doubtful Torah prohibition is lenient by Torah law and stringent only by rabbinic decree, the children are doubtful by rabbinic decree. However, according to the Rashba who holds that a doubtful Torah prohibition is stringent by Torah law, they are doubtful by Torah law. The practical difference is when these doubtful individuals perform the redemption of the firstborn; according to the Rambam, they are exempt from redeeming again, while according to the Rashba, they are obligated. Nevertheless, regarding service in the Temple, there is no practical difference, because initially, in any case, they are not permitted to serve, and after the fact, even a definite chalal does not disqualify the service, as the Rambam wrote in Chapter 6 of "Entering the Sanctuary."

A High Priest (Kohen Gadol) is forbidden to marry a non-virgin, as it is stated "a virgin" – and not a non-virgin. If he marries her, we force him to divorce her, but he does not receive lashes because it is a negative commandment derived from a positive commandment. Even if he had intercourse with her and her virginity was not yet removed, since the intercourse was such that could have removed her virginity, she is considered a non-virgin. If he had intercourse with her in an unnatural manner, she is also disqualified for the High Priest.

It is clear that children born from a non-virgin married to a High Priest are considered disqualified (chalalim) because there can be disqualification from a positive commandment. Likewise, he should not marry a minor or an adult woman initially, as it is stated: "He shall take a wife in her virginity" – "a wife" and not a minor, "in her virginity" and not an adult woman whose virginity has diminished, but rather a young woman. If he marries her, he does not have to divorce her because she will eventually become an adult while married to him.

Similarly, he should not marry a woman who lost her virginity due to an accident, but if he marries her, they remain married. If he betroths a non-virgin or a widow and then becomes the High Priest, he can marry her since he betrothed her permissibly. However, if he raped or seduced a young woman and then becomes the High Priest, he is forbidden to marry her because he did not betroth her. Nevertheless, if she bore him a child, the child is not disqualified, but if it was another man's rape or seduction, the child is disqualified.

If a widow from marriage falls before him for levirate marriage, he is forbidden to perform levirate marriage but should perform chalitzah because a positive commandment does not override a positive and negative commandment. If she is a widow from betrothal and is not yet a non-virgin and there is only a negative commandment from the Torah, he may perform levirate marriage and have initial intercourse, as the positive commandment overrides the negative commandment. However, the Sages decreed against initial intercourse due to subsequent intercourse.

It seems to me that if one performs levirate marriage with a widow from betrothal and she becomes pregnant and gives birth, the child is not disqualified by rabbinic law and is not similar to a chalutzah. After all, he performed a mitzvah. The same law applies to a divorced woman for a regular priest. If a widow falls for levirate marriage before a regular priest and he performs ma'amar but does not have intercourse until he becomes the High Priest, he is forbidden to marry her, as she is not similar to a betrothed woman. Even with a betrothed minor who becomes an adult under his betrothal before marriage, he should not marry her, as she is not similar to a widow since her body has changed. Nevertheless, if he marries her, he does not have to divorce her because she will eventually become an adult under his marriage.

Know that the Rambam wrote that it is forbidden for the High Priest to marry two women, but they disagreed with him on this, saying that this is only regarding the Yom Kippur service where it is stated "and atone for himself and for his household" – one household and not two women. But for the rest of the year, where is it stated that it is forbidden for him to have two wives? They brought proof from a verse in Chronicles that states, "Jehoiada took two women" – and he was the High Priest. They answered for the Rambam that he married the second one after the first one's death. Some say that it does not refer to Jehoiada but to King Joash, whom Jehoiada took two women for, as he guided him, as explained in the verse. All the matters in that section refer to Joash, and there is proof from the fact that this verse is not written in Kings, indicating that it refers to Joash, as the book of Chronicles elaborates on the matters of the Davidic kingdom.

There is no difference with a divorced woman whether from betrothal or from marriage, and even the mere scent of a divorce disqualifies her from the priesthood. And what is the "scent of a divorce"? For example, if he said to her, "You are hereby divorced from me but not permitted to any other man," even though such a divorce does not permit her to remarry, nevertheless, she is disqualified from the priesthood by Torah law, as it is written, "And a divorced woman from her husband they shall not take" (Leviticus 21:7), and the interpretation is that even if she is only divorced from her husband and not permitted to another, she is disqualified from the priesthood. We force him to divorce her, and the child is a chalal (disqualified from the priesthood). According to Maimonides in Chapter 10 of Hilchot Gerushin, this is a rabbinic decree, but nevertheless, we force him to divorce her as with all rabbinic prohibitions, and the child is a chalal by rabbinic decree. However, if he gave her a conditional divorce and the condition was not fulfilled, it is nothing and does not disqualify her. Even a priest himself is allowed to initially give a conditional divorce, and if the condition is not fulfilled, there is no divorce, and he may remain with her, as stated in Siman 145. There is not even a hint of a divorce here, for everyone knows that if the condition is not fulfilled, it is not a divorce at all.

An orphaned minor who was married off by her mother and brothers, and who can leave the marriage without a get (divorce document) merely by refusing and saying "I do not want him" - as the Sages ordained, as mentioned in Siman 155 - if she leaves through refusal, she is permitted to marry a Kohen, as this is not even similar to the scent of a get. However, if the husband gives her a get, she is prohibited to a Kohen. And even though it is not like a get since she does not need a get, nonetheless, it somewhat resembles a proper get, and the Sages prohibited her from marrying a Kohen. Therefore, if the husband who divorced her remarries her and she leaves him the second time through refusal, the refusal nullifies the previous get, and she is permitted to marry a Kohen. This is specifically when the same husband remarries her and she refuses him, but if after the get she marries another man and then refuses him, we do not say that the refusal of the latter nullifies the get of the first. This is the ruling of the Rambam, of blessed memory. And the proof for this is that she is prohibited to return to the first husband, just like a divorced woman who marries another man is prohibited to return to her first husband, as mentioned there, which implies that the get still applies. The Tur permits her to marry a Kohen, and the reason she is prohibited to the first husband has a different rationale, as mentioned there. And since there is a dispute among the poskim (halachic authorities) and it is a rabbinic prohibition, if a Kohen marries her, we do not require him to divorce her.

We hold that in matters of betrothal and divorce, we are concerned about a rumor when the rumor has been established in a court, and the details of these laws will be explained in Siman 46. We hold that for a rumor that comes after marriage or after betrothal, we are not concerned, whether the rumor pertains to an act after the marriage or to an act before it—we are not concerned about it, for we do not remove a woman from her husband based on a mere rumor. Therefore, if a rumor spreads that a certain Kohen divorced his wife and she is still living with him and serving him, we do not remove her, for it is a rumor that came after the marriage. However, if he dies and she marries another Kohen, she must be removed, for to this second Kohen, it is a rumor that existed before their marriage. We are not concerned about casting aspersions on the children of the first husband by forcing the second husband to divorce her, for on the contrary, people will say that since she was removed from the second husband and not from the first, it is evident that he divorced her close to his death, and there is no aspersion on the children.

And if a rumor spreads that a certain Kohen (priest) wrote a get (divorce document) for his wife, we assess: if in that city they do not call the giving of the get "writing" – then there is no substance to that rumor, because writing alone is nothing. But if they do call the giving "writing" – even though they also call writing alone "writing" – nevertheless, we are concerned about the rumor to prohibit her to a second Kohen after the death of the first, as mentioned. The reason we are stringent in this case is because certainly the rumor did not arise for no reason; rather, it is to express astonishment at the Kohen remaining with her. If their intention was only about the writing itself, there would be no astonishment. Therefore, their intention is certainly about the giving of the get. However, in a place where they do not call the giving "writing" – one cannot say that their intention is about the giving. The Rambam, of blessed memory, did not differentiate in this matter between whether they call the giving "writing" or not, but simply wrote that she must leave the second husband. The primary ruling follows the first opinion. And if a rumor spreads about an Israelite who divorced his wife and then died, and she married a Kohen – she must also leave the Kohen.

If a rumor spreads about an unmarried woman that she got betrothed and divorced, if both rumors emerged simultaneously, she is forbidden to the one to whom the rumor about the betrothal concerned if he is a kohen. However, if initially the rumor emerged that she got betrothed to this kohen, and after some time, a rumor emerged that he divorced her, we do not remove her from this kohen, as it is considered a rumor following betrothal, and when he dies, she is forbidden to another kohen. If a rumor spreads about an Israelite who betrothed a woman, divorced her, and then died, she is forbidden to any kohen in any case. More on this will be explained in Siman 46 regarding whether an Israelite is forbidden due to a rumor of betrothal.

Any rumor that comes with an explanation that breaks the rumor – we do not worry about the rumor, since it is a rumor with its refutation. Therefore, if a rumor emerges that there was a condition in the divorce, or that the get (divorce document) was thrown to her, but it is uncertain if it was closer to him or closer to her, and similar cases – we do not worry about the rumor. Furthermore, even if a rumor emerges that she was betrothed and divorced, and there is an explanation concerning the betrothal – she is still permitted to marry a Kohen, since without betrothal, there is no divorce. However, if there is an explanation concerning the divorce but not the betrothal – we worry about the rumor of the betrothal to forbid her to everyone, but we do not worry about the rumor of the divorce to forbid her to a Kohen after the death of her husband. This applies specifically when the explanation comes out immediately after the rumor; but if a clear rumor emerges and only later an explanation emerges – the clear rumor is not nullified by the later explanation, unless it is clarified in a court that the previous rumor is false. In such a case, even without an explanation, we nullify the rumor, as any rumor that is not upheld in court is not considered a rumor. Since it was later clarified in court that the rumor was false, we publicize it and nullify the rumor.

This that we have written, that with any rumor of betrothal or divorce, and an explanation emerges about the betrothal, she is permitted to marry a kohen because if there is no betrothal, there is no divorce—this is when the holding of the get (divorce document) was also only based on a rumor. But if he indeed divorced her, even if he divorced her only because of the rumor about the betrothal, and even if it becomes clear that the rumor was false, nonetheless, since ultimately she has the status of a definite divorcee, even though the get was only due to stringency, she is still disqualified from marrying a kohen. [This is the intention of the Choshen Mishpat in subparagraph 6, and according to the second explanation of the Beit Shmuel at the end of subparagraph 11], and see what I wrote in paragraph 18.

Rambam wrote: If there is a rumor about a woman that she has performed chalitzah [the ceremony for releasing a widow from levirate marriage], we do not take it into account. These are his words. Because a chalutzah (a woman who has performed chalitzah) marrying a Kohen (priest) is only a rabbinic prohibition, we do not concern ourselves with the rumor. There are those who disagree and prohibit her to a Kohen [Raavad]. And it appears to me that even according to this opinion, if she has married, she does not have to be divorced, because this is no worse than a case of doubt regarding chalitzah. The great later authorities agreed with the opinion of the Rambam, and this also seems to be the opinion of our teacher, the Rema, in paragraph 5, see there. Similarly, a chalutzah who did not need to perform chalitzah – her chalitzah does not invalidate her.

He also wrote: If there is a rumor about a virgin that she is no longer a virgin, we are not concerned about it, and she may marry a High Priest. If there is a rumor about her that she is a maidservant, we are not concerned about it, and she may marry even a priest. If there is a rumor in the city that she is promiscuous, we are not concerned about it. Even if her husband divorced her because she violated Jewish law or there were witnesses to an inappropriate behavior and he died before giving her the divorce, she is still permitted to marry a priest. We only prohibit a woman in these cases with clear testimony or her own admission. Thus concludes his words.

And Maimonides holds that we are only concerned with the rumor of betrothal and divorce when the prohibition is clear, but with a rumor of promiscuity, the prohibition is not clear, as they merely saw her behaving immodestly, and it is common for people to call an immodest woman a harlot. Similarly, for one who violates Jewish law or there were witnesses to an inappropriate behavior, it is still not clear that she committed adultery. And we are not concerned with a rumor of being a maidservant, as we do not disqualify a family based on a rumor. Similarly, we are not concerned with a rumor of her not being a virgin, as we also say that they merely saw her behaving immodestly [Rashi Gittin Chapter 89]. And there are those who dispute all this, but we are not concerned with a rumor of promiscuity for the reason explained [Raavad], and the same applies to a rumor of her not being a virgin [Magid Mishneh].

Some say that what we wrote in paragraph 15, that if he gave her a get (divorce document) even though it was clarified that the rumor of the betrothal was false, she is forbidden to marry a Kohen (priest) – this applies if they were at least engaged, but if there were no words of engagement between them, we do not concern ourselves with the get. Likewise, some say that specifically if she was divorced in a court that required him to divorce her because of the rumor, then she has the status of a divorcee even if the rumor was baseless. But if he stood and divorced her himself in the presence of witnesses because of the rumor of the betrothal and it was clarified that it was false, we do not concern ourselves with the get. And some say that if she married, she should not leave in any case when it is clarified that there was no betrothal at all, but there are those who disagree with this. Know that any Kohen who transgressed and married one of the women prohibited to him – we compel him by all means of coercion until he divorces her, and we forbid anyone to engage in business with him and similar strict measures until he divorces her. And a Kohen who divorced his wife – she should not live with him in the same alley as long as she has not married another. And when she marries another, it will be explained in Siman 119 that the more severe the prohibition, the greater the distance required. And if they were living in the same courtyard by rental or in a jointly owned courtyard – she is displaced because the burden on the man is harder than on the woman, and if the courtyard is hers – he is displaced, and there it will be further explained with the help of Heaven.

Which woman is considered a "zonah" (harlot) according to the Torah, for which a Kohen who has relations with her would receive lashes for being with a "zonah"? According to Rambam in Hilchot Issurei Biah, chapter 18, any woman who is not of Jewish descent, even if she converted or was freed, if she is less than three years and one day old, and likewise a Jewish woman who had relations with a man whom she is forbidden to marry by a prohibition that applies universally, excluding prohibitions specific to the priesthood, like a widow to a High Priest or a divorcee to a regular Kohen – she does not become a "zonah," for from priestly prohibitions, she becomes a "chalalah" (disqualified priest's daughter) and not a "zonah." However, with a universal prohibition, like those liable for karet (excision), or even those liable for negative commandments, such as having relations with a mamzer (illegitimate child) or a Natin (descendant of Gibeonites), or even those liable for positive commandments, like a convert from Egypt or Edom – when she has relations with him, she becomes a "zonah." Similarly, a woman who has relations with a man who has crushed testicles or a severed member becomes a "zonah" and is forbidden to the priesthood, and a Kohen who has relations with her receives lashes for being with a "zonah." If she was a priest's daughter, she is disqualified from eating terumah (priestly food).
