Rambam provides a general rule: a woman who has relations with a man whom she is forbidden to marry by a prohibition that applies universally, excluding priestly prohibitions because they do not apply universally as stated, and excluding a woman who has bestiality relations, even though it is punishable by stoning – she does not become a "zonah" because she did not have relations with a man. Similarly, a man who has relations with a menstruant woman (niddah), even though it incurs karet – she does not become a "zonah" because she is not forbidden to marry him. Similarly, a man who has relations with a prostitute (kedeshah), even though according to his opinion, it incurs lashes, nevertheless, since she is not forbidden to marry him – she does not become a "zonah." And in all these cases where she does not become a "zonah" – she is not disqualified from the priesthood, as according to his opinion, disqualification from the priesthood is tied to being a "zonah" or a "chalalah," and only from priestly prohibitions does she become a "chalalah," and from other prohibitions, she becomes a "zonah." The only exception to this rule is a woman who has relations with a "chalal" (disqualified priest's son) – even though she is permitted to marry him – nevertheless, she becomes a "zonah" because it is written, "He shall not profane his seed among his people," and we expound – just as he disqualifies a widow by his relations, so too his seed, who are "chalalim," disqualify any woman by their relations from terumah and the priesthood, and since they disqualify her from the priesthood, she automatically becomes a "zonah," as stated. Several of our Rabbis agree with Rambam's opinion: Rashi, Nimukei Yosef, the Ra'avad, and the Rashba.

However, our Rabbis, the Ba'alei HaTosafot [Yevamot 61a], the Ra'avad, the Rosh, and the Tur, disagree with the first opinion that holds that a zonah (a woman disqualified from marrying a kohen) is any woman who has relations with anyone prohibited by a negative commandment or a positive commandment. They assert that only those women who have relations with individuals punishable by karet (excision) are classified as a zonah. The general rule, according to them, is that a zonah is any woman who cannot be betrothed due to the prohibition, such as one who engages in relations with an ervah (a forbidden relative), thus becoming a zonah. However, one who has relations with someone prohibited by a negative or positive commandment, while she becomes disqualified from terumah (priestly offerings) and from marrying a kohen, does not become a zonah. Similarly, a woman who has relations with a chalal (a man disqualified from the priesthood) is disqualified from priestly offerings and marrying a kohen, but does not become a zonah, as this opinion holds that these are not interconnected.

The first opinion believes that from whatever name she is disqualified to marry a kohen, it must be due to her being a chalalah (a woman rendered unfit to marry a kohen) because there is no chalalah except from the prohibitions specific to kohanim, and necessarily she is also a zonah. However, this opinion holds that it is a separate prohibition. The primary verse concerns terumah, as it is written: "And if a priest's daughter becomes married to a non-priest, she may not eat of the sacred offerings" (Leviticus 22:12). From this, we learn that if she marries a non-priest, she may not eat of the terumah. We derive from another verse, "and she returns to her father's house" (Leviticus 22:13), that if she has relations with someone who disqualifies her, she is disqualified from terumah. The prohibition for a kohen is derived from a kal vachomer (a fortiori) from a divorced woman who is permitted to eat terumah but prohibited to a kohen. If she who is disqualified from terumah is certainly disqualified from marrying a kohen, then one who is disqualified from terumah is even more so disqualified from marrying a kohen. It is possible that there is no flogging for this negative commandment at all [see there, and in Sanhedrin 76b, and investigate further]. According to the first opinion, one is flogged for the prohibition of zonah.

There is another practical difference between these two opinions: according to the first opinion, since she is a zonah, the child born from her is disqualified from the priesthood [see there 44b], while according to this opinion, the child is not disqualified [see the Gra], and this requires further study.

According to all opinions, a yevama (a widow awaiting levirate marriage) who has relations with another man becomes a zonah (a woman prohibited to a kohen), since kiddushin (marriage) does not take effect with her, as it is written: "She shall not be the wife of the deceased to a stranger" – meaning, there shall be no legal status of marriage for her, and kiddushin does not take effect. Conversely, if a man has relations with his divorced wife after she has married another, even though it is a universally prohibited act, she does not become a zonah. According to the last opinion, she is not disqualified from eating terumah if she is a kohen’s daughter, since this disqualification is derived from the verse "And if a kohen's daughter becomes [married] to a stranger," and he is not a stranger to her originally. Similarly, an aylonit (a woman who is congenitally infertile) is permitted to marry a kohen and does not become a zonah, for we do not say that since she cannot bear children, the relations are considered promiscuous, as long as it was done in a marital context and permissibly, it is not considered promiscuity. Likewise, one who has relations with one of the secondary relatives forbidden by rabbinic decree, such as his chalutza (a woman released from levirate marriage) or a close relative of his chalutza, does not make her a zonah, since by Torah law she is permitted to him. Although we are stringent regarding lineage of kohanim even with rabbinic prohibitions, the prohibitions of kohanim are distinct, similar to the stringencies applied to kohanic lineage. There are also those who are uncertain about a yevama to the marketplace.

From here you learn that becoming a "zonah" (a woman forbidden to a priest) is not dependent on an act of forbidden intercourse, for one who has relations with a menstruant woman or one who has intercourse with an animal does not become a "zonah." And a woman married to a "chalal" (a man of priestly descent who is disqualified from the priesthood) has a permissible act of intercourse and yet becomes a "zonah" according to the Rambam. However, those who disagree with him still consider her disqualified for a priest, and it depends only on the defect according to the tradition we received from Moses at Sinai, according to the opinions that have been clarified. 

And a convert or a freed maidservant, even if she is less than three years and one day old—according to the Rambam and the Rosh, she is a "zonah" by Torah law even if she has not had intercourse, because they come from people steeped in licentiousness. And even though we learned from the verse in Ezekiel as mentioned in Siman 5, Paragraph 6, nevertheless they hold that by Torah law they are forbidden to a priest, and Ezekiel came and based it on a verse, as with many laws that Ezekiel derived, though they are from the Torah (Zevachim 18b). 

The Raavad and the Rashba hold that their prohibition is not by Torah law (Hilchot Issurei Biah 19:3). And the opinion of Rashi, of blessed memory, seems to me that when she is more than three years and one day old, her prohibition is by Torah law, and less than that is by rabbinic decree (see Rashi there 61a, s.v. ela, and in Kiddushin 78a, s.v. Rabbi Shimon, and according to what I wrote, it fits well that in Yevamot his intention is for one fit for intercourse and in Kiddushin his intention is that Rabbi Shimon permits until she becomes invalid by Torah law, and study carefully). (See Beit Shmuel, subsection 20, and the words of the Chelkat Mechokek, subsection 10, which are misprinted).

Any woman who has sexual relations with a man, making her a zonah (harlot) — whether it was coerced or consensual, whether it was accidental or intentional, whether it was in the usual manner or not in the usual manner — from the moment he has intercourse with her, she is disqualified due to being a zonah. This applies as long as she is at least three years and one day old, and the man is at least nine years and one day old, as this is the age at which they are capable of sexual relations. Some of our rabbis hold that if it was coerced, she does not become a zonah [Raavad and Rashba]. Nevertheless, she is disqualified from marrying a Kohen and is disqualified from eating Terumah, but she is not liable for lashes for being a zonah [Gra]. 

There are those who want to say that if she entered the chuppah (bridal canopy) but was not consummated, she is also considered a zonah as if she had intercourse — but this is not so. Although in all other respects we consider entering the chuppah as being fully married, regarding a zonah, which depends on a defect as the Rambam wrote [Hilchot Isurei Biah 18:4], there is no defect without intercourse. The proof is that the Rambam's position in all cases of forbidden relationships is that one does not receive lashes without both betrothal and intercourse. He explicitly wrote this in Hilchot Ishut 17. 

What constitutes a chalalah (disqualified woman) will be explained in Siman 7, with God's help. Be aware that a boy nine years old who disqualifies with his intercourse, if there is a doubt whether he is nine years old or not, we go stringently as in all cases of doubt. This is explicitly stated in the Gemara [Yevamot 68a], and the Rambam wrote similarly in Hilchot Terumot Chapter 5 [see Beit Meir].

Therefore, a woman who has had relations with another man – whether by force or willingly – is disqualified from marrying a priest (Kohen) and from partaking in Terumah. However, for her husband, if he is an Israelite, she is not forbidden if it was by force, as it is stated: "and she was not seized" – implying that if she was seized, she is permitted. But a priest's wife who was violated – is forbidden to her husband. And coercion is defined as any initial act of intercourse that was forced, even if later she consented, it is still called coercion (Ketubot 51b), because this too is considered coercion since at the beginning of the intercourse, the man imposed his desire on her (Rashi), and thus the beginning was forced without the desire of lust. And see what is written in Siman 7, Seif 1 regarding what constitutes coercion.

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote: If the wife of a kohen (priest) was raped, her husband receives lashes because of impurity, as it is stated: "Her first husband, who sent her away, may not marry her again after she has been defiled" (Deuteronomy 24:4). This includes all women who, if they had relations, are forbidden to return to their husbands. The Torah specifically exempts the wife of an Israelite who was raped, as it is stated: "But if she was not forced" (Deuteronomy 22:26), indicating that she is permitted to return to her husband. However, the wife of a kohen remains forbidden because she is considered a zonah (harlot). End of quote. 

His words are puzzling, as he begins with impurity and ends with zonah. In the Gemara (Yevamot 26b), there are two versions: According to the first version, the husband receives lashes for impurity and for zonah; according to another version, he receives lashes for impurity but not for zonah. Moreover, Maimonides himself ruled in the first chapter of the laws of forbidden relations, halacha 22, that the husband receives lashes for zonah. This requires further examination.

It seems to me that the explanation of his words is as follows: Regarding the prohibition of impurity, a kohen and an Israelite are equal. For if she willingly committed adultery, she is forbidden to both her Israelite and kohen husbands due to impurity. Since in the case of rape, there is no impurity, how can impurity apply to a kohen? They are equal regarding the prohibition of impurity. Therefore, it is certain that the prohibition is based on the verse concerning impurity, as mentioned. However, the nature of the prohibition is due to zonah, as even in the case of rape, she is called a zonah, as stated in section 23. 

Nevertheless, the verse regarding zonah does not explicitly state that even in the case of rape, she is called a zonah. In the case of impurity, the Torah clarifies that for a kohen, she is forbidden even in the case of rape and remains in the prohibition of zonah, which applies only to a kohen and not to an Israelite. 

[And he ruled according to the second version as is his manner throughout the Talmud. And that which is stated there, "thus, in the case of rape she is not called a zonah," is not according to the conclusion and is phrased as a question, concluding that "they were all included in 'after she has been defiled,'" implying that if so, she remains in her prohibition, which is the prohibition of zonah]. [In the discourse, we explained the distinction between the kohen husband and another kohen. Pay close attention].

The wife of a Kohen who tells her husband 'I was raped or one came upon me by mistake' – she is not forbidden to him, for we do not believe her and say that she has set her eyes upon another and is lying to release herself from her husband. And we do not say that she has rendered herself a forbidden entity (hefker), for she does not have the ability to do this as she is obligated to him, and by law, she is not believed [Ran and Nimukei Yosef at the end of Nedarim]. And she is still permitted to eat terumah since this presumption that she has set her eyes upon another is strong, and she did not originally come to forbid herself from terumah but rather to forbid herself to her husband, and it is assumed that she is lying [Ritva there in the laws]. And why should we strain ourselves to permit her to eat terumah? For if she is forbidden to eat terumah, a blemish would be cast upon her children [Gemara]. And Rambam in Chapter 17 of Terumot rules that she is forbidden to eat terumah [like Rava there]. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, Sotah Chapter 1, Halacha 3, it is explained according to the first opinion. And if she is believed by him that she is not lying – he is obligated to divorce her. Similarly, if one witness comes and says 'your wife committed adultery by force or willingly' – he is not believed for matters of sexual immorality require two witnesses. However, if the witness is believed by him – he is obligated to divorce her to avoid doubt, and this will be further elucidated with God's help in Siman 115. And if she says she was raped and one witness testifies in accordance with her statement, it is considered as if there are grounds to the matter and she is forbidden to him if there is no suspicion of collusion, and there it will be explained with God's help.

The Rambam wrote: A wife of a Kohen who tells her husband that she was violated, even though she is permitted to her husband as we have said, she is forbidden to any other Kohen in the world after her husband dies, since she has admitted that she is a zonah and has forbidden herself, becoming like a piece of prohibition. And if she marries, she does not need to be divorced unless this Kohen believes her former words. And her children are not chalalim when she marries, for the Torah gave the father credibility regarding his children and not the mother, for we say that she completely lied then. But if this Kohen believes her former words and must divorce her, it is possible that the children are chalalim. And if she gives an explanation for her former words and says that she lied, intending to release herself from her husband, she may originally marry a Kohen. Some are hesitant about this, but the primary view seems to be the first opinion.

This, that a woman is not believed to prohibit herself to her husband, applies when there are no grounds for suspicion. However, if there are grounds for suspicion, she is believed. The details of this will be clarified in Siman 115. Similarly, a woman whose husband warned her about a certain man and she secluded herself with him, and she did not drink the bitter waters of a Sotah, is forbidden to her husband even if he is an Israelite. If her husband dies, she is forbidden to a Kohen because she is a suspected adulteress, whether she refused to drink, her husband did not want her to drink, or there was testimony preventing her from drinking, or she was among the women who are not eligible to drink according to the laws of Sotah. There is also no difference whether her husband warned her or the court warned her, as sometimes the court must warn her according to the laws mentioned there. In all these cases, since she did not drink the bitter waters during the time of the Temple, or in the present when we do not have the waters, and it was not clarified with witnesses that she is pure, she is presumed to be a suspected adulteress and is forbidden to a Kohen. Her children from a Kohen are doubtful Chalalim (disqualified priests). Know that a husband is believed to say he knows his wife committed adultery and is forbidden to him. Although he is obligated to her as she is to him, and why is he believed and she is not? The reason is simple: he can divorce her against her will and does not need to lie to be rid of her, but she cannot free herself from him without his consent. Even if she says she finds him repulsive, and according to the opinion of the Rambam that we compel him to divorce her, without proof she is not believed. Therefore, we say she is lying and has her eye on another. Accordingly, in our times, when one cannot divorce against the other's will and one cannot marry two women because of Rabbeinu Gershom's decree, it is possible that he also is not believed. This will be clarified in Siman 177 with the help of Heaven.

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote: A Kohen (priest) who betrothed a woman, whether she is an adult or a minor, and after some time had relations with her, and he claimed that he found her to have been defiled by another man, she is prohibited to him out of doubt, as it is uncertain whether she was defiled before or after the betrothal. However, if an Israelite (non-priest) made such a claim, she is not prohibited to him, as there are two uncertainties – whether she was defiled before or after the betrothal, and even if it was after the betrothal, it is uncertain whether it was by force or willingly, as a woman who was coerced is permitted to an Israelite. Therefore, if her father betrothed her to an Israelite and she is less than three years and one day old, and he claimed that he found her to have been defiled by another man, she is prohibited to him out of doubt, as there is only one uncertainty – whether it was by force or willingly, and a doubt concerning a Torah prohibition is ruled stringently. End of quote. And our master the Beit Yosef copied this in section 14.

And even though with a girl less than three years old there is a double doubt (s’feik s’feika) — perhaps it was by force, perhaps it was willingly; and if you say it was willingly, perhaps she engaged in intercourse when she was younger, and the seduction of a minor is considered coercion [Yevamot 33b] — nevertheless, this is not a double doubt because everything is considered coercion, and there is only one doubt here — whether it was by force or willingly [Tosafot Ketubot 9a]. According to this, the prohibition applies only if she was married when she was older, but if she was married when she was younger, she is permitted to marry an Israelite in any case because she is considered coerced. However, the wording of the Rambam does not suggest this, as he follows his opinion in Hilchot Ishut 3:2, where he rules that if one has relations with a minor willingly, she is forbidden to her husband, as mentioned there. Similarly, in Hilchot Sotah 2:4, he writes this, and all the Poskim have already disputed him on this.

From his words there, it is clear that we do not say the seduction of a minor is coercion except when she was betrothed through rabbinic betrothal not by her father. However, in the Gemara in Yevamot, it is explicitly proven that it deals with Torah-level betrothal [Gra]. It seems to me that his words are correct, as it is explicitly proven in the Mishnah there that it deals with a minor who is not fit to bear children, and indeed there are minors who can conceive and survive [there 12b], and so the Rambam writes in Hilchot Ishut 19:14 [see there in Maggid Mishneh and in Hilchot Sotah 9:6]. According to this, the Sages did not say coercion except for minors so young that they are not fit to bear children, and if we knew the age limit, we would say that up to this age their seduction is coercion, and from then on their seduction is considered willingly. But we do not know this limit, and therefore we must be stringent with Torah laws in all doubts of Torah and lenient with rabbinic laws as per the law of s’feik s’feika leniency in rabbinic matters.

Accordingly, the Rambam correctly ruled in those two places that with Torah-level betrothal, she is forbidden to her husband, and with rabbinic betrothal, we are lenient. See what I wrote in Siman 68, Paragraph 8.

And this that is written that he found her as a "drusat ish" (one who had relations with a man) – its explanation is whether he claims "I found an open opening" or whether he claims "I found blood," but if she is a bogeret (mature woman) – he cannot claim "I found an open opening" as it is written in Chapter 11 of Ishut. And there are those among the Geonim who hold the opposite [Tosafot Ketubot 9], and the Rambam rejected their words there, and also the opinion of Rashi [there 36:] is like the Rambam. And this that is written that he came upon her after a time – his intention is that if he came upon her immediately after the kiddushin (betrothal), she is permitted even to a kohen, for an unmarried woman who had relations is not prohibited to a kohen. And similarly, if there are witnesses that after the kiddushin she was not intimate, even if he came upon her after a time – she is permitted even to a kohen [Beit Shmuel]. And the reason we do not always permit her by saying that she certainly was intimate before the kiddushin to maintain her status of being kosher and permissible to her husband, is because we can say the opposite – to maintain her status as a virgin and now she was intimate [there], and the presumption of the body is preferable to other presumptions [Tosafot there 45:]. And even though there is always a double doubt even in the case of a kohen’s wife – a doubt whether it was from a piece of wood or a man’s relations, and if you say it was a man’s relations, perhaps it was before the kiddushin? We can say that a piece of wood is not common [Hagahot Maimoniyot], and furthermore, if she was from a piece of wood, she would have claimed so as it is not a disgrace, and since she did not claim it, it is clear that she is certainly from a man’s relations [Tosafot there 9.].

Some of our rabbis have written that all of this only applies when he contradicts her, for then we say he is believed because he has made her forbidden to him with his words. The same applies if she is silent. However, if she says, "I was violated, and it happened before the betrothal," she is permitted to him because she claims with certainty and he is in doubt; in a case of certainty versus doubt, certainty prevails [R"Y and Ran]. And she has not made herself forbidden in such a case. This is also implied in the Jerusalem Talmud [ibid. 6]. But some of our rabbis disagree with this, and they hold that since there is only one doubt, we do not pay attention to her words [HaMeiri, see also Rosh]. They wrote that this is also the opinion of the Rambam, but I do not see a decisive proof from his words. On the contrary, from what he explained in Chapter 11 of Hilchot Ishut, it appears that he holds this way. Similarly, from what he explains further, it seems that if the majority of the city are fit, and their intercourse does not disqualify for priesthood, she is permitted post facto to a priest and does not have to leave him. Also, if she claims she was injured by wood, she is believed, and most poskim agree with this [ShMaK]. 

This is specifically when he says with certainty that he did not deviate, but otherwise, it is possible he deviated without realizing it [Ran]. The Rambam also wrote this in Chapter 11 of Hilchot Ishut. Some say that without intention, deviation is not common, but we ask him if he might have deviated intentionally, and if he says he did not deviate intentionally, she is forbidden to him [ibid. 10a, not in our texts]. Some say further that this applies only to a married man, but a bachelor is not believed because he is not experienced in this matter, and we punish him for his audacity [ibid.]. It seems this is the opinion of the Rif. However, if it is known that he is a frequenter of prostitutes, he is believed and punished for committing transgressions [Kesef Mishneh there in the Gemara]. If she claims she is still a virgin, witnesses are appointed to seclude with her again, and the matter will be clarified.

And know that what has been explained from our words is that if there was a presumption of permissibility, we would permit her even to a Kohen. And indeed, in other prohibitions when there arises a suspicion, many of the poskim do not rely on the presumption, as stated in Yoreh De'ah section 3. All the more so with genealogical issues, where we are very stringent and do not rely even on a single majority, and even in cases of double doubt, we are stringent as stated regarding the widow of a dough-kneader in section 2, paragraph 19. So how can we permit here based merely on a presumption when she is silent or denies? For in truth, when a disqualification has been clarified for us, it is proper to be stringent rabbinically, and all the more so with genealogical disqualifications. However, here the disqualification of this woman has not been clarified for us, and she denies it or remains silent, and we do not know if he is speaking the truth or merely casting aspersions. Rather, we came to prohibit her because he made her forbidden to him by a definite statement – in such a case, certainly if there is any presumption of permissibility, the definite statement is nullified. Conversely, when she admits and says with certainty that she was previously violated – then her certain claim is strong enough that we even validate her child with her certain claim, even against a majority of disqualified individuals, as stated in section 4, paragraph 30. And this will be further explained in section 68 with God's help.

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote: A single woman who was seen having relations with a man and he left, and they asked her, "Who was the man who was with you?" and she said, "A kosher man" – she is believed. Not only that, but even if she was seen to be pregnant, and they asked her, "From whom did you become pregnant?" and she said, "From a kosher man" – she is believed and is permitted to marry a kohen. In what case is this true? When the place where she had relations was a crossroads or in the corners of the fields where everyone passes by, and the majority of those who pass by there are kosher, and the majority of the city from which these passersby come are kosher, because the sages instituted a higher standard for lineage and required two majorities. But if most of the passersby would disqualify her, like Kutim or mamzerim, or similar, even though the majority of the place they came from are kosher, or if the majority of the people in the place are disqualified even though the majority of the passersby are kosher – we are concerned that she might have had relations with someone who disqualifies her, and she should not marry a kohen initially, but if she did marry, she does not have to leave him. This is the end of the quote. And even though it was explained there that even with a majority of disqualified individuals we validate the child when she claims with certainty – this is to avoid disqualifying the child from the congregation, but she herself who can marry an Israelite – we initially prohibit her from marrying into the priesthood until there are two majorities. And the fact that we validated in section 32 even herself with a certain claim – this is because she was already married, and furthermore, it was not clarified to us that she was disqualified as stated in the previous section. And it is simple that if a pregnant woman says she had relations with a kosher man and she is believed for herself – she is also believed for the child, for if she gives birth to a daughter – she is fit to marry into the priesthood. And all of this is when she says she had relations with a kosher man, but if she did not say this and remained silent – even after the fact she must leave the kohen if there were not two majorities [Beit Shmuel]. And if she claims she had relations with a kosher man – we do not remove her after the fact from the kohen even with a majority of disqualified individuals [Hagahot Maimoniot]. And it can be said that according to Rambam, if she did not say she had relations with a kosher man – we do not permit her to marry a kohen initially even with two majorities [Beit Yosef], for not claiming is not better with two majorities than claiming with one majority.

And there are among our rabbis those who hold that in the case of a definite claim that she was intimate with a kosher (permissible) man, she is permitted to marry into the priesthood even with a single majority. And if she does not make such a claim, whether initially or after the fact, she requires two majorities, and if not – she must leave [her husband] [Ramban, Rashba, Ran]. And there are those who say that even if she does not claim that she was intimate with a kosher man, she is permitted initially even with a single majority [HaMaor at the end of the first chapter of Ketubot holds that the entire sugiya follows Rabbi Yehuda and not Rabbi Gamliel]. This is a singular opinion, and we do not follow it.

And the reason we require two majorities ideally and not one majority – this is when there is at least a minority of invalids, but when there is no minority of invalids – we do not require two majorities. Therefore, in a city that is entirely Jewish or where the Jews have their own separate neighborhood – it is considered like an independent city, and we do not require two majorities. Similarly, if it is known that she committed adultery with a valid person but there is a concern that she might have also committed adultery with an invalid person – we also permit her ideally with one majority. And all this is if she willingly had relations, but if she was raped – her assertion does not help at all, because the reason her assertion helps is that we say a woman who commits adultery checks and commits adultery in a way that does not disqualify herself, as stated in Siman 4, Se'if 31, see there. But in the case of rape, checking does not apply, and therefore if it is known that she was raped, even two majorities do not help ideally. This is according to the opinion at the end of Se'if 34 that without her assertion, we do not permit her ideally even with two majorities, because according to the other opinions, we do not need her assertion with two majorities. However, if we do not know that she was raped, but she says she was raped – we permit her with her assertion ideally with two majorities, because if she wanted, she could have said she was not raped and willingly had relations. And all this is for herself, but regarding the child not being disqualified from the congregation – it helps in any case, as stated there in Siman 4. And when we permit the child to the congregation – we also permit him to the priesthood, as it is impossible to differentiate between them. Only if she is divorced – then it applies to the child ideally and post facto, because perhaps a priest had relations with her and the child is a chalal (disqualified priestly offspring). And although regarding herself there is no post facto since she is already disqualified from the priesthood, nevertheless regarding the child there is a distinction, and furthermore, for terumah (priestly tithes) there is a practical difference also regarding herself.

The rule that two majorities are effective initially – this applies when she had relations in a place where people move around and do not stay in one place. But if she had relations in the city, even if we knew that the one who had relations with her went to her, and we would say "whoever separates, separates from the majority," perhaps she went to him instead, and in any fixed situation, it is considered as half and half. Therefore, even if in the city everyone is fit except for one who is found to be disqualified – a Samaritan, a defiled priest, a mamzer, or a slave – she should not marry a priest initially in any case. However, if she already married, she does not need to divorce if she says she had relations with a fit person, because even in a majority of disqualified individuals, we validate post factum. Therefore, in a case where she does not say she had relations with a fit person and says she does not know if he was fit or disqualified, or if she was mute or deaf and we cannot rely on her gestures to distinguish between fit and disqualified – she is considered a questionable zonah. If she marries a priest, she must divorce, and her children are of questionable defiled status. Two majorities do not help at all unless the intercourse took place at a crossroads and not in the city. The Tur ruled that even in the city, we are not stringent with two majorities unless it is known that she went to the one who had relations with her. But if it is not known who went to whom, we permit her with two majorities even if she does not say she had relations with a fit person, and we assume that the one who had relations went to her. If it is known that the one who had relations went to her, even the Rambam agrees with this. And if we see that she became pregnant, and there are two majorities in this place according to the laws that have been explained, we do not suspect that she might have had relations elsewhere where there were no two majorities. Rather, we say that the promiscuity occurred here, and in all prohibitions, we do not transfer a prohibition from place to place.

It seems to me that, according to the opinion in section 35, when she claims with certainty, she is permitted based on a single majority. And based on what is written in section 34 of chapter 4, that the law of "established" is merely a stringency, since in the end there is a majority that suggests perhaps the one who engaged in relations came to her. And even if she went to him, it is considered as half and half, and consequently, it is a majority for permissibility. There is no difference whether she had relations in the city or in a place where people move around, except if she does not claim with certainty. But when she claims with certainty - there is no difference, unless it is known that she went to him. And as we explained there, we do not suspect that she may have committed adultery with her relatives, even if she is with them in the same house, unless she is suspected of them with a suspicion that has substance. And it was explained there in section 32 how the law is when she says she became pregnant by a certain man, and whether that man admits or not, and his statement only matters with regard to the child. But with regard to herself, the statement of the one who engaged in relations does not affect, and he is not considered a witness, for in the end he makes himself a wicked person. Only regarding the child, because the Torah granted credibility to the father, and without his admission, we do not consider him his child, as is explained there. But regarding herself, it is not necessary to say that if he is invalid and comes to disqualify her by saying he is the one who engaged in relations, he is not believed. Even if he is valid and comes to testify that he is the one who engaged in relations and that she is fit for the priesthood, if he is a priest, he is not believed to render her fit if without his statement she is not believed. This is because we suspect that perhaps he set his eyes upon her, and everything depends on the matter and according to the judgment of the court whether she is suspected of him or not. And know that a single witness is believed in prohibitions where the prohibition is not established, as is written in Yoreh De'ah, section 127. This applies when she does not contradict him, but if she contradicts him, a single witness in contradiction is nothing, as is written there.

[Laws of a Captive Woman and Who Is Considered a Halalah, containing 41 sections]

In Talmudic times, there were several nations with unruly conduct, such as the Arabs and similar groups, as is still found in some parts of Africa today. They would rob and capture people, taking them for ransom money. Therefore, a woman taken captive by them is presumed to have been violated and is forbidden to a Kohen (priest). For once she is in their hands, who would prevent them from assaulting her? Hence, even though a woman is not forbidden to her husband unless there are witnesses who testified that she committed adultery or through the warning and seclusion process, nevertheless, a captive is forbidden to a Kohen but not to an Israelite. This is because it is certain that she did not willingly engage in relations. Even though when she is at the mercy of those who might kill her, she might consent to them, which will be explained, this is not considered coercion. Coercion is only when she is forced into the actual intercourse but not when she is forced by other circumstances and consents to the intercourse, for this is considered full consent. And why is she not forbidden to her Israelite husband? Because most of the captors primarily intend to obtain ransom money, and the women know this and are not afraid they might kill them. Therefore, they are permitted to an Israelite but forbidden to a Kohen. Any woman older than three years and one day is presumed to have been violated. If she is unmarried, she is forbidden to marry a Kohen. If she is the wife of a Kohen, she is forbidden to her husband unless she has witnesses that testify she was not violated. The Sages were lenient regarding their testimony, as will be explained. The Rambam wrote in the 18th chapter of the Laws of Forbidden Relations that since there is only a doubt whether she was violated, and all doubts are permitted by Torah law, but by Rabbinic decree, a doubtful Torah prohibition is treated stringently, therefore they were lenient in her case. He follows his position that a doubtful Torah prohibition is lenient by Torah law. According to those who hold that by Torah law one must be stringent, there is another reason for leniency. This is because the virtuous daughters of Israel strive even in captivity to avoid being violated and employ all sorts of strategies and debase themselves in front of their captors to prevent them from setting their eyes on them. Therefore, their testimony is accepted leniently. Know that in our times, in all kingdoms, when a woman is imprisoned by the government for some crime, there is no concern that she will be violated by the guards there. This is because the government supervises to ensure that such a mishap does not occur and severely punishes anyone who attempts to violate them. At night, the women are locked in a separate room. Therefore, they are permitted to their Kohen husbands.

There are those who have written that since a woman does not become forbidden to her husband except by witnesses or by warning and seclusion, the Sages forbade the captive woman to a Kohen because they made a higher standard in matters of lineage [Beit Shmuel 1:1 and 34 in the name of the Maharik 160]. However, this does not seem to be the case from the Talmud and the decisors, for in the Gemara [Kiddushin 12b] it is said that they were lenient with a captive woman because she degrades herself, and the Rambam says the reason is because all doubts are permitted by Torah law. Furthermore, it is explicitly stated in the Gemara [Ketubot 13b] that a captive woman is considered as if there are witnesses that she was violated, because they are promiscuous and we are all witnesses that she was violated [Rashi], thus it is clearly a Torah prohibition but they were lenient in their testimony for the reasons we explained, and this is proven from several places [and Rabbi Dosa there 36a holds this way, and this is the approach of the Jerusalem Talmud which rules according to Rabbi Dosa and not according to our Talmud, and the Maharik's primary matter was written regarding seclusion but a captive woman is like witnesses, and the Beit Shmuel himself in 23 wrote that the decisors do not hold like him, and only according to the interpretation of the Yam Shel Shlomo in Tosafot Kiddushin there his words are correct, and all the decisors disagree with this, and scrutinize this].

A captive woman who married an Israelite and was found to have her virginity intact after he died — she is permitted to marry a Kohen, because it has been revealed that she is pure. Some are concerned that perhaps the captor had intercourse with her, which would prohibit her to a Kohen, while her physical signs of virginity remained intact. This concern does not seem valid, for why should we worry about such an uncommon occurrence? If the captor intended to complete the act, who would have stopped him? Presumably, he would have satisfied his desire. Therefore, she is certainly pure. However, who testifies to this? If we rely on the Israelite husband, his wife is like his own self, and just as she is not believed, so too is he not believed, as will be explained. We cannot say that he is believed only after his own death but not during his lifetime, because if that were the case, an Israelite man and his wife who were taken captive together would be believed to testify that she was not defiled, thus permitting her to marry a Kohen after his death, and we do not find this in the Gemara and the Poskim. Nevertheless, it appears to me that although he is not believed as a witness, he is still believed to say she was a virgin because he gains no benefit from this, and she is presumed to be a complete virgin. Consequently, she is permitted to marry a Kohen afterward based on this presumption. Additionally, it is possible that women saw her signs of virginity on the sheet, and they are believed to testify regarding a captive woman, as will be explained with God's help.

Everyone is considered credible to testify that she is pure—even a single witness, even a woman, even a relative. Even the five women who are not believed to testify that her husband has died, as mentioned in Siman 17—her mother-in-law, her mother-in-law's daughter, her co-wife, her yevamah (sister-in-law), and her husband's daughter—are believed regarding a captive. This is because, in the case of death, we are concerned that due to their hatred, they intend to cause her to remarry, and when her husband returns, she will be prohibited to both men. However, in this case, when they testify that she is pure, how can they cause harm? On the contrary, previously she was forbidden to her priestly husband, and based on their testimony, she will be permitted. 

We cannot say that they know there are two witnesses who testify that she was defiled, and they are testifying so that she will be with her husband, and when the witnesses come, she will be prohibited to her husband and her children will be disqualified as priests. For if that were the case, why would they need to testify? Without their testimony, she is already forbidden to her husband. And to suspect them of intending to harm her future children—we do not suspect them to such an extent. Moreover, disqualified children are only a detriment to the priestly father, but for her, it makes no difference because the disqualified child is a valid Israelite like all the children of Israel, only disqualified from the priesthood. 

[Note: A captive is not comparable to an agunah (a woman whose husband is missing), for in the case of an agunah, she herself is believed to say her husband died, which is not the case with a captive.]

According to the Rambam of blessed memory, any relative is believed to testify, even her adult son and daughter, and any minor, even if not a relative, is not believed to testify, except when speaking innocently (mesiach lefi tumo). This is evidenced by a case in the Gemara [Ketubot 27b] where a man, his wife, and their son were captured, and the son innocently said: "We were captured by the Arabs, my mother and I, I went to draw water thinking of my mother, I went to gather wood thinking of my mother," and the Sages allowed her to marry a Kohen based on his testimony. According to the Rambam, this son was a minor, hence he needed to speak innocently and not because of his kinship. However, most poskim (halachic authorities) disagree with him and maintain that a minor can testify if he is not her son, even if not speaking innocently, but her adult son and daughter are not believed to testify unless speaking innocently. The aforementioned case was not about a minor, but because he was her son, they did not believe him unless he spoke innocently. The Jerusalem Talmud [Ketubot 2:9] explicitly implies that even her minor son can testify, but this is not the approach of our Talmud. Similarly, a slave and a maidservant are believed to testify, even the husband's maidservant, but her maidservant is only believed if speaking innocently, as she is closely tied to her and not believed otherwise. The husband is not believed in any situation, even when speaking innocently, just like she herself, as his wife is considered like his own body. Even under oath, he is not believed [as demonstrated by Rabbi Zechariah in Halacha 9 there], because the reason a wife is believed to say her husband died is that she fears corrupting herself if she remarries and her first husband returns, as explained in Siman 17. But in the case of a captive, where there is no fear of corrupting herself, she is not believed even when speaking innocently, as in the case of the person involved, speaking innocently does not apply, and similarly, the husband, as he is like herself. Two captives who testify for each other are believed, and we do not suspect mutual favors, as leniency is applied in the testimony of a captive for reasons explained in Section 1. Nevertheless, some say that a Samaritan (Kuti) is not believed to testify, and even when speaking innocently, he is not believed. Although, to testify that her husband died, he is believed when speaking innocently, as noted there, but to testify about a captive that she is pure, his testimony is meaningless. The reason seems to be that testimony about a captive is as if he testifies that his hand almost never left hers, and if he was constantly alone with her, he is the greatest invalid for this testimony. Therefore, a Samaritan woman would be believed. Some are lenient regarding a Samaritan speaking innocently, and this is the conclusion of the great later authorities. His testimony could be that he spoke innocently, indicating that he and other men and women were always with her, and she was not alone with him for a long time. Testimony from hearsay is also valid for a captive. [The dispute between the Rambam and the poskim is written according to the Gra's commentary, and this resolves the difficulty raised by the Chatam Sofer. The words of the Beit Shmuel are insufficient, and take note.]

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 2 that a casual statement (mesiach lefi tumo) is only reliable to be lenient, not to be stringent. His explanation: When a non-Jew makes a casual statement and says she is impure, we do not consider her definitely impure, but she remains as she was before. Similarly, in the case of an agunah (a woman whose husband is missing), if a casual statement is made that her husband is alive, it is as if nothing was said, and she remains in doubt. The practical difference is when a single valid witness comes to testify that she is pure or that the agunah's husband has died, we permit her. However, if one non-Jew casually says she is impure and another casually says she is pure, we do not permit her, as Rema explicitly ruled in section 17 regarding an agunah. Even though there are those who are lenient there, we do not follow that opinion. Nevertheless, some say that in the case of a captive woman, even in such a case, she is permitted, as it is not comparable to an agunah who remains presumed to be married, and we assume her husband is alive. The non-Jew who casually says her husband is alive upholds her presumption, so how can we permit her through the casual statement that her husband is dead and remove her from her presumption where there is contradiction? But in the case of a captive woman, she has a presumption of being kosher, and we only forbid her due to the situation. Therefore, the casual statement that she is pure maintains her presumption, and the casual statement that she is impure does not matter to remove her from her presumption. This reasoning is sensible, as all disqualified witnesses are not believed to be stringent, and even a single witness is not believed to be stringent when there is contradiction, as will be explained. A single witness in contradiction is meaningless, and here she says she is pure. Although she is not believed, when there is a casual statement supporting her, she is believed, and the one contradicting her has no significance.

Some of our rabbis wrote that although all disqualified individuals are deemed fit to testify regarding a captive woman, nevertheless, a Torah-level thief and all those disqualified due to a Torah-level transgression are disqualified, just as they are in the testimony concerning an agunah (a woman whose husband is missing), as stated in Siman 17 [Hagahot Maimoniot, chapter 18 of Hilchot Edut, and Shevut Yaakov in the name of the Ritva]. Since such a person is brazen enough to publicly transgress the Torah, they are not deemed fit to testify regarding a woman [Rashi at the beginning of Rosh Hashanah], and the same applies to a captive woman.

A Kohen who testified about a captive woman that she is pure – he should not marry her, lest he had set his eyes on her. However, if he did marry her, it is explained in the Tosefta [Yevamot, Chapter 4] that he does not have to divorce her, as this is merely a suspicion. Another Kohen is permitted to marry her from the outset, and we do not say that because he wished to marry her he testified falsely [Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel], since for him it is only a mere suspicion. If he redeemed her with money and testified that she is pure – he is permitted to marry her from the outset, because if he did not know with certainty that she was pure, he would not have spent his money on her. Similarly, if it is not known at all that she was a captive, but only this Kohen knows and knows that she is pure – he is permitted to marry her [Beit Shmuel]. Likewise, the wife of a Kohen who was forbidden to him – this is when it is known that she was a captive, but if it is only known to the husband and he knows that she is pure – he is permitted to live with her. Even if there are witnesses that she was a captive but it is not known that he is a Kohen – he is permitted to marry her with the argument that he could have claimed he is not a Kohen [see Beit Shmuel]. If two Kohanim testify about her – one of them can marry her, as two are not suspected [Be'er HaYitev]. Similarly, if one Kohen testified about a married woman that she is pure – he is permitted to marry her after the death of her husband, as there is no reason to suspect him since she had a husband. Also, if the Kohen had a wife in a place where one does not marry two women, and then his wife died, he is permitted to marry her for this reason [there].

A captive woman is not believed regarding herself to say that she is pure – specifically when she does not have a "migo" (a logical argument that supports her claim), such as when there are witnesses who know that she was taken captive. However, if she says, "I was taken captive but I am pure," she is believed, because the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted. Even if there is one witness that she was taken captive, or even if he testifies that she was defiled, one witness regarding impurity is nothing except in the case of a sotah (a woman suspected of adultery) [Rashi on Ketubot 23]. And although in monetary matters we do not say "migo" to contradict a witness, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, siman 75, that is because in monetary matters one witness can obligate an oath, which is not the case in matters of prohibition [Bava Metzia].

If there were two witnesses who testified that she was taken captive, and one witness testifies that she was defiled and another contradicts him and testifies that she is pure, saying she was not secluded with a non-Jew until she was redeemed, even if the witness who testifies to her purity is a servant or maidservant - she is permitted. Even if the witness to her defilement came first, we do not say in this case that wherever the Torah believes one witness, it is as if there are two witnesses. Nor do we say to set one witness against the other and leave her in the presumption of being a captive, for the Sages were lenient with captives. However, regarding an agunah, it is not the same, as stated in Siman 17. And if two say she was taken captive and is defiled, and two say she was taken captive and is pure - she should not marry, but if she did marry, she need not be divorced.

A woman who declares herself impure, and one witness testifies that she is pure, is believed to prohibit herself to her husband. We are not concerned that she set her eyes on another man, because in any case, she is considered as captured, and the presumption that Arabs are licentious is no less than a basis for suspicion that she is believed. However, if two qualified witnesses testify that she is pure, she is not believed to prohibit herself to her husband, and she does not have the authority to remove herself from him. But if she is unmarried, she is believed to prohibit herself to a Kohen, as she establishes herself as a piece of prohibition. Similarly, she is forbidden from Terumah if she is the daughter of a Kohen. If she later provides a reasonable explanation for her initial claim of impurity and now retracts it, she is believed if the court deems the explanation appropriate.

If a woman says, "I was captured but I am pure," and the court permits her to marry, and afterward two witnesses come and testify that she was indeed captured – she may marry ab initio and does not need to leave her permitted status. Even if her captor enters after her and she is clearly in captivity in front of us in the hands of her master, but she managed to deceive the captor so he would not enter with her to the court in order that she would be believed according to the law because she has a "migo" (a legal presumption) – she still does not need to leave her permitted status. The sages did not adopt a stringent approach in these matters. This is not considered deception, as she acted properly since she knows she is pure, and once the matter has been permitted – it remains permitted. She will be guarded from now on until she is redeemed. Even though until now she was not guarded – from now on it is our obligation to guard her. Not only when she was initially permitted do we need to guard her, but even if she entered with the captor together, which is akin to having witnesses of her captivity since she is held by the captor and is forbidden to a Kohen – nevertheless, it is our obligation to guard her from now on. Even if she has been defiled, we are obligated to guard her so she does not become defiled again [Maharam Shif on Ketubot 23a]. However, if afterward two witnesses come and testify that she was defiled, even if she was married to a Kohen and had children from him – she must leave, and the children are disqualified (chalalim). If one witness testifies that she is defiled – it is nothing, as it has been said that one witness in matters of impurity is not considered. If two witnesses testify that she is defiled and two testify that she is pure, it seems to me that we establish the two against the two and the woman remains in her presumption of purity. Even though generally with two against two we are stringent – nevertheless, in the case of a captive woman, we are lenient. Not only if she was married to a Kohen does she not need to leave, but even ab initio she is permitted to marry. This is evidenced from the law explained in section 10. It is possible, however, that ab initio she should not marry when there are two witnesses of impurity.

As we said regarding a woman who claims, "I was captured but I am pure," and the court permitted her, she does not have to leave her husband even if witnesses later come and testify that she was captured. Similarly, even if the court has not yet permitted her but she married a kohen in front of the court and they did not protest because they had no reason to protest since she had a "migo" (a legal presumption), and later witnesses came and testified that she was captured — she does not have to leave him, for the fact that the court did not protest is as if they permitted her. However, if she married a kohen privately and then witnesses came and testified that she was captured — she must leave him, just as in the case of a kohen's wife where two witnesses testified that she was captured, she must leave him because she had no permission from the court.

Some say that even in this case she does not have to leave, as it is not similar to the case of a kohen's wife, because here she was single and could have married an Israelite; surely she is pure, for she would not leave a permitted situation and enter a prohibited one. 

Similarly, some say that if there are no witnesses that she was captured, and she did not come to the court to be permitted, and a kohen who knows she was captured and she tells him she is pure — he can marry her based on the presumption that she could have married an Israelite. 

There are those who question this, saying it is not a valid presumption, as perhaps she had an interest in him. Likewise, this reasoning casts doubt on the previous leniency. 

However, it is certain according to all opinions that in the case of a kohen's wife where the husband knows she was captured but does not know if she is pure — he is forbidden to live with her even if no one else knows she was captured. Since he knows and she has no presumption to claim she was not captured, on what basis can he believe her? 

However, if it is clear to him that she was not defiled, she is permitted to him as stated in Section 8.

A woman who does not have witnesses that she was captured, and she says before a Beit Din (rabbinic court) that she was captured but is pure, and she has witnesses that she is pure – we do not say to wait until the witnesses come, but rather we permit her immediately, for the sages were lenient regarding captives. Moreover, even if witnesses later come and say they do not know – she does not need to be separated from the permit [given by the Beit Din], even if the witnesses know she was captured. Additionally, even if there is a rumor that there are witnesses of her impurity – we do not pay attention to this and we permit her until the witnesses come and we hear what they say, for the sages were lenient regarding captives. And it should not be said, how can we permit her to a Kohen (priest) and maybe the rumor is true? For we can say that we permit her so that if she knows she was defiled, they will separate her from her husband when the witnesses come, and if she is not concerned, why should we be concerned, for according to the law, a mere rumor has no substance. However, a rumor that was strengthened in a Beit Din – certainly, it is proper to be concerned and to wait for the witnesses. And some are lenient even in this, but it is a great leniency, and it requires further investigation into the law.

The father who says, "My daughter was captured, and I redeemed her, and she is forbidden to a Kohen," whether she is an adult or a minor – he is not believed to render her forbidden to a Kohen. And even though the Torah granted the father credibility to say, "I betrothed my daughter to so-and-so" or "I betrothed my daughter in general, and she is forbidden to everyone," as written in Siman 37, nevertheless, in the case of a captive, the Torah did not grant him credibility. Similarly, if he says that she had forbidden intercourse – he is not believed, for he is only believed regarding betrothal. And even though through betrothal he has the means to disqualify her from marrying a Kohen by saying, "I betrothed her and divorced her," why should he not be believed to disqualify her through captivity or forbidden intercourse? It is not comparable because through divorce he only disqualifies her from marrying a Kohen and not from eating terumah, whereas in these cases, he would disqualify her from terumah as well. And even though if she is an Israelite woman, there is no practical difference in this matter, nevertheless, this is not a valid argument to believe him since this is a more severe matter. Moreover, he is not even considered a valid witness to join with another witness who testifies that she was captured, contrary to some opinions. He is not believed at all to disqualify his daughter or his wife, and he is only believed in what the Torah granted him credibility.

The wife of a Kohen who has been forbidden to him due to being taken captive, since the matter is uncertain – she is permitted to live with him in the same courtyard, provided that his children and household members are always with him to guard him. But if she is certainly impure – it is forbidden to live with her in the same courtyard, or even in the same alley, similar to a divorced woman as will be explained in Siman 119. And even according to the authorities who permit a woman who willingly committed adultery to stay even in his house because she is repulsive to him, nevertheless, with a captive woman it is forbidden because she was defiled by force and is not repulsive to him. And this leniency with a captive woman, even though the Gemara implies that the permission was because the husband knew she was not defiled, nevertheless, the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch did not differentiate in this matter since, in the end, the husband is not trusted and she is forbidden to him by law. Therefore, there is no difference whether he knows she is pure or not.

A city that has come under siege and been captured: if the besiegers surround the city from all sides so that not a single woman can escape without being seen and taken into their control, then all the women within are considered disqualified as captives, lest they have been violated by them—except for a girl who is three years old or younger. However, if it is possible for a woman to escape without being noticed, or if there is a hiding place within the city, even if it can hold only one woman, this saves everyone. How does it save? Any woman who comes to the court and declares, "I am pure," is believed even without a witness, because she has the "migo" (a presumption of credibility) that she could have said she escaped when the city was captured or was in hiding and thus was saved. Therefore, she can claim, "I did not escape, nor did I hide, and I was not defiled." But any woman who does not come to the court to declare her purity is presumed to be impure out of doubt. Some say she does not need to come to the court at all, because once there is a place of refuge, they are no longer presumed to be captives.

All this applies to a battalion of the same kingdom that settles in the city and is not afraid, so we are concerned they might have violated the women. However, a battalion from another kingdom that sweeps through and moves on does not render the women forbidden, because they do not have time to violate them as they are busy with plunder and fleeing. Nonetheless, if they are calm and confident and not in a hurry to flee, the women are forbidden. If, during their retreat, they take women into their control, even if the Israelites chase after them and rescue the women from their hands, the women are forbidden. Although the soldiers are preoccupied with their retreat, since the women were in their actual control, there is no greater captivity than this, and during their retreat, they defile the women because they are in their hands. This is the opinion of the Rambam in chapter 18 of Hilchot Issurei Biah and the Shulchan Aruch.

Some say that, on the contrary, in a siege by another kingdom, women are forbidden because there is no protection from the kingdom over the city. However, in a siege by the same kingdom, women are permitted because the kingdom ensures that nothing bad happens to any of the city's residents, provided that the protection around the city is good, such as having many soldiers guarding against robbers and looters entering the city. Otherwise, women are forbidden, as a time of war is considered like ownerless property [Rashi, Ketubot 27]. We do not worry that the soldiers themselves will commit evil deeds because the soldiers fear the kingdom. It seems to me that in practice, these opinions do not disagree. Certainly, in a siege by the same kingdom with an order from the king to protect the city's residents, even the Rambam agrees. On the contrary, according to the Rambam, it is not necessary for the protection to be so good, and without it, we do not worry [see Tosafot and examine closely]. If the kingdom abandons the city as they do to cities that rebel against the kingdom, this opinion also agrees that women are forbidden. Some say that in all circumstances, women are forbidden, whether in a siege by the same kingdom or another kingdom, because the evil inclination of sin is strong and we worry they will be violated [Rif, Rosh, Ramban, Rashba, who ruled like Rabbi Meir there]. Some are even stricter, saying that even if there is a place to escape, women are forbidden because they might be afraid to flee due to fear of the soldiers, but we do not hold this way [Beit Shmuel]. However, even according to these opinions, if there is fear of the king and his ministers over the people, preventing them from wrongdoing to the city's residents and punishing those who act inappropriately, there is no concern for the women. Therefore, in all the wars of our times, we do not worry about women being besieged because all the kingdoms of our times ensure that no harm comes to the city's residents, and if someone rapes a woman, his punishment is very severe.

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote: A woman who was imprisoned by gentiles for monetary reasons is permitted [to her husband]. If it was for life-threatening reasons, she is forbidden to a priest (kohen), and therefore, if her husband is a kohen, she becomes forbidden to him. When does this apply? When the power of Israel prevails over them, and they fear them. But when their power prevails, even if it was for monetary reasons, since she is under their control, she becomes forbidden unless there is a witness for her captivity. End of quote. And Rambam holds that even if she was imprisoned for life-threatening reasons, she is forbidden only to a kohen, but we do not fear that she willingly consented and would be forbidden also to her Israelite husband, for most Jewish women are modest and would not consent to such a thing. And if it was for monetary reasons, she is permitted even to a kohen, for they fear that if they defile her, they will lose their money since the power of Israel prevails. This is specifically when the Jew owes them money, as they fear losing their money. But if no money is owed to them and they captured her to ransom her for money, she is forbidden to her priestly husband, as this is considered true captivity, for in this case, they do not fear a loss since they are not losing from their own pocket.

Some say that even if they captured her in order to ransom her for money—she is permitted after the fact to her husband who is a Kohen, just like seclusion with a non-Jew, which is initially forbidden but after the fact, they do not separate her due to seclusion [as Rabina says in Avodah Zarah 23b and as the first answer of Tosafot and the Rosh], and this opinion has strong support in the Gemara [see Bava Metzia]. However, a captive woman who is forbidden to a Kohen is different, because since they acted like robbers, it is certainly likely that they violated her, but in the case of a capture for ransom, we do not forbid her after the fact, just like with seclusion, and even if their authority is strong, she is permitted according to this opinion [Beit Shmuel].

And even according to the first opinion that prohibits it even post facto, nevertheless, this is all when she was seized and is in their custody. But if she secluded herself with him for even a long time, and even if their power is strong, and even if she owes them money – we do not prohibit her because of seclusion, even though she acted improperly. And even if rumors of promiscuity spread about her, any rumor that arises after marriage is not considered to prohibit her to her husband. The reason is that since she is not in their custody, if he wishes to force her, she will cry out and they will rescue her. And although some want to say that if she stayed a long time, she is prohibited even post facto, nevertheless the main ruling is as I have written. The general rule is: even according to the first opinion, she is not prohibited to her husband the priest unless she is in their custody and stayed a long time, but with one defect – she is permitted post facto. And for this reason, it is possible to justify the practice of some respectable Jewish women who travel to courtyards and seclude themselves with them for a long time and travel to fairs without supervision, that as long as she is not in their custody by way of captivity, we do not worry they will force her as she will cry out and be rescued. However, this is all post facto and to not prohibit her to her husband the priest, but initially a prudent person should keep away from this unless she enters his house for a short time, for this is permitted even initially. Otherwise, you would not leave a daughter of our forefather Abraham, the wife of a priest, sitting with her husband, for it is impossible that she does not seclude with an Arab for a short time. And know that this reasoning which we have written, that since she is able to cry out she is not prohibited, is found in the Jerusalem Talmud there, and even a deaf-mute can hint and be rescued.

And our teacher the Rema wrote at the end of paragraph 11: "However, if she secluded herself for the sake of promiscuity, one should be stringent," end quote. Some say that his intention is regarding an unmarried woman who secluded herself for the sake of promiscuity, that she is forbidden to a priest, as it cannot be interpreted about a married woman since we do not forbid her due to seclusion even if she secluded herself for the sake of promiscuity, as written in Siman 175, see there. And some explained his words about a married woman, and what is clarified in Siman 175 that we do not forbid even in such a case, that is if she secluded herself with a Jew, and here it refers to secluding herself with a non-Jew, or there it refers to the wife of a Jew and here it refers to the wife of a priest, and although if she secluded herself willingly there is no difference between a Jew and a priest, nevertheless one should be stringent with a priest because they elevated the status of priestly lineage. And some also explained that it refers to a married woman, and certainly by law we do not force her to divorce as written in Siman 175, but our teacher the Rema said that the husband himself should be concerned and stringent. And it seems to me that our teacher the Rema spoke about the law, and it refers to a married woman in Siman 178, that no rumor of promiscuity had spread about her, but here it refers to a case where a rumor of promiscuity had spread about her as is evident from his previous words, and therefore it is like having grounds to believe that seclusion in this case also forbids a married woman to a Jew if the seclusion was for a long time. And it is likewise with an unmarried woman who secluded herself for the sake of promiscuity – certainly, ideally, she is forbidden to a priest, however, if she got married – she does not need to be divorced if she claims with certainty that she was not defiled, for it is no worse than if she claimed she was defiled by a fit man, which she is believed. However, if a rumor also spread and the rumor was confirmed in court – she must be divorced if she married a priest. And as for a married woman who secluded herself and said she was raped, this happened in ancient times – and some forbade her saying she is not believed with the claim of 'since I was not defiled, I was raped,' because she violated the law and secluded herself, and the Ra'avyah permitted her, saying that due to seclusion she did not lose her claim, for do all women know the law? Furthermore, a woman is not prohibited to her husband except through warning and seclusion – and this is the main ruling.

And regarding what Maimonides wrote, of blessed memory, that when a woman is imprisoned by non-Jews, she is forbidden to marry a Kohen, some of our Rabbis hold that she is also forbidden to her Israelite husband. This is because it is likely that she consented out of fear of death, thinking that by doing so she might save herself from death. Legally, we are concerned about this because it is human nature to become confused due to fear of death, except for one who is completely modest and would surrender herself to death – and this is not common [see Tosafot there 26b, and this that Rashi and Tosafot wrote that we are concerned she may have consented, their intention is not just a mere concern, but rather that legally we should be concerned as the Maharil wrote, and the words of the Bach Seif Katan 23 need further study]. If it is known that the woman is completely modest, she is permitted to an Israelite, and we do not concern ourselves that she may have consented [Yam Shel Shlomo there in the name of Sefer Mitzvot Katan]. There are those who wanted to permit a completely modest woman also to a Kohen, because she would surrender herself to death before being violated, but it is not to be permitted for this reason unless there are other factors for leniency [there in the name of Terumat HaDeshen].

Some of our rabbis have raised a difficulty with this, arguing that since the appeasement is due to fear, it constitutes coercion, so how can it be prohibited for a Jew? [Rashba there] Evidence for this is from what our Sages said [there 91b] regarding women who are kidnapped by thieves: even though it appears that these women assist them in their work and bring them bread and arrows, they are still permitted to their Jewish husbands, because we say that everything they do is out of fear. Thus, we see that anything done out of fear is not considered voluntary. Moreover, if that were the case, why would a captive woman not be prohibited to a Jew? We should be concerned that she might acquiesce out of fear of death [there].

It seems to me that there is no disagreement in principle, and certainly, everyone agrees that when she consents to intercourse in order to save her life from death, she becomes forbidden to her Israelite husband. For when the coercion is not directly on the intercourse itself, it is not considered coercion, as stated in Section 1. Otherwise, there would never be true consent in matters of divorce and other matters. 

However, this is only when she actively seeks him out by adorning herself before him or enticing him with words. But if she does nothing and he comes upon her, and out of fear she remains silent and does not resist him, this is considered coercion. Coercion and consent depend on the heart regarding the essence of the transgression. When she does not willingly consent in her heart, even if she remains silent, it is still considered coercion, for what else could she do? The proof is from Esther.

Accordingly, the Rashba who questions the opinion of our rabbis who prohibit, believes that they interpret the murderers as coming upon them and they remain silent, yet our rabbis still prohibited them. He rightly questions this, but their intention was that due to fear of death, she may try to get him to come upon her to perhaps save her life, as explicitly written [in another place]. 

Similarly, with women abducted by thieves and taken to the forests, who out of fear do everything they are commanded to do, this is considered complete coercion. And with a captive woman, why would she try to get her captor to come upon her? Most of those who come have monetary intentions. If his desire overcomes him to come upon her and she remains silent out of fear that he might kill her, it is still considered coercion, as mentioned. However, in the case where she is held by them and faces death, we fear that out of the terror in her heart, she might try to get him to come upon her in hope of saving her life. Only Maimonides and his followers believe we do not need to be concerned about this effort on her part, but in the main ruling, all agree.

And the proof for this is from the words of our teacher, the Rema, who wrote that there are those who say that in any situation where she believes she will be saved through ransom and return [to her husband], she is not forbidden to her Israelite husband, because she does not consent [to the act] even though she is imprisoned due to her own actions. These are his words. And behold, we are witnesses that even if she hopes to be released through ransom, nevertheless, if the assailant comes upon her, she will yield to him and not resist, as she would fear his anger. However, the allowance is because she does not endeavor for him to come upon her, since she has another means of rescue through ransom.

And what is considered to be because of danger to life? Either when they are sitting due to their own situation which involves a risk of death, or when they are imprisoned because of their husbands. For it was the custom in ancient times that even if there was a death sentence only on the man, they would imprison his wife and all his household as well, and they would be abandoned to anyone who wished, whether to kill them or to assault them. However, when they are imprisoned because of their husbands, they are not prohibited unless the judgment of death on their husbands has been finalized, for then their wives and all that they have are abandoned. In our kingdoms, this law does not apply at all, because the kings are merciful and do not have these repugnant judgments.
