And our master, the Rema, wrote that in ancient times during periods of rage and mass killing, our sages permitted the women to their Israelite husbands according to the opinion of the Rambam. And even according to those who disagreed, appeasement would not have helped then because there was mass killing.

There was an incident involving the wife of a Kohen who was imprisoned, and Jews were coming in and out to visit her. The Maharam of Rothenburg permitted her to her husband because in such a case, it is not considered a place of seclusion. It is possible that even if she was imprisoned for a capital offense, she would be permitted to her husband if she says she was not defiled. This is also implied by the wording of Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) in section 11. It appears that this depends on the discretion of the court, according to the circumstances of the place.

If a Jew converted to Islam along with his wife and then they both returned [to Judaism]—his wife is permitted to him, and we do not suspect that she committed adultery, for their wives are not abandoned and they watch over them. Even if her husband is a Kohen, she is permitted to him. However, if she alone converted, she is forbidden to her husband even if he is an Israelite, because it is certain that she committed adultery, and she requires witnesses or even one witness. It is permissible to be lenient with her testimony as with that of a captive, since it is not certain that she committed adultery. But she herself is not believed, and the testimony of her maidservant, son, and daughter seems to be accepted only if it is a spontaneous declaration, as it is not more credible than that of a captive. Even though some want to be lenient and say that we do not suspect that she committed adultery—this is not the accepted ruling, and all the great authorities of the later generations have agreed to this [see Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel and the Gra]. However, in times of persecution when they converted due to coercion, after the coercion has passed—they are permitted to their Israelite husbands, for certainly under duress they did not commit adultery. Even to Kohanim, if according to the context they were not given over to the persecutors to do with them as they pleased—they are permitted. And our teacher the Rema permits them even to Kohanim, though the later authorities are uncertain about this [see the Gra, section 35]. And a woman who was tempted and promised to convert but then recanted—she is permitted because of this even to her Kohen husband. However, if there was seclusion for a long time—in this case, one must assess according to the nature of the seclusion [see Beit Shmuel, section 32].

What is a "chalalah"? The Sages stated a major principle: there is no "chalalah" except from prohibitions related to the priesthood. Whether a priest (kohen) has relations with a woman forbidden to him by priestly law, causing her to become a "chalalah," or whether a child is born from such prohibited relations, the child is a "chalal." Even if this child marries a woman permitted to him, such as a "chalal" who marries a regular Israelite woman, she becomes a "chalalah," and any child born from this union remains a "chalal" for all generations.

However, from prohibitions that are universal, such as incestuous relations, or from those punishable by a negative commandment or a positive commandment, such as with a mamzeret, Egyptian, or Edomite woman, even if a kohen has relations with them, they do not become a "chalalah" but rather a "zonah" (harlot). Only upon a second act of intercourse does she become a "chalalah," since he has had relations with a "zonah," who is prohibited to the priesthood. Moreover, even from a prohibition punishable by karet (excision) that does not make her a "zonah," like one who has relations with a menstruant woman (niddah) who does not become a "zonah" as stated in Section 6, one might think that whenever she does not become a "zonah," she should at least become a "chalalah." Nevertheless, the Torah's decree is that a "chalalah" only results from prohibitions related to the priesthood alone [resolving the difficulty raised by the Beit Shmuel, Section 335].

Therefore, a Kohen (priest) who had relations with a zonah (a woman who engaged in prohibited relations) or a divorcee, and a Kohen Gadol (high priest) who had relations with them or with a widow, or if he married a non-virgin and had relations with her – they become disqualified forever. If he had a child with her, whether it was the Kohen who disqualified her or another Kohen – the child is a challal (disqualified from the priesthood), whether male or female. She herself becomes disqualified through his relations from the moment he begins the act, whether he did so unintentionally or intentionally, whether by force or willingly. This applies if the Kohen is at least nine years old and she is at least three years old. However, if a Kohen betrothed one of those forbidden to the priesthood and she became widowed or divorced from the betrothal – she does not become disqualified. But if it was from the marriage – Rambam wrote in Chapter 19 of "Issurei Biah" that even if she was not actually violated, she becomes disqualified, because any married woman is presumed to be non-virgin even if found to be a virgin. This implies that even if it is known she was not violated, she becomes disqualified. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot (Chapter 6, Halacha 3), it is explicitly stated that if he did not have relations with her, she does not become disqualified. Also, Rambam's language implies that since he wrote she is presumed to be non-virgin, it implies that if it is known she was not violated, she does not become disqualified. And this is what he meant by saying she might still be a virgin even if there was some intimacy. This is agreed upon by the major later authorities (Taz and Choshen Mishpat). Some wrote that we rule stringently in this case, that she becomes disqualified and her children are doubtful challalim (disqualified from the priesthood) (Taz and Beit Shmuel), but it is difficult to rule against the Jerusalem Talmud. (And they did not cite it, and what the Gra wrote that we rule according to Rav in Yevamot 57 and according to the explanation of Rabbeinu Tam requires further analysis considering what Rambam wrote in Chapter 7 of Terumot, and also the Tosefta clarifies this as well. Also, according to Rabbeinu Tam and Rav, it seems that this only applies to Terumah but how could she become a challalah without relations, as the Choshen Mishpat wrote, and it is not similar to the case of the ketubah and claim of virginity as Beit Shmuel wrote. Examine this well.)

The kohen himself who transgressed and had relations with one of the forbidden unions for kohanim – does not become desecrated. The reason is that the Torah sanctified the kohanim, and any violation of this sanctity through such relations results in the desecration of the kohen's sanctity from the woman and her offspring, preventing them from entering the sanctity of the kohanim. However, how is it possible that this kohen, who was born into the sanctity of kohanim, would lose his sanctity due to a transgression he committed? If so, we would also say that an Israelite who committed a transgression would no longer be considered an Israelite. Rather, even though he sinned, he remains an Israelite, and similarly, a kohen, even though he sinned, remains a kohen, as he was born a kohen.

A Kohen (priest) who marries a mature woman (bogeret) or a woman who lost her virginity due to an accident (mukat etz) does not make her a chalalah (disqualified woman), and similarly, if he has relations with a non-virgin without marriage, she does not become a chalalah. And even though there is a chalal (disqualified offspring) from violations of positive commandments as stated in Siman 6, nevertheless, since the positive commandment is derived from the verse "he shall take a virgin"—a virgin and not a non-virgin, it excludes marriage, but mere relations without marriage do not make her a chalalah [Rambam's commentary]. And know that a Kohen who marries a chalalah who became disqualified through violations of positive commandments is liable to lashes for "he shall not take a chalalah" [Maggid Mishneh there], although some of our Sages are uncertain about this [Tosafot there Avodah Zarah]. And all other disqualifications for Kohanim make them chalalim (disqualified) through relations even without marriage [Beit Shmuel]. And a woman who committed adultery while married to a Kohen—her children become chalalim because she becomes a zonah (harlot), and when she subsequently gives birth from the Kohen, they automatically become chalalim as stated [there].

A Kohen who has relations with any of the forbidden relations, or with a Yevama (widow bound to her deceased husband's brother) who went to the market (i.e., married someone else) where Kiddushin (betrothal) does not take effect as with forbidden relations, and she becomes pregnant from the first intercourse – the child is not a Chalal (disqualified Kohen), but she becomes a Zonah (harlot). However, with forbidden relations, there is no practical difference, as the child is a Mamzer (illegitimate), and the only practical difference is if the child is a female and a Kohen wishes to marry her, he must be cautioned because she is a Mamzeret (female illegitimate) and not because she is a Chalalah (disqualified Kohen). The main issue is with the Yevama who went to the market because the child is not a Mamzer, even rabbinically, as stated in Siman 159. And even according to those who hold there that the child is a Mamzer rabbinically – this is only in the case of marriage, as stated there. If this Kohen returns to have relations with her permissibly, such as with his wife's sister after his wife’s death or with a Yevama who went to the market or another Kohen with whom she is not forbidden – the child is a Chalal, because he has relations with a Zonah, which is a prohibition for Kohanim. However, one who has relations with a freedwoman, even if she becomes pregnant from the first intercourse – the child is a Chalal. And similarly, one who has relations with a Niddah (menstruant) – the child is kosher and not a Chalal, as stated.

And know that all this is the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, who holds that in any case where our Sages said that the offspring is kosher, such as a slave who has relations with a Jewish woman, the offspring, even if she is a daughter, is not disqualified from marrying into the priesthood, as stated in section 4, paragraph 13. This applies as well to all other cases of forbidden relationships punishable by negative commandments, and also to a yevamah (widow bound to marry her brother-in-law) who marries someone from the general population. However, there are those who say that while it is true that in all of these cases the offspring is kosher and not a chalal (disqualified priest), nevertheless, if the offspring is a female, she is disqualified from marrying into the priesthood. Similarly, in cases of forbidden relationships where the woman becomes a zonah (prostitute) – if the offspring is a daughter, she is disqualified from marrying into the priesthood [and this depends on the dispute between Rambam and the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) regarding whether a woman becomes a zonah from forbidden relationships, as stated in section 6, paragraph 19], except for the case of a niddah (menstruating woman), where the reason the daughter is disqualified from the priesthood is derived from a fortiori reasoning from a widow to a High Priest, whose prohibition is not equal for all. Nevertheless, since she is desecrated by his cohabitation, the offspring is disqualified from the priesthood, and all the more so in prohibitions that are equal for all Jews – when she becomes a zonah from his cohabitation, the daughter remains disqualified from marrying into the priesthood [Yevamot 45b]. However, a niddah does not become a zonah, and therefore, what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 17, that a non-Jew or a slave who has relations with a Jewish woman and she gives birth to a daughter, that daughter is disqualified from marrying into the priesthood, is not according to the Rambam’s opinion. Even according to their opinion – if she marries, she does not have to leave [Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel]. And so wrote Rashi in a responsum, that it is only a disqualification ab initio [there, and the dispute of Rambam with the poskim, for the Rambam rejects the Gemara in Yevamot 45b because in the conclusion there it is ruled that a slave who has relations with a Jewish woman, the offspring is kosher and there is no issue of disqualification from the priesthood, indicating that this sugya is rejected, and the Rif is uncertain about this, see there, and the Gra in subsections 53, 54, and 57, and in section 6, subsection 23, elaborates on this, and the Ramban’s opinion is unique, and examine this carefully].

A disqualified priest (chalal) who marries a fit woman (kesheira) - their child is a disqualified priest (chalal), and so is his son - all are disqualified priests for all generations. Even she herself becomes disqualified through his intercourse. According to Maimonides, in chapter 18, she is considered a zonah (prostitute), as mentioned in Siman 6, Se'if 19. However, if a fit priest marries a disqualified woman (chalalah) - the child is fit for priesthood because the Children of Israel are a purifying mikvah for the disqualified. Since there is both valid kiddushin (marriage) and no sin, the child follows the status of the father, who is not disqualified. Therefore, if this disqualified priest marries a fit woman and they have a daughter, and this daughter marries an Israelite, their children are considered fit.

A Kohen who has relations with a chalutzah – she and her offspring are considered chalalim (disqualified from the priesthood) by rabbinic decree, as the prohibition of a chalutzah to a Kohen is not from the Torah. However, a Kohen who has relations with one of the secondary relatives (shniyot) – she remains fit and her offspring from him are also fit, and the Rabbis did not decree that they should be chalalim, as a chalalah status only applies to Torah prohibitions related to Kohanim. Furthermore, they did not decree that the children should be mamzerim (illegitimate) by rabbinic law, as they did in the case of a woman who remarried based on the testimony that her husband had died, and then her husband returned, where the offspring from the second husband are mamzerim as stated in Siman 4. This is because they can only decree that the children are mamzerim when the mother was engaged in a Torah prohibition, not when there is only a rabbinic prohibition – it is impossible for the children to be mamzerim. But a Kohen who marries a pregnant divorcee, whether the child is from him or from another, and she gives birth while she is a chalalah – the offspring is fit, since they did not come from a drop of prohibited relations.

A priest who had relations with a woman who is a doubtful zonah (harlot) or a doubtful divorcee – this is a doubtful chalalah (disqualified priestly woman) and her offspring is a doubtful chalal (disqualified priest). We impose upon him the stringencies of both priests and Israelites – he does not eat terumah (priestly offerings), he does not become impure through contact with the dead, and he marries a woman who is fit for a priest. If he eats terumah or becomes impure or marries a divorcee – he is given rabbinic lashes. The same applies to a chalal of rabbinic origin – we do not allow him to eat terumah, but we give him forty lashes if he becomes impure or marries a divorcee, for according to Torah law he is a complete priest [Beit Yosef]. Some say that they were also stringent with a doubtful chalutzah (a woman who underwent the ceremony of chalitzah), but this is not clear, for they did not decree concerning a doubtful chalutzah, as if he married her he does not have to divorce her, as stated in Siman 6, Se’if 6, and how can we say that the offspring is a doubtful chalal? We have already written there that an error occurred in the book of the Tur, see there. But a chalal by Torah law – he is like a non-priest, and he marries a divorcee and becomes impure through the dead, for he is a complete non-priest, as it is stated, “Say to the priests, the sons of Aaron,” even though they are the sons of Aaron – until they are in their priesthood. It turns out that there are three types of chalalim: a chalal by Torah law, a chalal by rabbinic decree, and a doubtful chalal by Torah law.

In ancient times, a convert who married a female convert and had a daughter – she should not be married to a priest from the outset, even her daughter's daughter for many generations, even though her conception and birth were in holiness. However, if she is married, she need not be divorced, because according to the law she is permitted to marry a priest since her virginity was planted in Israel, meaning her conception and birth were in holiness. But since the priests practiced stringency upon themselves, therefore if she is married, she need not be divorced. But if her conception was not in holiness, even though her birth was in holiness – she must be divorced. If there is one side of Israel – either the father or the mother – the daughter is permitted to marry a priest from the outset, since one side is Israel and her conception and birth were in holiness.

The primary sanctity of the priesthood is upon the male descendants of the priesthood and not upon their females, as it is stated, "the sons of Aaron" – and not the daughters of Aaron. They are not forbidden from marrying those disqualified from the priesthood. Therefore, a female of the priesthood (a daughter of a priest) is permitted to marry a desecrated priest, a convert, or a freed slave. And even though a daughter of a priest may eat from the terumah and lesser sanctified offerings, nevertheless, regarding the sanctity of lineage, they are not like the males. And the proof is that even if they marry eligible individuals from Israel, their offspring are not priests, as lineage follows the father. However, wherever he (the priest) is forbidden to marry her, she is also forbidden to marry him.

A family in which there is a doubt regarding a challal (a person of priestly lineage who is disqualified from priestly service) or a doubt regarding a mamzer (a person born from certain prohibited relationships) or certainties – their laws are explained in Siman 2.

[The child follows the father, containing three sections]

Kohanim (priests), Levites, and Israelites are permitted to marry each other, and the child follows the father, as it is stated: "by their families, by their fathers' houses" (Numbers 1:2). Therefore, if a Kohen marries a Levite woman or an Israelite woman, the child is a Kohen. If a Levite marries a Kohen woman or an Israelite woman, the child is a Levite. If an Israelite marries a Kohen woman or a Levite woman, the child is an Israelite. Levites, Israelites, and chalalim (disqualified Kohanim) are permitted to marry each other because the status of chalal is only prohibited to Kohanim. The child follows the father; if he is a chalal, the child is a chalal, but if she is a chalalah, the child is not a chalal, as stated in Siman 7, Section 36, see there.

And similarly, Levites, Israelites, converts, and freed slaves are permitted to marry each other, and the child, according to the Tur, follows the status of the father, whether it is a convert who married an Israelite woman or an Israelite who married a convert, end quote. Therefore, if a convert marries an Israelite woman, the child is permitted to marry a mamzeret (a woman of illegitimate birth). The reason is that wherever there is a valid marriage and no transgression, the child follows the status of the father, as stated in Chapter 4. However, Maimonides wrote in Chapter 19 of Laws of Forbidden Relations that the child is considered an Israelite, and therefore prohibited from marrying a mamzeret. The Tur himself also wrote this in Chapter 4, and the reason is discussed there in paragraph 12, see there. What the Tur wrote here, that the child follows the status of the father, is relevant to the matter of not being fit to serve as a judge for a chalitzah (a ceremony releasing a widow from levirate marriage), as stated in Chapter 169. And an Israelite, Levite, or challal (a descendant of a disqualified priest) who married a convert or a freed slave—the child follows the status of the father. And if not for the words of the later authorities, I would say that the Tur holds like the Ra'avad in the chapter "Al Yedei," where it is written that the child is like an Israelite and not disqualified, see there and examine it well.

Any woman married in a forbidden manner – the child's status follows the more blemished of the two parents. If one of them is disqualified from the priesthood, the child is disqualified from the priesthood. If one of them is disqualified from the community, the child is forbidden to enter the community. The child of a maidservant or a non-Jewish woman is like them, whether she conceived from a fit person or from one who is disqualified. The reasons for these laws are explained there.

**[Laws of a Woman Who Causes Death to Her Husbands, consisting of seven sections]**

A woman who has been married to two men and they died, she should not marry a third man because of the danger, as she has already established a presumption that her husbands die. And even though, regarding monetary matters, a presumption is not established with less than three times, nevertheless, in matters of life-threatening danger we are cautious even with two times, as in the case of circumcision in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 263, where there is a dispute among the Tannaim [Yevamot 64b] whether a presumption is established with two times or three times. Therefore, in matters of danger, the Sages were stringent.

Regarding the primary issue of this danger, there is a dispute in the Gemara. One opinion states that it is caused by her "spring" (i.e., her nature), meaning that the woman's nature acts like a lethal entity, causing anyone who marries her to die. Another opinion states that it is caused by her "mazal" (fortune), meaning she has bad fortune that condemns her to live her life as an agunah (a woman bound in marriage unable to remarry), and anyone who marries her dies so that she remains an agunah [Levush]. Her bad fortune also means she will live without sustenance and her husbands die so that she lives in sorrow [Beit Shmuel].

There is a practical difference between these reasons: According to the reason of mazal, there is no difference between betrothal and marriage. According to the reason of "spring," there is no danger in betrothal because they have not yet consummated the marriage. Another practical difference is if the husbands did not die from a regular illness, but from an accident, such as falling from a roof or drowning in a river, in which case it is evident that the cause is not from her "spring." However, according to the reason of mazal, these deaths can also be attributed to her bad fortune.

But if the husband was old and died, there is no danger even according to the reason of mazal, for could he have lived forever? Similarly, if there was a plague and he died, since it is a widespread affliction, we do not attribute his death to her specifically but to the general calamity, as we find in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 321, where it states that in times of a widespread affliction, we do not attribute the death to a specific cause but to the general situation.

Regarding the law – most of the authorities agree with the reasoning that it is a matter of fortune [for Rav Ashi, the master of the Talmud, holds this way], and it also appears to be the opinion of our teacher, the Rema, who wrote 'or betrothed,' for according to the reasoning of affinity, there is no prohibition in betrothal as stated. Nevertheless, there are those who say that the reasoning of affinity is primary, and it appears to me that Rambam of blessed memory also holds this way in the end of chapter 21 of Issurei Biah, as he does not mention betrothal, and this is also the opinion of the Tur. I have not seen the earlier authorities explicitly mention betrothal, and if they held the reasoning of fortune as primary, why did they not mention it since this distinction is explicit in the Gemara? However, the second distinction in the Gemara regarding when one dies due to a reason, they also did not mention, and there is evidence to the contrary that they hold the reasoning of fortune as primary. If they had held the reasoning of affinity as primary, they should have mentioned that in such a case it is permitted. This is also the position taken by the Maggid Mishneh and our teacher the Beit Yosef, who rule according to the reasoning of fortune, and they did not elaborate on this matter due to the reason that will be explained [and in Ketubot 43a there is evidence for the reasoning of affinity].

In retrospect, if she married a third husband, Maimonides (Rambam), of blessed memory, wrote that she should not be required to leave him. Furthermore, even if she only became betrothed to him, we tell him to marry her. However, some of our rabbis disagree and hold that she should leave him because there is danger involved, and danger is more severe than prohibition. They were astonished by Maimonides' leniency in this matter. Yet, Maimonides explained in a responsum that there is no prohibition at all but rather a matter of superstition and fear that weak bodies might be harmed. Therefore, for someone who does not have a troubled heart, there is no concern in this matter. He also wrote that they used to tell these women that if they found someone willing to betroth them, they would not object, and they would betroth them in private and afterward marry them publicly. And the court would write the ketubah (marriage contract) and arrange the seven blessings. He wrote that the Rif, of blessed memory, and Rabbi Joseph ibn Migash ruled similarly, and he himself ruled likewise. Indeed, the Rif mentioned this matter very briefly in his halachic works (Ketubot, Chapter 4, and almost not at all in Yevamot, Chapter 6). Our rabbis held that all the discussion in the Talmud is only for those who want to be stringent. There are also other proofs, as we see in practice that there are those who marry a woman with this issue and live long lives, and generally speaking, in terms of luck, there is no luck for Israel, and a great merit can change one's luck (Tosafot Shabbat 156a). Some wrote that if she married three men and they died, if she married a fourth, even Maimonides agrees that she should leave him. However, this does not appear from his words that we have cited.

For all these reasons, many are lenient in this matter and combine various leniencies, such as if one of her previous husbands was somewhat ill even before she married him, we do not attribute his death to her. Additionally, if she is successful and prosperous, it is not a sign of bad fortune, and similarly, they find reasons to be lenient. The main reliance is on the opinions of the Rambam, the Rif, and the Ri Migash that we have mentioned, and it is appropriate to rely on these great rabbis even not in exigent circumstances. Our teacher, the Rema, also wrote that many are lenient in these matters and we do not protest against them, and we have also seen in our times that many are lenient in this regard, and since many are lenient, "The Lord protects the simple" [Shabbat 129b]. Heaven forbid if we were to forbid women, who have lost two husbands, from marrying again, it is very likely that they would fall into a bad path. Additionally, it seems to me that the main prohibition was only stated if the two husbands died immediately after marrying her, for in this case, there is certainly a sign either of her harmful nature or her bad fortune, but if they lived for several years, there is no reason at all to attribute their deaths to her.

Regarding the matter of the ketubah, our master the Beit Yosef wrote that if he was aware of her (previous marriages), she is entitled to a ketubah. If he was not aware of her (previous marriages), she is not entitled to a ketubah from the third marriage, but from the second marriage, she is entitled to a ketubah even if he was not aware of her (previous marriages). This is the end of his words. And it appears to me that this applies according to all opinions, that even those who are stringent in this matter still agree that from the second marriage, she is entitled to a ketubah. Even if he dies, the heirs are obligated to give her the ketubah because when he married her, there was nothing she could inform him of, and it turns out that the ketubah document is a binding obligation. Furthermore, even after his death, it was not clarified that he died because of her. They only prohibit her from remarrying due to a potential danger. How can we negate her definite obligation due to a mere concern, especially when she did not transgress at all? However, from the third marriage, even according to the Rambam who is lenient in this matter, she is not entitled to a ketubah if she did not inform him she had two previous husbands. For certainly, since he cares about this, and the matter is mentioned in the Gemara, it is a clear case of a mistaken transaction, and she deceitfully obtained the ketubah from him. It is possible that he can even force her to accept a divorce, and if not, he is permitted to marry another woman. But this requires further halachic clarification. [As mentioned above, this clarifies what the Beit Shmuel questioned, and it seems to me that this is the intention of the Bach. See there.]

Some say that similarly, a woman who has been divorced twice should not be married because her fortune caused her to be divorced. However, others say that there is no concern about this – and this is the main ruling, as in matters that come about through human action and choice, the concept of fortune does not apply at all. There are clear proofs that there is no concern at all regarding divorce. It also appears that if there was an interruption by a man from whom she was divorced between the two men who died, there is no concern of her being a "fatal woman" anymore. [This is also implied by Rivan in Tosafot to Ketubot 43].

A man who had two or more wives die on him – the Rosh, of blessed memory, ruled that there is no concern in this case. For if there was any concern, the sages would not have refrained from mentioning it. Furthermore, the two reasons do not apply here: the reason of "ayin hara" (evil eye) does not apply to a man, and the reason of "mazal" (fortune) also does not apply to him. The essence of "mazal" is not that this one dies because of the bad fortune of that one. This matter is not dependent on "mazal"; rather, "mazal" pertains to sustenance. This matter depends on the woman with her husband because he provides her sustenance. However, the man is not dependent on his wife for sustenance, such that we could say his "mazal" is bad and his wives die. For he can sustain himself without them. There are those who are doubtful about this [see Choshen Mishpat 3], and there are also those who explain the reason of "mazal" to include death, as mentioned in Section 1. According to the Rosh, of blessed memory, there is no concern even if his wives died from the same cause, such as in childbirth and the like [Beit Shmuel]. And it is obvious that when there is a reason to find a difference that does not exist in the woman he wishes to marry, like if the previous wives were virgins and he wishes to marry a widow or divorcée and the like – then there is no concern at all.

A woman who was divorced from her husband and married another man, or even was merely betrothed to him, even if he did not consummate the marriage – is forbidden to return to her first husband. If, after divorcing the second husband or if he dies, the first husband takes her back as a wife and has relations with her – he incurs lashes and is compelled to divorce her. But if he only betrothed her without consummation, or if he had relations with her illicitly – he does not incur lashes, as it is written: "Her first husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after she has been defiled" (Deuteronomy 24:4). The Torah is precise in saying "to take her," which implies acquiring her through betrothal, and "to be his wife" in a marital manner, implying consummation [Rashi on Kiddushin 78]. Similarly, if after the divorce she did not marry another man but illicitly had relations with another – she is permitted to return to her husband, as it is written: "And she departs from his house and goes and becomes another man's wife" (Deuteronomy 24:2). Her becoming another man's wife, which is through betrothal, is what prohibits her from returning to her first husband. And from where do we derive that if she was betrothed to another, even without consummation, she is forbidden to return to the first husband, as we do not call this "after she has been defiled"? Indeed, we learn this from the very text itself, for it is impossible to say that "after she has been defiled" refers specifically to when she had relations with the second husband, as it would be inappropriate to call this defilement since she married him lawfully [Tosafot on Yevamot 11]. Rather, the term "defiled" in the verse refers to a different matter, as will be explained in Section 2. Thus, the primary prohibition stems from "and she becomes another man's wife" – meaning she was betrothed to him.

The Rambam writes in Hilchot Gerushin, Chapter 11, Halacha 14: "Included in this prohibition is that any woman who has committed adultery while married to her husband is forbidden to him, and he receives lashes for her, as it says 'after she has been defiled'—and indeed she has been defiled, unless she was a wife of an Israelite who was raped. Therefore, any woman who becomes forbidden to her husband due to warning and seclusion, if her husband has relations with her, he receives rabbinic lashes. If he transgresses and takes her back after divorcing her, he must divorce her again." This is what he writes in Hilchot Ishut, Chapter 1, Halacha 22: "A man who warns his wife and she then secludes herself, and one witness testifies that she was defiled, if her husband is a Kohen and he has relations with her afterward, he receives lashes for her because she is considered a harlot, even though the primary testimony is not with one witness, she is already presumed to be a harlot." This clarifies that an Israelite does not receive lashes. However, the primary point is that the status of defilement is only established if two witnesses testify that she committed adultery, but through warning and seclusion, although she is forbidden to her husband as the Torah decreed in the case of a Sotah that a doubt is treated as certainty, she does not carry the status of defilement. Even if one witness testifies that she was defiled, one witness is not significant; only in the case of a Sotah did the Torah decree that one witness is credible because the Torah made the doubt like certainty, but she carries the status of a harlot who has strayed from her husband. We have already explained in Siman 6, Se'if 25 according to the Rambam that regarding defilement, both Kohen and Israelite are equal, but not so regarding a harlot. Therefore, it is written here 'when she committed adultery,' meaning there are two witnesses that she committed adultery, the Israelite also receives lashes because this is the primary status of defilement. But when she becomes forbidden through warning and seclusion, although she is forbidden by the Torah, there is no status of defilement on a doubtful Sotah. And even if there is one witness, there is still no definite status of defilement, only the status of a harlot, and a Kohen receives lashes for her but not an Israelite. Therefore, it is written here that he receives rabbinic lashes, and even when there is one witness, the law is the same. But a Kohen receives lashes with one witness because she has the status of a harlot, and without a witness—even the Kohen does not receive lashes.

And similarly, if she committed adultery with the first husband and married the second husband and he divorced her – she is permitted to return to the first husband, even if she was designated for him, since it was without betrothal. And even greater than this, our Sages said that a minor orphan girl who was married with rabbinic marriage to another, and rejected him, and then married another and was divorced, is permitted to return to the first husband since she left him through rejection and not through a get (divorce document) [Yevamot 108], for only a get forbids her to return when she married another and was divorced or widowed. Conversely, regarding the get that forbids, even if the get was not required by law but was given due to mere rumor of betrothal, whether from the first or second husband, and they gave her a get – she is forbidden to return to the first husband, for people do not know that the get was unnecessary and will say that he is taking back his divorced wife after she was married to another. And to announce that the get was unnecessary is of no use, for some will hear of the get and not hear of the announcement. And the same law applies to the orphan girl [ibid.] that when she left with a get and not through rejection, she is forbidden to return to him even though the get was not necessary, for our Sages were very concerned about the rumors regarding gittin (divorce documents) and kiddushin (betrothal) so that no blemish would befall the children. And although the children born from one who takes back his divorced wife are legitimate, for we expound "she is an abomination" but her children are not abominable [ibid. 11b], nevertheless, there is still a blemish of rumor.

In the case of a deaf-mute, there is no marriage according to Torah law; rather, the Sages instituted marriage for him, as stated in Siman 44. He marries through gestures and divorces through gestures. Therefore, if a deaf-mute divorces through gestures and she goes and becomes betrothed to another deaf-mute, she is forbidden to return to the first husband, as his power is not greater than that of a fully competent person, who, when he divorces and she marries another like him, she is forbidden to return to him. All the more so, if she marries a fully competent person and gets divorced, she is forbidden to return to the deaf-mute. However, the wife of a fully competent person who gets divorced and then marries a deaf-mute and is subsequently divorced is permitted to return to her fully competent husband, because since the marriage to a deaf-mute is only rabbinical, the Sages did not institute a weakening of the power of a fully competent person. And even though we are stringent regarding someone who remarries his divorced wife, even if the divorce was not according to Torah law, as we have stated, all this is because we are concerned about the gossip of people who might say it was a complete divorce. But in the case of a deaf-mute, everyone knows that his marriage is not from the Torah at all. Some have wanted to derive from the case of a deaf-mute to the marriage of a minor orphan girl, which also is only rabbinical, that if the first marriage was according to Torah law, for example, if her father betrothed her and she was divorced and then married another on her own, which is rabbinical, and then was divorced, she is permitted to return to the first husband [see Chelkat Mechokek and Beit Shmuel] - but this does not seem correct at all. One cannot compare a minor to a deaf-mute, because in the case of a deaf-mute there is no Torah marriage at all, but in the case of a minor there is Torah marriage through her father. Therefore, who knows if the marriage is from the Torah or rabbinical? It is not less than a divorce that involves a rumor. This is also implied by what will be explained in Siman 155 [and so writes the Beit Meir]. And regarding the law of living with one’s divorced wife in the same alley or courtyard, it will be explained, with God's help, in Siman 119. And know that in any case where there is no marriage at all, even rabbinically, like in the case of an insane person, if she marries him and gets divorced and then marries a fully competent person and gets divorced, she is permitted to return to the insane person [Beit Shmuel], because everyone knows that there is no name of marriage and divorce here, and it is just as promiscuity [and the Raavad in Chapter 11 of Gittin disagrees in the case of a deaf-mute, depending on the version in the Jerusalem Talmud, see Maggid Mishneh and Me'irat Einayim].

The Sages of blessed memory said (Gittin 45b) that one who divorces his wife because of a bad reputation, or because she is promiscuous with vows (and due to the sin of vows, children die in their youth (Shabbat 32b)), or because she appears to be an ailonit (a woman who cannot bear children) – he may never take her back. The reason is that the Sages were concerned that it might later be revealed that the bad reputation was false, the vow could be annulled, or she is not an ailonit, and in the meantime, she marries another and it casts doubt on the validity of the get (divorce document). He might say, "Had I known the truth, I would never have divorced her, even if I were given a hundred maneh," and the get would be considered a mistake, casting doubt on the legitimacy of the children from the second husband, making them mamzerim (illegitimate). And even though according to the letter of the law this is not an issue, because he did not explicitly say, "I divorce you on the condition that the bad reputation is true," or "on the condition that the vow cannot be annulled," or "on the condition that you are an ailonit" (Tosafot there 46a), and even though one might argue that it is obvious to all that his intent was clear that he is divorcing her for these reasons, nevertheless, we hold that revealing one's intent regarding a get is not effective, as stated in section 141. In these matters, the Sages were concerned about the potential illegitimacy of the children, as stated in section 3. Therefore, they say to him, "Be aware that one who divorces his wife for these reasons is forbidden to take her back forever," and consequently, it will be impossible for him to cast doubt, for everyone will see that he divorced her with full intent, not wanting her (and this is what Rashi means there in the commentary, explaining the reason that revealing his intent to everyone will not cast doubt, in accordance with Tosafot, and examine carefully).

According to the Rosh and the Tur, this only applies if, at the time of the divorce, he said to her, "I am divorcing you because of a bad reputation," and he repeated the matter by saying that if it were not for the bad reputation, he would not be divorcing her. The same applies to a vow or being an aylonit (a woman who cannot conceive); in such cases, if he is allowed to take her back, it would be a disgrace, as mentioned. But if he did not say to her, "I am divorcing you because of a bad reputation," he cannot cause any disgrace at all. Therefore, there is no concern even if he is allowed to take her back. Even if he said it but did not repeat it, there is no disgrace, for we hold that in all conditions, a double condition is required, and if he did not repeat it, the condition is null and the act is valid, as explained in Siman 38. Thus, even in a proper condition, if he did not double it, it has no substance, and all the more so in mere words, if he said it but did not repeat it—it is meaningless and does not cause disgrace. However, in a proper condition, it cannot be said here that if he explicitly conditioned that if the bad reputation is false, the divorce would not be valid, what good would it do if we say he should not take her back? In the end, she remains a married woman if the bad reputation is false. Nevertheless, some of our rabbis hold that even if he did not repeat it, he should not take her back. For although a double condition is required, in regard to causing disgrace, since he mentioned that he is divorcing her because of a bad reputation, it will cause disgrace even if he did not repeat the matter. Moreover, regarding the fundamental law of a double condition, many of the Geonim believe that it is only required as a stringency [the Gra], and not as a leniency, as mentioned in Choshen Mishpat Siman 207 and will be explained in Siman 38 [and the Rosh and the Tur do not hold this view, as mentioned there].

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, in Chapter 10 of Hilchot Gerushin, was even more stringent in this matter, that even if he did not tell her at all that he is divorcing her due to a bad reputation, he should not take her back, because of the suspicion. The Sages required him, in the case of a bad reputation or a vow, to say that he is divorcing her because of this, in order to chastise her so that she will not be accustomed to this behavior. And the court tells him, "Know that you will never take her back," and consequently, he resolves in his heart to divorce her in any case. And why do they tell him this? So that he will not cast suspicion, as was said to the earlier opinions. But in the case of an ailonit (a woman who cannot bear children), the Rambam did not mention that he should tell her, and it seems his reasoning is that this is evident and known to all when a man divorces his wife because she is not capable of bearing children, and it is as if he had told her. Additionally, in this case, chastisement is not relevant since she did not sin. However, to tell him that he will never take her back – even in the case of an ailonit, they need to inform him [according to the Maggid Mishneh and Beit Yosef].

Nevertheless, in truth, the Rambam is not stricter than the previous opinion, since ultimately he tells her that he is divorcing her due to a bad reputation or a vow in order to chastise her, and consequently, he may cast suspicion. And in the case of an ailonit, even if he did not tell her – it is as if he had told her, as mentioned above. And the Rambam ruled according to both interpretations, which are not necessarily contradictory in the case of an ailonit, and this is not the method of the Geonim to rule this way throughout the Talmud. And the fact that he omitted what Rabbenu Nissim mentioned, that this is only when he tells her, etc. – since he tells her in order to chastise her, it is effectively the same. And the Gra in his commentary elaborated that his reasoning is due to revealing one's intention, but it is questionable since in Gittin this is not the matter, and also the Bach in subparagraph 7 criticized the Maggid Mishneh and wrote that the implication of the sugya is not so. And it seems to me like the Maggid Mishneh, and the sugya necessarily follows the first interpretation, as the latter interpretation has no conflict there. And also the Yam Shel Shlomo in Chapter 4 of Gittin, Siman 69, ruled according to both interpretations, see there and examine it well.

The one who divorces his wife because she sees blood at every time of marital relations – he should not take her back, even if he did not tell her that this was the reason for the divorce, for it is assumed to be the reason since he cannot have relations with her [Be'er HaGolah]. And they tell him, "Be aware that you can never take her back" [Rashi, beginning of Niddah], in order to avoid casting doubt on the validity of the get (divorce document) if she gets healed [and so wrote the Levush in Siman 117].

In all these cases where it was said that one should not take her back, if he did take her back before she became betrothed to another—he should not divorce her. Since this is merely a concern, we do not separate a woman from her husband because of it, as we have stated in Siman 12. Moreover, even if he divorced her after marrying her, they permitted him to take her back initially, for otherwise, there would still be a blemish on the children she bore from him when he took her back. However, if she did not have children from him—he should not take her back, and betrothal is considered like marriage.

The one who divorces his wife because of a vow she made to divorce her – he is allowed to take her back, and the sages were not concerned to prohibit him from taking her back. This is because it is specifically with her vows that he could cause her harm and say, "Had I known that this vow could be annulled, I would not have divorced her," since its annulment depends on the husband. There are vows that the husband can annul, such as those causing personal affliction or matters between him and her, and there are those he cannot annul. Therefore, he can say, "Had I known that these vows are of the type I can annul, I would not have divorced her," and this would cast aspersions (on the divorce). But if it is his vow that depends on the annulment by a sage, how could he harm her? Everyone knows that a sage can annul a vow, so why didn't he annul it? Especially since this annulment involves a mitzvah to make peace between a man and his wife, and he cannot cast aspersions. Therefore, if the vow was indeed annulled, he is permitted to take her back. One should not say that it is the same for her vows, as a sage can annul all vows. It can be said that he cannot force her to go to a sage if she is not willing, but in annulment by the husband, her consent is not required, and he can cause harm as I have explained. Some say the reason there is no harm is that he vowed only to divorce her, and he indeed divorced her; he could have taken her back immediately and did not need annulment at all, so how could he harm her? According to this, if he indeed vowed to divorce her forever, harm could occur if an annulment is later found, and he is forbidden to take her back just like her vows. Some say that there is no harm because he did not say, "I am divorcing you because I believe there is no annulment for my vow," as with her vows when he said nothing. Even according to the opinion of the halachic authorities that no declaration is necessary, there is still a reason that Jewish women should not be promiscuous in vows, and this does not apply to his vow. According to this, if he indeed said, "I am divorcing you because of this vow," he could cause harm and is forbidden to take her back. In my opinion, the primary explanation is the first one, as the language of the halachic authorities implies that in any case, there is no harm in his vow, and this is also implied by the Talmudic discussion.

[A Married Woman Suspected of Adultery, Containing Fifteen Sections]
The Rambam writes in the second chapter of Sotah: Any woman who had a warning (kinuy) and seclusion (setirah) and did not drink the bitter waters because her husband did not want to give her to drink, whether she did not want to drink, or witnesses to her impurity came forward, or she confessed, or she was among those women who are not fit to drink, or the court warned her—since she became forbidden to her husband in any case—she is also forbidden to the man with whom she secluded herself forever, just as she is forbidden to her husband. If he (the suspected adulterer) went ahead and married her, she must be divorced from him with a get (bill of divorce) even if she had many children from him. It was learned from tradition that just as she is forbidden to her husband, so too she is forbidden to her adulterer. And do not wonder—when her husband does not want to give her the bitter waters and she stands and cries, "I am pure, give me the bitter waters," why is he able to forbid her to the suspected adulterer? Certainly, if she secluded herself with him after the warning, she is forbidden to her husband and also to the suspected adulterer when her husband divorces her—this is a decree of the Torah, and the Torah decreed that it is within their ability to determine if she is pure or not through the bitter waters, and this is with the consent of both. But when one of them does not consent, she remains in her prohibition. [Beit Shmuel]. And there is one who says that the court can compel him to give her the waters [there]—but this is not so, because once he says he does not want to give her the waters, even he himself can no longer give her the waters [Magid Mishneh from Tosafot Yevamot 95, and what the Avnei Nezer refuted their proof based on the reason of deferral, I am puzzled, for if he can retract, the court can compel him if she wants, as Beit Shmuel wrote, and this is not a deferral, and investigate this thoroughly].

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes that if a woman becomes forbidden to her husband because of her involvement with another man, she is also forbidden to that man, end quote. The explanation of his words is: The Torah decreed that just as she is forbidden to her husband, she is also forbidden to the adulterer. This is not only when there were witnesses to the warning and seclusion, but even if she became forbidden to her husband through witnesses to her misconduct, as will be explained, she is forbidden to the suspected adulterer [Gra]. Similarly, even if she is not forbidden by law, but her husband divorced her because of misconduct, she is also forbidden to the suspected adulterer. However, in this case, there is a distinction between whether she has children from him or not, as will be explained [see Beit Shmuel, subsection 3].

If the one who had relations with her did so by force and she is the wife of a Yisrael (non-priest), she is not prohibited to her husband. Some say that she is also permitted to the one who had relations with her after the husband dies or divorces her [Tosafot on Shabbat 56, and similarly in Ketubot 9]. However, if her husband is a Kohen (priest) and she becomes prohibited to him, she is also prohibited to the one who had relations with her [Beit Shmuel], even if he is a Yisrael. Nevertheless, if the one who had relations with her is a Kohen and her husband is a Yisrael, and she was forced and is not prohibited to her husband, she still remains prohibited to the one who had relations with her because of his priestly status, as he is not more lenient than another Kohen to whom she is prohibited.

However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 5 of Sotah, it is explicitly stated that even though she is permitted to her Yisrael husband if she was inadvertent, if he was intentional, she is prohibited to him. Similarly, and conversely, if she was intentional, even if he was inadvertent, she is prohibited to him, because she is prohibited to her husband. Inadvertence and coercion have the same ruling, and according to the Jerusalem Talmud, she is only permitted to the one who had relations with her if both were inadvertent. Some wish to say that the conclusion of the Jerusalem Talmud is not so [Mishneh L'Melech, Chapter 2 of Sotah, Halacha 12], but this does not seem correct [and so writes the Beit Shmuel and the commentators on the Jerusalem Talmud].

However, the Rosh wrote explicitly that it is not reasonable to prohibit her to the one who had relations with her if she is permitted to her husband [Chapter 6 of Yevamot 66]. And some say that even in a case where she is permitted to the one who had relations with her according to the law, she should be prohibited to him as a penalty [Beit Shmuel, Siman 159, Seif Katan 9], but if she marries, she does not have to leave him. And know that many of the great later authorities agreed that in any case where she is prohibited to her husband, she is also prohibited to the one who had relations with her. If another man had relations with her afterwards willingly, she is also prohibited to him, even though she was already prohibited to her husband. There are many proofs for this [Sanhedrin 41 and Sotah 25-26, and from Rabbi in Chapter "Keshem"] and some have tried to refute some of the proofs, but it is not a valid refutation.

Our Rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote that although we do not prohibit seclusion and thus she is permitted to the one with whom she secluded herself after the death of her husband, nevertheless, if the one who secluded himself with her knows that he had relations with her, she is prohibited to him according to the law [Ketubot 9], even though she is not prohibited to her husband because there are no witnesses and there was no warning and seclusion, and the court does not have the power to prohibit her to him. Nevertheless, if he knows the truth, she is prohibited to him. And there are those who say that she is also prohibited to her husband even without warning and seclusion if it is clear that she committed adultery, as will be explained, because this is like actual witnesses [and the Jerusalem Talmud may be saying this from a Rabbinic perspective, as we hold to differentiate between the husband and the one who had relations with her].

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote [there]: If witnesses came forward and testified that she secluded herself with this man, and they came and found an unbecoming matter, such as they entered after him and found her fastening her belt, or they found saliva above the canopy, and the like, if her husband divorced her because of such an unbecoming matter, she should not marry the one she is suspected with, but she is forbidden to him. If he transgressed and married her, and she had children from him, she does not need to leave him. If she did not have children from him, she must leave him. When is this said? When the city murmurs about her and the suspected person for a day and a half or more, and they say, "So-and-so committed adultery with so-and-so," and the rumor does not cease, provided that neither she nor he has enemies who would spread the rumor. But if there was no such rumor in the city or the rumor ceased not out of fear, if she married the suspected person, she does not need to leave him even if she has no children, even if one witness testified that she committed adultery with him, she does not need to leave him. According to his method, with witnesses of unbecoming behavior and a rumor that does not cease, she is removed from the suspect if they have no children, but if they have children, she does not leave him. From the husband, we do not remove her at all except with witnesses of impurity, for then even if she has several children, she must leave him. And there is no wonder—how is it possible that the husband does not remove her, but the suspect does, for the husband and the adulterer are equal, for wherever she is forbidden to the husband, she is forbidden to the adulterer as it is said? However, this is with definite intercourse the Torah decreed that wherever she is forbidden, she is forbidden to both, but in a doubt, we are stringent with the suspect and not with the husband. And only the husband can remove her against her will even nowadays in such a case, but we do not force him, nor do we advise him to keep her. And Rambam wrote in the 24th chapter of Ishut that she does not need a warning, for since there are witnesses of unbecoming behavior and a rumor that does not cease, she leaves without a ketubah. And more than this, it is explicitly understood there that it does not require a rumor that does not cease, but with witnesses of unbecoming behavior alone, she leaves without a ketubah. And there are many kinds of unbecoming behavior: when she secluded herself with him and they stayed long enough for impurity, and witnesses saw the unbecoming matter, such as she stood up from the bed and put on her trousers or fastened her belt, or they found fresh saliva above the bed, indicating that during the act she spat above the bed, even though it could be attributed to when she had intercourse with her husband, nevertheless, since it is fresh, it appears to have been when she was with the suspect. Similarly, if they saw the place of the shoes turned over by the bed indicating they removed their shoes and lay together in the bed, or they were coming out of a dark place, or they were pulling each other out of a pit indicating they were there and had intercourse, and the like, or they saw him kissing her on the mouth, or they saw them kissing each other, or they entered one after the other and locked the doors with a lock, and similar matters according to the observation of the court. And this is the opinion of Rif, Rambam, R"T, BeHa"G, Rashba, and the Itur.

Some of our rabbis hold that in this case, the husband and the suspected adulterer are equal: if there are witnesses of inappropriate behavior and a persistent rumor, she is also removed from the husband if they have no children. However, in one of these alone, either just witnesses of inappropriate behavior or just a persistent rumor, she is not removed from the suspected adulterer even if they have no children, but initially, it is forbidden for him to marry her. Even if there is merely a general suspicion, he should not marry her initially. However, if the rumor is due to enemies, it is meaningless, and even initially, she is permitted to the suspected adulterer according to all opinions. Know that whenever we mention witnesses of inappropriate behavior and a persistent rumor, it means that the rumor must not be due to the witnesses of inappropriate behavior, for otherwise, it is considered one matter. Some of our rabbis hold that with witnesses of inappropriate behavior, she is removed even from the husband but not with a persistent rumor, and from the suspected adulterer, she is removed with either one of them. If they have children, she is not removed neither from the husband nor from the suspected adulterer even with both of these factors. Some of our rabbis hold that even from the husband she is removed with either one of them if they have no children, as these opinions hold that these matters are close to being considered as witnesses of defilement. Since the witnesses or the husband himself have seen this disgraceful matter, she must be separated from him. Only if they have children, there is concern for the children's reputation, and they are presumed to be legitimate, as most relations are assumed to be with the husband. Therefore, we do not require her to leave to avoid casting aspersions on the children. Only with witnesses of defilement does she have to leave even if they have children, and similarly if the husband himself saw the defilement, as this is the Torah's decree. The primary ruling follows the first opinion in the previous section. However, according to all opinions, even in a place where the husband is not required to divorce her and he does so, it is forbidden for the suspected adulterer to marry her. If the husband divorced her based on a persistent rumor or witnesses of inappropriate behavior, and the suspected adulterer married her and they have no children, she is removed from him as well. This is also the ruling of our master, the Rema. Some say that with witnesses of inappropriate behavior she is removed, but not with a persistent rumor, according to those opinions that do not remove her with either one of them, as a persistent rumor is not considered significant even if the husband divorced her. Know that a persistent rumor is considered as such even if it was not confirmed in a court. Witnesses of inappropriate behavior must be valid and not those disqualified by Torah law from testifying in matters of immorality. A single witness regarding an inappropriate act is meaningless, for even if she indeed defiled herself, it is nothing. However, with actual defilement, if the witness is credible to the husband, the husband must be concerned about his testimony. But a single witness of inappropriate behavior is meaningless, and she is even permitted to the suspected adulterer. Nevertheless, with a persistent rumor, even those who permit with just a persistent rumor still require concern if there is also a witness of inappropriate behavior, and even if the witnesses are disqualified in matters of immorality.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: Two witnesses to an act of impropriety can combine their testimonies even if they saw the act at different times, and the impropriety seen by one was not seen by the other. And even though this is called "separate testimony," and in capital cases, such testimony is not valid as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 30, nevertheless, since in monetary cases such testimony is valid, we rule in this matter as we do in monetary cases because matters of prohibition are equated with monetary matters. And although it will be explained that for interrogation and investigation, we compare to capital cases because, from the Torah, even in monetary matters, interrogation, and investigation are required, and it was only abolished due to the concern of closing the door to loans, hence in matters of prohibition, we uphold the law, which is not the case with separate testimony. And even though for marriage witnesses do not combine as stated in Siman 46, that is because when they do not see together, they do not intend for the sake of marriage, and this does not apply in matters of prohibition. There are those who disagree and hold that even in matters of prohibition, separate testimony is invalid, and Rabbeinu the Rema did not bring this opinion at all, and Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef ruled accordingly in his great work in Choshen Mishpat there. Similarly, two witnesses to impurity combine even though the impurity seen by one was not seen by the other, and even though some of the great authorities hold that a woman should not be prohibited to her husband based on separate testimony, nevertheless, since our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, ruled this way, and so did the Maharshal and many of the later authorities, we hold this way in law and practice. Additionally, the disqualification of separate testimony in capital cases is derived from "he shall not be put to death on the testimony of one witness", which cannot be interpreted literally to mean there is only one witness since another verse states, "on the testimony of two witnesses the dead shall be put to death," but rather it refers to separate testimony. We do not derive monetary matters from this since in monetary matters one witness is effective for an oath, which leads to monetary payment, and in matters of adultery, one witness is also effective for a Sotah, hence we cannot disqualify separate testimony in matters of adultery even if we say it is ineffective for divorce and marriage. And even though for the heifer whose neck is broken, one witness is effective, this is not related to capital cases. (The explanation of the Jerusalem Talmud in the first chapter of Sotah does not distinguish between warning and seclusion as the Kesef Mishneh wrote, rather it infers from seclusion to warning and concludes that it depends on the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Sages, and the law follows Rabbi Akiva, and it applies to both, and see further).

There is much to scrutinize regarding what is considered an improper act, for seclusion alone does not render her forbidden even if they secluded themselves for the purpose of immorality, as seclusion alone does not prohibit. Likewise, mere suspicion does not prohibit when it comes to seclusion alone. However, if they locked the door – this is certainly considered an improper act [Bava Metzia]. The Maharshal wrote: if they saw them lying together clothed, as long as they did not see physical closeness, this is merely considered an act of impropriety, for this is not the way of adulterers. But if they saw physical closeness, it is considered actual impurity. Knocking on the door in her room or speaking to her with winks is not considered an improper act, and it appears that there is no general rule for this, but rather the matter of impropriety depends on the judgment of the court. However, the husband himself, when he wishes to purify himself, should be more stringent even if according to the law he cannot be compelled to divorce her.

The husband who divorces his wife due to an inappropriate matter, the one who was suspected should not marry her initially, even if after her divorce from her husband she marries another and is subsequently divorced from him. Even according to those who rule that we do not prohibit based on an inappropriate matter alone, even regarding the one suspected. And if she marries - she should not be divorced, even according to those who rule that we do separate her from the one suspected if she has no children from him, nevertheless since another has intervened she should not be separated even if she has no children from him. And some have written a general rule that in any place where by law she should be separated from the husband - the intervention of another does not help, but in a place where by law she should be separated from the one suspected and not from the husband - the intervention of another does help. And it is clear that when there are witnesses of impurity that she committed adultery with this one while she was under her first husband - then she should be separated from this one even if she has several children, for what does the intervention of another help with witnesses of impurity.

Regarding the ketubah, the law is clear that in a situation where, according to the law, the husband is compelled to divorce his wife, she does not receive her ketubah. However, if according to the law he is not compelled, but the husband himself is concerned and divorces her, he must give her the ketubah. Similarly, in any case where we said that ideally he should not marry her, but if he did marry her, he does not have to divorce her, if he then divorces her, he should not remarry her initially. What difference is there between the initial situation the first time and the second time?

One who is rumored to have had relations with a maidservant and she was subsequently freed, or with a non-Jewish woman who then converted – he should not marry her initially. Even though there is no prohibition if he comes to marry her, nevertheless, this will perpetuate the rumor. Therefore, since this is only due to concerns of gossip – if he marries her, he does not have to divorce her, even if it is certain that he had relations with her. And if he divorced her – she is prohibited from returning to him initially unless he has children from her, for then they permit him to marry her initially, as otherwise the gossip about the children would be worse. It appears that also in the case mentioned in section 9, if there are children, they permit him to marry her initially if he divorced her, where according to the law there is no prohibition after the fact, in order not to perpetuate the rumor about the children. Just as the law is with one rumored to have relations with a maidservant, so too with a slave who had relations with a Jewish woman and was freed – he should not marry her, and if he marries her, he does not have to divorce her, as we have written.

All those whom the sages said it is forbidden to marry initially – should not live together, even in the same alleyway, and certainly not in the same courtyard, and even more so not in the same house. And it is obvious that she should not serve him in any manner, for it is forbidden for them to be close together, as this would strengthen the suspicion, and furthermore, it is likely to lead to sin.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 5: "In any case where they warned him and he married, it is not considered 'after the fact,' and we remove her from him." This is indeed logical, for anyone who transgresses after being warned is not considered 'after the fact.' However, some have written to be lenient in this matter. And some say that in a case where it is forbidden by law to marry her initially—certainly it is not considered 'after the fact' if he was warned. But in a situation where the prohibition is only due to gossip, such as someone suspected of being involved with a maidservant—it is considered 'after the fact' [Bach and Beit Shmuel]. And in any case where they said if he married her, he does not have to divorce her, even if he only betrothed her and has not yet married her—some say he is permitted to marry her [Rivash], and similarly, the laws in section 10 are the same.

One who divorces a woman so that his friend can marry her, whether he takes money from his friend for this or wishes to fulfill his friend's desire – it is forbidden for the friend to marry her, as will be explained with God's help in Siman 143. This is a grave sin, for in the prohibition of remarrying one's divorced wife after she has married another, there is also this reason: to prevent those driven by lust from divorcing their wives so that another can marry them, and then they would divorce them and remarry them as before. Therefore, the Torah calls this a defilement and an abomination, for there is no greater abomination than this.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4: Some say that if witnesses come and testify that a man's wife committed adultery, they require investigation and interrogation. This is because, according to Torah law, even monetary cases require investigation and interrogation, but this was nullified for the sake of societal order, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 30. How then can we forbid a woman to her husband without investigation and interrogation? Some of our Rabbis hold that investigation and interrogation are only necessary when the Temple is standing and they come to execute her, but regarding the prohibition of being forbidden to her husband, investigation and interrogation are not required. Similarly, in matters of divorce and betrothal, investigation and interrogation are not required.

It seems that both opinions are correct in practice. It is certain that we need to investigate and examine thoroughly to ensure there is no absolute contradiction between the witnesses and that they all agree in their testimony that she committed adultery. If they contradict each other, such as if one says she committed adultery with Reuven and the other says with Shimon, their testimony is nullified. However, to follow all the detailed laws of investigation and interrogation as in capital cases, such as if one witness says he does not know in one of the interrogations, which would nullify the testimony, this certainly cannot apply to adultery. According to those who rule that with witnesses of indecent behavior and a persistent rumor, she can be removed from her husband, it is certainly clear that she would be removed in such a case. Even according to those who disagree, she cannot be permitted since both witnesses clearly testify that she committed adultery [see Noda BiYehuda, section 72].

A clear proof of this is that we do not have ordained judges, and by necessity, we are acting as their agents, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 1. How can we require the full rigor of investigation and interrogation as in capital cases when we lack the essential judges? [This is the intention of the Rashba as brought in Beit Yosef]. It also seems to me that if among the witnesses there is a relative or someone disqualified, their testimony is nullified even if there are a hundred witnesses, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 36. Nevertheless, if, according to the perception of the court, the matter is true, it is no less significant than indecent behavior. Otherwise, any cunning wicked person could introduce a relative or disqualified person among the witnesses to invalidate the testimony [see Tosafot, Makkot 6b, s.v. "L'ashehudi"].

One cannot accept testimony not in the presence of the wife and not in the presence of the husband, for testimony is not accepted not in the presence of the litigant, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 28. Similarly, if the woman married the one who cohabited with her and they come to prohibit her to him, the testimony must be accepted in his presence. However, if she has not yet married him, he is not considered a litigant even though she is prohibited to him, just as she is prohibited to priests because of her promiscuity. If testimony was accepted not in their presence, the court should strive to have the testimony retaken in their presence. If it is not possible to testify in their presence due to some reason, the testimony is valid post facto. Additionally, if the witnesses are afraid to testify in their presence, the testimony can be accepted initially not in their presence, as agreed upon by several of the great authorities.

[Witnesses from a Get and the Death of the Husband: Whether They May Marry the Woman, and It Contains Four Sections]
As explained in Siman 11, Section 10, the Sages were concerned about the appearance of impropriety. Similarly, there are other matters they were concerned about, and this concern applies to one witness but not to two, as the second witness would not agree to collude, as will be explained. Therefore, a messenger who brings a get (divorce document) from overseas and must declare "It was written and signed in my presence"—without this declaration, she is not permitted to remarry—he is forbidden to marry the divorced woman lest people say he had his eye on her and gave false testimony. However, in a case where he does not need to make this declaration, such as when both parties are in the same city and the witnesses to the get are present when the woman receives the get, as mentioned in Siman 161, he is permitted to marry her since her release is not based on his testimony. But if the witnesses to the get are not present at the time of its receipt and he must declare "It was written and signed in my presence," even if the matter is publicly known throughout the city as truthful, he still may not marry her. Similarly, in any situation where he needs to declare "It was written and signed in my presence," he should not marry her, as there will always be suspicion. However, if two people brought the get and made the declaration, one of them is permitted to marry her, as mentioned.

And similarly, a single witness who testified to a woman that her husband died – he should not marry her. Even if he did not testify with intent but was speaking casually, since she is permitted based on his words, there is room for suspicion, as among the public there is no distinction between intentional testimony and casual speech [and this resolves the question of the "Beit Meir" and see "Pitchei Teshuvah"]. However, if two witnesses testified that a woman's husband died, one of them is permitted to marry her, because it is not common for two people to sin for the sake of one, and there is no room for suspicion. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that although this is the law, nevertheless a pious person should distance himself from this, even if there are three or more witnesses. And there is someone who wants to say that this only applies to matters that require two witnesses by law; a pious person should distance himself from this because ultimately she is permitted based on his testimony as well. But in a case where two witnesses are not required by law at all, even a pious person need not distance himself from this [Noda B'Yehuda], though this is not implied by the language of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch.
