If a woman performed mi'un (refusal) or chalitza (levirate shoe removal) before a Beit Din (rabbinic court) – one of the members of the Beit Din is permitted to marry her, as it is said that two are not suspected, and certainly a Beit Din. Similarly, if a woman made a vow forbidding benefit from her husband and he did not annul it, and she came before a Beit Din to annul it based on an opening or regret and they could not find a way to annul it and she got divorced – one of them is permitted to marry her because they are a Beit Din. But an individual expert who can annul vows alone, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 228, who forbade it – he is not allowed to marry her due to suspicion that people might say he intentionally forbade her so that her husband would divorce her. And even though nowadays there is no individual expert, as stated there, nevertheless if she came before the individual expert to ask if it was possible to annul her vow and he said it was not possible and did not convene a Beit Din to annul it – he should not marry her, because she was forbidden based on his response. And in all these cases explained – if he married her, he does not have to divorce her, because this is only a mere rumor, as stated in Siman 11 regarding someone accused of relations with a maidservant. And some say that in the case of a get (divorce document) messenger and a witness testifying about the husband's death, even if he married her – he must divorce her, because there is a serious suspicion that, according to the rumor, she was never divorced or widowed. However, the eminent later authorities did not agree with this, arguing that it is unreasonable to force a woman to divorce her husband because of a mere rumor. Nevertheless, if he was warned not to marry her and he did so anyway – he must divorce her, and this is explained in Siman 12, and similarly if he betrothed her but did not marry her, it is explained there.

Each of these women who are forbidden to marry certain men are permitted to marry their sons or other relatives, as there is no concern that they will be taken away from their husbands for the sake of their relatives or sons, and there will be no scandal at all. Therefore, it is permitted for her to marry the son of the witness who testified for her or the son of the sage who forbade her to her husband, and all the more so to other relatives. Even to those men themselves, if others intervened—such as if after the testimony and prohibition, they married others and then became widowed or divorced—they are permitted to marry them, as there is no concern of scandal at all.

Similarly, even if others did not intervene but at the time of the incident, they had wives who later died, it is also permitted since there is no suspicion. Even in places where it is permitted to marry two wives, there is no suspicion that he wanted to marry this woman as well. However, if their wives were ill at the time of the incident and then died, it is forbidden to marry them, even in places where it is forbidden to marry two wives, because there will still be scandal. Even though most sick people recover, the way of the world is to suspect in such cases.

If they divorced their husbands afterward, if the husband regularly caused quarrels, which led to the divorce, it is forbidden for him to marry her, as people will suspect that he testified or forbade her intentionally and caused quarrels with his wife to divorce her. But if she was the one who regularly caused quarrels, there is no suspicion, and if there were quarrels before this, there is no suspicion. This is not comparable to when she was ill, where we suspect that people will say he set his eyes on her and feared his wife might die. Why not also worry about quarrels in such a case? Because in quarrels, there is certainly no concern, as many women quarrel with their husbands, and we are witnesses that they do not intend divorce. But when she is ill, the thought of death hovers over his mind, and besides, in the case of an ill wife, he has no wife, and his desire may overcome him, which is not the case with quarrels.

The Sages decreed that any woman who was divorced or widowed should not marry or become betrothed to another man until she waits ninety days, excluding the day she was divorced or widowed and excluding the day she becomes betrothed. This is to ascertain whether she is pregnant from the first husband or not, to distinguish whether the child is from the first husband or the second husband. For if she marries immediately and gives birth at seven months, we would not know if the child is from the first husband and born at nine months or from the second husband and born at seven months. They supported this on the verse (Genesis 17:7) "to be a God to you and to your descendants after you" – meaning that your descendants should be known to be yours, for the Divine Presence only rests on those who are certainly known to be descendants. Additionally, there is a concern for incest, because if she marries within three months and gives birth to a son, and it is assumed that he is from the second husband, he might marry the daughter of the first husband who he has from another woman, and in reality, the child is from the first husband and would be marrying his sister from his father. Similarly, if she gives birth to another son from the second husband, and he marries a woman and dies childless, this son might perform levirate marriage (yibbum) thinking he is his paternal brother, while in reality, he is only his maternal brother. And one who performs levirate marriage with his maternal brother's wife is liable to karet. There are additional concerns. (And Rav and Shmuel there do not disagree, as the Rif brings both opinions. See Beit Shmuel and it requires further investigation.)

And that which they decreed even regarding betrothal — because they strengthened the ordinance due to its frequent occurrence, given that it involves familial lineage, and a betrothed woman is close to intercourse. Moreover, even if it is clearly known that she is not pregnant from the first husband, such as if she was divorced or widowed from the betrothal — she must wait ninety days as we have said, even if she is young or old, barren or an ailonit (a woman who cannot have children), and even if her husband was far away or was a eunuch, ill, or imprisoned. Similarly, even if she miscarried after her husband's death, or even if we know that she is still a virgin, nevertheless, the Rabbis did not differentiate in their decree. And even a virgin from the betrothal must wait, and likewise, a yevama (a widow who is subject to levirate marriage) whose yavam (brother-in-law) died long after her husband's death and did not perform levirate marriage — still must wait three months after the yavam's death, as she is closer to intercourse than a betrothed woman since he can perform levirate marriage against her will. However, if a man remarries his divorced wife, she does not need to wait, as there is no concern in this case.

The waiting period for a divorced woman is calculated from the time the get (bill of divorce) is written. Even if the get was conditional or if she received the get after several years, nevertheless, the counting is only from the day of the writing, because after the writing, it is forbidden for him to be secluded with her, and therefore there is no concern. How can it be that the delivery would be long after the writing? Such as when he sent it through a messenger. There are those who say that the counting starts from the day of delivery, and our master the Rema wrote that it is proper to be stringent in this manner, and this seems correct to me, end quote. And certainly this is the case because since we are stringent even when it is definitely known that she is not pregnant, how much more so should we be stringent in such a case where she is still considered his wife until the delivery.

A single woman who became pregnant from Reuven, and Reuven admits that she became pregnant from him, and she went and got betrothed to Shimon and he divorced her, and now she wants to marry Reuven – she needs to wait ninety days after the divorce from Shimon, even though there is no concern at all since she is pregnant from Reuven, nevertheless, the Sages did not differentiate. And it is not comparable to one who remarries his divorced wife, which is known to everyone, but here, since she became pregnant from him through fornication, it is not known to everyone. And one cannot say the reason is that we are concerned that she may have fornicated with another as well, because if that were the case, she would need to wait twenty-four months as is the law with another's pregnant woman, which will be explained, rather we do not worry about this in a Rabbinic prohibition when both of them admit, as stated in section 4, but regarding the distinction, the Sages did not differentiate, as she is considered another's divorcee, and also the distinction, since it is based on a verse, is very stringent.

The one who refuses (ממאנת) does not need to wait, for the decree was only made concerning a divorced woman. And she is a minor who is not capable of becoming pregnant. Similarly, an unmarried woman who engaged in promiscuity, even if she is an adult, if it is not known that she became pregnant, she does not need to wait when she wishes to marry, because it is uncommon for her to become pregnant from promiscuity, as the promiscuous woman turns herself over after the act to prevent the seed from being absorbed and she is not included in the decree. The decree was only for a divorced woman and a widow, even if we know for certain that they are not pregnant. For this reason, even if she was raped, she does not need to wait because she turns herself over. Similarly, a captive woman does not need to wait, even though we suspect that the captor had relations with her, nevertheless, she turns herself over each time. 

However, some say that all these cases, if they are adults and capable of becoming pregnant, need to wait, for we do not rely on the reasoning that she turns herself over, as maybe she did not turn herself over well and the seed was absorbed. Therefore, according to this opinion, a married woman who was raped is forbidden to be with her husband until ninety days, for perhaps she became pregnant from the rapist and the child would be a mamzer (illegitimate). This is specifically if she was not with her husband for ninety days before the rape, for if she was, even if it is known that she is pregnant, we attribute it to her husband. It appears that this is only if she was with her husband recently, but if two months have passed since she was with her husband, she needs to wait, for it is possible to determine if she is not visibly pregnant a month after the rape, then she is not pregnant from her husband. And if she becomes visibly pregnant three months after the promiscuity, it is clear that she became pregnant from the adulterer. If we permit her immediately, it will not be clarified and we will attribute it to the husband.

A maidservant and a convert in ancient times, when they were designated for their masters during their gentile and servitude status, and they converted and were freed – they must wait even according to the first opinion in the previous section, and even if she does not wish to marry another but remains with her previous master – they must wait to distinguish between seed sown in holiness and previous seed.

And similarly, a Jewish man who has kept an unmarried Jewish woman as his designated concubine, and she wishes to marry another man—she must wait according to all opinions, even though this is considered licentiousness. For she is regarded by him as his complete wife, and it is likely that she is pregnant. If it is known that she is pregnant by him, and she was betrothed to another and then divorced, and she wishes to marry the first man—she does not need to wait, similar to the law of remarrying one's divorced wife [Chumash]. Nevertheless, if it is not known that she is pregnant by the first man—she must wait, as her case is not entirely similar to remarrying one's divorced wife. Otherwise, we would prohibit her to the first man as in the case of remarrying one's divorced wife after she was betrothed to another, which is forbidden to take her back. However, if she is pregnant by him—she is permitted [in my opinion]. And this is not similar to the law in section 4, for here, since it was public knowledge that she was designated for him, it is considered known to all that she became pregnant by him. And some say that it is similar to that law and she is forbidden without waiting even if it is known that she became pregnant [Yeshuot Yaakov and Beit Meir]. And it appears to me that the primary opinion is the first one for the reason we explained.

A woman who married by mistake and it becomes known that she is forbidden to the one she married, and the court removes her from him—if she is of age and capable of conceiving, she is forbidden to marry or return to her first husband without waiting ninety days in order to know whether she is pregnant from the one she mistakenly married. Even according to the first opinion in section 5, which states that in cases of promiscuity there is no need to wait, here it is different because she did not intend to act promiscuously and thought she was marrying legally, and she does not change her status. However, if she is a minor and not capable of conceiving, there is no need to wait. And even though we do not differentiate between an adult and a minor in terms of recognition as mentioned, in this case, since it is uncommon for her to marry by mistake, and anything uncommon the Rabbis did not decree upon, since there is no concern in the main matter.

A woman who was divorced and a flaw was found in the get (divorce document), and she was then divorced with another get, must wait three months from the time of the second get. If there was no flaw but merely a rumor of a flaw, and they required a second get because of the suspicion – some say that she also needs to wait from the second get, as the decree does not differentiate in this matter, and some say that in such a case, she does not need to wait from the second get but rather from the first get, as she is considered already divorced since she was divorced with a valid get. Nevertheless, it is proper to be concerned for the first opinion unless there are additional factors that make waiting impossible [Beit Shmuel]. Similarly, if she was divorced because of a mere rumor of betrothal, if the court required her to be divorced – she is considered divorced and must wait. However, if he divorced her on his own without the court's instruction – she does not need to wait [Beit Shmuel] if the court would not have required a get, such as when the rumor does not necessitate concern according to the law, as she is not considered divorced regarding the matter of waiting.

Even though the Sages prohibited getting married within the days of discernment (the waiting period), nevertheless, it is permitted to become betrothed, and writing the conditions (Tena'im) is of no consequence and is not comparable to betrothal. However, our master the Beit Yosef wrote that the betrothed should be made to swear not to enter the house of the betrothed until after the days of discernment, so that they do not come to a stumbling block. And even though if we were to be concerned about this, we would have to make everyone who becomes betrothed swear so they do not come to illicit relations, nevertheless, regarding the prohibition of discernment, one should be more stringent. However, from the words of our master the Rema, it seems that there is no need to swear; rather, it is sufficient to tell him that it is forbidden to enter her house until the days of discernment have passed. But from the words of the later authorities, it seems that they did not consider this a dispute and ruled that one must swear. And some say that even in the case of the twenty-four months of nursing another's child, the betrothed must swear not to enter her house for all twenty-four months (Chochmat Adam), but there are distinctions in this matter, and one should not learn from the discernment period, which is much stricter because it involves family lineage and is supported by a verse, unlike the nursing period of another, which does not require an oath. Entering her house with a guard is permitted even during the discernment period (Nodah B'Yehuda). However, if he swore generally not to enter her house, it is forbidden to enter even with a guard. And it seems to me that nowadays, the custom is not to make them swear even during the discernment period, and it seems that they rely on our master the Rema, who omitted the oath. (And the Beit Meir also wrote that nowadays there is no need to swear, see there).

The Sages further decreed that any woman who has been divorced or widowed and remains pregnant or nursing is forbidden to marry or even to become betrothed to another man until twenty-four months have passed, which is the time most infants nurse. The reason for this decree is that the Sages understood the mindset of women who are eager to marry a man, and if we permit her to marry before this time, she will employ various tactics to wean the child prematurely, putting the child in danger. Even if she marries and conceives again, her milk may spoil, causing her to wean the child prematurely and putting the child in danger. Therefore, they closed off this path so that she would not think about another man and would nurse the child properly. They also prohibited betrothal to distance her from marriage, similar to the decree regarding distinguishing between children. Additionally, from the outset of the law, betrothal is prohibited for the first reason we mentioned, that by this means she will wean the child prematurely. [This reason is written by the Rosh in the fifth chapter of Ketubot, siman 20, and this also reconciles what is in Yevamot, page 42, where the prohibition is linked to the one who marries, and in the name of the second reason, and in Ketubot 60, it is linked to her and does not mention the reason in Yevamot, as noted carefully.]

They were stringent in this matter that even if she gave her child to a nursemaid, it does not help, because we are concerned that perhaps the nursemaid will retract [Tosafot]. And even if she weaned him during this time, because we are concerned that perhaps she will wean him when he still needs to nurse [ibid], due to her desire to marry, she will do so, and the child will come to danger as mentioned. And even if the nursemaid swore not to retract or vowed before a multitude not to retract, as this cannot be annulled – nevertheless, it does not help, because since it is not apparent to the multitude, the vow or oath might be confused and annulled even without an oath [Rosh], and in this certainly there is a definite concern that she might retract. And even if she swore to a great person like those who walk in the king's court, who would surely fear to retract – nevertheless, it is forbidden because the matter is not apparent. And some say that if she swore and he married her – he should not divorce her since there is no concern with her, and most authorities disagree with this [Gra]. And likewise, even if the nursemaid gave a pledge, and even if two nursemaids were hired – it does not help at all [Ba'er Hetev] for the reason explained, and even if much money was deposited for her it is nothing. And we are not concerned that the woman might go astray, because since the Rabbis decreed due to the concern of the child’s danger – we do not pay attention to all the possible damages that might occur [Rivash].

If the infant died – she is permitted to remarry, and we do not suspect that she might intentionally cause his death, as this is not typical behavior for women. Even if it happened that one woman did so, we do not suspect this, as she was certainly insane [Gemara]. Similarly, if she weaned the infant during the husband's lifetime, even one day before his death – she is permitted to remarry, as there is no concern since she did not know the husband would die. Similarly, if she is unable to nurse her children, such as if she has dried-up breasts or her milk is poisonous and it is known to all that she cannot nurse – she is not considered a nursing mother of another, and even if she gave birth after the husband's death – she is permitted to remarry after the period of waiting. Similarly, if she gave her child to a wet nurse during the husband's lifetime three months before his death, which is the time the milk completely ceases – she is permitted to remarry, as all this is known and recognized by many. Similarly, if her milk ceased during the husband's lifetime and they hired a wet nurse for him – she is permitted to remarry, and she does not need three months during the husband's lifetime since her milk ceased, and the reason we required three months during the husband's lifetime is when her milk did not cease, but they hired a wet nurse for convenience. However, this is specifically when she does not nurse at all, but if she occasionally also gives the breast to the infant – she is prohibited until twenty-four months [the Gra]. And if her breasts dried up during the husband's lifetime or her milk ceased for any reason, if they hired a wet nurse during the husband's lifetime – she is permitted to remarry, and if not – she is prohibited, as she is still considered a nursing mother since there is no other wet nurse yet [see Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel, and examine this well].

And one should not ask regarding this – why in the decree concerning a nursing woman we only prohibited when there is a concern for her personally or when it is not evident to the public, but if there is no personal concern and it is evident to the public, we did not prohibit and did not decree due to other women, and in the decree concerning recognition (havchanah) we were stringent in every situation as explained? For it can be said that in a long period of twenty-four months they did not want to be so stringent, and moreover, in the matter of recognition there is a concern for lineage, and in lineage they were very stringent, and recognition they based on a scriptural verse. <small>[And the Talmud in Ketubot there that raises a difficulty from recognition is not to completely compare it as is evident from Rav Nachman himself who permitted to Rav Gamliel, but rather the explanation is how can we be lenient so much even in a case where there is a concern for this woman, whereas in recognition we are stringent even in a case where there is no personal concern according to Rabbi Meir, and this is the intention of the Tosafot there, and see in Maharsha]</small>.

It appears to me that even in a place where a nursing woman is permitted to remarry, such as when her breasts have dried up or if her milk is harmful, as previously explained, nevertheless, if she is pregnant, she is forbidden to remarry until she gives birth. This is because in the Talmud (Yevamot there) a different reason is given for a pregnant woman, that perhaps he will press and crush the fetus. And even though this reason is dismissed and it concludes that the reason for a pregnant woman is because typically a pregnant woman is considered as a nursing woman, and since it is one reason, we should permit it; nevertheless, the Rambam, of blessed memory, in Chapter 11 of Hilchot Gerushin, wrote this reason regarding a pregnant woman, indicating that he did not entirely dismiss it. Additionally, the Rabbis decreed regarding the pregnant woman of another and the nursing woman of another, and when she has dried-up breasts, she is not called the nursing woman of another, but the pregnant woman of another is called so, and thus she is included in the decree. And there are those who are uncertain about this, and it appears from the law as I have written. And from the Rambam himself, this law is proven, for why would he need the reason of pressing except in such a case. Therefore, in Ketubot there, he only mentioned the nursing woman because sometimes a nursing woman is permitted, but a pregnant woman is always forbidden, as it discusses her, and she knows if she has dried-up breasts or harmful milk. But in Yevamot, it discusses him, and he does not know, therefore they were combined, and examine this thoroughly.

Some of our rabbis have said that a divorced woman is permitted to remarry within twenty-four months because she is not included in the category of "nursing another's child," as she is not obligated to nurse the child. Rather, it is the father's responsibility to arrange for a wet nurse or to feed the child with milk and eggs. However, a widow, even though she is also not always obligated, such as when she does not seek sustenance from the heirs, still, since the child has no father to care for it, the sages made a decree that the mother must nurse the child [Rosh in Ketubot in the name of Rabbi Shimon the Elder]. Many of our rabbis disagreed with this because we do not find such a distinction in the Talmud. On the contrary, it implies the opposite—that there is no such distinction. This is also the opinion of the Rambam, and this is how the Gaon Rav Achai ruled in the Sheiltot. Furthermore, the Talmud [Yevamot] asks why this obligation was imposed on her when she could come to court and demand it from the heirs. It answers that a woman is embarrassed to come to court, and in the meantime, the child would be in danger. If so, it is even more so with a divorced woman who would be embarrassed to demand it from the divorcing husband in court. Moreover, they are forbidden to be together [Mordechai]. Additionally, the first reason we mentioned in paragraph 11 can also apply to a divorced woman.

There are those who are lenient regarding an unmarried woman who has given birth, allowing her to marry within twenty-four months. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote about this that one may be lenient with a promiscuous woman so that her husband will guard her. And although, according to the reasons explained, a promiscuous woman is actually worse than a divorcee or widow, since there is neither a father nor heirs to take responsibility for the child, nevertheless, it can be said that she is not included in the decree, as the decree was only made regarding the wet nurse of another's child where the father is known, but in the case of a promiscuous woman, the father is not known. Even if she claims to have conceived from a particular man, she is not believed if the man does not admit it. Additionally, in the case of a virtuous widow or divorcee, prohibiting her to remarry will benefit the child, as mentioned. But a promiscuous woman will not refrain from promiscuity, and all the concerns will return. On the contrary, if we do not permit her to remarry, the child will be in greater danger because she will not look after him, and she might even cause his loss due to her promiscuity. This is the intention of our teacher, the Rema, so that her husband will guard her, for once she has a husband and leaves her promiscuity, it will be more beneficial for the child than if we do not permit her. [His intention is not for her benefit, and this also explains the words of R’M of Tormos in the Hagahot Maimoniot on the one who performs chalitzah].

And if one admits that the child is his and wishes to marry her, he is believed, and she is permitted to marry him immediately. We do not worry that maybe the child is not his and he merely desires her, because since by law he is believed regarding the child being his as stated in Siman 4, how can we forbid her to him for twenty-four months? By law, she is not considered as nursing someone else's child but rather nursing her own.

The twenty-four months are according to the order of the months, one full and one deficient. The twenty-four months are excluding the day of birth and the day of betrothal, and the leap month is included in the count. The rule is that in a year we do not count the leap month, but in months, we do count the leap month, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 312. Since the Sages said that the period of nursing is twenty-four months, it follows that we also count the leap month within those twenty-four months. Nevertheless, some say that ideally, one should be concerned about the leap month as well, and the reason is that we also find that the Sages said the nursing period is two years (Gittin 75b), and in years the leap month is not counted (Gra). Even according to this opinion, if the twenty-four months are completed on the first of Adar II, there is no need to wait longer because the twenty-four months were completed before the leap month, and we are only stringent when the leap month is within the twenty-four months (Taz). Similarly, in any place where there is some reason to be lenient, we are lenient regarding the leap month (ibid.). Even in a situation where there is no reason to be lenient, if one married and considered the leap month within the twenty-four months, we do not remove or separate them (Levush), as the main ruling follows the first opinion. Note that in any case where it is forbidden to marry, it is also forbidden to marry a eunuch, even though there is no concern that she might become pregnant and her milk will spoil, nevertheless, the Sages did not differentiate (Beit Shmuel), and further, for the first reason we mentioned in section 11, this also applies here. It is permitted to become engaged, but the intended must be careful not to enter her house without a chaperone during the entire twenty-four months, as stated in section 10.

A widow who is nursing her son in a situation where she is obligated to nurse, such as when she is receiving sustenance, can say, "I will only nurse for a fee, and I do not want your sustenance. Give me my ketubah and I am not obligated to nurse." And even though she cannot remarry until twenty-four months have passed, nevertheless, she can refuse to nurse. However, if they offer her payment for nursing, they can compel her to nurse. This is explained in detail in section 80 with God's help. However, if the baby recognizes her to the extent that he will not nurse from another woman, it is obvious that they can compel her to nurse. This is further explained in section 95, paragraph 4. See there for more details.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in section 13 that there is no distinction whether she began to nurse or did not begin to nurse, end of quote. The explanation of his words: Some say that it is specifically when she nursed him during her husband's lifetime or afterward, but if she did not start nursing at all, she is permitted to remarry because she is not considered a nursing mother of another man’s child. To this, he (the Rema) said that it is not so—that she is always prohibited unless according to the details explained in section 17. According to this, a woman who gave birth at the time of her husband's death and does not want to nurse at all—nevertheless, she is considered a nursing mother of another man’s child, and all the more so if she was pregnant at the time of her husband's death, she is prohibited until 24 months after the birth, since she is considered a pregnant woman of another man. The reason of those who permit is because since the Sages said that a nursing mother whose husband died is only prohibited when she was nursing him at the time of her husband's death, to exclude if she did not put the breast to his mouth, she is not considered a nursing mother. Also, regarding a pregnant woman of another man, the Sages prohibited because generally, a pregnant woman is expected to nurse, and this is in general. But if at the time she was pregnant she expressed that she does not intend to nurse, such as by appointing a wet nurse and the like—there is no basis to say that a pregnant woman is generally expected to nurse, as she is not expected to nurse. However, to our Rabbis, the Rema, and the later authorities, this permission does not seem valid.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 14: "What we said regarding a divorced woman – there is an opinion that it is specifically if she nursed him before she was divorced until he recognized her, but before this time – no, because if she wanted, she could choose not to nurse him at all, even for payment. And there is an opinion that a woman whose husband died and left her pregnant and she gave birth and did not nurse her son – she needs to wait twenty-four months, and it seems from his words that the same applies to a divorced woman." His words require explanation. [See Beit Shmuel and Pitchei Teshuva].

It appears to me that the explanation is as follows: We have already written in section 16 that some permit a divorced woman [to remarry] because she is not obligated to nurse [her child], and many disagree with this. Some of our Rabbis hold that if she has already nursed the child until now and the child recognizes her, we compel her to continue nursing due to the danger to the child, for once the child recognizes the mother, it will not accept nursing from another. However, before the child recognizes her, they agree with the permissive view, and this is the opinion of the Rashba, of blessed memory. According to this, it can be said that even those who prohibit a divorced woman [to remarry] only do so if she has at least begun nursing, even if the child does not yet recognize her, as she is considered a nursing woman of a friend. But if she has not started nursing at all, she is not considered a nursing woman of a friend, so as not to create a third dispute regarding a divorced woman. Indeed, we do not find explicitly among the early authorities a prohibition on a divorced woman if she has not started nursing. However, the Rivash in his responsa ruled regarding a pregnant widow who had not started nursing and had hired a nurse that she is forbidden until twenty-four months, because there is a concern to make a decree lest she did not give [the child] to the nurse. This is the second opinion mentioned, and he brought this in his major work. According to this, this decree also applies to a divorced woman, for in principle, since she did not intend to nurse and did not start nursing, we should not prohibit her even in the case of a widow, as she is not considered a nursing woman of a friend and is not generally included among pregnant women who tend to nurse, as written in section 21. Nevertheless, they prohibited it, as per the opinion of our master the Rema there, and the reason is because we decree lest she did not give [the child] to a nurse since this is not evident, as written in section 12. Therefore, this decree also applies to a divorced woman according to those who prohibit it. Even so, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in his major work that he saw authorities permitting a divorced woman even if she had started nursing if the child does not yet recognize her, relying on the opinion of the Rashba, of blessed memory – and he did not object to them [and so wrote the Bach, although the Taz disagrees with this].

Some of the great Acharonim (later rabbinic authorities) wrote that in a situation where it is permitted to give a child to a wet nurse, one must give the child to an unmarried wet nurse and not to a married one. This is because the Gemara states the reason to avoid a married wet nurse is that she might become pregnant and her milk will spoil. Therefore, if the wet nurse is married, this concern exists as well, and this reasoning is sound. However, we do not find that the Halachic authorities have stated this, and on the contrary, in early responsa, it is found that they gave the child to a married wet nurse, and the great scholars of that generation did not object for this reason [Responsa of the Maimonides on Ishut, chapter 24]. Therefore, it seems that there is no strict requirement in this matter. The Gemara questions whether we should forbid any wet nurse to be with her husband because she might become pregnant, her milk will spoil, and the child will be harmed? And they answered that a father and mother are different because if the milk spoils, they will feed the child with milk and eggs, as parents generally have compassion for their children. This is not the case when she marries another man who will not have compassion for a child that is not his and will not provide milk and eggs. She would need to claim this from the heirs of her first husband and be embarrassed to claim it, and in the meantime, the child would be in danger [Yevamot 42b]. The Rambam explains that she can fix the spoiled milk with milk and eggs. Accordingly, this applies to the child from her first husband, as the second husband will not be concerned for him, and she would need to claim it from the heirs of the first husband and be embarrassed to go to court to claim it. However, a wet nurse who is hired and receives payment for nursing, presumably with the consent of her husband who hired her to nurse, as without his consent he could object, as mentioned in chapter 80, since she is receiving payment, both will consider the welfare of the child. If the milk spoils, she will not be embarrassed to claim money from those who hired her, and the husband himself will do all he can since they are receiving payment, and they are like a father and mother to the child. [Similarly, the Beit Meir wrote, and the words of the Noda BiYehuda in chapter 25 do not seem correct upon examination, and so wrote the Beit Meir].

In regard to these two matters - distinguishing and nursing - that the sages prohibited from marrying and betrothing, if one transgressed this, Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote: "If one betrothed within ninety days, he is excommunicated. If he betrothed and fled, he is not excommunicated. If he married within ninety days, they are separated until the time passes and he remains with his wife," end quote. And regarding a nursing woman, he wrote: "If he transgressed and married a pregnant or nursing woman within this time, he must divorce her, even if he is a priest. If he is an Israelite, he may remarry her after twenty-four months of nursing. If he married and fled and after a time returned and lived with his wife, there is no issue. If he betrothed a pregnant or nursing woman, he is not compelled to divorce her, but he should not marry her until after the nursing period or until the child dies," end quote.

According to his words, in the case where he betrothed within 90 days, excommunication alone suffices, and he is not compelled to divorce her. Consequently, he remains in excommunication until he divorces her or until the 90 days pass. Even if they did not excommunicate him until the 90 days had passed, they would still excommunicate him for the transgression he committed [Beit Shmuel]. If he fled, exile atones for his sin and he does not need excommunication [Magid Mishneh]. In the case of marriage, they separate them, and a get (divorce document) is not necessary, similar to the case of a nursing woman because it is a short period [Nemukei Yosef]. It is obvious that in the case of marriage, they would certainly excommunicate him, and there was no need to explain this because it is a fortiori from betrothal [Beit Shmuel]. This specifically applies when she is not pregnant, but if she is found to be pregnant, he remains in excommunication until she gives birth and nurses for 24 months or until he divorces her [Nemukei Yosef]. In the case of a nursing woman, if he went ahead and married her, because it is a long period, he is necessarily required to divorce her. Consequently, since he nullified his actions, he does not need excommunication [Beit Shmuel], and fleeing also helps there since by fleeing, he has revealed his intention not to be with her. In the case of betrothal, he is not compelled to divorce her but remains in excommunication until he divorces her or until the time passes [ibid. section 33], and Rambam did not need to explain the excommunication here as he relied on what was explained earlier.

And many of our rabbis hold that even in engagement, and certainly in marriage—whether in the case of a woman who needs to distinguish between her periods or a nursing woman—he would be excommunicated until he divorces her, even if she is a minor who is not capable of conceiving [Beit Shmuel, section 17]. In the case of a nursing woman, when he divorces her, he must give her the ketubah, and if he is a Kohen, he loses her permanently, but if he is an Israelite, he can remarry her after the required time if both agree, and he will write her a new ketubah. If she says she does not want to receive her ketubah now and will keep her ketubah until he remarries her, she has the right [Choshen Mishpat, section 111]. If he fled and later returned and lived with her after a while, it is not significant, and some say he is taught to flee because our intention is to separate them. Therefore, if he cannot flee, she should flee. This applies specifically if he betrothed her, but if he married her, we do not teach him to flee, and he is compelled to divorce her. If he fled without divorcing her, he did not act properly [Beit Shmuel, section 131]. Some say that this flight should be to such a distance that his return would be after three months in the case of distinguishing periods and after twenty-four months in the case of a nursing woman, but this does not seem to be the opinion of the authorities, especially nowadays when people travel by rail and there is no such distance that he could not return within the required time. If the court did not compel him until the time passed, even though he betrothed her in violation, we do not compel him again, because once the time has passed, it has passed. When he divorces her, she is forbidden to live with him even in the same alley, and certainly not in the same courtyard, even if his intention is to remarry her.

One of the great Rishonim wrote: If she transgressed and married within three months, we examine her with all types of examinations to see if she is pregnant. And even though Chazal said that we do not examine married women so that they do not become unattractive to their husbands, here, since she married in transgression, she should become unattractive and unattractive [Beit Yosef in the name of Ramah]. And what is her examination? Women examine her breasts, as usually there is a sign in a pregnant woman’s breasts. Additionally, there is an examination in her walking, as they make her walk on loose soil. If she is pregnant, her steps are more pronounced than those of other women [Rashi Yevamot 42].

Some say that all these matters apply when he betrothed her intentionally, but if it was done unintentionally – there is no need for a divorce, only to separate them. However, there are those who are stringent even in the case of unintentional betrothal. An unintentional act is defined as not knowing the prohibition. If one of them acted intentionally – they are both considered as having acted intentionally. And our teacher, the Rema, ruled in Section 10 that regarding a Kohen, who is forbidden to remarry her, one can rely on the lenient opinions and we do not require a divorce, but for an Israelite, one should not rely on the lenient opinions. And some say further that regarding a Kohen, even if he betrothed her intentionally, one can rely on the Rambam's opinion that a divorce is not required if he betrothed her. Consequently, if he married her during the waiting period, one can rely on his opinion that separation is sufficient, as stated in Section 25, and there is no need for a forced divorce. [And what the Bach writes in the name of the Taz in Subsection 17, that there is no difference between betrothal and marriage – this pertains to the waiting period, but regarding a nursing woman, even according to the Rambam, a divorce is required if he married her.] And if she committed adultery during the waiting period – she is punished only for the adultery and not for not waiting 90 days, because where there is a prohibition of adultery, punishing for the waiting period is irrelevant.

There are fools who transgressed and were punished for saying that in our times, when children are not nursed for two years, there is no need to wait two years [before remarrying]. Their mouths speak nonsense, for the Sages also knew that most children do not nurse for a full two years, but they were concerned for the rare cases where it could be a matter of life and death. Furthermore, the main reason, as we explained in section 11, is that the Sages understood the nature of women and that due to their desire to remarry, they might not take into account the well-being of the child, as experience shows. If you say that during the time when the child is still young, it is permissible to remarry, she will use all sorts of tricks to show that her child does not need to nurse for more than a few months, and she herself, due to her desire, will imagine this to be true. I tell you a great principle: our Sages of blessed memory, besides their great holiness and wisdom in the Torah of God, were also greater in natural sciences and worldly knowledge than all those who try to challenge their pure words. Anyone who doubts their words testifies about himself that he does not believe in the Oral Torah, even if he is ashamed to say it openly.

[Not to Marry a Woman During His Period of Mourning, and it contains 2 sections]

The Tur writes: It is forbidden for a man to become betrothed within thirty days of mourning. However, if he has young children and no one to care for them, he is allowed to marry even within the seven days, but he should not consummate the marriage until after thirty days. If he does not have children or has not yet fulfilled the commandment to be fruitful and multiply, it is forbidden for him to marry within the seven days. But after the seven days, he is permitted to marry and consummate the marriage, even if he is mourning for his father or mother. After thirty days, anyone is permitted to marry, even if he has fulfilled the commandment to be fruitful and multiply and does not have young children, even if he is mourning for his father or mother. Thus are the words of the Tur. 

And the Rambam permits betrothal even on the day of death, provided that no celebratory meal is held, as mentioned in Yoreh De'ah, section 392.

If one betroths a woman and mourning occurs, and he has not fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation, he is permitted to marry her within the thirty days of her mourning [Tur]. However, if he has already fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation, he must wait until after her days of mourning. With regard to betrothal, it is permitted in any case, but one should not make a feast. In Yoreh De'ah there are more laws regarding this; see there.

[Laws of Forbidden Relationships and Secondary Forbidden Relationships, containing 32 sections]

There are forbidden relationships that are prohibited by the Torah, and one is liable for karet for having relations with them. These are specified in the portions of Acharei Mot and Kedoshim, and no marriage can take effect with them. These amount to 22 forbidden relationships, including a menstruating woman (niddah), a married woman (eishes ish), a male (zachar), an animal (behemah), and 18 others that will be explained later. Additionally, there are secondary forbidden relationships – those that the sages prohibited. The Rambam wrote in the first chapter of Ishut that these are forbidden by tradition and their prohibition is rabbinic. They are called secondary forbidden relationships because they are secondary to the primary forbidden relationships, and each one is called a secondary relationship. There are twenty such women, according to his words. Some count them as 16, and some as 18, and the reasons for these counts will be explained later in section 24. 

The statement that they are forbidden by tradition, even though their prohibition is only rabbinic, is due to the fact that there is a hint to them in the verse concerning forbidden relationships, where it is written, "And you shall guard My charge" (Leviticus 18:30), implying that one should make a safeguard for My charge by prohibiting secondary relationships to prevent one from transgressing the primary forbidden relationships themselves. It is also received by tradition that Solomon decreed on them (Yevamot 21a), therefore they are called forbidden by tradition. 

Marriage can take effect with secondary forbidden relationships, and a get (divorce document) is required to dissolve the marriage.

Some are uncertain if a woman who was betrothed by one man and then betrothed by another needs a divorce from both men. Some say that even in cases of those forbidden by a negative commandment (lavin), there is uncertainty. For example, if one man betrothed a mamzeret (a woman of illegitimate birth) or other persons forbidden by a negative commandment, and then another man betrothed her, whether she needs a divorce from the second man if he is not under the negative prohibition, such as if he is also a mamzer, since perhaps, because she is not forbidden to him, his betrothal is valid.

Similarly, there is uncertainty regarding a secondary prohibition when the second man is not subject to the same prohibition, but if she is forbidden to the second man just like the first, it is obvious that only the first betrothal is valid. Some are uncertain even in this case and brought a proof from Rabbi Yosef Karo’s uncertainty in Siman 42 regarding betrothal before invalid witnesses by rabbinic law, and then another man betrothed her before the same invalid witnesses, if she needs a divorce from both. He ruled accordingly in practice.

However, the main ruling in cases of secondary prohibitions and those forbidden by a negative commandment is that since the Torah recognizes the betrothal, the second betrothal is invalid even if she is completely permitted to him. This is also inferred from what will be explained in Siman 44 that in cases of those forbidden by a negative commandment, the betrothal is entirely valid, and there is no doubt about this, as is evident throughout the Talmud.

Invalid witnesses by rabbinic law are not comparable to all these cases, because invalid witnesses are disqualified by the rabbis for all matters, even where they are required to testify by Torah law. We do not accept their testimony at all, making it like betrothing without witnesses. This will be explained further in Siman 44. But in cases of those forbidden by a negative commandment, where the Torah itself forbids and also states that the betrothal is valid, and similarly for secondary prohibitions, even though the rabbis forbade them, they are not stricter than those forbidden by a negative commandment.

It is not applicable to say that rabbinic enactments are akin to Torah law to the extent of considering her like an ervah (a woman forbidden by incest), as this leniency in Torah betrothal cannot be stated. Nor can it be said that one who betroths does so with the intent based on rabbinic conditions, since the rabbis did not say that the betrothal would not take effect.

However, if there is a doubt concerning a Torah prohibition and another man betrothed her, whether the second man also has a doubtful prohibition or is entirely permitted to her, she certainly needs a divorce from both. It has already been clarified that in all cases of ervah, the betrothal does not take effect, except for a niddah (a menstruating woman), where the betrothal does take effect because she is permitted after her niddah days, as it is derived from the verse (Leviticus 15:24) "and her impurity shall be upon him."

His mother is prohibited from the Torah, whether she was his father's wife or his father's concubine, and even if his father had relations with a prohibited woman and she gave birth to a son – his mother is prohibited. However, if his mother was his father's wife and he had relations with her, he is liable for two prohibitions – one for his mother and one for his father's wife [Sanhedrin 53a], whether during his father's lifetime or after his father's death. If this occurred with witnesses and warning, he is liable to stoning. If she was his father's wife, he is liable for two stonings, for both his mother and his father's wife, as it is written in Leviticus 20:11: "And a man who lies with his father's wife has uncovered his father's nakedness; both of them shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them," which implies whether she is his mother or not [Sanhedrin 54a]. Whenever it says "their blood is upon them" – the punishment is stoning, as we learn from the necromancer and the soothsayer, as it is written, "They shall stone them with stones; their blood is upon them" (Leviticus 20:27). If the father is alive and has not divorced her, he is also liable for the prohibition of a married woman and incurs three prohibitions, and if there were witnesses and warning, he is subject to strangulation as well, for the prohibition of a married woman is punishable by strangulation, as it is written, "And a man who commits adultery with another man's wife... the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death" (Leviticus 20:10), and we hold that any unspecified death penalty in the Torah is strangulation. However, in cases of intentional transgression, there is no practical difference between one death penalty and two, as if there are two death penalties, he is judged by the more severe one. The practical difference is in the case of inadvertence, where he would bring two or three sin offerings. Also, in cases of intentional transgression, there is a slight practical difference concerning his burial, to ensure he is buried among the most wicked [Yevamot 32b].

Secondary relatives on the mother's side include the mother of his mother and the mother of the mother of his mother, extending indefinitely upwards without interruption, because in this generation there is a Biblical prohibition, and they also decreed on the father’s mother, which is similar to the mother’s mother, as both are called “grandmother.” Even if he does not have a mother’s mother, nevertheless, his father’s mother is forbidden to him. Similarly, in any place where they decreed one because of the other, such as the daughter-in-law of his daughter, which will be explained that they decreed because of the daughter-in-law of his son, even if he does not have the daughter-in-law of his son, nevertheless, the daughter-in-law of his daughter is forbidden to him. And for the father’s mother, there is also no interruption, even the mother of the mother of the mother of his father, extending indefinitely upwards, is forbidden just like the mother of his mother.

However, the mother of one's maternal grandfather is not prohibited to him by rabbinic law, only she herself. Similarly, the mother of one's paternal grandfather is prohibited only she herself, but the mother of one's great-grandfather is permitted. Likewise, the mother of one's paternal grandfather's mother is permitted. This is the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, that the prohibition without interruption applies only to the mother’s mother’s mother without any male intermediary. Similarly, the prohibition regarding the father’s mother, which was decreed due to the maternal grandmother, applies without interruption. However, in a higher generation where a male intervenes, such as the maternal grandfather or paternal grandfather, only their mothers are prohibited. This is the approach of the Yerushalmi. But Rashi's opinion is not so, and he holds that any maternal line is always prohibited, even the mother of one’s great-great-great-grandfather is prohibited, as well as the mother of one's great-great-grandfather, and so on eternally. Similarly, the mother of one's paternal grandmother's father [Bach], and certainly the mother of one's great-great-grandmother, as the presence of multiple maternal ancestors tends to incline more towards prohibition due to the possibility of the maternal line.

The wife of one's father – it has already been explained that she is forbidden by Torah law, whether she is his wife from marriage or from betrothal, whether during his father's lifetime or after his father's death, and even if he divorced her – she is forbidden to him by Torah law during his father's lifetime because she is considered his father's wife, even if she is not his mother. However, if his father raped a woman – she is permitted to him, as she is not considered his father's wife. Even if she bore a child from him, she is still not considered his father's wife. The mother of his father's wife is permitted to him even by rabbinic law, and the daughter of his father's wife from another man is also permitted to him. Similarly, our Sages said that two step-siblings raised in the same house, for example, the son that Reuven had from Leah and the daughter that Rachel, Reuven's wife, had from Shimon – are allowed to marry each other. We do not worry about appearances, even though they seem like brother and sister since they were raised together, because it is known that they are step-siblings and not actual siblings.

These are the second-degree relatives regarding the wife of his father: the wife of his father's father, and this prohibition has no end, even if it is the father of the father of the father up to a hundred generations – his wife is forbidden due to the designation of "his father's wife," and the wife of our patriarch Jacob is forbidden to all of Israel because of this designation of "father's wife." However, the wife of his mother's father is not forbidden by rabbinic law, only she alone due to the decree concerning the wife of his father's father, as they are both called "great father." Therefore, even though the wife of his father's father's mother is permitted and we do not decree because of the wife of his father's father's father, nevertheless, such a close relative as his mother's father and his father's father are considered the same by the world, unlike higher up the lineage where generations are divided. Some say that the wife of his father's mother's father is forbidden to him, and even though the wife of his father's father's mother is permitted, nevertheless, the closeness from the father's side is decreed more strictly, and there are those who are uncertain about this [the Gra]. And there is one who says that also the wife of his mother's father has no end, as this seems to be the conclusion of the Jerusalem Talmud [there].

The wife of his brother is forbidden to him by Torah law, whether the brother is from his father or only from his mother. Only a brother from his father, if he dies without children, is his wife taken in levirate marriage. One who has relations with his brother's wife is liable to be cut off and to die childless, whether during his brother's lifetime or after his death if he left offspring. Regarding the wife of his brother from his mother only, even if he left no offspring, he is liable to be cut off and to die childless. We do not find a death penalty by the court for the wife of his brother, and there are no secondary prohibitions regarding his brother's wife. But the wife of his father's brother, who is also among the forbidden relations liable to excision as she is his aunt, has secondary prohibitions. By Torah law, only the wife of his father's brother from his father is forbidden, and her punishment is the same as the punishment for his brother's wife—excision and dying childless. The sages decreed even on the wife of his father's brother from his mother, and similarly, the wife of his mother's brother, whether from the father or the mother, was forbidden by rabbinic decree because of the potential confusion with the wife of his father's brother from the father, as they are similar and might be confused. There is no distinction in this forbidden relation and its secondary prohibitions, whether during the husband's lifetime or after his death.

His sister is one of the forbidden relations for which one incurs karet (a severe spiritual penalty), and there is no death penalty by the court for this. This applies whether she is his paternal sister or his maternal sister only, as it is written: "The nakedness of your sister, the daughter of your father or the daughter of your mother" (Leviticus 18:9). This is the case whether she was born from a marriage or from illicit relations. Even if his father had relations with a forbidden woman and fathered a daughter from her, she is his sister, and he incurs karet for being with her. Regarding this, it is said (ibid.), "born at home or born abroad"—meaning whether people say to his father, "Keep her," or "Send her away," she is forbidden to you [Yevamot 23, and see Rashi in the Chumash, though it requires further study]. There are no secondary prohibitions with his sister, and if she was born to his father lawfully, he is liable both because she is his sister and because she is the daughter of his father's wife [ibid. 22].

The daughter born from his father's maidservant and a non-Jewish woman – he is permitted to marry her, as their offspring are not considered his relatives, but rather hers, as stated in Siman 4, and she is not his sister. Nevertheless, it is initially forbidden for him to cohabit with her, because there are those who are uncertain and say that perhaps only according to Torah law does the offspring follow her, but rabbinically it is considered his seed. Therefore, it is proper to be stringent initially. Besides this, from any perspective, if she is still a maidservant – she is forbidden because she is a maidservant, and after she is freed – she is like a newborn child and it is clear that she is permitted [Levush], and similarly with a non-Jewish woman.

And all this applies to an ordinary maidservant. However, if his father had relations with his maidservant and bore a daughter from her, some of our rabbis hold that she is considered his full sister according to Torah law. This is not only the case if he married her, in which it is certain that he freed her, but even if he had relations with her illicitly, it is presumed that he freed her. Even if he claims that he intended it as an illicit act, he is not believed, because a person would not forsake a permissible act to engage in a forbidden one. The Rambam (Maimonides) of blessed memory brought this view in the name of some of the Geonim in the tenth chapter of Gerushin (Divorce) and disagreed with them, stating that the sages only said that a person does not treat his relations as promiscuous in the case of his wife whom he divorced and subsequently had relations with, but not in the case of an ordinary unmarried woman. See what I have written in Yoreh De’ah, section 267, and in Choshen Mishpat, section 279.

His daughter, his granddaughter (daughter's daughter), and his grandson's daughter are among the prohibited relationships for which one is liable to karet (excision). If done intentionally and with prior warning, they are executed by burning. His daughter is not explicitly mentioned in the Torah, but it is derived from the verse "The nakedness of your son's daughter or your daughter's daughter, you shall not uncover their nakedness," implying all the more so his daughter. Therefore, the verse concludes, "for they are your own nakedness," meaning they derive from the nakedness of your daughter or son. Burning is specified in the verse concerning a woman and her mother, as it states, "they shall be burned with fire, both he and they," and the Sages have derived from this also his daughter, granddaughter, and grandson's daughter (Sanhedrin 75). There is no distinction between his daughter from his married wife or from a forbidden union, even if he had relations with a prohibited relative and fathered a daughter, except for his daughter from a maidservant or a non-Jewess, as stated regarding his sister and similarly his granddaughter and grandson's daughter. One who has relations with his daughter from his marriage is liable for two offenses — for his daughter and for uncovering "the nakedness of a woman and her daughter" (Leviticus 18:17), although some disagree.

Secondary relatives: a daughter of his son's daughter, a daughter of his daughter's daughter, a daughter of his son's son, and a daughter of his daughter's son – are forbidden by Rabbinic decree and their prohibition does not cease even after a hundred generations. Similarly, the Jerusalem Talmud states that our forefather Abraham is forbidden to marry any Jewish women, and our foremother Sarah is forbidden to marry any Jewish men, because of the daughters of their sons and daughters. However, the Rambam (Maimonides) of blessed memory disagrees with this. Most of the decisors agree with the first opinion, because it is implied by the Jerusalem Talmud, and according to the Rambam, we would need to force an explanation for this [see Beit Shmuel and the Vilna Gaon].

The daughter of one's wife, the daughter of her daughter, and the daughter of her son are among the forbidden relationships (arayot) that incur karet (spiritual excision), as it is written: "You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter; you shall not take her son's daughter or her daughter's daughter" (Leviticus 18:17). The daughter in this context is from another man. If the transgression was intentional and with prior warning, the penalty is burning, as we derive from the case of a woman and her mother. However, according to the Rambam in Chapter 2 of Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah, the obligation of burning only applies during the lifetime of his wife, but after her death, the penalty is only karet. There are those who dispute this (see the Mishneh Torah).

This only applies to a legally married wife; if a man has relations with a woman illicitly and she bears a child from him, her daughter from another man is permitted to him. In these forbidden relationships, the term "taking" (kicha) is used, as in "If a man takes a woman and her mother" (Leviticus 20:14), and "taking" implies marriage. Even rabbinically, she is permitted to him after her mother’s death but not during her lifetime, to prevent illicit relations that would incur karet. If the first woman is married, he is liable for karet even if he has illicit relations with the second. With the second woman, marriage is not applicable since she is a forbidden relationship, and marriage does not take effect with her.

Even during her lifetime, if he marries her, he need not divorce her since this is only a rabbinic decree, but he must ensure that the mother does not come to his house. It is evident that if she is married, even if it is a prohibited marriage, since marriage takes effect, he is liable for karet if he has relations with her daughter or mother and all the related forbidden relationships.

Secondary relatives to them are: the daughter of the daughter of his wife’s daughter, and the daughter of the son of his wife’s son, and there is no limit for these prohibitions, even up to one hundred generations. According to the Rambam, there is a limit – one generation above what we have explained is permitted.

The mother of his wife, her mother's mother, and the mother of his wife's father are among the forbidden relations (arayot) for which one is liable to karet (excision). If one transgresses willfully and with prior warning, the punishment is burning, as it is written: "And a man who marries a woman and her mother, it is depravity; they shall burn him and them with fire" (Leviticus 20:14). It is impossible to say that this refers to his wife, for what sin has she committed? Rather, it refers to her mother and grandmother, and the explanation of "them" is her mother and grandmother, and consequently, the same applies to the mother of her father, for they are of one degree (of relation). This only applies to a woman who is married to him, but if he had relations with her in a promiscuous manner, her mother and grandmother are only forbidden rabbinically during her lifetime, as was explained regarding her daughter. According to the Rambam, after her death, they are subject to karet but not burning, and some say they are not even subject to karet, but only a general prohibition.

Secondary degrees of relation: The mother of his wife's mother's mother, and the mother of his wife's father's mother, and the mother of his wife's father's father, and the mother of his wife's mother's father. There is no limit to these prohibitions going upwards. According to the Rambam, there is a limit, for beyond the generation we have explained, they are permitted to him.

The sister of his father and the sister of his mother are also among the forbidden relations that incur karet (excision), but do not carry the death penalty by the court, whether the sibling relationship is through the father or the mother alone. There are no secondary prohibitions involved. A person is permitted to marry the daughter of his father's brother and the daughter of his mother's brother, and similarly, the brother of his father and the brother of his mother are permitted to marry his wife if she becomes divorced or widowed, and their own daughters.

It has already been clarified that the wife of his father's brother from the father is forbidden by Torah law and carries the penalty of karet. The secondary prohibitions include the wife of his father's brother from the mother and the wife of his mother's brother, whether from the father or the mother. Beyond this, such as the wife of his father's father's brother from the mother and the wife of his mother's mother's brother, whether from the father or the mother, are permitted. However, there are those who dispute this [see Beit Shmuel, section 16]. The wife of his father's father's brother from the father, the sister of his father's father, whether from the mother or the father, and the sister of his mother's mother are also permitted. There are several opinions that prohibit these as well, but the previous dissenting opinion is a solitary view. The wife of his mother's brother from the mother is also considered a secondary prohibition like all the other secondary prohibitions, and they compel him to divorce her if he marries her [Beit Shmuel].

The wife of one's son is a forbidden relation for which one is liable to karet (spiritual excision), and she is referred to as "his daughter-in-law" in the Torah. If one cohabits with her intentionally and after being warned, he is liable to stoning, as it is written, "their blood is upon them" (Leviticus 20:12), and we derive this from the cases of necromancers and diviners, as explained. This liability applies whether it is during his son's lifetime or after his death, and whether she was his son's wife from marriage or from betrothal. If one cohabits with her during his son's lifetime, he is liable for two transgressions – for his daughter-in-law and for a married woman [Sanhedrin 53].

Her secondary relatives: the wife of his grandson, and there is no interruption in this, and any woman from him is forbidden to Jacob our forefather. And the wife of his granddaughter is forbidden, and there is an interruption in this, for the generation above is permitted, because it is not similar to the wife of his grandson, where in this generation his daughter-in-law is forbidden by the Torah. But the wife of his granddaughter, where there is no Torah prohibition, it suffices that they decreed for one generation. And some say that also the wife of his great-grandson is forbidden by rabbinic decree [see Beit Shmuel, section 17]. And it has already been explained that the wife of the son of his wife is permitted to him, and the son of his wife is permitted with his wife. And the wife of his brother—whether from the father or the mother—is forbidden, whether he is his brother from his father's marriage or from illicit relations, and he is liable for karet. And two stepbrothers are permitted to each other as stated in section 6. And two stepbrothers who grew up together are each permitted to the wife of the other after death and divorce, and we do not worry about appearances that it looks like the wife of his brother because it is known that they are not related to each other, as stated there.

According to our Talmud, a man is permitted to marry his mother-in-law if she is not the mother of his wife, and a father-in-law is permitted to marry another wife he has if she dies or he divorces her. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is found that a man is forbidden to marry his mother-in-law, and our Rabbis in later generations have prohibited it. There was an incident where someone sought to marry his mother-in-law, prepared the meal, and Rabbeinu Tam of blessed memory spoiled his banquet. Similarly, a father-in-law is forbidden to marry his wife's [sister] <small>[the Gra]</small>. The prohibition appears to apply both during the lifetime of the father-in-law and after his death, but there is an opinion that if he marries her after his death, she does not need to be divorced, and this requires further deliberation <small>[see Noda BiYehuda, Siman 26]</small>. A man is permitted to marry the wife of his nephew or the wife of his niece if they are divorced or deceased, and he is permitted to marry his niece, as it is written in Siman 2 that it is a mitzvah to marry one's niece, see there.

The sister of one's wife is an erva (forbidden relationship) and is subject to karet (spiritual excision), but does not incur the death penalty from the court. There is no difference whether she is a sister from the father or only from the mother. She is only prohibited during the lifetime of his wife, even if he divorces her. However, if his wife dies, he is permitted to marry her sister. Anyone who divorces, even due to mere rumor, is prohibited from marrying her sister and all her close relatives who are considered erva. If he betrothed on a condition and the condition was not fulfilled, he is permitted to her sister and all her close relatives, as with a conditional get (divorce document), if the condition is not fulfilled, she is permitted even to a Kohen. There are no secondary prohibitions (shniyot) in this erva. The Rabbis did not decree a prohibition after her death because it is a significant distinction and there is no concern of confusing it with divorce. All secondary erva relationships, if one marries them, he is compelled to divorce them, even if he married them under duress; once the duress has passed, he is obligated to divorce her. Even if someone ruled permissively regarding any of the secondary erva relationships we considered, he is compelled to divorce her, for this is not a ruling but a mistake [see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 118]. Refer to Yoreh De'ah, section 157 regarding the principle of "let him be killed and not transgress."

This is what we wrote in section 1 about twenty secondary relatives according to the Rambam, and they are: the mother of his mother, the mother of his father's mother, the mother of his father, the mother of his father's father, the wife of his father's father, the wife of his father's mother, the wife of his paternal uncle from his father's side, the wife of his maternal uncle, the daughter-in-law of his son, the daughter-in-law of his daughter – which is the wife of his son's son and the wife of his daughter's son mentioned in section 21, the daughter of his son's daughter, the daughter of his son's son, the daughter of his daughter's daughter, the daughter of his daughter's son, the daughter of his wife's son, the daughter of his wife's daughter, the mother of his wife's paternal grandfather, the mother of his wife's paternal grandmother, the mother of his wife's maternal grandfather, and the mother of his wife's maternal grandmother. Those who counted sixteen do not disagree with all of this, but those ten secondary relatives we counted from the daughter of his son's daughter to the end, they counted as six, and the reason is that the daughter of his son's son and the daughter of his daughter's daughter when counted automatically include the daughter of his son's daughter and the daughter of his daughter's son, for they are on the same level, and likewise, the mother of his wife's maternal grandfather and the mother of his wife's maternal grandmother are included in the mother of his wife's paternal grandfather and the mother of his wife's paternal grandmother, for they are on the same level, thus reducing four from the twenty. Those who counted eighteen are those sixteen and two additional ones according to the opinion of the Rambam, and they are the wife of his maternal grandfather's father and also the mother of his maternal grandfather's father as mentioned in section 5. The wife of his father-in-law is not counted among the secondary relatives because it is only prohibited due to appearance (Marit Ayin), and similarly, his father-in-law being prohibited with his wife is also only due to appearance and is not comparable to other secondary relatives whose prohibition is due to the risk of confusing them with actual forbidden relationships. We counted eighteen forbidden relationships, and they are: his mother, the wife of his father, the wife of his brother, the wife of his paternal uncle, his sister from his father and mother, his daughter, the daughter of his daughter, the daughter of his son, the daughter of his wife, the daughter of her daughter, the daughter of her son, the mother of his wife, her mother, the mother of his wife's father, the sister of his father, the sister of his mother, the sister of his wife, and there are four more forbidden relationships not counted here – a menstruating woman (Niddah), a married woman (Eishet Ish), a male (Zachur), and an animal (Behemah). And know that his sister counts as two forbidden relationships – his sister from his father and his sister from his mother.

His wife went abroad, and they told him she died. He then married her sister, and afterwards, his wife returned. If his wife was married to him, she is permitted to return to him. There is no suspicion that people will say that the second woman was married to him and now he is marrying her sister while she is alive, because everyone knows that marriage does not take effect with the sister of one's wife, and he married her by mistake. Regarding the fact that he committed adultery with her, his wife does not become forbidden to him, even if he deliberately committed adultery with her, because adultery with his wife's relatives does not render his wife forbidden to him. Some say that if the relatives frequently visit him because of his wife, he is compelled to divorce his wife so that he does not come to sin, but many disagree with this. They argue that this poor woman, what is her sin, and why should we compel him to divorce her? Instead, he should be compelled not to allow them into his house.

And since everyone knows that he married her by mistake, it automatically follows that her sister does not require a get (divorce document) from him, and he is permitted to marry the relatives of the second woman, such as her daughter, granddaughter, and other forbidden relatives, as close relatives are not prohibited through promiscuity, as stated in section 16. Similarly, the second woman is permitted to marry his relatives, and if the first woman dies, he is permitted to marry her.
