There are those who say that rabbinically, it is forbidden to marry the relatives of the second woman during her lifetime, as explained in section 14 regarding his daughter, to prevent him from committing further promiscuity with her. However, there are those who disagree with this, arguing that here he did not intend to engage in promiscuity, so there is no concern for further promiscuity, as he married her by mistake based on witnesses. Nevertheless, there is reason to be cautious about this.

However, if his wife was only his betrothed (arusah) and they told him that she died, and he subsequently married her sister, and then his betrothed came back – he is prohibited to both of them. Both require a get (divorce document) from him, and consequently, the relatives of the second one are also forbidden to him, since she requires a get. However, if one of them dies, he is permitted to the other, because in this case, there is no reason to impose a penalty, as the sister of one's wife is always permitted after her death. The Rambam wrote in chapter 10 of Hilchot Gerushin that all these procedures apply, and similarly, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 27 that all the procedures mentioned in the chapters "Ha'isha Rabba" and "Ha'zorek" are applicable. These procedures will be explained further in Siman 17 with the help of God. It seems to me that there is a scribal error and it should say: "that all these procedures apply to her," meaning the second wife, because she did not investigate whether her sister had died or not. This is similar to the case of a woman who was told that her husband had died, and she married someone else, and then her husband returned; in such a case, we impose a penalty on her for this reason, as explained there. But what sin did the first betrothed commit, and why should we penalize her?

And why did they require a get (divorce document) for the sister of his betrothed? Because people might say that there was a condition with the first betrothal which was not fulfilled, and therefore he married her sister permissibly, and as a result she needs a get. And since she needs a get, it follows that his original betrothed, who is her sister, becomes forbidden to him so that people do not say that he married the sister of his divorced wife. However, with his wife who has been fully married, there is no such concern because there are no conditions in marriage. Even if he made some condition earlier, it is certainly waived at the time of consummation because a person does not engage in licentious intercourse. If the condition were not fulfilled, then the intercourse would be considered promiscuous. Therefore, it is clear to all that the second marriage is meaningless and is merely promiscuity. And even though if he made a condition at the time of intercourse, the condition stands, nonetheless, such a matter is not common. All this applies if he married her sister, but if he only betrothed her and did not marry her, a get is not required because no transgression has yet been committed, and therefore, we do not penalize them. This is also the law in the case where a woman was told that her husband died, and she became betrothed, and then her husband returned; we do not penalize her as stated in Siman 17. If one witness is deemed reliable to testify that his wife died and he marries her sister, there is a dispute among the poskim (halachic authorities) which will be clarified, with God’s help, in Siman 17.

And if they told him that his wife had died and he married her sister, and afterward they told him that initially, at the time he married her, his wife was still alive but now she has died – he is permitted to keep her as we have said. However, if a child was born while his wife was still alive – the child is a complete mamzer (illegitimate) according to Torah law because he was born from a forbidden relationship. But the children that he will have from her after his wife's death are completely legitimate since they permit him to keep her.

This which we have said, that if a man marries his wife’s sister, his wife does not become forbidden to him, applies only if her sister was unmarried. However, if her sister was married and witnesses testified that his wife and her sister’s husband had died, and he married her sister, and then it became clear that they were alive, then his wife also becomes forbidden to him. The reason is that the sister becomes forbidden to her husband; therefore, his wife also becomes forbidden to him. For a wife’s sister becomes forbidden to her husband based on what we have established in Siman 17: that if witnesses testified that a woman's husband died, whether two witnesses or even one, and the court permitted her to remarry based on the witness, following our established rule that one witness is credible to testify that her husband died, and we have established there that if she married another and then her husband returned, she needs a divorce from both, and she is forbidden to both. The reason she becomes forbidden to the first is that we are concerned people may say the first divorced her, and the second married her, and then divorced her, and it would appear that the first is remarrying his divorced wife after she was married to another. Since the sister of his wife becomes forbidden to her husband and needs a divorce from him, his wife also becomes forbidden to him because of the sister of his divorced wife. Although there are those who say that when she married based on the testimony of witnesses, she does not need a divorce from him, for there is no concern that people might say the first divorced her and the second married her, and thus she is forbidden due to the wife’s sister, and according to this, in the case of a married woman, we would have permitted his wife and the husband of his wife’s sister, because there is no concern that people might say, nevertheless we are concerned that perhaps her sister's husband will come without this man's wife, and people will say that his wife died and her sister’s husband divorced his wife and he married her, and she needs a divorce from him, and when she returns to her first husband, people will say that he married a divorced woman who had been married to another. And thus ruled the Rif, the Rambam, the Rosh, the Tur, and our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, and see what is written in Siman 159, note 23.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: If someone engages in illicit relations with his wife's sister, and then his wife and brother-in-law die – some say that it is forbidden for him to marry his wife's sister afterward, because just as she is forbidden to the husband, she is also forbidden to the adulterer, even though she was already forbidden to him in any case. And even though in the case of a non-Jew in a similar situation she would be permitted to him, as stated in Siman 178 – this applies to a non-Jew who is not subject to the laws of marriage at all. However, the wife's sister is fit for others, and she would also be fit for him to marry after his wife's death. Refer to what is written in Siman 11, Section 3, and from there also a proof for what is stated here.

As explained, through promiscuity her relatives do not become forbidden to him. Similarly, even if she was designated to him as a concubine, her relatives do not become forbidden, and we are not concerned about a betrothal. Even according to the Geonim, as explained in section 11, where with his maidservant we say that he freed her because he does not engage in promiscuous relations, a maidservant is different because the child does not follow him, unlike a free Jewish woman. However, if there are witnesses that she said he betrothed her in front of two witnesses and they went abroad, we are concerned about her statement and her relatives are forbidden. But if she said he betrothed her without specifying that it was in front of two witnesses, this means nothing, for even if he betrothed her privately, it is not considered a betrothal at all. We do not assume that this was her intention to say that he betrothed her with witnesses, for if that were the case, she would clarify her words. And it has already been explained that even if he betrothed her on a condition that was not fulfilled, he is permitted to her relatives. Similarly, if a father betrothed his daughter without her knowledge, and she was found to be of age, he had no authority to betroth her, this is not a betrothal at all, and her relatives are permitted. Even if she consented to the betrothal, since it was without her knowledge, refer to what is written in Siman 35 and Siman 37. This is specifically when there was no get (divorce document), but if there was a get, even if it was only due to mere rumor and not by law, her relatives are forbidden because of the name of the get, as explained. And in Siman 48, this will be further clarified, with God's help, see there. [And although in the responsa of the Rosh and the Shulchan Aruch it is explained that only her relatives are forbidden to him, it is clear that he is also forbidden to her relatives based on her statement since there is a presumption that she was designated for him].

The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 12 of Hilchot Issurei Biah: A Jew who has intercourse with a non-Jewish woman from other nations in a marital way, or a Jewish woman who has intercourse with a non-Jew in a marital way, they are liable to lashes from the Torah, as it says, "You shall not intermarry with them; do not give your daughter to his son, and do not take his daughter for your son" (Deuteronomy 7:3). This applies to both the seven nations and other peoples, as is explicitly stated by Ezra: "We will not give our daughters to the peoples of the land, nor take their daughters for our sons" (Nehemiah 10:31), end quote. And we have already explained in Siman 4, Seif 3, that according to the Rambam, the verse "You shall not intermarry with them" refers to all nations in their gentile state. Many of our sages disagree with him and hold that the verse refers to the seven nations in their converted state, but in their gentile state, there is no intermarriage at all. Consequently, according to the Rambam, one is liable only for marriage and intercourse, as he holds for all those liable to negative commandments. According to those who disagree with him, one is liable for intercourse alone with the seven nations in their gentile state, and in their converted state, one is liable for "You shall not intermarry with them" for marriage alone. With other nations in their converted state, it is entirely permitted, and in their gentile state, there is no intermarriage, and intercourse would be mere promiscuity. And it must be said according to the Rambam, even though there is no sanctified marriage, there is still a form of marriage (Beit Yosef), and other authorities do not hold this view. (See the Vilna Gaon in Se'if Katan 2, who wrote that according to the dissenters, one is liable with the seven nations in their gentile state only if he betroths and consummates, based on the language of taking, and it is questionable, as they do not have taking, and this is also the explanation of the verse according to Tosafot at the end of the chapter "Haomer”).

Nevertheless, it appears to me that even according to those who disagree with the Rambam, if she is in his house and he regularly has relations with her in the manner of a husband and wife, he is liable by Torah law. For it is explicitly stated in the Gemara [Sanhedrin 36b] that the Torah regards marital relations as being in the manner of marriage. It is strained to say that this is not according to the halacha. Therefore, even though they do not have a formal marriage, since it is in the manner of marital relations, he is liable by Torah law [as stated above and investigate further].

The Rambam writes that one who has relations with a non-Jewish woman in a casual manner is rabbinically liable because of the prohibition of relations with a non-Jewish woman [and some say also because of the prohibition of relations with a prostitute], and he receives lashes of rebelliousness. If he designated her for promiscuity, he is rabbinically liable because of the prohibitions of nidah, maidservant, non-Jewish woman, and prostitute. If he is a Kohen, even if he had relations with her in a casual manner, he is liable from the Torah because of the prohibition of relations with a prostitute and he receives lashes. And if the non-Jewish woman is married, there is a Torah prohibition because she is considered as a married woman, as it is written, "and cleave to his wife" (Genesis 2:24) – and not to another man's wife [Bach]. And some say that from the Torah, there is no prohibition at all [Rashba Kiddushin 21a]. 

And regarding what the Rambam wrote that a Kohen is liable because of relations with a prostitute, some poskim hold that this is only if she had relations once, then he is liable from the Torah because of relations with a prostitute, but if she has never had relations, she does not have the status of a prostitute. And even though it was explained in Siman 6 that a convert is liable because of the prohibition of relations with a prostitute, and a Kohen who marries her has the same status as one who marries a prostitute – this is because there is a concept of taking (marriage) and kinship that is more severe [there], as it is stated "a prostitute he shall not take." 

And the Rambam's distinction between having relations with her casually versus designating her for promiscuity is according to his version of the Talmud [there], but according to our version, there is no such distinction, and even if it was a casual relationship, he is liable for the four prohibitions mentioned. And if he designated her for promiscuity, as stated in section 2, it is a Torah prohibition. [The Rambam seems to have the version that the court of the Hasmoneans decreed on designating her, meaning specifically designated for him. But casual relations, meaning in a random manner, they did not decree. And see there in Rashi's commentary "Torah prohibition etc." and the Rambam explains "in a marital manner" as marrying her in a proper marriage, see there and examine carefully.]

A non-Jew who has relations with a Jewish woman, if she is a married woman – he is executed because a Jew is also liable for the death penalty for committing adultery with a married woman. If she is unmarried – he is not executed. However, a Jew who has relations with a non-Jewish woman, whether she is a young girl of three years and one day old or older, whether she is unmarried or married, and even if the one who has relations with her is a young boy of only nine years and one day old who is capable of intercourse, if he has relations with her deliberately – she is executed because she has caused a stumbling block for a Jew. This matter is explicit in the Torah, as it says, "Behold, these caused the children of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam" (Numbers 31:16), and it says, "And every woman who has known a man by lying with him, kill her" (Numbers 31:17) [Rambam]. And even though there is no proof from this verse, because there they were executed even if they had not had relations, only if they were capable of relations, because all of Israel stumbled in the sin of Peor through them. And the reasoning of causing a stumbling block is not found except with an animal, as it is written, "And you shall kill the animal" (Leviticus 20:15). Nevertheless, the Rambam understood that we learn from the war with Midian that when he has relations with her, her judgment is like that [the Mishneh Torah], and it is a fortiori argument from there, for there they judged them so because of the stumbling block for others, all the more so for the stumbling block itself.

Anyone who has sexual relations with a non-Jewish woman publicly in the presence of ten Jewish men, and it is not specifically required that the act itself be seen by them, as this is not possible, but rather they seclude themselves in a room for the purpose of intercourse – if zealots, who are zealous for the honor of God, encounter him, they should act swiftly and are praiseworthy. This principle is a law given to Moses at Sinai, and the proof for this is the act of Pinchas with Zimri. The zealots are only permitted to act during the act itself, as with Zimri, but if he has separated from her, they may not harm him, and if they kill him, they are liable for murder. If the zealot seeks permission from a court to kill him, they do not instruct him to do so, even during the act, and furthermore, if the zealot attempts to kill the perpetrator and the perpetrator escapes and kills the zealot to save himself, the perpetrator is not liable for his death. Regarding one who has relations with the daughter of a resident alien, the Rambam writes that zealots do not harm him, but he is punished with lashes for rebelliousness. There is no source for this in the Talmud, and it seems the reason is that the primary law is learned from Zimri with Cozbi, who was dedicated to Peor as stated in the Torah. Therefore, with a resident alien, who is not an idolator, zealots do not harm him, but he is punished with lashes for rebelliousness and is subject to the matters explained in section 3.

If zealots did not attack him and the court did not flog him, or if it was in private and no one knows — his punishment is explicitly stated in the tradition to be karet, as it says: "Judah has profaned the holiness of the Lord, which He loved, and has married the daughter of a foreign god. The Lord will cut off from the tents of Jacob any man who does this — awake and aware — and brings an offering to the Lord of hosts" (Malachi 2:12). If he is an Israelite, he will not have a wise person or a student among his descendants, and if he is a priest, he will not be able to bring an offering to the Lord of hosts. Thus, you have learned that one who has relations with a non-Jewish woman is as if he has married into idolatry, as it says "and has married the daughter of a foreign god," and he is called a profaner of the holiness of the Lord (Rambam). Our sages said that Abraham our father stands at the entrance of Gehinnom and does not allow anyone who was circumcised to enter. But this one, who has damaged the holy covenant, Abraham does not recognize him and he falls into Gehinnom (Eruvin 19a).

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote: This sin, even though it does not carry the death penalty by the court, should not be taken lightly in your eyes; rather, it involves a loss greater than any of the other forbidden relations. For a child from a forbidden relation is considered his son in every respect and is included among the people of Israel, even though he is a mamzer. However, a child from a non-Jewish woman is not considered his son, as it is stated: "For he will turn your son away from following Me" (Deuteronomy 7:4), meaning he diverts him from following after God. This matter causes one to cling to idolatry, from which the Holy One, blessed be He, separated us, and to turn away from following God and to betray Him. These are his words. And this is included among the forbidden relations, and its law is that one should be killed rather than transgress if it is in public.

A maidservant who was immersed for the purpose of servitude is prohibited to a free man, whether it is his maidservant or his friend's maidservant. One who has relations with her, according to the Rambam, is subject to rabbinic lashes, and according to many of the early authorities, this is a Torah prohibition due to the verse "There shall not be a promiscuous woman among the daughters of Israel, nor shall there be a promiscuous man" (Deuteronomy 23:18), as is stated in Siman 4, Se'if 3, where the Rambam holds that this prohibition applies to an unmarried Jewish woman, and Onkelos translated it concerning a slave and a maidservant. The early Geonim wrote: One who is caught with his maidservant, she is taken away from him, and they sell her and distribute her value to the poor of Israel, and they lash him, shave his hair, and excommunicate him for 30 days. Do not be surprised according to the Rambam's opinion, how it is possible that one who has relations with an unmarried Jewish woman is lashed by Torah law, and one who has relations with a maidservant or a non-Jewish woman is only subject to a rabbinic decree? For the matter of forbidden relationships is a decree of the Torah, and we have no revealed reason for all its details. Know that this is so, for if his mother-in-law is burned [forbidden relations with her], but if it is his mother, she is secondary to forbidden relationships.

Rambam wrote: Do not take lightly the sin of being with a maidservant, for this also causes the son to turn away from God, since the son of the maidservant is a slave and not from Israel, and it results in the desecration of the holy seed, making them slaves. End of quote. The law of zealots attacking does not apply to a maidservant, even in public, but in the case of a designated maidservant, Rambam also decrees lashes. And what is a designated maidservant? It is one who is half a maidservant and half free and is betrothed to a Hebrew slave – and she receives lashes, and he brings a sacrifice whether it was done unintentionally or intentionally.

If the child of a Jewish woman and the child of a maidservant became mixed up, both of them are considered slaves due to doubt and are prohibited from marrying a Jewish woman or a maidservant. Therefore, we compel the owner of the maidservant to free both of them and he receives a promissory note for their value from both of them. Neither one can claim that due to the doubt, he should not be required to pay, for the master can say, "If so, I will not grant you freedom and why should I lose out for nothing?" If the father and the master are the same person, when they grow up, they should free each other. The father gives the slave as a gift to the son and we compel them to do this so that they may be permitted to enter the congregation. If the children are females, both are doubtful maidservants, and if someone has relations with them and they give birth, the children are doubtful slaves and we compel them to free them. However, we do not compel the freeing of the females since they are not commanded in procreation unless they are treated as ownerless property as stated in Yoreh De'ah 267. Nevertheless, they cannot be enslaved because each one can claim that she is a free woman, and the burden of proof is on the claimant. If both are his daughters, for instance, if the father had relations with his maidservant and she gave birth to a daughter who got mixed up with his other daughter, he has the rights over them that a father has in any case. If one is a male and the other a female, their status is like that of two males since the male is commanded in procreation, and consequently, the female must also be freed.

The wife of a Kohen whose child was mixed with the child of her maidservant— all the laws that have been clarified apply to them. Additionally, both of them eat terumah because even a Kohen's servant eats terumah, and they receive one portion at the granary when they both come, but if one comes without the other, they do not give. It is obvious that if the servant belongs to another master who is an Israelite, both are forbidden to eat terumah. Both are also forbidden to become impure through contact with the dead due to the doubt regarding their priestly status. When they are freed, they marry women fit for a Kohen and do not become impure from the dead, and if they do make themselves impure, they are not lashed due to the uncertainty. They do not eat terumah because a freed Kohen's servant is considered like an Israelite, and if they eat, they do not pay the principal and the additional fifth like an Israelite, since we do not extract money in cases of doubt. Certainly, they do not receive a portion at the granary, and the terumah from their fields is sold to definite Kohanim, and the money belongs to them for the reason that has been clarified. They have no involvement with the sacred offerings of the Temple, except that when they bring a sacrifice, they can give it to any Kohen they desire, even if he is not from the designated watch, as per the law that a Kohen brings his own offerings. Therefore, even though they cannot offer it themselves, the members of the watch cannot force them to give it to them to sacrifice for the reason that has been clarified. Similarly, the firstborn of their flock does not need to be given to a Kohen but rather grazes until it becomes blemished, and then they eat it in its blemished state. They are exempt from giving the foreleg, the jaw, and the maw for the reason that has been clarified, and they are subject to all the stringencies of Kohanim and all the stringencies of Israelites. All the laws that have been clarified regarding the mixture of a son and a servant also apply to the mixture of the child of an Israelite with the child of a Samaritan in all relevant laws, and both are immersed for conversion, each being a doubtful convert, and they are forbidden to marry a mamzer. If they are females, they are forbidden to marry a Kohen, and the same applies to a maidservant.

[Laws of a Married Woman and All Laws of Agunot, with 262 Sections] A married woman (eshet ish) is included in the category of forbidden relations, and marriage (kiddushin) does not take effect with her, just as with all forbidden relations. When does this apply? When it is certain that she is a married woman. However, if there is a doubt whether she is betrothed or divorced, such as if the money for the betrothal or the get (bill of divorce) is in doubt whether it was closer to him or to her, or other types of doubts, or if there are two sets of witnesses contradicting each other, or even within one set of witnesses where one says one thing and the other says something else — this is a rabbinic doubt (safek d'rabbanan). In such cases, the kiddushin takes effect out of doubt, and she requires a get from both men. The same applies to rabbinically invalid divorces; if another man betroths her, she requires a get from both, from the first rabbinically and from the second by Torah law. We do not follow the principle of chazakah (presumption) to declare her status as unmarried when there is a doubt about the kiddushin and as married when there is a doubt about the get. Although by Torah law we follow chazakah, nevertheless, due to the severity of the prohibition of a married woman, the Rabbis were stringent and considered it a doubt. Therefore, when there is a dispute among the authorities about the validity of the kiddushin or the get, it is considered a doubt regarding a married woman, and she requires a get from both. Even if the majority of authorities lean to one side, we do not follow the majority in this case because sometimes, due to the severity of the prohibition of a married woman, we are concerned even for a minority view if it is a noticeable minority, unless it is against a single opinion that the vast majority of authorities do not consider, in which case we surely do not take that opinion into account, for otherwise there would be no end to the matter. Similarly, if Reuven betrothed her with chuppah and Shimon betrothed her with money or a document, she requires a get from both because there is a dispute among the authorities whether chuppah alone effects betrothal. However, if Shimon also betrothed her with chuppah, she does not require a get from him in any case, and only requires a get from Reuven. Further, it will be explained in Section 150 that even in a case where the get is invalid by Torah law and she marries another, and the child from this marriage is a definite mamzer (illegitimate), she still requires a get from both so that people do not say a married woman can be released without a get, as not everyone knows that the get is invalid by Torah law. But a definite married woman, for whom there was no rumor of divorce, we are not concerned about another's betrothal. Even if he betrothed her to take effect after her divorce and then she was divorced, she does not require a get from him, for a person cannot betroth something that is not yet in existence or not within his control, since she was a married woman at the time of the betrothal, as stated in Section 40. If she mistakenly thought she was single and married another, and then it was found that she was previously betrothed, she requires a get from both and is forbidden to both, as will be explained at the end of this section, God willing. Know that in any case of doubtful kiddushin where she requires a get from both, the first man is not permitted to marry her, lest people say he divorced her, she married another, and he then remarried his divorced wife after she had married another, as stated in Section 31. If the second man had relations with her before the first man divorced her, she is also forbidden to the second man, for through his relations she becomes forbidden to the first man, and just as she is forbidden to her husband, so she is forbidden to the adulterer, as stated there and in Section 46.

A woman who says to her husband, "You divorced me," and he says, "I did not divorce you" – our sages said that she is believed, because there is a presumption that a woman would not have the audacity to lie to her husband's face about something he knows to be false. Therefore, if a woman received betrothal from another man in the presence of her husband, she is considered betrothed to the second man, because she would not have the audacity to do so in front of her husband.

However, some say that this credibility is not for the purpose of allowing her to marry the second man or for allowing her to marry another man if she claims she was divorced, but rather to make us cautious and require a get (divorce document) from the second man [Ra'avad, Chapter 4 of Ishut and Ritva at the end of Nedarim]. It is not logical that due to the presumption that she would not have the audacity to lie, we would permit her to remarry without a new get. How can we permit a severe prohibition based on her statement in a matter where he contradicts her?

When a woman says, "My husband died," our sages said she is believed because it is a matter that can be verified if he is alive, and she would not ruin herself, as will be explained. But in this case, where it will never be revealed, it is impossible to say she is believed to marry another man. Rather, the matter is such that, due to this presumption, she becomes forbidden to her first husband if she extends her hand and receives betrothal from another. Although a woman is not usually believed to forbid herself to her husband, as stated in Siman 115 – this is in a matter where the husband does not know the truth to contradict her, such as if she says she committed adultery, the sages worried that she might have set her eyes on another man and did not believe her, as stated. But in this case, where she says something to his face that he knows the truth, and there is a presumption that she would not have the audacity to lie – she is believed to forbid herself to her husband.

Nevertheless, we do not compel him to give a new get, for how can we compel him? She says he already divorced her, and we do not believe her, otherwise, every woman could free herself from her husband with this claim, receive betrothal from another, and force him to give a get. Rather, she will remain an agunah (a chained woman) all her life until he agrees to give her a get, and she caused this loss to herself [Ritva], and certainly, she does not receive her ketubah. However, if she has not yet received betrothal from another – we compel her to stay with him unless he is a Kohen, who is forbidden to a divorced woman, and we are stringent due to her words [according to this view].

However, the Rambam, of blessed memory, in chapters 4 and 16 of Ishut, holds that this presumption (that a woman is permitted to the man she was betrothed to) is strong. This is also the opinion of several other poskim (halachic authorities). The reasoning is that, aside from it being a strong presumption that a woman would not be so brazen as to lie to her husband in such a significant matter where he knows the truth, it is also different from other cases where a woman makes claims to free herself from her husband. In other matters, even if she is lying, she still wants to get married lawfully, such as when she claims that she committed adultery or that he is repulsive to her. In those cases, she is asking that he be compelled to give a get (divorce) so she can remarry lawfully. But in this case, where she claims "he divorced me and I am permitted to marry another," if she is lying, she would remain in the prohibition of being a married woman her whole life, and her children would be mamzerim (illegitimate). No woman is suspected of doing such a thing [and this is the intent of the Rosh there].

This is why we need to give a reason for the woman’s credibility when she says her husband died, because in that case we do not suspect her of outright lying, but rather that she may be speaking based on hearsay or assumption, as will be explained. Her intention is not to marry unlawfully. But in this case, if she is lying, she is lying completely and would remain in the prohibition of a married woman her whole life, and her children would be mamzerim. No Jewish woman is suspected of this.

Furthermore, although she is believed, the court must certainly investigate and inquire from her when and where he divorced her and who the witnesses are. This is no less than when someone claims money from another; the court says to him, "Clarify your claim," as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 75. All the more so in matters of a married woman. Consequently, in most cases, the truth will be recognized and known, and if it turns out she is lying, her words amount to nothing. If, nevertheless, it does not turn out she is lying and it is not possible to clarify, such as if the witnesses died or went overseas, the Sages maintain that she would not be so brazen before her husband for the reasons explained. Even her ketubah (marriage contract) she takes, as we learn from the wording in her ketubah "when you marry another, you will take what is written for you." Since she is permitted to remarry, she takes her ketubah. Some say that for monetary matters, she is not believed.

Rambam wrote in Chapter 12 of Hilchot Gerushin: If a woman and her husband come, and she says, "You divorced me, and I lost my get," and he says, "I did not divorce you," even though she is known as his wife – she is believed, for it is established that a woman would not brazenly lie in the face of her husband. If the husband says, "I divorced my wife" – he is not believed, but we are concerned about his words, and she will be considered possibly divorced. Even if she admits that he divorced her – he is not believed, for perhaps he intends to harm her, or he divorced her with an invalid get and she does not know, or perhaps she would brazenly lie against him because he trusts her, and she does not know the severity of her prohibition. Therefore, we say to him, "If it is true, let us see it now – divorce her in our presence." So concludes his words. [And in the Tur, Siman 152, the version is more accurate, and according to that version, we explained there in Section 6.]

We learn from his words that her credibility is only established when the husband contradicts her because she would not have the audacity to lie in his presence. However, when he agrees with her and the presumption of audacity is removed, she is only believed stringently. Nonetheless, it is possible that this is specifically when he initiated by saying "I divorced you," but if she initiated by saying "You divorced me," even if he agrees with her, she is believed. Some are uncertain about this. Some write that she is not believed just as she would not be if he had initiated. Others write that she is definitely believed, and this is explicitly proven by his words in Chapter 16 of Hilchot Ishut, Law 27. 

In my opinion, it is clear that if both come from another city and say that he divorced her there, they are believed even if he initiated. The reason he is not believed in general is because a get (divorce document) is known by its public announcement. This applies only when both were in the city and we did not hear any rumor of a divorce, and therefore they are not believed leniently, only stringently, and we must consider all concerns mentioned by the Rambam because it is a surprising matter. However, if they came from another city and both agree that they were divorced, even though they were presumed to be husband and wife until now, why should we not believe them? Only in the case where the woman says "You divorced me" and he contradicts her, she is believed due to the presumption that she would not have the audacity to lie in his presence, as mentioned before. Therefore, she is believed even if they did not come from another city. According to this, in such a case where he does not contradict her, even if she initiated, since it is a surprising matter that we did not hear any rumor of a divorce, we cannot believe her leniently. The Rambam in Chapter 16 of Hilchot Ishut can be explained as referring to a case where they came from another city.

And this same law applies if she accepted betrothal from another man. If the husband said beforehand, "I divorced you" – she is not believed. Some say that even if he said afterward, "I divorced you" – she is also not believed unless contradicting him. According to our explanation, we should also differentiate between whether both were in the city or they came from another city, as we have written. And in section 152 we explained that the Rambam does not hold by the reasoning of "kol" (public rumor), see there.

In this presumption that a woman does not have the audacity to lie to her husband, there is no distinction between a betrothed woman and a married woman [Beit Yosef in Siman 152], and there are those who have doubts about this [Ezrat Nashim, and see Maggid Mishneh Chapter 4 of Hilchot Ishut].

If she initially said, not in her husband's presence, that she was divorced, and afterwards she said it also in his presence, there are those who are uncertain whether we apply this presumption, for perhaps because she said it previously, she is compelled to maintain her statement [see Darkei Moshe], and there are those who say there is no distinction in this and she is believed [Beit Shmuel], and this is also the conclusion of the great later authorities.

But if she spoke not in his presence or accepted betrothal not in his presence and he denies it, and in his presence she does not say "you divorced me" – we do not consider her previous statements at all. However, when she says in her husband’s presence "you divorced me" or accepted betrothal in his presence and afterwards retracts her words – she is not believed to retract, yet it seems that we are stringent to be concerned about her retraction. Similarly, if she provided a good reason for why she said so initially – she is believed to retract if the husband also says he did not divorce her, as a valid reason is effective in all matters [it seems to me].

If the second man to whom she was betrothed is a Kohen – her words mean nothing, for how can we believe she was divorced when she is forbidden to a Kohen [Ba'er Hetev], but nevertheless, if the husband also says she was divorced – it is obvious that she needs a get (divorce document) from the Kohen, for betrothal is effective in cases of a negative commandment and she is also forbidden to return to her first husband and needs a get from him as well, for the matter is weakened by her betrothal to the Kohen [it seems to me].

Also, if there is a reason to attribute her statement "I was divorced" to some mistake, such as it becoming known that there was a doubt about the validity of the get or something similar where she accepted betrothal from another and it is possible to attribute that she erred concerning the first betrothal and thought it was not valid – her words are nullified [Ezrat Nashim] and we examine the previous get or the first betrothal and determine the law [it seems to me].

If another man betroths her in the absence of her husband, the betrothal does not take effect until proof is brought that she was divorced prior to accepting the betrothal, because in his absence she might be bold in her assertions, and we do not even consider this stringently. However, some are stringent [Ran in the name of Ramban, Ketubot 2], but the majority of poskim do not hold this way. It seems clear that there is no dispute at all, for certainly if her husband comes and she admits that she was not divorced at all and he also says that she was not divorced at all, we investigate and examine her actions in accepting the betrothal and it is likely that some excuse will be found that she did so out of anger or something similar. However, if she persists in her claims even in the presence of her husband, certainly the betrothal is a concern and she requires a get from both men and is prohibited to her first husband. Even according to the opinion that if she says "you divorced me," even if she initially said it not in his presence and later said it in his presence, she is completely believed; nevertheless, in the case of accepting betrothal in this manner, certainly out of shame she will not uphold her lie and is not believed except stringently. See section 10.

The Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote that whenever the husband is in town when she becomes betrothed to someone else, it is considered as if it were done in his presence. There are those who disagree and hold that it must be literally in his presence. And certainly, even according to the Rosh, this is only regarding the acceptance of betrothal, which is a significant action, but when she claims she was divorced, it must be literally in his presence. There is an opinion that says there is no disagreement at all, for indeed when the husband is in town and she accepts betrothal from another man, and in the husband's presence, she brazenly claims she was divorced from him – this is considered as if it were done in his presence, for she knows that he will immediately come home and she will be forced to confront him. This is not comparable to when he is in another city, and in such a case, even those who disagree might agree with the Rosh. And if, upon the husband's arrival, she retracts her statement – the Rosh also agrees.

The Tur wrote in Siman 152 that when a woman receives betrothal without her husband's presence, and when the husband returns and she says, "You didn't divorce me," but then boldly claims, "You divorced me"—she is not believed, because she is asserting this to maintain her position. Since she committed a significant act, this is like what is stated at the end of paragraph 8 that receiving betrothal is not the same as saying, "My husband (divorced) me." However, this is certainly the case when he was not in town at the time of the betrothal, for if he was in town, it is explained that the opinion of the Rosh of blessed memory is that this is equivalent to being in his presence. If the Tur had disagreed with this, he would have mentioned his opinion as usual. Therefore, it is certain that this refers to when he was not in town.

The Rosh also wrote in a responsum: The statement that a woman who tells her husband "You divorced me" is believed—this applies only before she remarries another man. But if she has already remarried, she is not believed, because she would not make herself appear as promiscuous and thereby be forced to leave both husbands. And the same applies if she committed adultery; she is no longer believed [Beit Shmuel]. It appears that even if her husband was in town, we say that her impulse overcame her, and now she maintains her statement intentionally because of the great shame she faces. If the intention was specifically when the husband was not in town, the same ruling applies in the case of betrothal, as the Tur wrote, which we cited in the previous section. However, from the language of the Beit Yosef in Section 2, it seems that he holds there is one ruling for both, and the Rosh answered the question that was about marriage, but the same law applies to betrothal [and this is also evident in the Beit Shmuel, Section 6].

However, the Rashba of blessed memory, in his responsa brought by our master the Beit Yosef in Siman 152, explicitly wrote that even if she accepted the betrothal not in the presence of her husband, if afterwards when her husband came she brazenly claims in his presence that she was divorced, she is believed. And from the proofs he provided, it is evident that he also holds this way in the case of remarriage. [And his proof is from Ketubot 22b, where it questions "Would she be so brazen, etc.," and there it is discussing remarriage. According to the Rosh, it seems that the explanation is: the law that two witnesses say she was divorced certainly applies in all cases, even when they are in the same city, and in this case, she would not be so brazen. Examine this carefully.]

Some of the great authorities have ruled that if she is married, we should be stringent and consider the possibility that she might lie brazenly, and she needs a get (divorce) from both husbands, and we do not follow the lenient opinion of the Rashba, of blessed memory, which says she does not have to leave her second husband. However, if she was only betrothed, we are concerned with the opinion of the Tur, and she should not marry the second man. If she did marry him, it is possible she does not have to leave him. When it comes to verbal statements alone, if she first said something not in his presence and then said the same thing in his presence, if she is already married, she certainly does not have to leave him. If she is not yet married, there is a possibility that we should be cautious and not allow her to marry without a get. [R. Moses ben Habib in Ezrat Nashim, section 118].

The statement that a woman does not show insolence before her husband applies only where there is no one assisting her. However, when there is someone assisting her, she does show insolence, for example, if one witness supports her statement, she shows insolence. Some hesitate to say that based on the testimony of one witness, she does not show insolence. Know that in every case where we say she certainly shows insolence, the marriage of another man does not take effect with her. Nevertheless, she is disqualified from marrying a priest and from levirate marriage, for she has forbidden herself based on her own statement. And when one witness supports her, she needs a divorce from both men.

And so, some say that the idea that a woman does not brazenly lie in front of her husband applies only when there was no quarrel between them and she is not claiming her ketubah. But if there was a quarrel between them, she may indeed brazenly lie, and her words are worth nothing. Similarly, when she says, “You divorced me, give me my ketubah,” she is not believed even in his presence, and we say that the desire for money impels her to brazenly lie in front of him. However, from the words of Maimonides in Chapter 16 of Hilchot Ishut, it is understood that even if she is claiming her ketubah, she is believed. For he wrote there: A woman who says to her husband, “You divorced me,” is believed, for a woman does not brazenly lie in front of her husband. Therefore, if a woman produces a ketubah but does not have a get (divorce document) and says to her husband, “You divorced me and my get was lost; give me my ketubah,” and he says, “I did not divorce you,” he is obligated to give her the principal amount of the ketubah but not the additional amount. This is the end of his words. The Tur in Siman 152 wrote according to the first opinion, and since there is a dispute among the authorities, we are stringent in this matter.

And what is called "quarrel"? Some say specifically when she has previously been established as a liar, such as when she said, "You divorced me in front of so-and-so," and the witnesses came and contradicted her, she is no longer believed because we see that she has the audacity even in his presence. Certainly, in such a case, no one disagrees. However, from the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, it seems that it refers to all matters of quarrels. The other poskim did not mention the law of quarrel, and therefore, practically – we are stringent, and when she accepts kiddushin from another, she needs a get from both [and so it is written in Beit Yosef]. And know, in every place where we said that she needs a get from both and it implies that she is forbidden also to the second – this is when the first does not want to give her a get, but when he now gives her a get – she is permitted to the second, only forbidden to the first. Because she needs a get from the second, it is like one who remarries his divorcee after she was married or betrothed to another. However, she is permitted to the second only if she was betrothed, but if she was married – she is also forbidden to him. Because she needs a get from the first, it is as if she committed adultery under him and is forbidden to both.

And our master, the Rema, wrote that in our times, when there is an increase in insolence and licentiousness, we do not rely on the presumption that a woman would not have the audacity to lie in the presence of her husband, and we are stringent in this matter. According to this, there is no practical difference in all the laws that have been explained. However, this is not a general rule, for in cases where the court understands from the situation that the woman has indeed been divorced and the husband is merely being malicious and trying to deceive her and deny her freedom, we do not heed his words and she is believed even in our times. Many of the great authorities have written similarly, that in situations where there is a plausible explanation proving she has been divorced, she is believed even in our times. There are those who say that even according to the law of the Talmud, the presumption that she would not have the audacity to lie applies only if she said this in the presence of a court or an assembly of elders, but this is not implied by the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). Rather, even if she said this in the presence of two witnesses, it is considered a strong presumption, for if it were not so, the poskim would not have refrained from mentioning it. However, nowadays, there is no practical difference in this matter as mentioned.

In the testimony regarding a woman whose husband has died, our Sages of the Mishnah and Talmud were lenient in many ways and stringent in many ways. Our Rabbis gave a principle in this matter: They were lenient at the end of the testimony but not at the beginning of the testimony.

The explanation of the matter is as follows: they were lenient at the end of the testimony when it was completely clarified that he had died without any hint of doubt. They were lenient about who could testify about the death, and not only did they not require two valid witnesses, but even a single witness is trusted, and even those who are invalid as witnesses, such as a woman, a relative, a servant, a maidservant, or a Samaritan speaking casually. Not only that, but she herself is trusted to say, "My husband died." This is unlike any other prohibitions, for we hold that in a place where a prohibition has been established, a single witness is not trusted to remove the matter from its presumption, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, section 157. All the more so here, regarding the prohibition of a married woman, where there is a presumption of the prohibition of a married woman and a presumption of the husband's life. Nevertheless, they were lenient in this matter for reasons that will be explained to us with God's help.

In contrast to this, at the beginning of the testimony, meaning in the essence of the matter of his death, they imposed many stringencies to be concerned with even the smallest minority and with an uncommon minority, which they did not consider in all other prohibitions of the Torah. For example, if someone fell into the sea or a large river with his clothes and his trace was lost, based on the assumption he certainly drowned, nevertheless the Sages did not permit the agunah (a woman bound in marriage due to the unknown whereabouts of her husband) in this case. Similarly, they imposed great stringencies in such cases, which will be clarified before us with God's help.

The reason for this is that in the severe prohibition of a married woman, on which the entire lineage of Israel depends, if, God forbid, she is a married woman and marries another and bears children, the number of mamzerim (children born from certain forbidden relationships) in Israel will increase. Even if it happens to one out of thousands and she marries another and bears sons and daughters, the number of mamzerim will increase over the years to hundreds. It is already known in our times of such cases where the husband was not present for many years and his trace was forgotten, and based on the assumption he was already dead, but afterward, the husband came back. 

Such an incident happened in our times in the country of Ashkenaz, around the city of Mainz, where the husband was not present for more than fifteen years, and the wife sought to remarry. The prominent figures of the generation supported her because there was no quarrel between them, and they lived in love. Based on the assumption, there was no doubt that he had died, but the rabbi of Mainz stood firm that she should not remarry, and afterward, the husband came back. Similarly, there were several cases of those who drowned and were saved and came out of the water alive; in the Gemara, there are also such cases.

Therefore, those who speak falsehood should be silenced in their claims that the Sages were not concerned about the regulations of agunot. Who, like our Sages of blessed memory, made many significant leniencies for the sake of the regulation of agunot? Therefore, in what they were stringent, they knew why they were stringent, and one who questions them is as if questioning the Divine Presence.

And regarding the leniency that our sages of blessed memory allowed at the end of testimony, as they said, for the sake of the decree concerning agunot (women bound in marriage due to missing husbands), know that generally it is difficult for two valid witnesses to be present at the time of death. The reason our sages were lenient in this matter is because they said that due to the stringency they imposed at the end, they were lenient at the beginning. She investigates thoroughly and remarries, and a matter that is likely to be revealed, people do not lie about. For if, Heaven forbid, she did not thoroughly investigate his death and he is still alive, our sages penalized her by requiring her to leave both marriages, and any child from either marriage is considered illegitimate. And as it will be explained further, the stringencies that were imposed upon her, therefore, they were lenient at the beginning.

[In the beginning of the chapter "HaIsha Rabba," they said the reason is due to the stringency, etc., and this is the reason why she investigates thoroughly. And on page 93b and at the beginning of the chapter "HaIsha Shalom" and on page 116a, they said the reason is because it is a matter likely to be revealed, and they stated it in the form of a question whether the reason is because she investigates thoroughly or because it is a matter likely to be revealed. This means which reason is primary, as Tosafot explained there. But in truth, our sages relied on all these reasons for the sake of the decree concerning agunot. See there and analyze it well.]

And this is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 12 of Hilchot Gerushin regarding the reason why a woman herself is believed to say "my husband has died," because of the presumption that she would not ruin herself and make herself forbidden to her first husband, and thereby lose her ketubah from both this one and that one, and her children would be considered mamzerim, in a matter that is destined to be revealed to all. It is impossible to deny or claim otherwise, because if he is alive, he will eventually come or it will become known that he is alive. Similarly, if one witness comes and testifies that her husband has died, she may marry based on his testimony, because the matter is destined to be revealed, even if the witness is a slave, etc. And at the end of Chapter 13 of Hilchot Gerushin, he wrote: "Do not be troubled by the fact that the sages permitted a severe prohibition based on the testimony of a woman, or a slave, or a maidservant, or a Samaritan who speaks inadvertently, or testimony from another witness, or written testimony, without investigation and interrogation, as we have explained. The Torah only insisted on the testimony of two witnesses and other judicial procedures in matters where you cannot ascertain the truth except through the witnesses and their testimony, such as when they testify that this person killed that person or lent money to that person. But in a matter where it is possible to ascertain the truth without this witness, and the witness cannot escape if the matter is not true, such as this case where the witness testifies that a certain person has died, the Torah did not insist on it. It is unlikely that the witness would lie, therefore the sages were lenient in this matter and believed a single witness, even a maidservant or written testimony, without investigation and interrogation, so that the daughters of Israel would not remain agunot." End quote.

And the explanation of his words: According to Torah law, there is no need for testimony here since it is a matter that is destined to be revealed, and there is no uprooting of a matter from the Torah. Why then did the Sages ease this matter and not make a safeguard by not believing the testimony of a single witness? So that the daughters of Israel would not remain agunot (chained women). Nevertheless, they did not rely solely on the reason that it is destined to be revealed. They also relied on the reason that she would be careful not to ruin herself because they were stringent with her in the end. This is why they did not mention the reason of being careful in the testimony of one witness, because there the primary Torah law is that due to the reason that it is destined to be revealed, complete testimony is not required. And so agreed many of the great halachic authorities that the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, is that even according to Torah law, it is considered complete testimony because it is destined to be revealed. [And it seems to me that he explains the beginning of the chapter "HaIsha Rabba" that the reason is that due to the severity, everything is included, and it means that they were stringent with her in the end because it is destined to be revealed what happened, and she will not be able to justify herself, and therefore she will be very careful. And regarding the issues of yevama (levirate marriage), war, and quarrel, the Talmud asks which of the two reasons is the primary one upon which the Sages relied, and resolves the difficulty of Tosafot 93: "Ad," see there.] And see what is written in section 231 that many of the halachic authorities hold the opinion of the Rambam that the reason is only because it is destined to be revealed, see there.

And similarly, the great early authorities wrote, and this is their language: The Sages had a clear understanding that in a matter destined to be revealed and where the severity of the consequence is so great – certainly, the testimony is truthful, and if she scrutinizes and marries, she does so properly, and we are witnesses in the matter. Such publicity is considered everywhere as complete testimony, even from a Torah perspective. The Torah entrusted the Sages to determine what is well-known and evident as true to be considered as testimony. And when we say that the Sages were lenient regarding an agunah (a woman bound in marriage due to the uncertain status of her husband's death), this is what it means: The Sages, who are generally stringent in all matters, were lenient in this case to consider the publicity and treat it as clear testimony.

But there are some of our rabbis who hold that from the Torah this is not testimony at all, but rather it is a rabbinic ordinance that makes him trustworthy, and this is not considered uprooting a Torah law since it is reasonable to believe him—it is not considered uprooting a Torah law [Tosafot]. Moreover, we hold that anyone who betroths does so with the understanding that it is subject to the rabbis' authority, and the rabbis annul the betrothal from him [Rashi, Shabbat 145b]. However, when do they annul it—when it is true and properly verified. Therefore, even though from the Torah this is not testimony and she has no permission to remarry, nevertheless because of the reason that one betroths with the understanding that it is subject to the rabbis' authority, they permitted her to remarry. But if it was not properly verified and he is alive and she is close to being willful, why would they annul the betrothal? Would we make an ordinance for the promiscuous? [And this answers all the questions that were raised on this matter].

And do not be troubled by what is written according to the Rambam and some of the early authorities that the testimony of one witness is from the Torah. It will be explained in this chapter that a woman who remarries based on the testimony of one witness is not allowed to remarry except by the permission of a court. Also, the sages of the Talmud called a woman who remarries based on one witness "remarrying with the permission of the court." Yet, the testimony of one witness is considered as valid by Torah law just like the testimony of two witnesses. The reason is that with two witnesses, the matter is known to everyone that she is permitted, but with one witness, it is not known to everyone, and thus they need to consult a court [Tosafot, Ketubot 87b, s.v. "meklal"]. Therefore, it is called "with the permission of the court," meaning that the court has instructed that she is permitted, but the permission itself is from the Torah. Hence, the Rambam in the fifth chapter of his laws of testimony also calls this permission "from their words," since the permission is not so straightforward. There are some decisors who wish to say that the Rambam's opinion is that this permission is actually only rabbinic, but this does not seem correct [see Responsa Rivash, Siman 154 and 281, and the Maharik at the end of Shoresh 32, and see the Lechem Mishneh, and there are those who wanted to differentiate between a valid witness and an invalid witness, see Noda BiYehuda, Siman 33. However, we have not seen such a distinction among the early authorities, and according to the reasoning of "dika" (investigation), there is no distinction at all, and "dika" is because it is likely to be revealed as written. Therefore, it appears as I have written, and the interpretation of the Sifrei is an allusion like many interpretations of the Sifrei, and there is no difficulty from this on Rashi and Tosafot, and scrutinize well].

And do not be puzzled as to why, in the case of an agunah (a woman chained to a marriage), they were stringent regarding the substance of the testimony but lenient regarding the quality of the witnesses, whereas in monetary matters it is exactly the opposite? For we have already explained, with the help of Heaven, in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 284, Sif 4, that this is indeed the fundamental law. See there.

If a woman's husband went overseas and witnesses testified that he died, even one witness is sufficient, even if the witness is a relative, a woman, a servant or maidservant – as long as they are presumed to be credible, she is permitted to remarry. This includes even her son or daughter or her maidservant who testify on behalf of the agunah (a woman whose husband is missing) [Rashdam]. And even a witness who heard from another witness is acceptable, even if it is through many intermediaries, such as a woman who heard from another woman, even up to a hundred intermediaries, or a slave who heard from a maidservant, or a relative from another relative, or one invalid witness from another invalid witness up to a hundred. Since the Sages validated them for testimony due to the reasons explained, they are all valid from one to another. All those disqualified from giving testimony by rabbinic law, such as gamblers and the like, detailed in Choshen Mishpat, section 34, are valid to testify in matters concerning a woman. Testimony through intermediaries is acceptable as mentioned, even if the first witness, from whom the second witness heard, already died by the time the second witness testifies [Acharonim]. Even if the witness who testifies through an intermediary forgets who he heard it from, it is still effective and we do not suspect deception [She'erit Yosef]. Just as testimony through intermediaries is valid to be lenient, it is also valid to be stringent if the intermediary testifies that he heard that the husband is alive [Rashdam]. However, there are those who disagree and say that the Sages only trusted intermediary testimony for leniency, not for stringency [Ranach], but the primary opinion appears to follow the first view. The validation of intermediary testimony applies even if the first witness did not testify in court but merely mentioned in conversation that a certain person had died. The person who heard this can come to court and testify that he heard from so-and-so that the woman's husband had died, and such testimony is valid [Mahari and Aznei Yehoshua, section 26].

However, those disqualified by Torah law due to transgressions, as explained there in Choshen Mishpat, are not made fit by the sages for testimony regarding a woman, as they are not believed. And even though a relative and a woman are also disqualified from testimony by Torah law and are deemed fit for testimony regarding a woman, this is because their disqualification is not due to their wickedness but rather due to a decree of the Torah. Therefore, they were made fit for this, as they are not suspected. Similarly, those disqualified due to rabbinic transgressions, and even a rabbinic thief, were made fit by the sages, as they made the rule and they made the exception. However, those disqualified due to a Torah transgression, their testimony is nothing, not only those disqualified due to theft and robbery and other Torah prohibitions related to monetary matters, where they are suspected of giving false testimony for money as they commit other transgressions for money, but even those disqualified due to other Torah transgressions that do not relate to monetary matters are disqualified from testimony regarding a woman. There are those who say that only a wicked person due to violence, meaning his wickedness is in monetary matters, is disqualified because he is suspected of giving false testimony for money. But in other transgressions, he is fit [Nimukei Yosef, chapter "Zeh Borer"], but from the language of all the poskim (decisors), it seems there is no distinction, and so it is explained in the plain language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch.

Our Sages said (Sanhedrin 26b) that one who is suspected of illicit relations is disqualified from testifying for a woman [regarding her husband's death]. This is not only when witnesses testify that he committed fornication, but even if he is merely suspected of frequently being in seclusion with women and conducting his affairs with them (Nimukei Yosef), and he is accustomed to being with them and has a bad reputation (Rosh) — such a person is not at all credible to testify that a woman's husband has died. Due to his base desires, he is suspected of giving false testimony. Even if it is possible that he only violated a rabbinic prohibition by secluding himself with them, nonetheless, since his desire in this matter is great, he is suspected of giving false testimony (so it appears from the Talmud there). It seems to me that even in casual conversation, such a person is not trustworthy, because if his inclination is strong in this matter, who can know if he is speaking innocently or perhaps he is being deceitful? Therefore, even one who always secludes himself with unmarried women is disqualified from testifying for a woman (it seems to me).

Any individual who is disqualified from giving testimony according to Torah law, although disqualified from testifying regarding a woman (e.g., in matters of marital status), is nevertheless valid when speaking offhandedly. For example, a Samaritan is valid when speaking offhandedly. Even a Jew who is suspected of violating the entire Torah, as well as a Jew who worships idols, is valid when speaking offhandedly. All laws related to offhanded statements that are explained regarding a Samaritan apply to them as well. Similarly, someone who says they will worship idols, or someone who claims not to believe in the words of the Sages, or in reward and punishment, or in divine providence—these individuals are all disqualified from testimony regarding a woman except when speaking offhandedly. However, it is possible that these heretics are disqualified even when speaking offhandedly because they are suspected of causing others to sin. Therefore, the court needs to be very meticulous in examining their statements.

Even though they were very lenient regarding the testimony of a witness, nevertheless, based on a mere rumor that someone has died, even if the rumor is widespread and strong, as long as no one comes forward to testify about the death, it is nothing. For the reason they were lenient is because she (the woman) would be precise in the matter, and because a matter that is bound to be revealed, people do not lie about. In this case, even if she would be precise, the second reason does not apply since there is no one to testify. 

This will be explained further: when they heard the voice of a person saying that someone has died, and they went and did not find the person who said it, they permit his wife to remarry. This is because at least there was a person who clearly said that someone died, and the reason applies that for a matter that is bound to be revealed, people do not lie. And even though we did not find who said it, this is no worse than a witness who heard from another witness, even if the first witness has already died. At the time he said it, the reason that he would not lie about a matter bound to be revealed applied, and so it is here as well. But with a mere rumor, where there is no one to testify that someone has died, it is nothing.

Accordingly, if a single witness testifies that he heard that so-and-so died but did not say that he heard from specific individuals, only that he heard a rumor in general, we do not allow his wife to remarry. Even if he did not explicitly say that he heard a rumor but simply said that he heard, we assume that he heard a general rumor and it is not sufficient to permit her to remarry based on such testimony. [Mahari Ibn Lev, Part 3, Siman 89]. And this is what our master the Rema wrote in section 5 regarding testimony heard from another witness, that even if the witness did not specify from whom he heard but simply said that he heard, it is valid and we do not worry that the original witness might have been disqualified. This applies when he said he heard from someone but did not clarify from whom. In such a case, we do not suspect that the source might have been disqualified. But if he says that he heard without any specification, it is meaningless, and we suspect it might be just a rumor. [Meirot HaTzovot, Siman 26].

However, our master the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Joseph Caro) in his responsa concerning an incident where a certain Samaritan stated how he had true knowledge from reliable informants that a certain person had been killed, and a prominent authority wanted to be stringent because the Samaritan had said "I heard" without specifying from whom he heard it, fearing that he might have just heard a mere rumor. The Beit Yosef responded that there is no need to worry about this, for whenever the content of the testimony is clear and sufficient to permit a woman to remarry based on it, we should not invent doubts from our own minds, but rather permit the woman based on that testimony. End quote. It also seems to me that he only said this in a case where the Samaritan claims he has true knowledge from reliable informants, as there is no room for doubt about a mere rumor. However, in the case of "I heard" without further specification, even the Beit Yosef agrees <small>[and in the Kuntres Agunot, sections 139 and 148, this is a matter of dispute, and similarly, the Az Zenuim, section 136, does not agree with what I have said. Additionally, in the incident involving the Beit Yosef, there were other reasons to permit, as discussed there. What is written in Kuntres Agunot, section 233, from the responsa of Maharit is also not a proof, as in that case, they knew that the first informant was a Samaritan, but did not know who he was, as explained in Az Zenuim. Therefore, the primary ruling is not to permit based on "I heard" without further specification unless there are strong, clear indications that the report is true. See also Pitchei Teshuva, section 133]</small>.

This statement that we said, that a witness from another witness is believed and there is no need to investigate further – this applies when he says, "I heard from so-and-so that so-and-so died or was killed." But if he says, "I heard from so-and-so that it was as if he died or was killed," we do not permit based on this, because since he used a term of comparison, it might seem to him that the person died or was killed, and we need to investigate further to confirm the death or killing.

Even though all those who are disqualified are qualified for this testimony, as we have said, nevertheless, there are five women whom the sages have disqualified from this testimony because the sages know that these women hate her and want to cause her to be forbidden to her husband. It could be that he is alive and due to their hatred, they testify that he died to ruin her. These are: her mother-in-law, because she says that after her husband's death, her son will inherit all her labor, and she will control her assets. Even if she is not currently her mother-in-law, such as if the agunah's husband is not her son but from another woman, she still hates her because perhaps the agunah's husband will die, and she will perform yibbum with her son, and she will then be her mother-in-law, and when her husband dies, they will inherit everything she brought to her husband. Therefore, if the yevama is forbidden to the yavam, there is no such concern, and so too now when it is customary to perform chalitza and not yibbum. Her mother-in-law's daughter is disqualified because she says that this woman will inherit all her father's and mother's labor. Her co-wife is also disqualified; this is in places where two wives are taken who hate each other. Her yevama is also disqualified because she fears that she might fall to yibbum before her husband, and they will be co-wives. Therefore, if the agunah has seed from her husband, she would be permitted to testify because she is not in the status of yibbum. However, she might still be disqualified because she fears that her children might die, and she would then be permitted to yibbum. One cannot say how she could be disqualified from testifying that her husband died due to the concern of yibbum and they will be co-wives, for she testifies, and according to her testimony, she would perform yibbum with her husband if he left no seed. It can be said that her intention is to perform yibbum with her husband, and afterwards, when the husband comes, she will be forbidden to him. Even though we hold that if she performed yibbum in error, she is permitted to her husband, as stated in Siman 156, she says in her heart that she will be ashamed to return to him. Furthermore, perhaps her husband will perform chalitza with her, and she will marry another, and then when the husband comes, she will be forbidden to both. Similarly, her husband's daughter, who is her stepdaughter, is disqualified from testifying because she hates her as she takes her mother's place. Even in places where two wives are taken, and her mother is still alive, she is still disqualified because since her mother hates her, she also hates her. Regarding what we wrote about the mother-in-law when she is not currently her mother-in-law, and she is forbidden to the yavam, or in places where it is customary to perform chalitza, she is permitted to testify, there are those who disagree because the sages did not differentiate. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled leniently, and so have the later authorities.

It is obvious that all the women who are disqualified from testifying for her – she is also disqualified from testifying for them about the death of their husbands, since they hate her – she also hates them, as the water reflects the face, so the heart of man reflects man [Gemara 117]. This is specifically regarding disqualified testimony, but in a situation of "masiach lefi tumo" (speaking innocently), it could be said that they are believed, as they are not worse than Samaritans. Some are uncertain about this [see Aznei Yehuda 138]. It seems to me that in "masiach lefi tumo" they are believed, for in the case of bringing a get (divorce document), we hold in Siman 142 that they are believed because the main reliance is on the document and not on their testimony. Similarly, in "lefi tumo" we do not rely on their testimony, and the matter requires further investigation. [The Beit Shmuel in Siman 13 ruled to prohibit and his proof can be refuted, see Aznei Yehuda there and examine thoroughly].

These women who are invalid to testify due to enmity, even if we know they were friends with each other, are still not considered credible to testify because hatred is concealed in the heart. However, if they have already separated from each other, such as a mother-in-law whose husband has died and she has married another, and similarly in all the women we considered, once they have separated, they may testify, and we are not concerned about old enmity. Likewise, a daughter-in-law whose son has died and she has married another and she testifies about her new husband, she is credible. Some say that co-wives, even though they have separated, their hatred is severe, and she is not credible. This is not clear to me, for if so, we should disqualify any enemy from testifying for a woman whose husband has died, suspecting that he intends to harm her. Certainly, Israel was not suspected of this, as we hold in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 33, that an enemy is valid to testify, and we should not distinguish between women and men because of their perceived light-mindedness. How can we say such a thing about the daughters of Israel? Rather, we should only follow what the sages said and not innovate suspicions from our own minds.
