Likewise, males similar to these women, such as her father-in-law, her husband's son, and her husband's stepson, are credible to testify since the sages did not disqualify them. However, a brother-in-law is not credible to testify that his brother died in order to marry his wife, but if he has children and he testifies that she should marry another, he is credible. But if he left no children, he is not credible even nowadays when we practice chalitzah, for there is no reason to differentiate in this matter. All these women who are not credible to permit are likewise not credible to prohibit, and this will be further explained in this Siman, with G-d's help.

If a witness does not want to testify until he is paid a fee, his testimony is invalid, as it says in Choshen Mishpat, at the end of Siman 34, that one who takes payment to testify, his testimony is invalid. And even though we have validated all invalid witnesses for testimony regarding a woman, this invalidation is different because it is considered as having a personal interest, testifying for money. And even though someone with a personal interest is valid for testimony regarding a woman, as she herself is believed and there is no greater personal interest than this, and similarly, her husband's son is valid to testify, as it is written, and he has a personal interest to receive his father's inheritance, nevertheless, this invalidation is certain and his testimony is nullified from its own because he knew the testimony but did not want to testify except for a fee. This is not testimony, and one suspected of this, his testimonies are invalid until it is known that he did not take a fee for this testimony, and then his testimony is valid even if he has not repented. Similarly, if he returned the money to its owners and then testified on the same testimony, we accept it from him, as this is not an invalidation neither at the beginning nor at the end, but as long as he takes a fee, the sages penalize him by nullifying his actions.

However, if someone is sent to investigate the death or killing of a certain person to determine whether it is true that he has died or been killed, and he takes payment for this, and then he comes and testifies that the person has indeed died or been killed – his testimony is accepted. This is because he did not receive payment for the testimony itself, but for his effort and travel. However, this is only valid if they agreed to pay him for his effort regardless of whether his testimony would be effective or not. But if they agreed to pay him more if his testimony would be effective, then his testimony is invalid because he is receiving payment for testifying. What should be done if he was hired in this manner? When he comes to the court to testify, they should tell him that he will not receive the additional payment even if his testimony helps the woman, but he will receive the same amount as if his testimony had not been effective. This then reinstates the validity of his testimony, as stated in the sources. And all this applies to someone who receives payment for his effort. However, if he is paid specifically for his testimony, even if they explicitly pay him regardless of whether his testimony is effective or not – his testimony is still invalid, because he is, after all, being paid for testifying. There are those who wish to say that even if he is paid for his effort to investigate and inquire, if he receives more than what is necessary for this effort, it is considered as if he is being paid for testifying, and his testimony is invalid even if they pay him this amount regardless of whether his testimony is effective or not – but this opinion is not accepted. For what limit is there to this? Even if he receives a lot for his effort, what of it? He still receives it even if his testimony is not effective. And it is obvious that if he receives payment specifically for his testimony, his testimony is invalid.

If several witnesses testify to the death of a husband, and one of them is found to be disqualified from testifying for a woman, such as a thief according to the Torah or similar, we do not say that if part of the testimony is invalid, the entire testimony is invalid, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 36, even if they saw the event together with the disqualified witness and testified together. The reason is that these disqualified witnesses in the case of a woman’s testimony are only disqualified because they are suspected of lying. However, if we knew that they were not lying, we would accept their testimony. Therefore, when there is a valid witness with them, his testimony is true [Noda B’Yehuda, section 45]. And even though some have doubts about this, the main ruling is as stated, and several great authorities have agreed with this. Furthermore, this rule only applies in cases where two witnesses are required, for the Torah decreed that just as if one of the two is found to be a relative or disqualified, their testimony is invalid, so too if there are three [Makkot 6a]. But in the case of a woman’s testimony, even if there are two, their testimony is not invalid, for one valid witness remains, which suffices [in my opinion].

In any case where we have disqualified a witness from testifying in matters of a woman's status, there is no distinction between testifying about the core issue of death—where without his testimony she would be prohibited by Torah law—and testifying in matters where, by Torah law, his testimony is not required, but the Sages were stringent, such as in the case of someone who fell into water with no visible end and remained until his soul departed, and similar stringent cases that will be explained. In all these cases, the law is the same: disqualified witnesses are invalid for any matter of testimony regarding a woman.

It has already been explained that a witness who says, "I heard that so-and-so died," even if he heard it from a woman who heard it from a slave, this is acceptable testimony regarding a woman, and she can be remarried based on it. Even if he does not say from whom he heard it but just says generally that he heard it, it is acceptable, and we do not worry that the first witness might have been disqualified. However, some say that we should ask him from whom he heard it, and certainly, where it is possible to ask, we do ask [Taz and Beit Shmuel], for wherever it is possible to clarify, we clarify. If they asked him from whom he heard it and he said he doesn’t remember whether it was from a qualified or disqualified person, some prohibit, similar to one who heard from a non-Jew and does not remember if he was engaged in idle conversation or not, in which case it will be explained that she is forbidden to remarry. Others permit it – and this is the main ruling. It is not comparable to that case, for there the doubt is equally balanced, but here the majority of people are qualified, and we do not worry about the minority who are disqualified by Torah law [Aruch HaShulchan, Even HaEzer 17:92].

Even though for testimony from hearsay we do not investigate and inquire about the manner of death—since the one testifying does not know, as he was not present at the death and only heard from the first witness—and we are not obligated to send for the first witness, as our master, the Rema, ruled in paragraph 8 that the court does not need to send for him even if he is in the city, but rather rely on testimony from hearsay initially, nonetheless, if the witness himself testifies, or if a woman or a servant says, "So-and-so died, and I saw that he died," we ask him how he saw and how he knew. If he testifies clearly, he is believed. But if he testifies about things that mostly lead to death, we do not permit his wife to remarry, since one only testifies about a person's death when they saw him definitely dead without any doubt. Even if he saw him in agony for three days, he cannot testify about him. There is an opinion that one may testify about someone in agony, but this is not correct, as they were stringent about the essence of testimony even in very distant concerns, and many great authorities have contested this opinion. There is no difference whether he simply said, "So-and-so died," or "He died, and I saw that he died," for even if he just said, "He died," the implication is that he was present at the death, as he is the first witness. Therefore, in all cases, one must ask how he saw the death—whether it was by drowning, killing, or dying in bed—and how he knows that the deceased is indeed the husband of this woman. Also, one must ask how he knows for sure that he died, lest he saw things close to death but not definite death. If the court did not ask him, even though they acted improperly, they still permit the agunah (a woman bound in marriage) if the witness is not in the city. For if this would be an impediment after the fact, why did our master, the Rema, permit testimony from hearsay when the first witness is in the city?

And one should not wonder why for the first witness we ask him and for the testimony from hearsay we do not ask the first witness even when he is in the city according to what our teacher the Rema ruled. For certainly it is so, as we hold that we do not investigate the witnesses in cases of women with rigorous examination as will be explained due to the enactment for agunot (deserted wives). Therefore, when this second witness testifies that he heard from so-and-so that the person died – that is sufficient. If we were to call the first witness and ask him in detail, it would be like a rigorous examination. But when the first witness testifies before us, this is not considered a rigorous examination because the main thing is that we ask him. For even in monetary laws, we do not require rigorous examination, but we still ask the witnesses how they know the person is liable to the other. And although in monetary matters hearsay testimony necessitates that we send for the first witness, this is because in monetary matters hearsay testimony is completely invalid. But in testimony regarding a woman, where the Sages validated hearsay testimony, we are lenient with hearsay testimony in this particular aspect more than with the direct witness for the reason explained.

However, regarding testimony from a witness who heard from another witness, there are those who disagree and hold that if the first witness is in the city, the court must send for him and hear from him directly [Chesed Le'Avraham, section 18]. This seems reasonable, for since he is in the city, why shouldn't we clarify the matter, as this does not fall under the category of investigation and interrogation as mentioned. Some of the great authorities have strengthened the ruling of our teacher, the Rema [Beit Shmuel and Ezer Mikodesh]. However, we find that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in a responsum explicitly that if the witness is in a nearby place, we ask him; if not, the woman is permitted to remarry, end quote. However, this is certainly the case when the second witness clarifies his testimony as to how he knows of the death – there is no need to send for the first witness [Maharit Tzahalon], and this is the main ruling in the law.

Some say that even the woman herself, when she comes before the court and says her husband died, we need to ask her how he died, just as we ask a witness [Choshen Mishpat 397]. However, there are those who disagree, saying that we do not need to ask the woman herself, for we do not see that when a woman comes to court and says her husband died, she is asked how he died [Bava Metzia]. And logic supports this, because in a time of war, she might say it based on assumption, and similarly, a witness who says someone died might not have seen the actual death and left before it happened. But a man's wife, when he dies in his bed, would obviously not leave him and wait until he dies or recovers from his illness. In truth, the woman herself is not considered a witness; only a disqualified witness whom the sages validated is considered a witness in this context. But the woman is a party to the matter, and the sages believed her for reasons that have been explained. Therefore, she is not in the category of a witness that we need to question her how and what, unless there is a noticeable concern, such as in a war where she might be speaking based on assumption, and similar scenarios, as will be explained further, with God's help.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 5: If one hears the voice of lamenting women who mentioned him among the dead and eulogized him – they permit his wife to remarry. And there are those who say that it is not specifically two lamenting women or that they eulogized him, but even if there is one lamenting woman and she did not eulogize him, but merely mentioned him among the dead, they permit his wife to remarry, as it is stated in the Tosefta at the end of Yevamot: Even if one hears the voice of a lamenting woman mentioning him among the dead, there is no greater testimony than this. And it seems to me that it is true that one lamenting woman suffices, but specifically when she lamented him with a wailing voice, as it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud: If one hears the voice of a lamenting woman wailing for him among the dead, there is no greater testimony than this. And 'wailing' is an expression of 'crying' as it is written, "And the mother of Sisera wailed" (Judges 5:28), and this is the term 'mentioning' in the Tosefta, as we are accustomed to use the term 'mentioning' regarding the dead, which is a prayer for the soul of the dead. And specifically when there is a sage in the city who knows that she is lamenting for him and did not protest against her, for otherwise, it is not evidence, as perhaps she is lamenting based on an estimation of death.

From the law that has been explained, the poskim (halachic authorities) have derived that we should object to women eulogizing a person based on presumptive evidence indicating his death until the death is clearly confirmed through a ruling by a Beit Din (rabbinic court). Similarly, a wife is forbidden to eulogize or wear black as long as there is no testimony that permits her to remarry. Likewise, the children should not recite Kaddish, and relatives are forbidden to observe mourning practices until his death is confirmed by testimony that permits the wife to remarry. The children should not sign [documents] in a manner that indicates the deceased status, such as "the late" or "of blessed memory," to avoid potential complications.

There are those who wish to be stringent even in the case of someone who does not have a wife, to not observe mourning based on presumptive evidence, lest they do so for someone who does have a wife. However, this is not the main opinion, as we should not enact such decrees on our own accord (as Rabbi Yaakov Kuli also wrote in a responsum there). Similarly, no Beit Din should issue a certificate of testimony to a woman based on the testimony presented before them if that testimony is not sufficient to permit her [to remarry], for the Beit Din might make an error in permitting based on such testimony. Therefore, when this is given to the woman, it should be explicitly written that she is not being permitted to remarry based on this testimony alone and that it is given to her in case further clarification or more competent scholars of the generation determine that she is permitted to remarry based on this testimony. Similar caution should be exercised in all such matters.

Our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 6 that during times of persecution, women are permitted [to remarry] based on the testimony of repentant individuals who testify about what they saw during the time of distress, even though they abandoned the faith due to coercion. And those who abandoned the faith and frivolous individuals who returned in repentance but not with complete repentance – we do not rely on their testimony except in a situation where they are testifying without intent to benefit or when it is known that they testified without deceit and distortion, and everything is according to the matter of the witness and the perception of the judge, end of quote. And even though in all testimonies we require the beginning and end [of their status] to be kosher – this applies to inherent disqualifications, and furthermore, in the testimony for a woman, the Sages did not require the laws of testimony, and only if it is known that they will not lie is she permitted to remarry. Therefore, when they testify in their kosher state, even though at the time they saw the testimony they were not kosher, but nevertheless they were coerced then as well – we accept their testimony now. And so, many of the great authorities agreed that for the testimony of a woman we do not require the beginning and end [of their status] to be kosher. But if they have not yet repented completely – we do not accept their testimony except in a situation where they are testifying without intent to benefit, and even though from the language of the Shulchan Aruch that wrote "or it is known that they testified without deceit, etc." it seems that even without this situation they are kosher, we do not hold this way. Furthermore, the intention is when they testified without deceit and it is evident that they have repented completely, and for this reason, it concludes that everything is according to the perception of the judge and the matter of the witness. However, if at the time of witnessing the testimony they were not coerced and transgressed out of desire – they are disqualified even though they have now repented. Some, however, validate even this, because at the time of giving the testimony they returned with complete repentance, so they will not lie.

This which has been explained, that a wicked person in matters of Torah prohibitions is disqualified from testifying about a woman – this is when it is known that he is wicked. However, if through this testimony he makes himself wicked, such as if he says, "I killed this woman's husband," we accept his testimony and she may remarry. The reason is that we hold that a person does not make himself wicked. And that which we hold, that the admission of a party is like the testimony of a hundred witnesses – this applies to monetary matters and not to fines, punishments, or disqualifications [Rashi 25a]. Therefore, we split his statement and believe him that the husband was killed, but we do not believe him that he killed him. For he is testifying to two things: one, that so-and-so was killed, and the other, that he is the killer. In two things, we split his statement [Tosafot there]. And although we hold that if part of the testimony is invalid, the entire testimony is invalid, here it is impossible to say this, because what he says that he killed him is not really testimony but rather an admission [Nimukei Yosef]. Testimony is only called such when the matter pertains to others, and this matter does not pertain to the agunah if he killed him or another killed him. The testimony is only about what he testifies that this woman's husband is not alive.

Even with those who are disqualified from giving testimony, such as a slave or maidservant, we say that we split their statement. When they say "I killed so-and-so," we permit her to remarry [Bach and Beit Shmuel] because a person does not make themselves a wicked person. The same applies to a Samaritan who speaks innocently; when he says "I killed so-and-so," we permit his wife to remarry. And although the principle of "a person does not make themselves a wicked person" does not apply to him, nevertheless, since we also split his statement, it is not necessary to say it in his case because we do not take his words as formal testimony but as an innocent statement. Therefore, it does not matter to us whether he makes himself wicked or not. And even though it will be explained that a Samaritan in such a case is not believed for another reason—because we say that his intention is to instill fear so that people will be afraid of him and he is lying—this applies when we can attribute his words accordingly, such as when he tells a Jew, "Do my will, and if not, I will kill you just as I killed so-and-so," and the like, where it seems from his words that he is boasting. But when he simply says innocently, "I killed so-and-so," we do not suspect this [there].

Just as when someone says, "I killed so-and-so," we allow his wife to remarry for the reason explained, similarly, when he says this about his relative, such as Reuven who comes to the court and testifies that his son killed this woman's husband, we allow the woman to remarry. Even though we do not accept his testimony about his son, we still split his statement. And even though generally, if part of the testimony is invalid, the entire testimony is invalid, and in this case, the explanation we provided in section 51 does not apply, nevertheless, in the case of testimony concerning a woman, we do not say this, just as we do not require all the detailed laws of testimony.

Just as one witness is trusted in the testimony regarding a woman when he testifies in court, so too the agunah (a woman whose husband is missing and cannot be confirmed dead) herself, when she heard from someone who says, "Your husband has died," comes to court and says, "My husband has died," and she does not need further testimony. When they ask her how she knows, she says she heard it from so-and-so. The requirement for the witness to testify in court is because, without a court, it is not possible to permit her, not because his words are not valid without a court. Therefore, when she comes to court, the court permits her. And although the person who told her can retract his statement when he comes to court, because anything said outside of court is not valid, nevertheless, as long as he does not retract, why should we assume he will? However, if he subsequently comes to court and says that the husband did not die and that he lied to her, then it is obvious that he is believed even if she was already permitted, because since she was permitted based on his words, and now he retracts in court and legally he can retract, the permission is automatically nullified.

And similarly, if he comes to the court and says that she is lying and that he never told her that he (her husband) died, it is not only if he said this before the court permitted her to remarry, for the same rule applies in the case of a witness and a second-hand witness, as will be explained; but even if the court had already permitted her to remarry, they reverse their decision and forbid her (to remarry). This is the general rule: Any second-hand testimony, when the first witness comes and contradicts the second by saying he never told him, the first witness is believed [Ran in the name of Ramban, Chapter 7 of Ketubot]. 

Some have raised the objection that she should be believed with a "migo" (a type of legal presumption) that if she wanted, she could now say that her husband died without relying on the testimony of the witness, and she should be believed with the "migo" that the witness indeed told her. But it seems to me that this is nothing, because the witness himself also has a "migo" that if he wanted, he could say he told her falsely, for in court he can retract what he said outside of court [see Choshen Mishpat, section 17 and Beit Shmuel, section 23]. 

And this applies not only in the case of the woman herself but in all cases of second-hand testimony; however, as long as the first witness does not contradict her, she is believed in all that she says in the name of the witness. And even if she says that she heard from a witness that he drowned in the sea and the court permitted her to remarry, she is believed [Beit Shmuel, section 22], and we say that presumably the court permitted her correctly, as there were witnesses who saw him after he was brought up from the water, or similar circumstances.

There are those who are uncertain if a woman stated in a court that she heard from a servant or maidservant that her husband died and they permitted her to remarry, and afterward the servant or maidservant came and denied that they had ever told her this, whether they are believed or not. Similarly, if a valid witness testified in court about what he heard from an invalid witness, and the invalid witness came and denied it, whether the invalid witness is believed to contradict him or not. It seems to me that the invalid witness is believed to contradict him with the rationale that if he wanted, he could say that he told him or the woman and then retracted, because anything a person testifies outside of court, he can retract, as we have stated. 

Know that in the Treatise on Agunahs, Section 305, it is brought in the name of a great authority that if a valid witness testifies based on the testimony of an invalid witness, even if the invalid witness contradicts him by saying he never told him at all, the invalid witness is not believed, and so several other great authorities have written. However, it seems to me that the main ruling is as I have explained due to the rationale of migo (a halachic principle whereby a claim is believed because the claimant could have made a different, more advantageous claim).

There are those who question this by saying that if so, even if she marries someone else and the first witness comes and contradicts her, it would result in her being taken away from her new husband, which is not the way of pleasantness. It seems to me that certainly, once she has married, we do not believe him based on migo to remove a woman from her husband, as we do not say migo to take someone out of a situation. After she has married, the matter is concluded, and we do not pay attention to the first witness's words unless two valid witnesses testify that her husband is alive. However, as long as she has not married, the first witness is believed, whether valid or invalid, to contradict the one testifying in his name or to retract his testimony that was made outside of court.

However, in the opinion of our master Beit Yosef in his responsum (brought in the Treatise on Agunahs, Section 160), in the testimony of a woman based on hearsay, when the second witness testifies based on the first, the first witness cannot contradict him. But many of the great later authorities did not rule this way. However, it is clear that when two witnesses testify based on one, he cannot contradict them. But if he says that he told them and now, upon coming to court, retracts his words, it seems to me that their testimony is nullified because he can retract what he said outside of court, as we have stated. And when she testified based on a non-Jew who spoke without any ulterior motive (mesiach lefi tumo) and the non-Jew came and contradicted her or retracted, it is clear that we do not pay attention to his words. See what I have written in Section 106, that when the non-Jew retracts, it is a doubtful matter in law.

Our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote in section 9: A witness who estimates that someone is dead and a witness who states that he was killed, even though they contradict each other, since both agree that he is not alive, she may marry, end quote. Many disagree with him, as this is a contradiction in the investigative questions, which are the essence of the testimony. Although in the testimony of women we do not require the same level of scrutiny, it is clear that if they contradict each other in the investigative questions, their testimony is nullified. This is no less than in monetary cases, where we also do not require the same level of scrutiny, but still, if they contradict each other in the investigative questions, their testimony is nullified, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 30. Moreover, Rabbi Yosef Karo himself wrote in section 21 that if they contradict each other in the investigative questions, they are qualified witnesses, implying clearly that if the contradiction is in the essential questions, the testimony is nullified. And even though in the Mishnah (117b) we hold that in the case of two co-wives, where one says he died and the other says he was killed, they may marry, this is because a co-wife is not believed regarding her fellow co-wife, and her contradiction is not considered a contradiction, as will be explained in this section. But with witnesses, it is a contradiction in the investigative questions. This is also explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, distinguishing between co-wives and witnesses (see Gra, section 40, and Nodah BiYehudah, section 46).

However, the opinion of our master, the Beit Yosef, is that either he compares this to a contradiction in examinations, which is not the essence of the matter and is like a contradiction in a loan between a black maneh and a white maneh [Beit Shmuel], what difference does it make if he died or was killed? Or he holds that in women's testimony, even a contradiction in investigations does not concern us, for in any testimony that requires two witnesses, their testimony is nullified, but in women's testimony, where one witness suffices, surely one of them is testifying truthfully. This is similar to two sets of witnesses contradicting each other, where each comes independently and testifies, as mentioned in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 31, and the same applies to women's testimony when one witness contradicts another.

This is what is written in paragraph 21, "contradiction in examinations" is not precise, and the same applies to investigations. Indeed, some say that the Shulchan Aruch text should be corrected to "contradiction in investigations" [Bach], or it is possible that the seven investigations of time and place that we explained there in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 30, derived from scriptural verses, do not apply to women's testimony either. Proof for this reasoning is that if we say that in the case of death and murder among witnesses it is considered a contradiction and their testimony is nullified, we should also say the same for co-wives, since the reason their contradiction is not considered significant is because we say he is alive and she intends to cause harm, as will be explained. This applies only in a contradiction where one says he died and the other says he did not die, but in the case of death and murder, where each one testifies to permit her, if among witnesses it is considered a contradiction, it would also be considered a contradiction among co-wives [AzN in the name of Rachash]. Moreover, in the Mishnah it is taught: if one witness says he died and another says he did not die, she should not remarry. And if we say not according to our master, the Beit Yosef, it should teach a greater novelty, even when one says he died and the other says he was killed, where both agree about his death, she should not remarry. But certainly, in such a case, she may remarry [there]. The Jerusalem Talmud can be reconciled [see Noda B'Yehuda]. Therefore, in practice, many of the great authorities agree with the Beit Yosef, and even those who are stringent to initially consider the opinions of the dissenters, nevertheless, if she remarried, it is obvious that she should not be required to leave the marriage, and it is forbidden to cast aspersions on the marriage.

And we found in the responsa of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, that he ruled in a case of contradictory testimony where one says he died in one place and another says he died in another place, that this is not considered a contradiction, and he follows his approach. From this, it is clearly apparent that he holds that even a contradiction in the seven interrogations does not invalidate the testimony in the case of women’s testimony. It is clear that this is because, in any case, one witness is valid, and that suffices for women’s testimony, and certainly in other types of contradictions. However, for those who disagree with him, it is necessary to scrutinize whether the contradiction is in verification or in interrogation. It is obvious that whenever it is possible to reconcile the witnesses’ statements so that they do not contradict each other, such as if one says he was killed and another says he was drowned in water, it can be said that first they killed him and then threw him into the water. This one saw the killing and not the drowning, and that one saw the drowning and not the killing. Similarly, in other matters, we are obligated to reconcile their statements so that they do not contradict each other, even in a far-fetched manner. And behold, even in capital cases, we exert ourselves to reconcile their statements so that they do not contradict each other, as stated in Choshen Mishpat there. All the more so in women’s testimony. [And what the Beit Shmuel wrote at the end of section 25 regarding killed and drowned, that according to the Sha'ar ha-Gilgulim it is a contradiction, needs investigation, for it can be said as we have explained, and so it is written in the Ba'er Hetev in the name of the Keneset HaGedolah, and it is clear.]

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 10: If they heard a voice saying, "So-and-so has died," and they went and did not find anyone there, they may permit his wife to remarry. However, if they heard this voice in a field or a ruin, they do not permit based on that voice, as there is a concern it may be a demon since the voice came from a place where demons are commonly found. In the city, demons are not commonly found, only in fields, ruins, and pits [Jerusalem Talmud]. Even though in the Gemara [122a], it is said that if they saw a shadow of a shadow, meaning a double shadow, we do not worry about it being a demon because demons do not have double shadows, the Beit Yosef omitted this because the Tur wrote in the name of the Gaon that nowadays we do not rely on this sign as we are not proficient in it. And even though Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in Siman 141 concerning a bill of divorce brought this opinion, it seems to me that regarding a bill of divorce, it is necessary to have three people standing at a distance to observe, as one writes and the two sign, and with three, we rely that they can recognize a double shadow. But here, where one is sufficient, we do not rely on this, even if there are many people, as we do not differentiate. Additionally, there he wrote that the body is lying before us, and it is only impossible to recognize it, and concerning that body, there is no concern it is a demon, but there is a distant concern that the one who cried out was a demon and this body is not the one who cried out. This is a remote concern, so we rely on this sign. But here, where they did not find anyone at all, we do not rely on this sign [Beit Shmuel].

And in section 23, our master the Beit Yosef wrote: If they saw someone standing from afar and he said that he is "so-and-so, the son of so-and-so" or "so-and-so from such-and-such place," and that he was bitten by a snake and is now dead, and they went and found that his appearance had changed and they did not recognize him – they may allow his wife to remarry, end quote. And there are those who have the version "so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, from such-and-such place," for although in general it is sufficient to identify by the father's name or the place, nevertheless here, where they did not recognize the body because its appearance had changed – we are stringent in this matter and require both the father's name and the place. And regarding why we do not worry here about a demon, the reason is simple: since we see a body before us, we do not need to be concerned that the one who cried out was a demon and that this body is not the one who cried out, and why should we be concerned about such a distant suspicion? However, since our master the Beit Yosef was concerned about a demon even in such a case in section 141, it must be that we are dealing with a settled place where demons are not common. And in the Gemara there, they also did not worry about a demon in this law, and only in the previous law, when they did not find a person, did they worry about a demon.

And know that in the Gemara there, they asked about the previous ruling when no one is found there, should we be concerned that perhaps it is a rival wife who has come to disrupt or one of the other five women who hate her? And they answered that in times of danger, we write a get (divorce document) even if we do not recognize (the witnesses), and similarly for an agunah (a woman unable to obtain a divorce). If we do not accept their testimony, she will remain an agunah. Therefore, they were lenient in this matter. Hence, there are some Rishonim (early commentators) who said that according to the conclusion, because of the danger, we do not worry about a rival wife. Likewise, we should not be concerned about demons even in places where they are commonly found. But many of the Rishonim hold that although we do not worry about a rival wife, we should be more concerned about demons in places where they are commonly found. This is also the opinion of the Tur and our teachers, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch.

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, in Chapter 13 of Hilchot Gerushin, did not write at all about this law of Section 60 when no person was found there. He only ruled on the second law of Section 61, when they brought him up and did not recognize him, as he wrote that they permit his wife to remarry based on the voice they heard from him saying that he was bitten by a snake and died, without mentioning the matter of demons at all. Similarly, in Chapter 2 of Hilchot Mi SheNafal LeBor, regarding one who fell into a pit and said that anyone who hears his voice should write a get for his wife, he also did not mention this concern about demons. He only wrote that even if they brought him up and did not recognize him, it is valid, as this is considered a time of danger when they allow (the get) even without recognition, as noted there. Some say that his opinion aligns with the earlier view we brought, that just as we do not worry about a rival wife according to the conclusion, so too we do not worry about demons [Bach, and this is evident from Maran in Chapter 6 of Hilchot Gittin]. However, it is impossible to say this because if so, why did he omit this law about not finding a person at all, which would be more significant than the law he wrote about finding a person and not recognizing him. Some say that his opinion aligns with the opinion of the Gaon that we mentioned, and they questioned this because if so, he should have prohibited it in all cases. Indeed, the Maggid Mishneh [there] wondered why he omitted this law about not finding a person there [and the words of the Beit Shmuel in subparagraph 26 are not understood].

It seems clear to me that the Rambam, of blessed memory, holds that in the conclusion, when they said that in a time of danger they give [a divorce] even if they do not recognize [the body], the explanation is: This was permitted both in the case of a divorce and in the case of an agunah when they saw the dead body even if they did not recognize it. However, it is still necessary that some body be found. But if no body is found at all, we do not rely on merely hearing a voice. Consequently, the ruling in section 60 is rejected from the law. A clear proof of this is that even regarding a divorce, the Rambam required that there be a dead body. And in the Talmud [Gittin 66a], this is not mentioned at all, except that the conclusion requires this. And indeed, since there is a dead body, there is no concern about demons. However, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in section 141 hold that even when a dead body is found, there is a concern about the suspicion of demons. [And it needs further investigation according to this, why in Yevamot the question is only on the beginning of the Mishnah and not on the case of the silhouette, and in Gittin it refers according to the understanding that no person was brought up from the pit, and it appears from Rashi's commentary that even according to the conclusion this is so, and it appears similarly from the Jerusalem Talmud in Yevamot there, where it compares the case in Gittin to the beginning of the Mishnah, and examine this carefully.]

In these laws, it appears that even if the listeners did not recognize the voice as the voice of a specific person who is crying out, such as if his voice was not known to them – nevertheless, they permit his wife to remarry. And not only when a body is found, there is no need to worry about a remote concern that perhaps the one crying out was someone else and the body is not that of the one who cried out. But even in the first case where no person was found at all, since we heard that he clarified his name and his father's name or also his city's name – we do not worry about a demon in a place where demons are not commonly found. And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote: "A certain person has died," he shortened his words because mentioning the name alone is not sufficient as he wrote in section 23, rather he means a certain person, son of a certain person, or also from a certain place. And in section 141 regarding a get (divorce document) where his name is not clarified but he says anyone who hears his voice should write a get for his wife, indeed the Rambam wrote there "and it is known who he is," meaning they recognize who is speaking either by his appearance or by the distinctiveness of his voice. And if he does not mention his name but they recognize him by the distinctiveness of his voice that this is the voice of a certain person, son of a certain person – it appears that one can rely on this, and many of the great authorities agreed, but some of the great authorities questioned this, and the matter requires further analysis. And from the Rambam, it is not a conclusive proof.

And know, according to our rabbis who permit based on a voice even if no person is found there, there is no difficulty from the fact that we hold that based on an echo we do not permit, as mentioned in section 32. For truly, it is not comparable, as this voice is like testimony, either from the person himself or from another who informs of the matter. And there is no concern that perhaps it is a non-Jew speaking, for this too is a complete permit since it is like spontaneous testimony because he is announcing it with a voice without any question [see section 171]. Therefore, if he concludes 'they married off his wife' – this is not like spontaneous testimony as his intention is to marry her off, as will be explained [there]. It could be said that indeed it is speaking of a case where the listeners know that the voice is that of a Jew, but the poskim did not mention this, and if it were necessary for it to be specifically the voice of a Jew, they would have mentioned it, just like with writing that will be explained where they mentioned that it should be the writing of a Jew. And even though it can be said that this is not in the category of spontaneous testimony, as spontaneous testimony applies when one tells another that so-and-so died without any intended purpose but innocently, yet here where he stands himself and shouts that so-and-so died, necessarily he shouts with some intention and this is not innocent, it can be said that even this can be innocent, such as if he was his friend and is lamenting over him himself, and since it can be attributed to such a case – we do not worry further [this seems to me]. However, all this is according to the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, but according to what is explained in the opinion of the Rambam, we do not permit based on a mere voice according to his opinion.

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote: We have already said that hearsay testimony is valid for the case of a woman—when is this so? When it is heard from a person of sound mind, such as a servant or maidservant. However, if it is heard from someone of unsound mind or from a minor, he does not testify, and we do not rely on their words. If one hears from children who say, "We just came from the funeral of so-and-so, such and such eulogizers were there, and this sage and that one walked after the bier, and such and such was done with the bier"—one may testify based on their words and similar accounts, and it is permitted to marry his wife. These are the words of the Rambam, and they were copied in Shulchan Aruch, Section 13.

It is explained that the difference is that when a child says generally, "So-and-so died," his words are meaningless, whether he is speaking casually or testifying formally. However, when they recount an event related to mourning or a funeral or similar matters, it is a sign that their words are true. Additionally, it seems that even in such a case, one child alone is not believed, as it is written "children" in the plural. However, there is an opinion that this is not necessarily precise, as what difference does it make whether it is one or more? Nonetheless, it appears to me that they are certainly not believed as formal testimony but rather because of the casual conversation of children. However, without the context of the conversation, we say that they might have killed a locust and given it a name, as explained in the Talmud, for this is the way of children. But when they speak about matters of mourning and the funeral, it is clear that the matter is true. And since this is so, it is necessary that there be no fewer than two children speaking among themselves. However, it is also possible that when the child recounts what he saw to adults, it also has validity, and this requires further consideration. And even if they say, "So-and-so died, and we are coming from his burial," this also is not valid for the reason explained, unless they elaborate on such matters and similar ones.

And know that the Tur wrote in this language: Even if they heard from children who said "so-and-so died," whether they intended it for testimony or not, they permit his wife to remarry. And if they hear from them saying "we are coming from his burial," they do not rely on them to allow his wife to remarry unless they say, "such and such eulogizers were there and such and such people followed the bier," indicating something that shows the matter is true, end quote. And it appears from his words that when they say "so-and-so died," it suffices, but when they say "we are coming from his burial," they need to elaborate on this matter. For regarding death, there is no concern that they would attribute the name of a person to a locust, but in the case of burial, there is a concern, as a child might play and bury a locust and give it a person's name [Perisha]. However, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote that it is impossible to differentiate in this manner, and therefore he explained that what is written "and if they hear from them" is a scribal error and should say "if they hear from them," and it applies to everything, as he concludes that they need to elaborate on the matters [and so wrote the Bach]. And it is explicitly explained in the Kitzur Piskei HaRosh, which the Tur compiled [see there in Beit Yosef, chapter 6] that one needs to amend it to say "if" instead of "and," and his intention is that when they say "so-and-so died" or "we are coming from his burial," they need to elaborate on the matters, and so it is in the Kitzur Piskei HaRosh, see there [and according to this, the text is corrected].

However, regarding what he wrote, "whether they intended it as testimony or not," his intention is not that their testimony is effective, but rather the explanation is: whether their intention was for testimony or not, we accept their words. For although with a Cuthean, if he intended it as testimony, it is worse, nevertheless, with children, since we do not suspect them of lying, we accept their words as if they were speaking innocently, for the testimony of minors is essentially nothing. However, for those who hear from them, it does not matter whether they intended to hear from the children in order to testify in court or not.

Some authorities say that specifically for a minor who has reached the age of discernment, lengthy explanations are effective, but for one below this age, it is impossible to accept their words even if they speak innocently, just as with a mentally incompetent person whose speech has no validity. Similarly, if a minor who has reached the age of discernment recounts that he was present at the killing of a certain person, detailing how and why the killing occurred in a lengthy manner, his words are accepted and the agunah (a woman whose husband is missing and she cannot remarry) is permitted to remarry.

However, some authorities say that with a minor, it is only effective if he speaks innocently, not if he intends to testify, similar to a Samaritan. This is also the opinion of one of the great early authorities. But the opinion of the Tur is not so, as he explains in the Mishnah that whether the minor intends to testify or not, it applies to a minor. This is evident from the language of the Mishnah, which should have used the plural form if it intended otherwise. This understanding is also implied by other halachic authorities.

And the fact that children are reliable when elaborating on matters—it is specifically when they recount immediately after witnessing the death and the eulogy or the killing and its cause, such as when they say, "We just came from the eulogy of so-and-so, and thus and thus happened," as stated, and they recount before the court or before other people, and those people can testify even after some time [Bach]. This is also implied by the language of Maimonides, who wrote, "We just came." But if they do not recount immediately, their testimony is not valid at all, as it is not possible to establish their words when they recount an event that happened long ago. Even if they grow up afterward, they cannot testify about what they saw in their childhood. And although there are matters in which a child is believed in adulthood to testify about what he saw in childhood, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 35, and in testimony regarding a woman they were lenient, nevertheless, in this case, it is not due to stringency but because it is impossible to establish a foundation on their words, for perhaps it was some sort of joke and it seemed to them what it seemed. The measure of "immediately" is not specified and depends on the discernment of the court. Similarly, when they say, "We are going to bury and eulogize so-and-so," they are not believed even if they elaborate, as perhaps they will not go [Gemara], but only when they say, "We came from his eulogy," as stated. The general rule is that an idiot is never considered valid in his words when he is a complete idiot, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 1, or those who are extremely foolish, as explained in Choshen Mishpat there, and similarly an epileptic during his seizure is judged like an idiot, as stated there. The law regarding a deaf person will be explained further in Siman 73. And for a minor, it depends on the discernment when there is substance to his words, and this is in elaborating the matter. And even for those who hold that it requires "according to their innocence"—it is not literally "according to their innocence" like a Samaritan, but rather, even if by questioning he says only without intending to testify. The opinion of the Tur and most poskim is that even if he intends to testify, it is valid. Some of the earlier authorities hold that even after some time, his testimony is valid even if not immediately. According to this, if a minor testifies after some time, contradicting the testimony of a minor who testifies immediately, one should be stringent [Chakham Tzvi]. However, it does not seem so, and this is a singular opinion, and our master, the Rema, omitted this opinion, and it is possible that one should not be stringent in this matter [see Bach, Siftei Kohen 35 and Be'er HaGolah 87].

Regarding the deaf-mute, the Rambam wrote that if someone became mute and was tested in the manner used for divorce documents (gittin) and found to have coherent understanding, and he wrote that someone died, we rely on his writing, and his wife can remarry. This was cited in Shulchan Aruch, Section 12. The testing method for divorce documents is explained in Section 121, where we test him three times: once for "yes," twice for "no," and once for "no" and twice for "yes." However, this test is performed by nodding the head. Concerning writing, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 120 that according to the Rambam, a three-time test is not necessary. Therefore, in this case as well, if the test is done by nodding, it needs to be three times as in divorce documents, but for writing, once is sufficient. However, from the language of the Rambam, it seems that three times is required even for writing, since he wrote "in the manner used for divorce documents," and no other method is explained there. It is possible that even for divorce documents, three times is required for writing as well. We do not find that the Rambam was lenient with just once except in monetary matters in Chapter 29 of Sales, but not in matters of forbidden marital relations. And know that although regarding a divorce document, our master the Beit Yosef was stringent in Section 120 for a mute person to rely on his writing and brought different opinions on this, nevertheless, in the case of an agunah (a woman whose husband's whereabouts are unknown), he was lenient as they were lenient in agunah testimonies with any type of witness. Since we rely on his writing, all the more so we rely on his nodding, since for a divorce document, nodding is preferable to writing as written there.

It appears that if someone has become mute, an examination is effective—this applies whether he became mute due to illness or suddenly became mute while healthy (see Ran, Gittin chapter 7). However, he can still hear and is not like a deaf person who in every situation cannot hear or speak, for such a person is considered like an imbecile in all matters of Torah law. This is also the ruling in Gittin there (see there) and this is what the prominent Acharonim wrote (see Rashash, Ezras Nashim, and Maros Hatzovos). Even though one might say that even a completely deaf person can be examined and he is not comparable to an imbecile, and our sages explicitly stated (Yevamos 113a) that a deaf person has some level of understanding and is comparable to a minor, nevertheless it is difficult to be lenient in this matter since in the Gemara there is no leniency for an agunah except in the case of someone who has become mute (Gittin 71a) and a typical mute can hear. It is therefore impossible to be lenient with a completely deaf person, and even though there is no absolute proof from there (see there) it remains questionable in practice. Someone who speaks but cannot hear is considered fully competent (see Maros Hatzovos). Even though there are some opinions regarding other matters as written in Choshen Mishpat, section 235, nevertheless regarding an agunah, it is clear that he is considered fully competent. One who was born mute but can hear is judged like someone who has become mute. A drunk person who has reached the level of Lot's drunkenness is considered like an imbecile. A dying person, if he is fully conscious, his testimony regarding an agunah is accepted whether through speech or nodding. Someone who sometimes is sane and sometimes not, when he is sane, he is considered fully competent as it is written there regarding a get (divorce document).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 11: If it was found written in a document that a man died or was killed — his wife may remarry, even if the document is not validated. According to the Rambam, it must be known that an Israelite wrote it. Even if it is written in a Gentile's script, if it is known that an Israelite wrote it, and a Gentile is not trusted in his writing, for he is only believed when he speaks casually, and in writing, this is not casual, for presumably, it was written intentionally. Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, in his major work, wonders, why should the Gentile be disqualified if he wrote it casually? In truth, if he wrote to an Israelite that so-and-so died, this is not casual. However, if he wrote to a fellow Gentile about other matters and mentioned within that so-and-so died, this would be considered casual. One of the great early authorities permitted based on such a writing by a Gentile who wrote to his fellow, "Know that Yitzchak, who owes you money, has died, come to collect your money," and permitted based on this writing. Another great authority disagreed with him. The words of the one who permits seem correct, for he did not write about the death as a specific knowledge but incidentally so that his fellow could collect his money. It seems that even if he wrote to an Israelite, it would be considered casual, as this is better than casual, for he would not lie as the other would travel far based on his writing, and if he lies, there would be grievances against him. Similarly, it seems to me that if it was found in the ledger of a Gentile merchant that so-and-so the Israelite died, this would be considered casual, for he wrote it for his business accounts.

The matter of the document is not specifically when it is written in the language of a deed that he sends to the court this writing as testimony that so-and-so died, but even if it is a simple writing that he wrote as a memorandum, it also works. Most of the decisors agree to this, and it is also evident from the language "found written in a document," for if he sent it as testimony, it would not be termed "found" but rather written testimony as a new document, as explained. However, there is an opinion that distinguishes: if he wrote it as testimony, it works even as hearsay testimony, such as writing in his document that he heard from so-and-so that so-and-so died, while if it is a simple memorandum, it does not work unless he writes that he saw it himself [Beit Shmuel, section 127]. Nevertheless, we have not heard this distinction from the decisors, and on the contrary, from the source of the law from the language of the Jerusalem Talmud that allows marrying based on the testimony of one witness and hearsay testimony, and the like based on their writing [end of Yevamot], it is clearly proven that hearsay testimony also works in writing. And it cannot be said that it is specifically written testimony and not a simple memorandum, for it is clear from the Jerusalem Talmud that there is no distinction [otherwise, the baraitot would contradict each other, and this reconciles what the Ran says in the chapter "Mi She'achzo" and the Maggid Mishneh in chapter 13 that the Rif relied on the law of the deaf-mute in section 73. The Lechem Mishneh and the Beit Shmuel questioned why it is similar to the deaf-mute since he testifies based on the writing, and according to what was said, it is clear; otherwise, why did the Jerusalem Talmud create a dispute between the baraitot. Refer there and investigate]. And this is the intention of the Mordechai's gloss in chapter 2 of Yevamot for the one who scrutinizes his language, and refer to the Bach and the Chavat Yair section 21 in the responsa of the father of the Shach and the responsa of the Chavat Yair, and investigate].

And specifically when a person is signed on the document, but writing without a signature is nothing [Beit Yosef in the name of the Rosh], and even if it can be verified who the writer is, since he did not sign himself, it is not a valid clarification unless this writing is found among his account books, for then it is not customary to sign oneself. But in writing on a separate paper, even if it is written only as a memorandum, it is known that something not signed has no substance. However, if this writing is in the language of testimony, "I testify that so-and-so died," it may be effective even without a signature if the writing is verified, but still, it should not be relied upon because since he did not sign himself, it is considered a defect before us [it appears to me]. And if it is found in writing that a sign of death was written about this person like "deceased" or "the late" or "may he rest in peace" – it is nothing [Chavot Yair].

In regard to the ruling of our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo (the Beit Yosef), that there is no need for verification, there are those who disagree and hold that verification is necessary. Nevertheless, many of the authorities agree that in a situation where verification is impossible because there is no one who recognizes the signature, it is permissible without verification. For according to Torah law, no verification is needed; the verification of documents is rabbinic, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 46. In cases of an agunah (a woman whose husband is missing and cannot remarry), the sages were lenient.

Even though regarding marriage documents, our master, the Rema, ruled in Siman 42 that if the document was not verified, it is not considered at all, this applies when the action of the document is disputed. Then, indeed, verification is required by Torah law. However, in this case, where there is no one to dispute, verification is unnecessary. And even though the requirement for document verification is only rabbinic — this applies to a fully executed document that two witnesses have signed, not to a document signed by one witness, and certainly not to a document written merely as a memorandum. Nevertheless, since the sages were lenient with regard to agunah cases concerning testimony for reasons already explained, this testimony is considered complete testimony. Thus, since it is considered complete testimony, it does not require verification by Torah law.

Certainly, it is preferable to strive to verify the document initially, and even through one witness is sufficient. The reason that one witness is not usually sufficient for verification is that it is akin to hearsay. However, in the case of an agunah, hearsay is accepted. Nonetheless, when verification is not possible, it is permitted even without verification.

Some of the great authorities have said that the leniency established for cases where post facto validation is not required applies specifically to a letter found locally or when a Jew brings a letter signed by a single witness who testifies that a certain person has died. If there is a possibility of forgery, it will become clear who the forger is; thus, we are lenient even without validation, which is the recognition of the writer's handwriting. However, for a letter received through the postal service, where the postal worker receives sealed letters and does not know who sent them, and if there is a forgery in the letter, it is impossible to verify who the forger is—in such cases, we do not permit without validation.

This view does not seem correct because, according to it, we could only permit based on a letter brought by a person, not a letter found locally. Even in a letter found locally, if someone forged it, it would never be possible to identify the forger. This matter is clearly stated in all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) that we rely on such letters, and it is also stated in the Jerusalem Talmud: "If it was found written in a document that a certain person died," as mentioned in section 76. Therefore, it seems to me that this opinion is not the primary one.

However, it is certain that since it was established that initially, validation is required, and for a letter received through the postal service, it is easy to validate because every letter sent through the mail has a government stamp from the place it was sent. Therefore, it is possible to write to the rabbi or someone else there and ask them to verify the facts, and it is easy to find validation. But when it is impossible to validate, we rely on the letter even without validation because a woman examines the matter carefully and will not remarry in a situation likely to be revealed.

Jews serving in the king's army, when one of them dies and a document arrives sealed with the royal seal and signed by the army commander stating that a certain person, son of a certain person, with his appellation, has died—there have been several such incidents in the previous generation, and the great sages of the generation permitted their wives to remarry based on such documents, provided they conform to the state's regulations. That is, the document must be according to an official number, sealed with the government seal, and signed or written by the army commander along with additional signatures. Since falsehood would endanger their own lives before the king, we rely on this in cases of agunah (a woman whose husband is missing and cannot remarry). This is only when it explicitly states that he has died, but if it states that a certain person is missing, it is not permissible to rely on this, as he might have escaped or similar. However, if it states that he has died, we investigate the matter to the best of our ability and rely on the writing of the army commander with the royal seal following the regulations.

And regarding what the Rambam wrote that it is necessary to know that the letter is written by a Jew, our master the Rema wrote that it is proper to be stringent in this matter. And even if it is known that a Jew wrote it - if it can be said that he wrote so because a rumor had spread that the person had died, such as if he drowned in a body of water without a visible end or similar cases - we do not permit remarriage based on this letter, because we suspect that he wrote it due to the rumor that had spread. And the explanation of the matter is: when a rumor spreads about someone that he drowned or similar, it is the way of the world to say that he died, and from a legal standpoint, she is not permitted to remarry. Therefore, we are concerned that the one who writes that he died is writing based on this assumption because of the drowning or similar events. However, if there is a general rumor that he died and afterward someone writes that he died, there is no concern at all, because it appears that the rumor is true, but we do not suspect that he wrote so because of the rumor he heard. And so wrote our master the Beit Yosef in a response, and many great authorities agreed with this. However, there are some great authorities who were also concerned in this case that he wrote due to the rumor that had spread. And it seems that the primary opinion is the first one, for even in oral testimony, the law is the same. Therefore, if someone testifies that a certain person died and beforehand a rumor had spread that he died, we do not accept his testimony, and it is impossible to say this at all, as is evident from all the poskim. However, when he testifies before a Beit Din, it can be said that we do not suspect this, because the Beit Din asks him how he knows that the person died, and if he says based on the rumor, we do not accept his testimony. But in a general statement, it could be that he says so based on the rumor. According to this, if a witness testifies before a Beit Din that he heard from someone else that a certain person died, and beforehand a rumor had spread that he died, we do not accept his testimony, and this does not seem to be implied by all the poskim. Furthermore, since our master the Beit Yosef ruled this way, and it is explicitly implied from the words of our master the Rema, and many of the later authorities agreed with this, one who is lenient in this matter has not lost. However, in such a case, it seems that it is necessary at least to verify the letter to know who wrote it, and it is likely that through this it will become known whether it was written based on the rumor or not.

And there are some of the great authorities who have divided this ruling into three categories: The first – when a rumor has spread that a certain person drowned, and afterward someone else reported in a general manner that he died, or even if no rumor spread but the witness himself said that he drowned and afterward said that he died – everyone is concerned, for perhaps when he said he died, he meant through drowning, and we do not permit her (to remarry) until he explicitly states that the waters expelled him and he saw him dead in a manner that will be explained in this section, or if he said that he came out of the water alive and afterward died in his bed, and similarly in other matters close to death when a rumor spread, we judge in this manner.

The second case is when it has already become known that the person about whom this witness testified has died, having entered a place of danger where those who enter are likely to die. This matter has become publicized, and there is also a rumor that he died in that danger. If the witness testifies in general terms that he died, everyone agrees that there is a concern that he may not have seen him die and is testifying based on public consensus. In this case, we judge it similarly to the previous law.

And the third case – when a rumor spreads about a man who traveled from place to place and did not return home, and the rumor says he died, and afterward, one witness testifies that he died – in this, the great authorities are divided as stated in section 81. Even according to those who permit it, this is only when the testimony is solely about his death. But when the main testimony is about another matter and his death is mentioned incidentally – in this case, certainly, according to all opinions, we suspect that he is speaking based on the rumor. And this reasoning is sound [Marei Tzvi in the name of Seder Eliyahu]. And know that all this applies to one witness. But when two valid witnesses testify that he died – their testimony is accepted in any case, even if a rumor has spread and even if the matters were not clarified, for with two witnesses there is no concern [so it seems to me]. And we have already written what seems correct to us in section 81.

It is a simple matter that just as we have said that when someone drowns or there is a rumor, we no longer rely on a found document stating that a certain person has died or on verbal testimony, as we have explained all the opinions, similarly in such a case with a non-Jew who reports without intent to deceive that a certain person has died, if it is known that the person drowned – we do not permit based on his statement, because certainly he says so based on his assumption, and similarly in all such cases. And there is a doubt whether even afterward if he clarifies his words through our questioning him how he knew that the person died and he says things that according to the law would permit, nonetheless since the main permission comes through our questioning and a non-Jew reporting without intent to deceive is not through questioning as will be explained, it is not comparable to every case of a non-Jew reporting without intent to deceive that will be explained that even though afterward he clarifies his words through our questioning, we permit her – this is because the main permission was based on his previous words which were not through questioning, but in this case where his previous words do not permit her – perhaps it is ineffective for the main permission to come through questioning.

When there is a contradiction between witnesses, for example, if two valid witnesses come and testify that this woman's husband has died, and two other valid witnesses contradict them and testify that he did not die – the Sages stated [Yevamot 88b] that she should not remarry, and if she did remarry, she must leave. Even if the contradicting witnesses came after she had already married – she must leave, and the one who has relations with her is liable to bring a provisional guilt offering, similar to the case of doubt regarding whether one has consumed forbidden fat or permitted fat. However, if she married one of the witnesses who testified that her husband had died, and she herself asserts with certainty that her husband has died – if she married, she does not have to leave.

And the explanation of the matter is as follows: Behold, it is established for us that when there are two sets of witnesses contradicting one another – from the Torah, we must maintain the matter in its presumptive status, as in the law of any doubt. And rabbinically, even if there is a presumption of permissibility – it is forbidden. But when the presumption is towards prohibition – it is forbidden from the Torah. And behold, in the case of this woman who has the presumption of being a married woman (eshet ish), she is forbidden by Torah law, and one who cohabits with her is liable to a sin offering, as if he ate definite forbidden fat.

However, when she married permissibly based on the testimony of the first two witnesses, there is no sin offering required but rather a conditional guilt offering, for the first witnesses removed her from her presumptive status of prohibition based on their testimony. And although later others came and contradicted them, leaving the matter in doubt, it is like any doubtful prohibition, and therefore only a conditional guilt offering is required. And some say that in any case, there is only a conditional guilt offering, and the presumption of a woman is that she investigates thoroughly and would not marry without certainty regarding her status as a married woman. And even though the rationale of thorough investigation applies only when there is one witness who testifies that her husband died, but with two witnesses, we do not need her thorough investigation, nevertheless, when there are two sets of witnesses contradicting each other, she must investigate thoroughly; otherwise, we will be stringent with her in the end.

According to this, even if the two sets of witnesses came simultaneously, there is no sin offering but only a conditional guilt offering. And even though with a conditional guilt offering, it is established for us that one is not liable until the prohibition is fixed, meaning when there is a definite prohibition before us, such as when there are two pieces, one of forbidden fat and one of permissible fat, and he ate one of them and does not know which one he ate, but if there is one piece with a doubt whether it is forbidden fat or permissible fat and he ate it, he is not liable for a conditional guilt offering as the Rambam writes in the eighth chapter of Shgagot, nevertheless, here he is liable for a conditional guilt offering for it is considered as a fixed prohibition, for she was until now in the presumption of being a married woman. And even though regarding a sin offering we remove her from her presumption as stated – that is because we cannot consider it as definite forbidden fat, but regarding being called a fixed prohibition – certainly, there is no greater fixed prohibition than this, and he is liable for a conditional guilt offering even if she married and then witnesses came.

Indeed, if she marries one of the witnesses who permitted her, and she also asserts with certainty, even though if she had not married we would not allow her to marry, nevertheless, if she has married, she does not need to leave [the marriage]. The reason for this is that in any doubt concerning a prohibition, although we uphold the presumption and prohibit her, this is only for someone who is uncertain about the matter, especially when there is a presumption of prohibition. But for someone who says that there is no doubt in their mind and they know with certainty that this is permitted, they necessarily remove the matter from its presumption due to their clear knowledge. The Torah never equates doubt with certainty when there is a presumption of prohibition, and the court punishes and stones based on this presumption, as stated in Siman 19, but only for someone who is uncertain about the matter. However, if someone says with certainty that this is permitted, they necessarily remove it from its presumption. Even though for another person, they are not believed to remove the presumption of prohibition because there are those who contradict them, nevertheless, for themselves, they are certainly believed, as the Torah believes every person regarding their own matters of prohibition. And although regarding monetary matters we do not say that certainty (bari) is better than uncertainty (shema), this is because it concerns others. But in prohibitions and regarding oneself, one is believed. Therefore, if she does not say with certainty that he died, she must leave [the marriage], because for her, the witness is not believed to remove her from her presumption of prohibition. But when she also claims with certainty, she does not need to leave. What is this similar to? To two pieces, one of forbidden fat (chelev) and one of permissible fat (shuman). If Reuven comes and eats one of them, he is liable for a suspended guilt offering (asham talui). But if Shimon comes and says, "I placed the pieces or saw them being placed, and the forbidden fat was placed on the right and the permissible fat on the left," and there is someone who contradicts him, and he ate what was on the left side, should we obligate him to bring a suspended guilt offering? There is no doubt in his mind. 

[What the Ba'er Heitev wrote in Se'if Katan 158, that even if she was permitted based on the witnesses, she must leave, his intention is even if she had already married, as explained in the Gemara and as written by the Chazon Ish in Siman Peh.]

It is a clear matter that when two valid witnesses initially came to permit her, two who contradict them are not credible unless they are also valid. However, if they are relatives or disqualified from testimony according to all of the Torah, their words mean nothing against the two valid witnesses. This holds true when initially two valid witnesses testified, but if initially only one witness or two relatives or disqualified ones testified, and subsequently one witness or disqualified ones came and contradicted them, there are different laws regarding this, as will be explained further with God's help.

There are those who pose a significant question regarding this matter: even though we permit the witness who testifies to the death to live with her when she also claims with certainty, what shall we do concerning the children born from them? For them, there are two witnesses against two witnesses, and they are, Heaven forbid, in a state of doubtful illegitimacy (mamzerim). And it is impossible to say such a thing, for the Torah's ways are ways of pleasantness. If the children were in a state of doubtful mamzerut, our sages would not permit her to be with him. Furthermore, if after this person's death a priest (kohen) wishes to marry her, we would not allow it, as it is a case of two witnesses against two witnesses, making her a doubtful zonah (harlot) [see Beit Meir].

However, in truth, the sons are also eligible, and a Kohen would be permitted to marry her after the death of this one. A great principle in everything we judge, whether for permissibility or prohibition, is that if the matter has emerged as permissible due to a presumption or a clear claim, then all subsequent matters that follow are entirely permissible because the matter has already been deemed permissible. This is the main reasoning explained in Siman 4, Se'if 31, that her presumption benefits the daughter even though the daughter has no presumption.
