This is a great principle in all matters of presumptions and doubts, except in a case where there is no practical difference in what we are judging, like in a mikvah that was measured and found to be deficient. Since the mikvah itself does not matter, we then judge also the person immersing in it. [Refer to what is written in Sefer Or LeYesharim, Siman 39, and from Tosafot in several places, it seems there is a contradiction to this; however, it can be said that their words are according to the one who holds in Ketubot (13b) that according to the one who validates her, disqualifies her daughter, and consider this carefully].

However, it is certain that the witnesses who contradict them are forbidden to marry the daughter born to them, because according to their testimony, she is a married woman (אשת איש), and the daughter would be a mamzeret (a child born from a forbidden union). And indeed, everyone is believed to establish a piece of prohibition upon themselves, and certainly in such a case where she is forbidden to everyone except for the permitting witnesses. Similarly, if the man who married her dies, she is forbidden to marry another as long as it has not been clarified that the first husband is dead. However, once it is clarified afterwards, she is permitted even to a Kohen, as I have written.

If one witness says the husband died and another says he did not die, if the court had already permitted her to remarry before the second witness came – she does not need to leave her new marriage and she is allowed to marry anyone she desires. The reason is that we hold that in the case of one witness for a sotah (a woman suspected of adultery) when he testifies after warning and seclusion, and in the case of one witness for the eglah arufah (the heifer whose neck is broken) when he identifies the murderer, the Torah believes one witness as if he were two, as explained in the Rambam, Chapter 1 of Sotah and Chapter 9 of Rotzeach. Therefore, the second witness is not believed to contradict the first one. Wherever the Torah believes one witness, he is considered as two and the words of one do not stand against the words of two. And even though there, immediately when the witness testified, a second witness coming afterward is not believed to contradict him. So why do we require here that she was already permitted to marry? Because it is not the same. There, the Torah explicitly believes the one witness, and immediately when he testified, he is considered as two. But in the testimony regarding a woman, even according to the opinions that from the Torah one witness is believed, it is not exactly like the sotah or the eglah arufah. There, the Torah explicitly writes that one witness is believed, but in the case of a woman’s testimony, its basis is rabbinic. Therefore, as long as she was not permitted to marry, it is considered as if both witnesses came simultaneously. However, some of our sages hold that even in the case of the sotah and the eglah arufah, it is only when they ruled based on his testimony, and before this, it is as if both came at the same time. But the Rambam there and the Tur in Siman 178 did not rule this way. And even according to this, it is simple to distinguish that in the case of the sotah and the eglah arufah, where the court must give her the bitter water to drink or bring the eglah arufah immediately when the first witness testified, it is considered as if their ruling was completed that she should not drink or they should not bring the eglah arufah. But here, where she needs to marry, as long as the court has not permitted her, it is not considered a completed ruling. See what I wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 425, Se'if 75.

If the second witness comes before she is permitted to remarry, she should not marry, and if she does marry, she must leave the marriage, because she is in doubt whether she is still married. If she marries the witness who testified to her and she also says with certainty that her husband died, Rambam writes that she does not have to leave the marriage, comparing this to the case of conflicting testimonies, as implied in the Yerushalmi. However, some of our rabbis hold that one witness in opposition is meaningless, and it is certainly a prohibition, and one who has relations with her is liable for a sin offering and not a conditional guilt offering, and her certainty and the witness's testimony do not help, as we explained in section 88. Rambam holds that since one witness is valid in the testimony of a woman, although we do not permit her to remarry because of the opposing witness, it is still treated like a case of two against two in all of Torah law. However, if two witnesses come and testify that her husband is alive, it is obvious that she must leave the marriage even if she has married, and the children are considered illegitimate by all opinions, because in the presence of two witnesses, one witness is meaningless even in the testimony of a woman, even if she was permitted and married. According to Rambam, even if there is one witness against one witness, she should not be permitted to marry, but if she does marry, she does not have to leave the marriage, even though there is suspicion that the witness testified in order to marry her. Since there is such a suspicion with one witness, as we explained in section 12, nevertheless, she does not have to leave the marriage because of this suspicion, but initially, we advise against marrying her. Some want to deduce from the language of Rambam that if both witnesses come at the same time, she must leave the marriage, but if they come one after the other, even before she is permitted to remarry, she does not have to leave. This does not seem correct, because since he wrote earlier that only if she was permitted to remarry does she not have to leave, it follows that when he wrote later about both witnesses coming at the same time, his intention was that the second witness came before she was permitted to remarry. Even though some wrote this as law, it does not seem so from all the earlier authorities.

When they permitted her to marry based on one witness and then another came and contradicted him, it was clarified that she does not need to leave her first marriage and is permitted to marry. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 37 that nevertheless, because of "ill repute," she should not marry initially. And some say that this is not a matter of law but rather good advice, and according to the Rambam, there is not even good advice in this. Some of our Rabbis hold that initially, it is a complete prohibition because of "ill repute," and this is somewhat implied by the language of the Tur. But when two say he is dead and one says he is not dead, even if the one came before the two, she is permitted to marry initially, and there is not even "ill repute" in this.

All that has been explained regarding two against two and one against one applies only with valid witnesses. But concerning the testimony of women, relatives, and others who are disqualified and are only valid for the testimony concerning a woman, there are different rules. Sometimes they are equal to valid witnesses, and sometimes they are not. How so? If a woman, relative, or disqualified person says someone is dead, and another like them says the person is not dead, their status is like valid witnesses. There is a distinction between whether they permitted her to remarry before the second person came or not. If she married based on the testimony of the one who permitted her and she says she is certain he is dead – according to the Rambam, if she married, she does not need to be divorced, but according to those who disagree with him, she must be divorced. If two disqualified witnesses come and contradict the first disqualified witness, even if she has married, she must be divorced. Similarly, if one disqualified person says he is not dead and two disqualified persons say he is dead, even if they have not permitted her yet, they should permit her initially, and she may marry. If two disqualified persons say he is dead and two disqualified persons say he is not dead, their status is also like one against one; for disqualified witnesses, there is no difference in this matter.

And in this case, invalid witnesses are not similar to valid ones. For with valid witnesses, the only distinction is between one witness and two, but between two and more than two, there is no distinction either for permissibility or prohibition, as two are like a hundred. If a hundred valid witnesses come and testify that he died, and two valid witnesses come and testify that he did not die, if she married, she must leave. And likewise, the reverse: if two say he died and a hundred say he did not die, and she married one of those who permitted it and claims certainty, if she married, she does not have to leave. But with invalid witnesses, it is not so, as the greater number always outweighs the other side. With valid witnesses, since according to the Torah, "by the mouth of two witnesses shall the matter be established," whether it be two or a hundred, it makes no difference. But with invalid witnesses, whose testimony is nothing and were only deemed valid in the case of a woman's testimony, the majority opinion outweighs the minority, whether to be lenient or strict. How so? If ten women or ten close relatives and invalid witnesses say he died, and eleven like them contradict them, even if she married, she must leave, and even if she married one of her witnesses, she must leave [Beit Shmuel, sub-section 126]. And likewise, the reverse: if ten women and close relatives and invalid witnesses say he did not die, and eleven like them say he died, even if they did not permit her, they will permit her and she may marry, and similarly in all such cases. This applies to invalid witnesses against invalid witnesses, but for valid witnesses against invalid ones who contradict them, or vice versa, there are other laws.

How so? A valid witness says [the husband] has died, and many women or relatives and many invalid witnesses say he has not died. If they permitted [her to remarry] based on the valid witness before the invalid ones came, she does not have to leave her remarriage and she may marry, since the many invalid ones are considered only as one valid witness. But if they came before they permitted her, their status is like half and half, and she may not marry, and if she has married, she must leave [the marriage]. And if she married based on the witness and she says with certainty that he has died, our teacher Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in section 37 that she does not have to leave [the marriage]. It seems to me that those who disagree with Maimonides regarding one witness versus another witness also disagree about this for the reason explained, that one witness in contradiction is considered nothing [see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 118]. And some say that according to Maimonides, even if they permitted her based on the valid witness, if two invalid witnesses came and contradicted him, their status is like half and half, and even if she married, she must leave [the marriage], except when she married him and she says with certainty [that he died] [see Chelkat Mechokek, subparagraph 172].

A relative, an invalid witness, or a woman says that her husband died, or the agunah herself says "My husband died," and afterward a valid witness comes and says he did not die—even if they permitted her to remarry before the valid witness came, she may not remarry, and if she did remarry, she must leave her second husband. This is the opinion of the Rambam who holds that an invalid witness is less credible than a valid witness, even though according to Torah law, the testimony of a valid witness alone is not sufficient for anything except obligating an oath. Some of our Rabbis hold that in this case, an invalid witness is considered like a valid one, and if they permitted her based on the invalid witness or based on the agunah herself, and afterward a valid witness came and said the husband did not die, she does not have to leave her second husband. However, even according to the Rambam, this is only in the case of one invalid witness, where the valid witness is more credible. But if two invalid witnesses or two women came and permitted her to remarry based on their testimony, and afterward a valid witness came and said the husband did not die, in this case, she does not have to leave her second husband according to all opinions, because certainly in this case, the valid witness is not more credible than them.

And know that the agunah (a woman whose husband is missing and cannot remarry) herself can join with an invalid witness when she knows that her husband has died, and there is a significant practical difference in this, such as when a woman says he died and two women say he did not die. As we have explained, she must leave her second husband – this is when the agunah herself does not know anything. But if she also says she knows clearly that he died, even if she says this after she has remarried, she combines with the previous testimony, and it is considered as if there were two and two invalid witnesses. When she has remarried, she does not have to leave her second husband. Similarly, if she was permitted to remarry, she does not have to leave based on the earlier permission, as stated in section 96, where their status is like that of one witness and another witness. A Samaritan testifying unintentionally is treated like other invalid witnesses. If one Samaritan testifies unintentionally that he is alive and another unintentionally that he is dead, she should not remarry, and if she has remarried, she must leave. This is different from the case of a captive woman mentioned in section 7, paragraph 6, where we were lenient. In the case of a married woman, we must be more stringent. Some authorities are stringent in this matter, and some are lenient, and this will be further explained, God willing.

And regarding what we have written that the agunah herself can join with the previous witness even after she has remarried, nevertheless, the husband she has remarried does not join if he wants to testify that her first husband died, because he is a party to the matter and one's testimony is not valid for oneself. She herself is believed due to the reason that she is precise, but this reason does not apply to him. This is the intention of our teacher, the Rema, in section 37 at the end of the first gloss. However, there are those who disagree with him and hold that she is also not believed to join after she has remarried, and only before this can she join with the invalid witness.

Just as with disqualified witnesses we follow the majority opinion, so too with qualified witnesses who testify indirectly (i.e., through hearsay), even if they heard from others who are also deemed qualified — we follow the majority opinion, and their status in all matters is like that of disqualified witnesses. The reason is simple: just as disqualified witnesses are invalid for all aspects of the Torah, and only in the case of testimony concerning a woman's marital status have the sages been lenient without considering them fully qualified, so too a witness who testifies indirectly is not valid for the entire Torah, and only in the case of an agunah (a woman whose husband is missing and cannot be confirmed dead) have the sages been lenient. Therefore, their status is like that of disqualified witnesses, as will be explained.

Therefore, if two people testify that each one heard from someone else, for example, Reuven testifies that he heard from Levi and Shimon testifies that he heard from Yehuda that a certain person died, and two other people testify from their own knowledge that he did not die – their status is not like two against two, so that if she (the widow) marries one of the witnesses and claims certainty, she would not have to leave him. Rather, their status is like one against two and she must leave. If one witness testifies from his own knowledge that he did not die, their status is like two invalid witnesses and one valid witness contradicting them. If one witness testifies from the testimony of another that he did not die, their status is like two against one invalid witness, and she is permitted to marry initially. If two people testify from the testimony of another that he did not die, their status is like two and two invalid witnesses. If three people testify from the testimony of another that he did not die, we follow the majority opinion and the previous testimonies are nullified as in the case of invalid witnesses. Similarly, if initially two testified from the testimony of another that he did not die and three testify from the testimony of another that he did die, she may marry initially, and so in all similar cases.

And what has been explained, that two people who heard from a witness who heard from another witness are considered like two invalid witnesses – this is when each one heard from a different person separately. But if these two are testifying based on what they heard from one person, even if that person is valid to testify, they are not considered like two invalid witnesses but rather like one invalid witness. And even if a hundred people heard from one person, they are considered as one invalid witness. (Choshen Mishpat 489:289 and Beit Shmuel 127).

And one witness who testifies based on what he heard from an individual and one witness who testifies based on what he heard from many are equally weighed, and it is considered like one invalid witness (Choshen Mishpat ibid). Some say that one who heard from many is better than one who heard from an individual (Beit Shmuel ibid), and it is a doubtful legal matter since many great authorities have disputed this. If two testify that they heard from two, and one testifies that he heard from two – it is considered like two and one invalid witnesses (Noda BiYehuda).

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 42: "We do not remove a woman from her husband if there is a rumor that her first husband is alive." This implies that before she marries, we are concerned about a rumor. It must be said that this refers to a rumor that has been confirmed in a court, for without confirmation in a court, it is not considered a rumor, as stated in section 46. Nevertheless, after she has married, we do not remove her from her husband, because we are not concerned about a rumor that arises after marriage, as stated there.

It has already been explained in section 54 that testimony is only valid when given in a court of law, and anything spoken outside the court can be retracted when the person comes to court. There was an incident where someone contended about a certain woman, claiming that she was obligated to perform yibbum (levirate marriage). Later, he testified before the court that he had heard that the yavam (brother-in-law) had died a long time ago and that his initial claim was baseless. The court ruled that they could rely on his testimony because the initial statements were made outside the court. The ruling regarding testimony from hearsay, when the first witness retracts, is explained in sections 55 and 56, see there. Concerning a gentile who speaks casually (mesiach lefi tumo) about the death of someone, whether he can retract and claim he lied, it is an unresolved halachic question. For any witness whose testimony is only accepted in court, it can be said that as long as the testimony has not been examined in court, he can retract. However, in the case of mesiach lefi tumo, where formal court testimony is ineffective and only casual conversation is valid, it can be argued that once he has spoken casually, his testimony is finalized and he cannot retract, or it is possible that there is no difference. [See Kuntres Agunot, sections 156 and 158].

It has already been explained in section 36 that five women are disqualified from testifying that her husband has died because, due to their hatred of her, they are suspected of intending to cause her harm by enabling her to remarry, and when her husband returns, she will have to leave both her new husband and the original one. One of these women is her co-wife in places where it is customary to marry two wives. Therefore, if a man went overseas with his wife and left another wife here, and the distant wife came and testified before the court that her husband died, a woman is believed concerning herself, as has been explained, and she is permitted to remarry. However, regarding her co-wife, she is not believed, because a co-wife is not trusted to testify for her fellow wife, lest she intends to cause her harm as stated. Even if she herself remarries first, we do not say that if her husband had not died, she would not have forbidden herself to him, because we are concerned that due to her intense hatred for her co-wife, she wishes to forbid both of them to him, as Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines." One should not question that if so, she should not be believed even about herself due to this concern, but since she knows that she will not be believed regarding her co-wife, this concern is removed, for she only testifies about herself. And if it is difficult that if so, she should be believed also regarding her co-wife, it can be said that if so, the concern would return to its place [Jerusalem Talmud].

And not only is she not believed to permit her, but even to prohibit her she is not believed. Therefore, if there are two wives of one man, and one says "My husband has died" and the co-wife contradicts her and says "He has not died," the one who says "He has died" may remarry. Just as she cannot testify to permit her, so too she cannot testify to prohibit her. The same applies to all five wives; the law is the same. And even though she is presumed to be a married woman, nevertheless their words are considered nothing. Similarly, if the co-wives contradict each other and both admit that he is not alive, but one says he died and the other says he was killed, both are permitted. We do not consider this as conflicting testimony that nullifies their testimony completely and makes both of them forbidden, for since they are not testifying for each other, their contradiction regarding each other is not considered a contradiction. Each one testifies for herself and is permitted. Moreover, even with witnesses in such a case, Rabbi Yosef Caro ruled in paragraph 9 that both are permitted, and even those who disagree with him agree that in the case of co-wives, the contradiction is not considered significant for the reasons explained, as mentioned in paragraph 57. See there.

There is a doubt. Even though our Sages said that a co-wife is not believed, neither to prohibit nor to permit, nevertheless, when this co-wife testifies that her husband died and she herself took action and married another man, while she is not believed to be lenient for her co-wife to marry another, nevertheless, for stringency, perhaps she is believed, such as if they are the wife of a Kohen, her co-wife would be forbidden to eat Terumah, and if she committed adultery, the child would not be a definite mamzer to permit him to a mamzeret, and if she accepted Kiddushin from another, she would require a Get and would not be considered definitely a married woman. The logic supports this because since she herself took action, how can we not consider her co-wife at least as a doubtful married woman and not definitely? However, some say that since we rule in the Gemara [Yevamot 118a] that the co-wife is permitted to eat Terumah, and so writes the Rambam in Chapter 9 of Terumot, we see that we consider her definitely a married woman and not as doubtful. If another betrothed her, she does not need a Get from him [Beit Shmuel, section 134], and if she committed adultery, the child is a definite mamzer [Magid Mishneh, Chapter 12 of Gerushin]. However, it seems to me that there is no proof from this, as we can say that this is all until her co-wife took action and married, but once she married, why should we not be stringent? Nonetheless, on the main matter, some of our Rabbis disagree with the Rambam and hold that she is forbidden to eat Terumah, as for stringency, we are concerned with her words [Ra'avad there, and so it seems from Tosafot there, s.v. "Bat Yisrael," and their words tend towards what I wrote, and investigate thoroughly].

A woman who claims that her husband died is believed both to marry another and to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) with her husband's brother, since the principle that she is careful and likely to reveal the truth also applies if she were to do yibbum. Moreover, she can even collect her ketubah from her husband's estate, because although she is not trusted regarding monetary matters based solely on her word without witnesses, the ketubah is a Torah obligation, and every husband commits himself at the time of marriage that if she remarries, she will collect her ketubah. Since she is believed to remarry, it follows that she collects her ketubah due to his prior obligation. Therefore, this is only when it is known that the property belongs to her husband, but if it is not known, she is not believed to say that it is her husband's property, as she has no credibility in this regard. She is believed to say that the man who died before you is her husband, but she is not believed to collect her ketubah from this man's property since we do not know if this man had obligated himself to her. Although the Torah believes her for marriage and not for monetary matters, and she is only believed for the Torah-obligated ketubah and not for the additional ketubah, nor for the dowry properties and other things, the obligation that the husband commits to his wife that when she remarries she will take, applies only to the Torah-obligated ketubah. For other monetary matters, she needs two witnesses to testify before the court that her husband died. Just as she collects her ketubah, similarly, if she performs yibbum, the yavam (levir) inherits his brother's estate based on her word, as the Torah decreed that he shall establish a name for his brother in his inheritance when he performs yibbum with his wife. When she collects her ketubah, she must first swear, as is the law for all widows, as stated in Siman 100. Some say that through the process of gilgul she also swears that he died.

In what case does she take the ketubah? When she did not mention the ketubah, saying "My husband died, permit me to remarry." But if she comes and says, "My husband died, give me my ketubah," not only does she not take the ketubah, but we do not permit her to remarry, because we suspect that her sole intention was to take the ketubah and not to remarry, as she knows he is alive but wants to take money from his property. Some have inferred from the language of Maimonides at the end of Chapter 16 of Ishut that she has no intention to remarry at all, as he wrote, "If she subsequently remarries, she takes her ketubah." To me, this is puzzling, since she married without the permission of the court. And there are those among the early authorities who hold that even if she brought a single witness to testify that her husband died, we do not rely on it because we suspect him as well due to the mention of the ketubah. Our master, the Rema, brought this opinion, and how is it possible that when she marries on her own, she would also take the ketubah? This requires further investigation in terms of the law. (See Choshen Mishpat, Siman 82. It is possible that the Rema's opinion is also thus, and this is the meaning of "she has a witness" – that she brought him.)

If she mentioned both matters, saying "My husband died and permit me [to remarry] and give me my ketubah," since she mentioned the permission before the ketubah, it is assumed that her primary intention is for the permission. The mention of the ketubah is because it is customary for people to recount all their matters in court. However, if she mentioned the ketubah first, the Talmud leaves it unresolved, and all our rabbis ruled stringently that we do not permit her to remarry, and certainly, she does not receive her ketubah. However, the Rambam wrote that we permit her [to remarry] but do not give her the ketubah. He holds that the primary uncertainty in the Gemara is about the ketubah, but regarding the marriage, she is not suspect of remarrying while her husband is alive. Therefore, if she remarries, we do not object <small>[Beit Shmuel, section 131]</small>. This does not seem correct, for if so, the Rambam should have written in this manner. How could he write that we permit her, and how can we permit her initially when there is uncertainty? Some say that there is a printing error in the Rambam, and it should say we do not permit her <small>[The Vilna Gaon, section 140]</small>. And some say that even if she mentioned the permission first, we do not permit her initially <small>[The Rosh]</small>. However, if she remarried – it is obvious that she does not need to leave, for even if she remarried without the permission of the court, we rule that she does not need to leave, as will be explained.

The Rambam also wrote that even with the precedence written [in the Ketubah], one does not give her [the Ketubah payment]; nevertheless, if she seized her Ketubah, it is not taken from her. This follows his view that in all cases of monetary law disputes, seizure is effective, as he wrote in Choshen Mishpat in several places. And we have already explained there that some of our Rabbis disagree with him and hold that in cases of legal doubt, seizure is not effective.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in section 43 that even a woman who is a fool is believed to say that her husband has died, provided she knows the nature of marriage and widowhood. End of quote. The explanation of his words: Even a foolish woman who does not have the understanding and intelligence to comprehend the gravity of the situation she would face if she lies, and I would have said that in her case the principle of "she will investigate and will not permit herself" does not apply, he informs us that there is no difference. The reason can be said to be that, on the contrary, a woman like her is less likely to lie and deceive. And he does not refer to a completely insane woman, but rather to a foolish one. [And it seems to me that he learned from page 116: They said to Rabbi Yehuda, according to your words a clever woman will marry, etc., meaning a clever woman will scheme and thus get married, whereas a foolish woman who does not scheme will not get married, and the opposite is reasonable, and be exact in this matter].

We hold that in capital cases, there is a requirement for investigation and interrogation of the witnesses, but in monetary cases, there is no need for such investigation and interrogation, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 30. In matters concerning women's testimony, such as testifying that a husband has died, or in cases of marriage and divorce, there are elements of both capital and monetary law. This is because if someone cohabits with a married woman, he is liable for execution by strangulation, and there are also monetary considerations since the woman may need to collect her ketubah and other financial obligations such as sustenance and other matters. The Talmud at the end of Yevamot (122b) discusses to which category these laws should be compared, and all the poskim (decisors) concluded that we rule according to the opinion that does not require investigation and interrogation, similar to monetary cases.

However, this reasoning is not entirely satisfactory, as one of our Rabbis questioned. Even though there are monetary elements involved, there are also capital elements. And just because there are monetary elements, should we diminish its severity? According to Torah law, even in these cases, investigation and interrogation are required. It was only to avoid shutting the door in the face of borrowers that the requirement was annulled, as stated in Choshen Mishpat there. How can we be lenient in this case, especially since the reasoning of avoiding shutting the door does not apply here?

However, the Rambam, of blessed memory, in the end of Chapter 13 of Hilchot Gerushin, explains the reason: Due to the issue of agunot (women chained to marriages), the Rabbis were lenient, treating it as monetary law, just as they were lenient in matters of agunot with various types of witnesses. Additionally, the primary leniency regarding agunot is because she herself would be precise and there is a tendency for the truth to be revealed. Therefore, there is no need for the investigation and interrogation of the witnesses. This matter will be further explained in Siman 42, with God's help.

Therefore, even if the witnesses contradict each other in their examinations, their testimony is accepted. If they contradict each other in their interrogations, some say their testimony is invalid [Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel], for even in monetary cases, this is the law, as explained in Section 57. Others say that even if they contradict each other in their interrogations, their testimony is not invalid [Bach], as explained in Section 58. This is also the opinion of our master, the Beit Yosef, in a responsum, as explained in Section 59, and many of the later authorities hold this view [and it was wrongly written by the Beit Shmuel in Subsection 64 that this is an error], and there we explained a valid reason for this. Nevertheless, when the witness is before us, we inquire and ask him how he knows that the person is dead, as explained in Section 44. However, anyone who is stringent and inquires and investigates extensively, to the point that the testimony might not be accepted, is not approved by the sages, and so wrote the Rambam in a responsum [Beit Shmuel Subsection 65]. However, in a situation where there is concern about deception, it is obvious that we investigate and inquire extensively in order to uncover the truth. Some say that in such cases of suspected deceit, the law is like capital cases, that if one says "I do not know," their testimony is invalid. But the Rivash wrote that this is not an impediment, as only investigation and interrogation are required to uncover the truth, but it should not be like capital cases where the testimony is invalidated if one says "I do not know." It seems that the majority of the later authorities agreed with this opinion [see Noda B'Yehuda, Section 72]. [The Beit Shmuel in Subsection 63 wrote that in these times there are no capital cases, which is insufficient, and the clear reason is as explained. Also, what he wrote that the Rambam does not hold the reason of precision, we have already explained in Section 22 that this is not so, see there and examine carefully.]

It has already been explained that a woman who remarries based on the testimony of one witness, the testimony of a Samaritan speaking without self-interest, or her own testimony, the permission is not explicitly stated in the Torah. Rather, the Sages established this rule due to the problem of agunot (women unable to remarry because their husbands are missing). Therefore, in the Talmud, she is referred to as being married with the consent of the court. Even according to Rambam, whom we explained there permits it by Torah law, and many of our rabbis agreed as written in section 24, she is still considered married with the consent of the court because the permission is not so straightforward, and one needs to consult the court. Therefore, our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 39 that she should not remarry except with the consent of the court. However, if she remarried without the court's consent, meaning without their ruling, she should nevertheless not leave the new marriage. Just as when the court permits her to remarry based on the testimony of one witness and then another witness comes and testifies that her husband did not die, she should not leave her new marriage because the first witness is as reliable as two witnesses, as stated in section 93. Similarly, if she remarried without the court's consent, we do not pay attention to a witness who comes later and says her husband did not die, because her remarriage is no worse than the court's permission. Although she acted improperly by not waiting for the court's permission, she is ultimately permitted by law, and the Sages did not see fit to penalize her for this. Although there is an opinion that such a marriage is not considered as having the court's consent, since our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, established this as law, we follow this ruling. It is also evident from Rambam that he holds this view, as he ruled in a case of conflicting testimonies that if she remarried based on the testimony of the witness who permits, before the court permitted, and she confidently asserts her husband's death, she should not leave the new marriage. This shows that the court's permission is not a deciding factor.

And what is the jurisdiction of the Beit Din (rabbinical court)? Our teacher, the Rema, wrote there that the Beit Din must consist of three fit individuals who are not related to each other nor to the witnesses. This implies from his words that the jurisdiction of the Beit Din is that a fit Beit Din sits and permits her (i.e., declares her permitted). This is also found in several responsa from prominent later authorities. And some say that a fit and complete Beit Din is not required for this, as this is a ruling like all other rulings, and it suffices with one (judge), even if he is a relative, as with all rulings of prohibition and permission. Only for the acceptance of testimony from the witness is a complete Beit Din required, as is the law for all acceptance of testimony, and the practical difference is that the witness cannot retract later. But to permit her to the public, one wise man suffices, as with all other rulings. Additionally, even in the acceptance of testimony, a full Beit Din is not required, as in all acceptance of testimony, if there is no complete Beit Din, it is considered as hearsay. But in the case of an agunah, hearsay is acceptable, as it is written there in the responsum, and only to prevent the witness from retracting later is a full Beit Din required, but not for the permissibility of the agunah. And some have strengthened the words of our teacher, the Rema, that hearsay is acceptable in the case of an agunah because if we require fit witnesses, it might leave her an agunah. But for the acceptance of testimony before a Beit Din, why should we not require a fit Beit Din as in all acceptance of testimony? Additionally, there are also monetary laws involved in the acceptance of the ketubah, and it is obvious that a fit Beit Din is required. In any case, according to this, it does not affect the permissibility of the agunah.

And it appears to me that even regarding the permissibility of an agunah (a woman whose husband is missing and cannot be proven dead), it specifically requires a valid Beit Din (rabbinic court). According to the opinion explained in section 25, from a Torah perspective, she is not permitted based on one witness but only on the testimony of two valid witnesses. Therefore, her remarriage is based on the ordinance of the Beit Din. The Beit Din in each generation acts as the agents of the original Beit Din that enacted this ordinance, and it is as if the Beit Din of this generation permitted it, as through them, the communal statutes are maintained from the past [Rashi Bava Metzia 96b]. Hence, it is necessary for a valid Beit Din to convene to permit her.

Therefore, a woman who comes before us to marry and claims to be a widow, if she is not known here to be married to another man, she is believed by a migo (a legal principle) that she could have claimed to be single, just as she is believed to say she is divorced as stated in section 152. However, if she is indeed known to be married to another man, we do not allow her to remarry until she brings a document or evidence that she is a widow. If she has neither a document nor evidence and only states that her husband has died and she is believed, it is indeed necessary, ab initio, to convene a Beit Din to permit her, as is the rule for someone marrying based on one witness. However, in most cases, this is uncommon because when she is known here to be married to another man, naturally, when her husband dies, there are many clarifications. Unless he was killed or drowned, in which case she is not quickly permitted, and when she is permitted, it is done through a Beit Din [according to Perisha, section 152 in the name of Brit Avraham, and what I have written above].

It has already been explained that a Cuthean who is speaking casually is believed. What does "speaking casually" mean? It means he does not intend to testify to permit her, nor does he intend to speak for other reasons, such as boasting, instilling fear, or any other pretext, lest he has an ulterior motive or has been taught to say so. There is much caution needed here because it is easy to err. How do we know this? The Rambam wrote in Chapter 13: How so? If he was speaking casually and said, "Woe to so-and-so who died, how handsome he was and how much good he did for me," or he was speaking and said, "When I was on the road, so-and-so who was walking with us fell and died, and we were astonished at how he suddenly died," and similar things that show he does not intend to testify—he is believed. The Shulchan Aruch in section 14 copies this. Specifically, if it was not through a question, for if he was only asked what happened to so-and-so, or if he knew anything about so-and-so, and similar questions—his words are no longer effective. A general rule is that anything through a question is not considered casual, but if the Cuthean speaks on his own and then afterward is asked and examined until he explains the entire event, he is believed, and we marry based on his words, since the beginning of his words were not through a question, even if the end of his words delay. Similarly, it is specifically if he recounts in the market or before ordinary men or women in a homeowner's house, and then the listeners who heard these words come before a court and testify that they heard these things from the Cuthean, if the court sees that he spoke casually—they permit her. But if the Cuthean himself comes before the court and recounts such things—his testimony is void, because by coming to the court it is evident he intends to testify, and this is not casual. And if it happened that the Cuthean spoke such words before ordinary people, and they are not knowledgeable in the law and told the Cuthean to go to the rabbi and the court and recount before them what he told us—this does not harm at all, for we do not need his words spoken before the court, and the listeners come and testify before the court what they heard from him before he recounted before the court. And what the Rambam wrote that the Cuthean said "so-and-so," it does not mean just his name alone—for this is not effective, but "so-and-so the son of so-and-so" or "from such-and-such a city" and similar identifying marks to clarify who he meant, as will be explained.

It appears from the words of the Rambam, of blessed memory, that it is specifically when the non-Jew adds some additional statements to what he says about the death of a certain person, such as praising him or expressing wonder at his death, and the like. But if he only says "so-and-so has died," even though it clearly appears that he is telling it incidentally, it is still not considered incidental. Similarly, one of the great early authorities holds that if he did not say any additional words, but only "so-and-so has died," this is not considered incidental and we do not permit [the woman to remarry] based on this. Many of the poskim disagree with this and hold that the addition of words is not necessary at all. It seems that this is the opinion of our teacher, the Rema, who wrote there: "Similarly, if he said so-and-so has died incidentally, even if he did not say other things, it is still considered incidental." And there are those who are stringent. This implies that his opinion leans towards the lenient view. Similarly, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in his great book that all the courts in his city were accustomed to permit in such a case and did not heed the stringent opinion. The Rambam must be understood as not speaking precisely, but rather that this is the common way of speaking, for otherwise, why would he mention that so-and-so has died? And from the Rambam himself in law 25 there, it is also clear that there is no need for additional words.

In essence, it appears to me that there is no actual disagreement in the law. Certainly, if the gentile tells his friend who knew the deceased, or tells a Jew who knew the deceased, "So-and-so has died," there is no need for a connection of statements, as this is in line with how people naturally inform each other about the death of an acquaintance. Similarly, if the person speaking innocently was a friend of the deceased and even goes himself, sighs, and says "So-and-so has died," it is considered as speaking innocently. However, if a gentile comes to a Jew and says "So-and-so has died," and this Jew did not know the deceased, it is certain that without a connection of statements, the gentile intended to testify; otherwise, why would he tell him? But when there is a connection of statements, he mentioned the death incidentally as part of telling a story.

Additionally, as we said, when the gentile comes to the rabbi or the court and tells of the death of so-and-so, this is not considered speaking innocently but rather with the intention to testify, and it is not valid even with a connection of statements—this is when the gentile had no other business with the rabbi or the court, and it is certain that he came only to testify. However, when he had some other business there, his words are valid as they would be with others, and why should it be any different? Similarly, when the gentile knows that the deceased was close to the rabbi or the court and comes to tell them that so-and-so has died, it is also considered speaking innocently. [This explanation resolves several contradictions and various matters from responsa and the pamphlet on agunot (women unable to remarry), and study this well.]

In the Gemara at the end of Yevamot (122a), it states: There was an incident involving a group traveling on the road, and one of them fell ill. They left him at a gentile inn and continued on their way. Upon their return, as soon as the innkeeper saw them, she began to cry. They asked her, "Where is our companion?" She told them, "He died, and I buried him." They permitted his wife to remarry based on this testimony, as this is considered "mesiach lefi tumo" (reporting incidentally). 

From this, it is clear that the rule of "mesiach lefi tumo" requires that the gentile begins the conversation without being prompted by a Jew. Even if the gentile did not start speaking but rather began crying or the like, it is considered an initiation because the crying was incidental. Then, even if subsequently asked and she responds, it is still permitted, since she started incidentally, as mentioned in section 120.

The same rule applies conversely: if the Jew begins to cry, this is considered as the Jew starting the conversation, and the gentile's subsequent statement does not help, as it is no longer incidental. [Kuntres Agunot, section 20, and see there in section 186, and see there in Tosafot, and their proof from the Jerusalem Talmud needs further examination, as the Jerusalem Talmud does not establish that she cried, see there.]

If the non-Jew initiated the conversation, even though the beginning was not about the death of a specific person but about another matter and the death of that person came up through questioning, for example, if the non-Jew spoke about a group of thieves and a Jew asked what happened to the Jews, and the non-Jew responded that they were killed—it is considered as "speaking to one's own detriment" (מסל"ת) [Beit Shmuel 142, quoting Masat Binyamin]. According to this, the reverse is also true: if a Jew asked the non-Jew about another matter and the non-Jew, in his response, mentioned that certain Jews were killed, it is not considered "speaking to one's own detriment" since the Jew initiated the conversation [see Kuntres Agunot, section 244]. However, some of the great authorities permitted it in such a case, as in the incident where a Jew asked a non-Jew what happened to a certain ship, and he responded that it sank and there were three Jews on board—so-and-so and so-and-so—and three great rabbis permitted their wives to remarry when it was said that the water expelled them and they were buried [Be'er Haitev 147, quoting Rabbi Tzvi, the Alshich, and Rabbi Aaron Sasson]. Similarly, if a Jew asked a non-Jew where he came from and he responded concerning the death of a Jew [ibid., quoting Rashdam], since the question was not related to the permissibility of the wife, it is considered "speaking to one's own detriment" [ibid., quoting Maaseh Shmuel]. According to this, the reverse is also true: if the non-Jew spoke first about another matter and his response about the death of the Jew came through questioning, it is not considered "speaking to one's own detriment." There is proof for this opinion from the Jerusalem Talmud [Chapter 16, Halacha 5, where Reish Lakish said: "All who are asked and respond," and Rabbi Yochanan said: "All who mention a woman," and Mordechai explains that Rabbi Yochanan is stringent like our Talmud, indicating that even for the stringent view, without mentioning a woman, it is considered to one’s own detriment. See there and analyze thoroughly].

And so it is explained from the words of our teacher, the Rema, in section 15, where he writes that if they asked him first, "Where is our friend?" and he told them that he had died, this is not called "prompted by them." This implies that it is specifically when the question was about the person who was lost. But if the question was about another matter, and he responded about the lost person, it is considered "prompted by him." Otherwise, he would have clarified this point more distinctly. Therefore, it follows that even in the opposite case, even if the gentile was initially the one who brought it up but mentioned it not in relation to this matter, and the Jew asked about this matter, it is not considered "prompted by him." And this reasoning makes sense, because since we require "prompted by him" so that the gentile does not feel that they are intentionally asking about the matter of the dead person or his wife, other matters that are not directly related are considered as if they are not. There is no need to worry that because of the Jew's additional question, the gentile realized that they wanted to know about the lost person or his wife, as we do not need to worry about excessive concerns from our own reasoning. [And these are the words of Rabbi Yochanan in the Jerusalem Talmud there: "Whenever they mention a woman" – meaning even after the gentile started, and so wrote the Gra in his commentary, agreeing with this ruling. See there.]

In what was explained in paragraph 120, when a non-Jew begins to tell a story according to his straightforward manner that so-and-so died, then even if he subsequently provides details of the matter through questioning, it is permitted. Some say that this is specifically when he recounts the details in that same session through questioning, and since the main point was told straightforwardly, we do not need to be concerned that through the questioning of the Jew he added or omitted any detail, for he did not have time to do so. However, if after some time he recounts the details based on questioning, we are concerned that he may have fabricated or was asked to lie [Rashdam, Siman 43]. The practical difference is if the straightforward account initially is insufficient to permit, such as if he said straightforwardly that the person drowned in water without a visible end, and afterward, through questioning, he said that the water expelled him and they buried him – we do not permit her. And some say there is no difference in this, for why should we be concerned, and since his main statement was straightforward, we believe him in all that he responds through questioning, whether immediately or after some time [Masat Binyamin, Ra’am, Binyamin Ze'ev, see also Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 141]. And one who is lenient does not lose, for many permit it [and in Rashdam there it is explained that even in his generation they disputed him on this matter, see there].

And likewise, the opposite – when the gentile communicated his words through a question or testimony and his words were not accepted, and after some time he recounted this innocently, some say that since his words were not accepted previously, we should never accept them, and his innocent recounting is nullified even if he recounts innocently before other people [Dikduk HaMachazik Chaim section 30 from the language of the Rema] – and this is a great stringency. Why should it be, just because last year he was asked and was not believed, that he should not be trusted now when speaking innocently [ibid]? Therefore, it appears that if after some time he recounts innocently before other people – we can rely on him [And what is deduced from the language of the Rema can be simply explained, see there and reflect]. However, if the gentile comes to testify before the court – certainly it is difficult to rely on him another time even if he recounts innocently before people after some time [K.A. section 82], because once he came once to testify, it appears his intention is to permit, and how can we rely further on his words [And from this itself, it implies that in the first case there is no concern]. And similarly, there is doubt if initially he spoke innocently and afterward came to the court to testify if we say that the end proves the beginning that it was not innocent [ibid], and some want to differentiate between coming to the court to testify – in which case we do not say the end proves the beginning, and coming to the court to permit – in which case we do say the end proves the beginning. But it seems to me that they are the same, for coming to testify is like coming to permit, [as we hold according to Rabbi Yehudah in Yevamot 121b, and even though regarding this there is room to differentiate, nevertheless, from where do we say this, and therefore even though in the treatise on agunot there it was only written regarding intending to permit, I nevertheless wrote regarding intending to testify, and from the Machazik Chaim there it is also necessary to say so, and reflect].

There is no distinction in the case of "M'siach L'fi Tumo" (one who speaks innocently) whether he knows the Jewish religion or not, and we are not concerned to say that since he knows the Jewish religion, he may be deceitfully trying to permit the woman. The Rabbis made no distinction in this matter and relied on the woman to be precise and prone to revealing the truth [Maimonides' Responsa, on Women, Siman 9]. Even if it appears that according to his report we should be concerned that he may have monetary motives, such as if a gentile came and said to Jews, "Why don't you bring the murdered Jew lying in such and such a place? I would bring him with my cart if you give me a certain coin," on the contrary, since he is willing to bring the murdered person, it will be revealed immediately, so how could he lie [ibid.]. However, in a matter that is not likely to be revealed and we see a concern for monetary gain in his words, it is obvious that we should be concerned and not permit based on his words. Similarly, if there is another plausible explanation for his speech, such as an incident where a gentile said to a Jew, "Do this and that for me or I will kill you as I killed so-and-so," his intention was to instill fear [Gemara], and similarly in other types of plausible explanations that we can attribute according to the judgment of the Beit Din. But if he said, "It is appropriate to pay me well for this merchandise because I took the risk of the journey, as so-and-so was killed on this road," it is considered "M'siach L'fi Tumo," and we do not say that he intends to embellish his merchandise [Beit Shmuel, Siman 9]. For this alone, it would have sufficed to say that the road is dangerous. Similarly, if a gentile innkeeper said to a Jew, "Do not go out at night lest you be killed as so-and-so was killed," it is considered "M'siach L'fi Tumo" [ibid.]. Some are skeptical about this, suggesting that perhaps his intention is to clear himself from suspicion so that he will not be suspected of killing the person, since he is warning the Jew [ibid.]. It seems that everything depends on the context, and in these matters, one does not say that one case is similar to another; it depends on the judgment of the Beit Din [in my opinion].

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in Section 14: "And similarly, in a situation where there is concern for falsehood because he was taught to say so, one cannot rely on him," end quote. His intention is not that in every case of a straightforward statement (masl't) we should be concerned about this, for if so, we would never accept any straightforward statement due to such concerns. Rather, his intention is that if there are grounds for suspicion, such as if we knew that the woman had previously produced false witnesses and their falsehood was revealed, or if the non-Jew's story is something strange in the eyes of people, in that according to his story, he should have reported this a long time ago, or if we knew that the woman's relatives are promising money to the witnesses, or similar matters that, according to the perspective of the court, raise concerns about his testimony. Similarly, if the non-Jew retracts his previous straightforward statement, even though according to the law his retraction means nothing after his testimony has been accepted, still, if the non-Jew provides a good reason for why he initially said so and there are grounds for his words – we do not permit based on his previous words. And similarly in all such cases. [See Acharonim, Section 106].

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote: "Similarly, if one hears from the gentile courts that they said 'We killed so-and-so,' they are not believed, because they support themselves with lies to instill fear," end quote. Some of our Rabbis explained the reason, saying that they say this out of pride, claiming they kill according to law and justice [Rashi on Gittin 28]. There is a practical difference between the two reasons: if they say that the person was killed not by them but by other courts, according to Maimonides' reason, one may permit his wife to remarry, for instilling fear applies only when they make themselves appear fearsome. But according to the reason of pride, there is no difference, because they boast in general about their customs that they act justly. This is the intention of the Tur, who wrote that from Maimonides it seems that if not by their action they are believed, but from the Rosh it does not seem so, as the Rosh holds like the other reason we mentioned. [And this answers the question of the Beit Yosef, how he derived this from the Rosh, as the Tur inferred that Maimonides wrote "we killed" and the Rosh wrote "was killed," and pay attention to this.]

And so, there is also a practical difference when they say that he was killed unlawfully, for the reason of fear applies here, but there is no boasting in this, and on the contrary – there is a deficiency in that they killed unlawfully. And similarly, there is a practical difference when a non-Jewish official told this to a non-Jew, and the non-Jew told it to a Jew, for the reason of fear does not apply because the non-Jewish official does not instill fear in the non-Jew, but boasting does apply here, and it is possible that instilling fear also applies to the non-Jew, and similarly, it is possible that boasting does not apply to the non-Jew, and this requires further investigation for the law. And similarly, it is questionable whether boasting and fear specifically apply to the head of the judges, but not to the lower judges and their servants, whose law is like other non-Jews, or whether it also applies to them. And I found in the Responsa of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, that the servant of the non-Jewish official is believed, but the one appointed to kill is not believed.

And specifically the courts themselves, but other gentiles who report casually that a certain person was judged in the courts and the courts executed him – this is considered like other casual reports, and we allow his wife to remarry, because with ordinary gentiles, there is no concern of intimidation or boasting. We do not say that perhaps they heard it from the courts and there is boasting involved, as mentioned in the previous section, because we do not need to worry about such concerns and weaken the strength of the leniency as long as there is no substantial basis. This is not similar to what was stated in section 81 regarding someone who drowned and another said he died – we do not permit based on this testimony because we suspect he said it based on the drowning, there we have a substantial basis. But when there is no substantial basis, we do not attribute his statement to something that would invalidate his testimony [see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 40]. However, when there is a substantial basis, such as a Jew who heard from the courts and the gentile reported that he was killed by the courts – we attribute his words also to hearing from the courts [so it seems to me]. And some say that even if there is a rumor that he was judged in the courts and the gentile said he died, we say his report is because of the rumor [Beit Shmuel there], and according to what was mentioned there, there is no concern with the rumor, [and Beit Shmuel follows his method in subparagraph 31].

And this which has been explained, that through questioning it is not considered "speaking casually" (mesiach lefi tumo), there is no difference whether the respondent was the same non-Jew whom the Jew asked or another non-Jew who was present at the time when the Jew asked. But if a Jew asked a non-Jew, and there was no other non-Jew present at that time, yet the non-Jew who was asked then told another non-Jew about the matter that the Jew had inquired about concerning so-and-so, and this other non-Jew came before the Jew and casually reported that so-and-so had died – this is indeed considered "speaking casually," for the question asked by the non-Jew or what he conveyed from the Jew's question does not detract from it being casual. Similarly, if a Jew asked another Jew about so-and-so, and a non-Jew was present at the questioning and casually responded that so-and-so had died – this is considered "speaking casually" since the question was from a Jew and not from a non-Jew. However, if Jews were conversing amongst themselves about so-and-so, and a non-Jew came and asked them what they were talking about, and they told him about so-and-so the Jew, whether he was alive or dead, and he told them that he was dead – this is not considered "speaking casually" since his response was due to the Jew's question to him, even though he initiated by asking what they were talking about, still, he did not mention at all the matter of so-and-so's death, and therefore his report is through questioning. In contrast, when a non-Jew asks another non-Jew not in our presence, we do not worry about it since he reported casually to us. Similarly, when a Jew asks another Jew, even if the non-Jew was there, since he responded without being asked by him or another non-Jew, it is not considered as intending to testify but is casual. There are those who are uncertain about this and hold that there is no difference between asking a Jew and asking a non-Jew. The lenient has not lost, for there are those who are lenient even with a non-Jew since he was not asked, and this is also implied from the language of our master the Rema in paragraph 15. And though we are not lenient with a non-Jew, nevertheless with a Jew we may be lenient. From the language of the Jerusalem Talmud that we brought in paragraph 124, it is clearly implied that only when asking a non-Jew respondent is it not considered "speaking casually," but with another non-Jew it is considered "speaking casually," as is the plain meaning of the language of our master the Rema.

If a Jew is missing and a rumor is spread in the city and nearby villages, and an announcement is made that anyone who knows about this Jew should come forward and inform, and a non-Jew comes and says spontaneously that the Jew was killed or died – this is considered spontaneous testimony. Even though his statement was made because of the rumor and the announcement, nonetheless, since he was not specifically asked, it does not fall outside the category of spontaneous testimony. And even according to what has been explained, that there is no difference whether he was asked directly or someone else was asked, this is because he was present at the time of the question. But in the case of a rumor and general announcements, we do not consider it problematic.

However, if Jews are conversing together and a non-Jew comes and asks them what they are talking about, and they tell him that they are discussing whether a certain Jew is alive or dead, and he informs them that he is dead, this is not considered spontaneous testimony since they asked him. Even though it is not a direct question, since they told him they were talking about the Jew, it is considered as if they asked, as explained in section 125. 

But if the non-Jew says, "Aren’t you talking about so-and-so?" and they confirm, and he then tells them he knows that the person is dead – it seems this would be considered spontaneous testimony. Certainly, if the non-Jew comes and says, "Why aren’t the relatives of so-and-so inquiring about bringing him to burial, as I know he is dead," or if he says, "What are you talking about, perhaps you are discussing so-and-so?" and similar cases – this would be considered spontaneous testimony.

And what has been explained, that through questioning it is not considered "out of his simple conversation" (mesiach lefi tumo), some say that this is specifically when a Jew asked. But if a non-Jew asked another non-Jew, "How is the Jew, so-and-so?" or if he asked, "Do you perhaps know if the Jew, so-and-so, is alive or dead?" and he answered that he is dead – they permit his wife to remarry even though it is not "out of his simple conversation." The reason is that through questioning, he is not believed because perhaps his intention is to permit the wife to remarry or to testify about his death, and this is not applicable when the non-Jew is the one asking. And to suspect that the non-Jew is lying from the beginning – we do not suspect him, because if we do, what benefit is his integrity? We only suspect him when his intention is to testify, as he might add or subtract and it would not be considered testimony. But when the questioner is not Jewish, these concerns are removed. And this is only when there was no Jew present at the time of the questioning, for otherwise, we suspect that his intention is for the sake of testimony since the Jew hears the non-Jew's question. All the more so if the non-Jew asked in the name of a Jew, even if the Jew was not present at the time of the question – still, we do not permit her, because since he knows it concerns a Jew, we cannot rely on him. And if he did not tell the non-Jew that he is asking in the name of a Jew, even if the Jew requested to ask him, still, since the non-Jew who answered did not know this, it is possible that it is considered "out of his simple conversation." And even if this is the law, we do not find it except when a Jew heard from behind the wall the non-Jew's answer, and the non-Jew did not see him, for otherwise, how did we receive his answer? For if the first non-Jew told us the answer of the responder – it does not help, for with him it was through questioning. And if the second non-Jew later told us "out of his simple conversation," it helps in any case, even if initially it was through a Jew's questioning, as stated in Section 127.

If someone is apprehended for murder and confesses to the ruler that he killed a certain Jew—if he confessed due to torture, it is obvious that this confession is worthless, since a confession obtained under torture is not a valid confession. If he confessed without torture, his confession is valid. Even if it was due to the ruler’s questioning, it is still valid because in the case of a non-Jew, a confession obtained through questioning is valid, as we have written. However, it could be argued that the ruler’s questioning is different, and his response is like testimony, and in the case of testimony, it does not help [see Beit Shmuel, section 147]. It is obvious that if the ruler demanded from another non-Jew to testify that this non-Jew killed a certain Jew and he testified, it is not valid, because anything that comes in the form of testimony is not considered spontaneous [in my opinion].

If someone is apprehended for a reason other than the suspicion of killing this Jew, and during his confession before the authorities, he also mentioned that he killed a certain Jew, this is considered spontaneous, and there was an incident involving a murderer who was sentenced to death and said during his sentencing, "I have never committed any offense except once when I killed a Jew who was carrying such and such amount of money," and they permitted his wife to remarry based on this spontaneous confession [Mordechai, end of Yevamot]. There was also an incident involving someone suspected of murder who was judged before a judge, and the judge said to him, "Confess, and I will acquit you and release you," and he confessed that he killed a certain Jew, and they ruled that his wife could remarry [Maharik, root 121]. Even though it is possible that he confessed because the judge promised to release him if he confessed, nevertheless, if it were not true that he killed him, why would he bring upon himself such guilt? He should have known that it is the judge’s way to smooth talk him into confessing [there]. However, it is obvious that if the judge said to him, "If you do not confess, I will torture you," his confession is worthless, because he confessed to avoid torture. It is also known that Jews confessed during persecutions due to torture for things they did not do at all.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled in a responsum that specifically when one is tortured to confess to the killing of a particular Jew, his confession is not considered valid, as his intention is to free himself from the torture. However, if he is tortured generally to confess what he has done, and he confesses to killing a particular Jew, his confession is valid. This is because it is not customary to fabricate something one did not do and maintain that statement, for by doing so, he will not be freed from the torture. On the contrary, such a confession might cause them to torture him further to extract more confessions. If he had not confessed, he would likely be spared from the torture, for they would not torture him to confess to killing this Jew. But when they torture him to confess to the killing of this Jew, his confession is certainly not valid, even if he maintains his statement after the torture, because he fears they will torture him further if he retracts his confession. [Responsum of Beit Yosef, laws of Mesirat Nefesh, section 8]. And it is clear that a murderer who is not apprehended by the government, when he tells that he killed a particular Jew, is not believed, for his intention is to instill terror and fear so that they will give him what he requests.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote (in section 15): If an Israelite asked a gentile, and the gentile stated that someone had died and provided reasonable evidence, even though this is not considered unbiased testimony and she is forbidden to remarry, if she went ahead and married based on the ruling of a sage who permitted her, she should not be required to leave the marriage if there is evidence and reasonable indications that he died. This is his final statement. He made this like endless waters, which will be clarified that if she married based on the ruling of a sage, she should not leave. However, if so, there is no limit to these matters. For logically, if there are reasonable indications even without the gentile's statement, then what is the need for his statement here? Moreover, do we permit based on indications? Indeed, we are stringent in the essence of testimony to be concerned even for distant suspicions. In truth, some of the poskim (decisors) reject this law from being practical. It seems to me that the intention of Rabbi Moshe Isserles is not about an ordinary gentile, but similar to the laws we explained earlier, such as a murderer who was caught and confessed to killing a certain Jew. Even though the confession was due to an Israelite's question, since the murderer provided signs and indications about where he killed him and why he killed him for such and such money that was with him, and this matter is true, and he confessed when he was caught by the authorities, in this case, even though she is not permitted initially, if she married based on the ruling of a sage – she does not have to leave because the murderer confessed and brought severe judgment upon himself, which means he spoke the truth. [And it seems to me that the Beit Shmuel in section 149 also holds this way]. And some say that even without any statement at all and even without testimony, if there are indications that he died and a sage permitted her – she does not have to leave. There is no basis for these things, and God forbid to rely on this. [See Chokhmat Shlomo section 33 and Pitchei Teshuva section 177 where they discuss this based on the Radbaz and Mareh Tzovot].

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: If there is a doubt whether it was with deliberate intent (mesiach lefi tumo) or not – one should not permit his wife to remarry, as a doubt in a Torah law requires stringency. Similarly, in any case where there is a dispute in these laws – we follow the stringent opinion. And certainly, this is correct, as in all cases of doubt in Torah law we are stringent. Even in cases of a double doubt (safek sefeika), where we tend to be lenient in the entirety of the Torah, nevertheless, in the case of an agunah (a woman bound to her marriage) we must be stringent in matters of testimony itself. The primary reasoning behind the leniency of a double doubt is that the first doubt renders it an even fifty-fifty, and with the second doubt, the majority leans towards leniency. However, in the testimony regarding a woman, we are stringent even with a remote concern. Nevertheless, there are those who say that in a dispute among the authorities, we follow the lenient ruling. It seems to me that this is only when it appears to the sage that the opinion of the lenient authorities is primary based on the evidence he has. Hence, he can follow the lenient opinion, or if it seems to him according to the matter that one should be lenient, such as it appears to him that it was mesiach lefi tumo, and even though he does not have clear evidence for this, nevertheless, he is convinced in his heart that this is the case. The general principle is – one cannot establish fixed rules in these matters. However, it is clear that a sage should not rely solely on his own opinion but rather join with other God-fearing sages. If it seems to them that the matter leans towards leniency, they may permit it. But if the sage relies only on his own opinion – he is rebuked from Heaven. Regarding a double doubt in the case of an agunah, it will be further explained in this section.

One of the early Geonim gave a rule regarding this matter: whenever the doubt pertains to the fundamental question of whether he died, Heaven forbid, we do not take a lenient approach. However, if his death is almost certain and the doubt is only regarding the testimony—whether it is valid or not, such as whether the testimony was given spontaneously or not, or whether there is a contradiction in the testimony, or whether the witness is eligible to testify or not—we take a lenient approach. When the doubt is about the fundamental question of his death, we presume him to be alive. But when the presumption of his being alive is weakened, we then take a lenient approach regarding the testimony. Similarly, when the witness is before us, we investigate him thoroughly, and if his testimony is found to be improper, we invalidate it. However, if the testimony is indirect, such as if someone says they heard from another person, whether that person is Jewish or not, who saw the Jew either killed or dead, and it is impossible to reach the first witness to ask how he recognized that it was the Jew—whether by identifying marks, by sight, or perhaps he did not recognize him well, or perhaps it was after three days, or similar concerns—we lean towards leniency. [This is stated in the name of the Radbaz], and these are reasonable words.

A Kuti who speaks spontaneously based on what he heard from another Kuti who speaks spontaneously – we rely on his testimony, even if he did not explicitly state that the first one spoke spontaneously. We assume leniency in doubt and say that the first one surely spoke spontaneously. Since the one before us speaks spontaneously, we have no reason to suspect that the first one, whose statement he repeats, did not speak spontaneously. However, there are those who disagree and hold that it is necessary for him to explicitly state that the first one spoke spontaneously, because a regular conversation is not considered spontaneous unless it is clearly so. Therefore, it is necessary to know that the first person spoke spontaneously. Some want to argue that the testimony of a Kuti based on another Kuti is never valid, because a Kuti does not have the expertise to recognize whether the first Kuti spoke spontaneously or not – but this is an excessive stringency. Many of the decisors agree with the first opinion if it is impossible to verify how the first Kuti’s story was. This is also explained from what was clarified in the previous paragraph [see Choshen Mishpat 345, where it is written that those who disagree only do so if it is evident that the first one did not speak spontaneously, and so wrote the Mahratz, and so is evident from Ketzot HaChoshen, Siman 258. Review it carefully].

If a Jew testifies that he heard from a non-Jew that a certain person died, it is necessary for him to explicitly state that the non-Jew was speaking inadvertently (mesiach lefi tumo). Otherwise, even according to the opinion that permits relying on a non-Jew who heard from another non-Jew in an unspecified manner, in the case of a Jew who heard from a non-Jew in an unspecified manner, it is prohibited, because a Jew typically inquires about his fellow Jew, and it is assumed that the non-Jew responded to this inquiry [Beit Shmuel 161].
