Some say that even in the case of a Jew who heard from a non-Jew, it is valid in an unspecified manner [Taz and Kuntres Agunot, Siman 200], and on the contrary, even according to the stringent opinion regarding a non-Jew who heard from another non-Jew, there is room to be lenient for a Jew who heard from a non-Jew. For if the non-Jew was not speaking inadvertently, the Jew would not report it in an unspecified manner and would explicitly state that he heard it not inadvertently [there]. However, if we know that this Jew is an unlearned person and does not know the law that the non-Jew must specifically speak inadvertently, it is difficult to be lenient [this seems to me]. And if the non-Jew was speaking inadvertently and says that he heard a certain Jew testify about how a certain person died, we must deliberate on this matter, for perhaps since he is inadvertently reporting a testimony, it is not considered inadvertent [Beit Shmuel]. Some are lenient in this matter, and the law requires further investigation.

It is simple and logically understood that when it has been clarified regarding the types of witnesses who are trusted to testify that this woman's husband has died or was killed – this applies when the witness knows that the man about whom he is testifying was the husband of this woman, having recognized him and his wife during his lifetime. Now, when he testifies that the man has died and the sages believe him, the woman is consequently permitted to remarry based on his testimony. However, if the witness does not know at all that the person about whom he is testifying is the husband of this woman, it is not effective unless he testifies before the court that a certain person, the son of a certain person from your city, whose business was such and such, along with other distinctive signs, in a manner that leaves no doubt for the court about whom he is testifying, and they know that this man is the husband of this woman. In such a case, the woman is also permitted to remarry. Since the witness knows about whom he is testifying, having recognized him, it does not matter if he does not know that this is his wife. But if the witness did not recognize him either and only testifies that a certain person died in a certain place – clearly his testimony is worthless, for there are many people with the same names, and what kind of testimony is this? There are many detailed laws regarding this matter, as will be clarified with the help of Heaven.

The Tur wrote: If someone comes and says, "They told me that when you go to such-and-such a place, tell them that Yosef ben Shimon has died," and he comes and says so, and we recognize a certain individual known by that name—his wife is permitted [to remarry], even though he did not give a distinguishing mark by which we would recognize him, and we do not worry that it might have been another person with the same name. Some say this applies only when no one else with that name is established in that place, and also caravans are not common there. If one of these conditions exists, they do not permit [the wife to remarry]. And Rabbeinu Alfasi wrote that even if two people with that name are common there or caravans are common, they permit [the wife to remarry] unless both conditions for suspicion exist. And this is also the conclusion of our master, the Rosh, of blessed memory. And although Rabbeinu Alfasi is stringent regarding a lost get (divorce document) with one of these conditions for suspicion, as mentioned in Siman 132, nevertheless, regarding the testimony that a woman's husband has died, they were lenient, just as they were lenient with many leniencies concerning an agunah (a woman unable to remarry due to her husband's disappearance). Because due to the stringency imposed on her, she will investigate thoroughly before remarrying. But with a get, it is possible to write another get [Rosh, Chapter 3 of Gittin, Siman 3]. And even if an incident occurred where it was impossible to obtain another get, we still would not be lenient in this matter, because with a get there is no reasoning that she would investigate thoroughly, as she could say that she was divorced. In contrast, if her husband is believed to be dead and he comes back alive, her disgrace would be revealed. The sages did not establish leniencies for a get for the sake of agunot, because most of the time, there is no agunah situation, as it is possible to write another get. They did not establish [leniencies] for rare cases where it is not possible to write another get. [This is the intention of the Rosh, and it resolves the difficulty of Mar'eh HaTzofim; see there and understand].

And in regard to what the Tur wrote in the name of the Rif, that even if there are two people named Yosef ben Shimon known (to be in the area), if caravans are not common, it is permitted (to rely on the testimony of one witness regarding the husband's death). There are those who disagree with this, arguing that what does it matter if caravans are not common, since ultimately there is still another person with the same name? How do we know that the husband of this woman died, perhaps it was the other one who died? The Rif only permitted it when caravans are common and there are not two people named Yosef ben Shimon known, and not the other way around. 

And we cannot say that we know the other person is alive, because if so, it is obvious, and who would argue against this? However, if they testify about this (specific person), we surely know that he went on this journey and we do not know at all that the other person went on this journey – then it is reasonable to assume that the deceased is the one who went on this journey and not attribute it to the other, since we rely on what is common. But if the other person also went on this journey, even if it was a long time ago that he went, and the husband of this woman went on this journey recently, nevertheless we do not attribute it to him more than to the other.

And the words of the Tur can also be interpreted this way. And some say that even in such a case we attribute it to the husband of this woman, because it is reasonable to assume that the deceased is the one who went on the journey recently, and we do not need to be concerned that the other who went a long time ago also recently went on this journey. It is difficult to be lenient to such an extent. 

And there are those who say that if another Yosef ben Shimon is known in this city, we do not permit it in any way, and the Tur is referring to a case where another Yosef ben Shimon is known in the world but not in this city, but this does not seem plausible. The primary explanation is like the first resolution, and many great authorities have agreed with this.

And based on this, it is clear that the reason we rely on a man's testimony to permit a woman to remarry is when we know for certain that her husband traveled on this particular path. But if we have no knowledge at all whether he traveled on this path, it is not only when another person named Joseph ben Shimon is also known to be missing, making it impossible to be lenient, since both are in doubt, but even without the presence of two people named Joseph ben Shimon, the matter requires careful consideration whether leniency is permissible (see Ma'arot HaTzov'ot, end of section 19, note 4). And based on this, it is simple to differentiate between a get (divorce document) discussed in Siman 132 and our case here. Certainly, even with a get, if we knew that in this place such a get was written and the messenger took it on this path, we would also be lenient. However, in the case of the get, it discusses a situation where we had no knowledge at all if such a get was written in this place (and indeed, the Ramban wrote this in Milchemet Hashem on Yevamot there to explain the words of the Rif, and similarly wrote the Rashba, and see Beit Shmuel).

And our master the Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 18: If someone came and told us, "The court or some people said that when you go to such-and-such a place, tell them that Yitzchak ben Michael has died," and the messenger came and told us, and the messenger does not know who he is—since we know a certain person known by that name, his wife is permitted to remarry. We do not say that perhaps another Yitzchak ben Michael has died, provided there are not two people known by that name in that place, or if there are two, one of them is still alive. And it is clear that he holds that if there are two people known by that name, even if it is uncommon for caravans to travel there, we do not permit her to remarry, as is the opinion of those who disagree in paragraph 145. This also appears to be the opinion of the Rambam and Raavad in chapter 13, law 24 [and this can be derived from Rashi there in Yevamot]. And regarding what he wrote—that if one of them is still alive, we no longer worry—most of the authorities agree that we do not concern ourselves with the fact that his name is the same, since he is alive. And although some say that since there is another person known by that name, we worry about others who may also have that name [Rashba in Gittin 27], nevertheless, most authorities do not hold this way.

And our Rabbi the Rema wrote regarding this: Some say that all of this applies specifically when the witness mentioned the name of his city, but if he did not mention the name of his city, even though it is known that one person is missing – it does not help even if he mentioned his name, and there are those who are lenient. And some say that in a case where he mentions only his name, we require him to mention his city, but if he mentions his name and his father's name, we do not require him to mention the name of his city. And in a place where there are indications and proofs that this is the person – we can be lenient and rely on the opinion that says we do not require mentioning the name of his city. Many were astonished at this, for it contradicts the words of our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, who said that if someone comes and says that they told him when you go to such and such a place, say that Isaac the son of Michael died, he indeed mentioned his city as well, for they are informing the city that a certain person from their city died. If he is not from their city – why would they inform that city? It is unreasonable to say that even in such a case he must explicitly say "so-and-so from your city," for what sense does that make? Moreover, from his words, it seems that there are opinions that hold that there is no need to mention the name of his city at all. And some say that even just mentioning his name alone suffices, and this is something that cannot be said at all, for if one hears that Joseph died or Joseph the son of Shimon died, this woman will go and remarry, whereas in the world there are certainly many Joseph the son of Shimons.

Therefore, there are those who correct his words to say: They say that all this is specifically when the witness mentioned the name of the city [Maraot HaTzovot], but if he did not mention the name of the city, etc. – it is not valid, and there are those who are lenient that in a place where he only mentions his name, it is necessary to mention his city, etc. [Taz and he deletes the second "they say"], and he does not disagree with our teacher, the Beit Yosef, but rather he explains his words. And the explanation is: They say that it is specifically necessary to mention the name of his city, as in the case of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, where the name of the city is explicitly stated, or if someone comes and says that so-and-so from such-and-such city died. And there are those who are lenient that when he mentioned his name and his father's name, it is not necessary to mention his city. And this is implied from the version in the Tosefta at the end of Yevamot (14:11) where it is taught that one does not testify about him until they mention his name and his father's name, his name and his city's name. And there is a version in this Tosefta that says his name, his city's name, and his father's name [HaMagid Mishneh there, Hilchot 27], and the ruling is according to the first opinion that it is necessary to mention his city's name, for it is unreasonable to permit without mentioning his city's name, as there are many Yosef ben Shimon in the world, and they indeed wondered about those who hold this opinion [Taz, subparagraph 23].

And it seems to me that certainly there is no opinion to permit [a woman to remarry] based on [the husband's] name and his father's name alone, by saying that when someone says that Yosef ben Shimon died in a distant place, this would allow the wife of Yosef ben Shimon from this city to remarry. For there are many Yosef ben Shimon's in the world. The opinions brought by our master, the Rema, only differ if there are some indicative signs that slightly prove who this Yosef ben Shimon is, who is being testified about having died. Nonetheless, this is not a clear proof that the testimony is about the Yosef ben Shimon from this city who was lost, for example, if Yosef ben Shimon from our city was lost, and someone comes and says that around the city one named Yosef ben Shimon died or was killed. Those who permit it hold that we assume it is the Yosef ben Shimon from our city. Or if he says that in a certain city, Yosef ben Shimon died, and we know that the lost Yosef ben Shimon was recently in that place and no other Yosef ben Shimon was known by that name, and similarly, no other Yosef ben Shimon was lost from our city. Those who forbid it hold that this is nothing, and he must mention the name of his city since there is no clear evidence that his intention is about this Yosef ben Shimon. Therefore, it is not surprising that some permit [remarriage] even based on his name alone since it is more likely that the testimony is about him, and this is somewhat similar to "here he was found, and here he was." However, if there is estimation and proof that his intention is about this one, for example, if he says his trade was such and such, and he was found around the place of his trade, or he describes his clothing or physical signs, intermediate signs - everyone agrees that we do not need the name of his city.

[And this explains according to this what the Rosh permitted in the case of Makhluf ben Malul who was found near Fes, as brought by the Beit Yosef, that he was from Fes, and this answers the question of the Taz and the Chacham Tzvi.]

The designation of a family name is like the name of one's city and is even better, for in one city there can be a hundred family names. One's profession might also be like the name of one's city, as well as one's trade. It is possible that even inferior signs like "tall" and "short," "white" and "black" are like the name of one's city. Similarly, when referring to the surrounding area of a city, when one mentions a city in general, the intention is towards that particular city, for it is common practice that those who live around a city, when they say "city" without specification, mean the nearby city. Likewise, if Reuven asks Shimon, "Are you from such-and-such city?" and he answers "Yes," and then Reuven says, "Know that Levi has died or was killed," it is as if he said, "Levi from your city died or was killed," and all similar cases. There is no difference in all these matters between a witness testifying to a Jewish court and a non-Jew reporting informally. And from the Rambam, Chapter 13, Halacha 27, it is clear that mentioning his name and the name of his city suffices, see there.

A Jew or a non-Jew who is not suspected of lying comes and says, "A Jewish man died in such and such a place, he looked like this and that, and had these and those characteristics," and the characteristics are not distinctive but rather poor or average ones as will be explained in the detailed laws of characteristics in this section, and we do not know his name — we do not assume based on estimation that he is certainly a particular person from our town who went missing, until he says his name and his father's name and his town's name, or his name and his father's name or his name and his town's name according to the opinions clarified, or another distinctive characteristic. And if we knew that the missing person from our town was in that place where the witness says he died — it is possible that we permit based on average characteristics if no one else was known to have similar characteristics [in my opinion].

If someone comes and says, "This person who left with me from such-and-such city on such-and-such day died in such-and-such place," if it can be clarified through witnesses who the person is that left with him from here, they permit his wife to remarry. If it cannot be clarified, if it is possible to ascertain who the person is that left on that day, such as if the city gates are locked and everyone leaving the city is known to the townspeople, and it is clarified that all the people who left on that day are alive except for this one, they permit his wife to remarry even if he does not mention his name at all.

Maimonides Z"L wrote in the 13th chapter, Halacha 25: If a Samaritan and a Jew went out from us to another place, and the Samaritan came and spoke innocently and said that a man who went out with me from here has died – we allow his wife to remarry, even though the Samaritan does not know that man, provided he says, "I buried him." Similarly, if ten people went out together from one place to another, whether they are bound in chains or driving camels or involved in similar activities, and the Samaritan spoke innocently and said that ten people who went from such and such a place to such and such a place and were carrying such and such have all died and we buried them – we allow their wives to remarry. These words are as stated in the Gemara [122a], where these two incidents are mentioned, and in this language, that the Samaritan said, "I buried him" and "I buried them," and they allowed their wives to remarry.

And it is explained from the words of the Rambam, of blessed memory, that even though if the witness were a Jew it would suffice if he said merely "he died" or "they died," nevertheless, regarding a Samaritan, the Sages were stringent and required him to explicitly say both the death and the burial. There is one who sought to say that the Rambam's opinion in all cases of a Samaritan speaking offhandedly is that he must say "he died and I buried him," but his words were refuted because the Rambam wrote several laws regarding a Samaritan speaking offhandedly and did not mention burial at all, which implies that only in this case does he require burial. The reasoning is that since he does not mention his name but only a general description such as "the man who went with me" or "the people who went from such and such a place" without mentioning their names or the names of their cities, we require that he also say burial [Hagahot Maimoniot]. His reasoning is that since he does not mention his name, it is evident that the Samaritan does not recognize him. But when he mentions his name, it is evident that he recognized him, and a person is more meticulous regarding someone he knows than someone he does not know. Therefore, regarding someone he knows, when he says "he died" it is sufficient, for it is certainly true. But regarding someone he does not know, we are concerned that he might have made a mistake in his imagination and said that he died. However, when he says "he died and I buried him," it clearly appears that he is not speaking from imagination and it is true that he died [Kesef Mishneh]. And all this applies to a Samaritan speaking offhandedly, but for a Jew who testifies even in such a case, it suffices to say only "he died" and we are not concerned that he speaks from imagination [there]. Even though in war or at sea we are concerned about imagination even regarding a Jew, as will be explained with God's help.

Some say that the Rambam's opinion is to differentiate in cases of "mesiach lefi tumo" (speaking innocently) between different contexts. Wherever it appears that the non-Jew's intention is to inform the family members or relatives of the deceased that a certain person has died, as in the case in the Talmud where the non-Jew came and said, "Who is in the house of Chivai? Who is in the house of Chivai? Chivai has died!" – we do not require him to say that he buried him. Since he is making an effort to inform them of such a message, we are not concerned that he is speaking based on assumption. Or, for example, if he is mourning for him and says, "Woe for so-and-so my beloved" or "so-and-so the wise" or "so-and-so the diligent" and the like, and says that he died, he is being precise and will not speak based on assumption [it seems to me]. However, if he only says that so-and-so died, we are concerned that he is speaking based on assumption, and we require him to say that he buried him [there in the name of the Ritva]. It appears according to this opinion that the difference is between saying something connected with the death, which shows he is being precise, and merely saying that so-and-so died, in which case we are concerned about assumption.

And some say that the Rambam holds that in any case, there is no need to say "I buried him," and only in these narratives, when recounting that he went with him on the way or that Jews went on the way – in this case, it is necessary to say "I buried him" or "I buried them." The reason is because it is the way of people that when they go on a journey and one of them is lost or all are lost, and it is not known where they escaped to, it is assumed that they died. Therefore, if he does not say that he buried him or buried them, it is considered as if he is uncertain because they disappeared from him or they all disappeared. But when he also says about the burial, then there is no such concern, as he says that he buried him or buried them, and what is there to worry about further [there in the name of Ra'am]. According to this, it is possible that also among Israelites who testify, the law is the same, since we rely on the understanding of people [and this also seems to be his words there, see there well]. And some say that if he saw the death, we are concerned about uncertainty, but not if he did not see it.

From the words of our teacher, the Rema, in section 17, it is clarified that he considered the primary distinction to be whether or not the name of the deceased was mentioned, as he wrote in section 155. He also wrote that it is not specifically about saying "I buried him," but anything that implies certainty of death without saying "perhaps" is effective, end of quote. For example, if they moved him from place to place, or concealed him in dung or in a pit, and similar cases.

And all the reasons that were explained according to the Rambam do not settle well in the heart regarding the requirement to also say burial. In truth, the Tur ruled that for these actions, death alone suffices. The mention of burial in the Gemara was because that was how the incident occurred, as the Samaritans recounted, and not because the law requires burial to delay permission. This is also the opinion of several other decisors, and it appears that the authors of the Shulchan Aruch also held this as the primary ruling like the Tur. Nevertheless, they were concerned with the Rambam’s opinion, which is also the opinion of the Rif and several of our early authorities who were cautious of their opinion, of blessed memory.

If not for the words of our Rabbis, I would have said that even the Rif and the Rambam, who required stating "I buried him" here, do not do so out of concern for an assumption, as in the case of war or water which will be explained, since the Rif explicitly explained the reason they required saying "I buried him" due to concern for an assumption [in Chapter 15 of Yevamot (42.)], and in this case, he did not explain the reason. Therefore, it might be possible to say the interpretation is as follows: Certainly, if the gentile were to say, "This Jew who went out with me died in a certain city," that would be sufficient. Since he died in a city, it is assumed that the city's people buried him. But in these actions, it appears that he says he died on the way, and if he did not say "I buried him," then he is still lying on the way and needs to be buried. Therefore, those who bury him will recognize him by identifying marks or by visual identification if he is the Jew the gentile is talking about or not. Why should we rely on his words when it is possible to verify? And even in all prohibitions, we hold that wherever it is possible to verify, we verify, as it says in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 1, and certainly in the prohibition of a married woman. Therefore, when he says he has already buried him, we must rely on his words since it is impossible to verify further. And one should not ask that even when he did not say "I buried him," we should assume that he buried him. It is impossible to say so because if he had buried him, he would have reported it, as an ordinary gentile shouts and tells the whole matter, especially if he performed the kindness of burying the dead. Moreover, why should we say that he buried him? He is not obligated to do so. Certainly, for a Jew testifying in such a case, even without his statement, we know he buried him since he would not leave him without burial. But a gentile, if he had buried him, would explicitly state that he buried him [and see Eruvin 75:].

And regarding this, the Rambam wrote two rulings: The novelty is that it is not only one individual who is believed, but even concerning many people, for I might have thought that if according to the gentile's words they all died, there would have been a public outcry about it — nevertheless, he is believed. Additionally, the novelty is that it is not only if this gentile himself went out with the Jew that he is believed to say that he died, but even if the Jew went his own way and the gentile went his own way, as in the case of people who were taken out in chains, nevertheless, he is believed.

There are those who say that this is specifically when the non-Jew explicitly says that the person who left with him from here has died. But if he says, "A man who went with me has died," we are concerned that perhaps the one who left with him from here separated from him on the way and another man accompanied him and died [Taz]. And some disagree with this [see Beit Shmuel, section 153]. In truth, there is no dispute here, for certainly we require it to be evident from his words that he meant that specific person. This can be understood from the context and the arrangement of the non-Jew's words, even if he did not explicitly say, "the person who left with me from here." As long as it is implied from his language that he meant that specific person, we permit his wife to remarry. Without this, we do not permit it, and we do not strain the non-Jew's words to say that he meant another person when it is evident from his plain language that he meant that specific Jew. And it is obvious that when it is possible to clarify explicitly that he meant this person, we are obligated to clarify. However, when it is not possible to clarify, such as when the non-Jew has already left, we permit based on the plain language when it is clear that he meant that specific person [and this also appears from the author of Mareh Yechezkel]. There is no difference in this matter between a Jew testifying and a non-Jew casually speaking the truth [and this fits well with all the difficulties raised by the Taz, and this is the intention of the Rosh].

And know, that regarding what the Rambam wrote in the second ruling about ten men who were taken in chains, that he is believed [when he says they died], some say that this belief is only in such a case. But when they are not taken in chains, we do not permit [the wife to remarry] based on his statement that they all died, because we are concerned that perhaps all those [men] went to another world and these are other [men], or that one of them separated and another joined them [later], as [the sources] Chomat Shlomo and Turei Zahav say. Specifically, when there was a sign with these men, such as they were taken in chains or with camels or with other merchandise where they all traveled in one manner, in this case, we are not concerned that others were with the same matter itself, since this is like a clear sign from the number of people and their matters. But if he said generally "ten men went on a certain path and they were all killed," we are concerned that perhaps they are others or one of them is another person, as it says there. And there are those who disagree with this as well, see Beit Shmuel section 155. 

And it appears to me that there is no disagreement in this, for certainly we require that according to the simple meaning of his words and the arrangement of his statement, it should be evident that he is speaking about the same group that left from here. And when it is possible to verify, we verify. And it is a simple matter that based on the sign of the number of people alone, we do not permit an agunah [a woman bound in marriage], for although we wrote in Choshen Mishpat, section 262, that a number is considered a sign, nevertheless, it is clear that this is only an intermediate sign, because regarding monetary matters, we consider it a clear sign, but not for an agunah, as we wrote in Choshen Mishpat, section 267, paragraph 5, see there. However, if he specifies the exact place, it is considered a clear sign, as Beit Shmuel says. And also, if the gentile recognizes one of the group and says that this person whom he recognizes was killed with his entire group, we permit the entire group through his statement, as it says there. And this needs further examination.

When a person is found killed or dead outside of his home, his face and body marks are examined in order to testify about him. He is checked and observed even at night by candle light or moonlight. And although candle light is better for examination than moonlight, as is mentioned in Orach Chayim, Siman 433 – that applies to chametz because it needs to be checked in cracks and crevices. But this deceased person, when examined by moonlight and lying outside, the examination is good. However, if he is lying inside the house, it seems to me that he should not be examined by moonlight shining through a window into the house. Rather, a candle should be lit, because moonlight that comes into the house through a window is dim and not suitable for examination. There is someone who is uncertain whether one can rely on the testimony of a Samaritan who says he saw the dead or killed person at night and recognized him by candle light or moonlight. I do not understand the basis for such doubt. If it were thought that daytime examination is better, the poskim would not have omitted mentioning that ideally one should examine by day. And from the language of the poskim, it is clear that even ideally one can examine at night. Furthermore, if it were thought that a Samaritan is not trusted regarding night vision because he says “it seems to me,” we should also be stringent with a single witness due to this concern, just as we are stringent in cases of war and water, as will be explained.

There are two ways to identify a deceased person or a murder victim: through a distinctive mark and through visual identification (טביעת עין). Visual identification is preferred over marks [Chullin 96a], and reasoning supports this. A mark, even the most distinctive, such as an extra limb, might still be found on several people in the world, unlike visual identification, which recognizes the face. Recognizing someone's face means knowing that this particular person is unique in the world, as the Holy One, blessed be He, created all faces different from each other, and no one is identical to another [Sanhedrin 37a]. In the times of the Temple, when they judged capital cases, they only relied on visual identification and not on marks. For example, if two witnesses testified that Reuven killed a person and Reuven denies it, claiming that someone else killed and they mistakenly thought it was him, the court certainly asks the witnesses how they know it was Reuven who killed. It is obvious that if they answer they know him well through visual identification and saw him kill, his denial is disregarded. But if they say they do not recognize him through visual identification but knew that the killer had a distinctive mark like the one found on this person, and he stands and protests that he did not kill, but another person with a similar mark must have killed, it is clear that we do not execute him [Chullin 96a, see there in Tosafot s.v. "and not"; however, R. Yitzhak deals with complete visual identification, examine this well]. Similarly, regarding a lost item, the Halacha in Choshen Mishpat 267 is that witnesses are preferable to marks because witnesses testify through visual identification. Therefore, even if they did not explicitly testify that the item fell from this person but recognize through visual identification that the item belongs to this person, while the other person provides distinctive marks, it is nothing, as stated there in paragraph 8, see there.

Nevertheless, there is room for doubt when one witness claims that this deceased person is Reuven because he has a distinctive sign, and another witness claims that this deceased person is Shimon, and I recognize him with absolute certainty by facial recognition that he is Shimon. Should we consider them as contradicting each other and thus not permit the wife of Reuven nor the wife of Shimon to remarry? Or should we say that there is no contradiction here and permit the wife of Shimon to remarry because the second witness recognizes him with absolute certainty by facial recognition, and facial recognition is superior to signs? Presumably, Shimon also had a distinctive sign similar to Reuven, and there is no contradiction at all. It seems more likely that this is a contradiction because, since the one who recognizes him by facial recognition does not know about the sign, it is reasonable to assume that if Shimon had a distinctive sign like Reuven, the witness who recognizes him by facial recognition would know about it. Nevertheless, if the sign is in a concealed part of the body, it is possible that he recognized him well but did not know about the sign. This matter requires further investigation regarding the law.

Nevertheless, there are advantages to signs over facial recognition. Facial recognition does not apply to the entire body but only to the face and nose, as will be explained. Signs, however, can be on any part of the body. Moreover, facial recognition is only possible if one knew the person well and was close to them. But if one saw them once or even several times, that does not constitute complete facial recognition. As long as the eye has not had sufficient familiarity, it is not considered complete facial recognition. This is also the case with lost items, as stated in Choshen Mishpat there. However, a distinct sign, even if seen only once, is sufficient, obviously. Additionally, facial recognition changes over a long period after death. Therefore, after three days, one cannot testify based on facial recognition, as will be explained. But there are signs that do not have the ability to change, such as an extra limb or something similar.

Do not be troubled by our statement that visual identification is superior to signs, and that we trust any person with visual identification concerning an agunah (a woman whose husband is missing), even a non-Jew who speaks the truth. For even in monetary matters, which are less stringent, our Sages said that we do not return a lost item based on visual identification alone except for a distinguished scholar [Bava Metzia 23b]. This is not because not everyone is proficient in visual identification, but because we do not trust the person, and he might lie to acquire the object [Tosafot Gittin 27b]. Therefore, in prohibitions, where every person is trusted concerning himself, every person is trusted with visual identification, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, section 63. 

And although concerning a lost get (bill of divorce) we hold later in section 132 that we do not return it based on visual identification alone unless there is a supporting reason, and according to the Rambam, even with a supporting reason, it is only returned if there is also a distinct sign on the vessel, nevertheless, the reason is that visual identification of a get is not complete, since a person does not keep a get in his possession for long [Tosafot Bava Metzia 24b; and the Beit Shmuel's difficulty in subparagraph 68 is unfounded]. Therefore, only a distinguished scholar has the reasoning in the Gemara [Gittin there] that we return it because a distinguished scholar, if he was not certain, would not say so due to the fear of God within him. 

In truth, visual identification of a person is not comparable to visual identification of other items, for when a person recognizes another, the knowledge is clear since he sees him constantly and knows him as he knows himself. [See Beit Shmuel there; and see Ran in the chapter "Gid Hanasheh" regarding meat that was out of sight, what he wrote in the name of Rabbi Chananel. According to what I have written, it is clear, and examine this carefully.]

There are those who wanted to say that visual recognition (טביעת עין) is only effective with a Jewish person testifying and not with a non-Jew who speaks innocently (מסל"ת) [Choshen Mishpat 345], and the reason for this is that visual recognition requires significant examination. Therefore, when one intends to testify, he looks carefully and recognizes well, but when one speaks innocently without intending to testify, he only saw in passing, and it is impossible to recognize by visual recognition in mere passing [ibid.]. However, many disagree with this, and there are responsa from the early authorities that permit visual recognition by a non-Jew speaking innocently [see Beit Shmuel 276], and this is the primary ruling. The reason that makes sense is that anyone who speaks innocently about someone being dead or killed tells it as a novelty, and if he had not looked carefully and recognized, he would not have told it [and the proof is that according to Shmuel and Rabbi Levi (Ketubot 121): if one intended to testify, his testimony is valid, certainly there is no difference, and so according to Rabbi Yehudah as well, for they did not disagree on this matter].

It has already been explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 267, Se'if 5, that there are three types of signs (simanim): inferior, intermediate, and superior. The inferior signs are insignificant even regarding lost items. The intermediate signs are considered significant regarding lost items, but regarding the prohibition of a married woman, they are insignificant. In the Talmud, there is a doubt whether such signs that are used to return lost items are from the Torah, in which case they would also be effective regarding the prohibition of a married woman, or if they are a rabbinic enactment concerning lost items and do not help with the prohibition of a married woman. The conclusion of the Talmud is that they are rabbinic [Yevamot 120a, according to some opinions]. However, a truly superior sign is effective from the Torah, as there is no clearer testimony than this [Rashi Gittin 27b], and there is no need for a verse for this as it is clear based on reason [Shach there, Se'if Katan 7]. Some want to say that if intermediate signs are not from the Torah, then even a highly superior sign is not from the Torah, but rather a rabbinic enactment for the sake of easing the situation of agunot (chained women) [Shitah Mekubetzet Bava Metzia 28a]. Most of our rabbis do not hold this view, and it is clearly implied in the Talmud otherwise [there regarding appraisal]. On the contrary, some of our rabbis hold that even intermediate signs are from the Torah [as Rava says there, according to the general rule of the Geonim]. Though we do not hold this way, at the very least it remains a doubtful matter of law [as Rabbi Eliezer in Gittin 27b was uncertain]. However, a highly superior sign is certainly from the Torah. In the writings of the Rambam, it is not explicitly stated that one may marry off a woman based on a highly superior sign; moreover, from his words in Chapter 7 of Hilchot Nachalot, Law 3, it appears that even by a highly superior sign, one does not permit an agunah. Nevertheless, it is impossible to say this, as the interpreters of his words have agreed, as mentioned there. What Rambam calls a highly superior sign and writes that one does not permit an agunah through it – this is actually an intermediate sign, which regarding monetary matters is considered superior [and see what the Maggid Mishneh writes in Chapter 13 of Hilchot Gerushin, Law 21]. It seems more likely that the Rambam's opinion is that signs are from the Torah, even intermediate ones, but regarding a married woman they were stringent. Therefore, with a highly superior sign, it is obvious that it does not need to be stated that she is permitted [and so wrote the Mareh Tzovot in Se'if Katan 85, and likewise the Nodah B'Yehuda in Siman 32].

Some say that in a case of an intermediate sign, it is permitted where the prohibition is not from the Torah, such as with water that has no end and where it lingers until its life expires. Similarly, in everything that will be explained in this section, where most lead to death, they were only stringent in the prohibition of a married woman. And since its prohibition is not from the Torah, it appears that they rely on the intermediate sign. Furthermore, it is not clear that the signs are not from the Torah, and in any case, it is a doubtful matter of law as mentioned. Therefore, in matters of rabbinic prohibition, one may rely on this. And some say that even in a rabbinic prohibition of a married woman, one does not rely on the intermediate sign, lest one comes to rely on it in a matter that is prohibited by the Torah. And the first opinion seems more correct.

And there are those who say that even though a middle sign is nothing for an agunah (a woman bound in marriage), nevertheless, several middle signs together are considered a distinct sign. The reason being that a distinct sign is because such a sign is uncommon, and similarly, it is uncommon to have several middle signs together, making it like a distinct sign. And this is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote: that even a hundred non-distinct signs are nothing, and even to combine with other indicative evidence they are nothing. This is for inferior signs, as he did not mention middle signs at all. This is the opinion of many great ones [Bach 73], and it appears from the words of the Maharshal [Yam Shel Shlomo Chapter 16:6] who wrote that signs from his clothes and body combine together like a distinct sign, although clothing signs are nothing as will be explained, and yet in combination, they combine. And so wrote several great ones that two middle signs are considered like a distinct sign [Taz and Masat Binyamin and the responsa of later Geonim]. And although from the original ruling of our teacher, the Rema, it is evident that even middle signs do not combine, nevertheless, he may not agree with this, and therefore did not include middle signs [it appears to me], and this is found in his words in several places. And the conclusion of the later great ones is that this depends on the assessment of the sages of the generation. If according to these signs, no one out of a thousand would be found, it is properly like a distinct sign, and if not, it is nothing [Me'arat HaTzovot and Beit Meir], and this seems to be the primary ruling. And there is one who says that many inferior signs combine together to make them like a middle sign, and it appears to me also that it depends on the assessment of the sages of the generation as mentioned, and so is the law regarding the combination of other indicative evidence [Me'arat HaTzovot].

What is an inferior sign? Like tall and short, thin and thick, white and red, since such people are common, it is not a sign at all in other matters, and even if he is somewhat unusual, such as being taller than most tall people or shorter than most short people [Noda B'Yehuda]. However, if it is extreme, his height or shortness is considered a middle sign, and if it is very extreme until one out of a thousand is not found like him, possibly it is even a distinct sign [see Pitchei Teshuva 105]. And such should be judged for all inferior signs [it appears to me].

Large teeth in the middle of the upper jaw, even if they are somewhat different from the long teeth of other people, are considered a weak sign, because in this place it is common for many people to have large teeth. However, in other places, if the large teeth are different, such as in the lower jaw or the inner teeth, and if the number and exact location are specified and they are significantly different from the teeth of other people, it might be considered a distinct sign, and at the very least, it is certainly considered an intermediate sign. Some have written that a perforated tooth is considered a distinct sign, but it is not reasonable to rule this way in our time, as toothache has become common and many people have perforated teeth. Similarly, the length or shortness of the hair on the head or beard, whether black, green, or similar, is not considered a sign at all. Likewise, curly hair is not considered a sign at all because it is common. Additionally, if the head is bald or not clean-shaven, it appears not to be a sign at all. However, if the baldness is unusual or the leprosy on the head is unusual, it is considered at least an intermediate sign, and everything is according to the judgment of the sages. Similarly, if one is of striking appearance or limps on one leg, if such a condition is not common, it is considered an intermediate sign. The illness of bone fractures is considered a weak sign because it is common. Similarly, any unusual feature of a limb that is common among many people is considered a weak sign.

What is considered an intermediate sign? Anything that is not commonly found in many people but is not so rare that it is only found in one out of a thousand is considered an intermediate sign. A mole (shuma) on the body or head, which they call "bradavka" and is like a small persistent sore, was said by the Sages to not be a definitive sign even if it is considered a Torah-level sign [Yevamot 120a]. The reason is that a mole is common among those born at the same time under the same constellation [Rashi], meaning that it must necessarily be present in all people born at that time. Additionally, a mole tends to change after death [ibid.], and therefore it is not considered a sign at all. From this, we learn that any type of sign that is likely to change after death and is dependent on the birth constellation is not considered significant. Some say that a mole is a definitive sign, but because it tends to change after death, it is only considered an intermediate sign [Beit Shmuel and the Gra]. This implies that most of the time it does not change; otherwise, it would not even be an intermediate sign. However, it seems to me, based on the Talmudic discussion, that a mole is not even considered an intermediate sign [as the first explanation surely indicates, and there is no basis to differentiate according to the second explanation. See there and examine it carefully], and several prominent later authorities did not agree with this [see Mareh HaTzovot and Pitchei Teshuvah].

What is considered a significant identifying mark? Anything that is unusual and extraordinary and is found only in one out of a thousand [Beit Shmuel, Siman 172]. Therefore, a missing limb or an extra limb is a significant identifying mark, as is a noticeable change in one of his limbs, or a large bump on his nose which is a significant identifying mark. If it is not large, it is considered an intermediate identifying mark [in my opinion]. A deeply indented nose or something similar is a significant identifying mark, while a slight indentation is an intermediate identifying mark [in my opinion]. A mark on his body, hand, leg, or face is considered an intermediate identifying mark, but if he specifies the exact location, such as saying the mark is right next to his right eye, it is a significant identifying mark, as agreed upon by the leading later authorities [Taz]. Therefore, even with a mole, if he specifies the exact location, it is a significant identifying mark [Beit Shmuel, Siman 171]; some dispute this, but it appears that it is indeed a significant identifying mark. Similarly, with a scar or similar marks, if he specifies the exact location, it is a significant identifying mark, as this is akin to a hole next to a specific letter in a get (divorce document) as in Siman 132.

A crookedness in a finger and a mark on its side or upon it are considered a clear sign, and it is not necessary to specify which finger, for if one specifies which finger the mark is on, it restricts the location. Even without the crookedness, it is considered a clear sign as mentioned, and just the crookedness alone is considered an intermediate sign. If one specifies which finger, it seems to me that it is considered a clear sign. Similarly, a crooked neck is considered a clear sign. If one says that in their right or left eye there is something like a lens, it is considered a clear sign. A mouth that is crooked due to illness is considered a clear sign. Similarly, if the upper lip is cut so that the teeth are visible, it is considered a clear sign. Likewise, if the nails of the fingers are damaged, it is considered a clear sign, but only if the damage is significant. Minor damage is somewhat common and is only considered an intermediate sign.

One eye that tears – this is not considered a definitive identifying mark. Similarly, one who limps on their thigh, or whose legs are bent and twisted, some say this is not a definitive identifying mark, and I do not understand why – for it is not common even in one out of a thousand. If a mole is removed from its place and leaves a mark in its place – this is not a definitive identifying mark, but if the area is precisely defined – it is considered a definitive identifying mark, as I wrote concerning the mole itself. It appears to me that all the blemishes that disqualify priests listed in the seventh chapter of Bechorot, and which Rambam enumerates in the eighth chapter of Hilchot Biat Mikdash, are all at least considered a medium identifying mark, and many of them are considered definitive identifying marks, such as when the middle of the head is sunken or protrudes like an egg, or the side of the head protrudes in front of the face or behind it opposite the nape, or the head is wide and protrudes on both sides, or the neck is greatly sunken so that the head appears as if it is resting on the shoulders, or very long so that it appears to hang between the shoulders, and all similar cases. It is impossible to explain everything in writing, and the sages will see according to the matter and the principles explained, and God be with them to bring forth the true judgment of the Torah.

Some have written that if she married based on intermediate signs, she should not leave [her husband] (Beit Shmuel, sub-paragraph 70). This is perplexing, as our Sages only mentioned this in the context of water that has no end, as will be explained. Several of the great authorities have also expressed astonishment at this (see Mareh HaTzovot, sub-paragraph 193). It seems to me that with two signs, she definitely should not leave, as the combination makes them as a definitive sign, as explained in paragraph 171. Though ideally, one should be cautious about this as mentioned there, in a case of post facto, she should not leave. However, if she married based on one intermediate sign without the combination of other presumptions and proofs, it seems that she should leave. We have already explained in paragraph 169 that in the matter of visual recognition, there is no difference between a Jew testifying and a non-Jew testifying spontaneously. The same applies to signs.

When the body or the deceased is found without identifying physical features or facial recognition, such as when the body is so bloated that it cannot be recognized, or it has been eaten by wild animals or birds to the extent that recognition is impossible, and his clothes, which he was wearing or found near him, are found, even if we recognize the clothes as belonging to a certain person due to distinctive signs on the clothes, nevertheless, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled in section 24 that it is not considered as anything. This is because the sages taught in the Mishnah at the end of Yevamot (16:3) that testimony is only accepted for the facial features with the nose, even though there are identifying marks on his body or his clothes. The term "clothes" here refers to his garments. And even though identifying marks on his body are effective, as mentioned, nevertheless, identifying marks on his clothes are not effective, even if they are very distinctive. The reason, as explained in the Gemara, is that we are concerned about the possibility of borrowing. This means that the deceased found is another person, and the one whose clothes these are had lent his clothes to the deceased and then went away wearing other clothes. 

And even though this is a stringent ruling, the sages were stringent in this case because of the great leniencies they allowed for an agunah (a woman bound in marriage due to her husband's uncertain fate), and thus saw fit to be stringent in this matter. As long as it has not been clarified through bodily identification signs, they do not permit based on clothing signs. And even though in the Gemara there is another interpretation that refers to white and red clothes, which are poor signs, but in the case of distinctive signs, they permit based on clothing signs, still, since it is a doubt concerning a Torah law, we adopt the stringent position. Additionally, from another sugya (discussion) in the Gemara (Bava Metzia 27b), it clearly appears that we are concerned about borrowing, as it says there, after establishing the case with white and red clothes, it asks about finding the clothes tied in a pocket and suggests that if we are concerned about borrowing, etc., which indicates that the initial answer is the main one.

Although there is a presumption that whatever is found in a person's possession is considered his, and this is a strong presumption that works even against a "migu" (as stated in Choshen Mishpat, siman 99, see there), nevertheless, against this there is the presumption of a married woman, and it is a presumption against a presumption [Nodah B'Yehuda, siman 26]. Furthermore, this presumption does not apply here, because if we knew the man lying before us and were judging his clothes, it would be appropriate to say so, but here, where the body before us is unidentifiable and we need to judge based on the clothes on the body, it is not a complete presumption. Additionally, since we are concerned about borrowing, we must also be concerned about selling and losing [Chokhmat Shlomo, siman 142]. However, regarding selling and losing, we can say that we establish the clothes in the possession of the owner, but in the case of borrowing, even though they were lent, they still remain in the possession of the lender, meaning in the possession of the one who lent them, because even if they were lent to the body lying before us, they are not acquired by him and still remain in the possession of the lender. Further, although there is a presumption in this case, it does not help in the case of an agunah, because a majority is stronger than a presumption, and they were stringent even with a majority regarding death, such as in water without an end and various other matters that will be explained in this siman. Furthermore, even if it were a complete presumption, we are witnesses that a tiny minority in the world lend their vessels and clothes, and after all, we need a clear sign, and a clear sign is something found only one in a thousand. Since there is a tiny minority that lend their vessels and clothes, and logically they are less than one in a thousand, there is no clear sign here [in my opinion, and see Maharsha Gittin 27b, s.v. "simanim"].

All this we have explained according to the method of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who ruled straightforwardly that we are concerned about borrowing. In his great book, he wrote that this is the opinion of the Rif, the Rambam, and the Rosh. And although the words of the Rif and the Rambam are not explicitly clear, as they only copied the language of the Mishnah that identifying marks on the body and on the garments do not help, and it seems that the garments are analogous to the body, and one might infer from their words that prominent identifying marks are effective even on the garments, and so the Maggid Mishneh inferred from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 13, Law 21, and so the Nimukei Yosef inferred from the words of the Rif at the end of Yevamot. Nevertheless, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, holds that since they did not explicitly state that prominent identifying marks are effective on garments, it implies that they are not effective. Therefore, he also revised the words of the Tur, who wrote that even if there are identifying marks on the garments and on the body, we do not rely on them if they are not prominent, which implies that if they are prominent, they are effective even on the garments. However, he interpreted that it applies only to the body. There is evidence for his opinion from the fact that the Rosh wrote explicitly in the first chapter of Bava Metzia that in a case of uncertainty, we are concerned about borrowing. If the Tur did not agree with this, he would have cited his father's opinion. Similarly, the Tur himself ruled regarding a get (divorce document) in Siman 132 that we are concerned about borrowing, as mentioned there. This also seems to be the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 3 of Gerushin, Law 9, regarding a lost get, as mentioned there. And although from what I wrote in section 179, there is a distinction between a get, where there is no presumption that it belongs to him since it was lost and found not in his possession, and garments of the deceased, where there is this presumption since they were found with him, nevertheless, I do not see a reason to distinguish in this manner. Moreover, even in the case of a get found in a vessel, and the vessel is his, it is not effective, as mentioned there.

However, in truth, there is a significant dispute among our early and later sages in this matter. The Rosh and Rabbeinu Yerucham in Sefer Meisharim, the Rashba, the Maharam from Rothenburg in his responsa, Siman 370, the Terumat HaDeshen, the Mahari Weil, and the Bach hold that we are concerned about the issue of borrowing. <small>[And so it appears from Tosafot in Gittin 28 and Bava Metzia 27]</small>. But the Mordechai at the end of Yevamot, the Ritva, the Nimukei Yosef, the Ran in his commentary on Bava Metzia there, Tosafot in Yevamot <small>[120]</small>, the Shach in Choshen Mishpat <small>[Siman 65, Sif Katan 26]</small>, the Maharal of Prague, the Magen Shlomo in the responsa of the later Geonim, the Mahari Halevi <small>[there]</small>, the Gra <small>[Seif 83]</small>, and many other great authorities ruled that we are not concerned about the issue of borrowing, and that even the Rif and the Rambam hold this way. <small>[From what they wrote as the second explanation regarding the signs being rabbinic, and according to this explanation, there is no need to worry about borrowing. Furthermore, even if it were a Torah law, they said "either way, his vessels are white and red," and according to the approach of the Geonim to rule according to "some say" and "if you want, say" – and here all of these apply, see there]</small>.

Nevertheless, even those who are lenient—although they are clear about this as a matter of law—still, in practice, do not rely solely on the signs of clothing, but combine them with other factors. In this, it is possible that even the stringent ones agree, for surely, even according to the stringent opinion, this is not a matter of Torah law. Therefore, in conjunction with other factors, they can be combined. Hence, if even a moderate sign is found on the body, they permit it in conjunction with the signs of the clothing (see Yam Shel Shlomo, Siman 6, and Rabbi Yitzchak ben Lev, and see Beit Shmuel, Siman 69). Besides, this is proven by the Talmudic discussion, and logically it is clear: if you are concerned about such a situation, you must say that the deceased lent his clothes to the deceased lying before us, and this deceased also has the same sign as the lender. This is preferable to a definitive sign, and many great authorities have agreed with this in practice, and it is a correct reasoning. Similarly, if the prohibition is not from the Torah, such as in cases of water where there is no end [to the search] and similar situations where most lead to death, many of the poskim agreed that one can rely on the signs of clothing (and in the case of an individual question, some disagree based on the case where they found [the deceased] tied in a sack, but the Talmudic discussion proves this).

Some of the great authorities have written that even those who are stringent about the concern of borrowing only apply this stringency to identifying features of clothing, but not if one recognizes them by sight alone (Pnei Yehoshua, Bava Metzia 27b). Their reasoning is that with identifying features, we can also say, aside from the concern of borrowing, that perhaps this specific feature coincidentally appears on another person's garment. However, with visual recognition, we cannot say this, and thus we do not worry about borrowing alone, since there is a presumption that whatever is found in a person's possession is theirs. Nevertheless, we have already written in Section 179 regarding this reasoning and it was rejected there; see there. Additionally, this discussion is about a distinctive identifying mark, and it is highly unlikely that such a mark would be found on another garment. Therefore, visual recognition in this matter is no better than a distinctive identifying mark, and thus we have not seen any of the decisors make such a distinction. (See Machaneh Ephraim, end of Section 87, who leans towards this reasoning, but he brings from the Ramban that he explicitly does not hold this way; see there).

Some say that even those who are stringent regarding borrowing (clothing) – this is in the case of one or two garments, but if it is found in all his garments, we are not concerned about borrowing, for it is improbable that a person would remove all his garments and lend them to another [Maharim Padwa and Maharit, and Responsa of the Later Geonim, Section 61]. But there are those who disagree, saying that generally, we are concerned about borrowing in all garments [Bach in his Responsa and Maharim Lublin]. The great later authorities agreed to be lenient like the first opinion, for it is a wonder that someone would lend all his garments to others [Nodah BiYehudah, Second Edition, Chasam Sofer, and Maamar Tzedek], and it is obvious that if combined with some other matter, it certainly helps [Rabbi Akiva Eiger].

The Sages have said that there are certain items that people do not lend out, as it is not customary to lend them, and there is no concern of borrowing with them, such as a purse, wallet, or ring [Bava Metzia there], because people are particular about lending these items. A purse and wallet — because they are believed to bring bad luck, as people say that their fortune is sold [Rashi], and although divination is forbidden, nevertheless, people do not usually lend them, and this is a passive prohibition, without stating the reason as it is written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 179 [see Tosafot there and it needs clarification]. A ring is not lent because of the concern that someone might forge their signature, as in those days, it was customary to have one's seal on the ring. 

From this, the leading halachic authorities have derived that any item that is not customarily lent — one can permit through this object, and there is no concern of borrowing. Therefore, a tallit with tzitzit, whether large or small — there is no concern of borrowing, since it is a mitzvah that is personal and one does not lend it to another [Maharit], and certainly tefillin. Similarly, if one carries an amulet and it is found with him — there is no concern of borrowing, since he carries it for its protective qualities and does not lend it to another [there]. Likewise, if one carries something for his health and it is found with him — there is no concern of borrowing. Certainly, if he had a deposit of money, goods, or documents of others in his possession — there is no concern of borrowing, as he would not commit a transgression by giving them to another without the knowledge of the depositor [Beit Yosef]. 

Some say that even a shirt is not lent out by people, and similarly, any type of garment that is worn close to the body — but this is not clear. If one has documents and papers belonging to him, whether they are his certificates or his accounts — there is no concern of borrowing, as why would he lend them to another? Similarly, if he carries money in his purse and it is known that he took the money to buy merchandise and those same coins are found — there is no concern of borrowing [it seems to me] because we testify that he would not lend what he needs for his business. Should we suspect that it was stolen from him, and the person in possession of it is the thief, we do not assume that people are thieves, as it is written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 133, and we do not consider the person in possession to be a thief. 

Note that even though some authorities hold that there is a concern of borrowing with any item — we do not follow this, as the majority of authorities have ruled that with items that are not customarily lent, there is no concern of borrowing — and this is the main point from the Talmudic discussions, and this is how the leading later authorities have ruled.

Some say that in the case of items (such as clothing) where we do not suspect borrowing, as we have stated, this is when they are found on the deceased, who is wearing them or they are found in his pocket. But if they are found on the ground near him, this is not a sign that they belong to him, because we assume that they fell from someone else and not from this deceased person [Beit Shmuel, section 369]. And even though in the case of found items, we associate the fruits found near a vessel with the vessel, as we stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 262, nevertheless, in the matter of a married woman, we do not make such an association, just as an intermediate sign would be a definitive sign for found items but not for the prohibition of a married woman. However, many of the great authorities disagree with this, and they hold that if it is found near him, we do attribute it to the deceased, and we should not compare it to an intermediate sign because not all matters are the same. Especially since, generally, the deceased or the murdered person, due to the circumstances of his death or murder, throws off his clothes and items, and the measure of proximity depends on the visual assessment [see Pitchei Teshuva, section 195]. Additionally, there is the principle of proximity as derived from the Torah, as it is written (Deuteronomy 21:3), "The city nearest to the corpse," and although the rule is that we follow the majority even in the case of evident proximity, this applies if there were two corpses or murdered individuals far from this place; in such a case, we would attribute it to the distant ones due to the majority. But to generally follow the majority in such a case is not applicable, and proof of this can be found in the words of the Rambam in Chapter 9 of the Laws of Murderers, Law 6. And know that all of this applies when the body is found near the clothes and items, but to permit based on clothes and items that are not typically lent out, Heaven forbid to say so, unless they are found on the riverbank and subsequently the drowned person is found in the river, as will be explained with God's help. [And see what is written in Choshen Mishpat, section 325, paragraph 68, and analyze well].

It has already been explained that visual recognition is superior to signs, and visual recognition is not for the entire body but only for the face. Thus, the Sages taught in Yevamot: one testifies only regarding the facial features with the nose, for in this way the recognition of one person from another is evident, as it is written (Isaiah 3:9), "The recognition of their faces testifies against them." The face includes the forehead, the nose, and the cheeks themselves, and one does not pay attention to the eyes or the mouth. And although in the general sense of facial features the forehead is not included, nevertheless, facial recognition does involve the forehead. The Gemara brings a case of someone who stuck wax on his forehead and was not recognized, and similarly, if a person covers their nose, they will not be recognized, as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. Thus, the recognition mentioned in "the recognition of their faces" depends on the forehead and the nose, along with the cheeks themselves. And although for the recognition of a firstborn, the forehead alone suffices as mentioned in Choshen Mishpat, section 277, this pertains to recognizing a person when the majority of their head emerges from the womb, where the forehead indicates that it is a person. And regarding this, it is written in the context of recognition of a firstborn, but recognizing one person from another, i.e., distinguishing one face from another, is not sufficient with the forehead alone but requires the cheeks and the nose as well. And this is true according to Torah law, and although for one explanation in the Gemara it implies that, according to Torah law, for an agunah (a woman whose husband is missing), the forehead alone suffices, but the stringency of the Sages requires the face and nose as well. According to this, there would be practical differences in several matters between Torah law and rabbinic law regarding an agunah. Nevertheless, from the consensus of all the authorities, it is evident that the primary explanation is that even according to Torah law, recognition is not valid without the face and nose, and common sense also testifies to this, for with the forehead alone one cannot distinguish between people. The Jerusalem Talmud brings examples of many people who only covered their noses and were not recognized, all the more so without the face. [And furthermore, the general rule from the Geonim is to rule according to the latter explanation, and although the first explanation is also a decisive legal ruling, and perhaps because of this they reconcile, but in this matter, the primary ruling follows the "if you want, say" explanation, and Reish Lakish explicitly holds this way and disagrees, for Reish Lakish holds that a complete recognition is required for a firstborn, while Rabbi Yochanan believes that recognizing a person suffices. But according to the first explanation, they would differ in the practical sense, and the Mirrors of the Congregation elaborates on this, and it seems to me that the primary ruling is as I have written. Examine this well.]

One does not testify regarding him unless it is known that this corpse did not die earlier than three days from the time they recognized him. However, if it is more than three days, the corpse's appearance changes and it is possible that even though they recognize him as Reuven, he is not Reuven, and it merely seems to them that he is Reuven. And even though one might argue that if so, why should another person change to specifically resemble Reuven? One could say the opposite – that if it were really Reuven, he would have changed since it is known that after three days, the appearance changes. Therefore, it is possible that it is actually someone else, and just because they are searching for Reuven, they think he is Reuven. 

Some authorities hold that this is a biblical law, and in a case of doubt regarding three days, we are stringent, as is the rule with biblical doubts. Others maintain that this is a stringency of the Sages, and biblically, since they recognize him as Reuven, he is definitely Reuven, but the Sages were stringent in this matter. Therefore, in a case of doubt regarding three days, we are lenient, as is the rule with rabbinic doubts, as will be explained later, God willing. 

(It seems to me that the three days are full 24-hour periods, and in the new Sha'agat Aryeh, section 13, it brings from the three days of mourning that it is not full 24-hour periods. In his opinion, this is due to the change. I am puzzled by this because even if so, part of the day is considered like the whole day, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, section 69.)

In what case are these matters stated? On land. But someone who drowned in water, or even if he was killed on land and thrown into the water, even if he remained in the water for many days, if they recognized him as Reuven, they permit his wife to remarry, because in water, a body does not change except after a long time. The Jerusalem Talmud brings an incident where they retrieved a body from the water after seventeen days and recognized him because the cold preserves the body from changing. And in our Talmud, there's also an incident where they retrieved a body after five days, recognized him, and allowed his wife to remarry. (And although the Rif wrote five days, it is not a precise number, and only because that's how it is in the Gemara, so one must be precise.) It is also explained that the reason is because the water preserves the face from changing. One should not ask, since the Gemara explains that there is no difference in time, and implies that even if the body is lying in the cold on land, it still changes, so what is the difference with the cold in the water? It can be said that water, besides being cold, has the nature to preserve and maintain the form as it is. Additionally, even according to the Jerusalem Talmud which attributes the reason only to the cold, experience shows that the cold of the land is not comparable to the cold of the water, which is very strong, and the coldness of the water flow is distinct.

From this, the great poskim (decisors of Jewish law) have learned that in the northern countries during the winter, it does not change even over many days. For our eyes see that the cold of the rainy season in our northern countries, when the snow lies upon the ground and the cold is intense, the cold freezes and paralyzes for a long time, and the body becomes like stone, and it is impossible for it to change at all. And what the Sages of blessed memory said, that there is no difference between one time and another – this is certainly true in the Land of Israel and in Babylonia and throughout the East, where the countries are warm, and even in the rainy season, the cold is minor compared to the cold of the water. And so it is in most of the settled world. But in the north, we are witnesses that the winter cold is harder than the cold of water. And on this, the great scholars of the world relied in many responses and permitted it in practice. [See Beit Shmuel 178, and what Ramban wrote should be Raavan, and the Amudei HaShulchan 172 who elaborated on this, but I did not understand his reasoning and there is no disagreement here. The Jerusalem Talmud is straightforward and not referring to Eruvin 22b, and so ruled the Peri Megadim and he gave the reason because of the cold. Refer there and consider well.]

And all this is when we did not see that it changed. But if we saw that it changed, for example, its form became swollen, we do not testify about it, since what does it help that it was in the water, since in the end its features changed [Ba'er Heitev], and so it is proven from the discussion in the Talmud. And although some say that we do not worry about this, since if we recognize him, what does it matter if he became swollen, these words are not fundamental [Magen Avraham]. However, if the facial features did not swell, even if the body swelled, it seems to me that we testify about him if we recognize him, and it is not comparable to a wound that will be explained. See section 195.

And similarly, one who is in water, they testify about him even after a long time, as long as we have not seen him change when there is no wound on the entire body, such as if he drowned in water or died and was thrown into the water. But if he was killed by blows and wounds, and certainly if he was slaughtered – they do not testify about him, for so said our Sages of blessed memory, "the water draws out the wound," meaning that it aggravates the pain and causes swelling [Rashi], and even if the wound is not on the face but on other parts of the body, we are concerned that the face changed due to the wound on the body [Chayei Adam Siman 120], for the water, since it descends into the cavity of the wound, it flows and spreads throughout the entire body and changes its form.

Know that the Rambam, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG), and Rabbeinu Yerucham omitted the law concerning a wound. Rabbeinu Beit Yosef (B.Y.) wrote in a responsum that their reasoning is that it applies specifically if the wound is on the face. However, if the wound is in other places, it does not alter the face, and this did not need to be written because they already wrote that if the face is altered, one cannot testify about him. Since there is a wound, it is understood that the place of the wound has changed. 

And some say that they do not hold this at all and that according to the law, we follow the opinion that a wound invalidates [this is according to Abaye there], and it is impossible to say this since it is clearly proven that this opinion is held as law [Yevamot 47:]. However, the main reason is as written [Mareh Tzovot], and the law follows the opinion of the majority of decisors. Nevertheless, one can combine the opinion of the Rambam, SeMaG, and Rabbeinu Yerucham with other leniencies [there].

And if there is doubt whether it is a wound or not, we lean towards leniency [as stated in Beit Hadash in the name of the Rosh], and the reason is reasonable since we have not seen that his facial appearance has changed.

And know that I have explained this according to the opinion of the leading Acharonim [Chazon Ish and Ma'arot HaTzov'ot], but in truth, it is not explicitly explained in any of the Poskim that if the blow is on other parts of the body, the face will change because of this. On the contrary, in two places in the Gemara, it is explicitly implied that the water only damages the place of the blow [Baba Metzia 47b, Shabbat 120b], and so Rashi explicitly explains [Shabbat 121a], and so writes the Mordechai in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak of the Tosafists [there according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam].
