And logic supports this, for at the place of the blow, because of the pain and the opening of the wound, the water damages it, but what relevance is there to other parts of the body? And if it is because the water enters the hollow of the wound and washes through the whole body and damages the face, then even without a blow, there are many openings in a person, and certainly, water enters through his mouth and also through the openings of his nose, and according to this, the face would always change. Therefore, it is certain that there is no connection between these things. And also, the Tur, who wrote that if there is no blow, it can be explained that this refers to the face. According to this, there would be no disagreement at all in this matter, but rather that the Rambam did not need to bring this because of the reason explained, and the Tur brought it to teach that even if it seems that his appearance has not changed, nevertheless, since there is a blow on his face, certainly his appearance has changed. And according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, it must be so, [and this is also the opinion of the Pri Sha and the Taz].

There is an opinion that the principle of "water accentuating a wound" applies to a wound that existed during the person’s life and did not heal, but if it healed during their life or the wound occurred after death, such as from fish eating parts of the body, it is not relevant to say that water accentuated the wound. And the reason is logical, because the rationale for "water accentuating a wound" is due to the pain, and with a wound that occurred after death or if it healed, pain is not applicable. And our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, in his response, added that we only say "water accentuated a wound" when the person was thrown into the water while still alive with the wound, but if they were already killed on land before being thrown into the water, the principle of "water accentuating a wound" does not apply for the reason explained. And know that with a wound, even within three days of the killing or death, we do not testify about it, because once the face is disfigured due to the wound, it makes no difference whether it is within three days or after three days. And although there is someone who is uncertain about this, the main ruling is as I have written, and so it appears from the decisors.

It has been clarified that in the case of water, the body does not change even after several days; this is provided it was recognized immediately when it was brought up from the water. However, if it lay on dry land for some time after being brought up from the water before being seen again, it cannot be testified about. As our Sages have said (121a): "But if it stayed [out of the water], it will swell," because after they bring it to dry land, its appearance changes [Rashi]. And even if it is within three days of his death, killing, or drowning, it is of no use at all. It seems from the general language of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) that even if it was brought to a very cold place, it is of no use, for this is the nature of the body that as long it is in the water, it retains its appearance, but when it is brought up from the water and exposed to the air, its face changes. 

It appears that if they keep his head and face in the water, even if his entire body is out of the water, since his face is in the water, they can testify about him. This is also implied from several responsa. But in the opposite case, where the body was in the water and the head and face were out of the water, it certainly does not help, because we follow the reasoning. Although there are those who are uncertain about this, it seems this is the main view [see P.T. section 117]. And as I wrote in section 218, according to the Rambam (Maimonides), one witness alone is not sufficient for recognition.

And what is the measure of time it should be left on dry land for its appearance to change? In the Gemara, it is generally stated that if it was delayed, it would become bloated, but we do not know the precise duration of this delay. The version before us in the Rambam, Chapter 13, Law 22, states twelve hours, and it is clearly implied that before twelve hours it does not change. However, many of the decisors have written that this is a scribal error and it should say two hours, and some say one hour – and several of our Rabbis agreed to this [Ribash, Siman 377, in the name of Ramban and Rashba, and so wrote the Maggid Mishneh and Ran in his responsa]. Some say that since we find in the Gemara [115b] the term "immediately," it means literally immediately, but this is not a proof at all, as we find the term "immediately" in the Gemara [Gittin 27b] that is not literal, and since we find in the Gemara [Yevamot 121a] that it needs to be seen at the time itself, there is support for the opinion that the time is one hour, but even this is not a clear proof. From the language of the Rambam who wrote that if it was delayed after being taken out of the water and bloated, we do not testify about him, it is implied that only if we saw it bloated we do not testify about him. However, all the early authorities agreed that since it was delayed, it is presumed to have bloated even if the change is not noticeable, and if the change is noticeable, then even if it was not delayed, we do not testify about him. And this that the Rambam wrote "and bloated," his intention was "or bloated" [Mirat Hatzovot, Siman 303]. And specifically, if the face has changed, but for the rest of the body, we do not concern ourselves with it. And know that regarding the change, a great understanding is required to determine what is called a change, as it is inevitable that every dead or killed person or one who drowned, his face will change a bit. However, a change is considered when the change alters the appearance of the face significantly, such as when it bloats so much that there is no recognizable appearance of the face as it was in life [see Pitchei Teshuvah, Siman 117]. And there are those who say that when they placed him at the time he was taken out of the water in a cold place, as in the winter in our country, even if it was delayed a bit, we testify about him, but it is questionable if this can be relied upon. However, according to the method of Rabbenu Tam that will be explained, in any case, there is room to be lenient as will be explained with God's help.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 27: If they found him murdered and recognize him by sight but do not know when he was killed, some say that we assume he was killed within three days and testify about him, and some forbid. However, if a rumor spread saying "so-and-so died or was killed" and after three days they found him dead and recognized him—his wife is permitted according to everyone. And the reason for the dispute has already been explained in section 189, that if it is within three days, it is a Torah matter and we are stringent in cases of doubt, but if it is rabbinic, we are lenient. And some of the poskim wrote that it makes sense to be lenient in this, since we do not see any change in his appearance, and perhaps the concern of swelling is rabbinic. And the explanation of his words is—even if within three days it is from the Torah, that applies when we see a change that he swelled, but when we do not see a change, certainly there is no concern from the Torah, and some are stringent even in this. However, what Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote, that if a rumor spread she is permitted according to everyone, the commentators wrote that it is a scribal error, as she is only permitted according to the first opinion in any case—if the rumor is true, no further testimony is needed, and if the rumor is false, and this found body is not related to the rumor which has already passed three days—there is a doubt whether it is within three days or after three days, and she is permitted according to this opinion, indicating that the rumor does not detract. And some say she is permitted according to all opinions, for even though in a doubt of three days some forbid, nevertheless, we combine with this the rumor that it is true that he died since they recognized him. And Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef concluded this way from reasoning.

And one should not question the position of those who prohibit (remarriage) in a case of doubt within three days due to the concern that perhaps the deceased had died earlier, before the three days. Why do we not establish (presume) him in a state of life and say that he was alive until three days prior, as it is written in Yoreh De'ah, section 397, regarding a similar matter? For it can be said, on the contrary, that we establish the husband of this woman even now in a state of life, and this body is not her husband's but someone else's who had died earlier and whose appearance changed to resemble her husband's. Therefore, it is not appropriate to give him the presumption of life, since we do not know who he is and how many people die in the world at every moment. Additionally, she has the presumption of being a married woman, and moreover, there are disputes regarding this matter, as it is a presumption that has been weakened.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in Section 26: If there is a doubt whether he delayed or not, we go stringently, and even if she married, she must leave him. And all this applies to identifying him by visual recognition, but by clear signs, even if he delayed, they permit his wife, end quote. Provided that the signs are not those that can change after death, such as a mole and the like. And in a doubt whether he delayed, we go stringently, even according to the opinion that is lenient in the doubt of three days, since here it is only an hour, it is more likely that he delayed more than an hour [Chammach in the name of the Ran]. Nevertheless, if a witness heard from another witness who saw him dead after he was brought up from the water and did not clarify whether he saw him immediately or after an hour, we lean towards leniency assuming he saw him within the first hour [Bach, section 182], because since the first witness is not present and we do not know if he also had a doubt whether he delayed, we do not need to be stringent in this case. And similarly, when she is permitted by Torah law, such as when they stood over him for the time it takes for the soul to depart as will be explained, and she is only prohibited rabbinically, we can be lenient in a doubt whether he delayed [Pischei Teshuvah in the name of the Rashash]. And also what we have been lenient with a witness who heard from another witness, some say that this is only when she is permitted by Torah law [ibid.], and similarly, we can be lenient when combined with an additional identifying mark, and if the entire body is intact, we can be lenient when combined with the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam which will be explained later, and even if he definitely delayed, many great authorities were lenient based on the combination with the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam of blessed memory.

Everything we have written regarding the matter that one only testifies based on the face along with the nose, and that one only testifies up to three days – this is according to the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, and most of the decisors. However, in these matters, there is another approach by one of the distinguished early rabbis. This is the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 25: Rabbeinu Tam wrote that the rule that one does not testify unless the forehead, nose, and facial features are intact applies only when only the head is present. But if the entire body is intact, even if the facial features, forehead, and nose are not present, one can recognize the individual through clear recognition. The later authorities disagreed with him, end quote. And in section 28, it is written: And some say in the name of Rabbeinu Tam that the rule that one does not testify after three days applies only if the face is injured. But if the face is not injured, one can testify even after many days through clear recognition of the body and its form. The later authorities were not convinced by this, end quote. And the decisors disagreed in explaining the words of Rabbeinu Tam, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

Some say that his intention is that even if the entire body is whole, even if there is no face, forehead, or nose, one can testify based on visual recognition alone. Others say that his intention is that intermediate signs are also required [see Beit Shmuel, section 377]. Many things have been said about this. However, according to what we understand from the words of Rabbeinu Tam himself in Sefer HaYashar, section 491, the explanation is as follows: just as there are clear and unclear signs, similarly with visual recognition, there is complete visual recognition that is better than a clear sign, and there is incomplete visual recognition which is like a clear sign. Complete visual recognition is when the entire body is whole, and even if the face is injured, Rabbeinu Tam holds that this is complete visual recognition, which is better than a clear sign. When the entire body is not whole, meaning the head is severed from the body, this is incomplete visual recognition. And about this, it was taught that one can testify only about the face with the nose, even if there are signs on the body, and one can testify only up to three days. Although even without the nose, he can be recognized by visual recognition to say this is the form of so-and-so by the signs he has in the form, and the signs are signs of visual recognition, meaning it is recognized that this is the form of so-and-so. Nevertheless, without the nose and forehead, it is only like an intermediate sign, but with the nose and forehead, it is like a clear sign. Therefore, after three days, one cannot testify about him, because since the head is severed from the body, it changes after three days. But when the entire body is whole, even if the face is injured and there is no forehead and nose, they can recognize him by visual recognition that this is so-and-so by the signs of the entire body [Tosafot 121], meaning by the signs of visual recognition in the entire body, and not actual signs. Because when the entire body is whole, anyone who saw him alive, when looking at the whole body, will see with visual recognition by recognizing his signs, his image, and the outline of his limbs in the entire body that this is so-and-so, and even after a long time one can testify about him. And similarly, when he was raised from the water, where it is required that he be seen immediately, this is also when the head is severed from the body. But when the entire body is whole, even if the face is disfigured, one can testify about him even after a long time. And do not be troubled that since the head is severed, there is a wound, and it should not work even when in the water because the water preserves the wound, for it can be said that since the wound is not in the actual face, we do not concern ourselves with it, as stated in section 195. And also, according to what Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in a responsum that we brought in section 196, this is also satisfactory. This is the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam [and in the book Or LeYesharim, we elaborated on this with the help of Heaven].

And know, that although many disagree with his approach, nevertheless, many of our Rabbis only disagree with what Rabbeinu Tam holds, that when the entire body is intact even if the face is injured, one may testify by recognizing the body even after many days - in this they did not agree with him. However, when the entire body is intact and the face is not injured - they agree that one may testify even after a long time. And this is the opinion of our Rabbis, the Tosafists, the Rosh, and the Tur.

The Tur, after writing the entire opinion of Rabbi Tam that one can testify about the whole body even if there is no recognizable face, forehead, and nose, writes as follows: "And even if it was on dry land, if his face is not injured, one can testify about him even after several days through the recognition of his body and form. And even if his face was injured, in which case one can only testify about him within three days, if they found him killed and recognize him through visual identification but do not know when he was killed – it is assumed that he was killed within three days, and they can testify about him." His words mean that even if we do not agree with all of Rabbi Tam's words, it is nevertheless obvious that if the whole body is intact and the face is not injured, one can testify even after several days. The statement of our Sages that one can testify only within three days applies when the face is injured, even if the whole body is intact. This is unlike Rabbi Tam's opinion that if the whole body is intact, one can testify even if the face is injured, even after three days. The Rosh also wrote similarly in "Ha'isha Batra" (Section 3) that if the face is not injured, it is clear that they can recognize him through the visual identification of his body and form, as his form does not change so much and it is recognizable to the eyes. They can recognize a dead person through visual identification even after several days. This is also the language of the Tosafot, explaining that even if we do not agree with Rabbi Tam's opinion, nevertheless, if the face is not injured, it is obvious that one can testify even after several days.

And according to this, if his entire body is intact and there is no injury on his face, the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam is not a singular opinion, for Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur hold like him. Additionally, the commentators have inferred from the language of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, who wrote regarding the ruling of Rabbeinu Tam, "and the later authorities disagreed with him," that his words were not completely rejected, and Rabbeinu Tam's opinion is combined with other estimations and proofs. And know that according to this, what Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 28: "And some say in the name of Rabbeinu Tam that the ruling that one may not testify about him except within three days applies only when he is injured on his face, but if he is not injured on his face, one may testify even after several days" – according to what we have explained, this is not the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam. For according to Rabbeinu Tam, even if he is injured on his face, one may testify even after several days, as he explicitly explained in Sefer HaYashar. And this is the opinion of Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur, as we have written. (And since Sefer HaYashar was not printed in their times, they thus assumed this, and many things have been said about Tosafot. According to what we have written, it is simply understandable, and the bodily signs they wrote about are like visual identification of the body, which is akin to signs, and I found support for my words from the Maharik at the end of root 121, and investigate thoroughly.)

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in Section 28 regarding the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam that if the body is whole and not disfigured in the face, one may testify about it even after several days. For there are those who differentiate and say that anyone who was present when the person drowned in the water, even if the body is whole, may not testify about it. But someone who did not see the drowning and says he recognizes the person by sight and the body is whole – he may testify about it. End quote. This has no relevance to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, and it will be explained later, with God's help, in Section 221.

One does not testify about a person’s death unless it is a definite death, but one does not testify in cases where death is highly probable. It has already been explained that just as leniencies are applied in testimony, stringencies are also applied to the essence of the testimony, and even the slightest doubt is considered, even in cases with only a one in a thousand chance. This is due to reasons explained in section 20. Therefore, one does not testify that a death has occurred based on the condition of a gosses (a person in a death throe), for although the vast majority of gossesim die, since one in a thousand might live, one does not testify in such cases. This is contrary to the opinion that one can testify about a gosses after three days, and it is unthinkable to say so. This is also the opinion of the leading Acharonim (later authorities). 

Some say that in all matters where the Sages said not to remarry, if she did remarry, she must divorce, even in cases where death is highly probable, except in the case of water without a defined end. Some of the earlier authorities disputed this. However, this is not a general rule for all matters, for certainly there are cases where she must divorce if she remarries, and the decision depends on the understanding of the local wise men who are God-fearing.

If one falls into a lion's den that is very wide, and when he falls into it, he does not fall on the lions [Rabbenu Nissim] – we do not testify concerning him, because perhaps the lions were not hungry at that time, and since he is standing next to them, maybe they did not harm him. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it explains the reason that perhaps a miracle occurred for him like Daniel, but we hold that we do not mention miracles [Baba Batra 121:], and the Jerusalem Talmud holds that there is a Tanna who holds that we do mention miracles [Maharsha, s.v. "Ein"], and this follows the opinion of that Tanna, and it is possible that even the Jerusalem Talmud does not hold this as a practical halacha [and it seems to me that this is the intention of the Tosafot there according to the version of the Maharsha, see there and investigate thoroughly]. Based on this, if he fell on the lions – we testify concerning him, for they certainly killed him. Similarly, if he fell into a pit full of snakes and scorpions – we testify concerning him, because since he fell on them, they certainly killed him, and we do not say perhaps he knows how to charm the snakes, because since he trampled on them, they certainly harmed him [Gemara]. And in a lion's den in a place where they do not permit the wife to remarry, even if he is not found in the pit, we are concerned that perhaps he left the pit and went away, however, if human bones are found in the pit – his wife is permitted to remarry [Bach], though some dispute this, and it is not certain, and since this is not a common occurrence at all, there is no need to elaborate on this.

If someone falls into a deep fiery furnace or into a boiling cauldron filled with wine, oil, or water and remains there for a short while, witnesses can testify regarding his death. Similarly, in a less deep furnace, he must stay in it for a short time, because otherwise, he might have jumped out of the fire immediately. Likewise, if two of his vital organs were slaughtered or most of them, even if he stood up and fled, witnesses can testify that he has died, since he would certainly die soon. Any situation where it is impossible for him to survive and he must die shortly thereafter, witnesses can testify about his death.

However, if someone sees him crucified and birds are eating his flesh, even if he was stabbed or shot with arrows, witnesses cannot testify about his death. Some say this only applied in ancient times when they would hang a person by his hands and he could live for a long time, but in our times, when they hang by the neck, witnesses can testify that he was strangled immediately. This is reasonable, even though some disagree and bring evidence from the Jerusalem Talmud, which suggests that perhaps a noblewoman passed by and ransomed him, or there is concern that the rope broke. Nevertheless, this only applies if the rope broke at that moment. But if he remained hanging for a short while, it is clear that he was strangled. The concern of the Jerusalem Talmud is also only relevant for someone hung by their hands, because otherwise, sensory evidence shows that a person is strangled within a short time. Once he has remained hanging for a short time, he is considered strangled.

Similarly, if someone sees birds eating his flesh from a place that would cause death if removed, such as his brain, heart, or intestines, witnesses can testify about his death with certainty. Also, if someone saw him being hanged and after a day or two sees a person still hanging there, witnesses can testify that it is the same person and we do not say that perhaps the rope broke and another person is now hanging there. We assume it is the same person. Even according to the opinion that, in the case of a lost grave in a field where a grave was later found, we do not assume it is the same grave, in this case, it is clear. The concern is only rabbinical and a stringency applied to the prohibition of a married woman. Here, everyone agrees that we assume it is the same person. Additionally, there, the area is not confined, as the doubt applies to the entire field, but here, where the person was left hanging in a confined place and was found in that exact place, we certainly assume it is the same person.

It is stated in the Talmud [120a] that even if someone is seen as mortally wounded, meaning his flesh is cut and filled with wounds and sword bruises, one cannot testify about him. It is explained there in the Gemara that even if he is cut in a place that renders him a tereifah, such as his leg from the knee and above, the Tannaim are divided on this matter. Some permit it, and some prohibit it because it is possible that if the limb was cut with a knife heated in fire, he can survive because the burn can heal. Our Mishnah follows the opinion that prohibits it. The Gemara does not establish the Mishnah, which prohibits someone mortally wounded, in a place that does not render him a tereifah, such as cutting the hand or leg from the knee and below, because that would not be a novelty at all. It is explained there that if we know that it was cut with a heated knife, it is prohibited according to everyone.

The Rambam did not write at all about the law of someone mortally wounded. Many things have been said about this, and the primary reasoning seems to be that the Rambam holds that if the cut is in a place that renders him a tereifah, he will not live even if it was with a heated knife. Otherwise, many new laws in tereifah animals would arise. If the cut is in a place that renders it a tereifah, we hold that it is a tereifah. According to this view, if cut with a heated knife, it is kosher. However, in the Gemara, those who hold that with a heated knife, he can live also hold that a tereifah can live [for Rav who establishes it with a heated knife holds in Temurah 11a that a tereifah can live]. But we hold that a tereifah does not live more than twelve months, and therefore the Rambam omitted it. If it is cut in a place that does not render it a tereifah, there is no need to inform us that it is prohibited, and in a place that renders it a tereifah, it is certainly permitted after twelve months. Therefore, the Rif also omitted all the discussions of the Gemara. [Rashba, who holds that one can burn and live, implies somewhat in the beginning of "These are the Tereifot" that he also holds that a tereifah can live, following the opinion of the school of Rabbi Yishmael who holds this way. However, from the language of the Tosefta, where Rashba says it is kosher because it can burn and live, it implies that he holds that a tereifah does not live, and this is also apparent there 57b. Investigate this thoroughly.]

If someone falls into a body of water that has a definite boundary, his wife is permitted to remarry if he remained there for a certain amount of time on the riverbank until it was clear that the person has drowned and did not come out of the water. However, if he falls into a body of water that has no definite boundary, his wife is forbidden to remarry. What is considered a body of water with a definite boundary? It is one where someone standing on its bank can see all the shores of the water on all four sides, like a pond, a cave, or a small river where one can see all the banks of the river. If the drowned person were to emerge, he would be seen. Bodies of water with no definite boundary include all seas and large rivers because they extend far, and we fear that perhaps the current carried him far away, and he exited alive or entered a fish cave. Although this is a stringent ruling, the sages were strict in this matter for reasons explained in section 20. There is no difference in this ruling whether the person was naked or clothed, whether he could swim on the surface of the water or not, and whether he fell into the water or the water came upon him, such as if he was sitting in a lower chamber of a ship, and the ship sank to the depths. Even though it is highly likely that he drowned, since one in a thousand might be saved by quickly jumping into the sea, swimming, or sitting on a plank or mast and being saved, it is not possible to permit the wife to remarry. Anyone who permits her to remarry is excommunicated, as will be explained. If the time was not sufficient for it to be clear that the person has drowned, then even by Torah law, she is forbidden to remarry.

There was an incident where someone was tied by his leg and lowered into the sea, and when they pulled him up from the sea, they only brought up his leg. It was evident that the rope had snapped along with the leg and that the entire body had drowned. The Sages said that if the leg is from the knee and above, his wife may remarry, because when it is cut from the knee and above, even if the sea waves wash him ashore, he will not survive. Our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled in section 32 that she may remarry only after twelve months, because a mortally wounded person does not live for twelve months. This is also found in the Jerusalem Talmud. However, the Rambam and the Tur wrote simply that his wife may remarry, implying immediately, and they did not consider the Jerusalem Talmud, since it is not mentioned in the Gemara and is an excessive stringency. Since the sea is itself a place where survival is unlikely, this is a rabbinic stringency, and all the more so in such a case where he cannot live and the water exacerbates the wound, it is obvious that he will die immediately. In several matters, the Jerusalem Talmud is more stringent than the Babylonian Talmud, as mentioned in section 209. Nevertheless, in practice, one should rule according to our master, the Beit Yosef, because we do not find explicit dissent from the earlier authorities on this matter.

But if someone fell into the sea and afterwards a net was cast and a human leg was retrieved from the water, and there is no distinct sign on the leg to recognize that it is from the person who fell into the water, even if it is from the knee and above – we do not permit his wife to remarry. I say that it is the leg of another person, and it is not appropriate to say in this case "it is the one who was lost and it is the one who was found" as in the case of someone hanged in Siman 120, for there everything that was lost is what was found. But here a whole person was lost, and now a leg is found – it is not appropriate to say so. Additionally, in the sea there are many who drown. [It appears to me, see Pitchei Teshuva Siman 135]. And it is possible that if they stood by him until his soul departed, since the prohibition is only rabbinic – it may be permitted in such a case, and this requires further study. Similarly, it is possible that with an intermediate sign on the leg it may be permitted in such a case. [And what is written in Shulchan Aruch about a very distinct sign, it is possible that an intermediate sign is called distinct like in monetary matters, for what does it teach us with a distinct sign, and in the source of the law in the Maggid Mishneh it is not written distinct, see there in Chapter 13, Halacha 16].

Regarding the previous law, our master the Rema wrote that there are those who say that even a distinctive sign on his clothes is effective here, since they saw him drown in these clothes, end of quote. His explanation is that if someone was seen falling into the sea, and afterwards a leg with a garment or shoe was retrieved, and it is recognized by a distinctive sign or by a clear visual recognition that it belongs to the drowned person, it is obvious that she (the wife) is permitted to remarry. And although we are generally concerned about the possibility of borrowed clothing, in this case it does not apply, because how could he have taken off his clothes underwater and lent them to another person underwater. And even if someone drowned in his clothes, and after several days a dead person is found washed ashore wearing these clothes, and the dead person cannot be identified, still his wife may be permitted to remarry. Although it might be said that the drowned man had previously reached dry land and lent his clothes to another, and it is the other person who was washed ashore before us now, it is still a remote concern that two people would drown in these clothes and that he would have lent them to another person who also drowned in these clothes. And even though there are those who question this, nonetheless, regarding the concern of borrowing, since many disagree with the fundamental law of borrowing, and especially concerning borrowing all of his clothes, it is certainly permissible in such a case. And see Beit Shmuel section 98, Noda B'Yehuda section 28, and Maharit section 128, and the main ruling is as written, as ruled by Maharam Padua.

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 13, Law 9: If one witness says, "I saw that he died in war or in a collapse, or that he drowned in the great sea and died," and similar cases where most likely he died, if the witness says, "I buried him," he is believed, and she may remarry based on his testimony. If he did not say, "I buried him," she may not remarry, but if she did remarry, she does not need to leave her new husband. Similarly, if one witness testifies to a woman that her husband drowned in waters that have no end and did not emerge, and his memory was lost and his name forgotten, she should not remarry based on this testimony, as we have explained. If she did remarry, she does not need to leave her new husband. Even if it was a gentile speaking casually who said that so-and-so drowned in the sea, and she remarried based on his words, she does not need to leave her new husband. So ends his words. Our master, the Beit Yosef, copied this in Sections 33 and 34.

Explanation of his words: Behold, we hold that a woman is believed to say "my husband died" when she says he died in his bed, but if she says he died in war, she is not believed, as will be explained. The reason is that we say that in such a case she did not scrutinize properly and assumes he died because she believes it impossible for him to have escaped, considering that all who were with him were killed, and certainly, he too was killed. This is not limited to war; in any situation where the danger is great and most people are likely to die, if she says he died, she is not believed because we say she is only assuming. The Gemara (beginning of the chapter "Ha'isha Shalom") questions whether a single witness who testifies that he died in war is believed. The root of the doubt is that it was already explained in section 21 that a single witness is believed for two reasons: because people do not lie about matters that will eventually be revealed, and we explained there in section 23 that according to Rambam, this reason is from the Torah. Additionally, the Sages did not impose stringency in this matter to disbelieve a single witness because they relied on the woman herself to thoroughly verify her husband's death. Therefore, regarding a single witness in war, the doubt is whether the primary reason for permitting is because people do not lie about matters that will eventually be revealed, in which case the witness is believed because he does not assume, unlike the woman who might assume due to her desire to remarry, or if the primary reason is that the woman will scrutinize, and in war, she will not scrutinize properly (second interpretation of the Maggid Mishneh and third interpretation of the Lechem Mishneh). Furthermore, the Gemara states that waters are comparable to war. Not only if he did not emerge from the waters, in which case even two witnesses are not sufficient because we fear he might have emerged from another place, but even if she says "my husband drowned in the sea and immediately the sea cast him ashore and I saw him die," she is not believed because we fear he did not truly die and the waters confused her (Ribash, section 578), for we see many who drown and when pulled from the water appear dead, but after resuscitation and medical treatment, they live, and she is only assuming. And Rambam holds that when the witness did not say "I buried him," the doubt is not resolved, but when he says "I buried him," she is permitted to remarry (Gra, note 107), for in burial, we do not require her scrutiny. And although she herself is not believed when she says "he died in war" even if she says "I buried him" according to Rambam, as will be explained, implying that even in burial, we fear she is only assuming, here, since without burial the witness is not believed because she did not scrutinize, what does burial help? One could say that in truth, burial does not involve assumption since she buried him and looked at him. However, Rambam does not believe her in war even with burial because we suspect she might be lying (Beit Shmuel, note 146, see there), and we do not say the witness would lie. Know that this issue with waters also involves assumption, but this is in waters without an end. In waters with an end, there is no issue of assumption (Gra), for in waters without an end, the confusion is very great, but in waters with an end, they wait until his soul departs if he did not emerge, and then they testify about him (Rashba). Some say Rambam holds that even with a single witness, there is a concern of assumption (and so writes Rashi). However, in practice, there is no practical difference, for in the end, with burial, the witness is believed, and without burial, he is not believed, as will be explained in section 231.

According to the Rambam, the concern of "bedaimi" (uncertainty) applies specifically with one witness. Therefore, without the statement "we buried him," we do not permit her to remarry. However, with two witnesses, there is no concern whatsoever, and when they say he died in battle or in water, we permit her to remarry. With two witnesses, we do not need precise details, and there is no concern that they are speaking out of speculation. 

But the Rif holds that even with two witnesses, there is a concern of "bedaimi" and it is not effective unless they say "we buried him." However, it seems from his wording that the concern of "bedaimi," for which we require the statement "we buried him," is only in the case of battle. But in water, it is sufficient that they recognize him immediately when the water spat him out or when they took him out of the water. This is noted by the Hagahot Maimoniyot. The sages said that water is like battle, meaning somewhat similar, and in water, when they brought him up and saw him immediately, it is like "we buried him" in battle, as noted by the Lechem Mishneh. 

Some say that the Rif also requires the statement "we buried him" in the case of water. There are some of our rabbis who hold that with a single witness, there is no concern of "bedaimi" at all, even in battle, and there is no need to say "we buried him." Many of the early authorities hold this view, as they believe the question is resolved elsewhere. The opinion of the Rif and the Rambam represents a stringent view, but the laws and main sources in the Talmud do not support their position. Still, who would not take their great opinion into account, as noted by the Rivash in Siman 377?

According to the Rambam, we must say that the reason we permit remarriage when they brought him up from the water and immediately recognized his face without requiring "we buried him" at all, is in the case of two valid witnesses. But with one witness alone, even with recognition, we require the statement "we buried him." However, it is not specifically that they buried him; if they moved him from place to place and he had no life spirit within him, it is considered as if they buried him. It is also possible that the Rambam does not require the statement "we buried him" unless the water spat him out before the time it takes for his soul to depart. But if he was in the water for a long time, making it impossible for him to survive, we only require recognition, as it is obvious he could not survive. This is noted in the Ma'arechet HaTzov'ot. Therefore, in Halacha 22 regarding the law of delay, the Rambam does not mention at all that with one witness, it must also be said "we buried him," because there it discusses a case where he drowned a long time ago, as mentioned there, and "bedaimi" does not apply, as noted.

And so it appears to me to be the main point, that with this, what the Rambam wrote makes sense: "And similarly, a woman to whom one witness testified that her husband drowned, etc., and did not emerge, and his memory was lost, and his name was forgotten, she should not remarry; but if she did remarry, she need not leave [her new husband]." This is difficult, for what is he informing us? This is the same case, and on the contrary, the previous ruling contains a greater novelty — that even if he was seen dead, she should not remarry, and it must be that the sea cast him up; otherwise, how would one know he died? And certainly, if he was not seen to be cast up by the sea. Some want to say that he is informing us that even in such a case, if she remarried, she need not leave [her new husband] [Lechem Mishneh], but this is forced, for if so, he should have only said that if she remarried, she need not leave, as he said in the case of someone who speaks candidly. According to what I have said, it makes sense: in the first case, he informs us that if immediately after he drowned, the sea cast him up and he was seen dead, she should not remarry due to the concern that perhaps he did not die and might live, as was said. And in the latter case, he informs us that even if it was seen that he did not surface, and that means he delayed until his soul departed [Kesef Mishneh], he certainly died. This is a distant concern, that the waves carried him far away and he emerged from there, for his memory was lost, and his name was forgotten — nevertheless, she should not remarry [and the words of the Chacham Tzvi in section 62 are perplexing].

Some of the early authorities differentiate in this matter between one who saw the drowning and one who did not see the drowning. One who saw the drowning may say "it appears to me" due to the power of his imagination, which deceives him into believing that the person is certainly dead. Therefore, it does not help that he recognized him when he was pulled from the water by visual identification unless he says "I buried him" or something akin to burial, or if he provides an additional identifying mark besides visual identification, it is effective. It is not only someone who saw the drowning; the same applies to someone who knew about the drowning. However, one who neither saw nor knew about the drowning and recognized him immediately upon being pulled from the water by visual identification—no further proof is required [according to the Maor].

It appears that according to this explanation, the term "it appears to me" regarding drowning does not mean as we explained that he might still be alive and disoriented from the water, because if so, what would an identifying mark help with this? Rather, "it appears to me" means that perhaps it is another person, and it seems to him that it is this person because he saw or knew about the drowning. Since he provides an additional identifying mark, it is certainly him. Similarly, if he engaged in his burial or something akin to burial, such as moving him from place to place, he surely observed him well. There are those who differentiate even according to this explanation between knowledge and seeing, claiming that only seeing the drowning raises the concern of "it appears to me" and not just knowing about it. However, the primary opinion seems to be as I have written, that there is no difference between knowledge and seeing. [See Beit Shmuel, section 87, and Ma'arot HaTzovot, section 114, where it is explained in the responses of the Ramban and the Rivash that there is no difference].

The Tur has a different approach to all of this, and he holds that for someone who did not witness the drowning, the concept of immediate recognition is not applicable. Even if he did not see him immediately upon being brought up from the water but recognized him after a long time by sight recognition - we rely on him and permit her (the wife). However, for someone who did witness the drowning, it is not enough to see him immediately upon being brought up from the water; even in such a case, sight recognition without intermediate signs is not effective. This is the language of the Tur after he wrote the law regarding endless waters, that when someone falls there, we do not permit his wife: If one witness testifies that he saw him immediately after he was brought up and recognized him by signs on his body - he is believed, but by sight recognition alone - he is not believed. When is this said? When the witness saw him fall, etc., but another person who did not see him drown is believed even if he did not see him immediately after he was brought up, and even by sight recognition without signs, provided he saw him whole in his body. But if he is not whole, only the face with the nose - we do not rely on sight recognition alone without signs. These are the words of our teacher the Rema in Section 28, which we brought in Section 207. However, our teacher the Rema did not write that one who did not see the drowning does not need to see him immediately, because he was concerned about the words of other authorities who required seeing him immediately when he was brought up from the water. There is no difference in any manner except by a clear sign as we wrote above. And it also appears from the opinion of the Tur that with two witnesses, even if they saw the drowning, they do not need to see him immediately, because in the case of two witnesses, the Tur holds that the concept of "doubt" does not apply, as he wrote regarding the matter of doubt in war. And from the language of the Rosh, it does not seem so.

The foundation of the words of the Tur is based on what is written in section 200, where it is held that even those who disagree with the approach of Rabbeinu Tam (R"T), nevertheless, if the entire body is intact without injury, all agree with R"T that even after three days, one can testify about him. Similarly, if he was lifted from the water and delayed, because in the Gemara it is found that we need to see him immediately when he is lifted from the water, it does not agree to explain that it refers to a case where the entire body is not intact, as some of the poskim want to explain. If that were the case, he would be considered injured, and even in water, we cannot testify about him because water accentuates the injury. Additionally, it does not agree to differentiate that it is only when the injury is on the face that water accentuates the injury and not in other parts of the body, as stated in section 195. And although we wrote there that the opinion of the Tur can be interpreted in this way, nevertheless, from his language where he wrote there is no injury, it implies that he is referring to the entire body without injury. Therefore, he differentiates between one who saw the drowning and one who did not see it. And those incidents in the Gemara where we need to see him immediately are regarding those who saw the drowning. This is the approach of his father, the Rosh, in chapter "Ha'isha Shalom" section 3. And even though there are those who interpret the words of the Rosh differently, nevertheless, upon examination, it will be seen that his approach aligns with the Tur. Therefore, our Rabbi the Rema, who followed the approach of our Rabbi the Beit Yosef, who held that even with the entire body intact, it is only the opinion of R"T, as stated in section 206, therefore omitted the words of the Tur as stated that one who did not see the drowning does not need to see him immediately. [He wrote sections and because he was concerned about the opinion of Rabbi Chananel (R"Ch) in Tosafot 115: The beginning of the statement, although the Rosh himself did not hold this way, only the Tur was concerned because his words were words of tradition].

A sage who deliberately permitted [marriage] in the case of water that has an unknown source – he is excommunicated. If he did so unintentionally, such as he mistakenly thought this was the law regarding water with a known source and similar cases – what was done is valid, and if she married, she does not need to be separated, because water with an unknown source where it was left until it expired is only a rabbinic prohibition. How long is the duration – some say three hours, and some say two hours, but the main ruling is that there is no set duration, and it depends on the appearance, and many of the great authorities agreed with this. If she has not yet married – there is no permission at all. And if she married mistakenly thinking she was permitted – she does not need to be separated. However, if she married in a rebellious manner, such as if she was warned not to marry, or if one sage permitted and a greater sage prohibited – she must be separated, and this is the law in all matters where the majority lead to death and the sages prohibited it. We have already explained this in section 248, see there. [What the B'Sh wrote in section 263 is only if he is a well-known sage, it is difficult to understand from both perspectives – if she has not married, she should not marry, and if she has married, she should not be separated because she married mistakenly as she does not have the understanding of the sage's ruling.]

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in section 34 that all this applies when witnesses testify explicitly that someone drowned in an endless body of water. However, if they testify that he was on a ship that broke apart at sea or something similar, or even if they testify that he drowned but did not say he remained in the water long enough for his soul to depart, we are concerned that they might be using the term "drowning" loosely, as it is common for people to refer to such situations as drowning. Therefore, she would be required to divorce unless there is explicit testimony that he actually drowned and remained in the water long enough for his soul to depart. In such a case, testimony from a witness who heard from another witness (hearsay) is not sufficient unless the original witness explicitly stated how he drowned. Although we are lenient in several matters regarding hearsay, this leniency applies only when the language of the testimony indicates a situation closer to death than to life. However, in cases of drowning, it is more likely that he drowned in an endless body of water, and therefore, she should not remarry. Moreover, perhaps he did not remain in the water long enough for his soul to depart, and even if she remarried, she would need to divorce. If the witness explicitly states that he drowned in a body of water with an end but did not explicitly say he remained in the water long enough for his soul to depart, we are lenient with hearsay testimony. If the witness testifies that he saw him drown and remain in the water until his soul departed, but there is doubt whether it was an endless body of water or not, we also lean towards leniency, because even in an endless body of water, she would not need to divorce if she remarried. Therefore, it is considered a rabbinic doubt, and we rule leniently.

However, regarding the primary matter that was explained, that if he did not stand until his soul departed, it is a Torah prohibition and if she married, she must leave him, there are many who disagree with this and hold that even if he did not stand until his soul departed, it is considered that most who fall into water die, and she is permitted by Torah law, and if she married, she does not have to leave. And behold, in the Gemara [Yevamot 121b], there is a story brought where a Samaritan said that a certain person drowned, and based on this mistaken assumption, his wife went and married, and the sages said that if she married, she does not have to leave, even though he simply said that he drowned and did not say he stood until his soul departed. And even though it is possible to give a different reason, that because he was a well-known person and if he had come up from the water it would have become known, and so it is stated there in the Gemara according to one version, and in law there is no difference between a great person and an ordinary person, nevertheless, it is evident from common sense as well that anyone who falls into water and drowns, most of them die. And it is an explicit verse (Lamentations 3:54): "Waters flowed over my head; I said: I am cut off" [See M'rot Hatzovot section 137 which brings several poskim who hold this way].

However, it is certain that whenever it is clear that the person who said that he drowned is coming to inform of his death, it is certainly known that he is definitely dead, and presumably he remained there until his soul departed. According to this, the incident in the Gemara that we cited [there, section 134, in the name of the Maharit] makes sense. In any case, regarding a well-known person, there is room to be lenient after the fact in the case of complete drowning, even if he did not remain there the amount of time required for his soul to depart [there]. Everything depends on the judgment of the local sages with fear of God, for certainly one who falls into the water with his clothes on suddenly into the water is very unlikely to be saved, unlike one who falls in naked and can swim and reach the riverbank. It is impossible to explain everything that could possibly happen in such matters.

Our Rabbis, authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in paragraph 35: "There is an opinion that if [the husband] fell into water that has no end, she collects her Ketubah even though she is forbidden to remarry," end quote. And this is when two witnesses testified about his drowning, and even though we do not permit her to remarry – this is a stringency concerning a married woman. But regarding the Ketubah, even though in monetary matters we do not follow the majority, nevertheless in a case like this, we follow the majority, because the minority [chance of survival] is an extremely small minority [Gra]. However, with one witness, the ruling is the opposite; although the Sages believed him regarding the prohibition of a married woman, nevertheless, for monetary matters we do not extract money based on the testimony of one witness, and the heirs do not inherit based on his testimony, even in a case where she is permitted to remarry. She only collects her Ketubah from the conditions of the Ketubah, as stated in paragraph 110, see there. And there are those who disagree with this ruling and hold that in all cases where she is not permitted to remarry, she does not collect her Ketubah at all [Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 167].

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Gittin 28b) that a city under siege, a ship tossed about at sea, or someone going out to be judged are presumed to be alive. It is obvious that we do not testify about any of these cases that the person has died to permit his wife to remarry, for we consider them to be fully alive. Even if they sent a get, the get is delivered to their wives as stated at the end of section 141. If she remarries, she must leave the second husband, and her kiddushin (betrothal) from the second husband is invalid. However, if a ship is lost at sea, meaning it sank and it is unknown who among the people were saved and who drowned, or a city that was captured in ancient times when they used to kill everyone found in the fortress of the city, or someone going out to be executed, we apply to them the stringencies of both life and death concerning a get as mentioned there. Similarly, if she accepted kiddushin from another man, she requires a get from him out of doubt, but if she remarried, she must leave the second husband. If it is testified that her husband was lost at sea and not saved, this is the law of "water without end," and if she remarried, she does not need to leave. However, since the testimony was general about the loss of the ship and it is not known who was saved and who was not, if she remarries, she must leave because it is a complete doubt and she remains in the presumption of being a married woman. Even if his memory has been forgotten and lost, it does not help.

Some differentiate between a Jewish court and a non-Jewish court, but practically, there is no difference here, as many of the poskim do not differentiate, and this is evident from the simple language of the Rif there. It is proper to be stringent. The Rambam did not mention these laws regarding an agunah (a woman whose husband is missing and cannot remarry) at all. It is possible he relied on what he wrote concerning a get in Chapter 6 of Gerushin. The Rambam added there, based on the Jerusalem Talmud, that the same applies to someone dragged away by a wild animal, swept away by a river, or covered by a collapse, that we apply to them the stringencies of both life and death. It must be said that someone swept away by a river is not the same as someone who fell into water without an end, as being swept away by a river implies sitting by the riverbank and being swept by the water's current, which is easier to escape from than someone who fell into endless water. Therefore, this is a complete doubt.

Refer to what is written in section 132 and see Beit Yosef in section 141 on the words of the Rosh; this requires further study. Also, see Mar'ot HaTzov'ot.

It has already been explained that a woman who says, "My husband has died," is believed. However, our Sages stated that this is specifically when there is peace between her and her husband and peace in the world. But if there is war in the world, even if there is peace between her and her husband, or if there is strife between her and her husband even if there is peace in the world, she is not believed. The explanation is: when there is war in the world and she says he died in the war, we are concerned that she is speaking based on conjecture and relies on the fact that most people in such situations die, and therefore she says he has died. For example, if the first and last people in the group were killed and her husband was in the middle, she might say that since those were killed, her husband must have been killed as well. Therefore, she is not believed. And since the concern is due to conjecture and not because she might deliberately lie, if she says she buried him, she is believed according to most authorities, because if she buried him, she clearly saw that he died. It is not specifically that she buried him; similarly, if she moved him from place to place and clearly saw that he died, there is no longer a concern of conjecture.

However, the Rambam of blessed memory wrote that even if she says "I buried him," she is not believed. And some say that his reasoning is that when she says "I buried him," it appears she is lying because it is not customary to wait in a time of war and bury him [Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 146]. And some say that his reasoning is that in war, she is certainly in a hurry to escape for her life, but out of her great love for her husband, she would desire to bury him so he would not be cast like manure on the face of the earth. It is possible that out of great haste, she buried another man and thought it was her husband [Levush]. And some say that his reasoning is that since she strongly imagines that he died, she lies and says, "I buried him," so they would believe her more [Bayit Chadash]. And it appears to me that there is proof for the Rambam from the Jerusalem Talmud, which says that even if she says he died in his bed, she is not believed when it was a time of war, because we say that he died in the war, and she lies to say he died in his bed so that they would believe her more. And although in this, we do not hold like him as will be explained, because in our Talmud it is explained that if she says he died in his bed, she is believed, nevertheless, we do not say a distant dispute, for in any case, in war, she is not believed in any manner. However, most of the primary authorities do not hold this way, and so the Tur ruled that if she says "I buried him," she is believed. See there, and see what I wrote in paragraph 234.

And if one witness testifies that he died in war, the Rambam ruled that if he says, "I buried him," he is believed; but if he does not say, "I buried him," she should not remarry, and if she did remarry, she need not leave her second husband. Some say the reason is that without saying "I buried him," we are concerned that he is also speaking based on conjecture, but when he says, "I buried him," there is no concern of conjecture. And we do not suspect him of lying as we might suspect her. 

Even according to what we explained in section 217, that according to the Rambam, with one witness there is no concern of conjecture at all, it is still appropriate, because this ruling is a question in the Gemara. The doubt is whether the primary reason for the credibility of one witness is because it is a matter likely to be revealed, or because she will be meticulous. In war, she will not be meticulous, relying on the certainty that he was killed like many others who were killed. 

In truth, the primary reason is because it is a matter likely to be revealed, and many of the authorities hold that the Rambam's opinion in practice is that this reason is primary. Even according to what we explained in section 223, that the Rambam holds that both reasons are needed, and our reasoning here is that since the Gemara is in doubt, one cannot say that he decides definitively. Nevertheless, according to Torah law, he is certainly believed because it is a matter likely to be revealed. The reason of meticulousness is only a Rabbinic stringency, and therefore if he also says, "I buried him," there is no greater meticulousness than this. We do not know her meticulousness from his meticulousness, even though her meticulousness is due to the stringency we imposed on her in the end. However, in such a case where the witness was very meticulous, the Sages did not see fit to be stringent. Therefore, even without saying, "I buried him," if she remarried, she need not leave her second husband, because the question in the Gemara is a Rabbinic doubt. According to Torah law, he is believed in all cases because it is a matter likely to be revealed, and in a Rabbinic doubt we follow leniency. 

And so it is explicitly explained in the Jerusalem Talmud, where a case came before Rabbi with one witness in war, and he ruled similarly that she should not remarry, but if she did, she need not leave her second husband. And a collapse is considered like war.

And some of our rabbis hold that in the case of a single witness in wartime, even without burial, she may marry lechatchila (initially), because they compare it to water with a boundary where, according to their opinion, burial is not required as stated in Section 218 [Rashba and Raavad there]. However, the Rosh and the Tur agreed with the Rambam's opinion, because in water, it is not applicable to say "by conjecture," since one stands and sees all around him, but in war, it is applicable to say "by conjecture" [Rosh Chapter 15, Section 3]. And some say that it is not specifically "buried him," but even if he said he died or was killed, and I saw him afterwards and recognized him well by sight and saw that he died, he is believed, as if he said "I buried him" [Mordechai], and our teacher the Rema brought this opinion in Section 250. And some say that this opinion only permits in such a case for someone who did not see the killing [Chomat Shlomo, Section 163], comparing it to what is said in Section 220, distinguishing between someone who saw the drowning and someone who did not, and it is not conclusive [see Beit Shmuel, Section 154]. And all this is in the case of one witness, but with two witnesses, everyone agrees that burial is not required, because with two witnesses, it is not applicable to say "by conjecture." And even though the opinion of the Rif is that even with two witnesses "by conjecture" is applicable, nevertheless, many disagree with him, and so our teacher the Rema stated there. And regarding a Samaritan who reports and says he died in wartime, certainly it must be that he buried him, because otherwise, he might be speaking by conjecture. However, even in this case, there are those who are lenient, holding that "by conjecture" is only applicable to someone who intends to testify and permit, which is not the case with a Samaritan who does not intend anything [Gra, Section 156]. However, even in this case, there are those who say that the lenient ones only permit if he saw the killing [Chomat Shlomo], and it is difficult to rely on the lenient opinion without burial [there] unless combined with other leniencies.

And if she says he died in his bed – she is believed even if it was during a war. We do not say that if so, she should be believed when she says he died in war by a "migo" (a legal principle that if someone could have lied in a way that would benefit them more, we believe their less advantageous claim), because we can say that "migo" only applies when we suspect her of lying, and the "migo" is a sign that she is not lying. But in the context of war, we say she is not lying but rather speaking based on her assumption and is mistaken. How does the "migo" help in this case? [Tosafot, beginning of the chapter "Ha'isha Shalom"]. And even according to the Rambam, who also holds that if she says she buried him, she is not believed because we suspect her of lying, as stated in paragraph 230, nevertheless, this is not a good "migo" to say he died in his bed. Since it is known to everyone that there was a war, she fears that they will contradict her and say he died in the war and not in his bed [there].

And even if she said that he went to war, was struck, returned home, and died in his bed — she is also believed [Rashba there]. However, according to the Rambam, who holds that even if she buried him she is not believed, it seems that in this case, too, she is not believed [there]. Nevertheless, this is only according to the third reason we explained in section 230, that because of the power of imagination she lies, and it could be that in this case too her imagination misleads her. But according to the first reason that she lies, and according to the second reason that she might have buried someone else instead of her husband due to panic, it is obvious that in this case these reasons do not apply. And even according to the third reason, this is not exactly comparable to that case [Mareh HaTzov'ot subsection 177, and the commentator in the Jerusalem Talmud who proves this law from there, see there. It seems to me that he disagrees with the Babylonian Talmud as I wrote there, examine it carefully].

And our Master the Rema wrote that the same law applies when she says he died or was killed far from the war – she is believed, for it is only relevant to say "perhaps" when she says he died or was killed in the actual war. But if not in the war, even if he went there near the battlefield to plunder – she is believed, end quote. For those who are not standing in the battlefield are not killed; therefore, in a war of savages who, in their wickedness, kill even those who are merely accompanying and those who come near the battlefield, as occurred, unfortunately, in the decree of [the year] 5408 – there is no distinction among them, as anyone who was there is considered part of the war. And there are those who are uncertain about the ruling of our Master the Rema, questioning whether according to the Rambam, who does not accept the testimony even if she says "I buried him," this would also apply if she says he died or was killed far from the war. But in truth, it is not comparable, for in the war she is distressed, but far from the war she is not distressed, waits, and does not lie.

And know, from the words of our teacher, the Rema, we learn that even if she says he died naturally in war – she is not believed [there]. But there are those who disagree with this, since if she says he died not because of the war – she is believed [Yam Shel Shlomo], and it seems reasonable that she has a "migo" (a legal presumption) that if she wanted, she could have said he died in his bed, since there too he died naturally. However, there is no proof, because she is still anxious to flee from the place of war, and there is concern that she is speaking mistakenly, not having waited until he actually died. Nevertheless, if she buried him, it is possible that this would be effective in such a case even according to the Rambam [see Beit Shmuel, Siman 148].

There has not been a situation where a war occurred in the world that we were entirely unaware of, and she comes and says, "There was a war in such-and-such place, and my husband died in the war" – she should not remarry initially, but if she did remarry, she does not have to leave [her new husband]. There are those who say that if she remarried, she must leave [the new husband], but Maimonides ruled according to the first opinion. And even though in the Gemara this was an unresolved question, nevertheless, it is certain that from the Torah she is believed even in the case of war, as the concern of "perhaps it is similar" is only a rabbinic concern, and since in the Gemara it remains in doubt – it is a rabbinic doubt and thus lenient <small>[as is evident from the commentaries]</small>. And if she says, "I buried him" – there are those who say that in such a case, even according to Maimonides who prohibits [remarriage], if she says she buried him, she may remarry initially, and there are those who disagree with this <small>[see Beit Shmuel clause 150, and Marot HaTzovot clause 160]</small>. And if she says, "He died" without specification – if it is known that it was a time of war, we assume he likely died in the war and she is not permitted to remarry until she specifies that he died in his bed. But if it is not known to be a time of war, we assume she meant that he died in his bed <small>[Rashi 115]</small>.

And just as in times of war she is not believed even though there is peace between her and her husband, similarly if there is a quarrel between her and her husband, even though there is peace in the world – our Sages said that she is not believed to say "my husband has died" even when she says it over his bed. Two reasons have been given for this: the first – because we suspect her of lying due to her intense hatred and her intention to forbid herself to him <small>[Rashi 116]</small>, and thus it is impossible to permit her, as the primary reason she is believed to say her husband has died is because she would be meticulous in this matter so as not to forbid herself, but here, on the contrary, she intends to forbid herself to him. And even though she would also be forbidden to another man, it is worth it to her to be forbidden to the other in order to be forbidden to the first, as in the case of "Let me die with the Philistines" <small>[it seems to me]</small>. The second reason – because she says it out of assumption, and in any situation of danger that she saw, she does not pay attention to say perhaps he did not die and I should not remarry, because since she hates him, she is not so meticulous <small>[Rashi]</small>. And even if she says he died on his bed like any other person and she saw him die – we do not believe her in this, and it could be that he was in some danger and escaped from it <small>[it seems to me]</small>. And we rule stringently according to both reasons since the Talmud did not decisively rule according to any one opinion <small>[Rashba there]</small>. And this also appears to be the opinion of Maimonides, of blessed memory, who did not write any reason for this, and also because he did not differentiate between whether he started the quarrel or she started it, and in the Gemara there is a distinction in this regard: according to the opinion that she lies, it is only when she started the quarrel, as then her hatred for him is stronger, but if he started the quarrel and she loved him, she would not lie outright. However, regarding the assumption, we are concerned in all cases, as in a minor matter she would say it out of assumption, just like in times of war <small>[Tosafot]</small>. And so too, the Tur wrote that there is no distinction in this matter, see there. Maimonides did not mention this at all, which shows that he was concerned to be stringent according to both reasons <small>[and there is no need for what Kesef Mishneh wrote in the name of Ra'Em who interprets the opposite, and so too the Rosh wrote that we act stringently, see there]</small>.

And what is considered a quarrel? It is impossible to say that any general quarrel and disagreement is considered a quarrel for which she is not believed, for in most cases, a husband and wife argue from time to time, and yet their love remains strong. Moreover, the Sages have said [Yevamot 116b] that even if she says to her husband, "Divorce me," it means nothing, for all women say this when they are angry. So what is considered a quarrel? For example, if she says to her husband in his presence, "You divorced me in the presence of so-and-so," and we asked the witnesses and they said, "It never happened" [Gemara Yevamot], and since she was found to be contradicted by the witnesses, she can no longer be believed about anything. It is explained in the Talmud that only in such a case is she not believed to say that her husband died. However, if she says out of his presence, "My husband divorced me," and she is not believed by law, she is believed to say, "My husband died." Similarly, in our times, even if she says it in his presence, she is not believed because brazenness has increased in our times, as stated in section 17. However, if she says, "My husband died," she is believed as long as she is not contradicted by witnesses [Beit Shmuel, paragraph 240].

And there is a significant question to ask here: How can we say that when she is not contradicted, she is believed to say "my husband died," whereas we do not believe her regarding divorce? We suspect her of not being cautious about marrying when prohibited as a married woman and making her children from the second marriage mamzerim. So how can we believe her when she says her husband died? Rather, it must be said that in this case, she is afraid to lie. For regarding divorce, she can always cover her shame by denying it and saying, "You divorced me." But if she says "my husband died" and then he comes back alive, her shame will be revealed. Therefore, even when she is contradicted by witnesses regarding the divorce, we believe her about the death for this reason. However, even so, it is not comparable, because when she is contradicted by witnesses, her disgrace is revealed to everyone, and it is impossible to believe her at all. When she is not contradicted, even though we do not believe her, we also have not seen her falsehood explicitly, unlike when witnesses contradict her. Moreover, since it has been clarified that she hates him to the point that she was contradicted by witnesses, we estimate that she intends to prohibit herself to him in the manner of "let me die with the Philistines," as it says in section 238. Therefore, she is not concerned about her disgrace being revealed, and on the contrary, she wants to prohibit herself to him and there is no other way.

It is clear that in a dispute like this, she is not believed even if she says she buried him. Even according to those who rule that in the case of war she is believed when she says she buried him, this is only due to the concern of "inferred death," where in the case of burial there is no concern. However, in a dispute, where she intentionally lies as we have said, what benefit is there in her saying she buried him? For just as she lies openly about the death, so too she will lie about the burial. And it appears to me from the Talmudic discussion there that even according to the opinion that in the case of inferred death there is concern, this is not comparable to the concern of inferred death in war, where she is believed according to most authorities. The inference due to hatred is different [for otherwise, the Talmud would state this distinction, and this is the intention of Rashi in his commentary that "inferred death" in any danger is not precise, meaning even a slight danger is not like war].

And the Rambam wrote that even if one witness comes and testifies for her that her husband died, she should not remarry, lest she hired him. However, if she did remarry, she does not have to leave her new husband, since she has a witness, end quote. And they were astonished at him, questioning from where he derived this reason and suspecting the witness of false testimony. For if she is suspected, is all of Israel suspected? The Rambam's reasoning is that since she has already been established as a liar, and it was clarified that she hates him and intends to escape from him through various lies and schemes, as the witnesses contradicted her on the divorce, therefore now, when one comes and testifies for her that her husband died, which supports her escape from him according to the schemes she has made, there is concern that she hired and enticed him and gave him money to testify even in a matter that is likely to be revealed [Responsa of the Ra'avad in various places, beginning of Chapter 13]. And indeed, in the Gemara we also find a concern that she might hire witnesses [Gittin 67a], and although it is said there that they might speak but not act, in this case, where the permission is finalized through him, it is considered an action [Tosafot there] – this is with two witnesses, but with one witness, there is concern in such a case [and this clarifies what is in Ketubot 36b and Makkot 5a, see there].

However, they further challenged him: How does he derive a reason that is not found in the Gemara? After all, the sages of the Talmud [there] were uncertain about the credibility of a single witness in a quarrel, whether he is believed. If the reason a single witness is believed is because it is likely to be revealed, then he is also believed in this case. But if the reason is because she would be meticulous, then in this case she would not be meticulous. And this same language is also used regarding a single witness in a war.
