It seems to me that he was compelled to this explanation because the language of the Talmud, "she would not be meticulous," is difficult. What relevance does "not being meticulous" have here? On the contrary, it has become clear that she is trying to free herself from him through lies. And while in the case of war, "not being meticulous" is relevant because she might say things based on assumptions [and similarly in the case of Yevamah on 93b because she hates him], here where she is suspected of everything, what relevance does this language have? Therefore, he explains that the question of the Gemara is according to the opinion that the reason is based on assumptions. But according to the opinion that the reason is because she lies, the doubt is because she might bribe him. [And the Vilna Gaon in his commentary, section 147, wrote that this text should not be read at all; and according to what I have explained, there is no need for this forced interpretation, and consider this well.]

And the ruling that if she marries, she does not need to divorce, is because it is held that this concern is not from the Torah, for from the Torah, everyone is presumed to be of good standing. And it has already been explained that the fundamental reason for the Torah's allowance of a single witness is because it is likely to be revealed. Therefore, this doubt is rabbinic, and with rabbinic doubts, we are lenient. And thus, most of the authorities agree in practice that if she marries, she does not need to divorce. [And according to what I have written, all the difficulties raised by the early authorities are resolved.]

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in section 48 that if a woman's husband converted to Islam and left her as an agunah (a woman bound in marriage), it is treated as a case of dispute, and she is not believed to say "my husband died." However, some disagree with this, arguing that in the Talmud it is only said that she is not believed in cases of dispute where she wanted to unlawfully free herself from him and was contradicted by witnesses. But in this case, where her husband is wicked, she is nevertheless not suspected of intending to remarry unlawfully as a married woman. However, it is certainly true that even if we say this case is not similar to her claiming "he divorced me" and being contradicted, concerning her lying outright to remarry unlawfully, there is still a suspicion here since she hates him. This is agreed upon by several great authorities, and it is no less severe than a case of war where she says she buried him, which is subject to the dispute between the Rambam and the poskim regarding whether she is believed or not. Moreover, in a case with one witness testifying in a dispute like this that her husband died, the law will be like one witness in a case of war. Some say that with one witness, she may remarry initially. [And in the Beit Shmuel, section 141, what is quoted in the name of the Taz contains a textual error, for even if she remarries in a case of dispute from the Talmud, she does not have to leave her second husband.]

And one cannot say that in this case, the reasoning of precision does not apply at all, because the main concern is that she might forbid herself to him and to another. Here, even without this, she is forbidden to him since he has transformed. And even if she is not forbidden to him, certainly she would not be concerned about forbidding herself to him. We can say that she is precise so as not to forbid herself to the other man. It does not seem reasonable to say that the reasoning of precision only applies if she forbids herself to both the first and the second man. What kind of reasoning would that be? Several great authorities agreed that precision applies even if it only pertains to the second man [see Pischei Teshuva, section 168]. However, in practice, there is no significant difference in this matter, because on her own, she is certainly not believed. Only in the case of "I buried him" is there doubt, and one should not be lenient unless there is another reason for leniency [Mara'ot HaTzov'ot]. Regarding other types of disputes, even the most serious ones, it seems there is no room for doubt, and we must follow only what our Sages have stated, and this requires further investigation.

A woman who says, "My husband died under a collapsed building," is not believed, for a collapse is like a war, and she might be saying it based on an assumption. All the laws that were clarified regarding war apply here as well, whether she says, "I buried him" or "He died in his bed during the collapse," or if a single witness testifies that he died—it is all treated like war. Some say that even according to those who are lenient when she says "He died in his bed during the war," as mentioned in section 336, and consequently are also lenient in such a case during a collapse, nevertheless, if she says "He was killed" or "He fell from the roof and died," she is not believed. This is because although we do not suspect her of lying, since she did not stay there due to fear of the collapse and left him, she might be saying it based on an assumption and perhaps he did not die from that injury or fall. 

It seems to me that the collapse referred to by our Sages is when a collapse is common throughout the city, as was typical in ancient lands, where everyone flees the city. Therefore, it is like a war, and she might be saying it based on an assumption. But if it is the collapse of a single house, what relation does this have to war? After its collapse, they dig out all the people underneath it. Even though logically this seems correct, practically, it requires further deliberation.

[See Rashi, Bava Batra 115b, who wrote that "collapse" means the house fell on him or a storm wind caused all the houses in the city to fall, and in Taanit 19a, Rashi explained "collapse" as the walls and houses falling due to the wind, implying that "collapse" generally refers to the city, as is evident there.]

And similarly, if there was a situation of the release of snakes and scorpions in that place, and she said that a snake or scorpion bit him and he died – she is not believed, for this is also like war, since in her haste to escape she might say it based on her assumption, and we are concerned that perhaps she relies on the fact that most people who were bitten by this have died, so she assumes that he also died. All the laws of war apply to this situation as well. The "release of snakes" refers to when they were released among most people, but if one of them was bitten and his wife came and said that he died from a snake bite – she is believed, because she is not in a hurry to escape when the injury is not widespread. There are those who want to differentiate, regarding burial, between war and collapse or the release of snakes according to the Rambam, who holds that in war burial does not help, but in these situations, he would agree according to the first reason explained in paragraph 230, that in these situations this reason does not apply – but this is not so, for in these situations too, the panic is great just like in war, and there is no way to wait for burial according to the Rambam there [see Beit Shmuel section 156 and Ma'arot HaTzovot and Beit Meir, and investigate thoroughly].

During a plague – there are two opinions in the Gemara about whether it is like a war or not. The Rambam, of blessed memory, ruled leniently that it is not like a war and that she is believed. The Tur ruled that she is not believed. Some versions of the Rambam also say this, but in our text, it is clear that she is believed, and it is reasonable, as he states: "It is a well-known fact that during a plague, some live and some die. It is possible that strong young men might die from the plague while elderly sick people might survive. Therefore, we do not worry that she might have relied on the majority of those who died," end quote. Therefore, if she said she buried him, it seems that according to all opinions she is permitted to remarry, because according to the Rambam she is believed even without saying she buried him. According to the Tur, who holds that even in a war she is believed if she says she buried him. If she remarried, and similarly with one witness during a plague, it is a doubtful matter of law, and it appears that if she remarried, she does not have to leave him after the fact. We have already explained that the concern of "bed-dami" is only a rabbinic concern, and since there are two opinions in the Gemara and the legal authorities are divided on this matter, it is a rabbinic doubt, and we are lenient. Also, with one witness, it is possible to say that she may marry initially due to a double doubt – whether a plague is like a war, and even if it is like a war, there is a doubt about the law with one witness. However, some of the great authorities say that with an agunah (a woman whose husband is missing), one should not permit based on a double doubt, because many of the legal authorities hold that a double doubt does not permit in a case of a presumed prohibition, as stated in Yoreh De'ah 110. Also, even if we say that a double doubt is like a majority, because the first doubt makes it fifty-fifty and the second doubt makes it a majority, with an agunah, we do not follow a single majority and we are very stringent, like with water where there is no end, and similar cases. However, we have seen many of the great authorities of Israel who permit based on a double doubt with an agunah, and it appears that the reason is that there is no presumption of the prohibition of a married woman and no presumption of the husband's life, because the presumption is that a woman investigates and does not marry without certainty, which weakens these presumptions. The fact that the Sages were stringent even in a case of majority – this is in a case where the Sages said that in this matter they saw fit to be stringent because it is a common occurrence or for another reason known to them. But in matters where they did not explicitly say so, we do not have to be more stringent than in the entire Torah. Moreover, in a case where the prohibition is only rabbinic, like in the concern of "bed-dami," it seems clear that we can rely on a double doubt. Nevertheless, the practical ruling requires careful consideration.

However, regarding the primary law of a plague, it would seem logical to differentiate: in a standard plague, although many die, they are still buried properly, and people do not flee from them, so it is not similar to war. But there is a type of plague, may God save us, which is a contagious disease like it was in ancient times and is called the Black Death. People who exhibited symptoms of this disease were fled from, and there was fear of touching them or burying them by hand, but rather by dragging them. In this case, it is certainly like war. However, we do not find that the decisors made this distinction.

A woman who comes and says that her husband died of starvation is not believed, because she is speaking from conjecture. Since she knew he did not have anything to sustain himself, it became ingrained in her heart that he must have died. In fact, starvation is less severe than war, for in war, when she says he died in his bed, she is believed as we have said. But in the case of starvation, she is not believed even in such a case, because there is no basis to differentiate between dying in bed or not in bed; generally, one who dies of starvation does so in bed [Gra]. However, in contrast, it is lighter than war, because in war, even if she says she buried him, it is not accepted according to the Rambam as we have said. But in starvation, her testimony is accepted because she is not lying, and the urgency concerning burial is not comparable to that in war. Thirst is treated like hunger, so if she says he died of thirst, she is also not believed for the reasons explained. Regarding a single witness in a case of starvation, if he testifies that the husband died of starvation, it is not explicitly clear what the ruling is. It seems that the ruling should be the same as in war, as the witness would stand by his testimony until death because he is not in such a rush; perhaps the hunger did not affect him as much. Nevertheless, the permission for a single witness is due to the matter being likely to become known and due to her diligence, and she would not be diligent and would speak from estimation that he surely died. Therefore, she should not marry initially, but if she did marry, she should not be forced to divorce, just like in the case of war. If she says that he did not die from starvation because he had food to eat, but he had another illness and died or was killed, she is believed [Yesh Sh].

She said, "They smoked us out of the house," or "They smoked us out of the cave," – meaning that evildoers set the house or cave on fire, it filled with smoke, and I fled while he remained there and died – she is not believed. We say to her, just as a miracle was performed for you, perhaps a miracle was performed for him and he escaped from there [Gemara]. This does not mean a complete miracle, for we have already explained in section 209 that we do not mention miraculous events, but a kind of miracle where he found a place to escape. Even if we only know the event based on her word, we still do not permit her [to remarry]. This is not similar to the case of presuming someone dead from a war, which is a doubtful matter of law, for in that case she says he died, but here she explicitly speaks based on estimation [as explained in the Gemara]. 

If there was a fire and we see someone burned, and the woman cries out, "See, my husband has been burned" – she is believed even if he was burned to ashes such that no form is recognizable. This applies when no body part was found, and it is known that this body part is not from her husband’s body, so we attribute the ashes to her husband. However, if a body part is found that is known to belong to another body, she is not permitted, and we say that the one we saw burning is also another body, and her husband has fled [Gemara, see there in Rashi’s commentary, and this requires further study].

If she was in a place of a large fire, and many charred bodies were found such that it is impossible to recognize their forms, and we only know that the number of these bodies matches those who were in that place and are now missing – it is questionable whether their wives can be permitted based on the principle "found here and were here" or not [see Responsa of Nodah B'Yehudah, section 46], and in a pressing situation, one may permit.

She said, "Kutim or bandits attacked us, he was killed, and I was saved" – she is believed, even if it is known to us that they were attacked by them, for there is no suspicion of 'perhaps'. For specifically in a major war where spears and arrows are thrown at everyone standing there, she would fear for her life to stay there and would flee, and out of panic, she might say 'perhaps'. But in a bandit attack, which is a minor conflict where they only kill those they want to kill, she does not fear staying there, as she does not fear that they might kill her. For a woman carries her weapon with her, and the bandits do not kill her, either because they intend to fulfill their desires with her or because she is demure and does not stand against them, and they have mercy on her not to kill her. She stands until they kill him and does not say 'perhaps', and certainly would not lie.

It seems straightforward that she does not need to say "I buried him," and certainly, a witness regarding a small battle is believed without needing to say "I buried him," since even in a large battle, where she is not believed even if she says "I buried him" according to the Rambam, nevertheless, a witness would be a doubt. All the more so in a small battle where she is believed, certainly a single witness is believed. However, I have seen that some question this, and their reasoning is that although a woman is armed, the witness certainly fears standing there lest they also kill him, and therefore, why should we not be concerned that he might say it based on an assumption? Moreover, even for the woman herself, why should we not be concerned that she might imagine he is dead when he is not, similar to water, where we are concerned that one might imagine he is dead even though the witness does not fear standing there when he is taken out of the water, and nevertheless, we say this concern as stated in paragraph 217, and certainly here. However, from the straightforward understanding of the poskim, it seems to me that it is not comparable, for in water, it is the way of things that when one falls into the water, it may seem he is dead but in truth, the water merely confuses him. But in killing, it is clearly recognizable to everyone whether he is alive or dead, for as long as he has life in him, he will thrash about, and to be concerned that he is doing so to make the murderers think he is surely dead – this matter only applies as in times of decrees, G-d forbid, and there was a great war, but not in a small battle.

A fundamental principle in the release of agunot is that in any situation where the matter is not clearly permissible and requires the question of a scholar, even the greatest in Torah should not permit it on his own until two other great scholars of Israel agree with him. This has been the practice of all the great scholars throughout the generations, as is evident in all the responsa. Additionally, when a woman is permitted to remarry based on the testimony of one witness, a court of three is convened to release her, as stated in section 117; see there. This practice should not be changed.

A woman whose husband went to another country and [people] came and told her, "Your husband has died," and she married, and afterward her husband came back – the Sages penalized her in several ways, as will be explained. The main reason why the Sages believed a single witness is due to the presumption that she would carefully verify until she definitively knew that he had died. Since she did not verify carefully, the Sages penalized her. Nevertheless, even if she married based on the testimony of two witnesses and her husband returned, they also penalized her with all the penalties that will be explained. Although what could she have done, for while with one witness she should have verified the witness's words as stated, but with two witnesses, since the testimony of two witnesses establishes a matter in the entire Torah, why should we penalize her? Nevertheless, because of the great harm caused by marrying as a forbidden married woman and increasing illegitimate children in Israel, it is fitting for her to be penalized, so that all women will hear and be afraid. For after all, she is somewhat negligent since we see that the witnesses were false. Any woman connected to her husband should investigate thoroughly whether it is true that he has died or not. Even if she has not yet had relations with the second [husband], since she entered the wedding canopy with him, she is penalized. The same applies if she secluded herself with him after the betrothal. However, if she was betrothed and has not yet secluded herself with him, she is not penalized, as will be explained in detail with its reasoning, with God's help.

And what is the penalty? That she must leave both [husbands]. She is prohibited by Torah law from marrying the second one, and by Torah law she is permitted to the first one since she is considered coerced. Nevertheless, they penalized her that she must leave him and she needs a get (divorce document) from both. From the first one, she needs a get by Torah law, and from the second one due to the penalty. Additionally, we are concerned that people might say that the first husband divorced her and she married the second one lawfully, and now she is leaving him without a get. For this reason, she is rightly prohibited to the first one so that people do not say that he took back his divorcee after she married another. Therefore, if she did not marry the second but only got engaged, and the first one comes forward, she does not need a get from the second and she is permitted to return to the first. Since she has not yet committed a transgression, they did not penalize her. The concern that people might say the first one divorced her and the second married her also does not exist and, on the contrary, they will say that the engagement was a mistake. However, marriage will not be attributed to a mistake. If the second one who engaged her gave her a get, she is prohibited to the first one because people will say that the get was valid and she married the first one after she was divorced from him and engaged to another. There are those who disagree with this and this is also implied in the Mishnah. Similarly, if she secludes herself with the second one after the engagement, it is considered as if she married him. Also, if she engaged the second for the purpose of being a concubine, she is prohibited to the first one, for she is not lacking delivery to the chuppah (marriage canopy) since there is no chuppah for a concubine. Refer to what I have written in chapter 26 regarding whether it is permitted to marry a concubine. Additionally, if she engaged the second and did not marry or seclude herself with him, she is permitted to him if the first one dies or divorces her, and she is like any other divorced or widowed woman since she has not yet committed a transgression.

And furthermore, they penalized her such that she does not receive a Ketubah from either of them – she definitely does not receive from the second, and from the first it is a penalty. Even if the first husband takes her back unlawfully, she does not receive a Ketubah, and similarly, if the second husband takes her back unlawfully after she was divorced from the first, she does not receive a Ketubah. They also penalized her such that the fruits that both husbands consumed from her usufruct property do not need to be repaid, even though by law they are obligated. Since the husband receives the fruits in exchange for redeeming her and they are not obligated to redeem her because she is forbidden to them, nevertheless, they penalized her in this matter. Specifically, what the second husband consumed before the first returned is exempt from repayment because he thought she was his wife, but what he consumed after the first returned he must repay because he is like another man. The first husband, however, can continue to consume until he divorces her because she is his wife, even though he is not obligated to redeem her; nevertheless, they penalized her in this matter as well. Similarly, there is no need to repay what was worn out from her dowry property, even though a husband is usually obligated to repay, nevertheless, they penalized her in this matter and her legal status is like one who committed adultery under her husband as stated in Siman 115. This applies only to what is completely worn out, but what remains intact she takes, and some say she does not even take her existing worn-out items, but most authorities hold like the first opinion. For anything lost due to the penalty, seizure does not help, even if she seized without witnesses; nevertheless, if she admits, it is taken from her because the reason is due to the penalty. For anything that belongs to her, even if she seized with witnesses, it is not taken from her. Therefore, if she took a Ketubah or fruits from this one or that one, she must return them even if she took without witnesses, specifically what she took from the second after the first returned, but what she took before the first returned she does not need to return, since she took it lawfully because she did not yet know the first was alive. What we have written that fruits are taken from her, refers to sustenance she consumed from the second. If they are Kohanim and she died, neither is permitted to become impure for her, and neither is entitled to her found items or her earnings, nor can they annul her vows. If she is a Kohen's daughter, she is disqualified from Terumah; if she is a Levite's daughter, she is disqualified from receiving Maaser, even though Maaser Rishon is permitted to non-priests and a woman who committed adultery is permitted to Maaser, nevertheless, she was penalized in this matter and is also disqualified from marrying a Kohen forever. If she dies, her first husband inherits her because she is his complete wife, and if they die, the brothers of both perform Chalitzah for her if they died without children and are forbidden to perform Yibbum. The brother of the first performs Chalitzah due to Torah law and does not perform Yibbum due to the penalty, and the brother of the second is forbidden to perform Yibbum by Torah law and according to the law does not need to perform Chalitzah, but for appearance's sake, just as she needs a get from him.

The child from the second husband, conceived while still married to the first husband before he divorced her, is a mamzer (illegitimate child) according to Torah law. However, if she conceived from the second husband after the first husband divorced her or died, the child is a mamzer according to rabbinic law as a penalty. If the first husband had relations with her before the second husband divorced her or died, the child she would bear is also a mamzer according to rabbinic law as a penalty. Some say that the child from the first husband is always a mamzer according to rabbinic law, even if the relations occurred after the second husband divorced her or died. The primary opinion is the first one, as ruled by Rabbi Yosef Karo in Shulchan Aruch, section 56.

If her husband was abroad and they came and told her, "Your husband has died," and she remarried, and afterwards they told her that he was alive when she remarried and only now has died, the child she bore from him or conceived before he died is a mamzer (illegitimate) according to Torah law. However, any child she bears afterwards is not a mamzer, even according to rabbinic law. And although it was previously explained that such a child is a mamzer according to rabbinic law, this applies when the first husband has returned here. Since the Sages imposed a penalty that what she bears from him is considered a mamzer, therefore also what she bears from the second husband is considered a mamzer. But where the first husband died abroad and the issue of mamzerut does not apply to him, they did not impose the penalty regarding the second husband. However, some say that even in such a case, the child from the second husband is a mamzer according to rabbinic law. It appears that concerning other penalties that were explained, everyone agrees we impose the penalty on her, as if her husband had come here and the second husband divorces her and may not take her back forever.

And specifically, in the case of a woman whose husband went to a distant land, and she went and remarried mistakenly, they penalized her because she did not take care to find out whether he was alive or dead. But a married woman who remarried intentionally to another or committed adultery and bore a child and became pregnant by him after her first husband divorced her, even though she committed a sin, nevertheless, the child is not considered a mamzer (illegitimate) even by rabbinic law, for they are complete transgressors, and what sin has the child committed? But in a case where she did not intend to sin and stumbled, they rightly penalized her so that she would take care to thoroughly investigate whether the first husband was dead or not.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 58: A woman who was betrothed and made a mistake, thinking she was not betrothed and married another man – she must leave both this one and that one, and all these rules apply to her. However, if she was forced to marry or if the court mistakenly ruled and she married based on their ruling – she is considered coerced and is permitted to her first husband. And even though when she marries based on the testimony of two witnesses, she is also considered coerced and still penalized – it’s not the same, because there she was not forced to marry, but here she was forced to marry, and what difference does it make if it was coercion in relations or coercion in marriage? Moreover, with two witnesses she is also penalized so that she will be careful, as she is somewhat negligent as stated in section 256. Similarly, if the court mistakenly ruled – she is considered completely coerced because how could she be meticulous in the court's ruling? However, in the time of the Temple, she would have been obligated to bring a sacrifice according to the opinion that an individual acting on the court's ruling is obligated to bring a sacrifice, but she is not prohibited to her first husband because she is completely coerced. And even though marrying based on one witness is also considered like marrying based on the court’s ruling, and why is she prohibited to both? It is different there because the court's ruling based on one witness is because they assume she will be careful, and since she was not careful, there is a penalty, unlike other court rulings where there is no fault on her part, and there is proof for this from the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of the chapter "Ha'isha Rabba," see there. Nevertheless, there are those who disagree with this ruling, and it will be explained in section 31, with God’s help. [And with this, all that the Taz and the Bach wrote in section 172 is resolved, and the Rashba ruled based on reasoning as written in response section 10, see there, and also the Gra and the Beit Meir agreed with this, see there].

[The Law Regarding Whom Betrothal Takes Effect and Whom It Does Not, Containing Three Sections] There is no betrothal with forbidden relations (arayot), which includes those liable for karet (spiritual excision) and those liable for court-imposed death penalties; betrothal does not take effect with them. As it is written concerning the sister of a wife (Leviticus 18:18), "You shall not take a woman as a rival to her sister," meaning you shall have no acquisition with her. All forbidden relations are compared to each other, as it is written (Leviticus 18:29), "For whoever shall do any of all these abominations, the souls that do them shall be cut off." Thus, all arayot are compared to the sister of a wife: just as betrothal does not take effect with the sister of a wife, so too with all arayot [Kiddushin 67b]. Offspring from such unions are considered mamzerim (illegitimate), as mamzer status depends on the invalidity of betrothal, as stated in Section 4, Paragraph 13. However, with a menstruating woman (niddah), despite being liable for karet, betrothal does take effect. As it is written (Leviticus 15:24), "Her impurity shall be upon him," indicating that even at the time of her impurity, there is a state of being (existence) [there], and this state of being refers to betrothal that effectuates itself to him. Consequently, offspring from her are not mamzerim, as stated there.

However, with those who are liable for negative commandments or positive commandments, the kiddushin (betrothal) is effective, and it is considered a complete kiddushin even though they have committed a transgression and are obligated to divorce her. Nevertheless, the kiddushin is valid, and the children are not considered mamzerim (illegitimate), as it is written (Deuteronomy 21:15), "When a man has two wives, one beloved and the other hated," and is there hatred before the Almighty? Rather, it is referring to one who is hated in her marriage because she is from those liable for negative and positive commandments. The Torah states "when they are"—indicating that there is still an effective marriage (Yevamot 68a). Even in the case of negative commandments pertaining to priesthood, such as a widow to a High Priest or a divorced woman or a defiled woman to an ordinary priest, where the Torah increased commandments for priests, nonetheless, the kiddushin is effective as it is written (Leviticus 21:15), "He shall not profane his offspring" (Temurah 5a)—he causes them to be profaned but does not make them mamzerim. Since the offspring are not mamzerim, it follows that the kiddushin is effective, as these matters are interdependent, as stated. Therefore, we do not say in the case of negative commandments that the kiddushin is ineffective because any matter that the Torah says not to do, if done, is ineffective, since the Torah explicitly includes them (Yevamot 68a), except in the case of a yevama to the market, even though she is liable for negative commandments, the kiddushin is doubtful as stated in Siman 159. Similarly, with a non-Jewish woman and a maidservant, the kiddushin does not take effect because they are not suitable for kiddushin, and their offspring follow them as stated in Siman 4 and are not mamzerim. Certainly, this applies to rabbinic prohibitions such as secondary forbidden relationships and a chalutza (a woman released from levirate marriage) to a priest, where the kiddushin is effective, and all the more so, one who marries a woman in addition to his wife, even though he violated the enactment of Rabbeinu Gershom, the kiddushin is still effective. Know that wherever the kiddushin is not effective, a get (divorce) is not required if he betrothed her, except in the case of a married woman who was mistakenly married, thinking her husband was dead, and then the husband returned, she requires a get for reasons explained in Siman 17.

One might pose the following question: Since anyone who sanctifies (marries) does so with the consent of the Rabbis, as our Sages have mentioned in several places, and surely the Rabbis do not agree that one should sanctify through a prohibition and thereby annul the sanctification? The answer to this is that this reasoning can only be applied if the sanctification was entirely valid according to the will of the Sages, but afterward, there is a reason to annul it due to some cause, such as in the case of a claim of coercion in divorce at the beginning of tractate Ketubot, or the ineffectiveness of annulling a get (divorce document) not in the presence of the agent (Gittin 33), or the case of a get of a deathly ill person who should not be able to retract (ibid. 73), or even if the sanctification must be annulled immediately at the time of sanctification due to some reason, such as if he sanctified her against her will (Bava Batra 48), or in the case of a minor orphan who was sanctified and was not cohabited with when she matured, and another came and sanctified her (Yevamot 110), where in the essence of the sanctification there is no concern and they annul it for another reason. In this case, it is rightly said that anyone who sanctifies does so with the consent of the Rabbis, and the Rabbis annul the sanctification. However, in this case, where he sanctified initially in a prohibitive manner, whether by Torah law or rabbinic decree, and descended into sanctification initially not with the consent of the Rabbis, how can we say that he sanctified with the consent of the Rabbis? And even though he said "according to the law of Moses and Israel," it is certainly true that according to the law of Moses, sanctification is valid even with those who are liable for a prohibition (see Tosafot Bava Metzia 70a s.v. "tashich," and Taz Yoreh De'ah 117:1) (and see also Mordechai at the beginning of Kiddushin, see there).

[Execution Based on the Presumption of Forbidden Relations, containing six sections]
Someone who is presumed to have a familial relationship is judged based on this presumption, even if there is no clear evidence that this person is a relative. Floggings, strangulations, and stonings are carried out based on this presumption. How so? If it is presumed that she is his sister, daughter, or mother and he has relations with her in front of witnesses, he is flogged, burned, or stoned, even though there is no evidence that she is his sister, daughter, or mother other than this presumption. The Rambam writes in the first chapter of the Prohibitions of Forbidden Relations that the proof for this matter is from the Torah's judgment regarding one who curses or strikes his father, who shall be put to death. From where do we have clear evidence that this is his father if not by presumption? So too, other relatives are based on presumption. And in the Talmud [Chullin 11b], we derive from this verse that we follow the majority, for if not, perhaps he is not his father, but rather because most relations are with the husband. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud Kiddushin [Chapter 4, Halacha 10], it is derived from this verse for presumption, that is why they execute him, as it is clear this is his father. If it is only a presumption he is his father, and they execute, so too all who are presumed to be in forbidden relationships are executed. And it can be said that it is one matter, for this is a majority that comes from presumption. For when we say most relations are with the husband, there are no witnesses to this, but it is from presumption since they live as man and wife. And also, certainly, a son born before us with his father does not need presumption but rather the majority, that most relations are with the husband, so we do not worry that perhaps she conceived from another. But in the case of a son and his father who come before us from afar and live here with the presumption of father and son, in this case, the majority does not apply, only presumption. And the Torah that says, "he who strikes his father… shall surely be put to death" (Exodus 21:15) certainly refers to both a son born among us and a son with presumption [and this explains that in Sanhedrin 69a, and similarly written in Choshen Mishpat section 11, and see Beit Meir].

A presumption (chazaka) is a significant matter, for even the father, to whom the Torah has granted credibility regarding his children, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 277, and even to declare his son a mamzer (illegitimate), nonetheless, to remove him from his presumption, he is not believed, as stated in Siman 4, Se'if 41. Some say further that although he is believed to make his son a mamzer, this does not mean he is believed to say that his wife committed adultery with another man and that the child is not his; rather, it means that the child is his but was born from a prohibited relationship, making him a mamzer (Yam Shel Shlomo, Chapter 4 of Kiddushin, Siman 15, and similarly implied by Rashi there, 78). However, even according to those who say he is believed in all matters, nevertheless, against a presumption, he is not believed. And the Rambam, who wrote in Chapter 15 of Laws of Forbidden Relations, "A father who has established that this is his son and says 'this son of mine is a mamzer'—he is believed," it can also be said that he means to say that the child is his and a mamzer, as mentioned. And what is written afterward, that he is believed to say about the fetus in his wife's womb that it is not his and is a mamzer, this is because since the fetus has not yet been born, it has not been established as his son. And even if we say that his statement is taken literally and he is believed to remove the child from its presumption—this is from a presumption established by others. But if he himself has established the child as his son, he is not believed to remove him from this presumption, as stated there. And even in this case, the father is different, for the Torah has given him credibility, just as two witnesses can remove any matter from its presumption, for witnesses are certainly preferable to a presumption, so too is the father regarding his son.

And there was an incident with a woman who came to Jerusalem with a child on her shoulder, and she raised him with the presumption that he was her son. He subsequently engaged in relations with her, and they brought her to the court and stoned her. Therefore, if a man and a woman come from abroad, she says, "This is my husband," and he says, "This is my wife," if they are established in the city as husband and wife, they are killed if she committed adultery. The Rambam and the Tur wrote that it requires being established in the city for thirty days, for any presumption that is not based on an original strong presumption but rather on the nature of the matter itself is not valid for less than thirty days. More than thirty days, a person does not maintain a falsehood about something that is not as it appears, but up to thirty days a person can maintain a falsehood. Therefore, after thirty days, it is considered a clear matter without doubt. However, this only applies to others, but for themselves, they are believed immediately. For example, if both of them come and say they are husband and wife and she committed adultery – she is forbidden to him immediately, as they have made her a piece of forbidden matter for themselves. But if we have not seen them behave as husband and wife and only based on their words alone – an excuse is effective. If they give an excuse as to why they said so, we accept it if the excuse is good. But if we saw them behaving even for one day as husband and wife – then even an excuse is not effective.

However, if the woman, upon coming with the child carried on her shoulder, immediately states that this is not her child but that she took him to raise – this nullifies any presumption based on the child clinging to her, and the same applies in similar cases [Taz Yoreh De'ah 185]. And if a woman is presumed to be a niddah (menstruant) by her neighbors – her husband incurs lashes for relations with a niddah, as stated in Yoreh De'ah there. An excuse is effective for up to thirty days, but after thirty days it is not effective. However, if she wore her niddah clothes – an excuse is not effective even within thirty days, since she performed an action [Beit Shmuel and see Taz there]. In Yoreh De'ah 185:18 we explained that an excuse is always effective, see there.

Some of the great authorities have written that in such presumptions regarding lashes and prohibition, we follow such presumptions even without evidence to the presumption. However, concerning capital punishment by the court, we require evidence along with the presumption, for example, if he behaves with her as a man does with his wife and her child clings to her [Maharik chapter 87]. 

But the prominent later authorities have written that this does not seem to be the understanding of the decisors [Beit Shmuel and Beit Meir]. On the contrary, the Rambam wrote there regarding a woman who says she is married, she is not executed based on her statement alone until there are witnesses or a presumption. Hence, it is clear that she can be executed based on a presumption even if there is no evidence to support the presumption [Beit Meir]. However, one might say that a presumption after thirty days is considered like evidence.

Nevertheless, it appears to me that certainly, not all presumptions are equal. And indeed, concerning this presumption that the child clings to her, there is a dispute in the Talmud [Kiddushin 80a]. We hold that we stone based on such a presumption, but there is an opinion that it is not sufficient for stoning, yet it is sufficient for other matters [see Tosafot there]. 

And if we say that it suffices for stoning, then even a lesser presumption without evidence would be a distant dispute. Moreover, it seems there that the opinion which considers this presumption effective only does so when there is evidence, such as when the children cling to their mother. Indeed, the Jerusalem Talmud implies that it is effective even without evidence for stoning, but our Talmud does not hold this way. 

And since, according to the Jerusalem Talmud, it is effective even without evidence for stoning, certainly for us it is at least effective for lashes without evidence [see Maggid Mishneh, Laws of Prohibited Relations, chapter 20, halacha 10]. But for stoning, it is not effective without evidence. And what the Rambam wrote can also be understood to mean that there was some evidence, such as her behaving as a married woman and not as a single woman [and the proofs of Maharik there are clear from the distinction made by Rabbi Yehuda into two parts, see there].

And so too, there are cases where the death penalty is adjudicated based on a presumption. When two witnesses testify that someone had relations with a forbidden partner, they are not required to see the act of intercourse where the man inserts like a brush into a tube, but rather, once they see them engaged in a manner typical of those who engage in sexual intercourse – they are executed based on this observation, and we do not say, "Perhaps he did not have intercourse," because the presumption of this form is that he did have intercourse [Rambam, ibid.]. Even if the transgressors claim that they did not have intercourse, they are not believed, unless it is evident from the circumstances that they did not have intercourse, such as if immediately after lying upon her, they were separated, and similar instances [see Noda BiYehuda, section 23].

[Regarding Which Intercourse One is Liable for Forbidden Relations, and It Has 18 Sections]

One who has intercourse with any of the forbidden relations mentioned in the Torah, which are 18 in number as stated in Siman 15, Section 24, if done intentionally, he is liable for karet (spiritual excision), and if she also acts intentionally, she is also liable for karet, as it is written (Leviticus 18:29), "For whoever commits any of these abominations shall be cut off" etc. If they acted unintentionally – they are liable to bring a sin offering, and each one of them brings a separate offering. If one acted intentionally and the other unintentionally – the one who acted intentionally is liable for karet, and the one who acted unintentionally must bring a sin offering. There are some forbidden relations for which one is liable to the death penalty by the court in addition to the karet that applies to all forbidden relations, and these are detailed in Siman 15 there. However, the death penalty by the court is only applied with witnesses and prior warning, and even a Torah scholar requires prior warning even if he knows the law himself, as this is a decree of the Torah. This is what the Rambam wrote in Chapter 1, Law 3: "One is not executed or flogged until there is a warning, for the warning was given everywhere only to distinguish between intentional and unintentional acts." His intention is that there are many types of unintentional acts, such as not knowing that she is a forbidden relation, and such unintentionality can also occur with a Torah scholar. If one has intercourse five times with one forbidden relation, if it was in one session – he is liable for only one sin offering. If it was in five different unintentional acts, such as not knowing she is a forbidden relation and then having intercourse with her and finding out afterward and then forgetting again and having intercourse with her – he is liable for a sin offering for each and every intercourse. In cases liable for lashes, in such a scenario, if there were five warnings – he is liable for five sets of lashes. If there was only one warning – he is liable for only one set of lashes. If one has intercourse with five forbidden relations even though they are of the same kind, such as five of his sisters, even if it was in one session – he is liable for five sin offerings since the bodies are distinct, and similarly in cases liable for lashes.

The sexual prohibitions that do not entail the death penalty from the court, nonetheless, if there were witnesses and a warning, they are flogged, for all those liable for karet are flogged. One who has illicit relations with someone he is forbidden to by a negative commandment intentionally, with witnesses and a warning, is flogged. If it was done unintentionally, he is exempt from any punishment, for there is no offering for transgressing a negative commandment except in the case of a designated maidservant. If one has illicit relations with someone he is forbidden to by a positive commandment, he is not flogged, for there is no flogging for violating a positive commandment. However, prior to the act, they beat him until his soul departs so that he will not transgress the positive commandment. One who has illicit relations with one of the secondary prohibitions that we have enumerated there is beaten with disciplinary lashes. Similarly, in the case of a positive commandment, if the court sees fit to beat him with disciplinary lashes to distance people from transgressions, they have the authority to do so.

One who is coerced (an "anus") is exempt from everything, for the Torah exempts someone who is coerced, as it is written, "But to the girl you shall do nothing" (Deuteronomy 22:26). He is exempt from offering a sacrifice, from lashes, and certainly from the death penalty. And a woman whose initial intercourse was coerced, even if it ended with her consent, is exempt from everything, for her desire coerced her in this situation. Since the intercourse began under coercion, she was no longer able to refrain from deriving pleasure, for such is the nature of desire. In the end, she was still coerced, and what could she have done? Coercion applies only to a woman, but for a man, coercion does not apply. If he was coerced to engage in forbidden relations, if he did so with a flaccid organ, he is exempt, as will be explained. It is impossible to force him to perform with an erect organ, and if he does so, it is of his own volition. We do not say that he is coerced in this matter as we do for a woman when the initial act was coerced, for there the act of the transgression had already begun. But here, the beginning of the sin is of his own volition, unless he was ready to be with his wife and was coerced to be with the forbidden woman, in which case he is certainly exempt [Ra'avad]. Some say that in any case, since he was coerced, he is exempt in the laws of man [Hilchot Mishna], for this too is considered a type of coercion. However, this is only when there is a threat of death, but otherwise, he is liable. Rambam rules according to the first opinion. [See Tosafot Yevamot 53b, s.v. "they coerced him"].

In Siman 15, we explained all the illicit relationships, and a married woman is also considered an illicit relationship. Once a man betroths a woman, there are six women who become permanently forbidden to him, whether he marries her or divorces her, whether during his wife's lifetime or after her death. These are: her mother, her mother's mother, her father's mother, her daughter, her daughter's daughter, and her son's daughter. The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 2 of Issurei Bi'ah that if one has relations with any of these women during his wife's lifetime intentionally, with witnesses and warning, both of them are to be burned. If he has relations with them after his wife's death, they are liable to karet (spiritual excision) and not to a court-imposed death penalty, as it is stated, "They shall be burned with fire, both he and they" (Leviticus 20:14). What sin did his wife commit? Rather, the interpretation is that when both are alive, meaning his wife is also alive, and even if he divorced her, he and the forbidden relation are to be burned. But when she is not alive, there is no burning. And although this verse is written concerning his mother-in-law, the Rambam derived from it to include all forbidden relations that are prohibited through his wife. However, some of the early authorities disagree with him and hold that his mother-in-law after his wife's death is only generally forbidden and does not incur karet, while the other forbidden relations are subject to burning even after her death. There are those who are uncertain about this [see Maggid Mishneh, Halacha 7].

The sister of one's wife is forbidden to him during his wife's lifetime, even after he has divorced her. However, if his wife dies, he is permitted to marry her sister, as it is written: "And a woman to her sister you shall not take to be a rival, to uncover her nakedness while she is alive" (Leviticus 18:18). This applies whether she is her sister from her father or her mother, whether she is her sister from her father's marriage or from his illicit relations. For him, there is no prohibition except if he betroths a woman, then the seven forbidden relations to him are as explained. But if he was intimate with a woman (illicitly), her relatives, who are the seven women we have considered, are not forbidden to him. However, the sages prohibited him from taking any of them as long as the woman with whom he was intimate is alive, because she would come to visit her relatives, and he would be alone with her, becoming familiar with her, and might come to transgress by having intercourse with her. Moreover, even if he was merely rumored to have been with a woman, he should not marry any of her relatives until the woman rumored to be with him dies. If he married the relative of the woman he had illicit relations with, he does not have to divorce her. The Rambam wrote that if someone was rumored to have been with a forbidden woman or has a bad reputation with her, he should not live in the same alley or be seen in the same neighborhood as her. There was an incident where someone was gossiped about with his mother-in-law, and the sages gave him lashes of rebellion because he passed by her house. Some say this only applies to his mother-in-law because she is familiar with him due to her daughter and not with another forbidden relation.

One who has relations with a woman and her daughter in a promiscuous manner, or with a woman and her sister, and the like, it is as if he had relations with two unrelated women, because they do not become forbidden to each other except through marriage, not through promiscuity. Similarly, if his father, son, brother, or his father’s brother raped or seduced a woman, she is permitted to him, and he may marry her, as it is only said "wife" and here there is no marriage. Similarly, if his father or son married a woman, it is permitted for him to marry her daughter or mother [Rambam], and a person is permitted to marry the wife of his nephew if he died or divorced her, and a person may marry a woman and her niece or her nephew's daughter at the same time in a place where it is customary to marry two women [ibid.].

The male is considered fit for intercourse from the age of nine years and one day, and the female from the age of three years and one day. It is well known that a minor boy and girl are exempt from punishments. How long are they considered minors? The boy until he is thirteen years and one day, and the girl until she is twelve years and one day. Therefore, in all cases of prohibited relations, if both are adults, they are both liable to the death penalty or a sin offering. If both are minors, they are both exempt. If one is an adult and one is a minor, the adult is liable and the minor is exempt. Similarly, if one of them is deaf or mentally incompetent, they are treated as minors.

And a man who commits adultery with another man's wife (Leviticus 20:10), and we interpret "man" to exclude a minor [Kiddushin 19], for a minor who has relations with a married woman is exempt, and we do not say that since the woman is liable to death, if he is capable of intercourse, he should also be executed, as in the case of one who has relations with an animal [Tosafot there]. Likewise, they interpreted "another man's wife" to exclude the wife of a minor, and even though a minor cannot form a valid marriage and a verse is not needed for this, nevertheless, it is necessary in a case where a woman is waiting for levirate marriage to this minor, and he is already nine years and one day old, and I might say that her status is like that of a married woman, the verse informs us that she is not like a married woman because he was a minor. Similarly, one who has relations with the wife of a deaf-mute or an imbecile, their status is like that of the wife of a minor. And similarly, one who has relations with the wife of a tumtum or an androgynous, their status is like that of the wife of a minor. Similarly, a competent man who marries a deaf-mute or an imbecile, she is not a fully married woman, and one who has relations with them is exempt from death and from a sin-offering, and he is only given lashes of rebellion. Similarly, one who has relations with a woman who is doubtfully betrothed or doubtfully divorced is given lashes of rebellion. And a minor girl who was betrothed by her father to an adult man is a fully married woman, and one who has relations with her is liable to death when she is capable of intercourse. But if she was an orphan and was betrothed by herself or by her mother and relatives, this is only a rabbinic betrothal, and one who has relations with her is exempt from death, from a sin-offering, and he is only given lashes of rebellion.

It is stated, "And the daughter of any priest, if she profanes herself by playing the harlot, she profanes her father; she shall be burned with fire" (Leviticus 21:9). This does not refer to when she is unmarried, but rather when she is married. For a daughter of Israel who is married and commits adultery intentionally is liable to strangulation, but a daughter of a priest is liable to burning. However, a betrothed daughter of a priest has the same law as a betrothed daughter of Israel – stoning, since stoning is more severe than burning. It is impossible to say that the daughter of a priest is less severe than the daughter of Israel, and therefore, her law when married is burning [since burning] is more severe than strangulation. But the man who has relations with her does not have a changed law – he is liable to strangulation. For the daughter of a priest, there is no difference whether her husband is a priest or whether he is an Israelite, or even if her husband is a mamzer (a child born from certain forbidden relationships) or a Nathin (a descendant of the Gibeonites) or one of the other prohibited unions – her law is burning, as the Torah attributes it to her lineage. Therefore, the wife of a priest who commits adultery and she is the daughter of Israel – her law is not burning but strangulation.

One who has relations with a betrothed young woman who has not yet been married – both are subject to stoning, as explicitly stated in the Torah. However, if she was coerced, he is liable for stoning, and she is exempt. The obligation of stoning applies only when she is a young woman (na'arah) and not a mature woman (bogeret), a virgin and not one who has had relations, betrothed and not married, and still in her father's house. If she entered the wedding canopy, even if she has not yet had relations, or even if she has not entered the canopy but her father handed her over to the husband's agents who came to take her and she committed adultery on the way – her status is that of a married woman and not a betrothed one. One who has relations with a minor betrothed in her father's house – he is liable for stoning, and she is exempt. One who has relations with a mature betrothed woman in her father's house – both are subject to strangulation. If two men had relations with a betrothed young woman – the first is subject to stoning and the second to strangulation, since she is no longer a virgin. Therefore, if the first had relations with her in an unnatural manner such that she is still a virgin – the second is also subject to stoning. Note that in all forbidden relations, there is no distinction between natural and unnatural intercourse, as the scripture does not differentiate, except in the case of a designated maidservant, as will be explained. A betrothed young woman who was a convert or a freed maidservant, even if she converted or was freed when she was less than three years and one day old, her punishment is not stoning but strangulation, because the stoning of a betrothed young woman is written in the context of Israel, as it is written, "For she has committed a disgraceful act in Israel" (Deuteronomy 22:21).

Laws concerning defamation are explicitly stated in the Torah and elaborated in the Rambam, Chapter 3 of "Na'arah Betulah." According to the Rambam, if a man defames his wife by falsely accusing her of having engaged in sexual relations after she was betrothed but before they consummated the marriage, and it is found that she indeed committed adultery during this period, she is liable to be stoned. This is also the opinion of several of our authorities [see Tosafot Ketubot 45a in the name of Rashbam]. However, some of our authorities disagree and hold that she is not liable to be stoned unless it is found that she committed adultery while still in her father's house. If she committed adultery after leaving her father's house, she is to be punished by strangulation, like all other women.

In the case of a betrothed young woman who committed adultery, it is written that the stoning should take place at the gate of the city, and in the case of one who defames her falsely, it is written that she should be stoned at the entrance of her father's house. And so the Sages taught [Ketubot 44b]: If witnesses came to her husband's house and testified that she committed adultery while in her father's house, she is stoned at the entrance of her father's house, meaning, "See the offspring you have raised." And if witnesses came to her father's house and testified that she committed adultery while in her father's house, she is stoned at the gate of the city. However, the Rif and the Rambam have a different version in the latter case: If witnesses came to her father's house and testified that she committed adultery while in her husband's house, she is stoned at the gate of the city – for example, if she was in her husband's house between betrothal and marriage and committed adultery there and then returned to her father's house. But if she committed adultery in her father's house, she is stoned at the entrance of her father's house. And the statement "stoning at the gate of the city" refers to when she committed adultery in her husband's house. And this makes sense because the reason for stoning at the entrance of her father's house in the case of one who defames her falsely is so that people can see the offspring they have raised. Therefore, all the more so when witnesses came while she was in her father's house. According to the first opinion, it must be said that there is no need for evidence of the offspring they raised since everyone knows that she committed adultery in her father's house as she is still in his house. But in the case of one who defames her falsely, she is currently in her husband's house, and not everyone knows that she committed adultery in her father's house. Therefore, the Torah required her to be stoned at the entrance of her father's house so that everyone would know that the evil emerged from his house [and this is the intent of Rashi there in the commentary "See the offspring"]. And in the Tosefta, Chapter 10 of Sanhedrin: It is taught that a betrothed young woman who committed adultery is stoned at the entrance of her father's house – this is also explained according to the opinion of the Rambam. According to the first opinion, it must be said that witnesses came after she was at her husband's house [see Rashi there 45b in the commentary "at the entrance"].

Maimonides wrote: If witnesses came after she had matured or after her husband had relations with her, even though they testified that she committed adultery in her father's house when she was a young girl, she is stoned at the place of stoning, not at the entrance of her father's house. And they were astonished at him, for the entire matter of [the law concerning] defamation (motsi shem ra) pertains to when the husband had relations with her, as it is written, "I approached her and did not find evidence of her virginity" (Deuteronomy 22:14). And Maimonides himself wrote this in Chapter 3 of [the laws concerning] a young girl, so her stoning should be at the entrance of her father's house. It is possible that his intention is when the witnesses came without [the husband] defaming her. Or it is possible that his intention was that he only had relations with her the first time, so she is now considered a fully married woman. Therefore, even though her punishment has not changed to strangulation since she committed adultery previously, nevertheless, the entrance of her father's house is no longer relevant, and it is similar to a mature woman who has completely left her father's authority. [And this is understood from what is said there in the Mishnah 45, that after she matured, she and her conspirators are taken to the place of stoning, and the usual place of stoning is not at the entrance of her father's house. From this, he deduced regarding a fully married woman, as mentioned.]

And similarly, if her conception was not in holiness, even though her birth was in holiness, she is never stoned at the entrance of her father's house but rather at the entrance of the city gate, for she has no father. And likewise, anyone whose commandment is to be stoned at the entrance of the city gate, if the majority of the city are gentiles, they stone her not far from the entrance of the court, [see Tosafot there, s.v. "at the entrance of the court"]. And similarly, anyone whose commandment is to be stoned at the entrance of her father's house, and she has no father, or he has no house, they stone her at the entrance of the city's or the court's place of stoning, for the term "entrance of her father's house" is said as a mitzvah and not as a necessity. And even according to the one who holds that we need to follow the verse as it is written [Sanhedrin 45.], nevertheless here the verse revealed to include one whose conception was not in holiness, and this also means she has no father, thus it is not a necessity [Tosafot there 44., s.v. "there is no"].

It is written in Parashat Kedoshim (Leviticus 19:21), "And if a man lies carnally with a woman, and she is a bondmaid designated for another man, but she has not been redeemed, nor has her freedom been given to her, there shall be an inquiry; they shall not be put to death, because she was not free. And he shall bring his guilt offering..." etc. The tradition explains that this refers to a woman who is half-bondmaid and half-free, betrothed to a Hebrew servant. As it says, "they shall not be put to death, because she was not free"—if she were fully freed, they would be liable to death because she would be considered a fully married woman.

This case differs from all other prohibited relations in the Torah, where both the male and female offenders are equally liable. In this case, she is liable to lashes, as it says, "there shall be an inquiry," which implies examination, since they would examine a person to determine if they are fit to receive lashes or not. He, on the other hand, brings a sacrifice even if he acted intentionally, unlike other prohibited relations where no sacrifice is brought for intentional actions.

If he has relations with her multiple times, whether intentionally or unintentionally, he brings only one guilt offering. She, however, is liable to lashes for each act of intentional relations. But if he has relations with five different designated bondmaids even unintentionally and in one period of forgetfulness, he is liable to bring a guilt offering for each one, because they are considered separate individuals.

This case also differs in that for other prohibited relations, partial intercourse is considered as complete intercourse, but here there is liability only for complete intercourse, as it says "carnally," meaning intercourse capable of insemination. For this reason, there is no liability here for unnatural intercourse, unlike other prohibited relations.

Additionally, this case is unique in that the matter depends solely on her. The Sages taught (Kritot 11a): When the woman receives lashes, the man brings a sacrifice; if the woman does not receive lashes, the man does not bring a sacrifice. Therefore, if she acted unintentionally, was coerced, or is a minor not liable to lashes, he is not liable to bring a sacrifice. Her liability only exists when she is already a known bondmaid.

All these interpretations were derived by the Sages from the verses, as noted there. Hence, according to Maimonides in Chapter 3 of Laws of Prohibited Relations, if she is liable to lashes, he is liable to bring a sacrifice, even if he has not yet reached the age of maturity, as long as he is nine years and one day old, fit for intercourse. Although in all other cases a minor does not bring a sacrifice, here it is different because the Torah made it dependent on her.

There are those who disagree with this. Similarly, Maimonides in Chapter 8 of Laws of Theft, Law 11, states that a minor brings a sacrifice, explaining that it is impossible for his case to be without a sacrifice. We have explained this, with God's help, in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 367, Se'if 25, clarifying that if the minor desires atonement, he brings a sacrifice, but he is not forced to do so.

Maimonides wrote in the first chapter of "The Laws of Forbidden Relations": "The insertion of only the tip of the glans is called 'me'ara' (partial penetration), as it is said, 'He has exposed her source' (Leviticus 20:18), and the insertion of the entire organ is called 'gemar' (complete penetration). In all prohibited relations, whether one performs 'me'ara' or 'gemar', even if no semen is emitted and even if he withdraws without completing the act, once he has inserted the tip of the glans, both parties are liable to the death penalty by the court, or karet (spiritual excision), or lashes, or disciplinary lashes. Whether one engages in relations in the natural manner or in an unnatural manner, once he performs 'me'ara', both parties are liable to death, karet, lashes, or disciplinary lashes, whether they were lying down or standing. Liability is incurred upon the insertion of the glans. End of quote."

However, the insertion up to the glans is merely flesh and not the organ itself, as written in Siman 5, and this does not constitute intercourse. Even according to what is written there, that the lower part of the organ is considered the glans, liability is only for inserting the upper part of the glans [Beit Shmuel]. Some say that in truth, the insertion of the glans is called the tip of the organ [Taz], but in any case, regarding lashes, one is liable even in this manner [Beit Shmuel]. It is possible that to prohibit a woman to her husband, she would be prohibited in this manner even if there were no witnesses to the act of infidelity [see Chelkat Mechokek and Beit Shmuel]. However, from the language of Rabbi Moshe Isserles, who wrote, "A grown woman who was approached by a minor less than nine years old is not liable to the death penalty because of him, and it seems to me that she is also not prohibited to her husband," end of quote, it does not seem so. The insertion of the glans is not better than the intercourse of a minor, and the matter requires further investigation.

Anyone who engages in forbidden intercourse without an erection, but rather with a flaccid member, like the member of the deceased, such as the sick or someone born that way, such as a eunuch, even if he inserts the member with his hand—he is not liable for karet (excision) or lashes, and certainly not for death, because this is not considered intercourse. However, he disqualifies himself from partaking of terumah (priestly offerings), and the court administers disciplinary lashes to both of them [Rambam]. To her husband, she is forbidden in such a case, as stated in Siman 178 [Beit Shmuel]. 

One who has intercourse with a deceased woman is exempt. However, one who has intercourse with a sick woman, even if she is in the throes of death or is a terminally ill person whose majority of years have passed, if she is still alive, he is liable for her intercourse. Our sages said that one who engages in forbidden relations intentionally is liable because he derives pleasure [Sanhedrin 62a]. 

One is considered to be engaged in this if he did not intend the forbidden intercourse, such as if he intended his wife and the forbidden woman happened to meet him, or if he did not intend intercourse at all and he had intercourse. This liability is for a sin offering in cases of forbidden relations, but death or lashes do not apply in such cases, as it is considered a complete inadvertent act.

We have already explained that a female who is three years and one day old is suitable for intercourse, and one who has intercourse with her when she is a forbidden relation is liable for death, lashes, or a sin offering. But if she is less than three years old, her intercourse is not considered intercourse at all, and her virginity returns. More than this is said in the Jerusalem Talmud, first chapter of Ketubot: if she was three years and one day old and had intercourse, her virginity does not return. But if the court decided to add a leap year and it turns out she is not yet three, her virginity returns, and they derive this from the verse “I will cry unto God Most High; unto God that performeth all things for me” (Psalms 57:3). 

If she is less than three years old, her intercourse is nothing, for even if her father betroths her to a priest, she is permitted to him. But if she is more than three, she is forbidden to a priest and permitted to an Israelite even if she engaged in licentiousness willingly, for the seduction of a minor is considered coercion by most decisors [Beit Shmuel]. 

There is no distinction in forbidden relations between someone awake and someone asleep, therefore, if one was awake and the other asleep—the one awake is liable and the one asleep is exempt. One who has intercourse with a deaf-mute or an imbecile is liable, for they are suitable for intercourse like a minor older than three years and one day. But if both were minors or deaf-mutes and imbeciles—they are exempt. Nevertheless, they are beaten so they do not become accustomed to transgressions, as mentioned in Choshen Mishpat Siman 349 regarding theft.

The Sages taught in the Sifra on the verse: "You shall not approach to uncover nakedness" (Leviticus 18:6) – This teaches only that one should not uncover, but from where do we derive that one should not approach? The verse states: "You shall not approach a woman during her menstrual impurity" (Leviticus 18:19). This teaches only about a menstruant, but from where do we learn about all forbidden relations? The verse states: "You shall not approach to uncover nakedness." The Torah prohibits any form of closeness with forbidden relations, such as hugging and kissing, and certainly deriving pleasure from physical closeness or contact through limbs. If one does so with those liable to karet (excision), Rambam writes in Chapter 21 of Laws of Forbidden Relations that one receives lashes by Torah law, as it is stated, "You shall not follow the practices of the abominations," and it is stated, "You shall not approach to uncover nakedness" – meaning, you shall not approach actions that lead to the uncovering of nakedness. Some say one is not liable for lashes. One who performs any of these actions is considered suspect regarding forbidden relations and is disqualified from giving testimony concerning a woman. Likewise, it is forbidden for a man to rub himself against another man lustfully, and similarly for a woman with another woman. Thus, the Sages said (Shabbat 65a): women who engage in sexual relations with each other are unfit for marriage into the priesthood, and this is the practice of the land of Egypt, about which it is said, "Like the practice of the land of Egypt... you shall not do" (Leviticus 18:3), as this was their depraved custom. It is proper to give them disciplinary lashes since they engaged in a forbidden act. A man should be vigilant with his wife, sons, and daughters concerning such actions and should prevent women known to him to be accustomed to such behavior from entering his home. However, we hold that they are not disqualified from marriage into the priesthood because of this (Yevamot 76a).

[To distance oneself greatly from illicit relations, containing ten sections]

After the section on illicit relations, it is written: "Speak to the entire assembly of the children of Israel and say to them: You shall be holy" (Leviticus 19:2). Wherever you find a boundary against illicit relations, you find a boundary of holiness. The Holy One, blessed be He, commanded all of Israel, from the great to the small, to distance themselves greatly from illicit relations and to erect boundaries and safeguards around them. Because a person's soul desires illicit relations, many boundaries are necessary. Therefore, a person must distance themselves greatly from women. It is forbidden to wink at them with one's hands or feet, to signal to them with one's eyes, or to think about them. Concerning this, it is said: "And you shall not wander after your hearts and after your eyes, after which you stray" (Numbers 15:39). The eyes and the heart are two agents of sin. King David, peace be upon him, prayed about this: "Incline my heart to Your testimonies... Turn my eyes away from seeing vanity." It is forbidden to speak to them for the sake of desire or to jest with them, to treat them frivolously, or to gaze at their beauty. As King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 5:2-4): "For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, and her mouth is smoother than oil. But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a double-edged sword. Her feet go down to death; her steps lead straight to the grave." Even to smell the perfumes on them or on their garments is forbidden. It is forbidden to look at women who are engaged in washing clothes because their legs are exposed. If there is another way, one should not pass by the washing place. If there is no other way, one should close one's eyes to avoid looking at them. Concerning this, it is said (Isaiah 33:15): "And he who shuts his eyes from seeing evil" (Bava Batra 57).

It is forbidden to look at the colorful clothing of a strange woman if one recognizes her, even if the clothing is not on her, lest one come to have improper thoughts about her. If one encounters a woman in the marketplace or in the street, it is forbidden to walk behind her; rather, one should run and move to the side or go ahead of her so she will be behind him. Thus, the Sages said: "Better to walk behind a lion than behind a woman" (Berachot 61a). In places where the streets are narrow and it is impossible to move aside, one should force oneself and close one's eyes as much as possible. Someone who walks behind a woman in a river has no share in the World to Come (ibid.). One who hands money to a woman from his hand to her hand with the intention of looking at her, even if he has Torah and good deeds to his credit, will not be cleansed from the judgment of Gehinnom, as it is said (Proverbs 11:21), "Hand to hand, the evil person will not be cleansed" (ibid.).
