One should not pass by the entrance of a prostitute, even at a distance of four cubits, and should not say, "I will pass and subdue my inclination," for there is no guardian against the evil inclination. And one who looks even at the small finger of a woman with the intention of deriving pleasure from it – it is as if he looks at her nakedness. And it is forbidden to do anything that brings oneself into suspicion, and concerning this it is said, "Remove from you a deceitful mouth, and perverse lips put far from you" (Proverbs 4:24), "Keep your way far from her, and do not go near the door of her house" (Proverbs 5:8).

And it is forbidden to hear the voice of a woman singing who is not his wife, or to see her hair or parts of her body that are usually covered, and one who intends to do any of these things – they lash him with a disciplinary lash. And during the recitation of the Shema and prayer, it is forbidden even to hear the voice of his wife singing or to see her hair [Beit Shmuel], but it is permitted to hear the regular speaking voice of any woman [ibid.]. And if one is suspected regarding a particular woman – they warn him not to pass by the entrance of her house, and if he does so, they lash him [Chokhmat Adam]. And it is obvious that for other forms of closeness they lash him, and see there in Siman 22:3.

The daughters of Israel should not go with uncovered heads in the marketplace, whether they are single, such as widows and divorcees, or married women. And going with an uncovered head in the public domain is forbidden by the Torah, as it is written regarding a sotah, "and he shall uncover the woman's head" (Numbers 5:18) – implying that she does not go thus. And this will be further explained in Siman 115. Similarly, a virgin who has been intimate or betrothed but not yet married – some say she should cover her head, and some say she does not need to.

When a man needs to marry a woman, he is permitted to look at her to examine if she is beautiful so he may marry her, whether she is a virgin, widow, or divorced. Moreover, it is appropriate to do so, as it is forbidden to betroth a woman without seeing her first. Nevertheless, he should not look at her excessively in an immodest manner, as Job said (Job 31:1), "I made a covenant with my eyes; how then could I gaze at a virgin?" This is what the Sages said regarding a Torah scholar who goes to betroth a woman, that he should take an unlearned man with him. The reason is not that the Torah scholar is forbidden to see her, for if that were so, how could it be permitted for the unlearned man? Rather, the intention is so that she is not switched for another woman, as the Torah scholar might not be familiar enough to recognize her even though he saw her once, but the unlearned man would recognize if they switched her for another.

It is also permissible for a man to look at his wife even though she is a niddah (menstruant) and she is currently forbidden to him, and even though he derives pleasure from looking at her, since she will be permitted to him after some time, he will not come to sin. Therefore, our Sages permitted a niddah to adorn herself so that she would not become repulsive to her husband. However, he should not joke or act frivolously with her, and looking at her in a place of vulnerability is forbidden. If he transgresses this, he will have children who are not respectable. Similarly, it is forbidden to look at the covered parts of her body during her niddah days, as it says in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 195.

It is forbidden to make use of a woman at all, whether she is an adult or a minor, a maidservant or a freed woman, lest it lead to sinful thoughts [Rambam], and also to avoid habituating them to being among men [Rashi, Kiddushin 81a]. What kind of use is intended? Washing his face, hands, and feet—even pouring water for him to wash his face, hands, and feet—is forbidden, even if she does not touch him. Making his bed in his presence and pouring a cup of wine—any act that a wife does for her husband as a form of closeness is forbidden for another woman to do for him. This applies when it is done not in the manner of service, but in the manner of service, it seems there is no prohibition [it appears to me]. However, washing his face, hands, and feet is certainly forbidden in any manner, as it is considered excessive closeness. Some say that eating with him from the same dish is also forbidden, and this seems logical, as there is no greater form of closeness than this. Although there are those who are lenient regarding eating or handing something from his hand to her hand, this is only prohibited with his wife when she is a niddah, yet those who fear the word of God should distance themselves from such acts. However, this prohibition does not apply to his daughter or sister, as this does not constitute closeness of mind, for it is the way of the world and there is no concern of corruption from them. Some say the prohibition only applies in a place of seclusion, but in a place where many people are present, there is no prohibition. For this reason, some have the custom of being washed by maidservants in a bathhouse. Our master the Beit Yosef wrote that this is forbidden to even consider, and heaven forbid for an Israelite man to be washed by them. Some errant student must have written this. Some say that as long as it is not done in a manner of affection and only with the intention of a mitzvah, such as dancing with the bride, it is permitted. However, a person who guards his soul should avoid this, as there is a risk of coming to sinful thoughts, and it is a mitzvah that comes through sin. Some say that even with his wife, it is not proper to engage in excessive affection in public, such as examining her head and similar acts, as nothing is more beautiful than modesty. The general principle is that one who directs his ways and paths will never fail, but one who does not take it to heart will fall into the trap of the evil inclination, for it is stronger than him.

One should not inquire after a woman's welfare at all, even through a messenger, and even through her husband it is forbidden to send her greetings of peace. However, it is permitted to ask her husband how she is doing. The reason for not inquiring after a woman's welfare is that perhaps through asking after her welfare, even through a messenger, they might become accustomed to one another and develop affection [Rashi there]. According to this, the prohibition only applies to inquiring after welfare, which involves endearment and affection, but to say to her "Good morning" or similar seems to be permitted. To ask someone else how a particular woman is doing, some say it is only permitted through her husband and not through another [Chomat Shlomo], and some permit it [Beit Chadash]. To ask a woman about her husband's welfare is permitted [Maharsha Bava Metzia 87], though some wish to forbid it due to the concept of "a woman's voice is nakedness," but this does not seem correct, for general conversation is not forbidden with women, only a pleasant voice that gives enjoyment to the listener [there]. Writing in a letter "Send my regards to your wife" or "Tell your wife I send my regards" is forbidden, as this constitutes inquiring after her welfare through her husband, but to ask about her welfare in a letter is permitted, as one is asking her husband how she is. With one's daughter, daughter-in-law, and sister, it seems there is no prohibition at all in inquiring after their welfare, as there is no element of affection, since it is customary for a father to inquire after his offspring's welfare, and it is his duty, and similarly a brother to his sister. The fundamental principles depend entirely on one's perspective and fear of Heaven, and if one’s inclination is subdued and he has no improper thoughts at all, there is no concern in inquiring after welfare [Ritva there]. Therefore, we find that Elisha said to his servant, "Run now to meet her and say to her, 'Are you well?'" (II Kings 4:26), but from there no proof can be brought, as everything was done by divine instruction for he was a prophet [and it requires further study from Bava Metzia 87, except that it must be said that we learn from what is written in the Torah, and so also from Elisha there is proof].

One should not be surprised by the custom practiced in all Jewish communities when guests come to the host's house, and the host's wife honors them, feeds them, gives them drinks, and pours cups for them. There is no prohibition against this, and it is not considered improper use of a woman. Not only if the host is reclining with them, as she is serving before him, but even if he is not reclining with them, since she is not serving in a manner of closeness but rather out of hospitality and because all household needs fall upon her, there is no prohibition in this matter. Similarly, in an inn, when the innkeeper's wife pours cups for the guests, it is not a manner of closeness but rather of service.

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote [there]: One who embraces one of the forbidden relations for whom a person's heart does not feel guilt, or kisses one of them, such as his older sister or his maternal aunt and the like, even though there is no desire or pleasure at all, this is very disgraceful and is forbidden, and it is a foolish act. For one should not come close to any forbidden relation, whether they are an adult or a minor, except for a mother with her son and a father with his daughter. How so? A father is permitted to embrace his daughter and kiss her, and she may sleep with him in close physical contact, and similarly, a mother with her son, as long as they are minors. When they grow up and the son becomes an adult and the daughter becomes an adult, until her breasts have developed and her hair has grown, he should sleep in his garment and she in her garment. And if the daughter is embarrassed to stand naked before her father or if she is married, and similarly if the mother is ashamed to stand naked before her son, even if they are still minors, once they reach the stage of embarrassment, they should not sleep with them except in their garments. End quote. And our master, the Beit Yosef, copied this in section 7. The Tur wrote regarding the age of growing up: when the daughter is 11 years old and the son is 12 years old. However, if the breasts have developed before this time, it is prohibited even before this time [Maggid Mishneh]. Specifically, sleeping in close physical contact is prohibited, but embracing and kissing are permitted [Perisha]. However, when she is betrothed, it is forbidden even if she is completely a minor. Some say that the status of a granddaughter is like that of a daughter [Bach], and the same is true for a younger sister who is three years old [Maggid Mishneh], and all the more so for a son's daughter [see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 14]. If one comes to his son's house and his daughter-in-law's or to his son-in-law's and daughter's house and shows affection and esteem to their sons and daughters, and even takes them in his lap, with the intention of doing so for the sake of Heaven to bring joy to their parents, there is no prohibition in this, and thus the great sages practiced [end of Kiddushin]. The great principle stated by the Sages there is that everything should be for the sake of Heaven [see there in Tosafot what they wrote that we rely on this, meaning in a case related to the sake of Heaven, like the act of Rav Chisda, and similarly as mentioned in section 9 and the like, but not in another context].

[Laws of Prohibited Seclusion, containing 18 sections]
It is forbidden to seclude oneself with a forbidden relation, whether she is old or young, as this can lead to uncovering nakedness—except for a mother with her son and a father with his daughter, for desire does not dominate them as it does with other forbidden relations [Sanhedrin 103b], and with these one is permitted to live permanently. A brother with his sister is permitted to seclude themselves temporarily, but they are not permitted to live together permanently [Choshen Mishpat]. A husband with his wife who is a niddah is permitted to be together, since he will have permission with her after some time, and his inclination does not dominate him as much. The Torah testifies to this in the verse "enclosed in lilies" (Song of Songs 7:3) – that even when enclosed in lilies, no breaches will be made in them [Sanhedrin 37]. And as soon as she tells her husband, "I have seen blood like a red lily," he immediately separates from her [Tosafot]. A groom whose bride has become a niddah before he has consummated the marriage is forbidden to seclude himself with her, whether she is a virgin, a widow, or a divorcee; rather, she sleeps among the women and he sleeps among the men, because his desire is still strong since he has not yet been with her. Therefore, if he had consummated the marriage and she subsequently became impure, it is permitted to seclude himself with her, and this law is detailed in Yoreh De'ah, section 192. A single woman who is a niddah is considered a forbidden relation like any other forbidden relations.

The prohibition of seclusion is from the Torah, and thus our sages expounded [Kiddushin 80b] "If your brother, the son of your mother, or your son, or your daughter, or the wife of your bosom, or your friend who is as your own soul, entices you secretly, saying..." (Deuteronomy 13:7) to teach that a son may be secluded with his mother but it is forbidden to be secluded with any of the forbidden relatives in the Torah. To explain: Since it is written "your brother, the son of your mother, or your son, or your daughter, or the wife of your bosom," and it did not also write "your brother or your sister," rather because the enticement is in secret as it is written, and all these can be in secret since a son can be secluded with his mother, a father with his daughter, and a man with his wife, but not a brother with his sister [Pnei Yehoshua]. And it is also clarified in the Jerusalem Talmud there – "your mother in secret, your daughter in secret," a person may be secluded with his mother and reside with her, with his daughter and reside with her, with his sister but not reside with her, but occasionally it is permitted as it is written [see Beit Shmuel], and the prohibition also applies to those liable for negative commandments [there]. And one who is stringent regarding the seclusion with his sister – upon him shall come a blessing [Chesed le-Avraham], and the Rambam did not bring this even though it is explicit in the Gemara.

When the incident of Amnon and Tamar occurred, David and his court decreed a prohibition on seclusion with an unmarried woman, even if she is young and has not yet menstruated. For if she has menstruated, she is considered a forbidden relationship due to her menstrual impurity, as mentioned. Even though she is not a forbidden relation (erva), she falls under the category of seclusion with forbidden relationships. This does not imply that before this decree, complete seclusion was permissible, for it is obvious that such behavior leads to transgression. Even dancing together is prohibited, as it is written, "Young men and also maidens, old men with children" (Psalms 148:12), and it does not say "young men with maidens," which implies that it is entirely forbidden for a young man and a maiden to dance together. Similarly, at the end of Judges (21:20-21), it is written, "And they commanded the children of Benjamin, saying: Go and lie in wait in the vineyards. And you shall watch, and behold, if the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, then come out of the vineyards and catch you each his wife," etc. Why did they not command them to join the dances? Rather, it is certainly a complete prohibition and they did not allow the daughters of Shiloh to mix with them; therefore, they commanded them to hide in the vineyards. However, they decreed even temporary seclusion, similar to forbidden relationships. This is what Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch wrote, that it is included in the seclusion of forbidden relationships, meaning that even temporary seclusion is prohibited. As for Ruth secluding herself with Boaz, it was because she wanted him to marry her, as indeed happened.

Shammai and Hillel decreed against seclusion with a non-Jewish woman, even temporary seclusion, similar to forbidden relationships. Therefore, anyone who secludes himself with a woman whom it is forbidden to seclude with, whether Jewish or not Jewish, they both receive lashes of rebellion—both the man and the woman—and they are publicly shamed to disgrace them. Nevertheless, this does not disqualify the woman from marrying a priest, even if she secluded herself with someone whose intercourse would disqualify her from marrying a priest (according to the Tur). Except for a married woman, even if she secluded herself, she is not lashed, to avoid casting aspersions on her children, suggesting that someone else fathered them. If she sinned, what did her children do wrong, as this is only a suspicion of intercourse? Some say that he is lashed (according to the Bach), and some say that he is also not lashed (according to the Beit Shmuel), for if he is lashed, it will cast aspersions on her children, suggesting they are illegitimate. What is written in Siman 21, Se'if 3, that when one passes by the door of a suspected woman, he is lashed, refers to an unmarried woman.

And all of this applies when there are witnesses that he secluded himself with her or when he admits it, but she is not believed to say that he secluded himself with her. Even if one witness testifies to this, it is of no consequence if he denies it, for one witness in contradiction is of no consequence. Even if she claims and says that the child is his and he denies it – he is exempt even from an oath. Even if it is known that he had relations with her and he says that the child is not his – he is still believed, for the Torah believed him and we say that she committed adultery with others as well. This has already been explained in Siman 4. Nevertheless, in a situation where it appears to the court that he is secluding himself with her, even if there are no witnesses to this – they separate them and prevent them from living in the same courtyard and neighborhood, and they distance them from each other.

Any woman with whom it is forbidden to seclude oneself, if his wife is with him, it is permitted to seclude oneself because his wife guards him, and they will not come to any wrongdoing. Therefore, if a man’s work or business involves women and it is forbidden for him to be alone with them, what should he do? He should either engage in business with them while his wife is with him or find a different occupation. This allowance, where his wife is with him, applies specifically to Jews. However, with a non-Jew, since they do not adhere to this concern, a woman should not seclude herself with a non-Jew even if his wife is with him.

Additionally, one should not entrust a Jewish child, and all the more so a Jewish girl, to a non-Jew to teach them a trade or other matters, because they are suspected of homosexual relations. Even if they are not suspected of this, they are suspected of leading the child towards idolatry, and certainly if they are suspected of bloodshed. In Yoreh De'ah, Siman 153, it is explained that one should not place animals in their care. See there.

A woman whose husband is in town – we do not worry about her being alone with another man because the fear of her husband is upon her. However, some say that it is initially forbidden [Rashi]. If the man is familiar with her, such as if they grew up together, or she is his relative, or they have some acquaintance through business dealings or similar – it is forbidden for them to be alone together even in such a case when her husband is in town, and certainly if her husband has expressed jealousy towards him. Similarly, if there is an open door to the public domain and it is not locked – there is no prohibition after the fact regarding being alone, but if he is familiar with her or her husband has expressed jealousy towards him – it is forbidden for them to be alone together as stated.

According to the Rambam, of blessed memory, one woman is prohibited from being secluded even with many men unless the wife of one of them is present, as then his wife will keep watch and consequently, none of them will engage in promiscuity. However, when there are two women who are strangers, they are prohibited from being secluded. What is clarified, that many women with many men are permitted to be secluded, this applies only when there are no fewer than three women, but with two it is forbidden. And what is clarified in the Gemara, that a single woman may be secluded with many men when they are upright individuals because each would be ashamed before his fellow, this applies to completely righteous individuals, not to ordinary people. Similarly, one man should not be secluded even with many women according to the Rambam, unless his wife is with him.

But there are some of our rabbis who hold that one woman may seclude herself with two upstanding men in the city, and ordinary men are presumed to be upstanding. However, on the road or in a field, three men are required because one might need to relieve himself, leaving the second alone with her, and the same applies at night even in the city for this reason. With immoral men – even with ten of them, it is forbidden for her to seclude herself, because they are not ashamed of one another. Similarly, some permit one man to seclude himself with many women if he is not involved in dealings with women, for if he is involved with women, it is forbidden because he is familiar with them and is not ashamed of them.

Many women, not fewer than three, with many men—there is no concern for seclusion (yichud). If the men are outside and the women are inside, or the men are inside and the women are outside, and one woman separates and goes among the men, and they are licentious, and according to the Rambam, even if they are not licentious, or one man goes among the women and his business is with them, and according to the Rambam, even if his business is not with them—they are prohibited due to seclusion. [And see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 11, as mentioned in the name of the Bach].

It is permitted to seclude oneself with two yevamot (women bound to a levirate marriage) or with two co-wives, or with a woman and her mother-in-law, or a woman and her husband's daughter, or a woman and her mother-in-law's daughter, because they dislike each other and will not cover up for each other, and they will be afraid of each other to commit adultery. Similarly, it is permitted to seclude oneself with a woman who has with her a small girl who knows the concept of intercourse but does not yet give herself to intercourse because she does not yet have the inclination to commit adultery, as the woman will be afraid to commit adultery in front of her lest she reveal her secret to others. However, on the road, a small girl does not help, as she might turn with him to a secluded place and commit adultery, and certainly in a house where there is another room, it is forbidden. But to seclude oneself with that small girl herself is forbidden, as he might rape her. If the small girl is less than three years and one day old, there is no prohibition to seclude oneself with her. Similarly, a woman is permitted to seclude herself with a boy less than nine years old, as they only decreed against the seclusion of a man who is capable of intercourse and a woman who is capable. However, if the girl's father betrothed her, it is forbidden to seclude oneself with her, as her status is like a married woman and she is forbidden by Torah law, and there is no difference between one who is capable and one who is not.

An androgynous person should not be secluded with women because they have a desire for women. However, if they were secluded, they are not punished because their status is uncertain. But a man is allowed to be secluded with an androgynous person or a tumtum (one of indeterminate sex), as men do not have a desire for them, and the people of Israel have not been suspected of such behavior. See also what is written in Siman 24. Some say that an androgynous person should also not be secluded with a man.

The sages established that women should speak with each other in the restroom so that no man would enter and be alone with them. This was in ancient times when restrooms were in the fields and not in the city, where there was a concern of seclusion. However, in our times, when restrooms are in the city, there is no such concern. The sages also established that a woman should not walk in the marketplace with her child behind her, but rather the child should walk in front of her. The reason is that promiscuous individuals might attempt to seize the child in a hidden place, causing the mother to go after the child to retrieve him, during which time the wicked individuals who have grabbed him might assault her. All the more so, a daughter should not walk behind her, as there is a concern that she herself might be seized and assaulted.

It is prohibited to appoint even a trustworthy and upright person, even the most pious of the pious, to be a guard in a courtyard where there are women, even if he is standing outside. Even according to the opinion that one man is permitted to be secluded with many women, this is not comparable to being a constant guard, which is worse than someone whose business is with women. And even though he is standing outside, there is no guardian against sexual immorality. It seems that even two men are prohibited, because it is inevitable that one will leave or sleep, and the other will be secluded with them. Three men might be permissible, but according to the opinion of Maimonides (Rambam) in section 7, it might be that even three are prohibited, and this requires further investigation for a definitive ruling. The Sages also advised as a precaution that a person should not appoint a guardian over his household to prevent his wife from coming to sin. Had Potiphar not appointed the righteous Joseph as a steward over his house, he would not have come to that situation (Berachot 63a).

The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote: It is forbidden for a Torah scholar to reside in a courtyard where there is a widow, even if he does not seclude himself with her, due to suspicion, unless his wife is with him. These are his words. And in the Gemara, it does not state that it is only forbidden to lodge with her, and this is the opinion of the Ra'avad, of blessed memory. And this is also only when he eats from her provisions, but if he pays her for his food – it is permitted. And according to the Rambam, a temporary lodging is permitted, and only a permanent residence with her in the same courtyard is forbidden. 

The sages also said that a widow is forbidden to raise a dog because of suspicion, and a woman, even if she is not a widow, should not buy male slaves, even if they are minors, because of suspicion. According to the Rambam, it is only forbidden if they are of an age suitable for intercourse, but if they are very young – it is permitted. However, according to the Tur, it is forbidden even in this case, lest she raise them until they are of an age suitable, as the Tur wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 267.

One who does not have a wife should not hire a maidservant, whether she is a virgin or a widow, even if she has a son with her in his house when he lives alone, because the son will not be there at all times. Similarly, one who does not have a wife should not teach young children, because the mothers of the children come to the school and he will be secluded with them. Even in a place where there is no concern of seclusion, he will still be aroused by them. Likewise, a woman should not teach young children because the fathers of the children will come to her house on account of their sons, and they will find themselves secluded with her. Even if she has a husband, it is forbidden, because it is not the way of a man to always be at home. However, a teacher who has a wife does not have this concern. Not only when she is with him in the house where he teaches them is it permitted, for she does not usually leave her house, but even if he teaches in another house, it is permitted since his wife is in the city and can come to him at any time, and she watches over him. However, if she is in another city, it is certainly forbidden.

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote at the end of the Laws of Forbidden Relationships: "One does not expound on the secrets of illicit relationships in the presence of three people, because one of them will be preoccupied with asking the teacher questions, and the other two will be engaged in discussion with each other, and their minds will not be free to listen. And since a person's inclination is close to matters of illicit relationships, if he has a doubt about something he hears, he will tend to be lenient. Therefore, one should only expound to two people, so that one listener will free his mind and understand what he hears from the teacher." And with three, it is possible that two of them will not hear at all if the teacher says some prohibition (Rashi on Chagigah 11). Additionally, the Satan accuses Israel regarding illicit relationships, for Cain married his sister, and our forefather Jacob married two sisters. The teacher knows hidden reasons not apparent to other students, and if they do not hear the reason, they may come to err (Maharsha).

He also wrote: There is nothing in the entire Torah that is as difficult for most people to abstain from as forbidden sexual relationships and illicit unions. Our sages said [Yoma 75a], when the Israelites were commanded about forbidden sexual relationships, they cried and accepted this commandment with complaints and weeping, as it is said (Numbers 11:10), "crying in their families" – concerning familial matters. And our sages said [Chagigah there], theft and forbidden sexual relationships are things to which a person's soul lusts and desires. You will not find any community at any time that does not have individuals who are lax regarding forbidden sexual relationships and illicit unions. Our sages said [Bava Batra 165a]: most people are guilty of theft, a minority of forbidden sexual relationships, and everyone is involved in the dust of lashon hara (slander). Thus are the words of the Sages.

Therefore, it is proper for a person to subdue their inclination in this matter and to accustom themselves to greater sanctity, pure thoughts, and correct understanding in order to be saved from them. One should be careful of seclusion, which is a major cause, and all the more so from strolling with women and playing games with them, and certainly from dancing with them, God forbid. Similarly, one should distance themselves from frivolity, drunkenness, and lewd speech, and certainly from reading lewd books. Those who write and print them have no share in the World to Come, for they are significant causes. A person should not remain without a wife. Above all, it is said that one should direct their thoughts to words of Torah and broaden their knowledge in wisdom, for thoughts of immorality only prevail in a heart that is empty of wisdom. This leads to sinful thoughts, which are forbidden by the Torah, as it is written: "And you shall not follow after your own heart" (Numbers 15:39). And it is stated in the Torah: "A loving doe, a graceful deer—may her breasts satisfy you at all times; be intoxicated always with her love" (Proverbs 5:19).

[The Law Regarding the Prohibition of Wasting Seed, Containing Nine Sections]
A person created in the image of God should understand and comprehend with his knowledge and intellect that the desire created within man was not made for the sake of desire itself, for it is contrary to reason. As our Sages interpreted the verse "For He spoke, and it came to be" (Psalms 33:9) – this refers to woman; "He commanded, and it stood firm" – this refers to children. A woman is a vessel full of filth and her mouth is full of blood, yet everyone runs after her [Shabbat 152a]. She was only created for procreation, which is the preservation of the world. This is why the Holy One, Blessed be He, caused this desire to be strong in humans, so that His world would endure, as it is written: "He did not create it a waste, but formed it to be inhabited" (Isaiah 45:18). If the Holy One, Blessed be He, had not strengthened this desire in man, no one would engage in it due to its repulsiveness. And proof that it is not for any desire: immediately upon the emission of seed, the desire ceases entirely, and every person reflects: Where is my desire that I craved just a moment ago? Rather, one should understand that after the emission of seed for the purpose of procreation, there is no further need for it. Therefore, in the elderly who are no longer capable of procreation, their desire ceases, unlike the desires for eating and drinking, which even the very old still crave somewhat. Thus, it is a sacred duty upon a person to guard his seed so that it does not go to waste, God forbid, for it is holy. Natural scientists have already discovered through the microscope that in a drop of seed, the entire form of a human is present, and one who wastes it is as if he has killed a soul, God forbid.

Therefore, our Sages were extremely stringent regarding the evil eye, and this sin is more severe than all other transgressions in the Torah. All the more so for those who engage in self-pleasure and emit semen – not only is this a great prohibition, but the one who does this is considered to be in excommunication. Concerning this it is said, "Your hands are full of blood" (Isaiah 1:15), as if he has killed a soul. Similarly, one who intentionally causes an erection is in excommunication. Therefore, one must be very careful not to think about this, for such thoughts lead to the emission of semen in vain.

It is forbidden for a person to intentionally arouse himself or to bring himself to a state of arousal. If a person has an improper thought, he should divert his mind from frivolous matters to words of Torah, which are a beloved hind and a graceful deer, and they nullify evil thoughts. Therefore, it is forbidden for a person to sleep on his back with his face upwards; rather, he should tilt slightly to his side to avoid arousal, because when one sleeps on his back, the spinal cord heats up, through which the seed travels, and its source is in the brain. One should not gaze at animals, beasts, and birds when they mate with each other. However, those whose work involves this, such as animal breeders, are permitted even to insert them like a paintbrush in a tube, because they are engaged in their work and will not come to improper thoughts.

It is forbidden for an unmarried man to touch his genitals so that he does not come to improper thoughts, and even from below his navel, he should not put his hand lest he come to improper thoughts. And if he urinates, he should not hold his member and urinate. If he is married, it is permitted when his wife is with him and she is pure [Magen Avraham 63:14, and the Taz writes similarly there], and some say that even if his wife is not with him it is permitted [Beit Shmuel]. The opinion of the Tur is that even a married man is only permitted to hold from the corona downward towards the ground. In any case, whether married or unmarried, one should not extend his hand to the member at all except when he needs to relieve himself. Washing the member along with the whole body is permitted when washing in a manner of passing, but to linger much in washing the organ is not appropriate for perhaps it will cause arousal. Also, when washing, he should not look at his nakedness, which is disgraceful, and certainly, he should not gaze at the nakedness of his fellow. Additionally, the Sages prohibited riding an animal without a saddle so that the organ does not become heated from the flesh of the animal. [What is written in the Shulchan Aruch, section 6, about a saddle as a blanket is a scribal error, for a blanket causes heat as explained by Rashi in Niddah 14].

When engaging in marital relations with his wife, a man should not engage in intercourse internally and then ejaculate externally, thereby wasting his seed. This was the act of Er and Onan, whom the Lord killed because they wasted their seed on the ground, as it is written in the Torah of Moses. Therefore, if a woman has a blockage in her womb, and as a result, when her husband has relations with her, he ejaculates externally — this is forbidden. She should seek a cure for this condition or he should divorce her. However, it is permissible to have relations with a young girl or an ailonit (a woman who does not develop signs of puberty) since he engages in intercourse in the natural manner. This is only permissible if he has already fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation or if he has another wife in places where it is permitted to marry two women. But if he has not yet fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation, he should not marry a young girl who is not capable of bearing children, and certainly not a barren or elderly woman. 

Know that from the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in the first section, it appears that engaging in relations with a young girl pertains to the prohibition of wasting seed. This requires further examination and consideration.

A woman who has been told by doctors that if she becomes pregnant, she will die and it appears that she should engage in marital relations in the usual manner because of the danger, in such a case our Sages said (Yevamot 12b) that she may use a cloth. Rashi explained that she places a cloth in the place of intercourse when they engage in relations so that she does not become pregnant. However, Rabbeinu Tam holds that this is a complete prohibition, as it is considered like casting one's seed on trees and stones. Instead, he should engage in relations in the usual manner and afterwards she should place the cloth to absorb the seed, for she is not commanded regarding the destruction of seed. [And Rabbeinu Tam contradicts himself from Yevamot there to Ketubot 39a, and in Shitah Mekubetzet there it is written in the name of the Rosh, Ramban, and Ritva, and likewise in the Rashba in Yevamot and Ketubot there, and also the Mordechai at the beginning of Yevamot in the name of Rabbeinu Tam and Rivan wrote that there is no prohibition to place a cloth before intercourse, and also to place it after intercourse the Rosh wrote there is no prohibition, and also Rabbi Yitzchak in Tosafot Ketubot refuted his proof. Therefore, when there is a danger that she might become pregnant, one can rely and permit whether before intercourse or afterward, and it is explicitly implied this way at the beginning of Niddah.]

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: In the Talmud, in the chapter "Kol Yad," it implies that it is forbidden to wear pants unless they are made like leggings because it leads to the wasting of seed. And although it is possible to reject this by saying that in the Talmud it was only stated in their days when they had terumah (heave offering) and there was concern for bodily impurity, nevertheless, since the Rosh brought it in his rulings, it implies that even in our times it is forbidden. As for the custom to permit it in the bathhouse, one could say that for a short time they did not forbid it. These are the words of the Rema. 

It is clear that this was only said regarding pants that have a special pocket for the organ by itself, in which case heating is relevant. But regarding our pants, what heating is relevant? And it is obvious that in all generations, they did not go without pants [and so it is written in the Pri Tohar in the name of Atzei Arazim, and see Orach Chaim, Siman 91].

From his words it seems that they would go to the bathhouse wearing pants, but that is not the case in our times in our lands. Therefore, it is surprising that even some of the scholars and the God-fearing are not cautious and go to the bathhouse with their father, father-in-law, stepfather, or brother-in-law. And this prohibition is explicitly stated in the Gemara (Pesachim 51a) that it is forbidden to bathe with one's father, father-in-law, stepfather, or brother-in-law. And our master, the Rema, writes that it is permitted because they would go to the bathhouse wearing pants. But in our times, what permit is there for this?

And I thought to say that the Gemara says not to bathe with them, and in their times, bathing was usually in bathtubs, and this is forbidden so they would not sit in one bathtub, which leads to improper thoughts. But in our bathhouses, where they are just in one room, there is no concern. However, I saw in the Mordechai (there) in the name of Rabbi Meir of Rottenburg who considered this permit and rejected it based on reasoning that there is no difference in this matter. Nevertheless, the world possibly relies on this, but whoever fears the word of God should distance himself from this.

And bathing with one's primary teacher is also forbidden because of respect, and therefore if the teacher needs him to serve him, it is permitted as it is written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 242. Similarly, if the student was in the bathhouse before his teacher, he does not need to leave when his teacher comes. However, with one's father, father-in-law, stepfather, or brother-in-law, since the reason is due to improper thoughts, it is forbidden in all cases. And it is also taught in the Gemara there that in a place where the custom is that two brothers do not bathe together, they should also not bathe together, and so wrote the Rambam. But the Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not write this because now this is not the custom anywhere, and according to the law, it is permitted as the Gemara writes there. And I am puzzled by the Tur and the Beit Yosef that they did not mention this law at all, neither here nor in Yoreh De'ah. And I am even more puzzled by the Tur, who in the short decisions of the Rosh omitted it as well. Only the Rambam and Rema wrote it, as well as the Rif and the Rosh, and this requires investigation.

And to go to the bathhouse with a young son, there is a doubt whether it is permitted or not.

The early pious ones and the great sages, one of them boasted that he never looked at his own circumcision, and some of them boasted that they never gazed upon the form of their wife because their hearts were turned away from matters of vanity to matters of truth that capture the hearts of the holy. [Rambam]

[Laws of the prohibition of homosexual relations and bestiality, and that Israel is not suspected of such, with seven sections]
Homosexual relations and bestiality are among the forbidden sexual relations, and one is liable to karet (spiritual excision). If there are witnesses and a warning, one is liable to stoning, as explicitly stated in the Torah. Therefore, one who has relations with a male or brings a male upon himself, once there is penetration, if both are adults – they are stoned, as it is stated: "You shall not lie with a male as with a woman" (Leviticus 18:22), and in Kedoshim it is written: "If a man lies with a male as with a woman, both of them have committed an abomination; they shall surely be put to death; their blood is upon them" (Leviticus 20:13). Thus, both the one who lies and the one who is lain with are liable to stoning, and the prohibition "You shall not lie" applies to both of them – read it as "You shall not lie" and "You shall not be lain with" [Sanhedrin 54a], for the Torah does not punish unless it first warns with a prohibition. If one of them was a minor – if he is nine years old and one day, the adult is liable to stoning, and the minor is exempt. If he is younger than that – the adult is also exempt, and the court administers lashes of rebelliousness to the adult.

The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 1 of Hilchot Issurei Biah, Law 15: "One who has relations with an androgynous through his male organ is liable, and a tumtum is in doubt. Therefore, one who has relations with a tumtum or an androgynous through their female organ receives lashes of rebellion. An androgynous is permitted to marry a woman." His words clarify that the androgynous is considered as a male. Although, for the entirety of the Torah, he is in doubt whether he is a male or female, as the Rambam himself wrote concerning the impurity of childbirth in Chapter 10 of Hilchot Issurei Biah, and concerning valuations in Chapter 1 of Hilchot Erchin, and concerning the sighting of blood in Chapter 1 of Hilchot Mishkav uMoshav, and similarly in Chapter 2 of Hilchot Ishut and Nazir, nevertheless, here the Torah expanded its prohibition from the verse "And with a male you shall not lie as with a woman" to include from the location of his male organ when lying, his status is that of a male. Consequently, since this is the case, there is no prohibition in him marrying a woman. And what is questioned regarding Reish Lakish in Yevamot Chapter 2: refer to the Responsa of Nodah B’Yehudah, part 2, section 1, and Rambam in Chapter 7 of Hilchot Terumot and the Kesef Mishneh there. It is clear that according to the Rambam, an androgynous who has relations with a male is liable to death, and perhaps for all forbidden relations he is liable, or it is possible that the Torah only expanded his status specifically for the matter of male-male relations. But there are those who disagree and hold that ultimately an androgynous remains in doubt, and one is not liable for him at all, and he himself is not liable for anything, and he does not marry a woman. As found in the commentary of Rashi there in Chapter 3, who interprets the law according to Rabbi Yehuda in the Mishnah, and similarly the Rashba there, and see Kesef Mishneh and delve deeply.

One who has relations with an animal, or with a wild beast or bird, or brings them upon himself – both he and the animal are stoned, as explicitly stated in the Torah. Even though the animal has not sinned, nevertheless, since it caused a great stumbling block for a person, the animal is also killed, as it is written: "And you shall kill the woman and the beast" (Leviticus 20:16). There is no distinction between a man who has relations with an animal or brings it upon himself, or a woman who has relations with an animal or brings a male animal upon herself. There is no distinction between a large or small animal, as it is written (Leviticus 18:23) "with any animal" – even one day old, for a one-day-old ox is called an ox. And what is written "animal" – this also applies to wild beasts and birds, and throughout the Torah, it is so, just as in the labors of Shabbat. Also, with an animal, there is no distinction between natural and unnatural relations, as with a woman, for once he has initiated relations with the animal or the animal has initiated relations with him – he is liable.

One who engages in intercourse with an animal unintentionally, and a woman who causes an animal to engage with her unintentionally, the person is exempt - also the animal is not put to death. Although it is a disgrace before people when the animal is walking and they say, "This is the animal that so-and-so engaged with," nonetheless, the sages were uncertain [Sanhedrin 55b] whether the Torah commanded to kill the animal only when there is also a transgression, meaning intentionally. And since it is a doubt - the doubt concerning the life of an animal leads to leniency. However, it is disqualified from the altar in any case, and it appears to me that it is even forbidden for a common person because a doubt of prohibition is treated stringently and this is a doubt from the Torah. Similarly, regarding a non-Jew who engages with an animal, the animal is not stoned as Maimonides wrote in the ninth chapter of Kings, and although he is forbidden in this act since it is one of the seven Noahide laws and there is a transgression, nonetheless, the sages were in doubt whether the primary reason is due to disgrace, and for them, there is no disgrace. And although according to the Talmud's discussion it is clarified there that in one of them the animal is killed in any case, nonetheless, since in the end, it is a doubt for us in both, therefore Maimonides ruled leniently in both. However, it is certain that if one animal was engaged with by an Israelite unintentionally and by a non-Jew intentionally - then in any case, it is killed. And know that for a common person, it is not forbidden except by two witnesses and not by one witness and not by the owners, and it is not stoned by them except by two witnesses [Temurah 28b], and only for the altar is it forbidden in any case [there]. And it should not be questioned why it is not stoned by one or by the owners when they engage with it intentionally, since there is a transgression and disgrace, for this is not relevant to this, as just as a person is not killed without two witnesses, so too an animal, for as is the death of the owners, thus is the death of the ox [it appears to me].

Even though an animal is not stoned if the act was committed unintentionally, as we have said, nevertheless, if a minor who is nine years and one day old engages in intercourse with an animal, or a minor girl older than three years who has an animal brought upon her, even though they are not liable to the death penalty and their status is that of unintentional transgressors, the animal is still stoned because there is a transgression and disgrace. For they are not considered unintentional transgressors but rather complete intentional transgressors, except that the Torah spared the minors because their understanding is not yet complete. Therefore, the animal is killed [Sanhedrin there]. But if the boy is less than nine years and one day old and the girl is less than three years and one day old, the animal is not stoned because they are not considered fit for intercourse [there].

Even though seclusion (yichud) is prohibited with all forbidden relations (arayot), nonetheless, with a male (zachur) and an animal (behemah), there is no prohibition of seclusion because Israel was not suspected of such acts – of lying with a male or with an animal. However, distancing oneself even from seclusion with a male or an animal is praiseworthy, and the great sages would distance an animal to avoid seclusion with it. In places where there are many who transgress in this matter, one must be careful and avoid seclusion with them. In our countries, this is only considered an act of piety [Bach], but still, in any place, it is proper to prevent two single men from sleeping together. However, this is not the custom, and Heaven forbid, we have never heard of being concerned about this, but one who is careful about it will be blessed.

And know that with domesticated and wild animals, both the acts of mating and being mated (in a prohibited manner) are applicable. However, with birds, only the act of being mated is relevant, and the act of mating does not apply to birds [Rashi, Chullin 23a]. Regarding fish, it appears that mating with a human is not applicable at all. Additionally, only terrestrial species are included in the category of animals [Tosafot, Bava Kama 55a, s.v. atya, and see there Tosafot, s.v. hamanhig, and there is room for further investigation regarding the law].

[Not to engage excessively in conjugal relations and the conduct in this matter, as detailed in 13 sections]

Even in conjugal relations with his pure wife, a person should conduct himself with great sanctity, with pure thoughts and proper understanding. He should not act frivolously with his wife, nor should he speak obscenely, even in private conversation between them. As it is written, "And declares to a person what his conversation is" (Amos 4:13), and our Sages said (Chagigah 5b) that even light conversation between a man and his wife will be accounted for in judgment. He should not discuss other matters with her during the act or beforehand, so that his mind does not wander to another woman. If he did converse with her and immediately had relations, it is said about him, "And declares to a person what his conversation is." However, regarding matters of conjugal relations, he may speak with her to increase his desire to produce legitimate offspring. If he was upset with her and needs to appease her, he may speak with her to placate her.

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 21 of the Laws of Prohibited Relations: It is a measure of piety that one should not take this matter lightly and should sanctify oneself during marital relations, and should not deviate from the way of the world, and that this matter is solely for the purpose of procreation. One should not increase marital relations to be constantly with his wife, as this is highly improper and is the behavior of fools. Rather, whoever minimizes marital relations is praiseworthy, provided that he does not neglect the marital duty (onah) except with his wife's consent. This is the end of his words. The order of the marital duty will be explained in Siman 76, see there.

He further wrote in the fourth chapter of De'ot: Seminal emission is the strength of the body and the light of the eyes, and as long as it is emitted excessively, the body deteriorates, its strength diminishes, and one's life is lost. This is what Solomon said in his wisdom: "Do not give your strength to women" (Proverbs 31:3). Anyone who indulges excessively in sexual intercourse, premature aging comes upon him, his strength weakens, his eyes grow dim, a foul odor emanates from his mouth and armpits, the hair of his head, eyebrows, and eyelashes fall out, the hair of his beard and armpits and the hair on his legs increases, his teeth fall out, and many other pains besides these befall him. The wise physicians said that one out of a thousand dies from other ailments, and the thousandth dies from excessive intercourse. Therefore, a person must be cautious in this matter if he wishes to be well – he should only engage in intercourse when he finds his body strong and very healthy, and he has a strong erection not of his own volition, and he distracts himself with other matters, and yet the erection remains. If he feels a heaviness from his loins downward, as if the cords of his testicles are being pulled, and his flesh is warm – he should come to his wife, who is permissible to him. A person should not engage in intercourse when he is full or hungry, but after the food has been digested in his intestines. He should check his bowels before and after intercourse. He should not engage in intercourse standing or sitting, not in the bathhouse, not on the day he enters the bathhouse [in their very hot bathhouses], not on the day of bloodletting, etc. Thus are his words.

And even when one engages in marital relations during the designated time, he should not intend for his own pleasure but rather as one who is fulfilling an obligation, as it is a duty at its appointed time and to fulfill the commandment of his Creator in being fruitful and multiplying, and to have children who engage in Torah study and fulfill commandments in Israel. He should only engage in relations with her consent, and if she is not willing, he should appease her until she is willing. He should be very modest during the act and should not engage in relations in the presence of other people, specifically when they are awake, but if they are sleeping, it is not an issue. A partition does not help if he is aware, since the issue is one of modesty, and in the presence of animals, wild beasts, birds, or an infant who cannot speak, there is no prohibition. He should engage in relations in the middle of the night when no other voice is heard so that he does not become distracted by thoughts of another woman.

Our Sages said [Eruvin 63a]: "Anyone who sleeps in a room where a man and his wife reside, about him Scripture says, 'The women of My people you cast out from their pleasant houses' (Micah 2:9), because they are ashamed to be intimate in his presence." And even when she is a niddah, he should not sleep there, as he prevents them from speaking confidential matters. He should not say, "I will guard them so that they do not come to sin," for until now, who guarded them? The decisors omitted this, and I do not know why.

The Tur wrote in the name of the Ra'avad that there are four levels of intention in marital relations: The first and most proper of all is for the sake of procreation and fulfilling the positive commandment. The second is for the well-being of the fetus when she is pregnant, as our sages said that in the first three months, marital relations are harmful to the woman and the fetus, in the middle months, it is difficult for the woman but beneficial for the fetus, and in the last months, it is beneficial for both. The third is when his wife desires him or when he is about to travel, which is the commandment of conjugal rights. The fourth is when he intends to guard himself from sin – even in this there is reward.

It is stated in the Talmud [Gittin 70a]: One who lets blood and has marital relations will have weak children. If both let blood and then have relations, they will have children afflicted with ra'atan, which means they will be very weak because they have a creeping creature in their brain [Rashi]. This is specifically if they did not taste anything, but if they tasted something, there is no concern. Similarly, one who comes from a journey and immediately has relations will have weak children. This is specifically if he walked on foot, and similarly when he goes on a journey [Rambam, Hilchot De'ot 4], but if he travels by carriage, there is no concern, and on the contrary, it is a mitzvah to be intimate with his wife when he leaves for a journey and when he returns, as she longs for him then.

And one who comes from the bathroom should not engage in marital relations until he waits the amount of time it takes to walk half a mil – which is approximately one-sixth of an hour. If he engages in relations, it is said that he will have children who are epileptic [there]. One who engages in relations while standing – he will be seized by convulsions, which is the disease Karnefes. If he engages in relations while sitting – he will be seized by diarrhea, and similarly if she is on top and he is on the bottom, due to this illness, he will yawn [Aruch]. Furthermore, it is said that he will waste seed, as it is known that a woman does not conceive from standing. However, if it happens that he engaged in relations while standing and then withdrew, and she became pregnant – one cannot accuse her of adultery, for it is possible that she conceived while standing, as stated there. Additionally, it weakens his strength when he engages in relations while standing. Similarly, if he engages in relations in the usual manner and immediately stands up, there is also danger in this [there]. And marital relations is one of those things where a small amount is beneficial, but an excess is harmful [there]. And there are remedies mentioned in the Gemara regarding this matter, but we are not knowledgeable in the names of their remedies.

The verse states, "And I will purge from you the rebels and those who transgress against Me" (Ezekiel 20:38) – these are the children of nine categories: 

1. Children of fear – where a man imposes fear on his wife to coerce her to be intimate against her will, resulting in unworthy offspring.
2. Children of coercion – where a man forcibly rapes his wife, which is worse than instilling fear.
3. Children of hatred – where a man hates his wife.
4. Children of excommunication – where a man has marital relations while he is excommunicated.
5. Children of mistaken identity – where a man mistakenly believes he is being intimate with one of his wives but is actually with another, in places where polygamy is practiced (see Magen Avraham, Orach Chaim 240:9).
6. Children of strife – even if there is no hatred but there is temporary conflict and they do not reconcile before intimacy.
7. Children of drunkenness – where the man is drunk and does not pay proper attention to his wife.
8. Children of divorce intent – where the man has resolved in his heart to divorce his wife but is intimate with her.
9. Children of confusion – where multiple men have been intimate with her, as she was married to many men and was divorced and widowed multiple times, leading to many influences and resulting in unworthy offspring.

And children of brazenness – where the woman brazenly demands intimacy openly, but if she entices him with words of appeasement and decorates herself for him, it is acceptable (Nedarim 20).

It is forbidden for a man to coerce his wife for this, as it is stated, "He who is hasty with his feet sins" (Proverbs 19:2), and "Also, without knowledge, the soul is not good" (ibid.), resulting in unworthy children, and likewise one who has repeated relations without her consent (Eruvin 100b).

There is also in the Talmud one who says: "Why are people born lame? Because they overturn their tables, so that they are on top and it is below. Mutes – because they kiss that place. Deaf – because they talk during the act. Blind – because they look at that place" [Nedarim 20a]. And do not engage in much conversation with a woman, as it will ultimately lead to licentiousness. It is taught: "And so that His fear will be upon your faces" – this refers to shame, "so that you will not sin" (Exodus 20:20) – for shame brings about fear of sin. It is a good sign for a person if he is bashful, and anyone who is bashful does not quickly sin, and anyone who is not bashful, it is known that his forefathers did not stand at Mount Sinai [there].

Therefore, even though we hold [there] that whatever a person wishes to do with his wife he may do when she is pure—he may have intercourse with her whenever he wishes, kiss any part of her body he wishes, and have intercourse with her in the usual manner or in an unusual manner or through other means, provided he does not waste seed [Tur]—nonetheless, one who directs his ways should not do so, but rather should engage in relations in a manner conducive to procreation and childbirth, for it is impossible to ensure that seed will not be wasted, and this sin is very severe. And although there are those who permit even this when done occasionally and not habitually, it is difficult to say so [Beit Yosef], and one who guards his soul should stay away from this. And anyone who sanctifies himself with what is permitted to him is considered holy [the words of the Ba'er Hetev in section 2 are perplexing].

It is forbidden to engage in marital relations in markets, streets, gardens, and orchards, but only in a dwelling house, so that it does not appear as promiscuity and lead to habituation to promiscuity. One who engages in marital relations with his wife in these places is subject to disciplinary lashes. One should not engage in marital relations at the beginning of the night or at its end, but only in the middle, as explained in Siman 4. When traveling with his wife and staying in an inn without a private room, he should not engage in marital relations [but if he has a private room, it is permitted], only he should not sleep in the host’s bedding lest he see something inappropriate and be repulsed by it. During years of famine or other troubles, one should refrain from marital relations unless he has no children, it is the night of immersion, or his desire overcomes him.

It is forbidden to engage in marital relations by the light of a candle, even by darkening it with a garment. If it is Shabbat and the candle is lit, one should not engage in relations at all. However, if there is a partition, it is permitted even if the candle illuminates above the partition when it is darkened with a garment. If the candle is in another room, even if it illuminates their room, it is permitted. The light of the moon is not an issue, and one may darken it with a garment. It is also forbidden to engage in relations during the day, as it is considered brazen. If it is a Torah scholar and he darkens it with a garment, it is permitted, but this is only allowed in great need so as not to come to emit seed wastefully. To make a light partition on Shabbat for modesty in front of the candle might be permitted, as mentioned in Orach Chaim, Siman 315, see there. In a room that has books, it is forbidden to engage in relations until a partition is made, and they should not be visible above the partition. For tefillin, printed Chumashim, Gemaras, and legal codices, a double covering suffices, provided the second covering is not designated for them. Spreading a garment over a box of books is considered as a double covering, and the same applies to a mezuzah. However, for a Torah scroll and Chumashim made of parchment rolled up, only a partition suffices. See in Orach Chaim, Siman 240, that one should not engage in relations on a bed with an infant on it, and the head and foot of the bed should be oriented north-south. See there.

[It is forbidden to be with a woman without betrothal, containing fifteen sections]

The Rambam writes in the first chapter of Ishut: Before the giving of the Torah, a man would encounter a woman in the marketplace, and if he desired her and she desired him to marry, he would bring her into his house and have relations with her privately, and she would become his wife. Once the Torah was given, the Israelites were commanded that if a man wishes to marry a woman, he must first acquire her in the presence of witnesses, and then she becomes his wife, as it is stated, "When a man takes a wife and has relations with her" (Deuteronomy 22:13). This acquisition is a positive commandment of the Torah, and a woman is acquired in one of three ways – by money, by document, or by intercourse, etc. These acquisitions are called kiddushin or erusin everywhere. A woman who is acquired by one of these three means is called mekudeshet or me'oreset. Once the woman is acquired and becomes mekudeshet, even though she has not had intercourse and has not entered her husband's house, she is considered a married woman. Anyone who has relations with her other than her husband is subject to the death penalty by the court, and if he wishes to divorce her, she requires a get (bill of divorce). So are the words of the Rambam.

Explanation of his words: Regarding matters of marriage, the Torah writes that taking (קיחה) precedes consummation (ביאה), as it is written, "When a man takes a wife and comes to her and despises her" (Deuteronomy 22:13), implying that she becomes his wife even before consummation. Similarly, it is written, "When a man takes a wife and marries her" (Deuteronomy 24:1). It is explicitly stated in the Torah that betrothal (אירוסין) and marriage (נישואין) are two separate matters, as it is written in the portion of Shoftim, "And who is the man that has betrothed a wife and not taken her" (Deuteronomy 20:7). This taking is like an acquisition, as he acquires her for marriage in the presence of two valid witnesses. Therefore, regarding forbidden relations, we do not find the term "taking," only the term "lying with." In the case of those forbidden by negative commandments, such as prohibitions for priests, the term "taking" is used, because betrothal is effective for those forbidden by negative commandments, but not for those liable for karet. The four forbidden relations where the term "taking" is used—his wife's sister, his mother-in-law, his sister, and his brother's wife—are all for specific lessons: for his wife's sister and his mother-in-law, to teach that they are only forbidden if he betroths the first one, not if he lies with them without betrothal (Yevamot 97); for his sister, to teach about Cain, who was permitted to marry his sister (Rashi, Sanhedrin 58b); and for his brother's wife, to indicate that it refers to his paternal brother, as she is sometimes permitted if he dies childless (Torat Kohanim). However, for the children of Noah, we do not find any concept of betrothal at all, as it is written regarding Abimelech, "and she was married to a husband," which the Sages interpreted (Sanhedrin 24b) to mean that they have the status of married if they have consummated the marriage, but not if they have only entered the bridal canopy without consummation, and certainly they do not have betrothal. Before the giving of the Torah, we do not find that marriage involved both taking and consummation together. Similarly, our forefather Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in to her" (Genesis 29:21), indicating that his acquisition was through consummation. Thus, the Sages said (Bereishit Rabbah 18) that the children of Noah are liable for married women but exempt for betrothed women, as it is written, "and cleaves to his wife"—implying when he behaves with her in the manner of marriage (Rashi). (It is recorded there that even if he commits fornication without intention for marriage, she is considered married, but this understanding does not align with the Talmud's discussion about a child of Noah who designates, etc.; see there).

Therefore, a woman is not considered as a married woman unless she has been properly betrothed through kiddushin. However, if a man has relations with her in a promiscuous manner, not for the sake of kiddushin, it is considered as nothing. Some say that he is liable for lashes due to the prohibition of "There shall be no harlot" (Deuteronomy 23:18), and she is considered a "zonah" as mentioned in the Torah [Tur]. Most decisors hold that this only applies to a woman who is prepared to engage in promiscuous relations with anyone who desires. We have already clarified at the beginning of section 4 that this is also the opinion of the Rambam, that in a casual encounter she is not called a "kedeshah," for otherwise, one would not find a fine for a rapist or seducer, as a person cannot be lashed and also pay a fine. The Rambam himself writes this in chapter 2 of "Na'arah Betulah" and in the Book of Mitzvot [Negative Commandment 355]. Rather, the person transgresses a positive commandment, as a man is not permitted to be with a woman without kiddushin [Rivash, Siman 225]. Some say this is only a rabbinic prohibition [Chamat Magen] – and the main opinion is as stated. It is obvious that if she is of an age where she has a menstrual cycle, one who has relations with her is liable to karet (spiritual excision), and she is considered a forbidden relationship like all other forbidden relationships, as she has seen menstrual blood and has not immersed in a mikveh, as it is written: "And a man who lies with a woman during her menstrual period... both of them shall be cut off" (Leviticus 20:18). There is no difference in the prohibition of niddah (menstruant) whether she is unmarried or married, and this has already been explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 183.

If a man has relations with a woman in a promiscuous manner, this does not create any legal obligation for her to require a divorce, even if he had relations with her in the presence of witnesses. And what our Sages have said in various places, that a man does not make his sexual act one of promiscuity, applies to his wife whom he has divorced or to one he has betrothed conditionally and then had relations with her, for she is considered his wife. It is in regard to his wife that they said that a man does not make his sexual act one of promiscuity until he specifies otherwise. However, with other women, any man who engages in relations is presumed to be acting promiscuously unless he specifies that it is for the sake of marriage. Some of the Geonim ruled that any woman who has relations in the presence of witnesses requires a divorce, but Maimonides dismissed their words in chapter 10 of the laws of divorce, law 19, see there. And it is taught in the Tosefta at the beginning of Kiddushin: Any sexual act that is for the sake of marriage – she is betrothed, and if it is not for the sake of marriage – she is not betrothed. It implies that it must be explicitly for the sake of marriage.

Even if a man has relations with a woman with the intention of marriage between them privately, she is not considered his wife unless they seclude themselves before witnesses. He must summon witnesses to an outer room and say before them, "I am secluding myself with this woman for the purpose of betrothal," and then they enter the room, and he has relations with her, which constitutes betrothal through intercourse. There is an opinion that any time he marries her and it is known to all, it is as if there were witnesses at the time of intercourse, as stated in Siman 149 – but this is not so, for there it was only said regarding one who divorces his wife and then has relations with her again, not with a woman who was never his wife. This is merely promiscuity, and even if he regularly secludes her to himself, this is considered a concubine according to the Rambam, who prohibits it as will be explained with Heaven's help. [See Beit Shmuel] [and see Tosafot Yevamot 45b, who explain that since it is known to all that she immersed, it is as if they were present, etc., end of quote].

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 4 of the Laws of Kings that only a king is permitted to take a concubine and not a commoner, unless it is a Hebrew maidservant after designation, see there. And some of our Rabbis disagree with him, for we find in the Tanach several who had concubines and were commoners. However, this is not a proof, for it is possible that they were Hebrew maidservants after designation [according to the Gra]. However, in the Talmud, it is not found that a commoner is prohibited from having a concubine, and the reasoning of Maimonides will be explained before us with the help of Heaven.

What is a concubine (pilegesh)? Rambam writes that she is taken without kiddushin (betrothal) and without a ketubah (marriage contract) and she is exclusively for him. This is also the version we have in the Gemara (Sanhedrin 21a). Some of our rabbis hold that she does not have a ketubah but does have kiddushin (Rashi on Parashat Chayei Sarah), and it is also explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, Ketubot Chapter 5, Halacha 2, that one says they do not have a ketubah and one says they do have a ketubah but do not have the conditions of a ketubah. It is clear that they do have kiddushin. However, it is clear to all opinions that a concubine does not have the conditions of a ketubah like a man has for his wife, obligating him in her sustenance, clothing, and marital relations as with his full wife. Similarly, the husband does not eat her fruits, does not inherit her, and is not obligated in her redemption. A clear proof for this is that we also find before the giving of the Torah that they had concubines, as it is written, "And to the sons of the concubines which Abraham had" etc. (Genesis 25:6), and Nahor also had a concubine, as it is written, "And his concubine, whose name was Reumah" etc. (Genesis 22:24). Before the giving of the Torah there was no kiddushin at all, as it is written, so certainly, there was no obligation from a man to his concubine. From this, the reasoning of Rambam becomes clear, who prohibits a concubine, since the Torah decreed that a man should not take a woman without kiddushin, and consequently, according to his opinion, taking a concubine without kiddushin violates a positive commandment. Even according to Rashi, who holds that she does have kiddushin, since she does not have any conditions of a ketubah and throughout the entire Talmud it is clear that whatever a woman acquires, her husband acquires, and every woman has all the conditions of a ketubah, and it is not mentioned anywhere to establish this for a concubine, it is thus concluded that a concubine is prohibited. This is also evident from Bava Batra 49a and 51a, where it questions "It is obvious," and does not establish it with a concubine.

However, regarding the comparison made by the Rambam between the designation of a Hebrew maidservant and a concubine, there is room for inquiry as to what the connection is between the two. After all, a Hebrew maidservant is designated with the money used to purchase her, and he says to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me," as the Rambam writes in Chapter 4 of Laws of Slaves. Additionally, he is obligated to her with all the obligations a husband has to his wife, as it is written, "Her food, her clothing, and her conjugal rights he shall not diminish" (Exodus 21:10), and she is like a full-fledged wife.

It seems to me that the Rambam, of blessed memory, held that the designation of a Hebrew maidservant is not the same as the obligation of her food, clothing, and conjugal rights, but rather the rules for Hebrew maidservants sold and designated for marriage are similar to those for a concubine. The master designates her for marriage and she becomes like a concubine to him, and the same applies if the designation is for his son. Subsequently, it is written, "If he takes another wife, her food, her clothing, and her conjugal rights he shall not diminish" (Exodus 21:10), referring to the other wife, meaning when he marries a Jewish woman not through servitude, he is obligated to her with food, clothing, and conjugal rights, but not to the designated maidservant. And this is what is meant by "And if he does not do these three for her" – that is, designation for himself, designation for his son, and reduction of money. Thus the Rambam interprets this verse there, and therefore he does not mention the law of food, clothing, and conjugal rights because, in truth, she does not have them.

In the Mekhilta on Mishpatim, there is a dispute among the Tannaim, Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan. One says that the rule for daughters is food, clothing, and conjugal rights, and the other says that it is like the rules for Hebrew maidservants sold, and food, clothing, and conjugal rights only apply to a Jewish daughter betrothed not through servitude. Accordingly, the Rambam's comparison of designation to a concubine is appropriate, as she also does not have the obligations of a husband to his wife. And although he betroths her at the time of designation, since he does not give her anything at the time of designation, it is not similar to other betrothals.

And even if we do not follow the opinion of the Rambam and say that there is no Torah prohibition regarding a concubine, it is still forbidden to maintain a concubine, as the Tur writes in the name of the Rosh regarding an unmarried woman serving in the house of Reuven, where there is an unceasing rumor that he is secluded with her. Not only can her family members protest against him, as it is a disgrace to them for her to be his concubine, but even the Beit Din (rabbinical court) forces him to remove her from his house, as it is known that she is embarrassed to immerse in a mikveh, resulting in him engaging in relations with a niddah (a woman in a state of menstrual impurity). This is even more so according to the opinion of Rashi, who holds that a concubine must have a form of betrothal, and it is a complete prohibition to be secluded without betrothal.
