[And the Gra (Vilna Gaon) agreed with Rashi in his commentary, and for the Rambam, there is a way to reconcile; see there and analyze carefully.]

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that if a man designates a woman for himself and she immerses for him – some say it is permitted and she is the concubine referred to in the Torah, and some say it is forbidden and one receives lashes for it due to "There shall be no harlot" (Deuteronomy 23:18). And the esteemed later authorities challenged him, arguing that even according to the Rambam, who prohibits having a concubine, this does not warrant lashes, since the prohibition of "there shall be no harlot" that warrants lashes applies only to one who is promiscuous, but a concubine is only prohibited by a positive commandment because she lacks betrothal, as explained in section 7. Certainly, this is the primary opinion; however, it is possible that Rabbeinu the Rema's opinion is based on the teaching in the Torat Kohanim that states, "Do not profane your daughter to make her a harlot" (Leviticus 19:29) – this refers to giving one's unmarried daughter to another man not for the purpose of marriage, as well as a woman who gives herself not for the purpose of marriage. This is also found in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 76a). Since, according to the Rambam, a concubine is without betrothal and there is a positive commandment prohibition, it follows that it is akin to general promiscuity, which warrants lashes. And although the Rambam himself clarifies in the second chapter of "Na'arah Betulah" that this only applies when she is promiscuous with anyone who wishes to come upon her, as explained at the beginning of section 4, nonetheless, since the language of the Talmud and Torat Kohanim indicates that even when she is given to one person the rule applies, it is possible that the Rambam also did not mean specifically when she is promiscuous with everyone. This is also implied from the beginning of his wording there. Therefore, the Rema ruled as he did, but the matter requires further investigation for a definitive ruling.

A non-Jew who married a non-Jewish woman, or an apostate to idolatry who married an apostate woman according to their customs, and they later converted to Judaism but did not perform a new betrothal – there is no concern of betrothal at all, even if it was in the presence of valid witnesses, for there was neither "he gave" nor "he said," rather the priest gives each of them a ring. Even if there were witnesses to their seclusion, if he engaged in relations based on the original betrothal, she is permitted to leave him without a get (divorce document) even if she stayed with him for many years, as it is considered mere promiscuity, as mentioned in Siman 149. And some say that if he lived with her after this, we assume that a person does not engage in promiscuity, and even if she secluded herself with him afterwards in front of witnesses or it is known to all that they were secluded together – she requires a get. In the state of Spain during the times of persecution when Jews kept their faith secretly, they were stringent in every matter because they secluded themselves before many others like them – she is considered his complete wife. The ruling that there is no concern of betrothal applies only to those who act willingly. A Jew who married a non-Jewish woman and she converted, and they lived together without a new betrothal and ketubah, and afterwards he left her – she does not need a get, for even if he claims that he had relations with her for the sake of betrothal, since he did not seclude himself with her in the presence of witnesses, it is nothing. And one who lives with an unmarried Jewish woman promiscuously and they say they intended for betrothal, if there was one instance of seclusion with witnesses or it is known to all that they were secluded together – she requires a get.

A woman is betrothed through money, or a document, or intercourse, and all of these are based on Torah law. Through money – as it is written, "When a man takes a wife" (Deuteronomy 24:1), and "taking" (kicha) refers to money, as it is written, "I have given the money for the field, take it from me" (Genesis 23:13). Through a document – as it is written, "and she departs from his house and goes and becomes another man's wife" (Deuteronomy 24:2) – her becoming (married to the second man) is compared to her departure (from the first man); just as her departure is through a document, so too her becoming married is through a document. We do not compare her departure to her becoming married to suggest she could be divorced with money, for it is written, "and he writes her a bill of divorce" (Deuteronomy 24:1) – indicating that she is divorced only through writing. Through intercourse – as it is written, "When a man takes a wife and has relations with her" (Deuteronomy 24:1), and it is also written, "a woman married to a man" (Deuteronomy 22:22) – indicating that through intercourse she becomes his wife.

The sages prohibited betrothing a woman through intercourse due to promiscuity, for it requires designating witnesses for this, and it is an improper act. However, if one transgressed and betrothed through intercourse, he receives lashes of rebellion, but the betrothal is valid. Likewise, the sages prohibited betrothing a woman in the marketplace, even with money or a document, because this too is promiscuous. They also prohibited betrothing without prior engagement, as this is not the way of the upright and is considered promiscuous. The opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 3 of Ishut is that for these cases as well, one receives lashes of rebellion, but the betrothal remains valid. However, some of our rabbis hold that in these two cases (betrothing in the marketplace and without prior engagement), one does not receive lashes of rebellion, as it is not similar to the promiscuity of betrothing through intercourse. Additionally, in the case of intercourse betrothal, only the man receives lashes, as he is the one performing the act of betrothal. (See Choshen Mishpat, Siman 8 and Siman 87, where the Prisha reconciles this; see there.) (See the Makneh, who explains that the prohibition of betrothing through intercourse is because they prohibited betrothal, which is puzzling.)

A woman may be betrothed at any time—whether during the day or at night, whether with money or with a document—except on Shabbat and Yom Tov, when it is forbidden to betroth, as stated in Orach Chaim, siman 339. However, if one transgresses and betroths, even deliberately, the betrothal is completely valid. Indeed, even a transaction done in violation of Halacha is valid, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, siman 208. All the more so with betrothal, some authorities permit betrothing on Shabbat from the outset if the man has no wife and children, as mentioned in Orach Chaim there. Betrothal at night is permitted even from the outset, and this is the custom in all our countries.

A wedding canopy (chuppah) without betrothal (kiddushin) is not considered as betrothal – thus have agreed the majority of our rabbis, and even if she is pure, for more than three forms of acquisition we do not find for a woman, and so it appears from the straightforward reading of the Talmudic discussion at the beginning of Kiddushin. However, some of our rabbis wrote that it is a doubtful law, and she would require a divorce (get) out of doubt, and so it is ruled in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. Therefore, if she received betrothal from another, she needs a divorce from both. And if she was betrothed after the chuppah whether her status is as married or only betrothed – this will be explained with God's help in section 61, where it will also explain what a chuppah is and the law of a chuppah for a menstruant woman (niddah). In betrothal, there is no difference for all the decisors whether she was a menstruant or not, and even according to the Rambam who holds that a chuppah for a menstruant does not render her as married, in betrothal he agrees that it renders her as fully betrothed, and specifically for a chuppah he holds that we require a chuppah that is fit for intimacy and not for betrothal, and even in chuppah most decisors disagree with him [see what the Rambam writes in chapter 4 of Hilchot Ishut, halacha 12].

[The Laws of Betrothal with Money and the Appropriate Language for Betrothal, consisting of 42 sections] How is betrothal with money performed? He gives her, in the presence of two qualified witnesses who are not related to either the man or each other, a coin or something of equivalent value, which should not be less than a perutah (the value of a half barley weight of silver). The witnesses must see him give her the money or its equivalent and hear him say, "You are betrothed to me" or "You are engaged to me" or "You are my wife" or any expression that implies betrothal and is understood as such in that place, provided she understands that it is a term of betrothal. Rambam writes in Chapter 3 that he says to her, "You are betrothed to me with this," and our custom is to say, "You are betrothed to me with this ring according to the law of Moses and Israel." This is the preferred form of betrothal. However, if he did not say "with this" or "with this ring"—it does not invalidate it at all. The Tur does not mention this language at all. But if he did not say "to me" and just said "You are betrothed" without specifying to whom—she is certainly not betrothed, as it is not clear whom she is betrothed to, and unclear intentions are not considered valid intentions. "To me" means to be mine, and "betrothed" is a term of consecration, meaning she is forbidden to everyone else like a consecrated item for my sake. This is as if he said, "You are betrothed and forbidden to everyone else for my sake." But without saying "to me," he has not betrothed her to himself. All this applies when he betroths her suddenly without preparation. But if they prepared themselves for the betrothal—even if he did not say "to me," it does not invalidate it. For example, in our country where the betrothal takes place under the chuppah, it is understood that he is betrothing her to himself. This is no less valid than if he had discussed betrothal matters with her and then betrothed her immediately—even in silence, she is betrothed, as will be explained. Certainly, in such a case, and further details will be clarified in section 27.

In our country, the common custom is to perform the betrothal with a ring made of silver or gold, and specific witnesses are designated to observe the betrothal. It is proper to do so since there are many relatives present at the wedding ceremony [see Tosafot Makkot 7a, s.v. Shmuel]. He says to her in their presence, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this ring according to the law of Moses and Israel," and the witnesses see him place the ring on her finger. The use of a ring for betrothal has a proper basis in the wisdom of the Kabbalah [see Tikunei Zohar Tikkun 5 regarding the closed Mem representing 'help from offspring,' and examine this well]. The phrase "according to the law of Moses and Israel" has a foundation in the Talmud, which states in several places that anyone who betroths does so with the understanding of the Rabbis [see Tosafot Ketubot 3a].

Some say that one should not initially perform Kiddushin (betrothal) with a coin [Beit Shmuel], and the reason is similar to why one cannot acquire property through exchange with a coin, because its value is based on its form, and a coin's significance lies in its form, which is subject to change when the king decrees a new form [Bava Metzia 45b]. Similarly, with Kiddushin, one might say that a woman's intention is based on the form [Hagahot Mordechai, Kiddushin Chapter 1]. However, this reasoning holds no validity, as the primary method of acquiring through money is derived from the term "taking," as stated, and the main form of "taking" is with a coin. Whether or not the form is annulled, it is still considered money in the end. Exchange is different because it requires a specific item, similar to a shoe [see there in Rashi]. Additionally, it is explicitly proven in the Talmud and the poskim (decisors) that no one considers this an issue. Furthermore, from a logical standpoint, it is not acceptable at all, and the custom has already been to perform Kiddushin with a coin when there is no ring, and no one hesitates about this [according to my opinion]. One should not perform Kiddushin with a loan or a promissory note, and the details of these laws will be explained in Siman 28, with God's help. Similarly, some question whether in our times a perutah (a small coin) has any significance at all, and we have already explained in Choshen Mishpat Siman 190 that it is improper to say this, as all of the Sages' measures were received from Moses at Sinai, and even now a perutah has some significance as explained there. [And regarding a coin, the Avnei Miluim also wrote as stated, and the Mekneh in Siman 50 struggled with this, and there is no reason for it].

The custom is to sanctify with his right hand and place the ring on the index finger of her right hand, and there should be no interposition between the hands and the ring. Therefore, if they are wearing gloves, they should remove them. However, all this is not essential but rather for enhancement and as a sign of blessing, for even if he places it in her lap or within her domain, she is betrothed. The early authorities wrote that he should show the ring to the witnesses and the rabbi should ask them if it is worth a perutah (a minimal value), and they answer "yes." But this is not the custom. Nevertheless, it is certain that the witnesses should be careful to see how he places the ring on her finger. This is a strict law that the witnesses need to see the object with which she is being sanctified, as stated in section 42 when betrothing with an item ready before us. The custom is to place the ring on the finger next to the thumb, and legally there is no strictness about this.

The early authorities wrote that if one betroths a woman with land, she is betrothed, and all the more so with something attached to the land [Ran]. And this is the main ruling, for this also has monetary value, and in betrothal, we do not require the item to come into her possession at the time of betrothal, as even with "Give a maneh to so-and-so," she is betrothed, as stated in Siman 28. The witnesses need to see the item with which she is being betrothed only when it is present before them, but when she is being betrothed with something not before them, just as she does not need to see it at the time of the act, they also do not need to see it. And that which will be explained in Siman 32 regarding betrothal with a document, where there is a dispute among the authorities if she can be betrothed with a document written on something attached to the ground, is because betrothal with a document is derived from "and she shall leave and become," and just as a get (divorce document) is invalid if written on something attached, so too is a betrothal document, but not with monetary betrothal. Some of the early authorities wanted to say that one cannot betroth with something attached to the ground, but all our Rabbis did not agree with him [there]. And a clear proof for this is from the Tosefta in Kiddushin [Chapter 4], where it teaches that if one betroths with an Asherah tree, she is not betrothed because it is forbidden to benefit from it. This implies clearly that with a regular tree, she is betrothed [and so it appears in Tosafot, Kiddushin 5a, "since," see there].

It is obvious that kiddushin (betrothal) must be with the woman's consent. However, the fulfillment of a condition in kiddushin can possibly be valid even against her will. For example, if he said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me on the condition that I give you two hundred zuz," and he gave it to her—against her will, she is betrothed [Ran, Perek "Mi She'Achazo"]. In the case of a gift, giving it against one's will is not considered giving, but in the case of paying a debt, it is considered giving. And in the fulfillment of a condition, which is similar to a debt and a gift, we also hold that it is considered giving [like the opinion of Rava in Gittin 75]. Similarly, in the case of a get (divorce document), if he said to her, "This is your get on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz," and she gave it to him—against his will, it is a valid get [there in the name of the Gaon]. Some say that it is a doubtful kiddushin because we are uncertain whether it is considered giving or not [Rashba there], and similarly with a get [there]. In the matter of a get, it is explained in Siman 163 that the opinion of the Rambam is also that it is a doubtful case of law, and therefore, in kiddushin, it would also be doubtful. Some say that according to the Rambam, it is clear to him that it is considered giving, but he was stringent with a get because of the severity of the prohibition on a married woman. If she remarried, she does not have to leave [the second husband] [Magid Mishneh on Rambam, Chapter 8 of Divorce]. Therefore, in kiddushin, she is certainly betrothed, but it is proper to be stringent if she also accepted kiddushin from someone else to require a get from the outset. The opinion of the Rosh and the Tur there is that it is doubtful.

However, according to what our master the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Joseph Karo) wrote in the name of the Rashba (Rabbi Shlomo ibn Aderet) in Siman 143, there is a distinction between divorce (Gittin) and betrothal (Kiddushin). Even if we say that giving against one's will is considered giving, this means that the giver has fulfilled his obligation and has acquired what is in his hand. Therefore, the woman who has the bill of divorce (Get) in her hand and gave him the two hundred zuz has fulfilled her condition and acquired the bill of divorce in her hand. Similarly, one who swore to give a gift to his friend can give it against his will and be exempt. However, for the giving to be effective regarding those to whom it was given against their will - no, for it is impossible for a person to acquire for others against their will. Therefore, if a woman says, "Give me a maneh (a certain amount of money) and I will be betrothed to you," and the man swore to give it to her and gave it to her against her will - he has fulfilled his oath, but she is not betrothed. So it is written.

And according to this, there are those who say that in the case of betrothal, under any circumstances, she is not betrothed through giving against her will, because for her it is not considered acceptance against her will. However, in truth, there is no relevance to conditions in betrothal, for certainly in the essence of betrothal it is not considered acceptance when the giving is against her will. But when the betrothal is about something else and the giving of the money is merely a condition where he says, "on the condition that I will give you two hundred zuz," since he gave her even against her will, he fulfills his condition and the betrothal is valid if we say that giving against one's will is considered giving. There are those who wanted to differentiate between when he said it and when she said it – but there is no basis for these things.

Even with a condition, if he said, "On the condition that I give you two hundred zuz," and he gave her the equivalent value in goods against her will – there is no doubt at all. Since he changed from money to goods and also did so against her will, it is not considered a valid giving [Beit Shmuel in the name of Maharit]. And even though without being against her will, when he changed from what was stipulated, it is not considered a valid giving, as is written in Siman 143 regarding a get (divorce document). Nevertheless, if it was not against her will and she agreed to the other item, some say that it is considered a valid giving, as is written there. However, when it is against her will in such a case, it is not considered a valid giving. And there is someone who is uncertain and says that even against her will and with a change, it is considered a doubtful kiddushin [Beit Shmuel], and this is the main ruling that it is considered a doubtful kiddushin [and even Maharit did not write that it is definitely not kiddushin, see there]. And in Siman 143, this will be further explained with the help of God.

And there are those who say that even with a condition and without a change, sometimes it does not constitute a valid Kiddushin (marriage) when given against her will. For example, if he did not say "on the condition" but rather "behold, you are betrothed to me if I give you two hundred zuz," specifically with "on the condition" it is as if it is "from now" and the Kiddushin takes effect beforehand, and the two hundred zuz is to fulfill the condition. Then it is indeed doubtful whether the giving against her will is considered valid or not. But with "if I give," where the Kiddushin only takes effect at the time of giving the money, it does not constitute Kiddushin against her will, as explained in Section 7. These are reasonable words, for although regarding a get (divorce document) even with "if," it is doubtful whether it is considered "from now" or not, as stated in Section 144, this is because the time demonstrates that she was divorced then at the time of writing the get. But with Kiddushin, it is not considered "from now," as stated in Section 38. Therefore, it is possible to say that specifically when he betrothed her with money or cohabitation and said to her, "behold, you are betrothed to me if I give you two hundred zuz," but if he betrothed her with a document and it has a date written in it, it is doubtful Kiddushin like with "on the condition." However, in Section 32, it will be explained that a date in Kiddushin is insignificant.

And know, that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Siman 143, wrote in the name of his teacher that according to the opinion that giving against one's will is considered giving – even if the recipient did not accept it, it is considered giving. However, according to the opinion that it is not considered giving – against one's will is nothing. But if the recipient accepted it, even if he was forced to accept it, according to all opinions it is considered giving. Therefore, any case of doubtful betrothal that we discussed regarding giving against one's will is only when the recipient did not accept it. But if he accepted it, it is certainly betrothal even if the acceptance was against his will, and there are those who disagree with him in this matter. It appears to me that even according to his teacher's opinion, this is only in a condition of "on the condition that," but in a condition of "if," and all the more so when she says, "Give me a maneh and I will be betrothed to you" – it is not betrothal even if she accepted it, if the acceptance was against her will. For how is it possible to betroth a woman against her will? And "on the condition that" is different, for the betrothal has already taken effect and this is merely the fulfillment of the condition. [And from Rashi in Arakhin 32a, s.v. "against his will," that she deposited it in his house, etc., and from Tosafot in Gittin 75a, s.v. "implies," it appears like those who disagree with his teacher. See there and examine carefully.]

We have already written in Section 1 that she must understand that this is the language of betrothal. If she does not understand, it is meaningless, for a woman is not betrothed except with her knowledge. However, she is not believed to say that she did not understand, especially if it is a familiar expression like "You are betrothed to me," as it is likely that she knows. Nevertheless, if she says she did not understand, it is considered doubtful betrothal. If we know for certain that she did not understand, there is no betrothal at all. This matter depends on the circumstances; if it happened without preparation, it is possible that she did not understand. This matter depends on the judgment of the court according to the circumstances. All this applies when he did not first speak to her about matters of betrothal, but if he spoke to her first and then gave her something for betrothal, even if we know that she did not understand, she is betrothed, for even if he gave it in silence, she is betrothed, as will be explained.

If a man was speaking with a woman about matters of betrothal and in the course of the conversation, he gave her money or its equivalent in the presence of witnesses and she accepted it – this constitutes betrothal. It is certain that he gave it for the purpose of betrothal and she accepted it for the same purpose. Even though unspoken intentions are not considered valid, this is not an unspoken intention and it is as if he said, "Behold, you are betrothed to me," since they were engaged in matters of betrothal. All the more so, if he used the language of betrothal and she did not understand it, it is still considered betrothal since verbalization is not essential.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 3: If he was speaking with the woman about matters of betrothal and she agreed, and he then betrothed her without specifying or saying anything but merely gave her something or engaged in intercourse – since they were engaged in the matter, it suffices and there is no need for specification. 

He added the term “she agreed” – meaning she said “yes,” but if she was silent, it does not help. This is not implied by all the decisors. However, Maimonides’ intention was not necessarily that she must say "yes," because her statement does not affect the betrothal, which requires his declaration. Rather, his main intention was that we should know she consented to the matter of betrothal he discussed with her. In this, all the decisors agree that if we do not know of her prior consent and she accepted the betrothal, it does not help. Perhaps she did not accept it for betrothal, and in any case, this is not definite betrothal but doubtful.

Even with intercourse, although it may be apparent that she consented to the betrothal, if we did not see clear indications of her consent when he spoke with her, it cannot be considered definite betrothal but doubtful. Perhaps she intended merely for promiscuity, as it is not always said that a person does not engage in intercourse promiscuously, as stated in Chapter 10 of the laws of divorce, law 19. This is especially true for a woman of light mind.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles wrote: Some say that we do not need the conversation to be on exactly the same topic, but rather that the conversation should shift from one related topic to another, meaning that they are not discussing betrothal but matters relating to their marriage. This is implied in the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Maaser Sheni, Chapter 4. Practically, one should be stringent according to both opinions, and if she extended her hand and received betrothal from another man, she requires a get (divorce document) from both. Most of the authorities agree with the first opinion, as this is implied by the Talmudic discussion, and this is the opinion of the Rif, the Rambam, and the Rosh. According to the other opinion, it must be said that Shmuel and Rav Ashi refer to shifting from one related topic to another, and they consider the debate to be between Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Eliezer bar Shimon holds like Rabbi Yose, as explained by the Gra in his commentary on Section 11.

It is further written that some say we do not need to speak directly with her, but it is sufficient if the conversation occurs in her presence. This means that if he is speaking with others in her presence about the matter of betrothal and she remains silent, and from the context, he gives her something and she accepts it, this constitutes betrothal, and we presume she consents. However, from the language of the Rambam, which we cited in section 13, even according to what he wrote, it does not necessarily mean that she must explicitly say "yes." Nonetheless, we need clear knowledge that she consents. In such a case, certainly all the authorities agree as written there. There are those who hold that even if we do not have explicit knowledge that she consents, since she remained entirely silent, her acceptance indicates her consent. However, in practice, the law should be decided stringently that this is a case of doubtful betrothal. [And what was written that this seems implied by the Tur requires examination, as he previously wrote "with her" as mentioned there. See the glosses of Mordechai at the end of Gittin, where there is a dispute about this. The intention of the respondent is that if so, one could also inquire in a favorable manner, perhaps she can claim she did not understand, as per the opinion of the Maggid Mishneh cited in the Beit Shmuel section 5, which resolves the perplexity of the Vilna Gaon in section 13. Also, what was written in section 11 from the Tosefta in chapter 2, our version does not align with the Jerusalem Talmud, as mentioned there, and examine this closely.]

There are those who are uncertain when he first engaged her and afterwards gave her money without saying anything, whether this is also considered as speaking about matters of betrothal or not [Mei'ri, Kiddushin 3]. And it appears to me that this is a dispute among the early authorities regarding the concern of gifts (sablonot). For those who hold that the concern of gifts is that we are worried that with these gifts she was betrothed through an agent, they must hold that engagement is considered as speaking with her about matters of betrothal. And those who hold that the concern of gifts is that she was betrothed beforehand, there is no necessity for this [See Rashi 50a s.v. "we are concerned about gifts" who writes that one who engaged, etc., and the Tosafot wrote: "And if he engaged, what of it?" etc., see there].

There is uncertainty regarding a situation where a man spoke with a woman about matters of betrothal and then betrothed her in silence, whether this constitutes a definite betrothal. This may specifically apply when he spoke with her about the betrothal in front of witnesses, but if he spoke with her privately, even if the betrothal was performed in front of witnesses, since he did not say anything at the time of giving the item of betrothal, the witnesses do not know for what purpose he gave it to her—whether for betrothal or as a gift—and it is as if he betrothed without witnesses. Alternatively, it could be that since the witnesses saw the giving of the item of betrothal, it is sufficient. Regarding betrothal by document or cohabitation, it seems clear that the witnesses do not need to hear the discussion about betrothal matters, for even if they did not hear, they see the document which states "Behold, you are betrothed to me," and likewise if they witnessed the seclusion. However, with betrothal by money, there is uncertainty, and the matter requires further investigation to determine the law. [And regarding gifts according to Rashi's interpretation, there is no proof, because there the witnesses knew she was his betrothed, and from several responses, it appears that if the witnesses did not know the purpose of the giving, it is as if there were no witnesses, and this requires further investigation.]

He said to her, "You are my wife," "You are obligated to me," "You are acquired by me," "You are my betrothed," "You are mine," "You are under my authority," "You are taken by me" – she is betrothed if she understood his words. If she says she did not understand, she is believed, and there is a concern for doubtful betrothal. See what is written in Section 12. However, the man is not believed to say that he did not intend for betrothal, since these expressions are certainly expressions of betrothal. Nevertheless, in expressions of doubt which will be explained, he is also believed to say that he did not intend for betrothal but rather for work. Some argue that even in definite expressions, he is believed stringently to say that he did not intend for betrothal. The primary opinion is the first one, but if she also accepted betrothal from another person, she needs a get (divorce document) from the second one as a stringency. When he says that he intended for betrothal and she also says that she understood it was for betrothal, even if the witnesses did not know that she understood, it is still a definite betrothal. This is not like betrothing without witnesses, since they heard the expression of betrothal and know that the man intended for betrothal even if they did not know whether she understood. The main aspect of betrothal is from the man, and she also intended in her heart for betrothal. It is obvious that if they previously discussed marriage matters, it is definitely betrothal in any case, even if she did not understand that this was an expression of betrothal, since even silence is sufficient as stated, and there is no difference in these expressions whether said in Hebrew or in a foreign language.

There are expressions that are uncertain if they are terms of betrothal or not, such as if he said to her, "You are destined for me." In the context of a Hebrew maidservant, this is a term of betrothal. Similarly, if he said to her, "You are unique to me" or "You are my help" or "opposite me" in the sense of "I will make a helpmate for him corresponding to him," or "my rib," or "my enclosed one," or "under me," as these expressions are mentioned in the context of a man's relationship, as it is written, "And Hashem God built the rib... and closed up the flesh under it" (Genesis 2:22). Similarly, if he said, "my restraint," meaning that she should be restrained with him together, or "my possession" – she is betrothed in uncertainty. All these expressions can also be interpreted otherwise, that she should assist him in his household affairs.

And when do these constitute doubtful betrothal? When he first spoke with her about matters of betrothal, then it can be said that he intended betrothal, or perhaps he changed his mind from the matter of betrothal and is now pleasing her for household work. But if he did not first speak with her about matters of betrothal, these expressions mean nothing, for she certainly would not know what he was saying. Therefore, even if he intended betrothal, it is nothing. Hence, if she also said that she intended to become betrothed with this expression, it is a doubtful betrothal. And some say that if they were not previously engaged in matters of betrothal, even if both say they intended betrothal, it is nothing, for only when discussing matters of betrothal does silence also work, and in such cases, it helps if they say they intended betrothal and the expressions are not of retraction from betrothal. But to become betrothed with these expressions is impossible. And even if he spoke with her about matters of betrothal, if he says he intended for work and not for betrothal, he is believed.

One who says "You are my betrothed" is also considered doubtful betrothal, for regarding a half-slave woman it is written "and she is betrothed to a man" (Leviticus 19:20), as is explained in the Talmudic discussions. Rambam ruled that it is a valid expression, and it is written that he had a different version in the Gemara, and furthermore, according to what we maintain that this verse regarding the half-slave woman refers to someone who is half-slave and half-free, as explained in Chapter 4, it follows that even for a free woman this is an expression of betrothal. Although the expression "assigned to me" is considered doubtful, this is because "assignment" there means designation, as is evident in Jeremiah, and it is borrowed to mean betrothal. But the term "betrothed" has no similar usage in scripture, as Rashi explains. Onkelos translated it as "affixed to a man," and it is close to the expression "risked his life to die" (Judges 5:18), meaning she dedicated herself to this man, which is closer to the concept of betrothal. Nevertheless, in practice, we rule stringently according to the majority of decisors, and so ruled our master the Rema, that it is considered doubtful betrothal.

Rabbi Shlomo ben Aderet (Rashba) wrote in a responsum: If a man says to a woman, "You are my betrothed" – it is not equivalent to saying "You are my wife," for the term "betrothed" is not used for betrothal. A woman is not considered betrothed until she has been with her husband or has entered the chuppah (wedding canopy), and this was brought by our Rabbi, the Rema. All the later authorities agree that in any case, this expression is better than any of the expressions of doubt that have been clarified. It is definitely a case of doubtful betrothal even if he did not speak with her about matters of betrothal, and when they spoke about matters of betrothal – this expression is certainly considered betrothal. [And regarding a document – see in the Mekneh].

If he gave her money or an item of equivalent value and said to her, "Behold, you are my beloved" or "I am giving this to you out of love and affection" – we are concerned about the validity of the betrothal, because perhaps he meant that he is giving it to her so that there will be love and affection between them as a married couple. This is no less significant than expressions such as "dedicated to me" or "designated for me," and it could even be considered more significant. Even if they had not previously discussed the matter of betrothal, she would require a get (divorce document). However, from the wording of our teacher, the Rema, it does not seem to be so. Nevertheless, it is obvious that if they stated that they intended it as a betrothal, she would require a get. And if they had previously discussed the matter of betrothal and he used this expression, it appears to be a definite betrothal. There is an opinion that differentiates: if he said "so that there will be love" between them – it is a definite betrothal, but if he said "because of love" – it is only a doubtful betrothal, as its implication is because of love that already exists. According to this, even if he said "Behold, you are my beloved" – it would be a doubtful betrothal. And if they say that they did not intend betrothal at all, but rather promiscuity, perhaps they are believed.

In cases of uncertain expressions, our teacher the Rema wrote: Some say that although these expressions do not work unless he spoke with her about matters of betrothal, nevertheless, if she says that she accepted it for the sake of betrothal, it is considered doubtful betrothal. Even if he gave it to her in silence and did not speak at all, if both he and she say that they intended it for betrothal, it is considered betrothal. This is his concluding statement. It is clear from his words that in cases of uncertain expressions, it depends on her; if she says she intended it for betrothal, even if he says he did not intend, he is not believed. There are those who disagree and hold that he is also believed if he says he did not intend for betrothal, even if she says she did intend. If both of them and also the witnesses say that they intended it for betrothal, nevertheless it is only considered doubtful betrothal, requiring her to get a divorce. If she accepted betrothal from another, she needs a divorce from both. Some imply from his words that if the witnesses also testify that they intended for betrothal, it is considered definite betrothal if they had previously discussed matters of betrothal. If they were not engaged in matters of betrothal, it is not even considered doubtful betrothal, even if they intended for betrothal, and this is not correct.

And in the case where he gave her [the ring] without speaking with her about the matter of betrothal and gave it to her in silence, and both say that they intended it for the sake of betrothal, it is considered betrothal—the later authorities agreed that this is only doubtful betrothal. How can one say that when there was no conversation at all and he gave it to her in silence, it would be definite betrothal? This is akin to unspoken intentions, and it is more reasonable to say that it is not even doubtful betrothal. However, it is difficult to exempt them without a get (divorce document), and all the more so if the witnesses also understood it to be for the sake of betrothal. Similarly, if they had already reached an agreement and he then gave her [the ring] in silence, it can be compared to gifts given before betrothal. And if she was willing to be betrothed but they disagreed on details such as the dowry or other matters, and she stood and was betrothed in silence, it is also considered doubtful betrothal.

He also wrote that in a situation where there was no valid betrothal, even if he later says to her, "You are betrothed to me," he must take the money from her and give it to her again with the intention of betrothal. The explanation is as follows: for instance, if they completely stopped talking about the matter of betrothal, and he gave it to her in silence without intending it for betrothal, or with uncertain expressions, and they did not previously talk at all about the matter of betrothal, and after giving it to her, he said to her, "You are betrothed to me" — he must take it from her and give it to her again, and the initial giving is not sufficient to make it a definite betrothal. This is not similar to what will be explained in Siman 31 regarding appraisal, where it is not necessary to take it back from her — there, he had initially given it for betrothal, but it required appraisal, so the betrothal was effective from the start, like with money held in deposit, as will be explained in Siman 28, where if he betrothed her with his deposit that was in her possession and she said "yes," she is betrothed even if he did not take it from her, because the money was his. But here, what he gave her initially, she can claim she received it as a gift. Similarly, it is not comparable to a get (divorce document) as explained in Siman 136, where it is not necessary to take it back from her, because with a get, the concept of a gift does not apply. Although we hold that generally, when a person gives something to another, we do not assume it was given as a gift but as a deposit, as stated in Choshen Mishpat Siman 373, and thus even if she did not receive it initially as a betrothal, she cannot claim it was a gift but a deposit, and with a deposit, it is not necessary to take it back from her, as mentioned, nevertheless, this is not an absolute rule. Our master the Rema follows his view in Choshen Mishpat Siman 146, Section 18, regarding someone who paid twice for a piece of land, the seller can say that the second time he gave it as a gift. There, too, the later authorities challenged him. However, in our commentary there, Section 21, we explained his reasoning: because the seller could claim that after the first purchase, he repurchased the field from the buyer and then the buyer bought it back from him, and this money is the purchase money. Therefore, he can also claim that he gave it as a gift, for he would not give it as a deposit because the buyer might say he repurchased it from him a second time after buying it back, as explained there. Therefore, here too, she is believed to claim it was a gift, for he would not give it as a deposit because she might say she received it for betrothal. According to the opinion of our master the Rema, which we explained in Section 24, even if they did not speak at all and he gave it to her in silence, if they intended it for betrothal, it is considered betrothal. Accordingly, even in such a case, it does not suffice to be certain betrothal if he did not take it back from her, for the reason explained. Know that according to what we have written, the law is correct and resolves all the challenges posed by the great later authorities. However, it is certain that she requires a get from him, because the matter remains in doubt. [See the Gra in Subsection 21 who also resolved it, and in Choshen Mishpat there he challenged it, and according to our explanation, everything fits well, and examine it closely].

And furthermore, we hold in the case of [betrothing] his sister that the money is considered a gift, and the reason is that in the case of his sister we say that because of their closeness, he gave her a gift [Rosh, first chapter of Bava Metzia, end of siman 39]. Similarly, here, since he had previously spoken with her about matters of betrothal and also when he used ambiguous language, nevertheless, there is some closeness and love between them, we can rightfully say that he gave her the money as a gift, just like with his sister [See Lechem Mishneh, Chapter 6 of Laws of Acquisition, Halacha 20]. Furthermore, it seems to me that if she said that she received the money for betrothal, even if he does not agree with her, still the money does not return. And although it will be explained in Siman 50 that in any case where there is no betrothal, the money returns, nevertheless it is explained there that in a place where a get (divorce document) is required, the money does not return [See Beit Shmuel, there, siman 5]. Here, it seems that if she says she knows that he also intended it for betrothal, in any case, a get is required. Therefore, we are witnesses that he would not give her a deposit lest she claim this, and see what is written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 256, Se'if 7 [and examine this carefully].

It has already been explained in section 1 that if one says "You are betrothed" and does not say "to me," it is not considered a valid betrothal, because incomplete expressions that do not clearly indicate intent are not valid. When he does not say "to me," it is not clear to whom he is betrothing her. This is also the ruling regarding vows in Yoreh De'ah, section 206. This is the main ruling in practice, although some of our rabbis have been stringent and require a get (bill of divorce) [Hagahot Maimoniot, end of Gittin]. Their reasoning is that since regarding a get it is questioned in the Gemara (Gittin 85a) whether one needs to write "and this shall be to you from me a document of divorce," which implies that he is divorcing her with this get and it would be a clear expression, or if it is not necessary, and the matter was not resolved. Therefore, in a similar situation with betrothal, it remains a doubtful case of law. The first opinion holds that it is not comparable, because in the case of a get, even if "and this" is not written, it is clear that he is divorcing her because no one divorces someone else's wife. But regarding betrothal, it could be that he is betrothing her to someone else [Tosafot, Kiddushin 5a]. It is clear that if he was previously speaking with her about matters of betrothal, she is certainly betrothed, because in such a case, it is a clear expression that he is betrothing her. All the more so if they made preparations for the matter, like wedding festivities, she is betrothed as explained in section 1. [See Beit Shmuel, sub-section 14, that where there is additional evidence, one need not be concerned with dissenting opinions, but the Gra, sub-section 23, was very concerned with this opinion].

And similarly, if a man betrothed one woman with complete betrothal and said to another woman in her presence, "You are betrothed," but did not say "to me" – it is considered complete betrothal, requiring a get (divorce document) according to all opinions, because this is like indicative expressions, just as he betrothed the first one to himself, so also the second one. As we find regarding nazirite vows, if one says "I shall be" while a nazirite is passing before him, it is as if he said "I shall be a nazirite." Nevertheless, if she accepted betrothal from another man, she requires a get from both, and it is not similar to nazirite vows. In betrothal, one could argue the opposite: since he betrothed one woman to himself, he did not betroth the second one to himself, as it is not customary for people to marry two women, even in places where Rabbeinu Gershom's enactment has not spread. Similarly, if a man betrothed one woman and gave her two prutot (coins) and said to her, "You are betrothed to me," and said to another woman in her presence, "And you" – it is a doubtful matter whether there is an indicative expression for betrothal, as if he said to her, "And you also be betrothed to me," or there is no indicative expression for betrothal, and it is as if he said to her, "You should witness the betrothal of the first one." [Nedarim 6b, and see what I wrote in Siman 37, Section 15].

When "to me" is not said and both parties claim they intended for betrothal, one must be stringent and require a get (divorce document) [Rashdam]. Similarly, if there were prior engagement discussions between them, it is considered as indicative gestures and is deemed betrothal, although there are those who disagree [See Ba’er Heitev, subparagraph 16], and therefore it is considered doubtful betrothal. If she knew in advance that his intention was to betroth her, it is considered as if he was discussing betrothal matters with her [ibid, subparagraph 17 in the name of Radbaz]. If he was discussing betrothal matters with her in the presence of witnesses and then went to seek other witnesses to betroth her before them, the matter is interrupted and there are no indicative gestures here. However, if he told the witnesses in her presence, "I do not wish to betroth her before you, and I am going to bring other witnesses to betroth her," it is considered indicative gestures [ibid]. If the witnesses say that they discussed betrothal matters before them and the man and woman deny it, the witnesses are believed, and likewise the reverse. Nonetheless, she requires a get because, according to their statement that they discussed betrothal matters, they intended for betrothal, and in such a case, even if they did not discuss betrothal matters, she requires a get as I have written [It appears to me], and witnesses cannot retract their testimony once given before a court, as once they have testified, they cannot retract their testimony as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 29, and there are several detailed laws regarding this, see there. If the witnesses contradict the judges, there is a dispute among the poskim [See Ba’er Heitev, subparagraph 15], and in Choshen Mishpat, section 23, it is explained that the judges are believed because they are more meticulous, see there.

There is an opinion that if, when he gave her the money, he said to her "I am giving it to you for the sake of betrothal," it is as if he said "to me." This is not considered an unclear statement (yadayim she-einan mochichot) but rather is considered a clear indication of his intention. This would be different from someone who begins a statement and does not complete it, leaving his intention unclear, such as saying "Behold, you are betrothed" without adding "to me." However, in this case, where he said, "I am giving it to you for the sake of betrothal," it is clear from his language that he is the one betrothing and she is the one being betrothed [Rivash, Siman 266]. 

And although this language could also be interpreted to mean that he is acting as an agent for another or that she is accepting it on behalf of someone else, we still say that a person does not abandon a mitzvah that is incumbent on him and delegate it to others [ibid.]. The main reasoning that the lack of the word "to me" invalidates the betrothal is because his statement is incomplete. Since he mentioned "you," he should also have mentioned "to me." But here, he mentioned himself by saying "I am" and mentioned her by saying "to you."

However, there is an opinion that if Reuven said to Rachel "I give you this for betrothal," this is not considered a clear statement [Milchamot Hashem, Hilchot Ishut, Chapter 3, in the name of the Rashba], as she might be accepting it on behalf of another or he might be giving it on behalf of another. A clear statement is only when it is evident from the language that he is betrothing this woman to himself. Therefore, the main ruling is that this is only a doubtful betrothal, and indeed this is worse than not saying "to me." When "to me" is lacking, at least it is clear that this woman is being betrothed, but it is unclear whether it is to this man or on behalf of another. But here, even this is not clear. 

Moreover, the first opinion does not definitively rule that it is certainly a betrothal but rather states that she should not be released without a get [see there in Rivash and in Choshen Mishpat, Sk 14]. If he said "I give you for betrothal," there are those who say it is nothing, as it can be said he is giving for the sake of betrothal but not betrothing with this [see Beit Shmuel, Sk 16]. Others say this is a certain betrothal, like saying "to me." In any case, it remains a doubt, and she requires a get. If she accepted betrothal from another, she requires a get from both. If he said "Take this for betrothal for your daughter" or "on behalf of your daughter," it is nothing since he did not say "I give you" [ibid.], though some are stringent in this [Choshen Mishpat]. If he said "I give you with the betrothal of your daughter," it is considered a clear statement [Rashdam, Siman 60].

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that one must use language that indicates the future, such as saying "These are betrothals" or "They will be betrothals." But if he only says "They are betrothals," it is nothing. This is not specifically future language, as even present language is acceptable, because "These are betrothals" is present language. The essence of betrothal is in the present, as he is betrothing her at this moment, and this is the primary formula of betrothal when he says "You are betrothed to me." The intention is to exclude past language. And although in sales and gifts, as explained in Choshen Mishpat Siman 245, past language is effective because it serves as an acknowledgment, as mentioned there, this is the reason sometimes past language is effective, such as "I have given this field to so-and-so," but in betrothal, when he betroths her now with a ring or money or something of equivalent value in front of witnesses, acknowledgment of the past is irrelevant. Additionally, in sales, only the acknowledgment of the giver and seller is effective, but the acknowledgment of the buyer and recipient is not effective. In betrothal, the man stands in the place of the buyer and recipient, as he is acquiring her, as it is written "When a man takes a wife." Therefore, if he says "This money is betrothal," it is nothing. Even though this language is also present, it is present language that implies the past, similar to acknowledgment. But "These are betrothals" is present language that implies the future. Similarly, in the nullification of a get in Siman 141, see there.

Some say that since "kiddushin" (betrothal) is in the sacred language (Hebrew), which prohibits her to everyone else like consecration, just as there is no difference between saying "this loaf is consecrated" and "it shall be consecrated," so too there is no difference between saying "this money is for kiddushin to you from me" and saying "kiddushin to you from me" [Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel]. But in truth, this is not a proper analogy. Certainly, if the sanctity were to fall upon the money as it falls upon the loaf, it would be a good expression. But in truth, the sanctity falls upon the woman, not upon the money [Mekneh and Even HaEzer]. Saying "this loaf is consecrated" is similar to saying "you are consecrated to me," indicating that she will be consecrated just as the loaf is consecrated. When he says "kiddushin to you," it indicates that the money will be sanctified. However, when he says "they are for kiddushin," it is as if he says that this money will be for kiddushin [in my opinion]. Some say that if he says "you are consecrated to me" without "behold" – it is doubtful kiddushin [Mekneh]. It is obvious that if he spoke about matters of kiddushin, it is always kiddushin.

In several responsa, stories have been brought, and similarly, in our times, incidents have occurred with mischievous boys playing with young girls and, in a joking and mocking manner, betrothing them. It is impossible to ascertain that their intention was solely for jest, or sometimes one genuinely desires to betroth her to extract money from her father. Since she lacks the understanding to throw back at him what he gave her, if there are doubts regarding the betrothal, such as with the language used to betroth her, or the doubt is about another matter of this sort, one should not apply all the stringencies that are applied to betrothal, so that the daughters of Israel do not become abandoned. Therefore, if according to the majority of decisors the betrothal does not take effect, even though there are a minority of decisors who are stringent in this matter, one should follow the majority and invalidate the betrothal. Consequently, this should not be permitted based on an individual authority but rather based on three distinguished rabbis who are knowledgeable in the sources of the opinions and reasons. This is how all the great rabbis of previous generations have conducted themselves.

It is written, "When a man takes a wife," which teaches that the marriage (kiddushin) is effected when he takes her to himself and says to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me." But not when he takes himself to her, such as if he says to her, "I am your husband," "I am your man," or "I am your betrothed." There is no concern here because it is the man who acquires, not the one being acquired. Therefore, even if he spoke to her about the matter of betrothal, it is nothing, as it is worse than silence because he ruined it with his speech.

Some are stringent when he spoke to her about the matter of betrothal, and some say that it is a complete betrothal (see Beit Shmuel 19), because it is specifically with this language that it cannot effect betrothal, but it is not worse than silence, and it is proper to be stringent and require a get (divorce document). The opinion of the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch aligns with the first opinion.

If he said both phrases together – "Behold, you are my wife and I am your husband" – it seems to me that it is a complete betrothal, for as soon as he says "Behold, you are my wife," she is betrothed, and the rest of his words are only words of love. Some say it is a doubtful betrothal because the Torah was particular that he acquires her, and here he acquires her and also gives himself to her (see Mekaneh), but this does not seem right. Certainly, if he first says, "I am your husband," and then says, "Behold, you are my wife," it is a doubtful betrothal. But in the reverse order, it is definite betrothal, for in betrothal, within the time it takes to speak, he cannot retract. And even though some say this is only stringent (Rashbam Bava Batra 130), nevertheless, this is when he retracts from the betrothal. But when he adds to the language of betrothal, it is definite betrothal. Furthermore, the opinion of many poskim is that even leniently, within the time it takes to speak, it is like after the time it takes to speak (Ran and Rosh Nedarim Chapter 7). See what I wrote in Siman 49, but if he only said, "I am your husband," even if he betrothed her with a document and it is written in it, "Behold, you are betrothed to me," it is not a betrothal, as in a get (divorce document), which will be explained in Siman 141 (Ba'er Heitev in the name of Rachash).

And our master, the Rema, wrote: If one gave money to another and said to him, "Behold, you are my father-in-law," but did not say, "Your daughter is betrothed to me" – this has no effect, end quote. For the Torah says "When a man takes a wife," meaning that the taking should be for the woman and not for her father. According to this, it is similar to one who says "I am your husband," which is not effective even if he spoke with her about marriage matters, as has been stated. And some say it is not similar, for when one says "I am your husband," he has violated the commandment of the Torah. However, when he says "Behold, you are my father-in-law," he has spoken in a hinting manner that he wishes to acquire his daughter, but it is not a clear expression. Therefore, even if he did not speak with her about marriage matters, there is concern and one should be stringent, and certainly if he spoke about marriage matters. [ChM 28, and see the Gra, section 31].

If she gave him the money for the betrothal and she said, "Behold, I am betrothed to you," "Behold, I am engaged to you," "Behold, I am your wife," she is not betrothed, as it is written, "When a man takes a woman" and not when a woman takes a man. And even though she stands like the seller in a sale, and the seller says, "My field is sold to you," nevertheless, in betrothal it is a decree of the Torah that he must take her and not that she sells herself to him, for this is not a sale but a sacred union. Therefore, he must give the money, as he is the one who takes her. And if he gave her the money and she said, "Behold, I am betrothed to you," even though it is not definite betrothal, it is still doubtful betrothal. For it can be said that the Torah only insists that he must take her with his money but does not insist on who must say the declaration. And if it resembles a sale, it is on the seller to say, as mentioned. According to many authorities, from the Torah it is not betrothal at all, only rabbinically we are concerned for the betrothal to require a divorce [get] [Rif], for from the Torah it specifically requires his declaration [Ran]. However, according to the Rambam, it is considered a Torah-level doubt. Nevertheless, it can be said that even if from the Torah it is doubtful betrothal, she does not need a get from the Torah, for in all Torah-level doubts we need to establish the existing status, and she is presumed to be single [there], and the get is only rabbinical. However, this does not seem to be the opinion of all the authorities [see there], and the reason seems to be that even from the Torah she cannot be released without a get. For even though as long as she does not become betrothed to another, we can presume her to be single, but if she receives betrothal from another, she is prohibited from marrying him by Torah law due to the doubt of the first betrothal. For how can we nullify the betrothal due to her presumption, after all, she has left her presumption whether from the first betrothal or the second betrothal [it appears to me].

There are times when if he gives [the item for betrothal] and she says [the formula], it constitutes complete betrothal. For instance, if they were engaged in the matter of betrothal, no verbal formula is required at all, as even silence is effective, as we have written. Certainly, her saying something does not invalidate it. It is unlike the ambiguous phrases discussed in section 19, where even talking about betrothal matters only results in a doubtful betrothal because one could argue that he intended to hire her for work, as explained there. However, if she used an explicit betrothal formula, how does her speech spoil it? After all, it is not worse than silence. Similarly, even if they were not engaged in betrothal matters at all, and when she said, "Behold, I am betrothed to you," he answered "Yes" afterwards, it constitutes complete betrothal. In several matters, "Yes" is considered equivalent to explicit speech, as in the cases of naziriteship and oaths. Some say to be stringent in such cases where they did not speak about betrothal matters, considering it only doubtful betrothal, because sometimes "Yes" can mean "No," as written in Choshen Mishpat, section 221. However, this is not related, for certainly "Yes" generally means "Yes" literally. There, it is because the context proves it, as seen in Tosafot in Bava Kamma 93 and more so according to Rashi's explanation there, and see also Beit Shmuel. Additionally, some have explained that in cases where he gives [the item for betrothal] and she says [the formula], it is doubtful betrothal because perhaps his silence indicated agreement to her words, and silence is considered as agreement. Certainly, when he explicitly says "Yes," this is the opinion of most authorities.

If she gave the money to him and he said, "Behold, you are betrothed to me," there is no betrothal at all here. This is not similar to the case where he gave and she said [the formula], which is doubtful, because in that case, there is a reason to be concerned that we might say that silence is as acceptance or that the Torah only strictly requires the giving [of the money]. And if the stringency is rabbinic, it is because it resembles a sale where the buyer gives the money and the seller says, "My field is sold to you." But in the reverse case where she gave, there is no doubt at all. And even though one of the early authorities [Ba'al Halachot Gedolot] was stringent in this case as well, nevertheless all the decisors do not hold this way, as it is explicitly proven in the Talmud [Kiddushin 5a]. Nonetheless, some of the later authorities were concerned with his opinion to require a get [see Bayit Chadash and Choshen Mishpat].

However, sometimes when she gives and he says [the formula], it constitutes complete kiddushin. For example, if he is an important person, and she has honor in that he accepted a gift from her, and this pleasure is worth a perutah, then it is indeed as if he gave and he said [the formula]. For he gave her the value of a perutah in the pleasure of his acceptance from her. The general rule of kiddushin is that it is not necessarily with money or something worth money, but anything that provides her with something worth a perutah, such as sanctifying her with the pleasure of forgiving a loan, as will be explained in Siman 28. Similarly, here he sanctifies her with the pleasure of his acceptance from her.

And this is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 5, Law 22: She said to him, "Take this dinar as a gift and betroth me," and he took it and said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with the benefit I received from you as a gift" – if he is an important person, she is betrothed, for she has enjoyment from him deriving benefit from her, and with this benefit, she betroths herself to him. It is explained from his words that if, in a regular case, she gave and he said – it is nothing, even if he is an important person. For if she did not specify that she is giving it as a gift, it is assumed she is giving it for betrothal, and this does not work. Therefore, she needs to specify that she is giving a gift with the intention that he betroth her, and he explains his words that he betroths her with the benefit of receiving this gift. It implies from his language that if any part of this is missing, it is not a valid betrothal. But the Tur wrote: If she gave and he said, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with what I received from you" – if he is an important person, she is betrothed, for she enjoys that he receives a gift from her as if he gave her the value of a perutah. It is explained from this that she does not need to say anything, and he does not need to specify "with the benefit I received from you as a gift," but rather simply "with what I received from you," and many of our rabbis hold this opinion. However, there are those who question this, for if she is silent, who can say that she intends for betrothal? And thus, this is only a doubtful betrothal, even if he initially spoke to her about betrothal matters. And also, from the language of the Talmud, it is explained that it refers to when she said, "Take this maneh and betroth me." And also, according to the Rambam's opinion, it is understood that since she said she would be betrothed to him and he said to her, "with the benefit I received from you," it is as if he gave and he said, and what is the novelty in this? It seems to me that what the Rambam wrote, that she should say, "Take this dinar and betroth me" – his intention is not that she needs to say it at the act itself, for her saying it is nothing, but it helps as an acknowledgment from her that she intends to be betrothed to him through this giving. And if there is a prior indication of intent, it is also effective, such as if they arranged a match between them, and it was discussed between them that he would betroth her through her giving to him. In this case, certainly, the Tur also agrees that if there is no indication of intent for betrothal, and she simply gave him a dinar, what does it help what he says to her, for she did not intend for betrothal at all. And they only disagree in that the Tur holds that it is sufficient for him to say to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with what I received from you," and the Rambam holds that this is not sufficient for a definitive betrothal. For according to this language, it implies that he betroths her with his receiving from her, and the Torah states that he should give to her and not she to him. And the Tur holds that even in a regular case, its meaning is that with the benefit of his receiving from her, he betroths her, and this is equivalent to a perutah if he is an important person.

And what is called an "important person" requires a scholar's investigation as to who is not considered important to permit her without a get (divorce document). And according to reasoning, it appears that when he is considered important to her and she accepts his honor, there is no one who is not considered important. However, from the words of the Rambam who requires him to say, "Be betrothed to me through the benefit of my acceptance from you," and she previously said, "Here, take this and I will be betrothed to you," and nevertheless, he requires that he be an important person, it is apparent that it does not help that she considers him important to her [unlike the opinion of Etzem Yosef brought in Ba'er Hetev, section 29]. And some of our teachers explained that an important person is called someone who is not accustomed to receiving gifts [Rashi], and certainly one cannot release her without a get as long as it has not been clarified that this person is not at all considered an important person. And there is someone who wants to say that this law pertains specifically when she gave him a dinar (a type of coin), and not with a prutah (a smaller coin), and it does not seem reasonable at all to differentiate between these [as Abaye refutes on page 11 from the daughters of Rabbi Yochanan].

There are those who wish to say that since it is he who gives and she who says, if they were engaged in matters of betrothal, she is betrothed because it is as if he said it. Consequently, even if she gave and she said, and they were engaged in that matter, it is as if she gave and he said. And therefore, if he is an important person, she would be betrothed to him. However, this is not so. The reason that she is betrothed when he gives and she says, while they are engaged in that matter, is not because it is as if he said it, but rather the reason is that even in silence, it would be a betrothal. But when she gives and he says, for an important person, there must specifically be a verbal statement according to both the Rambam and the Tur, as is written. And the amount of the money for betrothal has already been explained to be a perutah or the value of a perutah, and this will be further clarified, with God's help, in Siman 31.

[One does not betroth with stolen items, a loan, or items prohibited for benefit, and if one betroths with a deposit, and it contains 97 sections]

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 5, Law 7: One who betroths a woman with stolen goods, theft, or by force, if the owners despaired and it is known that the person acquired the item through their despair, then she is betrothed. If not, she is not betrothed. End of quote. Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, copied this in Section 1, and Rabbi Rema wrote on this: If he betrothed her with Egyptian theft, she is betrothed. If he betrothed her with regular theft after despair alone, she is rabbinically betrothed. End of quote. All this needs clarification. From the words of the Rambam, it is clear that for both theft and stolen goods, it must be known that the owners despaired, but in general, it is not considered despair. However, we hold that even generally it is considered despair in theft (as the Rabbis of Bava Kama 114 hold), and as the Rambam himself wrote in Chapter 24 of Hilchot Keilim, Law 7, and as the Tur wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Section 368, and this is also the opinion of most decisors (see Shach there, Subsection 2). 

Some say that regarding betrothal by Torah law, we do not say that general theft is considered the owner's despair unless it is known that they despaired, then the betrothal is complete, and if she receives betrothal from another, she does not need a divorce. But as long as it is not known that they despaired, she needs a divorce from the other as well, but in any case, she is rabbinically betrothed and needs a divorce whether from a thief or a robber (Bach and Beit Shmuel, Subsection 1). The Rambam's language implies that if not, she is not betrothed at all. Moreover, in a robbery where by law there is no general despair, why should we require a divorce in general, and such a novel point should have been explained by the Rambam. Some say that what the Rambam wrote "if not, she is not betrothed" means that if it is certain they did not despair, and he is not referring to the general case (Chidushei Maharam at the end of Subsection 1). Therefore, it must be said that what he wrote "if the owners despaired" means each case according to its law – a thief even in general, and a robber when it is known, and his language does not bear this interpretation.

However, based on what I have explained previously in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 361, Se'if 5, that the Rambam contradicts himself in several places on this matter and omits all this debate about whether generic theft and robbery constitute despair (yeush) or not, and we explained there his reasoning: the reason that theft generally involves despair and not robbery is because in the case of theft, the owner does not know who stole from him to make a claim, unlike in the case of robbery [Rosh, Keilim Chapter 26, Mishnah 8]. According to this, there is no fixed rule in this law. If people saw the thief leaving the house and hiding the items under his cloak, even in the case of theft, the owner does not despair. Similarly, if a robber took something privately, the owner would despair. Only in cases affecting others do we assume that generic theft involves the owner's despair and not robbery. However, in matters related to the thief or robber themselves, such as if someone betrothed a woman with stolen or robbed items and similar cases, the thief or robber must know how they stole or robbed and whether the owner despaired or not, as explained there in Se'if 9. Therefore, it is appropriate for the Rambam to state "if the owners despaired," as the thief or robber themselves should know whether the owners despaired based on the nature of the theft or robbery.

And this that he wrote that extortion is considered like robbery, it is explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 34, that an extortionist is someone who takes his fellow's object against his will and pays him money for it. And even though it is explained there that his disqualification is only rabbinic, nevertheless, as long as the owner has not despaired, the object is not his, and he cannot use it to betroth a woman [see Beit Shmuel]. And this that his disqualification is not from the Torah is because he is not a complete robber since he pays money for it. And even though he transgresses "Do not covet" as it says there in Siman 359, nevertheless, since people do not perceive the prohibition of "Do not covet" unless it is taken without money [see Bava Metzia 5a], therefore, he is not disqualified as a witness from the Torah. Furthermore, on the contrary, when he transgresses "Do not covet," it is possible that then the betrothal is valid, since one does not transgress "Do not covet" unless he persuades the seller to sell to him as explained there. And in any case – if the seller despaired and agreed in his heart that the sale should be valid, then it is indeed his, and it is much better than robbery after despair, and the prohibition that he committed, he committed. And if he did not despair and intended to retrieve it, he still did not transgress "Do not covet" [see Makneh]. However, in the verse, extortion is considered actual robbery as it is written, "For the earth is filled with violence because of them" (Genesis 6:13), and our Sages said that the decree of the generation of the flood was sealed because of robbery. And in the Midrash [see Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer, Chapter 33] it is stated that extortion is less than the value of a perutah, and robbery is a perutah, see there.

There is another type of theft that Rambam, of blessed memory, did not consider – and that is oppression (oshek), because in matters of Kiddushin (betrothal), this does not apply. Oppression is when one owes another for rent or a loan and does not pay him, and the debt is not specified to this particular money or equivalent value. Even if he betroths with the money he borrowed from the lender, since the loan was given for expenditure, the Kiddushin is valid. Even if he designated an object to oppress him, meaning that the oppression would be collected from this object, and he betrothed the woman with it, it lacks the act of pulling (meshicha), and the object still belongs to him. If he already handed over the object to the oppressed, and the oppressed returned and deposited the object with him – this is outright theft and not oppression [see Bava Metzia 48].

And this which is written, "if the owners despaired and it was known that the item was acquired through despair," the phrase "and it was known that it was acquired" is redundant. There are those who want to explain that this means specifically when there are witnesses at the time of the betrothal that the owner despaired, but if at the time of the betrothal it was not known that the owner despaired, even though in reality the owner had already despaired before the betrothal – it is not considered betrothal, as it is like despair without knowledge. This has no relevance at all to despair without knowledge, for despair without knowledge is when it comes into the possession of the finder before despair. Rather, it is merely an analogy: just as in the case of a found item, if it comes into the possession of the finder before despair, it does not help that the owner despaired afterward. Similarly, with betrothal, the woman and the witnesses need to know that the money of the betrothal belongs to the one who is betrothing. Therefore, if they know that the betrothal money is stolen and they do not know about the despair, it is as if the betrothal is without witnesses, and also she does not rely on it. So, even though it is later revealed that the owner had already despaired, nevertheless it is not considered betrothal, because at the time of the act the betrothal did not take effect, and how can it take effect afterward?
