This law only applies if the woman and the witnesses knew that the money was stolen, but if they did not know at all, this law does not apply at all. However, according to what we hold, that an ordinary theft is considered despair, as we have written, it must be said that this applies only to robbery, and this requires further investigation.

And there are those who explain it thus: since we hold according to Choshen Mishpat, Siman 353, that mere despair (ye'ush) does not effect acquisition unless it is accompanied by a change of domain (shinui reshut) or a change of name (shinui hashem), see there; and what benefit is there in the owners' despairing? And some say that although mere despair does not effect acquisition, here, when the items are in the woman's possession, it constitutes despair and change of domain. Since she acquired them, he also acquires them [Ra'avad and the Ran and the Rashba, chapter 2, page 52:]. But there are those who say that since mere despair does not effect acquisition, she is not betrothed according to Torah law [Rosh in Bava Metzia, chapter 2], since at the time they are in his possession, they are not his, and he is giving her nothing. It is only rabbinically considered betrothal, to be concerned according to the opinion that holds that despair effects acquisition rabbinically [ibid.]. According to this, if Rambam holds this opinion, it is necessary to say that there was something additional to the despair, such as a change of name or something similar, that in such a case he acquires even when they are in his possession. This is why he precisely states, "if the owners despaired and it became known that he acquired that item through despair," meaning that aside from the despair, there was another factor by which he acquired it while it was in his possession – then she is betrothed [Gra and the Mikkneh].

It appears that this is the opinion of our master, the Rema, who wrote that if she was betrothed with stolen property after the owner had despaired of recovering it alone – she is betrothed by rabbinic law; these are his words. And the author (the Shulchan Aruch) wrote that she is fully betrothed after the owner’s despair (ye'ush). Some have tried to explain his words as referring to her own stolen property after the owner’s despair, where there is no change of domain, but this does not seem correct. Rather, it is certain that he (the Rema) holds that the words of the author, which are the words of the Rambam, refer to despair along with another factor. Therefore, he wrote that with despair alone, she is betrothed by rabbinic law, as it is written there. (And this is what they said in the Gemara there: “No one is concerned with Rabbi Shimon’s opinion.” According to this, it must be said that this refers to rabbinic betrothal. See there and examine further.)

And according to this opinion, there is no question regarding what will be explained in this section: that if one sells items that are forbidden to derive benefit from and sanctifies [a woman] with their money, she is considered betrothed because the money is permitted to the woman. This implies that even though the money is forbidden to him, since the money is permitted to the woman, the betrothal takes effect. Similarly, with stolen goods, we might say that even though he did not acquire them while they were in his possession, since she acquired them, she could be betrothed with them. Indeed, this opinion holds that when one sells items forbidden for benefit, the money is permitted to the seller himself. This is the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, in Chapter 8 of the Laws of Forbidden Foods, Law 16.

However, the language of the Rambam is difficult to interpret this way, for if so, what is the meaning of "and it is known"? Additionally, why does he conclude that he acquired that item through despair? He should have mentioned something added to the despair. Furthermore, most of the poskim (halachic authorities) agree with the first opinion that even when there is a transfer of domain, it is considered a valid betrothal, and we say that the betrothal and the acquisition happen simultaneously, just like with a divorce where we say that the divorce and the acquisition of the courtyard happen simultaneously, as mentioned in Siman 139. Therefore, it seems to me that the explanation is as follows: anyone who betroths a woman with any item is believed when he says that the item belongs to him. But a thief is certainly not believed to say that the owner despaired, for he is disqualified from all testimony. Thus, the Rambam informs us that if the owners despaired, meaning it is known that the thief acquired it through despair, that is to say, it is known to the witnesses that the owner despaired, but the thief himself is not believed to say that the owner despaired.

If this person performing the betrothal did not steal it himself but purchased it from a thief, he is certainly believed to say that the victim has already despaired, and it is considered despair and change of ownership in his hand, and it is acquired according to all opinions. However, according to the opinion of most authorities, as explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 353, we require that the despair occurs before the change of ownership. According to the Rambam, there is no distinction in this matter, as stated there. Nevertheless, in the case of the thief himself, if he betrothed with the stolen item before despair, even if afterwards, when it was in her hand, the owner despaired, the betrothal is not valid even according to the Rambam, who does not require despair before the change of ownership, because at the time of the betrothal, he gave her something that was not his. Even if he said "be betrothed to me after the despair," it is not effective. This is unlike the case of betrothing after thirty days, for now it is not his. [See Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 4.] And see what I wrote in Siman 31, paragraph 5.

And also the words of our master, the Rema, can be reconciled according to the opinion of most poskim (halachic decisors). This is what he wrote: if she was betrothed with stolen property after despair (of the owner) alone, she is betrothed rabbinically. You find a case of despair without a change of domain, such as when it was bought from the thief before despair, which is a change of domain before despair that does not work according to most poskim. And so our master, the Rema, ruled in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 356, and if she was betrothed with this after they despaired, even though for her it is despair and then a change of domain, nevertheless, for him, the item is never acquired according to what we explained there in Siman 353, section 5, that one who has the stolen item come to him before despair is similar to one who found a lost item before despair. Therefore, the betrothal is only rabbinic, but the straightforward reading of his words does not imply this. For the practical halacha, one should be concerned with all stringencies.

And also what our master, the Rema, wrote that if one betroths with stolen or robbed property from an Egyptian, she is betrothed, they questioned him since we hold in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 345, that there is no difference between theft and robbery whether from a Jew or a non-Jew. His words are only concerning the evasion of his debt, and also if he did not steal it but took it from a thief even before the despair of the owner, it is considered betrothal, since it is similar to the evasion of his debt because it came into his possession permissibly. But if the thief himself betroths, it is not a complete betrothal, and if another betroths her, she needs a get from both of them.

However, regarding the fundamental law of betrothal with stolen property, there are some of the great authorities who have questioned it based on what the Rambam wrote in Chapter 5 of the Laws of Theft, that if one acquires from a known thief, even after the owner has despaired and there has been a change of possession, one must return the money to the owner because he only acquires the item itself but is obligated to repay the money. Therefore, this woman must return the money of the theft, and with what is she being betrothed [Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 3]? 

It must be said that this refers to a thief who is not known [there]. However, according to what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 356, that even with an unknown thief, one must by law return the money, and it is only due to the enactment of the market that one is exempt from returning it, therefore, she is not betrothed by Torah law to one who holds that a Rabbinic acquisition is not a Torah-level betrothal [there], as will be explained in the law of acquisition by the presence of three parties. 

However, this is not comparable, for even according to this opinion, it is only in a matter where the principal acquisition is Rabbinic. But here, the woman has acquired the object by Torah law, and it is only by Torah law that she is obligated to return the money, and the Rabbis exempted her due to the enactment of the market. Since the Sages have already exempted her from payment, it is as if she has already paid, and the item remains hers even by Torah law [Avnei Miluim], for the victim has no claim against the woman regarding the item even by Torah law. 

And know that according to what we explained with the help of Heaven in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 353, paragraph 6, in the view of the Rambam, there is no difficulty at all, see there.

And similarly, according to the opinion that maintains that even if one buys from a thief who is not widely known as such, after the owner has despaired, if he bought it cheaply, he must pay the owners the full value [Sema, subparagraph 7], this requires analysis. For a woman is betrothed with a perutah and she returns the excess to him. However, it cannot be said this way, for if we say she must return the excess, the betrothal would be void, since she relied on the value of the item. Since the betrothal would be void, she does not need to return anything so that the betrothal is not void, as this is comparable to a buyer who bought according to the value of the item. Furthermore, we have already explained there in section 7 that the main opinion follows those who disagree with this view, see there.

However, one should scrutinize according to our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who explained that it is only because of the enactment of the market that there is no need to return the money. How does the enactment of the market apply to betrothal [purchase]? After all, no money was exchanged. And one cannot say that this enactment applies here as well, because otherwise no woman would agree to get betrothed, fearing that the betrothal money might be stolen or robbed. If so, we would say that betrothal should be valid even before despair (ye’ush), just as the enactment of the market applies to a purchaser before despair [ibid.]. Nevertheless, it seems to me that the enactment of the market does apply to betrothal. Not only according to those who hold, as stated in Siman 356, that the enactment of the market applies to gifts as well, and certainly betrothal is no less than a gift, but even according to those who hold that the enactment of the market applies only to sales, betrothal is like a sale. For she is essentially selling herself to him with the money of betrothal. The reason this enactment was not instituted before despair as in a sale is that there would be no benefit before despair. The enactment of the market before despair is that the owners take back the object and pay the purchaser the money he gave. But in the case of betrothal, even if we say that the owners would return to her the full value of the object, the betrothal would still be nullified because she was betrothed with the object and not with the money. Therefore, it is impossible to enact the market law in this case before despair. However, conversely, after despair and transfer of ownership, where the market law is that the purchaser does not have to pay, this enactment certainly applies to betrothal as well.

There is another question here: How could it happen that one would betroth a woman with stolen goods? For if the woman does not know that the betrothal was done with stolen goods, the betrothal would be nullified because she can say, "I do not want to be betrothed with stolen goods," as we find in the Gemara (53b) regarding consecrated items, where a woman can say, "I do not want the consecration to be effected through me." And if she knows that they are stolen, she is obligated to return the money (Beit Shmuel there), as stated in Choshen Mishpat, siman 356. However, it is explained there that this is only applicable if he acquired the item before the original owner had despaired of its return, not if he acquired it after the owner had despaired. Before the owner despairs, he is obligated to return both the item and the money, as stated there. After the owner despairs, perhaps there is no need to return the money either. But if we say that according to the law, one must return the money even after the owner despairs and the item changes possession, and only because of the ordinance of the market is there no need to return it, as our master the Beit Yosef holds, then if she knows they are stolen, the ordinance of the market does not apply (there), and see what is written there in siman 361, se'if 11.

Indeed, you truly find this both when she knew about the theft and when she did not know. For even if she knew about the theft, the majority of authorities hold that it is a complete acquisition after despair and change of domain, as is proven in the Talmud (Baba Kama 115a). We also clarified in the opinion of the Rambam there in Siman 153, Se'if 6, that he holds like most authorities. Only when one takes from a known thief, the Rambam holds that they enacted that he must return the money to the owners for the owners' benefit, as mentioned there. And even if she did not know that the items were stolen, she is still betrothed, for we also hold regarding consecrated items that she cannot say she does not want the consecration to be substituted through her, as the Rambam wrote in Chapter 8, Law 3 (the law follows Rabbi Yehuda in the Mishnah 52b, and so wrote the Ketzot and Avnei Miluim).

And it is obvious that if he informs her that the item is stolen and the owners have despaired, and she will have to return to the owners the value of the item, and he betroths her with the benefit of the use of the utensil since the utensil will remain with her, and she agrees and accepts – she is certainly betrothed, as there is value in this benefit. And if such a utensil is very common, in a way that this benefit does not have the value of a prutah, it seems to me that it would still be considered doubtful betrothal, because since she accepted it, perhaps the benefit is worth a prutah to her. But if he did not inform her that he is betrothing her with the benefit of the use of the utensil, if by law she was required to return the value to the owners – she is not betrothed even if the benefit is worth a lot, because women are not versed in the law to know that they need to return the value, and she thought that he is betrothing her with the entire item, and thus if she needs to return the value, it is considered a mistaken betrothal.

In Choshen Mishpat, Siman 356, our teacher the Rema wrote that in our times, any theft must be returned even after despair and change of possession according to the law of the land, see there. And the law of the land is a complete law from the Torah [Avnei Miluim]. According to this, if one betrothed a woman with stolen or robbed property in a place where the law of the land requires returning it, the betrothal is not valid. The reason this law is not mentioned here is that it relies on what was written there, and here it discusses the fundamental law. If the law of the land requires only the return of the money and the object remains with the thief, its ruling is as written in the previous section [the Beit Shmuel, sub-section 3, brought several new laws, and we wrote what seemed correct to us. Also, the Avnei Miluim deviated from his words, see there and analyze].

It appears that even in a situation where every theft is returned as mentioned – this is specifically when the victim demands it. However, when the victim does not demand it, such as when he is far away or does not want to litigate with the thief – it is considered complete despair (ye'ush), and she is betrothed if it comes into her possession after the despair [and so wrote the Pischei Teshuvah in the name of the Ketzot HaChoshen].

Maimonides wrote: If someone robbed a woman or stole from her or forcibly took something from her and then returned and betrothed her with the stolen, robbed, or forcibly taken items, saying, "You are betrothed to me with this," if there were prior arrangements of betrothal between them and she took it and remained silent, she is considered betrothed. But if there were no prior arrangements of betrothal, even if she remained silent when he gave her these items as betrothal, she is not considered betrothed. However, if she said "yes," she is considered betrothed.

This is because if there were prior arrangements of betrothal and she agreed to marry him, even though they did not finalize the details such as the giving of the dowry, now that he betroths her and she is silent, we say that she accepted it for the sake of betrothal and forgave him for taking her property. And because he intended to betroth her, we say that he agreed to the details as she stated, as explained in Siman 29. But without prior arrangements of betrothal, her silence is not evidence of forgiving the robbery. Why should she protest? She received what was hers, and his words mean nothing to her—she is not considered betrothed unless she explicitly says "yes."

Prior arrangements of betrothal are only considered if she essentially agreed to marry him. But if she had not yet agreed, even if matchmakers spoke between them, it means nothing. If they already made a formal commitment to marry, it is obvious that there is no greater prior arrangement than this, even if the time for betrothal had not yet arrived according to their agreement. There are those who are uncertain about this and want to say that prior arrangements of betrothal are only considered if she agreed to be betrothed to him now specifically. But from the language of Maimonides that we brought, it does not imply this, as he wrote that there were no prior arrangements of betrothal if they never discussed betrothal at all. Similarly, there are those who want to say that we are generally concerned about prior arrangements of betrothal, but this is not implied from the language of Maimonides and the decisors.

In the case of her own theft, there is no difference between before despair and after despair, as specifically in the theft of others, she is betrothed after despair because there is despair and change of possession in her hand. But in her theft, even though she has despaired, nevertheless, there is no change of possession when the theft is in her hand, as it is hers. However, rabbinically, she is betrothed after despair because rabbinically, despair effects acquisition as stated in section 6 [Bach and Choshen Mishpat 4]. According to the Tur in Choshen Mishpat, section 353, it is not a definite rabbinic acquisition but rather a doubt, and here too it is a rabbinic doubt about betrothal [Beit Shmuel 6]. Some say that if despair effects acquisition rabbinically, it is a biblical betrothal, because since despair effects acquisition rabbinically, it is considered as if the court declared it ownerless, and she is biblically betrothed [Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kama 67]. However, it is a legal doubt whether despair effects acquisition rabbinically, and according to this, it is a biblical doubt about betrothal [there]. The general rule is that something acquired rabbinically also results in a biblical betrothal, as will be explained in the law of three parties, but there are those who disagree as mentioned there. However, some say that theft is not comparable to other acquisitions in this matter because biblically it needs to be returned, so he betroths her with something that is not his [Beit Shmuel there]. But in truth, it seems comparable to all acquisitions, and since the court's declaration of ownerless property is ownerless, it is like a biblical acquisition if we say that in all rabbinic acquisitions she is biblically betrothed [Avnei Miluim 33]. This will be further explained with God's help.

Nevertheless, it is possible to say that theft is not similar to all rabbinic acquisitions, for in all acquisitions the item remains entirely his, whereas with theft, even after he acquires the object through despair, he is still rabbinically obligated to return the money for the object. Biblically, he is obligated to return the object itself. Consequently, this is not similar to all acquisitions [and perhaps this is what the Ba'er Hetev intended]. However, if he acquires the object also according to Torah law, such as acquiring the stolen item through a change in its form, it is no worse than ordinary theft where one can consecrate it after despair, and although he is obligated to return the value, this is no worse than any other debt [Choshen Mishpat, subparagraph 5].

And it seems more likely to say that in the case of theft from her, whether it is money or an object, even if he acquired it through a change of action, it is not considered a valid betrothal at all unless she remains silent. For she can say, "It was mine that I took back, and that is why I was silent when he betrothed me with it, because I did not care about his words." And we cannot say to her, "Why were you silent? After all, he acquired the object according to the law, and if you did not want to be betrothed to him, you should have protested the betrothal," for she can claim, "I do not know the law. Do women know the law?" [Gemara 13] And I only knew that he was a thief, and I took back my object or my money [see Beit Shmuel section 7 and the Magen Avraham], but nevertheless, she cannot be exempted without a get (divorce document) based on this reasoning, as will be explained with God's help.

And that which has been clarified that if he gives her a stolen item, she is betrothed even if she remains silent, and if he does not give a stolen item, she is betrothed if she says "yes" – this is specifically when he betrothed her at the time he gave her the stolen item. But if at the time of giving he did not say anything and after she received it he said to her, "Be betrothed to me with it," even if she said "yes" and he had previously arranged the betrothal – nevertheless, she is not betrothed, as it is assumed she accepted it for her stolen item. Even if he did not say to her "here is your stolen item" [as explained in Beit Shmuel, section 8], and even if she says that her intention was for betrothal when she received it, and he also says so – nevertheless, it does not help, as the sages established the understanding of a woman that she does not desire to be betrothed with her stolen item, unless he said to her at the time of giving "behold, you are betrothed to me" and he had previously arranged the betrothal or she said "yes." Similarly, if there was no prior arrangement and he betrothed her at the time of giving it to her hand and she did not say "yes" and after receiving it she said "yes" – it also does not help, because since she did not say it at the time of giving, it is certain she was not agreeable then [Beit Shmuel].

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that one must pay her for the thefts, meaning that in a case where the betrothal is valid despite betrothing her with something stolen from her, he must pay her for the theft. The reason is that what he gave her now is considered for the purpose of betrothal and not for the purpose of returning the stolen item. And even though we explained in Section 21 that if he jokes and she remains silent, we say that she forgave him for the theft, nevertheless, if he did not joke and she said "yes," he is obligated to pay her for the theft. This is because only if he joked previously do we say that due to their prior closeness she forgave him, but if he did not joke, even though now she agreed to be betrothed to him, she did not forgive the theft. However, there are some of our Rabbis who hold that even if he joked, he is obligated to return the theft to her, because, indeed, from where do we say that she forgave? And indeed, forgiveness is a weak claim in monetary laws. This is also implied in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 2, Halacha 1) that in the case of theft from her, the betrothal is valid, and the theft is considered an obligation upon him, and he is obligated to pay. Also, his intention was the same, for otherwise, the betrothal is nullified if he intended not to return the theft and she intended that he would return it. Therefore, it is certain that his intention was to return the theft to her.

And just as the law is regarding her stolen property, so too it is regarding her debt. If he returns her the debt that he owes her and says to her, "Take this sela that I owe you and behold you are betrothed to me with it," and the statement was made while the object was still in his hand, and he gave it to her and she took it and remained silent, if there were prior marriage negotiations between them – she is betrothed, and we say that she certainly agreed to accept it for betrothal and will collect the debt afterwards. For if not, she would not have remained silent but would have said to him, "I do not accept this for betrothal." However, if there were no prior marriage negotiations between them – her silence is not a sign of agreement, and she did not pay attention to his words unless she explicitly said yes. And if after he gave it into her hand, he said to her, "Behold you are betrothed to me with it," even if she said yes and there were prior marriage negotiations – she is not betrothed, because we testify that she accepted it for the debt and not for betrothal since he mentioned the debt at the time of the act. And even if he did not mention the debt, since he also did not mention the betrothal but gave it to her without specifying – she certainly accepted it for the debt. And if both of them say that their intention was for betrothal and he gave it to her without specifying – there is uncertainty whether this is similar to stolen property, where they are not believed, or not. It seems that she would need a get (divorce document) and it is not similar to stolen property, because with stolen property we say that since he is a wicked person, she is not believed to say she accepted it for betrothal, which is not the case with debt.

And even though a debt is similar to theft, nevertheless, they are not similar in all matters. For in the case of theft, even if he did not mention the theft at the time he gave it to her but only said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this" – she is not betrothed if she remains silent unless she consents, and if she does not consent – only if she says "yes." But with a debt, this rule does not apply unless he says to her, "Take this coin that I owe you and be betrothed to me with it." Because he mentioned the debt, we say that she certainly accepted it for the debt, even if she did not explicitly say "yes" or consent. However, if he did not mention the debt at all but gave her a coin and said to her, "Take this coin" and previously said to her, "Be betrothed to me with it," and she accepted it in silence and did not consent – nevertheless, she is betrothed, even though the time for repayment of the debt has arrived, and she cannot say, "I accepted it for the repayment of my debt." This is specifically with clear theft, where it is understood that her acceptance is for the return of the stolen item, as people strive to recover from a thief by any means possible. But with a debt, it is customary that a long time may pass, and if the conversation was only about betrothal, it is certain that she accepted it for betrothal and did not concern herself with the debt that she did not collect at that time. [And proof from page 13. And if it is difficult regarding the case of betrothal with theft, etc., and what is the difficulty, let it be established as unspecific, but it is certain that theft is different. And see Lechem Mishneh].

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote: If he returned to her a debt that he owed her and said, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this before you take it," and she took it and was silent, if there was betrothal between them – she is betrothed. If there was no prior betrothal – she is not betrothed until she says "yes." His words do not clarify that he first said, "Here is your debt," but rather immediately when he approached her, he said, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this." According to this, a debt is similar to robbery. However, it can be said that what he wrote, "he returned to her debt," means that he said to her, "Here is your debt," and then betrothed her. Many commentators have understood this to be his intention, as it appears from the language of the Talmud. However, some of our Rabbis are in doubt, thinking that perhaps if he said, "Here is your debt," and then said, "It is not my intention to give it to you as a debt but for betrothal," and she was silent and there was no prior betrothal – she is betrothed, because he explicitly retracted his initial words. Even though when he says, "Here is your debt and be betrothed to me with it," it is also considered an explicit retraction, it is not the same. Without an explicit retraction, she remained silent and did not bother to respond because he did not speak appropriately. If his intention was to also absolve the debt with the betrothal, it is obvious that she did not bother to respond and why would she do so? For in the case of prior betrothal, it is possible that she agreed in such a manner (as the Rashba holds, contrary to the Jerusalem Talmud in Section 26). But in the case where there was no prior betrothal, she did not consider his words at all. If his intention was to pay the debt later on, nevertheless, since he did not clarify his words, she did not bother to respond. But with an explicit retraction, if she did not agree to the betrothal, she should have responded, "I will not accept it for betrothal but for my debt."

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in this law that there are those who say she is certainly betrothed, and it is questionable because it is only a doubtful betrothal (as in Choshen Mishpat). And there are those who say that even with an explicit retraction, it is nothing because she did not care at all about his retracting words (interpreting that his retraction was indeed explicit, but from the Tosefta in chapter 2, it is clear that he said he would give the debt, and at the time of giving, he said he betroths her with it. This is the language of retraction, meaning at the time of giving, and the language of the Rambam is precise).

Some say that when the time for the debt repayment has not yet arrived, and he says to her, "Take your debt and you are betrothed with it," and she remains silent, even though he did not specify – she is betrothed [Bach]. And some say there is no difference in this case, because since he agreed to repay within the designated time, it is accepted as payment for the debt [Taz]. And there are those who resolve this matter by saying that certainly when he says, "Take this sela for your debt and be betrothed to me with it," it is as if it is after its time. But if he then says, "I am not giving it for your debt but for betrothal," and she remains silent, she considers and accepts it for betrothal, because the time has not yet arrived and he does not wish to settle the debt now, as he has retracted [Avnei Miluim], and this appears to be the main opinion. The same applies if he initially says, "I will repay your debt," and afterwards, at the time of giving, he says to her, "Be betrothed to me with it" – it seems to me that it is considered a retraction as explained according to the Tosefta.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 3: If a man asks a woman to lend him money with collateral, and she gives him the money, and when he gives her the collateral he says to her, "Be betrothed to me with this," and she accepts it and remains silent – it is a case of doubtful betrothal. And even though it is clarified in section 28 that in the case of debt repayment, if he does not mention the debt at all, she is considered betrothed, and certainly with collateral, nevertheless, with collateral, even without mentioning the word "collateral," it is like mentioning it, since in the same session they discuss that she should lend him with collateral, she lends him, and he gives her the collateral and says to her, "Be betrothed to me with this," it is like with a debt when he says to her, "Here is your debt and be betrothed to me with it," and she remains silent, she is not betrothed if he does not specify, and there is a doubt with collateral if it is also considered like a debt, and she is not betrothed, or perhaps it is not like a debt, because with a debt, since he owes her, she can say, "I am taking what is mine," but with collateral, even though he says to lend him with collateral, she does not yet have any ownership over the collateral, and it is not acquired by her at all, and at the moment he gives it to her, he is giving it only for betrothal, and certainly if the collateral is worth more than the debt. And even if we say that with collateral, no physical transfer is needed and money effects acquisition, still, it is only a general lien and the collateral itself is not hers, for he can repay his debt and retrieve the collateral, hence it is a case of doubtful betrothal when she remains silent, as perhaps she agreed to be betrothed with this collateral. And there is no difference whether he says to her, "Lend me with this collateral" or "with collateral in general," for even with "this collateral" it is only a lien, and with "collateral in general," since it was in the same session, it is like he said, "Take it as collateral and for betrothal."

He said to her, "Take this sela as a deposit," and before he gave it to her, he said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with it," and she took it in silence – she is betrothed, for this is not comparable to a debt or a pledge, and she does not receive anything that she could say, "I received it for my debt or for my pledge." And if she did not want to be betrothed, why did she remain silent? She should not have accepted it from him. She cannot say, "I did not pay attention to his latter words but only to the former, and I accepted it as a deposit," for she is not believed to say so, for what reason does she have to accept it as a deposit when he wants it for betrothal? However, if after she took it as a deposit, he said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with it," if she said yes, she is betrothed, for even with a deposit that is already in her possession, she can be betrothed with it, as will be explained. But if she remained silent, she is not betrothed, for silence after the giving of money is nothing, for if she remained silent, it was because she did not care to respond to him, as she had accepted it as a deposit, and why did she not throw it back at him? Because she was concerned that since she accepted it as a deposit and was obligated to guard it, if she threw it and he did not accept it and it got lost, she would be obliged to pay. And although in truth she would not be obligated if she threw it and said to him, "Here is yours before you," nevertheless, women are not knowledgeable in the law, and according to their reasoning, it seems to them that they would be obligated to pay. Therefore, she did not throw it at him.

What we have explained regarding a deposit, that silence after the giving of money is not considered an acceptance—this is the opinion of the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, as well as the majority of the poskim (halachic authorities). However, the opinion of the Rif of blessed memory is that it is a halachic doubt, and she would require a divorce (get) from him, and if he wishes to maintain the marriage, she would require another betrothal (kiddushin). The reason for the doubt is that she did not throw the deposit before him, and we do not ascribe it to her thinking that she is obligated to pay. [See Ran; the Rif also applies this to a deposit. According to the version of the Gemara, Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua only disagrees regarding a deposit, and this requires further study.]

In light of what has been explained, that when someone says to a woman with a deposit, "You are betrothed to me," and she takes it silently, she is considered betrothed, Rabbi Rema wrote that some say it is specifically when she takes it with her hand. However, if he threw the betrothal money to her, even into her lap, such silence is meaningless since she did not initially consent to the betrothal. The reason is that when she takes it with her hand, her silence is evidence of her consent—otherwise, who forced her to take it with her hand? But if he threw it into her lap, though for the purpose of betrothal it is considered as if she accepted it with her hand, still, her silence is not evidence of her consent. Why should she not remain silent, and what does she care about what he is doing? According to this, it is not only with a deposit that this law applies, but in all matters of betrothal, when a man approaches a woman and throws something into her lap in the presence of witnesses and says to her, "You are betrothed to me," and she remains silent, even if she did not take it and throw it back in his presence, it is not a betrothal at all, because we have no evidence that she consented since she did not accept it with her hand. Some say this is specifically when she immediately removed it from her lap, but if she did not immediately remove it, it is considered silence at the time of giving the money, and she needs a get (divorce). However, the Tur does not imply this, and so it seems to be the opinion of the great later authorities, and it also appears in section 30, see there.

There was an incident involving a man who betrothed a woman with a myrtle mat and was told that it was not worth a perutah. He then said, "Be betrothed to me with the four dinars wrapped inside it." When she took the mat, she did not know about the dinars, and when he said, "Be betrothed to me with the dinars," she did not throw the mat away nor did she say anything and remained silent. The sages said that this silence after receiving the money is not considered a valid betrothal at all. Since at the time of receiving it, the betrothal did not take effect, it does not take effect later through her silence unless she explicitly says "yes." Why did she not throw the mat away if she did not wish to be betrothed? Because she was afraid the money might get lost and she would have to pay for it, even though, in truth, this is not the law. Nevertheless, a woman might not be knowledgeable about this law and might think so; therefore, she did not throw the mat away, but not because she consented. Nonetheless, there is an opinion in the Gemara that worries about the betrothal due to this reason that she did not throw it away, as surely even a woman would not err in thinking she would have to pay, and therefore, her silence might indicate her consent, akin to her saying "yes." The Rif ruled that she requires a get (divorce document), and if he wants to maintain the marriage, new betrothal is required, as stated in section 33. However, Rambam ruled that she does not require a get for this reason, as the Gemara's primary ruling seems to be this way. Nevertheless, he requires a get for a different reason – perhaps the mat is worth a perutah elsewhere, as stated in section 31. The practical difference is that if it is something perishable, like food that spoils, she is not betrothed. Many poskim (decisors) follow Rambam's view, and indeed, they argue about considering the betrothal valid lest it is worth a perutah elsewhere, as his intention was not to betroth her with the mat but with the dinars [Rashba and Ran]. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch ruled like the Rif, and in the case of a deposit, they did not rule like the Rif for the reason explained in section 32. Therefore, if she knew she would not be liable for their safekeeping, even in the case of a deposit, it is considered a doubtful betrothal [see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 14].

Some say that in the case explained, when they told him it is not a valid coin and he said, "Be betrothed to me with the dinars inside it," it also applies if he did not say specifically, "Be betrothed to me with the dinars inside it," but simply said, "Here are dinars inside it" – she is also betrothed out of doubt. Similarly, our teacher Rema ruled in section 4. However, some disagree with this. For if he said, "Be betrothed to me with the dinars inside it," he is betrothing her now, and there is doubt in her silence as we have said. But if he did not say now the language of betrothal, what doubt is there? The first language of betrothal is nullified since she did not know there were dinars inside it, and how can she be betrothed now? Furthermore, some say that when he says, "Be betrothed with the dinars," he retracts from wanting to betroth her with the mat, and it is obvious that if he did not say the language of betrothal anew, it is nothing. Even if we say that his intention from the beginning was to betroth her with the dinars, initially his speech was in error because she and the witnesses did not know about the dinars, and how can she be betrothed now if he did not say the language of betrothal? It seems according to our teacher Rema that since everything was in the same context, it is obvious that it is no less than discussing matters of betrothal, and therefore, even if we say that he retracted his words, since he now said, "Here are dinars inside it," it is as if he is discussing matters of betrothal with her and gave it to her simply, which constitutes betrothal. Therefore, since her silence raises a doubt of consent, it is certainly a doubtful betrothal, and she requires a get (divorce document).

A woman who seized money from another man, and he asked her to return it to him, and she refused. He then said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this money," and she was silent and held onto the money — this does not constitute betrothal. This is because her silence after receiving the money is not significant, just as when the money came into her possession as a deposit, her subsequent silence is ineffective. Similarly, when the money came into her possession through theft, and on the contrary, theft is even worse. For with a deposit, mere silence does not help, but if she said "yes," she is betrothed. However, with money obtained through theft, even if she said "yes," it may not help unless she returns the stolen money to him and he betroths her with it. The reason is that we hold that if property was stolen and the owners have not despaired of recovering it, neither party can consecrate it — the thief because it is not his, and the owner because it is not in his possession. Consequently, this man, just as he cannot consecrate the stolen money, so too he cannot betroth a woman with it. According to this, even with a deposit, if she was asked to return it and she refused, it becomes like theft and he cannot betroth her with it. However, it is possible to say that she is betrothed if both parties agreed to the betrothal, for it is as if she returned the money to him and it became a deposit, and similarly, with consecrated property, if both parties agreed to consecrate it, it is consecrated. Since both agreed, it is like a deposit and it is consecrated.

The general principle regarding silence after the giving of money is as follows: If the object came into her possession not for the purpose of betrothal but as a deposit, or if she stole it from him, or even if it came into her possession for the purpose of betrothal but the betrothal did not take effect, such as when there was no prutah's worth in its external parts as in paragraph 35, or if the external object was not his and after it was in her possession he betrothed her and she remained silent – this is the silence after the giving of money. Since she did not say "yes," there is no indication of her intent to be betrothed to him. The reason she did not throw it in his face might be due to her fear of having to repay him as mentioned, and therefore, in each case, the law is as previously stated in the earlier paragraphs. However, if there is an indication of her consent to the betrothal, such as if the object was not in her hand but in her lap or in the hem of her garment or similar, and when he betrothed her with it, she took the object into her hand – she is certainly betrothed. Similarly, if he gave the object into her hand without specifying, and she accepted it, and after it was in her hand, he betrothed her with it and she was silent – she is certainly betrothed. This is not silence after the giving of money since it did not come into her hand for another specified purpose but rather without specification, and when he subsequently told her it was for betrothal and she remained silent, she considered and accepted it.

And with silence after the giving of money, some say that even "shadich" (an informal agreement) does not help [Ran], and the proof for this is the case of the mat. Since he consecrated her with the mat, it is obvious that it is not inferior to "shadich." Nevertheless, when he said, "Be consecrated with the dinars inside it," the Sages said that this is considered silence after the giving of money. The reason is that "shadich" only helps when the acceptance was initially for the sake of consecration, but it does not help because the money is hers from debt or theft. In this case, we say that since he made an informal agreement, she forgave him. But when the initial giving was for deposit and not for consecration, her silence does not indicate consent even if there was an informal agreement [Beit Shmuel], because just as she did not initially accept it for consecration, so too her silence was not for the sake of consecration. And in the case of the mat, even though it was initially for consecration, since the mat itself is not something appropriate for consecration, it is as if it was not for consecration at all. It is not similar to debt or theft, where there is enough for consecration, but something else prevents it [in my opinion]. And some say further that with silence after the giving of money without an informal agreement, even those who are strict about silence after the giving of money, as mentioned, nevertheless without an informal agreement, there is no reason to be strict at all [Maharamp], and though there are those who hesitate in this matter [see Taz]—nevertheless, this is the main opinion [Avnei Miluim].

From what has been explained, we learn that one can betroth a woman with a deposit that she is holding. Even though he is not giving her anything at that moment, it is as if he gave it to her since the deposit is in her possession. When he betroths her with it, the deposit becomes hers, and this is the money of her betrothal. The same law applies if he lent her an object and betrothed her with it—she is betrothed. All of this is when she says "yes," for if not, her silence after receiving the money would not be sufficient. Moreover, the sages said (M. 46): if a man says to a woman, "Be betrothed to me with the deposit I have with you," and she goes and finds that it was stolen or lost, if there remains from it the value of a prutah, she is betrothed; if not, she is not betrothed. We do not say that she only agreed to be betrothed with the entire deposit. If she knew the amount of the deposit, we say this, but if she did not know the amount, we say she agreed even with part of it. Some say that even if she knew the amount of the deposit, since he did not say to her, "Be betrothed to me with the entire deposit," her intention was also on part of it, and we should be stringent in practice according to this opinion. Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, ruled according to the first opinion, but in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is implied clearly like the second opinion.

In the case of a loan, the law is similar to that of a deposit. Although, according to the first opinion, it is impossible for betrothal to take effect with a loan if there is a deficiency, since she is aware of the amount of the loan, nevertheless, with a loan, she can be betrothed for another reason, as she is obligated to repay it. However, there must remain a minimum value (a perutah); otherwise, since she still owes the debt, it would be considered betrothing with a loan, and she would not be betrothed. But if a perutah remains, it is considered a loan and a perutah, and she is betrothed [according to the Bach and Prisha]. According to this, even with a deposit, if she is liable for its loss, according to the first opinion, she is betrothed even if she knew the amount of the deposit. Some disagree with this, arguing that although she is obligated to repay, she did not intend to be betrothed except with the entire deposit. The reason for betrothal with a loan and a perutah is that her mind is not on the loan but on the perutah. This is not the case with a deposit, where her mind is on the entire deposit [according to the Taz and Avnei Miluim]. In the case of a loan, it must be when he says, "Be betrothed to me with what you have in your possession" [according to the Avnei Miluim], for otherwise, she is truly not betrothed if there is a deficiency in the amount. [And regarding a deposit, the Rosh and the Tur find cases where she does not know how much it is]. In the case of a deposit, if only a perutah remains and she is betrothed with it as stated, he is not obligated to make up the balance, as he did not specify the amount with which he is betrothing her [according to the Tur].

A loan is not similar to a deposit. If someone had a loan with her, even if the time had come to collect it, and even if it were a documented loan, and he said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with the loan that I have with you," she is not betrothed. For a deposit is under the depositor’s control wherever it is, but a loan is given to be spent. And even if the loan is still intact with her, provided she has not used it, nevertheless, it is hers and not his. He only has a lien on her person and on her property to repay him, but the money is not his, so with what could he betroth her? And the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote, "because the loan is given to be spent, and there is nothing here that exists to benefit from now, since that coin has already been spent and its benefit has passed." His intention is not that if the coin were intact, she would be betrothed, but rather this is its explanation: since it is given to be spent, it is as though the coin were spent even if it is still intact, and the coin she has is not his but hers.

If she received money from him for an 'Iska' (a business partnership) which is half a loan and half a deposit, if he betroths her with the deposit portion, she is betrothed. Even if he betroths her with the 'Iska' generally, as long as there are two perutot, she is betrothed, since this is like betrothing with a loan and a peruta, where her intention is on the peruta. However, if he betroths her with the loan portion, she is not betrothed. There is an opinion that even with the loan portion she is betrothed, arguing that the reason why betrothing with a loan does not work is because it is meant for expenditure, and he is allowed to spend it and is not obligated to keep it available for her at all times. But concerning an 'Iska', where the recipient is forbidden to use it for another business and must use it for the 'Iska' as agreed, it is like a deposit. The primary opinion seems to be the first one, because, nevertheless, half of the loan is not under his control but under her control, and he only has a lien on it. With what, then, is he betrothing her now? The prohibition to use it for another matter is like a condition on the loan, but in any case, it is not under his control. Even with a regular loan, the borrower is not allowed to use the loan frivolously but must use it for business, as stated in Choshen Mishpat 67, although he is allowed to use it for any business he wants, whereas with an 'Iska', he is only allowed to use it for the agreed business. Nevertheless, they are one and the same.

Even if he had a document of debt against her and returned the document to her and the document is worth a perutah, she is not betrothed because he betrothed her with the loan, not with the document. And even if he said, "Be betrothed to me with this debt document," certainly his intention was not on the paper but on what was written in it. However, there are those who are stringent in this matter, and even if he did not say, "Be betrothed to me with this debt document," if it is worth a perutah and he returned the debt document to her, it is considered doubtful betrothal. This is because in the Gemara [there] there is a situation like this where they appraise the paper, and if it is worth a perutah, she is betrothed. And although in the conclusion it does not remain so, this is for another reason. But nevertheless, in terms of the law, perhaps it is so that his intention is also on the paper. And although there he specifically mentioned the document and said, "Be betrothed to me with this document," but when he did not mention the document at all, there is no proof from there. Nevertheless, perhaps even generally when he said, "Be betrothed to me with the loan that I have against you," and he returned the document to her, his intention was also on the document. Because in the term 'loan,' the document is also included [see Beit Shmuel, section 121]. And it is not similar to any two separate things, because the document is part of the loan. For when he settles his debt, he returns the document to him. And we have already explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 241, paragraph 3, that when one forgives the debt, even if he has the document in his hands, the document does not prevent the forgiveness. And we have explained there that it seems that when he forgives the debt, he is obligated to return the document as well. Hence, the document is not like another object. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Gittin, there is one who holds that forgiving the document is considered forgiving the debt. And even those who disagree there, this is because the main debt is referred to by the debt itself and not the document. But they agree that in the debt, the document is also included [it seems to me].

And what we have written according to the first opinion, that even if one says "Be betrothed to me with a promissory note," his intention is not on the paper itself, this appears to be the opinion of the Rambam [Beit Shmuel, section 20]. However, the Tur, who also holds like the first opinion, writes that if he says "Be betrothed to me with a promissory note" and gives it to her, we assess the value of the paper. If it has the value of a perutah, she is betrothed; if not, she is in a state of doubtful betrothal. Similarly, our master the Beit Yosef wrote this in section 8. And why is she in a state of doubtful betrothal if it does not have the value of a perutah? Because perhaps it has the value of a perutah in another place [Beit Yosef]. And although there is a difficulty with all that has been explained, and how can one betroth with a document, for the document is hers since the borrower pays the scribe’s fee as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 39? Some have explained that the document serves as collateral for the loan [Beit Shmuel, section 22], and just as one who betroths with her collateral is betrothed as explained, so too with a document. According to this, in the opinion that will be explained, even without returning the collateral to her, she is betrothed with a loan that has collateral, and similarly here, she is betrothed even without returning the document to her. However, it is impossible to say this, for it is agreed by all that one who betroths with a loan that has a promissory note is not betrothed, and it is not similar to collateral. Additionally, what similarity is there between a promissory note and collateral, for with collateral, the lender has an acquisition in the collateral itself, as will be explained, unlike with a promissory note. However, according to what the Rambam wrote [there] regarding the reason for collateral, that she is betrothed when the collateral is returned because she benefits from the collateral immediately, and thus derives benefit, it is possible to say the same for a promissory note. But according to other authorities who hold that she is betrothed even without returning the collateral, one cannot compare a promissory note to collateral. Furthermore, even according to the Rambam, it is difficult to say this, for with collateral, it is necessary that the benefit of using the collateral has the value of a perutah, otherwise, with what is she being betrothed, for the main collateral is hers. According to this, one would need to say that the benefit of using the paper is worth a perutah, which does not seem to be the case, for they only wrote that the paper itself is worth a perutah, implying that the benefit of using it is not worth a perutah. Therefore, it appears that the authorities are indeed referring to a case where the lender wrote the promissory note and not her, and according to the law in such a case, even when she repays him, he does not need to return the promissory note to her but only tear it up as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 57, and therefore, when he betroths her with it, it is a valid betrothal [and so wrote the Bnei Ahavah, chapter 5, halacha 13]. There are those who say that in every promissory note, the borrower needs to transfer ownership of the promissory note to the lender, and thus it is his [Avnei Miluim], but this does not seem to be the opinion of the authorities.

And just as one cannot betroth with a loan, so too, one cannot betroth with wages. For example, if he was hired by her and he is due wages for work he performed for her, and even if the time for the wages to be collected has arrived and he says to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with the value of these wages" – she is not betrothed. The reason is that we hold that wages accrue from the beginning until the end – for every perutah (smallest coin) of work he does, she becomes obligated to pay, and the payment is considered a loan to her, and with a loan, she cannot be betrothed. And even if we say that wages are only due at the end, nevertheless, here, since the work has already been completed, the money is considered a loan to her. [See Rashi 48b, s.v. b'schaar she'asiti, and see Gra, sec. 25, and it requires further investigation]. And even if he said to her, "Be betrothed to me with the wages for the work I will do for you," which he has not yet earned from her – nevertheless, she is not betrothed due to the reason that wages accrue from the beginning until the end, and for every perutah of work he does, it is considered a loan to her, even though we hold that wages are only paid at the end, as it is written in Choshen Mishpat, siman 339, nevertheless, the obligation accrues with each perutah of work he does, but the Torah does not require payment until the end of the term [Tosafot Bava Metzia 65a].

Even if he is a contractor and not a daily laborer, we do not say that a craftsman acquires the increase in value of the object and it is as if the object is his, and when he betroths her it is as if he betroths her with his own [object]. For we hold that a craftsman does not acquire the increase in value of the object, and the object belongs to her, and he is entitled to the payment for his work, which is considered a loan. And there are those who say she is betrothed, for we hold that a craftsman acquires the increase in value of the object. It has already been explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 306, Se'if 4, that although the primary ruling is that a craftsman does not acquire the increase in value of the object, as ruled by the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, nevertheless, in matters of prohibiting a married woman, one should be stringent. Therefore, in Se'if 15, both opinions are recorded. Additionally, it appears from the Jerusalem Talmud (Bava Kamma, Chapter 9) that we hold a craftsman acquires the increase in value of the object, and this is a dispute among the authorities. Some say it is a doubt in the law (Shach there, Se'if Katan 3). And there are those who say that even for a daily laborer, one could say he acquires the increase in value of the object, but we have already explained there that this does not seem to be the case. And know that all this applies when the craftsman only performs the labor, and the wood or stones or merchandise belongs to her. But if everything belongs to him, and he agreed with her to make her a garment or an object of his for a certain price, it is obvious that it belongs to him, and if he betroths her with it, it constitutes a complete betrothal.

Our sages said, even though with a loan she is not betrothed, nevertheless if he betroths her with the benefit of the loan, she is betrothed. And what is the benefit of the loan? When he extends the time of the loan for her. Our rabbis explained that this means: for example, she owed him a loan to be paid at a certain time, and he now extends the time for her for the future. This benefit is worth a perutah, for she would have paid a perutah to someone to work on her behalf to extend the time, or she would have given a perutah to him himself for the extension of the time. With this perutah, he betroths her and says to her, "Be betrothed to me with this benefit," for this benefit is worth a perutah. However, there is an issue of the appearance of interest here, for it is as if he is taking a perutah for the extension, since with this he is betrothing her. But it is not considered actual interest since he is not taking anything from her. Some of our rabbis hold that this is considered actual interest, for it is as if he is taking a perutah from her. This discussion refers to a case where she owes another person and the time to pay has arrived, and he comes and gives a perutah to the lender to extend the time for her, and with this, he betroths her. Therefore, it is not considered actual interest, for the Torah only forbade interest that comes from borrower to lender. All the more so, if he forgives her the entire loan and says to her, "Be betrothed to me with the benefit of this forgiveness," [it is valid].

And one should not wonder, how can the benefit of the loan be better than the loan itself, for even if he lends her money now and betroths her with it, she is not betrothed? And with the benefit of profit or forgiveness, she will be betrothed? Certainly, it is so that when he betroths her with the principal money, he is not giving her anything because it is already in her possession and it belongs to her. But when he betroths her with the benefit of forgiving a loan or extending the time, now he is giving her this prutah that the benefit is worth, as the benefit of a loan exists in its essence, and therefore she is betrothed with it. But the loan itself cannot betroth her, as we hold that a loan is given to be spent.

However, the Rambam of blessed memory in Chapter 5 did not agree with this explanation. He interpreted that if one betroths a woman with the benefit of a loan, she is considered betrothed. How so? For example, if he lent her two hundred zuz and said to her, "You are betrothed to me with the benefit of the time I am granting you to repay this loan, which will be in your possession for such and such days, and I will not demand it from you until a certain time" – she is considered betrothed. For she derives benefit from being able to use this loan until the agreed upon time. However, it is forbidden to do this because it is considered interest. And he (the Rambam) holds that as long as he does not give her something at that moment, she cannot be betrothed with it. It is not comparable to a deposit with which she can be betrothed without giving something, for the deposit is in his possession wherever it is, and when he betroths her, it becomes hers, and that is its giving. This is not the case with a loan, as what benefit is there in extending the time or the benefit of waiver? In the end, he is not giving her anything.

Even according to his interpretation, it can be said the same, for since he is lending her now, she is not betrothed because the money is meant to be spent and does not belong to her. He is only betrothing her with the benefit of the time, and in the end, he is not giving her anything in exchange for the betrothal. Since this is the case, even if the loan preceded the betrothal, what of it? They are one and the same [Ran]. It appears that his opinion is that just as if he betroths her with an item from which she can benefit through its use for a certain period, and the use is worth a specific amount, she is betrothed, similarly with money that is now ready to be lent to her, and he permits her to use the money for a certain period longer than a usual loan, this benefit is not considered a loan but rather the use of an item. This is specifically when the money is now ready before us, but if he already lent it to her, in the end, the benefit is from the loan, and it is no better than the loan itself [Nir Li].

Some of the early authorities explained that if the time for the borrower to repay has arrived and she has the money in hand ready to repay, and she willingly gives a dinar to someone to extend the loan period by one month, and he extends it in exchange for the betrothal – she is betrothed [Ra'avad there]. And it seems to me that in such a case, even the Rambam might agree that it constitutes betrothal, since the money is in her possession, and the loan period has already passed, the status of the money as a loan is nullified, and it is considered as benefiting from the use of the money, but this matter needs further examination. 

Know that in practice, we must take into account all opinions, as the first opinion is that of most of our Rabbis, and stringently, we must consider the Rambam’s view that if she accepted betrothal from another man, she needs a get from both. This is also understood from the words of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 10, see there. However, when she owes money to others and gives a perutah to the lender to extend the loan period, it appears to be a complete betrothal, and this is also implied from the arrangement of our Rabbi the Rema. [Regarding interest – see Beit Shmuel section 29, and it seems to me that there is a prohibition, relying on the previous words of the author].

There are those who say that with the benefit of forgiving a loan, even Maimonides agrees, that it is specifically in extending the time that he disagrees, as it is not better than the loan itself. But in forgiving the entire loan, it is certainly a great benefit [Beit Shmuel 128]. And certainly, it is possible to say so. However, there are those who are uncertain about this as well, because it is possible that even if he said to her, "With the benefit of the forgiveness, I betroth you," nevertheless, she has her mind on the money of the loan itself, and it returns to be like the loan itself [Ran], since it was given for spending and it is no longer in existence. Therefore, also in this, one should be stringent [as the Levush wrote].

Just as one cannot betroth her with her own loan, so too, one cannot betroth her with a loan of others, such as if he said, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with the loan that so-and-so owes me." However, the reason here is not the same as with her own loan, where the money was given for expenditure, as in the case of her own loan where she already acquired the money and he is not giving her anything new - it is clear that she is not betrothed. But with the loan of others, he is giving her something new that she did not have. Even though the loan is not tangible, it is considered a benefit to her as if it were tangible [Tosafot 47a]. However, there is another reason here. It is not only in the case of an oral loan where he said to her, "Be betrothed to me with the loan that so-and-so owes me," where there is no acquisition at all and with what is he betrothing her, unless it is in the presence of all three of them as will be explained. Rather, even with a loan in a document, and he transfers the document to her by writing and delivery as mentioned in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 66 - still, she is not betrothed. The reason is that since he can afterward forgive the borrower's debt, she does not rely on it because she fears he might forgive the debt [48a].

However, the Tur wrote that if the paper has the value of a perutah, she is definitely betrothed, and if not, she is betrothed out of doubt. The reason is that perhaps the paper has the value of a perutah in another place, and this is similar to what is written in her document. But some say that even if the paper has the value of a perutah, she is not betrothed, because the paper belongs to the borrower, and when he forgives the loan, she will be obligated to return the paper to him. Also, according to this opinion, if the paper is his and not the borrower's, she is betrothed when it has the value of a perutah. The Tur holds that she does not need to return the paper, and from his words, it seems that even when he did not say "be betrothed to me with this document," his intention is on the paper. In this respect, it is more stringent than her document of debt, and the reason is simple: since he transferred the document to her, it is as if he explicitly mentioned the document of debt. Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 13 that in the case of a loan with a document, she is betrothed out of doubt, and it seems that he holds that the doubt is whether she relied on it or not.

Even though betrothing with a loan does not effectuate a betrothal, nonetheless, with a loan that has a collateral, the betrothal is valid, whether it is her loan or someone else’s loan. The Rambam wrote in Law 14 the reasoning for her loan, which is that she benefits from the collateral from now, and thus, benefit has reached her hand. And regarding someone else’s collateral, he wrote the reasoning in Law 23 because the creditor has some ownership in the body of the collateral. There is no distinction between whether he took the collateral at the time of the loan or not at the time of the loan, because in all cases he has some ownership, and therefore he is liable as a paid guardian, as he wrote in Chapter 10 of Hiring. And regarding her collateral, it is obvious that there is no distinction, since the reason is that she benefits from the collateral from now, so what difference does it make whether he took it at the time of the loan or not. Moreover, since he wrote generally regarding someone else’s collateral as her collateral, it is clearly explained that there is no distinction. And this is why he needed to state a different reason for her collateral than for someone else’s collateral. One cannot say that he holds that with her collateral, she is betrothed even if he did not return the collateral to her, because he explicitly wrote there that it is specifically when he returns the collateral to her. Additionally, the reason that she benefits from the collateral from now only applies when he returns the collateral to her. However, certainly with someone else’s collateral, she would only be betrothed when it comes to his hand as collateral, but if it does not come to his hand as collateral, even though he can withhold it for his money, nonetheless, this is not considered a collateral that he has ownership in, as the Tur wrote. The Rambam holds that this only applies to someone else’s collateral, where the reason is that he has ownership in it, but with her collateral, where the reason is that she benefits from the item now, it could be that she is betrothed even if it does not come to his hand as collateral. And although the Tur wrote this regarding her collateral, nonetheless, according to the Rambam, we can say that the Tur himself holds that with her collateral, she is betrothed even without returning the collateral to her and even if he did not mention betrothing her with the collateral. For betrothing with a loan that has a collateral, he holds that she is betrothed because since there is a collateral, it is as if the loan is present and it is not like a regular loan that is meant to be spent. Therefore, if he said, “Behold, you are betrothed to me with the loan that you owe me on your collateral that is in my hand,” she is betrothed even though the collateral is still in his hand. Even those who hold that he must specifically return the collateral, hold that the reason is because it is like the benefit of forgiving a loan. These reasons only apply when there is a complete collateral, but according to the Rambam, it is possible that even without a complete collateral, she is betrothed.

It has already been explained that there are some of our Rabbis who believe that with her own collateral, she is betrothed even without returning the collateral to her. And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote that when the collateral is in her possession, it is as if the collateral was returned to her. And it seems to me that this is only according to the reasons explained, but according to the Rambam's reason that we brought, that she benefits from it now when it is returned to her, if the collateral was in her possession, this reason does not apply. However, with actual collateral, it is understandable even according to the Rambam, that she is betrothed because she acquires the collateral and it now becomes hers, for it is no worse than the collateral of others.

In the case of a pledge belonging to others, some of our rabbis have said that she is not betrothed unless the pledge was taken not at the time of the loan, for then he acquires the pledge by Torah law and can betroth with it since he has a legal acquisition in the physical pledge. However, he must inform her that it is a pledge, for otherwise she might think the object itself belongs to her and could later say that she did not intend to be betrothed with something that does not belong to him. But if he took the pledge at the time of the loan and betrothed her with it, she is not betrothed, for the Torah's statement that a creditor acquires a pledge applies only when it is not at the time of the loan. However, some of our rabbis hold that even with a pledge taken at the time of the loan, she is betrothed, since when the pledge is taken not at the time of the loan, he acquires full ownership until the pledge is redeemed. Therefore, at the time of the loan, his lien is strong enough to be considered money to betroth a woman with it. However, it seems to me that anyone who betroths with a pledge commits a transgression, for it is forbidden to use it as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 72, and this is like interest. If he betroths a woman with it, he benefits from it, and this is like interest. It is possible that it is permitted to betroth with it, for he is essentially betrothing her with the debt, and the pledge makes the debt as if it is present, and she will not use the pledge. This is of no consequence. Perhaps this is why the Rambam did not write the reason for a pledge belonging to others as he did for a pledge belonging to her, which is that she benefits from the pledge, because it is forbidden to use another's pledge.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that all of this applies to a pledge that he has from a Jew, but from a non-Jew – she is not betrothed, because a Jew from a non-Jew does not acquire a pledge [Pesachim 31b]. Maimonides (Rambam) did not differentiate in this matter because he holds that even a non-Jew acquires a pledge [Maggid Mishneh, Chapter 4 of Chametz], but we do not hold this way as explained in Orach Chaim, Siman 481. And even if the time for repayment has arrived and he has been given permission to sell it, nevertheless, as long as he has not sold it, it still belongs to the borrower, as is evident in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 73. And it is possible that in such a case she is betrothed, for what difference does it make if he sold it to others or gave it to a woman for her betrothal, and certainly one should be stringent and require her to receive a get (bill of divorce), and if she accepted betrothal from another man – she needs a get from both. And if at the time he pledged it to him he said, "If I do not repay you by such and such a time, the pledge will be yours from now," and the time arrived and he did not repay, and he betrothed her with it – it is a valid betrothal, even if he did not accept responsibility at the time of the loan, as is evident in Orach Chaim there. But if he betrothed her before the time arrived – she is not betrothed even if he did not repay at the time, for at the time of the betrothal it was not his, and he must take it from her and betroth her with it a second time.

There are those who ask why a pawned item is worse than a stolen item such that one cannot be betrothed with it. Indeed, the truth is that if he intends to steal it, she is betrothed. But when he does not intend to steal it, with what would she be betrothed [Beit Shmuel]? Similarly, if he sold the pawned item to another and the other person betrothed her with it, she is betrothed. For since the lender sold it, it is considered as if it were stolen. Therefore, even though the buyer did not know that it was a pawned item and if he had known, he would not have bought it, she is nonetheless betrothed, just as with one who betroths with a stolen item or sells the stolen item and the buyer betroths the woman with it. It seems to me that if there is a danger that he will be punished by secular courts for acquiring a pawned or stolen item and the buyer was unaware of this, the betrothal is not certain and is only considered doubtful betrothal. Perhaps it is not a betrothal at all, as I have written in section 19. Refer to it thoroughly, and the matter requires further study.

Even though one who betroths a woman with a loan, the betrothal is not valid, nevertheless, if he had a debt owed to him by another person and said to her in the presence of that person, "You are betrothed to me with the debt that is owed to me by this person" – she is betrothed, because she acquires the debt in the presence of all three parties. For although by Torah law this is not considered an acquisition, the Sages have already instituted that it should be considered an acquisition, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 126. 

There is an opinion that since this acquisition is only rabbinic, the betrothal is also only rabbinic.
