However, Rabbi Yosef Karo (the Beit Yosef) holds that by Torah law it is considered betrothal, because all rabbinic enactments regarding monetary matters are considered as if they are by Torah law, and this is proven in the Jerusalem Talmud (Ma'aser Sheni, Chapter 4, Halacha 3).

Even though ultimately he is betrothing her with a loan, since the debt is owed by others and he betroths her with it, she is betrothed by the benefit of the loan (Ran). This is not similar to her own debt, because a debt owed by others is something new to her, and her mind rests on the benefit and not on the money of the loan itself.

There are those who say she is not betrothed in the presence of all three parties, because we hold that if someone sells a debt to another and then forgives it, it is forgiven, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 66. Therefore, there is a concern that he might forgive the debt, and she does not rely on it. The first opinion holds that in the presence of all three parties, he cannot forgive the debt because the Sages strengthened the enactment of acquisition in the presence of all three parties. However, not in the presence of all three parties, even if it was a loan in writing and he transferred it to her by writing and delivery, it is only considered doubtful betrothal due to the reason that he can forgive the debt, as stated in Siman 54.

It appears to me that when one betroths a woman with a loan of others based on the principle of "ma'amad shloshtan" (the presence of all three parties), he must say at the time of the transaction to the borrower, "The money that I have with you as a loan, give it to this woman," for this is the essential law of "ma'amad shloshtan." And one should not say that when he tells her, "Become betrothed to me with the debt that this person owes me," it is as if he said it to the borrower, for the borrower’s consent is not required, as it is acquired even against his will, as stated in Choshen Mishpat there. Nevertheless, it is clarified there that nothing should be added to the enactment, and in the enactment, we do not find that this should be said to the recipient, but rather to the borrower or the trustee. The fact that the poskim (decisors) did not mention this is because it is an obvious matter. Nevertheless, in practice, there is room for doubt, for perhaps regarding betrothal, when he says to her in the presence of all three, it is as if he says it to the borrower, and this requires further investigation for the law.

And just as we explained regarding a rabbinic acquisition, which is not effective according to Torah law, that one can become betrothed with it, like the acquisition of "Ma'amad Sheloshtan" (when three parties are present), similarly, there is a question about an acquisition that is effective according to Torah law but not effective rabbinically. For example, in the case of the acquisition of money, where Reuven bought merchandise from Shimon and gave him money but did not yet take possession of the merchandise. According to Torah law, money effects acquisition, but rabbinically, only taking possession effects acquisition. If Shimon then betrothed a woman with this money, is she betrothed or not?

There is an opinion that she is betrothed, because the rabbinic enactments were not meant to override Torah law leniently (Sema, Siman 198, Se'if Katan 3). However, if this is the case, we should also consider when another man betroths the woman after the first man, we should still be concerned about the second man's betrothal. And we have already explained in the name of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, that she is fully betrothed to the first man. 

In truth, we explained in Choshen Mishpat, there Siman 1, that in matters of acquisitions, this is not considered an uprooting of a Torah law, because this is not among the commandments, and all merchants can establish any form of acquisition they desire, as we explained there in Siman 241. The main element of acquisition is the mutual consent of the buyer and the seller, which is why an "asmachta" (conditional commitment) does not effect acquisition. Why should a rabbinic enactment be less effective than the merchants' practices? Moreover, since it has already been established, there is no mutual consent regarding the money, and therefore, it appears to me that in any case, we cannot entirely dismiss the issue of doubtful betrothal.

However, if the seller is permitted to use the money, as explained there in Siman 195 – it is obvious that it would be a complete betrothal, as stated there in Se'if 7. We also explained there that when the sale is canceled according to the rule of "Mi Shepara" (the curse for one who reneges on a deal), it is obvious that it is not a valid betrothal.

And if the seller received the money from the buyer and betrothed a woman with the item he sold to the buyer, it appears that the betrothal is valid because, according to Rabbinic law, the item has not yet left his possession. However, some say that if another man comes and betroths her, we are concerned for the betrothal of the second one as well, because according to Torah law, the first man betrothed her with stolen property. And even though we have explained that in matters of acquisition we follow the enactment of the Sages, nevertheless, because according to Rabbinic law he is obligated in "Mi Shepara" (a curse invoked on one who reneges on a deal) if he wishes to retract the sale, the item is not completely his before he receives the "Mi Shepara," and therefore we are properly concerned for the betrothal of the second one. Consequently, it may also be said regarding the previous law when he betrothed her with the money, that since if the buyer wishes to retract the sale, he cannot do so without the "Mi Shepara," the money is considered somewhat his before the buyer receives the "Mi Shepara," and we are concerned for his betrothal.

And if a person sold an item to his friend and the buyer had already taken possession, and afterward a defect was found in the merchandise or there was an overcharge greater than one-sixth, and in the meantime, the seller betrothed a woman with the money, if the seller was unaware of the defect or the overcharge – it is clear that the betrothal is valid. Even though the seller is obligated to return the buyer's money, he need not return the exact same money and can return other money. However, if the seller knew of the defect or the error, it is possible that this could be considered as betrothing with stolen property, and in practice, we should be stringent as there is no clear ruling on this matter [see Maggid Mishneh there].

And if the buyer betrothed a woman with the item and afterward a defect was found in it, if they knew of the defect at the time of the betrothal – the betrothal is valid because they accepted it knowingly. If they were unaware of the defect – then the betrothal is not valid since she did not consent to the defect. However, if it is discovered after the betrothal that there is a complete voiding of the sale, which does not concern the woman – it appears that it is a doubtful betrothal [in my opinion].

Even though if one betroths a woman with a loan, she is not betrothed, but if he betroths her with a loan and an available perutah or another available object - she is betrothed, as her intention is on the available perutah. And even if the loan was a large amount, we do not say her intention was on the loan <small>[Rashi, Sanhedrin 19b]</small>. There is no difference whether the loan preceded the perutah or the perutah preceded the loan, as the Rambam writes in Chapter 5, Law 16. This applies specifically to a loan and a perutah, but if he betroths her with two available items, one of which effects betrothal and the other does not, such as betrothing her with two perutahs, one his and one stolen, there is no proof that this constitutes betrothal. Such betrothal is certainly invalid as there is no greater mistaken betrothal than this, since she did not consent to be betrothed with less than two perutahs. However, with a loan and a perutah it is different, because the loan is essentially forgiven to her, and there is no mistake here. If her intention was to be betrothed also with the loan, the betrothal would not take effect. We say her intention was only on the available perutah, and the loan is merely like a condition, as if he said "on the condition that you forgive me the loan" <small>[Rashba, Responsa, Section 1733]</small>. But if he betroths her with two items, one of which does not effect betrothal, such as stolen items or items prohibited for benefit, there is no betrothal. This is not comparable to a sale where one sells an item not yet in existence along with an item in existence, where the acquisition takes effect on the item in existence, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Section 209, or "acquire this and the donkey" in Section 210. There, they are two separate matters, but here, the woman is one entity and she did not consent to be betrothed with only one of the items. Nor is it relevant to say that half of her is betrothed and the betrothal extends to her entire being, as she did not consent to be betrothed partially <small>[and the words of the Avnei Miluim require further examination]</small>. The reason we say her intention is on the perutah is because a woman's mind in grasping betrothal is only on what is immediately available to her, and what is not immediately available is considered merely a condition.

And similarly, as explained in Section 16, a craftsman does not acquire ownership through the improvement of the vessel. If he betroths a woman with the wages of his work, it is considered as a loan and she is not betrothed. However, if he added a perutah's worth of his own labor and betroths with the vessel, she is betrothed, as it is considered a loan and a perutah. Some say that this is specifically when he added some tangible thing to the work, such as a stone, wood, or nail of his own that remains visible. But if he gave money of his own for the work, this money is also considered a loan. However, it is clear that if he bought something specific with his money and added it to the work, it is not considered a loan, for since he purchased it with his money, it belongs to him. Nevertheless, if he gave his own money just to enhance the work or something similar that is not specific, it is considered a loan. Similarly, if he added his own dye, it is considered doubtful betrothal since it is not substantial.

Just as there is a distinction in loans between one's own loan and the loan of others, where in the case of another's loan, if he handed over the loan for the purpose of betrothal in the presence of three, she is betrothed. Similarly, with wages, if someone performed work for another and became entitled to a perutah in payment for the work, if he betrothed her with this perutah in the presence of three, it is as if he betrothed with another’s loan in the presence of three. Even if the work is not yet completed but the employer accepted it with a transaction and committed to paying him, he can betroth her with this in the presence of three. 

There is an opinion that regarding wages, as long as he has not returned the object he rented, it does not have the status of a loan at all, and it is even worse than a loan within the time frame. However, when he returns the object, it retroactively becomes a loan and does not have the law of the presence of three because the debt is not yet clarified, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 126. Nevertheless, according to what we explained there in section 2, at the end of the time the obligation is clear even if he has not returned the object. Therefore, since the employer accepted it with a transaction and committed to paying, it is indeed relevant here to the presence of three as stated.

There is a need for careful consideration regarding the law of betrothal, as perhaps one should be stringent also according to the opinion of those who disagree.

And regarding an artisan who is a contractor, when he made an item for her, as we wrote in section 47, if he betrothed her with the wage for his work, the main ruling is that she is not betrothed, because we hold that an artisan does not acquire through the enhancement of the vessel. However, in matters of betrothal, one must be stringent according to those who say that an artisan does acquire through the enhancement of the vessel. 

Some say that this only applies when he has already returned the vessel to her but betroths her with the wage that is due to him. But if he has not yet returned the vessel and at the time of returning it he betroths her with the wage of the vessel, she is betrothed according to all opinions. This is similar to a loan that has collateral, as explained in section 56. And even though we require that it be explicitly taken as collateral, as mentioned there in the name of the Tur, nevertheless, the fact that he retained the item with him is considered as if it was taken as collateral, because any artisan who holds onto a vessel is as if he has collateral for his wage. 

Some say that this is true only if he revealed his intention to hold it as collateral for his wage, for otherwise, it is not considered similar to collateral. And some say further that even revealing his intention is not effective unless she demanded the item and he told her that he would not give it to her until she paid, as this is explicitly like collateral. And some say further that even in such a case, it is not effective, because the law of an artisan is not like that of a lender with collateral. Collateral is only when it comes into his hand as collateral for a loan, which the Torah considers as somewhat of an acquisition of the collateral itself. 

And it is clear that one should be stringent in matters of betrothal according to all opinions. Some of the early authorities said further that the opinion that is stringent in saying that an artisan acquires through the enhancement of the vessel, thereby making it a valid betrothal, applies only if at the time he returned the item to her he said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with the wage of this vessel". But if he said it to her before returning it, it is nothing. And consequently, according to those who hold that an artisan does not acquire through the enhancement of the vessel, it is also ineffective in such a case, contrary to the first opinion that considers it as collateral. However, the primary ruling in this matter requires proof. And we have already explained that it is only due to the stringency of betrothal that we are concerned with the opinion that an artisan acquires through the enhancement of the vessel, and therefore there is no need to elaborate further on this.

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 7: If one betroths a woman with less than a perutah or with a loan and then has relations with her in the presence of witnesses without specifying anything further, she requires a get (divorce document), because it is assumed that he relies on this act of intercourse and not on the invalid betrothal, as it is presumed that an upstanding Jew does not engage in intercourse promiscuously. Now that he has the opportunity to make it an act of mitzvah (commandment), he will do so. This is the end of his words. And although Rambam does not hold this view regarding a single woman, as he writes in Chapter 10 of Hilchot Gerushin, nevertheless, in cases where the framework of betrothal was entered into, but the betrothal was invalid according to the law, we still say that he does not engage in intercourse promiscuously. Some have inferred from Rambam's language that the betrothal through intercourse is definite [Magid Mishneh], but many disagree, holding that it is only a doubtful betrothal, and if she accepts betrothal from another man, she requires a get from both. Even regarding Rambam's opinion, there is no clear indication that he intends it to be considered definite betrothal [Kesef Mishneh]. Additionally, not everyone is expert in the law that betrothing with a loan does not constitute a valid betrothal, and thus his intention might be for the intercourse to serve as betrothal. This also appears from the language of the Talmud [Ketubot 74a] and the Jerusalem Talmud [Gittin Chapter 8, Halacha 9] that the principle of "a man does not engage in intercourse promiscuously" is only to require a get from him, as discussed there. In Siman 31, this will be further elucidated, with additional details provided in Siman 42, God willing.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Yosef Karo), wrote in section 17: If someone enters his friend's house and takes a utensil or food item or something similar and uses it to betroth a woman, and then the homeowner comes and says, "Why didn't you give her this item, which is better than what you gave her?" – she is not betrothed. This is because the homeowner only said this to avoid embarrassment, and since he betrothed her with his friend's property without his friend's knowledge, it is considered theft, and she is not betrothed. If he betrothed her with something the homeowner doesn't care about, such as a date or a nut, she is betrothed out of doubt. This is the language of the Rambam.

It appears that the reason given – that the homeowner only said it to avoid embarrassment and did not genuinely intend to give it – is not needed to explain why the betrothal is not retroactively valid. Even if we assume he spoke genuinely, since it was not taken with the homeowner's knowledge, it is theft, and one cannot betroth with stolen property. Even someone who borrows without the homeowner's knowledge is considered a thief, all the more so in this case. The reason is needed to explain that if we say he genuinely consented, the betrothal would take effect from now on if the item is still present, and he could take it back and give it to her in front of witnesses. To this, it is said that even from now on, it is not effective because he did not genuinely consent.

This reasoning also has practical implications if he took it in front of the homeowner and betrothed her with it, and the homeowner said, "Why didn't you give her something nicer?" If the homeowner's statement was genuine, she would be betrothed. But since we say he did not genuinely consent, she is not betrothed. See the commentaries of the Chelkat Mechokek and the Beit Shmuel, where it is explained that even for future betrothal, it would need to be done anew, as the Beit Shmuel himself writes in section 31, subsection 1. Even according to the Rashba, it must subsequently be stated, "Behold, you are betrothed to me," as explained there. This will be further clarified in section 31, subsection 5, with God's help.

All that we have written is according to the opinion of the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch. However, in my humble opinion, these matters are perplexing. How can we say that she is not betrothed even for the future because he did not have complete intention? From where do we derive such a leniency? Perhaps he did have complete intention, and at the very least, it should be considered a doubt of betrothal. Indeed, some of our sages explained this matter in the Gemara (Kiddushin 52b) that the one who betrothed her with the food had some connection since he was a partner in the profit from this food (Rashi) or he had previously authorized him to take from this food, but did not specify to take from the best (Tosafot), and he took from the best. Even in this case, it seems to me that their intention is not that it is certainly not a betrothal, but rather that the Sages said it is not a definite betrothal. Even though in the Gemara there is a version at the end of the discussion that she is not betrothed, this version is not found in the Rif and the Rosh. And even according to our version, one can say that she is not definitely betrothed. Although the language is distant, it is clearer according to the version of the Rif and the Rosh, and according to their view, it applies only to the past and not to the future. But the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch, who did not interpret it this way, indeed for the past it is certainly not a betrothal, but for the future, why should it not be a doubt of betrothal, since perhaps he had complete intention? Especially since in betrothal there is also somewhat of a mitzvah, how could they definitively rule that he did not have complete intention? And also, what they wrote that in a case where the owner of the item is not particular, it is a doubtful betrothal even for the past – this is perplexing. How can it be in a person's power to betroth a woman with someone else's property without his knowledge? (The Noda B’Yehuda also wonders about this).

Therefore, it appears to me that the Rambam is also referring to retrospect, and this is the matter: Certainly, it is not the manner of a stranger to come into another's house and take something for himself, and if a person like this is found, the homeowner would not tell him, "Go to the better ones," but rather, it refers to a friend who regularly comes and goes in his house, and they are dear friends, and it is the custom of this one to enter the home of the other frequently and take what he wants, and the homeowner is not particular about it and knows this from before. Nevertheless, this person who came without the homeowner's permission as usual and took something of the owner's and betrothed a woman with it – she is not betrothed, because in the end, he took it without permission and is like a thief. Even if he is not particular about what he eats there or uses his utensils, but to give to others – he is certainly particular. And even if he later told him, "Go to the better ones,” he said it out of etiquette because of their closeness, but in truth it is like theft. Even if he later agrees, it is still retrospectively like unknowing despair (see Tosafot Bava Metzia 22a s.v. "If etc." and "If you say etc."). And when he told him, "Go to the better ones,” and he then betrothed her with it, it is a doubtful betrothal. But retrospectively, it is certainly not a betrothal. Therefore, the Rambam needed to say that his statement was to avoid embarrassing him, because this has implications for the future as well, so that the betrothal should not be definite. Therefore, in a matter that the homeowner is not particular about at all and knows that this frequent visitor always takes it – she is betrothed out of doubt, because perhaps it is as if he commanded him to take it.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: "A guest who is sitting with the host and takes his portion and betroths a woman with it – she is betrothed." This is the end of his words. And even though we hold that guests are not permitted to take from what is before them and give it to the host's son or servant without the host's permission, as stated in Orach Chaim section 170, and certainly they should not give to others, therefore some say that it is only a doubtful betrothal. And some say that this applies only when each person has not yet been given their portion before them, but when each person has been given their portion before them – it is considered like their own, and they are permitted to do with it as they wish. There is some evidence for this from tractate Derech Eretz chapter 9. See there. (See also the commentary of the Gra section 150 and the Magen Avraham section 170, and the words of the Beit Shmuel section 146 require investigation, and be precise).

There are those who say that guests who are dining at the table of a host, even if they have selected their portion and it has been placed before them, and the host took from what was placed before them and betrothed a woman with it – she is betrothed as long as they have not put it into their mouths [Be'er Heitev in the name of Maharit]. And although we have written that when each one’s portion is placed before him it is considered as his own, this is true when he has done some action with his portion, for just as he can put it into his mouth, so too can he give it to another, and this is his acquisition. But as long as he has not done any action with his portion, it is still considered as the host’s portion [in my opinion]. And it seems to me that this is with a guest who eats for free, but a guest in an inn who pays for his meal, as soon as his portion is placed before him, he acquires it and the host has no rights to the portion, for the table before him is considered his for the duration of his stay in the inn, and the table acquires his portion for him. However, with many guests, as long as each one’s portion has not been clearly specified, it is not yet considered as his own. Nevertheless, there is a doubt if the host has a share in this as long as each one’s portion has not been clearly specified, and this requires further investigation for a definitive ruling.

If there was merchandise between him and his friend, and he divided it without his friend's knowledge and betrothed [a woman] with his portion, since it requires the appraisal of a court and his division is meaningless as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 176, she is not betrothed. This is because he cannot take for himself whatever he wants and leave whatever he wants. Even if he gave her all the merchandise in his portion and it is worth more than a perutah, she is still not betrothed, because she does not desire to be betrothed except with all the merchandise, unless he specified and said, "Be betrothed to me with the portion that I have in this merchandise." For he betrothed her with this portion, and he only has half of it since his division is not a valid division. It seems to me that if she knew he divided the merchandise without his partner’s knowledge, it would be considered a doubtful betrothal, for she knows that his division is nothing and she accepted it with what he has in this. Although women are not experts in law, nevertheless, in such a case, we do not say this leniently. This is not similar to what is written in section 32, for there she did not accept it for betrothal at all but as a deposit, see there. Similarly, if the partner later came and agreed to the division and the betrothal had not yet been consummated, it would be a doubtful betrothal, for it could be said that it was retroactively revealed that he betrothed with what was his. There are those who say this is similar to unintentional abandonment, but in truth, this law depends on retroactive clarification. If we say there is retroactive clarification to be stringent in Torah law, we say it is clarified retroactively that this is his portion. Even if it was consumed, it would be a doubtful betrothal. All this applies to merchandise that has good and bad parts, but with a type of merchandise where all items are equal and he divided it without his partner’s knowledge and betrothed with his portion, she is betrothed. For this is like the division of money, where a partner can divide without the other's knowledge, as stated in Choshen Mishpat there, and specifically if he divided it equally by measure or weight in a way that does not require court appraisal.

One who betroths a woman with a borrowed ring or other borrowed object without informing her that it is borrowed – she is not betrothed, for she accepted the object with the understanding that it was hers, and indeed it is not hers since she must return it to its owner, thus it turns out that he betrothed her with an item taken by theft [Rosh, Chapter 1, Section 20]. If he informed her that it was borrowed and did not inform the owner of the object that he intended to use it for betrothal – she is not betrothed unless he borrowed it for a specific period, for otherwise, the owner can take it back immediately. Although we generally hold that a loan without a specified term lasts for thirty days, this is not the case with borrowing objects, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Section 341. And even according to those who say there that an unspecified borrowing also lasts for thirty days, this applies only to the borrower himself. It is obvious that he does not have the authority to lend it to another, as this would be akin to outright theft [Avnei Miluim]. However, if he borrowed it for a specified period, although the borrower does not initially have the right to lend it to another, after the fact, it is not considered theft [there, and Beit Shmuel, Section 148]. Some are uncertain about this, arguing that since a transgression was committed, she can claim that she does not wish to be betrothed through a transgression [Mikneh and Kereb Nateanel, Section 98]. Therefore, it is necessary that permission was given to lend it to another, and this seems to be the implication from the wording of the Rosh there. In practice, this is considered a doubtful betrothal. Additionally, another condition is required: he must inform her that the object is borrowed until a certain time, and that the enjoyment of adornment during that time is worth a perutah – then she is betrothed. And although she must return the object after the time, which is similar to a gift on the condition to return, as will be explained in the beginning of Section 29 that she is not betrothed, nevertheless, she is betrothed because he gives her what is his, and that thing he gives her in a complete gift [Beit Shmuel].

Some say that even if all these conditions are met, it is only a doubtful betrothal, as it resembles a gift given on the condition that it be returned [Tur in the name of Baal Ha'itur]. Since he betrothed her with the object without specifying, even though she knew it was borrowed, her intention is on the item itself. And since the item must be returned to the lender, it is like a gift given on the condition that it be returned. The first opinion holds that since she knows it is borrowed, her intention is only on the benefit of its use. Therefore, if he explicitly says, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with the benefit of using this object," it is effective according to all opinions, because the benefit remains with her and the item itself was not given to her at all. This is not similar to a gift given on the condition that it be returned. In such a case, there is no need to inform her that it is borrowed, since he is not betrothing her with the item itself but with the benefit of its use for a certain time. If he betrothed her explicitly with the item itself, according to all opinions, it is not a betrothal [Bach]. Some say that even when he betroths her explicitly with the benefit of its use, he must inform her that it is borrowed. Otherwise, since she thinks it is his and he betroths her with the benefit of its use, his intention according to her understanding is to betroth her with the item for her use. And since the item must be returned, it is like a gift given on the condition that it be returned. But when he tells her it is borrowed, she knows he is giving her all he has in the item, and it is not similar to a gift given on the condition that it be returned [Even HaEzer 61]. This does not seem correct, because even with a gift given on the condition that it be returned, she is legally betrothed, except that the Sages decreed it invalid because it resembles an exchange, as stated in the beginning of section 29. Therefore, when he betroths her with the benefit of its use, even if she thinks it is his, it is not similar to a gift given on the condition that it be returned, which would be like an exchange. However, some say that when he betroths her with the use of the object, he must say, "with the benefit of using the object," which is like the benefit of a loan where she would need to give a coin to appease him to borrow it, and he betroths her with this coin. But if he simply said she should be betrothed "with the use of this object," it is not effective, as this is like betrothing her with the payment for its use, which is like a loan, as the rental of an object is like a loan [Ketzos HaChoshen].

And know, that what we have written, that some say that even with all the conditions they are only doubtful betrothals, there are those who disagree with this and hold that when all the conditions are met, according to everyone they are definite betrothals. The authorities who disagreed, only disagreed if he borrowed without a specified time. Therefore, some say that they are only doubtful betrothals because he can take it back at any time he wishes, and some say that she is betrothed because they hold that a general borrowing is for thirty days [Beit Yosef and Bach]. And according to this, since we hold in practice that a general borrowing is not for thirty days, it is clear that it is only doubtful betrothals. And according to what is written in subsection 70, that after it is clear that he cannot lend, it is far from even being doubtful betrothals. But in practice, we do not rule leniently, and it is considered doubtful betrothals.

Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 20: "If one gives his fellow a gift on the condition that it be returned, and the recipient went and betrothed a woman with it – she is betrothed." And even though when one betroths a woman on the condition that the betrothal be returned, she is not betrothed as it is written in section 29, this is due to the decree concerning exchange as explained there. But when one gives a person a gift on the condition that it be returned, it is entirely his, as he is granted ownership through a complete acquisition. The condition to return it is merely a stipulation, as stated in Choshen Mishpat section 241, paragraph 11. Therefore, he can also consecrate it, as stated there, and thus he can also betroth a woman with it. 

And if it is questioned that since he stipulated to return it, and if he does not fulfill the condition, the gift is nullified, and since he betrothed a woman with it and cannot return it, the condition is not fulfilled, and the gift is nullified, making the betrothal an act of theft, because in consecration, it is established that the item must be returned when consecrated as stated there, and here the woman will not return it? It can be said that here too, he can either later purchase it back from the woman and return the item or leave it with the woman and repay the giver with money equivalent to the item's value. For even according to the opinion that in the condition of a get (divorce document) the item itself must be returned specifically, and this is the ruling as stated in section 143, this is only in the case of a get because it is said that the intent is to cause distress. But with an ordinary person, what difference does it make if it is the item itself or its monetary value? 

Therefore, if he does not fulfill his condition and does not return the money to the giver, he betroths with theft retroactively. Nevertheless, it will always remain a doubtful betrothal because whenever he returns the money, the betrothal will retroactively take effect. And it is a simple matter that when he betroths her with this, he gives her the item permanently, because if he also gives it to her on the condition that she return it, it is not a betrothal.

One who rents a utensil or object from his fellow and betroths a woman with it is treated as one who borrows a utensil as explained. If he did not inform her that it was rented, she is not betrothed. If he informed her and the usage is within the rental period as agreed upon, she is betrothed. Some are uncertain whether renting is better than borrowing, because in the case of borrowing, if he betrothed her with the object itself, she is not betrothed, as stated in Section 78. However, in the case of renting, she is betrothed, since renting for a day is considered a sale. Nevertheless, it can be argued that even in renting, she is not betrothed, because not in all matters did the Sages say that renting is considered a sale. This is also implied from the words of Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) in Section 19, who equates renting to borrowing entirely. In any case, some say that renting is effective when he gives her the object itself and she knows it is rented, because even if it is not considered a sale, why should he not be able to transfer his rights to another? Indeed, regarding renting land, one can also initially rent it to another, as stated in Choshen Mishpat Section 312. In the case of renting movable objects, although one should not initially rent it to another due to the risk of loss, still, the rights he has should be effective when he transfers to her the rights he has in the object itself. Since he paid money, he has rights in the object for the entire rental period. This requires further study.

Everything we have explained regarding consecrating (kiddushin) with a borrowed vessel applies when the owner of the vessel was not informed that the borrower intended to use it for kiddushin. However, if the owner was informed, our sages have ruled that the kiddushin is valid in any case, even if the woman was not informed that the vessel was borrowed. The reason is that we assume the lender, since he lent it for the purpose of kiddushin, fully intended to give it in a manner that would be effective for kiddushin. If it would not be effective as a loan, it would be considered a gift, or at the very least, a gift on condition that it be returned. The woman would acquire the vessel and then return it to him or pay him its value, as is stated in the law regarding a gift on condition of return. 

Therefore, there is doubt if the borrower did not return the value to the lender whether the kiddushin is definitely valid because we say he intended it as a complete gift, or it is only doubtful kiddushin. From the language of the Tur, it seems he also is uncertain about this, and therefore it is only doubtful kiddushin. A similar example is mentioned regarding an etrog owned by the community, where one fulfills his obligation with it, as stated in Orach Chaim, Siman 658.

It is specifically when he asked from the husband himself, but one should not borrow a utensil from a woman who has a husband without the husband's knowledge, for whatever the woman acquires, the husband acquires. Nevertheless, our Rabbi the Rema wrote that if one borrowed a utensil from a woman who has a husband and sanctified with it – we are concerned about the sanctification and it is considered doubtful sanctification. And now the custom has become somewhat lenient in this regard, that if the groom does not have a ring, they borrow from another woman standing there at the time of the chuppah even without the husband's permission, because presumably the husband is not particular about giving a gift on the condition that it be returned. And there is no reason for this leniency, for in a case of financial loss we do not say that a person is pleased to do a mitzvah with his money, as it is written in Orach Chaim section 14 and section 437. However, it seems to me that there is a correct reason for this leniency, for certainly with utensils and items that are not related to her body, she indeed has no permission, and in this our Rabbi the Rema says only that we should be concerned about the sanctification, meaning it is doubtful sanctification since perhaps the husband is pleased. But with a ring or other item related to her body, they are hers and the husband has no connection to them, and creditors do not collect from them as it is written in Choshen Mishpat section 97, and even consecration does not collect from this as Maimonides wrote in chapter 3 of Arachin. And although after his death we assess this towards her ketubah as it is written in section 99, the reason is that he only granted her as long as she is under him and not when he dies, and certainly he did not grant her to give them to others. However, against her will they are hers, for even after his death they cannot be taken from her as written there, only they are calculated towards her ketubah value. And similarly, when she gives to others, it is calculated towards her ketubah value when he dies. But nonetheless, since they are hers, why shouldn't she be able to do with them as she pleases? And all the more so if the ring being borrowed is her wedding ring, it is obvious that it is entirely hers, for the sanctification does not revert to the husband as it is written in section 50. Therefore, this custom has a place according to the law.

According to what has been explained, every person who arranges a wedding must be careful to ask the groom if the ring belongs to him or if he borrowed it, and if he borrowed it, he must ask him if he informed the lender that he intends to use it for marriage, also if he borrowed it from the husband or from a woman who has a husband [Beit Shmuel]. And based on what was said, in items that belong to her body, the husband's consent is not effective without her consent, and ideally, one should avoid using a borrowed item for marriage [Responsa of the Rosh], and it is better to marry with a coin than with a borrowed ring, and if someone else gives the groom a ring as a gift, they should ensure that the groom lifts the ring three handbreadths as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 198. The one who performs the marriage is not believed to cast aspersions on the marriage by saying that he stole the ring or borrowed it without the owner's knowledge, for no person makes himself wicked [Drisha], and borrowing without knowledge is considered theft. And if he sold him an item on the condition that he will pay him another item like it - this is a complete sale, but he must acquire it by pulling or lifting it, each according to its form of acquisition, and if he sold it to him for money, the giving of the money is not essential, provided they make a decisive agreement, for without a decisive agreement, he did not acquire it as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 200.

Sanctification using items forbidden for benefit – she is not sanctified because it is not considered to have monetary value, and even though there are some items whose mitzvah is to be burned and their ashes are permitted for benefit, and thus if the ashes have the value of a perutah she would be sanctified with it, and likewise there are forbidden items from which one may benefit in an unconventional manner, and if such benefit has the value of a perutah she would be sanctified with it. However, since she believes she is being sanctified with the primary item and in a conventional manner, the sanctification is automatically void, for even if he sanctified her with a maneh and it was found to be missing a dinar, she is not sanctified. But if she knew it was from items forbidden for benefit and in such a way it has the value of a perutah, it is possible she is sanctified [and so it appears in Tosafot]. Some say that even unconventional benefit is only permitted for a sick person and not for a healthy one, for the Sages only said one does not get lashes for forbidden benefit in an unconventional manner, but there is still a rabbinic prohibition [Ran there], and this is only according to the opinion that even with rabbinic prohibitions she is not sanctified, therefore she is not sanctified due to unconventional benefit. What is permitted for a sick person is not considered monetary value to effect sanctification, for otherwise all forbidden items would be permitted for a dangerously ill person. According to the opinion that with rabbinic prohibitions she is sanctified, she requires a get, and similarly if the ashes have the value of a perutah, she requires a get [see Beit Yosef and Chelkat Mechokek]. There is an opinion that in all forbidden items, if she knows it is prohibited for benefit, he can sanctify her because she can sell it to a sick person [Beit Shmuel], but this is problematic because the sale itself is forbidden even to a sick person, and benefiting in an unconventional manner, nevertheless, the sale is in a conventional manner [and so writes the Makneh, and so it appears from Ritva], and even if she herself is sick and permitted to benefit in an unconventional manner, there is still doubt if the sanctification is valid, for although regarding her it has the value of a perutah, regarding him it does not have the value of a perutah, and moreover, monetary value is only considered what is valuable to everyone, unless he says to her, "You are sanctified to me with the benefit you have from being healed by this," and this benefit has the value of a perutah [Maggid Mishneh in the name of Ritva], and this seems to be the main halachic ruling. Know that chametz on Pesach, although we hold in Orach Chaim 445 that its ashes are forbidden, nevertheless, concerning the stringency of sanctification, we are concerned it might be from those burned and its ashes are permitted [Beit Shmuel there].

Therefore, one who betroths with items of orlah, kilayim of the vineyard, an idol, a stoned ox, a beheaded calf, pigul, notar, and impure things, and with the birds of a leper that are taken for the purification of the leper, one of which is slaughtered and the other is sent away, even though the sent one is permitted for benefit since the Torah did not say to send it to cause stumbling to people, nevertheless, from the slaughter of its counterpart until the sending it is also forbidden [Tosafot 57.], and with the hair of a Nazirite, and with a firstborn donkey whether before or after its neck is broken if it was not redeemed with a lamb, with meat and milk, with un-consecrated animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard, and with wine used for libation – she is not betrothed. Similarly, a priest who betroths with his portion from the Temple, whether from the most sacred offerings or from the lesser sacred offerings – she is not betrothed, even though the priests eat them, nevertheless, they do not own them but rather they belong to the Most High, and when they receive them, they receive them from the table of the Most High, and the Torah only gave them the right to eat them and not for any other matter. Similarly, an Israelite who betroths with a thanksgiving or peace offering – she is not betrothed for the reason explained, and there is no difference whether it is alive or after slaughter. And one who betroths with the hides of sacrificial animals after the blood is sprinkled – it seems she is betrothed. Similarly, one who betroths with the remnants of a meal offering – she is not betrothed, and one who betroths with second tithe before redemption whether unintentionally or intentionally – she is not betrothed, because before redemption it is the property of the Most High.

A firstborn animal in our times, after it develops a blemish, is certainly considered the property of the priest, as he is permitted to sell it and even feed it to a non-Jew. However, an unblemished firstborn animal in our times is treated like other lesser sanctified offerings from the time of the Temple, and is not considered the property of the priest, as it is forbidden to shear it or use it for labor. Some say that a firstborn animal in our times, even if unblemished, is considered the property of its owner [Rosh, Chapter 1 of Bava Kamma, Section 15 in the name of some], and therefore, if a priest used it to betroth a woman, the betrothal is doubtful. It is not similar to other sanctified offerings, because from the moment it is born, the priest acquires it, as we learned in the Mishnah, Chapter 1 of Ma'aser Sheni, and so ruled our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Yoreh De'ah, Section 306, that this is the main legal ruling [the Gra], but here, due to the severity of the prohibition of a married woman, he wrote that she is doubtfully betrothed. Invalidated sacrificial animals, such as those that developed a blemish before being redeemed, are prohibited for benefit, but once they are redeemed, they are permitted. [In the Jerusalem Talmud, Nedarim, end of Chapter 5, it says that one who betroths with a Torah scroll is not betrothed, even with his own Torah scroll, and this requires further investigation].

There are some of our rabbis who hold that there is no difference between Torah-prohibited benefit and rabbinically-prohibited benefit, and in all of them, the kiddushin (marriage) does not take effect. For although they are only rabbinically prohibited from benefit, nevertheless, in the end, it is not considered property since it is worth nothing [Rashi Pesachim 7a and Ran end of chapter 2 of Kiddushin], and so it appears in the Jerusalem Talmud [chapter 1, halacha 1]. Therefore, if someone betroths a woman on the eve of Passover during the sixth hour with chametz (leavened bread), which is rabbinically prohibited from benefit, and even if it is hardened chametz, which is only rabbinically prohibited from benefit even during Passover itself and is a double rabbinic prohibition – nevertheless, she is not betrothed. This also appears to be the opinion of the Rambam at the beginning of chapter 5 [HaMaggid Mishneh]. 

However, there are some of our rabbis who hold that any rabbinic prohibition that has no basis in Torah law, if one betroths a woman with it, she is betrothed. Therefore, with rabbinic chametz and rabbinic hours, as mentioned – she is betrothed, for this is like it has no basis in Torah law. But with Torah hours and rabbinic chametz, or rabbinic hours and Torah chametz – this is considered having a basis in Torah law and she is not betrothed [Tosafot Pesachim there and Rosh Kiddushin there]. 

And there are some of our rabbis who hold that with Torah chametz and rabbinic hours, one must be concerned about the kiddushin, for maybe they made a mistake about the hour and thought it was the sixth hour when in reality it was only the fifth hour, which is still permitted from benefit even rabbinically [Ramban]. But with Torah hours and rabbinic chametz, there is no concern for the kiddushin and no concern for a mistake, for even if they err, they will not err between a Torah prohibition and a complete allowance. Furthermore, the mistake between before noon and after noon is not so common. [What the Ba'er Heitev wrote in subsection 92 in Chullin in the Temple courtyard, this is according to Rabbi Shimon and we do not hold like this].

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 21: If one betroths with rabbinically prohibited items of benefit that have no basis in Torah law, she is betrothed. But if it is chametz that is prohibited by Torah law during rabbinic hours, or chametz that is rabbinically prohibited during Torah hours, it is doubtful if she is betrothed. And if it is entirely biblically prohibited items, such as chametz that is biblically prohibited during Torah hours, she is not betrothed, end quote. His words are perplexing, for regarding chametz that is rabbinically prohibited during Torah hours, there is no one who holds that we should be concerned about the betrothal [Chametz, Bedek HaBayit, and the Gaon of Vilna]. Furthermore, it is explicitly stated in the Gemara Pesachim there that we do not need to be concerned about the betrothal, and to say that he was concerned with a singular opinion that holds that chametz on the eve of Passover until nightfall is only rabbinically prohibited from benefit — if so, we should say the same for biblically prohibited chametz. Moreover, this is an opinion rejected by all the poskim [commentaries on Shulchan Aruch] [Bedek HaBayit Section 53, see there in detail]. Additionally, it is difficult regarding his ruling that for rabbinically prohibited items with no basis in Torah law she is betrothed and did not consider the opinions that they are not betrothal, and he should have ruled that this is a doubtful betrothal [Gaon of Vilna].

And it seems to me that his words are correct, for indeed we do not find explicitly among any of our rabbis who would say that in cases of rabbinic hours or rabbinic chametz, the marriage is not valid. And since the Rosh explicitly ruled that in such cases the marriage is valid, and according to the Rambam’s opinion, he also holds this, as he wrote in his great book, therefore he ruled so. And this that he ruled that in cases of rabbinic chametz and Scriptural hours it is a doubtful marriage, is because Rashi's opinion is that the Talmud in Pesachim deals with Scriptural hours and rabbinic chametz, where we do not worry about the marriage, and it somewhat implies from his words that the opposite, we do worry about the marriage. And the reason is that when the main prohibition is Scriptural but the Sages brought the prohibition earlier, it is considered as Scriptural. But with chametz that is essentially rabbinic, that Scripturally there is no prohibition at all, it is like it has no basis in the Torah. And all this is to explain the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, but in practice, in all cases, it is a doubtful marriage even in something that has no basis in the Torah. 

[What the Beit Shmuel and other later authorities wrote that according to Rashi in two rabbinic prohibitions she is not betrothed, is not so, for Rashi explains in Pesachim that “Kordyan wheat” is complete chametz, and the Ketzot HaChoshen already objected to them in Chapter 2, Section 2, Note 7, see there, and there is proof for this from Rashi there 21b, s.v. from six and onwards, that if it was after six, what would he come to teach us, etc., end quote. And according to the Beit Shmuel, it teaches us a lot, and since Rashi strained the language of “from six and onwards” and did not explain it simply with rabbinic chametz, it seems that he holds that in such a case the marriage is valid, as I wrote, and the words of the Beit Yosef are well understood, and study it carefully].

Some have asked how it is possible to say that one can be betrothed with something whose primary prohibition is rabbinic, for after all, since it is rabbinically prohibited to derive benefit, it would seem she is receiving nothing. And indeed, one who betroths with the presence of three, where the acquisition is rabbinic, it is considered a valid betrothal. Similarly, in the reverse, in matters where the Sages prohibited benefit, the betrothal is not valid [Beit Shmuel, sec. 52]. However, from acquisitions, there is no proof at all, for rabbinic acquisitions are not less valid than the acquisitions practiced by merchants, which are considered Torah-level acquisitions as stated in section 63. Nevertheless, regarding other rabbinic prohibitions, it seems to me that it depends on the dispute between the Rif and other poskim regarding one who betroths with witnesses who are rabbinically disqualified, whether we should be concerned about the validity of the betrothal. This will be explained in section 42 with God's help, where the Rif indeed holds that such betrothal is not valid because one who betroths does so based on the authority of the Sages. Those who disagree with him maintain that we do not say this to nullify betrothal unless explicitly stated by the Sages. But regarding all rabbinic prohibitions and disqualifications, there is no proof that the betrothal is entirely nullified, for perhaps in such cases the Sages did not enact their decree. After all, there are betrothals that take effect even in transgression, such as those involving prohibitions of negative commandments. Similarly, one could say regarding rabbinic prohibitions and disqualifications that although it is forbidden, the betrothal still takes effect. However, from the Jerusalem Talmud, it appears that in cases of rabbinic prohibitions of benefit, the betrothal does not take effect, as stated in section 88 [and I am puzzled by the Beit Shmuel who cited the Rif, for indeed the Beit Yosef in section 142 ruled not like him].

All items prohibited for benefit, even if they are of Torah origin, if one transgressed and sold the prohibited item and received money for it and betrothed a woman with that money – she is betrothed. For even though he committed a transgression by benefiting from items prohibited for benefit, nevertheless, the money itself does not become prohibited. Only with idols and the produce of the Sabbatical year does the verse reveal that the money is seized by the prohibition, but not with other items prohibited for benefit. And although initially the money is certainly forbidden to him, nevertheless, if he betrothed a woman with it, she is permitted to benefit from it, as it is not considered money of prohibited benefit with regard to her. And even though he benefits by her becoming betrothed to him, they were not so stringent in this matter, as the money does not become seized by the prohibition of benefit. And according to Torah law, it is permitted for him initially, and though by rabbinic law it is forbidden for him to benefit from the money initially – nevertheless, she is betrothed. But with idols, if he sold them and betrothed with their money – she is not betrothed for the reason explained.

When is she considered betrothed? When he sold them to a gentile or to a Jew who knew that these are items forbidden for benefit. However, if the buyer did not know at all that they were forbidden for benefit and the seller took their value and betrothed a woman with it – this is a doubtful betrothal, for it is near to saying that the betrothal did not take effect at all, since he must return the money to the buyer and it is as if it were stolen in his hand. This is also implied in the Jerusalem Talmud. However, it is possible to say that since the money came into his hand through a transaction, this money is considered as a loan in his hand and he can use it and repay with other money [Rosh and Ran there]. But when the buyer knew that these were items forbidden for benefit and he took them – it is obvious that the money belongs to the seller, for he took them. [What the Rosh wrote "gift money" is a common phrase and does not apply to all places, for he consented to buy them and did not worry about the prohibition, and it is not similar to recognizing that it is not his, for he must return it against his will, and it answers the question of the Beit Shmuel section 158, and furthermore, it is at least like a loan as the Avnei Miluim wrote in the name of the Ritva. Also, see Tosafot Bava Batra 92b s.v. "if etc." that it is not similar etc.].

One who betroths with terumot and ma'aserot—if he is an Israelite, even though they come from his own produce and he has the benefit of discretion to give them to any Kohen he wishes, nevertheless, the Rambam ruled in Chapter 5 that she is not betrothed, because the benefit of discretion is not considered monetary value. However, some say that the benefit of discretion is considered monetary value, and she is betrothed. Many great authorities agree with the Rambam, and we have already explained there in Section 13 that at the very least, this is a legal doubt, as it is evident from the Talmud in Bechorot that it is considered monetary value. However, a Kohen who betroths with terumah and a Levite with the first tithe, she is betrothed, because the gifts to the Kohanim are considered their actual property, and they may do with them as they wish. This is not comparable to consecrated items which are considered as having been acquired from the divine table, but the gifts to the Kohanim were given by God to Aaron and his sons to be their actual property. Therefore, a Kohen who betroths with terumah, terumat ma'aser, challah, bikkurim, the foreleg, the cheeks, and the maw, the first shearings, the five sela'im of pidyon haben, the redemption of a firstborn donkey, with the stolen property of a proselyte, a field of inheritance, and a field of dedication, she is betrothed, and even ideally he may betroth with them. Similarly, a Levite with ma'aser, and an Israelite who is poor with the poor tithe. But a wealthy person who betroths with the poor tithe of his field, she is not betrothed, even though if he wished he could renounce his possessions and become poor and it would be fit for him, nevertheless, as long as he has not renounced his possessions, it does not belong to him, and furthermore, every poor person is commanded to separate from his field and give it to others. An Israelite who inherits terumot and ma'aserot from his mother's father who was a Kohen, they are considered his, and even though he is not permitted to eat them, he can sell them. Even if he inherits untithed produce and separates terumot and ma'aserot from them, they are considered his, because gifts that have not yet been separated are considered as if they have been separated, provided that the work on the produce had been completed for terumot and ma'aserot during the Kohen's lifetime and the Kohen had acquired them during his lifetime.

One who betroths a woman with consecrated property of the Temple treasury inadvertently – she is betrothed, and he must repay the principal and an additional fifth to the Temple and bring his guilt offering, as is the law for anyone who commits an inadvertent misappropriation. However, if he intentionally betroths her – she is not betrothed, because with intent, the consecrated property is not desecrated, and he is not liable for misappropriation, as the law of misappropriation only applies to inadvertent actions. 

If one betroths a woman with produce of the Sabbatical year, with the ashes of the red heifer, or with water drawn for the ashes of the heifer – she is betrothed, even though it is forbidden to take payment for the sanctification of the water and sprinkling. Nevertheless, since one can take payment for drawing and bringing the water, when he betroths with the water and ashes themselves, she benefits from them since she can receive a prutah from someone who needs them due to the labor of drawing and bringing. Some say she is not betrothed with the water and ashes themselves unless he betroths her with the payment for bringing the ashes and water or with the payment for drawing the water.

Similarly, one who betroths a woman with the dung of an ox that was to be stoned – she is betrothed, even though it is forbidden to benefit from it, its dung is permitted because it is not significant compared to the ox. However, one who betroths with the dung of calves designated for idolatry – she is not betrothed, because their dung is also forbidden for benefit, as it says, "and nothing of the banned property shall cling to your hand" (Deuteronomy 13:18). But one who betroths with the hide of an ox that was to be stoned – she is not betrothed, because the Torah also forbade its hide for benefit.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in paragraph 21: A congregation that established a regulation and made an agreement among themselves that anyone who performs a kiddushin (betrothal) without a quorum of ten, or something similar, and one transgressed and performed the kiddushin - we consider the kiddushin valid and she requires a get (divorce document), even though the congregation explicitly stipulated that such kiddushin would not be valid and they declared his property ownerless, nonetheless, we should be stringent in practice, end quote. The explanation of his words: Not only is it that if they imposed a prohibition on this, it is of no effect, since their prohibition is not stronger than a Torah prohibition and kiddushin is valid in cases of negative commandments, but even when they established and declared his property ownerless, since the declaration of a court is considered valid, and all the prominent people of the city in their city are like a great court as it is written in Choshen Mishpat section 2, nevertheless, it is difficult to annul kiddushin, because some say that a court's declaration of ownerlessness is only effective in the court of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi who had the power to annul property, but others do not have this power, and even though the principle of "you shall only go by the judge who will be in those days" applies, this is only when there is no one as great as them in the generation, but if there is someone as great as them in the generation, we do not have the authority to annul property [Mordechai, first chapter of Bava Batra in the name of Rabbeinu Tam].

Moreover, he wrote: A woman who vowed to derive no benefit from a certain person or from anything given to her without the presence of certain individuals, and someone transgressed and betrothed her—she is not considered betrothed, as it is as if he betrothed her with items from which she is prohibited to derive benefit. This applies specifically when he betrothed her with money, but if he betrothed her with a document—she is considered betrothed. This is only when she said that anything given to her without the presence of certain individuals shall be "like consecrated" or "like forbidden," but if she did not use the comparative "like" and instead said it will be "consecrated"—there is doubt whether she intended actual consecration, in which case her words mean nothing since a person cannot consecrate something not in their possession, or if she intended it to be like consecration. Therefore, she should not be released without a get [divorce document] [Choshen Mishpat in the name of the Rashba]. 

And what he wrote regarding being betrothed with a document being valid—the reason is that we rule that if a get is written on items from which deriving benefit is prohibited, it is valid. Even though it is written in the get, "and he shall place it in her hand" (Deuteronomy 24:1), since this placement is not monetary, it is still called placement even when it involves items from which deriving benefit is prohibited. Similarly, betrothal with a document does not require monetary placement and is called placement of a betrothal document. However, in Siman 32, the Rema himself wrote a dispute on this matter, and some say this refers to rabbinic prohibitions of benefit, while the latter refers to Torah prohibitions of benefit [see Choshen Mishpat]. There is support for this from the Jerusalem Talmud in the first chapter of Kiddushin. However, it cannot be said so, as the Jerusalem Talmud also differentiates in Gittin, and we do not rule so as written in Siman 124. Therefore, some say that here it does not refer to certain betrothal but to monetary betrothal, which is certainly not valid. Hence, he says that betrothal with a document is valid, meaning stringently it is considered betrothal and not leniently, as stated in Siman 32 [Beit Shmuel, note 156]. However, it is obvious that she is forbidden to marry the one from whom she vowed not to derive benefit and needs a get [there]. 

Additionally, it is possible to distinguish here from Siman 32 that in the context of vows, we follow the common language. Generally, when she said anything given to her, she intended only money and items, as that is called giving in common language, and betrothal with a document did not come to her mind [it seems to me]. Besides this, the primary halacha is that if betrothed with a document involving Torah prohibitions of benefit, it is considered betrothal [the Gra] just like with a get. However, in practice, due to the severity of a married woman, he was concerned in Siman 32 to also bring the second opinion, but the halacha is proven in the Talmud that gittin and kiddushin are equal in this matter [see Gittin 10a. Something not found in Kiddushin, and scrutinize this]. Even if the Jerusalem Talmud differentiates between rabbinic and Torah prohibitions of benefit, the primary is our Talmud, and in my humble opinion, it can also be interpreted that in Torah prohibitions, she is betrothed and divorced [what is stated there from now even with Torah prohibitions, etc., is said calmly, and what is stated about what is the difference between it and a document, etc., adds another proof to this and refutes that proof, but the first one remains, and scrutinize this]. 

From these words of the Rema, one can learn that in places where there are lawless Jews, and there is a concern they will seize young women and betroth them, and due to panic or light-mindedness, she will not protest or immediately discard the betrothal document, they should be taught to forbid upon themselves anything received from others without their parents' knowledge with vows and consecration. The concern of being betrothed with a document is rare, and many great individuals have done so.

[Methods of Giving Money, and If It Was Not Given Completely or Given as Collateral, with 42 Sections]
The money for the betrothal must be given to her as an absolute gift, and if he gave it to her on the condition that she returns it – it is not a valid betrothal. And even though in general, for the entirety of the Torah, a gift given on condition to return it is considered a gift, as it is written in Orach Chaim section 658 regarding the etrog, because the gift is considered a permanent acquisition like all gifts, and the condition to return it is just a condition like any other condition – nevertheless, in betrothal, the Sages stated that she is not betrothed. The reason is that a woman cannot be acquired through exchange, because the woman does not acquire herself through it since she receives nothing, for the cloth returns to the owner. Similarly, a gift given on condition to return is like an exchange, where she receives nothing. This is also clarified from the language of the Rambam in Chapter 5, Law 24, where he writes: "If a man says to a woman, 'Behold, you are betrothed to me with this dinar on the condition that you return it to me,' she is not betrothed whether she returned it or not. Because if she did not return it, the condition was not fulfilled, and if she did return it, she did not benefit, and nothing reached her hand." End quote. And even though it is possible that she may have derived some benefit until she returned it, nevertheless, she was not betrothed through this benefit but through the item itself.

Therefore, if he gave her a gift on the condition that she returns it, and he said to her, "With the benefit that you enjoy during the time, you are betrothed to me" – it is considered betrothal, as the benefit remains with her. And so wrote our teacher, the Rema, in section 1. And although regarding an exchange transaction itself, even if he wants to leave the kerchief with her, it is not considered betrothal, since an acquisition is made through an item even if it does not have the value of a perutah, as stated in Choshen Mishpat section 195, the acquisition of exchange is not included in "when a man takes" as written in the Torah regarding marriage. And most of our rabbis agreed [Tosafot and Ran at the beginning of Kiddushin]. It seems to me that for this reason, the Rambam did not need to mention at all the law of exchange, because a woman is not betrothed through it since it is not included in the acquisition of money that is encompassed in "when a man takes a wife." And just as there is no need to mention other types of acquisitions used in sales that are not applicable in betrothal, so too there was no need to mention this. Nevertheless, with a gift on the condition to return, which is not truly an exchange but similar to an exchange, if he betrothed her through the benefit, she is betrothed, and this has no relation to exchange at all [it seems to me].

From the words of the Rambam, it is explained that a gift on condition to return does not even have the slightest hint of betrothal [Yam Shel Shlomo]. However, some of our Rabbis hold that, by Torah law, a woman can be betrothed with a gift on condition to return, since it is still called a gift. But the Sages decreed and nullified such betrothal due to the concern that people might say a woman can be betrothed through barter (chalipin). Since this resembles barter when the item is returned to him, they made this decree [Tosafot, Rosh, and Ran]. According to this, it seems that even if he betroths her with the benefit she enjoys within the time period, since he mentioned it as a gift on condition to return, there is still the decree of barter. And it appears to me that this is the reason of Rabbeinu Yerucham [brought in Beit Yosef], who mentioned two opinions on this matter there. But from the words of Rabbeinu Rema, who did not bring the other opinion at all, it is evident that he holds that according to all interpretations, since the benefit of use within the time period was mentioned, there is no longer the decree of barter, and the law remains in question. [The difficulty raised by the Chavatzelet HaSharon in section 3 we resolved in section 28, paragraph 77, see there]. [See the Vilna Gaon in section 2, who holds that according to Tosafot and the Rosh, even with benefit, she is not betrothed, and therefore, in practice, one should be stringent].

And regarding the acquisition by exchange, there are those among the Rishonim (early authorities) who hold that when the Sages said a woman cannot be acquired through exchange, this refers to a standard exchange where the buyer transfers a cloth to the seller, and the seller transfers to him in return his merchandise that is located somewhere, thus effecting a transaction. The buyer then becomes obligated to pay money according to the value of the merchandise. Similarly, in this case, the man betroths her with an object but does not give it to her immediately; he gives her the cloth as an exchange acquisition to transfer the object to her, and she transfers herself to him and becomes obligated for the object. This type of exchange is not in the category of money but in the category of acquisition. However, if he betroths her with this cloth as an exchange acquisition, she is betrothed by it, because once she has taken hold of a cloth measuring three handbreadths by three handbreadths, she can take it, and this is not in the category of acquisition but in the category of money (Tosafot Rid and Shita Mekubetzet). Nevertheless, the majority of the early authorities do not imply this. On the contrary, the general principle of exchange acquisition where a woman is not betrothed by it means he gives her his cloth as an acquisition, and she transfers herself to him. Conversely, if he betroths her with another object and transfers the object to her through the acquisition of the cloth and says to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this object, and I am transferring it to you through the acquisition of the cloth," it could be that this constitutes betrothal, and this will be clarified with God's help in this section (Avnei Shoham, subparagraph 2). As for what is written in the Mordechai, it seems to me that his intention was that he did not mention exchange at all. Likewise, some say that in the case of a gift on the condition of return, she requires a bill of divorce (see HaMelech HaMashiach, subparagraph 1), but in the words of our Rabbis, it is explicitly stated to the contrary, that even those who hold that from the Torah it constitutes betrothal, nevertheless, the Rabbis nullified the betrothal (as the Beit Shmuel wrote there).

There are those who say that what was explained, that betrothal on condition to return is not valid – this is specifically when the condition is doubled, for if not, the condition is void and the act stands [Bach] as stated in Siman 38. It is explained in Choshen Mishpat Siman 207 that any condition that is not like the condition of the tribes of Gad and Reuben is not a valid condition. Also, it is necessary to have all the laws of conditions, such as "yes" before "no" and the condition before the action, as mentioned there. However, for those who maintain that on condition (alone) does not require all the laws of conditions, as mentioned there, it is valid even without doubling the condition. And even for those who do not maintain this, nevertheless, in a compelling assessment that he only gave on this condition, the laws of conditions are not needed, and it suffices with mere expression, as stated in Orach Chaim Siman 658 regarding the Etrog [Beit Hillel]. 

It cannot be said that in the case of the Etrog, there is certainly a compelling assessment that he gives it on condition to return because he needs it himself for the next day, but here there is no compelling assessment, for here too there is a compelling assessment that he only gives it to betroth her with it since he explicitly says so. And if he betroths her with a small coin, there is no compelling assessment, but if he betroths her with a significant amount, which is not common for betrothal, there is certainly a compelling assessment when he says so [see Beit Shmuel]. 

Also, it cannot be said that since in betrothal, the condition to return does not work, there is no compelling assessment, and on the contrary, there is more reason to say that he intended a complete gift [see Avnei Milu'im]. If so, why did he say at all on condition to return? We must see that he did not concern himself with this, or he does not know the law. How can we judge this matter of assessment due to the primary law of betrothal, and indeed on this we are judging.

However, there are some of the early authorities who do not hold by the reasoning of estimation in this matter, and they also wrote regarding the etrog that a doubled condition is necessary [Rosh, Chapter "Yesh Nochalin" Section 48]. Nevertheless, even if we say that without a doubled condition the condition is nullified and the act remains valid, the marriage still does not take effect, because the woman did not rely upon it and did not know that the act remains valid and the condition is nullified, as she thought she would have to return it [Beit Shmuel]. For do women learn the laws? It is as if one betroths with someone else's loan, where she is not betrothed because she does not rely upon it, thinking that the debt will be forgiven, as stated in Siman 28, Section 54; and here too, she did not rely upon it. This is not similar to all the conditions in Siman 38, where we hold that if the condition is not doubled, the betrothal is valid and the condition is nullified, because there the betrothal is complete and the condition is not intrinsic to the betrothal. But here the condition is intrinsic to the betrothal [ibid.]. However, it could be said that even according to her understanding, it is a gift on condition to return, which according to Torah law would be a valid betrothal, but the Rabbis invalidated the betrothal because it resembles an exchange. And here, the truth is it is not a condition to return and does not resemble an exchange, but she thought so, hence the betrothal takes effect [ibid.]. Nevertheless, since according to her understanding there is no betrothal according to Rabbinic enactment, and also according to the opinion of the Rambam that we mentioned, even according to Torah law there would be no betrothal, it could be said that there is no betrothal – and therefore it is a doubtful betrothal [so it seems to me].

Some of the great authorities have said that in any case where a double condition is required, if it was not expressed as a double condition, although the action is valid, the condition must still be fulfilled because of one's word. This is similar to the concept of hiring. They brought proof from the law of conditional release (halitzah), which will be explained in Siman 169, where there is no condition in halitzah. Nevertheless, it is explained there that she must pay him due to the concept of hiring, and this is analogous [see Ketzot HaChoshen Siman 241 and Even HaEzer, Ketzot HaChoshen Siman 1]. According to this, in any matter, it would not be considered a valid betrothal since she is obligated to return [the money].
