However, it does not seem reasonable to say this, for if so, the power of a double condition would be weaker than that of a single condition. In a double condition, if he wishes, he can fulfill his condition along with the action, and if he does not wish, he will not fulfill either the condition or the action. In a single condition, the action is valid regardless, and if we say that the condition is also valid regardless, the power of a double condition would be significantly weaker than that of a single condition. The proof from halitzah is not a proof at all, for in halitzah, the matter concerns the woman alone and does not concern the man at all. Because of the commandment, he has the option to perform levirate marriage (yibbum) and not halitzah, and only she misled him because she does not wish to marry him, and he troubled himself to perform halitzah. Therefore, she is certainly obligated to pay him like any other hire. But in betrothal and in buying and selling, where the matter concerns both of them and both desire the matter, what relevance does hiring have? Furthermore, even in halitzah, she is not required to pay him according to the condition but according to the estimated trouble, and in halitzah, there is trouble. But what relevance does this have to betrothal and buying and selling? Also, none of the early authorities appear to support this view [and also the Netivot HaMishpat there rejected this, see there].

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 1: But if a woman gave another a gift on the condition that it be returned to her after 30 days in order to betroth her with it within the 30 days, and he gave it to her within the 30 days for betrothal – she is betrothed. And the commentators wrote that this statement that she gave it to him in order to betroth her is not necessary at all, for even if she only lent it to him for his own use and he betrothed her with it – she is betrothed. The main reason for those who are stringent about betrothing with a borrowed item is because it resembles a gift on the condition to return, as explained in section 28, paragraph 78. Here, this is not applicable because it belongs to her and she will not return it [Taz, Choshen Mishpat, and Beit Shmuel]. They also wrote that it was unnecessary to state that the gift was for 30 days, for even if she gave it to him as a plain gift on the condition to return – he can betroth a woman with it, as stated there in section 80. The decree of exchange is only when he betroths her on the condition to return, but someone who has a gift on the condition to return can betroth [there].

It appears to me that the primary ruling follows the words of our teacher, the Rema, that if the gift was not until 30 days and at any time she returns it to him, it is truly hers – then with what does he betroth her? For this is exactly like betrothing her with her own object, which is not a valid betrothal since at any moment she returns it, it is as if the time for returning has arrived. And this is not similar to someone who betroths a woman with an object that another gave him as a gift on the condition to return it. And the necessity to state that she gave it to him in order to betroth her, certainly if he betrothed her within 30 days and she said "yes," or even if she was silent and he said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with the benefit of using this object" and the benefit is for up to 30 days – she is betrothed even if she did not give it to him in order to betroth her. But if he said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this object" and she was silent and accepted it, if she did not give it to him in order to betroth her – this is nothing, for he betrothed her with the object and the object is hers, and if for the usage – he did not betroth her with the usage, for in the case of another’s gift, we say that the object will remain with her forever and he will pay the giver as stated there, but not when the object is hers. However, if she gave it to him in order to betroth her – even in such a case she is betrothed because her primary giving was in order to betroth her and it is as if they explicitly stated that he would betroth her with the benefit of the usage. Nevertheless, if it was not until 30 days – it is not effective, for it is as if she said to him, "Betroth me with my object" since at any moment the time for returning has arrived. [And with this, it is clear why this was not mentioned in the responsum, for there it discusses when she said "yes," and the Rema teaches the halacha, and see Avnei Miluim and Mekaneh for what they wrote about this, and examine it well].

There are those who say that it is specifically when he gives it to her so that he may betroth her and there was no condition attached. However, if he gave it to her as a gift on condition that he would take her in betrothal with it – she is not betrothed, because she explicitly conditioned that if he does not betroth her with it, the gift would be nullified. Thus, he is not giving her anything, for either way it is hers. There are those who disagree, saying that this is like saying, "I am giving you this object as a gift on condition that you will acquire another object from me with this gift I gave you," which certainly works. Similarly, here he gave it to her on condition that he would take her in betrothal with this object. It seems to me to conclude that if he gave her the gift for a fixed time on condition that he would betroth her within that time, it is like a regular condition and she is betrothed. But if he gave it to her simply on condition that he would betroth her with it, then at the time of the betrothal, that is, when he fulfills the condition, it is the time of returning, and it is truly hers. With what is he betrothing her? As stated in the previous section. However, if the gift is for a fixed time, he betroths her with the benefit of usage he has until the time, and if this has the value of a perutah – she is betrothed.

Even though it is necessary to give her the money for the betrothal, nevertheless, our sages said that sometimes, even if another person receives the money for himself, she can be betrothed with it. How so? She said to him, "Give a maneh (a specific amount of money) to so-and-so, and I will be betrothed to you." When he gave it to him, he said to her, "Be betrothed to me with the maneh that I gave to so-and-so" – she is betrothed even though she did not receive any benefit. This is similar to a guarantor who becomes obligated to the lender even though he himself did not borrow from him; nevertheless, since he instructed to lend to so-and-so, it is as if he borrowed it himself. Likewise, when a woman instructs him to give to so-and-so, she becomes obligated in marriage, and it is as if he gave it to her.

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 5: A woman who said, "Give a dinar to so-and-so as a gift and I will be betrothed to you," and he gave it and said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with the benefit of this gift that I gave at your request" – she is betrothed, even though she did not receive anything, because she benefited from her will being done and that so-and-so benefited because of her. End quote. 

And it appears that the Rambam did not mean specifically that he should specify at the time of the betrothal saying "with the benefit of this gift that I gave at your request," but even if he said "with the amount (money) that I gave to so-and-so" in a general way, as I have also written, it is effective. Rather, the Rambam explains what constitutes the betrothal and why it is effective due to the benefit, and the benefit is significant. Just as a guarantor obligates himself because of the benefit that another is loaned money at his request, so too she is betrothed by this benefit that he gave to so-and-so at her request. 

And it is customary in such betrothals to explain the reason for the betrothal, but this explanation is not essential. Moreover, even if he said generally "Be betrothed to me" [as Rashi explained], it is also effective according to the Rambam and other decisors. Just as in all other betrothals, when he gave her the ring and said generally "Behold, you are betrothed to me," even if he did not say "with this ring," it is effective, so too in this betrothal if he says it generally. However, it seems to me that in such a case, he needs to say it immediately upon giving it to so-and-so. But if there was a slight delay in between, he needs to specify and say, "Be betrothed to me with the amount that I gave to so-and-so" [as the Rosh said] or "with the benefit of this gift," etc., as the Rambam said. Otherwise, it does not at all appear that he is betrothing her with anything [and according to what I have written, Rashi, the Rambam, and the Rosh do not disagree].

According to what has been explained, the act of betrothal (kiddushin) is specifically when he says to her, "Be betrothed to me," but without his statement, it is not effective. However, some of the early authorities have said that even if he did not say anything, it is effective, because since she said to him, "And I will be betrothed to you," and he gave her [the item] based on her statement, it is not inferior to speaking with her about the matters of betrothal, which is effective even though he did not specify [Ran in their name], as mentioned in Siman 27, Seif 13. It is not similar to a case where he gave and she said [the statement of betrothal], which is not effective as mentioned there, because there he gave first and it is not evident that he gave it as a betrothal, and the proof of the betrothal comes from her statement. Thus, it turns out that the act of betrothal is completed by her statement, and therefore it is not effective. But here, he performs the act of betrothal entirely, for with this giving she is betrothed without any other statement, since her statement is like speaking with her about the matters of betrothal, which is effective even in a general situation [there]. The reason of the Rambam, Rashi, and the Rosh is that it is obvious that if he gave and she said [the statement of betrothal], it is not effective to be a definite betrothal, even if she said it at the moment he gave it into her hand. And although he gave it to her with that intention, it is still not effective, because it is not similar to speaking with her about the matters of betrothal, where he also spoke. But if he did not say anything, even though his giving indicates that he agrees with her words, it is not effective, for this is similar to her silence after the giving of money, which is also not effective even if he said and gave in a case where we need her statement [there].

From the words of our master, the Rema, who wrote about the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, which are the words of the Rambam, "And if they were engaged in that matter, even though he gave it without specifying, she is betrothed," it appears that these early authorities do not disagree at all with the previous opinions and they also agree that without his speech, it does not work at all. They are really referring to a case where they previously spoke about matters of betrothal and he also spoke about this, for in such a case, all agree that the statement is not essential. And know that when they spoke about matters of betrothal, she does not need to say, "Give to so-and-so and I will be betrothed to you"; saying "Give to so-and-so" alone is sufficient. However, this is only when she initiated the matter of betrothal, but when he initiated speaking about matters of betrothal and she responded, "Give to so-and-so," it is not a certain betrothal, for it is similar to "Give them to my father or your father," which will be explained in Siman 30 that it is not a betrothal. And perhaps in such a case, even if she concluded with "and I will be betrothed to you," it is not a certain betrothal, and we specifically need her to be the one to initiate.

And our Rabbi the Rema wrote that all of this is specifically when she began by saying, "Give a maneh (a specific amount of money) to so-and-so," but if he first said to her, and she responds, "Give to so-and-so" – see below in Siman 30, Se'if 8, end quote. And it means that it is explained there that in such a case, it is not considered a valid betrothal. And it is clearly understood from his words that there is no difference whether she concluded with "and I will be betrothed to you" or not. Because if he was the one who initiated, even if she concluded with "and I will be betrothed to you," we say that she was mocking him, for otherwise, what relevance does this have to Siman 30? However, logically, it would seem to differentiate that if she did not conclude with "and I will be betrothed to you" but only said "give them to so-and-so," it would be considered as mocking and as if she is saying "give them to whomever you want, and I have no interest in the betrothal." But if she concluded with "and I will be betrothed to you," this would not be considered as mocking. Nevertheless, from the words of our Rabbi the Rema, it does not seem so [and this is also evident from Rashi, Tosafot, and Ran as I wrote in the previous section]. And in any case, it seems that his intention is that it is not a definite betrothal, but it is at least a doubtful betrothal [and this is clearly implied in the Rosh as I wrote, and in general, it is a question on the Beit Shmuel as I wrote, and even more so from the words of the Rema].

Furthermore, he wrote: If a woman says to a man, "Lend a maneh (a certain amount of money) to so-and-so, and I will become betrothed to you," and he lends to so-and-so and says to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with it" – it constitutes betrothal just like with a gift. However, if he extended the loan period based on her request and betrothed her with it – she is not betrothed. This is because the reason for this betrothal is akin to the reason for a guarantor, as mentioned in Section 11. And even with a guarantor in such a case, he is not obligated, as a guarantor only becomes obligated when the loan is given based on his guarantee, not based on the extension of the loan period. A guarantor who guarantees not at the time of the giving of the money is not obligated, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Section 129. 

There is a question regarding this, as, after all, the benefit of extending the loan period is equivalent, as mentioned in Section 28 regarding betrothal with a loan. Therefore, the other party benefits from her action, and she benefits from his action, so what is the difference between this and lending based on her request, and what does this have to do with being a guarantor? Additionally, in Choshen Mishpat there, it is not clarified that extending the loan period does not make one a guarantor, unless he guarantees the entire principal not at the time of the giving of the money, but why should extending the loan period not make one a guarantor?

There is an opinion that says if he tells her, "Become betrothed to me with this benefit that I extended the loan period for so-and-so based on your request" – she is betrothed. But if he just says, "Become betrothed to me with the benefit of extending the loan period" without specifying "with this benefit" – she is not betrothed. At the beginning of the loan or gift, even if he did not specify the benefit, it is assumed that she is being betrothed with the benefit. However, for extending the loan period, he needs to specify, and this is what Rabbi Rema is addressing. There is no valid reason to differentiate in this, for if she benefits from the extension of the loan period for so-and-so just like with the loan itself, why not say that it is assumed his intention is to betroth her with the benefit?

And it appears to me that this is not intended to be compared exactly to the law of a guarantor, for if that were the case, we would say that if she accepted [the betrothal] with a formal acquisition in such a manner, it would be considered betrothal just as in the case of a guarantor where one becomes obligated in such a manner, as it is written in Choshen Mishpat there. And in such a case, it would need to be explained, for it is a great novelty that a formal acquisition would cause betrothal even though a woman is not betrothed through barter. Rather, the explanation is as follows: Certainly, if the woman initially came to him and said, "Extend time for so-and-so and I will be betrothed to you," she would be betrothed, for there is no difference between a loan and extending time. However, our teacher the Rema is dealing with a case where this person demanded repayment of the loan and pressed for payment, and she saw his distress and said to him, "Extend time for him and I will be betrothed to you." This is not considered a monetary benefit for her, for she only did this to save the borrower from distress. And even if it is possible that she entered into a guarantor agreement, such as by accepting with a formal acquisition, nevertheless, this is not relevant to betrothal because this is not considered a benefit for her but rather saving the borrower from distress. Therefore, even if he said to her, "Be betrothed to me through this benefit," it is nothing. [And therefore, the Rashba in his responsa compared it to a strangler, even though there is no relation between the two, as the Ketzot Hachoshen explains, rather to explain the reason that there is no benefit here, and examine this carefully.]

Nevertheless, in practice, one should not be lenient against the opinion of the great later authorities, and such a case would be considered a doubtful betrothal. Additionally, who can say that in such a case it is not called a benefit? Perhaps relieving a friend's distress is considered a greater benefit than the loan itself. The reason of our master, the Rema, seems to be that performing a mitzvah such as relieving a friend's distress is not considered monetary compensation in the context of betrothal. Nevertheless, in practice, one should not be lenient in this matter, and it would be a doubtful betrothal.

And as we have explained, sometimes a woman is betrothed even though she herself did not receive the money for the betrothal. We derive this from the law of a guarantor. Similarly, our Sages stated that sometimes a woman is betrothed even though the man did not give the money for the betrothal but another gave it to her. We derive this from the law of a slave, as just as a slave can purchase his freedom with money, even if others gave the money on his behalf, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 267, so too if another man gave her a maneh (a specific amount of money) and said to her, "Take this dinar of mine and with it be betrothed to so-and-so" – she is betrothed when she accepts it, but only if that so-and-so appointed him as an agent to betroth her [Rashi], for otherwise, who gave him the authority to betroth her on his behalf? This does not fall under the category of "benefiting someone in their absence," as it is not necessarily a benefit since sometimes he does not wish to marry her, and he also incurs obligations to her for sustenance, clothing, and marital relations, and moreover, he may not want to be prohibited from marrying her relatives [Rashba]. And even if he did not appoint him as an agent but that so-and-so later said to her, "Be betrothed to me with the maneh that so-and-so gave you" – she is betrothed [Rambam].

From these two laws, we learn a third law: sometimes, even if he did not give and she did not receive, the betrothal is still valid. How so? If she said to another person, "Give a maneh (a sum of money) to so-and-so and I will be betrothed to him," and this person gave the money to the so-and-so and the so-and-so betrothed her and said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me through the benefit of this gift that I received at your request"—she is betrothed. This is because this benefit is worth a perutah to her, similar to what was explained in Siman 27, Se'if 39, where she gave him something and he betrothed her through the benefit of that gift he received from her. There, it was explained that it applies specifically when he is an important person. Here, it applies even if he is not important, because in that case, she gave him money from her own funds, so if he is not important, with what would she be betrothed? But here, since others gave him the money based on her instructions, she is rightfully betrothed through the fulfillment of her command. This itself is explained by the Rambam.

He said to her, "Be betrothed to me with a maneh" and he gave her a pledge on the maneh – she is not betrothed. Thus our Sages said, "There is no maneh here, there is no pledge here," meaning that the woman is acquired with money, and the money is not present, so how can she be betrothed? The pledge does not take the place of the money since it will not remain in the woman's possession. Therefore, if he said to her, "Be betrothed to me with this pledge and the pledge will be yours" – she is betrothed because he gave her a right to the body of the pledge. It is like the pledge of others by which a woman can be betrothed, as it is stated in Siman 28, Se'if 56, because a creditor has ownership of the body of the pledge, and this case is similar. However, some of our Rabbis hold that even in such a case it does not work here. A person can encumber his property for something he is already obligated for, like a creditor, but for something he is not yet obligated for, the encumbrance on his property does not take effect. When he said to betroth her, he was not yet obligated to her, similar to a gift when he says to give a gift. See what is written in Se'if 25.

However, even according to this opinion, if he gave her collateral and said to her, "Acquire with this collateral the obligation of a maneh and be betrothed to me with it," she is betrothed [Ran in the name of Raavad], because before the betrothal he obligated himself to the maneh, and a person can obligate himself, and consequently the collateral becomes encumbered, and the betrothal is valid as it is akin to the collateral of others. There are some of our Rabbis who hold that even in such a case it does not work [ibid. in the name of Ramban, and so wrote Rashba], explaining that when the Sages said, "There is no maneh here, there is no collateral here," it means that since that maneh with which he betrothed her is still with him and the money of betrothal that is attached to the husband is not considered money of betrothal, it is as if there is no collateral here. Even though the collateral was acquired for the obligation of the maneh, still she is not betrothed with it because since the maneh is not with her, the collateral is also nothing [ibid.]. According to this, other obligations would also not work, such as if he gave her a document for the maneh, it is nothing because the maneh is still with him, whereas according to the initial opinions it does work [Chomat Shlomo, section 8], and therefore it is a case of doubtful betrothal [ibid.].

According to what has been explained, the words of our master, the Rema, are puzzling. He wrote that it is certainly the case that if he gave her a document for the dinar, it does not constitute kiddushin. Then he wrote that if he said to her, "You are betrothed to me with this dinar, and you will acquire the collateral itself that I am giving you for this," then she is betrothed. And according to the earlier opinions, she is betrothed when he gives her a document, while according to the last opinion, even acquiring the collateral itself does not help. How could he write two contradictory statements? And indeed, the commentators have already been puzzled by this [Beit Shmuel and the Gra, subparagraph 14].

And it appears to me that his words are correct, for in a contract given to her for the dinar without collateral, she is not betrothed according to all opinions since there is no tangible item here to say that through this item she is betrothed. For even according to the opinions that do not worry about it being tied to the money of the betrothal, nevertheless, this applies when there is some tangible item worth money and she has a lien on the actual item like collateral. But this document, how does it help for betrothal? And it is not similar to a document of others, for if not for the reason of forgiveness, she would be betrothed with it as stated in Siman 28, Se'if 54. This is because something new is added for her by others, and although there is no tangible item, nevertheless, she has something new, meaning money with others as stated there. But this new thing added for her is complete with the one who betroths, and he has not yet given it to her, so with what will she be betrothed? And even if the paper is worth a perutah, there is no betrothal here, for he did not betroth her with the document itself, but with the money, and he gave a document for the money. [See Choshen Mishpat, Siman 68, and it requires further study.]

And this is what he wrote, that when he told her "you will acquire the body of the collateral," she is betrothed. He holds that in this, everyone agrees, and our rabbis only disagree regarding the lien on the collateral for the reasons that were explained. But if he said that she should acquire the body of the collateral, it is considered as if it is entirely hers, even though if he pays her the dinar, she will be obligated to return the collateral to him; otherwise, it would not be considered collateral. Nevertheless, as long as she has not returned it, it is as if it is entirely hers, and when she does return it, it will be like a sale. And that which we wrote in section 21 that when he said to her "the collateral will be yours," there are those who disagree with this. Rabbi Rema does not hold this way and only disagrees when mentioning the lien. If he did not say "you will acquire the body of the collateral," but rather "do not return the collateral to me until I give you such and such amount," some say that it is like he said she should acquire the body of the collateral, and others disagree. And only regarding a gift does this work, that she should not return it until he gives her the gift, but not regarding betrothal, and this seems to be the main view.

If a man says to a woman, "Be betrothed to me with a maneh (100 dinars)," and he gives her immediately one dinar and no more, she is immediately betrothed when she takes the dinar. He is obliged to complete the remaining ninety-nine dinars. This is similar to saying, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this dinar on the condition that I will give you a maneh," in which case she is betrothed from now. For anyone who says "on condition" is as if he says "from now." We do not say that they did not intend to complete the betrothal until the maneh is given, because if so, she would not have accepted one dinar from him, and he would not have given it to her. Rather, it is certain that they intended this for the sake of betrothal, and the rest is a condition.

And although he did not mention the laws of conditions, we judge it as if he stipulated and doubled the condition, as per the Rosh (First Chapter, Siman 9), and all the laws of conditions. Moreover, according to those who hold that "on condition" does not require the laws of conditions, as stated in Siman 38, even those who do not hold this way, still in this case, there is no need for the laws of conditions. It is better when he did not mention an explicit condition, but his actions demonstrate his intent, than when he mentions a condition not in the manner of the condition written with the children of Gad and Reuven (Rashba, Gittin 75). And this is based on what is written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 207, Se'if 5, that there are matters where an indication of intent is sufficient, and no condition is necessary.

Even according to those who disagree and hold that an indication of intent is not better than a condition that was not doubled (Ramban and Ran there), they still agree in this case. For indeed, this is not in the category of a condition, since he did not separate the dinar from the ninety-nine dinars. He said to her, "Be betrothed to me with a maneh," but we say that since she accepted one dinar, it indicates that they did not want to wait for the completion of the betrothal until the entire maneh was given. But how can we say that the laws of conditions are required, and if not, the condition is void and the act remains, and she would be betrothed even if he did not subsequently give her the ninety-nine dinars? Did he betroth her with a dinar? It is understandable that in all conditions, we uphold the words of the betrothal and annul the condition. But here, we would need to annul the main words of the betrothal, and that is impossible. Therefore, we say that the betrothal is valid immediately, and he is obligated to give her the remainder, and if he does not give it, the betrothal is annulled. The practical difference is that she cannot retract, and he can give her the remainder against her will (See Even HaEzer, Siman 14, and Siman 1, and as I have written in Siman 7, and it seems to me as I have written).

In what case is she betrothed with one dinar? When he said to her, "Be betrothed to me with a maneh" without specifying. But if he specified and said to her, "Be betrothed to me with these one hundred dinars," she is not betrothed until she receives the entire maneh. And the dinar she received, even though she did not receive more at this time, it was not her intention to be betrothed with it until the entire maneh is given. Similarly, even if he said to her, "Be betrothed to me with a maneh" without specification and began counting into her hand, even if he stopped in the middle and paused for a long time and she remained silent, we do not say that she consented to be betrothed with part of it. Since it is the way of the world to count one after another, certainly her intention was for the entire amount, and she was not concerned about the interruption in the middle. She knew that the betrothal would not be completed until he counted all of it into her hand. This is the opinion of the Tur and our teacher the Rema, and this is also indicated by the Talmudic discussion.

But Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote in chapter 7: "In what case are these words said? When he said to her, 'You are betrothed to me with one hundred dinars' without specifying. But if he specified and said to her, 'You are betrothed to me with these one hundred dinars' and began to count them into her hand, she is not betrothed until he completes the hundred. And even with the last dinar, both can retract from each other." End quote. He holds that we require two things: that he says 'these' and that he counts them into her hand. But without these two things, she is betrothed with the previous dinar. And so wrote our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 7. 

And some say that even according to Maimonides, the main thing depends on his saying 'these dinars,' and then, even if he did not count them into her hand, she is not betrothed until the completion of the hundred. But if he said 'with a maneh' without specifying, even if he was counting and stopped and she remained silent, she is betrothed with just one dinar. [Chamor Mishna and Beit Shmuel] 

And some say that according to Maimonides, we specifically need both conditions. And even if he said 'these dinars' without counting, she is betrothed with just one dinar, and all the more so if he said 'with a maneh' without specifying and was counting. [The Gaon of Vilna] And this is also implied in the Tosefta that the Rif brought. And the reason is because they hold that she should have said, when he stopped giving, that she does not agree to be betrothed with less. And since she remained silent, it is assumed that she agreed, expecting the betrothal would be completed immediately and the rest given later. But if he said 'with these dinars' and was counting or 'with this maneh' and was counting, it is obvious that she did not bother to respond. [It appears to me that this explains what is said there: 'what are we dealing with here?' It refers to a specific maneh in the Baraita, and Rav Ashi came to differentiate, and the halacha is like the anonymous opinion in the Talmud].

In a situation where she can retract, such as "with these dinars" or counting and proceeding according to the Tur, and according to the Rambam "with these dinars" alone for the first opinion, and in both cases for the second opinion – even with the last dinar, both can retract unless he said to her that what I have not completed will be on me as a loan and she explicitly agreed, then the betrothal is finalized. Specifically, if she said "yes," but if she was silent, even if she did not say "no," this is not a definite betrothal. This will be further explained [It seems to me that what is mentioned in Shulchan Aruch, section 7, regarding the lacking dinar means what has not been completed and is lacking, and this addresses the Gra's question in subparagraph 21, see there].

"In these 'dinars' or he counts and continues to the Tur, and according to the Rambam in both together as written, the same applies if he gave all of them into her hand and she counted them and found that one dinar was missing or one of them was made of copper or some other inferior material – she is not betrothed unless she recognized initially that the dinar was inferior or made of copper and presumably consented to it, or after seeing it, she thought and accepted it. There is no difference whether it is one copper dinar or many dinars, if she thought and accepted, she is betrothed. Similarly, if he said to her, 'Be betrothed to me with this maneh' and she saw what was in his hand, and it was evident that there was not a full maneh, such as if many were missing, and she thought and accepted them into her hand – she is betrothed [Beit Shmuel, Section 17]. In this case, when a copper or inferior dinar is found and she can get rid of it with difficulty, she is betrothed, and he should replace it. However, if he did not replace it, it does not invalidate the betrothal [ibid.]. But in the case of a copper dinar, it seems that it is impossible even with difficulty to get rid of it as a dinar if the recipient is informed that it is made of copper, and there is no betrothal. Only an inferior silver dinar might be possible to get rid of with difficulty to someone who is not so particular [it appears to me]."

In this ruling where a dinar is missing, or it is made of copper and thus inferior to the previous ruling, when a man says to a woman, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with one hundred dinars," without specifying further, some authorities say that the law is like when he gives her one dinar, that she is betrothed, and it is a fortiori case (kal vachomer): if we say that with one dinar she consents to be betrothed, all the more so when one dinar is missing from a hundred. Others say that on the contrary, if a dinar is missing, it is worse, and she is not betrothed. Specifically, when he gives her only one dinar, we say that she consents to be betrothed with that dinar, and the remainder he will pay her when she demands it. But if only one dinar is missing, she will be embarrassed to demand it from him, and therefore she does not fully consent and is not betrothed until he completes the payment of the dinar, and before this, she can retract. It seems that according to this opinion, it is not specifically one dinar missing, for the same applies if slightly more than one dinar is missing as long as it is not a substantial amount, she will be embarrassed to demand it. It is difficult to define the exact amount for which she will be embarrassed to demand <small>[see Rashi 47a s.v. "kesifa" etc., that it refers to a small amount etc.]</small>. The opinion of the Rambam seems explicitly to be like the first opinion, see there <small>[and see Lechem Mishneh there]</small>.

There are those who say that even according to the first opinion, there are some of our Rabbis who hold that it is specifically if the groom accepted upon himself the dinar as a loan that she is betrothed, but otherwise she is not betrothed. And there are some of our Rabbis who disagree with this [see Beit Shmuel subparagraph 13]. It appears to me that everyone agrees with this, that according to the first opinion, there is no difference between whether he accepted upon himself the dinar as a loan or not, because according to this opinion, if a dinar is missing, it is as if he only gave a dinar. And there, even if he did not accept it upon himself as a loan, it remains as a loan by default, and similarly here [and what Rashi wrote on 47a about a missing dinar when he said "I will take it as a loan," because that is the wording of the baraita there, and see in the first chapter 8a he did not write so, and what is the difference between them, analyze this carefully].

Some of our Rabbis hold that in a situation where the woman could retract, even if she did not explicitly retract but remained silent – the betrothal is annulled automatically [Ramban and Ran]. And some of our Rabbis hold that it is specifically when she explicitly retracts, but if she remains silent, the betrothal is not annulled [Rashi]. Therefore, there is an opinion that what was clarified in section 29, that when she consents and says "yes," the betrothal is finalized – this applies only according to the latter opinion. But according to the former opinion, that the betrothal is annulled, her consent does not help unless he betroths her anew and she says "yes" [Beit Shmuel, section 16]. Similarly, according to the latter opinion, if he betroths her anew and she remains silent – it is a doubtful betrothal, because it can be said that she relied on his previous statement, and her silence is not like silence after the giving of money, since the betrothal was not annulled, contrary to the opinion of some who dispute this [ibid.]. But according to the former opinion, that the betrothal was annulled, it does not help at all even if he betroths her anew when she remains silent, because since the betrothal was annulled and the money is considered a deposit in her hand, what does her silence help? This is considered silence after the giving of money [ibid., section 19].

However, from the words of our teacher, the Rema, in section 7, it is understood that even according to the first opinion, there is a doubt about the betrothal when he betroths her anew and she remains silent. Additionally, it is implied from his words that when she consents and says "yes," it is effective even according to the first opinion, even without him betrothing her anew. It appears that his reasoning is that indeed, this is not a complete nullification of the betrothal according to the first opinion; rather, it is that the previous betrothal was not fulfilled. This is not similar to a deposit, where silence after the giving of the money is considered acceptance. Therefore, even when she consents and says "yes," even if he did not betroth her anew, it is effective according to all opinions and is not less valid than discussing matters of betrothal. We consider the money in her possession as betrothal money. This also seems reasonable; however, in practice, one should be stringent according to all opinions.

The one who says to a woman, "Be betrothed to me with this dinar on the condition that I complete for you a maneh," and she says, "On the condition that you complete for me two hundred," and he stipulated according to all the conditions of a stipulation, or according to the opinion that holds that with "on the condition" there is no need for the conditions of a stipulation as written in Siman 38, and they did not agree between them. Afterwards, when they made claims against each other, he betrothed her and gave her the dinar without mentioning the condition. If the man claimed against the woman, they should follow the woman's words and he must complete for her two hundred. If not, she is not betrothed. If the woman claimed against the man, they should follow the man's words and he must complete for her only a maneh, for it is assumed that whoever made the claim agreed to the words of the other. This is similar to buying and selling as written in Choshen Mishpat Siman 221.

If initially they agreed between them and were ready for the betrothal, and one of them wanted to add or subtract, and they separated from each other, and afterwards the other party claimed and betrothed her without specifying, we do not say that he agreed to fulfill the other's wish. Rather, it is based on the initial agreement, and the second party certainly also had this intention since they initially agreed. This is also the law in buying as written there. However, we have already explained in Choshen Mishpat there in Seif 3 that some disagree with this, and according to this, there is doubt regarding betrothal in this law. Even according to what is written there that the main opinion follows the first view, it is due to complaints as written there, and in betrothal, complaints are not relevant. Therefore, the law is uncertain.

In all this main law, it seems to me that it speaks when he betrothed her afterwards with the dinar, there was proof that he betrothed her based on the first condition, such as when it was close to the original statements or they mentioned that he betrothed her based on the first condition. But if the matter was prolonged and he betrothed her afterwards with a plain dinar, from where can we say that he betrothed her based on the first condition? Perhaps he betrothed her without any condition, and therefore the law is uncertain.

If a man betrothed a woman with an object, and within that object there was another object, if he said, "Be betrothed to me with this" – it is obvious that she is betrothed with both items. If one of the items does not belong to him – she is not betrothed. However, if he only mentioned the outer object, if the two items are not commonly used together – it appears that she is only betrothed with the object he mentioned and not with the other. But if they are commonly used together, it depends on the context. For example, liquids in a vessel that are typically used together: if he betrothed her with a drinking cup and only mentioned the cup, the Sages said that if the cup was full of water – she is betrothed with both the cup and the water, and they combine to meet the value of a perutah, because the water is secondary to the cup and it is assumed he intended the water as well. If it was filled with wine – the wine is not secondary to the cup, and she is betrothed with the cup but not with the wine. If it was filled with oil, which is more significant than the cup and people commonly refer to what is within the cup by the name of the cup itself – she is betrothed with the oil and not with the cup, because it is assumed he intended the more important item. According to this opinion, if the oil has the value of a perutah, she is certainly betrothed, and if not, she is not betrothed, but it is doubtful betrothal as with anything that does not have the value of a perutah, as we worry it may have the value of a perutah elsewhere, as stated in Siman 31. However, some of our Rabbis hold that if the cup is full of water – she is betrothed with the cup and not the water, as water has no significance to assume he intended it. With wine, she is betrothed with the wine and not the cup, as it is customary to drink the wine and return the cup. If it was filled with oil, which is used for a long time – she is betrothed with both the cup and the oil. According to these principles and the opinions clarified, each case of two items together should be analyzed. One should be stringent according to both opinions because they are from the great early authorities. Some say this distinction regarding the cup applies when he betrothed her not during a meal or drink, but if he betrothed her during a meal or drink and said "Be betrothed to me with this cup" – it is certainly intended only for the wine in the cup, as that is the common practice. The same applies to other beverages. Similarly, if he said "Be betrothed to me with a cup of wine" – even not during a meal, his intention is only for the wine, and if it turns out there was no wine but another beverage, she is not betrothed. Also, if he was dining in someone’s home and betrothed the host’s daughter with the cup before him, in any case, his intention is for the beverage and not the cup, since the cup is not his.

Some of the great authorities ruled in a case where someone took a chicken and placed it in a vessel or a garment and consecrated it in this unspecified manner, that we say according to all opinions that it is consecrated with the chicken and the vessel. If one of them is not his, it is a doubtful consecration [Kenesset HaGedolah]. According to reasoning, it appears that this matter is similar to a cup with wine in it. It seems that everything depends on the local customs and the common language used, and the significance of the items. The sages of the place should decide this according to their understanding, and in a case of doubt, it is clear that one should be stringent in all matters.

In the Gemara [9a], a story is brought of a man who was selling necklaces of jewelry. A single woman came and said to him, "Give me one necklace," and he said to her, "If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me?" She answered him, "Give, you should give." Similarly, there is a story of a man who was drinking wine in a shop, and a single woman came and said to him, "Give me one cup," and he said to her, "If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me?" She answered him, "Give, you should give." Similarly, there is a story of a man who was throwing dates from a palm tree, and a single woman came and said to him, "Throw me two dates," and he said to her, "If I throw them to you, will you be betrothed to me?" She answered him, "Throw, you should throw." He did so, and the Sages ruled that they are not betrothed because she did not agree to his words. Her intention was, "Give me and do not play with me about anything else" [Rambam, Hilchot Ishut 4]. There is no difference between food and drink and jewelry or any other item [Tosafot], as such an answer indicates that she does not wish to be betrothed. The same applies if she did not repeat her response, such as if she said "Give" or "Throw" or something similar [Gemara]. But if she responded "Yes" and he gave it to her, she is betrothed. If she did not respond at all but accepted in silence, the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book is that she is betrothed. Many disagree with him and hold that only if, at the time he gave it to her, he said again, "Behold, you are betrothed to me," and she accepted in silence, she is betrothed. But if he asked her beforehand, "If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me?" and she accepted in silence, it is nothing [Bach, Chelkat Mechokek, and Beit Shmuel]. This is also clarified from the words of our teacher, the Rema, in Siman 10. 

And what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in the Shulchan Aruch, "If he said at the time he gave it to her, 'Behold, you are betrothed to me,' and she accepted, she is betrothed," this implies that he also requires him to say it again at the time of giving because she previously responded "Give," indicating she did not want to be betrothed. Therefore, it is necessary for him to say words of betrothal again. But if she did not respond at all previously and accepted in silence, even if he did not repeat his words, she is betrothed when she accepts in silence. He wrote similarly in a response. [And it is brought in the Tur, Berlanach, Siman 3, see there].

And our teacher, the Rema, explicitly wrote in his major work like those who disagree with him, and according to this, one must say regarding what is written in the Shulchan Aruch, "And if he said to her at the time he gave it to her, 'Behold, you are betrothed to me,' and she accepted, she is betrothed." His intention is not specifically about the previous words of the Beit Yosef, only when she responded initially "Give," but even if she did not respond initially "Give," if he did not say to her a second time "Behold, you are betrothed to me," her acceptance in silence means nothing. [And this resolves the difficulty raised by the Choshen Mishpat in section 22]. And what he wrote afterwards, "And if she accepted in silence but then said 'Give me' or 'Throw [it to me]' or something similar – she is not betrothed," end of quote. The explanation of his words seems to be that when she answered him "Give," he gave it to her and said to her "Behold, you are betrothed to me," and she did not respond at all but said once again as before "Give me," it is worse than if she had remained completely silent. And I am puzzled, for the Ran explicitly wrote that she is betrothed in such a case, see there, and the opinion of the Rashba is that even if he said to her at the time of giving "Behold, you are betrothed to me," and she accepted in silence, she is not betrothed, because initially she responded "Give," meaning she is not interested in the betrothal. It does not help that he repeated and said to her at the time of giving the language of betrothal when she was silent, unless she explicitly consented to the betrothal, see there. And conversely, the Rashba holds that if the first time when he asked her if she would be betrothed to him if he gave it to her, she did not respond "Give" but remained silent – she is betrothed, according to the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, as we have written [see the Gaon of Vilna's commentary in section 26 where he explains the Rashba's opinion in this way].

Furthermore, Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: All this applies when she initiated by saying "Give me a little." But if he initiated by saying "If I give you, will you be betrothed to me?" and she responded in a playful manner "Yes" and accepted from him – it is considered a doubtful betrothal. His words are perplexing: What does "playful manner" mean? It is true that some of our sages hold that when the Sages said that when she responded "Yes" it is of no consequence, this is when she initiated by asking him, for her words were not related to betrothal at all. However, if he initiated the conversation and said to her in a questioning manner "If I give you, will you be betrothed to me?" and she responded "Give" – it can be said that this is a betrothal, for we say that her intention is to agree to his words [Ran, and this is also found in Tosafot]. Some are uncertain about this [Mordechai], and some say that it is not a betrothal, since he said it in a questioning manner. If she really agreed to his words, she should have responded "Yes," and since she said "Give," it is a sign that she does not agree to the betrothal [Rashba]. Furthermore, even if he reiterated at the time of giving "Behold you are betrothed to me" and she remained silent, she is not betrothed according to this opinion as written [there]. However, the term "playful manner" is not found in the decisors, and what is the nature of this playfulness? And if she said "Yes," why would it not be a betrothal [see Chamat Hamelach]? Some wish to emend his words to say that she said to him "Give" or "Give me" [Gra], and some want to say that his intention was that she responded in a doubled language "Give, give," which is a playful manner. But if she said "Give," it is a betrothal [Beit Shmuel]. This is not clear, as it is proven from the Talmud and the decisors that there is no difference between a doubled language and a single one, and in a doubled language, what relevance does playful manner have? This requires further investigation.

And it seems to me that his words are directed at the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, which are the words of the Rambam, who wrote that if she said "yes" she is betrothed, but if she said "give me" or "throw" or words whose intention is "do not jest with me with these words, but rather give me only" – she is not betrothed, end quote. The Rambam understood that her saying "give" or "throw" implies "do not jest with me," because in truth it is a matter of jest that she requests something from him and he answers her with matters of betrothal. And our teacher, the Rema, follows his own reasoning in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 521, that there is a "yes" which is like a "no" in a matter that seems strange, see there. And since there are authorities who are stringent when she did not begin to request from him but he was the one who initiated, and there are those who disagree with this as mentioned, therefore he was stringent and ruled that in a case where he initiated, it is a doubtful betrothal. To this he added stringency by saying that not only when she answered "give me" or "throw" is it only a doubtful betrothal, but even if she answered "yes" but in a jesting manner or with doubt, it is also only a doubtful betrothal. And this is its explanation: but if he initiated and even if she answered "yes" in a jesting manner, it is only a doubtful betrothal because there is a "yes" which is like a "no," and all the more so when she answered "give" or "throw" as mentioned. And this is included in the words of the Rambam who wrote words whose intention is "do not jest with me," and consequently when she answered "yes" in a jesting manner or with doubt, it also implies "do not jest with me." And for the halacha, one should be stringent according to all the opinions that have been explained, for all of them have reasonable explanations in logic and in the Talmudic discussions.

Some of the great authorities have questioned whether, if when she asked him to give her [something] he did not respond in the form of a question but in the form of a decree, such as if he said, "I will give you and you will be betrothed to me," and she was silent and accepted it, or if she said to him, "Give" or "You shall surely give," that it is possible she is betrothed. And even according to the authorities who rule that it is not effective if he subsequently said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me" – this is because he initially spoke to her in the form of a question. However, if his initial response was in the form of a decree, it would be a valid betrothal, and it appears that it would be a doubtful betrothal.

[To where should the betrothal be given, with 33 sections]

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 4, Law 21: One who betroths a woman with money or a document does not need to place the betrothal directly into her hand. Rather, if she agrees to receive her betrothal and he throws it either into her hand, into her lap, into her courtyard, or into her field, she is betrothed. This is also written in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. And even though regarding a get (divorce document), some of our Rabbis were stringent that she is not fully divorced until the get comes directly into her hand [Tosafot Gittin 78:], and Rabbi Rema also ruled this way in Siman 139, nevertheless, with betrothal, they did not see fit to be stringent in this manner. Being stringent could lead to leniency if we cast doubt on the betrothal. Since according to the primary law she is fully betrothed, even giving it into her courtyard, the Sages did not see fit to be stringent in this case. However, with a get, there is no harm if we say she is not yet fully divorced [in my opinion]. Additionally, with a get, they were stringent because it is a disadvantage for her, and it can be given against her will according to the law, unlike betrothal. Thus, with a get, the stringency is merely an added precaution by the Sages and not with betrothal [HaMagid Mishneh, Chapter 5 of Divorce Law 13]. See what is written in Section 13.

It is explained from the words of the Rambam that before he throws her the betrothal money, she needs to consent to his throwing it to her. However, if she did not explicitly consent before he threw it, and he threw it and she remained silent – it is not considered betrothal as long as it did not come into her hand directly, even if it came into her domain, because her silence is not proof that she consented, as it is written in Siman 28, Seif 34. However, if she consented to the betrothal, even if she did not explicitly consent to the throwing, and he threw it into her domain – she is betrothed, contrary to the opinion of some who disagree. Nonetheless, if she explicitly said "place the betrothal money into my hand" and he threw it into her domain – there is no betrothal, since he deviated from her instructions. But if he threw it into her hand – it appears that she is betrothed, because the term "give" includes all forms of giving, whether by handing or by throwing, unless she explicitly stated not to give it to her by throwing.

And this that the Rambam wrote that within her courtyard it constitutes betrothal, the Tur wrote that we require the courtyard to be guarded with her knowledge, and then she is betrothed even if she is not standing next to the courtyard, see there. And even though with a get (divorce document), we require two conditions—that it be guarded with her knowledge and that she stands next to it as it says in Siman 139—this is a stringency with gittin because it is a detriment to her, and also with a get it will be explained there with God's help, and not with betrothal. And the Rambam, who did not mention this, some say he holds that with betrothal, even if it is not guarded with her knowledge and she is not standing next to it, she is betrothed. And even though with a gift we require one of these conditions as the Rambam wrote in Chapter 4 of Hilchot Zechiyah, nevertheless, betrothal is more significant. And some say that the law of betrothal is like the law of a gift, and the Rambam relied on what he wrote in Hilchot Zechiyah, but there is room to question this because an ordinary field is not guarded as it says there, but one could say that with a field we indeed require her to stand next to it. And it seems to me that the practical law is to be stringent like the first explanation, because in the Gemara (Bava Metzia 11a) there is a case where with sale and gift, since there is another person transferring it, we do not require a guarded courtyard or for her to stand next to it, and therefore, even though the Rambam did not rule this way, nevertheless, with betrothal, he might have been stringent. (And possibly this is the reason of the Maggid Mishneh, and even though the Beit Yosef in Choshen Mishpat Siman 200 wrote that according to Rav Papa, we also require it to be guarded with the knowledge of the giver, see there, this is according to the Rosh who ruled like Rav Papa, see there and be precise.)

According to the Tur, the courtyard must be guarded with her knowledge. If it is guarded with his knowledge and not with hers, one might say that it is still effective based on what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 200, regarding a gift. Even if it is guarded with the knowledge of the giver, the recipient acquires it, and the same should apply here. However, it is possible to differentiate because in betrothal, we require that the money comes from his hand to hers and that he relinquishes all his power over the betrothal, as this is the essence of the betrothal. Therefore, it does not help if it is guarded with his knowledge, and it is considered a doubtful betrothal [see Choshen Mishpat, Siman 200, Sifkat 2, and Beit Shmuel, Sifkat 3]. And indeed, there are those who disagree with this [see Shach there]. Furthermore, in the case of a found item, everyone agrees that it must be guarded because there is no other intent to transfer it, as we wrote in our work, Siman 3. Therefore, in betrothal, even though there is another intent to transfer it, she does not rely on him as in a gift where she wants the money to be clearly in her hand. Therefore, it is considered a doubtful betrothal. [See Taz and Beit Shmuel, and the question of the Avnei Miluim, Sifkat 3, is not difficult at all, and study this well].

If she was standing in the domain of her husband, he needs to place it into her hand, or into her lap, or into one of her vessels over which he is not particular about the location, such as her basket, which is a vessel that women use to place needles and tubes and the like. Even though this is like the buyer’s vessels in the domain of the seller, where the buyer does not acquire it, or it is a doubtful legal status as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 200, nonetheless, she is considered betrothed because he is not particular about the location of such a vessel of his wife, just as he is not particular about the location of her lap. However, if he placed it in a different vessel, even if he placed it on her bed and she was sitting on the bed, she is not definitely betrothed unless the bed is ten handbreadths high, in which case it creates its own domain. And regarding the legs of the bed standing on his property, he is not particular about this, as stated regarding divorce in Siman 139. If it is not ten handbreadths high, she is doubtfully betrothed. And if the bed is his, she is not betrothed in any case unless he lent her the domain, as its law is explained there, and the same applies to betrothal. See there.

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote: If she was standing in a domain that belongs to both of them and he threw her betrothal items with her consent, but they did not reach her hand or her lap - this is considered a doubtful betrothal. Even if she told him, "Place my betrothal items in this specific place," and that place belongs to both of them, this is still considered a doubtful betrothal. These are the words of the Rambam, and our teacher, the Beit Yosef, copied them in Section 3. Rambam holds that even though a courtyard jointly owned by partners does not acquire from one another, nevertheless, concerning betrothal, if she has a share in the courtyard and he is agreeable that she be betrothed, it is possible that it is like her courtyard. Therefore, it is a doubtful betrothal. However, some of our teachers disagree with this and hold that even for betrothal, a jointly owned courtyard is nothing, and she is not betrothed. The reason our teacher, the Rema, did not correct this is that he relied on what he wrote in Section 9. Regarding the law, according to the opinion of the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch, she requires a get (divorce document).

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 4: If she is standing in an alleyway or at the sides of a public domain and he throws it into her four cubits – she is betrothed. But if it remains within his four cubits – she is not betrothed, even if she enters his four cubits because he preceded her in them, he has acquired them and they are his. And the explanation of the matter is: In Choshen Mishpat, section 243, it is explained that the Sages decreed that any four cubits in which a person stands are considered as his courtyard regarding acquisitions. This applies specifically in an alleyway and at the sides of a public domain because everyone has permission to linger there and place their belongings there. Therefore, whoever precedes within the four cubits, it is considered as his courtyard. However, this does not apply in a public domain or in the property of others because a person does not have permission to linger there. Also, in a shared courtyard, this was not decreed because one cannot take permission from the other partner. And even though some say that this was decreed only in the case of a found object to avoid disputes, as mentioned there in section 268, nevertheless the majority of Poskim hold that this was decreed for all acquisitions, as mentioned there in section 200, paragraph 8. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch hold that also regarding betrothal, it is considered as her courtyard if she precedes him within the four cubits, and similarly regarding divorce, as stated later in section 139.

Even though this acquisition is only rabbinic, nevertheless, she is betrothed by it according to Torah law because the court has the power to declare property ownerless [Ran, Chapter 8 of Gittin], and thus the place becomes like her courtyard by Torah law. Furthermore, anyone who betroths does so with the understanding of the rabbis [Ramban there]. This does not mean the betrothal is rabbinic; the betrothal is by Torah law since the rabbis made it like her courtyard. Rather, if he did not betroth with the understanding of the rabbis, one might say his intention is for the betrothal to take place in a courtyard that is valid by Torah law. But since he betroths with their understanding, the betrothal is completed by Torah law in the courtyard established by the rabbis. [This reconciles all that is stated by the Avnei Miluim in section 5]. We have already explained in Siman 28, Se'if 61, in the name of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, that all rabbinic acquisitions are also acquisitions by Torah law for all matters, and this is proven in the Jerusalem Talmud in Ma'aser Sheni, see there. Also, regarding the four cubits, it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud Peah [Chapter 4] and Jerusalem Talmud Gittin [Chapter 8] that even those who hold that a gift does not establish the four-cubit acquisition, nevertheless agree concerning gittin, see there. And it is obvious that the get is by Torah law, and one cannot say it is only in gittin because anyone who betroths does so with the understanding of the rabbis, and the rabbis annulled the Torah betrothal with this get and not with betrothal. This is certainly the case, for if they annulled a Torah betrothal with such a get, all the more so they complete a Torah betrothal with such conditions since he betroths with the understanding of the rabbis. [See Avnei Miluim, and to my humble opinion, the main point is as stated].

The decisors did not bring any disagreement regarding this law of four cubits, and it is clear to them that according to all the decisors, this law is agreed upon. And even though the Rambam, of blessed memory, did not bring at all the law of four cubits regarding betrothal, it is because he relied on what he wrote in Chapter 5 of Laws of Divorce [Gra 26, and so it appears from Maharshal and Beit Shmuel]. On the contrary, according to the Rambam, four cubits are effective even in a public domain as he wrote there, and the reason is because of the decree concerning agunahs [Beit Shmuel 5]. And for this reason, they also instituted it in betrothal, even though in betrothal the issue of agunah does not apply, nevertheless, we compare betrothal to divorce [there]. But the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, even though in divorce they ruled in Siman 139 that four cubits are effective even in a public domain, nevertheless, in betrothal they hold that it is not effective [there], and all of this is according to the opinion of the great later authorities.

However, I found that one of the early authorities explicitly wrote that the four cubits rule does not apply even to bills of divorce [Nimukei Yosef, first chapter of Bava Metzia], and also the Rif, of blessed memory, in the eighth chapter of Gittin did not write this law. It also seems to me that the Rambam, of blessed memory, did not hold that the four cubits rule applies to bills of divorce, and certainly not to betrothal. The four cubits rule he wrote about there pertains to a different matter. In bills of divorce and betrothal, there is another form of acquisition that does not pertain to monetary laws, namely when she can guard the bill of divorce or the betrothal and he cannot guard it, as will be explained. In this, there is no difference between a public domain and a semi-public domain, as it pertains to the law of guarding. Only regarding bills of divorce, we hold that the document must be close enough to her that she can bend down and take it, and even in this, the Rabbis were stringent that she should not remarry until the document reaches her hand, as the Rambam wrote there. But in betrothal, we follow the law that as long as she can guard it and he cannot, it constitutes betrothal, as will be explained. The four cubits mentioned by the Rambam in the context of a bill of divorce is so that she can bend down and take it, and it pertains to the law of guarding. Indeed, they were stringent that if the husband entered the four cubits before her, it is not a valid divorce, even if she could bend down and take it, as he wrote there in Law 15. Therefore, in Law 12 there, regarding if her hand was like a basket, he wrote that if he threw the bill of divorce on her hand and it fell within her four cubits, she is divorced when the document rests, because it is considered as if it were in her hand, and even more so because she can bend down and take it [and this resolves the Tosafot’s question in Gittin 78b 'let it be,' see there and examine well]. Therefore, in betrothal, the Rambam did not mention the law of four cubits because it is included in the law that she can guard it and he cannot. If she indeed cannot guard it, she is not betrothed by the law of four cubits. And what they said in the Jerusalem Talmud that there is a four cubits rule in bills of divorce, they meant it as a theoretical law, not for practical application, as it says there. Indeed, the Jerusalem Talmud is very stringent regarding the actual acquisition of the four cubits, requiring that he says he intends to acquire, as it is written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 268, Section 5, see there. And our Talmud does not hold this [Bava Metzia 10a]. Therefore, in my humble opinion, even though the law of four cubits in betrothal is explained in the Shulchan Aruch and later authorities without dispute, one should act stringently in practice. If another man betrothed her, she would need a divorce from both. Also, if he threw the betrothal in a public domain within her four cubits, it is a doubtful betrothal [Beit Shmuel]. Even though, according to what I wrote, there is no betrothal here either way, since according to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, this law does not apply in a public domain, and according to the Rambam, he does not hold this law at all as I wrote. Nevertheless, since the great later authorities decided so, God forbid to dispute them leniently. However, in Siman 139, we explained that in the case of a bill of divorce, the Rambam agrees that fundamentally she has four cubits, but because of stringency, they invalidated it, see there.

According to the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, within her four cubits, even if both of them can guard the betrothal, she is betrothed. And even though with a get (divorce document) we are stringent in this manner in Siman 139, it is a stringency specifically for a get, but with betrothal it is valid. In any case where the get is valid by Torah law and only invalid by Rabbinic law, then in betrothal she is certainly betrothed. Just as if he preceded her into these four cubits, she is not betrothed even if she also subsequently entered these four cubits. Similarly, if she preceded, she is betrothed even if he also subsequently entered these four cubits, for the rule in the law of acquisition of four cubits is that whoever precedes in them, they become his property. And although with a get we are stringent even in this manner, it is a stringency specifically for gittin as mentioned. And if both of them came into these four cubits simultaneously, it is like a courtyard owned by both of them, as explained in Section 6. And in Choshen Mishpat Siman 268, it is explained that there is a dispute whether four cubits acquire for a person only when standing or even when walking, and it is clear that in betrothal we should always be stringent in this matter. And although in the Shulchan Aruch it does not bring this opinion which differentiates between standing and walking, nevertheless, we should be stringent. And similarly, although we explained there in Section 4 that there is no practical difference in law, nevertheless, in betrothal we do not rely on this, and we should be stringent in all matters.

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote in the fourth chapter of the Laws of Marriage: If they were standing in a public domain or in a domain that belongs to neither of them and he threw her the betrothal money, if it is closer to him – she is not betrothed, if it is closer to her – she is betrothed. If it is equally distant, or if it is uncertain whether it is closer to him or her, and the money was lost before she could take possession of it – she is in a state of doubtful betrothal. What defines closer to him and closer to her? If he is able to guard it and she is not able – it is closer to him. If she is able to guard it and he is not able – it is closer to her. If both of them are able to guard it or neither of them are able – it is equally distant. These are the words of Maimonides, and similarly, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 5. And although we do not find in any place that acquisition depends on guarding, nevertheless, the Sages decreed so in the case of divorce documents because of the decree concerning chained women (agunot), and it was not possible for them to differentiate between divorce documents and betrothal documents because it is written "and she departs and becomes" [Ran, Chapter 8 of Gittin]. And although in divorce documents we rule that it is not a complete divorce until it reaches her hand, Maimonides holds that this is a stringency they imposed in divorce documents, but regarding betrothal she is fully betrothed. And according to this reasoning, the entire basis of this law is a rabbinic decree. And although we have already explained that in every rabbinic acquisition the betrothal is of Torah status, nevertheless, according to those who disagree, they are only rabbinic betrothals. [See Choshen Mishpat, sections 5 and 7].

However, some of our Rabbis have offered a different rationale for this, stating that since, according to Torah law, a get (divorce document) can be given against the wife’s will, therefore the get is effective even when it is near her [Rashi there 78b]. Consequently, it would also be a valid transaction in betrothals, because the verse states, "And she shall depart and she shall be [another man's wife]" [there]. According to this reasoning, it can be said that this is a full-fledged law. The reason they were stringent with gittin (divorce documents) until the get reaches her hand is a stringency specific to gittin, lest people come to say that a distant get is close [Rashi there]. Consequently, with betrothals, there is no need to be stringent about this. For in the case of a get, there could be a problem if people say she is divorced and she remarries another, but with betrothals, it is not problematic if people say she is betrothed. And although there could be an issue if she accepts betrothal from another man, this is not common because someone who is betrothed does not usually accept betrothal from another man. Furthermore, there is no concern for the opposite, that people will say a close betrothal is distant and she is not betrothed, for even if we say she is not betrothed until the betrothal reaches her hand, they might still say a close one is distant and it is not a betrothal. According to Torah law, they are certainly betrothal [in my opinion]. This rationale we have explained can apply to all the stringencies imposed in such matters concerning gittin, but not in betrothals.

And regarding what he wrote that neither of them can guard it, this constitutes a doubtful betrothal; the intention is not that both together cannot guard it, for if so, it is obvious that it would not be a betrothal. Rather, the intention is that each one individually cannot guard it, but both together can guard it. In chapter 139, it will be further explained with the help of Heaven. According to this, when it is written that both can guard it, the meaning is that each one can guard it individually. And the statement of this law in a public domain is not to exclude an alleyway or the sides of a public domain, for it is a fortiori from the public domain, but to exclude his courtyard and hers. In his courtyard, she is never betrothed, and in hers, she is always betrothed if the courtyard is guarded or she is standing beside it. And the comparison of a domain that does not belong to both of them to a public domain is because the law is the same for both regarding the acquisition of sales.

And regarding what is written about a doubt whether it is closer to him or to her, some of the early authorities explained that this specifically applies to two sets of witnesses, one set saying it is closer to him and the other set saying it is closer to her, which constitutes a biblical doubt. And although from the Torah, in a case of two against two, we maintain the status quo, nevertheless, rabbinically, she cannot be released without a get (divorce document) since there are two witnesses saying it is closer to her (Yevamot 31). However, with one set of witnesses where one says it is closer to him and the other says it is closer to her, one could say that we maintain her status as unmarried. Similarly, if both have a doubt whether it is closer to him or to her, we maintain the status quo. Some say that even with one set of witnesses where one says it is closer to him and the other says it is closer to her, the sages decreed that it is a case of doubtful betrothal (Chamach and Beit Shmuel). 

But in Siman 47, it will be explained that in such a case, if she marries, she does not need to leave her second husband. However, initially, she should not marry because since it is known that he threw the betrothal, it weakens the presumption of her being unmarried. According to this opinion, even if both are in doubt whether it is closer to him or to her, she should initially not marry because her presumption is weakened. If she did marry, she does not need to leave. However, one could argue that since both are in doubt, there is no concern of betrothal at all, as it is like betrothing without witnesses (see Beit Shmuel, section 9). 

But according to this, even in a case where one witness says it is closer to him and the other says it is closer to her, there should be no concern, as we hold that betrothal with one witness is not considered a betrothal. This is the opinion of most authorities, but certainly, this is not like a definite betrothal without witnesses but rather like any doubt whether there are witnesses or not. By law, we maintain the status quo, but since her status is weakened, she should not marry initially. 

Some differentiate between whether the witnesses saw the place where the betrothal fell and are uncertain if it is closer to him or to her, which constitutes a case of doubtful betrothal, and if they did not see the place at all but only saw the throwing and do not know where the betrothal reached, whether closer to him or to her, it does not even constitute a case of doubtful betrothal (Avnei Miluim). But I have not clarified this distinction (also, the Tosafot in Ketubot 23 do not imply this). However, with two sets of witnesses, even if she marries, she must leave rabbinically (Tosafot there).
