Some say that even with two sets of witnesses, if she marries, she does not need to leave (Rivash, Siman 266) because we also combine the presumption that a woman examines carefully before marrying with the presumption of being unmarried. The examination is because she fears that her witnesses might be disqualified, so she is careful. This is also explained in the Jerusalem Talmud in Yevamot (Chapter 10, Halacha 3). (Also, the Tosafot according to the answer "there are those who say" hold this, and the Rashba there writes that the sugya is according to the opinion that two against two is a biblical doubt).

A side street (simta) is a place designated for those standing there at that time, and it is similar to the courtyard of both of them [Rashbam Bava Batra 76b]. It is a private path or a protruding entrance from a public domain, and people have permission to place their belongings there, similar to a shared courtyard that is not made for the walking of the public [ibid. 84b]. Similarly, a corner adjacent to a public domain, which is ownerless and the public can use to ease congestion [Rashi Bava Metzia 10a], and similar such places should be judged according to the situation. 

A synagogue and a study hall—some say it has the same status as a side street regarding the four cubits [Rivash], and some say it has the status of a shared courtyard [Beit Hillel], as proven in Yoreh De'ah, Section 224, see there. There is an opinion that the primary view is the first one, that even though in other matters their status is certainly like a shared courtyard, nevertheless, regarding divorce and betrothal, which are commonly done in a synagogue and study hall, their status is like a side street [Beit Shmuel 9]. According to this, in our country where it is not common to perform divorces and betrothals there, their status is like a shared courtyard. 

It is possible to say that during prayer time their status is like a shared courtyard, and outside prayer time their status is like a side street, and this requires further consideration. The courtyard of the synagogue also seems to have the status of a side street.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 6: "If he threw her the betrothal money, even into her lap, and she did not take it but remained silent—there is an opinion that says it is nothing, since from the outset she did not consent to be betrothed to him." This aligns with what is stated in Section 2, that if she did not explicitly consent beforehand for him to throw it to her, and he threw it and she remained silent, it does not constitute betrothal. As our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 28, that it is only when she took it in her hand, but if he threw the betrothal money to her, even into her lap, her silence is meaningless since she did not initially consent to be betrothed to him. We explained there in Section 34 that it is only when she took it in her hand that her silence serves as evidence of her consent. Some say that since he used the language of betrothal and she was silent, it constitutes a complete betrothal, and it is only when she immediately threw the betrothal money from her lap that it does not constitute betrothal, but if she did not throw it away, it does constitute betrothal. According to this, it must be said that in our teacher, the Beit Yosef's ruling, the intention is also that she threw it away. Many disagree with this opinion.

And for the one who holds this opinion, there is an apparent proof from what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Siman 42, Se'if 1: that if a man forcefully took a woman's hand without her consent and betrothed her, and she did not throw away the betrothal (money), she is considered betrothed, even though it initially was under duress and he gave it to her without saying anything, since he initially spoke to her about betrothal. And if we say that if she threw it when she did not consent, we are not concerned that she didn't throw it from her lap, then similarly, the betrothal should not be valid since he took her hand forcefully. Why then should the betrothal be valid just because she didn't throw it away?

However, in truth, these cases are not comparable, because there it speaks of a case where she initially consented to be betrothed to him, as is evident from the language of our teacher, the Rema, and also from the source of the law. Additionally, it is not the same because when the betrothal is in her hand, even though it was given to her against her will, once the coercion ceased, she should have thrown it from her hand. This is not the case when it was in her lap; she did not worry about throwing it away since it was not directly in her hand. Although according to the law there is no difference between her hand and her lap regarding the acceptance of the betrothal, nevertheless, regarding the fact that she did not throw it away afterward, logic suggests making this distinction. Nevertheless, in practice, it is possible to be stringent even though according to the essence of the law, it is as stated. [The Taz and the Bach in Siman 28 are stringent, and also the Chochmat Shlomo wrote that they contradict each other, and the one who corrected the Taz also holds this way, and the Chatam Sofer there refuted his words, see there.]

In the case of a get (divorce document), it is established that if the husband says to his wife, "Take your get from the ground," it is considered as if he said nothing, because we require "and he shall place it in her hand" (Deuteronomy 24:1). Some say that the same applies to kiddushin (betrothal): if he says to her "Take your kiddushin from the ground," it is not considered kiddushin. Even though for kiddushin we do not require the giving to be directly from his hand to hers—since if he betrothed her with a deposit that was already in her possession, she would be betrothed—nevertheless, we do require that it come from his hand or the hand of his emissary to hers, even if not in the context of kiddushin. Similarly, if he betroths her with something that is considered as if given to her, it is still considered as giving, but if he says "Take it from the ground," it is not valid kiddushin, as there is a comparison between get and kiddushin based on the verse "and she departs and becomes [another man's wife]" (Deuteronomy 24:2) [Mahari"l in his response].

Some say that it is considered complete kiddushin, and we do not require the giving to be from his hand to hers in kiddushin [Rashdam, Ranach, and Avnei Miluim], since the comparison of "and she departs and becomes" applies only to kiddushin with a document. What benefit is there to a deposit already in her possession that did not come into her possession as kiddushin? Moreover, do we not find cases where a deposit was not handed directly from his hand to hers? If there were truly a distinction, the Talmud and the legal authorities would have explained it [in my opinion]. Also, from what is explained in Siman 28, Se'if 37 regarding a woman who grabs money, it is also proven that we do not require the giving to be from his hand to hers, as it is clearly implied there that if she says "Yes," she is betrothed, even though the money did not come from his hand to hers [Avnei Miluim]. 

There are some great authorities who are uncertain about this law [R. Yosef ibn Lev, Rashbash, and Beit Shmuel, subsection 1], and certainly, in practice, it is considered a case of doubt in kiddushin. Even though the primary opinion seems to be the second one, in practice, they cannot be considered definitely betrothed but rather betrothed in doubt, and if another man betroths her, she requires a get from both.

He said to a woman, "Be betrothed to me with this dinar," and she took it and threw it in front of him into the sea or into the fire or into anything that is lost and said nothing – she is not betrothed, for this proves that she does not desire the betrothal. And although she is obligated to pay him and one might say that she intended the betrothal and came to test him to see if he would not get angry, nevertheless, we do not say this, for such an action proves that she does not desire him, and out of anger, she destroyed it and will be obligated to pay. All the more so, if she threw it in front of him to a place where it is not lost, it is not a betrothal, for this is like saying, "Take what you gave me, I do not desire you."

The halachic authorities did not distinguish in this matter between "shadich" and "not shadich," and it implies that even if they had previously spoken about matters of betrothal, she is not betrothed. However, logically, there seems to be a distinction, and certainly, if at that very moment she threw it from her hand, it is not a betrothal in any case. But if she delayed a moment and then threw it in his face, if they had previously spoken (shadich), it would at least be a doubtful betrothal, for perhaps at the moment she received it, she consented and then changed her mind. But if they had not spoken (not shadich) and she held it for some time and then threw it, it would be a doubtful betrothal. But if she did not hold it for some time, even though she did not throw it immediately upon receiving it, it is not a betrothal, for there is neither a verbal expression of betrothal on her part indicating her consent nor an action, and on the contrary, her action shows she did not consent, it is not a betrothal. And the law of "within the time it takes to speak" does not apply in this case, for we hold that in betrothal, "within the time it takes to speak" is like "after the time it takes to speak." Since she threw it within that time, her action of throwing nullifies her action of receiving. But if she delayed until after that time, it is certainly a doubtful betrothal. But if they had previously spoken (shadich), even within the time it takes to speak, it would be a doubtful betrothal, unless she threw it right at the moment she received it.

There is a doubt if he betrothed her with an object and at the moment she received it, she tore it but did not throw it from her hand, whether we say that this is also an indication that she does not want the betrothal, or perhaps since she did not throw it from her hand, it is considered a valid betrothal. And in practice, it seems that it is a case of doubtful betrothal.

Some say that if they are standing in her domain and he threw the betrothal (money), since it is still in her domain – she is betrothed, unless she explicitly said that she does not want to be betrothed to him. This is also the law if he threw it close to her or within her four cubits [Tur]. However, there are those who question this [Beit Shemuel], arguing that what more could she have done after he threw it in front of her? There is no greater indication of her disinterest in the betrothal than this. This matter requires further study, as it seems that this is similar to the law detailed in section 17, see there. Nevertheless, practically, this remains a doubtful betrothal since there are significant authorities who are stringent in this matter [and also the Chacham Tzvi agrees with the Tur].

He said to a woman, "Be betrothed to me with a maneh" (a specific amount of money), and she responded, "Give it to my father" or "Give it to your father" or "Give it to so-and-so," and he gave it to them, we do not say that her intention is to be betrothed through this. Rather, her intention is to mock him by saying "Give your money to others." Even though she instructed him to give it to her father, it means nothing. Even though at the moment he gave it to her father he said to her, "Be betrothed to me with the maneh that I gave to your father," and she remained silent - it means nothing. Specifically, if he gave it into her hand and she accepted it silently, she would be betrothed. But in this case, what does she have to speak of, since it did not come into her hand? And how do we know that her intention was not for them to receive it on her behalf and thereby become betrothed? Because if so, she would have responded, "My father or your father or so-and-so will receive it on my behalf." This is not similar to the case of "Give a maneh to so-and-so and I will be betrothed to you" in Siman 129 where she is betrothed, because there she initiated the conversation and it is not appropriate to say she intended to mock. But when he initiated and she responded in this manner, it is as if she is mocking him, as Rashi and Tosafot explained. Some say that in the case of "Give a maneh to so-and-so" even if she did not complete the phrase with "and I will be betrothed to you," she is betrothed when she initiated the conversation, as noted in Beit Shmuel Seif Katan 13. Refer to what I wrote in Siman 29 Seif 14, and this requires further study.

However, if she responded to him, "My father will accept for me" or "Your father will accept for me" or "So-and-so will accept for me," and when he gave it to them he said, "Acquire these betrothals for so-and-so," or if they heard when she told him that they would accept it for her, then upon their acceptance it is as if it reached her hand, even if he did not say again to her, "Be betrothed to me with the money I gave them." Even if she said, "So-and-so will accept for me," and that person is a stranger, we do not say that she is merely pushing him off and does not desire the betrothal. Rather, we say that her intention is truly to be betrothed through that person's acceptance, for if not, she would have said, "Give it to so-and-so."

And know that when she said, "So-and-so will accept for me" or "My father and your father will accept for me," the intention is not that she is making them her agent to accept the betrothal on her behalf. For if so, she would need to tell them, "Be my agents to accept the betrothal money on my behalf," and not tell another person, "Tell so-and-so to accept my betrothal." In such a case, it could be said that it is merely a matter that cannot be entrusted to an agent. Rather, the reason is that since she told him that they will accept it, it is as if it was given into her hand.

And in truth, we hold that she can appoint an agent to accept [the betrothal] on her behalf even not in his presence, and this is not similar to one who says "Tell so-and-so." Rather, the truth is that this is not like agency but more like a condition, for in such a case she becomes betrothed to him. And indeed, in the Baraita there it is taught in the language of a condition, but the poskim omitted this because it is not a complete condition but rather that in such a case she agrees. And what the Maknah wrote in the name of the Chelkat Mechokek and the Beit Shmuel that she made them agents to accept is not clearly explained in their words, and their intention is as I have written. And understand this well.

It is stated in the Talmud that if a man says to a woman, "Be betrothed to me with a maneh" and she responds, "Place it on a rock" – she is not betrothed. However, if the rock belongs to her – she is betrothed, and if the rock belongs to both of them – it is a doubtful betrothal. Some of our rabbis have explained this literally, that if the rock belongs to her, she is betrothed because it is considered like her courtyard and as if she received it in her hand (Rashi). And if the rock belongs to both of them, even though in a jointly-owned courtyard, one cannot acquire from another, here it can be said that since she has a share in it, when she tells him "Place it on the rock," her intention is to become betrothed. And he too, since he wants to betroth her, grants her a place in that rock, and she acquires it. Or perhaps, since the rock is not entirely hers, it is considered merely a pretense (Ran and Maggid Mishneh). This is also the opinion of the Rambam, as written in section 6, see there. According to this view, which is based on the principle of 'courtyard,' the rock must be under her control or she must be standing beside it, and similarly, it refers to a rock owned by both of them (this seems correct to me).

And some of our rabbis interpret that this ruling is not based on the principle of a courtyard, for if it were based on the principle of a courtyard, there would be no doubt in the case of a courtyard that belongs to both of them, as it is certain that she would not be betrothed, since partners' courtyards do not acquire from each other. Here, it refers to a case where there is another form of acquisition, such as if he subsequently threw it into her lap and she remained silent. In this scenario, we say that when she said, "Place it on the rock," she was merely rejecting him, meaning she did not desire him and told him to place it wherever he wished. Consequently, his throwing it into her lap would also be ineffective since she indicated her lack of interest in him. However, if the rock belonged to her, we say she did not intend to reject him, and on the contrary, she consented. In this case, even if he did not throw it into her lap, she would still be betrothed by the principle of a courtyard [Choshen Mishpat]. Therefore, if the rock belonged to both of them and he subsequently threw it into her lap, there is doubt whether her intention was to reject him or she consented [Rosh]. 

From the words of the Tur, it implies that if the rock belonged to her, even if he did not place it on the rock at all but threw it directly into her lap, she is betrothed. Although one could argue that she insisted on it being placed on the rock and not in her lap [Yam Shel Shlomo], it can also be said that there is no insistence in this case, as she could take it from her lap and place it on the rock herself [there]. And so it is with all similar cases that will be explained. Know that according to this opinion, it only applies when she said, "Place it on the rock," and nothing more. But if she added "and I will be betrothed to you," there is no doubt, and she is betrothed if he threw it into her lap, as she was not merely rejecting him [in my opinion]. However, according to the previous interpretation, even if she said, "and I will be betrothed to you," it means nothing in the case of an ordinary rock since it is not hers, and with what could she acquire it [Ran in the name of Ramban]? Certainly, according to the law, the first opinion does not disagree with this one when he throws it into her lap. This opinion only disputes the first one in the case of a courtyard that belongs to both of them, as mentioned.

Some of our rabbis also hold like the previous opinion that in a courtyard owned by both, there is no acquisition, and they explain in a different manner that the reason does not depend here on the acquisition of the courtyard, but rather if the rock is hers, her mind is settled, and if it is not hers, her mind is not settled. And in the case of a rock owned by both, there is doubt whether her mind is settled or not [Tosafot]. And even though there is no acquisition in a rock owned by both, and what benefit is there in her mind being settled, and what doubt is there in this [Piskei Yeshivot], nevertheless, this opinion holds that if she says, "Place the money on the rock and I will be betrothed to you," she is betrothed by the law of a guarantor, similar to "Give the money to so-and-so." According to this, if her mind is settled, she would be betrothed by the law of guarantee even though there is no acquisition [Makneh]. However, many of our rabbis agreed that the law of guarantee only applies when she commands to give to a person but not in placing it on a rock or throwing it away, as there is no law of guarantee in this [Rosh there and Ran in the name of others, and also Ramban who disagrees regarding throwing away agrees in the case of a rock, see there]. Nevertheless, in practice, one should be stringent since many great authorities hold that there is a guarantee in such a case [Rosh].

Some of our rabbis have written that if she says simply, "Place them on the rock," she is not betrothed even if he places them on her rock. However, if she specifies the rock, such as saying, "Place them on a certain rock" or "on my rock," she is betrothed [Tur in the name of the Rema], because when she says to place them on the rock, she is rejecting him. And there are those who say that no one disagrees with this, and that all the poskim agree with this [Cheshek Shlomo], but it does not appear that way from the language of the poskim and from the words of Rabbeinu the Rema [and so it appears from the Levush and the Mishna Shlomo], and in practice, it is clear that one should be stringent according to all opinions. According to this opinion, regarding a rock that belongs to both of them, it can be said that there is doubt as in the previous opinion from the law of surety [so it appears from the Gra, section 10], or it is possible that it holds like the first opinion that regarding a rock that belongs to both of them, it is considered an acquisition in terms of betrothal, and this also seems to be the understanding from the arrangement of the language of Rabbeinu the Rema in section 9, see there. [From the Levush it is explained that the opinion of the Tosafot and the Rema are one, see there, and this is like the Gra].

There are those who hold that in a situation where it is clear that she does not want the betrothal, as previously explained, then the betrothal is not valid even if it later comes into her possession. And it is not considered that she threw it away from her hand as we said about throwing it into her lap. And even though in section 18 we differentiated between it coming into her hand and into her lap, where she should have thrown it away from her hand, nevertheless, here she can say that she received it as a gift. Still, there is a question regarding the law, where does she get the right to say that he gave her a gift, for he said that she should be betrothed to him with it. And the Beit Shmuel compares it to a case where someone gives a gift, but it is not the same, as in that case she had previously asked for a gift. Therefore, it seems to me that one should be stringent in this matter. There is also a question on the Beit Shmuel in section 17 where he wrote this in the name of the Rema, and the Rema wrote about it being in her lap. And what he wrote, that if he said at the time of giving to her hand that she should be betrothed to him, then she is betrothed, is obvious, and what is he teaching us?

Our Sages further stated there that if a man says to a woman, "Be betrothed to me with this loaf of bread," and she responds, "Give it to a dog," she is not betrothed. However, if the dog belongs to her, she is betrothed. If a dog is running after her to bite her and she says, "Give it to this dog," it is considered a doubtful betrothal because perhaps with the benefit that she saves herself from the dog through this loaf, she fully commits and consecrates herself to be betrothed to him, as this benefit is certainly worth a perutah. Alternatively, since he is obligated by the Torah to save her, it is a duty imposed on him. This law also applies according to the opinion in Section 27, where he gave it to her afterward into her lap. Her saying, "Give it to the dog," is like saying, "I do not desire you," and the giving into her lap does not help. If the dog is hers, she is betrothed even if he did not place it into her lap. Similarly, if the dog is running to bite her, it is a doubtful betrothal even if he did not place it into her lap, for the reasons explained. According to the first explanation in Section 26, which understands it by the principle of ‘courtyard,’ there is a difference between a rock and a dog. If she said, "Place it on the rock," she is not betrothed if the rock does not belong to her, even if she said, "And I will be betrothed to you," because with what will she be betrothed, as explained in Section 27. However, if she said to give it to a dog that does not belong to her, she is betrothed if she said, "And I will be betrothed to you," as this is like giving security to destruction, which is comparable to giving security to a person. There are those who disagree with this, as will be explained, and some say that even with a rock, security is applicable, as explained in Section 28.

The sages also said there that if a man says to a woman, "Be betrothed to me with this loaf of bread," and she replies, "Give it to a poor person," she is not betrothed, even if this poor person is dependent on her for support due to a mitzvah (commandment), because she can say, "Just as I am obligated to support him, so too are you obligated to give charity," and it is not considered as if it was given into her hand. And why, in the case of a dog running to bite her, did we say it is a doubtful betrothal even though there is also a mitzvah to save her, because it is possible that saving her life is very important to her and she fully intends to betroth herself <small>[Ran]</small>. And it seems that in the case of a poor person, if she said, "And I will be betrothed to you," she is betrothed even if he is not dependent on her, since she explicitly stated that she is betrothed by the benefit that he gives the loaf to the poor person, as this benefit is worth a perutah (a minimal amount of value) to her and is no less than giving a maneh (a substantial amount of value) to another person. Similarly, in the case of a poor person dependent on her, if she replied simply, "Give it to the poor person," and later stated that her intention was to be betrothed by this, it would be a doubtful betrothal, and even if he is not dependent on her, it seems that the law is the same. And in this law of the poor person, according to the opinion in section 27 here, even if he later placed it into her lap, she is not betrothed, because by saying "Give it to the poor person," she rejected him, showing she has no desire for him. It is straightforward that if she said, "Give it to my creditor," and he gave it to him, she is betrothed. However, some differentiate between whether the creditor is pressing her to pay or not, and between a non-Jewish creditor – it is betrothal, and a Jewish creditor – it is a doubtful betrothal, and I do not know why <small>[see Be'er Hetiv, section 9, in the name of Rashdam]</small>.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 11: If she first said, "Give a loaf to the dog" or "Place a coin on the rock and I will be betrothed to you" — some say that it is treated as if she said, "Give a coin to so-and-so," as mentioned earlier in section 29, and one should be stringent in this matter. The reasoning behind this opinion is that, just as she is betrothed through the principle of surety (arvut) when giving a coin to another person, there is also a principle of surety in giving to the dog or placing the coin on the rock, as stated in section 28. Others say that in both cases there is no principle of surety, for surety only applies to giving to a person and not to placing on a rock or giving to a dog or to waste [Ran in the name of others]. And some say that there is no surety with the rock, but there is surety with the dog [there in the name of Ramban], because since the item is lost through her speech, there is surety. From the words of Rabbi Moshe Isserles it appears that he mainly holds that in both cases there is no surety; however, one should be stringent regarding betrothal according to all opinions, as the Rosh also wrote [Chapter 1, section 13], and see what is written in Choshen Mishpat section 380, paragraph 4.

[One cannot betroth with less than a perutah’s worth, nor with precious stones, and it contains 42 sections]

One cannot betroth with less than the value of a perutah, and even if the woman consents, it does not help, because it is not considered money at all [Tosafot Gittin]. There is a doubt regarding an item that is not worth a perutah if the woman can say, "To me, it is worth a perutah," similar to the five sela'im for the redemption of the firstborn, where the priest can say the same, as mentioned by the Tur in Yoreh De’ah, section 305. Alternatively, it is possible that for monetary value, one can say "To me, it is worth more," but for something that is not money at all, it cannot be considered as money [Ran]. However, there are opinions that say this applies specifically if it is genuinely worth five sela'im to this particular priest, such as if he typically pays more for such an item than its usual value. Accordingly, if it is worth a perutah to this woman, but the witnesses do not know that she usually pays more, there is no betrothal, as it would be like betrothing without witnesses [ibid.], but Rambam and the Tur there do not agree with this; see there. Therefore, there is doubt in all cases if the woman says that to her, it is worth a perutah [and what the Beit Yosef wrote there according to the Rambam, that it must be worth it to any person, was refuted by the Shach and Taz; see there].

Nevertheless, if he betrothed her with an unspecified object, there is no need to appraise it beforehand if it is worth a perutah. Rather, since it is indeed worth a perutah, she is retroactively betrothed from the moment the betrothal was given. And it is not necessary to say when the value of the object was not specified at the time of betrothal, but even if he specified and said to her, "Be betrothed to me with this object that is worth fifty zuz," or if he said to her, "Be betrothed to me with fifty zuz, and here are these items in their value," and its value was not appraised beforehand, if it is later found to be worth fifty zuz, she is retroactively betrothed from the moment the betrothal was given.

There is a doubt if the value of the object is less than a sixth, which is considered a waiver in buying and selling, whether this law also applies to betrothal. And if he said, "Be betrothed to me with fifty zuz, and here are these items in their value," certainly there is no waiver in this case. Similarly, if the object is worth a perutah but less than a sixth is lacking in its value, it is clear that it is not considered money. However, if he said, "Be betrothed to me with this object that is worth fifty zuz," and it is lacking less than a sixth, there is a doubt about this.

It seems that in betrothal, this does not apply. The reason for a waiver in buying and selling, as the Tur writes in Choshen Mishpat, siman 227, is that this is the way of buying and selling, where exact precision cannot be achieved, and it is customary for people to waive less than a sixth, but in betrothal, which is a rare occurrence to betroth with an object and specify its value, it cannot be said that it is customary for people to waive. Moreover, since we see that these people are meticulous and do not follow the usual custom in betrothal, it is certainly unlikely that she would waive. Furthermore, the reason we do not require an appraisal beforehand, even though a woman is not knowledgeable in appraisals and we might think that she does not rely on its value, nevertheless we do not say this but rather assume she relies on it. If we say that even less than a sixth she is betrothed, she certainly does not rely on it, as it might be worth slightly less, making it a sixth or slightly more. Since it is impossible to be precise to the exact amount, it must certainly be of full value. However, in practice, this matter requires further investigation.

This is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 7, Halacha 18: If he said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with these clothes that are worth fifty dinars," and they were made of silk and similar materials that a woman desires, if they were worth fifty, she is betrothed from the time of acquisition, and there is no need for appraisal in the market, and afterwards she becomes betrothed in order to assure her mind. Rather, since they are worth what he said to her, she is betrothed from the first moment. But if they are not worth it, she is not betrothed. 

It is explained from his words that specifically with items that a woman desires, there is no need for prior appraisal, but with items that a woman does not desire, prior appraisal is needed. And it is also implied from his words that even with items that require appraisal, if they were not appraised, the betrothal is not nullified, but rather it does not take effect until they are appraised. However, some of our Rabbis hold that if appraisal is required and it was not done, the betrothal is not valid at all.

However, some hold that there is no need for appraisal in any matter. And some say that even according to the Rambam, in a place where appraisal is needed, the subsequent appraisal does not help unless he betroths her anew. Rather, he means to say: in a matter that does not require appraisal, we do not say that it should be appraised and then he should betroth her since it does not require appraisal. But in a place where appraisal is required — it should be appraised and then he should betroth her, and if he betrothed her without appraisal, the subsequent appraisal does not help.

However, it is certain that in a case where an item requiring appraisal was not appraised initially but was later appraised, and then he consecrated her anew—she is betrothed, even though he did not take the item back [Rashba]. Also, if she was silent and did not say "yes," but did not throw the item from her hand—she is betrothed. This is not like being silent after the giving of money, for here, since she initially accepted it for the sake of betrothal, it is better than merely matchmaking [Beit Shmuel]. And we have already explained in Siman 27, Se'if 25 that this is not similar to the ambiguous expressions discussed there, where it is necessary to take the betrothal from her when consecrating her again; refer to it there.

There is an opinion that if one betrothed with stolen property, the betrothal is not valid as stated earlier in section 28, and if afterwards he purchased this item from the person he stole it from – the betrothal becomes valid from that moment as long as the item is still in the woman's possession [Beit Shmuel there, subsection 163, in the name of the Ritva]. However, according to the opinion of our Rabbis, it was explained that in a matter that requires evaluation and was not evaluated, the betrothal is not valid at all. Therefore, even in the case of theft followed by a purchase, the betrothal does not take effect [Beit Shmuel, subsection 1].

It seems to me that even according to the one who holds, in the opinion of the Rambam, that the betrothal takes effect once the item is evaluated as stated, nevertheless, in the case of theft followed by a purchase, they agree that the betrothal is not valid. For in the case of evaluation, the item is his, but she does not trust its value until it is evaluated, so it can be said that she trusts it once evaluated, and the betrothal takes effect. But in the case of theft, where the item was never his, how can the betrothal take effect later? There are no witnesses who saw the betrothal, for at the time the witnesses saw, there was no betrothal at all. How is this related to evaluation? I am bewildered by the opinion that holds that the betrothal takes effect later in the case of theft. This is not comparable to what is stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 374, regarding one who steals a field and sells it, and then purchases it from the original owner, where it is established that the field remains with the buyer. There, the reason is that the original owner prefers to maintain his credibility. But in the case of betrothal, this does not apply [Tosafot Kiddushin 63].

Even though in the case of betrothal, it is certainly preferred that the betrothal be valid, nevertheless, what does it help? As we have explained, even though there is no acquisition, it is like saying, "This field is acquired by you when I will purchase it," which does not help, as a person cannot transfer ownership of something that has not yet come into existence. The reason is due to the reliance of the mind, as explained there. But in the case of betrothal, which requires witnesses, it does not help. If the witnesses see that it was theft, there is no betrothal at all, and if they do not know, it is obvious that it does not help. Also, the other reasons we explained there do not apply at all in the case of betrothal.

And even in the case of theft where the owners have despaired, if the change of possession occurred before the despair, we explained in section 28, paragraph 10, that it does not help even according to the Rambam, who does not require the despair before the change of possession, since at the time of the betrothal, the item was not his [and so writes the Beit Shmuel there, subsection 4], and certainly in such a case.

It appears to me that none of the early authorities hold this view regarding theft. The statement that it is effective refers to a case where one enters his fellow's house and betroths a woman using the homeowner's property, and the homeowner subsequently says, "Go to the more beautiful ones," indicating that he is pleased with this. In such a case, they hold that since the homeowner revealed his intention retroactively, it is not considered theft, and the betrothal is valid from that point onward [as the Ritva wrote in Kiddushin 52]. However, in the case of outright theft, they do not hold this view. Even this ruling is not clear [as the Ritva concludes that in his opinion, this is not the case]. We have already explained in that section, paragraph 71, that even if he said so with complete sincerity, he must betroth her again afterward, as noted there [and what is written there in subsection 44 brings this in the name of the Ritva. However, his words there in subsections 43 and 53, and in this section, subsection 1, are not straightforward. The careful reader of the Ritva there will see that he does not hold this view for the law, and certainly not in the case of outright theft].

We have already explained the opinion of the Rambam that for items which a woman does not desire, an appraisal is necessary. Some of our Rabbis hold a different view in this matter: that for all items which most people are knowledgeable about their value and the money involved is small, an appraisal is not needed. However, for precious stones and pearls and the like, where most people are not knowledgeable about their value and sometimes make significant errors in their estimation, and he says to her, "Become betrothed to me with this precious stone worth fifty zuz" – an appraisal is necessary, for she does not rely on the fact that it is worth that much [Rosh]. According to this, there is only concern when he states its value, but if he betrothed her without specifying the value, there is no concern. Yet, some of our Rabbis hold that even without specifying the value, there is concern, for she does not rely on it, as she is always mistaken, even if he tells her that he is betrothing her with whatever its value might be; she thinks it is worth a lot and is mistaken in this. Therefore, in all cases, an appraisal is necessary [Ran in the name of R"T, and so it appears in Tosafot 9a. Otherwise, what is the objection from the garnet, and also according to the alternative opinion (7b) they also disagree about any amount, see there].

Our Rabbis have written that the reason the custom has developed to betroth with a ring that does not have a stone is because if it had a stone, it would require an appraisal, as mentioned. According to the opinion of the Rambam, they were not concerned, or it is possible that a ring without a stone is also something that the woman desires. Certainly, it is proper to fulfill even the great opinion of the Rambam and to betroth with something that the woman desires, and it is possible that this is why our teacher the Rema wrote in section 2 that under the chuppah, it is customary to ask the witnesses if the ring is worth a prutah so that the bride knows she is being betrothed with something worth a prutah, end quote. In this way, even according to the Rambam, it is satisfactory since they appraised the ring. However, in our country, it is not customary to ask the witnesses.

He also wrote that it is customary to cover the faces of modest brides who are not particular about what they are betrothed with, end quote. This means that by covering their faces, it is as if they are saying, "Betroth me with whatever you wish as long as it is worth a prutah." This custom is widespread throughout the country, and according to this, it is also satisfactory according to the Rambam. And even though according to this, why is it not customary among us to betroth with a ring that has a stone? It can be said that one cannot rely on this alone, because if she knows there is a stone, she will always be mistaken in her mind to think that it is worth a lot and the betrothal will not be valid according to the other Rabbis. As it is written in Choshen Mishpat section 227 regarding deception, even if one says "on condition that there is no deception," there is still deception if it is worth much more than stated, because one can say, "Since I saw it was worth more than you said, I knew you only said that to calm me." Therefore, the woman would also be mistaken about this even if the witnesses say it is only worth a prutah, and even if her face is covered and she appears not to be particular, as mentioned, this is beneficial according to the Rambam and the other Rabbis regarding all items. But with a ring with a valuable stone, every woman knows its high value, and these measures would not help according to the other Rabbis. She would still say that even though her face was covered, she knew it was worth a lot, and an appraisal would be needed before the betrothal. Therefore, the custom among us is to cover the bride's face and also not to betroth with a ring that has a valuable stone in order to satisfy all opinions.

And there is a significant question to ask here: After they cover the bride's face and the witnesses of the betrothal do not see whom he is betrothing, why do we not suspect that it is as if he is betrothing without witnesses? However, among us there is no concern about this, since it is known that this virgin was brought to the chuppah and it is established that she is indeed the one being betrothed, and we rely on presumptions [Even HaEzer]. Nevertheless, this is based on knowledge without direct sight, which is effective in monetary law as stated in Choshen Mishpat, end of section 30, but not in capital cases. And in divorce and betrothal, knowledge without direct sight is also effective since the witnesses of divorce and betrothal derive the principle from monetary law [there and Mekneh, section 42]. Furthermore, this is also considered a form of sight since she is later revealed, and everyone sees her, similar to if witnesses saw someone with a covered face committing murder—would they not be able to bring that person to court and testify against him [see Pitchei Teshuvah]? Additionally, this is considered actual sight when the entire body stands before the witnesses, as there is an inherent recognition of the body even without the facial features according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, as explained in section 17. Moreover, among us, when they give her to drink from the cup of betrothal before the betrothal, her form is necessarily revealed to some extent, and this is considered actual sight [so it appears to me]. [And the intention of the Maharit, who distinguishes between the sight of the betrothal and the sight of the woman, means her recognition, but there is sight, and this answers the question of Even HaEzer].

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: If he betrothed her with a ring that has a stone or with a plain ring and it was found to be made of copper, even though it is not customary to betroth in this manner, we still suspect the betrothal is valid. Even if the witnesses under the chuppah said it was gold and it was found to be copper, although from a legal standpoint it seems she is not betrothed, nonetheless, one should be stringent in practice, end quote. He wrote that therefore it is customary to ask the witnesses if the ring is of proper value and also to cover the bride's face as mentioned, because in such a case, even if it is found to be copper, there is no erroneous betrothal. There is no difference whether he betrothed her with a ring that is actually copper or with a gold ring that was found to be copper, as long as it is of proper value.

The explanation of his words is that according to our custom, all betrothals are considered valid in any case, and even without this, we suspect the betrothal is valid since he betrothed her with a ring without specifying its value. Even though the witnesses said it was gold, nonetheless, he did not deceive her but rather the witnesses deceived her. Indeed, there is no practical difference in this, and she can claim she relied on the witnesses, which is as if he himself deceived her. However, in practice, it is difficult to annul the betrothal without a get (divorce document). This is why Rabbi Moshe Isserles wrote that one should be stringent in practice even though from a legal standpoint it seems there is no betrothal. Nevertheless, according to the custom of covering her face, even from a legal standpoint, one should be concerned since it is as if she is saying she does not care. In any case, if someone else comes and betroths her, it seems she would need a get from the second as well since the witnesses explicitly said it was gold. And if he betrothed her plainly or with a ring that has a good stone – it is clear that she is fully betrothed according to our custom of covering her face.

And know that some have written that one should not betroth with a coin, and we have already explained in section 27 that this is not so.

Rambam of blessed memory wrote in Chapter 4, Law 19: If one betroths a woman with less than a perutah, she is not betrothed. If he betroths her with a utensil or food or something similar worth less than a perutah, she is doubtfully betrothed and requires a get out of doubt, for perhaps this item is worth a perutah elsewhere. From here you learn that anyone who betroths with an item of equivalent value, if it is worth a perutah in that city, it is a definite betrothal. If it is not worth a perutah, it is a doubtful betrothal. It seems to me that if he betroths her with a dish or vegetable that does not last, and similar items, if they are not worth a perutah in that place, she is not betrothed at all because this item will not reach another place before it spoils and loses its value and will not be worth a perutah. And one cannot say that even if it is worth a perutah elsewhere there is any concern, for the witnesses see that he betroths her with less than a perutah and it is like betrothing without witnesses. It can be said that since the witnesses also have this doubt, it is a betrothal with witnesses, as some say that Rambam holds that if it is known to be worth a perutah elsewhere for something that lasts, it is a definite betrothal. And it must be said that the witnesses also knew this, for otherwise it would be like betrothing without witnesses regarding definite betrothal. And some say that Rambam does not hold that it is a definite betrothal for reasons to be explained.

Some of our Rabbis have said that this concern that perhaps a perutah's worth exists elsewhere is not a Torah-level concern, because certainly in all transactions, only the place and time of the transaction as it stands there at that moment are considered. Even with respect to consecrated property, they said that consecration only applies in its place and time [Arakhin 24]. The reason for the stringency is that perhaps there is a person from this place for whom the name is worth a perutah, and if he sees that we are not concerned about the betrothal, they will also not be concerned in their place [Ran]. According to this, there is no difference between something that will spoil before reaching there and something that will not spoil. Furthermore, for this reason, even if there are witnesses that a perutah's worth exists elsewhere, the betrothal is not definite since it is not worth a perutah here, but it is a case of doubtful betrothal. And it is not like other doubts, but merely a stringency of the Rabbis. Also, according to the Rambam's reasoning, we should not ask why we are concerned about the doubt that it might be worth a perutah elsewhere and establish her presumption of being single. For it can be said that since an act of betrothal was performed with her, her presumption is weakened. Additionally, this is something that can be clarified, and we do not rely on a presumption.

There is an opinion that explains the reasoning of the Rambam, that the sanctification (of marriage) is valid when the item is worth a perutah (minimal value) in another place. Since it is worth a perutah in another place, it is as if she says, "To me, this is worth a perutah" [see Ran, Beit Shmuel, and what I wrote in paragraph 1, and it is correct]. And even though we wrote in paragraph 1 that even if she says "to me, this is worth a perutah," it is still doubtful, this is when it is not known if it is worth a perutah in another place. But when it is known, she can say so [Beit Shmuel]. And one should not say, "How do we know she agrees to accept it as worth a perutah?" Certainly, she does, since she accepted it for the sake of marriage, and everyone knows that a woman does not get married for less than a perutah, it is assumed that she accepted it as a perutah since it is worth a perutah in another place [Avnei Miluim]. 

And regarding what we wrote in paragraph 11 that the witnesses also need to know that it is worth a perutah in another place, some say that this is not necessary, since the witnesses before us see with what she is being sanctified, and in a place of high value, there are witnesses that this item is worth a perutah. We should not consider the witnesses before us as testifying about half a matter, since they testify about everything they saw, and they cannot see more, just as three sets of witnesses combine to establish a chazakah (presumption) in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 145 [Beit Meir, and see Avnei Miluim]. 

In my opinion, the main point is as I wrote in paragraph 11, that this is not similar to the case there, where the witnesses do not contradict each other. But here, according to the witnesses before us, there is no sanctification, and what is the use of having witnesses at a distance who say that it is worth a perutah there [and what the Avnei Miluim wrote in subparagraph 7 is not understood].

And one should not ask how it is possible to say that the reason is that it is as if she says, "To me, it is like money," for if so, we should say the same for something that does not last. Why, then, did the Rambam differentiate between something that lasts and something that does not last? It can be said that indeed this is so, as stated in section 1, that this matter is not within the capability to make money from something that is not money at all, as mentioned there. Consequently, regarding something that spoils before it reaches there, it is not money at all.

There are those who are uncertain regarding the opinions of the poskim who hold that even if a perutah's worth (a small coin) in another place is not considered a valid Torah-level kiddushin (betrothal), and some hold this view even regarding the Rambam, as mentioned at the end of section 11. The reasoning is that one must consider the specific time and place. If the woman needs to travel immediately to the place where the perutah's worth is valid, the question arises whether the kiddushin is valid according to all opinions, or if even in such a case it is only considered a doubtful kiddushin. From the language of the earlier authorities, it seems that in any case it is not considered a definite kiddushin. 

Even though in the case of ma'aser sheni (second tithe) it is established that a woman cannot be betrothed with it because it is considered sacred property, as stated in Siman 28, section 86, if not for this reason, the Talmud states that she could be betrothed with it. Ma'aser sheni has no value in the province until it is brought to Jerusalem, but nevertheless, the kiddushin takes effect immediately when she is betrothed with it in the province. This is because its primary mitzvah is to be eaten in Jerusalem, and when she is betrothed with ma'aser sheni, she knows she must go to Jerusalem to consume it. This is similar to betrothing a woman on a fast day with food, even though it has no current value, she accepts it knowing she will eat it in the evening and understands the necessity. Similarly, with ma'aser sheni, everyone will pay a perutah for it because they know it can be eaten in Jerusalem. However, an item that is not a perutah's worth here will not have anyone willing to pay a perutah for it, even if it is worth a perutah elsewhere. 

Therefore, the practical ruling is to be stringent in all cases and consider such a kiddushin as doubtful.

There are those who say that if one betrothed with an etrog that is not worth a perutah, but only because of its mitzvah value it is worth a perutah – she is not betrothed [Birkei Yosef in the name of Maggid Mishneh], and there are those who are uncertain about this. It seems to me that certainly if for all of Israel it is worth a perutah because of its mitzvah value and it is sold in the market for a perutah – she is definitely betrothed, for what difference does it make if its value is because it is needed for eating or because it is needed for a mitzvah; in the end, it is worth a perutah. And if for everyone it is not worth a perutah even because of the mitzvah because it is very common, and for her it is worth a perutah because she says, "To me it is worth a perutah because of the mitzvah," if she truly cannot obtain another for the mitzvah – it is certainly better than a Kohen who says, "To me it is worth five selaim" as we brought in section 1, even though for everyone it is not worth a perutah. However, if she can also obtain another but says that for her, because of the preciousness of the mitzvah, it is worth a perutah – it seems like the first opinion that she is not betrothed, for the value of a mitzvah is not considered money, for even a superior mitzvah is not called money compared to a non-superior one if it cannot be sold at a higher price [as proven in Bava Kamma 78b, and see Pitchei Teshuvah section 1 who compared this to what Chacham Tzvi said, but according to my words this is not a comparison, and the main proof of the great ones from Rambam at the end of chapter 4 of Mamrim was rejected by Noda Biyhuda in section 67 with good reasoning, see there. Nevertheless, it seems to me that the law is as I wrote, but in practice, it requires further investigation].

It is clear that the concern that it might be worth a prutah (minimal value coin) elsewhere applies only when it was sanctified without specification. However, if he told her that this item is worth a prutah and it turns out that it is not worth a prutah here, even though it might be worth a prutah elsewhere, she is not betrothed. For even if he said it was worth one hundred maneh (large sum of money) and it turns out to be worth less, she is not betrothed. There is no doubt about this. Nevertheless, there are those who have doubts about this, and it requires further investigation [see Pischei Teshuvah, subsection 6].

In regards to the concern that perhaps it (something) has a status of a permitted entity in another place, even though there are some early authorities who ruled that we do not worry about this [Bahag], nevertheless, all our early authorities and the Geonim ruled that we do worry about this. Therefore, this opinion is not mentioned at all in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, and even if it is in a distant place where it is permitted, we are concerned about it [as mentioned in the Gemara]. There is no distinction between whether it can be sustained or not, as we have explained that according to most of the early authorities, this is a rabbinic concern and there is no distinction in this regard. Even according to the Rambam, it only applies when it is absolutely impossible for it to be sustained in any way. However, a fresh fig that can be dried and transported – even according to the Rambam, we are concerned about it [Beit Yosef], and likewise with anything similar. However, regarding something that by all appearances is not considered permitted in any place, there is no need to be concerned about it, especially since according to most authorities this is only a rabbinic concern, and practically, this requires careful consideration.

The statement that she is doubtfully betrothed because perhaps this matter is worth a perutah elsewhere means that she needs a get (divorce document) to permit her to marry others. If he wants to maintain the marriage, she needs another kiddushin (betrothal). Even if it is known that the item is worth a perutah elsewhere, since according to most authorities, this is only rabbinic kiddushin. Some say that there is no need for another kiddushin, just like with the kiddushin of a minor, which are rabbinic, and when she grows up, he consummates the marriage with intercourse, and the same applies here. However, with the concern that perhaps it is worth a perutah elsewhere, these are not even fully rabbinic kiddushin, but merely a concern. Even though the reason for a minor is that a person knows that from the Torah, a minor's kiddushin is nothing, so when he consummates the marriage when she grows up, he does so for the sake of kiddushin, here too, a person knows that kiddushin worth less than a perutah are not Torah kiddushin and will consummate for the sake of kiddushin. Some say that in any case, there is no need for another kiddushin because even in the case of mistaken kiddushin, there is no need to remarry, as intercourse acquires and there is no need for another kiddushin. This is not the opinion of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, and it is also written in Siman 42 that in the case of doubtful kiddushin, he must remarry, see there. Furthermore, regarding what we wrote that a person knows that a woman cannot be betrothed for less than a perutah, there is a dispute in the Gemara about this, and therefore, in any case, he should remarry initially, because according to the Rambam, this entire matter is doubtful kiddushin, and it is obvious that according to the Ba'al HaMaor he needs another kiddushin.

When betrothing her anew, it is necessary to betroth her with a whole prutah, and we do not say that the amount less than a prutah from before can be combined to reach a prutah, for they do not combine with each other according to the majority of authorities. The initial betrothals are considered rabbinic betrothal and the money belongs to her, and she does not need to return it to him as stated in Siman 50. Therefore, she has already acquired it. Only according to the Rambam, who considers it doubtful betrothal and the betrothal returns as stated there, can they be combined. However, if the earlier amounts have already been consumed, it is considered a loan and they do not combine. [Avnei Nezer]

If another man comes and marries her with complete kiddushin (betrothal) - the first man should divorce her, and the second man should marry her. However, the second man should not divorce her and the first man marry her, as a decree lest people say that it is permissible to remarry one's divorced wife after she has been married to another. Because once the rumor spreads that the first man betrothed her and then the second man betrothed her and she returned, they will say that the first man divorced her, the second man married her, divorced her, and then the first man remarried her. And even though it was explained in Siman 10 regarding the betrothal of a deaf-mute, that since it is only Rabbinic, they were not stringent with this decree, this is because a deaf-mute does not have any Torah-level kiddushin at all. But in a case where there is Torah-level kiddushin, even though in these kiddushin there is no Torah-level kiddushin, nevertheless we decree, as it is written there in S'if 4 regarding a minor, see there [and this also resolves the question of the Beit Shmuel, S'if 9].

And this, that she is permitted to the second [man]—specifically if the second did not have relations with her before the divorce from the first [husband]. But if he did have relations with her, she becomes prohibited to the first [husband] as is the law for a married woman who committed adultery, and consequently she is also prohibited to the second [man]. For just as she is prohibited to the husband, so too she is prohibited to the adulterer. And although the main issue with the first [man] is only rabbinic according to most authorities, nevertheless it is judged as in the case of Torah-level marriages, as we wrote in section 46: when a rumor arose that she is married, even though the rumor was not substantiated by witnesses. See there. And it is not specifically that he had relations with her, but even if he secluded himself with her, we say "these are the witnesses of seclusion, these are the witnesses of relations" [see there in Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 18]. And the general rule is that in any case where she requires a get from both [men], we judge it similarly. And some say further that even if she married the second [man] based on the ruling of a sage, she is prohibited to both this one and that one. And even if we say in cases of doubtful betrothal that if she marries another she does not need to leave him, because the child is presumed permissible, as we establish her status as single and it is not comparable to cases of two against two witnesses where we rule she must leave, this doubt is more severe than doubt in betrothal [see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 10]. The reason is that since the matter of betrothal was present, but the doubt is in its validity, her presumption is weakened as we wrote in section 30, paragraph 15. And some are lenient in this [see Even HaEzer, subparagraph 12]. The main ruling follows the first opinion, as Rabbi Rema ruled in paragraph 4, but from what we wrote in section 17, paragraph 262, it is clear that it is according to the lenient opinion. See there.

Nevertheless, regarding the child born from the second husband before the first husband divorced her – the child is legitimate, and he (the second husband) is obligated to divorce her. Since the first marriage is only a concern due to the possibility that a perutah (a small coin) was worth more in another place, we do not consider the child from the second husband to be a mamzer (illegitimate). This is unlike the case where the sages penalized a woman who heard that her husband had died, married another man, and then it turned out that her first husband was still alive, in which case the child is a mamzer from both (men). In that situation, they penalized her because she married while still technically married to her first husband, and she should have been more careful, as stated in Siman 17. Therefore, if it indeed becomes known that there was a perutah's worth in another place, and certainly if it becomes clarified that there was a perutah's worth in another place, the children from the second husband are considered doubtful mamzerim. However, without this, even according to the Rambam, as some interpret his words to mean that it is a doubtful betrothal, there is no Torah prohibition, and the children are legitimate. Even if it becomes known that there was a perutah's worth in another place, at the time of the betrothal it was not known to the witnesses, and it is like a betrothal without witnesses. But if, at the time of the betrothal, it was known to the witnesses, then indeed the children are doubtful mamzerim, as I have written in section 26.

If the second man also betrothed her with something worth less than a perutah, she is permitted to the first man and does not require a get from the second man in any case. If it is worth a perutah in another place, then she is betrothed to the first man, and if not, neither betrothal is valid. If she received a get from the second man, she is forbidden to his relatives as it is written in Siman 15 that in any case where she received a get, even if it is unnecessary, this is the law, and thus she is forbidden to the first man. If the second man betrothed her with something else worth less than a perutah, she requires a get from the second man according to the law, as it could be that the first man's item is not worth a perutah in another place and the second man's is. Some say that in such a case, she is permitted to the first man and we do not concern ourselves with the get of the second man, as in Siman 46 where there was a rumor of betrothal from this one and that one. Similarly, in this case, according to the same logic, all the more so in the first case where the second man betrothed her with the same item with which the first man betrothed her, she is permitted to the first man. Even according to the Rambam, who considers it a doubtful Torah prohibition, nevertheless he holds that a doubtful Torah matter is lenient according to Torah law. Although she is certainly forbidden to his relatives so that people will not say he is marrying the relative of his divorcee, and she is also forbidden to his relatives as per Siman 15, nevertheless, to return to him, there is no concern that people will say he is remarrying his divorcee after she married someone else. However, it is not similar to Siman 46 where it was just a rumor and people will say that it was clarified that the rumor was false, but here there was an actual betrothal, just not worth a perutah, so it can be said that it is more severe. Nevertheless, there is no clear proof for this, and since the main ruling here is a rabbinic doubt according to most authorities, it is possible to be lenient in this matter.

Rabbeinu Meir HaLevi, as cited by the Tur, writes: If one betroths with something about which we do not know now whether it was worth a perutah at the time of betrothal or not, we follow the current value. If it is worth a perutah now, the betrothal is certainly valid until it becomes clarified by witnesses that it was not worth a perutah at the time of betrothal. And if it is possible to clarify through witnesses that it was worth a perutah at the time of betrothal, we are concerned about their testimony and do not permit her [to marry another] even if the witnesses are very far away. Not only if it is known that there are witnesses who know, but even if a rumor spreads that there are witnesses who know it was worth a perutah, we are concerned about it. However, we do not prohibit her based on the testimony of a woman or a relative who says they knew it was worth a perutah at that time.

And we are concerned about the rumor even when it has not been confirmed in a court of law [Beit Yosef], and even though any rumor that has not been confirmed in a court is considered nothing, as we wrote in Siman 46, this applies to a rumor concerning the essence of the betrothal. However, when the betrothal is certain and the doubt is about its validity, we are concerned [so it appears to me]. And also regarding the doubt of mamzerut (illegitimacy) mentioned in Siman 23, it applies even to a rumor not confirmed in court, for the reason we explained. And if the matter now is not public knowledge and we do not know how it was at the time of the betrothal, it is automatically a doubtful betrothal, for even if at the time of the betrothal it was not publicly known, we are still concerned that it might have been known elsewhere. The general principle is that we should never worry that the transaction changed at the time of the betrothal from what we see now, and we follow the present state [Choshen Mishpat 11].

There is an opinion that in transactions we do not follow the present value, because transactions are always subject to change, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 227, Se'if 12. According to this, even if the current value is not a perutah, it is not definitely a valid kiddushin (marriage), because if she is betrothed to another afterward, she would not need a get (divorce document) from the first one, since it is definite that she needs a get because perhaps it wasn't worth a perutah at the time of the kiddushin. However, it seems to me that the primary opinion follows the simple understanding of the Tur, that we follow the present value. And although market prices tend to change, nevertheless, since the majority of people do not betroth with less than a perutah, it is sufficient for us to say that if the current value is less than a perutah, we should be concerned that maybe at the time of kiddushin it was also not worth a perutah. But if the current value is a perutah, we should not be concerned that at the time of kiddushin it was not a perutah, as it is evident that we rely on the present status supported by the majority. 

A proof for this is from what we hold in Siman 37 regarding a girl who betrothed herself in the evening of the day she transitions from na'arah (young girl) to bogeret (mature girl), and her father betrothed her in the morning, that the father's kiddushin is not valid, because there is no contradictory presumption, we follow the present status since she is a bogeret now, and in the morning she was also a bogeret. All the more so when there is a majority that supports the current status. And although the presumption of being unmarried contradicts the current status, the majority is preferable to the presumption. 

And the reason we do not follow the presumption in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 251, regarding a gift from someone on their deathbed where the giver claims they were on their deathbed and the receiver claims they were healthy, and the burden of proof is on the receiver even if the giver is now healthy, is because of the presumption of ownership that the giver has. It cannot be said that here too there is a presumption of ownership if we say it was worth less than a perutah and the money should return to him, because less than a perutah is not considered money, and additionally, we have already explained that the kiddushin is not retracted. However, from the language of our master Beit Yosef in the Bedek HaBayit, it also seems that it is not a definite kiddushin. Further investigation is needed for the ruling, and all the more so if he betrothed her with an item and told her it was worth a maneh (100 zuz) and it was not appraised at the time, and afterward it was appraised whether it was found to be worth a maneh or not, it is considered doubtful kiddushin.

It is self-evident that when one betroths a woman with three or four items, each of which individually is not worth a perutah, but together they are worth a perutah, if he betroths her with all of them, she is betrothed. However, if he says, "Be betrothed to me with one of them," she is not betrothed, only in a state of doubtful betrothal, perhaps one of them is worth a perutah elsewhere, as previously mentioned. Even if he betroths her with all of them but betroths her with each one individually, they do not combine, because he divided the act of betrothal among each one. Therefore, if a man says to a woman, "Be betrothed to me with this date, be betrothed to me with this one, be betrothed to me with this one," if one of them is worth a perutah, she is betrothed; if not, she is not betrothed, only in a state of doubtful betrothal, perhaps one date is worth a perutah elsewhere. But if he said to her, "Be betrothed to me with this one and this one and this one," they all combine, so if together they are worth a perutah, she is betrothed; if not, she is not betrothed, only in a state of doubtful betrothal, as previously mentioned.

And it is explained from this that when one says "with this one and this one and this one," it is as if he combined them together, similar to when he says, "Be betrothed to me with these." And so wrote Rambam in Chapter 5, Law 27. And although in Chapter 7 of Shevuot he ruled that when one swears an oath "I owe you nothing, nor you, nor you," it is as if he specified each one separately, and similarly in an oath "I owe you nothing of wheat, barley, and spelt," and he ruled similarly in Chapter 4 of Nedarim, however, Rambam holds that even though this language specifies each one separately, nonetheless, this language also includes them together, and when there is not a perutah in each one, we say that his intention is to include them all together. Especially in betrothal, where it does not take effect with less than a perutah, it is certain that his intention was to include them all together. Only when there is a perutah in each one do we say that it tends more to specify than to include. And so it is explicitly in the Jerusalem Talmud Kiddushin Chapter 2, Halacha 1, and in the Jerusalem Talmud Shevuot Chapter 5, Halacha 4. And although it does not seem so in our Talmud (46a), Rambam held that even in our Talmud there is someone who disagrees with this (Shevuot 38a, where Rabbi Yochanan says that a perutah from all of them combines, meaning also in wheat, barley, and spelt when there is not a perutah in each one, Rabbi Yochanan says so there in the Jerusalem Talmud and disagrees with Rabbah there, resolving the difficulties of Kesef Mishneh, Lechem Mishneh, Beis Shmuel, and others. Note this well).

Sometimes, even when a man says, "Be betrothed to me with this one and this one and this one," they do not combine to equal a perutah (the minimal value for betrothal), for example, if she eats each one as he gives it to her until she finishes them all as he concludes his words. Since the betrothal is not completed until she receives them all, and she has already eaten them before they were acquired for her betrothal, therefore all the dates until the last one are considered a loan to her. This is not comparable to one who says to a woman, "Be betrothed to me after thirty days," where she is betrothed even if the money was consumed, as stated in Siman 40, since it is not considered a loan because he gave it to her for betrothal and she consumed her own property. But here, since the betrothal is not completed until the last one, it is considered a loan, except for the last one, which is not considered a loan because at the time she ate it, the betrothal was already completed, and she consumed her own property. Therefore, if the last one is worth a perutah, she is betrothed; otherwise, she is not betrothed except in doubt. Even if all the previous ones before the last one are each worth a perutah, we do not say that his intention was for the first ones and that he is betrothing with a loan, for it has already been explained in Siman 29 that one who betroths with a loan and a perutah, his intention is on the perutah.

But if he did not say to her, "Be betrothed to me with this one and this one and this one," but rather said to her, "Be betrothed to me with these," and she ate them one by one, they all combine to form the value of a perutah, including those she ate, because since he completed all the words of the betrothal before he gave her anything, therefore, immediately when he gave her the first one under the context of betrothal, it came to her hand, and she ate from what was hers. Similarly, if he said, "With this one and this one and this one," and completed all his words before she accepted them all, they combine even if she ate them one by one for the reason explained, since he completed the words of the betrothal before giving her anything, it is as if she eats what is hers. Some say that we require that all be handed to her before she eats anything, but if he handed her the first one and she ate it, and then handed her the second one and she ate it, and so on, they do not combine even if he completed his speech before she ate anything, because the main completion of the betrothal is in her receiving it in her hand. As long as they have not come to her hand, it is like a loan one by one. However, when he said, "Be betrothed to me with these," even if she ate the first ones before he handed her the last one, they still combine because he did not divide them in his speech—they are all as one. Yet, some disagree even in this <small>[Shach]</small>. The first opinion holds that the main thing depends on the completion of his speech, and when his speech is completed, they all become hers, and she eats from what is hers, even if she did not receive them all at once and ate them one by one <small>[See the Vilna Gaon, note 14]</small>.

If one betroths half a woman, she is not betrothed, as it is written, "When a man takes a wife" (Deuteronomy 22:13), and not half a wife. Therefore, if he says to her, "Half of you is betrothed to me," she is not betrothed. And even though betrothal is a term of sanctification and in the case of sanctification, we hold that if someone says, "Half of the animal is an offering," the sanctification extends to the whole animal, as Rambam writes in the fifteenth chapter of Hilchot Korbanot, nonetheless, here we cannot say this, since she has to consent to be betrothed to him, and if she does not wish to be wholly betrothed to him, how can the betrothal extend to her entirety [Gemara]. However, if he says to her, "Be betrothed to half of me," she is betrothed, for his intention is not to half of his body but rather to mean that he will take another wife, as a man is permitted to marry two wives according to Torah law. And although after the enactment of Rabbenu Gershom it is forbidden to marry two wives, nevertheless, the betrothal is valid, as it is not worse than those who are prohibited by negative commandments, whose betrothal is valid. But a woman cannot be married to two men [Gemara]. It seems to me that if he explicitly says, "I am only betrothing you to half of my body and not to all of it," she is not betrothed, and in his case, the sanctification cannot extend to his whole being, for she is betrothed to him and not he to her, as she becomes forbidden to all men like holy property and not he to all women by Torah law, as explained. Nevertheless, in practice, it requires further investigation, as I have not found this ruling explicitly mentioned in any of the decisors. And all the more so, if he says to a woman, "Behold, you are betrothed to me and to Shimon," she is not betrothed. And if he says, "Half of you is betrothed to me," even if he later says, "The other half of you is also betrothed to me," it is as if he said nothing [Chazon Ish], as when he stated it in two separate times, his statement is interrupted, and neither part takes effect. However, if he says at once, "Half of you and half of you," there is a doubt concerning the betrothal, as will be explained.

The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 3: If he said to her, "Half of you is betrothed to me with a perutah and the other half with a perutah," or if he said to her, "Half of you is betrothed to me with half a perutah and the other half with half a perutah," she is betrothed.
