If he said to her, "Half of you is betrothed to me with a perutah today and the other half with a perutah tomorrow," or "Both halves of you with a perutah," or "Your two daughters to my two sons with a perutah," or "Your daughter is betrothed to me and your cow is sold to me with a perutah," or "Your daughter and your land to me with a perutah" – in all these cases, she is doubtfully betrothed. And many of our Rabbis disagree with him regarding his ruling that if he said "Half of you with a perutah and half of you with a perutah" or "Half of you with half a perutah and half of you with half a perutah," she is certainly betrothed, as "both halves of you with a perutah" is preferable to this, which he said in one statement, and nonetheless it is doubtful, and certainly in such cases, it is only doubtful betrothal. Additionally, the language of the Talmud that states a woman is not betrothed in halves implies in all forms. Therefore, they ruled that even in these cases, it is only doubtful betrothal. Similarly, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch ruled in section 7 there, and in practice, we follow the majority of decisors. However, the Rambam's reasoning is that certainly a woman is not betrothed in halves, but when he says "Half of you and half of you," his intention is not to betroth her in halves but rather he is enumerating and proceeding [gradually] <small>[Ran]</small>, and this reasoning is found in the Talmud. This is akin to saying "I betroth your head, your hand, your foot, and all your limbs," where it cannot be said that he is betrothing her in halves but rather enumerating all her limbs. This is unlike saying "Both halves of you with a perutah," where, by including them in one statement and yet dividing them, it is possible that his intention is to betroth her in halves. And regarding his ruling that "Half of you today and half of you tomorrow" is doubtful, it is because it can be said that anything not betrothed in one day, even if said in one time, interrupts the matter and is considered betrothal in halves <small>[there]</small>.

Some of our Rabbis have said that the case of "half of you and half of you" being a doubtful betrothal only applies when he uses the language of engagement or other expressions that are effective for betrothal. However, if he uses the language of betrothal, she is certainly betrothed. The reason is that it has been explained in section 32 why we do not say that when someone says "half of you is betrothed to me," the betrothal should extend to the whole of her, just as it does with sacrifices, because it also depends on her consent. This only applies when he says "half of you," but when he says "half of you and half of you," and she agrees to be fully betrothed, the betrothal extends to the entire part of her from the first half. However, all the decisors do not differentiate in this matter, and the reason might be that it is possible that at the time he said "half of you," she did not consent to be fully betrothed, and only afterward, when he said "and half of you," she consented to the second half. According to this, when he says "both halves of you" with a prutah and uses the language of betrothal, it is effective. Similarly, if she says that at the time of the first half she consented to be fully betrothed, it is effective. However, this does not seem to be the opinion of the decisors.

But in truth, this is not necessary, as the reason given there—that it depends on her consent—is not sufficient. For ultimately, since she also consents to half, we would say that her sanctity extends to all of her. Rather, the main reason is that since by his speech the sanctification does not extend to all of her but only due to her consent, it becomes a sanctification because of her and not because of him. It turns out that she sanctifies herself to him, and the Torah says that he shall sanctify her, not that she sanctifies herself to him [Beit Shmuel in the name of Maharit, and likewise wrote the Rashba]. And although in all marriages her consent is necessary—for certainly it is so that without her consent it is impossible to sanctify her—nonetheless, he sanctifies her entirely, which is not the case with the phrase "half of you," where he only sanctifies half of her, and this is not a valid sanctification. And although by his speech the sanctification could extend to all of her, he cannot do so because it also depends on her. It turns out that by his speech he did not sanctify her [and the Avnei Miluim's objection to this is unfounded]. According to this, in any language of halves, even if we say that she consents to all of it, nonetheless, since by his words it is only in halves and depends on her, it turns out that by his speech he did not sanctify her [and Tosafot Rid, cited by the Avnei Miluim, in siman 18, answers to differentiate between two opinions. If split into one opinion, it is difficult to differentiate, and perhaps their intention is similar to what was mentioned].

Some of our rabbis say that when it is stated "half of you today and half of you tomorrow," it is at least a doubtful betrothal. This is when he said it to her at one time, meaning in one continuous statement. However, if he said to her "half of you today" and nothing more, and after some time said to her "half of you tomorrow" — it is obvious that this is not a betrothal. This is also implied by the language of the Talmud and the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). Similarly, when one says "half of you with half a prutah and half of you with half a prutah" or "half of you with a prutah and half of you with a prutah," it refers to a case where he gave her the entire prutah or the two prutot at once and said it to her in one continuous statement. But when he divided them into two separate givings and two separate times, it is nothing. It is necessary for the second statement to be made within the time frame of "toch k'dei dibbur" (the time it takes to say a greeting) to the first. There is someone who wants to say that it must be immediate, but if not immediate, even if said within "toch k'dei dibbur," it does not help, because we hold that in betrothal, "toch k'dei dibbur" is not considered as one continuous statement in regard to retraction. This does not seem correct, because all these cases are doubts, and the rule that we hold "toch k'dei dibbur" is not considered as one continuous statement is for stringency and not for leniency, and what practical difference does this make?

And this, that he wrote "your two daughters to my two sons for a perutah" — the doubt is whether we follow the giver and the receiver and there is monetary value, or perhaps we follow the betrothed and the ones being betrothed and there is not a perutah for each one. It refers to young daughters where the betrothal is by the father, but if they are adults and appointed the father as an agent to receive their betrothal, it is obvious that a perutah is needed for each. The agent is not superior to the sender. Even though sons are not under the father’s authority and necessarily appointed their father as an agent, and there is no perutah given by each, nevertheless, the giver does not need to be concerned as long as the receiver receives a perutah. Some say this is only when the father gives the money on their behalf, making him one giver, but if the two sons gave the father a single perutah to betroth for them, this is not betrothal, as one does not betroth with less than a perutah. However, when the father gives a perutah, we consider it as if each of them gave a perutah, and since the receiver has a perutah and the giver also gave a perutah, it is a doubtful betrothal. Therefore, this can also be found with adult daughters, such as when they said "Give the betrothal money to our father and we will be betrothed to them," which works by the law of a guarantor, as mentioned in Siman 29. Moreover, in such a case, it might be certain betrothal even if we say we follow the ones being betrothed, since by the law of a guarantor, it is as if each received a full perutah. This requires further study for the law, but in practice, we are stringent, and it is considered a doubtful betrothal.

Some of our rabbis say that in the case of "your two daughters to my two sons," where it is a doubt whether it constitutes a valid betrothal, this only applies when it has been specified to whom each daughter is betrothed, such as Rachel to Reuven and Leah to Shimon. Otherwise, it would be a betrothal that is not fit for consummation [Tosafot]. And even though we hold that a betrothal that is not fit for consummation is still considered a betrothal, as mentioned in Siman 41, nevertheless, in this case, since each of the sons appointed the father as an agent to give the betrothal on his behalf, it is certain that his intention was for a betrothal fit for consummation. Otherwise, it would be a deviation from the agency [Maggid Mishneh, Chapter 7]. According to this, if both sons said to the father, "Betroth for us the two daughters of so-and-so," it would be a valid betrothal. There is, however, an opinion that implies that in any case where the betrothal is not fit for consummation, it would still be a valid betrothal. Therefore, in practice, it is considered a doubtful betrothal [see Beit Shmuel, Section 16, who wrote that Tosafot wrote according to Rava], and see what I wrote in Siman 35, Section 53.

And with "your daughter and your cow for a perutah" there is uncertainty. Do we say that his intention is to give half a perutah for your daughter and half a perutah for your cow – and she is not betrothed? Or perhaps your daughter is betrothed with a perutah and your cow through pulling (meshichah), for he knows that less than a perutah cannot betroth a woman [Rashi], and presumably that is his intention even though his wording does not imply this. Additionally, movable property is not acquired with money but only with pulling [Tosafot]. Similarly, with "your daughter and your land for a perutah" there is the same uncertainty as with the cow, and although land is acquired with money, because of the first reason there is still doubt. Therefore, if he said, "your daughter and your cow for two perutot" – it is definitely betrothal because there is a perutah for the daughter, and although the cow is not acquired with money, she is betrothed, for we hold "acquire you and a donkey," where half is acquired, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 190, look there. All the more so if it is "your daughter and your land for two perutot" she is betrothed. [See Beit Shmuel, Se'if 17, and his words are puzzling for we hold that half is acquired as stated, and it can be reconciled according to the words of the Ran brought in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 41, Se'if 4, look there and examine it well.]

Some of our Rabbis hold that the case of uncertain betrothal with "your daughter and your cow for a prutah" or "your daughter and your land" applies when he has taken possession of the cow or the land. In such a case, one might say that the entire prutah is for the betrothal. However, if he did not take possession or hold onto them, it is obvious that the prutah is for both and she is not betrothed at all. Nevertheless, it is proper to be stringent. And all the legal authorities did not mention this, for if at the time of giving the prutah he took possession or held onto them, it is clear that his intention was that the prutah should be for the betrothal. If he took possession or held onto them afterward, there is doubt about his intention at the time of the betrothal. Therefore, if he has not yet taken possession or held onto them, perhaps he will still do so. Additionally, perhaps at the time of the betrothal his intention was to take possession or hold onto them but he has now changed his mind. Even if we say that if he took possession or held onto them at the time of the act, it would be an uncertain betrothal and not definite, for maybe his intention was to acquire the cow or the land with half a prutah and by taking possession or holding onto them, then even if he did not take possession or hold onto them, perhaps his intention was so at the time of the act, and now he has changed his mind. In any case, the doubt remains unresolved. Additionally, it is possible that if we follow the recipient who betroths with half a prutah since the prutah came into the recipient's possession, as in the case of "your two daughters for my two sons" that has been explained, even though there is a distinction, there is still doubt in this matter.

The Sages taught: If one betroths two women with a perutah's worth or one woman with less than a perutah's worth, even if he sent gifts afterward – she is not betrothed. We do not say that he knew his betrothal was invalid and therefore sent gifts for the sake of betrothal (Rashi). Rather, we say he sent them because of the initial betrothal, and there is not even a doubt of betrothal unless there is a concern that it might be worth a perutah elsewhere, such as if he betrothed her with money, which by Torah law requires the value of half a barleycorn, and all the more so if he betrothed her with a coin or according to the Rambam with something that does not endure. Even in a place where they are concerned about gifts, as mentioned in Siman 45, nevertheless here we are not concerned, because the gifts were sent for the previous betrothal. (See Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 20, where he quotes the Bedek HaBayit that with money less than half a barleycorn, even if it is worth a lot, it is nothing. The Beit Yosef there wrote in a language of possibility, and the matter needs investigation for the halacha).

Even though with gifts we do not worry about betrothal, nevertheless, if he betrothed her with less than a perutah and then cohabited with her in the presence of witnesses of seclusion - she needs a get (divorce document). Thus, our Sages said [Ketubot 74a]: "If one betroths with a loan and cohabits, with a condition and cohabits, with less than a perutah and cohabits - she needs a get from him because a person does not make his cohabitation promiscuous and he intended to cohabit for the sake of betrothal." Therefore, it is not comparable to gifts. And from the language of the Rambam in the seventh chapter, it is implied that with less than a perutah and with a loan it is definitely betrothal. Similarly, from the language of our teacher the Beit Yosef here in section 9, who wrote that she needs a get, it is evident that he certainly intended to cohabit for the sake of betrothal. According to this, if another man came and betrothed her, she does not need a get from him. However, many of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) hold that this is only doubtful betrothal, and if another man betrothed her, she needs a get from both of them.

It is surprising regarding our teacher the Beit Yosef, who in his book Kesef Mishneh wrote there that even according to the Rambam it is not definite betrothal, and here he ruled that it is definite betrothal. Similarly, in his major work, it is surprising regarding our teacher the Rema, who wrote here: "And the same applies to a minor who betrothed and grew up with her, she needs a get because he certainly cohabited for the sake of betrothal when he matured." Even though there are no witnesses to his seclusion or his cohabitation [Gra], since they lived together as husband and wife, it is considered as witnesses as stated in section 26, and it will be further explained in section 43. Earlier in section 28, the Rema himself wrote in section 16 that with less than a perutah and cohabited, it is doubtful betrothal. But here he compares it to a minor who grew up, which is certainly betrothal when they lived as husband and wife.

For practical halacha, the later authorities concluded that with less than a perutah and cohabited, it is doubtful betrothal. Even if she secluded herself with him and we do not know that he cohabited, she needs a get, because we say that the same witnesses of seclusion are the same witnesses of cohabitation [Beit Shmuel]. I think to reconcile the words of our teachers, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, that certainly if he betrothed her with less than a perutah and cohabited once by chance, she needs a get out of doubt. Here, we are discussing a case where he betrothed her and cohabited with her as husband and wife, in which case it is clear that it is definite betrothal since he knew that he betrothed her with less than a perutah. This is also implied from the words of our teacher the Rema, who wrote that specifically in such a case where everyone knows that the betrothal of a minor or with less than a perutah is nothing, therefore he cohabited for the sake of betrothal. But in a place where there is a mistake, other betrothal is needed. This is explained in the source of the law [Teshubot Maimonides] in a case of a man who had several sons from his wife, and in the end, it was discovered that the betrothal ring was not worth a perutah. They ruled that he needs to betroth her again, because since he did not know that other betrothal was needed, it did not occur to him to betroth her with his cohabitations.

The general rule is that any doubtful betrothal and he knew about it and cohabited once, we say that a person does not make his cohabitation promiscuous, and she needs a get. However, if another man betrothed her, she needs a get from both of them. But if he lived with her as husband and wife and it was publicly known, it is definite betrothal, which is stronger than the presumption that he does not make his cohabitation promiscuous. All this is when he knew that it was not betrothal, but if he did not know at all, other betrothal is needed. However,

[How are betrothals by document conducted? This contains 15 sections]
It has already been explained in Siman 26, section 12, that betrothal by document is derived from the verse "and she departs and becomes [another man's wife]" – just as her departure (i.e., divorce) is by document, so too her becoming (i.e., betrothal) can be by document. Therefore, in betrothal by document, most of the rules of a get (divorce document) apply, as will be explained. How is betrothal by document conducted? He writes for her on paper, even if it has no monetary value, "You are betrothed to me," "You are betrothed to me," or "You are my wife," and hands it to her and says to her, "You are betrothed to me with this document according to the law of Moses and Israel." If he does not say it – it is still considered betrothal. In truth, among the halachic authorities, it is not found that in betrothal by document a statement is required, and logic dictates this, for in betrothal by money, when the parties are engaged in the matter, the statement is not essential as written in Siman 27, and all the more so with a document where the language of betrothal is written, a statement is not necessary. However, in the Gemara [48a] it implies that he needs to say to her, "Become betrothed to me with this document," and certainly, initially, he should say it, as this is the proper manner of betrothal. Nevertheless, it does not invalidate the betrothal if she and the witnesses know it is a betrothal document and he gives it to her – it is sufficient [so it seems to me] [see Beit Shmuel, section 3]. If she is a minor or a young girl and is being betrothed by her father through a document, he writes "Your daughter is betrothed to me," and if he wrote "You are betrothed to me" – it is also considered betrothal [Chelkat Mechokek, section 5], and in Siman 37 it will be explained who receives the betrothal and other specific laws regarding this. If she is an orphan and is being betrothed by her mother or brothers with rabbinic betrothal, it appears that he must specifically write "You are betrothed to me" and give it to her.

The marriage contract (shetar kiddushin) is written by the husband, and even though she is the one who transfers herself to him, and in a sales contract the seller writes "my field is sold to you," nevertheless in marriage, it is a tradition from Moses at Sinai that the husband, who is acquiring, writes "behold, you are betrothed to me," as it is written, "when a man takes a wife"—which implies that he must take her and not that she acquires herself to him. Similarly, when betrothing a minor or a young woman through the father, as has been mentioned, even though it is written "I gave my daughter to this man" (Deuteronomy 22:16), which seemingly implies that he is transferring his daughter to him, the tradition has come that the document must be written by the husband, who is acquiring, stating "your daughter is betrothed to me," and just as in a divorce the husband writes, so too in betrothal. And even though in the Jerusalem Talmud (Kiddushin 1:2) it is explained that even if the father of the girl wrote a document saying "I, so-and-so, betrothed my daughter to so-and-so," it is also valid, nevertheless in the Babylonian Talmud and the poskim it is clearly implied that it is essential that only the husband writes it. And also in the Jerusalem Talmud, it seems that it is only said in the context of betrothal through the father because it is written "I gave my daughter," but even in this case, we do not follow this opinion, and what is written "I gave my daughter" means "with my consent I gave," because for a minor and a young woman the consent of the father is required, but not for an adult woman.

It is necessary to give her the document in the presence of witnesses, just like a get (divorce document) which requires delivery witnesses, as the primary witnesses are the delivery witnesses, for we hold like Rabbi Elazar who says that delivery witnesses effectuate the get. The same applies to marriage, as they have the same law, and there is no need for witnesses to sign the document. However, regarding a get, it is explained in Siman 133 that if witnesses sign the get and it is delivered to her privately without witnesses, some say it is valid and some say it is invalid, and the same applies to marriage, and the reason is explained there with God's help. Additionally, it is explained there that ideally, there should also be signing witnesses, and as our custom is to have signing witnesses on the get and to deliver it in the presence of delivery witnesses, the same applies to marriage. Nevertheless, if after the fact there were no signing witnesses, it is valid according to all opinions, both for a get and for marriage.

And since we hold that delivery by witnesses effects the acquisition, therefore, even if it is written on something that can be forged, such as on pottery or the like, it is still valid, as in Gittin, Siman 124. However, some say that this is specifically when there are no signed witnesses, as then there is no concern. But if witnesses also signed on the document, it is not valid on something that can be forged, as we are concerned that they may rely only on the signed witnesses, and it will be possible to forge it, and this will be explained with the help of Heaven. Additionally, it needs to be written in ink or any substance whose mark endures, as in Gittin, and this is explained in Siman 125. It seems that all the precautions necessary in writing a get (divorce bill), such as not writing it through a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor, and other laws explained there, also apply to a marriage document, because we learn the marriage document from the get.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: If it was written in his own handwriting and there are no witnesses, she is doubtfully betrothed. And the meaning is, even if he gave it to her privately, where there are neither signing witnesses nor delivery witnesses. The doubt is that although in divorce and betrothal it is impossible without witnesses, as matters of sexual prohibitions require at least two witnesses, nevertheless, we hold that a divorce document (get) written in his own handwriting without witnesses and not delivered in the presence of witnesses is valid by Torah law, and if she remarries, the child is legitimate. This is because the Torah made it dependent on his writing, as it is written, "and he writes for her a bill of divorce" (Deuteronomy 24:1), thus it is valid by Torah law if written in his own handwriting. Therefore, some say that the same applies to betrothal. And although this is not similar to divorce since a divorce can be written without her consent and thus depends mainly on the husband's writing, unlike betrothal which requires her consent as well, still, since the betrothal document is derived from the divorce document, the law is the same as in a divorce document. However, there are those who disagree, and even with a divorce document, it is invalid rabbinically and she should not remarry with it, as stated in section 130. Certainly, with betrothal, she needs another betrothal, but in such a betrothal, she is doubtfully betrothed and requires a get (divorce document).

And it is necessary to explain this law: It is certain that the Torah's requirement of handwriting for a get (divorce bill) for witnesses is for the signing witnesses, as the Torah stated that his handwriting is as valid as the handwriting of the witnesses. However, this does not pertain to the witnesses of delivery. Consequently, there is no practical difference in this law, for if there were no witnesses of delivery, according to the opinion that without witnesses of delivery it is invalid, as mentioned in section 3, it is also invalid here, even if we consider them as signing witnesses. This is only relevant to those who hold it is valid without witnesses of delivery. And since for us it is a doubt, it is a doubtful marriage. If there are witnesses of delivery, it is certainly valid in any case [see Chumash Meir and Beit Shmuel]. Therefore, our teacher the Rema was precise to write that it is doubtful marriage and did not write that some say it is valid and some say it is invalid, because even according to the opinion that it is valid, it is only doubtful marriage since there are no witnesses of delivery. There is no practical difference in this law, except that one should not say that there is no doubt in such marriages, for there is a doubt, but to be certain marriage, it is not, even according to the opinion that validates with his handwriting.

And according to this, there are those who wish to say that in such a case of betrothal (kiddushin), it is a case of a double doubt (safek sefeika) – a doubt whether the law follows the opinion that a person's handwriting is considered like the handwriting of witnesses, and if you say it is, there is a doubt whether the law follows the opinion that the signatures of witnesses are valid without the delivery of the document in their presence. And it is a double doubt that also reverses: a doubt whether the signatures of witnesses alone are sufficient, and if you say they are, a doubt whether a person's handwriting is considered like witnesses, and it would be a double doubt leading to validation. However, it appears to me that this is not a double doubt and is not similar to other cases of double doubt where the uncertainty is about the fundamental act, whether it was done this way or that way, and if you say it was done this way, perhaps in this case it is also valid. But here, the act is clear to us and the doubts are about the law. Therefore, when we come to judge this woman, it is a single doubt – whether she is single or married. And what difference does it make whether this doubt or that doubt, it is like a double doubt from the same source. Therefore, the main ruling follows our master the Rema that this is a case of doubtful betrothal.

If a marriage document (shetar kiddushin) comes before us, written in handwriting, and it is not known whether there were witnesses to its delivery or not, we do not assume that it was certainly done according to halacha and that there were witnesses to its delivery. For it can also be said conversely, to establish her status as unmarried and say that there were no witnesses to its delivery, and she remains unmarried according to the opinion that invalidates a handwritten marriage document. Rather, she is in a state of doubt regarding her marital status, and the kiddushin is rabbinically invalid until it is clarified that there were witnesses to its delivery. However, if a marriage document comes before us signed by witnesses, we assume that there were certainly also witnesses to its delivery, and she is married according to all opinions. We do not say that perhaps there were no witnesses to its delivery, which would invalidate it according to the opinion that requires witnesses to the delivery. If she accepted kiddushin from another man, she needs a get (divorce document) from both men, for a get is valid in such a case as well, as mentioned in Siman 133.

The marriage contract must be written by the scribe with the intention for the specific woman, just as with a divorce document where it needs to be written for her sake. If it was written without this intention, she is not betrothed. It is only written with the woman's consent, and although in the case of a divorce document her consent is not required—because she can be divorced against her will—nonetheless, if it was written without her consent, there are sages who validate it because since we derive the law from divorce, it should be completely analogous to divorce. However, there are sages who invalidate it, arguing that in this context, the comparison to divorce does not apply due to the reason explained. Therefore, if it was written without her consent, she is in a state of uncertain betrothal. If she accepted betrothal from another man, she needs a divorce from both. However, if the second man also betrothed her with a document that was written without her consent, she is not betrothed to the second man in any case [in my opinion].

Our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote that there is an opinion which states that the names of the man and the woman must be mentioned in the marriage document (shtar kiddushin), just as they must be mentioned in a get (divorce bill). Certainly, this is the case since we derive it from a get. The Rashba also wrote that even though the Gemara does not mention the names, it is obvious that this is the case, and it is explicitly implied in the Jerusalem Talmud. However, if the names were not mentioned, it seems to me that a get would still be necessary to release her, even in a case where there is no concern about forgery, such as if he stipulated that he is betrothing her with a document and not with money. This is because some early authorities hold that even in a get, if the names were not written, it is still valid for us who hold that the delivery of the get by witnesses effects the divorce, and it does not need to be self-evident within the document since the witnesses know the parties involved. If so, all the more so with kiddushin, where it is impossible to release her without a get. Even though the halachic authorities did not bring this opinion at all in the laws of gittin, and it is unthinkable to rely on it for any leniency, nevertheless, regarding a marriage document, where it is not explicitly stated that the names must be mentioned, it is unthinkable to release her without a get. Therefore, it seems to me that this is why our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote "there is an opinion" to indicate that this is only a stringency to be concerned about and not a leniency. Additionally, the Rashba in a responsum appears somewhat uncertain about this, even though he ruled decisively in his novellae. Nonetheless, in practical terms, he seems to have been concerned about this.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: If one writes on something attached to the ground or on items forbidden for benefit, some say it is invalid, and some permit it. End quote. All the great authorities agree that if it is attached to the ground, it is completely invalid, because although one can consecrate with money even if it is attached, as explained in the Tosefta we brought in section 27, subsection 5, but for a marriage contract (ketubah) derived from a divorce document (get), it is invalid. Those who initially permitted it also reconsidered and straightforwardly ruled it invalid [Choshen Mishpat 7:7 and Gra 9]. Conversely, regarding items forbidden for benefit, many authorities hold that it is valid, just as a get written on forbidden items is valid. Some differentiate between a Torah prohibition and a rabbinic prohibition, and we have already explained our view on this in section 28, subsection 97. Practically, one should be stringent.

Time – There is no need to write the date in a marriage contract (shtar kiddushin), as even in a divorce document (get), it is valid according to Torah law without a date, and it is only the Sages who instituted writing the date in a get. In a marriage contract, they did not institute this because most people perform kiddushin (betrothal) with money. Therefore, even for those who perform kiddushin with a document, they did not institute [writing the date] (Yevamot 31b). Furthermore, the primary reason the Sages instituted writing the date in a get is due to concerns of promiscuity, as stated in Siman 127. In a kiddushin document, this concern does not apply because if there were an issue, it could be erased, and she would be presumed to be single. However, in a get, it should not be erased because she would be presumed to be a married woman, and the date would reveal when she committed adultery, but this is not the case with kiddushin (ibid).

And even if he betrothed with a disqualified document, such as one written not for her or with another disqualification, nevertheless, we evaluate the paper to see if it has the value of a perutah – she is betrothed if he betrothed her in the presence of witnesses. If not, she is betrothed out of doubt, perhaps the value of a perutah is found elsewhere. And even though he betrothed her with a document saying, "I betroth you with this document," still, as long as he did not say, "I am not betrothing you as monetary value, only as a document," we can say his intention is also for the betrothal money, and he means "I betroth you with this document as monetary value," similar to if he said, "I betroth you with this ring." It is explicitly explained by the poskim that when it has the value of a perutah, she is certainly betrothed by the monetary value, and we say that her intention is also on the paper, and this is also implied in the Talmud, as well as explicitly in the Jerusalem Talmud, brought by the Rif in the first chapter, though the Rambam omitted all this, and I do not know why. Perhaps he explains it specifically if he betrothed her with monetary value, but it does not seem so, and it requires further investigation. Nevertheless, it seems to me that if she or he says that their intention was not at all to be betrothed by the paper as monetary value, it is only a doubtful betrothal even if it is worth a perutah. [And perhaps the Rambam holds that we need to ask them, and they are believed when they say their intention was not on the paper unless they say their intention was on the paper, and if so, there is no innovation in this and therefore he omitted it.]

If he betrothed her with a document and said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this document and the paper is mine," she is not betrothed, because the letters are considered to be floating in the air and he has given her nothing. We require that he give her the document itself, similar to a get (divorce document), which is invalid in such a case, as stated in Siman 143. Similarly, if he said to her, "On the condition that the paper is mine," Rabbi Rema rules that she is not betrothed. However, there is an opinion that it is at least doubtful betrothal, because since he said "on the condition," it does not constitute a reservation in the document but rather a condition. This makes it a condition and an action in the same matter, and any condition and action in the same matter nullifies the condition and validates the action. Nonetheless, from Rabbi Rema's words in Siman 38, Paragraph 4, it is evident that he does not agree with this ruling, as explained there. The Gra (Vilna Gaon) similarly writes in his commentary that it is only taken into account as a stringency. This will be explained further with God's help. 

If he said to her, "On the condition that you return the paper to me," in the case of a get (divorce document), it is effective as stated in Siman 143. In the case of betrothal, it also seems to be effective because a gift given on the condition to return it is still considered a gift. Although it is explained in Siman 29 that it does not work with monetary betrothal, nonetheless, with betrothal by document, where the essence of the betrothal is not in the value of the paper, it is effective. This is because the letters are not considered to be floating in the air, as at the moment of betrothal the paper is hers. This will be explained further with God's help.

If someone stole a piece of paper and wrote a marriage contract (shtar kiddushin) on it and betrothed a woman with it, and the original owner has not yet despaired of recovering it – it seems that this is not a definite betrothal, because since the paper is not hers, it is no better than when he says "the paper is mine," in which case she is not betrothed. However, it could be argued that since the paper has been altered by the writing, he has acquired it through this change and should return its value to the owner, making the paper his, and the betrothal valid. This requires further investigation, because if he wrote in a way that the writing can be erased, this is considered a change that reverts to its original state, and he has not acquired it.

[And in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 267, Se'if 68, we clarified that two women cannot be betrothed with one document, as with divorce documents (gittin), and there is clear evidence for this from Gittin 9a: since it does not ask "and furthermore, there is no other case," see there and analyze it carefully.]

[Laws of Betrothal through Intercourse, containing 11 sections]

It has already been explained in Siman 26 that betrothal through intercourse is explicitly mentioned in the Torah: "When a man takes a wife and has relations with her" (Deuteronomy 24:1). It is also explained there that the Sages prohibited betrothal through intercourse because it is considered immodest, but this prohibition does not invalidate the betrothal. 

How is betrothal through intercourse performed? The man secludes himself with the woman in the presence of two witnesses and says to her in their presence, "Behold, you are betrothed to me through this intercourse that I will have with you immediately." The witnesses then leave, and he has intercourse with her for the sake of betrothal. The witnesses do not need to see the intercourse itself, as it is improper; rather, they need to see the seclusion. Even though they do not see the intercourse, since they see the seclusion, they are witnesses of the seclusion and thereby witnesses of the intercourse. 

Even though in the cases of betrothal through money or a document, the witnesses need to see the actual act of betrothal, in this case, the seclusion is considered equivalent to the intercourse itself, as if they saw the intercourse. This is because fire in tinder does not smolder without igniting, and he is familiar with her. Additionally, it is impossible to see the actual act of intercourse, and even in cases of execution for adultery, witnesses are sufficient even if they do not see the actual act of penetration. Furthermore, it is sufficient if they see behavior typical of adulterers, even though one could argue that perhaps he only had external contact; nonetheless, they are executed based on that appearance.

If one asks, "Why is it that for mere seclusion they are not executed, even if they say they secluded themselves to commit the act, yet for betrothal, seclusion is sufficient even if they did not see this appearance?" The answer is that it is not comparable. In the case of seclusion for a forbidden act, it is possible to argue that they repented and did not commit the act; therefore, they are not executed unless the witnesses saw them lying together, which clearly indicates they did not repent. However, in the case of permitted intercourse, it is obvious that when they secluded themselves, he certainly had intercourse with her—who would prevent them? Therefore, it is considered as if the witnesses actually saw the intercourse. Although it is immodest, it is not a transgression, and the immodesty already passed from the moment they secluded themselves.

Therefore, it seems to me that if one betroths through intercourse one who is subject to a negative commandment (lav), we do not say in this case that "these are the witnesses of seclusion, these are the witnesses of intercourse," and she is not betrothed unless they saw the actual intercourse, just as in the case of illicit relations where they are executed as we mentioned. And one cannot say that in the case of a death penalty, we assume they retracted, but not in the case of a negative commandment, because what difference is there between a negative commandment and a karet (excision) prohibition, both are from the Torah. Or it is possible to say that since witnesses were appointed for this betrothal, we say it as in the case of permitted betrothal, and the matter requires further investigation for the law. Similarly, there is doubt regarding secondary incest prohibitions and a chalutzah to a priest, even though their prohibition is rabbinic, and see what I wrote in Siman 18, se'if 3, and all the more so if one betroths a menstruant through intercourse, which is subject to karet.

If he betrothed her in the presence of witnesses to seclusion, and they secluded themselves and stayed together for the amount of time it takes for intercourse, and then they came out and he or she said that he did not have intercourse with her and there is no betrothal – it appears that we are concerned about this and it would be considered doubtful betrothal. Even if both of them say that he did not have intercourse with her, nevertheless, they are not believed to release her without a get (divorce document). However, it cannot be said with certainty that he did have intercourse with her and it is definite betrothal; not only if they both say so, but even if one says he did and the other says he did not, we say that it is possible that he indeed did not have intercourse with her, as we say regarding a levir and his sister-in-law that up to thirty days a person restrains himself, as we will say later in section 167, and therefore here too we should be concerned that perhaps he did not have intercourse with her, and therefore it is doubtful betrothal.

In Siman 20, it is explained that for all prohibited relationships, liability is incurred with partial penetration, even if full intercourse was not completed. Regarding the intercourse of betrothal, the Sages stated [Yevamot 10.] that anyone who engages in intercourse intends for complete intercourse. Elsewhere, the Sages said [Yevamot 55b] that a woman is acquired for her husband with partial penetration. Our Rabbis explained that if he completes the intercourse, he intends to acquire her only with the completion of intercourse. Therefore, if before he completes, she extends her hand and accepts betrothal from another man, she is betrothed to the second man. But if he only performed partial penetration and withdrew, he acquires her with partial penetration. Similarly, if he initially stated that his intention is to acquire her with partial penetration, he acquires her with partial penetration even if he completes the intercourse. And if before the completion of the intercourse she accepted betrothal from another man, she is betrothed to the first man. Some distinguish between the intercourse of betrothal, which only acquires her with full intercourse, and the intercourse after betrothal, which establishes the marriage with mere partial penetration since she is already acquired to him [Rif]. Some of our Rabbis said that certainly, also in betrothal, partial penetration is like complete intercourse, similar to prohibited relationships. And what the Sages said "completion of intercourse" in betrothal means the completion of partial penetration, as partial penetration has a beginning and an end. This partial penetration is the insertion of the glans, and there is a beginning and end to this [Rabbeinu Tam]. Our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, only brought the first opinion, implying that this is the primary ruling.

Sexual intercourse that effects acquisition for marriage has no distinction whether it is in the usual manner or not in the usual manner. Since he had full intercourse with her for the purpose of marriage—even if it was not in the usual manner—she is betrothed to him. Similarly, for all forbidden relations, there is no distinction between the usual manner and not the usual manner, as it is written, "the lyings of a woman" (Leviticus 18:22)—the different types of lying are likened to each other. However, if he had intercourse with her with a flaccid member, he has not acquired her, for this is not considered intercourse, as written in Siman 20, Se'if 17. Also, if he had intercourse with her without intent, as if engaged in casual activity without intending intercourse, it appears that he does not acquire her. And although regarding a sacrifice he is liable since he derived pleasure, as written there, nevertheless, for marriage, we require the intention to acquire her. Furthermore, in an intentional case, he is not liable at all if it was casual, as written there. Also, a virgin less than three years and one day old is not betrothed through intercourse, for her intercourse is not considered intercourse at all, as written in Se'if 37. Likewise, accidental intercourse does not effect acquisition in a woman, and certainly not coerced intercourse.

In the case of betrothal through money, it has been explained that the declaration is essential. If he did not say to her "Behold, you are betrothed to me," it is nothing unless they spoke about matters of betrothal. And in the case of betrothal through a document, we explained that the declaration is not essential. Regarding betrothal through intercourse, it seems that its law is like betrothal through money. Only in the case of a document that contains the language of betrothal is the declaration not essential. However, in the case of intercourse, it is like money, and without a declaration, it is considered mere licentiousness. We do not say that a man does not make his intercourse licentious, for Rambam has already written in the tenth chapter of the laws of divorce that we only say this presumption in the case of his wife who was divorced or in the case of betrothal on condition and he had intercourse [with her]. But if they are engaged in matters of betrothal, it seems that the declaration is not essential, as in the case of betrothal through money. There are those who are uncertain about this since the witnesses do not see the intercourse. It seems in such cases that the declaration is indeed not essential, because if the witnesses were invited to witness the seclusion, even according to Rambam, it is clear that we say a man does not make his intercourse licentious. This is no less than the case of betrothal on condition and subsequent intercourse, and certainly according to those who disagree with him. If they designated one witness for the intercourse, for those who are concerned about betrothal with one witness as in Siman 42, there is concern here as well.

In the act of betrothal through cohabitation, the woman becomes only a betrothed (arusa) similar to the betrothal through money or document, and she does not become a married woman (nesuah). And even though a married woman is one who has had intercourse and here too she has had intercourse, nevertheless, since this is intercourse for the sake of betrothal, she does not become a married woman. All the differences that exist between a betrothed woman and a married woman apply to her as well. And these are the words of the Rambam in Chapter 10: "A betrothed woman is forbidden to her husband by rabbinic decree as long as she is in her father's house, and one who has intercourse with his betrothed in his father-in-law's house is given lashes of rebellion. Even if he betrothed her through intercourse, he is forbidden to have intercourse with her a second time in her father's house until he brings her into his house and secludes with her and designates her for himself, and this seclusion is called 'entering the chuppah,' and this is called marriage everywhere," end quote. Similarly, the differences in Torah law between a betrothed woman and a married woman, such as if he is a Kohen he does not become impure for her as stated in Yoreh De'ah section 373, and also that he does not inherit her – these apply also to betrothal through intercourse. And even though the reason for impurity and inheritance is because it is written "his close relative" (Leviticus 21:2) and a close relative is bodily closeness [Rashi, Bava Metzia 18a, and see his language in Ketubot 53a, "he does not inherit her"], and in betrothal through intercourse there is bodily closeness, nevertheless, since this intercourse is not for the sake of marriage but for the sake of betrothal and he is still not permitted to her as the Rambam wrote, this is not considered bodily closeness. For even according to Torah law, there is a difference between a betrothed woman and a married woman as it is written "Who is the man that has betrothed a woman and not taken her?" (Deuteronomy 20:7) and this includes all kinds of betrothal, whether through money, document, or intercourse – thus the Torah considers her as not yet taken [in my opinion], and see what I wrote in section 55.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that some say it is specifically if he had relations with her in his father-in-law's house, but if he brought her into his home and had relations with her, or he had already betrothed her and then had relations with her—her status is like that of a married woman. This means that when he brought her into his home and betrothed her through intercourse, the betrothal and marriage occur simultaneously, as bringing her into his home is considered marriage, as is evident from the language of the Rambam in the previous section. Similarly, if he had already betrothed her with money or a document, even if he had relations with her in his father-in-law's house for the sake of marriage—it is like she is married. And this that we hold that one who has relations with his betrothed in his father-in-law's house receives lashes, as written—this is when he did not do it for the sake of marriage but rather in a promiscuous manner. However, if it was for the sake of marriage, he does not receive lashes, and she becomes a married woman through this intercourse. And even if he did not recite the marriage blessings, the blessings do not impede the marriage. And that which our Sages said, "a bride without a blessing is forbidden to her husband like a menstruant" [Tractate Kallah 1:1], the intention is regarding the marriage itself, but the blessings are initially required, and post facto do not impede, like all blessings.

Behold, this distinction made in betrothal through intercourse between having intercourse with her in her father-in-law's house and bringing her into his home is not implied by any of the early authorities and is a singular opinion [Ran, Perek HaMadir], and he himself did not definitively rule this way [as he wrote in a tentative language]. The general principle of the Talmud implies that any intercourse not accompanied by a wedding ceremony, which is the intercourse of betrothal, is merely engagement in all cases [otherwise in Gemara 10: regarding the matter of Ben Bag Bag, it would establish that it was without a wedding ceremony and he had intercourse with her in his home. The Makneh brought proof against the Rema from Tosafot Yevamot 59, s.v. "ha" see there, and it can be refuted that it refers to a case not in his home, and also the Gra disagrees with him, see there].

However, regarding the ruling that intercourse following betrothal makes her considered as a married woman if he intended it for marriage—this is certainly true. Even if he betrothed her through intercourse and then had intercourse with her again for the purpose of marriage, she is considered married. Although only the wedding canopy (chuppah) establishes marriage, the chuppah is merely preparation for intercourse, and certainly, intercourse itself suffices. Additionally, many authorities hold that the essence of the chuppah is seclusion, as written in Siman 55. This applies to the chuppah itself if he intended it for marriage and not merely for licentiousness. Nevertheless, some say that in the house of her father-in-law it is not effective unless he brings her into his house and secludes with her. I do not understand this, as since he secluded her for the purpose of marital intercourse, what difference does it make whether it is in his house or not? This is also evident from the language of the Rambam, who wrote: "One who has intercourse with his betrothed for the purpose of marriage after betrothing her—once he has intercourse with her, he acquires her, and she is considered married and is his wife for all matters." This clearly implies that in any place where he has intercourse with her for the purpose of marriage, she is considered fully married.

The Rema also wrote: "There are those who say that if a single man has relations with a single woman in the presence of witnesses, we are concerned that he may have intended it as a form of betrothal, since it is presumed that a person does not make his act of intercourse one of promiscuity. However, if he is already known to act promiscuously or if he has another wife, we are not concerned. There are some who are lenient in all cases. See further in Siman 149 and Siman 166 and earlier in Siman 15." And even according to those who hold that this presumption applies only to the man and not to the woman who is being cohabited with, and it is obvious that when she is in a state of niddah, this presumption does not apply since he is transgressing a severe prohibition. The essence of this dispute hinges on the words of the Rambam in Chapter 10 of Hilchot Gerushin and Chapter 4 of Hilchot Nachalot, where the Rambam disputes some of the Geonim who said that we always apply this presumption to every person and in every situation. The Rambam holds that this is said only regarding his wife who has been divorced, as stated in Siman 149, and we have already written about this in Siman 15, Section 11. Also, in the case of his maidservant who bore him a son and he treats him as a son, and he is a Torah scholar and known to be meticulous in commandments, see there in Hilchot Nachalot. Know that what our master the Rema wrote, "in the presence of witnesses," does not mean that he designated witnesses for his seclusion, for certainly in such a case even the Rambam agrees that we are concerned for betrothal. Rather, it means that he did not designate witnesses, but witnesses saw from outside, as is clarified in the source of the law in the Mordechai, Chapter 3 of Kiddushin. See what is written in Siman 149, Section 13 regarding the opinion of the Rema.

[The Law of the Blessing of Betrothal and Whether Ten are Required, Containing Thirteen Sections]
One who betroths a woman must recite a blessing, just like all commandments that require a blessing. This is the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us regarding forbidden unions, and prohibited to us betrothed women, and permitted to us married women [Ran] through chuppah and betrothal. Blessed are You, Lord, Who sanctifies His people Israel through chuppah and betrothal." And why do we not recite a shorter blessing: "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to betroth a woman," like we do with other commandments? Furthermore, where do we find such a blessing that mentions what God has forbidden to us? After all, we do not bless "Who has forbidden to us a limb from a living animal and permitted to us the slaughtered animal." And why mention forbidden unions here? Additionally, why mention chuppah here when we bless the blessing of betrothal in the house of betrothal and without chuppah [Rosh, Chapter 1 of Ketubot, Section 12]? This was the custom in Talmudic times—to betroth first and then, after some time, bring her to chuppah. Even today, this is the custom in Eastern countries.

However, the essence of the matter is as follows: Certainly, this blessing is not an actual blessing of the commandment, as it is impossible to bless in the manner appropriate for a blessing of a commandment. One cannot bless at the time of betrothal with "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning betrothal" because one does not bless on a commandment whose completion is not its final act, as the betrothal still lacks the transfer to the chuppah (wedding canopy). Even at the time of entering the chuppah, it is impossible to bless concerning betrothal and chuppah since the betrothal was done a long time ago. And when someone comes to perform betrothal and marriage together, they also did not see fit to establish a separate blessing so that there would be a uniform blessing format for all cases. Additionally, it is clear that this blessing is not a blessing for the performance of a commandment because the commandment of procreation is about fulfilling the mitzvah. If someone takes a concubine and fulfills the mitzvah of procreation, he is not obligated to betroth a woman. Similarly, one who marries an elderly woman, an infertile woman, or a woman who cannot bear children, as well as a man who is naturally unable to have children but marries, they still recite the wedding blessings even though there is no obligation in this mitzvah since it does not fulfill the mitzvah of procreation. Even one who marries a woman for the sake of procreation, since it is possible to fulfill the mitzvah of procreation without betrothal, it is not comparable to slaughtering, where one is not obligated to slaughter and eat, and even so, when he slaughters to eat, he blesses. There, it is impossible to eat without slaughtering, but here, it is possible to fulfill the mitzvah of procreation without betrothal.

However, because our Sages did not want this commandment to be fulfilled without any blessing at all, they instituted a blessing for the sanctity of the entire Jewish people. This means that the Holy One, Blessed be He, chose them and sanctified them concerning marriage. We give praise that He sanctified us with His commandments, separated us from the nations, and commanded us to sanctify a woman permitted to us and not one of the prohibited relationships. They mentioned the prohibition of betrothals and the permissibility of marriages under the chuppah and kiddushin to prevent anyone from mistakenly thinking that the blessing of kiddushin was established to permit her to him. Therefore, they mentioned the chuppah to say that only the blessing of the chuppah permits the bride. For this reason, they also mentioned the chuppah before the kiddushin to indicate that the permissibility of the marriage is through the chuppah that follows the blessing of kiddushin. Some say that the primary version is "chuppah with kiddushin," meaning chuppah with kiddushin preceding the chuppah. Because the "bet" is soft according to the rules of grammar, like the letters "beged kefet" when following a vowel, scribes mistakenly wrote "and kiddushin" with a "vav." Additionally, since our custom is to perform betrothal and marriage together, bringing the couple under the chuppah and then reciting the blessing of betrothal, it is fitting to also mention the chuppah before the kiddushin. Since the final permissibility is through the chuppah, they mentioned the chuppah first.

Therefore, we conclude it with a blessing, even though it is a short blessing, similar to Kiddush, which we conclude with a blessing because it is somewhat lengthy, even though it contains only one concept. Similarly, in this blessing, even though it contains only one concept, nevertheless, since it is somewhat lengthy, we conclude it with a blessing. It was also established in the language of sanctity, like the Kiddush of Shabbat and Yom Tov. Just as in the Kiddush, two things are mentioned: the act of creation and the Exodus from Egypt, making it considered lengthy, so too in this blessing, which includes the sanctity of the entire people of Israel and the sanctity of the union, it is considered lengthy. The explanation of "Who sanctifies His people Israel through the chuppah and kiddushin" is also as we have said. Some say that this refers to the chuppah and kiddushin of the entire people of Israel, who were sanctified to the Holy One, Blessed be He, at the time of the giving of the Torah. The chuppah was Mount Sinai, which He held over us like a barrel, and we stood under the mountain as under a chuppah. The kiddushin was the giving of the Torah, as explained by Ramban. It is indeed true that from then we were sanctified, and this union also comes in sanctity and is connected to the blessing of betrothal of this union. According to this, it makes sense that the chuppah preceded the kiddushin, as the holding of the mountain was before the giving of the Torah, as explicitly stated in the Torah.

The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 3, Law 23: Anyone who betroths a woman, whether by himself or through an agent, must recite a blessing before the betrothal, either he or his agent, just as one recites a blessing before performing any commandment, and afterwards he betroths. If he betrothed without reciting a blessing, he should not recite the blessing afterward because this would be a blessing in vain; what has been done is done. These are his words. Some say that the blessing is recited after the betrothal, because the woman might retract and the blessing would be in vain [Raavad]. This requirement to bless before performing the mitzvah applies when the mitzvah is in the hands of the one reciting the blessing [Hagahot Maimoniot]. However, the main ruling in this matter follows the Rambam, to bless beforehand [Responsa of Rashbash], and this is the custom of all Israel. Yet, in the case where he ruled that if one did not bless beforehand, he should not bless afterward, we do not hold like him, and one blesses afterward as well. This is not considered as after the act because the main completion is the chuppah (marriage canopy), and it is still considered as before the act. Moreover, according to what has been stated, the main blessing is not on the betrothal itself but on the sanctity of the entire Jewish people, and in this, it is not relevant to say "before the act." Especially according to our custom, where one person recites the blessing, it is obvious that he can recite it afterward as well [Chomat Shlomo and Beit Shmuel].

Even when one betroths with intercourse, he should ideally recite the blessing before the act, which means he blesses in front of the witnesses of seclusion and in front of ten men according to those who require ten for the blessing of betrothal, as will be explained. Afterward, he secludes himself with her and has intercourse with her. Although it is not proper to bless the mitzvah unless it is ready to be performed, and at the time he is with her in bed it is impossible to bless due to "and there shall be no indecent thing in you" (Deuteronomy 23:15), in truth, for this reason, it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Berakhot 9:3) that for betrothal by intercourse, one does not bless before the act. Nevertheless, since this is not stated in our Talmud, we do not follow the Jerusalem Talmud, and furthermore, there is a dispute in the Jerusalem Talmud itself on this matter. And this is called "before the act" since it cannot be done otherwise.

In concluding the blessing, the Rambam states: "Blessed are You, O Lord, who sanctifies Israel," and no more, for since it is not currently the time of the wedding canopy according to their custom, how can one conclude with "under the wedding canopy"? Nevertheless, many of our rabbis have written to conclude "who sanctifies His people Israel through the wedding canopy and betrothal," and this is the custom throughout the diaspora. Since earlier we say "and permitted us... through the wedding canopy and betrothal," we should also conclude the blessing in this manner. One should not challenge this practice even when the betrothal is a long time before the wedding canopy, for the blessing pertains to the sanctity of the entire people of Israel, as mentioned. Additionally, in this marriage, since the betrothal without the wedding canopy is ineffective, it is necessary to mention it. The Rosh wrote that this is indeed the custom.

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote that the groom himself must recite the blessing, and if he consecrates through a messenger, the messenger must recite the blessing. This is logical, as the mitzvah is his, and he must bless over it. However, some say that another should recite the blessing so as not to embarrass someone who does not know how to recite it, as they instituted for the reading of the Torah that another reads and not the one who is called to the Torah for this reason. Similarly, in the Temple, when bringing the first fruits, one had to recite the passage "Arami Oved Avi" (Deuteronomy 26:5), and they instituted that it be recited by prompting even for one who knows how to read for this reason. Here, it is even more preferable because the blessing is upon the sanctity of all Israel, and all are equal in it. However, if there is no one else who knows the blessing, the groom should recite it himself. Additionally, we find with Rebecca that others blessed her and not Eliezer, who was Isaac's messenger, as it is written, "And they blessed Rebecca" (Genesis 24:60). The Vilna Gaon explains that in Tractate Kallah (1:1) it is derived concerning the blessing of betrothal, but the plain meaning of the verse does not refer to the blessing of betrothal, and it is merely an allusion.

The Rambam wrote that it is customary to recite this blessing over a cup of wine or beer, and one should first bless over the cup and then recite this blessing. If there is no wine or beer, one recites the blessing on its own. Technically, there is no need for a cup for the blessing of betrothal, as the requirement for a cup is only for the blessing of marriage. However, for betrothal, people have the custom similar to the blessing of circumcision, as stated in the Tur Yoreh De'ah, section 265, because one does not say a song except over wine, and it causes its own blessing [Berachot 42]. In many places, wine is brought, and blessings are made over it even though it is not necessary to drink it [Rashi, and see there in Tosafot]. They give the groom and bride a little to drink, and the one reciting the blessing fulfills his obligation this way. And although for blessings over enjoyment, the one reciting must taste, nevertheless, since it was instituted over a cup, it is like Kiddush and Havdalah, where one can fulfill others' obligation with the blessing over the wine as our master the Beit Yosef wrote regarding circumcision there [in my opinion]. It seems that if the one reciting wants to drink it, there is no objection, and it is acceptable, although it is not customary. And even though it would be better, since the cup is not essential, nevertheless, since it was established as obligatory to bless over the cup, it is like Kiddush and Havdalah [in my opinion]. There is no need to drink all or most of it; a taste suffices, for there is no obligation of a cup by law as with Kiddush and Havdalah, where one must drink all or most of it.

The blessing of betrothal ideally requires ten men, which means that in addition to the witnesses of the betrothal, another eight or seven men are needed, as the groom is also counted in the quorum, similar to the blessings of marriage [see Choshen Mishpat section 7, and this requires further investigation]. Even relatives can be included in the ten if they are adults. If ten men are not available, it does not invalidate the blessing because the Talmud does not explicitly state that ten men are needed for betrothal. However, in the Sheiltot of Rabbi Achai Gaon [Parashat Chayei Sarah], it is explicitly stated that ten men are needed, while from Maimonides it appears that ten are not required [what is written in the Tur as "Rabbi Hai Gaon" is a printing error, and it should say Rabbi Achai Gaon, see Beit Yosef].

If the blessing of betrothal is not recited at the time of the betrothal and the wedding takes place later, the blessing is missed and should not be recited at the time of the wedding because its time has already passed. Even according to what we have written that if the blessing was not recited before the betrothal, it may be recited afterwards, this applies immediately and on the spot, like in our regions where betrothal and wedding occur together. But when the betrothal is at an earlier time, it is not relevant to recite the blessing at the time of the wedding. Nevertheless, there are Geonim who ruled that if the blessing was forgotten at the time of the betrothal, it should be recited together with the wedding blessings. Since it concludes with "and permitted us the betrothed," it pertains also to the wedding [Mordechai]. Additionally, just as we hold that one who did not recite the blessing after a meal can recite it as long as the food has not been digested, so too here, even if much time has passed, as long as the permission is not completed the blessing can be recited. And since the permission is not completed except through the chuppah, the blessing can be recited at the time of the wedding [Rosh in the name of R"Y]. And some say that the custom is even initially not to recite the blessing at the time of betrothal but only at the time of the wedding under the chuppah [Mordechai, and this is the intention of the Rema in section 3 when he writes "and so is the custom," and so wrote the Gra in Sk"Y, and see ChM"Ch Sk"D, and it is explicitly stated in the Mordechai as written, see there].

If they did not recite the blessing at the time of the betrothal and recite it at the time of the wedding, Rabbi Rema writes that some say he should betroth her again under the chuppah so that the betrothal is close to the blessing. And even though it is ruled in Siman 36 that if an agent betroths, the sender should not betroth again to avoid people saying the first betrothal is invalid and causing confusion, here they did not worry about this. Specifically, when it is done by an agent, there is a concern that people might say that betrothal by an agent is ineffective, but not when he betroths her himself. See what is written in Siman 36, Se'if 10.

And even in a place where the blessing of betrothal was already recited at the time of the engagement, nevertheless, some say that it should be recited again under the chuppah (wedding canopy) without mentioning God's name and sovereignty [see Chiddushei Maharam Chaviv, Siman 6], and he should say, "Blessed are You, Lord, who has sanctified us," etc., without pronouncing the name as it is read [see Avnei Shoham, Siman 6]. This rule applies only in a place where everyone conducts the betrothal under the chuppah, as is our custom, and he betrothed and recited the blessing beforehand and now is betrothing her anew under the chuppah according to the custom. Therefore, he recites the blessing again for the sake of those present, so they do not say that he betrothed without a blessing. However, in places where everyone betroths beforehand and he already betrothed and recited the blessing, what need is there to recite it again [Chiddushei Maharam Chaviv]? Therefore, in our country, when it happens that someone betrothed a woman before the chuppah, he should also betroth her under the chuppah. If the betrothal blessing was not previously recited, it should be recited under the chuppah with God's name and sovereignty. If it was already recited beforehand, it should be recited under the chuppah without mentioning God's name, as stated above.

The man can appoint an agent to betroth a woman for him with money or a document, and the agent will tell her, "You are betrothed to so-and-so," as it has already been explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 182, that throughout the Torah, a person's agent is considered like the person himself. And even though for a mitzvah that is incumbent upon a person's body, he cannot appoint an agent—just as he cannot appoint an agent to put on tefillin for him—nevertheless, we have explained there that the preparation for the mitzvah can be done through an agent. And the betrothal with money or a document is considered a preparation for the mitzvah, as the mitzvah itself is procreation, as stated in Siman 34, Se'if 2. Therefore, in betrothal through intercourse, agency does not apply at all. One can appoint an agent either to betroth any woman for him or to betroth a specific woman. Nevertheless, it is not advisable from the outset to appoint an agent to betroth any woman for him [Beit Shmuel], because if the agent dies before it is known whom he betrothed on his behalf, he would be prohibited from marrying any woman, as will be explained, with the help of Heaven.

And specifically when he is unable to perform the betrothal himself, but when it is possible for him to betroth her himself – it is forbidden for him to betroth through a messenger. And so our Sages said: it is forbidden for a person to betroth a woman until he sees her, lest he find in her something unseemly and she becomes repulsive to him, and the Merciful One said, "Love your neighbor as yourself" [Leviticus 19:18]. Therefore, when he does not know her, it is forbidden for him to betroth through a messenger if it is possible to betroth her himself. If it is not possible, the commandment should not be annulled because of this, and if he knows her, it is permissible for him to betroth her through a messenger. Nevertheless, there is a greater mitzvah to betroth her himself even if he knows her, if it is possible to betroth her himself, for the mitzvah is greater when performed by oneself than through a messenger, as with all commandments. Similarly, it is a greater mitzvah for a father to betroth his daughter himself and not through a messenger. And the reason we are not stringent about this and make matches without the groom seeing the bride is because before the betrothal he sees her, and if she does not find favor in his eyes, the match will be annulled. Other reasons have also been written on this matter. However, initially, it is certainly more proper for the groom to see the bride before the match, because if not, even if before the wedding she does not find favor in his eyes, he will be embarrassed to break the conditions. In our country, the custom has now spread that they see each other before the conditions, and it is a proper custom built on the foundation of law and peace.

We hold that in all matters of agency, an agent can appoint another agent. Since the agent of a person is like the person himself, he can appoint another agent. Furthermore, we hold that verbal instructions cannot be transferred to another agent. This means that only agency involving an action, such as delivering a get (divorce document) to a wife, allows the first agent to appoint a second agent. However, agency involving verbal instructions, like appointing an agent to write the get, does not give the agent the power to appoint another agent, as verbal instructions do not have the power to be transferred to another, as stated in Siman 120, and as we explained in Choshen Mishpat Siman 294.

Therefore, in the case of agency for betrothal, if the husband gives the agent money or a document to betroth a woman with that money or document, the agent can appoint another agent if he is unable to do it himself, such as if he falls ill or encounters another impediment, and he transfers to the second agent the betrothal means given to him by the husband. However, if the husband did not give him the betrothal means but merely told him to betroth her with any money he chooses, he cannot appoint another agent because this is considered verbal instructions.

Some say that in all cases of betrothal, an agent cannot appoint another agent, even if the husband gave the agent money or a document, because transferring the betrothal means is considered verbal instructions and is not like a get, where once the get is in the agent's hands, it is considered an action since he can deliver it against her will. But betrothal, which depends on her consent and she might refuse, is considered verbal instructions. 

Others differentiate between money and a document. They say that with a document, which must be used to betroth her, it is not considered verbal instructions. But with money, which can be exchanged for other money, it is considered verbal instructions. 

In the Jerusalem Talmud, Gitin Chapter 3, Halacha 5, it is explicitly stated according to the opinion that an agent cannot appoint another agent in betrothal, as it is raised as a question there and not resolved, and this also seems to be implied at the beginning of Chapter 4. And although our Talmud does not imply this, since it is not explicitly stated in our Talmud that an agent can appoint another agent, and the Jerusalem Talmud explicitly states that he cannot, we hold according to the Jerusalem Talmud. 

Nevertheless, it seems to me that our Talmud explicitly implies the opposite, as a gift is similar to betrothal in that one cannot force someone to accept a gift. And in our Talmud, it is said (Gitin 29) that a gift is like a get, and this is also the ruling in Choshen Mishpat there. This requires further investigation. 

[Also, the Jerusalem Talmud can be interpreted to mean that even in betrothal, an agent can appoint another agent, and the question "What is the difference?" is a rhetorical question, and the answer "Everything is in his power to divorce" means that because of this we might have distinguished, but it teaches us that we do not distinguish. However, at the beginning of Chapter 4 there, it cannot be interpreted this way. And there is a distinction between a gift and betrothal, as a gift is a benefit and one can confer a benefit in someone's absence, making it as if it has already come to his hand, unlike betrothal. This requires further investigation.]

Everyone is eligible to be an emissary for betrothal, whether a man or a woman, even a relative or someone otherwise disqualified, except for a deaf-mute, an insane person, and a minor, because they lack mental capacity, and a non-Jew, because he is not part of the covenant, and a slave, because he is not subject to the laws of betrothal. There is an opinion that a slave is valid to be an emissary for delivering a divorce document (get), and Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in Siman 141 considered this opinion as creating a doubt, see there, and certainly the same applies to betrothal.
