The reason he did not bring this opinion in this Siman is that most of our Rabbis disagree with it, and the main ruling is as such, but due to the stringency of the matter, we need to be concerned for this opinion as well, and because this opinion is in the context of divorce documents, where it is the Talmudic discussion, therefore Rabbeinu Beit Yosef relied on it there. [And so it appears from the Gra in Sk' 14, and what the Beit Shmuel wrote in Sk' 14 that the Beit Yosef wrote there that the same applies to betrothal, is not found there, and in any case, the law is true, and the words of the Avnei Miluim in Sk' 9 are not fundamental, because according to most opinions, even in a get, the verbal declaration is essential as written in Siman 136, and conversely, in a betrothal contract, if she knows what is written in the contract, the verbal declaration is not essential as written in Siman 32, and his words are perplexing, and scrutinize them well.]

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in paragraph 6: If someone sends a letter via a non-Jew to another Jew in a different location and appoints him as his agent to betroth a woman for him, some say that its status is like that of a get (divorce document), and some say that regarding betrothal, according to all opinions she is betrothed by Torah law. Certainly, even regarding a get, it is valid by Torah law in such a case, and those who are stringent about a get do so only out of stringency, as stated in section 141, where the matter is explained with God's help. And the custom has already spread to send a get by postal service, and all the more so regarding betrothal there is no concern, and so agreed the great Acharonim. Nevertheless, where there is no pressing need, one should not do so, but according to the law, there is no concern about this. And to send a letter by which the agent will betroth her with his money, there is no concern about this.

We hold that a messenger can serve as a witness in matters for which he is a messenger, and even though a person's messenger is considered like the person himself, the messenger is not disqualified from being a witness. This is because the party involved is disqualified from being a witness due to personal interest in the matter, whereas the messenger does not have a personal interest, so why should he be disqualified? On the contrary, he is an even better witness and strengthens the testimony since the matter was carried out through him. Therefore, when someone sends a messenger to betroth a woman for him and there is another person in whose presence the messenger betroths her, there are two witnesses to the betrothal. And if he appoints two messengers to betroth her, no other witnesses are needed, as they are both his messengers and his witnesses. The same applies to a divorce document (get) and monetary matters, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 121.

Even if the agent receives payment for his agency, he is not disqualified from testifying in this matter [Ran there], provided that his payment is fixed whether he completes the task or not. However, if there is a difference in his payment depending on whether he completes the task or not, it is obvious that he is disqualified from testifying, for there is no greater bias than this, as he desires for the betrothal to be valid and to receive greater payment. And since an agent can become a witness, if there were two agents who testified that they betrothed her on behalf of the sender and she denies it, she is not believed and she is fully betrothed.

The Tur writes: This applies when there is no monetary denial, such as if he betrothed her with a document or even with money and they say that he gave it for the sake of betrothal and she says it was for safekeeping. But if there is a monetary denial where she says that she did not receive anything at all – they are not believed, for they are considered interested parties in their testimony. For if it were as she says, they would be obligated to return what was given to them to the sender. And since there is a contradiction, they are required to take an oath, and any witness who needs to take an oath is not a valid witness. However, Rambam did not differentiate in this way, for it can be said that since from the Torah law there is no need for an oath and the Torah’s oath is only in a case of partial admission, therefore, even though rabbinically they are obligated to take an oath, it is not sufficient to disqualify their testimony. Therefore, in practice, if there is a contradiction between them, it is a case of doubtful betrothal, and so ruled our teacher, Beit Yosef, in paragraph 2. And one should not be surprised at Rambam’s reasoning, for after all they are interested parties in their testimony since rabbinically they are obligated to take an oath, and if they do not wish to take an oath, they must return the money, and there is no greater interest than this. One can say that if Elijah were to come and say that the witnesses gave her the money for betrothal, she would indeed be betrothed. The deficiency is on our part due to our lack of knowledge; therefore, one cannot remove her from a case of doubtful betrothal. Furthermore, there is no complete interest in their testimony, for if they do not testify about the betrothal and say he did not give them money to betroth her, they must take an oath against him, and if they testify, they must take an oath against her. In any case, they must take an oath, but their disqualification is not due to the interest, but because we say that any witness who needs to take an oath is not a valid witness, and this disqualification is only rabbinical [Choshen Mishpat, section 3].

Some of our rabbis maintain that in the case of betrothal with money, even if the woman acknowledges it, it is only considered doubtful betrothal. The reason is that since the testimony would not be effective without her acknowledgment, as the Tur writes, the entire testimony is validated by her acknowledgment, making it like a betrothal without witnesses [Ran and Rashba]. According to this opinion, when an agent serves as a witness in betrothal, it only applies to betrothal with a document and when the document does not contain an explicit statement. If it does contain an explicit statement, it is treated like money. Indeed, there is a dispute in the Jerusalem Talmud on this matter, and its conclusion seems to rule that if there is no contradiction between them, it is considered definite betrothal. The Rosh [Chapter 2, Section 4] brings this, but the Tur and Shulchan Aruch do not mention this opinion at all. Nevertheless, leading later authorities are inclined to be concerned with this view, and according to this, in all cases of betrothal with money, it is considered doubtful betrothal [see Choshen Mishpat, Siman 2 and Beit Shmuel, Siman 3]. 

It appears to me that even according to this opinion, if there is one witness testifying that the money was given to her for the sake of betrothal, there is no doubt, for in this case, one cannot impose an oath, as a supporting witness exempts from an oath, as written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 75. Therefore, even if she contradicts, it can be said that in such a case it is betrothal. Some say that even this does not help according to this opinion, because since they are only credible through the supporting witness, their testimony does not have the status of testimony [Beit Shmuel, end of Siman 5]. This is not clear, for if so, in any testimony where witnesses are disqualified and others testify to validate them, such as conspiring witnesses, we would also say that the first testimony is nullified because their validity is only through others. Certainly, their testimony stands once the disqualification is removed, and the same applies here. It is not comparable to the primary opinion that if she acknowledges them, it is not definite betrothal, because this is due to the fact that the main issue depends on her acknowledgment and there are no witnesses. But when it does not depend on her acknowledgment, and their disqualification is due to the obligation of an oath, when there is a witness who removes the oath, they remain valid [and this is also evident from the Maharik, brought by the Beit Shmuel himself].

However, when the messenger is one person and he has another person who testifies with him regarding the betrothal, even though this witness also assists and exempts him from an oath, there is still reason to doubt this because in such a case, the primary testimony relies on one of the witnesses of the betrothal. And in testimony, we require that the matter be concluded based on two witnesses equally [Choshen Mishpat, end of section 3]. Nevertheless, it is clear that for stringency, we should consider them as fit witnesses [as in the case of the Maharik, section 28, regarding being concerned about gifts given by a messenger and a witness. There is difficulty with the Beit Yosef who questioned him, and also difficulty with the Beit Shmuel who brought this leniently, and analyze carefully].

And some say that for another reason, an aiding witness does not help here, for our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 87, Se'if 6, that an aiding witness only exempts when the defendant makes a claim that can be believed without a migo (a form of legal argument), but if he is not believed except by force of a migo, which is based on another claim, he must swear as if he made the other claim, end quote. Therefore, they are still considered interested parties in their testimony, for they are compelled to say that they gave the money to the woman. If they say that they returned the money to the sender, they would have to swear, for in this case, they do not have an aiding witness. Thus, it is better for them to say that they gave it to the woman, for in this case, they have an aiding witness and are exempt from an oath. If they say this, they would still need to swear that they gave it to her, for a witness who requires an oath is not a valid witness.

And it seems to me that this is not comparable, because there, both claims are made by one person, such as in the case of a pledge where a person can exempt himself by claiming "I returned it" and "It was stolen," and for one claim he has a supporting witness but not for the other. However, here, the husband is not contradicting them and says as they do, and only she contradicts them. And since they have a supporting witness against her, they are properly exempt from an oath and are not considered as having a vested interest. Additionally, this is not a complete "miggo" (presumption) that should be judged like all other "miggots," as we explained in our work in Choshen Mishpat, section 296, paragraph 4, see there [and besides, the Shach disagrees there, see there].

There are those who say that if the husband initially exempted them from an oath at the time he sent them, allowing them to be trusted to say whatever they want - in any case, the marriage is certain [Choshen Mishpat 2], because there is no need for an oath at all even if he contradicted them, since they can say, "We returned it to the sender and he exempted us from an oath." But if the husband wants to exempt them from an oath now, it is not effective as it says in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 121, because one can say that due to the benefit of being exempted, they are testifying for him [Sema there, Siman 24]. And there are those who hesitate even if he exempted them earlier [Beit Shmuel, Siman 3], and there is no valid reason for this hesitation, and so it is implied from several major Rishonim that it is effective, and also in Choshen Mishpat there is no other opinion on this [and the Beit Shmuel's precision is not understood and in many places there is such in the Shulchan Aruch, and it is evident from Mordechai and Ritva in Perek 2 of Kiddushin, and there are those who validate even if he exempted them afterward, see Avnei Miluim, Siman 6].

And similarly, if he went with the agents and stood from afar and saw that they carried out their mission, it is effective, for now there is no need for an oath. However, according to the opinion of our teacher, the Rema in Choshen Mishpat there, it is a matter of doubtful betrothal, and how can valid betrothal be made based on it? This implies that the betrothal is completed only by the husband's declaration and not by witnesses. Therefore, if there are witnesses that the husband saw the agents, they are certainly witnesses to the betrothal, for now we do not need the husband's statement. Similarly, in the matter that was explained that the husband is exempt from an oath, there need to be witnesses for this, for otherwise it would imply that all the essentials of the betrothal are completed by the husband and not by witnesses, and they are not valid betrothal, as it is when completed by the woman, according to the opinion explained in paragraph 9, and this requires further examination in practice. It turns out that betrothal by agents is not valid betrothal unless they betroth with other witnesses, and if they themselves are the witnesses, they should betroth by a document that does not involve a perutah, and in this case we will not be stringent to say perhaps there is a perutah elsewhere. And if they betroth with money, there need to be witnesses that the husband handed it to them and that they handed it to her for the sake of betrothal, and then there is no doubt about the betrothal.

If all acknowledge the betrothal but she says she was betrothed with a prutah and they say she was betrothed with a maneh that the husband gave them to betroth her with – the agents must take an oath of heset that they gave her the maneh, and she is exempt from taking an oath since even according to the agents' words, the money was given to her for the purpose of betrothal, and it belongs to her. Why should she take an oath [Beit Yosef in the name of Re'i]? And although since the witnesses require an oath, they are not complete witnesses for the betrothal as mentioned, and according to this, she should return the betrothal money and why not take an oath, indeed the betrothal money is not returned in any case, for in any case, it is a case of doubtful betrothal and how can we say she should return the betrothal money and they will come to say there is no betrothal at all and seize betrothal with her sister as mentioned in Siman 50, therefore we do not allow her to return the betrothal money and hence she does not need to take an oath [Mekane].

The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 3, Law 15: Anyone who appoints an agent to receive betrothal must do so in the presence of witnesses. However, a man who appoints an agent to betroth a woman for him does not need to do so in the presence of witnesses, as there is no need for witnesses in the man's appointment of an agent except to verify the matter's truth. Therefore, if the agent and the sender admit to it, witnesses are not needed, similar to an agent for delivering a divorce document or an agent authorized to separate tithes for him. In all such cases, a person's agent is like the person himself and does not require witnesses. This is the end of his words.

And behold, he also ruled similarly in Chapter 6 concerning divorce, that an agent for delivery does not need witnesses, but an agent for receiving does need witnesses. The Rambam likened betrothal to divorce in this matter. However, in Chapter 9 of laws concerning divorce, Law 32, he himself explained that when there are no witnesses signed on the divorce document, then two witnesses are needed for the agency. Therefore, in betrothal, where there are no signing witnesses, why should we not require witnesses as in the case of a divorce document? This is the question of the RaMACH that the Kessef Mishneh cited, as mentioned by the Maggid Mishneh in the Mishneh Torah.

It appears to me that according to the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, it is certain that there is no relevance to witnesses in the context of agency throughout the entire Torah. Even in matters of divorce (gittin) and betrothal (kiddushin), although there is no matter of a forbidden relationship (davar she-be'eravah) with fewer than two witnesses, this applies at the time of the betrothal or divorce when the agent is betrothing or divorcing her, but not at the time of the agency. However, when she appoints an agent to receive the betrothal or the divorce, she needs two witnesses for the agency, not because of the agency itself, but because her body was initially forbidden to the entire world, and after the divorce, she is permitted. In betrothal, it is the opposite. Therefore, how is it possible for her status to change from forbidden to permitted or from permitted to forbidden in a matter that requires testimony without the hearing of witnesses?

Even though the agent of a person is like the person themselves, and it is as if she received the betrothal or the divorce, nevertheless, in the end, the witnesses did not hear any verbal statement from her. How can her status change from forbidden to permitted or from permitted to forbidden without hearing witnesses? But the husband's body does not change at all, as he is always permitted to all women. The main issue of his forbidden relationship is only at the time of the betrothal and divorce, when she becomes forbidden to the entire world or permitted to the entire world. And he also forbids himself to her relatives or other forbidden relationships through betrothal and is released from his obligations through divorce. This is similar to other acts of agency, but his body does not change from forbidden to permitted or from permitted to forbidden.

The requirement for witnesses of the agency in the case of a divorce without witnesses of the signing is a different matter. According to our established law, witnesses of delivery (mesirah) finalize the divorce. The verse "and he shall write for her" refers to writing the get (divorce document) for her sake, and if it is not written for her sake, it is not a valid get at all. Therefore, even though there are two witnesses at the time of delivery, the main validity of the get also depends on it being written for her sake. Who testifies to this? When there are signed witnesses on the get, it is as if they testify that it was written for her sake. But without witnesses, who testifies to this? Therefore, two witnesses are required to hear when she appoints him as an agent to deliver this get, and it is as if they know that it was written for her sake, like the signed witnesses.

And regarding what the Rambam wrote, "If the agent and the sender admit, there is no need for witnesses," our master the Rema wrote that an admission is only considered valid if made in the presence of witnesses, in the manner of a formal admission. This means that he must say, "You are my witnesses," or make the admission in a complete and formal manner and not just in casual conversation, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 81. And even though the claims of "I was jesting with you" or "so as not to make an oath" do not apply in matters of betrothal as they do in monetary law, nevertheless, one can give another pretext, such as to ensure that someone else does not precede him, or something similar. There are those who want to say that this applies only to the agency of receipt and not to the agency of delivery, but this is not the main opinion and there is no distinction in this matter. The fundamental law is that this only applies in cases of contradiction, when the sender denies appointing the agent. However, if he admitted before witnesses that he appointed the agent, he can no longer deny it, even if the witnesses were not present at the time of the appointment. According to his opinion, agency for delivery does not require witnesses, but for receipt, witnesses are required at the time of the appointment, as stated.

Some of our sages maintain that even for the delivery of a marriage proposal, witnesses are required, as any matter of marital status cannot be established with fewer than two witnesses. However, for a get (divorce document), witnesses are not necessary for the delivery because the get itself serves as proof, which is not the case with betrothal. According to this, if the betrothal is done through a document, witnesses are also not required for betrothal. It seems to me, however, that this is only when witnesses sign the document, but if he instructs to betroth her only with witnesses of delivery, it is invalid.

Nevertheless, the Tur rules in Siman 141 that even for the delivery of a get, witnesses are required. According to this, witnesses are also required for a betrothal document, and although there might be reasons to differentiate, in practice it does not seem appropriate to distinguish, and if there were no witnesses, it would be considered doubtful betrothal according to this opinion.

Some of our Rabbis are inclined to say the opposite, that in the case of betrothal, even for a receiving agent, witnesses are not required. This is not comparable to a get (divorce document), which is intended to permit her, and cannot be done without witnesses. In the case of betrothal, since she is forbidding herself, just as the husband's acknowledgment of the agency suffices, so too does her acknowledgment. However, we should be concerned and stringent, and consider this opinion about receiving agents without witnesses, thereby requiring a get (divorce document). This is also the ruling of our teacher, the Rema, in that location.

If someone sends a messenger to betroth a woman and the messenger claims that he betrothed her, and the woman also says that she was betrothed, but the witnesses to the betrothal are not present, and the messenger and the woman say that the witnesses have died or have gone abroad, even though she is presumed to be a married woman because of the presumption that a messenger fulfills his mission, nevertheless, if another man comes and betroths her, she requires a divorce from both men. This is because we only rely on the presumption that a messenger fulfills his mission to be stringent, not lenient.

And even though a man and woman who come before us and are presumed to be husband and wife cannot have their betrothal to another man take effect, even without witnesses, relying only on their behavior as husband and wife, these presumptions are not comparable. In that case, the presumption is based on their own actions, but here the knowledge of the husband's status comes only from the presumption that the messenger fulfilled his mission. Therefore, even if there are witnesses that the husband appointed the messenger, since there are no witnesses to the actual betrothal, we are concerned about the betrothal by the other man.

However, if they were living together as husband and wife, even though he did not see the witnesses of the betrothal, since they subsequently lived as husband and wife, we are not concerned about the betrothal by the other man. We do not investigate the presumption of how the betrothal occurred because it is known to all that they are husband and wife. Consequently, the presumption that the messenger fulfilled his mission is strengthened.

Rabbi Moses Isserles (the Rema) wrote: If there are no witnesses in the matter and the sender denies having appointed the agent, some say she is in a state of doubtful betrothal, while others say she is not betrothed at all—and the latter opinion appears to be the main one. The reason is that any single witness in a case of contradiction is considered nothing, and even though he performed an act and betrothed her in the presence of witnesses, nevertheless, since he (the sender) denies and says that he did not appoint him as an agent and there are no witnesses before us that he appointed him as an agent, this is nothing. Even if a father received the betrothal for his adult daughter and she denies that she made him her agent—she is not betrothed when there are no witnesses before us regarding the agency, and all the more so with another person when the woman denies that she made him her agent to receive it, for it is a great principle that a single witness in a case of contradiction is not believed. However, if there is another witness for the agent who testifies like him, or if there are two agents who are fit to testify—they are believed, for an agent can become a witness as has been stated.

And regarding his ruling leniently, it is difficult [to understand] (Chamudei Daniel and Beit Shmuel), since he performed a significant act to sanctify her, it is difficult to release her without a get (divorce document). It seems that we compel him to give her a get, because she is forbidden to others, as she does not know whether he is telling the truth or the messenger, and this is not similar to the case of testimony by secondhand report, where if the first witness contradicts the second, the second is not believed. For the messenger is not a witness but rather claims he was appointed as a messenger and testifies about himself, not about others (Beit Shmuel, sub-paragraph 11). And even though the sender can say, "I will not give a get because I do not wish to forbid myself to her relatives," nevertheless, since she has not committed any wrongdoing and the messenger stands and asserts that he was appointed as a messenger, we compel him to give a get. However, if she dies without a get, the sender is not forbidden to her relatives even according to the primary opinion, since he denies the agency, and only concerning the woman herself, who cannot contradict him, she is considered doubtfully betrothed (ibid.). And all this applies to the agency of betrothal with money, but regarding the agency of betrothal with a document, it is treated like a get, as will be explained in section 141, where it is deemed like a third party and the betrothal is doubtful (so it seems to me, and see Beit Shmuel).

The Tur writes in the name of the Rosh that even if one was not explicitly appointed as an agent but merely expressed his desire for a certain woman and told another to arrange the match for him, and that other person went and betrothed her without explicit appointment as an agent—she is betrothed to him. However, if he did not tell him to arrange the match and the other person betrothed her for him—she is not betrothed, and we do not suspect that he made him an agent. This applies whether the one performing the betrothal is his father or a stranger. Even if he later agrees to the betrothal, it is meaningless. And it is clear that according to those who hold that agency requires witnesses, he must express his desire before witnesses and request that he arrange the match. The reason that explicit agency is not required for betrothal seems to be because one can benefit a person in his absence, and since he requested that the match be arranged, it is as if he appointed him as an agent. Benefiting someone without their knowledge is considered as agency. However, if he did not request the match, even though he expressed his desire, it is meaningless. Expressing one's desire in betrothal does not have the same status as in divorce, as will be explained in Siman 141. Therefore, it is not effective even if he later agrees to the betrothal because the previous action has no substance. But if he requested that the match be arranged, it is considered as true agency, as stated.

Rabbeinu Meir HaLevi also wrote: If a father presented the matter before his son, indicating that he wants to betroth a woman to him, and the son remained silent, and then the father went and betrothed her to him – this constitutes a valid betrothal. This is because, out of respect for his father, the son remained silent, effectively appointing him as his agent to betroth her. However, with another person in a similar situation, it would be a doubtful betrothal, end quote. The reason is that when the agent presented the matter before the principal, indicating his desire to appoint him as his agent to betroth her on his behalf, and the principal remained silent, it is uncertain whether he agreed to appoint him as his agent and his silence is considered as consent, or perhaps he did not agree and did not bother to respond. But with a father, it cannot be said that he did not bother to respond, and his silence is considered as consent. The reason he did not explicitly appoint him as his agent is due to the embarrassment of having to tell his father to act as his agent. There are those who disagree and hold that even with a father, it is only a doubtful betrothal, for it is possible to say that the son remained silent not out of embarrassment but because he did not consent or was uncertain about the matter. Although we have explained that with another person, it can be said that he did not bother to respond at all, but with a father, it cannot be said so, still, to consider it a definite betrothal is difficult.

And know, that although this opinion differs from that of the Rosh which we brought in the Talmudic discussion [where the Rosh interprets it as referring to the son and the Ramah interprets it as referring to the father], nevertheless, in practice, it is possible that they do not actually disagree. This is also implied by the language of the Tur, and it could be that even the Rosh agrees that when the agent expresses before the sender his willingness to be an agent and the sender remains silent, it constitutes a doubtful betrothal. And although our teacher, Rabbi Yosef Karo, in his major work, wrote that they disagree, nevertheless, in the Shulchan Aruch it implies that he retracted this, as he arranged both laws in sections 4 and 5 without mentioning a disagreement [and so the Beit Shmuel also wrote that they do not disagree], and even in his major work, his intention is that according to the Rosh this law is not proven, but nevertheless, one can say that they do not disagree in practice.

It is straightforward that if the agent denies his agency and she claims that he betrothed her on behalf of the sender, and there are no witnesses, she has rendered herself as a "piece of forbidden meat" (i.e., she is forbidden to others), and he must give her a get (divorce document). However, we do not force him to give a get if he does not acknowledge the agency of the agent.

A messenger who deviates from his mission - his mission is nullified, as stated in Choshen Mishpat there. And not only in the case of a complete deviation, such as if he was instructed to betroth her on a condition and he betrothed her unconditionally or vice versa, but even if he changed the location, for example, if he was told "Betroth this woman for me in a certain place" and he betrothed her in a different place - she is not betrothed, because he can say that in this place it is agreeable to me for her to be betrothed since I have many friends there and they will not speak ill of me, unlike in another place (Gemara 50). All the more so if he changed something regarding the condition. However, if he was told "Betroth this woman for me, and she is in such-and-such place" and he betrothed her in a different place - she is betrothed, because it was not said out of insistence but merely to indicate her location, as he did not say "Betroth her in such-and-such place" but rather "and she is in such-and-such place." The same law applies to the mission of delivering a divorce document, as stated in Siman 141.

If someone appoints an agent to betroth a specific woman for him, and the agent goes and betroths her for himself, this is considered deceitful behavior. Rambam in Hilchot Ishut, Chapter 9, Halacha 17, writes that such a person is called wicked, similar to a poor person who is turning over a cake (to eat it), and another comes and takes it away. However, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch do not write that this person is called wicked, because they follow their reasoning in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 237, that in the case of a gift or found object, the person is not called wicked. And betrothal is not worse than that. The Rambam's opinion is that in any situation, such a person is called wicked. Nevertheless, what was done is done, and if she knew that the agent betrothed her for himself and she agreed and accepted, she is betrothed to the agent. Even if he was not appointed as an agent but was told, "When you go there, betroth that specific woman for me," and he went and betrothed her for himself, this is still considered deceitful behavior because the person relied on him and he deceived him, even though he was not specifically appointed as an agent to go on his behalf, but rather incidentally when he went on his own business to betroth her on his behalf. It seems to me that in such a case, even according to the Rambam, he is not called wicked but rather a deceiver.

The translation of the passage:

And specifically, if he betrothed her with his own money, but if he betrothed her with the sender's money – there is no betrothal here, because it is considered theft in his hand, and one who betroths with stolen property, she is not betrothed, as stated in section 28. And some say that this is specifically when the agent does not have other money now to replace the sender's money and give it to the sender, or even if he has and there is a concern to replace it, such as if the sender's money is of better quality or if he betrothed her with an object of the sender, but if he betrothed her with the sender's money and the agent has other similar money to give to the sender – she is betrothed [Beit Shmuel section 21], because in this case it is not considered that he betrothed her with stolen property since he betrothed her with his own. And there are those who disagree with this, saying that this is only applicable when someone deposits money and it is permitted to use it and return other money to the depositor, but in the case of an agent, he is a complete thief and has no permission to replace it, and wherever the money is, it belongs to the sender unless he gave him permission to use and replace it [Mekneh]. And it appears that they do not disagree, for certainly if the sender gave him tied-up money, he has no permission to replace it, but if he gave him open money and the sender knows that the agent also has money and he mixes it with his own money, and it is not the custom of the world to be particular about this money or that money – certainly the main opinion is like the first opinion. And if you ask, when he betrothed her with the sender's money, why shouldn't she be betrothed to the sender like in a sale in Choshen Mishpat section 183? There, we say that the seller transferred ownership to the sender, but in betrothal, how can she be betrothed to the sender when he did not betroth her on his behalf [there and Even HaEzer, and see Taz and Drisha, and what Beit Shmuel wrote that one cannot betroth with a coin, we have already written in section 27 that this is not so, and the Even HaEzer also wrote so].

Behold, this is not a novelty at all when the agent betroths her for himself, that she is betrothed, for why should she not be betrothed to him? Just because he acted deceitfully, should she not be betrothed to him? Rather, even if when he came to the woman, he told her that he came to betroth her on behalf of his sender and all his words until the betrothal were as such, and at the time of the betrothal, he betrothed her for himself, and she understood that he betrothed her for himself and did not object – she is also betrothed. And we do not say that since until the moment of the betrothal their intention was for the sender, therefore we should say that when he said "for me," it meant on behalf of his mission to betroth you for the sender, and even though they changed their minds, it is considered "matters of the heart" – we do not say this. For the interpretation of "for me" is literally "for me," and this is not "matters of the heart." And since both of them say that their intention was for the agent – she is properly betrothed to him when he betrothed her with his own money, as was written.

However, if she says that she did not understand at all that he was marrying her to himself, and she thought that he was marrying her to the one who sent him – she is not betrothed to the agent. Certainly, she accepted the betrothal based on what he initially told her, that he was betrothing her to someone else, and she is believed when she says so. It is also clear that she is not betrothed to the one who sent the agent, as the agent did not betroth her on his behalf. Therefore, she does not need a get (divorce document) from either of them [Taz]. There is someone who is stringent and requires a get from both, but there is no reason for this [Beit Shmuel], except perhaps due to the concern of onlookers [Prisha], who might say that a married woman is being released without a get. Therefore, if this matter became known to all the onlookers at the time of the betrothal – that the agent deviated from his instructions and she did not consent to be betrothed to him – it is obvious that there is no concern here [and what the Tur did not mention is because it is obvious].

If the agent says, "Behold, you are betrothed to me," and then immediately says that he made a mistake and intended to betroth her on behalf of the sender, Rabbi Rema writes that he is believed when he claims he made a mistake. There are grounds to support the claim of a mistake because he is the agent of the sender, and there is a presumption that an agent performs his agency. Until the betrothal, he spoke with her on behalf of the sender, so how could he suddenly betroth her for himself? It is likely that she would not agree to be betrothed to him, and no sensible person would do such a thing. Therefore, he is believed. 

Regarding the status of the betrothal, some say that she is betrothed to the first one, meaning the sender, and "to me" refers to my agency, as stated in section 31. This applies if he says that he said "to me" without any intention, and it is automatically interpreted as referring to the agency. However, this interpretation does not seem to be supported by the authorities. Certainly, he must betroth her again on behalf of the sender because the initial betrothal is invalid. She is not betrothed to the sender, nor is she betrothed to the agent himself, even if there is no issue with the money, such as if he mixed the sender's money with his own or if the sender instructed him to betroth her with his own money. Since he said he made a mistake and he is believed, as a mistaken consecration is not a consecration, just as if he intended to say "terumah" and said "ma'aser" instead, and the like. Additionally, she says that she does not wish to be betrothed to the agent, and the circumstances support this, making the betrothal invalid.

However, some say that the agent must swear that he made a mistake and did not intend to betroth her for himself. It appears to me that this only applies if she does not protest and it is acceptable to her to be betrothed to the agent. But if she protests and says she does not want him, and he did not speak with her on his behalf or did speak but she did not agree, and she remained silent because she did not understand that he was betrothing her for himself, then his oath is irrelevant. She is believed, as explained, and even if he intended to betroth her for himself, it is of no consequence.

Therefore, what our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote that there are those who are stringent and require a get (divorce document) from the agent – this is only when there is no clear proof that the agent made a mistake, and there is no clear evidence that she did not agree to the agent, such as if he spoke with her and perhaps she might consent to marry him, and she did not explicitly tell him that she does not desire this. These matters depend on the opinion of the local court to investigate and inquire thoroughly. And when it is evident from all sides that he made a mistake in his words – she does not require a get without cause, and the agent can betroth her again on behalf of the sender. But if the matters are not so clear, it is certainly difficult to release her without a get from the sender, and this also appears from the source of the law in Mordechai, Chapter 3, see there, and this is agreed upon by the great later authorities.

And know, regarding what was explained that if someone transgressed and betrothed her for himself, he is considered deceitful or wicked according to the Rambam – this applies if the woman would have consented to be betrothed to the sender. But if she did not consent at all to be betrothed to the sender, only to the agent, then it is proper that he betrothed her and this is not deceit at all. However, if there is time to inform the sender that she does not consent to be betrothed to him, it is proper to inform him. And if he fears that by the time he informs him, someone else might precede him, then this is also not necessary.

The Sages said (Nazir 12b) that if someone tells his agent, "Go and betroth a woman for me," without specifying a particular woman, and the agent dies and it is unknown whether he betrothed a woman or not, the presumption is that he did betroth a woman, because there is a presumption that an agent completes his agency. Since it is not known which woman he betrothed, he is forbidden to any woman who has relatives that are forbidden to him as incestuous relationships, which are six forbidden relationships: her sister, her daughter, her granddaughter (daughter's daughter), her grandson's daughter, her mother, and her maternal grandmother. When detailed, they are seven forbidden relationships, because a sister is counted as two — from the father and from the mother. He cannot marry a woman who has such relatives, because perhaps his agent betrothed her sister, or her daughter, or her mother. But a woman who does not have such relatives is permitted to marry him, and there is no concern for secondary forbidden relationships because their prohibition is rabbinic. Therefore, if he wants to betroth a woman who has such relatives, he has no solution unless these relatives come and say that they were not betrothed by his agent. Some say that their statement does not help to permit her, and only if they marry other men is it clarified that they are single and permitted to him. The reasoning behind this dispute will be explained further with God's help in section 40, as noted there.

Our Sages further stated that even if a woman has such close relatives, if these relatives were married at the time he appointed the agent, even if later, before the agent’s death, they became widowed or divorced in a way that he still had time to betroth them, nevertheless, he is permitted to marry this woman, and we do not suspect that the agent betrothed one of her relatives. They explained the reasoning that since at the time he appointed the agent they were married, a person appoints an agent only for something that is currently possible, not for something that is not currently possible. There is a version in the Gemara that says he cannot appoint an agent for this. Therefore, our early Rabbis wrote that anything a person himself cannot do, he cannot appoint an agent to do. He cannot appoint an agent to betroth this woman after she gets divorced because since he cannot currently betroth her, he cannot appoint an agent now for this. If the agent betroths her on his behalf, it is invalid because the agency is not in effect. He would need to appoint the agent after she becomes widowed or divorced when he himself has the ability to betroth her. Some say that from a legal standpoint, he could appoint the agent, but it is not customary to appoint an agent for something that one cannot currently do, and we do not concern ourselves with this. However, if he did appoint the agent for this, the agency is valid. We have already explained this dispute in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 182; see there. It depends on the different versions in the Gemara as we have written.

The reason for this prohibition, which our sages forbade for all women, is according to some of our rabbis because it is a penalty for commanding him to betroth any woman without specifying a particular woman. For he should not have involved himself in a situation of potential prohibition and possible error. For according to the law, there is no prohibition here, as there is no absolute presumption that an agent does the agency, since it does not depend on him, and perhaps the woman will not agree to be betrothed on behalf of the sender. Additionally, how can we forbid him from all women, as we should follow the majority, and the majority of women in the world are not relatives of the woman who was betrothed to the agent. And one cannot say that any fixed situation is considered as if it is half and half, for from the Torah, the law of fixed applies only when the prohibition is distinct by itself and the permission by itself, like in the case of nine stores explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 110. And you should know that this is only a penalty, for otherwise, all minors whose fathers are far away would be forbidden forever due to the concern that perhaps their father accepted betrothal for them through an agent. Rather, it is certainly only a penalty, and it is a penalty for him, but not for others.

But there are some of our rabbis who hold that it is a definitive law, that all minors—even if their father has died—are permitted, because they are presumed to be single, and the presumption that an agent fulfills his mission does not remove them from their presumption. Furthermore, there is a presumption about the father that when he betroths his daughter, he will inform her and many people, and he will not be silent so that she would become corrupted. However, when this man comes to betroth a single woman, and we are concerned that perhaps the agent has betrothed one of her relatives, although each of the relatives has a presumption of being single, their presumption does not help this one who wants to be betrothed, since the relatives are not before us that we might say their presumption would be effective. Indeed, if the relatives come and say, "We were not betrothed," they are certainly permitted because of their presumption of being single to be betrothed to others. And since they are trustworthy about themselves, they are also trustworthy regarding this one [Ran, Chapter 6 of Gittin, in the name of Ramban]. The presumption that an agent fulfills his mission is a strong presumption, for most women desire to be betrothed, and more than a man desires to marry, a woman desires to be married. And there is also a definitive law about this, that the prohibition is evident to itself—that is, known married women—and the permission is evident to itself—that is, all single women are permitted because of their presumption of being single. And we are in doubt about the relatives of this one, whether they are from the singles or the married [It appears to me, and see Ran there who questions how one witness is believed, and it can be said that they are believed about themselves because of their presumption, and consequently, she is permitted because the prohibition is removed. Pay careful attention].

There is a practical halachic difference between these two opinions: according to the reasoning of the law, she is permitted when the relatives say that she was not betrothed. According to the reasoning of a penalty, their statement does not help, because according to the law she is permitted even without their statement, so what would their statement add? Therefore, it only helps if they stood and betrothed, for they would not perform a forbidden act, and then it is necessarily impossible for us to prohibit her to him. This is the basis of the two opinions we wrote in Siman 36. Another practical difference: if he did not pay attention and betrothed a woman, according to the reasoning of a penalty, the betrothal is valid because according to the law she is permitted. According to the reasoning of the law, it is a doubtful betrothal, because perhaps he betrothed her sister or another forbidden relation and his betrothal does not take effect with her. Until it is completely clarified that all her relatives are unmarried, then the betrothal is a valid betrothal. [See Beit Shmuel 31].

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 11 that there are those who say that if a man instructed a messenger to betroth a specific woman and the messenger died, he is immediately forbidden to marry her relatives based on the presumption that a messenger carries out his mission. However, there are those who disagree. The reason for the dispute is as follows: According to the reasoning of a penalty, if he instructed the messenger to betroth a specific woman, the penalty does not apply as it does when he gave a general instruction. Therefore, he should not be forbidden to marry her relatives. However, if the reasoning is based on law, just as he is generally forbidden to marry all women, he is likewise forbidden to marry her relatives when he specified. Nevertheless, all the great later authorities dispute the Rema. They hold that even according to the reasoning of a penalty, here it is a definite law, and only in a general instruction do we impose a penalty on him forbidding all women. But when he specified a particular woman, it is clear that we say the presumption that a messenger carries out his mission applies, and he is forbidden to marry her relatives. And even if we say that we do not apply the presumption of a messenger carrying out his mission leniently, we certainly apply it stringently. Consequently, her relatives are forbidden to him by law due to the doubt.

And it appears to me like the words of our master, the Rema, that according to the law, there is no need to be concerned at all, even according to the opinion that we say there is a presumption that an agent completes his agency even for leniency. For here, it is not in his control at all, and even if in a general case there is reason for concern because many women wish to marry, but when specifying a particular woman, who says she consented to be betrothed to him? And even though nevertheless, from the Rabbis, there is reason to be concerned that perhaps she consented, still it is clear that if this woman wishes to marry another, we cannot forbid her due to the agency of this one, for she has the presumption of being unmarried and she stands and declares that she was not betrothed to the agent of this one. And according to this, if we say that the presumption of this woman also benefits her relatives, it is clear that there is no prohibition on him to betroth the relatives for the reasons explained, except that according to the one who holds that in the case of a general woman it is completely forbidden by law with all women, it is explained that he holds that the presumption of this woman does not benefit another. And if so, there is reason to forbid them at least from the Rabbis, but according to the one who holds it is a penalty, he does not hold this reasoning. And if so, they are permitted - whether due to the reason of presumption or because the presumption of completing the agency does not apply here as mentioned, and a penalty does not apply here since he specified the woman. And our master, the Rema, said well. Nevertheless, in practice, it is proper to be stringent according to all opinions until the matter is clarified.

If one appointed an agent and then nullified the agency before the betrothal, the agency is nullified. However, if the nullification occurred after the betrothal, the nullification is ineffective, even within the time it takes to say the words of the betrothal, similar to the laws of divorce as discussed in Siman 141. For in the matters of divorce and betrothal, it is established that the time it takes to say the words is considered as if it were after that time, as mentioned in Siman 38 and Siman 49, and this is the opinion of the majority of the decisors. However, according to the opinion that this is only a stringency, as mentioned there, certainly one must be stringent that if she accepted betrothal from another man, she would require a divorce from him. And if it is not known whether the nullification was before or after the betrothal, it is considered a doubtful betrothal.

This nullification is specifically verbal and in the presence of two witnesses, and it must be explicitly nullified. A mere expression of intent is not effective because we hold that an expression of intent in the case of a divorce document is not valid, and the same applies to betrothal. Perhaps here an expression of intent is effective as a stringency since it is still before the betrothal and it is similar to monetary laws where an expression of intent is effective in several matters, but matters of the heart are certainly meaningless. Ideally, the nullification should be in the presence of the agent himself, as the Sages decreed regarding a divorce document, as written there, to prevent complications and they prohibited nullifying it not in the presence of the agent. Nevertheless, after the fact, if it was nullified, it is nullified even not in his presence. 

And perhaps you will ask, what concern is there in betrothal if it is nullified not in his presence? In the case of divorce, there is a concern that she will not know about the nullification and will marry someone else, but in betrothal, what concern is there if she thinks she is betrothed? However, here too there is a concern. If she thinks she is betrothed, she might accept betrothal from another and not worry about the first betrothal, when in fact she is single. Additionally, since she believes she is betrothed, she will remain single and not marry another, preferring to remain with the one she believes betrothed her ("better to sit with a friend"). Or, the betrothal may reach her before it is nullified, and she might think it has already been nullified and marry another.

Rambam and the Tur did not write this law at all because these concerns are indeed uncommon, as is evident. Also, in the Gemara, this is not mentioned regarding betrothal. However, from the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Gittin, it seems so, and this is how our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, ruled, and this is our established practice. 

[And even though according to our Talmud in Gittin 33a, according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nachman, whose opinions we follow, and based on the reasoning explained there, this does not apply to betrothal, nevertheless, according to the reasoning of the Jerusalem Talmud, there is a concern, and consider this carefully.]

If someone appoints an agent to betroth a specific woman on his behalf, and the agent goes and betroths her for him, but the sender himself betroths one of her close relatives who are prohibited to marry each other (like her mother, daughter, or sister), and it is not known which of them was betrothed first – both need a get (divorce document) and are forbidden to him. However, if it is known who was betrothed first – she is the one who is betrothed to him, and the second one does not need a get because betrothal does not take effect with a close relative. Even if the agent betrothed her first, we do not say that it is evident that the sender does not want the agency to take effect because he immediately betrothed her close relative; certainly, he nullified the agency in his heart. This is because we have already explained that revealing one's intention in one's heart is not significant. If he explicitly nullified it, and we know that the nullification occurred before the agent's betrothal – it has already been explained that the agent's betrothal is nullified, and consequently, the sender’s own betrothal is a definite betrothal. If it is not known whether the nullification occurred before the betrothal or not – the matter returns to being doubtful, and both need a get and are forbidden to him.

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 9, Law 18: If someone appoints an agent to betroth a woman for him and the agent goes and betroths her, the agent says, "I betrothed her for myself," and the woman says, "I was betrothed to the first one who sent him." If the agent did not act with witnesses, the agent is forbidden to marry her relatives, and she is permitted to marry his relatives. The woman is forbidden to marry the relatives of the one who sent the agent, and the one who sent the agent is permitted to marry her relatives. If the agent is established by witnesses, she is betrothed to the first one. If she says, "I do not know to whom I was betrothed, whether to the sender or the agent," if the agent is not established by witnesses, she is betrothed to the second one. If it is established that he was the agent, both must give her a divorce. If they wish, one gives a divorce, and the other marries her. End quote. His source is from the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 3 of Kiddushin, and he made this ruling akin to the case where a man says to a woman, "I betrothed you," and she says, "You did not betroth me." He is forbidden to marry her relatives, and she is permitted to marry his relatives, as stated in Siman 48, that anyone who admits to the betrothal makes himself forbidden to the relatives as with forbidden relationships where betrothal does not take effect. And all this applies when the witnesses to the betrothal are not present or do not remember how it happened. The details of the laws concerning the giving of divorce will be explained there, with the help of Heaven.

And one should not wonder why, when a man did not appoint a messenger with witnesses, it is permissible for the sender to marry her relatives. After all, he says that he appointed the messenger, and she claims that she was betrothed to the messenger. One could say that there is no reason to prohibit the sender from marrying her relatives, for the primary reason for the prohibition is because of the agency. Here, the messenger stands and claims that he annulled the agency and betrothed her to himself. The messenger has the power to permit the sender to marry her relatives, and she does not have the power to prohibit him. This situation is no different than any woman who claims that Reuven betrothed her, and Reuven denies it. Here, too, the messenger, who stands in place of Reuven, denies it. Nevertheless, some of our Rabbis disagree with this and hold that he is also prohibited from marrying her relatives.

And similarly, regarding his ruling that if the agent was established with witnesses, she is betrothed to the first [principal], and the agent stands and protests, even though he made me [an agent] with witnesses, I rescinded my agency and betrothed her to myself [there is a difficulty]. How can we permit her to the principal? However, when we scrutinize his words, he did not say "if he made him with witnesses," as he said at the beginning "if he did not make him with witnesses," but rather, in truth, there is no difference whether he made him with witnesses or without witnesses. Being established is another matter, such as if he brought witnesses with him or a validated document that this agent was made with witnesses. Since the agent himself exerted effort before the betrothal to bring proof that he is the agent of so-and-so, he is not believed to say that his intention changed at that moment. And since she claims with certainty that she was betrothed to the principal, we believe her, and the agent's words are nothing, and it is like a claim against what is established for us and against the presumption. Nevertheless, it is certain that the agent is forbidden to her relatives [according to the Rambam], for he made himself like a single witness. And it is possible that he is also compelled to give a divorce, as it is written in Siman 48. Some of our Rabbis disagree about this and hold that there is no difference between being established and not being established, and even if he is established, she is not betrothed to the first one with this betrothal. Rather, the agent is compelled to give a divorce, and he is also compelled to betroth her again on behalf of the principal. [See Beit Shmuel on Siman 37, and it seems to me that the intention of the Rema is as I have written, and with this, we avoid all doubts. Examine this well.]

And regarding the ruling that if she says, "I do not know to whom I was betrothed," if there is no established testimony, she is betrothed to the second one. If there is established testimony, both must give a get (divorce document). The reasoning is simple: when his agency is not established, and he claims with certainty while she is uncertain, he is believed, for there is no reason not to trust him. However, when there is established testimony, the presumption is that she contradicts him. Therefore, both must give a get, as the matter is balanced: he claims with certainty, and his agency is established. No one disputes this ruling.

If, after the agent (shaliach) said, "I betrothed her to myself," he retracted and said, "I thought I had betrothed her to myself, but I remembered that I betrothed her to my sender," if this is established by witnesses, then we say that there is a presumption that an agent carries out his agency, and he is believed to retract and say that he was mistaken. The agent is permitted to her relatives, and the betrothal is certainly valid for the first one. However, without being established by witnesses, it is indeed possible that he withdrew from his agency as he initially stated, and he is not believed now to retract, and he remains prohibited to her relatives, and the first one requires a new betrothal. And when she said, "I do not know," and the agent retracted, if it is established by witnesses, it seems it is no worse than if she had contradicted him initially. But without being established, the law is not as it was previously decided that she is betrothed to the second one; rather, certainly in this case, he is believed to retract, and she is not betrothed to him and needs a get (divorce document) from him and also from the first one, or the first one should betroth her anew.

Some say that if an agent betroths a woman without specifying, meaning he goes to the woman and says, "So-and-so appointed me as an agent to betroth you," and after some time he betroths her unspecifically, and the agent claims he intended it for himself while she claims she intended it for the sender, if the agency was not well-known, the sender is allowed to marry her relatives as the agent claims because we believe him that he intended it for himself. The agent, however, is forbidden to marry her relatives, and she is permitted to marry the agent’s relatives. But if there were witnesses attesting to the agency, the sender is also forbidden to marry her relatives because the agent’s objection is not considered sufficient to nullify the agency [Raavad there]. It is possible that, in practice, even Rambam agrees with this ruling, but this requires further investigation. [And the Raavad explains the Yerushalmi in this way; it is puzzling why the Shulchan Aruch does not mention this at all].

If the agent (shaliach) says, "I betrothed her on behalf of the sender," and she says, "You did not betroth me" – the sender is prohibited from marrying her relatives based on the agent's word, even if there are no witnesses. Since the agent says he fulfilled his mission and there is a presumption that an agent fulfills his mission, it is as if the man told the woman, "I betrothed you," and she says, "You did not betroth me." And be aware, both the sender and the agent can cancel the agency with their verbal declaration. Even if a kinyan (formal act of acquisition) was made, they can still cancel the agency. If they swore not to cancel the agency and then canceled it, the cancellation is valid, but they have violated their oath. However, they are not believed to say they canceled unless we know clearly that they did, because a person does not make himself a wicked person. Further details will be explained in the laws of divorce, G-d willing.

It has already been explained in section 58 that if an agent deviates from their mission, the agency is nullified. There are those who are uncertain if a rabbinic betrothal or a doubtful betrothal constitutes a deviation from the mission, for certainly the intent of the sender was to perform a complete betrothal. Similarly, if he betrothed her with betrothal that does not permit consummation [Maggid Mishneh, Chapter 7, Law 20]. And in section 31, paragraph 38, we wrote that there is a dispute on this matter, and in practice, it is considered doubtful, see there. And even though logically it would seem that this is certainly a deviation from the mission [there], nevertheless, one could argue the opposite, that certainly if he deviated in some action, it would be considered a deviation. But if he did not deviate in action but according to the law it is considered a deviation, this is not a deviation in the mission, for he was not instructed on how to act according to the law, but it is merely an indication of intent that we are witness to the fact that certainly he only desired clear betrothal. And we hold that an indication of intent in a divorce document is not significant, and similarly in betrothal. Therefore, practically, it is a doubtful legal matter and is considered doubtful betrothal [even though the proof of the Maggid Mishneh from page 52 of Rabbi Taviumi can be refuted by saying that he did indeed betroth one of the daughters for him, as in the case of the sisters in the Mishnah there. Similarly, the proof of the commentator from page 64b can be refuted, see there. Nevertheless, it can be argued logically as stated, and scrutinize well].

[Laws of Agency for a Woman, containing 19 sections]

Just as a man can appoint an agent for betrothal, so too a woman can appoint an agent to receive betrothal. And as soon as the agent receives the betrothal, she is betrothed, just as with a divorce where a woman appoints an agent to receive it. She is required to appoint the agent in the presence of witnesses, even according to the Rambam who does not require witnesses for agency in general. Nevertheless, for the agency of receiving, he agrees that witnesses are needed. The reason for this matter is explained in the previous section, section 17. All the more so according to other authorities who require witnesses even for the man’s agency. However, if she did not appoint the agent in the presence of witnesses and the agent received the betrothal, it is proper to be stringent and require a get (divorce document) because there are those who say that for betrothal, even for the agency of receiving, witnesses are not needed, as mentioned there in section 20.

Just as it is a greater mitzvah for a man to perform a commandment himself than through an agent, as stated there in section 2, so too it is a greater mitzvah for a woman to perform it herself than through an agent. And although a woman is not commanded to be fruitful and multiply, she still has a mitzvah because she assists her husband in fulfilling his commandment. We have already explained in section 1, paragraph 6, that even one who is not commanded to be fruitful and multiply still performs a mitzvah when they fulfill it, for it is the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, to increase the settlement of His world, as stated there in section 4. And regarding all women, it is obvious that there is a mitzvah, for it is impossible to fulfill the mitzvah without them (and this answers the question posed by the people there), but this is not a mitzvah imposed on the individual. Therefore, it is certainly a greater mitzvah for a woman to perform it herself than through an agent. However, there is no prohibition if she is betrothed through an agent without seeing him, for although with a man there is also a prohibition, as stated in the previous section there, because perhaps she will not be pleasing in his eyes, with a woman we do not worry about this, for a woman is generally agreeable to any match. And since she consents to be betrothed without being present, she will not despise him.

In all matters of betrothal, the law concerning a woman with her agent is the same as the law concerning the agent with the man. If the agent deviates from their mission, the mission is nullified. If she told the agent, "Receive the betrothal in a certain place," and he received it in another place, she is not betrothed. If she told him, "He is in a certain place," and he received it in another place, she is betrothed, because she was merely indicating the place, as we have explained regarding his own mission. Similarly, any deviation nullifies the mission. Only in the matter previously clarified, where an agent can appoint another agent, there are those who say that in the case of an acceptance mission, it is not so, for the reason that 'words cannot be entrusted to an agent,' as explained there in Section 3.

How does the procedure of betrothal through a receiving agent work? Rambam wrote in Chapter 3, Law 18, that if the woman’s agent receives the betrothal, the groom says to him, "Behold, so-and-so who sent you is betrothed to me," and he responds, "I have betrothed her to you," or "I have engaged her to you," or "I have given her to you as a wife," or any similar expression. If the agent says "Yes," it is sufficient, even if he remains silent. If they were engaged in that matter and he gave the agent (the money) without specifying or saying anything, it is sufficient, and she is betrothed. End quote.

The requirement that the agent must say "I have betrothed her to you" or say "Yes" – some say the reason is that otherwise we might suspect that he revoked his agency and received the money as a deposit and not for betrothal (Bach). There is no clear reason why we should be concerned about this.

Others say the reason is because it is written, "I have given my daughter to this man" (Deuteronomy 22:16), and he is like an agent from his daughter, implying that he needs to say he is giving [transferring ownership], but this also does not seem reasonable, as the verse means he gave her willingly.

Others say the reason is that with the woman herself, her silence is clearly an agreement to the betrothal, because since she is prohibited to everyone else, she would have protested if she was not agreeable to the betrothal. But the agent does not care about this, and his silence does not indicate agreement to the betrothal, therefore his statement is necessary (Avnei Miluim). This is also difficult to understand, as the agent stands in the place of the woman, and there is no greater proof of his agreement than his acceptance of the betrothal, as no one forced him, and for the woman herself, it is also the acceptance that serves as proof of her agreement (and what Maran wrote, see at the end of the discussion).

Therefore, it appears to me that the rationale of the Rambam is certainly if the witnesses to the betrothal know that this man is a messenger from the woman, there is no need for his declaration at all. The requirement for the messenger's declaration is because of the witnesses. For, it is understandable when they see a man betrothing a woman, there is knowledge and evidence. But when they see a man betrothing a woman through another man and they do not see the woman and do not know about the agency, if they do not hear from the man statements acknowledging his agency, there is no clear knowledge and it is like betrothing without witnesses. Therefore, it is required that he says "So-and-so is betrothed to you" or says "Yes," for this is akin to knowledge from him that he is a messenger from the woman. Therefore, if they discussed the matters of betrothal beforehand, nothing else is needed since the witnesses know that he is a messenger.

Some say that what the Rambam wrote, that if he was silent, it is effective when they are engaged in that matter, means that the husband's silence is effective just like when he betroths her, as it is effective when engaged in that matter by the act alone without any speech. However, this does not apply to the agent, for with the agent, the saying is essential. But most of the authorities agree that it applies even to the agent, that when engaged in that matter, neither the husband's nor the agent's speech is needed. And it is obvious that according to the reasoning we have explained, it is so, as there is knowledge and evidence here. This is also explicitly implied by the Rambam's wording, for if it only applied to the one who betroths, it would be a redundant expression. And according to the version we have of the Rambam, "And if they were engaged in that matter," it further implies that after the fact, his speech is not required at all, even if they were not engaged in that matter.

In the case of betrothal with a document through an agent, the Rambam writes that the document must be written with the agent's knowledge, since a betrothal document must be written with her knowledge, as stated in Siman 32. Therefore, when she appoints an agent, her agent is like herself, and certainly if it is written with the woman's knowledge, it is effective. However, some of our Rabbis hold that it is not effective with only the agent's knowledge but requires her knowledge, that she commands the writing of the document. In this case, we do not say that her agent is like herself, just as in a get (divorce document) we require the knowledge of the grantor specifically, that the scribe must hear directly from the husband, and even if the husband says, "Tell so-and-so to write it," it is invalid. Similarly, in betrothal, we require the knowledge of the grantor specifically, who is the woman, and not her agent's knowledge [Ran and Maggid Mishneh]. According to the Rambam, one could say that there is no connection between these cases. For in a get, since the husband must write the get, he himself must instruct the scribe to write it. But in a betrothal document, the woman does not write it; the man writes it. We only need to consult her opinion, and her agent's opinion is like hers. Additionally, the invalidity of "tell so-and-so to write" in a get is due to a decree, as stated in Siman 120, or due to "words" (mili) as will be explained there, but in betrothal, none of this applies to the woman since she does not write it. Furthermore, in a get, even through an agent, the agent's name is not mentioned in the get, whereas in betrothal, it is written, "So-and-so, whom you sent, is betrothed to me." Since the agent's name is mentioned, her knowledge is effective [according to the Rambam]. Nevertheless, we learn from all this that we require her knowledge in the betrothal document, meaning she must agree to the writing of the document. It is not enough that she agrees to the betrothal in general, for here she sent an agent to receive the betrothal, and still, we require the knowledge of her agent or her knowledge according to the authorities who disagree with the Rambam [Bach, subparagraph 3]. And it is simple, even according to the Rambam, that if the man appoints an agent to betroth the woman, the writing of the document is not effective with the agent's knowledge but only with the man's knowledge, as in the case of a get, as we have explained [this seems correct to me].

And just as the husband can revoke the agency, so too can she. If she retracted and canceled the agency before receiving the betrothal, it is nullified and she is not betrothed. If it is unknown whether she canceled the agency before the betrothal or after receiving the betrothal, she is considered to be in a state of doubtful betrothal.

And similarly, if her agent received betrothal from one person and she herself received betrothal from another, and it is not known whether the betrothal her agent received preceded hers or hers preceded, she is forbidden to both and requires a divorce from both. If they wish, one can give a divorce and the other can marry her, and she needs another betrothal because perhaps the betrothal of the other one preceded, and the previous betrothal did not take effect. And all this applies when the two betrothers are distant from each other. But when they are close relatives, such as if the agent betrothed her to Reuven and she herself was betrothed to Reuven's son or brother, both must give a divorce and she is forbidden to both of them. For how can she marry one of them? Perhaps the betrothal of the other preceded, and she was divorced from him, and thus she is a forbidden relative to the second. And all the laws of nullification that apply to a man also apply to a woman.

One who betroths through an agent should not betroth again at the time of the wedding, so as not to cast aspersions on the original betrothal by suggesting that the agent's betrothal was invalid. And even though we ruled in Siman 34, Se'if 12, that if the man himself betrothed, he is permitted to betroth her again, nonetheless, in the case of betrothal through an agent, they were concerned as mentioned there. However, some say that if the first betrothal was without ten [people present], he is permitted to betroth her again himself in the presence of ten, as it is evident that he is doing so because he wants to betroth her in the presence of ten, and not because there is a concern about the agent’s betrothal. Similarly, this is specifically when there are witnesses to the agent's betrothal, for then he is not permitted to betroth her again. But when there are no witnesses present, and only the agent and the woman say that she was betrothed with witnesses, in such a case there is no concern if he betroths her again, since there are no witnesses to the agent's betrothal.

It has already been explained in Siman 35 that a woman is fit to act as an agent for betrothal and can receive betrothal on behalf of her friend. Moreover, even if she receives betrothal for herself, she can still receive it on behalf of her friend. The one who is betrothing can say to her, "You are betrothed to me, and so is so-and-so betrothed to me." Even though they become co-wives and in all testimonies where a woman is fit, a co-wife is not believed, nevertheless, her agency is valid because she acted as an agent. This is because the reason she is not believed is due to suspicion of causing harm, but in an action she performs on behalf of her friend, there is no concern of harm (see Tosafot). 

Some say further that even if, at the time of receiving the betrothal, Rachel from Jacob said to Leah, "Receive also for me betrothal from Jacob," and Leah did not answer her but received it, and Jacob said in giving her the betrothal money that he is betrothing both of them—then the second one is also betrothed. We do not say that since Leah did not explicitly say she is receiving on behalf of Rachel, Rachel is not betrothed. On the contrary, since Leah did not say she does not want to receive on behalf of Rachel, we say she consented to receive also on behalf of Rachel even though they become co-wives. But if she explicitly received on behalf of Rachel as well, it is obvious that there is no doubt about this, and it is not a novelty at all (Rosh). 

From this, there is proof of what is written in Siman 6, that even if the agent did not respond "yes," it is still a valid betrothal (Chumash Menachem, note 8).
