However, it can be said that this is not a proof, for here it is better since she is certainly betrothed, we say that her friend is also betrothed, which is not the case with an agent who receives only on behalf of the one who sent him alone (Beit Shmuel, note 2).

A woman who is an agent to accept betrothal on behalf of her friend, and when the betrothal was given to her, he said to her, "And you as well" or "And so you," and she was silent and accepted it—both are betrothed. However, if he did not say to her "And you as well" or "And so you" but rather just "And you"—this woman who accepted the betrothal is doubtfully betrothed, as perhaps he only intended to see what she would say, as if he said to her, "And what do you say about this matter?" Therefore, even though she accepted it and was silent, it can be said that she is still contemplating this matter, as he is asking her, but she has not agreed now to the betrothal. Therefore, it is a doubtful betrothal because it can be said that they intended for betrothal. This is specifically when there are two prutot, not less. And if he betrothed Rachel and Leah was standing there, and he gave a pruta to Leah and said to her, "And you"—this is a complete betrothal. This is because when Leah received it on behalf of Rachel, we can say that when he said to Leah "And you," it is as previously mentioned, and she did not bother to respond since she was to accept on behalf of Rachel. But when Rachel accepted it herself and he said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me," then when he gave it to Leah and she accepted it and he said to her "And you"—it is obvious that both intended for a complete betrothal. Otherwise, why would he give it to her and why would she accept it?

From a logical perspective, it appears that this uncertainty when he says to her "and you" exists when he gives her two prutot and says to her at the time of giving, "Behold, so-and-so who sent you is betrothed to me, and you" or "and you too" regarding definite betrothal. But if he gave her the two prutot and said to her, "Behold, so-and-so who sent you is betrothed to me," and then paused even for less than the time it takes to speak and then said to her, "and you" or "and you too"—her betrothal is not valid. Firstly, because we hold that in betrothal, within the time it takes to speak is not considered as speaking, and moreover, since he gave her the two prutot on behalf of her friend, her friend has already acquired all the money, even if it is a thousand dinarim, so with what would he betroth her? However, from the language of the Tur who wrote: if she is an agent to receive betrothal for her friend, and after he gave the betrothal into her hand, he said to her "you too"—both are betrothed, but if he said "and you"—she is doubtfully betrothed, it clearly implies that even in such a case it is effective. We must say that this ruling that within the time it takes to speak is not considered as speaking in betrothal applies only to retraction, and our teacher the Beit Yosef also wrote this in his book Bedek HaBayit. And even though, if so, since regarding retraction it is not considered as speaking, the money belongs to the other woman, with what would he betroth her? We must say that it refers to a case where he intended from the outset for this, so the other woman did not acquire all the money. But if he did not intend from the outset but changed his mind to betroth her as well, even if the decision was within the time it takes to speak, he still has nothing with which to betroth her, as the money belongs to the other woman. And if we say that he added money for her, then it is obvious that it would be a betrothal even with "and you" alone, as was written regarding two women and two acts of giving in the previous section.

Jacob betrothed Rachel and said to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me," and gave her two prutot. Then he said to Leah, "And you too," and she agreed – both are betrothed, since Rachel accepted [the betrothal] for herself and for Leah [Ran and Rosh Nedarim 6:]. Even though Rachel was silent and one might question whether she accepted [the betrothal] on behalf of Leah as well, since Leah did not previously appoint her as an agent, one could say that if Leah did not agree to this, she should have responded, "I only accept [the betrothal] for myself." Why was she silent when Jacob said to Leah, "And you too"? It must be that she agreed. However, if he only said to Leah, "And you," it is a doubtful betrothal. Although it is more likely to interpret his words as meaning "And you too," since it is also possible to interpret it as saying, "And you observe the betrothal that I am doing with Rachel," even though this is a far-fetched interpretation, nonetheless, these are not explicit betrothal words regarding Leah, but rather like an implicit intention for betrothal, and it is a doubt whether there is an implicit intention for betrothal or not. And even though implicit intentions that are not clear are not considered implicit intentions according to most of the authorities, as we wrote in Siman 27, Seif 1 and Seif 27 there, but with clear implicit intentions that are considered implicit intentions for all matters, only in betrothal are we in doubt whether there is an implicit intention for betrothal or not.

And know that this law we have written is according to the explanation of our Rabbis in the Talmudic discussion there, and it is a doubt in law whether there is a "hand" (partial expression) for betrothal or not. According to this, in the law written by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Siman 27:4, if one betroths a woman and says to another woman in her presence, "You shall be betrothed," without saying “to me,” it is a case of doubtful betrothal there. We have explained the reason there in Siman 28 according to the words of our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, that the doubt is because maybe he intended to betroth her on behalf of another. However, according to what we have explained here, that it is a fundamental doubt in the law whether there is a "hand" for betrothal or not, the reason is simple. Even though it is evident ("hands that clarify"), there is still a doubt whether there is a "hand" for betrothal or not [and so wrote the Gra in Seif Katan 24]. However, in truth, it is one matter, for since there is a doubt about another intention, even though it is a far-fetched interpretation, since there is a possibility to doubt it, it is not explicit betrothal but rather "hands" (partial expression), and it is doubtful whether there is a "hand" for betrothal or not. But if there was no doubt in his words, it is not a "hand" but complete betrothal. Also, the law we wrote in Seif 12 is according to the explanation of the Rambam in Chapter 4 of that Talmudic discussion. The doubt there is also because of the fundamental doubt whether there is a "hand" for betrothal or not [and it is problematic with the Rosh who omitted this in his rulings in Kiddushin Chapter 1:62 and in Nedarim there, whether there is a "hand" for betrothal or not. Similarly, the Ramban in the laws of Nedarim did not write this, and on the contrary, from the Rosh in Kiddushin there, it appears that with evident "hands" there is a "hand" for betrothal. It can be said with difficulty that it is all one matter, and it needs further study, and be diligent and understand].

Some of the great authorities have said that ideally, it is not appropriate for a father to act as an agent for his adult daughter to accept betrothal on her behalf. Their reasoning is that since, in the case of a minor or a young girl, the father has the authority to betroth his daughter even without her consent, people might mistakenly think that the same applies to an adult daughter and that her consent is not required at all. However, all the great authorities disagreed with this, arguing that it is an unfounded decree and is not found in the Talmud. On the contrary, it is explicitly stated otherwise [Kiddushin 41a], and it does not appear there that this applies only after the fact (i.e., not ideally). Nevertheless, it seems to me that when she appoints him as an agent, he should not appoint another agent, even if we say that in betrothal an agent can appoint another agent. This is because if the father's agent comes to accept the betrothal and says that he is the father's agent, there is a definite concern that listeners will mistakenly think that the father is appointing an agent to accept betrothal on behalf of his adult daughter and will not realize that he is a second agent and that the father is also an agent of his daughter [and perhaps this is what the Rashba was referring to in such a case].

There are those who say that, nevertheless, if it indeed happened that a father accepted betrothal on behalf of his adult daughter without her knowledge, she requires a get (divorce document) out of doubt, since perhaps she agreed to her father's betrothal. Certainly, according to the strict law, there is no doubt of betrothal here, as we do not suspect that she might have consented. However, due to the severity of issues concerning forbidden relationships, we require a get <small>[Chamudei Daniel]</small>. If we explicitly heard that she objected, she does not need a get. If we saw from her some indication that she agreed, it is definitely considered a case of doubtful betrothal, and it depends on the judgment of the court according to the situation <small>[See Beit Meir]</small>.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 12: A woman does not appoint an agent to receive the betrothal (kiddushin) from the agent of the husband, and if she does, it is considered a doubtful betrothal. And regarding a get (divorce document), there is a dispute as mentioned in Section 141, and for those who prohibit it, the Talmud provides two reasons (Gittin 63b) – either because it is a disgrace to the husband, as it appears that he is insignificant in her eyes since she does not receive it herself, or because of the concept of "her courtyard that comes afterwards," meaning that we decree that after the husband gives the get into the courtyard of another, she will acquire the courtyard and people will say she is divorced. This is akin to appointing an agent from another agent, and in this case, it is clear that it is not a valid get because we require it to be placed in her hand or her domain at the time of giving. The practical difference between these two reasons is that for the first reason, it is a concern of a Torah prohibition, and against this, if the husband knows about it and does not object, it is permitted even initially. For the second reason, it is a rabbinic prohibition, and his knowledge does not help. 

Now, the second reason does not apply to kiddushin at all, because for kiddushin, we do not require it to be placed in her hand or domain directly, as even with a deposit, she is betrothed. According to this, it is puzzling about Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef, who in Gittin brought both opinions, and in kiddushin, which is more lenient, he decisively ruled to forbid it. It is possible to say that he holds that in kiddushin, everyone agrees that the husband objects to this, specifically in a get, where they are separating, some hold that he does not care if it is not significant to her, but in kiddushin, he certainly cares, and this reasoning makes sense. (And in Yevamot 34, it discusses with their knowledge, and this resolves all that was questioned there).

There are those who say that although it has been clarified that a woman can act as an agent for her friend even in cases where they are co-wives to each other, nevertheless, a man's own wife cannot act as an agent for another woman to receive betrothal from this woman's husband, for a woman's hand is like her husband's hand and the betrothal does not leave his domain [Bava Metzia]. This reasoning is logical – and in practice, it is advisable to be stringent. Similarly, in the case of a get (divorce document), a man's own wife cannot act as an agent to receive it on behalf of her co-wife – and in practice, it is advisable to be stringent.

[All the laws of the betrothal of a minor girl and a maiden, containing seventy-two sections]

A daughter is under her father's authority for all the days of her childhood and maidenhood until she becomes an adult. The father can betroth her without her consent to whomever he wishes, as it is written, "I gave my daughter to this man" (Deuteronomy 22:16). The verse refers to a maiden, as it is written there, "and they shall bring out the maiden" etc., and the money of the betrothal belongs to the father, for he has rights over her in all matters, such as her found objects and the work of her hands. Similarly, her ketubah (marriage contract) belongs to him if she is widowed or divorced from the betrothal, as it is written, "in her maidenhood in her father's house" (Numbers 30:17), indicating that all the benefits of her maidenhood belong to her father. However, once she is married, her father no longer has authority over her, for she has transferred from his authority to that of her husband, and his authority over her is terminated even if she is still a minor. [See Tosafot, Ketubot 46b, and the discussion there. We have explained according to the truth, and therefore the Tur wrote the laws of her found objects and the work of her hands here; scrutinize well.]

And similarly, her earnings belong to her father. If she is dependent on his table, he takes all her earnings. If she is not dependent, he takes the excess over her sustenance. If her earnings are not sufficient for her sustenance or she does not earn at all, it will be clarified in Siman 71 whether he is obligated to sustain her. Similarly, if she finds a lost item, it belongs to the father even if he does not sustain her. Although some of our Rabbis hold that if he does not sustain her, the found item belongs to her, nevertheless, most of the authorities agree that her found item always belongs to him, as cited in Rashi on Ketubot 47a, "mishum." This is also mentioned in Choshen Mishpat Siman 74. According to Maimonides in Chapter 17 of Hilchot Gezela, and the Tur there, even if she is sold as a maidservant, her found item belongs to him. Similarly, if she becomes widowed or divorced from the betrothal, the ketubah belongs to him. However, from the marriage, he has no right to it, even in her minority.

Therefore, a father can accept betrothal (kiddushin) for his daughter from the day she is born until she matures (becomes a bogeret). Even if she were deaf or mentally incompetent, if the father betroths her, she is considered a fully married woman (eshet ish) according to Torah law. Even though she will never achieve full mental capacity, since the Torah grants the father the right to accept betrothal for his daughter during her childhood and adolescence, there is no difference between a competent girl and one who is deaf or mentally incompetent. Nevertheless, when she becomes a bogeret, even though in other respects she may be like a minor, regarding betrothal, she is considered an adult, and no more under her father's authority than a competent girl; the father no longer has rights over her from the time she becomes a bogeret.

The father can betroth his daughter through money or a document, or through sexual intercourse (kiddushei bi'ah). He secludes her with witnesses present and says, "I hereby hand over my daughter to you for betrothal through intercourse," and the man says, "Your daughter is hereby betrothed to me through this intercourse that I will have with her." However, betrothal through intercourse is only valid if the girl is at least three years and one day old, for if she is younger than this, the intercourse has no legal significance. Even if the father handed her over for betrothal through intercourse, she is not considered betrothed.

There is no validity to a betrothal with a fetus, and if the pregnancy is recognizable, the betrothal is valid according to the Rambam, as will be explained in Siman 40. Similarly, there is no validity to a betrothal with a stillborn. What has been clarified is that from the day it is born, the betrothal is valid if it is known for certain that the pregnancy was completed. However, if it is not known for certain, it is only a doubtful betrothal, because perhaps it is not a stillborn. But with a definite stillborn, the betrothal is not valid even while it is alive, for it is considered as dead. It is worse than a fetus with a recognizable pregnancy, because there, when it is born, it will be a living being, but the stillborn is considered as dead. Nevertheless, if the father of the stillborn accepted the betrothal, and afterwards the betrothing party betrothed her sister, even though according to the law the betrothal with the sister is certainly valid, it is proper to be stringent and require another betrothal once the stillborn dies. Also, it is forbidden for him to have relations with her sister while the stillborn is alive [see Chiddushei Maharach Or Zarua, Siman 2]. However, the primary law is as stated [and practically, one should be stringent according to what the Ramban wrote in the opinion of Rashi; see Beit Shmuel, Siman 2, and in the Ketzot HaChoshen and Even HaEzer, and it appears to me that Rashi also holds this way, and according to the distinction, Rabbi Yosef said this, which is merely a jest, because if not for jesting, he would have asked plainly, and there would be a distinction for the mother of the mother. Thus, Rabbi Yosef also holds that it is not like a living being, and he only asked Rabbi Zeira in jest, and therefore he said to his sister not to think that Rabbi Zeira was truly asking according to the law, and with this, everything is clarified. Pay close attention].

There is one who is uncertain whether a gift given to a minor girl or a young woman belongs to her father, like a found object or the money of betrothal, or not. And there is one who holds that it does belong to her father. However, we find that the Rashba wrote in a responsum (cited in Even HaEzer) that the gift does not belong to the father. And it is logical that the Torah only granted the father rights to a found object, which another person did not intentionally transfer to her. But regarding a gift given to her, it is certain that the donor did not intend to transfer it to the father, since he did not give it to him. How, then, could it be transferred to the father? It is not comparable to a slave, whose gift belongs to his master, because it is evident to all that a slave cannot own anything independently of his master. But in the case of a daughter, this is not evident to all. Even a wife, whose hand is like her husband’s hand, does not transfer the principal of a gift to her husband; he only consumes its produce. (This also invalidates the proof of the Beit Shmuel from Tosafot; examine this closely.) However, in the case of a minor girl who does not have the capacity to safeguard the object, her gift belongs to her father, for certainly the donor did not give it to her except to bring her joy, and his primary intention was for the father, as we explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 274, Seif 4. See there.

When the daughter reaches adulthood, her father no longer has control over her, and she is like all other women who can only be betrothed with their consent. The time when an ailonit (a woman who does not develop signs of puberty) reaches adulthood will be explained in Siman 155. All the signs of childhood, adolescence, and adulthood will be explained there, as well as whether the testimony of women is valid for this matter. Refer to Siman 169 for who is reliable in counting the years. It appears from the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) that the father is also not trusted regarding the count of years, like all other relatives, as explained there, that it is not valid. This matter of the father being trusted to prohibit his daughter, which will be explained in this Siman, applies when the years are verified independently of him, in which case he is trusted to say, "I have betrothed her."

Just as reaching the age of majority removes a girl from the authority of her father, so too does marriage. If she was married while still a minor, with her father having married her off, and she then became widowed or divorced during her father’s lifetime, she does not return to her father’s authority even if she is still a minor. However, if she became widowed or divorced from betrothal, she returns to her father's authority until she reaches majority. From marriage, even if she entered the wedding canopy but had not yet consummated the marriage, she is considered married. 

From where do we learn that a married woman does not return to her father's authority? From the laws of vows. As it is written, “And the vow of a widow or a divorced woman, everything that she has bound upon herself shall stand against her” (Numbers 30:10), indicating that she does not return to her father's authority. Based on this, it is possible that if the father handed her over to the husband's messengers and she died, she does not return to her father's authority, as is the case with vows. This matter requires further study regarding the law.

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 3, Law 13: If she was betrothed before she became of age without her father's knowledge, she is not betrothed, even if her father later agrees to the betrothal. Even if she becomes a widow or is divorced from that betrothal, she is not forbidden to a priest. Both she and her father can object, whether she was betrothed in his presence or not in his presence—she is not betrothed. It appears from his words that if at the time of the act the father agrees to the betrothal, even if he did not explicitly tell her to get betrothed, it is considered a valid betrothal. However, if he agrees afterward, it does not help, and we do not worry that perhaps he had agreed at the time of the act. And not only when it was not in his presence, because he did not know about it, but even in his presence, since he remained silent, it is certain that he did not agree at that time, and his later agreement is just a change of mind and therefore does not help. Even if he accepted a get (divorce document) from the one who betrothed her, which would be a clear sign that he later agreed—she is not forbidden to a priest.

There is an opinion that holds, according to the Rambam, of blessed memory, that if she was betrothed in the presence of her father and he remained silent, and afterward he consented, it constitutes a valid betrothal [Maharik 32], because the end proves the beginning, indicating that he had consented at the time of the act [Lechem Mishneh]. And all the more so, if he explicitly consented at the time of the act, it constitutes a valid betrothal. Nevertheless, even if we know that he consented at the time of the act, both the father and the daughter can later object. And although the father can betroth her against her will, that is when he betroths her of his own accord. But when he did not betroth her, and she betrothed herself only with his consent – she can later object [Kesef Mishneh]. Similarly, he can also object afterward even though he consented at the time of the act. This is what the Rambam wrote, that both she and her father can object, meaning that even if we know that he consented at the time of the act, they can still object later [as explained above in the intention of the Kesef Mishneh, and there is no need for the words of the Lechem Mishneh; see there and examine carefully].

And when we know that he was agreeable at the time of the act, even if the betrothal was not done in his presence, nevertheless, since he knew that she was being betrothed and he was agreeable, the betrothal is considered complete, even according to the opinion of the Rambam, unless one of them protested afterward, as we have stated. And one should not ask, if the betrothal was complete at the time of the act when he was agreeable, how can it be nullified afterward by their protest? And if it was not complete at the time of the act, when will it be completed, since according to the Rambam, it does not help if he agrees afterward? Therefore, it is necessary to say that it was completed at the time of the act, so how can the betrothal be nullified afterward based on their protest? It can be said that certainly the betrothal is completed immediately, but this is like a conditional betrothal that neither of them will protest afterward, and even though this was not explicitly stated, this is the case according to the matter, since he gave her the betrothal and not to her father, it is considered as an explicit condition that if one of them regrets afterward, the betrothal will be nullified [as stated according to the opinion of the Rambam of blessed memory].

However, many of our rabbis disagree with him and hold that even if he knew nothing about the betrothal and afterwards, when he heard about it, he consented – it is considered a valid betrothal from the moment he heard and consented. And even if he did not consent immediately upon hearing but remained silent and did not protest, and later consented, this demonstrates retroactive approval, and it is considered a valid betrothal from the time of hearing, even if the money was consumed before he heard. And although one might ask how the betrothal can take effect at the time of hearing when the money was already consumed, it can be said that this is akin to betrothing a woman with money on the condition that the betrothal takes effect after 30 days; she is considered betrothed after 30 days even if the money was consumed, as stated in Siman 40, see there. And although he did not say to her, "Be betrothed to me after your father consents," it is effectively as if he had said so, since the betrothal depends on the father's consent.

And some of our rabbis are of the opinion that when the father consents, the betrothal is valid from the time he betrothed her. The reason is that since he later consents, it is as if he said to her, "Go and accept your betrothal" [Rosh]. Furthermore, every man wants to marry off his daughter, and it is a privilege for him, and one can bestow a privilege upon a person in their absence [Ran]. And if he did not consent, the betrothal is not valid because it is not a complete privilege [ibid.]. According to this reasoning, it is effective even for a minor, even according to those who hold that he cannot say to his minor daughter, "Go and accept your betrothal" as will be explained in this section. And it is also effective according to this reasoning even if she explicitly stated at the time of accepting the betrothal that she does not intend to act as her father's agent [Beit Shmuel there], for according to this reasoning, since it is a privilege for him, one can bestow a privilege upon a person in their absence and there is no need for her agency, for it is as if he said to the one betrothing her, "Accept the betrothal on behalf of my daughter."

Some say that if the money has been consumed, the betrothal is not valid. Their reasoning is that they hold the betrothal takes effect from the moment the father hears and consents, and if the money has been consumed by then, with what will she be betrothed? This is not similar to the case of betrothing her after thirty days as discussed in Siman 40, because there, since she knows that the betrothal will not take effect until thirty days have passed, the money is not considered a loan to her, as explained there. However, here, since she does not know when the betrothal will take effect, it follows that as soon as the money is consumed, it becomes a debt upon her. Subsequently, when the father hears and consents, it is as if he is betrothing her with a loan, and she is not betrothed.

And according to these opinions that were explained, it is effective even if the father consents afterward—immediately upon his consent, the betrothal is valid, either from the time of his consent or from the time of the betrothal, according to the opinions explained. And it does not help to delay afterward. However, if the father has not yet consented and she retracts and objects to the betrothal, the father's later consent does not help. And certainly, if the father objects, it is not a valid betrothal. 

And one should not question why her objection is effective since the father later consents and he can betroth her against her will. The answer is that since at the time of the betrothal he did not consent and she retracted before his consent, the entire act of accepting the betrothal is nullified and his later consent does not help. And if he wishes to betroth her against her will, he must personally accept the betrothal from the one betrothing afterward, but her acceptance is nullified.

And know that in all these laws, there is no difference between whether her father betrothed her beforehand to this man or not. In a place where we said that the betrothal is valid according to all opinions as explained, it is valid even if he did not betroth her at all, for the reasons explained. And in a place where the betrothal is not valid, it is nothing, even if he betrothed her himself initially. And even though most authorities hold that the betrothal is valid even if he consented afterwards, it would be appropriate to say that if he betrothed her, the betrothal is valid immediately because he certainly consented. It is not worse than what will be explained, that if he revealed his intention that he wanted to betroth her to someone and she betrothed herself to him, we are concerned about the betrothal. However, we do not say this because, although he desired the match, he still wanted to betroth her himself [Beit Shmuel, 16]. This concern about revealing intention is when the father is present at the time of the betrothal [see Beit Shmuel, 24]. Therefore, if he betrothed her and the father was present at the time of the betrothal, we are certainly concerned about the betrothal, and it is considered a doubtful betrothal [in my opinion].

There is an opinion that when betrothal is arranged, we always have to be concerned about the possibility of Kiddushin (marriage) [Bach], and it seems to me that this is reflected in the words of the Rambam who does not mention arranging betrothal at all. One could say that he holds that without arranging betrothal, there is no concern for Kiddushin at all, and when it is arranged, there is a doubt of Kiddushin even if the Kiddushin was accepted not in the presence of the father, and the Rambam considers it as if he consented at the time of the act. According to other authorities, even if he consented afterward, it is considered definite Kiddushin even without arranging betrothal. However, in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 11, it is explained according to the first opinion. Nevertheless, in practice, we should be stringent because there are those who say that even if the father heard and remained silent and did not object, it is as if he consented [Mordechai, chapter 2]. Although most authorities disagree with this and all the great authorities agree that only explicit consent [Bach, subparagraph 161] constitutes Kiddushin, there are also some of our early authorities who hold that when the father is far away, we surely have to be concerned that he might have consented. Therefore, all the more so, we should be stringent in all cases of arranged betrothal to say that it is a doubtful Kiddushin. Some of the early authorities hold that for a minor, like the Rambam, even subsequent consent does not help, even if arranged betrothal took place. For a young woman, even without arranged betrothal and even if he did not explicitly consent when he heard but remained silent and did not object, it is considered complete Kiddushin [Shitah Mekubetzet in the name of Riaz]. However, we have not found any authority among the poskim who agrees with this. Nevertheless, for a young woman, there are those who are stringent and require a get (divorce document) and to announce that the get is merely a stringency. Why is there a need to announce? So that people will not say she is a complete divorcee and that Kiddushin cannot take effect with her sister [see Bach, subparagraph 19, and there is a need for further study as the majority of the poskim explain otherwise, and the Rosh writes this as a possibility].

In the case of a minor who was betrothed without her father's knowledge, in a situation where we have said that it is not a valid betrothal – she does not even require refusal (mi'un). But if a minor, and all the more so a young woman, was betrothed without her father's knowledge and also married without his knowledge, many of our Rabbis agreed that she requires both a get (divorce document) and refusal if she is a minor. The refusal is to publicize that the get is not a complete get so that people will not say that betrothal cannot be effective with her sister. Consequently, in the case of a young woman, an announcement is required as stated in the previous section. Our Master, the Beit Yosef, ruled in section 11 that even if she was married, her status is like she was only betrothed, as also stated by the Tur. The Rambam did not mention this law at all [and I am puzzled by the Yam Shel Shlomo in chapter 2, section 9; see there and examine it carefully]. It appears that he did not have this version of the law in the Gemara [and this is the intention of the Beit Yosef, and for no reason did the Ba'er Hetev wonder in section 10]. The reason why the poskim (decisors) hold that if she was betrothed and married without knowledge, it is worse than if she was only betrothed, is because since the father remained silent in both matters, she is considered as an orphan during her father's lifetime or he has renounced his right over her or his silence is considered as agreement. For in the case of only betrothal, it can be said that he was very angry and therefore remained silent, but for all this (i.e., both betrothal and marriage), he would not remain silent [Ran]. This only applies when the father is in the city or close to her, but if he is far away, there is a different law, which will be explained later [and so it is in the Gemara: if she was betrothed without knowledge and married without knowledge and her father was here, see there 45:].

A minor who was betrothed without her father's knowledge, and the father did not hear about it at all or he was far away, and in the meantime, the daughter grew up and left her father's authority and remained silent without protesting the betrothal. If her husband had relations with her after she grew up, it is obvious that she is fully considered a married woman for all intents and purposes, as it is certain that he intended the relations as a form of betrothal, knowing that the betrothal of a minor is invalid. Even if he did not specifically appoint witnesses for their relations, since the matter is public knowledge, it is as if there were witnesses. However, if he explicitly had relations not for the sake of betrothal, it is considered licentious relations [Responsa Rashba], but we do not suspect him of this [ibid.]. Even if he did not have relations with her after she grew up, she is still in doubt concerning her marital status, as her silence upon reaching adulthood is considered as agreement to the betrothal. This is not comparable to the father's silence, who might have been angry, which is not applicable in her case. This is similar to an orphan betrothed by her mother, where upon growing up, the betrothal becomes effective even without relations, and it is considered doubtful betrothal as will be explained in Siman 155. Even though some say it is not comparable, as there it is at least rabbinically binding betrothal, unlike when her father is alive, nevertheless, in practice, it remains doubtful marital status, especially according to those who say that when the father is far away, the betrothal is rabbinically valid even during her minority like an orphan. However, if the father is present and remains silent and she grows up without protesting, it is still considered doubtful betrothal, and this is the ruling of our teacher, the Rema, in Siman 11.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in Section 12: "A minor girl who betrothed herself to someone whom her father had expressed a desire for her to marry—we are concerned that he may have consented." And it must be said that this refers to a situation where it was done in his presence and he expressed his desire for her to accept the betrothal, or even not in his presence in such a manner when he explicitly stated that he wishes for her to accept the betrothal. Otherwise, what advantage is there over a matchmaker, which is ineffective as stated in Section 15? The Tur concludes that it is considered a betrothal as long as she has not been betrothed to another, and he strives to betroth her to the second one. And the Tur's opinion is that this concern that he may have consented is not because it is as if he made her a proxy to accept the betrothal, for if so, how could he retract since she accepted the betrothal on his behalf, and one's proxy is like oneself? According to the opinion that in such a case agency is effective even for a minor, as will be explained. Rather, the Tur holds that he did not object to her acceptance, but it is not a complete betrothal. Therefore, when she is betrothed to another, the betrothal she accepted is nullified. Our master, the Beit Yosef, omitted this because he holds that the reason is that it is as if she is his proxy, and immediately upon her accepting the betrothal, he cannot retract. (See Choshen Mishpat, Section 23, and Beit Shmuel, Section 24, and according to what is written, everything is clear. And from Kiddushin 45a, there is no proof at all, for there he did not express his desire for her to accept the betrothal. See there and examine it well.)

She was betrothed with her father's consent but married without his consent. If the father comes and objects to her marriage, her marriage is annulled, and she is considered only betrothed. Therefore, regarding all matters where there is a difference between a betrothed woman and a married woman, such as inheritance if she dies—since with a married woman, the husband inherits his wife, but with a betrothed woman, he does not—and similarly, if he is a priest, he becomes impure for his married wife but not for his betrothed one. There are also differences in the marriage contract and burial. If she married without her father's consent, even though her father himself betrothed her and she is considered married by Torah law, it is not considered a complete marriage either when her father is present or if he went to distant places because the marriage is not complete since the father can object.

Some say that even if the father died before she married and she married after his death, she is not considered fully married since the betrothal is by Torah law, but the marriage is not, making it worse than the betrothal and marriage of an orphan. However, Rabbeinu Tam (R"T) of blessed memory disagreed with this view and said that since the father has died and there is no longer a concern that he will object, it is a complete marriage. She is not under the authority of her brothers, and they cannot object like the father could. No person bequeaths the rights over his daughter to his sons, and it is considered a complete marriage, and the husband inherits her.

Some of the early Geonim said that just as the Rabbis instituted that a minor orphan could be betrothed and married by her mother and brothers, or by herself alone, as mentioned in Siman 155, so too they instituted that if someone went on a long journey and left his home, the mother or brothers could betroth her to someone they see fit for her. This would constitute betrothal and marriage by rabbinic decree, and if she wishes to leave him, she requires refusal (mi'un) like all minor orphans. If she grows up and does not refuse, the betrothal grows with her. If the father returns even while she is still a minor, no new betrothal is needed, as her betrothal is valid by rabbinic decree, unless he wishes to make it a Torah-level betrothal, which he can do. However, the blessings should not be recited because they would be in vain since they were already recited by rabbinic ordinance. This is what the Talmud says regarding a minor who was betrothed without her father's knowledge—that it is not a valid betrothal at all, and does not even require refusal—this applies when the father is here or nearby, but not when he is far away. Some interpret this to mean that this applies when he left his house empty and left due to financial constraints, certainly it is agreeable to him that his wife betroths their daughter to a suitable match. It is obvious if his wife is a woman of valor whom he trusts in all her endeavors, then this minor is like an orphan in her father's lifetime. But if he is a merchant and traveled far away for business and stayed there for a long time, certainly he does not want her to be betrothed without his knowledge.

However, there are some of our rabbis who disagree with all these matters, as we do not find this ordinance in the Talmud. On the contrary, in the entire discussion regarding a minor who was betrothed without her father's knowledge, there are many questions and issues, and how could it be that the Talmud did not mention that it refers to a case where the father is far away and she has permission to betroth herself? Therefore, they ruled that such a betrothal is invalid, and she does not even need to perform mi'un (refusal) to leave him. Nevertheless, one should not prohibit her to him and remove her from him, as this is not considered promiscuous relations, and she is not considered single to him because it was done in the manner of betrothal and marriage. Moreover, even if the father came and objected to the betrothal, as long as she has not betrothed someone else, she is permitted to remain with him, and their cohabitation is not considered promiscuous. If she stayed with him until she matured and he cohabited with her after she matured, the betrothal is completed and is considered Torah-level betrothal, provided the father did not accept betrothal from another man for her while she was a minor. However, if he did not cohabit with her after she matured, it is not even a doubtful betrothal. This is not similar to what is stated in paragraph 18, where immediately upon the father's objection, the betrothal is completely nullified <small>[Beit Shmuel 32]</small>. If the father betrothed her to another man before she matured, she is taken away from the first and given to the second. It seems that she does not need a get (divorce document) from the first; however, from the words of our teacher, the Rema in paragraph 14, it is understood that she does need a get from him. It is possible that his reasoning is due to appearances, as everyone saw how she was with him for a long time like husband and wife, and it would be a scandal if she were to leave without a get. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote that in practice, one should be stringent according to the first opinion.

And there are some of our rabbis who added to say further that on the contrary, when her father is far away, it is worse than when he is here, and they do not allow her to remain under him because there is concern that perhaps he accepted betrothal for her and she is a married woman. However, the great rabbis did not agree with him, for if so, if her father died while far away, she would be prohibited all her life. Rather, certainly we do not concern ourselves with this, for we maintain her in the presumption of being unmarried and do not fear that she was betrothed, just like the wife of a priest whose husband is far away and she eats terumah by Torah law and we do not fear that he died, for we maintain him in the presumption of being alive. Similarly, at all times she is permitted to the one who betrothed her, for at all times we maintain her in the presumption of being unmarried. And on the contrary, some say exactly the opposite — that whenever her father is far away, if she betrothed herself to another, it is a doubtful betrothal by Torah law, for we fear that perhaps if the father heard, he would agree, and she would be in doubt of being betrothed. For what the sages said, that we do not fear that the father agreed, applies when he is here and not when he is far away. According to this opinion, she would not leave even through refusal but only through a divorce. However, most of the decisors do not hold this way, as we have explained.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 14: There was an incident where a man divorced his wife and stipulated that she would care for his daughters, provide for them, raise them, and marry them off, and so she did. However, the father came and objected to the marriage of his minor daughters, and it was ruled that if he had instructed her to marry them off and raise them, whatever she did was valid, and he could not object, provided that he had so instructed her in the presence of witnesses, because a receiving agent requires witnesses as mentioned earlier in section 35. But if he said that she would have the authority to marry them off when they grew up and she married them off while they were still minors, her actions are invalid, and he can object since she deviated from his instructions. And even if he did not object, there is no marriage at all, even according to those who are stringent in cases of doubt, since she violated his instructions, and she can leave without the need for refusal according to all opinions. However, when he said to raise them and marry them off, we do not say that his intention was only to marry them off when they are adults, but rather he said two things to her – to raise them, meaning to bring them up, and also to marry them off even when they are minors. And it seems to me that this is because he said three things – also to provide for them as mentioned. But if he only said to raise them and marry them off, it is possible to say that his intention was only to marry them off when they are adults, and therefore it is considered doubtful marriage. And one should not ask that even though he made her a receiving agent for the marriage, why not be concerned that he might have revoked her agency before she married them off? For it can be said that certainly, if he claims so, we are concerned about it, and although we do not believe him with certainty, nonetheless, it is only considered doubtful marriage. However, in this case, he did not claim this but only objects now, and he does not have the ability to object as they ruled. And it has already been clarified in section 35 that even in agency without witnesses, one should be stringent, but with witnesses, it is considered a valid marriage.

Just as a father can betroth his daughter himself, he can also betroth her through his agent, but there is a greater mitzvah for him to do it himself than through his agent, as stated in Siman 35. Similarly, he can betroth her through her own agency. The sages said: A man can say to his young daughter, "Go and accept your betrothal," and even more so with a young woman. All the previous laws that have been explained, regarding a situation where she accepted betrothal without his knowledge and he consented, are considered valid betrothals, as it follows that she can accept the betrothal with her father's consent. Otherwise, what benefit would his consent provide?

However, it is necessary to explain the reason why her acceptance [of the betrothal] is effective by his command. While it makes sense for a young woman to be his agent to accept the betrothal, a minor girl is not within the law of agency. So how does her acceptance help? Some of our rabbis hold that this is not actually a matter of agency. Rather, when he tells her, "Go and accept your betrothal," it is as if he is giving her his right, which the Torah granted him, to accept betrothal on her behalf. She can then accept the betrothal from whomever she wishes [Rashba]. He relinquishes all his authority over her, and she is in her own authority as an adult. Even though a minor does not have the legal capacity to acquire on her own, it has already been explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 243, that with the intent of another person, a minor can have the legal capacity to acquire [Tosafot there]. According to this opinion, since this is not a matter of agency but rather a relinquishment of authority from her, it is not necessary to tell her in the presence of witnesses. It can even be said privately between them [and Rema in Siman 7 does not agree with this reasoning].

Some of our Rabbis hold a different reason for this, that just as a woman who says, "Give to my dog and I will be betrothed to you" or "Give on top of the rock and I will be betrothed to you," and the rock belongs to her – when he gives, it constitutes betrothal. Similarly, this young girl is not inferior to a dog or a rock [Raavad and Ramban]. And even though in that case, she said this to the one betrothing her, and here, the father did not speak at all with the betrother, nevertheless, since he said to her, "Receive your betrothal," it is as if he said, "Whoever gives you a maneh, I consider it as if they gave it to me," and it is as if he said to the betrother, "Give to my daughter and she will be betrothed to you." This opinion holds that with a rock or a dog, by giving to the rock or the dog, she becomes betrothed through this alone, as stated in Siman 30, Section 26, see there. And this opinion does not hold as stated there in Section 27 that it must be given later into her lap, for according to this opinion, what benefit does her receipt provide? Nor does this opinion hold that a rock is under the law of a courtyard, as stated there, because if so, the father would need to stand beside it, as the law of a courtyard requires it to be guarded with his knowledge or that he stands beside the courtyard [and see what is written in Section 32]. Rather, they hold the reason of surety, as stated there in Section 28, that this is like "Give a maneh to so-and-so," see there. And here too, it touches upon the law of surety. Therefore, even if he commanded the betrother to give to another young girl who is not his daughter, and through this his daughter would be betrothed to him – it would also constitute betrothal [Beit Shmuel, Section 7]. However, the reason of surety only suffices for betrothal with money and not for betrothal with a document. And indeed, some say that this law is only for betrothal with money [see Ran, First Chapter, s.v. "wrote"]. But there is another reason here that it is as if it reached his hand, and this is like "Whoever gives you, I consider it as if they gave to me" [Beit Shmuel]. And most of the authorities do not hold this reasoning [this is the opinion of Tosafot Rid, that even with a get (divorce document) such a thing works, see Avnei Miluim, Section 3, who also writes this, and it is difficult on the Beit Shmuel, and according to this opinion, indeed this law does not apply to a document, and this is also implied by the language of Raavad quoted in Rosh, First Chapter, Section 15, see there. However, the Baraita explicitly states there also a document, and it seems they hold like Tosafot Rid, and this is the difficulty of the Rosh there, as Ran writes, and examine this well].

And some of our Rabbis have said that this entire law is based on the concept of agency (שליחות), and even though a minor cannot serve as an agent, this applies when the agency is to benefit someone else, because the disqualification of a minor from agency is due to the fact that "man" (איש) is written in all matters of agency, such as in divorce (גט), tithes (תרומה), and Passover (פסח), and this is specifically to benefit another through his agency. But in the case of the betrothal of a minor girl, where she benefits herself through the agency of her father, her agency for herself is effective as if her father had accepted the betrothal on her behalf, because a minor can acquire when another person grants it to him. This is as explained by the Rosh there. 

Similarly, it is implied from the language of the Rambam in Chapter 3, Law 14, that this law is based on the concept of agency, and it is not surprising that a minor can be included in the concept of agency, for in truth, this is not complete agency but rather a form of acquisition, and acquisition also involves agency. Yet, a minor acquires through the intention of another granting it to him, and similarly here, the father grants her the betrothal and makes her an agent to acquire it for herself. This reason almost aligns with what we wrote in Section 26. 

According to the reason of agency, it should be said to her in the presence of witnesses, for agency of acceptance requires witnesses as written in Section 35. However, even without witnesses, one should be stringent as written there, and if it is evident to all that she is preparing herself for the wedding and to accept the betrothal, and the father is also involved in the preparation, this itself is like a statement in the presence of witnesses, as is evident in the Rivash, Section 479. 

There is no difference in all this between a young girl and a minor girl, and this is the main ruling. Although some dissent and say that a minor girl cannot accept her betrothal and only the father must accept it, and only in the case of a young girl can the father instruct her to accept the betrothal, nevertheless, the law is not so, and the majority of the decisors do not hold this view. This is also clear from several Talmudic passages, as seen in Beit Shmuel, Section 8. Certainly, according to this opinion, all the passages refer to a young girl, as explained by the Ran according to the Ramban, and the passage of Rav Nachman on page 19 refers specifically to Rabbi Yosef.

Nevertheless, since there are those who disagree regarding a minor girl, our teacher, the Rema, wrote that in order to avoid disagreement, the father should hold the minor's hand when she receives the betrothal or stand next to her when she receives it, as it is as if he received it himself. And this method is preferable even according to those who believe that a minor girl has the power to receive her own betrothal, as the reasoning is that she is like the father's courtyard, and as it is written in Section 27, he must also stand next to her, as it is written there. According to the reasoning of the courtyard, it also works for betrothal by document [and in Section 32 we questioned this]. Our teacher, the Rema, concludes that this is preferable to him receiving it himself, for there are those who say it is forbidden to betroth one's minor daughter, as will be explained shortly, since the prohibition is because it might be against her will. But if it is her will to be betrothed, there is no prohibition [see Beit Shmuel, Subsection 11], and consequently, when she receives it herself, it is clear that it is her will.

How is the language of betrothal expressed? When the minor (girl) receives the betrothal on the instruction of her father, he says to her, “Behold, you are betrothed to me,” and he can also say, “Your daughter is betrothed to me” if the father is standing next to her even though he gives her the betrothal, since the authority comes from the father. Even if her father is not next to her and he says, “Your daughter is betrothed to me,” it is considered betrothal since she stands in place of her father [Beit Shmuel, section 10], and although there is some hesitation about this [Hagahot Maimoniyot], and certainly the language is not straightforward, nevertheless, there is no impediment to the betrothal in this case. All the more so when the father tells the groom, “Give my daughter the money for betrothal and she will be betrothed to you,” in which case, according to all opinions, she is permitted to receive her betrothal not in the presence of the father [Beit Shmuel, section 9], since when he says to her, “Your daughter is betrothed to me,” it constitutes betrothal, as it is based on his instruction. And if the father receives the betrothal of his daughter, it is obvious that he must say, “Your daughter is betrothed to me” and not any other language when she is a minor or adolescent. However, if she is of age and the father is her messenger, he can also say, “Behold, you are betrothed to me,” as he speaks to the messenger as if to the sender, since a person’s messenger is like himself [ibid., section 10]. Nevertheless, it is certainly not a proper language at all, and there is hesitation about all of this when the language is not accurate [this is according to what is stated in Hagahot Maimoniyot, section 11].

In the case of betrothal by a document, when the woman receives it in her childhood or adolescence, according to those who hold that betrothal by a document is also permissible for her to receive by her father's command, the betrother must write in the document, "Your daughter is betrothed to me" specifically. And at the time he gives it to her, he says to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me." However, to write in the document "Behold, you are betrothed to me" is not correct, just as in a divorce document executed by an agent, it must be written in the name of the woman. Similarly, in the betrothal of a minor where the father is the one delivering her for betrothal, it must be written specifically in his name [Ran], and so ruled our teacher the Rema. However, there are those among our teachers who are certain that even if in the document it is written, "Behold, you are betrothed to me," it constitutes a complete betrothal [Ramban], as it is not similar to a divorce document executed by an agent, where the agent has no connection to the divorce document. In contrast, with betrothal, on the contrary, she is the primary party, only that the Torah granted the father permission. In practice, it seems the primary view is this one [see Gra, Section 22], and even our teacher the Rema only ruled thus ideally, as he concluded in his words that if these matters were altered, she is still betrothed. And if one betroths by a document and the father receives the document, if she is a minor or adolescent, it must be written "Your daughter is betrothed to me." If she is an adult, and the father is her agent, it must be written specifically "Behold, you are betrothed to me," to speak with her as in a divorce document, and if he changed it, it is not a betrothal. And when he hands the document to the father, he should say, "Your daughter is betrothed to me" [Bach, Section 10]. However, some say that even in the case of a minor, if it is written in the document "Behold, you are" it is also considered betrothal [there in the name of Ra'am], and this seems to be the main opinion. Nevertheless, in practice, one should be stringent in betrothal according to all opinions.

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 7 that when they send the young girls to another place and the father is not with them when they receive the betrothal, since he prepared to bring her to the chuppah and the betrothal, it is as if he is holding her hand at the time of receiving, end quote. And it is no less than if he consented before the betrothal, for according to everyone, the betrothal is valid. And this is only if she is betrothed with money, but with a document, the matter is difficult unless it is based on the principle of agency. For concerning the principle of courtyard (acquisition by property), we require that he stands next to her, as it is written in section 29. And even this is not satisfactory, for indeed it is a courtyard that is guarded without his knowledge when she is awake and not when she is asleep, and it is also a mobile courtyard. And it is explicitly stated in the Talmud that it does not have the status of a courtyard for this reason. (And see there in the Rif, and scrutinize carefully).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 8: It is a mitzvah not to betroth one's daughter while she is still a minor until she grows up and says, "I want to marry so-and-so." However, there are those who say that in our times, it is customary to betroth our minor daughters because we are in exile and do not always have the means to provide a sufficient dowry. Additionally, we are few in number and do not always find a suitable match. And so is the custom, end quote.

But in our times, we do not betroth minors, and we have never heard of anyone who betroths a minor, and that is proper. For in the Talmud (Kiddushin 41a) it is stated that it is forbidden to betroth her while she is a minor. And although when she consents there is no prohibition, nevertheless, it is not proper. And thus, the simple custom in our times and in our region is not to betroth minors.

The father who gave permission to his agent to betroth his daughter, and he himself went and betrothed her to someone else, and his agent betrothed her to another – whichever of them preceded, the betrothal is valid. If it is not known which one preceded, she is forbidden to both and requires a get (divorce document) from both. If they wish, one can give a get, and the other can marry her, but she requires a new betrothal, for perhaps the other’s betrothal preceded and was not valid, as stated in Siman 36, Se'if 9 regarding the agency of a woman. Similarly, if the betrothers are relatives forbidden to each other, she is absolutely forbidden to both, as stated there.

If, after he sent an agent to accept the betrothal of his daughter, he appointed another agent to accept her betrothal and did not explicitly annul the agency of the first, and each of the agents went and accepted betrothal on her behalf, she requires a get (divorce document) from both, even if we know who received it first, because there is doubt whether his intention was to annul the first agency or not. 

There is an opinion that if it is known that the betrothal by the second agent preceded, she does not need a get from the first, because if he annulled the first agency, then the first betrothal is invalid, and even if he did not annul it but thought that the first agent might not find someone to betroth her, since the second agent's betrothal preceded, it implies that the first agent did not find someone, and therefore the second betrothal is valid.

However, it can be said that he did not appoint the second agent except in the case that the first did not find anyone at all, but if the first did find someone, even after the second’s actions, the first’s actions would be valid and not the second’s. Accordingly, the doubt returns as before.

And one cannot say that if we hold this reasoning, then in the case where he himself betrothed her before his agent, his betrothal is valid and not the agent's, we should also say that he did not betroth her himself unless the agent did not find anyone at all, but if the agent did find someone, the agent's betrothal should be valid. It can be said that against his own action, we do not apply this reasoning.

Even if the second agent did not betroth her at all, but only the first did, it remains a doubtful betrothal, as he might have annulled the agency.

One cannot argue that with the sending of the divorce document, even if he appointed multiple agents, we do not say that the earlier ones are annulled as stated in section 141, for it is not similar. There, all the agents are for one matter – to receive a get from a specific person. Similarly, if all the agents are for one person to receive betrothal from him, we do not say that the agency is annulled. But here, he appointed agents to receive betrothal from anyone they deem fit, and it is impossible for all of them to be agents.

Be aware that this law of two agents also applies to a man who appointed two agents to betroth a woman on his behalf, or a woman who appointed two agents to accept betrothal on her behalf, as these doubts regarding the annulment of the first agency also apply.

A daughter, upon reaching maturity, leaves her father's authority. The time of her maturity is six months after the days of her youth, which begin when she brings forth two pubic hairs at the completion of twelve full years. From then, she is called a "na'arah" (maiden) until six full months have passed. Rambam wrote in Chapter 2 of Ishut that from the beginning of the completion of the six months and onwards, she is called a "bogeret" (mature woman). This implies that she will never reach the days of maturity in less than six months, and many of our rabbis agreed with this, as it is evident from our versions in the Talmud [Kiddushin 79a and Ketubot 39a]. Some of our rabbis hold that sometimes she can be a "bogeret" in less than six months if she brings signs of maturity [Rashi]. They also hold that what the sages said [Niddah 67b] about the signs of the breasts are signs of maturity. There is a dispute about this, with the halacha being decided in the Talmud that the law follows all opinions to be stringent, meaning that any of the signs she brings makes her a doubtful "bogeret." However, Rambam, in Halacha 7, holds that all of these are signs of youth, and regarding maturity, he did not write any signs at all. According to him, there is no doubt in the world about maturity. But all our rabbis disagree with him, and so reads our version in the Talmud [there] and the Tosefta in Niddah [Chapter 6] that there is a dispute about the signs of maturity. The Rif also wrote this in Chapter 13 of Yevamot [and it is perplexing regarding the Maggid Mishnah there who wrote that this is the law, see there]. According to this, there is also doubt about maturity, and all of this has practical implications for the law that will be explained further, with God's help.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 5: If her father betrothed her in the morning and she betrothed herself in the evening, and both were on the day that completed six months of her youth, and they examined her and found her to be a bogeret (mature woman) – she is presumed to be a bogeret and the father's betrothal is invalid. There is an opinion that says this is so even if she does not contradict him by claiming that the signs of maturity appeared in the morning. Another opinion holds that this is only if she contradicts him, but if she does not contradict him, she needs a get (divorce document) from both.

The explanation of the matter is: Our Sages hold that on this day, when she completes the six months, she can develop signs of maturity either in the morning or in the evening. On that day, she has neither the presumption of youth nor the presumption of maturity. It is not only if the father accepted the betrothal in the morning and she did not accept it at all that the father's betrothal is invalid because we assume her to be single, but even if she also accepted betrothal in the evening, since she is now showing signs of maturity, we do not worry about the father's betrothal. We say that since she is a bogeret now, she must have also been a bogeret in the morning. We do not take a stringent approach to consider it a doubt because we follow the current status, and this itself is like a presumption to follow the present time and say that since it is so now, it was likely also so earlier when there is no other presumption to contradict it. This is also proven in the Talmud, and additionally, the signs of maturity typically appear in the morning.

Based on this, if she herself accepted the betrothal in the morning without her father's knowledge, and her father did not accept the betrothal at all, and in the evening she was found to be an adult (bogeret) – it can be said that it is only a doubtful betrothal and we do not say that we follow the present state, but rather we follow her status of being unmarried and say that she just now showed signs of maturity and not in the morning [and so writes the Beit Shmuel]. However, according to the reasoning we wrote that it is customary for signs of maturity to appear in the morning – even in such a case, the betrothal would be valid [and see Yam Shel Shlomo, Chapter 4, Siman 17, although there is a printing error there].

All that we have written is according to the first opinion, which holds that even if she does not explicitly say that she brought the signs (of maturity) in the morning, we still follow the current situation. Nevertheless, if she clearly states that she did not bring the signs in the morning, we are concerned for her statement and it becomes a doubtful case of betrothal. And this is the main ruling, for although by law we follow the current situation for the reasons explained, still, since she claims with certainty against this, how can we not be concerned for her statement? After all, a certain claim is a strong claim, and only against a presumption of possession do we not consider a certain claim. All the more so, to be stringent, how can we not be concerned for a certain claim? And if the father also claims with certainty that she did not bring the signs in the morning, we certainly would be concerned for his words. The term "contradiction" that the Tur and Shulchan Aruch use does not mean that this one claims this and that one claims that, for everyone agrees it is a doubt. They used the language of the Gemara in a manner that does not align with this opinion. The second opinion holds that this is not a complete presumption to follow the current situation, and it remains a doubt unless she claims with certainty that she brought the signs in the morning, which then becomes a complete presumption. But if she does not claim with certainty, we act stringently.

And know that the Rambam, of blessed memory, omitted all these laws, and his reasoning, it seems to me, is that he follows his own reasoning that we wrote in section 36, that there are no signs for adolescents (bogrot), and there is no doubt in the matter that from the beginning of the day she is an adolescent as it is explicitly stated at the beginning of chapter 2. According to this, all the discussions on this matter are irrelevant because it cannot be otherwise. He holds that this is precisely the dispute in the Talmud there, and the halacha is decided accordingly. 

[For the explanation of what Rav said, "From now on she is an adolescent," etc., it is not due to some reason but because that is the truth, meaning from now on she is an adolescent, and on the day that completes six months, she is certainly an adolescent in the morning as well. Shmuel does not agree with this. This answers Tosafot's question in the comment "And Shmuel," that the entire discussion in the sugya is according to Shmuel and not according to Rav, and therefore the Talmud had to conclude the sugya by ruling according to Rav there. This resolves all the difficulties raised against the Rambam, of blessed memory.]

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch further wrote in section 6 that if within the six months of maidenhood her father betrothed her without her knowledge and she herself betrothed herself without her father's knowledge, and signs of maturity were found, it is a doubt and she requires a divorce from both, end quote. And this law applies only according to those who hold that even within six months she can mature, as it is written. But according to those who do not hold this, this law does not apply at all. However, it can be said that according to all opinions there is place for this law, and it is said that when one of the signs of maturity is found, we say that she had been a maiden six months prior and we did not observe. And the proof for this is that many of our Rabbis hold that there must necessarily be six months between maidenhood and maturity, no more and no less. Therefore, what the Sages investigated regarding the signs of maturity, what doubt is there in this? Rather, the doubt is that when we find signs of maturity, we say that indeed she showed signs of maidenhood six months prior, and even if there were no two hairs then, we say they fell out. However, according to this, the doubt cannot be less than twelve years and six months, because before twelve years signs of maidenhood are not valid. But our Rabbis, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, seem to hold clearly that signs of maturity can also be within six months, according to the opinion of Rashi. And what the Beit Shmuel wrote in subsection 5 that the Rif also holds this opinion, according to what is written there is no proof.

Accordingly, if within the six months her father alone betrothed her or she betrothed herself alone, it is also a case of doubtful betrothal when it is later found that she has signs of maturity. The reason is that even though we can say that if her father alone betrothed her, it is a complete betrothal due to the presumption of her being a maiden within this time, nevertheless, opposite this, there is a presumption of her being unmarried. And if she alone betrothed herself, even though we should say that it is not a betrothal at all since these two presumptions help to nullify the betrothal, still it is a case of doubtful betrothal because the presumption that we follow the present contradicts these presumptions and weakens them, as we say regarding impurity that all impurities are based on their present state, as explained by the Rambam in chapter 18 of the Laws of the Fathers of Impurity. And Tosafot in Eruvin 35b hold that this only applies to terumah and holy items, but the Rambam does not hold this way. And regarding betrothal in the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rav Nachman, we rule like Rabbi Yehuda that we do not follow the present because of the opposing presumption of property, as it says there according to Rav. And the Rambam would explain what is said there, but here who would say to establish the body, etc., meaning here the presumption does not apply as it is obvious that she was a mature woman from the morning, as it cannot be otherwise. And study this well.

Rambam writes in Chapter 3, Law 14: Any woman who is in doubt whether she is a bogeret (mature woman), whether her father alone betrothed her or she betrothed herself, is considered doubtfully betrothed. Therefore, she requires a get (bill of divorce) out of doubt. The doubt is whether she is twelve years and six months old or not, or even if she is much older and there is a doubt whether she brought forth two hairs before six months, according to Rambam, there is no inherent doubt regarding her maturity as written. The reason she requires a get out of doubt and we do not establish her status based on a presumption, such as if signs of maturity are found in her now, and according to Rambam there is no need for signs at all but rather that she has reached the age of maturity, the reason we explained in the previous section. And if signs of adolescence appear in her a month or more after twelve years, we say that presumably at the end of twelve years she also had signs of adolescence and therefore now she is a bogeret. However, there are those who disagree with this.

And since according to most of the authorities, except for the Rambam, there are signs of maturity, it is necessary to explain them. And we learn in Niddah (47a): The Rabbis taught: These are the signs of maturity: Rabbi Eliezer the son of Rabbi Tzadok says, when the breasts move. Rabbi Yochanan the son of Beroka says, when the tip of the nose becomes distinct. Rabbi Yehuda says, when the crown of the head becomes prominent. Rabbi Shimon says, when the palm of the hand becomes fleshy – and the law is according to all of them to be stringent. And if she exhibits one of these signs but not all, she is in doubt as to whether she is mature. And the Rif wrote in the thirteenth chapter of Yevamot that if she exhibits one of the signs and betroths herself during her father's lifetime, her betrothal is valid and she requires a get (divorce), and her father cannot annul her vows. And if her father betroths her without her consent, she requires a get. End of quote. According to the Rambam, all these are signs of adolescence, as he wrote.

If a man betroths his daughter without specifying which one, for example if he says "My daughter is betrothed to you" without clarifying which daughter [Rashi 64b], or if the man who is betrothing says to the father "One of your daughters is betrothed to me" [Rashi 51a], or if the man who is betrothing says "Your daughter is betrothed to me" and the father responds "One of my daughters is betrothed to you" – adult daughters (bogerot) are not included. Therefore, if he has only two daughters and one is an adult, the younger one is betrothed. The reason, the Sages explained, is that it is not necessary to say that if the adult daughter did not give permission for the father to accept her betrothal, it is obvious that there is no concern for her since she is not under his authority to betroth. Even if she gave him permission to accept her betrothal, and even if she said that the money for the betrothal should be his, she is not included because a person does not neglect a mitzvah imposed upon him – which is the betrothal of minors and maidens – and perform a mitzvah not imposed upon him, as the adult daughter is not under his authority to betroth. This applies specifically if she appointed him as an agent to accept betrothal generally and did not specify "from so-and-so," but if she said "from so-and-so" and he accepted from him, she is also in doubt of being betrothed, and other adult daughters are not included. If he has two or more minor daughters or maidens, they are all prohibited and all require a get (divorce document), even though these are betrothals that are not handed over to consummation. We hold that they are considered betrothal, as it is stated in Siman 41.

And there is a question here: why do we say that the older daughters are not included even when she made him her agent, because it is not a mitzvah incumbent upon her, and as for the young girls, it is a mitzvah incumbent upon her? On the contrary, it has already been clarified that there is no mitzvah to betroth a young girl, and there is even a bit of a prohibition as mentioned in section 33. And the prophet Jeremiah who said (Jeremiah 29:6), "Give your daughters to men," was not referring to young girls, for he also said there, "and take wives for your sons," and the betrothal of a minor is nothing and is not within the father's authority for betrothal. Rather, its meaning is about the effort, and this is how the Sages explained it in Ketubot [52b, and see Rashi there in Kiddushin and it requires study]. And when an older daughter made him her agent, there certainly is a mitzvah to betroth her, so how can we say that the older daughters are not included? Besides, it is not customary for people to marry off the younger before the older, and Laban said this, so how can we say the opposite? In truth, one of the great early Rabbis wanted to say that when one says "your daughter is betrothed to me," his intention is only for the older one for the reason we explained [Tosafot, Ketubot 52b], but the Sages of his generation did not agree with him, and he himself did not rely on this in practice. And it requires a reason why [and the Ritva wrote that it does not refer to minors, and it requires study to understand how this can be, and examine it carefully].
