And the answer to this – since we see that this man, when he said generally "your daughter is betrothed to me," or this father, when he said generally "my daughter is betrothed to you," without specifying which daughter, they have deviated from the norm of ordinary people who do not act this way, as it is madness not to specify which daughter is being betrothed. Therefore, we must delve into the depths of Torah law based on the understanding of this language and not consider matters of common decency since this man has deviated from common decency. Consequently, the minors and adolescents are included in this language, and we interpret his words as the language of the verse "I have given my daughter to this man," excluding the adults, as the section dealing with a man who brings a bad name (Deuteronomy 22:13-21) does not apply to adults. Since minors and adolescents are included, even if we say that adults are also included, he has done nothing beneficial because it would be a betrothal not fit for consummation. Therefore, we say that this man intended only what the Torah allowed him to betroth, which are those under his authority, and he did not consider the adults. However, when he made him an agent to receive betrothal for this man, it is obvious that his intention was also for her, and therefore she is also included, and all of them are forbidden and need a get (divorce document). Nonetheless, if he has other adult daughters, they are not included and are permitted based on the reasoning we have explained, and we do not say that his intention was only for this adult based on estimation since he has deviated from ordinary people as we have said, we do not make estimations in his case. And if there was an engagement with this, it will be explained to us with God's help.

The Tur wrote: If a man arranged a match for his eldest daughter and he had other daughters, and the matchmaker said to him, "Your daughter is betrothed to me," and he made him a messenger to receive the betrothal – his intention is not on the other daughters, and she is betrothed with definite betrothal. Even if he did not arrange a match and said, "Your eldest daughter is betrothed to me," and he has daughters only from one wife – certainly his intention is on the eldest, and she is definitely betrothed. End quote. And there are those who disagree even in this case when he said simply, "Your daughter is betrothed to me," as since he did not specify, we are concerned that perhaps his intention was on the one he did not arrange a match for, and it is a doubtful betrothal (as explained by the Maggid Mishneh, Chapter 9). However, if he said, "Your eldest daughter," there is no one who disagrees, as this is considered a clear specification, unless he has two eldest daughters from two different women, as will be explained in Section 54. See there.

It is taught in the Tosefta of Kiddushin [Chapter 4]: Two brothers who betrothed two sisters, one does not know to whom he betrothed, and the other does not know to whom he betrothed—they are both prohibited due to doubt. If they were involved in the matter with the intention of the elder brother for the elder sister and the younger brother for the younger sister, I say—the elder sister was not betrothed except to the elder brother, and the younger sister was not betrothed except to the younger brother, end of quote. We learn from this that being involved in that matter is considered as if it were explicitly stated, and even according to the one who disagrees regarding engagement, as we have written, nevertheless, if they were involved with the elder sister for the elder brother and the younger sister for the younger brother, and he betrothed without specifying, it certainly takes effect [Ran, Chapter 2]. Some are stringent even in such a case [Beit Yosef in the name of Ra'avad], and they hold that the betrothal is valid for all, and they all require a get (divorce document), because even if it is clear to us that the intention of the one betrothing was for the elder sister, his thought does not nullify the words he expressed, for unspoken thoughts are not considered significant since he changed the wording from the common form which clarifies betrothal [ibid.], and from the Tosefta there is no proof, for there it speaks about a case where from the beginning each one betrothed one of them known, and now they got mixed up, and therefore we follow what they were initially involved in, but in a case of betrothal without specifying, it is possible that we do not follow their presumed intention [Ran].

And this is the opinion of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in Section 16 where they wrote: If a man has two daughters, even if both are minors, and he made a match for one of them with a man and after some time received betrothal from him, and the man said, "Your daughter is betrothed to me," both daughters are forbidden to him and they both need a divorce from him. Even if he immediately clarified within the time period of "within speaking" and specified "your daughter, so-and-so," it is not effective. And in all such cases where the betrothal could not lead to marital relations, we compel him to divorce her. [The conclusion that adults are not included in this matter is superfluous; see there.]

It seems clear to me that the statement that being occupied with it also does not help does not mean being occupied with that exact matter, for it is obvious that in such a case it helps, as even in silence she is betrothed when they are engaged in that exact matter, as stated in Siman 27. Rather, it means that they were previously engaged in discussing her betrothal. Additionally, it seems to me that the fact that being betrothed does not help, this is only when it was done through mere speech. However, if the betrothal terms were written in a condition document as is customary among us, and it was publicized according to custom—certainly, he intended for her and not for another. Nevertheless, in practice, this requires further study since our Rabbis were very stringent on this matter. Also, the statement that retraction does not help even within the time it takes to say a few words, this is when he clarifies that his intention was for a specific woman and he did not make a verbal mistake by saying it in general, but rather he explains his intention. However, if he says that he made a verbal mistake and intended to say your daughter but erred in his speech—certainly he is believed to say within the time it takes to say a few words that he made a mistake.

[Note: The small print sections refer to commentaries and further clarifications from other sources, which have been left out of the main translation for clarity.]

There are those who say that if Reuven told Shimon, "One of your daughters is betrothed to me," and afterwards said that he betroths her with the consent of the father, so that whichever daughter the father desires, she will be betrothed, and the father said, "I intended for this one" – he is believed. However, it seems to me that all [the daughters] are forbidden. It is not only if he said it in general terms and afterwards explained his intention, which would be considered mere thoughts and worse than what has been explained, but even if he said at the time of the act, "One of your daughters is betrothed to me – whichever one you desire," and the father said, "I desired this one," it is also considered mere thoughts. Moreover, there is a concern of retroactive clarification (brerah), and even without this, our Rabbis were stringent even with adult women when they made him an agent, and the decisors were also stringent with a matchmaker. How can we be lenient in this case? [And the Rema in Darkei Moshe, section 13, came to reconcile the words of the She'iltot, but not for practical ruling, and therefore omitted this ruling in the Shulchan Aruch].

Reuven betrothed one of his daughters, explicitly mentioned by name, to a minor. Afterwards, Shimon came and said, "One of your daughters is betrothed to me." Some say that even the one betrothed to the minor is included in the prohibition because the betrothal of a minor is not valid betrothal. Others say that only the completely unbetrothed ones are included in this, but anyone upon whom there is a designation of betrothal, even though by law it is not a valid betrothal, is not included in the doubt. And this appears to be the main ruling. Additionally, the Beit Yosef did not write this as a final law, but rather in connection to the responsa of the Rosh, and the texts are not precise, as is evident there.

If a man has two sets of daughters from two wives, and the oldest of one set and the oldest of the other set are not of the same age, and similarly, the youngest of one set and the youngest of the other set are not of the same age—for example, he married the second wife after the first had already given birth, or the first wife died before he married the second wife, and all the daughters are still minors and maidens who are under the authority of their father to be betrothed—if he says to the betrother, "I betrothed one of my daughters to you," all are forbidden. However, if he says, "I betrothed my oldest daughter to you," if he said this at the time of the betrothal, even though this wording also contains ambiguities, as it could be interpreted to mean the oldest daughter of his first wife who is the oldest of the oldest, or it could mean the oldest daughter of the second wife who is the oldest of the youngest, or it could mean the youngest daughter of the first wife if she is older than the oldest daughter of the second wife, such as if the oldest daughter of the second wife was born after the youngest daughter of the first wife and she is called the oldest in comparison to the daughters of the second wife—in this ambiguity, all the daughters of the first wife are included, as they are all older compared to the daughters of the second wife. Nonetheless, the Sages said that all are permitted except for the oldest of the oldest, who is the oldest daughter of the first wife. The reason is that a person does not put himself into a situation of doubt to say something that might lead him to have to ask the sages, and when he says "oldest," he means the oldest of the oldest.

And similarly, if he said, "I betrothed to you my younger daughter," and I do not know if it is the youngest of the young ones, who is the younger of the second wife, or the youngest of the older ones, who is the younger of the first wife, or the older of the young ones, who is younger than the youngest of the older ones - all are permitted except for the younger of the second wife who is the youngest of the young ones, due to a reason that will be explained. And all of this is referring to a case where, at the time he betrothed her, whether older or younger, it was clear to him whom he was betrothing, but afterward, he forgot. Therefore, we say that he certainly intended the oldest of the oldest and the youngest of the youngest, because a person does not put himself in a position of doubt to mention the term "older" unless it is the oldest of all, so that if the matter is forgotten, there will be no doubt [Rashi's version]. Similarly, with the younger one, the sages deduced from the language of the Mishnah that it refers to such a case. And it is also clear from the language of Maimonides [Chapter 9, Halacha 9] who wrote that at the time of the betrothal he told the husband, "I betrothed to you my older daughter," even though it could be said that she is the oldest of the oldest or the oldest of the young ones, etc. - all are permitted except for the oldest of the oldest. And it is clearly implied that the doubt arose afterward. And one must also explain the language of our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 17, who wrote: And he told the betrothed at the time of the betrothal, "I betrothed to you my older daughter," and he does not know, etc. Meaning, now he does not know. And according to this, it is clear that even if the betrothed says that at that time he intended another, he is not believed [and so wrote the Tosefot Yom Tov, Chapter 3].

And if at the time of the betrothal, when he says, "I have betrothed you, my eldest daughter," and they ask him which eldest one, and he says, "I do not know, I simply said it," by logical reasoning, it is clear that they are all forbidden because he himself does not know whom he betrothed. However, from the Talmudic discussion [there], which questions the opinion that betrothal not leading to marital relations is not a valid betrothal from this Mishnah according to Rabbi Meir, who prohibits all the daughters except for the youngest of the young ones, and this is betrothal not leading to marital relations. The Talmud resolves that the case is where he knew at the time of the act and later forgot. It is explicitly clear that according to the opinion that betrothal not leading to marital relations is a valid betrothal, it would be valid even if the doubt was at the time of the act. And we hold that it is a valid betrothal, and we hold like Rabbi Yose, who disputes Rabbi Meir and holds that all are permitted except for the eldest of the eldest. Therefore, even if the doubt is at the time of the act, all are permitted. However, this is against logical reasoning unless he says that his intention was according to the language. Therefore, it appears to me that certainly in such a case all are forbidden except for the youngest of the young ones. The Talmud could have said "and according to your reasoning" as the Talmud's style in many places [and it is possible that this is indeed what it means there, see and examine it].

A mature girl (bogeret) is not included among the daughters since she is not under his (the father's) authority. And there are those who say that even if the mature girl appointed her father as an agent to receive her betrothal and he told the one betrothing, "I have betrothed my oldest daughter to you" – the mature girl is not included [Beit Yosef according to the Tur]. And although, on the contrary, we explained in section 48 that even when he says "my oldest daughter" in the context of betrothal, he does not mean another, and certainly when she appointed him as an agent, as agency is preferable to betrothal as stated there, and even if she is a mature girl as implied by the Tur, nevertheless, this applies when he has only daughters from one wife, for then the title "oldest" applies only to the oldest of all of them, even if she is a mature girl, since the others will be called by their names. But when he has two sets of daughters from two wives, then the title "oldest" applies to the one after the mature girl and she is called the oldest in relation to the second set. Therefore, the mature girl is not included [Beit Shmuel, section 242]. However, there are those who say that certainly without appointing him as an agent, she is not included, but if she appointed him as an agent, as explained in section 45, she is also included, and therefore, here too, if he said "the oldest," he meant her and not others [Chomat Shlomo, section 37 and Beit Shmuel there].

And since it is a case of doubt in law, the mature girls and the eldest among the mature are forbidden, and thus the great later authorities have agreed [Mikneh and Even HaEzer]. There is someone who wants to be even more stringent that if there is only one mature girl among the daughters, even if he did not appoint her as an agent, nevertheless, when he said "the eldest," all the daughters of the first group are forbidden, as well as the eldest of the second group. Because, necessarily, "eldest" is not specific, as there is a mature girl who is older than her, therefore, there is a doubt regarding all the daughters of the first group that they are considered older in relation to the daughters of the second group, and also the eldest of the second group [Mikneh]. There is some proof for this in the Talmudic discussion [from the case of the minor according to Rabbi Meir, who said "except the eldest among the eldest," and see Pnei Yehoshua, commentary on the fourth chapter: "However," and examine it carefully].

If all the daughters are of age and they all appointed him as an agent, if he accepted betrothal for his daughter without specifying, all of them are forbidden and need a get (divorce document). If he said "the eldest," the eldest of them is betrothed and the rest are permitted. If he said "the youngest," the youngest of them is betrothed and the rest are permitted. If one of them appointed him as an agent, when he said "my daughter" without specifying, she is betrothed and the rest are permitted. If he said "the eldest," and the youngest one appointed him as an agent, the eldest is permitted by law because he cannot betroth her, and the youngest who appointed him as an agent needs a get because perhaps he intended her and called her "eldest" due to her importance.

If Reuven had five sons and they all appointed him as an agent to betroth on their behalf, and Shimon had five daughters, whether minors, adolescents, or even adults, and appointed him as an agent to accept betrothals on their behalf, and Reuven said to Shimon, "One of your daughters is betrothed to one of my sons," even though it is impossible to consummate the marriage at all because we do not know who is the one betrothing and who is the one being betrothed, and if one of the sons were to approach one of the daughters, it could be that he would approach a forbidden relation, such as the sister of his wife, nevertheless, we hold that betrothals that are not fit for consummation are still considered betrothals. Therefore, each of the daughters needs five bills of divorce from each of the sons, and if one of the sons died, each of the daughters needs four bills of divorce and chalitzah from one of them, because perhaps she is the betrothed of the deceased, and each stands in this uncertainty. Similarly, if two or more died, it suffices to receive a bill of divorce from each of the living and chalitzah from one of them, because in any case, one chalitzah suffices. If the five are not brothers, then bills of divorce alone suffice. If some of them are brothers and some are strangers, from the strangers a bill of divorce suffices, and from the brothers, chalitzah is required from one of them if one of the brothers died, because perhaps she is the betrothed of his brother.

The father who says, "I have betrothed my daughter, but I do not know to whom," or if he does not say to whom — this daughter, if she is a minor or a young girl, is forbidden to everyone in the world until it becomes known to whom she was betrothed. For the father is believed to prohibit his minor or young daughter since the Torah has given him the authority to betroth her, and it is within his power to betroth her. Anything that is within a person's power, he is believed [regarding it], as is the case with all prohibitions. The Torah explicitly believes him, as it is written, "I have given my daughter to this man" (Deuteronomy 22:16). Were it not for him saying "to this man," she would be forbidden to everyone in the world. If he dies and it is not known [to whom she was betrothed] — she remains in her prohibited status.

If after he said "I betrothed her and I do not know to whom" or did not say to whom, and then says "I betrothed her to so-and-so" or "I remembered to whom I betrothed her," even though he says this after some time has passed, he is believed. And even though after a lapse of "kedei dibur" (the time it takes to say a greeting) one is not believed to retract, and with betrothal we are stringent even within "kedei dibur," here it is not a retraction but rather an explanation of his original words or a recollection, for he necessarily betrothed her to someone, and therefore he is believed even after some time. Even if it becomes known to him only after she has matured or if he says after she matured "I betrothed her to so-and-so," he is believed. And even though after she has matured he has no authority over her, nevertheless, to explain his original words, why shouldn't he be believed? For if another person comes and says "I betrothed her," he is believed, as will be explained, and the father is no less credible than another person. And even though the reason another person is believed is because he fears the father might contradict him, as will be explained, nevertheless, we can say that the father also fears that witnesses might contradict him if she was betrothed to another, so he also fears to lie. Moreover, to explain the matter, no reason for his credibility is needed. And it seems to me that if he did not forget but did not say at the time of the act to whom he betrothed her, and later on he says to whom he betrothed her, he needs to provide some reason why he was silent until now and did not say to whom he betrothed her.

It appears to me that the father's credibility to state to whom he betrothed his daughter is only effective if that individual has died, permitting her to the general public. However, to permit her to that specific individual, what relevance does the father's credibility have? For logically, if that individual claims he betrothed her, it will be clarified that he is believed only if the father does not contradict him. And if that individual denies and says, "I did not betroth her," certainly the father's words will be of no consequence at all. It would be like a woman who claims, "You betrothed me," and he says, "I did not betroth you," as will be clarified in Siman 48. There is no remedy for this except to request a divorce from him, as stated there.

And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in section 20 that there are those who say that if the groom stood before him initially and he did not recognize him, and afterward he said he recognizes him – he is not believed. And it is not specifically that he initially stated explicitly that he does not recognize him, but rather since he did not say simultaneously "I betrothed my daughter to this man," he is not believed anymore after the time it takes to say a brief statement ("kdei dibur") to say "I betrothed her to this man," but within that time, it is as if he is concluding his words [Beit Shmuel]. And from the precise language of our Rabbi, the Rema, it seems to me that it is specifically if he says afterward that he recognizes him from before, therefore he is not believed after the time it takes to say a brief statement because his credibility is weakened since he did not say it simultaneously as mentioned, but if he says afterward that initially he did not recognize him and now he reconsidered and recognized him – he is believed, for there is no flaw in this.

There are those who say that what has been clarified, namely that he is not believed after the time it takes to speak [to invalidate a claim] when the groom is present, unless two people come, each saying "I betrothed her," thereby rendering her forbidden to both, as will be explained. But if only one person claims that he betrothed her, what does it matter whether the father is believed? He is believed to say that he betrothed her even if the father does not recognize him, as will be explained. And there are those who reject this, arguing that the case speaks of a situation where the groom did not immediately say, "I betrothed her." In such a case, he is not believed to say later on that he betrothed her, because he did not state it immediately, and we must rely on the father's credibility. But it seems to me that only the father is not believed afterward because his credibility is weakened by the fact that he did not say these things together initially. However, in the case of the groom who did not speak at all and was not asked, what deficiency is there in the fact that he did not say it earlier? Nevertheless, it is clear that there is a practical difference in the father's credibility even with one groom, for instance, if the groom did not speak at all and went away and died. In such a case, if the father were believed, she would be permitted to others. But now that he is not believed, she remains in her prohibition.

If the father does not know to whom he betrothed her, and someone comes and says before the father, "I betrothed her," and the father does not deny it, he is believed to marry her and she is permitted to him. He does not need to betroth her again when he marries her. And even though for matters of sexual prohibitions, two witnesses are required, this is to remove her from her presumptive status. Here, however, he is maintaining her presumptive status by saying, "I am the one who betrothed her" [Ran]. And why do we not suspect that he is lying? Because we say that a person would not have the audacity to claim before the father that he is the one who gave the betrothal if it were not true, as he would fear that the father might deny it and he would be disgraced in front of everyone. Therefore, it is certainly true since the father does not deny it. But if the father denies it, it is obvious that he is not believed to marry her. There is an opinion that he is not even believed to require her to receive a divorce from him [Tur], since the father's denial removes the presumption that a person would not be brazen enough to lie. Consequently, for matters of sexual prohibitions, two witnesses are required, since she cannot be permitted to another after he divorces her because the father denies it. His divorce is only to prevent her from becoming forbidden to another due to this person's claim. Certainly, he is not believed to prohibit her based on his word alone [N"L].

If two men come and each one says, "I betrothed her" – both of them must give her a get (bill of divorce). If they wish, one can give a get and the other can marry her. However, he needs to betroth her again when marrying her, since she has already been divorced from another. We are concerned that perhaps the one who divorced her is the one who betrothed her, and since he divorced her, she requires a new betrothal. If he is a Kohen, she is forbidden to him. If one of them married her before the other gave a get, she is forbidden to him because it is considered an act of promiscuity. She is also forbidden to the second one, as perhaps he is the one who betrothed her, and this was an act of promiscuity, making her forbidden to both the husband and the paramour.

One should not ask why she is permitted to others after both have divorced her, given that we have seen that one of them is brazen and lying. Why not suspect that both are lying? It can be said that since both of them give her a get to permit her to others, no person sins without benefit. Therefore, certainly, one of them knows that the other betrothed her, and she will not come to sin. The reason one gives a get is that he has no other option since he claimed to have betrothed her. Furthermore, the presumption that a person is not so brazen remains strong. Even if there is one who is definitely brazen and lying, what of it? If one is brazen, does that mean the other is as well? We say that one of them is telling the truth, and one is lying, and we do not know who is who.

It seems that even if later one of them retracts and admits to the other, we compel him to give a get. On what basis can he retract, unless he gives a good reason for saying so? Even in such a case, it is difficult to release her without a get from him.

If someone comes and says, "I betrothed her," and marries her, and afterwards another comes and says, "I betrothed her," and the father says, "I do not know," nevertheless, he is not believed to prohibit her to the first one. Since she was permitted to the first one, she has a presumption of permissibility, and one witness is not believed to remove her from this presumption. Therefore, some say that even if the first one has not yet married her, but the court permitted her to marry, the second one is also not believed for the reason we explained, that as long as the court permitted her, she has a presumption of permissibility [see Yevamot 117:]. Unless two witnesses come and contradict him, in which case, even if she is already married, she must leave, and even against the father they are believed, and she is forbidden to both [Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel]. However, according to what our teacher, the Rema, wrote at the end of Siman 17, that when she marries based on a court's mistaken ruling, her status is like one who was coerced, it is possible to say that here too, her status is like one who was coerced, and she is not forbidden to her husband when it becomes known who the betrother is [Even HaEzer]. However, there are those who disagree with this, as written there in Siman 262, and see what is written in Siman 31, Section 22.

The father who says about his daughter while she is still a minor or a young woman, "I betrothed her and divorced her" – is believed to disqualify her from marrying a kohen. And even though the Torah only believed the father regarding matters of marriage and not for other matters, such as in the case of a captive where he is not believed, as stated in Siman 7, nevertheless, regarding the priesthood, he is believed. Because since he is believed about the betrothal, she is thereby automatically forbidden to a kohen due to the prohibition of a married woman. And regarding his claim that he divorced her – this is valid if he says it immediately following the statement that he betrothed her, as he is believed by virtue of a "migu" (a presumption) that if he wanted, he could have simply not said that he betrothed her, and thus she would remain prohibited to a kohen as a divorcee. However, if he claims this after a delay, since she was established as a married woman based on his word, he is not believed to later say that he divorced her, as a retrospective "migu" is not applied, as stated in Choshen Mishpat Siman 82 in the principles of "migu". This is not similar to the case where he is believed to later specify to whom he betrothed her, as that pertains entirely to the matter of the betrothal and clarifies his initial words. But when he says she was divorced, he is breaking the betrothal, and he is only believed by virtue of a "migu" [Beit Shmuel]. The same applies to any statement that breaks the betrothal, such as if he says there was a condition in the betrothal that was not fulfilled or the witnesses were disqualified – he is only believed if it is said immediately following the initial statement, as explained [Chomat Shlomo]. One should not ask, isn't it the case with betrothal that even immediately following the statement is considered as after a delay? This pertains to the act of betrothal itself, which cannot be retracted, but regarding a statement that contradicts his initial words, he is believed by a "migu" if it is said immediately, as explained in Siman 47 regarding a woman who says "I was betrothed" and immediately following says "I am single," see there [Beit Shmuel].

A father's credibility is only during the years of his daughter's minority and adolescence, but after she has matured, he is not believed to say that he betrothed her when she was a minor or adolescent. Even if he says that he betrothed and divorced her during her minority, he is not believed to disqualify her from marrying a priest, as the Torah only granted him credibility while she is under his authority. And even though we hold that a father is believed regarding the ages, as the Rambam writes in Hilchot Ishut 2:23, that a father who says, "This son of mine is nine years and one day old, this daughter of mine is three years and one day old" is believed to obligate someone who has relations with them to bring a sacrifice, but he is not believed for lashes or punishments. "This son of mine is thirteen years and one day old, this daughter of mine is twelve years and one day old"—he is believed regarding vows, evaluations, consecrations, and dedications, but not for lashes or punishments. Therefore, if he says when she is mature that he betrothed her when she was a minor, he should be believed with the argument that if he wanted, he could say she is still a minor or adolescent. Some say this is only when there are witnesses regarding the ages, but otherwise, he is believed with this argument. However, it seems to me that in any case he is not believed, because since it was clarified that he is not believed for lashes or punishments, how can we believe him with the argument that he betrothed her when she was a minor and she is a married woman, obligating the death penalty for someone who has relations with her intentionally, or that he divorced her and obligate lashes for a priest who marries her? And it cannot be said that he would not be believed for this but only for unintentional actions and for a sacrifice—it is impossible to say this, because when the Torah believed him regarding his daughter's marriage, it believed him for everything, as explained in the section of "Motzi Shem Ra." Since we cannot believe him for everything, we do not believe him at all. Furthermore, some of the early authorities said that since this credibility granted by the Torah is a novelty that a single witness is believed, it only applies to this novelty and he is not believed in other matters to disqualify her by the argument.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 27: If a father says that he betrothed his daughter and then betrothed her to another, and he says that the first betrothal was with invalid witnesses according to Torah law and is therefore null - he is believed. And in his larger work, he brought this from a responsum of the Rashba, and our teacher the Rema wrote on this: It seems to me that he is believed only within the time it takes to say a few words, as is the law in section 69 regarding "I betrothed her and divorced her," where after the time it takes to say a few words, he is not believed to cancel the betrothal. And the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, are indeed puzzling. There is someone who says that the father is believed in all matters even after the time it takes to say a few words, except for divorce, where he is not believed [Bach]. But it has already been clarified that this is not so, and this is also against reason. There is someone who says that regarding invalid witnesses, he is believed because it is like an explanation for the betrothal, and in explanations, he is believed even after some time [Taz]. However, this is not so, for every explanation must be clarified in court that it is indeed an explanation, as written in section 46 [Mekane]. And it is possible to say that certainly, he is not believed after the time it takes to say a few words to remove her from the status of a married woman, but here, where he betrothed her to another, he is not removing her from the status of a married woman but only concerning the first betrothal. The Beit Yosef holds that he is always believed since he is not removing her from her status. Or it is possible to say that certainly when he said earlier that he betrothed her to someone, he is not believed later to cancel his words. And here, it is stated that he said simply that he betrothed her, as can be understood from his words, and afterward, when he betrothed her to another, he was capable of saying even about the first betrothal that it was invalid due to witnesses, and therefore, he is believed by a "migo" (a legal presumption) - and this is not a "migo" retroactively. Since at the time of accepting betrothal from the other, he says that the witnesses of the first betrothal were invalid, he has a "migo" to say that he betrothed her to the second one.

A woman who said, "I betrothed myself and I do not know to whom," and one comes and says, "I betrothed you"—he is believed to give her a get (bill of divorce) to permit her to the whole world, but not to marry her. This is different from the case of a father where it was clarified that he is believed to say, "I betrothed her," because he fears the father who would not deny him. However, regarding her, he does not fear because even if he is lying, she will cover for him due to her strong desire, and there is no presumption of fear here. Therefore, even after he divorces her, he is forbidden to marry her because we suspect that they might conspire to divorce and remarry. But since we forbid her to him forever, there is no concern anymore, and he is believed to permit her to others, for a person does not sin without benefit. And since this is only a suspicion, if he marries her even before the divorce—we do not take her away from him. Similarly, if there is only one witness who says he betrothed her—he is permitted to marry her initially. And even though in a place of a presumption of prohibition, one witness is not believed except in matters within his control, as stated in Yoreh De'ah 127, here he does not remove her from her presumption but clarifies the matter. Therefore, if two come and each says, "I betrothed her"—one witness is not believed to clarify, for one witness in contradiction is nothing. And the fact that the Sages believed him to permit her by giving a get, the same applies if he died before giving the get, there is no difference. And some say that if two come and each says, "I betrothed her," if they wish—one gives a get and one marries, like with the father, and this needs further investigation for the law.

[Laws of Conditional Betrothals, containing 102 sections]
        One who betroths a woman on a condition: if the condition is fulfilled, she is betrothed; if not, she is not betrothed and does not require a get (divorce document). This applies whether the condition was made by him, such as giving her a maneh (a specific amount of money) or similar, or by her, where she must fulfill the condition. If the condition is made properly according to the legal requirements of conditions, as will be explained in this section, then it is valid. If not made properly, the condition is null, and the act of betrothal stands in all respects. [And that there is no reliance (asmachta) in the condition will be explained in section 42, paragraph 11.]

If the condition was not fulfilled due to a circumstance beyond his control (an unavoidable accident), nevertheless, the betrothal is nullified. Although the Torah exempts one who is coerced from liability, this applies to matters between him and God, not to matters between him and another person. What does the other person care about his unavoidable accident? Even though in the case of divorce (gittin) there is a concept of coercion, the sages nullified the claim of coercion for the sake of order, as stated in Siman 144, and a get (divorce document) is also between the husband and wife. However, it is not the same, since a get depends solely on his will and not on her will. Therefore, when he is coerced, there is a claim of coercion. But this is not the case with betrothal, where a woman is not betrothed except with her consent. She does not agree to the betrothal unless the condition is fulfilled [Ran, Chapter 3]. This reasoning is also written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 21, and its source is from the Jerusalem Talmud [Chapter 3, Halacha 2], where Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish disagree on this reasoning, and the law follows Rabbi Yochanan. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, Rabbi Yochanan himself instructed his daughters at the time of his death to follow the opinion of Resh Lakish, lest the matter come before a judge who might rule according to Resh Lakish, leading to confusion.

There is a doubt whether we say that there is no claim of coercion (ones) in all types of conditions (tenaim) in marriage, or if this applies specifically to conditions that are for his or her benefit, such as the giving of money or other benefits. But a general condition that does not involve benefit, for example, if he said, "You are betrothed to me on the condition that I come here within 30 days, and if I do not come, the betrothal is nullified," and he was coerced and did not come – whether the betrothal is nullified and there is no claim of coercion, or if there is a claim of coercion and the betrothal is not nullified. Similarly, the reverse case, if he said, "On the condition that I do not come here within 30 days, and if I do come, the betrothal is nullified," and he intended to come and nullify the betrothal but was coerced and did not come – whether there is a claim of coercion and the betrothal is nullified, or there is no claim of coercion and the betrothal stands. There is also a doubt whether, even if we say that according to the law there is a claim of coercion in such cases, there might be a rabbinic enactment that there should be no claim of coercion, similar to the laws of divorces (gittin).

Some of the early authorities wrote that if a man said, "You are betrothed to me if I do not come from here until a certain day," and he was prevented by circumstances beyond his control and did not come, there is a claim of coercion, and she is not betrothed. There is no remedy for this from the sages concerning divorce, and conversely, if he said, "You are betrothed to me if I come," and he was prevented and did not come, in this case, there is certainly no claim of coercion, neither in divorce nor in betrothal from the outset. Since the condition was not fulfilled, even though it was due to coercion, the condition was still not met. Proof for this is brought from the case where a man said, "This is your divorce on the condition that you give me my cloak," and the cloak was lost. The sages said that she cannot give the money equivalent to the value of the cloak and the divorce is void. In this case, she was coerced, yet it is clear that if the condition was not fulfilled, even due to coercion, there is no claim of coercion.

And it follows that according to this opinion, the law is like the first opinion, that in any condition where the fulfillment of an act, such as giving money or other benefits, is required, and if the person was coerced and did not fulfill it, the claim of coercion does not hold legally, even in divorce cases of this kind. Even in a case where the condition is not related to a benefit, such as "if I come," and the person was coerced and did not come, the claim of coercion is not valid. The enactment that the Sages decreed regarding divorces, that there should be no claim of coercion, only applies when the condition was the absence of an act (e.g., he should not come) and the condition was fulfilled due to coercion. In this situation, legally, there is a claim of coercion, for it cannot be said that the condition was fulfilled since it was fulfilled due to coercion, and this is not considered fulfillment. Therefore, in betrothal, there is a claim of coercion, but in divorces, the Sages decreed that there should be no claim of coercion.

But there are some of the early authorities who wrote that this question was asked of the ancient Gaonim whether the claim of duress applies to betrothal, and they replied that it is a doubtful matter of law [Ran, end of the third chapter of Gittin in the name of the Itur, and Magid Mishneh, chapter 9 of Divorce in his name]. And there is someone who wanted to say that they do not disagree with the first opinion, and as we have written, if the condition was not fulfilled due to duress, in this case, certainly there is no claim of duress, for what does it matter if it was due to duress; after all, the condition was not fulfilled. And this, that the Gaon replied that it is a doubtful matter of law, is when the condition was fulfilled due to duress, such as if he said "Behold, you are betrothed to me on the condition that I do not come until a certain day," and he was compelled and did not come. According to the law, there is a claim of duress, but in divorce, the Sages enacted that there should be no claim of duress, and the Gaon was uncertain if the Sages also enacted this in betrothal or not [Avnei Miluim].

However, it is not so, for we find that they also asked the opposite case regarding a man who betrothed on the condition, "If I do not come by such-and-such time, the betrothal will be null," and he did not come. They asked before Rav Shmuel, the head of the academy, whether coercion applies to betrothal. From this, it is clear that there is a question also when he was coerced into fulfilling the condition, unless we say to differentiate between a condition that pertains to his benefit or her benefit and a general condition that does not pertain to benefit. According to the doubt we mentioned in paragraph 3, if we say so, then for the law regarding a condition of giving money or other benefits, and he was coerced and did not fulfill it, according to all opinions, the claim of coercion does not apply. However, from the words of the later authorities, it seems they do not hold this distinction. There are several proofs to this reasoning that regarding something that pertains to benefit, certainly, the claim of coercion does not apply.

In all matters, one can stipulate any condition they wish, except for conditions that contradict what is written in the Torah or are impossible to fulfill. Similarly, it seems to me that one should not stipulate a condition in betrothal that must be maintained for the entirety of one's life, such as "on the condition that you do not drink wine all your life" or "that I do not drink all my life." Just as it is not possible to stipulate such a condition in a divorce, as stated in Siman 143, because it is not considered a proper severance if she remains tied to him her whole life, so too in betrothal, it is not a proper union if it depends on a condition that must be upheld forever, and if the condition is violated, they would separate. However, one should deliberate whether this applies only to divorce, as the Torah states "severance," and this is not considered severance, but not to betrothal. Nevertheless, the prevailing opinion is that the same applies to both divorce and betrothal [see Rashi and Tosafot, s.v. “kol”], though the poskim (halachic authorities) do not mention this. In all other conditions, one can stipulate in both betrothal with money or a document and in betrothal through intercourse. And even though we hold that there is no condition in chalitza, as stated in Siman 169, because any act that cannot be done through an agent cannot have a condition, and betrothal through intercourse cannot be done through an agent, nevertheless, since betrothal with money or a document can be fulfilled through an agent and can include a condition, the same applies to betrothal through intercourse, as all forms of betrothal are compared to each other [Ketubot 74]. Furthermore, it seems to me that in betrothal with a document on condition, the condition should not be written in the betrothal document itself, as is done with a get (divorce document), as stated in Siman 147.

Stipulating against what is written in the Torah, how so? If one stipulates on the condition that he will not be obligated to her in the mitzvah of conjugal relations – his condition is null and the marriage is valid, because a person does not have the power to nullify something from the words of the Torah. However, in monetary matters, his condition is valid. For example, if he said to her, "on the condition that I will not be obligated to provide you with sustenance and clothing" – his condition is valid because this is not a transgression of the Torah's words, as every person has the right to waive his own money. And this is specifically when she forgives him, but if he said "on the condition that you will not have any claim for sustenance and clothing on me" – this is also considered stipulating against what is written in the Torah [as brought in Ketubot 56 based on the Rashba], and this is also proven in the Talmud [Bava Metzia 51b]. Some say that even if one stipulates against a rabbinic matter that is not monetary, his condition is null, because whatever the rabbis established, they established similarly to the Torah. And there is one who wants to say that in rabbinic matters, even in monetary matters, his condition is null, because they made their words stronger than those of the Torah, but all the poskim disagree with this [Beit Shmuel, Section 13], and only regarding the ketubah alone did the sages decree thus, so that it would not be easy to divorce her, as mentioned in Section 66, and he can stipulate that she will sustain and support him [Tosefta Ketubot, Chapter 4].

He said to her, "On the condition that you eat pork" or "on the condition that you commit another sin" – this is not considered a condition against what is written in the Torah, because she has the ability not to eat and not to be betrothed to him, and it is considered something within her control since she has the capability to eat. However, if he said to her, "On the condition that another person commits a sin" – this is not a valid condition, because the other person may not agree, and it is not within her control for the other person to fulfill it, making it like a condition that is impossible to fulfill. There is no difference between a biblical prohibition and a rabbinic prohibition. But if he made a condition with her regarding someone else's property, such as "on the condition that another person gives me his courtyard" or "on the condition that another person marries his daughter to my son" – this is a valid condition, because it is within her control to ensure that the other person fulfills it by increasing the dowry and gifts until he agrees.

A condition that is impossible to fulfill – how so? For example, if he said to her, "On the condition that you ascend to the sky" or "descend to the depths" or "swallow a reed of four cubits" or "bring me a reed of one hundred cubits" or "cross the great sea by foot" – this is not considered a condition. Thus, the Sages have said (Gittin 84a) any condition that is impossible to fulfill in the end and was stipulated from the beginning is merely considered as exaggeration, and the matter stands. Even if it is possible to do this unnaturally, only through names (i.e., mystical means) and the like (Tosafot there), it is not called possible to fulfill it. Similarly, any such matters. But if he said to her, "On the condition that you give me one hundred maneh," it is considered possible to fulfill, even if she is poor, since it is within the capability of other wealthy people to fulfill this matter; we do not follow her status. The same applies to similar cases. Many other laws of conditions will be clarified in Siman 143, there.

If he stipulated with her two conditions and one of them is contrary to what is written in the Torah or impossible to fulfill, it is clarified from the words of the Rambam (Chapter 6, Halacha 10) that one condition is nullified and the other remains valid. This is also implied by the language of the Talmud, and we do not say that just as one condition is exaggerated, so too is the other. Rather, one condition remains valid and the other is nullified. This is similar to "acquire you and the donkey," where we hold that he acquires half, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 190. And know that although it is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud (Bava Metzia, end of Chapter 7) that an obligation is considered a monetary matter, and so it is in the Tosefta of Kiddushin (Chapter 3), nevertheless, our Talmud does not follow this approach, as bodily distress is not subject to waiver, and this is the ruling of all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law).

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote: One who betroths on a condition and after several days retracts the condition, even if he nullifies it privately between himself and her without witnesses, the condition is nullified and she is betrothed unconditionally. Similarly, if the condition was made by the woman and she nullifies it privately between herself and him, the condition is nullified. Therefore, one who betroths on a condition and then consummates the marriage unconditionally or has relations unconditionally, she requires a get (divorce) even though the condition was not fulfilled, because perhaps he nullified the condition when he had relations or when he consummated the marriage. 

And there are those who say that the condition must be nullified specifically in the presence of witnesses, and similarly, if he consummates the marriage unconditionally in the presence of witnesses, then she requires a get, but without this, it is not effective. And there are those who say that the nullification of the condition is only effective in matters of money, for money can be waived, and it is as if he said, "I have received it." But in other conditions, nullification and waiver are not effective, like one who betrothed on the condition that she has no defects or vows, the betrothal is immediately nullified if she has defects or vows upon her, and what benefit is there in nullifying the condition? In matters of money, waiver is effective even after the stipulation, as if the condition had been fulfilled.

The Rambam's opinion is that since the condition was made for his benefit, his intention is not that the kiddushin (marriage) be immediately nullified, but rather that the matter depends on whether the defects or vows become known. And as long as he did not object to them, she is considered betrothed. However, if he did object to them, she is not betrothed, even if he later forgives it, because the moment he objected, the kiddushin were nullified. This is not comparable to what will be explained about "on the condition that I am wealthy" and he is found to be poor, or poor and he is found to be wealthy, for even if she said that in her heart she intended to be betrothed to him, she is not betrothed. In such a case, since she said in her heart that she did not object at the time of kiddushin, and nevertheless they verbally stipulated this condition, things that are in the heart are not valid. However, in this case, he objected at the time of the act but made the matter dependent until it could be settled. Therefore, afterward, when he objected and then reconciled himself to the defects and vows, the kiddushin were finalized. There is no concern of retroactive clarification, as stated in section 68.

According to the Rambam, witnesses are not needed, because since the reasoning is due to waiver, as we have written, even between him and her alone it is effective. And even if he brought her into the chuppah alone and did not consummate, we say maybe he waived, and all the more so if he brought her in and consummated. Nevertheless, even if he brought her in and consummated, we do not say he definitely waived, but it remains a doubt of kiddushin, and if another man betrothed her, even after the consummation, she requires a get (divorce document) from both of them. For even though he consummated, there is a concern that perhaps he consummated based on his condition and thought the condition would be fulfilled. Therefore, if it became known before the consummation or the entry that the condition would not be fulfilled and he brought her in and consummated, it is considered complete kiddushin. However, she does not have a ketubah because regarding the ketubah, it stands on his first condition.

And those who disagree with him hold that it is not due to forgiveness, but rather that when they cohabit, we say that he betroths her anew through this cohabitation, and similarly with the entering into the chuppah (bridal canopy). According to this, it is indeed necessary to have witnesses, as all betrothals require witnesses [Rosh]. And some say that if he brings her into the chuppah without cohabiting, it is nothing [Ran], for according to this reasoning that the concern is because he betroths her anew, this only applies to cohabitation and not to entering the chuppah, but there is a concern for the opinion that betrothal also occurs with the chuppah. In practice, we must be concerned for the opinion of the Rambam [there], and our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 35, only mentioned the opinion of the Rambam, and even if he cohabited or brought her into the chuppah immediately after the betrothal, she requires a get (divorce document) because since the reasoning is due to forgiveness, we are concerned that he forgave immediately [and Rashi and Tosafot in Ketubot 73, s.v. but they hold like those who disagree, and the Rif and Rambam ruled like Ulla in the name of Rabbi Eliezer in Ketubot 74, that if he cohabited, everyone agrees, and when they disagree, it is about bringing her into the chuppah without cohabiting, and the halacha follows Rav, see there].

If before the consummation he explicitly stated that he relies on the initial condition – it seems that according to all opinions, a get (divorce document) is not required. There are those who are stringent even in such a case, fearing that perhaps at the moment of the act he forgave [the condition] (Shiltei Giborim), but this does not appear to be the opinion of all the poskim (halachic authorities) (see Chomat Shlomo and Beit Shmuel there). And in the case of betrothal without specifying conditions and later discovering vows or blemishes – this will be explained in Siman 39.

Some say that if one betrothed a woman on a condition that extends over a certain period of time and married her within that time, the condition is certainly nullified, and the betrothal is not dependent on it. Even if the condition was not fulfilled within the set time, she is betrothed [Ran, 3rd chapter, according to the Jerusalem Talmud]. The reason is that since they did not wait until the time of the condition's completion, it is certain that they nullified the condition so that the betrothal is not dependent on it. Nevertheless, if the condition relates to a monetary matter, such as on the condition that he gives her a sum of money within a year from the day of betrothal and he married her within the year, even though the condition of the betrothal is nullified and the betrothal is not dependent on it, still, the money is an obligation upon him to pay [there], if he admits that he did not pay. If there is a dispute between them, it will be clarified before us with God's help.

However, the poskim (Jewish legal decisors) did not bring this law at all, and it seems to me that they do not hold by this law because in our Talmud they said that if one betroths on a condition and then has relations, she needs a get (divorce document) due to the doubt that he may have waived the condition. And if she accepted betrothal from another, she needs a get from both, as we wrote. According to the Jerusalem Talmud, he certainly nullified the condition. Although one could say that our Talmud does not speak of a condition extending over time but rather of conditions such as blemishes and vows, where he did not know she had them and thought she did not have blemishes and vows, therefore it is only doubtful betrothal. But with a condition extending over time, he knows that it is still possible to violate the condition and, nonetheless, marries her, certainly waiving the condition. Nevertheless, from the language of the Talmud that says "if one betroths on a condition and then has relations, she needs a get" and the get is due to the doubt, it implies that in all matters of conditions, the law is the same. And also, the Jerusalem Talmud can be explained differently [it is in chapter 3, halacha 2 and they explain that Rabbi Abahu's retraction is not a retraction from his words, but rather the condition was that whoever retracts from the betrothal until a certain time should give such and such. And he married her within the time, and Rabbi Eliezer said to him, "Go and give," meaning sustenance, and he responded, "I did not acquire a wife," meaning she still has the right to retract, and he agreed with him and said whoever retracts should give as per their condition. It questions what this adds and answers that he made it a court enactment, meaning he strengthened the condition not to be like an 'asmachta' but like a court enactment. According to the Ran's explanation, it is difficult what he meant by "she does not retract," since the condition was upon him. See there and examine well].

If a disagreement arises between the man and the woman regarding the fulfillment or nullification of a condition, for example, if he betrothed her on the condition "that I give you a maneh," or "that I speak to the ruler for you," or "that I go to such and such a place," and he says, "I gave it to you," "I spoke to the ruler," "I went to such and such a place," and the betrothal was completed, and she says, "You did not give it," "You did not speak," "You did not go," and the betrothal is nullified; if the condition was set for a specific time or was a condition of refraining from an action, such as "on the condition that I do not go or do not speak," and he says, "I did not go," "I did not speak," and the betrothal was completed, and she says, "You went," "You spoke," and the betrothal is nullified, or in any similar case, or if the condition was upon her, whether to do something or refrain from doing something, and there is a disagreement between them — some of our rabbis hold that in matters of betrothal she is believed, and in matters of divorce he is believed, as the burden of proof lies on the one who seeks to extract [something from the other] (Rashba in the name of Ramban). 

And it seems that the intention is that in betrothal, where he seeks to establish the betrothal and keep her with him, and she seeks to nullify the betrothal and separate from him as before the betrothal, the man is considered the one extracting from his fellow, for he is seeking to remove her from her previous status and bring her under his authority, therefore she is believed. But in divorce, it is the opposite: she seeks to remove herself from his authority under which she has been until now, thus she is considered the one extracting, and the burden of proof is on her. And if he claims that the condition was fulfilled, it is as if he says to the woman, "I betrothed you," and she says, "You did not betroth me," he is prohibited from marrying her relatives, and she is not prohibited from marrying his relatives (Beit Shmuel). Consequently, the reverse is also true: if she says the condition was fulfilled and she is betrothed, and he says it was not fulfilled, he is believed and she is considered the one extracting, seeking to impose the obligations of a husband to a wife on him, and the burden of proof is on her, making it as if she says, "You betrothed me," and he says, "I did not betroth you," and she is prohibited from marrying his relatives. 

This is also explained in the Jerusalem Talmud: when the time arrives, he says, "I gave it," and she says, "I did not receive it," Rabbi Yose says that since he seeks to prohibit her to him, he must bring proof. And there is no difference in the disagreement between a condition to perform an action and a condition to refrain from an action, contrary to the opinion of some who say that in the case of refraining from an action, even if the other party denies and claims that he transgressed and performed the action, he is not believed, and we do not suspect that he actually transgressed. This is not so, and the words of the Beit Shmuel there are perplexing, for the Ran only wrote this concerning a get [divorce] and it seems so from the Rema at the end of this section, and this was also contested by the Beit Meir and Sha'ar HaMelekh.

The primary ruling here seems perplexing to me. If according to his words, she is a married woman because the condition was fulfilled, what benefit is there in her denial? And what does this have to do with the principle of "the burden of proof is on the claimant"? That principle applies only to financial matters, not to prohibitions. Furthermore, one cannot argue that she has a presumption of being single, since it has already been clarified in Siman 30 that once an act of betrothal is performed, the presumption of being single is removed. This situation is similar to a case where someone betrothed a woman conditionally and then had relations with her, where we rule that she needs a get (divorce document) and has no ketubah (marriage contract). This implies that financial matters and prohibitions are separate, so how can we permit her without a get?

Therefore, it seems to me that the intention of the Yerushalmi and the poskim is to say she is believed, and we do not force her to be his wife. Nevertheless, we do not permit her without a get and we compel him to give a get, since according to his words, she is a married woman. Conversely, if she claims the condition was fulfilled and he denies it, we also compel him to give a get. Even though we rule that if she says "You betrothed me" and he says "I did not," we do not compel him to give a get but merely request him to do so, that case is different because he denies it entirely. Here, however, there was a betrothal between them, and the dispute is over the condition; certainly, we compel him to give a get since according to her, the condition was fulfilled.

Therefore, it must be that both are prohibited to their relatives in all situations, not as stated in the previous section. (However, in the Ran in the name of the Ramban, it is written that she is believed and permitted to marry others, but this language does not appear in the Rashba, and this requires further investigation. Nevertheless, it seems clear to me as I have written.)

If one says the condition was fulfilled and the other does not deny it but says "I don't know," our master, the Rema, writes in section 39 that there are those who say that for any condition requiring an action, neither party is believed to say that the condition was fulfilled unless there are witnesses. However, for a condition requiring inaction, each party is believed if the other does not contradict him. And there are those who say that even for a condition requiring action, one is believed as long as the other does not contradict him. End of quote.

And it is necessary to explain the reasoning of the first opinion as to why he would not be believed even in a case of "kum va'aseh" (a proactive action), since the second party does not contradict him. They wrote the reason that it is similar to one who says, "You lent me a maneh," and the other says, "I do not know." Even though the principle of "a certain claim versus an uncertain claim, the certain claim prevails," nonetheless, to extract money from its established status, we do not say that the certain claim prevails, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 75. Here too, his certain claim cannot remove it from its previous status. Nevertheless, it remains a doubt regarding the betrothal even according to this opinion, for in that case, if someone wishes to fulfill his obligation to Heaven, he must pay and also must swear that he does not know, as stated there. And although one might differentiate that in that case, the uncertain claim is weaker because he should have known, thus he is obligated to swear and also to pay if he wishes to fulfill his obligation to Heaven, whereas here, the uncertain claim is better since why should he know whether the condition was fulfilled or not. Nonetheless, on the contrary, one could say that since she has no reason to know, how can we say we do not concern ourselves with his words? This is certainly the reason for the second opinion that considers the betrothal certain, and therefore, even according to this opinion, it remains a doubt regarding the betrothal.

We find in the Tosefta (Chapter 3) that there is a dispute regarding this matter. It is taught there: One who says to a woman, "Behold, you are betrothed to me on the condition that I speak on your behalf to the authorities," she is immediately betrothed until he says, "I did not speak"—these are the words of Rabbi Meir. But the Sages say: If the condition is fulfilled, she is betrothed, and if not, she is not betrothed. Thus, Rabbi Meir holds like the second opinion that we presume he will fulfill the condition, and certainly if he says he fulfilled it. And the Sages hold like the first opinion that we need to know clearly that the condition has been fulfilled; otherwise, it is a doubtful betrothal. The law follows the Sages.

If the condition was passive (i.e., not to do something) and he claims he fulfilled it, according to all opinions, he is believed. If he claims he violated the condition and did what he was supposed not to do, he is also not believed to invalidate the marriage, to say he actively violated it, and to remove the action from its previous presumption. Some say that even if both of them claim they violated the condition actively, they are not believed [Beit Shmuel, Section 169], but this does not seem correct, for they have the capability to separate from each other by writing a divorce. However, according to this, even when he himself says he violated the condition, why should he not be believed by this logic according to Torah law, since he can divorce her against her will? Thus, it should be said that this is like a presumption that cannot be uprooted, and therefore, it could apply even if both of them say so. In a condition of an active action, if he says he did not do it and thereby invalidated the marriage, he is certainly believed. If both of them say the condition was fulfilled, it seems they are believed to make the marriage certain, for they have the capability to consecrate each other, and furthermore, they can waive the condition [there]. In any case where we said he is not believed or both are not believed, it means they are in a state of doubtful marriage, and if she accepted marriage from another, she needs a divorce from both. It appears to me that a condition dependent on another person and not on him, such as "on the condition that so-and-so goes to a certain place" or "does not go," according to all opinions, he is not believed without verification through witnesses in any situation, even in a passive condition where he claims he did not do it, since it is not within his control. For even in other prohibitions, he is not believed in matters not within his control, as written in Yoreh De'ah, Section 127, and certainly in matters of a married woman.

How is the law of a condition? The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 6 that any condition in the world, whether in betrothal, divorce, buying, selling, or other monetary laws, must have four elements. These are the four elements of any condition: it must be doubled, the affirmative must precede the negative, the condition must precede the action, and the condition must be something that can be fulfilled. If the condition lacks one of these, the condition is null and void, as if there were no condition at all. Instead, she would be betrothed or divorced immediately, and the sale or gift would take effect immediately, as if no condition had been made at all since one of the four elements is missing. All of this we learn from the condition of the Children of Gad and the Children of Reuben, with whom Moses our teacher made a condition, and the Torah took care to write all these details, indicating that they are essential. Some add that the condition must be in one matter and the action in another matter, and this will be explained further with God's help.

A double condition, how is it? He should double the statements and say, "If you give me a maneh, you are betrothed to me, and if you do not give, you are not betrothed," as the scripture doubled the statement, "If the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben will pass over... but if they do not pass over" (Numbers 32:29-30). The affirmative should precede the negative, meaning he should say, "If you give, you are betrothed, and if you do not give, you are not betrothed," and he should not say the negative first, "If you do not give, and if you give." If he mentioned the negative before the affirmative and then repeated the negative after the affirmative, such as saying, "If you do not give, you will not be betrothed, and if you give, you are betrothed, if you do not give, you are not betrothed," it is considered as if he mentioned the affirmative before the negative, and the initial negative is not considered at all. This is because the Sages instituted regarding a conditional get (divorce document) of a deathly ill person to initially avoid starting with a negative outcome, as mentioned in Siman 145. The leading later authorities concluded that the main concern is not to end his statements with the affirmative. Therefore, even if he mentioned the affirmative before the negative, if he concluded with the affirmative, such as saying, "If you give, you are betrothed, and if you do not give, you will not be betrothed, and if you give, you are betrothed," the last statement is taken into account, and the condition is nullified. This matter is not related to "taking the first statement" or "taking the last statement" but rather that anyone making a condition—the main factor is what he concludes his words with.

However, the essence of this law puzzles me, for if we had not found the "yes" preceding the "no" in the condition of the children of Gad and the children of Reuben, we would not have said this logically. And even though we do not derive from there except what it is logical to say [Tosafot Ketubot 74], still the "yes" preceding the "no" is not from logic [Mikneh 61], for why should the "yes" precede the "no" rather than the "no" precede the "yes"? Nonetheless, we do not require it exactly as it is written, and if the "no" precedes the "yes" but then the "no" is said after the "yes," we do not mind as it is written. Therefore, even if the "yes" is said again after the "no," what difference does it make to us since the "yes" came first? And where do we learn to say that the primary focus is on what he concluded with, for this is not logical [indeed, according to the Tosafot Yeshanim in Kiddushin 62, Shmuel's law regarding a dying person is proven from the verse "clean," examine and you will find, but according to the Tosafot there and the Ritva, it is not so, and examine carefully].

And know that it is considered as the fulfillment of the matter we are dealing with, even if it is against the will, as in the case of a get (bill of divorce) for a seriously ill person, it is considered "if I die" – valid, and "if I do not die" – invalid, even though the will is that he should not die. Nevertheless, the act of the get is only due to the death, and similarly in all such cases. But in a matter that one is compelled to do from both sides of the issue, like in the case of giving a sotah (suspected adulteress) the bitter waters to drink, which the Torah decreed she must drink, it is rightly considered valid if she was not defiled since that is our will. This is according to Tosafot there and not according to the Yad Rama and Ritva. Many great authorities agreed with this, and we have already explained this in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 207, Se'if 2, see there. (And this resolves the question of the Taz in the introduction to Yoreh De'ah).

And regarding a condition prior to the act, the Rambam differs with the other decisors. According to most decisors, the condition applies also to the speech (the act of speaking), meaning that the condition must precede the speech of the act. He should say, "If you give me a maneh, then you are betrothed to me, and if you do not give, you are not betrothed." But if he said, "You are betrothed to me if you give me a maneh, and if you do not give, you are not betrothed," where the speech of betrothal precedes the condition, the condition is null even if he gives the money for the betrothal afterward. The Rambam explains that "condition prior to the act" means prior to the act of betrothal, such that he first states the condition and then gives the money for the betrothal. If he reversed the order, giving the money for the betrothal first and then stating the condition, the condition is null, and she is betrothed, and the condition is void.

And this is the language of the Rambam there: How so? If one says to a woman, "If you give me two hundred zuz, you are betrothed to me with this dinar, and if you do not give me, you will not be betrothed," and after stipulating this condition he gives her the dinar – the condition is valid, etc. But if he said to her, "You are betrothed to me with this dinar," and he gave the dinar into her hand and completed the condition and said, "If you give me two hundred zuz, you will be betrothed, and if you do not give, you will not be betrothed" – the condition is nullified because he preceded the act and gave it into her hand and then stipulated, and although everything was within the same statement – she is immediately betrothed and does not need to give him anything, end of quote. And even though this is not a novel idea at all, for we hold in Kiddushin that within the time span of "within the same statement" is not considered as such – this is all when one reconsiders within that time span, but with a continuous statement, certainly if not for the fact that the act preceded, the condition would be valid. [This is the intention of the Beit Yosef to resolve the Tur's question, as later authorities have also written].

And behold, even though the Rambam, of blessed memory, when placing the act before the condition, also placed the speech of the act first, nevertheless, it is implied from his language that he was only particular about the actual act not preceding the condition, but regarding the speech of the condition, we are not concerned, according to the Maggid Mishneh. According to his view, several conditions in the Gemara, where the speech of the act was placed first, can be reconciled. According to the view of all the decisors, it must be said that it is not precise, just as the Talmud does not mention a double condition in all conditions. According to the Rambam, one cannot conceive of the act preceding the condition except in the case of betrothal with money or a document, but not in the case of betrothal through intercourse, where the condition is stated before the witnesses of seclusion prior to the intercourse. The fact that the Rambam also placed the speech of the condition before the act, even though it is not a hindrance according to his view, seems to me to be because he holds that the manner of fulfilling the act is at the time of the speech of the act. Therefore, since the fulfillment of the act must follow, it is necessary for the speech to follow as well. When placing the act before the condition, it is necessary to place the speech of the act first as well. Nevertheless, this does not hinder. [And in this, what was questioned on him from Gittin 75 is resolved: "Rava raises an objection, etc." And there, in the ordinance of Shmuel, we require the condition first, etc. Look there and examine further.]

And even though the language of the Mishnah is "Any condition that has an action at its beginning, its condition is nullified" [Baba Metzia 94a], which seems to support the view of the Rambam, of blessed memory, nevertheless, all our early sages, the decisors, and the commentators disagree with him, and the law follows the majority, but one should be stringent and consider his opinion.
