And according to their view, if at the beginning of his words he presents the condition before the action, but in the repetition, he presents the action first, such as if he said, "If you give me two hundred zuz, you will be betrothed to me, and you will not be betrothed if you do not give," it appears that this is effective and is called a condition before the action [Magid Mishneh Chapter 6 and Maharit in his novellae], for in the repetition we are not concerned. And even though there are those who are uncertain about this, nevertheless, this appears to be the main view. And although in the condition of the children of Gad and the children of Reuben, even in the repetition, Moses our teacher presented the condition before the action, certainly, that is the usual way of speaking but not a requirement, for the reason that one must present the condition first is because when one presents the action first, it is fulfilled without the condition. But in the repetition, when he says that the action will not be fulfilled, how can we say that the action is fulfilled without the condition because he first said that the action will not be fulfilled?

Some authorities say that we do not require a condition to precede the act except in a situation where the act is performed immediately in that same setting. However, if the act will be performed after some time, such as in the case of a gift where Reuven instructed to give a sum of money from his assets to Shimon on a condition and the act precedes the condition, we do not concern ourselves with it [Shach Choshen Mishpat 253:16].

This reasoning somewhat aligns with the Rambam's view to be stringent about the essence of the act itself, although Rambam was not particular about the spoken words at all. This opinion, however, is particular about the spoken words like most of the decisors. Nevertheless, this is only when the act is performed immediately. Therefore, if the spoken words of the act precede, the act is fulfilled immediately. But when the act has not yet occurred, what difference does it make if the spoken words of the act precede the condition? There are some early authorities who did not make this distinction [Maor in the second chapter of Beitzah; Ramban and Raavad there disagree with him, see there].

Some say further that even if he gave the money of betrothal into her hand but did not say anything to her, and afterwards he said to her, "If you give me a maneh, you are betrothed to me," and he repeated his condition – it is considered a condition, even though he gave the money of betrothal first, because when he gave it to her without specifying, it is not a betrothal but a deposit. Afterwards, he precedes the condition to the act, and the money becomes betrothal money. Therefore, she needs to say "yes" as is the law of a deposit, as explained in Siman 28 [Beit Shmuel, section 2]. According to the Rambam, in such a case, even if he precedes the speech of the act, it is considered a condition, since the act of betrothal occurs after the speech, as before this it was a deposit. However, if at the time of giving he said, "You are betrothed to me," no condition is effective even within twenty-four hours, as we have written. The same applies to a gift [Taz]: when he gives a gift, he acquires immediately, and no condition is effective afterward, even within twenty-four hours [see Beit Shmuel there who wrote, and afterward he said, etc., and it is not accurate that one must precede the condition, and his words are according to the Rambam. See Bach in section 101].

There is a doubt among some whether only for a condition pertaining to the future all the laws of conditions are required, or also for a condition pertaining to the past, such as "Behold, you are betrothed to me if I did such and such" or "if you did such and such," whether it is necessary to precede the condition with the action and to double the condition or not. It can be said that specifically for a future condition we say that the nullification of the condition, which will come after the action, does not nullify the action unless the condition was made according to its laws. But for a past condition, what need is there for the laws of conditions? From that moment it becomes clear whether the action will be fulfilled or not. This is no less than "from now" which will be explained that the laws of conditions are not needed because the action takes effect from now, and similarly, the clarification is from now [Mishneh Lemelech, Chapter 6]. However, we see with the condition of a Sotah, which pertains to the past: "if a man lay with you, if a man did not lay with you," and we require the doubling of the condition [ibid]. And some of the great authorities concluded that for the past we do not require the laws of conditions [‘Divrei Emet’ and ‘Yad HaMelech’], as this is like a condition that cannot be fulfilled, for a future condition can be fulfilled or nullified by him, but for the past, what was, was, and he cannot fulfill or nullify it. And indeed, for Sotah, we do not require all the laws of conditions, only the doubling is needed, and we do not learn a negative from a positive, but not all the laws of conditions. And Maimonides in the laws of Sotah did not mention the laws of conditions at all, see there. And there is a halachic inquiry about this, as this distinction is not found among the early authorities, and also it seems from their words that there is no distinction between past and future [for otherwise, Tosafot would not question anything, Tractate Sotah 62b, s.v. hanaki].

A condition that can be fulfilled, how is this? It has already been explained in Section 11, and there is no difference whether the condition is on the man and woman or on others. And even though when it is on another, it is not in his power to fulfill it, nevertheless, it is considered as if it is in his power since he can increase the dowry and gifts until the condition is fulfilled, as mentioned in Section 10. The Tur wrote that it is required that the action can be fulfilled by an agent, and we have already explained in Section 8 that this rule does not apply to betrothal. The Rambam did not mention this detail at all in the laws of conditions, as this is only relevant to the law of chalitzah, and he explained this law there. In other matters of the world, there is no practical difference, for in monetary laws there is nothing that cannot be fulfilled by an agent, and so too with divorces and betrothals, even betrothal through intercourse, because the acts are compared to each other as mentioned there. Regarding vows and oaths, even though they cannot be fulfilled by an agent, there is no practical difference in this, for we do not find that the Sages required the laws of conditions in them. It is only regarding the principle of "from the negative you hear the positive" that exists in vows that this is a matter of logic, even if all the laws of conditions are not required. (See Rambam, Chapter 1 of Vows, Halacha 20 and the notes there, and according to what was explained, it is understood. Contemplate this well.) (And it is not similar to the doubling of the negative because that precedes and the negative is well understood, and nevertheless, the Sages compared them since they are matters of the same kind. Contemplate this well.)

A condition involving one matter and an action involving another matter, how so? This is when the condition is not related to the essence of the action, such as if he says, "If you return to me the paper on which the get (divorce document) is written, you are divorced, and if you do not return it to me, you are not divorced." The condition contradicts the action, for if she returns the paper, how is she divorced? We learn this also from the condition of the children of Gad and the children of Reuben, where the condition was if they crossed the Jordan, and the action was to give them a portion on the other side of the Jordan [Gittin 75a]. 

And some say that this is specifically in a case where he did not say the phrase "on the condition" that you return the paper to me, for if the get is not valid until she returns the paper, the condition contradicts the action. But if he said "on the condition" that you return the paper to me, and we hold that anyone who says "on the condition" is as if he says "from now," then the get is valid immediately and the condition will be fulfilled afterward, and the condition does not contradict the action – it is not considered a condition and action on the same matter [there in Tosafot, s.v. "the condition"]. 

According to this, the same law applies to kiddushin (betrothal). If he gave her a dinar for kiddushin and said, "If you return the dinar to me, you are betrothed to me" – this is not a condition because the condition contradicts the action. But if he said "on the condition" – it is valid kiddushin. However, for kiddushin, for another reason, it is not valid kiddushin as a gift on the condition to return, because it resembles an exchange, as written at the beginning of section 29, see there. But for kiddushin with a document on "on the condition," it is valid kiddushin.

And so it appears from the Tur, who wrote about a condition and an action in one matter: "If the dinar with which I betroth you is mine," and he did not write a greater novelty, even "on condition." And although in the case of betrothing with money, even "on condition" does not work because it resembles an exchange transaction, but in the case of betrothing with a document, "on condition" does work. Similarly, the Tur ruled regarding a divorce in Siman 143: "on condition that you return the paper to me" – the condition is effective, see there [what the Beit Shmuel wrote in subsection 7 on the Tur – it requires further examination].

And so it is implied by our teacher, the Rema, who wrote at the end of Siman 32 regarding betrothal with a document, that if one says "on the condition that the paper is mine" – she is not betrothed. However, it implies that if he says "on the condition that you return the paper to me" – she is betrothed, as it is written there in Section 14, see there. However, one can say that this is because he holds that we do not require at all in the laws of conditions this detail, as some hold, as will be explained, or because he holds that all the laws of conditions do not prevent [the betrothal] to be stringent, as will be explained. And this law is a doubt regarding betrothal, and he only mentioned there what is clear to us that it is not betrothal, as his opinion will be explained in Section 45, with the help of Heaven.

Some of our Rabbis hold that even in the case of "on the condition that you return it to me," it is also considered a condition and an act in one matter [Tosafot 6: s.v. lo according to the first answer, and the Rosh in Bava Batra, chapter 12, siman 48]. However, they hold that we do not require at all this rule of a condition and an act in one matter in the laws of conditions [there]. This also seems to be the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, who did not consider this rule in the laws of conditions. Therefore, in the case of "on the condition that you return it," it certainly works, as if he said "from now." Without "on the condition," it does not work. And there is no need to learn this from the condition of the children of Gad and the children of Reuben, because it is a simple reasoning that since he says, "If you return the paper to me, you will be betrothed to me," then when are the betrothals effective? At the moment she returns the paper to him. So with what is she betrothed? And we only needed to learn from the children of Gad and the children of Reuben in the case of "on the condition." But we do not hold like this as I have written, and therefore the Rambam did not need to mention this, just as he did not need to mention in these rules the rule that if one stipulates against what is written in the Torah, his condition is null, for this is clear from reasoning that a person does not have the ability to make a condition that will violate a Torah commandment. Similarly, he does not have the ability to impose a condition to completely nullify the act, such as saying, "If you return the paper to me, you are betrothed or divorced," and this is nothing but an exaggeration of words, and the condition does not work, and the act remains valid. Nevertheless, this requires further investigation, for we find that the Rambam wrote in the Laws of Divorce, chapter 8, that if he said, "This is your get, and the paper is mine," she is not divorced. But if he said, "on the condition that you return it to me," she is divorced. And he did not mention what the law is if he said, "if you return the paper to me" [and the Kesef Mishneh in chapter 7 of Gittin wrote as I have mentioned in the opinion of the Rambam, and this requires further investigation, as the Beit Shmuel, siman 7, wrote that according to the Rambam, she needs to fulfill the condition].

And according to what we learned, that also in "on the condition" it is considered a condition and an act as one thing, but we do not require that the condition be separate from the act, the law in "on the condition" is that it is a condition. If she later returns the paper to him, the condition is fulfilled, and she is betrothed or divorced. If not, she is not betrothed and not divorced. This is similar to "take this etrog on the condition that you return it to me", which is explained in Orach Chaim, Siman 658. However, there is someone who says that also in "on the condition", the condition is nullified, and there is no need to return the paper. He holds that "on the condition" is also a condition and act as one, and we learn from the condition of the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben that this is not a condition, the act remains, and the condition is nullified [see Beit Shmuel there according to the Rosh in Perek Nosen, though this is not definitive as the Ketzos HaChoshen writes there].

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 4 that there are those who say that the condition must be regarding one matter and the action regarding another matter. But if everything is regarding one matter, it is not considered a condition, and one should be stringent according to his words. According to this, there is no clear ruling except in the case where he said, "This is your divorce document and the paper is mine," in which case she is not divorced. The same applies to betrothal. However, if he stated it in the language of a condition, whether he said, "on the condition that the paper is mine" or "on the condition that you return the paper to me," or whether he used the language "if the paper is mine" or "if you return the paper to me"—in all these cases, it is considered a doubtful betrothal or a doubtful divorce in every aspect, whether she returned the paper to him or not. If she returned it, one might say that perhaps we do not require the condition and the action to be in two different matters, and it is a valid condition, and when the condition is fulfilled, she is betrothed or divorced. And regarding "on the condition," there is also a doubt whether this is a condition in one matter and the action in another, and when the condition is fulfilled, she is betrothed or divorced. Or perhaps it is a condition and action in one matter, and we require them not to be in one matter, and the condition is nullified. Consequently, when the condition is fulfilled, she is not divorced. Only one might say that in the case of "on the condition that you return it," she is betrothed and divorced even if the condition is fulfilled, because since we hold that anyone who says "on the condition" is as if he said "from now," the paper was hers, and what difference does it make to us if she returned it afterward? And if she did not fulfill the condition and kept the paper for herself, it is also a doubt, for perhaps we hold that we require the condition to be in one matter and the action in another, and this is all in one matter, and the condition is nullified, and the action is valid even if the condition was not fulfilled. Or perhaps we do not require this, and it is a valid condition, and if the condition was not fulfilled, the betrothal and divorce are nullified. And in "on the condition that you return it," there is further doubt whether this is not considered in another matter, as mentioned.

This that we explained in the previous section regarding the words of our teacher, the Rema, we explained according to the understanding of one of the great later authorities [Beit Shmuel, subsection 8]. However, according to this, how did our teacher, the Rema, rule earlier in section 32 that when he betroths with a document and says to her "on the condition that the paper is mine," she is not betrothed? After all, this is a case of doubtful betrothal. And we already brought there in subsection 14 someone who holds this opinion, but how is it possible for him to contradict himself from there to here?

Therefore, it seems to me that our teacher, the Rema, holds that in practice we follow the Rambam's opinion that we do not need the conditions and the act to be in separate statements. However, as a stringency, one should be concerned for the opinion that requires them to be separate. But all this is only in the case where one says, "on the condition that you return the paper to me," since "on the condition" is like "from now" and it is possible for the betrothal to take effect because at the time of betrothal the paper is hers. According to the Rambam, this is a complete condition, and if she does not return the paper, she is not betrothed. For those who argue, the condition is nullified and the act stands even if she did not return it. This applies specifically to "on the condition that you return," but in the case of "on the condition that the paper is mine" or "if you return the paper to me" or "if the paper is mine" – in all these cases it is like saying "this is your divorce and the paper is mine," and she is not divorced. The same applies to betrothal. 

The reason for this is that since the betrothal or divorce does not take effect until the paper is returned, it is not considered a betrothal or divorce at all, because on what basis would they take effect? This is not only according to the Rambam, who holds that we do not need the condition and the act to be in separate statements, and thus it is a condition, and since the condition takes effect, the betrothal does not, as there is nothing for it to take effect on. Even according to those who argue that the condition is nullified and the act stands, we do not say this, as it would be like uprooting the matter entirely. This is the opposite of what we wrote in section 41, where in such a case even the Rambam agrees the betrothal is valid because it is considered as if she was exaggerating in her words. But according to this reasoning, it means she was joking, and it is not within the realm of divorce or betrothal at all. 

Therefore, the Rambam in chapter 8 of Hilchot Gerushin only wrote that in the case of "on the condition that you return the paper to me," the get (divorce document) is valid. But in other cases like "if" or "on the condition that the paper is mine," she is not divorced. Similarly, in the Gemara, only the phrase "on the condition that you return" is mentioned [Gittin 75a]. In practice, one should be stringent for all opinions [as it is close to the opinion of the Maharam Halawa, and his words need examination, as his conclusion contradicts the Tur, and also as it is stated, this is not the opinion of the Tur].

The opinion of the Rambam and several of our rabbis is that in all matters we require a double condition and all the legalities of conditions—whether in matters of marriage and divorce or in monetary laws. There are some of our rabbis who hold that in monetary laws we do not require the legalities of conditions, as we have already explained this in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 207, see there. However, there are some of our rabbis who maintain that according to the fundamental law, we do not follow Rabbi Meir, who requires a double condition and all the legalities of conditions, except in divorce and marriage due to the severity of forbidden relationships. They bring proof from the Yerushalmi (Chapter 3 of Kiddushin), and also, in all the conditions mentioned by the sages of the Talmud, not all the legalities of conditions are detailed. But most of our early rabbis disagree on this and hold that according to the fundamental law, we do require that any condition lacking the legalities of conditions invalidates the condition and the action remains valid. Whenever the Talmud mentions a condition, all the legalities of conditions are required, and the Talmud did not mention this everywhere because it was not coming to teach us this novelty (Tosafot, Sukkah 41). The Yerushalmi explains that although by law, without the legalities of conditions, the condition is invalid and the action remains valid, nevertheless, due to the severity of forbidden relationships, we are stringent that if she accepted betrothal from another, she needs a get (divorce document) from both (Tosafot, Gittin 75). Without this, the Yerushalmi’s approach does not align with our Talmud, as our Talmud holds according to several poskim that in a case of "on condition," the legalities of conditions are not required at all, while the Yerushalmi holds that even in "on condition," the legalities of conditions are required (see there in the commentary of the Meharsha).

And this is what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: "There are those who say that the requirement of these four conditions [for a valid condition] applies only where it results in a stringency, but not where it results in a leniency." And even if the four conditions are not present, it is considered a doubtful betrothal and a doubtful divorce, and if another man betroths her, she needs a get (divorce document) from both [men]. And even though there are those who say that only a double stipulation and a stipulation where the positive condition precedes the negative condition are not required according to this opinion, nevertheless, a stipulation that precedes the act and a stipulation that is possible to fulfill are required according to this opinion, because logic dictates so. And even if we do not derive it from the condition of the children of Gad and Reuven, nevertheless, how is it possible to stipulate a condition that is impossible to fulfill, and this is merely an exaggeration of words. And similarly, when the act is at the beginning, especially according to the Rambam, who considers an act to be actual, how is it possible for the stipulation's words to come and nullify the act. Nevertheless, since our rabbis, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, wrote that according to this opinion not all four conditions are required, we are obligated to be stringent in this matter. However, it is possible that they hold that a stipulation preceding the act is considered as the speech of the act itself, as explained. But in the actual act, according to the Rambam, it is possible that they also agree that when the act is at the beginning, the stipulation cannot come and nullify it. Nevertheless, since this is not explicitly clarified in their words, we should not be lenient in matters of forbidden relationships. And also, in a stipulation that is impossible to fulfill, it appears from the Rambam that according to all opinions, a stipulation must be possible to fulfill, as he did not require the laws of stipulation for "from now" and "on the condition that" as will be explained. And nevertheless, he wrote that it must be possible to fulfill. Therefore, it is difficult to be lenient in matters of forbidden relationships in something that is not explicitly and unanimously agreed upon by all the poskim.

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote: Anyone who says "from now" does not need to double his condition nor precede the condition before the action, but even if he precedes the action, his condition is valid. However, he must make a condition on something that is possible to fulfill, and if he makes a condition on something that is impossible to fulfill – it is as if he is exaggerating in words and there is no condition. And anyone who says "on the condition" is like saying "from now" and does not need to double the condition nor precede it before the action. Since the action takes effect from now, it inherently takes effect with the condition he made. But a condition with "if," since the condition comes to nullify the action from taking effect from now – it is not a valid condition unless he doubles it. Likewise, other laws regarding conditions apply. And that the Rambam did not mention that we do not need "from now" to have the affirmative before the negative, it seems to me that he did not need to mention it because since we do not require it to be doubled, it follows that the affirmative or negative order is not relevant here; this only applies in the doubling of the condition. And there are those whose words imply that even with "from now" we require the affirmative before the negative, but it seems to me as I have written. And even if one says "there will not be a marriage from now if you do not give me two hundred zuz, and if you give me, the marriage will be from now" – it also works according to the Rambam and the authorities who follow his approach, that with "from now" and "on the condition" we do not require the laws of conditions, except for something that is impossible to fulfill because it is considered as exaggerating in words.

However, many of our rabbis disagree with the Rambam and hold that even with "from now" ("me'achshav") and "on condition" ("al menat"), we require a doubled condition (tenai kaful) and all the laws of conditions. And even though in the condition of the children of Gad and the children of Reuven the condition was not "on condition" but rather "if they pass over, if they do not pass over," nevertheless, there is no difference between them. For although he conditioned the existence of the act from now, nevertheless, everything depends on the fulfillment of the condition, and if the condition is not fulfilled, the act is void. Therefore, even in this case, the condition comes to nullify the act, and consequently, it requires the laws of conditions; otherwise, its power to nullify the act is not strong. The Tur wrote that his father the Rosh agreed with this opinion, and our master the Beit Yosef brought both opinions without deciding between them. Consequently, one should be stringent in every aspect. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is explained that even with "on condition," the laws of conditions are required. It is possible that the Jerusalem Talmud holds that "on condition" is not like "from now," and according to this, with "from now," it is possible that the Jerusalem Talmud would also hold that the laws of conditions are not required. But in the Jerusalem Talmud Gittin, it is clearly implied that it also holds that anyone who says "on condition" is considered as if he said "from now." Therefore, the Jerusalem Talmud holds like those who disagree with the Rambam.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that there are those who say that even if one did not specify all the conditions of the stipulation but merely stated generally that the stipulation is like the condition of the children of Gad and the children of Reuben, it is considered a valid stipulation. Since he says that the power of this stipulation should be like the power of their stipulation, it is automatically as if he specified all the details of the conditions. Nevertheless, the condition must precede the action and must be stated explicitly. He should say, "If you give me two hundred zuz, you are betrothed to me like the condition of the children of Gad and the children of Reuben." If he says the reverse, "You are betrothed to me if you give me two hundred zuz like the condition of the children of Gad and the children of Reuben," it does not work because he says it in reverse, and we see that he did not stipulate like their condition. This law, when he said "like the condition of the children of Gad and the children of Reuben," is agreed upon as effective as if he specified all the details of the conditions. And although some of the earlier authorities did not decisively rule this law clearly, nevertheless, the Rosh ruled so explicitly in his responsa as the Tur wrote in Choshen Mishpat at the end of Siman 241. See also what I wrote in Choshen Mishpat Siman 207, Paragraph 6.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 7: If a man betroths a woman and either he or she retracts immediately, even if they retract within the time it takes to speak, their retraction is meaningless, and she remains betrothed. This was quoted in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 34. From this language, it implies that the betrothal is definite, and if another man betroths her, she does not need a get (divorce) from the second man. However, some of the early authorities said it is a doubtful betrothal, and if another man betroths her, she needs a get from both men. This is a stringency they applied to divorce and betrothal, for although in all other areas of Jewish law one can retract within the time it takes to speak, nevertheless, due to the severity of matters of forbidden relationships, they were stringent in this case. 

But Maimonides and many of the early authorities held that fundamentally, one cannot retract even within the time it takes to speak. The reason is that in other matters that are not as severe, when a person performs them, he does so without full intention, thinking he can retract within that time. However, with divorce and betrothal, which are very severe, a person only performs them with full consent, and therefore, retraction is not effective even within that time. Additionally, even a condition cannot be imposed if the act was performed first, as stated in Section 31, and certainly, the matter cannot be entirely nullified. And although for Maimonides, this is specifically if the act was performed first, but not for speech, nevertheless, this applies to imposing a condition and not to complete retraction. See what is written later in Section 141, Paragraph 141.

Nonetheless, I am uncertain even regarding this, whether the inability to retract even within the time it takes to speak (toch kedei dibbur) applies even when the act of betrothal has not yet occurred. For example, if he says to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this dinar," and within the time it takes to speak he says, "Here, take the dinar as a gift or as a deposit," and then he gives her the dinar. Or perhaps this inability to retract only applies if he retracts within the time it takes to speak after giving the dinar, but if the giving occurs afterwards, they can retract. From the language of the earlier authorities, it somewhat implies that it is only after the act of betrothal that he cannot retract. This is also implied by the words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Siman 141, Section 59, see there. However, before the act, he can retract, and when he immediately gives it into her hand, it would be according to the second statement. And although in the case of a condition he cannot say after the act according to most of the earlier authorities, this is a scriptural decree that we derive from the condition of the children of Gad and the children of Reuven. But regarding a complete retraction, perhaps he can retract, and this needs further analysis in practice.

[There is no proof from the fact that the Talmud considers it together with the blasphemer, as there the speech is the act, and from the tearing in Nedarim, Chapter 7. There is proof to the contrary, see there.]

Specifically regarding the matter of the betrothal itself, within 24 (seconds) is considered like after the duration of speaking, but a witness about the betrothal can retract within 24 (seconds) as in all testimonies [Rivash, Siman 267]. Similarly, if she said she was betrothed and retracted within 24 (seconds), she is believed, as stated in Siman 47.

It has already been explained in paragraph 13 that they can nullify the condition, and the kiddushin (betrothal) are completed even without the fulfillment of the condition. There is a difference between nullifying a condition of kiddushin and nullifying a condition of divorce: a husband can nullify any condition of divorce, but in kiddushin he can only nullify a condition that was to his benefit, such as "on the condition that she has no defects" or "that she gives me two hundred zuz." However, a condition that was to her benefit, he cannot nullify, and the kiddushin are not completed until he fulfills it, unless she nullifies it. The reason is simple: divorce depends solely on his will, while kiddushin depend on the will of both. In paragraph 13, several opinions about nullifying conditions are explained; see there.

Just as they have the ability to nullify the condition, so too they have the ability to add to it or subtract from it. Therefore, the Rosh ruled in the case of one who went overseas and betrothed on the condition, "If I come back within twelve months, you will be betrothed to me from now." Before he left, they both agreed to extend the time, and twelve months passed without him returning, but he returned before the new extended time — the betrothal is valid. Any act done on condition can have the condition nullified, added to, or subtracted from, because we learn from the condition of the children of Gad and the children of Reuben that a condition has the power to nullify the act. If not for this derivation, a condition would not have the power to nullify the act. But we derive it from them, and you only have what is derived. Since the act and the condition are separate entities, and the act can stand without the fulfillment of the condition, we learn from the children of Gad and Reuben that it is possible to nullify the condition, which is an independent act and merely speech, and speech can nullify the speech of the condition while the act remains valid (Responsa of the Rosh). Even if the money was consumed, the betrothal is retroactively valid when the second condition is fulfilled, and they can also change from this condition to another condition (It seems to me). This all follows the opinion of the Rambam, which we explained in section 13 and according to the reasoning explained in section 14, and not according to those who disagree with him there. This is why our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled this law in section 37 and did not consider the opinion of those who disagree, because he holds in the matter of nullification as the Rambam does, and he did not bring the opinion of those who disagree in section 35, as we wrote there.

And there are those who challenge our master, the Beit Yosef, who ruled this law from what he himself wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 228, Se'if 39, regarding someone who swore to pay his fellow by a certain time: the lender can say, “It is as if I have received payment.” However, extending the time is not allowed unless it was stipulated that he could extend it [Taz]. In truth, the source of this law in Yoreh De'ah is from the Rashba, and he indeed disagrees with the Rambam regarding the annulment of a condition, as he wrote in Se'if 13, that he holds that not every condition can be waived, except in monetary matters. According to this, indeed, for the Rambam, the condition could also be extended. Alternatively, it can be said that even the Rambam agrees that, just as in Kiddushin (betrothal), a man cannot extend the time without the woman's consent when the condition benefits her, so too in an oath, it is as if God is the second party, and without His consent, one cannot change anything in the condition, except for the waiver where the lender says, “It is as if I have received payment,” thereby fulfilling his condition and being released from his oath. But to leave the condition in place and change something in it is not within human capacity since there is an oath involved [see Avnei Miluim and Mekaneh on this matter, and it seems to me as I have written].

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 7: One who tells a woman, "Behold, you are betrothed to me on the condition that my father agrees" — if the father agrees, she is betrothed; if he does not agree, or if he remains silent, or if he dies before hearing of the matter, she is not betrothed. [If he tells her] "on the condition that my father does not object" — if the father hears and objects, she is not betrothed; if he does not object or if he dies, she is betrothed. If the son dies and then the father hears, we instruct the father to say "I do not agree," so that the betrothal is nullified and she will not fall before a levir for levirate marriage. This is the end of the quotation.

And his opinion is clear that when one says "on the condition that he agrees," the intention is that he explicitly agrees and says "I agree." If he said at the time he heard it that he does not agree, the betrothal is nullified even if he agrees afterward, because the condition was based on the initial statement. Otherwise, she would always be forbidden until he dies, as he might agree later. And even if he did not say at the time of hearing that he does not agree, but remained silent – the betrothal is immediately nullified. Otherwise, if he remains silent forever, she would be forbidden until the father's death, and this is not logical. We assess that their intention was that if at the time of hearing he says "yes" – the betrothal stands, and if he is silent or, all the more so, if he says "no" – the betrothal is immediately nullified. Therefore, he equated the law of not wanting to silence, and in both cases the betrothal is nullified.

And when he says "on the condition that he does not protest," the intention is also at the time of hearing, for if he protests at the time of hearing, the betrothal is nullified and nothing will be effective afterward. If he remains silent at the time of hearing, the betrothal is immediately valid, and his protest will not be effective afterward. Therefore, if the father dies before hearing, the betrothal is valid because he can no longer protest. It does not seem correct to say that the condition meant that he must hear and not protest, because if so, he should have said "on the condition that he hears and does not protest." Since he said only "on the condition that he does not protest," his intention was solely on the absence of protest and not on hearing. 

This is what is written, "If the son dies and afterward the father hears, they instruct him to say 'I do not want.'" The intention is not that they instruct him afterward, for certainly, if he was silent at the time of hearing, it is no longer effective. Rather, the intention is that they instruct him at the time of hearing while they are engaged in that matter, or within twenty-four hours of his hearing, and he should protest then. 

If he said "on the condition that he remains silent," the law is the same as when he said "on the condition that he does not protest." However, in the case of "on the condition that he remains silent," protest is not effective even within twenty-four hours of his hearing. For immediately when he was silent, the betrothal is valid, and in betrothal, within twenty-four hours is considered the same as after twenty-four hours, as explained. But in "on the condition that he does not protest," protest is effective within twenty-four hours, for this is the implication of the phrase "that he does not protest immediately," and one must necessarily allow a short time for his protest, which is within twenty-four hours, for this is the way of people. But in "on the condition that he remains silent," the intention is immediately upon his hearing.

And it appears to me that according to this, also in "on the condition that he consents," which means that he says "yes," it also means within twenty-four hours of his hearing, for what difference is there between this and that? It is possible that it is not the same, for in the condition that he must consent, he must consent immediately upon hearing, and no time at all is given to him. And in "that he does not protest," the intention is that he does not protest after some deliberation and consideration, which is within twenty-four hours, or as long as they are engaged in that matter. And "on the condition that he remains silent" also means immediately.

(Note: The commentary of the Rambam and the Rosh is as explained by the Rashba and the Tosefta, which is puzzling. If within twenty-four hours it is effective as explained, it could be resolved, but there it is explicitly stated that perhaps he will consent after an hour.)

Many of our Rabbis disagree with the Rambam and hold that when he says "on the condition that my father says 'yes,'" it does not refer to the moment of hearing, but rather whenever the father says "yes," the betrothal is valid. Even if the father initially says he does not consent, whenever he later consents and says "yes," the betrothal becomes valid. This is also taught in the Tosefta [Chapter 3]: "on the condition that the father consents," even if the father says "I do not consent" – she is betrothed, because the father might consent at a later time. This means she remains in a doubtful state of betrothal indefinitely until the father dies without ever consenting, since no specific time was set for his consent. Any condition that is tied to an action and has no set time, as long as the action can still be carried out, the condition can still be fulfilled [Ramban, Rashba, Ran].

And if he said "on the condition that he does not object," even if the father initially agreed when he heard it – she is not betrothed with certainty because he might object later, and if he objects – the betrothal is immediately nullified even if he later says "I agree." Therefore, when the son dies, we teach the father to say "I do not want" even if he had already heard and agreed, so that the betrothal will be nullified, and she will not require levirate marriage. And why do we say that in the case of "on the condition that he does not object," since he objected, the betrothal is immediately nullified, but in the case of "on the condition that he says yes," his objection is not effective when he says "yes" afterward? Because there the condition was an act of commission that he should say "yes," and therefore as long as the condition is fulfilled, it is effective. But "on the condition that he does not object" is a condition of omission, and any condition of omission, as long as an action is done, the condition is nullified as long as no time was set for the condition. Similarly, in "on the condition that he says yes," since he said "yes" and the condition was fulfilled, it is not effective even if he later retracts, just as it is not effective in the condition that he does not object, which is an omission, when he retracted and did it, even if he later agrees. And in "on the condition that he does not object," when he initially agreed, we said that he can object and nullify the betrothal because his agreement does not affect the condition, just as in "on the condition that he says yes," we do not consider it if he did not initially agree. We need to look at the wording of the condition, and when the wording of the condition is fulfilled when the condition is an act of commission, or when the wording of the condition is nullified when the condition is an omission and he nullifies it, then the condition is fulfilled or nullified, and we do not consider what was before or what will be after.

However, if the condition was "on the condition that he remains silent," there is a different ruling. If he remained silent at the time he heard, she is certainly betrothed, even if he protests afterwards. And although this is also a case of "on the condition that he does not protest," why does his protest afterwards work in that case but not here? Because he phrased the condition in the language of action and not in the language of inaction. Its ruling is like the condition of action, similar to "on the condition that he says yes." Once he says yes, the betrothal is finalized. Likewise, "on the condition that he remains silent," once he remained silent, the condition is fulfilled and the betrothal is finalized. And if the father died before he heard, the betrothal is finalized. See what I have written in section 59.

Furthermore, there are those who disagree with the Rambam, for he holds that when one says "on the condition that my father approves," it means that he must say "yes," while they believe that it means that he remains silent and does not object [Rosh and Tur, and this is also implied by Rashi and Tosafot]. And there are those who say further that "on the condition that he approves" is equivalent to "on the condition that he does not object" [Ramban]. And we hold stringently that one who says "on the condition that he approves" should be stringent according to all opinions: as "on the condition that he says yes," as "on the condition that he remains silent," and as "on the condition that he does not object" [Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 19].

In relation to what we have written, that in the case of one who says "on the condition that he does not object," even if he initially consents, if he later objects, the betrothal is nullified, our teacher, Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema), wrote in clause 10 that there are those who say that if he says "yes" once, he can no longer object. This is the opinion of the Tur. It seems to me that the Tur does not definitively consider this as a valid betrothal but rather as a doubtful one. For indeed, his father, the Rosh, was in doubt about this, and from his words, it appears that he leans more towards the opinion that he can object. How then could the Tur not bring his father’s opinion at all? Rather, the Tur’s intention is also regarding a doubtful betrothal. And according to the Beit Yosef and what we have written, it is clear. For the practical law, there is no difference because there is a dispute about this, and it is automatically a doubt. However, in the case of "on the condition that he says yes," even the Tur agrees that if he objects initially, and then says "yes," it is certainly a valid betrothal, because the condition is an affirmative action. Additionally, the condition itself proves this, for if the intention was that the betrothal would be nullified upon the first objection, why state that he should say "yes"? It should state that he should not object. Therefore, certainly the meaning is that as long as he says "yes," even after his objection, it should be a valid betrothal. This is also explicitly stated in the Tosefta that we brought. It is possible that even according to the Rambam, who holds that the intention is for the first time he hears it, as we have written, this only applies to "on the condition that he consents," not to "on the condition that he says yes." However, the commentators on his words did not write this. Consequently, the practical law in all cases is a doubtful betrothal. All these laws also have implications in the conditions of monetary law.

If he said, "On the condition that you will say 'yes'," and she heard and remained silent, according to the Rambam the betrothal is nullified, but according to other authorities, it is in a state of doubt until the father dies, in case he might still say "yes." Therefore, if the son dies, she is prohibited to the general public according to those authorities, because the father might say "yes" and she would then be obligated to the levirate marriage. However, to the yavam, she is permitted in any case, because if the father says "yes," then according to those authorities, she is a yevamah, and according to the Rambam, it is as if he is a stranger. Similarly, even if he does not say "yes," according to those authorities, it is no worse than a stranger. Therefore, if she performs chalitzah with the yavam, she may marry another. This is also stated by the Tur in the name of the Ramah. There are those who say that she should not perform chalitzah but should undergo yibbum [Beit Yosef] because perhaps the father will never say "yes," and her chalitzah would not be valid, making her permitted to a Kohen, and she would then require an announcement regarding her status to the priesthood, as we are concerned about this in Siman 156. However, it seems to me that it is not comparable, because there, there is a remedy to wait until the matter is clarified, as stated there. But here, she can never marry another until the father dies, and it is possible that she does not want to marry the yavam, or he does not want her. Therefore, it is necessary for her to perform chalitzah, and if she requires an announcement, we will make one then [and with this, we can understand what Rashi wrote in Yevamot 119: "to her companion forever"].

Based on what has been explained, according to all opinions, if the father said "on the condition that he remains silent" and he remained silent at the time of the hearing, she is betrothed even if he later objected. Our teacher, the Rema, writes that nevertheless, if he was not at home when he heard and when he came home he objected, it is considered an objection because his initial silence was due to not being at home. However, there are those who disagree with him, arguing that this only applies to the betrothal of his daughter, which was accepted without his knowledge because he was not at home. In such a case, it is reasonable to say that he has until he returns home to object because he does not need to object and reveal his opinion when he is not in his place. But the son is not under his father's authority; it is merely a condition. And since he did not say "on the condition that he remains silent in my presence," as soon as he heard and remained silent, wherever he was, the betrothal is valid. However, it is certain that if the son did not inform him of the betrothal on the way and only upon arriving home did he find out, then it is only then considered the time of hearing. For as long as he did not know that the son relied on him, why should he remain silent or object? And it is possible that this is what our teacher, the Rema, meant. Similarly, even if he heard that the son relied on him but did not know the details and upon coming home he found out the details, it also seems that this is considered the time of hearing, for without knowing the details, why would he object or remain silent and agree?

In Ketubot [73b], it was taught: "I am hereby engaging in intercourse with you on the condition that my father consents." Even if the father does not consent, she is betrothed. Rabbi Shimon says: if the father consents, she is betrothed; if the father does not consent, she is not betrothed. The Talmud explains that the first Tanna holds that "on the condition that he consents" means "on the condition that he remains silent," and he did remain silent. Rabbi Shimon, however, holds "on the condition that he says 'yes,'" and he did not say 'yes.' And in Gittin [25b], the Talmud establishes this dispute based on a different reasoning. The first Tanna holds that a man does not make his intercourse promiscuous and intends complete betrothal even if his father does not consent [Rashi]. Rabbi Shimon does not agree with this; therefore, if the father consents, she is betrothed, and if not, she is not betrothed. The Talmud establishes that Rabbi Shimon holds by the concept of retroactive clarification (bererah); therefore, even though at the time of intercourse it is uncertain whether the father consents, we say that from the moment of intercourse it is considered betrothal once it is clarified afterward that the father said, "I consent" [there]. This is not like other conditions where a person conditions something within his power to fulfill and intends to fulfill it when he conditions it; and once the condition is fulfilled, the divorce or betrothal is retroactive, and it is not because of bererah. But a condition that is not within his power and at the time of the condition is uncertain, and the condition is fulfilled by itself, is bererah [there, and so the Tosafot wrote in Yoma 56b, s.v. de-Rabbi Meir, and in Sukkah 24b].

The Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch did not bring this law at all. It seems to me that the reason is that they hold according to the sugya in Gittin, and the halacha does not follow the Tanna Kama because it is proven in Ketubot there that only when one betroths on condition and then consummates, we are concerned that he may have waived his condition, as I wrote in section 13. But if one betroths through intercourse on condition, he certainly does not waive it, and we do not hold like Rabbi Shimon, because we hold that in biblical matters there is no retroactive clarification. Therefore, they did not write this in the laws of betrothal through intercourse. For in betrothal with money, when he says "on condition that my father approves," we do not need the reasoning of retroactive clarification, because with money she can be betrothed with that money also afterward when the father approves, and we do not need to say that it was clarified retroactively. But in betrothal through intercourse, the betrothal must take effect at the time of the act, for afterward the intercourse no longer exists, and we are necessarily brought to the law of retroactive clarification. And even if we say that even here the betrothal takes effect retroactively since anyone who says "on condition" is as if he says "from now," nevertheless, it is not similar to all other retroactive clarifications where the matter is revealed afterward only about the past time. But in this case, the matter is revealed only afterward for the future time, and therefore, since it takes effect for the future, the betrothal certainly takes effect without any retroactive clarification, and therefore it also takes effect retroactively. Therefore, although in Ketubot there they disagree on the language "on condition that he approves," what it means, the poskim did not concern themselves with it because of the sugya in Gittin. [This resolves the difficulty of the Beit Shmuel in section 18 and the difficulty of the Panim Me'irot in Kiddushin 63, "on condition," see there and analyze carefully].

Any condition that has a set time for its fulfillment, if the time passes and the condition is not met, the betrothal is nullified. Any condition that does not have a set time, the time is indefinite. Therefore, if he says to her, "Be betrothed to me with this coin on the condition that I give you a maneh (a certain amount of money)," whenever he gives the maneh, the betrothal is fulfilled. If he states that he does not wish to fulfill his condition ever, we do not force him to fulfill it, and the betrothal is nullified and does not require a get (divorce document). Nevertheless, a conscientious person should not marry her without a get, because perhaps later he will say that he wants to fulfill the condition and thus cause her problems with a second husband. Although according to the strict law, this is nothing even to those authorities who disagree with the Rambam regarding the condition "on the condition that my father agrees," and they hold that even if initially he said "I do not want," if he later says "yes," the betrothal is valid as we have written, this applies to a condition that is not in his power to fulfill immediately. But for a condition that he can fulfill immediately and he says he does not wish to fulfill it, the betrothal is nullified immediately. However, there is still room for suspicion, and this suspicion can cause her harm.

But if he says they should fulfill [the condition] and now he does not yet desire to fulfill it but wishes to fulfill it after some time, indeed, he has the right to do so. Nevertheless, we wait for him only up to twelve months, as is the law for someone who demands to marry, where such a time is awaited. After twelve months, if he does not fulfill [the condition], although the betrothal still hangs in the balance, we nonetheless write him a letter of rebellion and treat him according to the law of a rebel, which will be explained in Siman 77. If he dies before the condition is fulfilled, even a chalitzah is not required, and she is permitted to a Kohen. However, if she waived the condition during his lifetime, the betrothal is immediately completed as if he fulfilled it. Some say that even after his death, if she waived the condition, the betrothal is retroactively valid and she is considered a married woman [Beit Shmuel, Siman 62]. 

All these matters apply when he did not consummate the marriage before the condition was fulfilled. But if he consummated the marriage before, she is immediately betrothed even if the condition was not fulfilled, because presumably, at the time of entering the chuppah, she waived the condition, and he must give her the ketubah. And even though we explained that if he betrothed her on condition and consummated the marriage without specifying, it is only doubtful betrothal, this refers to a condition where it is not known whether it was fulfilled, such as defects and vows and the like. But in this case, where she knows the condition was not fulfilled and agreed to enter the chuppah, it is certain she waived the condition [ibid, Siman 63]. Some say that even here it is doubtful betrothal [Bach and Chamudei Daniel].

He said to her, "Be betrothed to me with this perutah (small coin) on the condition that I work for you as a laborer" or "I will speak on your behalf to the authorities." If there are witnesses that he worked for her as a laborer or spoke on her behalf to the authorities, she is certainly betrothed, and she cannot claim that she did not need this work or these words spoken. Since he performed the work in the manner of a laborer or spoke to the authorities in the accustomed manner, if the matters are known regarding what is spoken to the authorities, and if they are not known, she also cannot say she did not need these things, for he fulfilled his condition. Since she benefited from these matters or the work, she is certainly betrothed. Similarly, if she admits that he fulfilled the condition, her admission is as valid as witnesses. If she denies it and there are no witnesses, she is believed regarding herself. If she does not deny it and there are no witnesses, she is doubtfully betrothed. We have already explained these laws from Section 20 to Section 25. See there. [See Choshen Mishpat 20 and 21, and Beit Shmuel, and see Beit Yosef who sought to distinguish between the Tosefta and the Tosafot, but Choshen Mishpat did not agree, and so wrote the Ketzot HaChoshen.]

And this specifically applies when the betrothal was with someone else's money and this statement and action were a condition. But if he betrothed her with this, such as if he did not give her anything and said to her, "Be betrothed to me in exchange for my working with you as a laborer or for speaking on your behalf to the authorities" – she is not betrothed even if he worked and spoke. The reason is that we hold that the payment for labor extends from the beginning to the end, and for each perutah's worth of work or speech, she remains in debt, and it is considered as if he betrothed her with a loan, and she is not betrothed, as stated in Siman 28, Se'if 46.

He said to her, "On the condition that I have a hundred zuz," if it is known through witnesses that he has a hundred zuz, meaning they saw a hundred zuz in his possession, even if they do not know for certain that it belongs to him, there is a presumption that whatever is in a person's hand belongs to him unless it is known that it belongs to others. Similarly, if we saw a hundred zuz with him and the presumption is that it belongs to him, she is definitely betrothed. If it is known that he does not have it, she is not betrothed. If it is not known whether he has it or not, she is betrothed out of doubt, even if he says he does not have it, because we are concerned that perhaps he retracted from the betrothal. Since he initially betrothed her with this condition, it is likely that he has it, and now he is retracting. Therefore, it is a doubtful betrothal. Even if she also says that he does not have it, it does not help, and it remains a doubtful betrothal, for the reason explained. It is not like other conditions where if both admit, the betrothal is nullified, because in this case, it appears as a retraction, as explained.

If he says to her, "On the condition that I have a maneh (a specific amount of money) with so-and-so," if it is known by witnesses that he has a maneh with so-and-so, then she is definitely betrothed. If it is not known, she is betrothed doubtfully, even if that so-and-so says he does not have it with him, and even if he and she both say they do not have it, it is still doubtful betrothal for the reason explained. If that so-and-so says he has a maneh with him, and he (the groom) also says so, and she says she does not know, it is only doubtful. But if she also says that he has a maneh with so-and-so, it is as if they both say the condition has been fulfilled, and she is definitely betrothed. 

In these laws, when the condition was that he has it, even if she denies it certainly and says he does not have it, it does not help to annul the betrothal, even according to the one who holds that in other conditions she is believed to say the condition was not fulfilled, as mentioned in section 20. But in such conditions, she is not believed for the reason explained unless there are witnesses, and even one witness does not help to remove the doubt of betrothal.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in section 16: "On the condition that a certain person says that I have a hundred [zuz] in his possession"—if he says he has it in his possession, she is betrothed; if he does not say he has it in his possession, she is not betrothed." Their words mean that even if it is later verified by witnesses that I have a hundred [zuz] in his possession, if he does not say it, she is not betrothed. There is no doubt here since the condition was not fulfilled because he did not say it. Conversely, it seems to me that if he says he has it in his possession and it is not verified that he has it, these are only doubtful betrothals when she says she does not know for certain, as we said. We cannot say that the condition was only on his statement, as it appears from the Tosefta [Chapter 3], from where this law originates, that this is an additional condition to the verification that he has a hundred [zuz] in the possession of that person. Furthermore, it seems to me that everything depends on the context. If the conversation between them was that he has a hundred [zuz] in the possession of that person and that he will betroth her on this condition, and she did not agree until that person also says so, and he betrothed her with this language, "on the condition that a certain person says," it is certainly in addition to the verification. But if there was no prior conversation between them and at the time of betrothal he said this language to her, since that person said he has it in his possession, it is a definite betrothal, as the condition was fulfilled. However, this is only when he indeed has a hundred [zuz] in his possession, as it does not depend solely on the statement but rather that they believed him on his word.

He said to her, "On the condition that I have a maneh (a specific sum of money) in such-and-such a place," if it is verified that he has it in that place, or if both agree, she is certainly betrothed. If he does not have it in that place, she is betrothed out of doubt, for perhaps he does have it there and is merely trying to cause mischief and retract from the betrothal. This is all based on the reasoning previously explained, unless there are witnesses that he does not have it in that place; in that case, the betrothal is nullified, even if he has the maneh in another place, even in a place close to the specified location. Since the condition was specifically about that place, there is certainly a concern that she desires to go only to that place. Therefore, if it is known that there was no specific insistence on that place, if it is discovered that he has it in another place, the betrothal is likely valid, and at the very least, it is a doubtful betrothal.

And even if he said to her another expression, "On the condition that I show you a maneh (a specific amount of money)", the intention is not to show her someone else's maneh, but rather his own maneh. Until he shows her his own maneh, she is not definitively betrothed, but rather in a state of doubtful betrothal. This is because when he said, "On the condition that I show you," this is an additional condition that even if it is known through witnesses that he has it, she is not satisfied until she sees it with her own eyes. Therefore, even if there are witnesses that he can show it to her, she is not betrothed until he shows it to her. And as long as he has not shown it to her, it is not even a doubtful betrothal because the condition has not been fulfilled. However, it is within his power to show it to her whenever he wishes, as no time was set for the condition. He must show her his own money and not someone else's. Even if the money is in his possession as part of a business transaction from someone else and he is dealing with it as if it were his own, it is of no consequence, as this was not her intention. Some say that even if he has a share of the profit amounting to a maneh from this business transaction, since the profit has not yet been divided, it is not considered his. There is an opinion that this applies only when the time for division has not yet arrived and the profit is still integrated into the principal. However, if the time for division has arrived, it is considered his even if it has not yet been divided. And although a business partner is considered like a worker and can divide whenever he wishes, even within the time, as stated in Choshen Mishpat 176, here it is in a situation where it is impossible for him to divide, such as when he received it with another person, and then he cannot divide before the time. It is possible that even if he has no partner, it is not considered his until the time for division arrives, because although he has the power to divide, as long as he has not divided, it is not considered his. Who knows if he will agree to divide, or the business partner might find a pretext not to divide. This does not apply when the time for division has arrived, as then it is considered his.

He showed her a maneh of his own, but it is mortgaged to a creditor – she is betrothed. This is specifically when he did not mortgage it to the creditor from the present time, and therefore we are not concerned about the mortgage, as all people have mortgages, and it is not similar to a business deal where he has profit but they have not yet divided, which does not help, because there they were not yet his and had not yet come into his possession. But this maneh is always his, and it is currently his, and the mortgage does not cancel it from being considered his. However, if it is mortgaged from the present time, it is not considered his, because if he does not pay, it belongs to the creditor from the present time and is not his. Therefore, it is a doubtful betrothal. 

And if he has a maneh from wages due to him, if he has already completed the work – it is considered his, but if not – it is not considered his, as wages are only paid at the end. And if he has money as a gift from someone, if the giver transferred it to him through another person – it is considered his, but if not – even if he promised to give it and surely will fulfill it, nevertheless it is not considered his because he has not yet acquired it.

Some say there is a distinction between saying "on condition that I have" and "on condition that I show you." In the case of "on condition that I have," if he did not have it at the time of the betrothal, she is not betrothed even if he later earned or found something. But in the case of "on condition that I show you," even if he did not have it at the time of the betrothal and later earned or found something and showed it to her, she is betrothed, since he said "on condition that I show you," implying that he would show it to her later, and he did show it to her. However, if he said "on condition that I show you a maneh that I have," it does not help if he acquires it later, because he said he has it, which means he must have it at the time of the betrothal. 

There is also a distinction in that, in the case of "on condition that I have," even if it is not verified that he has it, the betrothal is in doubt because we are concerned that he might have it. But in the case of "on condition that I show you," this is not the case, and we are not concerned that he might have shown it to her, because here there is no actual deed, and we are concerned out of doubt. But in the case of "show you," there is an actual deed that he must show her, so why should we be concerned about this? 

It is also not similar to "I will do work for you" or "speak to the authorities," where, even though these are positive actions, we are concerned. In those cases, she cannot contradict him, and perhaps he did indeed do the work and speak, and it is not customary to do these things in front of witnesses. But in the case of "show you," since she says he did not show her, why should we be concerned? It is also customary to show things in front of witnesses. It seems that even if he claims he showed her and she denies it, she is believed. However, according to what is written in section 21, she needs a get (divorce document), and we compel him to give a get. 

Now, even though some disagree and hold that even in the case of "on condition that I show you," he must have the maneh beforehand, and it does not help if he acquires it later, because otherwise there would be no limit, and whenever she asks him to show it to her, he could say he still has time to show her (as per Beit Yosef in the name of the Rosh), and he means that he might still earn or find something. However, the Tur did not bring this opinion at all, nor did our master the Rema. The reason is that there is certainly a limit, because if she asks him to show it to her and he does not, the betrothal is void, since the condition is "on condition that I show you," meaning that whenever she asks him, he is required to show it to her. 

Nevertheless, as long as she does not ask, he has time forever, as long as no time was set in the condition. And even if he earns later, the betrothal is valid when he shows it to her (according to Beit Shmuel in the name of Rashal). Similarly, if he said "on condition to bring you a maneh," it is like "show you," and even if he earns later, it helps as long as it is his. But if he said "to bring you a maneh that I have," he must have it beforehand, just like "on condition that I show you a maneh that I have" (according to Chochmat Shlomo).

He said to her, "On the condition that I have a beit kor of land," if there are witnesses that he has it, she is certainly betrothed. If not, she is betrothed doubtfully, perhaps he has it and says he does not to deceive her, as explained regarding the maneh in section 73, for he said it in a manner that suggests he has it. If he said, "on the condition that I have a beit kor of land in a certain place," if he has it in that place, she is certainly betrothed. If not, she is doubtfully betrothed, perhaps he has it there and intends to deceive her, and there is a particular concern about this location over another because she might specifically want to go to that place, or perhaps the produce growing on that land is better than on other land. Therefore, if it is known that there was no specific insistence on that place, it is judged like the maneh as we explained. Some disagree regarding land, arguing that we do not suspect he might have land there that is unknown, and this is not similar to the maneh, because if he had land in that place, it would be known to all. Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, did not bring this opinion at all in section 20 [see the Gra, section 32].

He said to her, "On the condition that I show you a plot of land (a 'beit kur' of soil)" – she is betrothed only when he actually shows it to her, and it is not sufficient for him to bring witnesses who testify that he has it, as we have said regarding money. In this case, it is effective even if he acquires it later, which is different from "on the condition that he has it," as we have said regarding money. However, he must show her land that is specifically his and not someone else's, even if he rented it from others or holds it as a sharecropper or tenant, and even if he holds ancestral land that has been in his family for generations and will be passed to his descendants. Nevertheless, it is not valid because it is not his, and if it deteriorates, the landowner has the ability to evict him. But if the land is his—even if he pays taxes from it—she is betrothed because the land is his, though the practical difference is if all the people in the place pay taxes from their property, then even if he only has a precise 'beit kur,' she is betrothed because she knew he pays taxes. But if not everyone pays taxes, the betrothal is not certain until he has a 'beit kur' of land that does not incur taxes, meaning he must have more than a 'beit kur' so that the excess value covers the tax. If not, she is not certainly betrothed but it remains in doubt. The Sages did not distinguish between superior, average, and inferior quality land.

The area of a "beis kor" (a field measurement) must be suitable for planting throughout its entirety. If it contains deep crevices that are ten tefachim (handbreadths) deep and four by four wide, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 218 regarding sales, or rocks that are ten tefachim high and four by four wide, if the crevices are filled with water, they are considered like rocks and are not measured with it because they are not suitable for planting. The beis kor must be measured separately from the crevices and rocks. However, if the crevices do not contain water and are suitable for planting, they are measured with it. And even though it is explained there in Choshen Mishpat that even if they are not filled with water, they are not measured because a person does not want to pay for a field that appears to be in two or three places, this reasoning does not apply to a woman (in the context of marriage contracts), as she does not care since he (the husband) will take the trouble to gather the produce. Nevertheless, if the beis kor is truly in separate locations that are completely divided, they do not combine, and it must be in one place. Although she does not mind the interruption of crevices and rocks, it is still considered one field, unlike when it is in completely separate places. And if the field contains a cistern filled with water, even though it is not suitable for planting, it is measured with it because it is necessary and beneficial for the field. Only crevices filled with water are not measured because they do not suffice to irrigate the field and do not enhance it, unlike an actual cistern. If the crevices and rocks are less than ten tefachim, they are measured with the beis kor because they do not have a distinct status and are called the basins of the land into which water drains, and the rocks are called the ridges of the land, which is the way of most lands. However, if there are many such bad spots in the beis kor, it is certainly not considered land. It appears to me that the measure is a beis four kabin and that they are absorbed within five kabin within most of the field, as stated in Choshen Mishpat there regarding sales. In cases of doubt, it is considered a doubt in betrothal here.

The Sages taught in a Mishnah in Kiddushin (48b): If one betrothed a woman and said to her, "On the condition that I am wealthy," and it turns out he is poor, or even the opposite, "On the condition that I am poor," and it turns out he is wealthy; "On the condition that I am a Kohen," and it turns out he is a Levi, or "a Levi," and it turns out he is a Kohen; "On the condition that I am a Natin," and it turns out he is a Mamzer, or "a Mamzer," and it turns out he is a Natin; "On the condition that I am a resident of the city," and it turns out he is a resident of a large town, or "a resident of a large town," and it turns out he is a resident of the city; "On the condition that my house is near the bathhouse," and it turns out it is far, or "far," and it turns out it is near; "On the condition that I have a maidservant" or "a grown daughter," meaning an important one, or he said to her, "On the condition that she has a maidservant" or "a baking daughter," and it turns out he does not have, or "On the condition that he does not have," and it turns out he has; or he said to her, "On the condition that he has a wife and children," and it turns out he does not have, or "On the condition that he does not have," and it turns out he has—in all these cases, the betrothal is nullified. Similarly, if she said, "In my heart, I intended to be betrothed to him even if the condition is not fulfilled," she is not betrothed. It does not matter whether she accepted the betrothal herself or whether she appointed an agent to accept it under such conditions and the agent deviated from his mission—she is not betrothed. We do not say that she gave the agent discretion and that there is no strictness regarding this, because since she stipulated on the condition, there is strictness unless she explicitly said at the time of the betrothal, when he stipulated the condition, "Even if it is not as you said, I am agreeable," and he did not respond to her negatively—then she is betrothed in any case. Similarly, if the condition was on her with such matters and it turns out that she deceived him—the betrothal is nullified even if he now says, "In my heart, I intended to betroth her in any case," because thoughts in the heart are not considered matters unless he explicitly said at the time of the betrothal after stipulating the condition that even if it is not so, he agrees—then his betrothal is valid.

In all the matters that have been clarified and similar ones, even though there are things that are not understood as to why the stipulation was made, and on the contrary, there are cases where the condition could be found to be praiseworthy, such as "on the condition that I am poor and was found to be rich," nevertheless, since there was a condition between them, we are not to seek reasons and the condition must be fulfilled as stipulated. If it changes, she is not betrothed, for every person has a mind that is not comprehensible to others and may choose the worse over the better, and may be particular about something that no other person would be particular about.
