This is also implied in the Tosefta [chapter 2], where it was taught: "On the condition that I am Joseph" and he was found to be Joseph and Simon; "on the condition that I am a perfumer" and he was found to be a perfumer and a tanner; "on the condition that I am a city dweller" and he was found to be a city dweller and a villager—she is betrothed. "On the condition that I am only Joseph" and he was found to be Joseph and Simon; "on the condition that I am only a perfumer" and he was found to be a perfumer and a tanner; "that I am only a city dweller" and he was found to be a city dweller and a villager—she is not betrothed. Thus, we see that even a change in name from Joseph to Simon is a matter of concern, even though there is no apparent reason why she should be particular about it. This is also evident from the language of Rashi [Ketubot 49b, s.v. "a resident of the city"], and the Talmud there, which considers the reasons according to Rabbi Shimon.

But some of our Rabbis have written reasons for all these matters as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, that it could be that there is a concern about a change in condition even if the change is for the better. For example, if [a man] was poor and was found to be rich, [the woman] can say, "I do not want the excessive expenses and the great bother that come with the wealthy, as everyone seeks things from him and bothers him" [as explained in the Jerusalem Talmud]. Similarly, from a metropolis to a city – there is a reason that in a metropolis there are all the pleasures that a person seeks, which are not found in a city, and from a city to a metropolis – there is a reason that in a city there is more tranquility than in a metropolis, where there is not as much noise as in a metropolis. And if [his] house is far from the bathhouse and it is found to be close – there is a reason that she can say she desires to be jumping and moving about in her going and returning and for this, a long path is needed. If he stipulated that he has a wife and children and he does not – she can say her desire was for companionship and not to sit alone. And in the matter of lineage, like from a Levite to a Kohen, and from a Kohen to a Levite, from a Mamzer to a Natin and vice versa – if the deception was to a lower status, she can say she specifically wanted someone of distinguished lineage, and if the reverse – she can say she does not want someone of distinguished lineage lest he become arrogant over her. Similarly, with a maidservant and a daughter, if he stipulated that he has and he does not – she is particular because she needed companionship and wanted an important maidservant or a capable one, and the reverse, when he said he does not have and he does – it is obvious there is a concern as she does not want an important one, lest she speak ill of her, and due to her importance, people would believe her.

And based on this, some of the great later authorities have written that every condition requires some strictness when there is a change, but if there is no strictness at all due to the change, the betrothal is not nullified because of the change. Therefore, the case in the Tosefta about changing the name from Yosef to Shimon doesn't make sense—what strictness is there in this? However, it appears to me, with all due respect, that in every condition a person sets, there is, according to his understanding, some strictness, even if for most people there is no strictness at all. Nevertheless, since he set this condition, it must necessarily be fulfilled, and if not, the betrothal is nullified. The Jerusalem Talmud, on the contrary, teaches us not to say that these conditions are like the words of fools and we should not pay attention to them, because since he set conditions contrary to common sense, it tells us that it could be that this man or woman, according to their lowly understanding, has some strictness about it. There is no condition in the world where, according to the one setting it, there is no strictness. Even regarding names, there are those of lowly understanding who are strict about names, believing that one name indicates good and another should be avoided, and there is nothing in the world where, according to the one speaking, there is no strictness.

We also learn from the Tosefta that we do not follow estimations when it comes to conditions, but rather the exact wording of the condition itself. For instance, between a perfumer and a tanner, there is a significant difference. According to estimation, when one says "on the condition that I am a perfumer," it seems that she desires a profession involving pleasant scents, and it is certain that she does not want a foul-smelling profession like a tanner. Nevertheless, the Tosefta rules that if he did not say "I am only a perfumer" but said "on the condition that I am a perfumer," he could still be a tanner if he is also a perfumer, and similarly in all such cases. The general principle is that we do not interpret conditions but follow the exact wording.

We also learned in the Tosefta: "On the condition that I am poor," and he was poor and became rich; "on the condition that I am rich," and he was rich and became poor. "On the condition that I am a perfumer," and he was a perfumer and became a tanner; "on the condition that I am a tanner," and he was a tanner and became a perfumer. "On the condition that I am a city dweller," and he was a city dweller and became a town dweller; "on the condition that I have children," and he had children and they died; "on the condition that I have no children," and he had none and then had some – she is betrothed. "That I am only poor," and he was rich and became poor; "that I am only rich," and he was poor and became rich; "that I am only a perfumer," and he was a perfumer and became a tanner; "that I am only a tanner," and he was a tanner and became a perfumer; "that I am only a city dweller," and he was a city dweller and became a town dweller; "that I am only a town dweller," and he was a town dweller and became a city dweller; "that I have no children," and he had children and then they died; "that I have children," and he had none and then had some – she is not betrothed. This is the rule: anything that is fulfilled at the time of betrothal, even if it is annulled afterward – she is betrothed; and anything that is not fulfilled at the time of betrothal, even if it is fulfilled afterward – she is not betrothed. And it seems clear that there is a printing error in the second clause from "that I am only a perfumer" to "city" – and it should read: "that I am only a perfumer" and he was a tanner and became a perfumer, "that I am only a tanner" and he was a perfumer and became a tanner, "that I am only a city dweller" and he was a town dweller and became a city dweller, "that I am only a town dweller" and he was a city dweller and became a town dweller, etc. as it should be. And this change in the Tosefta in the wording of the second clause from the first, where initially it states "on the condition that I am" and later "that I am only," teaches us that even if he said "that I am only," and one might think that the main concern is for the future and not for the time of betrothal, it teaches us that its law is like "on the condition that I am," that the main condition is at the time of betrothal.

And similarly, if he said to her, "Be betrothed to me with this cup of wine," and it was found to be honey, or "with this cup of honey," and it was found to be wine – she is not betrothed if the cup was covered and she did not see what was inside it, even if she said in her heart she intended to be betrothed to him as he said. However, if the cup was uncovered – she is betrothed, since she saw that it was not as stipulated and accepted it, thus she consented. Nevertheless, the Rashba wrote in a responsum that one should not rely on this, and there is no conclusive proof that these are definite betrothals, and therefore he should betroth her again. It seems clear that in the case of an uncovered cup, if she said she intended in her heart to be betrothed to him since she saw what was inside – there is no need for another betrothal. Similarly, if he said to her, "Be betrothed to me with this gold dinar," and it was found to be silver, or "with this silver dinar," and it was found to be gold – the law is the same as with the cup. If he said, "Be betrothed to me with one dinar," and it was found to be two dinars – she is betrothed, for this is not a change, as two hundred includes one hundred. However, if he said, "There is only one dinar here," and it was found to be two – it seems this is a change. But if he said, "Be betrothed to me with a silver dinar," and it was found to be gold – she is not betrothed in any case, for this is a complete change, even though gold is worth much more than silver. In this case, we do not follow estimation but rather the spoken words.

If he betrothed her without stipulation and wants to annul the betrothal, claiming, "I thought she was a Kohenet and she is actually a Levite, or a Levite and she is a Kohenet, wealthy and she is poor, poor and she is wealthy," or if she claims, "I thought he was such and such and he is not," even though there is strong evidence that they thought so, nevertheless, since they did not stipulate, thoughts of the heart are not considered and she is betrothed. Except in the case of defects and vows, which are a doubt in betrothal as mentioned in Siman 39, because all people are particular about this and it is considered as if it was an explicit condition, and similarly in the case of an ailonit (a woman who is unable to conceive). However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 3, Halacha 4, there is a dispute, and some hold that if there is evidence that he thought so, the betrothal is valid only stringently and not leniently. Thus, one should be concerned about this in the case of a married woman.

Our Sages said: If one stated, "on the condition that I know how to read," he must read the Torah and translate it into the Targum of Onkelos the Convert. Some say that if he knows how to read and translate three verses, it is sufficient. It appears to me that nowadays, when we do not translate in public during the Torah reading, the intention of "knowing how to read" is that he knows how to read with the cantillation marks, as is customary among our Torah readers. And if he said, "on the condition that I can read," he must know the Tanach with precise grammar. Certainly, he must know how to translate the Torah as stated [by the Chochmat Shlomo], and this was in the time of the Talmud as mentioned.

He said, "On the condition that I know how to recite the Mishnah," he must know the Mishnayot. It's possible that even if he only knows part of the Mishnayot, it suffices, and this requires further study for the final ruling [there]. This is according to the explanation of the Rambam. According to Rashi, it means that he recites the laws given to Moses at Sinai. Some say that if he knows the Midrashic interpretations of the Talmud, which are the interpretations the Talmud derives from the verses of the Torah, like Sifra and Sifrei, she is betrothed. The primary opinion is the first one [the Gra]. If he said, "On the condition that I am a Tanna," he must know how to read the Mishnah, Sifra, Sifrei, and the Tosefta of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Oshaya. The reading means understanding the plain meaning and being well-versed in them. It appears to me that this also depends on their language and order of study. However, in our language, when one says "on the condition that I can recite," it is like saying he can study, and there is no fixed measure for this, except that he is considered among the householders who study.

He said, "On the condition that I am a student": anyone who can be asked one thing from his studies and can answer is called a student and she is betrothed, even if the one thing is from the laws of the festival that they teach publicly close to the festival so that all the people will be knowledgeable about them, and even if he knows the tractate Kallah – it is sufficient [see Tosafot Shabbat 114]. And if he said, "On the condition that I am a scholar": anyone who can be asked a matter of wisdom in the Torah, meaning a matter that depends on reasoning in any place and can answer it, for it is a sign that his intellect is straight and he is a scholar in the Torah. We require "in any place" because since it depends on his intellectual reasoning, it does not matter whether it is in this place or another [see Chochmat Adam]. Nevertheless, we follow the majority of his reasoning, for if in a few instances he does not hit the truth in his reasoning, he is not a scholar, and indeed in all matters we follow the majority [it seems to me]. Also, in this matter, it appears to me that according to our languages, if these words have another indication, one must follow the intention of the language that is customary among the people of the country.

He said, "On the condition that I am strong," we do not say he must be like Avner ben Ner or Yoav ben Tzruya, but rather anyone whose peers fear him because of his strength. "On the condition that I am wealthy," we do not say he must be like Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom or Rabbi Akiva ben Yosef, but rather anyone whom the people of his city honor because of his wealth. It is known that in a small city, one is called wealthy with a smaller sum, whereas in a large city one is not called wealthy with such a sum. Therefore, it depends on the place where he lives.

He said, "On the condition that I am righteous"—even if he is completely wicked, she is nevertheless doubtfully betrothed, for perhaps he had thoughts of repentance in his heart. The reason we are concerned about this is as stated in Section 73, that it is a strong presumption since he made this condition, there are grounds to believe that it is true. Even if he still possesses stolen items and has not returned them to their owners, nevertheless, perhaps he has resolved in his mind to return them. In any case, the matter of doubtful betrothal remains. If he is presumed to be of intermediate character, it is also considered doubtful betrothal. If he is presumed to be righteous, it is a complete betrothal. Although a righteous person would not say about himself that he is righteous, as this would be arrogance, nevertheless, in the matter of betrothal, when the woman only agreed under this condition, it is not arrogance, and a person knows their own soul. There are those who say that if he claims he had thoughts of repentance in his heart, he is believed to make the betrothal certain since she cannot contradict him. However, this does not seem correct, for how can we believe a completely wicked person to make the betrothal certain?

He says, "On the condition that I am wicked"—even if he is completely righteous, it is still a doubtful betrothal, for perhaps he contemplated committing sins. And even though a bad thought is not considered by the Holy One, blessed be He, as equivalent to an action, perhaps he contemplated idolatry in his heart, for such a thought is indeed considered equivalent to an action. Similarly, thoughts of heresy and denial of the words of our Sages render him completely wicked, even if he does not perform evil actions. And why do we suspect this? Because it is likely, as stated in the previous section.

Similarly, in all matters such as if he consecrated [a woman] "on the condition that I am an accountant," "on the condition that I am a miller," "on the condition that I am a scribe," "on the condition that I am a painter," "on the condition that I am a tailor, or a shoemaker, or a blacksmith, or any other type of craftsman" – if he is recognized in his town as an expert in this wisdom or craft, even though in large cities where there are great sages and master craftsmen his wisdom and craft are considered insignificant, nevertheless, since in his place he is considered a sage or craftsman – the consecration is valid. And if not – it is doubtful consecration, for nevertheless, she should not be released without a get (divorce document), because perhaps others are not aware of his wisdom and craft, for it is no less than "on the condition that I am righteous" and he is found to be wicked, and everything is due to the reason we explained that there is a presumption (raglayim ladavar) for it, unless the man is known to be deceitful, in which case it is possible, with the concurrence of all the sages of the place, to annul the consecration.

In Sections 13 and 54, it is explained that it is possible to nullify the condition and that the betrothal (kiddushin) will take effect even without fulfilling the condition. A condition that benefits one party can be nullified by that party alone. If it benefits her, she alone can nullify it. Specific laws regarding this are detailed there. However, to nullify the betrothal and withdraw from it, even if the condition is fulfilled, there is a difference between a condition of "if" and a condition of "from now" or "on the condition that," which is considered like "from now."

How so? If he gives her a coin and says, "If I give you a maneh (a specific amount of money) within 30 days, you will be betrothed to me with this coin," the betrothal does not take effect until he gives her the maneh. Therefore, before this, she can withdraw from the betrothal, and fulfilling the condition will not help. Consequently, if another person betroths her before the condition is fulfilled, she is betrothed to the second person, as this is considered an explicit withdrawal on her part since she accepted betrothal from another. Certainly, he can withdraw from the betrothal if the fulfillment of the condition falls upon her, and fulfilling the condition will not help. His withdrawal, however, must be explicit, stating that he withdraws from the betrothal. Betrothing another woman does not affect anything, as he can marry as many women as he desires.

It seems to me that even nowadays, with the ban of Rabbeinu Gershom against polygamy, this does not nullify the first betrothal. One who wishes to withdraw from the betrothal must do so in the presence of witnesses; otherwise, he will not be believed. If the party responsible for fulfilling the condition wishes to withdraw, he does not need to do anything other than not fulfill the condition.

And there is no distinction in this matter between betrothal by money and betrothal by document, for in all cases when the betrothal is nullified, no get (divorce document) is required at all. Even in the case of betrothal by document that includes a date, where in such cases regarding divorces we are stringent as stated in Siman 143 because we say that the date on the document proves its validity and it might be considered as if it were effective immediately, as explained there. But in matters of betrothal, we do not say this, as there is no difference between one form of betrothal and another. Additionally, the sages did not establish a requirement for a date in betrothal documents as stated in Siman 32. Also, in the case of betrothal through intercourse, the betrothal is nullified if the condition was not fulfilled, and even though according to this it would seem that the intercourse was promiscuous, nevertheless, since they nullified the betrothal, it is nullified.

However, regarding the conditions of "from now" and "on the condition," there is a different ruling. Since upon the fulfillment of the condition the betrothal takes effect retroactively, therefore her retraction does not help if he fulfills the condition. And if she accepted betrothal from another man before the condition was fulfilled and afterwards the condition was fulfilled, the betrothal from the second man is null. And if he said to her, "on the condition that I give you a maneh within 30 days," if he gave it to her within 30 days, the betrothal is retroactively valid. If he did not give it to her within 30 days, she is not betrothed. And if she accepted betrothal from another man within those 30 days, she is in a state of being both betrothed and not betrothed until the 30 days are completed. If the 30 days pass and the first man did not fulfill his condition, the first betrothal is annulled, and the second betrothal becomes fully valid, and she does not require a get (divorce document) from the first man. If the first man fulfills his condition, she does not require a get from the second man.

There is also a difference between a condition of "if" and "from now" and "on the condition that," for in a condition of "if" where the betrothal will take effect upon the fulfillment of the condition, it is impossible to betroth her except with money. Even if the money is consumed before that time, the betrothal remains valid for the reason that will be explained in Siman 40. However, with betrothal by document, there are those who say that the betrothal does not take effect until the document is in his possession at that time, as stated there. According to this, it is obvious that with betrothal by intercourse, he cannot betroth her, for the intercourse will not be at the time the betrothal takes effect. But with "from now" and "on the condition that," he can betroth her with any form of betrothal he wishes, since the betrothal takes effect retroactively. And what we wrote in Siman 99 regarding betrothal by intercourse, that if the condition is not fulfilled, the intercourse is considered licentious, this is only with "from now" and "on the condition that," but with a condition of "if," he cannot betroth her by intercourse. This will be explained there, with God's help.

In Siman 137, it is explained that if a man says to his wife, "You are divorced except for with regard to so-and-so," it is not a valid divorce because we require a complete severance, and this is lacking. However, if he said, "On the condition that you do not marry so-and-so," it is a valid divorce because this is like any other condition. Regarding betrothal, if a man says to a woman, "You are betrothed to me except for with regard to so-and-so," meaning she will be prohibited to everyone except him, but to so-and-so, she will be considered single and his betrothal to her would take effect to prohibit her to him—many of our Rabbis opine that this is not a valid betrothal at all, because betrothal is compared to divorce as it is written, "And she departs and becomes," and this is also the plain meaning of the Gemara (Gittin 82b). However, the Rambam of blessed memory, in Chapter 7, was stringent in this matter and wrote that it is a doubtful betrothal, and so ruled our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Siman 39. Therefore, in practice, she requires a divorce from him and is prohibited to marry a priest.

[Betrothal on Condition of No Vows or Blemishes and Who Must Bring Proof; with 22 Sections]
A man who betroths a woman and says to her "on the condition that you have no vows" and it is found that she has vows – the betrothal is null and void and does not require a get (divorce document). However, not all types of vows fall under this category. Our sages have said: Which vows are included? Those that cause affliction to the soul, such as a vow not to eat meat, not to drink wine, or not to adorn herself with colorful garments, and even just one of these [Ketubot 72b], because these cause significant affliction to the soul and make her repugnant to him. It is not only colorful garments; the same applies to other types of garments that women typically adorn themselves with [Bedek HaBayit]. Similarly, if she vowed not to eat bread – it is obvious that this causes significant affliction to the soul. The same applies to matters between her and her husband in major issues that most people usually care about, such as "I am forbidden to all Jews" or similar matters; in such cases, a get is not required [See Chomat HaChaim Section 1].

However, if other types of vows are found upon her, even if they cause a small amount of personal affliction, such as a vow not to eat apples or similar matters, and also in small matters between her and him – she requires a get (divorce) and a ketubah (marriage contract). And even though he stipulated generally "on the condition that she has no vows," which implies any type of vow, nevertheless, this language only refers to matters which most people are particular about, and not to what some meticulous individuals are particular about in minor matters. And even if it is known that this man is exceedingly meticulous, still, his meticulousness is considered significant only in matters that people generally are particular about, and in matters that people are not generally particular about, his meticulousness is not considered significant. He should have stipulated this explicitly. And since he said generally "vows," this language includes only what the majority of people consider significant. And even though when she vows during the marriage, he can annul any type of affliction, even the smallest, as it is written in Yoreh De'ah, section 234, this is because it is not proper for her to vow while married to him. But if she vowed before she came into his possession, most people are only particular about significant matters of personal affliction and matters between her and him.

However, if he explicitly betrothed her on the condition that she has no vows upon her, it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that even if it is found that she vowed not to eat carobs, which people usually do not eat at all, she is not betrothed since he specified "any vow." Thus, the poskim (Jewish legal decisors) have written. There is room for doubt whether this applies only to matters related to personal affliction, even if it is a minor affliction, but anything not related at all to personal affliction, which the husband cannot annul, is not included even in the term "any vow." We say "any vow" includes something that has a bit of affliction or is between the husband and wife, but for other vows, he did not intend. Alternatively, it is possible that if any kind of vow is found upon her, the betrothal is nullified. The Jerusalem Talmud and the poskim cited carobs as a significant example, and common sense suggests that the phrase "any vow" includes everything, as many people are particular about any kind of vow since the sin of vows is great, and it is written, "It is better that you do not vow" (Ecclesiastes 5:4). The fact that the husband cannot annul his wife's vows, except those of personal affliction or between them, is a decree of the Torah. However, in this case, his condition certainly intended to cover all kinds of vows. Nonetheless, in practice, one should not be lenient, and she requires a get (divorce document) without a ketubah (marriage contract) [this is my opinion].

If vows are found upon her that invalidate the betrothal and he wishes to waive the condition, the condition is nullified, and there is no need for a new betrothal, as the original betrothal remains valid. This is because any condition made at the time of betrothal can be waived, as stated in Siman 38, paragraphs 13 and 54. However, this applies if he did not object upon hearing it. But if he objected immediately upon hearing, the betrothal is immediately invalidated, and waiving the condition is no longer effective. This will be explained in Siman 60, where it is stated that she needs to be betrothed anew in case of a mistaken betrothal. And even though it is explained there that some opinions hold that waiving is effective only in monetary matters, the main legal ruling is that it is possible to waive any condition, as our masters, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, have ruled there.

And there is a question about this: How can we say that when vows are found upon her, the betrothal is nullified and she is permitted to marry without a divorce? For if she goes to a sage and he annuls her vows, then the betrothal remains valid, as will be explained. So how can we permit her to marry? Perhaps she will later go to a sage who will annul her vows, and it will be found that the first betrothal is valid, and her children from the second husband will be mamzerim (illegitimate)? 

There are some of our Rabbis who hold that the annulment by a sage is effective only if he annulled it before the betrother became aware of the vows. But if he became aware before the sage annulled them, the betrothal is immediately nullified [Tosafot there, 74b: s.v. HaChacham]. According to this, it can be said that we permit her to marry if the vows were known to him before the sage annulled them.

There are early authorities who said that we do not need to be concerned about this, for she will certainly not do such a thing and will not go to a sage to annul it, as she would not want to ruin herself and make her children mamzerim. Therefore, once she is permitted to marry and has married, there is no longer any concern [Shitah Mekubetzet].

There is proof for this reasoning from later in Siman 143 regarding a conditional divorce, where we are not concerned that she might violate the condition actively and ruin herself. Some also say that the moment the court permits her to marry, the betrothal is immediately nullified, and even if she goes to a sage and he annuls the vows, the original betrothal does not take effect again [there in the name of the Ra'ah].

However, in the Jerusalem Talmud of "HaMadir" there is a dispute regarding this matter. There are those who hold that she is permitted without a get (divorce document) because she will not ruin herself, as mentioned. And there are those who hold that she is indeed forbidden without a get because she might annul her vow. Therefore, although it appears clear from our Talmud (the Babylonian Talmud) that a get is not required, and this is also the ruling of the Rambam and many of the early authorities, nevertheless there are some decisors who are concerned with the opinion in the Jerusalem Talmud and have written that she should not remarry without a get. And so wrote our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, at the end of Section 1, that there are those who are concerned she might go to a sage and have her vow annulled, and therefore she is forbidden to remarry without a get. And even those early authorities who hold that she is permitted without a get wrote that in practice one should be cautious of the Jerusalem Talmud. And although in Section 143 we rule that we are not concerned she will ruin herself, nevertheless, in this case, we need to be cautious because her intention might not be to ruin herself but rather to escape the punishment of vows, and it would not occur to her that by this she is ruining herself.

And even though it could be said that the Yerushalmi is referring to a case before it became known to the husband, but after it became known, there is no longer a concern because the betrothal is nullified. And there is proof for this from our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, who were concerned about the Yerushalmi, as it is written, and in section 2, they ruled that after it became known to the husband, she can no longer be permitted [to remarry]. And if one were to think that the Yerushalmi is also referring to after it became known to the husband, why were they concerned about the Yerushalmi? Nevertheless, it does not seem so, and several of the earlier authorities held that the Yerushalmi does not distinguish between before the husband's knowledge and after, [Ran and Sh'ma'ta Kadma]. And logic dictates this as well, for how could it be said that it refers to before his knowledge, for even without the concern of the sage's annulment, she cannot marry because maybe the husband, upon hearing, will forgive the condition and she will be retroactively betrothed, as is written in section 38, clause 54. And it is forced to say that we assume that he will not forgive because he is strict in this matter, for how can she be permitted to marry initially based on this? Rather, certainly, the Yerushalmi does not distinguish between before and after knowledge. And that which our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, were concerned about the Yerushalmi even after his knowledge, truly they held that there is no concern in this matter, but they were stringent in betrothal matters due to the severity of the issue, as they were stringent in the main concern of the Yerushalmi that perhaps the sage will permit her, for surely our Talmud does not hold of this concern, and so too the Rambam, of blessed memory. Nevertheless, because of the severity, they were concerned about this, and therefore, even after his knowledge, they were concerned about the Yerushalmi, although they did not hold this way in practice [as it appears to me, and see Chom'at Chemed and Beit Shmuel].

If she had vows upon her and went to a sage who annulled them, she is considered betrothed, for the sage uproots the vow from its foundation as if it never existed at all. When does this apply? When the sage annulled it before the husband became aware. But if the husband became aware before the sage annulled it, the betrothal is immediately nullified. Do not be surprised by this reasoning, for even after becoming aware, she can annul it through a sage, uprooting it as if it never existed. Certainly, he betrothed her with the understanding that if he does not wish to annul the betrothal because of the vows, the betrothal should remain valid. And where he became aware before they were annulled, he immediately wishes for the betrothal to be nullified, lest she cannot find a sage to annul them. However, where they were annulled before he became aware, he certainly does not wish to nullify them due to the vows, for now there is no concern. And it is simple that this only applies when he heard and objected, but if he did not object, it is as if he waived the condition. But if she annulled it before he became aware, even if he objected when he heard, his objection is of no consequence, for there are no vows upon her since they were uprooted from their foundation. Even if he claims that his intention at the time of betrothal was that if she had vows, even if she annulled them, he would not want her, we do not heed him. We say that he now finds a pretext to nullify the betrothal, and at the time of betrothal, his intention was only if the sage did not annul them before he became aware. However, if he explicitly spoke thus at the time of betrothal, everything depends on his condition.

And know that in the Gemara there, there is a distinction made in this matter between an important woman and an unimportant woman. For an unimportant woman, she needs a get (divorce document) out of doubt even if she nullified the vows before her husband became aware of them, whereas an important woman does not need a get. The explanation of the matter is as follows: This reasoning that we wrote that since the sage uproots the vow from its root, it is as if there were no vows upon her at all and most people do not care about this, this reasoning is not clear, and for every person there is doubt whether this is worthy of concern or not. Consequently, she requires a get out of doubt according to the opinions of people. And all this applies to ordinary women. But regarding an important woman, there is no doubt in this matter, and every person’s opinion is that for an important woman, when there is doubt, there is no doubt, and the betrothal is annulled because it is better for him than a doubt, for in a doubt she would need a get, and he would be prohibited from marrying her relatives, and this is not acceptable to him. Therefore, he resolves in his mind at the time of the betrothal that if there are vows upon her, even if she annuls them, the betrothal will be annulled. And according to this opinion, for ordinary women, she requires a get out of doubt, but for an important woman, she does not require a get.

However, according to the law, since according to the first opinion there is no difference between an important and an unimportant woman, and both are fully betrothed, and according to the second opinion, an unimportant woman requires a get (divorce document) out of doubt, and an important woman does not require a get, it follows that even an important woman requires a get out of doubt. The doubt is whether we hold according to the first opinion or according to the second opinion. Although by this she will be prohibited to his relatives, what does it matter to us, since according to the first opinion she is fully betrothed? If she accepted betrothal from another man, whether she is important or not, she requires a get from the second man as well, due to the doubt. This is because perhaps we hold according to the second opinion that for an important woman the first betrothal is completely nullified, and for an unimportant woman it is also only a doubt, and therefore she requires a get from the second man.

And this is what our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 2: If there were vows upon her and she went to a sage and he annulled them – she is betrothed, etc. And there is one who says that if she is an important woman, even if the sage annulled the vows before they became known to the husband – it is doubtful if she is betrothed. And the doubt is because of our uncertainty regarding whose opinion we follow. According to the first opinion – only if it became known to the husband before the sage annulled the vows, she is not betrothed. According to the second opinion we brought – even if the sage annulled the vows beforehand, she is not betrothed. Therefore, according to the law, there is one who says that it is doubtful betrothal with an important woman because there is a doubt that we might follow the second opinion. And the same applies to a non-important woman, it is doubtful betrothal for the reason we have explained.

[And this is the intention of the Shach, and the Bach's wonderment about him is unfounded, and with what we have explained, the question of the Chokhmat Shlomo is also resolved, and also all the efforts and scrutiny of the Beit Shmuel and the meticulousness of the Makneh, and pay close attention.]

If a man betrothed a woman on the condition that she has no vows upon her, and then had relations with her without specifying, it has already been explained in Siman 38, Se'if 13, that even if it is found that she has vows, according to the Rambam, she still requires a get (divorce document) due to the concern that he may have forgiven the condition, and the initial betrothal would take effect. There is no need for witnesses of seclusion nor for another act of betrothal. Even if he brought her into his house but did not have relations, she still requires a get. Some say the concern is that he may have betrothed her through this act of relations, and according to this, the concern for betrothal only applies from this point forward, and witnesses of seclusion are required, and this only applies to relations and not to bringing her under the chuppah (wedding canopy). Refer there to what is written in Se'if 16.

However, the Tur in Siman 38 wrote the words of the Rambam, and in this Siman, he wrote that if one betrothed on condition and had relations without specifying, and there are witnesses to the seclusion, she requires a get out of doubt, even if he had relations immediately after the betrothal, because a man does not make his relations promiscuous and had relations for the sake of betrothal. However, she does not have the rights to the ketubah (marriage contract). If she married another, she requires a get from both. This is in accordance with the opinion of some authorities, and they have already questioned him on this [Beit Yosef and Bach there, note 159]. It seems clear that the Tur holds like the opinion of some authorities and did not bring the words of the Rambam earlier except for the matter of forgiving the condition, which is the main point of the Rambam's words there. But in what the Rambam concluded, that according to this, if he had relations and brought her under the chuppah, we are concerned for forgiving the condition, he does not agree with him and relied on what he wrote here. This is also evident from the words of his father, the Rosh, of blessed memory [and the words of the Avnei Milu'im there, note 17, are perplexing, for if so, why did he not write here about bringing under the chuppah, and also he explicitly wrote that he had relations for the sake of betrothal].

And also with regard to blemishes, it will be explained that if he betrothed her on the condition that she has no blemishes and then had relations without specifying, the law is as stated: she requires a get (divorce document) but does not receive a ketubah (marriage contract), and the get is given out of doubt. If another man comes and betroths her, she also needs a get from the second man. However, if he remained with her after consummating the marriage for a considerable amount of time as a husband with his wife, she is certainly considered betrothed, whether concerning vows and blemishes or other conditions, and she is entitled to a ketubah. And although the initial ketubah is nullified, how can she collect? It can be stated that his intention was that if he does not object afterward, her ketubah is validated [Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 7]. Similarly, the betrothal is certainly finalized when he remained with her because it then becomes clear that he does not object [there]. This is not a matter of retroactive clarification, and see what is written there in paragraph 68.

One who betroths a woman on the condition that she has no blemishes, and one of the blemishes that disqualify women, as will be explained, is found in her – she is not betrothed. However, if another blemish is found in her, other than those blemishes, even if he says he is particular about even that – she is considered betrothed. For since he said "blemishes" in general, the intention is only for the blemishes that most people are particular about. Therefore, something that people are generally not particular about, his particularity is not considered as such, as it is written in Nedarim. Therefore, if he said on the condition that she has "no blemish at all" – even other blemishes would prevent the betrothal, just as in Nedarim when he said "any vow."

The translation of the passage:

What are the blemishes that disqualify women? All the blemishes that disqualify priests from performing service, as enumerated by the Rambam in Chapter 8 of "Bi'at Mikdash," also disqualify women. Additionally, women have further disqualifications that do not apply to priests. These include: a bad odor from the body, even if it is a slight odor and she is not otherwise dirty, as someone who is dirty is also disqualified as a priest; sweat; bad breath; and some say even the smell of the nose, as the smell from the nose is worse than from the mouth, because bad breath can be mitigated by keeping pepper in the mouth. For smell from the nose, a man can also be compelled to divorce, as stated in Siman 154, and certainly for a woman it is considered a blemish. A deep voice, as a deep voice in a woman is considered a blemish, as it is written "For your voice is sweet" (Song of Songs 2:14), but the extent of this depth is not defined. It seems that if her voice is markedly different from other women in depth and roughness, it is considered a blemish. If her breasts are larger than her peers by a handbreadth, it is a blemish. If there is a handbreadth between her breasts, it is also a blemish. Similarly, if a dog bites her and it leaves a scar, even if the wound has healed but the mark remains, it is considered a blemish. There is uncertainty if this blemish applies only to exposed parts of her body or even to covered parts. Since the poskim did not differentiate, it seems it applies to the entire body. A mole on the forehead is considered a blemish, and even though it is also a blemish for priests, this applies to a large mole the size of an Italian issar or a small one with hair. For a woman, even a small mole without hair is a blemish. When we say on her forehead, it does not mean the exposed part of the forehead, as then he would have seen it and not minded, but rather a mole under her hair that is sometimes seen and sometimes not. If it is never seen, it is not a blemish. Some say that a large mole the size of an issar or with hair is a blemish anywhere on the body, but this is not implied by the Rambam in Chapter 7, who wrote that a large mole the size of an issar or with hair is a blemish only on the face and not the body.

And this that we said that in an exposed place where he did not see and did not care, even though he stipulated that there should be no blemish, we must say that his intention was only regarding what he saw. But there are poskim (halachic authorities) who disagree with this and hold that even a blemish in an exposed place, as long as she has not entered the husband’s domain, we can say that he did not see it, and only after marriage do we say this [Beit Shmuel]. And this is also implied from the Rambam whom we brought, for the face is an exposed place, and nevertheless, he wrote that a large wart or one with hair is a blemish. Likewise, he did not mention there any difference between a blemish in an exposed place and a hidden place, and only in chapter 25 of Ishut regarding the ketubah did he mention this, which refers to after marriage, see there. [And so too wrote the Maggid Mishneh and in the Darkei Moshe and Beit Shmuel who hold this way, see there].

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in section 4: "If there is a bathhouse in the city, even hidden blemishes do not annul [the marriage]. In what case does this apply? When it is customary for the daughters to go to the bathhouse openly. However, in a place where the daughters only go to the bathhouse at night and in secret, even visible blemishes annul [the marriage]." This is when he betrothed her through an agent and did not see her, for if he saw her, it has already been clarified that he has no claim concerning visible blemishes. This is also according to those who disagree and the Rambam, as we have written, that even a bathhouse is not a proof after betrothal, and only after marriage do we say that if there is a bathhouse, he has no claim even concerning hidden blemishes.

An epileptic, if the condition occurs at regular intervals, it is considered a hidden blemish. If it does not occur at regular intervals, it is considered a visible blemish. Additional laws regarding blemishes will be explained in Siman 116. A woman who urinates in her bed during sleep is considered to have a blemish, as is a leprous woman [Beit Yosef]. Some say that she must be given her ketubah and can only be divorced against her will, and this is not included in the decree of Rabbenu Gershom [Taz]. For a man who urinates in bed, some say it is not considered a blemish [Beit Shmuel], but this is questionable, for it appears to be a significant blemish. There are those who say that what was clarified regarding the bathhouse, when there is one in the city, even hidden blemishes are not nullified, does not apply to all blemishes. For epilepsy and bad breath, there is no difference whether there is a bathhouse in the city or not, since one can easily avoid detection. Similarly, sweat and a deep voice are not noticeable in the bathhouse for this reason [Chamat Chamudot]. Besides the blemishes we have mentioned, there are certainly other blemishes, such as contagious diseases, and if doctors say she has a hidden disease or something similar, it is also considered a blemish. Some say that if her nose is much larger than other people's, it is considered a blemish, but this is questionable.

He betrothed her on the condition that she has no blemishes, and she had blemishes. She went to a doctor and he healed her, even if it was before the husband became aware of the blemishes – nevertheless, she is not betrothed. This is not comparable to vows, where a sage can annul the vow from its inception, making it as if it never existed. This is not the case with blemishes, which are only healed from now on, and he betrothed her on the condition that she has no blemishes, and she had them. However, it is not only for this reason, since in the case of a man, such a situation would constitute a valid betrothal, as will be explained. Rather, it is because, in the case of blemishes in a woman, there is a concern, even in such a situation, that she is still repulsive to him when he remembers that she had blemishes. But with vows, there is no such concern since they are annulled retroactively. Similarly, in the case of blemishes in a man, there is no concern in such a situation because a woman is generally accepting of any man. Additionally, it is more of a disgrace for a woman to have had blemishes, even in the past, than it is for a man. Therefore, if the woman stipulated that he has no blemishes and he had blemishes and went to a doctor and was healed – she is betrothed for the reasons explained.

There are those who are uncertain regarding the condition that a woman has no blemishes and it becomes known to her before she is healed whether the betrothal is nullified, as stated in Nedarim, that a woman, when it becomes known to her husband before a sage releases her, or it is possible that specifically the man is particular about a minor matter and immediately when it becomes known to him, he says he does not want a woman with vows. But the woman is not particular even with blemishes if there is a remedy for the blemishes. However, in the case of vows, when she stipulated on the condition that there are no vows and it becomes known to her before the sage releases him, some say she is certainly not betrothed because in the case of vows there is no disgust. And this that we explained that when it becomes known to him before the sage releases her, she is not betrothed is because he assumes that perhaps there is no release for her vows and immediately nullifies the betrothal, and this reasoning applies to her as well. However, there is no proof for what is said, that he nullifies the betrothal due to a minor particularity and not her, so too with this reasoning one could say that he assumes this and not her, and even if she assumes this, she still does not nullify the betrothal because of this until she sees if there is a release for his vow, as we said that she waits to know if there is a remedy, which is also hidden from her, and she still waits, and the same applies here. Therefore, it is a doubtful betrothal.

Nevertheless, if he betrothed her on the condition that she has no blemishes and it was found that she had blemishes and a doctor healed them, she is retroactively betrothed. It is possible that even if it became known before she was healed, it is effective since the condition that she has no blemishes has been fulfilled, and it cannot be said that she is repulsive in his eyes because according to his condition, he is not concerned with the past [Terumat HaDeshen]. And although we have said that there is no strictness in the language, this is in the opposite case, but nevertheless, one cannot interpret the condition more than the language can bear [see Beit Shmuel]. The same applies to vows if he said in the future tense that she should have no vows. However, it can be said in both cases that if he found out before the annulment or before the healing, he thought there was no annulment or healing and immediately nullified the betrothal, and therefore in such a case, the betrothal is doubtful. Some say that in any case, the betrothal is doubtful even if he said she should have no blemishes and the doctor healed her before he found out, because there is no strictness in the language [Bach and Chavat Yair].

The Tur wrote: If defects are found in her after she was betrothed and she is still in her father's house, and the father claims that the defects developed after the betrothal and it is due to her luck – he must bring proof, and if he has no proof, she leaves without a ketubah, and even the betrothal money must be returned. If the defects are not found until after she enters his house – then the father is believed, and the husband must bring proof that the defects were present before the betrothal. However, if he brings proof that the defects were in her father's house after the betrothal, it does not help him. When is it said that the father must bring proof? In the case of a young girl, but for a mature woman, even if she is in her father's house – the husband must bring proof. There are further opinions on this matter that will be explained with God’s help in Siman 117, where most authorities agree that regarding the betrothal, she needs a get in all cases, and the distinction is only regarding the ketubah. Therefore, it is not relevant to this Siman, and although there are those who dispute this, nevertheless, this is the opinion of most authorities. Therefore, our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, did not write this law except anonymously.

[The laws regarding betrothal after a certain time, after childbirth, and similar cases, containing 28 sections]

One who says to a woman, "You are betrothed to me after thirty days" and gives her the money for betrothal now – for all thirty days she is completely single, and if she is the daughter of a priest (Kohen) married to an Israelite, she may eat terumah. After thirty days, she is fully betrothed, and if she is the daughter of an Israelite married to a priest (Kohen), she may eat terumah according to Torah law, even if the money has been consumed. This is unlike a loan, where betrothal with a loan does not effect betrothal, and unlike a deposit, where the value must remain. A loan is given to be spent, and it is as though nothing was given to her. A deposit remains in the possession of the depositor. But this money was given for betrothal and it belongs to her, and she consumes it from her own property. Since it was originally given with the intention of betrothal, even though at the time the betrothal takes effect the money is no longer there, she originally acquires herself with that money (Ran).

And even though we hold in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 196, regarding one who says to his friend, "Pull this cow and it will not be acquired until after thirty days," that it is not acquired, because there the acquisition is through pulling, and after thirty days there is nothing tangible with which to acquire it; but here, the money is considered as if it is present, for the reason we have explained. And if she retracts, she must return [the money]; it is as if he gave it to her after thirty days. According to this, some say that if he betrothed her with a document and it is not present after thirty days, whether it was torn or lost or is not in his possession, the betrothal is not valid. And certainly, if he betrothed her through intercourse with the intention that the betrothal would take effect after some time, she is not betrothed. And only if the paper of the document is present, it would be considered like betrothal through money to be stringent, as we have written in Siman 28. See there.

If he retracts within thirty days or she retracts, such as if they say "we do not wish for the betrothal" – the betrothal is nullified because one statement nullifies another statement. And even though we have established that a statement cannot nullify an action, and here there is an action of giving money, nevertheless this is not considered an action because until the betrothal takes effect, it is considered merely a statement, similar to when one sends a divorce document to his wife and can still nullify it, as stated in Siman 141, see there. If she retracts, it is obvious that she must return the betrothal money. If he retracts, some say she does not need to return it, because if we say that until the betrothal takes effect the money is still in his possession, then if it were consumed, why would she be betrothed? This ruling that she must return the money when she retracts is for another reason, and by extension, the money remains a debt upon her since the prevention (of the betrothal) was from her side. Others say that even if he retracts, she must return the money, because he gave it to her only for the purpose of betrothal, and since he no longer wishes for the betrothal, she is obligated to return it. And if the money was consumed, it is as if it were still present when there was no retraction.

One might question the status when they retract from the betrothal and the money or the betrothal document is still in her possession, and afterwards, before the thirty days are completed, they revert and agree again. Do the initial betrothals remain valid, and do we say that the agreement nullifies the retraction, or perhaps, once they retracted, the initial betrothals were nullified, and we do not say that the third agreement validates the first agreement? In the case of betrothal with money, it is certain that there is no doubt that there are no betrothals, because in a situation where the money remains hers after the retraction, it is necessary to give her new money to betroth her again. If she needs to return the money to him after the retraction and she hasn't returned it yet, then the money is considered a debt, and betrothal with a loan is not valid. However, in the case of betrothal with a document, one might question when the document is still in her possession. [One could resolve this from the fourth chapter of Gittin, from the dispute between Ran and Rashba regarding whether one can divorce again with the same document, as mentioned in Siman 141, but there is no proof from there for a betrothal document in the woman's possession, and scrutinize carefully.] [Afterwards, I saw in the novel ideas of the Rashba that retraction after retraction is not effective.]

Some of the early authorities wrote that the retraction of betrothal needs to be specifically in the presence of two witnesses. However, if the retraction is done privately, even if it was heard from behind a fence that she is annulling the betrothal, it is considered merely as a thought and not as a spoken declaration [Ritva]. The reasoning is that the ability to annul the betrothal stems from the principle that a spoken declaration can annul another spoken declaration, as stated. Therefore, just as the declaration of betrothal was in the presence of two witnesses, so too, the declaration of annulment must be in the presence of two witnesses, similar to the annulment of a get (divorce document), which also requires two witnesses, as stated in section 141. However, this law is not explicitly mentioned in all the legal sources, and the matter is questionable in practice. Certainly, if she annulled it in his presence or he in her presence, it would indeed be considered an annulment, for there are opinions concerning a get that argue that if the annulment is done in the presence of the messenger, two witnesses are not needed, as stated there. However, it is definite that if the annulment was done in the presence of two witnesses, even if not in the presence of the other party, it is valid. Similarly, if he annulled it in the presence of two witnesses without her being there, it is valid.

One may question whether, if either he or she claims after thirty days that they annulled [the divorce] within thirty days in the presence of two witnesses, and those witnesses have since gone overseas or died, they are believed by virtue of a "migo" (a legal presumption). For he has a "migo" that if he wanted, he could have divorced her, and she has a "migo" that [she can claim], "You divorced me," which is credible according to the Talmudic law. Or perhaps this is not a good "migo" because it is not convenient for him to say that he divorced her in order to avoid being prohibited from marrying her relatives if she is a distinguished woman. And even if she is not distinguished, maybe he now desires to marry one of her relatives. [And from Ketubot 75, there is no proof, see there.] Additionally, her "migo" is not a complete "migo" because it would require brazenness (due to the confrontation). Therefore, it seems in practice that she should not be exempted without a get (divorce document) when there are no witnesses that the divorce was annulled, and certainly not when they contradict each other. However, if both admit that it was annulled, it is possible they are believed. Nevertheless, in practice, one should be cautious in this matter [see Pitchei Teshuva, section 3 who quotes Shaar HaMelech].

If one consecrates a woman for thirty days and stipulates that afterwards she will be free without a divorce – it is ineffective, and she remains betrothed forever. For although consecrating [an item] for a period is valid, nonetheless, even in consecration, we hold that the sanctity does not dissipate automatically. Even if, in consecration, it reverts to the secular without anything after a time, nevertheless, the sanctity of a woman does not end without a divorce. And it is also established in Gittin that if one divorces a woman for thirty days, she remains divorced forever because once it is decided, it is decided. All the more so with betrothal, as the betrothal extends indefinitely. Some say that this applies to betrothal with money, but with a document, there is a doubt regarding the betrothal, as explained in Siman 137, where concerning a divorce document, there is a doubt if she is divorced, and the same applies here with a betrothal document. There is a doubt if the betrothal takes effect at all in such a case, as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud.

One who betroths a woman to take effect after thirty days, as it is stated, and another comes and betroths her within those thirty days – she is betrothed to the second one forever. And the Rambam wrote in Chapter 7 that the reason is because at the time the second one betrothed her, she was not betrothed, and the second one’s betrothal took effect, making her a married woman. After the thirty days, when the first one’s betrothal would come into effect, they would find her already a married woman, and it would be as if the first one had betrothed a married woman, in which case the betrothal does not take effect. From this language, one could infer that if the second one dies or divorces her within the thirty days, the first one’s betrothal would take effect. This is also stated by the Tur, who mentions that there are some earlier authorities who hold this view. And even though in a case of retraction, the betrothal is completely nullified because it is an explicit retraction, here, where she accepted betrothal from another, one could say that her intention is not to completely retract from the first one’s betrothal, but rather her intention is still that if possible, the first betrothal should take effect.

There are some of our rabbis who disagree on this matter and hold that the first betrothal is nullified immediately when the second betrothal occurs, even if she is later divorced from the second husband or he dies. Moreover, they argue that acceptance of betrothal from the second is more significant than retraction, since retraction is merely verbal while acceptance of betrothal is a substantive act [Rosh, Chapter 3; Rashba]. However, the first opinion is clarified in the Jerusalem Talmud, which also explains that if the second husband dies and leaves a brother, to whom she is bound by levirate marriage, the first betrothal does not take effect after 30 days since she is still bound by the second betrothal. Some of our rabbis were stringent even in this case, reasoning that the Jerusalem Talmud holds that betrothal does not take effect with a yevamah [like Rav in Yevamot 92b], but we hold that it is a doubt, as stated in Siman 44, and therefore the levirate bond does not prevent the first betrothal from taking effect, and she requires a divorce from the first and halitzah from the brother of the second. According to this opinion, it is forbidden to perform levirate marriage before the first husband divorces her, but afterward, it is permitted to perform levirate marriage as in the case of a yevamah who was betrothed to another inadvertently, where the other man divorces her and the yavam performs levirate marriage, as stated in Siman 159. This case is not worse than an inadvertent betrothal [in my opinion].

There is an opinion that since it has been clarified that if she was consecrated (betrothed) after thirty days, she is considered consecrated even if the money was consumed, the same applies if she returned the money to him and did not nullify the betrothal, it is still considered a valid betrothal [Even HaEzer 32:2]. We say that he gave it to her as a gift, as Rabbi Isserles (the Rema) wrote in Yoreh De'ah 305 regarding the redemption of the firstborn, that if the money was returned, it is as if it was consumed. 

In my opinion, certainly if it was explicitly given as a gift, it is no less valid than if it was consumed. However, if she returned it without specifying, even if she said she is not nullifying the betrothal, her words mean nothing. For with what is she being betrothed, since she returned the money to him? It is not comparable to when the money is consumed because she derived benefit from it and it was given for the sake of betrothal, so it is indeed a valid betrothal. But if she returns it, with what is she being betrothed? Equating the return to consumption is incorrect. Just as consumption does not help in the case of the redemption of the firstborn according to Rabbi Isserles, so too, return does not help. However, to say that just as consumption helps, so too does return, this is not a valid argument. In any case, it remains a doubtful betrothal. 

There is also a doubt if she did not benefit from the money, for example, if it was stolen or lost from her within thirty days, do we say that only if she benefited from it, the betrothal is valid, or perhaps even in such a case the betrothal is valid [The Ritva implies that the main factor is the benefit, as discussed in Ketubot 6 regarding a loan, but the Rashba in the third chapter clarifies that the betrothal is due to her obligation to return the money if she does not want the betrothal, which is considered as the benefit of debt forgiveness, so even in such a case it is a valid betrothal. According to this, there is also doubt if it was lost due to an unavoidable accident, and see Pitchei Teshuva 1 quoting Rabbi Akiva Eiger who also doubted the law in the case of an unavoidable accident. Based on what has been said, there is also doubt if it was lost without an unavoidable accident].

The one who says to a woman, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this peruta from now and after thirty days," and another comes and betroths her within those thirty days – she is doubtfully betrothed to both of them. Therefore, both of them must give her a get, whether within the thirty days or after the thirty days. The reason for this matter is because there is a doubt regarding the first one who said, "from now and after thirty days," as to his intention. If his intention was "from now, provided that I do not retract within thirty days," then if he does not retract within thirty days, the betrothal of the first one takes effect from the first moment, and the betrothal of the second one is nothing. Or it is possible that by saying "and after thirty days," he was retracting from his initial words of "from now" and his intent was that the betrothal should not take effect from now but only after thirty days, and thus the betrothal of the second one takes effect and that of the first one is nullified. Therefore, there is a doubt for both of them, and she requires a get from both.

Therefore, if one betroths a woman from now and after thirty days, he can retract within the thirty days regardless of the situation. If his intention was that it would be effective only if he does not retract, then he has retracted. Even if his intention was that the betrothal would take effect after thirty days and he retracted from "now," it has already been explained that one who betroths for after thirty days can retract. However, she cannot retract, because perhaps his intention was conditional upon him not retracting and the condition was dependent on him and not her. Therefore, if she retracts within the thirty days, she requires a get out of doubt, because perhaps he retracted from "now," and she can also retract, as it is written (see Beit Shmuel, section 6).

However, there are some of our rabbis who explain that there is another doubt regarding his words, for perhaps his intention was from now if it will be after 30 days [Ramban and Rashba], and according to this, he also cannot retract if he does not die before the end of the 30 days. Therefore, even if he or both of them retract, a get (divorce document) is required out of doubt. Similarly, if he dies within the thirty days and did not retract, there remains a doubt regarding the kiddushin (betrothal) and she requires chalitzah (ceremonial release from levirate marriage). But if he retracted and died within the thirty days, the kiddushin is nullified according to all opinions. It is clear that if he said "from now, but she will not be betrothed until after 30 days" or "from now if he reaches 30 days" – then it is certainly conditional [Beit Shmuel] if he does not retract within 30 days, and he can retract, but not she. It is possible that "if he reaches 30 days" means if he lives until 30 days as we have said, and this requires further investigation for the legal ruling.

There is a question among the poskim (halachic authorities) regarding their opinion in section 38 that even in a case of "from now" a double condition is required. How, then, can it be said "from now and after 30 days" with the intention of making it conditional, since he did not make a double condition? If his intention was to make a condition, then the condition is automatically void and the action stands, making it a complete kiddushin (betrothal) from now, and he cannot retract. If we say that he did make a double condition, then how can we say there is a doubt that he might retract since the condition was explicitly doubled? Also, we cannot say that indeed it was stated without doubling the condition and if his intention was to make a condition, the condition is void and he cannot retract, as this does not seem to be the opinion of all the poskim.

The answer to this is that such a condition, where he stipulates that he will not retract from the kiddushin within 30 days, is not similar to other conditions and does not require a double condition, since it relates to the essence of the kiddushin. It is not comparable to the condition made by the tribes of Gad and Reuben, nor is it considered as a condition and action on the same matter which would inherently be flawed, as mentioned there. This is because his desire is to fulfill the kiddushin and he makes this stipulation on the matter itself, which is two opposites in one issue. This is different when the condition is truly about retracting from the kiddushin, for who can force him to agree to the kiddushin, and it is merely a matter of settling his mind.

Also, according to the interpretation of our Rabbis in section 13, it is similar, as it is not a secondary condition but rather if he lives, for if he does not live, why would he need the kiddushin and why would she require chalitza (ritual release from levirate marriage) unnecessarily. This is also a matter of settling his mind to see what will happen to him, and it does not require a double condition. For this reason as well, there is no concern of retroactive clarification (brerah) here, as the reason we wrote there in section 67 does not apply here.

And what we have written, that both of them give a get (divorce document) whether within thirty days or after thirty days, so wrote the Rambam in Chapter 7 and in Shulchan Aruch, Section 3. And although the first one should not give a get within thirty days, because even if we say it is a condition, the betrothal is not completed until thirty days, and certainly if it is a retraction, the betrothal did not begin at all within the thirty days. On the contrary, if it is a retraction, this get itself is a retraction, and what use is it to write it in vain? And if it is a condition, the get is also valid, because when the time arrives, it becomes clear that at the time of writing the get, she was betrothed and was subject to divorce.

And the second one, who divorces within thirty days, is because he betrothed without any time condition at all. And if "from now" of the first one is a retraction, then she is betrothed to him immediately, because both have retracted from the first betrothal and his get is a get. And if the first one is a condition, then the second betrothal is nothing. And if no one else came and betrothed her, it is possible that he cannot divorce her within thirty days, because perhaps it was a retraction and the get is not valid at all [Me’iri, Chapter 6 of Gittin].

And therefore, when the thirty days are completed, the betrothal will take effect, and they will think she is divorced. Nevertheless, it seems that another get is not needed after thirty days, because since it is a retraction, both have retracted from the betrothal. Is a get worse than a retraction? But the get is unnecessary if it is a retraction, but the get is necessary because of the uncertainty of the condition. And therefore, even if it is a retraction, they have retracted from it [there].

But some say that from the first one, a get within thirty days is not effective because of the doubt that perhaps his intention was a condition, and there is no get until the completion of the betrothal. Therefore, since the betrothal is not completely finished before thirty days, the get is not valid at all. And when the thirtieth day arrives, and he has not retracted and he is alive, she is a married woman and needs another get [Rashba in his Responsa, Section 907].

And this requirement that both must give her a get (divorce document) applies when she wishes to marry another man. However, if she wishes to be with one of them, the other gives her a get, and she is permitted to the second. This is also stated by the Tur, see there. Some say that only the first should divorce her, and she is permitted to the second, but not the other way around [Beit Shmuel in the name of the Rashal], so that it should not be said that the first divorced her, the second married her, divorced her, and then the first remarried her, as we are concerned about this in Siman 31, see there. However, here this concern does not apply, because it cannot be said that the first divorced her within 30 days. Whether his intention was conditional or for retracting, in any case, the kedushin (betrothal) is suspended and standing until the completion of the 30 days, and it cannot be said that the second married her within the 30 days. Nevertheless, it is proper to be stringent [see Beit Shmuel, Siman 26].

The Rambam writes: If one says to a woman, "Behold, you are betrothed to me from now and after 30 days," and another comes and says, "Behold, you are betrothed to me from now and after 20 days," and another comes and says, "Behold, you are betrothed to me from now and after 10 days," even if there are a hundred in this sequence, the betrothals of all of them are effective, and she requires a get from each one because she is doubtfully betrothed to all of them. And so it is written in the Shulchan Aruch. From the end of the wording, it is implied that she is doubtfully betrothed to all of them, meaning to this one or that one, because it is uncertain whether "from now" is a condition and the first betrothal is effective, or a retraction and the last betrothal is effective. Even though from this perspective, for the intermediates, in any case, a get would not be required, and indeed the Rosh rules this way as the Tur writes, nonetheless, it can be said that the Rambam holds that this phrase is not uniform among all people. Therefore, it can be said that this one intended it as a condition and this one as a retraction, and thus there is doubt whether the first and last intended it as a retraction and the intermediate intended it as a condition, and his betrothal is effective. There is no limit to these doubts; therefore, even if a hundred betroth her in this manner, she requires a get from all of them. Some of the early authorities hold this as well.

Indeed, what is said that the betrothal of all of them takes effect on her – from this language it implies that it is not because of the doubt that it is unknown whose betrothal took hold, but rather that all of them truly have a partial betrothal. For there are those who actually rule that anyone who says "from now and after a while" initiates the betrothal, though it is not finalized. Therefore, if afterwards another person betroths her with this language, his betrothal also partially takes effect, and so on up to a hundred. And although it is impossible for a woman to be half betrothed, this is certainly true as long as he retains something of the woman's person. However, here he did not retain anything of the woman's person, but rather they all complete [the betrothal]. [Tosafot 60b].

And there is a practical difference in law between these cases. If there is a doubt, a get (divorce document) is not required unless the second groom set his time before the completion of the first groom's time, and similarly for all of them. But if the second groom set his time after the first groom's time, his kiddushin (betrothal) does not take effect, because the first groom's kiddushin takes effect upon the completion of his time, whether it was a condition or a retraction. However, if the kiddushin of all of them are effective, there is no difference in this matter because the first groom left room (ravaḥa) for anyone who betroths her within thirty days [Ran]. 

From the wording of the Rambam, it appears that this applies specifically in this order, when the time of the last groom ends within the time of the previous one. However, according to what was said, there is a doubt, as perhaps one intended it as a condition and the other as a retraction, even due to doubt she needs a get from the second groom even if his time was after the first groom’s time. This is because perhaps the first groom's was a retraction and the second's was a condition, and since the second groom betrothed her on the condition that he would not retract until his time ended, and he did not retract, the first groom’s kiddushin, which was a retraction, is null and void. This is because the second groom's kiddushin preceded them, as his kiddushin was from now and this was before the completion of the first groom’s time [see Chommat Chemed section 9].

It appears that the Rambam interprets that according to the opinion in the Gemara that the betrothals of all of them take effect on her, it is not a definite betrothal. For, in truth, it is difficult to say that several betrothals take effect on one woman. Rather, the intention is also due to the doubt, that perhaps for this one it was conditional and for that one it was a retraction, as we have said.
