And this is what he wrote, that all of them are in this order; the intention is not that the time of the second is absorbed within the time of the first, but rather it means that all of them are in this order, that each one said "from now and after some time." [And see the Mishneh Torah and Kesef Mishneh, and this is what is said in the Gemara that each one leaves space, meaning that there is a gap between each one to take effect for either this one or that one for the reason explained, and consequently all of them take effect on her out of doubt regarding the divorce, like a candle among bricks. And see Rashi there and the Maharsha, and according to what we have said, it fits well; scrutinize it carefully.]

If one betroths a woman with a document stating "from now and after thirty days," the document must remain in the possession of the woman after thirty days. Although if it were a condition, this would not be necessary, because once the thirty days are completed, the betrothal is considered finalized retroactively. Nevertheless, there is a concern that she may have retracted her consent, and thus the betrothal would only take effect after thirty days. Furthermore, according to the opinion that the betrothal is only fully effective after the thirty days (and not a complete acquisition until then), even if it were a condition, she would not be fully his wife beforehand, even if the condition was fulfilled, because the betrothal of a second man would still be effective during that time. Therefore, according to this opinion as well, the document must be in her possession at the time the acquisition is completed. Refer to the Ran and Beit Shmuel at the end of Siman 108, and to what I wrote in Siman 146 and in Choshen Mishpat Siman 197, where it is explained that in a case of "from now," the acquisition is complete even if she is standing in the public domain after thirty days, because the acquisition had already been completed then. However, regarding betrothal, according to this opinion, it is not complete until the end of the designated time. [It is unclear why betrothal should differ from any other matter, and according to what I wrote about the Rambam's opinion, this opinion also agrees with this, and further study is needed.]

Any woman whom one cannot presently betroth, because the betrothal does not take effect with her – one cannot betroth her now even for a future time when the betrothal would take effect, as this is considered a case of something that has not yet come into existence. Therefore, if one says to a woman, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this coin after I convert" or "after you convert" or "after I am freed" or "after you are freed" or "after your husband dies or divorces you" or "after your sister, who is my wife, dies" and similar cases – she is not betrothed even when the time arrives, even if the betrothal coin is still with her then, and she does not require a get (divorce document) and would need a new betrothal if he wishes to marry her. Furthermore, she must return the betrothal money to him. We do not say that he gave it to her as a gift, as in the case of betrothing his sister, because in that case everyone knows that the betrothal does not take effect with his sister, and certainly he gave it as a gift. But here, he mistakenly thought that the betrothal would take effect when the time arrives and did not give it as a gift. Therefore, when the time arrives, he can betroth her with this money and does not need to take it back from her, as it is considered a deposit. When the money is then in her possession, he should say to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this money." [As explained in Beit Shmuel, section 9] [See Choshen Mishpat, section 209, where it is stated that if one says, "It will be acquired by you when it comes into existence" – it is acquired, but in betrothal, this does not apply, as the main element is the speech, and the speech must occur afterward. Consider this carefully.]

If one person betroths a woman to take effect after thirty days, and another comes and betroths her within those thirty days, and says, "After your husband dies" – she is considered betrothed because he can betroth her now within the thirty days. Even if the first one said, "From now and after thirty days," and the second one betroths her after the first one dies, she still needs a get (divorce document) from the second one as well. This is because if the second one betrothed her within the thirty days, she would be betrothed in doubt, perhaps the first one intended to retract, as has been stated. Therefore, even if he said "after he dies," it is also a doubt. [Bach and Chamasani].

If a woman is subject to levirate marriage (yibum), her betrothal (kiddushin) is valid out of doubt, as stated in Siman 159. Therefore, if someone says to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this perutah after your yavam releases you," she is doubtfully betrothed, because perhaps the betrothal takes effect now, and it also takes effect later out of doubt. Similarly, if he betroths her now, she is also doubtfully betrothed. Consequently, it is forbidden for the yavam to perform yibum with her before this man gives her a get (divorce document).

The one who gives two prutot to an unmarried woman and says to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me today with one, and with the other after I divorce you," she is currently betrothed, and when he divorces her, there is a doubt regarding the betrothal. The doubt is whether we say that since the betrothal takes effect now, it also takes effect after he divorces her, or perhaps it does not take effect. And even though according to the principle we established, that anyone who can betroth now can also betroth later, and he can indeed betroth her now, it is different there because that same betrothal he makes for later he can do now. But here, that second betrothal he makes now for later cannot be done now, for he is engaging her now with a different betrothal, and that second betrothal cannot take effect now. Therefore, it is possible to say that after the divorce, it also does not take effect.

And there is a question regarding this: We hold that if someone tells his friend, "This field that I am selling to you now, when I later buy it back from you, it will be sanctified" – the sanctification takes effect (Ketubot 59b), and thus ruled the Rambam in Chapter 6 of Hilchot Erchin, based on the reasoning that because he can sanctify it now, he can sanctify it for a later time. 

However, one must differentiate, as it is stated, because in the case of a woman, there is another sanctity now, and with sanctity, the sanctification takes effect even if there is another sanctity now, as the Rambam writes in Chapter 4 of Hilchot Me'ilah, that if someone says, "These plants are a sacrifice until they are cut down," and then redeems them, they revert and become sanctified because he sanctified them now and also sanctified them for after they are redeemed.

Nonetheless, the sages (Nedarim 30a) asked this question and differentiated that with plants, it is specifically when he redeems them that they revert and become sanctified, because since the plants did not leave the domain of sanctity or his domain, it makes sense that they would revert and become sanctified. But if another person redeems them, they do not revert and become sanctified.

And similarly with a woman, when he divorces her, she leaves his domain, which is akin to another person redeeming them. And even though she also agrees that the sanctity should take place even after the divorce, nevertheless, the act of sanctification depends on him and not on her, as it is written, "When a man takes a wife" and not "when a wife is taken by a man." Therefore, when she says, "I sanctify myself to you," it is nothing, as stated in Siman 27. Only her consent is needed, but he is the one who sanctifies her. Therefore, when she is divorced, she completely leaves his domain, which is akin to another person redeeming them (Ran there).

And all this we have explained according to the opinion of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch in section 7, who ruled that it is a doubtful kiddushin (betrothal). However, Rambam in Chapter 7 and also the Tur ruled that it is definitely kiddushin, and so ruled the Rashba for the reasons explained, that this is very similar to hekdesh (consecration). And even though in the Talmud it remains in doubt, nevertheless, we derive from another sugya (Talmudic discussion) that we brought, which does not make the fine distinctions we explained. And a woman, since she is agreeable to this, can also be betrothed now and also at a later time. And Rabbi Yosef Karo follows his own opinion, as he wrote in his major work that it is possible that Rambam's intention was also doubtful kiddushin. But the earlier authorities did not write so. However, in practice, there is no difference, since we follow the stringent view that disputes Rambam, and if she received kiddushin from another, she also needs a get (divorce) from him. Therefore, it is possible that they did not write Rambam's opinion in the Shulchan Aruch. And know that even according to Rambam, if they wanted to retract the second kiddushin, they can retract since it is like betrothing a woman for a later time. And it is possible that even if he said "from now," she can retract, even though with "from now" she cannot retract, that is because the kiddushin takes effect from now. But here, it cannot take effect from now because of the first kiddushin, and therefore it is possible she can retract. And it is clear that if one gives a prutah to his wife and says, "Behold, you are betrothed to me after I divorce you," it is nothing, for he cannot betroth her now as she is already betrothed, and therefore in this matter, her status is like saying this to another man's wife, which does not work because he cannot betroth her now, and similarly in this case.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 7: "If one tells another, 'If your wife gives birth to a female, she will be betrothed to me with this,' it is as if he said nothing. However, if his friend's wife is pregnant and the pregnancy is noticeable, she is betrothed. It seems to me that he must betroth her again after she gives birth through her father so that the betrothal will be without any defect." Thus he concluded. He holds that what the sages said, that if the pregnancy is noticeable she is betrothed, is not according to the opinion that a person can acquire something that does not yet exist. Rather, even according to us, who hold that a person cannot acquire something that does not yet exist, she is betrothed, for the noticeable pregnancy is considered as if it already exists. Many disagree with this, and therefore, according to the law, it is a doubtful betrothal, and so ruled our master the Beit Yosef in section 8. And even though in Choshen Mishpat section 209 regarding acquisition he did not make this distinction, we have already explained there in section 6 that due to the severity of the prohibition of a married woman, he was concerned with Maimonides' opinion, as stated there. However, Maimonides himself wrote in Chapter 22 of Sales that if one grants something to a fetus, it is not acquired, and he did not differentiate between a noticeable pregnancy and a non-noticeable one. Therefore, it seems that according to the main law, he also holds that even a noticeable pregnancy is considered as something that does not yet exist. It is only due to the severity of the prohibition that he was concerned about this, and therefore required the woman to be betrothed again after she is born. Accordingly, if he subsequently betrothed her sister, both would require a get (divorce document) because it would be a doubtful betrothal for both. Know that although the commentators on Maimonides and several poskim (decisors) understood from his words that he holds that a noticeable pregnancy is not considered as something that does not yet exist and she is fully betrothed, this is because they did not have his commentary on the Mishnah where he explicitly explained that it is a stringency in betrothal, and according to the law, even a noticeable pregnancy is considered as something that does not yet exist. Similarly, Rabbi Ovadia wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah in the name of Maimonides that this was the version of the Mishnah they had before them, as stated there.

[The Law of Betrothal that is not Conducive to Marital Relations, Containing Eight Sections] A person may betroth multiple women at once, provided there is the equivalent value for each one individually. He can say to them, "You are all betrothed to me with this money," or he can list them by their names. One of them can receive the betrothal on behalf of all of them if they agree, and she is considered their agent for receiving the betrothal, as a woman can serve as an agent for her friend even in a situation where she becomes a rival to her, as stated in Siman 36, Se'if 11. Refer there for more specific details on this matter. It appears to me that in the case of a betrothal with a document, one cannot betroth two women with a single document. This is similar to the requirement that two women cannot be divorced with a single bill of divorce, as it is written, "and he shall write for her" and not "for her and her fellow," as mentioned in Siman 130. Betrothal with a document is comparable to a bill of divorce, as stated in Siman 32. Therefore, if one wishes to betroth them with a single document, it must be written in the manner explained there concerning a bill of divorce. This should be carefully considered in practice.

We hold that betrothal (kiddushin) which does not permit consummation is still valid betrothal. The explanation is as follows: for example, if someone betrothed one of two sisters, or one of a woman and her daughter, or another close relative (ervah), and said, "One of you is betrothed to me," even though he cannot consummate the marriage with either of them because one might be forbidden to him (ervah), as he might have intended the other one at the time of the betrothal, and he is not believed to say, "I intended this one." Nevertheless, the betrothal is valid, and both require a get (divorce document) and are forbidden to him forever, as one might be the sister of his divorcee, and he must treat both according to all the laws of forbidden relatives. Similarly, if he said to a father, "One of your daughters is betrothed to me," and the father accepted the betrothal, or if two or three sisters or other close relatives where one made the other a messenger to receive her betrothal and he gave it to her hand and said, "One of you is betrothed to me," all require a get and he is forbidden to them. Or if two sisters were standing and he gave a coin to this one and a coin to that one and said, "One of you is betrothed to me," it is the same. But if two sisters were standing and he gave a coin to one and said, "One of you is betrothed to me," it seems that the one who received the coin is the betrothed one, since there is no concern regarding the other one, as he did not give her anything, and she also did not make her a messenger to receive the betrothal.

And there is room for doubt if one said to a father, "One of your daughters is betrothed to me," and one of them was forbidden to him by a prohibition, such as being divorced from engagement while still under her father's authority and he is a Kohen. Do we say that he certainly intended the permissible one and not the forbidden one? Or since the betrothal is effective for her, it is also not considered available for consummation. It seems that this is the case, because since he did not specify the other by name, perhaps his intention was the divorced one. Otherwise, why did he not specify her by name?

Even though betrothal that is not intended for consummation is still considered betrothal, nevertheless, if one betroths two women at the same time, such as two sisters, or a woman and her daughter, or other forbidden relations, and says, "You are both betrothed to me," it is not a valid betrothal, and neither of them requires a get (divorce document). The reason is that just as if he betroths one of them and then betroths the second one, the betrothal would not be valid, so too when he betroths them both at the same time. There is a general rule that whatever cannot be done sequentially cannot be done simultaneously (see Tosafot, Eruvin 49b, s.v. "Mai"). The Rambam, in his commentary on the Mishnah, wrote that the reason is because it is written, "And a woman to her sister you shall not take as a rival" (Leviticus 18:18). The Torah says that when they have become rivals to each other, you should not have a valid acquisition even with one of them. And we learn all forbidden relations from the case of a wife's sister. Although the verse is not explicitly referring to this situation, since the verse speaks of a prohibition punishable by karet (excision), which is only when one marries one of them first and then cohabits with her sister, we still derive from it that since the Torah said that betrothal does not take effect with a wife's sister, therefore, if one betroths both of them at the same time, the betrothal does not take effect with either. Because if the betrothal would take effect with one and not the other, why would you assume one over the other since he betrothed both? And for the betrothal to take effect with both is impossible, for each one is the sister of his wife, and therefore the betrothal does not take effect with either (as explained, the rationale of the Rambam and the Raavad, and the Talmud, Eruvin 50a, rejects this reason stating that the verse does not speak explicitly about this, but we derive it implicitly. The Talmud resolves it according to Rabba's principle that whatever cannot be done sequentially cannot be done simultaneously, as mentioned, even if one does not generally follow Rabba's view, one is compelled to do so here due to Tosafot's question in Eruvin).

If someone sanctified many women at once and among them were two sisters or a woman and her daughter, and all the women appointed one of them as an agent to receive the sanctification on their behalf, if he said "those of you who are fit for marital relations are sanctified to me" – then all are fully sanctified to him except for the two sisters or the woman and her daughter, for he explicitly excluded them by saying "fit for marital relations" and they are not fit even if he sanctified only one of them without specifying who she is. If he said "one of all of you who is fit for marital relations is sanctified to me" – each one is sanctified in doubt, for perhaps he intended her, and the two sisters do not need a divorce even though he sanctified one of all of them, and it is not worse than sanctifying one of two sisters. Nevertheless, here where he said "fit for marital relations" his intention is proven to exclude them, for if he intended one of them, she is not fit for marital relations. Some say that in such a case the sisters also need a divorce, and this is like sanctification that is not meant for marital relations since he said "one of you." The opinion leans more towards the first view for the reason we explained, but in practice, we should be stringent in sanctification. If among the women there were those prohibited by negative commandments and he said "fit for marital relations" it is doubtful if they are included since sanctification takes effect with them, or perhaps they are not considered fit for marital relations. And a menstruant is certainly called fit for marital relations after she becomes pure.

And if he said, "All of you are betrothed to me" – according to several of the poskim, the non-Jewish women are betrothed and the sisters are not betrothed. This is similar to what we hold in Choshen Mishpat, siman 190 regarding "Acquire it and the donkey," even though the donkey is not subject to acquisition, nevertheless, the man acquires half of it. Similarly, even though the sisters cannot be betrothed together and the betrothal does not take effect on them, nevertheless, the betrothal takes effect on the non-Jewish women. However, the opinion of the Rambam in chapter 9 and several of the poskim is that the betrothal does not take effect on any of them, and it is not comparable to "Acquire it and the donkey" because they are two separate statements. But since he said "all of you" and included them all in one statement, it is impossible to uphold half of the statement. According to this, if he said, "The sisters and the non-Jewish women are betrothed to me" – the non-Jewish women are betrothed. However, there is another distinction between this ruling and "Acquire it and the donkey," because there, there are two acquirers, the man and the donkey, and it is unreasonable to say that since the donkey did not acquire, the man also did not acquire. But here, the husband is one acquirer and he only wants to acquire all of them, and if not all of them, he does not want even some of them [this is the intention of the Ran and the Maggid Mishneh, and it resolves the difficulty raised by the Lechem Mishneh]. According to this, even if he divided them into two statements, they are not betrothed according to this opinion. And why do we not follow the seller's intent in "Acquire it and the donkey"? Because with respect to this acquirer, the seller's intent is also fulfilled since he only intended to transfer half to him.

And since there is a dispute among the authorities on this matter, therefore, non-Jewish women (who are sisters) are betrothed in doubt, whether he included all of them with the phrase "all of you" or whether he said "the non-Jewish women and the sisters." If he said, "One of all of you is betrothed to me," they are all betrothed in doubt, both the non-Jewish women and the sisters. If he said, "All of you and one of the non-Jewish sisters," they are certainly betrothed, and both sisters require a get (divorce document) [Bach and Shach]. This is not similar to the case of "acquire you and a donkey," because if it were known which of the sisters he betrothed, the betrothal would be complete for her as well. Now, due to the lack of this knowledge, both sisters require a get in doubt, but the non-Jewish women are certainly betrothed.

And so too is the law if among the women he betrothed there was a maidservant or a non-Jewish woman or one who is prohibited to him, such as a married woman, his daughter, or his sister, and the like, and he said, "The one among you who is fit for marital relations is betrothed to me" – the other women are betrothed. And if he said, "All of you are betrothed to me" – the other women are betrothed out of doubt, as explained in the reasons given.

Only with consent can one perform betrothal, and the witnesses must see the betrothal. In it, there are 51 sections.

The Rambam writes at the beginning of chapter 4: A woman can only be betrothed with her consent, and if someone betroths a woman against her will, she is not betrothed. However, if a man is coerced until he betroths against his will, she is betrothed. The reason is that although it is obvious that betrothal must be consensual from both the man, as it is written "When a man takes a woman," and from the woman, as we require the consent of the transferor [Rashi 44:] and she transfers herself to him, as it is written "She shall go and become another man's wife," implying her consent [Rashi Yevamot 19:], nevertheless, just as in buying and selling where the consent of both the seller and buyer is required, and even so, we hold that if a man was coerced to sell his field and he received the money for the field himself or said "I am willing," the sale is valid as stated in Choshen Mishpat section 205, unless he gave prior notice of his unwillingness. Without such a notice, we say that due to the coercion, he resolved to transfer ownership since he received the money. Similarly, if a woman who is like a seller of herself was coerced to accept betrothal and received the betrothal money herself or other forms of betrothal, when she said "I am willing," we say that due to the coercion, she resolved to transfer herself, and this is considered consent even though it was through coercion. And even though the rationale for sale is explained there that the reason he resolved to transfer ownership is because he received the money, and thus in betrothal by document and intercourse, she receives nothing, and it is like a gift where it is not acquired as stated there, and even with money betrothal, it is understandable if he betrothed her with a lot of money, but if he betrothed her with a small coin, it is not reasonable to say that because of the money she transferred herself to him. However, the truth is that in betrothal, it is like receiving money since he obligates himself in her sustenance, clothing, and marital relations [Tosafot Bava Batra 48:], and also because any woman prefers being married to being single [Nimukei Yosef there], therefore it is like a sale. And similarly, when a man is coerced to buy a field, the Rambam holds that the sale is valid when he says "I am willing," and all the more so in selling a field, as it is better for a person to buy than to sell [Gra]. And similarly, when he is coerced to betroth, it is like buying a field, and since he said to her "You are betrothed to me," it is like saying "I am willing" [Maharam Alashkar], and his betrothal is valid by law. This is similar to acquiring a field where he benefits from the produce, and here too, he benefits from her as she is obligated to his work and he establishes offspring from her. And even though he is obligated to her sustenance, still her benefit is greater than his expense, and even with a field, there is an expense.

And this is by law, but the sages decreed that when a man coerces a woman to accept a betrothal, the sages annul the betrothal because he acted improperly (Bava Batra 48b). However, when a man is coerced to betroth and she acted improperly, Maimonides holds that the sages do not annul the betrothal because it is not necessary; he can divorce her against her will. If he does not desire her, he can divorce her. But she, who cannot divorce against his will, compelled the sages to annul the betrothal (Hagahot Maimoniyot). Even nowadays, when there is the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom not to divorce against her will, and so we would have to annul the betrothal if he was coerced. However, Rabbeinu Gershom did not decree in such a case, and he can divorce her according to Torah law (Taz).

And this is the opinion of the Rambam and those who follow his approach. However, many of our rabbis hold that if a man is coerced into betrothing a woman, the betrothal is not valid according to the law. They also hold that even in the case of acquiring a field, only if he was coerced to sell is the sale valid, but if he was coerced to buy a field, the acquisition is not valid, as Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Choshen Mishpat there. And even though buying is certainly preferable to selling, nevertheless, buying is always done willingly, whereas selling fields is mostly done under duress, because if he did not need the money, he would not sell. Therefore, even when coerced to sell, the sale is valid [Bava Batra 47b]. And even though coercion of oneself is not comparable to coercion by others, nevertheless, due to the coercion, he resolves and transfers ownership upon receiving the money. But in the case of buying, we do not find any element of coercion at all. Therefore, even when coerced to betroth, which is similar to acquisition, the betrothal is not valid according to the law. Moreover, it is worse than acquiring a field, as taking a wife against his will is more severe. And since there is a dispute among the authorities as to whether coercion to betroth a woman results in doubtful betrothal. And know that monetary coercion is also considered coercion [Mikneh] even if he was not physically coerced. Coercion is only considered when he was coerced regarding the betrothal itself, but if he was coerced in another matter and as a result of that other coercion he agreed to betroth, this is not considered coercion at all, and this is complete willingness as written there in section 7, and see further in section 134. And if he declared a pre-emptive protest (moda'ah), his protest is a valid protest [it seems to me].

Do not be surprised by this matter that we said that from a legal standpoint, one who betroths a woman by force and she subsequently accepts the betrothal, she is considered betrothed. This is clearly explained in the Scripture at the end of the Book of Judges. After the war with the tribe of Benjamin, when most of the tribe was killed and they feared that the tribe would be eradicated, and they had previously sworn not to give their daughters to them as wives, it is written that they commanded the sons of Benjamin, "Go and lie in wait in the vineyards and watch; and behold, if the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, then come out of the vineyards and seize for yourselves each man his wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin," etc. (Judges 21:20-23). And the sons of Benjamin did so, and they took wives according to their number from the dancers whom they seized, etc. This was done according to the instruction of the Sanhedrin and the entire people of Israel. And behold, they forced the women whom they seized from the vineyards. Nevertheless, since they subsequently accepted the betrothal, even though it was by force, their betrothal is considered complete. [Regarding what the Avnei Miluim questioned about those who disagree, asking where we find that in cases of coercion one would drink from his own cup, and he wrote that the obligation to heed the words of the sages is only a postponement, he did not mention the words of the Rambam at the end of Chapter 2 of the Laws of Divorce, see there].

If a man betroths a woman while he is in a state of "dozing but not fully asleep, awake but not fully awake" – his betrothal is valid, as he is not considered as one who is fully asleep and he is still sound in his understanding. This state is defined as when he is slightly dozing, and if someone calls him, he responds. Even though he may not be able to respond to something that requires reasoning, nevertheless, if reminded, he recalls and says yes or no. But in a lesser state, such as being deeply asleep, he is considered as fully asleep. There is no difference between the beginning of sleep and the end of sleep. When one is in this intermediate state of "dozing but not fully asleep, awake but not fully awake," he is considered fully awake and is obligated in all commandments. He fulfills the obligation of reading the Megillah and eating the Pesach offering in this state, and also acquires his yevama (levirate wife) in such a state.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in section 1: If a woman first said "Marry me" and he threw the betrothal money into her lap and said to her "Behold, you are betrothed to me," and she shook her clothes within the time frame of "toch k'dei dibur" (a brief period after the act, typically considered as the time it takes to say a greeting) to throw off the betrothal money and claimed that she initially intended it only as a joke – nevertheless, she is considered betrothed. We do not follow the context or indicators that suggest she did not intend for betrothal. Even though it is explained in section 30, sub-section 20, that if she threw it away within "toch k'dei dibur," it is considered as nothing, and even if it was a case of doubt, as mentioned there, nonetheless, here, since she initially said "Marry me," we are concerned that she genuinely accepted it when he threw it into her lap, and immediately within "toch k'dei dibur" retracted. In matters of betrothal, retraction does not help even within "toch k'dei dibur," as explained in section 38, sub-section 51. From the language of Rabbi Moshe Isserles, it implies that it is a definite betrothal. And even though we have explained there that some authorities believe that within "toch k'dei dibur" is only a stringency in betrothal, and therefore according to this, it would only be a doubtful betrothal, nevertheless, our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 34, seem to hold that this is the fundamental law, as explained there. And even though she did not say "Marry me" at the time of the throwing of the betrothal money, still, since she did not explicitly say "Give the betrothal money into my hand," but said "Marry me" generally – she is betrothed even by throwing.

However, it is impossible to say that his intention was for definite betrothal, because without this, since she says that her intention was only for jest, even though we do not follow assumptions and proofs in matters of betrothal, nevertheless, this is only due to the gravity of betrothal [see Gra, subparagraph 4]. Therefore, even without a reason for retraction within 24 hours, it is only a doubtful betrothal. And although the fundamental law is that unspoken intentions are not considered, nevertheless, where it is evident that her intention was only for jest, it is considered significant, as in many matters we follow assumptions where the assumption is certain, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 246. And in matters of betrothal, even with a certain assumption and clear testimony that she only intended it as jest, nevertheless, we do not follow the assumption. This is also explained in the source of the law [Responsa of the Rambam, Issurei Biah, section 61]. Therefore, our master the Rema did not state because unspoken intentions are not considered, but because we do not follow assumptions in betrothal, which explicitly implies that only in betrothal do we not follow assumptions. If it were due to unspoken intentions, then in all matters we hold that unspoken intentions are not considered. Rather, certainly, even in matters where in other areas we follow assumptions, in betrothal we do not follow, and this is certainly only due to the gravity of forbidden relations, as stated. Therefore, it is only a doubtful betrothal [and the words of the Noda B'Yehuda, section 59, are puzzling, as he only brought the beginning of the Rambam's responsa, but it is explicitly clarified there as stated, see there].

Nevertheless, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that since our teacher, the Rema, did not write that it is a doubtful betrothal or that we are concerned about the betrothal, but simply stated that she is betrothed, it implies that even in a case where there is a strong presumption, it is also considered definite betrothal. And the language he used, that we do not follow presumptions and proofs in betrothal, is not just out of stringency, for he also used this language leniently in section 4, see there. Rather, the fundamental law is that in matters of divorce and betrothal, we do not follow presumptions even if they are very strong, whether leniently or stringently. In divorce and betrothal, we only follow the explicit action and not the thoughts, even if we know with certainty that the thoughts are contrary to the action.

A proof of this is that in the Talmud, there is a dispute about whether or not an expressed intention (gilui daata) in the context of divorce documents (gittin) is significant, and we hold that it is not significant [Gittin 34a], as mentioned in the end of section 141. Even those who hold that it is significant agree that unexpressed intentions (devarim shebalev) are not significant in matters of divorce and betrothal [there 32a in Tosafot s.v. MaD]. Rather, they hold that in a case where one's intention was revealed to everyone before receiving the get (divorce document) that it is not intended as a complete get, it is significant, and she is not divorced [there]. However, we hold that even in such a case, it is not significant, and she is fully divorced and permitted to remarry. There is no clearer proof than this. The incident brought by the Talmud there involves a man who gave a get and canceled it twice, and they forced him to give it a third time, instructing the witnesses to plug their ears until after the get was given so they wouldn't hear him canceling it again [there]. This is a clear proof, yet we do not follow this even leniently. The laws of gittin and kiddushin (betrothal) are the same. Another proof is from a get given by a dying man to prevent his wife from needing to perform levirate marriage and not out of hatred. According to our custom, we do not give conditional gets but rather a plain get, and they engage in matchmaking as mentioned in section 145 [there]. When he recovers from his illness and does not want to marry her, or she does not want to marry him, should we invalidate the get? This is a clear proof that he divorced her only due to fear of death, yet we do not consider this, because according to the act, it was a complete get [and the known get in the days of Maharam Lublin, which was validated by Maharshal and all the greats of the generation, as mentioned by Bach in section 148, was based on a known proof].

And the reason for this, it seems to me, is because divorces (gittin) and marriages (kiddushin) are not like monetary laws where the matters are upheld between themselves and witnesses were created only to prevent falsehood. However, in divorces and marriages, even if the act is done properly, without witnesses the act has no substance. Since the matter depends solely on the witnesses, they must see the act as it is and not investigate the thoughts of the heart, even with a strong presumption (umdena demukhach). If we were to follow the presumption, we would be following their own judgment and not the testimony of the witnesses, and this cannot be the case with divorces and marriages.

For this reason, it seems to me that there is difficulty among some of the early authorities regarding how a woman can be betrothed or divorced on a condition, such as if she does this or if I do that, since we hold that any "if" condition is considered an "asmachta" (a conditional commitment), and an "asmachta" does not effect acquisition, as our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in his great book in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 207. Some have said that the rule that an "asmachta" does not effect acquisition applies only when it is in the manner of a penalty and not when it is in the manner of a condition, as we wrote there in Se'if 24. Others say that the reason is that since it is something that a person is strict about, if he had not fully resolved to betroth or divorce, he would not have said it [as noted there in the Beit Yosef]. Some say that any condition set by a person himself does not constitute an "asmachta" [as noted there]. However, none of these explanations align with the principles and laws that we hold regarding the laws of "asmachta." According to our understanding, the matter is clear: the primary reason for the rule of "asmachta" is due to unspoken intentions — we are witnesses that he did not fully resolve in his heart, but rather thought that this matter would turn out as he had in mind, and he did not fully commit, as the Rambam wrote in Chapter 11 of Hilchot Mechira and the Tur there in Se'if 16. All this applies only to monetary laws which depend on the agreement of the heart, and when the presumption is strong that he did not resolve in his heart, it is not a valid acquisition. But in the case of divorces and betrothals, which depend on the testimony of witnesses, we do not follow the unspoken intentions of the heart, even with a strong presumption, and therefore the law of "asmachta" does not apply to them at all.

However, this matter requires great consideration. Certainly, if the witnesses do not perceive at the time of the writing of the get (divorce document) and the betrothal that it is not genuine, even though we know clearly through compelling evidence that they did not intend it sincerely in their hearts, we should not be concerned with what is in their hearts. But if, according to their actions, it appears to the witnesses clearly that it is only done in jest and mockery, it certainly cannot be considered definite betrothal. Even for doubtful betrothal, much deliberation is needed in such a case. Therefore, our teacher the Rema did not write that if she initially said "betroth me" in jest and mockery, it is obvious that these are not definite betrothals, and it is possible that they are not even doubtful betrothals. Rather, she said simply "betroth me," and according to the witnesses' perception of her statement, it was not in jest and mockery. Therefore, it is considered a betrothal even if she said she only intended it as a joke and there are indications and proofs to this. Nevertheless, it is considered a betrothal. [And in Tosafot in Gittin there, they compared it to monetary law, see there. It is possible that this applies only according to Rava, who holds that a revealed intention is significant, as all their words there are according to Rava and not Abaye. This requires further study, see there.]

Although this appears to us to be the case based on the Talmudic discussions and the language of our master, the Rema, nevertheless, since this is not explicitly found in the words of the decisors and there are some indications to the contrary—those decisors who sought other reasons for the asmachta, as we mentioned, if they held according to our reasoning, the reason would be straightforward. And even though this is not a definitive proof, one should not take action to be lenient based on this reasoning. Additionally, regarding the ruling of our master the Rema, one should be stringent in practice and consider it a doubt concerning betrothal. And I believe there is a dispute among the decisors regarding this reasoning that we wrote [see Beit Shmuel section 12, implying that the Rashba holds like our reasoning, while the Mordechai disagrees with this; refer there and scrutinize carefully].

Our Rabbi, the Rema, also wrote: If a man took a woman's hand forcefully without her consent and betrothed her, and she did not throw away the betrothal money, she is considered betrothed. Even though initially it was through coercion and he gave it to her without saying anything, since he initially spoke with her regarding betrothal, she is considered betrothed. We have already explained this in Siman 30, Se'if 18, that even though many poskim (halachic authorities) hold that if he threw the betrothal money into her lap and she did not initially consent, we do not consider it a betrothal even if she did not throw it away immediately, nevertheless, here it is considered a betrothal because he initially spoke with her about betrothal matters. Even though he betrothed her forcefully, since she did not throw it away, perhaps she later consented, and we are concerned about the betrothal. Additionally, placing it in her lap is not the same as putting it in her hand, as explained there.

However, according to this, it would only be a case of doubtful betrothal, but from the wording of our teacher, the Rema, it implies that it is a certain betrothal [and so it appears in Beit Shmuel, section 3]. It is possible to say that his intention is not about a complete coercion, but rather that they spoke about matters of betrothal, and she did not refuse the essence of the betrothal, but she was still unwilling to accept the betrothal. He then took her hand forcefully and inserted the betrothal ring into her hand. Consequently, if she truly did not wish for this, when he withdrew his hand, why did she hold onto the betrothal ring? It is not comparable to a case where it was thrown into her lap, because when he forcefully placed it in her hand and then withdrew his hand, if she had not willingly held it in her hand, it would naturally have fallen from her hand. Therefore, it is certain that she consented, and thus, it is a certain betrothal. This is why it is written "and she did not say anything," because since he spoke with her about matters of betrothal, even if he did not say "Behold, you are betrothed to me," she is betrothed, as it is written in section 27 [and although in Hagahot Maimoniot at the end of Gittin, which is the source of the Rema, it is explicitly mentioned there only that she requires a get (divorce document), nevertheless, his words can be interpreted in this manner, and in any case, the ruling should be stringent].

He further wrote: If he owed her money and she said to him, "Give me my money," and when he began to give it to her, he said, "Behold, you are betrothed to me," and she threw the money from her hand – it is not a valid betrothal. There is nothing novel in this, for even if she threw it without him owing her, she is not betrothed as stated in Siman 30, and in the case of a debt, even if she threw it, she is not betrothed as stated in Siman 28. Some say that if she did not throw it, even in the case of a debt, the betrothal would be valid because he did not say to her, "Here is the money I owe you," as written there [in the Beit Shmuel, subsection 4], and this is the novelty that our Rabbi, the Rema, is conveying to us. However, I do not understand, for since she said, "Give me my money," it is as if he said it, for she explicitly stated that she is accepting it for the debt. Furthermore, what relevance does this have to this Siman? Some say that the novelty is even if she was standing in her own domain, and when she threw the money from her hand, it was still in her domain [according to the Bach]. Some say the novelty is that we are not concerned about the rumor that she was betrothed, for this is not a rumor since the witnesses saw her throw it from her hand [according to the Drisha and Prisha]. All these matters are not relevant to this Siman but rather to Siman 30 and Siman 46, and it is also not such a novelty.

And it appears to me that our master, the Rema, is referring to the above case where she said "marry me" or they initially spoke about matters of marriage. It was explained that if he threw the money for marriage to her, even if he threw it immediately, it would still be considered a valid marriage because she initially consented, as mentioned in section 6. Similarly, it was explained in such a case where he gave her the money against her will and she did not throw it away, it is considered a valid marriage, as mentioned in section 14. Therefore, I say that in a case where they initially discussed marriage matters and he owed her money, and she said to him, "Give me my money," and he began to give it to her and she accepted it and threw it away, there is no suspicion of marriage. This is not similar to the previous case, where we are concerned that the initial acceptance was with consent and she immediately changed her mind. But here, the initial acceptance was for the debt, so we are not concerned, even though she initially said "marry me" or they discussed marriage matters. And it is not only if he gave her the entire debt at once and said to her, "You are betrothed to me," that there is no concern, because she requested what was due to her, and he gave her everything that was due. And it is possible that in such a case, even if she did not throw it away, we would not be concerned. However, practically speaking, it is difficult to be lenient in this. But even if he initially gave her a little, and I would say that this giving was not considered for the debt but for the marriage, since she initially consented and immediately changed her mind and threw it away, and in any case, it should be considered a doubt of marriage and we should compare it to the previous law, it comes to teach us that even in such a case, there is no concern of marriage. [And see Chelkat Mechokek, section 3, and Beit Shmuel, section 4, and I have written what seems correct to me].

If one betroths without witnesses, we do not consider his betrothal valid. Even if he betrothed her with one witness and there is no contradiction between them, the accepted principle is that matters concerning marital status require no fewer than two witnesses. This is derived from the verses in the context of divorce and betrothal: "because he has found some unseemly thing in her," and it is written, "by the mouth of two witnesses... shall a matter be established." Just as there, two witnesses are required, so here two witnesses are required as well. Even though in monetary matters, when both parties agree, witnesses are not required, monetary matters are different because a person has the authority to do whatever he wants with his money. Additionally, in monetary matters, if it affects someone else's debt, he is not believed without witnesses. In betrothal, it always affects others because he becomes forbidden to her relatives and she becomes forbidden to his relatives, and she also becomes forbidden to the entire world. If another man comes and betroths her, his betrothal is not valid. Although this is not considered harming others since no one has any claim over this woman, if we say that there can be betrothal without witnesses, it would result in a situation where someone could be liable for the death penalty without witnesses. How so? Reuven betroths Leah without witnesses, and later Shimon has relations with her. If we say that Reuven and Leah are believed and their betrothal is valid, we would need to execute Shimon for having relations with a married woman, which is impossible. Therefore, we must require witnesses for the betrothal to execute Shimon for having relations with a married woman who until that moment was presumed to be unmarried. Consequently, it is impossible to say that betrothal has any validity without witnesses. Betrothal cannot be partially valid, such that it would not be valid to execute Shimon but would be valid for her to be considered his wife. Therefore, the clear halacha is that betrothal without witnesses is nothing, and she remains unmarried as before. Even for betrothal through intercourse, witnesses are required, meaning witnesses to the seclusion, which are considered witnesses to the intercourse, as stated in section 33. Except for betrothal through a written document in his handwriting, some say that witnesses are not required, as we learn from divorce that his handwriting is like witnesses, as stated in section 32. However, most authorities disagree with this.

There is a question regarding this matter: How can we say that a matter of forbidden relations requires at least two witnesses, and if someone betroths a woman without witnesses, the betrothal is not valid at all, even if it is true that he betrothed her? This is not because they are not believed. If so, if a married woman committed adultery and there are no witnesses, only the husband saw her committing adultery, should we also say that she is not forbidden to him since there are no witnesses? It is obvious that she is forbidden to him. The answer to this is that in the case of betrothal, the act of betrothal itself forbids her, and the Torah decreed that there is no betrothal without witnesses. This is not the case with adultery, where the act of adultery itself forbids her and not the witnesses. Witnesses are only needed for credibility, and consequently, if the husband saw it himself, she is forbidden to him. [See Tosafot Ketubot 9a, s.v. "Umiy"].

When someone betroths in the presence of one witness, it is also considered nothing according to the views of the Rif, the Rosh, the Rambam, and the majority of the halachic authorities. However, there are those who are stringent in this matter and write that we need to be concerned about the betrothal. Similarly, our teacher, the Rema, was concerned according to the stringent opinion, except in cases of agunah (a woman whose husband is missing and cannot remarry) or pressing circumstances, where one can rely on the lenient opinions, which are the majority. The reason for the stringent opinion is that in the Gemara, the Amoraim debated this issue, and the halacha was not conclusively decided. Therefore, we are concerned with the opinion that even with one witness, we are concerned about the betrothal.

However, the main issue needs to be understood according to those who hold that we are concerned about the betrothal. After all, the clear halacha throughout the Talmud is that matters of sexual prohibition require at least two witnesses. It seems that this opinion holds that the requirement of two witnesses is relevant to a woman who is already prohibited, such as a married woman, and you are coming to forbid her to her husband, like in the case of a suspected adulteress, or to permit her to the public, like in the case of a divorce or the death of the husband. In these cases, we require two witnesses because the main issue of sexual prohibition is written in the section on divorce. However, for an unmarried woman who is coming to be betrothed, it is considered a transaction like all other transactions, since the husband acquires her. Therefore, even though betrothal is mentioned in this section, we do not learn the matter of "testimony" from the "testimony" written regarding death and sacrifice, but rather from the "testimony" of monetary matters, as it is written in the verse, "For any iniquity or for any sin" (Deuteronomy 19:15), and we expound in the Sifrei, "For any iniquity" – this refers to monetary matters, "and for any sin" – this refers to sacrifices. Since the acquisition of betrothal is similar to the acquisition of monetary matters, and regarding monetary matters, we derive that one witness suffices for an oath, and we learn this from the same verse, therefore, there is a reasoning that even with one witness for betrothal, we are concerned about it. Hence, they used the term "concerned," meaning that it is not a complete betrothal but rather a concern of betrothal.

And also, the concern for betrothal with one witness is only when they agree with the testimony of the witness, but if they deny it, it is nothing. Even if one of them denies the witness, it is nothing because one witness in contradiction is nothing. And even though in monetary matters it obligates an oath, here an oath is not applicable [Rashi]. Some say that when he denies the witness and she agrees, or vice versa, the one who agrees must be concerned about the betrothal according to this opinion. This is specifically when the one who denies says that there was no betrothal at all. But if he admits it yet says that he intended it as a joke, then the one who agrees also does not need to be concerned [Bach]. And even though with two witnesses he is not believed to say that he intended it as a joke, nevertheless, against one witness he is believed with a migo (legal presumption) that if he wanted, he could have denied it completely. However, some disagree with this, as we do not approach it from the standpoint of credibility but rather because even if he intended it as a joke, thoughts in one's heart are not considered significant [Chomat Shlomo and Beit Shmuel]. According to this, even in such a case, the one who agrees must be concerned about the betrothal. Nevertheless, the first opinion should be upheld, as it is obvious that if two witnesses were aware that their intention was merely a joke, it is not a betrothal at all, and it is better than an overt declaration, as stated in Section 12. However, if they are not aware, we do not follow conjecture. Similarly, with one witness, if he was aware that their intention was a joke, it is obvious that there is no concern for betrothal. Therefore, we say that the one who denies and says he intended it as a joke is believed to contradict the witness with a migo, and we also say that the witness was aware that his intention was a joke, and consequently, the one who agrees also does not need to be concerned [Nir Li].

There is no difference between a witness who says that she was betrothed in his presence alone, or who says that she was betrothed before two witnesses and he alone saw it, while the others say they did not see it. This is specifically when the witness does not contradict them by saying that they did see it. However, if he says that he and another person were invited to witness and both saw the betrothal, and the second person contradicts him, if the second person denies the entire event, we consider one against one, and she retains her presumption of being unmarried and can marry initially, as stated in Siman 47. But if the second person acknowledges the event but says the betrothal was not valid, for example, one says he was a relative to the groom and the other says he was a relative to the bride – she should not marry initially because her presumption of being unmarried has been weakened, as stated in Siman 30. However, if she marries, she need not divorce. There are those who are stringent even if the second person denies the entire event if she does not deny and says it could be that he was a relative to her. If she says the betrothal was in front of two witnesses, even if the two deny it, she has made herself forbidden. Similarly, if he says so, he has made himself forbidden to her relatives. If there were three present at the event and one says she was betrothed and two say she was not, she can marry initially if she does not contradict the two. If one witness says, "She was betrothed in my presence and in the presence of another person," and that other person is not here – we should be concerned for his words, and if she marries, she need not divorce because, after all, there is only one witness. Even according to Rema, who is stringent even with one witness alone, he is lenient in cases of hardship and distress, and there is no greater hardship and distress than if she marries, for if we require her to get a divorce, she will be forbidden to the second husband. If one testifies to the betrothal and another testifies that he heard from another who saw the betrothal – they combine, and she is betrothed. The law of two against two will be explained in Siman 47, with God's help.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote: Similarly, if one betrothed a woman in front of two witnesses and one of them was a relative, it is as if he betrothed in front of one witness. And even though we hold in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 36, that if one of the witnesses is found to be a relative or disqualified, the entire testimony is invalid, here it refers to a situation where the valid witness does not become invalidated, such as when they were not joined together for the testimony or the valid witness did not know of the disqualification, as mentioned there. Additionally, according to the opinion that invalidation only occurs when the testimony and declaration in court happen together, and here there was no declaration in court, it follows that at the time of the betrothal, the valid witness was not invalidated. Moreover, since the primary concern with betrothal in front of one witness is just a stringency because we are cautious with betrothals, it naturally follows that we should be cautious about all stringencies. Therefore, even if a relative or disqualified person is found, one should be concerned initially that perhaps it was in a manner where the valid witness was not invalidated according to one of the opinions regarding this law. Know that betrothal in front of one witness is considered even if he betrothed her a hundred times in front of a hundred people one by one, since there were not two present at one time, it is considered betrothal in front of one witness, and in a pressing situation or a case of potential abandonment, one can be lenient with this.

From the words of our master, the Rema, we learn that even those who are concerned about the validity of a single witness for marriage, nonetheless, regarding the testimony of relatives or disqualified individuals, no one is concerned. Similarly, the testimony of women, even if there are a hundred of them, is not considered. The proof of this is that in cases where the Torah accepts a single witness, such as in monetary cases for an oath, still, relatives, disqualified individuals, and women do not obligate an oath. Similarly, in cases where the Torah believes one as if he were two, such as in the case of a suspected adulteress (Sotah) and the decapitated calf (Eglah Arufah) to testify that she was defiled after seclusion and that the murderer was found, the Torah believes only a valid witness and not a relative, disqualified individual, or a woman, as is explained in their respective laws. And this is what the Sages said [Yevamot 88:] that a hundred women are considered like one witness, meaning not as one valid witness but, on the contrary, in a negative sense that a hundred women do not have the credibility of two witnesses. If one witness contradicts them, they are not believed, but are considered as one witness who can be contradicted by another. This is unlike a valid witness, where one witness is not believed to contradict him because he is trusted as two witnesses. However, in truth, their status is not even as one witness. And this that they are believed in the case of Sotah not to have her drink and in the case of the decapitated calf not to decapitate it, is because in those cases no testimony is needed at all, as even if they heard from a bird flying the law would be the same, as explained in Tractate Sotah.

Since a betrothal without witnesses is considered invalid, even if one betroths in the presence of witnesses, both the man betrothing and the woman being betrothed must see the witnesses. It is not strictly necessary to see them, but they must be aware that there are witnesses observing the betrothal. However, if the witnesses saw them but they were entirely unaware of the witnesses—such as if the witnesses saw them from a window and the witnesses could see them but were not seen by the man or woman—then she does not need a get (divorce document) from him, and it is as if the betrothal was without witnesses.

Some say that even if the man and woman intended a complete betrothal, it is still invalid in such a case because it is considered a betrothal without witnesses [Beit Shmuel in the name of Maharit]. Others also say it is not a valid betrothal, but not for the reason previously explained; rather, because we are certain that they did not intend a betrothal since they did not see witnesses [Chelkat Mechokek, section 7]. Therefore, even if they contradict the witnesses by claiming that no betrothal occurred at all, it makes no difference to us, since even without their contradiction, it would not be a valid betrothal due to our certainty that they did not intend a betrothal.

The practical difference between these two reasons is in a case where invalid witnesses were present at the time of the betrothal, and the man and woman did not know that they were invalid. Hence, they intended a betrothal. If valid witnesses were standing at a distance and saw the betrothal without knowing that the invalid witnesses were present, according to the first opinion, since they were unaware of the valid witnesses, it is not a valid betrothal. According to the latter opinion, since they intended a betrothal, it is considered valid [Beit Shmuel, section 11].

However, from the words of our teacher, the Rema, a different ruling is clarified in this matter. He wrote regarding this law that even if the witnesses heard her say that she accepts the betrothal, she can claim, "I knew that there is no betrothal without witnesses, and I intended to mock him." But this is specifically when she says that she intended to mock in general. However, if she denies receiving anything and the witnesses testify that she did receive it, she is no longer believed to say she intended to mock, and it is considered betrothal. End of quote. It is clearly different from the previously explained opinions, as it is specifically when she says she intended to mock in general and does not contradict the witnesses. But if she says she intended for betrothal or completely denies the witnesses, it is considered betrothal. And it seems that he holds that wherever witnesses are required, it is not incumbent upon the parties to know that there are witnesses, but as long as they intended the matter and there are witnesses who saw the matter, the matter is concluded. The practical difference is in a case where they would not be believed if they knew about the witnesses, but if they did not see and did not know about them, they are believed, like in the claim of intending to mock, as he wrote. And this is the opinion of our teacher, the Rema.

And there is a question in this matter, for according to this, what does it help that she says "I intended it as a joke," since unspoken intentions are not considered significant? Moreover, according to what is written in Section 8 that in matters of divorce and betrothal, we follow the action and not the intention, even if she intended it as a joke, it should be considered a valid betrothal just as when witnesses see something and say "we intended it as a joke," it is considered nothing as written there. 

The answer to this seems to me to be as follows: In all testimonies except for financial matters, knowledge and observation are required, as the Rambam writes in Chapter 17 of Testimonies, but knowledge without observation or vice versa is nothing. Therefore, if they did not see the witnesses and did not know of them, it is considered observation without knowledge when she says she intended it as a joke. 

The explanation is that we already explained in Section 12 that if the witnesses sensed that she intended it as a joke, it is not considered a valid betrothal, and therefore if they knew of them and did not sense that she intended it as a joke, it is considered unspoken intentions, and more than a mere disclosure of intent it does not become, and therefore it is a valid betrothal. However, when they did not know of them, we say that if they had known there were witnesses, the witnesses would also have sensed that she intended it as a joke, for the sense of a joke is based on her movements and gestures, and we say that if she had known there were witnesses, she would have increased her gestures so that the witnesses would understand that she intended it as a joke. Consequently, her intention would be like observation without knowledge, and it is not valid testimony. [And with this, everything is clarified].

The first opinion holds that in any testimony that requires witnesses, just as the witnesses need to see the matter, so too the parties involved need to know about the witnesses. The reason, it seems to me, is that since the Torah decreed that if a man and a woman betroth each other privately without witnesses, it is nothing, and if they think that there are no witnesses, then the act of betrothal they performed is not according to the Torah's decree. And while thoughts in the heart are not considered significant and revealing one's intention is not a matter of importance, nevertheless, this is more than just revealing one's intention. This is akin to saying explicitly that they did not intend for a betrothal as decreed by the Torah, for even if they intended for betrothal, they did not intend for a Torah-sanctioned betrothal, since the Torah decreed that there is no betrothal without witnesses, and they wanted to perform a betrothal without witnesses. It is evident to all that they did not know about the witnesses, hence there is no betrothal here. This is also the reason for the second opinion, that we are certain they did not intend for a betrothal as decreed by the Torah, as mentioned, since they did not know about the witnesses. There is no practical difference between these opinions except as mentioned in paragraph 25.

And know that from the language of our early sages, this law is not conclusively determined, and there are aspects supporting both sides. From the words of the Rashba, of blessed memory, who wrote in Gittin [8a], it seems reasonable that if he saw the witnesses, but if they see and are not seen by him, a get (divorce document) is not required because a person knows that without witnesses, she is not considered betrothed. Therefore, when he had relations, it was not for the sake of betrothal but merely for promiscuity. This is also written by the Ran there. From this language, it somewhat implies that if he had relations for the sake of betrothal, it would be considered a betrothal according to the opinion of our master, the Rema.

However, in Kiddushin [43a], the Rashba, of blessed memory, wrote: This is specifically when he betrothed her in the presence of two who are with her, but if he hid witnesses behind a fence and she was not aware of them, it is not valid. For perhaps if she had been aware of them, she would not have accepted the betrothal. But now that she thought there were no witnesses, she accepted them because she knew that a betrothal without witnesses is not taken seriously and she wanted to mock him. This slightly implies the opinion of those who disagree. However, this language can also be reconciled according to the opinion of our master, the Rema. Similarly, it is implied from the language of the Rivash in his responsa [266], where he wrote that whenever she does not see that there are witnesses, it is not proof that she accepted the betrothal, even if they heard her say so, because she thought there were no witnesses, etc. This clearly implies that if she had accepted the betrothal, it would be considered a betrothal. And regarding this, he brings the language of the Rashba from Kiddushin there. Thus, it is evident that he holds the opinion of our master, the Rema [see Beit Yosef].

Testimony of separation: Our sages stated (Makkot 6b) that it is invalid for capital cases but valid for monetary cases. What is testimony of separation? It is when one witness sees from one window and another witness sees from another window, and the witnesses do not see each other. The Rambam also writes this in Chapter 4 of Hilchot Edut. Regarding divorce (gittin) and marriage (kiddushin), it is not explicitly clarified what their status is. It seems to be likened to capital cases, where only in monetary cases, where witnesses are created primarily due to falsehood and we only need to know the act, do we not worry about the separation of witnesses. But in divorce and marriage, where without witnesses, the act is meaningless, the witnesses need to see each other. Moreover, the reason why in monetary cases separated testimony is valid is because one witness is sufficient for an oath (Tosafot there), but in divorce and marriage, where one witness is meaningless, separated testimony is also meaningless. However, according to this, whoever is concerned with one witness in marriage would obviously consider separated testimony valid. 

What was clarified in Siman 11 regarding witnesses of indecency, who are combined even if they did not see at the same time, is because the act itself renders her forbidden, and the witnesses only testify to this. Since the matter is revealed through two witnesses, she is automatically forbidden to her husband. Similarly, in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 30b), there is an opinion that even in testimony about two hairs (indicating puberty), it is valid in such a manner because we only need to know that two hairs have grown. But in divorce and marriage, where without witnesses it is nothing, and the main validation of the divorce or marriage is through the witnesses, it does not help to have one after another as stated in Section 23 and as our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 2. Therefore, separated testimony is also nothing. 

Additionally, the opinion in the Talmud (Gittin 33b) that if one instructed two to sign a divorce, it is valid even if he told each one separately, this only pertains to making them witnesses. But when they actually testify, it is not valid if they are not together. And what is explained in Siman 130, that the rule that the witnesses of a get (divorce document) do not sign separately is only a decree and not from the primary law, is because at the time of signing the act of the get is not completed until it is handed to her, and then indeed the delivery witnesses need to be together as stated in Siman 133. Even according to the opinion there that if it was delivered between him and her with only signing witnesses, it is valid, this is because we consider the signed witnesses as if they are present at the time of delivery, and thus they are both together since they are both signed on it now. 

And although this seems correct to me according to the law, practically one should be stringent, and if one betrothed a woman based on separated testimony, it is considered doubtful betrothal (see Beit Shmuel, Siman 133, Sk 1 and Gra, Sk 3, where it is unclear how these relate to each other, and the words of the Beit Shmuel in Siman 11, Sk 13 are also unclear, see there, and see Noda BiYehuda, Siman 72, his words are not clear to me).

If one sanctifies (betroths) in front of witnesses, even if he did not say "you are my witnesses" – she is betrothed, since the witnesses do not need to be designated as such, as it is written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 39. Rather, since they saw the act, they can testify about it. According to this, even if specific witnesses were designated, others who saw the act can testify. Nevertheless, it is proper to designate witnesses for the betrothal under the chuppah, and this is the practice in many holy congregations, which is very proper for several reasons:

Firstly, because most of those standing there are preoccupied with the festivities of the bride and groom and do not pay attention to the main act of betrothal to ensure that two witnesses see it as required by Torah law.

Secondly, because most of those standing close to the bride and groom are relatives and therefore disqualified from being witnesses, and those who are qualified to be witnesses are standing far away. Due to the crowding, they do not see the act of betrothal at all, resulting in betrothal without witnesses.

Thirdly, according to several authorities, when relatives and non-relatives see a testimony together, even the non-relatives are disqualified, as in the case where one is found to be a relative or disqualified. When witnesses are designated, the relatives do not disqualify them, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 36.

It is proper for the groom to designate the witnesses, but due to embarrassment, it is not feasible to impose this on him. Therefore, it is proper for the officiating rabbi to designate the witnesses. The custom is to designate the cantor and the sexton because they stand close to the bride and groom. If one of them is a relative, another should be designated. 

[And regarding the matter in Keritot 12b and in Tosafot there, it seems that it is not about the testimony of sight but about the hearing of a lengthy matter, and in such a case, without the intent to testify, one will not remember accurately after some time. See also Pischei Teshuva, section 11].

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that the witnesses must see the actual giving into her hand or into her possession. But if they did not see the actual giving into her hand, even if they hear him say "Be betrothed to me with such-and-such an item" and afterward it is found in her possession, it is not considered a betrothal until they see the actual giving. We do not rely on assumptions and proofs in this matter, end quote. The intention is not due to doubt that perhaps the item did not pass from his hand to hers, but even if it is clear that it did pass from his hand to hers, it is not considered a betrothal. This is evident from the source of this law in a case where two people stood behind a fence and heard Reuven say to Leah "Be betrothed to me with this etrog," but they did not see the actual giving. The Rashba ruled that there is no concern of betrothal here, even if she admits that she took it for the purpose of betrothal, because visual and factual testimony is required, end quote. Reuven and Leah must be aware of the witnesses, for otherwise, even without this, there is no concern of betrothal, as stated in section 25. This is a proof to what is written in section 5 that divorces and betrothals are not like monetary laws and we do not rely on assumptions, even if they are compelling, it is still nothing. It is also a proof to what is written in section 27 that in divorces and betrothals, there must be knowledge and visual testimony, and this is knowledge without visualization. And if you ask why in betrothal through cohabitation is it sufficient to have only witnesses to seclusion, which is knowledge without visualization? Certainly, in the case of betrothal through cohabitation, this is also considered visualization because it is impossible to see the act itself, and when they see the seclusion, it is as if they see the cohabitation. However, in the case of money or a document, actual visualization is required. And the Rashba also wrote in section 1193 that we require both knowledge and visualization, see there. And know, the witnesses do not need to recognize the woman, but later, if she denies the betrothal and says it was not her, she is believed. See Be'er Heitev subsection 12, and this is obvious.

As explained earlier, it is also proven from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 3 of Ishut and Chapter 10 of Gerushin that only in the case of intercourse do we say that the witnesses of seclusion are the witnesses of intercourse. But for other forms of betrothal, the witnesses must see the betrothal itself. However, some of the early authorities were uncertain about this, suggesting that just as in the case of intercourse it is not necessary to see the act itself, so too in the case of betrothal with money, if the witnesses saw something indicating that he gave her [the money], it is considered as if they saw the betrothal itself (Maharam of Rothenburg in Mordechai Chapter 3 and at the end of Gittin, and in Responsa of the Rambam, Women Section 61). According to this, we would need to say that the witnesses of betrothal can be valid through knowledge without actual seeing (Beit Shmuel, Section 12), just as in the matter of investigation and interrogation, the laws of betrothal are like monetary laws which do not require investigation and interrogation, as will be explained. Similarly, according to this opinion, betrothal is determined by estimation, contrary to what was written in Section 8 and Section 27 (and there is a difficulty with the Beit Shmuel, as he himself retracted in the end of the responsa in all places according to the words of the Rambam, see there. Perhaps he intended as we have brought, and examine this carefully).

However, in truth, there is no proof at all from inquiry and investigation, for the Rashba, who ruled that certainty and direct evidence are required as he himself wrote, also ruled that inquiry and investigation are not necessary [see Responsa, Section 566]. And what relevance does inquiry and investigation have here? Inquiry and investigation need to be conducted in a court, and from a legal standpoint, we do not have a court at all since we do not have ordained judges. Rather, we act as their agents, as stated in Choshen Mishpat Section 1, and we only carry out their agency in essential matters, as stated there.
