And since there is no necessity for inquiry and investigation, we do not act as their agents. However, in a case of necessity, such as if fraud is suspected, inquiry and investigation are indeed required, as will be explained. But the testimony of witnesses, which is still required by Torah law just as in the times of the Temple, surely needs to be as in capital cases, and indeed it is more stringent than capital cases. For in capital cases, even without witnesses, the act remains an act, but to testify in court requires witnesses. However, in cases of divorce and marriage, the act does not hold at all without witnesses, and it is obvious that certainty and direct evidence are required. This is clearly implied in the Rambam, Chapter 17 of Testimony, and since direct evidence is required, we do not rely on estimation. And that which the Sages said that the witnesses of women are not investigated through inquiry and investigation is because since she needs to receive her Ketubah, it is similar to monetary laws [at the end of Yevamot], implying that from the outset no inquiry and investigation is needed. This applies to the testimony of a woman whose husband died, but not to divorce and marriage. And even regarding the testimony of a woman whose husband died, the Rambam wrote at the end of Chapter 13 of Divorce that the reason is because of agunah (a woman chained to her marriage) and not from the outset of the law, see there. Nevertheless, in practice, it is difficult to be lenient with significant estimation in marriage, and she requires a Get [and likewise, from the Tosafot at the beginning of Chapter 4 of Gittin, who say that we follow significant estimation in divorce and marriage, even though one could refute this by saying that they wrote this according to Rava, and we follow Abaye, nevertheless, in practice, one should not be lenient].

Our teacher, the Rema, also wrote: If someone betrothed a woman through a hole in the wall, for example, if she extended her hand through the hole and someone came and gave her betrothal, and the hole is narrow and it is impossible to see her at the time of betrothal, and she says that she did not hear that she was being betrothed – she is believed with the claim (migo) that she could have said that it was not her hand but another's, provided there are no witnesses contradicting her, end of quote. 

There are those who interpret his words to mean that if she says she heard when she was being betrothed, the betrothal is valid even though the witnesses did not see her at all because the hole is narrow, and it is similar to witnesses of intercourse who do not need to see directly and it suffices with witnesses of seclusion. However, it has already been explained that our teacher, the Rema, holds that one cannot learn from intercourse to money and documents. Therefore, it must be said that since they saw the hand extended into the hole, it is considered as if they saw her directly, even though they did not know from which body it came. Or it is possible that they knew that this woman was standing on the other side of the wall near the hole, and still, she has the claim (migo) that she could say that at the moment of betrothal someone else came and extended her hand into the hole. 

Even though the witnesses say that it was possible to hear the betrothal, still, since they do not say that she definitely heard, this is only a suspicion, and we say (accept) the migo in place of the suspicion of the witnesses. Similarly, even though the witnesses say that a moment before the betrothal she was standing by the hole, still, it is not certain that she extended her hand into the hole, and therefore it is a good migo. Nevertheless, it is called direct witnessing since they saw the hand, and also there is real knowledge because they knew that this woman was standing there a moment before, and even though she did not see the witnesses, since she knew of the witnesses, it is as if she saw them. Or it is possible that even if they did not know at all if this woman was standing there, still, it is called knowledge and witnessing because of the hand, since they knew and saw this hand, it is as if they saw the whole body and had knowledge. For even if they see the woman and do not recognize her, it is not complete knowledge, and still, it is certainly called knowledge and witnessing. Hence, seeing only the hand is also called knowledge and witnessing, but this requires further investigation in practice.

However, in the responsa of the Rashba, it is explicitly stated that the witnesses need to know to which body the extended hand belongs. He wrote that since the second witness says he did not recognize whose hand it was, there is only one witness, as there.

Additionally, it is written that any testimony that has not been investigated in a court is not considered testimony regarding betrothal. Therefore, even if witnesses said outside of the court that she was betrothed, they can retract in court and say she was not betrothed, and vice versa. Witnesses of betrothal do not require interrogation and investigation unless it appears that there is deceit involved. Hence, it is clear that what was written, that any testimony not investigated in court is not considered testimony, refers to cases where interrogation and investigation are necessary, such as in a deceitful matter [see the Gra, note 18]. It must be said so, as it deals with the retraction of witnesses, and it is obvious that in such instances, interrogation and investigation are required. And it is clear that if she contradicts the witnesses, interrogation and investigation are necessary. Therefore, it is explained in Siman 11 that to prohibit a woman to her husband, interrogation and investigation are required because she contradicts them. Here, where the witnesses themselves retract, it is obvious that even if she does not contradict, it is considered a deceitful matter and requires interrogation and investigation [regarding what the Beit Shmuel wrote in note 14, it is unclear why her contradiction is necessary].

Additionally, it is written: If it is found written in a document "So-and-so betrothed so-and-so" and witnesses signed it, as long as the document is not verified, there is no need to be concerned about the betrothal, contrary to the opinion of those who are stringent in this matter. And some say that indeed one should be stringent in this matter, for according to Torah law, witnesses who sign a document make it as if their testimony has been investigated in a court, and according to Torah law, it does not require verification [Shach Choshen Mishpat 46].

However, the main opinion follows our teacher, the Rema, that this only applies to a document found in the possession of the litigant. But here, if the man and woman admit to the betrothal, it is certainly considered betrothal. Here, it must necessarily be referring to a case where they deny it and claim that the document is forged and was not found in their possession. In such a case, it is clear that according to Torah law, verification is required [Avnei Miluim].

Even if the document is in his possession and he claims he betrothed her, if she denies it, it is meaningless, for a betrothal document must be in the possession of the woman, similar to a get (divorce document). This is not comparable to a document that a lender produces against a borrower. Even if this document is not a betrothal document but rather a document of evidence of the betrothal, where the witnesses testify that he betrothed her on a certain day and in a certain place with money or an equivalent value, it is still not comparable to a document in the possession of a lender. There, the document is from the Torah, and the primary loan is based on the document. However, a document of evidence of the betrothal is not primary, is not customary, and is not included in documents considered as if their testimony has been investigated in court. On the contrary, since this betrothal document deviates from custom, there is no greater deficiency than this. In a place of deficiency, it is clear that verification is required by Torah law [see Choshen Mishpat 10:10 and 10:11].

However, in the case of an actual betrothal document that is in her possession and she denies it, it appears to be similar to a document in the possession of a lender, which does not require verification by Torah law.

It also appears from the words of our teacher, the Rema, that when a document is ratified, it constitutes a valid betrothal, and similarly, if it can be ratified, it is as if it is already ratified. However, there are those who disagree and hold that we do not rely on a document that was written without the woman's knowledge, as this is not considered a proper document but merely a memorandum. Testimony must be given orally and not in writing, and this is not similar to monetary documents as discussed in Choshen Mishpat, chapter 28, which are merely considered memoranda (see Rashba, responsum 1009, and see also Choshen Mishpat, subparagraph 10). According to this, if it is written in the document, "The woman told us to write, sign, and give it to so-and-so who is betrothing her, to be in his possession as proof that he betrothed me," it is considered a valid document (see Choshen Mishpat, subparagraph 10). However, there are those who say that even in such a case, it is not a valid document for the reason we mentioned, that only promissory notes have a basis from the prophets by divine command, as it is written, "Write in a book and sign it and summon witnesses" (Jeremiah 32:44). But a document as proof of betrothal cannot be written, for the Torah says, "From their mouths and not from their writings" (based on the words of Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg). This is not related to what is written in chapter 17, paragraph 75, about finding written in a document, "So-and-so died," for there, a document is not required, only a mere notification, and witnesses are not needed, as explained there. See further what is written there in paragraph 78.

It seems to me that the intention of our teacher, the Rema, is that if the marriage document is not confirmed, there is no need to be concerned at all. But if it is confirmed, then there is a need to be concerned and to search for the witnesses, and the matter will be clarified accordingly. If someone presents a marriage document and the witnesses say that he once asked them to forge a marriage document, this document is also presumed to be forged [Beit Shmuel]. However, if the witnesses testify that both parties asked them to write the document, then it is certainly a valid marriage. Nonetheless, the court must investigate and examine the witnesses to ensure they are not known to be wicked, since this individual is suspected of seeking out fraudulent witnesses. It is appropriate for the court to remove such stumbling blocks and not to give room for criminals to harm and defile the daughters of Israel [Rashba, cited in Beit Yosef].

If someone spreads a rumor that he betrothed a certain virgin and claims he has witnesses who are not currently in town, we do not heed his words, even if he says they will come today or tomorrow, or even if he mentions the names of the witnesses [Beit Shmuel, section 16]. Even if she is his betrothed, we do not pay attention to him [ibid], unless there is a rumor that she was betrothed according to the conditions of a valid rumor, as will be explained in Siman 46. Similarly, if the court understands from the circumstances that it is possible she was betrothed, then they are concerned about his words and wait for the witnesses. But without this, there is no need to be concerned.

This is not comparable to what is written in Siman 157 about someone who died with the presumption that he had no brothers, and a rumor emerged that he had brothers, and the witnesses who know about this rumor are in another country. In that case, we are concerned about the rumor even if it has not been confirmed by the court, and she is forbidden to remarry until the witnesses are questioned. There, she was already his wife and was permitted upon his death, and since there is a rumor, she is not properly permitted yet. This is different from the case of betrothal, where this woman has no connection to the one spreading the rumor. Even if she is his betrothed, so what? She is not yet bound to him by betrothal. Moreover, in that case, there is no one to suspect, but here, we suspect the one who seeks to extract money from her. If we start being concerned about such rumors, many ruffians will spread rumors about the virgins of Israel. Therefore, if the court does not see a genuine reason to be concerned based on their understanding, there is no need to be concerned at all [and this resolves the difficulty raised by Avnei Miluim, section 13].

Rambam wrote in Chapter 4: If one betroths with witnesses who are invalid according to Torah law, she is not betrothed. If the witnesses are invalid according to rabbinic law or there is doubt whether they are invalid according to Torah law, if he wishes to marry her, he must betroth her again with valid witnesses. If he does not wish to marry her, she requires a get (bill of divorce) from him due to doubt. Even if the woman denies it and contradicts the witnesses, saying, "You did not betroth me," we force her to accept a get. Similarly, in all cases of doubtful betrothal, if he wishes to marry her, he must betroth her again certainly, and if he does not wish to marry her, she requires a get from him due to doubt. Consequently, if someone else comes and betroths her, she is betrothed to the second one out of doubt and requires a get from both of them if they do not want her, or the first one should divorce her and the second one should marry her. However, for the second one to divorce her and the first one to marry her is forbidden. Although according to the law it is permitted, we nonetheless decree against it lest people say that the first one divorced her, someone else betrothed her afterwards and divorced her, and then she married the first one, as stated in Siman 31.

And that which was written regarding a case of doubt—if he wishes to marry her, he must betroth her again with valid witnesses. Although, in a case of doubtful divorce, the Rambam ruled in Chapter 10 of the Laws of Divorce that if he wishes to marry her, he does not need another betrothal, the reason is simple: in the case of betrothal, when there is a doubt, she is presumed to be single, and therefore, he must betroth her anew. However, in the case of doubtful divorce, she is presumed to be a married woman [as mentioned in the name of the Maharik]. Nevertheless, even in a case of doubtful betrothal, he does not recite the blessing of betrothal again [as mentioned in Beit Shmuel, Section 17], for blessings are not essential.

And regarding what is written that we compel her to accept a get (bill of divorce), it seems the intention is that she is not believed to contradict the witnesses and remarry without a get. In the Tur, the version is "and we compel him to give a get," and similarly it is written in the Shulchan Aruch, section 5. It is not understood, if he is willing to betroth her again as written, why we should compel him to give a get. It must be said that the intention is when he does not want to betroth her, and consequently she does not belong to him, and she also cannot be betrothed to another. Therefore, we compel him to give a get. It is also possible that even if he wants to betroth her anew, if she contradicts the witnesses, her status is as if he says to a woman "I betrothed you" and she says "You did not betroth me," we compel him to give a get. And even though she is not believed to contradict the witnesses, nevertheless, since according to the witnesses it is only a doubtful betrothal, there is reason to say that we compel him if she does not agree to him and contradicts the witnesses. However, the great later authorities did not write this.

And that which he wrote regarding questionable disqualification in cases of rabbinic invalidation, his intention refers to rabbinic disqualifications and not to maternal relatives. Even though in chapter 13 of Testimony he wrote that maternal relatives are disqualified by rabbinic law, his intention is not that they are only disqualified by rabbinic law, as all the early authorities have agreed that there is no difference between paternal and maternal relatives. Rather, it is the Rambam's way to call anything not explicitly stated in the Torah "rabbinic," meaning that the scribes received this tradition all the way back to Moses at Sinai, just as he refers to betrothal through money as rabbinic. Nevertheless, there is one who holds that maternal relatives are only disqualified by rabbinic law [see Beit Shmuel, section 16], and this also seems to be implied by our teacher, the Rema, in Choshen Mishpat, section 33. Refer there.

And that which is written, that if someone else betrothed her, she requires a get (divorce document) also from the second one, there are those who say that this applies only in a case of doubtful betrothal. However, if one betrothed her in the presence of witnesses who are disqualified by rabbinic decree, there is no need to be concerned about the second betrothal since, according to Torah law, the witnesses are valid. Nevertheless, our master the Beit Yosef, in his great book, holds that even in the case of witnesses disqualified by rabbinic decree, she requires a get also from the second one. Even if both (the first and the second) betrothed her in the presence of witnesses disqualified by rabbinic decree, she requires a get from both, since as long as the first betrothal is not finalized, the second betrothal also takes effect, necessitating a get from the second one. For indeed, some of our great Rabbis hold that when one betroths in the presence of witnesses disqualified by rabbinic decree, the betrothal is nullified, as anyone who betroths does so with the understanding of the Rabbis. And although we do not rule in this manner, nevertheless, certainly for the second betrothal, there is concern, necessitating a get from him. This is also explicitly implied by the wording of Maimonides, of blessed memory, and there is no room for doubt in this matter.

The laws regarding disqualified witnesses are explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 33, and further in Siman 34. There it is explained that one who violates an oath of expression, some say that he is only disqualified if it was an oath regarding the past, because at the moment the oath left his mouth, it was false. However, for an oath regarding the future, he is not disqualified. And some say that even according to those who disqualify him as a witness, it is only by rabbinic decree [see Beit Shmuel there if the testimony of disqualified witnesses was not accepted in their presence].

Some say that when we state that betrothal conducted by witnesses who are disqualified by rabbinic decree is a matter of concern, this refers to standard Torah betrothal. However, in the case of rabbinic betrothal, such as when someone betroths a minor orphan with the consent of her mother and brothers, or even if she is not an orphan but her father is distant, there is no need to be concerned about the betrothal at all, even if the witnesses are disqualified by rabbinic decree. However, if the father consents upon hearing about it, according to the stringent opinion in section 37, it certainly constitutes betrothal. But as long as we do not know that the father has consented, there is no Torah betrothal here.

Witnesses who became disqualified after the betrothal, but at the time of the betrothal were still qualified, according to the law, if others testify about their testimony at the time of the betrothal, the betrothal is valid. However, the disqualified witnesses themselves cannot testify in court about the betrothal after they have been disqualified, even though they were qualified at the time of the betrothal. Since they are now disqualified, their testimony is not accepted. Nevertheless, it is proper for the court to investigate other witnesses. [See Responsa of the Rivash, Siman 266, and Divrei Rivot, Siman 185. The Ba'er Hetev, in Siman 14, quotes them as saying that the betrothal is invalid, but he did not quote accurately and caused a stumbling block. It is a mitzvah to erase it.]

One who has illicit relations, even though he is deemed a complete wicked person, there are those who say that if he was a witness to a marriage, we take the marriage into account. This is because his desire overwhelms him in this matter more than in other transgressions, and therefore we do not have the power to disqualify him in the serious matter of illicit relations. [This is according to the opinion of the Rif and Rabbeinu Tam in Sanhedrin 26b who believe that someone under suspicion has actually committed the act, but according to those who follow Rav Nachman and our version, it is not said. Examine this well.]

There are some of our Rabbis who hold the opposite view, that in other transgressions a person is not disqualified by mere suspicion. However, one who is suspected of sexual immorality, even though there are no witnesses that he committed the act, but there is mere suspicion, and certainly he is not disqualified from Torah law for all testimony, nevertheless, for testimony regarding a woman – he is disqualified both in matters of marriage and divorce, and also to testify that her husband died – he is disqualified [Rashi], because his inclination overpowers him in this matter and he cannot be a witness in these matters. And one who secludes himself with those forbidden to him – is disqualified by rabbinic decree [Bach], and one who embraces and kisses them – according to Maimonides in the first chapter of the Laws of Testimony, he is disqualified by Torah law, and Maimonides did not mention any of these laws in the Laws of Marriage nor in the Laws of Testimony [see Beit Yosef on Tur, Choshen Mishpat, section 34].

And know that, in my humble opinion, it appears from the Talmudic discussion that what we have explained applies only when one comes to testify about the betrothal or the divorce. Therefore, we do not believe him because he is suspected of lying due to his impure desires. However, if he was a witness at the time of the betrothal, then certainly the suspect is valid according to the Torah. But the leading later authorities did not understand it this way (see Choshen Mishpat 15:15 and Beit Shmuel 21), and it is clear that one should always be stringent. There is much to scrutinize in our times regarding witnesses for divorces and betrothals, as those who are promiscuous in any transgression, even a minor one, are indeed disqualified from being witnesses.

Rabbi Moses Isserles wrote: "If one consecrates [a woman] in front of those disqualified from giving testimony by Torah law due to their wickedness, such as in front of forced converts or other wicked people, some say we should be concerned about the validity of the consecration, lest they have repented. Others are lenient." And the great later authorities wrote that they do not disagree in practice, for certainly, if a wicked person shows no signs of purity and does not strive in his Judaism, we are not concerned that he might have repented. But those who strive to emerge from their upheaval and afterwards repent, their end proves their beginning, that their heart was always towards Heaven, and therefore we are concerned that they might have contemplated repentance in their hearts. 

There was an incident in the presence of Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (Rashi), with a forced convert who consecrated in front of his fellow forced converts and they repented, and he said that a bill of divorce is needed, lest they had contemplated repentance in their hearts. And it is further written that those forced converts who had to turn due to fear, since they could not save themselves and secretly observed the commandments—they are fit to give testimony. 

And know that all this is not relevant in our times, since the kings of the nations are benevolent and would never force a change of religion. Therefore, someone who is wicked is wicked of his own accord and not out of coercion, and how could we suspect that he might have contemplated repentance in his heart? This explanation is only relevant to earlier times when they afflicted Israel to force a change of religion. And even though one who consecrates "on the condition that I am righteous," even if he is completely wicked, we are concerned that he might have contemplated repentance, as stated in section 38, this is because he said "on the condition that I am righteous," and there are grounds to believe that his thoughts are for good. But this does not apply to ordinary wicked people without coercion.

[Laws of the Betrothal of a Minor and If They Grow Up, Containing Nine Sections]

A minor who betroths or marries a woman does nothing, and she does not need a get (divorce document) from him. If he dies, she does not require chalitza (ceremonial release from a levirate marriage), as the actions of a minor are considered null. Although the Rabbis instituted marriage for a minor girl to prevent her from being treated promiscuously, they did not institute marriage for a minor boy. On the contrary, it is forbidden to marry him off while he is still a minor. Therefore, in the case of a minor girl who was betrothed rabbinically while she was an orphan and then grew up, the betrothal becomes rabbinical when she reaches adulthood, as explained in Siman 155. However, for a minor boy, even after he grows up, the betrothal does not become valid unless he has intercourse with her or they seclude themselves after he has grown up. Hence, if a minor boy betroths, they must wait until he grows up and then he must betroth her anew. However, if they are already married, he does not need to divorce her, and she is permitted to remain with him until he grows up. For this reason, the Sages instituted that his intercourse should not be considered promiscuity (Mordechai Yevamot Chapter 6), because since it is in the context of betrothal and marriage for him, it is not considered promiscuity, even if she is an adult (Rosh). This is why the Sages instituted marriage for a deaf-mute, as explained in Siman 44, because he will never reach the status of marriage. But a minor boy will reach the status of marriage when he grows up. See what I wrote in Siman 1, Section 11.

Even though a minor sent gifts after he became an adult, and even in a place where we are concerned about the significance of gifts as mentioned in Siman 45, nevertheless, it is nothing, and we are not concerned that perhaps he sent them for the sake of betrothal. For certainly, he sent them with the intent of affirming the original betrothal. And this that we said, that if the husband consummated the marriage after he became an adult, it counts as a valid betrothal, the reason is that he is aware that the betrothal from his minority might be nothing, so he intended and consummated the marriage for the sake of betrothal, so that the intercourse would not be promiscuous. But for gifts, why should he be concerned? And also for intercourse or seclusion, it is specifically when there are witnesses to the seclusion that they secluded themselves after he became an adult [Rosh HaMadir, end of Siman 11]. And if he lived with her after he became an adult in the manner of husband and wife, there is no need for witnesses of seclusion, because since it is publicly known, it is as if there are witnesses, as mentioned in Siman 149, and see what is written at the beginning of Siman 26.

If he upheld it when he matured – her original ketubah is valid and there is no need to write her another ketubah. And even though the ketubah document given during his minority is not valid at all, nevertheless, since the ketubah is a rabbinic enactment, his document is effective even if written during his minority. Therefore, she is entitled to only the basic amount – one hundred if she was a widow and two hundred if she was a virgin, according to the law. However, any additional amounts that he wrote for her during his minority are not valid, as his obligation is not binding at all. All of this is when he wrote her a ketubah during his minority. But if he did not write her a ketubah during his minority, when he matures, he only writes her one hundred, because at that time she is not a virgin. There are those who disagree with this [Cheshek Shlomo], and the logical reasoning supports this because truly, the ketubah he wrote for her during his minority is not valid except due to the rabbinic enactment. Therefore, what difference does it make whether he wrote it or not? Certainly, if when he matured, he tells her before they have relations, "I will only give you a ketubah of one hundred," and she consents, it is definitely effective. But in general, he must give her the same amount as all virgins [there]. And the reasoning of the first opinion could be that if he wrote it during his minority, the sages uphold his ketubah. But if he did not write it, from where does the obligation come? The sages did not enact it during his minority, and he did not write it for her. His obligation only starts when he matures, and she is now a widow [and although the Beit Shmuel's proof in subsection 4 from Tosafot can be refuted, and see Even HaEzer, nevertheless, the first reasoning has a halachic basis, and the proofs of the Cheshek Shlomo are not decisive. On the contrary, from the Tur it implies the opposite, and what he wrote that he does not collect from the ketubah document, etc., means only from the ketubah document alone. See there and examine carefully].

There are those who have a doubt regarding a minor who betrothed a woman and said, "Behold, you are betrothed to me after I become an adult," or an adult who said to a minor, "Behold, you are betrothed to me after you become an adult." The question is whether since at the time of the betrothal they are minors, it is ineffective and is considered as something not yet in existence, similar to "after you are freed" in Siman 40, or whether it is different, because a matter that is lacking only in time is not considered as something not yet in existence [Maggid Mishneh, Hilchot Ishut, Chapter 4], since time will inevitably come. We found that one of the early authorities explicitly wrote that it is considered as something not yet in existence [Mordechai, Bava Metzia, Chapter 1], and this indeed seems correct, since if he is unable to betroth her now, how can he have the power to betroth her at a later time? Moreover, the main reasoning that a matter lacking only in time is not considered as not yet in existence is not universally accepted. Additionally, in this case, it is not just a matter of time, since they also lack the action of bringing two pubic hairs. Even though this seems clear, nevertheless, in practice, since many great authorities are in doubt about this, it is considered a doubtful betrothal. All the more so if he betrothed her on the day he completes 13 years, as at night he will have completed 13 full years, it is considered a doubtful betrothal. In the context of sacrificial offerings, we hold that lacking time on the same day is not considered lacking time [Zevachim 12a], although even this is not universally agreed upon, since some authorities hold that even regarding sacrifices, lacking time on the same day is considered lacking time [Tosafot, Menachot 5a]. Furthermore, this applies only to something that will be suitable on that same day and not on the next. In any case, this is certainly considered a doubtful betrothal, and it might even be considered a definite betrothal if we say that on that day when they bring two pubic hairs, it is effective [see Tosafot, Niddah 49b]. Even though it seems from the Talmud [Yevamot 34a] that betrothal in such a case, when betrothing after they become adults, is effective, it can be explained that it refers to a case where he betrothed her on the previous day [Rashi, there]. Furthermore, the discussion there follows the opinion that a person can transfer ownership of something not yet in existence, which is not the accepted ruling [as stated there in the name of the school of Rav and Rav Huna, as written in the first chapter of Sanhedrin, and Rav Huna holds that a person can transfer ownership of something not yet in existence in Yevamot 93b].

And there is someone who asked why a minor does not have the power to betroth a woman, for we hold that when someone else grants it to him, he has the power. Here, the woman is granting herself to him. The answer to this is twofold: Firstly, it is a scriptural decree, as it is written, “When a man takes a wife,” and wherever it says “man,” it excludes a minor. Secondly, if it were within the power of the woman to grant herself to a man by saying, “Behold, I am betrothed to you,” it would be fitting. However, we hold that this does not work, and he must take her, as it is written, “When a man takes a wife,” and not that she takes herself to the man. Rather, since she agrees to the man’s betrothal, she nullifies her own will and desire, and makes herself ownerless to the husband, and the husband brings her into his domain. According to this, it is not someone else granting it, but like someone acquiring from ownerless property.

One of the early authorities wrote: A minor boy of eleven years old whose father betrothed a woman for him—she requires a get (divorce document), because it is considered a benefit for a person even without their presence [Maharik Shoresh 32 in the name of Rabbi Yosef Barzilai]. And our master, the Beit Yosef, rejected this from the law and wrote that these are astonishing matters, and certainly it is so, for what benefit is there since he becomes obligated to her support? Additionally, he becomes forbidden to her relatives, and furthermore, it is forbidden to betroth a woman until one sees her, lest he finds something in her that he finds displeasing. All the more so with a minor who lacks understanding; certainly, there is concern that when he grows up she will not be pleasing in his eyes, so what benefit is there? And indeed, the sages said that it is forbidden to betroth one’s young daughter until she grows up and says, “I want this particular man,” and all the more so for a man. And in several places in the Talmud, it is explicitly stated that a minor cannot perform kiddushin (betrothal), and this matter is not mentioned by any of the early authorities.

And it appears that the one who wrote this did not intend it to apply to Torah-sanctioned marriages, and also did not intend that if, in his minority, he does not want her, she would require a get (divorce). For it is explicitly asked in the Jerusalem Talmud, Ketubot [Chapter 9]: "Is there divorce for a minor?" Rather, the case there refers to a situation where he remained with her for half a year after he reached adulthood [as explained in the Maharik]. And it seems that he did not seclude himself with her during his adulthood but did not explicitly protest. Nevertheless, many great authorities wanted to nullify the marriage, but he was stringent and required a get. And this is what he meant: that one can benefit a person not in their presence, meaning certainly, according to Torah law, the marriage is nothing, and even the Rabbis did not institute marriage for a minor. But since we find everywhere that every minor is pleased with his father's actions and desires to fulfill his father's will, therefore, in the case of a fire on Shabbat, a minor who comes to extinguish it is not prevented because he acts with his father's consent [Shabbat 121a], knowing that extinguishing the fire pleases his father and he does it for him [Rashi]. And regarding found items, we also say that at the moment he finds it, he is pleased for his father [Bava Metzia 12b], and when he lifts it for his father, he lifts it [Rashi], as the son is attached to his father and the daughter to her mother. Any matter that pleases his father also pleases him. Therefore, in such a case, if he reached adulthood and did not protest immediately upon reaching adulthood, it is considered a benefit for him, and the marriage stands. This can be inferred from the Mishnah in Ketubot [Chapter 9]: "A minor whom his father married off, her ketubah remains valid because he upheld it upon reaching adulthood." Why does it teach that his father married him off? It is because, otherwise, it is forbidden to marry off a minor, but if his father married him off, there is no prohibition because he is pleased with what his father did. Therefore, if he reached adulthood even by one day and did not protest, the marriage stands. And what we wrote in section 2, that we are not concerned with the marriage even if he sent gifts after reaching adulthood, this applies when he married her by himself and not through his father. And even in this, they disagreed with him [as written in the Maharik there, and do not refute me with what is written there: "Moreover, since he did not protest until the age of 13 and a half, who says he did not consent, etc., after he grew up, etc.," meaning one point is that since he did not protest, the marriage is valid even without explicit consent, and furthermore, etc. See there and examine carefully].

Some of the great authorities have stated that if a minor is married to a woman by his father a year before reaching the age of majority, he has a marriage from a Rabbinic standpoint. The statement that a minor does not have a marriage until he reaches full maturity only applies without his father's consent. However, with his father's consent and within a year of reaching maturity, there is a Rabbinic marriage [Bach, Siman 1]. Without his father’s involvement, it would be considered mere promiscuity. But when his father marries him off, he is taught not to engage in promiscuity and is guided in the proper way [ibid.]. There is support for this from the praise the Sages gave to those who marry off their sons close to their maturity, which some of our rabbis interpreted as within a year of reaching majority. However, many disagree, maintaining that the Rabbis did not institute marriage for any minor. This is also inferred from Maimonides in the twenty-first chapter of Issurei Biah, understanding “close to their maturity” as after they have matured. Even according to those who interpret it as before maturity, it does not mean that the marriage is Rabbinically valid, but rather that their intercourse is not considered promiscuous. However, the betrothal and marriage themselves are meaningless during their minority [Chomat Shlomo and Beit Shmuel, Siman 1, Seif Katan 4]. Similarly, Mordechai wrote in the sixth chapter of Yevamot that the Rabbis did not institute marriage for a minor, even close to his maturity. For the Sages said that if a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor marries a woman and dies, their wives are exempt from chalitzah and yibbum [Yevamot 69b], and similarly, they do not require a get (divorce document). This statement about marrying them off close to their maturity pertains to the idea that their intercourse is not considered promiscuous and does not require a get. End of quote. For more than a hundred years, due to the severity of the times, hundreds of minors and minor girls were married off. Based on the ruling of the great authorities of the generation, led by the Vilna Gaon, all these marriages were annulled without a get. Although some of the great authorities had reservations about this, the majority of the great authorities of that generation permitted it without a get.

However, for a minor girl, the Sages instituted a form of betrothal when she has no father, allowing her to be married based on the decision of her mother and brothers or based on her own decision. Additionally, they instituted that if she wishes to leave him, she does not need a divorce document (get), so that the choice remains in her hands, and she can refuse and leave him. The details of how refusal (mi'un) is done and until when she can refuse will be explained in Siman 155. Similarly, a minor girl who is no longer under her father's authority, such as if her father had married her off and she was subsequently divorced, can enter into a rabbinic marriage. Additionally, a court can decide to marry off a minor girl just as her mother and brothers can, and they can stipulate that if she refuses, she will lose all that she has. However, they do not have the authority to marry off a minor boy. If he betroths a woman and there is a doubt whether he is an adult or a minor, it is considered doubtful betrothal. The same applies to a minor girl. Even though one might say to maintain their previous status and consider them minors, nonetheless, since they will inevitably mature over time and most adults develop two pubic hairs, the presumption of permissibility does not apply.

[Laws of Marriages of Deaf-Mute, Insane, Drunk, Eunuch, Androgynous, and Forbidden Relationships, and Those Who Are Half-Slave or Maidservant, Containing Seventeen Sections]

A deaf-mute man and a deaf-mute woman are not subject to marriage according to Torah law, because they lack full mental capacity, as their intellect is weak and not clear. Therefore, whether they marry someone like themselves, or a deaf-mute man marries a hearing woman, or a deaf-mute woman marries a hearing man – their marriage is not valid according to Torah law. However, the sages instituted a form of marriage for them. Consequently, if a deaf-mute man marries a hearing woman and a hearing man then betroths her, she is considered fully betrothed to the hearing man. If the hearing man has relations with her, she is forbidden to both of them as an adulterous wife who is forbidden to both her husband and the adulterer. Even though her prohibition to the hearing man is only rabbinic, she is still considered a rabbinic prostitute, and he has relations with a rabbinically forbidden married woman. However, since according to Torah law the betrothal by the hearing man is valid, he must divorce her. And since she is also forbidden to the deaf-mute man, he too must divorce her. Although it is explained in Siman 28, Section 61 that rabbinic acquisition is effective even according to Torah law, this applies to monetary transactions where the rabbinic acquisition is considered as if it were actual money. This is not the case with a deaf-mute, who has no valid acquisition according to Torah law.

And specifically when a fully competent man (pikeach) has relations with her, but if he only betrothed her – he gives her a get (divorce document) and she is permitted to marry a deaf-mute (cheresh), and we are not concerned that people might say that the deaf-mute divorced her, and she was betrothed to the fully competent man, then divorced, and then returned to the first husband. For we do not make such a decree in the case of the marriage of a deaf-mute, which is only rabbinically ordained. Similarly, if a fully competent man betrothed a deaf-mute woman, and then another fully competent man betrothed her – both betrothals are effective, and even though the second one is also only rabbinic betrothal, nevertheless the betrothal is effective, as it is written in Siman 42, Se'if 44 regarding two who betrothed before witnesses disqualified by rabbinic law. And even according to the one who argues there, he agrees here that the acquisition of the deaf-mute woman is somewhat of an acquisition and somewhat reserved, and since there is a reservation in her acquisition, consequently the second betrothal is also effective rabbinically, as it is written similarly in Siman 40, Se'if 18. And even though regarding two new yevamot (widows subject to levirate marriage) it will be explained in Siman 171 that the intercourse of the second does not invalidate the first, this is because both acquisitions from the deceased brother are equal. But here, in betrothal, since there is a reservation in her, it is obvious that the second betrothal is effective rabbinically, and this resolves the question posed by the Makneh. Similarly, if a deaf-mute man married a deaf-mute woman and another deaf-mute betrothed her, she needs a get from the second and is permitted to the first for the reason explained. There is an opinion that wants to prohibit her to the first in such a case, and similarly if a fully competent man betrothed a deaf-mute woman and then another fully competent man betrothed her, for fear that people might say he is taking back his divorced wife after she was betrothed to another. This is not similar to when a deaf-mute marries a fully competent woman and then another fully competent man betrothed her, where she is permitted to the deaf-mute, because there everyone knows that the second betrothal is Torah law and the first is rabbinic betrothal. However, when both are rabbinic betrothal, we indeed make such a decree. Nevertheless, the primary opinion seems to be the first one, and so it is in the Jerusalem Talmud.

A fool, whether male or female, does not have valid betrothal (kiddushin) either by Torah law or Rabbinic law. For, specifically with the deaf, they established marriage because they have some degree of understanding, and there could be peace in the home. But fools who have no understanding at all, why would they establish marriage for them? Therefore, whether a fool marries a mentally competent woman or a mentally competent man marries a fool, there is no valid betrothal or marriage at all.

Therefore, only a complete fool, like those who are insane, who have no understanding and run in the streets and marketplaces and the like, are not considered married. But if his mind is clear, even though it is very poor and weak, the betrothal is valid. And if he is sometimes a fool and sometimes mentally competent and we do not know when he is in his right mind, we are concerned about his betrothal.

If his understanding is confused and he does not fully comprehend anything, some say that there is a concern for betrothal [Chemdas HaMishpat and Beis Shmuel], for although for testimony and ritual slaughtering we consider such a person a fool, nevertheless, for betrothal he is not called a fool unless he is a complete fool. 

Accordingly, even someone whose mind is deranged and whose understanding is confused in one matter, but in other matters he asks and answers appropriately, and also the very simple-minded who do not recognize matters that contradict one another, and also those who are bewildered and hasty in their understanding, although for testimony they are considered fools as Maimonides wrote in Chapter 9 of Testimony, nevertheless, for betrothal it is considered doubtful betrothal. For in terms of name, the deaf and the fool are the same, but for betrothal, the deaf and the fool are different as mentioned. Therefore, for betrothal, it must be a complete fool so that his betrothal is not valid at all. 

Certainly, those fools that the Sages in Chagigah [3b] considered as such, like one who goes out alone at night, one who sleeps in a cemetery, and one who tears his clothing, although they do this out of foolishness, nevertheless, regarding betrothal, they are not called fools. However, their betrothal is not certainly valid, but doubtful, and if she accepted betrothal from another, she needs a get (divorce document) from both [in my opinion].

A drunk person who betroths – their betrothal is valid even if they are very intoxicated, and similarly if she was intoxicated. For a drunk person's transactions are valid, but if they reached the level of Lot's intoxication – their betrothal is not valid because they have no awareness at that level. Much investigation is needed to determine whether they were at this level of intoxication, as sometimes it appears so but is not upon further investigation. All this applies after the fact, but ideally, it is proper for the groom and bride not to drink any intoxicating beverages before the betrothal, even a little. For this reason, it is customary to fast on the day of the wedding as stated in Siman 61, in order that they be fully sober. In Siman 121, it will be explained that we do not rely on our own recognition of intoxication. See there.

A eunuch who betroths, whether he is a natural-born eunuch or a man-made eunuch, such as one with crushed testicles – the betrothal is valid. Even though a man-made eunuch is subject to a negative commandment, betrothal is effective with those who are subject to negative commandments. Similarly, an ailonit (a woman who does not develop female secondary sexual characteristics and is infertile) who becomes betrothed – the betrothal is valid even though she cannot bear children, and not only if he knew she was an ailonit, but even if he did not know and it was a mistaken transaction, nevertheless, the betrothal is valid, and she requires a get (divorce). Some say that if he did not recognize her and she is found to be a definite ailonit, the betrothal is not valid even rabbinically, and it is worse than other defects, because for such a defect no man would forego. Her signs are that she has no breasts, or intercourse is difficult for her, or her voice is deep like a man's, or she does not have elevated and rounded flesh above that place – with one of these she is considered an ailonit. However, from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 2 of Ishut, it appears that he holds she must have all these signs to be a definite ailonit, and if she is a doubtful ailonit, even according to this opinion, she requires a get. And in the case of a eunuch, even if he did not know and he is a definite eunuch, according to all opinions, she requires a get, because a woman is willing to accept any man. The Rambam's opinion is like the first opinion that even a definite ailonit who was not recognized requires a get.

The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 4: A tumtum and an androgynous who betrothed a woman or were betrothed by a man—these are doubtful betrothals and require a doubtful divorce, end quote. And although in Chapter 1 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations he ruled that an androgynous is liable for sodomy like a male, it is not because he is certainly a male, but because the Torah included him from the verse "And with a male you shall not lie" (Leviticus 18:22), that from the place of his maleness he is liable for sodomy like a male, as stated in Siman 24, Section 2, look there. But in truth, he is a doubtful male, doubtful female. And this which he wrote that if they betrothed a man they need a divorce, and similarly, a tumtum needs a divorce—there are those who disagree with him, arguing why they need a divorce since they are not fit to marry [Raavad]. And some say that the reason of the Rambam is in order not to be liable afterward when he comes upon the androgynous through his female aspect as coming upon a doubtful married woman [Magid Mishneh and Beit Shmuel]. And similarly with a tumtum. And I am astonished—is it necessary to give a divorce in order to prevent someone from committing a more severe transgression, and behold, one who comes upon them commits a severe transgression and is flogged with lashes of rebellion as stated there. Therefore, it seems to me that on the contrary, we require a divorce so that they will not think that the betrothal is valid and will come upon them. Therefore, we require a divorce to separate them so they will know it is a great prohibition to come upon them. And know, that some of our Rabbis hold that an androgynous is certainly a male as the Tur wrote, but the decisors in many places concluded like the first opinion [Gra], and certainly a tumtum when torn and found to be a male—he is certainly a male, and similarly in the opposite case. But an androgynous has male and female characteristics and is always considered doubtful.

If one betroths any of the forbidden relatives, the betrothal is invalid because betrothal does not take effect with them, and there is no need for a get (bill of divorce). This is not similar to the cases of a tumtum (a person with indeterminate sexual characteristics) or an androgynous person when they are betrothed, where the Rambam (Maimonides) required a get, as he wrote that their betrothal is uncertain. However, with forbidden relatives, everyone knows that betrothal does not take effect. 

Regarding a menstruating woman, although she is considered forbidden (erva), if she is betrothed, the betrothal is valid, as it is written, "And her impurity shall be upon him" (Leviticus 15:24), indicating that even during her menstruation, the betrothal is valid. The word "shall be" (tehi) signifies existence [Yevamot 49b]. Even initially, one can betroth a menstruating woman. However, the Rambam wrote in Chapter 4 that it is not proper to do so, following his view that a wedding canopy (chuppah) with a menstruating woman is forbidden. Therefore, betrothal should not be done in a manner that would not be fitting for a chuppah. However, we do not follow this opinion as stated in Siman 61, and nonetheless, those who are meticulous strive to perform the betrothal in purity, in accordance with the Rambam's view, as mentioned there.

Similarly, if one betroths a secondary forbidden relationship or those forbidden by negative or positive commandments, the betrothal is valid, as betrothal takes effect with those forbidden by negative or positive commandments. This is certainly true if one betroths a woman while already married, even though this violates Rabbeinu Gershom's ban, it is still a valid betrothal. However, if a widow is betrothed to a man who is not her brother-in-law, although this is a negative commandment, there is doubt whether the betrothal takes effect because it is written, "The wife of the deceased shall not marry outside to a stranger" (Deuteronomy 25:5), and perhaps the Torah's intention is that there should be no betrothal to a stranger. In the case of the co-wife of a widow, certainly, the betrothal takes effect as stated in Siman 162. However, the co-wife of a forbidden relative is like the forbidden relative herself, and betrothal does not take effect with her.

If one consecrates a Kuthite (Samaritan) woman or a maidservant, it is nothing, for they are not eligible for consecration. Similarly, if a Kuthite or a slave consecrates an Israelite woman, it is nothing, as it is written regarding a slave, "Stay here with the donkey" – implying with someone who is like a donkey. The same applies to a maidservant. Concerning Kuthites, it is written, "You shall not intermarry with them." Additionally, it is said regarding a beautiful captive woman, "After that, you may go in to her and be her husband," implying that initially, she is not eligible for marriage. Moreover, they only have the status of a woman who is consorting with a man, not betrothal and marriage.

A Jew who has converted to Islam and betrothed a Jewish woman, or the reverse, their betrothal is fully valid. For even though they have sinned, they are still considered Jews, and all their legal status is like that of Jews, and she requires a get (divorce document) from him. Moreover, even the offspring he fathered after his conversion are considered complete Jews. If that offspring betroths a Jewish woman, or a Jew betroths a female from that offspring, it is a fully valid betrothal. Likewise, the offspring of their offspring until the end of all generations are considered Jews. This applies specifically to offspring fathered with a Jewish woman or a female apostate. However, if they fathered a child with a non-Jewish woman or a maidservant, the child is not Jewish but rather non-Jewish or a servant, for even a fully Jewish man who has relations with a non-Jewish woman or maidservant, the child is like her. And a female apostate who has offspring from a non-Jewish man or servant, the child is considered a complete Jew as stated in Siman 4, and if he betroths a woman, it is a fully valid betrothal. It is written in the Responsa of Maimonides [Women, Chapter 12], a response by Rabbeinu Natan, the author of the Aruch, as follows: You asked about a converted Jew who has a young daughter or a girl; if her father can accept her betrothal or not. This occurred in ancient times, and they said she is betrothed, and the one who accepted the betrothal can accept the divorce. But if he accepted the betrothal when he was a Jew, it is obvious to us that he cannot accept the divorce while he is converted. End of quote. See what is written in section 11.

The Samaritans whom Sennacherib settled in the Land of Israel and who converted out of fear of the lions, as described in the Book of Kings, even though our Sages considered them complete Samaritans in all respects, nevertheless, if one betrothed a woman, she requires a get (divorce document). This is because it is possible that our Sages' ruling was only as a stringency and not as a leniency. Even though we find that our Sages [at the beginning of Yevamot] regarding the ten tribes who assimilated among the nations considered them as complete idolaters even concerning betrothal, nevertheless, since we do not find this explicitly stated about the Samaritans in the Talmud, we are concerned about their betrothals. The Tur also wrote in the name of Rav Yehudai Gaon and Rav Shmuel Resh Kalah that a get is required, see there. It is obvious that if afterwards an Israelite betrothed her, she would also require a get from the Israelite, because perhaps even as a leniency their status is not like Israel, but if one Samaritan betrothed her after another Samaritan, she does not require a get from the second one in any case, since either the first betrothal is valid or neither of the betrothals is valid [so it seems to me].

There are those who say that what we have stated, that even his offspring whom he fathered after he converted, when they are born from a Jewish woman or someone similar, their status is as Jews, and if he betroths, his betrothal is valid, this applies only if it was not under coercion as in the early days during times of persecution. But if it was willingly, his offspring do not have the status of Jews [Ba'er Heitev section 8 in the name of Ben Habib and Rashdam]. However, there is no basis to these statements, for in what way is their Jewish status nullified? Even though their father's betrothal was not according to Jewish law, nevertheless, the offspring are Jewish, born outside of proper betrothal. And there are those who further say that if he converted and betrothed a woman, his betrothal is only valid rabbinically [ibid. section 17 in the name of Re'im]. However, there is no reason for this; if he betrothed in the presence of valid witnesses, why would his betrothal not be valid according to Torah law, knowing he is a convert? The Talmud explicitly states [Yevamot 47b, Bekhorot 30a] that if he betrothed, his betrothal is valid. It is true that some of the early authorities wrote that what the Sages stated, that his betrothal is valid, is only for stringency and not for leniency [Hagahot Maimoniot, chapter of the one who releases in the name of Rabbeinu Shimshon]. But from the words of most of our sages, it is clearly understood to be the opposite. Also, the Tur wrote that although some say that a public Sabbath desecrator and an idolater are considered like a full idolater and his betrothal is not valid – this is not acceptable. So wrote the Tur. And so it is clear from the Rambam and all the decisors, and so our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, ruled in section 9 [and I have seen in the Rashdam's end and there is no foundation to his words, and he also did not base his responsum on this, only that the betrothal was without witnesses. And it seems they learned this from what the sages said about the Ten Tribes, but from where do we derive this, for it is derived from the verse at the beginning of Yevamot].

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 4: One who betroths a woman who is half-slave and half-free is not fully betrothed until she is freed. Once she is freed, her betrothal is completed just like the betrothal of a minor who has grown up and there is no need to betroth her again. If another man comes and betroths her after she has been freed, it is a doubtful betrothal for both of them. And who is the "designated maidservant" mentioned in the Torah? It is one who is half-slave and half-free and was betrothed by a Hebrew slave. And one who is half-slave and half-free who betroths a free woman, it is a doubtful betrothal. And they were puzzled by this, for since her betrothal is completed after her release, why is she doubtfully betrothed to both if another man betroths her? Some want to say that according to Rambam, he is unsure whether the first betrothal is completed or annulled, because in the Gemara there is a dispute about this [Gittin 43b]. However, this does not seem to be the correct understanding of his words, for if so, he should have said it is a doubt, as he wrote regarding one who is half-slave. Rather, the explanation of his words is as follows: He ruled according to the opinion that the first betrothal is completed. And the intention is not that it is completed without any action, for without any action, even after the release, she is as before, betrothed but not fully married, punishable by a mere prohibition and not by death. This is the "designated maidservant" mentioned in the Torah who is liable to lashes, and the one who has relations with her brings a guilt offering, whether unintentionally or intentionally. And when are the betrothal and marriage fully completed? When she stays with him for some time after the release as husband and wife, and it is known to all that he has relations with her. Even if there are no witnesses to their seclusion, since they live as husband and wife, she becomes fully married. This is similar to a minor, as written in Siman 43, Section 2, regarding a minor. This is also the opinion of Rambam regarding a minor, as written there in Halacha 8 [see there in the Mishneh Torah]. Therefore, if another man comes and betroths her immediately after she is freed, it is a doubtful betrothal for both of them. The doubt is whether we say that since the first betrothal is only a mere prohibition, the second betrothal takes effect, or since she is half-betrothed to the first for a prohibition, the second betrothal does not take effect for this half, and consequently not for the other half either, for betrothal does not take effect on half a woman [and he explains the doubt of Rav Chisda there not like Rashi nor like Tosafot in the words "either way," but as he wrote. This also resolves Tosafot's difficulty in the words "completed," and also resolves the Ra'avad's objection brought by the Kesef Mishneh. The Tur made a dispute between Rambam and the Rosh, but according to what I wrote, they are the same, and this is the intention of the Beit Shmuel in Section 15, but what he wrote in Section 16 that we are unsure if it is completed or annulled, according to what I wrote, there is no need for this, and examine well].

From what has been explained, we learn that one who betroths a woman who is half slave and half free needs to give her a get (bill of divorce), as she is betrothed with a prohibition that is a negative commandment, and to obligate him in a sacrifice for having relations with her. If before giving her a get, she was set free and then another man betrothed her before the first man lived with her as husband and wife, she requires a get from both of them. This is because there is doubt if the second betrothal took effect or not, as mentioned. Alternatively, one of them could divorce her and the other could marry her with complete betrothal. Even the second man is permitted to divorce her and the first can marry her, and we do not worry that people might say the first man has taken back his divorcee after she was betrothed to another, because everyone knows that the first betrothal was not complete like other betrothals, as mentioned [Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel]. This is also evident from the language of the Tur. However, our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote that the first should divorce her and the second should marry her. If both of them died, the brother of one of them performs chalitzah (ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage), and the brother of the second either performs chalitzah or levirate marriage. However, the first brother does not perform levirate marriage, because perhaps she is the yevamah (widow) of the second. But the second brother can perform levirate marriage in any case — if she is indeed his yevamah, then he is performing levirate marriage properly, and if not, she has already been released from the first and is permitted to the general public. This is not a case of the wife of two deceased men, which will be explained in the laws of yibbum (levirate marriage) as forbidden to be taken in levirate marriage, because in any case, only the betrothal of one of them is valid. Therefore, even if the brother of the first betrothed her after her release and they died, she is permitted to their third brother, as she is not the wife of two deceased men [Gemara].

And all of this applies when the second man betrothed her immediately after she was freed, before they lived together. But if the first man lived with her after her release as husband and wife, the original betrothal is completed, for he knew that he had betrothed only half of her, and consequently, his intention was that his betrothal would be completed through his intercourse with her in entirety. Moreover, he knew that even for the betrothal of the half that was free, it was not initially a complete betrothal, but only a prohibition and not a death penalty, as with all betrothals, and now he completes the betrothal as in all other cases of betrothal.

If another man betroths her before she is freed, it seems clear that the betrothal of the second man does not take effect, because whatever potential for betrothal exists has already been taken by the first man [Beit Shmuel]. However, some say that the betrothal of the second man does take effect, because in the case of a married woman, betrothal does not take effect due to the liability of death penalty, but in this case, where there is only a prohibition (lav), betrothal takes effect as it does with all those who are subject to prohibitions [Avnei Miluim, Note 4]. In my opinion, the primary view is the first one, that we do not find a concept of marriage after marriage. Since the Torah decreed that betrothal does not take effect with a married woman, there is no difference between a married woman who is liable for the death penalty and one who is liable for prohibitions. Furthermore, in the Gemara, they were uncertain whether, after she is freed, the first betrothal is completed or nullified. If we say that before she is freed there is betrothal after betrothal, we would have to say that even after she is freed, the first betrothal remains in place and the second betrothal also takes effect, which would not be less significant than before she is freed. Therefore, it is certain to the Sages that in any case, betrothal does not take effect after betrothal, and thus before she is freed, the second betrothal certainly does not take effect. Only after she is freed were they uncertain because the second betrothal is stronger than the first, and therefore there is reason to say that the first betrothal is nullified.

And this is what the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote: concerning a half-slave and half-free man who betroths a woman, it is considered doubtful betrothal. The doubt arises because perhaps, just as we hold that if a man says to a woman, "Be betrothed to half of me," she is betrothed, as stated in Siman 31, so too here, he betroths her with his half that is free. Or perhaps it is different there because she perceives his entire body, and when he says "to half of me," he means he will take another wife, which is not the case here because she does not perceive his entire body, as the half that is a slave is not eligible for betrothal.

And why did we say regarding a half-maidservant that the betrothal is definite and warrants lashes? This is because the Torah decreed so, as it is written, "And she is a woman who is an engaged maidservant" (Leviticus 19:20), and the tradition teaches us that it refers to a half-maidservant and half-free woman [Ran]. And why don't we derive the law of a slave from a maidservant? Because it is a novel concept, as these betrothals differ from all other betrothals in the world, where general betrothals are subject to the death penalty, but these betrothals are only subject to a negative commandment, and we do not derive from a novel concept [in my opinion].

There is one who says that the reason is because the primary acquisition is through the man; therefore, we require that he betroths her, not that she be betrothed to him. Hence, with a half-slave, the aspect of slavery does not betroth the aspect of freedom, similar to the shofar, where one does not fulfill the mitzvah by blowing it himself for this reason, as stated in Orach Chaim, Siman 589. However, with a half-maidservant, he only betroths the half that is free, and she becomes nullified to him, and even the aspect of her servitude can become nullified, as this is not a valid acquisition [Avnei Miluim].

And this reason is not sufficient, for it is not comparable to a shofar, where a man needs to blow, and here a half-man is blowing. But in betrothal, it is not obligatory that he betroths her, and in the other half, the betrothal is valid, and we do not need the aspect of his servitude at all. And if the concern is that when he has relations with her, the aspect of slavery will be used in a prohibited manner – indeed, this is true, as our Sages said in Yevamot [45b], but we see that this is not a reason for our Sages to doubt the betrothal [Gittin 43b] and annul it for this reason, as these matters are not related. And the primary point is as I have written.

And there is a question regarding these laws as to why they were written by the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, since we hold that we compel the master to free him, as it is written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 267. And behold, he is considered entirely a free man, so how can this law be understood? The answer is that we find this case when the second half belongs to minor orphans, who cannot be compelled. Additionally, even though we compel the master, as long as he has not written a release document, his status is not that of a fully free man. There is a doubt in the Gemara if one who is held back from receiving a release document has the status of a free man or not. We have explained this above in Siman 4, Se'if 17, see there.

[The Laws Regarding the Concern of Betrothal through Gifts and Writing a Ketubah, with 22 Sections]

Our Sages of blessed memory said that there is a concern of betrothal with the gifts that the groom sends to the bride, and there are detailed laws regarding this as will be explained. However, regarding the primary interpretation of "gifts," our early sages disagreed. Rashi of blessed memory explained that there is a concern that the gifts themselves might have been sent for the purpose of betrothal. The Rif and the Rambam explained that we are concerned that he might have betrothed her beforehand since the sending of gifts is a sign of prior betrothal. There are practical differences in the law between these two interpretations.

How so? According to Rashi, there is no concern of "Sablonot" (gifts given in the context of betrothal) unless he sent them with witnesses, and there were also witnesses present at the time of giving them into her hand. In such a case, even if he did not explicitly state that he is giving them for the sake of betrothal, since they had previously discussed marriage arrangements, as will be explained, it is as if they were discussing matters of betrothal. Thus, even if he gave them in silence, it constitutes betrothal, as stated in Siman 27, Se'if 16. This opinion holds that since there were prior discussions of marriage arrangements, it is as if they had spoken about matters of betrothal, as referenced there. 

There are those who are stringent if he sent the gifts with witnesses, even if there were no witnesses at the time of giving them. Their reasoning is that just as we hold regarding betrothal through intercourse that the same witnesses who observe the seclusion (yichud) are considered witnesses to the intercourse, so too here, we say that the same witnesses who observe the sending are considered witnesses to the giving. At the moment the betrothal takes effect, no witnesses are needed. 

Even though it is explained in Siman 42 that this applies only to intercourse, whereas with money, the witnesses need to see the giving of it into her hand, it must be said that here, since the presumption is that an agent fulfills his agency, it is similar to the witnesses of seclusion in the case of intercourse. There are others who are even more stringent and say that even without witnesses to the sending, we are concerned for betrothal if it is established that he sent the gifts in a place where it is customary to send rings or similar items after the marriage arrangements. This is considered as if we ourselves witnessed that he sent them for the sake of betrothal, provided that the majority betroth with such gifts. This is an excessive stringency, and if there were no witnesses at the time of sending the gifts, there is no need for concern. However, if he sent the gifts through someone, there is no need to be concerned at all for this opinion. Even though we are stringent with betrothal witnessed by one person, in this case, we need not be stringent with gifts, as it is merely a minor concern.

But according to the Rambam's opinion, we are concerned even if he did not send with witnesses, since the concern is that perhaps he had already betrothed her. And only when they admit that he sent [gifts] to her are we concerned about betrothal. And even though if so, since they say that he did not betroth her previously, they should be believed by virtue of "the mouth that forbids is the mouth that permits," nevertheless, this is like a "migo" in the place of witnesses [Choshen Mishpat 1], since it is discussed in a place where the custom is to betroth before sending gifts, as will be explained – they are not believed to claim against the custom even when they have a "migo," since a "migo" in the place of a custom is not said as it is written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 82, in the principles of "migo." And according to this opinion, if he says that he betrothed her with the gifts, then there is no longer a concern that he had betrothed her previously, for he claims in his interest that he betrothed her, and since he claims that he betrothed her with the gifts, it is like a clarification that he did not betroth her previously. And for the concern of the gifts themselves being for betrothal, we are not concerned according to this opinion [Beit Shmuel 1], since this opinion does not hold this concern at all because since he did not specify that they were for betrothal, and silence during engagement is not akin to being engaged in that matter [Tosafot 56b] as it is written in Siman 27, Se'if 16.

And conversely, there is a difference when there are witnesses that she was not betrothed previously – according to the view of the Rambam, this concern is removed, but according to Rashi, it does not help since the concern is that he may have betrothed her now with the gifts. Regarding betrothal agreements, it is the opposite: according to Rashi, without an intermediary there is no concern of gifts, but according to the Rambam, it appears that even without an intermediary, this concern exists. However, from the words of our teacher, the Rema, it is understood that even according to the Rambam, we are not concerned if there is no intermediary, because otherwise, we would have to be concerned about betrothal for anyone who gives a gift to an unmarried woman in the presence of witnesses. But from the words of several authorities, it is understood that according to this view, even without an intermediary, we must be concerned about betrothal [Beit Shmuel, section 7], because this concern only applies to things that it is customary for the groom to send to the bride, but for other items, this concern does not exist. It is not customary to give an unmarried woman gifts that the groom sends to his bride, and if indeed he gave her such items in the presence of witnesses, we certainly are concerned about betrothal [Avnei Miluim, section 5]. According to this, a distinction arises between this view and that of Rashi, because according to Rashi, we are certainly concerned about betrothal with anything he sent her [it seems to me].

There is another practical difference: if one sends betrothal gifts to a minor after her father's death, according to the Rambam, there is a concern that perhaps her father had accepted the betrothal, whereas according to Rashi, there is no such concern, and refusal (mi'un) is sufficient [Beit Shmuel]. It is also possible that refusal is not needed at all for the concern of betrothal gifts. Similarly, if the woman sent him betrothal gifts, according to Rashi, there is no concern, but according to the Rambam, there is a concern [there]. Additionally, if the groom himself did not send the gifts but his father did, according to Rashi, there is no concern, but according to the Rambam, there is a concern [there]. 

Likewise, if the gifts were sent on Shabbat or Yom Tov, when it is prohibited to betroth a woman, there is no concern according to Rashi, but there is a concern according to the Rambam [there]. Another practical difference is that according to Rashi, there is no concern unless he sent the gifts without specifying their purpose, in which case there is a concern that perhaps his intention was for betrothal, but if he explicitly stated that they were betrothal gifts, there is no concern. According to the Rambam, the concern remains that perhaps he had betrothed her initially. Some say that even according to Rashi, there is no concern when the gifts were sent without specification unless they were sent with affectionate language, in which case there is a concern for betrothal. According to this, if he explicitly sent them as a gift, even if he used affectionate language, there is no concern for betrothal [there, section 5, see there]. 

When he explicitly sent them as betrothal gifts, and certainly if he used the language of a gift, there is no concern, even if he said that the groom is sending to the bride, there is no concern, because the terms groom and bride apply from the time of the engagement. Know that according to Rashi, in any case where there is a concern for betrothal, even if both parties say they did not intend for betrothal, and even if they swore to this effect, we do not pay attention to them, and she requires a get, similar to the Rambam's position if they say that she was not betrothed initially as mentioned.
