And with what has been explained, that when he sent on Shabbat and Yom Tov we do not worry about the betrothal, some say that in any situation where we would have to be concerned that he committed a transgression if his intent was to betroth through the sending of gifts, such as if there is a prohibition in the city not to betroth with less than ten people present, and the like – we do not worry that he sent them for the sake of betrothal. However, according to the Rambam, we should be concerned. There is also an opinion that when there is a prohibition in the city not to betroth with less than ten people, even according to the Rambam, we do not worry that he already betrothed her, for if he had betrothed her in the presence of ten, it would have been publicly known, and we do not need to worry that he betrothed her with less, as stated by the [Chiddushei HaMeiri]. 

Similarly, with what has been explained that if the father of the groom sent the gifts, there is no concern for betrothal, even if the messenger said, "The groom sent this to you," it means nothing, for what effect does his statement have? However, if the groom stood by when his father sent the gifts, and the groom was silent, or if the father said, "Take this to the bride in the name of the groom," he has certainly granted him the gifts. Therefore, based on what is written in Siman 35, that if the father presented before the son and the son was silent, it is a case of doubtful betrothal, if the messenger delivered the gifts to the bride in the name of the groom, and in places where most people betroth first and then give gifts – some say that we should be concerned about betrothal, and even if there is a minority who betroth and then give gifts – it is possible we should be concerned.

There is another distinction: according to Rashi, there is no concern of betrothal unless the bride herself received the gifts. However, if her father, mother, brother, or other household members received them, the concern is removed. But according to the Rambam, there is no distinction since the concern is about the past time. Some say that even according to Rashi, there is a concern that perhaps she appointed an agent to receive the gifts for the sake of betrothal. However, according to this, if the groom said, "Give the gifts to the bride," and she handed them to someone else, there is no betrothal, because even if he intended betrothal, the agent deviated from the intention of the sender. Certainly, if the groom said, "Give the gifts to one of her household members on behalf of the bride," there is no concern. This situation only arises when he gave them without specifying [this is my understanding]. And know that according to Rashi, there is no difference whether the groom sent the gifts through an agent or gave them to her himself. In a situation where we are concerned, we are concerned even if he sent them through an agent, and in a situation where we are not concerned as will be explained, we are not concerned even if he gave them to her himself. This is unlike those who are stringent and say that if he gave them himself, we are always concerned even in a situation where there is no legal reason to be concerned about the gifts, and certainly, according to the Rambam, there is no distinction in this.

In what cases do we worry about gifts (sivlonot)? The Rambam writes in Chapter 9: In a place where the custom is to send gifts to the betrothed woman after she is betrothed, and witnesses come and testify that they saw gifts being brought to her, we are concerned that she might have been betrothed and she requires a get (divorce document) out of doubt, even though the majority of the people in the city do not send gifts except before the betrothal. But in a place where the custom is for everyone to send gifts first and then betroth, if they saw gifts, we are not concerned (for betrothal). It is clear from his words that when he writes "in a place where the custom is," he means that even if the minority have this custom, we are concerned for the minority in the stringency of a married woman, just as they were stringent in several matters such as water without an end and similar cases [Rosh]. Additionally, this majority is different from other majorities because the nature of the matter is such, but here it is only a custom and sometimes a person follows the minority custom. Therefore, in the case of the prohibition of a married woman, they were stringent to be concerned [Ramban]. However, this is specifically when the minority regularly do so, but where even the minority do not do this consistently and only occasionally betroth and then send gifts, it is not even considered a minority [Rashba]. For if the entire city always does the opposite, sending gifts first and then betrothing, even if sometimes they happen to send gifts after the betrothal, we are not concerned about the gifts.

And know that from the language of the Rambam, it becomes clear that it is specifically when witnesses came who saw the gifts, but based on their own testimony, they are believed to say that he did not betroth her previously, unlike what is stated in paragraph 3. However, our teacher the Rema wrote this regarding the language of the Rambam, which is the language of the author. It seems that he holds that the Rambam did not specifically mean witnesses. And indeed, the language of the Rema can be interpreted that the stringency is when he did not send them with witnesses, but nevertheless, for the sending itself, witnesses are required. However, the great later authorities wrote explicitly as stated in paragraph 3, and it must be said that they hold that the Rambam did not intend to exclude only if they deny that he sent gifts at all, for then witnesses are required, and even one witness is not valid because one witness in a case of denial is worthless. But when they admit, one should be stringent [so it seems to me].

Therefore, some say that if there are no witnesses and only their own admission, they are not believed that there were no prior betrothals except in a place where the majority first betroth and then send gifts, but we do not consider this for the minority in such a case [Taz]. The reasoning supports this because they have a "migu" (a legal presumption), and specifically where the majority first betroth and then send gifts, they are not believed with a "migu" against the custom of the majority, but against the minority, it is obvious that they are believed with a "migu." However, from the language of our teacher, the Rema, it does not seem so unless we say, as mentioned, that his intention is that there is no need to send with witnesses, but witnesses are needed for the sending (of gifts). Nevertheless, according to the law, some are stringent even in such a case if when they initially said they sent the gifts they did not say that there was no prior betrothal. Therefore, even if they said so afterward, they are not believed with a "migu" because it would be a retrospective "migu" [Beit Shmuel, paragraph 3].

And know, from the language of the Tur it becomes clear that according to Rashi's opinion, we are stringent with gifts (sivlonot) only in a place where the majority sanctify (i.e., perform Kiddushin) and then give gifts. For in such a case, there is a concern that the gifts were sent for the purpose of Kiddushin and not as mere presents, according to the custom. But for a minority, we are not concerned. And logic supports this, for indeed it would be an excessive stringency to worry about Kiddushin when it was not mentioned at all, and it is sufficient to be stringent with the majority and not with the minority. And this is also Rashi's opinion in the Gemara. Nevertheless, there are those who are stringent according to Rashi's opinion even in the case of a minority, and therefore it is appropriate to be stringent in practice even in such a case [there, section 4]. And this also seems to be implied from the language of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: Some say that all gifts sent immediately after the betrothal, within a day or two, are of no concern at all, and even if he sends her gifts later as well, since he sent her gifts initially, we see that he sends gifts first and then betroths, and we are not concerned about these gifts. His words mean that, according to Maimonides, there is certainly no concern immediately after the betrothal that perhaps he had betrothed her earlier, because if so, it would have become public knowledge, given that it is a short time after the betrothal. And although it is possible that he betrothed her privately [Ketubot 23], in this case, there is no concern for that, since the betrothal was public, and why would he betroth her privately? Therefore, concerning these gifts, there is no worry, and consequently, there is no concern for all his gifts, since we see that this man first sends gifts and then betroths. 

Some of the great authorities have said that this only helps if most people first send gifts and then betroth, and only a minority first betroth and then send gifts – this reasoning is effective against the minority. But if most people first betroth and then send gifts – this reasoning is not effective. According to Rashi, who is concerned that the gifts themselves might be for betrothal, there is no proof from the short time after the betrothal. However, if the groom and bride were in the same city and he sent the gifts through a messenger, there is proof that they are not for betrothal, because if he intended them for betrothal, why did he not give them to her himself? This concern for gifts sent through a messenger applies when they are not in the same city. However, according to Rashi, there is no difference between gifts given immediately after the betrothal and those given later [see Beit Shmuel, section 8; Even HaEzer, sections 6 and 7; Makneh; and Tosafot Gittin 64, s.v. "Ba'al" – study this well].

However, from the words of our master, the Rema, it appears from the arrangement of his words that according to all opinions and in all places, there is no need to be concerned in this manner. His reasoning is that it is not customary to perform the betrothal immediately after the engagement, and since the primary concern regarding gifts (sivlonot) according to Rashi's opinion is a distant concern that we should worry about betrothal when the language of betrothal was not mentioned at all, and even according to the Rambam, it would be a great stringency to remove this woman from her status as single based on something for which we have no evidence and only because of the stringency of a married woman do we act stringently in this matter. Therefore, since it is not customary to perform the betrothal immediately after the engagement and it becomes clear that it is customary to send gifts before the betrothal, there is no longer a concern regarding his gifts, as it has been clarified that this man is among those who send gifts and then perform the betrothal. Nevertheless, since the latter authorities were stringent in this matter, it is difficult to be lenient in practice [see Chavatzelet HaSharon, subparagraph 6, and Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 9; their words are not conclusive to one who examines the Maharik, and the Rema did not derive this directly from there but rather relied on the great opinion and proof for his view from there as is his custom, and pay close attention].

It is further written: All concerns regarding gifts are only to initially necessitate a get (divorce document), but if she has already married, she does not need to leave (her new husband), and we are lenient in cases of doubt. And the great authorities have also written that this only applies in places where the majority first give gifts and then betroth, for when the minority first betroth and then give gifts, we are lenient and not strict against the majority. However, there are those who are lenient in cases of doubt even against the majority, stating that a matter dependent on custom is not considered a complete majority, and it may be from the minority. And since this is only a general concern and she is presumed to be single, we cannot consider her a married woman based on a general concern when they themselves say that they did not betroth her beforehand and did not intend the gifts for betrothal. Nonetheless, in practice, one must deliberate on the matter, and it is difficult to be lenient unless according to the judgment of the great authorities of the region based on the situation. However, in our countries, where everyone first gives gifts and then betroths, as will be explained, it is certainly permissible to be lenient in cases of doubt regarding gifts, unless the groom states that he intended them for betrothal.

Regarding the concern of gifts (sablonot), we should be stringent according to the stringencies of both approaches—of Rashi and of the Rambam. And although most of the earlier authorities wrote like the Rambam, nevertheless, we should also be stringent according to Rashi's approach. It has already been explained in section 6 that in a place where there is a prohibition, if one intended the gifts for the sake of betrothal, we do not worry about it. Therefore, if the man who sent the gifts subsequently married another woman, we no longer worry about the gifts, for if he had betrothed her, he would not marry another woman and transgress the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom [Beit Shmuel, Section 16]. 

Similarly, we are only stringent about gifts if it has been clarified that he sent the gifts, but if there is only a rumor that he sent gifts, we do not worry about betrothal. And even though we are concerned about a rumor of betrothal as stated in section 46, nevertheless, since the rumor of betrothal that we are stringent about is only a stringency and also the concern of gifts is merely a stringency, we do not apply two stringencies [Chochmat Adam]. This is specifically when they deny the rumor and say that he did not send anything at all, but when they admit that he sent but it was in a place where most people send gifts and then betroth, they are believed with a miggo as stated in section 10. However, since there is a rumor, the miggo is nullified, for we do not say miggo to contradict a rumor as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 150 [Mekaneh].

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote: Nowadays, the custom in all the provinces of Israel, Egypt, and Turgama is not to be concerned about gifts (sablonot), except in Constantinople where they are concerned about them. The reason is that in his days, in all these places, everyone would first give gifts and then perform the betrothal. According to this, in all our regions where the custom is widespread that engagements are made, gifts are sent, and then after some time the betrothal and chuppah (wedding canopy) are done together, it seems clear that one should not be concerned about gifts. Even if someone claims that he intended the gifts for betrothal, it seems that one should not be concerned, because the one who makes a claim against the custom has to bring proof, especially since she also has the presumption of being single.

However, from the words of our teacher, the Rema, it does not seem so, as he wrote: "And some say that one should be stringent even in a place where everyone first gives gifts and then betroths, unless there is another reason to permit it. And it seems to me that if the groom states that he only sent the gifts as mere presents – according to everyone, there is no need for concern in such a case, and indeed, it happens every day that engagements are broken off and the gifts are returned, and it is not customary to require a get (divorce document) since in these places nowadays everyone first gives gifts and then betroths, and the groom does not claim that he sent the gifts for the sake of betrothal." These are his words. It is clearly explained that if the groom claims he sent the gifts for the sake of betrothal, even if the bride denies it, we are concerned and may require a get. In truth, many of the great authorities disagree with this and hold, as I wrote, that since everyone first gives gifts and then betroths, we do not pay attention to his words. All the more so in our country, where betrothals are conducted under the chuppah (wedding canopy) and not even one in a thousand betroths before the wedding – it is obvious that there is no concern regarding the gifts.

And it seems to me that in our regions, even our teacher, the Rema, would agree that there is no concern even when the groom claims otherwise. The reason he is stringent, even though everyone waits and then sanctifies, is explained in the source of the law. It is because there might be a minority who sanctify and then wait [Choshen Mishpat]. This only applies in regions where they sanctify a long time before the wedding ceremony. But in our regions, where everyone sanctifies under the wedding canopy, this concern is completely removed. 

And what he wrote, that it is common practice to return from engagements, applies equally to all places—even when they sanctify before the wedding ceremony. In such cases, there is a concern if the groom claims that he intended it as a sanctification. But in our regions, he is not believed without proof. Also, from the Levush it is clearly understood that his conclusion, “and the groom does not say that he sent for the sake of sanctification,” does not mean if the groom says so. Rather, it means that no groom says such a thing, and consequently, even if someone does say so, he is not believed. However, from his previous words, it does not imply this. Therefore, it appears as I have written.

Just as we are concerned about gifts, so too we are concerned about the ketubah (marriage contract). If he wrote her a ketubah and it reached her hands, it is considered as definite betrothal, for it is obvious that they do not give a woman a ketubah before betrothal. And even if it has not yet reached her hands, and even if the majority of the people in the city write the ketubah and then betroth, if there is a minority where the established custom is to betroth and then write the ketubah, we are concerned that he might be from the minority and she has already been betrothed. And even though there is a reason to attribute the writing of the ketubah to something else, such as there being no available scribe in the city and it happened that a scribe was available to write it, and therefore he wrote it not because he betrothed her, nevertheless, due to the stringency regarding a married woman, we do not rely on this unless it is clarified with witnesses that he did not betroth her. Or if the matter of the ketubah is revealed solely by himself and he says that he did not betroth her, he is believed with a "migo" (a legal principle where a claim believed in one context is believed in another) against the minority, as we stated regarding gifts.

And if it is the custom of all the people in the city to write the ketubah (marriage contract) before the betrothal, as is the clear custom among us, there is no concern regarding the betrothal. And it appears to me that even Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema), who was stringent regarding gifts even in a place where everyone gives gifts and then performs the betrothal, would agree regarding the ketubah if everyone writes it before the betrothal. There, he was stringent due to the possibility that we might not be well-versed in the custom and there might be some who betroth beforehand, as he wrote. But with regard to the ketubah, the custom is clear to write it before the betrothal in all our lands, and even regarding gifts, the law is the same in our country, as I wrote in paragraph 17.

The concern of a ketubah (marriage contract) arises even when there was no formal betrothal, provided it is known that it was written with the consent of both parties. For once they agree to write a ketubah, it is obvious that there are matters of betrothal between them. However, if it was not written with the consent of both parties, we are not concerned with the ketubah unless there was a formal betrothal [Beit Shmuel]. And know that in a place where we are not concerned, we are not concerned even for both matters together. For example, if he sent her gifts and also wrote her a ketubah, if it is a place where everyone gives gifts first and then betroths, and everyone writes a ketubah and then betroths – we are not concerned [there].

It is clear that if there is a certain custom in a city, we follow the custom. If there was a custom and it was nullified, we follow the current practice. If there was never a fixed custom in the city or it is a new city where people have gathered from many places, and the nearby towns have different customs, we treat it as a fifty-fifty situation and are concerned about betrothal. If it is known that everyone came from one region where there is a fixed custom, we follow that custom. If someone comes from a place where they are not concerned about giving gifts as a sign of betrothal to a place where they are concerned, we follow the custom of the place he came from, unless he has been here for thirty days, in which case he is considered like a resident of this city [as mentioned there]. Even though we hold that one applies the stringencies of the place to which one has come, as stated in Orach Chaim 496, this applies to the stringencies of prohibitions. But here, since the concern is that he might have betrothed, if he came from a place where they are not concerned about gifts as a sign of betrothal, there is no concern about betrothal through gifts. Therefore, even if he does not intend to return, we do not consider it. Only if he has settled here for thirty days, it is assumed he has become aware of their custom, and thus he also follows their custom, and there is a concern about betrothal [so it seems to me].

[Laws Regarding Rumors in Betrothal and Whether the Rumor is Nullified, Containing 26 Sections]
A woman about whom a rumor has spread that she is betrothed to a certain man and she is single, the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 9, Law 22 that she is considered betrothed even though there is no clear evidence. Any rumor that has not been confirmed in court is not taken into consideration. What kind of rumor would confirm that she is betrothed? For example, if two people came and testified that they saw candles lit, beds made, and people coming and going, and women rejoicing with her and saying, "So-and-so was betrothed today." If they heard them saying, "So-and-so will be betrothed today," it is not taken into consideration, as perhaps they gathered to betroth her but the betrothal did not take place, until it is heard that she was betrothed. Similarly, if two people came and said, "We saw something like an engagement celebration and heard festive sounds and heard from someone who heard from someone else that so-and-so was betrothed in the presence of certain individuals," and the witnesses then went to another country or died, this is considered a rumor that confirms her betrothal, end of quote.

Explanation of his words: The general noise in the city is of no consequence unless this noise is substantiated in a court by valid witnesses who testify that they themselves saw the preparations for the betrothal according to common custom. Even though they do not know about the actual betrothal itself, having only heard it from women or from someone who heard it from someone else, and the witnesses to the betrothal have died or gone away – this is called a "rumor," because it is akin to having a basis since they themselves testify that they saw the preparations with their own eyes. The difference between hearing from women or from one witness, although legally they are the same, is clarified in his words: hearing from women means that they themselves saw the betrothal, whereas one witness may not have seen the betrothal himself and did not hear it from two witnesses but from one witness who saw the betrothal. Therefore, when it comes to women, he wrote that they should say "she was betrothed today," but for a witness, he did not write this. The women, having seen the betrothal themselves, need to say that it was today, but the witness who heard from them does not say he saw it himself but heard it from someone else, so how can he know when the betrothal occurred? The reason why women must say they saw it themselves and it is not enough for them to say they heard it, it seems to me, is because the testimony of one witness is considered valid by Torah law for obligating an oath, therefore his hearsay testimony is effective for a rumor. However, women have no substantial standing unless they say they saw it themselves. Another possible explanation of his intention is that since for a witness he added that these witnesses themselves heard the general noise in the city about the betrothal, it suffices if he also testifies as a secondary witness. In any case, we learn from his words that even for a witness, it is necessary that they see the preparations for the betrothal.

And some of our rabbis hold that in the case of hearsay testimony, it is not necessary that the witnesses see the preparations for the betrothal. The reason is that hearsay testimony is, at any rate, a clear matter regarding the rumor that has spread, for they testify that so-and-so testified from so-and-so and so-and-so from so-and-so. Even though this is not valid testimony for legal matters, nevertheless, regarding the rumor, it is considered a clear matter. However, when women say, "So-and-so was betrothed today," this is not considered a clear matter but rather just a general rumor. Therefore, we require that these people see the preparations for the betrothal, and it would be considered as having a basis, so that it does not need to be a clear matter.

There are some of our rabbis who hold that hearing from women and seeing the preparations is a more reliable sign of the voice than hearing testimony from a witness who heard from another witness. If the voice went out at the time, it is of no use at all to have heard from a witness who heard from another witness. Rather, it is specifically when they saw the preparations—candles lit, beds made, and women saying "So-and-so was betrothed today." But if the voice went out afterwards, it is sufficient to have heard from a witness who heard from another witness. [Rashba in his responsa, brought by Beit Yosef].

And regarding what the Rambam wrote, that it is sufficient if they say they heard from so-and-so, some of our Rabbis are of the opinion that we specifically require that they heard from two people. However, it is not necessary that both heard from the same two people; rather, even if one heard from one person and the other from another person, it is still valid, because we do not require witnesses of the betrothal itself. Nevertheless, the rumor must emanate from two people who heard from two sources. But if two people heard from one source or one person heard from two sources, it is not considered a rumor. 

It is possible to say that there is no practical disagreement: according to the Rambam, who ruled that we also need them to witness the preparations for the betrothal, it is sufficient if two people heard from one source. Without witnessing the preparations, the Rambam would agree that we need two people who heard from two sources. Likewise, our Rabbis would agree with the Rambam that if they saw the preparations, it is sufficient if two people heard from one source, as this is no less valid than the women's statements. They interpret this as referring to a case where the preparations were not witnessed, as explained. 

Moreover, regarding what the Rambam wrote, that if the later witnesses went to another country or died, it is still considered a rumor, there are those who disagree and hold that it is specifically if they went to another country that it is considered a rumor, because there is a fear that they might return and contradict the testimony. But if they died, it is not considered a rumor. This also seems to me to be according to the Rambam's interpretation that it refers to witnessing the preparations, and all would agree that even if the witnesses died, it is still considered a rumor.

In the Gemara, it is explained that it is only when people say that a specific woman was betrothed to a specific man that it constitutes a rumor. However, if they do not mention to whom she was betrothed, it is not considered a rumor. Specifically, for the rumor to be valid, people need to say it this way, but the women or witnesses do not need to express it this way, as is also evident from the language of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). Furthermore, the Gemara clarifies that if the rumor arose in another city that she was betrothed, it is not considered a rumor. The poskim did not need to explain this because from their writings, which state that the court needs to investigate the evidence of the preparations, it is implicitly understood that this pertains to this city and not another city. Therefore, the women or witnesses do not need to explicitly say "in this city," as it is understood. However, if they explicitly say that she was betrothed in another city, it is not considered a rumor.

And this is the language of the Tur: "A single woman about whom a rumor emerged that she was betrothed, we are concerned about it and she needs a get (divorce document), provided that the rumor is clear and established in a court. This means that when the rumor emerged, the court investigated it and found it to be true. But if it is not clear or not established in a court, then no. And what is considered a clear rumor? For example, if witnesses came and testified that they saw candles lit, beds made, and women rejoicing for her and saying, 'So-and-so was betrothed today to so-and-so,' etc." End of quote. It implies from his words that the women also need to say that she was betrothed to so-and-so today. And it is possible that the Tur also agrees with what was explained, that the Tur is dealing with a rumor that emerged that she was betrothed in general, as is evident from his words, and therefore requires that the women say 'to so-and-so.' But the Rambam, who wrote that the rumor emerged that she was betrothed to so-and-so, does not require the women to say 'to so-and-so.' Also, what the Rambam and the Tur required, that the women say she was betrothed today, is because the rumor did not mention 'today.' Therefore, our master the Beit Yosef, who wrote, 'A single woman about whom a rumor emerged that she was betrothed today to so-and-so in this city,' wrote in the women's statement that they say 'So-and-so was betrothed' and did not mention 'today.'

The general principle is that we do not concern ourselves with a rumor unless it has been substantiated in a court (Beit Din), where the court has investigated the matter and heard that there is substance to the rumor, as we have said. There are four things that must be present: they must say "she was betrothed" in the past tense, they must say that the betrothal took place "today," they must say "to so-and-so," and they must say "in this city." According to what we have explained, the phrase "she was betrothed" is only necessary either in the rumor or in the testimony of the women. As long as the rumor has not been substantiated in a court, we do not concern ourselves with it. Even if they say there are witnesses in a nearby place, we do not prevent her from marrying. However, this depends on the understanding of the God-fearing court. But if there is a strong presumption that she was betrothed, such as if she is known in the city to have definitely been betrothed, then we do not need it to be substantiated in a court, for we execute punishments based on presumptions. It is only for a mere rumor that we require the court's investigation. The court should continue to investigate the rumor as long as she has not married another man in order to clarify whether there is substance to it. But once she has married another man, we do not investigate the rumor further, for a rumor that arises after marriage is not taken into consideration, as will be explained.

There are those who say that the type of rumor that a court needs to investigate is specifically when there is a loud and widespread rumor in the city that "so-and-so was betrothed." However, if there is no loud and widespread rumor in the city, it is not considered a rumor. Otherwise, no Jewish woman would remain single, as two irresponsible individuals might go to a gathering and say that someone was betrothed, and one person would hear and testify on their behalf, and then two others would hear from that one, and two more would hear from those two, and it would never end. Therefore, it needs to be a loud and widespread rumor in the city, as people do not accept a loud and widespread rumor unless there is substance to it. When this is combined with the testimony of two people who say they heard it, then we are concerned about the betrothal [Bach in the name of the Maharal of Prague]. Indeed, this is also indicated by the language of the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, especially according to the Rambam, who wrote that even with witnesses, they need to see the preparations for the betrothal. This clearly shows that one should not rely on mere hearsay [Beit Shmuel]. There are also those who say that in the case of women's statements, it is necessary for them to be rejoicing with her and saying "she was betrothed," but if they are rejoicing with him and saying that he betrothed her, it is not considered a rumor, although this is not conclusive [as the Talmud and the poskim state the general practice, and see Beit Shmuel, subsection 3].

These two [witnesses] who testify before the court that they saw the preparations and heard the women saying [that the husband died] or heard it from someone else, as was explained, need to be valid witnesses. Although we are concerned about a rumor even if it hasn't reached the level of testimony that they went overseas or that all the clarification relies on the women's statements and the preparations, nevertheless, how can we rely on these matters based on witnesses who are not valid for testimony? This is also implied by the language of the Rambam and all the decisors. And indeed, the Tur brought in the name of one of the earlier authorities that even if a woman heard from two [witnesses], we are concerned about the rumor. This is a singular opinion that has not been clarified, and besides this, there is a printing error in the Tur in this entire matter, see there. [See Beit Shmuel, section 5, who brought proof from R. Shimon in the Talmud that valid witnesses are not needed, but this is difficult to understand since R. Hananel and R. Shimon were not referring to the first witnesses but rather to from whom they heard, see there in Rashi and Tosafot. It is clear that Rabbeinu Tam follows R. Abba and R. Shimon follows Ulla, see there and examine well.]

Even when a rumor has spread, and the court has investigated and verified that there is substance to the rumor and there is a concern that she may have been betrothed, this is only if there was no explanation accompanying the rumor that refutes it. In such a case, even if she denies and says she was not betrothed, she would still require a divorce (get). However, if an explanation accompanied the rumor and was heard at the same time as the rumor of her betrothal, she is not considered betrothed. Instead, we ask her, and we rely on her words, since there is no clear evidence and the rumor is not strong.

And what is considered a valid excuse (to dismiss a rumor)? The Rambam wrote: If a woman was betrothed conditionally or there is a doubt about the betrothal, the rumor does not hold, end quote. The Tur wrote: For example, if a rumor spread that she was betrothed conditionally or that the betrothal was uncertain whether it was closer to him or to her, or even if there is reason to dismiss the rumor such as if there is doubt whether the betrothal was worth a perutah or perhaps it was performed by a minor – we do not concern ourselves with the rumor, end quote. The explanation of his words is that an excuse can be of two types: either the people explicitly state the excuse, such as a conditional betrothal or an uncertain betrothal whether it was closer to him or to her, which is like saying themselves that there is doubt about the betrothal, or even if the people do not explicitly cast doubt but through their story it is possible to cast doubt, like those cases mentioned in the Gemara where a rumor spread that a betrothal was done with unripe dates and therefore if we were to assess them they might not be worth a perutah, and similarly a case where a rumor spread that one of a certain person's sons betrothed a certain woman and that person had both adult and minor sons, and therefore it is possible that one of the minors betrothed and there is no valid betrothal here. For the main concern about the rumor is due to slander and not from the essence of the law, and since there is merely an opening to say there is no valid betrothal here, the people will say that certainly the court examined this well and found that there is not worth a perutah and that a minor performed the betrothal.

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, did not mention this second pretext, and some say that this is also included in his words when he wrote "questionable betrothals" [Beit Yosef], but it does not seem so in the Tur [Beit Shmuel, section 11]. And it seems clear to me that the Rambam has a different opinion on this matter. For behold, in the Gemara it is said regarding these two cases that even according to the one who says we do not nullify a rumor, in this case we do nullify it, because people will say that certainly the court examined and found that there was no betrothal. And this has no relevance to a pretext, for when there is a pretext in the actual words of the people, such as a condition or a close doubt to him or her, there is no need to nullify the rumor at all. Rather, immediately we do not take the rumor into consideration. And there is also a stringency in this, that if the pretext did not emerge together with the betrothal, even if over time a pretext emerged and people say that it was conditional or a close doubt to him or her, it does not help, for a pretext is required at the time of the rumor, as will be explained. But these two cases are not considered a pretext at all, and if the people themselves do not cast this doubt, whether he is not suitable or he is a minor, we are concerned about the rumor, and she needs a get (divorce). However, for this, nullification of the rumor is required, meaning that the court announces that there is no substance to the rumor, which is the interpretation of the Talmud that we nullify a rumor, meaning by announcement. But the Rambam ruled that we do not nullify a rumor and omitted the entire dispute about nullifying a rumor, and also the Rif did not mention nullifying a rumor. Therefore, we do not nullify a rumor, but in this matter, it is preferable to a pretext that emerges together with the rumor, for this pretext is effective even if it emerged over time, and people say that it could be that he was not suitable or the one who betrothed was a minor. And the reason is that in a pretext about a condition or a close doubt to him or her, we do not accept it if it emerged over time, for why did they not say it at the time of the act? And since the rumor has become established, we do not pay attention to the pretext. But in a pretext that he is not suitable, even at the time of the act when the rumor emerged, they said with what did he betroth her? And similarly, when he is a minor, at the time of the act, they said that one of the sons of so-and-so betrothed her, and the minor is included. However, if the people themselves do not clarify the permissibility, we do not rely on nullifying the rumor. But if over time they clarify the permissibility, we accept this as a pretext, for the rumor has not become so established. This is not the case with a condition or a close doubt to him or her, which is a completely new matter, for the rumor has already become established, and we do not accept the pretext after time [and its source is from what Rabbi Zeira said, that in the place of a pretext we consider the pretext, meaning in a place where even according to the words at the time of the rumor there is a pretext, like these two cases mentioned above, we consider the pretext even from now until ten days, for on the contrary, it stands there, and it is automatically proven that the law is not according to the one who says we nullify a rumor even in these cases mentioned above. And even though the commentators did not write this, this is what appears to me, and scrutinize well].

And this law that we have written according to the Rambam, the Rambam explained subsequently, where he wrote: If a rumor spread that she was betrothed to so-and-so and after some days they provided an explanation, if it appears to the court that it is indeed so, they rely on the explanation, and she is not considered betrothed. But if not, since the explanation was not heard at the time the betrothal was heard, they do not concern themselves with the explanation. These are his words, and similarly, it is written in the Shulchan Aruch, section 4. 

To explain, if it appears to the court that it is indeed so, for instance, if the rumor that spread supports this explanation, like the cases we mentioned where they said at the time of the rumor with what she was betrothed, and afterwards, they clarified themselves with the explanation that it was not valid, and similarly with a minor as we wrote – they rely on this and she is not considered betrothed, because the rumor did not become established. But if not, for instance, if the explanation is something new, like a condition or a doubt close to him or her, where the rumor at the time of the betrothal does not support this interpretation – they do not concern themselves with the explanation since the rumor has already become established. This is the intention of the Tur, who wrote about the Rambam in the language of dispute, that in truth, he disagrees with the Tur as we explained in these two cases.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 3 like the Tur, that even in these cases, it is permitted immediately and there is no need to state a pretext. And in section 4, he copied the words of the Rambam that we brought, and therefore, it is impossible to interpret what he wrote, "if the matter appears to the court," about these cases, because according to the Tur, no pretext is needed for them. And it is also impossible to interpret it as referring to a condition or a close doubt to her or him, because in such a case, it is not relevant to say that the matter appears to the court, for how would this be apparent. And some say that the intention is, for example, if initially the rumor spread that he betrothed her by throwing, and the pretext came out that he was close to her [Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel]. However, in my humble opinion, there is no need for any pretext according to the Tur, for what is worse than if he betrothed her with inferior dates, where one can say they are not worth a perutah even though they might be worth a perutah, or with one of the sons of so-and-so, where one can say it was the minor even though it could be interpreted as the adult. And similarly, with throwing, since it can be interpreted that he was close to her even though it could be that he was close to him, nevertheless, there is room for doubt, and why should a pretext be necessary.

Therefore, it seems to me that our master, the Beit Yosef, explains that it applies to all kinds of excuses. Even if a rumor spreads that she was betrothed without any conditions, and afterward a rumor spreads that it was conditional or that the betrothal was done by throwing (an object) and it was close to her, the excuse that came afterward is valid, provided that the court has thoroughly clarified that this is indeed the case — that he betrothed her conditionally and the condition was not fulfilled, or it was certainly close to her. This is what he wrote, "if it appears to the court that this is so," meaning that the court was informed that this is indeed the case according to the excuse. The reasoning is that in the Gemara, there is a dispute whether we nullify a rumor or not, meaning when it becomes known that the betrothal is not valid betrothal. However, we are stringent and do not nullify a rumor. Therefore, although we do not nullify it ourselves, if such an excuse comes from the people, certainly we nullify the betrothal. But the great later authorities did not write this, and therefore, it is proper to be stringent in practice.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: If it is later clarified that the rumor was false, such as when the witnesses upon whom the betrothal was attributed come and say, "It did not happen"—then the rumor is nullified. Some say that in our times, rumors are not nullified. And we have already explained that the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam is also that rumors are not nullified, and there are supports for this from the Talmud as explained in section 13. Additionally, Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef did not mention this at all. Rabbeinu the Rema holds that since the concern of a rumor is only a rabbinic concern, we follow the lenient opinion. Nevertheless, he was cautious of the opinion that in our times rumors are not nullified because the Talmud attributed this to the customs of various places, and we do not know from which places we are [see Chomat Shlomo]. Even in places where rumors are nullified, it only applies when the witnesses upon whom the rumor was based come and say the matter is false. However, if the witnesses who spread the rumor come and say it is false, we do not pay attention to them since they are retracting their original statements [see Beit Shmuel]. Some say that even in such a case it is effective because initially it was only a mere rumor. Certainly, if through investigation and inquiry it is found that their statements are false, it is effective [see Bach]. Know that in any case of a rumor, if the witnesses upon whom it was based are close to the city, it is not considered a rumor until the witnesses are questioned [see Beit Shmuel], especially when the court sees that the rumor is gaining strength.

He also wrote: If he sent her gifts in a manner that does not raise suspicion, even if a rumor arises that she is betrothed, we do not concern ourselves with the rumor, since it is customary to refer to such gifts as betrothal gifts. This means that the court does not need to investigate the rumor, even if a general rumor arises that she is betrothed, because this is akin to a rumor with its refutation. Since it is known that he sent her gifts, we attribute the rumor to them. Without the gifts, the court would be obligated to investigate the rumor, as mentioned in paragraph 8. However, if the court investigated the rumor and found it to be substantiated, such as witnesses testify to preparations for a betrothal and women are rejoicing and saying she is betrothed, or witnesses testify that they traveled to a far place where the betrothal actually took place, then certainly we are concerned about the rumor. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that in any case where there is no need to be stringent, one should not be stringent about rumors at all, in order not to give power to the wicked who might spread rumors about the daughters of Israel to make them agunot or extort money from them. Therefore, in a case where there is no need to investigate the rumor because there is something to attribute it to, it is proper for the court not to investigate at all, unless it appears to them that there is substance to the matter. And it is clear that if the court sees that the hand of the wicked is involved in spreading the rumor, they are obligated to use all means to silence the rumors so that the daughters of Israel are not treated as ownerless property.

A rumor emerged that she is betrothed to a certain man, and the rumor was substantiated in accordance with the law in such a way that she would require a get (divorce document). Another man then came and definitely betrothed her in our presence. We then reexamine carefully the betrothal of the first man which was based on a rumor. If clear witnesses come with clear testimony that the first betrothal was a complete betrothal, then the second betrothal is null, because betrothal does not take effect with a married woman. This is specifically if she accepted the betrothal from the second man not in the presence of the first man, for if she accepted it in the presence of the first man, it is obvious that she would need a get from the second man, as a woman does not have the audacity to accept betrothal from another man in the presence of her husband, and it is as if she is saying "you divorced me," as stated at the beginning of section 17. However, she is also not permitted to the second man according to what our master the Rema wrote there, that we are stringent in this matter. But if she accepted it not in his presence, she does not need a get from the second man if the betrothal of the first man is definite. And why is the court obligated to reexamine the first rumor which was already examined? Because if the rumor stands as it was, she is prohibited to the first man as will be explained. Therefore, we reexamine, and perhaps the first betrothal will be found to be definite, and she will remain with him, and we will not need to force him to divorce her.

If the court re-examined the situation and found no new information regarding the first betrothal and the rumor persists as before, the sages stated that we compel the first man, whose betrothal was rumored, to divorce her, and the second man marries her because his betrothal is certain. Nevertheless, he must betroth her anew, as perhaps the rumor about the first betrothal was true and therefore the first betrothal would take effect. However, the reverse situation, where the second man divorces her and the first man takes her back, is forbidden, as people might say that she was divorced by the first man, betrothed by the second man, and divorced again, and thus it would seem that the first man is remarrying his divorced wife after she was betrothed to someone else.

If the second man divorced her and the first man took her back, it is possible that post facto, he does not need to divorce her, as there is a double doubt: perhaps the first man did not betroth her, and the rumor was false, and she is permitted to him; and even if we say he did betroth her, perhaps he did not divorce her, and therefore the second man's betrothal and divorce are null. However, initially, he should not take her back. It is also possible that even post facto, he needs to divorce her, because since the reason is due to the suspicion of the world and public opinion, we do not rely on a double doubt. See what I wrote in Siman 31.

All this applies when the second man did not marry her before the first man divorced her. If he did marry her and had relations with her, she is forbidden to him by Torah law if the first man's betrothal was valid, like a married woman who committed adultery, who is forbidden to both her husband and her adulterer. She is forbidden to both the first and second men, and both must give her a divorce, and she is forever prohibited to both of them. If it was only a chuppah (bridal canopy) and no relations, we do not consider it.

All of this applies when the first betrothal was public and the second betrothal is certain. But if the second betrothal was also public, such as when there was a rumor that she was betrothed to a certain man and the court investigated the rumor and confirmed it according to the law, and afterwards another rumor emerged similar to the first one that she received betrothal from another, and the court also investigated this second rumor and confirmed it according to the law – in this case, one divorces and one marries, whether it is the first or the last, and even though there is also a concern here that people might say that he is remarrying his divorcee after she was betrothed to another, nevertheless, since from the second there is only a mere rumor, they were not stringent in this matter.

If a rumor spreads that she was betrothed to someone and he divorced her, we do not concern ourselves with prohibiting her due to the betrothal, since the rumor and its refutation come together. However, she is prohibited to a Kohen due to the rumor of the divorce if the rumor is substantiated in a court of law as per the proper procedure. And if a rumor spreads both about the betrothal and the divorce, but the rumor indicates that the divorce was conditional – some say that this is also considered a valid explanation since there is a basis for annulling the betrothal, similar to if the rumor indicated that the betrothal was conditional and the condition was fulfilled, thus making it a valid divorce [Ramban]. Others say that this is not considered a valid explanation [Raavad], and it is not comparable to the condition of the betrothal where we say that the condition was not fulfilled and she remains presumed to be single as before. However, if there was a clear rumor regarding the betrothal and she left the presumption of being single, then to rely on the divorce being conditional and the condition having been fulfilled – there is no proof to rely on in this case [Beit Shmuel, Section 11].

The Sages said: Any rumor that arises after marriage, and even after betrothal, we do not take it into consideration. The explanation of this matter is: Specifically regarding an unmarried woman, if a rumor arises and the rumor is substantiated in a court, we take the rumor seriously and she requires a get (divorce document). But if she is betrothed, and certainly if she is married, even if her husband is an Israelite and would not be prohibited from her if the subject of the rumor were to divorce her (for example, if the rumor was that he had betrothed her before she was betrothed to her current husband), nevertheless, we do not take the rumor into consideration and she does not need a get from the subject of the rumor, so that she should not become despised by her husband. For a rumor is merely a suspicion and we only took it seriously regarding unmarried women. The same applies to the wife of a Kohen who is living with her husband and a rumor arises about her that she was divorced or a harlot – we do not take the rumor into consideration, for we do not remove a woman from her husband except with clear testimony [Rashi].

There is a question regarding this matter – how do we find a case for this ruling, given that we hold that any rumor that has not been substantiated in a court is nothing, even concerning an unmarried woman? Therefore, regarding a betrothed or married woman, the court should not investigate the rumor, and consequently, it is nothing? The answer to this is that indeed, the Sages commanded that the court should not investigate a rumor that emerged about a betrothed or married woman, and even if they investigated and found the rumor to be substantiated, we do not concern ourselves with it. It is possible that they are obligated to investigate in case they find clear testimony, but this does not seem to be the opinion of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). Furthermore, even if the rumor emerged while she was still unmarried but was not substantiated in court until after she became betrothed, the court does not investigate the rumor to substantiate it. Even if witnesses say they heard from so-and-so and so-and-so who have gone overseas, and even if they say this before the court, it is still just a rumor and not clear evidence. Similarly, if they say they saw preparations and women are saying she has been betrothed – this is not legally valid testimony. Why should we amplify the rumor and make it more of a slander? Therefore, it is better not to investigate it unless clear witnesses come forward.

Regarding what we have explained that we do not worry about a rumor that follows an engagement, our teacher the Rema wrote: However, if she later admits that she was betrothed to the first man, she is forbidden to her [current] husband, since the rumor emerged initially. These are his words. And even though we hold that a woman is not believed to prohibit herself to her husband, nevertheless in this case where the rumor supports her, she is believed. But the leading authorities of the later generations dispute this, as it is proven from several places in the Talmud that a woman is not believed to prohibit herself to her husband even when there is some support [like the incident at the end of Nedarim], unless there is clear evidence or compelling circumstances that clearly indicate so. The explanation in the responsa of the Rosh is clear, as the Chasam Sofer wrote in section 17 that his intention is regarding the ketubah, that the rabbi has the ability to cause her to lose it if he wishes to divorce her, and see what I wrote in section 48.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in his major work in Siman 42 in the name of the Rashba, that one who spread a rumor of betrothal regarding a single woman is compelled to clarify his words or to give a get (divorce document), see there. However, this is not an absolute rule, for on the contrary, sometimes the one who spreads the rumor is punished in order not to cast aspersions on the daughters of Israel, as the Rashba himself wrote in a responsum that we do not pay attention to a rumor, see there. Rather, everything depends on the matter, as it is written there, that everything is entrusted to a God-fearing court that understands that there is substance to this, they compel him to clarify or to give a get. But if they do not see any substance to this, on the contrary, they punish him and silence the rumor [and it is questionable about the Chavot Yair Siman 17 who brought this as a definitive law]. And it has already been explained that we do not pay attention to a mere rumor, and the Rosh wrote in a responsum that if it happened that based on a rumor he gave her a get and she became betrothed to another and he died, she is forbidden to return to the first one, because people will assume that the get was valid and will say that he is taking back his divorced wife after she was betrothed to another, and see what is written in Siman 10 and 48.

[Witnesses Contradicting Each Other or a Woman Retracting Her Testimony, and this Contains Eleven Sections]
Two witnesses say, "We saw that she was betrothed," and two others say, "We did not see that she was betrothed" – she is considered definitely betrothed. Even if she denies it, and even if all of them live with her in the same courtyard, this is not considered a contradiction because "we did not see" is not evidence, as it is possible that the betrothal was performed in private. This is customary for people to betroth in private to avoid others preempting them or when betrothing a woman who is not suitable for them. Therefore, even if she marries one of those who say, "We did not see her betrothed," she must leave him. If all of them were present at the same event and say, "We did not see," it is as if two say she was betrothed and two say she was not, which will be explained later. What we said, that "we did not see" is not evidence, specifically applies in one courtyard where it is possible that those did not know about the betrothal. But if they live in the same house and say, "We did not see," it is as if they say she was not betrothed, as it is improbable to perform it so secretly that those in the same house would not notice. Similarly, if these two say she was betrothed in front of everyone and those two say it is false, "we did not see the betrothal" – it is also as if they say she was not betrothed.

If two people say she was betrothed and two people say she was not betrothed, whether the contradiction is about the essence of the betrothal and they say she never had even a doubt of betrothal, or whether they agree on the essence of the betrothal, such as everyone agreeing that betrothal was thrown to her but two say it was close to her and two say it was close to him, and she also says she was not betrothed – she should not marry, and if she marries she must leave. And even though according to Torah law we should establish two against two and maintain her in the presumption of being unmarried, nevertheless, the Sages were stringent in any case of two against two even after the fact. However, if she married one of the witnesses who contradict the betrothal and she also says with certainty that she was not betrothed – she does not have to leave. The reason is that in any case of two against two, even when there is no presumption of permissibility, it is a doubtful prohibition and one is obligated in a conditional guilt offering like a doubt concerning forbidden fat or permitted fat, and in all doubts a person is trusted to say with certainty that there is no doubt of prohibition, and all the more so here where there is also a presumption of permissibility. Therefore, she does not have to leave, and we have further explained this in Siman 17, Se’if 88, see there.

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 9: If one witness says she is betrothed and she says she was not betrothed, she is permitted [to marry someone else]. If one witness says she is betrothed and another witness says she is not betrothed, she should not marry [someone else], but if she does marry, she does not have to leave [the second husband], since she says she was not betrothed. And this is the end of his words.

Now, what Maimonides wrote about her contradicting the witness and being permitted, and it is clear from his words that even initially she is permitted—this is a clear law throughout the Talmud that one witness in contradiction is nothing <small>[Yevamot 65b]</small>. Therefore, even if the witness says she was betrothed in the presence of two witnesses, it is nothing when she contradicts him. For if the witness had said she was betrothed only in his presence, even without the reason of contradiction, it is nothing, for Maimonides holds that if one betroths with one witness, we are not concerned with his betrothal. 

But what he wrote, that if there is also a witness who contradicts him, she should not marry initially, requires a reason. For if there is a witness who says like her, would it be worse? The commentators wrote that Maimonides holds it is certainly worse, for when there is a witness who contradicts the witness, she would brazenly say she was not betrothed. Therefore, initially, she should not marry. And this is what the Sages said <small>[Ketubot 23a]</small>: One witness says she was betrothed and one witness says she was not betrothed, she should not marry, but if she marries, she does not have to leave. And this is also when she says she was not betrothed. For if she says she was betrothed, it is obvious that she makes herself a piece of forbidden meat, and even if she says she is uncertain whether she was betrothed or not, and even if she marries, she must leave, for she is concerned for herself as possibly betrothed <small>[Maimonides' Commentary]</small>. Therefore, even if she says she was not betrothed, and without the witness who supports her, she would be permitted initially. 

But because of the witness, it is worse as stated. And according to this, we must say that only when the witness first said she was not betrothed, and then she said like him, but if she first said she was not betrothed, she is immediately permitted. And the reasoning of brazenness does not apply, for she did not know there was a witness who said like her. 

According to this, we come to a new law: the rule that one witness in contradiction is nothing is only when the contradicting witness did not precede the other witness. But when the contradicting witness preceded, we must be concerned initially.

However, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote: If one witness says she was betrothed and another witness says she was not betrothed, if he (the second witness) says there was never any doubt of betrothal – she may marry ab initio. And if he threw her betrothal [money] and one says it was closer to him and one says it was closer to her – she should not marry, but if she did marry, she need not divorce.

And this is the opinion of most of our early sages, that a single witness against a single witness in matters of betrothal is nothing, for she remains presumed to be unmarried. However, if both admit that betrothal was thrown to her but the one permitting the marriage says it was closer to him, the presumption of her being unmarried is weakened. Therefore, she should not initially marry [Tosafot there]. Additionally, it is easy to err between what is close to her and what is close to him, and hence we are stringent that she should not initially marry [Ran there]. Similarly, if there was preparation for the betrothal, such as lit candles and arranged beds, but one says the betrothal was not completed – the presumption of her being unmarried is weakened, and she should not initially marry [Tosafot]. In these cases, our sages said [there] that when there is a single witness against a single witness in matters of betrothal, she should not initially marry, but if she did marry, she need not divorce.

It is obvious that according to this opinion, it discusses a situation where she also says that she was not betrothed, or that she says she does not know at all about the betrothal in a manner that she does not need to know, such as when one person says that her father accepted betrothal for her when she was a minor and another person disputes this [Raavad]. But if she herself is doubtful about the betrothal and says that she is uncertain whether there was a betrothal or not, they agree with the Rambam that she makes herself a doubtful prohibition. Or it is possible that when she says she does not know whether it is closer to him or to her, her words are as if they are nothing, and if she marries, she does not have to leave [and as it is also stated by the Raavad and so writes the Magid Mishneh, see there]. This is not considered as being concerned about doubtful betrothal, which would be the case if there was no witness claiming that it is closer to him, and it would certainly be a doubtful betrothal. But with one witness against another witness, and she remains in her presumed status of being permitted in terms of not having to leave, her statement that she does not know does not remove her presumed status unless she says as the witness who claims that she was betrothed [see Beit Shmuel section 6 who refutes the words of the Perisha, and it requires further study as it seems the main point is like the Perisha, and what Tosafot writes that "we know," meaning since both say so, what difference does it make whether it is two or a hundred or a thousand, and examine this carefully].

And according to these opinions, it seems that even with one witness in a situation of contradiction, the law is the same. For example, if one person says she was betrothed and she denies the essence of the betrothal—one witness in contradiction is nothing and she may marry ab initio. However, if she also admits that there were preparations for betrothal but claims the betrothal was not completed, and the witness says it was completed, or if she admits that he threw the betrothal to her but says it was closer to him and the witness says it was closer to her—she should not marry ab initio. For this opinion holds that there is no difference with one witness in contradiction whether the party involved denies it or whether another witness contradicts it. Therefore, just as with a witness who contradicts in such a case, she should not marry ab initio; similarly, with her own contradiction, she should not marry ab initio. [See Rashi on Kiddushin 65b s.v. "one witness in contradiction" where there is one witness who contradicts him, and see Yoreh De'ah, Siman 127, Se'if 1 in the gloss, and the Shach, Se'if Katan 14, and scrutinize well.]

And also regarding the words of the Rambam, we can interpret his intent in a case where one person says she is betrothed and another says she is not betrothed, that it is referring to a situation where both agree that he threw [the betrothal object] but they disagree whether it was closer to him or to her [Ran]. According to this, he does not differ from other decisors, and the explanation of his words is that when she contradicts the witness, it could be a contradiction regarding the main matter. However, when ordinary people contradict each other on a matter that does not concern them, it is unlikely that the contradiction is about the main issue, but rather about its details. 

Additionally, it can be interpreted from his words that he is referring to a situation where she is silent, and therefore, initially, she should not marry because he holds that the single witness in contradiction, as the Sages said, is of no consequence, only in the contradiction of a party involved and not in the contradiction of a witness. Or he holds that since she is silent, her presumption is weakened. This is what he wrote, that if she married, she does not have to leave [the marriage], for she says she was not betrothed. This means that it is as if she says she was not betrothed because she married, and his language is precise when he wrote "for she says," and he did not explain that she actually says it, but through her marriage, it is as if she says she was not betrothed [in my opinion].

She herself said, "I have been betrothed," and there are no witnesses before us to testify to this. If she then retracted and said, "I am single" within the time it takes to say a greeting (toch k'dei dibur) – she is believed. And even though we hold that in matters of betrothal, retraction within toch k'dei dibur is ineffective, this applies to the act of betrothal itself; retraction within toch k'dei dibur is not effective. However, regarding a statement, it is effective. But after toch k'dei dibur, she is not believed and is forbidden to be betrothed to another. However, if she gives a plausible explanation for her initial statement, such as saying she initially claimed to be betrothed to prevent unworthy men from pursuing her, and we see truth in her words – for example, if she is very beautiful or wealthy and attracts many suitors – she is believed. Even if she was betrothed previously and then provided a plausible explanation, she is also believed, for a good explanation completely nullifies her previous statement, indicating she was entirely single. But if she did not provide a plausible explanation, or if she did, and it does not seem genuine to us – she is not believed.

Therefore, if she accepted betrothal from another, it is a case of doubtful betrothal. The Rambam writes that therefore he should give her a get (bill of divorce), and she will be forbidden to him and to everyone else until her original betrothed comes. There are those who want to say that witnesses can testify that this is her betrothed, but this is not so, for if that were the case, why would we require a get from the one who betrothed her here? After all, betrothal does not take effect with a married woman. Rather, the intent is that the one who comes will say that he betrothed her earlier, and therefore without a get from the second one, she is not permitted to him. However, with a get, she is permitted to the betrothed in any case, for if it is true that she is his betrothed, it is good, and if not, she is considered single. We do not suspect that the one who comes is lying outright and that she will agree to his words. There are those who want to say that even if she does not admit to him and says that she is single and did not accept betrothal from him, she is still permitted to him. Since he says that she is his betrothed, his original words are confirmed, and what do we care? However, there is room to question this, for she is considered married in our view, and now that she denies it, it is as if she is saying, "I was not betrothed to you but to another." For when she says, "I am single," we do not believe her, and this requires further inquiry regarding the law.

Some say that all this applies when she says "I was betrothed" without specifying to whom. However, if she says "I was betrothed to so-and-so," she is no longer believed to say "I am single," even within twenty-four hours and even if she gives a good reason [Beit Shmuel]. She is forbidden to everyone until that person comes or until he dies, because she is not believed to harm him and release herself from him. And some say that within the time it takes to speak (a brief moment), she is believed even in such a case, since it is only a matter of speech, and only after that time is she not believed even with a good reason, because how can she negate his rights? And even though she has a "migo" (a legal presumption) that she could have said she was not betrothed, this is a retrospective migo, and the migo that "you divorced me" also does not apply, because even if she had said so, she would still be forbidden to another [ibid.]. However, if the man denies it and says that she was not betrothed to him, she is believed with a good reason to retract, but without a good reason, it is like saying "you betrothed me" and he says "I did not betroth you," as will be explained in Siman 48 [in my opinion].

[He said to her, "I betrothed you," and she denies it, or vice versa, and it contains thirteen sections]
One who says to a woman, "I betrothed you in the presence of so-and-so and so-and-so, and they have gone to a distant land" [Tur], and she says, "You did not betroth me" — he is forbidden to marry her relatives, such as her mother and sister and other relatives who are forbidden due to the betrothal, for he has rendered himself a piece of prohibition. However, she is permitted to marry his relatives because he is not believed to forbid her. Furthermore, even if he were to cohabit with one of her relatives, she would not be disqualified from marrying a priest, for just as he is not believed regarding the woman, similarly he is not believed regarding her relatives, and only he has committed a prohibition [Pischei Teshuvah].

Some say that this is specifically when he said, "I betrothed you in the presence of so-and-so and so-and-so," but if he said, "I betrothed you" without specifying, he is not forbidden to her relatives, for he can explain his words as meaning that he betrothed her without witnesses. Similarly, the Rosh wrote in a responsum concerning Reuven's concubine who said, "Reuven betrothed me," that her words mean nothing unless she says that he betrothed her in the presence of witnesses, as stated in Siman 15, Se'if 32 (see Beit Shmuel). However, there is a doubt as to whether the Rosh ruled this way only regarding a concubine, but for a man, and certainly for a Torah scholar who knows that there is no betrothal without witnesses, if he says simply "I betrothed you," it is presumed that he meant a proper betrothal, and he is not believed to say afterwards that it was without witnesses (see Chochmat Shlomo). This also seems to be implied by the Rambam and Shulchan Aruch, who wrote simply "one who says 'I betrothed you'," and if we say that in an unspecified case, he can claim that he did not intend witnesses, why did they write their statements so generally? Moreover, in the Gemara (65a), the Talmud did not explain it this way, but rather stated that if it were not so, one could ask the witnesses (and on the contrary, from Rava's question there it is proven that even in an unspecified case, we presume a proper betrothal; see there and examine it carefully). And what the Rambam and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Se'if 5 about all those cases, when he claimed witnesses, will be explained with God's help.

When he says "I have consecrated her" – he becomes forbidden to her relatives, even if witnesses come and contradict him. For in any case where a person makes something forbidden to himself, he is believed about himself more than a hundred witnesses, as it says in Yoreh De'ah, Section 1, regarding a slaughterer who says, "I did not slaughter this animal," and witnesses contradict him, nevertheless it is forbidden to eat from it due to the principle that he has made it forbidden to himself. Similarly, one of the early authorities ruled in the case of a captive woman who says, "I am impure," and witnesses contradict her, that she is believed to forbid herself to a Cohen. However, if he retracts his statement and admits to the testimony of the witnesses, although generally retraction without a valid reason does not help, in this case where the witnesses contradict him, his retraction is effective even without a valid reason.

And similarly, if a woman says to a man, "You betrothed me," and he says, "I did not betroth you," he is permitted to marry her relatives, but she is forbidden to marry his relatives. This applies after they die, for while they are alive, this ruling does not apply at all. Before he divorces her, she is forbidden to everyone, not just his relatives. And after he divorces her, he is also forbidden to her relatives because of the divorce, as will be explained. Only if she dies is he permitted to her relatives, and if he dies, she is still forbidden to his relatives.

He says, "I betrothed you," and she says, "You did not betroth me but betrothed my daughter" – he is prohibited from the mother's relatives for the reason explained, and the mother is permitted to his relatives as mentioned. He is permitted to the daughter's relatives, and the daughter is permitted to his relatives, as the mother is not believed concerning the daughter, and only the father is believed to prohibit his daughter, as the Torah gave him the authority, as it is written, "I have given my daughter to this man," and not to the mother. Moreover, the father is only believed concerning a minor or a na'arah (young girl), but not concerning an adult woman. Even rabbinically, the mother is not believed to prohibit her daughter based on her word. Conversely, when he says, "I betrothed your daughter," and she says, "You did not betroth her but betrothed me" – he is prohibited from the daughter's relatives, and the daughter is permitted to his relatives. He is permitted to the mother's relatives, and the mother is prohibited from his relatives for the same reason.

And there is a doubt when someone says "I betrothed your daughter" and becomes prohibited to the relatives of the daughter, if this is specifically when he says he betrothed her with Torah-sanctioned betrothal, such as if she is an adult, or even a minor but he claims he betrothed her through her father and the father died or went to a distant land. However, when he says he betrothed her only through her mother or brother, which is a rabbinic betrothal, is he not prohibited to her relatives? Or is he prohibited to her relatives even in a rabbinic betrothal?
