And it appears that the primary view is that he is indeed prohibited to her relatives, because the reasoning that a person is trusted upon himself more than a hundred witnesses applies, whether in a Torah-sanctioned or rabbinic context.

Maimonides and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: All those who claim betrothal – when the claimant argues that there were witnesses but they have traveled to another country or have died, but if they admit that the betrothal was without two witnesses – there is no betrothal. Explanation: Initially, they stated betrothal in general terms, but the court is obligated to investigate and inquire about how the betrothal took place. Therefore, if he or she says that there were witnesses and they have traveled, it is considered one witness. If they admit that it was without witnesses, there is no betrothal [and it reconciles the apparent contradiction between the beginning and the end of the statement]. According to this, it is like the opinion in paragraph 2 that one is believed to clarify their words. However, it can be said that this applies specifically to the woman or the man if he is unlearned, but for a scholar, it would be as if he contradicts himself because he knows that there is no betrothal without witnesses. It can also be explained that it refers to the initial statement, as usually in such a contradiction where one says "I betrothed you" and she denies it or vice versa, it is unlikely that there was no matter of betrothal between them, and one claims there were witnesses and the other says there were none, or vice versa. Therefore, if they admit that it was without witnesses, meaning the one asserting the betrothal admits to the denier that it was without witnesses – there is no betrothal. But in a case where one says "I betrothed you" and the other says "you did not betroth me," it is not considered, because this is an unlikely scenario. Nevertheless, if we interpret it this way, we learn that at that moment one can clarify their words. Surely, if he says "I betrothed you," initially he would say it generally, for if he said he betrothed without witnesses, he is claiming nothing. If he says it was with witnesses, how can he later say it was without witnesses? Therefore, certainly, if he says it generally and she responds it was without witnesses and he admits to her words, and similarly when she claims and he denies it, this is the meaning of the word "admit" they wrote, meaning he admits to the denier. Hence, we learn that at that moment one can admit to the denier in such a case. But if he said generally "I betrothed you" and she said generally "you did not betroth me" and they parted ways, whether he can later clarify his words that it was without witnesses or find other invalidities in the betrothal without a good reason why he erred initially when he stated betrothal generally – it is questionable [and the opinion of Ba'er Heitev in Section 1 is that one can clarify their words and it implies in all cases, and so it seems from what is written in Shulchan Aruch Section 15, Paragraph 30, unless we differentiate between a woman and others. However, for a woman and someone who is not a scholar who can err in the law, certainly, one can clarify as written in Paragraph 2].

There is a doubt whether it is specifically when he said in a court, "I betrothed you with witnesses" or she said in a court, "He betrothed me with witnesses," that they become forbidden to their relatives and also require a divorce as will be explained. But if they said this with witnesses outside the court, they can retract their claims when they come to court, similar to monetary claims where anything claimed outside the court is considered nothing as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 80. Or perhaps matters of prohibition are different, as in monetary matters a person does not reveal his claims except in court, but not in matters of prohibition. However, this is certainly the case when he admitted before witnesses with a complete admission that he betrothed her with witnesses or she admitted with a complete admission even not in court—they cannot retract their statements, for in such a case, even in monetary matters, the law is the same as stated there in Siman 81.

In any case where we have said that a woman tells a man "You betrothed me," and he says "I did not betroth you," we ask him to write her a get (bill of divorce) if he does not want to marry her, for she would be forbidden to everyone else. However, we cannot force him to give a get since he denies it. We also cannot force him on the grounds of the principle of Sodom, that she benefits and he does not lose, because he can claim that he would suffer a loss by being prohibited to her relatives. Therefore, we ask him to give her a get to permit her [to others], and then he becomes prohibited to her relatives since he gave her a get. Writing "You are not my wife" is like an admission that she was his wife, and consequently, he is prohibited to her relatives. Even if it is not considered an admission from him, nonetheless, people will say that the sister of a divorcee is permitted [to marry him].

If they did not ask him to give her a get (divorce document) but he himself initiated giving her a get, it is considered an admission on his part that he betrothed her, and he is obligated to give her a ketubah (marriage contract) according to the poskim (halachic authorities) who hold that a betrothed woman is entitled to a ketubah as stated in Siman 55. And so our sages said [there], if he gives a get on his own initiative, we compel him to give her a ketubah. According to the Rambam and the Geonim who hold that a betrothed woman is not entitled to a ketubah, but if he wrote her a ketubah, then he is certainly obligated to give it to her when he gives a get on his own initiative and not when he was asked to. And even though, if so, how can he claim he did not betroth her? This can also happen in a place where they write the ketubah first and then perform the betrothal, and he claims that the ketubah was written but the betrothal was not completed [HaMaggid Mishneh]. And even if he gives the get on his own initiative, if he is a scholar and knows that she is forbidden to everyone else and clarifies at the time of the get that he writes it so she will not be agunah (chained woman) – he does not give a ketubah [there].

But in the case where he says "I betrothed you" and she says "You did not betroth me," we do not require him to give a get (divorce document) since she is permitted to marry others, and obviously, we do not ask her to accept a get since he is not forbidden from marrying multiple women. Even now, according to the enactment of Rabbeinu Gershom, the Light of the Exile, it also appears that a get is not required because she contradicts him and he has no wife, so he is permitted to marry another woman. However, sometimes she can compel him to give her a get, such as when people refrain from marrying her because of the slander he spread about her that he betrothed her, she can compel him to give her a get. Nevertheless, she is not prohibited from marrying his relatives even after the get, since she insists that she does not need the get but only seeks it to remove the concern of those who refrain from marrying her, and this is considered a get that is not needed and does not prohibit her from marrying his relatives, [Mordechai], thus ruled Rabbeinu the Rema. There are those who disagree with this, as it is certain that she is prohibited to a Kohen, and therefore also to his relatives, for otherwise people would say that a divorced woman is permitted to her ex-husband's relatives, not everyone knows that this is a get that is not needed by law [there]. Rabbeinu the Rema himself ruled in Siman 10 that even if she was only divorced due to a mere rumor and married another and he died or divorced her, she is prohibited from returning to the first husband, all the more so in matters of forbidden relations. It seems to me that his reasoning for being lenient here is because in this case it is public knowledge that she is seeking to marry, as is customary when she sends to arrange a match for herself, and everyone knows she is single, but over time she saw that people still refrain from marrying her because of his claim, as who would want to marry a woman about whom someone says she is his wife. Even though everyone knows she is permitted by law, people customarily avoid arranging a match with such a woman. Therefore, it is as if it has become public that the get is merely for the sake of removing doubt. Nonetheless, one should not be lenient in practice [see Chamudei Daniel and Beit Shmuel].

There was an incident where a man said, "I betrothed my sister-in-law (my wife's sister) in the presence of so-and-so, but they have gone overseas. I betrothed her before I betrothed my wife, and I did not divorce her, and she was married to another man." Rabbeinu Tam ruled that he is not believed to prohibit his sister-in-law to her husband as long as he does not bring witnesses. Furthermore, even if she also says that he betrothed her, she is not believed to prohibit herself to her husband as long as she is still with him. However, if he divorced her, she is prohibited to him because she has made herself forbidden to him by her own admission.

Additionally, Rabbeinu Tam ruled in this matter that even if one brings witnesses that he betrothed her before he betrothed his wife, nevertheless, if the sister of his wife was betrothed in his presence, she is not prohibited to her husband. This is similar to the case where a woman says "You divorced me" as stated in the beginning of section 17. Otherwise, she would not have the audacity to accept betrothal from another man in his presence. However, as mentioned there, in our times where there is chutzpah, one should be stringent and not lenient in this matter. All of this applies to the sister of his wife. However, he becomes prohibited to his wife, for according to his words, she is an ervah (forbidden relation) to him, and he is believed regarding himself. We cannot suspect him of hating her and wanting to prohibit her to himself since he can divorce her whenever he wishes. Therefore, in our times, when one cannot divorce his wife against her will due to the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom, the light of the exile, he is not believed to prohibit her to himself, as is the case when a man accuses his wife of adultery, which will be explained in section 115. [There is room for inquiry, even before the decree, whether his intention might be to exempt her from the ketubah, and in this case, he does not have the miggo (advantage) of divorcing her].

[The Law of One Who Betroths One of Five Women, and Each Claims He Betrothed Her, Containing Eight Sections]

Our Sages stated (Yevamot 118b): If a man betrothed one of five women and does not know which one he betrothed, and each woman claims, "He betrothed me," if he wishes, he may take all of them according to Torah law, which permits marrying multiple women. If he does not wish to marry all of them (Rashi), he must give a get (bill of divorce) to each one and is forbidden to marry any of their relatives. He places one ketubah (marriage contract) among them and withdraws, and they may either divide it among themselves or wait until one of them proves that she is the one he betrothed. This is similar to the law of a deposit, as explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 300, where one person claims, "I am the owner of the deposit," and another person also claims, "I am the owner of the deposit," when the deposit was given without the owner's knowledge. In such a case, the deposit is placed between them, and the depositor withdraws. Even though when the deposit was given with the owner's knowledge, the depositor must give to each claimant due to his negligence in not verifying the owner, similarly, it is clear that he should have verified which woman he betrothed. Nevertheless, in this case, it is as if they did not demand it from him, as explained in the name of the Sma (Siftei Cohen) (commentary on Choshen Mishpat 312:12), who states that there is no need to pay both claimants even if he wants to act ethically because he can excuse himself by saying, "I did not consider that another person would claim the deposit." All the more so, he can say here, "I did not consider that another woman would claim I betrothed her," and he is exempt even to act ethically (in my opinion). This is why when they demand it from him, he is liable due to his negligence for not knowing that a deposit might be held for a long time, causing him to forget the owner, and he should have written down the owner's name (there). However, with a woman, this does not apply, and it is similar to the law of a purchase, as explained in Siman 222, where the item is placed between them, and the seller withdraws (in my opinion, and as it appears in Yevamot there, and examine this well).

And this is the case when he betrothed with money or a document and the document was lost. But if he betrothed through intercourse, which is a rabbinic prohibition to betroth through intercourse as stated in Siman 26, and each woman says, "He betrothed me," the Sages fined him that he must give a Ketubah (marriage contract) to each and every one of them. Since he committed a prohibited act and degraded them by betrothing through intercourse, he must absolve himself from the transgression and give to all of them [Rashi]. This is analogous to the case of theft explained there in Siman 365, where one stole from one of five people and does not know from whom, and each one says, "He stole from me," he pays each and every one of them because of the fine for committing a prohibited act. And even though in that case it is a Torah prohibition and here it is a rabbinic prohibition, there is no difference in this regard. Moreover, here he degraded them with the betrothal through intercourse.

And there are those who question, for it was clarified there regarding theft that each person must swear, so why do all the women take without an oath [Beit Shmuel], and indeed the Sages compared betrothal through intercourse to theft [there]. And there is one who says that the reason is that if he were to claim with certainty that he betrothed this one, he would swear against the others and be exempt. And since he claims uncertainly and he is obligated to take an oath by Torah law because he admits to one of them and would be required to take an oath and cannot swear and must pay, unlike in the case of theft where the Sages decreed that the victim swears and takes [Korbanei Netanel there]. However, this is not in the category of "because he cannot swear, he pays," for it is certain that he is obligated to only one ketubah, and moreover, four of them are certainly deceitful [see Sema, Siman 300, Se'if Katan 1]. However, in truth, it is not comparable, for here he must give a get to each one, and since he gives a get, he must also give the ketubah. Moreover, an oath does not apply here as it does in the case of theft where each one claims money, whereas here they are not claiming the ketubah but rather that he should marry them, and he does not want them and divorces them, and thus he must give the ketubah.

There are those who say that if he wishes to take one of them, he is exempt from giving a ketubah to the remaining ones, as it is similar to a case where one says "You owe me money," and the other responds "I don't know," in which case he is exempt from payment, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 75. For indeed, when he does not wish to take one of them, it is not similar to that case, since he knows he is obligated to one of them, but when he wishes to take one of them, it is exactly similar to that case. The decisors did not mention this at all and it also appears to be the opposite of what we wrote in Siman 1. Therefore, it seems to me that even in such a case he is obligated, for when one wishes to act righteously, he is also obligated in a case of uncertainty, as stated there. And it is only from the perspective of the court that they cannot obligate him, and here, it is not a matter of strict law but merely a penalty. And since by divine law he is obligated in such a case, all the more so here, he should be obligated by the penalty law. Furthermore, since he is obligated to give the get by strict law, he is consequently obligated to give the ketubah as well, as stated.

This obligation that the Sages imposed to give them a ketubah is fine according to the opinions that an engaged woman is entitled to a ketubah. But for those who hold that she is not entitled to a ketubah, what relevance does a ketubah have here? Therefore, the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in chapter 9 that here we are dealing with a case where it is known that he wrote her a ketubah but the ketubah was lost. For if it were not lost, it would be known from the ketubah to whom she was betrothed, or there are witnesses that he stipulated to give her a ketubah, in which case he is obligated even if he did not write it for her [Ra'avad], or they made a formal acquisition to give a ketubah, or the ketubah is intact but the woman's name is not mentioned in the ketubah or their names are the same [Hagahot Maimoniyot].

And the Tur also wrote, for example, when the ketubah was lost, and according to his opinion in Siman 55 that a betrothed woman has a ketubah, this would not be necessary. Therefore, some say that even according to those who hold that a betrothed woman has a ketubah, nevertheless, since this is only a penalty for one who betroths through intercourse, the sages did not penalize him unless he wrote to one of them [Drisha and Prisha]. However, this is not implied by all the authorities [Beit Shmuel], and the Tur relied on what he wrote there. And it comes to teach us that even though here each one claims she lost the ketubah, and the claim of loss is a weak claim, for in a case of a lost and found document, we do not return it to the lender as stated in Choshen Mishpat Siman 65, and certainly here where all four are definitely lying. Nevertheless, since it is a penalty, the sages penalized him even in such a case.

If a man betroths a woman and then immediately retracts by saying that the money should be a gift, even if it is within "toch k'dei dibur" (the brief period it takes to say a greeting), his retraction is meaningless, and she requires a get (divorce document). This is because, in matters of betrothal, retraction within "toch k'dei dibur" does not work for the act of betrothal itself, as stated in Siman 38. Some say that even to be stringent we do not consider it as if it were spoken [there, in the name of the Rivas], and there are those who disagree about this, as explained there in Siman 51. See also later in Siman 141, Sif 141.

The Sages said [Gittin 6a]: "Anyone who is not proficient in the laws of divorce documents (gittin) and betrothal (kiddushin) should not engage in them to issue rulings, for it is easy to err and permit a forbidden relationship, thereby increasing the number of illegitimate children (mamzerim) in Israel." Some say that this prohibition applies specifically to issuing rulings, but arranging a betrothal is permitted since it does not involve issuing a ruling. However, arranging a divorce document, which involves many details, is forbidden unless one is knowledgeable in the laws of divorce [Taz]. Others say that even arranging a betrothal should not be done initially by one who is not knowledgeable in the laws of betrothal [Shvus Yaakov]. It is written that there was an ordinance from the early French Geonim in the days of Rabbeinu Tam that no one should arrange a betrothal except one who has been chosen as a rabbi and teacher in the community [Pitchei Teshuva in the name of Kenesset Yechezkel]. In a place where there is a city rabbi, no one else can arrange a betrothal, even if he is a Torah scholar, unless the rabbi grants him permission [see Noda BiYehuda, second edition, Even HaEzer, section 82].

[When the engagement gifts and betrothal gifts are returned, and the annulment of engagements, in 22 sections] It is simple and logically understood that all the gifts a man gives to his wife, whether given after the marriage, after the betrothal, or after the engagement prior to the betrothal – these gifts are entirely hers. Even if the husband dies or divorces her, the gifts remain with her, as written in Siman 99. Even if he divorces her because he hates her, we do not say that the gifts should be returned to him on the grounds that he only gave them out of love, and now that he hates her, the gift should be annulled. This is not a logical argument; otherwise, anyone who gives a gift to a friend out of love, and later becomes his enemy, would have the gift annulled. Would any person who gives a gift be required to ensure that the recipient remains their friend forever?

However, this applies to marriage, but from betrothal, if he divorces her or dies – the gifts return to him or his heirs. The reason is that it is a clear presumption that he gave her the gifts only on the condition to marry her, but if the marriage is annulled, the gifts are returned to him. This applies to all kinds of gifts of money, gold, jewelry, utensils, and clothes that have not worn out, as will be explained, except for types of food and drink, which are not returned for reasons that will be explained in this section. There is no difference in the gifts whether he sent them to her before betrothal after they were engaged, or whether he gave them to her after betrothal, for there is no reason to distinguish between them. However, a gift he gave her before the engagement seems not to return to him, for it is considered a general gift, unless he explicitly stated that he is giving it to her on the condition that she marries him.

And this applies to other gifts, but the money for betrothal, whether he betrothed her with money or with an equivalent value, even if he betrothed her with a thousand dinars, the betrothal money is not returned to him after the engagement. Whether she retracts and compels him to divorce her, or he retracts and divorces her, or he dies, or she dies, or even if he divorces her because she is forbidden to him for some prohibition [there in subparagraph 1] – the betrothal money is not returned to him, and it is considered an unconditional gift from which there is no retraction. And although it is obvious that in the case of betrothal there is an understanding that he gave it to her only on the condition of marriage, nevertheless, the sages said this for the reason that people should not say that the betrothal is nullified and that betrothal can take effect with her sister [Bava Batra 145] or with any other relative of hers who is forbidden to him even after her death, like her mother and the like.

Therefore, if the betrothal was a mistake – it is obvious that the betrothal is annulled. Similarly, if a minor was betrothed through her mother and brothers and she refused him, it does not concern us if people say that betrothal is effective with her relative; on the contrary, it is better that they say so than to say that it is not effective, for indeed it is effective. Likewise, if the betrothal was conditional and the condition was not fulfilled. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote that even in a case of doubtful betrothal, the betrothal is annulled. The great Acharonim [Chacham Zvi and Beis Shmuel] were astonished at him, for in a case of doubtful betrothal, a get (divorce document) is required, and out of doubt her relatives are forbidden to him. Why should we not decree in this case also that the betrothal should not be annulled, so that people do not say that betrothal is certainly effective with her sister? And behold, a minor's betrothal is rabbinic, and the betrothal is only annulled through refusal, as we have said, and not through divorce, even though her relatives are only forbidden to him rabbinically. All the more so in a case of doubtful Torah-level betrothal.

However, the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, are correct, for since by law the betrothal is valid and only because of the decree it is not valid, it is sufficient to decree certainly on the betrothal and not on doubt. It is not similar to a minor who goes out with a bill of divorce, for there, whatever the Sages instituted, they instituted in the manner of Torah law, and in any case, it is certainly a rabbinic betrothal. Moreover, in a case of doubt, there is a decree to the contrary; if the betrothal is not annulled, people will say it was certainly a betrothal and will think that betrothal does not take effect with her sister, when in truth it does take effect out of doubt. And since there is a decree on both sides, it is better to maintain the law as it is.

Furthermore, there is no decree here according to what one of the early authorities wrote, that in the case of doubtful betrothal, if she marries, she does not have to leave her husband because we establish her as having the presumption of being unmarried [Kesef Mishneh, Chapter 4, in the name of the Maharik]. Therefore, there is truly no concern even if they say that the betrothal would be valid with her sister, unlike Rabbinic betrothal, where if she marries, she must leave according to Rabbinic law [Even HaEzer]. And although this is not the practical ruling, it is not only in the case of two against two witnesses—where although Biblically we would uphold the presumption, Rabbinically she must leave as stated in Siman 16—but even in a general doubt without contradictory witnesses, such as two saying he threw her betrothal money and it is uncertain whether it was closer to him or her, she must also leave because she loses her presumption of being unmarried since a betrothal act was performed on her, as stated there regarding one against one witness. Nevertheless, it is clear that this is only Rabbinic, for Biblically even a challenged presumption remains a presumption. Therefore, we do not decree in this case since it is merely a Rabbinic stringency. However, for a minor, in Rabbinic betrothal, it is certainly Rabbinic [so it appears to me], and thus the Mordechai rules [in the glosses at the end of Chapter 3] that in cases of doubt, the betrothal is annulled. See there.

Even though we have said that in cases of mistaken betrothals the money of the betrothal is returned, nevertheless, if someone betroths his sister, the money is considered a gift. Although there is no greater mistake than this, in a mistake that it is impossible to make, this rule does not apply, since everyone knows that betrothal does not take effect with forbidden relations (arayot) and this is not a mistake but a deliberate act, and he gave it as a gift. And this rule of returning the money in a mistaken betrothal applies in cases where the mind is genuinely mistaken, such as when her husband went overseas and they told her he died, and she accepted betrothal, and then her husband returned, and similar cases. But not in cases of betrothing a forbidden relation. Similarly, if someone betroths a married woman knowing her husband is alive, the money is also considered a gift. We do not say that only for a relative does he intend it as a gift and not for someone who is not related to him. And even though some of our Rabbis were uncertain about this, nevertheless, the law does not differentiate in this matter as we explained with the help of Heaven in Choshen Mishpat, siman 356, paragraph 7. See there.

Rabbi Moses Isserles (Rema) wrote that all of this only applies to engagements, but regarding marriages—the betrothal (kiddushin) remains valid. According to the reason explained, which is to prevent people from saying that it was a mistaken betrothal and that the betrothal would then be valid with the sister, this concern only exists with betrothal and not with marriage. People would never say it was a marriage by mistake, as this is highly uncommon. Additionally, conditions do not apply to marriages, as any conditions would have been waived at the time of the marriage (see Tosafot Yevamot 107). Nevertheless, his words are puzzling because this reason is only needed for after the engagement, where all gifts are returned. But after marriage, where all gifts remain with her as we have explained, why do we need this reason? Is betrothal worse than all other gifts that are not returned to him (see Chamat Hamadlik 5)? Even the ketubah must be given to her, so certainly the money of the betrothal is not returned. And it cannot be said that this refers to a rebellious wife against her husband, as this does not seem to be the intent of his wording. Some say this refers not by law but in a place where according to the enactment, when she dies, the husband does not inherit her and everything is returned to the dowry givers. In such a case, the betrothal money is also taken from her heirs and returned to him. Others say that even if he dies, the custom in several communities is to include the betrothal ring in her ketubah. But aside from the fact that this has no sound reasoning, since all other gifts he gave her certainly are not returned, why should the betrothal money be worse than all other gifts (see there)? His wording does not support this.

It seems to me that our master, the Rema (Rabbi Moses Isserles), holds that kiddushin (betrothal) is inferior to all other gifts, for it is not a gift but an acquisition, as he acquires her with the money of kiddushin, just as a woman is acquired for her husband with money or its equivalent. Certainly, according to the basic law, just as someone who buys land with money and then the seller repurchases it from the buyer, the seller returns the money he received; so too, when he divorces her, it is as if she is buying herself back from him so that she is no longer under his domain, and she should return to him the money of kiddushin, which is the betrothal money. However, due to a decree, our Sages said that it should not be returned, as we have explained, and this decree applies only to betrothal and not to marriage. The reason that the poskim (decisors) referred to kiddushin as a gift is a common expression because in the Talmud (Ketubot 76b and Bava Batra there), there is a dispute among the Tannaim whether kiddushin returns after betrothal or not. The reason for their dispute is that one who holds that it does return considers it superior to all gifts since it is like the price of a purchase. One who holds that it does not return, either holds that even though it is like the price of a purchase, due to a decree, we do not remove it, and this is relevant only after betrothal and not after marriage, or he holds that nevertheless, it is not similar to a purchase because he gives it to her completely out of love, and according to this, even after marriage, it does not return. The Amoraim (Sages of the Talmud) also argued about this in Bava Batra there: one opinion is that even according to the basic law, it does not return (Rabbi Pappa there who said the halacha, etc.), and according to this, even after marriage, it does not return; another opinion is that the reason is only due to a decree (Amimar there, and he deals with the whole matter, and study it well). According to this, only after betrothal does it not return, but after marriage, it is like the price of a purchase. Our master, the Rema, ruled according to this Amora, for according to him, these Tannaim do not disagree on the basic law, and all agree that it is like the price of a purchase. Therefore, it is correct that our master, the Rema, ruled that from the marriage, it returns (see Mordechai, chapter HaOmer at the end of the chapter in the gloss, and in Beit Shmuel section 1, and according to what we have explained, everything is clear and there is no dispute among the Tannaim on the basic law, and study it well).

And that which we wrote in section 2 that the gifts always revert after the betrothal, and certainly after the engagement before the betrothal, the Rambam wrote in Chapter 6 of Zechiyah: If one sends gifts to his father-in-law's house, whether many or few, whether he ate there a betrothal meal or not, whether he died or she died, or if the man retracted - all the gifts are returned except for food and drink, and similarly a few utensils that he sent for her to use in her father's house. If she used them and they wore out or were lost, they are not repaid, but if they are still intact, everything is returned and he can collect them in a court of law, for it is known that he only sent them for adornment purposes. If she retracted, everything is returned, even the food and drink, and she pays their value at a discount. And the Geonim have already agreed that if the value of the food and drink was six, she pays back four if she retracted, for he did not give her this gift except with the understanding that she would not retract.

However, the Tur writes as follows: "And the gifts that he sent, sometimes they are returned and sometimes they are not returned. How so? If he sent her clothes and fine linens, items that are meant to be used in her father's house and she could use them until they wear out, and she used them in her father's house, similarly if he sent her types of food or drink, if he ate and drank in his father-in-law's house an amount worth a dinar when he sent them, since it is customary to feed him when he sends a gift – then she does not need to return them even if they are still extant and even if they are worth a hundred maneh. If he did not eat there at all or ate there less than a dinar's worth – she needs to return them. In what case is this stated? When he retracts. But if she retracts – even a small bundle of vegetables must be returned, even if he ate there, and when she pays him, she deducts one-third of their value and pays two-thirds. If he sent her silver or gold vessels and clothes that are not meant to be worn out in her father's house – they are returned in any case even if he ate there. If they sent him to eat in his house when he sent the gift or if he sent the gift through his messenger and they fed the messenger, it is a question whether this is considered as if he ate there, and it is not resolved. Additionally, it is a question whether if he ate there an amount worth half a dinar whether he waived the other half, and further it is a question whether the enhancement of the gifts’ value is returned with the gifts when they are returned, and it is not resolved. Therefore, we do not extract from uncertainty and they are not returned." So writes the Tur.

And according to the opinion of the Tur, so is the opinion of most of our rabbis, and the opinion of the Rambam (Maimonides) is a singular opinion. Even the Rif does not hold like him, for according to the Rambam, even if one did not eat there, the food, drink, and few used items that wore out do not return. According to the Tur, these do not return unless one ate there at the time of the gifts [see Beit Yosef], because through the act of eating, one forgives all these. And if he ate food worth a dinar, no less, because a dinar was a significant currency during the time of the Talmud [Kiddushin 12a, Arakhin 23b]. Additionally, he disagrees that according to the Rambam, if they did not wear out, in any case, they return, but according to the Tur, if he ate food worth a dinar, these items do not return even if they are intact. And if he gave a gift of money, it is also like items made to be used up, for they were given to be spent [Nimukei Yosef, Chapter 9 of Bava Batra].

And there are some authorities who disagree with the Tur on one particular point, as according to the Tur, regarding garments and clothing items that can be used until they wear out, if they have been consumed there – they do not return even if they are still intact and not worn out. However, there are those who disagree with him, stating that in this case, it is a doubt in the law. According to the authorities who hold that possession is effective in cases of doubtful law, if someone has taken possession, we do not remove it from him, except for small ornaments such as various scarves, women's ties, and shoes, for in such items, one forgoes even if they are intact. This is what the terms "Yeba and Savtacha" in the Gemara there refer to, and the Tur explains that this refers to garments and clothing items as mentioned by the Beit Yosef. The Beit Shmuel's wonderment at the Tur is unnecessary, and furthermore, the Tur holds that possession is not effective in cases of doubtful law as stated in Choshen Mishpat in various places.

Items that are not typically subject to wear and tear: when she sells them, it is considered as if she has stolen them, and she must repay their value at the time of the theft. Regarding the appreciation of gifts, there is a legal doubt as to whether the appreciation is collectible in certain gifts that depend on consumption. If they are consumed, they are not collectible, but if not consumed, they are collectible. In these cases, there is doubt if they appreciated after being given to her and then wore out before returning, whether we say that since at the time of giving, his intention was for them to be consumed and to remain with her, she should only pay their value at that time, or perhaps since they were not consumed and remained in his possession until the time of return, she must return the appreciation, and it is a legal doubt, and the one who seeks to extract money from another carries the burden of proof and the appreciation is not returned. 

But in gifts that do not depend on consumption and are always returned like items not subject to wear and tear, there is no doubt at all. For if they are still extant, she collects them with their appreciation, and if she sold or gave them away, it is clear that she must pay what they appreciated before disposal. If they appreciated after disposal, she is nothing more than a thief, and all thieves only pay the value at the time of the theft, and certainly the appreciation is not returned. Even if they sold them and profited with the money received for them, it is clear that they are not obligated to return the profits since the profits were not for the groom’s benefit. 

Know that if there are a few small gifts that are made to be worn out, if they are numerous, such as sending her four pairs of small garments that certainly would not wear out in her father's house, they are considered numerous gifts and are collectible in any case.

The Rambam, of blessed memory, also wrote: "My teachers instructed that if it is the custom of the country for each person to make a feast and feed his friends or distribute money to servants and the like, and he did as everyone does and then retracted – he must pay for everything, because he caused him to lose his money, and anyone who causes another to lose money must compensate him. This is provided that he has witnesses to how much he spent, for this is not a case where he can take an oath and collect." This is the end of his words. The Rambam, of blessed memory, compared this to all the laws of indirect damage and causing harm. Others disagreed with him on this, arguing that any loss of money that the owner incurs knowingly, even if it resulted in damage, he is exempt. To what is this similar? To someone who sells garden seeds and they do not sprout – he does not reimburse the expenses, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 232, and as it is taught in the Tosefta: if someone sells wine to his friend and it turns out to be bad and it spoils, he must provide the value of the wine, not the value of the vinegar that the buyer turned it into [Raavad and the Gra, section 9]; this is not related to indirect damage and causing harm. But according to the Rambam’s opinion, this is not comparable to all those cases, because there he intended to profit and incurred expenses, but here he did not intend to profit but to act according to the custom of the country, and therefore, the one who retracts is obligated to pay the other all the expenses [Magid Mishneh]. Therefore, although this is no more than indirect damage for which one is usually exempt, in this case, it is considered as if he incurred the expenses on his behalf, since it is the custom of all the people in the country to make a feast and incur expenses. Hence, it is the law to pay for everything as if it were a direct cause of damage, as if he instructed him to incur these expenses, and it is not considered indirect damage for which he would be exempt [Bayit Chadash].

According to the Rambam, the law is clear in our region: when people get engaged and write preliminary agreements or conditions, and travel from place to place, and both parties incur significant expenses, if one of them subsequently backs out, they must reimburse all the expenses incurred by the other party, as verified by witnesses, estimates from experts, or a court. Those who disagree with the Rambam do not collect these expenses. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled in the Shulchan Aruch like the Rambam, and it appears to be the established custom in all courts that the party who breaches the agreement reimburses the expenses of the party who upheld the agreement. Often, they reach a compromise between them. [What the Beit Shmuel writes in section 7 about at least a third, I do not understand the relevance of this reduction, as it only applies to gifts of food and drink for the bride and her family’s household.]

Regarding gifts, it appears that all types of presents that the groom sends to the bride are considered as not meant to be consumed and always return even if he retracts. As for food and drink that he sent—according to the Rambam, if he retracts, they do not return, but if she retracts, she pays a third less. According to the Tur, they do not return if he retracts unless the groom ate there an amount worth a dinar. However, the current custom is not for the groom to personally bring gifts to the bride's father's house and eat there. It seems that what they do now during the engagement, making a feast and rejoicing together, is considered like eating a dinar at the bride's house. Nevertheless, according to the opinion that will be explained, before the betrothal, in any case, everything returns. There is no practical difference now between the Rambam and the Tur according to our custom, where the betrothal is at the time of the wedding.

And our master, the Rema, wrote that some say all this refers to what was sent after betrothal, but before betrothal, after engagement — everything is returned. There are those who disagree, end quote. The later authorities ruled according to the first opinion that everything is returned [Taz and Beit Shmuel], and according to this, even when he withdraws, all the gifts he sent her are returned to him. Even gifts that have been consumed must be paid for, even if the cancellation is on his part, because he gave them with the understanding that if he withdraws, she will repay him, and certainly if she withdraws. However, we have never heard in our time that they would rule this way, that she must pay for consumed gifts or delicacies that he sent her when he withdraws. It is possible that our engagements, which involve prohibition and penalty, are considered like betrothal [Bava Metzia], and it is possible that the people of the country adopted the ruling of those who disagree. One of the great ones already wondered about this, how it is possible that she should pay when the cancellation is on his part [Chomat Shlomo section 11, and the answer of the Beit Shmuel section 9 comparing it to “he did not eat” in the Talmudic times is insufficient, because in their times, without the eating of a dinar, there was no bond of love, which is not the case now, where the engagement agreements bond them to each other in love].

Our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote in Section 4: If one arranges a match for his daughter with another and sends him clothing and jewelry, and then the engagement is broken off and the groom or his father-in-law withdraws – he must return what was sent to him. Just as the gifts that he sent to her are returned, so too must what she sent to him be returned, for it is understood that they were only sent with the intention of proceeding to marriage. This is the same reasoning for both parties. The Talmud and the legal authorities mentioned the case of the groom sending gifts to the bride because it is customary for the groom to send gifts to the bride [as noted by the Gaon of Vilna], but the law is the same for gifts sent by the bride or her father to the groom.

The general rule is that when an engagement has been established and then the engagement is broken off, all the gifts that are still in existence, which were given to each other and are items that do not wear out, such as pearls, precious stones, and valuable items, are returned to each other. This applies regardless of who broke off the engagement. Items that do wear out, such as shoes and similar items, as well as cash gifts that were given to each other, according to the Rambam, if they are still in existence, they are returned; if they are not still in existence, they are not returned. However, the party that broke off the engagement must compensate the other party even for gifts that wore out or were lost, and also for food and drink expenses up to one-third, and also for the expenses of the engagement agreement according to the local custom. Similarly, the party that broke off the engagement must pay the matchmaking fees if the custom is to pay them before or immediately after the engagement agreement. We have already explained that there are some who disagree with the Rambam on specific details. Regarding the expenses, the ruling follows the Rambam straightforwardly, as our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, only brought his opinion on this matter. Additionally, regarding the ruling that the party that broke off the engagement must compensate the other party even for gifts that wore out or were lost, there is no disagreement. The only point of contention is regarding items that wear out: if they are still in existence, they are always returned, and if they are not in existence, they are not returned if the party who was supposed to return the gifts did not break off the engagement. On this, the Tur and the poskim disagree, distinguishing between whether the items were consumed or not, as we have explained. However, we have already clarified that in our times, consumption as it was in their times in the bride's house is not relevant.

The penalties that are written in engagement agreements, as is the custom among us to write in the conditions a penalty for the party that breaches the agreement to the party that upholds it, amounting to half the dowry, and this has been the practice since ancient times. According to the law, it would seem that there is no substance to this because they are considered an "asmachta" (a conditional commitment that is not legally binding), as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 207. Indeed, our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote in section 6 that when they want to make promises in engagement agreements, they do so in a manner that it should not be an asmachta, meaning they create a document in which one party owes the other a certain amount. After obligating himself to this amount, he makes a condition with the bride's father that if he fulfills the engagement and enters the wedding canopy with his betrothed, the debt will be forgiven. Then, they create another document in which the other party owes this amount and makes a condition with him that if he brings his daughter to the wedding canopy with this betrothed, the debt will be forgiven. They place these two documents in the hands of a third party. This follows the approach of the Rambam in Chapter 11 of Hilchot Mechirah regarding all kinds of asmachtot. We have explained these matters in Choshen Mishpat, there in section 47. In our times, this practice is not customary. (The half dowry penalty written – it seems that the intention is half the dowry of the bride, as this is called a dowry and not of the groom).

In truth, many of our early authorities have written that in engagements (shidduchin), there is no issue of asmachta (a stipulation that one does not intend to uphold), as Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that some say all penalties made in engagements do not involve asmachta, and this is the common custom to collect penalties made in engagements, as stated in Choshen Mishpat 207. We explained there in section 48 the reason, because it is appropriate for the one who retracts to be liable for a penalty for the shame caused to the other party. And even though we do not adjudicate cases of shame in our times as stated there in section 1, nevertheless, when one obligates himself to pay for the shame, there is no issue of asmachta. However, an acquisition (kinyan) is required because mere words are insignificant, and therefore it is necessary to acquire upon the penalty. But one should not make an acquisition with a sudar (handkerchief), because currency is not acquired through exchange unless one acquires something equivalent to money in a specific item or in what he possesses, whether land or movable property. Some say that no acquisition is needed since it is payment for shame, similar to "if one plows and does not work, he pays the best" which does not require an acquisition. And our master, the Beit Yosef, himself brought this opinion in Choshen Mishpat there, that there is no asmachta in engagements for this reason, and he did not explain it here because he relied on what was written there. We explained there that it is possible the acquisition made at the time of the conditions also benefits the penalty of half the dowry, and even though currency is not acquired through exchange, it is possible that since the acquisition benefits other obligations like food and clothing, it also benefits currency. This requires further study in practice. Moreover, since it is customary to gather many people at the time of the conditions, it is considered a significant court, and the acquisition is as if it were from now, in which case there is no asmachta. Additionally, in engagements, since it is the custom of the world to acquire with a sudar, it is acquired by law even without "from now," and the one who retracts is obligated, since the matter depends on custom, similar to situmta (a customary form of acquisition). In any case, according to all our authorities, there is no asmachta in penalties of engagements. 

[What is written by the Shach in section 14 in the name of the Maharik, that even if no penalty was made, it is likely that one must pay for the shame, is not found in any other authority.]

Only financial penalties made at the time of the engagement are not considered an asmachta (a conditional commitment that is not legally binding). However, if financial penalties are made before the wedding – those penalties are considered an asmachta. Nevertheless, before the wedding, even if one consents to marry but wants to change some of the conditions, they are obligated to pay the penalty. Otherwise, anyone could easily find ways to nullify some of the conditions, and thereby the engagement would be nullified, bringing shame to the other party. However, if one of the parties wishes to delay the wedding, we are not concerned with that, as the penalty does not apply to delays, unless the court sees that it is a scheme to cancel the engagement. Many times, one party wishes to cancel the engagement but is afraid of the penalty and seeks schemes to pretend they do not want to cancel. The court must understand this and obligate them to pay the penalty. (What the Beit Shmuel wrote there in the name of the Maharit, that even if one swore on the conditions, it does not apply to delaying the time – this needs further examination).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote in section 6 that this only applies if the penalty documents have already been written. However, if they performed a kinyan (formal acquisition act) on the condition to write the documents, and before they were written one of them retracted and protested in front of witnesses against writing the documents, he has the right to protest the document, as stated in Choshen Mishpat sections 39 and 243. Consequently, since he stipulated that the documents should be written and protested against their writing, he is exempt from both the engagement itself and the penalty, as the kinyan for writing the document is not valid because it is merely a verbal commitment. Therefore, since it was contingent on the writing and the writing is canceled, the matter itself is also nullified. If he did not stipulate "on condition," although he can protest the writing of the document, the engagement must still be completed due to the kinyan. 

Know that in Choshen Mishpat section 243:7, we explained that even if the document was written, as long as it has not been delivered to the recipient, if he protested against delivering it, the gift is also nullified. This is because saying "on condition that you write" implies writing and delivering, as writing without delivery is nothing. Since he retracted from delivering it and the gift was contingent on this, the gift is nullified. The Rema relied on what is written there. It is possible that according to our custom, after writing the conditions and performing the kinyan, they read the conditions publicly and break utensils as a sign of joy, they cannot retract after the reading of the conditions. This is considered the finalization according to the custom and the main aspect of shame, and this is also the essential ruling according to the law.

If they accepted a formal acquisition (kinyan) concerning the marriage alone, meaning to perform the marriage on a certain day, some say that this is considered a mere "acquisition of words" and the acquisition is void since there is nothing substantial upon which the acquisition can take effect [Sema there, subsection 12]. Others say that the acquisition is indeed valid [Taz there]. We have explained there in section 8 that the primary legal opinion appears to be that the obligation of marriage constitutes a personal obligation, as the husband commits himself to provide her sustenance and clothing, and she obligates herself to perform work. This is no less valid than a rental of one's services. See there.

Some say that if they wrote an outline and made a formal acquisition, even though they did not explicitly state that they would write the contracts, it is as if they said it. Because it is certainly their intention, as it is a simple custom that after writing the outline, they write the conditions. Therefore, each party can retract after writing the outline and can object to writing the conditions, and the engagement is nullified, and they are exempt from the penalty (Taz and Beit Shmuel). However, if they deposited a promissory note with a third party, the obligation is finalized, and they are liable for embarrassment. If the conditions were already written in brief and given to a scribe to write them in full, neither party can retract, and they are liable for embarrassment (Beit Shmuel). In our times, the custom is not to first write an outline and then immediately write the conditions, but either to write conditions alone or only an outline stating that it holds the power of conditions. However, it is certain that for us, the main conclusion is the public reading of the conditions and the breaking of the vessels, as stated. And when an acquisition is made during engagements, even in general terms without stating that it is for the purpose of writing, it implies writing and reading. Therefore, as long as the conditions have not been read publicly, they can retract from the engagement without penalty, and this is the custom.

If he made the transaction in secret in the presence of witnesses and instructed the witnesses not to reveal the matter, and then one of the parties objected to the witnesses that they should not write it down – he is exempt from the fine and can object, since it was done in secret and there is no issue of embarrassment. This is specifically when no others were present at all, but if others were present, even if they were only relatives of the parties, embarrassment is applicable. However, it has already been explained that according to our custom, until after the reading of the conditions, they can retract without a fine.

It is obvious that the obligation of a penalty for breaking off an engagement or altering its details applies only when one cancels it of their own free will. However, if the person was compelled to cancel it due to some form of coercion that, in the eyes of the court, constitutes coercion, we are witnesses that the commitment was made only under the assumption that no coercion would occur. This is a significant presumption, and even financial coercion is considered coercion. Therefore, if someone's financial situation declines and they cannot fulfill the promised details, and the other party is unwilling to accept anything less, the engagement is annulled and both parties are exempt from the penalty. This applies similarly in all such cases, and even regarding an oath, a significant financial loss is considered coercion, as stated by our teacher, the Rema, in Yoreh De'ah, section 232.

And there is no obligation of a penalty even on one who changes willingly except for one who obligated himself. However, if the prevention is not from the obligating party, he is exempt from the penalty and from returning the expenses to the other party. Only the gifts are to be returned to each other as explained. Therefore, among us where it is a simple custom that the father of the groom and the father of the bride write the conditions and obligate themselves, and afterwards the prevention was from their wives who one of them delays the completion of the match or fulfilling the details, and all the more so if the groom or the bride do not want the match without their fathers' persuasion, the fathers are exempt, as our Rabbi the Rema wrote that one who arranged for his daughter or his granddaughter or his relative to marry a certain person and then the daughter does not want, the arranger is exempt from the penalty because this is called coercion even though he did not condition it, provided there is no deceit in the matter. And look later at the end of Siman 77, where it is explained that a betrothed woman who says the groom is repulsive to her, her father is not obligated to give what he promised her. And even though we do not rule like the Rambam and force to give a divorce with the claim of "he is repulsive to me" as explained there, nevertheless he is not obligated to fulfill what he promised. All the more so, before the engagement, even though in our time it has become customary in many places that the groom and bride themselves sign the conditions, nevertheless the main obligation is on the fathers and they are not obligated if the prevention is not from themselves. And if the other party suspects that his hand is involved in spoiling the matter, he can impose on him an acceptance that he did not incite this and that from his side there is no prevention at all. And even if perhaps giving money to the son or daughter would make them agreeable, he is not obligated to do so, because this is considered complete coercion, and also the guarantors are exempt. And he did not need to condition this because generally the children agree to their parents' wishes and this or that who deviated from the norm, even though it is not complete coercion that is not common at all, nevertheless it is also not very common that there is exemption in money in such a case. And even the trustee who holds a promissory note or cash to give to his son-in-law is exempt, and the trustee does not give it because we testify that his intention was only if his daughter agreed. And likewise, if the father of the groom is the trustee and the groom does not agree, the law is the same. And even if there was also an oath about this, he is exempt if he needs to spend a lot of money until they agree, because it is a clear assessment that he did not swear with such an intention to spend a lot of money to appease them.

And so too with other unforeseen circumstances that occur, where it is not possible to fulfill the details that were promised, such as if one has lost his wealth. Similarly, if a father promised a dowry for his son of a certain amount and the father dies, the heirs are not required to fulfill this and are exempt from the penalty. Also, the betrothed son is exempt from the penalty, for there is no greater unforeseen circumstance than this. And even if the father left enough to cover the promised amount, the heirs are not obligated to give it to the betrothed if it exceeds his share of the inheritance, as the betrothed did not acquire the money during the father's lifetime. Even though in the conditions they made a formal acquisition (kinyan sudar) to uphold all the details, the acquisition is not for the betrothed son to immediately acquire the dowry, but rather for the father-in-law who betrothed his daughter to his son. The father promised a certain amount to his son, and if he does not give this amount, he will pay a penalty to the other side. And for this, they made a formal acquisition (kinyan sudar), but the son did not acquire any right. Therefore, even if it was written that he obligates himself to give, he is exempt if he becomes poor or dies, and the groom only receives his share of the inheritance. Similarly, if the father of the bride promised a dowry for his daughter of a certain amount and he loses his wealth, it is considered an unforeseen circumstance and he is exempt. Similarly, if he dies and the inheritance falls to his male sons, they are not required to fulfill their father's commitment, as the daughter did not acquire anything during his lifetime, as we said regarding the son. However, they are required to give her according to her share, a tenth of the estate, or according to the estimate of the father’s intention. Therefore, if at the time of the commitment he was in a better financial state than at the time of his death, that estimate which he made himself is nullified, as he was in a better state at that time.

And it is obvious that if the father of the groom or the father of the bride deposited the dowry they promised and committed to in the conditions with a third party, the son acquires it during the lifetime of the father, and it is not considered part of his inheritance, just as a gift given by a father to one of his sons is not considered part of the inheritance after the father's death, and he acquires it for himself. Similarly, if the father of the bride deposited the dowry and died, the daughter acquires it during his lifetime, and his heirs have no claim to it, even if the money is in the hands of a third party. For specifically in a general agreement, they are exempt because the son does not actually acquire the dowry; therefore, if he dies or other unforeseen events occur, they are exempt from the penalty.

And even if they did not deposit the money but only obligated themselves through a promissory note, our Rabbi, the Rema, also ruled that the heirs are obligated to pay, and a claim of coercion does not help, for a claim of coercion does not help in the case of a loan. Similarly, if the acquisition was made at the time of the engagement, where the son or daughter received the property themselves, the heirs are also obligated to pay. However, for money, the symbolic act of acquisition does not apply, since currency is not acquired through barter. The act of acquisition is only effective for dowry items, whether movable property or real estate, unless nothing is left from the father, in which case it is obvious that the heirs are not obligated to pay from their own pockets. This applies specifically to a promissory note regarding the dowry, but if a promissory note was given for a penalty, the heirs are exempt, for since they are exempt from the penalty, what benefit does the promissory note provide, as they have no obligation for a penalty. Similarly, if there was a complete obligation to the daughter or son by mere verbal commitment, according to the ways that will be explained in section 51, where one can be bound by words alone, and they died, the heirs are obligated to pay.

And similarly, sometimes even the one who is liable is exempt from the penalty, even if his situation has not changed, such as a father who sent his son to find a match for his daughter and gave him a power of attorney for these matters, and the son deviated from the details and the father refuses and does not want the match - both are exempt from the penalty [Bach 16]. However, if the son did not deviate from the details and the father does not want to fulfill it - he is liable for the penalty, for the agent of a person is like the person himself.

Similarly, if one party is compelled to change some detail and the other party does not agree to it, even if the change is minor – for example, if two people became engaged while they were living in the same city with the assumption that the marriage would take place there, and one is forced to leave the city and wants the other to follow to perform the marriage, but the other does not agree – both are exempt from the penalty. This is because one was compelled and the other wishes for the marriage to occur in the city. However, if one leaves the city without being compelled, they are liable for the penalty, and the other is exempt.

If they do not live in the same city and did not specify in the conditions where the marriage would take place, the groom is obligated to come to the bride's location to marry her, as this is the customary practice and the way of men to seek out women. If there is a fixed custom regarding the wedding expenses, they should follow that custom if it was not specified in the conditions.

And sometimes one party is exempt from the penalty if they do not want to carry out the engagement, even without a change in their situation and without any coercion, and even if the other party wants to fulfill all commitments. For example, if the betrothed has corrupted their behavior either towards Heaven or towards people, the betrothed woman can retract and is exempt from the acquisition, the oath, and the obligation of the contract if it was given. Even if she knew that his behavior was somewhat corrupted before the engagement, if it worsened afterward, she can retract (Beit Shmuel, section 12). Even if the contract was placed in the hands of a third party and returned to the betrothed man, it is as if nothing was done, for she has no obligation to fulfill the conditions. Similarly, if the betrothed woman corrupted her behavior and the betrothed man does not want to continue, he is exempt from everything. It is obvious that if one of them goes insane, the other can retract, and similarly, if one of them becomes ill, it is obvious that they did not consent with this in mind.

Moreover, the Rosh ruled regarding Reuven, who betrothed his daughter to Shimon with a formal transaction and an oath, and they deposited documents with a third party. Afterwards, it happened that the sister of the betrothed converted to Islam, that Shimon can retract and is exempt from the transaction, the oath, and the obligation of the document, which includes penalties agreed upon between them. If the third party returned the document to the betrothed, it is of no effect. This is also the ruling of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 5. Even if the betrothed's sister merely committed adultery while being a married woman, or even if she was single and became pregnant from promiscuity, which is a significant blemish, the betrothed can retract [Taz and Shach]. The reasoning is that it is a significant presumption that he did not agree to such a great blemish. Anything that, in the eyes of the court, significantly changes the status of one party to such a degree that it is a great disgrace in the eyes of people, the other party can retract. It is impossible to detail everything in writing because it depends on the values, location, circumstances, and lineage of the families involved. It is evident that if the betrothed becomes blemished, the betrothed woman can retract, and vice versa.

And our master the Rema wrote that some say all this applies before betrothal, but after betrothal, his field was destroyed, end quote. For even regarding blemishes, we say this, and all the more so regarding other matters. And he is obligated to give her the ketubah if he wishes to divorce her. Also, as explained with the case of the betrothed sister, his field was destroyed. And although a person has free choice and can choose to do good or evil, nevertheless, his field was destroyed. And in our regions, where we do not betroth before the wedding, this law has no practical difference.

What is written in the conditions "and due to quarrel and dispute, it shall be as per the enactment of ShUM" – this refers to the husband's inheritance rights if she passes away after the wedding, and it will be explained in Siman 53. Additionally, we write in our conditions "that the penalty shall not release" etc. – this refers to the situation where even if one party wishes to pay the penalty and break off the engagement, nevertheless, there is a significant deterrent from the enactment of the ancients if he is not coerced and no change has occurred in the other party. And even without the enactment of the ancients, since in all conditions a kinyan (acquisition) is made, it is clarified in Choshen Mishpat Siman 12 regarding two who accepted arbitrators with a kinyan and a penalty, and after the arbitration one said, "I will pay the penalty and not fulfill the arbitration" – his words carry no weight. All the more so in conditions between a groom and bride.

The Tur wrote: Rabbi Yosef stated that all penalties that are made regarding engagements, where one who retracts will be liable to the other party for such and such an amount, are not considered an asmachta (a non-binding commitment). Therefore, if each party made a contract upon themselves and deposited it with a third party under the condition that whoever retracts will give it to the other party, the third party should act upon their trust.

The Tur further writes that if each party gives a pledge to the other for the penalty they would incur, saying to each other, "If I retract, I will give you such and such, and this object is in your possession as a pledge for the penalty I would incur if I retract" – this is invalid. For in this manner, the pledge is not acquired as long as there is no actual obligation. A person can encumber their property for something they are already obligated for, but for something they are not yet obligated for, the encumbrance does not take effect. Instead, it is necessary to transfer it with a symbolic act of acquisition (sudar), not as an asmakhta (reliance) in a reputable Beit Din (court), so that he becomes obligated by law if he retracts. Then he will give him the object as a pledge, and the encumbrance will take effect on the pledge since he is obligated to the penalty if he retracts. Alternatively, he can say, "If I retract, you will acquire such and such amount of money in the essence of this object." End of quote.

And even though he himself wrote that there is no issue of "asmachta" (a conditional commitment) in betrothal agreements, it is different here because he reveals his intention that he does not rely on the penalty but prefers to pledge an object. However, there is no pledge here unless he says "you shall acquire the actual object" or he becomes obligated by law [Rashal and Bach]. Furthermore, while it is true that there is no issue of "asmachta" in this case, nevertheless, this pertains to his obligation, but the pledge does not acquire if he wants to collect from the pledge unless he did as stated [Taz]. According to this reasoning, the obligation remains on him, and he can withhold it as a pledge, but he does not acquire the actual pledge to sell or give it as a gift or the like. However, according to the first reasoning, the obligation is also nullified.

The laws of matchmaking are explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 185. Our custom is to pay the matchmaker immediately after the conditions (tanaim) are made, and even if the match is later canceled, the matchmaking fee is not returned. The custom is that the initiator receives half and the one who completes the match receives half. Those who are involved in the middle, according to strict law, get nothing. Nonetheless, the custom is to give them something as well, for it is impractical to adhere strictly to the law in this matter. The matchmaking fee is taken from the total amount of the dowry. There are places where they pay five percent — two and a half percent from each side, and there are places where they pay six percent. There are those who, when there is no river separating the parties, pay four percent, and each place follows its custom. It is certainly forbidden for any party to bring in a relative or friend as a matchmaker when other matchmakers have already begun the work, as this is almost outright theft and is no less severe than a poor person turning over a cake (to claim it as theirs). Nonetheless, some are not particular about this, but this is not a sound practice. If the matchmaker initially stated that they would work for free, they receive no matchmaking fee. If two people swore to each other that they would marry and one of them reneged, or if only one person swore, this is explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 236.

[b]Matters Acquired by Verbal Agreement, and If They Are Given in Writing, and This Contains 13 Sections[/b]

Our sages said (Ketubot 102b): "How much are you giving your son? - Such and such! How much are you giving your daughter? - Such and such!" They stood and betrothed - they have acquired. These are the matters acquired by verbal agreement, for with the pleasure that they are marrying each other, they resolve and transfer to each other. And although mere words are generally not effective without a formal act of acquisition, this is because for mere words a person does not rely and does not resolve in his heart to transfer. But in a situation where it is clear to us that he fully intended in his heart to transfer, it is considered an acquisition, similar to what is stated in Choshen Mishpat 204 regarding the sale of a stolen field, where the acquisition is invalid, and the thief subsequently repurchased it from the original owner, the field remains in the possession of the buyer from the thief because the sages assessed his intention that he meant to uphold the sale to the buyer. And even though unspoken intentions are not considered, nevertheless it acquires, and we explained there the reason is due to reliance on the mind, and we also explained there the reason that this pleasure of holding him as a trustworthy person is considered by him as receiving money, and this is his acquisition as if he received money. Similarly, the sages understood that this pleasure from the engagement is so significant to them as if they made a formal acquisition, and they resolve and transfer to each other, thus it is considered a complete acquisition.

From the words of all the decisors, it appears that this law applies only at the time of betrothal. However, from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 11 of Hilchot Mechirah, it is explained that this law also applies at the time of marriage, see there. And furthermore, it is explained there that even though transferring something undefined to another person does not acquire ownership even with a formal acquisition, nevertheless, in this case where it is acquired by mere verbal agreement, it also applies to something undefined, see there. And in Chapter 6 of Hilchot Zechiyah, it is explained that it is necessary that the item being agreed upon is within the person's possession, for otherwise, a person cannot transfer ownership of something that does not yet exist, see there. This means that the acquisition by verbal agreement is not superior to a complete formal acquisition. The reason that something undefined can be transferred by verbal agreement is because, according to the Rambam, the reason something undefined cannot be acquired is due to a lack of certainty, but with verbal agreement, there is certainty, as he wrote. However, with something that does not yet exist, the reason it cannot be acquired is not due to certainty but because a person does not have the power to transfer ownership of something that is not in existence or in their possession. Therefore, it is obvious that verbal agreement is certainly not superior to formal acquisition. This is the intention of the Beit Shmuel, section 4. Therefore, since it is explained in Choshen Mishpat, siman 60, that a person can obligate themselves even regarding something that does not yet exist, it follows that with something acquired by verbal agreement, one can also obligate themselves even regarding something not in their possession or something that does not yet exist. Some of the early authorities disagreed with the Rambam and held that things acquired by verbal agreement are effective even for something that does not yet exist and is not in the person's possession, see Hagahot Maimoniyot, Chapter 23 of Hilchot Ishut. But the Tur and Shulchan Aruch rule like the Rambam. Perhaps those who disagree hold that with something that does not yet exist, if it is said that it will be acquired when it comes into existence, it is acquired. Therefore, with things acquired by verbal agreement, it is as if it was said so. However, we have already explained in Choshen Mishpat, siman 209, section 9, that the main legal ruling is that even in such a case, it is not acquired, see there. And see what we wrote in siman 66, section 8.

And even though we have written that in the manner of obligation it is effective even for something that has not yet come into existence and is not in his possession, this is all when, at the very least, the thing will eventually come into his possession and then it will be within his power to fulfill. But when the thing will never come into his possession, such as when he promises something concerning another, like a father who decides that his son will do something, such as going to a certain place or giving something or going after the bride, or similar matters that do not depend on the father but rather on another person or the son — his decision is meaningless.

There is no distinction whether the son or daughter is a minor or an adult – in all cases, the parents are obligated by mere words. However, this is only what the Sages said regarding the first marriage, where the son is a bachelor who has not yet married, and the daughter is a virgin who has not yet been betrothed. In such cases, the parents' joy is great, and from their abundant joy for their son and daughter, a person's intention is entirely towards their son and daughter, and they effect the acquisition through mere words. But this does not apply to second marriages.
