And some say that if for one of the parents it is the first marriage and for the other the second marriage – for example, a bachelor who marries a widow or a widower who marries a virgin – then for the one for whom it is the first marriage, their son or daughter acquires [the benefit], but for the second marriage, they do not acquire it unless a formal acquisition is made as in all monetary laws.

And similarly, this is specifically regarding a father who made a commitment concerning his son and daughter. However, regarding his granddaughter or even his grandson – a mere statement is not sufficient to establish an obligation, and certainly not for his grandson’s son or granddaughter. Even though a person’s affection extends also to his grandchildren, nevertheless, the primary joy of a person is only with his sons and daughters. Similarly, a mother who made a commitment concerning her son or daughter – it does not establish an obligation with a mere statement, as this power is only in the hand of the father. Certainly, a brother who made a commitment concerning his sister or other relatives does not have this rule unless he made a commitment to a poor relative to help him, as this is like charity and he is obligated to fulfill it due to the principle of a vow. Even if the gift is substantial, in the case of a small gift, even if he promises it to a wealthy person, there is an issue of lacking faithfulness if he does not fulfill it, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 249. However, this is not considered a binding acquisition, and if he retracts, we do not have the power to compel him. But for a poor person, even if he is not a relative and even if the gift is substantial, if he promised it – even not at the time of betrothal – we compel him to fulfill it due to the principle of a vow.

And since the sages (Chazal) have said this regarding the parents of the betrothed, how much more so regarding the betrothed themselves. Therefore, a man and a woman who were betrothed, and he said to her, "How much are you bringing to me? ... Such and such," and she said to him, "And how much are you giving me" or "writing for me? ... Such and such," and they stood and sanctified (i.e., got married) – these are matters that are acquired by mere speech, and whatever they promised at that time they must fulfill as if it were a formal transaction. Even if he agreed to provide for her daughter for five years, the daughter has acquired it because he committed by mere speech. And there is no difference between a first marriage and a second marriage, for their joy is great even in a second marriage, and from the joy, they finalize and transfer ownership by mere speech alone.

Some of our rabbis believe that things acquired through verbal agreement only hold if the betrothal happens immediately following the conditions without any interruption. This is implied by the language of our Sages, "and they stood and betrothed," suggesting that the betrothal occurred directly out of the discussions. Alternatively, even if the betrothal took place later, as long as the conditions were mentioned during the betrothal, it is considered as if the betrothal happened directly out of the discussions [Tosafot Ketubot 109]. However, if the betrothal occurred later and the conditions were not mentioned, or if there was an interruption after the betrothal, the conditions are not acquired by verbal agreement. According to what I have mentioned in the name of the Rambam, that even during marriage it is effective, it seems he does not hold this view unless we force an interpretation that even before the betrothal they interrupted and then mentioned it during the marriage. But this does not seem correct because, in truth, some of our rabbis disagree [Shitah Mekubetzet in the name of R"Y] and hold that as long as the betrothal was based on the original conditions, it is valid. The Talmud's use of the phrase "and they stood" proves nothing, as this is its usual language [Ketubot 73, 107]. However, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch follow the first opinion, and according to this, this law does not apply to us since we betroth under the chuppah and it is not customary to mention interruptions close to the chuppah. Some say further that it is necessary for them to agree together, meaning that one party should ask the obligated party, "How much will you give?" and he should respond, "Such and such." But if they acted without mutual agreement, with each party stating independently, "I will give such and such," this is merely idle talk and has no legal standing.

The Sages of blessed memory [there] stated that matters which are acquired through verbal declaration are not meant to be written down. This means that we do not say that since a standard acquisition is formalized through writing, witnesses can also write a document for these matters acquired by verbal declaration and collect from encumbered property with it. We do not say this; it is not to be written without the instruction of the parties involved. When it is written according to their instruction, it can be collected from encumbered property, but without their instruction or if it is not written at all, it can only be collected from unencumbered property. Therefore, if it is written in the document "In our presence, the witnesses, so-and-so said to so-and-so, 'How much are you giving?'" etc., it can only be collected from unencumbered property. But if it is written "In our presence, the witnesses, so-and-so said, etc., and so-and-so and so-and-so told us to write and sign and give it to each one," it is considered a complete document and can be collected from encumbered property [see Hilchot Mechira 6:8]. And if they themselves wrote promissory notes with their own signatures, even if witnesses validated their signatures, if the matter itself was not validated, it is considered an oral loan and cannot be collected from encumbered property, and they are believed to claim repayment as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 69 [this appears to me].

And some of our rabbis explained that it was not given to be written – that even if they are commanded to write, they do not collect it from encumbered property, for the Sages did not strengthen the power of things acquired by verbal agreement except for free property and not for encumbered property. However, for free property, no writing is needed at all [see Rosh there, chapter 3, and in the commentary on Mishneh Torah]. And this seems to be the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 6 of Laws of Acquisition and the Shulchan Aruch in this section [and see there in the glosses and in the Maggid Mishneh, and there is a difficulty with the commentary of the Kesef Mishneh in subparagraph 5, and what was written in the previous section in the name of the Maggid Mishneh we wrote according to the opinion of the Kesef Mishneh and it does not seem so, and see Beit Yosef].

The difference between the ruling in this section and the ruling in the previous section is that there, the son does not acquire immediately, nor does the daughter, because the ruling there is only a penalty clause against the other party, that if he does not fulfill, he pays a fine. Therefore, if he is prevented or dies, the heirs are exempt from paying as stated there in section 30. The ruling in this section, however, is that when acquired by verbal agreement, it is immediately acquired by the son or daughter, and if he dies, the heirs are obligated to pay, and no compulsion exempts them. Similarly, when not acquired by verbal agreement but the father agreed and made a full acquisition obligating himself to give such and such to his son or daughter, it is immediately acquired and is like any other debt. Even if the bride’s father dies before the wedding, it is collected from the heirs, even from encumbered properties, like any other debt. And why is it not the same in the previous section? Because there, the acquisition is only against the other party to obligate a penalty as stated there, but here the acquisition is for the son or daughter. And a symbolic acquisition (kinyan sudar) only works for movables and real estate, not for money, as currency is not acquired by barter. It requires an acquisition through land, and one should not accept in the acquisition to give to his son or daughter, for an acquisition of "I will give" is not effective, as stated in Choshen Mishpat section 245, but an acquisition of obligation upon oneself to give.

There is another practical difference between this section and the previous one. In the previous section, when the father dies, the heirs do not need to give [the gift] because the stipulation is nullified. Rather, the son or daughter takes their portion as heirs, just like the other heirs. However, in this section, or when they acquired a complete transaction from the father obligating himself, as we said, they do not deduct from their inheritance portion because they acquired it during the father’s lifetime and it is like other gifts that a father gives his son or daughter during his lifetime. And we have already written that a transaction of "I will give" does not help. Therefore, if he said "I will give such and such" and accepted with a transaction, and similarly the groom who stipulated to give a specific amount in the ketubah and at the time of the marriage they retract – they cannot be coerced because a transaction of "I will give" does not help. And even though there are those who hold that a transaction of "I will give" does help, nevertheless, it is at least a doubtful law, and one cannot take from the one who is holding [the money]. They are only obligated to fulfill it due to the penalty imposed on them at the time of the conditions, as is customary and as we wrote in the previous section. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that therefore the custom is to make new conditions before the marriage, meaning that then they are fully obligated not because of the penalty. However, among us, this is not the custom [see Beit Shmuel who elaborates extensively in subparagraph 20, and we have already explained in the previous section paragraph 38, and what is written in Choshen Mishpat subparagraph 12 is questionable, and also the symbolic transaction that customarily done among us is nothing for money because currency is not acquired through exchange, see there and understand].

There was an incident where a father arranged a match for his son and later demanded from the other party to pay the dowry they had promised. The other party responded, "You are not my counterpart," as the money belongs to the groom. When the groom demanded it, he replied, "You were not present at the time of the conditions, and you only know about it through your father; therefore, you have no claim against me," and evaded both the dowry and the penalty. Rabbeinu Tam responded that the groom should write an authorization for his father, and then the other party would be obligated to pay the father because he is the groom's agent, and the other party cannot dismiss him.

All that is agreed upon in the conditions must be fulfilled before the wedding, even if it was not specified when the dowry will be given. The father of the bride cannot tell the groom to marry her first and then he will give it, because it is a strong presumption that the commitment is intended for the fulfillment of the marriage. However, the groom cannot demand that the dowry be given directly into his hands; the father can say he will deposit it with a third party until he sees how he treats his daughter. This is the usual custom, to deposit the dowry with a third party for a certain time after the wedding, and anyone who acts without specification does so according to the custom, unless explicitly stated in the conditions or before witnesses that it will be given directly to him before the wedding. If the father of the daughter sees after the wedding that his daughter does not have a pleasant life with her husband and that her husband causes her frequent quarrels, he is not required to give him the dowry, even if he swore to give it, as stated in Choshen Mishpat section 73. Similarly, when the money is with a third party, it should not be handed over to him, as there is concern that he will cause more quarrels once the money is in his hands. However, if the father is making excuses not to give the money to his son-in-law, the court will take the money and give it to the son-in-law. These matters depend on the judgment of the court. The groom must pay for writing the conditions if only one document was written, but if two documents were written, each side pays for their own. It is also a simple custom among us that both sides share the expenses of writing and similar matters.

[One who commits money to his son-in-law and does not want to give it to him, and there are six sections]
The sages taught [Ketubot 108b]: One who commits money to his son-in-law and then goes bankrupt, she (the daughter) can say, "What can I do? Either marry me or release me!" The explanation is: whether he committed a dowry to his daughter through a penalty as stated in Siman 50, or he transferred it to her through a complete acquisition as stated in Siman 51, or he committed it in a manner that it was acquired merely by verbal agreement as stated there, or he committed it in a manner that it was not acquired either by verbal agreement, acquisition, or penalty [as stated in the Tur], and based on this commitment, the groom betrothed his daughter. Afterwards, he (the father) went bankrupt, meaning he does not heed his words and speaks to him disrespectfully, saying "Take mud off my feet" and mocks him, or says "Hang me on a tree, I have nothing to give you," or he died or went far away and there is no one to demand from [Ran]. And the betrothed does not wish to either marry her or release her with a get until the father fulfills what he committed – the daughter can compel him (the betrothed) either to marry her or to release her, for why should she remain an agunah (chained woman) due to her father’s wrongdoing? And if she cannot compel him to marry her without the dowry, nevertheless, she can compel him to do one of these two – either marry or release. It is obvious that if he (the father) obligated himself with a complete obligation as in Siman 51 and he has assets – the court can extract from him by force what he committed, and even if he is not present, the court can descend upon his assets and collect from them. Only if he is impoverished, or they cannot collect, or he is not obligated by law as stated – she can compel him (the betrothed) either to marry or release [see Ran]. There is no difference whether the father committed in the presence of the daughter or not [see Beit Shmuel].

And if she pledged herself and does not fulfill it, the Rambam wrote in chapter 23 that if she pledged herself and did not have the means, she must remain until she finds what she pledged or until she dies. And why does she not free herself by rebellion [meaning, he rules in the case of "I find him repulsive" that we compel him to give a get]? It is because the rebellious woman who is betrothed, the husband wants to marry her, but she does not want to. However, in this case, the husband does not want her until she gives the dowry she pledged, and she wants him, as she says to him either marry or release. This applies to an adult woman, but a minor who pledged herself – we compel him to give a get or marry without the dowry, end quote. And some say that she should also be treated as a rebellious woman [Rif], however, according to what is established in Siman 77 that even in the case of a rebellious woman, we do not compel him to divorce her, there is no practical difference in this. Nonetheless, the opinion of the Rambam and the Rif is that if she pledged herself and she is an adult, even if she has nothing to give him, she cannot force him, but she must remain until her hair turns white or she acquires what to give him.

However, there are those who say that even if she agreed to the marriage on her own and at that time was able to fulfill it, but later her circumstances changed and she can no longer fulfill it, she can claim "What can I do? Either marry me or release me" [The Rosh and the Meor like Admon in the Baraita]. However, the Tur differentiates in this matter, stating that this is only if she agreed in the presence of her father, as she can then claim that she assumed her father would provide for her, and now what can she do? [This explains Admon's language in the Mishnah, ponder this well]. Nevertheless, it can be said that even according to the Tur, if she agreed on her own without her father's presence, and at that time she was able to fulfill it, but later her circumstances changed, she can also compel him either to marry her or to release her. The Tur only states that if at the time of the agreement she was not able to fulfill it, then she cannot compel him if she agreed without her father's presence [This also explains the language of the Mishnah, see there and ponder this well].

Even if her father stipulated [a certain condition], when can she compel him? When she does not have the means to provide what her father stipulated. However, if she has the means, she must provide what her father stipulated and cannot say, "Marry me or release me," nor can she claim, "What do I have to do with my father's stipulation?" For according to the fundamental law, we do not compel him when the hindrance is from another party [as that is the rationale of the sages there]. Rather, we hold that since she is coerced, we do not want to cause her to remain agunah (a chained woman). Therefore, if she is not coerced and is able to fulfill [the stipulation], but insists on strict adherence to the law because she did not make the stipulation, we also strictly adhere to the law and do not compel him. This is the main ruling in the law [see Beit Shmuel, subsection 3, where it also implies this in the responsa of the Rambam, and see Bayit Chadash] [see Maggid Mishneh, chapter 23, halachah 16, where it states that even if he swore to marry her, he is exempt].

All these matters only apply after betrothal and before marriage. However, before betrothal, as is our custom after the conditions are set, this law does not apply, for the conditions are torn up and the match is annulled if one of the parties does not fulfill their agreement. After marriage, one certainly cannot betray his wife because he was not given what was agreed upon; rather, he is obligated in all matters that a man is obligated to his wife. Even if she herself made the agreement and cannot fulfill it, it is forbidden to betray her once he has married her. Nevertheless, when the father made the agreement and does not want to fulfill it, and he has the ability to do so, the court can extract from the father all that he agreed upon, even after marriage [Beit Shmuel]. It has already been clarified in section 2 that a person should not quarrel over the dowry even if it was agreed upon, and by this he will see a sign of blessing. See there.

One who committed to giving a dowry to his daughter and his son-in-law demands it from him, claiming that he gave it to his daughter – this is not a valid claim, for it is well known that the intention of the commitment is to give it to the couple. And one who swore to provide for his son-in-law and at that time was wealthy but later became poor – he is obligated to sell his possessions and other items and provide for his son-in-law because he swore, except for his residence and personal utensils. However, the son-in-law is cruel if he puts his father-in-law through such hardships and ought to forgive him.

The Law Regarding One Who Commits to His Son or Daughter and Whether It Is Acquired, and When She Falls Before a Yavam, and If the Daughter Dies, with 24 Sections
The sages taught (Ketubot 66a): One who commits money to his son-in-law, and his son-in-law dies, and his brother wishes to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) and she is willing to undergo yibbum, nevertheless, he can say, "I wanted to give to your brother, but to you I do not wish to give." Even if the first brother was an ignoramus and the second a scholar, he can still say this. And even though the commitment was made in a manner that it was acquired according to the law, such as through a formal transaction or by standing and sanctifying (the marriage), which are acquired through verbal agreement, nevertheless, he can say this. The reason is that anyone who commits during the conditions or at the time of betrothal does so with the intention that the marriage will take place, and the commitment is not fully acquired until the marriage. Since he (the son-in-law) died before the marriage and she marries another, even if she marries the deceased brother through yibbum, we have no power to compel the father to fulfill the commitment, because he can say that he did not commit to this marriage.

The Tur writes in the name of the Gaon that this specifically applies when a father pledges to his son-in-law, but if he pledged to his daughter, for example, if he said at the time of the betrothal, "I am giving my daughter such-and-such amount," the daughter acquires it even if the son-in-law dies. He cannot then say, "I only pledged this to my daughter on the condition that the marriage with the son-in-law would take place," because in any case, he pledged it to his daughter and she has acquired it. This is the end of the quotation. The explanation of his words is: Certainly, the daughter does not acquire it before her marriage, and if she dies and has a son or daughter, they do not inherit this money, for it is clear that the pledge was only on the condition that she gets married. The practical difference between pledging to his son-in-law and pledging to his daughter is that if she performs levirate marriage (yibbum) with the brother of her betrothed, the father cannot say, "I wanted to give it to your brother, not to you," because he pledged it to his daughter and the betrothal remains valid. This is implied from the language used, specifically when she performs levirate marriage with the brother, as it comes from the betrothal of the deceased brother, and the father pledged it to his daughter at the time of the initial betrothal, so the betrothal still stands and there is also marriage. However, if the son-in-law dies and she gets betrothed and married to another man, the father is not required to fulfill the pledge, as he pledged at the time of the initial betrothal, and that betrothal has been nullified. This is also evident from the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 2.

This distinction that we wrote between one who pledges to his son-in-law and one who pledges to his daughter does not appear to be implied by the Rambam in Chapter 23 of Hilchot Ishut, where he wrote: "A father who pledged a gift for his daughter has not acquired it for her until her husband takes her in marriage, and similarly, the son has not acquired it until he takes her in marriage, for anyone who pledges does so with the intention of marriage. Therefore, one who pledges money to his son-in-law and dies before the marriage, and she falls before his brother for levirate marriage, the father can say to the yavam, 'I wanted to give it to your brother, but I do not want to give it to you.' Even if the first one was unlearned and the second one is wise, and even though the daughter wants him." Thus, he wrote this law that there is no need to give to the yavam regarding one who pledges to his daughter. The language of the Rambam was copied by our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Section 1, and therefore he wrote in Section 2 the distinction between one who pledges to his son-in-law and one who pledges to his daughter in the name of "there are those who say," because the Rambam does not hold this way. [See Shitah Mekubetzet in the name of the Ritva, who explains that the distinction of the Gaon between his son-in-law and daughter is based on his interpretation in the Yerushalmi, which the Rif rejected, and it is necessary as we have said; and although in the Tur it is not possible to say this, see Bach and examine it closely.]

The leading later authorities wish to align the opinion of the Rambam with that of the Gaon, and they wrote that when the Rambam said "the father who stipulates through his daughter," his intention was that he stipulated to his son-in-law to give him when he marries his daughter. However, regarding stipulating to his daughter, he agrees with the opinion of the Gaon [Chomat Shlomo and Beit Shmuel]. But this does not seem so; if so, why did he change the language that he wrote himself in that same law? Moreover, he wrote "and similarly one who stipulates for his son," which implies that his daughter is analogous to his son. Furthermore, if the Rambam's intention was that he stipulated to his son-in-law to give him when he marries his daughter, what does he mean by "for anyone who stipulates only stipulates with the intention to marry"? It is obvious since he explicitly said so according to their interpretation. And even though it can be said that their intention is that he did not say this explicitly but we say that this was his intention, what explicit language did the father use? If we say that he said, "I stipulate to my son-in-law through my daughter" – this is not a language at all. And if he only said, "I stipulate to my son-in-law," then why did he write "through his daughter"? Rather, it is certain that he said, "I stipulate to my daughter," and the Rambam's intention was that there is no difference between stipulating to his son-in-law and stipulating to his daughter. And this that he wrote "through his daughter" is also his language in the earlier laws, see there. [See Mekaneh, who also struggled greatly with this.]

From the words of the Rambam, who equates the commitment for a son with that for a daughter, we learn that just as when one commits to give a dowry for his daughter at the time of betrothal, he is only obligated if she marries that specific groom, so too, when one commits to give a dowry for his son at the time of betrothal, he is only obligated if the son marries that specific bride. If she dies and he marries another woman, even one better than her, the father is not obligated to fulfill his commitment. [And so writes the Beit Meir]. This is also the law regarding commitments made at the time of engagement, according to our custom. Logic dictates this as well, since the intention is for this specific couple and not if he marries another or she marries another. This is the primary ruling in law.

If a father pledges money to his son-in-law and his daughter dies, even if the father gave the money to the son-in-law before the wedding, since the marriage did not take place (because she died beforehand), the father takes the money back from the son-in-law, even if they were already betrothed. All the more so if they were not yet betrothed. Not only does he take back the money from the son-in-law, but even if his daughter left behind offspring, the son-in-law does not inherit her. The reason is, as stated, that anyone who pledges money does so with the intention that the marriage will take place, and this is a well-established presumption.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 3 that there is an opinion which states that this applies specifically when one stipulates for his son-in-law. However, if one gives to his daughter without specification for her marriage and does not mention that she should marry a particular person, she acquires that gift. Thus, even if she becomes betrothed and the betrothal is later annulled due to the death of the groom, the father cannot retract the gift. This means that he is not stipulating for his daughter at the time of the betrothal but rather giving to her or committing according to the laws of commitment with a certain amount of money. There is no difference between stipulating or giving it to her without specifying whom she should marry; it belongs entirely to her. If she dies and leaves offspring, they inherit it. However, if he specified that she should marry a particular person and she did not live to marry him, then her heirs do not inherit it, and the money returns to the father. Yet, in this case, her right is stronger than the stipulation made at the time of betrothal, as it was explained that the father is only obligated to give if she marries that groom and not another. In this stipulation, the father commits even if she marries another. Even if he gave or stipulated for her when she was betrothed or engaged to someone, we do not say that his intention was only if she marries that person. We do not say this, as long as he did not specify, and the stipulation was not made at the time of betrothal or at the time of the conditions.

In Yoreh De'ah, section 253, it is explained that if someone vows money to a female orphan to marry her off and she dies, her heirs do not acquire the money, as stated there. This is even more so than with his own daughter, where it has been clarified that in such a case, her heirs do not acquire the money, and certainly, this applies to someone else. However, in Choshen Mishpat, section 253, it is explained that if a person on their deathbed commanded to give two hundred zuz for her dowry and she died before getting married, her heirs do acquire the money. Rabbeinu the Rema writes there that there are those who disagree and hold that her heirs do not acquire the money, as stated there. In Yoreh De'ah, it is written that there are those who disagree, and this is the first opinion mentioned in Choshen Mishpat. Indeed, it can be said that in Yoreh De'ah, everyone agrees that specifically a person on their deathbed who distributes after their death intends it as a complete gift to the recipient, but someone who vows himself for the marriage of a certain woman certainly only intends it for the marriage, and if that does not happen, he did not vow. However, for the actual law, there is no practical difference, since Rabbeinu the Rema ruled there even for a person on their deathbed that the primary law is that the heirs do not acquire the money, as stated there. [And in the Mordechai, in the chapter "Even though," it seems to follow the Rema, as stated there.]

However, it has been clarified in Yoreh De'ah that as long as the orphan girl is alive, the money belongs to her, and it must be given to her immediately; one does not wait until her marriage. Accordingly, it seems even more so in the case of a commitment to one's daughter that he must give it to her immediately. It is possible that this applies specifically to a vow made to an orphan girl, as she is presumably poor and needs to prepare clothes and other items for marriage. If the money is not given until after the marriage, with what will she marry? Therefore, it must be given to her immediately. This is not the case when making a commitment to one's daughter, which is intended to bring the money into the husband's household; why should it be given immediately? This seems to be the main point, and it is also evident from what is stated in Siman 51, that it must be given before she enters the husband's household, and the father cannot say, "Enter and then I will give it." Hence, it is clear that immediately after the commitment, he is not obligated to give it, and this is not comparable to the case of the orphan girl for the reason we have explained.

All the laws that have been clarified are only applicable after betrothal, but after marriage, according to the opinion of the Rambam, Rashi, and other great early authorities, even if the father has not yet transferred the dowry and all that he promised his daughter before the marriage, he is obligated to transfer it after the marriage. Even if his daughter dies, he must transfer it to the husband according to Torah law because the husband inherits his wife. Once he has married her, the money is his, and when his wife dies, he inherits her. This is clear and applies specifically when the obligation is binding by law, such as when it is acquired through a verbal commitment or formal acquisition and obligation. However, if the obligation is not binding by law but was merely a promise, or even if there was a penalty attached but not the main obligation, as discussed in Siman 50, and it was not given before the marriage, and she married and then died – he is exempt even from the penalty. According to this, there is a significant difference between after betrothal and after marriage. After betrothal, even if the dowry is in the hands of the betrothed, if she dies, it is returned to the father. After marriage, even if the dowry is still with the father, it is taken from the father and given to the husband even if she dies, according to Torah law, unless there is an enactment otherwise, as will be explained. Even before the chuppah, if the father has handed over the dowry to the husband's agents and she dies, the husband inherits her as the Rambam states in Chapter 22. Even if the dowry is still with the father, as mentioned in Siman 57, see there. Similarly, regarding what has been explained that the yavam (levirate husband) does not need to be given – this is all if she was widowed from the betrothal, but if from the marriage, the yavam inherits and takes from the father all that was promised, as mentioned.

But Rabbeinu Tam disagreed with them and held that even after the marriage, if the father has not yet transferred the dowry and the daughter died, the husband does not acquire it even according to Torah law. This is because there is a strong presumption that what the father allotted to his daughter or son-in-law is only for the benefit of his daughter, meaning when the money comes into her possession and there is benefit to the household. However, as long as the money has not come into the possession of the husband, the husband does not acquire it, for he did not obligate himself under such conditions [and he explains the matter in Ketubot 47 after the marriage]. And since there is a dispute among the poskim (halachic authorities) on this matter, we do not take the money from the father even if many years have passed since the wedding. As long as the dowry has not been transferred, the husband does not inherit it, and even if he has children from her, and even if the husband has died, the children do not inherit it. For as long as the money has not come into the possession of the son-in-law, he does not acquire it according to Rabbeinu Tam's opinion, who follows the presumption as mentioned. Therefore, we do not take from the one who holds it out of doubt.

According to Rabbeinu Tam, even if the money was placed in the hands of a third party by mutual agreement, meaning that it was entrusted by both parties, there are distinctions in this case. If the money was entrusted with the condition that it should not be given to the husband until a certain time, and the daughter dies within that time, the husband does not acquire the money. However, if the third party was appointed for the benefit of the couple, meaning to profit for their benefit, even if a time was set and the daughter dies within that time, the husband acquires the money because it is considered as if it has come into his possession, since the daughter benefited from the profit. Moreover, even if the third party is not permitted to deliver the money to the couple without the knowledge of both parties, it is still considered as if it has been collected. Even if there has not yet been a profit, since we consider it as if it is in the husband's possession, we are not responsible for the profit, as the assumption of benefit is removed, and it is as if the daughter enjoyed it. If the money was simply entrusted to the third party without a set time or for profit, and the husband could have taken it from the third party but did not until the daughter died, they should divide it. This is because it is doubtful whether, in this manner, it is considered as if the husband has collected it since the father gave it to the third party without any condition, or perhaps since it has not yet come into the husband's possession, he has not acquired it, so they should divide it. And some say further that even if the father-in-law agreed to invest the money for the benefit of the couple, even if it is still in the father's possession and she dies, the husband acquires it for the reason explained.

Even if the father made a document for the money and converted it into a loan, as long as he has not handed it over, he has not acquired it according to Rabbeinu Tam, due to the presumption we mentioned. Therefore, even though in all other obligations by document it is as if the money has come into the hands of the one to whom it is obligated, here it is different because of the presumption. There are those who say that with the conversion into a loan, the husband has acquired it, and it is a doubtful law. Therefore, we do not take it from the one who holds it <small>[Be'er HaGolah, section 9]</small>. And some say that we do take it out based on the principle of double doubt: perhaps the law is according to the first opinion, and even if it is according to Rabbeinu Tam, perhaps in this case Rabbeinu Tam would agree. However, money is not taken out based on double doubt, as it is no better than a majority, and we do not take it from the one who holds it even with a majority, as we do not follow the majority in monetary matters <small>[see Be'er HaGolah]</small>. And some say that in a document that is entirely handed over, if the father gave it to his son-in-law, the husband has certainly acquired it, for he can hand over the debt document to another, and the other would claim it from him. If the father would then claim it back from his son-in-law due to the presumption, the son-in-law is still considered the holder <small>[Turei Zahav, and see Be'er HaGolah]</small>.

And if the father provided a guarantee for the dowry for his son-in-law, the son-in-law acquires it even when it is still in the father's possession. In such a case, the father decides and conveys it even before his daughter benefits, as it is as if it has already been transferred from his hand to the son-in-law. All the more so, if he placed collateral in the hands of the son-in-law for the dowry. Some say that even with a guarantee, the son-in-law does not acquire it because the guarantor is only obligated in a case where the borrower himself can be claimed against. But here, where it is not possible to claim against the father due to an estimation, how can we take it from the guarantor? And since it is a doubtful legal matter, we do not take from the one in possession. Do not wonder why we said in all doubts not to take from the one in possession, but in a doubt concerning an intermediary, they divide. Indeed, that is the case, and when we need to take from the father, we do not take due to doubt. But when it is in the hands of an intermediary, both are considered possessors and they divide it.

In the primary ruling we stated that one does not take away from the one in possession due to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, if the groom seized it, we do not take it away from him. And even according to the opinions of the poskim that holding does not help in a case of doubtful law, here it is different because the groom can say "I hold by the first opinion," and although it is not possible in every case to claim "I hold by," for if so there would be no end to the matter, and if one finds an individual opinion, he would say "I hold by this opinion," here it is different because the first opinion is the view of Rashi and the Rambam and other great Rabbis of ours, and certainly he can say "I hold by their opinion," and so ruled Rabbeinu Rema. And there are those who say that holding only helps before the doubt arises, that is, before his wife died and he seized it against their will, and they did not want to give it to him, but after her death, holding does not help. However, there are those who say that holding does help, and so the great later authorities ruled in practice that even after her death, holding helps.

In what case does the husband not acquire according to Rabbeinu Tam's opinion? The dowry that the father wrote to give him, and even if the father designated money, movable property, or real estate for his daughter, not to be fully transferred to the husband but rather that the assets remain hers and the husband enjoys the produce, which is called 'nichsei melug,' and if they have not yet come into her possession under both their authorities, the husband has not acquired them. However, gifts given in honor of the groom and bride, if they have not come into the groom's possession, he has acquired them. But gifts that the father gives are like a dowry based on the presumption that he gave them only so that his daughter would benefit from them. The general principle is: anything the father gives reverts to the father as long as the husband has not yet acquired them, as there is a strong presumption that he gave them only so that his daughter would benefit from them, and if they have not come into his possession, she has not yet benefited. However, gifts that others gave her or an inheritance that came to her from elsewhere, it is obvious that the husband inherits them, even according to Rabbeinu Tam, immediately after the wedding, as there is no such presumption. All these matters clarified according to Rabbeinu Tam's opinion apply only if the money and items have never once come into the groom's possession. But if they came into his possession even once, even if he returned them to the father, he has acquired everything, because once they have come into his possession, even for one day, they are considered entirely his, and he inherits his wife according to Rabbeinu Tam.

All these laws that have been explained are according to the fundamental principles of Torah law regarding the husband's inheritance. However, the great sages of past generations, from the time of our early rabbis, who witnessed the sorrow and anguish of the fathers of women who died after their wedding and their husbands inherited them, resulting in the loss of both lives and money, made enactments regarding this. And anyone who marries a woman does so with the understanding of this custom, for in matters of money, a person has the right to forgo his money. Since there is an enactment that the husband should not inherit her, it is as if it were explicitly stipulated at the time of the betrothal that everything given should be returned to the father. Our rabbis relied in these enactments on what our Sages expounded in the Torat Kohanim (Sifra), "And your strength shall be spent in vain" (Leviticus 26:20) – this refers to one who marries off his daughter and she dies during the seven days of feasting, thereby losing his daughter and his money. Therefore, they enacted measures to avoid such a curse. There were many enactments in this matter, until they enacted and re-enacted, as will be explained before us with God's help.

The first ordinance was in the days of the French sages, headed by Rabbeinu Tam, and this was agreed upon by the sages of Narbonne and the great scholars of Lombardy. Concerning anyone who marries a woman and she dies within a year without a surviving child, he must return all the dowry and the woman's jewelry to those who gave them or to her heirs, everything that remains in his possession from the dowry that has not worn out. He should not scheme to deduct anything except for the expenses of her burial according to her honor, not according to his desire. Even if the husband possesses his wife's dowry and has benefited from it, he must return it by the time set by the court, which is within thirty days.

The second ordinance is called 'The Ordinance of Shu"M' after the three great communities in Ashkenaz – Speyer, Worms, and Mainz. At that time, all the communities made an ordinance that if any man or woman were to marry and one of them were to pass away without offspring within two years of marriage, half of the dowry would return to the heirs of the deceased [there]. These two ordinances were brought by our teacher, the Rema, and this is what is written in the conditions: "And due to Adur, it will stand as the ordinance of Shu"M." Even if it is not written, it is as if it were written since this is the established custom, and even for an orphaned girl who is married, the custom is the same [Choshen Mishpat, section 17]. Only what is intact returns, but what has been spent or lost is exempt, provided that it was not squandered after her death except for burial expenses. What was spent on medical treatments and burial expenses is deducted for him, and if he had a loss in business with her money, it is also deducted for him. If he also had his own money, the loss is calculated on both [Beit Shmuel, section 17] according to the value of the money, for it is not similar to two who put into a purse as explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 176 [Neharot]. If he deducted a tithe from the dowry sum, it is also deducted for him [there].

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that some say if the groom wants to sell his properties within two years, the heirs can object, and even if she also agrees to the sale, nevertheless, the heirs can object for the reason that she might die within this time and it will revert to them. This ruling is very puzzling; because of the possibility that she might die and they would inherit her, should we prevent them from selling? If so, any future heir could prevent their testator from selling their properties. It is possible that this applies only to those who give the dowry and their heirs, like the father of the bride and his sons, as it seems from the source of this ruling. However, we have never heard that they conduct themselves this way, to worry about death and prevent the couple from doing what they wish with their properties, and this requires further investigation.

This was approximately one hundred and twenty years ago when, at a gathering of the sages of the country and the leaders of the lands, they established that for three years everything, including the clothing of the wife, would be returned to the donors of the dowry and to her heirs. And until today, this custom is firmly established in our country without any doubt. They added to the enactment of ShUM (the sages of Speyer, Worms, and Mainz), but in our language, this enactment is included in the enactment of ShUM which is written in the conditions because that was the language of the enactment. And one should not deviate from this custom because from the greatest to the smallest, everyone accepted this throughout the country to the point that many people think it is a strict law. It is also common knowledge that everything is returned to the donors of the dowry if she did not leave surviving offspring, meaning a child who lived for thirty days and survived a little after her death [Bach, subparagraph 14]. If the son or daughter lived even one day after her death, the husband takes everything because the child inherits it, and then the father inherits from his son or daughter. There is no distinction in the enactment whether the child lived long or died immediately after her death. And we have already written the procedures of the return, that gifts which were not due to the father are inherited by the husband, and the father's gifts are taken back. And even though in Siman 118 it will be explained that there are those who disagree about this, nevertheless, since in the language of this enactment it is explained that even her clothing is returned, how much more so her gifts and all her adornments. Only the expenses and losses incurred will be deducted, as stated.

The assets and money that revert due to the enactment—some say they revert to the dowry givers, meaning this is without question that if a father gave his daughter a dowry and she died within three years, the dowry returns to him, and if the father died, it returns to his heirs. However, if the dowry givers were relatives or distant people who do not inherit from her—in this, the decisors are divided on to whom it returns, whether to the dowry givers or to the heirs. Some say it should return to the dowry givers and some to the heirs, and from the language of the enactments, it implies the first opinion. And there are those who decided that if the dowry giver was a relative, even though there is a closer relative who is her heir, nevertheless, it returns to the dowry giver. But if the giver is an outsider, in this case, "your strength should not be spent in vain" does not apply—it returns to her heirs. However, when the women themselves bring in the dowry, this enactment was not made, as it says there, and her husband inherits, for "your strength should not be spent in vain" only applies when others give. And the later authorities wrote that this is the simple custom with an orphan girl who has inheritance money from her father due to the tenth of the assets or she is an heir, and it is written in the conditions "due to enhancement and dispute it should stand as the enactment of Shum," and thus this enactment should be upheld.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that regarding the ordinances there is no distinction between one who promises for his daughter or his son and dies, end quote. This means that even if a father promises a dowry for his son and the son dies within the period of the ordinance without leaving any surviving offspring, the dowry returns to the father, and the widow does not collect her ketubah from these funds. Some say that the ordinance was not intended to deprive her of her ketubah, and some say that even according to the ordinance, it applies only to the basic ketubah amount of one hundred or two hundred [zuz] which is from the Torah, but regarding the additional third on the dowry, they did not make an ordinance, and she always collects the additional third on her dowry. From the language of the ordinance of Shu"M that we cited in section 19, it implies that the ordinance was for both. And it seems to me that even according to our custom where the ordinance is for three years as we wrote, nonetheless regarding her ketubah, if he dies, even for those who practice, one should not act beyond the ordinance of Shu"M, because in this matter it seems that the ordinance was not renewed. It is obvious that the intercalated month is included in the year.

There are also some theories by the great scholars regarding these enactments, but since they do not have solid foundations, it is not necessary to elaborate on them. A general principle to be aware of is that when there is any doubt concerning these enactments, one should adhere to Torah law or reach a compromise agreeable to both parties. May God bless His people with peace, life, and blessing so that they will not need these enactments, Amen and Amen. Further elaboration on this will be provided in Siman 118 with the help of God.

The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote at the end of chapter 20: If someone instructed to give his daughter a certain amount of money for her support and to purchase land with it, whether he was on his deathbed or in good health, and he died, and the money is in the hands of a trustee, and the daughter said, "Give it to my husband to do with it as he pleases," if she is of age and married, she has the right to decide. If she is still betrothed, the trustee should do as instructed originally. If she is still a minor, even if married, her wishes are not heeded, and the trustee should follow the father's instructions. This is the end of his words. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch also ruled similarly, stating that it is a mitzvah to fulfill the words of the deceased. For an adult married woman, the father's intention was likely only for the trustee to hold the money until she marries, since once married, the husband has the rights to the produce [Rashi Ketubot 69:]. However, for a minor, her wishes are not followed because she lacks mature intent and might change her mind upon reaching adulthood. In a case where the trustee does not follow her wishes, even if she says that her husband will use the money to purchase land as per the will, her wishes are still not followed for the reason explained [Tosafot Yom Tov there]. For an adult married woman, even if she explicitly says that her husband should do as he pleases, her wishes are followed as stated.

And the father's commandment was not that she should not acquire the money now but to buy a field with it. For if he had said so, even without the reason of the commandment to fulfill the wishes of the deceased, they would not listen to him, as she would not have acquired the money except in this manner. Rather, he now granted her the money but commanded that a field be bought for her with it. Therefore, if not for the reason of the commandment to fulfill the wishes of the deceased, they would give her the money immediately as it is entirely hers. According to this, if he indeed told her that she should not acquire the money but to buy a field, even if she is an adult and married, the trustee should act and buy her the field, and the husband will consume the produce.

And if the trustee acquired the field, and afterwards she wants to sell it and give the money to her husband – she has the authority to do so. However, if her father left her land and died, and she says that whatever her husband wants to do, he can do – the husband does not have the authority to sell the land, for she herself does not have the authority to sell land inherited from her father until she is twenty years old, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 235. But land that the trustee acquired may be sold, for she did not inherit this from her father, and in this case, she does not need to be twenty years old, as stated there.

Some of our rabbis hold the opinion that even land acquired by the third party (the intermediary) cannot be sold, and it is possible that the reason is that since he commanded to purchase the field, its status is like an inheritance, and she is not permitted to sell it for less than the value of twenty (currency units). However, most of the great earlier authorities hold like the first opinion, and thus they wrote in the name of Rabbeinu Hai Gaon. Moreover, there are authorities who hold that even in the case of an inheritance, it is permissible to sell.

A grown son or daughter for whom the father left money with a trustee—the trustee should give it to them after his death, and we do not say that he made him an executor over them. It is only for minors that we say his intention was for guardianship [Shitah Mekubetzet there in the name of the Gaon], unless the father explicitly instructed what the trustee should do with it and that it should not be given in any other manner, in which case he is obligated to fulfill the father's instructions. And our master the Rema wrote that even when money is entrusted for his daughter, some say that it must have been entrusted initially for that purpose, end quote. This is based on what is explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 252, that we only say "it is a command to fulfill the words of the deceased" when it was initially entrusted for that purpose, as mentioned there. However, there are those who say that in a case where it is for the benefit of his daughter not to give it to her husband, we say "it is a command to fulfill the words of the deceased" even if it was not initially entrusted for that purpose [Derush veChiddush]. And there are those who disagree [Beit Shmuel]. Some of the great authorities have written that what we stated, that in the case of an adult from the betrothal period, the trustee should act as the father instructed, applies when he left other heirs, so she has no right to the money except through the trustee's authority and therefore it must be fulfilled according to the trust. But if she is the sole heir, then only if she is a minor should the trustee fulfill the will, but not if she is an adult, as she immediately acquires the money by inheritance, and inheritance overrides the trust. For this money was not given to the trustee as a gift but as a deposit, and Torah inheritance applies to all the money wherever it is, and even if the father explicitly instructed "do not give it to her until she marries" or "until a certain time," they should give it to her because he is making a condition contrary to what is written in the Torah, and his condition is null [Shitah Mekubetzet in the name of the Tosafot Rid]. However, from what is stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 253, regarding one who says "give a shekel to my son every week," if it is sufficient for them, they do not give them more—it does not imply this, as mentioned there [and also in this topic of entrusting, which resembles this, it does not imply this, as mentioned there. This requires further investigation for the ruling].

Engaged is considered a married woman in full, and one who intentionally has relations with her is liable to the death penalty. Her death penalty is more severe than that of a married woman, for a married woman is punished by strangulation, whereas an engaged woman is punished by stoning. The betrothed man cannot release her except through a bill of divorce. Nevertheless, it is forbidden for the betrothed man to have relations with his betrothed before the wedding ceremony. This is what the Men of the Great Assembly established in the blessings, "and has forbidden to us the betrothed women" – that the betrothed man should not have relations with his betrothed before the wedding ceremony and blessings. This prohibition is Rabbinic, similar to the decree on a single woman. One who has relations with his betrothed in his father-in-law's house is given lashes of rebellion. Thus, our sages said, "A bride without a blessing is forbidden to her husband as a menstruant woman" (Tractate Kallah), and even seclusion with her was prohibited by the sages, similar to the decree on seclusion with a single woman (Beit Yosef). Likewise, a betrothed couple is forbidden to have seclusion, for anyone forbidden in relations is also forbidden in seclusion (Chomat Henoch). Therefore, some say that they should not live together lest they become repulsed by each other, and even in engagements without betrothal this should be feared. More so, there is concern that they will not control their desires and come to sin, and furthermore, they might even come to a sin punishable by excision since she is considered menstruant if she is of age. Therefore, one who fears the word of the Lord should distance himself from this and similar situations.

Even if he betrothed her through intercourse, he is forbidden to have intercourse with her a second time until the time of marriage, for we hold that intercourse effects betrothal and not marriage, as stated in Siman 33. And marriage is effected through the chuppah. However, what constitutes the chuppah is a matter of dispute among the authorities, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 10 that a betrothed woman is forbidden until he brings her into his house, secludes with her, and designates her for himself. This seclusion is called "entering the chuppah," and it is called marriage everywhere. One who has intercourse with his betrothed for the sake of marriage after having betrothed her, once he has penetrated her, acquires her and she becomes married, and she is his wife for all matters. Once the betrothed woman enters the chuppah, she is permitted for him to have intercourse with her at any time he wishes, and she is his complete wife for all matters. From the moment she enters the chuppah, she is called married even if she has not had intercourse, provided she is fit for intercourse. But if she is menstruating, even if she has entered the chuppah and secluded with him, the marriage is not completed, and she remains as a betrothed woman. End of quote.

From his words, it is clear that the essence of the chuppah (bridal canopy) is seclusion for the sake of marriage. This seclusion must be with preparation and designation to be together as husband and wife. Therefore, he must bring her into his house, seclude himself with her, and set her apart for himself. Bringing her into his house is the preparation, and the setting apart is the designation to live with her always. The seclusion serves in place of consummation, even if he has not had relations with her, as long as she is fit for relations, as it is written. But if the seclusion is not permanent, even if it is with preparation and designation, such as bringing her into his house for a few days and then she returns to her father's house, even if they have secluded themselves, it is meaningless.

It is obvious that even if the seclusion was not in his house, such as designating a place on the way to seclude with her and set her apart for himself to take her from there to his house, from that point onward she has the status of a married woman, as stated in Siman 57. When he secludes himself with her, he must recite the Blessing of the Bridegrooms at the place of the marriage, which is the place designated for seclusion or where he brings her into his house. The blessing is recited before the marriage. However, the blessings are not indispensable post facto, as stated in Siman 33. The statement "a bride without a blessing is forbidden" refers to without marriage, as a typical marriage includes a blessing. Conversely, the Bridegroom's Blessing alone is meaningless, as Maimonides states: If one betroths a woman and recites the Bridegroom's Blessing but does not seclude himself with her in his house, she is still betrothed; the Blessing of the Bridegrooms does not effectuate marriage, only entering the chuppah does. If one betroths and enters the chuppah but does not recite the Blessing of the Bridegrooms, she is fully married, and he can recite it even after several days.

And this is what he wrote: that if he has relations with her for the sake of marriage, she becomes married. It is clear from his words that through intercourse for the sake of marriage, she becomes married even though he did not bring her into his house. According to his words, we need to differentiate: what the Sages said, "one who has relations with his betrothed is flogged," this is when his intention was not explicitly for the sake of marriage. But with the intention of marriage, she becomes married through this intercourse. And one cannot say that his intention is in the preparation to bring her into his house, for if so, there would be no need for intercourse, and mere seclusion would suffice. Rather, it is certain that he holds that since the Sages established that through seclusion with preparation and intent she becomes married, and seclusion is only necessary because of intercourse, then certainly through the intercourse itself, no preparation or intent is needed.

And it is possible that there is no need for witnesses of seclusion for this intercourse, and it is not comparable to the act of betrothal through intercourse, which requires witnesses, for there it is the beginning of the acquisition. And the intercourse of marriage is similar to the intercourse with a yevamah (a widow awaiting levirate marriage). And behold, even in the primary act of intercourse, it is less stringent than the intercourse of betrothal, where there, according to the Rif and the Rambam, complete intercourse is required, as stated in Siman 33, Section 4. However, with the intercourse of marriage, the Rambam wrote that arousal suffices [and his source is from Yevamot 55b, as the Rif wrote there, and see Ran on the first chapter with the words "we recite in the Gemara 'they asked'"]. And the intercourse of marriage or the chuppah, since they are known to all, serve as witnesses, as stated in Siman 149, and see what is written in Siman 26, Section 5.

Some say that the chuppah (marriage canopy) is not seclusion, but rather whenever the husband brings the bride from her father's house to his house for the purpose of marriage, even if he does not seclude himself with her, as it is written, "But if she vowed in her husband's house" (Numbers 30:11), which implies that as long as she is in her husband's house, she is under his authority [Ran, beginning of Ketubot]. And likewise, the sages taught [Ketubot 48a] that she is always under her father's authority until she enters her husband's authority for marriage, which signifies that the essence of marriage is her entering her husband's authority. 

And the Rambam holds that it is true that her entering his authority constitutes marriage – but with seclusion, for the common practice is that when he brings her into his house, he secludes himself with her. However, this opinion also agrees with the Rambam that the primary element is seclusion, as is evident in Siman 57; see there. [And in Ketubot 11b, the sages taught: "If he married her, etc., and there are witnesses that she was not secluded, etc." This is not difficult according to the Rambam based on what the Tosafot wrote, that he does not rely on them. On the contrary, it is proof for the Rambam, for if not, what is the significance? But it can be refuted, and the Rambam in Chapter 11 omits this aspect of witnesses, and it will be explained with God's help in Siman 67.]

And some say that the chuppah is when the father hands her over and brings her into a house that has been specially prepared for the chuppah, such as decorated sheets. Some make it with roses or myrtles, and there the couple secludes themselves [Beit Yosef, Siman 61, in the name of the Atur]. This is the meaning of "entering the chuppah," which refers to a designated place similar to a canopy where the groom and bride sit with the groomsmen. And in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of Sotah, it is stated that wedding chuppahs are decorated sheets and gold crescents hanging from them [there]. This clearly indicates that there was a special and adorned place for the chuppah.

And the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote [Sukkah 2:68]: "It is a matter of inquiry what the chuppah is, whether it is the place where they bless the wedding blessings, which is the beginning of the marriage, and therefore they call it chuppah. It is impossible to say this, because sometimes they bless it in the street of the city when the people are numerous. Rather, the main place where the groom and bride sit is called chuppah, and not a place made temporarily. And there they bless the wedding blessings all seven days, and it is customary in Ashkenaz to make a canopy and a seat for the groom and bride, and it is called chuppah." End quote. And this is similar to the previous opinion, and there is support for this from scripture [Joel 2:16] "Let the groom go forth from his chamber, and the bride from her chuppah," indicating that there is a fixed place for this time called chuppah, as it is written (Psalms 19:6) "And he is like a groom coming out of his chuppah," meaning from the tent where the chuppah is, as it is written before "He set a tent for the sun in them."

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that there are those who say that the chuppah is when a cloth is spread over their heads at the time of the blessing. End quote. This opinion has been dismissed [see Choshen Mishpat 7:6], however, the intention of this opinion is similar to our custom where poles are erected and a canopy is spread over them, and it is called in common parlance "chuppah." It is set up in a special place, such as the courtyard of the synagogue or something similar, and the bride and groom, along with the attendants, are brought under it, and there the blessings are recited.

It is also written that according to one opinion, the wedding canopy (chuppah) of a virgin begins when she goes out with a veil, and for a widow, it begins when they seclude themselves, end quote. This is found in the Mishnah, where it states that a virgin goes out with a veil and her head uncovered [Ketubot 2:1]. They used to bring the virgins from their father's house to the wedding house with their hair on their shoulders [Rashi]. The "veil" (hinuma) is the scarf on her head hanging over her eyes, and sometimes she dozes within it because her eyes are not uncovered, and therefore it is called "hinuma" because of the drowsiness [Ketubot 17b]. Some say that the chuppah is when she is handed over to the groom before the blessing [Mordechai, beginning of Ketubot]. These two opinions do not mean that as soon as the veil is placed on her, she is considered married, or as soon as she is handed over to the groom, but the intention is according to our custom where the bride is seated, her hair is braided, and musicians play before her. The groom comes and covers her face with a scarf, and from there they go to the chuppah. This is the hinuma and the handing over to the groom. For us, it is obvious that she is not considered married since she has not yet been betrothed, and there is no marriage before betrothal. Rather, this is the beginning of the marriage, which is completed after the betrothal and blessings. These opinions also only intend to describe the beginning and order of the marriage process [as it appears to me; see Mordechai there and Chomat Hadat, section 9; be precise].

It is further written that the current custom is to call the chuppah a place where a canopy is spread over poles, and the groom and bride are brought under it publicly, and the kiddushin (betrothal) is performed there, and the blessings of betrothal and marriage are recited there. Afterwards, they are brought to their home and they eat together in a private place. This is the chuppah as it is practiced now. According to this, the main completion of the chuppah is when they eat together in a private place, which is considered seclusion (yichud). Therefore, one should prevent many people from going there [Bach], and even one person should not enter there, for otherwise it is not the proper seclusion for intimacy. Thus, one should prevent anyone from entering there to ensure complete seclusion [Beit Shmuel, paragraph 5]. According to this, in our times, since it is not the custom for the groom and bride to eat together in one room without anyone entering, but rather all the attendants and guests of the wedding are present, it is necessary to understand what constitutes the chuppah that makes her considered married now.

And I found one of the early authorities who wrote about this, and this is what he said: "It seems to me that the matter is as follows: The father initially gives his daughter to her groom to be his wife among his circle of friends, and this is called 'marriage'. After she stands for a day or two to prepare the needs of the feast and clothing, he would designate a house to rejoice there with his groomsmen and friends and to make a feast in order to consummate the marriage that night. They would bring the bride into that house, and that designated house is called the 'chuppah'. This is what was said in the Jerusalem Talmud, 'Not only is it a chuppah but a house that has a chuppah,' meaning that even though they have not yet placed her in the canopy but in a house that has a canopy, she immediately eats terumah. Therefore, I say that our chuppah is the bringing of the bride into a house that has decorated sheets. From the time of marriage, which is from the time the father gives her to the husband, he inherits her, but he does not become ritually impure for her or annul her vows until she enters the chuppah. Once she enters the chuppah, she is his wife in all respects, except that it is forbidden to have relations with her until the seven blessings are recited. Also, if he has relations with her after the marriage without a chuppah, he does not acquire her for these matters, because without a chuppah it is considered promiscuity, etc." Thus he wrote. [Brought in Shaar HaMelech in the treatise on Chuppat Chatanim].

From these words, it becomes clear that marriage (nissu'in) and the wedding canopy (chuppah) are two separate matters. This can also be inferred from the language of the Mishnah, which states (Ketubot 48b): "She remains under the authority of her father until she enters the authority of her husband for marriage." Furthermore, it states (Ketubot 57b): "A woman does not eat terumah until she enters the chuppah." The change in language indicates that they are two separate matters. However, none of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) have mentioned this distinction. In the words of the Rambam, which we have cited: "This seclusion is called entering the chuppah, and it is called marriage everywhere." This clearly shows that they are one and the same. Similarly, in the Mishnah that states "until she enters the authority of her husband for marriage," it must be referring to the chuppah, as this pertains to the matter of terumah. Rashi explains there that it means entering the chuppah for the sake of marriage. There are those who indeed have the version "until she enters the chuppah" (Tosafot). However, we find in the Gemara (Ketubot 49b) in the Baraita: "One who has relations with a married woman, once she has entered the authority of her husband for marriage, is liable to strangulation," and it is inferred there that this applies even though she has not yet entered the chuppah. Thus, it shows that they are two separate matters. It must be said that the term 'marriage' is a comprehensive term that spans from before the chuppah to after the chuppah. The beginning of the marriage is not yet the chuppah, and the culmination of the marriage is the chuppah.

It appears to me that all the authorities do not disagree at all. Indeed, the concept of a chuppah is not written in the Torah, only the concept of marriage is written, as it is stated, "And who is the man who has betrothed a woman and has not taken her" (Deuteronomy 20:7). This is the taking of marriage. According to the fundamental law of the Torah, when a man has relations with a woman for the purpose of marriage so that she becomes his complete wife, she is considered married, as Maimonides wrote. However, it is not the custom of the Jewish people to engage in relations publicly, and if one does so, witnesses are required for the seclusion for the purpose of relations. Even if it is possible that witnesses are not needed for this, as stated in section 5, the matter will still be public since they need to bless before the marriage and immediately after with the seven blessings. Therefore, our sages established that the chuppah should be part of the marriage. This has always been the case, even during the time of the prophets, as it is written, "As a bridegroom comes out of his chuppah" and "And a bride from her chuppah." Certainly, Moses our teacher instituted this practice for Israel.

And the explanation of "chuppah" is derived from the expression "He hovers over him all day long" (Deuteronomy 33:12), indicating a covering and separation from others. In the Aggadah, our sages said [Baba Batra 75a] that in the future, the Holy One, Blessed be He, will make seven chuppot for every righteous person, meaning coverings of honor to distinguish them from others, as it is written: "For over all the glory there will be a chuppah" (Isaiah 4:5). This established the practice of making an honorable chuppah and reciting seven blessings over it, thereby completing the marriage, and the consummation is not delayed because everyone understands the bride's purpose in entering the chuppah. However, there is no need for witnesses of seclusion or ten people for the marriage blessings, and it is inappropriate to consummate immediately. Any type of chuppah customary to be made is considered the acquisition of marriage as long as their intention is for marriage and they are separated from others, standing together in one place for the purpose of marriage, such as when he brings her into his home and they seclude together as Maimonides wrote. It seems to me that even Maimonides did not intend complete seclusion, meaning that they be alone in one room, but rather that they be together as husband and wife, standing next to each other and reciting the seven blessings. Therefore, the opinion we wrote in Section 6 that chuppah is not seclusion but bringing her into his home for the purpose of marriage, also essentially agrees with Maimonides. It is obvious that this opinion also agrees that if he brings her into his home and is not with her, this is nothing, and it is clear that he must be with her and recite the seven blessings. However, according to what all the poskim (decisors) wrote in Maimonides' opinion that he requires complete seclusion in one room without anyone else, this opinion disagrees with him. But according to our understanding of Maimonides, both opinions are essentially the same.

And similarly, if they have adopted different types of chuppahs, like in paragraph 7, where they make a special and decorated place for the groom and bride, or like in our practice where they set up poles with a spread canopy, and under this the attendants bring the groom and bride, and beforehand they seat the bride and the groom covers her, and upon returning from the chuppah they walk together and sit at the table close to each other, and this is a sign of marriage and everyone knows that this is a preparation for consummation in the usual manner, there is no need to worry that at this moment it is not possible for them to consummate, because this was intentionally done so that the sensation would not be too intense as mentioned. 

And the Rosh, of blessed memory, who was concerned because the place of the chuppah is temporary, also agrees, for they designate a place where they are together before the chuppah and after the chuppah, hence the entire matter is considered the chuppah, and as soon as they recite the seven blessings, she is fully married. 

And this is what one of the early authorities differentiated between marriage and chuppah, as we wrote in paragraph 12; his intention is also that the beginning of the marriage is the place where they sit before the chuppah, and there he covers her head, which symbolizes taking her into his domain, but this is not the completion of the chuppah. 

And it is not better than handing her over to her husband, which is effective only for matters of inheritance as stated in Siman 57, and the completion is under the chuppah, for that is when the marriage is completed, and the sign of the completion of the marriage is when they bless them with the blessings.

The general principle is that, according to the fundamental law of the Torah, marriage is through intercourse intended for the sake of marriage or its preparation. The chuppah (wedding canopy) is the preparation for this, and what constitutes this preparation depends on custom. Since this act is called chuppah and the blessings are recited, the marriage is completed, and the ultimate preparation of all chuppahs is that from this moment forward, the bride enters his domain and is ready to be with him as husband and wife. Therefore, Rambam required that she be pure, because since the essence of the chuppah is for the sake of intercourse, we need her to be fit for intercourse. However, most of the poskim (halachic authorities) disagree with him.
