They hold that, just as we do not require her to be fit for intercourse at the very moment of the chuppah, since ten people will certainly be there for the blessings and it is impossible for him to have intercourse then, we say that she should be fit for intercourse after some time. Therefore, what difference does it make whether it is after an hour or after a day or two?

And the fact that we establish the chuppah (wedding canopy) in the courtyard of the synagogue has a significant reason. The main purpose of the chuppah is the transition from the authority of the father to the authority of the husband, which occurs if the husband takes her to his house. However, our custom in many instances is to do everything at the house of the bride’s father, and sometimes the bride’s father also takes them to his house for a certain period. So, how is it evident that she has transitioned from her father’s authority to her husband’s authority? Therefore, we set up the chuppah in the courtyard of the synagogue, which is a communal place, and at the time of the chuppah, the community's intention is to transfer this land to this groom, similar to the community's etrog (citron) which, at the time of the blessing on the first day of the festival, is considered as each person's own. Once this land is considered his, it is as if he brings her into his domain. The poles and the spread-out canopy that we call the chuppah truly serve this purpose, as it covers the groom and bride and separates them from other people to indicate their union with each other. The fact that the groomsmen also stand under the chuppah is all for the sake of connecting the groom and bride, and therefore, they stand close to each other.

Furthermore, it appears to me that even according to the Rambam and those who follow his approach that the blessings are not essential, similar to any blessing that is not essential, this applies only to a wedding canopy (chuppah) that is akin to consummation for the purpose of marriage or actual seclusion in a closed room suitable for consummation at that moment. However, all other chuppahs that are merely preparations to signify the completion of the marriage for this couple—until the seven blessings are recited over them, the marriage is not completed. Perhaps this is the reason why some decisors hold that the blessings are essential under the chuppah, and therefore it is necessary to recite the blessing of the bridegroom before the completion of the marriage. 

[And regarding the primary matters that we have explained, the Gra also wrote in Siman 9 that there is no need for seclusion at all, only that she be in his domain, see there. And we have explained that the Rambam also holds this view. See Rashi, Kiddushin 10a, s.v. "this and so forth," "and she is married, obviously," "any pure person in your house shall eat it," see there. And see Yevamot 110 in Rashi, s.v. "father of the chair in the canopy," and the assumption is like other chuppahs where he has not yet consummated, see there and understand it well.]

There are those who say that it is proper that at the time of the betrothal, according to our custom where the betrothal (Kiddushin) is done at the time of the chuppah (marriage canopy), the groom and bride should not stand under the canopy spread on poles, which is the chuppah, but should stand in front of it. Then, when they begin to bless the seven blessings (Sheva Brachot), they should stand under the chuppah [Beit Yosef]. The reason is so that the chuppah does not precede the betrothal. However, we have not seen anyone who is concerned about this. According to what the great authorities have said, the primary aspect of the chuppah is the seclusion that follows in a modest place. Therefore, there is certainly no concern in this matter [ibid.]. Even according to our custom, there is no concern in this, as we have already explained that our chuppah is because they accepted upon themselves that this is the chuppah and the completion of the marriage, and she becomes his wife completely. This is after they have completed the seven blessings, as we have said, that then it is the completion of the chuppah and not before. Therefore, the betrothal precedes the chuppah, as before the blessings there is no chuppah. The fact that the preparations for the marriage are before the betrothal is of no concern.

Since a betrothed man and woman are prohibited from being secluded together, our master the Rema wrote that a betrothed man who is with his betrothed in one house should recite the seven blessings, lest they become secluded. And even though blessings without a wedding canopy are not effective at all, nevertheless, according to what the Rambam wrote, that if his intent is for marriage, a wedding canopy is not necessary, therefore they recite the seven blessings. For then, it is obvious that if he has relations with her, he intends for marriage and will not abandon the permissible and engage in the forbidden. Additionally, according to the opinions that the blessings are essential, it is necessary to recite them. Moreover, since they are together in the house for a long time, it is like a courtyard belonging to both of them, and their seclusion is considered marriage, making her permitted to him after the blessings. All of this is according to their custom, where betrothal has already taken place, but according to our custom, where the betrothal occurs at the time of the wedding canopy, the blessings are not effective since the betrothal has not yet occurred. Therefore, the betrothed man should distance himself from his betrothed until the time of the wedding.

We have already written in the name of the Rambam that if someone betroths a woman and recites the wedding blessings but has not yet secluded himself with her in his home, she is still considered betrothed. The wedding blessings do not effectuate the marriage; only entering the chuppah (bridal canopy) does. However, if he cohabits with her for the purpose of marriage, it is valid as we have written. The Rambam's intention is that if he does not cohabit with her or immediately seclude himself with her, the blessings are in vain.

And likewise, if he betrothed and brought her to the chuppah but did not recite the blessings of the grooms, she is still considered fully married, and he can recite the blessings even after several days. And although all blessings must ideally be recited prior to the performance of the mitzvah, nevertheless, since these blessings do not explicitly mention the marriage, they can be recited afterward as well. However, the blessing for betrothal must be recited before the betrothal, like all blessings that must be recited before fulfilling the mitzvah.

Several of the poskim (halachic authorities) wrote that there is no chuppah (bridal canopy) for a widow, and their basis is from the Jerusalem Talmud. It will be explained with God's help in Siman 64 that there is no proof from the Jerusalem Talmud. It is obvious according to the Rambam's opinion, who holds that the chuppah is the seclusion, and likewise according to those who maintain that the chuppah is the transfer into the husband's domain, why should there be a difference between a virgin and a widow? However, according to those who maintain that the essence of the chuppah is the house that is designated for the residence of the groom and bride, or with the decorative sheets, and likewise according to those who maintain that the essence of the chuppah is the spreading of the canopy or the veil, certainly since these are not done for a widow, she does not have a chuppah. The primary acquisition for her is through seclusion suitable for marital relations. Similarly, according to our chuppahs, where a widow's marriage to a widower is not made public, she does not cover her head, they do not have attendants or musical instruments, and they are not led to the courtyard of the synagogue. Rather, they set up poles with a spread fabric in the house and he sanctifies her (marries her) and they recite the seven blessings – this is not an acquisition of chuppah and it is necessary to acquire her through seclusion suitable for marital relations. This will be further explained with God's help in Siman 64.

Before entering the chuppah, one must write a ketubah, and only afterward is it permitted to be with his wife. For our Sages have said that it is forbidden to be with one's wife even for one hour without a ketubah. This is the ruling of the Rambam, and it is brought by Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in Section 3. 

One should not ask why it is obligatory to write it before the chuppah; why not write it after the chuppah, before consummation? One could say that the Rambam is consistent with his view that the chuppah must be fit for consummation, and without a ketubah, it is not fit for consummation [Hilkhot Ishut 10:7]. According to this, since we do not hold like him in this matter, as stated in Section 61, it would be permitted to write it afterward. 

However, Rabbeinu the Rema did not correct this because, according to our custom, we interrupt with the reading of the ketubah under the chuppah between the blessing of betrothal and the blessing of marriage. Therefore, even without the reason of the Rambam, it is necessary to write it before the chuppah, and this is the custom.

But the ketubah (marriage contract) alone does not effectuate marriage. Therefore, if someone betroths a woman and writes her a ketubah, but she has not yet entered the chuppah (marriage canopy), she is still betrothed and not married, because the ketubah does not effectuate marriage. If he dies or divorces her, Rambam wrote that she collects the principal amount of the ketubah only from unencumbered properties and not from encumbered properties. She does not collect any additional amount (even if it was written in the ketubah). Rambam’s reasoning is that the ketubah is not considered significant because it was written only on the condition that he would marry her. Therefore, the principal amount of the ketubah is like an oral loan, and she collects only from unencumbered properties. However, if he betrothed a woman and did not write her a ketubah and he dies or divorces her while she is still betrothed, she does not receive anything, not even the principal amount, because the enactment of the principal amount of the ketubah was not established until marriage or until it is written. This is the opinion of Rambam.

Some of our Rabbis hold that a betrothed woman (arusah) is entitled to a ketubah, as it is demonstrated in several places in the Talmud. If he did not write one for her, she can collect from unencumbered properties, but if he did write one for her, she can collect even from encumbered properties, as with all written contracts. However, without writing one for her, it would seem that even according to this opinion, she cannot collect from encumbered properties. However, the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote that even without writing one for her, she can collect from encumbered properties by the stipulation of the court (Ketubot 4:6). It appears from the words of the Rosh in another place that he was uncertain about this ruling (ibid. 5:5). Moreover, even if he wrote one for her at the time of betrothal and then wrote another at the time of the marriage, the first lien is considered waived (ibid.), and she can only collect from the time of the marriage. All of this pertains to the basic ketubah, but regarding the additional ketubah, all agree that even if he wrote one for her, she cannot collect from the time of the betrothal, for it is a strong presumption that he wrote it only with the intention to marry her. The poskim have written that the custom follows Maimonides (Rambam) that a betrothed woman does not collect a ketubah, as in all the places in the Gemara where it is stated that a betrothed woman has a ketubah, Maimonides establishes that it is when he wrote one for her. This is also the opinion of the Geonim, since in the Gemara it was questioned whether a betrothed woman has a ketubah or not, and it was not resolved there (Bava Metzia 17a), it is not possible to collect a ketubah.

If a man betroths his daughter and she becomes widowed or divorced from the betrothal, even several times, before she reaches the age of maturity—her ketubah belongs to her father, for she does not leave her father's authority except through maturity or marriage. Therefore, if she marries and then becomes widowed or divorced from the marriage, even before maturity and even if she is a minor—her father has no claim over her, not even over the first ketubah written from the betrothal. We do not follow the writing of the ketubah to say that since it was written under the father's authority, it should belong to the father. Rather, we follow the collection [of the ketubah], and the collection is after the marriage. [Rashi Ketubot 43].

A betrothed woman who died—if the betrothed was a Kohen, he does not become impure for her, as it is written, "except for his close relative" (Leviticus 21:2), and this refers to a close blood relative. A betrothed woman is not considered his close relative, even if he betrothed her through intercourse, since she is forbidden to him until the marriage. If he died, she is not obligated to become impure for him, even though it is a mitzvah to become impure for all close relatives; nonetheless, for the betrothed, it is not a mitzvah. However, there is no prohibition for her, even if she is a Kohenet (a female descendant of Aaron), because the daughters of Aaron were not commanded regarding impurity, as it is written, "Say to the priests, the sons of Aaron" (Leviticus 21:1) — and not the daughters of Aaron.

And similarly, regarding inheritance – when she dies, he does not inherit her because in the context of inheritance, it is also written "his flesh," and since he does not inherit her, he is also not obligated to bury her. Rather, her father inherits her and her father buries her. And if there is no father, her heirs will bury her. Even if nothing remains from her inheritance, the betrothed man is not obligated to bury her or to incur expenses. Even if she was married to him in a place where, due to a regulation, he does not inherit her as mentioned in Siman 53, he is not obligated to bury her. In places where he inherits half of her dowry, some say the burial is the responsibility of both of them [Chamudei Daniel], and some say it is solely the husband's responsibility [Beit Shmuel].

Similarly, the betrothed man is not obligated to provide sustenance for his betrothed, because as long as she has not been married and he is not obligated in her marital relations, he is likewise not obligated in her sustenance and clothing. Unless she is a minor orphan who is being supported by her brothers, in which case the betrothed man is obligated to provide for her sustenance. Since she does not have sustenance from her brothers except until she is betrothed or until she matures, and this one has not matured to support herself but is a minor or a young girl, and no one wants his betrothed to be disgraced and go begging at the doors. Therefore, even if he says he does not care about this, we compel him to support her, and he becomes obligated by rabbinic decree. This is the opinion of the Rambam. However, some say that the betrothed man is not obligated to provide her sustenance even in such a case, and she is sustained by her brothers [and it depends on the version there in Gitin 53]. It is obvious that a merely matched woman has no status of a wife even like a betrothed one, and even if he wrote her a Ketubah, it means nothing if they retract before the betrothal, since he wrote it only with the intention to betroth and marry her [Chochmat Adam]. All the more so for other matters, she has no status like a betrothed woman.

[How Much Time is Given to a Betrothed Woman When the Betrothed Man Demands Marriage, and in it are 11 Sections]
A betrothed woman whose betrothed demands marriage, and no time for marriage was set at the time of the betrothal, and she says she needs time to prepare her clothing, jewelry, and all that she needs – she is given twelve months from the day of the demand to provide for herself and to make her preparations. Afterwards, she must marry and cannot delay any longer. If she says that even after this time she is still not properly prepared, he can compel her to marry. If she refuses, a letter of rebellion is written against her if her intention is to cause him distress, as explained in Siman 77, where it will be explained with God's help.

There is no difference whether he is a bachelor or a widower, and he cannot say that since he is not a bachelor, he is not so particular about the preparations, for she can say that his affection for her is greater than that of a bachelor [Yerushalmi, Chapter "Even Though"]. And there is also no difference whether he demanded immediately after the engagement or many years after the engagement, and he cannot say that since much time has passed, why did she not prepare herself, for she can say that since at the time of the engagement we did not set a time, therefore, as long as he did not demand, I did not prepare myself. And there is no difference in this regard whether she has a father or not, but there is a difference in her age, as will be explained.

How so? If a girl is betrothed by her father and the husband demands marriage while she is still a minor, we do not respond to him at all until she grows up. Not only can she delay the marriage, but even her father can delay it until she grows up and becomes a young woman. The betrothed cannot say to the father, "What difference does it make to you? What are you worried about if she consents?" The father can reply, "She currently lacks understanding, and I fear that after the marriage, she might regret it and come to me, and I will need to provide her with new ornaments and clothing" (Gemara, Ketubot 57b). If all parties agree for her to enter the marriage, the court does not prevent them. Nevertheless, it is not proper to do so, as it is even a commandment not to betroth a minor until she grows up, as stated in Siman 37. However, aside from the father, no one else can prevent the marriage if she consents, not even her relatives. Even if the father has died, she does not return to them. Although she is ill and it appears that he is hastening to marry her to inherit her, as in a place where there is no Takkanat Shum, or he imagines she will live for years and he will eventually inherit her, nevertheless, since she consents, he can marry her. Some of the great authorities wrote that the relatives can prevent the marriage if the father is not present, because they are fit to inherit her and the marriage would only be a rabbinic marriage. But Rabbeinu Tam disagreed with them and ruled as mentioned (See Mordechai, Chapter 2 of Kiddushin and Hagahot Maimoniot, Chapter 22, where this is explained. It is perplexing as it states there that twelve months have passed, and so Rema wrote in Darkei Moshe, but this is not mentioned in Shulchan Aruch. See there). (Also, see Siman 37, Seif 13 in the Rema. It is complex and requires careful study).

And know that what we have written, that in her youth we do not respond to her at all until she grows up, so it seems to me from the language of the Rambam in Chapter 10 and from the language of the Shulchan Aruch. And in the Gemara (Ketubot 57b) it states: "We do not arrange a marriage for a minor girl, but we do arrange a marriage for her when she is grown." And so writes the Tur. From this language, it appears that the betrothed can compel this even in her youth, to set a time now for her to marry when she grows up, after twelve months. But the Rambam omits this, and it seems to me that he interprets it as not an obligation that the betrothed can compel this, but rather that there is no prohibition in the matter. And this is also implied in the Gemara, which raises the question "Isn't it obvious?" and answers that we are not concerned that she might become frightened now and become weak, thus it teaches us. And if we were to say that the betrothed can compel this, what was the question? Rather, it certainly teaches us that there is no prohibition, and we are not concerned that she might become weak. (And with this, the question of the Tosafot there, s.v. "bagrah," is resolved, and their words are puzzling as the Maharsha wrote, and according to what I have written, it is clear, and examine it well). (And look there in Rashi, s.v. "but etc., without betrothal etc.").

If she was summoned during her youth, she is given twelve months from the time of the summons. We derive this from Rebecca, as it is written, "Let the young woman stay with us a few days" (Genesis 24:55), and "days" means a year, as it is written, "his redemption shall be a year" [Talmud]. And even though Rebecca was a minor, as explained in the Aggadah, in earlier generations the time of maturity was earlier than in our times [Tosafot Sanhedrin 69a]. The Torah refers to her as a "young woman," but a minor is also included in the term "young woman" [Ketubot 44b]. There is no conclusive proof from this, and it is merely an allusion. Since she is given twelve months, it naturally follows that the marriage will occur after she reaches maturity, as there is only a six-month difference between youth and maturity.

If she was demanded in her maturity (i.e., after reaching adulthood) — she is not given twelve months from the time of the demand but twelve months from the time she matured. And if she was demanded six months after maturity, then she only has six months from the time of the demand. The reason is that immediately upon her maturity, she begins to prepare herself. This is the opinion of the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch. However, some of our rabbis hold that this is only if she was betrothed after she matured, as it is assumed that she starts preparing her adornments immediately upon maturing so that if she finds a husband, everything will be ready. But if she was betrothed before maturing, she does not bother to prepare since she is already betrothed [Tosafot], and therefore she is given twelve months from the time of the demand. However, this opinion is not brought in the Shulchan Aruch [see Beit Shmuel]. Similarly, if she was betrothed on the day of her maturity, she is given twelve months from the time of the betrothal, which is the time of maturity, even if she was demanded afterward.

And this is when twelve months have not passed since she reached maturity, but if twelve months have passed since she reached maturity and then she became betrothed, we only give her thirty days from the time of the demand because she has already prepared her needs. Some say that the thirty days are counted from the time of the betrothal [Rashi], but the decisors agreed with the first opinion. And if twelve full months have not passed since her maturity before the betrothal, we complete twelve months from the time of maturity [Tur], and if twelve months are completed within thirty days from the time of the demand, we complete thirty days from the time of the demand [there] [and in Beit Shmuel section 2 there is a scribal error].

All this applies when she is a virgin, but if she is a widow or divorced from a marriage, she is only given thirty days from the time of the claim, and according to some, from the time of the betrothal, as stated. If she became betrothed to another and several months passed after the claim and he died and she became betrothed to another, we do not count from the time of the first one [Beit Shmuel]. However, if the first one claimed her during her youth and twelve months passed, she would be an adult for six months, and consequently, she only has six months from the second one. For if the first one claimed her after she matured, we also count from the time of her maturity, as stated [there, and what is mentioned that even in her youth the claim is valid, we have already written that it does not seem so from the Rambam, and investigate further].

Just as a period of time is given to a woman when the husband is summoned to support himself, so too is a period of time given to a man to support himself and to prepare for the needs of the wedding when the woman summons him. And how much time is given to him is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud, where his rule is the same as hers according to his circumstances: if he is a bachelor, even if he marries a widow, he is given twelve months; and if he is a widower, he is given thirty days. In his case, there is no distinction based on his age since a man, even an older one, does not begin to prepare himself before being summoned. 

And Maimonides wrote: "And how much time is given? The same as is given to her: if twelve months, then twelve months; and if thirty days, then thirty days." From his wording, it seems that it does not depend on him at all but on her: if she is a virgin, even if he is a widower, he is given twelve months; and if she is a widow, even if he is a bachelor, he is given only thirty days. He did not consider the Jerusalem Talmud because our Talmud proves his point <small>[since it questions Rabbi Huna and resolves it because of him, see Ran]</small>. Furthermore, it is logical because the time given to him is for preparing the wedding necessities, so why would he need twelve months for that? According to Maimonides, it makes sense that if she needs twelve months, then naturally he will not hasten to prepare until her time. According to the Jerusalem Talmud, it must be said that his preparation is not just for the wedding but also for his other needs, for which he needs more time. The Rosh and the Tur ruled according to the Jerusalem Talmud.

The time arrived that was given to the woman, and she did not want to marry to cause him distress – we judge her as a rebellious wife as it is written. And if the time that was given to him arrived and he did not marry her – he becomes obligated in her sustenance even though he did not consummate the marriage, and even if he dies before the marriage, she is sustained from his estate all the days of her widowhood [Ran on Perek 4 of Ketubot]. And since she is sustained by him, it seems that her earnings belong to him. However, there is no proof, for it is possible that they penalized him to sustain her without taking her earnings, similar to the case where we judge her as a rebellious wife. 

If there was a delay due to an unavoidable circumstance, such as if he fell ill before the time arrived or she fell ill or she became a niddah and was not fit for marriage, or if the time arrived on a day when marriages are not conducted – he is not obligated to provide her sustenance. And even though she can say to him that it was his bad luck that caused it, nevertheless, he is considered an unavoidable circumstance. But if he fell ill after the time arrived, he has already become obligated in her sustenance and does not become exempt now even though he is currently an unavoidable circumstance. And if she fell ill after the time, it is uncertain if he is obligated in her sustenance. There is no difference regarding becoming a niddah whether it is at her regular time or not at her regular time. When the unavoidable circumstance passes and he does not marry her – he becomes obligated in her sustenance [Beit Shmuel].

In our times, when the betrothal (kiddushin) is done at the wedding, none of these laws are relevant. If the wedding date was set at the time of the engagement and one of the parties does not want to marry on the agreed-upon date, the other party has the right to break off the engagement. If no date was set and one party demands marriage, a suitable time frame is given according to the need and as deemed appropriate by the court. The time frame mentioned in this section is not applicable here since possibly only after betrothal is such a time relevant, not before betrothal. [See Beit Shmuel, section 4, on the obligation of support, and it needs examination what obligation is relevant; the engagement can be broken off and another engagement can be made.]

[The Law Concerning When the Bride is Delivered to the Husband or His Agents for Marriage, and it Contains Five Sections]
We have already explained in Siman 55 what constitutes a chuppah (marriage canopy), through which a woman becomes fully his wife in all respects. However, we clarified there that the term "marriage" is also applied before the chuppah, as the term "marriage" extends from the time she leaves her father's house to her husband's house, and the completion of the marriage is the chuppah. The sages accepted that there are matters in which she is considered his wife from the time she leaves her father's authority to her husband's authority, even though the chuppah has not yet been completed, as will be explained. This is regarding inheritance according to Torah law, where the husband inherits his wife from the time of marriage when the dowry is with him or even with her father, according to the opinions explained in Siman 53. As the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote at the beginning of Chapter 22 of Ishut: "The husband precedes everyone in inheriting his wife. And from when does he merit her inheritance? From when she leaves her father's authority, even though she has not yet entered the chuppah, since she has come under her husband's authority, he inherits her." End quote. And similarly, if she committed adultery, her death is by strangulation and not by stoning like a betrothed woman, as it is written, "to play the harlot in her father's house" (Deuteronomy 22:21) – excluding when the father has delivered her to the husband's agents [Ketubot 48:], and certainly when she has been delivered to the husband himself, even before the chuppah. Also, regarding the annulment of vows, the husband annuls her vows without the father's partnership, unlike a betrothed woman, as stated in Yoreh De'ah Siman 234. Furthermore, even if the husband dies before the chuppah, she is considered married for the purposes discussed and is regarded as a widow from the marriage, and thus she does not return to her father's authority [ibid. 49]. However, for other matters, such as eating terumah, finding lost objects, and similar issues, she is not considered married until after the chuppah. Similarly, he does not become impure for her if he is a kohen, and he does not mourn for her until after the chuppah. Also, her earnings do not belong to him until after the chuppah [Rashi]. What we have written, that regarding vows she is considered married, there is no disagreement about this [and what the Ba'er Heitev wrote in the name of Rashi, it is clear that Rashi wrote this according to Shmuel, but the Tana D'bei R' Yishmael has already ruled as the Tosafot wrote there].

Therefore, if a woman became betrothed and her father handed her over to her husband or to the husband's agents who were sent to take her and bring her to him, or if the father sent her to her husband and they encountered the husband or his agents and handed her over, and she died on the way before entering the chuppah (marriage canopy), although the dowry is still in her father's house, her husband inherits her according to Torah law, following the opinions of Rashi and the Rambam as stated in Siman 53. According to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam there, this is specifically when the dowry is in his possession. This is the Torah law, but according to the rabbinic enactment, he does not inherit her even after the chuppah for any period, as stated there.

Rambam wrote: Similarly, if the father or the father's agents went with the husband and the husband entered with her on the way to a courtyard and secluded himself with her there for the sake of marriage and she died – behold, her husband inherits her. But if the father is still with the husband to bring her to the husband's house or the father's agents went with the husband's agents or with the husband, even if the husband entered with her to a courtyard to lodge on the way where travelers lodge in the same inn, since the father or his agents are with her and he has not yet secluded himself with her for the sake of marriage, if she dies, her father inherits her, even though her marriage contract is in the husband's house, end of quote. And behold, it is certainly true that if he secluded himself with her explicitly for the sake of marriage, she is considered fully married not only for inheritance but for all matters, even for eating terumah, as Rambam holds that seclusion for the sake of marriage is considered as the wedding canopy, as stated in section 55. And only in this chapter, Rambam is dealing with the laws of inheritance [and proof from the Rashba who wrote: And if you say, according to the objector who thought that she entered explicitly for the sake of marriage, how can it be taught regarding inheritance, etc., for there is nothing after the wedding canopy, end of quote, and therefore Rashi was precise in his commentary where he says that the handing over, etc., and means that it does not refer to explicit marriage, see there].

The Tur wrote: If the father handed her over to the husband's agents, etc., or if the husband had a courtyard on the way and she entered with him and secluded herself with him, it is assumed that they entered for the purpose of marriage, and he inherits her, etc. However, if the father went with the husband's agents, etc., or if she had a courtyard on the way and she entered with him, it is assumed that she entered only to lodge and did not leave the father's domain, and even if her dowry is in the husband's possession, the father inherits her. These are the exact words. And this is a different law from what the Rambam wrote, as the Tur is dealing with a case where they did not explicitly speak either for the sake of marriage or not for the sake of marriage. Therefore, in her courtyard, it is assumed that it was not for the sake of marriage, and in his courtyard, it is assumed that it was for the sake of marriage. However, this is only regarding inheritance, since it is not clearly known that it was for the sake of marriage. The Rambam did not deal with this at all, even though this law is mentioned in the Gemara. However, the Rambam wrote the laws that derive from this, that if it is explicitly for the sake of marriage, she is fully married, and if it is explicitly not for the sake of marriage, it is nothing, even for inheritance. But in a case of ambiguity, it depends on the circumstances: in her courtyard, it is assumed that he did not consent to marriage because it is degrading for him unless it was explicitly for the sake of marriage, and in his courtyard or that of both of them, it is assumed to be for the sake of marriage unless it was explicitly stated that it was not for the sake of marriage. Legally, the Rambam does not disagree with this. [And so wrote the Maggid Mishneh. See Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 2, who wrote that in his courtyard, when they seclude themselves, it constitutes a wedding canopy (chuppah) and he acquires everything, and this does not appear so from the Tur and the Rashba. And it also appears this way from the Ran and the Talmudic discussion. What Rashi wrote is according to the one who posed the question, and scrutinize it well.]

This rule regarding transferring to his domain is not specifically limited to when she has a father and is a minor or a young woman, but equally applies if she is an adult who has already left her father's domain, or an orphan or a widow from a marriage who went by herself from her home or her father's home to her husband's home and died on the way. In such a case, the husband does not inherit her. However, if the husband or his agents received her to bring her to her husband's home and she died, the husband inherits her according to Torah law. All the laws that were explained apply to her as well.

Know that even according to the Rambam, who holds that the chuppah of a niddah is not a valid chuppah, nonetheless, transferring to his domain for the purpose of inheritance is effective even when she is a niddah, for this rule is not derived from the laws of cohabitation. Therefore, even for a widow, according to many poskim who hold that she does not have a valid chuppah, nevertheless, transferring to his domain for the purpose of inheritance has the same law as for a virgin.

Therefore, in truth, some say that the reason a widow does not have a valid chuppah is when he does not go with her. In earlier generations, they did not make a chuppah on poles as is customary now, but rather there was a special marriage house where the groom and bride would come, and there was no relevance to transferring to his domain since they did not go together but each came separately. However, now that the groom goes with the bride from our chuppah to the marriage house and there consummates the marriage, he acquires her even when she is a widow.

However, if it is a matter of transferring to his domain, it has been explained that this is effective only for inheritance. And so it was decided in the Gemara. Additionally, even now it is not customary for the groom to go with the bride when she is a widow. Rather, each goes to the designated house, where they perform the betrothal and bless the seven blessings, and from there either he takes her to his home or she returns to her home for some time and then later travels to her husband's home.

[How much a person should give to his daughter, and it contains seven sections]

Our Sages of blessed memory said (Ketubot 52b): It is written in Jeremiah (29:6) that the prophet sent to the exiles, "Take wives and beget sons and daughters, and take wives for your sons and give your daughters to men." It is understandable that a son is under his father's control, for it is the way of a man to seek a wife. However, how can daughters be under his control, since it is not the way of a woman to seek a man (Rashi)? Rather, this is what it means: to dress her, clothe her, and give her something so that men will be eager for her and come to marry her. And how much? Both Abaye and Rava said up to a tenth of his property. Thus, it is a commandment from the Sages, based on the Torah, to provide one's daughter with a dowry, clothing, and coverings so that men will be eager to marry her.

And there it is taught [Ketubot 67b] – Someone who marries off his daughter without specifying, should provide her with no less than fifty zuz, etc., and similarly, someone who marries off an orphan girl should provide her with no less than fifty zuz. If there is money in the fund, they should support her according to her dignity. And it seems that these fifty zuz are only for clothing, as it is taught there [Ketubot 64b] that even the poorest of Israel should not provide his wife with less than fifty zuz worth of clothing per year. And so wrote the Rambam in Chapter 13 of the obligations of a man to his wife, and he wrote there that this amount depends on the time and place.

According to this, what Rambam wrote in Chapter 20: "The sages commanded that a person should give a small portion of his assets to his daughter so that she can get married with it, and this is called sustenance. One who marries off his daughter without specifying should not give her less than the clothing that is provided to the wife of a poor man in Israel, as it is written in Chapter 13." This is referring to a case where the father is poor, but if he is wealthy, he should give her according to his wealth, end quote. It appears clearly that the rule stated to give a small portion of his assets so that she can get married with it is the rule we brought in section 1. Why didn't he write one-tenth of the assets? Because we hold that it is not specifically one-tenth, as will be explained in Chapter 113, that orphans who marry off their sisters from their inheritance assess how much the father would have given them, and if we do not know his estimation, we give her one-tenth of the assets. Therefore, he wrote generally that he should give a small portion of his assets according to his desire. The second rule that he wrote, not to give her less than the clothing provided to the wife of a poor man in Israel, is the Mishnah we brought in section 2, and he explains that this is only regarding clothing. Why didn't he write fifty zuz? Because he follows his reasoning in Chapter 13 that this amount depends on the place and time.

And this is what the Tur wrote in this chapter: One who marries off his daughter without specifying should not provide her with less than clothing worth fifty gold coins of the local currency. In what case is this said? In the case of a poor person. But a wealthy person must provide according to his status. These are his words. And he only wrote the law of clothing; why did he not write the first law? Because in his opinion it is not relevant to practical matters, as he explained in chapter 111 regarding the Ketubat Benin Dichrin (special inheritance clause for sons from a first marriage), which the Geonim nullified because the ordinance was made so that a person would eagerly give to his daughter as much as to his son. And now they customarily give them more and more. These are his words. And this is for a dowry, called "parnasa" in the language of the sages, as Rashi explained: "For the dowry, we assess the father of the orphaned daughter who is about to get married, and we give her a dowry according to our estimation of her father, whether he was generous or frugal." These are his words. But the law of clothing needed to be mentioned because in this matter it is possible that they would not be excessive, or this is relevant to the extremely poor that he should not provide her with clothing worth less than this amount.

According to this, what our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, said: The sages commanded that a father should give a little from his assets to his daughter, and this is called "parnasah" (support). When a man marries off his daughter, he should not give her less than the clothing that is decreed for the wife of a poor man in Israel. When does this apply? When the father is poor. But if he is wealthy, he should give her according to his wealth. These are the words of the Rambam (Maimonides), and there are two laws: he must give her parnasah, which is the dowry, and clothing is a separate matter. And what is written in the Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah, Siman 250 regarding the community leaders who marry off an orphan, they should not give her less than fifty zuz – this refers to clothing, and they are not obligated to give her a dowry if there is a strain on the charity funds.

Clothing – One must provide her with what she needs for the year for both summer and winter, but only what she needs for one year. In the time of the Mishnah, this was sufficient with fifty silver coins of the province. Nowadays, it depends on the prices and customs of the region. Some say that he can be compelled to do this [Ba'er Hetev], and if he is wealthy, he can be compelled to give according to his means [ibid.]. Others say he cannot be compelled [Beit Shmuel], and regarding the amount of the dowry, it is obvious that he cannot be compelled to give the amount of the dowry, and he is only compelled to marry them off [ibid.], for it is a positive commandment from the words of the Prophets, as emphasized by the prophet Jeremiah, as it is written [and in the Ma'aseh Rokeach, the difficulty of the Makneh is answered, where he assumed that the fifty silver coins were the dowry, as mentioned there. We have clarified with the help of Heaven that this is for clothing, as proven from the Rambam and the Tur].

If a father made a condition with the groom to bring her in naked, the groom should not say "When she comes to my house, I will dress her," but rather he must dress her while she is still in her father's house, for it would be degrading for her to come to his house without honorable clothing, and it would also be disgraceful for the father. How is this condition fulfilled? Whether through a legal acquisition or by stipulating at the time of the betrothal, and it is considered a matter acquired by verbal agreement as stated in Siman 51. For us, since the betrothal is at the time of the wedding canopy (chuppah), the groom must obligate himself with a complete commitment through a legal acquisition at the time of the conditions. However, if the groom did not obligate himself to dress her and the father is poor and does not provide her with more than the value of 50 zuz for clothing, even if the groom is wealthy and would be required to dress her in clothing worth much more than this amount, nevertheless, she cannot compel him to give her clothing beforehand. He can say, "When you come to my house and the obligation will be upon me, I will dress you then according to my honor."

[Law regarding a father who marries off his adult son at home and whether he acquires it, containing four sections]
Our sages said that there are three laws which the sages received as Halakha (law) without reason [Bava Batra 144], and this is one of them: If a father marries off his adult son at home – he has acquired it. Specifically, an adult, specifically a virgin, specifically his first wife, and specifically if he marries him off first. The explanation of the matter: A father who marries off his adult son and has not married off another male child before him, and there is no concern regarding a daughter [Tur], and he marries him to a virgin, and for this son, it is his first marriage, and he designates a specific house where he does not live because he lives in another house, and the father clears out this house of all his belongings and possessions, leaving nothing there, and makes it into a wedding house for his son [Rashi, Gittin 14] – the son acquires that house. This is a Halakha without reason, yet there is some reasoning for it – they estimated the father's intention that out of his great joy, he granted him the house. And since he cleared the house of all his belongings and the son has no other place to live, the son's mind relies on it, and it is reasonable that he gave it to him [Tosafot]. This is like a law from Moses at Sinai that this acquisition is without a document and without a formal act of acquisition [Nimmukei Yosef].

And specifically, if he cleared the house so that nothing at all remains in it, not even a small jug of oil or a shoe or any small item, but if he left even a small item like an empty jug or any small thing worth only a perutah – the son does not acquire it because this is not a clear indication that his intention is to transfer ownership. Therefore, there were some sages who intentionally left some item of their belongings there so that it would not appear as if they were transferring ownership of the house.

If a father designated a house for his son for the purpose of marriage, and the house has an upper floor or an anteroom in front of it, and it contains all the details that were clarified so that the house is acquired by the son, we do not say that the upper floor or the anteroom is also his. Rather, only the house is acquired, and the upper floor and anteroom remain with the father. Even though the anteroom is necessary for the house, since it was not explicitly given, it is not acquired. Similarly, if there were two houses, one inside the other, and he married him off in one of them, he did not acquire the second house. Even if he married him off in the inner house, and therefore it is necessary to pass through the outer one, still, he acquires the inner house but not the outer one. Since this is a law without a reason, we only follow what is explicitly stated. [See Rashbam there, in the beginning of "Two Houses," who wrote that if he acquired a house and an anteroom, etc., according to the general rule of the Geonim, he acquired the anteroom. But Tosafot and the poskim did not explain it that way. See there in Tosafot, who wrote the opposite.]

And likewise, if he designated household items for his son's wedding, the son acquires them. And if he designated a house and household items for him, even if the house was not acquired—for example, if he retained some of his own items there or if he had a storage of merchandise there—we do not say that he also did not acquire the household items. Rather, the household items are acquired, and the house is not acquired. These laws also apply in our times [Beit Shmuel].

The Tur wrote: It is customary for young men, when one of them marries, for his friends to send him gifts in order to support him with the expenses incurred for the wedding. They come and eat with him during the seven days of festivity or part of them. When they get married, he reciprocates by giving them what they had done for him, sending each one of them according to what they had sent him, and he eats, drinks, and rejoices with them. This is called "shoshvinut" – which means friendship. These are the words of the Tur.

And this has the status of a loan, that if one sent to his friend and he (the recipient) later got married and the friend did not send back to him, he can claim it in court. However, he cannot claim it before he gets married. Moreover, if the one who received wants to return it before he gets married, he can say: "I will not accept from you now until I get married because I want to rejoice with you in the same way that you rejoiced with me." And it is similar to a loan in this regard as well – that there are times when the borrower is not permitted to repay without the lender’s knowledge, such as if he lent him in a settled area, he cannot repay him in the desert against his will, as it says in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 74. And this is also the case with this groom, it is like repaying in the desert, which diminishes his honor.

And even when the groom cannot demand repayment unless he celebrated in the same manner as the first one, but if he changes the celebration from how the first one was, he is not obligated to repay him, because he can say, "I do not wish to do for you other than what you did for me." Some say that whether the change is in the reduction of joy from the first one, such as if the first one married a virgin and he married a widow, he can say to him, "When you marry a virgin, I will repay you." Similarly, if the first one celebrated publicly and this one wants to celebrate privately, either because it is a time of distress or because he wants to minimize expenses, he can say, "When you celebrate publicly, I will pay you." Conversely, if the second one seeks to increase the joy, such as the first one married a widow and he marries a virgin, or the first one celebrated privately and he wants to do so publicly, the first one can say to him, "When you do as I did, I will repay you," and not in any other manner. [Rashbam Bava Batra 145:] And some say, specifically when he seeks to decrease the joy from the first one, but when he seeks to increase the joy, the first one cannot say this to him [Tur in the name of the Ra'ah].

If the second person wants to return to the first person more than what he sent him—it is permitted, and there is no issue of interest because he did not give it with the intention of interest, as he could have reduced it if he wanted to, but rather it is out of great joy and friendship that he increased the gift. And if the Sabbatical year passed between the first person's wedding and the second person's wedding—the Sabbatical year does not cancel the debt because we do not apply "he shall not exact" in this case since he cannot demand payment until the time comes for the second person to marry and return the gift. Therefore, if the second person married and did not demand from the first person and then the Sabbatical year passed—he can no longer demand from him because once the second person married, he had the ability to demand payment, and when the Sabbatical year arrived, "he shall not exact" applies.

Sometimes the money given as shushbinus (wedding gifts) returns to the heirs, as will be explained. When it does return, the firstborn does not receive a double portion, because the firstborn only receives a double portion in what is already in possession, not what is expected to be received. This is not considered in possession since if he had not married, he would not have been obligated to pay him. For this reason, the yavam (brother-in-law who performs levirate marriage) also does not receive a portion in it. For example, if one became a shushbin (best man) for his friend, and in return, his friend became a shushbin for him, and they celebrated together, but before he could repay him, the groom died and his brother performed levirate marriage with his wife, the yavam does not acquire it. This is because the yavam does not take what is expected, as stated in Siman 163.

Reuven who sent Shimon a wedding invitation gift, Shimon is not obligated to return it unless he is invited to eat, drink, and rejoice with him. However, if he is in the city or nearby enough that he could know that Reuven is getting married, he should come on his own to eat, drink, and rejoice with him and repay him. If he does not come, he must pay him in full even though he did not eat with him, since he obligated himself by not coming on his own. However, the Rambam wrote that this applies in a place where the custom is not to invite each individual, but rather everyone who hears comes on their own. But if the custom is to invite, then he must be invited. If he was invited and did not come, he must pay in full, but if he was not invited, he is completely exempt.

If he was not in the city or nearby in a manner that he did not know if this man took a wife, the groom needs to notify him to come. If he did not notify him, he pays him what he owes him, but deducts what he would have eaten had he been there, and pays the remainder. And do not wonder why we said that when he is in the city and the custom is to call, and they did not call him, he is exempt from everything? For certainly, it is because when he is in the city and they did not call him, it is as if they insulted him, as if they do not want his recognition, so why should he pay him? But when he is not in the city, the reason they did not notify him is because they did not want to trouble him to come from a distance, for that is the way of the world [it seems to me]. And how does he deduct for him? If he owed him a zuz, he pays him nothing, because he would not have fed him for less than a zuz. If he owed him a sela, he deducts half a sela, for thus is the custom: one who sends a sela feeds him for half a sela. From a sela and above, each one deducts according to what is appropriate to feed someone who sends such a gift, for according to the abundance of the gift, they prepare for each one.

Reuven who sent wedding gifts to Shimon and Reuven died before the wedding, or if he married and died during the days of celebration—Shimon is not obligated to repay the wedding gifts to the heirs, because he can say, "Give me my friend and I will rejoice with him as he rejoiced with me, and since I cannot rejoice with him, I am exempt." Therefore, if the days of celebration were completed and he rejoiced with him and then Reuven died—Shimon is obligated to repay the heirs. Similarly, if Reuven invited him and he did not come, or if Shimon was not in town and therefore was not informed, and the days of celebration were completed and then Reuven died—Shimon is obligated to return the wedding gifts to the heirs, either entirely or with deductions as specified.

And similarly, if Shimon dies and afterward Reuven marries a woman and the days of celebration are completed, whether the heirs of Shimon are obligated to pay Reuven – Rambam, of blessed memory, ruled that it depends on the custom. In a place where they have the custom to collect from the heirs, they compel the heirs to pay with a deduction for his (Shimon’s) consumption. In a place where there is no custom, they do not pay anything. The reason is that since Shimon has died, it is uncertain whether his assets were obligated or not, since perhaps because Shimon cannot rejoice with him (Reuven), his assets were not obligated, and the heirs are exempt. Therefore, it depends on the custom, for in cases of doubt we do not extract money. Tur wrote similarly. And there are those who say that the heirs of Shimon are always obligated to pay, since the delay is not due to Reuven, but rather from Shimon. Reuven can say, “What am I at fault for the delay? It is not from me” [Ramban]. However, the main opinion is like the first one [Maggid Mishneh], for Shimon is also not at fault. But if Shimon dies after Reuven marries and after he rejoiced with him, or he was able to rejoice but did not come – according to all opinions, the heirs of Shimon are obligated to pay whether in full or with a deduction as mentioned, for his assets were already obligated during his lifetime to pay.

And in a case where the heirs are obligated to pay when their father owes for what was sent to him, it is not only if this obligation is for something sent for his own wedding, but even if he incurred the obligation because something was sent for one of his sons’ weddings, where the father married him off and prepared for him the needs of the wedding and feast – the heirs are obligated to pay back. And not from the inheritance of this son to whom it was sent, but it is repaid from the general estate, as the obligation was on the father since he was the one who married him off. And there is a general principle regarding this – even though the heirs repay the debt of their father, nevertheless, they do not have the status of wedding guests who would be able to rejoice with this groom. Rather, only this son, for whom it was sent to the father, can rejoice, and not the others, even though the payment comes from the general estate.

The sages taught in a Mishnah [Bava Batra there]: The repayment of wedding gifts (shoshvinut) can be claimed in court, but sending a friend jugs of wine and jugs of oil cannot be claimed in court because it is considered an act of kindness. The Rambam explains that this means: the shoshvinut that can be claimed in court is only when one sent cash, but if one sent various kinds of food and drink, it does not have the status of shoshvinut that was explained, even if it was sent at the time of the wedding and one rejoiced with him, because the enactment was only regarding cash. However, many of our rabbis explain that there is no difference in this matter, and what was taught that jugs of wine and oil cannot be claimed in court is when they were not sent at the time of the wedding, or even if they were sent at the time of the wedding but the sender did not go to rejoice with him, because in this case there is no status of shoshvinut. The reason the Mishnah mentions jugs of wine and oil is because typically, when one wants to eat there and rejoice with him, one sends cash and the groom prepares with it, but if one does not want to eat and rejoice there but intends to benefit him, one sends him types of food and drink. However, according to the law, there is no difference between cash and types of food and drink.

The Tur wrote: If one of the brothers made a wedding present (shushvinus) for his fellow during their father's lifetime, and the father gave him what he sent, and the father died, and the one for whom the wedding present was made comes to repay, if the father specified this when he sent it, saying, "Go and make a wedding present for so-and-so," now when it is returned, it is to him alone. But if he did not specify anyone and just said, "One of you should make a wedding present for so-and-so," and this one stood on his own and did it, it is returned to all of them and they divide it equally as with other loans of their father. And he does not need to return everything at the first marriage he marries, but the first who marries pays his portion due to him. And regarding the joy of the one who sent together with the brothers, the Ramah wrote: If they all rejoiced with him, when he returns to each one, he needs to rejoice with him. And if he cannot rejoice, he must deduct from his portion. But if only one of the brothers rejoiced with him, he only needs to rejoice with the one who rejoiced with him. And if he cannot rejoice, he deducts from his portion. But for all the others, when they marry, he gives each one their portion and does not deduct anything, end of quote. [This is the explanation of the Tur on the Baraita there regarding sending a wedding present to his father, see there. And according to the Rambam in Chapter 9 of Inheritances, there is a different explanation of this, which is explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 286, see there.]

If someone sent a gift of "shushbinut" (a type of wedding gift) to his friend and the friend refuses to accept it, and the giver insists until the friend swears to take it, this is considered a valid gift and cannot be taken back, since the friend did not want to accept it but was compelled to do so. The same applies to similar cases. All the laws of "shushbinut" that have been explained are not practiced among us, and even in the time of our master, the Beit Yosef, this was not practiced, which is why he did not include these laws in his pure table, as he himself wrote.

[The Wedding Canopy Regarding What Makes the Marriage Valid and Wedding Customs, Consisting of 21 Sections]

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 10, Law 2: Once the betrothed woman enters the wedding canopy (chuppah), she is permitted to be with her husband whenever he desires, and she is considered his complete wife in all respects. Once she enters the chuppah, she is called "married," even if they have not yet engaged in intercourse, provided she is fit for intercourse. However, if she was menstruating (niddah), even if she entered the chuppah and was secluded with him, the marriage is not completed, and she is still considered betrothed. End quote.

And in Law 6, he wrote: If he betrothed her and brought her into the chuppah but did not recite the wedding blessings, she is considered fully married, and he recites the blessings even after several days. A niddah should not marry until she becomes pure, and the wedding blessings are not recited for her until she becomes pure. If he went ahead and married her and recited the blessings, he does not recite them again. End quote.

It is explained from his words that the chuppah of a menstruant woman does not constitute marriage. In the Gemara (Ketubot 56a), it is a question raised by Rav Ashi: If she entered the chuppah and then menstruated, what is the law? If you say that the affection of the chuppah acquires (the status of marriage) – (this applies) to a chuppah that is fit for consummation, but a chuppah that is not fit for consummation does not (acquire the status of marriage), or perhaps there is no difference? The matter remains unresolved. Therefore, it is ruled stringently, and according to this, the Rambam should have written that it is a doubt. And while concerning prohibition there is no practical difference, nevertheless concerning monetary matters, such as inheritance, there would be a practical difference: if he seized it, it is not taken from him, as in all cases of doubt in law. And indeed, the Rambam holds in all unresolved cases in the Talmud that seizure is effective, as he wrote in Choshen Mishpat in many places (and so it is written in the book "Tekfo Kohen," Siman 8, and so it is written by the "Urim Ve'Tumim" there). Moreover, if the husband is in possession of the dowry, the wife's heirs do not take it from him. From his (the Rambam's) words, it does not seem so, since he ruled that the chuppah of a menstruant woman is not a marriage. And it is possible to say that concerning inheritance, there is no practical difference in this case, as he certainly inherits her according to what is written in Siman 57, that if the father gave her over to the husband's agents, he inherits her even if she is not fit for consummation, as it is written there in Se'if 5. All the more so, in the chuppah of a menstruant woman, which is not worse than this, for he has taken her into his possession. And according to this, also concerning vows and if she died by strangulation, her status is also like that of a married woman, as it is written there in Se'if 1. But this does not seem so from his (the Rambam's) language. The Maggid Mishneh explicitly wrote that he does not inherit her. And some say that the Rambam follows his reasoning in the first chapter of Hilchot Nachalot, that in a case of doubtful divorce, the husband does not inherit her, and all the more so in doubtful betrothal. There is no proof, as certainly in those cases seizure is effective, and where do we derive that seizure is not effective? And indeed, many authorities disagree with his fundamental ruling, as it is written in Siman 90, and all the more so, even according to the Rambam, seizure is effective. It is obvious that in the case of seizure, a doubtful divorce is no less significant than if the house fell on him and his wife, as will be explained there (and so wrote the "Beit Shmuel" there, Se'if Katan 20, that legally seizure is effective, and the "Chamudei Daniel," Se'if Katan 14, compared this to the case of the house falling, as explained there).

And it appears to me, when we scrutinize his language in the sixth law where he wrote: "And a menstruating woman should not marry until she becomes pure, and one does not recite the blessing until she becomes pure, but if he went ahead and married and recited the blessing, he does not recite the blessing again," why did he write that she should not marry until she becomes pure? He already wrote this in the first law, where it only deals with the law of the blessing. Furthermore, why did he change his language from "chuppah" (marriage canopy) to "nissuin" (marriage) and he should have said "she should not enter the chuppah until she becomes pure"? Additionally, why did he rule that one does not recite the blessing again since the chuppah of a menstruating woman is nothing and she is like a betrothed woman, and it is like reciting the marriage blessings for a betrothed woman, which are blessings in vain? Why not recite the blessing again after she becomes pure? See what I wrote in section 20.

The truth is that according to what is stated in Siman 55, the main aspect of marriage is that he takes her into his domain, to his house, and lives with her as husband and wife, as it is written, "And who is the man who has betrothed a woman, and has not taken her?" (Deuteronomy 20:7). The "taking" refers to bringing her into his domain, and this constitutes marriage. However, the custom of the chuppah (bridal canopy) has been established, and from that moment she is considered fully married, such that even if she departs from his domain for several days, since it is after the chuppah, she is still considered fully married. Therefore, according to the Rambam, who states that the chuppah is consummation for the sake of marriage or seclusion for the purpose of consummation for the sake of marriage, as mentioned there, the Rambam refers to this type of chuppah. Consequently, when she is a niddah (menstruant) and not fit for consummation, even her seclusion is meaningless and does not qualify as a chuppah. However, this is specifically if one of them dies immediately or if they separate from each other. But if he takes her into his domain, even though the chuppah was not a valid chuppah, she must nonetheless be considered fully married, since he has taken her into his domain, which is the essential aspect of marriage according to the Torah.

Accordingly, the words of the Rambam are well explained. In one ruling, he wrote that if she entered the chuppah in her state of niddah, the marriage is not considered finalized in the event that one of them immediately dies or they separate from each other. In another ruling, he wrote that she should not marry until she becomes pure, meaning he should not take her into his domain until she becomes pure, and they do not recite the blessings for her until she becomes pure. However, if he transgressed and married her and recited the blessings, he does not recite the blessings again because she is married by force of circumstance since he has taken her into his domain, which is the essence of marriage. The doubt in the Gemara is only whether the chuppah is considered a chuppah. But afterwards, when he takes her into his domain, she is married by force of circumstance. Accordingly, there is no practical difference regarding inheritance except in a distant case, such as if she died at the moment of the chuppah, which is entirely uncommon. Therefore, the Rambam wrote that the chuppah of a niddah is nothing because the marriage is not finalized through it. Consequently, from any perspective, if they separate willingly, they have shown their intention to annul what they had planned to do with the chuppah, and this too is uncommon. If he took her into his domain and then she died before she became pure, it is obvious that he would inherit from her as a married woman. [And from the Beit Shmuel, section 62, it is explained that seizure is effective, but it seems to me as I have written.]

Many of our sages disagreed with him and held that the marriage canopy (chuppah) of a menstruating woman (niddah) is a complete chuppah. The question in the Talmud is only regarding the addition to the ketubah discussed there, as the presumption is that it was only written due to the affection of consummation or for a chuppah that is fit for consummation, and not for one that is not fit for it. Alternatively, this might also be considered as the affection of consummation. However, for all marital acquisitions, the chuppah of a niddah is a complete chuppah and thereby completes the marriage. And we hold that even for those who are prohibited, such as those forbidden by negative commandments, they still have a chuppah (Yevamot 57b) even though there is always a transgression in their consummation. All the more so the chuppah of a niddah, which will be permissible after a few days, is considered a chuppah (Ran, Chapter 5 of Ketubot). However, according to Maimonides, there is no difficulty from this, as Maimonides explains that there is a chuppah for those who are prohibited even without betrothal, as he wrote in Chapter 7 of Terumot: a widow who was betrothed to a High Priest or a divorcee to a regular priest, since they are guarded for a forbidden consummation, they do not eat terumah. Similarly, if they entered the chuppah without betrothal, they do not eat, as the chuppah disqualifies them from eating. And indeed, a chuppah without betrothal is certainly nothing, as Maimonides did not consider a chuppah as part of the acquisitions of betrothal, but there the reason is different, because since they were secluded in the chuppah, it is like consummation, and they are disqualified from eating terumah (explaining like Rashi there, and similarly the Rashba wrote there that since the chuppah exists for consummation, the Rabbis decreed, see there).

And furthermore, there is no connection between them, for the Torah explicitly states that there are marriages among those who are prohibited by negative commandments. Since there are marriages, it follows that there is a chuppah (wedding canopy) [and this is also consistent with the explanation of Tosafot there] that the chuppah is the marriage. However, in permitted marriages, just as the sexual relations are permitted, so too the chuppah, which is a prerequisite for sexual relations, must be permitted. The chuppah is not more significant than the sexual relations themselves. But in prohibited marriages, just as the sexual relations are forbidden and yet the Torah states that they have marriages, so too they have a chuppah. One cannot say that the Torah did not actually state that there are marriages among those prohibited by negative commandments, and if it is because the kiddushin (betrothal) takes effect, how do we know that they also have marriages? This is explicit in the Torah in the context of war arrangements, as it is written, "And who is the man that has betrothed a woman and has not taken her? Let him go and return to his house" (Deuteronomy 20:7). The taking is the marriage, as it is written, and we expound [Sotah 44a] "and has not taken her" – to exclude a widow to a High Priest, a divorced woman or a chalutza (a woman who underwent chalitza) to a common priest, who do not return, indicating clearly that they have marriages. However, since these are prohibited marriages, they do not return from the battlefield. One cannot say that the Torah excluded them by stating that they do not have marriages, as this does not seem to be the case [and this is also evident from Rashi there, and it is explicitly evident from Rambam, Kings 7:8, who includes them with one who remarries his divorced wife, and this resolves all the difficulties raised by the Lechem Mishneh, who struggled greatly with this issue. See Chapter 10 of Ishut, and also see Sha'ar HaMelech there. According to what we have said, everything is explained with the help of Heaven].

They further challenged him, as in the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Yoma, Chapter 1, it says regarding the High Priest that they prepare another wife for him in case his wife dies, and they permitted him a rabbinic prohibition to marry her on Yom Kippur. However, on Yom Kippur, she is not fit for consummation. This challenge is also not valid at all. Besides the fact that one should not compare an incidental prohibition of Yom Kippur to the inherent prohibition of a menstruant woman [as also stated in Shaarei Metz], it is obvious that he would not bring her into the chuppah on Yom Kippur, as he would not have the time to leave the Temple, and they relied on the primary Torah marriage that we wrote about in Siman 55, which means bringing her into his house and domain. Even though according to the Rambam it is also forbidden when she is not fit for consummation, as we mentioned in Halacha 6 that we brought, this is certainly only a rabbinic prohibition. Therefore, just as they permitted him for the sake of the atonement of all Israel to marry her on Yom Kippur, they also permitted him to bring her in even when she is not fit for consummation, as it cannot be done otherwise. In truth, in our Talmud in Tractate Yoma, Chapter 1 [13a], they said he should bring her in before Yom Kippur and divorce one of them conditionally. Additionally, from the Jerusalem Talmud, it seems that it is sufficient if he betroths her and there is no need for marriage [as also stated by Tosafot in Yoma, there, s.v. "v'lechada," see there].

According to Maimonides, even when there is a rabbinic prohibition preventing the consummation of the marriage, one should not perform the chuppah. Therefore, he wrote that the ketubah must be written before entering the chuppah, and afterward, it is permitted to be with one's wife. Based on this, even when she is ritually impure due to finding a stain or when she is in her days of purification, and she immersed before her days of purification, since the prohibition is only rabbinic, it is still forbidden to perform the chuppah. It is possible that in the case of a rabbinic prohibition, if the chuppah is performed, according to Maimonides, it would still be considered a valid chuppah.

However, many of our Rabbis disagree with him and hold that the question in the Gemara is only regarding the additional Ketubah amount that he wrote for her due to the affection of consummation – for this she is still considered betrothed, but for all other matters, she is considered fully married. And some say further that even regarding the additional amount, the doubt in the Gemara is only if he brought her to the chuppah while she was ritually pure, and during the chuppah she became a Niddah, as the language of the Talmud implies "she entered the chuppah and became a Niddah," which implies she became a Niddah after the chuppah had started. In this case, it is certainly possible that for all matters the chuppah is invalid because it was a mistake, as he intended for a pure chuppah and she turned out to be impure. Therefore, according to this opinion, if the bride is impure, she should inform the groom that she is impure, because otherwise it would be a mistaken chuppah. But if she was impure beforehand and the groom knows this and brings her to the chuppah, there is no doubt at all in the Gemara [Mordechai in the name of R"i]. But some say the opposite, that the doubt in the Gemara is necessarily when she became a Niddah beforehand, because otherwise, since she entered the chuppah in purity, he has already acquired her at the beginning of the chuppah, as the end of the chuppah is the beginning of consummation, and the chuppah acquires at its beginning [Rosh]. According to the first opinion, we can say that the intention was that she prepared to enter the chuppah while pure, and when she started to enter, she became a Niddah, so there wasn't even the beginning of the chuppah. Additionally, although the end of the chuppah is the beginning of consummation, who says the chuppah acquires at its very beginning? Maybe it acquires in its middle, before its end. Throughout all Jewish communities, it is accepted like the Rabbis who disagree with the Rambam, and they bring to the chuppah even if she is not in purity, except for a few individuals who are concerned with the opinion of the Rambam. However, even they cannot precisely determine if she will become a Niddah immediately before the chuppah. But according to what is written in section 5, even according to the Rambam she is fully married even if the chuppah was not in purity, as he later brings her to his home, which is the main part of the marriage. And they recite the seven blessings for them, even though they committed a transgression according to the Rambam, as explained there.

In my humble opinion, the legal authorities do not disagree with Maimonides (Rambam) at all, as I have written in Siman 55 that according to Maimonides, the primary aspect of 'chuppah' (marriage canopy) is either intercourse for the purpose of marriage or seclusion for the purpose of marriage. In this, it is obvious that no one would disagree that seclusion is only called seclusion if it is suitable for intercourse. Furthermore, when she is impure, he is forbidden to be secluded with her. For the other legal authorities who hold that the 'chuppah' is bringing her into his house for the purpose of marriage or an 'apiryon' (bridal litter) or covering the bride's head with a veil, or our types of 'chuppahs', and do not require seclusion suitable for intercourse at all, therefore, we do not worry if she is impure. Hence, according to what we have explained there, Maimonides would also agree to all these types of 'chuppahs' and there is no disagreement at all. Furthermore, I say that regarding Terumah (priestly tithe), where it is stated in the later Mishnah that she does not eat Terumah until she enters the 'chuppah', this 'chuppah' is certainly according to Maimonides that it must be suitable for intercourse, and even when he has intercourse with her.
