For in the Gemara there it is explained that the later Mishnah holds that an external examination is not considered an examination until he secludes himself with her and examines her himself, and therefore he must have intercourse with her or at the very least seclusion suitable for intercourse. From this, Maimonides derived to explain that the term 'chuppah' in the Gemara refers to seclusion suitable for intercourse. [And even according to Ulla there in Ketubot 57b, we can say that according to the later Mishnah we require an internal examination, and it appears so from Maimonides in Chapter 6 of Terumot, where he wrote Ulla's reasoning and wrote until she enters the 'chuppah', and according to him, 'chuppah' is seclusion suitable for intercourse. This resolves the question of the Rosh there in Siman 66, regarding this Mishnah, it is obvious that there is no issue there, and also the question of the Kesef Mishneh in Siman 5 is not difficult at all since the 'chuppah' there is only the one suitable for intercourse according to his view, and if he agrees to the other types of 'chuppahs', it is obvious that there is no issue at all, and examine this carefully.]

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 11 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations regarding the law of a woman who was asked to marry and agreed, that she needs to observe seven clean days, as she may have seen blood due to arousal, and he wrote that she is forbidden to marry until she counts and immerses. However, this applies to regular people, but in the case of a Torah scholar, she is permitted to marry immediately and count the clean days and immerse afterwards, as the Torah scholar knows that she is forbidden and will be careful not to approach her until she immerses.

Some have objected, questioning how one could make a wedding canopy for an impure woman [Raavad]. Others have resolved that since this is not a Torah prohibition, it was not treated stringently [Beit Shmuel Section 2, citing Maggid Mishneh]. However, it cannot be said so, as we have already explained that according to his view, one must be careful even with rabbinic prohibitions, as he himself wrote that they should write the marriage contract before the wedding canopy as he stated. And it is possible that he holds that this is not even a rabbinic stringency, but rather a stringency that women took upon themselves, as is evident from his words there, where he also wrote that all these are excessive stringencies that the daughters of Israel have adopted and are not comparable to all rabbinic prohibitions. However, according to what was mentioned earlier, Maimonides would agree that in other weddings we do not insist on her purity, it fits simply [see there in Kesef Mishneh and Beit Yosef, Tur Yoreh De'ah, Section 192, who questioned why Maimonides did not write in Chapter 10 of Laws of Marriage that a Torah scholar is permitted to marry a menstruating woman, and see what he answered, and his words are perplexing unless we say that he holds as written that he agrees in other weddings, and examine this carefully].

Nevertheless, even so, it is necessary to understand: according to the Rambam, who holds that "chuppah" is seclusion, how could he seclude himself with her, for she is prohibited to him according to the stringency? There are those who permit seclusion because she is not a nida and he is a Torah scholar [Magid Mishneh], but our teacher, the Beit Yosef, disagreed and held that it is prohibited to seclude oneself with her. If so, what kind of chuppah is this [Beit Shmuel]? It is possible to say, for example, that he betrothed her through intercourse [as the Beit Shmuel wrote regarding if she became a nida], in which case it is then permitted to seclude with her since he has already had intercourse. However, it is difficult to say this because since we are discussing a Torah scholar, how could he betroth through intercourse, for Rav would flog one who betrothed through intercourse. According to what I have written, that the Rambam would agree with other forms of chuppah, this is clearly simple.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Yosef Karo), wrote in section 1: Once the man brings his betrothed into the chuppah (marriage canopy), even though they have not yet consummated the marriage, she is considered his wife in every respect, and if she becomes widowed or divorced, she collects the principal and additional amounts of her ketubah. In what case does this apply? When she is fit for cohabitation. However, if she was a niddah (menstruant) and then he brought her into the chuppah and secluded with her – she is not considered his wife, but in all matters she is still like a betrothed woman since she was a niddah. Some say that this is specifically regarding not reducing the additional amount of the ketubah, but in all other matters she is considered married. This is the end of the quote. The first opinion is the view of the Rambam, and the "some say" is the view of those who disagree as mentioned. It seems clear that the primary ruling is like the Rambam [and so wrote the Beit Shmuel in section 62]. In section 2, he wrote: It is proper that she should not marry until she becomes pure. This is the end of the quote. Therefore, it is surprising that the phrase "it is proper" implies a stringency and enhancement of the matter, whereas according to the Rambam, it is essential. Furthermore, according to the Rambam's definition of chuppah as seclusion fit for cohabitation, how can the betrothed seclude with her while she is a niddah? He has not yet consummated the marriage, and generally, grooms do not consecrate with cohabitation. Hence, what is the meaning of the phrase "it is proper that she should not marry until she becomes pure," as there is no other way, and moreover, our teacher the Beit Yosef himself wrote in section 55 that the chuppah is seclusion fit for cohabitation as stated there. According to what was written, even the Rambam would agree in other forms of chuppah, and in these, she does not need to be pure. Therefore, he only wrote the phrase "it is proper" for enhancement alone [and it is forced to say that it refers to the desire for the seven clean days, and furthermore, even in this they are forbidden to seclude].

Additionally, it seems to me to say that even according to the Rambam, who requires that she be fit for cohabitation, nonetheless, if she is able to go to the mikveh after the chuppah, such as when the time for her purification has arrived even though she has not yet immersed – it is permissible to perform the chuppah and seclude with her even though he has not cohabited with her. We are not concerned about a mishap occurring in a short time, for she will immediately immerse after the chuppah. According to this, it is possible to say that what our master the Beit Yosef wrote, "It is proper that she should not marry until she has purified," does not mean when she is still in her days of menstruation, but rather before her purification. [And this reasoning, that we are not concerned about a short time that he might come upon her, is also written by the Noda B'Yehuda, Second Edition, Yoreh De'ah, Siman 122].

And our master, the Rema, wrote that now the custom is not to be meticulous and not to wait. Nevertheless, it is good to inform the groom beforehand that she is a Niddah. For most of the world has adopted the opinion of the poskim who disagree with the Rambam. And what he wrote—that it is good to inform the groom—is not according to the Rambam’s view, but rather according to the explanation we clarified in section 10, so that it should not be a mistaken betrothal. [And from the Beit Shmuel, section 8, it is implied that this is also according to the Rambam, and it requires further investigation, as the Beit Meir wrote there.]

Furthermore, it is written in Section 1 that according to the Rambam, the ketubah must be written before the chuppah so that the chuppah will be one that is fit for consummation. According to the opinion that the chuppah of a menstruant is considered a valid chuppah even though it is not fit for consummation, the same applies if the ketubah was not written. Nevertheless, it is preferable to write it beforehand. This custom is observed even by those who do not follow the Rambam, for we interrupt by reading the ketubah between the blessing of betrothal and the blessing of marriage, as will be explained, and therefore the ketubah must be before us.

Furthermore, it is written: A gravely ill woman, even if she is brought under the chuppah with her bed so that her husband may inherit her, this is not considered a valid chuppah at all, since she is not fit for marital relations. Therefore, her husband does not inherit her. This applies in places where the customs of ShUM are not practiced. Nevertheless, it does not help even according to those who do not follow Maimonides, for although we do not require a chuppah fit for marital relations, we do require a woman who is fit for marital relations. Everyone understands that the purpose of the bride entering the chuppah is for marital relations, and since she is never fit for such relations, according to all the poskim, she is not considered married. This is not similar to a woman who is merely sick, as explained at the end of Siman 56, where she is still fit for marital relations.

Additionally, he wrote: If he brought her to the wedding canopy (chuppah) and did not recite the blessings of the grooms, it is considered a complete chuppah because the blessings are not an absolute requirement and he can say them even several days later. Ideally, he should recite them before he has seclusion with her. Refer to above, Siman 55. Nowadays, the custom is to recite the blessings under the chuppah before they have seclusion. And he follows his view in Siman 55 that after the chuppah, the groom and bride have seclusion. And we have already explained that according to our custom, the blessings are a fundamental law, and this completes our chuppah as stated in Siman 55, section 19. Moreover, since he immediately takes her under his authority, this is the essential marriage according to the Torah as stated in section 4. Therefore, the blessings are at the time of marriage, and it has already been clarified that there are authorities who believe that the blessings are an absolute requirement. We have explained in Siman 55 there that in our type of chuppah, according to all opinions, the blessings are an absolute requirement. Refer there.

Additionally, he wrote: If one betrothed a woman by mistake and subsequently had a marriage with her, and afterwards it became known that the betrothal was in error, even if he betroths her again, there is no need to recite the seven blessings (Sheva Brachot) again, and the initial blessings suffice, end quote. The reason is not because it is permissible to have a wedding before betrothal, for certainly a wedding that precedes betrothal is not valid at all [see Melamed LeHoil, Chapter 10], but the reason is explained in the source of the law in Mordechai [in glosses on Kiddushin] in the name of the Rashba, author of the Tosafot. The subsequent marital relations will constitute the marriage, and the previous blessings will apply to them. Moreover, the blessings are not indispensable, similar to the case of a minor who marries a woman. The Sages did not institute marriage for him, yet when he grows up, the seven blessings are not recited for them, but once he has marital relations in his adulthood, the marriage is completed. This is also the ruling of Rashi [there], and it appears to align with the words of the Rambam we brought in Section 3. Nevertheless, there are those who are hesitant about this and hold that if it is clear that the betrothal is not valid, new blessings must be recited after the betrothal [Bach, section 7, in the name of Rabbi Moses Minz and the Bach]. In the source of the law that did not require blessing, there were additional reasons to uphold the previous betrothal, but the language there does not indicate this. The matter requires further investigation, and in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient.

Several beautiful customs have been established by the Jewish people for their weddings: It has become customary to fast on the day of the wedding, as it is stated in the Aggadah that the sins of the groom are forgiven [Jerusalem Talmud, Bikkurim]. Since it is a day of forgiveness, it is appropriate to fast and to pray for mercy that he will live a tranquil life with his spouse and that they will produce a righteous generation in the eyes of God and man. Additionally, the fast helps prevent drunkenness and ensures that their minds are clear during the sanctification (kiddushin) – for this reason, it is not necessary to complete the fast. Similarly, a father who accepts the sanctification of his minor daughter should also fast for this reason.

The common practice is that if the wedding is held during the day, the groom and bride eat and drink after the ceremony. From this, it seems that the second reason is considered primary. Furthermore, there is an indication from the custom that when the wedding continues for several hours into the night, they fast until after the ceremony. According to the first reason, they would not need to fast after nightfall. There is no need to formally accept the fast during the Mincha (afternoon) prayer beforehand since everyone follows this custom, as is evident in Orach Chaim 562. Even if the wedding is held during the day and the fast is not completed, the groom and bride should still pray the "Aneinu" prayer during Mincha, as implied there. It is also customary for them to confess their sins during the Mincha prayer.

On days when fasting is not customary, there is no need to fast either. This applies specifically to days mentioned in the Talmud, such as Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, and certainly Purim, Isru Chag (the day after a festival), the 15th of Av, and the 15th of Shevat. However, during the days of Nisan, fasting is customary, and in Orach Chaim 573, it is also stated that fasting is observed on Lag BaOmer, the three days of restriction, and between Yom Kippur and Sukkot since these days are not mentioned in the Talmud. If fasting is very difficult for them, they should not fast, but they should be careful not to drink intoxicating beverages or indulge in excessive eating and drinking on that day [Beit Shmuel].

Additionally, it has become customary to hold the wedding ceremony under the open sky as a good sign that their offspring will be as numerous as the stars of the sky. Recently, there are those who have come to change the customs of Israel and to emulate others by not wanting to hold the wedding under the sky, but their position is weak, and the position of those who maintain the customs of Israel is strong. Another custom is to break a glass under the wedding canopy in memory of Jerusalem, which will be explained in detail in section 65, see there.

[The laws of the Blessing of the Grooms, containing 42 sections]

The blessing of the grooms for marriage consists of six blessings, which are as follows:
Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, who created everything for His glory... Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, Creator of man... Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, who created man in His image, in the image of His likeness, and prepared for him from his own self an eternal building. Blessed are You, Creator of man... May the barren one rejoice and be glad at the ingathering of her children into her midst in joy. Blessed are You, who makes Zion rejoice with her children... Grant perfect joy to these loving companions, as You gave joy to Your creation in the Garden of Eden of old. Blessed are You, who grants joy to the groom and bride... Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, who created joy and gladness, groom and bride, etc. Blessed are You, who grants joy to the groom with the bride.

The custom when reciting blessings under the chuppah is to first bless over the cup, "Borei Pri HaGafen" (the Creator of the fruit of the vine) or "Shehakol" (the Creator of everything), and then to recite the blessings. During the seven days of feasting, in the Grace After Meals, the blessings are recited first and then the blessing over the cup. The reason is that the blessing over the cup is more frequent, and what is frequent takes precedence. During the meal, when the blessings are recited after the Grace After Meals, it should not appear that the cup is for the Grace After Meals; therefore, the blessing over the cup is delayed to indicate that it is for the blessings of the bridegrooms. Even according to our custom, where there are two cups as will be explained, it is still more recognizable when the blessings are recited afterwards. Furthermore, during the meal, since the marriage has already preceded, and the marriage itself causes the cup to come, the Grace After Meals does not require a cup. Additionally, the main reason for the meal is because of the marriage; therefore, the blessings come first and the frequent practice is overridden.

These blessings that were arranged concerning matters of marriage start from "Who formed man" and onward, as that blessing begins to speak of both of them. "Who formed man" – speaks of the male, "and established for him from himself an eternal structure" – this refers to the female. "May she rejoice exceedingly" – because we need to elevate the memory of Jerusalem at the height of our joy, as it is written, "If I do not elevate Jerusalem above my chief joy" (Psalms 137:6). "Gladden the beloved companions" – a blessing for the groom and bride that they should succeed in joy and good-heartedness, and "Who created" for the sake of all Israel, and "beloved companions" refers to the groom and bride, blessing them that they should rejoice "as You gladdened Your creation in the Garden of Eden of old" – like You gladdened Adam the First when he was in the Garden of Eden. And why do we conclude the first blessing with "Who gladdens the groom and the bride" and the last one with "with the bride"? Because the joy of the first blessing is not about the joy of the wedding itself, for it is a prayer in which we pray and bless that they should be joyful and successful all their days, therefore we do not conclude it with "Who gladdens the groom with the bride," as that would imply man with woman, but rather, Blessed is Hashem who gladdens both of them forever with sustenance and all good things. And in the last blessing, we praise the Holy One who created the wedding of the union of man and woman through joy and happiness, therefore we conclude "Who gladdens the groom with the bride," which is an expression of the joy of man with woman. The blessing "Who has created all for His glory" is not from the order but for the gathering of the people who gather there to perform a kindness in memory of the kindness of the Creator who acted with Adam the First, who became his Best Man and attended to him, and this gathering is an honor to the Creator, and this blessing was established for that purpose. From the time of the gathering, it is fit to bless, but since there is a blessing over the cup, they arranged it to be recited over it. And the blessing "Who forms man" was established for the first formation of Adam the First [Rashi Ketubot 8a].

The first blessing begins with "Blessed" even though it is adjacent to the blessing over the cup, because it is not part of the sequence as mentioned, and it stands as its own blessing. Additionally, during the meal it precedes as mentioned, and since it is a short blessing, if it did not begin with "Blessed," its nature as a blessing would not be evident. This is also the reason for the blessing "Yotzer HaAdam" which is not considered adjacent to its counterpart and would not start with "Blessed" [Tosafot]. "Asher Yatzar" begins with "Blessed" because it is the first blessing of the current union [Rashi] as mentioned, and therefore it also concludes with "Blessed" like all primary blessings in a series [ibid]. Furthermore, if it did not start with "Blessed" it would appear as if it were a single blessing with "Yotzer HaAdam" [Tosafot]. "Sos Tasis" does not begin with "Blessed" because it follows the long blessing of "Asher Yatzar" and thus only concludes with "Blessed" as is the rule for a blessing adjacent to its counterpart. Similarly, the blessing "Sameach Tesamach" and the blessing "Asher Bara" begin with "Blessed" because they are said individually when there are no new faces present as will be explained, thus they are not adjacent to their counterpart, and they conclude with "Blessed" because they are long and also because they are the last in the order of the blessings.

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 10: If there is wine available, one should bring a cup of wine and first bless the wine, then arrange all the blessings over the cup, resulting in the recitation of the seven blessings. In some places, it is customary to bring a myrtle branch along with the wine, bless the myrtle after the wine, and then recite the six remaining blessings, end quote. The Tur wrote in the name of Rabbeinu Nissim Gaon: If one is in a place where wine is not available, he should take raisins, soak them in water, squeeze them, and bless over them. If raisins are not available, he should bless over beer with the blessing of "Shehakol," since it is essential to have a cup. However, for the blessing of betrothal (Erusin), if wine is not available, even if there is beer, one blesses without a cup, as it is not an optimal mitzvah. But for the seven blessings of the wedding (Sheva Brachot), one must bless over a cup with the blessing of "Borei Pri HaGafen," or "Shehakol" on beer if no wine is available at all, end quote.

There is room for doubt regarding the words of the Rambam if he also holds that the cup is essential. This is because he wrote "if there is wine," which implies that if there is no wine, it is not essential—this applies to wine, but beer is required. Alternatively, he might hold that the cup is not essential at all. This seems to be his intention since he did not mention beer at all. However, the halacha is that the cup is essential, as the Tur wrote. [And also, the Maggid Mishneh seems to have adopted this view, and this is the intention of the Chayei Adam, and the Beit Shmuel mistakenly critiqued him in subparagraph 2.]

And why is it that for the blessing of betrothal the cup is not essential, but for the blessing of marriage it is essential? It appears from the words of our sages that because it is traditionally accepted that we require seven blessings for the bridegrooms, and here there are six blessings, but with the cup there are seven blessings. And just as it has been traditionally received from Moses our teacher that we need to rejoice for seven days of feasting [Jerusalem Talmud, Ketubot, Chapter 1], and there is a hint for this in the Torah as it is written, "Fulfill the week of this one" (Genesis 29:27), so too has the tradition of seven blessings come to us. However, what the Tur wrote that for the blessing of betrothal, if there is no wine, one should not bless on beer and should bless without a cup, Maimonides in Chapter 3 did not write this, and as it is written in Siman 34, if there is no wine, one should bless on beer. And the Tur himself also ruled this way there, as it says, that ideally, also for the blessing of betrothal, a cup is needed.

In our practice, where the betrothal (kiddushin) takes place at the time of the wedding ceremony (chuppah), two cups are necessary: one for the blessing of betrothal (birkat erusin) and one for the blessing of marriage (birkat nisuin). We recite the blessing over the wine (borei pri hagafen) on each cup separately, as they are not connected to each other. Additionally, there is an interruption with the betrothal since the groom betroths the bride after the blessing of betrothal. Rashi of blessed memory instituted the practice of reading the ketubah (marriage contract) after the betrothal to create a significant interruption between the blessing of betrothal and the blessing of marriage, and this is our established custom.

Regarding the final blessing (bracha acharona), if the same person recites both blessings and drinks from both cups, one final blessing suffices for both, which is recited after the second cup [Chochmat Adam 15:16]. However, some say that a separate final blessing should be recited for each cup due to the significant interruption, as mentioned [Hagahot Maimoniyot, Hilchot Ishut 10:3]. Nonetheless, for us, this distinction is not relevant since it is not our custom for the person reciting the blessings to drink; rather, the groom and bride taste a little. The custom mentioned by Rambam to bring a myrtle (hadas) is not our practice, and it is possible that this is done intentionally so that the blessings of marriage (sheva brachot) are seven blessings, no more and no less.

Even though in the blessing of betrothal, the Rambam wrote in Chapter 3 that the groom himself should recite it, nevertheless, regarding the blessing of marriage, it is implied from his words in Chapter 10 that another person recites it. The reason is simple: the blessing of betrothal is like other blessings on commandments, and it is upon the one performing the commandment to recite it. However, the blessings of marriage are blessings for the groom and bride, that they should be successful, as it is written – and therefore, it is necessary for others to bless them. However, it has already been explained in Chapter 34 that even for the blessing of betrothal, our custom is that another person recites it. And our custom is that the groom and bride stand under the chuppah facing east, and the one reciting the blessing stands facing west so that he blesses them face to face, as all blessings are face to face like the priestly blessing. And the bride is positioned to the right of the groom, as it is written (Psalms 45:10), "The queen stands at your right hand, etc."

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote: "One must recite the blessing of the bridegroom's benedictions in the bridegroom's house before the marriage," thus were his words. Similarly, the Tur wrote: "The bridegroom's benedictions are recited before entering the chuppah," thus were his words. They were precise in saying that the blessings should be recited before the chuppah and the marriage, as all commandments are blessed upon before performing them. According to this, it is puzzling regarding our custom of reciting the blessings after standing under the chuppah. However, our custom is based on a line of reasoning that "before performing" only applies to the blessing of betrothal, which is like other blessings on commandments. But the blessings of marriage, which are prayers on behalf of the bridegroom and the bride for their success, what relevance does "before performing" have to this? After all, during the seven days of celebration, we recite the seven blessings in the presence of new faces. And what Maimonides wrote about blessing before the marriage follows his view, as we wrote in Siman 55 that chuppah means seclusion suitable for intimacy, and therefore it is necessary to bless beforehand, for if they bless during the seclusion, it is not considered seclusion. But in our chuppahs, it is actually better that they enter the chuppah and then bless them for their success. The Tur also wrote to bless before entering the chuppah because he also holds that chuppah means seclusion, as he wrote in Siman 61. [And the words of the Beit Shmuel in section 1 are not clear to me, as to what connection the blessing of betrothal has to marriage. And what he wrote that the Tur holds like the Rosh, it is true that in this Siman he copied the words of the Rosh for some matter, but in Siman 61 he wrote that it means seclusion, see there.]

One does not recite the "Blessing of the Grooms" except with a quorum of ten adult free men, and the groom is included in the count. Since these are blessings of joy and he is in a state of joy, why should he not be included in the count? This applies whether they are recited at the time of the wedding or at the feast after the Grace After Meals. Although these blessings are not like sacred matters such as Kaddish and Kedusha, which cannot be recited with less than ten people, nevertheless, since we say "who created all for His glory" which honors those assembled and we mention the rebuilding of Jerusalem, it is not respectful to mention them with less than ten people, as it is derived from the verse about Boaz, as it is written (Ruth 4:2), "He took ten men, etc." However, one should not learn from this verse that we need ten excluding the groom, as this is not logical at all. Therefore, during other meals when there are no new faces and only the "Who created joy and gladness" blessing is recited, ten are not required. Nevertheless, three are needed, as it is not less than the requirement for the Grace After Meals, for any additional blessing beyond the established blessings of the Grace After Meals is not recited with less than three. However, the "Blessing of Betrothal" does not require ten, as stated in Siman 34, as it is a mitzvah blessing like all other mitzvah blessings. But initially, ten are also required there, as stated. It is possible that three are also required there, as three are necessary – the groom and the two witnesses of the betrothal.

Some say that in a place where it is impossible to gather ten [men], one should not marry a woman there and should go with her to a place where there are ten because of the blessings [Beit Yosef in the name of the Rashba]. However, many disagree with this, as there is no reason to say so, since the blessings are not indispensable after the fact. One can bring her under the chuppah without the blessings, and they can bless after several days when ten are available, if they gather within the seven days of feasting. It is possible that even after a long time, the seven blessings are recited since they have not yet been said. This is also indicated by the language of the Rambam in chapter 10, who wrote that if the wedding blessings were not recited, they can be recited even after several days. See there [And in the Yam Shel Shlomo I found that after the seven days of feasting, they should not recite them]. During the meal, only the blessing "Who created" is recited, but at the time of the chuppah, it is not recited alone because at the time of the chuppah, only the seven blessings were instituted. [What the Beit Yosef wrote in the name of the Rashba requires investigation, as the Rashba did not say not to have the wedding, but rather not to bless with fewer than ten. See there in the responsa.]

It appears to me that if the blessing of the grooms (Sheva Brachot) begins with ten [people] and some of them leave, they may complete it even with less than ten. For even in the case of Kaddish and Kedusha, the law is the same, as it is stated in Orach Chayim, Siman 55, and certainly in the case of the blessing of the grooms. Furthermore, it is taught together in one Mishnah in the third chapter of Megillah, and their laws are certainly the same. There are those who wish to say that if the blessing of the grooms is recited with less than ten people, it is valid post facto and does not need to be recited again. This does not seem to be the opinion of all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). [See Noda B'Yehuda, Siman 56, who brought proof from Tosafot, and one who examines the Jerusalem Talmud of Megillah will find no proof from there, and so wrote his grandson in the book Yad HaMelech.]

If there are two grooms together, one recites the wedding blessing for both of them, as well as the blessing of betrothal, even if the grooms are not together but there is intention for both of them, as mentioned in Yoreh De'ah section 265 regarding circumcision, and like two groups eating separately where one recites the grace after meals for both as long as they see each other. Some say that one should not recite the blessing for two grooms together due to the evil eye. Each group of the grooms brings them in separately so it is clear there are two weddings and one does not bless for one in the presence of the other to distinguish their weddings [Beit Yosef in the name of Rashba]. And so, the custom is to make a separate canopy for each and to bless for each one. However, in the seven blessings after the meal, one can bless for many grooms together if they ate together, as the concern is only at the time of the wedding.

Maimonides, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: A man may marry multiple women at once on the same day and recite the wedding blessing for all of them together. However, he must celebrate with each one with the joy appropriate to her: if she is a virgin, seven days; if she is not a virgin, three days. And we do not mix one joyous occasion with another, as it is stated. Just as one does not marry during Chol HaMoed because we do not mix one joyous occasion with another, as stated in section 64. And even though there, they are two different kinds of joy, and here, it is one kind of joy, nevertheless, since in the Jerusalem Talmud (beginning of Moed Katan) we learn from the verse about Rachel and Leah, "Complete the week of this one," it implies that even within one kind of joy, we do not mix one joyous occasion with another so that one's heart can be fully dedicated to one mitzvah. Nowadays, this law does not apply, as we do not marry two women [and therefore Maimonides in the Laws of Marriage brought the Jerusalem Talmud's verse in relation to the previous law].

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote that one should not perform weddings for two sisters together, and some say that even for two non-related women, one should be careful not to perform their weddings simultaneously due to potential jealousy, lest one be honored more than the other. However, this caution is not widely observed, and on the contrary, some intentionally arrange weddings of poor women with those of wealthy women for the sake of the mitzvah. These are his words. 

This is unrelated to the matter discussed earlier regarding one blessing for two grooms; here the issue is mixing one celebration with another. Therefore, one should not perform weddings for two sisters in the same week. This is stated in the Mordechai [Moed Katan, Chapter 1]: "One does not mix one celebration with another," as derived in the Jerusalem Talmud from the verse "Complete the week of this one...," and therefore the early authorities had the custom not to perform weddings for two daughters or two sons or a brother and sister together. These are his words.

And regarding what he wrote that even two non-related women should not have their weddings at the same time, it means on the same day, because it is taught in Tractate Semachot that one should not praise two brides together unless there is enough for both, and even if there is enough, it is forbidden due to jealousy—if one is beautiful and the other is not, there will be jealousy between them, and similarly if one is honored more than the other. In this regard, our teacher, the Rema, says that this caution is not observed. However, in the case of two sisters or two brothers or a brother and sister, one must certainly be careful.

We hold that for a virgin, the celebration of the marriage lasts seven days, while for a widow, the celebration lasts three days, as will be explained in Siman 64. The blessings—for a virgin, all seven days, and for a widow, only one day. Thus, the Sages said (Ketubot 7a), "One day for blessings and three days for rejoicing." For a virgin, all seven days we recite the blessings after the meal, following Birkat Hamazon. When there are new faces (guests who were not present at previous meals), we recite all the blessings. Without new faces, we only recite the blessing "Who created." It has already been explained that the seven blessings require ten men, while "Who created" suffices with three. However, some say that even "Who created" is not recited throughout the seven days unless others besides the household members are invited, as this constitutes a wedding meal. But if he eats with only his household members, it is not considered a wedding meal, and "Who created" is not recited. Similarly, "the joy in His abode" is not said (Chokhmat Adam, section 8). This is the custom, and although there are dissenters, the prevailing custom follows this opinion. For a widow, no blessing is recited on any of these days, not even "Who created." However, "the joy in His abode" is said for all three days, as will be explained in Siman 64.

Some of our rabbis have written that just as it is forbidden to recite both Kiddush and Birkat Hamazon over one cup due to the principle of not bundling commandments together [Pesachim 102b], so that it should not be a burden, similarly, at a wedding meal, one should not recite the Sheva Brachot over the same cup used for Birkat Hamazon [Tosafot there]. Instead, one brings a cup and recites Birkat Hamazon over it. After completing Birkat Hamazon, he places it before him and brings another cup and recites the Sheva Brachot over it. He then places this cup down and takes the cup over which he recited Birkat Hamazon, and recites the blessing over wine or Shehakol on it. It is explicitly stated in Massechet Sofrim (Chapter 19, Halacha 11) that two cups are required and the blessing extends to the second cup as well, since his intention is also on it. The custom is that the one who blesses drinks the majority of the cup, mixes the two cups together, and gives this to the bride and groom to drink. 

However, there are some rabbis who say that all blessings should be recited over one cup, as the case of Birkat Hamazon and Kiddush involves two separate matters and the principle of bundling commandments applies there. But here, it is a single matter because Birkat Hamazon leads to the wedding blessings [Tosafot there]. The Tur writes that in Ashkenaz and France, the custom followed the first opinion, while in Spain, they followed the second opinion. Therefore, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in Siman 9 that the prevailing custom is to bless over one cup, as he was in Spain. Our teacher the Rema wrote that in these regions, the custom follows the first opinion, and some say that even for just the "Asher Bara" blessing, two cups are required. This is the conclusion, and it is appropriate to follow this practice [Bach]. In places where some poetry is recited before Birkat Hamazon, such as "Doi Haseir" or "Nodeh Lishmecha," it is said over the cup of Birkat Hamazon. "Doi Haseir" is only recited when the Sheva Brachot are said, and when only "Asher Bara" is said, "Nodeh Lishmecha" is recited [Beit Shmuel, Sk 11]. It has already been explained that for betrothal and marriage, two cups are required because they are two separate matters, as there can be betrothal without marriage, and the reading of the ketubah interrupts between them.

Maimonides, of blessed memory, writes in Chapter 2 of the Laws of Blessings that after the four blessings of Birkat Hamazon, in the house of a groom they recite the blessing for the groom after these four blessings at every meal that is eaten there. However, this blessing is not recited by slaves or minors. How long do they recite this blessing? If a widower marries a widow, they recite it only on the first day. But if a bachelor marries a widow, or a widower marries a virgin, they recite it all seven days of the wedding feast. This blessing that is added in the house of the groom is the last blessing of the seven blessings of marriage, etc. Thus, it is explicitly stated in his words that even the "Asher Bara" blessing is not recited for a widower who marries a widow all three days. And so it is clarified by all our early sages who wrote that for a widower who marries a widow, the blessing is only on the first day when they recite the seven blessings, and thereafter they do not recite even "Asher Bara". This is also clearly proven from the Talmudic discussion [there, where it questions on Rosh Hashanah, etc., whether it is concerning a widower, it is only one day, or if you want to say concerning a widower, one day for the blessing and three days for rejoicing, see there, and it did not answer for the blessing of "Asher Bara"].

And so it is explicitly clarified from the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 13, that even for a widower who marries a widow, we say "the joy is in His abode" for all three days. Refer there. He did not mention "Who created" [a specific blessing], which implies that its blessing is only for one day, even for "Who created." And the reason we say "the joy is in His abode" is because, according to the Talmudic law, we say "the joy is in His abode" for a virgin for twelve months, as will be explained. Therefore, it is appropriate that for a widow, during her three days of joy, we say "the joy is in His abode," but we do not bless "Who created." And I also found this explicitly in the words of the Maharshal, of blessed memory, in his book Yam Shel Shlomo on Ketubot, which was recently printed, where he wrote in chapter 1, section 12, as follows: From the fact that it says one day for blessing and three for joy, it implies that we do not bless more than one day, even "Who created," etc. End quote. And similarly, it is written in the Shita in the name of the Raavad, as follows: And a widow who marries a widower, one day, and this applies to the blessing of the grooms, but regarding "the joy is in His abode," it seems that a bachelor and a widower are the same, etc. End quote. Thus, it is only regarding "the joy is in His abode" that we say it within the three days of his joy, and not for any other blessing.

The Tur wrote: It seems that even for a widow marrying a widower, the seven blessings are only recited on the first day, even if there are new faces. The blessings "Who dwells in joy" and "Who created" are recited all three days of their rejoicing and are said even if there are not ten people present. Some say that even "Who created" requires ten, but this was not accepted by the Rosh of blessed memory. This is the end of his words. This is a singular opinion against the Rambam and all the decisors. Furthermore, it seems clear to me that there is an error in the words of the Tur, as he copied this from the Rosh's words and it is not mentioned there. Also, in the abridged rulings of the Rosh, which the Tur himself authored, this is not mentioned. Additionally, if our master the Beit Yosef did not mention this opinion in his great book, and none of the commentators on the Tur mentioned this, it is clear that the correct text is: "Who dwells in joy" is recited all three days of their rejoicing. Therefore, he added "in the days of their rejoicing," meaning that since their rejoicing lasts three days, "Who dwells in joy" is recited all three days, as stated by the Raavad whom we brought. But what relevance does the blessing "Who created" have to the time of rejoicing, and what connection is there between joy and this blessing? Because the Tur later brought a dispute about whether ten are required for "Who created" or not, the proofreaders erred and wrote "Who created" earlier as well. In any case, it is clear from the law that "Who created" is not said all three days for a widower marrying a widow. Even if this is the Tur's opinion, it is a singular opinion, and it seems more likely that there is a scribal error in the Tur, as it is known that many errors were found in the Tur's books, as the Beit Yosef wrote in his responsa at the beginning of the Tur Orach Chaim. Also, according to the Talmudic discussion, it cannot be said otherwise, as written.

I have seen that one of the great later authorities, based on the words of the Tur that we brought, ruled that a widower who marries a widow should recite the blessing of "Asher Bara" all three times [Beit Shmuel 17]. And after him, all the abridged legal codices followed suit, and it was also printed in the prayer books. However, in my humble opinion, it is clear that one should not recite it, and it is close to being a blessing in vain. Therefore, it is simple that one should only recite "Shehasimcha Bim'ono."

It has already been clarified that with a virgin bride, when there are new faces, all seven blessings are recited for the entire seven days. But when there are no new faces, only the blessing of "He who created" is recited. What constitutes new faces? According to the Rambam, of blessed memory, new faces are defined as those who did not hear the blessings at the time of the wedding ceremony. However, if they did hear them then, even if they have not yet eaten at the meal, they are not considered new faces. This is as he wrote in the second chapter of Berachot regarding the blessing of "He who created," which we have brought, and these are his words: This applies when those eating are the ones who were present at the wedding blessing and heard the blessings. But if those eating are others who did not hear the wedding blessings at the time of the wedding, the seven blessings are recited for them after the Grace After Meals, in the same manner as they are recited at the time of the wedding, provided there are ten, and the groom is included in the count. End of quote.

From the simplicity of his words, it seems that the reason we need to recite the seven blessings when there are new faces is so that the new people who have not heard the wedding blessings will hear the blessings to fulfill their obligation. But it cannot be said so, for are these people obligated in the blessings? Rather, the main point, according to the Rambam of blessed memory, is that these blessings are to bless the couple so that they will succeed, and incidentally, a blessing is given in honor of the people gathered and to recall the destruction of Jerusalem, as mentioned. This obligation is incumbent upon every Jewish person who comes to enjoy the wedding festivities to bless the couple during their seven days of celebration. The one who blesses and the others who hear and respond "Amen" — it is as if all those present have blessed the bride and groom. And since they have blessed them once, they have fulfilled their obligation. Therefore, when there are new faces who have not yet heard the blessings, it is as if they have not yet blessed the couple and are obligated to bless them. Hence, one stands and blesses, and they hear and respond "Amen" and fulfill their obligation. This is what the Rambam wrote "they bless for them," meaning they bless for them so that they fulfill their obligation to bless the bride and groom. Even if there is one person who has not heard, they bless for him. And when he wrote "and there should be ten," he did not mean that the new faces should be ten, but rather that ten people should be present during the blessings, for there are no wedding blessings with fewer than ten, as mentioned in Chapter 10 of Ishut. And so agreed the great later authorities [Bach and Chomat Shlomo, section 9] that even for one person they recite the blessings.

However, most of our rabbis have interpreted "new faces" in a different manner, that even people who were present at the time of the wedding ceremony and heard the blessings, if they have not yet eaten the wedding meal, are considered "new faces," and the seven blessings are recited for them after the Grace After Meals. Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote that this is the clear custom. According to this opinion, there is a different intention in "new faces," for since their days of joy are all seven days of the feast, it is appropriate to bless them every day of the seven days of the feast. Indeed, in Tractate Sofrim, Chapter 19, Halacha 11, it is stated that they were accustomed throughout the seven days of the feast to say the seven blessings over a cup in the presence of "new faces" even without a meal [see Beit Yosef]. However, we do not recite the blessings without a meal, as this is explicitly implied in the Talmud. When there are "new faces," it is considered a new and beautiful joy to say the blessings. Without "new faces," the joy is not as great, and the main joy is during the meal. Therefore, when there are "new faces" at the meal who have not yet eaten, it is an additional joy, and all the blessings are recited. According to Tractate Sofrim, there is a new joy every day when there are "new faces." But if there is no new joy, such as when there are no "new faces" or according to the Talmud, if they are not at a meal, there is no place for the seven blessings, as they were only instituted for a new joy. Therefore, they need to be recited always at the first meal, even if they were recited at the time of the wedding and there are no "new faces" who did not hear the blessings, because the meal is considered a new joy in contrast to the joy of the wedding, unlike the opinion of the Rambam.

And therefore, some say that they are not considered "new faces" unless they are important people for whom additional food and drink are prepared. And even if, at present, no additional food and drink are prepared for them, but they are worthy of such, this is considered "new faces" [Bach and Beit Shmuel]. The reason is that since we require a new joy, it is not considered new if they are not important. But when they are important people, it increases the joy of the wedding participants, and it is appropriate to recite the Sheva Brachot. Therefore, even if additional food and drink are not prepared for them, what of it? It does not depend on the abundance of food but on the honor of the new people for whom it is fitting to increase the provisions. However, according to the Rambam, even if the new faces are not important, blessings are still recited for them, as he wrote.

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 7 that some say if there are new faces present, even if they are not eating there, one should recite the blessings for them both at night and during the day. This opinion seems to be based on the tractate Sofrim, which we mentioned, where any new faces present on that day who were not there the previous day are considered a new joy, and one must recite the Sheva Brachot (Seven Blessings). Since this day is considered a new joy that did not exist yesterday, it follows that the entire day and the preceding night are suitable for reciting the Sheva Brachot, since this day is considered a new joy. Therefore, during all the meals of this particular day, the Sheva Brachot are recited because there is an increased joy on this day due to the new faces, even if they are not eating there. According to this opinion, the joy is not dependent on the meal but on the people. However, our custom is not to recite the Sheva Brachot without a meal, but the joy is not dependent on this, according to the tractate Sofrim. Even according to this opinion, the blessings are not recited throughout the entire day and night unless the new faces are present at the time of the blessings, since the primary joy is because of them.

Our early sages wrote that Shabbat is considered like new faces, for even if there are no new people who have not yet eaten, nevertheless on Shabbat and Yom Tov meals we recite the seven blessings. The days themselves are considered like new faces, based on the Midrash: "A psalm, a song for the day of Shabbat"—the Holy One, blessed be He, said, "New faces have come here," and Yom Tov and Shabbat are alike in this regard. This is based on the opinion of most of our sages that the reason for new faces is because it is like a new joy. It is obvious that on Shabbat and Yom Tov additional joy is added due to the extra soul, and it is customary to increase joy and portions on Shabbat. Therefore, we recite the seven blessings, for certainly Shabbat is considered more important than any of the most important new faces, as is proven in Tractate Shabbat, that Shabbat is greater than all the guests.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that this [requirement] applies specifically to the evening and morning meals, but not to the third meal, and thus the custom has spread, end of quote. The reason is simple: just as with new faces, the importance of joy because of the guests is when more food is prepared for them or is deemed appropriate to prepare for them, so too on Shabbat, the evening and morning meals where significant foods are prepared are considered as having new faces. However, for the third meal, it is not customary to increase the amount of significant foods, and most of the time, the third meal is eaten just to fulfill one's obligation, and consequently, it does not carry the importance of new faces. Nevertheless, according to the opinion stated in section 27, it is obvious that the seven blessings are also recited for it, but most of the authorities do not hold by this opinion, and our teacher, the Rema, did not bring it, except in places where it is customary according to this opinion, but he did not bring it as a practical ruling everywhere.

Regarding the third meal, our teacher the Rema wrote that in these regions it is customary to recite the seven blessings during the third meal. This might be because it is customary for new faces to arrive, and some say it is because it is customary to deliver a sermon, which is considered like new faces. Now, however, it is not customary to deliver a sermon, and even if no new faces arrive, the seven blessings are recited. Perhaps this is based on the opinion mentioned in section 27. However, it appears that according to the law, based on our custom of making the third meal with an abundance of good food and drink, it is not inferior to the morning meal for the reason mentioned in the previous section. Therefore, if there truly is not an abundance of food and no new faces and they still wish to say the seven blessings, they should only do so if new Torah insights are shared at the table, which would take the place of the sermon and bring additional joy, for "the precepts of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart." Only then can the seven blessings be recited.

The seven days of feasting begin immediately after the Sheva Brachot that were recited initially, meaning the blessings recited at the time of the chuppah (wedding ceremony), not from the first meal. Therefore, when the chuppah was during the day and afterward the meal was at night, the day before the night is also counted in the seven days of feasting. Even if several days passed from the chuppah to the first feast, such as if the chuppah took place and they immediately traveled with his bride to another city and stayed on the way for several days, nevertheless, the seven days are counted from the day of the chuppah [Responsa of the Rosh, general section 26]. And some say that these seven days need to be from hour to hour, and this is a mistake, and so agreed the great Acharonim [later authorities] [Kenesset HaGedolah and HaFla'ah].

It has already been explained that for a virgin, [the blessing is recited for] seven days, and for a widow, one day. This is specifically regarding a widow marrying a widower, but if a widow marries a bachelor, [the blessing is recited for] seven days. And even though regarding the celebration, some say that if she is a widow, even if he is a bachelor, the celebration does not exceed three days, as stated in Siman 64, nevertheless, regarding the blessing, it is seven days if one of them is either a bachelor, even if she is a widow, or she is a virgin, even if he is a widower. For the celebration depends only on her, as stated there, but the blessing depends on both of them.

And this that in the case of a widow marrying a widower, one day for a blessing – the intention is for the first meal, and there is both a leniency and a stringency in this matter. The leniency is that even if the meal extended to the second or third day, since there was no meal until now, the Sheva Brachot (seven blessings) are recited. The stringency is that if there were several meals on the day of the wedding, the Sheva Brachot are only recited at the first meal. Similarly, with a virgin bride, the Sheva Brachot are not recited at a second meal even if it is on the first day, unless there are new faces present, as we have said, and this is the opinion of most authorities. Some are uncertain in the case of a widow marrying a widower when the wedding ceremony was during the day and the meal was at night, that the Sheva Brachot should not be recited because the day of the blessing has already passed, but our Master, the Beit Yosef, ruled in his work Bedek HaBayit that they should be recited, because there is no wedding without Sheva Brachot at one meal. And even though the general principle is that in cases of doubt concerning blessings one should be lenient, it seems that the custom is to recite them, especially if there was no proper seclusion during the day suitable for marital relations, which is the main aspect of the marriage for a widow, as we have said in Siman 64, it is certain that the blessings should be recited at night. Similarly, if the meal began during the day and concluded at night, the blessings should be recited according to all opinions. Nevertheless, it is preferable from the outset to ensure that for a widower and widow, the wedding ceremony and the meal should be on the same day.

And from the language of the Rambam that we brought in section 19, it seems that he rules regarding a widower and a widow, when there are no new people who have not heard the blessings at the chuppah, that for the first meal, we do not say the seven blessings, only the blessing "Who created." According to his view, for a widower and a widow without new faces, the seven blessings are not recited, only "Who created." Just as with a virgin, when there are no new faces who have not heard the blessings at the chuppah, we do not recite all seven days of feasting, only "Who created," so too with a widower and a widow on the first day. For the first day of a widow and the seven days for a virgin are equivalent. And indeed, according to the Rambam, it could be that even for a virgin, we do not recite the seven blessings at all, except at the chuppah, when there are no new faces who have not heard the blessings. [See Beit Shmuel section 5, who wrote that according to the Rambam, we bless the entire day as per the opinion in section 27, but this cannot be said, as he explicitly wrote it is specifically for those who have not heard the blessings, and the first day he wrote is the language of the Talmud, and its interpretation is the first meal. However, most poskim do not agree with the Rambam as written.]

Our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 10: Some say that if the groom leaves his chuppah, even if his bride is with him and they go to eat in another house, the blessings of the groom are not recited there. This applies when he intends to return later to his chuppah, but if he goes completely to another house with all the company and that house becomes the main place, that too is called a chuppah and the blessings of the groom are recited there. Similarly, sometimes the groom and bride go to another city; if it is within the seven days and they do not intend to return, the blessings of the groom should be recited there, end quote. The reason is because the sages said (Sukkah 25b) that there is no joy except in the chuppah, implying that outside the place of the chuppah, joy is not applicable. Therefore, if they temporarily move to another place, the blessings are not recited, not even "Who created joy and gladness" and "that joy is in His abode" (Tosafot there). Some say that "that joy is in His abode" is recited, as according to the Talmudic law, this is recited even before the chuppah, as will be explained (Ran).

However, the entire essence of this law was established only when there is a fixed location for the chuppah for the groom and bride along with the attendants for all seven days of the feast, such as the canopy that is made in Ashkenaz, as mentioned by the Tur. This is one of the chuppahs we explained in Siman 55. Therefore, when they leave there occasionally, there is no joy. But for us, where the chuppah is in the street and afterwards there is no fixed place for the seven days of the feast, it is clear that wherever the groom and bride and the group assemble and eat and rejoice, that place is like the place of the chuppah, as if they went completely to another house or city without the intention of returning, that place becomes the place of the chuppah, as mentioned. Similarly, for us, since we are not accustomed to establishing a fixed place for the seven days of the feast, therefore, wherever they assemble becomes the place of joy.

Some of the great authorities have also said that even in a place with a fixed canopy, if they went temporarily to another place, even with the intention of returning to the canopy, the exemption applies only if they eat in another place out of necessity, like in a sukkah or something similar, and there is no joy there at all. But if they rejoice there, such as if the groom and bride and the group are invited to a feast by one of their friends or relatives, the blessings are said there, even if they intend to return to the canopy. Although the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch does not indicate this, nevertheless, according to our custom, the law is certainly like this since we do not have a fixed canopy for all seven days of the feast. 

Regarding what is written that when they go to another city, it becomes the fixed place, it is clear that this is only within the seven days of the chuppah, but after seven days it is nothing. There is someone who wants to say that if they immediately went to another place after the chuppah, that place becomes like the chuppah, and the seven days of the feast begin from the time they arrived there. However, there is no logic at all to say this, as mentioned in Siman 31, and this is the opinion of all the authorities, and this is the main law according to our teachers, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch.

Note that the seven days of the feast are not subject to the principle of "day and night." For example, if the chuppah was on Wednesday close to evening, the seven days extend until the end of the next Tuesday, and at the beginning of the next Wednesday night, the seven days of the feast are over, and the blessings and "joy in His abode" are not said. On Wednesday morning, Tachanun is said.

The members of the wedding party who did not manage to all eat together with the groom in one room and were divided into many houses, if some of them can see each other – it is obvious that they are all obligated in the blessings for the groom. If they can all hear the one who is blessing near the groom, they have all fulfilled their obligation. If not, they should bless separately when there are ten together. Even if they ate in houses that are not open to the place where the groom eats – they all recite the blessings for the groom. Not only if the servers at the groom's table also serve at their table, since it is established in Orach Chaim 195 that the server joins for a zimun, all the more so regarding the matter of considering it as one meal for a wedding. Even if there are different servers at their table, since those in the other houses began eating when those eating with the groom began, and not exactly at the same moment, but rather meaning that they all came for the celebration but due to the constraint of space they separated into different rooms, and they are all considered as one to bless the blessings for the groom because they are all eating from the meal prepared for the wedding canopy. Since they all cannot hear the blessings from the one blessing at the groom's table, they should bless the seven blessings separately. Even though the groom and bride will not hear the blessings from them, this does not matter. The custom of bringing the bride to hear the blessings is not essential but a beautiful custom, since the blessing is for the success of both, it is fitting that they should stand to hear the blessings, but it is not essential.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 12: The servants who eat after the wedding feast — some say that they do not recite the Sheva Brachot, and some say that they do recite them, and this view seems more correct. And it seems that there is no practical disagreement, for certainly if the servants eat afterwards just to satiate themselves without an elegant table setting to honor the bride and groom, such as singing before them or dancing and the like, this is not considered a wedding feast and there is no need to recite the blessings. But if they eat with dignity in honor of the bride and groom, they are no different from other guests and need to recite the Sheva Brachot, even if they start eating after the main wedding party has finished. In any case, it is still considered a wedding feast. This matter should be understood based on the specific circumstances [and in the Yam Shel Shlomo, section 20, it was ruled that only "Shehasimcha Bim'ono" should be recited, see there, and according to our understanding, there is no dispute here].

The blessing "Shehasimcha Bim'ono" (That the joy is in His dwelling) is not an independent blessing and is included at the beginning of the Grace After Meals invitation. One says, "Let us bless that the joy is in His dwelling from Whom we have eaten," and with ten [people present], "Let us bless our God that the joy is in His dwelling, etc." There are those who err and say, "that the joy is in His dwelling 'and that we have eaten' from His [bounty]" – and this is a mistake, for we do not bless on joy but on eating; rather, we mention the matter in the context of the invitation: "Let us bless our God that the joy is in His dwelling," meaning that the joy is not from us but from His dwelling. In what should we bless Him? We bless Him for what we have eaten from His [bounty], but we do not bless for joy, as this does not pertain to the matter of the Grace After Meals. Furthermore, it would have to say "that we rejoice from His dwelling," but it is a narrative to remind us of the matter.

And the reason we say the phrase "His dwelling" is because from there the Holy One, blessed be He, blesses Israel, as it is written: "Look down from Your holy dwelling, from heaven, and bless Your people" etc. (Deuteronomy 26:15), and in the prayer of Moses (Psalms 90:1) it says "Lord, You have been our dwelling place throughout all generations," and the essence of the song of the ministering angels day and night is out of respect for Israel <small>[Chagigah 12b]</small>. Therefore, we mention this during the joy of a wedding. It was not instituted for any other mitzvah meal except for weddings. One of the great scholars wanted it to be said at the conclusion of a tractate since there is no joy like the joy of Torah, and he ruled thus, but the joy was disrupted in great places, attributing it to his attempt to innovate something that our ancestors, of blessed memory, did not institute <small>[Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kama, Chapter 7, Siman 37]</small>. It seems to me the reason is quite the opposite: they instituted it at weddings because if we consider it, there is no complete joy in a wedding. If man were to exist perpetually as an individual, there would be no need for marriage and procreation, but because man exists only through his species, he must marry and procreate, for he is destined to die, and his offspring will remain in his place. Therefore, one of the sages broke a precious glass at his son's wedding canopy, and some said "Woe to us that we die, woe to us that we die" <small>[Berakhot 31a]</small>, as I have explained. Therefore, we say "that the joy is in His dwelling," meaning that in this world there is no complete joy, only above there is complete joy, as it is written "Strength and joy are in His place" (I Chronicles 16:27). But the study of Torah is complete joy in this world, as it is taught in Avot: "One hour of repentance and good deeds in this world is better than all the life of the world to come," and certainly the study of Torah, which is equal to all the commandments. Therefore, it should not be said then that the joy is in His dwelling, for we also have complete joy at that time. And at a circumcision meal, it is also not said because of the infant's pain <small>[Ketubot 8a]</small>. And at the redemption of the firstborn meal, some say to bless "that the joy is in His dwelling" <small>[Yam Shel Shlomo, there]</small>, but our teacher the Rema in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 305, wrote not to bless, based on that, and this is the custom.

And since it is not a blessing in its own right, therefore it is recited even not during the seven days of feasting, but at any time when meals are made because of the wedding. Therefore, one who dines in the house of the bride and groom from when they begin to engage in the needs of the wedding with the meals and their preparation, they recite "the joy is in His dwelling" and the diners also respond "Blessed is the One whose joy is in His dwelling" or "Blessed is our God" when there are ten diners. And this blessing is recited until thirty days after the wedding, whether they invite guests generally or specifically for the wedding. From thirty days onwards until twelve months after the wedding, if they invite guests to eat because of the wedding, meaning for the joy of the wedding, they say "the joy is in His dwelling." But if they invite them generally, they do not say it. At the engagement meal, they do not say it [Beit Yosef], but some say that it is recited. And what was explained that even before the wedding ceremony it is recited, this is in a place where the betrothal happens a long time before. Since the engagement already took place, they recite "the joy is in His dwelling" immediately when they begin the preparations as was mentioned. But in our country where the betrothal happens at the time of the wedding, it is not recited before the wedding. And even at the meal that is made the night before the wedding, they do not say "the joy is in His dwelling" because there is not even engagement yet [Darchei Moshe in the name of Kol Bo], and these laws apply to a virgin.

All of this is according to the law of the Talmud, but nowadays, due to our many sins, all joy has been diminished. We do not say "the joy in His dwelling place" except during the seven days of the wedding feast, neither before the wedding ceremony nor after the seven days. Even if one makes a meal explicitly for the sake of the wedding, and even within thirty days, and even during the seven days of the wedding feast—it is only said when others are invited. But if one eats only with the members of his household, we do not say "the joy in His dwelling place," as it is written in the blessing of "He who created" [Choshen Mishpat 8:8]. Regarding a widower who marries a widow, our master the Beit Yosef decided based on his own reasoning that since for a virgin, according to the Talmud, it is said even after the seven days of the wedding feast, therefore, during the three days of joy for a widow, we say "the joy in His dwelling place," but "He who created" should not be said, as it is written in paragraph 22.

[Laws of the Mitzvah of Marital Relations and Its Preparation, with 12 Sections]

The virgin, when the time for her wedding arrives, should prepare herself for the purification necessary for the mitzvah of marital relations. Her father should caution her to always be mindful of the laws of niddah (menstrual purity), emphasizing that neglecting these laws constitutes a severe transgression. The consequences of such neglect include the punishment of karet (spiritual excision) and losing her place in both this world and the World to Come. Additionally, failing to observe these laws properly could permanently damage her progeny and bring her close to heavenly punishment. As it is taught: "Women die in childbirth due to three transgressions: not being careful with niddah, etc." (Shabbat 31a).

If she observes these laws properly, her reward will be very great, and she will be fortunate in both this world and the next. Her mother or close relatives should teach her the proper methods of checking and maintaining the required purity, ensuring she understands the necessity of distancing herself from her husband during her niddah period. This includes not passing objects directly to him or receiving them from him, and not eating from the same dish, in accordance with all the laws detailed in Yoreh De'ah, Chapter 195.

Eight days before her wedding, even if she is in her days of purity and even if her menstrual period has not yet arrived and she has never seen blood, she should perform an examination in the evening with a clean cloth, inserting it into that place and checking in all the crevices and folds. It is better if she leaves the cloth there throughout twilight and at the beginning of the night she should remove it. If it is clean of blood, she should start counting seven clean days and check herself every day twice; at the very least she should perform one examination during these seven days as mentioned there in Siman 196. She should go to the mikvah before the wedding, and before her immersion she should check herself, and if she finds herself clean of blood, she should immerse and recite the blessing for the immersion. Afterwards, she should enter the wedding canopy and fulfill the mitzvah of marital relations. On the day she confirms her purity, she should wear white, meaning a clean dress, as is the custom of virtuous women, descendants of Abraham our forefather, whose ancestors stood at Mount Sinai and their impurity ceased.

And if she is in her days of impurity and during the time of the wedding canopy she is not pure, she must be cautious with the groom as the law of a Niddah with her husband, and even more stringent than her. For with a Niddah, she is permitted to be secluded with her husband because the Torah testified about us that we will not come to transgression, God forbid (Sanhedrin 37a), but she is forbidden to be secluded with her husband. Rather, he sleeps among the men and she sleeps among the women. The reason is because he has not yet had relations with her and their desire is strong, and we are concerned about transgression, God forbid. They should not be secluded together even during the day in the same room until her time of purity.

And even an elderly widow, from whom the menstrual cycle has already ceased, must perform a hefsek tahara (a check to ensure she is free of menstrual blood) and count seven clean days. This is as our Sages said (Niddah 66.): If she was proposed to for marriage and she accepted, she needs to count seven clean days, whether she is older, younger, a child, or elderly. This is because we are concerned that due to excitement she may have seen blood and did not feel it. She counts the seven days starting from the day after the proposal, and even if she checked herself and found that she was pure, we do not take this into consideration due to the aforementioned reason. If the time for her wedding was set and, due to some reason, the wedding was delayed and a new date was set, the previous seven days are nullified, and she must perform a hefsek tahara and count seven days again from the new set date, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 192, along with other detailed laws on this matter.

The one who has intercourse with a virgin in the context of fulfilling a mitzvah, once he completes the act, he must withdraw immediately, even if she is a minor who has not yet reached the age to see menstrual blood and has never seen blood before. This applies even to a mature woman whose hymen has been fully worn away, since we are concerned that perhaps some menstrual blood might have mixed with the blood of the hymen. And although even with a fully mature woman who finds blood during intercourse, if she has a wound, we attribute it to her wound, as it says in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 187, and there is no greater wound than this, nonetheless, since this intercourse is for the sake of a mitzvah, we are stringent. Moreover, attributing it to a wound is only to avoid prohibiting her to her husband forever, but with regard to the need for purification, we do not take this into account. Even if she checked and did not find blood, she is still considered impure, as she might have seen a drop of blood the size of a mustard seed which was covered by the semen, for there must necessarily be blood due to the hymen, and it is certain that the semen covered the blood. Therefore, this applies specifically if he had a complete intercourse, but if he only had partial penetration and withdrew without finding blood, some are lenient. And he completes that intercourse in the usual manner without concern, and he is also permitted to withdraw from her even with a live organ, although finding blood during intercourse prohibits withdrawing with a live organ, as the withdrawal is pleasurable for him like the intercourse itself, and he must wait until the organ dies, as it is written in Siman 185, that one who withdraws with a live organ is liable to karet. Nonetheless, in this case, we are not concerned since the primary matter is merely a stringency.

This law that has been explained is derived from the Talmud, and thus the Sages said [Niddah 65]: "Rav and Shmuel both said: The law is that one performs the mitzvah of marital relations and then separates." According to Maimonides in Chapter 5 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations, the Talmudic law applies only to a mature woman who has already begun her menstrual cycle, whereas for a young girl who has not yet reached the time to see blood, it is due to the stringency that the daughters of Israel imposed upon themselves, as mentioned there in Chapter 11. Maimonides explained that as long as she sees blood due to the wound, she is impure, meaning even after the second and third immersion in a mikvah. Furthermore, as long as her hymen is not completely torn and she finds hymenal blood, she is impure. However, during the second intercourse after her purification from the first one, if she does not find blood, she is pure, and we do not suspect that there might be hidden semen, as it is not a necessity that she will see hymenal blood again, unlike the first time as explained. And one should not say that if so, even in the case of a mature woman during the first time we should not worry if she does not find blood, because indeed in a mature woman, her hymen is already torn. For our eyes see that even older women have hymenal blood, and in a mature woman, her opening is not closed as much as in a young girl or a maiden [see Ketubot 36: Rashi s.v. ה"ג and Tosafot there].

After the initial marital intercourse, she should wait until Thursday for her next act of intimacy, like any woman who has had intercourse and then saw blood. She should then cease her impurity in the evening with a proper examination and by wearing white garments. She should count seven clean days, checking herself each of those seven days, and afterward, at night, she should go to the mikvah for immersion. During these days, he should treat her as a complete niddah regarding physical separation, but she is permitted to be alone with him like other women because he has already had intercourse with her.
