In this respect, she is less stringent than a complete niddah, as with a complete niddah, it is forbidden for him to sleep on her bed even when she is not in it, and it is also forbidden to sit on her bed. However, the bride, after the initial marital intercourse, is permitted for him to sleep on her bed after she has gotten up from it, even if the sheet still has blood on it, and certainly, he may sit on her bed when she is not sitting on it, as it says in Siman 193. Some say that in this respect she is also less stringent than other niddahs because we attribute the stain to the initial intercourse even within the first three days, unlike a complete niddah, as it says in Siman 196. However, some are stringent in this matter, treating even a stain with stringency, even though stains are rabbinic in nature. The detailed laws about this are explained there [see Beit Shmuel, note 3].

In the Gemara, the halacha is established that it is permitted to consummate a marriage with a virgin for the first time on Shabbat, and there is no issue of causing a wound, nor of creating an opening, nor of causing her distress. Even though blood is released and this constitutes a wound, and every wound involves the potential for taking a life, and it also involves creating an opening, and creating an opening on Shabbat is liable for the prohibition of building, nonetheless, there is no prohibition here. Certainly, if the blood of the virgin's hymen were absorbed within the walls of the womb and its release involved a wound like all blood within human flesh, it would indeed be considered a wound. However, this blood is stored like a deposit, standing in place, and is not absorbed. Rather, the opening is locked before it, and it is opened for it to come out. And regarding the opening, there is no intention to open it. Even though it is a "psik reisha" (an inevitable outcome), since the opening is unavoidably created, nonetheless, every act on Shabbat that is destructive does not incur liability, as all destructive acts are exempt. And this opening is considered destructive for him, as a virgin is valued more highly than a non-virgin. Even according to the opinion that holds that one is liable for a destructive wound, since the blood is stored, it is not considered a wound. Additionally, the Rambam in Chapter 8 of Shabbat rules that one is exempt for a destructive wound. And even though all exemptions on Shabbat are usually "exempt but prohibited," nonetheless, in a place of mitzvah (commandment), they did not decree. Furthermore, this is not considered a "psik reisha" as will be explained.

Moreover, even if we say that the blood of the membrane connects and it is a complete opening and not a destructive act, this is only if it were a "pesik reisha" (an inevitable outcome) and he intended to release the blood and open the opening. But in truth, he does not intend this but rather for his own enjoyment, and his intention is not for the blood or the opening. And since he does not intend for this, we hold that an unintentional act is permitted. And this is not a "pesik reisha" because many times it can happen that during intercourse the opening is not made and the blood is not released. And even if he is not skilled in avoiding it, it can still happen naturally. Therefore, since it is not inevitable, it is considered an unintentional act and not a "pesik reisha". [This is the approach of the early authorities who interpret that most are skilled in avoiding it, meaning it is known to most people that it is possible to avoid even for those who are not skilled. Not like the Babylonians who think that one must be skilled to avoid it, as mentioned in Tosafot Ketubot 6a in the name of many of our teachers. And consequently, what the Hagahot Ashri and Agudah and Shla wrote is dismissed, as well as what the Taz wrote in Orach Chaim there. And it is a complete leniency from the outset.]

The Ba'al HaMaor writes at the beginning of the laws of Ketubot that after the first intercourse, when he finds the signs of virginity, he must bless. And this is his language: "And when he takes out the cloth, he is obligated to bless. If there is a cup and myrtle, he blesses with them 'Borei Pri HaGafen' and 'Borei Atzei Besamim,' and then says: 'Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who planted the nut in the Garden of Eden, the rose of the valleys, so that no stranger will overpower the sealed fountain. Therefore, the beloved doe kept her purity and did not break the law. Blessed are You who chose the offspring of Abraham.'" And he likened [the woman] to a nut, as with a nut the edible part is covered until the time of its breaking, so too the daughters of Israel have their virginity sealed until their marriage. And "rose of the valleys" – because Israel is compared to a rose, and it alludes to the blood that they guard themselves from during their menstrual period from coming close to their husbands, as it is said, "She is enclosed with roses" [Sanhedrin 37.]. And the rest of the matters are understood. And he concludes with the offspring of Abraham, the first father who out of great love for God kept the entire Torah before it was given, especially in matters of menstrual impurity, as is famous in the legend regarding the verse "Knead it and make cakes" (Genesis 18:6). And some say that this blessing should not be said as it is not found in the Talmud, and some say to bless without mentioning the name and sovereignty, and also without a cup. And this blessing is not observed nowadays. In ancient times, the custom was to make a meal of fish after the mitzvah intercourse so that they would be fruitful and multiply like fish. Therefore, it was called "mitzvah intercourse" because from then on she was fit to conceive, as a woman does not conceive from the first intercourse. And now this meal is not customary, and there are places where they distribute cheese.

One does not recite the Shehecheyanu blessing upon marrying a woman [Shach Yoreh De'ah 28], and it appears to me that the reason is that Shehecheyanu is not applicable here; rather, the blessing of HaTov VeHaMeitiv (Who is good and does good) is appropriate since the joy is for both of them, similar to when a man's wife gives birth to a son, where he recites HaTov VeHaMeitiv as stated in Orach Chaim 223. This is a blessing to God who has benefited them, and this type of blessing is found in the wedding blessings such as "Who created man" and "Who established", which is a blessing to God for him and for her, as well as the blessing "May You bring joy". Therefore, HaTov VeHaMeitiv would be redundant. Additionally, it can be said that for the blessing of engagement one does not recite Shehecheyanu because there is no complete joy, and at the time of the wedding one does not recite it because the process began at the engagement. Therefore, even when the engagement and wedding are together, Shehecheyanu is not recited because they are two distinct events, and one can be engaged for a long time before the wedding, as was customary in the time of the Talmudic sages. Hence, the Shehecheyanu blessing was not established for this occasion.

When the mitzvah of marital relations extends until after the seven days of feasting, and a meal is made on the night of her immersion, it is clear that the seven blessings are not to be recited, nor the "He who created". There are those who say to recite "the joy in His dwelling" at that time – but even this has no basis in law. However, since this does not involve mentioning the Name of God, we are not concerned. Nevertheless, it is better not to make a meal at that time because it is customary for the sons of Israel to keep the time of immersion concealed, and this is not similar to when the mitzvah occurs on the day of the wedding. Therefore, they should not make a meal at all [see Pischei Teshuva, section 62, subparagraph 20]. Additionally, those who have the custom that the groom sanctifies her anew in front of witnesses at that time – this has no reason or sense, for even according to the Rambam, the betrothal of a menstruant is valid, and regarding the wedding canopy of a menstruant, we do not follow his opinion. As I wrote in section 55 and section 62, even the Rambam agrees that our wedding canopy is effective even when she is in her state of niddah, see there.

[The time for the marriage of a virgin and a widow and their celebration, containing 18 sections]

The Rambam, of blessed memory, writes in Chapter 10: The Sages instituted that anyone who marries a virgin should rejoice with her for seven days, and he should not engage in his work or conduct business in the market, but rather he should eat, drink, and rejoice. This applies whether he is a bachelor or a widower. If she is a non-virgin, there should be no less than three days of rejoicing, as the Sages decreed for the daughters of Israel that he should rejoice with the non-virgin for three days, whether he is a bachelor or a widower. End of quotation. 

His opinion is that the rejoicing is not connected to the wedding blessings, for the wedding blessings are recited all seven days when he is a bachelor, even if she is a widow, as is written in Section 62. The rejoicing depends only on her. The reason is that the seven blessings are related to the matter of the union; therefore, when one of them has never been married before, they have seven blessings for all seven days. However, the rejoicing is only for the sake of the woman, that he should make her happy, as she is primary and he is secondary to her. Therefore, the time of rejoicing depends only on her. If she is a virgin, her rejoicing is for seven days. If she is a widow or divorced from marriage and is a non-virgin, her rejoicing is only for three days, for the joy of a virgin is greater than that of a non-virgin, as a woman does not make a covenant except with the one who made her a vessel.

But there are some of our rabbis who hold that, while it is true that the joy is on account of the woman, nevertheless, if he is a bachelor, even if she is a widow, their joy lasts all seven days. For how is it possible that they would recite the seven blessings for them, and he would then rise early to his work? Therefore, the days of joy are not fewer than the days of blessing. And even if the seven blessings are not recited, such as when there are no new faces, and even the blessing "Who has created" is not recited, such as when only the household members are eating, nevertheless, since these days are the days of blessings when others would be in their joy, it is impossible that they would not be days of joy. And so is the custom.

And this that the Rambam wrote that he (the groom) does not engage in his work nor in his trading, this is not explicitly found in the Talmud, but it is explicitly stated in the Midrashim [Pirkei D’Rabbi Eliezer, Chapter 16]: A groom is likened to a king; just as a king does not do work, so too a groom does not do work; just as a king does not go to the market alone, so too a groom does not go to the market alone. And so wrote our teacher the Rema, that a groom is forbidden from doing work and is forbidden to go alone in the marketplace. And it seems that the Rambam interprets that the restriction is not about going out alone but rather about engaging in business transactions, and this seems correct, for if it were only about going out alone, why specify the market over other streets? And if you question that if it is about business transactions, what is the meaning of “not going out to the market alone,” certainly it means that if he has any partnership in business, the partners can engage, but he alone should not engage in work or trading [see Pitchei Teshuvah, Section 1]. However, many of the early authorities interpreted that there is also a prohibition for a groom to go out alone in the marketplace without engaging in business transactions, and not just the marketplace but any place where many people are present so that he is not seen alone. And the sages in the Talmud said that a groom requires protection [Berachot 54b], and since he needs protection, it follows that he should not go out alone. And it also appears in the Talmud that he should not do work, although it is not explicitly stated there that it is forbidden, it implies so [Ketubot 5a, he gets up early for his craft and goes]. And the language of the Talmud implies that he needs protection even in his home and even during the day requires protection [Kessef Mishneh there]. And it is also stated in the Agada that the groom should wear honorable clothes all seven days of the feast, and everyone should praise him all seven days of the feast, and his face should shine, as it is written “and he like a groom coming out of his chamber” [Pirkei D’Rabbi Eliezer there], and there should be feasting and joy before him all seven days of the feast [Yalkut Shoftim], and the bride also needs protection [Gemara].

The Torah states, "When a man takes a new wife, he shall not go out to the army, nor shall he be charged with any business; he shall be free for his house for one year, and he shall bring joy to his wife" (Deuteronomy 24:5). This joy is not literal joy, as that is only during the seven days of the wedding feast and for a widow, three days. Rather, this refers to matters of war, as it is written, "He shall not go out to the army, nor shall he be charged with any business," meaning he is not even to provide water and food, as explained in Sotah 44a. "He shall be free for his house" includes one who builds a house and dedicates it, plants a vineyard and redeems it, who are also exempt. "And he shall bring joy to his wife that he has taken" includes his yevamah (levirate wife), who is also exempt from all these (Sotah 43a). Additionally, in the plain meaning of the verse, the joy mentioned here is not about feasts and cessation of work, but rather to delight her and fulfill her wishes as much as he can. So too, it is written in the Sefer Yereim, Mitzvah 190: We learn that in the first year a man marries a woman, he is obligated to bring her joy, as it is stated, "and he shall bring joy to his wife," in any manner that he knows brings her happiness. This mitzvah applies both in the Land of Israel and outside it, as it is a personal obligation, etc. The concept of this joy is similar to what is written, "And you shall rejoice in all the good" (Deuteronomy 26:11) and similar expressions. Some suggest that in the first year, he should not go on business trips to other cities, but this has no substantial basis, as I have explained. This applies to both a virgin and a widow, except for one who remarries his divorcee, as she is not considered new. (Also, none of the poskim (decisors) have cited the words of the Yereim, and possibly they hold that it only pertains to matters of war, and this requires further study).

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that a woman can forgo her joy, end quote. The commentators on the Shulchan Aruch explained that this is only regarding eating, drinking, and rejoicing with her, but regarding the cessation of work, her waiver is not effective. Some say that according to the Rambam, where the joy is only for her sake, her waiver is effective. However, according to those who hold that even a bachelor who marries a widow has a seven-day celebration, her waiver is not effective [Ba'er Hetev]. This does not seem to be the opinion of Rabbeinu the Rema. The main opinion appears to be as one of the great authorities wrote, that for a virgin, the prohibition of work is intrinsic and her waiver is not effective, but for a widow, the ordinance is for her sake, as is evident from the language of the Talmud: "The sages enacted for the daughters of Israel that he should rejoice with her for three days" – in this case, her waiver is effective. This is what Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in paragraph 1 concerning a virgin, that the groom is forbidden to work, and in paragraph 2 concerning a non-virgin, that she can forgo [Makneh]. And note that the term "non-virgin" used by the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch refers to a widow from marriage, because from betrothal she is still considered a virgin. However, from marriage, she is presumed to have been consummated, and even if it is known that she was not consummated, it seems that from marriage her status is that of a non-virgin. A virgin who gave birth out of wedlock or conceived and miscarried or was proven by witnesses to have had relations – there is a doubt whether her joy and blessing are like that of a virgin since she was never married, or since she is not a virgin her status is like that of a widow. This seems to be implied by the term "non-virgin" used by the poskim, and the matter requires further study.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah at the beginning of Ketubot: A virgin is married on the fourth day, and a widow on the fifth day. The reason for a virgin is that the court sits on Mondays and Thursdays, therefore she is married on Wednesday and the consummation occurs at night. If he does not find her to be a virgin, he will rise early to the court, and it may be clarified that she committed adultery after betrothal and is forbidden to him. However, if a day or two passes after the consummation, his temper will cool, and he will not go to the court, which could lead to a stumbling block. Therefore, the Gemara states that in a place where the court sits every day, a woman may be married on any day. Similarly, in our case, since the claim of virginity does not apply regarding prohibition, as the betrothal and marriage occur simultaneously, she can be married on any day. The reason the Mishnah did not permit marriage on the first day is because on the second day he would rise early to the court. The Gemara explains that this is for a different reason – so that he will have three days after Shabbat to prepare for the banquet, and on Wednesday, he will marry her. However, if he has already prepared, he can marry her even on the first day according to the Mishnah's ruling. For us, she can be married on any day. The Mishnah did not explain the reason for a widow, but the Gemara provides two reasons. One is that since her joy lasts three days, the Sages were concerned that he would not rise early the next morning for his occupation. Therefore, they mandated that he marry her on Thursday, so he would be at home on the next day and the following day, due to Friday and Shabbat, and he would rejoice with her for three days. Another reason is so that he will consummate the marriage on the night of the sixth day, upon which a blessing was given to man. For man was created on the sixth day, and God blessed him to be fruitful and multiply. The virgin consummates on the night of the fifth day, when a blessing was also given to the fish created on the fifth day, and God blessed them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters" (Genesis 1:22).

Our early rabbis were meticulous in noting that the Mishnah only explained the reason for a virgin, and even for a virgin, it only mentioned the reason related to prohibition. This teaches us that for other reasons, a special day for marriage was not fixed. The reason for a blessing is merely good advice, and the reason for preparing the feast, although it is a requirement, if it has already been prepared, one may marry on any day he wishes. Therefore, our sages said that in a place where the court sits every day, a woman may be married on any day if the needs of the feast are prepared and he is not particular about the day of the blessing. However, nonetheless, for a widow, it appears from the Talmudic discussion that someone who is a craftsman or a merchant should only marry on Thursday for the reason that he should rejoice with her on Thursday night and the Sabbath. However, the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) did not mention that there is a prohibition for a widow to marry on a day other than Thursday, and indeed, it is common practice for marriages to take place on any day.

However, from the words of the Rambam, it is apparent that this reason is not primary. He wrote there in Hilchot Ishut 15: "In a place where the court does not sit except on Monday and Thursday, a virgin marries on Wednesday so that if he has a claim of non-virginity, he can rise early to the court. The custom of the sages is that one who marries a widow marries her on Thursday so that he will be with her on Thursday, Friday, and Shabbat, and then he goes to his work on Sunday." The Rambam attributed this to the custom of the sages and not as a fundamental law. Therefore, the Mishnah did not explain the reason regarding a widow, and also the Gemara, which permitted in a place where the court sits every day to marry on any day, did not refer only to a virgin, for they said "a woman marries on any day" and did not say "a virgin marries on any day" – from here we learn that it applies to all women. (And so wrote the Ran and the Ritva that because of the urgency of the blessing, they did not designate a specific day, and so it is written in Shitah Mekubetzet).

And there is an explanation for this: Indeed, why did the sages worry that one might rise early for his work, since it is forbidden to work? If it is because he might not obey – what can be said for someone who marries a virgin and is forbidden to work for seven days? However, the main point is this: Certainly, God forbid to suspect any Jewish person of violating the words of the sages. But in truth, the primary celebration for a widower and a widow is only one day. Just as their blessing is only one day, so too their joy is only one day, and according to the law, he is permitted to rise early for his work the next day. The sages were concerned for her distress and therefore instituted that he should rejoice with her for three days. And because this was a new ordinance, they arranged that he marry her on Thursday, so he would rejoice with her for three days as mentioned. Thus, after they established this and it became customary that work is forbidden for three days, it was then practiced that on any day he marries, it became customary not to work for three days. [And perhaps this is the intention of Rashi of blessed memory on page 5, s.v. "the next day," see there and in the Shittah Mekubetzet, and examine closely].

We have written this according to the opinion of the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch, but the Tur wrote: The Sages established that a widow should marry on Thursday and consummate the marriage on Thursday night, so that he will be happy with her for three days—Thursday, Friday, and Shabbat. This applies to a craftsman, but an idle person who does not have to worry about going to work can marry on any day. For a virgin, they did not establish a specific day for marriage because there is no concern that he might leave her and go to work. The reason is that his joy is great, and he will not go to work all seven days. According to this opinion, it is forbidden for a widow marrying a widower, if he is a craftsman or a businessman, to marry on any day other than Thursday. This is also the opinion of the Tosafot and the Rosh. It is surprising that our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, and the later authorities only brought the opinion of the Rambam, and also our custom of marrying on any day is difficult, as they did not take this opinion into consideration. Perhaps, as explained, if her forgiveness is effective, then there is no concern. Even if he goes to work early, she would presumably forgive him. It is unlikely that he would act against her will, and if she does not give him permission, he would not do so. Although the Sages were concerned that he might act against her will, since according to the Rambam it is entirely permissible, and according to the Tur it is an improbable scenario, therefore, they were not concerned. Nevertheless, it requires further investigation in practice. However, if they discussed before the marriage that he would immediately travel after the marriage, it is certainly permitted, as she is considered to have forgiven and waived her joy, which has been explained as permissible.

Maimonides wrote: "One does not marry women on Friday or on Sunday, as a decree lest it leads to the desecration of the Sabbath in the preparation of the meal, as the groom is preoccupied with the meal." This is his exact language. However, the Tur and the Rosh permit it, as the conclusion of the Talmudic discussion does not concern itself with Sabbath desecration, for it is assumed that all necessary preparations for the meal are made beforehand. The Tur wrote that based on this, it is permissible to make meals both on the Sabbath and on the night following the Sabbath. Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote that the custom has spread to marry women on Friday, provided one prepares the wedding feast three days before the wedding. This is their exact language. Nowadays, we do not adhere strictly to this either. It seems to me the reason is that although our sages said that the rabbis were diligent in enacting the decree for the daughters of Israel that the groom should toil in the meal preparation for three days, this was all in their time when the groom would prepare the meal. But now, our custom is that the bride prepares the meal, so we do not worry about Sabbath desecration, as only the groom is concerned about fulfilling the bride's wishes by increasing the preparations, since women are particular about this. But since the bride prepares the meal, we do not worry about Sabbath desecration because the groom is not particular about it. This is also understood from Maimonides' language, where he concludes that the groom is preoccupied with the meal. This means that since the groom is preoccupied with the meal's preparation, we are concerned about Sabbath desecration. Therefore, our custom is correct even according to Maimonides. Nevertheless, we see with our own eyes that during the winter days, it is very appropriate not to hold a wedding on Friday because the days are short, and the wedding is delayed. However, we do not have the authority to protest.

[Maimonides wrote about Sunday; in the Talmud, it is proven that even according to his opinion, the prohibition is only on the night following the Sabbath. See there, page 5, Rashi's commentary beginning "there is ample time." Perhaps he adopted the first explanation there that it concerns oneself, etc. According to this explanation, it must be said that what is taught on the night following the Sabbath refers to the entire Sunday. Otherwise, what is the question from Yom Kippur? See there. In the Jerusalem Talmud, at the beginning of Ketubot, it is explained that one does not marry women on Friday or on the night following the Sabbath out of respect for the Sabbath. See there. This is Maimonides' source, and I am puzzled that he did not bring this, and it requires further study.]

If the groom does not want to make a feast and the bride's relatives want him to make a feast, they can compel him to make a feast according to his and her honor. This is the ruling of all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). According to his honor means that if his family is wealthier than hers and they make more lavish feasts than her family, he is obligated to make it like his family's standard. According to her honor means the opposite, as the principle is that she ascends with him and does not descend with him. It is clear from this that not only the bride herself can compel him to do this, but even her relatives can, such as if she remains silent. If she says she does not care, it is not reasonable that her relatives can compel him, but it is possible that even in such a case they can compel him by saying that even though she does not care, it is still a disgrace to the family.

However, nowadays, when the bride makes the feast, we do not have this problem. It seems that according to our custom, the groom and his family can compel the bride to make the feast according to his and her honor because if they care about this, why shouldn't they be able to compel her just as her family can compel him? This seems to be the main ruling in practice. Similarly, all matters of wedding celebrations that are customary, if one side wants to object to not doing it, they do not have the power to do so. For example, if she is a virgin and he is a widower, and she wants to have the festivities customary for virgins, such as musical instruments and the like, and he does not want it, she can compel him. Conversely, if he is a bachelor and she is a widow or divorcee, he can compel her to make the festivities customary for bachelors.

It is customary not to marry women except in the first half of the month when the moon is waxing and increasing, and not when it is waning. This is not considered divination but merely a good omen, similar to how kings are anointed by a spring so that their reign may continue, and just as wine is poured through pipes before grooms as a good sign that the union will increase. This is not considered following the ways of the Amorites, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, section 179. Some months have the custom not to be stringent about this – Elul, Tishrei, and Adar. It is better not to be stringent at all about this, as it is written, "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord, your God" (Deuteronomy 18:13). For the signs of blessing for fish and humans mentioned in the Gemara are not strictly observed, even more so for something not mentioned in the Gemara at all. It is possible that because Israel counts by the moon and is compared to the moon, they were accustomed to be particular. Additionally, the stringency is not to avoid the waning period but rather for a good sign to marry in the waxing period. Nonetheless, it is better to be stringent about what is mentioned in the Gemara.

It has already been explained in Orach Chayim, Siman 339, that it is forbidden to betroth a woman on Shabbat. Even if one betrothed her on a weekday, it is forbidden to bring her under the wedding canopy on Shabbat. Although through betrothal she is already his wife, since through marriage he acquires her found items and her work, it is like acquiring an acquisition on Shabbat. Therefore, he should bring her under the wedding canopy before Shabbat, and he may consummate the marriage with her for the first time on Shabbat, as mentioned in Siman 63. And although it is said that the additional ketubah amount is acquired from the time of the first marital relations, we do not say that this is like making an acquisition on Shabbat, because the husband is not the woman's acquisition; rather, the woman is the husband's acquisition, and he already acquired her at the time of the wedding canopy. However, when the wedding canopy was for a menstruant and she then immersed, it is possible that according to the Rambam, who holds that the wedding canopy of a menstruant is not valid and the acquisition is through the first marital relations, one should not consummate the marriage with her on Shabbat. However, it has already been explained that most authorities disagree with the Rambam, and in Siman 55, we explained that it may be said that even the Rambam agrees with the other authorities. See there [see Beit Shmuel, Sk 5].

Many of our rabbis have written that this acquisition through chuppah (marriage canopy) applies only to a virgin, but for a widow, chuppah does not effect acquisition; rather, it is through seclusion for the purpose of intercourse that he acquires her rights to her findings and her handiwork. Therefore, he must seclude with her before Shabbat so that it does not appear as if he is making an acquisition on Shabbat. This is also the conclusion of our rabbis in the Shulchan Aruch in this section and in Orach Chaim section 339. In truth, the Talmud does not mention this distinction between a widow and a virgin regarding the acquisition through chuppah, and the Rambam does not mention it either. However, the words of these rabbis are founded on the words of the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Ketubot, where it is stated: "Those who marry widows must marry them while it is still day on Friday." This implies that the law of a widow is different from that of a virgin. The explanation is that for a virgin, chuppah effects acquisition, and since the chuppah was on Friday, he can have intercourse with her on Shabbat. But for a widow, it is necessary for him to bring her in, meaning to seclude with her while it is still day, because chuppah does not apply to her. According to this, for those who hold that chuppah for a virgin is also seclusion fit for intercourse, as stated in section 55, it must be said that for a widow, even this does not help because this is considered chuppah, and for a widow, there is no chuppah. Therefore, actual intercourse is required while it is still day. The term "to bring them in" in the Jerusalem Talmud refers to actual intercourse.

And even though there is no proof at all from the Jerusalem Talmud, for it is not because there is no "chuppah" (marriage canopy) for a widow but rather because the Jerusalem Talmud holds there that it is forbidden to have intercourse with a virgin for the first time on Shabbat due to causing a wound, and therefore when it says "those who marry widows" it refers specifically to the chuppah, meaning bringing her into the chuppah, and the same applies to a virgin except that a virgin's chuppah is not done on Friday because she is not fit for intercourse on Shabbat. In truth, there is no difference between a widow and a virgin [according to the Gra and similarly written by the Maharit], nevertheless, since our early sages adopted the interpretation of the Jerusalem Talmud to differentiate between a virgin and a widow, we should not deviate from their words.

In my humble opinion, it appears that all the halachic authorities do not disagree at all, according to what is written in Siman 55, that there are many types of chuppot (wedding canopies), and from the Torah, all are considered chuppot according to the customs of the people in that place. Even the Rambam agrees with this, as mentioned there. It is certain that if the custom is that chuppah is seclusion (yichud) appropriate for marital relations, as the Rambam wrote, this chuppah also applies to a widow. Why should there be a difference between them? However, if the chuppah is sitting in a canopy for the seven days of feasting, as the Rosh wrote in Sukkah (Chapter 2), and similarly the Tosafot wrote there (25b, "Ein"), or if the chuppah is bringing her to his house for marriage, or spreading a cloth over the bride's head, or the hinuma, or according to our custom with a canopy spread on poles in the synagogue courtyard, and the bride is seated and her hair loosened, and the groom throws a covering over her, and they are led to the chuppah and then back from the chuppah to the groom's house with celebration – certainly, these chuppot do not apply to widows. As we see, even though poles are set up and a cloth spread, it is done privately in the house, and the couple stands under the poles without attendants and without celebration, and only the betrothal and blessings are arranged, and then they immediately leave. This is not considered a chuppah that would be a form of acquisition because, for a widow and widower, it is not customary to make such preparations and celebrations. Certainly, her chuppah is only seclusion appropriate for marital relations. This is what the Jerusalem Talmud says about widows – for virgins, it is obvious that chuppah is done during the day because there are many preparations, as we see. But for widows, whose chuppah is a short time of seclusion appropriate for marital relations, and can be done at night, the Jerusalem Talmud advises doing it before the day ends. Therefore, the Rambam, who holds that chuppah is seclusion appropriate for marital relations, did not mention a distinction between a widow and a virgin. Our rabbis, the Tosafot, the Rosh, and other early authorities who hold that chuppah is sitting in a canopy for the seven days of feasting, and the Jerusalem Talmud because this is the custom of the world, therefore wrote that there is a distinction between a widow and a virgin. They also agree that for seclusion appropriate for marital relations, it suffices for a widow, as this is her chuppah. When they wrote that there is no chuppah for a widow, they meant the chuppah done for a virgin does not apply to a widow, as we see even now. Therefore, in practice, if he wishes to be with her on Shabbat, they must seclude themselves before the day ends in seclusion appropriate for marital relations. But if he does not wish to be with her on Shabbat, or she is impure, this is not necessary, and her chuppah acquisition will occur when he is with her after Shabbat. This is the halacha. However, one of the early authorities already wrote that there is a danger in having the first marital relations with a widow on Shabbat, even if they secluded themselves before the day ends (Magen Avraham, in the name of Maharil). Therefore, some great rabbis instructed to have marital relations before the day ends with only minimal intercourse. It has become customary to advise against having the first marital relations with a widow on Shabbat due to the danger. An incident occurred in the previous generation with a great rabbi who permitted this and regretted it greatly afterward. This is what I was taught in my youth by one of the great rabbis (See Beit Shmuel, who quoted the Taz and rejected it, reasoning that there is no preparation).

One does not marry women during Chol HaMoed, neither virgins nor widows, and does not perform levirate marriages, as it is written (Deuteronomy 16:14), "And you shall rejoice in your festival" – and not with your wife (Moed Katan 8b). One does not mix one joy with another, just as one does not perform mitzvot in bundles so that one's heart can be focused on one mitzvah, likewise, one’s heart should be focused on one joy (Tosafot there). We learn this from Solomon, who, when he finished building the Temple, celebrated for seven days before the festival so as not to mix this joy with the joy of the festival (there 9a). In the Jerusalem Talmud, it is derived from the verse "Complete this week" (Genesis 29:27), and the practical difference according to the Jerusalem Talmud is that even with one type of joy, such as marrying two women at once, one does not mix them, as written in Siman 62. However, it is permitted during Chol HaMoed to remarry one's divorced wife if he divorced her from marriage because this does not bring so much joy, and therefore "the joy in His dwelling" is not said for all three days (Beit Shmuel Siman 62:17). But if he divorced her from the engagement, it is forbidden to marry during Chol HaMoed because this is complete joy since he has not yet married her. But on the eve of the festival, it is permissible to marry even a virgin, even though her joy lasts seven days, the main joy is one day (Gemara). Regarding making the feast on the festival, some prohibit it and some permit it, as written in Orach Chaim Siman 546, and therefore the custom is not to marry at all on the eve of the festival (Magen Avraham there).

[It is a mitzvah to bring joy to the groom and bride, consisting of five sections]
It is a great mitzvah to bring joy to the groom and bride, to dance before them and to say that she is beautiful and graceful, that a cord of grace is drawn upon her, even if she is not beautiful. This is not considered falsehood because it can be said that she is beautiful in her deeds. Additionally, there is a notion that even if she is not beautiful, a cord of grace is drawn upon her, making her appear beautiful. However, if she has a defect, one should not say that she has no defect as this would be an outright lie; rather, one should remain silent on this matter. Similarly, one should praise her for a quality she possesses, for there is no person who does not have some virtue.

Our Sages said (Ketubot 17a) about Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai that he would take a branch of myrtle and dance before the bride, saying, "A beautiful and graceful bride." And it is stated in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (chapter 17) that the dogs did not consume the palms of Jezebel's hands because she would dance before the bride and groom. And our Sages said, "Anyone who benefits from a wedding feast and does not bring joy to the groom transgresses five voices." If a deceased and a bride meet each other, the deceased is moved aside to give way to the bride, and the bearers of the deceased should turn to another path. All this is to endear her to her husband. Furthermore, the honor of the living takes precedence, as it is taught in Tractate Semachot: "If a deceased and a bride are present, the bride takes precedence. If a deceased and a circumcision are present, the circumcision takes precedence, because this is the honor of the living and that is the honor of the dead." Therefore, Ramban of blessed memory wrote that in all matters, the needs of the bride take precedence over those of the deceased, whether it is for burial or any of his needs or for sustenance from the charity fund. (Shitah Mekubetzet there, and the wording of Tractate Semachot is not before us in chapter 11).

Joy is achieved when men dance separately and women separately. Heaven forbid that men and women should dance together. David said, "Young men and also maidens, old men together with youths" (Psalms 148:12), and he did not say young men with maidens. Anyone who does so kindles the fire of Gehenna for themselves, and their punishment is great. It is even forbidden to dance with the bride. It is also forbidden to gaze at the bride's face for even a moment with excessive looking. Some permit looking at her jewelry or her uncovered head, while others forbid even this. Only a casual glance is permitted, not a fixed stare, so that one does not arouse the evil inclination within oneself.

We interrupt Torah study for the sake of bringing a bride to the wedding canopy, and even one whose sole occupation is Torah study is obligated to interrupt [his study]. However, this obligation applies specifically when he sees them entering the canopy and is required to honor them by attending. But if he merely knows that there is a wedding in the city, he is not obligated to interrupt his study and go there. The essence of the mitzvah is to accompany her to the canopy. However, if there is a mixture of men and women, it is better not to go. Therefore, they should accompany the groom when he is being led, and not the bride, because it is a mitzvah that comes with a transgression. For this reason, if many women are also accompanying the groom, it is better not to go.

It is written, "May my tongue cling to the roof of my mouth if I do not remember you, if I do not raise Jerusalem above my highest joy" (Psalms 137:6). And memory is an active deed [see Megillah 18a]. Therefore, one must perform some act to remember the mourning for Jerusalem. Our sages said this is the ashes of the burnt substance placed on the heads of grooms, and it is placed at the spot of the tefillin, as it is written (Isaiah 61:3), "to bestow on those who mourn in Zion a crown of beauty instead of ashes" [Sifrei Devarim 3:23]. Therefore, the custom in Ashkenaz is to place ashes on the head of the groom before the chuppah and then immediately remove it. In Sephardic communities, it is customary to place a crown made of olive leaves on the groom's head because the olive is bitter, as a remembrance of the mourning for Jerusalem [Tur]. And there are places where the custom is to break a glass after the seven blessings, and this is the custom observed in these regions where the groom breaks the vessel over which the blessing of betrothal is recited. Each region follows its own custom, and there is no concern of wastefulness in this practice because it is done in remembrance of Jerusalem. May the Almighty grant us the merit to see its rebuilding, Amen and Amen.

What should a man find in his wife that would warrant divorcing her and not living with her. This section contains thirty-five paragraphs:

It is written: "When a man takes a wife and marries her, and it happens that she does not find favor in his eyes because he has found some unseemly thing in her, he writes her a bill of divorce, gives it in her hand, and sends her out of his house. She departs and becomes another man's wife." (Deuteronomy 24:1-2)

The Mishnah at the end of Gittin states that Beit Shammai says a man should not divorce his wife unless he has found some unseemly thing in her, interpreting the verse literally: "if she does not find favor in his eyes because he has found some unseemly thing in her."

Beit Hillel holds that even if she spoiled his dish, he may divorce her, interpreting the verse to mean either "an unseemly thing" or another matter in which she has wronged him.

Rabbi Akiva says that even if he found another woman more beautiful than her, he may divorce her, interpreting the verse to mean "if she does not find favor in his eyes" due to beauty, or because he has found some unseemly thing in her.

The halacha follows Beit Hillel: if she has wronged him, he may divorce her, but he should not divorce her merely to take another more beautiful than her (Tur).

The prophet Malachi said, "For I hate sending away," and our Sages said (Gittin 90b), one said, "If you hate her, send her away," like Rabbi Akiva (Rashi), and one said, "The one who sends away is hated before the Omnipresent" (ibid.), and they do not disagree; this applies to the first match, and this to the second match. For Rabbi Eliezer said, "Anyone who divorces his first wife, even the altar sheds tears for him," and he expounds this from the scripture there. And specifically when he divorces her against her will, but if he divorces her willingly, we have no issue (Beit Yosef). And according to this, for us who have the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom against a forced divorce, this law does not apply (Aruch HaShulchan, Even HaEzer 119:2 that even in such a case, one should not hasten to divorce her).

According to what we have explained, it is clarified that Beit Hillel only spoke regarding the first marriage, but concerning the second marriage, they hold like Rabbi Akiva that even if he finds another woman more beautiful than her, he can divorce her. However, from the words of the Tur, it is explained that according to Beit Hillel, whether it is the first marriage or the second marriage, he should not divorce her because of another woman more beautiful than her, as the verse "if he finds some unseemly thing in her" applies to both cases (Perisha). And even in the second marriage, he should not divorce her unless she ruins his food and similar cases where he has a resentment towards her, and in this, the prophet says, "If you hate her, send her away." And it makes sense that for another woman more beautiful than her, it does not apply to say that he hates her (Bach). However, in the first marriage, even though the Torah permits him to divorce her in such a case, he should not hasten to divorce her and the one who sends her away is hated, unless he finds some unseemly thing or promiscuity in her. And this is also clarified from the words of the Rambam in the 10th chapter of the Laws of Divorce, law 21, see there. And this is also the intention of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 3 (and this is what the Rema glossed: "But without this, etc." to clarify the intention of the Beit Yosef that he does not rule like Beit Shammai, and this resolves what the commentators questioned, and this is the intention of the Gra, and study it well).

Some say that this prohibition only applies to a married woman and not to a betrothed woman, as a betrothed woman can be divorced in any situation. This understanding aligns with the plain meaning of the verse, which speaks of after marriage as it states, "When a man takes a wife and marries her." This also aligns with the words of Beit Hillel in the Mishnah, who said, "Even if she burned his food," which happens after marriage when she cooks for him. Nevertheless, some say there is no difference between a betrothed and a married woman (both opinions are in the Mishneh Torah, see there). According to this opinion, it must be said that the verse and the Mishnah speak in the usual manner. Additionally, some say that the first match is only when she was a virgin, as a woman makes a covenant only with the one who made her a vessel (Sanhedrin 22b). In this context, our sages said (ibid.) that the altar sheds tears for him. But if she was not a virgin, her status is like a second match (Pri Chadash), because even though for him it is the first match, for her it is not (Beit Meir). There are those who infer from Rashi's words at the end of Gittin that a virgin, even when she is not his first, is considered like a first match, and his first wife, even if she is not a virgin, is considered like a first match (Noda BiYehuda) (and see Taz and Maharshal, and according to what was said, it is clear, and examine this thoroughly).

There are those who say that the primary ruling that one should not divorce his wife unless he finds in her a matter of sexual immorality is according to Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. When she has acted immorally against him, it is neither a Biblical prohibition nor a Rabbinic prohibition but rather good advice (Maggid Mishneh there in the name of Kenesset HaGedolah and several other great authorities). However, from several of the great early authorities, it appears to be a complete prohibition. The Rashba, of blessed memory, wrote in his responsa (section 18) that the reason no blessing was instituted for divorces is because there are divorces that are sinful, such as when he does not find in her a matter that permits him to divorce her according to the law. Therefore, even in a case where it is a mitzvah to divorce, no blessing was instituted because the Rabbis did not differentiate (between cases). Hence, it is clear that he holds it to be a complete prohibition. Also, the Rivash wrote in his responsa (section 127) that if a father tells his son to divorce his wife, he does not have to listen to him, as if he tells him to transgress a Torah commandment, he does not have to heed his words. Hence, it is clear that he holds this to be a Torah prohibition. This is also evident from the Jerusalem Talmud, which questions Beit Shammai's position, asking why we need the verse stating that her first husband cannot take her back, as she is already forbidden to him due to sexual immorality. It answers that it is to impose a prohibition, indicating that it is a Torah prohibition. Additionally, it implies this in our Talmud, where Rav Pappa asked Rava whether, if he found neither sexual immorality nor any other matter and divorced her, the divorce would be valid. Rava answered that since the Torah revealed in the case of a forced divorce that he cannot send her away and must remain standing ready to take her back all his life, it implies that regarding other women, what he has done is done. If there were no Torah prohibition, what is the question? It is certainly a complete prohibition. However, the Torah nevertheless commanded that if he transgressed and divorced her, the divorce is effective (and Rava follows his reasoning in Temurah 4a, where if one acts, it does not take effect, according to Abaye there is no problem at all; see Tosafot there, s.v. vehashta, and examine it well).

The general principle is that if a man divorces his wife because he found another woman more attractive than her, this constitutes a Torah prohibition, even in the case of a second marriage. However, if he developed hatred towards her because she wronged him, even if it was just by burning his food, and certainly if he hates her due to some defect or undesirable trait she possesses, he may divorce her in a second marriage. But in the case of a first marriage, he should not hasten to send her away, because the altar sheds tears for him, unless he found in her a matter of sexual immorality or she is not modest like the proper daughters of Israel, such as if she violates Jewish law. In such a case, it is a Torah commandment to divorce her, as it is stated, "because he found in her a matter of sexual immorality, and he writes her a bill of divorce and sends her from his house" (Deuteronomy 24:1). This applies even according to Beit Hillel (Tosafot). A woman who was divorced because of licentiousness should not be married by another man if he is a proper person. The Torah calls him "another man," as it is written, "and she leaves his house and becomes the wife of another man" (Deuteronomy 24:2), and it does not say "a second man," to imply that she is not suited for the first husband, because he expelled wickedness from his house, and this one brought it into his house. The second husband merits that if he divorces her, as it is stated, "and the latter man hates her" (Deuteronomy 24:3), and if not, she buries him, as it is stated, "or if the latter husband dies" (Deuteronomy 24:3). This is fitting for death, as the first expelled wickedness from his house, and the second brought wickedness into his house (Talmud).

And similarly, a bad wife to her husband, such as one who curses him or causes him distress by refusing to eat with him, and similar situations where he experiences distress from her—even in the first marriage, it is a mitzvah to divorce her, as it is stated (Proverbs 22:10): “Drive away the scoffer, and strife will go out.” And a bad wife is as troublesome as a rainy day (Yevamot 63b), which is a day of hail and wind, as it is stated (Proverbs 27): “A constant dripping on a rainy day and a contentious wife are alike.” 

And all these matters apply initially. However, after the fact, if he divorced her under any circumstances, the divorce is valid, and he is not obligated to take her back. Only in a case of coercion did the Torah reveal that he stands ready to take her back, but not in other situations (end of Gittin). The decisors omitted this because it is obvious, and furthermore, it is possible that we only need this reasoning for those who hold that anything the Torah says not to do, if done, does not take effect, as it says in section 5. And the decisors believe that if done, it does take effect. As for the principal ruling that if done, it takes effect, the law is not clear (see Beit HaBechirah, Chapter 6 of Bechorot, and Melamed LeHo'il Chapter 8 of Loans and Borrowing, and Magen Avraham Chapter 1 of Theft, and the Tur wrote this as he holds like Rava).

The Tur wrote: "But if he finds in her a matter of immorality or immodesty, it is a mitzvah to divorce her, as it is written, 'Expel the scoffer and conflict will depart.'" And our sages said that this verse refers to a bad woman, as it is written. However, regarding immorality or immodesty, it is a mitzvah from the Torah, as explained (by the Beit Yosef). Also, the language of the Shulchan Aruch in section 4 is somewhat imprecise, as it equates the law of a bad woman with that of an immodest woman. However, the Talmud proves that regarding an immodest woman, there is a positive commandment from the Torah to divorce her. Similarly, the language of the Rambam is puzzling in this regard because he also wrote in Chapter 10, Law 22, "A bad woman in her behaviors and who is not modest like the virtuous daughters of Israel, it is a mitzvah to divorce her," as it is said, "Expel the scoffer and conflict will depart." However, he did not write that it is a mitzvah from the Torah to divorce her. It must be said that he holds that what our sages said, that it is a mitzvah from the Torah to divorce her, is only according to Beit Shammai. For according to Beit Hillel, it is not specifically about immorality, as even if she burned his food (he can divorce her) (as explained by the Lechem Mishneh). And one should not ask how it is possible to say that according to Beit Hillel there is no mitzvah from the Torah to divorce her in the case of immorality, for it is forbidden to be with her. It can be said that although it is forbidden to be with her, he is not obligated by the Torah to divorce her, but he should distance himself from her and take another wife. This is also clarified from the words of the Rambam at the beginning of the laws of divorce, where he wrote that from the Torah, divorce is not a mitzvah at all, even in a place where she is forbidden to him. For he wrote that there is a positive commandment to divorce with a written document, as it is written. And similarly in the Sefer HaMitzvot, mitzvah 222, it is written: "He commanded us to divorce with a document in any case when one wishes to divorce, as it is said, 'And he writes for her...'". It is clear from his words that there is never a mitzvah to divorce, and the mitzvah is only when one wishes to divorce, to not divorce except with a document. This is like the mitzvah of slaughtering, that when one wishes to eat meat, it is a mitzvah to slaughter. However, from the words of the Rashba, which we brought in section 5, it is clarified that there is a mitzvah to divorce one who is fit to be divorced. This is also clarified from Tosafot at the end of Gittin, where they wrote that even according to Beit Hillel, it is a mitzvah from the Torah to divorce an immodest woman.

Maimonides wrote (there): A man should not marry a woman with the intention of divorcing her, nor should she sit under him and serve him while he intends to divorce her. So wrote the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. This means that whether one marries initially with the intention of divorcing or later decides to divorce after marrying her and continues to engage with her, it is forbidden. In Chapter 21 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations, he wrote: "It is forbidden for a man to marry a woman with the intention of divorcing her, as it says: 'Do not plot harm against your neighbor who lives trustfully near you' (Proverbs 3:29). However, if he informs her at the outset that he is marrying her for a limited time, it is permitted."

From his words, it is understood that the reason for this prohibition is because she is unaware of his intention. But if he informs her that he is marrying her for a specific period, it is permitted. Accordingly, even if she is living with him, it is not forbidden to engage with her unless he does not inform her of his intention to divorce. But if he informs her, it is permitted. Some of the great authorities have written this (Chomat HaChaim, section 1), though there are those who disagree (Beit Shmuel in the name of the Pri Sha).

In the responsa of the Geonim, it is clarified that if he informs her, it is permitted (Perach HaChaim). It must be said that he does not hate her, for if he hates her, it is forbidden to engage with her lest the children be considered children of a hated woman. This is only when he wants to divorce her for other reasons, and it is not considered "children of a divorced heart" which applies only if at the time of intercourse he intends to divorce her and not if he decides to divorce her later (Beit Shmuel).

And know that from the words of the Tur, it is understood that even merely being together without intercourse is also forbidden due to "do not plot harm against your neighbor." So wrote the later authorities (Beit Shmuel and Perach HaChaim). There are some who are uncertain about this (Maggid Mishneh and so wrote Chomat HaChaim).

However, there are some of our Rabbis who hold that marrying a woman for a limited time, even if she is informed, is forbidden. And that which is found in the Talmud where they would announce "Who is available for the day?" is explained to mean that he would not be intimate with her. If he were to be intimate with her, he would marry her permanently (this is according to the explanation of Tosafot and the Raavad in Chapter 11 of Issurei Biah, as mentioned by the Yam Shel Shlomo in Chapter 4 of Yevamot, Section 6, and further supported by the conclusion there in 37a; examine this carefully). Therefore, whether he marries her initially for a limited time or whether he intends to divorce her from the outset, it is forbidden for him to be with her, even if she is informed, because we consider this as "Do not devise evil against your neighbor," even though the end of the verse, "while he lives securely with you," does not apply when she is informed and consents, for she is living securely without deceit. Nevertheless, there is still a devising of evil (Yam Shel Shlomo there).

According to the Torah, a man can only divorce his wife voluntarily, while a woman can be divorced whether it is her will or not. However, Rabbeinu Gershom instituted a decree in the "Herem de-Rabbeinu Gershom" that a man should not divorce his wife against her will, and this decree has spread throughout the world and will be further clarified. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote that according to Torah law, even if the husband cannot pay the ketubah and dowry, she cannot use this as a reason to prevent the divorce. Rather, she should be divorced and then claim from him what he owes her, as stated. The source of this ruling is from the responsa of the Rosh, who ruled similarly in the case of a woman with epilepsy, that even after Rabbeinu Gershom's decree, she cannot prevent the get because of the ketubah, as written in Siman 117, Se'if 25.

The Rashba in his responsa wrote (as brought in Beit Yosef) that he heard in the name of the Gaon that a man is not permitted to divorce his wife if he does not have the means to pay her ketubah. Similarly, I found this in the responsa of the Rif. And so wrote the Tashbetz, and there are many proofs from the Talmud that without the ketubah, he cannot divorce her. For the Sages expounded on the verse, "The Lord has delivered me into the hands of those I cannot withstand" (Lamentations 1:14) — this refers to a bad wife whose ketubah is large (Yevamot 63b). And they also said in Eruvin (41b) that a man with a bad wife and a large ketubah, who cannot divorce her, will not see the face of Gehinnom (hell). Similarly, in Gittin (58a), it is mentioned about a man who suspected his wife and wanted to divorce her but could not because he did not have the means to pay the ketubah. It is also explained in Midrash Bereshit (Parasha 17) about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Gamla, who had a bad wife and did not divorce her until they lent him the ketubah amount, after which he gave her the ketubah and divorced her.

It seems to me that they do not disagree in practice, for it is certainly valid that he can live with her even if she is a bad woman and he suffers from her, and the Torah has given him permission to divorce her or if he hates her; and in the case of a second marriage without the ketubah, he cannot divorce her. All the more so in the time of the Talmud, when he could marry another woman. But when she has a defect, such as being epileptic or similar conditions that human nature cannot tolerate — in such cases, even with a man, we would compel him to divorce her. We do not consider her ketubah. All the more so when she is promiscuous, where the law dictates that it is a mitzvah to divorce her, we do not consider the ketubah. This also appears from several of the great later authorities (and this is also what is inferred from the Chavat Yair, section 5, and so writes the Peri Chadash, although the Beit Shmuel, section 6, did not write so; nevertheless, this seems to be the primary halachic ruling).

Rabbeinu Gershom Me’or HaGolah and the great scholars of his time decreed a ban against divorcing a woman against her will. This enactment spread throughout the world, even in places where Rabbeinu Gershom’s ban against marrying two women did not spread. Even if one wishes to give her the ketubah, one should not divorce her in our times without her consent. However, if he divorced her with her consent and a defect was found in the get (divorce document) requiring a new get, he may give it to her against her will since she initially consented and accepted it. But as long as she has not accepted it, even if she initially agreed to accept it and then recanted, he should not give it to her against her will, except in a case of a mitzvah, such as fulfilling the commandment of procreation, as Rabbeinu Gershom did not enact a ban in such a case. There are those who disagree and hold that Rabbeinu Gershom did include such cases in his decree, and this has already been explained in Siman 1. Also, if she develops defects that are unbearable, Rabbeinu Gershom did not enact a ban in such cases, as explained in Siman 117. It has also been clarified in Siman 1 that to permit marrying two women, one needs permission from one hundred rabbis. But in a case where one is allowed to divorce against her will, it seems that there is no need for one hundred rabbis.

In a situation where one must choose between two options—either to divorce against her will or to marry another woman while still married to his first wife—it seems preferable to divorce against her will. This prohibition is temporary, while having two wives would involve a long-term prohibition. Although neither situation is forbidden where it is stated that in such a case Rabbeinu Gershom did not enact his decree, nevertheless, why should he remain with two wives? There is an opinion that having two wives is less severe than divorce against her will, arguing that the prohibition of two wives was only until the end of the fifth millennium, as stated in Siman 1, while the prohibition against forced divorce is eternal (Noda B'Yehuda Siman 1). Furthermore, it could be said that the prohibition of having two wives did not spread throughout the entire world, whereas the prohibition of forced divorce did. Nonetheless, it seems to me that this is not the case because, in places where they permit this, there is no prohibition at all since Rabbeinu Gershom did not enact his decree in such cases. Nevertheless, why should we perform an action that would make it appear to onlookers that a man has two wives? This requires further investigation (see Noda B'Yehuda who also cites the opinion of the Gaon of Lisa who disagreed with him, and see Raan Yoma Chapter 8 regarding someone who is seized by a ravenous hunger, where it is better to slaughter an animal than to feed him non-kosher meat, even though non-kosher meat is a lighter prohibition than slaughtering, nevertheless, he would be transgressing with every olive-sized portion he eats).

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: If he divorced her against her will in our times and she married another, the man is no longer called a transgressor. His words mean that as long as he has not taken her back, he remains under his excommunication. However, since she has married another and he cannot take her back, the excommunication is lifted from him, and he is no longer called a transgressor. Refer to Yoreh De'ah, section 334. Nevertheless, for the transgression he committed, he needs absolution (three times) or repentance. It is obvious that as long as she has not married and she wants him to take her back, he is compelled to do so if he is not a Kohen (see what is written in section 24).

And a great question arises for the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) regarding the opinion of Rava in Tractate Temurah: if one performs an action that should not take effect, why should a get (divorce document) be valid against the woman's will after the enactment of Rabbeinu Gershom’s decree? After all, even in rabbinic matters there is reason to say that if one performs the action, it does not take effect (Ketubot 1:). And all the more so regarding the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom, which is akin to a Torah prohibition. It could be argued that since we find in matters of kiddushin (betrothal) that kiddushin is effective even with those who are prohibited by a negative commandment, even though the Torah forbids it, it proves that the Torah commands that kiddushin should be effective even if done in prohibition. And since divorce is compared to betrothal, it follows that in the matter of a get itself, the Torah reveals in the case of one who rapes a virgin that if he divorces her, the get is valid, even though the Torah says he may not send her away all his days. This proves that in matters of get, if it is done, it is effective. But he is obligated to take her back because the Torah decrees so for all his days, standing and returning. But in other matters, we do not force him to take her back even though he committed a sin. And what we said in the previous section, that we force him to take her back, is not strictly from the law but from reasoning, so that a sinner does not profit. However, it is obvious that the get is valid, even according to the opinion that if it is done, it does not take effect (and so wrote Tosafot in Temurah 5b, s.v. "Meitivi," etc. And if you say, etc., one can answer, etc. See there. And I do not understand their question there 6a, s.v. "Vehashta," see there. And perhaps their intention is that he should take her back. And see the sugya, where it is proven explicitly that the get is valid even according to Rava, and all the more so according to the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom. And investigate this thoroughly). And see what I wrote in section 24.

In the Gemara (Gittin 75a), it discusses a case where a man says to his wife, "This is your get (divorce document) on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz." There is a dispute whether, if she gives it to him against his will, it is considered a valid giving or not. This will be clarified in Siman 143; refer there. One might question whether we should derive from the essence of the get, as it is written, "and he shall place it in her hand," and nevertheless, according to Torah law, a woman can be divorced against her will, as it is written, "and he shall send her out of his house." If so, the Torah has revealed that giving against one's will is considered giving. However, in truth, it is not similar. The dispute is about something that is the recipient's property, like the woman who is the husband's property, and she gives him the money to fulfill the condition and release herself from his ownership. One can indeed say that it is impossible to release ownership without his consent. But the man is not his wife's property, and she only has an obligation to him for sustenance, clothing, and marital relations. He can indeed release her from this obligation even without her consent. (Rashba there, and the Pri Chadash's objection is unnecessary. His intention is as I have written, and so writes the Beit Meir. Examine this well).

And since a woman can be divorced against her will, as her consent is not required, therefore a minor and a deaf-mute can also be divorced by receiving a get (divorce document), even if the marriage was a Torah marriage, such as through her father. All the more so with an orphan who was married off in her minority, which is only rabbinic marriage. Similarly, a deaf-mute marriage is only rabbinic, as stated in Siman 44, unless she was betrothed when she was of sound mind. And even though a minor and a deaf-mute do not have complete understanding, nevertheless, since the woman’s consent is not required, they can receive their get. However, if the minor has a father, it will be explained in Siman 141 whether she can receive the get herself, see there. Also, a minor who is too young to understand the concept of a get cannot receive a get, and this will be explained there with the help of Heaven.

But a woman who has become mentally incapacitated and has no understanding at all, if she does not know how to guard her get (divorce document) at all, even according to Torah law he cannot divorce her, and the husband is obligated to all her requirements as we wrote in Siman 70, see there what we wrote in Seif 16. And if she knows how to guard her get but does not know how to guard herself from immoral individuals, according to Torah law she can be divorced. However, the sages instituted, in order to prevent her from being treated in a wanton manner, that he should not divorce her, and consequently he must guard her. Since the sages imposed this upon him, therefore he is exempt from providing her with sustenance, clothing, and marital relations, and he leaves her and marries another woman, and he feeds and provides for her from his own resources, and he is also not obligated for her medical care. However, if it is possible to cure her mental incapacitation, certainly the husband is obligated to cure her (Beit Shmuel, Seif Katan 10, also according to the opinion of the Rambam). And this is the view of the Rambam at the end of Chapter 10 of Hilchot Gerushin.

But there are some of our rabbis who hold that even if she cannot guard herself, he is obligated to provide for her sustenance and all conditions of the ketubah, except for her conjugal rights, since it is impossible to have relations with her. For if we say that he is exempt from all obligations, then what benefit did the sages achieve with their enactment? Furthermore, since the sages said that he should not divorce her, she is not worse off than a woman who is divorced but not divorced, whose husband is obligated to provide for her sustenance (Tur in the name of the Ra'ah). And it seems that according to this opinion, he is obligated for all her medical needs, even those not related to her madness. However, from the language of the Tur and the Ra'avad there, it does not seem so. And for us, who are prohibited from divorcing a woman against her will, even the Rambam agrees that he is obligated to all obligations (Choshen Mishpat, Siman 9).

The current custom regarding a mentally incompetent person is to permit him to marry another woman based on the authorization of one hundred rabbis and with royal permission (see there, section 112). Some have written that it is necessary to designate a ketubah (marriage contract) for her and to prepare a get (bill of divorce) through an agent, and to obligate him in all the conditions of the ketubah as well (Bach). However, there are those who question this, arguing how it is possible to hold the rope at both ends, and how we can obligate him in the ketubah and the obligations of a husband to his wife (Chamot). Additionally, there are those who question the validity of the tripartite get, asserting that it is impossible to release her with such a get when she recovers, and the agent cannot deliver the get based on the principle stated by our sages (Nazir 12b) that anything a person cannot do himself at present, he cannot appoint an agent to do. Since she is not currently eligible to receive a get, neither can an agent act on her behalf (Melamed LeHo'il, chapter 6, in the name of the wise men of Kushta). Many great rabbis have discussed this, and we ourselves have written about this in Choshen Mishpat, section 182 (see there). In practice, it is difficult to rely on such a get, and therefore, when she recovers, it is proper to write her another get.

If one transgressed and divorced her in her insanity, if she does not know how to guard her get, it is not a valid get at all because, according to Torah law, she is not subject to divorce. However, if she knows how to guard her get but does not know how to guard herself, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled that she is considered divorced, and he must send her out of his house and is no longer obligated to care for her. He gives her the ketubah. Some say that even in retrospect, she is not divorced, because the Sages decreed not to divorce her. According to this opinion, in our times, when there is a prohibition against forced divorces (the ban of Rabbeinu Gershom), she is certainly not divorced (Beit Shmuel).

And all this applies to a person who is always mentally incapacitated. However, when someone is sometimes sane and sometimes insane, and he divorced her when she was sane because he thought she would remain that way forever and not return to her insanity, we do not undo the action since at the time of the act he did not knowingly violate the decree of the Sages. Nevertheless, according to the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom, this is only the case if he divorced her willingly. But if he divorced her against her will, it is not a valid divorce according to this opinion, which holds that violating the decree of the Sages does not constitute a valid divorce (see the commentaries of the Chochmat Shlomo, section 16, and the Beit Shmuel, section 13). 

Do not be troubled by the fact that our teacher, the Rema, ruled that if he divorced her against her will and she remarried, he is no longer considered a transgressor, as stated in section 16. How can it be said that it is not a valid divorce? It can be explained that indeed, the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom was for the benefit of the woman, and since she remarried, it reveals her intention that she is content, thus the divorce is valid. But if she did not remarry and cries out that she is not content, certainly according to this opinion it is not a valid divorce, and we compel him to take her back, as I have explained there (that it is not a valid divorce is akin to a penalty).

It was taught in Ketubot (28a): A man who divorces his wife should not allow her to remarry within his neighborhood, because she is familiar with his gestures and signals, and they might come to commit a transgression (Rashi). And if he is a Kohen, she should not even live in the same alley as him, even if she has not remarried (ibid.), lest he come to have relations with her, and a Kohen is forbidden to have relations with a divorced woman. However, an Israelite, as long as she has not remarried, she can live in his neighborhood (ibid.). An alley is larger than a neighborhood, for a neighborhood consists of only three houses. When she has remarried, it is more stringent for him, and it is sufficient to distance her to a neighborhood. But when she has not remarried and he is a Kohen, whose prohibition is more lenient because she is single, they were strict with him to distance her from the entire alley (Tosafot, and this is also apparent from Rashi; examine it well).

And some of our Rabbis hold that a neighborhood is greater than an alley and they were more stringent regarding living arrangements because it is a prohibited relationship (erva), and without marriage to a Kohen they were not so stringent, and distancing as in the case of an alley is sufficient (Rosh and Ran). And a Jewish divorcee who remarries and then becomes a widow or is divorced again, her status is like that of a divorcee to a Kohen (Rosh), for this too is a prohibition by a negative commandment, although there are those who are hesitant about this (Ran in the name of R"i) and hold that even in an alley she is permitted to live with him because without sanctification there is no prohibition of remarrying one's divorcee after she married another (there). However, in the same courtyard it is certainly forbidden for them to live together, and according to this opinion, we have no proof that a Jew who divorced his wife and she did not remarry would be forbidden to live with him in the same courtyard (SeMaG).
