But from the decisive authorities, it is explained that this too is forbidden, as will be clarified, and it is not similar to a captive woman whom the Sages permitted to live with in the same courtyard, provided they do not seclude themselves, as stated in Siman 7, Se'if 16, for there the reason is due to the matter being in doubt, as stated there (and this is also evident from Rashi).

However, Rambam of blessed memory writes in Chapter 21 of the Laws of Divorce, Law 27: "One who divorced his wife from the state of marriage should not reside with her in the same courtyard lest they come to promiscuity. And if he was a Kohen, she should not reside with him in the same alleyway (mavoy), and a small village is considered like an alleyway." His words indicate that he did not learn from the Gemara that she should not marry in his neighborhood, but rather that one who divorces his wife should not reside with her in the same courtyard. However, in his neighborhood, she is permitted to reside (according to the Maggid Mishneh). And according to him, even the divorced wife of an Israelite who has not remarried is forbidden to reside with him in the same courtyard, as mentioned, and it is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud in the chapter "HaZorek" (see there), and this is the law we follow. The measure of a small village has not been clarified as to its size (see Aruch Hashulchan, Section 19). The prohibition of an alleyway applies only to an alleyway closed on three sides, as was the case in the time of the Talmud, but in an open alleyway, where many people pass through, they are permitted to reside even if she has remarried. If he divorced her because she is forbidden to him, even if she has not remarried, it is forbidden to reside with her as if she has remarried to another. And if it is a Torah prohibition, such as a suspected adulteress or one who sees blood due to intercourse, it is forbidden to reside even in an alleyway. If it is a rabbinic prohibition, such as a captive woman, it is forbidden in the courtyard but permitted in the alleyway (see there, Section 22 and see Gra, Section 16). And regarding other rabbinic prohibitions, some say it has the same law as a captive woman and some say it has the same law as if she has remarried and divorced, and only in the case of a captive woman was the leniency applied (see Beit Shmuel, Section 16).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 7: "If a public thoroughfare separates between their houses, even if there are no other Jews in the city besides them, it is permitted." End of quote. The explanation of his words, it seems to me, is as follows: It has already been clarified in section 26 that when she marries another man, we are very strict with her, to the extent that even in a large neighborhood she is forbidden to live with him, and certainly in a cul-de-sac. This is the opinion of the Tur. And in section 27, it was explained that in an open alleyway where a public path passes between them, it is also permitted. It seems reasonable that this is only in a place where there are other Jews besides them, because then they will be afraid to seclude themselves. But if they are the only ones in the city, it is forbidden even in an open alleyway, because they can easily seclude themselves. This is what he means by saying that if a public thoroughfare separates between their houses, meaning that they live opposite each other, that is, he lives on one side and she on the other side, and a public thoroughfare separates them, then it is permitted even if there are no other Jews besides them. Because, if they want to seclude themselves, one of them would necessarily have to cross the width of the public thoroughfare, and this would be noticed by even the non-Jews in the city. But if they both live on the same side, they can easily seclude themselves by passing along the sides of the public thoroughfare, which is not so noticeable, and therefore in such a case, it is forbidden even in an open alleyway. And even if they live far from each other, there is an opinion that says the prohibition is only when they live house next to house and can pass through the wall between them, but if one house separates between them, it is considered that a public thoroughfare separates them (Chokhmat Shlomo, section 20), and he was challenged on this (in section 21). And it seems to me as I have written (and this is also implied by the language of the Hagahot Asheri. Otherwise, he should have said "if they are not adjacent to each other." And the Rema combined the words of the Hagahot Asheri with those of the Terumat HaDeshen. See and analyze well).

Reuven divorced his wife, and she went and married another man and had children. The divorcer (Reuven) also married another woman and had children with her. The children are permitted to marry each other, and there is no concern that because they are related by marriage, they will come to a prohibition. All the more so, it is permitted for the daughter of the divorcer to marry the brother of the divorced woman, and the brother of the divorcer to marry the sister of the divorced woman (according to the Chida in the name of the Kenesset HaGedolah). We should not increase decrees beyond what the Sages have stated.

The Sages said (there) that if she had a loan with him, she appoints an agent to claim it, and she should not claim it herself. According to the Rambam, this applies to all divorced women, whereas according to Rashi, it is only when he is a Kohen, and according to the Halacha, we follow the Rambam. And even though they do not seclude themselves privately, nevertheless, since they conduct business together, there is a concern that they might become close and seclude themselves, and he may come upon her. Therefore, any type of business should not be conducted together when they need to speak together and negotiate, and similarly, lending each other money after the divorce is forbidden unless through an agent. If a divorced woman comes with her ex-husband to court, they are excommunicated or given lashes of rebellion. Similarly, if they live in the same courtyard (according to the Rosh, Ran, and Tur, when they come to court, they are not given lashes unless he was a Kohen or she remarried, and see Shach, subparagraph 17, and in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 334).

The prohibition applies only if they are engaging in business together, such as coming to court or other dealings. However, there is no prohibition against entering incidentally into a house where his ex-wife is present, and it is permitted to enter her house incidentally even if she has remarried, as long as he does not reside there and does not engage in business with her (as is evident in Pesachim 110b). There are those who are stringent even in this case (Beit Yosef). The reason is that he might be drawn towards her. It seems to me that even according to this stringent opinion, one should only be stringent if he stays there for an hour or two and there are not many Jews present. Otherwise, there is no concern (as is evident in Beit Yosef, see there, and the precise explanation of Chokhmat Shlomo 24, and pay close attention).

It is permissible for a man to provide sustenance for his divorced wife when she has no means of support, and indeed, it is considered a greater mitzvah than supporting other poor people because of the commandment "and do not ignore your own flesh." It is found in Midrash Bereshit (Parashat 17) about a man who gave money to his divorced wife for sustenance, and as a result, rains came down. However, he should not give it to her directly to avoid having dealings with her; rather, he should support her through an intermediary. And even though it says there that he gave it to her directly, in truth, this was not proper behavior. The proof is that it was reported to Rabbi Tanchuma that he committed a sin by speaking with his divorced wife, and when Rabbi Tanchuma asked him why he did so, he replied that his compassion was aroused.

When both are in one courtyard and one of them needs to leave the courtyard because there is a prohibition against them being together, who must defer to whom? The Sages said (there) that she must defer to him, because moving a man is harder than moving a woman. It is obvious that this is when they have equal rights to the courtyard. But if the courtyard belongs to her, he must defer to her. And only when the courtyard belongs to both of them or if they are living there as tenants, then she must defer to him. And after the divorce, when she must defer to him, if she wants to remarry, they will need to distance themselves from each other from the entire alley and neighborhood as explained. No one from the alley where the first one resides may marry her unless he accepts upon himself to distance himself from this alley and neighborhood. For she must distance herself from him and not him from her, as we have said. Consequently, if someone wants to marry her, he too must distance himself. (Chokhmat Adam and Beit Shmuel)

All these matters apply only if she was divorced from marriage, but if she was divorced from betrothal, she is permitted to live with him in the same courtyard and to summon him to court, for his heart is not familiar with her, and there is no concern for impropriety. Therefore, if it is known that they were accustomed to being together and his heart is familiar with her even from betrothal, all the laws that we have mentioned apply. Similarly, a yavam and his yevamah after chalitzah have the same status as a betrothed couple, and if his heart is familiar with her, they are forbidden to live together. This is the ruling of the Rashba in his responsa (Siman 209, cited in Beit Yosef). The prohibition of chalitzah is like the prohibition for a kohen, for there is also a negative commandment in her case.

It was taught in Simchot chapter 2: Beit Shammai say that one who divorces his wife should not reside with her, neither in an alley nor in a courtyard. If the alley belongs to both of them, he should turn his entrance to another side. And if the courtyard belongs to both of them, they should move away from each other, and a woman should move away from a man. In what case are these words said? When they were married. But concerning a priest's wife, even if they were not married, these words apply from marriage, but not from betrothal. And similarly, one who performs chalitzah for his yevamah should not move away because his heart is not familiar with her. End of quote. (According to the Rambam, this refers to an alley, but in any case, it is forbidden in a courtyard. And the equation of a priest's wife to marriage is not according to the opinions explained, and it can be reconciled, and pay attention to this.) (In the Jerusalem Talmud, the beginning of Kiddushin, it is written throughout the section (Malachi 2), "the Lord of Hosts," and here (in the verse "because he hated sending away") it is written "the God of Israel," to teach you that the Holy One, blessed be He, designated His name in divorces only in Israel alone).

The woman can only be divorced through a written document, as it is written: "He shall write for her a scroll of severance and place it in her hand and send her from his house." This means he must write a document that releases her and permits her to everyone, and he gives it to her and tells her that it releases her. This is what is called a "get" (Tor). "Get" is a term for a legal document, and all legal documents are called "gitin" in Aramaic. The term "scroll of severance" is translated as "get peturin." We do not need to specify "get of a woman" because in most places where "get" is mentioned alone, it refers to a woman's get (Tosafot, beginning of Gittin, and similarly Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah, chapter 2, and Tosefot Yom Tov).

In the explanation of "and he writes her a document of divorce," the Tannaim in the Gemara disagree, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Meir holds that the signing witnesses effect the divorce, while Rabbi Elazar holds that the delivery witnesses effect the divorce. The explanation of the matter is that Rabbi Meir holds that "and he writes her" refers to the signing, as the essence of the document is the signatures (Rashi 3a), as it is written in Jeremiah (32:44), "And write in the book and sign it and attest it with witnesses." Therefore, all the requirements for the get (divorce document), such as being written for her sake and not being attached (to anything), apply to the signatures of the witnesses, and we do not care at all if the writing of the get was for her sake or attached. Thus, Rabbi Meir would say, even if one found a written get lying in the trash, and it was signed for his and her sake and given to her, it is valid (there). Hence, according to Rabbi Meir, a get without signed witnesses, even if delivered in the presence of witnesses, is not a get at all. However, even according to Rabbi Meir, some of our rabbis hold that delivery witnesses are required at the time of giving the get to the woman, as there is no matter of intimacy with fewer than two witnesses (Tosafot 4a, s.v. "for we hold," and Rosh 9:7). In practice, this does not make a difference, as we do not follow Rabbi Meir, as will be explained.

And Rabbi Eliezer holds that "and he writes her" refers to the writing of the get (divorce document), meaning that when the get is written, either by him or by the scribe according to his instructions, it must be written for her sake and while detached (from the ground). All the invalidations of the get pertain to its writing and not to the signing of the witnesses. There is no need for witnesses to sign the get according to Torah law; the sages instituted the requirement for witnesses to sign the get for the betterment of the world, lest the witnesses of the delivery die or go overseas, and the husband would contest and claim he did not divorce her. Therefore, the sages instituted the signing of witnesses (Gittin 36a), because with signed witnesses, he cannot contest. 

And there is no question that according to Rabbi Eliezer, a get is invalid without witnesses of delivery, and the husband could still contest by saying he delivered it without witnesses. This is not the case, because with signed witnesses, we assume that everything was done properly (Tosafot and Rosh there). This is what Rabbi Eliezer would say: Even though there are no witnesses on it, if it was given to her in front of witnesses, it is valid, for the witnesses sign the get only for the betterment of the world (Gittin 86a). And this is what is written in Jeremiah: "Write it in a book and seal it" which is a good counsel, teaching us (Rashi Gittin 36a), so that we would not need to bring the witnesses of delivery. The law is decided according to Rabbi Eliezer, as we hold that the law follows Rabbi Eliezer in matters of divorce (Gittin 4a). However, even among the followers of Rabbi Eliezer, our early sages disagreed, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

The opinion of Rashi, Tosafot, HaMaor, the Rosh (Chapter 9, Section 7), and the Tur in Siman 133 is that a get (divorce document) without witnesses to its delivery is not valid at all, even if the witnesses signed it for his and her sake, for there is no matter of ervah (sexual prohibitions) with less than two witnesses (and also according to Rabbi Meir, as stated). Therefore, according to Rabbi Eliezer, even though "and he writes" from the verse refers to the writing and the Torah does not explicitly mention witnesses to the delivery, without witnesses it is nothing. The Torah decreed that in every matter of prohibition, it shall be established by the testimony of two witnesses, and we have explained this with the help of Heaven in Choshen Mishpat, the beginning of Siman 241, see there. And Rambam, of blessed memory, in Chapter 1, Halacha 10, explained this and this is his wording: "And from where do we know that he should give it to her before witnesses? As it says, 'By the testimony of two or three witnesses, a matter shall be established,' and it is impossible that today she is forbidden and the one who comes upon her is liable to death by the court, and tomorrow she will be permitted without witnesses, etc." End quote.

And one should not ask based on this (question), as we have learned (Gittin 86a) that according to the Torah, if a get (bill of divorce) is written in his own handwriting and there are no witnesses, neither signature witnesses nor delivery witnesses, the child (from a subsequent marriage) is legitimate. How can it be permitted without any witnesses at all? For the Rashba, of blessed memory, already wrote in Kiddushin (65b) as follows: "There, the reason is because the Torah compared a get to monetary matters, as it is written 'and he shall write her' (Deuteronomy 24:1), which implies that as long as he writes it for her, it is considered a valid document, similar to a monetary document." And we explained in Choshen Mishpat there, in the matter of the reason that in monetary matters, the admission of the party is like the testimony of a hundred witnesses because it does not impose a liability on others. That is to say, a person can do whatever he wants with his money. Similarly, with a get, the matter of the get depends only on the husband alone, who can divorce her against her will, and therefore his handwriting is like the testimony of a hundred witnesses, similar to the admission of a party in monetary matters. See there.

Our Rabbis also wrote that even after the enactment that witnesses should sign the get (bill of divorce), nevertheless, one can initially give a get with only witnesses of delivery and without any signed witnesses at all. The enactment that witnesses should sign was not made so that lacking signed witnesses would invalidate the get rabbinically or that one would be required to do so initially, but rather they instituted and taught to do so in order that there would be no need for witnesses of delivery. However, if one wishes initially to rely on witnesses of delivery, he may rely on them. And so Rashi explained (Rosh, Chapter 4, Siman 12).

However, according to the Rif and the Rambam in Chapter 1, they have a different approach to all of this, and the Raavad and the Ramban (in the Sefer HaZechut) and the Rashba and the Ran (in Chapter 9) agree with them. The Rif there elaborates to prove that even according to Rabbi Eliezer, the intention is not that only witnesses of delivery validate (the get), but rather that also witnesses of signing validate it. Ideally, it should be done with witnesses of delivery. Nevertheless, even if only witnesses signed the get and he delivered it to her privately, the get is valid because it has signed witnesses on it, similar to Rabbi Meir's opinion. According to Rabbi Meir, there is no need at all for witnesses of delivery, unlike what was written in Section 2. Rabbi Eliezer added that even with only witnesses of delivery it is valid; however, it is also valid with only signed witnesses. The Sages did not say that according to Rabbi Eliezer, even witnesses of delivery validate it. In truth, the validity of signed witnesses according to Rabbi Eliezer is not similar to Rabbi Meir's approach. According to Rabbi Meir, it is valid even if the get was not written for her sake, as we explained, whereas according to Rabbi Eliezer, if it was not written for her sake, it is completely invalid. Their primary dispute depends on this: Rabbi Eliezer interprets "and he writes" to refer to the writing of the get, while Rabbi Meir interprets "and he writes" to refer to the signing of the witnesses. However, we say that even according to Rabbi Eliezer, if the witnesses signed on the get and signed it for her sake, we consider these witnesses as if they were witnesses of delivery (as explained by the Ran there).

And one should not question this method by asking how it is possible to permit a matter of prohibited relations without witnesses, since Rambam himself wrote this, as mentioned in section 4. However, the answer is that the witnesses who signed the get (divorce document) are considered as if they were present at the time of delivery. Since there are witnesses to the essential matter and the get is found in her possession with these witnesses, it is known that the husband delivered it to her, and it is as if they themselves are testifying to the delivery (Ran there). Do not be troubled by the fact that Rambam wrote in chapter 3 of Testimony that accepting testimony in writing is only Rabbinic, but according to Torah law, it must be verbal testimony, as we have already explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 28, paragraph 17, and in section 29, paragraph 1, that this applies only to documentary evidence like a loan document, but not to documents of acquisition, and certainly not to gittin (divorce documents) and kiddushin (marriage documents), where the Torah commanded that divorce must be through a get with signed witnesses, which is considered as if they are testifying before us. The same applies to betrothal by document, as it is compared to divorce in the matter of a document of betrothal, as mentioned in section 32, paragraph 3.

And according to this opinion, a significant question arises: For it is established that according to Rabbi Eliezer, a conditional intent (al menat) validates the bill of divorce (get), and thus one may write a get even on a material that can be easily forged, as Maimonides writes in Chapter 4, Law 2, and in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Siman 124. And according to the previous opinion that without conditional intent it cannot be a valid get at all, it is understood that the woman coming to remarry must bring witnesses of delivery (eidim mesira), and if there is forgery, they will recognize it (Rashi 22b). But according to this opinion, that even according to Rabbi Eliezer we rely on the witnesses of signing (eidim chatima), how is it permissible to write on a material that can be easily forged, for according to Rabbi Meir it is forbidden, as stated in the Talmud there. However, in truth, Maimonides of blessed memory addressed this when he wrote that one may write on a material that can be easily forged, provided that it is given to her with witnesses of delivery. His intention is that if we rely solely on the witnesses of signing, it is certainly forbidden to write on a material that can be easily forged (Chidushei Maharach Siman 124, Sec 2). And you should know that this is so, for even according to the first opinion, after the enactment that they sign on the get and there is no need to bring witnesses of delivery when she comes to remarry, why is it valid on a material that can be easily forged? Rather, it must be that when it is written on a material that can be easily forged, when she comes to remarry, she is not permitted unless the witnesses of delivery are present. And this is what the Tur wrote there: even though it is on a material that can be easily forged, it is valid, provided that the witnesses of delivery are present. And it will be explained with God's help in Siman 124, see there.

On the contrary, the primary proof of the Rif, of blessed memory, is from this ordinance that witnesses should sign the get (bill of divorce) so that she will not need to bring the witnesses of delivery. If we say that without witnesses to the delivery it is not a valid get at all, what benefit is there in this ordinance, as who can say that it was given to her with witnesses of delivery? And what we wrote in section 3, the reason we rely on the signing witnesses, as they certainly acted properly, is still difficult, as even the signing witnesses are not present before us. And if you say that without witnesses to the delivery, they would not sign the get, this cannot be said because we hold that a get can be written for a man even if his wife is not with him. And still, who testifies that it was not given to her without witnesses of delivery (Ramban and Ran)? And according to the first opinion, the reason must be that even without this, one could ask why a get is written for a man without his wife; we should be concerned that he might write it in Nisan and not give it until Tishrei, and it would be an early get and invalid. Rather, it must be said that we are certain that a person does not bring calamity upon himself, and he will surely give it to her on that same day (Tosafot Bava Batra 167). And if so, according to this, it also makes sense that since a person does not bring calamity upon himself, he will surely give it to her properly with witnesses of delivery, as everyone knows that matters of sexual immorality require at least two witnesses. 

And you might say, if so, why do we need the ordinance of signing witnesses, since based on what we have explained, we should permit it even without signing witnesses? It can be said that certainly if we knew that the husband wrote this get and gave it to her, we would say so. But since there are no witnesses at all, we say that she herself wrote it or commanded it to be written. And when there are signed witnesses, we do not worry about this because the witnesses would not sign without the husband's command. And when the get is in the husband's handwriting, from the Torah it is certainly valid, but rabbinically it is invalid, and if she marries, she must leave him. This is one of the three invalid gets where the child is still legitimate but if she marries, she must leave him (Gittin 86). And the proof of the Rif from the scribe's writing and why it is invalid, who is it worse than if there are no witnesses at all, he wrote in the name of a Gaon that it is like a forged document internally, and Rabbi Ephraim, his student, disagreed with him as the Maor wrote. However, what Rabbi Eliyahu asked about why they did not also say that witnesses of delivery finalize it, we answered well in section 7 with God's help, and be precise in your studies.

And even according to the first opinion, there is a question, for in the Talmud it is said that even according to Rabbi Eliezer, who does not require it to be written for her sake, nevertheless, if invalid witnesses signed it, or if it was signed not for her sake, it is considered as if it were internally falsified and invalid. And this is the established law. What concern is there in this? And while in the case of invalid witnesses, there is a concern that the delivery might also be in their presence (Rashi 10a, s.v. "admits"), but in the case of it not being for her sake, what concern is relevant here, since it is necessary to have witnesses for the delivery? According to the Rif and the Rambam, it is understandable that there is a concern that one might rely solely on the signing witnesses. But according to the first opinion, it is difficult. And it must be said that we decree regarding signing because of writing, for if the signatures are not done for her sake, people might also say that the writing does not need to be for her sake (Tosafot 4a, s.v. "admits"). From the words of the Rambam, in Chapter 1, Law 17, and Chapter 3, Law 8, it is clear that in the case of an internally falsified document, there is no need for any reason that would cause damage, but it is inherently invalid, as we hold like the Sages that even with explicitly stated names, it is invalid because there is something inherently wrong in the signing of it (and when the witnesses are distanced from the writing, he validates there because the invalidity is not inherent in the signatures; and from his words there in Law 18, it is proven that he does not hold the opinion of Tosafot, and certainly not the concern that we have mentioned, that we might rely solely on the signing witnesses). And know that from Gittin 6b: "Who is the Tanna? Rabbi Yochanan said not like Rabbi Eliezer, etc. This needs investigation according to the Rif, who, according to his opinion, Rabbi Eliezer can also rely on the signing witnesses. And it is possible to say that this is what Abaye answers there, and it means that it is impossible to say that it requires giving for her sake since it is possible to rely solely on the signing witnesses, and investigate this well.

The Rambam wrote at the beginning of Chapter 2 (of Hilchot Gerushin): "That which is said in the Torah, 'and he writes her a document of divorce and gives it into her hand,' whether he (the husband) writes it with his own hand or instructs another to write it for him, and whether he gives it into her hand or instructs another to give it to her, it is not stated 'and he writes' except to indicate that she can only be divorced through a written document, and 'gives' to indicate that she should not take it herself." And this is clear in the Mishnah and Gemara (Gittin 7b) that the husband does not need to write it himself, but rather the scribe can write it by the husband's command. It is impossible to say that the Torah intended for the husband himself to write it, for throughout the entire Torah, a person’s agent is considered as himself. Additionally, in this verse, it is written, 'and he shall send her out of his house,' from which we derive that the husband can appoint an agent (Kiddushin 41a). Although this applies to the giving of the get, from which we also derive that the woman can appoint an agent and that an agent can appoint another agent, the writing of the get requires the scribe to hear directly from the husband, as will be explained. Nevertheless, it is no less than any other agency in the Torah. Even according to the opinion that agency is not required for writing, 'and he writes' does not refer to the husband but to the scribe. The requirement for the husband to instruct the scribe and the witnesses to sign is not due to agency but because if the husband does not command, it is not considered written for her sake and is therefore invalid (Tosafot Gittin 22b, s.v. veha). One should not question from where we derive this, as there is also proof from the Torah. In every place where it is written, 'and he writes,' it does not require that he himself writes but that it should be written. Thus, it is written regarding the mezuzah, 'and you shall write them on the doorposts of your house.' Do we say that every Jew is obligated to write his own mezuzah? Rather, the scribe writes it. A greater proof is from the portion of Tavo, where it is written, 'And Moses and the elders of Israel commanded the people, saying...and you shall set up great stones...and you shall write upon them all the words of this law...' Did every Jew write on the stones? Rather, since it was by the command of Moses and the entirety of Israel, individuals wrote and it is considered as if they all wrote. Similarly, when the scribe writes by the husband’s command, it is considered that the husband wrote it. One might ask why the scribe writes a mezuzah by himself without the command of the homeowner, while a get requires the husband’s command. This is because we require it to be written for her sake, and without his command, it is not considered for her sake, as explained. (And regarding the stones, it seems from Joshua 8 that he wrote them, and the entire Torah was written by Moses himself, and therefore it is stated, 'write for yourself,' meaning you and no other. In the end of Beshalach, where it is written, 'write this for a memorial,' it does not state 'for yourself' because there it alludes also to the act of Amalek, which is in the Prophets, and the act of Haman in Esther, as stated in the Mechilta and Megillah 7a. Pay close attention to this.)

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 1: The get (divorce document) must be written by the husband or his agent, end quote. It is clear from his words that agency is required in the writing of the get, and "and he shall write" refers to the husband. This is also explicitly evident from his words in his major work in section 123, see there. Similarly, this is implied by the Tur there, who wrote that he should write it himself or his agent, see there. According to this, what the Tur wrote at the beginning of this section, "This get must be written by the husband or he must instruct a scribe to write it," end quote, his intention is also in the capacity of agency.

However, there are some of our Rabbis who explicitly wrote that agency is not required for writing [the get] (Rashba, 22b; Ran, there). The term "and he shall write" does not refer to the husband but rather to the scribe. The prohibition against the scribe writing without the husband’s command is because, without his command, it is not considered written for her sake, as a woman is not presumed to be in a state of divorce. There is proof for this from the beginning of Zevachim, where it is explained that if we said a woman is presumed to be in a state of divorce, it would be valid even if the scribe wrote it without the husband's command (Rashba). However, since she is not presumed to be in a state of divorce, without the husband's command, it is not considered written for her sake, even if he intends for her sake and her name, because this intention is not sufficient without his command (there). 

Our Rabbis, the Tosafists, are uncertain about this matter. In one place, they wrote that agency is required for writing (9a, s.v. "even though"), and in another place, they wrote two opinions on this (22b, s.v. "and this"). The Rosh, of blessed memory (there), also brought two opinions, but his conclusion seems to be that agency is required (see there). Regarding the Rambam's opinion, it is not decisive (see there; however, from his words in Chapter 3, Halacha 16, it appears that he does not require agency, see there and examine carefully). 

There are practical differences in law between these two opinions, which will be explained with G-d's help in Siman 123, see there. Additionally, there is a disagreement among the early authorities whether we require "sons of severance" in the writing of the get, and this will also be explained with G-d's help there.

Furthermore, it seems to me that there is a practical difference between these two opinions regarding a deaf-mute's get (divorce document). Rabbeinu Yerucham wrote that a deaf-mute's get has a different formula than standard gittin (divorce documents). In standard gittin, the husband speaks on his own behalf, but in a deaf-mute's get, the court speaks for him, as will be explained in Siman 121. Some understand from his words that a get is written like other gittin, and the formula of Rabbeinu Yerucham is an addition to all gittin, as mentioned there (Beit Shmuel in section 9 and Tzemach Tzedek in Siman 68 quoting Tosefot Yom Tov). However, many disagree with this and hold that this is the specific formula for a deaf-mute's get and nothing more (Shu”t Beit Ya’akov Siman 123 and other great authorities). It is also explicitly stated in the words of Rabbeinu Yerucham that this is an enactment of the Geonim. It seems to me that certainly, if the writing of the get requires agency, a deaf-mute cannot have the scribe write like all other gittin because a deaf-mute cannot appoint an agent. Therefore, the court must write based on his gestures, and it becomes a Rabbinic get that nullifies Rabbinic kiddushin. However, if agency is not required but merely the husband's command, then the scribe can write based on his gestures just as he would based on the command of a hearing person. This opinion seems baseless because even if agency is required for the writing, a deaf-mute can appoint an agent for his get, which is Rabbinic, as some have suggested. This has no basis at all, and throughout the Talmud and the decisors, it is clear that one who cannot appoint an agent cannot do so even in Rabbinic matters (as is explicitly stated in Tosafot Gittin 64b s.v. "Shani" see there, and the words of the Beit Shmuel who wrote this opinion are astonishing. Investigate this thoroughly).

It seems to me that even according to the authorities who hold that agency is not required for the writing of a get (divorce document), nevertheless, when the husband instructs the scribe to write it, it is considered as if he is appointing him as an agent. And these authorities are only saying that it is possible to instruct even someone who is not fit to be an agent, as will be explained in Siman 123, or if the husband himself is not fit to appoint an agent as per the previous law. But in a case where it is appropriate, it is considered agency. For even in any appointment of an agent, it is not necessary to explicitly say to the agent, "I am making you my agent for such-and-such," but rather to simply tell him, "Go and do it." And indeed, in the case of terumah (tithing), it is considered agency when one says, "Whoever wishes to separate terumah, let him come and separate it" (Nedarim 36b), even though in terumah, it cannot be done without agency (and what the Ran wrote there is regarding vows, because he is not designating him specifically, as Tosafot wrote in Gittin 66, and the commentator there). And from the Tur itself, there is clear proof for this. For he requires agency in the writing of the get, as he wrote in Siman 123, and nevertheless wrote here, "or instruct the scribe to write it," which implies that through the instruction, the scribe becomes an agent. Therefore, in all the arrangements of gittin, when the husband tells the scribe, "Write me a get," etc., it is considered as agency. And therefore, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Siman 154, in the order of the get, do not mention agency there, because this and that are the same. And regarding the agency of the get, it is explained there in Siman 97 that he should say to him, "I appoint you to be my agent to deliver the get," etc., in order to inform him that he is making him an agent for delivery, as explained there in Siman 25. See there.

Since the husband must write the get (bill of divorce) himself or through his agent, it follows that the parchment, ink, and quill must belong to him, and he must also pay the scribe's fee. This is also taught in the Mishnah (Bava Batra 167a) that the husband gives the scribe's fee. Nevertheless, our Sages said (ibid. 168a) that nowadays we do not practice this way; rather, the wife gives the scribe's fee. This is a rabbinic enactment for the sake of preventing agunot (women unable to remarry because their husbands refuse to grant a divorce), lest the husband refuse to pay the scribe and leave her unable to remarry. Therefore, they enacted that she should pay the scribe, and the Sages transferred ownership of that money to the husband (Gittin 2a), making it as if he had paid him, since the authority of the court can confiscate property (Rashi). (And what is said, perhaps the truth is as the Ramban and the Ran wrote there.) And this is what we learned in the Mishnah (Gittin 22a): the woman writes her get and transfers it to her husband, who then gives it back to her for the divorce (Rashi). From the language of the Rambam in Chapter 2, Law 4, who wrote "the woman gives the scribe's fee in every place," it seems that after the enactment, it is required that she pay the scribe's fee for all gittin (divorces). However, in the Get Procedure of the Rosh, brought by the Tur at the end of Chapter 154, it is written that the husband should pay the scribe's fee, but if the woman pays it, the get is still valid. This implies that even after the enactment, ideally, the husband should pay the scribe's fee, but if he refuses and she pays it, the get is valid because the Sages transferred that money to the husband to prevent her from becoming an agunah (Beit Yosef). This is also explained in the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, which wrote that they permitted the woman to pay the scribe's fee (and similarly, the Hagahot Maimoniot in the name of Sefer HaTerumot). Indeed, the words of the Rambam are puzzling, as it seems that if the Sages enacted that the get is valid if she pays, it does not mean it is obligatory. Therefore, it seems to me that the Rambam also meant that she is permitted to pay. A proof for this is that the Tur also wrote in this chapter that for the sake of preventing agunot, the Sages enacted that the woman should pay the scribe's fee and then transfer it to the husband. This must mean that she is permitted to do so, not that it is obligatory, as is evident from the Get Procedure he wrote in Chapter 154. Therefore, the intention of the Rambam is also that she is permitted to do so. And when the Rambam wrote "in every place," he meant that one should not say that since the Sages only permitted it for the sake of preventing agunot, it only applies where there is a concern of becoming an agunah, such as when she wants to travel abroad and seeks a get. But in a case where there is no such concern, the Sages did not permit it. Therefore, he says that in every place, she can pay the scribe's fee after the enactment. (The Beit Yosef and the Gra in their commentary, Section 5, understood the words of the Rambam literally and created a dispute between him and the Rosh. However, it seems to me as I have explained.)

From the language of the Talmud and the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) that we have brought, it is clear that when the woman gives the payment, she does not need to now transfer the payment to the husband. Rather, the Sages have transferred it to him. And this is the language of the Shulchan Aruch in Section 1, where it is written that the Sages instituted that the woman gives the scribe's payment and they transferred it to the husband. However, the language of the Tur that we have brought is problematic in this matter, for he wrote that the woman should give the scribe's payment and transfer it to the husband. His language implies that she now needs to transfer it to him (and the Perisha wrote that this is not precise, and this requires further examination).

The Tur wrote that the husband must write [the get] etc., and even if his agent writes it, it must belong to the husband. Therefore, the scribe must give the ink and parchment to the husband as a gift before writing, and the husband must pay him. However, due to the decree concerning agunot (chained women), the Sages instituted that the wife may pay the scribe. The Rosh similarly wrote in the order of the get that the scribe gives the parchment and ink as a gift to the husband, for we require that the get be his, and the husband pays the scribe. If the wife pays, the get is still valid. 

The explanation of the matter is that although the Sages instituted that the money the wife gives to the scribe for his payment automatically includes the parchment and ink, nevertheless, the scribe must gift the parchment and ink to the husband. Even if the husband himself pays the scribe, the scribe must gift the ink and parchment to him, as the money given to the scribe does not acquire the parchment and ink for the husband, since money does not acquire movable items without an act of drawing them (meshicha). Therefore, the scribe must hand the parchment and ink to the husband and say, "I give this to you as a gift," and the husband must lift them a tefach (handbreadth) to acquire them through lifting (hagbahah). It appears to me that he must lift them three tefachim because in Choshen Mishpat, siman 198, there are two opinions regarding lifting, one of which requires three tefachim to remove the status of lavud (connected). 

What the Tur and the Rosh wrote about giving them as a gift is not precise, as they could also be acquired through purchase, since money is taken for them. However, they used definitive language because sometimes the scribe only takes payment for his labor, and the parchment and ink he gives for free. Additionally, if the scribe writes for free, he certainly has the authority to do so and there is no prohibition, as he can say, "It is as if I have been paid." In that case, he must give them only as a gift.

And there is no need to question after the sages have granted him the money for the sake of the validity of the get (divorce document), automatically they have also granted him the parchment and the ink, since without this the get would not be valid. And it cannot be said that the decree of the sages was only regarding the scribe's fee and not the parchment and the ink, for it is explicitly proven in the Talmud (21a) that the matter of a woman writing her get also pertains to the parchment, as seen there (the Talmud brings this regarding a tablet, and so too the Tosafot there 20b: s.v. "a woman" in the name of Sefat Emet), for it can be said that the sages only decreed that her giving should be like his giving. And since in his giving, it is necessary for the scribe to grant him the parchment and the ink, her giving is not superior to his giving, and why would the sages decree that it should be as if the scribe granted him the parchment and the ink, since there is no impediment to the get being given, for the scribe is able to grant it, and there is no concern of causing her to be an agunah (a woman chained to a marriage). Additionally, it is possible to say according to the precise wording of the Tur and the Rosh that certainly where she is giving the scribe's fee according to the decree of the sages, there is no need for the granting of the parchment and the ink, for the sages enacted a complete decree so that no further acquisition is needed. But in a case where he is giving the scribe's fee, where there is no decree of the sages, it is necessary for the scribe to grant him the parchment and the ink, for money does not effect acquisition as written. And according to this, what they wrote that the scribe should give the parchment and the ink as a gift to the husband applies only to their statement that follows that the husband needs to pay the scribe's fee, and not to what they wrote afterwards regarding the decree of the sages that she should give. However, all the great later authorities did not hold this way in their writings, and in every matter, it is necessary to effect acquisition. And this is also implied, for if not, they should have explained it so, for it is not the way of the decisors to obscure but to clarify. Therefore, the first answer must be said.

And there is still a great question to ask about this: why is it necessary to transfer ownership of the parchment and the ink, since the scribe is the agent of the husband? Even for those authorities who do not require agency in the writing of the get (divorce document), as we explained in section 16, that by his command it is considered agency, and certainly according to the Rosh and the Tur who hold that agency is required, as stated in section 14, and the principle that a person's agent is like the person himself. Therefore, when the scribe gives the parchment and the ink according to his agency, it is as if the husband himself is giving it. This is explicitly proven in Choshen Mishpat, section 183, that when one sends an agent to buy something and the agent buys it with his own money, the item is acquired for the sender even though the money was not formally transferred by way of acquisition. The reason is that everything the agent does is as if the sender himself did it. Furthermore, above in section 35, subsection 3, it is explained that when one sends an agent to betroth a woman and does not give him money for the betrothal but tells him to betroth her with any money he wishes, he cannot appoint another agent in his place because matters (mili) cannot be transferred to an agent. This clearly shows that when the agent gives his own money for the betrothal, it is considered as if it were the sender's money. Similarly, the money for betrothal must be the husband's, just as the parchment and ink for the get must be, and nevertheless, we say that what the agent gives is considered as if the sender himself gave it.

However, the explanation of the matter is as follows: Certainly, when the husband appoints someone as an agent to complete the entire matter, such as when he says to three people, "Write and give a bill of divorce to my wife," even if they write it from their own initiative, they stand in his place, and his agent is like him. But if the matter is not completed by this agent, such as when he tells a scribe to write the bill of divorce and the delivery will be by another person, or the husband himself will deliver it, then this agent is not an agent for all matters like the husband himself and does not stand in his place except for what he accepted upon himself, which is only to write the bill of divorce and not to acquire the parchment and ink based on his agency, unless he explicitly transfers it to him. And this is what we have learned (Gittin 66a): One who was cast into a pit and said, "Anyone who hears my voice should write a bill of divorce for my wife," those who hear can write and give it without any transfer, because in the case of one cast into a pit, when he says "write," it is as if he said "give," as will be explained. And since he made them agents to complete the matter, they stand in his place.

And this is what the Tur wrote in the name of the Ramah: "If a man tells witnesses, 'Write a get (divorce document) and give it to my wife,' they do not need to transfer ownership of the paper to him before writing it. Rather, even if they write it from their own resources and give it to her, since they are acting on his behalf, when they give it to her as his messengers, it is as if they gave it to the husband, and subsequently, the husband gave it to his wife. Since they are acting as his agents in delivering it, he effectively acquires it for the purpose of divorcing her, and thus the husband's acquisition and the wife's divorce occur simultaneously." This is the end of his words. The explanation is that since he appointed them as agents to deliver it to her, and at the time of delivery, the agent is like the husband himself, it is as if the husband delivered it to her. Consequently, it is considered as if at that moment he transferred it to the husband, and his acquisition and the divorce occur simultaneously. However, when they are not his agents for delivering the get, this reasoning does not apply.

However, according to this, the husband acquires the parchment only at the time of giving, which means that at the time of writing, the parchment was not his. And behold, the Tur and the Rosh require that the parchment be transferred to the husband before the writing. It is possible that they wrote this as an enhancement (hiddur), that it is better to transfer it before the writing. But if it was transferred to him after the writing, it is still valid, for the main requirement is that at the time of giving, it should be his. Indeed, there are those who hold this view (as the Beit Yosef wrote in the name of the Ramban, that if the parchment belongs to her, there is no need to transfer it to him before the writing, only before the giving). The Levush also wrote similarly, stating: if it was written first and then given to him, it is still valid, but it is better to give it to the husband first so that the scribe does not forget to give it to the husband afterwards. (According to the Rema, there is no need to distinguish between the completion of the act and part of the act, as he wrote in section 22. Rather, because giving it to the woman is like receiving it for the husband's benefit, and the husband gives it to her, as his agent is like himself. The Drisha also wrote this. However, from the language of the Mordechai at the end of the chapter "Hakkabel" in the name of Rabbeinu Yoel, it seems to me as I have written. And the Bach wrote that Rabbeinu Yoel's opinion is like the Rema. The Bach also wrote that regarding the primary giving of the parchment and the ink, even according to the Rosh and the Tur, it is not a disqualifying factor after the fact. This is difficult to understand, and it does not seem so. The Beit Shmuel and the later authorities also did not take this view, and the Levush wrote similarly).

And as the Rosh and the Tur said, so wrote several of the poskim. And these are the words of the Mordechai in the laws of divorce: The parchment, ink, and quill must belong to the husband, and he should give them to the scribe. If he does not have them, others may purchase them for the husband because we require "and he wrote and gave." Similarly, if the scribe wrote on his own parchment at the husband's command, it is valid, provided that he gives it to him afterward to be his. Nevertheless, it is preferable to give it to the husband first, lest the scribe forget to give it to him afterward as a gift. If the quill belongs to others, it is not invalid because the owner of the quill does not mind since nothing remains from the quill in the get, unlike the ink. So wrote the Sefer HaTerumah and the Hagahot Maimoni in chapter 3, who stated that we need not be concerned about the quill at all. The Tur and the Rosh also did not mention the quill. It turns out that according to our Rabbis, even after the fact, it is invalid if the scribe did not at least transfer ownership of the parchment and ink to the husband before giving the get. Ideally, he should transfer it to him before writing the get. Some are stringent from the outset also regarding the quill, but after the fact, there is no invalidation with the quill.

However, the Rambam, of blessed memory, did not mention at all the requirement of transferring ownership of the parchment and the ink. Also, at the beginning of the laws of divorce, where he lists the things that invalidate a get (divorce document), he does not mention at all that the parchment and ink must belong to the husband. It is also difficult to say that by mentioning in chapter 2 that the woman pays the scribe’s fee, he implies that the parchment and ink are included in the scribe's fee, for even if this is true, he should have mentioned that the parchment and ink must belong to the husband, just like if the scribe writes for free. Therefore, it seems to me that he holds the opinion we wrote in section 21, that since the scribe is his agent, it is as if the agent is like himself, and even if he did not transfer ownership of the parchment and ink to him, it is considered as his own. Alternatively, it could be that it was obvious to him that everything must be the husband's, and he did not need to mention it. Also, he holds that everything is included in the scribe's fee, as we wrote. This is also the opinion of the Ramban and the Ran, of blessed memory, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

And these are the words of the Ramban, of blessed memory, on what the Sages said, that she pays the scribe, and the Sages established that the scribe should transfer ownership to the husband. He wrote, and from this it is understood that the ink, the parchment, and the quill all belong to the scribe. Therefore, the bill of divorce (get) is valid, and there is no concern because he sells everything to the husband for the same currency that she gives to the scribe for the get, whether it is for the parchment, the ink, or his effort and toil. And the Sages transferred ownership to the husband, not as those who are meticulous say, that everything should be literally transferred to the husband, but rather the Sages transferred it to him, and even though he did not physically pull anything, it is valid, etc. For what is written "and he shall write" means by his hand or by his messenger, excluding her or her messenger. Therefore, since the Sages transferred the money of the scribe to the husband, this is not "and she wrote" but it is valid because he becomes the husband's employee and agent with this currency. However, if everything belonged to the woman, even though we learned that the woman can write her own get, maybe she needs to actually transfer the get itself to the husband, for the Sages only established the transfer of the scribe's money, etc., but they did not establish the transfer of her property to the husband, etc. And so it appears from the words of Rashi that she indeed needs to give it to the husband or his messenger to acquire it. However, she writes it with her own property and transfers it, and she does not need to transfer it initially, for in the writing, the husband’s messenger is involved when he says "write," and thus it is considered as if he wrote it. And regarding "and he shall give," we require it to be his. Therefore, she transfers to him the written and signed get, and he divorces her with it. So Rashi, of blessed memory, explained. End of the words of the Ramban, of blessed memory (brought in Beit Yosef).

And these are the words of the Ran (in the second chapter): We learn that the husband does not initially need to provide the parchment, the ink, and the quill from his own resources, as some authors have written in the context of preparing gittin (divorce documents). Rather, with that single coin that the Rabbis instituted, the scribe acquires the parchment and transfers ownership to the husband, as he (the scribe) acts as his agent and acquires it for him. However, if the parchment belongs to the scribe, some have written that the husband or his agent must formally acquire it because the scribe does not acquire it on behalf of the husband when it is his own. Others, however, say that this is not necessary, for with the payment she (the wife) gives to the scribe, the Rabbis have instituted that the husband acquires the parchment, the ink, and the scribe's effort and labor. Nevertheless, when she herself writes the get (divorce document), the Rabbis did not institute such a provision, etc. So ends his words.

From these words, it is clarified that when she pays the scribe's fee, if the scribe buys the parchment, no transfer of ownership is required because he acts as her agent and acquires it on her behalf. However, if the parchment initially belongs to the scribe, according to the Ran, a formal transfer of ownership (hakna'ah) is necessary because something in a person's possession cannot transfer to another's possession without a formal act of acquisition, not even through oneself. Some say that even in this case, no transfer of ownership is needed because the Rabbis granted it to him, which is the opinion of the Ramban as mentioned. 

Consequently, if the husband pays the scribe's fee and the parchment initially belonged to the scribe, according to all opinions, a formal transfer of ownership is necessary because the Sages did not establish a remedy for this situation. If the scribe buys the parchment now, no transfer of ownership is required because he acts as the husband's agent and acquires it on his behalf. When the woman provides the parchment, she needs to transfer ownership to him at least before giving it. 

In this matter, the Ramban and the Ran differ from the Rosh and the Tur and other authorities. According to the Rosh and the Tur, the scribe's fee granted by the Sages does not enable him to acquire the parchment and the ink. Therefore, in every situation, it is necessary to transfer ownership to the husband. According to the Ramban and the Ran, the fee includes the acquisition of the parchment and the ink. They also differ when the husband pays the fee.

Our masters, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 1: The get (divorce document) must be written by the husband or his agent, and even if his agent writes it, it must belong to the husband. Therefore, it has become customary, when the husband is present, for the scribe to give him the parchment and ink as a gift before writing. Some say that even the quill and other writing tools should be given as well, and the husband pays the scribe's fee. Because of [the concern for] agunot (deserted wives), the sages decreed that the wife pays the scribe's fee, and it is transferred to the husband. This is written to indicate that this custom is dependent on practice and applies only when the husband is present. However, if he is not present, such as when he is in a hurry to go abroad and said to three people, "Write and give a get," or if he was thrown into a pit and said, "Write a get and give it to my wife," there is no need for this transfer (Rema). This clearly implies that they hold like the opinion of the Ramban, which we mentioned, that the transfer is not essential, as the scribe's fee includes and is effective for transferring the parchment and ink. It is only customary to make the transfer to fulfill the opinion of the Rosh and the Tur.

There is a question here because, since it is uncommon, they did not require an act of acquisition at all, even though there is no payment to the scribe. It must be said that the reason is as the Tur stated in the name of the Ramah, that wherever one is an agent for delivering the get (divorce document), no act of acquisition is needed, as he wrote. Therefore, they hold the view of the Tur and not of the Ramban. However, in truth, the Ramban must also agree with this reasoning, for the Ramban himself wrote evidence from one who was thrown into a pit, that no act of acquisition is needed, as mentioned there. 

And there is someone who wrote that the Ramban does not hold the opinion of the Ramah (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 2), but this is not clear, for the Ramban himself brought this evidence. Therefore, the Shulchan Aruch did not mention the acquisition of the parchment and ink except when the woman writes, as mentioned in Siman 123, where everyone agrees, as written. And similarly, if the scribe writes for free, certainly an act of acquisition is needed, and they did not mention this because it is obvious that how else would he acquire it if not through an act of acquisition? Or it is possible that they hold, as written in the opinion of the Rambam, that an act of acquisition is never needed except when she writes, for even if he writes for free, in any case, his agency is like her own, as mentioned in paragraph 26 (and all the words of the Beit Shmuel in subparagraph 2 need examination, and the Tevuot Shor of the Gaon of Lissa already questioned him).

And some have asked, based on what was stated, that when the paper belongs to her, according to all opinions, she needs to transfer ownership, and it was explained that the transfer of ownership is effective even after writing. And behold, there is a requirement of transfer of ownership between writing and delivery, and we should invalidate it just as we invalidate when it is cut from something attached [to the ground] between writing and delivery, as will be explained, because it lacks cutting (Ran in the Mishnah that a woman writes her own get). And they answered that specifically cutting, which is a deficiency of an act in the body of the get, invalidates, but not the transfer of ownership, which is not in the body of the get (there, and it requires further investigation from Chullin 135. And it can be resolved). Moreover, the Torah only excluded something that cannot be at the time of delivery, such as something attached [to the ground], because if it is cut at the time of delivery, it would be like taking your get from the ground, unlike transfer of ownership, which can be at the time of delivery itself (Tosafot Gittin).

If one stole paper or parchment and wrote a bill of divorce on it and gave it to her, it is valid even before the owner has despaired of recovering it, for he acquired it through a change of name and a change of action, and he is only liable for the value to the owner, and the bill of divorce remains valid according to the law in her possession. This is not considered a reversible change when the writing is erased, even on parchment where erasure is possible, because erased parchment is still called erased parchment (as explained in Maharshal, Choshen Mishpat 4:4). However, if one stole a written bill of divorce, such as if he instructed a scribe to write a bill of divorce on the scribe's parchment and paid him for it, and after the scribe wrote it, he stole it from him and did not pay him, and used it to divorce his wife, she is not considered divorced, for there is no change. This is only before the owner has despaired, but if he gave it to her after the owner had despaired, it seems to me that she is divorced, for when it came into her possession, it involved both despair and a change of ownership. Even though before she received it, the bill of divorce was not his, nevertheless, the transfer of ownership and the bill of divorce come together. In practice, this matter requires further consideration.

If the scribe willingly gave him the get (bill of divorce) and agreed with him that he will pay him at a later time, even if he has not yet paid him, the get is not considered stolen in his possession, since the get was given to him willingly, he just owes him money (Choshen Mishpat 5). However, if the scribe gave him the get on the condition that he would pay him immediately and he did not pay, certainly the get is considered stolen in his possession (ibid). 

There are those who want to say that even if a specific time was set for payment, she should not remarry until he pays or the time passes and the scribe does not object. Otherwise, there is concern that the scribe might go in and out demanding the money, and the sale would be retroactively annulled if he does not pay him, resulting in the get not being his, and it would not help that she agrees to pay the scribe, because if the get were hers, she would need to transfer it to him, as the Rabbis did not establish a transfer for something that is hers, as explained (Taz 3).

There are those who disagree with this, as it is explained in Choshen Mishpat 190 that when one sells his field due to its poor quality, even if he goes in and out demanding the money, the sale is not annulled. And there is no sale due to poor quality more than a parchment on which a get is written, which is of no use to the scribe at all. Therefore, the transfer is not annulled because of this (Pitchei Teshuva in the name of the Geonim). Furthermore, it is explained there that if he converted it into a loan, the transfer is completed even if he goes in and out demanding the money. Therefore, if he says, "The pulling will acquire it for you, and the money will be a loan with you," he acquires it immediately (see there).

Thus, here with a get, where the scribe knows he needs to deliver it to the wife, and the get must belong to the husband, certainly his intention is to transfer it immediately (so it seems to me), and the money will remain a loan. Nevertheless, in practice, it is certainly proper to be careful to pay the scribe immediately. And it seems clear to me that even if initially he did not acquire the get, such as if it was stolen in his possession as mentioned, if he later paid for the get and it became his, he can take the get immediately from the woman and re-deliver it to her in the presence of witnesses, and she will be divorced then.

There are those who have written that regarding a stolen get (divorce document), it is stated that if he has not paid for it, it is still considered stolen in his possession. Sometimes, even if he has paid for it, it is still considered stolen, such as if he took it against the owner's will. In such a case, even if he paid for it, it is considered stolen. And even though we hold that if someone is coerced into selling and says "I want to" (the sale is valid), this is only if he explicitly says "I want to," but not if he does not say "I want to," as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 205.

However, in truth, this ruling does not apply to a get. If he stole the paper and wrote the get on it, he acquires it through the change (in the paper) as has been explained. And if he stole a written get, in any case, how was it written? If it was not written by the husband's instruction, it is invalid anyway because it is not written for her sake. And if it was written by the husband's instruction, the scribe was willing to be his agent for writing the get and, consequently, when he paid him according to the agreed amount, it became his (the husband's). Unless we say that afterward, the scribe retracted from his agency and wishes to keep the get for himself for personal purposes, and also if he did not transfer ownership of the paper to the husband before writing the get, this requires further investigation.

And all of this applies when the scribe wrote on his own parchment and with his own ink. However, if the parchment and ink belong to the husband and he hired the scribe for his writing, and the scribe wrote the get (divorce document) and it was stolen from his hand and not paid for, then it depends on the dispute explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 306, regarding whether an artisan acquires ownership through the improvement of an object or not. This is a matter of legal uncertainty as discussed there. Some say that in the case of writing a get, the concept of an artisan acquiring ownership through the improvement of an object does not apply. Just as it is said in Bava Kamma 99a regarding wool and dyes, if the wool and dyes belong to the employer, the artisan only takes a wage for dyeing, because the improvement comes from the dyes and not from the artisan who dyed it (Rashba there). Similarly, in the case of a get, when the paper and ink belong to the husband, the scribe has no involvement in the improvement of the object, as the ink is what enhances it, not the artisan. Therefore, even according to the opinion that an artisan acquires ownership through the improvement of an object, in the case of a get, he does not acquire it (Turei Zahav). According to this, if the ink belongs to the scribe, then this principle might apply. However, it is possible to say that in the case of a get, this principle does not apply at all, because the idea of an artisan acquiring ownership through the improvement of an object only applies if the improvement is universally valuable, such as wood to make into a vessel or wool to dye, which is considered an improvement for everyone. But in the case of a get, the improvement is only for this particular husband and not for others. What ownership could the artisan have if not for his own purposes, and this improvement would exist even without the writing? Nevertheless, the matter requires further study and consideration.

However, regarding the signatures of the witnesses, it is certainly the case that the principle of "the craftsman acquires through the improvement of the vessel" does not apply. Therefore, if they were hired for a certain amount for signing and they signed without receiving the payment, there is no concern about this even according to the first opinion. The reason is that while it is permissible for the scribe to take payment for his writing, it is forbidden for the witnesses to take payment for their testimony. The allowance for witnesses to receive payment is due to compensation for their time or other reasons explained in Siman 130, and this does not pertain to the essence of the get (bill of divorce). However, it could be argued that although it is forbidden to take payment for testimony, perhaps taking payment for signing so that the document endures for a long time might be permitted, but this requires further investigation because a get does not need to endure for a long time. Nevertheless, as I have written, the principle of "the craftsman acquires through the improvement of the vessel" does not apply at all to a get for the reasons explained in the previous section.

The sages taught in the Mishnah (Bava Batra 167a) that one may write a get (divorce document) for a man even if his wife is not with him, as they write and sign it for him, and he can use it to divorce his wife whenever he wishes. Even though his wife is not present when the get, written and signed, is given to him, it does not require her consent, as she can be divorced against her will (Rashbam). According to this, following Rabbeinu Gershom's decree that it is forbidden to divorce a wife against her will, a get is not written for a man if his wife does not consent to the divorce. This is the custom in all Jewish communities, and those who write and sign a get without the wife's consent are penalized. However, if the man has distanced himself from his wife to a faraway place and has left her in a state of being unable to remarry (agunah), if the court in the man's location clearly knows that his intention is to trap her in this state, it is a mitzvah for them to endeavor to send a get through an agent to the court in the wife's location. The court will call the wife, and if she agrees to accept it, they instruct the agent to deliver it to her. Alternatively, if he is overseas and it is difficult to send an agent, the practice has been to send a get via postal mail, appointing an agent where the wife resides, who will act as an agent on his behalf without him being present, as will be explained in detail in Siman 141. The court arranges the get and sends it via postal mail to the court in the wife's location, and if she agrees to accept it, the agent delivers it to her. This is the custom.

One might ask, according to the Talmudic law, we write a bill of divorce (get) for a man without his wife being present, even when they are both in the same city. Why are we not concerned that he might give her the get at a later time, making it predated, and a predated get is invalid? The answer to this is that we are not concerned about this because it is established that a person does not bring misfortune upon himself before its time (Tosafot, Gittin). Presumably, his intention is to give it to her immediately. Furthermore, a get that is given publicly and requires witnesses to its delivery creates a public knowledge (kol) that she was divorced after the time of the writing (Tosafot, Bava Metzia 19a). The words of the Nimukei Yosef in Bava Batra are somewhat puzzling, but according to what the Nimukei Yosef writes in Bava Metzia, his words can be reconciled. However, this is not the opinion of the Tosafot in Bava Metzia in the passage beginning "When" (d.h. eimat).

When writing a get (divorce document) for a man, even if his wife is with him, the witnesses need to recognize that this man is named such-and-such, and this woman is named such-and-such, and that this woman is his wife. They also need to know that the names of his father and her father are correct (as stated in the Mishneh Torah, Hilchot Gerushin 2:3). The reason for this is because we are concerned that perhaps it is another man, and he intends to collect the ketubah for another woman (as explained by the Rashbam). Even if they recognize the man, if they do not recognize the woman, we are concerned that perhaps she is not his wife but rather another woman whose husband has the same name, and he will give the get to the other woman so she can collect the ketubah (as explained by the Tosafot). However, regarding the prohibition, there is no concern that he will give the get to another man's wife and render her permitted unlawfully, because the witnesses of the delivery need to recognize them at the time of the delivery (as stated there). So why is recognition required at the time of writing? Certainly, there is no concern for this, and the other will divorce her with a valid get. The concern is that after she collects her ketubah, he will deliver this get to her again, and she will collect the ketubah a second time, since we hold that if she produces a get without a ketubah, she can collect her ketubah, as stated in Siman 100. Therefore, even if they recognize them, if they do not recognize their names, we are concerned that they might have switched their names, and we do not rely on writing based on subsequent questioning (as stated by the Beit Yosef). Rather, they need to recognize them before the writing.

Some say that the scribe also needs to recognize them (the couple) because he needs to hear from the husband and write it for his sake and for her sake. Therefore, ideally, he should recognize them before he writes (Chamudei Moshe). Similarly, the Rambam wrote in Chapter 2, Law 3, see there. And this is the main ruling, as we hold according to Rabbi Eliezer that the primary requirement is the writing (Gra).

When his wife is not with him, it is necessary to know that he has a wife named such-and-such, because otherwise there is still a concern that he may write [a get, a bill of divorce] for another woman whose husband's name is the same as his, as mentioned (Beit Shmuel). And know that in all this, even when it has not been established in the city that there is another person with the same name, we still worry that there might be (such a person). And if it has been established that there is another person in the city with the same name, it is possible that we need to investigate the wife of the second person, perhaps her name is also the same as the wife of this one, and then there is a different ruling in this matter. And so the Sages said (there) that when there are two people in the city whose names and their wives' names are the same, one cannot divorce except in the presence of the other, because we worry that one might write a get and give it to the wife of the other and divorce her on his behalf (see Tosafot there, s.v. "VeLichush"). And this will be explained in Siman 136, with God's help.

This concern about recognition is only rabbinic, for according to Torah law we do not worry about this at all. Therefore, the Sages said (Gittin 66a) that in times of danger, such as when a person is close to death, or thrown into a pit, or sitting in prison, or sent to distant places, and similar circumstances, they write and give the get (bill of divorce) even if they do not recognize [the husband], for they do not delay the get because of this. It appears to me that nevertheless, after giving the get into her hand, they should clarify everything as much as possible. For although we do not delay the writing and giving of the get due to concerns of agunah (a woman who cannot remarry), afterwards, why not clarify when it is possible to clarify? However, if even afterwards it is not possible to clarify, we do not make her an agunah because of this, and we permit her to remarry (so it appears to me).

And since this concern is only of Rabbinic origin, therefore, if after the fact they wrote and signed without recognition, if it is later clarified that this is indeed a man and his wife whose names are such and such, we do not say that since they were not recognized at the time of writing it is not for their sake, but rather there is no disqualification in this and it is valid after the fact (Chokhmat Adam 8). And it is possible that even if it is not clarified later, nevertheless, since we see that the woman has the get in her hand and her name and her husband's name are as written in the get, we do not prevent her from remarrying, because since it is impossible to clarify now, there is no greater time of danger than this, that she should remain an agunah forever (Tur Gittin).
