And this is not comparable to the case where it is established in the city that there are two men whose names and their wives' names are the same, as will be explained in Siman 136, where even after the fact it prevents until she brings proof that she was divorced in the presence of the other, because there is still a concern that perhaps the other wrote it and lost it, and this one's wife found it (Rashi 24b), and this concern is a Torah-level concern (Tur Gittin), as it implies in the Talmud (Yevamot 116a), that in matters where a person is careful, we do not worry about it falling, but in matters where one is not careful, we do worry about it falling, see there. Moreover, even if we say that this is not a Torah-level concern, nevertheless, it is considered as having a defect before us when there is another couple with the same names as this couple, but in general, where this is only a concern in general, we say that even after the fact it does not prevent. However, from the general language of the Poskim it implies that we do not permit without recognition, because in any case it needs to be clarified that the witnesses of delivery knew that this is the man and his wife and their names are such and such. For although in a time of danger the Sages permitted giving without recognition, but not in a time of no danger, they do not permit even after the fact, and so it is proper to instruct, and we do not leniently permit in the prohibition of a married woman, even in Rabbinic matters (so it seems to me).

Since it is of rabbinic origin, it does not require complete testimony for recognition. It suffices even with the testimony of one witness, or even by a woman or a relative, because it is a matter that is likely to be revealed, and therefore we are not stringent with the testimony for recognition that is of rabbinic origin. Thus, our sages said (Yevamot 39a) regarding the recognition in the matter of chalitza, which will be explained in Siman 169. Also, the agent (shaliach) is believed, even though he has a vested interest since he receives payment for his agency. Nevertheless, because it is a matter likely to be revealed, he is believed (Beit Shmuel). 

Anyone who has been established in the city for thirty days as a husband and wife, and their names are known, we do not suspect them further, and testify based on this. The custom is to write the father's name based on the individual's testimony, and similarly, the mother's name, even if the parents' names have not been established for thirty days (ibid). Some say that the parents' names also need to be established for thirty days (Aruch HaShulchan, Siman 10, quoting the Beit Yosef). The leniency regarding writing the parents' names based on the individual's testimony does not have a sound reason to differentiate. It is possible that since, post facto, it is valid even without the parents' names, although if there is a mistake it is invalid, we are not stringent in this matter. Additionally, if the parents did not reside here, it is difficult to find testimony on this most times, and it is like a place of danger. Therefore, we rely on them alone. 

There is an opinion that specifically when he gives her the get (divorce document) in our presence, and we know that this is his wife, we rely on the parents' names based on the individual's testimony. But if he does not divorce her in our presence, we do not rely on his recognition of the father's name (Taz). These words are reasonable because relying on his own name alone is like being established in the same town for two years, where there are many people named Yosef in the marketplace. Therefore, we need testimony on the father's name and do not rely on him alone.

A scribe should not write it, and witnesses should not sign it until the husband tells them to write and sign it. Without his command, it is not considered done for its specific purpose. All the more so according to those who require agency in writing, the husband should instruct the scribe in front of witnesses and tell the witnesses, "Listen to what I am commanding him" (Choshen Mishpat, Siman 11). It is clear that there is no need to worry about this after the fact (ibid.). Additionally, in the procedure of the get (divorce document) as explained in Siman 154, this is not mentioned. 

The reason it is required initially, in my opinion, is because according to Rabbi Meir, the main thing is the witnesses signing the get. They need to know that the get was written by the husband’s command. Even though Rabbi Meir does not require the writing to be for its specific purpose at all, since we hold like Rabbi Elazar that the main thing is the writing of the get, and the Sages also established that witnesses should sign the get, as explained, we are stringent initially according to both opinions. After the fact, it is not mandatory because neither according to Rabbi Meir nor Rabbi Elazar is this required, and it is merely an additional stringency. We are accustomed to be stringent in matters of divorce beyond what is required by law, as evident in the Talmud (Gittin 72b, Tosafot s.v. "Hachi," Gittin 84a, Tosafot s.v. "Mistabra," Gittin 85b, Tosafot s.v. "Af Al Gav," and Rosh Chullin 69d). This is because we are concerned about erring courts, as explained there. Rashi (Gittin 85b, s.v. "Min") gives another reason for this, so that the matter is permitted and no invalidity arises, as explained there and by the Ran (Gittin 7:7).

When the husband instructs them to write and sign, the scribe himself writes as per the instruction, and the witnesses, whom he instructed, sign themselves. They cannot delegate this task to others to write and sign. Even if he told the Great Court, "Give a get (divorce document) to my wife," they must write and sign it themselves and cannot instruct others to do so. Certainly, if he told them "write and give," it is forbidden for them to appoint agents in their place. Although we hold that an agent can appoint another agent even without explicit permission from the sender, in the case of writing and signing the get, an agent cannot appoint another agent. This is because we hold that matters (mili) cannot be transferred to an agent. The explanation is that when there is an action involved, such as giving the get to an agent to deliver to the wife, the agent can appoint another agent in his place. However, since the sender only gave verbal instructions, these instructions cannot be transferred to another (Rashi). This disqualification is from the Torah. If the husband gave such a get, instructing the scribe to write and the witnesses to sign, and they instructed others who wrote and signed and then delivered the get to the husband who gave it to his wife, the get is void from the Torah. This is the ruling of the Rambam in Chapter 2, Law 5, who concludes that since the husband did not instruct those who wrote it, it is not considered "for her sake." It is also clear from the Talmud and all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) that this is a disqualification from the Torah. If they wrote it themselves and instructed others to sign, the get is not void but disqualified rabbinically. Its status is like that of a get signed by invalid witnesses, as explained in Siman 130, which is disqualified but not void (Beit Shmuel, Section 7). We hold like Rabbi Eliezer that the main aspect is the writing. If the husband told the court to write and they instructed another to write and signed it themselves, we have a doubt in the Talmud (end of Chapter "Haketel") whether "write" refers to the writing of the get, and those who instructed the writing performed an act that cannot be transferred to an agent, making the get void. Or, perhaps his intention was regarding the signatures that they should sign themselves, and the writing is as if he said to tell another to write, whose ruling will be clarified before us. According to several poskim, this is only a rabbinical disqualification, as will be clarified with G-d's help. Some hold that it is a doubt, as will be clarified.

It seems to me that even if the husband gave the scribe parchment and ink and told him to write a get (divorce document) for his wife, and the scribe instructed another person and he wrote it, the get is invalid. This too is considered a matter of "mili" (non-transferable verbal instructions). Although he handed over the parchment and ink, which are not "mili," nevertheless, his instruction to write is considered "mili." Additionally, some of the early authorities wrote that whenever the matter is not completed by the agent, it is considered "mili" and cannot be delegated to another agent. The agency for delivering the get is the completion of the matter, but the writing is considered "mili" because the matter is not completed until the get is delivered (Mordechai there in the name of the Sefer HaChochmah). See also what is written in Siman 141, section 117 regarding the explanation of "mili" according to the Sefer HaEitur.

If a husband says to two or three people, “Tell a scribe to write and witnesses to sign [a get],” it is explained in the Talmudic discussion at the end of [the chapter] “HaMekabel,” and several of our Rabbis have also written that in this situation, the concept of “matters cannot be delegated to a messenger” does not apply. This is because he has not delegated mere “matters” to them; rather, the husband himself is appointing the scribe and the witnesses as agents, even not in their presence. A person can appoint an agent not in the presence of the agent (Ramban, Rashba, and Ran there). According to Torah law, the get is valid, and it should not be invalidated on the grounds that the husband told these people to instruct the scribe and witnesses. This is not analogous to testimony from hearsay (עד מפי עד), because in hearsay testimony, witnesses testify that they heard from others that Reuven borrowed money from Shimon, where the testimony was not originally given to the current witnesses but to the first ones. Here, however, the main testimony is given only to the scribe and the witnesses, and the initial individuals are merely agents of the husband to instruct them to prepare the get (Tosafot 67a, s.v. “Amru”).

However, it is explained there in the Talmud that there is a rabbinic disqualification for a different reason. If the scribe signs himself as a witness on the get (divorce document) along with another witness, when it is said that the get is valid, it is necessarily saying that "they said" (amru) is invalid. For if we say that it is valid, it could lead to a problem where the get would be invalid according to Torah law. This would occur if he tells two or three people to tell the scribe to write it and for certain individuals to sign it. They might be embarrassed in front of the scribe because the husband did not designate him as a witness, and due to this embarrassment, they might tell the scribe that the husband instructed him to sign himself as a witness along with one of the other witnesses. Since the husband did not command this, the get would be invalid according to Torah law. But if we say that it is forbidden for the scribe to sign himself as a witness, then this concern does not exist, and saying "they said" (amru) is valid. Therefore, these two matters are interdependent: if we say that "they said" (amru) is valid, then a scribe signing as a witness is invalid due to this concern explained above. And if we say that "they said" (amru) is invalid, then a scribe signing as a witness is valid. Thus, it is found that these two laws cannot both be validated, for if one is valid, the other must necessarily be invalid.

Since the Rif and the Rambam in Chapter 9, Law 27 ruled that a document signed by a scribe and a witness is valid, therefore they ruled that "he said that they said" is invalid. Furthermore, their opinion on this matter will be explained later. Some of our Rabbis hold that a document signed by a scribe and a witness is invalid, as the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in Siman 130. According to this, they would validate a document if it was said, "he said that they said." Nevertheless, the Rosh (Chapter 9, Law 6) wrote in the name of Rabbeinu Yitzchak the Elder, the author of the Tosafot, to invalidate both. This is not a contradiction of two stringencies that negate each other, for if it was clear to us that a document signed by a scribe and a witness is invalid, we would indeed say so. However, this law is not clear, and due to doubt, it is invalid. Therefore, it is proper to be stringent in both laws, and out of doubt, invalidate both. This seems to be the opinion of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, who wrote in Siman 130, Paragraph 18, that one should be careful not to have the scribe sign as a witness because there are those who invalidate it. In this Siman, Paragraph 4, they wrote that if he divorced her through "he said that they said," she is doubtfully divorced. Therefore, if both of these situations occurred in one get (divorce document) - a scribe and a witness signed it and "he said that they said" was used - the get is invalid. If he gave two gets, one through "he said that they said" and one signed by a scribe and a witness, one of them is valid according to this opinion. This will be further clarified in Siman 130, with God's help, and also regarding "he said that they said," it will be explained further before us.

And these are the words of the Rif (there): He said to two [people], "Write a get (divorce document) and give it to my wife," and they told a scribe, and he wrote it and they signed it—she must leave. And even if he said to them, "Tell the scribe to write it and the witnesses to sign it," the get is invalid. For it was taught in the chapter that follows: They said to him, "Shall we write a get for your wife?" He said to them, "Write it." They told a scribe, and he wrote it, etc.—the get is invalid unless he says to the scribe, "Write," and to the witnesses, "Sign." And Rav Ashi concluded that all of this follows Rabbi Yossi, and it is said in a way that does not leave room for doubt. And it is clear from his words that he equates the case where one says "Tell [the scribe]" and the case where one does not say "Tell [the scribe]." Therefore, he does not hold that saying "Tell [the scribe]" is a rabbinic prohibition because of the decree concerning the scribe and witnesses, for in the case of a rabbinic prohibition, if she accepted betrothal from another, the betrothal would be valid and the child would not be a mamzer, as is written in Siman 150. And if she remarried, she would not have to leave, as is written there. So how can he equate the case of saying "Tell [the scribe]" with not saying "Tell [the scribe]?" Furthermore, from the ruling that the get is invalid, and as it is taught in the Mishnah according to the conclusion of Rav Ashi, and the Rambam has already established for us in Chapter 10 that it is invalid from the Torah, it is certain that the Rif holds that Rav Ashi ruled entirely according to Rabbi Yossi. And Rabbi Yossi does not differentiate between saying "Tell [the scribe]" and not saying "Tell [the scribe]." And even in the case of saying "Tell [the scribe]," Rabbi Yossi holds that it is merely verbal directives and cannot be transferred to an agent (and so wrote the Ran and the Yesh Shlomoh at the end of the chapter of "Hamekabel" that Rabbi Yossi holds this, see there). Just as in the case of not saying "Tell [the scribe]," we say that it is merely verbal directives that cannot be transferred to another, even though in all other cases of agency, an agent can appoint another agent, nonetheless, in verbal directives, it is not so. Similarly, in the case of saying "Tell [the scribe]," we say that verbal directives cannot be transferred to an agent. The principal does not have the power to transfer verbal directives to another through an agent. And Rav Ashi disagrees with the conclusion of the chapter "Hamekabel" that holds that in the case of saying "Tell [the scribe]," verbal directives are not applicable. And the Rif ruled according to Rav Ashi, who is later, and also the Mishnah he brought is after "Hamekabel," and it was a dispute and then it was stated anonymously, and the law follows the anonymous opinion. Since this Tanna stated it anonymously according to Rabbi Yossi, we rule according to him. And even in the case of saying "Tell [the scribe]," the get is invalid from the Torah because of verbal directives. This ruling is not dependent on the scribe and witnesses. And so ruled the Ba'al HaMaor and Rabbeinu Chananel, as the earlier authorities wrote.

And also the opinion of the Rambam appears explicitly in this manner. He wrote in Chapter 2, Law 6: "If he said to two or three [people], 'Tell the scribe to write a get [divorce document] for my wife, and tell the witnesses to sign it,' and they told the scribe and he wrote it, and [they told] the witnesses and they signed it, or if he said to two [people], 'Tell the scribe to write a get for my wife and you sign it,' this get is invalid, and this matter is greatly deliberated because it is close to being a null get," end quote. And it appears to me, in my humble opinion, clear that the Rambam also holds like the Rif, that even when one says "tell," matters of agency (mili) apply, as is explicitly proven from his words in Chapter 4 of Zechiya regarding a gift. He wrote there that a gift is like a get [divorce document], where a person cannot transmit agency matters to a messenger. How so? If he said to three [people], "Tell so-and-so and so-and-so to write and sign a gift document and give it to so-and-so," it is nothing, etc., end quote. And if it enters your mind that he holds that in saying "tell," agency matters do not apply, and a get is invalid due to the decree of "signed by the scribe and a witness," this has no relevance to monetary law, as indeed the Tur ruled in Choshen Mishpat Section 244 that in a gift, when one says "tell," the gift is valid, see there. But certainly, he fundamentally holds like the Rif that even in saying "tell," agency matters apply, and the get is null from the Torah. However, due to the severity of the prohibition of a married woman, he also considered the Talmudic discussion at the end of Chapter "HaMekabel," which holds that agency matters do not apply in saying "tell," and the invalidation is only rabbinic due to the decree of "signed by the scribe and a witness," and we are stringent that even if she received kiddushin [betrothal] from another, she needs a get. But fundamentally, he holds like the Talmudic discussion of "Mi SheAchzo" according to Rav Ashi, who ruled like Rabbi Yossi. And this is also evident from the words of the Maimonidean glosses there: "Behold, he ruled completely like Rabbi Yossi, etc., because agency matters are not transmitted to a messenger, etc., and even in saying 'tell,' etc.," end quote. And so wrote the Maggid Mishneh there: "It appears from this according to Rabbi Yossi that even in saying 'tell,' it is not a get because agency matters are not transmitted to a messenger, and we say the get is null," end quote. And many of the great ones have labored over the words of the Rambam, of blessed memory (see the commentaries and what is written in the name of the Radak and Rabbi Moshe Alshakar). In my humble opinion, there is no doubt in the matter, and he holds like the Rif. See what I wrote in Choshen Mishpat there and in our book "Even HaEzer" Section 82.

The Ramban and the Rashba, of blessed memory (there), also hold that in the case of "tell [the scribe] to write the get," the get is nullified by Torah law, but for a different reason, not because of "mili" (untransmittable matters). They hold that in the case of "tell [the scribe] to write," it is not considered "mili." Rather, the reason is that since a get (divorce document) requires intent (lishmah) and it is also required that "he writes it for her," meaning that the husband must write it for her, the scribe and witnesses cannot write and sign it unless they hear it directly from the husband himself. He cannot appoint them as his agents in their absence. Although in all other matters a person can appoint an agent not in the agent's presence, nevertheless, in the case of a get which requires intent and must be written by the husband, he cannot appoint an agent in his absence. According to this opinion, not only in the case of "tell [the scribe] to write" is the get nullified, but even if the husband states in front of the court, "I am appointing so-and-so the scribe to write a get for my wife and so-and-so and so-and-so to sign it," it is of no effect at all.

The Ran and the Ra'ah questioned this opinion: If so, how does the Talmud derive that Rabbi Yose holds "mili" cannot be transmitted to an agent? Perhaps he holds that in all matters they can be transmitted, but a get is different because of the reason explained. Additionally, how does the Talmud validate "tell [the scribe] to write" by Torah law, and it is only invalid due to a rabbinic decree? Even though "mili" is not applicable here, it is still nullified for the reason explained. Furthermore, how can it be said that there, regarding "mili," Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yose disagree, with Rabbi Meir holding they can be transmitted and Rabbi Yose holding they cannot, and the law follows Rabbi Yose? If so, Rabbi Meir must necessarily not hold the reason explained, as he validates even without "tell [the scribe] to write." Therefore, how do we know Rabbi Yose holds the reason explained, as he only disagrees on the grounds of "mili"? How can we disagree with Rabbi Meir on something for which we do not find any other disagreement? Additionally, the main point is puzzling: because it requires intent, he cannot appoint an agent in his absence?

It appears to me that their intention is as follows: Certainly, according to the opinion that matters can be entrusted to an agent, there is no distinction between an agency for an action and an agency for words, and speech is as strong as action. Therefore, it is also strong in this regard, that one can appoint an agent not in their presence. However, Rabbi Yossi, who differentiates between an agency for an action and an agency for words, holds that the power of words is not as strong as the power of action. Consequently, in this matter as well, the power of an agency for words is not sufficient to appoint an agent not in their presence. And although in other matters of agency for words, it is possible that one can appoint an agent not in their presence, nevertheless, regarding a get (divorce document), concerning the writing which requires intent for the sake of the specific person, and it is upon the husband to write it, the agency for words in a get is not strong enough to be effective not in their presence to fulfill the requirement of intent as if it were written by the husband. Additionally, according to Rabbi Yossi, not everyone agrees with this, as certainly the passage at the end of Tractate Kiddushin does not agree with this reasoning, as they validate from the Torah saying "tell [others] to say," but Rav Ashi in the seventh chapter holds this way. And they explain that what the Rif compared "tell [others] to say" to "not saying 'tell [others] to say'" is not from the reasoning of matters but from this logic, and all according to Rabbi Yossi (as it appears to me).

And there are among our Rabbis those who hold a different opinion on this matter, that certainly in the case of "tell them" (i.e., appointing through an intermediary), the concept of "mili" (non-transferable verbal directives) does not apply, and it is invalid because "tell them" is considered valid due to a rabbinic decree from the time of the Scribe and Witness. However, this invalidation is only in a general case when one says, "Tell so-and-so to write and so-and-so and so-and-so to sign." But if one says, "I appoint so-and-so as the scribe to write the get and so-and-so and so-and-so as witnesses to sign," and you tell them that I have appointed them for this, it is valid even ab initio. For a person can appoint an agent even not in their presence, and there is no concern of the decree of the Scribe and Witness to worry that due to the embarrassment of the scribe, he would sign as a witness against the husband's directive. Certainly, they would not do so and thereby increase mamzerim (illegitimate children) in Israel out of concern for the embarrassment of the scribe, as everyone knows that deviating from the husband's directive invalidates the get. This concern we had with "tell them" is because whenever he said so, they might err in thinking that the husband entrusted them with the matter to change the agency according to their discretion. And when he says, "so-and-so and so-and-so should sign," it is merely showing them the place (indicating whom to appoint). Otherwise, why would he depend on their statement? He should have said, "I appoint them." But when he truly appoints them, they will not err (Ran and Ra'ah there and the Ra'ah is even more lenient and distinguishes between when he says "of your own accord" and when he specifies, but the Ran dismisses this - see there). (It can be said that when he appoints them as agents, even the Rif and the Rambam agree that this is not "mili," and so writes the Shiltei Giborim - and this requires further study. However, according to the Ramban and the Rashba, it is not a valid get, as written, and the Radach in Beit Gimel wrote that from the Rambam it is evident that when he appoints not in their presence, it does not work - see there. And his words are not necessarily conclusive - see there).

Rambam wrote in Chapter 2, Law 16: "If someone became mute, but his mind is sound, and they said to him, 'Shall we write a get (bill of divorce) for your wife?' and he nodded his head, they test him three times intermittently. If they asked him about something that requires a 'no' and he indicated 'no,' and about something that requires a 'yes' and he indicated 'yes,' they may write and give the get. They must test him thoroughly to ensure his mind is not disturbed. Likewise, if he wrote with his hand, 'Write and give a get to my wife,' they may write and give it to her, provided his mind is settled. The law for someone who became mute is not the same as for a deaf person."

His words mean that if someone was initially of sound mind and then became deaf, since the original marriage was valid according to Torah law, the sages did not permit relying on his writing because a deaf person lacks mental competence. However, if someone became mute, meaning he is dumb but he hears and does not speak, he is considered competent in all matters, and we only need to ascertain his intention. Therefore, his writing is effective. It implies that, certainly, someone who is fully competent who wrote in his own handwriting, 'Write a get for my wife,' is considered as if he spoke. More on this will be clarified with the help of Heaven.

And it is also evident from the Talmudic discussion (71a) that verbal speech is not specifically required for a get (divorce document). Even though verbal testimony is required for giving testimony, this is because of the Torah's decree, as it is written "by the mouth of two witnesses," and we expound "from their mouth and not from their writing." But in other matters, writing is equivalent to speech (there). A proof from the get itself is that we do not require verbal speech, as they permitted it through nodding of the head as it is written. Another proof is that in testimony it is written "if he does not tell," and nevertheless, if not for the verse "from their mouth and not from their writing," I would validate written testimony as well, implying that writing is considered telling. And even though we exclude a deaf-mute from chalitzah because they cannot say "he shall say" (Yevamot 104b), saying certainly must be with the mouth (Tosafot Gittin there). Furthermore, in chalitzah it is written "and she shall answer," and we derive (Sotah 32a) from "the Levites shall answer" that it must be in Hebrew, and from there we also learn that it must be with the mouth like the Levites (there). According to this, it is possible that saying could also be in writing. Therefore, in a get, where neither speech nor saying is written, it is certain that we only require his intention and will, and writing is sufficient.

However, the Tur wrote: "The scribe should not write and the witnesses should not sign until they hear [the instruction] from his mouth." Even if he is deaf, as long as he can hear but cannot speak, or even if he is fully competent and wrote them in his handwriting to write and sign, they should not do so until they hear it from his mouth. And so wrote several of our Rabbis: the Rosh, the Rashba, the Ran, the Mordechai, the Beit Yosef, the SeMaG, the SeMaK, and the Hagahot Maimoniot. And it is explicitly stated in the Tosefta Gittin (Chapter 2): "If a scribe writes it with the specific intention and the witnesses sign it with the specific intention, even if they wrote it and signed it and gave it to her, it is invalid until he tells the scribe to write and the witnesses to sign." Not only that, but even if he wrote in his own handwriting to the scribe to write and to the witnesses to sign, even if they wrote it and signed it and gave it to her, it is invalid until they hear his voice saying to the scribe to write and to the witnesses to sign. The Tosefta does not refer to a deaf person, and it must be said that what is stated in the Gemara (82a) that it is necessary to hear his voice excludes the opinion that a deaf person who can communicate in writing is valid. This is not specifically about a deaf person; the same applies to a competent person who is mute—it is not valid. And this is why nodding is effective, as the Tur wrote in Siman 121. The Rosh wrote in a clear Mishnah (Ketubot Chapter 19) that nodding might be preferable because it shows bodily intention, or alternatively, if he became mute and cannot communicate otherwise, they were lenient due to the difficulty. The first explanation suggests that writing is not effective by Torah law, and the second explanation suggests it is effective by Torah law, and only the Rabbis decreed about it. According to this, if he became mute, writing might also be effective. However, from the Tur, it is clarified that the first explanation is primary, and so wrote the Rashba there that nodding is preferable to writing, and it is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that nodding is like a voice.

However, regarding the opinion of the Rambam, it is possible to say that only in the case of one who has become mute does handwritten communication suffice, and not in the case of someone who is fully capable, and this is for a rabbinic reason: they did not decree in a situation where it is impossible for him to speak verbally. And this is somewhat implied from the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in the Shulchan Aruch, section 5, where after he writes the opinion of most poskim (halachic authorities) that handwritten communication does not suffice, whether in the case of a fully capable person or one who has become mute, he writes: "And there are those who permit in the case of one who has become mute to write and sign through handwritten communication, etc." This is the opinion of the Rambam. And one of the poskim wrote similarly (Beit Yosef in the name of the Riva). And even though in his major work he wrote that this does not seem correct to him, for if it were so, he would have clarified it, and on the contrary, since he permits in the case of one who has become mute, all the more so in the case of a fully capable person. Therefore, perhaps in the Shulchan Aruch, he was cautious about this because it is not explicitly stated in the words of the Rambam (and see Maggid Mishneh there, and examine further). And it is possible that he was concerned about the Tosefta we mentioned, and he holds that the Tosefta only invalidates in the case of a fully capable person because he has the ability to speak, and this requires further investigation.

In my humble opinion, it seems for a different reason to differentiate between someone who has become mute and a fully competent person. Certainly, the writing of a fully competent person standing before us is better than that of someone who has become mute. However, this scenario cannot apply in practice. Why should he write if he can speak? The law concerning a competent person is only necessary in practice when he is at a distance. In that case, he writes to a specific scribe in a specific place to write a document and to specific witnesses to sign it. Since he is not present before us, it is indeed worse than someone who has become mute and stands before us. When he stands before us, writes, and hands his written document to the scribe and witnesses, it is indeed considered as if he spoke because they see and understand each other. But a competent person who is at a distance and sends his written document, even though they recognize his handwriting, they do not see him and he does not hand them his document directly—how can this be considered as if he spoke? This also seems to be the precise meaning of Rashi’s language (Gittin 71a, s.v. “cheresh”) where he writes “and he handed them [the document]...”. According to this logical reasoning, it is also clear why Rambam did not write the law regarding the writing of a fully competent person, because it is not applicable. If he is present, he can speak. If he is not present, it is certainly worse than someone who has become mute. Hence, we should interpret the Tosefta as indicating that the prohibition is because he is not present. The Tosefta refers to a fully competent person writing from a distance. When it states “until they hear his voice,” it means he should be in close proximity and thus able to speak. “Hearing his voice” is not literal, as even motioning is sufficient for someone who has become mute. But for a fully competent person, why should we rely on motioning when he can speak? Thus, hearing his voice is necessary. From this reasoning, it is also clear why motioning is better than writing. Certainly, logically, writing is better than motioning, as writing clarifies his intent without doubt, as noted by several early authorities (the Itur and Avodat Yisrael). However, for someone who has become mute, motioning is better, whereas for a fully competent person, it is worse because he is not present. Although I have not found this distinction in any poskim, it seems logically correct.

Furthermore, it is explicitly clear from the words of the Rambam, of blessed memory, that written consent (ketav yad) is preferable to nodding (herchanah). For with nodding, a verification is required three times, but with written consent, no verification is mentioned. The reason is simple: with written consent, there is no doubt about his intention, whereas with nodding, there is doubt. This is why "give" is mentioned regarding written consent and not nodding, because with written consent, he can write "write and give," unlike nodding, where everything is nodding. And certainly, when asked, "Shall we write a get for your wife?" they remind him to write and give, and the Talmud and the poskim did not need to mention this. Or it is possible that it is similar to being thrown into a pit, where "give" does not need to be mentioned. However, some have written that in the case of writing when one has become mute, if we permit it, verification three times is required, just as with nodding (Beit Yosef in the name of the Ran). But from the words of the Rambam, it is implied as we have written (and it is explicitly clear from his words at the beginning of Chapter 29 of Hilchot Mechirah, see there).

And regarding the fact that the Rambam, of blessed memory, did not mention someone who speaks but does not hear, the Gemara treats them with the same law as someone who has become mute, that is, one who hears but does not speak, and one who speaks but does not hear, and both are treated as fully competent for all matters. The poskim (decisors of Jewish law) have labored over this, and in my humble opinion, the reason is clear: it is not relevant to mention the law of nodding and writing for someone who speaks but does not hear, since he can speak. Why would we need his nodding or writing? He can simply speak. And when we need to ask him something, we can ask through nodding or writing, but he himself can speak. This is the same reason writing is not mentioned for a fully competent person, as stated in Siman 61. 

And know that the Rambam, at the beginning of chapter 29 of Hilchot Mechira, wrote that someone who speaks but does not hear sells and buys movable items through indication, like a fully deaf person. Do not question why he does not speak, as it is stated regarding a get (divorce document), for it is undoubtedly not the same. In transactions, where it is necessary to hear the terms of the deal, they must communicate through indication. But in the case of a get, the husband does not need to hear anything from the scribe and witnesses, and they need to hear from him. Therefore, what do we need his indication for? He should speak with his mouth. (See there in the Maggid Mishneh and the Kesef Mishneh).

And according to this, in practice, for a fully competent person who sends his handwriting to instruct someone to write and others to sign, we do not find an explicit allowance. This is not only according to the Tur, the Rosh, the Rashba, the Ran, Mordechai, the Behag, Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, Sefer Mitzvot Katan, and the Hagahot Maimoniot, but also according to Rabbeinu Tam who holds similarly, and this is explicitly stated in the Tosefta that it is invalid. Even according to the Rambam and Baal Ha'itur, it is not explicitly stated in their writings that it is valid for a fully competent person. Only Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, in his great book, wrote that according to their opinions, it is valid for a fully competent person. And we have already written in Section 61 about the concerns regarding this. Nevertheless, I have seen in the responsa of the great Acharonim that in a situation of severe agunah, they permitted it through handwriting (Asher BeYehoshua, Siman 114 and 115), when the woman would remain an agunah if not for this method. It is possible that they hold that even those who invalidate it, this is only rabbinically, while biblically it is certainly valid, as proven by the Talmudic discussion as written in Section 58. Also, the second discussion (82b) only excludes a completely deaf person for whom it is ineffective. Furthermore, the Tosefta, which is not brought in the Talmud, is not considered in a case of agunah. And the citation from the Jerusalem Talmud is also not explicitly clear. Indeed, it is true that it differentiates between writing and nodding because nodding is like a voice. However, at the end of the Jerusalem Talmud discussion (Chapter 1 of Terumot, Halacha 1 and in Hatekabel), it is explicitly implied that for a fully competent person, if we know that he genuinely commands in writing to write a get, it is written. As Rabbi Yossi the son of Rabbi Bun stated: "We are standing with a healthy person; why isn't it a get?" and he answers: "I say he is occupied with his documents," end quote. This can be interpreted as follows: initially, the Tosefta we brought earlier was cited, and it previously differentiated, in the case of one who became mute, between writing and nodding. The difficulty is that the Tosefta speaks about a healthy person; why is it invalid through his writing? It is understandable in the case of one who became mute, who is not fit for speech, that we can say his writing is not like speech, since he cannot speak. But in the case of a healthy person who is fit for speech, what is the difference between speech and writing? Moreover, in the case of one who became mute, it is possible that we cannot rely on his writing as he may not be of complete and settled mind. But in the case of a healthy person, what do we have to worry about? The answer is that even in the case of a healthy person, I say he is occupied with his documents, meaning he did not write this genuinely to act upon it, but rather as someone merely occupied with documents and papers without precision.

(And the Pri Megadim interprets differently, that it refers to nodding, and his interpretation is perplexing. The Korban Netanel interprets as I wrote). In my opinion, this is a significant support when there is no other option. And since our rabbis who invalidate it do so only rabbinically, and according to the Rambam and Baal Ha'itur, as explained by Rabbeinu Beit Yosef, they explicitly permit it. The Talmudic discussion also proves this, and as we explained, the conclusion of the Jerusalem Talmud is that it is only due to the concern of being occupied. Therefore, if through the exchange of letters we know that his true intention is to write a get, it is permissible in a situation of severe agunah. Especially since many great authorities in previous generations have already ruled this way. However, now that the Jewish people are scattered across all corners of the earth, and it is unlikely that three Jews will not be found with him, it is better for him to command them there in his place to write and sign the get and send it via mail. For it has already become widespread in our times to send a get via mail, as will be explained in Siman 141. And when this repair is available, it is clear that it should not be permitted through handwriting. Heaven forbid to permit this, since many of our rabbis invalidate it in such a case, and some

He said to ten people, "Write a get (divorce document) for my wife." One of them can write it on behalf of all of them, for his intention wasn't that all of them should write it, as this is not customary among people. Rather, his intention was that from these ten people, whoever wishes to be his agent to write the get can do so. There is, however, an opinion that if two or more people write different parts of the get, the get is invalid, as it is written "and he shall write" in the singular form (Choshen Mishpat section 16). Even though in the Gemara (26b) it is clearly proven that one can write the format of the get and the essential part of the get can be written by another, one could say that for the format we are not stringent, but for the essential part, if two people write it, it is invalid (Beit Shmuel section 9).

However, in truth, we cannot say this, as "and he shall write" is in the singular form. According to Rabbi Meir, "and he shall write" refers to the signatures, which necessarily implies two people, yet it is still written in the singular form (Tosafot Gittin). Furthermore, how is it possible to write in the plural form, since the primary obligation is on the husband, and it is upon him that "and he shall write" is stated? But if he commands a scribe, it becomes as if the scribe is his agent, and why shouldn't he be able to make two or more agents? Additionally, the language of the Gemara (end of the chapter "HaMekabel") regarding this law, which says "one writes on behalf of all of them," implies that it is coming to teach a leniency, that we do not require all of them to write. Nevertheless, in practice, this requires further investigation, as the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch invalidate it.

Even if he said, "All of you write," his intention is not that all of them should write, but rather that all of them should be present at the time of the writing. Therefore, one of the ten writes in the presence of all of them. But when he did not say, "All of you write," it is not necessary for all of them to be present (Beit Shmuel). And there is no need to ask: if we say that two or more are permitted to write one get, why not say that his intention was literal, that all of them should write a little bit? For indeed, it is not to be assumed that a person would intend to perform an act of madness, but rather we assume that he wanted all of them to be present at the writing in order to publicize the matter. Moreover, even according to the opinion that disqualifies a get written by two people, he agrees that it is valid if written in the template style, as we have written. And if so, we still do not say that all of them should write the template little by little. Rather, certainly, it cannot be said so. Regarding the signatures, when he only said "write" or "all of you write," our master the Beit Yosef in his great book holds that they should not sign, since he did not mention signing (and so wrote the Bach and the Shelah in chapter 6, section 16). But there are those who disagree with this, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 9, Law 26: "If one says to ten people, 'Write a get (divorce document) for my wife,' one person can write it on behalf of all of them. If he says, 'All of you write,' one of them writes in the presence of all of them." And then he wrote, "If one says to ten people, 'Write a get and sign it and give it to my wife,' one of them writes, and two sign, and one of them gives it to her, etc. If he says to them, 'All of you sign,' all of them sign." This is also the opinion of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 8. One of the witnesses is prohibited from writing the get even though, according to Maimonides, a scribe who signs as a witness is valid. Nevertheless, there are those who invalidate it, as mentioned in Section 130. But to deliver the get, the scribe can serve as a messenger (Beit Shmuel, Subsection 10), and similarly, one of the witnesses can serve as a messenger to deliver the get. However, it seems this is only when the messenger does not need to declare "It was written and signed in my presence," such as when the get and the authorization are validated as will be explained in Section 142. But when it is necessary to declare "It was written and signed in my presence," it is not appropriate for them to be messengers, because when the scribe is the messenger, he cannot say "It was written in my presence," but rather "I wrote it," and when one of the witnesses is the messenger, he would need to say "I signed it," which does not follow the sages' enactment. Nevertheless, it is possible to say there is no concern in this, for certainly this is not considered changing the format established by the sages. The language of the sages was generally established when the messenger is another person, so why should it be any worse when the writer or witness is the messenger and says "I wrote" or "I signed"? However, for a witness, it certainly seems forbidden as the sages said (Gittin 15b) "either all in the validation of the get or all in the enactment of the sages," and see there in Tosafot, and it will be explained in Section 142 with God's help.

According to the words of the Rambam and the Tur that we have written, our master the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Yosef Karo) writes that if one only says "write" and not "write and sign," they should not sign. This is what the sages taught in the Mishnah (66b): If one says to ten people, "write and give a get (divorce document) to my wife," one writes and two sign. If he says "all of you write," one writes and all sign. This is a truncated language, and it refers to a situation where he also said "sign" (and so wrote the Bach and the Yam Shel Shlomo). And what we have taught in the Baraita there: If one says to ten people, "write," one writes with the consent of all. If he says "all of you write," one writes in the presence of all. This does not refer to our Mishnah, and it is a separate law. They should not sign, since he did not mention signing. And in the Mishnah, according to their words, it refers to when he said "write and sign." When he said "all of you," it is not necessary to write in the presence of all, but all must sign. Or it is possible that since he said "all of you write and sign," the writing must also be in the presence of all. The Rambam only refers to a case where he says "all of you sign."

But there are some of our Rabbis from whose words it is understood that the Mishnah and the Baraita are one and the same (Ran), that when one says "write a get for my wife," it includes both the writing and the signing. However, many later authorities were puzzled by this, as it is clear from many places in the Talmud that when one says "write," his intention includes also the signing. Moreover, it is very forced to say that the language of the Mishnah is fragmented (Beit Shmuel, note 11; Maggid Mishneh, Chapter 2, Law 2; Pri Chadash; and Gra). And there is someone who says that when one says "write and give," it is certainly understood that his intention is also to sign, and they must specifically sign. But when he says only "give," they can give only through witnesses of delivery. And if he says only "write," they can only write and not sign (Gra and Turei Zahav). And there is someone who says that it is clear from many proofs that even in "write" alone, signing is included (Pri Chadash, but the Beit Meir rejected his words and concluded in accordance with the opinion of the Gra and Turei Zahav). And they wrote that Rambam himself was not precise in this matter in all places, as there are places where he explained "write and sign" and places where he wrote only "write," intending also the signing (and see Pri Chadash). Nevertheless, in practice, it is difficult to be lenient against the plain meaning of the words of Rambam and the Tur, and against three great authorities who agreed thus. Therefore, one should be stringent in this matter in all cases, as per both opinions (so it appears to me).

He said to ten people, "Write and sign a get (divorce document) for my wife," and listed them by their names, Reuven, Shimon, Levi, etc. Whether he listed all ten or only some of them, it is considered as "all of you" (כולכם), and all ten must sign. Even when he listed only some of them, we say that his intention was for all of them, but it was burdensome for him to list all their names. This appears from the words of the Rambam there. However, from the words of Rashi and the Ran (at the end of the chapter "HaMekabel"), it is clear that if he listed only some of them, only those listed need to sign. It is also clear from the Talmudic discussion there that this is due to doubt. But from the Rambam it is clear that it is entirely considered as "all of you," and if not all sign, the get is void. This is contrary to the Talmudic discussion (Ran there). However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is clear like the Rambam, and the Rif omitted all of this, which requires further study there. According to our Talmud, she would be doubtfully divorced. It is a simple matter that in any case where it is considered "all of you" in writing, one must write in the presence of all of them. And so it is taught in the Mishnah that in the case of "all of you," if one of them died before signing or before writing, the get is void because his words were not fulfilled. This will be further clarified.

The Tur wrote: If one says, "All of you sign," then everyone must sign. And if two sign first, they are considered witnesses, and the rest as a formality. Therefore, if the rest are invalid or if they signed on different days, even within ten days, it is valid. If one died before signing, it is invalid. If one of the first two was invalid, it is invalid, specifically if he signed before the others. But if the others signed below first, and then the invalid one signed above, it is valid due to the valid ones below. The Rema wrote that initially, a relative or invalid person should not sign with them, even at the end, even if two valid ones signed on the same day and the relative or invalid one afterward. If it was signed after the fact, after two valid ones signed on the same day, it is valid, but if one says "all of you" for witnesses, it is not valid unless all are valid and sign on the same day. And some of our Rabbis hold that even if "all of you" is said generally, they are all considered witnesses and must all be valid and sign on the same day (which is ruled in Yevamot 18b because Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds so). And Rabbi Moshe Isserles wrote that one should be stringent according to this opinion, regarding the relative or invalid person, as it is certainly invalid by Torah law. But regarding the others signing not on the same day, it is possible to be lenient (Choshen Mishpat 26), as an early invalidation is only rabbinic. Know that according to the first opinion, where the rest are for formality, it is valid even if they signed after the get (divorce document) was received, as every condition fulfilled after giving is considered. She may remarry initially, even if they signed after she married another man, though she must leave the latter because the get is only effective upon condition fulfillment. Nonetheless, the get is valid, and she must divorce him and can marry another (there, 22). Also, regarding the others signing not on the same day, there are those who doubt this, even though it is only rabbinic, since major Rishonim (the Bahag, Behag, Tosafot, Rashba, and Rivash) rule that all are witnesses, one cannot be lenient even rabbinically (Beit Shmuel 17). Even according to the first opinion, each must sign in the presence of all, as get witnesses sign only in each other's presence, as stated in Siman 130. Hence, if one dies before signing, the get is void even if one dies after signing but before everyone else signs, because the remaining ones would not sign in the presence of the deceased. However, this invalidity is only rabbinic, as signing not in each other's presence is rabbinic (Choshen Mishpat 23). Some say this is only initially, but after the fact, it is valid even if they did not sign in each other's presence (there, in the name of the Ran). Some hold that those for formality do not need to sign in the witnesses' presence (Beit Shmuel 15, in the name of Raavad and Ramban). Hence, the get is only invalid if one died before signing, but if he signed and then died, it is valid (Choshen Mishpat). There are other opinions regarding those for formality, to differentiate if invalid ones signed above or below, but it is unnecessary to elaborate, as the main law is to be stringent according to those who hold all are witnesses, and no relative or invalid person should sign anywhere. If one did, the get is invalid, so there is no practical difference in this law (Nodah BiYehudah elaborates on this, and Beit Shmuel 14, Choshen Mishpat 45).

By the decree of the Sages, when one instructs many people to write a get (bill of divorce) for him, or to sign it, or to deliver it to his wife, he must explicitly say, "Each one of you shall write a get for my wife," and similarly, for the signatures, he should say, "Any two of you shall sign a get for my wife," and for delivering the get, he should say, "Each one of you shall deliver a get to my wife" (end of chapter "HaMekabel"). The reason is to avoid complications that may arise if he were to say, "All of you write," or "All of you sign," or "All of you deliver," which would require all of them to sign, and the writing and delivery would have to be in the presence of all of them, which is likely to lead to errors. Therefore, they instituted this practice. And even though, in general, if he tells ten people to write, one writes, and similarly for the signatures, two sign, and for delivery, one delivers, since he did not say "all of you," as explained, then why do we need this decree? Nevertheless, the Sages instituted it to ensure clarity in his instructions (Siman 448). However, even after the decree, if he says "All of you sign," it is invalid unless all of them sign, and this is obvious (Beit Shmuel).

The husband must be of sound mind until the giving [of the get]. There are 33 sections:

The one who divorces must be of sound mind at the time he commands the writing of the get, and if he was not of sound mind, his command is not a command. Therefore, if someone has been seized by an evil spirit, which is a sickness that confuses the mind, and he said, "Write a get for my wife," his words are meaningless, and we do not write it, even if he later recovers, unless he commands it to be written after he has recovered. His previous words are meaningless, and even if they wrote it based on his previous words and signed it and gave it to his wife, it is a nullified get according to the Torah (as stated in Beit Yosef), because since his words are meaningless, it was not written by the command of the husband (Pri Chadash). Even an examination does not help in this case because he is presumed by us to be insane for sure (Beit Shmuel). However, it appears to me that if they examined him and he responded properly, and they wrote it and gave it to her, she would be in a state of doubtful divorce, for how can we be lenient with the prohibition of a married woman in a case where he responded properly, and perhaps the evil spirit did not control him as we thought, and therefore we follow the stringent view, and it would be a doubtful case (and what the Beit Shmuel wrote in subsection 1, that if they wrote the get it is nullified, does not refer to his previous words; see there and examine carefully).

If he was healthy at the time he commanded it to be written and then was seized by madness, it should not be written while he is in his illness. If it was written and given during his illness, the Tur writes that it is nothing, whether he died from the illness or recovered. From his words, it is clear that according to Torah law, it is not a valid get (divorce document) at all, even though the command was given while he was healthy. However, the Rambam in Chapter 2, Law 15 writes that if it was written and given before he recovered, it is invalid. From the fact that he did not write that it is null, it is clear that its invalidity is Rabbinic and not from the Torah. The great later authorities (Bach, Chavot Yair, Beit Shmuel, and Gra) agreed that since he was healthy at the time of his command, even though the writing was done while he was insane, it is only a Rabbinic invalidity. They were puzzled by the Tur's opinion. In my humble opinion, it seems that there is no disagreement at all. The Rambam is referring to a case where he said, "Write and give," as is clear from his words, and the giving was done by others. Therefore, he wrote "write and give," meaning through others. Since the command was given while he was healthy, its invalidity is only Rabbinic. But in the Tur's words, it is clear that he only commanded the writing. Therefore, he specified, "If they wrote and gave it during his illness, it is nothing," meaning they wrote it and he gave it. Since the giving was done while he was insane, it is obvious that it is nothing. (And what is written in the print "and they gave it" also means that he gave it. It seems more likely that the first "vav" is a printing error. Therefore, the Rambam wrote "write and give," and the Tur changed the language of the giving.)

And our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, differentiates that the Rambam is referring to a case where we have the means to heal him, and therefore he is not disqualified from a Torah perspective. The Tur, however, is referring to a case where we do not have the means to heal him. Based on this, the Shulchan Aruch in section 2 presents these matters without distinction. However, all the great scholars refuted his words, as in the Gemara (70a) this distinction is not according to the halacha. Moreover, neither the Rambam nor the Tur mentioned this distinction at all, which indicates that they do not hold this distinction. Rather, even in a case where we do not have the means to heal him, his disqualification is only rabbinic.

If a person was healthy when he instructed to write [a will], and before it was written he was seized by madness and it was not written, if he later recovered his health, one writes based on his original instructions and there is no need to ask him again. Moreover, even if during his madness he objected to writing it, we do not pay any attention at all to what he said during his madness, and such an objection holds no weight (Tur).

Similarly, a drunk person who has reached the level of Lot's drunkenness and says "write [a document]," it is not written because he is not of sound mind at all. And the Rambam writes there, "If he has not reached [that level], it is a doubt." According to this, if someone is very drunk, even though it is clear to us that he has not reached the level of Lot's drunkenness, nevertheless it is a doubt. However, according to the Tur, there was another version in the Rambam which states, "The Rambam writes... if it is doubtful whether he has reached the level of Lot's drunkenness, it is a doubt." It is explained that it is only because we are uncertain if he has reached the level of Lot's drunkenness, but if it is clear to us that he has not, even though he is very drunk, the get [divorce document] is valid because we hold that a drunk person who has not reached the level of Lot's drunkenness, his transactions are valid, and if he commits a capital offense, he is executed for it (Eruvin 65b). However, our teacher Beit Yosef in his major work wrote that even according to the Tur's version, if someone is very drunk, we might consider the possibility that he has reached the level of Lot's drunkenness. I am puzzled by this because since the court executes him for a capital offense if he has not reached the level of Lot's drunkenness, even though he is very drunk, certainly for a get we should not be concerned. However, it is possible to say that indeed the great court has the capability to recognize if he has reached the level of Lot's drunkenness and they rely on them for capital punishment, but not for a get because we cannot rely on our recognition. Even though it is stated in the Gemara there regarding lashes as well, and for lashes it does not require the great court, it still requires a competent court and their capability is sufficient. But for a get, there is no requirement for it to be done by the court, for not everyone who divorces does so in a court (Arachin 23b). Therefore, we certainly should not rely on our recognition.

And know that according to what we have stated, this is what the Rambam wrote in Chapter 4 of Hilchot Ishut: if a drunk person betroths a woman, the betrothal is valid, even if he is very drunk. However, if he reaches the level of Lot's drunkenness, the betrothal is not valid. This aligns with the understanding that we must be stringent in cases where someone is very drunk, as they might have reached Lot's level of drunkenness, and we are not experts in determining this (Beit Yosef). Similarly, when it seems to us that someone has reached Lot's level of drunkenness, we must be concerned that perhaps this is not the case, and therefore we proceed stringently in all matters. Refer also to what is written in Siman 44, Se'if 4.

From these words, it is clear that on the day of the get (divorce document), it is proper that neither the divorcing husband nor the divorcing wife drink any intoxicating beverages, even a small amount, in order to avoid any doubts. And so have several great authorities written (Shach and Beit Shmuel, section 2). However, if one drank a small amount, the get should not be withheld because of this, if the get is necessary. There is an opinion that it is proper for them to fast on that day (Ba'er Heitev in the name of Taz), but we have never heard of this custom. We only warn them not to drink intoxicating beverages, and so is our custom.

In the Gemara (70b), it is explained that if someone commands to write a get (divorce document) and at the time of its writing he goes to sleep, it is acceptable. Even though he is not of sound mind during sleep, nevertheless, since he does not lack any action and can be awakened, it is considered as if he is awake. Based on this, one of the great authorities wrote that if someone commands to write a get and was not drunk, but during the writing he became very drunk, it is also acceptable. Even though a drunk person is comparable to someone who is possessed by an evil spirit or to an idiot, as stated, nevertheless, since the Gemara differentiates between sleep and possession by an evil spirit — because a sleeping person does not lack any action, while someone possessed by an evil spirit requires an action to be cured — and a drunk person also does not lack any action, his status is like that of someone who is asleep (Beit Shmuel, subsection 2). However, I am astonished because it is clearly explained in the Talmud (Eruvin 64b) that if someone drinks more than a quarter-log, neither sleep nor travel will help him. Moreover, we find in the Talmud that they would make remedies for drunkenness by anointing with oil and salt on the palms of the hands and feet (Shabbat 66b). How can we say that he does not lack any action? Therefore, it is forbidden to be lenient in this matter, and if this happens, it is a doubtful divorce.

It was taught in the Tosefta (Terumot Chapter 1): Someone who is sometimes a lunatic and sometimes sane, meaning intelligent, this is the rule: Whenever he is a lunatic, he is considered a lunatic in all respects; and whenever he is sane, he is considered intelligent in all respects. End of quote. This is also brought in the Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 28a). Similarly, Maimonides wrote regarding testimony in Chapter 9 of Testimonies, and these are his words: "Someone who is epileptic, at the time of his seizure, is disqualified (for testimony), and when he is healthy, he is qualified. And whether it is someone who has seizures from time to time or someone who always has seizures without a fixed time, as long as his mind is not always disturbed. For there are epileptics whose minds are disturbed even when they are healthy. One must be very cautious regarding the testimony of epileptics." End of quote. Therefore, how much more so must one be very cautious regarding the divorce of someone who is epileptic.

Based on this, what is stated in Shulchan Aruch, section 3: Someone who is sometimes healthy and sometimes insane, when he is healthy, he is considered fully competent in all matters, and if he divorces during that time, his divorce is valid. Even if he is generally healthy but not completely sane, it means even though he is weak and the signs of his illness are still noticeable in his body, he has not fully recovered but is like a person recovering from an illness. Nonetheless, during his period of health, he is considered fully competent for that time (Beit Yosef in the name of Rashba). It seems to me that this is not the case for all types of mental illnesses, such as epilepsy, according to the words of the Rambam that we have brought. Certainly, we need to see that he has almost returned to his strength, and similarly, we need to examine other matters that are similar to this illness. The words of the Shulchan Aruch are only referring to a person whose madness has clearly left him, and he is as rational as any other person. Therefore, even if he is still weak and his illness is noticeable, nevertheless, in his rationality, he is healthy and strong. This requires careful examination.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in his great book in the name of the R"i and the Rema that when we do not know with certainty the time when a person is healthy and the time when he is insane, it constitutes a doubt, and it is clear. The explanation of his words is that when the time of his health is not known, meaning that his illness and health do not have a fixed time, if we do not know clearly that at the time he gave the get (divorce document) he was healthy, such as when the court did not investigate him thoroughly, we should not validate the get based merely on an assumption that the observers said he appeared to be healthy then, since it was not thoroughly investigated. Certainly, if he was not completely sane and his strength was still weak, as stated in the previous section, we should not validate the get in such a case when there is no fixed time. But when he has a fixed time, then during his period of health, we assume him to be in a state of health since that is his pattern (and this is also the intent of the Ba'er Heitev in se'if katan 4). 

I have seen someone who wrote that when his illness does not have a fixed time, his get should not be validated even during his period of health (according to the P'ri To'ar in se'if katan 2). However, one cannot say this since the Rambam clearly wrote that there is no distinction between epilepsy with a fixed time or without a fixed time, as stated in section 9. Furthermore, the language of the Tosefta that we brought does not indicate this either. What logic is there to make such a distinction? Rather, it is certain that when there is no fixed time, we need to investigate very thoroughly (and also from Rosh Hashanah 28 it is clearly proven so, see there and pay close attention).

And when he is healthy and permitted to divorce, as we have stated, even though we know that he will return to his madness, we do not concern ourselves with it, since he is presently healthy. This is not similar to what is stated in Siman 119 regarding a woman, where she should not be divorced even during her lucid periods if she sometimes is sane and sometimes insane, because there the rabbinic ordinance is that they should not treat her with disregard during her insanity. And after the fact, even for a woman, such a divorce would be valid as stated there in section 24. But for a man, this does not apply. The signs of insanity are explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 35, and see what we wrote there in section 7 regarding the opinion of those who disagree with the Rambam and hold that only the signs mentioned in the beginning of Chagigah in the Gemara are considered insanity and not in other matters. Their words have been rejected by most of the poskim, and we have explained that it is possible that they too agree with the Rambam, as mentioned there. (See also in this Siman and in Beit Shmuel, subsection 9).

Melancholic individuals who do not engage in any madness but merely sit in sadness, avoiding social gatherings, and do not seek food, though when given food they eat, and do not initiate conversations, though when asked they respond with few words, and do not speak irrationally—there is a question as to whether they are considered insane or not. According to logic, this does not exhibit signs of insanity but rather a condition of sadness alone, and it depends on the discernment of the court to understand his ways and behaviors (and see Rashi on Chagigah 3b: "I heard it as an illness that seizes from sadness," end quote, and this is not considered insanity, see there and in Pis'chei Teshuvah).

It is very, very important to be cautious with a deathbed get (bill of divorce) when the person commands to write a get, that he should be of sound mind at the time he commands the scribe to write and the witnesses to sign, and at the time the scribe writes and the witnesses sign, he should be of sound mind the entire time of the writing and the signing. For the scribe is the husband's agent, and since at the time of writing he is not of sound mind, how can his agent write? And even according to those authorities who hold that agency is not required in writing, nevertheless, when he commands him to write and the scribe acts on his behalf, it is necessary that he himself be of sound mind and fit to write himself. And even at the time of the witnesses' signing, if he was deranged, our master the Beit Yosef writes that the get is null and void. And even when there are delivery witnesses, it is as if it is inherently forged, and though this is only a rabbinical invalidation, nevertheless, the get is null and void from the Torah (Tiferet Gedaliah). The reason is that since he commands them to sign, there must be a law of agency, and since the law of agency is nullified because he is deranged, the get is null and void (there).

However, to my humble opinion, it is perplexing to state that it would be invalid by Torah law if he was not sane at the time of the signing. For it is understandable regarding the writing, which is his responsibility to write the get (bill of divorce), and he has it written by the scribe, that it is necessary for him to be fit for writing at the time the scribe writes. But concerning the signing of the witnesses, even if we say that it is his responsibility to have the witnesses sign, it is sufficient for him to be of sound mind at the time he commands them to sign. But at the time of the signing, what does his mental state matter to us? After all, he is not the one signing the get, but the witnesses are signing, just as in any testimony. And how can we say that the get is invalid by Torah law? Indeed, none of the early authorities mentioned at all that he must be sane at the time of the signing, only at the time of the writing and the giving. Even in the Shulchan Aruch, section 4, the signing is not mentioned at all. Similarly, our teacher, Rabbi Yosef Karo, in his great book where he extensively discusses this matter, does not mention this at all. Only at the end of his words did he write as follows: "And in a case where it is clarified to us that he was insane at the time of the command, or at the time of writing and signing, it is invalid according to all opinions." From the fact that he did not write "or at the time of signing," it appears that his main intention was regarding the writing, and the common phrase includes them together because there is nothing that interrupts between the writing and the signing. Also, the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch did not mention the signing at all. Therefore, the matter requires further investigation regarding the law.

All the more so, at the time of giving the get (divorce document), the person must be of sound mind (Levush). If he became mentally unsound between the writing and the giving, it does not affect the validity, and there is proof from what has been explained about one who said, "Write a get for my wife," and then was seized by an evil spirit and said, "Do not write it," and then recovered. We write it based on his initial words, as stated in section 4. This implies that the seizure by the evil spirit did not nullify his initial words, and all the more so it does not nullify the act of writing the get (Beit Yosef). Even if he became mentally unsound in the middle of the writing and stopped writing, when he recovers, they finish the writing (there). And so it is explained by all our early authorities that one only needs to be of sound mind at the time of writing and giving, and any interruption due to lack of mental soundness in between does not concern us, as our master the Beit Yosef elaborated in his great work, see there.

And this is what our Rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot, wrote (Gittin 72b, s.v. hatam): "And concerning a will of a deathly ill person (shechiv mera), Rabbi Yitzchak says that one must be careful that there is no deterioration between the writing and the giving, etc." Their intention is not that the deterioration in between invalidates the get (divorce document), but rather this is the explanation: If after writing it, he deteriorates and gives it to her while in a deteriorated state, even though he later recovers, we do not say that it is revealed that he was of sound mind when he gave her the get and that it was just a temporary insanity and the get is valid. Rather, we are uncertain, perhaps he was insane at the time of giving, and she is doubtfully divorced (Beit Yosef). Or their intention is that they are obligated to see before the giving that he is of sound mind at the time of giving. And if we did not see and later saw him in a deteriorated state, we are concerned also for the time of giving, as it does not apply to establish the presumption (chazaka) of the time of writing that he was of sound mind and say that he was also of sound mind at the time of giving. Since he is prone to deterioration, he does not have a presumption (see Maharshal and Pnei Yehoshua there). And this is what is written in the Order of Writing a Get according to the Rosh, z"l (of blessed memory): "And if a deathly ill person commands to write a get for his wife, the scribe must be careful that the sick person is of sound mind and settled from the beginning of the writing until the completion of the giving. For if his mind becomes disturbed in between, even if his mind later returns to him, the get is invalid." This is a printing error, and it should say "until the completion of the writing" (Beit Yosef). And similarly, the Tur in the end of Siman 154, who copied this order from the Rosh, wrote explicitly "from the beginning of the writing of the get until the completion of the writing." And similarly, Rabbeinu Yerucham copied it this way and not as it says before us in the Rosh. And this is also implied from what is written that the scribe should be careful. And if according to the version before us, the caution is on those arranging the get, but concerning the time of writing, this caution applies to the scribe who writes it. And nonetheless, Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in Darkei Moshe, section 1, that since also in the order of the get found in our hands it is written like the language of the Tosafot and the Rosh, it is good to be cautious according to their words. And this is also written by the great later authorities (Bach, Siftei Kohen, section 5), and only in a post-facto situation can one be lenient. And I do not understand their words—what relevance is there to "initially" and "post-facto"? Is it in our hands that the mind of the sick person should not be interrupted in the middle? And if we say that their intention is that if he becomes insane in the middle, they should initially arrange another get, this is even more puzzling. And who says to us that in the second one it will not be the same? And furthermore, how can we not be concerned about the case where there might not be enough time to arrange another get properly? Therefore, their words are not clear to me, in my humble opinion, and the main point is as Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef said.

In my humble opinion, I find it appropriate to uphold the version of Tosafot and the Rosh that is before us, as they do not contradict all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). We must distinguish between a case where the sick person only instructs to write and sign, and he himself gives the get (divorce document). In that case, we are not concerned if there was a disruption between the writing and the giving. Tosafot and the Rosh refer to a situation where the sick person said "write and give," making the agent responsible for both the writing and the giving. In such a case, there is a rationale to say that if there was a disruption between the writing and the giving, it is not a valid get. The intention is not that the get itself is invalid but that the giving is invalid, and therefore, another agent needs to be appointed for the giving once he recovers, or he himself should give it, for reasons that will be explained with God's help.

For behold, there are some of the great authorities who question everything explained in the Talmud and poskim (decisors) that a person has the ability to say, "Write and deliver a get (divorce document) to my wife."
