How can he appoint an agent for the delivery while the get is not yet written? For we hold that anything a person cannot do himself at present, he cannot appoint an agent to do (Nazir 12b). And before the writing, he is unable to deliver the get to his wife, so how can he appoint him as an agent? And one cannot say that because it is within his power to write it, it is considered something he can do now, for the Tosafot there explicitly wrote that even for something within his power, since it requires an action, he cannot appoint an agent (see Noda BiYehuda, Drush 13). However, the simple answer is that certainly if he were only appointing an agent for the delivery alone, he would not be able to do so. But since he is appointing for both the writing and the delivery, it is all considered one act of agency from the beginning of the writing until the completion of the delivery (see his son's gloss there and in She'elot U'Teshuvot Sho'el U'Meshiv, section 86). To what can this be compared? To one who hands over a get to an agent to deliver to his wife who is several days' journey away, even though he cannot hand it to her now. Nevertheless, since the agency begins from this moment, we do not question it (ibid.).

And based on this, a person on their deathbed (shechiv me'ra) who says, "Write and give a get (bill of divorce) to my wife," and then becomes incapacitated after the writing, thereby voiding the agency of giving the get. And even though the agency was not completely voided when he became incapacitated in the middle, as we have written, this is only in the middle of the writing or in the middle of the giving, where it is not completely voided but only temporarily interrupted. However, when he made an agency together for both the writing and the giving, and the agency was interrupted between the writing and the giving, the giving is considered a separate agency. And if we consider it a separate agency, then the agency he made before the writing does not help, because he himself cannot do it. Thus, it is necessary either to appoint an agent for the giving when he recovers or to deliver it himself. This requires further deliberation because I have not found any of the poskim (decisors) who discuss this matter, and therefore it remains a question in practice.

According to what has been explained, any sick person who is commanded to write a get (divorce document) for his wife requires an examination both at the time of writing and signing and at the time of giving it. However, the examination is not like the examination for someone who has become mute, as will be explained in this section, where it is necessary to examine him three times intermittently. Specifically, when someone has become mute from speaking, such an examination is needed. But a sick person who speaks only requires a minor examination to see if his mind is settled upon him, so that he is not like those sick people who speak without knowing what they are saying (Beis Yosef). And so our teacher the Rema ruled in paragraph 4, and there is no disagreement about this matter. And if he does not know what he is saying, his status is like that of a fool (ibid.). And one should not ask, since he speaks and knows what he is saying, why is any examination needed at all? For it can be said that because he is sick, he is prone to mental changes, therefore we are concerned about him. Furthermore, in truth, this very thing itself is his examination, that when he speaks and knows what he is saying, a get is written for him.

And if they did not examine him and wrote and gave her a get (divorce document), our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in his major work that it might be valid after the fact (bediavad), as this seems to be the implication of the language used by Tosafot and the Rosh, who wrote that one needs to be cautious about this. It implies that it is merely a general caution and specifically if he did not become mute. But if he became mute, even after the fact, one cannot validate without examination, as will be explained (Rema in Darkei Moshe, and there is a question on the Beit Shmuel, section 5, who disputed this. See there, for the Rema is also referring to a case where he became mute. See there). However, in truth, even if he did not become mute, it is always possible to clarify afterwards according to the state of his illness, and those who attend to him during his illness can know well if he was of sound mind during the time of writing and giving. And it has already become the custom that every rabbi who comes to arrange a get for a sick person examines him thoroughly and does not rely on others, and supervises him throughout the entire time of writing, signing, and giving.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (end of chapter 7): "If a man became mute, and they said to him, 'Shall we write a get for your wife?' and he nodded his head, they test him three times. If he responded 'no' to 'no' and 'yes' to 'yes,' then they may write and give [the get]." And even though we require that they hear his voice instructing the scribe to write and the witnesses to sign, the Jerusalem Talmud explains that nodding is equivalent to hearing his voice. It is clarified in the Gemara (70b) that the three tests must be done intermittently, meaning they wait an hour after the nodding and then ask him the same question again (Rashi). They also wait an hour after the second question. The questions of 'no' and 'yes' are asked as follows: one 'no' and two 'yeses,' two 'nos' and one 'yes.' This testing is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud: how do they test 'no' and 'yes'? They say to him, 'Shall we write a get for your wife?' He says 'yes' (meaning he nods his head). [They ask] 'For your mother?' He says 'no.' 'For your sister?' He says 'no.' 'For your daughter?' He says 'no.' And so on. The need for one 'no' and two 'yeses,' and two 'nos' and one 'yes' is because we are concerned that if he is asked 'no' and 'yes,' 'no' and 'yes,' and he nods his head once 'no' and once 'yes,' and so on, perhaps he is afflicted with a condition that causes him to nod his head unintentionally sometimes for 'no' and sometimes for 'yes.' But if he nods two times 'no' and one 'yes,' and so on, then it cannot be attributed to such a condition, and it is certain that he is responding intentionally.

It is also stated in the Talmud there in a Baraita that they ask him if he wants them to bring him fruits from the tree that grow in the summer, and this is asked during the rainy season. And in the summer, they ask him about fruits that typically grow during the rainy season. From this, they understand if he is in his right mind or not, because when he says "yes" regarding fruits that typically grow at this time and "no" regarding fruits that do not typically grow now, it is a clear sign that he is in his right mind. If not, he is not in his right mind. They do not ask him simply to bring these or those fruits, because generally fruits can be preserved in honey from the summer for the rainy season or vice versa, but rather, they ask him if he wants them to pick them from the tree (Tosafot). The examination from the Baraita does not contradict the examination that was explained earlier, as the previous one is also a good test. However, the examination from the Baraita is a better test since he does not mistake the summer for the rainy season. Therefore, in this examination, there is no need for alternating questions or for one "no" and two "yes" as in the previous examination. Three times "no" and three times "yes" are sufficient. Additionally, they do not ask him about wearing warm clothes in the summer or cool clothes in the rainy season, as there is no clear evidence from this, even if he answers "yes" for "no" and "no" for "yes," because he might be feeling cold in the summer or hot in the rainy season. However, from fruits, there is clear evidence (Gemara and Tosafot). All that has been explained follows the approach of Rashi and Tosafot there in the discussion.

However, the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 2, Law 16: "One who has become mute, but his mind is sound, and they said to him, 'Shall we write a bill of divorce for your wife?' and he nodded his head, we test him three times intermittently. If he responded to 'No' with 'No' and to 'Yes' with 'Yes,' they may write and give [the bill of divorce]. They must test him thoroughly to ensure that his mind has not become deranged." End of quote. It seems from his words that the Talmud and the Jerusalem Talmud did not specifically require these tests, and he also did not mention what is said in the Talmud, that one 'No' and two 'Yes' are sufficient. Additionally, it seems from his words that three questions are enough because he holds that the Talmud was not specific, as the main thing is to remove any doubt and clearly know that he is responding with understanding. This is included in his statement that "they must test him thoroughly." Anyone can perform these tests as they see fit, as long as it removes any doubt (as it is found). It also appears that he does not interpret "intermittently" as Rashi does, meaning with an hour's delay, but rather "intermittently" refers to alternating 'No' and 'Yes.' None of the later authorities mentioned Rashi's hour delay. Nevertheless, it is proper to be concerned and stringent according to Rashi's opinion if there is time for this (as it is found in the glosses of the Maharil and the Mordechai, who suggest being concerned for Rashi's opinion, as well as in the Beit Shmuel in section 7). It seems to me that an hour is not specifically what we call an hour, one twenty-fourth of a day, but rather a pause in time.

The Tur states: If someone becomes mute and they ask him if he wants a get (divorce document) to be written for his wife, and he nods his head to indicate "yes," they test him with other questions. They ask him something that requires an appropriate response. If they see that his mind is settled and he gestures appropriately for "no" and "yes," nodding for "no" and for "yes," then he nods "yes" three times for each, they write and give the get. They should not test him with three consecutive "yes" or three consecutive "no," but rather one "yes," two "no," two "yes," and one "no." They should not test him with things available at that time, but in the summer, they ask him if he wants winter fruits, and in the winter, if he wants summer fruits. If he answers "yes," he is certainly a fool, but if he answers "no," he is wise. However, if they ask him in the summer if he wants to wear warm clothes suitable for winter and he answers "yes," he is not presumed to be a fool, for perhaps he feels cold. Similarly, if he answers "yes" in the winter about summer clothes, it can be attributed to the possibility that he feels hot, and she is doubtfully divorced. Thus are the words of the Tur.

And what he wrote about testing him with other matters, his intention is that the examination should not be related to the matters of the get (divorce document) as per the opinion of the Jerusalem Talmud, but rather the examination needs to be about other matters (Bach and Avnei Yehoshua, and examine closely). And Rashi's delay also seems that he does not hold this opinion (there), and he required that the examination specifically be about fruits (there). It also appears from his words that only when he answers "yes" about fruits that are not in season, he is certainly a fool, but if he answers "no" about fruits that are in season, he is not held to be a fool, as perhaps he is answering with reason but simply does not wish to eat those fruits. However, according to this, why did he write that if he answers "no" about fruits that are not in season, he is perceptive? From where do we know that his intention is perceptiveness, that he knows they are not found now? Perhaps his intention is that he does not wish to eat them. But indeed, even so, his intention is at least perceptiveness, as he answers properly and knows what is being asked of him. And the Tur did not mention that they should ask him about picking fruits from the tree because he understood that even in general fruits, when spoken about, the intention is not about those preserved in honey. And he was precise and wrote "one yes and two no's, and two yes's and one no," to exclude asking him the single "no" after two "no's" so that there would not be three consecutive "no's," as this is not truly intermittent. And our master the Beit Yosef did not concern himself with this, as is evident from his words in Section 5, see there (Avnei Yehoshua, note 7).

Furthermore, it appears to me that the Tur did not specifically refer to the inspection of fruits, but his main intention was to test him with other matters and with things that are not available at certain times in order to know through this if he is of sound mind. It is unreasonable to say that only the inspection of fruits constitutes a test and not other things. The proof for this is that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, copied his language in the Shulchan Aruch but omitted the inspection of fruits. However, from the language of our teacher, the Rema, who wrote "and some say that we test him through fruits, etc., if he wants them to be picked for him from the tree," it seems that we specifically need the inspection of fruits. And it seems to me that in our country, we do not follow this test, and it is entirely impossible to practice this, as no fruits grow here during the rainy season.

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that when do we require three examinations? When one becomes mute out of good health, as then the concern is great that perhaps he is not in his right mind. But if a sick person becomes mute, one examination is sufficient because it is certainly due to his weakness that he became mute and not that he lost his mind. However, several of our early sages did not mention this distinction in practice, and Rambam also did not mention this, nor did the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. Rashi in the Mishnah explained that the person became mute due to illness. See there (Beit Shmuel), and we can say that the explanation is that the muteness is due to an illness that has now developed in him.

If they did not examine him for becoming mute according to the law and he gave her a get (divorce document), she is also considered doubtfully divorced. Some say that this specifically applies if he became mute while he was healthy, but if he became mute due to illness, it may be permitted after the fact in a situation of potential agunah (a chained woman) (Beit Yosef). There are those who disagree with this (Beit Shmuel, section 5). In practice, one must deliberate on this and understand the nature of the illness.

And specifically, in the case of someone who became mute, his nodding and signaling are effective if they tested him and found that he is of sound mind but simply cannot speak. Similarly, a person who was born mute but can hear, and does not speak, is considered like a fully competent person, and we rely on his signaling for matters concerning a divorce (get). However, a deaf person who cannot hear or speak, who is considered like a fool, cannot divorce his wife through signaling if he married her when he was fully competent. Similarly, if a levirate widow (yevama) falls to him from his brother who was fully competent, since both the marriage and the levirate bond are from the Torah, and he is not of sound mind to dissolve the bond with a get. But if he married a woman while he was deaf, even if she is fully competent, he can divorce her through signaling, because just as he married her through signaling, he can divorce her through signaling, and for this reason, no testing is required. Similarly, a person who was born mute does not require testing, because he also married through signaling. Some say that both a deaf person and a mute person require testing (see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 9, for both opinions). A deaf person is not the same as a fool in this regard, because a fool has neither valid marriage nor divorce, but a deaf person has a weakened intellect, and therefore the Rabbis instituted marriage for him, unlike a fool, as explained in Siman 44. The laws regarding a written document are explained in Siman 120. Note that signaling must be specifically with his head and hands, but a movement with his mouth, meaning the movement of his lips, is not effective because it is not as clear a sign as signaling (Rashi, Gittin 59a). However, if he married through such movement, it is possible that he can also divorce through such movement (see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 9). Refer also to Choshen Mishpat, Siman 335.

The dying person, according to Rashi and Rach, is considered as dead and cannot divorce even though he is sound of mind. One of the early authorities wrote a reason for this, since our Sages said (Kiddushin 78b) that when he is dying, he cannot give a gift, as it says in the Gemara. And regarding a get (divorce document), it is written "and he shall place it in her hand," and we require that he be capable of giving (as explained there in the Rosh in the name of Rabbi Judah of Bonia). And although it is stated in the first chapter of Ohalot that a dying person is considered alive in all respects, inheriting and passing on inheritance, obligating levirate marriage, and exempting from levirate marriage, all of this applies to matters that happen automatically and not to actions such as giving a get or a gift, in which he is considered dead. However, Rabbi Judah the Elder, the author of the Tosafot, and the Rosh of blessed memory disagreed with them. This is also the opinion of the Rashbam of blessed memory (Baba Batra 127b) that a dying person can only not give a gift because he lacks the strength to speak, but when he can speak, it is clear that he is considered alive in all respects, as proven from the Mishnah in Ohalot and other numerous proofs. Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in his great book that according to this opinion, even a dying person who cannot speak, if there is time to examine him, can divorce through signaling and nodding. Some say that this is only when he can speak, but a dying person who cannot speak cannot divorce (Mordechai and Sefer Mitzvot Gadol). Rabbi Moshe Isserles wrote that one should be stringent according to this opinion, and it is not comparable to what will be explained regarding one who has slaughtered the signs, who can divorce through signaling, and there is no greater dying person than this. There, since he was slaughtered while in his full strength, his mind is clear, unlike the dying person whose mind is not clear when he loses the power of speech (Chokhmat Shlomo, section 10), or because he is dying from illness and has lost the power of speech, he is considered dead (Beit Shmuel, section 10). The Radbaz ruled in his responsa (volume 4, section 206) that if he can speak, they write a get for him initially, and although in Gittin we are stringent with several stringencies, this case is different because it cannot be otherwise. And it is clear from his words that when he cannot speak, they do not rely on his signaling.

The Sages said (Gittin 66a) that if someone slaughtered two of his windpipes or the majority of them and signaled and said, "Write a get for my wife," they should write and give it. Similarly, it is taught: If they saw him injured or crucified and he signaled and said, "Write a get for my wife," they should write and give it. There is no need to say "write and give" because he is in danger, like someone thrown into a pit, where it suffices to say "write" alone. And even though he will die immediately, as long as he is alive, he is considered alive. Thus, the Sages said there: "He is alive and destined to die." Similarly, it is taught in the Tosefta (Gittin, Chapter 4): A healthy person who said, "Write a get for my wife," and then climbed to the top of the roof and fell, they write and give it to her as long as he has breath in him. Thus, even if he fell to his death, as long as he is alive, he is considered fully alive. The early authorities were uncertain whether such cases require examination, and therefore, our teacher the Rema ruled that an examination is required three times as explained if he cannot speak. And one might ask, how do we know that his intention is for a get to be written? Indeed, it is when we asked him, "Shall we write a get for your wife?" and he nodded (Tosafot). There are those who say that if the majority of the windpipe was slaughtered and they wrote without examination, it is valid after the fact (Bach). It is a great wonder to say this because we witness that it is very difficult for him to maintain his intention throughout the writing and giving of the get. And know that there are those who wrote that in every place where examination is mentioned, we are not proficient in this (Bach), but this does not seem to be the opinion of all the decisors and the Shulchan Aruch. This matter requires careful consideration (Chachmat Shlomo and Beit Shmuel). Indeed, it is difficult to say that in a case of potential agunah (a woman unable to remarry), we would not rely on our examination.

When one commands to write a get (bill of divorce) and there was a mistake, whether it is possible to write another get. There are 19 sections in this:

If a man said to a scribe and witnesses to write, sign, and deliver a get to his wife, and from them also be the messenger to deliver it to her, and they wrote, signed, and delivered it to her, and it was found that the get was invalid either by Torah law or rabbinic law (Beit Yosef), they can write and sign another get and deliver it to her even without the husband’s command regarding the second get. And even though the witnesses and the scribe, once they have performed their mission, cannot perform another mission without the knowledge of the sender because he only appointed them for one matter, nevertheless in this situation, they can write another get because they have not yet fulfilled their mission, as he commanded them to write a get and not just a mere shard (Gittin 63b). And one should not say this is only reasonable when the invalidity is by Torah law and it is certainly a mere shard, but when the invalidity is by rabbinic law, it is not a mere shard because by Torah law she is divorced, and if she accepts betrothal from another, she needs a get from him, and it is not a mere shard. However, in truth, regarding the mission, it is indeed a mere shard because it is clear that when the husband commanded them to make a get, his intention was for a valid get also by rabbinic standards so she can remarry with it, for otherwise what benefit is it to her and him? Therefore, in this regard, it is considered a mere shard, and they can write another get without his knowledge.

And similarly, even if the get (divorce document) was written and signed properly but was lost before it was delivered to her, they also write another get. For in this case, too, they did not complete their mission perfectly, as they were commanded to give it to her, and when it was lost, they did not give it to her (Gemara). And Maimonides in chapter 2 omitted the case of it being lost, which is puzzling, as no one disputes this matter. It must be said that he holds it as a fortiori from a get written improperly (Beit Yosef). But in the Gemara, it implies the opposite—that the case of being lost is of greater significance. Refer there (and see Lechem Mishneh, and the words of the Maggid Mishneh are puzzling, as how could Rabba's reasoning be entirely contrary to Rav Nachman?). However, in truth, if we are precise in his words, he did not omit it at all, for he wrote there: "he said, etc., and the get was found to be invalid or improper, they write another get even a hundred times until a valid get reaches her hand." Thus, since he wrote "until it reaches her hand," it follows that as long as it has not reached her hand, such as if it was lost or for another reason, they write another get (Pri Chadash). And it is not specifically lost by itself, but even if they lost it by their own hands, they also write another get (there), for in any case it did not reach her hand. And it is possible that for this reason Maimonides did not explicitly write "lost" but rather "until it reaches her hand" to include also losing it by their own hands.

And this is specifically when he made them emissaries also for the delivery, but if he instructed them only to write and sign, and to hand the get to another emissary who would deliver it to her—whether he said "write it and give it to an emissary" or "write it and give it to an emissary who will deliver it to her"—there is a question in the Gemara there if they can write another get when it is lost from the hand of the emissary, for they have fulfilled their mission. And even when he said "and he will deliver it to her," it can be said that the intention is not that they are obligated to remain until it is delivered to her, but that it is the way of people to tell all their words, expressing their desire that the emissary deliver the get to her, and it remains unresolved. Therefore, in such a case, they do not write another get, and if they wrote and sent another get through this emissary, she is doubtfully divorced. This explanation follows Rashi’s interpretation there, and the Rosh also wrote similarly (Ketubot 6:6) that in these two cases when it is lost, it is a doubtful matter of law. And although from the language of the Tur it seems that the doubt is only in the second case when he said to them "and he will deliver it to her," but in the first case there is no doubt that they certainly cannot write another, and there is justification for this in Halacha (according to the Geonim in "If you say so"), nevertheless, it cannot be said conclusively as proven from the Rosh (Beit Yosef), and in both cases, it is a doubt.

However, the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote there: If the husband said to them, "Write and sign [the get] and give it to the agent to bring it to her," and they wrote and signed it and gave it to the agent, and the get was found to be invalid or disqualified, they should not write another [get] until they consult with the husband, for he did not appoint them as agents for the divorce itself, and perhaps he only wanted them to write and give it to the agent alone, etc. And if they wrote another get, etc., it is a doubtful divorce. End of quote. The question in the Talmud is explained to refer to a case where the get is found to be disqualified, but from Rashi, the Rosh, and the Tur, it appears that the question is only about a lost get. However, regarding a disqualified get, what relevance does it have to say they completed their agency, since they did not write it according to the law? Furthermore, from the Rambam, it seems that it is specifically when he said to bring it to her that there is doubt, but in the first case where he only said to give it to the agent, there is no doubt. Certainly, they cannot write another get even if it is found to be disqualified in its writing. The reason of the Rambam must be because since he only commanded them to deliver it to the agent, and in the act of delivery to the agent, she is not yet divorced, therefore, the husband might not be concerned even if it was written disqualified, because even with a valid get she is not yet divorced, and he did not make them agents until she is divorced. But when he said to bring it to her, there is doubt that perhaps his intention was until it reaches her hand. And it seems that according to the Rambam, if it was lost in any case, it is clear that they cannot write another get since it was written according to the law. (Beit Yosef and Avodat HaBayit, section 7).

And some say that Rashi and the Rambam do not disagree regarding the distinction between a lost and a found invalid get (Jewish divorce document), as Rashi does not specifically mention a lost get, as the same rule applies to a found invalid get, which is a case of doubt. Similarly, when the Rambam mentions an invalid get, the same applies if it is lost (Rabbeinu Yerucham, Book 3). However, this does not seem correct, as the reasoning is not the same. Rather, it is certain that in the case of a found invalid get, according to Rashi, the Rosh, and the Tur, one can definitely write another get. But in the case of a lost get, according to the Rambam, one certainly cannot write another get (Beit Yosef).

There are those who wish to equate the opinions, that which the Rambam wrote regarding a disqualification found in a get (divorce document), this applies when the disqualification was found after it was handed to the messenger and the disqualification occurred after it was given to the messenger. This is similar to it being lost, since it was handed to the messenger in a valid state. However, if the disqualification existed beforehand, even the Rambam agrees that they can write another one (Beit Shmuel, section 7). This does not seem to be the case from his words, as he wrote in a similar manner beforehand, and there it means that it was written in an invalid state. Additionally, in the Talmud, this issue is mentioned before the law of it being lost. For this reason, Rashi explains it as referring to a lost document. If the Rambam meant a disqualification that occurred in the messenger's hand, why would he mention a law not found in the Gemara? It would have been better for him to write about it being lost. Therefore, it is evident that the Rambam intentionally wrote this because it is obvious to him that there is no doubt in the case of a lost document, as he wrote. Certainly, in practice, one must be stringent according to both opinions (and even though the Maggid Mishneh implies like the Rivash, nevertheless the main opinion follows the Beit Yosef). From our teacher, the Rema, in section 2, it appears that he holds the main practice according to Rashi and the explanation of the Beit Yosef that we have written, and he was very concise there.

It is obvious that even according to Rashi, who explained that if a defect is found in a get (bill of divorce) in any manner, another get can be written. This applies only if [the husband] said, "Write and give [the get]" or "Write and give [the get] to the agent who will deliver it to her." However, if he instructed the scribe to write and the witnesses to sign, and he took the get from them and personally handed it to the agent to deliver the get to his wife, and it was found to be defective, they cannot write another get without the husband's permission. This is because the agent was made an agent only for this specific get that was handed to him, and not for another one (Choshen Mishpat 6). Even if he did not explicitly make him an agent for this specific get but made him an agent in general and handed it to him, he cannot accept another get without the husband’s knowledge (Beit Shmuel 8). Ultimately, when he handed it to him, he did not appoint him as an agent except for this get. And if he told the agent, "Deliver this get, and up to a hundred gets, until one of them is valid," according to the opinion of the Rav, it is treated like the scribe and witnesses, as will be explained later (ibid.).

According to the laws that have been clarified, anyone who writes a get (bill of divorce) for his wife and delivers it to her personally, and the get is arranged as customary where the officiating rabbi instructs the husband to tell the scribe, "Write a get for my wife," and the witnesses to sign, as will be explained in the order of the get in Siman 154, and the husband says so, and a defect is found in the get, the husband does not need to instruct the scribe again to write it. Rather, the scribe himself writes another get, because the husband appointed him as an agent to write a get and not merely a worthless piece of pottery. The Rosh of blessed memory wrote (there) that this is specifically when a clear defect is found. However, if there is doubt whether the get is valid or not, due to stringencies that have been adopted beyond the letter of the law, the scribe cannot write another get, because according to the basic law, the scribe has fulfilled his agency. Therefore, when another get is required, the husband needs to instruct him to write another get. Similarly, if there is doubt for the officiant whether there is a defect in the get according to the law or not, the husband needs to instruct, for how can the scribe write on his own, perhaps there is no defect, and he has already fulfilled his agency.

And because of this, our Rabbis, the Tosafists (63b) and the Rosh there, and other early authorities, wrote that it is good to instruct the husband to tell the scribe and the witnesses to write and sign the get (divorce document) so that it will be valid according to their opinion without any doubt. Then, if some minor issue is found that does not invalidate it according to the law, they can write and sign another get without the husband's permission, since he had already given them permission for this.

Therefore, our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, established this in the order of the get (divorce document) at the end of Siman 154. They wrote there in paragraph 15: The husband should hand the parchment, etc., to the scribe in the presence of witnesses and say to him before them, "Write me a get for the sake of divorcing my wife, so-and-so, etc., and I give you permission to write the get from one to one hundred until one is valid without any doubt, whether in the writing or in the signing, according to the opinion of such-and-such a sage or to whomever he shows it, etc." End of quote. And similarly, in paragraph 16, it is written that he should say the same to the witnesses, that they should sign for him up to one hundred gets until one of them is valid according to the opinion of such-and-such a sage. See there. And this is the practice of all those who arrange gets.

And it is very puzzling to me because several of the early authorities wrote that it is not proper to do so, due to the concern of retroactive clarification (bereirah). This means that we would need to say it was clarified retroactively that this get (bill of divorce) which the rabbi validated was indeed the husband's intention. And we hold that in matters of Torah law, there is no bereirah, as written in the glosses of Mordechai on Gittin in the name of Rabbi Yosef Kolon. And so wrote the Kol Bo, and the Beit Yosef in his major work in this section also wrote similarly in the name of Rabbi Yechiel, and added that the source of this matter is from Rabbi Yehudah the Elder, the author of the Tosafot, who holds that we follow bereirah. However, the Rambam, Rabbeinu Tam, and several other early authorities ruled that in matters of Torah law, we hold that there is no bereirah.

Moreover, it is puzzling to me that in this chapter, section 1, it is written in the Shulchan Aruch as follows: Therefore, if the husband leaves the city, he should state that he gives them permission to write and sign a get (bill of divorce) from one to a hundred, provided that one of them is fit both in writing and in signing according to the opinion of the rabbi in the city without any doubt, and to anyone who sees it. However, if the husband is in the city, one should not rely on this, and the husband must repeatedly instruct the witnesses and the scribe each time. And so is the custom, that he repeatedly instructs them as he did initially. He also transfers to them the parchment and the ink if the scribe no longer has any left from what was originally given to him. And the reason one does not rely on this is due to the principle of "bereirah" (retroactive designation), as mentioned in the Beit Yosef. If so, later in the order of the get, which deals with an ordinary get where the husband is in the city and is not in a hurry to leave, why did they establish this in the order of the get?

It appears to me that our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, hold that there is necessarily no concern of "bererah" (retroactive clarification) in this matter. How can one say that Rabbi Yochanan, the author of the Tosafot, follows his own reasoning that we hold there is "bererah"? After all, the Tosafot in Gittin (24b) write in his name that even one who generally holds there is "bererah" agrees that in matters of divorce we hold there is no "bererah," since it is written "for her sake," implying that it must be clarified at the time of writing. Therefore, it is certainly not relevant to this issue at all, as the Maharshal wrote (in Yam Shel Shlomo, Gittin, Chapter 6, Siman 5), and these are his words: “It does not seem to me at all appropriate to compare this to the matter of 'bererah,' since it is stated that it should be valid according to the opinion of the rabbi. Therefore, it is as if he explicitly clarified that the first ones are nullified and only the last one will complete his agency.” (And similarly, the Gaon of Prague wrote there). 

And even though, upon closer examination, there is a concern of "bererah" because we require the get (bill of divorce) to be written for her sake and for the sake of severance, meaning that the scribe should write it with the intention that the husband will divorce her with this get. And since he did not make him an agent for writing except in a manner that the rabbi agrees to this get, therefore, at the time of writing, he writes to divorce her in a manner that the rabbi agrees. And even if it is valid and the rabbi does not agree, he will not divorce with it, and this is truly "bererah" (retroactive clarification) that after showing it to the rabbi and the rabbi agrees to this get, it becomes clarified that this get was written for the sake of divorce. 

However, in truth, one must say that this is not a complete condition, and he is not making an exact condition. The primary intention of the condition is that he appoints him an agent to write as many gittin as he wishes, and it depends on his will to show it to the rabbi. Additionally, this condition is like other conditions in a get, and if so, in every condition in a get, we should also say that once the condition is fulfilled, it is a get retroactively. Why do we not say there is a concern of "bererah"? However, Rashi already wrote (Gittin 25b) that "bererah" does not apply to conditions in a get because it is within his power to fulfill them and his intention is to fulfill them when he makes the condition, and once the condition is fulfilled, it is a get retroactively. There is no concern of "bererah" there. And similarly here, the scribe can write a valid get, and the rabbi will certainly not seek pretexts to invalidate it, and thus, there is no concern of "bererah" (so it appears to me).

Therefore, in the order of the get in Siman 154, they wrote to practice this way due to the concern that they might write a second get and forget to obtain permission from the husband. There is a concern that the get might not be entirely invalid, so according to the law, they do not have permission to write another get without his command. The concern of clarification does not hold according to the reasons we have explained. However, in this Siman, which deals with the essence of the law, they wrote that if the husband leaves the city, it is necessary to say this. How will they act if there is a concern about the get and he has left the city? Afterwards, they wrote that when the husband is in the city, it is not advisable to rely on this, and he should command again. Since there are those who are stringent due to the concept of clarification, and in matters of the get they are very meticulous to fulfill all opinions, therefore, when he is in the city, he should command again. He should not say this formula, since we are making him command again; how can he say this formula which contains this concern? This is also what the later authorities wrote. One should not say, "If so, why did they arrange this formula in the order of the get? Why not be concerned initially for the concern of clarification to fulfill all opinions?" Because it can be said that they were more concerned about the possibility that they might forget to tell the husband to command them to write another get due to the concern of clarification, since in their opinion there is no concern of clarification at all.

And all this is to justify their words, but in truth, I have seen and heard from great authorities who very much doubted this matter and instituted not to say this version. And so I practice, for why should we involve ourselves in the dispute of the early authorities? After all, in the end, when another get (divorce document) is required, we do not rely on the first arrangement, and the husband is commanded again to write and sign. Therefore, it is unnecessary, even for one who does not hold this concern, except when the husband is in a hurry to leave, in which case it is necessary to arrange in this version. (Also, the Tevu'ot Shor in section 7 wrote that it is better not to say this version at all, but rather to say that he should write as many gittin (divorce documents) as he wishes. And since it is impossible to say according to the version of the Shulchan Aruch, why should we say this at all? And so, the Gaon Rabbi Eliyahu Mordechai Halevi from Pinsk told me that he and his predecessor, the Gaon Rabbi Mordechai of blessed memory, did not arrange at all in this version.)

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that some say that when we say that the witnesses and the scribe have fulfilled their agency and need to be instructed again, this is only if the document has already been signed and invalidated. But if it has not yet been signed, another scribe can write it, and the husband does not need to instruct again. However, the custom is to be stringent in all matters. End of quote. And they wondered about this: what is the relation of the scribe to the witnesses, for the scribe has already fulfilled his agency (Taz, and these are also the words of the Beit Shmuel, section 6). This is only satisfactory for the one who holds that the witnesses of the signing effectuate the document (i.e., the main thing is the signatures, and the writing without the signatures is nothing). But for us, who hold that the witnesses of the delivery effectuate the document, the main thing is the writing (ibid., and also the Yam Shel Shlomo there criticized the Rashbatz, see there). Furthermore, the source of the law is from the Tashbatz as written in the Beit Yosef, and he did not write this as a law, remaining doubtful about it, see there. Therefore, when he concluded that the custom is to be stringent in all matters, this is not a stringency but the essential law itself (Taz).

And it appears to me that his opinion is indeed correct, that certainly if there was a commandment for the scribe to write independently and for the witnesses to sign independently, they are indeed two separate delegations. But since they are commanded together to write and sign, it is all considered one delegation. And as long as they have not signed, the delegation is not completed at all, and this has no relevance to "matters of a document" (inyanei shtarot), for ultimately, he commanded them together to write and sign. And the proof for this is from what the Nimukei Yosef wrote (in Gittin, and brought in Sema, Siman 79, Seif Katan 10) that a document that was signed by one witness and then lost or erased, they can write another document, for as long as the second witness has not signed, it is considered that they have not fulfilled their delegation. Hence, it is explicitly stated that even though this witness has fulfilled his delegation, nevertheless, since he commanded both of them, as long as the second has not finished, it is considered even for the first that his delegation is not completed. And similarly, regarding the scribe and witnesses. Therefore, even here, there is an opinion that even if one witness has already signed the get (bill of divorce), as long as the second has not signed, it is still considered that they have not fulfilled their delegation and they are permitted to write another get (Choshen Mishpat 32:2). However, according to the custom that has been adopted to be stringent in every matter, it implies that even if only part of the get was written and it became invalid, nevertheless, he has fulfilled his delegation for the part that he wrote, and the husband needs to command again (ibid.). And according to the custom, even in the case of a complete invalidation that according to Torah law another could be written, nevertheless, the custom is to be stringent.

He further wrote that even in a case where, according to the law, they need to ask the husband and he commands them to write another get, such as when it is not invalid according to the law but only due to an extra stringency, nevertheless, if they wish to write another get and give her two gittin, they have permission and do not need to ask the husband. The reason is simple: if the first is valid, she is divorced with the first, and if it is invalid, then his opinion is not needed and she is divorced with the second. However, it will be explained later that two gittin should only be given out of necessity, therefore, this is not a good solution (Beit Shmuel, section 2). And know that what our teacher, the Rema, wrote—that when the husband retracts and commands to write another get, he transfers ownership of the parchment and ink to them—the language is not precise, for does the husband need to transfer ownership to them? It appears to me that it is a scribal error, and it should say "he transfers ownership to him," meaning the scribe transfers ownership to the husband.

There is an opinion that the scribe should be cautious, after the rabbi has reviewed the get (bill of divorce) and found any deficiency in it, such as extending a letter or letters that have been blurred and their form is no longer recognizable, not to make any corrections without the rabbi's permission. This is because it might be valid according to the rabbi's opinion, and the scribe has already fulfilled his duty. Therefore, in some forms of gittin (bills of divorce), the husband initially instructs the scribe that the get should be valid in the eyes of the rabbi and anyone to whom it is shown, so that the scribe also has the authority to make corrections after having considered the rabbi’s opinion (Choshen Mishpat, Siman 1, quoting Darchei Moshe). This custom, however, has never been adopted, and especially for those who do not follow this format as we have explained, the scribe has no authority to correct anything in the get without the husband’s permission. Nevertheless, one of the great authorities has wondered about this, reasoning that since it is valid even without correction, what harm is there if the scribe corrects it on his own? And if it is invalid without the correction, then the opinion of others is not needed at all, as the scribe has not yet fulfilled his duty. It must be that it is indeed not valid without the correction, and the rabbi mistakenly ruled it valid. In such a case, if the scribe corrects it without the rabbi’s permission, it does not help, because the husband instructed him to make it valid according to the rabbi’s opinion (Turei Zahav). Therefore, in places where this format is not practiced at all, it is preferable that the scribe himself has the authority to make corrections in any matter as we have stated.

Laws regarding who is eligible to write a Get (divorce document) and the law concerning it being written on Shabbat. This section contains 18 paragraphs:
Rambam of blessed memory wrote (Hilchot Gerushin 3:15): Everyone is eligible to write a Get except for five: a non-Jew, a slave, a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor. Even a woman herself can write her Get. A Jew who has converted to idolatry or publicly desecrates the Sabbath is considered like a non-Jew in all respects. Why are these five not allowed to write a Get? Because the writer must write it for the sake of the man who is divorcing and the woman who is being divorced. A non-Jew writes on his own accord, a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor do not have legal capacity, and a slave is not subject to the laws of divorce and marriage, therefore he is disqualified like a non-Jew in all respects. If one of these five writes the Get, it is not a valid Get, even if valid witnesses signed it and it was delivered to her by valid means. End of quote.

From his words, it is understood that he holds like the poskim (decisors) we mentioned in Siman 120, Se’if 14, that we do not require agency (shelichut) in the writing (of a get, a Jewish bill of divorce). Otherwise, why would he explain these reasons? For all of these invalidations, there is a simple reason that they are not fit for agency. It also appears that he holds that even though we do not require agency in the writing, nevertheless, the writer must be eligible for the law of divorce. Therefore, he wrote that the reason for invalidating a slave is that he is not within the framework of gittin and kiddushin (divorce and marriage), meaning he is not eligible for divorce. Some of our rabbis hold that in matters where we do not require agency, we also do not require eligibility for the law of divorce. The Talmud (Gittin 23b) invalidates a slave from being an agent for delivering a get because he is not within the framework of divorce and marriage, as delivering a get requires agency. Therefore, regarding a slave, even if he has agency, he is not eligible for divorce. But for the writing of the get, if we say that agency is not required, then eligibility for the law of divorce is also not required (Tosafot Gittin 22b, s.v. "Veha" first explanation, and the Rosh, Ran, and Rashba there). Therefore, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not write these reasons because they hold that agency is required in the writing, as mentioned there.

And this is why the Rambam needed the reason regarding a gentile that he writes with his own intention, and it does not suffice for him with the reason that he is a slave. Indeed, the reason is that for a gentile himself, it is sufficient with the reason that he is not someone who is subject to "karet" (spiritual excision). However, because he wrote that one who publicly desecrates Shabbat is considered like a gentile, it is impossible to say this reason, as he is certainly someone who is subject to "karet." Even though he has sinned, he is still an Israelite. Therefore, he also needed to give another reason for a gentile, that this reason applies also to one who desecrates Shabbat (see Beit Shmuel, section 5). According to this, the Rambam's statement makes sense, that if any of these five wrote, it is not a valid get (divorce document), and it implies that from the Torah it is not a get. It is difficult because if he wrote it with the invalidity of a gentile due to writing with his own intention and not for its sake, it is still questionable, as perhaps his intention was for its sake. But in truth, its invalidity is because he is not someone subject to "karet" (Beit Yosef). According to this, according to our rabbis who hold that even someone subject to "karet" is not required in writing, the invalidity of a gentile would be questionable (ibid). And know that a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor are considered people subject to "karet," for they indeed are subject to "karet" once the minor grows up and the deaf-mute and the imbecile recover. However, they are not of sufficient understanding at all to write for its sake, and thus it is invalid from the Torah.

According to this, in the case of someone who desecrates Shabbat, where the reason is only because he acts on his own accord, it appears that it is not definitely invalidated by Torah law but is a doubtful invalidation. Perhaps he wrote it with proper intent, and it is possible that this is why the Rambam was precise in his language, stating that if the get (divorce document) was written by one of these five (categories of people), it is not a get, to exclude the one who desecrates Shabbat, which is a doubtful case, as we have written.

Therefore, in practice, for a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor, according to all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), the get is invalidated by Torah law. For a non-Jew and a slave, according to those who hold that agency is required in writing, and certainly for those who require the ability to sever (the marriage), it is also invalidated by Torah law. Even according to the Rambam, who does not require agency in writing, since he requires the ability to sever, it is also invalidated by Torah law. According to the poskim who do not require the ability to sever, in the case of a non-Jew it is a doubtful invalidation because perhaps he did not write on his own accord. In the case of a kosher slave, he does not write on his own accord, and so wrote the Ramban and the Rashba, as the Maggid Mishneh and the Beit Yosef mentioned in their names. And the one who desecrates Shabbat is a doubtful invalidation according to all opinions, as we have explained (as it appears to me).

And regarding what was written, that the woman herself writes her own get (bill of divorce), the Tur wrote in the name of the Ramah that it is specifically when the husband initially tells her to write it, as it needs to be written by him or his agent; otherwise, it is invalid. This follows his (the Ramah's) opinion that agency is required in the writing, and the same applies to another person (as stated by the Chamudei Daniel and Bais Shmuel). The Tur informs us that not only in the case of another person, even if one does not require agency, without the husband's directive, it would not be considered written with proper intent, as explained in Siman 120, that a woman is not ordinarily positioned for divorce (as stated at the beginning of Zevachim). Even if she is positioned for divorce and certainly writes it with proper intent, since agency is required, the husband must command her. The Rambam did not mention this because he does not require agency in the writing, as he wrote. Nevertheless, it is certain that according to him, the husband still needs to instruct her, and if he did not, it might be a doubtful case in law. It is not similar to another person for the reasons we explained, and this requires further investigation. What the Rambam writes about a woman doing it for the sake of demonstration is to show that even she can write it. But regarding the proper intent, it can be argued differently, as we wrote (this seems to me).

The Tur also wrote that when she writes her get (bill of divorce) and transfers it to her husband, and he then returns it to her, this is certainly correct, and all the early authorities explained this. Although the Sages granted him the compensation for the writing, nevertheless, when the parchment belongs to her, she needs to transfer it to him, for the Sages did not grant from what is hers, as stated in Siman 120, Section 29. And even when she transfers it to him after the writing, it is still valid and not considered lacking an action, as stated there in Section 32. And the Rambam did not need to mention this, as it is an obvious matter, and he was not dealing with this. He only stated that she is allowed to write it and the parchment can be his (see Beit Shmuel, Subsection 2). And the Shulchan Aruch wrote exactly in the language of the Tur, see there Section 1.

The Rambam further wrote there: If one of these five writes the form of the get (divorce document) and leaves the place for the essential parts—specifically, the place for the man, the place for the woman, the place for the date, and the place for the phrase "you are permitted to any man"—and a competent Israelite writes these essential parts for the sake of the woman, this is a valid get. It is permitted to allow a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor to write the form of the get initially, provided that a competent adult Israelite oversees them. However, a non-Jew or a slave may not write the form of the get initially, even if a competent Israelite oversees them, etc. These are the words of the Rambam (as explained in the Gemara 23a, where it is clarified that Rav Huna and Shmuel do not disagree and both require a competent adult overseeing and leaving the place for the essential parts. See there).

The explanation of his words is that, according to the fundamental law, there is no concern with the form at all, as writing with specific intent (lishma) is required only for the essential parts (toref). Therefore, the Sages permitted, for the benefit of the scribes, to write standard forms of bills of divorce (Gitin) as stated there in Law 7, and this is an explicit Mishnah (26a). Hence, after the fact (bediavad), if one of these five wrote the form, we are not concerned. However, initially (lechatchila), we do not permit them to write even the form, as we decree the form because of the essential parts (toref). Initially, even the form needs to be written with specific intent (lishma), and only for the benefit of the scribe did they permit this. However, an adult standing over them and teaching them to write with specific intent (lishma) allows even the form to be written initially, as it is written with specific intent (lishma). With a non-Jew or a slave, an adult standing over them does not help, as they act according to their own understanding. For the essential parts (toref), an adult standing over them does not help even for a minor, a deaf-mute, or an imbecile (cheresh, shoteh, v'katan). This seems to be only rabbinic, for from the Torah, why would it not help? With a non-Jew or a slave, if they wrote the essential parts (toref) with an adult standing over them, it appears it is a doubtful invalidation from the Torah, as perhaps they did not act according to their own understanding (and the Beit Shmuel wrote similarly in Section 65).

And there are some of our Rabbis who hold that with a non-Jew, even after the fact, a form is invalid by rabbinic law. And some say that with a minor, deaf-mute, or mentally incompetent person, if an adult stands over them, they can write even the essential parts. But with a non-Jew and a slave, it is invalid because they act on their own understanding. And in a form, all of them can write from the outset even without an adult standing over them (for they hold that these are two separate issues of Rav Huna and Shmuel and do not disagree, and examine this carefully). And there are those who hold that if an adult stands over them, a minor, deaf-mute, or mentally incompetent person can write even the essential parts, and without an adult standing over them, even the form is invalid (for they hold that there is a disagreement, and the law follows Rav Huna, see there). And there are those who hold that the form can be written even without an adult standing over them, but the essential parts are invalid even with an adult standing over them (for they hold that there is a disagreement, and the law follows Shmuel, see there). And according to the authorities who require agency in writing, it is obvious that the essential parts are invalid in all cases (and the explanation of Rav Huna is according to Rabbi Meir, see there in the Tosafot in the second interpretation). And it is a simple matter that in practice, one should be stringent according to all opinions. And know that what they wrote that the location and time are included in the essential parts, even though it is only rabbinic, nevertheless, they treated it as if it were a Torah law (Beit Shmuel section 6). And see what I wrote in Siman 124, section 32, and the same applies here, see there.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in paragraph 1 that the husband should not initially write the get (bill of divorce) himself, nor should he instruct the scribe on how to write it, but should simply tell him in general to write it. And some say one should be stringent that even a relative should not initially write it if it is possible for someone else to do so. Ideally, the scribe should write with his right hand, but if he is left-handed, he should write with his left hand. This concludes his words.

Here is the translation of the passage:

And behold, that which is written that one should not instruct the scribe on how to write [the get], the reason is simple: perhaps he will change some of his words in a way that does not render the get invalid, but still, it would invalidate the get since it was not written as he was instructed and thus deviated from his mission. And that which is written that a near relative should not write it from the outset, even though there is no reason for this as our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wondered in his great book, nevertheless, there is a slight concern that the relative might be exchanged as a witness. However, this is indeed a weak reason, for we should not enact decrees from our own understanding. Also, that which is written that he should write with his right hand, there is a great reason for this, for since the Torah states "and he shall write," and the standard way of writing is with the right hand, it follows that a left-handed person should write with his left hand, which is considered his right hand, as is the case with tefillin. Consequently, one who is ambidextrous should preferably write with his right hand, and after the fact, there is no disqualification if he wrote with his left hand, for writing with the left hand is still considered writing for an ambidextrous person, as it is taught regarding the obligation of Shabbat (Shabbat 103b): one who writes two letters, whether with his right hand or his left hand, is liable, and the Gemara establishes this for an ambidextrous person. But for regular people, one is not liable when writing with the left hand, and so ruled the Rambam in chapter 11 of Hilchot Shabbat. According to this, a regular scribe who wrote with his left hand renders the get invalid. Nevertheless, the prominent later authorities have written that in cases of potential agunah or if the get has already been given, it should not be invalidated even if the scribe is not ambidextrous (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 4, and Chelkat Mechokek). The reason is that we should not compare this to Shabbat, for Shabbat requires a skilled labor (there), and there is proof from what the Beit Yosef ruled in Orach Chaim, siman 32, regarding tefillin written with the left hand, that if it is impossible to obtain others, they are valid, see there. However, even the ruling regarding tefillin is not explicitly clear in the early authorities, see the Tur and Beit Yosef, and further investigation is needed regarding practical application.

However, what is written that the husband should not ideally write [the get] himself is perplexing, for the primary commandment of the Torah is that the husband should write for her a bill of divorce and he is given permission to instruct someone else to write it. But to forbid him from writing it himself from the outset is very perplexing. Yet, the reason given is because the Tur wrote in Siman 126 in the name of the Itur that there are many precise details in a get that the sages said, as will be explained there, and this is only when the husband writes it himself or instructs the scribe to write it in such and such a manner, because the husband might say he intended to invalidate it. But when he instructs the scribe to write it generally, there is no concern with many of the precise details. According to this, it is better that he does not write it himself, so that if any of the precise details are changed, he might not have the ability to invalidate it (Beit Yosef). Therefore, this ruling is like an ordinance and not from the strict law, and this is not a sufficient reason (Taz). Another reason can be added, as we learned regarding the recitation of the first fruits (Bikkurim, Chapter 3), initially, anyone who knew how to read would read, and one who did not know would be prompted, and they refrained from bringing because of the shame. They instituted that everyone should be prompted. Similarly, if permission is given to the husband to write it himself from the outset, it could be that someone who cannot write himself will refrain from divorcing because of the shame, and sometimes there is a mitzvah in the get or a remedy for an agunah. Therefore, they instituted that even one who can write should not write it himself. Additionally, another reason is that it is taught (Gittin 86) that if he wrote it in his own handwriting and there are no witnesses on it, the get is invalid, but if she remarries, the child is legitimate. Therefore, perhaps witnesses will not be required for it, and he will want to free himself from her and write it himself and give it to her. Hence, they distanced it so that the husband does not write it himself.

It is taught in the Tosefta (Shabbat chapter 12): "A minor holds the quill and an adult holds his hand and writes; the adult is liable. If an adult holds the quill and a minor holds his hand and writes, he (the adult) is exempt." Thus wrote the Rambam in chapter 12 of Shabbat, see there. From this, we learn that the one who holds the writer's hand and guides it on the parchment is considered the writer, and not the one holding the quill. Therefore, also in a get (divorce document), if the minor holds the quill and the adult holds the minor's hand, the get is valid, and vice versa, the get is invalid. And even though earlier it is taught there: "One holds the quill and one holds his hand and writes; the one holding the quill is liable, the one holding his hand and writes is exempt," it appears explicitly the opposite, that the main issue is the one holding the quill. However, it must be stated that there is a scribal error, and it should read: "the one holding the quill is exempt, the one holding his hand is liable," as is proven from the Rambam we brought (and so is written in the glosses of the Gra). The Rambam did not bring at all the first clause. However, it is questionable whether it is only when the one holding the quill cannot write by himself that the one holding the writer's hand is considered the writer, or if even when he can write by himself, since the act of writing is done by the one holding his hand, the one holding the quill is not considered the writer at all, and his hand is considered as the quill. And this seems to be the main interpretation (and this is evident from what is written there: "he intended to assist him," etc., and there, too, there is a scribal error corrected by the Gra. Pay close attention).

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 3 of Laws of Divorce, Law 19: "If one writes a bill of divorce on Shabbat or Yom Kippur unintentionally and gives it to her, she is considered divorced. If they wrote and signed it on the same day intentionally and gave it to her, she is not considered divorced, for the witnesses are disqualified by Torah law. If they wrote it on Yom Tov intentionally and it was delivered to her in the presence of valid witnesses on Yom Tov, it is a disqualified bill of divorce."

Explanation: It has already been explained that one who publicly desecrates Shabbat is disqualified from writing a bill of divorce. Even according to those who hold that for the first offense one is not yet disqualified (Tosafot Chullin 14), this applies to a single act of transgression, such as slaughtering an animal on Shabbat or writing two letters. However, in the case of a bill of divorce, which contains many words, one is disqualified if they wrote more than two letters (Beit Shmuel, section 8). Even though regarding the death penalty, any action done in one instance and one warning is considered one act of labor, nevertheless, regarding the status of being like a non-Jew, every two letters completed are considered a separate act of desecration. However, if written unintentionally, the bill of divorce is not disqualified, similar to a transaction done in prohibition, where the transaction remains valid as written in Choshen Mishpat, section 208. Even though cooking on Shabbat unintentionally is prohibited on that day to prevent benefiting from Shabbat labor, as written in Orach Chayim, section 318, nonetheless, this does not apply to a bill of divorce, as it is forbidden to divorce on Shabbat. If one divorces, what is done is done, as written in section 339. Study there thoroughly.

And know that the same law applies if the witnesses signed mistakenly; it is also valid. What difference does it make in this case? The Rambam did not need to mention this (says the Pri Chadash). It is possible that the Rambam intentionally did not mention the witnesses because even if the witnesses signed deliberately and the get (divorce document) is invalid, nevertheless, since the scribe wrote it mistakenly, if there are valid delivery witnesses, its invalidity is rabbinic, as it is considered internally forged and is not nullified by Torah law. The practical difference is that if she accepted betrothal from another man, she would need a get (divorce document) from the second man as well.

And regarding what he wrote: "If they wrote and signed it intentionally, the get (divorce document) is invalid because the witnesses are disqualified by Torah law," this was unnecessary, for the get is invalid by Torah law due to the scribe's writing. It appears more correct according to the version of the Rambam brought in the Tur, which states: "If they wrote and signed it on a festival intentionally," etc., and see there. And on a festival, this reason is necessary, for if it were only because of the scribe's writing, it would not be invalid. Although he is a wicked person, nevertheless, one who publicly desecrates Shabbat is considered like a gentile, but one who desecrates a festival is not. In the Shulchan Aruch, the version is "on that day or on a festival," see there. And this reason is necessary because of the festival, as stated. And regarding what he wrote: "If they wrote it on a festival intentionally and it was delivered to her in the presence of valid witnesses, it is invalid," his intention is: if they wrote and signed it, referring back to the earlier discussion, and it is invalid because the witnesses are wicked, making it like a document that is internally falsified. But if the witnesses did not sign or signed unintentionally, the get is valid, as stated, for it is not disqualified because of the festival for writing the get. And so wrote the great later authorities (Avnei Shoham, section 8, and Chayei Moshe, sections 11 and 12).

And know that on Shabbat, a get (divorce document) is nullified if it was written intentionally, specifically if written publicly. But privately, its status is not like a gentile (Pri Megadim). However, there is a doubt regarding what is considered public in this context. Is it specifically ten Jews, as in the matter of sanctifying God's name, or is it sufficient if another Jew sees and does not conceal himself from desecrating Shabbat to be considered public? This is explicitly implied in the Talmud, Eruvin 69. See there. Consequently, it is clear why Rambam did not mention this law when discussing public desecration of Shabbat, as in the matter of a get, it is necessarily public since the husband, wife, and witnesses know about it. In the previous law, he mentioned that one who desecrates Shabbat publicly is disqualified from writing a get, as in other matters, when one desecrates Shabbat, it can also be done privately, between oneself, without anyone seeing. This is not the case when the desecration involves the writing of the get itself. The great later authorities have also written that this law applies to public desecration (Choshen Mishpat 11, Beit Shmuel 8, and Pri Megadim). It is difficult to understand, as public desecration for the sanctification of God's name is learned from a verse in the last chapter of Sanhedrin, "And I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel." See there. But regarding Shabbat desecration, since the reason is due to brazenness, what difference does it make if it is ten or less? And from Eruvin there, it seems as I have written, and further study is needed for the law.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that one should not perform a divorce at night, and if a divorce is carried out at night, some say that the get (bill of divorce) is invalid. Therefore, after the community has prayed the evening service, even though there is still plenty of daylight, one should not carry out a divorce. Refer later to the end of section 154. The author means that it was explained there that in pressing circumstances, even at night, one can write and give the get. See there, as in truth, there is no valid reason not to divorce at night, and from the Gemara it appears explicitly that this is not the case (see the end of Chapter 7, "When the sun sets," and analyze it closely). They wrote that the reason is certainly that the writing of the get and the signatures of the witnesses are also initially permitted at night, and it is only the giving of the get that they wrote should not be done at night, similar to how the Sages prohibited chalitzah (the ceremony where a widow releases her brother-in-law from the obligation to marry her) at night, which is considered a legal matter as stated in Siman 169. And the same applies to the giving of the get because in chalitzah it was written that since through it she takes her ketubah (marriage contract), it is considered a legal matter (Nimukei Yosef on Chapter 48). Similarly, here, by the get, she takes her ketubah, and it is considered a legal matter. However, in truth, it is not comparable because in chalitzah, from the death of her husband, she is entitled to her ketubah, but until the chalitzah, she does not take it because perhaps her brother-in-law will marry her. But with a get, until she receives the get, she has no claim to the ketubah, and the obligation begins only after the get is given. Furthermore, chalitzah requires a court, while with a get, the Sages said that not everyone who divorces does so in court (Arakhin 23). Certainly, a get given by an agent to deliver to the woman, which requires stating "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," and requires a court, should not be delivered at night (Noda BiYehuda). Nevertheless, since this matter was stated by the earlier authorities and Rabbi Moshe Isserles brought it, we do not arrange a get at night unless in pressing circumstances. (And what the Noda BiYehuda wrote from Rashi at the beginning of Sanhedrin is no proof at all because Rashi's intent was on chalitzah, see there. And in the arrangement of the get, it will also be explained regarding the court matter).

**The Law Regarding What Materials a Get (Bill of Divorce) May Be Written On. It Contains 46 Sections:**

Our sages said (Gittin 2a) that a get written on items prohibited for benefit (issurei hana'ah) is valid. The phrase "and he shall place it in her hand" (Deuteronomy 24:1) does not imply the same type of giving as in monetary payments, where the item must have value. Rather, it refers specifically to the giving of a get (Gittin 20b). This is only valid after the fact (bedi'eved), but initially (lekhatchilah), it is certainly forbidden to write a get on items prohibited for benefit, as this would involve deriving benefit from prohibited items (Tosafot, Gittin 20b, s.v. "bichtivat"). This is also the language of the Shulchan Aruch, section 1. However, Rambam wrote in the beginning of chapter 4 that a get may be written on anything, even on items prohibited for benefit. This is also the language of the Tur, and it implies that even initially one may write on such items. Perhaps the reason is that he does not intend to benefit (Bach). Even though, in the end, he inevitably benefits (Perisha), it seems to me that if the husband himself writes the get, it is certainly forbidden initially, because his intent is for the get, and he benefits. But their intention is when the scribe writes it and does not take payment, and he derives no benefit from the get (Atzei Gilad). Even though it causes the husband to benefit from items prohibited for benefit, we do not find that causing (grama) is forbidden in this context. Furthermore, even if the scribe writes on something of monetary value, he could transfer ownership to the husband as a gift without taking money from him, and there would not even be an indirect benefit. There are those who want to say that their intention is that from the perspective of the get itself, there is no prohibition; the prohibition is only due to benefiting from prohibited items, and they also agree that initially it is forbidden (Perisha). This does not seem correct, as although sometimes found in the Mishnah, it is not the way of the poskim (decisors). From the Gemara, it also seems that it is permitted initially, as Rabbi Eliezer said, "We also learned [that a get may be written] on an olive leaf," and that case is initially permitted. Therefore, both are true: the Tosafot are referring to the husband himself, as proven there by the writing on the slave, while Rambam and the Tur refer to the scribe. The message sent from there refers to the husband himself. Thus, there is no difficulty with Rabbi Eliezer’s statement, "We also learned," etc., even though it is not similar. See there and examine carefully.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes: "However, regarding something that needs to be eradicated from the world and requires burning, if one writes a get (bill of divorce) on it, the get is invalid," end quote. Many are puzzled by this, as its source is from the Ran who writes, "In all items prohibited for benefit, even though they are considered as if their measure is crushed, we do not say this except in matters that require a specific measure, like a shofar or a lulav. However, regarding those that must be eradicated from the world, for those who say that anything destined to be burned is considered as already burned, it implies that it is not a valid get, as it is as if it does not exist," end quote.

The explanation of his words is that even though in the Talmud we only find the concept of "crushed measure" in relation to objects like an Asherah tree or a condemned city, which the Torah commands to destroy, as it is written, "You shall surely destroy," etc., we do not find this for other items prohibited for benefit. Nevertheless, our sages, the Tosafists, wrote (Sukkah 35a) that this concept also applies to other items prohibited for benefit that are commanded to be burned, like Orlah (fruit from a tree within its first three years) and similar cases. The Rashba also wrote this, resolving the question raised by the Gra.

Therefore, I say that even though the concept of "crushed measure" exists, nevertheless, a get is valid because we only apply this to items that require a specific measure, like a shofar or a lulav. In every matter, there are points, lines, and surfaces, and a surface only exists in an object with three dimensions, which are six sides (Hilchot Mechira, Chapter 17). Therefore, the sages said (Eruvin 80a) that a lechi (side post) from an Asherah tree is valid, even though a lechi requires a height of ten tefachim, because anything that does not require a measure of its dimensions but only its length is considered like lines and is permitted in all matters (ibid). A get is similar to a lechi.
