Further, for those who say that anything destined to be burned is considered as already burned, i.e., Rabbi Shimon, who holds throughout the Talmud that anything destined for a certain purpose is considered as if it has already been used for that purpose, it is certainly not a valid get. This is worse than the concept of "crushed measure" because it is considered as already burned and does not exist in the world at all (and there is a difficulty with what the Gra wrote in his second gloss, "and it is not, etc.," as everyone agrees that "crushed measure" exists, but they do not hold that it is considered as already burned).

Therefore, the words of our master, the Rema, are puzzling, because the Ran only wrote this according to Rabbi Shimon. However, throughout the Talmud, the Sages dispute Rabbi Shimon, and the law follows the majority. Some want to say that the Rambam, of blessed memory, rules according to Rabbi Shimon, but this is not so, as there are many proofs that he does not rule according to Rabbi Shimon (Peri Chadash, and so writes the Gra). And the proof is that he ruled there that the side post of an idolatrous tree is valid; therefore, they ruled not according to our master, the Rema (the Gra, the Chochmat Shlomo, and the Peri Chadash). However, from the side post, there is not such a strong proof, because it can be said that he holds that the side post of an idolatrous tree is valid because, although it is crumbled and ground, nevertheless, if one were to stick the crumbs to the wall, the side post would be valid (Tosafot there). But a bill of divorce requires one book and not two or three books, as it is stated in the Talmud.

And based on what we have explained, it appears to me that his words are correct, and a different intention is hidden in his words. It is not because of the principle that anything destined to be burned is considered as already burned, for we certainly do not follow Rabbi Shimon in this matter. Rather, the interpretation is as follows: just as our sages said regarding a shofar, a lulav, and the act of chalitzah from a city condemned for idolatry or from an asherah tree, that since the Torah commanded that they be burned and removed from the world, even though they are not literally considered as if already burned, nevertheless they are considered as fragmented, as if their measurement is shattered, and they do not have the required measurement. Similarly, regarding a get (divorce document), although we do not require a specific measurement, the Torah still said it should be one document and not two or three, and since this is considered as shattered, it is like having multiple documents within it. This is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote: something that needs to be eradicated from the world and needs burning, like an asherah tree, as it says "and their asherah trees you shall burn with fire," and a city condemned for idolatry, and offerings to idols, in all of which the Torah decreed that they be eradicated from the world and burned (as Rashi wrote in Rosh Hashanah 28 and Sukkah 31 and Yevamot 103). He holds according to the majority of the poskim that in other prohibitions of benefit, even though the mitzvah is to burn them as stated at the end of Temurah, we do not say that their measurement is shattered. (And his intention is not according to the Ran, as some commentaries on the Shulchan Aruch misunderstand. And know that what Rashi wrote in Rosh Hashanah there in the commentary "since it is destined for burning, it is considered as already burned," he did not mean according to Rabbi Shimon but regarding the matter of considering the measurement as shattered. See there and understand well.)

It is permissible to write a get (bill of divorce) on something that can be forged, meaning that something can be erased from the writing and it is not noticeable that it was erased. And even though other documents are invalid if they can be forged, as it is stated in Choshen Mishpat 42 due to the concern that something might be erased from the document and something else written in its place, nevertheless, a get is valid. The reason, the sages said (Gittin 22b), is because we hold like Rabbi Eliezer that the witnesses of delivery finalize the get, and from the Torah, it is not required to have witnesses sign the get. For if it was required by the Torah to have signing witnesses, it would necessarily need to be evident within the document itself that no forgery could be done (Tosafot). But since the witnesses of delivery are the main factor and it is delivered in their presence, it is impossible to forge it, for they read the get at the time of delivery to the woman, and if there was any forgery from any condition, they would know and not allow it to be given to her (Rashi). And even after a long time, the get is valid, and even after a long period when she brings the get, she is permitted to remarry and collect her ketubah, and we do not worry that perhaps it was forged because she needs to bring the witnesses of delivery (there) and they remember what was written in it. And even though we hold that a forgery within itself is invalid even for us, this is not considered a forgery within itself, because since it is recognizable by the witnesses of delivery, it is not called a forgery (Beit Shmuel, subsection 3).

And there is a question regarding this matter: According to several authorities, the document is valid with the signatures of the witnesses alone, even if it was delivered to her privately, as will be explained in Siman 133. And even according to those who invalidate it in such a case, nevertheless, according to all opinions, when she brings the get (divorce document) to the court to remarry, she does not need to bring the witnesses. For this reason, Rabban Gamliel the Elder instituted that witnesses sign on the get so that she would not need to bring the witnesses. So, how do we validate something that could be forged, as it is possible to forge it? The answer to this is that certainly, when it is written on something that can be forged, she is required to bring the witnesses. This is what the Tur wrote: "And the witnesses must be present before us," as mentioned there (and also what Rashi wrote, which we brought, his intention is the same as the Tosafot wrote).

And these are the words of the Rambam in Chapter 4: "And one may write on something that can be forged, provided that it is given to her in the presence of witnesses of delivery." And so it is written in the Shulchan Aruch. And it means that the Rambam holds that even with only witnesses to the signing, it is valid, as he writes there. Therefore, he says that in this case, specifically, it is required to give it to her in the presence of witnesses of delivery. Consequently, when she comes to remarry, she must also bring the witnesses of delivery.

From a logical perspective, it appears that if she brings witnesses of the signatures and they testify that there was no forgery, it is also permitted. For what difference does it make if it is witnesses of delivery or witnesses of signatures? However, the Tur wrote that witnesses of signatures, even if they are before us, are invalid. See there. The reason must be because he holds that any bill of divorce (get) without witnesses of delivery is invalid. Therefore, here, where it was written on something that can be forged, its presumption is weakened, and we are concerned that perhaps there were no witnesses at the time of delivery (Beit Yosef in the name of the Rosh). According to this, for the Rambam, who does not require witnesses of delivery, this concern is removed, and witnesses of signatures when they testify are effective (there). However, it is possible to say that even according to the Rambam, it is invalid here without witnesses of delivery, because it is considered forged internally, not truly forged. If so, even witnesses of delivery would not help, but for this matter, it is considered forged, and we do not rely on witnesses of signatures alone, only specifically on witnesses of delivery (Chovat HaMechokek). Furthermore, here we should decree when witnesses of signatures come before us, lest they do not come before us, but only witnesses who recognize their signatures. This is the validation everywhere, for then we surely are concerned that perhaps she did some forgery or perhaps forged the signatures to the extent that it appears to the validators that they are the signatures of the signed witnesses. When it is written on something that can be forged, its presumption of validity is weakened (Beit Yosef). Therefore, even according to the Rambam, it does not help when there are no witnesses of delivery before us (and so wrote the Beit Shmuel, section 3, and not like the Chovat HaMechokek, section 2, who wanted to be lenient according to the Rambam, and his reasoning is not understood. And examine this matter thoroughly).

And since it is written on a material that can be forged, therefore it is permissible to write on "diftara," which is parchment that has not been fully processed and can be forged. Similarly, it is permissible to write on erased paper. And it is not only when the entire paper is erased and both the get (divorce document) and the witnesses' signatures are on the erased part that it is valid, but also for other documents there is no concern that one might erase and write whatever he wants, for if so, it would be written on paper that has been erased twice and the signatures on paper that has been erased once, and everyone would recognize the forgery. And it is possible that in such a case, there is no need to bring delivery witnesses at all (see Beit Yosef and Choshen Mishpat, section 3). However, even if the get is written not on the erased part and the witnesses sign on the erased part, then surely the get will also be erased and rewritten, and it will not be recognizable, since both will have the erasure only once. Nevertheless, since we do not permit without bringing delivery witnesses, there is no concern, as they will remember, as mentioned. Similarly, if the get is on the erased part and the witnesses not on the erased part, it is also valid because there are delivery witnesses (and in this case, even according to Tosafot, Ran, and Rosh, delivery witnesses are needed, as in other documents it is invalid as mentioned in Choshen Mishpat, section 45, and in this way the language of the Mishnah in Gittin 21b is understandable: "We do not write on erased paper"—according to their view, the language needs examination, since it refers to witnesses, see Tosafot 22a, s.v. "not," and according to what was said, it is clear, see and pay attention).

And so it is taught (Yoma 19a) that one may write on an olive leaf even though it can be forged. Tosafot and the Ran wrote that the sages permitted writing only on an olive leaf, which is something that lasts, because an olive leaf is thick and endures for many days. For although they permitted writing on something that can be forged, nonetheless, it must be something that can endure. And so it is taught in the Tosefta (Chapter 2) that writing on olive leaves, gourd leaves, carob leaves— on anything that endures—is valid. Writing on beet leaves, leek leaves, onion leaves, vegetable leaves—on anything that does not endure—is invalid, etc. This concludes the text.

However, the Rif, Rambam, Rosh, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch did not mention this, and it could be said that it is not because they do not agree with the Tosefta, but since they wrote that one may write on an olive leaf, it is implicitly understood that on other leaves one should not write. And even though there are leaves of gourd and carob on which it is permitted to write, they did not bother to elaborate on this because it is not common at all. Nevertheless, from the Rambam, there is evidence that he does not agree with the Tosefta from the fact that he permits writing with a mark on leather even though it does not last, which will be explained in Siman 125. And in the Tosefta, this is invalidated. Therefore, the Magid Mishneh wrote that the Tosefta was dismissed from the halacha because it was not brought in the Talmud. (See there, in Chapter 4, Halacha 7.) And he dismissed the Tosefta due to the Yerushalmi according to his version, which will be explained there with God's help. And also, regarding the leaf, he simply wrote "leaves," and so it is written in the Shulchan Aruch.

Furthermore, it appears to me that from the Jerusalem Talmud on this matter, it rejects the Tosefta. The Jerusalem Talmud questions regarding an olive leaf: Is it not like a torn piece of paper? Rabbi Zeira said: Even if one writes, "I, so-and-so, am divorcing my wife," it is valid. So the interpreters explained that the question is because it is impossible to write the entire get (bill of divorce) on one leaf, and one would need to write on several leaves, and the Torah says "a book" (sefer) and not two or three books. However, not only does the language not agree with their interpretation, but the rule that a book must be one and not two or three books is not found at all in the Jerusalem Talmud, and Rambam did not bring it up either, as will be clarified later in this section with God's help.

Therefore, it appears to me that the explanation of the Jerusalem Talmud is that it does not hold like the Tosefta that an olive leaf is preferable; rather, it is like any leaf. Hence, the question is: Is it not intended to be torn and does not last? The answer is that a get does not need to be lengthy; even six words suffice for it to be valid. And a leaf does not typically break into many pieces, just into parts, and it will remain whole for the measure of six words. This is true for any tree leaves. Therefore, Rambam did not specify an olive leaf but just leaves in general. However, the Rif, Rosh, and Tur did mention an olive leaf.

Nevertheless, for practical halacha, it is clear that one should not deviate from the Tosefta. (And this is what the Jerusalem Talmud meant afterward: "And it comes out like Rabbi Eliezer; if he elaborates, it is invalid, and if he does not elaborate, it is valid." According to what I have explained, this means that if he elaborates at length, like "so-and-so from such a place or standing today, etc.," it is invalid because such a large piece will not endure. But if he does not elaborate and only writes six words, as mentioned, it is valid. Consider this carefully.)

And similarly, one is permitted to write on pottery and on anything he wishes, even on living beings, except on something attached (to the ground), which is invalid because it is written "and he shall write and give" and we derive that it must be something that is not lacking anything between writing and giving except for giving. This excludes something attached, which requires cutting and giving (Gittin 21b). Therefore, even when writing on living beings, one must give her the entire living being in its entirety and not cut off only the part where the get (bill of divorce) is written and give it to her, for if so, it would require cutting (Gittin 21b). Similarly, regarding anything on which the get is written, one must not cut off the part that was not written upon after writing, for this reason, as will be explained with God's help in sections 23 and 24.

There is a question regarding this matter: it is written in a bill of divorce (get) using the expression "book," as it says, "and he shall write for her a document of severance." In the passage regarding the Sotah, it is likewise written, "the priest shall write these curses in a book." Why is it that for a bill of divorce any material is acceptable except for something attached, whereas for a Sotah (Sotah 17a) it is taught that it cannot be written on a tablet, paper, or diftera, but only on a scroll, as it is stated "in a book," meaning parchment (Rashi)? Even though in Gittin it is taught that "book" only explicitly means a book, how do we know it includes any material? The verse states "and he shall write for her," implying any material (see there). But if so, we should also interpret the verse regarding Sotah in the same way (and see Tosafot there, s.v. "not"). Although in Gittin one could say that the principle of general and specific, and general again applies, since "and he shall give" returns and generalizes (Tosafot), in truth, this derivation is not according to the halachic ruling, but according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi there (as it says there: and the Rabbis, what do they do with "and he shall write"? See Rashi and scrutinize well).

Indeed, the Jerusalem Talmud in Sotah there poses this question and answers that in the case of Sotah, it is written "in a book," and therefore it must be written on parchment. However, regarding a get (divorce document), where it is written "and he shall write for her a document," it implies it is referring to the recounting of matters (as per the Rabbis of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi). This elucidates the depth of Rashi's words in Gittin there, s.v. "if he wrote in a book," and s.v. "and he wrote for her, what does he do with it," which at first glance are puzzling, but according to the Jerusalem Talmud, his intention is with good reasoning. The words of Tosafot in Sotah there also require further investigation. Pay close attention (and understand it well).

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in section 2: "One may write on any detached item, and some say it must specifically be on something that is durable. But if one writes on an onion or vegetable leaf and the like, it is invalid." And behold, in the Tosefta we brought, it also says the term "invalid" and not "nullified." And even though according to the Tosefta it appears that it is nullified from the Torah, it is possible that the Tosefta does not differentiate between the terms "invalid" and "nullified" as it is evident in the Tosefta in all laws there. However, the poskim (decisors) who were precise with this language, it seems to me that Rabbeinu the Rema wrote this precisely because according to the Rambam and the Beit Yosef it is not specifically an olive leaf as we explained in section 12. Therefore, he wrote "invalid," and the practical difference is that if she received kiddushin (betrothal) from another, she would also need a get (divorce document) from him according to the Rambam and the Beit Yosef (as it appears to me).

Additionally, he wrote that ideally, it should be written on parchment that is properly prepared for Torah scrolls, tefillin, and mezuzot, but it does not need to be processed for the sake of its sanctity. However, this is not a strict requirement, and even if it is written on paper called "papyrus" in any script, it is valid. The explanation of his words is that the parchment should be prepared as it is prepared for Torah scrolls (according to the Chayei Adam), as writing a get (divorce document) on parchment processed for the sanctity of a Torah scroll is prohibited since it has no sanctity. It just needs to be well-processed like the parchment for a Torah scroll. And although writing on diphthera (unfinished parchment) is also valid, as mentioned, it is better to use parchment initially so that it is not prone to forgery and does not require bringing witnesses for delivery. When he writes that any script is valid, he does not mean any script other than Ashurit script, as it is clearly written in section 126 that only Ashurit script is acceptable, except in cases of agunah (a woman chained to her marriage) or pressing circumstances. Rather, the meaning is that one does not need to be meticulous about perfect script as is required for a Torah scroll, as is explicitly stated in Darkei Moshe.

And behold, now in all the communities of Israel, they initially write on paper called papel (Papi'r). And we must consider: In matters of divorce documents (Gittin), we are stringent with numerous stringencies. So why do we not insist on following the directive of our master, the Rema, to write initially on parchment (Klaf)? Parchment is readily available among us, and this is not a time of exigency. The great authorities, Rabbi Moses ben Habib in his book "Get Pashut" and the Taz, have already addressed this issue. Rabbi Moses ben Habib states: "We have neither seen nor heard of anyone being concerned about this even initially. The custom in Jerusalem, may it be built and established, and throughout the Land of Israel, as well as Gittin from overseas, is that they are written on our paper called papel." Similarly, the Bach testified in section 126 that all Gittin from Salonika, Egypt, and other places in Turkey are not written on parchment. Our papers cannot be forged, for if any letter or word is written over an erasure, it is immediately noticeable and apparent to all who see it. Therefore, it is permissible to write Gittin on paper just as on treated parchment, and there is no need to bring delivery witnesses before us, as certification witnesses suffice. This is clear. The Taz writes: "It appears to be more kosher to write on papel since our parchment can be more easily forged by scraping because it is thick and strong, unlike paper, where scraping is impossible without it being noticeable. Even though the custom in these lands was to write on parchment, during the decrees in the lands of Wallachia and Ukraine, where many needed to give a divorce out of necessity and parchment was not available, they became accustomed to writing on papel, and from there it spread to other places." Similarly, many authorities wrote (see "Pri Tohar"). Therefore, it is forbidden to change from the custom, and one should only write on good and smooth paper, not on simple paper called Bibola or Raschazana, which is not smooth and has pits, making the writing uneven. It also appears to me that one should be cautious not to write on large and thick papers like parchment, for it might be possible to erase on them without it being noticeable, leading to forgery, and requiring delivery witnesses constantly. Instead, one should write on Schreib or Regal paper, and this is how we conduct ourselves in our country.

He writes on the hand of the slave and gives her the slave, or on the horn of the cow and gives her the slave and the cow in the presence of witnesses. But he should not cut off the hand of the slave or the horn of the cow and give it to her. If he wrote and then cut it off and gave it to her, it is not a valid get (divorce document) according to the Torah, because we require that there should be no interruption between the writing and the giving, as we have explained. And even though regarding slaughtering, a tooth or a nail is considered attached when they are attached to a living animal, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, section 6, it is different there because it is not relevant to give the entire living animal, as there is no concept of giving there. Therefore, certainly the tooth and the nail are nullified to the living animal and are considered attached. This is not the case with a get, where he gives her the entire body, and the entire body is not attached. And the concern that he might cut off the horn from the cow is not considered, because it is not customary to cut it off. Certainly, he is not allowed to cut off the hand of the slave. Also, the slave does not need to be bound, as this is only relevant in a transaction involving the slave, which is because of the concept of a moving courtyard, which does not acquire. But with a get that is written on him, this is not relevant, since he gives her the entire slave. And if he engraved the get on the hand of the woman, she is not divorced because he has not given her anything.

The writing of a get (divorce document) by a person is considered writing that can be forged, and it always requires witnesses to the delivery. However, if it is written as a tattoo, which is never erased, it does not require [witnesses to the delivery] (Gemara 20b). And although there is a prohibition against tattooing, nevertheless the get is valid, just as if it were written on items forbidden for benefit (Tosafot). Furthermore, from the Torah, there is no prohibition unless one writes and tattoos with ink and with kohl, as it is taught in Makkot (21b). However, there is a rabbinic prohibition (there).

Some say that one must explicitly give her the servant and the cow, meaning that when he hands her the servant and the cow upon which the get (divorce document) is written, and says to her, "Here is your get," he must also say to her, "And they are yours." But if he gives her the servant and the cow and merely says, "Here is your get," it does not imply that he gives her the entire servant and cow, but rather only the hand and the horn (i.e., the part upon which the get is written), and the get is invalid (according to the Ran in the name of the Ramah and the Rashba). The reason is that it is not reasonable to assume that the entire body is nullified to the hand and the horn; on the contrary, the hand and the horn are subordinate to the body, and he has given her nothing (as explained by the Ran in the Mishnah). Other poskim (decisors of Jewish law) do not mention this, and it does not appear this way in the Jerusalem Talmud either. For it says (Yerushalmi, Chapter 2, Halacha 3) regarding the Mishnah that if he wrote on the horn of a cow and gave her the cow, etc., the Mishnah is when he says to her, "Here is your get." But if he says to her, "Here is your get, and the rest for your ketubah," she has received both her get and her ketubah at once. Hence, it is explicit that even when he says to her simply, "Here is your get," the get is valid, as his intention is for the entire body. This requires further study, and therefore one should be stringent according to both opinions. In the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, this matter is not mentioned at all (and in the Beit Yosef it is brought).

The Jerusalem Talmud further inquires there: If he handed her the divorce document (get) in a manner that in a sale transaction the cow (or other object) would be acquired by the buyer, does this mean that if he handed her the get in the same manner, it would be like a sale and she would acquire the get, making the get valid? Or perhaps, since it is written in the context of a get "and he shall place it in her hand," it must be entirely in her hand? See there. The explanation seems to me as follows: In the acquisition by handing over (kinyan mesirah), we hold in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 198, that it does not require the buyer's domain at all, nor does it need to be handed over from hand to hand; rather, once the buyer has grasped it in the presence of the seller or by his command, it is considered a valid transfer. Therefore, in the case of a get in such a manner, it would not be considered "and he shall place it in her hand." Or perhaps, since in the context of acquisition it is valid, the get would also be valid. The question remains unresolved. (And this resolves the difficulty raised by the Sha'ar HaKolel there).

Some of our Rabbis hold that the Torah only disqualified a get (divorce document) when it is lacking cutting between the writing and the giving in the case of living beings or something attached to the ground, where one removes something from its growth. However, a detached item is not considered lacking cutting. For instance, if one wrote on a large parchment and the get was written on part of it, and he intends to cut out that part and keep the rest for himself, it is not considered lacking cutting. They wrote in the name of Rashi, of blessed memory, that such a case came before him, and he validated the get (Tosafot 21b in the name of Rashbam and Rosh, and the Tur in the name of Rashi, and it is implied from his language 22b, "lest he cut it," see there). But all our Rabbis disagree with this, and also Bahag disqualifies it, as do all the decisors. The Tur wrote that this is specifically when it is cut from a large parchment that it is considered lacking cutting, but if it was cut a small amount just to beautify it, it is not considered lacking cutting. Nevertheless, the Rosh wrote in the order of the get that the scribe should cut the parchment to the measure of the get so that he does not need to cut it further. Therefore, if the scribe made a mistake in the get after writing part of it and starts over on the same parchment, he should first cut off the part he wrote. This is the end of his words.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 3: If they wrote [the get] on a large piece of paper and cut it after writing, before giving it, it is invalid. But if he cut off a little to beautify it, it is not considered cutting. And as long as he did not cut off much more than the writing of the get, it is considered for beautification. However, initially, everything should be cut before writing, even the holes made to line it up and other things; everything should be cut before the lining because the lining is a necessity for writing. End of quote.

And behold, regarding what is written that if a large piece of paper is cut after writing, it is invalid, there is an opinion that it is nullified by Torah law (Beit Shmuel, section 10). However, it seems to me that it is precisely written "invalid" and not "nullified," for indeed, according to the opinions that invalidate, they invalidate by Torah law. Nevertheless, since the opinions of Rashi and Rashbam are lenient, even though we do not follow their lenient opinions, still, to be stringent, we certainly need to take their opinions into account. And also, the Tosafot write there in the name of Rabbeinu Tam that he was stringent in this matter, which also implies that it is said only to be stringent and not to be lenient. Therefore, it is appropriately written "invalid" and not "nullified," for if she received kiddushin (betrothal) from another, she needs a get (divorce document) from him as well (in my opinion). And regarding what is written that for its smoothness it is valid, there are those who say it is proper to cut it into thin pieces, for then it appears that the smoothness was done and not for the sake of the parchment (Gaon of Prague and Knesset HaGedolah in the name of the Biyurim of the SeMaG), and it is proper to do so initially.

Rabbeinu Nissim wrote in the name of Rav Hai Gaon, of blessed memory, that it is not considered lacking cutting (פסול מחוסר קציצה) except in a case where, before writing, it was intended to cut from it; in such a scenario, it is not allowed to cut from it after it has been written. However, if there was no intention to cut, we do not concern ourselves with it. The poskim (decisors of Jewish law) did not bring this ruling, but nevertheless, it is clear that we should be stringent according to his words. If there was an intention to cut, even a small amount, it is forbidden to cut afterwards, for we cannot say that the Gaon's intention was only regarding a large cut and not a small one; since it depends on his intention, whether large or small, it is ultimately considered lacking cutting. We learn from his words that even if it was intended to cut but was not cut afterwards, it is not invalidated, for the thought alone does not invalidate it. And regarding whose intention it depends on, it appears that it depends solely on the owner's intention, as the paper must be his. However, the later authorities wrote that whether it is the intention of the owner or the intention of the scribe to cut, it invalidates if they cut after the writing, even a small cut, and we should be stringent (Atzei Geza, Gevurat Peretz, and Pitchei Teshuva).

It is permitted to write the get (divorce document) on a large piece of paper, even if much of it will remain blank, and we do not worry that one might come to cut it after it has been written (Ran). There are those who require that in such a case, one should write in the middle of the paper and the remaining blank areas around it serve as an aesthetic margin. However, if one writes at the top of the paper and leaves a large blank area below, we decree that one might come to cut it (Geonim’s Responsa). The language of the Ran certainly indicates the opposite, and only with a perforated pot did the Sages decree the possibility of cutting, as will be explained, but not with something detached, and certainly not with the horn of a cow, where they did not decree the possibility of cutting as it is stated (and even the Geonim’s Responsa itself concludes leniently there and is brought in Pitchei Teshuvah, note 9). Nonetheless, it is proper practice to write on one sheet and not on two folded sheets in the manner of folding paper, as in such a case there might be concern that the scribe will cut the empty page for himself unintentionally (and the Geonim’s Responsa is also lenient here, but it seems to me as I have written). Similarly, the common practice is to write on one sheet and not on a folded one, and it should not be excessively large. This is what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch have written: it is good to cut the paper to the size of the get, meaning it should not be excessively large, so that one does not come to cut it.

The Tur and the Rema wrote that even though the document contains other matters, if he gives her everything, it is valid. The explanation is that what is written on the paper, even if the get (divorce document) has other matters written on it, does not invalidate the get if he gives her the entire paper, including the part where the other matter is written, so that there is no need to cut it. However, it appears to me that this only applies when the other matter is written before the get, after the get, on the sides, or on the back. But if another matter is written in the middle of the get, it is certainly invalid because it confuses the meaning of the get. On the contrary, from the original law, one might say that only writing on the back does not invalidate it, but writing before it or on the sides does. However, there is no reason to differentiate, and this is clearly implied by the language of the Tur and the Rema. But in the middle, it is certainly invalid (its source is from Nedarim 19b: "A certain man... he took a Torah scroll... Rabbi Yochanan said, 'What is the concern? If it is because of the words...,' and from this, there is proof that it is only because of... as the Beit Yosef wrote, and there Rashi explained that perhaps he wrote her a get outside... see there and examine it carefully).

One may not write a get (bill of divorce) on something attached to the ground, even if he gives her the attached item as it is and it does not require cutting off. Nevertheless, we require that it be given into her hand, and there is no giving into her hand here because something attached cannot be given from hand to hand, but rather through acquisition by strength, money, or a document, and not by hand-to-hand giving. The Jerusalem Talmud derives this from the word "book" (sefer), just as a book is detached, so too everything must be detached. The Rashba of blessed memory brought this reasoning, and even though "book" comes to mean a recounting of words, nevertheless, since it uses the term "book," it implies that it needs to be detached. The Rosh of blessed memory wrote the first reason (chapter 2, section 23), and something attached is considered invalid by Torah law, and the get is null and void. The practical difference between the two reasons concerns a perforated pot, which will be explained, and its law is like that of something attached and given from hand to hand. According to the first reason, its law is not like other attached items, but according to the Jerusalem Talmud, its law is like other attached items. (Beit Shmuel, section 11).

Just as something attached (to the ground) is invalid, so too, something that was detached and then reattached to the ground and nullified to the ground is considered fully attached (Beit Yosef). However, if it was not nullified, it is not considered attached. Yet, if it took root to the extent that it requires cutting, even if it was not nullified, it is invalid (ibid.). Even if it was written and signed while detached, and after signing, it was reattached (and nullified), and later detached and given, it is invalid. And it is not only if it took root after writing and signing, but even if it did not take root, it is still invalid because it lacks an action from the time of writing until the time of giving, as we require "and he wrote and gave" without any missing action from the time of writing until the time of giving (Tur). However, the Rashba validates in such a case (the Tur did not bring his opinion).

It has already been explained that the main aspect of a get (Jewish divorce document) is the writing, and therefore, if the writing was done while attached (to the ground) and it was detached before the signatures and signed while detached, the get is invalid. Even the form (the non-essential part of the document) should not be written while attached, and if, after writing the form, it was detached and the essential part was written while detached, signed, and given to her, it is valid. All the more so, if the form was written while detached before cutting and then it was cut, it is valid. This is because writing the form while attached is permitted after the fact. Regarding a scribe who writes the forms of gittin, it will be explained in Siman 131 that many authorities invalidate even after the fact. In the case of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor, it is permissible even initially to write the form, as explained in Siman 123. The reason is simple: regarding scribes (adults), which is a common matter, they prohibited even after the fact as a decree because of the essential part. Concerning attached (writing), which is not so common, they prohibited initially and permitted after the fact. Regarding deaf-mutes, imbeciles, and minors, which is entirely uncommon, they allowed it according to the law even initially. However, it has already been clarified in Siman 123, Section 9, that there are those who invalidate even after the fact. It must be said that writing while attached is less common than writing by deaf-mutes, imbeciles, and minors. Also, know that even regarding attached writing, the opinion of the Ramah is to invalidate rabbinically even the writing of the form, similar to the scribes, as the Tur writes in his name. However, this is a singular opinion and is not the accepted ruling. (See Avnei Shoham, Section 15, regarding writing the form initially on the horn of a cow.)

In Siman 123, Se'if 9, we explained that although the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) included the need for a date in the main part of a document, even though it is of rabbinic origin, they nonetheless treated it with the same severity as if it were of biblical origin. It appears that this is said only as a stringency and not as a leniency. For example, if the date was written on an attached piece of material and the main part on a detached piece, it is certainly invalid according to rabbinic law, but it is not nullified to the extent that if she accepted betrothal from another man she would not require a get (divorce document) from the first man. Our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, was uncertain about this, and it requires further investigation. (And the main point seems to me to be because the date is included in the main part according to Rashi in Bava Metzia 7b: s.v. "shtar," and not because it has the status of the main part; investigate this well.)

It is well-known throughout the Talmud that a perforated pot, whatever is planted or rooted in it, is considered as if it is planted or rooted in the ground. A non-perforated pot is considered as if the contents are detached. For a perforated pot, there is no difference whether it is situated on the ground or on supports that create an air gap between the pot and the ground (Tosafot Gittin 7b s.v. dilma and Shabbat 81a: see there). This applies to clay pots. Regarding wooden pots, some authorities say they do not require perforation; even if not perforated, they are considered as if they are (Tosafot there). Others say the opposite. The main point is that clay certainly requires perforation, but regarding wooden pots, some say that perforation does not help at all (Tosafot Menachot 84b). The status of being considered like the ground, in the case of a perforated pot, applies only to what is planted or rooted in it, but the pot itself is always considered detached. Therefore, one can write a bill of divorce on the pot itself, even if it is perforated, and hand the entire pot to the woman, and we are not concerned that the place of the bill may break off, thereby making it incomplete, because certainly the pot will not be damaged, and it is not customary to break it (Tosafot 21b).

But if the get (bill of divorce) is written on the leaf of a perforated pot, the get is invalid according to Torah law. And it is not necessary to say that if he gives her the get while it is still connected to the ground and the nourishment has not been interrupted from the ground, it is considered fully attached. But even if he lifts the pot from the ground and gives it to her, causing the nourishment to be interrupted and it is considered detached, nevertheless the get is invalid. For although it is not invalid according to Torah law, as this is not considered a cutting from something attached and it is not considered lacking detachment because such detachment is not discernible at all and does not require any further action, just like the act of all detached items (Ran there), nevertheless, rabbinically it is invalid. This is because we decree that perhaps he will cut the leaf from the pot, and then it would be considered lacking detachment. For it is common to cut the leaf, and if he cuts it, it would certainly be invalid according to Torah law. And it is not necessary to say, according to most authorities who invalidate even a detached item that is lacking cutting, but even according to those who say that the invalidity of cutting is only with something attached, nevertheless, here we decree that perhaps he will cut it while it is still on the ground, and it would be considered lacking cutting from something attached (Ba'er Hetev, subparagraph 12).

There is an opinion that according to the first reason we explained in section 29, the disqualification of something attached [to the ground] is because there is no "and he shall place it in her hand," as we require it to be given directly from hand to hand. If he wrote [the get] on a leaf of a perforated potted plant and gave her the entire pot without severing its nourishment, and she made an act of acquisition, she is considered divorced because the pot is something that can be given from hand to hand (Beit Shmuel, subsection 12). And even though the giving of the pot is meaningless since its nourishment has not been severed and it is considered attached [to the ground], nevertheless, the acquisition is through the act of possession, and still, "and he shall place it in her hand" is applicable because it is lifted and given from hand to hand. However, this does not seem correct, because with a get, we require that the acquisition be through giving from hand to hand (so writes the Taz), and all the more so according to the opinion that the disqualification of something attached is because it is not similar to a book, the get is certainly invalid.

Some say that the same rule applies to a non-perforated pot, which is considered as detached. Nevertheless, if one writes on its leaf and gives her the whole pot, it is also invalid according to the authorities who hold that even when detached, the Torah invalidates it due to the need for cutting it off, as there is also a decree lest one might cut it. This is not comparable to writing on a large sheet of paper where we do not decree lest one might cut off a part, because cutting a leaf is done easily and there is a common practice to cut leaves; therefore, it is decreed (Choshen Mishpat 13). And some say that when it is non-perforated, it is considered like all detached items, and we do not decree lest one might cut it; therefore, if one writes on the leaf and gives her the whole pot, it is valid (see Bayit Chadash). It appears that the primary opinion is like the first one, as the author of the second opinion is the Rashba in his novellae (21b), and he himself is uncertain about this, see there. And know that when writing on pottery, which we validated when it is perforated, and certainly when it is non-perforated, she always needs to bring witnesses of delivery before us when she comes to marry with this get, because pottery is something that can be forged, and in such a case, witnesses of delivery are needed as written in paragraph 5.

It has already been explained in Section 2 that a get (Jewish divorce document) written by a slave requires an "Al Menat" (condition) because it is considered writing that can be forged. However, if it is written with a tattoo, "Al Menat" is not required because once it is tattooed, it cannot be forged. It is also explained there that such writing involves a Torah prohibition or a rabbinic prohibition, as mentioned there. Nevertheless, the get is kosher because we do not suspect the scribe of being a wicked person, except for someone who desecrates the Sabbath, as mentioned in Section 123. However, the witnesses who signed it with a tattoo must have done so unintentionally, because if they did so intentionally, the get is invalid, as even with a rabbinic disqualification, the witnesses are disqualified (Beit Shmuel, Subsection 16). Similarly, even if the witnesses signed regularly without a tattoo, since the get is written with a tattoo, the get is invalid without "Al Menat" for another reason—it is like a get written on an erased surface with witnesses signing on the paper (Be'er HaGolah, Choshen Mishpat, Subsection 18). Some argue this point, saying that in the case of writing on an erased surface with witnesses signing on paper, there is a concern of forgery, but when written with a tattoo, it cannot be forged (Beit Shmuel there). There is also an opinion that we are concerned that perhaps the get was originally written regularly and then forged and tattooed (Be'er HaGolah). However, why should we be concerned about such a possibility, since when the get comes before us now, there is no concern of forgery (Beit Shmuel). Additionally, there is no concern that someone might erase the signatures and forge the get because this would certainly not be done, as it would then be impossible to verify the signatures (there). Therefore, the matter requires further investigation for a definitive ruling, and from the Tur it appears as the first opinion mentioned there.

When does a woman become divorced through a writ (get) written on the hand of a slave? In the case of a slave who is established to be hers, and the writ is written as a tattoo, and she claims that she transferred ownership of the slave to him before the writ and then he transferred it back to her. However, in the case of a slave that is established to belong to him (the husband), and the writ is written on his (the slave's) hand, and she claims that the husband gave her the writ with this slave, and the husband is not present, and there is no witness before us, since it is written as a tattoo, no witness is needed as stated. Nevertheless, it is considered a doubtful writ. The reason is that if they were to come to litigate about the slave in monetary law, and she would claim that he sold or gave the slave to her, and he (the husband) would claim that the slave came into her possession on his own, the law would side with him. For it is established that living beings that can walk are not judged like other movable property, where the possessor can say 'you sold or gave it to me,' but rather it stays with its owner, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 135. Since regarding monetary matters, we cannot establish her possession of the slave when the owner is not here, and they agree on this, how can we permit her through this writ? (Talmud Gittin 20b). Therefore, it is considered a doubtful writ. The same applies to writing on the horn of a cow, in which case it is also doubtful. Specifically, this applies to a case where it is established to belong to him. But otherwise, even when it is not established to belong to her, since the husband does not have possession of the slave or the cow, we establish them in her possession, and consequently, she is divorced. Similarly, in a place where possession is effective, such as after three years or similar cases where possession is effective as explained in Choshen Mishpat, she is also divorced. The general rule of this law is that when the monetary claim is removed from her, we have no basis to invalidate the writ from her possession.

There is someone who posed a significant question regarding this matter. If so, even if it is not established that it belongs to him, and even if it is established that it belongs to her, how is she divorced? After all, necessarily, before the get (divorce document) it must be the husband's, and if so, it would be as if it is known to us that it is his (Beit Shmuel section 17). The answer to this is that since even if the husband claimed that she transferred ownership of the servant to him and he wrote the get on him and did not hand it over to her, he would not be able to take the servant from her. For she would be believed to say truthfully, "I transferred ownership to you, but on the condition that you divorce me with it," and she would be believed in any case to take the servant from him because living beings do not have an established possession. Consequently, it follows that the get is also valid since the servant is in her possession, and only if the husband comes and says that he did not give her the get, she would not be divorced, and the servant would remain with her. And as long as he does not come and contradict her, we consider her to be in the status of a divorced woman (Taz). Likewise, there is someone who questioned what we wrote, that after three years, she is divorced, and indeed a woman does not have an established possession in her husband's property. The answer to this is that if so, how can we consider her divorced with any type of get that she brings, for indeed she does not have an established possession in the item on which the get is written if we are certain that it belongs to the husband. Rather, certainly, since there is a dispute between them, as we see in any case that he wrote a get, such a woman has an established possession in her husband's property, as he does not trust her (there).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 7: If the get (bill of divorce) is engraved on a tablet and the witnesses are on it, and it is found in her possession, and she says that she gave it to him and he returned it to her, even though it is established that the tablet is hers, she is divorced. This is because a woman herself can write her get, as our master concluded. Similarly, the Rambam wrote in chapter 4 and the Tur, and its source is from the Gemara (20b). There is no novelty in this except to inform us that we should not say that a woman does not have the capacity to transfer ownership to another in such a way that the other can immediately transfer it back to her. It might be thought that her transfer of ownership to him is not valid, and thus it would turn out that he divorced her with something that is not his. Therefore, we are informed that she knows how to transfer ownership even in such a case. 

And one should not ask: Did not the Rabbis grant him the fee for the get from her property, as stated in Siman 120? If so, why do we need her transfer of ownership, since we have already written there in paragraph 27 in the name of the Ramban that the Sages only granted him ownership if she gave money, but when the parchment is hers, the Rabbis did not grant him ownership. See there.

It appears to me that what the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote, stating that she says she gave it to him, does not mean she needs to explicitly say that she gave it to him. In truth, Maimonides did not mention this, and the language of the Tur also seems to support this view. The reasoning supports it as well, because her statement neither adds nor detracts. Certainly, we say that it is assumed they acted in this way because, otherwise, the witnesses would not have signed it. The mention that she says it is merely customary language. It is possible that this is why they wrote that the witnesses signed it, for in essence, the get (divorce document) is valid even without signing witnesses, as written in Siman 133. Certainly, from the reasoning we explained, they wrote this, because otherwise, we would not believe her.

However, from the words of the Tur, it is clear that even without witnesses, we say it is assumed she gave it to him. The Tur did not write that the witnesses signed it but that she needs to bring it in front of the court. If the witnesses’ signatures are inscribed in a way that they cannot be forged, even if the court is not present, she is divorced. Nonetheless, we can say that even though the Tur did not initially mention that the witnesses signed it, his intention aligns with our explanation. He means that, in any case, if she brings it in front of the court, it is valid because the witnessing witnesses would not allow the delivery of the get unless she had given it to him. If the witnesses’ signatures are inscribed and cannot be forged, we rely on the signing witnesses, as we explained.

Maimonides and the Shulchan Aruch conclude that the woman herself writes her get, meaning this is from the Mishnah in Gittin (22b), from which the Gemara brings proof that a woman knows how to transfer ownership. Maimonides further concludes that the get is only valid with its signers if there are no witnessing witnesses. He needed to state this because, otherwise, it would be possible to ask the witnessing witnesses if she transferred it to him if we always required her to bring it in front of the court. However, because when there are witnessing witnesses, we do not require her to bring it in front of the court, and the signing witnesses are not present to ask them, we therefore need to rely on the presumption that she certainly transferred it to him.

If one engraved the get (divorce document) on a plate of gold and gave it to her, if he gave it to her without any specific stipulation, he cannot consider the value of the gold plate as part of the payment for the ketubah (marriage contract), because this was given to her as a get. What he owes her for the ketubah he must pay separately. However, if he said to her, "This is your get and your ketubah," she is divorced, and she has also received her ketubah to the extent of the value of the plate. One cannot argue that, in this case, the letters of the get are "floating in the air," because the entire plate counts as the payment for her ketubah. We require that the object on which the get is written belongs to him, and this does not belong to him, but it is as if he said, "Receive your get and forgive me your ketubah" (Chikrei Lev and Beit Shmuel). This is specifically when she accepted the get willingly, for otherwise, how could he force her to forgive the ketubah (ibid.), unless she explicitly says she forgives it (Atzei Ganim). There is an opinion that this applies only when he uses this specific language, but if he said, "This is your get and you will pay your ketubah from the gold it contains," this is not a valid get, as this language cannot be interpreted as forgiveness (Givat Pinchas). There are those who disagree (Turei Zahav), and it is also explained in the Tur, who used the language of payment, that this implies, "This is your get on the condition that you will be paid from the gold it contains," meaning she will return the obligation of her ketubah. This is also considered forgiveness (Atzei Ganim). If he gave it to her without any stipulation, even if there is a large part of the plate where the get is not written, it cannot be counted towards her ketubah, because the get must be written on something that is considered his (Gemara 20a).

He should not give her the get (bill of divorce) while the writing is still moist; instead, he should wait until the writing and signatures have dried well, lest it be considered a writing that can be forged. However, it is not only for this reason, as it is permitted to write on a material that can be forged, and she must bring [evidence] as explained. But there is another reason: it is as if he wrote on a non-enduring material (as stated in Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel), for while it is moist, the writing can be erased, and this is a problem even after the fact, as will be explained in the next section. Therefore, if he gave it to her while it was still moist, there is doubt whether the get is invalid or not, because it is not really applicable to consider this non-enduring, since it will immediately become enduring. This requires further investigation (as Beit Shmuel section 21 states that his opinion leans towards invalidating it, while Choshen Mishpat's opinion is to validate it). Initially, we are careful that the witnesses do not sign until the writing has dried, as stated at the end of section 130; this is merely a stringency. Regarding signatures, it will be explained at the end of section 133 that there is no issue even after the fact.

Some say that if one throws sand on the writing in the manner done to dry it, or if one throws gold dust on it, the get (divorce document) is invalid because it is like writing over writing. However, if one throws sand and then removes it, leaving the writing as it was before, it is valid, as stated in Orach Chaim, Siman 32. There are those who question this matter fundamentally and hold that this does not fall under the category of writing over writing, and the case of throwing gold dust mentioned in Orach Chaim there refers to covering it so much that the ink is not visible at all. But with a small amount of sand, there is not much concern (as per the Pri Toar). Nevertheless, all scribes are careful not to put sand or other types of dust on the get but rather dry it in the sun or by a fire.

And know that in the Gemara (2b), it is an established law that the Torah says "one book" and not two or three books. If the get (divorce document) is written on two papers, it is not a valid get. And this that we learned in the Mishnah in Gittin (87b) that if part of the get was left and written on the second sheet, it is valid – there it is talking about one piece of parchment in two columns, like the scrolls of the Torah (Tosafot). And this that we learned in Sotah (18a) that if it was written on two pages, it is invalid – that is because the Torah says "one book" and not two or three books, which refers to two separate pieces of parchment (there). And although we hold that "book" comes to mean a count of words, and therefore we do not specifically require parchment as in the case of Sotah, as I wrote in section 15, nevertheless, we also expound this teaching (there), for the text does not depart from its plain meaning, that "book" is written in the singular form.

And based on this, I am very astonished at the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch for not mentioning this law anywhere. Only our teacher, the Rema, in Siman 130, section 7, wrote that if two pieces of parchment are glued together by glue, the get (divorce document) is invalid due to doubt. See there. His reasoning is because of the issue of "two books." How could they omit a clear law from the Talmud without dispute? It is far-fetched to say that they hold like Rashi in Sotah there, who explains that even one piece with two columns is invalid in the case of Sotah because of the issue of "two books." See there. Consequently, from the Mishnah in Gittin there, it is proven that this law does not apply, and we would have to say that the words of the Gemara are according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi (21b), who does not interpret "book" to mean the recounting of things, as explained there. And we hold like the Rabbis that it refers to the recounting of things. If so, how does the Gemara there question plainly, "And let it derive from 'one book' that the Torah said, etc.?" This requires further study.

With what materials a get (Jewish bill of divorce) can be written, the correct writing method, and the parchment. This section contains one paragraph:

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Gittin 19a) that a get can be written with ink, sap, red dye, gum, vitriol, and any substance that is lasting. It cannot be written with liquids, fruit juice, or anything that is not permanent. Ink is defined as "kiag-ros" and in the Arukh it is defined as "al-midar." Sap, according to Rashi, is "orpimant" and others interpret it as "epermant." Another interpretation is that it is a type of soil found on the island of Zamm in the sea of Ikar and in the land of Greece. Red dye, according to Rashi, is a red color called "minio." Some interpret it as "rathel menig," and Bartenura explains it as a root herb called "sama," while "sikra" is a stone that dyes red. Gum is a type of resin called "goma," and vitriol, as explained in the Gemara, is "charta daushkafi." Rashi interprets it as "adramant," and Tosafot and Rashbam interpret it as a green earth called "vitriol," which is also called "zag" in Arabic. Another interpretation is "copper water," and they are all the same.

The Rambam writes in the beginning of Chapter 4: "One may only write a get (bill of divorce) with something whose mark endures, such as ink, red dye, gum, and vitriol, and similar substances. But if it is written with something whose mark does not endure, such as beverages and fruit juices and the like, it is not a valid get." These are his exact words. However, he omits "sam" (a type of ink) which is mentioned in the Mishnah, and I do not know why. It seems that in the Mishnah available to him, "sam" was not included, and it is also not found in the Mishnah of the Jerusalem Talmud. See there. There is no practical difference in law because anything whose mark endures is valid. The Tosefta (Chapter 2) adds nut shells, pomegranate peels, congealed blood, and congealed milk. See there. It seems to me that there is some scribal error in the Tosefta, because it appears that congealed blood and congealed milk are not substances that endure. Besides this, according to the context of the Tosefta there, there must be some error. See there. And it seems that the nut shells refer to the outer green and soft shell, because the hard inner shell is not suitable for writing. Even though in the Tosefta of Shabbat (Chapter 12) the text is the same as in the Tosefta of Gittin, it is also evident there that it is a scribal error. See there (because it concludes with the rule: "If one writes with something that does not endure, etc." According to our version, it does not consider these things as substances that do not endure in writing, and why would it consider them so there? See there. Therefore, certainly the shells are enduring, and blood and milk are not enduring. Pay attention and understand).

The language of the Rambam is that it requires something whose mark stands, as he wrote, and so is the language of the Shulchan Aruch. But the Tur wrote that one may write the get with anything whose mark is recognizable, etc. End of quote. And some say that they disagree on the law, that according to the Tur, it does not need to last and endure for a long time, but anything whose mark is recognizable at the moment is valid (Bach, Beit Shmuel). And it is a great wonder to say this, for the Mishnah required something that endures. Moreover, even with fruit juice, it is recognizable, but it is invalid because it does not endure. Therefore, it is clear that the Tur also requires something enduring (Pri Chadash and Gra). And this that he wrote "whose mark is recognizable," on the contrary, his intention is that even over a long time, we need its mark to be recognizable. Meaning, certainly over time the writing is not as good as at the time of writing, yet we still need the mark to be recognizable even after time. And similar to this is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 11 of Shabbat, law 15, who wrote, "The writer is not liable until he writes with something that marks and endures," etc. See there. And furthermore, it can be said in his intention that we need it to endure and be recognizable, for there are things that endure but are not recognizable, like gallnut water on gallnut-treated parchment, as will be explained, and similarly myrrh water which absorbs into the paper and is not recognizable from outside, and this writing does not help (there).

It was taught (there) that if one wrote with lead, with black ink, or with any black substance, it is valid. The Rif and the Rambam, of blessed memory, copied this language there and wrote that these substances should not be used initially. The Tur disagrees, stating that they can be used initially as well. The Tur wrote that "lead" (evar) means lead filings mixed with water, meaning that one scrapes the lead into water and blackens it (Rashi), and it becomes like ink. However, if one wrote with lead itself, which they call "plumbum," the get (divorce document) is invalid according to Torah law (Beit Shmuel 2). "Black ink" (shachor) is made from charcoal, meaning that one grinds the charcoal in water, mixes it with water, and makes ink from it. But if one wrote with the charcoal itself, it is not a valid get. "Shichor" is adramant (iron gall ink) according to the Tur and based on the Talmudic discussion there and Rashi's explanation, see there.

However, Maimonides (of blessed memory) leaves it ambiguous and does not differentiate between "avra" and "maya d'avra" (embryonic fluid), and some say that his opinion is the opposite: that with "avra" it is valid, and with "maya d'avra" it is invalid. Similarly, with "shachor" (black), the Bach and the Lechem Mishneh interpret that the Talmud distinguishes between "avra" and "maya d'avra," stating that "maya d'avra" is invalid, as well as with "shachor." He explains that the Talmud's distinction between "avra" and "maya d'avra" is the opposite of Rashi and the Tur, and on the contrary, "avra" would be written, and "maya d'avra" would not be written. This is not a logical opinion at all, but rather Maimonides holds that both are valid. The Talmud's distinction is not according to the law (as Rav disagrees with Shmuel, see there) (Beit Yosef, the Gra, and Pri Chadash). It is also clarified from the words of our teacher, the Rema, who wrote in section 2: Some say that with "avra" it is valid, meaning pieces of "avra" mixed with water, but if written with "avra" itself, it is invalid. One should be concerned about this initially. Since he wrote that only initially one should be concerned about this, it implies that in retrospect, both are valid. Practically, we need to be concerned about all opinions, whether with "avra," "maya d'avra," or charcoal; it would be a doubtful get. Note that the Aruch interprets "shachor" differently, that it is an iron tool used for inscribing, and "shichor" he interprets as charcoal. According to the Aruch, using this tool is valid at least in retrospect. Practically, it would be a doubtful get, as according to Rashi and the Tur, it does not refer to the tool but rather as written.

As has been explained, any kind of ink is valid for writing a get (divorce document), as long as the writing endures for a long time. There is no difference between black ink, red ink, or green ink. However, white ink is certainly not valid, as white ink on white paper is obviously not sufficiently visible. Nevertheless, our teacher the Rema wrote that ideally, it is customary to write it with good ink, of the sort used for writing books, and one should not deviate from this practice. However, in a situation of potential agunah (a woman unable to remarry due to an unresolved previous marriage) or pressing circumstances, one may write with any type of ink. 

There are those who cast doubt on a certain type of very good ink, which is shiny and called "glanz" (glossy). They write that when this ink dries, after a day or two, the letters fall off the paper and it is as though they were never there. However, this is not correct, as the impression of the ink is always noticeable. Furthermore, it does not disappear on its own, except due to some external reason, and this does not qualify as non-enduring. We have never heard of this issue, and on the contrary, scribes seek out such ink even for writing Torah scrolls, tefillin, and mezuzot. We have seen Torah scrolls from many years ago, and the ink still shines, and we do not know the reason for this doubt.

Additionally, it is written in the name of the "Seder HaGet" that there are those who are stringent and say that the scribe should read each letter first before writing it, as is done with Torah scrolls. However, the requirement to read each letter is considered an excessive stringency and lacks a clear rationale. Even with a Sefer Torah, it is not necessary to read each letter, only to read each word, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 274. Perhaps this is a textual error, and it should state "read each word," as it is in the "Seder HaGet" of Rabbi Michal, son of Rabbi Yosef, which was printed in the Shulchan Aruch after the completion of the laws, see there in Section 78. And in Yoreh De'ah, it is explained that even when writing from another text placed before him, he must still read each word before writing it. However, in Orach Chaim, Siman 32 regarding Tefillin, it is explained that when writing by heart, one must read each word first, but not when writing from a text, because he is accustomed to them (Magen Avraham, Siman 142). According to this, in the case of a Get (bill of divorce) written from another Get, there is room to be lenient, as the scribe is certainly familiar with the format of the Get. Nonetheless, with a Get, the main aspect of this requirement is an additional stringency, as the witnesses read the Get before signing it, and the Rabbi reads it before and after the giving of the Get. If there is any deficiency, it will be noticed. Since this is not a strict legal requirement but rather a matter of stringency, it is certainly proper to be stringent initially for the scribe to read each word before writing it, even when writing from another Get, and this is the custom.

One may write it with gallnut water, provided the parchment is not treated with gallnut, for on such parchment the gallnut water is not noticeable, and if one writes with it, it is not a valid bill of divorce (get). The same applies to all similar cases, as the legal authorities have written. The explanation of this matter is as follows: the ink that scribes make is from gallnut water, vitriol (which is called copper water), and gum arabic. These are well-cooked together, and some also add the soot that accumulates on utensils, which is called "rus." This is the standard ink referred to in the Mishnah, as stated in section 1, which in German is called "kierg-rus," as written in the order of the bill of divorce by Maimonides that we have cited. It is known that the primary element that sustains the writing is the gallnut water, which is called "gals." However, by itself, it is not black, and if one writes with it on a white surface, the writing will not be noticeable. Therefore, if the parchment is treated with gallnut, it is white, and writing with gallnut water alone will not be visible. But when it is not treated, it is black, and the writing is noticeable. The same applies to all similar matters. In the Gemara there, it mentions "mei treya," which Rashi explains as rainwater, or alternatively, water in which fruit that resembles gallnuts has been soaked.

It seems clear to me that on our paper, writing with gallnut ink alone is not considered writing at all, because our paper is white and gallnut ink alone is not distinguishable on it as it is on gallnut-treated parchment. And one cannot say that it is only on gallnut-treated parchment that it is not distinguishable because gallnut does not add to the gallnut. And ostensibly, the language of the Talmud also indicates this, as it says there that gallnut ink on top of gallnut ink is not visible, and the language of the Tur also indicates this. Nevertheless, follow the reason and the sense perception testifies to this, and it is a matter that requires further investigation as far as the law is concerned. And know that in the procedure of the get (divorce document) according to Maharam that we mentioned, in letter 32, it is written that when writing the get with gallnut ink, the parchment should not be gallnut-treated, even if other substances mentioned are mixed in, end quote. These statements are surprising, because sense perception testifies that when gum arabic and copper sulfate are mixed in, the ink blackens and is visible even on white parchment that has not been treated, and our parchments are good and processed better than gallnut treatment. And nevertheless, Torah scrolls are written with such ink and it is clearly visible. And thus I found one of the great authorities who wrote this clearly (Noda B'Yehuda, second part, and the words of Rabbi Shabtai, regarding the Tosafot on Gittin 19. And we do not hold like this, see there and analyze).

We learn in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 2, Halacha 3): "And he wrote"—excluding if he engraved; "and he wrote"—excluding if he dripped; "and he wrote"—excluding if he poured. Now, engraving will be explained later, and "dripping" refers to making dot-like shapes in the form of letters. There is a dispute there: one opinion says that if the dots are merged, meaning if one passed the quill over them and they became like complete letters, it is valid. Another opinion says that even in such a case it is invalid because it is not considered writing since it was not originally written in the proper form of a letter. Pouring is explained there as pouring ink which is absorbed into the paper, making the letters indiscernible from the outside. The law regarding engraving has been written by the poskim, as well as the law regarding pouring, since they have written several laws of this nature that the writing must be discernible. However, the law regarding "dripping" is not mentioned at all, which is perplexing, as there is no explicit disagreement in our Talmud on this. It is possible they held that since the Talmud brings the baraita of "and he wrote"—excluding if he engraved (20a)—and does not bring the case of "dripping" from the Jerusalem Talmud in one baraita, it implies that the Talmud does not hold like that. And the reason it does not bring "pouring" is because it is superfluous, as the Talmud had already explained that law earlier. Moreover, there is proof from the fact that we hold by a get (divorce document) that if someone does not know how to sign, we tear a blank piece of paper for them and fill the tears with ink, as is written in Siman 130. Certainly, in such a case, it is considered writing. And although in the case of a get this was permitted because of the agunah (a woman who is chained to her marriage) issue, nevertheless it proves that such writing is valid at least post-facto, and certainly "dripping" is better than this. The Jerusalem Talmud indeed questions this law of tearing paper and filling it with ink, arguing that this is considered the first writing. It answers that they widen the tears and the witnesses do not fill the entire width of the tear. Therefore, it properly invalidates "dripping." But our Talmud, which permits even without widening, certainly considers "dripping" valid. This requires further study for the halacha, and if such writing occurred, the get would certainly be considered of doubtful validity when given to her.

The Rambam writes in Chapter 4, Halacha 7: "One who cuts on the leather in the shape of a letter or marks on the leather in the shape of a letter, it is valid." And in the Jerusalem Talmud, the version reads: "One who cuts on the leather in the shape of a letter, it is valid; one who marks on the leather in the shape of a letter, it is invalid." And the Rambam himself in the Laws of Shabbat, Chapter 11, also writes the same: "One who cuts is liable, and one who marks is exempt." The Rashba and the Ran have already wondered about his ruling that considers a get valid when it is marked on leather. And in the Tosefta, the version is the opposite: that cutting is invalid and marking is valid. Certainly, this is corrupted. All that has been written regarding the Rambam's words does not make sense. In my humble opinion, it appears clearly from the words of the Tur that there is an error in the Rambam's texts, for the Tur brings in his name: "One who cuts on the leather, etc., or marks on the tablet, etc." And this is engraving, as will be explained.

And these are the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 5: "If one tears on leather in the shape of letters, it is valid. But if one imprints on leather in the shape of letters, it is invalid. And some say the opposite. And there are those who deem both valid." And the opinion that says the opposite follows the version of the Tosefta. It has already been explained that the main opinion follows the version of the Jerusalem Talmud (according to the Gra). And those who deem both valid follow the version of Maimonides. The main opinion follows the first view. Nevertheless, in practice, all these cases are considered a doubt in the validity of a get (divorce document).

This that is written in the Torah "and he shall write for her a scroll of cutting off" (Deuteronomy 24:1) — engraving on wood and stone is also considered writing, for regarding the tablets it is written several times the term "writing" and they were engraved on the stones, as it is written "engraved on the tablets" (Exodus 32:16). And in the portion of Tavo, regarding the stones set up across the Jordan, it is written "and you shall write on the stones" (Deuteronomy 27:8). Even though it is possible that there it was writing and not engraving, nevertheless, it is certain that on stones, engraving is preferable to writing, for writing cannot be a complete writing, unlike engraving, as proven in the Talmud Menachot (34b). And it seems that for a get (divorce document), it is only valid with engraving and not with writing on stones, for although we do not require complete writing in a get as will be explained, nevertheless, we require something that endures, as explained. And writing on stones is not something that endures, as proven there in the Gemara (see Tosafot there, s.v. "and you shall write," where they explain that complete writing does not apply to stones because they do not endure).

Engraving is valid in a get, whether on stone or on metal plates, as long as the body of the letter is engraved. This can be done either by engraving from the inside, making the letters recessed and the surrounding area raised, or by engraving the letter from the outside, making the letters raised and the surrounding area recessed. There is no difference between whether the letters are recessed or raised, as long as an action is performed on the body of the letter itself. However, if no action is performed on the letters themselves but only around them and within them, leaving the letters formed passively, the get is invalid.
