This is what is stated in the Gemara (2b): "If one engraved the interior [of the letters], it is invalid; if one engraved the exterior [of the letters], it is valid." Engraving the exterior means performing an action on the letter itself, while engraving the interior means performing an action within and around the letter without touching the letter itself. Just as engraving the exterior is valid whether the letter is recessed or raised, so too engraving the interior is invalid whether the interior of the letters is recessed, making the letters raised, or the interior is raised, making the letters recessed. Even if one made a seal and engraved the get with the seal, as is done with coins, this is also considered engraving the interior and is not a valid get according to the Torah, as it is not considered writing at all (Gemara, ibid.).

And since "chiseling out" (i.e., forming letters by removing ink) is invalid, therefore, if a drop of ink falls into a letter and the letter is no longer recognizable, one cannot remove the ink and correct the letter, as this would be considered "chiseling out." Since the letter was nullified by the drop of ink, when one removes the ink and the letter remains, it is considered as if he is forming the letter by chiseling out and not by writing the letter itself. This is also written in Orach Chaim, Siman 32 regarding a Torah scroll, tefillin, and mezuzah. There is no difference between wet or dry ink, contrary to those who wish to be lenient with wet ink. Most halachic authorities agree with this. Even if the drop fell after the letter was completed (Beit Shmuel), if it is in the significant part and the form of the letter is altered, one cannot remove the ink. However, if the form of the letter is not altered, one may erase the drop of ink, as this is not considered "chiseling out" since the letter was recognizable (Beit Yosef). See what is written in Section 19.

And our master, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 8 that some are stringent even if the letter is recognizable, and this is the custom. This is only initially, but in retrospect, it is valid in a pressing situation or in a case of potential abandonment (Achronim). There is no valid reason for this stringency even initially, since if the letter is recognizable, it has no relevance to "chok tochot" (engraving through removal). It appears that the initial stringency is due to the requirement of "hekef gvil" (surrounding parchment), and even though it is not essential in a get (divorce document), initially, "hekef gvil" is required even in a get (and this is also implied in Nodah B’Yehudah, section 85, who explains this). The truth is that from the primary source (Maharik, root 98), it is understood that this also relates to "chok tochot". The interpretation is not that if a drop fell on a letter and the letter remains intact, there is no reason to be stringent. The intent is when the legs of the letter "hei" or "kuf" slightly touch their roof, and it is clear that the touch happened afterward, and the "hei" and "kuf" are recognizable. However, since the touch makes the letter imperfect, this is what is referred to by saying that even if the letter is recognizable, meaning it is clear that this was not from the initial writing. Therefore, it is certainly appropriate to be stringent because of "chok tochot". The general principle is that "the letter is not recognizable" means when a drop fell and altered the entire shape of the letter. "Recognizable" means the letter is clearly recognizable, and its imperfection is visible, caused by the drop of ink and not from the initial writing. However, in any case, since correcting it to remain a letter requires scraping off the drop, it becomes "chok tochot". One should only be lenient in a pressing situation when the get has already been given, or in a case of potential abandonment even if it has not yet been given.

And for this reason, since when the letter is recognizable, it is merely a stringency, therefore there is one who writes: if a drop of ink fell and did not change the shape of the letter, and the scribe hastened before the ink was absorbed into the paper and sucked the ink with his tongue and wiped it off the get (bill of divorce), and it is not noticeable that there was an erasure, it is permissible even initially. For even if it had dried, it would not have changed the shape of the letter, and he would have been permitted by law to scrape it off. Therefore, when it has not yet dried and he licked it with his tongue, it is permissible even initially. But if, when it dries, it would change the shape of the letter, it is not permissible to lick it while it is still wet. And all this is specifically when black ink fell into the letter. But if something not so black, like coffee or something similar, fell, and the writing is still recognizable, but it diminishes its appearance, there is no concern in this, and he wipes it off and inks it. However, if it appears as an erasure to the eye, one should be stringent, for we are stringent regarding erasures in a get, as will be explained with God's help.

There is no remedy for a get (divorce document) that becomes invalid when a letter gets damaged. In a Torah scroll, there is a remedy to erase and write on the erased spot, but in a get, it is forbidden to write on the erased spot due to concerns of forgery. It is forbidden for a get to have any erasure or smudging, even between letters, because of the concern of forgery (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 11). However, in a situation of potential agunah (a woman unable to remarry because her husband refuses to grant a divorce), there is a remedy for any mistake, even a complete mistake, to scrape and write on the erased spot. Even for us who do not validate any erasure, it is still valid in a pressing situation (ibid.). This is what the Taz did in practice in a pressing situation (ibid.). Even if the error is noticed after writing the entire get, it is still possible to erase and write. And although this is not in the proper sequence, the sequence is not a requirement for a get; it is only a requirement for tefillin and mezuzot that they be written in sequence (ibid.). It is incumbent upon the rabbi arranging the get to understand if this is a pressing situation for this get or not. For the main law regarding the deficiency of a letter, see what I wrote in chapter 126, paragraph 1 (and study this carefully).

And know that we wrote in section 15 that if an entire letter is damaged and its form is altered, if one removes the ink and the letter remains as before, it is considered "carved from within." This is agreed upon by all the authorities. However, there are those who say (Bach) that the get (divorce document) is nullified by Torah law in such a case, but many disagree with this. From the responsa of the Rashba (section 511), it is explained based on the Jerusalem Talmud in Megillah that "carved from within" by Torah law applies specifically before the letter is formed. But if it was written properly according to halacha, and afterwards, due to damage, its form was altered and the damage was removed, and the letter remained as before, it is not invalid by Torah law (Bava Metzia). Additionally, it is unlikely that the get would be nullified by Torah law due to the lack of a letter or even a word, and even in the essential part of the get, it would not be nullified by Torah law. For there are several repeated phrases in the get, as explained in section 126, section 61, see there.

There are those who say that if a drop of wax falls on a letter or within a letter, even though the letter is not recognizable, one can scrape off the wax and remove it, and this is not considered as engraving from within (Pri Chadash and Magen Avraham in Siman 32, Se'if Katan 23). However, there are those who lean towards being stringent, considering this as well to be engraving from within (Pitchei Teshuvah, Se'if Katan 13, in the name of Ginat Veradim). This also seems to be implied from what is written in Orach Chaim, Siman 340, that if one removes wax from a notebook and there is enough space to write two letters, one is liable. It appears to me that when the wax is still soft, one can scrape it off, as this is merely considered a cover and is not similar to wet ink, because when ink falls on a letter, even when it is wet, it all becomes one, which is not the case with wax. However, when the wax has dried and thereby nullified the letter, scraping it off would be similar to engraving from within, and this requires further investigation.

If a drop of ink falls on a letter and it appears as though it is part of the letter, and the letter is still recognizable to a child who is neither wise nor foolish, but the top or leg of the letter becomes thick, it is not invalid. Even if it is left as it is, it is valid because there is no required size for the letter. Consequently, it is also permissible to fix it and scrape off the thickness, contrary to those who would want to invalidate it even in such a case (Pri Megadim). Similarly, if a small thorn-like protrusion extends from the body of the letter in a way that does not alter the form of the letter at all, but merely protrudes, it is also valid (ibid.) and one may scrape off the protrusion.

There are letters that do not require scraping in their correction but only adding a bit to the shape of the letter, such as the letters Kaf, Bet, Dalet, Resh, and others. This is not considered 'etching from the inside' (Rivash 66). It is clear that if one made a mistake and wrote a Bet instead of a Kaf or a Dalet instead of a Resh, one can add to the thickness and make it into a rounded shape, and similarly, in the reverse case, one can add to the thickness and make an angle. This disqualification only applies to Tefillin and Mezuzot when they have already been written afterward because it is not in their proper sequence, but not in a Torah scroll, and certainly not in a Get (Pri Chadash). However, if one scrapes from the thickness of the letter to make it rounded like a Resh or to make an angle like a Dalet, this is certainly considered 'etching from the inside.' But when one adds to its thickness, it is considered writing. However, if a drop of ink falls inside the Bet and it looks like a Pe or its form is ruined, and similarly, any other letter whose form is ruined even though it has not changed to another letter, it is invalid, and there is no remedy to scrape the ink because this is precisely 'etching from the inside' (Beit Yosef, Orach Chayim 32).

If he made a divided letter that appears as two separate letters, and there was a letter "shin" on the side of the division, there is a solution: erase one of the three heads and make another head, extending it slightly so that it no longer appears divided. However, if he initially made a fourth head for the "shin" and extended it, and then erased one of the three heads, this is considered as engraving from within (chak tochot), which is not valid, contrary to those who permit it even in this case (three times and Pri Chodosh). Similarly, if he wrote two words as one and there is an extra letter between them, he should erase it so that they appear as two separate words (ibid). It also seems that he can scrape the thickness of the letter to make it thin so that it appears as two words, and conversely, he can add to its thickness to make it appear as one word, as there is no fixed measure for the thickness or thinness of letters. This is also not considered as engraving from within because the letter remains as it was, only becoming thicker or thinner, and the intention is not for the essence of the letter but to bring it closer to or farther from the other letter (so it appears to me).

There are those who wish to say that if the leg of the letter "heh" is attached to the roof by a very thin hair-like thread, and a child who is neither wise nor foolish still reads it as a "heh," it is permissible to detach the hair-like thread. However, many great authorities disagree, arguing that when we see a change in the letter, it is not dependent on the child's reading (see what I have written in section 126, clause 60, and examine it closely). The validity of the letter is not dependent on its thickness or thinness, for what difference does it make whether it is thick or thin? It is invalid (according to Radak, Pri Chadash, and Atzei Yehuda). Similarly, if two letters are joined together in such a way that the form of one letter is completely lost, there is no remedy to scrape off the connection, as this constitutes "cutting from the inside." However, in a Torah scroll, there is a remedy to completely scrape off the leg of the letter and rewrite it. In a get (bill of divorce), where it is forbidden to write on an erased area unless in a case of pressing need and potential for marital strife, there is no remedy other than to write a new get if there is no pressing need. Similarly, if one needed to make an open "mem" and his hand extended and closed it, he cannot scrape off the connection, as this would be "cutting from the inside." Rather, he must scrape off the entire protrusion, and there is no need to erase the entire "mem" (according to Beit Shmuel, section 13). In a Torah scroll, one rewrites on the erased area, but in a get, there is no remedy unless it is a pressing need, as mentioned. Some are stringent about the essential parts of the get even in cases of potential marital strife, but one can be lenient in cases of marital strife and pressing need (according to Beit Shmuel there and in Tiferet Gittin).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 16: If the legs of the letters "hei" and "kuf" touch, it is to be invalidated even post facto. However, if a child can read it, some permit it in a case of hardship (agunah). Ideally, one should not separate it with a knife, but rather write another get (divorce document). This applies specifically not in a case of hardship, but in a case of necessity where there is a concern for agunah, it may be corrected according to the opinion of the Rabbi. And see Beit Yosef, section 32 for how to correct it, and see Shulchan Aruch, section 154, paragraph 45. End of quote.

Explanation of his words: If the legs of the letters 'hei' and 'kuf' touch, it does not suffice even if a child can read it, as it is stated that any letter which does not have the form of the letter as it was given to Moses at Sinai does not have the status of a letter (Beit Shmuel). However, in a case of potential "agunah" (a woman unable to remarry because she cannot obtain a religious divorce), if a child can read it and the get (divorce document) has already been given without correction, it is valid in a pressing situation because we rely on the child’s reading. Even those who are stringent in section 24 agree in a case of potential "agunah" and pressing circumstances where another get cannot be obtained. Furthermore, he says that if the get has not yet been given, initially, if there is no concern of "agunah," it does not help even if one erases the entire leg and rewrites it properly, because although this is effective in a Torah scroll, in a get it does not help since it is forbidden to write on an erased area. Certainly, separating the touching parts with a knife is forbidden due to the prohibition of "cutting within the letters." However, if there is concern of "agunah" and it is necessary to correct this get, one should not separate it with a knife due to "cutting within the letters" but should erase the entire leg as stated in Orach Chaim section 32, and even though it is necessary to write the leg on the erased area, and currently, the custom is not to validate any erasure in a get as will be explained, nevertheless in a case of "agunah," the get is valid without validation. For it is permitted to write on something that can be forged when given to her with witnesses of delivery as stated in section 124, and therefore all disqualifications due to concern of forgery, when given with witnesses of delivery, are valid in a case of "agunah." All the stringencies mentioned in this section due to concern of forgery only apply when there is no concern of "agunah" (Chiddushei Maharam Halava 25), and even in the main part of the document, it is valid as stated in section 154.

Even before the signatures, one can only correct [a mistake] in a case of potential agunah (a woman unable to remarry due to the husband's absence or refusal to grant a divorce). And although one can correct the joining of letters before the signatures even if it is not a case of agunah, as will be explained, nonetheless, the joining of the letters hei and kuf, which is a correction in the essence of the letters themselves, cannot be corrected even before the signatures if it is not a case of agunah. Although in a Torah scroll one can correct this, and similarly in tefillin and mezuzot, where one scrapes off the entire leg [of the letter], in a get (divorce document) it is different, since it is forbidden to write on the scraped or erased part, as is written. According to Rabbeinu the Rema, as will be explained, even the joining of letters cannot be corrected if it is not a case of agunah. However, in practice, one can be lenient with the joining of letters even if it is not a case of agunah, but not with the essence of the letter itself.

The Tur writes that some require making decorations (ziyyunin) on the letters שעטנ"ז ג"ץ in a get (divorce document), but in Sefer HaTeruma it is written that it is not necessary and it is better to refrain from making them. His words: Since it is not customary to make decorations, one should not change the custom in order not to cast aspersions on earlier gittin (divorce documents). Furthermore, many scribes might make them like sticks on the letters, not knowing how to do them properly, and thereby spoil the writing so that the letters are not legible. Therefore, it is better to desist and follow the custom. Similarly, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG) wrote (Beit Yosef) and the Shulchan Aruch ruled in section 7 that if someone wants to make decorations, they can be stopped. If one made decorations in a pressing situation, the get is valid (Chakhamat Adam, subparagraph 10). But if not in a pressing situation, another get should be written because of the suspicion regarding earlier gittin. Note that the concern about casting aspersions on earlier gittin only applies to something that is merely an extra stringency, but if it seems necessary according to the basic law to change, we do not consider the concern of casting aspersions on the earlier ones (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 10).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 6: "It is customary to be stringent that the letters be surrounded by parchment, and if there are joined letters, one should scrape between them to separate them." His words mean that, by strict law, there is no need for the letters to be surrounded by parchment in a get (divorce document), as there is in a Torah scroll or phylacteries, because it is written "and you shall write," requiring complete writing. Therefore, each letter must be surrounded by parchment. However, for a get, complete writing is not required. Nevertheless, it is customary to be stringent even in a get because the letter does not appear properly when one letter is joined to another. Therefore, we are lenient when one letter is joined to another to separate them, and this is not considered engraving from the inside, as it does not touch the body of the letter. Also, ideally, we require the letters to be surrounded by parchment, as in a Torah scroll. This, which we said that by strict law there is no need for the letters to be surrounded by parchment and it is valid even if one letter is joined to another, is only if the shape of the letter is not altered by this, and a child can read it. But if the shape of the letter is altered and a child cannot read it, it is invalid by strict law (Hilchot Mezuzah 4:6 and Hilchot Tefillin 6). However, it is uncommon for the shape of the letter to be altered by the joining of one letter to another, and therefore they did not write the law of the change of the shape of the letter in the case of the joining of one letter to another (and this resolves the precision of Beit Shmuel 7). But if the shape is altered due to the falling of ink into the letter, one cannot remove the ink, as this would be considered engraving from the inside if the shape is altered, and all the authorities agree on this (and the words of Beit Shmuel require further study).

However, our teacher, the Rema, wrote that there are those who say that one should not separate letters if they are touching, and this is the customary practice. Yet, there are those who are lenient in a pressing situation to correct it before the witnesses sign when the husband commands it to be corrected. The explanation of his words is that even if the shape of the letter has not changed and a child can still read it, nonetheless, it should not be separated except in a pressing situation. This is not comparable to a Torah scroll where even initially scraping off ink is done so as not to have to store away something with sanctity. But with a get (divorce document), which does not have sanctity, one can write another one (Choshen Mishpat 28). This is merely an extra stringency. Therefore, in a pressing situation, one can separate the letters, but this is only before the signing. After the witnesses have signed on an invalid document, what use is the correction? (Choshen Mishpat 29). Also, without the husband's instruction, one cannot correct it, as the scribe has already fulfilled his mission. However, this is an excessive stringency, since if it is valid without correction, there is no need for correction at all. And if it is not valid without correction, the scribe has not yet fulfilled his mission and can correct it even without the husband's instruction, as stated in Siman 122 (Gra, Choshen Mishpat 8). It is possible that his intention is that surely the scribe can correct it even without the husband's instruction, but someone else cannot correct it without the husband's instruction, as the husband did not make him a messenger for someone else (as is evident from Choshen Mishpat 29, which states, "But without the husband's instruction, who can correct the get except the scribe"). In truth, from the wording of the Rosh in his responsa, it is evident that even after the signing and without the husband's instruction, it is permissible to correct in a situation of potential marital strife if the shape of the letter has not changed. Also, it is permissible to hand it to her without any correction at all. Therefore, for a get sent to the woman's location, one can rely on this leniency (Choshen Mishpat 29).

The main points of our teacher, the Rema, who was stringent in this matter, are very puzzling, for even though touching the letters with one's feet is forbidden by law, nevertheless he was lenient in a case of potential agunah (a woman chained to her marriage), as mentioned in section 25. Therefore, some say that there is an error in his words, and it should say: "and there are those who are lenient in a pressing situation or to fix it beforehand, etc." This means that in a pressing situation, they are completely lenient, either to give it as it is without correction or for someone else to correct it even without the husband's instruction. If it is not a pressing situation, it should be corrected before the signatures and with the husband's instruction (Taz). In any case, his intention was to practice as the great later authorities agreed (Chacham Tzvi, Beit Shmuel, and Taz) that in a pressing situation it is valid in any case, whether to give it to her without any correction or for anyone to correct it even without his instruction and after the signatures, and all this is when the form of the letters has not changed.

And know that in every place where the poskim (halachic decisors) wrote to correct [the text] before the signatures, ideally, one should also correct it before completing the writing of the get (bill of divorce) according to the law of Moses and Israel, so that it will not be lacking in action between the writing and the giving (Taz). However, this is merely an added stringency, as another lacking action is referred to as the lacking of the writing itself. Nevertheless, ideally, it is proper for the scribe, before he writes "according to the law of Moses and Israel," to review the get and correct what needs to be corrected.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 4 that it is not considered "cutting out letters" unless the entire letter is made in this way. However, if it still requires fixing to make the letter kosher, it is not considered "cutting out letters." This is surprising, as he is lenient in this matter, whereas in other issues like the joining of letters where it is not fundamentally required by law, he was stringent, and similarly, if a drop of ink falls into the letter and the letter is still recognizable, he was stringent, as he wrote. And in the matter of "cutting out letters," which is a Torah prohibition, he was so lenient. What difference does it make whether it is the whole letter or part of the letter? It is not considered a letter until it is entirely correct. Indeed, there are those who disagree with this and hold that even part of it invalidates (Pri Hadash and it appears in Mordechai's responsa 61, see there). It seems to me that Rabbi Moshe Isserles was not referring to the fundamental law of "cutting out letters" and his words were mistakenly printed in section 4 regarding the law of "cutting out letters." This actually belongs to section 8 regarding the law when a drop of ink falls into the letter. In this case, he correctly said that since the letter was written correctly but was invalidated by the drop of ink, upon removing the ink it returns to being a letter. And we have already explained in section 19 that from the Torah, since it was written correctly, it is not considered "cutting out letters," but rather a rabbinic prohibition. According to this, certainly, if a drop of ink falls and ruins the letter, and even after removing the ink it still requires completion by writing the letter itself, this is not considered "cutting out letters."

Some say that based on this, if a little ink falls, one can add ink and make a yud or a vav from the ink that fell and the ink that was added, and it is not considered engraving from within, even though the beginning of the letter is from the ink that fell. Nevertheless, as long as it is necessary to assist in completing the letter, it is valid (Beit Shmuel, section 5, in the name of Beit Yosef). However, there are those who disagree with this (Peri Chadash), arguing that there is no difference between part of a letter and the entire letter. Similarly, if part of a letter was written without the proper intention, it is also invalid (ibid.). Moreover, according to the previous ruling as we explained, it is not comparable, because in that case the letter was originally made in a valid manner, which is not the case here (it seems to me).

It is further written there that some authorities say that ideally, one should be stringent and not write with an iron quill to avoid coming to a situation of engraving. And even though there is no concern in this, even if one comes to a situation of engraving, since one is engraving the letter itself and it is valid as explained, nevertheless, there is a concern that one might come to a situation of engraving the inner parts (Be’er Heitev). Furthermore, it is preferable from the outset not to engrave at all but rather to write (the Vilna Gaon). Additionally, there is concern that the paper might be thin and the point of the quill might engrave into the paper and pierce the letter with a perforated hole, causing some of the letters to be partly in holes and partly in ink. Sometimes, the crack and the hole might be close to the letters, and they would not be surrounded by parchment (Gufei Torah). It is obvious that in a pressing situation where there is no other quill, one should not withhold the get (bill of divorce) for this reason, as there is no substantive halachic basis for this stringency, and it is merely an additional precaution.

And behold, in no place do they write with an iron quill. However, what our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 22, that there are those who have written that one should be careful not to write the get (divorce document) with a quill of a feather, but only with a reed—this we have neither seen nor heard, and it is almost impossible for the writing to come out well. The Ba'er HaGolah wrote that a pious man in Vilna commanded to write with a reed, but it did not succeed for him. And also in Yoreh De'ah, section 271, he wrote similarly about a Torah scroll. However, neither do we practice this with Torah scrolls. But in the days of the Talmudic sages, it appears that they wrote Torah scrolls, tefillin, and mezuzot with a reed (Taanit 20b).

Many of the great authorities have agreed that a printed get, if it is intended for her and given to her, is valid, since printing is akin to engraving, and engraving in the letters themselves is valid, as it is written. Furthermore, this is not engraving but actual writing, for what difference does it make if one presses the pen onto the paper or if one presses the paper onto the lead letters (see Beit Shmuel and Taz in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 271, Peirush HaRosh, and other sources). It is clear that this is specifically when the printer is a Jewish adult who intends it for her and for her sake, and if any one of these is missing, it is not a valid get. However, the signatures of the witnesses are not valid through printing because their actual signatures must be recognized, and therefore they must be written by hand (Peirush HaRosh).

It appears to me that although a get is valid even by engraving, as it is written, nevertheless, if the husband instructed the scribe to write and he engraved, or vice versa, it constitutes a change in his agency and is invalid. Even though, according to the language of the Torah, writing and engraving are the same, as in the tablets and the tzitz (headplate), where engraving is referred to as writing, in common language, it is not so. However, in practice, there is room for doubt in this matter, as one could say that this is not a change since the husband does not care between the two. This is similar to what the Sages said in other matters, that he is merely showing him a place. Therefore, in practice, this matter requires careful consideration, and one should be stringent.

From a logical standpoint, it appears there is no doubt that even though engraving in the actual letter is considered writing, as explained earlier, nevertheless, embroidering, weaving, or sewing letters in a get (divorce document) is not considered writing at all. You should know that the Torah refers to such activities in the context of the Tabernacle’s construction as “embroidering” and “weaving,” and embroidery is considered needlework (Yoma 72b). This is not comparable to engraving, which the Torah refers to as writing in several places, as mentioned there and as implied in Gittin (20a). However, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 23 that if one embroidered, wove, or made letters in the get with needlework, some say it is not considered writing. This clearly implies that some say it is considered writing. He wrote in his major work that according to Rashi in Gittin, it appears that embroidery is not considered writing only when it is laid on the garment with both ends tucked in. But real embroidery on the garment itself is considered writing, as he mentioned there. This is also somewhat implied from what he wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 283, that just as it is forbidden to write verses, so too it is forbidden to engrave them on wood or gold or to embroider them on garments, as he brought this from the responsa of the Rambam. According to this, if this were to happen in practice, it would be considered a questionable get. Certainly, this is merely a stringency without basis, as why should we compare this to writing? The stringency regarding embroidered verses is due to the disrespect of sacred texts. However, according to what Rashi explains in Yoma that in embroidery, they first form the shape with dye, it would indeed be a questionable get because of the dye. And this resolves the question of the Gevurot Ari on the Beit Yosef. Since it is highly unlikely that they would weave or embroider a get for its intended purpose, there is no need to elaborate on this. In practice, it is clear that if such a case occurs, one should be stringent in all aspects.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 15: "There should be no blurring, and it should not be written on an erased surface." The reason is due to the concern for forgery. Therefore, one must be careful that no liquid or moisture falls on the paper because when writing on it, it appears erased. And if rain falls on the writing, the get (divorce document) is not given, because it becomes blackened and can be forged. Similarly, one should not write on an erased surface for this reason (Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel).

Therefore, if a fly comes and drags the ink, one should not erase it but leave it as it is, unless the letter is damaged. There should be nothing erased or anything that can be forged between words or letters. Therefore, nothing should be written on any scraped surface (there). One should not write on any hole because the ink does not go over it, making it appear erased or scraped. If the hole is next to the letter and not in the letter itself, there is no concern in this (Choshen Mishpat).

However, all these matters are not by strict law, for it has been clarified in Siman 124 that it is permissible to write on something that can be forged when witnesses are present before us, and only initially one should be careful lest the witnesses die (Beit Shmuel). Therefore, in a case of potential agunah, it is valid (there), and similarly, if the get has already been given, there is no need for another get (in my opinion), as it is merely a stringency due to the concern that the witnesses might die, as stated. And in truth, there is also a remedy for this by affirming the erasures and crossings out. But even in this, the custom is to be stringent not to make any affirmations in the get. The reason is that the language of the get should not be altered from the customary practice, and also because it is necessary to write twelve lines and no more. If they affirm what is written on the erasure and crossing out, it would be necessary to add to the language and the lines (Beit Chadash and Get Pashut). Therefore, the one arranging the get must be careful and understand that if it is possible to write another get, the original get might be invalidated and the woman will remain an agunah. One should not be stringent in all this, since by strict law, it is permissible to write on something that can be forged.

And these are the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 19: A get (divorce document) in which a letter or word was erased or written between the lines, if it is from the body of the get, it is valid. But if it is from the essential part (the "toref"), it is not a get. If he later clarified at the end of the get that a certain letter is hanging or written on the erasure, even if it is from the essential part, it is valid like other documents, and the validation should be written before "in accordance with the law of Moses and Israel." Nowadays, however, the custom is to be stringent and not to validate an erased get. And we have already explained the reason for this. In a case of preventing a woman from becoming an agunah (a chained woman) or after the fact, it is valid even if not validated, since there is a presumption (Bach and Shach). It has already been clarified that the date is also considered part of the essential part (toref). Know that the non-essential part of the get that is relevant to its continuation, without which there is no connection to the matters, is obviously also part of the essential part. Also, in the essential part, what is not required by Torah or Rabbinic law, like redundancy in language, is included in the non-essential part. Thus, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled in his responsa (section 9). The general rule is that the essential part is considered to be the place of the name of the man and the woman, as well as the wording that proves he is divorcing his wife, and the place where it states "you are permitted to any man" and the place of the conditions according to several authorities, and this is the main opinion (Peri Chadash). It has already been clarified that we consider the date part of the essential part stringently but not leniently. Similarly, the place of writing the get and the place where the man and woman stand are considered part of the essential part stringently but not leniently. However, from the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 123, clause 3, it is clearly implied that they are not at all part of the essential part. See there and it requires further study.

And Rambam wrote in chapter 4, and the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch [also wrote], that the writing must be clear and well-defined so that children can read it—children who are neither very intelligent nor foolish, but average. The writing should not be distorted or confused, lest one letter resemble another and the meaning be altered. If the text has the potential to convey two different meanings or if the writing is distorted or confused to the extent that it could be read as conveying a different meaning, since it is being read in the context of divorce and there is an implication of divorce, it is invalid. This means that the get (bill of divorce) is not nullified because it can also be read as a statement of divorce and it implies divorce (Beit Shmuel, section 30). The Tur brought the words of the Rambam in this language: "Since it can be read as conveying another meaning, even though it implies divorce and contains elements of divorce, it is invalid."

It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that there is a substantial difference between the two expressions. For instance, the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote there regarding the expressions that one must be cautious with the wording of the get (divorce document), such as the elongation of the vavs and other expressions that will be explained in Siman 126. If they are altered, the get is invalid, as stated in the fourteenth rule. The Raavad, of blessed memory, and similarly the Tur wrote there that this only applies when the husband objects, and it will be explained there with God's help. Therefore, according to the Rambam's reasoning, he wrote, "Since it is referred to regarding divorce, etc.," meaning that even though its primary meaning indicates divorce, since it can be understood for another matter, it is invalid. The Tur, according to his reasoning, wrote, "Since it is referred to for another matter, etc.," meaning that its primary meaning is explained for another matter, even though it also implies divorce, it is invalid. This excludes the precise expressions that will be explained there, that even if altered, as long as its primary meaning is for divorce, it is not invalid unless the husband objects. (However, if so, he should not have written this in the language of the Rambam, and it is possible that his version was like this, and this requires further investigation).

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 18: The get (bill of divorce) must be readable in the place where it is given, even to a child who is neither wise nor foolish. And there are those who say that it must also be readable in the place where it is written. This is certainly true regarding the change of names, where the primary consideration is the place of giving. However, even with the change of names, it must also be written according to the place of writing, as explained in section 129 (Beit Shmuel). Moreover, how can witnesses sign a get that is not readable to them, and what difference does it make if it is readable in another place (Chokhmat Shlomo)? Therefore, if it is not readable in the place of writing, it is certainly invalid (there). All the more so if it is not readable in the place of giving. There are those who want to say that for this matter, the primary consideration is the place of writing. This is not similar to the change of names, where the primary consideration is the place of giving, because if it is written only according to the place of writing, it is not known at all in the place of giving who the divorcer is, and they might think it is a different person. This is different from a change of letters, where it is known that each country has some variation in the form of the letters from other countries. When they see this form in the place of giving, they know that in the place of writing it is written in this way. This is not considered a change at all, and on the contrary, it should initially be written according to the place of writing (Get Pashut). However, in practice, it is difficult to rule this way, because ultimately, if it cannot be read in the place of giving, it is certainly an invalid get. This requirement to write according to the place of writing applies when it can also be read in the place of giving, but the form is according to the place of writing. In this case, it is certainly written according to the form of the place of writing. But if it cannot be read at all in the place of giving, it is an invalid get. Therefore, it must be readable in both places (as explained clearly).

When showing a letter to a child who is neither wise nor foolish, it is not necessary to cover the sides of the letter that are in doubt; rather, show it to him as it is. If he can read it, it is valid. Some say that the child must know the letters but not the combination of words, and some say that even if he knows the word itself, it is still acceptable (Tosafot, Perek HaMevi). This is also evident in the Talmud (Menachot 29a and see Beit Yosef, Siman 34). However, if we see that the form of the letter is not as it should be, it is invalid, even if the child reads it correctly, as stated in Orach Chaim 32, that the child's reading only helps with the length of the letter (Magen Avraham, Siman 20) and similar cases. Nevertheless, regarding a get (divorce document), our teacher the Rema wrote in Siman 16 that one must be careful that everything which should touch does touch, and nothing that should not touch does not touch, similar to a Torah scroll and tefillin. If something that should touch does not touch, such as the back of the tzadi and the yud in the aleph, and similar cases, some say that even if a child who is neither wise nor foolish reads it, it is invalid even post facto. Some say that in cases of potential aguna (a chained woman unable to remarry), such a get may be validated if the child can read it. If it is in the template of the get, even without a case of potential aguna, one may be lenient, end of quote. And so it is written in Siman 126.

Additionally, it is written: According to the opinion that holds that if the Aleph of "Yisrael" is written together, some say it is valid if it is in a form, and in a case of agunah (a woman bound in marriage) one should be lenient. If the tip of the Yud on the Aleph touches also from the front like so, it is valid. If the letters spread out due to the moisture of the ink, which they call "giplasin," to the extent that they appear to be connected, and nevertheless it seems that the letters are not touching, it is valid. So it is concluded.

And behold, what is written in the Lamed-Alef of Yisrael, if it is in the form, it is valid, meaning that "according to the law of Moses and Israel" is the form, unlike names such as Eliyahu Yisrael, which are the essence (Beit Shmuel). And even in the form, one should not be lenient except in cases of agunah or in pressing circumstances. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Siman 126, Se'if 19, permits it completely in the form. See there. And what is written about the tip of the Yud on the Alef, if it touches, it is valid, meaning specifically the tip of the Yud, which is the bend on the left side when it touches (there). And similarly, in the Yud on the right side, when its tip touches, it is valid. But if the Yudin themselves of the Alef touch and it is not recognizable that it is an Alef, then certainly in the essence it is invalid, and in the form, only in pressing circumstances and in cases of agunah it is valid. And what is written about the letters not touching in the Giplasin is valid, even though it looks like erasures, since everyone sees that it is due to the moisture of the ink. But if the letters touch each other, it is certainly invalid, even if it happened after the writing (there). And although it is clarified that in the attachment of letters, one can be lenient in pressing circumstances to correct before the witnesses sign, this applies to one letter or more, but not in the entire get, as it nullifies the form of the get. And even in most of it, it should not be validated (as it appears to me).

From a legal standpoint, it is not required to rule lines on a get (divorce document) because ruling lines in Torah scrolls, tefillin, and mezuzot is for the sake of neat writing, and a get does not require such neat writing, as stated by the Beit Yosef. However, it is customary to rule lines on a get, and it is also customary to rule lines on the sides so that the lines of the get are even, not one long and one short. If no lines were ruled at all, it is still valid. One should be careful not to rule lines with lead, because it colors and is considered writing on top of writing. The lines should be ruled outside the writing area so that the letters do not appear to be broken if the lines are too deep. Nevertheless, one should not rule lines with lead, because even from the inside the color is visible, which is not the case when ruling with iron or a reed (see Chochmat Shlomo, subparagraph 14). In Tractate Soferim, it is taught that lines are ruled with a reed for a Torah scroll (see chapter 1, halacha 1), and all the lines should be ruled before writing.

It is customary to make it twelve lines, corresponding to the number of the word "get," and there are other reasons for this. Similarly, it is customary to make a thirteenth line and divide it into two, that is, two half-lines, and they are also ruled before writing. The witnesses sign on them, one below the other.

It has already been clarified that if one did not score lines [on the parchment], it is still valid. The same applies if he added or subtracted from the twelve lines. However, there are those who say that it should only be validated in a case of potential agunah (a woman unable to remarry due to her husband's disappearance) coming from a distant land where caravans are not common. The decisors have already agreed that in all the stringencies of this section, it is valid in a case of potential agunah, even if the get (divorce document) has not yet been given or has already been given, even if it is not a case of potential agunah (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 19).

When writing on parchment, our teacher, the Rema, writes in paragraph 12 that one should write on the flesh side and not on the hair side. If one writes on the hair side, some disqualify it. However, it seems to me that in a situation of necessity, one should not be stringent. He also writes that when the scribe writes initially, he should be careful not to touch the ruling lines on the sides. It is customary initially to leave a margin on the sides of about half a finger's width, at the top about a finger's width, and at the bottom enough to hold with one's hand or more. In all these matters, there is no disqualification after the fact, even not in a situation of necessity, in my opinion.

The custom is that the letters should not extend beyond the lines on the right and left. If one writes outside the lines, some say that even a single letter that goes outside invalidates [the document]. In cases of potential agunah (a woman who cannot remarry) or pressing circumstances, there is room to be lenient. This is the ruling of our master, the Rema. The reason for being stricter here than with a Sefer Torah is due to the concern of forgery. Therefore, in cases of potential agunah, even if many letters extend outside the line, it is valid (Choshen Mishpat and Beit Shmuel section 121). Some are lenient with a single letter if the get (divorce document) is written, even if not yet given (Bayit Chadash). All of this applies to the essential part of the document, but for the non-essential part, it is not invalidated by this at all (Beit Shmuel). Because this is an excessive stringency (Tashbetz), there was an incident involving two words in the non-essential part that went outside the line, and two great Sephardic sages ruled them valid (Pitchei Teshuva section 125). They wrote that if there is space at the end of the line to write two letters, one should mark it with ink (there). This is all due to the concern of forgery, so that someone does not write whatever he wants there. This is not the custom (there), but it is a good custom to follow.

The custom is to make it so that its length is greater than its width. The length is referred to as from top to bottom, and the width is referred to as from right to left, according to the way lines are written. The reason is that it is called a "book of severance," and a book's length is greater than its width. And even though the "book" of a get (divorce document) is for recording matters, nonetheless, initially, people are meticulous about this as well. However, if it was not written this way, it does not invalidate it at all, and one may use it for a divorce initially (Radvaz and G"F). Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 13 that the length being greater than the width includes the lower margin, meaning that it is not necessary for the writing alone to have its length greater than its width, but rather we measure the entire length of the paper. And even though there are those who say that initially one should be meticulous that the writing alone should be longer, nonetheless, we are not meticulous about this even initially (G"F), because if we were meticulous about this, the writing would not be properly aligned.

It is customary to extend the lines, meaning that one should lengthen the final nun (ן) or final kaf (ך) of the upper line to reach the line below it, or the head of the lamed (ל) on the lower line to reach the line above it. If this was not done, there are those who say it is invalid. However, in cases of potential agunah (a woman bound in marriage due to her husband's disappearance or refusal to grant a divorce), one should not be stringent, as it is explicitly proven from the Talmud that extending the lines is not required (Gra). There is no valid reason for this stringency; the primary reason is to prevent forgery between the lines (Beit Shmuel, section 33). According to Talmudic law, it is permitted to write on something that could be forged, and it is only we who are stringent in this matter. Therefore, this is a stringency upon a stringency, and only outside of agunah situations is it correct to be stringent, since this custom has already been adopted. However, when there is concern that the get (divorce document) might be invalidated, we do not worry about this stringency. It is proper to be careful that the final nun (ן) in the word "פטורין" at the end of a line should be slightly curved to the right, so that the head of the lamed (ל) in the word "וישראל" above it can be extended, ensuring that it too will be connected (Chochmat Adam).

Since it is customary to scratch out the lines, the scribe must be careful not to extend the top of a letter below into the space of the letter above or vice versa. If he does so and the shape of the letter changes, such as extending the top of a "lamed" into the space of a "dalet", making it appear like a "he", it is invalid. However, if he extends the top of a letter into the space of an "aleph" or similar letters where no mistake is likely, it is not invalid. Nevertheless, ideally, one should be careful even in such cases (Choshen HaMishpat 39). The primary consideration depends on the change of the letter's form, as stated.

If the scribe needs to correct letters, for instance, if they are not touching where they are supposed to touch, or if they are too short and need to be lengthened, and similar situations, ideally, he should correct them before writing according to the law, so that there will not be any missing action after the writing before the delivery (Taz). And even though we have already explained that it is not considered missing an action in the writing itself, nonetheless, ideally, we also strive for this. If he corrected them afterward, there is no objection, but at the very least, he should correct them before the witnesses sign, because after the signatures, what does the correction help since it was signed when it was invalid (Choshen Mishpat, section 27). Therefore, it is essential to know if it is a complete correction such that without it, it would not be a valid letter, or if it is not a complete correction, in which case there is no objection (in my opinion). And when correcting, the scribe himself must do the correction since he is the agent of the owner, and not someone else (ibid.), unless the owner currently commands someone else to correct them (Beit Shmuel, section 25). And after the fact, it is effective even after the witnesses have signed as mentioned in section 30.

It is taught in the Tosefta at the end of Gittin: If [a get] was torn, it is valid; if it was ripped, it is invalid. If it was torn with a court-ordered tear, it is invalid. If it decomposed or rotted or became like a sieve, it is valid. If it was erased or smudged but its outline remains, if it can be read, it is valid; if not, it is invalid. End quote. And it is written in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 2, Halacha 3): A hide that was torn is valid; if it was ripped, it is invalid, unless it was not torn with a court-ordered tear. But if it was torn with a court-ordered tear, it is invalid. What is a court-ordered tear? Between the writing and the witnesses. End quote.

And the Rashba, of blessed memory, explained in the chapter "Hanikabel" (Gittin 64) the Tosefta as follows: "Nikra" (torn) means it is valid for divorce, as the tear does not invalidate it. However, "Nitkara" (torn) means it is invalid. And what is "Nitkara"? For example, if it was torn with a court's tear, it is invalid for divorce because it is like a mere shard. Even with witnesses of delivery, it is invalid for divorce because this is not considered a get (divorce document) at all, but like a shard. And what would be the benefit of it being on condition? And thus, the entire Tosefta should be understood. Similarly, the Jerusalem Talmud explains that "Nitkara" is a court's tear and is invalid, and "Nikra" is a tear that is not of the court. However, according to the words of the Raavad in chapter 4 of Gittin (halacha 15), it seems that he does not explain it concerning the validity and invalidity of giving the get when it is torn, but rather concerning the collection of the ketubah. The get came into her possession whole and proper, but now she brings before us a torn get and demands the ketubah. If it was torn with a court's tear, we say that she has already collected her ketubah, and therefore they tore it with a court's tear. If it was not torn with a court's tear, she collects her ketubah with it. And it is implied from his words that giving a torn get is invalid even if it is not torn with a court's tear. See there.

However, from the words of the Rambam there, and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 20, it seems that they interpret like the Rashba, and these are their words: "Similarly, a get (divorce document) that is found torn crisscross, which is a court-ordered tear, this get is invalid like other legal documents. But if it was torn and it is not a court-ordered tear, it is valid. If it was decayed or rotted or became like a sieve, it is valid. If it was erased or blurred and its outline remains, if it can be read, it is valid; if not, it is not a get. In what case are these words said? When the get was delivered by the witnesses of the signing, and there are no witnesses of delivery. But if there are witnesses that the get was delivered to her in their presence and it was valid, it is valid even if the essential part of the get was on an erasure or between the lines, or if it was torn crisscross when given to her in their presence." End of quote.

It is explained from their words that from a legal standpoint, there is no invalidation of a get (divorce document) even if it is erased and blurred, as long as its imprint remains—that is, the writing and letters are recognizable. Similarly, even if it is torn with a court's tear, it is still a valid get and she can be divorced with it. The requirement for witnesses of delivery to acknowledge the court's tear is because without this, we are concerned that it was not given with the intention of divorce, as it might have been intentionally torn by the court to invalidate it, as is customary. What is written that the witnesses should testify that it was valid at the time of delivery refers to when its imprint does not remain, and they testify that at the time of delivery the imprint was present. Without this, it is obvious that it is not a get at all. Even if its imprint remains, if it cannot be read, it is not a get at all, even according to the Rambam. In this, they disagree with the Rashba, who holds that if it is torn with a court's tear, it is completely invalid. Note that what the Rambam wrote, that a court's tear is crisscross, and the Jerusalem Talmud says between the writing and the witnesses, is because our Talmud (Bava Batra 168b) holds this way. Perhaps both are true, as in our Talmud there is another opinion, and we hold by both opinions. It is possible that we also hold like the Jerusalem Talmud.

In any case, we have learned from the words of all our rabbis that a tear not made by a court does not invalidate a get (bill of divorce) at all, and it is permissible to give it to her. And it is not only if it was torn not in the middle of the letters but between lines or between words—if it is not between the text and the witnesses, which is considered a court tear according to the Jerusalem Talmud as mentioned—but even if it was torn within the letters and split them into two, if the letters have not changed, it is valid. Although in a Torah scroll we invalidate this because it requires a surrounding of parchment, for a get it has already been explained that it does not require a surrounding of parchment. Even according to the Raavad, who interprets differently, we do not explicitly find that he invalidates such a case (and the Beit Shmuel wrote similarly, section 136). However, this is only post facto or in pressing circumstances, but ideally, one should not give it if it was torn within the letter, for even writing on erasure or scraping we are stringent, as explained (there). As for a tear between lines or between words, there is no need to be stringent even initially. Regarding other documents, the laws of tearing are explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 52, see there.

The text of the get (bill of divorce) and the precision of its letters. It contains 63 sections:

This is the wording of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 1: A get can be written in any script and in any language, whether it is the script of non-Jews or the script of Jews, such as Provencal and the like. But if part of the get is written in one language and part in another, it is invalid. However, there are those who validate it. It seems to me that even according to the one who invalidates, he would agree that if part is in Hebrew and part in Aramaic, it is valid, as both were given at Sinai and are considered close in language and thus like one language. Therefore, it is customary now to write part of the words in the get in Hebrew and most of it in Aramaic. Alternatively, since most of it is in Aramaic and only some words are in Hebrew, this is not considered part in another language. Additionally, it is specifically referring to the essential part, but what is added in the essential part, such as "You are permitted to any man" or other words, are not necessary and are merely customary redundancies. This is how I justify the custom. The custom is to write it in Aramaic and in Ashurit script, and not to validate other scripts except in cases of agunot (chained women) and pressing circumstances, such as if it was brought from distant places and caravans are not common. So is the conclusion.

And behold, that which is written that one may write [a get] in any script and in any language, all the decisors agree without dissent that there is no sanctity in a get that would disqualify it if written in other languages or scripts. This is also evident in the Talmud (Gittin 19b) and the writing of the nations is considered writing even regarding the laws of writing on Shabbat. If one writes inadvertently on Shabbat, they are obligated to bring a sin offering; if done intentionally, the punishment is stoning. This is not like what someone wished to claim, that the prohibition of their writing on Shabbat is not from the Torah, God forbid to say so. The great authorities have already refuted him (Beit Shmuel 31:1, Magen Avraham Orach Chaim 340:10, and Avodas Zarah 306), and so wrote Rashi and the Ra'av (Shabbat 103a), and there is an explicit Mishnah there. So too ruled the Rambam in Chapter 11 of Shabbat. The error arose from what is written in Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim 306:11, where the intention is to command a non-Jew to sign, as speaking to a non-Jew is rabbinically prohibited, as Eliyah Rabbah explains in Levush there and in his book Aderet Eliyahu.

And this that they wrote, whether it is the script of a Jew, such as Provençal, its interpretation is what we call Rashi script (three times), and it has more novelty than the script of other nations, which are agreed upon to write the letters in such and such a way. But Rashi script is similar to Hebrew script in a small quality with several differences, and there would be room to say that it does not have the status of script at all, and to Ashurit it is a disqualified script. And it comes to teach us that it is considered script. And similarly, our scripts that we write in letters and accounts. And indeed, there are those who hesitate about the Provençal script, as our master the Beit Yosef wrote in his great book, but he objected to them. And those who hesitate hold that when one writes a form that leans towards Ashurit, one must write actual Ashurit, and if not, it is not script. However, from his words there it is clear that Provençal does not lean at all towards Ashurit, and this is the script that they called Mishkei. But in the book Get Pashut, he wrote that Provençal is Rashi script. However, according to the law, all scripts are valid as long as it is a script that has spread in the regions. And all the more so Rashi script, as all books are printed in this script.

It appears to me that if it becomes necessary, in a case of potential agunah (a woman who cannot remarry because her husband has disappeared or refuses to grant a divorce), to write in our modern script that we use for letters and accounts, the writer must be very careful to ensure that each letter is complete. For example, the letter 'Aleph' should not be written in a way where the final stroke is not connected to the first stroke, as it would not be a proper Aleph. Similarly, care must be taken with other letters, except for 'He' and 'Kof,' which in Hebrew script are also divided into two parts. For example, the letter 'Kof' in our script has a form that is written like this: <example> and it is better to write it like this: <example> or like this: <example>. One must also be careful not to write two letters together, not to write letters in a distorted manner (which is called "gitzokt" in Yiddish), and not to use abbreviations. In any script, one must be very meticulous.

It appears to me that all this applies to script, but regarding another language, one should not write at all, even in a case of agunah (a chained woman), and not due to the law itself, but because we testify that it is almost impossible to translate the language of the get (bill of divorce) as established by the Sages into other languages without errors. Additionally, we have never heard in our times of writing in another script. However, currently, since Jews are dispersed and scattered around the globe, and it is possible that there is no scribe there who knows how to skillfully write in Hebrew in Ashurit script, if there is a pressing need, one should write the holy language according to the formula of the get in our script, and one should not cause the daughters of Israel to be agunah because of this. (And see Even HaEzer 130:10, where it is written that Ashurit script, even if not straight and beautiful, is preferable to provincial script. This is somewhat perplexing to me.)

And the reason for all this is that, as already explained in the previous section concerning several matters wherein we are stringent with a get (divorce document) similar to a Torah scroll because it is called a "scroll of severance" (ספר כריתות), therefore we are also stringent regarding the Assyrian script and the Holy Language. However, in a situation of a chained woman (agunah), none of this is an impediment, for "scroll" refers to the enumeration of matters, as mentioned there (and see Beit Yosef).

And these are the words of the Rambam in Chapter 4, Law 9: Any language in which the get (divorce document) is written, the scribe must be careful with the words of the get so that their meaning does not imply two different matters, such that the reader might say, "Perhaps he intended this or that," and its meaning is not a language of divorce, or "Perhaps he intended this matter," and its meaning is a language of divorce. Rather, the words should be without doubt in that language, implying only one matter—that he divorced and sent away so-and-so. Similarly, the writing itself must be clearly explained in the script in which it is written, so that even children who recognize that script can read it, and they are neither foolish nor wise, but average. The writing should not be crooked or confused, so that one letter might resemble another and the matter would be changed. End of his words. His words are clear and do not require explanation.

And what they wrote that if part of it is in one language and part of it is in another language, it is invalid — this is also from the words of the Rambam there. Based on this, they have labored greatly to find a reason for the text of our get (divorce document), whose main part is in Aramaic and part of it in Hebrew. And all the reasons they wrote have points of contention (as stated in the responsa of the Rema, siman 126 and elsewhere). The Tur also wrote this law in siman 130. Some have written the reason that 'a single book,' the Merciful One said, and not two or three books, and two languages are like two books (as stated there). However, it is impossible to say this at all, for what is the connection to two books? Moreover, we have already written in siman 125 that the Rambam did not bring the law of two books at all, see there. However, the main law is from the Tosefta at the end of Gittin, which teaches: a get written in five languages and signed by five witnesses in five languages is invalid. And regarding witnesses, it will be explained in siman 130, with God's help. And the Rambam holds that it is not specifically five languages; the same applies to two languages, as there is no reason to differentiate in this matter. The reason is simple: the content does not appear continuous and good when changing languages in the middle of the matter, as is well known by experience. Therefore, it is invalid but not nullified, as this is not a Torah-level invalidation. According to this, there is no question at all about the text of our get, as these two languages, Hebrew and Aramaic, connect very well in language. All the holy Talmud and all our sages wrote their books combining these two languages, and it is almost impossible to write otherwise. It is known that anyone who tries to force themselves to write a large matter in Hebrew alone or in Aramaic alone will toil greatly, and it will not be beautifully expressed (and see there what is written similarly in siman 7, but he wrote it for the reason that in the Torah and Prophets, Aramaic is found, and according to our words, it is straightforward).

And this is the formula of the get (bill of divorce) that is written in all our regions: On such and such a day of the week, on such and such a day of the month of a certain month, in the year such and such from the creation of the world, according to the counting that we count here in... the city that sits on the river of such and such. I, [name], the son of [father's name], who is standing today in... the city that sits on the river of such and such, willingly and of my own accord, without being forced, release, discharge, and divorce you, [wife's name], the daughter of [her father's name], who is standing today in... the city that sits on the river of such and such, who has been my wife from before now. And thus I release, discharge, and divorce you so that you are permitted and have authority over yourself to go and marry any man that you desire, and no man will protest against you from this day and forever. And behold, you are permitted to any man. And this shall be for you from me a document of release, a letter of discharge, and a bill of divorce, according to the law of Moses and Israel. And the witnesses sign, each one on a separate line beneath the text: [name], the son of [father's name], witness, [name], the son of [father's name], witness.

The reason why we write the days of the week as "in Sabbath" and the days of the month to the moon is certainly more appropriate to write with a "lamed" according to the style of the language. However, because there is a potential mistake with the days of the week, for example, if one writes "on the third day of the Sabbath," it might be misunderstood as the second day, and for the Sabbath, it is the third. Therefore, we write "in Sabbath" to avoid mistakes. This is not the case with the days of the month, as the counting is indeed from Rosh Chodesh (the New Moon). And why do we write "in Sabbath" and not "to the week"? Because "week" also includes the Sabbatical year in the language of the Sages (Gittin 17b), and also because "week" is written in marriage as "fulfill the week of this one." They did not want to mention it in a divorce document (Gittin). Additionally, we, the children of Israel, count every day towards the Sabbath due to its great sanctity. As it is stated in the Mekhilta, "Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy," etc., you should count towards the Sabbath (Ramban in his commentary on the Chumash). Similarly, we say in the Song of the Day, "Today is the second day in the Sabbath," and similarly for all the days.

And know that on the days of the week, we do not mention the day except for "on the first day of the week," "on the second day of the week," and in the days of the month, we mention the day by writing "on the eleventh day of the month of so-and-so." For in truth, there is no need to mention the day at all, except because in the days of the month there can be confusion at the beginning of the month if they write "on the second day of the month of so-and-so" or "on the third day of the month of so-and-so," people might say it does not refer to the days of the month but to the weeks, that it is the second or third week of the month of so-and-so. And in a get (divorce document) the language needs to be clear; therefore, they add the day or days up to ten days of the month, as will be explained. And this is why they write "of the month" and not "of the new moon" because it is written "the expelling of the months," for "new moon" is called because of the renewal of the moon. Therefore, they write the clear language. And in the Torah, it is written all as "month," there is a great reason for this. For in the Torah, the names of the months are not mentioned, only their numbers: "the first month," "the second month," "the third month," "the seventh month." And it is impossible to write "in the seventh moon" because is there a change in the moon between the seventh and other months? Therefore, it is written in the language of "month," meaning the seventh renewal of the year, that in each month it renews, and twelve times a year it renews. For this reason, it is written "the first renewal," "the second renewal," "the third renewal," "the seventh renewal," unlike in a get where they mention the name of the month. Therefore, they write clearly "the moon" that serves in the month Iyar, Sivan, etc. And proof of this is that in the place where the name of the month is specified, it is written "moon." In I Kings 6 it is written, "In the fourth year, in the month of Ziv," and in the eleventh year, "in the month of Bul," which is the eighth month, etc. There it is explicitly stated that when the name of the month is specified, it is written "moon," and when it is counted, it is written "month." And although several months are specified in the Bible and still it is written "month," nevertheless it is a good reason and a great proof from the verse in Kings that we brought (it seems to me).

On the first day of the week, one should write "on the first day of the week" and not "on the first of the week." If one wrote "on the first of the week," it is valid (Rashdam). Similarly, in all matters clarified, if one wrote "to the month" instead of "to the moon" or wrote "in the moon" instead of "to the moon," or in the days of the week wrote "week" instead of "Shabbat" or wrote "to Shabbat" instead of "on Shabbat," after the fact, it seems to me that it is valid (and so writes the Geonim). For it is not relevant to invalidate after the fact, as it is not considered a change, but ideally, one should be meticulous for the reasons explained.

And this is why, ideally, we write "on the first day of the week" and not "on the first" because it is written in the account of Creation, "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." Likewise, in the days of the month, it is written in the portion of Bamidbar, "on the first day of the second month." The reason why throughout the Torah it is written regarding months as "the first month" has a significant reason, because "first" is a term of importance from the root "head," as it is written, "This month shall be for you the head of months; it shall be the first for you of the months of the year." And in the plain sense of the verse, the explanation is that because this month is for you the head of all the months due to the miracles that occurred in it, therefore, it remains forever for you the first of the months of the year. And it is possible that we intentionally do not write the term "first" to indicate that it is not the head of the days (and ponder this well). And this that the Tanna at the end of Tractate Tamid repeated in the song that the Levites would say in the Temple: "on the first day they would say," and similarly in the Baraita of Tractate Rosh Hashanah (31a), and similarly in the Baraita at the end of Tractate Sukkah regarding the songs of the festival, this is because they considered all the days as first, second, third, etc. And in the account of the sequence, certainly, it must be said first, second, third, etc. However, when we are speaking only about this day, we write "on the first day of the week." And this that we say after the prayer "the song of the day" and we say "today is the first day in the week," on which the Levites would, etc., it would be more correct to say "today is one day in the week," but in order not to deviate from the language of the Mishnah and the Baraita, we say it this way (so it seems to me).

On the third, fourth, and fifth days, the word is written with a full "yud" in the middle. On the second and sixth days, it is written without a "yud" in the middle, as this is the case in most of the scriptures. If there is an occasional exception, there is an interpretation for it. The general rule for writing names and words in divorce documents (gittin) is to follow the majority of the scriptures. This is also explicitly stated in the Masorah of Parashat Naso: every first instance is written with a full "yud," every second without, every third with a full "yud," every fourth with a full "yud," every fifth with a full "yud," every sixth without, every seventh with a full "yud," every eighth with a full "yud," and every ninth with a full "yud" (The Gra, Siftei Chachamim 3).

The names of the months are as follows: Nisan is written in full with two yuds, as it appears in the Scroll of Esther. Iyar is written with two yuds, as it is in the Targum, and if it is written with one yud, it is invalid unless in a case of pressing need. This is the ruling of Rabbeinu the Rema in section 7. He further wrote that some refrain from giving a bill of divorce (get) in Iyar, but in a case of pressing need, they give it and write it with two yuds. Thus, the custom is clear to initially write Iyar with two yuds (three times). Similarly, we do not refrain from arranging a get in the month of Iyar. This was also ruled by Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in section 23, as there is no doubt in the matter. As for the statement that if it is written with one yud, it is invalid unless in a pressing need, this is certainly correct because it is truly pronounced with a chirik and a kamatz, "Iyar," and when written with one yud, the yud is silent. In a pressing need, it is valid because in the common language, people indeed say "Iyr," and there is no confusion with another month. Nevertheless, the great authorities wrote that if the mistake is discovered on the same day, another get should be written with two yuds. If several days have passed, another get is not necessary.

Sivan is full [30 days] and so it is in Megillat Esther. Tammuz is full [30 days], and it is written "on the fifth of the month" (Ezekiel 8:1). Av – we do not write "Menachem Av," and what is customary to write so in letters and when blessing the new month is only for consolation, so that we may merit, with God's help, the coming of the Messiah. However, its name is only Av, as it is in the Talmud at the beginning of Tractate Rosh Hashanah, see there. And if one wrote "Menachem" alone, some say it is valid post facto, since it is well known and recognized that the month of Av is called Menachem (three times). However, I am uncertain about this, because although it is true that in the books of the Sephardic sages and their agreements, it is customary so, among us it is not customary.
