Some write both together, and this certainly seems to me that if "Menachem Av" was written, it is valid post facto, since this is how we bless the month in all our regions, and it is also written in letters.

Elul is a full month and is written with a vav, as it is in Nehemiah (6) and in the Mishnah at the beginning of Rosh Hashanah and in Chapter 9 of Bechorot. Tishrei has one yud at the end and no more, as it is in the Mishnah there. MarCheshvan has one vav, as it is in the Mishnah and the Gemara in the first chapter of Ta'anit and in other places. If one writes only "Cheshvan," it is valid (three times), as it is called in common parlance, and also in the calendars, it is printed as "Cheshvan," and there is no mistake. It appears to me that if one writes it with two vavs, it is also valid, as the extra vav does not change the pronunciation, and there is no mistake. One must write "MarCheshvan" as one word. If one writes it in two words, like "Mar Cheshvan," there is a doubt (there), and even if we say that it is valid in two words, there is a doubt if "Mar" is written at the end of a line and "Cheshvan" at the beginning of the line (there). It seems that "Mar" is a separate word, as some explain that in this month rain falls, and "Mar" is an expression of raindrops, as it is written, "Behold, the nations are as a drop (mar) from a bucket" (Isaiah 40:15). Or it can be said that in the Jerusalem Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 1:2) and in the Midrash Bereshit (Chapter 48), we say that the names of the months came up from Babylon, and it can be said that they made this month’s name in memory of the beginning of the sin, for because of this sin, the ten tribes were exiled, and afterward Judah and Benjamin, and the head of the sinners was Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who changed the festival of the seventh month to the eighth month, as it is written in Kings. And "Mar" in Aramaic means change, and thus they hinted at "Mar Cheshvan," meaning that he changed it to Cheshvan, and by the way, they hinted that this caused bitterness to all of Israel. However, in truth, we do not expound on names, and if it is written in two words or in two lines, it is a doubt, though the inclination is to permit it, and in a case of potential non-marriage, one may be lenient.

Kislev without a yud at all, as it is written at the beginning of Nehemiah and in Zechariah (7), and although in the Mishnah and Gemara throughout the entire Talmud there is a yud after the lamed, and so it is in Targum Yonatan there, nevertheless the scripture is primary. And if it is written with a yud after the lamed, it is not to be invalidated because of this (Pri Chadash and Gra) since there is no strictness in this matter. In Aramaic, there needs to be a yud after the lamed because the lamed has a tzere, and every tzere draws a yud in Aramaic. Tevet, Shevat, Adar are simple in scripture, Mishnah, and Gemara with three letters each and no more.

It is proper to read the get (divorce document) according to the vowels of the letters. There are some months for which, according to common pronunciation, the vowels are not as they are in the text. Therefore, it is necessary to specify: Nissan - the samekh has a kamatz; Iyar - both yuds have a kamatz; Sivan - the vav has a kamatz; Elul - the lamed has a cholam; Marheshvan - even though the vowelization of the vav is not clear to us, it seems it has a kamatz; Kislev - the lamed has a tzeirei; Tevet - the bet also has a tzeirei; Shevat - the bet has a kamatz; Adar - the aleph has a chataf patach and the dalet has a kamatz.

There is an opinion that if one wrote "Marḥeshvan" as "Bul" and "Iyar" as "Ziv" and "Tishrei" as "Ethanim," it is valid because it is written that way in the Scriptures in Kings (Pri Megadim). However, it is questionable to me, since the common people do not understand this, and in a get (divorce document), it needs to be understandable to everyone. Furthermore, did they really call the months that way in the days of Solomon? It is merely a nickname for the months. Therefore, in practice, one should deliberate on this matter.

There is also an opinion that if the name of the month was not mentioned at all, but instead, one wrote "the first month," "the second month," "the third month," etc., it is valid (Gaon of Prague), since everyone knows that Nisan is the first month, Iyar is the second, and Sivan is the third. This is considered as if it is explicitly stated. In the entire Torah and the Prophets, it is written this way, as the names of the months came up from Babylon as it is written. In a case of potential hardship (like a woman unable to remarry without a get), it is certainly permissible. But in a case not involving hardship, one should not be lenient unless she was already betrothed or married (in my opinion).

When the year is a leap year and one divorces in Adar, it is necessary to explicitly state which Adar it is. In the first Adar, one should write "First Adar" or "the first" (Choshen Mishpat 21); in the second Adar, one should write "Second Adar." If one wrote simply "Adar" in the first Adar, it is valid, but in the second Adar, it is invalid, because "Adar" generally refers to the first Adar, as agreed upon by most authorities, as stated in Yoreh De'ah Siman 220 and Choshen Mishpat Siman 43. Although it is clarified there that according to the Rambam in Hilchot Nedarim Chapter 10, when one knows the year is a leap year, "Adar" generally refers to the second Adar, and indeed, some say that in a divorce document, it is invalid even in the first Adar if it simply states "Adar," since we are concerned about the opinion of the Rambam (Bach and Shach in Yoreh De'ah Siman 220). 

They were puzzled as to why the Shulchan Aruch did not bring this opinion at all in Siman 7, but many great authorities agreed that regarding a divorce document, if it was written simply in the first Adar, it is valid, and we do not concern ourselves with the opinion of the Rambam. This is because even according to the Rambam, it is only considered a postdated get (divorce document), and according to most authorities, a postdated get is valid, as will be explained in Siman 127 (Beit Shmuel 19, Taz, and Perach). Although according to the Rambam, a postdated get is invalid as stated there, its invalidity is only rabbinic. Additionally, there is a double doubt (safek sefeika): maybe the halacha is that the first Adar is simply "Adar," and even if one says that the second Adar is simply "Adar," there is a doubt that maybe the halacha is that a postdated get is valid, and it is also a reversible double doubt (Perach). Furthermore, there is another doubt that maybe the scribe did not know the year is a leap year, and in such a case, even the Rambam agrees that simply "Adar" refers to the first Adar, as stated there. One should write "the first" in full (Choshen Mishpat 22, who also wrote like Beit Shmuel, but his words lack clarity and understanding).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 4 that on Rosh Chodesh (the New Moon) one should write "on the first day of the month of a certain month," and there are those who say to write "on the first of the month." Because of this, some refrain from giving a get (divorce document) on Rosh Chodesh. And behold, what is written as "on the first day" is a scribal error, and it should say "on the first day" (Cheshek Shlomo and Beit Shmuel, subsection 8). And so it is written at the beginning of Haggai "on the first day of the month," and as it is written regarding the first day of the week. Their dispute is whether to write "day," for those who say not to write "day" as in the days of the week. However, we have already explained in Section 11 that deliberately writing "day" is so that there should be no mistake in the week, as mentioned there. And certainly, it is an excessive stringency to refrain from giving a get on Rosh Chodesh (Gittin) when Rosh Chodesh is one day. All the later authorities agreed that only when there is a necessity, a get is given on Rosh Chodesh (Cheshek Shlomo and Beit Shmuel, subsection 8). And thus testified the Bach, who saw gittin given in ancient times on Rosh Chodesh, and it was written in them "on the first day." This is the main ruling; however, if one wrote "on the first of the month," it is also valid (Gittin).

They also wrote in section 6 that if one writes a get (divorce document) on the first day of the month of Iyar, he should write "on the thirtieth day of the month of Nisan," as it is the New Moon of Iyar. This applies to all New Moons that span two days. On the second day of the New Moon, he should write "on the first of [the month of] so-and-so," since its reckoning is from the second day. However, some say that a get should not be given on any New Moon, and it is good to be cautious about this unless there is a concern of causing the woman to be unable to remarry (agunah). This is certainly a correct stringency, to not give a get on the first day of the New Moon because one needs to mention both the previous and the current month. Even though Rabbi Yosef Karo in his major work wrote that there is no need to be concerned with these stringencies at all, nevertheless, this is the practice in all Jewish communities: if it is not a case of agunah, a get is not arranged on the first day of the New Moon. However, on the second day, it is like a one-day New Moon, and one writes "on the first of [the month of] so-and-so." The language in the Shulchan Aruch is not precise about this. Similarly, the phrase "on the first" instead of "on the first day" is sometimes preferred, especially when the New Moon is two days, so as not to suggest it is the first day of the New Moon. When one writes "on the first of the month," it is clear that it refers to the number of days in the month. Nevertheless, it does not seem necessary to differentiate in this matter. It has already been clarified that all these details do not invalidate the get after the fact. If on the first day of the New Moon, he wrote only "New Moon of so-and-so" or "New Moon of so-and-so, which is the thirtieth of the previous month," the get is also valid. However, without this, a get is not arranged on the first day of the New Moon unless in a case of agunah, as mentioned. Certainly, on the second day of the New Moon, if he wrote "New Moon of so-and-so," it is valid, and also if the New Moon is one day, since on the first day of the New Moon, it is really not the New Moon but belongs to the previous month. Nevertheless, it is valid because in common parlance it is called the New Moon, and Hallel and Musaf are recited. Certainly, on the second day of the New Moon or when the New Moon is one day, it is indeed the New Moon.

In the numbering of the days of the month, one writes in the masculine form: "on the second day," "on the third day," "on the fourth day," "on the fifth day," "on the sixth day," "on the seventh day," "on the eighth day," "on the ninth day." The feminine form is used without the "hey" [suffix]: "three," "four," "five." For the second day, one writes "two" (feminine form). "Month" is masculine in all of the scripture, and "year" is feminine, as it is written at the beginning of Bamidbar: "on the first day of the second month in the second year." Note that for the word "eight," there is no difference in gender except in the vowelization: in the masculine form, the "nun" is with a kamatz, and in the feminine form, it is with a segol, and "eight" is written without a vav. If one writes "eight" in full (with a vav), it is valid, and similarly for "three" written in full (with a vav), it is valid because the word is clearly recognizable and the meaning does not change. Additionally, in the Masorah, "eight" and "six" are sometimes written in full, as well as "three" and "four" occasionally according to the tradition. Also, if one does not write the prefix "on the" before "second day," "third day," etc., but just writes "second day," "third day," it is valid. In Jerusalem, this is written initially (three times). If one exchanges the masculine form for the feminine or vice versa, it is valid after the fact, even not in pressing circumstances. Similarly, if one writes only in abbreviations like "11th," "12th," it is also valid if it is vowelized to understand that it is a number (three times). Even not in pressing circumstances, it is valid (Beit Shmuel, section 13). Some say only in pressing circumstances (Levush).

Until ten, we write "days," and from ten onward, we write "day" – on the eleventh day, on the twelfth day, etc. And even though "ten" is a feminine term and "two" is a masculine term, nevertheless, this is the style of the language, as it is written: "eleven days from Horeb, etc." and similarly in Esther it is written: "in the twelfth month, etc." on the thirteenth day of it. This is why until ten we write "days," and from there onward "day," for this is the style of the language, as it is written in Parashat Behaalotecha: "You shall not eat it one day, nor five days, nor ten days, nor twenty days." There are those who say that from twenty onward we write "days," but there are those who disagree. And the custom is to write "day," as is proven from the scripture we brought (referenced in the commentaries). If one wrote "day" instead of "days" or "days" instead of "day," it does not invalidate the document after the fact, especially in pressing circumstances, as this is not considered a change at all.

In counting the years, one should use the feminine form: "In the year five thousand six hundred and forty-five from the creation of the world," and similarly, two, three, four, six, seven, nine, ten without the final "hey" (ה) at the end. Similarly, eleven, twelve, etc., up to twenty, and from then on: twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three, the lesser number being in the feminine form. And so it should always be, for the lesser number is in the feminine form and the greater number is in the masculine form, the opposite of the days of the month (see Avnei Shoham, note 14). This is the style of the language regarding years in the Tanach, as it is written, "In the six hundred and first year," etc., and many similar examples.

There is also a difference between the number of days in the month and the years. In the days of the month, we write the smaller number first, such as on the twenty-first day, while in the years, we write the larger number first, such as in one hundred and twenty-seven years. This is the way it is in the Scriptures: "a hundred years, twenty years, and seven years," and many others like it. But in the days of the month, the smaller number comes first, as we count the days of the Omer. It is also written in the Torah: "On the fifteenth day of the seventh month." However, all of this does not invalidate it after the fact. If one wrote the smaller number first in the years or the larger number first in the days of the month, it is valid because there is no strict requirement in this matter. We find in the Talmud (Yoma 55a) that in numbering, the custom of places varied: some placed the smaller number first, and some the larger. Similarly, in the Scriptures, we sometimes find the smaller number first in years, as in Kings (1 Kings 6:1): "And it was in the eightieth year and the four hundredth year," etc. Note that "eighty" is written in full with a vav, even though "eight" is deficient, as I have written (in Hilchot Mechirat Chametz 13), that if one wrote "sheni" and "shishi" in full, it is valid. However, I have a difficulty with this because, according to the reading, it relates to "shinaim" and the language of joy, even though they are also written in the Scriptures without yods. Nevertheless, according to the reading of people, perhaps this is correct, and it requires further contemplation for the law. Additionally, "shishu" in the Tanach, which is a term of joy, is written with a full yod in Lamentations and at the end of Isaiah.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 8: "There are versions of gittin (divorce documents) in which it is written 'how I, so-and-so,' and this is not proper intent. One should be careful not to write the word 'how.'" In the text of the get (divorce document) according to the Rif and Rambam, it is written 'how,' and the Rosh objected to this, stating that this is only relevant for other documents when witnesses write 'how this matter occurred before us.' But for a get, which is in the language of the husband who says that he is now divorcing his wife, there is no need to write it, only that 'at this time I am divorcing my wife.' However, if it was written 'how,' it is certainly valid, as this version is also found in the Gemara (85b) (Choshen Mishpat Ḥelkat Meḥokek and Beit Shmuel, section 22). Nevertheless, the Rosh holds that the language found in the Gemara is not the actual language of the get, but rather the Gemara explains the subject matter that Rava instituted regarding 'from this day and forever' as explained there. And you should know that this is so, for the writing of the get is in the second person, whereas in the Gemara it is in the third person. Therefore, it is certain that only the subject is stated there and not the exact text of the get.

Additionally, it is written that there are versions in which it is written "and to the places of your fathers," and one should be careful not to write them. This means that in the text of the get (divorce document), they would write "and any other name and epithet that I have and that my fathers have, and to my place and to the places of my fathers," and similarly for a woman, they would write "and any other name and epithet that you have and that your fathers have, and to your place and to the places of your fathers." The Rosh, of blessed memory, objected to this, questioning why they had the custom to write this, since they do not mention the place of the father and the dwelling place of the woman's father. Among us, the custom is not to write any place names of birth and residence at all, for reasons that will be explained in Siman 128, and we also do not write "and any other name."

It is stated in the Gemara (85b): Abaye said, "One who writes a get (divorce document) should not write 've'din,' which implies 'and this judgment,' but rather 've'dan,' meaning 'and this document.' This means that in the get it should be written, 've'dan di yehei leichi minai,' etc., which means, 'And this document which shall be for you from me' (Rashi). If he writes 've'din' with a yud, it implies, 'It is a judgment that I divorce you,' but if it is not a judgment upon me to divorce you, you will not be divorced (there). Even though we find several instances of 've'din' with a yud in the Talmud, where its meaning is 'this,' like 'din garma de'ashiraya bir' (Berakhot 5b) and 've'din kiyumaihon' (Bava Batra 161a), and throughout the Jerusalem Talmud, 'mai kadin,' and regarding the verse, 'and one called to another' (Isaiah 6:3), the Targum translates as 'and they receive from each other,' and regarding the verse, 'these you may eat' (Leviticus 11:9), the Targum translates as 'these you may eat,' nevertheless, the husband can contest and say that it was deliberately written this way to cause her harm, as will be explained. And even though according to the Rambam it is invalid even without the husband's contest, as will be explained, this is because it deviates from the standard formula established by the Sages (Hilchot Gerushin 4:14). Note that the Rambam there wrote another concern about 've'din,' as follows: the reader might read 've'din' to mean, 'a judgment will be between me and you,' etc.

Abaye also said there that one should not write the word "Igeret" (letter) with a Yod because it implies "Gag" (roof) as "Igeret" in the sense of roof is customarily written with a Yod since it is not written in Hebrew. But "Igeret" in the sense of a letter should be written in Hebrew without a Yod, as it is written "on all the words of this Igeret (letter)" (Tosafot). And some say that the explanation is that he should write "Ve'igeret Shibukin" and not "Igeret" without a Vav at the beginning, because that would imply a general letter which a person sends to his friend. Rather, it should be "Ve'igeret" with a Vav, which implies it refers to a get (divorce document) and the matters mentioned above (Tosafot in the name of R. Yitzchak). And the Rambam wrote that one should not write "Igeret" lest the reader read "Im zanit" (if you committed adultery), meaning "Digrat" in Aramaic is an expression of a prostitute, and the reader might read it as two words "I geret" (if you committed adultery), then it will be a get, and if not, it will not be a get.

Additionally, it is stated there not to write "limehak" with a yod, which would imply "li mehak" (meaning "this number shall be mine and onwards" according to Rashi), but rather to write "lemehak" without a yod, as it concludes "to marry anyone" etc., meaning she has the permission to go and marry whomever she wishes. Similarly, do not write "limehak" which implies "to mock," meaning it is necessary to ensure that the foot of the letter he (ה) has space between its foot and its roof, so that it does not appear as a chet (ח), which would imply "limehak" (to mock), meaning "I am mocking you" (there). And because the letters aleph, chet, he, ayin, and resh are interchangeable, it is therefore necessary to be more cautious about this so that the intended meaning does not change, and this applies to all instances of the letter he (ה).

Also there, "די תיהויין די תיצבייין" should be written with three yuds, implying "תהויין" and "תצביין," meaning five yuds need to be written: three yuds at the end of the word, one after the dalet, and one after the tav. "די" means "that," and similarly with "די תיצבייין." This is the interpretation of the get (divorce document) that he writes to her, such as "פטרית" (you are released), etc., "די תיהויין" (that you shall be) "רשא ושלטא" (free and empowered) etc., to any man "די תיצבייין" (that you choose). This means that now, by this get, I have released you so that you shall have the authority to marry whomever you desire. Therefore, if he writes only two yuds at the ends of "די תיהויין" and "די תיצבייין," it would imply that it refers to general men. Furthermore, the reader might interpret it as plural, as if he is speaking to two women, and thus it would result that he is not divorcing this one but another. However, when he writes with three yuds, there is no such mistake. Post facto, it is not critical if he did not write a yud between the tav and dalet, and similarly between the tav and hei (as in Choshen Mishpat, section 131), as mentioned in section 50.

Some say that "די תיהוייין" is one word, and similarly "די תיצבייין," while others say that they are two words. Therefore, one should be careful to write "די תיהוייין" on one line and similarly "די תיצבייין," and also not to distance the word "די" too much from them (Levush) so that it is possible to read them as one word or as two words. This is the custom. If "די" is written on one line and "תיהוייין" on another line, it is considered as two words, and similarly if they are greatly distanced. However, in a case of necessity or if the get (divorce document) has already been given, it is valid since there is no change in the meaning of the get (Taz and Beit Shmuel, Section 25). Moreover, the main opinion is that they are two words, and similarly in the translation "די" alone (Gra, Section 20). (Also, the Chaim Mikol HaMitzvos, Section 32, disagrees with the Rema, as the Rosh wrote that even one word is not a mistake, and certainly two words are not, see there).

Additionally, it is stated there: "And the 'vav' of 'teruchin' and the 'vav' of 'shevikin' and the 'vav' of 'kedei' – if one does not elongate them, they appear like 'yuds'. This implies 'teruchin' meaning 'divorced women of the world' and 'shevikin' meaning 'abandoned women of the world', and it does not belong to her (Rashi). And if one does not elongate the second 'vav' of 'kedei', it will imply 'and like' meaning 'for nothing' and 'without any purpose' (ibid.). And Rambam wrote that 'teruchin' and 'shevikin' imply that she left and divorced him, and 'kedei' implies 'under this condition I will exempt you'. The intention is not to elongate them excessively so they do not appear as other letters, but to elongate them slightly more than other 'vavs', and this is the custom. The main thing is that they should not appear as 'yuds' (Tosafot). Certainly, for all 'vavs' one must be careful that they do not appear as 'yuds', but in these particular words, extra caution is needed because they imply a change in meaning."

One should write "תרוכין" and "שבוקין" without the first yud. If they were written with yud's, the Talmud would not instruct to extend the vav, as their meaning is clear even without it (Rosh). However, "פיטורין" should be written with a yud after the peh, and therefore there is no need to extend the vav, because without the yud it means "exemption" and "obligation." Some say that "פטורין" should also be written without the first yud, because when writing a bill of divorce "פטורין," there is no confusion with "exemption" and "obligation," and this is the practice. Therefore, one should also extend the vav of "פטורין." Do not be perplexed as to why the Talmud does not warn about this, because in truth, the Talmud (Sotah 35b) differentiates the language of "פטורין" between the Babylonians and the people of the Land of Israel; these write it with a yud and those without a yud. Look there, and we follow those who do not write it with a yud.

And know that these three terms: "Shevukin," "Tirukin," and "Peturin" (which mean release, dismissal, and divorce, respectively) are written in a Get (bill of divorce) three times. Initially, they write: "I have wished, etc., and released, dismissed, and divorced." In the second instance, they write: "And thus, I have dismissed, released, and divorced." In the third instance, they write: "And this shall be for you from me a document of dismissal, a letter of release, and a bill of divorce." And your mnemonic is "Shevukin, Peturin, Tirukin," "Peturin, Shevukin, Tirukin," "Tirukin, Shevukin, Peturin." If there is a change in this, it does not impede the matter. This is the ruling of our master, the Rema, in section 12. See there.

The reason for these expressions and their variations, it seems to me, is as follows: In the Torah section about divorce, the term "divorcee" is not used; instead, the terms "sending away" (shiluach) and "cutting off" (keritut) are used. The term "divorcee" (gerusha) is mentioned elsewhere, such as with priests: "A woman who is divorced from her husband they shall not take" (Leviticus 21:7). There are three aspects to a get (bill of divorce): First, initially, they were connected by their marital bond, and now this bond is severed by the get. This is what the Torah means by "and he writes her a document of keritut," which Onkelos translates as "a bill of release" (get peturin). Thus, "peturin" is a term for keritut (cutting off). 

The second aspect is that he sends her away from his house, as it is written, "and sends her away from his house," since they cannot remain together, and with this, the matter of the get is completed. This is the term "veshavkit" (you are released) written in the get, meaning that he allows her to leave his house. The term "divorcee" (gerusha) is similar to "sending away" (shiluach), except that "shiluach" is a respectful term for the moment, while "divorce" (gerushin) is a term of disgrace, as it is written, "and he drove them out from Pharaoh's presence" (Exodus 10:11). Therefore, in the case of Adam and Eve when they sinned, it is written, "He sent him out" (Genesis 3:23), and afterward, "He drove out the man" (Genesis 3:24), meaning He first sent him out of the Garden of Eden temporarily, and then the Scripture informs us that He drove him out permanently.

Therefore, in the actual section, the term of disgrace "divorce" (gerushin) is not used, but rather the term "sending away" (shiluach), which is the same. In the case of priests, the term "divorcee" (gerusha) is used because they are not to take them due to their sanctity. This is the term "teruchin" in the get, as Onkelos translates "divorcee" (gerusha) as "terucha." 

This is the order of the wording in the get: "I, so-and-so, desire, etc., and release, and send away, and divorce you," meaning I wish to send you away from my house, sever the bond between us, and divorce you permanently. Then, "who had been my wife from before," etc., meaning until now you were my wife and we were connected, and now I have severed the bond and sent you away and divorced you permanently. "Release" (peturit) is mentioned before "send away" (shavkit) because it first states that they were connected; therefore, it immediately says that now the bond between them is severed.

In both instances, "send away" (shavkit) is mentioned before "divorce" (teruchit) because "sending away" is written in the actual section of the get itself, and "divorce" is written elsewhere. At the end of the get, it writes, "and this shall be for you from me a document of severance, a letter of release, and a bill of release." The entire matter of "and this shall be" is to make it clear with what he is divorcing her, as it is stated in the Mishnah and Gemara (Gittin 85b). The explanation is that with this document he divorces her. 

Behold, the Torah calls it a "document of keritut." Tradition teaches that it is not an actual book (sefer), but rather it refers to the enumeration of matters, as it is stated in the Talmud (Gittin 21a). Additionally, tradition teaches (ibid.) that a document severs, and nothing else severs; she is only divorced through a document. Therefore, the Sages had to mention these three names: sefer (document), iggeret (letter), and get (bill), because "sefer" is written in the Torah. Since tradition teaches that it is not an actual book, they called it "iggeret" (letter). To avoid saying "just a letter," they also called it "get," meaning a document, because without this, he cannot divorce her. Therefore, they connected these three names to the three names of the get. They prefaced "sefer" because it

Abaye also said there that one should not write "le'itnesba" with an aleph, but rather "le'itnesba" with a hey, because if it is written with an aleph, it might be read as "lo titnasei" (do not marry) according to Rashi. However, if one omits the hey from "le'itnesba" and writes "litnesba," it is valid, because as long as the meaning does not change, there is no concern. Even if the entire word "le'itnesba" was omitted, it is valid post-facto, as it is only part of the form (Beit Yosef in the name of Ramban, and see there). Furthermore, even without this word, the meaning remains the same, as he writes to her that she may be permitted, etc., to go to any man she desires to marry. An invalid document is only one that has a different meaning, such as if it is written with an aleph, which can be interpreted as "do not marry." But otherwise, we do not worry about it. In this manner, one must be cautious with every language and every writing to ensure it does not have dual meanings. And it has already been established that one should only write in the language ordained by the Sages and in Assyrian script.

A major principle is written by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 20, that since we recognize the style of the text, it should not be invalidated due to the omission of a single letter. In a copy [of a document], even if more is missing, it is still valid (Beit Shmuel, subsection 30). Anything that is clearly a scribal error is valid regarding the date, such as if the "shin" of "Shishi" (sixth) or the "resh" of "Revi'i" (fourth) is missing. Although the date is considered essential, it is not exactly as essential as the main content. However, regarding his name and her name, it is certainly invalid (this is the intent of the Beit Shmuel), for in the essential parts, one must be meticulous about omissions and additions as prescribed by Torah law (ibid).

Therefore, if he wrote "on the fourth, twenty days of such-and-such month" and omitted the word "on Wednesday," it is valid, for the term "the fourth" has no other meaning except in relation to the days of the week. And some say that even if the fourth day was the twenty-first of the month, it is valid after the fact. The reason is that since "the fourth" has no other meaning except the days of the week, and it is known that the fourth day was the twenty-first of the month, it is evident that there was a mistake in the setting of the month. This is also explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 43, regarding documents. However, our teacher, the Rema, even though he did not make any corrections in Choshen Mishpat, here, because of the stringency of Gittin (divorce documents), wrote in Siman 21 that there are those who disagree and invalidate in such a case, as some also disagree regarding names (as the Siftei Kohen wrote there in subparagraph 7). And even if he wrote the day of the week correctly, the day of the week does not add or detract, as our Sages said (beginning of Rosh Hashanah) that the days of the week are not mentioned in the Torah, for even if he did not write the day of the week at all, there is no concern for this. The main thing is the day of the month (as stated in the Responsa of the Rivash, Siman 117).

It is written "yetiḥi" with three yuds, "lichi" with two yuds, as it is written "hailichi et hayeled hazeh" etc. "Antati" without an additional yud after the aleph (Beit Yosef), and "anash" should not be written with three yuds. "Yimach" (he will protest) is written with either a heh or an aleph. The primary opinion is that with an aleph it means protest, but with a heh it refers to the verse "timcheh et zecher" (you shall blot out the memory of Amalek). If it is written with a heh and the get (divorce document) has already been given, it is valid. If it is written "yimchi" with a yud, it is invalid unless in a pressing situation or where there is concern of "agunah" (a woman who cannot remarry because her husband's whereabouts are unknown). Some say it is valid in any case (the Gra, note 30, and what is mentioned that once in Daniel it is written "yimcheh" with a heh, as the Beit Yosef wrote, I do not know its source).

If he wrote "Israel" with an aleph-lamed as one word, it is not invalid post facto, as it has already been given, or in place of a potential agunah (a woman unable to remarry). This has already been explained in the previous section that we count but do not reckon. If he wrote "reckon," it is not to be invalidated in pressing circumstances. And even if it is customary to write so initially, it is not to be invalidated, for it is found twice in the Tanach spelled with a full vav — in Jeremiah 33 and in Psalms 147, counting with one yod. This is also how it appears in many instances in the Targum of Numbers. It seems that if it is written with two yods, it is not to be invalidated, as there is no change in this. In the Gemara (Bava Kamma 5a), there are several instances with two yods. The same law applies if he wrote "to reckon" instead of "reckon," it is also valid. Similarly, if he wrote "the count we count in such-and-such place," it is also valid, and likewise any similar cases.

A place that sits by a certain river is written with one word and one yud (י). If it is written in two words and with two yuds (יי), it is still valid, even not under pressing circumstances. It is written "in a certain town which is called such and such," for a city is referred to in the feminine form, as it is written, "Behold, this city is near" (Genesis 19:20), and there are many such examples in Scripture. It is written "Anisana" full with a yud, which is a sign for the one speaking on his behalf. If it is written without "Anis" it is also valid initially, because the intention is the same, and sometimes the language usage varies.

The custom is to write "דהוית" (that you were) as one word, but if one writes "די הוית" (that you were) as two words, it is acceptable. If one does not write "מן קדמת דנא" (from before) but only writes "דהוית אנתתי" (that you were my wife), or omits the word "אנתתי" (my wife) or the word "דהוית" (that you were), it is still valid, since "אנת אנתתי" (you are my wife) was written earlier. In the phrase "ובנפשיכי" (and in yourself), the custom is to write it with two yods, but if it is written with one yod, it is valid, as some authorities hold that it should be written initially without an additional yod after the shin, because with a yod it implies two souls. However, this is not the main opinion (see there). Regarding "ולהתנסבה" (to be married), the custom is to write it without any yod, but if a yod is written after the hei, it is valid, as some say it should ideally be written with a yod, but the custom is not to do so. Some have the custom to write "מן שמי מן יומא דנן ולעלם" (from my name from this day and forever), and some say not to write "מן שמי" (from my name), and this is the custom in these countries.

It is necessary to write "and you are permitted to any man" for this is the main essence of the get (divorce document), and so it is taught in the Mishnah (Gittin 5b): the essence of the get is "you are permitted to any man." In the earlier versions of divorce documents, this was not written (Tosafot 26a, s.v. v'tzarikh), and this is also implied by Rashi's version of the get (Gittin 5b). Their reasoning was that since various phrases are written in the get now, such as "you are dismissed and released and removed" and these are repeated three times, and also "you are hereby authorized and empowered to go marry etc.," it is no longer necessary [to write "you are permitted to any man"]. In the time of the Mishnah, they did not extend the text so much. Nevertheless, some of our Rabbis wrote that if "you are permitted to any man" is not written, it is close to saying that if she marries, she must leave (Ramban). The reason is that although it is true she is permitted to marry anyone she desires, it has been clarified in Siman 137 that if he says to her "except for your adulterous relations," it is considered a reservation in the get, and similarly, here one could say that he only permitted her for marriage and not for adultery, in which case she would still be considered a married woman and it would be a reservation in the get. Therefore, it is written "you are permitted completely." And if you ask why indeed they instituted writing "to marry," one could say that since they write "you are permitted," they did not worry about this. However, most of the poskim (halachic decisors) do not agree with this (Gittin 5b, Pri Chadash, and it is also implied from the Vilna Gaon in Siman 148), as the concern for adultery is only when it is explicitly stated so. Additionally, since he writes for her "dismissals and releases and removals," it implies for everything. Therefore, if she marries, she does not need to leave. Also, if it is a place of agunah (where the husband has traveled far and it is impossible to obtain another get), she may marry initially. Similarly, if he wrote "you are permitted to any man" but did not write "to go marry," if it is a place of agunah where another get cannot be obtained, she may marry (Gittin 5b).

One should be careful to write "muteret" (permissible) with a vav, because if the vav is omitted, it is possible that it would be invalid even after the fact, as it could imply that she permits herself to another man (Levush and Beit Shmuel 136). And although it is possible to read it with a shuruk (a vowel sound that does not draw a vav like a cholam male), nevertheless, it appears more likely to people to read it with a patach, indicating she permits herself to another man. All of this applies to those who invalidate the absence of "harei at" (behold you are...). However, according to most poskim (decisors of Jewish law), there is no concern in a case of agunah (a woman unable to remarry). (Also, the Gra 150 challenged this, and I do not understand his intent when he wrote that the "tav" is with a dagesh, and what of it? After all, "muteret" with a patach also has a dagesh. This requires further investigation.)

And our master, the Rema, wrote in section 41 that, ideally, it is good to be careful to write "you are hereby permitted" in one line. However, if the divorce document (get) has already been written in two lines, it is valid to give it. The reason, ideally, is so that it can be read all at once without interruption, for if there is an interruption, one might think that the hearer believes she is not permitted to marry anyone (Levush). Therefore, the reader should ensure not to interrupt the reading (Beit Shmuel). In truth, the primary reason is very weak and lacks substance (Gra). In the Gemara, we explicitly find the opposite, as it says to write "you are hereby" below and "permitted" above (Gittin 88b, and the Gra also wrote this, and the Terumat HaDeshen himself wrote that he did not know of any concern regarding this, as brought in the Beit Yosef). Nevertheless, ideally, one should certainly be careful to write "and you are hereby permitted to any man" in one line since it comes from the mouth of our master, the Rema, and so is the custom.

One must be careful to write "Hodan di Yehavi" etc., so that the meaning is clear ("Yadayim Mokhichot") that this document is a divorce, and it should not be said that the divorce was verbal and the document is merely for evidence. Indeed, the Gemara (85b) remains in doubt whether "Vedan" is essential or not, and in cases of doubt regarding prohibitions, we are stringent. Most authorities also write this, even though it does not seem so from the Rambam. Additionally, the word "Minai" is essential even post facto, so that it is clear ("Yadayim Mokhichot") that he is divorcing her and not another man, as we say at the beginning of Nedarim (5a). It is puzzling that the Shulchan Aruch does not mention this (Gittin 3:5), as most authorities require "Vedan" and "Minai," and if one of them is missing, it is a doubtful divorce (ibid.). One should write "Minai" without a Yud after the Mem, as with a Yud it resembles heresy. If it was written with a Yud, it is not invalid post facto, as the continuation of the text clarifies the intent that it is from him. "Di Yehavi Likhi" is written in two words, and this is the custom. However, if it was written as one word "Diyehavi," it is valid, and even if only "Dehavi" was written, it is valid in pressing circumstances to prevent being chained (Agunah). The pronunciation of "Vedan" is with a Tzeirei, and "Minai" is with a Chirik under the Mem and a Kamatz under the Nun, and the Aleph with a Chirik. "Dehavit" is with a Tzeirei under the Vav (Levush).

It has already been explained that one needs to lengthen the vavs in the words "teruchin," "shevukin," and "peturin," and that there should be five yuds in the words "tehavuyin" and "teitzaviyin." One should not write a yud individually or in a letter. The Rambam wrote in Chapter 4, Halacha 14, as follows: If one wrote in this manner and did not lengthen these vavs or did not write the extra yuds, or wrote the yuds that we said should not be written, this is an invalid get (divorce document). Similarly, anything like this in any language is invalid. This is the end of his words. The Shulchan Aruch, in section 22, also writes this, and they wrote that aside from the two additional yuds in "tehavuyin" and "teitzaviyin," which is merely a custom, they concluded their words. And it means that if "tehavuyin" and "teitzaviyin" are not written with the dalet in the place where it should be, which means like "she will be" or "that you will want" (Rosh), and according to this, one should not be particular about the yud between the tav and the heh (there), nor about the yud between the tav and the tzadi (and these are the two additional yuds in each one, understand this well). They also wrote that some say that if one did not write "tehavuyin" properly but wrote "zot tehei resha" instead, it is better. This is the end of their words.

And this is the opinion of the Rambam, that with these changes, the get (divorce document) is invalid. And even though they are only minor concerns, it is still considered a deviation from the form established by the Sages (according to the Maggid Mishneh). If she remarries, she does not have to leave (her second husband). However, the Raavad wrote there in the name of the Gaon that all these meticulous details are only relevant if the husband comes and contests (the validity of the get). The wording of the Maggid Mishneh is: "And the rabbis wrote that all these meticulous details of Rav are relevant when the husband himself wrote it, or if a scribe wrote it based on his (the husband’s) dictation. And afterward, the husband comes and contests it, saying, 'I am the one who invalidated it with these meticulous details and intended to ruin it.' But if the husband told the scribe and witnesses to write the get, even in a general manner, and the scribe and witnesses made a mistake in one of these letters, and the husband does not contest it, the get is valid and she can remarry with it. If witnesses are available, they should testify before the court that it was a scribal error." Similarly, Rabbeinu Hai wrote: "If the husband gave permission to the scribe to write a complete get and they made mistakes in all or some of these matters, if the scribe is present, he should correct it. If not, and she marries with this get, we do not make her leave. Certainly, if she comes to remarry and the husband contests it, saying, 'This is the document I said...' etc., and I intended to invalidate it, we do not let her remarry. But if she has already married, we do not make her leave." And Rabbeinu Nissim responded similarly, based on a tradition from the Gaon: "If the husband himself wrote the get, and she remarries and the husband contests, she must leave. If the woman claims it was a scribal error, she must bring proof. But if there is no contest from the husband and there is a scribal error, and he instructed to write a get in a general manner, since he wanted to divorce with complete intent, a second get is not needed. Any error that comes from the scribe’s hand, the husband’s contest is not valid." This is also the opinion of the Geonim, etc. And I have written these opinions, but I cannot decide between them. This is the conclusion of the Maggid Mishneh. The Ran also wrote similarly, and the Tur brought this as well, but he did not write that if she remarries, she must leave. See there.

According to the commentators, this is the explanation: in a case of two negative factors regarding the husband's contestation and the fact that he or the scribe wrote it at his direction, even if she has married, she must leave him. In a case of two positive factors, where the scribe wrote it and the husband instructed him without specification and did not contest it, even initially she may marry. In a case of one positive and one negative factor, such as where the husband wrote it but did not contest it, or the scribe wrote it and the husband instructed him without specification but the husband contested it, she should not marry initially, but if she has married, she does not have to leave (Taz, Lechem Mishneh, Peri Chadash, Rabbi Yosef Ben Lev in his responsa, and others). According to Maimonides, the Raavad, and the Tur, it is always understood that if she married, she does not have to leave.

Indeed, from the conclusion of the words of the Maggid, it appears that this is not entirely a singular opinion. Therefore, it is possible to interpret that the Raavad and Rabbeinu Hai do not hold at all that if she marries, she must leave [her husband], even in cases with double suspicion. Thus, the Tur did not mention this at all, and this is only the opinion of Rabbeinu Nissim in the name of the Gaon. Similarly, the Raavad did not mention this in the name of the Gaon, for he stands by the words of the Rambam, and if it were conceivable that there is a situation where if she marries, she must leave, he would have mentioned it, as the Rambam does not hold at all that she must leave. Also, the interpretation is not that if the husband objects in any manner, she should not marry, but only specifically regarding his writing or the scribe writing on his behalf. And when it is written that the husband does not object, the intention is that either the husband does not object, or it is a dividing "vav" (and).

This is the explanation of the view of the Rishonim that all these precisions apply in a case of a double defect. But if he told the scribe to write it generally, and the scribe erred, or even if he wrote it himself and there is no objection, it is valid and she may remarry with it. If witnesses are available, it is good for them to testify that it was a scribal error and not an intentional corruption. The words of Rav Hai mean: if the husband gave permission to the scribe to write a complete get (divorce document) and the scribe erred, etc., if the scribe is present, he can correct it even without asking the husband, and then we do not pay attention to the husband's objection. But if the scribe is not present and someone else must correct it, it is necessary to ask the husband for permission to correct it, as stated in Siman 125. If they did not do so, we do not allow her to remarry, because the husband might come and object. However, if she married, she does not have to leave him, even if he wrote it himself (this is what Rav Hai referred to when he said, "and he wrote," meaning clearly that he wrote it himself, and in this case, he concludes that she does not have to leave). But if he objects before she marries, even if it is not his writing, we do not allow her to marry. Rabbeinu Nissim added that if he wrote it himself and objects, even if she married, she must leave him. If the woman brings proof that there was no intention to corrupt at the time of writing, we do not pay attention to his objection. But if there is no objection from the husband, even if he wrote it himself, we have no concern about this, and she can remarry. Similarly, if he instructed to write it generally and the scribe made an error, his objection does not matter. This is what he wrote: "and there is an error from the hand of the scribe," etc., which is a dividing conjunction. According to this, there are several opinions on this matter; what one is stringent about, the other is lenient, and vice versa (see Gittin 65 where other opinions are also brought about this explanation, not as the previous interpretation, and also see Beit Shmuel 32, which shows that he is uncertain about the intent of these words) (and also from what is written in Siman 123, Paragraph 12, it is clear as well).

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Yosef Karo), in section 22, after bringing the opinion of the Rambam, wrote as follows: "There are those who say that if the husband does not contest, the get (divorce document) is valid, and there is one who says that the husband's contest is not effective unless he wrote it himself or the scribe wrote it at his dictation." And he was very brief. But in any case, it seems clearly as I have said, since he did not bring at all the opinion that if she remarries she must leave, it implies that he holds this is a singular opinion and we do not follow it. Moreover, we learn from his words that according to the Raavad, which is the opinion that without contest the get is valid in any case, even if written by the husband. And according to the other rabbis, which is the "there is one who says," if written by the scribe, the contest is not effective at all, but if written by him or the scribe at his dictation, the contest is effective. And without contest, even in this case, it is valid. Accordingly, the Rambam is the most stringent of all, and even according to him, if she remarries she does not have to leave, as he wrote in chapter 10.

Indeed, the words of the Rambam, of blessed memory, are very stringent. What the Maggid Mishneh wrote, that his reasoning is because it deviates from the form that the Sages established, this itself we do not find except regarding the issue of "before me it was written and before me it was signed," where it is stated in the Gemara as such. But in this matter, where the Sages only warned us to do so, from where do we derive that this is considered a deviation from the form established by the Sages? For example, in the enactment of Rabban Gamliel, where witnesses must sign the get, nevertheless, if they did not sign and gave it to her in the presence of two witnesses alone, the get is valid. Similarly, with only signing witnesses and without the presence of others, as stated in chapter one and will be explained in section 133, there is no greater deviation from the form than this, and yet it is ruled as valid. Therefore, certainly in a place where the Sages themselves did not say it is considered a deviation from the form, we do not say so. Moreover, from his own words in that chapter, law 9, another reason is heard, that this is only because of the suspicion of others. He wrote that every language written in the get must be such that it does not imply two different matters, lest the reader say perhaps it was intended for this and that, etc. Hence, he was concerned about the suspicion of the reader. And it seems to me that he interprets the Gemara in all the warnings not to imply different meanings, meaning that the reader should not perceive different meanings and cast suspicion on the get.

And know that regarding the lengthening of the vavs in the form of a get, the great later authorities agreed that Rambam does not invalidate them unless they are made small like yuds. But if they are made as vavs, even if they are not lengthened to match other vavs, there is no concern with this (Beit Shmuel se'if katan 32, Taz se'if katan 24, Pri Chadash, and Get Pashut se'if katan 66). Nevertheless, they should be lengthened before the signatures of the witnesses or at least before the delivery of the get, and specifically, this should be done by the scribe himself, but another should not correct it unless instructed by the husband. For in a situation that is not pressing, the get should not be delivered without lengthening the vavs, as the Tur wrote in the name of the Rosh: "If the get was given to her and the vavs were not lengthened, and the husband is far away, I would not invalidate it because of this. Similarly, if there is a concern of chained wives, such as the get being brought from a distant place, the vavs should be lengthened because it is assumed that the husband instructed to write it according to the correct procedure of the sages, and if the scribe did not write it properly, the husband would be agreeable to correcting it. And on this one can rely in a pressing situation." And this applies to a get that is sent, but when the husband is present, another person should not correct it without the husband's instruction, as written in Siman 125. Similarly, if a yud was written like a vav or the hey was written like a chet, they should be corrected before the signatures and at least before the delivery. They should be corrected in a manner that there is no concern of chiseling out the letters, as written there. And even though in such a case there may be scraping or writing over an erasure, it is valid according to the law, as writing on something that can be forged is permissible. And even though we do not write this way, as written there, if it is in a manner that it is impossible to write another get, they should do so, as this is a disqualification from the law of the Gemara. And one who knows the laws of gittin knows how to correct, and it is impossible to explain everything in writing.

The text of the get (divorce document) according to the Rosh includes the phrase "and any name, whether given to the individual or the place." This is his wording: "I, So-and-so son of So-and-so, from such-and-such a place, who resides, etc., and any other name and nickname that I have and for my place, etc." End of quote. 

However, we do not write "and any name" in any context, as stated in sections 128 and 129. Regarding the Rosh's wording, our sages, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in this section, paragraph 30, as follows: "It is customary to write 'who stands in such-and-such a place' before 'and any name,' and some say to write the nickname before 'who stands in such-and-such a place.' This is the custom in these countries. It is customary to write 'So-and-so son of So-and-so' and not 'Bar So-and-so,' but if 'Bar' is written, the get is valid. It is customary to write 'and any name that I have and for my ancestors.'" End of quote. And with us, we do not write "and any name" at all, except in the reverse manner as stated there.

In a get (divorce document) for a betrothed woman, it is written "who was my betrothed." If he wrote "who was my wife," it is valid because a betrothed woman is also called his wife, as he effects betrothal even with this expression, as stated in Siman 27. Some say that the reverse is also true: if he wrote to his wife "my betrothed," it is valid after the fact. However, there are those who invalidate this (Levush), and it is proper to be stringent in practice (and the Taz, who also rejected the Beit Yosef's proof, wrote like the Levush).

The shin and ayin whose yuds do not touch them, being separated from the body of the letters, and similarly the yuds in the aleph and tzadi that do not touch the letter, our master the Beit Yosef ruled in paragraph 17 that if a child reads them properly, even if they are in a problematic state, they may be deemed acceptable in a situation of agunah (a woman who cannot obtain a divorce). And similarly, if the legs of the heh are attached to its roof, he ruled that if a child who is neither clever nor foolish reads them properly, they may be deemed acceptable in a situation of agunah, even if they are in a problematic state, and one should separate them with a knife. And we have already explained this in the previous section, paragraph 45, that regarding this matter we are more lenient with a get (divorce document) than with a Torah scroll, as in a Torah scroll the reading of a child does not suffice for this matter, but with a get we rely on it because there are many forms of expression for a divorce, and to the eye of the observer, as long as the child reads it correctly, it is not considered a significant change in a pressing situation. Nevertheless, it is proper to correct it before the signatures, and in any case, before the delivery. And what our master the Beit Yosef wrote about separating with a knife, it seems to me that he did not mean this literally, as this would be considered erasure from within the letter, but rather that he should scrape the leg and write it correctly, and he relied on what was written on these matters in the previous section (it seems to me).

Furthermore, it is written in section 20: Since we recognize the manner of the text, it should not be invalidated due to the omission of a single letter. End quote. His intention is even regarding the essential part of the document. It is written in section 49: If a single word is missing from the template, it is not invalidated because of this. End quote. Why then is it necessary to inform us about a single letter? Certainly, this means that even in the essential part, if the omission of the letter does not cause a change in meaning, it should not be invalidated. Therefore, our teacher, the Rema, wrote that all the more so if the second "vav" of "u'k'du" is omitted and it is written as "u'kd" since the meaning does not change, the omission does not invalidate it. The same applies if there are additional letters, as long as the meaning does not change. However, if the meaning does change, it is invalid. Therefore, some say that if it is written "l'briyat alma" with a "heh" at the end, the get (divorce document) is invalid because "alma" means a young woman. However, some permit it in a pressing situation. End quote. According to the first opinion, the get is invalid even if the husband does not contest it because the term "alma" with a "heh" more closely implies a young woman than the word "olam" (world). But if it is written "l'alma" with an aleph, it is valid (Beit Shmuel 141). Many prominent authorities validate it with a "heh" in pressing situations when it is not possible to obtain another get (Get Pashut 167, Pri Hadash also validates it even not in cases of potential agunah, see there).

It is an established law in the Gemara (Bava Batra 162a) that one does not derive legal principles from the last line in documents, as elucidated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 44. Therefore, the scribe must be careful not to have on the last line phrases such as "a bill of divorce," "a letter of dismissal," or "a writ of release," but only "according to the law of Moses and Israel." Consequently, it is customary to make the letters very large, because the preceding content cannot be written due to the aforementioned reason. Ending in the middle of a line is not appropriate because there is a concern that the witnesses might sign on this line, and then one cannot derive legal principles from the preceding line. This would invalidate the phrase "this is your bill of divorce," which is the main part of the get (divorce document) as explained. Therefore, it is necessary to extend these letters considerably to end at the end of a line. However, if it is impossible to write another get and there is a concern of leaving the woman in a state of "agunah" (a woman who cannot remarry), it is not invalid even if "this is your bill of divorce" is written on the last line. In such a case, we do derive legal principles from the last line, as we hold that where "valid and confirmed" is written, we do derive from the last line, as stated in Choshen Mishpat there. "According to the law of Moses and Israel" in a get is akin to "valid and confirmed" in other documents. However, ideally, one should not rely on this because some of the early authorities questioned it, but in a pressing situation, there is room to be lenient (see Beit Yosef and Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 29).

In Siman 134, it will be explained that the husband needs to annul declarations. Nevertheless, it should not be written in the get (divorce document) that the declarations are annulled because no condition should be written in a get, as stated in Siman 147. Consequently, one should not question all the concerns mentioned in this Siman and the previous one regarding the fear of forgery. What concern of forgery could there be for us, given that nothing is written in the get except the fixed formula? It can be said that regarding the names of the man, the woman, the fathers, and the places, there is a concern for forgery. Additionally, the reason we do not write conditions in the get is due to stringency, as stated there. Therefore, it is impossible that because we have accepted this stringency upon ourselves, we should be lenient in another matter.

It is necessary to write the date on a get, and the laws of a predated or postdated get, consisting of 49 sections: The sages instituted that a date must be written on a get. How so? By stating: "On such and such a day of the week, on such and such a day of a certain month, in such and such a year according to a certain reckoning." And why did they institute this? After all, it is not a document of collection (Rashi 17a) that would indicate when to collect, for the collection of a ketubah does not require a date, since as soon as she presents the get, she collects her ketubah. And if it is due to sustenance, to reclaim what she borrowed and consumed before the date written in the get, if there is no date, he might claim that she was already divorced and thus not entitled to sustenance. This reason does not require a date, as she can bring witnesses to the court who will testify about the time of her divorce (Ran and Tosafot there), or they can write her a separate document stating that she was divorced on that day (there). Moreover, one cannot say that the institution of the date was for the issue of the three months she must wait before remarrying, and if there is no date, she might marry earlier and claim she was already divorced. This reason clearly does not require a date, as when she wishes to remarry, we will ask her to bring proof of when she was divorced (in my opinion). Similarly, one cannot say that the institution of the date was to determine when to take the fruits of her property that were in his possession. Without a date, he might consume them, and when she demands them in court, he could claim that he divorced her just now. This reason does not require a date, as we establish that the husband has the right to the fruits until the moment the get is given to her, even if the get was written much earlier. Therefore, whatever he consumes until the moment of giving is consumed lawfully, and to prevent him from consuming the fruits after the giving, a date is not necessary, since she can come immediately after the giving to the court and reclaim whatever is in his possession from her property (Ran there), or she can ask the witnesses to write for her the date of her divorce (Tosafot). For everything that is in her favor, a date is not required for the reasons explained.

Indeed, the ordinance was established. The Sages said (there), "Because of a safeguard against promiscuity," for sometimes a man is married to his relative, and she commits adultery under him, and he wishes to cover for her. So, he gives her a get (divorce document) after the adultery and does not write the date on it, and she will claim, "I was divorced before the adultery." And so it is in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 4 of Gittin (Halacha 3): "Why did they establish a date in the get? Because of an incident that occurred: There was a man who was married to his niece, and she committed adultery while she was still married. He went and predated the get, saying, 'It is better that she be judged as a single woman rather than as a married woman.'" This is the end of the quote, and it is brought by the Rif and the Rosh there. And the explanation is: Before they established writing the date in the get, the witnesses did not pay attention to the time, and it was possible for him to write it earlier, and she would agree to this because it was to her benefit. But after they established the date, he could not predate it because the witnesses would not sign it, and likewise, the delivery witnesses would not allow giving such a get. And indeed, before the ordinance, it was not necessary to predate it, for he could write her a get without a date and give it to her. And when they would testify in the court about her adultery, she would produce her get and claim, "I was already divorced and single at that time" (Rashi). And we do not say, "Presume her to be married and only now divorced," since she is divorced before us. On the contrary, we presume her to be of valid status, not having committed adultery while married (Ran). (There is a difficulty with what the early authorities wrote in the name of the Itur, that the Jerusalem Talmud does not hold this reasoning of 'perhaps he will cover for her.' It is true that in Chapter 2, it gives the reason of 'fruit,' but in Chapter 4, it gives the reason of 'perhaps he will cover for her,' as mentioned. And it must be said that his intention was regarding Rabbi Yochanan, that in our Talmud, he gives the reason of 'perhaps he will cover for her,' and in the Jerusalem Talmud, he gives the reason of 'fruit').

And one should not ask, this reasoning makes sense when the Holy Temple was standing and they would judge capital cases, but in our time, what difference does it make? Indeed, even in our time, it is his will to cover for her so that the child will not be a mamzer, and furthermore, she will not be forbidden to him if she committed adultery before the divorce. However, if she committed adultery after the divorce, she is permitted to return to him (Rosh there). And one should not ask, according to this, why do we need the reason to save her from death? It can be said that without the reason of saving her from death, they would not have instituted the time period, for even without the time period, when he wishes to take her back, we would say to him, bring proof that she committed adultery after the divorce, and similarly, when the son wishes to marry a woman, we would say to him to bring proof. Therefore, the main institution was in order to save her from death, and since they decreed for this reason, we uphold the institution for the reasons that have been explained as well (there).

However, there is a significant question regarding this matter: How is it possible that the primary ordinance was established to save her from death, when in fact one is not executed without a warning? And the witnesses who warned her, if they know that she is still a married woman, his cunning by giving her a get (divorce document) will not help since the witnesses know that she is still married. And if they do not know, without this she is not executed, as it would be a doubtful warning for the witnesses. It can be said that the concern is always that the witnesses might not know, and if it is because of a doubtful warning, it is established that a doubtful warning is considered a warning, as the Rambam wrote in Chapter 16 of Sanhedrin. Furthermore, the master of the discussion in our Talmud, who says the reason is Rabbi Yochanan, and he holds that a doubtful warning is considered a warning (Makkot 15b). Moreover, the truth is that this is not a doubtful warning, for a doubtful warning is only called such when the doubt exists for the transgressor as well. But when the transgressor is clear about it, even though the warning witnesses do not know, it is called a definite warning since the warning is only given to distinguish between inadvertent and deliberate transgression. And since the transgressor knows, it is a proper warning (Tosafot Pesachim 63b). And with this, what is said to Rabbi Lish Lakish in Gittin there becomes clear: Adultery is not common, and why does he need to say this? Doesn't he hold in Makkot there that it is not considered a warning? But if it were a definite warning, he would be compelled to this reasoning. Pay close attention to this.

And if she was divorced with a get (bill of divorce) that does not have a date, she should not remarry. However, if she did remarry, she does not have to leave her second husband, even if she has no children from the second marriage. This is because it is one of the three invalid gittin (bills of divorce) mentioned (in Gittin 86a), where it is taught that if she remarries, the child is legitimate, and the Gemara rules there that if she remarries, she never has to leave (the second husband). And one should not ask, according to this, what did the Sages accomplish with their decree, since if he wants to save her from death, he can write her a get without a date, and she can claim that she committed adultery afterward. Although this is a flaw compared to other gittin, we still cannot execute her if she claims that she was divorced before the adultery (Beit Shmuel 1). However, the benefit is that since it is initially forbidden for her to remarry, the scribe will not want to write it, and the witnesses will not want to sign it (Rashi). And nowadays, it is obvious that even if such a get is obtained, we will not believe them to take her back, and we will not consider the child legitimate due to the flaw compared to other gittin that are written according to the enactment of the Sages (Beit Shmuel).

And know that there are some of our rabbis who hold that according to Rabbi Eliezer, who says that "delivery of the document effects the divorce," a get (divorce document) is valid without a date. Just as they instituted that the witnesses should sign the get for the betterment of the world, and nevertheless, it is valid even without the witnesses' signatures as stated in Siman 133, so too the date, which was also instituted for the betterment of the world, the get is valid even without a date, and she may marry l'chatchila (ideally) based on the witnesses of delivery who will testify about the get and the date (Rashbam, Bava Batra 172b, and Tosafot there, and Hagahot Maimoniyot, Chapter 1, Note 50, in the name of the Itur). However, all the early authorities did not write this, and do not compare different rabbinic decrees to one another. Moreover, here the betterment of the world is due to the concern of mamzerut (illegitimacy), which is not comparable to the betterment of the world regarding the signatures, which is for the protection of the woman. And in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, this opinion is not mentioned at all (see Beit Yosef and Beit Shmuel). There are those who say that when there are signed witnesses, it is certainly invalid according to the majority of the poskim (decisors), but when there are no signed witnesses at all on the get, it should be validated in a case of agunah (a woman who cannot remarry) because it is impossible to come to cover-up, as she will necessarily have to present the witnesses of delivery when she wishes to remarry, as stated in Siman 124, and they will be asked when the divorce took place (Tosafot Gittin and Gilyon Maharsha). However, from the general language of the poskim, it does not seem so, and this requires further investigation for the halacha. Also, from the Jerusalem Talmud, it does not seem so (for it says in Chapter 2, Halacha 2, that according to Rabbi Shimon, who validates a get written by day and signed by night and holds like Rabbi Eliezer that "delivery of the document effects the divorce," there is a distinction between wanting to have witnesses sign or not, which clearly implies that according to the first opinion, in any case, it is invalid. See there carefully).

And there is someone who asked a great question according to the opinion of the authorities that if a man sets his eyes on divorcing his wife, he can no longer inherit her (this is the opinion of the Rashbam in Bava Batra 146 regarding the case of the "Toteranit"). If so, what did the Sages ask, why did they institute a date in divorce documents? One could say it is so that if the woman dies between the writing of the get and its delivery, he will not inherit her. And if he sent the get from overseas and before it reached her hand the woman died, if there was no date in it, it could be claimed that she died before the writing of the get, and by the date it is clarified that she died afterward. And we certainly take into account the possibility of her death. Rather, it is certain that we do not hold by this opinion (Gra, Even HaEzer 2). According to this, one could question our master the Rema in Siman 90, Section 5, who ruled that if a man rebels against his wife, he does not inherit her when he does not treat her in the manner of a husband. And consequently, from the time of writing the get he does not treat her in the manner of a husband, as it says there in Section 24. If so, this has implications for inheritance. However, according to what we have explained there, this only applies when he does not abide by the law or the court does not attend to this. This is understandable, because in such cases it is not common, and in the majority of cases, the court attends to it and he abides by the law and inherits her until the delivery of the get.

Since a get (divorce document) without a date is invalid, all the more so if the date is early, it is invalid. And thus it is taught in the Mishnah: if it was written during the day and signed at night, it is invalid; but if it was written at night and signed during the day, it is valid (Gittin 17a), because the night follows the day. Rambam rules in Chapter 1, Law 25, that even if they were engaged in that matter, it is invalid. And although in other documents and in a ketubah, if they are engaged in that matter, it is not considered early, as it says in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 43, nevertheless, in a get, it is invalid. In other documents, it is valid because when they are engaged in that matter, the voice (report) goes out from the time of the writing (Rashi Gittin 18a), but in a get, it is not dependent on the voice, and until it is delivered to her, it is impossible, and there is a concern for covering up adultery (Beit Shmuel, section 3). However, the Rosh (Chapter 2, Siman 7) disagrees and holds that if they are engaged in that matter, it is also valid for a get, for this is implied by the simple reading of the Talmudic passage, that it also applies to a get, that as long as they are engaged in that matter, it is considered as one day (and also the Rashba there and the Shitah Mekubetzet in Chapter 2, Siman 9, disagreed with the Rambam, and furthermore, there are those who explicitly have the text in the Gemara there: "They only taught that a get written etc., only when they are not engaged in that matter etc.").

The Rambam further wrote there that just as an early-dated get (divorce document) is invalid, so too a get with a post-dated time written for the future is invalid. However, all the early authorities disagreed with him regarding a post-dated get, as there is no concern of covering up adultery in such a case. On the contrary, it extends the time of her marital status. Some say that the Rambam's reasoning is that we decree against a post-dated get because of an early-dated get (commentary), but this is difficult, for how can we impose decrees on our own? Others say that his reasoning is because the woman will lose the produce (benefits) from the time the get is given until the date written in it, as the husband will consume the produce even afterwards. When she takes him to court, he will say to her, "Show me your get, which states you were divorced at such-and-such a time."

Furthermore, there is also concern about the possibility of covering up an act of infidelity if the get (divorce document) is postdated, as the Ran (Rabbeinu Nissim) of blessed memory wrote. He explains that one might write the date of the get several days later, and the woman could present her get and claim that she was divorced before the act of infidelity, even though the date on the get does not prove it. This is because it is evident that the get is postdated, and it is considered like a get without a date. There is proof for this from Yevamot 116a, where it is stated that we are concerned lest it was delivered via a flying camel (i.e., in an unlikely manner). Why not consider that it might be postdated? This is what the Kesef Mishneh wrote there.

The halachic authorities who permit a delayed get (divorce document) say that it is valid for her to remarry immediately and there is no need to wait until the time specified in the get (Raavad there). However, the husband may eat the fruits (benefits) until the time specified in the get, and she may not collect her ketubah (marriage contract payment) beforehand (there). Others say that the divorce does not take effect until the specified time (Tosafot 17a, d.h. "Reish Lakish"), and according to this opinion, the Rosh, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch rule in section 9.
