One must be stringent and consider both opinions regarding whether she accepted betrothal from another man (Beit Shmuel, section 15). 

It is clear that practically, one should also be concerned for the Rambam's opinion that a delayed get is invalid, and she should not be allowed to remarry without another get. Perhaps, in a situation of potential agunah (a woman unable to remarry), one may rely on the majority of poskim who disagree with the Rambam and validate a delayed get according to the specified time. 

Know that what we wrote according to the first opinion, that she has no fruits or ketubah until the time of the get, applies if the get was delayed with her consent, as it is like she forgave him until the time of the get. But if it was written without her consent, she collects the ketubah immediately, and he does not eat her fruits immediately (Rosh, section 5). 

This is according to the first opinion that the get takes effect immediately, but according to the second opinion, she certainly does not collect her ketubah before the specified time in the get, as how could she collect her ketubah if the divorce has not yet taken effect? Also, he eats the fruits until the specified time in the get (there). 

Therefore, the concern regarding the fruits in section 9 is removed, and regarding the concern of promiscuity mentioned in the previous section, it can be said that there is no concern, since it is known that the time was delayed, they will investigate thoroughly to ensure she engaged in promiscuity before the divorce, unlike a get without a specified time, where they would not consider it at all (Bach and Beit Shmuel).

That which is written earlier is invalid. Some say that specifically, an earlier date invalidates [the get] when the date of the get precedes the signatures, such as if it was written and signed in Marcheshvan but it was written in it as Tishrei. Similarly, according to the Rambam, if it was written and signed in Tishrei and it is written in it as Marcheshvan, it is invalid. However, if he was standing in Tishrei and wrote the get for her sake according to the law and it was written in it the date of Marcheshvan, and the witnesses signed on it, and the get was written before them on the same day as written in the get, it seems to be valid. For we do not consider it earlier or later since the date written in the get and the signing all occurred on the same day. This is what the Rambam wrote: "Until they sign it at the time of its writing," meaning at the time written in the get, not on the day of its writing. And that which we say that if it was written during the day and signed at night, it is invalid, is specifically when it was written with a date and signed at night after the date. This is the explanation of the commentator on the Rambam there (and the Beit Yosef brought it in Bedek HaBayit and there is a deficiency there, see there. And know that this is not the Maggid Mishneh, for the Rivash already wrote at the end of Siman 117 that in the first three chapters of Gittin, the Maggid Mishneh is missing. And the language also proves this).

The explanation of the matter is that we do not insist that the writing itself should not precede the signatures, but rather on the date written in it. Therefore, if it was written previously and the date was written several days later and the witnesses signed on the day the date was written, the get (divorce document) is valid. Now, according to those who hold that a postdated get is valid, this is not a novelty at all. Only according to Rambam, who invalidates a postdated get, and it could be said that only if it was written for a future date is it invalid, we learn that since the witnesses signed on the day of the date, it is not called postdated. And even though we hold according to Rabbi Eliezer that "and he writes her" refers to the writing of the get and not to the signatures of the witnesses, nevertheless, since there is no delay in the signatures, there is no defect here.

Now, the Rambam wrote regarding an early-dated get (divorce document) that it is invalid, and similarly about a late-dated one according to his view. He established a general rule in Chapter 10 that in any place where he wrote "invalid" and not "null," it is invalid rabbinically. However, it disqualifies her from marrying a kohen by Torah law, and she should not marry initially, but if she did marry, she does not need to divorce. A new valid get is written and given to her, and the child is legitimate. There is a doubt whether its status is exactly like a get without a date, where even if she has no children, she does not need to divorce, or not. Some say that in this case, it is more stringent than a get without a date, and if she has no children, she should divorce (Ran, Chapter 9, s.v. "an early-dated get"). Others say there is no difference, and even if she has no children, she does not need to divorce (ibid., in the name of some opinions).

However, the Tur wrote as follows: "My father, the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote in a responsum: If a woman was divorced with an antedated get (bill of divorce) and its invalidity was not known until after another man betrothed her, the second betrothal does not take effect and she does not need a get from him, and she is permitted to return to the first husband." End quote. His words are perplexing—how can he be so lenient? After all, its invalidity is only rabbinic. And even though the date is considered a significant part of the get, as the Tur wrote in Siman 123, it is clear that this is only a stringency and not a leniency, as he wrote there. And already our master, the Beit Yosef, expressed wonder about this in his great book. There is someone who says that the reason is that since the invalidity was not known until after the second betrothal, it is considered a mistaken betrothal, because if the second man had known that the get was invalid, he would not have betrothed her (Bach). But it is impossible to say this, as a mistaken betrothal only applies in cases where there was an explicit condition, such as betrothing on the condition that there are no defects and similar cases, but not in cases where nothing was specified (Taz). And is this prohibition more serious than other prohibitions punishable by lashes, where even if he did not know that she was prohibited, the betrothal takes effect and she requires a get? How much more so with secondary prohibitions related to forbidden relations, as is evident from what was explained in Siman 116. And how much more so with an antedated get, which is a rabbinic issue. There are those who wish to say that the reason is because the witnesses who signed the antedated get were disqualified (Gra in the name of Ginat Veradim).

However, this only applies if the witnesses knew that it was predated, and they themselves were the witnesses of the delivery. If they did not know, then they are not disqualified. Even if they knew, if there were other valid witnesses of the delivery, it is only a rabbinic disqualification. All of this is not explained in the words of the Rosh (there). There are those who wish to differentiate between betrothal and marriage (there in the name of R. Yitzchak Minz), but these words have no basis as is evident from several places (there). There are those who wish to provide a reasonable explanation for this, that it is certain since the disqualification was not discovered until after the second betrothal, it shows that it was not done intentionally by the husband but rather due to the scribe's error. The husband certainly told him to write a valid get as is customary, and thus this is a deviation from the husband's agency, nullifying his agency, and it is as if it were not written under the husband's authority and is therefore not for its intended purpose, making the get invalid from the Torah (Gittin 3:45). (And the Yam Shel Shlomo in Chapter 2, Section 12, rejected this answer with both hands and wrote that these are erroneous words – refer there. And according to what was said, there is a good rationale in this matter).

Based on this, it is possible to say that other legal authorities would agree with this, and all the laws they explained earlier that the disqualification is rabbinic, this is when the husband is aware of the disqualification. But if he is not aware, then the scribe has deviated from his agency. However, according to the words of Maimonides in Chapter 2, Law 9, that if he did not appoint an agent to deliver the get to the wife, but only for writing and signing, they do not write another get even if it is found invalid or disqualified, and we say that his agency is completed, see there. It is impossible to uphold this law, and although in Siman 122 we explained Maimonides' opinion differently, see what is written in Section 6, nevertheless, it is impossible to establish this law as halacha because all the authorities did not mention this, and even the Rosh himself did not explain this reason. And our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, rejected it from halacha, as Rabbi Moshe Isserles wrote in Section 2, and these are his words: "And an early-dated get, although it is invalid, if she was betrothed to another, she needs a get from the second and is forbidden to return to the first," end quote. And he did not differentiate between whether the husband knew about the disqualification or not. And the great later authorities also rejected this law, therefore we do not hold this way. And in practice, even if he did not know about the disqualification, nevertheless, she is forbidden to return to him after being betrothed to another and needs a get from the second. There is an explanation for this: since the husband did not care to check at the time of delivering the get to his wife whether it was valid or not, we say that he accepted and received everything the scribe did in his writing, and it is considered that he completed his agency (also the Beit Yosef did not agree with this law, see there, and therefore it is forbidden to rule like this responsum).

The Tur writes: If a woman was divorced with a get (divorce document) that does not have a date, she should not remarry. However, if she did remarry with it, she does not have to leave her new husband, even if she has no children. If the date was predated, it is invalid. Nevertheless, if it was written during the day and signed at night or even within ten days, the ruling of the Rosh is that it is valid in pressing circumstances where another get cannot be obtained. The Ramah writes that it is invalid. According to this, the Rosh's opinion differs from that of all other authorities. He differentiates between a completely predated get, where the date written is earlier than the actual writing and signing, and a get written in Marheshvan with a date in Tishrei. In such cases, he is very stringent, and if the husband did not know about the get, it is invalid by Torah law. If she betrothed another man, she does not need a get from him, as stated in paragraph 15. However, if it was written during the day and signed at night or within ten days, he is lenient and considers it valid in pressing circumstances. This is based on the Talmudic discussion (Gittin 19a), where there was an incident where witnesses did not sign until later, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi allowed it, saying that Rabbi Shimon, who disagreed with the law of a get written during the day and signed at night, is reliable in pressing circumstances when the husband has gone away or she is already remarried (Rashi). His reasoning is that there is a difference between a predated get that is written falsely and one that is written during the day and signed later, which is written truthfully (Beit Yosef). Some say that the distinction is whether the witnesses know that it is predated, in which case it is valid in pressing circumstances, and if they do not know, it is invalid by Torah law (Maharim Mintz). This distinction does not seem logical (Beit Shmuel). Some differentiate between when the husband knows that it is predated, in which case it is valid in pressing circumstances, and when the husband does not know, in which case the get is invalid by Torah law (Beit Shmuel). The reasoning is that if the husband does not know, it will cause problems regarding the fruits, as she will seize the fruits sold from the date written in the get. But if he knows that it is predated, she will rightfully seize the fruits since he intended to divorce her (Beit Shmuel). This reasoning does not seem correct, as the Rosh would not invalidate the get by Torah law for this reason. Moreover, it is clear from the Tur's language that the Rosh's leniency in pressing circumstances does not apply to a predated get. Therefore, the primary opinion is that if the get is written falsely, it is invalid by Torah law because it deviates from the husband's agency. But if it is written truthfully, it is valid in pressing circumstances.

Accordingly, according to the Rosh and the Tur, there are three distinct legal categories regarding precedence: When the document was truly written earlier and the signatures or the delivery happened afterward, it is valid in a pressing situation. If it was written with an earlier date, it is invalid even in a pressing situation. However, if the husband knew about this, it is not void according to Torah law, and she requires a get (divorce document) from the second husband if she received betrothal from him, and she is forbidden to return to the first husband. If the husband was unaware of this, it is void according to Torah law. We have already written that the decisors dispute him on this matter (and similarly, one can interpret the intention of the Beit Shmuel in subparagraph 4 as ruling for the law and not on the words of the Tur; see there and scrutinize).

And behold, in this law regarding a document that was written truthfully but the signatures were delayed, where the Rosh and the Tur permit it in pressing circumstances, many authorities agree with this (as mentioned in Beit Yosef). However, the Rif and the Rambam do not see it this way, and therefore their opinion is brought in Shulchan Aruch, Section 2, under "there are those who say." Certainly, in pressing circumstances, one may rely on these our Rabbis.

Accordingly, the law is that if the earlier marriage was valid, even in a pressing situation, it is invalid and not nullified by Torah law, whether the husband knew about the invalidity or not. If another man comes and marries her, she needs a get (divorce document) from him and is forbidden to return to the first husband. However, if the second husband does not want to divorce her, he can keep her (see Beit Shmuel section 5 and examine further). This follows the rulings of rabbinic invalidities as stated by the Rambam in chapter 10, that if she married, she does not have to leave, and the child is legitimate. A proper get is written for her, and she remains with her husband. See there and it will be explained in section 150. However, this is specifically when the husband knew about the invalidity. But if he did not know, she is taken away from the second one as well, because we must be concerned with the opinion of the Rosh that we mentioned, that if the husband did not know, the get is nullified by Torah law, and she is forbidden to both. This is also agreed upon by the great later authorities (Gilyon Maharsha and Beit Meir, not like the Beit Shmuel section 5 and as it appears from the Rema in section 2 who wrote that she needs a get from the second husband but did not write if she is forbidden to him or not, because in this case, there is a distinction between knowing and not knowing).

And when it is known from the invalidation that we said that if she married, she does not need to be divorced, some say that this applies even if she has no children, similar to a get (divorce document) without a date. And some say that it applies only if she has children, as explained in section 11. And regarding a get written during the day and signed at night or after several days, or given after several days, according to the Rif, Rambam, and Ramah, its status is like an early get that was written invalidly as we explained. But according to the Rosh, Tur, Aitur, and the glosses of Maimonides (Chapter 1), and Rabbeinu Yerucham, and it also seems to be the opinion of Rav Hai Gaon (as cited in the Rosh), it is valid in a time of necessity.

However, what is considered a pressing situation (sha'at hadchak)? The Tur writes that it is when it is impossible to obtain another get (bill of divorce), and Rashi of blessed memory explained (Gittin 19a) that it is when the husband went on his way or when she has already remarried, end quote. It could be interpreted that if she remarried, even if the first husband is in the city, there is no need to provide another get so that she will not be disdained by her current husband (Gra, section 9). In this case, it is more lenient than other disqualifications by the Rabbis because we rely on Rabbi Shimon who holds that this is a valid get.

One might question whether, if the get is given through a messenger and the husband has already gone overseas, this also constitutes a pressing situation, and if we can initially give her the get. The great authorities agreed that this too is considered a pressing situation, and the messenger is instructed to give her the get (as cited in the name of the Maharit and the Rachash). However, if it is possible to obtain another get, even from a distance, she is not permitted to remarry with this get (as cited there), even if it has already been delivered to her, provided she has not yet remarried. It is obvious that if she has merely become engaged to someone else, this alone does not constitute a pressing situation.

If the get (bill of divorce) is written during the day but they didn't manage to sign it until the night, and it is written in the get before the signing that "this get was written on such-and-such a day and the witnesses did not manage to sign it until the night," and then the witnesses sign afterwards, it is valid. This is because there is no longer a concern about adultery or the fruits of the land, since it is explicitly stated that it was signed the next day. The same applies if it is signed several days later, as long as it is specified before the signatures that it was signed on such-and-such a day. This is also valid in other documents, as written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 43. Similarly, if one witness signs on the day it is written and the second witness does not manage to sign until the night, and it is written between the signatures that "this get was written and signed on such-and-such a day and the second witness did not manage to sign until the night," it is also valid, as written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 44. Certainly, this is only valid after the fact (b'diavad), and it should not be done initially (l'chatchila), as it adds more than twelve lines to the get. However, in the case of a deathbed (sh'chiv me'ra), where it is seen that there is not enough time to write another get at night and she would remain bound to her levir (brother-in-law), they can initially do so. It is also possible that in a situation of potential being chained (agunah), such as when it is estimated that afterwards he will not agree to give the get and she will remain an agunah, they can also rely on this initially. However, this is an uncommon situation where his mind would change in such a short time. Certainly, it is better to write and sign at night, even though it is not customary to give a get at night, than to sign on another day after the get was written, even if it is written in the get that "this get was written etc."

And they asked in the Gemara (18a): For bills of divorce that come from overseas, which are written in Nisan but do not arrive until Tishrei, what benefit did the Sages achieve with their decree? Meaning, how did the Sages invalidate a predated bill of divorce? After all, a bill of divorce sent by a messenger from a distant place is necessarily predated, as its delivery is far removed from the time of writing and signing. This raises concerns about covering up infidelity and regarding the fruits (profits), as she could claim them from buyers who purchased from him until the delivery, by presenting her bill of divorce and asserting that she was divorced from the date written on the bill. In truth, the husband is entitled to the fruits until the time of delivery, as we have said, and she would be wrongfully seizing them. 

The Gemara resolves that bills of divorce brought by a messenger have a public awareness (a voice), as it becomes known that the delivery happened after the writing date. People will investigate to determine the actual day of delivery, thus avoiding any issues. You might ask, if so, why is it necessary to write the date on a bill of divorce sent by a messenger? Indeed, the date creates public awareness, as people see from the date that the delivery did not occur on the day of writing (Tosafot). Without a date, there would be no attention to the matter. 

Furthermore, one might question why a predated bill of divorce is invalid, as the witnesses know it was not delivered on the writing date, and this also becomes publicly known. This is not a valid question because the Sages did not rely on public awareness except in the case of a bill of divorce sent by a messenger, where it is unavoidable (Ran). For a bill of divorce sent, the matter is more widely known than for a bill written locally.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5 that a get (bill of divorce) not delivered on the day it was written cannot be validated except by sending it to her via a messenger. This ruling was also written by the earlier authorities. There is someone who wishes to say that based on what we wrote, the reason that the sages did not want to rely on the leniency except in the case of gets that are sent, where there is no alternative, and therefore does not agree with this ruling, since it is possible to give another get (Beit Shmuel, subsection 6). However, this is not necessarily a reason to invalidate it after the fact, as it is clear that initially, one should not do so, as our teacher the Rema wrote that it is customary to be stringent and write another get. But after the fact, it should not be invalidated, since it was sent via a messenger. And what we said, that the sages did not want to rely on the leniency except in the case of gets that are sent, is definitely true. The sages did not want to establish this ruling for all earlier gets. If there was no necessity from sent gets, the sages would not have validated it in any case. But since, due to sent gets, they had to establish this and rely on the leniency where there is no alternative, it follows that this ruling is effective for any get sent via a messenger, and it cannot be invalidated, since it is a rabbinic enactment. However, initially, one should not do so if it is possible to write another get. But after the fact, it is clear that it is valid (and so wrote the Beit Meir).

And know that this ruling applies only to a case where the earlier date was written in a kosher manner but its delivery was delayed. However, if the date was truly earlier, meaning it was written with a preceding date, this remedy to send it via a messenger does not help. Even in cases of divorce documents sent from afar, if the date of writing is earlier, the document is invalid just like any other predated divorce document, as the Sages did not make a remedy for those who write falsehoods. This is also agreed upon by the great later authorities (Bach, Beit Shmuel 6:6 at the end of his words, Gra, Beit Meir, and Taz). The Ran writes: "And if you say, why is a predated divorce document invalid? Since its time precedes its delivery, it has a voice, etc." Therefore, it seems to me that only in divorce documents that come from distant lands do they rely on the voice because of the agunah (a woman whose husband is missing and cannot remarry) and similarly in the case where one deposits a divorce document for his wife and he goes on his way. His intention refers to a truly earlier document written with a preceding date, as one of the great authorities (Taz) also wrote: "The main ruling is that a truly predated document, or one written by day and signed by night, is invalid and has no remedy. But a document where there was a delay between writing and delivery by the husband has a remedy to send it via a messenger. If it is easily possible to give another divorce document, he should write another one." And this is as we have written.

Nevertheless, there is another detail in this matter as written by one of the great Acharonim (end of section 13), and these are his words: "In my humble opinion, regarding the law, if an early get (divorce document) is one that was written on the tenth of the month and they wrote in it the fifth of the month and similarly if they intentionally predated it, and it has signed witnesses, this get should not be validated through a messenger because the get is invalid due to the witnesses signing falsely and they are thus disqualified, etc. However, if that get does not have signed witnesses or even if it does have signed witnesses but the predated time in the get was not intentional at all, such as if they erred in the calculation of the month or they wrote the day of the declaration that the husband instructed them, etc., in a manner that the signing witnesses are not disqualified, in such a case, even though it is entirely predated as it was written on the tenth of the month and they wrote in it the fifth, it should be validated and given through a messenger, because anything given through a messenger has a public awareness and there is no concern for illegitimate relations or for fruits (issues of property rights), etc." This is his conclusion, and perhaps one can rely on this in cases of agunah (a woman unable to remarry due to her husband's absence or refusal to grant a divorce), and so it should be ruled in times of necessity (as it appears to me).

And they asked in the Gemara (17b) about the decree regarding the time of writing it and placing it in one's pocket, what is the law? And they answered: A person does not bring misfortune upon himself in advance. Refer there for the explanation of the matter: What did the Sages achieve with their decree, as we hold that one may write a bill of divorce for a man even if his wife is not with him. Given this, he can keep the bill of divorce in his pocket and give it to her later, and he can cover up her infidelity. And they answered that people do not usually do this—to bring something that is not good forward before its time. And if one does so, it is assumed that immediately after writing it, he will give it to her (Tosafot, s.v. "until," refer there). And if indeed the matter is prolonged, there is a remedy to send it through a messenger, as it is written.

And based on this, it is puzzling regarding the Rambam, of blessed memory, at the beginning of Chapter 2, where he wrote: "Similarly, if one told a scribe, 'Write me a bill of divorce for my wife,' and told witnesses to sign, they write and sign, and give it to him, and he divorces with it whenever he wants." This implies clearly that he permits ab initio (from the outset) to divorce with it after some time. How can this be said, for there is a concern of promiscuity, and this is the main reason for the enactment of the Sages regarding writing the date?

However, I found one of the early authorities (Nimukei Yosef, Chapter 1 of Bava Metzia) who wrote in this language: "Even if it is certain that it was written in Nisan and he placed it in his pocket and did not give it until Tishrei, it is valid." And so wrote the Rambam, of blessed memory, and the Ramban, of blessed memory, agreed with him. It is not similar to other documents for two reasons: First, in a bill of divorce, it is uncommon to predate because a person does not bring misfortune upon himself. For this reason, it is taught that ab initio, one writes a bill of divorce for a man even though his wife is not with him, and we do not worry that he will predate it. Therefore, if it happened that he did so, it is not invalid. This is not the case with other documents where a person might predate them. Additionally, the main purpose of writing a bill of divorce is for divorce, and for divorce it is entirely valid. Because of an uncommon concern, it is not invalidated for divorce. However, other documents, etc."

And it is explained the intention of the Rambam, interpreting what the Sages said that a person does not bring misfortune upon himself, meaning that it is an uncommon matter. Therefore, if it happened incidentally, we do not worry about it (and there is no need for the forced explanation of the Beit Shmuel, Section 7, and the minister did not remember Joseph, see there and analyze thoroughly).

According to this, there is a dispute among the early authorities regarding a situation where someone wrote a get (bill of divorce) for his wife and it remained with him for several days. According to Rambam, Ramban, and the Nimukei Yosef, he is permitted to give it to her himself because it is an uncommon situation and the Rabbis did not decree against it. However, according to Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur, the only solution is to deliver it through a messenger. Since our teachers, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, only mentioned this opinion, this is the ruling we follow. However, in a case of potential agunah (a woman who is unable to remarry), and it is impossible to deliver it through a messenger, we can rely on the opinion of our teachers who permit him to give it himself (as also written by Beit Meir). Similarly, a person can escrow a get with a third party to be given to his wife after some time, and there is no concern of it being predated (Talmud, ibid.), as in such a case, the matter becomes known.

It is implied from Rashi (17: s.v. ad) that a woman who comes to seize property from buyers who purchased from her husband after the time of the get (divorce document) needs to bring proof as to when the get reached her hand. However, all of our rabbis disagree with this. They say that this only applies to a get that is found, which has a defect because it might have fallen from its owner and was not properly guarded. But for any woman who brings a get, we say that it was presumably delivered on the day it was written, and she does not need to bring proof unless there is a defect in it. This is also the ruling in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 5.

Some say that just as the Sages permitted a get (divorce document) to be delivered by an agent after some time, so too if the husband himself brings it to the place of the wife, we do not worry about it being antedated, as the matter is public knowledge, just like when delivered by an agent. There is no concern of it being antedated (Yam Shel Shlomo, Chapter 2, Section 5; this is also written by the Mahara'i). There is an explicit Baraita (Gittin 5a) that states: If he himself brought his get, he does not need to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed." It is clear from there that the husband can bring his own get, and it is assumed that it is not on the day of the writing of the get. Thus, we see that we do not worry about it being antedated in this case (ibid.).

If one instructed two or three people to write a get (divorce document), sign it, and deliver it to his wife, but the matter was delayed and they did not write it on the day they were commanded, even if a long time passed, and they went to another place, or if they wrote it on the same day but it was found not to be written according to halacha, and they need to write another get, they should not write the date as the day the husband commanded them, nor the place he commanded them, but rather the date of the day they are writing now and the place they are currently in.

For example, if they were in Jerusalem when the husband instructed them and it was in Tishrei, and it was delayed until Nisan and they are now in Lod, they should write the date as Nisan and the place as Lod.

This is also the law regarding other documents, except for acquisition documents, as mentioned in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 43. Even though the get is in the language of the husband, and how can they write in Nisan in Lod, "I, so-and-so," when he was not in Lod in Nisan? For other documents that are in the language of the witnesses, it makes sense since they are currently in that place, but the get is in the language of the husband. We say that since they are his agents, and an agent of a person is like the person himself, if not, how could they write, "I, so-and-so"?

Since they are like him, they can properly write in Nisan in Lod, as they are currently there. The explanation is that the husband commanded them to write a get for his wife, and it is as if they write in Nisan in Lod on behalf of so-and-so. However, the format of the get is not like this because "he shall write" refers to the scribe writing on behalf of the husband and in the language of the husband. This is also explicitly proven in Yevamot 116 regarding a get found in Sura that was written in Sura, "I, Anan bar Chiya," etc., and he was actually in Nehardea. The Gemara there says that the matters were entrusted, and examine this well.

And know that in other documents, there are some authorities who required mentioning in the document the place where the matters were also delivered (Rashbam Bava Batra 172, and Nimukei Yosef and Mordechai there). And they write: "In such-and-such a place, we wrote what we saw in such-and-such a place." Based on this, there is someone who says that it is necessary to write at the end of the get (divorce document), before "according to the law of Moses and Israel," in this language: "This get was instructed to us by the husband, so-and-so, in such-and-such a place at such-and-such a time, to write a get for his wife, so-and-so, and its writing was delayed until such-and-such a day in such-and-such a city, according to the law of Moses and Israel," and the witnesses sign. And if they did not do so, there is concern to invalidate it because it appears like falsehood, according to the opinion of these authorities we mentioned. But in a pressing situation, where it is a case of a chained woman (agunah) and it is impossible to obtain another get that would be written with this formula at the end of the get, one can be lenient and rely on the opinion of those who permit writing simply, "in Nisan and in Lod" (Gra, section 222).

In my humble opinion, it appears that one should not write this even initially, as it is prone to error. There is clear evidence from Yevamot that we cited, where the get (divorce document) was a standard get like all other gittin, as is proven there. It is not similar to other legal documents, which are in the language of the witnesses. When they write a record of testimony that occurred before us on a particular day in a particular place, where someone told us something, there is indeed concern that it might appear false, as he did not say it to them on that specific day and in that specific place. But with a get, which is in the language of the husband and written by the scribe on his behalf, it frees his wife from that day. How can they write in the get “this get was commanded to us, etc.” as if they are the ones writing the get? Is it not the husband who writes the get, and the scribe is like the husband himself? The scribe’s presence in a specific place on a specific day is like the husband’s presence. Furthermore, in the get, it does not say “on a specific day in a specific place I am here,” but rather “on a specific day in a specific place I free my wife.” The truth is that on that day and in that place, he frees her, as the scribe writes the get on his behalf on that day in that place. Therefore, all the decisors did not mention this (as it appears to me).

And if they did not do so, but rather wrote the place that the husband told them and the time that he told them, it is considered like all rabbinic disqualifications that were explained in Siman 150. This is also explicitly indicated in the Gemara (Perek). Similarly, the Rivash (Siman 382) wrote so, and so did the Ramban and the Ra'ah of blessed memory. The reason is that it appears like a lie. And even though we hold that we do not worry about something appearing like a lie (Ketubot 85b: Gittin 26b), not all lies are similar to one another (there). However, if they did not change their place but only delayed writing and wrote today as the husband commanded them, since it was delivered by a valid messenger, it is acceptable after the fact (Gittin 20:20). For this is not a complete predated document since the husband indeed commanded them on that day. But when they are in a different place, since they are compelled to write the place where they are currently standing, it is impossible to validate it if they wrote the day the husband commanded them. For if they write the place of writing and the time of the command, there is no greater discrepancy than this, and it is disqualified. But when they did not change their place and are standing in the same place where the husband commanded them, certainly, ideally, they should write the day of writing. However, after the fact, if they wrote the day of the command and it was delivered by a valid messenger, it is acceptable (there).

It has already been explained that, ideally, one should write all the details of the time: the day of the week, the day of the month, and the year. However, mentioning the day of the week has no basis, as it is not found anywhere in the Tanakh. Therefore, if it is not written, it does not invalidate the document at all (Beit Shmuel, subsection 11). The Rambam wrote even more in Chapter 1, Law 26, and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 7, that a get (divorce document) which does not have the exact date but rather states "the first or second Shabbat of a certain month" or "in a certain month" or "in a certain year" without specifying the month—even if it writes "in a certain Sabbatical year"—is valid. This is explicitly stated in the Gemara (17b), and they asked, "If so, what did the Sages achieve with their enactment?" They answered that the benefit is for the previous Sabbatical year, so that if she committed adultery, they would judge her accordingly. Otherwise, even if the exact day is written, there is still a concern that she might commit adultery in the morning, and in the evening he would write her a get, and she would claim that she was divorced in the morning. Thus, the benefit is for the previous time.

And one should not ask, "What benefit is there in this ordinance? After all, if she commits adultery, he will write her a bill of divorce in such-and-such a year or even more, in such-and-such a Sabbatical year, and her adultery will not be clarified." It can be said that generally, the husband's knowledge of the adultery does not occur soon after the act because surely she committed adultery in secret. And even if it becomes known, he is not concerned that it will be revealed to the court. Most of the time, months and years will pass before it becomes known to the court. Therefore, in most cases, there is benefit from the time period (Mahar"m Schiff). The sages did not want to impose excessive stringency in their ordinance, and as long as there is some time, it suffices. It appears to me that nowadays, the time of the Sabbatical year is irrelevant, as this applies only when Sabbatical years and Jubilees are counted, and they would write in the third Sabbatical year of the Jubilee. But now, this is not a valid indicator at all. And more than a Sabbatical year will never be a valid indicator, such as writing a specific Jubilee year, which means nothing. Furthermore, it seems to me that a month without a year is meaningless, even if he writes the day of the month and the week, because it is not clear in which year it is (and this is evident from Rashi's commentary, who explained that writing the month without the year is not valid, as he wrote there).

And there are some of our rabbis who hold that even initially one can do so, to write "the second week of the month of a certain month of a certain year" or just "the year" (Rashi and Rashba). But from the language of Rambam, it implies that it is only valid post facto. And there is doubt regarding his intention: whether he means that it is valid after it has already been given, or even if it was written this way, it can be given (and this is also found in Beit Yosef, see there, and in the commentary of the Shach, section 12). The Rif and the Rosh omitted this law, and I do not know why.

The Rambam, of blessed memory, also wrote: "Similarly, if it says 'today I have divorced you,' it is valid, as it implies the same day the get (divorce document) was issued." This is what he wrote, and similarly, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote there that "today" implies the day that this get is issued (Bava Batra 172b), and we consider it as a complete time (Rashbam). And since the witnesses see it in her hand and it is written "today," it is considered as having a date written in it (there). Even if the year is not written at all, it is valid (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 13). There are some of our rabbis who hold that "today" by itself is meaningless because it does not specify a clear time. Rather, it means as a condition that the get will not take effect until the day it is clarified in the court that it was in her hand (Ramban there), or it will be clarified by the witnesses of delivery on the day it was given to her (Shita Mekubetzet in the name of Ri'az, chapter 2 of Gittin). According to this, the court or the witnesses need to write for her in a document that it was clarified to them that on such-and-such a day he divorced her, and then she is divorced (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 13, and Atzei Gittin).

The Rambam also wrote that if the date was cut off from the get (divorce document) and he gave it to her, it is valid. Many disagree with him, arguing that if so, what did the Sages accomplish with their ordinance? Certainly, this ruling is like all rabbinic invalidations, such as a get without a date. The Rambam, of blessed memory, holds that since it is an uncommon situation, the Sages did not decree upon it. This follows his reasoning regarding a get in the husband's hand, that he can give it to her whenever he wants, and we are not concerned about the date because it is an uncommon matter, as we explained in section 30. Similarly, in this case, because it is not common, when it happens that someone does this, we do not prohibit her. However, most authorities disagree with this. It is surprising that our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 8, wrote that the Rambam's opinion is primary, and the later authorities have criticized him for this. (The Rambam interprets what the Sages said in Gittin 17: "the decree regarding the date, etc., for a trickster," meaning that it is an uncommon matter, and when it happens, we are not concerned about it and permit her).

In the days of the Talmudic sages, they would write in documents and bills of divorce according to the years of the reigning kings for the sake of governmental harmony. If one deviated from this practice, the bill of divorce would be invalid. However, nowadays, since even the nations no longer count by the years of the kings in their documents, this practice has been nullified for many hundreds of years. The entire world uses other systems of counting, and all Jews worldwide count from the creation of the world. Therefore, all the legal authorities have written that if a scribe omitted the count from the creation of the world, it is still valid, because everyone knows that our reckoning is from the creation of the world. This is also the ruling in the Shulchan Aruch, section 10 (Tosafot Avodah Zarah 10b, s.v. "Sifra").

And the Rambam wrote in the first chapter: "And all of Israel has already adopted the practice of dating bills of divorce either from the creation of the world or from the reign of Alexander the Macedonian, which is the era of contracts. If one dated it according to the reign of the ruling kingdom at that time in a country where that kingdom has authority, it is valid." These are his words. Now, the era of contracts has already been abolished. If one were to date a bill of divorce according to it now, its status appears to be as the Rambam wrote earlier: "If one dated it according to a kingdom that does not rule that country, or according to the building or destruction of the Temple, if it is customary in that place to use such dates, it is valid. If it is not customary, it is invalid." These are his words. And since it is no longer customary to use the era of contracts, it is invalid. However, there is no proof from this, for if so, why does he validate it if dated according to the reigning kingdom at that time in a country where it is no longer customary to date as such? Rather, it is certain that the reason for invalidity is because we are concerned that the ruling power might object. Although nowadays we do not write according to their years, nonetheless, writing according to a kingdom that does not rule that country or according to the building or destruction of the Temple might cause objection, unlike the era of contracts, which would not cause objection (as it appears in Beit Yosef, there). Similarly, there is no objection in places where it is customary for the people to write in a particular manner (there). There are those who argue that nowadays, since there is no objection, there should be no invalidity on account of objection (there). From this, it appears that if one were to date a bill of divorce according to the era that the nations count by now, it would be valid, though this requires further investigation. The decisors did not address this issue at all, because nowadays everyone dates according to the creation of the world.

In the enumeration of years from the creation of the world, there are four categories: thousands, hundreds, tens, and units. For example, now they write five thousand, six hundred and forty-five. Our master, Rabbi Yosef Caro, wrote that if one omitted the thousands and hundreds and just wrote the specific year, it is still valid. Even if one omitted the creation of the world, it is still valid. He also wrote that if one omitted the five thousand and only wrote thousands, it is valid. Furthermore, he wrote that if one wrote the general and the specific small unit but omitted the middle specific unit, for example, if one wrote five thousand and forty-five and omitted six hundred, it is invalid. However, if she has married, she does not need to leave him. Some say that she requires a valid get (bill of divorce) from the first husband and can then stay with the second. This is similarly ruled in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 43, see there.

And behold, what is written about omitting the thousands and hundreds, that it is valid, the reason is straightforward because the intention is known to everyone. And evidence is that even in letters, when they write the year, they do not write at all the count of the thousands. Therefore, even when omitting the hundreds, everyone knows the intention. And some say that even if he omits the tens, for example, if he writes the year as five, it is valid (Beit Shmuel section 118). However, in my humble opinion, there is room to question this, for our teacher the Beit Yosef in Choshen Mishpat there in the Shulchan Aruch omitted this, and also in his great book there, he wrote that his opinion tends to validate but nevertheless he is uncertain about it and did not write this in the Shulchan Aruch. So how can we validate this in a get (divorce document)? And reason testifies that this has no meaning for the readers. And so one of the later authorities wrote that in such a case, it is invalid (Turei Zahav), for in this case, there is certainly a concern to cover up her infidelity, as one might say it refers to ten years earlier.

And this which he wrote by skipping five, it is valid. The reasoning is straightforward: everyone understands that the term "thousands" refers to five thousand, for it cannot mean two thousand. If it were so, it should have been written with two Yuds, "אלפיים" (alpayim). And although in the Torah it is written with one Yud, nevertheless, in human writing, another Yud is needed (Beit Shmuel). Additionally, there is no mistake that it was written three thousand years earlier.

And that which is written, omitting the middle detail, is invalid. The reason is that people are not accustomed to writing in such a manner, and it appears as if it were indeed early. It should not be compared to what is written in Siman 126 regarding when one confuses the day of the week with the day of the month, where it is valid, because from the day of the week, it is evident that there was an error of one day in the month. This is not the case here. And even though it is certain that if we consider this detail to pertain to six hundred years earlier, the day of the week would not align with the days of the month, it is not evident from it, because most people are not aware of calculations from centuries ago (Beit Yosef).

And this is what is written: "If she has married, she does not need to leave him." It appears that even if she has no children, she does not need to leave him, and she also does not need a get (divorce document) from the first husband. This is different from a completely predated get and all rabbinic invalidations, where she would need a get even if she has married, as stated in Siman 150. This is because there are several reasons to permit it. One reason is that the lack of thousands does not invalidate it, so why should the lack of hundreds be worse? Additionally, everyone understands that the hundreds are missing, and no one would think that it was written many hundreds of years earlier. Furthermore, since the tens and units of this year are visible, it is as if it is proven from within that it is not predated. At the very least, it is not worse than a get without a date, where she does not need to leave him even if she has no children. However, there is an opinion that is stringent, like with all rabbinic invalidations, requiring her to have a kosher get from the first husband and then she may remain with the second husband (as the Beit Shmuel also wrote). It is clear that if the units are missing, it is considered a completely predated get (Levush and Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 21), as it certainly appears clearly that it was written in earlier years, and its ruling is as stated in paragraph 21 there.

It is necessary to mention in a get (bill of divorce) the place of the husband, the wife, and the witnesses. And there are forty-eight sections on this:

It is necessary to mention in a get the place where it is written and signed, and this is why we write "on such and such a date, in the city of..." etc. This is a rabbinic enactment to write the place where the get is made. According to the Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur, and it also appears from the Rambam, the main concern is the place of the witnesses and not the place of the scribe. What concern is there with the scribe? But with the witnesses, it is a good enactment for the preservation of the world, lest a challenge arise, so we may know who the witnesses are in order to validate it through them (Levush). If we do not write the name of the city, who will know who the witnesses are? Indeed, there are many Yosef ben Shimon in the world. However, we cannot say the reason is to be able to refute their testimony by saying, "You were with us." It is necessary to write the place where they were at the time of writing the get because we hold that the essential act of divorce is through the document, and the signing of the witnesses is only for the betterment of the world (there). As for the witnesses of the delivery, there is no benefit in writing the place, for perhaps it was delivered in a different place, and those witnesses cannot be refuted. Therefore, the first reason seems correct (Tosafot and Rosh in the corresponding place; see there).

However, there are some of the great early authorities (Semag, Sefer HaTerumot, and Hagahot Maimoniot, Chapter 1) who hold that one must also be particular about the location of the scribe, and this is also implied by the plain language of the Gemara (Perek: which says "but for the scribe"). According to the first opinion, if the scribe writes in Tiberias and the witnesses sign in Sepphoris, one should write Sepphoris in the get. According to this opinion, everyone must be in the same place, as it is not possible otherwise. Certainly, one should not write the location of the scribe separately and the location of the witnesses separately, for the enactment was not made in this way. Necessarily, they must be in the same place (and with this, the words of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch at the end of Section 1 are understood; see there). As for the reasoning of those who hold this opinion, it can be said that indeed the entire get is in the language of the husband, and the location of the husband is explained in the get. Therefore, there is no reason to mention the places of the witnesses as well, except that the matters of the get need to be clarified because it needs to be written and signed for him and for her. Therefore, it is necessary to clarify in which place this significant matter was written and signed. Just as the scribe must also recognize the man and the woman, as stated in Section 120, so too regarding the place where they are standing, the scribe is equal to the witnesses. The first opinion holds that it is not comparable to recognition, where it is necessary to recognize them because he must write it for him and for her, and if he does not recognize them, it is not considered for him and for her. However, the location where he stands is not relevant at all (and see Beit Shmuel, section 4). Furthermore, the truth is that the get is in the language of the husband, but he writes according to our counting and speaks with the witnesses, therefore the location of the witnesses is written (there, section 1). But with the scribe, he does not speak; rather, he is his agent to write.

And if the location of the witnesses and the scribe is not written at all, the leading later authorities (Beit Shmuel, Gra, and Taz) agree that the get (divorce document) is valid. For certainly, the sages did not establish a regulation to invalidate the get because of this, and it is not similar to a case where there is no date, where there is a concern for potential misuse. But in this case, there is no concern for misuse; rather, it is a good regulation, as we have explained. And it is simple that if the get has not yet been given and there is time to rewrite another get with the location of their standing, then another get should be written.

And there is a question regarding this matter: some of our Rabbis hold that for anything that does not need to be mentioned, if there is a change, it does not invalidate (Tosafot, Perek [chapter]... D.H. "VeSham"). Therefore, since a change in the place where the witnesses stand invalidates it, as will be explained, it is necessary that the deficiency is a hindrance. The answer to this is that this general rule only applies to something where the falsehood is not evident from it, such as a change in the place of birth, which will be explained later, where it was their custom to write it since not everyone knows the birthplace, and it is not something noticeable. But in the place where the witnesses stand, where the falsehood is evident from it, for example, if they come to disqualify the witnesses and say they are false witnesses since they were with us in a certain place, certainly, the change invalidates it even though the deficiency is not a hindrance (Gemara Paragraph).

Therefore, if they changed the place of their standing and wrote that it was written in another place, the get (divorce document) is invalid even in pressing circumstances (there). And if she remarried, she does not have to leave (her new husband) as with all rabbinically invalid documents, whose rules will be explained in Siman 150. This is the opinion of the Rambam and the Rosh, and this is also the plain ruling in the Shulchan Aruch, section 1, and no other opinion is mentioned. But this is the language of the Tur: If the place of the witnesses' standing was changed, Rabbi Chananel wrote that if she remarried, the child is a mamzer (illegitimate). And so wrote the Ra'avad, that even if she remarried, she must leave (her new husband), but the child from the second (husband) is legitimate, but from the first (if she returned to him without a get from the second), the child is a mamzer. This does not seem correct to the Rosh, of blessed memory. And Rabbeinu Tam ruled that the child is legitimate, but she should not remarry with it initially. According to Rashi, she may remarry with it initially, and this is also the opinion of the Rif. End of quote. And it means that when the get was already given.

And behold, what is stated that according to Rabbi Chananel, the child is a definite mamzer, does not mean that he would be permitted to marry a full mamzeret, as this is only rabbinic. Rather, his intention is that the child is a rabbinic mamzer (Bach), as he holds that this is considered a change from the established norm set by the sages, and the child is a mamzer by their ruling. In the first case, when she remarries without a get from the second husband, the child is a Torah-level mamzer, because according to Torah law, she is fully divorced, and the second marriage is considered a complete marriage. And this is what is written, that according to Rashi and the Rif, she may initially marry him, not that it is explicitly stated in their words, but the Tur inferred this as their intention, and there is no clear proof for this from the study of the issue. And so wrote one of the greats (Gra on Even HaEzer 4:4 in the name of Ra'am), and our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, took as primary the opinion of the Rambam, Rabbeinu Tam, and the Rosh, and this seems to be the main opinion (Gra). And there are those who were concerned with the opinion of the Ra'avad that she should leave (Beit Shmuel 4:3 and Taz 4:3), and this needs to be considered, for they wrote that even Rav Hai Gaon agrees with the ruling of the Shulchan Aruch.

And know that there is someone who says that a change is considered not only a complete change, such as writing a different city, but even if he writes the name of the same city with a slight change, like the city of Tunis if he writes "Tunas" or the city of Lepanto if he writes "Lipunat," the get (divorce document) is invalid (Get Pashut 3:3). Similarly, one of the greats wrote about a city named Pilitz, and they wrote "Pilz," which is considered a change of name (Noda BiYehuda Part 1). However, there are changes that one need not be so particular about after the fact or in a case of preventing a woman from becoming an agunah (a chained woman who cannot remarry) or in a pressing situation (Get Pashut), like in Constantinople if he wrote "Kushtantin," replacing a 'd' with a 't', or if he wrote "Kushtantin," it is valid as the change is not so noticeable. But "Tunas" and "Tunis," the change is noticeable. Similarly, the city of Ishkupi, where they did not write the yud after the aleph, was validated (there). Therefore, those who sit in judgment should be precise regarding changes, which to validate and which to invalidate (there). However, there are some of the greats who hold that these changes are not considered changes but rather as if the name of the place was not written at all, and this seems correct (Beit Meir and others), and this requires further investigation.

In truth, it appears that if, according to the reader's pronunciation, it seems like a completely different city, it is certainly considered a change. However, if according to his pronunciation it is recognizable as the city, but it is written with an error, there is no concern about invalidating it after the fact. According to this, everything depends on the discernment of the Beit Din (rabbinic court). Additionally, we observe perplexing practices in the writing of city names. For instance, in my hometown, which everyone calls Babruysk—both Jews and non-Jews, and it is written that way in all scripts and languages, including royal documents—they write "Babruysk" in the get (divorce document). Similarly, in the city where I am currently, Navahrudak, they write in the get without an aleph between the dalet and the kuf, which is puzzling since the kamatz (vowel) pulls towards an aleph, and in every language, they pronounce the dalet with a kamatz. Moreover, according to the writing they use, there would be three consecutive shva vowels, which is impossible as is well known. Therefore, it must be that the reader reads it with a kamatz even without the aleph, and it seems that more likely they read it with a patach, which would be considered a name change. When I first came here, I contemplated this matter extensively but refrained from changing it because all the great authorities before us wrote it this way. It must be, by necessity, that since it is known that they wrote it this way in the get, everyone understands that this is not considered a change.

It is written in the Mordechai, Parashat HaMegarash, a responsum of Ritzba and Rashba, authors of the Tosafot, and these are their words: Regarding a get (divorce document) that was brought from the land of the Ger (Germans) etc., and what they call Borzish and we call Baorish, it seems to me that since it is evident from the place of residence of the man and the place where the get was written that it came from the land of the Ger, and their language is to speak in a simplified manner, there is no need to be particular at all. End of quote. 

And we learn from the words of our Rabbis that the reason we hold that the name of the place of delivery is primary is when the names are distinct. But with one name, where according to the dialect, it changes slightly in letters and pronunciations from one country to another, and in the place of delivery it is known that in the place of writing they speak this way and they know that this is the name of the city or river where they call it one way and here they call it another way, there is no need to be particular at all if they wrote it according to the pronunciation of the place of writing.

They further wrote there, and these are their words: "What they wrote about the river YIR, and we customarily write about the river KIR, since there is no letter in the place of the foreign language, thus a yod is equivalent to a kuf." End of quote. And the matter is sealed (see Ahash and Gaf, section 3). It seems to me that the explanation is certainly if there was another letter there in the place of writing under the kuf of the place of giving, it would be a complete change of name (like Nafata and Tafata, section 3). But since in the place of writing there is no other letter under the kuf, rather the kuf is missing, thus a yod is equal to a kuf, meaning that it is the same when it starts with a yod as if it started with a kuf. Everyone understands that it is the same river called here KIR, but in the name they omitted the kuf and took a shorter language YIR, which is a shortened form of the name. This is what is meant by another letter in place of the foreign language, that is, in place of the foreign kuf (as it appears to me).

The Darkei Moshe wrote in the name of Mahari"v that if a get (divorce document) is written within the suburbs of a city, it is written "standing here" because the suburbs of the city are considered like the city itself (end quote, Beit Shmuel, section 1). It seems that the explanation is as follows: if there is a wall around the city or the houses themselves are adjacent to each other around the city to the extent that it is obvious that this is the end of the city (as explained by Rashi at the beginning of chapter 5 of Eruvin), and behind the wall there are still houses within the suburbs of the city, that is, within seventy and two-thirds cubits, and the person who is divorcing or being divorced is standing there, they can write in the get "standing in such-and-such a city" or "standing in such-and-such a place." Similarly, if a get is written there, they can write the name of the city, because within the suburbs of the city, it is considered as the city itself. It implies that beyond the suburbs of the city, one should not write the name of the city, even if it is within the city's boundary, because what relevance does the boundary have to the city? The same law applies concerning vows, as it is taught (Nedarim 56b): one who vows not to enter a city is permitted to enter its boundary but prohibited from entering its suburbs. The Gemara there explains, as it is written, "And it came to pass when Joshua was by Jericho," and it is impossible to say he was in Jericho itself, for it is written, "Now Jericho was tightly shut up," but he was in the suburbs of Jericho. It is impossible to say he was in the boundary of Jericho, for concerning the boundary it is written in the Torah, "And you shall measure from outside the city on the east side two thousand cubits," meaning that outside the city is called outside and not the city itself. See there.

And it is necessary to be precise according to this, regarding what is written in Joshua (21:11) "And they gave to the children of Aaron... and they gave them the city of Arba... it is Hebron in the mountain of Judah, and its surrounding fields and the fields of the city and its courtyards they gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh as his inheritance." And at the beginning of Judges it is written "And they gave to Caleb Hebron as Moses had spoken..." And it must be that it was far from Hebron much more than its outskirts, for it was beyond the pasture lands, and the pasture land itself is a thousand cubits as it is written in the book of Numbers, and the pasture land itself is called outside the city as it is written there "And the pasture lands of the cities which you shall give to the Levites, from the wall of the city and outward a thousand cubits around." And nonetheless it is called in Judges Hebron. And so the sages said (Baba Batra 122b, Makkot 10a) that there is a question there on the verse in Judges, how did they give it to Caleb, for it was a city of refuge. And they answered that they gave him the outskirts of the city, villages, fields, and courtyards that were adjacent to it and were called by its name, they gave to Caleb (Rashi). And it must be said that this is not a general principle, for this is only generally speaking, that outside the outskirts is not like the city, but if they are called by the name of the city, even if very far, they have the name of the city upon them, not because they belong to the city, but because they are called by the name of the city. And so it was in Hebron, that they called even the villages around it by the name Hebron. And so the sages said there in Makkot about the city of Kedesh, that one was a large city, a fortified city, and a medium city adjacent to it that they also called Kedesh by its name.

Additionally, it seems to me that there is no difficulty regarding the distance from Hebron to Jericho at all. This distinction of "within the outskirts" and "beyond the outskirts" applies only to a city that has a surrounding wall or where the houses themselves are contiguous with each other, forming a wall around the city. In such a case, it is appropriate to refer to an area as "outside the city." However, in a city that does not have a surrounding wall, and the houses are not contiguous, how can one define "outside the city"? Who can determine where the edge of the city is? According to this, it makes sense that Jericho was surrounded by a wall, as is evident there, whereas Hebron was a city of refuge, and cities of refuge are prohibited from being surrounded by a wall, as indicated in Makkot (where it questions about fortified cities). And this is explicitly stated at the end of the tractate Arakhin that cities of refuge do not have a surrounding wall. Therefore, even if it is very far, it is still called by the name of the city. Nevertheless, it is impossible to say this because in Nedarim, no distinction is made between a city with a wall and a city without a wall. Additionally, it is derived from the verse "you shall measure from outside the city" written regarding the cities of the Levites, and their cities did not have a surrounding wall as indicated in Arakhin. Therefore, it is certain that once the houses of the city are completed, that is the edge of the city, and all houses beyond that are considered outside the city. All that is beyond the outskirts is not included in the city. The main point is as the first answer: in Hebron, even the villages, the courtyards, and the fields were called Hebron. Similarly, we find in the beginning of Gittin, Lod and the village of Lodim, and in Makkot, there is Selikum and the village of Selikum. This will be explained later that regarding a river, anything within the city's boundary is written as being on that river because the city's utilities come from it, as will be explained. There is no proof for houses standing outside its outskirts. This is also what the Mordechai writes in the chapter "Mi She'Achzo" that outside the outskirts of a city is not included in the city's name, even if it is within the boundary (see there in the gloss that begins "Some say").

And even though in the Responsa Maimonides on the Laws of Marriage, Siman 22, it is written in the Responsa of the Rashba, who was one of the Tosafists, that everything within the techum (Sabbath boundary) is considered as the city, and he brought proofs for this. However, he himself wrote there that he does not rely on these proofs, and his main reasoning is based on logical inference regarding a river and mills that the name of the city is called upon them. Therefore, he does not disagree in our case, because this does not apply to houses, as he wrote. And I have seen someone who relied on this to permit within the techum all that is written with the name of the city, but this is not clear at all. Certainly, if they have no other name but the name of the city, they write the name of the city initially, as is written in Hebron. But if it does not have the name of the city, it seems to be a change of place. And this also appears to be the opinion of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, as mentioned there. And it is puzzling that he did not mention this at all in the Shulchan Aruch (and the Gra in Siman 26 permits in pressing circumstances even outside the techum and is lenient within the techum after the fact, as mentioned there. And this is puzzling).

If there is a necessity to write [a document] outside the boundary of the city, and this place does not have a specific name, it seems that one should write "according to the count that we count here, near..." or write "here, on the side of...". In the Gemara, we find this language (Yevamot 115b): "That get (divorce document) was found in Nehardea, and it was written on the side of Kalonya town, etc." However, it is possible that the city was called by two names, "the side of Kalonya" (and perhaps this is what Rashi means there, for otherwise, what is he teaching us?) (and from the Maimonides' responsa mentioned above, it appears in its simple form). And whatever was written is valid. Similarly, if the husband stands there at the time of writing the get, he should write "standing near..." or "standing on the side of...town that is located, etc." Likewise, if the wife stands there, he should write "standing near" or "on the side of" (as it appears to me if that place does not have a specific name, and even if it is outside the boundary, since it is subordinate to the city).

And now, in our times, in many cities there are suburbs at the edge of the city that have their own names, whether they are contiguous with the city or separated from it by some distance. For example, in my city where I am currently, there is a small suburb separated from the city by about half a Sabbath boundary and it is called Perashika. In the city of Navahrudak, if someone were to ask a resident where they live, they would answer Perashika. And if they asked in the form of a question, "Do you live in Navahrudak?" they would respond, "No, I live in Perashika." Even in the royal courts, it has this name. However, the courts are not a proof, for every part of the city has its own name because it is the law of the government that every street should have a name. 

It seems to me that if it is necessary to write the name in a get (divorce document), one should write, "according to the count that we count here in Perashika adjacent to Navahrudak city" or "in Perashika next to Navahrudak city," and if one wrote only Perashika, it seems it is valid after the fact. But if one wrote only Navahrudak, it appears another get is needed. However, perhaps in a situation of preventing a chained wife (agunah) and in pressing circumstances, one can rely on it, since in other places this name is not known at all. When a person living in Perashika travels ten parasangs away and is asked where they are from, they will say from Navahrudak. And when they are asked where they came from, they will say from Navahrudak. And when asked where they are traveling to upon their return, they will say to Navahrudak. This is only as a part of the city, and practical consideration is needed in this matter.

One writes [the name of the place] whether it is a large city or a small city, or even a small village (Gra, section 10), as "metah" means place. However, this is according to Tosafot's interpretation in Eruvin (21a). But according to Rashi's interpretation there, there is no proof. It seems to me that it is better to write "in the village of so-and-so," as Onkelos interpreted "the villages of Jair" (Chavvoth Jair) at the end of Parashat Matot. Similarly, where it is written, "He captured Kenath and its villages," he interpreted it as "Kenath and its villages." Additionally, it seems to me that if it becomes necessary to write [the name of] a village, one should write "the village of so-and-so near the city of so-and-so," because it is known that there are many villages with the same name, and it is not clearly recognizable where the get (bill of divorce) was written. And one writes "in the city of so-and-so" or "in so-and-so city," and this is our custom.

When it becomes necessary to write a get (divorce document) in the fields' courtyard houses, it appears that it should be written according to the counting that we count here in a particular courtyard near a particular city, a settled place. And if it is necessary to write a get in inns along the way, standing alone without a village nearby, it should be written according to the counting that we count here in... as they call it, near a particular city, a settled place, etc. What we call in our language "inns" does not have a specific word in either Hebrew or Aramaic, and therefore only its name should be written. When writing in all these, near a particular city, it is not necessary to write the name of the river that is in the village, courtyard, or inns. Usually, there are no rivers there, and if there is, its name is not clear. Therefore, it is better to write the proximity to the city, as mentioned. The city's proximity is known to all the villagers and estate owners, to which city they belong. It is certain that one should avoid as much as possible writing a get except in a city where gittin (divorce documents) are regularly arranged. However, sometimes in the case of a get for a dangerously ill person, it is necessary to arrange it in the place where the sick person is lying, and therefore we have explained these matters. If the word "settled place" was skipped, it is valid, and they wrote that if the entire region is named after the city, as there is the region of Babylonia and a city named Babylon, when writing in the city of Babylon, they write in the region of Babylonia (Darkei Moshe and Beit Shmuel, section 7). The settled place, etc., precedes the name of the place itself. And in the city, our custom is to precede the name to the settled place, and the reason is that the settled place needs to be adjacent to "sitting on the river," meaning the city sitting on a particular river. This is not the case with the region; it is impossible to write thus, because it implies that the entire region sits on that river. After the fact, there is no strictness in either case when written early or late (in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Megillah: family by family refers to villages, region by region refers to cities, and city by city refers to large towns).

There are versions that wrote "whether in names, whether in cities, and any name that I have and my place," due to the concern that they might have another name. Nevertheless, if it is known that there are two names, one should not rely on this and should explicitly write "such-and-such place that is called such-and-such." Our custom is not to write "and any name" whether in names or in cities. If a city has two names, we explicitly write "that is called" as mentioned. One should not write a yud next to the mem because the dalet is with a shewa, and after a shewa, it is not possible to have a yud. However, if one wrote a yud, "d'yimetkaria" (that is called) is valid, and we pronounce the dalet with a hirik. We write "d'metkaria" with an aleph or "d'metkaret," since a city is considered feminine, as it is written, "behold, this city is near." Similarly, if a river has two names, we write the second one "d'metkari," and for a river, we write without an aleph because a river is considered masculine, as it is written, "the name of the one river, the name of the second," and "the fourth river is the Euphrates." Even though "river" in the plural is "neharot," as it is written, "the rivers lift their voices," and throughout the Tanach, except for twice in Habakkuk where it is written "neharim," still in the singular it is considered masculine. Some say that if the river is called in the masculine form, we write without an aleph, and if it is called in the feminine form, we write with an aleph. There are rivers called in the masculine form, those ending with a final nun appear (likely), and there are those called in the feminine form, those whose ends do not have a final nun appear (likely). After the fact, there is no hindrance in any of these.

If a city or river has two names, one at the place where the get (divorce document) is written and one at the place where the get is given, when the get is sent by a messenger from place to place, their status is like that of the husband's names, as will be explained in Siman 129. The primary consideration is the place of delivery, and regarding the place of writing, one writes "which is called." However, in this case, it is not similar to the name of the husband.
