For the husband's name, if he made the place of writing primary and the place of delivery secondary, some disqualify it, as mentioned there. But with the name of a city or river, this is not disqualified after the fact or in a pressing situation, because the husband's name is critical by Torah law. Therefore, any alteration disqualifies it, even if it is not a complete change. This is not the case with the name of the city or river, which is not required by Torah law. Therefore, if it is not a complete change, such as making the place of writing primary, the get is not disqualified (Gra, paragraph 30). And we have already explained in paragraph 9 that as long as the name is the same but the pronunciation differs from the place of writing to the place of delivery, and it is a known name that their language is different in their pronunciation, there is no concern about this. See there.

And our master, the Rema, wrote in section 3: "If a city has two names, one known among the Jews and one in the language of the nations, the name that the Jews call it is primary, and they write according to the meaning of their language. If the two languages are similar to each other, and the name given by the Jews is merely an abbreviation, such as a city that the nations call 'Haradesh' and the Jews call 'Radesh', they write only the Jewish name. But if not, they write both names, the Jewish name first and then the name by which it is called by the nations." His words seem to indicate two cases: when it is merely an abbreviated name, they write only the Jewish name; and when there are two distinct names, they write the Jewish name as primary and then the name by which it is called by the nations (and so it is written in the glosses to the Shulchan Aruch). But if so, why did he elaborate so much, which is not his usual style? And what does he mean by 'they write according to the meaning of their language'? What relevance does 'meaning' have in this matter?

It appears to me that there are three categories of distinctions. Sometimes the name is the same for us and for them, but according to their pronunciation, the name changes, like the city of Nowhardak in our language, and the nations call it Nowogrodek. This is not due to a change, but because their pronunciation substitutes a "hey" for a "gimel," as is known, and the "nun" and the "vav" are pronounced with a "kamatz" according to their language, where the meaning is "new city." There is no actual change here, but due to the difference in pronunciation between our language and theirs, some letters and vowels differ. In such a case, we write only the Hebrew name. This is what is meant when it says, "we write according to the meaning of their language," meaning according to the meaning of the Hebrew language alone, and the meaning of their language is not written at all, since there is no actual change in language but a necessity of pronunciation. 

Then it says, "And if the two languages are close to each other," meaning there is an essential difference between the languages not because of pronunciation but because they are close to each other, like "Radish" and "Radish" (in different dialects). Here too, we write only the Hebrew name for another reason, that this is like an abbreviation of the name and a nickname, which is acceptable even initially according to many authorities, as will be explained in Siman 129. All the more so for a city that they call with a "gimel" and Israel with a "kuf," like the city of Rothenburg or Rotenburg, we write only with a "kuf" because this is from the first category we mentioned. Furthermore, it says, "But otherwise, we write both," meaning that when the change is not in pronunciation and is not an abbreviation of the language, it is a complete change, and we write both names.

They posed a question on our master, the Rema, that according to what is written in the "Ra'adish" and "Ra'adish," since it is an abbreviation of the name, there is no need to mention "Ra'adish" at all. Yet, at the end of the laws of Gittin, he wrote the wording of a get (divorce document) from the town of Kazmer which is called Kazmiraz, and this too is merely an abbreviation of the name. Similarly, in Poznan, they write "called Poznani," which is also just an abbreviation of the name. Indeed, the Levush did not mention "Ra'adish" and "Ra'adish" at all but wrote that when it is an abbreviation of the name, there is no need to write it at all. He wrote that indeed, in the town of Poznan, they did not need to mention "called Poznani." Some have written to differentiate that "Kazmiraz" is their way of stressing the "z" at the end, and similarly, "Poznani" is their way of stressing the "n" at the end, and therefore it is considered another name, and both must be mentioned (Beit Shmuel, section 9). I do not understand this; is it because they stress the letter that it is not considered an abbreviation? It is clear to everyone that this is an abbreviation. One can possibly suggest another reason for this: Certainly, when it is an abbreviation of the name where the extended form has no other meaning except for the elongation, like "Ra'adish" and "Ra'adish," there is no need to write both. But when the elongation has another meaning, both need to be written. Therefore, in Kazmer and Poznan, both need to be written, as it seems the town was named after its founder, who was called Kazmer, a name still common among them. When they say Kazmiraz, it is as if they are saying "of Kazmer," meaning it belongs to Kazmer. Similarly, it is so in Poznan, and therefore both need to be written (as explained above).

There are those who say that it is not necessary to mention anything at all, only the name of Israel alone (three times the name), as in the name of the divorcer that will be explained in Siman 129. For the get (bill of divorce) is a matter of Jewish law, and among Jews, it needs to be known, and we only need our name alone. For this reason, even according to the words of our teacher, the Rema, we do not care whether the majority of the city are Jews or not, for even if the Jews are a minority, the main thing is the name of Israel, and it is written in their language "d'mitkarei" (called), because the get is among Jews. Therefore, why should we mention any other name in the get at all (and it is written that from the Maharai and the Maharik there is no proof for this)? However, in truth, it is not comparable to the name of the divorcer, as the Jews gave him the name, which is not the case with a city. The founders of the city were the nations, and they called them names initially, and the name they gave it when they founded it has not ceased from among them. Therefore, it is impossible not to mention this name at all. This is also the simple custom in all countries. In my previous city, which in our language is called Zivakai and in their language is called Nova Zivkav, we write Zivakai "d'mitkarei" Nova Zivkav. This is also the custom in all countries.

Indeed, it is a straightforward matter that if only the Jewish name is written, it is valid even initially, and there is no need to write another get (divorce document). However, if only the non-Jewish name is written initially, it is certainly necessary to write another get. Nevertheless, if she has already received the get and it is difficult to obtain another one, it appears that it is valid after the fact, as it is not worse than a nickname. In the region of Raissin, there is a city where they write only the non-Jewish name in the get, and in the previous generation, one of the great rabbis protested against this, but they did not change their custom. They may have relied on the opinion of several great halachic authorities who maintain that a nickname is valid even initially for both the husband and the wife, as mentioned in Siman 129, and even more so for the name of the city. Since they have always practiced this way, they did not want to change it to avoid casting aspersions on the earlier gittin (divorce documents). Although this does not necessarily cast aspersions, since it is technically valid, they did not want to change it (see Pitchei Teshuva, subsection 13, and according to our explanation, it is clear, and examine it well).

And this is regarding names: we write "nicknamed" as stated in Siman 129. In the case of a city, we write only "called," because for a city, a nickname is not as applicable as it is for a person. Additionally, for a person, they were first given their primary name and afterward nicknamed with a secondary name. But for a city, which is named after the nations that call it, how can we write "nicknamed" when, in most cases, they are the founders of the city and they gave it its name initially? Furthermore, it will be explained later that if one writes "nicknamed" or "called," it is kosher, but not the other way around. Therefore, for a city, we write only "called," and similarly for a river.

By law, it is not necessary to write the name of the river by which the city sits, as it is not such a significant identifier (Levush). However, it has become customary to write it to distinguish it from another city with the same name. Therefore, even if it is not known that there is another city with the same name as this one, the name of the river is written (Beit Shmuel). In the Talmud, we find a get (bill of divorce) that was written with the name of the river (Gittin 27a): "Shuiri of the city on the river bank." Similarly, we find a get that was written without the name of the river (Yevamot 115b). Therefore, if the name of the river was not written, the get is valid (Beit Yosef). However, if it is known that there is another city with the same name, then by law, the name of the river must be written, and if it was not written, there are those who consider invalidating it (Gaon of Vilna, section 33). Nevertheless, in a case of potential agunah (a woman who is unable to remarry), the get should be deemed valid (ibid.), since even if the place of writing the get was not written at all, it is valid post-factum, as mentioned in section 3, and certainly in this case. In a place where the name of the river is written on all gets, and one get was written without it, there are those who consider invalidating it in any situation, because an observer might say that the get was written in a different place (ibid.). It is obvious that in a case of potential agunah, the get is valid (ibid.), as even an observer will assume that in this get, the name of the river was omitted. Why would one think it is a different city? Even if it is known that there is another city with the same name, and the name of the river is written on all gets, and in this get it was not written, it still seems to me to be valid in a case of potential agunah for the reasons explained.

And even if the name of the river was changed, our teacher, the Rema, ruled in section 4 that it is valid because anything that does not need to be written, if it was altered, is valid (Gra's commentary, section 22). Now, according to what was stated in section 4, if the change is noticeable to everyone, this ruling does not apply. And indeed, I found someone who invalidates the change of the name of a river (Radach, Section 4). Nevertheless, most of the great later authorities validate it in a case of potential agunah (a woman unable to remarry), such as the Levush, B"S, and Gr"P. This is not comparable to the name of a city mentioned in the Talmud which must be written correctly, as certainly, the change invalidates it. This is not the case with the name of a river. Nor is it comparable to what will be explained—that if one wrote a river outside the boundary, some invalidate it because after all, this river does not belong to the city, and the city is without the river. So, when it is written that it sits on a specific river, it constitutes a change in the city. However, the change in the name of the river, it is true that the city sits on the river, and there is no change in the city, only in the river, which should not invalidate it (Levush, B"S). This requires further investigation for a definitive ruling.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that any river which is outside the city's boundary should not be written at all, even if they derive some benefit from it. Even after the fact, if it was written, some invalidate it. Even if it is within the boundary but outside the city's extension, it should not be written unless all the city's needs are supplied by it.

From his words, it seems there are three distinctions regarding a river: If it is within the city or its extension, if the city's residents use it somewhat, such as for soaking flax, washing, or grinding, it can be written in a bill of divorce (get). If they do not use it at all, it should not be mentioned (as is evident in Beit Shmuel, section 14), as the term "sitting" implies usage. Some say that within the city's extension, it can be written in any case (as mentioned there in the name of Maharim). If it is outside the city's extension but within the boundary, it should not be written unless all the city's needs, such as drinking water, are supplied by it. It is obvious that if the city's residents drink its water, even according to those who hold that anything outside the extension should not be written, in such a case it can be written.

If it is outside the boundary, it should not be written at all, even if all the city's needs are supplied by it, and if it was written, some invalidate it, as it has no connection to the city. However, some permit it in such a case (as Beit Yosef cited in the name of Kol Bo), and certainly if it is visible from the city, it is valid. It appears to me that if they drink its water, it is valid according to all opinions because it is the lifeline of the city, and it can be said to be "sitting" even if it is outside the boundary. Similarly, within the boundary and outside the extension, even if they do not use it for all the aforementioned purposes but only for one or some other usage, and it is already customary to write the river in bills of divorce of that city, one should not protest against them.

If there are two or three rivers, all of them are written as "situated on such-and-such river and such-and-such river," and there is no need to write "on such-and-such river and on such-and-such river," because why should we mention "river" with each one? However, there are templates of divorce documents that write "river" with each one, and this is proper to avoid the error of thinking that the river has several names. And this is the custom, and we write all the rivers, even if the majority draw from one and the minority from the other. Nevertheless, we write all of them. And the reasoning is that even the minority of the city is still part of the city. Similarly, if one is used for many purposes and the other for few purposes, we still write all of them unless one has no use at all, in which case it is not written. And it is written "ditva" with one "yod" and as one word, meaning "the city situated on such-and-such river." And if it is written "di yitva," it is also valid, as this means "the city which is situated on such-and-such river."

Even a river that dries up when the heat is intense, nevertheless, it is still called a river when it has water, as it is written: "And the river will dry up and be parched" (Isaiah 19:5). And in the Gemara, it states: "The river has stopped flowing" (Bava Metzia 77a). I found that the Maharik (Responsa, Shoresh 137) ruled similarly. It is clear that when there is no water in it, at that time, it is not possible to write it in a get (divorce document) (ibid.). A city situated on the shore of seas, they write "situated on the shore of the sea," but they do not customarily write the name of the sea, and I do not know why. It seems to me that a city situated on two seas should write "seas" in the plural form. There is doubt regarding a river that does not flow but is like a reservoir and is called "Azirea," whether it is proper to write "river," since "river" implies flowing. Perhaps it is better to write "situated on waters of so-and-so." In Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt speedily in our days, they write "on the waters of Shiloach." There are those who say that if it is not within the city's boundaries, one should not write "on the shore of the sea," which implies on its bank, unless it is visible in the city (Responsa, Shoresh 145). I do not know if this is the custom, for it seems that a sea, which is more well-known than a river, and everyone knows that this city is situated on the sea, and it is well-known due to commerce, there is no need to be meticulous about this. Nevertheless, in practice, it requires further investigation. However, there is no need to elaborate on such matters, for certainly, every city in which gittin (divorce documents) are written, they have been careful and acted according to the great teachers of that time, and one should not question them (so it appears to me).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote that a city whose water supply comes from wells should write "from the waters of the wells," and a city whose water supply comes from springs should write "from the waters of the springs." In one instance, they write "wells" without a vav. If the spring water is hot, they write "from the hot spring waters." If there are flowing wells in the city, it is written that it sits "on the waters of the cisterns," which is valid. If the city is situated on a river, neither "wells" nor "springs" should be written, but rather "the river." There are those who disagree and hold that all sources of the city's water supply should be written, and this is the custom in these regions, as will be explained in the example of the get (divorce document) that I wrote at the end of Siman 124. If a city has only cisterns and ponds, they should not be mentioned at all to avoid distinguishing between gittin (divorce documents) written before and after they were made. End of quote.

The explanation of the matters: a pool is considered gathered water, and a well is called living water that flows. And so it is stated in the Talmud (Eruvin 23b), and similarly in the Scripture (Proverbs 5:15): "Drink water from your cistern, flowing water from your well." The difference between a river and a spring is that a river has a flow beyond the place of its source, like the nature of rivers, and a spring does not extend beyond its source. So it is taught in the Gemara (Shabbat 121b): "Rivers that flow and springs that bubble, etc." The difference between a well and a spring is that a spring flows on its own and the water is close to the ground, whereas a well is also a spring, but one digs deep into the ground until they bring forth living water that flows, as we dig our wells and build within the well so that the dirt does not fall and block it.

And this is what they wrote, that when it comes to hot springs, they write "on the hot spring waters" in several places, but it is not customary, and even in the holy city of Tiberias, they do not mention "hot" (three times), as there is no obligation to mention all the specific signs. And this is what they wrote, that if one writes "cisterns" instead of "wells," it is valid, even though throughout the Talmud we say "cistern" is one thing and "well" is another, as it is written. Nevertheless, since the Talmud in Beitzah (39a) holds that "cistern" means a spring, as mentioned there, it implies that the term "cistern" applies to a spring and certainly to a well. And it seems to me that the reason is that certainly in the holy tongue (Hebrew) there is a distinction, but in Aramaic, "well" is without an aleph, as Onkelos translated every "well" in the Torah as "bira." Therefore, even if one writes "bor" with a vav, it is valid, as most of the get (bill of divorce) is in Aramaic. And at the end of Middot, it also proves that the term "cistern" applies to "well," as mentioned there (and be precise).

And if one wrote "on wells of springs," there are those who want to invalidate it (Beit Yosef in the name of Maharik). And similarly, if one wrote "on springs of wells" (Get Pashut section 52). And I am very puzzled by this, for in the text of our get (divorce document), we only mention springs and not wells, as written in section 154. And the custom is simple and well-known that among us, most of the water usages come from wells, and there are places where there are no springs at all. And even in places where there are springs, they are very few. And it is far-fetched to say that we rely on what has been explained that it is permissible with a change in the name of the river, for how can one initially rely on this? Rather, it is certain that we know that a well is also included as a spring. And a clear proof of this is that Rashi, of blessed memory, in Eruvin (104b) explained that a cold well is a spring, as referenced there (and also a proof from there that "bor" or "bir" means a well, as referenced there, and be precise). And even though in our common language we call it a "well" and not a "spring," nevertheless, everyone knows that a well is a spring, for in truth, they are springs that flow from deep in the ground. Furthermore, in the Talmud Beitzah that we brought, it was considered to say that a "bor" and a "spring" are one and the same, and certainly a "well" and a "spring" (and so wrote the Beit Shmuel section 16, even though in section 14 he brought the words of the Maharik).

And this is what they wrote: In a city that has only cisterns and lakes, these should not be mentioned at all in the get (divorce document), so as not to differentiate between the earlier gittin and the later gittin, in order not to cast aspersion on the earlier ones. In truth, there is no relevance to this concern of casting aspersion regarding something that is not necessary to mention if they are mentioned later, as some of the great authorities have written. Rather, the explanation is as follows: It is obvious that even previously, they did not live without water, for it is impossible for humans and animals to live without water. Rather, it must be said that they were supplied by the waters of a neighboring city (three parsangs away), and they would write in the gittin that it was from a certain city that was supplied by the waters of a certain city. Later, for the benefit of the city, they made cisterns and lakes, and they are still being supplied by the waters of the neighboring city. Therefore, it is not appropriate to change the previous formulation. But if now they are not being supplied by the waters of the neighboring city but only from the cisterns and lakes, it is obvious that these should be written in the get: "such-and-such city that is settled by the waters of cisterns and lakes." Similarly, in Jerusalem, the holy city, it is written: "settled by the waters of Shiloach and by the waters of cisterns" (there). And if another river was added, the new river is also written, and there is no concern of casting aspersion on the earlier ones (as per the Levush, and this is the intention of the Gra in his commentary that disagrees with the Beit Shmuel, and examine this thoroughly).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 7: If two rivers flow into each other and are close to a city, if one of their names is lost, we only write the name of the remaining one. If both names are known, we write both names. If there is any doubt, we only write one name since it is better to risk omitting a name than to risk changing a name. 

It is known that usually small rivers flow into larger rivers, and from his words, it seems that even if the larger river's name is lost, we only write the smaller one's name. However, in the original ruling from the responsa of Maharik, Section 106, it is explained differently. The Levush also wrote: If two rivers merge before reaching a city, and one is large and the other is small, and the small one loses its name from the point of merging onward, it is obvious that we only write the name of the larger river. If the larger river loses its name and most of the locals call the river by the smaller river's name, some say that we should write both names. This is because we see that the main and majority of the water comes from the larger river, but since the locals call it by the smaller river's name, we need to mention both names.

It is possible that Rema also agrees with this, and he only wrote generally because it is usually the case that the smaller river loses its name. This is also implied in the Beit Shmuel, Section 18, and not like the Gra. When he wrote "if there is doubt," it means that some call it by the smaller river's name and some by the larger river's name, which is a doubt. In such a case, we only write the larger river's name since it is the primary one, and we don't write both names because if the larger one is primary, it would be a change. However, the reverse is not a concern, as the larger one won't be dismissed, and the only concern is the omission of the smaller river's name from the get if both are primary. It is also known that even if there are actually two rivers and only one is written, it is still valid since the omission of a river's name does not invalidate, unlike a change which some believe does invalidate even where an omission does not. This is the opinion of the Sefer HaTerumot as mentioned in Beit Yosef.

Additionally, in his work Darkei Moshe, he wrote that the custom has spread to write the names of two rivers in a divorce document, as there is no concern that there might be another city with the same name and with similar rivers. However, in a place where there are not two rivers and there is a concern for causing a woman to become an 'agunah' (a woman who is chained to her marriage), or after the fact, there is no need to worry (Beit Shmuel section 118). We also do not worry about this even initially. In my city, there is only one river, and nevertheless, divorce documents have always been written, for certainly there would be no greater cause for 'agunah' than if we did not write a divorce document in the city. There are many places that have only one river and they write divorce documents. If there is a river whose name consists of two words, like "Raagin Shforg" or something similar, it is still considered one word and should not be written in two words (ibid.). If there is a river or city that is pronounced with a soft "kaf" (a letter in Hebrew that can be pronounced as either a hard 'k' or a soft 'kh'), even though we pronounce it like a "chet" (another Hebrew letter, similar to a hard 'h'), nevertheless, it should be written with a "kaf" and not a "chet," because in some regions they pronounce "chet" like a "hey" (another Hebrew letter, a softer 'h'), and this would constitute a change. Further details on this matter will be explained in section 129 (ibid.).

A city that has no river, spring, or well, only gathered water, and sometimes it dries up, and then they drink from the water of the nearby city, should always write also the nearby city regarding the water, even when the water here has not dried up, since many times they use water from the other city. And they should write from a certain city which is situated on gathered water and which is supplied from the water of a certain city (Hagahot Maimoniyot and as explained by the Gaon of Posen, section 54, and it must be in his intention that they mention the gathered water in the city as well, and examine this thoroughly). And a new city that has a river but no known name, and has springs and wells, should write that it is situated on river water and on spring and well water (Nodah B'Yehudah, section 116). However, it is unlikely that a river would have no name, and certainly in a new city, when they need to begin arranging gittin (divorce documents), they need to consult the leading rabbis of that time, and they will establish the names.

It is necessary to write in the get (divorce document) the name of the husband's city and the name of the wife's city. It is evident from the Talmud that they were accustomed to write the name of his city and the name of her city (Gittin 20a: "But we require his name and her name and the name of his city, etc." and in the Mishnah: "If he changed his name or her name or the name of his city, etc."). Regarding the explanation of the name of his city and her city, it can be interpreted in three ways: 

1. The name of the place where the husband and wife are standing at the time of the writing of the get, similar to the name of the city of the witnesses and the scribe as has been explained.
2. One can say it refers to the city where they reside, and if the get is written in another place, it must be written that he is from such-and-such place and she is from such-and-such place.
3. One can say it refers to the place where they were born. 

In truth, the Rosh wrote in Chapter 8, Section 9, and the Tur wrote that in Ashkenaz and France they were accustomed to write all three: the place of birth, the place of residence, and the place of standing, due to the concern of cases where there might be two people named Joseph son of Simon.

And some of our rabbis hold that the primary factor is the place of residence, and it is essential (Rashba in his responsa, section 113, in the name of the Ra'avad). And there are those who are uncertain about this (Rashba there, concerned with the opinion of the Ra'avad, and in section 108, he permits it after the fact if it was not written, see there). And some of our rabbis hold that it is not essential to mention the place of residence (there, in the name of the Itur and the Rosh, and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, and Rabbeinu Yechiel, and the Riv, and the Nimukei Yosef, chapter 2, and this is also the opinion of the Tosafot, see there). Nevertheless, they wrote that ideally, if it is possible to write the place of residence, it should be written, but it is not essential at all. And the place of birth is not needed at all. And also in France, where they tended to write it, they wrote in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak haZaken that many times when the place of birth was not clear to them, he would tell them not to write it at all (Tosafot, Pesachim).

And behold, our simple custom is not to write either the place of birth or the place of residence, but rather the place where they are standing at the time of the writing of the get (bill of divorce). In a get sent from place to place, we do not write at all the place where the woman is standing. The reason, as written by the author of Terumat HaDeshen, section 142, is that since our places of residence are unstable, as we are exiles and wanderers, we do not write it at all. We rely on the majority of the poskim (decisors) who hold that the name of the city refers to the place of standing. Even though in a get sent we do not write at all the place where she is standing because we do not know where she is standing at the moment, and therefore there is no name of her city at all, still, there is no concern with this. For the reason that they used to write the name of his city and her city in the times of the Sages is not a requirement, and there are many proofs for this. One of them is from what is taught in the Mishnah (26a): "One who writes forms of gittin (bills of divorce) must leave blank the place of the man, the place of the woman, and the place of the time." And it does not teach the name of his city and the name of her city, from which we learn that it is not a requirement (Gra, note 3). The main reason they instituted writing it is because of two men named Yosef ben Shimon (same name), and since they write the place where the husband is standing, there is no concern that it will be taken to the wife of another Yosef ben Shimon (Gittin 10). And also, in most cases, the place where he is standing is his place of residence. Even if it happens that the husband is not in the city at the time of writing the get, and she is also not in the city, and it is necessary not to write the place for both of them, there is still no concern according to most poskim, as mentioned. Even according to those who require the name of the place as essential, they agree that in a case where it is impossible to write the name of their place, it does not invalidate the get. Otherwise, how could it be said that one who has no fixed place cannot divorce his wife? (ibid.). The Sages did not want to establish in a get sent that we should know at the time of writing the place where the woman is standing and write "standing in such-and-such place," because in most cases, it would be a hindrance to the get. There is no greater misfortune for agunot (women unable to remarry) than this. (What is written in the Shiltei Giborim in the name of Riaz in chapter 8 is puzzling).

And this is the opinion of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 2, who wrote as follows: One writes the name of his city and the name of her city, but one does not write the place of birth. And although if one changes this it does not invalidate [the document], nevertheless, it is better not to write [the place of birth] so that no mistakes will occur and it will not appear as a change. Furthermore, one does not write the place of residence because we are exiles and wanderers, and our place of residence is uncertain. However, one writes the place where the man is currently standing, if he is present in a particular city at the time of the signing of the get (divorce document). If he is not present there, one does not write his place at all. Similarly, for the woman, if she is present at the place of the signing of the get, one writes the place where she is currently standing in a particular city. If not, one does not write her place at all. If one wrote the place of birth or the place of residence and did not change it, it is valid. This is not a novel ruling; rather, it teaches us that ideally, one should not deviate from the custom of not writing the place of birth and residence, but post facto, we are not concerned about this.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that if the place of standing was changed, some permit it just like in the case of the place of birth, because anything that does not need to be written, even if it was changed, is valid. And there are those who invalidate it. In a pressing situation, one should be lenient. However, if the place of residence was changed, it is invalid according to all opinions, and even if she was married, she must leave him. And his words require explanation, for according to what has been explained, there is no hindrance after the fact if the name of their city was not written at all. If so, why does the change in the place of residence invalidate it, according to the principle that anything which does not need to be written, a change does not invalidate it? Furthermore, how is it possible to permit a change in the name of the city, as there is an explicit Mishnah that states: "If he changed his name and her name, the name of his city and the name of her city, she must leave both him and the other," etc. See there.

However, the explanation of the matter is as follows: There are some authorities who hold that any alteration invalidates a document, even in matters that did not need to be written at all, such as the place of birth (this is the opinion of Sefer HaTerumot as cited in Beit Yosef, and according to Rema in Darkei Moshe, the Raavad also holds this way). However, the majority of authorities permit this, and therefore the opinion of those who invalidate in such cases was not brought in the Shulchan Aruch. Nevertheless, even those authorities who permit alterations in matters that do not need to be written, say that this is only in matters where the alteration is not noticeable to the public, like the place of birth, since not everyone knows where a person was born. But the place of residence, which is noticeable to everyone, an alteration would make it appear as if the document is forged and it would be invalid (see Beit Yosef). This is the opinion of those who invalidate. But those who permit hold that even in such cases it is valid, since it does not need to be written (this is the opinion of Tosafot, the Rosh, and other authorities). All of this applies when the place of residence is also written, which is the primary name of his city and her city as stated in the Mishnah. Since there is no alteration in this, we do not worry about the alteration of the place of standing. Additionally, the alteration of the place of standing is only noticeable temporarily, while the alteration of her place of residence is always noticeable. Therefore, an alteration in her place of residence is invalid according to everyone, because this is the primary name of his city and her city as stated in the Mishnah, as it is written.

And according to this, it is necessary to say that our teacher, the Rema, did not mean according to our custom where we only write the place of residence and rely on that as the name of the city and town, as it is written. For if so, how could it be possible to validate by changing the place of residence, since it is explicitly taught that a change invalidates? Rather, it is certain that his words are according to the ancient times when they would also write the place of dwelling. And so wrote one of the great Acharonim (Turei Zahav, subparagraph 5), and he said that when there is no person in the place written in the get whose name is the same as this, even for us it is valid. It needs further study, for based on what we wrote, even in such a case, there is reason to invalidate. And study this well.

But the main points are perplexing: How is it possible that our teacher, the Rema, wrote in the Shulchan Aruch that a change in the place of standing is valid in a pressing situation, and it would not be his intention for us? Is there a greater stumbling block than this? Therefore, it seems to me that he holds that it is also valid for us. He holds that when we write the place of standing, it is not our intention that this is the city or town mentioned in the Mishnah, for the intention of the Mishnah is certainly only the place of residence, as the language plainly suggests. However, because our place of residence is not firmly established for us, we are unable to mention it, as we have written. Moreover, the sages did not say this as an absolute requirement, as explained in section 42. The fact that we write the place of standing is not from the enactment of the Mishnah, but we practice this way because we cannot write the place of residence. Therefore, in a pressing situation, we rely on the authorities who hold that as long as there is no need to write it, the change does not invalidate it, even in something recognizable to the public. Furthermore, the recognition is only temporary, as we have written. And although in most cases the place of standing is the place of residence, since we do not mention that they live there, we do not worry about it. Therefore, in a get (divorce document) that is sent, we do not mention the place of the woman's standing at all, as we have written. Similarly, if the husband is not in the place where the get is written at the time of writing, we do not mention his place of standing at all, as we have explained. Therefore, even the change does not invalidate it in this case.

And behold, we have written all this to justify his words, but practically it appears to me that Heaven forbid to rely on this, for from all the early authorities it is explicitly proven that when they validated with a change of standing place, it was when they also wrote the place of residence. But for us, it is impossible to validate in practice even if she was married. And I saw one of the great ones in his book (Perek Yud, Gemara Perek Hazorek) who validated in practice in a pressing situation when we noted the woman's standing place. However, to me, this is difficult (also the great Nodah B'Yehudah in the second section, Siman 109, has reservations about this, and nevertheless, he did not explicitly invalidate but wrote that if such a case came to him, he would not hasten to validate or invalidate and would deliberate on it. And regarding the great Perek Yud, he wrote that an elder has already ruled, and therefore I do not say about this neither prohibition nor permission, and it requires further study).

Laws regarding the names of the man and woman, their nicknames, and the names commonly found in our country, comprising 132 sections:
One must write the name of the man and the name of the woman in a get (divorce document), and this is from the Torah. If their names are not written, the get is invalid according to the Torah, even if it is handed to her in the presence of witnesses, for it says "a scroll of severance" indicating a narrative of severance. It is impossible to narrate the severance without writing his name and her name (Ramban and Ran Gittin 20). This is included in the Rambam's language at the beginning of the laws of divorce, among the ten essential things for a get, where he writes that one should not divorce except in writing, meaning that their names should be written in the document. He did not need to explain this because of its obviousness (addressing the precision of the Geonim). This is also the opinion of all our Rabbis, and so wrote Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in section 11 that if the names of the man and woman are not written in the get, it is invalid and the children are considered mamzerim (illegitimate), end quote. Most of the great later authorities agreed with this (Gra, note 19; Beit Meir; Turei Even, note 15). This is what Tosafot writes in Gittin 20 in the commentary beginning "Ha" that according to Rabbi Meir, it is invalid from the Torah, meaning that according to Rabbi Meir, it is necessarily from the Torah, and it can be inferred that the Rabbis do not disagree in this matter, as explained in "Hazorek" in a changed case, and certainly if not written at all. The Beit Meir also wrote this, and the later authorities' effort on this matter was unnecessary; scrutinize this well.

And know that in the Mordechai, Chapter 3, it is written in this language: Rabbeinu Yoel HaLevi wrote, "If I were not afraid of my colleagues, I would say that even if the names of the man and the woman were not mentioned in the get (bill of divorce), etc., according to Rabbi Eliezer who says 'on condition' constitutes a valid divorce, and we hold according to him. Since the witnesses stand before us and say that the get was delivered into her hand from her husband, what need is there to mention their names, etc." This is the end of his words. However, his opinion stands alone and has no support among the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), and the proofs he brought are not proofs at all (according to the Gra). Indeed, this reasoning is very perplexing. What is effective according to Rabbi Eliezer regarding 'on condition' even when it is not evident from the document itself, this is when the names were written but there exists another person with the same name or it is possible to forge, and in such cases, we say the witnesses of delivery know. But when no name at all is mentioned in the get, on what basis are they 'on condition'? Their entire testimony is verbal, and it is not a written divorce. It is also not similar to a nickname that is valid because it is like the actual name. But what relevance does a get have without any names at all? (And with this, all his proofs are nullified, see there). Nevertheless, some of the great Acharonim (later authorities) were concerned about this opinion as a stringency, perhaps the invalidity is only rabbinic (Lechem Mishneh, Chapter 1, and Gittin Chapter 3). According to this, if she was divorced without names and then married another, she would require a get from both (the first and the second husbands), and this needs further investigation.

Nevertheless, even according to what is clear to us that from the Torah the names are essential, there is a doubt if his name is written in the get (divorce document) and her name is not written but instead it is written generally "you, my wife," should we say that it is considered as if there is no name at all, or is it possible that since his name is specified in the get and the community knows that she is his wife, it is considered a valid get from the Torah, and its invalidity is only rabbinic. And there is someone who wrote that her name is also from the Torah, for otherwise, there would be no enumeration of matters between him and her (Tosafot Gittin). And it appears to me that if he has only one wife, it is possible that it is from the Torah like a specified name, but if he has two or more wives, there is no enumeration of matters. Practically, it is necessary to be stringent in every case.

The Tur wrote in the name of the Rosh, of blessed memory, that if the name of the woman's father is not mentioned in a get (divorce document), it is valid. The same applies if the name of the husband’s father is not mentioned (Beit Yosef). Similarly, the Shulchan Aruch states in Section 9 that if the name of the father of the man or the name of the father of the woman is not mentioned, the get is valid. Therefore, in the case of a convert (in ancient times) or a foundling (whose parentage is unknown), only their names are written. However, some say that this is specifically when their place of residence or their current location is written, for otherwise, how would it be known who is the divorcer and who is the divorcee (Kenesset HaGedolah in the name of Radbaz)? According to this, in a get that is sent where the woman's location is not mentioned, the name of her father must be mentioned. Additionally, there are those who are concerned that the Rosh, who validated such a get, did so because in their times they would write the place of residence, which served as a good identifier. But in our times, when only the current location is mentioned, and there are many transients from various places, this does not serve as an identifier at all since there are many identical names in the world. Therefore, in our times, it is not sufficient to omit the mention of the fathers' names (Nodah BiYehudah, Section 113).

Indeed, our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, left the matter unspecified, and even in their time, they only wrote the place where they stood. From this, it is evident that there is no distinction in this regard, and the truth is that we hold according to Rabbi Eliezer that intent (kavanah) is what validates (koretet), and they know who the husband and wife are. We do not require that it be self-evident from the text, and it is not worse than something that can be forged, which is permitted for us for this reason. Therefore, even if the place where they stood is not written, it is sufficient to validate it with their names alone, because since it includes his name and her name, and the witnesses know who they are, that is sufficient (there). This is also explicitly implied in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 2, Halacha 3), where it states: "Even if he writes, 'I, so-and-so, am divorcing my wife,' it is valid." End quote. And it can also be deduced from this that her name is not required, since it does not say "my wife, so-and-so." However, it is possible that a concise expression was used, or that one word is missing in the Jerusalem Talmud. But regarding the names of the fathers, it is certainly a good proof, for otherwise, it would not have been omitted, as the entire essence of the law is that a get (bill of divorce) does not require lengthy wording. See there (in my opinion).

And know that the Levush wrote in this ruling that if the father's name is not mentioned, some say it is valid and some invalidate it. End of quote. And I do not know who the invalidating opinion belongs to. It seems that his intention is regarding the words of the Terumat HaDeshen, Siman 138, from which it appears that he invalidates it (and it is brought in Beit Yosef, and the Ba'er Heitev in subsection 17 rejects his words without proofs, see there). Therefore, in practice, one should be cautious in this matter. And it is obvious that this is only in a situation of extenuating circumstances and in a situation of potential agunah (a woman chained to her marriage), but otherwise, even according to those who validate it, one should not do so and must write the fathers' names with their titles and not change it. (And it seems to me that the Terumat HaDeshen does not disagree with the Rosh, but holds that one should differentiate as explained in subsection 4).

He changed his or her name, for example, if his name is Abraham and he wrote Isaac, or even if he wrote Abram or Abram instead of Abraham (three times); similarly, if a woman's name is Nefata and he wrote Tafata (Gittin 63b), and any similar case, even though he wrote "and any name that he/she has," nevertheless, the get (divorce document) is invalid according to Torah law. This is also the opinion of all the decisors, and even if it was delivered under a condition (Bach, sub-section 5), what benefit is there in a condition when the get is written with a different name? There is someone who wants to say that according to the Tosafot, the invalidity is only rabbinic (there), but it does not appear reasonable to me (this is the Tosafot that we mentioned in section 1, and according to what we wrote there, it is not specifically referring to Rabbi Meir; analyze this thoroughly).

And even if he changed his father's name or her father's name, the get (divorce document) is also invalid. And although if he did not write the father's name at all, it is valid, as we wrote, and it was explained in the previous section that anything that is not essential, its change also does not invalidate. Nevertheless, in this case, it is not similar to that. Firstly, it was also explained in section 4 that this rule only applies to something not recognized by many, but for something recognized, this rule does not apply. And even if we do not say this, it is impossible to validate it because if his name is Yosef ben Shimon and he wrote ben Shmuel, it is another person who is divorcing. Furthermore, what is required by law to be written, even though it is not essential after the fact if it was not written, nevertheless, since it needs to be written, certainly the change invalidates it, like the change of place of residence in section 44 (the Gra). And all this is when he did not establish himself with this change of name. But if he had previously established himself here with the change of his name or her name or the parents' names, there are other laws, and they will be explained before us with G-d's help in section 88.

And it was found in one of the early authorities who wrote that a change in the father's name does not invalidate the get (divorce document) (Itur, Article 7), for he holds that even initially it is not necessary to write the father's name (Gittin 4:5). This is a singular opinion and is nullified in the face of the majority of our early and later authorities who ruled that even if she remarries, she must leave him. And so ruled our teacher, the Rema, in section 10, see there, and there is no doubt about this.

However, there is an opinion that this invalidation due to the change of the father's name is not from the Torah but rather rabbinic in origin. It is not similar to the change of his name or her name (as mentioned there, subparagraph 149). And even though in all rabbinic invalidations we hold that if she married, she does not have to leave him, as stated in Siman 150, nevertheless, there are invalidations in which the Sages saw fit to be stringent, such that even if she married, she must leave him (as mentioned there). The proof that this invalidation is only rabbinic is that the Rosh wrote in his responsa that the reason for the invalidation due to the change of the father's name is because observers might say that another man divorced her. And since it is only because of what observers might think, it is clear that this invalidation is only rabbinic (as mentioned there). I have also seen some great authorities who wrote that this is only rabbinic.

However, from the responsa of the Rosh, there is no proof at all, for there it deals with a case where, out of embarrassment, he intentionally changed his father's name from Shimon to Shmuel, as is evident from his words (Klal 17, Siman 12), where he wrote that he divorced his wife using the new name. And there he wrote, asking how one could change his father's name. And similarly, it seems in the Tur. And there is one who wrote that the incident was where he changed his name to that of his grandfather (see Beit Yosef, s.v. "V'katav Od"). But this one, who mistakenly or intentionally wrote a different name for his father, this is not the one who is divorcing. And if it is because people know that this is the one who is divorcing, then if so, even if he changed his own name, we would also say that since people know that he is the one divorcing, it would not invalidate the divorce from the Torah. But certainly, since a different name is written in the get, it is not a valid get at all, and the fact that people know does not help. And if he changed his father's name, similarly, it is clear in the get that Yosef the son of Shmuel divorced, and not Yosef the son of Shimon. And what would the fact that people know help in this case? However, practically, one should be stringent, that if another man betrothed her, she requires a get from the second one as well. (And the main point in the words of the Gaon Pnei Yehoshua, who wrote that in such a case the Sages were stringent and she must leave [both husbands], is perplexing, for it is neither from the Mishnah nor the Gemara. And see the Chiddushei HaGrach, Siman 119, where it appears that his opinion, and that of the Gaon Rabbi Meshulam, is that the matter is not clear whether it is rabbinic. See there.)

There are many detailed laws regarding someone who has two names, as will be explained with God's help. However, in the explanation of two names, there are also several categories. The first is when a person is called by two names from birth, which is common among us. The second is when there is essentially one name, but it has a nickname, as is customary among us. For example, someone who is called "Leib" has the sacred name "Yehuda" or "Aryeh," and someone who is called "Wolf" has the sacred name "Zev" or "Binyamin," and someone who is called "Ber" has the sacred name "Dov" or "Yissachar," and someone who is called "Michel" has the sacred name "Yechiel," and similar cases. The third category is when a person is given one name from birth, but due to illness, another name is added, as is customary among us. The fourth category is when some people call him by one name, and others call him by another name, as it is stated in the Gemara (34b) about the woman who was mostly called "Miriam" and occasionally "Sarah." The fifth category is when in one place he is called by one name and in another city by another name, and the get (divorce document) goes from one city to another, and there is the name of the place of writing and the name of the place of giving.

A fundamental rule to know is that the two names mentioned in the Gemara and in the early authorities are of the fourth and fifth categories. It is known that in the days of the Sages of the Talmud and the early authorities, no one was called by two names at all, as we see in the Babylonian Talmud, the Jerusalem Talmud, and Midrashim, where there is no Tanna or Amora who had two names. What we find as "Abba Shaul" is actually one name, "Shaul," and "Abba" is a title, like "Rav" or "Rabbi." Also, among the early authorities, we do not find (except for Tosafot Ketubot 98b s.v. "Amar") any use of nicknames in their times. Furthermore, a name change due to illness was a complete change of name, replacing the old name with a new one, unlike our custom of adding a name. And indeed, in the Torah, we also see name changes without adding a name, like Sarai to Sarah, Abram to Abraham, Hoshea to Yehoshua, and our forefather Jacob when God said to him, "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel," we do not find in the entire Tanach that he was called by both names, but either Jacob or Israel. The name Jacob was not completely removed because that is what God wanted, as the Sages explained (Berachot 13a). These are the general rules, and now we will explain their details with God's help.

And know that the text of the get (divorce document) according to the Rambam, of blessed memory, in Chapter 4 is as follows: How I, so-and-so, son of so-and-so, from such-and-such a place, and any other name and nickname that I have and that my fathers have and that my place, etc. And this is the text of the Bahag (Baal Halachot Gedolot) according to what is stated by the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG) and the Rosh in Chapter 4. And according to the Rif, the text before us in Chapter 9 is: How I, so-and-so, son of so-and-so, and any name that I have, and it does not write 'and nickname.' And so it is before us in the printed Bahag, and according to the text of the Rif, he does not write 'and any name' but only his name and her name, and not the name of their fathers, see there. (And in the Bahag before us, there is confusion about this, see there.) And the Ramban, of blessed memory, testified that this is the true text of the Rif, of blessed memory, as stated by the Ran. And this is how they write in Ashkenaz according to this text (Rosh).

And the reason for this formulation is based on what is taught (34a) that Rabban Gamliel the Elder instituted that one should write "So-and-so and any name he has" and "So-and-so and any name she has" for the sake of societal order. This means that if later it is discovered that he or she has another name, it will be included in "and any name." They did not worry about the opposite concern, that perhaps he has no other name, and the observer who sees "and any name" will not say that this is not the person granting the divorce, since this is the formulation of all divorce documents, and there will be no objection to it (so it appears to me). And the formulations that also add "nickname" are for the same reason—lest they have some nickname. Moreover, it is common in Ashkenaz that the nations call Jews by nicknames close to the Hebrew language, and it is not appropriate to write on that nickname "who is called." Therefore, they customarily write "and any name and nickname," which includes everything (Rosh). This that in the formulation of the Rif, it only includes his name and her name alone, and not the fathers' names, is because it is merely a concern and in the institution of Rabban Gamliel, it was only found regarding their names alone. Therefore, they did not worry to write also the fathers' names, and moreover, it was explained in the previous section that the fathers' names do not invalidate post facto, see there.

But Rabbeinu Tam, of blessed memory, did not agree that this should be a general formula, because sometimes it could lead to a problem when one has only that name written in the get (divorce document) and no nickname. And when writing in the get "and all names and nicknames," it might appear that this get belongs to another person who has both a name and a nickname (Tosafot, Rosh, and Sefer Mitzvot Gadol). And even though this is a general formula, how can we write "and all names and nicknames" since he does not have another name or nickname (it seems to me). The decree of Rabbeinu Gershom was only for someone who indeed has another name, as explained in the Mishnah and Gemara there, that the decree was made for this reason. The intention is not to write "and all names," but rather to write the second name he has, as stated in the Talmud (35a): "Acha bar Hada who was also called Ihya Mari," and as the details of the laws in this matter will be explained. And this is the formula of the get according to Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, Rabbi Yitzchak of Prague, and Sefer HaTerumot, where "and all names" is not written in the get formula, and this is the common custom in all our regions.

The first opinion holds that if so, what was Rabban Gamliel's intention in saying "Mr. So-and-so and any other name he has"? Let him briefly say that the correction is to write all the names (Ran). According to the last opinion, it can be said that he intentionally states this so that the primary name is written first and the secondary name is written afterwards, as "called" or "nicknamed," as will be explained with the help of Heaven (so it seems to me).

However, from what is stated in the Gemara there, the case where she was called Miriam and somewhat Sarah, meaning that a minority of the people in her city called her Sarah (Rashi), and in the Rif, the version is that the majority called her Miriam and a few called her Sarah. And the Nehardeans say that in the get (divorce document) it should be written "Miriam and any other name she has," and not "Sarah and any other name she has." This clearly indicates the first opinion, because according to the latter opinion, they should have said "Miriam who is also called Sarah" and not "Sarah who is also called Miriam." We must say that indeed this is the intention, and the Talmud uses the language of the Mishnah. This is also clarified for me from the Rashba's commentaries there. And if it is difficult, since it explicitly mentions both names, what difference does it make if he writes Sarah first or Miriam first? One could say that in any case, the main name should not be written with "who is also called" (there).

It can also be said that according to our version, it can be interpreted that most people would call her Miriam, but a minority would occasionally call her Sarah. In such a case, it is possible that it is not necessary to write that she is called Sarah, since even the minority only occasionally calls her Sarah. Therefore, it is necessary to write "and any name." Even according to the version of the Rif, where the minority always called her Sarah, it can also be said that it is not necessary to write that she is called Sarah, because the phrase "called" implies that either everyone or at least the majority calls her that, and not when only a minority of people call her that. Therefore, it is necessary to write "and any name." This is not similar to what will be explained regarding when a person has one name in the place of writing and another name in the place of giving, where it is necessary to write in the place of writing "called" that name, because in that place everyone calls him by that name, so the term "called" is appropriate. However, when only a minority of the city calls her by another name, it can be said that the term "called" is not applicable, and this requires further consideration.

In the Jerusalem Talmud, it is stated regarding the ordinance of Rabban Gamliel in this manner: Rabbi Yossi said, "That which you have said applies to the past (after the fact), but ideally, one must act according to what Rabbi Ila said in the name of Rabbi Avin: If a name becomes known in another place, one must mention all three names." And the conclusion is: After the fact, it is sufficient to write "and any other name" when there is one name in the place of writing and another name in the place of delivery. This is the ordinance of Rabban Gamliel concerning after the fact. However, ideally, one must specify the names according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam. Moreover, if there is even a third name, all three names must be specified. It is clarified according to this that the interpretation of the ordinance is like the first opinion, and ideally, one must act according to the latter opinion.

And it appears, in my humble opinion, that the first opinion also agrees that when someone has two names or a nickname, it must be specified. Certainly, all names need to be detailed. However, they hold that the phrase "and any name" should also be written because Rabban Gamliel's enactment was to write it in this way to validate it post-factum, at the very least. Therefore, it must be written. Additionally, it is possible that he might have another name or nickname unknown to us. Indeed, this is the opinion of the Raavad, as the Ran writes in his name, and these are his words: "But from the words of the Raavad, it appears that Rabban Gamliel the Elder enacted that one should write 'So-and-so,' meaning both names he has in the place of writing and the place of giving. And because he was also concerned about aliases and nicknames, he enacted that one should write 'and any name he has,' thus writing 'So-and-so, who is called So-and-so, and any other name,' etc." End quote. In our opinion, even though the Rif and the Rambam do not interpret the enactment in this manner, they agree with the practical ruling.

And so, conversely, according to Rabbeinu Tam, of blessed memory, if after the fact one did not write all the names but only the primary name along with "and any name," it is also valid. The proof for this is from what will be explained in the reverse case, where we also write "and any name." Furthermore, if one wrote only the primary name by itself, it is also valid, as will be explained. However, if one wrote only the secondary name, even if "and any name" was written, it is not valid. More detailed laws on this matter will be explained with the help of Heaven.

However, from the words of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in Section 1, it somewhat implies differently from what we have stated, as our master Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote: "If one of them has two names, they write the name they are most commonly known by, and write 'so-and-so, and any name he has, divorces so-and-so, and any name she has.'" This implies that there is no need to specify the names according to the Rambam. And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) annotated, "And some say that one should not write 'and any name he has,' but if he has two names, he should write 'so-and-so, also known as so-and-so,' and this is the custom, and it should not be changed. And even if the get (divorce document) was written, it should not be used for the divorce unless both names are written." Thus, it is clear that even post facto, it is not valid. However, one could say that this applies when the get has not yet been given, but if the get has already been given, it is valid (as the Beit Shmuel wrote in Section 2). This is certainly the case because as long as the get has not yet been given, it is still considered initially, and it should not be changed from the customary practice.

And also in the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, there is room for scrutiny. For he himself wrote in section 16 that one writes "Yehuda who is called Leon," and in section 17 he wrote that one writes "Chaim who is called Bibant," and in section 19 regarding a name that was changed due to illness, he wrote that one should write the current name first and then the old name with "who is called" in between. Hence, it is clear that he holds that all names must be specified. However, his intention is clarified based on what he wrote in section 12 about someone who has one name in Judea and another name in the Galilee, and his language is: "Initially, one should write all the names that one has, or write the name he has there and include 'and any other name' to encompass names from other places." Hence, it is clear that he holds that either way is the same and there is no advantage of one over the other. Therefore, he did not concern himself to be precise about this in all places. Sometimes he writes that one should write "and any other name" and sometimes he writes that one should specify the names, since he holds that the law is the same for both. But from the Jerusalem Talmud which we brought, it is understood that initially it is better to specify all the names. (And from the language of the Beit Yosef, it implies that when one specifies all the names, there is no need to write "and any other name," even though in his place they wrote "and any other name," but the law is clarified to us as it appears to me).

And now we will explain the details of the two names that we elaborated on in Section 12, and first, we will explain the fourth and fifth details which are in the Talmud. We will explain the fifth detail which has two names in two places, and this is what it says in the Gemara (34b): If a man had two wives, one in Judea and one in Galilee, and he had two names, one in Judea and one in Galilee, and he divorced his wife in Judea using his name from Judea, and his wife in Galilee using his name from Galilee, she is not considered divorced until he divorces his wife in Judea using his name from Judea and the name from Galilee together, and his wife in Galilee using his name from Galilee and the name from Judea together. If he went to another place and divorced using one of the names, she is considered divorced. But you said that the name from Galilee must be with him—rather, we learn from this that this applies when the name is established and when it is not established. So concludes the Gemara.

And the explanation of the matter is when he sends a get (bill of divorce) to his wife who is in another place, and it is known here that in the place where the get is given he has another name, he needs to write in the get the name of the place of giving. Regarding the place of writing, he should write "who is called" or "and every name" according to the opinions that have been explained, because the main point is the place of giving. This is when it is known that he has another name in that place. But if it is not known in the place of writing that he has another name in the place of giving, and they wrote the name from the place of writing and sent her the get and she received it, even if it later becomes known that he has another name in the place of giving, the get is valid. We rely only on the name he is known by. Therefore, only in Judea and Galilee do we need to specify the names because there they knew that he might have another name in another place. But if he went to another place and in that place it is not known that he has another name, even if he sent the get to the place of the second name, the get is valid as we have said. This is the opinion of Rashi and Tosafot. The reason is that the place of giving is the main point, since the main purpose of the get is to permit her to marry others, and we need to write the name by which he is known in the place where she is permitted. And although from the Tosefta in Chapter 6 of Gittin it appears that the place of writing is the main point, and it also somewhat implies this in the Jerusalem Talmud, nevertheless our Talmud is the main authority, and most of the decisors agreed to this.

And it is necessary to explain this: if the primary concern is the place of delivery, because the woman is permitted there, as stated (as stated by the Rosh), and also because those in the place of delivery who do not recognize the place of writing will cast aspersions on the children from her second husband, saying that she was not divorced by her (first) husband (Tosafot and Rosh). If so, why is the get (bill of divorce) valid when it is not recognized in the place of writing, and it has a different name in the place of delivery? Ultimately, in the place of delivery, where it is called by a different name, it is not recognized that this woman is permitted, and they will cast aspersions on her children from her second husband. The truth is that, according to the fundamental law, when they do not know, there is no concern in this matter, for in the place where the get was written, it is called by that name as written in the get, and the people of the place of delivery will assume that presumably, the husband of this woman is called by that name in the place of writing, for no one divorces the wife of another (see Nedarim 6a). Therefore, the get is valid according to the fundamental law and also to avoid aspersions. However, when it is known in the place of writing that it has a different name in the place of delivery, it is impossible not to write the primary name of the place of delivery, for they themselves know that in the place where the woman is permitted, it does not appear at all in the get that her husband is divorcing her. Therefore, even post facto, it is not a valid get if they did not write the name of the place of delivery. And also, the people of the place of delivery, when it becomes known that the people of the place of writing knew that it has a different name in the place of delivery and did not mention it in the get, they will say that certainly another man divorced her, for if she had been divorced by her husband, they would have mentioned this name since they knew of it (and the Turei Zahav, section 8, wonders about this).

And if he did not write it as such, the Tur writes that the get (divorce document) is invalid, and if she remarried with it, the child is a mamzer (illegitimate). All thirteen ways mentioned in the chapter "HaZorek" apply to it, because this is a complete change of name. It appears that this is only when the name of the place of giving is not mentioned at all. Even if he wrote "and all names," since this name is the main one, it cannot be included in "and all names." However, if he also specified this name and wrote concerning it that it is called, even though he made the main name the place of writing, nevertheless, since he also explicitly mentioned the name of the place of giving, it is valid post facto (bediavad). This also seems implied by the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book. See there.

But our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 4 that if one made the place of writing primary and wrote based on the place of giving, which is called by another name or any nickname, it is invalid. End of quote. And it is questionable where he derived this from, and the later authorities (Beit Shmuel in sub-section 7 and Bayit Chadash) have already questioned him. There are those who permit this even initially (Bayit Chadash), and it is a significant leniency for certainly, initially, one should write based on the place of writing which is called, and not based on the place of giving (Beit Shmuel). But after the fact, it does not seem to invalidate (there). And even more puzzling is that it is written in the Shulchan Aruch that Beit Yosef wrote that this is implied from the language of the Tur. On the contrary, the Tur and Beit Yosef only wrote regarding "and any nickname" and not when specifying the name there. However, his reasoning appears as I explained in section 23 that they hold that "and any nickname" has the same ruling as specifying the name there. And since they invalidated with "and any nickname," it follows that specifying the name is also invalid. And although this is their opinion, in practice, one can say that it is not equivalent to the ruling of the great later authorities (and also the Gra in sub-section 12 and the Mishneh Lemelech in chapter 3, law 13 wrote that the main ruling is according to those who permit it there).

And if they did not write the place of writing but only the place of delivery, there is one who says it is also invalid (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 6). This is derived from the language of the Talmud that we brought, which says "until he divorces his wife who is in Judea with a name from Judea and a name from Galilee with him," implying that the place of writing is also essential. And even though according to the Rif and the Rambam, initially it is not necessary to specify it but to include it in "all names," nevertheless, this is as if they mentioned it explicitly according to their opinion. But if they did not write it at all, neither specifically nor inclusively, it is not valid. Furthermore, according to the Raavad that we brought, it must be specified, and we explained that possibly the law agrees with him. Additionally, the Tosefta holds that the primary importance is the place of writing, and since the language of the Talmud also implies that it must be mentioned, it cannot be valid if it is not mentioned at all. And even though in "all names" the primary and secondary, when only the primary is mentioned, the secondary does not invalidate it, this applies when both names are in one place. But here, where the place of writing is the primary, it certainly invalidates it. Nevertheless, if she has married, there is doubt if she should leave, since the primary name was written in the get, and this requires further investigation for the law.

From the words of the Rosh and the Tur, it is clarified that the requirement to write two names and that it is essential even post facto is only when the people of one place do not recognize at all the name of the other place. However, if in one place they know that there is another name from the other place, it is valid post facto if they wrote only the name from the other place that is also known to the current place. This is simple, but initially, it is certainly necessary to specify all the names, as written in section 19 from the Jerusalem Talmud, see there.

And know that in what we have written, that when it is not known in the place of writing that he has another name in the place of giving, it is valid with just the name in the place of writing. The Rosh and the Tur wrote: "But if he is not known by two names, and it is not known in the place of writing that he has another name in the place of giving, and also in the place of giving it is not known that he has another name in the place of writing, it is only necessary to write the name of the place of writing, and not any other name and nickname, etc." End of quote. The explanation of the matter is that it is not only if in the place of giving they know the name of the place of writing that it is certainly valid, as we have written, but even if the people in the place of giving do not know the name of the place of writing, it is also valid, even if it is later revealed that he has another name there (Beit Yosef). And when they wrote that it is not necessary to write except the name of the place of writing, it is not meant in the first instance, but certainly only valid after the fact, as is evident from the end of their words. And what they wrote in the language of the first instance, it is necessarily so, since they do not know of another name, and their intention is that it is not necessary to be concerned that perhaps he has another name in the place of giving, and it is not necessary to write every name and nickname due to this concern. And even if it is later revealed that he has another name, it is valid after the fact, as they wrote at the end of their words. And the Bach and the Taz endeavored to explain the words of the Rosh and the Tur in another way, but the matter is simple as the Beit Yosef wrote. And what they questioned, why is it valid when the other name is not known, and similarly the Taz was astonished in paragraph 8, we have already explained with the help of Heaven in section 26, especially since this is only rabbinically mandated; the child is considered a mamzer with just the name of the place of writing, as the Beit Shmuel wrote in paragraph 8.
