And it is obvious that all of this only applies to names of places of writing and giving, but when the writing and giving take place in the same location, or if the name is the same in both places, even though in another place it has another name, we do not concern ourselves with this. However, ideally, it is certainly proper to write all the names as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, and so wrote the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG), see there. All these matters we have explained follow the opinion of Rashi, Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur.

But some of our Rabbis hold that there is no difference whether it is known at the place of writing that he has another name at the place of delivery or whether it is not known. For even if it is not known, if it is later revealed that at the place of delivery he has another name and they do not recognize the name from the place of writing, the get (divorce document) is invalid. And this is what our Sages said, that without it being established, we are not concerned about it. The explanation is, specifically when he is established by another name at the place of delivery. But if he is not established at the place of delivery by another name, but his name is the same as the name from the place of writing, or it is known that at the place of writing he is called by that name, even if it is later revealed that in some place he had another name and this name is completely unknown, we are not concerned about it since it is neither the place of writing nor the place of delivery. And this is the opinion of Sefer HaTeruma, the SeMaG, Ra’aviah, and the Mordechai. And for practical halacha, certainly one should not deviate from the opinion of these Rabbis. And the Rambam of blessed memory and the authors of the Shulchan Aruch did not mention any of this at all. Their reasoning and explanations will be clarified to us with the help of Heaven.

There is another interpretation brought by the R"an, of blessed memory, which is the opposite of the opinions previously explained. He holds that if a person has been established in the place of writing with two names—meaning that he is sometimes called by one name and at other times called by the name of the place of giving—then even if the name of the place of giving is written, she is not divorced. However, if he has not been established with two names in the place of writing, meaning that he is only called by one name, even though it is known that he has another name in the place of giving, one should only write the name used in the place of writing.

However, the R"an, of blessed memory, himself elaborated and explained according to Rashi and Tosafot. According to all interpretations, a name used in other places, not in the place of writing and giving, is not considered at all after the fact. The names used in the place of writing and giving, both his and hers, as well as the names of their fathers, need to be explicitly detailed. The primary focus is the name of the place of giving. 

Regarding the name of the place of writing, they should write "who is called" for a male and "who is called" for a female. After the fact, if they wrote according to the name of the place of writing, any name is valid. But if they wrote according to the name of the place of giving, it is invalid. According to our Rabbi, the Rema, writing "who is called" for the place of giving is also invalid. However, most of the great authorities disagree with him on this, as mentioned in paragraph 28. Ideally, all the names in all places should be written, as derived from the Jerusalem Talmud.

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, in Chapter 4, did not mention any of this, but rather wrote that if a man has two names, and similarly if a woman has two names, when he divorces her, he writes his name and her name by which they are most commonly known and recognized, and he says "So-and-so, and any name he has, divorces So-and-so, and any name she has." And if he writes his nickname and her nickname, it is valid. If he writes a name that is not well-known, and writes "any name he has," it is invalid. These are his words. He did not mention any distinction between the place of writing and the place of giving. It appears that his opinion is that the primary decree of Rabban Gamliel was that if someone has an additional name, whether this second name is here or elsewhere, the main rule is to write the primary name and add "and any name," and it is upon the witnesses to understand what is the primary name and what is supplementary. Regarding the place of writing and giving, since the Talmud equates the place of giving to the primary, and the Tosefta equates the place of writing to the primary, it seems they do not disagree, and there is no strict requirement about which name to write and "any name" since both are primary. (Gittin, end of Chapter 16). There was no need to specify that without establishment, one does not need to write "and any name," since it seems that Rabban Gamliel's decree was to write in every get "and any name" due to this concern. Therefore, even without establishment, they write. The Talmud explains according to the basic law, and from the fact that the Rambam wrote that if one writes a name that is not well-known and writes the primary and "any name," it is invalid, we learn that its invalidity is only rabbinic, as stated at the end of Section 31, and it is not similar to an absolute change of name (as explained by the Beit Shmuel, Section 8).

Our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 4 that the primary factor is the place of giving, according to the majority of authorities. Similarly, they wrote in section 12 that ideally, all names that a person has should be written, even if they are not commonly used at the place of writing and giving. Alternatively, one should write the name he is known by at that location and include "and any other names." If only the name he is known by at the place where both parties are standing was written, and "and any other names" was not included, it is still valid, even though it is known that he has another name elsewhere (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 22). However, if the name from another place was written along with the name from the place of writing and giving, the get (divorce document) is invalid according to Torah law (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 23). This is not similar to the case where the name of the place of writing was written along with the name of the place of giving and "and any other names," which is only invalid rabbinically, as there is at least the name of the place of writing. But if the name from an entirely different place was written, it is considered a complete name change (Beit Shmuel, ad loc.).

And behold, they also did not mention a distinction between when the name was established and when it was not established. According to them, if the name was established at the place of giving and it has another name, if it was written at the place of giving with "and any name," then the get (divorce document) is invalid. Therefore, they should have explained that if it was not established, the get is valid. It seems clear that they were concerned with the opinion of our Rabbis, which we brought in section 33, that even if the name was not established, if it was later known that it had another name at the place of giving, the get is invalid, even if they wrote "and any name," as long as it was not explicitly mentioned. Therefore, they omitted this law entirely.

And now we will explain the fourth detail mentioned in Section 12, when a person has two names in one place, where some call him Reuven and some call him Shimon. Now, if half and half call him by these names, it is simple that one should write one name and the other as "also known as" or "and any name" according to the view of the Ba'al HaMaor, and he can choose which name he wants to write explicitly and the other as "and any name." However, if the majority of people call him Reuven and the minority call him Shimon, one must write "Reuven also known as Shimon" or "and any name," and not the other way around, as it is stated in the Gemara that we brought there regarding the case where the majority called her Miriam and the minority called her Sarah, and the Sages ruled "Miriam and any name she has," not "Sarah and any name she has." And we have already explained in Section 17 that according to Rabbeinu Tam, we do not write "and any name," according to our custom, but rather each name explicitly. The intention of the Talmud is also "Miriam who is called Sarah," and not "Sarah who is called Miriam." See there.

There is doubt whether the intention of the Talmud is that even after the fact, it is essential if he wrote "Sarah and any other name she has," or if this requirement is only from the outset. The doubt is whether we compare the minority (of people who call her by an alternate name) to the place of writing and the majority (who call her by the primary name) to the place of giving. If so, the law is that if he wrote "Sarah and any other name," the get (divorce document) is invalid. But if he wrote "Sarah, who is called Miriam," the get is valid, as mentioned in section 28. However, it is possible to say that this is better than the situation with names, because in the case of names, in the place of giving, they do not recognize the name written in the get at all, but here, the majority also knows that the minority call her by the name written in the get. This is similar to what was explained in section 30 and is valid after the fact, even with just the minority name. This also appears from the novelties of the Rashba, of blessed memory, there; see there.

But the Tur does not agree with this, as he wrote in the name of the RaMaH as follows: "When one divorces in his location, he writes the main name specifically and the secondary name inclusively. If he wrote the secondary name specifically and included the main name, there is a doubt if she is divorced." And I found that the MaHarShaL in his book (Yam Shel Shlomo, Chapter 4, Section 16) wrote as follows: "And regarding what he wrote, etc., there is a doubt if she is divorced. I do not understand why, although we say 'Miriam and all names' but not 'Sarah and all names,' this wording seems to be only initially required, and where do we get the idea to invalidate it after the fact? At most, it is only invalid so that she should not remarry, but if she did remarry, she does not need to leave. And even this is only according to their interpretation, etc. But according to our opinion, this is only a stringency initially. However, if he wrote 'Sarah who is also called Miriam,' it is certainly valid, and so ruled the RiVaSh." And in such a case, it is certainly valid as written in the previous section. But if he wrote 'Sarah and all names,' one should be concerned for the opinion of the Tur, and there is a doubt if she is divorced. And this also seems to be implied by the words of the Rambam that we brought and by the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, in Section 2: "If he wrote the name they are not generally known by and wrote all the names he has, it is invalid." This implies that even two names in one place, like Sarah and Miriam in the Gemara, and according to their opinion, it is invalid by rabbinic decree. And regarding rabbinic invalidations, it is explained in Section 150 that if she remarried, she does not need to leave, and this requires further investigation.

The essence of the Tur's words is puzzling. He himself wrote at the beginning of this section that one should write the main name and all nicknames and appellations, but one should not write the secondary name and all nicknames, etc. This applies initially, but after the fact, even if only one of them is written, it is valid. It is explicitly stated that even if only the secondary name alone is written, it is valid. And similarly, Rabbi Isserles (Rema) wrote at the end of section 1: "If only one name was written, even if it is the secondary name, and he divorced her with it, it is valid." How then does the Tur contradict himself? Rather, it must be said that he was quoting the opinion of the Ra'avad, which he did not hold by. And since Rabbi Isserles ruled not like the Ra'avad, we follow his ruling. However, Rabbi Yosef Karo in his major work wrote the opinion that without "and all nicknames" it is preferable. It seems that Rabbi Isserles also holds this way, for otherwise, he would have corrected it in section 2. This opinion does not seem reasonable at all (Gra in his commentary, section 7, and similarly in the Bais Shmuel, section 3). Therefore, according to the law, writing only the secondary name alone is invalid, as it also appears from Maimonides (there). It is not similar to the appellation, which is valid because everyone recognizes it and it is known to all, and not to the secondary name (there).

When writing the two names in the get (bill of divorce), one should initially write the primary name followed by the secondary name which he is called by. If he did the opposite, it is valid after the fact since both names are explicitly mentioned. From the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 2, it implies that even initially there is no strict requirement in this matter. However, some say that if it is not a case of preventing a woman from becoming an agunah (a chained woman) and the get has not yet been given, another get should be written, as it is clarified from the Talmud that one should write the primary name followed by the secondary name which he is called by, and not the opposite (Beit Shmuel, subsection 4), and this is the main ruling.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 14: "One who has two names, they write 'Reuven who is called Shimon.' If they wrote 'Reuven Shimon,' there is an opinion that it is invalid." End of quote. The explanation of his words is such: for example, if he has one name in the place of writing and another name in the place of giving, or even if both names are in one place, and these people call him Reuven and those people call him Shimon, like the case of Miriam and Sarah in the Talmud, the laws are explained that one must write on one of them 'who is called' according to the details that have been explained. Therefore, if one wrote both names together, it is invalid, because since he is not called by both names together, people might say that one is the divorcer (as per the Mahari"k Shoresh 98). And even if the people of this place know that in another place he is called Shimon (as stated in Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 24), and similarly, in one place where these call him Reuven and those know that there are people who call him Shimon, nevertheless, it does not help, because ultimately, he is not called by both names together.

And know that in his large book, he wanted to differentiate that when the two names are in two different places, it is invalid, but when they are in the same place, where some call him Reuven and others call him Shimon, it is valid if he wrote Reuven Shimon. However, from the language in the Shulchan Aruch, it implies that in all cases it is invalid (and so wrote the Gra in subparagraph 62). And his reasoning in his large book is because he saw that the Mahari ben Lev, the author of Teharet Hakodesh, validates in such a case, therefore he wanted to differentiate, but in the Shulchan Aruch, he ruled in a general manner like those who invalidate and did not differentiate in this matter because there is no reasoning to differentiate in this. Therefore, he wrote that there are those who say it is invalid because in his opinion, the author of Teharet Hakodesh disagrees in this matter (there). However, the truth is as our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in his book Darkei Moshe, paragraph 16, that even the Teharet Hakodesh agrees that it is invalid in all cases. And the validation mentioned there is explained that his name was changed due to illness, and when they called him up to the Torah, they called him by both names together, Reuven Shimon. Therefore, even though most people called him by only one name, some called him Reuven and others Shimon, nevertheless, since they called him to the Torah by both names together, the author of Teharet Hakodesh validated it. Consequently, in all cases, it is invalid if there is no one who calls him by both names together. (The Levush gave another reason for this invalidation, and the Gra has already wondered about him there, as in the Beit Yosef the reason we explained is clear).

And now we will explain the first detail in section 12: someone who is called by two names together. In the time of the Talmud and the early authorities, this was not common at all, and therefore they did not mention it, as stated there. But among us, it is very common, such as someone who is called Avraham Yitzchak, both names together. It is clear that it should be written this way in a get (divorce document), and this is the simple custom. If he wrote "Avraham who is called Yitzchak," it is completely invalid, because this is a total change (Beit Shmuel 24 and Get Pashut 63). And this is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote on the words of the Shulchan Aruch in section 14: "But if he is called by both names together or is called up to the Torah this way, it is valid" – end quote. They were puzzled by him because his wording implies that only after the fact is it valid if both names are written together. There is no puzzlement at all, for he is referring to a case where most people call him by one name, some call him Reuven and others Shimon. On the words of the Shulchan Aruch, he stands, and therefore, he says that if he is called by both names together or is called up to the Torah this way, meaning that there are those who call him by both names together, or even if no one calls him by both names, but when called up to the Torah, he is called by both names together, in such a case it is valid only after the fact. These are his words in his book Darkei Moshe, which we brought in the previous section, and it is clear (and so it appears from the Taz and Get Pashut there).

And if only one name is written in the get (divorce document) while everyone calls him by both names, the decisors have not clarified its ruling. It seems to me that it is not similar to a nickname or an abbreviated name, which will be explained as kosher, because in that case, everyone calls him by that name when they want to use a nickname or abbreviate his name. However, with one name, there is no one who calls him by that name. Even those who permit the secondary name would agree here that it is invalid, because with the secondary name, at least a minority of people call him by the secondary name, which is not the case here where no one calls him by only one name.

But if some people call him by one name and they wrote this name, it seems to me that it is valid after the fact. Even those who invalidate the secondary name do so because most do not call him by that name at all. But here, since most call him by this name in conjunction with the other name, and some call him by this name alone, it is no worse than an abbreviated name which is valid after the fact or a nickname, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

There is an opinion that if someone is called by two names, Reuven Shimon, and in the get (divorce document) it is written Shimon Reuven, the get is invalid (Gittin 63:3). In my humble opinion, this does not seem correct. Certainly, where the meaning of the name is altered to the ear of the listener, such as if someone named Yom Tov would have it written as Tov Yom or Shem Tov as Tov Shem, or a woman named Bat Sheva written as Sheva Bat, and the like, it is certainly invalid. However, in the case of Reuven Shimon or Avraham Yitzchak, and the like, where it is clear to the ears that the one written as Shimon Reuven is the same person called Reuven Shimon, why should it be invalid because of this? A proof for this is found in the scripture where names are sometimes listed in one order and other times in the reverse order, such as "These are the generations of the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 2:4) and "on the day that the Lord God made earth and heaven" (Genesis 2:4), and similarly, "Aaron and Moses" (Exodus 6:26) is also "Moses and Aaron" (Exodus 6:27). Although these are separate people and separate matters, and this is not proof for one person, still, the verse begins one way and ends the other, indicating that there is no strictness in this matter. And although there are Talmudic interpretations that teach that they are considered equal, nonetheless, ultimately, this is the way of the scripture, and the matter requires further study for a definitive ruling.

There is an opinion that one should be careful with someone who is called by two names, to write the two names on one line and not on two lines (T"G in Likutei Shemot, letter Aleph). And if they were written on two lines and it is a pressing situation where it is not possible to write another get easily, the get is still given to her even at the outset (there). For truly there is no reason for this [restriction], and only in names where there is doubt whether it is one name or two names, like Yedidya and Aminadav and such that will be explained, should one be careful. But not in distinctly separate names like Reuven Shimon and such. Only ideally, since they were given to him at birth as two names, they are considered as one name in this respect, not to separate them onto two lines. However, it is obvious that they should not be written completely together as one word (there), but each name should be written as a separate word. Not like the one who wanted to say to write them completely together (there). And know that all these two names that we have explained, where he is called by two names, is when he was given two names at birth. But if a name was added to him due to illness, there are different laws for this. And similarly, if sometimes he is called by one name or he is called up to the Torah by one name, or conversely, he is called up to the Torah by two names and is called by one name. And if he signs himself differently from how he is called, there are different laws for this, and it will be explained before us with God's help.

And now we will explain the second detail from section 12 concerning nicknames. Because there are many details in this matter, we will first quote the words of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, and then explain them with the help of Heaven. And these are the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 15: "One who has two names, and the second name is derived from the first in a manner of a diminutive, such as Yitzchak (Isaac) and Chakin, Aharon (Aaron) and Arnin, and similar cases, does not need to write the diminutive name at all, unless there is someone whose name is specifically Yitzchak or Aharon." And our master, the Rema, commented on this: "The same applies to Yaakov (Jacob) and Yaakil, Peretz and Partzin. It seems that the same applies to Avraham (Abraham) and Avralan, and similar cases. However, if one wants to write it, it does not harm. However, any shortened name that is a name in its own right, such as Elchanan and Chanan, and similar cases, should be written."

In Section 16, our master Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote: If the second name derives from the Hebrew name, such as Yehuda Leon, we write "Yehuda, known as Leon." If it does not resemble the Hebrew name at all, we write "nicknamed." And our master the Rema wrote: The explanation of his words is that Leon means lion, and Yehuda is called this because of the phrase "Yehuda is a lion's cub." Accordingly, we should write "Yehuda, known as Leib." But some say that whenever both names are in Hebrew, we write "known as," and if one is in a foreign language, we write "nicknamed," regardless of whether it derives from the name or not. Therefore, we write "Yehuda, nicknamed Leib," and similar cases. This is the practice in these regions. Any family nickname should not be written at all, whether it is in Hebrew or a foreign language, and this is the accepted custom.

Additionally, our master the Rema wrote there: One who has a Hebrew name by which he is called up to the Torah, and also has a name in a foreign language, the Hebrew name is considered primary, and the second name is written as "also known as." The same applies to a woman; the Hebrew name is considered primary. Furthermore, he wrote: There are those who say that if one has two names and is accustomed to using both, but one is more primary, it is written as "so-and-so also known as so-and-so." If one is not accustomed to the second name, it is written as "who was called." (This is the correct version three times, and the variant reading "also known as" is in the present, while "was called" refers to the past; see there.) Additionally, he wrote: Any nickname that is derogatory to the divorcer is not written in the get. Therefore, if he has repented, it is not written for him. Any name or nickname that he has, and any nickname that he is not called by exclusively, but is called with his primary name, does not need to be written. However, if the gentiles call him by the nickname alone, even though Jews do not call him that, some say that it is written "and any name and nickname," although in other divorces it is not written this way. The same applies to a family nickname. In my opinion, the nickname should not be written at all, just as it is customary with family nicknames.

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 17: If the second name is in a foreign language and it is all one, such as Chaim Bivant (which is Chaim in our language), we write Chaim who is called Bivant. Any nickname we write "the one called," whether it is in Hebrew or in a foreign language. And Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: It has already been clarified that this is not the custom. And in section 8, Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote: Now the custom is that in all divorce documents we write "and any name that I have and my ancestors and my place." And Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: In these countries, the custom is not like that, but if he has two names, we explicitly write as said. And in section 1, he similarly wrote not to write any name he has, but if he has two names, he writes "so-and-so who is called so-and-so," and this is the custom and should not be changed. And we have already explained this in section 15, see there.

A fundamental principle that needs to be known is that the term "d'mitkarei" (called) applies to all types of names and nicknames, for that is how he is called. However, the term "ha'mechuna" (nicknamed) only applies to a name that is somewhat related to the original name, as will be explained. If there is no relation at all, for example, if his name is Reuven and they call him Shimon, if one writes "ha'mechuna," it is completely invalid because there is no connection between the name Reuven and the name Shimon. It is necessary to write "d'mitkarei." Even if we say that "ha'mechuna" refers to the person and not to the name, it still does not apply because "ha'mechuna" implies a nickname and not a completely different name. Therefore, when in doubt whether to write "ha'mechuna" or "d'mitkarei," one should write "d'mitkarei" and not "ha'mechuna." This is also the ruling of all the great authorities (as the Beit Shmuel similarly concludes in subsection 30).

In the explanation of the term "kinui" (nickname), several interpretations are offered. The primary interpretation is that it refers to a change or concealment and hiding of the original thing. We find in Job (32:21-22): "Let me not, I pray you, respect any man's person; neither will I give flattering titles unto man. For I know not to give flattering titles..." meaning, I will not respect any man by changing my words and covering them, but I will reveal my words because I do not know this trait of concealment and hiding. And in Isaiah (44:5), we find: "And surname himself by the name of Israel," meaning, even though he did not behave like an Israelite, he will call himself Israel. This too can be understood as the language of concealment and hiding, that he will hide his true self and say, "I am Israel." Similarly, with Cyrus (Isaiah 45:4), "I have surnamed you, though you have not known me," meaning, I have named you as my servant and my anointed, though you have not known me. (However, there it can also mean a language of establishment and foundation, as in "a plant which Your right hand has planted.")

In the language of the Talmud, we find a nickname used derogatorily, such as "Ayin kol" (evil eye) or "Ayin Kutz" (thorny eye). Similarly, with nicknames for vows and oaths: for a nazirite vow, "Nazik" from "nazir"; for an oath, "Shakuka" from "shevuah"; and for vows, "Konam" (prohibited) becomes "Konas" or "Konech" (Nedarim 10a). The gist of the idea is that the name is slightly altered from its original, but it is still recognizable as stemming from the original name. This is not complete concealment.

However, in Ezra (6:13), we find: "Tattenai, governor of the region beyond the river, Shethar-bozenai, and their companions," and its explanation is those similar to them, meaning these officials and those of similar rank. Here it is a language of similarity. (And in Shevuot 36a, we find) regarding the Mishnah of "Yikach" (take), Rav Chisda sat before Rav Yitzchak and said, "This Mishnah follows our teaching." He replied, "Kenah (reversed)," and Rashi explained: reverse your words against others, etc., so that you do not curse me. This shows that it is a language of reversal.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, holds that one should not write the nickname unless the nickname is not exactly similar to the proper name. For a nickname implies concealment and hiding, and when it is exactly similar—even if it is in a foreign language, like "Byivant" and his name is Chaim—how can this be a nickname, for this is his proper name? Therefore, for us, someone whose name is Baer and his sacred name is Dov, or Wolf and his sacred name is Zev, or Binyamin, for Binyamin is also like a wolf as per the verse "Binyamin is a ravenous wolf," or someone whose name is Leib and his sacred name is Aryeh or Yehuda, for Yehuda is like a lion as per the verse "Yehuda is a lion's whelp." It is necessary to write "Dov known as Baer," "Zev known as Wolf," "Binyamin known as Wolf," "Aryeh or Yehuda known as Leib," since this is his actual name. But when it is not his actual name and it derives from his name, like Shlomo who is called Zalman, or Yechiel who is called Michal, or Raphael who is called Foa (Avraham), one writes the nickname. However, when the nickname is a completely different name that does not relate to the proper name, one does not write the nickname. The name Zalman derives from the name Shlomo, which was called Salaman by the gentiles, and it is a play on words, and then they called Salaman, Zalman, according to the changing pronunciations from country to country. Similarly, Michal derives from the name Yechiel, which was initially called Ikel to shorten the name, and then according to the change in pronunciation, it was called Michal. Similarly, Foa for Raphael was a shortened name. Our master, the Beit Yosef, holds that there is no difference between Hebrew and foreign languages; rather, everything depends on what has been explained.

However, our master the Rema (Rabbi Moses Isserles) holds that any nickname in a foreign language can be written as the nickname, even if it resembles a proper name, since it has changed from one language to another. The meaning of the nickname is like "and their nicknames" in Ezra, which we brought, meaning a term of similarity as we have written. Therefore, it is written "Dov nicknamed Baer," "Zev or Binyamin nicknamed Wolf," "Aryeh or Yehuda nicknamed Leib." And this is the common custom among us. Even more so with names like "Shlomo Zalman" or "Yechiel Michel" or "Raphael Pua," where the nickname is written, which does not completely resemble the original name. Even according to our master the Beit Yosef, the nickname is written. Similarly, with all shortened names, if it is necessary to write the shortened name, as will be explained, the nickname should be written. There is no need to question our words according to our master the Rema, that the nickname is derived from "and their nicknames" in Ezra. From where do we know that for an absolutely dissimilar name we write the nickname? The truth is that for an absolutely dissimilar name, certainly everyone agrees that this is the main nickname, like most of the nicknames in the Scriptures and the Talmud, which we brought, which imply concealment and hiding. Nevertheless, even for a very similar name, the term "nickname" applies, as in Ezra.

And this distinction between a foreign language and the Holy Tongue, that when the nickname is in the Holy Tongue, we do not write "nicknamed," but in a foreign language, we do write "nicknamed," it seems to me that the reason is as follows: Whenever the nickname is in a foreign language, it certainly has some similarity to the original name, like a shortened form or a transformation from one language to another or the like. But when the nickname is in the Holy Tongue, it has no connection to the original name and is entirely a different name. And what relevance does the term "nickname" have in this context, as I wrote. According to this, there is a doubt regarding someone whose name is Yehuda and is called Aryeh or someone named Binyamin and is called Ze'ev, how to write it. According to the principle of our master, the Rema, it should be written as "nicknamed," but there seems to be no reason not to write "nicknamed" since from Yehuda comes the name Aryeh and similarly from Binyamin, Ze'ev. It seems that the reason is that this is considered one and the same name in all respects, and therefore it is not appropriate to write "nicknamed," as it would be like writing Yehuda nicknamed Yehuda or Binyamin nicknamed Binyamin. The proof for this is that our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote regarding Yehuda who is called Leon, and Leon in their language is like Leib in ours, and it is difficult because it does not exactly resemble the name Yehuda since Leon means lion, and Yehuda is named after a lion. This is a concealment and covering of Yehuda. But certainly, Yehuda and Aryeh are considered exactly the same name without difference, and similarly Binyamin and Ze'ev, as they share the same reason. This is what our master, the Rema, wrote, and there is no difference whether it derives from the name or not. His words, meaning whether it is exactly like the original name, such as Yehuda Leon as mentioned, or not exactly like the original name, contrary to the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, as mentioned.

And know that although the reasoning we have written, that every foreign (non-Hebrew) name has some resemblance to the original name, even though in most names it is certainly so, nevertheless, it is not an absolute rule. Also, what we have written in the explanation about deriving from the name, although according to the depth of the Shulchan Aruch it seems so, nevertheless, from the words of the Darkei Moshe (section 18) that states there is no difference whether the foreign name is a translation of the Hebrew or not, it is clear that even if there is no connection between the foreign name and the Hebrew name, one writes "known as". There is clear evidence from what is written there in section 24, "Moshe, known as Levi," and there is no connection between them. Similarly, there are names among us such as Shimon, known as Zimmel, and Meshulam, known as Zalman (Beit Shmuel, section 29), and also Aveli, which is a nickname for Avraham (in the section on men's names, letter Aleph), and Elimelech, known as Pilta (there), and Eliezer, known as Lieberman (there), or Bukash, or Pavoli, or Feibush, or Lippman (there). Similarly, Yissachar, known as Ber (there, letter Yud). Also, in the names of women, most foreign names are derived from the original name, as we have heard and seen in the name books. Nevertheless, there should be no absolute rule in this matter, because there is one nickname for several names. Therefore, every foreign name is written as "known as," since the Hebrew name is nicknamed by this foreign name, and this falls under the term "known as." Every sacred name (a name from the Torah) is written as "called," since it is also a standalone name. Therefore, in the case of Elchanan, called Chanan, one does not write "known as," even though it is certainly derived from Elchanan. Nevertheless, since Chanan is also a standalone name, it is not appropriate to say that Elchanan is known as Chanan, as there is Chanan without Elchanan. This is also evident from all the name books, and this is the custom in all our regions.

And this which is written that one should not write a family nickname at all, the reason is simple: since the entire family has such nicknames, it is not a distinguishing mark at all (Levush). And that which is written that if one is called to the Torah by a Hebrew name and also has a name in a foreign language, the Hebrew name takes precedence, and for the other name, we write "called" (dim'kari), his words contradict what he wrote earlier, that for the foreign name we write "nicknamed" (dem'khune). The later authorities wrote that he did not delve into the difference between "called" and "nicknamed," but rather he meant to teach us that the Hebrew name is primary. However, in truth, one should write "nicknamed" (Taz, Nekudat HaKesef, and Beit Shmuel, section 30). This is a significant difficulty, that he did not be precise about the matter he was discussing. There is someone who says that here he is discussing a case where the nickname is also a proper name, which is independently called a name, and it is like a Hebrew name, so one does not write "nicknamed" but "called" (Gehilot Ephraim, section 82). There are those who differentiate between when the nickname was from birth and when it was added later, and their words were rejected (Avnei Shoham and Gehilot Ephraim there). There are those who say that here it is discussing a case where at birth, he was only given the nickname, and later his name was changed to a Hebrew name due to illness. In such a case, "nicknamed" does not apply, since this was his original name. Therefore, even though the name changed due to illness is primary as will be explained, nevertheless, it is impossible to write "nicknamed" on the original name, but rather "called" (Gehilot Ephraim there and Noda BiYehuda, section 119). And although this is certainly the case according to the main law, nevertheless, this is not the implication of his words, because if it were so, he would have explained it.

In my humble opinion, it seems that the explanation is as follows: Certainly, if the foreign name (la'az) is based on the Hebrew name, even if it does not directly derive from the Hebrew name, we write "nicknamed" because this foreign name is associated with the Hebrew name. But if a person has two names, one Hebrew and one foreign, and the foreign name is not based on the Hebrew name but rather the person was given two distinct names such that sometimes they are called by one name and sometimes by the other, this is what is being taught here: Even though most of the time they are called by the foreign name, and we might have thought to write the foreign name first and then the Hebrew name as "called so-and-so," still the Hebrew name is primary because it is the name used for being called to the Torah. Therefore, we write the Hebrew name first and the foreign name as "called so-and-so," and it is inappropriate to write "nicknamed" since it has no connection to the Hebrew name, as stated in section 54. Furthermore, it says an even greater novelty: the same applies to a woman in such a case — the Hebrew name is primary, and we write the foreign name as "called so-and-so," even though most people call her by the foreign name. With a woman, there is no concept of being called to the Torah. According to this, his words are precise, and it is clear that for a woman, this applies only if at least a minority call her by the Hebrew name, giving it precedence over the foreign name. However, if even a minority do not call her by the Hebrew name, it is considered a forgotten name and is not written at all. But for a man, since there is the matter of being called to the Torah, if he is called to the Torah by the Hebrew name, and even if he is also called to the Torah by the foreign name, we do not write the Hebrew name at all, as it is considered a forgotten name (as the Beit Shmuel also wrote in section 31, that the Hebrew name is primary even if it is used by a minority).

And this is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote afterward: "There are those who say that someone who has two names, if he is accustomed to both, but nevertheless one is more primary, they write 'Ploni who is called Ploni.' If he is not accustomed to the second name, they write 'who was called.'" This means that it has been clarified that the Hebrew name is primary even though most people call him by the other name. This applies to a Hebrew name against a foreign name. But when both names are Hebrew or both are foreign, and he is not called by both together, but sometimes by this name and sometimes by the other name, if one name is more primary and he is mostly called by this name, they write this name and for the second name, 'who is called.' This is like the case in the Gemara where most people called her Miriam and a few called her Sarah. However, if he is not accustomed at all to the second name, meaning even a minority do not call him by the second name, and it has not been completely forgotten, otherwise, it would not need to be mentioned at all, but rather, occasionally he is called by this name, they write 'who was called' and not 'who is called' because 'who was called' refers to the past (as it seems to me). A derogatory nickname is not written at all because the Torah's ways are pleasant ways. Therefore, in the case of a penitent, we do not write 'all names,' even though in the reverse case we do write them according to our custom, as it is written (and this is also proof for what I said that the Rema is referring to when the nickname is not associated with the Hebrew name at all, because a derogatory nickname certainly does not belong to the Hebrew name, and similarly, in the reverse case, examine this carefully).

And this which is written, that any nickname which is not called by that nickname alone, but rather they call him with the primary name, there is no need to write the nickname—the reason is simple: since they always mention the prominent name with the nickname, it is not considered a nickname regarding bills of divorce. The reason why we write the nickname in the divorce document is to recognize that this is the person divorcing, so that they do not think that this Reuven mentioned in the document is not the one divorcing, because many who are called by a nickname do not know that his name is Reuven. Therefore, in any case where they always call him by the prominent name with the nickname, there is no need to worry about this (Terumat HaDeshen, Siman 235 and Gittin, Siman 85). And some say that both should be written together (Prisha, Siman 45).

However, regarding what he wrote that if the non-Jews call him only by the nickname, some say that we write "and all names and nicknames," even though in other divorce documents we do not write it. He concluded that it should not be written at all. This raises a question, as he himself wrote in section 14: "If he is called by one name among Jews and another name among non-Jews, we write the Jewish name and 'also known as' the non-Jewish name. But if the names are almost identical, we only write the Jewish name," as discussed earlier in section 128 regarding rivers. How then can he write here not to mention the non-Jewish name at all? Even those who hold that we should mention it do not specify explicitly but write "and all names." 

The truth is that in section 14, it is discussing when he has two distinct proper names, one among Jews and one among non-Jews (section 86). Therefore, we write "also known as" and not the nickname, since the non-Jewish name is a proper name in its own right and not a nickname for the first name. (This is proof for what is written in section 61.) Or when both names are foreign names (section 25), it is not appropriate to use "also known as" since each name is a proper name in its own right. But here it discusses where the primary name is the Hebrew one and the nickname is for the Hebrew name. Since the Jews call him by the primary name with the nickname, there is no need to mention the nickname at all, not even to include it as "and all names," because there is no confusion for the reason explained in the previous section.

One should not ask how we write only one name when it was explained in section 45 that when he is called by two names, both must be written. Here, since he is called by the proper name with the nickname, why not write both? The answer is that it is different when both names are proper names in their own right, in which case certainly both must be written. But here, where one name is only used with the nickname, there is no need to mention the nickname at all, as everyone knows who he is, as was written. And what was written in section 14 that if the names are almost identical, we only write the Jewish name, means when even the non-Jews call him by the Jewish name, but according to their pronunciation, it changes slightly, like calling Aaron "Aran," Michal "Michael," and Moshe "Mashey." In such cases, there is no need to mention this at all, as it is considered a shortened version of the name.

And what is written in Section 15 concerning the matter of the name of youth when it is derived from the first name and does not need to be written at all, like Yitzhak Hakin, and in our language Itsa, Itzik, Itzka, Aharon Arnin, and in our language Ara, Arka, and for Yaakov, Yakil or Yankel, as is customary to call in our place the name Yaakov, or Peretz, Pertzin, or Avraham Avrelen, or Avramil, Avramka, and similarly for Shmuel, Mula, Monya, Shmulik, and likewise in the names of women, it is customary to call Bila, Bilka, Bilyata, Piga, Pigala, Basha, Bashka, or Bashinka, and all such things which are only names of youth. And usually, people themselves are not called by the name of youth (see at the end of the names of men that in women it is not so). Therefore, there is no need to mention it at all, because everyone knows that this name of youth that they call him is the name that is written in the get. But what our master the Rema wrote there, and I quote: "However, any abbreviation of a name that is a name in itself, like Elchanan Hanan, we write it, and similar to this," end quote. It is necessary to ask, what is the matter of the abbreviation of a name to the name of youth? However, he [the Rema] holds that they are all the same. And it seems that we found in the Mordechai who wrote in Chapter 4 in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, and I quote: "And there is no need to write a nickname that is an abbreviation of the name, like Bila, Bilta, Shmuel, Muel, Margaliyot, Margalota, Tzipora, Pora, Binyamin, Bonami, because this is neither a nickname nor a change," end quote. And the owner of the Hagahot Maimoniot in Chapter 4 calls this a name of youth (brought in Beit Yosef). From here we learn that this and that are one and the same. And the truth is that for a youth, they do not insist on calling him by the actual name, only by the abbreviation of the name. And sometimes it is a name of affection and endearment, like they call Berela, Leibala, and in women's names, Pigala, Bilka. But for an adult man and in his presence, they call him by the actual name, and this is a way of respect. And it is not necessarily that they abbreviate the name, for Bila, Bilta, Margaliyot, Margalota, are extensions of the name, but they call this by the borrowed name, the abbreviation of the name, or the name of youth. Therefore, they do not write it because it is not a name at all. And therefore, if this abbreviation is a name in itself, like Elchanan, who they call Hanan, they write it, and similarly in all such cases.

And this ruling that if one wishes to write the abbreviated name, it is not harmful—this is the primary ruling in practice. Even though there are those who want to say specifically not to write it (Ranach) and their reason is that perhaps it will not be written correctly (G"F, Se'if 171), and also perhaps someone who sees it will question it (there), nevertheless, we do not worry about this. For why should we be concerned that it will not be written correctly, and the observer will not question it, thinking that there was another person in the city with the same name, and the abbreviation is for a sign (there)? Furthermore, sometimes there is doubt whether this is an abbreviation of the name or a completely separate name, and in this case, it is certainly correct to write it (Bach, Se'if 128). Additionally, there are abbreviations that have another sacred name, and therefore, the Maharshal (in Yam Shel Shlomo, Siman 28) ruled regarding Yaakov Yaakil that one should write Yaakil because he has another sacred name, Elikim. And although from the language of Rabbeinu the Rema it seems that even in this case it is not necessary to write the abbreviation, for this is the novelty he added to the words of the author, therefore, certainly, if one wishes to write it, they write according to the ruling of Rabbeinu the Rema. And thus have the later authorities decided, especially regarding women's names, as will be explained.

And know that from the language of the Shulchan Aruch it somewhat implies that the need not to write the abbreviated name is specifically when they also call him by the primary name. And even though most people call him by the abbreviated name, nevertheless, they write only the primary name. And all the more so for a man who is called to the Torah by his primary name, and likewise he signs himself with his primary name. But for a woman, if everyone calls her by the nickname, the primary name becomes like a forgotten name, and they write only the nickname, even though it is an abbreviation and a name from her youth. Similarly, for a man, if they call him to the Torah by the nickname, as is common now where there is no fixed reader to know the calling of the names, and likewise if he signs himself with the nickname, they write only the nickname (as mentioned, and this is also implied from the Geonim in section 26). And even if there is doubt about this for the one arranging it, it is better to write only the nickname, for writing the nickname is valid after the fact, and according to many great halachic authorities, it is even initially valid, as will be explained later with G-d's help. And a general rule regarding names is that whenever there is some doubt about the primary name, they write only the nickname. What difference does it make if it is a nickname from youth or an abbreviation of the name? In the end, everyone calls him that, and we do not expound on names, but rather write them as they are called. And it is impossible to clarify everything in writing, and if the arranger is a learned and knowledgeable Torah scholar, he will understand how to write. And more will be explained about this with G-d's help.

And now we will explain the third detail from Siman 12, when someone was ill and their name was changed. The poskim (decisors of Jewish law) were very stringent about name changes, considering it of utmost importance. We have already explained that the change of name for an ill person in their times was not as is customary among us, where we add a name to the existing one and call the person by both names together, and likewise, the person signs their name and is called to the Torah with both names, as is known. In their times, it was a complete name change, where the previous name was removed and another name was given, similar to "your name shall no longer be Jacob, but Israel," etc. This is explicitly seen in a response from a Sephardic authority (cited in Get Pashut, Siman 93), which states: "Concerning a get (divorce document) of a person on their deathbed, they wrote his name as Matzliach, and three days before writing the get, they made a prayer for him and changed his name, calling him Chaim," etc., end quote. Likewise, in a responsum from the Mabit, it states about a person on their deathbed whose name was changed from Yitzchak to Chaim, etc., see there. This is also brought by Beit Yosef in the following language: "An incident came before the R"P with someone who was ill, and they changed his name during his illness," etc., see there. Therefore, our custom of adding a name to the ill person's original name is not a name change but rather an addition of a name. Accordingly, all the laws that are discussed regarding the name change of an ill person according to the opinions of the poskim are based on their practice of completely changing the name. However, according to our custom, there is a different law in this matter, which will be explained in Siman 82 with God's help.

And behold, regarding the change of name according to their custom, if everyone was calling him by the new name, there would not be any effort for the decisors in this matter, and it is simple that they write the new name. However, due to the habit that everyone is used to his first name, even after the change, there are many who will still call him by his first name. The earlier authorities ruled that the changed name is primary, and regarding the first name, they write "who is called," even if the majority call him by the first name and the minority by the changed name. Even if the first name is Hebrew and the changed name is a foreign language, nevertheless, the changed name is primary, and regarding the first name, they write "who is called." This is not similar to the majority calling him Miriam and a minority calling him Sarah, and similarly for a Hebrew name and a foreign name, it was clarified that the foreign name is secondary. Here, since they intentionally changed his name to another name, it is obvious that the second name is primary in all aspects.

Therefore, some say that it is not specifically when the name is changed due to illness, but also if the name is changed due to another reason that necessitated the change, the second name becomes primary just as with a name change due to illness (and this is also found in the Responsa of the Rema, Siman 84). And some say that it is only a name change due to illness, because the tearing of the harsh decree is severe with this name, and not for a name change due to another reason (and this is found in the Maharik, Shoresh 98). The main ruling seems to be that certainly, with any name change, we follow the change. However, this is not comparable to illness, because with illness, we follow the name even if only a minority call him by the changed name and make it primary. But with any other name change, we follow the majority; if the majority call him by the changed name, we write "formerly known as" for the first name. But if the majority call him by the first name and a minority by the changed name, we write the first name and "formerly known as" for the changed name. (And this is also indicated by the words of the Taz, Siman 27, and the Magen Avraham, Siman 92, except that they hold that when the change is due to fear of danger, it is similar to a name change due to illness. And in the words of the Beit Shmuel, Siman 33, there is an error; see there and examine thoroughly.)

And these are the words of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, section 18: Someone whose name was changed because of illness, even though he is always called by his original name, nevertheless, the name of change is primary, even if it is a foreign name and the original name is Hebrew. And we write it first, and afterwards "known as so-and-so" with the original name. This is specifically when he is sometimes called by the second name, but if he is never called by the second name at all, we write only the original name. There is an opinion that requires two gittin (divorce documents) with both names. If he has a prominent name by which he is called up to the Torah and signs his writings and documents, that name is primary. If he is called up to the Torah with both names, we write the second name as primary and the first name as "known as." However, for the person signing himself, if he has two names, he should sign with both names without "known as." These are their words.

And behold, this is a simple matter: that which was stated that even though they always call him by his first name, nevertheless, the name of the change is primary. It does not mean that they do not call him at all by the name of the change, and it is like a forgotten name, for in such a case it is obvious that the name of the change is not primary. Not only that, but they do not write it at all, as explained in their own words. And some say that not only is there no need to mention it in such a case, but it even invalidates the get (divorce document) if it is mentioned, since the name of the change has been completely forgotten (Gra, Even HaEzer 129:6). And so it is clarified from the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, where he brought the words of the notebooks about a woman whose name was Rivka and her name was changed due to illness and she is called Chana, and the whole world calls her by the name Rivka, which is her first name, that the name Chana should not be written in the get at all. And it is obvious that the name Rivka is not worse than a nickname, etc. Thus the words of the notebooks. And it is written about someone who was called at birth Chaim, and afterwards they call him by the name Bybant, etc. And if they do not call him at all by the name Chaim, they write only Bybant alone. And if they also wrote the name Chaim, it implies from the notebooks about a woman whose name was Rivka and changed to Chana that she is not divorced. Thus the words of the notebooks. Hence, it is held in the opinion of the notebooks that if they also wrote the name Chana that was forgotten, she is not divorced. And from this, it is learned about the name given at birth that when it is forgotten and they wrote it, even if they also wrote the name by which he is called, she is not divorced. And that which they wrote that they always call him by his first name means that generally, they always call him by his first name, however, a minority call him by the name of the change.

However, regarding invalidating the get (divorce document) by mentioning also the forgotten name, this matter is perplexing. Since the commonly used name is also mentioned, what harm does the forgotten name cause? Even though this name has fallen into disuse, it was indeed his name at some point, and the get clearly identifies who is divorcing. Furthermore, what our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote—that she is not divorced—seems to imply that according to Torah law she is not divorced, which is an impossible assertion. Moreover, from where did he derive such an inference from the booklet? On the contrary, from the fact that it is written that the name Rivka is no worse than a nickname, it is explicitly proven that they validate the name Rivka alone, and do not invalidate it if they also wrote the name Hannah. Therefore, it seems to me that there is a printing error in his great book where it is written "And if he also wrote the name Chaim," and it should say "And if he only wrote the name Chaim." This is certainly the case, as with the forgotten name alone she is not divorced according to Torah law. Another proof is that if it were as written before us, why did our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, not bring this ruling in the Shulchan Aruch? Moreover, he wrote that there are those who require two gets in a case where he is not called by the forgotten name at all. How can we say that this name invalidates it? Additionally, there is proof from the words of the Maharshal (Yam Shel Shlomo, Chapter 4, Siman 24) who wrote in the opinion of the Terumat HaDeshen that a name of illness, even if he is not called by this name, is still considered, as it is like a sign. Therefore, it seems to me, even though the Levush also wrote that if they wrote in the get also the forgotten name, it invalidates the get—regarding a name of illness that has been forgotten, it does not invalidate the get. Also, regarding the main matter that a forgotten name invalidates the get if they wrote also the commonly used name and did not write both together but rather as "called," I am perplexed as to why it would invalidate it. This requires further investigation for the halachic ruling.

This, that the illness is considered primary, is specifically when the divorce is in the place of writing the get (divorce document) or even in a get sent from place to place, provided that in the place of giving, the name change is known. However, if in the place of giving it is not known at all that his name has changed and he is called by his original name, the original name known in the place of giving must be written first, and the name change should be written as "also known as" (Beit Shmuel Section 34). For it has already been explained that the place of giving is primary. Some say that the name change is written as primary, and the original name as "also known as," and they write for the place of giving that his name has changed due to illness (Yam Shel Shlomo Section 24). And some say that one should not rely on this (Beit Shmuel there). And this seems to be the primary ruling (and the Yam Shel Shlomo there that permits this in such a case, but it is not necessary to do so from the outset, therefore the primary ruling follows the Beit Shmuel).

And regarding what was written that there are those who require two gittin (divorce documents) for two names, he explained his words in his major work in two ways. The first way is according to the simple understanding of his words in the Shulchan Aruch, that even if one is never called by the second name, nevertheless, two gittin are required. The reason is that since it is not proper to write the second name even as secondary in one get if one is never called by it, however, since we see that a name of illness is so significant that even if only a minority call him by it, it is treated as primary as we have written. Therefore, even if he is never called by this name at all, nevertheless, it should be written in a separate get, and post facto, we are not concerned about this (Beit Yosef). The later authorities have decided that even initially, two gittin are not required for a name of illness that has been forgotten, but rather, the name he is called by is written and that is sufficient (Beit Shmuel, sub-paragraph 35, and Turei Zahav). And so should be the ruling, for there is great effort and concern of confusion with two gittin, as will be explained with God's help.

The second case is written about a sick person whose name has been changed, and who divorces while he is still ill. The new name is not yet established, neither through being called up to the Torah nor through his signature. It is impossible to write one get (divorce document) with the new name as the primary name according to the rules of a name given due to illness, because it is not yet established. Writing the previous name as the primary name and the change as an alias is also impossible, for we have a rule that the name given due to illness is primary. Therefore, two get documents should be written (Beit Yosef). However, after the fact, if he divorced with only the previous name, it is valid (Ba'er Heitev on this section). Initially, there are those who say to write the previous name and "any other name he has" (Gittin Peirushim 293), and this is also appropriate to do in our times when we do not write "and any other name" in the get. Nevertheless, for such a get, it should be written initially. If he divorces after three or four days when it has become well-known that his name has been changed, there is doubt as to which name is primary. Initially, two get documents should be written, but after the fact, whether he wrote the previous name and "any other name he has," or he wrote the changed name and "any other name he has," it is valid (there). And it seems to me that as long as the changed name is not established, it is necessary to specifically write the previous name with "any other name" (and see Piskei Teshuvot section 50 where it mentions the Get Mesudar and it is an all the more so reasoning, see there).

A sick person who had their name changed and subsequently died from the illness, it appears that the name change is not mentioned at all. Regarding whether his son or daughter would need to mention their father's name in their bills of divorce, they should only refer to his original name. Because he died from his illness and the name change did not help him, he remains known only by his first name. Additionally, since he died from the illness, he was never established by this new name. This is also the ruling of one of the great authorities (Rabbi Yeshaya, grandson of the Shelah, in his responsum Chut HaShani, and it is cited in Pitchei Teshuvah, section 50, note 50).

And this which is written, that if he has a well-known name by which he is called up to the Torah and with which he signs his writings and documents, that name is the main one, it appears clearly from the arrangement of his words that even if his name changed during his illness, if he is called up to the Torah and signs himself with the previous name alone, even if everyone calls him by the changed name, nevertheless, the name he establishes for himself for being called up to the Torah and for his signature is preferred over all the other names, and they write it as the main name and the changed name as the secondary name (Magen Avraham 298). And if he is called up to the Torah by this name and signs with the other name, there are those who say that we follow the majority; if his being called up to the Torah is more frequent than his signatures, this name becomes the main one and the signature name as the secondary name, and if his signature is more frequent than his being called up to the Torah, we make the signature name the main one and the Torah name the secondary name (ibid). And if both are equal, the changed name is the main one (ibid). And there are those who say that when his being called up to the Torah and his signature contradict each other, the changed name is always the main one (Taz 130). And in other names not related to illness, if his being called up to the Torah and his signature contradict each other, we combine this with what the public calls him; if they call him by the name he is called up to the Torah, we make that the main one and the signature name secondary, and if they call him by the signature name, we make that the main one and the Torah name secondary. And if they call him by a third name, we prioritize the name the public calls him and the other two as secondary, and we prioritize what is more commonly used by him as explained (ibid).

And this is what our master, the Rema, wrote: If one is called up to the Torah with both names, the second name is considered primary, and for the first name, we write "also called." His intention is not that we call him by both names together, for if so, one would need to write both names together, and what relevance would "also called" have here? Rather, it means that sometimes he is called by the original name and sometimes by the changed name, and therefore the changed name is primary (Gra, section 99). One should not ask, according to this, how he concludes: "but until the signature itself, if he has two names, he should sign with both names without 'also called.'" For in such a case, how would he sign himself as Reuven Shimon? After all, he is called either Reuven or Shimon. The answer is that even in such cases, he can sign himself with both names together. This is clarified in the larger work of our master, Beit Yosef, where it says: "And this law was written by Maharik, etc., and he wrote that one must write 'so-and-so, also called so-and-so,' and he objected to a bill of divorce where the two names were written without 'also called' between them." Also, in Terumat HaDeshen, section 134, it is written that one must write 'also called.' However, if one comes to sign a bill of divorce, he should sign 'Yaakov Moshe son of so-and-so' without needing to sign 'also called.' The reason for distinguishing between the divorcer and the witness, etc., is that the witness specifying his names in the bill of divorce is only for the sake of societal order (Gittin 36), and it does not apply to saying he is called by two names. This is not the witness, for in any case, he is valid for testimony (Beit Shmuel, section 146), and whoever he may be, he is valid. But for the divorcer, if they say it is someone else, they will say about this man's wife that she is still married.

Additionally, it can be explained that this refers to someone who is called to the Torah with both names together, but people only call him by one of the names. Some call him by the original name and some by the changed name. This is to teach us that even in such a case, the changed name is primary and the original name is written as "also called." Even if the original name is used first when he is called to the Torah, we do not take it into account. This is explicitly explained in the responsa of the Mahari"v, section 182, and this is his wording: "Someone whose name was Yosef and his name was changed to Yisrael due to illness, and everyone calls him Yisrael. Only when he signs, he signs Yosef Yisrael, and when he is called to the Torah, he is called Yosef Yisrael. We write Yisrael, also called Yosef, because the name given due to illness is primary." And this statement that everyone calls him by the name from the incident was indeed the case. But it is also true if a minority calls him by the changed name, as previously explained. According to this, it can be said that even the statement that he signs with both names is only in such a case. However, it has already been explained according to the great book of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, that in all cases when someone signs with both names together, it is valid. (And the Gaon there questioned this, saying that since the original name is used first when called to the Torah, it should be written first in the get as well. He follows his opinion that when two names are used together, if the last name is placed first, it is invalid. But we have already explained in section 48 that in my humble opinion, this does not seem to be the case, as explained there).

There are those who have raised a significant question regarding this matter: since we follow the name used for being called up to the Torah, how do we reconcile what the poskim (decisors) have written that the name change is primary? If he is called to the Torah by the changed name, there is no need for the reason of a name change due to illness. And if he is called to the Torah by the previous name, we have ruled that the previous name is primary (as stated in the responsa "Lechem Rav"). In my opinion, this is not a question at all, as the poskim indeed state that the name change due to illness is primary and should be given precedence. Therefore, in the case of a woman, or a man who lives in a settlement and is not called to the Torah and does not sign documents, the changed name should be given precedence. Likewise, in places where they do not call people to the Torah by name but simply call "Kohen," "Levi," "Shelishi," or in many places where there are no fixed cantors who know how to call people to the Torah, as we see in our times in many places where they do not know their right from their left in calling a person to the Torah, sometimes calling them by one name and sometimes by another, one should not establish a rule based on the name used for being called up to the Torah. The changed name is primary. Even in places where they are knowledgeable, the poskim indeed state that the changed name is primary. Consequently, one must be careful in signing to use this name as primary, and the cantor must be careful to call him to the Torah by this name. However, if he signs his name with the previous name and is called to the Torah by the previous name, although this is not proper, since he himself has uprooted the changed name, we do not follow the changed name because he has personally nullified it (as it appears to me).

All these laws were explained according to their custom, where the name of the illness is completely changed. However, according to our custom, we add a new name to the previous one, so that the person is called by both names. For example, when his name was Reuven and they added the name Shimon, we say in the prayer for changing the name of the sick, "and his name in Israel shall be Shimon Reuven." In a get (divorce document), both names must be written together. If afterwards everyone calls him only Reuven, and he signs and is called to the Torah with both names, we write Shimon Reuven who is called Reuven. If it is written Shimon who is called Reuven, it is invalid. If it is written Shimon Reuven without "who is called Reuven," it is valid (Tur, Even HaEzer, Hilchot Gittin, Siman 129, Seif 2). If there are those who call him by both names, even if they are a minority, it seems to me that it is not necessary to write "who is called" at all, for as has been explained regarding the change of name due to illness, it is strong enough to make it the primary name even if a minority calls him by the new name. Similarly, for this matter, it is possible that nonetheless, ideally, we write "who is called Reuven," since the majority call him that.

One of the great authorities wrote (there, section 11): A woman whose name was Frida, and due to illness her name was changed to Sarah Frida in accordance with local custom where the first name is not removed but rather an additional name is given. Now, some call her Frida Sarah, some Sarah Frida, some just Sarah, and some just Frida. It should be written as Sarah Frida, who is called Frida Sarah, and who is called Frida. End of quote. And it seems to me that it should also be written as "and who is called Sarah" (see there, subsection 8, where a reason is given that there's no need to write Sarah separately, but in my humble opinion the reason is not sufficient; see there and scrutinize).

Additionally, it is written there that if the majority call her "Freida Sara," it should be written "Freida Sara who is called Freida." However, it seems to me that since the minority call her "Sara Freida," it should primarily be written "Sara Freida who is called Freida Sara," as it is written in Section 82, that for this matter as well, the name change due to illness is significant, even if only a minority call her that.

Additionally, it seems to me that according to our custom, where we add a name even if there are some who call her by both names but the majority call her only by the previous name, if the scribe made a mistake and wrote only the first name, it is valid in a pressing situation. This is because what the halachic authorities wrote—that if the name change is not mentioned, the document is invalid—applies when the first name is completely uprooted, in which case the main name is not mentioned at all in the get (divorce document). However, according to our custom, where the first name is not uprooted at all and the majority call her only by this name, this name is not lesser than a nickname. Much deliberation is warranted in this matter.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in section 18: Someone whose name has been changed due to illness and has a nickname based on the second name, we write the second name with its nickname before the first name. If he also has a nickname based on the first name, we also write that at the end. And if his name has been changed twice, we write the third name first, then the second, and then the first, writing each name with its nickname.

The explanation of his words according to their custom is that the primary name is the first name, but the world mostly calls him by the first name and a minority by the changed name. It is explained that we write the changed name as primary and the first name as secondary. Therefore, if the changed name has a nickname, we write it with its nickname and then the first name. If the first name also has a nickname, we also write that at the end, like someone whose name was Yehuda and his nickname was Leib, and the changed name is Dov and his nickname is Ber, we write Dov known as Ber, called Yehuda known as Leib.

Similarly, if his name has been changed twice, we write the last name and its nickname, then the second name and its nickname, and then the first name and its nickname, for the last name is always primary. In this case, we do not write "called" on the first name, like someone who has two nicknames, as it is explained that we write "known as so-and-so" and "known as so-and-so" for the names, since the nicknames are equivalent and one does not negate the other. But here, the last name negates the first, except that many still call him by the first name, so it does not apply to write "called" except "called" meaning that many still call him by his previous name.

And all this is when they call him by his first name. But if they do not call him by it, there is no need to write it at all. Similarly, if he is called by his nickname and the sacred name has been removed from him, such that they do not call him by it, and he does not sign with it or go up to the Torah with it, we do not write the first sacred name but only his nickname. And so with all his names in similar cases.

And all this is according to their custom, but according to our custom, where we add names as stated, and we call him by both names, and each name has a nickname, we write both sacred names together and also the nicknames together. For example, Dov Yehuda, also known as Ber Leib. If his name was changed twice and another name was added, such as Tzvi, also known as Hirsch, and we call him by three names, we write Tzvi Dov Yehuda, also known as Hirsch Ber Leib. If one of these names was annulled, we do not mention it at all, as has been explained. And this is the law for all names, as will be further explained with God's help.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 10: "Joseph son of Simon who changed and wrote 'Joseph son of Samuel' is invalid. And there is one who says that if she has married, she need not leave, but only if he is established by the second name. Otherwise, she must leave." End quote. The explanation of the matter is that the Tur brings an incident that happened with one whose name was Joseph son of Simon, and his father changed and shamed to mention him, and called himself Joseph son of Samuel. And it seems this was the name of his grandfather (see Beit Yosef). The Rosh of blessed memory invalidated the get (bill of divorce) since the observer might say another is divorcing her because her husband's name was Joseph son of Simon, and this is Joseph son of Samuel.
