End quote of the Tur. And he means that although the father's name does not invalidate a get, as the Tur wrote earlier, nevertheless the change invalidates it. And we do not say that any non-essential change does not invalidate, for this applies only to changes like place of birth and the like, which are not recognized by many. But a change of the father's name, which is recognized by many, invalidates it, as this reasoning is written in section 8. See there, and we have written other reasons there as well. See there.

And even though this invalidation is only rabbinic, as is evident from its language, and with a rabbinic invalidation we hold in Siman 150 that if she married, she does not have to leave, nevertheless here she must leave. There are rabbinic invalidations for which they were stringent to say that she must leave, as it is written in Siman 10, see there. And we have already written in Siman 11 that from this there is no proof, for the change of the name of his father is only rabbinic. It could be said that it is from the Torah, and here there was no intentional or accidental change, but rather he intentionally maintained his father's name as another name or signed himself with his grandfather's name out of shame. If you ask, why then is the get invalid, and why not say that just as a person can change his own name, he can also change his father's name? However, certainly this is not comparable. Every person can change and exchange his own name, but not his father's name, and it does not help that he maintained his father's name as another name. Therefore, she must leave. There is an opinion that says that since his father's name was established in change, if she married, she does not have to leave, and they brought a responsum from Rashi who ruled this way (see Beit Yosef).

And behold, from what was written in the name of "Yesh Mi She'Omer" (there are those who say), it appears that the primary ruling is according to the first opinion. However, we see that our master, the Beit Yosef, in his responsa (Siman 9), was asked about such a case and responded that if she has not yet married, even if she has been betrothed to another, we do not rely on this get (divorce document), and the first husband writes her another get in the name of the true father. Only if she has married do we rely on this opinion, because if she requires a get from the first husband, she would necessarily have to leave the second husband, as is the law for one who has married in prohibition, and she must leave both husbands. Therefore, due to necessity, we rely on this opinion. However, in truth, we hold that in all rabbinic disqualifications, the first husband divorces her, and she remains with her current husband, as the Rambam wrote in chapter 10, and so too the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Siman 150. According to this, even if she has married, the first husband gives her another get, and she remains with her current husband. Our master, the Beit Yosef, concluded the matter by stating that in the case of the Rosh, it was only a rabbinic disqualification. However, in the Shulchan Aruch, he wrote generally that if he changed his father's name, it could be that he changed it deliberately, and this could be a Torah-level disqualification. Since this law is not clear, he left it ambiguous.

One who has converted to another religion (a "Kuti") — it would seem that one should write their primary name as their Jewish name and their secondary name as their Kuti name. However, Rabbeinu Tam, of blessed memory, ruled that this name should not be mentioned in a get (divorce document) written according to the law of Moses and Israel (Tosafot 34b, Rosh, Ran, and all the poskim). Instead, only the Jewish name should be written. Some say this is only when the Jewish name has not yet been forgotten, meaning people remember that he had this name. But if it has been forgotten, the Jewish name is not written (Beit Yosef). Others say that even if it has been forgotten, it should still be written (Beit Yosef citing Maharik), because this is not analogous to any other forgotten name, as in this case everyone knows that he had a Jewish name. Even if they do not know what it was, they will assume that the name written in the get was probably his original name (Responsa Radach Beit 4). There are those who compromise, suggesting that both the Jewish name and the Kuti name should be written (Gra, Siman 24). This is the main ruling, as also in other cases of conversion, our master the Beit Yosef ruled in paragraph 5 that if the primary name is written as the Kuti name and the secondary name as the Jewish name, it is valid, and certainly the opposite is valid. However, the main legal principle is that there is no difference here between whether the Jewish name has been forgotten or not (and so wrote Taz, subparagraph 6, and this is also the conclusion of Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 10, and so wrote Turei Zahav).

Our custom when dealing with a convert is to write the name "Israel" and all aliases and nicknames that he has. Even though in all other divorce documents we do not write "and all aliases," in this case, we do. If the convert has a nickname, we write the name with the nickname first and then "and all aliases." However, if one wrote the name of a non-Jew and all aliases that he has, the get (divorce document) is invalid. Nevertheless, if one wrote the name of a Jew who is called by a certain name, the get is valid, as long as the explicit name of Israel is written. If a person’s father has converted, when the son writes a get, he does not need to write the name of his father and all aliases, because since it is not obligatory, we should not embarrass him (Taz and Beit Shmuel). However, the Maharshal and Maharam Padua in their responsa wrote that one should write "and all aliases" and inform the one giving the get, and this matter requires further investigation according to the law (based on Pitchei Teshuvah, note 13). One should write "and all aliases that I have" after his name and not after his father’s name.

In ancient days, a convert needed to write the name of "Israel, son of Abraham our father" and not just "son of Abraham" lest it be thought that his father's name is Abraham. If "our father" was not written, he must write that he is a convert, and if he did not do so, it is invalid (Beit Shmuel, section 39). Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 6 that a convert who wrote his gentile name is valid, even if it was forgotten from him. These words require explanation because, certainly, with only this name it is impossible to validate the get (bill of divorce); rather, his intention is that this name was written primarily and also the name "Israel" with which he is known. However, from the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, it appears simply that with this name alone it is valid. Its source is from the Tosefta in chapter 6 of Gittin, where it is taught that a convert who changed his name to a gentile name is valid, and similarly, you say regarding a female convert. The Tosafot and the Rosh brought this Tosefta, but the Rif and the Rambam did not mention it. Indeed, it can be said that it does not mean that they changed their name only in the get, but that they changed their name even before the get, and it comes to teach us that since they wish to be called by this name, it is valid when written so in the get. One of the early authorities explained this in a responsum (Radach, house 4), and this is implied from what is taught later in the Tosefta there: Gittin coming from overseas, even if their names are like gentile names, are valid because Jews overseas have names like gentiles. However, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch explained it simply that only in the get was this name written, and there is a question here: why, in the reverse case, if a gentile name alone is written, it is invalid, but for a convert, it is valid? The answer is that a convert writing the name he had before he became a Jew is not prevented by the Torah of Moses, as the Torah did not obligate a gentile to convert, unlike the reverse case. Even if this name has been forgotten, it is valid because it is known that he necessarily had some name before he converted, and people will not say he is someone else. This is not similar to any name that has been forgotten, as we wrote in section 91. However, in practice, it is certainly difficult to validate a forgotten name, and more so it is puzzling that our teacher, the Beit Yosef himself, in his great book, rejected this matter, but in the Shulchan Aruch he wrote it simply and validated it, and this requires further study.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Gittin 87b): "If he wrote his nickname or her nickname, it is valid." The Rambam in Chapter 3 and the Shulchan Aruch in Section 1 copied the words as they are without explaining what the nickname is. From this language, it is evident that it is only valid post facto. However, some of our Rabbis hold that it is also valid initially with his nickname and her nickname (Tosafot 34b, Rosh, and Ran in Chapter 9 in the name of Rabeinu Tam and Rach) because they have a version in the Mishnah that states, "If he wrote his nickname or her nickname, it is valid, and so the meticulous people of Jerusalem would write." This is the version of the Jerusalem Talmud, as it is explained there that the meticulous people would sign with this initially. But in our version, it is written about the meticulous people first, referring to a different matter. This is the version of the Rambam, and therefore he ruled that it is only valid post facto.

And what is "ḥanikha"? Rashi explains that it is the surname of the family, as he wrote: "the family nickname." And it means, for example, that the family name is Lipshitz and the family name is Shapiro. And it was written: a man from the Lipshitz family divorced a woman from the Shapiro family, and their special names were not mentioned at all. And in the get it was written: "I, from the Lipshitz family, standing, etc., release you, my wife, from the Shapiro family," and she was divorced on these terms. Otherwise, how would we know which family member divorced (Mordechai Chapter 3)? And according to this explanation, the explanation of "ḥanikha" in the Mishnah is as the Baraita in the Gemara (page 88) where we learned: The Rabbis taught that the surname of the fathers in gitin is valid up to ten generations. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says up to three generations, and the Rif and the Rosh ruled according to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar because the verse supports it: "When you beget children and grandchildren" (Deuteronomy 4:25). And so we learned in the Tosefta (chapter 6): If he wrote using the name of his grandfather, it is valid; if he used the name of the family patriarch, it is invalid. If they were called by his name, it is valid.

However, it seems to me that it is impossible to say, even according to Rashi's explanation, that the Mishnah and the Beraita are one and the same. For in the case of a family surname, such as the Lipshitz family that we mentioned, it is not relevant to differentiate between generations, since all generations have the same designation, as is well known. Rather, it is certain that the Beraita refers to something else and does not deal with the family surname shared by all members. Instead, it refers to a situation where the head of the family had a well-known and recognized name, such as a scholar or a wealthy person, and he wrote in the get (divorce document) "I am from the seed of so-and-so," and the Tanna Kamma holds that up to ten generations, the matter is recognized. However, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that beyond three generations, the matter is not recognized, and the get is invalid as mentioned. According to this, the language of the Tosefta that we brought is precise: if he wrote in the name of his father's father, meaning from the seed of so-and-so known to be his grandfather, it is valid. If he wrote in the name of the family patriarch who is more distant than three generations, it is invalid. If they were known by his name, meaning that the entire family adopted this name as a family designation and in the world, they are called by this name, such as the Lipshitz family and similar cases as in the Mishnah, it is valid (as mentioned above).

However, the Rosh and the Ran, of blessed memory, wrote in the name of Rabbeinu Chananel and Rabbeinu Tam, of blessed memory, that the "nickname" mentioned in the Mishnah is a completely different matter from that of the Baraita. The Mishnah deals with the nickname of the man and the woman themselves, and its explanation is similar to the nickname of a name as explained in this section, such as someone whose name is Yehudah and his nickname is Leib, or Dov and his nickname is Baer. Similarly, the nickname of a woman, such as her name is Miriam and her nickname is Miryasha or Mirusha and the like. According to this, it can be said that in practice they do not disagree, and all agree that the nickname of the man himself is written initially, but the family's nickname is only written after the fact (and see Beit Yosef, subsection 1). This is also proven by the Tur, as mentioned there (and what he writes is sufficient, meaning after the fact).

And from the general wording of the Rambam, of blessed memory, it is proven that he also interprets the surname of the person himself. And so he explicitly writes in his commentary on the Mishnah, see there (Avodah Zarah 1:8 and Geirim 3:4). But he only accepts this retrospectively, and there is someone who says that the Rambam allows it from the outset (Tosafot Yom Tov, Peah 9:8). According to the style of his language, it is proven as such, see there. And our master, the Beit Yosef, was astonished at him in his great book that he did not mention at all the matter of the surname of the family up to three generations, see there. And this very astonishment can also be wondered about him, that he did not mention this at all in the Shulchan Aruch. And it seems to me that our master, the Beit Yosef, questioned the surname of the family up to three generations and no more. On the contrary, the more generations it is established, the more significant the surname becomes. He struggled greatly with this, and therefore he omitted it. And although in section 96 we have correctly explained the matter, he was not comfortable with it. As for the opinion of the Rambam, it seems to me that in section 95 we wrote that it refers to when he did not write his name at all, but only the surname of the family, see there. And indeed, this is what the Mordechai wrote in the first chapter of Gittin. But there are early authorities who explained that it refers to when he also wrote his name but instead of "son of so-and-so," he wrote the surname of his grandfather, who was the head of the family, and up to three generations it is valid. Beyond that, it is considered a name change and is invalid (Shibolei HaLeket, chapter 4, in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak ben Avraham). And the Rambam was in doubt about this, therefore he did not write it at all. It is also possible to say that he holds, as we wrote in section 96, that it does not refer to the surname of the family but to the name of the grandfather who was known and recognized, and he wrote "from the seed of so-and-so," as implied by the Tosefta we brought. Therefore, since in our time it is generally not customary to write this way and it is not a sign in our days, he did not write about this law at all.

One does not write in a get (bill of divorce) "Rabbi" or "Sage" or "Prince" even if he or his father held such titles, nor her father. It is not necessary to state that one does not write such titles for oneself since the get is in the language of the husband, and it is not customary for a person to refer to himself with an honorific title. Even for the father’s name, one only writes the name itself, "So-and-so, son of So-and-so." Additionally, one does not write "son of the holy one," even if he was holy and was martyred for the sanctification of God's name, because no title is written in a get. However, if it was written "So-and-so the Wise" or "the Rabbi" or "the Prince," it is valid post facto. This is not only where it is true, but even if he is not actually of that status and is not called by that title, the get is still valid because his name was explicitly written. Even for his own name, it is valid (this is explicitly stated in Shulchan Aruch, Section 7). We are not concerned that people will say he has two names and that this is not the one divorcing, since everyone will understand that he wanted to describe himself in this way, and who can protest against him? We find in the Gemara that a person can describe himself in this manner (Pesachim, Chapter 7).

And there is someone who asked a question about this, for we find in the Gemara (Ketubot 85b) the case where someone said, "My property to Tuvia," etc., and then Tuvia came, and then Rav Tuvia came. It was said, "To Tuvia, but not to Rav Tuvia." (This is the intention of the Beit Shmuel, section 13.) According to this, it seems that if someone is worthy of being called "Rav," it constitutes a change of name if "Rav" is omitted. And there are those who ruled this way (Shiltei Giborim, Chapter 8 of Gittin). However, this is not a question at all, for we see that throughout generations, this has not been the custom in Gittin, even concerning the father's name. And this is the main point, for in the case of Tuvia, it is said there, "If it is someone who is familiar with him, meaning accustomed to him, they call him without the title 'Rav.'" And who is more familiar than a son with his father? And the Get (divorce document) is in the language of the husband. And one cannot say that on the contrary, the son, since he is obligated to respect his father, certainly needs to call him "Rav." One cannot say this, for we find in the Talmud that they did not refer to their fathers with a title, only by their actual name, as in Pesachim (112a), "I say to Yochai, my father," and in Gittin (14b), "Rabbi Dostai, son of Rabbi Yanai, who said, 'Who gave to Yanai, my father, a son like me?'" and in Bava Batra (56b), "Rabbi Yosei said, 'When Abba Chalafta went, etc., to learn Torah.'" And we also see from Maimonides, of blessed memory, in his introduction to his great work and in his introduction to his commentary on the Mishnah and in its conclusion, where he signed himself, "Moshe son of Maimon," even though his father was great in Torah, as he brought in Chapter 11 of Shechita, the law of ten, etc. It is thus explicit that the respectful way is to refer to one's father only by his actual name. However, as a distinction in the case of two Yosef ben Shimon in one city, if one’s father is a Rav and the other’s is not, one should write "the Rav" (Beit Shmuel there and Nachalat Shiva). Nevertheless, we have never heard of anyone writing this way.

According to the basic law, it is not necessary to write "Kohen" or "Levi" [in a document], and it is evident from the Talmud (Bava Batra 172a) that in the time of the Tannaim, they did not practice writing "Kohen" in documents unless to distinguish him from another person with the same name. However, the simple custom in all regions is to write "Kohen" or "Levi," and they also write it for the father of the bride if he is a Kohen or Levi. It somewhat implies in the Talmud (Ketubot 24b) that in the time of the Amoraim, they wrote "Kohen" in documents. Since the custom is simple to write it, if it is not written, some say it is invalid because once it became customary to write it, its absence would imply that he is someone else. Others permit it, arguing that since it is not required by the basic law, it should not be assumed he is someone else. The ruling in practice is that if the divorcer is a Kohen or Levi and it was not written, even if the get (divorce document) was given, if it is possible to give another get, it should be given unless it is a pressing situation where it is impossible to give another get. In such a case, or if the get has not yet been given and it is a pressing situation where it is impossible to write another get, this get may be given. However, for the father of the bride, if he is a Kohen or Levi and it was not written, if the get was already given, it is valid even if it is possible to write another get, as there is less concern regarding the names of the fathers in terms of their titles (Beit Shmuel, section 14). Know that it is simple that "Kohen" and "Levi" are written next to the father's name, and it is not necessary to write it separately for him and separately for his father, as it is understood that if his father is a Kohen or Levi, he is as well (ibid.).

If they wrote "Kohen" for someone who is not a Kohen or "Levi" for someone who is not a Levi, it is clear that the get (divorce document) is invalid. And even though any matter that does not need to be written, a change does not invalidate it, it has already been explained in section 8 that we do not say this except in a case where the change is not noticeable to the public. However, in this case, it is obvious that people will say it is someone else. Also, regarding the father of the woman, if they wrote "Kohen" or "Levi" and he is not, the get is invalid even in a pressing situation. And so have ruled the great authorities of the world (Noda B'Yehuda, siman 89 and the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger, siman 116). And although there is an opinion that leans towards validating it in a pressing situation (Pri Tevuah, subsection 21), God forbid to rely on this.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in section 7: "If there is doubt whether he is a Kohen or not, two gittin (divorce documents) should be given." This is his final word. Now, regarding the one who is divorcing himself, doubt does not apply, for there is no person in Israel who does not know this. Rather, the intention is about the father of the woman who does not know if her father is a Kohen or not. Generally, there is no need for concern, for the majority of people are neither Kohanim nor Levites. It is only intended when it is said that it seems he is a Kohen or Levite and it is not clear. In such a case, two gittin should be written. The same applies to the one who is divorcing himself when it happens that he does not know for sure and it seems to him that he is a Kohen or Levite (as the Taz wrote in section 11 and the Pri Tohar in section 17). Furthermore, it is written that in a get (divorce document) one should not write "Ploni bar Ploni" but rather "Ploni ben Ploni," because "bar" can imply "outside" (as stated in Beit Shmuel). However, post facto, it does not invalidate the get even if it has not yet been given, for most of the language of the get is Aramaic, and in Aramaic "bar" is used. Ideally, there should be some concern (this seems correct to me).

If the one granting the divorce is a Kohen or Levi and his father's name has a nickname, he should write "the Kohen" or "the Levi" before the nickname, for example, Ploni ben Yehuda the Kohen or the Levi known as Leib. The same applies to the father of the woman. The reason is that if he writes "ben Yehuda known as Leib the Kohen," people might think that the nickname is "Leib the Kohen." Therefore, he should write "the Kohen" after his sacred name. There is no concern that the nickname will be distanced from the actual name, as we find in the verse, "And they took Lot and his possessions, the nephew of Avram." But if he has two names that are written as one who is called by both, he should write "the Kohen" afterward, as there is no concern that people will think he is called by that name, because he indeed is called by it. However, a nickname is not relevant in this case. It seems to me that even for a nickname, if it was written afterward and the get (divorce document) was already given, there is no need to write another get, even if it is not a pressing situation. Similarly, if it is a pressing situation, there is no need to write another get even if it has not yet been given, as the concern is minor (and this is also indicated in the Beit Yosef, see there).

Our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 19 that there is an opinion which states that when giving two gittin (divorce documents) to a woman, one should not give both at once but rather one after the other. One should only give two gittin out of necessity. The first get should be the one deemed more valid by the rabbi, with all its questions and readings according to the order of the get, and afterwards, the second get should be given also according to the order of the get. The reason for giving two gittin should be explained to those present at the time of the giving, and the husband should be instructed to have the intention to divorce with each of the gittin. If both are given consecutively in the same order, it is valid. So concludes the matter.

Explanation of the matter: Giving two bills of divorce (gittin) at once raises several concerns. The first concern is that he might intend to divorce her with the get (bill of divorce) that is not the primary one according to the law (Beit Yosef in the name of the Rivash). The second concern is due to the issue of selection (bererah), as we hold that in matters of Torah law, there is no selection. Since it was not clarified at the time of giving the get with which one she is being divorced, there is a concern regarding selection (Rema in Responsa, Siman 84, section 22). The third concern is that Tosafot wrote in Sotah (18a) that it is forbidden to divorce with two gittin, as the Torah said "a book of divorce" and not two or three books (there). This is why they wrote that one should not give two gittin except in a pressing situation, because in giving two gittin, even one after the other, there is a concern, as the witnesses of delivery do not know with which one he is divorcing her. Such a concern is found in the Gemara (76b) regarding two people who sent two gittin and they got mixed up, that he gives both to this one and both to that one. And Rabbi Yirmiyah said that according to Rabbi Eliezer, who said “on condition” constitutes a valid get, it does not help because they do not know with which one he is divorcing her, and this is not a clear giving, and we require a giving for her sake. And even though Abaye rejected this and said that we only require writing for her sake and not giving for her sake, and this is the halacha as stated in Siman 132, nevertheless, in gittin, the sages were concerned for all opinions, and there is reason to be concerned for Rabbi Yirmiyah's view. Therefore, one should not give two gittin except in a pressing situation, and if it is possible to resolve with one get, how good it is.

Now, regarding all these concerns, we must discuss the first concern—that he might intend to divorce her with what is not fundamentally valid according to the law. This is relevant when someone gives two bills of divorce without specification. However, anyone who gives two bills of divorce clearly states that his intention is to divorce her with the bill that is fundamentally valid according to the law, and there is no concern about this. Therefore, the third concern about "two or three books" does not apply here, because that applies when he intends to release her with both of them. But here, where he explicitly says that he intends to release her with one of them, it does not fall under the category of "two or three books." Nevertheless, one might say that we are concerned he might forget to tell the rabbi arranging it to instruct him to say that he intends to release her with one of them. And although this is a remote concern, we still need to be cautious. Yet, even in such a case, the concern of "two or three books" does not apply, since only one of them is valid. Still, we might say that according to most opinions from the Torah, both are valid, and the concern returns to its original place. However, we have already written in Siman 122 that the Rambam does not hold the opinion of "two or three books," as he did not bring this ruling in all of the laws of divorce, and we explained his reasoning there.

And the concern for retroactive clarification (brerah) also does not apply here, as there is no need for the giving to be done with specific intent, as it is written: "and he gives her both [documents] and divorces her with this one that is valid." There are many commandments that, due to doubt, both options are performed with the intent to fulfill one of them, similar to those who wear two pairs of tefillin at once, as written in Orach Chayim, Siman 34, where it is instructed to intend to fulfill the commandment with one of them. And even though the husband does not know with which get (divorce document) he is divorcing her, what difference does it make? After all, she is certainly divorced with one of them. A clear proof is from the law of two people who sent two gets that got mixed up, which we have brought up. Additionally, in the case of a get given by a person on his deathbed, when he says, "This is your get from today if I die," when he dies, the get is effective. The husband does not know at the time of giving the get when it will take effect, yet we do not worry about retroactive clarification. All the more so in this case, where he knows he is divorcing her with one of them but does not know which one is the primary get. However, the early authorities indeed questioned why in the case of "from today if I die" there is no concern for retroactive clarification and answered that in something destined to be clarified from the outset, as it will be clarified when he dies, retroactive clarification does not apply. Some have answered that retroactive clarification only applies to two separate things, but in a condition on one thing, even according to those who do not hold by retroactive clarification, it is effective. According to this, in our case, where there are two things and it will never be clarified, there is a concern for retroactive clarification. However, in truth, since she is certainly divorced with one of them, retroactive clarification does not apply at all, as at the time of giving it is clarified that she is divorced with one of them. And this reasoning is brought in the poskim. There is someone who was concerned with two gets at once due to the issue of interposition (chatzitzah). This is not understood, as the same type does not interpose with itself. Furthermore, she receives both of them with both her hands, and the valid get is attached to one of her hands. If she were to receive it with one hand and it rests on her palm, it would still be a valid get. And even if she receives it with one hand, the valid get is also attached to her fingers, as she takes both gets with her fingers, and necessarily one of the gets is attached to one of the fingers. Unless we say that perhaps the husband placed them on her palm and the one resting on her hand is the invalid one.

And also, the primary reason for distancing from two gittin (divorce documents) is because the agents (messengers) might not know which one of them effects the divorce. Besides, the law is not like this, as I will further explain. It is not similar to two gittin from two different men that got mixed up, where the one that is not his (the husband's) was not written in his name or for her. This is different here, as both were written in his name and for her, but there is a doubt regarding the names. In such a case, it is well known to the agents that she is certainly divorced with these two gittin, and both belong to her. However, the primary divorce takes effect with the get (divorce document) that was written according to the law. In conclusion, these reasons are indeed weak, but since our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, were concerned about this, it is impossible to go against their words.

Therefore, they wrote that initially, the more kosher-looking get (divorce document) should be given with all its questions until its completion. Otherwise, before the get is finalized, we still fall into some of the concerns that were explained. Therefore, one get is completed and the second is begun. This is not a concern because when the second get is given, it nullifies the first get, as the husband does not have the power to nullify a get once it has been given to the woman. Therefore, with a get through an agent, it is certainly difficult to send it through two gets, as it appears like the nullification of a get. Also, we should not worry that when the rabbi himself arranges the second get, it would seem like he is invalidating the first get, as the rabbi certainly does not say that the first get is invalid, but rather that he has a concern and doubt. Therefore, he arranges a second get.

Some of the great authorities have added a good enactment in this matter, for even according to the ruling of the Shulchan Aruch, some concerns remain. If the husband knows from the outset that he must give two bills of divorce (gittin), it will not be clear to him with which one he is actually divorcing her. Therefore, they established that neither the husband nor the witnesses nor the scribe should be informed that two gittin are necessary. Instead, one bill of divorce should be arranged according to the law, and afterward, it should be said to them, "I see some concern in this get (bill of divorce); therefore, it is good to write another one." This way, all concerns will be resolved (Gittin 76:7 and Noda BiYehuda 90). Although there is a concern that the husband might say, "Had I known I had to give another get, I would not have divorced her," (and the Gittin passage there is concerned about this), this is not a real concern. When the rabbi arranges the second get, the husband says that he gives it willingly and nullifies any prior declarations. So, how can he later contest it? If the husband indeed does not agree to give a second get, the rabbi arranging the get must persuade him, either with money or with words, until he agrees. If not, the rabbi will not arrange it against his will. If we worry that the woman might not be able to remarry, since the primary get was arranged first according to the law, if the husband stubbornly refuses, we will permit her to marry with the first get, just as we are cautious with all enactments regarding agunot (chained women). Therefore, it seems to me that one should certainly avoid arranging two gittin. When the necessity arises, it should be done as mentioned: not revealing the need for a second get initially and arranging the get that seems more legally sound first, and afterward arranging the second get with the husband's consent.

Regarding names and nicknames, it has already been clarified that for a sacred name, one writes "who is called" and it is not specifically limited to Hebrew, but any Hebrew name found in the Tanakh and in the Talmud is written as "who is called." For a foreign name, one writes "nicknamed" and for a woman's name, one writes "who is called" and "nicknamed" with a kamatz. There is no difference in writing "nicknamed" between a man and a woman, except in pronunciation – for a woman with a kamatz and for a man with a segol. If only the nickname is written without the Hebrew name, it is valid, as it is stated: "If one wrote his or her nickname, it is valid." According to many of our rabbis, this is even valid from the outset. Therefore, the custom in cases of doubt about the sacred name, such as someone whose name is Leib and whose Hebrew name is uncertain if it is Yehudah or Aryeh, is to write only the nickname. Many great rabbis have adopted this practice. However, the validity of the nickname alone applies only if everyone calls him by that nickname, as the Tur states: "If his nickname is known and recognized everywhere, and everyone calls him by it, except when signing a document or reading in a book where he is called by his prominent name, then the nickname alone suffices even from the outset." This means that even post facto, we do not validate the nickname alone if not most people call him that way and it is not frequently used, as the Raavad states in his comments on the Rambam: "If one wrote his or her nickname, it is valid," he wrote: "This is only if he is more accustomed to that nickname." But when writing the Hebrew name, one writes "nicknamed" or "who is called" even if only a minority calls him that way, as is evident from the case of most people calling her Sarah and a few calling her Miriam in the Gemara, which is clarified in this section.

One who has two Hebrew names and each name has a nickname, such as if his name is Yehuda Dov and his nickname is Leib Ber, one writes "Yehuda Dov, also known as Leib Ber," and similarly in all such cases. If only one name has a nickname, such as if his name is Moshe Yehuda and they call him Moshe Leib, there is an opinion that one writes "Moshe Yehuda, also known as Leib" (Beit Shmuel, Section 24). However, some disagree with this because "also known as" refers to the person and not the name. Therefore, how can we write "also known as Leib" if they call him Moshe Leib? Instead, one should mention both names, and consequently, it is impossible to write "also known as" since there is also a Hebrew name. Rather, one should write "Moshe Yehuda, called Moshe Leib," and this is the primary ruling (Nodah B'Yehudah, Section 119 and Teshuvot Geonim, Section 7). Similarly in all such cases, except if they only call him by the name Leib, then one should write "also known as Leib."

If someone has two names from birth, and he is called to the Torah and signs with both names, but in everyday life he is only known by one of them, such as his name being Abraham Isaac but he is only called Abraham, then they write "Abraham Isaac who is called Abraham." After the fact, if "who is called" was not written at all, and it was simply written as "Abraham Isaac," it is still valid. Similarly, if only "Abraham" is written, it is also valid if everyone calls him only Abraham, as it is no less valid than a nickname. However, if only some people call him by one of the names, it is invalid if only "Abraham" is written. In such a case, it is not necessary to write "who is called" at all (Yoreh De'ah 129:2). Conversely, if he is called by both names and is called to the Torah by one name, it is necessary to write "Abraham who is called Abraham Isaac" (ibid. 129:3). What is stated there, that it is also permissible to write "Abraham Isaac who is called Abraham," is not clear, as "who is called" is only relevant to what he is called in everyday life.

Someone whose name in the Torah reading is Yechiel Avraham but is commonly called Michael Avraham, and similarly, someone who goes up to the Torah with the name Yehuda Moshe but is called Leib Moshe, should write "Yechiel Avraham, who is called Michael Avraham" and similarly "Yehuda Moshe, who is called Leib Moshe," and so on for all similar cases. One should not place the sacred name before the secular name, since he is first called by the secular name (Shulchan Aruch, section 7). If someone is commonly called Yehuda Leib and signs his name that way but goes up to the Torah only with the name Yehuda, initially one should write "Yehuda, who is called Yehuda Leib," but after the fact, if he wrote just Yehuda, and it is a pressing situation or the get (divorce document) has already been given, it is valid (Shulchan Aruch, section 8). If it is impossible to determine how people call him, such as someone named Elchanan Zev but is called Chanan by people, if we knew that he is called Chanan, it is obvious that we should write "who is called Chanan." But if it is impossible to determine whether he is called Chanan or Chana, we should not write "who is called" at all, but just Elchanan Zev, since that is how he goes up to the Torah and signs his name (Shulchan Aruch, section 10). The general rule is that it is better to enter into a doubt of a deficiency rather than a doubt of a change, because the former does not invalidate while the latter does.

There was an incident involving a man named Yehoshua whose nickname was Heschel, and he would be called to the Torah with that name and sign his name as such. However, in his youth, there was some confusion and he was occasionally called Hershel. To this day, some people call him Heschel and some call him Hershel. It was ruled that both nicknames should be written, "Yehoshua, also known as Heschel and also known as Hersh" (there, section 12). The name Hershel should not be written because it is a diminutive form. Know that even if someone signs their name regularly with both their given name and nickname, as is customary among us—for example, Shlomo Zalman or Tzvi Hirsch or Yehoshua Heschel or Yechiel Michel—it should not be written in the get (divorce document) as both names together. Instead, it should be written as "Shlomo, also known as Zalman," and similarly for the other names, unless everyone calls him by both names together, such as "Shlomo Zalman." In that case, it should be written "Shlomo, called Shlomo Zalman." One should not pay attention to the non-expert cantors who call people up to the Torah using both their name and nickname, because expert cantors do not do this, as one is called to the Torah only by their sacred name.

One of the great authorities wrote that if there is a woman whose name is Shasya Tova, and almost all the inhabitants of the city call her Tova alone, but some people, including those from her household and family, call her by both names together, it is preferable to write two gittin (divorce documents). In one, write "Shasya Tova, who is called Tova," and in the other, write "Tova, who is called Shasya Tova." However, if only one document is written and it states "Shasya Tova, who is called Tova," and she is divorced, and it is difficult to obtain another get (divorce document), it can be validated. Similarly, if it is written "Tova, who is called Shasya Tova," or if it is written only "Shasya Tova," it can be validated when it is difficult to obtain another get. But if it is written only "Tova," it should not be validated except in a case of great necessity to prevent a woman from being left in a state of agunah (a woman who cannot remarry because her husband refuses to grant her a divorce or is missing). And so it is in all similar cases (there, section 15). In my humble opinion, it is questionable why he was so stringent (and examine this closely). The writing of the name Tova will be explained with God's help in the section on women's names in this chapter's conclusion.

Additionally, it was written: One whose name is commonly Nachum Shoel and signs as such, and is called to the Torah by the name Menachem Shoel, if it is known that the divorcer’s family calls him Nachum, and his sacred name is Menachem, and especially if it is known that this was the name of the deceased after whom he was named, one should write Menachem Shoel, also called Nachum Shoel. However, if this is not known and there is doubt that perhaps from the cradle he was called Nachum, as he signs, one should be stringent and give two bills of divorce: the first as Menachem Shoel, also called Nachum Shoel, and the second as Nachum Shoel, also called Menachem Shoel. In retrospect, if he divorced using the name Nachum Shoel alone, it is valid, as this is not worse than using a nickname. It is straightforward that if he is also called to the Torah by the name Nachum Shoel, initially one should only write Nachum Shoel, even if it is known that the name of the deceased after whom he was named was Menachem Shoel, and from the cradle he was also called by this name. Nevertheless, the name Menachem has been forgotten, and it should not be written. Similarly, for a woman whose name is Meryasha, although it is commonly derived from Miriam, if she does not sign her name as Miriam, one should not write Miriam at all, but only Meryasha, following the principle we have written that it is better to risk a potential lack rather than a potential change. This applies to all similar cases, as there is a general rule in divorce documents regarding names.

Furthermore, it is written (there, section 29): A woman named Frida Baila, and that is how a minority call her, while the majority call her simply Baila. If her usual practice is to sign letters as Frida Baila, this is considered primary, and one should write "Frida Baila, who is called Baila." If they wrote just Baila, it is also valid, as this is an abbreviation of the name. If she does not sign at all or signs only as Baila, two gittin (divorce documents) should be written: one as "Frida Baila, who is called Baila," and the other as "Baila, who is called Frida Baila," end quote. In retrospect, it is obvious that writing just Baila is valid. If everyone calls her only Baila, then even initially, one should write only Baila, as the name Frida is considered a forgotten name.

Additionally, it is written (there, section 36): If someone's name was Yaakov Yehoshua and his daughter came to get divorced, and they investigated his signature and saw that he signed himself as Yaakov Yoshua, and it is known that this was the signature of his ancestors from whom he was named, and there is a doubt whether they signed this way due to tradition or because of the abbreviation of the name, it is good to write two bills of divorce: one in the name of Yaakov Yehoshua and the other in the name of Yaakov Yoshua. And if the bill of divorce is through an agent or in a pressing situation, it is permissible to be lenient with one bill of divorce in the name of Yehoshua alone. And specifically, it must be clarified that he was called to the Torah with the name Yehoshua (there, section 137).

Every name that is in the Holy Tongue (Hebrew) ends with a "hey" (ה) at the end, and every name that is not in the Holy Tongue is written with an "aleph" (א) at the end. Many instances in the Tanach (Bible) are like this: Ezra, Amsha, Ala, Uza, Machida, Charsha, Sisera, Chativa, Peruda (Ezra 1). Nevertheless, we also find names ending with a "hey" such as Dalia, Tovia, Asna (there). Therefore, women's names end with an "aleph" at the end, like Bila, Alka, Basha, Chasha. Even though the "lamed" in "Bila" is pronounced with a "segol" (vowel sound like "e"), and similarly the "kuf" in "Alka" and the "shin" in "Basha", and every "segol" draws the eye, this is in the middle of the word and not at the end. Therefore, the name "Galia", even though the "gimel" and "lamed" are pronounced with a "segol", nevertheless, after the "gimel" we write an "ayin" and after the "lamed" an "aleph". Similarly, with all similar cases. This is why we find in the Talmud (Gemara) that Chuma, the wife of Abaye, and Chova, the wife of Rav Huna, end with a "hey" because the name is in the Holy Tongue. The same applies to male nicknames: any nickname in the Holy Tongue is written with a "hey", and if it is not in the Holy Tongue, it is written with an "aleph" at the end (Shulchan Aruch, section 34). However, if one changes and writes a "hey" instead of an "aleph" or an "aleph" instead of a "hey", it is valid (Beit Shmuel, subsection 50). But initially, one should be very careful since we see in the names of the Talmudic sages that they all end with an "aleph": Rava, Ravina, Rav Huna, Rav Chisda. And this is why "Rabbah" ends with a "hey" because in the Holy Tongue there is such a word, "and God saw that the wickedness (רבה) of man was great" etc. Therefore, any foreign name derived from the Holy Tongue, like Sarah being called Saya, is written with a "hey" (Beit Shmuel, general rules, section 15). Similarly with all similar cases. Nevertheless, we do not write "called" but rather "nicknamed" because after all, it is a nickname (there, section 14).

Any nickname in a foreign language, such as in the German language, when there is doubt whether to write it with a Tav (ת) or a Tet (ט), it should be written with a Tet (ט), because the Tav (ת) can be pronounced softly and it would result in a change of the name. Similarly, for anything of this sort, and any word where there is doubt whether to write it with a Chet (ח) or a Kaf (כ), such as Michal or Ikal, it should be written with a Kaf (כ), because in some places the Chet (ח) is pronounced like a Heh (ה), resulting in a change of the name. There is no concern that the Kaf (כ) will be pronounced with a dagesh (making it a Kaf) and thus also change the name, because certainly, they will not pronounce it with a dagesh, as if that were the case, it should have been written with a Kuf (ק) (as noted in the Beit Shmuel, Section 147). Similarly, for anything of this sort, even if there was a change after the fact, it is still valid. Initially, one should not create doubts because of this, unless the doubt is clear.

A fundamental rule regarding names is that one always goes by the name that they are called, and it should not be changed from how they are called unless it is known that it is an abbreviation of the name or a diminutive name. However, with the primary name, one does not make interpretations of names to say that it is called by such and such a reason, and consequently one would need to change the writing of this name from how it is called, for it is easy to make mistakes and invalidate the get (divorce document). Rather, one writes it as it is called. Even if the name is like the names of non-Jews or if that name indicates some defect, we do not say that they certainly did not give him such a name. Rather, one does not change from how it is called (Beit Shmuel in his general rules, section 1). Similarly, if it is known how he signs his name, there is no change at all unless he is an ignoramus who signs with errors. If his name is not known, one follows the name written in the ketubah (there). And know that nowadays, one should not look at the ketubot because many write them without precision regarding the name.

It has already been explained that an abbreviation of a name does not need to be written; only the primary name should be written. However, there is no objection if one wants to write both the primary name and the abbreviation, such as "Yitzchak, also known as Itza," and similar cases. Therefore, when there is any doubt whether it is an abbreviation of the name or not, both should be written. If the abbreviation of this name is another sacred name, both should certainly be written. Similarly, if this sacred name has another nickname, the abbreviation should also be written. However, if the abbreviation is embedded within the primary name, such as Eliezer (Leizer) or Elazar (Lazar) or Yitzchak (Itzak), and similar cases, the abbreviation does not need to be written at all since it is essentially one name. 

For someone who has both a sacred name and a secular name, if the sacred name is mentioned first, the secular name is written as "known as." If the secular name is mentioned first, the sacred name is written as "called." The order depends on knowing which name was primarily given at birth, and generally, the sacred name is the primary one. When there is doubt whether to write "called" or "known as," "called" should be written. If both names are secular and the person is not commonly called by both names but rather by one or the other, it is obvious that "called" should be written since "known as" is only used when this nickname refers to a sacred name.

It is not appropriate to write diminutive names such as Berela, Leibeli, or Velvela unless the person is commonly called by these names in their presence and does not object. If the majority of people call him by these names in his presence, it should be written, but for a minority, it is not a concern even if he does not object. The same applies to women's names, as will be explained at the beginning of their section.

One should not place vowel points in a get (divorce document), even for names that can be read in two ways when they are not vowelized. Nevertheless, one should not place vowel points, and if one did, it appears that it does not invalidate the get. However, when there is doubt whether to write a vav or a soft bet, it is better to write a vav, because a bet can be read with a dagesh (dot) and there would be a change. Generally, when a vav is needed at the beginning of a word, two vavs are written, like "Volf." Therefore, the city of Vilna is written with two vavs, and likewise the city of Warsaw. Similarly, in the middle of a word, if the vav is in place of a bet, like "Zanvil" (Zanvil), it is written with two vavs. If it is in place of a soft peh, it is written with one vav.

In foreign languages, the kamatz pulls an aleph after it, but not the patach. However, this is not a strict rule, as in the city of Warsaw and Danzig, which are pronounced with a patach and pull an aleph (as the Taz writes in several places), while in my city of Novardok, it is the opposite: after the patach they write an aleph, and after the kamatz, they do not. (Rashi in Ketubot 69b s.v. "yenachem" explains similarly.) The chirik pulls a yod after it, as does the tzeirei, like Beila, Reizel, and similar names, where a single yod is written. Two yods are not written unless the yod is felt after the patach, like in the names Braiena, Traiena, and similar cases. One should not ask, according to the rule we mentioned, why "Chaya" is written with one yod—this is because two yods are only when the patach pulls them, and not when the yod has its own point, unless the yod is with a tzeirei, like in "Chayei Avotai" or with a chirik, like the name "Chaim," which is written with two yods (and the Taz, in the name of Pia). The segol pulls an ayin in the middle of the word, while at the end of the word it comes with an aleph, as it is written. The mappik pulls a vav. Know that all these rules are according to the majority, and there are exceptions. This is also true in the Holy Tongue, as is well known.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Siman 32 that one should not write the name of a man or a woman in two lines, but in one line it is possible to write some names that can bear this, similar to "Chedar Laomer" and "Immanuel." And if he wrote one word, he has not lost. And the name "Yedidiah" if divided into two words, is valid, provided it is in one line. And "Peda Tzur" and "Ami Nadav" are considered one word, end quote. There are those who ruled practically that initially, one should write these names as two words in a manner similar to one word, as written in Siman 126 regarding "Di Tehoyeiyn" and "Di Teitzavieyn." And only the name "Yedid Yah" would appear more like two words than one word, and "Peda Tzur" and "Ami Nadav" would appear more like one word than two words. And if, after the fact, they were written as one word completely or as two words completely, the get (divorce document) is valid (Gra, Siman 134). And the name "Yom Tov" is similar to "Yedidiah," and likewise "Shem Tov" (there). Indeed, any name that ends with a closed mem or a long nun is certainly two words and only needs to be written in one line (there). In two lines, it is certainly invalid. Therefore, in the name "Ben Tzion," he should write it as two words but not completely as two words. And in these names "Yom Tov," "Shem Tov," and "Ben Tzion," even if they were written in two lines and the get has already been given and it is a case of potential agunah (chained woman), they should be validated (Taz, Siman 3). And the name "Bat Sheva" some say it is indeed one word (Yam Shel Shlomo and Beit Shmuel in women's names, letter B') and this is also implied in the Gemara (Sanhedrin 102a). And there are those who say it is two words (Taz, there, letter D' in the name of Sifsei Shlomo) and should be written in one line and appear as two words. And if, after the fact, it was written as one word, one can rely on the first opinion (there). And the names "Avigdor" and "Shneor" are one word, and likewise "Aviezer" (Yam Shel Shlomo). And there are those who disagree regarding the name "Aviezer" (Taz, letter A' Siman 16). Therefore, it should be written as one word and appear somewhat as two words. And "Avi HaEzri" is written in two words and in one line (Beit Shmuel, there).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (known as the Rema) wrote at the end of this section: Any nickname that changes due to the language of the countries, such as "Leib," which in some countries is spoken as "Lib" in a lighter language, and in some places is spoken as "Leiba" or "Liova." Similarly, the nickname "Wolf," which is called in these countries "Wolf" and in other countries "Wolfa" or "Wolflin" or "Wolflain," or the nickname "Mendel," where some say "Mandel" and the like. Also, in the pronunciation of words, such as in some countries where they say "Gomprecht" or "Gomprecht," or the languages differ in the pronunciation of the "B" or "P" or "V," such as "Zanvil" or "Zanvil," "Faifish" or "Vayvish," where some countries speak more softly. We follow the language of the people in the country where the get (divorce document) is given, and there is no need to be particular about how the names and nicknames are written, as each person writes according to the language of their country. Hence, the order of gittin (divorce documents) differs in this matter, and the main point is as I have written. This is how it seems to me to instruct. However, if the language of the countries is not known, one should not deviate from what is found in the words of the ancients. Nevertheless, retroactively, if one changed in any of these matters, it is valid as I have mentioned. All of this applies to foreign languages, but the names found in the scripture are not subject to changes in the language of the countries and are written as they are in the verse. For example, the name "Yosef," which some call "Yozef" and some call "Yasef," is written everywhere as "Yosef." For a name that is sometimes written fully and sometimes without certain letters, we follow the majority.

And after the words of our teacher, the Rema, it is clear that one should not pay attention to the specific writing of names by the authors who list names. Rather, one needs to understand and comprehend the language spoken in the country where the get (divorce document) is written. Therefore, we will only bring a few names, and they are the names commonly found in our region, Lithuania and Reisin, where the pronunciation is similar in both regions, and also in Little Russia. However, the pronunciation in the region of Volhynia, Podolia, and a bit from the region of Ukraine differs from ours. Similarly, the pronunciation of the people of Poland differs from ours, and certainly the regions of Germany, Austria, France, England, America, as well as Spain, Portugal, Holland, and other countries, should not learn from what is written here about their pronunciations. And you will see there that in Sha Pesha, they call it in Volhynia and Poland "Basil Pesil" and many similar cases. The general rules of names we have already explained with the help of Heaven, and these laws are the same in all countries.

And these are the names common among us: Abraham, Abba, Avli, Aaron, Aryeh, Ariel, Ara, Arka, Artza, Elijah, Eliyahu, Eliezer, Elazar, Avigdor, Uri, Alexander, Isser, Elchanan, Isaac, Elimelech, Ephraim, Elkana, Eliakim, Aviezer, Itzel, Isaac, Itzchok, Asher, Antshil. Benjamin, Binosh, Baruch, Ber, Beril, Brona, Bunem, Bendit, Binya, Binka, Benya, Bezalel, Ben-Zion, Boaz, Berach, Berachiah. Gad, Gedaliah, Gronem, Getzil, Gutiel, Gutman, Gershon, Gershom, Gera, Gabriel, Gimpel. David, Dan, Daniyah, Danka, Daniel, Dadka, Dov. Hillel, Hoshil, Hoshka, Haasha, Heshil, Hoshia, Hirsch, Hersh, Hertz, Hertzil, Hendil, Henoch. Valk or Falk, Wolf, Velvel, Volya, Veltsik. Zebulun, Zechariah, Zev, Zalman, Zussman, Zusha, Zisel, Zimel, Ziskind, Zelik or Zelig, Zeka, Zavil, Zanvil. Chaim, Chaykel, Hezekiah, Chatzkel, Hananiah, Hlawna, Hloina, Chanan, Chanya. Tuvia, Tobias, Tedres, Todros, Treitel, Tadiel. Isaac, Joseph, Yosef, Judah, Yuda, Yudel, Yudka, Issachar, Jacob, Jonathan, Yonatan, Yasil, Yashka, Yakil, Yohanan, Yechiel, Yekutiel, Yerachmiel, Joshua, Yosua, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Yedidiah, Israel, Yom Tov, Yiracham, Joel, Yozel, Yozef, Jonah, Yania. Katriel, Caleb. Leib, Levi, Levik, Lipa, Lipman, Lizer, Lazar, Lemil, Lapidot, Liakum, Lima, Lima. Moses, Meir, Michael, Mikhail, Mordechai, Menahem, Mendel, Mendel, Mencza or Mentza, Menkin, Menkil, Manasseh, Menos, Menya, Menuch, Meshulam, Mattathias, Muniya, Manya, Mulya, Melech, Meitza, Meika. Nathan, Neta, Noah, Nachum, Nachman, Nehemiah, Nissan, Nathaniel, Naphtali, Nasha or Nashka. Saadia, Sender, Sinai. Akiva, Obadiah, Ozer, Ezra, Azriel, Ever, Amram. Phineas, Pina, Pinka, Peretz, Pesach, Pisha with Tzirei, Pishl, Pishka, Palti, Paltiel, Feivel, Feibush, Feitl, Polt. Tzvi, Zadok, Tzemach. Kusha, Kushka, Kulya, Kapil, Kalonymus, Kalman, Kim, Kodesh. Reuben, Rubtsa, Ruba. Saul, Shoel, Shukel, Samuel, Shmelka, Shachna, Solomon, Shalom, Shabtai, Shepsil, Simcha, Shemaria, Shemaril, Shimon, Samson, Shamsul, Schneur, Sheptil. Tanchum, Tania. And now we will explain them in detail with the help of God.

Abraham does not need to write "referred to as Avramil" or "Avramka" or "Avramka" because all these are abbreviations of the name and also names of diminutives. But if he is referred to as "Avar" or "Avarlin," some say it should be written because it does not resemble Abraham so much, and some say it is not necessary (Beit Shmuel on Names and TaZ). It seems more correct that these should be written, as it is not similar to "Avramil" or "Avramka," as a distinguished person would not be called by these names in his presence, but "Avar" is called in his presence, and "Avaril" seems to me to be a diminutive name. However, if someone is called "Aba" and his holy name is Abraham, it is necessary to write "Abraham who is called Aba" since it is a Hebrew name and not a foreign name. Even though he signs as "Abraham Aba," nevertheless, they should not be written together because it is merely a nickname for Abraham. This double-signing is similar to signing "Dov Ber," "Ze'ev Wolf," or "Yechiel Michel" (TaZ, letter Aleph, subsection 36). If his nickname is "Avali," they write "Abraham referred to as Avali," even though some say it is not necessary to write the nickname at all (Taz), but the main principle is to write it (see there). For Aaron who is called "Ara" with a kamatz under the aleph or with a patach, or "Arka" or "Arza," it is not necessary to write the nickname because it is merely an abbreviation of the name and also not respectful (and similarly in Beit Shmuel). Likewise, "Aril" does not need to be written, and for Aryeh, his nickname is usually "Leib." However, this is not a general rule as there are those who are called "Aryeh" and have no nickname at all, and the officiant needs to inquire about this.

Rules of the witnesses of the get and their signatures: how and what. It contains 63 sections:
It has already been explained at the beginning of section 120 that we follow Rabbi Eliezer who says that the condition (of the get) effects the divorce, and from the Torah, there is no need at all for witnesses of the signature. Only as a decree from Rabban Gamliel was it instituted for the betterment of the world. And after the fact, if the get was given with the condition alone, it is valid. This will be further explained in section 133. However, ideally, it should not be deemed valid without witnesses of the signature, for the sages instituted it. And although we wrote there that according to several of our rabbis, the decree was not to invalidate it without this, nevertheless, since it has become customary to sign witnesses on all gittin, if this get is given without witnesses, there is no greater disparagement than this. Therefore, as long as she is not remarried and there is no concern for her becoming an agunah (a woman bound to her marriage), they should write another get (Yam Shel Shlomo, Chapter 4, section 41; similarly, Beit Meir).

And even though the signing of witnesses is only due to enactment, nevertheless, there must be two fully valid witnesses as in any testimony of the Torah. And even one invalid witness invalidates the get (divorce document), as the Rambam writes in Chapter 1, Law 17: “If its witnesses from within are invalid, even if one is invalid and one is valid, and it was given to her in the presence of two valid witnesses, it is invalid, as it is found to be forged from within.” These are the words of the Rambam. Similarly, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in this chapter, Section 17. And thus the Sages said (4a), Rabbi Eliezer agrees with respect to a get that is forged from within that it is invalid. The reason is that perhaps one might come to rely on it (Tosafot), and it is invalid by Rabbinic decree, and see what I wrote in Section 49.

It is questionable if a document is signed by only one valid witness, whether it is considered internally falsified because it lacks two witnesses. Logically, it would seem that it is valid post facto and is not worse than a document without any witnesses at all. In such a case, there is no concern that someone might rely on it, as everyone knows that one witness alone is not sufficient. I have seen that some rule accordingly (Ba'er Heitev, section 131).

However, from the words of Maimonides in Chapter 3, Law 8, it appears otherwise. He brings the opinion of those who hold that a document internally falsified invalidates the get (divorce document) according to Torah law. He disputes this, saying that its invalidity is only rabbinical, and he considers even a document signed by only one valid witness to be invalid. It is evident that rabbinically it is invalid in any case, and I have seen those who hold this view based on Maimonides (Lechem Mishneh, Chapter 1, Law 17).

Nevertheless, it seems to me that the primary opinion is the first one, that there is no reason to invalidate it in this case. Furthermore, from the words of Maran Kessef Mishneh there, it seems that Maimonides holds that whenever the invalidity is not evident, such as when signed not for its sake, it is invalid rabbinically. But when the invalidity is evident, such as when there is a space of two lines, it is valid post facto. Therefore, with only one witness, its invalidity is certainly evident. Hence, it seems to me that certainly, according to those who hold it is invalid by Torah law, this too is invalid by Torah law since there is only one witness. But for those who hold that its invalidity is only rabbinical, it is invalid only when there is a concern for error. Maimonides did not write this among the invalid cases, but according to the opinion that its invalidity is by Torah law, not explaining that, according to him, there is no invalidity at all.

However, in practice, one should be stringent, as his words do not clearly indicate this. (It is puzzling that the Ba'er Heitev did not mention the words of Maimonides or the Lechem Mishneh).

The laws regarding disqualified witnesses are explained in Choshen Mishpat, sections 33 and 34. In the context of gittin (divorce documents), we are even more stringent initially, avoiding having certain individuals sign as witnesses even if they are technically valid according to the law due to their relationship, such as a second-degree relative to a third-degree relative. Even more distant relatives are not allowed to sign initially. Similarly, a relative who has become distanced, who is technically valid by law, or mere in-laws who are valid for testimony, are not allowed to sign a get. It is preferable to find a scribe who is not a relative of either the husband or the wife. According to those authorities who validate a scribe's writing as equivalent to testimony, it is essential to ensure the scribe is not related to them. All this is applicable when possible, but when not possible, it is not a concern.

Additionally, it is customary that the scribe should not be a relative of the witnesses, since the witnesses testify that the husband instructed the scribe to write, and although they are testifying about the husband, not the scribe, it still appears as though they are testifying about a relative. This is especially true if the scribe is paid a significant fee for writing (according to the Avnei Nezer). None of the individuals involved should be related to the rabbi overseeing the get process, and none of the witnesses should have a physical defect. It is advisable to be stringent about all these matters initially if possible. The Maharil was meticulous about having proper witnesses and a proper scribe, although in urgent situations, he was not strict about the scribe.

If one witness is a relative of another, they are disqualified by law. It is appropriate to avoid having a witness who is a mamzer, or one with a crushed testicle, or one who has undergone amputation, or an uncircumcised man whose brothers died due to circumcision, even though they are technically valid for testimony by law, as stated there. Someone suspected of licentious behavior, who is used to being secluded with women and has a bad reputation, is disqualified by law from testifying about a woman's status due to his strong desire for her to be single and available to him. Although this primarily relates to testifying that her husband has died or divorced her (Rashi, Sanhedrin 26a), and not signing a get in front of us, it is certainly not appropriate to have him sign a get. Even in urgent situations, it is advisable to avoid using this witness.

And behold, all that is mentioned are stringencies and enhancements regarding a get (divorce document), and in pressing circumstances they are not essential. Particularly regarding the closeness of the rabbi arranging the get, it is an excessive stringency, for the arranger does nothing except instruct them in the order of the get (as is implied in Darkei Moshe section 17). Nevertheless, since we are stringent in requiring a court for a get, it is obvious that there should be many stringencies, for a close relative judge is invalid by law. Similarly, witnesses should not be relatives of the judges, as stated in Choshen Mishpat section 33. Even those who disagree in monetary matters, as stated there because we do not require testimony in monetary cases that can be refuted, agree in other prohibitions.

According to the law, it is permissible for other people to act as witnesses for the delivery (of a document) who were not the signing witnesses, and they are not disqualified due to the concept of "a matter and half a matter" as explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 30. For just as in the testimony of possession for three years, three sets of witnesses are valid because it is impossible to observe three years all at once and they must necessarily be separate, as we explained there in Siman 16, similarly, the signing (of a document) necessarily precedes its delivery. Furthermore, witnesses for the delivery do not need to be signing witnesses, for according to all opinions, it is valid with only witnesses for the delivery. According to the Rif and the Rambam, it is even valid with only signing witnesses, as stated in Siman 120. Therefore, these are two separate testimonies (Sanhedrin 6a, and see there in Tosafot s.v. "mitoch"). Nevertheless, the custom is to be stringent initially in this matter as well, as Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote at the end of Siman 1: "The custom is also to take signing witnesses for the delivery, and they will see that the husband instructed the scribe to write, so that everything is done in the presence of one set of witnesses." He also wrote that the witnesses should sign only with the husband’s ink and quill, like the scribe, as stated above in Siman 120. This is obvious.

From the decree of Rabban Gamliel, the witnesses signing a document must clarify their names in their signatures (36a). By the letter of the law, it was not necessary to clarify their names. The sages originally taught (ibid.) that the witness would write, "I, Ploni, signed as a witness," not meaning specifically "Ploni Reuven" or "Ploni Shimon," but just "Ploni" (as evident from Rashi). In the Tosefta, the version is clearer: "I am a witness, I signed as a witness" (ibid.). When it was necessary to validate their signatures, they had to compare with other documents where their signatures appeared to ensure consistency because it was not known who the witnesses were (Rashi). Therefore, Rabban Gamliel decreed that they should clarify their names for the betterment of society so that their signatures could be easily validated. Hence, they would sign "Reuven ben Yaakov witness" or even without the father's name, simply "Reuven witness," or without the name, just "ben Yaakov witness." This is how the sages explained in the Mishnah (7b): "Ploni witness" is valid, "ben Ploni witness" is valid, "Ploni ben Ploni" without writing "witness" is valid (ibid.). Now we are stringent and require writing "Ploni ben Ploni witness." However, if one only wrote "Ploni" without "witness" or "ben Ploni" without "witness," it is invalid because we suspect it was not written for the purpose of testimony at all. But when both his name and his father's name are written, it is certainly for the purpose of testimony. This is the ruling of all the authorities and in Shulchan Aruch, section 11. (One should not be mistaken by the language of the Jerusalem Talmud on this Mishnah, which seems to allow all forms even without "witness," as it is evident that the text is corrupted, and the conclusion there implies otherwise. See there in detail.)

This disqualification by name alone without a witness, or by the name of the father as mentioned, is valid when there are no witnesses (see Beit Shmuel 22). One should not ask that in the absence of witnesses, it is anyhow disqualified according to many authorities as mentioned in Siman 120 and Siman 133. It can be said that certainly, this is so; however, in all divorce documents, when she comes to remarry, we permit her based on a single witness alone, as we say that presumably there were also witnesses, for this is the main decree according to those authorities who disqualify without witnesses. In this divorce document, when there is no witness signed, we do not permit her to remarry unless she brings witnesses before us (as stated there). It seems to me that even if he did not write his name at all but signed "I am a witness" as before the decree of Rabban Gamliel, it is also valid if she brings witnesses before us. It should be treated no differently than a divorce document without any witnesses at all, for there is no reason to consider this as a forgery from within since it is not a forgery but merely not done according to the decree. And we should not rely on this signature. However, according to the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam, who validate with witnesses' signatures alone, as mentioned there, certainly, the get (divorce document) cannot be validated if there were no witnesses at all unless they signed according to the decree, and the get is rabbinically disqualified (as it seems to me). But I have seen that the Rashba of blessed memory (in the Sholeach 36) wrote, "However, in retrospect, it is possible that the get is not disqualified even according to Rabbi Meir, for they only decreed so that witnesses would be available to validate it and not that something else would result from it, neither for prohibition nor for monetary matter, and if for this reason, why should the get be disqualified?" And so wrote Rabbeinu Yerucham (brought in Beit Yosef). And since according to Rabbi Meir it is valid, all the more so according to us who hold according to Rabbi Eliezer. The Rashba also wrote that the decree of stating names in witnesses was only according to Rabbi Meir and not Rabbi Eliezer. And from the words of the Rambam and the Tur and all the authorities, it does not seem so. Furthermore, the main decree of Rabban Gamliel regarding the signing of witnesses is according to Rabbi Eliezer, so that there should be no need to bring witnesses, as explained in the Talmud, that through the witnesses' signatures the get is validated. And when names are not specified, the validation will not be easy, and it is possible that even the Rashba did not say otherwise but that according to Rabbi Eliezer there is no hindrance in the matter, and it is merely like lacking witnesses. This is certainly so, as written (Beit Shmuel 1 who wrote, "And this is the reasoning of the Rashba and Rabbeinu Yerucham who wrote that there is no need to specify their names," and the Beit Meir was puzzled by this, and according to what I have written, it is clear, and the words of the Beit Shmuel are correct, and what he wrote, that it is not difficult, but it does not seem so to one who examines his innovations there, but it seems that even initially there is no need).

And know that what we have written, that before the enactment, the witness would not specify his name at all, so explained Rashi and the Rashba there, and it is explicitly proven from the Tosefta that we brought. And I have seen that there are those who understand the opinion of the Tur that he interprets that even before the enactment, he would sign his name, and Rabban Gamliel's enactment was to also write his father's name (Beit Yosef). And according to this, we must say that what is stated in the Gemara there, "Initially, he would write, 'I, so-and-so, signed as a witness,'" this is like any so-and-so in the Talmud, meaning his name is specified. And I am very puzzled because there is an explicit Mishnah (Gittin 7:6) that says "so-and-so is a valid witness," and according to this, we must forcefully explain and say that the Mishnah was taught before the enactment. And indeed, there is someone who wrote this (Lechem Mishneh, Hilchot Edut 4:10). And according to this, we must say that the entire discussion in the Talmud there, which questions "and let Jacob be a valid witness," is also according to what was before the enactment (there). And these matters are very puzzling, and I do not know the basis for such an understanding in the opinion of the Tur, for he brings the Mishnah as it is there.

And it is puzzling regarding the Rambam who did not bring at all the laws of the Mishnah but wrote in Chapter 1, Law 24, as follows: "Even though the witnesses' signatures on a get (divorce document) are by rabbinic decree, they instituted that the witnesses should specify their names in the get." And in Chapter 4, in the format of the get, he wrote: "So-and-so, son of so-and-so, a witness." And why did he not clarify that "so-and-so, a witness" is valid, and similarly "the son of so-and-so, a witness," and similarly "so-and-so, the son of so-and-so" without "a witness"? And more difficult than this, why did he not clarify that "so-and-so" alone or "the son of so-and-so" alone is invalid? And I have seen someone who raised a difficulty against him (Lechem Mishneh, and what he means is that he follows the method of the Tur alone, which cannot be said, as his words are problematic. See there).

However, in my humble opinion, it is clear that Maimonides, of blessed memory, had a different version of the Mishnah, as I have seen in several mishnayot where the version "So-and-so, a valid witness, the son of So-and-so, a valid witness" is written, not just "a valid witness."
