This is explicitly proven from his words in his commentary on the Mishnah there on the previous Mishnah, where he wrote: "Because a person signs his name on testimony in three ways: either he writes only his name, such as writing 'So-and-so,' or he writes 'the son of So-and-so' without his name, or he writes his name and 'witness.'" Thus, it is clear that he holds that even writing only one's name without 'witness' and without the father's name is valid. Therefore, in this case where he wrote that they instituted that witnesses should specify their names, it includes everything—however it is written, it is valid. And in chapter 4 on the formula of the get (divorce document), he wrote that it is customary to initially write in the most proper manner, as we do. According to this, those who hold that writing only "the son of So-and-so" is valid will find it acceptable in all forms. However, if he signs only his name or his father's name—even if we do not hold like the view of the Rashba in section 8, that according to the Rashba it is valid even before the enactment (and it must be said that his version of the Gemara there, which raises the difficulty of 'and it should be valid with Yaakov as a witness,' does not include two answers but only the latter answer).

There was someone who asked a significant question: since the primary purpose of specifying their names was to ensure the validation of the signatures, and now the court immediately takes the get from the woman and keeps it with them, as we will explain later in the order of the get in Siman 154, why do we still need to specify the names of the witnesses? One cannot say that it is truly unnecessary, because our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, established this rule even though they held that the get does not remain in the woman's possession (Beit Shmuel, Siman 1) and it is torn up. This is not a question at all, because if Rabban Gamliel's enactment was only for a woman's get, it would be fine, but in truth, his enactment was for all documents (Tosafot at the beginning of Gittin). The Mishnah states that witnesses sign the get, and every document is called a get (there), as the enactment for the betterment of the world regarding the validation of the document applies to all documents. This is also clearly proven in the Talmud there (36a), which raises a question from the verse in Jeremiah, which refers to a deed of purchase and sale (as explained in the Shach, Choshen Mishpat, Siman 28, Sif Katan 14), and in other documents. Certainly, even now, it is a significant enactment so that it can be validated. Consequently, it is impossible to be lenient with a woman's get compared to other documents, except when there is a special provision for an agunah (a woman who is unable to remarry), such as with witnesses who cannot sign, as will be explained in this Siman. But regarding specifying the names, there is no provision for an agunah, for what loss is there if they sign according to Rabban Gamliel's enactment? Therefore, it is still practiced today.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 11 that some say that since it suffices if one writes "Yosef" up to "son of Yaakov," there is no need to write further. If there was a mistake or a change in it, it should not be invalidated, as we mentioned above in section 128 in similar cases. However, one should only rely on this in pressing circumstances or in cases of potential hardship. Indeed, we already explained there in section 4 that the general rule stated by the authorities, that a change does not invalidate in cases where a lack does not invalidate, only applies to matters where the change is not apparent to everyone, such as the place of birth. But in matters where the change is apparent to everyone, the change invalidates, as noted there. However, this applies only to the man and woman who might cast aspersions on the get (bill of divorce), claiming that someone else divorced her or that another woman was divorced. But regarding witnesses, even if they claim that the witness is a different person, what of it? The other person is also fit to testify. This is not the same as changing the witnesses' standing place, where the falsehood is evident to all. Not all authorities agree with this; some invalidate in all cases, as noted there in section 45. Also, some hold that any change that should be ideally written invalidates, even if the lack does not invalidate after the fact, as written in section 129, subsection 8 (Gra, note 27). Therefore, one should certainly only rely on this in pressing circumstances or in cases of potential hardship. It seems that if there was a mistake in his name, it should also be validated in cases of hardship or pressing circumstances, as even "son of Yaakov" alone is valid (Beit Shmuel, note 20). However, some invalidate a change in the witness's name (there, in the name of Rashach). Note that wherever a mistake does not invalidate, a hollow letter engraving also does not invalidate (there). Similarly, if there was a mistake in the word "witness," it also does not invalidate, as it is not necessary (there). The requirement to sign as a witness is only in a woman's get, since the entire get is in the husband's language, and thus he writes "witness," meaning "I testify to this." It is not a requirement, and a mistake does not invalidate it, nor does hollow letter engraving, as noted.

A witness should not sign his name or his father's name with the title "Rabbi" or "Sage," but rather with his personal name and his father's name. Similarly, he should not sign with his nickname, but only with his formal name. If he has a different name in another place, he does not need to sign with that name, but only with the name by which he is known here, as stated in section 129, paragraph 79. Any matter that has even a slight doubt about how it should be written should not be signed initially, because one should not initially enter into uncertainties without necessity. Therefore, if a witness's father's name is confused, it is not signed, and the same applies to all similar cases. Initially, one must be cautious with the witnesses' signatures in all matters that one is cautious about in writing a get (bill of divorce), such as requiring complete writing, surrounding parchment, and all similar matters (language of the Rema).

The witnesses must sign below, under the last line, one below the other. If they signed above, before the get (bill of divorce), or on the sides, or behind it, it is invalid. Thus, the Sages taught in the Mishnah (Gittin 87b). This law applies to all documents, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, the beginning of Siman 45. This is a rabbinic enactment to prevent falsification by writing anything they want below. Even if falsification is not possible, such as when it is written "valid and established" or in a get "according to the law of Moses and Israel," or if one witness signs below and the second signs above, on the side, or behind it, it is invalid because it was not done according to the enactment of the Sages, as stated there (Tosafot, beginning of Chapter 3 of Gittin, s.v. "Pashut" and similarly in Shach, Siman 1). Furthermore, the Sages decreed that they should sign one below the other and not on the same line, due to the concern that someone might cut off everything above the signatures and write before them that Reuven borrowed money from him, making it a document with its witnesses on one line, which can be collected upon, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 44. Even though it is explained there that if the document ends in the middle of a line, they can sign one after the other, in a get it is not possible to do so because twelve complete lines are written (it seems to me).

Similarly, one should not leave a space equivalent to the size of two lines between the writing and the signatures, as is done with other documents. If such a space is left, the Tur wrote that the get (divorce document) is invalid, and even with witnesses, it is invalid. This is more stringent than the issue of potential forgery, which is valid with witnesses as it says in Siman 124. Here, there is a concern that the woman might fill the space with some condition favorable to her, and the flaw will not be noticeable at all (Beit Shmuel, Section 2). However, the Rambam in Chapter 1 rules it valid with witnesses. There is a challenge to his ruling since there is such a concern (as noted by Avnei Miluim and Lechem Mishneh). It appears to me that his reasoning is that it is no worse than a document that can potentially be forged, and indeed, the forgery here is less likely. At the end of the get, it is written "according to the law of Moses and Israel," which is considered firm and established as in other documents. If she adds a condition in the two-line space, the forgery will be noticeable. Although she could write "according to the law of Moses and Israel" again, it would be like two firm and established statements, as explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 44. However, this would be surprising as it is not initially intended to be done that way, as mentioned there. Therefore, people would not rely solely on an uneducated person. Consequently, for this reason, we do not validate a space of two lines without witnesses alone, even if “according to the law of Moses and Israel” is seen once. However, when there are witnesses, why should we not validate it? But, as explained, if they signed above, to the side, or behind it, everyone agrees that it is valid with witnesses, as it is evident to us that there are no witnesses, and necessarily she must bring witnesses, and it is like writing on a document that could be forged (Beit Shmuel, Section 6).

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 2 that one should begin at the top of the line so that no blank space remains in the margin of the get (bill of divorce) before the signatures. This is perplexing to me because the reason for this invalidation is only relevant if the witnesses are signed on the same line one after the other, to prevent forgery by making a document appear as though it and its witnesses are on one line, as stated in section 15 and clarified in Choshen Mishpat section 45. Since it has been clarified that the witnesses sign one below the other, this concern no longer exists. Regarding the Tur, there is no difficulty because he indeed did not write this law that they must sign one below the other. On the contrary, in the order of the get according to the Rosh, it is explained that they can sign on the same line. But regarding the Shulchan Aruch, which wrote this in section 1, it is difficult. It seems to me that even if they are written one below the other, there is still a concern if a blank space remains, for perhaps someone will cut above and write on the blank space "I, the undersigned, owe Reuven a maneh," and it would become a document with the borrower's signature. However, this concern is about the witness himself, that the witness would not be summoned. When they sign on one line, the concern is about someone else who might make a document with witnesses. Therefore, regarding concerns about others, we do not rely on the fact that no blank space remains before the signatures, for perhaps they will not be careful about this. Thus, we also require the additional safeguard that they sign one below the other. This law is good advice for the witness himself (and therefore the Rema did not comment on section 2, and take note of this).

The witnesses must initially be careful that the one who signs first on the get [divorce document] should sign first, and after him, the second should sign. For if the second signs first, there will remain two lines between his signature and the get, and it will be invalid at that moment. Nevertheless, after the fact, if the last one signed first and then the first one, it is valid, and there is no need to write another get, even if it is possible to write another get.

And nothing should be written between the get (divorce document) and the signatures of the witnesses that is not relevant to the get, because there is concern that perhaps the witnesses only signed on that matter. Even if nothing significant is written, but merely a greeting, we are concerned that perhaps they only intended to sign on the greeting. Thus, our Sages said (Bava Batra 176a): “If it is written as ‘hello,’ it is invalid, but if it is written as ‘and hello,’ it is valid.” The explanation is that if the greeting is written without a connecting vav (the Hebrew letter for "and"), we worry that their signature is only on the greeting. But if it is written with a connecting vav, it is valid, because the vav connects it to what is above, and they signed on everything. The Rambam (Maimonides) wrote in Chapter 4 of the Laws of Divorce that if the get is delivered conditionally, in any case it is valid. And if he gave it to her only with witnesses (as he holds that witnesses alone also make it valid), and it was written as ‘hello’ without the connecting vav, she is in a doubtful state of being divorced. And even though one could say that since the testimony is not clarified and proven from the get itself, it is as if there are no witnesses at all, and it is not a get, nevertheless, one should rule stringently that it is a doubtful get (Ran, Chapter 9 of Gittin). However, in a case where it is clear that the witnesses did not intend to sign this get, and there is no conditional delivery, even according to the Rambam, it is not a get at all (Beit Shmuel, Section 4).

Even when signing below, the backs of the signatures need to face the get, meaning they should sign in the same direction as the writing above. However, if the feet of the signatures face the get, meaning they turned the paper upside down and signed, the get is invalid. Even if only one witness signed this way, it is invalid, because such a signature is considered nothing, leaving only one valid witness. If it was done by minors (under the age of majority), it is valid, as this is not considered internally forged but rather as if there were no witnesses at all.

Our master, the Rema, wrote in section 7: "If one glued two pieces of parchment together with adhesive and wrote a get (divorce document) on them, it is invalid out of doubt." And the reason for the invalidation is because the Torah said "a book" and not two or three books. And so our Sages said (20b): "And the adhesive does not make them like one piece of parchment." And behold, we have already wondered in Siman 124 about the Rambam, the Tur, and the Beit Yosef who did not mention this law anywhere, and see there what we wrote about this. And our master, the Rema, took the straightforward meaning of the Talmud, that with two books it is invalid by Torah law. However, in practice, if one wrote the get on two pieces of parchment and gave it to her, we go stringently in all aspects, and it is a doubtful get. For how can we not be concerned about the opinion of these great rabbis, from which it seems they did not hold this law? And certainly, as we explained there, according to Rashi (Sotah 18a), it is clear that this statement of our Sages is not the halacha except according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi alone, see there. But Tosafot took this as the halacha, see there.

However, it is also astonishing regarding our teacher, the Rema, for in the matter of Tefillin we hold that gluing or sewing makes two pieces of parchment as one (Menachot 34b), and so write the Tosafot there (32a, s.v. D'ilma). And although concerning a Shofar we hold in Orach Chaim 586 that gluing does not make it as one, this is because the addition is noticeable (Tosafot Sotah 17b, s.v. K'tava), and indeed there has been astonishment about this (Beit Shmuel, sub-section 8). And that which we hold in Yoreh De'ah 288 regarding a Mezuzah that if it was written on two pieces of parchment and sewn together, it is invalid, this is when they were sewn together after the writing because the writing was done in an invalid state. But if they were sewn together before the writing, it is valid, as is evident from the language of the Rambam in the fifth chapter of Hilchot Tefillin. See there.

However, in truth, his words are correct, as it was a doubt in the law. Even regarding a single parchment of tefillin, there are some poskim (decisors of Jewish law) who hold that joining and sewing is ineffective (Magen Avraham, Orach Chaim 32:52 in the name of Bach). We do not find that Rambam, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch wrote the law that joining and sewing would be effective. The distinction we mentioned in mezuzah between sewing after writing and before writing is also not clarified in halacha. On the contrary, in Menachot, according to the one who permits only with joining, it is also permitted after writing (and so wrote Beit Meir). However, in truth, there is no proof from there, as the main mitzvah is placing it on the hand as it is written in the Torah, and at the time of placing, it is one unit, as opposed to mezuzah where it is written "and you shall write them," requiring at the time of writing that it be one unit. Similarly, in a get (divorce document), where it is written "and he shall write for her a scroll of severance," it requires at the time of writing that it be one unit. Thus, it is certainly a doubt in the law. From tefillin in Menachot, there is no proof at all that it does not need to be entirely one unit. The proof is that in the conclusion, he retracted and held that even joining is not required, and only hanging the parchment is sufficient. If we come to compare it to impurity, we find a dispute among the Tannaim in such a case whether it is considered connected or not (Keilim 3:5 regarding joining an earthenware vessel, and in the first chapter of Tohorot 1:1 regarding joined loaves for the purpose of ritual impurity).

And know that it is not considered "two or three documents" unless they are separate. Even if they are glued together or sewn, it is a doubtful matter of law. But if it is on a single piece of paper or parchment, if the get (divorce document) is written on two pages, it is considered one document, as it is taught (Gittin 87b): If part of the get was left and written on the second page, and the witnesses signed below, it is valid. This is specifically when there is no concern that there were two gets, and the end of one and the beginning of the other were cut and joined together, such as when it is evident from the beginning and end of the paper that nothing was cut from it, and the scribe intended to complete it on the second page to avoid suspicion that he started writing it, then changed his mind and canceled it, and later decided to complete it (Rashi there, Gittin 88a, and Tosafot, s.v. "and perhaps," examine closely). But if it is not evident, even if we knew that it was delivered to her with witnesses, it is a doubtful divorce, as perhaps there were two gets and parts of each were cut. However, if witnesses testify that it was one get from the start and it was delivered to her with witnesses, it is valid. Even according to the Rambam, who permits ex post facto without "and signed" (witnesses signing), here it is invalid without "and signed" because it is somewhat like forged from within, though not entirely forged, for if so, even with "and signed" it would be invalid. Rather, it is as if no witnesses signed on it (Taz and Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 7).

We hold that two women cannot be divorced with one get (bill of divorce), as it is written, "and he shall write for her," and not for her and her companion (Gittin 87a). Even two women from one man cannot be divorced with one get, such as if he were to write, "I, Reuven, have divorced Rachel and Leah." This is explicitly proven in the Talmud there, where it is compared to a slave, and with slaves, two slaves from one master cannot be freed with one document, as proven there. This is also the ruling in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 267, Se'if 59. However, there is no invalidation if they are written on one sheet of paper. Even if on one page it is written, "Reuven divorced Rachel and Shimon divorced Leah," it is also valid. It is only invalid if they wrote, "We, Reuven and Shimon, divorced our wives Rachel and Leah." Even if they wrote it this way, if they later specified "Reuven divorced Rachel and Shimon divorced Leah," it is also valid, as will be explained. This is an explicit Gemara there. According to this, it is evident that in the case of two women from one man, if he wrote, "I, Reuven, divorced Rachel" and "I, Reuven, divorced Leah," it is also valid, and it is a fortiori from two men. The general principle is that the man and his wife must be specified separately and not mixed together. (And according to this, the Gemara there regarding slaves answers and does not say that we establish it with two documents. It could have answered similarly, but the truth resolves that due to another matter, it must be established with two documents, as explained in Gittin 42b.)

However, there are many detailed laws and disputes among the halachic authorities, as will be explained with God's help. The words of the Rambam in Chapter 4, Halacha 18 are as follows:
        
Five men who wrote one bill of divorce for their five wives—if they wrote it collectively, such as writing: "On such-and-such a Shabbat, so-and-so divorced so-and-so, and so-and-so divorced so-and-so," and each one of them said to his wife, "You are hereby divorced," and the entire format of the bill of divorce is included, and two witnesses signed below, this is a valid bill of divorce and it should be given to each one of them individually. If there is no individual delivery at all, whoever receives this document is divorced. But if it was written: "On such-and-such a Shabbat, so-and-so divorced so-and-so," and the bill of divorce was completed, and then another bill of divorce was started on the same document, writing: "On such-and-such a day, so-and-so divorced so-and-so," and the second bill of divorce was completed, and so on until all the divorces were completed, and the witnesses signed below—if this document was given individually to each one of them, they are all divorced. If there is no individual delivery, and this document was found in the possession of one of them, if it was the one whose divorce was last and the witnesses are associated with it, she is divorced. If the document was found in the possession of one of the earlier ones, she is in doubt whether she is divorced.

If they wrote: "We, so-and-so and so-and-so, divorced our wives, so-and-so and so-and-so," and completed the bill of divorce, even if it was delivered individually to each one of them, it is not a valid bill of divorce, as two women cannot be divorced with one bill of divorce, as it is stated: "And he shall write for her," not for her and her companion. If they subsequently specified within the bill of divorce, writing: "So-and-so divorced so-and-so, and so-and-so divorced so-and-so at such-and-such a time," these are valid.

This is the end of the Rambam's words, and it is also recorded in Shulchan Aruch, Sections 9 and 10.

Explanation of the matter: In the Mishnah, it is taught (Gittin 86b) that when it comes to general documents, all of them are valid, but when it comes to the specific form for each one, only the last one is valid. The Gemara explains that a "general document" refers to a situation where the same date is written for all, and a "specific form" refers to a situation where a separate date is written for each individual. This does not mean different dates, for if that were the case, it would be considered predated. Rather, the same date is repeated, such as "on the first day of the week" for each one. 

The Rambam holds that it is not specifically only about the date, because if it were, what would be the meaning of the term "specific form" mentioned in the Mishnah? Rather, a "general document" refers to the date along with the specific form of the get (divorce document). When it is for each individual separately, only the last one is valid. However, when there is one specific form for all, it follows that there is one date for all, and this is the general rule that all are valid. The reason is that when there is one specific form for all, it follows that the witnesses' signatures apply to all. But this is when it is written at the beginning, "so-and-so to so-and-so," and similarly for all of them with a connecting "vav" (and). Otherwise, it is no better than a simple greeting mentioned in section 19. However, when there is a specific form for each, even if the beginning has a connecting "vav," since these are five separate lengthy matters for each, we are concerned that perhaps the witnesses only signed the last one.

And there are some of our Rabbis who disagree with him, for in their opinion, when there is one template for all, it is preferable, as they are all valid, as stated. And those who disagree with him hold that not only is it not preferable to have a separate template for each, but that it is entirely invalid, for whenever there is one template for all, it is considered as if two women are being divorced with one get (Tur and Ramah). And this that they said, that in all cases they are valid, also refers to having a template for each one, except that the second template began without repeating the date, such as writing "On Sunday, So-and-so divorced So-and-so" with all the details of the get, and afterwards writing "And similarly, So-and-so divorced So-and-so" with all the details of the get, and so on. In this manner, they are all valid. But if after concluding the first get, he began with "On Sunday, So-and-so divorced So-and-so" and finished the details of the get, and then began again with "On Sunday..." and so on, in such a case, only the last one is valid. (And the Beit Shmuel, Siman 10, wants to interpret that Rambam’s opinion is also like this, but it is not so, as is evident from his words, and as is apparent from the commentators, and so wrote the Bach).

And also, regarding what Rambam wrote, that when one writes, "We, so-and-so and so-and-so, divorced our wives, so-and-so and so-and-so," if he later specifies, "so-and-so divorced so-and-so, and so-and-so divorced so-and-so," it is valid. There are some of our Rabbis who hold that since he began in an invalid manner, specifying them afterward does not help, and this is called "two women in one get" (Rashba). And even though it is explained thus in the Gemara, it is not according to the halacha, for the Talmud interprets this according to Reish Lakish, and the halacha follows Rabbi Yochanan there. And most of the poskim agree with the Rambam that in this case, we do not find that there is a dispute.

And Rambam, of blessed memory, established a general rule that what was explained, that only the last one is valid, applies when there is no condition. But if there is a condition, all are valid because the reason for invalidation is that we suspect they might have signed only the last one. And when there is a condition, there is no need for witnesses of delivery (עדי מסירה), and this fits with his view that when there are witnesses of the document (עדי חתימה), there is no need for witnesses of delivery, as will be explained in Siman 133. But according to those who hold that witnesses of the document are not sufficient, it needs to be explained this way: Certainly, when there is a condition before us, all are valid. And what we said that only the last one is valid, the matter is thus: Any get (bill of divorce) that comes before us with signed witnesses does not need to bring witnesses of delivery, as we assume there were witnesses of delivery, as this was the essential enactment of Rabban Gamliel, as explained. But a get without signed witnesses must bring witnesses of delivery before us who testify that it was handed over in their presence, or other witnesses who testify that it was handed over in the presence of witnesses of delivery. And this get, which is a form for each, is only valid for the last one, meaning that the last one does not need to bring witnesses of delivery, but the previous ones are like without signed witnesses and need to bring witnesses of delivery. And this is explicitly implied in the Tur, see there.

And with regard to that which we said, that at the same time for all of them, they are all valid and divorced by it, the Tur wrote: either one of them should take hold of it for all of them, or it should be given to each one as needed. And it appears to me that his intention is certainly at the time of the divorce, each husband must give it to his wife, and then the other gives it to his wife, and so on for all of them. Or one can be an agent for all the women to acquire it on their behalf. And that which the Tur wrote, this refers to when they come to marry and need to show the get as proof (so it seems to me). And that which the Rambam wrote, "all of them are valid," means that whoever the get comes from, she is divorced, meaning that one first brings it, then gives it to the second, and the second to the third, and so on for all of them, and they are all permitted to remarry (Beis Yosef). And some say that only the first who shows the get is divorced, and she cannot hand it over to another (D'var Avraham and Taz), and this explanation is very forced. However, even according to this opinion, if the woman comes and the get is in her hand, we do not need to ask her if perhaps another handed it to her (Beis Shmuel, sub-paragraph 12). And that which the Rambam wrote, valid for all of them, it should be given to each one with the condition, the reason is simple. Although according to his view it is valid only on a biblical level as the Maggid Mishneh wrote, but ideally, even according to his view, it needs to be on a conditional basis (Beis Yosef). And as will be explained with God's help in Siman 133. And that which the Rambam wrote, that it is only valid for the last one when the get comes from the hands of the first ones, it is doubtful whether she is divorced, the reason is simple because it is not clear that the witnesses signed on the first ones, and therefore it is doubtful. And there are those who asked why the last one is valid since we say that perhaps the witnesses only signed on the last one, and the last one would be without a date and invalid (Beis Shmuel, sub-paragraph 16). And this question is according to the Tur's view that each one has her own form and the date is only on the first one, and for example, it was written without the conjunction "and" and in this case only the last one is valid. However, it is not a question because although we are concerned that the witnesses only signed on the last one, nevertheless, from where do we know to be concerned that the writings were on separate days? And certainly, when it is written above a certain day and many matters are written in it, we assume they were all written on the same day.

Additionally, the Rambam of blessed memory wrote: "If one wrote two bills of divorce on two separate columns of the same scroll, side by side, and there are two witnesses at the end of this bill of divorce and two witnesses at the end of that bill of divorce, it is valid. And whenever this scroll leaves the hand of the husband, she is considered divorced." And it has already been explained that according to him, it is valid even without "al menat" (conditional stipulation), and one can hand it to the other, and at the time of acceptance, each one accepts it, as was written in section 31. And according to those who maintain that "al menat" is always required, the practical difference is that it would not be necessary to bring "al menat" before us.

It is further written: If there were only two witnesses, and they come under this get (divorce document) and under that get, if it leaves the hand of this one, where the witnesses are named with her get, she is divorced. But if it leaves from the hand of the second, where the witnesses are not named with it, it is not a get until he delivers it to her in the presence of witnesses. According to those who hold that witnesses are always necessary, the implication is that she must bring witnesses before us, as we have written.

He also wrote: If one wrote two bills of divorce on two separate sheets, one above the other, and the witnesses signed between the two bills of divorce, such that they appear at the end of the first and above the second, if the document was delivered from the hand of the one where the witnesses are considered at the end of her bill of divorce, she is divorced. The one where the witnesses are considered at the beginning of her bill of divorce above, she is not divorced. He further wrote: If the top of one sheet is joined to the top of another sheet, and the witnesses are in the middle, such that the witnesses are at the beginning of both bills of divorce, both are invalidated. However, if they were delivered to them with witnesses, both are valid. And for those who require intent, the practical difference is that they would need to present the intent before us, as it is written. The Shulchan Aruch does not mention any of this because these matters are clarified from the preceding rulings as well.

It has already been explained that when Reuven is written up to the point of "kosher" and similarly with the son of Yaakov up to the point of "therefore," the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch write that if two gittin (divorce documents) are written on two columns on one scroll next to each other, and the witnesses sign underneath one another, such that one witness's name is under the first (column) and his father's name is under the second (column), and similarly the second witness's name is under the first witness's father's name, and the names of the witnesses are signed underneath, it is valid. However, if Reuven the son is written under the first (column) and Yaakov the witness is under the second (column), the second (document) is invalid. But if Reuven is written under the first (column) and the son of Yaakov the witness under the second (column), the second (document) is also valid. This is the end of the quotation.

Explanation of the matter: Initially, the general principle was established that if witnesses are associated with it, it is valid. Subsequently, it is explained how this works. If Reuven is signed under the first, the first is valid because we combine this with that of Yaakov's witness until under the second, since it is read in order. However, the second (document) is invalid because we do not combine Reuven, the previous one's son, with the second, as it is necessary to read from the second one. For example, if we know that the signature of Yaakov the witness is from Reuven his son, otherwise we would assume that Yaakov himself signed on the second one, making it valid with Yaakov the witness (Talmud). Also, the first one is valid because we combine the father's signature with the son's, as it is read in its proper order, as mentioned. Therefore, if the son of Yaakov the witness is signed on the second, both are valid—the second due to the son of Yaakov the witness, and the first due to the combination of the second. All this applies in the absence of “on condition” (a stipulation), but with “on condition,” we do not concern ourselves with it. For those who always require “on condition,” it matters in that it would require bringing witnesses that there was a stipulation, as mentioned (and see Beit Shmuel, section 9).

The witnesses of the get (Jewish bill of divorce) should not sign separately, each one must be in the presence of the other at the time of signing. They do not need to see each other while signing, and each one does not need to see the other, but they must be present in the place where the other is signing (Kenesset HaGedolah). Nevertheless, our custom is to be stringent that both of them stand together, right next to each other. The first signer sits, holds the quill, and says to the second, "Listen, so-and-so, how I am signing the get in the name of so-and-so, and his wife, so-and-so, for the purpose of divorce." The second witness observes while the first signs. Then the second witness sits and performs the same procedure, and the first stands next to him, as will be explained in the order of the get, with the help of Heaven. If they sign separately, the get is invalid.

And the reason for this law, the Sages said (Gittin 10b), is that we decree lest he say to ten people, “All of you write a get (bill of divorce) for my wife,” where the law is that one writes and all sign, as stated in Siman 120, Se'if 69. All the more so when he says, “All of you sign,” according to all opinions, they all must sign, as stated there in Se'if 68. If not all of them sign, the get is invalid because it depends on the husband's insistence (Rashi). Therefore, if we do not require that each one be in the presence of the other, it could happen that not all will sign, leading to corruption. But when we require that they all be present together, naturally, they will all sign and it will not lead to corruption. One should not question why we should be concerned about this, for certainly when he says “all of you,” all will sign. For it can be said that it is not only according to the opinion that all are considered witnesses, as stated there in Se'if 71, and all must sign on the day of writing, and if not, it is invalid. Certainly, there is a great concern that they might not realize that all are required to sign on that day, thinking that only two are witnesses and the rest are for a condition and can sign even the next day or subsequent days, following the law of conditions. But even according to the opinion that the truth is that two are witnesses and the rest are for a condition and can sign on another day, still, not everyone is well-versed in the law and may think that it is not necessary for all ten to sign, knowing that two witnesses suffice. Therefore, the Sages required that the witnesses of the get must sign in each other's presence, and naturally, since they will all gather, they will all sign on that day. Additionally, there is a concern that he might say “all of you sign” to the witnesses, in which case, according to all opinions, all are considered witnesses and must sign on that day, and in this, it is easy to err, as stated (Ran in the name of Ramban there).

And know that we follow this rule only stringently and not leniently. For example, if we need to validate the signatures and we can only find validation for one witness, we do not say that since one cannot sign without the other, it is necessarily the case that the first also signed as a witness, and it is considered as if it is validated. We do not say this, and we need to find validation for the second witness as well (Rema in Darchei Moshe, note 11).

Some say that the reason witnesses do not sign [the document] one not in the presence of the other is when there are two witnesses or more, and the husband designated them beforehand. However, if he only designated two witnesses and they signed in each other’s presence, and initially he did not intend to have more sign, but later decided to add another witness or witnesses, they can sign even though they were not present with the first two witnesses. (Tosafot, Chapter 2, s.v. "Tzei.") 

There are some of our Rabbis who disagree with this and invalidate [the document] even in such a case when the third was not present with the first ones, because the husband revealed his intention that he does not want the divorce to be finalized until the additional witness also signs, hence his status is like that of the first two witnesses (as mentioned by Rabbeinu Elchanan). 

It is clear that one should be stringent in this matter. However, the Tur and the Rema only brought the first opinion, and the matter requires further investigation for a definitive ruling (see Ran at the end of Chapter "Hazorek" and the commentary of the Gra, note 28, and examine further).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 18 that one should be careful not to have the scribe sign as a witness because there are those who invalidate this practice. His words imply that his legal opinion is otherwise, because indeed the Rif and the Rambam in chapter 9 permit the scribe to sign as a witness. However, he was concerned about the opinions that invalidate it. We have already explained this in section 120, clause 50, that this law depends on the principle of instructing someone to tell the scribe to write and particular individuals to sign. If this is valid, then necessarily the scribe signing as a witness is invalid because we are concerned that, out of embarrassment, the scribe, not being designated by the husband as a witness, might alter the instructions and command the scribe in the husband's name to sign. This is invalid according to the Torah because another was designated as a witness. But if "instructing someone to tell" is invalid, this concern does not exist, and the scribe signing as a witness is valid. Therefore, the Rif, Rambam, and Shulchan Aruch there invalidate the scribe signing as a witness in the case of "instructing someone to tell" but permit it otherwise. They were concerned about the opinions that hold "instructing someone to tell" is valid, and consequently, the scribe signing as a witness would be invalid. Moreover, we explained there in clause 51 in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak of the Tosafot that these two laws are not dependent on one another and both could be invalid. Indeed, in the Talmud (66a), there is another concern with "instructing someone to tell" that one might hire witnesses to say in the husband's name to the scribe to write and to the witnesses to sign. According to the primary law, "instructing someone to tell" is valid, and consequently, the scribe signing as a witness is invalid. Therefore, the ruling is to be stringent in all cases (see Beit Shmuel, section 29, who elaborates on this).

The witnesses who sign the get (divorce document) need to know how to read the get and sign it. Before they sign, they read the get and then sign, because otherwise, what are they signing? This will be explained in the order of the get. There is a doubt in retrospect if they did not read it before signing. It seems that since they were present at the writing of the first line and heard the scribe write it for his and her sake, they know what they are signing, and the reading is not indispensable after the fact. However, since the main witnesses are the delivery witnesses, for them, it is clear that reading is indispensable (Gittin 19b), as stated in Siman 135. However, it has already been clarified that, for us, the signing witnesses are considered the main witnesses. Since they know that this is the get, their reading is not indispensable after the fact. This also implies from what our teacher, the Rema, wrote there: "And if they testify well that this is her get," meaning if they know clearly that this is her get, their reading is not indispensable after the fact. And the reasoning is so: after all, is the reading a commandment? Rather, it is so they know what they are signing. All this is when they know how to read, but if they do not know how to read the get, their signature is nothing. However, the Sages instituted a solution for this because of concerns, as explained with the help of Heaven.

In regard to other legal documents, it is explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 45, that ideally, it is not sufficient for two people to read before the witness. Instead, the witness is obligated to read the document himself. In a situation of ex post facto (bediavad), there is a disagreement among the authorities, as mentioned there. In the case of gittin (divorce documents), the sages permitted others to read the content of the get and explain it to the witnesses due to the concern for agunot (women who cannot remarry because their husbands are missing). The witnesses are then permitted to sign. The Tur writes that even if one person reads before them, it is sufficient. However, in practice, one should not rely on this. According to Tosafot, it is only effective with two people, and this seems to be the opinion of the Rambam as well. This is also the conclusion of the later authorities (Beit Yosef, Beit Shmuel, subsection 26).

And know that Rambam wrote in the first chapter, "and that they recognize the language of the get," meaning, even though they do not know how to read, when the language of the get is read to them, they understand. But if they do not understand the language and the reader needs to translate it for them from one language to another, it does not help. However, the Tur wrote that even if they do not recognize the language of the get, the reader should translate it to their language. And the reason of the Rambam can be explained that if they do not understand the language, it is like testimony from one who heard it from another (Beit Yosef), and they brought proof for the Rambam from the Jerusalem Talmud in Gittin (Chapter 9, Halacha 8), where it is explained that the witnesses need to know how to read the get themselves. However, for the Tur, it is also fine, since it can be said that it refers to other documents (Shabbat Kodesh there), and it is necessary to say so, as from the Jerusalem Talmud it is clearly understood that they need to read it themselves (Avnei Shoham, section 27, who refutes this in another way and does not require this). (And the Shach in Choshen Mishpat, section 45, sub-section 3, ruled like the Tur).

The Sages also were lenient regarding gittin (divorce documents) with witnesses who do not know how to sign; they would make an impression for them on the paper with saliva or something similar, which does not last, and they would trace over the impression. For if they were to make an impression with something that lasts, their signature would be invalid, as writing over writing is not considered writing (Tur). And some say that even with something that does not last, it is initially forbidden to make the shape of the letters for them, as this is considered writing over writing, and there is a concern they might do so with something that lasts. It is only valid after the fact if they made an impression with something that does not last (ibid.). Initially, they only permitted tearing a blank piece of paper in the shape of the letters, and they would fill in the tears with ink in a manner that the ink follows the tear, as in the way of writing (this is implied by the language of the Rema, paragraph 16, see there).

And know that in the Jerusalem Talmud Gittin (Chapter 2, Halacha 3) and Shabbat (Chapter 12, Halacha 4) it raises a difficulty on this: "Is it not the handwriting of the first one?" and resolves it by explaining "when he widened the tear for them," meaning that if they were to fill all the tears with ink, how would they confirm their signatures? (Tosafot 9a) For they wrote in the form of the tears, and it resolves it by stating "when he widened the tear for them and did not fill it entirely," thus their writing retains its original form. However, this requires further investigation, as the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) omitted this. Consequently, it is also explained that in the case of saliva marks, one must widen them (and the explanation that tearing paper means another paper to place on the parchment as Tosafot wrote there, and Mordechai in Chapter 2 explained on that paper, and this is similar to Rashi's explanation of marking it, see there and examine it carefully).

In this leniency that was granted regarding divorce documents, the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in the first chapter as follows: "It is a leniency that was granted in the matter of women's divorce documents so that Jewish women would not remain agunot (chained wives), since the signing of witnesses on the get (divorce document) is rabbinic, as it is written." It is clear from his words that they only granted leniency when there are witnesses of delivery, for in such a case their signatures are rabbinic. And certainly according to the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) who hold that it is impossible without witnesses of delivery. Therefore, what he wrote, that if they recorded in something that endures, their signatures are nothing, means that it is as if there are no witnesses of delivery, and it is valid post facto as it is written in Siman 133. It is not reasonable to say that this is considered as forged from within. Therefore, it is a wonder about the Tur who wrote in the name of the Ramah that if they recorded for them in what the bottom one wrote, it is not a get, and if she was divorced with it, she is disqualified from marrying a kohen, as it is written. And he himself holds in Siman 133 that without witnesses of delivery, it is nothing, and necessarily there are witnesses of delivery. So why is it not a get? There are those who say that he holds that it is worse than without signatures because we decree it due to writing (Beit Shmuel, sk 28). But it is impossible to say this, for if so, it is only a rabbinic disqualification, and how did he write that it is not a get at all, but only disqualified for a kohen? Furthermore, from where do we derive to decree this? For we do not find this reasoning except in the case of not for its sake (Tosafot, beginning "modah"), and even in this, many poskim disagree. Additionally, in all such cases, he should not have written conclusively. And it appears to me clearly that he wrote this according to the opinion that holds that witnesses of delivery alone suffice, and perhaps the Ramah holds so in practice. And since there are no witnesses of delivery, it is certainly not a get, and only for a kohen one should be stringent.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Siman 14 that if a get (bill of divorce) was written in one script and its witnesses signed in another script, it is valid, provided that the witnesses recognize the language and the script of the writing. This is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 4, and their intention is that the witnesses need to read it. If they do not recognize the language and the script, how can they read it? Consequently, if others read it before them, it suffices that they recognize only the language (Beit Shmuel, se'if katan 25). According to the opinion of the Tur that we wrote in Siman 44, this is also not necessary. Additionally, he wrote that if one of the witnesses signed in one script and the other witness in another script, it is valid. And although we invalidate such a case in writing, as written at the beginning of Siman 126, we are lenient in signatures. Furthermore, each witness's signature is considered a separate writing. Know that in all matters where we are stringent by law in writing, we should also be stringent in signatures, especially in the case of "chak tochot" (engraved letters), which are invalid. However, in cases of touching letters and similar instances, we may be lenient in signatures in pressing situations.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (10:): All documents that are processed in non-Jewish courts, even though their signatories are non-Jews, are valid, except for bills of divorce for women and emancipation documents for slaves, because they (non-Jews) are not capable of performing these separations. A bill of divorce that is processed in non-Jewish courts and has non-Jewish witnesses signed on it, even if it was written by a Jew and delivered in the presence of Jewish witnesses, since the signatories are disqualified from testimony, it is considered internally forged, and the bill of divorce is invalid. Even one disqualified witness invalidates the bill of divorce, as stated in Section 2, and its invalidity is by rabbinic decree. From a legal perspective, it is a complete bill of divorce, and its invalidity is due to a rabbinic decree. Therefore, if he gave her such a bill of divorce, the betrothal would take effect (Ran there).

As we have already written in section 3, if the invalidity is apparent and people will not rely on it, the get (divorce document) is valid. Therefore, some of our rabbis hold that the reason why Kuthian witnesses invalidate a get in courts, even when written by a Jew and with Jewish witnesses, is only when the Kuthian names resemble Jewish names. In such a case, we are concerned that people might rely on them, and it would be considered internally falsified. However, when the names are unique to Kuthians, which the Gemara refers to as distinctive names, there is no concern that they will be mistaken for Jews, and people will not rely on them. Thus, the get is valid (Rosh and Rashba in the name of the Raavad, ruled according to R' Shimon there). Some have written that, ideally, we do not validate it, but only post facto is it valid (there in the name of R' Chananel). The opinion of the majority of poskim is to invalidate even post facto, as they decreed distinctive names due to non-distinctive names (like the first Tanna of the Mishnah who also holds like R' Eliezer there). This is the opinion of the Rif, the Rosh, and the Rashba, and it is likewise concluded in the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 19. This also clarifies the opinion of the Rambam who generally ruled to invalidate, and so is the law (Chapter 6 of Avadim).

And there is a question regarding this among the poskim (Jewish legal decisors) who validate with prominent names as it is written. If so, why do they only validate when it is done in courts, as implied in the Mishnah? Even if it is done among non-Jewish laypeople, since the writing is by a Jew, with Jewish intent, and the signatures are prominent names, what reason is there to differentiate between a court and laypeople in a get (Jewish divorce document)? However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, a reason is provided for this, because a public announcement is made in courts, meaning that in courts we rely on the fact that everything is done properly, that the writing is by Jews, with Jewish intent, and that it was only done in the presence of the court and with their signatures. But when it is done among laypeople, we do not rely at all on the fact that it was done properly. Therefore, in all cases it is invalid (Ran and Ramban in Milchemet Hashem). For us, there is no practical difference in this matter as it is written.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 19, after writing the law about a get (divorce document) from non-Jewish courts, which is invalid in all cases, wrote as follows: "But if a woman brings before us a get with which she was divorced to remarry, and the names of the witnesses are like the names of non-Jews, if they are names that Jews never use at all, she may remarry with it, as it is certain that they are Jews, for they would not have signed the get with such names unless they knew they were Jews. But if they are names that somewhat resemble Jewish names, we are concerned that the signers of the get may have erred, thinking they were Jews, and perhaps they are non-Jews, and she may not remarry with it." And so wrote several of the early authorities in explaining the sugya (discussion) (11b in the case of Reish Lakish from Rabbi Yochanan) that permits with distinctive names. According to their view, that it is invalid even with distinctive names, it is necessary to explain this way. And the poskim (decisors) who permit with distinctive names interpret the sugya according to its straightforward meaning, that when we see in the get distinctive names, we permit the get even if we know they are non-Jews.

And it is quite perplexing to me the approach of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. The first perplexity is that if these are established names, how can they be Jewish? I found one of our Rabbis who answered this question, saying that it is not absolute that there cannot be a Jewish name like that, only that it is uncommon (Ritva). The second perplexity is that if we are concerned that the document might have been made invalidly, there are many concerns regarding a get (divorce document), and yet our Sages were only concerned with the writing being for the sake of the specific person, and even this, according to the halacha, we do not hold by. And the requirement to say "in my presence it was written" and "in my presence it was signed" is not due to this concern, but because witnesses are not readily available to validate it (as Rava says at the beginning of the tractate). The Rashba, of blessed memory, in his novellae there, also raised a similar question, and wrote: “It is difficult, how can it be that they stand before the husband and the scribe and they do not recognize if they are Jewish or not, that they would rely on them and sign them?” And he did not answer anything. Furthermore, it is even more perplexing to me that at the end of section 142, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote regarding an agent who said "in my presence it was written" and "in my presence it was signed," that even if the names of the witnesses are like the names of non-Jews, we do not concern ourselves with them, and if the husband comes and objects, we do not pay attention to him. And it is clear that even if they have names that are not established, he cannot invalidate it, for if otherwise, it should have been explained. And it is also clear from there, from the source of the law in the Jerusalem Talmud as it says there. And how in this law do we concern ourselves with invalidating it in a place where there is no objection at all? Indeed, in the Rambam, this law is not found at all. And it is clear to me that he explains regarding the validation of the get with established names, even though he holds that even with established names it is invalid, as it seems from his words in chapter 6 of the laws of slaves. Nevertheless, in a pressing situation and in a place of potential agunah (a woman unable to remarry), it is possible to validate it and rely on Rabbi Shimon who holds this way, similar to what our Sages said regarding another law: "It is permissible to rely on Rabbi Shimon in a pressing situation" (Yevamot 20). And I found one of the great ones who wrote this reasoning in his own name (Yam Shel Shlomo chapter 1, section 25). Therefore, since this is not a fixed law, the Rambam of blessed memory omitted it (Aruch HaShulchan, first chapter, section 11, who also wrote regarding an agent similar to a woman, and the words of the Kesef Mishneh do not seem correct).

It seems to me that the primary ruling according to our Rabbis is not to entirely invalidate the get (divorce document), but rather to indicate that there is an obligation to investigate the matter. As we generally say, whenever clarification is possible, we clarify. The intention here is that if the names are well-known, we validate them without further inquiry, since it is certain that they are Jews and there is no mistake in this regard. However, for names that are not well-known, there is a concern that obligates us to verify this matter. But when it is impossible to verify, we do not invalidate the get post facto in cases of significant hardship or exigent circumstances.

Additionally, all of this applies to a woman who brought the get to us or to a messenger who does not need to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" and is unaware of this matter to testify about it. However, a messenger who needs to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed"—since he acted according to the regulation of the sages, it is assumed that everything was properly validated. Therefore, we do not worry even if the husband comes and objects, as stated in Siman 142.

Nevertheless, I have not found support for my words among the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). Therefore, in practice, one should not rely on this reasoning I have written. However, it seems clear to me that only if it is known that they were Jews, and the concern is only rabbinic, we can rely on what is written (see Beit Shmuel at the end of section 30, and examine all his words carefully).

The Sages taught in a Mishnah (86a): There are three types of invalid bills of divorce (gittin), but if a woman remarries based on one of them, the child from the second marriage is legitimate. These are: if it is written in the husband's handwriting but has no witnesses; if it has witnesses but no date; or if it has a date but only one witness. These three types of bills of divorce are invalid, but if a woman remarries based on one of them, the child is legitimate. Rabbi Eliezer says: Even if it has no witnesses, as long as it was given to her in the presence of witnesses, it is valid, etc., because the witnesses do not sign the bill of divorce except for the betterment of the world (tikkun olam). The first opinion is that of Rabbi Meir, who holds that the witnesses' signatures finalize the divorce. Nevertheless, if it is in the husband's handwriting, it is valid by Torah law even without witnesses, as it is written, "and he writes for her." And although matters involving forbidden relationships require at least two witnesses, the husband's handwriting is regarded as equivalent to a hundred witnesses. The Torah includes this in divorce as it does in monetary matters, where the admission of a litigant is like a hundred witnesses, as it is written, "and he writes for her," implying that any writing from him effects the divorce (Rashba, Kiddushin 65a). We have explained the reason for this in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 241, see there. This ruling applies both according to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer. By rabbinic decree, such a bill of divorce is invalid, but if she remarries, she need not leave her second husband, even if she has no children from the second marriage (Tur).

The invalidity due to the date has already been explained in Siman 127. If it has a date but only one witness, if there were witnesses present at the time of delivery, according to our ruling that follows Rabbi Eliezer, it is not invalid. If there were no witnesses and it was given to her privately, if it is in the husband's handwriting, it is invalid by rabbinic decree, but if she remarries, she need not leave her second husband, as in the first case. If it was written by a scribe, Rambam writes in Chapter 1 that it is not a bill of divorce at all, see there.

Here are the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 20: "If he gave her the get (divorce document) privately, even in the presence of one witness, it is not a valid get. In what case is this said? When the get was written by a scribe. But if the husband himself wrote the get in his own handwriting and one witness signed it and he gave it to her, this is an invalid get but it disqualifies her from the priesthood." This is the language of the Rambam in Chapter 1, Laws 13 and 14; see there. And this refers to a situation without a condition (stipulation). Therefore, if it is in the handwriting of a scribe, it is not a get at all. But if it is in the handwriting of the husband, if she remarries, she does not have to leave her new husband, also without a condition and without a witness, for the reason that has been explained. Even without a signed witness, because one witness neither adds nor detracts, and it was only written because of the beginning, where it was necessary to mention it, so that it would not be said that a document written by a scribe and one witness is like two witnesses. And when it says "and disqualifies her from the priesthood," it is an additional matter, for since we hold that if she remarries she does not leave, all the more so it disqualifies her from the priesthood. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, himself erased this from the books for this reason; see there. But this is his way in the Shulchan Aruch, to copy the Rambam's language as it is, even if it is problematic.

And know that what we have written, that a document written in his own handwriting, if she marries, she does not have to leave him, this applies both according to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer, according to the opinions of the Rif and the Rambam, who both hold that Rabbi Eliezer also agrees that witnesses sign the document, as stated in Siman 120 and will be explained in Siman 133. And indeed, this is the case, for Rabbi Eliezer agrees with Rabbi Meir. And even according to the Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur, who hold that Rabbi Eliezer believes that only on the condition (that witnesses sign) does it effect the divorce, and not by the document itself, it appears to me to be simple that just as for Rabbi Meir, a document in his own handwriting stands in place of the condition, so too for Rabbi Eliezer it stands in place of the condition. What reason is there to differentiate in this matter? This is also evident from the words of the Chidushei HaRashba in Yevamot (31a) and in Kiddushin (65b), and so wrote explicitly the Ra'avad in his commentary on the Mishnah in this Mishnah. And this is also evident from the words of the Tur in his book Kitzur Piskei HaRosh, who wrote on this Mishnah that if the husband wrote in his own handwriting, if she marries, she does not have to leave him, also according to the Rosh. And this can also be deduced from Rashi's commentary on the Mishnah (see there and examine it well), and it also appears from the Yerushalmi.

According to this, what the Tur wrote at the end of this section is as follows: "A get (divorce document) without witnesses, even if it is recognized as the husband's handwriting, or there is only one witness, even if the writing of the get is recognized to be in the hand of the court scribe, or even if it is the husband's handwriting, is invalid. However, if she married with it, she should not be required to leave him, even if she has no children." End quote. There is a question raised about the scribe's handwriting and one witness—why should she not be required to leave him (Beit Yosef)? However, the truth is that in the Gemara, there is a distinction between an expert scribe and a non-expert scribe. For an expert scribe, the handwriting is considered like a witness from the Torah, and it is only invalid rabbinically. Therefore, if she married, she should not be required to leave him. This is why the Tur precisely mentioned a court scribe, who is an expert scribe (Bayit Chadash). Nevertheless, in any case, it can be said that the intention is without stipulation, because if there is a stipulation, in any case, it is valid (Beit Yosef).

However, the commentators on his words explained that without "Upon the condition" (al menat), even if it is in the husband's handwriting, it is not a valid bill of divorce (get) for us, since we follow Rabbi Eliezer's opinion. According to the Tur, Rabbi Eliezer does not agree with Rabbi Meir that even a debt document (shtar chov) is valid, but only specifically "Upon the condition." The Tur speaks about a woman who presented a bill of divorce before us, and we do not know if it contained "Upon the condition." Therefore, if it was in the husband's handwriting or from a distinguished scribe and one witness, if she remarried, she does not need to leave the new marriage because we assume that there was "Upon the condition" (Beit Yosef). Some have challenged this by asking why we assume validity when there are no two signed witnesses, perhaps there was no "Upon the condition" (Beit Yosef). However, one could say that just as we assume there was "Upon the condition" with signed witnesses, so too with the husband's handwriting or a distinguished scribe and one witness (Beit Yosef). Nevertheless, they all agree that according to Rabbi Eliezer, who says "Upon the condition" validates, it does not work without "Upon the condition," even in the husband's handwriting. This is also the opinion of the Beit Shmuel (Section 31 and in Section 20 where he made a distinction between the Beit Yosef and the Beit Shmuel, but it is not so, as the Beit Yosef wrote according to the Rambam's view that Rabbi Eliezer also holds "Upon the condition" validates, and the Beit Shmuel follows the Tur that only "Upon the condition" validates).

And there is some proof for this approach from the words of the Rosh there, who discusses the issue of the Amoraim in this Mishnah, whether she should go out or not. What practical difference does it make for us, since we hold like Rabbi Eliezer? He answers, because in the case of the three types of bills of divorce mentioned in the Mishnah, there is a bill of divorce with witnesses but no date, and in this Rabbi Eliezer does not disagree. It seems from his words that in the case written in the husband's handwriting, Rabbi Eliezer does disagree and holds that the child is a mamzer (illegitimate). This is also implied from what he wrote there, that the criterion for severance is only with conditions, and without them it is not a valid get (divorce document) at all. However, the main issue is very puzzling, that in the husband's handwriting there should be a difference between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer, aside from what is proven from several Rishonim who do not hold this way. As I have written, it seems to me that there is no proof from the Rosh at all, because he is not addressing this law of the husband's handwriting, but rather coming to reject the Rif’s opinion that Rabbi Eliezer also holds that conditions effect severance. He elaborates on this matter, stating that Rabbi Eliezer holds that only conditions effect severance, not witnesses, and this is what he said that only in the case of no date does Rabbi Eliezer not disagree, meaning that even if there are conditions, she should not remarry. But in other laws, if there are conditions, she may remarry initially. And so explicitly wrote the Ba'al HaMaor in the name of Rabbeinu Ephraim, a student of the Rif, who disagreed with him in this wording. But to say the opposite, that according to Rabbi Eliezer, the husband's handwriting does not work from the Torah, we have not heard from their words. The words of the Tur can also be interpreted in their straightforward manner, as I have written, as is evident from his words in the Rosh's rulings that we have written. This is why he did not write in the language of the Mishnah and wrote even if it is recognized as the husband's handwriting, implying that the woman brought it before us. Certainly, if the act is before us, we would not allow her without conditions. In the Rosh's rulings, he wrote in the language of the Mishnah, but not with the intention that we assume there were conditions. However, in practice, my opinion is nullified, and when such an incident occurs, we should be stringent in all aspects. According to the Rif and the Rambam, she should certainly not leave. In my opinion, the same is true according to the Rosh and the Tur. According to the commentators, if she married, she should leave, and the child is a mamzer according to the Rosh and the Tur. Therefore, in practice, she should leave, and the child is a doubtful mamzer, unless we rely on the Rif and the Rambam, and this requires further investigation.

The witnesses of a get (divorce document) should not take a lot of money, more than what is appropriate for their lost time, as we hold that one who takes payment for testimony invalidates their testimony. Some say that an agreement is made with the witnesses that if they invalidate the get, they will have to pay, and because of this, they can take a lot of money. Alternatively, it is because they are forbidden to marry the divorced woman, as stated in Siman 12. According to this, some are meticulous to find witnesses who are not Kohanim, since a Kohen is anyway forbidden to marry a divorced woman (Rema in Darkei Moshe). However, we have not seen this practiced, and the reasoning is weak. For just because they are forbidden to marry her, it does not mean they are not commanded to testify (Taz). Furthermore, if so, we should seek out unmarried witnesses, since in our community it is forbidden to marry two wives. Additionally, the first reason is not customary among us to make agreements with the witnesses to pay if they invalidate. Indeed, the main allowance is because they are not obligated to go and see the testimony, and the commandment is that when one sees testimony, it is a mitzvah and obligation to go to the Beit Din and testify, as stated in Choshen Mishpat Siman 28. Therefore, because they are invited to go and sign the get and be witnesses, they can take as much payment as they want, as many great authorities have written. Certainly, the one arranging the get can take as much as he wants, as stated in the order of the get in Siman 154. It has already been clarified that the custom is that the signing witnesses are the primary witnesses. However, if others who are present at the time of the get are the delivery witnesses, they are forbidden to take payment, as they are not invited to come and witness the testimony, but came of their own accord. From a legal standpoint, the scribe can also be one of the delivery witnesses, even though he is invalid for signing (Beit Shmuel at the end of Siman 29).

According to the primary law, it would seem that if the witnesses signing the get (bill of divorce) have not yet grown a full beard, it is necessary to check if they have grown two pubic hairs, and we do not rely on their age to assume that they have developed the signs of maturity. This presumption is only for stringency and not for leniency, as stated in Siman 169 regarding chalitzah (the ritual of removing a shoe). However, I found that our master the Beit Yosef, in his great book, wrote in the name of the Condresim, the Sefer Mitzvot Katan, and the Kol Bo: If the signing witnesses are presumed to be of age, it is sufficient because the main witnesses are the witnesses of the delivery, and at the time of delivery, there are many mature men present. From their words, we learn that the witnesses of the get do not need to be specifically appointed by the husband for the purpose of testimony; rather, as long as they see the delivery from his hand to hers, they are valid witnesses. Nevertheless, it is customary l'chatchila (ideally) for the husband to command them to be witnesses.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 22: "There is an opinion that says the get (divorce document) must be dried before the witnesses sign it." End quote. There is no reason for this, and it has already been explained at the end of section 124 that the get should not be given to the woman until it has dried, because as long as it hasn't dried, it is considered as a document that could be forged. But regarding the witnesses' signatures, what difference does it make? And so have many of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) written, that there is no reason for this (see the Beit Yosef there, and similarly the Radbaz). However, since these words came from our teacher, the Beit Yosef, it has become customary to be stringent in this matter as well, unless it is a pressing situation where the day might pass, or similar cases, in which case this stringency need not be observed.

The writing and signing [of the get] must be for his sake and for her sake. And there are 21 sections on this topic:

It is required that the writing of the get and its signing be for the sake of the man who is divorcing and for the sake of the woman who is being divorced, as it is written: "And he shall write for her a document of severance and place it in her hand." The word "for her" (לה) is extra and comes to teach that it must be done for her sake. And although it is needed for the derivation that it should not be for her and her companion, as it is written in Siman 130, section 25, there are two "and he shall write for her" (וְכָתַב לָהּ) written. Consequently, since it needs to be for her sake, it is obvious that it also needs to be for his sake, and there is no need for a separate derivation for this, as the simple meaning of the verse implies this, that "and he shall write" refers to the husband. And when he himself writes, he certainly writes for his sake. Therefore, throughout the Talmud, we only mention "for her sake." Accordingly, when the scribe writes at the instruction of the husband, he must write for his sake and for her sake and for the sake of divorce, not merely for the sake of writing. This applies to all procedures of gittin (divorce documents), and the signatures must also be for his sake, for her sake, and for the sake of divorce.

A get (bill of divorce) that was written not for its intended purpose or for her sake is invalid according to Torah law. Even for the priesthood, such a get does not disqualify her, and another man's betrothal does not take effect on her at all (Beit Shmuel). If it was written for its intended purpose but signed not for its intended purpose—even if one witness signed for its intended purpose and the other did not—the get is rabbinically invalid under all circumstances, even when it was conditional. This is considered as if it were inherently forged (Gemara, 4). One should not ask what problem could arise from this, since with invalid witnesses, there could be an issue if we rely on them. But with respect to a lack of proper intent, what concern is there even if we rely on them, since they are valid and the get is valid through conditional means? It can be said that we decree the signing due to the writing, meaning if they do not sign with the proper intent, we might decree that they will also not write with the proper intent (Tosafot there).

Furthermore, not only according to the Rif and the Rambam, for whom even according to Rabbi Eliezer it is valid with witnesses alone, this is certainly a major forgery, for what is written for her [the woman] for her sake [i.e., the sake of the divorce] applies also to the signatures of the witnesses. But even according to those who disagree and hold that without stipulation it is nothing, and that the witnesses' signatures are not essential from the Torah, nevertheless, since this get (divorce document) is validated by its signatures, we say that it was certainly done properly, for this is the main ordinance of Rabban Gamliel—that the witnesses should sign the get. And since they make it a valid get, it is certainly part of the writing of the get. Therefore, since they signed it, if they did not sign for her sake, it is considered inherently forged (Rashba there, and this is what the Shulchan Aruch says in section 6: if it was given to her without stipulation, etc., this is according to the view of the Rif and the Rambam).

There are some of the Geonim who hold that if the signatures are not properly executed, such as if they signed not for the sake of the get, or if one of the witnesses is disqualified, or even if only one witness signed it, the get is nullified by Torah law, even if it was written for the sake of the get and delivered in the presence of valid witnesses. The Rambam, of blessed memory, in Chapter 3, Law 8, disagreed with them, and his words are as follows: "This does not appear to me to be correct, but rather as a falsehood, not a definite falsehood. And since it was delivered in the presence of valid witnesses, it is only disqualified by rabbinic decree." End quote. The Rif in Chapter 9 also brought this opinion of the Gaon and ruled not according to him. It appears that the opinion of the Gaon is that according to Rabbi Eliezer, the get is validated either by witnesses of delivery (a.m.) or by witnesses of the signing (a.h.), as per the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam.
