And he (the Gaon) holds that since he made the witnesses sign the get, he revealed his intention to validate it by witnesses of the signing alone. And even if he later also takes witnesses of delivery, it is merely for additional validation. And since his intention was to make the get valid by witnesses of the signing, the get is disqualified by Torah law when the signatures are not according to the law of the Torah. And although Rabban Gamliel instituted witnesses of the signing for the betterment of the world, it can be said that the Gaon holds that Rabban Gamliel instituted that there should be witnesses of the signing and not witnesses of the delivery because they are preferable for validation purposes, and then the signatures become a Torah requirement. And even though it is explicitly proven in the Talmud that when he made Samaritans sign, the disqualification is only rabbinic, and therefore there are those who hold that with prominent names it is valid (10:), this is certainly so, because since he made Samaritans, who are known not to be valid witnesses, it is clear that his intention was not to validate it by witnesses of the signing. But when he began to make Israelites sign, his intention was to validate it by witnesses of the signing. And since they are disqualified, or they did not sign for the sake of the get, or only one witness signed, the get is disqualified (and this resolves the difficulty of the Gra in subparagraph 8, and also what he wrote there that even if there are no witnesses of the delivery, it does not need to be for the sake of the get by Torah law, etc., is difficult according to the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam).

And our master the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Yosef Karo) in section 6 brought the opinion of the Gaon (Rabbi Elijah of Vilna) in the name of "some say" and considered his words stringently in the case of "not for its sake". This is because he did not consider his words in section 130 regarding one valid witness and one invalid witness, where he wrote in section 17 that the get (divorce document) is invalid and did not bring the opinion of the Gaon that it is not a get. And some have challenged him on this (see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 7). It seems to me that according to what we have explained, it is clear that whenever a disqualification is found in the witnesses or in one witness who is not fit to testify, he did not consider this opinion because since he is not fit to testify, certainly the husband's intention was not to validate the get by a single witness alone, and even if he does not know of the disqualification, nevertheless if he knew, he would not have intended it. But in the case of "not for its sake", where the witnesses are valid, it is certainly possible that the husband wanted to make the get valid according to Torah law based on the signatures, and therefore they invalidated it. Thus, he considered this opinion stringently. And we have already explained there in section 3 that when only one valid witness signs, it is not invalid even rabbinically (and so wrote the Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 7) and that there are those who disagree with this, see there.

And since the main aspect of the get (Jewish bill of divorce) is that it must be written for the sake of the specific individuals involved, therefore all the decisors have written that one must be very careful when the husband instructs the scribe to write the get. He should say in the presence of the signing witnesses, "Write a get for my sake, for so-and-so, and for the sake of my wife, so-and-so daughter of so-and-so." Similarly, when he instructs the witnesses to sign the get, he should tell them to sign it for his sake, for her sake, and for the sake of the divorce. It is customary that they respond, "So it shall be done," and this is not an absolute requirement. Likewise, the scribe should verbally declare when he begins writing that he is writing it for the sake of so-and-so, the wife of so-and-so, and for his sake. Similarly, each of the witnesses should declare when beginning to sign that they are signing for his sake, for her sake, and for the sake of the divorce, and they should specify their names. Thought alone does not suffice, and this requirement is binding even after the fact (Bach Commentary, sub-section 8). Some say that verbal declaration is not absolutely necessary and that thought alone suffices after the fact (Taz Commentary). Regarding a Torah scroll, it is clarified in Yoreh De'ah, section 274, that one must verbalize it, and so it is written in Orach Chaim, section 32, regarding the preparation of tefillin. Some of the early authorities were uncertain whether writing a Torah scroll requires verbal declaration or if thought alone suffices (Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah, there). However, it is certain that if the husband instructs them to write and sign for his sake and for her sake, even if they did not verbalize it, it is assumed that they acted with his intention. But if the husband did not instruct them explicitly, it remains a doubtful matter of law even if he instructed them to write a get for his wife, since he did not explicitly state that it should be written for his sake and for her sake, there is doubt whether the woman is not considered to be in a state of divorce. Or perhaps, since he told them to write a get, it is assumed that his intention was according to the law (as it seems to me). Additionally, it appears to me that if the husband simply told them to write a get for his wife, and they wrote and signed explicitly for his sake and for her sake, this suffices.

And know that in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch and in the order of the get (divorce document), it is explained that when the husband instructs the scribe and the witnesses, he tells them, "Write a get for my wife, Plonit." Similarly, with the witnesses, it is not explained that he needs to say, "Write a get for my wife, Plonit, and for my sake." When the scribe begins, he needs to say for his (the husband's) sake and for her (the wife's) sake, and similarly, when the witnesses sign. And it must be said that when the husband instructs, he does not need to say for his own sake as well, since he is instructing to write a get for his wife's sake, it is automatically included for his own sake. However, it is better for the husband to clarify his words clearly as stated, and this is the simple custom. And proof of this is in the order of the get at the end of Siman 154, section 16, where in his instruction to the witnesses it also states for his own sake. Refer there. Additionally, they have added there that he should say to them, "Be witnesses and sign this get that the scribe Ploni ben Ploni is writing." Refer there. And similarly, the custom is to mention the scribe, and it is not an impediment.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in paragraph 7 that the scribe, when writing, should write consistently and not intermittently in order to ensure that he writes with the proper intent, just as he started. However, after the fact, if he wrote intermittently, it is still valid. For ideally, we are concerned that if he stops, he might not continue to write with the proper intent, and we would have to rely on what he said at the beginning of the get (Jewish divorce document). Ideally, it is certainly not proper to rely on this, but after the fact, we do rely on it. He also wrote that some say that the preparation of the parchment and the cutting of the quill, as well as the lining of the parchment, should all be done with the proper intent. However, if these things were done without the proper intent, it is not invalid. For the obligation of proper intent applies only to the writing and the signatures, and ideally, it is merely an enhancement to strengthen the matter of intent.

He further wrote in section 9 that if the witness began to sign part of his name and did not say it was for his name and for her name, and then remembered and said it, there are those who validate it. But if he completed his name and did not say it was for his name and for her name, there is no remedy (Beit Shmuel, section 10). Even though "Ben Yaakov" as a witness is written correctly, nonetheless, when his name is written incorrectly, it is considered as if it is internally falsified. However, if only part of his name is written, it does not fall under the category of internally falsified since it is not a complete word. And even though his entire name is not written correctly, it is still not considered as falsified and is validated with "Ben Yaakov" as a witness. Therefore, it seems to me that if he only signed "Reuven" as a witness and signed part of his name not for its intended purpose, the get (divorce document) is invalid (as it appears to me, and see Beit Shmuel and Teshuvot Geonim, and according to our words, there is no disagreement, and scrutinize this). However, what does "not for its intended purpose" mean? Either he explicitly intended it not for its purpose, or by default, which is considered as not for its purpose, or even if he intended in his heart for its purpose but did not express it verbally, and the husband did not explicitly tell them to sign for its purpose. But if he explicitly told them to sign for its purpose and intended it in his heart, it is sufficient, or possibly even by default, it is done with the husband's intention, as written in section 6. One should be stringent in practice unless in a time of need, in which case one may rely on what is written in section 6, since if there is intent from the husband, it is not invalid by Torah law, but only a rabbinic concern.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Yosef Karo), wrote in Section 8: "There should be two witnesses to the signing present at the time when the get (divorce document) begins to be written, so they know it is written for its proper purpose and recognize it at the time of signing." And it is explained that it suffices for them to be present only at the beginning of the writing of the get. The language of the Tur is: "The witnesses who sign need to be there when the scribe writes it and recognize that this is the get that the scribe wrote for its intended purpose. However, even if they are only there at the beginning of the writing and heard that he began to write it for its intended purpose, it is acceptable." From the Shulchan Aruch, it seems that even ideally, they only need to be present at the beginning. However, in the order of the get in Section 21, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in this language: "They need to be present at the time of writing the line containing the names of the man and the woman and the date, and they should hear that it is being written for his and her intended purposes." These statements do not contradict each other, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

For in the Gemara, we do not find at all that the witnesses must stand while the scribe writes. This is only found in the case of a messenger who must say "It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence." Even regarding the messenger, the Sages said that he need not stand except for the writing of one line when he heard that it was written for its specific purpose; this suffices (Gittin 5b). And Rav Ashi said there that even if he only heard the sound of the quill or the scroll, he can say "It was written in my presence." The Rif ruled accordingly. There are those who are stringent and rule specifically according to the first opinion. However, Rashi of blessed memory explained that the first opinion refers to the line where the names of the man and woman and the date are written (Gittin 15a). All these matters pertain to the messenger and not to the witnesses. However, it is certain that the witnesses must know that the scribe wrote it for its specific purpose, for otherwise, on what basis are they signing? Furthermore, they must recognize that this is the get (bill of divorce) that the scribe wrote for its specific purpose.

Therefore, ideally, it is proper for witnesses to be present during the writing of the get (divorce document), but after the fact, it is not an absolute requirement at all, as Mordechai wrote in the order of the get, and these are his words: "And if there are no witnesses present during the writing of the get, it appears that it is valid, for generally, since the husband instructed the scribe in the presence of witnesses to write it for her sake, it is presumed that he wrote it for her sake and properly, even if he does not recognize the handwriting of the scribe, for most of them are proficient. The sages did not require witnesses to be present during the writing of the get except for cases where it is necessary to state 'before me it was written' to prevent the husband from casting aspersions on the get. But when the husband himself gives it, there is no concern that it was not written for her sake. Nevertheless, it is good for witnesses to be present during the writing of the get, and this is the common practice." (This is brought by Beit Yosef in his work.) In this way, the words of the Tur are clarified. Our master, Beit Yosef, because we see in the Gemara that even for a messenger, they were strict not to stand over the writing more than one line, so as not to cast aspersions on earlier gittin, therefore, he did not want to be stringent about witnesses more, since there is no source for witnesses in the Talmud. On the contrary, he did not want to write explicitly 'the first line' but rather 'the beginning,' so as not to completely resemble the law of the messenger in the Gemara, but it is understood that 'the beginning' refers to the first line. In the order of the get, he considered the opinion of Rashi that we brought. All these matters are stringencies and not the fundamental law. (See Beit Yosef there.)

Additionally, it is written in Section 5: A get (divorce document) that was written without specific intent (lishma), even if one subsequently passed a quill over it with the proper intent, it is not a valid get. However, some say that we are concerned about it. The explanation of the matter is that we hold that writing over existing writing is not considered writing. This is established in regard to Shabbat, as the Rambam writes in Chapter 11 of the Laws of Shabbat, and similarly regarding the sanctification of God's name, where if it was not sanctified initially, passing a quill over it with the proper intent does not help. The sages also said this is not the optimal way (Gittin 20a). The intention is that it is invalid. When it is said that it is not the optimal way, implying that it is at least valid, this is referring to the opinion of those who disagree, saying that even according to them, it is not the optimal way. But according to us, it is completely invalid, as it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Shabbat Chapter 12). I am astonished at the codifiers of the law who did not bring this ruling in the laws of writing a Sefer Torah, tefillin, and mezuzot in Yoreh De'ah and Orach Chaim (except for the Beit Yosef in his book in the laws of Yoreh De'ah, Section 276, who brings this, but it requires further investigation). Some say that we should be stringent about this, but not lenient, because in the Talmud (Gittin, ibid.) there is an opinion that differentiates between the sanctification of God's name and other matters. Therefore, in practice, it is clear that we should be stringent regarding the prohibition of a married woman (and see Tosafot, Shabbat 104b, s.v. "אמר").

The Tur writes that the writing and signing of the get (divorce document) must be done for the sake of the specific man and woman, whether it is the main part or the form. Therefore, the scribe should not write forms of gittin to have them available whenever he wants, and when they come to divorce, he writes the main part with their names. Even after the fact, if it was already written, the Ramban wrote that it is invalid for divorce, and so wrote the Rema. Even if she got married with it, she must leave the marriage. The Rambam, however, permits it even initially for divorce if it was written. The Rosh also wrote similarly, and his words are: "It appears to me that it is only invalid initially, but after the fact, if it was already written, it is valid for divorce. Nevertheless, it is good to be stringent and divorce with another get if the husband is present." This is the wording of the Tur.

And behold, those who hold that it is valid after the fact (bediavad) consider this matter similar to the writing of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor as in Siman 123, and the matter of something attached (to the ground) as in Siman 124, where after the fact, we do not decree concerning the form (tofess) due to the essential part (toref) – see there. However, according to our version in the Rambam, Chapter 3, even initially (lechatchila), they permitted scribes to write the form and leave the essential part, and they did so for the benefit of the scribes – see there. And those who invalidate even after the fact hold that this is worse than something attached and the writing of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor, which is not common at all. And in the case of a scribe, if we permit it after the fact, they will do so regularly. And this also seems evident from the Talmudic discussion (26b), where Rav ruled according to Rabbi Eliezer, and those who validate believe that even Rabbi Eliezer invalidates only initially, and the Rambam completely dismisses this due to the discussion in the second chapter, where we do not decree the form due to the essential part. Also, concerning the writing of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor, there are those who invalidate even after the fact, as mentioned in Siman 123 – see there. However, what the Tur wrote, that according to those who invalidate, even if she married, she must be divorced, this is not consistent with what is written later in Siman 150, that in all rabbinic invalidations, if she married, she need not be divorced (see Beit Shmuel, subsection 2). And perhaps in this case, they saw fit to be stringent because it is a common matter, or those who hold this opinion also believe that in all rabbinic invalidations, she must be divorced, as some hold – see there. (And in the Shulchan Aruch, these laws are not mentioned at all, and perhaps they hold that it is like the writing of a deaf-mute and something attached, and there was no need to repeat it again).

It is obvious that even if part of the essential text (toref) is written explicitly not for its intended purpose, it is not a valid get (divorce document). There are those who have doubts about the phrase "You are permitted to any man" when it is written not for its intended purpose, as before this phrase there is a similar language. In the ancient forms of gittin (divorce documents), sometimes this phrase was not written at all (Tosafot 26a, s.v. "Vetzarich"). However, in the Gemara (85a), it is explained that the primary part of the get is the phrase "You are permitted to any man," and one should be stringent (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 1). It has already been explained in Siman 123 that the date is also considered part of the essential text of the get for stringency purposes; refer there.

There are several types of "improper intent" (shelo lishma) that can occur with a get (divorce document): The first is when it was not written for the purpose of divorce at all. The second is when it was written for someone else. The third is when it was written for this person but for his other wife. The fourth is when he told the scribe, "Write it, and for whichever wife I choose, I will divorce with it." In the first three cases, the get is void according to Torah law. In the fourth case, according to Rambam, it is considered a doubtful divorce, as will be explained.

The first scenario is as follows: A scribe who wrote divorce documents for himself in order to learn the craft or practice, and he specified the name of a man, the name of a woman, and the name of a city. If someone came and found this document with the same name as the husband, the same name as his wife, and the same name as his city, and he took it and used it to divorce his wife, it is not considered a valid divorce document according to Torah law. This is because it was not written with the intention of divorce at all. Even if the scribe intended for the specific man and woman, since the husband did not instruct him, it is not considered written for their sake at all (Tosafot 22b, s.v. "Veha"). Rather, it is considered unspecified and invalid according to Torah law, as the woman is not designated for divorce (ibid.). Furthermore, it is explained in Siman 120 that even if the husband instructed Reuven to write a divorce document and Reuven instructed Shimon, it is not a valid divorce, because matters of this nature cannot be transferred to an agent. Certainly, it is invalid if there were no instructions at all.

The second scenario is as follows: Reuven wrote a get (divorce document) to divorce his wife, and he wrote it with his and her names. He then reconsidered and decided not to divorce her. A fellow townsman found the get and said to him, "My name is the same as yours and my wife's name is the same as your wife's name. Give me this get," and he gave it to him, and he divorced with it. Even though it was written for the sake of divorce, it is not a valid get at all according to Torah law, because it was written for someone else and not for him. And one should not ask: since the first person could not have divorced with it either, because we hold that if there are two people named Yosef ben Shimon in the same city, there needs to be a distinguishing mark on the get to differentiate between them. In truth, the Talmud (24b) establishes that since there are witnesses and they know that this person delivered it to this woman and she is his wife, it is sufficient. And although it will be clarified in Siman 136 that they need to divorce in the presence of the second person, nevertheless, what of it? At the time of the divorce, he did so, and the details of this law will be explained there with God's help.

The third scenario is when someone has two wives with the same name, and he writes a bill of divorce (get) for the older one but then changes his mind about divorcing the older and uses it to divorce the younger. This is not a valid get according to Torah law, because even though it was written for the man who is divorcing, it was not written for the woman who is being divorced with it. Additionally, in this case, when he initially decided to divorce the older wife, it must have been clear to everyone that the get was written specifically for her (Gemara). There is an opinion that, ideally, even in such a case, it must be explicitly clear from the get itself whom he is divorcing (Beit Shmuel, note 3). Similarly, in the previous law, the get must clearly differentiate between this Yosef and another Yosef, and this will be explained in detail in section 136, with the help of Heaven.

The fourth scenario is when a man has wives with the same names and he tells the scribe to write a get (divorce document) and specifies that he will decide later which one he will divorce. The scribe writes the get with this in mind, and the man subsequently divorces one of them. Our sages said there is no retroactive clarification (brerah) in matters of Torah law. We would need to say that it was clarified afterward that the get was written for this specific woman, and we hold that there is no retroactive clarification in Torah law. Therefore, according to the principle that there is no retroactive clarification in Torah law, as ruled by the Rambam (Maimonides) in several places, it seems that the get is nullified from a Torah perspective. However, the Rambam ruled that she is considered to be in a state of doubt regarding her divorce status and is disqualified from marrying a kohen (priest). If she accepted kiddushin (betrothal) from another man, she would need a get from both men. The reasoning is that there is concern regarding the prohibition of a married woman, perhaps the principle of no retroactive clarification in Torah law is not so clear-cut. Some of the early authorities ruled that there is retroactive clarification even in Torah law. However, some of our rabbis held that even if we generally rule that there is retroactive clarification in Torah law, in this case, there is no retroactive clarification because it is written, "And he shall write her a document of divorce" (Deuteronomy 24:1), implying that it must be specified at the time of writing. Nonetheless, the Rambam was stringent, as did the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 4. The same applies if he told the scribe to write a get for whichever wife would first exit the house, as this depends on the decision of others. This too is a doubtful divorce since, in a case of doubt, we do not rely on retroactive clarification, even though it depends on the decision of others, which is generally more lenient regarding retroactive clarification than when it depends on his own decision. Nonetheless, it remains doubtful. In the Talmud, some compare this to other cases, while others distinguish it based on the differences we have discussed.

### The Law Regarding Writing a Get Before Marriage and a Lost and Found Get. This Section Contains 27 Paragraphs:

If a man told a scribe to write a get (divorce document) for his fiancée, saying that once he marries her, he will divorce her with it, and then he marries her and divorces her with that get, the get is valid. This is not considered as something that has not yet come into existence because he has the power to divorce her even now. And even though the get states "my wife" and not "my fiancée," we maintain that even for a get given to a fiancée, if it is written "my wife," it is valid, as stated in section 126. The reverse is also true, as mentioned there.

From the Torah, this is certainly a valid get (divorce document). However, by rabbinic decree, there is a deficiency in it because we hold by the ruling in Siman 148 that any get where the wife secluded herself with her husband after the writing of the get should not be used for her divorce. This is a precaution lest she becomes pregnant and there will be rumors that she conceived from him after he divorced her, as those who see the date on the get will say that the get preceded the birth. Similarly, since she married after the writing, it is certain that she secluded herself with him. Nevertheless, in truth, even with this get, she should not be divorced initially, but if she was divorced with it after the fact, it is a valid get (Rashi, Yevamot 52.). This is also our ruling in Siman 148; see there. This is also the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 3. There are those who say that it refers to a case where the date written is after the marriage, which is the time of giving (Tosafot there), and according to this opinion, even if she was divorced, she should not remarry (there). I am perplexed by our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who wrote in Section 1 like the second explanation, while in Siman 148 he ruled like the Rambam. The Rambam does not differentiate between this get and an old get, see Chapter 3, and how could he not mention his opinion at all (and perhaps because of the Baraita in Gittin 26b; see there, and analyze it well).

And behold, according to the first explanation, in any case, the get (divorce document) is predated and invalid, and it must be said that he gives it to her through an agent, and with an agent, predated does not apply as is written in Siman 127 (double-sided). Additionally, it can be said that everything happened on the same day – the get, the marriage, and the divorce – or that it was written in the get not the date of the day but the date of the week or the month, which is also valid as is written there. And there is no question that there would not be a rumor here that her get preceded her son; it can be said that it refers to the get of his betrothed, and there would be a rumor about the child (Tosafot). Also, according to the second explanation, it can be scrutinized that the get is postdated, as it is written for a different time than the day of the writing, and according to the Rambam, it is invalid as is written there. However, since it is not given to her until that day, there is no concern in this (Beit Shmuel section 1 and Tosafot, beginning of “because”).

However, if he commanded to write a get (bill of divorce) for a woman in general, to divorce her with it when he marries her, it is not a valid get because it is a matter that has not yet come into existence. Just as a person cannot transfer ownership of something that has not yet come into existence, similarly, he cannot either betroth or divorce with something that has not yet come into existence, when it is not currently within his power to betroth or divorce her (Yevamot 52b and 93a). This is also the ruling of the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 2. And if he said, "Write a get for my yevamah (sister-in-law, in the context of levirate marriage), and when I perform yibbum (levirate marriage) with her, I will divorce her," and he performed yibbum and divorced her with this get, she is in a state of doubtful divorce. The doubt is whether her status is like a betrothed woman, since she is bound to him, or perhaps, since he has not yet betrothed her, her status is like a regular woman.

The Tur wrote as follows: He instructed to write a get (divorce document) to divorce a woman in general when he marries her; Rambam wrote that it is not a get, and for a yevamah (a widow awaiting levirate marriage), it is a doubtful get. And our master, the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote that even for a regular woman, it is a get according to the opinion that a person can transfer ownership of something that has not yet come into existence. And these words are astonishing because it is a well-established law that a person cannot transfer ownership of something that has not yet come into existence (Beit Yosef). There are those who explained that although we hold this way, nevertheless, it has the scent of a get and disqualifies her from marrying a kohen, since there are those in the Gemara who believe that a person can transfer ownership of something that has not yet come into existence (Bach). And since many authorities hold this view, we must be cautious with a get (Kidushin 150, Chapter 5 of Yevamot). This is not sufficient because if so, why did the Tur not also worry about this in the case of kiddushin (betrothal) in Siman 40 regarding one who betroths a woman with something that has not yet come into existence, such as "after you are freed" or "after your sister dies", etc. Moreover, in all aspects of Torah law, once a halacha is decided, we do not worry about the other opinion, and this halacha is clear throughout the entire Talmud. Indeed, in the Shulchan Aruch, this was completely omitted for this reason, and I have seen other explanations, but they are distant (unconvincing).

It appears to me that the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote that the reason is because she was not subject to divorce at the time of the writing of this get (bill of divorce), and it turns out that it was written not for the purpose of divorce. According to this, it is as if it were not written for her sake and is not a get at all. But the Rosh and the Tur do not hold this reasoning; rather, they believe it is because it was not in existence yet. In Choshen Mishpat, section 209, there are two opinions regarding the acquisition of something not yet in existence, and whether an explicit acquisition for when it will exist is valid. Some say it is acquired, and some say it is not acquired. These two opinions are found in the Mordechai at the beginning of the chapter "Yesh Nochalin." It appears to me that the Rosh and the Tur hold like the first opinion, and the proof is that the acquisition of something not yet in existence and an acquisition for when it will exist are the same. The Tur wrote there in section 210 that one who grants an acquisition to a fetus for when it is born, it is acquired, and the Rosh agrees with this. Therefore, it is clear that in the case of a get where he says to write a get to divorce her when he marries her, it is similar to this, and it is clear that there is a concern to be stringent. This is what is inferred according to the one who says, etc., meaning in such a manner. But in section 40 in Kiddushin regarding something not in his control or her control, like his or her release or the death of her sister, it certainly does not help in any way, like granting to a fetus when it is not pregnant, as mentioned there. Do not be troubled that the Gemara explicitly says in Yevamot (52a) that it is not a get, for it can be said that the author of that statement holds like the one who says that even when it will be born, it is not acquired in the case of a pregnant woman, which is a dispute in the Gemara (Bava Batra 142a). The Rosh and the Tur rule like the other opinion, and therefore they are stringent. Therefore, in practice, it is certainly proper to be stringent.

If two men with identical names and whose wives also have identical names sent two bills of divorce, and they became mixed up, one should give both bills of divorce to each woman in the presence of witnesses. This way, in any case, each woman will receive her bill of divorce. If one of the bills of divorce is lost, the remaining one is invalid and should not be given to either woman. If it was given to one or both of them, it is considered a doubtful divorce. In these cases, even according to the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam, who usually hold that the testimony of the witnesses of the delivery is sufficient, here the attestation must be from the writing, since the two bills of divorce have identical names and nothing distinguishes them from each other. According to those who require proof from the content of the bill of divorce, even with attestation from the delivery, it can be said that there must be some distinguishing mark within the bill itself, and at the time of delivery to the messenger, it was clear. However, when the messenger delivers them before the witnesses of the delivery, they do not know which bill belongs to which woman (as explained by the Beit Shmuel section 3). This will be further elucidated in section 136, with God's help.

The one who brings a get (divorce document) from one place to another and is an agent to deliver the get to the woman, and the get falls from him on the way in a place where caravans are frequent, where there are many passersby on this route, there is concern that perhaps another man also lost a similar get with the same names, since in the world there are people with identical names for the man and the woman. Even if the name of the city is written in the get, there is concern that perhaps there is another city in the world with the same name as their city, and there is a couple there with the same names as this couple. Clearly, our Sages stated (Gittin 27a) that we are concerned about two people with the same names. All the more so if it is known in the city where the get was written that there is another couple with the same names as this couple, then even if caravans are not frequent, there is concern that perhaps the other man also wrote a get for his wife, and it fell from him or from her or from his agent (Rosh, there). One should not ask what the "all the more so" is, as in the case of frequent caravans and not known, there is concern for the falling of a get from many people from the entire world, and in the case of known and not frequent caravans, there is only concern for the falling of a get from an individual with the same name as mentioned. There is more concern for the falling of a get from many people than from an individual, as the truth is that in the Talmud (Baba Batra 172a) we conclude that there is no difference between the falling of a get from many people and from an individual (Bach). Furthermore, there is more concern for the falling of a get from an individual that is known than from many people, and to be concerned for a city with the same name as this city, and for identical names in this city for the couple in this city.

And specifically, this applies in a situation where in the place where the get (divorce document) was written, another couple with the same names was established (Tur). But if in that place there was no establishment, even though in the place where the get was found, a couple with the same names was established, there is no concern because the name of the city is written in the get, and we know that this city has a different name. Consequently, it is understood that if the name of the city is not written in the get, then even if a couple with the same names was established in the place where the get was found, it is considered established. (And what Rashi explained there in the sugya, his intention was regarding the city where the get was written, as explained explicitly in Bava Metzia 18. See there, and not like Bach. Nevertheless, the law is correct as stated by Maimonides.)

Therefore, in these two scenarios, whether caravans are common and there is no established presumption or there is an established presumption and caravans are not common, and certainly in both together, if the get (bill of divorce) is found immediately after it was lost, such as if it was seen a little while before, the get is valid, as there is no concern in this case. "Immediately" means that no one passed by from the time of the fall until the time of the finding. If it is found not immediately, and it has a clear identifying mark, such as a hole next to a specific letter, or he recognizes it by sight as his get, or even if it does not have a mark or recognizable sight on the get itself, but it has a clear mark or recognizable sight on the container in which the get was found, and he finds it still in that container and knows he did not lend it to another person from the day he placed the get in that container, or he finds it tied to his pocket, wallet, or his ring, and he recognizes these by sight even if he does not remember if he lent them to another, we are not concerned, as people do not typically lend their pockets, wallets, and rings (Bava Metzia 27b), because we worry about divination and with a ring we worry about forgery (ibid.). Or if he finds it in his house among his household utensils, even if it is in a house where many people frequent, and if he found it on the ground there would be a concern, nevertheless among his household utensils there is no concern (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 9). In all these cases, even if there is an established presumption and caravans are common, and he finds it after a long time, the get is valid and can be handed over to the woman.

But if it is not found immediately, such as when one does not know whether someone passed by there or not, and there is no distinguishing mark or seal on the get (bill of divorce) or on the vessel, it is invalid. We are concerned that this get might not belong to him but to someone else with the same name, and it was dropped. Even if witnesses testify that the other person known by this name was not in town when the get was written, it is still invalid, even when caravans are not common, because the names were established to be the same. 

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that even if the passerby on this road was only a non-Jew, it is still invalid. Although a non-Jew is not fit to be an agent for delivering a get, we are nevertheless concerned that the husband or wife or the agent entrusted it to him based on a distinctive sign, or that the husband sent it through his hand to be delivered to a Jew and instructed that Jew to receive the get from him, which is permitted in such a case as stated in Siman 141 (Bayit Chadash).

The Tur wrote, "And similarly, if he saw that a person passed there, even if caravans are not common and there is no established certainty of two people named Yosef in the same town, etc." His words are puzzling, for even without an established certainty and without frequent caravans, it is valid even for a long period, as is evident from the Talmudic approach and the decisors, as explained there. Also, regarding our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who copied this language in section 4, it is puzzling. The Bach and Beit Shmuel (subsection 10) have already expressed astonishment about this. Some have explained that it means "or" as a disjunctive, meaning either it is not established, etc. However, this is not implied by the language. Moreover, if so, this has already been clarified in his previous words. (And regarding what the Bach wrote, "What novelty is there in this?" – this indeed is not a novelty, see there).

Therefore, it seems to me that the Tur is expressing his own reasoning because the Jerusalem Talmud is very stringent on this matter. Even if two people with the same names have not been established, and even if they checked thoroughly in all possible ways, due to another concern, the Jerusalem Talmud states (Chapter 3, Halacha 3) that we are concerned that perhaps this man had two bills of divorce, one valid and one invalid, and he lost the valid one and discarded the invalid one. And at the time he found it, we say that he found the invalid one. And it explains there that due to the stringent nature of marital laws, they were very strict. Therefore, even though our Talmud does not consider this stringency, nevertheless, since it is also explained in our Talmud that "immediately" means that no one has passed by there, and the Tur explains that it is specifically when it is known that no one has passed by there that we validate in all cases. But if it is not known, it is invalid if it has been established that people pass by or if caravans are common. And this is when it is not known. But if it is known that someone has passed by, we are stringent even if caravans are not common and it has not been established. (And what the Rosh wrote, "but if someone passed by," means that it is possible that someone passed by, and in this way, we can somewhat reconcile the words of the Beit Yosef, who was puzzled by the Bach. Contemplate this well.)

And know that it is taught in the Tosefta (Chapter 2) that if a get (divorce document) was lost and found after some time, even if one recognizes its identifying marks, it is invalid because identifying marks are not sufficient for gittin (divorce documents). This is the end of the quote. Do not be troubled by what is stated that if there is a distinctive identifying mark it is valid, as the Tosefta is referring to a non-distinctive identifying mark, as is proven in the Jerusalem Talmud there which brings a baraita that there are no identifying marks for gittin and explains this as referring to when one says how many lines were in this get, but if one says that a particular letter was dotted, it is considered an identifying mark. It appears that this baraita is the same as the Tosefta that we brought.

Even if the matter has been established and caravans are common, and he does not have a distinctive sign, if the witnesses of the signing of the get (divorce document) say, "We have never signed another get with the same name as this man and the same name as this woman," even if they do not testify about the signatures on this specific get that it is their handwriting, such as when the get is not before us and therefore it could be someone else's, nevertheless, we return it to him. The reason is that we do not suspect him of lying deliberately to cause a married woman to stumble. The fact that we do not return it to him without the detailed conditions explained, even if he stands and cries out that it is his, is not because we suspect him of deliberate lying, but rather we say that because he knows that he lost such a get, it is clear to him that this get is his, and he does not believe that another person also lost such a get. Indeed, these are significant stringencies that they were stringent specifically with regard to a get and not in other matters, as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. Therefore, he says so. However, in this case where the witnesses say that they have never signed except on one get, we would need to assume that he is lying deliberately, and this we do not suspect. Nor do we need to worry that it might belong to someone else and that there are other witnesses with the same names as these witnesses, for such a distant concern we do not need to worry about (Talmud). Therefore, this is specifically in a situation where it has not been established that there are other witnesses with these names. But if it is known that there are other witnesses with the same names as these, it is not valid until they testify about the handwriting on this get that it is theirs, or the witnesses say, "We recognize this get by a distinctive sign it has, such as a hole next to a specific letter or by its seal."

And know that the witnesses are believed based on a clear sign or distinctive writing, even after they have seen the get (divorce document) with this sign, and they say that this was the get they signed on, they are believed. However, what we have said that he is also believed based on a clear sign or distinctive writing is only when he himself found it, as he has the "migu" (presumption of honesty) to say that he did not lose it. But if someone else found it and he provides the sign, he is not believed unless he states the sign before he saw it, not after he saw it. This is not because we suspect him of lying intentionally but because, as we said, since he does not care about the matter and knows that the get was lost, he might state the sign inaccurately. One should not ask, "If so, what benefit is there in the 'migu'?" since 'migu' only helps when there is a suspicion of lying, not when we say he might be mistaken. In truth, we find that even in such cases 'migu' is effective because he claims with certainty (Tosafot Shevuot 45b s.v. "mitoch" and Yevamot 97b). According to this, distinctive writing is not believed at all when someone else found it, because distinctive writing cannot be verified before seeing the get. Even though it is found in the Gemara that a Torah scholar is believed with distinctive writing, this applies to monetary matters. But regarding a get, it is doubtful in the Talmud whether he is believed because of this (in the discussion of Rabba bar Bar Chana). Moreover, in our times, it is difficult to judge a Torah scholar regarding the prohibition of a married woman.

However, this specifically applies when the husband himself lost the get (bill of divorce) before giving it to his wife or his agent sent to deliver it lost it and receives payment for the agency, then they are not believed based on a distinguishing mark or explicit sign after they have seen the get if someone else found it. But if another person who has no financial interest says that he has a distinguishing mark or an explicit sign, he is believed even afterward like witnesses (Beit Shmuel, section 13). And although neither the husband nor the agent is suspected of lying intentionally, as stated, nevertheless, because the agent is concerned about the payment for his agency and the husband is concerned about the payment for the scribe, not wanting to have to pay again, they might say something that seems plausible with little examination when they have no compelling reason otherwise, as stated.

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: "If there are not two known Yosef ben Shimons, and caravans are not common, one can return it without a sign even if it stayed there long enough for a person to pass by." This is also the language of the Tur. However, this is not specific, as even after a long time it is valid, as is evident from the Talmud. It is possible that according to their opinion, which we explained in paragraph 13, that if it is known that a person passed by there, we are stringent in every case. Therefore, for a long time, which is like it is known that a person passed by there, one should be stringent. However, it requires further investigation, as the Talmud does not imply this.

Everything mentioned is according to the opinions of the Rosh and the Tur, and similarly, this is the opinion of the Rif. However, the Rambam, of blessed memory, in Chapter 3, Law 9, has a different approach regarding the matter of being established and the prevalence of caravans. His words there are as follows: If one brings a get (divorce document) and it is lost, and it is found, if it was lost in a place where caravans are not common, even if it is found after a long time, it is presumed that the get that was lost is the same get that was found, and she can be divorced with it. If it was lost in a place where caravans are common, if it is found immediately and no one has yet passed by or if it is found in a vessel in which it was placed and it has a distinctive mark in its length and width of the get it was wrapped in, it retains its presumption and she can be divorced with it. If another person in that place has the same name as in the get, there is a concern that this get found might belong to the other person, since someone passed by even if they did not stay. If she is divorced with it, she is doubtfully divorced. But if no one passed by, it retains its presumption even if there are two people with the same name established there. This is the end of the quotation.

He distinguishes between places where it is established that caravans are frequent and places where they are not. He is more stringent in places where it is known that caravans pass, even if only one person has passed through there, while in places where caravans are frequent, it is required that a person remains there for a certain amount of time. He is also stringent in cases where something is found in a vessel, requiring not just the identifying marks of the vessel but also the identifying marks of the document (get). The early authorities have already disputed his view, as the Talmudic discussion indicates that both places where it is known that caravans pass and places where caravans are frequent are treated equally. They also question why the identifying marks of the vessel alone are not sufficient. Some explain his words to mean that when he says "it is established," he is referring to places where caravans are frequent. He holds that in both cases, we are stringent if a person has passed through there, but if it is only established without a person passing, there is no concern, even for a long time. In places where caravans are frequent, he is more stringent than places where it is merely established, but the stringency of a person passing through is only if the person stayed there (this is how the commentator explains, and it is not the same as what the Meiri wrote in Chapter Four as quoted by the Rivash in section 117). Following this explanation, our master, the Beit Yosef, adopted this opinion in the Shulchan Aruch in the name of "some say," see there (similarly, it can be inferred from the words of the Ran, see there).

And it is impossible to say this at all, for according to their words, it is stricter when caravans are frequent than when it is established. We have already brought in the name of the Rosh that on the contrary, it is more stringent when it is established than when caravans are frequent. Furthermore, such an opinion is not found at all in the Talmud. It is true that some of the early authorities ruled like the opinion in the Gemara that we need both, and this is the opinion of the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot and Rav Hai Gaon, as the poskim wrote. However, they hold that even when caravans are frequent alone, it is valid even for a long time, just like when it is established alone. Moreover, generally, the Rambam follows the approach of the Rif, as is known. Therefore, it is certain that his intention is as was said, that he rules stringently in one of them. The Ra'avad, the Rashba, and the Tur also understood his words this way, as is evident from their writings (and so wrote the Lechem Mishneh in Chapter 8). However, they wondered about his stringency in established cases more than in frequent caravans and also why he did not suffice with the principle of "the nature of the vessel" as was mentioned.

And it appears to me that the reasoning is as follows: The Rif brought in the name of a Gaon who ruled that as long as a person did not stay there, and the Rif wrote, "It seems to us that we act stringently, that no person passed there. But if a person did pass and it was established that there were two dry lands, we are concerned, etc." And the Rambam holds that specifically in the case of "it was established" he disagrees with the Gaon, but not in the case of frequent caravans, as "it was established" is more stringent, as mentioned in the name of the Rosh. Moreover, the reasoning is that in the case of "it was established," since it is known that there is another person with the same name, it is a great concern. But in the stringency of frequent caravans, what applies to calling it frequent caravans when one man passed? At the very least, when a person stayed there, during this time it could be that several people passed during this stay, and this provides grounds for this stringency (and see Beit Yosef who wrote similarly). And that which is written that we require that he also has distinguishing marks on the get (divorce document) is simple, for as it is mentioned in the Mishnah, "If he found it in a pouch or in a wallet, if he recognizes it, it is valid," it is explained straightforwardly that we require also recognition of the physical get itself. This is more stringent than other matters, as we brought from the Jerusalem Talmud, and they only made stringent regarding the distinguishing marks of the get in its length and width, as this is not a definitive sign. The reason for this can be explained, as it is unlikely that he would not recognize it, for it is assumed they are meticulous in placing the get in the container in a specific order. Why would he not recognize it by the way it is placed?

The words of our master, the Rema, are very perplexing in this matter. He wrote that there are those who say that if the name of the city is mentioned in the get (divorce document), there is no need to be concerned about the presence of caravans, as there is no concern about two cities having the same name. This is based on the responsa of the Rosh, section 45. And many have already expressed their astonishment at him, for on the contrary, from the responsa of the Rosh there, it is explicitly stated the opposite. He wrote: "And this is when caravans are not common, and there is no established presumption. Therefore, the name of the city helps unless there is another city that has the same name and caravans are not common. Then, even in a place where another Joseph son of Simeon has been established, we are not concerned. But if caravans are common, we are concerned that there might be another city with the same name." These words are the opposite of his statement. And what is even more perplexing is that in his book Darkei Moshe, he wrote that this is implied in the Gemara, in the chapter 'Kol HaGet,' but in the Gemara there, it is explicitly stated the opposite, that we are concerned about two caravans (Beit Shmuel, section 64, and Gra, section 15).

And I have seen someone who explained that the case of caravans being common concerning the suspicion of "two Yosefs in one city" is not similar to the case of caravans being common concerning the suspicion of "two cities with the same name." For the concern of identical names, even if only caravans from the surrounding cities are common, we certainly worry about identical names. However, to be concerned about another city with the same name as the city on the get (divorce document), the caravans must be common from a much greater distance, because in the nearby cities, their names are certainly well known (Bava Metzia). And in the Gemara, when they were concerned about two caravans, there were people coming from afar (there). And although regarding the law, it is a reasonable matter, nevertheless, this is not sufficient. For in such a case, it should have been explained and not left ambiguous. Furthermore, this is not explained in the Rosh at all.

And in my humble opinion, it seems clear that he had a different version in the responsa of the Rosh, as the version in the Rosh's responsa before us is not like the version brought by the Beit Shmuel. If we say this, his words are correct, for indeed, when we scrutinize the words of the Rif, Rambam, Tur, and many other poskim, we do not find any of them mentioning the concern of two identical towns; they only mention two Joseph ben Simon, except for the Rashba in his novellae there. And this is what he said, that this is also implied in the Gemara, and indeed it is so, for what they said there — "we are concerned about two caravans" — is not a halachic ruling but a question (Tosafot Bava Batra 172b). On the contrary, this statement was made by Rav Huna, who asked Rabbah, and he explained that we are not concerned unless caravans are frequent and it has been established. And he mentioned there in the case of "established" only two Joseph ben Simon and not two caravans. Furthermore, according to Rabbah, it is certain that just as we are not concerned about two Joseph ben Simons in frequent caravans unless it has been established, similarly, we are not concerned about two caravans in frequent caravans unless two caravans have been established. Therefore, even the Amoraim who argue against him and believe that we should be concerned in one of them, where do we get the idea to make such a distant distinction to also worry about a town with the same name, and that there would also be a pair with identical names as this pair? And this is what he said, that this is also implied in the Gemara, meaning that we do not find in the entire sugya a concern for two identical towns, only for two Joseph ben Simons. And what is at the beginning of the sugya is merely a question, as mentioned, and it is explained that we are not concerned. This seems clear in his intention (and the Pitchei Teshuva also brought that the Chatam Sofer debated this matter, and I do not currently have the Chatam Sofer's book with me).

The Tur wrote, "When do we adopt a stringent approach in one aspect of concern? When two people with the same name have been established, or when caravans are frequent regarding a bill of divorce, because it is possible to write another. But concerning death, where witnesses testify that Yosef, the husband of so-and-so, has died, his wife is permitted to remarry unless caravans are frequent and two people with the same name have been established in that city." And this is explained at length in Siman 17. Some of the Rishonim wrote another distinction: In the case of death, since we know that the husband of this woman was on this route, we say "here he was found, here he was," and we do not worry about someone else unless it has been established otherwise. Similarly, for a bill of divorce, we are not stringent except in the case of a messenger who brought a bill of divorce from a distance, where we cannot say "here he was found, here he was," because the bill of divorce was not established in this place. However, if the bill of divorce was indeed lost in the place it was written, even if it is found after some time and in a place where caravans are frequent, we do not worry about someone else unless it has been established that another person has his name and her name, and we say "here he was found, here he was" (Nimukei Yosef, Chapter 15 of Yevamot in the matter of Yitzchak and Rabban Gamliel). Similarly, the Ramban wrote in the Milchamot there, see there.

And know that everything stated in this section applies only when the husband acknowledges that he wrote the get (bill of divorce), and similarly when she provides a clear identifying mark on the get and claims that it fell from her. In such cases, even if he does not acknowledge, these laws will be clarified in section 153. However, in this section, which deals with a case where the get fell from the hand of the messenger and the concern is that it might be a different get, it necessarily refers to a situation where the husband acknowledges. If he does not acknowledge that he wrote the get, the get is not returned to the messenger under any circumstances. If the husband says, "I wrote the get and gave it to this person for safekeeping," and this person says, "You gave it to me for the purpose of divorce, and I am the agent to receive it on behalf of your wife," there are many detailed laws about this which will be explained, with God's help, in section 141, and it is not relevant to this section at all.

The Law that a Get Requires Witnesses of Delivery. It Contains Nine Sections:
It has already been explained that we hold according to Rabbi Eliezer who says that the essential part of the get (divorce document) is the delivery, and the fact that witnesses sign the get was instituted by Rabban Gamliel only for the betterment of the world to provide it with validation. Therefore, if after the fact there were no witnesses at all, only witnesses to the delivery, the get is valid. Nevertheless, at the outset it is forbidden to do so without witnesses to the signing. Even for us, who tear up the get and it is not in the woman's possession, and the reason for validation no longer applies, since it has become customary in all gets to have witnesses sign, if we change this get to be without witnesses, there is no greater defamation than this, as stated at the beginning of Siman 130 in the name of the She'iltot. Additionally, I found that the author of the Terumat HaDeshen in Siman 232 adds another reason, that since there are several anonymous Mishnayot and Baraitot that follow Rabbi Meir who says that the essential part of the get is the signing, and a get without signing witnesses is like a mere shard, we remove ourselves from all disputes so that it will be fully permissible and not cast any defamation at all on the marriages of the daughters of Israel. End of quote. After the fact, it is valid without signing witnesses.

There are those who write that all this applies when the husband did not instruct the witnesses to sign. But if he instructed them to sign and they did not sign, and he gave the get (divorce document) only in the presence of witnesses, the get is invalid according to Torah law (as brought in Meshiv Nafesh and cited in Pitchei Teshuvah). He brings proof from the Talmud (Gittin 19b) regarding writing ink over red dye, that even according to the opinion that considers the upper writing as writing for Shabbat, one should not rule thus for gittin. If the signatures were only rabbinic, why not rule thus? Rather, certainly when the husband instructed to sign, the get is invalid according to Torah law without the signatures. Additionally, there is proof from the Jerusalem Talmud (Gittin 2:2) regarding a get written during the day and signed at night. Rabbi Shimon validates it, and Reish Lakish explains that he holds like Rabbi Eliezer, who does not require witness signatures at all. Once the get is written, it is completed. It states there that when he wants to have witnesses sign, the get is not complete until after the signatures. Hence, when he wants witnesses to sign, it is not a get without their signatures. In my humble opinion, Heaven forbid to say this. Certainly, if he sends through an agent and instructed the scribe to write and the witnesses to sign, and they did not sign, and the agent gave her the get without witness signatures, he deviated from his agency, and the get is invalid. But if he gives it to her himself, even if he initially instructed the witnesses to sign, he later consented to give it without witness signatures. The Jerusalem Talmud only says that when he wants witnesses to sign, the get is not complete until after the signatures, and if signed at night, it is considered predated. This is certainly the case. From our Talmud, it is clear there is no proof since it can be said it refers to when given by an agent. Furthermore, according to the Rif, it is valid with only the witnesses to delivery. Additionally, even if it is rabbinic, one should not act on it, as if it is not written, it is considered forged from within.

And furthermore, it is written that now, when the husband commands to write a get (divorce document), his intention is that it should be written properly according to all customs, even those that have no basis in law at all. And if they did not do so, the get is invalid. He expressed surprise at several great authorities who were lenient in times of necessity regarding several matters (see there). And I say that the great authorities ruled correctly. Certainly, if some specific detail was explicitly mentioned and they did not do so, there is indeed a concern. But in a general sense, the instruction is to write the get according to the opinion of the rabbi who arranges it and according to the law. Why should we say that the get is invalid, God forbid, due to something that has no basis in law at all? (see Rashi Bava Metzia 96b s.v. nim'alu).

And even regarding something that was spoken about before the writing of the get (divorce document) to do such and such, if afterward he agreed without that matter, it appears to me that it is within his power to do so. The proof is from the laws of conditions that will be explained in Siman 143, where it is stated that he has the ability to nullify the condition even after the giving of the get. And even though the condition is stipulated after the writing of the get, before the writing it is forbidden as stated in Siman 147, nevertheless, according to many poskim (halachic authorities), even before the writing it is valid as stated there (see Beit Yosef). We do not find a distinction in this matter that a condition made before the writing cannot be nullified. The proof is from the Mishnah at the beginning of Chapter 9 which states that if a condition was written into the get and afterward he erased it, it is invalid because it was not written for the sake of a complete severance (Tosafot, 4b). According to the opinion in the Gemara there that it is invalid only if written but valid if stated orally even before the essential part, it is clearly implied that if he retracted and nullified the condition, similar to erasing it, it is valid. And logically this is so, for as long as the get has not reached her hand, it is not considered an act at all, just mere speech (Tosafot, beginning of Chapter 4, s.v. "Rabbi Shimon"), and he can nullify the speech, as one speech nullifies another. All the more so in a matter that has not been done at all, like if he told the scribe to write and the witnesses to sign, and after the writing he does not want them to sign. Their signing depends solely on his speech, so why can't he nullify his speech? This is also explicitly stated by a certain posek who wrote that if the husband told three to write and sign, and one of them died, in a pressing situation and a place of potential chaining (agunah), they should not sign at all on the get and it should be conditional only (Beit Shmuel, Siman 130, Se'if Katan 29).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that the get (divorce document) must be handed over to the woman in the presence of both witnesses together. This excludes the case where it was handed over in the presence of one witness and then handed over again in the presence of another witness (Beit Yosef). Some have written that this is only required initially, but after the fact (bedi'eved), their testimonies can be combined, just as in monetary law where it is established in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 30, that their testimonies can be combined. Only in cases of capital law (dinei nefashot) is separate testimony invalid, while in other prohibitions, it is the same as in monetary law (Beit Shmuel and Gra). In any event, the get is not invalid (Beit Shmuel). Some are uncertain whether the get is invalid or invalidated (Bayit Chadash).

In truth, the matter is not the same for all prohibitions and monetary law, where we only need to know the action, and separate testimony can be combined, except in capital law where it is a scriptural decree. However, for witnesses of gittin (divorce) and kiddushin (marriage), where witnesses are required for the matter itself, separate testimony is not considered testimony at all. It is clearly stated in Siman 42 that kiddushin is not valid if one witness saw the betrothal in the morning and another witness saw it in the evening, unless someone is stringent about betrothal with one witness. Therefore, what is the difference between this and gittin? The reason a get is valid in such a case, as implied in the Gemara (Gittin 33b), is that at the time of signing, the get is not completed until it reaches her hands when both witnesses are signed on it. But in monetary matters, where the get is completed at the time of delivery, without two witnesses, it is nothing, just like in kiddushin (Turei Zahav). Certainly, if there are witnesses on the get and it is handed over in the presence of one witness and then in the presence of another, the get is not invalid, as according to the Rif and Rambam, witnesses alone are sufficient, as will be explained. However, without witnesses, it seems that this is not a get at all in such a case. Nonetheless, practically, one should be stringent, as perhaps just as there are those who are concerned about betrothal with one witness, so too should we be concerned about divorce with one witness (Taz and Beit Shmuel). At the time of delivery, the man and woman must see the witnesses, just like in kiddushin (ibid.).

The opinion of the Rif, of blessed memory (Chapter 9), is that regarding the view of Rabbi Eliezer that "on condition (with witnesses) I have severed," it means even "on condition I have severed," and he agrees with Rabbi Meir that even "with signatures alone I have severed." And when witnesses signed on it and he delivered the get (divorce document) to her in private, it is a valid get according to Torah law. He derives this from the enactment of Rabban Gamliel, for if you would think that without "on condition" it is nothing, what benefit is there in "with signatures alone"? For if she brings the get before us, we would still be concerned that it was delivered to her without "on condition." Rather, it must certainly be that "with signatures alone" suffices. This is also the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 1, the Raavad, the Ramban, and Rabbeinu Yerucham. It also seems that the Rashba somewhat agreed with this. 

And if the question arises, how is it possible for her to be divorced without witnesses? Explain that we consider the signed witnesses as if they were standing before us. There are some of the early authorities who explained the matter this way: it is certainly the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer that only "on condition" severs, not "with signatures alone." Nonetheless, he agrees that "with signatures alone" is effective without "on condition" because the delivery severs, as long as there are witnesses at the time, whether they testify about the delivery itself or about the essence of the matter. Hence, what Rabbi Eliezer agrees that "with signatures alone" is effective even though it was not given "on condition" is not because "with signatures alone" severs, but because the delivery severs since there are witnesses about the essence of the matter. These witnesses of "with signatures alone" are considered "on condition" since the get emerges from his hand through these witnesses, and it is known that the husband delivered it to her. Thus, it is as if they themselves are testifying about the delivery (Ran there).

However, it is the opinion of Rashi, Tosafot, the Rosh, the Ma'or, Rabbeinu Ephraim (a student of the Rif), the SeMaG, the Sefer HaTerumah, and the Mordechai that without "on condition" it is nothing, and only "on condition" constitutes the act of severance and not "on testimony." And this is what Rabban Gamliel established: since the get (bill of divorce) is issued from the hands of witnesses, and the witnesses are established, it is certainly delivered to her properly "on condition." Moreover, they added that even according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that "on testimony" constitutes the act of severance, nevertheless, it must be delivered to her in the presence of two witnesses, as there is no matter of intimacy less than two witnesses (Tosafot 4a, s.v. "For we hold" in the name of Rabbeinu Tam and Rosh, Chapter 9, Section 7). And since this is a dispute among the authorities, the law requires us to be stringent according to all opinions, and initially, all opinions agree that we need both "on condition" and "on testimony," and so is the custom in all the communities of Israel. It has already been explained in Siman 130 that initially, we take one set of witnesses to be both the signing witnesses and the delivery witnesses, and not two sets, due to the concern of "a matter and not half a matter." And post facto, there is no concern about this, as it is not considered "half a matter," as explained there.

And be aware that our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, initially ruled in Section 1 according to the opinion of the Rif, that it is sufficient for a creditor alone to be valid after the fact. He then wrote: "And there are those who say that if it is known that it was given without the stipulation, even though it is signed by witnesses, it is invalid." This is the opinion of the Geonim, which the Rambam brought in Chapter 1, who held that it is invalid but not null. He did not mention at all the opinion of all those authorities who hold that without the stipulation, it is not a get (divorce) at all (see Beit Shmuel, Section 3). It is possible that since practically there is no practical difference, as it is impossible to completely nullify the get because of the opinion of the Rif, rather it should be invalidated because of the other opinions, and there is no practical difference in this law. One should not err in thinking that if it is only Rabbinically invalid, we rule that if she married, she does not have to leave according to Section 150, for certainly in this invalidation it is not applicable to say so. Nevertheless, it should have been clarified further, and there is a practical difference regarding if he betrothed her sister, her mother, or her daughter; according to the Rif and the Gaon, the betrothal is complete, and according to Rashi and Tosafot, there is no betrothal at all, and if another person betrothed this ervah (forbidden relation), she requires a get from him, and this requires further investigation.

It is necessary that the signatures also be dry at the time of the giving [of the get] so that there will not be any writing that can be forged. However, there is no hindrance after the fact regarding the signatures, only concerning the get itself (Taz), as stated in Siman 124. It is customary to gather ten people at the time of the giving of the get in order to publicize the matter that she is divorced, and the judges, the scribe, and the witnesses are included in the count, as well as relatives, and there is no hindrance at all in this matter, as is evident.

### Laws of Annulment of Declarations Regarding a Get. Containing 33 Sections:

It is a well-known and agreed principle that any action a person takes, if it was not done willingly but under duress, is considered null and void. Even for a transgression committed under duress, one is not punished for it, as it is written, "But to the girl you shall do nothing" (Deuteronomy 22:26). All the more so with the giving of a get (divorce document), which must be done willingly by the one granting the divorce. If he was forced to give the get, the get is null and void by Torah law, even if he did not issue a formal protest (moda'ah) beforehand. The get is void because he was compelled to give it. The same law applies to a gift, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 205. We have explained this in Siman 205, Section 10. 

One should not ask, "But there are cases where individuals are compelled to give a get, as taught in the Mishnah (Tosefta, Avodah Zarah), and these are the ones who are forced to divorce?" Indeed, in truth, it is taught (Arakhin 21a) that in cases where the law mandates coercion to give a get, we compel him until he says, "I want to." Once he says, "I want to," he is considered to be acting willingly.

And there is a question regarding this: How can it be considered his will when he says "I want to," when in fact he is being coerced to say so, and therefore it should be considered duress? The answer to this is written by the Rambam in the second chapter, and this is his language: We do not say someone is under duress unless it is a situation where he is pressured and compelled to do something that he is not obligated to do by Torah law, such as one who was beaten until he sold or gave something. But someone whose evil inclination overpowered him to neglect a mitzvah or to commit a transgression, and he was beaten until he did something he was obligated to do or refrained from doing something forbidden, this is not considered duress. Rather, he coerced himself with his own evil intention. Therefore, this person who does not want to give a divorce, since he wants to be part of Israel and wants to observe all the mitzvot and avoid all transgressions, and his evil inclination overpowered him, once he is beaten until his inclination is weakened and he says "I want to," he has already given the divorce willingly. And this is what the Sages said (Baba Batra 48): because it is a mitzvah to listen to the words of the Sages, meaning that when he says "I want to," he has resolved in his heart to give the divorce because he is performing a mitzvah, since the Sages obligated him to do so (Rashbam).

Therefore, if he was coerced unlawfully, meaning he is not obligated according to the law to give a get (divorce document), and the court forced him to give a get, even if he said "I am willing" and did not issue a protest (moda'ah), or he issued a protest and then nullified it, the get is invalid according to Torah law. However, it still has the semblance of a get and disqualifies her from marrying a kohen (priest) because we decree (a prohibition) due to the case where it is lawful (Bach, commentary 13). Similarly, even someone who, according to the law, should be forced to divorce, it is forbidden to do so through non-Jews, but must be done through a Jewish court. If non-Jews coerced him to divorce, even though he is obligated to do so according to the law, the get is invalid. Nevertheless, it disqualifies her from marrying a kohen.

Our sages explained (Gittin 88b) the reason is because it might be confused with a lawful get given by a Jewish court, so they decreed that it disqualifies her from marrying a kohen. But according to Torah law, it is not considered a get at all, as it is written "before them" and not "before non-Jews" (Gittin 88b). Therefore, if non-Jews unlawfully coerced him, meaning he was not obligated by law to divorce, it does not even have the semblance of a get, and she is not disqualified from marrying a kohen.
