We do not decree in the case of unlawful coercion by Jews because that itself is a decree due to lawful coercion, as explained (Rashi Gittin 88b). We should not decree a decree upon a decree. Certainly, the case of lawful coercion by non-Jews or unlawful coercion by Jews is not confused with lawful coercion by Jews, as they are equal in this matter, unlike the case of unlawful coercion by non-Jews which is not confused with lawful coercion by Jews (Gittin 88b), since there is no similarity at all. (Regarding the disqualification from marrying a kohen, if she marries another man, see Bach and Torah Gedolah).

And how does one proceed when the law dictates that he is obligated to divorce, but we do not have the strength to compel him? If it is necessary to compel him through secular courts, the Beit Din (Jewish court) should request that the secular courts compel him in such a way that they say to him, "We are compelling you until you do what the Beit Din of Israel tells you to do." Then, it is considered as if he were compelled by Israelites. This is what the sages taught in the Mishnah there: a coerced get (divorce document) by Israelites is valid, but by gentiles, it is invalid. However, if gentiles beat him and say to him, "Do what the Israelites tell you," refer to there. (And all these matters should not be done without the permission of the government).

And this is the language of the Tur: The Rama wrote specifically in this language, but if non-Jews coerce him and say to him "Give a get," even though a Jew tells them to coerce him, it is invalid. However, the Rosh, of blessed memory, did not agree, for since a Jew tells them to coerce him, even if the non-Jews say to give a get, it is valid. The explanation of his words is that if a Jewish court requests them to coerce him and they coerce him to give a get without mentioning to him that he should do what the Jews command him, the Rama holds that this is as if they themselves coerced him. The Rosh holds that since it was at the request of the Jews, it is as if the Jews themselves coerced him. It is possible to say that they do not disagree, for certainly if the Jew is present at the time of the coercion and he hears that the Jew requests them to coerce him, and they coerce him, it is exactly like coercion by Jews and falls under the reasoning of the Rambam that we mentioned in section 2. However, if the request was not in his presence and the coercion was not in front of a Jewish court, and the non-Jews did not mention the name of the Jew at all but just said "Give a get," even if he knows that this is at the request of the Jews, it is as if they themselves coerced him. Alternatively, it is possible to say that this is their disagreement: what we wrote in section 3 that coercion by non-Jews according to Torah law is not a valid get, the words of the Rambam do not imply this, but that it is only invalid rabbinically. And although from the sugya in Gittin it is understood that according to Torah law it is not a get, from the sugya in Bava Batra it is understood that it is only invalid rabbinically (Beit Yosef). The Rambam took into consideration that sugya, and according to this, it can be said that if according to Torah law it is invalid, certainly it is necessary to mention "do what the Jews tell you." If the invalidity is only rabbinically, it is sufficient if it is known that the coercion came through the Jews. However, it does not seem that the Rosh holds that its invalidity is only rabbinically (see Jerusalem Talmud on this Mishnah, and it is difficult in its explanation. It seems to me that their disagreement depends on this, and one should delve into it).

Rabbeinu the Rema writes in section 8: "Even if he received money for giving the get (divorce document), we do not say that because of this he consented." His words mean that it has been explained in Choshen Mishpat there that there is a difference between a sale and a gift. In a sale, even if we know he was coerced, nevertheless, if he did not make a pre-emptive declaration (moda'ah), the sale is valid. But in the case of a gift, even without a pre-emptive declaration, the gift is void. The reason is that in a sale, since he takes money, he finalizes the transaction despite the coercion, which is not the case with a gift. It is explained there that a get (divorce document) is treated like a gift. Therefore, I might say that also in the case of a get, when he receives money for the get, he finalizes the divorce. It comes to teach us that in the case of a get, we do not say this, for it is not a monetary matter that he would consent to for money. Therefore, if we only know about his coercion, or even if we do not know about his coercion but it is known to us that she is coerced, even if he did not make a pre-emptive declaration and received money, it is nevertheless not a valid get until he says after the coercion has been removed that he is giving the get willingly. This will be further explained, with God's help, in section 33.

All these matters apply when he did not issue a declaration of protest (moda'ah). But if he did issue a declaration of protest, even if Jews coerced him lawfully and he said "I am willing," it is ineffective until he nullifies the declaration of protest. This is explicitly implied in the Gemara (end of Chapter 5 of Arakhin) that saying "I am willing" is ineffective when there is a declaration of protest. The reason is simple: just as if he is forced to give a get (divorce document) unlawfully and says "I am willing," it is meaningless, as explained, that "I am willing" is only effective where the law mandates the divorce, for it is a mitzvah to heed the words of the sages. But where coercion is not lawfully mandated, his saying "I am willing" is ineffective, for just as he is forced to give the get, he is also forced to say "I am willing." Similarly, with a declaration of protest, even if we do not know of his coercion, and certainly if we do know of his coercion and he issues a declaration of protest, he is compelled to give against his will. Just as he is compelled in giving, he is also compelled in saying "I am willing." Even if we do not know of his coercion, he is certainly coerced since he issued a declaration of protest. And you might say, if so, what benefit is there in nullifying declarations of protest? This matter will be explained further ahead.

What is the declaration of duress? The Tur wrote that if one made a declaration of duress before two witnesses and said, "This get (bill of divorce) that I wish to give to my wife—know that I am being coerced to give it, and therefore I declare before you that it should be nullified," then it is nullified. This is true even if he did not perform a formal acquisition (kinyan), even if they do not recognize his coercion, and even if he is not telling the truth and is not actually coerced. Since he nullified it, it is not a valid get. And even if he gives it afterward, we do not say that the declaration of duress he made is nullified unless he explicitly states that he is nullifying the declaration of duress. Then, it is nullified and does not require a formal acquisition. 

It is clear that the nullification of the declaration must be done willingly. This means that if he was coerced regarding the get, they are obligated to remove the coercion from him, and he will do as he wishes and nullify the declaration of duress he made. For if he is still coerced, his nullification is of no use; he is coerced concerning both the get and the nullification of the declaration of duress. If we do not know of his coercion at all, but he merely made a declaration of duress, then when he nullifies the declaration, it clearly appears that he is giving the get willingly. Otherwise, who is forcing him to nullify the declaration of duress?

This is not similar to the statement "I am willing" that we explained does not help if he made a declaration of duress, because we say that he is coerced to make this statement, as we said. Certainly, as long as he does not explicitly nullify his declaration of duress, we say that he surely has some coercion forcing him to also say "I am willing." Otherwise, who forced him to give the get and to make a declaration of duress beforehand? But when he explicitly nullifies his previous declaration and we do not know of his coercion, we say that surely he had some coercion initially and now it has been removed. Otherwise, who forced him to explicitly nullify his previous words? 

If indeed we see that he has some coercion, his nullification of the declaration is of no consequence, as we said. But when we do not know of any coercion and he explicitly nullifies his previous words, why should we suspect? There is no declaration of duress here at all. This is different from the statement "I am willing" when he did not explicitly nullify his previous declaration of duress. We say that his initial words still stand since he did not explicitly nullify them. If it were true that his previous coercion was removed, he should have nullified the declaration he made to uproot the declaration of duress.

And these are the exact words of the Rambam in Chapter 6, Law 19: "If someone said to two people, 'The get (divorce document) that I am writing for my wife is void,' and afterwards he wrote a get and gave it to her in the presence of two other people, it is void. This is the declaration of intent to annul the get. Similarly, if he said to them, 'Any get that so-and-so will write for me is void,' or 'Any get that I write in the court of so-and-so is void,' or 'Any get that I write from now until twenty years from now is void,' then the get is void. Likewise, if he said in front of two people, 'Any get that I write for so-and-so, my wife, is void,' and anything that I use to annul this declaration is also void, and afterwards he wrote and gave the get to her, even though he annulled the declaration before writing the get, the get is still void. Therefore, what is the corrective measure for this? The witnesses should say to him before writing the get, 'Declare before us that all the declarations you made that would cause the get to be void when they are fulfilled are themselves void,' and he says 'yes,' and afterwards he tells them to write, sign, and give it to her. They should not allow him to leave until the get reaches her hand, so that he does not go and annul it. Neither the one who makes the declaration nor the one who annuls the declaration needs to make a formal acquisition." These are his exact words.

We learn from his words that a declaration of duress (moda'ah) regarding a get (divorce document), even if we know for certain that there is no compulsion and he does not mention any duress at all but rather nullifies it before its writing, it is nullified unless he nullifies his declaration. Most of our rabbis agree with this, and this is also how it is stated in the Shulchan Aruch. Some of our rabbis wrote that we specifically require a declaration that mentions duress, but without mentioning duress, if he says "the get that I will write will not be a get," this is not a nullification because since he is not under duress at all, we assume that he fully intended it at the time of action, and a prior nullification before writing does not help unless he nullifies it after writing (Rashbam Bava Batra 40). This can be explained logically: since he is not under duress but nullifies it before writing, what is the context of his nullification? If we say that he nullifies the scribe and witnesses, then when he says again "write it," he reinstates them as his agents, and we hold that one statement nullifies another statement, especially according to those who say that agency is not required in writing the get. If we say that he nullifies it to be like a mere shard, there are those who hold that even after writing, he cannot nullify it forever so that he would not be able to use it to divorce again (as per the version in the books, Chapter 4 of Gittin: the document itself is not nullified, and Tosafot there s.v. "hatam," and this is the opinion of Ramban and Rashba as per the Maggid Mishneh in Chapter 6, Law 21, and Rambam does not hold this way, see there). However, we can say that the context of the nullification is to nullify the agency of the scribe and witnesses, so it is as if they wrote it not by his command, and it is invalid because it was not written for its intended purpose. When he then says "write it," it implies he is commanding them of their own accord and not his own until he says "I retract my initial nullification" (Ramban Bava Batra there). From the words of the Tur that we brought, it somewhat implies that one must mention the language of duress, and even if we know he is not under duress, he still must mention the language of duress. This also somewhat appears from the language of the Shulchan Aruch. However, it is not logical to say this, and therefore we can say that it is customary to say this before the witnesses, for if not, they would ask him if he does not want the get, then do not give it, hence he customarily says he is under duress.

And regarding what the Rambam wrote, that when one nullifies [the get] before two [witnesses] and then rewrites it before another two [witnesses], this is a nullified get — his intention is not that if it is given before the original two [witnesses] it is valid, as this is not a logical assertion at all. Rather, he is stating the common occurrence that those two witnesses before whom it was nullified would not involve themselves with the get, knowing it was nullified. This is unlike other legal documents, where witnesses can sign both the protest and the sale or gift document (see Bava Batra 42b). There, it does not lead to confusion, unlike with a get. Certainly, if he wishes to give the get before them, they would not agree until the protest is nullified. Additionally, it is clear to me that if someone delivers a protest regarding a get before witnesses, the witnesses are obligated to come to the court and report it in order to prevent stumbling blocks.

And this is what he wrote: "Any get (divorce document) that so-and-so writes for me is null." It appears to me that this means that he is only nullifying the get that so-and-so will write for him or the court of so-and-so, but if another person writes it, he is not nullifying it. And it comes to teach us that even in such a case where he is not entirely nullifying it but only nullifying the writing of so-and-so, this too is considered an advance declaration (moda'ah). Afterwards, he informs us that he can nullify it for a specific time, such as for twenty years. For although one might say that since he is not nullifying it entirely but only nullifying the writing of so-and-so or for a specific time, it is merely an expression of words, for what difference does it make to him if this person or that person writes the get, or what difference does it make if it is before or after twenty years? Nevertheless, since it depends on his will, he can make an advance declaration in any manner.

However, in the matter he wrote that when one issues a declaration of protest (moda'ah) concerning the get (divorce document) and also about the nullification of the declaration of protest that he will make, the nullification of the declaration of protest is ineffective, and the get is invalid. The remedy for this, he wrote, is to say before witnesses that all the things he declared, which would cause the nullification of the get, are hereby nullified. His words are not understood at all – what kind of remedy is this, since he issued a declaration of protest on all the nullifications he will make? And indeed, Rashba, of blessed memory, already raised an objection to him and wrote that there is no remedy for this except by disqualifying the witnesses, meaning that he should nullify all the declarations and also disqualify any witness who would testify that he issued a declaration of protest before him. And since he disqualifies any witness in this matter, even if they testify, we will not accept their testimony. And if you say, what benefit is there regarding the prohibition if they testify, and perhaps they already testified – it can be said that as long as he disqualifies his witnesses, he also completely nullifies the declarations. And so we practice, as will be explained with the help of Heaven. However, this remedy is not complete, for in the end, what can be done if he indeed does not completely nullify?

Indeed, the words of the Rambam are also explained well according to what we have clarified in Section 8, that it is certainly necessary to know that now there is no coercion upon him (or in the case of one who is compelled by law, we say that he desires to fulfill the command). However, one must completely retract his previous statements and nullify all that he said before. As long as he has not fully retracted, even if he says "I want," we say that he is compelled. In contrast, if he completely retracts, there remains no speech to suspect the nullification of the get (divorce document). Therefore, if he delivers a notification to nullify the notification, he must completely retract the language he used and nullify the delivery of the notification of the nullification. However, there is a concern that he might have also given a notification regarding this as well. Therefore, the Rambam of blessed memory says that he should include all previous statements in a general manner, whatever they may be, and say that he nullifies all statements that could cause the nullification of the get. Consequently, there is no concern left for us, for we know that now he is freely willing, and he has nullified all his previous words, leaving nothing for us to be concerned about. Even if we say that perhaps some thought remains in his heart, it is established that an expressed intention (gilui daata) in a get is not significant. Moreover, we do not see anything other than his previous words, which he has nullified. The Ran of blessed memory (in Chapter 4) also writes similarly, that according to the words of the Rambam of blessed memory, no concern remains. The Rambam only stated that one must completely nullify all previous statements. (According to what I have written, the words of the Maggid Mishneh are also understood there).

And also the Rosh of blessed memory wrote there similarly, and these are his words: "And if he issued a declaration (moda'ah) and said, 'Even if I nullify it, it will not be nullified,' if he then nullified the declaration and the declaration of the declaration until the end of all declarations, everything is nullified. Just as the nullification of one declaration is effective, so too is it effective for many declarations and for all conditions he stipulated." And these words of his are interpreted according to what I have written. It is only surprising why he was puzzled by the words of the Rambam of blessed memory. And similarly, the Tur, after bringing the words of the Rosh, wrote contrary to the Rambam, etc. For in truth, their intention is the same, only the Rambam expressed it differently. And the conclusion of the Rosh in the words of the Rambam also appears as I have written, except that the Tur did not bring them. (And see Beit Yosef who brought the language of the Rosh).

And behold, according to the law, certainly there is no need to annul a declaration of intent unless we have reason to fear that the husband is divorcing against his will. If it is known that he is divorcing voluntarily, there is no need to annul the declaration of intent, as he is not suspected of causing harm in Heaven's eyes or of making a declaration (Bach). However, nonetheless, all our early rabbis wrote that it is proper to annul declarations of intent for every get (divorce document). Thus, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch concluded in section 3: "It is customary to require the annulment of declarations of intent even for one who divorces voluntarily. However, if he forgot to annul the declaration of intent, the get is valid since he is divorcing of his own free will." This is also written in the Leket Yosher that once he forgot to annul the declarations and said he is not concerned about it because he knows the get was given with the husband's consent.

The text of the nullification is written in Section 2, and this is what it says: Therefore, one must nullify before writing the get (divorce document) any declaration (moda'ah) that he has made and say thus: "I hereby nullify any declaration that I have made regarding this get, and I also nullify anything that would cause, when those things are fulfilled, a nullification of this get. And I also testify about myself that I have not made any declaration regarding the get that would cause it to be nullified because of it. And I disqualify any witness or witnesses who would testify that I made or said anything that would cause this get to be nullified or to weaken its validity because of that declaration or statement." And some say it is sufficient if he says that he nullifies any declaration and any declaration of a declaration until the end of all declarations. And this is the custom. However, it is better initially to be stringent and to say according to the first opinion. And here they brought all the opinions that we have explained, and what they wrote that it is better to be stringent according to the first opinion, their intention was either to disqualify witnesses or to follow the wording of the Rambam (Rema and Beit Shmuel, Section 4), and according to what we have explained, the words of the Rambam are like the words of the Rosh, and understand this well.

A declaration must be made before two witnesses (Bava Batra 40a). Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 1 that even if it was not delivered in the presence of two witnesses together, but rather to each one separately, as long as they are valid witnesses, it is acceptable. This is because the requirement for two witnesses is only necessary to ascertain the truth, except in cases of capital law where the Torah decrees that separate testimonies are invalid, and similarly in matters of divorce and marriage where the witnesses are essential to the very act. 

However, if a declaration was made before one witness or before relatives or invalid witnesses, it is not effective, as it was not given willingly. If we say that one witness or relatives are not credible, this is a decree of the Torah that one witness or relatives are not credible even if we are certain they speak the truth. But what relevance does this have to the declaration? Since the declaration was made, what does it matter if the witnesses are invalid? We can say that if it was not made before two valid witnesses, it is considered as thoughts in the heart, and thoughts in the heart are not considered as significant. Even if he expressed it verbally, it is only considered an expression of intent, and we hold that an expression of intent in matters of divorce is not significant, as stated in Section 141. 

Alternatively, it is possible that since it was not delivered before two valid witnesses, he did not intend a full declaration. However, it is possible to say that this is specifically if we do not believe the invalid witnesses or the single witness, but if we know their words are true, we might need to take it seriously due to the severity of the matter. This requires further investigation. It seems more likely as stated earlier (see Rivash, Section 232, though it is not conclusive) and in Section 32, the matter of expressing intent before writing the divorce document will be explained.

It is also written in Section 3 that it is customary to nullify any declarations before the writing [of the get] and after the writing before the delivery. The reason for this is that we are concerned that the get might have been nullified after the writing or during the writing. Although this second nullification is effective only according to those who hold that the get itself cannot be nullified, but for those who hold that the get can always be nullified, the second nullification is of no benefit. Therefore, there are those who have the custom not to allow the husband to go until after the delivery, so that he does not nullify it upon leaving. Nevertheless, it is customary to nullify even after the writing. Indeed, Maimonides wrote there that they should not allow him to leave until the get reaches her hand, for he holds that if he nullifies it after the writing, the get is nullified forever. As we explained in Section 10, according to Nahmanides and Rashba, this is effective.

Anyone who issues a protest (moda’ah) against a get (divorce document) receives lashes of disobedience because he causes the creation of mamzerim (illegitimate children) among Israel. For the get reaches her hand and she remarries based on it, and then witnesses come and testify that he nullified the get before them or that he issued a protest before them prior to the writing of the get, and the child is found to be a mamzer. Even if he nullified the protest at the time of giving [the get], we are still stringent with him, for there is concern that there are those who know about the protest but do not know about the nullification, and they will spread slander. Certainly, it is appropriate to be stringent in this matter. Some say that lashes of disobedience are only administered if he was coerced properly and issued a protest (Beit Shmuel, Section 11). This seems to be implied by Rashi's commentary (Kiddushin 12b, d.h. "and on"), but from the words of the Maggid Mishneh (Chapter 6, Law 26), it does not seem so (for what does he argue with Rashi). The main ruling is that if he was coerced in any way, it is not appropriate to punish him for issuing a protest. However, it has already been clarified that issuing a protest is effective even without any coercion, and in such a case, it is certainly appropriate to punish (and Rashi's statement is taken in the usual manner).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 10: "A bill of divorce (get) where the husband delivered a preemptive protest (moda'ah) about its delivery, and he then gave it to her, and afterwards he voluntarily nullified it and said to her, 'Divorce yourself with the get I already gave you,' he does not need to take it back from her." End quote. And certainly, his intention is solely with respect to delivering a protest that he was coerced and did not mention the nullification of the get. For if he mentioned the nullification of the get, according to Maimonides (Rambam) and several other authorities, the get is nullified and he cannot use it again to divorce her, as stated in Siman 141. It is clear that the get must be intact in her possession or under her authority at the time he tells her to now divorce herself, etc., because the primary effectiveness of the get is now, not from before. One might ask, if so, if he tells her tomorrow, it would be considered predated. But it can be said that since it was written and delivered on the day of writing, we do not worry about this, and this requires further clarification. The Levush wrote that the get takes effect retroactively, and this requires further analysis.

It has already been explained that if it is known that he is under duress, even if he did not declare a protest beforehand, the get (divorce document) is invalid. What is considered duress? This includes financial duress, such as being forced to give a get if he does not pay a certain amount of money, and physical duress, such as being beaten, imprisoned, or threatened with imprisonment. This specifically refers to duress from others, but self-imposed duress is not considered duress. As our Sages said (Bava Metzia 48b), "Perhaps self-imposed duress is different from duress by others." What is considered self-imposed duress? For example, if he loves his wife and she hates him and causes him distress to the point that he gives her a get, since the get itself is given willingly, this is considered self-imposed duress. Otherwise, most gittin (divorce documents) would be considered given under duress, as when one divorces, there is usually some compelling reason for it. Therefore, as long as the get itself is not given under duress and no protest was declared beforehand, the get is valid.

And similarly, if a husband agrees with his wife to give a get (divorce document) and the agreement was made of his own free will, and the third party holds a sum of money with the condition that if he retracts from giving the get, the third party will hand over the money to her or impose a financial penalty to the lord of the city, this is not considered coercion since he is divorcing willingly. Even though he is compelled by the potential loss of money if he does not divorce, it is not considered duress because he acted willingly. The penalty he agreed to was made willingly to strengthen his resolve to divorce, and it is not considered duress. We find a similar case in the Talmud (46b) where a man declared all fruits of the world forbidden to him if he would not divorce his wife. Would we say he was under duress because of the vow? Certainly not, because he made the vow willingly, so it is considered full willingness (Beit Yosef in the name of the Ra'ah). All of this applies when he does not regret the get. However, if he regrets it and wants to retract from the penalty, and he is coerced because of the penalty and is compelled to divorce due to the potential loss, this is considered full duress even if he did not make a formal declaration of duress because he does not want the get (Beit Yosef in the name of the Responsa of the Rashba). I am uncertain if even annulling declarations would help as long as the financial coercion is not removed, for as long as he cries out that he does not want to divorce but is compelled by the money held, the annulment of declarations is ineffective as long as the duress exists. When someone is under duress, there is no need for a formal declaration of duress. The only solution is to give him the money and then he will divorce willingly, or he should retract his refusal and state that he wants to divorce with complete willingness. Even in this case, there is doubt if financial coercion is considered the same as physical coercion, such as if he is beaten to divorce. Even if he says a thousand times that he divorces willingly, he is still considered coerced by the beatings to say so. Furthermore, the Maharik (root 63) ruled in the case of a man imprisoned to force him to divorce his wife, and then released from prison, that if they can still imprison him again if he does not divorce, it is still considered duress. It does not help until this duress is removed so that he is assured he will not be imprisoned even if he does not divorce. If we say that financial duress is exactly like physical duress, we need to remove this duress from him. However, in truth, it does not seem entirely correct to equate the two, and the matter requires further examination. See section 26.

If the coercion was not directed at the one giving the divorce but at others, for example, if another person was beaten, and by divorcing his wife, the other person was saved from the beatings, this is not considered coercion. Coercion is defined when it is on his own body, not when it is on another's. For in this case, he is acting of his own free will, even though his compassion was aroused due to the suffering of the other person. Nonetheless, the divorce is given of his own free will (as stated there in the name of the Tashbetz). Except in the case of a father for his son or a son for his father, where such coercion is considered as if it is on one's own body, like one body (Beit Yosef). However, there are those who disagree even in this case (Tashbetz). In my humble opinion, one should be stringent in this matter.

All coercion is only considered coercion regarding a get when they mention the get during the coercion, saying to him, "If you do not divorce, we will beat you or take your money" or something similar. However, if the coercion does not pertain to the get, and they force him to do something else, and the husband himself, in order to escape this coercion, says he will divorce her knowing that this will remove the coercion from him, it would seemingly not be considered coercion regarding the get, since he divorces her of his own volition. This is specifically when the coercion for the other matter is lawful. But if they coercively force him unlawfully regarding another matter, and from that coercion, he divorces, it is possible that the get is considered coerced, and this requires further investigation (as mentioned there in the name of the Rashba). Refer also to what is written in Siman 154, Section 13, and in the Responsa of the Rivash, Siman 127.

And know that our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 4 as follows: "But if he accepted penalties upon himself if he does not divorce, it is not considered coercion since he linked his divorce to another matter and can pay the penalties and not divorce. However, there are those who are stringent even in such a case (Rashba), and it is good to be stringent from the outset and exempt him from the penalty. But if he already divorced because of this, etc., the get (divorce document) is valid since initially, he was not coerced into it." And I am very puzzled that he made a dispute between the opinions, and it is clearly explained in the great book of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, that there is no disagreement at all. The first opinion is when he did not retract from the get (divorce), and the second opinion from the response of the Rashba clearly explains that he retracted from the get and the penalty but was compelled because of the penalty, as there. And this is what we explained in section 23, and the Rashba explicitly invalidates in such a case, as there. And it also clearly appears from the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, there that there is no disagreement, as there.

And it appears to me that his opinion is that when he has not retracted, it is certainly not considered coercion according to all opinions, even though he is compelled because of the money which the trustee is holding as a penalty or similar situations, since he imposed the penalty willingly. The two opinions he brought up are when the divorcer retracted, but the trustee does not want to return the penalty money to him unless he divorces her, and he divorces her. The stringent opinion is that of the Rashba, which we brought, and the first lenient opinion is not from the author mentioned in section 23 but rather a response from the Maharik, which our rabbi Beit Yosef brought. And these are his words: If the trustee has money in his hands for this purpose and the trustee does not want to give the money until he divorces, it is not considered coercion, etc. These are the exact words of the Maharik, root 63. And Rabbi Rema explains that it refers to when he retracted, and it is also evident from the words of the Levush at the end of this section who brought this response in these words. And some say that even in this case, it is not coercion, as they wrote: If the trustee has money in the hands of the trustee for him to divorce, and he wants to retract, and the trustee does not want to return the money to him until he divorces, it is not considered coercion, for coercion is only considered when it comes because of others and not when one brings coercion upon himself. And see in Maharik, root 63. These are the exact words of the Levush.

And regarding the law, I am astonished at how it was decided retrospectively against the opinion of the Rashba who completely invalidates it. And these are the words of the Rashba: "You asked about Reuven, the husband of Leah, and Leah's relatives who had agreed that Reuven would divorce Leah his wife and they consented to each other with a penalty of a thousand dinars and that he would divorce her at a set time. Afterwards, Reuven regretted it and refused the matter, and they pressured him due to the penalty until he went to the treasurer to negotiate with him and he did not accept it, and because of this fear he divorced, but he was not proficient in issuing a preemptive declaration. Should this divorce be considered coerced? My answer is that this divorce is coerced and invalid as long as it is known that it was under duress, even though he did not issue a preemptive declaration, etc." End quote. And even if the Mahari"k explicitly disagreed with the Rashba, it is difficult to rule against the opinion of the Rashba, especially since the Mahari"k did not bring him up at all, and necessarily either he did not see the Rashba's words or his intention was not when he retracted and gave under compulsion. And what our teacher the Rema brought in this matter, that even if one divorced due to an oath, it is not considered duress when he swore to divorce, and this is from the responsa of the Ritva brought by our teacher the Beit Yosef at the end of Siman 154, and even this is not relevant to this case, for there too it does not deal with retraction, but rather one who swore to divorce and divorced, and the Ritva says it is not considered duress since he swore willingly, see there. And it will be further explained. But what relevance does it have to one who retracted on the divorce and the penalty and was compelled because of the penalty to give a divorce, for there is no greater duress than this. And from the words of the Levush, it is implied there that he differentiates between setting a time for divorce and not setting a time, and this is not understood at all (and also the Rema does not hold this as written by the Ba"sh in subsection 8).

Indeed, from the simple wording, it implies that it is speaking of a case where he did not retract, but in this itself, there is cause for concern. Since he imposed a penalty if he does not grant the divorce, this itself appears as coercion. This is explicitly evident from one of the great Acharonim who questioned how, according to Rabbeinu the Rema, arrangements are made for a divorce and securities are set for penalties (Even HaEzer 134). However, according to this, I do not know who is stringent in this matter that it says "there are those who are stringent." One cannot say that he refers to those who are stringent in giving a divorce when he swore to give a divorce, which seems like coercion, because certainly, they also agree regarding a monetary penalty. For in the case of an oath, one could say he is compelled because of his oath, but with a monetary penalty, he is not compelled if he wishes to lose his money. The main ruling is as stated in paragraph 23, as it is explicitly derived from the Talmud that we brought in paragraph 23, and it will be further clarified with God's help.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: If the husband swears to give a get (divorce document), they need to release him from the oath first so that it does not appear as coercion. However, if he provides a guarantee, it is acceptable since it does not resemble coercion. This is his wording. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: The same applies if he made a formal acquisition to divorce, etc., and even if he divorced because of an oath he made on his own to divorce, the get is valid since he was not initially coerced into it. This is his wording.

The explanation of these matters is as follows: There are those who are stringent regarding someone who swore to divorce, considering it akin to coercion. This is not similar to what our Sages said (Gittin 46b): "May the fruits of the world be forbidden to me if I do not divorce you," as it is clear that this is not coercion because he based his vow on something else, on the fruits, and it is not coercion since he can choose not to eat the fruits and not divorce. But in the case of swearing to divorce, where he linked the get to his oath, it is considered akin to coercion (Beit Yosef in the name of the Ran). Therefore, when he provides a monetary guarantee or something else, it is similar to what our Sages said, and this is not considered coercion at all.

However, the Ritva in his responsa (brought in Beit Yosef, end of section 154) explicitly explained that those who are stringent in this matter do so not because of the fundamental law, for certainly, anything a person willingly accepts upon himself is not considered coercion, as with the vow of fruits in the Gemara. Rather, they are stringent initially, but after the fact, there is no concern. This is also the ruling of MaharaL ben Chaviv (there in Beit Yosef).

This is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote: If he divorced because of an oath, the get is valid. All of this provides clear evidence for what we have written above. As for what he wrote: If he made a formal acquisition to divorce, this is obvious as it is merely a stringency, for the acquisition has no reason in this matter, as Rambam wrote in Chapter 5 of Sales, Law 11, see there. And if he made a penalty in the acquisition, the penalty does not apply either, as it is like "acquiring a donkey and half of it," (Terumat HaDeshen, section 173). However, regarding "acquiring a donkey and half of it," we hold that he acquires half, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 210, and as Rambam ruled in Chapter 22 of Sales. Nevertheless, regarding a get, this does not matter (it is only concerning the fundamental matter that Terumat HaDeshen analogized it to "acquiring a donkey and half of it," this requires further analysis, and scrutinize it well).

The halachic authorities in the laws of divorce only discussed the case of one who took an oath to divorce and did not discuss at all the case of one who took an oath not to divorce. In reality, this latter case is more concerning than the former. For according to the opinion that anything the Torah says not to do, if one does it, it does not take effect, there is a significant concern that the get (divorce document) would be invalid. It is known that this ruling—that if one does it, it does not take effect—has not been definitively resolved in halacha, whether it does or does not take effect. However, this is understandable as the Tosafot wrote (Temurah 6a) that in the case of one who took an oath not to divorce, even according to the opinion that if one does it, it does not take effect, here it does take effect because it is not a prohibition decreed by the Torah but rather an oath from his own mind, see there. Nevertheless, the halachic authorities should have been concerned about this, as many of the early authorities disagree on this matter, and it seems this is also the opinion of the Rambam (as explained by Maggid Mishneh, Chapter 9 of Laws of Loans). We have already elaborated on this in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 208, Section 3, see there. And our teacher, the Rema, contradicts himself on this matter between what he wrote in Choshen Mishpat there and what he wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 232, and we have explained this there with G-d's help. Therefore, in arranging the get, we have the divorcer state that he has not taken an oath to divorce and also that he has not taken an oath not to divorce, etc. And one of the great rabbis in the generation before us (Chatam Sofer) has already addressed this issue.

Some say that only an explicit declaration of intent (mesirat moda'ah) nullifies the get (divorce document), but if he did not explicitly declare his intention but only hinted at his intention to make a declaration, it has no effect (Beit Shmuel, Section 1). Indeed, the established law is that revealing one's intention regarding a get is not significant, as stated in Siman 141. However, it may be argued that this applies only after the writing of the get; simply revealing his intention does not help unless he explicitly nullifies it, as a verbal declaration cannot nullify an act. But before the writing, it is possible that revealing his intention may have an effect (Bach). Even though before the get reaches the woman it is not yet considered an act (Tosafot 32b, s.v. R. Shimon), nonetheless, regarding the revealing of intention, it might be considered an act. This is also implied by the language of the Talmud (Bava Batra 40b) that the declaration about a get is merely a revelation of the matter. However, this is only in regard to not needing to know his coercion, as the revelation of the matter indicates that since he made a declaration, he is presumably coerced (as the Rashbam writes there). But the declaration must always be explicit, especially according to what is written in Siman 42, Section 10, that gittin (divorces) and kiddushin (marriages) depend solely on witnesses, and we do not follow the thoughts of his heart at all. This is unlike monetary matters where witnesses are created only to prevent falsehood, and it is necessary to know the intentions of his heart. This is not the case with gittin and kiddushin. For this reason, we explained there that there are no legal principles of asmachta (reliance on conditions) in gittin and kiddushin. For this reason, the Sages ruled that revealing one's intention regarding a get is not significant. However, we have already explained there that the early authorities who sought another reason why there is no asmachta in gittin and kiddushin did not accept this principle. Nevertheless, regarding the revealing of intention, it is clear from several authorities that they did not consider it significant even before the writing of the get, as is evident from the Rashbam's commentary. Nonetheless, in practice, this requires further investigation (Pitchei Teshuva, Section 1), but in a pressing situation, one may be lenient since the Beit Shmuel ruled thus, and it is also clear from the Rashbam.

It has already been explained in section 6 that even if money was received, we do not say that he agreed, see there. However, from the words of the Rashbam there, who wrote that since he is not receiving money for this get (divorce document) that he is giving, if it were agreeable to him, why would he submit a protest, etc., it somewhat implies that if he receives money, it is not considered a protest if we do not know of his coercion. And from the responsa of the Rashba (brought in Beit Yosef), who wrote that this get is coerced and invalid as long as the coercion is known, even if he did not submit a protest, because the submission of a protest is only relevant where he received money, etc., and they coerced him, and he divorced, these are not valid divorces because there is no money involved. And if you wish to say, etc., that since he accepted upon himself a penalty of a thousand dinars and by giving the get he gained this money, it is considered as receiving money, it is not so, because this is not considered as receiving money but as avoiding a monetary loss, which is significantly worse, etc. It is explicitly implied that if he receives profit money, the get is valid even though he is coerced if he did not submit a protest. And it is implied from the words of our Rabbis that whether he submitted a protest and we do not know of his coercion, or we know of his coercion and he did not submit a protest, receiving money is effective. Therefore, it can be said that what our Rabbi the Rema wrote in section 8, that giving money does not help, is specifically when we know of his coercion and he submitted a protest. But if one of these is missing, giving money is effective, and it is treated like a sale. Nevertheless, regarding the law, it appears to me that if the submission of a protest was due to a monetary concern or the coercion was due to a monetary concern, certainly if they gave him money, we say that he agreed. But if the coercion was physical and the coercion was not removed from him, certainly giving money does not help, even if he says he agreed in exchange for the money as long as the coercion is still upon him. And similarly, if he submitted a protest and we do not know of his coercion but according to the assumption, the protest was due to another matter, not because of a monetary concern, giving money also does not help, unless he explicitly says that he agreed in exchange for the money. Since there is no clear coercion upon him, as soon as he says he agreed, if he revoked his protest, it is effective even without giving money. And if they gave him money, perhaps his statement "I desire" (to give the get) is effective even if he did not explicitly revoke his protest. (See Ba'er Hetev section 14 and Pischei Teshuva section 16, and I have written what appears correct to me, and scrutinize well).

It is necessary to read the get (bill of divorce) before its delivery and after, as well as additional laws. This section contains fifteen paragraphs:

The witnesses before whom the get is presented, who are the witnesses of delivery (which is the essential part of the get), must read it before the delivery (Gittin 19b). This requirement is indispensable even after the fact, because if they do not read it, they do not know if a get was given to her or something else. It appears that here the Sages did not permit others to read it and tell them, as is allowed with the signing witnesses in Siman 130. The distinction is clear, as the Sages were lenient with signing witnesses, as the Rambam explains in Chapter 1, because the signing witnesses are a rabbinic enactment. We have explained this there in Siman 47. But the delivery witnesses are required by Torah law, and therefore immediately before its delivery—which is the completion of the get—they must read it themselves. However, some say that when the head of the Beit Din (rabbinical court) and his scribes read it in front of them, and they fear him, they can rely on them (Ran, Chapter 2), and this reasoning is logical. For indeed, with other documents, it is also valid in such a case, as stated in Choshen Mishpat Siman 45, and we should not be stricter with a get than with other documents. And with the signatures, they were more lenient than with other documents, as stated there in Siman 43.

Based on what was said, it can be inferred that according to the Rif and the Rambam, a bill of divorce (get) is valid with the signatures of the witnesses alone, provided that the witnesses themselves have read the get. We do not impose an additional stringency requiring them to read it themselves because, according to Torah law, it is valid even without the additional reading (as implied in Beit Shmuel, Section 1). However, the simple understanding of the language of the Poskim does not suggest this leniency. It can be argued that they were lenient only regarding signatures because not everyone is capable of signing their own name, therefore they were lenient in this case. But in the case of reading, which everyone is capable of, and many can read, there should be no leniency. Additionally, with signatures, the completion of the get is not at the time of signing but at the time it is handed over to the woman, so the Sages were lenient. However, with reading, which completes the get, there was no leniency. It also seems clear that even if the witnesses of the signing are the same as those who read the get and they had already read it before signing, they are still obligated to read it again close to the time of delivery. This is implied by all the early authorities and the Shulchan Aruch, who wrote this rule without qualification, even though the custom is that the signing witnesses are the same as the delivery witnesses.

All the early authorities agreed that it is good to read it [the get, Jewish divorce document] before giving it and after giving it. So also wrote the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. The reason seems to be that we are concerned that perhaps after the husband took it into his hand, he switched it with another paper (as is evident in the Rosh, Chapter 2, section 16). And even though this concern is remote, nevertheless, at the completion of the get, there should be no doubt. However, after the fact, if it was not read after giving it, it does not invalidate [the get]. Moreover, even if after reading it before giving it, the husband took the get and hid it in his bosom, we are not concerned that he switched it and she is permitted to remarry (Tosafot and Rosh). However, ideally, in such a case, there is certainly an obligation to read it again according to the law (and the Rosh is uncertain about this).

And similarly, if they did not read it before the giving and they read it immediately after the giving, it is also valid (there) because what is there to be concerned about? And there are those who object to this (Mordechai in the name of R"M Chapter 2) because we require that at the time of giving the witnesses know that it is a get. Refer there, and this opinion was not brought by the legal decisors. And it seems to me that they do not argue at all because certainly if the witnesses were present at the making of the get, in its writing and signing, and they knew that the matter was a get, everyone agrees that what does it matter if they did not read it before the giving since they read it afterwards. However, if they knew nothing at all about the matter of the get and they were called from the market to be witnesses on the get and they did not see it nor read it, certainly there is reason for concern unless they read it within the time of speaking after the giving (as it appears to me). And know that the primary matter is not the reading of the get because there is no commandment to read it, and the primary matter is to know that this paper is the get that this man wrote for this woman. Therefore, if the witnesses examine well that this is her get, nothing more is needed. (And what the Rema wrote, "And similarly, if they testify," is a printing error, and it should say, "if they examine," as written in the Tur’s gloss).

Our custom is to conduct it diligently such that the officiating rabbi reads the get (bill of divorce) after it has been written and signed, and the husband once again annuls any previous statements, as mentioned in Siman 134. The rabbi reads the get along with the witnesses, and then the rabbi asks the scribe if it was written for his sake and for her sake, and for the purpose of divorce, and if the husband commanded him to do so. He asks the witnesses if they heard from the husband that he commanded the scribe and if they heard from the scribe that it was written for his sake, etc. Afterwards, he asks each witness if they signed in the presence of each other and if they signed for his sake, etc., and if the husband commanded them to do so. He asks the scribe and the witnesses if they recognize the writing of the get that they wrote and their signatures that they signed. Afterwards, the get is handed over to the woman in the presence of the witnesses. Then, the get is received back from her, and the rabbi reads it again with the witnesses, and once again asks the scribe and the witnesses as mentioned. This is the conclusion of the get, as mentioned in the order of the get in Siman 154.

If they read the get (bill of divorce) and gave it to the husband or his agent, and he placed it in his hand and then gave it to her, ideally, they should read it a second time before giving it to her. However, after the fact, if they did not read it and gave it to her and it was then thrown into the sea or fire and it is impossible to read it after it was given, she is nevertheless divorced. Since they read it initially, we do not worry that it was switched, as he is not suspected of such deceit. Moreover, even if the husband claims after the get was burned or lost that it was switched and a different document was given to her, he is not believed, and she is considered divorced. This is because she had been established as divorced from the time she received the get, and he is not believed to remove her from this established status. If his claim were true, he should have said so immediately at the time of the giving. Therefore, it is certain that he now regrets and is searching for excuses unless he now shows us the get in his possession, which would then be clear proof that he tells the truth and she would require a new get. Even in such a case, he is only believed as long as she has not remarried. However, if she has remarried, he cannot render her forbidden to her new husband since she was established as divorced, and his claim cannot remove her from this status. We would say that she returned the get to him to extricate herself from the second husband, and they conspired together. Similarly, even if she has not remarried and he is a Kohen (priest), he is not believed to take her back because of this suspicion that she returned the get to him. Therefore, if we know that the document given to her was burned and he now shows it in his possession, he is believed in all matters, even if he is a Kohen and even if she has remarried, and she must leave both this one and that one. What we said that he is not believed if she has remarried applies when the get was not burned or lost but was not read after being given to her. Since there could be a defect if the get remains in her possession, she might return it to him to extricate herself from the second husband or to return to him if he is a Kohen. Therefore, it is good and proper that our custom is not to leave the get in her possession, and the court takes it and tears it up.

If they did not read the get (divorce document) before giving it to her, and then it was thrown into the sea or burned, and it turns out that it was not read at all, neither before the giving nor afterward, she remains in a state of doubtful divorce in every respect until he divorces her with a clear get. Even if she remarries, she must leave [her new husband], for she is presumed to be a married woman (eshet ish) and has not been certainly divorced. A doubtful divorce does not remove the certainty of her presumed status as a married woman. Even if the husband says the get was valid, he is not believed to establish her as a definite divorcee. Her status is as that of a husband who says, "I divorced my wife," which makes her a doubtful divorcee, as will be explained in Siman 152. Although there, the reason she is not a definite divorcee is because of a flaw, since every get has a public notice (kol), and this one does not, as mentioned there, here she was divorced and there is a public notice. Since the witnesses did not read it either before the giving or after, and the get was lost, she cannot be established as a definite divorcee. On the contrary, even if we say that there he is completely believed (see Bava Batra 135a), here he is not believed because there is a flaw before us, as the witnesses did not read it at all and now it is lost. Conversely, even if the husband says that it was not a get at all and that he gave her a different document, he is not believed to make her definitely not divorced, for in any case, from the time of giving, she was presumed to be a doubtful divorcee. Therefore, she remains in a state of doubtful divorce in every respect.

This is what we have said: If they did not read it at all, it is considered a doubtful divorce. This is when the get (divorce document) was burned or lost. But if the get is later found in her possession, she certainly should not remarry with this get initially, since it was not read either before the handing over or immediately after the handing over. Nevertheless, if she did remarry, she should not be made to leave (her second husband), since the get is still in her possession. Even if she showed the get after she had already married the second husband, she should not be made to leave (her second husband). This is because it only serves as proof that she was divorced then. Nevertheless, if she has not remarried, we do not allow her to marry with this get because of the deficiency that it was not read immediately after the handing over. However, we do not make her leave her (second) husband because of this deficiency. This is the opinion of most of the decisors.

However, the Tur wrote as follows: "If it was not read at all and was lost, and he says that what he gave her was not a get (bill of divorce) but merely a document, she should not remarry and is disqualified from marrying a kohen. If she did remarry, she need not leave her second husband." And the Rambam wrote: "Even if the husband says it was a valid get, she is considered doubtfully divorced." So concludes the Tur, who is very lenient, even if it was burned and not read at all, that she need not leave her second husband (and this is like the first explanation of Tosafot Yom Tov: s.v. Tzrichi, and consider it well). His reasoning is that it is not comparable to a husband who says "I divorced my wife," where she is doubtfully divorced, because there is a clear flaw since there is no public knowledge of this get. But here, there is public knowledge; only the witnesses failed by not reading it. And since it is known to the witnesses that he wrote her a get and at the time he handed it to her he said, "This is your get," and he did not protest within twenty-four hours claiming he was joking and did not give her the get, and he is not suspected of causing her to sin in the eyes of Heaven, she is presumed divorced before us, and he is not believed to forbid her to a second husband. (And this is the "some disagree" that the Rema wrote, as mentioned by the Beit Shmuel, section 5, and the Gra, section 6, wrote that on the contrary, even if she has the get in her possession, if she remarried, she must leave her second husband. And this is the opinion of the Rashba, and like the second explanation of Tosafot there. These matters are perplexing because the second explanation deals with a case where it was burned, as explained in the Gemara, and the Rashba's intention is also when it was burned, as the Rema explicitly wrote in the Darkei Moshe, note 1, and the language of the Beit Yosef is somewhat imprecise there. Consider it well).

There is a type of ink that, over time, gets absorbed into the paper, making the letters completely unrecognizable. There is also a type of dye that, when applied to the paper, reveals the absorbed letters and makes them visible (Rashi 19b). Similarly, if one applies pomegranate peel water to the paper, it reveals the letters (Tosafot). If a get (divorce document) was written with such writing and the writing is recognizable at the time of delivery, the get is valid. This is not considered writing that cannot endure, because it does endure, only that it gets absorbed over time and can be brought out, as mentioned. But if at the time of delivery the writing was absorbed, it is not a get. This is also clear from Rashi's explanation there, and Tosafot explicitly write so as well: "If at the time of delivery it was seen that the paper was blank, then even if it was definitely written with gallnut ink, it is not a get, because at the time of delivery the letters were already absorbed." This is clearly implied by all the early authorities. The Levush was stringent, considering it a doubtful get even in such a case, arguing that perhaps the Torah does not require the writing to be recognizable. But this reasoning is puzzling, also from a logical standpoint (and the Beit Shmuel in section 6 also questioned him and wondered why he did not bring evidence from Rashi and Tosafot).

This writing is called in the Gemara there "water letters" and it is stated there that if he gave her a blank piece of paper and said to her, "This is your get," and the witnesses did not see at the time of giving whether the letters were discernible or not, and afterwards they checked the paper with a dye and the letters were revealed, it is a doubtful get. If they checked and the letters were not revealed, it is nothing, for it is clear that it is a blank paper. If they did not check it at all and the paper was burned, some say it is also a doubtful get (Tosafot, s.v. "and Shmuel") and so ruled the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. Some say that if they did not check it, since they saw it was a blank paper, we do not consider it at all unless they checked it and the letters were revealed, then she is doubtfully divorced (Rashba).

The Tur wrote: If he gave her a blank piece of paper and said, "This is your get (divorce document) if it is not examined, etc." or "if it is examined and the writing is revealed," she is in a state of doubtful divorce, etc. The Ramah wrote: If it was burned or lost before being examined, there is no concern at all, and she is permitted even to a Kohen. The Ramah's opinion aligns with the view mentioned in the previous paragraph (Beit Yosef). Some say that the Ramah's opinion is in accordance with the first opinion and does not disagree with the Tur. The reason for the stricter ruling when it was not examined is that the paper is present before us and can be examined. Therefore, we are stringent even if it was not examined. The opinion mentioned in the previous paragraph is lenient even in this case, and both opinions agree that if it was burned or lost, she is permitted because it is impossible to examine it (Bach in the name of Rashal). All these laws apply when the witnesses saw that it was a blank piece of paper. Nonetheless, we are stringent if, when examined, the writing is revealed, as perhaps at the time of giving the get, the letters were discernible, and the witnesses did not scrutinize it properly. Or even if they did scrutinize it, it was not immediately at the time of giving the get. In such a case, we are concerned that perhaps at the time of giving the get, the writing was discernible and then became absorbed. Even if it was not examined, we are concerned that the writing might have been revealed if it had been examined, according to the opinions explained. However, if the witnesses saw the letters clearly before the giving of the get, it is obvious that she is in a state of doubtful divorce in any case, according to all opinions, even if it was burned or lost (Avnei Shoham, sub-clause 6, and the words of the Bach, who wrote that the case involves initial reading, and therefore he questioned it; see there, and it requires further investigation).

He threw her a document in the presence of witnesses into her domain and said to her, "This is your divorce." They searched the place where he threw it and did not find a divorce document, only a mezuzah or another document. We do not consider this a divorce at all, not even stringently, because we say he definitely did not throw her a divorce document but rather the mezuzah or the document that was found. It is explained in the Talmud (19b) that this is specifically in a place where mezuzot or documents are not commonly found. However, if such items are occasionally found in that place, it is considered a doubtful divorce, because perhaps what he threw was indeed a divorce document and mice ate it or dragged it away, and the mezuzah or document was there beforehand. I am puzzled by the legal decisors who did not mention this condition, for it is stated explicitly in the case where he threw it among her barrels, and Rav Nachman said, "A mezuzah among barrels is uncommon," clearly indicating that if it were common, we would be stringent. Perhaps they wrote in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch that he threw it among barrels, which itself implies it is a place where such items are uncommon. Nevertheless, they should have explained this, and this requires further investigation. Similarly, it is difficult regarding the Rambam in the first chapter; perhaps they explain that the Talmud refers to a case where the witnesses read the divorce document beforehand, then he placed it under his garment and gave it to her. Therefore, in such a case, if mezuzot are common among the barrels, we would be stringent. But if they did not read it at all, we are not stringent even if such items are common because the concern that mice took it is a distant concern. Practically, we should be stringent in all cases (see Ran who wrote two explanations, and scrutinize this carefully).

And specifically, if only one mezuzah or one document is found, but if two mezuzahs or two documents are found, and we saw that he only threw one document (Rashi), and therefore necessarily one item was also there before, we are stringent in all matters, and she is in doubt as to whether she is divorced due to the concern that mice may have dragged it away. And even if the get (divorce document) was read beforehand and two mezuzahs or two documents were found afterward, she is still only in doubt as to whether she is divorced, and not definitively (Levush and Bach). There is an opinion that says in such a case, she is certainly divorced, but this is not clear (there). How can it be made into a definitive get since it was not found? And how can we attribute the dragging by mice to be lenient (see Pesachim 9a, and examine it closely)?

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch write that this applies only if the get (bill of divorce) was not read initially. However, if after they read it and determined it was a get, the husband took it from their hands and threw it into her courtyard or among the barrels, even if only a single mezuzah or document was found, it is considered a doubtful divorce. Certainly, their intention is that he put it into his garments or the witnesses momentarily looked away, for otherwise, they clearly saw him throw her the get, so why would it be doubtful? It is possible they hold that due to the severity of the prohibition against a married woman, we are stringent in every matter and say that they did not observe properly, and perhaps within a moment it was switched, because the concern of mice is difficult to apply leniently in the prohibition of a married woman. In any case, it is apparent from their words that if it was read, we are stringent in every matter, even if mezuzot are not commonly found among barrels, and even if only one was found. This contradicts what we wrote in Section 13, and the Rambam is generally stringent in doubtful cases. Refer to what we wrote in Siman 139, that she is not permitted until it actually comes into her hand.

What language should the husband use when giving the get to her? This section contains 22 paragraphs:

The get (divorce document) must be given directly into her hand. Although, according to the fundamental law, it is also effective if placed in her domain, it is not literally her hand. The Sages explicitly stated (beginning of chapter 8), "Her hand" only refers to her hand. From where do we derive her roof, her courtyard, and her enclosed area? The verse states "and he shall place it" in any case, implying that it need not specifically be in her hand. It only needs to be similar to her hand in that it is guarded with her knowledge (Rashi). The very definition of "hand" is a domain, as in the phrase "and he took all his land from his hand" (Rashi, Bava Metzia 10:). It is explicitly taught: if one throws a get to his wife, and she is inside her house or courtyard, she is divorced. Nevertheless, the ruling is that she is not permitted to remarry until she receives the get directly in her hand, as will be explained in Siman 139. The Aruch writes in the entry "Get" that our Rabbis accepted that even if it was thrown into her courtyard, she is not permitted to remarry until the get reaches her hand (Tosafot 78:), and there is proof from the Jerusalem Talmud (chapter 8, halacha 2), which states that the most proper way is until it is given directly into her hand. Similarly, in our Talmud (there), Shmuel told Rav Yehuda, "Do not act until the get reaches her hand." Even though the Tosafot explained that this applies only to transactions in the public domain, such as when it is close to her and similar cases, and not to transactions in her courtyard, according to the acceptance of the Geonim, the straightforward meaning of the words stands.

And the reason, it seems to me, is clear based on what is stated there in the Jerusalem Talmud. It raises an objection from Rav against Rav. Here, Rav says that within her four cubits she is divorced, and there Rav says that we specifically require the extension of her hand, meaning that she can extend her hand and take it. It resolves this by stating that here it is for the law and there it is for practical ruling. That is to say, according to the basic law, she is divorced when the get falls within her four cubits, even if she cannot extend her hand and take it. However, in practice, it is specifically required that she be able to take it. And on this, it concludes that the most proper practice is until it is placed in her hand, but by law, this is not necessary. However, practically, it is stringent with a get. The reason for this is that in several matters, the Sages were stringent with gittin beyond the basic law, as stated in the Talmud (85b) regarding the enactment to write "from this day and forever," even though by basic law it is not required, as explained there. Rashi explains there that this is to remove any doubt so the matter will be clear and no blemish will fall upon the families of Israel. And they were concerned about errant courts that might misunderstand the phrase "and he placed it in her hand" to mean her actual hand, as in several places they were concerned about errant courts, all the more so with a get (Yevamot 106b, Bava Batra 138b, and see there in Rashbam to the phrase "and he resolved").

And know that there are some great authorities who express doubt, suggesting that perhaps we require the entire get (divorce document) to be in her hand literally, meaning that no part of the paper should protrude from her hand, but rather it should be entirely concealed in her hand. Based on this, I have heard of those who are stringent, folding the get multiple times until it is possible to conceal it entirely in her hand. They bring proof from the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 2, Halacha 3), which states there: Or is it different because it is written "and he shall place it in her hand" until the entire get is in her hand. This implies that the entire get should be literally in her hand. However, aside from the fact that our ancestors never practiced this, and there is no reason for it, and no one would mistakenly think that in the acquisition by hand, the entire object needs to be concealed in the hand—there is no need for proofs for this. Additionally, there is a concern of casting aspersions on earlier gittin (divorce documents), and further concern that due to the multiple foldings, the letters may become blurred. The Jerusalem Talmud never intended this, as will be explained with God's help.

And this is what it means: for it is based on the Mishnah that writes the get (divorce document) on the horn of a cow and gives her the cow. And there, Rabbi Zeira asks: if he gave it to her by delivery, what is the law? By the measure of the law, you would say that the transaction is acquired, and here you would say so, or is it different because it is written "and he shall place it in her hand" until it is entirely in her hand. And the explanation of the matter is that certainly, according to the basic law, she is divorced. And even though he cannot deliver the cow to her hand directly like he delivers a paper on which the get is written, since she cannot lift the cow and take it in her hand, he can still transfer it to her through another form of acquisition, such as pulling or delivery. However, because the Jerusalem Talmud in the eighth chapter that we mentioned is stringent in practice, requiring specifically her actual hand, Rabbi Zeira asks regarding such a get written on the horn of a cow, what should be done with it. In this case, only pulling or delivery can be used for the transaction. And the Jerusalem Talmud in Kiddushin (Chapter 1, Halacha 4) holds that it can only be acquired by delivery and not by pulling, as is the plain meaning of the Mishnah in the first chapter of Kiddushin (25b), which is also the opinion of Rashi there. Therefore, Rabbi Zeira asks: if he gave it to her by delivery, what is the law? Meaning, in this case, another form of acquisition is not possible, as stated by the measure of the law. Meaning, according to the basic law, there is no question because since you say the transaction is acquired, meaning, as it is taught that a large animal is acquired by delivery, and here you say so, meaning, there is a question in astonishment. Or is it different because it is written "and he shall place it in her hand" until it is entirely in her hand, meaning that the question is according to what we were stringent in the eighth chapter, that in practice she should not be permitted until it is given directly into her hand. And with a cow, it is impossible to give it directly into her hand. Therefore, he asks if they were also stringent in this case in practice or if they were not stringent because it is impossible to do so. Thus, we revert to the basic law. And when it says "until it is entirely in her hand," the intention is not that it should be entirely contained in her hand, but rather that the entire get should be in her hand directly, not just in her possession. Therefore, it is unthinkable to be stringent and act so. Especially since we also have the custom that after receiving the get, she places it under the cloak on her heart and walks four cubits this way.

I have also seen that there are those who rely on the words of our teacher, the Rema, in this section, paragraph 1, where he wrote that it is customary for the husband to fold the get (divorce document) like a letter and give it to her so that she can hold the entire document in her hand when he gives it to her. They interpret his words to mean that the entire get should be hidden in her hand without any edges of the get protruding. (See Pitchei Teshuvah, section 139, note 4, who wrote that this is not a new concept, as the Rema had already mentioned it.) However, this is not the correct understanding. Rather, his intention is that if the get is not folded like a letter, she will only grasp a small part of the get, but by folding it like a letter, the main part of the paper will be entirely in her hand, as is known. The concern was for the possibility of a mistaken court, as they explained in the Jerusalem Talmud, and as we have explained, they were concerned for the possibility of a mistaken court.

And a clear proof of this is from what all the early authorities wrote, that the woman should be careful not to close her hands while the husband is holding the other end of the [divorce] document. And these are the words of the Mordechai, chapter 8: "And according to this, sometimes the husband holds the get at one end and gives it into her hand while still holding the other end, and she closes her hand tightly before the husband has let go of his end of the get, and it is like the get is in her hand and he is pulling it. However, after the fact, etc." End of quote. And if you were to think that the entire get must be enclosed in her hand, how could you find such a case? Rather, certainly this has never been the custom, and we should not change from what our Rabbis have always practiced. And in Siman 139, this will be further explained with God's help (and this is also the intention of the Tosafot on 78a in the commentary beginning with "if", and pay close attention).

The one who divorces must have the intention at the time he gives her the get (divorce document) that with this get, he releases her from him.
