She must also know that by receiving this get, she is released from him and permitted to any man. Therefore, he must say to her at the time of giving it in the presence of witnesses, "This is your get," or "This is your divorce," or something similar. If he handed it to her and said nothing to her, and they had not previously discussed the matter of the get, Rambam writes in Chapter 1 that it is a questionable get, and it is explained that from a Torah perspective it is still a get. The Tur writes that it is not a get, which implies that from a Torah perspective it is not a get, similar to the case of betrothal explained in Siman 27 where it is not a betrothal at all. According to Rambam, the distinction is clear: for betrothal, her consent is needed, but for a get, her consent is not needed at all. Although from the Torah it is required that she be sent away and not return, and if she does not know, she might return to him, it can be said that after some time, they will inform her that it is a get. For it is obvious that she needs to know afterward that she was divorced from him so that she does not return to him. (This is the intention of the Rema in Section 5 in the name of Tosafot in the chapter "Hazorek" (and what is written in the chapter "Hamegaresh" is a typographical error) 4:78, beginning with the words "it is not"). What the Beit Shmuel writes in Subsection 3 in the name of Tosafot that it must be at the time of giving is not found in Tosafot, and the Taz writes similarly. He unnecessarily created a disagreement between Tosafot and Rambam. Also, the words of the Gra in Subsection 10 require examination. The words of the Rema are correct, and ensure to understand this well.

This applies when he was not speaking with her about the matter of the get (divorce document), for then the declaration is crucial, either by Torah law or rabbinic law, as we have said. However, if he was speaking with her about the matter of the get, and in the course of the conversation he gave her the get and she accepted it, even though he did not say anything, she is fully divorced. The same law applies to betrothal, as we have stated in section 27, and it is explicitly stated in the Mishnah (Gittin 4:4). The reason for the declaration "this is your get" is because otherwise it is not evident at all that he gave it to her for the purpose of divorce. But since they are discussing the matter of the get, the context indicates that he gave it to her for the purpose of divorce, as it is written, "a document of severance and he shall place it in her hand," meaning he should give it to her as a document of severance (Rambam).

And our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 5: One must give it to her as an act of divorce, but if he gave it to her as a promissory note, she is not divorced unless he subsequently says, "This is your get," or informs the witnesses in advance. And our master the Rema wrote on this: Provided that the woman knows she is being divorced with it or that the witnesses inform her afterwards. The main ruling regarding giving it as a promissory note is in section 138, and here it seems to me that it teaches us that since it is written in section 1 that when he spoke with her about the matter of the get, the statement is not an impediment. This is only when he gave it to her simply, as this is considered as if he said it. But if during the conversation about the get, he said to her, "Take this promissory note," even though it is likely that he said it out of embarrassment since they were discussing the matter of the get and he gave it to her, nevertheless, since he explicitly said it is a promissory note and his giving it is in the form of giving a promissory note, it is not a get until he subsequently says to her while the get is still in her hand, "This is your get," or informs the witnesses in advance that his intention is for it to be a get, but out of embarrassment, he tells her it is a promissory note. In such a case, even if he was not speaking with her about the matter of the get, she is divorced as will be explained in section 138. And the words of our master the Rema are based on this, that he wrote to inform the witnesses, for indeed it is certainly sufficient to inform the witnesses regarding the essence of the get, as we do not require her consent. Nevertheless, if she does not know she is divorced, she will return to him, and from the Torah, we need her to be sent away and not return (Yevamot 113b). And his words are accepted by all opinions (and the words of the Ba'er Hetev section 3 and the Gra section 10 require further examination as I wrote in section 7).

Even though saying "this is your get" is sufficient, nevertheless, ideally, he should say to her "this is your get, accept this get, and you are hereby divorced by it from me from now, and you are permitted to any man." This is explained later in the order of the get in Siman 154. All this is to clarify matters: that it is a mitzvah for her to receive it and that he is divorcing her from now and not from tomorrow. The phrase "you are permitted to any man" is because this is the essence of the get, and even in Talmudic times, they were accustomed to say so (Tosafot Gittin 78a, s.v. "eino"). The main thing is that the husband needs to understand the meaning of the words he says to her, and likewise, everything he says to her should be explained clearly (Rema). Therefore, our custom is that when the husband says these words, we interpret each statement in the spoken language so that both he and she understand, and there is no doubt in this matter. We also have the custom of folding the get like a letter and giving it to her so that she can hold the entire paper in her hand. For if he were to give it to her unfolded, she would hold only its edges, and the husband would hold it above her hands while she extends her hands and brings one hand close to the other with the hands open at the top. The two witnesses stand right beside them, and the rabbi who arranges the get instructs the husband to say the order of "this is your get, accept it, etc." and explains the words in the spoken language, speaking directly and looking at her face as if speaking directly to her. After completing all the words, he gives the get into her hands, and she closes her hands and raises the get above her head, places the get under the garment on her chest, and walks around the house with the get, walking not less than four cubits. She then hands the get to the court, and they read it again as explained, and then they tear the get as will be explained later in the order of the get.

It is written: "and he shall send her out from his house," and not that she should send herself out (Kiddushin 5a). This means that the woman is the acquisition of the husband, and not the husband the acquisition of the wife. Therefore, just as in marriage, he must say "Behold, you are betrothed to me," and not "Behold, I betroth myself to you" or "I am your husband," as stated in Siman 27, so too in divorce, he must separate her from him and not separate himself from her, such as by saying to her "I am not your husband" or similar expressions. The Tur wrote that it is not a valid get (divorce document) even to disqualify her for marrying a kohen. If he said to her such a phrase and spoke with her about the matter of the get, there is a disagreement. The Tur wrote that even in such a case, it is not a get at all. His reasoning is that this is worse than silence because he separates himself from her, and the Torah decreed that this is not effective. Some say that she is divorced, as it is certainly not worse than silence. Others say it is a doubtful divorce (Beit Yosef in the name of the Rosh). The primary opinion seems to be like the first opinion (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 2).

And these are the words of our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, in Section 3: When he gives her the get (bill of divorce), he should say to her, "Behold, you are divorced from me with this get and permitted to any man," or "Behold, you are sent away from me." And if his agent gives it to her, he should say, "Behold, you are divorced from so-and-so with this get, and behold, you are permitted to any man." And if he said to her, "I am not your husband, I am not your man," there is someone who says that it is not a get, even if he was speaking with her about matters of her get, as it is written, "and he sends her away," and not that he sends himself away. And there is someone who says that if he was speaking with her about matters of her get, it would be considered a doubtful divorce. And that which is written in Section 27 regarding betrothal, it only mentions the first opinion. It can be said that in the case of a get, there is concern for this opinion because within the get are written effective expressions, and possibly in such a case, at the very least, it would be a doubtful case (Beit Shmuel).

In truth, the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in the first chapter in this language: "How does one write for her? Behold, you are sent away. Behold, you are divorced. Behold, you are to yourself. Behold, you are permitted to any man," and similar expressions. She is divorced, and the essence of the get (bill of divorce) is: "Behold, you are permitted to any man." But if he wrote for her: "I am not your husband. I am not your betrothed. I am not your man," this is not a get, as it is stated: "And he sends her away," and not that he sends himself away. Similarly, one who writes to his wife: "Behold, you are a free woman," this is not a get. End of quote. Thus, he invalidated these expressions only in the writing of the get. And it also appears from the words of the Rif, of blessed memory, in the first chapter of Kiddushin (as the Ran, of blessed memory, wrote there) that our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in his great book that certainly they also agree that whenever he said these expressions, she is not divorced; but because in the Gemara (Gittin 85b) it was said these expressions on the Mishnah of the essence of the get: "Behold, you are permitted to any man," which they explained as referring to writing, they also explained these expressions as referring to writing. End of quote. And we must deliberate on this, for how do we know when the get is written properly and only in his speech he did not say as necessary, that the get should be entirely invalidated?

And even more so, his words are puzzling when he wrote that those expressions were stated regarding the Mishnah about the essence of the get (divorce document), but in truth, those expressions were not stated there at all. Rather, they are found in the first chapter of Kiddushin, as mentioned there. And regarding this Mishnah, it is only stated in the Gemara that if a man said to his wife, "You are free," it means nothing. And Rashi there explained that if he said to his wife to write in the get, "You are free," etc., then indeed, Rashi explicitly indicated that saying means writing, and it implies that the saying does not invalidate the get. However, one can say that in the case of saying "You are free," it certainly does not harm if the get is written correctly because it neither adds nor detracts. But if he says, "You are not my wife," it is worse because this is the opposite of what the Torah says, "He shall send her away." But even in this case, it is difficult to understand our master the Beit Yosef who wrote in section 4: "If he said to her, 'You are on your own,' it is a get, but if he said to her, 'You are free,' it means nothing." Why did he not explain that this is only if it is written in the get? Moreover, the Rambam included them in the same law as he wrote. Therefore, it is certain that our master the Beit Yosef holds that this phrase invalidates the get even if it is written correctly. And where did he get this from, since Rashi explicitly says the opposite? And it is true that in Kiddushin it is stated with this phrase, and similarly in Gittin: "He gave it to her and said, etc., 'You are not my wife, you are not my husband, you are not my betrothed,' there is no concern," implying that the saying invalidates. However, just as Rashi explained in Gittin regarding "You are free" that it means writing, we should also explain here. And furthermore, since the Rambam changed his wording from that of the Talmud, it seems that he intentionally wrote so, because otherwise, it is known that he always preserves the language of the Gemara. In conclusion, the words of our master the Beit Yosef are wondrous to me, and his words align with the opinion of the Rosh and the Tur, but according to Rashi and the Rif and the Rambam, it is certainly a doubtful get, and one should be stringent regarding the prohibition of a married woman (as it appears to me). And know that a minor who is divorced by her father, as mentioned in section 141, he needs to say, "Your daughter so-and-so is divorced from me, and she is permitted to any man" (Kenesset HaGedolah). And the phrase "I have no business with you" does not work in a get (Beit Yosef).

Our sages stated (Baba Batra 167b) that in a city where there are two men named Joseph, they do not divorce their wives except in the presence of one another. The reason is that we are concerned that since a man can write a get (divorce document) even if his wife is not with him, they might write a get for one Joseph, and he might take the get and deliver it to the wife of the other Joseph, whose name is the same as his wife's. Even though he is obligated to give it in the presence of witnesses, and they will know if she is his wife or not, it can be said that he will give it in the presence of witnesses who do not scrutinize carefully to see if she is his wife, since they know his name and her name and will not suspect that he is giving it to another man's wife. Therefore, when they come to testify that this woman was divorced, they will testify that this woman received a get from her husband, named so-and-so, and the court will not investigate whether they made a mistake. But because they decreed that they should not divorce except in the presence of one another, the court always investigates this matter, and the witnesses are careful (Tosafot there and the beginning of Chapter 3 of Gittin, see there well). They did not want to establish that the witnesses must recognize only by name that this woman is the wife of so-and-so, because this is not a good ordinance, as it would be difficult to find witnesses (there). This is the opinion of our teachers, the Tosafists, of blessed memory.

However, in Siman 120, Section 40, we explained that the witnesses must recognize that this is his wife, see there. Nevertheless, it can be said that in the case of two men named Yosef son of Shimon, we do not rely on this. Additionally, there is a concern that the ketubah might be collected a second time, as mentioned there. Therefore, even if a get (divorce document) is issued by the hand of one, she is not divorced until she brings proof that he divorced her in front of another or brings a document that this is the one who divorced his wife.

And there is a question about why our sages established this requirement that they must divorce in each other's presence. After all, we learn in the simple get (172b) concerning documents with two people named Yosef ben Shimon that they should write an identifying mark, meaning to write the name of the grandfather or whether he is a Kohen or Levi, etc. According to Rabbi Meir, who holds that the signatures of the witnesses are what finalizes the get, it is necessary to do this, for we require it to be evident within the document who is divorcing. Why do we not do the same according to our view, which follows Rabbi Eliezer who holds that the handing over of the get finalizes it, and we would not need them to divorce in each other's presence?

The answer is that, in truth, the Talmud means to say that according to Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that the handing over of the get finalizes it, we do not need this, and it suffices that they divorce in each other's presence. However, in reality, it is not so. The Rashba wrote (in the third chapter of Gittin) that even if an identifying mark is written to differentiate between them, we still do not rely on this, and it is specifically required that they divorce in each other's presence. The reason is that perhaps the witnesses of the handing over are not familiar with the identifying mark.

And know that there is an opinion which states that even for us, one must write a distinguishing mark to differentiate between each one. Although we follow the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer, nevertheless, ab initio, we should fulfill the requirements of the get (divorce document) also according to Rabbi Meir (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 4). And indeed, in many matters, we are concerned with the get even when it is not according to the strict law. However, after the fact, we do not worry about this, and if the get has already been given, she may remarry with it (ibid.). Nevertheless, there are those who say that even according to Rabbi Meir, it does not need to be explicitly evident from the document itself (Ran, chapter 3). It seems from the language of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) that we do not need to write a distinguishing mark for us, as the conditions themselves create the separation, since they did not mention this at all. However, in practice, it is explained from the words of our teacher, the Rema, in paragraph 6, that one must write a distinguishing mark, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

And likewise, it seems reasonable that the reason our Sages required that they divorce in each other's presence is when the names of their wives and the names of their wives' fathers are also identical. Otherwise, what concern is there? This is also written by the Tur, who says: "And if there is someone in the city whose name is the same as his, and his wife's name is the same as his wife's, he cannot divorce except in the presence of the other, lest he write a get (divorce document) and give it to the other's wife whose name is the same as his wife's, thus prohibiting her to her husband." Similarly, the Rambam writes in Chapter 2, Law 3; see there. This is also implied in the Talmud (beginning of Chapter 3); see there.

However, our teacher, the Rema, was stringent in this matter. He wrote that some say that if the names of the divorcing men are the same, even if the names of the women are different, nevertheless, they should write an identifying mark for the divorcer, either by his nickname or whether one is a Kohen and the other is not a Kohen. Therefore, it is customary to deliver the get (divorce document) in public, so that if there are two men in the city with the same names, the get will be witnessed. This is not a matter of strict law but rather a general stringency that is customary in divorce matters, as it is customary to be stringent in many things related to gittin (divorce documents). The reason is that perhaps one of them has another wife with the same name as the other man's wife (Beit Shmuel). And although it is forbidden for us to marry two women, nevertheless, perhaps he transgressed and took two wives. All of this is merely a stringency. According to the law, he also agrees that it is not necessary (as mentioned above, and the words of the Beit Shmuel, section 4, are not clear to me). Furthermore, it seems clear to me that in such a case, only an identifying mark is required, and not that they should divorce in each other's presence. For if we say that they must divorce in each other's presence, how could we rely on divorcing in public? Perhaps one is not present. Rather, it is certainly merely an added precaution. This is also implied in the Terumat HaDeshen, section 6.

The Ritva writes (at the end of the first chapter of Bava Metzia): I have a difficulty. Since there are two men named Yosef ben Shimon established in the city, how can one write a get (divorce document) for a man when his wife is not with him, to send it through a messenger? One can say that this applies when the witnesses do not recognize the wife, but if they do recognize her, then certainly he can divorce her without the presence of the wife of the other man, etc. And here, due to the concern of a woman becoming an agunah (a chained wife who cannot remarry), the Rabbis were lenient, so that if the messenger recognizes her, he can give it to her, and they rely on him as if he were two witnesses. This is what we say about two men named Yosef ben Shimon living in one city. However, when they are not living there at the time of the divorce, the Rabbis were lenient to allow the get to be given through a messenger who recognizes her or that it should not be given to her except in the presence of witnesses who recognize her. This seems correct to me, and so did our teacher instruct us. And from his words, it is clear that he holds like the opinion of the Tosafot that we wrote in paragraph 15 and not like what we wrote in paragraph 16 and in Siman 120, paragraph 40. It also becomes clear from his words that there is no need for a distinguishing mark to differentiate between them, because otherwise, this would not be a question at all why they were lenient through a messenger, even though they are stringent also in this matter as we wrote in paragraph 17. And indeed, I am puzzled as to why we need to be lenient in this matter, since it is possible to do so with a distinguishing mark (and see Tosafot at the beginning of Gittin, s.v. derabbanan, and examine it well).

Our Sages taught in the Mishnah (Beitzah 36b): We do not judge, sanctify, perform chalitzah, or perform yibbum on Shabbat and Yom Tov due to the decree that one may come to write. All the more so, we do not divorce on Shabbat and Yom Tov because the essence of a get (divorce document) involves writing, and therefore it was not included in the Mishnah (Ran there). Moreover, it follows logically that if these actions, which are mitzvot, are prohibited, all the more so a get, which is not a mitzvah, as stated in Siman 119, Se’if 8. And in the Tosefta there, it is also taught that we do not divorce on Shabbat and Yom Tov. 

Even if the get was written before Shabbat and it is not dated earlier, such as being written for the current month or to be sent by a messenger, nevertheless, the Sages permitted it if the situation necessitates it, such as if he is ill and his illness has taken a turn for the worse, and he wishes to divorce her to exempt her from chalitzah. If the get was written before Shabbat, the Sages permitted him, if the get is in his possession, to transfer ownership of the place where the get is located along with the get to her, thus making the get in her possession. They did not permit moving it and giving it to her by hand because the get is muktzeh (set aside, prohibited to move on Shabbat), as anything not usable on Shabbat is considered muktzeh. The get is only usable for divorce, which is prohibited on Shabbat. Although it could be used to cover a bottle, it is still considered muktzeh because before the divorce, one would not use it for other purposes to avoid damaging it, making it akin to muktzeh due to monetary loss, which is the most stringent form of muktzeh. Therefore, they permitted the transfer of the place, which is also a rabbinic prohibition of moving muktzeh, as we find that the Sages were very strict about the prohibition of muktzeh more than other rabbinic prohibitions (see Shabbat 94b in Rashi s.v. Le'afukei and examine carefully).

One should not ask that since they permitted him to divorce, it should not be muktzeh, for indeed, just because they permitted something to a sick person does not change the status of the object. All this applies when it is possible without moving the get. But if it is not possible, such as if it is not in his domain, they permitted him to take it by hand and give it to her (Gittin 77b and see the Rosh there). Rabbi Rema wrote that some say that nowadays, when we write the Oral Torah, it is permitted to move a get on Shabbat, for one can learn many laws from it and can give it to her in any manner. And an objection is raised, for in the Gemara there the incident was with Rava, and it was already permitted in his days to write the Oral Torah. One can answer that this opinion holds that there the get was in a different place and needed to be transferred through a public domain, and therefore Rava required transferring the place and not because of the prohibition of moving (as indeed the Rosh there wrote in the name of the Rashbam) (even though its source is from the Mordechai and he holds otherwise, nevertheless Rabbi Rema brought it according to the opinion of the Rashbam).

He must release her with a complete release without any reservation. There are thirteen sections on this:

The Torah calls a divorce document a "book of separation," and therefore the divorce document must separate them so that she does not remain connected to him in any marital matters at all. Therefore, if a man divorces his wife and says to her at the time of giving the divorce document, "Behold, you are permitted to all men except for a certain man," whereby she would remain prohibited to that man as if she were still married, or "except for a certain man," both expressions have the same intent. Similarly, if he says "except for a certain man," it is not a valid divorce document and she is forbidden to remarry. However, regarding the priesthood, she is disqualified (from marrying a priest). If he (the husband) is a priest, he is forbidden to take her back, and if he dies, she is prohibited from marrying a priest because regarding priesthood, even the scent of a divorce disqualifies, as it is stated in Siman 6, see there. And explicitly, it is stated in the Talmud (Gittin 84b) that even though in the Jerusalem Talmud (Gittin 9:1) there is a dispute about this, in our Talmud it is a clear law that the scent of a divorce disqualifies for the priesthood (The Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 1, writes that in the Jerusalem Talmud it is stated that it is not a divorce even for the priesthood, see there. And indeed, even in the Jerusalem Talmud, there is a dispute about this, see there. And in the Rashba’s commentary, it is explained that there are those who do not hold this opinion, and pay attention to this matter).

If someone writes in a get (Jewish bill of divorce) the phrase "except for so-and-so," the get is invalid even if this phrase is written after the essential part of the document, and it has no validity at all, as will be explained in section 147. Even if this phrase is said verbally before the essential part is written, the get is also invalid. The manner of its invalidity, whether completely or doubtfully, will be explained there, with God's help.

Conversely, if the get is written correctly and after writing but before giving it, the husband says that he does not wish to permit her to marry so-and-so, and at the time of giving the get he does not mention this and says to her generally, "You are permitted to any man," the get is completely valid. However, if he mentions this restriction at the time of giving the get, it does not entirely invalidate the get. What should be done? The Sages there have said that he should take the get back from her and give it to her again, saying, "You are permitted to any man." The early authorities explained that this specific phrase must be used, but if he says, "This is your get," it is not effective because once he said "except for so-and-so," it could be thought that this is still his intention. Therefore, it is necessary to explicitly say, "You are permitted to any man" to nullify his previous words (Ran). This is also implied by the language of the Tur.

However, Maimonides, in chapter 8, halacha 17, wrote that it is sufficient to say, "This is your get," and he holds that the Sage's use of this particular phrase is not exclusive. There is no concern that his intention remains with his previous words; otherwise, why would he take back the get from her? It is certainly his intention to permit her to any man.

And one should not ask why it is necessary to take it from her and return it to her and say at the time of its return "You are hereby, etc." and why he cannot say it to her while the get is still in her hand from the first giving, similar to when he gives it to her while she is asleep or when he gives it to her as a document of loan, where it is necessary to say to her afterward "You are hereby, etc." and there is no need to take it back from her, as will be explained in Siman 138. This has already been questioned in the Gemara there (84b), and they answered that it is not comparable because in those cases the initial giving is nothing, but here the first giving was effective in disqualifying her from marrying a kohen, as it is written. Therefore, if he does not take it back from her, the declaration would not be effective since she has already acquired it for the purpose of disqualification from the priesthood. But in those other cases, she has not acquired it for anything (Rashi). And even though, on the contrary, since with the first giving she acquired it for the purpose of disqualification from the priesthood, the power of this get has been weakened, and how can he divorce her again with it, since a woman cannot be divorced twice with one get? One can answer that indeed, if he had given it to her only for the purpose of disqualification from the priesthood, we would say so, but he gave it to her to permit her to everyone, and his words were not fulfilled because he said "except for so-and-so," which is not a valid severance. Therefore, the first giving is not yet complete, and it is considered as one giving. However, since there was still some benefit in the giving concerning the disqualification from the priesthood, it is not sufficient without taking it back and giving it again (I learned this from the words of the Rashba in his commentary there). (And what the Talmud says, "since she acquired it," is not precise because if so, what benefit would there be in the return.)

All this applies specifically when he says "except for so-and-so," but if he says "on the condition that you do not marry so-and-so," since he did not use the language of "except," which would imply a reservation in the get (divorce document), but rather used the language of condition, it is like any other condition, such as "on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz," and the get is valid. This is the opinion of the Rambam, Ra'ash, and Tur, as is clearly implied by the conclusion of the Talmud (beginning of chapter 9). Not only in the case where he says "on the condition that you do not marry him," where he only made a condition regarding marriage but in terms of fornication, she would not be considered to him like a married woman, and thus it is a complete severance from his marriage, but even if he says to her "on the condition that you do not have intercourse with him" or "on the condition that you do not be with him," where she is not permitted to him in any way, nonetheless, since he used the language of condition, it is not a reservation in the get but merely a condition like any other conditions. See what I wrote in paragraph 10.

However, there are some of our Rabbis who are stringent in this matter and hold that it is not explicitly proven from the Talmud that this is the definitive law. It is considered a doubtful case in matters of rabbinic law, and we follow the stringent view (Rashba in the name of Ramban, Ra'ah, and Ri'az). Even in a case where it is conditional that she should not remarry, it is a doubt, and certainly, one should be stringent regarding a prohibition related to a married woman. Therefore, if the husband suspects someone of having an interest in his wife, he should be careful not to say anything during the giving of the get (divorce document) either explicitly or conditionally. Instead, he should inform the court, and they will ensure that the person he suspects does not marry her after he divorces her. Even Rambam, who permits a condition that she should not remarry a particular person, holds that this is only for a set period, such as up to fifty years, or something similar. However, if it is indefinite, implying forever, the get is invalid. There are those who disagree with him, and it will be clarified in Siman 143 with the help of Heaven.

If this individual who said "except for so-and-so" regarding the get (divorce document) refers to someone with whom marriage is not valid for him, such as if she is a forbidden relative incurring karet (excision) or even a forbidden relative by a negative commandment where marriage is not valid, like a slave or similar, the get is valid. This is because this does not constitute an exclusion in the get, since without his exclusion, marriage with that individual is not valid. Excision only applies in matters where there is a possibility of a valid marriage (Yerushalmi). Therefore, if there is a possibility of a valid marriage with her, even if she is forbidden to him, whether due to priestly prohibitions, such as a widow to a High Priest, a divorcee to a regular priest, or a zonah (harlot) and chalalah (disqualified priestly lineage), or due to general prohibitions for all Jews from a negative commandment, such as a mamzer (illegitimate child) or netin (Gibeonite), or an Ammonite or Moabite convert, or an Egyptian or Edomite, since there is a possibility of valid marriage with her, it is considered an exclusion and the get is invalid. This is an explicit Mishnah (Chapter 5).

And if this person was of limited understanding, his betrothal does not take effect, and only when he grows up does it become valid, and the get (bill of divorce) is invalid. This is the opinion of most of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). There are those who say that she is doubtfully divorced. This dispute depends on the version of the Talmud there, whether the question was resolved or not. Similarly, if he said to her, "except for one who is yet to be born," since he is not yet in the world, it is a question that remains unresolved according to all opinions. Even if he exempted an unborn child who would be male, it remains doubtful. Likewise, if he exempted the sister's husband, who is currently forbidden to him (as she is his wife's sister), and if the sister dies and he can marry her, it is a question that is unresolved according to all opinions. This is not similar to exempting his brother, which is considered in the Mishnah there, as he is also suitable if this one dies without children, and he must perform levirate marriage. It is not considered an exemption. Certainly, it is not considered so, because once he divorces her, she cannot come to levirate marriage and remains forbidden as his brother's wife. Furthermore, since he will die, she is then permitted to his brother, and all the days of his life, she is forbidden to his brother, hence it is not a valid get, similar to the condition "that you will not drink wine all my life," which is not considered a valid severance according to one Talmudic opinion (Yoma 13b). Even though we do not rule this way in practice, as I wrote in Siman 143, nonetheless here it is worse, since all the days of his life, it is not considered an exemption in the get, unlike in the case of the wife's sister. (This is my humble opinion).

And similarly, if he said to her, "except for your adultery," meaning that she is permitted to marry, but for adultery, she would be treated as a married woman, this too is a doubt, since she is still bound to him regarding adultery. Or maybe, since for marriage she has separated from him, this is not considered a reservation. And similarly, if he said to her, "except for not in the usual manner," it is also a doubt. And similarly, if he said to her, "except for your inheritance, except for your terumah, except for the annulment of your vows," meaning that regarding the marital relationship he divorces her completely, except that he reserves the right to inherit her when she dies, or if he was a Kohen that she would eat terumah (according to the Tosefta), or that he would have the ability to annul her vows, this too is a doubt. And similarly, if he reserved "except for the document and intercourse," meaning that she would not be betrothed except with money, this too is a doubt, for all of these are questions that were not resolved in the Talmud there.

And know that in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 7, Halacha 3), it implies that if he divorces her and retains for himself her earnings or the consumption of her fruits, it is considered a retention in the get (divorce document). According to this, it seems that it would be a doubt like all other doubts we have explained. However, in our Talmud, this is not considered at all, and the Talmud only considers matters of Torah law. It is possible that her earnings and fruits, since they are only by rabbinic decree, are not considered a retention at all and are merely a monetary condition. Further investigation is required for the ruling (and see there in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 9, Halacha 2, in Shabbat, beginning of the Halacha "but"). It is also possible that regarding retention, the Jerusalem Talmud also agrees that it is not a retention, as the Jerusalem Talmud there speaks concerning another matter. Nevertheless, for the ruling, one should be stringent.

And this that we have written, that if he reserved her for licentiousness, it is a doubt; nevertheless, conversely, if he reserved her for marriage and permitted her for licentiousness, this is not a doubt but certainly a reservation (Beit Shmuel, section 5), for the primary intent is marriage. However, if he reserved someone who is forbidden to him, it is not considered a reservation, as we have written, even if he reserved her for licentiousness. For licentiousness pertains to him as well, it is not considered a reservation (ibid.), for all his reservation is only for licentiousness, since marriage does not apply to him. But according to the conclusion of the Talmud there, there is much to ponder on this (as it says there, perhaps if he transgressed and married her, and see Beit Shmuel and it requires further examination, and study it well).

He said to her, "You are permitted to every man except Reuven and Shimon," and then he took the get (divorce document) from her and handed it back to her and said, "You are permitted to Reuven and Shimon," this constitutes a doubtful divorce. The doubt arises whether his intention was to include Reuven and Shimon, or if perhaps her understanding reversed the matter, permitting her to Reuven and Shimon and forbidding her to the rest of the world (Gittin 82b). It seems that even if he later clarifies his intention, it does not help, as this is indicated in the Talmud, and in all cases, it remains doubtful. And although according to the Rambam in Chapter 8, it is certainly a valid get (for he rules according to the 'yesh omrim' following the opinion of the Geonim), nevertheless, most poskim (decisors of Jewish law) disagree with him, and his opinion is not brought in the Shulchan Aruch at all, because it is impossible to be lenient in matters of prohibited relationships (ishut) against the opinion of many of our early authorities.

Even according to the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, nevertheless, if at the second instance when he gave it to her he said to her, "Behold, you are permitted to Shimon," it would be a doubt, because perhaps he did not permit her to Reuven, or it is possible that his intention was also for Reuven, and he only mentioned Shimon because he had mentioned him previously. And since he nullified his last statement, all the more so the first one. Therefore, it remains a doubt. And even if he said "also to Shimon," it is still a doubt whether his intention was "also to Shimon and all the more so to Reuven," or "also to Shimon" includes everyone in the world except Reuven, who remains prohibited. And if he subsequently said in his second delivery "to Reuven," the Rambam ruled that it is not a definite divorce, because he only permitted her to Reuven and not to Shimon (even according to the above opinion), as it is only when Shimon is mentioned last that we can say his intention was all the more so for Reuven who was mentioned first, which is not the case in the reverse. However, according to most of the poskim, it remains a doubt in all the laws that we have explained. And similarly, if in his second delivery he said "also to Reuven," it is also a doubt like "also to Shimon" (Tosafot there in chapter three). This also seems to be the implication from the Rambam there in law eight, see there.

If he divorces her for a future time, for example, if he says to her, "You are divorced after thirty days," she is divorced when the time arrives. There are many detailed laws regarding this, which will be explained in Siman 146. However, in the opposite case, where he divorces her for the present time but not for the future, there is a dispute among the halachic authorities. The Rambam (Maimonides) in Hilchot Gerushin, Chapter 8, Halacha 9, writes: "If he stipulates and says, 'Today you are not my wife, and tomorrow you are my wife,' she is not divorced, even though he has severed the marital bond today. Therefore, in a get (divorce document), we write, 'from this day and forever.'" This correction is found in the Talmud (Gittin 85b). And even though earlier (on 83a) there was a question resolved that once the bond is severed, it is severed forever, and for this reason, Rosh ruled that she is fully divorced. The phrase "from this day and forever" is included in a get to exclude this ruling, as stated there, to enhance the get so that no doubt is cast upon it. But from a strictly legal perspective, this is not necessary, as Rashi explains there. Nevertheless, the Rambam does not agree with this and holds that since the Talmud states to exclude this ruling, it indicates that this is the definitive law. This is also implied by the Rif. Consequently, since there is a dispute among the halachic authorities, it is considered a doubtful divorce. This is what Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in the Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 148:5: "If he says to her, 'Here is your get, and you are divorced from me today, and tomorrow you are my wife,' she is doubtfully divorced." This is also agreed upon by the earlier authorities (such as the Ran and the Maggid Mishneh). Some wish to say that the doubt arises because we do not know his intention—whether he intended to divorce her completely today and remarry her tomorrow, or whether she should not remain divorced at all. However, this is baseless; the doubt arises due to the differing opinions among the halachic authorities regarding the Talmudic passages. This is what the Beit Shmuel means in his commentary. Additionally, in the Jerusalem Talmud, Kiddushin, Chapter 3, Halacha 1, it is explicitly stated like the Rambam.

The Law Regarding the Manner in Which a Get (Bill of Divorce) Is Transferred from His Hand to Hers. It Contains 26 Sections:
Even though it is written, "he shall write her a bill of divorce and place it in her hand," the giving by the husband is not comparable to the receiving by the wife. For in the case of the wife’s receiving, even if she did not take it directly in her hand but it was placed in her domain, she is divorced, as will be explained in Siman 139. We have explained the reason in the beginning of Siman 136, because it does not say "and he shall place it in her hand," and "her hand" implies her domain, as in "and he took all his land from his hand." We only require that it be similar to her hand, which is guarded with her knowledge, as mentioned there. However, his giving must be directly from his hand or from his agent, who is like him. If he placed the get in his own domain and said, "Take this get from my domain," it is nothing. Similarly, our Sages said (Gittin 78a), "Take your get from the ground," it is nothing, even if the ground is his. From the fact that it says "and he shall place," it clearly implies that he needs to place it, not that she should take it, as with the sprinkling of the blood of sacrifices, where it says "and he shall place" and it must be done by hand, as explained there, that he should take it with his finger. Similarly, in the guilt offering of a leper, it says "and the priest shall place" and it must be done by hand. This is not comparable to the giving of priestly gifts, where the term "and he shall give" is used, such as "and he shall give to the priest the shoulder, etc.," where it does not require giving by hand specifically, because there it means a gift. Therefore, it requires the measure of giving, which is not the case with the giving of a get, which does not mean a gift, for even if it was written on something prohibited for benefit, it is valid (as explained in Tosafot Gittin 20b, s.v. dilma). Similarly, the giving of the blood of sacrifices does not mean a gift, and therefore it specifically requires giving by hand, directly by the body.

And there is a significant question regarding this matter. It has already been clarified in Siman 136 that they permitted a person on their deathbed to divorce on Shabbat by transferring ownership of the domain where the get (divorce document) is placed, and the domain is transferred along with the get as one. This is explicitly stated in the Gemara (beginning of chapter 8), and indeed, it is not handed directly to him. One cannot say that this is only rabbinically ordained and that they were lenient for a person on their deathbed, as our sages explicitly said that if someone says "take your get from the ground," it is not valid, which implies this is a Torah law. This is also clarified by all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). And our rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote regarding this matter of transferring ownership of the domain that this is not similar to "take your get from the ground" because since the get goes from the husband's domain to her domain, it is as if he gave it to her. End of quote. And this needs investigation, because is her domain better than her hand? For if she takes it into her hand from his domain, it is not effective, so how would it be effective for it to come into her domain from his domain? We must say that their intention is that since the domain itself comes into her domain along with the get, it is better than if she had taken it into her hand from his domain, where the domain itself did not enter her hand (and their intention is that the domain comes into her domain).

And the reason for this is indeed so, for we must scrutinize why the Torah decreed that her domain be like her hand, while his domain is not like his hand. Rather, it is certain that his domain is also like his hand. The reason it does not help if she takes from his domain is because the Torah decreed that he must give her the get (divorce document) and not that she should take it from him. Therefore, when the domain is transferred to her domain together with the get, it is as if he gave her the domain along with the get, and it is as if it was given into her hand because his domain is like his hand. For this reason, it does not help even if she took it from his hand or his body unless he performed an act of giving, such as bringing his body or hand closer to her. And all this is because we require that he give and not that she take for herself, as will be explained before us with God's help (and the Pnei Yehoshua there remains in question regarding the words of Tosafot, see there).

Even if the get (bill of divorce) was placed on his hand and she was standing next to him and took the get from his hand, it is not a valid get because he did not assist in giving it, as we explained that we require him to give it and not her to take it. However, if he brought his hand close to her, it is considered a valid get since he performed an action by bringing his hand close, which is like giving it. There is an opinion that just bringing his hand close is not sufficient, as we require both bringing his hand close and assisting in her taking it (Bach). In truth, there is a dispute among the early authorities on this matter. The Rashba and Ran wrote that when he brings his hand close to her and she takes it, it is a valid get (refer to chapter 88). The Rosh (ibid, section 5) wrote that according to the Ri, if his hand was open and he brought it close to her and she took it, it is not a valid get because we require both that he assists in her taking it and that he brings the get close to her, as discussed there.

And the explanation of the matter regarding the reasoning behind their dispute, it seems to me, is as follows: The Torah decreed that he must give her the get (divorce document) and not that she should take it from him, as it is written. Similarly, the Rambam wrote in Chapter 1, Law 12. Therefore, it is necessary that an act of giving be performed. Those who validate the proximity of his hand hold that this constitutes an act with his body by bringing his body closer to her. However, those who invalidate it hold that the proximity of the body is not considered an act. There is proof for this from what our Sages said (Sifri Chapter 5 and Zevachim 105b) that a deficiency in proximity is not considered a deficiency in action, and consequently, proximity is not considered an act. Those who validate it argue that even though it is not an act, it is still considered giving. Our master, the Beit Yosef, seems to fundamentally hold the opinion of the Rosh, see there.

And similarly, if his hand was closed with the get (bill of divorce) inside it, and he opened his hand and she took it from inside, even so it is not a valid get. For although he assisted in her taking it by opening his hand, since he did not bring his body closer to her, it is ruled by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 1, that this is not a valid get according to all opinions. The reason is that although he performed an action with his body, nevertheless, this is not considered an action with the get itself, and in the end, she is the one who took the get. However, if he opened his hand and brought his body closer to her, then the opening is considered an action with the get due to his proximity to her. And this is the opinion of the Rosh that we mentioned, which requires two conditions: that he assists her in taking it and also that he brings the get closer to her. The intention is that he assists her in taking it by opening his hand, but this alone is not considered an action with the get. And since he brought his hand closer to her, it follows that the opening of the hand is considered an action with the get.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 1: If the get (divorce document) is stuck under his belt on his waist, and he tightens his waist and it becomes loosened, and he leans towards her and she takes it, it is considered as if he gave it to her. But if he tightens his waist without leaning towards her, or if he leans towards her without tightening his waist, it is not considered a giving. And there is an opinion that if the get was tied to his hand or his thigh, and he bends towards her with his body or extends his hand until she pulls the get off him and he says to her, "This is your get," it is considered a valid get.

Explanation of the matter: Certainly, what is written "and he shall place it" is not specifically meant to be in his hand, and the same applies if he placed it with any other part of the body; it is also considered placing, for what difference does it make? Therefore, when the get (divorce document) is stuck under his belt, if he tightens his belt and does not lean himself towards her, even though he performed an action with his body, it is not considered an action with the get, like opening his hand as explained. And similarly, if he leaned himself but did not tighten his belt, it is merely an approach and not an action. This is like having an open hand and bringing himself closer to her, which does not help according to the Rosh.

But if he tightens his belt and also leans himself towards her, it is like a closed hand that opens and brings his hand towards her; this is considered placing. And all of this is according to the Rosh. Consequently, according to the Rashba, he agrees with the Rosh if he tightens his belt and does not lean himself. But if he leans himself towards her and does not tighten his belt, he holds that it is considered placing, like bringing his hand closer with an open hand as explained.

Consequently, the same law applies when the get is tied on his hand or on his thigh, and he bends towards her with his body or tilts his hand until she pulls the get from him. This is like bringing his hand closer with an open hand; according to the Rashba, it is considered placing, and according to the Rosh, it is not. It is explained that there is an opinion that argues even on leaning himself without tightening his belt, but on tightening without leaning, he does not argue.

This is why he did not write the opinion of "some say" on leaning himself without tightening his belt. And why should he depict this law when it is tied on his hand or thigh? Because this is the language of the Rambam, as explained. And it appears that the Rambam holds like the Rashba, and therefore it is written in the language of the Rambam. From this, we also learn about the law of leaning himself without tightening his belt, that both are the same.

And these are the words of the Rambam, may his memory be blessed, in Chapter 1, Law 12: A get (bill of divorce) that was lying on the ground and he said to her, "Take your get from the ground," and she took it, or it was tied to his hand or his thigh and she pulled it off from him, even though he said to her after it came into her hand, "This is your get," it is not a valid get, as it is stated, "and he shall place it in her hand," and not that she should take it by herself. And behold, neither he nor his agent gave it to her. But if he inclined his body to her or extended his hand until she pulled the get off from him and he said to her, "This is your get," it is a valid get. End of quote. And from this, our teacher the Beit Yosef learned that his opinion is like that of the Rashba, may his memory be blessed, as he wrote, and so did the Tur hold in the opinion of the Rambam, see there.

And the Tur writes: "But if he holds the get (bill of divorce) by one end and extends it to her, and she takes it from the other end, it is considered a valid get." End of quote. This means, even according to the Rosh, the reason being that there are two actions involving the get itself in this case: he holds it by one end and also brings the get closer to her by extending it. Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, in his major work, holds that this is considered only as bringing it closer and not as an action involving the get. Therefore, he wrote there that according to the Tur, even according to the Rosh, who requires two actions, this is only in a case where she needs assistance to take it. But if she does not need assistance for taking it, such as in this case where bringing it closer alone suffices.

And in the Shulchan Aruch, this matter was not mentioned. According to this, it is difficult to understand from where it is known that Rambam holds like the Rashba. Perhaps, in his own ruling, even the Rosh would agree that no assistance is needed in taking it (Bach). However, it can be said that if it is tied to his hand, it certainly needs assistance because it is tied (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 2). But in truth, his words are puzzling. For by holding it by one end so that she takes it from the other end, it is considered assistance in taking it, and there are two actions (Bach). This is not comparable to the case where the get is placed in his open hand, where he did no action involving the get. But by holding it by one end, it is indeed considered assistance and an action involving the get. Moreover, according to what has been written, it does not depend at all on whether assistance is needed or not, but rather this is the fundamental law: that bringing it closer alone is not considered giving. (Especially since we brought clear evidence from the Talmud in section 5 that bringing it closer is not considered an action, see there).

Some interpret the words of the Tur to mean that he holds one end of the get (divorce document) and extends it into the hollow of her hands, and before he releases the get from his hand, she grasps the other end, so that even if she does not take it, the get is in her hand by virtue of his giving it (Tur 503). However, it cannot be said this way, for if so, it is a complete giving, and what is the Tur teaching us? What relevance does this have to the cases previously explained, which are all inferior forms of giving? Rather, it is certain that this too is an inferior form of giving, and if she had not taken hold of the other end, the get would not have reached her hand, as he holds one end and not over the hollow of her hands. This is also how the commentators of the Tur understand it, and this is the main interpretation (and the Tur 503 wants to reconcile the words of the Beit Yosef this way, but it cannot be said so, for the Beit Yosef states that here there is only proximity and not a complete giving, as explained there, while according to the Tur 503, it is a complete giving).

The matter is clear that if one declares "Your get is null" when it is placed on the ground, and similarly in all the laws that have been clarified where this does not constitute a giving, the husband must take the get back from her hand and give it to her again with a complete giving and say at the time of giving, "This is your get." And in a case where we have said that it is considered a giving, such as when her hand was closed and she opened it and brought her hand near, or when he tightened his loins and leaned his body towards her, or according to the opinion that mere closeness is effective—even if he did not say to her at the time he brought his hand or body closer, "This is your get," but said it after she had taken the get, it is still effective, for the statement "This is your get" is effective even after the get has come into her hand (Ra"n, Chapter 8).

However, what has been clarified in Siman 136, that when they are engaged in matters of the get, the statement is not essential at all, and even if he gave it to her in silence, it is still a get, this is only with a complete giving and not with the deficient givings that have been clarified (there). And the reason is clear, for when he gave it to her directly from his hand to hers and they were discussing the matters of the get, it is indeed like saying "This is your get." But in a deficient giving, such as when he tightened his loins and leaned his body and she took it, the action does not prove the finality of the get, and perhaps he did it in jest. Therefore, if he explicitly said after she received it, "This is your get," it proves that it was the finality of the get. But if he did not say anything, the action does not prove that it was intended as the finality of the get, and in any case, in practice, one should be stringent even if he did not say anything, and in deficient givings when they are engaged in matters of the get (Avnei Shoham, Siman 1, and according to what I have written, even the Rambam would agree with this reasoning, and in practice, it should be treated as a doubtful divorcee, and pay attention carefully).

Know that there are those who want to say that if one declares "Your get is null" when it is placed on the ground, it is as if he said nothing, yet in any case, she is disqualified for the priesthood, for it is no less than the smell of the get which disqualifies for the priesthood (Bach in the name of Mahari"l, and so wrote Knesses HaGedolah). And there are those who say that if her hand was closed and she opened it and he leaned his hand towards her, there is no need for a statement and being engaged in that matter is effective. And what has been clarified, that a statement is specifically needed, is only in the case where he tightened his loins and brought his body closer (Beit Shmuel, end of Siman 2). And one cannot say so, for according to the reason we have explained, in any deficient giving, a statement is specifically needed, for without a statement, there is no proof that his intent was to finalize the giving of the get. And so wrote the great authorities (Atzei Tzvi, Siman 2, in the name of Bais Meir and Ginas Veradim). And in practice, one should be stringent and treat her as a doubtful divorcee (and what Beit Shmuel wanted to attribute to a scribal error in the Rosh requires further investigation).

It is obvious that when the husband gives the get (divorce document) into her hand, he must withdraw his hand from the get and not hold onto it. For if he still holds onto its edge, he is still attached to the get, and this is not a proper severance. Therefore, our Sages said (Gittin 78b) regarding a get that is tied with a string or cord, and he gives her the get while the string remains in his hand, if he can pull it and bring it back to himself—meaning that the string is strong and when he pulls the string, the get follows—it is not a valid divorce, for this is not a proper severance. But if not—meaning that the string is weak and thin, and if he pulls the get, the string will break and the get will remain in her hand—then she is divorced, and it is not considered as if he is holding the get. For the string is not part of the get and does not have the power to pull the get after him, and it is a proper severance.

There are differing opinions among the early authorities regarding this matter. Some say that it is specifically when the get (divorce document) is heavy and the string is so thin that even if the get is placed in her hand and she does not close her hand, the string will break upon pulling it. In this case, she is considered divorced. But if the get would follow the string when her hand is open, and she only closed her hand after he gave her the get, it is ineffective and is not considered a valid giving. The reason is that at the time of giving, it could have been pulled away, and her act of closing her hand was done by herself, making it akin to "take your get from the ground." Others say that this is indeed considered a proper giving since he initiated the giving, it is properly termed "and he gave," even though she completed the giving. (These two opinions are found in the Rosh, Ran, and Rashba, but in Tosafot, only the prohibitive opinion is mentioned. See there, and so too is it written in the Kesef Mishneh there.)

There is a need to explain the reasoning behind the two opinions. The opinion that permits holds that it is not worse than the deficient forms of delivery that have been explained, such as if he tightened his belt and leaned his body, and she took the get (divorce document). Since the primary act of taking was done by her, it is valid. All the more so in this case where he placed the entire get into her hand, and she merely completed the act of giving. Those who prohibit would argue that in this case it is worse, because as long as he can pull the get back to himself, it is not considered as giving at all. It turns out that until she closed her hand, it cannot be called giving at all. Therefore, when she closed her hand, she performed the entire act of giving. This is not similar to the case where he tightened his belt and leaned his body, where at the moment she took the get, he was performing an action by tightening and leaning. In contrast, at the moment she closed her hand, he was not doing anything. It is also not similar to the case where a man says to a woman, "This is your get, but you will not be divorced by it until after thirty days," where the effect of the divorce happens after thirty days, and at that time he did not place it in her hand. It must be said that since he gave it to her before the thirty days, it is considered giving even now. In that case, before the thirty days, it was a complete giving. Therefore, even if there is an interruption in between, when the time arrives and the get is in her hand, she is divorced by the initial giving. However, here initially there was no giving at all because as long as her hand was open, he could retract it. When she closed her hand, she performed the entire act of giving. (Rosh)

Behold, the Rosh and the Tur agreed with the words of those who prohibit, and consequently, according to most of our gittin (divorce documents) which are written on paper, if there is only a thin thread tied to the get and it is in her hand, it is not a get. For certainly, he can pull it back to himself, and the fact that she holds it tightly does not help, as it is written, unless her hand is clenched, and he thrusts the get into her hand with force, so that if he pulls the thread, it would break. Then she is divorced (Tosafot there), for he performed the entire act of giving, and she did nothing.

Therefore, all our Rabbis have written that one must be very careful when giving a get (bill of divorce) to ensure that the woman's hand is open until the entire get is placed in her hand, and he should not hold onto its end. Only afterwards should she close her hand. If she closes her hand before he has completely placed the get and is still holding onto its end, it is as if the get is in her hand and the string is in his hand, which does not constitute a valid get. Nevertheless, the Tosafot and the Mordechai wrote that in such a case, the get is valid after the fact (bediavad), as it is no worse than if he had tightened his belt and leaned his body, which has been clarified there. It is questionable whether they wrote this because they hold according to the opinion that permits if she closed her hand and the string is in his hand, as has been explained. According to the ruling of the Rosh and the Tur, even after the fact it would be invalid. Or it might be that even according to the opinion that prohibits, they allowed it in this case.

It would seem at first glance that this is only according to the opinion of those who permit it, since logically there is no difference between them. However, according to this, it is difficult because the Rosh and the Tur hold like those who invalidate it. And how did the Tur write that when the husband holds one end and she is at the other end and he extends it to her, it is considered a valid get (as written in section 10)? This is exactly the same law that when she holds the other end, one end is still in his hand and this is not considered a severance. And when he releases his end and she receives it, she has performed the entire act of giving, so how is she divorced? Indeed, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, is puzzled by this. It seems that for this reason he omitted the Tur's ruling in the Shulchan Aruch. Our teacher, the Rema, in his book Darkei Moshe, distinguishes between whether the grabbing was with the husband's consent or without his consent, because if it was with his consent, it is considered giving. According to this, it could be that what Tosafot and the Mordechai wrote—that it is valid after the fact—also applies according to those who invalidate it. Based on this, it is written in the Shulchan Aruch, section 2: "All of this only applies when she grabbed without the husband's consent. But if the husband instructed her to grab, and even if he extended the get to her and she took it from the other end, it is a valid get." However, this reasoning is perplexing because if the reason that in such a case it is not considered giving, then what does his consent help?

In my humble opinion, it seems appropriate to distinguish between these two cases. Indeed, if we say that the placement into her hand requires that her hand be open until he removes his hand from the get (bill of divorce), and not that she should hold one end of it while he holds the other end, then certainly the Sages should have clarified this. For most transfers occur in such a manner: when one person gives to another, this one holds one end of the object and the other holds the other end, and the giver removes his hand after the receiver has grasped it with his hand and fingers. Therefore, it is certainly called a valid giving, because as long as he holds one end of the get, it is not called giving at all, and it is still considered in his hand. When he removes his hand, the giving takes effect, and the removal of the hand itself is the act of giving as per common practice. This is not the case when the get is tied with a string, and the entire get is in her hand, and it does not help because of the string tied to it. Certainly, it does not help if he releases the string from his hand after she grasps it, because essentially, nothing has changed in the get. According to this, the words of the Tur do not contradict each other. According to this, the words of the Tosafot and Mordechai are also understandable, even according to those who prohibit, for these cases are not similar. And the Tosafot did not mention the opinion of those who permit at all, and even though some want to force their view that they brought both opinions, nevertheless, a careful examination will show that this is not the case (as the Ketzot HaChoshen writes in section 29). Also, the Bach wrote almost similar reasoning to reconcile the words of the Tur (see there). (The words of the Beit Shmuel are not clear to me.) Nevertheless, in practice, one should be stringent regarding the prohibition of a married woman, but in a case of potential agunah (a woman unable to remarry), perhaps one can be lenient. For even if we do not say so, we have many of our Rabbis' opinions who are lenient regarding a get tied with a string when she grasps it, and we have the opinion of Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) that with the husband's consent, it is indeed considered a valid giving. From the Rambam, there is no conclusive proof regarding this (see there, chapter 5, law 16).

If he gives her the get (bill of divorce) while she is asleep, the get is not finalized. For although we do not require her consent, she still needs to be aware that she is being divorced. And she is in a worse state than a deaf-mute woman, for a deaf-mute woman knows how to guard her get, but a sleeping woman has no awareness at all (Rosh, Chapter 8, Section 4). Therefore, it is not a valid get until she wakes up from her sleep and he tells her, "This is your get." There is no need to take it from her and give it back to her, for the giving was done by his hand. However, it does not take effect while she is unaware, and now that she is aware and knows that this is a get, he only needs to tell her that he is divorcing her. But it is necessary that the get be in her hand when she awakens and he tells her. If the get is not in her hand when she awakens, it is not a valid get until he takes it from her and gives it back to her and says, "This is your get." This seems logical, for the giving to her while she was asleep is not considered a giving since it fell from her hand when she woke up (ibid). However, if she takes it herself when she wakes up, it does not help, since it fell from her hand while she was asleep (Tur). And if it did not fall from her hand while she was asleep, he only needs to say to her, "This is your get," and without this, it is not effective. Even if he said to the witnesses, "See the get that I am giving her," it is nothing, even if the witnesses tell her afterward, it is not effective since she was asleep. Similarly, even if he talked to her about the matter of her get before she slept, it is nothing (Beit Yosef).

If he (the husband) gave the get (divorce document) to her agent, even if she is asleep at the time of its receipt, it is still a valid get since the agent is awake and he is considered as her. Otherwise, for every agent of receipt, we would need to ensure that she is awake at the time of receipt, and we do not find this requirement anywhere (Ran there). However, if he gave her the get in her courtyard while she is asleep, some say it is not a valid get, since the courtyard is considered an extension of her hand, and she needs to be awake as if she were receiving it in her hand. Additionally, the courtyard needs to be guarded with her knowledge, and furthermore, without her hand, there is no courtyard (Rashba, end of chapter 8). This is also the ruling of Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) in paragraph 3. Nevertheless, there are those who disagree (there in the name of his teacher), arguing that in truth, the courtyard is also considered an agent, as stated in the Talmud, and it is not inferior to an agent (Bava Metzia 12). Certainly, the courtyard must be guarded with her knowledge, and it can be guarded with her knowledge even while she is asleep if it is enclosed and locked with the key in her possession. Moreover, it is not applicable to say that she does not have a hand since she will have a hand when she awakens, and we can wake her from her sleep. It is not comparable to an insane person (as the reasoning of those who disagree is explained there). One should be stringent according to both opinions (although in Bava Metzia there it is explained in Rashi that for a get, it is only considered due to her hand, see there).

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (78a): If he said to her, "Take this document," and she read it and found that it was her get (divorce document), it is not a valid get until he says to her, "This is your get." Even if they had initially spoken about the matter of the get, it is ineffective (Ran), because without speaking about it or without saying "document," it is nothing (ibid.). The Talmud explains (55a) that if he first said to the witnesses, "See this get that I am giving her," and then gave it to her in their presence and said to her, "Take this document," she is divorced. The reason for this, the earlier authorities explained, is not because her intention is needed, but because when he says, "Take this document," we are concerned that perhaps his intention was not truly for it to be a get, and he does not intend to divorce her with this giving. However, when he first told the witnesses, "See this get that I am giving her," it clarifies that he gave it to her with the intent of it being a get so she would be divorced immediately upon this giving. The reason he said to her, "Take this document," was to avoid embarrassment, and once it becomes known to her that this is her get, she is divorced, even if they had not previously been involved in the matter of the get.

And from the words of the Rambam of blessed memory in Chapter 1, Halacha 9, we learn another reason for this, and thus he writes there: "And from where do we know that he must give it to her specifically as an act of divorce? As it is stated: 'a scroll of severance, and he shall place it in her hand' - he must give it to her as a scroll of severance. But if he gave it to her as a promissory note or a mezuzah, etc., it is not a get (divorce document). And if he subsequently said to her, 'Behold, this is your get,' it is a get. If he said to the witnesses, 'See, this is a get that I am giving to her,' and then said to her, 'Take this promissory note,' it is valid because he informed the witnesses that he is giving it as a get, and the reason he called it a promissory note is because he was embarrassed before her." End quote. And similarly, it is stated in the Sifrei (Deuteronomy, Pisqa 269): "And he shall place it in her hand and send her away from his house - until he says to her, 'This is your get.' From here they said, if one throws a get to his wife and says to her, 'Take this document,' etc., and she reads it and it is her get, it is not a get until he says to her, 'This is your get.'"

The practical difference between the previous reason and the reasoning of the Rambam is that, according to the previous reason, it is a doubtful divorce since we do not know whether his intention was for the sake of divorce or not. According to the Rambam, even if his intention was clear, it does not help until he explicitly tells her or the witnesses that he is giving it as a divorce, and this is a scriptural decree. In practice, it is clear that one should be stringent according to the first opinion. Perhaps the teaching from the Sifrei is merely an asmakhta (a scriptural support), as there are many teachings in the Sifrei that are only asmakhta (as Tosafot, Shabbat 91a). Nonetheless, all the laws in that section of the Sifrei are from the Torah.

Some say that the effectiveness of telling witnesses "See the divorce document that I am giving her" only applies if he did not say this to them in her presence. However, if he said it to them in her presence and afterward gave it to her and said, "Accept this promissory note," she is not divorced. This is certainly the case, for we see that he is not ashamed to tell her that he is giving her this divorce document. Since he later told her that it is a promissory note, perhaps he nullified his earlier statement and did not give it to her as a divorce document to effect her divorce now. Furthermore, it does not help even if he subsequently says to her, "Here is your divorce document," because we fear that he nullified the divorce document, and he is not using it to divorce her, as we explained in chapter 141. This is not similar to the case where he said, "Accept this promissory note," and did not first tell the witnesses, where it is effective if he says afterward, "This is your divorce document," because there we assume that he said so out of embarrassment, and we do not worry about the nullification of the divorce document. But here, there is no embarrassment, and perhaps he completely nullified it (Beit Shmuel, section 8). Therefore, the law regarding this divorce document is that she needs a second divorce document, and if she accepted betrothal from another man, she needs a divorce document from both men, and she is disqualified from marrying a Kohen if they die without giving her another divorce document (Tur in the name of the Ramah).

When he said to her, "Take this document of debt," it does not take effect until he says to her, "This is your get [divorce document]," as it is stated. There is no need to take the get from her hand and give it back to her, for it was a proper giving; it was only that he did not clarify that he was divorcing her. Nevertheless, the get must certainly be in her hand or in her possession when he subsequently says to her, "This is your get," for that is the main act of the get taking effect. And some say that specifically when he previously said, "Take this document of debt," there is no need to take it from her and give it to her again, for he only gave it to her for safekeeping. But if he said to her, "Acquire this document of debt," and she acquired it through the previous giving for the purpose of using it, it does not help if he subsequently says to her, "This is your get," unless he takes it from her hand and gives it back to her (there) and says to her, "This is your get." And even though she had acquired it, she consented to give it back to him.

The laws regarding the acceptance of the get into her hand or her possession. There are 53 sections in this:
