The phrase written in the Torah, "and he shall place it in her hand," is not to be taken literally as only her hand. The same applies if the get reaches her lap, her courtyard, or to her agent whom she has appointed, making his hand like her hand. This is what our Sages said (beginning of chapter 8): "Her hand" implies only her hand, but from where do we derive her roof, her courtyard, and her enclosed yard? The verse states, "and he shall place it," in any case. "Hand" here means possession, as it is written, "and he took all his land from his hand," as mentioned at the beginning of section 136. The Jerusalem Talmud derives this from the fact that "and he shall place it" is written twice in the section of the get. Even though anything a woman acquires, her husband acquires (since he eats the fruits of all her property), thus the get is still in his possession, this question has already been asked in the Talmud, and they answered that her get and her courtyard come simultaneously. This means that through the get, the possession of the courtyard comes to her together with the get. Evidence for this is that a slave also goes free with a deed, and how can he be freed by receiving the deed into his hand? For the hand of a slave is like the hand of his master. Rather, his deed and his hand come simultaneously, and here too, her get and her courtyard come simultaneously. This applies specifically to a courtyard of Nichsei Melug, but a courtyard that she brought to him as Nichsei Tzon Barzel, the get is not completed because it still lacks collection (Beit Shmuel and Beit Chadash). If he threw it into a courtyard of Nichsei Tzon Barzel, it seems to me that she is doubtfully divorced, for he can say, "Take your courtyard and your get."

And the Rambam wrote in the beginning of Chapter 5 that whether it is her courtyard that she owns, or a courtyard that is rented or borrowed by her, it is all considered her domain. Once the get (divorce document) reaches her domain, she is divorced. This is the end of his words. Similarly, it is written in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. And even though the sages said (Pesachim 6a) that rental is not a complete acquisition like sale, nevertheless, regarding acquiring an item in the rented place during the period of the rental, it certainly acquires, and it is explicitly stated in the Mishnah (Ma'aser Sheni Chapter 5, Mishnah 9) that it is possible to acquire in the rented courtyard anything placed there, and it acquires for him (according to Rashi in Bava Metzia 11b, s.v. "and its place"). This is also proven from several places. Someone raised an objection that the Rambam ruled in Chapter 6 of Rental that in a rented courtyard, the manure in the courtyard is acquired by the landlord. However, we have already explained with the help of Heaven in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 313, Section 6, that this is only regarding manure due to the reasons explained there, and not regarding other matters. It is clear that regarding acquisitions, the domain of the borrower and the renter acquires everything. (And the Ketzos HaChoshen also wrote similarly there. The words of the Shach there require further study. And with this, all that the Bais Meir wrote is resolved. Refer there and examine carefully.)

The courtyard has two modes of acquisition, through the principle of "hand" and through the principle of "agency." The Sages said (Bava Metzia 12a) that regarding a bill of divorce, since it is a detriment to her, it cannot be acquired through the principle of agency, as it is not agreeable to her to be her own agent. Therefore, it is acquired through the principle of "hand." And since the acquisition is through the principle of "hand," it must be like her hand, meaning she must be present in the courtyard and it must be guarded with her awareness, similar to her hand. Therefore, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: "When is this the case? When she is standing in her courtyard and it is guarded with her awareness. But if she is not standing there, even though it is guarded with her awareness, she is not divorced," as the Tur wrote, because we require it to be similar to her hand, as explained. And even though when she is standing there it is automatically guarded with her awareness, why did they need to state "and it is guarded with her awareness"? In truth, the Rambam did not mention this, because we can find a case where the courtyard is large, and she is in the east of the courtyard and the bill of divorce is in the west, and it is not guarded with her awareness (Beit Yosef). This specifically applies to a courtyard without partitions, but if it has partitions, it is considered guarded with her awareness even in such a case. There is proof for this from the Talmud (Gittin 77b), and this resolves the question of the Taz. Pay close attention to this.

And this that they wrote that she was standing in her courtyard, the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote "beside her courtyard" there, and similarly is the language of the Talmud there. Also, this language can be interpreted as "beside her courtyard and from the inside," but outside it does not help. And this opinion was brought by the Maggid Mishneh in Chapter 17 of Laws of Theft, law 8; and our teacher, the Rema, wrote thus in Choshen Mishpat, siman 200, seif 1, there. And it is astonishing regarding our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who wrote "beside the courtyard" there, and here he wrote as the language of the Tur. And perhaps in the case of a get (divorce document) he saw fit to be stringent. However, practically speaking, since the majority of opinions hold that even from outside, beside the courtyard, it is considered an acquisition regarding a get, there is no need to be concerned with the other opinion except as a stringency (and see Tosafot Eruvin 92b, s.v. "Isha", and the Terumat HaDeshen who questioned this and there is no difficulty, see there and study it well).

Since the reason for a get (divorce document) involving a courtyard is because it is considered like her "hand" and not because of agency, as it is a disadvantage for her, as we have stated, and therefore she must be present in the courtyard. One might say that when she requests the get and says that it is to her benefit, and the get is thrown into her protected courtyard with her knowledge, she should be divorced even if she is not in the courtyard, and it should be like a gift that she acquires in such a manner, because in the case of a gift, the courtyard has the status of agency. Nevertheless, the early authorities ruled that even in such a case, she must be present in the courtyard because the essence of divorce is a disadvantage for the woman, and even if she desires the divorce, we are concerned that she might change her mind (Rashba and Ran there). This is also stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. However, in practice, in such a case, it seems it would be a doubtful divorce.

And know that the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) wrote that in the case of a yavam (a man bound by levirate marriage), if he throws her a get (divorce document) into a guarded courtyard with her knowledge, and she is not standing beside it, it is a case of doubtful divorce. It is close to saying that it is satisfactory to her and it is a merit for her, and its law is like a gift (Ran and Maggid Mishneh there). It is implied from their words that in the absence of a yavam, she is certainly not divorced. However, it could be said that this is not specifically stated, and the same law would apply to any get where there is doubt whether it is satisfactory to her. The reason they mentioned the case of a yavam is because the Talmud discusses it in a different context (Chapter 16 of Yevamot) whether we say it is a merit for her. And it seems to me that this is the opinion of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in Section 3, where he wrote that if it was given in her courtyard without her knowledge and she is not standing beside her courtyard, it is a doubtful divorce. And the later authorities questioned him, saying that this doubt is only in the case of a yavam. According to our understanding, it makes sense since we follow the rationale that perhaps even in this get it is satisfactory to her. And how can we be lenient in the prohibition of a married woman? However, if we know for certain that she does not want to be divorced, he also agrees that she is not divorced. And he (Beit Yosef) is referring to a standard get, and therefore it is certainly necessary to be stringent, as perhaps this get is satisfactory to her.

The Tur wrote in the name of the Ramah that she needs to be standing in the courtyard when the get (bill of divorce) is given into it. But if he threw the get into her courtyard and afterward she came there and he said to her, "This is your get," even though the get is still lying there, she is not divorced until she takes it from there and he says to her at the time she takes it, "This is your get," because the first giving is nothing (Beit Shmuel, section 3). Alternatively, until he takes it from there and gives it to her for her to be divorced with it, we require that she be near the courtyard at the time of the giving of the get into it and at the time he says to her, "This is your get." Similarly, in a case where we said that her get and her courtyard come simultaneously, we require that she be standing in the courtyard at the time of giving. And if she was there at the time of giving the get and at the time he said, "This is your get," even if she left in between and returned, we do not consider it a problem. The reason for this is that it needs to be similar to her hand: just as her hand is with her both at the time of giving and at the time of saying, so too must the courtyard be (Beit Yosef). But in the middle, we do not consider it a problem since the matters of the get are only at the time of giving and at the time of saying.

The Rashba, of blessed memory, wrote there that if she said to him, "Throw my divorce document into my courtyard and my courtyard will acquire it for me," she is divorced even if she was not standing next to the courtyard. For a courtyard is not inferior to an agent, and she has effectively made the courtyard her agent to receive [the document]. An agent does not need to be standing next to her, as we have written. And it explicitly states this in the Jerusalem Talmud (first chapter), and the Ran and Maggid Mishneh agreed to this in their commentary on the fifth chapter, second law. Additionally, he wrote that if the document was already placed in her guarded courtyard and she was not in the courtyard, and he said to her, "This is your divorce document," and she said, "Let my courtyard acquire it for me," she is also divorced. The explanation of his words is certainly in such a case alone, one cannot say she is divorced, for at the time he threw it there, the courtyard was neither his agent nor her agent. This is merely like placing it in her hand as a deposit. Thus, afterwards, when she says, "Let my courtyard acquire it for me," how can she be divorced? For he needs to say to her, "This is your divorce document." His intention is that indeed he said to her afterwards, "This is your divorce document," and it is like the first case where she says, "Let my courtyard acquire it for me," and then he throws it to her and says, "This is your divorce document" (Ran). What he placed in her courtyard beforehand is considered as a deposit in her hand, and see what I have written in section 11.

In my humble opinion, the words of the Rashba do not contradict the words of the Tur, as they are discussing entirely different matters. The Rashba is speaking about a courtyard that is the woman’s agent to receive the get (divorce document), and an agent does not need to be standing next to it, as he wrote. The Tur is discussing a courtyard that acts as an agent for delivery, meaning it acquires on her behalf as an extension of her hand, and therefore, it is necessary for her to be standing in the courtyard at the time of the delivery of the get, because she did not make the courtyard her agent to receive it. But the Rashba is discussing a case where she made the courtyard her agent to receive it, and it rightfully acts as an agent. And when the Sages said that in the context of a get, the courtyard functions as her hand, this means that she did not make the courtyard her agent to receive it—that is, she did not say "my courtyard should acquire for me," but rather, it acquires as an extension of her hand.

Our master, the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Joseph Caro), in his great book, brought these words of the Rashba and wrote that it is evident from his words and from the words of the Ran that they disagree with the Tur and hold that it is not necessary for her to stand next to her courtyard at the time the get (divorce document) is given into it. See there. Based on this, he wrote in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 2, after bringing the words of the Tur, that some disagree, and his intention is towards the Rashba and the Ran. I am very puzzled as to the connection between these matters, and he also did not bring these words of the Rashba in the Shulchan Aruch because it seems to him that the Rashba was not clear on this law, as he wrote in his great book. However, the Ran and the Maggid Mishneh do not seem to interpret it this way. See there. For us, this law is not relevant at all, as we do not appoint an agent for acceptance as stated in Section 141, and we also do not permit giving a get to her domain but only to her hand, as will be explained and as stated at the beginning of Section 136. See there. (With difficulty, one can reconcile the words of the Beit Yosef, but it requires further study and scrutiny.)

And know that what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote, that if she came to her courtyard after the get (bill of divorce) was placed there, she is not divorced until she takes it from there, etc., it is necessary to understand what benefit there is in her taking it herself, since the initial placement was ineffective. This is similar to saying "Take your get from the ground." I found that one of the commentators on the Tur raised this question (Bet Yosef). However, it appears that Rambam holds similarly, as he wrote in Hilchot Gerushin chapter 5: if the get was placed in the hand of a non-bound slave, it is invalid until the get reaches her hand. It implies that if she takes it from the slave's hand, it is a valid get (Magid Mishneh), and it is not like taking the get from the ground (see Beit Shmuel section 29, and further investigation is needed). It seems to me that our Rabbis hold that since the truth is that a courtyard also has the status of agency, but regarding a get, because it is a disadvantage to her, it only has the status of her hand, as written. Therefore, when she herself takes it from the courtyard, and she takes it willingly, it reverts to the status of agency, such that her receiving it is like receiving it from her agent's hand and not from her own ground. The same applies to the slave. And that which the Sages said, "Take your get from the ground," means nothing — this is referring to her ground, not his ground, for the reason explained. However, in terms of the law, since the Rashba and Ran disagree with this regarding the slave and hold that he must take it from the slave and give it to her, and if she took it herself, they are uncertain if it is like "Take your get from the ground," as will be explained, therefore, the same applies to the courtyard in our case — it is also ineffective according to their opinion. When she takes it herself, she is in doubtful divorce status, and I am amazed that our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, did not discuss this at all (and perhaps the Beit Shmuel section 29 also intended this but was very brief, and what the Taz wrote requires further investigation, see there and scrutinize).

If she was standing in her courtyard at the time he threw her the get (divorce document) and he did not say anything, and afterward he said, "This is your get," it is valid (Beit Shmuel section 2). This also becomes clear from the words of the Tur. Similarly, if he gave her the get as a deposit and afterward said to her, "This is your get," she is divorced and there is no need to take it back from her and give it to her again (ibid.). However, if he placed the get outside the courtyard and the wind pushed the get into the courtyard, even if she is standing in the courtyard, it is not effective until he takes the get and gives it to her and says to her, "This is your get" (ibid. section 1). If she was standing by the courtyard and he threw the get into the courtyard without her knowledge and said to witnesses, "See the get that I am giving her," the Rashba is uncertain about this (ibid.), but he leans more towards the opinion that she is divorced, for she can be divorced by means of her courtyard even against her will (see his comments on chapter 288).

It is stated in the Gemara (Eruvin 92b) regarding two courtyards adjacent to each other, one large and one small, where the large one is breached into the small one, so that the entire width of the small one is open to the large one: the small one is considered subordinate to the large one, but not the other way around. Therefore, when both courtyards belong to her, and she is standing in the large one, if her husband throws a get (divorce document) to her into the small one, she is considered divorced, since it is as if she is standing in the small one because the entire small one belongs to the large one. But if she is in the small one and the get is in the large one, she is not considered divorced, because the large one is not subordinate to the small one. And we do not say that the woman is considered as if she is standing in the large one, because she does not intend to acquire the get (according to Rashi).

None of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) mentioned this ruling at all, perhaps because they hold that even if she is standing at the edge of the courtyard and outside, it is still considered as if she is standing next to the get. Therefore, there is no practical difference in this ruling, because even when she is standing in the small one, she is still standing next to the large one. They hold that this sugya (section of the Talmud) contradicts the sugya in Gittin 88a, which says that standing next to it is sufficient (see Tosafot there).

It is also possible to say that this ruling applies only if she does not intend to enclose the small one. But if she intends to enclose it, we cannot consider it as one courtyard, because anything that is intended to be enclosed is considered as enclosed. And although for other matters considered by the Talmud this detail is not scrutinized, for the matter of a woman's prohibition (i.e., divorce), it is certainly something to be scrutinized. It is difficult to establish and clarify this matter, and therefore the poskim omitted it. When such a case occurs, she is in a state of doubtful divorce.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (79a): If she was standing on the roof, and he threw [the get] to her, once it reaches the airspace of the roof, she is divorced. This means that his courtyard and her roof acquire for her by the law of courtyard, and even the airspace of the roof acquires. If an incident occurred to the get before it rested on the roof, such as being erased or burned, she is divorced, as once it reaches the airspace of the roof, it is as if it has rested. The Gemara establishes that this is specifically for a roof that has a railing around it, for airspace does not acquire unless it is within partitions; otherwise, it is not protected from the wind that might blow it away before it rests. Even without a railing, if it is within three handbreadths of the roof, it is considered as if it is resting due to the principle of lavud, which considers it as if it is attached. Some say that within three handbreadths, even if it is not protected from the wind, it is considered protected because of lavud (Maharshal). Others say that in this context, it is considered protected (Maharam). This seems reasonable, as even when it is resting in a courtyard, it must be protected. One cannot say that even above three handbreadths is acceptable, as above three handbreadths without partitions, the airspace does not acquire without partitions, even if it is protected. However, if we say that unprotected from the wind does not disqualify it as a courtyard that is not protected, since it is protected for other purposes, we could say that below three handbreadths she is divorced even if it is not protected from the wind (Avnei Shoham at the end of section 5 states this). But this is not a logical argument, as it is still not protected. Also, it does not seem to be what Rashi implies there. However, from Rashi it is clear that if it were protected from the wind, she would be divorced even without partitions. According to this, it must be that above three handbreadths it is impossible to be protected from the wind. Yet Rashi explains that we require airspace destined to rest, and Pnei Yehoshua questions this, as it is a question in Bava Metzia 12a. It is not difficult at all, as without partitions it is certainly not as if it has rested. Examine this well.

And it has been explained that when there are partitions or within nine handbreadths, she is considered divorced even if it was erased or burned before it was placed. This is specifically when the get (divorce document) preceded the fire, and it was fit to be placed if not for the fire that came after it was thrown. But if the fire came first, it is nothing, for it was not fit to be placed at all. And even though within three handbreadths is considered as if it is resting, this is when it is fit to come to actual rest, then within three handbreadths is considered as if it were placed. But not when it is not fit to be placed at all. The same law applies to erasure, when the thing that caused the erasure came after the get was thrown. And it is specifically when it was erased or burned during its descent to the roof. But if it was erased or burned during its ascent upwards, even if it was within the partitions or below three handbreadths, it is not a valid get. For during its ascent upwards, it is not called giving into her domain, and during its descent, it is called giving into her domain (Levush and Beit Shmuel, subsection 6. And the reason it is not mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch is because it is almost impossible for this to happen, and consider well).

And if it was not erased or burned and was placed on the roof, some say that the validity of the get begins also from the moment the get ascends above when it is within the partitions or within three handbreadths (Beit Shmuel, subsection 7). And some say that even in such a case, the validity of the get does not begin through its ascent above (Bach), and this also seems to be implied by the language of Rashi; see there.

According to the Rambam, of blessed memory, there is another method in this matter, and this is his wording: If she was standing at the top of her roof and he was below in his courtyard and he threw it up to her, once it reached the airspace of the walls of the railing or at least within three handbreadths of the roof, she is divorced, provided that it comes to rest. But if it was erased or burned before it reached her, even if it was erased or burned after it reached the airspace of the walls or after it reached within three handbreadths of the roof, such as if the wind blew it away and it was erased or burned, since it did not come to rest, it is not a valid get (divorce document) and she is not divorced. End of quote. This will be explained in Sections 19 and 21.

We also learned there in the Mishnah: When his roof and her courtyard are involved, he is above and she is below, and he threw it to her. Once it leaves the domain of the roof, if it is erased or burned, she is divorced. The Gemara establishes this case when the walls of the courtyard are higher than the parapet of the roof, and as soon as it leaves the domain of the roof, it enters the domain of the courtyard. Therefore, she is divorced since it is within the walls of the courtyard. This is specifically when the get (divorce document) preceded the fire, as stated in section 15. Additionally, the Gemara teaches that this applies only when it is erased while descending, but not when erased while ascending. Rashi, Tosafot, and all the commentators explained that this means if he stands on the roof and throws it from his hand to pass over the parapet, he throws it upward. Then, after it passes over the parapet, it descends downward into the courtyard. Therefore, if it is erased while still ascending, even if it leaves the boundary of the roof and enters the airspace of the courtyard, it is not considered a valid get unless it is while descending after it has begun to descend (Tur).

But the Rambam of blessed memory explains that this is what it means: specifically, when it is erased while descending, meaning in the case of the latter clause where the roof is his and the courtyard is hers, and he threw it downward, which is its natural movement as it descends. If it is erased or burned, she is divorced even though it did not come to rest because it was going to come to rest. However, if it is erased while ascending, meaning in the first clause where the roof is hers and the courtyard is his, and he threw it to her roof, and the husband needed to elevate the get in a manner not in its natural movement, as long as it did not come to rest at the end, she is not divorced. And even if it is erased while descending towards the roof, because the husband's power was not in a manner of resting, which is in descent (according to the Maggid Mishneh), therefore the Tanna did not teach in the first clause that if it is erased or burned, she is divorced, because in truth she is not divorced until it comes to rest. And perhaps you will ask, if so, why do we teach that once it reaches the airspace of the roof, she is divorced? The practical difference is if another man betrothed her while it was still in the air before coming to rest, whether the betrothal is effective, or if the husband died before it came to rest, in any case, her status is that of a divorced woman, or if he nullified the get in the interim (ibid.).

Nevertheless, it is perplexing to me that if the manner of its descent to the roof is not considered the force of the husband, how can she be divorced even when it rests on the roof? After all, it did not come through the husband's force. However, in truth, such a case is considered secondary force (Tosafot Shabbat 99b, s.v. "or"). Regarding Shabbat, one is liable (Bava Kamma 70b). Therefore, if it descends to the roof, why should she not be divorced, considering secondary force is like primary force? And even though regarding those liable for exile, secondary force is not like primary force, as proven in the Talmud (Makkot 8b) and as the Rambam writes in Chapter 5 of the Laws of Murder, nevertheless, for other matters, secondary force is like primary force, as the liability for exile differs from other laws (see Chapter 2 of Bava Kamma). Additionally, it seems to me that this secondary force is also considered like primary force concerning exile, but there it is a different matter. In truth, some say the Rambam's intention is that even initially, when it descends via descent, she is divorced, and the Rambam's intention is regarding ascent (Ran and Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 7). However, the Rambam's language does not indicate this (Gra, subparagraph 8), and many agree with the former interpretation, as is stated in Shulchan Aruch, paragraph 5.

In my humble opinion, there appears to be a different intention in his words when we carefully examine the matter, such as when the wind blew and carried it off, and it was erased or burned, etc. Why do we need to know how it was erased or burned? Also, the commentators stated that in the latter part of the Mishnah, he rules according to all the authorities, but this does not seem correct to me. For the language there in Halacha 4 is: "If it was his roof and he was above it, and she was below in her courtyard, and he threw her the get (divorce document), once the get leaves the boundaries of the roof and reaches the boundaries of her place where she stands, she is divorced." And in Halacha 5, it says: "If he threw it into her domain, into the fire and it was burned, or into the water and it was erased, or it was lost, it is not a get. But if it reached her domain and rested, and then the fire came and burned it, it is a valid get." Thus, it is written explicitly that it must rest first. And indeed, they questioned this language (Lechem Mishneh), and it is even more puzzling that he did not mention at all in Halacha 4 the law of it being burned or erased, and why did he write this in a separate Halacha?

Therefore, it appears to me that the Rambam does not distinguish between the beginning and the end, but in a different way, he distinguishes regarding the essence of the erasure and burning between descending and ascending. The explanation is as follows: since the fire and water were not originally there, as stated in Halacha 5, but rather the wind brought them from another place, consequently when the fire encountered the get (bill of divorce) while it was still in the air, the wind lifted it upward, as this is its nature. And since it was burned in an upward manner, the burning was during its ascent, it does not help that it was close to the ground because initially it was not intended to rest there due to being lifted by the wind upwards. Therefore, whether on the roof or in the courtyard, it does not help, and there was no need to mention this rule for the courtyard since it was mentioned for the roof. And descending is considered when the get was placed directly on the roof or the ground of the courtyard, and consequently, when the wind struck it, the fire and water struck it in a descending manner, because otherwise, they would not have snatched the get, as is evident. Therefore, in Halacha 5, it is written separately that it specifically applies if it reached her domain and rested, etc., and it is precisely written generally "her domain," which includes both the roof and the courtyard. And what the Sages said that it specifically applies in a descending manner, the explanation is that the wind with the fire or water was in a descending manner, meaning it was placed on the roof or in the courtyard, and the wind with the fire or water descended to the ground and received it. And what is stated in the Mishnah, "erased or burned," is a separate matter and does not refer to the previous case. Alternatively, it does refer to the previous case and it means that even if it was erased or burned after it was placed, nevertheless, the get is valid from the moment it descended into her domain.

There is an opinion that if both the courtyard and the roof belong to her, and he threw [the divorce document] to the roof, she is not divorced as long as it is in the airspace of the courtyard. Even though the airspace is hers, nevertheless, since it is not destined to come to rest in the courtyard, she is not divorced (Beit Shmuel, end of section 7). These are surprising matters, for it is explicitly stated in the Talmud there that if both the roof and the courtyard belong to her, the airspace of the roof is not required. See there. Only the Rashba, of blessed memory, wrote in his novellae that this is specifically when the document descends, but not when it ascends, for an ascending trajectory is not considered a valid transfer, as he wrote there. And know that all these laws apply when the get was not within her four cubits, but within her four cubits, nothing else is required, for four cubits acquire [the document], as will be explained with God's help (there). This is according to the law but not in practice, as will be explained before us with God's help. Additionally, according to the law, the airspace of four cubits does not acquire the get, as it is a question in the Talmud (Gittin 78b) that is unresolved. See there. There are many details in the law of four cubits, as will be explained with God's help.

If the courtyard belongs to her and there is a pole fixed in the courtyard that is higher than the courtyard's boundary, and he throws the get (divorce document) onto it, she is not divorced because it is not destined to rest on the ground. The wind will blow it outside the boundaries. And even though regarding Shabbat, if he threw from the public domain and it rested on the pole, he would be liable, since the pole certainly has the status of a private domain like the entire courtyard, in the case of a courtyard, it needs to be protected. Here, it is not protected. And even according to the opinion we explained in section 14, that within three handbreadths of the roof, even when it is not protected, it is a valid get, it is different there because the roof is very wide and she is standing there, and it is considered protected (see Maharsha 79a, s.v. "these words" and what Tosafot says there, s.v. "if she was standing there", and see Rashba and be precise). But on a pole, it is not protected at all. And even if there is a basket on the pole, if it is not deep and wide enough to protect the get from the wind, she is not divorced. This is also implied in the Gemara there.

The Rambam wrote there in Halacha 10: If one threw a get into her domain, and it passed through her domain where she was standing and fell outside of her domain, even if it passed close to the ground within three handbreadths, she is not divorced until it comes to rest in her domain. This is also written by the Tur, who holds that airspace where it will not come to rest is not considered as if it has come to rest. Even though in the Talmud (Bava Metzia 12a) there was a question that was not resolved regarding airspace where it will not come to rest—whether it is considered as if it has come to rest or not—there are indeed some of the early authorities who ruled here as well that she is doubtfully divorced (Ramban, Rashba, and Ran). 

This is not similar to a case where a fire preceded the get, where she is certainly not divorced, because there it is not fit to come to rest at all. Similarly, it is not comparable to a case where the get was burned while it was rising upwards, where it is certainly not a valid get, because in the case of rising upwards, it is not considered at all as if it is going to come to rest (Tosafot). 

Also, what was explained in section 14, within three handbreadths close to the roof, is considered as if it has come to rest because, by its force, it was fit to come to rest on the roof if not for the fire and water that jumped. Within three handbreadths, it is considered as if it has come to rest. But here, by its force, it was not fit to come to rest, because by the force of its throw, it fell outside of her domain. Therefore, it is a doubtful case in the law. This is also the case regarding monetary laws, as written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 268. 

However, the Rambam z"l holds that it is certainly not considered as if it has come to rest. He ruled this way in Chapter 4 of Maaseh HaKorbanot, because in Zevachim (25b), it is explained that this is the fundamental law (see Beit Shmuel, section 9). Therefore, also in monetary laws, he did not bring this law as a doubt, as the Maggid Mishneh wrote. Regarding the Tur, it is puzzling because in Choshen Mishpat there, he wrote that it is a doubt. 

Know that when it rolls on the ground and goes outside her domain, it is explicitly implied in Bava Metzia there that it is considered as if it has come to rest. Nevertheless, the Rashba z"l wrote that regarding a get, it is not a proper giving because in many aspects, a get is different from monetary matters (see Beit Shmuel, section 10). According to this, it is possible to reconcile the opinion of the Tur that in the case of a get, he agreed with the Rambam. It is clear that in practice, we follow the stringent opinion, and she is doubtfully divorced. (In Bava Batra 85a, it is clear from the get to a transaction in the opposite way, that since in the case of a get it is good, all the more so in monetary matters.)

Two courtyards, one inside the other: the outer one belongs to him and the inner one belongs to her, and the walls of the outer courtyard are higher than the walls of the inner courtyard. He threw her a get (divorce document) into her inner courtyard, and the get was still in the air opposite the inner courtyard and above its walls, such that if the wind were to blow it, it would fall into the outer courtyard. Nevertheless, she is considered divorced, for the walls of the outer courtyard always guard the inner courtyard. It is as if the outer courtyard is obligated to guard the inner courtyard (Rashi 79b). 

One might question: Even if we consider that the outer courtyard is obligated to the inner courtyard, since if the wind blows it, it would fall into the outer courtyard, it should not be better than a courtyard belonging to both of them. In truth, it can be said that in a courtyard belonging to both of them, she is divorced. This is not explicitly discussed in the Poskim (decisors of Jewish law), but logically, it seems so, for she has the right to place her belongings there. Just as regarding acquisition, it is explained in Choshen Mishpat 200 that a person's vessels acquire for him in a courtyard belonging to the seller and the buyer because the buyer has permission to be there, so too it appears regarding a get. Moreover, the Rashba (of blessed memory) wrote that in this case, we consider the walls of the inner courtyard to extend upwards, as if the get reached the airspace within the walls of the inner courtyard. 

And the main ruling is that even if the get is burned or erased while still in the air, she is divorced according to most Poskim, as we have explained in section 14, if it was on a downward trajectory. According to the Rambam (of blessed memory), it is significant that the get begins its effect from the moment it is in the air, as we have explained his opinion in section 19.

However, concerning the core of this law when one throws a get (divorce document) into a courtyard that belongs to both of them, it is not explicitly clarified in Choshen Mishpat there, except that the buyer's vessel acquires there, and without vessels, nothing is mentioned. According to the conclusion of the Gemara (Bava Batra 84b), in a simta (an alleyway), the buyer does not acquire without his vessels; the same applies to a jointly owned courtyard, as the Gemara compares the two. We have already written this in Choshen Mishpat, section 14, see there. Therefore, with a get as well, she is not divorced. However, it is possible to say that since regarding the buyer's vessels in the seller's domain, a get is more lenient than acquisition, as in acquisition according to the Rambam, he does not acquire, and according to other authorities, it is a doubtful law, as we wrote there in Choshen Mishpat. And regarding a get in her bed, she is divorced in such a case because the husband does not object to the location of her bed, as will be explained before us. Therefore, it is possible to say that also in this matter, a get is more lenient than acquisition. And even though we wrote in section 25 that on the contrary, a get is stricter than acquisition, it can be said that concerning outside her domain, it is stricter, but concerning within her domain, it is more lenient than acquisition because he does not object to her. Therefore, it seems to me that she is doubtfully divorced.

And our Sages said there that the law clarified regarding courtyards—that if the inner one belongs to her and the outer one belongs to him, she is considered divorced, as explained—is not the same with baskets. If there are two baskets, one inside the other, and the inner one belongs to her and the outer one belongs to him, and he throws [the get] into the inner one, even though it reaches the airspace of the inner basket, she is not considered divorced until it rests on the ground of the inner basket. This is because the partitions of a vessel are not made to preserve the airspace, as a vessel is only made to hold things within it (Rashi). In other words, the airspace does not acquire by the law of domain, but by the law of lifting, it does acquire. (And this resolves the Tosafot's question from Avodah Zarah 71a, and similarly, Rashi there is precise—study that carefully.) And some say that once it reaches the airspace of the partitions of the inner basket, she acquires it and it is a valid get, but before it reaches this airspace, even though it has reached the airspace of the outer partitions, it is not a get (Tosafot). And the Tur wrote similarly there.

However, this is specifically when the outer basket does not have a bottom and the inner basket is standing on the ground. But if the outer basket has a bottom, it is not a valid get, because it is considered like the vessel of the buyer in the seller's domain, which is a doubtful case in Choshen Mishpat there, and here too it is a doubtful divorce (Tur), because since the inner basket is standing within the outer basket, the outer one is considered the husband's domain, even though the baskets are in her courtyard (Ran there). And this is the opinion of most authorities.

However, the Rambam, of blessed memory, has a different opinion on this matter, and his words are as follows: "How so? Two baskets, one inside the other; the outer one belongs to him and the inner one belongs to her. If he throws her the bill of divorce into them, even if it reaches the airspace of the inner one, she is not divorced until it rests on the side of the inner basket. In what case does this apply? When the basket is tilted on its side and has no bottom. But if it has a bottom, even if it rests on its bottom, she is not divorced, because the woman's vessel in the husband's domain does not acquire the bill of divorce for her unless he is not particular about its location." Thus are his words. It explains that the baskets are situated in the husband's courtyard, and he follows his reasoning that the buyer's vessel in the seller's domain does not acquire for the buyer, as stated in the beginning of chapter 4 of Mechira, see there. However, if it has no bottom and the bill of divorce rests on its side, it is not considered a vessel, and the husband is not particular about its location, as will be explained similarly. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 9, only copied the words of the Rambam and did not consider writing according to most of the decisors because it is an uncommon matter. Also, the Rif, of blessed memory, omitted all these laws. However, I am puzzled by the Maggid Mishneh's explanation that the baskets are in the husband's domain. Why do we need the outer basket? It is possible that it teaches us that even if her basket is within his basket, nevertheless, when her basket has no bottom, not only is he not particular about it being in his domain, but even about it being within his basket, he is not particular, since it is not a vessel. In my humble opinion, it also seems that according to his explanation, it refers to the baskets being in her domain, and when it has a bottom, it is considered as being in his domain due to his basket, similar to the previous explanation.

If she was standing in his courtyard and he threw the get (divorce document) to her there, she is not divorced, even if the get fell near her, it is still considered in his domain and has no effect. Even if it fell into one of her vessels, it is considered like the vessel of a buyer in the seller's domain, making it a doubtful get. According to the Rambam, it is not a get at all, as he wrote. Therefore, even if her bed was there and she was sitting on it and the get fell on the bed, she is not divorced until the get reaches her hand. However, regarding her small vessels, the Sages said that a person does not mind his wife's small vessels being in his domain, and she is divorced if the get falls on her small vessels, as if he had transferred ownership of the ground on which the vessel stands to her. Similarly, if the bed was ten handbreadths high, making it a separate domain, and its legs were in his domain, the Sages said that people are not particular about the space under the legs of the bed, at least regarding his wife (Tosafot), even if they are particular with others, and she is divorced. Additionally, if the bed is suspended in the air and it fell on it, she is divorced because he does not mind the air in her vessel, at least regarding her bed. But if the bed is less than ten handbreadths high and stands on the ground, he certainly minds, and the bed is considered part of his domain, like the vessel of a buyer in the seller's domain, making it a doubtful divorce. According to the Rambam, she is certainly not divorced. If the get fell into her lap, she is certainly divorced because her lap is considered like her hand. Even if it fell on her garments that drag on the ground, a person does not mind his wife regarding the place of her garments that she wears, even if they drag on the ground (Tosafot 78a). Specifically, we said that a bed ten handbreadths high is not particular about the space under its legs, not with other vessels. The reason is that a bed that is ten handbreadths high is convenient to use underneath (Rashi), and it is considered as standing in the air, not with other vessels. Therefore, if the bed is fenced until close to the ground, it is also doubtful (as inferred from Rashi there). The measure of small vessels that one does not mind their place is not clarified. In the Jerusalem Talmud, it implies that all its uses are included, and in our Talmud, it is explained as like her basket, which is a vessel in which women place their spinning and needles, and also a small vessel in which she eats dates. From this, we learn an example. All this is from the basic law, but practically, only her hand and not her domain, as will be explained. Even when it falls on her garments, it is not permitted because sometimes she borrows garments and the lender minds (Beit Yosef in the name of Rabbeinu Peretz there).

It has already been explained that in a place that is borrowed or rented to her, if the get (divorce document) falls there, she is divorced. Therefore, if the husband lent her his courtyard and she acquired it with a valid acquisition, and he threw the get into it, she is divorced, because it is considered as hers. And the Sages said (beginning of chapter 8) that one who lends a place to another does not lend more than one place, not two places. However, a small object standing in the courtyard is not considered a separate place and is nullified to the courtyard. If the get falls there, she is divorced. But a large object standing there is considered a separate place, and if the get falls on it, she is not divorced. And what is the definition of this matter? The Tur wrote: If there is in the courtyard a distinct place for itself that has four cubits by four cubits, even if it is not ten handbreadths high, or if it does not have four by four cubits but is ten handbreadths high, or even if it does not have four by four cubits and is also not ten handbreadths high but is distinct by name for itself, it is considered a separate place and is not included in the borrowed courtyard. And similarly, it is stated in the Shulchan Aruch. Consequently, if it falls on a chair or a table or a bed and the like that are standing in the courtyard and belong to him, she is not divorced, as these are not nullified to the courtyard. Only a small piece of wood or a small stone and the like are nullified.

And it is understood that when he lent her this courtyard, and he had another courtyard next to this one, and the get (divorce document) fell into the other courtyard, she is not divorced. The sages said there that with roofs it is not so; if he had two roofs next to each other and he lent her one roof and the get fell on the adjacent roof, she is divorced. The reason is that since the usage of roofs is not fixed, people are not particular about using one roof and then another (Gittin 79b). From the Talmudic discussion there, it seems to me that this applies specifically when there is no parapet for each roof separately. Then he does not mind if, having given permission to use this roof, she uses the other as well, since the roofs are connected without interruption, and it is all considered one roof. But if there is a parapet separating the roofs, or an airspace interruption, or he said to her, "I am only lending you one roof," she is not divorced if it fell on the other roof. And if he lent her a place in the courtyard, he did not lend her the roof (see Beit Shmuel 118). There is uncertainty regarding places with minimal usage, like a ruin; if he lent her the place, whether the adjacent area is included as with a roof or not, and this requires further investigation.

All that is stated in these two sections reflects the opinion of the Tur and most of the legal authorities, but Rambam, of blessed memory, has a different opinion on this matter. He wrote there in Halacha 9: "If the husband lent her a place in his courtyard but did not designate it specifically for her, and he threw her the get (bill of divorce) and it reached within four cubits of her where she is standing, she is divorced. If the get rolled and fell onto a beam or a rock far from her, if the place where it fell does not have four cubits by four cubits and is not ten handbreadths high and does not have its own designation, it does not separate into its own domain, and it is as if she and it are in the same place. If it has one of these three things, it separates into its own domain, and he lent her one place, not two places, and she is not divorced until the get reaches her hand." End quote. Regarding roofs, he wrote in Halacha 11: "If she was standing on her roof and he threw it to her and it fell on another adjacent roof, if she can extend her hand and take it, she is divorced, for although the residences are divided above just as they are divided below, people do not care about such a place." End quote.

The commentators have exerted effort to explain his words, and in my humble opinion it seems simple that the Rambam holds that if one loans her the entire courtyard, there is no distinction between a large item and a small item, as even a large item is nullified to the courtyard when it stands there, for he has loaned her the entire courtyard. However, the discussion is about when he loans her a place in the courtyard solely for receiving her get (divorce document), and the usual space of a person is four cubits. Therefore, wherever she stands, she has four cubits, and when the get falls within her four cubits, she is divorced. But if the get rolls onto a beam or a rock, the ruling is as follows: if she is standing on the beam or the rock and the get is also there, then the get and she are in the same place. However, if she is standing in the courtyard and the get falls onto the beam or the rock, and the get is within her four cubits but the beam or rock extends much further, it depends on whether they have an independent designation or are eighteen handbreadths high or four cubits wide. If the place of the get is separate from her place, she is not divorced. If not, the get and she are in the same place, and she is divorced. When it is written that it is far from her, the intention is not that it is far from her four cubits, for if so, it is nothing anyway. Rather, it means that the rock and the beam are far from her and she is not standing on them, and they extend beyond her four cubits. And regarding roofs, he holds that if he loans her this roof, how could it include the other roof? It doesn't make sense at all. Rather, he explains that she was standing on her roof and he threw the get to her there, but it fell close to her on the other roof in a manner that she could extend her hand and take it. Thus, we say that this is not like "take your get from another domain," but rather like throwing it into her domain, as the owner of the other roof does not object to this. And since the get is close enough for her to extend her hand and take it, she is divorced. There is an opinion that this applies only if she is standing on her roof, but if she was standing on another's roof and he threw the get to her roof, she is not divorced (Beit Shmuel, section 19). This is certainly so, for how can she be divorced if it fell in another's domain and he intended to throw it there? Only when he threw it to her roof and she is standing there, but did not aim to throw it directly to her but close to her, and she can take it, it is considered hers regarding not saying that it fell in another's domain. This is only according to the Rambam, but according to the Tur and all the other authorities, even in this case it does not help. Therefore, according to the law, she is in a state of doubtful divorce.

The sages taught in a Mishnah (78a): If she was standing in the public domain and he threw it (the get, divorce document) to her, if it is closer to her, she is divorced; if it is closer to him, she is not divorced; if it is halfway, she is both divorced and not divorced. The same applies to betrothal. Rav explained in the Gemara that her four cubits is considered closer to her, and his four cubits is considered closer to him, because the acquisition of four cubits is a rabbinic enactment (Bava Metzia 10a), as explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 243. Nonetheless, this also applies to a get, because since the sages instituted this as being like her courtyard, "hefker beit din hefker" (property declared ownerless by a rabbinical court is ownerless) (Ran). Even though it is established there that in the public domain the rabbis did not institute the four cubits, only in a side street and the sides of the public domain, nonetheless, for a get they instituted it even in the public domain due to the concern of agunah (a woman unable to remarry) (Rosh). It appears that this is the view of the Tur, who wrote in Siman 30 regarding betrothal that in the public domain the four cubits do not take effect, but here he wrote "public domain," so it must be said that for agunah they were lenient. However, this is problematic, as the Mishnah equates betrothal to divorce. Some indeed say that they are equal because it is written "and she departs and she becomes" (Ran). Therefore, even though the main enactment was for a get due to agunah, they were nonetheless compelled to equate betrothal to divorce. However, our rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote there (s.v. Rabbi Yochanan) that in truth, even here, the intention is not the public domain but rather a side street and the sides of the public domain. And one must say that what they called the public domain is because it is not a private domain, and there are similar examples in the Talmud. They also wrote to distinguish that in a place where she cannot guard it, they did not institute it in the public domain, but when she can guard it, they did institute it in the public domain. It has already been explained in Choshen Mishpat and earlier in Siman 30 that the one who comes first acquires the four cubits, and the one who comes after has no claim to them at all.

There is another clarification in the Gemara from Rabbi Yochanan that it is considered "close to her" when she can guard the get (divorce document) and he cannot, and when he can guard it and not she, it is considered "close to him." Additionally, Rabbi Yochanan holds the ruling of the four cubits (as previously explained), but in her four cubits, even if he can guard it as well as she can, she is divorced by the law of the four cubits. Outside of the four cubits, she is not divorced unless she can guard it and not he (Tosafot). However, it appears to me that according to Rabbi Yochanan, there is no necessity to say that the four cubits apply in divorce documents also in the public domain (although if so, it is difficult to understand why Tosafot were compelled to their explanation; examine this closely). This acquisition of guarding applies only in divorce and betrothal, as Rabbi Yochanan himself said there, "They said it regarding divorce and not for other matters," and betrothal cannot be separated from divorce because it is written, "And she departs and becomes" (see there). The reason in divorce is that it is an acquisition because she is divorced against her will, and since it is acquired against her will, if she can only guard it, it is valid as a get (Rashi). Some say that it is not by law but because of the regulation to prevent agunot (chained women), and betrothal cannot be separated from divorce for the reason explained (Ran).

It is further stated there in the Gemara: Shmuel said to Rav Yehuda, "Sharp one, so that she can bend down and take it, and you should not perform an action until the get (divorce document) reaches her hand." And from Rashi's explanation, it becomes clear that "so that she can bend down and take it" is a legal ruling, and he disagrees with Rav and Rabbi Yochanan, and holds that "near to her" is only considered if the get is placed right next to her feet in such a way that if she bends down to the ground, she can take it. And this statement, that one should not perform an action until the get reaches her hand, is due to stringency and not from the essence of the law. According to this, for Shmuel, she is not divorced either within four cubits or by guarding. However, the Rosh explains that Shmuel also agrees that the get is acquired within four cubits, and this statement, "so that she can bend down and take it," is due to stringency. The Ran explains that in an alleyway or the sides of a public domain, she has four cubits concerning a get, and only in a public domain are there no four cubits, and according to the law, it needs to be so that she can bend down and take it. And even according to Rashi, it seems that the law follows Rabbi Yochanan. However, it is possible to say that in a public domain, even Rabbi Yochanan does not hold of the ordinance of four cubits as stated. However, regarding guarding, according to the Rosh, certainly, the get is effective by law when she can guard it and not him. And according to Rashi, it is a dispute as stated.

The Tur writes: "If she was standing in a public domain and he threw it within her four cubits, she is divorced. In which case is this said? When the husband is not standing with her within her four cubits. But if he is standing with her within them, even if she preceded him and acquired them, she is not divorced until it reaches her hand. Similarly, if he threw it to her in a public domain and he is far from her, even if she can guard it and it is not she herself, she is not divorced until it reaches her hand. If two say it reached her four cubits and two say it did not reach, she is doubtfully divorced. And Rabbeinu Chananel wrote that even if he threw a get into her courtyard, she is not permitted to others until it reaches her hand. The Rosh of blessed memory was astonished at his words, and as I have written, this is his agreement."

It is explained from his words that within four cubits she is divorced when the husband does not come into them, but when the husband comes into them, she is not divorced until it reaches her hand, and similarly, guarding does not help. And there is someone who says that his intention is not for a public domain proper but for an alleyway and the sides of a public domain, and he relied on what is written in Siman 30 (Beit Yosef). However, what he wrote that when he comes into her four cubits, even if she preceded, she is not divorced, and similarly with guarding, his intention is not that it is not a valid get at all, for the Rosh explicitly wrote that this is only because of stringency and not by law. Rather, his intention in practice is that they do not permit her to remarry in such a case, but certainly she is forbidden to a Kohen, and if another person betroths her, the betrothal is valid, for by law it is a complete get. And that in betrothal he was not stringent in practice, we explained there the reason in Siman 30, section 11, and there in section 10, we brought the opinions of the early authorities who hold that by law, the four cubits do not help in divorce; see there. However, the language of the Tur, who wrote that it is not a get, is very puzzling, for this language implies that by law it is not a get, and this requires further investigation.

The words of the Rambam, of blessed memory, are very complicated. He wrote: "If he threw it to her in a public domain or in an area that belongs to neither of them, if it is closer to him, she is not divorced. If the get (divorce document) is halfway between them, or from halfway to her side, until it is closer to her, she is doubtfully divorced. If it is close enough to her that she could bend down and take it, it is invalid until the get reaches her hand, and only then she may remarry with it ab initio. How is it considered closer to him? If he can guard it and she cannot guard it, that is considered closer to him. If both of them can guard it, or neither can guard it, that is considered halfway between them. If he arrived first and stood, and then she stood across from him and he threw it to her, if the get is within his four cubits, she is not divorced, even though she could bend down and take it. If she stood first and then he came and stood across from her and threw it to her, even if it is halfway between them, since it is within her four cubits, it is an invalid get until it reaches her hand." End of quote. The earlier authorities (Rashba, Ran, Maggid Mishneh, and Kesef Mishneh) have already struggled with his words and raised difficulties. Refer to there. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in paragraphs 13 and 14, copied his words as they are, refer to there.

In my humble opinion, it appears that Rambam's view is that all these Amoraim do not disagree at all. The proof of this is that Rav explains that "close" is defined as four cubits, and in the Jerusalem Talmud, Rav also says this regarding this Mishnah, and afterwards, Rav says that it depends on the outstretching of the hands, that she can stretch her hand and take it. This is similar to our Talmud, which states "enough to bend and take it." The Jerusalem Talmud questions Rav against Rav and resolves it by saying that one instance refers to the law and the other to practice. Similarly, Rabbi Yochanan, who says in our Talmud that it depends on guarding, says in the Jerusalem Talmud that it depends on the outstretching of the hands. Consequently, it must also be said that one instance refers to the law and the other to practice. Accordingly, they all agree with Shmuel that in practice, it must be "enough to bend and take it." Furthermore, he is stringent in practice until it reaches her hand, and so it is in the Jerusalem Talmud. We have already explained this in the beginning of chapter 136. All the words of Rav, Rabbi Yochanan, and Shmuel are true and do not contradict each other. Certainly, it is considered close when he can guard it and not she, or when he reached it within four cubits. Although in a public domain or a domain that does not belong to either of them, four cubits were not instituted, nevertheless, regarding a get (divorce document), they instituted it due to the necessity and for the sake of preventing agony, as explained. Consequently, since they instituted it, whenever he reaches within four cubits or even more than four cubits and he can guard it and not she, she is certainly not divorced. When she reaches within four cubits or even more and she can guard it and not he, by the letter of the law, she is certainly divorced. All the more so if it was close enough for her to bend and take it, nevertheless, due to stringency, the Sages invalidated the get until it reaches her hand. In a case of equal possibility, such as when both grasped the four cubits together, or both can guard it, or neither can guard it alone but together they can guard it, she is considered doubtfully divorced. This is different from what we wrote in chapter 30, section 10, regarding Rambam’s opinion.

And according to this, all his words are properly aligned. Initially, he wrote that if it is closer to him, she is not divorced, and if it is exactly halfway or from halfway to closer to her but not including, then it is a doubtful divorce. And if it is closer to her, even such that she can bend and take it, and certainly within four cubits and in her guarding, it is invalid. This is what Shmuel said: "Do not act until the get reaches her hand." Similarly, in the Jerusalem Talmud, the clearest among them is until the get reaches her hand. Afterwards, he explains what is considered closer to him and explains the two ways: the law of guarding as mentioned. Then, he explains the law of four cubits when she first stood to seize the four cubits, and in both cases, it is not a get at all. Afterwards, he explains that when she first stood to seize the four cubits, even though by the fundamental law it is valid, nevertheless, the get is invalid until it reaches her hand. The same applies when she can guard and not him, and this did not need to be clarified at the end of his words since it was already explained that even if she can bend and take it, it is invalid, and certainly in guarding. This needed to be clarified in the four cubits to indicate that he holds like Rav that she has four cubits for the get, and only due to the stringency did the sages invalidate it until it reaches her hand. Although our early and later sages did not interpret his words this way, nevertheless, since according to their interpretation his words are problematic as they all questioned him, and according to our interpretation, his words are clear with divine assistance, therefore we explained according to our humble opinion. Concerning betrothal in the last part of the fourth chapter of Ishut, he only mentioned guarding there because he holds that in betrothal, there were no regulations as in gittin, we establish the primary explanation of closer to him and closer to her and ruled like Rabbi Yochanan that the law follows him against Rav and Shmuel. Earlier in chapter 30, we elaborated on this with divine assistance, see there in sections 10, 11, and 12 (see also the glosses on the Shulchan Aruch, sections 22 and 23, the second one, and according to what we said, it is not so, and examine closely).

Maimonides, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: If her hand was inclined, meaning she held her hand slanted and not upright like a partition, nor extended in the manner in which one extends a hand to receive, and he threw the get onto her hand and it fell to the ground, if it fell within her four cubits and rested, she is divorced. And the question arises: Do we not permit according to the four cubits rule as has been clarified? However, there is no problem at all, since he threw it onto her hand, and therefore, even though it did not rest in her hand and fell within her four cubits, she is divorced (as explained by the Kesef Mishneh in Hilchot Gerushin 13). For the reason we do not permit by the four cubits is merely a stringency, and therefore, when he intended to throw it to her hand and the get touched her hand, even though it did not rest in her hand and rested within her four cubits, she is divorced.

The Tur writes: If it did not come to rest within the four cubits but rather rolled immediately outside of them, it is questionable whether the airspace of the four cubits acquires it or not, and this is unresolved. Therefore, she is in doubt whether she is divorced. These are his words, and similarly it is stated in Shulchan Aruch, Section 15. And it is true that this is a question in the Gemara (Gittin 78b). However, I am puzzled because in the case of rolling, it is explicitly stated that it is considered as if it has come to rest (Bava Metzia 12a). It must be said that they hold that in the case of a get (divorce document), it is different, as rolling is not considered a valid giving. We have already mentioned this reasoning in Section 25 in the name of the Rashba. And Rashi precisely explained in Gittin there that it did not come to rest because it was burned, and it is possible that his intention was to exclude the case of rolling. And the Rambam did not mention this, as we have already written there that he holds that it is not considered as if it has come to rest. See there, Subsection 25, and in my opinion, this is unnecessary, and the author was stringent regarding rolling.

It has been clarified that if someone throws [a get] onto her hand and it falls within her four cubits, she is divorced. This applies when she is standing in a place where the get is not likely to be lost. But if she is standing near a fire or on the riverbank, and he throws it onto her hand and it falls into the fire or into the water, she is not divorced, because from the outset it was destined to be lost. And even if we say that airspace where it is not destined to rest is considered as if it has rested, this only applies when it is fit to rest but went far away. However, if it is not fit to rest at all, such as when it is burnt or lost, it is certainly not considered as if it has rested, and it is as if it was intended from the outset to be lost. (And this is the intention of Rashi there in the comment beginning "on the riverbank.")

And regarding the practical Halacha, we have already brought what Shmuel said to Rav Yehuda: "Do not perform an action until the get (divorce document) reaches her hand." And it is further stated that there was an incident where the get was close to her, and the Sages required chalitzah for the divorced woman when the husband died. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is also mentioned that the most correct approach is that the get must reach her hand. This view was brought by Tosafot and the Rosh, and all the early authorities in the name of the Aruch and Rabbeinu Chananel, who wrote: "We have received from our teachers that even if the get was thrown into her courtyard, she does not become permitted to others until the get reaches her hand." The basis of their words is according to this Jerusalem Talmud. Tosafot and the Rosh rejected this, stating that this only applies to a public domain and not to her courtyard, for in the case of throwing into her courtyard, we permit it both in theory and in practice. And according to their view, it appears that only in the case of throwing into her courtyard or her house do we permit it in practice, but in the case of throwing into an alley or the sides of a public domain, we do not permit it in practice. However, the Ran wrote that this Jerusalem Talmud only applies to the four cubits in a public domain, for by law, four cubits do not acquire in a public domain, and it was only regarding a get that they instituted this. But in cases where the law allows acquisition, the Jerusalem Talmud was not stringent. And according to this, even in the case of throwing into an alley or the sides of a public domain, we should permit it in practice. Nevertheless, both he and the Rashba wrote that one should be concerned with the words of Rabbeinu Chananel, for they are words of tradition.

And these are the words of our master, the Rema, in section 14: But if he threw it to her within her four cubits and the husband does not enter there, she is divorced. And all this is according to the law, but initially, one should not divorce even by placing the get into her courtyard or into her garments, but only into her hand directly, and her hand should be open from the beginning of the giving until the end. And even after the fact, one should not permit her to marry another until the get has come into her hand directly. And it is customary that after he gives her the get, she should close her hands and place it under her garments, and she should be careful that no one assists her in receiving it, and there should be nothing, such as a ring, in her hand at the time of receiving it. So are the words of the Rema. And this is the simple custom. And it is implied from his words that, according to the law, even in a public domain, her four cubits acquire it for her, for he is referring to the words of the Mechaber, who is discussing a public domain and a domain that does not belong to either of them (see in the Nimukei Yosef in the first chapter of Bava Metzia on the Mishnah "He saw the lost object" where he writes, "And we hold that in the case of a get, four cubits do not acquire it," and I do not know his intention, whether it is according to the law or only a stringency, and see what I wrote above in section 30, paragraph 10, and be precise).

And it is obvious that we only say it is not a valid divorce (get) until it reaches her hand as a stringency, but not as a leniency. In a place where there is a dispute among the halachic authorities, it is considered a doubt whether she is divorced. However, regarding what Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote, that even after the fact, she should not be permitted to marry another until the get reaches her hand directly: if it is a place of hardship where it is impossible to obtain another get, and he threw it into her courtyard or into her garments, should she be permitted to remarry?

In the Responsa of the Rivash, sections 205 and 206, it is explained that she should not be permitted to remarry if he threw it into her four cubits, even in an alleyway, and only if she already remarried should she not be forced to leave her new marriage. And in a public domain, it seems from his words that one should be even more stringent, because several authorities hold that the four cubits were not established at all in a public domain, neither for a get nor otherwise. Also, the Bach wrote that the intention of the Tur was only regarding an alleyway and not an actual public domain.

However, if he threw it into her garments that are in her lap, it appears that in a place of hardship, she may be permitted, as this was not mentioned by the earlier authorities, and it is a distant decree to say that perhaps the garments are not hers. And it seems to me that in practice, if such an incident occurs, they should consult with the great authorities of the generation at that time, and they should deliberate on the matter.

And regarding what we wrote in section 45 that if the get (divorce document) did not rest within four cubits but rather rolled beyond them, it is considered a doubtful divorce, our teacher the Rema wrote in section 15 that all this applies when she is not standing in her own domain. But if she is standing in her own domain, even if it fell from her hand and rolled beyond four cubits, she is divorced, because it only rolled within her domain. However, for us, since we do not effect a divorce through her domain as we have explained, if the get fell from her hand, it is necessary to divorce her again. Therefore, she should raise her hands when receiving her get so that it does not fall from her hand, and also her hands should be three handbreadths above the ground. Thus it is explained from his words that even in such a case we are stringent in practice, and if he did not divorce her again and it is a case of preventing her from remarrying (agunah), there is a need to consider this. However, among us, it is not customary to divorce in the woman's domain, and the arranging of the get is done in the rabbi's house. It is obvious that also according to the law, one should be stringent if it falls from her hand, because it is a domain that is not hers. According to several legal authorities, they did not establish four cubits in such a case as we have written, and it is obvious that one should not be lenient in this matter.

It has already been explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 202, that a servant is considered like a courtyard, except that it is a moving courtyard. Therefore, it is required for the servant to be bound. In the case of a courtyard, it must be guarded with her knowledge, whereas a servant guards himself. Therefore, it is required that he be asleep and she is sitting next to him and guarding him with her knowledge. Hence, the Sages said (Gittin 78a) that if he gave the get (divorce document) into her servant's hand and he (the servant) was asleep and also bound, and she was next to him, it is a valid get.

The opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 3 of Hilchot Mechira is that it is not necessary to have both conditions (asleep and bound), but that being bound alone is sufficient, because then he is not considered a moving courtyard and is also regarded as being guarded with her knowledge. When he is bound, it cannot be said that he guards himself. Also, being asleep alone is sufficient according to the Rambam, because when he is asleep, he is considered guarded with her knowledge and is not a moving courtyard since he stays in one place. However, being only asleep is invalid rabbinically, because there is a decree lest he not be asleep. But being bound alone is not subject to such a decree because it is not common (see Beit Shmuel, Siman 27).

Therefore, the Rambam ruled in Chapter 5 that being bound alone is sufficient for her to be divorced, but only being asleep is invalid, even if she is sitting next to him. However, Rashi, Tosafot, and all our Rabbis hold according to the first opinion that both conditions (asleep and bound) are necessary (Tosafot Bava Kama 12a). Hence, it is surprising that our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, in Sections 16 and 17, wrote the opinion of the Rambam as the main one and the first opinion under "some say." Nevertheless, for us, there is no practical difference in this matter, as it has already been explained that even in a courtyard, she is not permitted until it reaches her hand, and certainly with her servant (and the Tur had a different version in the Rambam, see there).

Since it has been explained at the beginning of this section that the reason a get (divorce document) is effective in her courtyard, even though what a woman acquires is acquired by her husband, is because her get and her courtyard come simultaneously, therefore, if he placed the get in his courtyard and then sold her the courtyard or gave it to her, since she acquired the courtyard through a document, money, or possession, she is divorced because her get and her courtyard come simultaneously. However, if he placed it in someone else's courtyard and that other person sold or gave her the courtyard, she is not divorced because when the husband placed the get in the courtyard, it was not hers to acquire through her courtyard, and when the courtyard came into her possession, it did not come from the husband, so it cannot be considered as giving her the get and the courtyard simultaneously (Rashi 21a). Nevertheless, we do not decree about his courtyard because of another person's courtyard (Gemara there).

And the same law applies to his slave. If he gave the get (divorce document) into the slave's hand while the slave was bound and asleep, according to Rambam, it suffices for the slave to be bound alone, as it is written, "And she was sitting next to him," and he sold the slave to her or gave him to her and wrote her a gift deed over him.
