Since she acquired the slave, she acquired the get and is considered divorced. However, if the slave was not bound, she acquires the slave but not the get and is not divorced until the get reaches her hand. Some say that the husband does not need to take it from the slave and give it to her. There are those who are uncertain about this, perhaps it is like "take your get from the ground" since the initial giving was not a proper giving (Beit Shmuel, section 29). The first opinion holds that it is not similar to "take your get from the ground" because the giving to her courtyard was valid, but the courtyard did not have the power to acquire it. Therefore, in this context, the initial giving is considered a giving. We have already written something similar in section 11, see there. The main ruling is that she is in a doubtful state of being divorced.

Laws of Agency in Divorce: Agent for Delivery and Agent for Receipt – containing 29 sections:
We maintain throughout the entire Torah that a person's agent is like himself, as we have explained at length in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 182, with the help of Heaven. In the matter of divorce, the Torah explicitly wrote this, and thus the Sages expounded (beginning of Chapter 2 of Kiddushin) that in the context of divorce, it is written, "and she shall be sent out of his house" (Deuteronomy 24:1). It should have written "and he divorced her," but this comes to teach us that the husband can appoint an agent. And from the fact that it is written "and she shall be sent" with a "hey" (indicating the feminine), it is expounded that the wife can appoint an agent. And we further expound "and she shall be sent" without specifying the "hey" as if to say that she will send, and it is written again "and she shall be sent" to teach us that an agent can appoint another agent. The husband's agent is called an agent for delivery, as he stands in the place of the husband to deliver the get (divorce document) to the wife, as if she received it from the husband himself. It is not considered a get until it is delivered to the wife—that the get reaches her hand. Therefore, the husband can retract it before the get reaches her hand. When he delivers it to her, he says to her: "This is your get that your husband is sending to you, and with this get, you are divorced from your husband and permitted to all men." All the laws concerning the giving of the get and its declaration when the husband gives it to her apply equally to his agent. The scholar arranging the get joins with two others to form a court, as will be explained in Siman 141. They meticulously ensure that the get is written properly, as will be explained in the procedure of the get in Siman 154, with the help of Heaven.

And the agent of the woman is called an agent for receiving, and he stands in her place. From the moment the husband delivers the get (divorce document) to her agent, she is divorced from him and permitted to marry any man. His status is equivalent to the woman's in every matter, such as if the get was thrown into his yard or within his four cubits. There is an opinion that just as a woman cannot appoint an agent to receive her get from the husband's agent due to the disrespect it implies towards the husband, who might say she is dishonoring him by not receiving it herself from his agent, as explained in Siman 141, similarly, one should be concerned about the disrespect to the woman, who might say the husband is dishonoring her by not giving it directly to her agent but rather to his yard (Taz). However, these matters are not necessarily conclusive (Beit Shmuel Section 2). For us, there is no practical difference in this matter since we do not practice the appointment of an agent for receiving, as will be explained there. According to the law, it remains a doubt since it is a question in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 6, Halacha 2 and see Maaseh Rokeach at the beginning of Chapter 6, who also wrote similarly).

When the husband delivers the get (bill of divorce) to his agent, he should say to him: "Receive this get for my wife, [name], and she will be divorced by it from me from now, and permitted to any man." And in the get, he should write: "You are permitted to any man," because in the writing of the get, it is necessary to speak in the second person, as we consider the agent like the wife herself. And only in his verbal statement is it necessary to clarify his words about whom he is divorcing, as how could he say to him, "You are divorced"? But in its writing, it is like all other gittin (bills of divorce), just as in the case of a delivering agent, it is written in the husband's language, as if speaking in the second person. Also, the parchment and ink do not need to be given to his agent, as the agent of a person is like the person himself (Siman 141:1).

We find among the early authorities (Sefer HaTerumos and Hagaos Maimoniyos Chapter 6) a formula for a document that they would write for an agent of acceptance in the following language: "We, the Beit Din, were convened as a court of three, and before us came [Name] from such-and-such a place situated by such-and-such a river, and he divorced his wife [Name], who had appointed an agent to accept her get (bill of divorce) in the presence of witnesses, from the hand of her husband [Name]. And he said to him, 'Accept this get for my wife [Name], and she is hereby permitted to marry any man.' And prior to giving it, he nullified before us any declaration he might have made, stating that if he had issued any declaration, it would be null and void. And he imposed no conditions on the get but divorced her with a complete divorce. We read the get and found it valid and in accordance with the law. And because we saw that [Name], daughter of [Name], from [Name], son of [Name], her husband, had given the get into the hand of her agent of acceptance, we wrote this document for her to be in her possession as evidence and proof. This document is strong and established on such-and-such a date, etc., [Name], judge; [Name], judge; [Name], judge."

Rambam wrote in chapter 6 that a messenger to receive a get (divorce document) must be appointed in the presence of two witnesses, and there must also be two witnesses who testify that the get reached the hand of her messenger. Additionally, the first witnesses who saw her appoint the messenger can also serve as witnesses for the receipt of the get from the husband's hand. This is explicitly stated in the Mishnah (63b): a woman who says, "Receive my get for me," needs two sets of witnesses—two who say, "In our presence, she said," and two who say, "In our presence, he received," etc. This is not considered half a matter, since they saw all they could see at that time (Rashba). Furthermore, once she appoints him as a messenger, his hand becomes like her hand, such that when the husband gives him the get, it is as if she herself received it. Therefore, those who saw the messenger receive it have effectively seen her receive it from her husband (cited in the name of Ramban). This is considered valid, and all the more so if the witnesses before whom she spoke are the same ones who witnessed the receipt of the get by the messenger from the husband, this is certainly acceptable. We do not say that they are liars, questioning how they could be present at the woman's statement to the messenger and later in a different place when the husband handed the get to the messenger (Tosafot).

However, regarding an emissary for delivery, the Rambam wrote that witnesses are not required at the time of appointing him as an emissary, as it is already explained in Choshen Mishpat there that agency does not require witnesses or a formal act of acquisition. But the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote (at the beginning of "HaSholeach") that in the Jerusalem Talmud there it is stated that an emissary for delivery must be appointed in the presence of two witnesses, and the emissary does not count as one of the two. And in our version of the Jerusalem Talmud, this is not found. And regarding the law, it can be said that they do not disagree, as the Rambam explained in Chapter 9, Law 32, that specifically when witnesses are signed on the get (divorce document), witnesses for the agency are not required. But without this, witnesses are needed. And according to this, it can be said that the Jerusalem Talmud refers to a situation where there are no signed witnesses on the get. However, from the Rosh it is understood that in all cases witnesses are required. And the Tur in Siman 141 wrote that the Rambam disagrees with the Rosh, and also in the Shulchan Aruch there, in Section 11 and Section 13, both opinions are brought.

And behold, the reasoning of the Rosh is straightforward, for even though it is true that all agency does not require witnesses, nevertheless, in matters of marital status, nothing can be done without witnesses. However, according to the Rosh, one cannot say this. It is true that this is the opinion of the Raavad in the third chapter of Ishut and the Ran at the beginning of the first chapter of Kiddushin, who also ruled that in matters of agency for Kiddushin, witnesses are required, just as Kiddushin itself requires witnesses. But the Rosh there agreed with the words of the Rambam that for agency of the man, witnesses are not required, and for agency of the woman to receive Kiddushin, witnesses are required. And even regarding the agency of the woman, he hesitated to say that witnesses are not required, as the Tur wrote earlier in Siman 35 and gave the reason that witnesses are required only for the completion of the matter, not for the agency itself. Therefore, why did he require witnesses for the get, both for the agency of the man and for the opinion of the Rambam, one of the greats (Chapter 10 of Gittin 63: beginning with "the woman") labored greatly because since the get is before us in the hand of the agent and the woman admits that he is her agent to receive it, why should he not be believed with a migu (a legal principle allowing one to be believed if they could have lied more effectively) that if he wanted, he could have handed it to her? And this that the Mishnah required witnesses is because it is dealing with a case where the get was torn, as explained there, that there is no migu. But where there is a migu, why should he not be believed, for in the Talmudic discussion (Gittin 64a), it is explained that wherever there is a migu, he is believed. And one cannot say that because we hold that witnesses of the condition (of the divorce) are required to know at the time of the delivery of the get to the agent that the divorce was completed, and if there are no witnesses to the declaration, how will they know of the condition that this woman was divorced? For one cannot say this, for if so, we would require that the witnesses to the declaration also be present at the time of the delivery of the get. Otherwise, the witnesses of the delivery would still not know, and no authority has written such a thing. And also in the Talmud (beginning of the chapter "HaMekabel"), it is proven explicitly that this is not required, and the Mordechai explicitly wrote there, and one must say that the witnesses of the condition only need to know from the delivery of the get. Therefore, why are witnesses needed for the agency? And in truth, there are those among the early authorities who wrote that as long as the get is in the hand of the agent, witnesses are not required at the time of the agency (Ran according to Rashi in the discussion of "the husband says for safekeeping," and similarly wrote the Maharshal there). But all the decisors did not differentiate in this matter, and it is explicitly implied from the Rambam, the Tur, the Shulchan Aruch, and most decisors that witnesses are always required for the agency to receive the get.

However, with the help of Heaven, we clarified in Siman 35, Se'if 17, the reasoning of the Rambam, of blessed memory, that it is certain there is no connection between witnesses and agency, even in the cases of divorce and marriage, contrary to the opinion of the Rosh, which we mentioned, that only at the conclusion of the matter are witnesses required. The reason the Rambam required witnesses for her agency, both for divorce and marriage, is different. Since initially, this body was forbidden to the entire world and afterward permitted, and in marriage, the opposite—how can it be that this body transitions from prohibition to permission or from permission to prohibition without witnesses? And although her agent is like her, still, witnesses did not hear anything from her directly. However, for the husband's agency, nothing is required because his status does not change at all; both before and after, he is permitted to all women. The matter of immorality related to him only occurs at the time of marriage and divorce, when she becomes forbidden to the entire world or permitted to the entire world, and witnesses are needed at the conclusion of the act. But his agency is like any other agency that does not require witnesses. The reason witnesses are needed when there are no signatory witnesses on the get is for a different reason: the primary validity of the get depends on it being written for her sake and other matters, and who testifies to this? Therefore, when there are signatory witnesses, they testify. But without signatory witnesses, it is indeed necessary to have witnesses at the time the get is handed over to the agent, and they know it was written properly. And there, in Se'if 19, we wrote that in the case of a get, even the Raavad agrees with the Rambam that no witnesses are needed for his agency because the get itself proves it. But the opinion of the Rosh, of blessed memory, requires further investigation as to what difference there is between the agency of marriage and the agency of divorce. (And the Rosh in Perek 2 of Kiddushin, Siman 7, wrote, "If we can differentiate between a get that comes to permit and marriage that comes to prohibit, etc., this requires further investigation," and he did not explain a reason for differentiating).

It seems to me that according to the Rosh, it must be so, because the main reason why the husband is not believed to deny when the get (divorce document) is in the hands of the agent is due to the principle of "migo" (since if he wanted, he could have given her the get). How can we remove her from the presumption of being a married woman through a "migo," when a "migo" in the presence of a presumption is an unresolved issue in the Talmud (Bava Batra 5b)? Therefore, even if he does not deny, she would only be permitted based on his admission, and it turns out that the permissibility depends on him and not on witnesses. How can we permit a married woman through a permissibility that depends on him and not on witnesses? Therefore, witnesses are also required for his agency so that he cannot deny, as the witnesses will contradict him, and it turns out that the permissibility depends on the witnesses. But in the case of marriage, on the contrary, she is entering herself into a prohibition, and she is believed about herself to prohibit, just like if she says "you betrothed me" and he says "I did not betroth you," she becomes prohibited to the whole world based on her admission. And even though in the discussion (64a) it is proven that when there is a "migo" he is not believed, the Rosh writes there (siman 8) that this is when the get is in the woman's hand, and therefore she has already left the presumption of being a married woman (and what he writes there that it is possible even if it is in the hand of a third party, is written because she can claim that the get was in her hand). So too must we say according to the other poskim that in every case a "migo" is effective, and here it is a "migo" in the presence of the presumption of being a married woman. But since there is already a written and signed get, it is as if she has already left the presumption of being a married woman when we can say that she has already been divorced by the agent, and her presumption of being a married woman is weakened, and the "migo" is effective. The main laws of this will be explained, God willing, in siman 141.

How is the language of an agent for acceptance? For example, when she says to her agent in the presence of witnesses, "Receive my get (divorce document) from my husband, so-and-so," or "Take my get from my husband, so-and-so," or "Carry my get," etc., or "Acquire my get," etc., or "Let my get be in your hand from my husband, so-and-so," in all of these cases she must say "for me." Without saying "for me," it is not sufficient for the agency of acceptance. However, saying "Receive my get" is effective (Beit Shmuel, section 3), as this is the primary language of acceptance. It seems to me that the same applies when she says it in a foreign language that is effective. Moreover, it is necessary to explain it to her in a foreign language so that she can say it in a language she understands, because if she does not understand the matter, it is meaningless (and the Yam Shel Shlomo is uncertain about "carry my get," see there).

Just as a woman can appoint an agent to accept [a get, a divorce document] on her behalf, so too, she can appoint an agent to bring her get by saying to the agent, "Bring me my get." The law regarding this is the same as the law regarding an agent for the husband to deliver the get: it is not considered a get until it reaches her hand. We should not question the situation by saying that if her agent is like her, she should be divorced upon his acceptance of it, and if he is not like her, how does she become divorced? For indeed, he is neither his agent nor her agent. For if the husband truly appoints him as his agent to deliver the get, it is impossible [for it to be effective]. But if the husband says he does not want the agent to be his agent but rather her agent, how does she become divorced? In truth, he is the woman's agent, but she does not want the get to take effect upon his receipt of it, but rather upon her own receipt of it (there, sec. 4).

However, a husband cannot appoint an agent for acceptance, meaning he cannot tell another person, "Take this get and acquire it for my wife, so-and-so," because the get is a disadvantage for her, and one cannot impose a disadvantage on a person in their absence. It is impossible for someone to be her agent for acceptance without her knowledge. Furthermore, it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 1 of Gittin, that even if her husband is afflicted with boils, and it is presumed that it would certainly be a benefit for her to be divorced, it still amounts to nothing, because a woman would prefer any husband over none. Similarly, it is stated there at the beginning of Chapter 6 that even if there were quarrels between them and she was crying out to be divorced, as long as she did not appoint an agent for acceptance herself, we say that perhaps she has reconciled and changed her mind. This is the opinion of the Rosh and the Tur. Some say that in a case of quarrel and she is crying out to be divorced, she is considered possibly divorced (Ran, Chapter HaMekabel).

And know that the Tur brought in the name of the Itur that when we know that she wishes to divorce and the husband tells someone, "Take possession of it for her," she is divorced through his acceptance even if he did not make him an agent to accept it. For he wrote in the name of the Geonim: If he said to him, "Take possession of this get for her," and then wants to retract, he cannot. And he explained their words that since he said to him, "Take possession of it for her," and she desires it, she is divorced. But against her will, she is not divorced. And the Tur challenged him on this, see there. And these matters are puzzling, for even if one did not heed the words of the Jerusalem Talmud, in our Talmud (end of chapter 16 of Yevamot), there is a question regarding one who grants a get to his wife in a place of conflict. And according to most of the decisors, the question is resolved that it certainly does not work. And according to some, it remains in doubt, as I wrote. But how can we say with certainty that it is a get? And it must be said that he interprets it: Since the Talmud did not say that she cries out to be divorced, as in the Jerusalem Talmud, it implies that the question is whether we know that there was conflict between them, and yet we did not hear from her that she wishes to be divorced. But if we heard, she is divorced, for it is a benefit for her. And this is a singular opinion, and all the decisors hold that even if we later hear from her that she is agreeable to the acceptance of her get on her behalf, it does not work unless we knew at the time of the acceptance of the get that she currently wishes to be divorced (Nimukei Yosef there). And explicitly, it implies this in the Jerusalem Talmud, see there. And in any case, she is in doubtful divorce status.

And similarly, when delivering a divorce document (get) to a wife in a situation where there is a brother-in-law (yavam) so that she will not be obligated to undergo levirate marriage (yibbum) after his death, there remains an unresolved question. Perhaps she loves the yavam and prefers to undergo yibbum (as discussed in Yevamot). There was an incident in the house of Rashi, of blessed memory, regarding a student who fell ill and had a fiancée in a distant place. He requested Rashi, of blessed memory, to accept a get on behalf of his fiancée, but Rashi refused because this is a question unresolved in the Gemara (Mordechai there). Even in a case where the yavam is a minor and she would need to wait many years for him to perform yibbum, there is a disagreement among the early authorities (Rishonim) whether it is possible to deliver a get on her behalf without her knowledge (there).

And it seems to me that since the doubt in the Gemara is whether she might love the yavam (levir) and prefer to undergo yibum (levirate marriage), therefore in our times and in our country where yibum is not practiced at all and we only perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage), it is certainly a merit for her, and we can act on her behalf without her presence. I found that this is also the ruling of the Maharshal, of blessed memory, in Yam Shel Shlomo on Yevamot, chapter 15, section 21. He also wrote there that if the yavam has a wife already, and in our country it is forbidden to marry two women, it is certainly unreasonable—even if yibum were practiced—that she should expect the yavam's wife to die so that he could marry her. Therefore, it is a merit for her. Although initially there is some hesitation, according to what he ruled that if both parties want yibum, we do not object to it, nevertheless, he ruled that after the fact, if she received a get (divorce document) on her behalf, chalitzah is not required. And it is obvious to us that we have not heard of yibum at all, and it is a merit for her, and in pressing circumstances, it seems to me that we can rely on this.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 5: If her husband has turned into an idolater and we know that she is pursuing a get (divorce document), some say that the one who turned can grant her a get, but there are those who disagree even in this case. Similarly, if the yavam (levirate husband) has turned and the husband grants her a get so that she does not fall before the yavam. And if his wife has turned, he should grant her a get through another, as mentioned above in Section 1. And even if she later retracts, she does not need another get. The same applies to a woman who is forbidden to her husband; he grants her a get through another, but some are stringent in this matter. This concludes his words.

And behold, what was stated that there are those who disagree even in the reverse case, his intention is regarding the Ran in his responsa who wrote that even if she demands a divorce, we still are concerned that she may have changed her mind. One of the great authorities elaborated to prove that in the reverse case there is no disagreement at all, and only when she demands a divorce, we do not rely on saying that she truly desires it in a situation of quarrel or similar matters, but not in the reverse case where it is certainly to her benefit even if we did not hear from her. And so ruled Rashi, of blessed memory, in practical halacha (Taz). Similarly, this is the ruling of the Maharshal in Yam Shel Shlomo there. 

And what was written regarding a woman forbidden to her husband, there are those who are stringent to grant her a get (divorce) in Siman 1, he did not bring this opinion at all. It must be said that there, in the reverse case, he was not concerned with this opinion, and here regarding a woman forbidden to her husband, he was concerned (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 7). However, in truth, it is very surprising to be concerned with this opinion whose reasoning is to consider the opinion of the Rif in the first chapter of Gittin that even in a case where it is beneficial to grant on her behalf, it is only regarding that the husband cannot retract, but the completion of the get and the emancipation is specifically when the get and the emancipation come into her hand and the hand of the servant (Maharik, root 141). And this is indeed a singular opinion, besides that most decisors disagree with the Rif, and even the Rif would not hold this in the reverse case and the reverse where it is a complete benefit (Atzei Yehuda who elaborated on this and his words appear to be the main ruling).

It appears to me that in the laws that have been clarified, such as in cases of someone afflicted with boils, in the case of a dispute, in the case of a yavam (levirate marriage), or in the case where the doubt is whether she consented at the time when the other party acquires on her behalf, and even if she cried out earlier to be divorced, perhaps she has now changed her mind as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. According to this, in our times when iron wires have spread throughout the world, which we call telegraph, through which people can communicate over long distances, if the rabbi in the husband's location asks the rabbi in the wife's location whether the wife wishes to appoint someone to receive the get (divorce document) on her behalf, and he responds that she consents and requests that the get be received on her behalf, it is as if she is standing before us and requesting to appoint someone to receive the get on her behalf. However, the rabbi in the husband's location should not arrange the get until the following day to mitigate the concern that she might have changed her mind. If it is delayed until the next day, the rabbi should ask again via the telegraph. It also seems (according to what the Be'er Heitev writes in Siman 65) that even if someone is appointed to receive the get on her behalf and then they ask on the same day if she agrees and she responds affirmatively, it is acceptable. Nevertheless, it is better to ask beforehand. In my opinion, in cases of potential agunah (a woman who is chained to her marriage), one can rely on this, and the best and correct way is that she appoints a specific person as her agent to receive it. The reason for this, as brought in the name of the Rashba, is that there is a doubt whether if she says "whoever the husband wishes to give it to shall be my agent to receive it," there might be a concern of bereira (retroactive designation). Therefore, it is better if she specifies a particular person.

If someone sends a get (divorce document) to his wife through an emissary for delivery, and there is a concern that he might annul the get or the agency, he should be made to swear with all severity and all the curses in the Torah and the Mishneh Torah that he will not annul the get or the agency. In addition, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 11 a good enactment to avoid any concern or dispute: initially, the emissary should be appointed as an emissary to receive the get, to acquire it on her behalf, relying on our sages who permitted acquiring the get for her when it is reversed. As he wrote, the husband should hand the get to the emissary and say to him, "Acquire this get for my wife, [her name] daughter of [her father's name], and she is thereby divorced from me and permitted to anyone." Then the rabbi should say to the husband, "Your wife is already permitted to anyone, but I ask you, for the sake of clarity, to take the get from the emissary and give it back to him to be an emissary for delivery. Say to him in these words: 'Deliver this get to my wife [her name], and your hand shall be as my hand, your mouth as my mouth, and your actions as my actions, etc., and she will be divorced from me and permitted to anyone.'" Consequently, there will be no concern about its annulment since he knows she is already divorced. Even if he annuls it or dies, she will not require yibum (levirate marriage), and we can rely on the fact that he was initially an emissary to receive it and she was already divorced. This is specifically when the emissary was first an emissary to receive and then an emissary to deliver, as mentioned, but not the reverse, because the agency for receiving cancels the agency for delivery, as he himself annulled the delivery (Bach and the Gra). This will be explained in section 28.

It is obvious that if a woman appointed an agent to receive a get (divorce document) on her behalf, and the agent went to the husband, and the husband said, "I do not want you to be an agent to receive it, but rather to be my agent to deliver it," and the agent agreed, the agency for receiving the get is nullified and he becomes an agent for delivering it, as it depends on the will of the husband. Furthermore, even if the husband did not explicitly say "I do not want [you to be an agent to receive it]," but rather handed him the get and said, "Deliver this get to my wife, so-and-so, and give it to her, and your hand will be like my hand," etc., thereby clarifying that the get will not take effect until it reaches her hand, it is understood that the agency for receiving the get is nullified and he becomes an agent for delivering it. It is necessary to clarify what expressions denote delivery and what expressions denote receiving.

In Section 10, it clarifies the terms of acceptance. If the husband says to the agent these terms or if he says, "Acquire it for her," or "Here is this get for you," it is also considered as if he said "acquire" (Gemara 63b). In the Gemara, the term used is "here," which is like saying "here is." However, if he says "bring and give it to her," the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch ruled that this removes it from acceptance and makes him a messenger for delivery. If the get does not reach her hand, she is not divorced because "bring" certainly does not mean "acquire." And even though regarding the payment of a debt, we hold (first chapter of Bava Kama) that "bring" is like "acquire," nevertheless, regarding a gift and a get, we hold (fourth chapter of Gittin) that "bring" is not like "acquire" because in something given willingly, his intention with "bring" is not for the agent to acquire on his behalf. Only regarding debt and deposit, which he is obligated to give, is "bring" like "acquire." Thus, the Rambam ruled in Chapter 4 of Zechiyah that regarding a gift, "bring" is not like "acquire." Now, if he only said "give it to her," it would seem to say that the agency of acceptance is not removed, for regarding a gift, the Rambam ruled there that "give" is like "acquire," and since the Talmud compares a gift to a get, also in a get, "give" is like "acquire." The Rambam here only wrote about when he said "bring and give it to her" and not "give it to her" alone. But the Tur explicitly wrote "bring or give it to her," making him a messenger for delivery. They already questioned him, for he himself in the Tur Choshen Mishpat Siman 125 ruled like the Rambam that in a gift, "give" is like "acquire." (See Beit Shmuel Subsection 9 and Chelkat Mechokek Chapter 6 Halacha 10, and the Gra Subsection 18, and study this well).

However, in my humble opinion, it seems that the words of the Tur are clear, and also the intention of the Rambam in what he wrote "go and give," means "go or give." This is also elucidated from the Tosefta (at the beginning of chapter 4 in the words of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel) and from the Jerusalem Talmud (chapter 6, halacha 1 in the words of Rav Nachman) that "give" is not the same as "acquire" in the context of a get (divorce document). There is also proof from the Babylonian Talmud (in the comments there). The statement in the Gemara that a gift is like a get regarding "go" but not like "acquire" is certainly true, as a gift is like a get in the context of "go," but a get is not like a gift in the context of "give it to her," because a gift is a complete acquisition, unlike a get. On the contrary, this is the intention of our sages there; we hold that the agent for a gift is like the agent for a get regarding "go," but not like "acquire." In other words, although in "give" they are not similar for the reason we mentioned, nevertheless in "go," they are similar. The reason is simple: the term "give" itself is a term of gifting, but in the context of a get, the term gifting does not apply, and "go" since "give" was not stated, even in a gift it means to deliver it to the recipient, just as in a get it means to deliver it to his wife.

However, there are some of our rabbis who hold that when a husband says "go to her" or "give to her," it is uncertain whether this is considered as if she has already acquired the get or not. Therefore, if the husband dies before she receives the get, she is subject to yibbum (levirate marriage) out of doubt and must perform chalitzah (a form of releasing the obligation of yibbum) but not yibbum (actually marrying the brother-in-law) (Rashba and Ran at the beginning of chapter 6 and Rivash). This seems to be the straightforward interpretation of the Talmudic passage there. And this is the opinion of Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) in section 6, even though he only mentioned "give," it certainly applies to "go to her" as well, as is clear from the source of the law (as Beit Shmuel also wrote in subparagraph 10). Know that all these expressions are only if the sender did not say anything else besides these expressions, but if he concluded his words and said, "and your hand shall be like my hand," etc., in any language he used, it is obvious that he has nullified the acceptance and made the agent a messenger to deliver (the get) (there).

The husband cannot appoint an agent to accept the get (divorce document) without her consent. Therefore, when he appoints an agent to deliver the get to his wife, even if he uses the language of acceptance, such as saying "accept this get for my wife," we say that his intention is for the agent to deliver it. Once the get reaches her hand, she is divorced. This is a teaching in the beginning of the chapter "Hatekabel." We do not say that it is not a get at all, even when it reaches her hand, because he did not appoint the agent for delivery but made a mistake in thinking that he could appoint an agent for acceptance. No one makes such a mistake, and certainly, his intention is for delivery. Therefore, he said "accept and deliver it to her," and the agent knows this and agrees to be an agent for delivery.

Similarly, when she appoints an agent for acceptance and the agent says, "I do not consent to be an agent for acceptance, but accept this get for her," we say that his intention is also for delivery, and he means "accept and deliver it to her" (Beit Shmuel, section 8). This must be so, because it is impossible for his intention to change in a single moment. There are those who want to say that it is a retraction from what he said, "I do not consent" (Lechem Mishneh, chapter 6, halacha 10), but this does not seem correct. Nevertheless, in practice, one should be stringent (see there, where he questions the language of the Rambam and derives his ruling from it, and it is not difficult at all. It is known that the Rambam always adopts the language of the Talmud).

The woman's agent who came to receive a get (divorce document) from the husband and said to him "I am an agent of acceptance," and [the husband] said to him, "Take it as she said," meaning to say, "I do not nullify your agency, whether she appointed you as an agent of acceptance or as an agent of delivery, you are as she said," and he brought the get. If she then says to him, "I only appointed you as an agent of delivery," even if the get reached her hand, she is not divorced. This is because it nullifies the agency she made, and he did not agree to the trouble of delivery. Since she did not appoint him as an agent of acceptance, and he did not agree to delivery, even though he handed it to the woman, it was settled afterward. However, at the time he received the get from the husband, he did not agree to delivery.

However, in the reverse case, where the agent comes to the husband and says, "I am an agent for delivering [the get] from your wife," and the husband responds, "Here, take it as she said," meaning as explained above, and he brings the get and says to her, "I appointed you as an agent for receiving [the get]," as soon as the get reaches her hand, she is divorced. This is because he did not nullify the agency she established but rather diminished it; she said [an agent for] receiving, and he said [an agent for] delivering, and receiving is less burdensome than delivering. Therefore, he agreed even to delivering. But if before the get reached her hand, the get was burned or she accepted betrothal in the meantime, it would be a doubtful divorce. Perhaps his intention was specifically as she said, and from the moment the agent received it, she was divorced. The Talmud is uncertain about this language, whether his intention was, "Here, take it as she said," meaning, "I believe you that this is what she said," in which case, before the get reaches her hand, she is certainly not divorced because he appointed the agent for delivering; or his intention was specifically as she said, and he was an agent for receiving, and thus when it reaches her hand, she is certainly divorced, and before that, she is doubtfully divorced. This is the ruling of all the authorities, and although the Rambam did not mention this, it must be his intention as well (as the Kesef Mishneh wrote).

And regarding what was explained in section 25, that she appointed him as a messenger for bringing, but he said to receive, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 8 that if the husband did not say "Take this" as she said, but instead gave him the get and said to him "Go and give it to her" or "Acquire it for her," once the get reaches her hand, she is divorced. Their words are very perplexing, for since the messenger told him that he is a messenger to receive, and the husband said "Acquire it for her," which is a term of receiving, certainly his intention was only for receiving. And since she did not appoint him for receiving, she is not divorced at all. There are those who have explained that since he said "Acquire it for her," his intention was for what is beneficial to her, and since if we say that he is not a messenger for bringing, she would not be divorced, and she wants to be divorced, therefore we say his intention was for bringing (D’var Pashut). This is not understood at all, for certainly the words of the husband are as they sound, and how can we interpret his intention leniently? Even with "Go and give it to her," there is a doubt according to the poskim whether "Go" is like "Acquire" or not, as written in section 22. Perhaps his intention was to "Acquire" relying on the words of the messenger (Beit Shmuel section 11). It is explained in the Gemara that "Go" is effective (Gittin 63a: it resolves, no, etc., and bringing is like receiving). All the poskim wrote this. But regarding "Acquire it for her," there are indeed those who disagree (see Beit Shmuel section 12 and examine thoroughly). However, the Gemara discusses when he said "Go and give it to her" (ibid.), and in this case, it is certainly clear that his intention was for bringing since he told him to give the get into her hand. Therefore, it seems to me that the intention of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch is also when he said "Go and give it to her" or "Acquire and give it to her," but they abbreviated the language. In such a case, it clearly seems that his intention is for bringing, and in practice, she would be doubtfully divorced. (And with what was said, the opinion of the Itur brought by the Ran and Ramban there, who were puzzled by it, can also be explained. See there and examine thoroughly.) According to this, it can be said that those who are stringent with "Go" or "Give," but with "Go and give it to her," they agree that it is not like "Acquire." This requires further study.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 10: If one made him (the agent) an agent for receiving (the get), and the agent said this to the husband, and the husband gave the agent a document of sending, and afterwards gave him a document of receiving, if he gave him the get when he gave him the document of sending, he thereby nullified the agency of the woman. Afterwards, when he gave it to him for receiving, he nullified the agency of sending, and the husband does not make an agent for receiving. There is no agency here at all, and she is not divorced through this agency. Rather, he should return and give it to him for the purpose of receiving on behalf of the woman. But if he did not give him the get except at the time he handed him the document of receiving agency, she is divorced immediately when he gave the get into his hand. For since he did not give him the get initially, the woman's agency was not nullified. End of quote.

Explanation of his words: Although the agency (of delivering the divorce document) depends on his (the husband's) will, nevertheless, he cannot annul the agency of the wife. For even if he makes him (the agent) an agent for delivery, and the divorce document (get) does not take effect until it reaches her hand, acceptance is included within delivery. This is because the agent needs to receive the get from him (the husband) and then deliver it to her. Therefore, even if he made him an agent for delivery at the time of giving the get and afterward changed his mind and made him an agent for acceptance, the get certainly does not take effect at all, even when the agent delivers it to her hand. The reason is that the agency for delivery was annulled by himself (the husband), and he does not have the power to make an agent for acceptance. The agency that the wife made is of no benefit because at the time of giving the get to the agent, it was not given for the purpose of acceptance. However, if he (the husband) received the get back from the agent and gave it to him again for the purpose of agency for acceptance, which the wife made, she is divorced immediately upon its acceptance. This is because the essence of her agency was not annulled, as we have stated, and it was only lacking the giving of the get for the purpose of acceptance. Even though initially he wanted specifically delivery and wrote a document of delivery, this does not matter because the get was not given to the agent at that time, and the giving of the get was for the purpose of acceptance, she is divorced immediately and there is no need to take it again. The main issue depends on the time of giving the get to the agent (as we have explained according to the words of the Gra, section 22). Some say that if he initially gave the get for the purpose of delivery, it is of no benefit at all when he afterward made him an agent for acceptance, even if he takes the get back from him and gives it to him again. This is because immediately when he made him an agent for delivery, the agency for acceptance was completely annulled (Taz and Beit Shmuel, section 16), and this also appears to be the implication in the source of the law in the Rivash, section 329. See there.

The Laws of Agency and Revocation of Agency, consisting of 168 sections:

Since it has been clarified that a man appoints an agent to deliver (a get, a religious divorce document) and a woman appoints an agent to receive it, it follows logically that when the husband sends the get via an agent to deliver it, she can appoint an agent to receive it directly from the husband's agent. Nevertheless, there is a dispute in the Gemara (Gittin 63b) regarding this, with one opinion prohibiting and one permitting it. The reason for the prohibition is either due to the dishonor to the husband, as it may be perceived that she holds him in contempt by not receiving it herself, which is not comparable to any other agent receiving it directly from the husband, who knows and does not object; but through his agent, he might object (Rashi). Consequently, if the husband knows and does not object, such as when he tells his agent to deliver it to her or to her agent, there is no concern at all (Tosafot). However, there is another reason for the prohibition, which is a rabbinic decree due to the case of a courtyard acquired afterward. That is, it has been clarified in Siman 139 that if the get is placed in another person’s courtyard and then she acquires the courtyard from that person, it is not a valid get, because at the time it was placed in the courtyard, it was not hers, and when it became hers, she did not receive it from her husband. Similarly, in this case, if he handed it to his agent and afterward she appointed her agent, it is similar to the aforementioned case. According to this reason, if she appointed her agent first and afterward he appointed his agent, it is not comparable to that case. But according to the reason of dishonor to the husband, there is still a concern of dishonor when he does not know about her agent. Therefore, if he knows about her agent and she appointed her agent first, there is no concern for either reason.

And the halachic ruling is that the Rif, the Rambam, the Rosh, and other early authorities ruled according to the opinion that permits, as it is evident in the Talmud there (which states: "If Rabbi Chanina's view were correct..."). However, the Baal Halachot Gedolot, the Rashba, and Sefer HaTerumah ruled according to the opinion that forbids, and similarly in the name of Rabbeinu Tam. Therefore, it remains a halachic doubt, and she is considered to be doubtfully divorced. Thus, the Shulchan Aruch brought both opinions without making a definitive ruling. Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in his major work that certainly one should be concerned for the opinion of those who forbid, and so wrote the Ran there. (The Beit Shmuel, in section 4, brought from the responsa of the Rivash, siman 55, that it is better to rely on those who permit than to send through a non-Jew, and there is a difficulty since the Rivash wrote this because in that place they were accustomed to rule in all matters according to the Rambam, as he wrote there. But for us, it is a dispute among the authorities. Conversely, regarding sending through a non-Jew, it will be explained in this siman that we are accustomed to permit sending through the postal service. Therefore, this matter requires further analysis.)

There is a significant question to be asked here: even without all the concerns, how is it possible to permit her to appoint an agent to receive it from the husband's agent without his knowledge? It is forbidden to change the husband's instructions. For example, if he said to give it to her in a specific place, it is forbidden to give it to her elsewhere, as will be explained. All the more so, if he said to give it to her, how can one give it to her agent and change his instructions? They answered that certainly if he told his agent, "Give this get (divorce document) into my wife's hand," it is indeed forbidden to change this. The permission is only when he said, "Give this get to my wife," which does not specifically mean into her hand (Beit Shmuel, section 3 and Vilna Gaon, section 5). And it is true as found in the responsa of the Rashba (section 1007) and all the earlier authorities did not mention anything about this. The Rashba himself hesitated there but wrote that it is necessary to say so, although the reasoning is puzzling since even when he says, "Give it to my wife," it implies her hand specifically. What seems correct to me is that in the Jerusalem Talmud (beginning of chapter 6), it states: "And he shall place it in her hand" - I only have her hand; from where do we derive her agent's hand? From where do we derive his agent to her agent? Hence we learn from "and he shall place" repeated twice. Certainly, the main derivation is only for an agent to another agent, as the concept of agency itself is derived from "he shall send her away" as mentioned at the beginning of section 140. Certainly, the derivation is when he said, "Give it to my wife." If he explicitly said "to my wife" or "to her agent," there would be no need for a verse since it is logically understood as mentioned in paragraph 1. Rather, certainly the Torah includes that even if he said, "Give it to my wife," the agent can give it to her agent. Nevertheless, the distinction between saying "into her hand" and saying "to my wife" is also valid. How do we include even such a case?

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in Section 1: If a woman tells her agent to receive the get (divorce document) from her husband, he should not receive it from the husband's agent. However, if she says, "Receive the get from my husband," he can receive it from the husband's agent. This is according to the opinion of those who permit an agent to receive the get from another agent. But according to those who prohibit this, it is forbidden in all cases due to the disrespect to the woman, as she might say, "I am of little worth in his eyes since he does not give it directly to my agent," and perhaps in such a situation, she did not appoint him as an agent to receive it (Taz and Bach, subparagraph 4). And when she says, "from my husband," it is forbidden even according to those who permit it, as it is written.

Even according to those who permit it, it is only to appoint another agent after the agent of the husband has received the get (divorce document), but not to make the husband’s agent also her agent to receive it, such as if she says to him, "You are hereby my agent to receive the get for me." And some say that even if she only said to him, "Receive it" without specifying "for me," it is also understood as if she said to be her agent to receive it. Or even if she said to him, "Let this get be a deposit with you," it is also considered as if she said, "Be my agent to receive it," because the husband did not give it to him as a deposit, and presumably her intention was for him to receive it on her behalf and keep it as a deposit. She does not have the ability to do this, and the sages (in Gittin) explained the reason is because the agency does not revert back to the husband, meaning the agent cannot switch from being the husband’s agent to the wife’s agent as long as he has not completed the husband’s agency. And before he hands it to her, the agency of the husband has not yet been completed (according to the Maggid Mishneh). Any agent who becomes an agent for the one he was sent to, thereby interrupts the first agency before he had the opportunity to return to the sender and say, "I have done your agency." An agency that is not fit to return and report is not considered an agency (according to Rashi). The sages ruled there that it remains in doubt, and if the husband dies before the get reaches her from the agent, she performs chalitzah (ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage) and does not undergo yibbum (levirate marriage). But if the get reaches her hand, she is definitely divorced, and we do not say that since she made him her agent to receive it, the husband’s agency was nullified, because it does not help even if he hands it to her. The agent did not intend to nullify the husband’s agency, but thought it would be effective if he became her agent to receive it. Once it is known that it is not effective, he completes the husband’s agency.

Some authorities say that the ruling in the Talmud, which considers it a doubtful get (divorce document), is not because there is a doubt whether the agency must revert back to the husband or not. Certainly, it must revert back. If from the outset of the agency, it was not fit for the agency to revert, such as if the husband told the agent, "You will be my agent for delivery until halfway, and then she will appoint you as her agent for acceptance," it is definitely not valid. This will be clarified similarly in Siman 142 (see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 23). Rather, the doubt is whether, at the initial stage of the agency, it was fit for it to revert, and perhaps we only require this at the initial stage of the agency (Rashba in his novellae there).

It appears to me that the reason for this requirement that the agency should return to the sender is because an agent of a person is like the person himself. Just as the sender himself would not have the capacity to be appointed as an agent to accept the get (divorce document) from his wife, since the get must necessarily leave his possession, so too, the agent he appointed, who stands in his place, cannot be made an agent by the wife before completing his mission. If this were allowed, the get would never actually leave the husband's possession. Therefore, there is a doubt whether, from the beginning of the agency, it is necessary for the agent to completely replace the sender until the mission is completed or not. It seems from the Talmudic discussion that this principle does not apply only to a get, but to all matters. Accordingly, if Reuven wants to give a gift to Shimon and appoints Levi as an agent and tells him, "Take this item to Shimon," and then Shimon appoints Levi as an agent to accept it on his behalf, it is not effective.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (64b): A betrothed young woman, she and her father can receive her bill of divorce. This means she or her father. She, because she is of age, and her father, because as long as she has not married or reached full maturity, she is still under her father's authority (Rashi). And although she can receive her bill of divorce herself, nevertheless, she does not have the ability to appoint an agent to receive it, only her father can appoint an agent and not she (Kiddushin 44b). Her power is not strong enough to appoint an agent. The reason is that her receiving the bill of divorce herself is only as an agent of her father, for in truth, she is under her father's authority. And regarding betrothal, she cannot receive it without her father's consent, as we wrote in Siman 37. However, concerning a bill of divorce, the Torah considered the father's mind, that he is not particular if she receives it, since a bill of divorce can be given against one's will (Ran there). This is only with the delivery of the bill of divorce. But for her to appoint an agent to receive it of her own will, certainly, the father would not agree to this. It seems that with the father's consent, she can act, just like she can receive betrothal with her father's consent, as we wrote there.

When she is married, even if she is a young girl (na'arah), she can appoint an agent to receive [her get] and not her father, because with the marriage, she has completely left his authority. Similarly, when she matures (becomes a bogeret), even if she is still betrothed, or if her father has died, she can appoint an agent, for she is an adult and leaves her father's authority upon his death. This applies to a young girl (na'arah), but a minor (ketanah), even if she is married and her father has died, cannot appoint an agent, for a minor cannot appoint an agent. Therefore, a minor who is married has no remedy through an agent to receive [the get], but rather the husband or his agent must deliver the get into her hand directly and not into her father’s hand, because she is married. However, when she is betrothed, the father can appoint an agent to receive [the get] even if she cannot. See what I wrote in paragraph 15 and it requires further investigation in Siman 173, paragraph 34.

And a minor betrothed girl, when the husband or his agent delivers the get (divorce document) into her hand, our rabbis dispute this. There are those who say that although a betrothed young woman (na'arah) can receive her get, either she or her father, and a minor girl also, when her father dies or she marries, she can receive her get. Nevertheless, a minor betrothed girl whose father is alive, only her father can receive her get and not she herself. This is the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam. And it is also explained in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 6), which states there that a minor's father receives it and not she herself. However, our rabbis, the Tosafists (Kiddushin 64b), hold that she can also receive her get. And Rashi, of blessed memory, initially held that only her father and not she herself could receive it, but later retracted this position, as it appears there. For it seems that since a young woman (na'arah) is still under her father's authority, this minor girl, when she has no father or is married, has the power to receive her get. So why, when she has a father, should her status differ from that of a young woman? The reason for the first opinion could be that as long as there is an adult, a minor cannot perform any act.

And more than this, there are those who say that even if the father grants her permission to receive her get (divorce document), it is not effective, for whenever there is an adult, we do not leave anything to a minor (according to the Ra'avad and the Ritva). And there are those who say that even according to those who forbid it, it is only without her father's consent. But with her father's consent, even a minor can receive her get (according to the Ramban and the Rashba). 

Proof of this is that in the matter of betrothal, certainly she has no hand (to act independently), yet a person can say to his minor daughter, "Go and receive your betrothal." The first opinion holds that this applies specifically to betrothal with money, where the benefit reaches her hand, but not with betrothal by document, and certainly not with a get, which returns to him (the father). However, we have already explained in Siman 37 that even with betrothal by money, there are those who disagree and hold that he cannot tell her to receive her betrothal (there).

And it is clear that in all these disputes, it is a case of doubtful divorce. If she received betrothal from another after receiving a get, she would require a get from both men if the second betrothal was through the father. And if the husband dies, she would perform chalitza and not yibbum (levirate marriage) (as per the commentary on the Shulchan Aruch, which implies that the primary opinion is that she has a hand, but this is questionable since it is explained otherwise in the Jerusalem Talmud, and all these authorities disagree. Therefore, it appears to me that it remains a doubt as stated).

And what has been explained, that a minor girl when she is married or when her father dies can receive a divorce document (get) by herself, does not apply to a complete minor who has no understanding at all, for the Torah says "and he sends her out of his house" (Deuteronomy 24:1), and not when he sends her out and she returns. Therefore, an insane person cannot have a divorce at all (Yevamot 113b), and she needs to have the understanding to guard her divorce document. And thus, the Sages taught (Gittin 64b) that anyone who cannot guard her divorce document cannot be divorced. The Sages explained there that the measure is anyone who can distinguish between her divorce document and something else. This means that she has the understanding that if they give her a nut, she takes it, and if they give her a pebble, she throws it away. And some say that it means when she reaches the age of minors, around six or seven years old, each according to her level of understanding, as is written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 335. At this stage, she knows to guard her divorce document and does not return to her husband's house. But less than this measure, she cannot receive a divorce document and is not divorced at all.

Some say that any minor girl who has not reached this age (of maturity), even the father cannot accept her divorce document, as she has not yet reached the stage of divorce for reasons that have been explained. And some say that the father can always accept her divorce document, for the father will keep the get (divorce document) and will not allow her to return to her husband's home, and he will also guard her from promiscuity. This also seems to be the implication from the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 6, end of Halacha 2). In practice, it is considered a doubtful divorce. Any minor girl who has the ability to receive her get also has the legal status of a courtyard (regarding divorce), so if the get is placed in her courtyard, she is divorced. And even though a courtyard also has the status of an agent, and a minor cannot appoint an agent, the Sages said (Bava Metzia 10a) that the courtyard of a minor is considered as an extension of her hand. Similarly, she has the four cubits (regarding the get), even though it is only a rabbinic enactment. Nevertheless, since she has a courtyard, she is also included in the enactment of the four cubits. See what I wrote in Siman 139.

Some say that when a minor girl is divorced by her father, the husband must write the get (divorce document) as if speaking directly to the father but in the third person regarding the daughter. How so? He should write, "I am releasing, etc., your daughter, Plonit, who was my wife." And some say that the wording should not be changed from that of all other gittin (divorce documents), since the father stands in her place. Therefore, in practice, it is proper to be stringent and write two gittin, as is stated in the order of the get in Siman 154, and this is what the great authorities have instructed. However, after the fact, if he only wrote one get like all other gittin, it is valid (Beit Yosef in Bedek HaBayit).

And know that what we wrote in section 9, that a minor cannot appoint a messenger, is a straightforward law throughout the Talmud that a minor cannot appoint a messenger. The reason is because it is written regarding agency, "a man" in the context of Passover and divorce (Rashi Bava Metzia 10b, s.v. "and does"), or because it is written regarding terumah, "also you" – just as you are people of intelligence, so too your agents must be people of intelligence (Raavad, Terumot 6:9). According to this, the words of the Rambam there are very puzzling, where he wrote, "A minor cannot appoint a messenger to receive her divorce, even though her courtyard can acquire her divorce document like an adult's, because a receiving messenger requires witnesses, and one does not testify about a minor, who is not of complete intelligence." The Raavad already contested this (and what the Maggid Mishneh wrote is very difficult, as the Lechem Mishneh wrote). 

And what seems clear to me is that the Rambam's reasoning is sound and necessary. It is true that for all agency, an adult is specifically required. However, regarding a woman being divorced, since it is written in the context of a get (divorce document), "and she shall be sent away," and we derive from this that the woman can appoint a messenger, as we wrote at the beginning of section 140. A woman being divorced can also be a minor if her father accepted betrothal for her, as though the Torah explicitly wrote that a minor being divorced can appoint a messenger, like "and he shall place it in her hand" written there, which includes even a minor. And even what we derive from "in her hand" to her courtyard also includes a minor. Therefore, the sages said that a courtyard applies to a minor, implying that the entire passage discusses even a minor. Thus, the verse "and she shall be sent away" also includes a minor, and the Torah permits a minor to appoint a messenger for a get. 

Why then did the sages say that a minor has no agency even for a get? And behold, regarding a courtyard, there is a discussion in the Talmud (Bava Metzia there) that only for a get does she have a courtyard and not for other matters. Thus, we should say the same regarding agency, that only for a get does she have agency and not for other matters. And even according to the opinion there that we derive other matters from a get, and this is the ruling of the Rif there, we should also say regarding agency that we derive from a get to all matters that a minor has agency. Therefore, the Rambam explained that regarding agency, it is impossible to say that the Torah's intention includes a minor due to the witnesses (and with this, all his words are precise and all the questions of the Lechem Mishneh are resolved there, and study it well).

It has already been explained in Siman 140, Section 5, that a "Shaliach Kabbalah" (an agent appointed to accept a get, a Jewish bill of divorce, on behalf of a wife) requires two sets of witnesses: two who witness the appointment of the agent and two who witness the acceptance of the get from the husband. Even if the witnesses to the appointment are the same as the witnesses to the acceptance, we do not say that they are liars (i.e., suspect their testimony) because it is unusual for them to be present at both events. Similarly, if one of the witnesses testifies regarding both the appointment and the acceptance, and the second witness testifies separately about the appointment and separately about the acceptance (so that there are three witnesses: one for the appointment, one for the acceptance, and the third joining both), it is valid because the entire matter is considered one testimony. Nevertheless, when there are two sets of witnesses, we do not say that they are testifying about half of a matter, due to the reasons explained there. Concerning a "Shaliach Holacha" (an agent appointed to deliver the get to the wife), it has been clarified there that, according to the Rambam, no witnesses are needed at the time of the appointment, whereas according to the Rosh, witnesses are required. In practice, we follow the Rosh. However, at the time of delivering the get to her hand from the agent, witnesses are certainly required. Furthermore, three witnesses are needed, as will be explained in Siman 142.

And behold, regarding the reason why witnesses are needed at the time of appointing the agent to accept [a get], we have explained there. And we also explained the reason for the dispute between the Rambam and the Rosh there. The reason why witnesses are needed when the acceptance agent receives the get from the husband is straightforward, as we hold that "with witnesses, it is as if it is written and signed." Just as when the get is given directly from the husband to the wife, witnesses are required, so too when it is given to her agent.

Consequently, according to this reason, according to the Rif and the Rambam, as explained in Siman 130, when there are signed witnesses on the get, the witnesses of delivery are not indispensable after the fact, and it is only initially that witnesses are needed. But according to Rashi, Tosafot, and the Rosh, without witnesses, it is nothing, and even after the fact, it is indispensable.

However, there is another reason for this: It is necessary to have witnesses for the acceptance so that they can later testify about the acceptance of the get. Otherwise, who would believe them that they received the get from the husband? Yet, according to this reason, there is a distinction between when the get is lost from the agent's possession, in which case witnesses are certainly required, and when the get is in his possession, in which case witnesses are not needed. This is similar to a woman bringing a get signed by witnesses, where witnesses of delivery are not needed, as this was an ordinance of Rabban Gamliel that witnesses should sign the get for the betterment of the world, as stated in Siman 120 and Siman 130.

Similarly, for a delivery agent, when he hands over the get to the woman, witnesses are also needed for the reasons explained. And in this case, there is another reason: since he needs to say "It was written and signed in my presence," which requires a court, as stated in Siman 142.

It is obvious that when the husband hands over the get (divorce document) to the agent of acceptance, he should not hand it over until the agent clarifies that he is an agent of acceptance from his wife. However, it does not invalidate if the clarification is after he has given the get to him, as it is merely a matter of revealing the fact. Nevertheless, initially, it is proper that he should not hand over the get until he first clarifies that he is an agent of acceptance. The manner of clarification can be either through witnesses or through a document of acceptance agency, as will be explained later, with God's help. But an agent of delivery who brings the get does not need witnesses to testify that he is an agent from the husband, as the get is signed in his hand. Even to testify that it was written and signed for her sake, the Rabbis trusted the agent, as it is stated in Siman 142. Nonetheless, the common custom is that he also brings a verified authorization from a court that the husband appointed him as an agent, as will be explained, with God's help. However, after the fact, the authorization is not indispensable.

In all these cases where two witnesses are required, the agent can also be considered as one witness, and he, together with another witness, makes two for the testimony. This applies to the execution of the agency, whether for delivery or receipt, and whether for the handing over of a get (divorce document) from the husband to his agent, or from his agent to the woman. For we hold that an agent can become a witness (Kiddushin 43b), as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 121, and also above in Siman 35 regarding marriage, see there. This is if the agent is eligible to be a witness, such as not being a relative or disqualified, and not a woman, although everyone is fit to be an agent as will be explained. This is the opinion of the Tur and the Itur, but the Rosh wrote (end of Chapter 4) that an agent cannot become a witness in these matters, except in the case of a delivery agent when he hands over the get to the wife, and three are required as stated in Siman 142, then the agent is one of the three (Arba'ah Turim, Even Ha'ezer, Siman 4). But if two are sufficient, he is not one of the two. The reason is that the agent stands in the place of the man or the woman and is considered like the party themselves. This is because in monetary matters an agent can become a witness since a person's money is not like their body (Sanhedrin 10a), but in matters of prohibition, an agent cannot be a witness. And that which it is said regarding marriage that an agent can become a witness, and likewise for divorce, the Sages said (Kiddushin 43b) that an agent can become a witness, this is when two are agents. This is the language of the Talmud there: He said to two, "Go and betroth a woman for me," they are his agents and they are his witnesses. Likewise for divorce, see there. Since he sent two, his intention was to make them witnesses, for if it were only for agency, why would he need two? But when he sent one, his intention was to make him like himself, and he cannot be a witness. And that which the Sages said there, that an agent can become a witness, even if it is one agent, this is in monetary matters for the reason I wrote. And that which is explained there in the Talmud, that one who holds an agent can become a witness does not hold the view that he is like the person themselves, see there, this is in monetary matters.

This is what we have written according to the opinion of the Rosh, and this seems correct to us in our humble opinion. Otherwise, the words of the Rosh are puzzling since the source of his ruling is from the Jerusalem Talmud (beginning of chapter 4), which holds that the messenger does not count as one of the witnesses there. And why should he be concerned with the words of the Jerusalem Talmud since in our Talmud it is explicitly ruled that a messenger can become a witness? And indeed, there are those who interpret the Jerusalem Talmud differently (see Rashba there). But for the Rosh, this is difficult. And there are those who say that this is a stringency from the Rabbis and not from the essence of the law (Beit Yosef). And I am puzzled why one should be concerned with a stringency in a place where the Gemara was not concerned with it. Furthermore, if so, we should also be concerned with this stringency in matters of Kiddushin (betrothal). Therefore, it seems to me that the Rosh holds this distinction that we have written, that in our Talmud, this law is not found in Gittin and Kiddushin, only with two messengers. And indeed, the Rosh in the beginning of chapter 2 of Kiddushin did not write this law there, only with two messengers. See there.

And the reason why the Rosh, of blessed memory, was compelled to this [position] is because the Jerusalem Talmud itself rules at the beginning of the second chapter of Kiddushin that a messenger can become a witness, and here it rules that he does not count as a witness. Therefore, we are forced to make this distinction. And there is proof for this from the Jerusalem Talmud itself. It states there at the beginning of the second chapter of Kiddushin: "Beit Shammai say that the messenger does not count as a witness, and Beit Hillel say that the messenger counts as a witness." And the Jerusalem Talmud questions, "How is this possible?" and answers, "He sent two [messengers], etc." There is no explanation for this (see the commentators there). In my humble opinion, the difficulty is as follows: How is it possible to say that a messenger counts as a witness when the Jerusalem Talmud holds in the fourth chapter of Gittin that the messenger does not count among the two [witnesses]? And it answers, "He sent two," meaning that with two messengers, they become witnesses (and regarding the annulment of a get, it says there that he counts among the two; see there. And the reason is simple, for he himself can also annul [the get]).

And regarding the law, most of the decisors disagree with the Rosh, and even according to the Rosh of blessed memory, it is possible that it is merely a stringency (as the Bach wrote). Nevertheless, heaven forbid to disregard his opinion in practice. And according to what is written, even in matters of marriage one must be careful that the agent is not one of the two witnesses. And when he appointed two agents, the later authorities agreed that according to all opinions, they become witnesses (see Beit Shmuel at the end of section 11), whether in matters of divorce or marriage, and the Talmud explicitly supports this, as written. Similarly, when the husband's agent delivers the get (bill of divorce) to his wife and three are required, the agent is one of the three. The reason three are required is due to the confirmation of a court, and this is only rabbinic. And in rabbinic matters, we say he becomes a judge, and so it is in the Talmud (5a). And regarding the nullification of the get, it is also stated in the Jerusalem Talmud there that he is counted among the two for the reason written in the previous section.

And regarding the matter that an agent for receiving needs witnesses when the get (divorce document) is handed to him, the Rambam wrote: "In what case are we discussing? When the get was lost or torn. But if the get is in the hands of the agent for receiving, there is no need for witnesses, whether the husband gave it to him privately or in the presence of witnesses. Its presence in the hands of the agent for receiving is as if it were in the hands of the woman herself. Nevertheless, he should not give it to him initially without witnesses, just as with the woman herself." And he follows his reasoning that after the fact it is valid even without witnesses when there are signing witnesses, as he wrote in section 17. And for the second reason mentioned there, so that they may later testify about the receipt of the get, it also does not apply when it is in the hands of the agent, similar to when it is in the hands of the woman. But according to our Rabbis who hold that witnesses are essential, here too witnesses are needed at the time of giving. However, to bring witnesses that the get was received in the presence of witnesses is not necessary, since the get is in the hands of the agent.

And this is what the Tur wrote, that if the signatures of the witnesses on the get (divorce document) are validated, there is no need to bring witnesses before us; rather, the messenger should state that he received it in front of two witnesses, etc. And similarly, our master the Beit Yosef in section 10 only copied the beginning of the words of the Rambam, that if the get comes from the hand of the reception messenger, there is no need for receipt witnesses. This means that it is sufficient for the messenger to say that he received it in front of witnesses. And all of this is regarding the receipt witnesses. But for the statement witnesses, before whom the wife appointed the messenger of reception, they are always needed, even if the get comes from the hand of the messenger (see Magen Avraham and Beit Shmuel section 12). And more will be explained with the help of Heaven.

And according to this, in the opinion of the Rosh who requires witnesses also for a messenger of delivery, it would also seem that the messenger needs to bring witnesses that the husband appointed him as a messenger. What difference is there between delivery and receipt? This is not found anywhere, and on the contrary, from the words of the Rosh at the beginning of Gittin, it is explicitly understood that there is no need to bring witnesses for this unless the husband disputes it, and it is a case where the messenger does not need to say "in my presence and in my presence." And indeed, some of our Rabbis hold that when the get is in the hand of the messenger, there is no need for witnesses of the statement (Rashi 64a s.v. ve’amai and Ran there). However, it may be said that it is not similar, for the messenger is certainly trusted in all matters. But regarding a messenger of receipt, in order for the woman to be divorced immediately upon his receipt, it is necessary to bring witnesses for this. For indeed, the fact that he is trusted because the get is in his hand pertains to the husband, as it’s certain he gave it to him. Similarly, he is trusted when the get is already in the woman’s hand. However, as long as the get is in his hand and we consider her divorced, on what basis do we hold her as divorced when the woman is not present to confirm she appointed him as a messenger? Even if she acknowledges she appointed him, he would be trusted from the time of her acknowledgment but not from the time the get came into his hand.
