One cannot say he would be trusted through a migo (claim of credibility) that if he wanted he could have handed it to her, for this is not a migo at all, as perhaps she does not want to receive it from him without the husband's knowledge. Therefore, to consider her divorced from the time of his receipt, it is necessary to bring witnesses that she appointed him as a messenger (and the Ran also wrote there that he is not trusted for her to be divorced from the first moment, see there). According to this, it may be said that they do not disagree at all. See Beit Shmuel section 12 and examine well.

And know that from the words of the Tur that we brought, it is explicitly implied that when is it not necessary to have witnesses that the get was handed over in their presence? Only when the signatures have been authenticated. But without authentication, it implies that witnesses are needed even when the get is in the hands of the agent. However, from the words of the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch, it does not imply this, as the Rambam only required authentication when the husband disputes and claims it is forged, as he wrote in Chapter 12, see there. And here in Chapter 6, he does not deal at all with authenticated documents. And so it is in the Shulchan Aruch. Also, from the Talmudic discussion, it is implied this way. Furthermore, it is surprising about the Tur himself, for later in this section, he wrote that authentication is needed only when there is a dispute. And these are his words: "She appointed an agent to receive it in the presence of witnesses, and the get is in his hand, and the husband claims it is forged, it should be authenticated by its signatures or by witnesses of delivery," end quote. So how does he require authentication here even without a dispute, even when the get is in the agent's hand? And also, our master the Beit Yosef in his book in the section beginning "He questioned him" found it difficult, for he himself wrote in Section 142 that authentication is not needed as long as the husband does not dispute it. And the Ra'avad holds in Chapter 12 that authentication is always required when the agent does not say "it was written and signed in my presence," but the Rambam holds in Chapter 7, Law 24, that without a dispute, authentication is not needed. And the Tur there holds like the Rambam. So why did he write here that authentication is needed? And his wording is not consistent.

Therefore, it seems to me that the Tur introduced a different ruling, and the essence of his words is as follows: Initially, he wrote the ruling from the Mishnah that a messenger designated to receive (a get) requires two sets of witnesses. Afterwards, he brings the Rambam's opinion that this is specifically when the get is lost, but when the get is in the hand of the messenger, there is no need for witnesses to validate (the delivery). He wrote that this is according to the Rambam, but according to our custom, witnesses are always required, except that they do not need to be presented before us since there are signed witnesses, and the law regarding the messenger is the same as regarding the woman herself. He then wrote that the requirement to bring two witnesses who saw the delivery pertains to a case where the recipient is not recognized, etc. But if the signatures have already been verified, there is no need to bring witnesses before us, etc. His words mean that even when the get is lost, if the signatures have already been verified, there is no need for witnesses to the delivery, just as in the case of the woman herself. If her get is lost, as long as the signatures were verified once, she is permitted, even if we do not know if there were witnesses to the delivery, because once we know that witnesses signed, we can assume they acted properly, which is the main ordinance of Rabban Gamliel. The same applies to the messenger. This will be clarified in the case where the get is lost, and there are no witnesses who saw it in her hand, that even the husband's admission does not help (and in the Shulchan Aruch, this is in section 56). This is truly the case when the signatures have not yet been verified.

All these matters apply when the husband does not contest it. But if he comes and contests, claiming it is forged, even if she appointed an agent with witnesses, and there are witnesses testifying to this, and the get (divorce document) is in the agent's hand, it still needs validation. Either the signatures must be validated, or witnesses must be brought who saw it being delivered in their presence. For even if the get was in the woman's hand and the husband claims it is forged, it requires validation. This is why the Sages instituted that an agent for delivery should say "It was written and signed in my presence," so that if the husband contests it, we do not heed him, for the Sages trusted the agent, as stated in Siman 142. And in a place where there is no need to say "It was written and signed in my presence," if the husband contests it, the signatures must be validated. Consequently, for an agent of acceptance, where the statement "It was written and signed in my presence" is never relevant, it always needs validation when the husband contests it, whether the get is in the woman's hand or in the agent's hand (see Beit Shmuel, section 74).

And if the husband does not contest the claim of forgery, but admits that he wrote it, and only says that he did not give it to the messenger for the purpose of divorce, but as a mere deposit, and the messenger says that he gave it for the purpose of divorce so that she would be divorced upon receiving it, the Rambam rules in Chapter 12, Law 11, that the messenger is believed. He further writes that if the get (divorce document) is found in the possession of the woman and she says that this messenger gave it to her, and the messenger says that he indeed gave it to her and that the husband gave it to him for the purpose of divorce, and the husband says he only gave it as a deposit, the messenger is believed, and she is considered divorced. He makes no distinction whether the man and the woman are in the same city or not, as in such a case it would seem that the husband would be believed, for if he intended it for divorce, why would he give it to a messenger and not deliver it to her himself? There is an opinion in the Talmud (64a) that supports this reasoning. Nevertheless, the ruling follows the opinion that the messenger is believed (as per Rabbi Chananel and Rif).

The reason for this matter is that the status of the agent is like the status of the trustee, who is always believed as long as his trusteeship is in his possession, as it is written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 56. However, his credibility is not based on the principle of "miggo" (a legal presumption that if someone had an alternative option that would have been more beneficial, and didn't take it, their current claim is believed) that he could have handed it over to her, because this is not considered a "miggo" at all. First, she might not want to accept it from him without the husband’s knowledge. Additionally, even if he did hand it over to her, if the husband claims that he did not hand it over for the purpose of divorce, how would she be believed? Furthermore, perhaps he handed it over in the presence of witnesses as a deposit, and there is no "miggo" to contradict witnesses. Rather, his credibility stems from the fundamental law that a trustee is believed, because when the trusteeship is handed over to him, it is given on the condition that he will be believed in everything he says. If he says it is for divorce, it will be for divorce (Tosafot, s.v. "Shalish"). He is not relying on the possibility that the witnesses might contradict him, because the witnesses might die or travel overseas (there). However, it appears to me that if witnesses come and contradict him, asserting that it was indeed given only as a deposit, he is not believed, and she is not divorced. As it has already been explained there in Choshen Mishpat, the trustee is only believed against one witness, not against two witnesses. However, what we are saying is that as long as no witnesses come to contradict him, he is believed, and she is divorced according to the opinion of the Rambam.

However, according to what the Rambam himself wrote in Chapter 16 of the Laws of Loans, Law 8, and I quote: "A document that was in the hands of a third party etc., and he said it is paid, he is believed even though the document is validated, because if he wished, he could have burned or torn it," end quote. It is clearly stated that it must be within his power to uphold his words. Several other early authorities have also written similarly, and it is evident in the Talmud (end of the chapter "Ze Borer"). Therefore, if we say, as mentioned, that he did not have the ability to deliver it to the woman, why would his power be greater that we should believe him? Consequently, one must say that the Rambam holds that he could have delivered it to the woman, because since witnesses testify that she made him her agent for receipt, she would certainly accept her get (divorce document). The Rambam holds that she would be believed when her get emerges from his hand, and he does not claim it is forged. Furthermore, it cannot be said that he is believed by a migo (a reason to believe him because he could have made a different claim) that if he wanted, he could have said it is forged. Firstly, this is not a good migo because she could find witnesses to validate it. Additionally, anyone against a third party is not believed even when he has a migo. This matter requires further examination, and it is difficult to determine the law. Refer to what I wrote in paragraph 45.

And there is a question regarding this matter: It is explained in Choshen Mishpat there that the trustee is believed only when the litigant acknowledges that he is a trustee, and without this acknowledgment, he is not believed. And according to the opinion mentioned there, when the litigant says, "I handed it to you for safekeeping," he is not considered a trustee (Shach there, Se'if Katan 5). Here, the husband says, "I gave it to you for safekeeping." Indeed, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch there ruled that even when they contradict him, he is believed. However, according to those who disagree, it is difficult. One could say that the safekeeping of a get (divorce document) is not similar to the safekeeping of money, because in the case of money, there is no concept of trusteeship at all. But in the case of a get, why was the get written, and why was it entrusted to him? Certainly, the husband also acknowledges the main point that he wants to divorce her but claims that there was some condition between them, and the messenger contradicts him on this. Therefore, even according to the husband's words, there is still a concept of trusteeship (there).

And this is what the Rambam wrote: If the get (divorce document) is in the possession of the woman, and she and the agent say that it was given to her for the purpose of divorce, but the husband claims that he gave it as a deposit, the agent is believed. Even though a trustee is only believed when the deposit is still in his hands, here the husband is not believed, whether the agent was appointed to receive the get or to deliver it. Since she could have given it to him directly, it is as if it is in his hands (Beit Shmuel 183). This is different from a monetary deposit, where if the deposit leaves the hands of the trustee, he is not believed. Here, the woman and the agent are considered as one person, because the main function of the get pertains to the woman and not to another. When the agent takes it, he takes it to deliver it to her, and even when he is an agent to receive it, his hand is like her hand, and he delivers it to her as proof. The husband is believed regarding an agent for delivery when he did not testify in front of us to dispute the get; this is only when he claims it is forged, in which case she needs to verify it, but not with claims of deposit or other claims, such as that the get was lost or stolen. In such cases, the judgement reverts to the law of a trustee, who is believed whether the get is in his hands or in the woman's hands, since the husband admits to the primary validity of the get (as mentioned above).

And all this is the opinion of the Rambam and the Rif, but many of our Rabbis disagree with them and hold that the agent is only believed if the husband and wife are not in the same city. In that case, he has the status of a trustee, as we have said. However, if both are in the same city, the husband is believed because there is evidence that he did not entrust the divorce document for the purpose of divorce, as otherwise, he would have given it to her directly (as Rav Huna said there). And although a trustee is generally believed everywhere, in such a situation, it is as if witnesses contradict him. Therefore, even in the case of an agent for delivery, when both are in the same city, even if he says "in my presence it was written and signed," the husband cannot claim it is a forgery, as the sages established. Nevertheless, if the husband says he gave it as a deposit, he is believed because of the reason explained—that he would have given it to her directly (as is found in Tosafot s.v. "the husband," who ruled that the husband is believed, and so wrote the Ran in his first answer, and similarly in the Rashba's novellae). It is unreasonable to say that just as the sages established that by saying "in my presence it was written and signed," the husband cannot claim forgery, so too, he should not be believed when he says it was given as a deposit. This cannot be said, for even in cases of forgery, if witnesses come and contradict the agent, the agent is not believed, for the sages did not establish their decree against two witnesses, as written in Siman 142. This reasoning that he would have given it to her directly must be considered as two witnesses, for otherwise, why is the agent not believed? Indeed, against one witness, the trustee is believed, as written in Choshen Mishpat Siman 56. Therefore, it must necessarily be considered as two witnesses (as explained in the reasoning of Tosafot and the Rashba, for otherwise, what compelled them to say so? Consider this well).

Therefore, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that for this reason, it is proper to be careful not to divorce through an agent to deliver the get (divorce document) when the husband and wife are in the same city, as there is a potential for mishap. If the husband claims that he did not give the agent the get for the purpose of divorce, he would be believed because, according to this reasoning, there is no difference between an agent to receive the get and an agent to deliver it, as mentioned. However, according to our custom, every agent to deliver the get has a validated authorization with witnesses and a Bet Din (rabbinical court) confirming that the husband appointed him as an agent. This concern is thereby removed, and he can appoint an agent even within the same city, and this is the practice.

And besides this, there are those who say that this flaw, where he gave the get to her, only applies to a receiving agent. Since the agent’s hand is considered like her own hand, and she is divorced immediately, why did he not give it directly to her? However, for a delivering agent, this is not a flaw at all, as he did not wish to give it to her directly so that she would not be divorced immediately. Therefore, he gave it to the agent, perhaps intending to cancel the get before she receives it (Ran). According to this reasoning, there is no need to be careful at all about appointing an agent in one city as a delivering agent.

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 55 that even according to those who disagree with the Rambam and hold that in one city the husband is believed, this is specifically when he claims he gave it as a deposit. But if he claims that he appointed her as an agent to deliver it and wants to retract before it reaches her hand, he is not believed. The reason is that in such a case, the reasoning does not apply that if he had intended it for divorce, he would have given it to her, because even by his own words, he gave it into her hand for divorce. This is only according to what has been said, that there is no distinction according to this opinion between an acceptance agent and a delivery agent, as it can also be said in the case of delivery that he gave it to her. But according to those who say in the previous section that in the case of a delivery agent we do not say so because he did not want her to be divorced immediately, it follows that even if he says he gave it for delivery, the husband is believed. For it is only in the case of acceptance that we say he should have given it to her, but not in the case of delivery. And the claim of delivery is like the claim of giving it as a deposit (Beit Shmuel, section 177).

And regarding the second ruling of the Rambam, when the get (bill of divorce) is in the woman's possession and she and the agent claim it was given for the purpose of divorce, while the husband claims it was for safekeeping, it seems at first glance that according to those who disagree, in this case as well, they would hold that if they are in the same city, the husband is believed (as the Beit Shmuel writes in section 83). However, from the phrasing of Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef, it does not appear this way. The first ruling he wrote in section 55 and there he mentioned the opinion of those who disagree, while this ruling he wrote plainly in section 56 without bringing the dissenting opinion. Therefore, it seems that when the get is in the woman's possession, it is more preferable. And there are some of the Rishonim (early authorities) who intend to say that this is what the sages said, that if it were given for divorce, it would have been given directly to her hand. This does not mean that the husband would have given it to her hand, but rather that the agent would have handed it directly to the woman so that it would be in her hand as proof. Therefore, if it is indeed in the woman's hand, the husband is not believed (Ran there in the third answer, that in such a case even Rabbeinu HaMeiri agrees). However, from all the Rishonim it does not seem this way, and even the one who said this reasoning did not say it as a ruling (since he provides other answers). Therefore, it seems he was not precise in this matter and relied on what he had previously brought from the opinions of those who disagree (and although the Beit Shmuel's proof from section 57 can be refuted, as there the woman herself does not know for certain, nevertheless his words are correct and this seems to be the main point, and study it well).

Additionally, the Rambam wrote there in chapter 12: If the get (divorce document) was lost, even though the husband says he gave it to the agent for the purpose of divorce, and the agent says he gave it to her, she is in a state of doubtful divorce. This is because she had the presumption of being a married woman, and there is only one witness here along with the husband. Even if the woman says that she received it in front of the husband for the purpose of divorce, and the agent says he gave it to her, since the husband and the agent are supporting her, it is possible that she is being brazen and perhaps she was not divorced. End of quote. This informs us that even though when the get is present, whether in the hand of the woman or in the hand of the agent, she is permitted even if the husband denies it. If the get is before us, even if the husband also admits it, she is not divorced because there is no means to remove her from the presumption of being a married woman since there is neither a get nor witnesses. However, when the get is present, the get itself removes her from the presumption of being a married woman, and the husband is not believed, as it is written.

It is further written there: A receipt agent who received a get [divorce document] for a woman and sent it to her in the presence of two witnesses, and the get reached her hand, and she took it, and the get is now in her possession, but she does not know whether her husband sent it to her, or her receipt agent, or her husband's agent. She is considered divorced, as we have explained. If the husband comes and disputes it, claiming that he did not write it or that it is a null get, it must be validated by its signatories, for the witnesses testify that the get given to her came from the hand of her agent, whose hand is like her own hand. And even though she does not know, the witnesses know. If it is not validated, she is not divorced.

This teaches us the great strength of a get when it is physically present. For if the get were lost, even if everyone agrees, it is nothing, as we have written. When it is present, even if the woman herself does not know how she was divorced, and the agent is not present, nevertheless, as long as the husband has not come and disputed, nothing further is needed, since there are witnesses that the agent sent it to her. And even if the husband comes and disputes, only the validation of the signatures is needed, as they signed on this get, and witnesses testify that this get came from the hand of her agent. Therefore, even if the husband says he gave it as a deposit, he is not believed according to the Rambam's opinion. According to the opinion of those who disagree, he is believed when they are in the same city. However, as long as the husband has not come and disputed, we assume she is divorced, even according to the dissenting opinion. There is one who says that according to the dissenting opinion, she is not assumed to be divorced even without the husband's dispute. The great early authorities inclined more towards this view than the first view (The Rosh holds the first view, and the Ritva and Hameiri disagree, as the Beit Shmuel wrote in section 188).

It is a simple matter that everything explained, whereby the agent is trusted as well as the woman, is only applicable when we have witnesses before us that she appointed him as an agent to receive [the get]. Even if the husband does not know that she is an agent to receive [the get], nevertheless, he gives the get to the agent in a manner such that if he is an agent to receive it, she is immediately divorced upon his receipt of it (Beit Shmuel 12 and 78). This is the power of a trustee because they trusted him according to Rambam, even when they are in the same city, and according to those who disagree, when they are in two different places, as we have written. It is also necessary that the agent explicitly says that it was handed over to him in the presence of witnesses, according to those who hold that without this it is nothing, and according to Rambam, there is no necessity for witnesses after the fact, as we have written several times. This requirement for witnesses that she appointed him as an agent is for an agent to receive [the get], but for an agent to deliver [the get], no witnesses are needed. Once the get reaches her hand, she is divorced (Beit Shmuel 78), as long as the husband does not come and contest it. If he contests, it can be validated by its signatures. If the agent is in a place where he needs to declare "before me it was written and before me it was signed," the husband cannot contest it, as will be explained in Siman 142, with the help of Heaven.

And know that, according to logical reasoning, it appears that in any case where we said that the agent is believed when the get (divorce document) is in his hand or in the hand of the woman, the same applies even if now the get is not in his hand but there are witnesses who saw the get in his hand—it is also considered as if the get is now in his hand, for witnesses are credible in all matters. And this is explicitly implied by the words of our Rabbis, the Tosafists (Gittin 64a, s.v. Tenach), who wrote that we only need witnesses who saw the get in his hand, whole and not torn. However, our teacher, the Rema, wrote in sections 55 and 57 that some say it is specifically when the get comes from his hand, but if the get is not in his hand, he is not believed, even if there were witnesses who saw it in his hand. 

And the reason can be explained because the entire credibility of the agent is due to his status as a trustee, and we hold that a trustee is only believed when his trusteeship is in his hand. But when it is not in his hand, even if we know through witnesses that it was in his hand, his credibility as a trustee is nullified. Only if it is in the woman's hand is it considered as if it is in his hand, for the reason we wrote in section 33. But if it is not in the hands of either of them, it is not considered as the status of a trustee. 

And the words of the Tosafists can be explained to mean that as long as the husband does not contest, we do not need the credibility of the trustee. But if he contests, the fact that there are witnesses who saw the get in his hand does not help (and this is also implied in the Beit Shmuel, section 179, who agrees with the Rema. Therefore, even though the Gra, section 107, rejected his words, it seems that the ruling is according to the words of the Rema).

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 11: A delivery agent does not need witnesses if the agent and the sender both acknowledge [the delivery]. If the sender disputes [the delivery], it is a doubt. Some say that a delivery agent must be appointed in the presence of witnesses. When does this apply? When the husband’s agent does not need witnesses if he delivers a get (divorce document) signed by witnesses. However, if there are no witnesses signed on the get and the agent delivers it in the presence of witnesses, it is a doubtful divorce. And these two opinions we have already explained in section 140, paragraph 6: the Rambam holds that no witnesses are required for a delivery agent, while the Rosh, based on the Jerusalem Talmud, holds that witnesses are required. We have explained there the reasons for both opinions with Divine help. And regarding what is written that without signed witnesses it is a doubt, this is what the Rambam wrote. We have explained there in paragraph 8 that when there are signed witnesses, they serve as testimony that it was written for her sake. But without signed witnesses, who testifies to this? Although they believe the agent when he says "in my presence it was written," this is only when there are signed witnesses or at least when he was appointed as an agent in the presence of witnesses. Then certainly the witnesses acted according to the law. But without any witnesses at all, on whom can we rely regarding the primary writing of the get according to the law? He did not rule it as a definite invalidation, but as a doubt. Perhaps the agent alone is trustworthy also regarding the primary writing, and we rely on the scribe who wrote it for her sake, as our Sages said at the beginning of Gittin, "The scribes of the judges are well-versed."

However, regarding what he wrote that if the sender denies it, it is a doubt, his words are puzzling. What are we dealing with? If the sender claims it is forged, certainly the signatures need to be verified. Or is it when the agent said "in my presence," then the husband is not believed to claim it is forged? And if the husband claims he gave it as a deposit, it has already been clarified that when the get is in the hands of the agent or the woman, he is not believed to say he gave it as a deposit. And if we say his intention is when the husband and wife are in the same city, then there is a dispute between the Rambam and the Rosh whether the husband is believed when he says he gave it as a deposit, as we have explained. And our master, the Beit Yosef, himself wrote this dispute in section 55 regarding an agent to receive, and the same applies to an agent to deliver, as is evident from his words there. In such a case, he should not have left it vague but rather explained it. And it is possible to say that it refers to when the get has already been given to the woman in the presence of witnesses, and now the get is not in her possession, but the witnesses saw it earlier in the hands of the agent when he gave it to the woman. And we have explained in section 42 that there are two opinions on whether its status is like when it is now in the hands of the agent or not (and this is also what the Beit Shmuel explains in subparagraph 14, interpreting the words of the Beit Yosef there).

However, this too does not seem clear to me, for how can one generalize matters? Therefore, it appears to me things as they are: Even though we have already explained that even with a delivery agent, when the get (divorce document) is in the hands of the agent, the husband is not believed according to the Rambam, even when both are in the same city, and according to the Rosh, when they are in two different places, there is still room to examine this matter. Why should the husband not be believed with the argument that if he wanted, he could nullify the get? In the case of an agent for acceptance, which is explained in the Talmud, it makes sense that when the get is in the hands of the agent, she is already divorced, and the husband has no argument. But with a delivery agent, she is not yet divorced, and he has the ability to nullify it.

And indeed, we have explained in section 31 that against a third party, he is not believed even with an argument, and this is the opinion of several early authorities. Likewise, with a delivery agent, the husband is not believed when the get is in the hands of the agent. Nevertheless, this is not explicitly stated in the Talmud or the Rambam, and certainly, there is room for doubt in this matter. Therefore, even though it appears from the words of the Shulchan Aruch in section 55 that it holds the same for a delivery agent, that the husband is not believed, it is not explicitly written so. Hence, it is written here that if the sender denies, it is a doubt, even when the get is in the hands of the agent. For perhaps where there is an argument, the agent is not believed. And here, it is referring to when the get is still in his hands and not in the woman's hands. For if he had already delivered it to her, there is no argument like with an agent for acceptance. (And even though its source is according to the explanation of the Beit Shmuel there and the Gra in section 25 from the Hagahot Maimoniot, chapter 3 of Ishut, where it is written after the woman has accepted it, and so too the Ba'al HaGoleh wrote, and the Gra questioned him there. Nevertheless, it appears to me his intention is as I have written, and he did not mean otherwise. And understand this well.)

And know that according to this opinion, which requires witnesses for the sending agent, our master the Rema wrote: However, the agent is believed to say that he was appointed with witnesses, and no testimony is required for this. And the custom is to require authorization and witnesses for the authorization that he was appointed as an agent. And certainly, this is the opinion of the Tur and several early authorities, that the agent is believed to say he was appointed with witnesses. However, in my humble opinion, there are those who disagree with this, as will be explained in the following section, with God's help.

Our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 13: "There are those who say that the messenger of delivery and the messenger of receipt do not need to be appointed in the presence of witnesses, and there are those who disagree." And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote that this is a repetition of what was already written in section 11. And it is almost impossible that he would write the same law twice in succession. In my humble opinion, a different intention is hidden in his words. His intention is not regarding the appointment of the messenger, but rather, even according to those who require witnesses, and even according to the Rambam who does not require witnesses, nevertheless, when there are no witnesses signed on the get, witnesses are required, as has been explained. Nevertheless, if the messenger is believed to say that he was appointed with witnesses, there is also a disagreement about this. The Tur and several of the early authorities ruled that he is believed to say that he was appointed with witnesses, as mentioned in the previous section. However, in the responsa of the Rosh, section 45, siman 10, it is explicitly implied that in a case where the messenger does not need to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," the messenger is not believed to say that he was appointed with witnesses unless he brings proof of this, as mentioned there (so too wrote the Maggid Mishneh, chapter 6, law 4, and the Beit Shmuel, siman 142, se'if katan 7). Therefore, he was precise in section 11 to say to appoint him with witnesses, and here he wrote to appoint him with witnesses, meaning to appoint him in the presence of witnesses who will testify that he was appointed as a messenger with witnesses.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 13 that there are those who say that if a messenger of delivery gave her the get (divorce document) in private, he cannot return to give it to her in the presence of two witnesses because she is considered divorced since the get is in her possession with its signatures. However, there are those who say it is invalid. Nevertheless, if the get is validated with its signatures while in her possession, she does not need to bring it before us; she only needs to state that she received it in the presence of two witnesses as required. The same applies to a receipt messenger from the husband. This concludes his words.

Explanation of his words: As explained earlier in Siman 133, the Rif and Rambam hold that witnesses of delivery are not essential. If the husband gives the get (divorce document) to his wife privately, it is valid as long as there are signed witnesses on the get. Rashi, Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur, however, invalidate it without witnesses of delivery. According to this opinion, it is obvious that if an emissary delivers the get without witnesses, it is invalid. Even according to the Rif and Rambam, an emissary is worse. Rambam writes in Hilchot Gerushin 6:15, “If the emissary gave her the get privately, he must take it back and give it to her in the presence of two [witnesses],” and he does not require the husband himself to take it back and give it again in the presence of two. He also writes, “If he died, since the get is validated by its signatures, it is a valid get.” This is what the Rema wrote—that if it is impossible to give it to her again, for example, if he died, the first opinion is that of the Rambam, and the second opinion that invalidates it. This seems to be the opinion we mentioned in Siman 6, that even though only witnesses of delivery establish it, it is still valid even with signed witnesses when given privately because the signed witnesses are considered like witnesses of delivery since the get comes from the husband with these witnesses, and it is known that the husband gave it to her. Therefore, this is only when the husband himself gave it to her and not when an emissary gave it to her, since it is not clearly known that the husband gave it to her. Hence, even according to the Rif, it is invalid with an emissary. This is somewhat evident from the Ran in chapter 9. The one who cited both opinions in the Tur is mistaken as it is not found there at all. The Gra in comment 29 explains that this is the dispute in Siman 133. If so, what is the novelty here? Therefore, I think as I wrote. This is what he wrote—that she does not need to bring witnesses of delivery before us, and it is enough for her to say that she received it in front of two witnesses. This is according to all opinions, like when the husband gave it to her. And he wrote, “And similarly, when the emissary of the husband received it.” He means that when the get is in the hands of the emissary, he is trusted to say that he received it from the husband in the presence of two, and no witnesses are needed for this, as explained in Siman 24.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 14 that both a messenger for acceptance (שליח קבלה) and a messenger for delivery (שליח הולכה) do not need to hear directly from the principals that they are being appointed as a messenger. Therefore, both the man and the woman can appoint in the presence of witnesses a messenger who is in another location, and the witnesses can write and sign that so-and-so was appointed as a messenger. And all the early authorities agreed on this, and it is evident from the Talmud in various places. Explicitly, we say (Gittin 30a) regarding a messenger of the court, which will be explained in Section 142, that one can appoint a messenger whether in his presence or not in his presence (Beit Yosef). As for what is explained in Section 120 that one cannot instruct a scribe and witnesses to write and sign not in their presence and that they need to hear from his mouth, this is because "matters of agency" (מילי) cannot be transferred to a messenger. However, the delivery of the get (divorce document) is not considered "matters of agency". And there are opinions that say that appointing not in their presence is valid (Ran, end of Chapter "Hamekabel"), but we do not hold this way, as stated there.

And based on this ruling, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 35: If a husband sends a get (divorce document) through a non-Jew to be handed to a certain person, and the husband appoints that person in writing to be a messenger to deliver the get to his wife, it is kosher because the non-Jew is merely performing a mechanical action. And the Rosh and the Tur wrote that this is the custom in Ashkenaz and France based on the ruling of Rabbeinu Tam, of blessed memory. This is for the reason explained, that the husband can appoint a messenger not in his presence. And our master the Rema wrote on this, and these are his words: However, there are those who disagree and hold that a messenger for delivery cannot be appointed through writing, and I have not seen it practiced this way. And he was very brief, and the matter needs to be explained.

And behold, the Rosh, the Rashba, and the Ran brought in the name of the Geonim (at the end of chapter 2 of Gittin, see there) and this is what they said: "The Ba'al HaMaor wrote: The sages asked before Rav Haninai Gaon whether a Kuti (Samaritan) could be a messenger to receive the get (divorce document) and to deliver the get. What is the law regarding tying the get with one thread and telling a Kuti to bring this thread to a specific Jew who will then give it to the woman? He answered: No, and if he gave it into her hand or the hand of her Jewish messenger, it is valid. But in the hand of a Kuti, it is not valid, because when the get leaves the hand of the husband, it must reach the hand of the wife or the hand of a Jewish messenger who stands in place of the husband, or the hand of a messenger appointed by the wife who stands in her place. And the sages of the present say that even though a Kuti delivers the get, if he gives it to a Jew and that Jew gives it to the woman in the presence of witnesses, we do not marry her off initially because a Kuti is not eligible for this matter. But if she was married, we do not force her to divorce because of Rabbi Shimon's statement in the Mishnah that all are valid. And Rabbi Zeira said that Rabbi Shimon followed the reasoning of Rabbi Eliezer who said that conditional divorces are valid, and the law follows Rabbi Eliezer." End of quote.

The Rosh was astonished by their words, and this is what he wrote: "Their words are astonishing because if the husband appointed the non-Jew as an agent and told him to appoint the Jew in his place, it would be invalid. A non-Jew cannot act as an agent, and he is also not a party to divorce. But here, since the non-Jew is merely performing a monkey's task and the husband, by his writing, appointed the Jew in that place as the agent, why should the get (divorce document) be invalid? Thus, it is customary in Ashkenaz and France, according to the words of Rabbeinu Tam, to send a get and betrothal through a non-Jew, and he appoints a Jew in that place as an agent by his writing." This is the end of the words of the Rosh. The Rashba also copied the words of the Geonim and did not dispute them. The Ran also did not dispute them, only wondering what the relevance of Rabbi Eliezer was. And the Magid Mishneh also brought their words in Chapter 6, Law 6, and did not dispute them at all.

It seems to me that our Rabbis did not intend to interpret it according to the explanation of the Rosh, of blessed memory. Rather, this is the interpretation: The husband did not write to the Jew nor inform him via witnesses that he is appointing him as an agent to receive the get (bill of divorce) from the non-Jew. Nor did he appoint the non-Jew as an agent to deliver it to the Jew so that the non-Jew would make the Jew his agent. Instead, he told the non-Jew, "Give this to the Jew," assuming that the Jew would deliver it to his wife. The husband's intention was to make the Jew his agent, but he did not explicitly inform him that he was appointing him as his agent. Therefore, the Gaon did not validate it, since the Jew was not appointed in writing as an agent. This is considered as if the non-Jew is the agent, who then makes the Jew an agent. The Rabbis of today validate it because the Jew understands that the husband is making him an agent, knowing that a non-Jew cannot be an agent. I found this reasoning explicitly in the Mordechai, Chapter 2. It states in the responsa of Rashi, of blessed memory, that there was an incident where someone wanted to send a get to his wife through a non-Jew or to make him a recipient, and he said that it does not work unless he tells a Jew. The Ra'avyah wrote that this is specifically where the non-Jew is the one delivering or receiving. However, if the non-Jew hands it to a Jew, it is permitted from the outset. This is similar to what is mentioned in the chapter "HaMekabel" (Bava Metzia 10:5) that a person knows he cannot appoint an agent for receiving and will intend it for delivery. Similarly, here, a person knows that there is no agency for a non-Jew and will not err. All the more so when it is explicitly stated that he appointed the Jew as an agent. Thus, it is clearly stated as we have said.

And this is what the Gaon wrote, that a Cuthean (Samaritan) should not be involved at all, and if he gave it into her hand or the hand of her Jewish agent, this is all in general terms. However, when he informed the Jew that he was making him an agent to deliver it to his wife, certainly the Gaon agrees. And there is clear proof for this, for in the Halachot Gedolot it is written after this as follows: "And an agunah (a woman whose husband is missing) who comes to the court and says, 'Be witnesses for me that so-and-so who is overseas I made an agent to receive my get from my husband,' and the court overseas writes this down and makes that person an agent to receive the get, and the husband gives it to him. If after the get falls into the agent's hand, it is torn or burned, this agunah is divorced." This means that she requests the court in her location to inform the court in the husband's location that she made so-and-so her agent to receive the get, and they do so, and the husband gives it to that person as an agent to receive it, she is divorced by his receipt. It is explicitly stated that through writing she can make an agent to receive the get, and certainly an agent to deliver it through writing. Therefore, certainly the Gaon is referring to a situation where she did not inform the agent, as he wrote (and it is strained to say that this law written by the Halachot Gedolot is according to the Sages, who now say otherwise).

And this is what the Ran, of blessed memory, questioned: What is the relevance of Rabbi Eliezer here? According to our explanation and as the Mordechai wrote, their words are very precise. Behold, in the Mishnah regarding all documents processed by non-Jewish courts, even if the signatories are non-Jews, they are valid, except for bills of divorce (Gittin) and emancipation of slaves, where Rabbi Shimon even permits these. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon holds like Rabbi Eliezer, and even the Tanna Kamma holds like Rabbi Eliezer, but they argue regarding well-known names (9:). Rashi explains that the Tanna Kamma disqualifies rabbinically even with delivery witnesses because they might come to rely on the signing witnesses, while Rabbi Shimon holds that since they are well-known names, everyone knows they are non-Jews and will not rely on them. This is the opinion of the Rabbis now, as certainly, initially, we do not marry her off because a non-Jew is not eligible for severance (divorce). 

And according to the simple meaning of the husband's instruction to the non-Jew to deliver it to an Israelite who will then deliver it to his wife, it appears that the non-Jew is acting as an agent, but he is not eligible for severance and unfit for agency. Nevertheless, we do not force her to leave if she married, because just as Rabbi Shimon said with non-Jewish signatories that it is valid since with well-known names people will not err and rely on them, and they will not permit without proper intent, therefore even according to the Rabbis of Rabbi Shimon, we rely that she should not leave because everyone knows that the non-Jew is unfit for delivering a get, and presumably the husband's intention was that the Israelite would be his agent, and the non-Jew is merely performing a superficial act, as the Rosh wrote. This is precisely the words of the Mordechai that we brought.

There are those who want to bring proof that it is forbidden to send [a Get] through a non-Jew from the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 3, Halacha 3) in the Mishnah which discusses one who brings a Get and it was lost. If it was found immediately, it is valid, and it explains that this is only if no person passed there. It questions what the law is if a non-Jew passed by, and it concludes there that it is valid. This implies that we are not concerned that a non-Jew would deliver the Get. However, this is not a proof at all, for certainly most Gittin are sent through a Jew. Since in that case it is a remote concern that we should worry that the found Get belongs to another whose name is the same as his and her name is the same as hers, therefore, to be concerned for a minority in such a remote concern, surely there is no need to be concerned. Moreover, indeed the Jerusalem Talmud rejects this, and it is valid for another reason. On the contrary, there are those among the decisors who hold that the conclusion of the Jerusalem Talmud is that even if a non-Jew passed, it is invalid (Beit Yosef in Siman 132), as we explained in Siman 132, Section 11, see there and what we wrote in Section 13.

And there are those who wish to be stringent in this matter, reasoning that this is akin to "Take your get from the ground." This is only a surprising statement, as this invalidation only applies when the woman takes it from the ground herself, because the verse states "and he shall place it in her hand" and not that she should take it herself, as Maimonides wrote in Chapter 1 and as clarified in Siman 139. But if his agent hands it to her, what difference does it make from where he takes it? His agent is like him, and it is as if he himself took it and placed it in her hand. Indeed, although this reasoning is mentioned in Tashbetz, it was later rejected for other reasons (see there, Part 3, Siman 326). There are many proofs to this, and it does not need to be explained, as it is self-evident that this is not in the category of "Take it from the ground" at all (and so writes the Pitchei Teshuvah).

Here is the translation of the provided passage from the Aruch Hashulchan:

And indeed, in practice, Rabbeinu Tam and the Rosh explicitly permitted it, as well as the Rashba, the Ran, and the Maimonides, who brought the words of the Ba'al HaMaor according to our interpretation. This has no relevance at all to this law that specifies in writing a particular person in a particular place as the agent. And even without this, the conclusion of the Ba'al HaMaor is that if she marries, she does not need to leave. Mordechai in the name of the Ra'avyah explicitly permitted it, as did the Tur, Beit Yosef, Radbaz, and Tashbetz, and similarly the Yam Shel Shlomo in the second chapter permitted it unanimously. The Radbaz and Tashbetz acted as such, as is clear from their responsa. Only our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote that there are those who disagree and hold that one should not appoint through writing. His intention is towards the words of the Ba'al HaMaor, and according to what we have written, it is not relevant at all. And what he grasped from the words of the Geonim, that their reason was because one should not appoint an agent through writing, we have brought from the Ba'al HaMaor himself that he permitted through writing for an agent to receive, and what difference is there between an agent to receive and an agent to deliver? On the contrary, logically, an agent to receive is more stringent, as in the matter of agency itself, according to the Rambam, for delivery, witnesses are not needed, and for receiving, they are required. And if the reason is because "take your get from the ground," we have already refuted this reason.

Furthermore, how is it possible to say that agency through writing does not work? Firstly, writing is considered like speech, as demonstrated in the Talmud Gittin (71a) and in Tosafot there. And even for the writing of a get (divorce document), writing is effective according to several authorities. And even for those who prohibit writing a get through written instruction, it is not because of the concept of agency, because according to several authorities, agency is not needed for writing; rather, it is merely a stringency, as we explained in Siman 120, Se'if 4, see there. And it is evident in the case of agency that it is not necessary at all to hear directly from his mouth, but as long as we know that he agrees, he becomes his agent, for we hold that one can benefit a person in his absence, and benefiting, according to most authorities, is considered agency. And concerning a get itself, the Sages were uncertain (Yevamot Chapter 16) if one can grant a get to his wife in the presence of a yavam (levirate brother). The question is whether it is considered a benefit or a detriment, see there. Therefore, it is clear that one can benefit her through agency even without her speaking or writing, and all the more so, writing is effective.

Furthermore, since it is explicitly stated in the Gemara that one can appoint an agent to deliver the get (divorce document) whether in his presence or not (30a), how can it be prohibited to do something that is explicitly permitted in the Gemara? Therefore, it seems to me that the opinion of our master, the Rema, is as follows: since in matters of divorce, we are stringent in several aspects beyond the fundamental law, we should not permit something that is not explicitly found in the Gemara. And what we have brought from the Gemara, that it ruled whether in his presence or not, refers to when it is done in a court, as there is a strong authority of the court so that it will not be possible to deny and claim it is forged. And what he wrote, that one should not appoint an agent for delivery in writing, refers to his own handwriting without the authentication of a court, because afterward, he could deny and say he did not write it and it is forged. Furthermore, he could claim it was done in jest. This reasoning is also found in the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate Terumot, Chapter 1, Halacha 1. But through a court, he indeed agrees that it is possible to appoint an agent in writing.

And further he wrote, "I have not seen this practice," end quote. And certainly, it is so, for it is possible to appoint a Jewish agent. However, even in the previous generation, when, due to our numerous sins, the Jewish people were scattered from one end of the world to the other and across the great sea, it was almost impossible to send an agent to deliver the document to the place where the woman is. And because the sages of the generation saw that Jewish daughters would remain agunot (chained women), they permitted sending a get (divorce document) via the post. And now, in our days, this is a simple practice in all Jewish communities without any objection. And the practice is as follows: First, the Beit Din (Jewish court) in the place of the woman writes to the Beit Din in the place of the man to summon the man and arrange for him a get according to Jewish law, and to appoint a specific person in the place of the woman as an agent to deliver the get to his wife. The man declares before the Beit Din before writing the get, and also afterward, "I hereby appoint so-and-so, son of so-and-so, from such-and-such place as an agent to deliver the get to my wife, so-and-so, daughter of so-and-so, and his hand shall be like my hand, etc. And I give him permission to appoint an agent in his place, etc." And he says this before two witnesses. They write the authorization that before two witnesses, he appointed so-and-so, son of so-and-so, as an agent to deliver it, etc., according to the format of the authorization that will be explained. But instead of writing in the authorization "so-and-so delivered the get of separation to so-and-so," it should write "appointed," since he is not delivering the get into his hand. The witnesses of the authorization sign, and the Beit Din certifies them. Consequently, since this agent cannot say "it was written and signed in my presence," the get must be validated by its witnesses, and the Beit Din in the place of the woman must recognize the signatures of the Beit Din in the place of the man. This is the benefit of what we wrote: first, the Beit Din in the place of the woman writes to the Beit Din in the place of the man so that they respond to their letter beforehand and inform them that they will do so. This letter will reach the Beit Din in the place of the woman before the get and the authorization arrive, and consequently, afterward, they will recognize the signatures of the Beit Din when they compare their certification on the authorization to their signatures in their letter. This is a complete validation without concern of forgery. The husband will send the get and the authorization to the agent in the place of the woman, and they will write distinct signs on the get, like a hole near a particular letter, and thus the agent will deliver it to the woman in the presence of a Beit Din of three and witnesses, as will be explained in the order of the get, Siman 154. However, many questions that are explained in the name are not relevant to ask since the agent did not see the writing of the get and the signatures. The rabbi arranging the matter will understand all that is relevant to ask and what is not, as it is difficult to specify everything in writing.

And know that I have seen someone write that it is better for the husband to appoint an agent at the place of writing [the get, the Jewish bill of divorce] in the manner of all agents, so that the agent will deliver the get to his wife, bring it to her location, and hand it over to her. He grants him permission to appoint an agent and for that agent to appoint another agent, in the manner of all agency. Afterwards, this agent will appoint the man who is in the place of the wife as his agent in his place. By doing this, we gain the benefit that the first agent, when he appoints in front of a court in the place of the husband the man who is in the place of the wife as his agent, will be able to say "It was written and signed before me," and he will appoint the man as an agent not in his presence. He will not need, according to the law, to say "It was written and signed before me," but rather he will say, "I am an agent of the court," and they will write the second authorization in the manner in which they write from the first agent to the second agent, and they will also write that he appointed this agent in his place to appoint so-and-so who is in the place of the wife as an agent.

It is not clear to me at all, because since the husband knows for certain, and also his agent knows, that he has no intention whatsoever to deliver the get to the wife's location and to hand it over to her, there is nothing that appears more deceitful than this. This is merely a subterfuge. Even in monetary laws, we follow an evident assessment, as it is written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 246. All the more so with a get, when there is an evident assessment that what he is saying he has not resolved in his heart, and he has no intention at all in this matter, and he also does not have the ability to travel to the wife's location. How can we rely on the idle words he speaks with his mouth when he has no intention at all to do what he says he will do? This is not like unspoken thoughts that are not considered, which is when his intention is unknown to all. But when his intention is known at the time of the act, this is not unspoken thoughts (so wrote the Tosafot, beginning of Chapter 4). Additionally, whenever we can know his intention from ourselves, even without his revealing his intention, it is not considered unspoken thoughts (there). Here, everyone knows that he has no intention at all to go across the sea or on such a long journey. And the rule that revealed intentions in a get are not significant is regarding the husband in the matter of cancellation, not regarding the agent. This is not a revealed intention but rather an explicit matter known to all, and something known to all is like having witnesses about it (Beit Shmuel, Siman 26, S.K. 1). Additionally, regarding an oath, which the Torah ties to the expression of the lips, nevertheless, our sages have said (Shevuot 26b) that if his heart contradicts his mouth, such as if he swore not to eat wheat bread but intended barley bread, the oath does not take effect at all, as it is written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 210. All the more so with an agency, where we are witnesses that he has no intention at all to travel far to the place of his wife, his words spoken with his mouth are not considered at all. Additionally, it is taught in Terumot (Chapter 3, Mishnah 8) that if one intended to say "Terumah" but said "Ma'aser," or intended to say "Ma'aser" but said "Terumah," he has said nothing until his mouth and heart are aligned, as it is written, "You shall observe the utterance of your lips," and it is also written, "Every generous-hearted person," which requires resolving in the heart and expressing with the lips (Raavad). In our case, it is also clear that he must resolve in his heart what he says, otherwise, what kind of agency is this? And we are witnesses that he has not resolved in his heart at all. Therefore, such a practice should not be done; rather, the husband should appoint an agent at the wife's location, and there is no need here to say "in front of me" because there is an authorized power of attorney, and the court in the wife's location will recognize the signatures of the court that authorized the power of attorney through correspondence before sending the get, as we have explained with God's help (but the custom is through two agents).

All are eligible to act as an agent for the delivery of a get (divorce document), whether a man or a woman, whether for its delivery or receipt. And even though a man is not involved in the receipt of a get and a woman is not involved in the giving of a get, nevertheless, a man can receive a get for his minor daughter, for just as the Torah granted him the right to receive her betrothal money, so too he can receive her get from betrothal. Additionally, a woman can sometimes be sent by her husband with her own get, and he tells her, "Be my agent to deliver this to the court in such and such a place, and they will appoint an agent to deliver this get to you," as will be explained in Siman 142. Thus, it is found that a man can also be involved in the receipt of a get and a woman in the delivery of a get (beginning of Perek HaMekabel). And if a man's wife receives the get on behalf of her co-wife, see what is written at the end of Siman 136.

The following are disqualified from delivering a get (divorce document), whether for bringing it or for receiving it: a deaf-mute, an imbecile, a minor, a Samaritan, and a slave. Similarly, a blind person is disqualified from bringing a get in a place where it is necessary to say "It was written and signed in my presence," because he cannot see the writing and the signatures, and how can he say "It was written and signed in my presence"? This will be explained in Siman 142. The reason these individuals are disqualified is because they are not capable of acting as agents, as it is written in Choshen Mishpat Siman 182. Although a slave is fit to act as an agent in other matters, since he is obligated in mitzvot like a woman and is a member of the covenant, as stated there, nevertheless, regarding gittin (divorce documents) and kiddushin (marriage), he cannot be an agent because he is not subject to the laws of gittin and kiddushin (Gittin 23b), as kiddushin does not take effect on him. The case where a woman is divorced through her own slave, as stated in Siman 139, is not due to the agency of the slave but rather due to the principle of "her courtyard" (Tosafot there).

And know that according to most of the authorities, a slave is disqualified both from conveying and receiving [a get, a Jewish bill of divorce]. However, there are some of our Rabbis who hold that a slave is only disqualified from receiving [the get] but not from conveying it. Since he is capable of acting as an agent and his disqualification is only because he is not included in the laws of divorce, he is only disqualified from receiving it because through his receipt the woman becomes divorced. But for conveying it, he is merely like any other agent, and he is indeed capable of being an agent (this is the opinion of Rabbi Yitzchak of Vienna as mentioned by the Ran and the Maggid Mishneh in chapter 6). And although from the Talmudic discussion there it seems to imply this way, nevertheless, we do not rule this way, and it is considered a singular opinion. Also, in the Jerusalem Talmud (chapter 2), it is explained according to the first opinion. Nevertheless, in practice, one should be stringent and consider it a doubtful divorce (Beit Yosef). This is also implied in the Shulchan Aruch, section 31, which states that there is an opinion that if the slave is an agent for conveying, it is considered doubtful. Thus ruled the Rashba to be concerned for the opinion that validates it, and therefore [the woman] is disqualified from marrying a Kohen. If she accepted betrothal from another man, she would require a get from him.

In section 17, it is explained that there are five women who are not trusted to say that her husband has died because we suspect that they might lie due to hatred in order to cause her harm. These women are: her mother-in-law, her mother-in-law's daughter, her co-wife, her yevamah (sister-in-law through levirate marriage), and her husband's daughter. Similarly, they are not trusted to bring her divorce document because they might intend to harm her by having the husband come and contest it, and meanwhile, she would marry and then have to leave both this one and that one. When is this said? In a place where it is not necessary to say "in front of me it was written and in front of me it was signed." But in a place where it is required to say "in front of me it was written and in front of me it was signed," they are able to bring her divorce document, because after the statement "in front of me it was written and in front of me it was signed," the husband is not believed to contest it, as stated in section 142. Therefore, it cannot be said that their intention is to harm her, as she will not be harmed further (Gemara there). This will be further explained there with God's help. If her co-wife is made an agent to receive it, refer to what is written in section 65 (Tosafot Gittin 77b s.v. yadah).

And similarly, all relatives are fit to be agents for a get (divorce document) whether for delivering it or for receiving it, as an agent is not a witness and an agent is like the person themselves. Similarly, a female agent [is permissible]. Therefore, what difference is there between a close relative and a distant one? And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 33 as follows: "There is an opinion that where possible, initially the agent should not be a relative of either the man or the woman, nor of the judges before whom the get is given." And the custom now is not to be stringent in this matter, because sometimes it is a benefit for agunot (women unable to remarry) when she cannot properly pay the fee for the agency, one of her relatives volunteers to be the agent, as has happened several times. However, in a situation where there is no impediment due to financial reasons, it is certainly a mitzvah to heed the words of our teacher, the Rema, if possible.

And regarding those disqualified from testimony due to their wickedness, the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 6, Law 7, that those disqualified by rabbinic decree due to transgression are fit for delivering a get (divorce document), but those disqualified by Torah law due to transgression are unfit for delivering the get. If they do deliver it, it is invalid. This applies when the get has been validated by its signatures, but if the validation relies solely on the testimony of someone disqualified by Torah law, it is not considered a valid get. And all the early authorities were astonished by this position: if the get is validated by its signatures and there is no need for the bearer to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," why should it be invalid if the wicked person delivered the get? Moreover, even if the validation relies on such a person, why should it not be considered a get at all? It should suffice that the woman cannot remarry based on his statement, but how can it be said that the get is entirely nullified? After all, it is merely a doubt whether he is lying, and it might be validated by its signatures and be kosher (Rashba 5:). The commentators (Hagahot Maimoniyot and Kesef Mishneh) explained that the intention is that as long as it has not been validated, it is not a get at all. Nonetheless, if she accepted betrothal from another, she would need a get. However, from his wording, it does not seem so (Beit Shmuel 146), and therefore, the opinion of most of the decisors is that if it is validated by its signatures, it is entirely kosher. What difference does it make if he is wicked? After all, he is a member of the covenant and fit for delivering the get. When it is not validated, it is a doubtful divorce, and we are concerned about forgery. If she accepted betrothal from another, she would need a get from him (ibid.).

And the Rambam, who disqualified it entirely, stating that it is not a get (divorce document) at all, must be referring to a case where there was no validation on it. In such a severe case, validation is required by Torah law, and as long as it has not been validated, it is like a mere shard of pottery, and therefore it is not a get at all (see Beit Shmuel end of section 146). Alternatively, it could be referring to a case where the husband claims it is forged, which follows his reasoning in chapter 7 that when the husband claims forgery and there is no validation, in a place where one does not need to declare "in front of me it was written," the get is nullified by Torah law. Also, many disagree with him, as will be explained in section 142, but in any case, he follows his reasoning that in such a severe case of Torah law, the declaration "in front of me" is of no consequence, and therefore he wrote that it is not a get (see Maggid Mishneh there). Alternatively, it could be referring to a case where there are no witnesses that appointed him as an agent, and it was explained that according to the Rambam, he is believed to say that he was appointed as an agent, but in such a severe case of Torah law, he has no credibility at all, and therefore it is not a get at all (see Gra sub-section 71).

And these are the words of the Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah (Chapter 2): "Anyone disqualified from giving testimony due to a transgression of Torah law is disqualified from delivering a get (divorce document) if it has not been ratified by its signatures, and we do not rely even on his statement of 'in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed.' But if it has been ratified by its signatures, it is valid." And from this it is clearly explained like the first answer in the previous section. However, in what he wrote that if it is ratified by its signatures, it is valid, it contradicts his words here where he wrote that it is invalid. And it seems to me his intention is thus: if it was delivered ratified, such as with the authorization customary among us and similar cases, it is completely valid. But if when it was delivered it was not yet ratified and he was disqualified by Torah law according to his view, as he wrote, then even though it was later ratified and is valid by Torah law, nevertheless, it is disqualified by rabbinic decree because it was not valid at the time it was delivered. And this is precise in his language when he wrote "in what case are these words said? When the get was ratified," meaning when it was ratified afterwards. And in his commentary on the Mishnah, it is implied from his language that it was delivered ratified. And this is clearly explained from the language of the Ra'avad (and these are his words: "And if the get is ratified by its signatures, they are fit to deliver it"). And it is possible that all the poskim (decisors) agree with him on this, that any get delivered without ratification is disqualified by rabbinic decree even if it was later ratified, because it was disqualified at the time of its delivery to the woman. And the Rosh is one of those who disagree with the Rambam, as the Tur wrote, and he wrote in this language (Chapter 2, Section 26): "And if they were disqualified by Torah law, they are disqualified from delivering the get in the Diaspora, etc. And if it was ratified, even if they did not repent, it is valid, etc." It is clearly implied that it was delivered ratified (and according to this, what he wrote there, and not like the Rambam, according to our explanation, they do not disagree at all, as is evident from his words in the commentary on the Mishnah).

The language of the Shulchan Aruch, Section 33, is as follows: Even those who are disqualified by rabbinic decree due to transgression are qualified to deliver a get (divorce document), but those disqualified by Torah law due to transgression are disqualified from delivering the get unless the get is validated by its signatures. There are some who disqualify even if it is validated by its signatures. This refers to the opinion of the Rambam (Maimonides). According to what we have explained, it can be said that the Rambam also agrees that if a get is validated, it is valid, as is evident from his words in his commentary on the Mishnah. The great sages of the world have already permitted, in pressing circumstances, a validated get delivered by a transgressor of Torah law (Pitchei Teshuvah Section 31, citing the responsa of the later Geonim). According to our explanation, this permission is straightforward even according to the Rambam. However, one who wished to initially permit delivering the get without validation and to validate it afterward for some reason he had (as mentioned there), this does not seem acceptable at all. According to what has been written, all the authorities agree with the Rambam that such a get is invalid, as it was delivered by someone disqualified. And a significant reasoning is that because it was delivered by someone disqualified, when it is later validated, it becomes a complete validation (Beit Shmuel, Section 144). One must be stringent according to the law to recognize the signatures, and without this, it is not permissible at all, even for those who are lenient with the recognition of signatures, as will be explained. For a transgressor of Torah law, there is a concern of forgery, and it is also appropriate to be stringent and require clear signs on the get, such as a hole next to a particular letter. Without validation, it is nothing according to the Rambam from the Torah, and according to other authorities due to doubt, as written (the question of the Beit Shmuel there to the Rosh requires further investigation, as the Rosh certainly agrees that if it is validated, he is believed to say he is the agent).

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote there: The law of one who abandons the faith is like the law of those disqualified from testimony by Torah law. This is because he is still considered a member of the covenant and is fit for agency. However, there are some of our Rabbis who hold that he is not a member of the covenant and his status is like that of a non-Jew (Tosafot Sanhedrin 72b), and this also appears to be the opinion of the Rambam (Beit Shmuel, section 47). According to this, it is forbidden to send a get (divorce document) through him, and if it was sent, it is invalid even if the get was confirmed. Therefore, one who publicly desecrates the Sabbath, even in rabbinic prohibitions, is completely disqualified from being an agent for a get, because we always consider one who publicly desecrates the Sabbath as someone who abandons the faith, and one must be very careful about this. (And the Magen Avraham in section 189, sub-section 1, wrote that one who abandons the faith does so out of spite, and without spite, he is not disqualified. According to this, it might be possible to be lenient with someone who desecrates the Sabbath not out of spite. And similarly, in the Knesses Hagedolah, end of chapter 2 of Gittin, he wrote this in letter 78. One should deliberate on this matter and take note carefully.)

It is a clear matter that for any testimony, we require the beginning and the end to be valid. Therefore, if the messenger was a minor when the get (bill of divorce) was given to him, even if he reached the age of majority afterward at the time of its delivery, or if he was deaf and then regained hearing, or if he was insane and then became sane, or if he was a slave and then was freed, it is invalid. However, if the beginning and the end were valid, even if there was a defect in the middle, it is valid—for example, if the get was given to him while he was of sound mind, and he became deaf and then regained hearing, or he was sane and then became insane and then became sane again, it is valid. This does not apply to a minor, a slave, or a Samaritan, but for a blind person in a place where he needs to say "in my presence it was written, and in my presence it was signed," it is not the same. Only if he was not blind at the time of the writing is it valid, even if he is blind at the time of the delivery of the get, because a blind person is not disqualified except for the fact that he cannot say "in my presence it was written, and in my presence it was signed." And since at the time of the writing he was not blind, he is completely valid. And for disqualification due to sin, it is the opposite: if the end is valid, such as if he repented before the delivery, even though he was wicked at the time the get was given to him to deliver, it is valid, because a wicked person is valid for agency; we are just concerned that he might lie. And since he repented, there is no concern (Beit Shmuel, section 148).

The agent can receive payment for his agency as much as he wants, for even witnesses of a get (divorce document), who are prohibited by Torah law from taking payment for their testimony, as we explained earlier in Siman 130, may receive payment for going to the court to be available to testify, which is permitted. All the more so, an agent who is not a witness, since even a relative is valid as we have explained, and his effort is considerable to go to the place of the woman and deliver the get, or for an agent of acceptance who needs to go to the place of the husband to receive the get, he is permitted to take as much as he wants for his service. However, it is proper for him to make the deal with the husband or with the wife beforehand regarding the payment for his agency, and not rely on making it afterwards, because perhaps they will not agree, and the husband might say, "Had I known I had to pay this amount, I wouldn't have sent him," and thus the agency would be nullified. Similarly, the wife might say this regarding an agent of acceptance, which would result in the nullification of the agency. Likewise, the agent himself might say, "Had I known they wouldn't pay me this amount, I wouldn't have agreed to the agency," and thus his agency is nullified. Therefore, it seems to me that if a situation arises where they did not arrange a fixed payment for the agent beforehand, they should not discuss payment at all until the get is delivered to the woman, or in the case of an agent of acceptance, until the get is received from the husband. After the completion of the get, there is no concern of nullifying the agency. However, it is still improper for them to say, "Had we known, we would not have agreed to this," as it casts a bad impression. Therefore, it is obligatory to arrange payment beforehand when appointing the agent. All the more so, when they have made a fixed deal, the agent should not ask for more upon arriving at the woman's place, for the reason we have explained. Some are concerned about this being considered as having a personal interest, and one with a personal interest is invalid to testify (based on Pischei Teshuva, Siman 130). Even though this is not testimony as we explained, nevertheless, when he needs to say "in my presence" (regarding the writing and signing of the get), it is akin to testimony, as the Sages trusted the agent when he testifies that it was written and signed in his presence. The great later authorities dispute whether one with a personal interest is valid in this case or not. When he requests more than his agreed payment, he certainly has a personal interest. To me, it seems that if his main reliance is on the authorization as per the law of the Talmud, certainly when he has a personal monetary interest, it is hard to rely on him, as perhaps due to wanting to increase his payment, he might lie. But according to custom, where there is a written authorization, the main reliance is on the authorization, and the statement of "in my presence" is not a legal requirement. There is no concern when the authorization has been validated (based on Noda B'Yehuda, Siman 129, and Pischei Teshuva there). However, due to the concern of nullifying the agency, one must certainly be cautious in this regard.
