Agency does not require a formal transaction (kinyan), yet it is customary for the husband to perform a symbolic act (kabalat sudar) as a declaration that he has firmly resolved in his heart to carry out this matter. Therefore, if he states earnestly and with full intent that he has resolved to do this, no formal transaction is needed. Similarly, it is our custom for the agent to perform a symbolic act (kabalat sudar) and to state earnestly and with full intent that he has resolved to be an agent to deliver the get (bill of divorce) to a specific woman. The husband also performs a symbolic act (kabalat sudar) and states his intent, although according to the letter of the law, no formal transaction is necessary. All the more so for an agent appointed to receive a get, where both the woman and the agent must perform a symbolic act (kabalat sudar) and state firmly that they have resolved to do so. Do not be surprised at the stringency, for even in monetary matters, Maimonides (Rambam) wrote in the fifth chapter of the laws of sale, law twelve, that the custom in most places is to perform a formal transaction and declare, "We have made a formal transaction with so-and-so who appointed so-and-so as an agent," etc. This formal transaction, while not legally effective, serves to show that the statement is not frivolous but made with full intent. Therefore, if one states earnestly that he has resolved to do this, nothing else is needed. All the more so should we be stringent and perform a transaction and declaration in matters of divorce, and this is the established custom, which should not be changed.

If the husband or the agent is young, it is good to scrutinize whether they have brought signs of maturity, for a minor cannot appoint an agent nor be appointed as one. If they have a beard, there is no concern at all. When it comes to the agent, by law, it is certainly necessary to scrutinize. However, for the husband, it is not required by law, because in any case, if he has not brought two pubic hairs, his betrothal is invalid. Nevertheless, it is good to require and scrutinize also regarding him. There is also some concern by law that perhaps the delivery of the divorce document (get) will be delayed, and he will grow up and seclude himself with her afterwards before the get is given (Darkei Moshe). And even though if he secludes himself with her, he cannot give her the get because people might say the get preceded the conception of the child, this is only a rabbinic concern. By Torah law, the get is valid, and even rabbinically, if he divorced her with this get, she may remarry ab initio, as will be explained in Siman 148, see there. And regarding a woman who appoints an agent to receive the get, by law, it is necessary to ensure and scrutinize that she is of age and has brought signs of maturity, because the betrothal of a minor by her father is a Torah betrothal. If her years are not known to others and only known through her father, she needs a significant number of black and large hairs so that their tips can be bent back to their roots, and this will be further explained regarding chalitzah in Siman 169, see there. Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 25, and these are his words: "But there is no need to be so meticulous with the witnesses of the signing, for the act of signing constitutes the main act of divorce, and it is customary that many adults are present at the giving of the get. According to the custom of designating witnesses, it is necessary to ensure that they are adults." And all the more so according to our custom, where the witnesses of the signing are designated ones, it is necessary to scrutinize that they are adults and have brought signs of maturity.

And even though by law the agent is believed, as has been explained, nevertheless the custom from ancient times is to make an authenticated authorization, as stated in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. The form of the authorization document and the procedure for delivering a get (divorce document) through an agent will be explained, with God's help, in section 154 regarding the order of the get. The purpose of the authorization is that witnesses testify about the agency and the court authenticates their signatures. And when the husband and wife are in the same city, by law authorization is needed according to several authorities who hold that the husband is believed when he says he gave it as a deposit, as has been explained (Beit Shmuel, section 31). Additionally, there is a benefit in the authorization, for by law an agent cannot appoint another agent in his place unless he was compelled, as will be explained, but in the authorization it is written that he gave him permission to appoint an agent and an agent of an agent even without compulsion.

And since according to the law the authorization is not essential, therefore, if the authorization is lost, damaged, or corrupted, and it is an urgent situation, we give the get (divorce document) without the authorization. The agent is trusted to say that he was appointed as an agent in the presence of witnesses, just as he is trusted to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed." However, ideally, the authorization should be written meticulously, and care should be taken not to write abbreviations in it and not to change anything from the words written in the get. For example, if the name "Zanvil" is written in the get with a "bet," it should not be written in the authorization with a "vav." Similarly, any other such cases should be handled with care. The witnesses to the authorization should not be relatives of each other, nor to the man or woman, nor to the witnesses of the get. And even though in retrospect it may be acceptable if they are related to the witnesses of the get, as their testimonies are unrelated—witnesses of the get testify about the get and witnesses of the authorization testify about the agency (Beit Shmuel, section 34)—many great authorities did not want to permit this (Kenesset HaGedolah).

And if the witnesses to the authorization were found to be disqualified, our teacher the Rema ruled in section 24 that the entire agency is nullified, for they are testifying to the essence of the agency and that the husband appointed the agent in their presence. This is not similar to other disqualifications of authorization. Even though, in the absence of an authorization document, he is believed to say that the husband appointed him as an agent, nevertheless, if this was done in the presence of disqualified witnesses, it is even worse (Beit Shmuel, section 35). Seemingly, it appears that only the agency itself is nullified, and if he subsequently brings another authorization, it is valid. However, in his book Darkei Moshe, he wrote that the get (divorce document) is invalid. Perhaps his reasoning is that it is evident that those who arranged the get were ignorant, and it is impossible to rely on them for the entire get (there). If it is clarified that the disqualification became known later and the court did not know beforehand, and there is no suspicion on them since they are not Torah scholars, nevertheless, the agent must be reappointed, for since the first agency was done with disqualified witnesses, it must be redone. He should appoint him anew in the presence of qualified witnesses. Thus, the great later authorities ruled, and it is correct (Atzei Gera, Ginat Veradim, and Pithei Teshuvah, section 14).

And in the authorization document, the name of the city with its rivers is written, just as in a get (divorce document). Similarly, all the nicknames of the man and the woman are written, just as in a get. Some say that the nickname of the agent is also written, while others say not to extend the authorization with unnecessary words. Some say there is no need to worry about extending it with words that pertain to the essence of the agency, since anyone can write according to the clarity of their language, and it is not a fixed ordinance by the Sages. Nevertheless, the wording of the authorization has already been printed in the order of the get, and from it, one should neither detract nor add. This is the practice of all the rabbinical courts in Israel, and it will be explained in detail with the help of Heaven (G-d).

The custom is that the rabbi who arranges the get (divorce document) validates the authorization, and some say that it should be validated by three [people], and this is the common practice and should not be changed. However, if in the place of the woman only one signature out of the three is recognized, it suffices. Some are lenient after the fact even if no signature is recognized at all (Beit Shmuel 136). Additionally, even if the authorization is not validated, it is valid (ibid.), for the witnesses signed on the document make it as if their testimony was investigated in a court. But it is difficult to rely on this, and one should rely on the opinions that hold that court validation does not require further validation (Taz 3). According to this, one should only validate when the authorization is validated by a court, but in the place of delivery, the signatures are not recognized. But if it is not validated at all, one should not rely on it (ibid.), unless it is a pressing circumstance, for in such a case the agent is believed even without authorization.

Therefore, for a get sent via postal service where the agent does not say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," as explained, and by law, authorization and validation are required, it is necessary to recognize the signatures of the validating judges, or at least one of them. We have already written in section 62 a solution for this, that through prior exchange of letters, the signatures can be recognized. Rabbi Rema wrote there that some have the practice of writing a letter from the place of delivery to inform if there is any change in the authorization. And it means that the authorization is not written in Ashurit script but in our script. Therefore, if the writing differs between the place of delivery and the place of writing, the authorization should be written in the script of the place of delivery so that they recognize if there is any change from the get to the authorization.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote in section 30 that a delivery agent who brings an authorization document which states that he is also an acceptance agent—if the agent does not deny the authorization but claims that he was appointed as both a delivery and acceptance agent, then the agency is valid, and he becomes a delivery agent who gives the get (religious divorce document) to the woman. However, if the agent says that he was never appointed as an acceptance agent, then the authorization contradicts him, and the entire agency is nullified, and the get itself is invalid. This is because it indicates that the organizers of the get were unlearned and did not know that the husband does not typically appoint an acceptance agent. Thus, there are several concerns of invalidity. Similarly, whenever it is evident that the organizers of the get were amateurs, this is problematic. There is an objection to this position: if so, even when the agent claims that he was appointed as both an acceptance and delivery agent, the organizers of the get were still unlearned, for they did not give him authorization for the delivery agency and should have informed him that he was also an acceptance agent. One could say that we judge them favorably, assuming that their primary intent was for the acceptance agency. Therefore, they wrote the authorization, assuming the husband would agree to the acceptance agency, and no further effort was necessary. Consequently, even if the husband did not agree, they did not bother with the delivery authorization and maintained the original intent that the agent is trustworthy. However, this only applies when the agent was appointed by the woman, for otherwise, what relevance is there to the acceptance agency? Even this is very strained because how could it be imagined that the authorization for acceptance agency should come from the woman? How did they write such authorization? It is possible to say that he was not precise in his language, and he did not mean authorization but rather a document of acceptance agency, as we wrote in section 140, subsection 4. However, this is also difficult because this document is written after the acceptance agent received the get from the husband. This requires further investigation. Some have explained that indeed he was only a delivery agent, and what was written regarding acceptance was merely to strengthen his position. This explanation does not hold, as what strengthening is relevant here? Therefore, this requires further study, and it is difficult to rely on this as definitive law.

Since we do not practice the method of agency for receiving a get (divorce document) for reasons that will be explained and are not described in the procedure of the get, we will clarify here the entire procedure: A woman, when she wishes to appoint a messenger for this purpose, should appoint him in the presence of two kosher witnesses who are not related to each other, nor to the woman, nor to the man. She should say to him in their presence, "You, [so-and-so], accept my get from my husband, [so-and-so], and your hand shall be as my hand, and your acceptance as my acceptance, and you shall acquire it for me and receive it for me. The moment the get reaches your hand, I will be divorced from him and permitted to all men." The messenger responds, "I will do so," and both of them accept this with a kinyan sudar (formal act of acquisition) and say with full heart, "We have said and decided to do this matter," to strengthen the matter as stated in section 77. Afterwards, the witnesses write a document of authorization in the following format:

Testimony of the witnessing that took place before us, the undersigned, on a certain day of a certain month in a certain year from the creation of the world according to the count that we count here in such and such a city situated on such and such a river, how a certain woman, the daughter of a certain man, who is presently residing in such and such a city situated on such and such a river, appointed before us a certain man, the son of a certain man, to be her agent to receive her divorce from her husband, a certain man, the son of a certain man. And in our presence, she said to this certain man, her agent, "Receive my divorce from my husband, a certain man, the son of a certain man, and let your hand be like my hand and your reception like my reception, and merit it for me and receive it for me, and as soon as the divorce reaches your hand, I will be divorced from him and permitted to any man." And what was done before us, and what we heard and saw, we wrote and signed as a testimony to the appointment of the agent to receive her divorce, and everything is valid and established. The words of a certain witness and the words of a certain witness. And Mordechai wrote in the chapter "HaMekabel" that although there was a kinyan (formal acquisition), the kinyan should not be written in the authorization (Darkei Moshe, section 24, and see Beit Yosef in the name of the Itur).

The witnesses who sign this document should be well-known individuals whose signatures are recognizable in the place where it is given. If this is not the case, the local court should verify their signatures and issue a certification that they recognize the witnesses’ signatures or that the witnesses signed in their presence. However, the signatures of the court members also need to be recognized in the place where the document is given, as the certification itself requires validation. This stricter requirement is based on the law, and it is not comparable to the leniency applied in the case of an authorization for delivery, where leniency is allowed when it is impossible otherwise. In that case, the agent is trusted because the document is in his possession, which is not the case with a get (divorce document) (see Beit Shmuel, section 38). The commentators have written that in this matter, one should be stringent and ensure that all three signatures are recognized (Levush, Darchei Moshe, and Bach). However, some are lenient in this matter because the validation of documents is of rabbinic origin (Beit Shmuel, citing Rashbatz). To validate the signatures, three individuals are required, in accordance with the rules of a court (ibid.).

When the agent comes to the place of the husband and the husband consents to the agency of acceptance, he should write the get (divorce document) in the usual manner with the annulment of declarations, and they should be careful not to write the location of the woman's standing. The witnesses should sign, and then the husband should convene a kosher court that is not related to one another, nor to the husband, wife, or the agent. Although according to the law there is no concern regarding the agent's relationship, the court should recognize the signatures of the authorization or the signatures of the court that validated the authorization, as mentioned. They should read the authorization, and then the husband will bring the get, they will read it, return it to the husband, and he will annul all declarations and disqualify witnesses who might testify to something that would invalidate the get, as mentioned in Siman 134. He will give the get to the agent in the presence of delivery witnesses and say to him, "Accept this get for my wife, [name], daughter of [name], and she is hereby divorced from me and permitted to any man." The agent receives it, lifts it up, and hides it under his garment close to his heart, just like the woman herself would. Afterward, the court will receive the get from his hand, read it with the witnesses, as the law requires reading also after the delivery. The Tur wrote in the name of the Ra'avad that one should be careful not to impose any condition in the get. The reason is that there may be witnesses who know about the get but do not know about the condition, and they will go and testify before the woman that she is divorced, and she will remarry, but the condition will not be fulfilled, making the get invalid and her children illegitimate (Beit Yosef). This reason is weak, for the woman will not remarry until the arrival of the agent, who knows about the condition, and he also brings a document from the court as will be explained. Some say the reason is that the woman can claim she only appointed the agent if he would accept without a condition, and she did not consent to the condition. Therefore, if she said he could accept on condition, it is permissible to impose a condition (Bach and Taz). However, our custom is not to impose any condition in the get.

After the agent receives the get (divorce document), the Beit Din (rabbinical court) will write down their testimony and hand it over to the agent. We have already written its formula in Siman 140, Section 4, see there. The husband will also write under the signatures the following language: "I, so-and-so, who is present today in the city of such-and-such, located on the river such-and-such, have divorced my wife, so-and-so, daughter of so-and-so, and I divorced her in the city of such-and-such, located on the river such-and-such, by the hand of so-and-so, son of so-and-so, who is my agent before the Beit Din of so-and-so, so-and-so, and so-and-so, who are signed in the document above. And I divorced her with a complete divorce, nullifying all previous declarations and without any conditions, as written above. And their document and signatures are genuine, and because everything is true I have also written this document to serve as proof and as my testimony, so that I will not have any opportunity to dispute this matter. And everything is valid and established." He signs it in his handwriting, "Declaration of so-and-so, son of so-and-so." They will hand everything over to the agent, and the signatures of the judges in the place of the husband must be recognizable to the Beit Din in the place of the wife, or two witnesses must testify that they saw the agent receive the get from the husband. However, according to the law, the agent is trusted when the get is in his hand, as has already been explained regarding when the husband claims it was given as a deposit. But for a claim of forgery, witnesses are needed, because only for an agent of delivery, when he says "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," did the sages believe him, and not for an agent of receipt.

And because it is known that verifying signatures is not an easy matter, from one place to another, and especially since it has been explained that all three signatures need to be recognized, therefore the Tur wrote in the name of the R"F that it is proper to avoid divorcing through an agent of acceptance at all. And so it is written in Shulchan Aruch, Section 29, and this is the custom. Nevertheless, if it is not possible in any other way, she can make an agent of acceptance if they recognize the signatures of three judges (Bach, Taz, and Beit Shmuel, Section 40), and they permitted it in practice for someone who was sometimes of sound mind and sometimes not. And through an agent of delivery, it is not possible, for perhaps at the time of the agent's delivery to her, he would be of unsound mind. And they permitted that the woman appoint an agent of acceptance in place of the husband during his lucid period, and she would return to her place, and during his lucid period, he would hand the get to her agent of acceptance (there). And this is because she did not receive the get from the husband himself during his lucid period because his lucid period was short, and there was not enough time at the moment (as it should be, for otherwise why would they have done so; rather, certainly as we said, and the woman could not stay there and left it to her agent, so that when the time was sufficient, he would receive the get from him). And even though he became of unsound mind between her making an agent of acceptance and the get, we do not concern ourselves with it, for even if he became of unsound mind between the writing and giving, we explained in Siman 121, Section 16, that it is valid, and all the more so in this case.

The Bach, of blessed memory, in his responsa brings in the name of the sages of France that a woman can appoint a shaliach kabbalah (agent to receive a get) in her place, provided that two witnesses accompany the agent to testify about the agency. Now, with ordinary people, certainly there is no issue, as it has already been explained that even an agent in another place can be appointed by her not in his presence. However, for those who sometimes are well and sometimes not, there are many concerns about this, as perhaps at the time she made him an agent, she was not of sound mind (see Pitchei Teshuva, section 22). Some prohibit it and some permit it. Therefore, it seems to me that in our times, when communication through wires spans the whole world, and people can communicate from a distance in an instant, this can be easily arranged. First, the rabbi in the husband's location will speak with the rabbi in the wife's location about the situation, and she will appoint a man in the husband's location as an agent to receive the get and designate a specific person. This can be done when she is of sound mind, and when she is well, they will arrange the get, and the agent will receive the get on her behalf. There is no concern for any forgery, as they will inform each other through the wires that she appointed so-and-so as an agent to receive the get in the presence of two witnesses, and afterward inform that the agent received the get according to halacha. Nevertheless, in practice, this needs careful consideration, and it should be done according to the agreement of several decisors who understand the situation and ensure that everything is according to the law of the Torah.

A husband who appoints an agent to deliver [a get, a Jewish bill of divorce] must say to the agent, "Give this get to my wife," and according to the law, this suffices. However, the custom is to add and say, "And let your hand be as my hand, and your actions as my actions," etc., as will be explained in the order of the get. The husband has the ability to appoint an agent solely for the delivery of the get or to appoint an agent for the writing, signing, and delivery, as it is taught (Gittin 65b): "If someone says, 'Write a get and give it to my wife,' they should write and give it," meaning that he says to three people that one should write, two should sign, and they should give it, as stated in Siman 120. One of them becomes the agent for the delivery, for his intention is not that all of them should be agents unless he says "all of you," as will be explained. Additionally, it is not invalid if the scribe or one of the witnesses acts as the agent, for everyone is qualified to be an agent, as stated.

Not only that, but even if he shortened his words and did not use the customary language of a get (divorce document) as is familiar among people, such as if he said to them "expel her," which is a term for divorce, or "send her away," a phrase from "and he sends her from his house," or "release her," a term for a letter of release, or "dismiss her," a term for a book of dismissal, or if he said "write a letter and give it to her," as this too is a term for a get, similar to how they write "a letter of release" (Rashi). Regarding the term "letter," he must say "write and give," for otherwise, it is not a term at all. In all these expressions, if he had previously spoken with them about matters of her get, they can write a get and give it to her. For if he had not spoken with them about the matter of the get, how would they know what he meant? Even the term for divorce could be interpreted as expelling her from his house, as it is written, "Expel the maidservant" (Ra’avad and Beit Shmuel, section 20).

But if he said to them, "Release her," "Support her," "Do for her according to the law," "Do for her according to custom," or "Do for her properly," he has said nothing. And the Rambam wrote in Chapter 2, Law 10, that if they wrote and gave it to her, it would be a void get (divorce document), because he holds that these expressions do not at all imply the language that indicates a get. However, Rashi explained there that these expressions are questionable, like "Release her," whether it means release through a get or release from obligations, and similarly "Support her," whether it refers to the needs of the get so that she will not require levirate marriage, or actual support, meaning providing for her needs. Likewise, "according to custom" and "properly," whether it refers to the law of the get or the law of sustenance (and the Ran and the Ra'avad similarly wrote). According to this, it seems that if they gave it to her, it would be a doubtful get. However, from the language of the Mishnah, "he has said nothing" implies clearly that there is no doubt in this matter, and this is also indicated by the Jerusalem Talmud and the Talmudic discussion, which says there are expressions that are doubtful, as will be explained. It implies that in these cases there is no doubt at all, and this is indeed the truth. Even though these expressions can also be interpreted as referring to a get, nevertheless, since the straightforward meaning of the language implies another matter, even if his intention was for a get, it is only considered as unspoken intentions. And even if he spoke with them previously about matters of her get, this is not similar to betrothal when giving it into her hand, where there is no need to explain. Similarly, when he spoke with her about the matters of the get and then gave her the get plainly, it suffices because he is giving her something, and the matter is evident. But in his speech when he tells others, if the language more likely leans towards another matter than a get, it is considered as unspoken intentions, even if he previously spoke with them about the matters of the get. And the expressions that will be explained as doubtful are because they frequently indicate the language of a get, as will be explained (and in the Gemara, there is a distinction between "Pitre'u" and "P'taru," and in our texts, there is no distinction).

And if he said to them, "Release her," "Dismiss her," "Permit her," or "Leave her," it is effective for her, but it remains a doubt. It is a question in the Gemara if "Release her" is exactly like the expression in a bill of divorce, where the intent is the same, and it indicates the language of a get (bill of divorce). However, since the term "release" is not written in the get, perhaps it is not effective (Rashi). Similarly, the term "dismiss her" is like the biblical language "and she shall leave his house," but there is doubt because, in the biblical language, it implies that she leaves on her own and not that he dismisses her (ibid.). Likewise, "permit her" is the expression "you are permitted to any man," but still, it could also be interpreted regarding the annulment of vows, and it is not a clear expression (ibid.). "Leave her" is like "permit her," and similarly, "it is effective for her" implies more the language of the get, meaning to benefit her so that she becomes free from her marital bond, but still, it is not a clear expression, and it remains a doubt.

One who says "Write a get (bill of divorce) for my wife" and does not say "Give it," they should write it and give it to him, but not give it to her, because he did not make them emissaries to divorce, only to write. And if they gave it to her, it is not a get, because if he wanted them to give it to her, he would have said "Give it," and his intention was only that the get be ready in his hand, and when he wishes, he will divorce her. This is said regarding a healthy person and also when there was no alarming reason. But if he was ill and had been sick for three days, or was in danger because his illness suddenly worsened even before three days, or was taken into custody by the authorities even for monetary matters, or they are leading him away and he cannot delay, or he is in haste to depart overseas or to go on a caravan to the desert, or if he was seized by thoughts of death due to his lack of health and made a will because he fears death, in all these cases, even if he only said "Write a get for my wife," they write and give it to her, because it is known and understood that his intention was to write and give it to her, but due to his haste and worry, he did not finish saying "Give it."

And sometimes the same rule applies to a healthy person, as the sages taught in the Mishnah (66b): There was an incident with a healthy man who said, "Write a bill of divorce for my wife," and then he went up to the roof, fell, and died. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said, "If he fell of his own accord, it is a valid bill of divorce; but if the wind pushed him, it is not a valid bill of divorce." For if he fell by himself, it is evident that his intention was thus, and the end proves the beginning, and it is like the case of one who is dangerously ill or similarly in distress, and he is very agitated. But if the wind pushed him, then his intention was not originally for this, and his status is that of a healthy person. And if he fell by himself, even if they have not yet written it, they write and give it as long as he has life in him, provided they check that he is of sound mind, as stated in section 122. And if there is doubt whether he fell by himself or the wind pushed him, if he fell immediately, it is a sign that he fell by himself, and it is a valid bill of divorce. But if he did not fall immediately, it is doubtful. However, if it is certain that he fell by himself, even if he did not fall immediately, it is a valid bill of divorce, and we do not say that initially he did not intend to fall. However, from the language of Maimonides in Chapter 2, Law 13, it is understood that only if he fell immediately is it a valid bill of divorce. And if he fell immediately, we assume that he fell by himself unless it becomes known to you that the wind pushed him. And see there (and the comments of the Maggid Mishneh, and the Beit Yosef, and the Gra, section 141, and I do not know why they rejected the words of the Beit Yosef, and scrutinize it well).

And so, we have learned there: If someone was thrown into a pit and he said, "Whoever hears my voice should write a get (divorce document) for my wife," they should write it and give it, provided he specified his name, his wife's name, his city's name, and her city's name, for he has designated the agency to whomever hears his voice. But if he did not use this language and instead said, "Whoever wishes to write, may come and write," it is a doubtful matter whether this is effective or not (Beit Shmuel, section 127). And even according to those authorities who hold that agency is not needed for writing, nevertheless, he still needs to command the scribe to write (ibid.). And certainly, regarding the giving of the get, clear agency is required. However, the language "whoever hears my voice" constitutes clear agency for whoever heard his voice.

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote there, "And this is provided that they know him," see there. And some have explained that this means, "And this is provided that they know that this person, whose name is such, is the husband of the woman whose name is such" (see Lechem Mishneh and Kesef Mishneh on the Ran). And some have explained that this means, "And this is provided that they know him to be a human being" (Hagahot Maimoniot, letter chaf). And the Rambam concluded that even though they brought him up from the pit and did not recognize him, this is still a valid get (divorce document), for this is akin to a time of danger when they write and give even though they do not recognize. 

And know that in the Gemara there it is stated that specifically if they saw the reflection of a reflection, meaning the shadow of a shadow, otherwise we are concerned that it might be a demon. Therefore, when they saw the reflection of a reflection, this concern is removed because demons do not have the reflection of a reflection. And so have all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) ruled. The Rambam, of blessed memory, did not mention this at all, and the commentators have written that according to the conclusion of the Talmud, since it is like a time of danger, this is not necessary. However, most poskim do not hold this way, for only concerning another matter did the Talmud state this, but in general, they need to see the form of a man and his reflection of a reflection. 

Otherwise, we are concerned that it might be a demon, for it is the way of demons to be found in pits, also in the city, and also in the fields and forests. According to the second explanation we wrote regarding the words of the Rambam, it can be said that the Rambam's intention is also this. Practically, we cannot rule this way now, for it has already been clarified in Siman 17 that we are not experts in the reflection of a reflection, see there. All the more so, we need to know that the get was given to her while he was still alive and sane, which is not common at all. For if when they brought him up from the pit he was still alive and sane, he could command afterward. And if he is not alive or not sane, it is uncommon to know that he was alive and sane the entire time the get was written and given.

It has already been explained in Siman 120 that when someone tells ten people to write a get (divorce document) for his wife, his intention is not that all of them should write it, but rather that one should write it on behalf of everyone, unless he says "all of you write," in which case one writes it in the presence of all of them, as explained there. The same law applies to the case where someone is thrown into a pit and says "anyone who hears my voice," even if there are many people present, it does not need to be done in the presence of all of them. Rather, one writes and two sign, for even though he said "anyone who hears," it is not as if he said "all of you," and his intention is only that whoever hears his voice should do it, not that everyone should necessarily do it.

And similarly, regarding the delivery of the get (divorce document), if many people stood together and he said, "Bring the get to my wife," his intention is not that all of them should bring it, but rather that whichever one of them wishes to can bring it on behalf of everyone. However, if he said, "All of you bring it," it is not valid until all of them bring it, meaning that one brings it in the presence of all, that they all go with him (Gemara, end of chapter 6). Therefore, the Sages decreed (there) that one who tells many people to bring a get to his wife should explicitly say, "Each one of you should bring the get to my wife," so that there will not be a problem with the statement "all of you," for if one is missing, the get will be invalid. And it is similarly explained in section 120 regarding the writing of the get, see there.

He said to three people, "Two of you sign the get (divorce document)," and among the three were a father and his son, who cannot sign together, as well as other relatives. The father should sign with the other person or the son with the other person. We do not say that he certainly only intended the father because we do not honor the son in the presence of the father; rather, he intended both of them. And so said the Sages (Gittin 66a): "The law is that people appoint a son in place of a father as an agent." Similarly, regarding the delivery of the get, if he said to three people, "Two of you deliver this get to my wife," and among them were a father and his son, the father and the other person or the son and the other person are able to deliver it. Only in the case of delivery can the father and son deliver it together, as relatives are not invalidated from delivering a get. Nevertheless, there are those who say that the father and son should not deliver it, not because of invalidation, but because we say that the husband certainly did not want to trouble both of them together (see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 30, in the name of the Maharshal). This also appears to be implied by the language of the Tur.

It is obvious that when a messenger brings a get (divorce document) to the woman, he must recognize her as the wife of the husband who sent him. If he does not recognize her, he should give it to her based on the testimony of two witnesses who confirm to him that this is indeed the wife of the sender. For even a blind person can be a messenger when he does not need to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," even though he cannot see her and his recognition is only by the sound of her voice (Gittin 23a). All the more so, another person can rely on witnesses who recognize her. This will be explained, with God's help, in Siman 142, Section 49.

If a man tells an agent, "Take this get (divorce document) to my wife," and the agent replies, "I do not know her," or he says, "I am embarrassed to give it to her," and the husband then says, "If so, give it to a certain person who knows her, and he will give it to her," the first agent does not become an agent for divorce. He should not deviate from his agency, and he cannot either give the get to her or appoint another agent in his place. Rather, he should hand the get to that certain person, and that person will be the agent for divorce and will give it to her, or he may send it through another if he becomes ill or is prevented, as will be explained. If the first one gave her the get or sent it through his own agent, it is a doubtful divorce. For although it is certain that any agent not appointed for divorce cannot change his agency, as mentioned, nevertheless, since the husband initially wanted him to be the agent for the divorce but he did not agree at that moment, and later he did agree, there is doubt whether he may be considered an agent appointed for divorce (this is according to Rabeinu Tam's version in Tosafot, Gittin 29b, s.v. ה"ג). And know that an agent not appointed for divorce cannot appoint another agent, this applies when it is without the husband's knowledge. But with the husband's knowledge, he can appoint another agent.

If one appoints an agent to deliver a divorce after a certain time, it is considered as if the divorce can be given from now, and he appoints the agent because it can be given. Therefore, if he sent a get (divorce document) through an agent and told him not to give it to her until after thirty days, if the agent falls ill or encounters an unavoidable circumstance within those thirty days, he can appoint another agent to deliver it after thirty days. This is like any agent who can appoint another agent in such a case. If he possesses authorization (reshoot), even if it is not written that he can appoint another agent, he can still do so without an unavoidable circumstance, for the main purpose of the authorization was presumably for this, as for an unavoidable circumstance, no authorization is needed (Bach, subparagraph 151). Some are stringent and say that the get should not be handed to the second agent immediately because we are concerned that he might change the agency and give it to the woman immediately. Instead, he should appoint him as an agent to deliver it after thirty days, and the get should be deposited in the court until that time, or he should inform the court of his agency, and they will appoint an agent after thirty days (Rama in the Tur, and it seems to me that he also agrees with depositing it in the court as mentioned, following the rationale). This is according to Rashi’s opinion, which will be explained, that when it comes to an object, he cannot appoint an agent because we are concerned that the second agent might change the instructions of the husband, for whenever there is any condition in the agency, there is this concern, as will be explained. Know that whenever a get is handed over for after a certain time, the husband must state and stipulate that the woman is trusted to say that he did not come within the time and reconciled with her and nullified the get, as will be explained. Therefore, when a get is handed over to an agent for after thirty days, this stipulation must be made. This applies only to a married woman and not to a betrothed woman, for regarding a married woman, the sages said that people's minds are such that since she is dear to him, he will surely seek to nullify it. Therefore, this condition is necessary, and when it is stipulated, this concern is removed, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

If someone sends a get (divorce document) through an agent and tells him, "No one else should deliver it to her except you," and the agent gives it to another person who then delivers it to her, it is obvious that it is not a valid get since he explicitly stated that no one else should deliver it. Even if he told him simply, "Take it to her," and certainly if he said, "You take it to her," the agent should not send it with someone else as long as he is able to deliver it himself. However, if the agent becomes ill or is otherwise unable to deliver it, he may appoint another agent, even if he was told, "You take it," and certainly if he was merely told, "Take it," since he did not specify that no one else should deliver it. If he explicitly stated that the agent may appoint another agent, the agent of the agent may appoint another agent, even if the original agent did not become ill or face any other impediment, because that is his intention. If the agent becomes ill or is otherwise unable to deliver it, he does not need explicit permission. Some of our Rabbis hold that if he said, "Take it," without further specification, the agent may send it with another person even if he did not become ill or face any other impediment. However, if he said, "You take it," the agent should not send it with another person unless he becomes ill or faces an impediment, or if he explicitly stated that he may appoint another agent. (This is the opinion of Rabbeinu Chananel in the Tur, and most authorities agree with the first opinion.)

And the reason for this law is that certainly, according to logical reasoning, an agent would not have the authority to appoint another agent in his place without the principal's permission, for who gave him this power? However, since the Torah decreed that an agent can appoint another agent, as stated at the beginning of section 140, it must be that the intention of the Torah is in a general sense. If the principal gave him explicit permission to appoint another agent in his place, it would obviously be allowed and there would be no need for a scriptural text for this. And similarly, if the principal explicitly told him not to appoint another agent in his place, it is clear that he cannot do so. Therefore, the Torah certainly refers to a general case, and according to Torah law, any agent can appoint another agent in his place, even if he did not become ill or was not compelled. For according to the Torah, there is no logical reason to differentiate in such a case. And what we said, that without illness or compulsion he should not appoint another agent in his place, this is a rabbinic decree because there are people who are particular about this, and when they hear that an agent appointed another agent, they might cancel the entire agency. But in the case of illness or compulsion, no one is particular (Ran Chapter 3). The second opinion holds that in a general case, people are not particular even without illness or compulsion.

According to what has been explained, when one sends a messenger or appoints a second messenger according to the first opinion, if he appointed a proxy in his place without becoming ill or being coerced, and the second messenger delivered the get (divorce document) to the woman, the get is not nullified by Torah law but is invalid rabbinically. However, there are those who say that the intention of the Torah is also such that a messenger can appoint another messenger only when it is known that the husband does not object. But if he objects, he cannot appoint another messenger. And according to this, when we say that without illness or coercion people object, even by Torah law the get is void (see there in the Ran for two reasons). And according to this, in practice, one should be stringent according to both reasons. Our Rabbis, the Tosafists (29b, s.v. Rashbag), hold this opinion as well. And according to this opinion, even if the husband did not explicitly state that he should appoint another messenger in his place but revealed his intention that he does not object, he can appoint another messenger in his place even without illness or coercion (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 54). This should not be done in practice, but according to our custom, where they write a power of attorney, it is explicitly stated in it that he can appoint another messenger in any case, as will be explained in the order of the get in Siman 154 (what the Beit Shmuel questioned in subparagraph 55 is not difficult at all, for in the Gemara it is explicitly stated what the sender said, and it is not similar to the question of the Ran, see there and examine it well).

Just as the first agent can appoint a second agent, so too can the second agent appoint a third agent, and so on indefinitely. Since the Torah has given permission for an agent to appoint another agent in his place, it makes no difference whether it is the first, second, or third agent. The law of the second agent is the same as the law of the first agent: he cannot appoint another agent unless he falls ill, is coerced, or if the husband explicitly states that he can appoint another agent. Even if the husband only explicitly permits the first agent, the second agent is still included, for they all derive their authority from the husband, as will be explained (in my opinion).

Now, logically, it would seem to say that the second agent can appoint a third agent even without having fallen ill or being coerced. This is because in the case of the first agent, we require that he fell ill or was coerced since the husband appointed him and possibly prefers him over others as long as he has not fallen ill or been coerced. However, in the case of an agent of an agent, since the husband is not aware of them, what difference does it make to him whether it is the second or third (Ran there)? Indeed, there are those who hold this view (Ramah in the Tur), but the majority of poskim do not agree because one cannot confer more authority on the second agent than on the first (Ran there). This is also how it is concluded in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 39.

When a first agent appoints a second agent in a situation where it is necessary to say "It was written and signed in my presence" ("Befanai Nechtav u'Befanai Nechtam"), as will be explained in Siman 142, this must be done in front of a court, and the first agent must declare in their presence "It was written and signed in my presence," because this serves as a form of validation, and validation requires a court. The second agent will then say, "I am an agent of the court," as is mentioned there. If it is a situation where it is not necessary to say "It was written and signed in my presence," or if the document is already validated, in which case it is also not necessary to say it, as mentioned there, it is not required to appoint the second agent in the presence of a court. Nonetheless, the Rosh and the Tur wrote that it should be done with witnesses, as they maintain that an agent for delivery must be appointed with witnesses. Consequently, according to the Rambam, who holds that it is not necessary to appoint with witnesses, it is possible that in this case as well, it can be done privately, and so wrote the prominent later authorities (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 157, and the Gra, subparagraph 83).

In my humble opinion, it seems from the way our teacher, the Beit Yosef, rules in paragraph 40 that witnesses are required, that according to the Rambam, witnesses are also necessary. Even though the actual agency does not require witnesses – this applies to the husband himself when he appoints an agent. But when an agent appoints another agent, on whom does the second agent rely? The second agent relies on the first agent who is the husband's agent. How can the first agent alone be trusted? Even though the Sages trusted the agent, this is during the delivery of the get (divorce document) to the woman, at the completion of the get, and we rely on the actual get. But at the time of appointing the second agent, when the get is not yet completed, there is no logic to rely on the get, neither at the time of its writing nor at the time of its delivery. Therefore, when appointing with witnesses, the witnesses are relied upon. However, in the Rambam, Chapter 7, Law 21, it is explicitly stated that he can appoint an agent privately, see there.

Every agent stands in place of the husband, for they derive their authority from the husband. Therefore, if the first agent appoints a second agent and the second agent dies before delivering the get (divorce document), the first agent may take the get from the heirs of the second agent and deliver it to the woman or send it through another agent. We do not say that the first agent's agency is nullified as soon as he hands it over to the second agent, for just as the husband could take it from the heirs, so too can his agent (Taz 25). Even if the second agent is still alive, the first agent can take it from him and deliver it to another or to the woman (ibid.), for since the husband has said that his hand should be as his own hand, it is as if he stands in the husband's place. Moreover, even if he has already delivered it to the woman but failed to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," he can take it back from the woman and re-deliver it, saying "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," as stated in Siman 142 (see Beit Shmuel 25). The general principle is that as long as the get has not been properly delivered to the woman, the agency is not complete. The same law applies from the second agent to the third, and from the third to the fourth, and so on forever, as they all have the same law and all derive their authority from the husband.

Although we have said that the power of the first agent still exists as long as the second agent has not delivered the [get] to the woman, nevertheless, if the first agent dies, we do not say that the agency of the second agent is nullified. Since the husband is still alive and the first agent has transferred his power to the second agent, the second agent now stands in the place of the husband. Similarly, if the second agent designates a third agent, the third agent stands in the place of the husband, and so on indefinitely. However, we mean to say that as long as the first agent is alive, he has the ability to reclaim his power because he stands in the place of the husband. But if he does not reclaim it, the second agent stands in the place of the husband. Therefore, if the husband dies before the [get] is delivered, all the agencies are nullified, and none of them are permitted to deliver the [get] to her, as they all derive their power from the husband, as has been stated.

If a "shaliach kabbalah" (an agent appointed to accept a get, a Jewish divorce document) can appoint another agent in his place, just as with a "shaliach holacha" (an agent appointed to deliver a get), the Tur brings three opinions in the name of a Gaon. He writes that without the woman's instruction, he cannot appoint another agent in his place. However, if she instructed him that he can appoint another agent in his place, he can do so. In the name of the "Itur," it is written that in any situation, an agent can appoint another agent. In the name of the "Ramah," it is written that in any situation, he cannot appoint another agent, even if he was given permission, because it is considered a matter of "mili" (personal matters), and "mili" cannot be transferred to an agent. The Tur is puzzled by this, arguing that if he was given permission, it is not considered "mili," similar to the case discussed in Siman 120. The commentators are also puzzled by the Tur's position. Rav Yosef Karo (Rabbeinu Beit Yosef) wrote in his major work that the "Itur," who permits appointing an agent in any situation, does not mean that the agent himself would accept the get from the husband and thereby effect the divorce. Rather, he means that the agent can appoint another agent to accept the get from the husband and give it to him (the original agent), and as soon as the get reaches his (the second agent's) hand, the woman is divorced.

Behold, the opinion of the Ramah is clear that he holds this is like mere words since the agency only involves mere words and is very similar to what is stated in Siman 120 regarding one who instructs a scribe to write a divorce document, that he is not permitted to instruct another to write it, because mere words are not transferred to an agent. And what the Tur questioned, that in the case of "tell them" mere words do not apply, and if so, when he instructs him, why should he not be able to make an agent, is not difficult at all. For the Tur follows his reasoning above in Siman 120 and in Choshen Mishpat Siman 294, that in the case of "tell them," mere words do not apply, and many of our Rabbis think so, for that is the straightforward understanding of the passage at the end of the chapter "Hakebel." But we have already explained in Siman 120, Sections 52 and 53, that the Rif and the Rambam hold that even in the case of "tell them," the reasoning of mere words applies, based on the passage "Mi She'achzo" there. And the Ramah was concerned for their opinion, as is evident from the words of the Tur himself in Siman 120, where he wrote that the Ramah ruled in the case of "tell them" that it is a doubtful divorce, and if it was certain to him that in the case of "tell them" the reasoning of mere words does not apply, there would be no doubt of divorce, but rather a Rabbinic disqualification due to the decree of "Chatham Sofer," as we have explained there in Section 50. But the Ramah was concerned for the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam (and see Beit Chadash).

And regarding the reasoning of the Gaon, it seems simple that he also holds that it is a matter of "mili" (verbal directives) and in the case where he says "say," he holds like most of the authorities that "mili" does not apply. Therefore, he ruled that without a specific directive, one cannot appoint an agent, but with a directive, one can. The reasoning of the Itur seems to be that he holds that this has no connection to "mili" at all, for in truth, the matter is astonishing. After all, we expound "and she sends," teaching that a woman can appoint an agent ("and she sends" teaches that the agent can appoint another agent, as in the beginning of the second chapter of Kiddushin). According to the previous opinions, it must be said that this refers to the man or when she appoints an agent for delivery and the husband also appoints him as an agent, then the agent can appoint another agent, but not in the case of an agent for receiving. However, the Itur holds that "mili" is only when he commands to write, as this is like mere words, but when he commands to receive something, this is not "mili" at all, for there are many types of agency in such a manner. The primary example of agency in Terumah is that he does not give him anything but sends him to separate his Terumah. Similarly, here she sends him to receive her get. This also seems to be implied by the words of the Rashba, who wrote (Gittin 29) and we hold like Rava who said "mili" cannot be transmitted to an agent, meaning since he said to them to write, these words that were transmitted to them cannot be transmitted to others. Thus, it is clear that this applies only to writing (and from his words at the end of the chapter "Hiskabel," brought in Beit Yosef, it is not so, see there). Similarly, it is explicitly stated in Mordechai at the end of the chapter "Hiskabel" in the name of Sefer HaChochmah that receiving the get or receiving Kiddushin is not "mili" for this is a complete action, see there. And in Shulchan Aruch, section 44, this opinion is not brought at all. In practice, one should be stringent according to all opinions. According to the Gaon who permits with her directive, he can appoint an agent even without duress and does not need to appoint him in the presence of a court, only in the presence of two witnesses. And when the second agent receives the get from the husband, she is immediately divorced (the Beit Yosef brought the responsa of Rabbi Shmuel ben the Tashbetz who permitted in practice according to the Itur's opinion, and it is also explicitly stated there that immediately when the second agent receives the get from the husband, she is divorced, and there is a difficulty on the Beit Yosef).

There are those who say that if a woman appoints two agents for receiving her get (divorce document) one after the other, the second one nullifies the first one. Similarly, if the husband appoints two agents for delivering the get, one after the other, unless it is evident from the appointment of the second agent that they still desire the first one (Ramah in Tur). However, the Rosh and the Rashba of blessed memory ruled that even if she appoints ten agents, whether simultaneously or one after the other, as long as the get reaches the hand of any one of them, she is divorced. Her intention was not to nullify the previous agent but rather that if the agency does not succeed with one, it will succeed with another. And this is the ruling we follow, as stated in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 44. The same applies to a husband who appoints agents for delivering the get.

And even more than this, Rashi of blessed memory ruled regarding a woman who appointed an agent to receive her get (divorce document), and the agent delayed in his mission. She then appointed another agent, and this second agent received a get that was not valid. When the first agent heard about this, he reaffirmed his mission, went to the husband, and received a valid get. Rashi of blessed memory permitted her to remarry because the first agent's mission was not annulled by the appointment of the second agent. We do not find an annulment of an agency through mere indication of intent, and even if there was an indication of intent, we hold that mere indication of intent is not considered significant in matters of gittin (divorce documents). All the more so, there was no indication of intent here at all; rather, she was simply eager to obtain a get. We are witnesses that she is content with her divorce wherever it may occur since she was actively seeking the divorce. 

We find an even stronger case regarding the Passover offering: when an agent was appointed and the individuals sought to perform it themselves, nevertheless, the agency of the agent was not annulled (Pesachim, Chapter 9). All the more so, the agency of the first agent is not annulled when a second agent is appointed (Mordechai, beginning of Chapter "HaSholeach").

And similarly, in the case of appointing multiple agents at once, it is not a matter of retroactive clarification, where we would say that it is clarified that she intended for this particular agent, as there is no retroactive clarification here at all. She intended for all of them, for anyone who would receive a valid get from her husband. However, the Rashba of blessed memory wrote that if she said, "Whichever one of you the husband chooses to give it to shall be my agent to receive it," it is possible to say that this does involve retroactive clarification (as the Beit Shmuel writes in Siman 61), since she made the agency dependent on the husband's choice. It is then considered retroactive clarification, as we say in all cases of retroactive clarification in the Talmud, that it is clarified retroactively that she appointed this one as her agent. And we hold that in matters of Torah law, there is no retroactive clarification, as I wrote in Siman 140, Se'if 17, see there. And even though it could indeed be said that this is not a matter of retroactive clarification, since we do not need a retroactive clarification, because if we know that it is a benefit for her, she can acquire the get in her absence and without her knowledge (as in Yevamot, Chapter 15). And since she says that whoever the husband chooses shall be her agent to receive it, he will then be her agent to receive it and acquire it for her without her knowledge, since she expressed her desire for this, and it is a benefit for her. However, nevertheless, it could be said that from the perspective of benefiting her without her presence, she cannot be divorced, because perhaps at that time she did not maintain her previous intention, which would be considered a benefit for her. Therefore, we must rely on her prior agency, and there is a concern of retroactive clarification in this matter.

It has already been explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 182, that an agent who deviates from his instructions nullifies his agency. This is certainly true regarding the agency of a get (divorce document), whether it is an agent for delivery or an agent for receipt. If the agent changes any detail from the instructions of the sender, his agency is nullified and it is not a valid get. Therefore, the agent must be extremely careful not to deviate from his instructions at all. Additionally, it is proper and correct to ensure that the sender does not impose upon the agent tasks that might be subject to change, so that the get does not become invalid. Also, there is a concern that the change might go unnoticed and the woman might marry based on this invalid get, resulting in the get being void and her children being considered mamzerim (illegitimate). There are further specific laws regarding what constitutes a change.

Our sages taught in the Mishnah (65a): "If one says, 'Give this get (bill of divorce) to my wife in such-and-such a place' and it was given to her in another place, it is invalid. If he says, 'Behold, she is in such-and-such a place' and it was given to her in another place, it is valid." And in the Gemara (29a) it is stated: "When he tells the agent, 'Do not divorce her except in the house,' and he divorces her in the attic, or if he says, 'Do not divorce her except with your right hand,' and he divorces her with his left hand, it is not a valid get." And so is the language of Maimonides in Chapter 9 and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 45. It is explicitly explained that regarding location, it is considered a change even if he did not say "Do not give it to her except in such-and-such a place." However, regarding house and attic, or right hand and left hand, it is not considered a change unless he says, "Do not give it except in this manner." The reason is simple: in matters where logic dictates that there is no strictness in the change, such as house and attic, or right hand and left hand, if he merely says, "Give it to her in the house" or "with your right hand," we do not say that he is particular about it, for what particularity is there in this? It is not considered a change unless he says, "Do not give it except in this manner." However, regarding location, there is certainly a strictness, for with regard to the get, some people slander and say, "What did so-and-so see to divorce his wife?" Therefore, we say that even if he did not say "Do not give it to her except in such-and-such a place," he is also speaking with strictness, and we say that in this place he is comfortable being embarrassed and not in another place (Beit Shmuel, Section 62). Also, in this case, if he says, "Behold, she is in such-and-such a place," it is explicitly proven that his intention is not with strictness but merely indicating where she is currently located. From this, one can infer for all matters. Therefore, the custom among us is to tell the agent, "Give it to her wherever you find her," as it is written in the order of the get. (And know that if not for the words of the earlier authorities, one might say that in the Mishnah it is only invalid, and in the Gemara there it is not a get. But they also wrote regarding the Mishnah's ruling that it is not a get, and it must be said that the Mishnah does not distinguish between invalid and null, according to the general rule of Maimonides in Chapter 10. Nevertheless, it remains a question how we can say, "If it was given in another place, the get is null," for perhaps he did not say it with strictness, and we should be stringent. However, we do not have the power to argue against the earlier authorities, even to be stringent. Pay attention to this.)

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote there: "If he said to give it to her on a specific day and it was given to her within the specified time, it is not a valid get (divorce document). If he said not to give it to her except on a specific day and it was given to her either before or after, it is not a valid get because he was precise about the specific day." And the Tur wrote that it is implied from his words that when he says to give it to her on a specific day, it can be delayed, provided it is not given earlier. The reason is simple: the matter of the get is a matter of affliction, as is common in the Talmud; a person does not advance affliction upon themselves (Gittin 18a), and therefore, it is certain that the husband does not wish to advance the giving of the get, but delaying it does not concern him (B"Sh, section 63). If he said not to give it except on a specific day, it is a strict stipulation in every respect (H'M wrote that it is from the Tosefta, but I did not find it). And in Siman 144, it will be explained that even delaying it has some authorities that invalidate it, see there in section 26, and so should be ruled.

Similarly, in the case of a woman who instructed her agent to accept her get (divorce document) in a specific place and he accepted it in a different place, it is not a valid get for the reason we explained, that she does not wish to be embarrassed in a different place. However, if she said, "Bring me my get from such-and-such a place," and he brought it to her from a different place, it is valid (Siman 5) because when she says "bring me my get," he is not her agent for acceptance, rather the husband makes him an agent for delivery. Since she is not divorced by his acceptance, there is no concern if he brings it from a different place (Ran there). Moreover, since the husband needs to appoint him as an agent, it does not depend on her. In truth, there is nothing novel here, and it is an established Mishnah that does not require explanation. The version of the Rambam is more correct, as he reads in the Mishnah: "Bring me my get in such-and-such a place or to such-and-such a place" (Hagahot Maimoniot), meaning that when the husband makes him an agent for delivery, he will deliver the get to that place. There is a reason to say that in a different place she would not wish to be embarrassed and receive her get; thus, it teaches us that since he is the husband's agent and not hers, there is no concern about this. However, even this is not a novelty at all, for it also depends on the husband. Moreover, since she accepted it in a different place, she has now consented to this, and we do not need her prior consent, as he is not her agent.

The sages said there that even if she said "Receive my get for me in such-and-such a place" and he received it in another place, sometimes it is valid. The effect of the get only occurs when it reaches the specified place. For example, if she said, "Receive my get for me in Mata Mechasya" and sometimes he finds it in Babylon, it is clear she did not care in which place he receives it. One cannot say she only desires one of the two places, because if so, she would have said "Receive my get for me in Mata Mechasya or in Babylon." Rather, it is certain that she does not care about the place at all. However, according to this, why specify a place at all? She could have just said "Receive it for me" or "in any place you find it." Rather, she certainly meant this: receive the get in any place, but the effect of the get will not occur until it reaches Mata Mechasya.

And there is a question regarding this matter: if so, the get (divorce document) would not take effect at all, because when the husband hands over the get to the agent, the get does not take effect. How then could it take effect when it reaches Mata Mechasya? This is similar to "Take your get from the ground," which is not a valid get, because in Mata Mechasya he is not receiving it directly from the husband. Indeed, some of our rabbis have written that it must be referring to a case where the husband, when giving the get to the agent, says, "You will be my agent to deliver it to Mata Mechasya, and there you will appoint another agent to deliver it, and from that agent, she will receive it as an agent for receiving" (Tosafot there in the first answer). In such a case, it is as if the husband is handing it to him in Mata Mechasya. However, since the Rif, the Rosh, the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch in section 50 are silent on the matter, it implies that they hold that in all cases it is permissible. The reason is that the get’s effect is always from the moment the husband hands it over, but it is like a condition that she will not be divorced until it reaches there. This is similar to saying to a woman, "This is your get, but you will not be divorced with it until after 30 days" (Tosafot there and Ran). And it must be that the husband knew of this language and agreed to it, for it depends on him to impose a condition on the get (this seems to me, and it also appears from the language of the Ran there). Nevertheless, there is no need to tell the agent that she must be trusted to say that he did not appease her, as this only applies when he set the time, in which case he could contest that his intention was that perhaps he would appease her. But when she set the time, we do not worry that he will contest (Beit Shmuel section 64).

The Tur wrote: If the husband said to the agent, "Take such-and-such an item from her," if he did not insist that the agent take the item first, even if the get (divorce document) reached her hand first and afterwards the agent took the item, it is considered a valid get. Therefore, the agent can send it through another person. However, if he insisted that the agent take the item first, it is not a valid get unless the item reaches his hand first. Therefore, he should not send it through another person, because even if she gives the item to the second agent first, it is not a get since the item did not reach the first agent first. And even if, after the second agent received the item and gave her the get, the item came into the hand of the first agent, it is not a get because the get did not reach her as a formal divorce. Rather, the first agent should take the item from her and then give her the get as a formal divorce after the item has reached his hand. This is the opinion of the Tosafot and the Rosh (Gittin 29b) that when the agency of the get is conditional on the item, the get should not be given until the agent receives the item from her. Not only if there was a change where she received the get before giving the item, even if she gave it afterwards, and even to the first agent, it is not a get because they deviated from the agency. For he intended to cause her distress and dominate her by delaying the get until she gives the item. But even if there was no change with the second agent who received the item and then gave her the get, it is also not a get because since the get was conditional on the item, his intention was not for the item to be in the hand of anyone other than the first agent and for it to be in his hand before giving the get. Therefore, it is necessary that after the item comes into the hand of the first agent, he must receive the get from her and then give it to her. However, when the get is not conditional on the item, and he says to give her the get first, he can send it through another person. Even though with the item he has no permission to give it through another person, this does not apply to the get, for with the get he is permitted to appoint an agent as with all gittin (divorces). And similarly, when the get is conditional on the item and the first agent received the item from her first, he is allowed to appoint an agent for the get. (And this is also implied by the language of the Shulchan Aruch, section 51, and some say when he told him to take, etc., this is the opinion of the Tosafot).

However, the opinion of Rashi and the Rambam in Chapter 9, Law 35 is not so. According to their view, even if the get (divorce document) is conditional upon the object, if the second agent received the object first and then gave her the get, she is considered divorced. This is because it is not critical that the object be in the hands of another person, as it is assumed that he is trustworthy since the first agent trusted him. The main concern is that the object should not remain with her when she receives her get. Since the second agent did this, it is a valid get. However, initially, the first agent should not appoint a second agent, as he might not fulfill the husband’s instructions properly since he did not hear them directly from the husband, which could lead to complications. This applies to any condition the husband sets with the agent; the agent should not appoint a second agent as he might change the condition, as will be explained. If the get was not conditional upon the object and the husband authorized giving her the get beforehand, there is no concern even initially in appointing a second agent. Even though regarding the object it is possible that the husband does not want it to be in the hands of any other person, regarding the get, this does not apply since the get is not conditional upon the object. (This is explicitly stated in Rashi there, and it is also clarified in the Rambam there in Law 37, where it says: "If he said, 'Give her the get and take…', he should not send it through another person since he does not want his deposit to be in the hands of another. But if he did send it, it is a valid get whether…")

And according to this, I am very perplexed because since the husband is particular that the object should not be in the hands of another, therefore when he attached the get (divorce document) to the object, how can it be a valid get through the second agent? For the first agent altered his agency since he attached the get to the object, and there is no greater change than this. Therefore, we must say that not all particularities are the same. For although he is particular that the object should not be handed to another person, nevertheless, since it is common for people to trust their objects to others, his particularity is not so significant as to be considered a change concerning the get. However, this particularity that the object should not remain in her hand at the time of receiving the get is a significant particularity for most people, for when he divorces her, he certainly intends to vex her. And this is also evident from the precise wording of Rashi and the Rambam, of blessed memory (as Rashi wrote "to vex her by keeping her in suspense until she gives [the object]"—see there. And the Rambam, of blessed memory, when discussing attaching the get to the object, wrote that most people are particular about it, and in the case where he did not attach it, he wrote that it is not his will, etc.—see there and examine thoroughly).

The two approaches we brought are also mentioned by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 51, and their intention is clarified as we have written (and the words of the Beit Shmuel in sections 65 and 66 require further examination, and the Ketzot HaChoshen has already questioned him in chapter 3, letter 20; see there also regarding his challenge to the Tur, which also requires examination, and scrutinize this matter). There is also a third approach by the Ramban, of blessed memory (brought in the Yam Shel Shlomo, chapter 3, section 12, and partially in the Beit Shmuel there), and he holds that even if one said, "Give her the get and take from her the object," his intention is also that the object should be taken first (as per the Tosafot's question in the commentary "Take" and he does not agree with their answer; scrutinize this). However, regarding the get, this is not invalid since he did not condition the get upon the object, and the practical difference is only with respect to the payment for the object. According to this, even if he said, "Take the object and give me the get," and he or his messenger changed and gave the get first, this is also not invalid for the get and it is not considered a condition on the object unless he said, "Take the object and then give her the get," since by saying "and then give her the get," he conditioned the get upon the object.
