In such a case, if the messenger only sent the get through a second messenger, the get is invalid, even if the second messenger did not change anything, because this itself is considered a change as we wrote at the beginning of the previous section. The Maharshal in the Yam Shel Shlomo there agreed with this approach to some extent; see there. And the ruling is clear that one should be stringent according to all the approaches.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 52: Any condition that the husband stipulated with the agent, such as "Do not divorce her except in the house or in the attic," or similar conditions—if the husband did not authorize the agent to appoint another agent, he cannot initially send it through another person, lest the second person may not be meticulous in fulfilling the agency, and the get (divorce document) will be invalid. And even though this concern is not explicitly clarified except according to the opinion of Rashi and the Rambam, as I have written, nevertheless, the matter is stated generally according to all opinions, as it also seems logical.

And our master, the Rema, wrote: However, if he appointed a second agent, even if he did not tell him the condition or changed it, if the condition was fulfilled, the get is valid. And one should not say that since he did not tell him the condition or changed it, it is considered a deviation and the agency is invalid, for it is not so. Since, in the end, the condition as commanded by the husband was fulfilled, the agency is not considered altered. What is this similar to? To someone who sent an agent to buy wheat for him, and he wanted to buy barley, but ultimately bought wheat. This is not a change in the agency, for the matter was fulfilled as per the sender's command. Also, one should not say that since the second agent changed from the first agent’s command, the agency is invalid, for it has already been explained that everything depends on the husband, and when the husband's command is fulfilled, the agency is fulfilled.

Additionally, he wrote that if she stipulates to waive all rights that she has over him, even though legally there is room to discuss what is included in "all rights," nevertheless, it is proper to be stringent regarding a get (divorce document) that she should waive all rights she has over him, and afterwards, they can discuss what is included in this. Similarly, anything of this sort. The explanation of the matter is that she should not waive specifically this right and that right and not some particular right, because perhaps they will not be precise in the legalities, and the get will be invalid. Rather, she should waive everything according to its plain meaning, and afterwards, they can discuss what is included in its plain meaning. Likewise, one must be careful that if there remains any debt between them, whether this one owes that one or that one owes this one, or any claim, they should explicitly state that this does not pertain to the get, so that even if the matter is not fulfilled, it will not affect the get. And this is our practice.

It has already been clarified that if the husband said "Do not divorce her except you [yourself]," he cannot appoint a second agent. Therefore, there is an opinion that if he said, "Do not divorce her except with your right hand," he cannot send her with another hand, even if he becomes ill, as it is as though he specified that no one else should divorce her except him. And thus ruled our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, in section 46. There is an opinion that if he becomes ill, he can appoint a second agent (Ramah in the Tur), but the law does not follow this opinion (as this is only according to the opinion of Rabbi Chananel that we brought in section 106, and most authorities do not hold this view, as we wrote there).

A messenger who brings a get (divorce document) and must say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" (b'fanei nichtav u'b'fanei nichtam) — if he did not say this, the get is invalid, as will be explained in Siman 142. If it is a place where it is not necessary to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," as will be explained there, he gives it to her, and she is thereby divorced and permitted to remarry, even if the signatures of the witnesses are not recognized. She can collect her ketubah from unencumbered property but not from encumbered property unless the signatures are verified, as with all documents from which one cannot collect from purchasers without verification of the document. However, for the permission to remarry, the verification of signatures is not required unless the husband or witnesses contest and claim it is forged. Consequently, she collects her ketubah from unencumbered property, for this is the condition of the ketubah: "When you marry another, you shall take what is written for you" (Rosh, beginning of our tractate).

And the reason the Sages were lenient in this matter, that it does not require verification, is because according to Torah law, witnesses signed on a document are considered as if their testimony was investigated in a court. It is the Sages who required verification for other documents, but for a divorce document (get), due to the concern for agunot (chained women), the Sages were lenient (Talmud) to believe the agent in the place where he must say "it was written and signed in my presence," so that his statement would be regarded as verification by two witnesses. For if we required two witnesses for verification, it would often be difficult to obtain them, since the get comes from another place. Consequently, even in a situation where it is not necessary to say "it was written and signed in my presence," they trusted the agent without verification due to the concern for agunot. Furthermore, there is no concern that the husband intended to harm her by writing an invalid get, as he is not suspected of causing her harm by the hands of Heaven (Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Gittin, see there). Additionally, there is no concern that the woman herself made an invalid get and hired the agent, as we strictly enforce that if it is found that the get is invalid and she remarries based on it, she must leave both husbands and she has no ketubah from either, and the child is a mamzer from both. Due to the stringency we imposed on her in the end, we were lenient with her at the beginning, allowing this get to remove her from the status of a married woman (Rosh, chapter 1, section 8, and Ran there). And as this reasoning is stated in section 17, that for this reason they believed her to say "my husband died," how much more so with a get, where the writing proves itself. According to Torah law, it is as if their testimony was investigated in court, as stated.

All this is when there is no dispute about the get [bill of divorce], but if there is a dispute from the husband or from two witnesses—since one witness disputing is nothing, as there is no dispute with less than two (Gittin 9a), and one witness in contradiction is nothing—and if two witnesses testify that the get is forged, even if she remarried, she must leave, and the child is a mamzer [illegitimate]. Even if the signatures were verified by the get's own witnesses or others testify about their signatures, it does not help, as it is two against two, and she remains in the presumption of being a married woman, as will be explained in Siman 152 (Beit Shmuel, Siman 69, see there). And if the husband comes and disputes, claiming that he did not divorce her and the get is forged, the get should be verified by its signatories. Once verified, his dispute is not considered, for the witnesses contradict him, and even if other witnesses testify about the signatures of the get's witnesses that their signature is true, he is not believed to say that they signed falsely. But if the get was not verified and the witnesses are not known, Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 7 that she must leave, and the child is a mamzer. If the get was lost, she is considered doubtfully divorced, and the reason is that although the verification of documents is rabbinic, nevertheless, when the husband claims with certainty that it is forged and she cannot contradict him, she is presumed to be a married woman (Magid Mishneh). Furthermore, there are opinions that in a case where a party claims forgery, verification is required by Torah law (Beit Shmuel, Siman 70), and automatically, if the get was lost, she is doubtfully divorced, as it is unknown whether there was verification when the get was present or not. For this reason, it does not help even if she contradicts him with certainty (in my opinion). Nevertheless, if another man comes and betroths her, she needs a get from the second one as well, even if the get was not lost and no verification was found, as there is concern for those authorities who hold that even when the party claims forgery, no verification is required by Torah law (Beit Shmuel, Siman 71).

It has already been explained that there are five women whom the Sages of Blessed Memory have identified as hating a particular woman and are suspected of causing her harm, and they are not trusted to say that her husband has died, as stated in Siman 17. The same applies to bringing her a get (bill of divorce). Specifically, in a case where it is not necessary for the agent to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" (b'fanei nechtav u'b'fanei nechtam), we are concerned that the get might be forged and the women might intend to cause harm. However, in a case where the agent must say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," this concern is removed, for they have no ability to cause harm since once the agent says this, the husband is no longer believed to challenge it, as stated in Siman 142. And how would they cause harm? We would not believe the husband in his challenge, and to suggest that their intention is to have two witnesses declare the get forged is not plausible, for how would they know that they could obtain such witnesses (see Tosafot 23b, s.v. Adrabba, and it must be said according to their intention that Abaye did not worry about this for the reason we explained. Understand this well). If it is a place where it is not necessary to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" and they did say it, some say they are trusted because the law is established in Siman 142 that it is effective and the husband's challenge is not valid, and some say they are not trusted, for although the law is so, women are not well-versed in the law and think that their statement is not effective in a place where it is not required to say (both opinions in the Ran at the end of the second chapter). But in a place where it is required to say, everyone knows that the husband's challenge is not effective. And these are the five women: her mother-in-law, her mother-in-law's daughter, her co-wife, even if she was married to another man (Yerushalmi, Yevamot, Chapter 15, Halacha 4), for the hatred still lingers between them, her yevamah (sister-in-law), even if she is her sister, and there is no concern of yibum (levirate marriage), the Rabbis did not differentiate, and her husband's daughter, as already explained in Siman 17.

It has already been explained in Siman 90 that as long as she has not been divorced, even if he intends to divorce her, nevertheless, all the obligations of a husband to his wife apply to them. Therefore, if one sends a get (bill of divorce) to his wife, and it is not a get until it reaches her hand, he is obligated to provide her sustenance and all conditions of the ketubah (marriage contract) until it reaches her hand. Additionally, she may eat terumah (priestly gifts) if she is the wife of a Kohen until the get reaches her hand. And if the husband dies before the get reaches her hand, the get is invalid because there is no get after death. In the case of a receiving agent, he is obligated to provide her sustenance and all conditions of the ketubah until the get is handed to her agent. However, she is prohibited from eating terumah immediately once the agent leaves her presence, as it is possible that the agent met the husband outside the city and received the get from him (Rashi there). This is merely a stringency that the sages imposed regarding terumah (see Tosafot there, s.v. "Hiskabel").

Some say that in our times, when it is forbidden to divorce a woman against her will, and we hold that there is no agency for a sinful matter, if a man sends a bill of divorce (get) through an agent to divorce her against her will, and she is divorced against her will, the divorce is invalid (as per Noda BiYehuda, Siman 75, and Ketzot HaChoshen). They hold that when there is no agency for a sinful matter, the action is nullified if it can be reversed. However, many disagree and hold that the action remains valid because the Talmud only mentioned this in the context of liability, not in the context of nullifying the action. In practice, this is a doubtful matter of law, and we adopt a stringent approach rather than a lenient one. Many great authorities have been uncertain about this, and we have already explained this in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 182, Section 13. Refer there.

It has already been explained in Choshen Mishpat there that an agency can be annulled merely by speech, by saying "I annul the agency," just as its establishment was by speech, so too its annulment is by speech. And it appears that even if the agency was accepted through a formal acquisition, it can be annulled merely by speech. This is also implied from the general language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 59, that since the acquisition does not constitute an obligation, it does not prevent the annulment. Moreover, it is essentially a mere verbal commitment. Even if one swore not to annul it and then annulled it, the annulment is valid, and he is considered to have sworn falsely. This is also clarified by the earlier authorities who wrote that in the reverse situation, one should not rely on his oath and he should make an agent for receipt. Similarly, our teacher, the Rema, wrote in this section, indicating that the annulment is effective even when one swore not to annul it. (And I found this explicitly in the Mordechai, at the end of chapter 3 of Kiddushin, regarding acquisition, for it is also considered as a mere verbal commitment, see there):

Therefore, if someone sends a get (bill of divorce) to his wife and cancels it before it reaches her, it is considered canceled. However, after it reaches her, he cannot cancel it because she is already considered divorced. Even if we see that he intended to cancel it before it reached her, we maintain that revealing one's intention regarding a get is not significant, as will be explained later. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch write that even if he cancels it within the time it takes to say a greeting (toch k'dei dibur) after it reaches her, it is ineffective. And although normally we consider toch k'dei dibur as immediate, the sages explicitly stated (Nedarim 87a, Bava Batra 130a) that regarding gittin (bills of divorce) and kiddushin (marriage consecration), toch k'dei dibur is treated as if it is after that period, as explained in Siman 49 concerning kiddushin. It appears to me that according to the Rambam and several other Rishonim, this is fundamentally the law because these matters are done with deliberation and intention, and therefore, one cannot retract even within toch k'dei dibur (Ran there). However, some of our rabbis hold that this is merely a stringency that the sages imposed concerning gittin and kiddushin (Rashbam and Nimmukei Yosef there). According to this, it is understandable why in Siman 49 we follow the stringency. However, here, where we lean towards leniency and say it is a valid get, why should we not consider the opinion of these rabbis? We have already written something similar in Siman 38, section 51.

By law, one can nullify the agency even not in the presence of the agent, as stated in Choshen Mishpat there. And since, regarding a divorce document (get), a great mishap can occur from this—where the agent, unaware of the nullification, might deliver the get to her and she will remarry with it—therefore, Rabban Gamliel the Elder decreed that one should not do so, but rather, if he wishes to nullify it, he should do so in the presence of the agent or the woman (Mishnah, end of Chapter 4). And if he cannot go himself, he should send an agent to the agent or to the woman to inform them of the nullification. And although he decreed thus, nevertheless, if it happened that the husband nullified the get not in their presence, it is nullified (as per Rabbi) and the Sages did not uphold their words to say that the nullification not in their presence is ineffective.

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 6, Law 16: "Anyone who annuls (a get) in the presence of others must annul it in the presence of two (people)," end quote. It is explicitly clear that when annulling in the presence of the woman or the agent, two are not required. This is also evident from the words of the Tur, who wrote: "Initially, one should only annul it in the presence of the agent he sent or in her presence, but after the fact, even if he annulled it in the presence of two others, it is annulled, and there is no need to annul it in the presence of three," end quote. This is also implied by the words of the Shulchan Aruch, Section 60, see there. It is similarly clear from the words of our Rabbis, the Tosafists (32b, s.v. "and Rav Nachman, etc." and "You might say, what difference does it make now, etc."), and from the words of Rashi, of blessed memory, there (s.v. "in the presence"). However, some of the poskim wrote that if the agent went to annul the agency of the get, he must annul it in the presence of two (Ritva, brought in Beit Yosef). This is explicitly evident in the Jerusalem Talmud (beginning of Chapter 4), which states: "If the agent went to annul the get, he must annul it in the presence of two, and the agent shall bring two with him," end quote. And it must be that the agent annulled it in the presence of the woman or her agent; otherwise, why would he send an agent? He should have annulled it in his place (this is also found in Beit Yosef). It is surprising that all our Rabbis did not take the words of the Jerusalem Talmud into consideration.

It appears to me, in my humble opinion, that the Rambam and all the decisors do not disagree with the Jerusalem Talmud. Specifically, when the husband himself annuls the get (divorce document), witnesses are not needed if he annuls it in front of the wife or the agent. This is what they wrote: that anyone who annuls in front of others needs to do so in front of two witnesses, but in front of the wife or the agent, two witnesses are not needed. However, the husband's agent, even when annulling in front of the wife or the agent, requires two witnesses. Otherwise, how can we believe one person when he comes and says the husband annulled the get? Indeed, there are some early authorities who wrote that the husband's agent, when coming to annul the get, needs two witnesses to attest that the husband appointed him as an agent to annul it before it reaches the wife. Otherwise, we must suspect a conspiracy (Mordechai, beginning of the chapter "HaSholeach" in the name of the Riva). And certainly, in such a case, he is like the husband himself and does not need to annul it in front of two witnesses. But the Jerusalem Talmud is speaking where there are no witnesses that he is the husband's agent. Therefore, how can we believe one person? And to this, the Jerusalem Talmud says that it needs to be annulled in front of two witnesses, including the agent. Meaning, since the wife or the husband’s agent hears from two witnesses that the husband annulled the get, she remains presumed to be a married woman, and the get is annulled. For according to two witnesses, a matter is established, and anything done in front of two witnesses is considered truthful (see Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer, Chapter 4, Section 3, who raises a difficulty with the Riva, and according to our explanation, it is resolved. Pay attention and understand). (See Beit Yosef and Bach, Section 292, and according to our explanation, it is not so. See there).
Certainly, please provide the passage from the Aruch Hashulchan that you would like translated.

One may ask a significant question: why does annulling a get (divorce document) not work when done before one witness or by oneself? According to the Rosh, who holds that appointing an agent requires two witnesses, it can be understood that annulling also requires two witnesses. However, according to the Rambam, who does not require the appointment to be made before witnesses, why is annulling more stringent than the appointment itself? And if it is because we do not rely on the annulment unless it is before two witnesses, the Talmud and the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) clarify that even if it is certainly known that it was annulled, if it was not annulled before two witnesses, the annulment is not effective at all.

What appears to me from the words of the Tosafot is that, according to Torah law, the annulment is indeed effective. However, the Sages established their decree that it should not be effective due to the great potential for damage that could arise. If one annuls the get before one witness, not in the presence of the agent or the wife, it is certain that it will not become known, and she will marry another man, and her children will be considered mamzerim (illegitimate). And even though, in the presence of two witnesses, it is not certain that it will reach her ears, as explicitly stated in the Talmud, nonetheless, in most cases, it will become known, similar to someone who sells a field with witnesses, as it creates publicity. However, here we are concerned that even with two witnesses, it may not become known (as Tosafot states). Nonetheless, in most cases, it will become known, but with fewer than two witnesses, it will certainly lead to damage. Even before Rabban Gamliel's decree, it was not effective with fewer than two witnesses, as proven in the Mishnah. This decree preceded Rabban Gamliel's decree (and this is the intention of the Tosafot, who wrote that even Rabbi agrees here, saying, "What power does the court have?" meaning that this decree was already established, resolving the difficulty raised by the Maharsha. Examine this closely and see Malmad Hatalmidim, chapter 6, halacha 18, and the glosses there, though their words are not clear to me).

There are two types of annulment: the first is the annulment of the agency, and the second is the annulment of the essence of the get (divorce document), which nullifies it from being a get, making it like an ordinary piece of paper. There is a practical difference between them. In the annulment of the agency, just as the principal can annul the agency, so too the agent can annul his own agency if he no longer wishes to be an agent, as it is stated in Choshen Mishpat there. However, in the annulment of the get, the agent cannot annul it, since he did not write it by his own command, and only the husband can annul it. Additionally, there is a practical difference in that, in the annulment of the agency, the husband can later use the same get to divorce if he is agreeable to the agency, since the essence of the get was not annulled, only the agency. When they agree again, the agency resumes as before. However, in the annulment of the get, the get becomes invalid forever, since it was annulled from being considered a get.

And indeed, there are some of our Rabbis who hold that the husband has no ability at all to nullify the essence of the get (bill of divorce), for how can his speech nullify the act of writing, since we hold that speech cannot nullify an act (Kiddushin 59b, Tosafot there, and Ran in the fourth chapter of Gittin). Similarly, the Rosh there is uncertain about this, and the Ramban and Rashba also hold that he cannot nullify the get, but they wrote that in practice one should be stringent. However, the Rambam explicitly wrote in chapter 6 that he can nullify the get and the get is invalid forever. So too, the Tosafot in Gittin (32b, s.v. hatam) wrote that the get is not considered an act as long as it has not been delivered to her and is only considered as speech, and speech can nullify speech. Similarly, the Mordechai in the name of the Itur in the end of the third chapter of Kiddushin wrote likewise. And since this is a dispute among the Rabbis, we follow the stringent opinion in every matter, that if he nullified it, it is nullified forever and she is a married woman. If she accepted Kiddushin from another man after receiving this get, she requires a get from both men. This is also how it is ruled in the Shulchan Aruch, section 66.

And these are the words of Maimonides there, in Law 21: “If one sends a get (divorce document) with an agent and then annuls the get, he may still use it to divorce whenever he wants, because he did not annul it as a get but only as far as the agency is concerned. Therefore, if the get was in the husband's hand and he annulled it, such as by saying, 'This get is annulled,' he can never use it to divorce, and it is like a broken shard. And if he divorced with it, she is not divorced. Similarly, if he specified at the time he annulled it and it was in the agent's hand and he said, 'The get I sent is annulled as a get,' he can never use it to divorce.” So are the words of the Shulchan Aruch. It is clear from his words that when the get is in the agent's hand, even if he said, 'I annul the get,' his intention is not towards the get but towards the agency, unless he explicitly said, 'I annul it as a get.' And this is explicitly proven in the Talmud (beginning of chapter 4). And the reason for leniency is because the language of annulment applies more to the agency than to the get, since the language of 'valid' and 'invalid' applies more to the get. Therefore, as long as he did not explicitly say, we assume it pertains to the agency (so it seems to me). And know that even according to those who say that the essence of the get cannot be annulled, this is only when it is fully written, but as long as its writing is not completed, everyone agrees it is considered only as speech (as is evident from Tosafot, chapter 8, s.v. 'And perhaps,' and as is evident from Rashi there, for Rashi holds at the beginning of chapter 4 like the Ran, and as the Maggid Mishneh wrote in chapter 6, law 21. Nevertheless, in practice, I am uncertain, for according to the other two explanations in Tosafot there, this is not necessary, and it is only according to the first explanation of Rabbeinu Ezra. Look there and examine carefully).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in section 60 that the husband is not believed to claim that he has nullified the get (bill of divorce) unless the agent or the wife admits it, or he has witnesses who attest to the nullification. It seems that this applies when the get is already in the hands of the wife, for otherwise, why should he not be believed, since he could nullify it now? Even if we say that when the get is in the hands of the agent, the husband is not believed, even with a migo (a logical argument that he could have made a stronger claim), as this reasoning is mentioned in this section (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 91), this applies when he disputes the agent from the outset and claims that he gave it to him as a deposit and not for divorce. But when he admits that he gave it to the agent for divorce but later nullified it, why should he not be believed? This is better than a migo because his current words are like a complete nullification, as he says that he nullified it, and he has the power to say that it is nullified. But when the get is in the hands of the wife, we indeed need their admission or witnesses; otherwise, how can the husband remove her from the status of being divorced?

If one questions how we can believe the agent when he admits that the husband nullified it, since he makes himself wicked by giving it to the wife after the nullification (as questioned by Beit Shmuel there), it can be answered that the agent can justify himself by saying that he did not know that this language was one of nullification or something similar. Moreover, the reasoning that a person does not make himself wicked applies only when he alone speaks about himself and not when another person says something concerning another, and he admits to it, even though by this he makes himself wicked. Nevertheless, we do not find that we should not believe the words of another for this reason. And furthermore, even though we do not follow leniently in this matter, certainly, we should go stringently and believe them.

One should not say, if so, how does this apply to witnesses, for when there are witnesses, it is obvious that we believe them even leniently. It can be answered that certainly, this is so, for also when she admits, it is obvious that she is not believed leniently, for example, if he is a kohen, she is forbidden to return to him, and we do not believe them that it was nullified (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 92), for perhaps both of them are retracting the get and saying that it was nullified, but in truth, it was not. Similarly, if she received betrothal from another, she is not believed to prohibit herself to the second one (there). And with witnesses, they are believed in any case (and the words of Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 91, are not clear to me, especially since he himself brought that the Rashba wrote so, and I did not find this in the Rashba also what is mentioned by Rema from the Hagahot Ashri, I did not find).

Furthermore, it is written that some say that the two individuals before whom the agency is nullified must be together, but not separately. However, if the get itself is nullified, even after it has been written, it is effective even if done separately. The reason is that nullification before the two individuals is akin to a court, as we have learned in the Mishnah that one would establish a court and nullify it. The Gemara explains that two individuals suffice, and since they are like a court, they must be together. This is unlike testimony, where it is possible to accept testimony from one not in the presence of the other (this is the intent of the Gra in section 120, and similarly, this should be the understanding in the words of the Beit Shmuel in section 194, although his language requires scrutiny). However, when nullifying the get itself, there is no need for a court, as the one who writes it is the one who nullifies it. The ordinance mentioned in section 146 pertained only to the nullification of the agency, but for nullifying the get itself, only witnesses are needed, and it is treated like any other testimony that is valid even if not in the presence of the other. The reason this was not instituted may be explained by the fact that it is uncommon to nullify the get itself. Why would one nullify the get, rendering it impossible to retract it, as we have said? It is better for him to nullify the agency so that he can retract it if he wishes. You should know that this is correct, for many of our rabbis hold that nullifying the get itself is entirely ineffective, as we have stated. Therefore, even according to those who say that nullification is effective, it is certainly uncommon, and they did not see fit to institute a regulation for something uncommon (this is my opinion). There are those who interpret that this refers to after writing and before handing it to the agent, which is like giving notice and can be nullified even if not in the presence of the other. But after appointing the agent, he can only nullify it in the presence of both, even when nullifying the get itself (Tur and Beit Yosef). According to what I have written, this is unnecessary. Nevertheless, it is proper to be stringent according to both interpretations (as it seems to me).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 61: If one sent [a get] through two or through ten [agents], he can initially nullify the agency of one not in the presence of the other. Those whose agency has been nullified are void, and they cannot act as agents unless they are appointed again. For ten who were made agents, whether to write and deliver the get or to deliver it, if he nullified some of them, not all are nullified. There is an opinion that if one of them is nullified, all of them are nullified. End of quote.

The explanation of his words is that it has already been clarified regarding the ordinance of Rabban Gamliel that one should not annul (a get) not in the presence of the messenger or the woman, due to the concern that she may not know about the annulment and may remarry. And only after the fact, if he annulled it, it is annulled. Therefore, when he sent (the get) through two or more (messengers), he does not need, even initially, to annul it in the presence of all of them, because there is no concern here. The one in whose presence it is annulled will no longer be a messenger, and the one not in whose presence it is annulled is permitted to be a messenger, because by annulling some of them, not all are annulled, and the others who were not annulled are permitted to be messengers, and there is no concern here. Consequently, this law also applies when ten were made messengers to write a get, for we hold that one writes and two sign. If he annulled three in their presence, the other three can write and give, and there is no concern. But to annul not in his presence is forbidden initially, lest the one who was annulled does not know about his annulment and will act as a scribe, witness, or messenger. Most of the decisors agreed to this, and this is also derived from the Talmudic discussion (Gittin 33b: the law follows Rabbi in both cases, testimony, etc., is not entirely annulled, and if those go and write and give, they may write and give, and when he said all of you write or all of you bring, it is obvious that even according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, he can annul, for it will not lead to concern, as established by Rav Ashi there).

And this is what was written: "There are those who say that all of them are nullified." This is the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 6, Law 18, where he writes: "If one said to ten people, 'Write a get (divorce document) and give it to my wife,' he can nullify it for one without the presence of the other, and even in the presence of two others. If he sent the get by the hand of two people, he can nullify it for one without the presence of the other, and even if there were ten, if he nullified it in the presence of one of them, the get is nullified." And the Raavad and the Ramach have already questioned his words, for since he ruled that nullifying it in the presence of one nullifies all of them, how can he nullify it for one without the presence of the other? Those who were not present for the nullification will not know, and they will write and give it, and she will remarry. And one cannot say that it refers to the case where he said 'all of you,' which would require all of them to sign and give it, thus preventing any wrongdoing since those who were nullified in their presence would know of the nullification and would not sign and give it. Firstly, because he does not mention at all that it refers to 'all of you,' and furthermore, because he wrote that he can nullify even in the presence of two others, and in this case, even if it were 'all of you,' it could lead to wrongdoing since not all would know of the nullification. Moreover, the primary ordinance of Rabban Gamliel was that one should not nullify except in the presence of the messenger or the wife. How then did he write that he can nullify in the presence of two others? And if we say his intention was that after the fact, if he nullified it, it is nullified, what is this language of 'he can nullify' that he wrote, which implies even initially? Furthermore, if that was his intention, why did he need all this elaboration? He should have briefly said that after the fact, if he nullified it not in the presence of the messenger or the wife, it is nullified. And besides, his words are against the Talmudic discussion that we brought, and many commentators have labored greatly to reconcile his words with great difficulty, and his words were not satisfactorily settled (see there in the Lechem Mishneh).

In my humble opinion, it seems clear that the Rambam had a different approach to this entire matter. Nowhere in his writings on this topic does he mention the decree of Rabban Gamliel, who ordained that the get (divorce document) should not be voided in the absence of the messenger or the wife. Only in law 26 does he write that someone who sends a get to his wife and then voids it in front of two others is punished with lashes of disobedience because he causes the possibility of mamzerim (illegitimate children), etc. This is based on the Gemara in Kiddushin (12b) where Rav would punish someone who voids a get, and Rashi explains there that this applies even when voiding it in the presence of the messenger. The Rambam did not agree with this explanation, and Tosafot also wrote similarly. Therefore, the Rambam did not mention Rabban Gamliel's decree at all, because since we hold like Rabbi who says that if he voided it, it is void, there is no difference whether he voided it in their presence or not. Initially and after the fact, it is not relevant to mention this matter. Initially, one should certainly not void a get, even in the presence of the messenger, as Rashi explains. Though he does not agree with Rashi that one is punished in such a case, certainly it is not proper to void a get. Proof of this is that he himself wrote later in the same chapter, law 20, that when a person writes and gives the get himself to his wife, they should not let him leave until the get reaches her hand, so that he does not void it. This shows that we are concerned with preventing the voiding of a get to the best of our ability. However, with a get given through a messenger, we cannot prevent this, and therefore the Rambam did not distinguish between these cases. He only wrote the basic laws of voiding and mentioned punishment only if voided not in their presence. This is based on the words of Rav in Kiddushin, or perhaps Rav's words are in accordance with Rabban Gamliel's decree, but there is no practical difference. The term "can void" does not imply initially, as the Gemara in Bava Metzia (49a) clarifies, where it says that if one says to his friend "I give you a gift," he can retract it, and it questions "can" is obvious, rather say "permitted to retract." Thus, "can" does not mean initially, and Tosafot also wrote this (37a, s.v. Rabbi) that "can" does not mean initially. When it says that if he voided it in front of one person the get is void, even though the Gemara clearly states that it is not entirely void, it is simple that Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagree in two Baraitas on two issues: voiding makes it void, and whether one can void it not in the presence of the other. Rabbi is lenient in both, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is stringent. Initially, the Talmud wanted to say that the second law does not depend on the first, meaning even Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that if voided it is not void, would agree here that it is not entirely void, and others can write and give it as we explained. But Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel also disagrees here and holds it is entirely void or for another reason, as explained in the Talmud. But this does not relate to the dispute of if voided it is void. All this is according to those who hold that in one case the law is like Rabbi and in one like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. But according to the conclusion of Rav Nachman, who rules the law is like Rabbi in both cases, all these reasons are unnecessary. The simple reason is that if voided it is void, like the first dispute, even though it could lead to problems, as partial voiding voids the entire agency. And indeed, they punish him as explained. But the law remains that it is a complete voiding of the get. Therefore, the Rambam specifically mentioned this law, even in front of two others, to teach us that it is not a separate dispute but the same as the previous one. Do not question why the Rambam needed to write this law at all since he already wrote that if voided it is void. One can say that he needed to write this law for two reasons: first, to teach us that the entire agency is void, so we do not mistakenly think the reason is as initially thought. Second, because there is another establishment that anything done in the presence of ten needs ten to

We have already mentioned what our Sages said in Kiddushin (12b) that Rav would flog one who nullifies a get and one who declares a protest against a get. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 67: "One who sends a get to his wife and then nullifies it in front of two others, and similarly one who declares a protest against the get, is flogged with disciplinary lashes because he causes the creation of mamzerim," end quote. And we have already written that Rashi of blessed memory explained this also applies to one who nullifies in front of the messenger, but the Rambam and Tosafot do not hold this view, as we have written. However, it is certain that even according to them, one should initially avoid nullifying a get in any manner, for it is not reasonable to create a distant dispute where according to Rashi, one would be flogged, and according to them, one could initially do so. Rather, it is certain that they also agree that one should not initially nullify, as we have written.

Therefore, the common custom is that when a person sends a get (divorce document) through an agent, they make the husband swear that he will not issue a protest or nullify the get. This is explained in the order of the get in Siman 154, Section 26, see there. Concerning a wicked person who has repented, some say he cannot appoint an agent to deliver the get to his wife because we are concerned he might nullify it. Even if he accepts upon himself with an oath and prohibition not to nullify it, it does not help, as we are concerned he might violate his oath. Some say that the early authorities found a solution for this by initially making the agent an agent for receiving, who says to him, "Acquire this get for my wife, so-and-so, daughter of so-and-so, and with it, she will be divorced and permitted to any man." This is because it is certainly a merit for her, as it is written in Siman 140, see there. Afterward, he takes back the get from the agent and makes him an agent for delivery, saying, "Deliver this get to my wife," etc. This is the custom. Therefore, even if he might nullify the get, we rely on what was previously an agent for receiving, as mentioned there. However, caution must be taken not to initially make him an agent for delivery and afterward an agent for receiving, because the agency for receiving nullifies the agency for delivery, as we explained there with the help of Heaven.

The halachic ruling in the Gemara (34a) follows Abaye, who states that an indication of intent regarding a get (Jewish bill of divorce) is not significant. The explanation is that when a get or its agency is annulled, it is annulled through an explicit verbal declaration. However, if the annulment is not explicitly verbalized, even if the intent to annul is clear, it is ineffective. For example, if the agent informs the husband that he has not yet delivered the get, and the husband responds, "Blessed is the good and beneficent," indicating his gratitude that the get was not delivered, it is clear that he wishes to retract the divorce. Nevertheless, the agent can still deliver the get, as an indication of intent is insignificant.

Moreover, even if the husband ran after the agent and it was clear that his running was to annul the get, but he did not reach the agent before the get was delivered, the get is not annulled and is valid, allowing the wife to remarry. Similarly, if the husband sent another agent to annul the get by intercepting the first agent, but the first agent delivered the get before being intercepted, the get is valid (as explained by the Beit Shmuel, section 197).

This specifically applies when the husband instructs an agent to annul the get but does not annul it himself in the presence of witnesses. If he annulled it himself, it has already been established that the annulment is effective even without the presence of the agent. Additionally, if the husband tells the agent to return the get and he will provide another one, it is merely an indication of intent and does not annul the get. If the agent delivers the get, it is valid. However, if the husband explicitly tells the agent not to deliver the get, or writes to him not to deliver it, this constitutes a valid annulment. For the purpose of annulment, writing is considered equivalent to speaking.

Do not be astonished by this ruling and do not find it difficult, for even in monetary matters we follow a clear presumption, as it is stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 246, and all the more so in matters of prohibition. However, we have already explained in Siman 42, Section 8, that in matters of divorce and marriage we do not follow even a clear presumption, because in monetary matters witnesses were not created except for falsehoods, and it is dependent on the agreement of the heart to buy, sell, and give. But in divorce and marriage, which are not valid between a man and his wife except by the testimony of two witnesses, the matter is established only by what the witnesses heard from his mouth, and we do not follow the thoughts in his heart. However, we have already written there in Section 13 that it seems to me there is a dispute among the early authorities on this reasoning, see there. Additionally, there is another reason according to what the Tosafot wrote (at the beginning of Chapter 4) that thoughts in the heart are not considered significant matters even where it is known to us that he was coerced into not revealing his thoughts, and thoughts in the heart do not become significant matters except where we can understand his intention by ourselves without him revealing it explicitly. Therefore, revealing intention in a get (divorce document) is not significant, for we do not know his intention by ourselves that he desires and needs its nullification, for he himself commanded to write and give it. (And it is also possible that they wrote this only according to Rava, as is evident from the beginning of their words, but it also fits according to Abaye, as is evident from their language that they spoke according to the law, see there.)

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in section 62: If a man sends a divorce (get) to his wife and tells the messenger, "If the woman desires to come to me, I will accept her, and if not, release her with the get," and then the husband leaves that city, and afterwards the woman comes with the messenger to that city, the messenger can give the get. This is because the woman did not come to the husband, as he left the city before she arrived. Even if the husband were in the city, if he cannot reconcile with her, the messenger can give the get. The initial statement, "If she comes to me, I will accept her," is considered just words and does not constitute a binding condition; it is merely an expression of intent, which is inconsequential. This ruling is derived from the responsa of the Rosh, as brought by the Tur, who ruled accordingly in practice. This situation is considered only an expression of intent since he did not say, "If she comes, the get is void." This applies specifically when, initially, he sent the messenger simply to give her the get, and later told the messenger, "If she desires to come here, I will accept her." In such a case, it is merely an expression of intent. However, if at the time he appointed the messenger or within 24 hours of the appointment, he said, "If she desires, etc.," then it is not merely an expression of intent, and the agency is established on that condition. Therefore, if he is in the city and she comes and he cannot reconcile with her, he cannot give her the get (according to Taz and Beit Shmuel, section 198). Furthermore, we learn from their words that when the husband makes a condition that she should come to him, and he was in one place at that time and subsequently moved to another place, she needs to come to the new place where he currently is. It is not sufficient for her to come to the place where he was when he made the condition, because he did not say she should come "here," but rather "to him," meaning to wherever he may be.

There is a difference in the language of nullification; in some cases, it is effective, and in others, it is not. The general principles are that the language of nullification must indicate future action and that it should imply that he is nullifying it, not that it is inherently invalid (Beit Yosef). For how could it be invalid when there is nothing inherently invalid about it, and it is merely a fabricated claim? Therefore, the Sages said (32b): if he said, "This get (divorce document) will not be effective, will not permit, will not release, will not send, will not divorce, it shall be clay, it shall be like clay," his words stand, for this is a language indicating future action. But if he said, "This get is not effective, does not permit, does not release, does not send, does not divorce, it is clay, it is like clay," he has said nothing, for this is the language of the past. Similarly, if he said, "This get is invalid," he has said nothing, for it does not imply that he is nullifying it but merely that he is declaring it invalid, which it is not (Rashi). Similarly, if he said, "It is not a get," he has said nothing for the same reason. However, if he said, "This get is null" or "I do not want it," this is a nullification, for "I do not want it" implies that he desires it to be nullified. Similarly, "it is null" implies future action, and although it also has a past connotation, it primarily implies future action, and we presume his intention is for the future to achieve his purpose (Gemara). If he said, "This get is null" without adding "it is," or if he said, "This get is null," pronouncing "null" with a patach (a vowel indicating past tense) instead of a tzeirei (a vowel indicating future tense), it is a doubt, and we err on the side of stringency.

The Tur writes in the name of the Ra'avan: "If one says, 'It shall be invalid,' it is nullified even though he cannot invalidate the body of the get (divorce document), because when he says 'it shall be,' it is a future-oriented language. This means it shall be invalid for use in divorce, similar to someone saying 'it shall be like a shard.' Even though we see that it is not a shard, we say it shall be like a shard regarding divorce. Similarly, when he says 'it shall be invalid,' he means it shall be invalid for divorce." And so too writes Rabbi Meir Cohen: "When he says 'it is invalid,' it is effective, similar to saying 'it is like a shard.'" The Tur writes that this is not comparable, because saying 'it shall be a shard' or 'it is like a shard' is a term that cannot apply to the get at all. Therefore, we must interpret his words to mean it shall be like a shard in the sense that it cannot be used for divorce. And since his words imply a future meaning, they are effective. But if he says 'it shall be invalid' or 'it is invalid,' since this term can apply to the get, meaning it shall be invalid, and this is not invalid because he cannot invalidate it from now, therefore it is nothing. These are the words of the Tur. And some say that according to the Tur, it is also a doubt (Bach and Beit Shmuel, section 161). And even though this is not implied from his language, nevertheless, in practical halacha, it is certainly a doubt since there is a dispute about this, and we follow the stringent opinion.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 64: "If one says 'You shall not go out permanently,' it is null and void, and it is as if he said 'Today you are not my wife, and tomorrow you are my wife.'" This is perplexing, for in the case of "Today you are not my wife, and tomorrow you are my wife," according to the Rosh, she is divorced, and we hold that it is a questionable divorce as stated in section 137. It is only according to the Rambam that she is not divorced, as stated there. So how could he write that in this case it is a null divorce? Since he compares it to the case of "today," he should have ruled it as a questionable divorce. Indeed, in the source of this law in the responsa of the Ran (cited in the Beit Yosef), it implies that he ruled it as questionable because only according to the Rambam is she not divorced. The Ran's own opinion in this case of "today" is that it is questionable as stated in chapter 9 of Gittin. It is possible to say that his opinion is that even though when one says "Today you are not my wife," etc., we hold it as questionable, but when he says before giving the get that "this get shall not be permanent," it is worse because he has essentially reserved something in the get itself, which is no worse than nullifying it. Nevertheless, in practical law, it seems to me that it is questionable. Perhaps there was a printing error, and it should read "If one says 'You shall not go out permanently,' it is questionable," as it should be. Also, it seems to me that the phrase "it is null and void" is not appropriate at all.

And regarding these expressions that do not serve to invalidate the get (divorce document), the Tur and Shulchan Aruch write in section 65 that if he did not initially reveal his intent to invalidate it and said expressions that do not serve to invalidate the get, nevertheless, it is an objection to its validity, and it needs to be validated by its witnesses. So too wrote Rashi there and the Ra'avad in the Tur. The Tur concluded that certainly if he initially revealed his intent to invalidate it and said one of these expressions, they are nothing since they are not expressions of invalidation. However, if he did not initially reveal his intent to invalidate it and said one of these expressions, since we can interpret his words as an objection to it, if it is not validated by its witnesses, he is believed. And if the messenger subsequently gave it to the woman, it is nothing. But if it is validated by its witnesses, it is valid. This is the end of his words. Some have asked regarding expressions in the past tense that do not serve to invalidate, why he should not be believed with a migo (a type of legal presumption) that if he wanted, he could invalidate it now, as this reasoning was stated in section 150. In truth, it is not analogous, for there he says that he has already invalidated it, and he is rightly believed with a migo. But here, he is not saying that he invalidated it previously; rather, he is invalidating it now in the past tense, thinking it is effective. What relevance does migo have to this (so it seems to me, and see Beit Shmuel section 179)?

And know that all these expressions that are effective for nullification and those that are not effective have been explained according to the words of the Talmud and the decisors when he nullified in Hebrew or Aramaic, as they spoke in the time of the sages of the Talmud. Regarding our foreign languages, one must understand the matter by translating from Hebrew or Aramaic into the foreign language. However, the general principle is the same: the past tense is not effective unless he says that he has already nullified it, in which case he is believed before giving it to the woman or to her agent to receive it, due to the principle of "migo". Nonetheless, in this case, we are stringent. If the nullification is in the future tense or present tense, the nullification is effective. It is impossible to detail everything in writing according to our foreign languages, and it is up to the court to understand the matter and the language, each case according to its circumstances.

Any agent who brings a get (divorce document) is not suspected that the husband may have canceled it or given a protest. Similarly, there is no concern that the husband might have died, leaving the woman bound to yibbum (levirate marriage) if he has no children. Even if the husband was left elderly or ill, we rely on the previous presumption (chazakah). In the case of illness, this is not against the majority since, on the contrary, most sick people recover. However, if the husband was left in a dying state (goses), the get should not be given to her because most people in this state die. Even if he is alive, if he is not of sound mind at the time of giving the get, it should not be given to her, as stated in Siman 121. If it was given to her, it is a doubtful divorce (safek megureshet). Additionally, some say this applies specifically to illness by divine cause, but if it is by human cause, such as being beaten to the point of becoming a treifah (mortally wounded), his status is like that of a goses. It seems to me that all this applies when no information has come that he canceled it, gave a protest, or died. But if some information has come, even if not confirmed by witnesses, the get should not be given until the matter is clarified. However, according to our custom where protests are canceled and witnesses disqualified as stated in Siman 134, there might be no concern for a protest. Nevertheless, for cancellation, there is concern, even if he swore not to cancel it, perhaps he violated his oath.

This that we have written, that if an elder is left (a Get), we do not worry about death, this is an explicit Mishnah (28a). And it was stated on this in the Gemara: Rabba said, they only taught this with an elder who has not reached the age of strength, which is eighty years old, but if he has reached the age of strength, we worry about death. And this is a stringency that they were stringent with Gittin because of the severity of (the prohibition of) a married woman. But in other matters, such as one who sends his sin-offering from overseas, even if he has reached the age of strength, we do not worry about death (Tosafot Yoma 55b s.v. "veHatnan" see there). And Abaye raised a difficulty from a Baraita that even a hundred-year-old is given in the presumption that he is alive, and it concludes in a refutation, and the law is not according to Rabba. And similarly, the words of the Rif and the Rambam, of blessed memory, lean this way, as they did not bring Rabba’s ruling. And so ruled the Rashba and the Rosh. And it similarly implies in the Jerusalem Talmud. However, in the Gemara there is another resolution: since it is a division, it is a division, meaning from eighty to one hundred we worry about death, and from one hundred, since it is a division, it is a division, and we do not worry about death. And so ruled the Tur in the name of the Ramah. And so ruled the Raaviah (Beit Yosef). Therefore, in practice, one should be stringent. And also our teacher the Beit Yosef in section 68 brought this opinion in the name of "there are those who say" see there. However, Rashi, of blessed memory, explained that specifically up to ninety years one should worry about death and no more. And it seems he was compelled to this from the language of the Baraita "even up to one hundred years," and it implies that certainly before this. Therefore, he explained that from ninety to one hundred one does not worry about death either. And it could be said that the reason is that since it is written "and if by strength, eighty years," it implies that beyond this is not common. And up to ninety is all included in eighty, but from ninety and onwards is not common at all. Consequently, since it is a division, it is a division. And according to this, for Rashi, from ninety even Rabba agrees. Nevertheless, in practice, one should be stringent according to the Ramah and Raaviah, of blessed memory. (And so it is implied from the Shulchan Aruch that did not mention Rashi’s words).

A city that is surrounded by a military force from the same kingdom and is under siege, or a ship that is being battered in the sea and is on the verge of sinking but has not yet sunk, and it is unknown what has happened to it, and one who goes out to be judged in capital cases—these are presumed to be alive. If they are Kohanim, their wives may eat Terumah. If a get (divorce document) of one of them is in the hands of a messenger, he should deliver it on the presumption that the husband is alive, and she will be presumed divorced. However, if the city has already been conquered, or if it is surrounded by a military force from a different kingdom that does not have mercy on the city's inhabitants, or if a ship has been lost at sea, or if one goes out to be executed by the laws of the nations, or if someone is dragged by a wild animal, swept away by a river, or a building collapses on them, we apply the stringencies of both life and death. A Kohen’s daughter married to an Israelite, or an Israelite's daughter married to a Kohen, shall not eat Terumah. If a get of one of them is in the hands of a messenger, he should not deliver it to his wife; if he does, she is in doubt whether she is divorced. If it is known that the husband died before the get reached her, it is not a valid get, as there is no get after death.

Regarding one who goes out to be executed by the laws of the nations, the Rambam in Chapter 6 writes that in Jewish law (during the time of the Temple), he is considered certainly dead (according to the second interpretation in Gemara 28b). The Rosh and the Tur rule the opposite—that in Jewish law, we apply the stringencies of both life and death. In the laws of the nations, if the final ruling of the supreme judge is signed, he is considered certainly dead (according to the first interpretation there). The Rashba ruled stringently in both cases, and so did the Tur in the name of the Ramah. The statement we made about a siege by a different kingdom, where we apply the stringencies of both life and death, is from the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 3, Halacha 4). The Rashba interprets the Jerusalem Talmud differently, saying it refers to a city that has already been conquered, where we apply the stringencies of both life and death. The Jerusalem Talmud says that this is true within the same kingdom, but with a different kingdom that the first kingdom fears, even in such a case they are presumed to be alive. These things are not common in our times, and circumstances have changed so that even during conquest, the inhabitants are protected from harm. The kings of our times are merciful. Someone standing in the line of battle is certainly considered under the stringencies of both life and death, and everything depends on the situation. Not all wars are the same, and not all places are the same. The court must understand the situation, and if they cannot determine it, they should rule stringently.

**Laws of Stating "In My Presence It Was Written and In My Presence It Was Signed." There are 68 sections:**

The sages taught in the Mishnah at the beginning of Gittin: One who brings a get (divorce document) from overseas must state, "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed." "Overseas" refers to outside the land of Israel (Rashi), as the Mishnah was taught in the land of Israel. Why was this required? The Gemara establishes that it is because witnesses are not readily available to verify the signatures on the get. If the husband comes and claims that the get is forged, the necessary witnesses for verification may not be available, and the woman would remain an agunah (a woman who is unable to remarry). Therefore, the sages instituted that the messenger must say, "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," and the sages made this statement as a form of verification so that the husband would not later be believed if he claimed it was forged. The sages trusted the messenger as if he were two witnesses and strengthened this decree, making the get invalid if the messenger did not say "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," as will be explained further. If they did not strengthen this decree, it would not be upheld, and many women would remain agunot due to the lack of verification. Therefore, the sages were compelled to reinforce this decree. However, in the land of Israel, where witnesses are readily available for verification, this statement is not required. Regardless, if the messenger in the land of Israel also says "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," it is effective just as it is overseas, as will be explained.

And one should not question that if we come to be concerned about the husband's challenge, then what have they achieved with their ordinance, since the statement of the agent is valid only if the husband challenges by saying it is forged. The sages trusted him like two witnesses when he says that the scribe wrote it and the witnesses signed it in his presence, and it is not forged. But what can we do if the husband claims that it is true the witnesses signed, but he intentionally had invalid witnesses, such as relatives or other invalids, sign it to disqualify her? This was asked in the Jerusalem Talmud (beginning of the tractate, see there). And they said there that he is not suspected of causing harm under Heaven, but only in court he is suspected of causing harm. And since he knows that if he comes and challenges, his challenge will be null, he will also have valid witnesses sign. This means that no Jewish person is suspected of causing her to fall into a situation of being a mamzer under Heaven, but only of causing her distress in court by saying it is forged, because he knows she will not find validation. The claim of forgery must be accepted from him since it applies to all documents. If we do not accept the claim of forgery, the world will be filled with forgeries. Therefore, when they enacted that the agent's statement is in place of validation and it is known that his claim of forgery will not be accepted, he will not come and challenge, causing harm under Heaven, as he is not trusted to cause harm under Heaven. And we are witnesses that if it is not forged and he had the witnesses sign, he had valid witnesses sign (as explained in the Jerusalem Talmud).

And also, one should not ask: if the reason is for verification, why is it necessary to say "it was written in my presence"? After all, the verification of the document is only through its signatories, as with all document verifications, which testify only to the signatures of the witnesses. This is addressed in the Gemara at the beginning of Gittin, because this verification is different from other document verifications. In all verifications, two witnesses are required, but in the case of a get (divorce document), the sages trusted the messenger as though he were two witnesses. Therefore, they instituted that he should also say "it was written in my presence" as a recognition so that people would not come to confuse this with the verification of ordinary documents, thinking that the verification of a document is sufficient with one witness. And why indeed did the sages trust the messenger alone as two witnesses? Because of the ordinance regarding agunot (women who cannot remarry because their husbands are missing or refuse to grant a divorce), so that she would not have to trouble herself with the verification of two witnesses.

And if one asks, with what authority did the Sages believe a messenger as if he were two witnesses? Thus, our Sages stated there that from the Torah, there is no need for validation at all, for witnesses signed on a document are considered as if their testimony had been investigated in court, since Israelites are not suspected of forging documents. And it is the Rabbis who required validation for all documents, and therefore, they said that validation is necessary. They also said that the messenger is believed in this matter as two witnesses because in their enactment, they could establish that he would be believed as two witnesses. And why did they enact this? Because of the ordinance concerning agunot, as it is written. And we have already explained this matter in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 29, see there. Therefore, there is no need to ask why one witness can release a woman from the presumption of being married, for once the get (divorce document) is in her hand, signed by witnesses, she is released from the presumption of being married based on the witnesses signed on it, since from the Torah, it is as if their testimony was investigated in court. Consequently, since there is no presumption of prohibition on her, one witness is believed, as it is written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 127. However, due to the matter of validating documents, two witnesses were required, and the Rabbis enacted that for the purpose of validation, one is sufficient, just as one is sufficient for the essence of the prohibition.

And since the reason is due to verification, as witnesses are not commonly available to verify it, therefore whether one brings a get (divorce document) from outside the Land of Israel (Chutz La'aretz) to the Land of Israel or from the Land of Israel to outside the Land of Israel or from one country to another outside the Land of Israel where caravans are not common, one must say "It was written and signed in my presence." However, within the Land of Israel, from one province to another, it is not necessary to say this, and the reason is that there caravans are common. In the time of the Temple, caravans of pilgrims were common, and even after the destruction, since there are fixed courts in the cities as per Ezra's decree that they sit on Mondays and Thursdays to judge (beginning of Ketubot), caravans are common traveling to the places of the courts to adjudicate with one another (3:). Similarly, within the same province outside the Land of Israel, it is not necessary to say this, as caravans traveling from place to place are common (Hagahot Maimoniot, Chapter 7). The rivers in the Land of Israel and the islands in the great sea of the Land of Israel, which is not the Atlantic Ocean but what is called the Middle Sea that extends from Jaffa to Spain, and all the islands in this sea that belong to the Land of Israel are considered like the Land of Israel regarding the requirement to say "It was written and signed in my presence" (8:). This was also explained by Rambam in the first chapter of Terumot. Similarly, Babylonia is considered like the Land of Israel concerning gittin because there are many yeshivot there, and caravans travel between them frequently, making it easy to verify. From Babylonia to the Land of Israel or from the Land of Israel to Babylonia, it is not necessary to say this for the reason explained, and this pertains to the situation in the time of the Talmud (6a).

All of this is according to the Talmudic law, and so wrote the Rambam in Chapter 7. But nowadays, even in the Land of Israel, caravans are not frequent, and certainly not in Babylonia. Even in the Land of Israel, from province to province, the law requires the declaration "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" (בפ"נ ובפ"נ). So wrote our teacher, the Beit Yosef, at the end of Section 1, and furthermore, nowadays, in all places, even within the same province, from place to place, and even within one city, from neighborhood to neighborhood, and from house to house, the messenger must say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed." The reason is that we find in the Talmud that Rava required in his city of Mechoza the declaration "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" from house to house. He explained the reason because the people of Mechoza were busy with commerce and did not stay long in their homes and did not recognize each other's signatures. This is called "not commonly found to verify it." The Tosafot wrote there that from here Rabbeinu Tam rules that nowadays, in all places, the declaration "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" is required, because nowadays in all places people are busy and distracted like the people of Mechoza. This is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 1: "And nowadays, the one who brings a get (divorce document), even from house to house in one city, must say 'in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed.'" Refer above to Section 141, where it says not to deliver it when the husband is in the city, and the reason is that the husband can claim it was given as a deposit. We have already explained there in Section 35 that for us, who write an authorization, there is no concern about this.

And it turns out that among us, there is no situation where one does not need to say "in front of me it was written and in front of me it was signed." However, when the get (divorce document) is validated according to law in a Beit Din (Rabbinical Court), certainly there is no need to say "in front of me" because the declaration serves in place of validation and it has already been validated. Accordingly, some say that when the agent has an authorization and it specifies who the witnesses of the get are, this is considered as if it has been validated by its signatories, and therefore the agent does not need to say "in front of me." So wrote the Rashba in his responsa and the Mordechai (end of Chapter 6). Rav Rema wrote that there are those who disagree and say that authorization is not considered validation, and the custom is that the agent says "in front of me it was written and in front of me it was signed" even when he has authorization, and this should not be changed. The later authorities wrote that the dissenting opinion is merely a stringency (Beit Shmuel, Siman 141, subparagraph 44, and so wrote the Noda B'Yehuda, Siman 128, brought in Pitchei Teshuvah, subparagraph 5).

However, in my humble opinion, it appears that our master the Rema and the prominent later authorities have abbreviated this matter, and there is no disagreement at all. They hold that the reason for the permissibility is because they maintain that when there are two witnesses signed on the authorization and they testify about the witnesses of the get (divorce document), it is as if two people brought the get, and there is no need to say "in front of me it was written and in front of me it was signed," as will be explained. Those who dispute this, such as the Rivash in Siman 318, indeed disagree. He states that this is neither a validation of the get nor a rabbinic enactment, as mentioned there. This is also the opinion of the Ramah in the Tur, although he holds that it is as if two people brought the get. Nonetheless, this only applies when the agent delivers the get to the woman in the presence of these witnesses, so that it is a complete matter—they testify about the delivery of the get to the agent and the delivery by the agent to the woman. But if there are other witnesses for the agent's delivery to the woman, it is a partial matter.

In the Shulchan Aruch itself, this is ruled in Siman 12, and it will be explained further. Therefore, I say that neither the Rashba nor the Mordechai, who also validate, disagree about this. The Rashba writes in his responsa, Siman 561, that anyone who brings a get, even if it is not validated, is believed to say "in front of me it was written and in front of me it was signed," and there is no need for witnesses that the husband appointed him as an agent; rather, anyone who brings a get suffices with this. One can understand that if witnesses were required, it would not be necessary to say "in front of me it was written and in front of me it was signed," for if there are witnesses, it is as if it was brought by two people, etc.

It can be said that his intention is when the witnesses are present, as per the opinion of the Ramah, but with written witnesses it does not help. The Mordechai deals with written witnesses, but they were validated by a court, which is the essence of document validation. This is the standard in all the Talmud. The Rivash would also agree to this, as is explicitly clear from his language that we quoted. This aligns with "it will be validated by its signatories" that we learned in the Mishnah. The Mordechai writes at the beginning of the chapter "HaGet," and further mentions that if you have the signatures of the court and the witnesses, etc., why would it be necessary to say "in front of me it was written and in front of me it was signed," for even if the husband comes and objects, there are the signatures of the witnesses and the court. This is from the responsa of Rabbeinu Tam, as mentioned there. And who would disagree with this?

Therefore, it seems to me that when it is stated that there is a dispute regarding this matter, it does not refer to the validity of a court when there is an authorization, as no legal authority would disagree on this. Rather, they refer to when there are only the signatures of witnesses, as some hold that even this alone is sufficient, similar to two people bringing it. The Rashba explains that even two witnesses in writing are effective. Additionally, the reasoning of the Ra'ah, who is concerned about "half a matter," is not held as the law, but rather as a stringency, as evident from the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Section 17, who wrote at the end of the section: "There are those who require that it be delivered in the presence of the witnessing agents themselves," end quote. This is the opinion of the Ra'ah, and he was only concerned as a stringency. In Section 12, he also considered this opinion, but it is not held as the law, as will be explained with G-d's help.

And based on this, it appears clear to me, in terms of the law, that although the established custom is that even when the messenger brings authorization with witnesses and it is validated by the court, he still says "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," and Heaven forbid to change this practice. Nevertheless, if it happened that he did not say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," there is no concern at all, and the get (divorce document) is valid since it contains the validation of documents. And explicitly, our sages said (Gittin 15b), "either entirely through the validation of the get or entirely through the enactment of the sages," meaning the statement "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed." Since the get is validated, the enactment of the sages is not necessary. And the intent of our master the Rema is only when there is no validation of the court on the authorization, only witnesses alone. But the custom he wrote about is certainly in all cases, even when there is court validation, and it should not be changed. And the primary law is as I have written, especially when the signatures of the judges are not recognized in the place of delivery, it is certainly proper to be stringent if it is not a case where a woman would be left chained (agunah).
