In such cases, one should be lenient as our master the Rema wrote at the end of this section, see there.

And also, as it was explained in section 6, that nowadays in every place, one must say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" (Befanai Nechtav U'Befanai Nechtam) because today everyone is as mobile as the people of Mehoza, it also appears that this is merely a stringency. And you should know that this is indeed the case, since the Rif, the Rosh, and the Rambam in chapter 7 did not mention at all the case of the people of Mehoza who are mobile (see Hilchot Gittin there, notes 1 and 2, and it requires further study. It seems to me as the Rambam wrote in his commentary on the Mishnah, beginning of chapter 4 of Rosh Hashanah, that a medina is a city. Analyze this well). But for another reason, it appears to me that nowadays, by strict law, one must say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" even in the same city, because our writing in documents and letters is in the script of Meshita and not in Ashurit script. In this case, it is relevant that some people recognize the signatures, knowing that this was written by one person and that by another person. But with a get (divorce document), where the custom is that the witnesses sign in Ashurit script, no one recognizes their signatures except for the rabbi in front of whom they sign. How can it be said in this case that the witnesses are available to validate it? Therefore, it appears to me that nowadays, by strict law, one must say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" even in the same city when there is no established authorization, as explained.

And know that there is another explanation in the Gemara, according to the opinion that the ordinance of saying "befanai nechtav u'befanai nechtam" ("It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence") was established for two reasons. The first reason is for validation, as we have stated, and the second reason is because in the Diaspora they are not proficient in the requirement that the get (bill of divorce) must be written for the sake of the husband and the wife, as they are not Torah scholars (Rashi). Therefore, they required the messenger to say "befanai nechtav u'befanai nechtam," and consequently, we ask him if it was written for her sake (there). This is why they did not require him to explicitly say "in my presence it was written for her sake," because they were concerned that if we increased the number of words he must say, he might forget to say "for her sake" and would deviate from the formula established by the Sages for gittin (Gittin 3, Rashi there). Therefore, they only required him to say "befanai nechtav u'befanai nechtam," and the court would ask him if he knew that it was written and signed for her sake. Furthermore, even if they did not ask him if it was written for her sake, we assume that he is testifying that it was written for her sake (Tosafot 2: d.h. lefi). The reason they were more concerned about "for her sake" than other disqualifications has a reason (there). In fact, in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is stated that they were concerned about all disqualifications because they are not proficient in the precise details of gittin. Our Talmud focused on the disqualification of "for her sake" because it is the main and common issue, unlike other types of disqualifications like being written while attached (to the ground) and the like, which are not common. There are further explanations on this (Ran at the beginning of Gittin and Rashba).

And behold, all of our early sages concurred according to the Talmudic discussion that this reasoning was dismissed from the law and the reason is solely for the sake of establishing the matter. However, one of our sages held that the law also follows this reasoning (the Ra'avad in Sefer HaZechut, and it is brought by the Ran and the Rashba), and he has proofs for this which the early sages refuted. Yet, there is one proof from the Gemara (5b): Rabbah bar bar Hana brought a get (divorce document) where half was written before him and half was not written before him. He came before Rabbi Eliezer to ask if he could say "it was written and signed in my presence," and Rabbi Eliezer said to him that even if only one line was written for its sake, it suffices, meaning that even if the agent was present only at the time of writing the first line and heard it being written for its sake, it is no longer necessary to be present, as it is assumed that the rest was completed for its sake (Tosafot). This implies that the reason is because of "for its sake." However, there is no proof from this because this means that if he was present only during the first line, which is the main part that needs to be "for its sake" because it contains the name of the man, the woman, and the date, he can say "it was written in my presence," as if the entire get was written in his presence because this is the essential part of the get that needs to be "for its sake." But the reason is not due to a concern of "for its sake" (Ran). However, this is correct according to the opinion that in the first line is the entire essence of the get and it is necessary to be present (Rashi beginning of chapter 2), but most of the poskim do not hold this way, as will be explained with God's help. And it can be said that on the contrary, this is proof to the opposite if we examine why it is necessary to be present for the entire signing but for the writing, it suffices to be present for the first line, as will be explained. Rather, it is certainly because the main reason is for the sake of confirming the matter, and "it was written in my presence" is so that it should not be confused with the validation of other documents, as explained. Therefore, they were lenient regarding the writing. Nevertheless, how does he say that it was written in his presence when only the first line was written before him? Rather, it is certainly because the declaration of "for its sake" is in the first line when the scribe at the beginning of the writing says, "I am writing for the sake of so-and-so." Therefore, it is considered as if the entire writing was for its sake. According to this, when he says one line for its sake, it is not because of a concern of "for its sake," but rather he is stating the reason why one line suffices, because it is for its sake, meaning the first line, which is written for its sake (as it seems to me).

According to this, what is explained in the arrangements of Gittin (divorce documents) that the emissary must hear how the scribe writes it for the purpose (of the specific woman) and that the witnesses sign it for the purpose, and that when bringing the get (divorce document) to the woman, the court asks him if it was written and signed for the purpose, as it is written in Siman 154, this is merely a stringency to fulfill this opinion that holds that the ordinance was also for the purpose. However, according to most authorities, there is no need to ask the emissary at all about the purpose, and consequently, the emissary also does not need to be concerned that perhaps it was not written or signed for the purpose. And so the sages said at the beginning of Gittin that generally the scribes of the judges are learned and know that it needs to be for the purpose. And only according to the one who holds that the ordinance was for the purpose do they worry about this. But since we hold that the reason is for validation, we are not concerned at all about the issue of the purpose, as everyone is proficient that it needs to be for the purpose.

It is specifically the messenger for delivery who must say "It was written and signed in my presence" (Rashi), but a messenger for receipt does not need to. The reason is that since the concern is that the husband may come and contest (the validity of the get), there is no need to worry about his contesting unless it is given to a messenger for delivery. This is because at the time the get leaves his hand, he has not yet completed the divorce, so we are concerned that he might reconsider and contest. However, when he gives it to her or her agent for receipt, at the time the get leaves his hand, he completes the divorce, and there is no concern that he might come and contest. The woman is permitted to remarry even though the get was not verified, because whenever there is no concern of the husband's contesting, there is no need for the get to be verified. However, if the husband comes and contests, it should be validated by its signatures, and this is similar to what we learned in the Mishnah that one who brings a get within the land of Israel does not need to say "It was written and signed in my presence," and if there are objections, it should be validated by its signatures (Ran).

And since the messenger must say "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," therefore, he must stand by during the scribe's writing and the witnesses' signing, and see how they write and sign it for his [the husband’s] sake, for her [the wife’s] sake, and for the sake of divorce. Afterwards, when he delivers it to the woman, he says in the presence of two [witnesses], "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," and immediately upon his saying this, he delivers the get [bill of divorce] to her in their presence, and she is thereby divorced. His statement is like the validation of a court regarding all documents, such that if the husband comes and claims it is a forgery, we do not pay attention to him. And although the witnesses of the get are not known to us, nevertheless, we rely on the messenger as we would on two witnesses who testify to the validity of the signing witnesses. Know that what we have written, that the delivery must be in the presence of two, is because the messenger joins to make a third, as a court is required. If the messenger is a relative or a woman, he must give it in the presence of three. Further details on this will be explained with God's help.

And the Rambam wrote there in Law 5: A messenger who brings a get (divorce document) from one place to another in the Diaspora, or from the Land of Israel to the Diaspora, or from the Diaspora to the Land of Israel, if the messenger was present at the time of the writing and signing of the get, he must declare before two [witnesses], "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," and afterwards he should give it to her in their presence, and she will be divorced by it. Even if the witnesses are not known to us, and even if the names of the witnesses are like the names of non-Jews, we do not concern ourselves with them. And if the husband comes and stands and disputes it, we do not pay attention to him. These are the words of the Rambam, and similarly is written in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 1. 

However, this is surprising in what is said that if the names are like the names of non-Jews, we do not concern ourselves with them. For in the Gemara (Gittin 11b), it is explicitly explained that this is only regarding gittin that come from the Diaspora, because most Jews in the Diaspora have names like those of non-Jews, and we do not concern ourselves that they might be non-Jews. But not in the Land of Israel. And if so, how did the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch, which are also discussing gittin that come from the Land of Israel, write that we do not concern ourselves with this? (And similarly, the Lechem Mishneh raised this question, and his answer is forced, see there.) 

On the other hand, it is difficult, for the messenger, when he says "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," the Rabbis trusted him as if there were two [witnesses]. And if so, it is as if two witnesses testified about the witnesses of the get that they are valid. Therefore, it seems clear to me that the Rambam explains the sugya (Talmudic discussion) as referring to when there is no declaration "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," such as when the messenger was not present at the time of writing and signing. But when he says "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," there is no concern. And for this reason, he carefully wrote "he must declare," etc., and even if, etc., meaning that in such a case, we do not worry about invalid witnesses. (And one should not question that the Talmud says gittin that come from Medinat HaYam (overseas), and it must be said "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," for it can be said that it refers to a woman who comes with her get or a messenger of acceptance who does not need to say "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," as explained.)

There are those who say that the credibility of the messenger is only when the husband disputes the validity after some time has passed, but not when he disputes it immediately at the time of the messenger's declaration of "It was written and signed in my presence" (Beit Shmuel, subsection 2). The reason is that the credibility of the messenger is because, according to Torah law, it is as if the testimony has been investigated in a court, as we have mentioned. And there are some poskim (decisors of Jewish law) who hold that this is only when there is no dispute, but when there is a dispute, it requires validation according to Torah law. We have already mentioned this reasoning in Choshen Mishpat, beginning of Siman 46. Therefore, if at the time of giving the get (divorce document) there was no dispute and the messenger has already said "It was written and signed in my presence," she is presumed to be single, and the husband is not believed in his dispute until two witnesses come. But if the husband disputes it at the time of the act, and Torah law requires validation, then the messenger's declaration is not credible until two validating witnesses come (there). However, this situation is almost non-existent, because if the husband comes a moment before the delivery of the get, there is no need for a dispute since he can annul it himself. And perhaps the language of the dispute includes elements similar to annulment. And if he comes after the delivery, the messenger has already said "It was written and signed in my presence," and the declaration is close to the delivery, as we have explained, and she is presumed to be single. What difference does it make between a short time and several days? And if we say he came within the duration of speech, it is established in Gittin and Kiddushin that it is as if it is after the duration of speech, as we mentioned in the previous siman. It can only be said if he did not say "It was written and signed in my presence" at the time of the delivery, and he needs to take it from her and say "It was written and signed in my presence," as will be explained. And in the meantime, the husband comes and disputes (Atzei Gittin). According to Rambam's opinion in chapter 3 of Testimonies, that all documents are rabbinic, how can we say that according to Torah law it is as if the testimony has been investigated in a court, while according to him, there is no testimony at all by Torah law in a document? But we have already explained in Choshen Mishpat, beginning of Siman 29, that this applies only to evidentiary documents, but in acquisition documents, and in Gittin and Kiddushin, Rambam agrees that by Torah law there is testimony in a document. See there.

It is clear that when the agent states "before us" and "before us," she can collect her ketubah even from purchasers. And even though in a situation where there is no need to say "before us," she does not collect from purchasers because the husband can contest, and she cannot collect from purchasers until there is proper verification according to the law. She can only collect from unsold properties due to the condition of the ketubah that states, "when you marry another, you will take what is written for you." However, from purchasers, she does not collect. Nevertheless, when the agent says "before us," she can collect even from purchasers because the husband will not be able to contest afterward. However, this applies only to the basic ketubah, which is a Torah obligation. The additional amount of the ketubah cannot be collected from purchasers because the addition is not part of the ketubah's condition. It is possible that even from the husband himself, she cannot collect the addition if he contests until witnesses come to verify it, as with all documents. The agent's credibility may only apply to the basic ketubah and not to the additional amount (Hilchot Ishut 7:7 in the name of the Ramban, as well as the Ran and Avnei Shoham, section 2). However, when there is an authenticated authorization, it seems that she can collect everything, even from purchasers, because this is a complete verification (ibid.).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 3 that just as there is no need to validate the get (divorce document) when one says "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," there is similarly no need to validate the witnesses of the agency. Rather, he is believed to say that the husband appointed him as an agent with witnesses, even if the signatures of the witnesses of the agency are not recognizable, or even if he has no witnesses at all regarding the agency. As long as he says the husband appointed him properly as an agent, he is believed.

His words mean that just as the sages believed him to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," they also believed him to say that the husband appointed him as an agent, since the get is in his possession and it is not possible to contradict him. This also seems logical to me, for if he were not believed to say that he is the husband’s agent, it would result that the agent would need to validate his agency documentation. If so, why did the sages, to prevent a situation of chained women (agunot), believe the agent regarding the validation of the get? Just as the agent would validate his agency documentation, he would validate the signatures of the get. But certainly, because witnesses are not readily available, the sages believed him regarding everything (Rosh).

And know that all this is only necessary if we say that an agent for delivery does not have the status of a trustee, and only an agent for receiving has the status of a trustee (Beit Shmuel, Section 141, Paragraph 80). However, according to what we established in the previous section, that there is no distinction, and in all types of agency he is believed because a trustee is believed, as our master the Rema wrote there in Section 55, it is clear that the agent is believed as a trustee. Even if the get is now in the woman’s hands, he is also believed, as stated in the Rambam, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch there in Section 56 (refer to what the Beit Shmuel wrote in Paragraph 7, and this requires further study. But in my humble opinion, the matter is clear as I have written, and examine it well).

In a situation where the agent must say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" (בפ"נ ובפ"נ), even one of the five women who are not trusted to say her husband died and to bring her divorce document (get) can serve as an agent because we suspect their intention is to mislead. However, when it is necessary to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," she can be an agent. The reasoning for this we explained in the previous section, paragraph 137. And in a place where it is not necessary to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," if the agent says it, it is effective in that the husband cannot later contest it. We do not say that since in this place the sages did not institute that it must be said, his statement is ineffective and requires validation like all other documents. We do not say this because since the sages instituted that the agent is trusted as two witnesses with his statement, there is no reason to differentiate in trustworthiness between different places. This is when the agent was present at the writing and signing. But if he was not present, he cannot say it. In a place where it is not necessary to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," he gives it to her as such, and if the husband contests, it is validated by its signatories. The agent can also be one of the three for validating the get. In a place where it must be said "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," he should not give it to her until the get is validated. If he gave it without validation, it is invalid until validated because he cannot say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed." If the husband contests and it cannot be validated, according to the Rambam, in chapter 7, the get is void. If she married, she must leave, and the child is certainly a mamzer (illegitimate). According to the Tur, it is a doubtful mamzer. We have already explained this in section 141, paragraph 136. If the get is lost, she is doubtfully divorced. We have also explained there that it is obvious that the sages trusted the agent's statement "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" to dismiss the husband's contest. But if the husband brings witnesses who testify that the get, which the agent said "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," is forged, the get is void. If she married, she must leave, and the children are mamzerim. If two say it is forged and two say it is not forged, its law is like two who say she was divorced and two who say she was not divorced, and it will be explained in section 152. In this case, the agent is not like a complete validation.

And since the statement of the agent "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" (B'fanai Nechtav U'fanai Nechtam) is considered like a validation, and all validation of documents is done in a court of law which consists of three judges, therefore, when the agent delivers the get (divorce document) to the woman and says "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," he must give it to her in the presence of three judges. However, the sages have said that it is sufficient in the presence of two, as the agent himself is considered as one of the three, since we hold that an agent can act as a witness. Likewise, in rabbinic matters, a witness can act as a judge, as is written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 7, and the validation of documents is rabbinic, as is written. Therefore, the agent joins the court. According to this, if the agent is a woman or a relative or disqualified person who is not fit to serve in court, he must give it to her in the presence of three qualified men. There are those who wish to say that here the sages were lenient, and even if the agent is a relative, he can join the three. This is based on the Ran in the name of some authorities, and therefore they only mentioned a woman. However, this is not the primary view, and it does not seem to be the opinion of our rabbis. (See Tosafot there, s.v. "he teaches," etc., and one of them holds that the same applies to a relative.)

The Tur writes in the name of Rabbeinu Peretz, and similarly Rabbeinu Rema rules in section 4, that one should be stringent even when the messenger is neither a relative nor disqualified, to deliver it to her before three others, and this is the custom. And this stringency has a basis also according to the Talmud (Gittin 5b) where there is an opinion that maintains this due to the concern that if a woman brings a get (bill of divorce), it might be given in the presence of two, and it would not occur to differentiate. And the Talmud rejects this by stating that when a woman brings a get, it is known, and they do not rely on it. And now, due to our many sins, in our times, we all know that those who arrange gittin (divorces) are few who know the laws from the sources in the Talmud and the poskim (decisors), and even the Maharshal in his generation complained about this, and all the more so in our generation. They do not realize that if the messenger is a relative, the law changes, and therefore, Heaven forbid to deviate from this.

It is also written that some are stringent and require two additional witnesses for the delivery of the get (bill of divorce), and these witnesses should not be relatives of the judges, nor of the man or the woman. Additionally, the three judges who are present should not be relatives of the witnesses of the get nor of the messenger. The reasoning behind this is that although the judges themselves can also serve as witnesses since hearing is not greater than seeing, and moreover, in rabbinic matters a witness can become a judge as has been explained, nonetheless, because by custom the get is delivered in front of three judges for the reason that has been explained, it is not apparent at all that they are the witnesses for the delivery. This could lead to a problem in cases where a court is not needed for validation, such as where there is no need to declare ‘in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed’ or where the get is already validated. People may mistakenly think that even two witnesses are not needed for the delivery. Therefore, the custom is that there should always be two witnesses for the delivery, even when there are three judges present. Additionally, these three judges might not be meticulous in observing the actual handing over of the get into her hand, as they consider themselves as a court for validation and focus on hearing the declaration of ‘in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed’ and might not pay attention to the actual delivery. Therefore, we require two other specific witnesses for the delivery, and they will observe the delivery of the get from the messenger into her hand.

Additionally, he wrote that there are those who are stringent and say that the rabbi who takes payment for arranging the giving of the get should not be one of the three sitting as judges; rather, he should seat three others, and the rabbi should ask all the questions and arrange the giving [of the get]. The reason is clear, as we hold that one who takes payment for judging invalidates his judgments. Since his statement is for validation and requires a court, it is considered a judicial act, and it is improper to take payment for this. Therefore, it is better that the arranger who takes payment not be one of the court. This is not comparable to a standard get where we also stringently prefer not to give it at night and to have three [judges], yet he himself wrote in the order of the get that it is simply permitted to take payment. This is because, in that case, it is merely a stringency, and in times of necessity, they give it at night and do not require a court. However, in the case of an agent, according to the Talmudic law, it requires court validation, as mentioned. Furthermore, in that case, the rabbi takes payment for the effort to instruct the scribe and witnesses on how to write and sign, not for the act of giving itself. This differs from the agent who brings a written get before us, where there is only the labor of the giving, and it is not proper to take payment. What surprises me is why our master the Rema did not mention this later in Siman 154 in the order of the get. It seems to me that this is not the practice, perhaps because now there is much labor for the arranger in asking questions to the agent and the woman, in reading the authorization and its details, as will be explained there. Therefore, taking payment could be said to be for the labor, not for the act of giving itself or for the statement "in my presence." This requires further investigation.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch (Section 5) wrote that those who give it in their presence do not need to sit, and when the messenger says "it was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence," he needs to stand. There is an opinion that initially, they should sit when he says "in their presence it was written and in their presence it was signed," and initially, it should be given during the day and not at night. Certainly, it seems that initially, they should sit because this is the correct procedure, as it is written that the judges sit. The first opinion perhaps holds that this is like the conclusion of a judgment and not the beginning of a judgment, and for this reason, it is valid even at night after the fact, as it is written in Choshen Mishpat (Section 5), and therefore, even initially, there is no need to sit. Additionally, since the main law is for the sake of validation, and in the validation itself, we are lenient in several matters, as written in Choshen Mishpat (Section 46). It seems to me that there is no disagreement at all, as the first opinion holds that since the judges are also witnesses and the delivery is more important than the statement "it was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence," therefore it is good to act like witnesses and stand. The "there is an opinion" perhaps holds by the stringency explained in Section 24, where they take two witnesses for the delivery aside from the three, and the three remain as the court alone. Certainly, it is proper that they sit as a court, and so the simple custom among us is that the three sit and the messenger and witnesses stand, and there is no need to change this.

The prominent later authorities have written that a divorced woman needs a document from a Beit Din (rabbinic court) stating that she is divorced, and the rabbi alone is not believed to testify to this by himself, as he is removing her from the presumption of being a married woman. Therefore, she requires an act of the Beit Din, and she can show it wherever she goes to prove that she is divorced (Taz and Shach, subsection 8). This is why it is customary that when a woman receives her get (divorce document) and travels to another place, she receives a document from the Beit Din stating that she is divorced, and this is called a "ptur" (release). And it is clear that this is necessary in a place where she was presumed to be married. However, in a place where she is not presumed to be married, she is believed by herself to say, "I am divorced." But in a place where she is presumed to be married, she cannot be permitted to remarry without a Beit Din of three that are signed on her release. And even though there are those who are lenient to rely on the signature of the rabbi alone, Heaven forbid to rely on this. And even with the signatures of two, whom we can consider as witnesses testifying in writing as explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 28, where there are those who are lenient to accept testimony from writing, nevertheless, it is not to be relied upon in practice in the matter of the prohibition of a married woman. Especially nowadays, when the mail travels all over the world every day, it is possible to verify through the confirmation of a Beit Din of three, and there is absolutely no room to be lenient at all. (And regarding the recognition of the signatures of the Beit Din, one may rely in pressing circumstances on the words of the Rema at the end of this section, see there).

We have already written in section 16 that the messenger says "in my presence it was written, in my presence it was signed" and immediately hands her the get (divorce document). Similarly, Rambam wrote in Chapter 7, Law 5: "He says 'in my presence it was written, in my presence it was signed' and then gives it to her in their presence." This is also the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 1. It is clear that when he says "and then," it means immediately within 24 hours, as it is explicitly proven in the Talmud (Gittin 5:) that it must be specifically at the time of giving. However, the language of the Tur is: "He shall say 'in my presence it was written, in my presence it was signed' at the time he gives it to the woman or immediately within 24 hours." The Beit Yosef copied this language in section 6 (and see the commentary there). It seems to me that it is all the same, and the main point is that if it is possible to synchronize the statement and the giving simultaneously, that is best. This is what the Tur meant by "at the time he gives it." However, not everyone can achieve this synchronization, so at the very least, they should be close to each other, and it does not matter whether the statement comes before or the giving comes before. Therefore, Rambam takes the usual approach where he speaks first and then gives, and the Tur, who wrote "or immediately thereafter," means either before or after. The words of the Shulchan Aruch do not contradict each other. This is what we find in the writings of our teachers, the Tosafists (Gittin 5: s.v. "he shall take it"), and the Rosh there, who are uncertain if the statement made before the giving is effective; their intention is before the time of speech. The doubt is that although it is proven in the Talmud that it must be at the time of giving, perhaps the intention is in the same setting even after 24 hours, or perhaps it must be specifically within 24 hours. The poskim do not disagree on this matter at all (in my opinion), and this is also implied in the Mordechai there.

And one should not question, since the declaration is in place of verification, why indeed did the sages make a stringent ruling in this matter, and verification could take place even after a long period, and even with regard to the get (divorce document) itself, if verification is required it would be valid if verified after a long period. The answer to this is that since the leniency allowing the declaration of the messenger to be considered as two witnesses is due to concerns of "Agunah" (a woman who is unable to remarry because her husband's whereabouts are unknown, or he refuses to grant a divorce), as mentioned, and she becomes free to remarry upon receiving her get, therefore they were stringent in this matter to ensure that the declaration is made immediately upon her receipt of the get, to recognize that it is due to her receipt of the get that they were lenient in considering his declaration as equivalent to two witnesses (this seems correct to me).

Therefore, if he gave her the get (divorce document) and did not manage to say "in front of me it was written and in front of me it was signed" before he became mute, the get is invalid and cannot be rectified until it is verified by its signatories. Even if he can write that "in front of me it was written and in front of me it was signed," it is not effective. Even though generally writing is considered like speaking, in this case the ordinance was specifically that he must speak with his mouth. The reason for this ordinance is that since they were lenient in considering him as two witnesses, they were stringent in other matters. Therefore, if the messenger can speak, his writing does not help, even though regarding testimony there are opinions in Choshen Mishpat, Section 28, that if he is capable of speaking, his writing is effective. Nevertheless, in this case, they were not lenient. This is also clarified from the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book. The leniency regarding testimony about her husband's death in writing, as explained in Section 17, is because it is impossible otherwise since the one testifying in writing will not come here to testify orally. But a messenger delivering a get and standing in the place of the wife, why should he not speak with his mouth? And if the concern is that he might become mute, this is an uncommon occurrence. The leniency in Section 121 regarding a mute person writing "write a get for my wife" according to the Rambam is because it is impossible otherwise and because there it is not testimony but merely revealing his intention and desire to divorce. Even though our master, the Rema, was lenient in Choshen Mishpat, Section 46, Paragraph 7, regarding verification in writing, this is for complete verification and not for the statement "in front of me" that the sages were lenient to consider his statement as two witnesses. Therefore, they were stringent that he must testify specifically with his mouth (see Beit Shmuel, Subsection 11, who wrote that the Rivash in Section 240 contradicts himself to what he wrote in Section 413, but there is no contradiction, as he differentiates between complete verification and a messenger as explained). Know that although one of the early authorities explicitly wrote that it is effective for a mute person to say "in front of me" in writing (Ran, Chapter 1), nevertheless, it does not imply this from most of the early authorities. This is also clearly seen from the words of the Rambam and the Tur, and our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled accordingly (Aruch HaShulchan, Chapter 1, Section 9, and in Tosafot, s.v. "if you say," it is clearly explained that writing is not effective, and so it appears from the Maharsha and the Maharam there).

And this is the language of the Shulchan Aruch, section 7: If one delayed saying it more than twenty-four hours or did not say it in the presence of the woman, or gave it to her privately, even if she is married, it is taken from her and given to her again in front of two witnesses, and he says before them "It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence." If it was not taken from her, it is invalid until it is verified by its signatures. Therefore, a mute person cannot bring a get (divorce document), even though he can write "It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence," because it needs to be said verbally. Some say it needs to be said in the Holy Tongue, meaning "It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence." If he is unlearned, they teach him word for word and inform him of the meaning in the vernacular. However, after the fact, if he said it in the vernacular, it seems to me that it is valid. If the agent did not say "It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence" and the husband died, there is no remedy to take it from her and give it back to her and say "It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence." There is no remedy other than to verify it by its signatures. This is the language of the Shulchan Aruch.

And behold, what they wrote that the declaration is effective even after a period of time is indeed clarified in the Tosefta, Chapter 2, where it states: "One who brings a get (divorce document) from overseas and did not say 'It was written and signed in my presence' (b'fanai nechtav u'b'fanai nechtam), he may accept it from her even after three years, etc." This is further clarified in the Gemara (Gittin 5a): "What should he do? He should take it from her and give it back to her and say 'It was written and signed in my presence.'" This applies even after a long period of time, and consequently, even if she remarried, the get is valid, because this is in place of the validation, and the validation can occur even after a long period of time. However, it is necessary to take it and give it to her, as this was the enactment - that the declaration must be specifically at the time of giving. This is not comparable to a complete validation, as we have explained. Therefore, when the husband dies, there is no remedy, even if she has not remarried, because the declaration must be made at the time of giving, and how can he give it to her when the husband is already dead? It would appear as a get given after death. But when he is alive, even if she remarried, it still pertains to the husband, as the giving of the get to her is still relevant. Therefore, when he dies, there is no remedy except with a complete validation, in which case it is not necessary to take it back from her and give it to her again, as we have stated. Additionally, when the husband dies, the agency is nullified, and he is not believed to say 'It was written and signed in my presence' (b'fanai nechtav u'b'fanai nechtam), as stated in the Beit Yosef in the name of the Rivash.

And that which they wrote, or that he did not say [the declaration of] "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" before the woman, it is not because she needs to hear this declaration. Rather, it means that since it needs to be said within 24 hours of the delivery, it must be said in her presence, because otherwise, it would certainly not be within 24 hours. The explanation is that if it was not said in her presence, it is certainly after 24 hours. (See Taz, subparagraph 5, and the Gra, subparagraph 24, and according to what I have explained, it is clear and investigate further.) However, what is written, or that it was given to her privately, this only follows the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam in Siman 133, that after the fact, even without the stipulation, it is sufficient. Therefore, just because of the declaration "in my presence," it needs to be taken and given before two [witnesses]. But according to the other authorities, without this, the get (divorce document) is nothing, as is written there. And according to this, they should have explained that what they wrote, "even though she married," etc., is not for the other authorities, for indeed she married in prohibition, and this requires further investigation. And perhaps they relied on what is written in Siman 133 and there is no need to explain it here.

And what they wrote that for a mute it does not help to write it, we have already explained this in section 30. And it is not specifically a deaf person, for the same applies to a hearing person, as we wrote there. However, what they wrote that it must be said specifically in the Holy Tongue (Hebrew) has no reason, for are these matters of holiness? And even in matters of holiness, many things are valid also in a foreign language, as it is taught in Sotah chapter 7. And what they cited that this is implied by the Rosh, certainly his intention is what the Rosh wrote in the first chapter (section 63) that one should not say anything other than the language that the sages instituted. Certainly, this is so, that one should not say a different version like "I know" which is the writing and signing and the like. But in which language, what importance is there in the matter? And it is true that our teacher the Rema himself in his book Darkei Moshe (section 7) also doubted this, and therefore he wrote in the Shulchan Aruch that if it was said in a foreign language it is valid. But still, whoever said that it must be only in the Holy Tongue, from what reason did he say it? And it seems to me that he said well, for behold in the Talmud (3a) they asked the one who says that the reason is because of "for its sake", why did they not institute to say "before me for its sake" and "before me for its sake"? And they answered that it would come to confuse him, meaning if we increase the words, he will not say it as the sages instituted. Behold, it is explicitly stated that the sages estimated that with more than four words, there could be an error in his words. And it is a known fact that the Holy Tongue is a language where a small amount holds much, unlike all other foreign languages. Therefore, if he says "before me and before me" in a foreign language, it will be more than four words and there could be an error. And according to this, it is well said that it should only be said in the Holy Tongue (and even though this is according to Rava, in reasoning they do not disagree).

And know that there are some of the early authorities who hold that when one does not say "before me it was written and before me it was signed," it is not necessary to specifically take it from the woman and return it to her in the presence of two witnesses and say "before me it was written and before me it was signed," unless there are no witnesses to the delivery before us. But when the delivery witnesses are before us, it is sufficient for him to say before them, "The get that I gave before you to such-and-such a woman was written and signed before me" (Rosh and Mordechai in the name of R' Yitzchak of Kinon). And there are those who are even more lenient to say that even if there are other witnesses who were present at the time of the delivery, even if they were not designated as delivery witnesses, the agent can say before them as well, "The get that I gave to such-and-such a woman in the presence of such-and-such witnesses was written and signed before me" (Tur in the name of the Ramah). However, from the majority of our rabbis, it does not appear so, and this opinion is not brought in the Shulchan Aruch. The proof brought from the Jerusalem Talmud is not decisive at all. Look there (the proof of R' Yitzchak of Kinon from what is stated there in order to establish her as divorced before two witnesses, and it can be said that this means that it is necessary to establish her by returning the giving of her get to her hand. Look there and examine carefully).

If the agent did not say "Before me it was written and before me it was signed," and it was not taken from her to return to her and say "Before me it was written," as mentioned, and the get was not validated by its signatures, even if there is no objection from the husband, the get is invalid because it was not done according to the sages' ordinance, and she should not marry with it. Even if she has already married, she must leave (Tur). However, the child is not a mamzer (illegitimate) (ibid). Even though Rabbi Meir holds (Gittin 5a) that without the declaration "Before me it was written," the child is a mamzer, as Rabbi Meir says: anyone who deviates from the formula established by the sages in gittin, the child is a mamzer, and in the Jerusalem Talmud it appears that the law follows him, nevertheless, in our Talmud it appears that the law does not follow him in this case. This is also the implication from Maimonides and all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). On the contrary, according to the principle that Maimonides established in chapter 10, which will be explained in section 152, that wherever we say a get is invalid, if she married, she does not have to leave, we should say the same here, that if she married, she does not have to leave (see Beit Yosef). However, regarding this ordinance, it is clarified from the Talmud and the poskim that the sages strengthened the ordinance, so if she married, she must leave. In the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, it is clarified that according to Maimonides, she does not have to leave, see there, and it requires further study. However, if the husband came and objected and it was not validated, Maimonides wrote in chapter 7 that it is not a get, and if the get was lost, the child is a doubtful mamzer. From the words of the Rosh and the Tur, it is clarified that even if the get was not lost, and the husband came and objected and it was not validated, she is doubtfully divorced, and the child is a doubtful mamzer, see there. One should be stringent according to all opinions regarding if she received kiddushin (betrothal) from another, that she needs a get from the second one as well, and we have already spoken about this (see Beit Yosef).

It has already been explained that the validation of signatures is equivalent to saying "It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence." However, our custom is that even though there is an authorized validation, the messenger still says "It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence." But, according to the law, it is not mandatory. The method of validation is elucidated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 46, where five methods of validation are discussed. It is also explained there that even when there is a court validation of the signatures, it is still necessary to recognize the handwriting of the court, but in the case of a get (divorce document), we are lenient even with the recognition of one of the judges, as our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Siman 141, Section 24.

And know that at the end of this section, it is even more lenient, that even without the recognition of the signatures of the judges at all, it does not invalidate the get (divorce document) after the fact. And even without the statement "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed." And these are the words: "There are those who say that if the agent brings the get that is validated by its signatures, even though the signatures of the validating judges are not recognized, nevertheless, in a pressing situation and to prevent the woman from being chained (agunah), one should be lenient and rely on it, even though the agent did not say 'In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed,' since it is impossible to return and say it. One should rely on the signatures, for by Torah law, witnesses who sign a document are as if their testimony has been examined in a court of law." And the conclusion is: by Torah law, no validation is needed at all, and only by rabbinic decree is validation required. Therefore, we are lenient in this matter when there is validation, even though the signatures of the validating judges are not recognized. And we rely on the authorities who hold that the signatures of the validating judges do not need to be recognized (Beit Shmuel, section 142). And according to this, it seems that this leniency applies specifically when there is no challenge from the husband. But when there is a challenge and he claims that everything is forged, it is necessary to recognize the signatures of the validating judges. And perhaps in such a case, even in a situation of pressing need and agunah, it is not effective at all until the signatures of all the validating judges are recognized, for it has already been explained that when there is a challenge, many authorities hold that validation is required by Torah law.

It has already been explained in Siman 140 and 141 that an agent can appoint another agent if the first agent becomes ill or is compelled, and even at the instruction of the husband, even if he is not ill or compelled. How does one act when it is necessary to say "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" and the second agent cannot say this because the get (divorce document) was not written in his presence? The sages taught in the Mishnah (Gittin 29b): One who brings a get from overseas and becomes ill, appoints an agent in a court and sends it, and says before them "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed." The last agent does not need to say "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," but rather says, "I am an agent of the court," and it is presumed that the court acted properly (Rashi). When the second agent becomes ill and appoints a third, he also appoints him in a court and says, "I am an agent of the court," and this continues indefinitely. When the last agent delivers the get to the woman in the presence of a court, he also says, "I am an agent of the court." All these declarations must be made at the time of the transfer of the get to the second agent and from the second to the third, or immediately thereafter, within the time span of "while speaking" (toche kedei dibur), as has been explained concerning the transfer of the get from the agent to the woman. This was the enactment: the first agent, when handing over the get, whether to the woman or to a second agent, must say immediately "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed."

And why is a Beit Din necessary? Because even when the agent delivers it to the woman, a Beit Din is needed. The requirement for giving it in the presence of two witnesses is explained by the fact that the agent also joins the Beit Din. Therefore, in this case as well, if the agent is fit to be part of the Beit Din (i.e., he is not a relative or disqualified, and is not a woman), then it is sufficient to have two witnesses, and the agent joins as the third member. This applies as well when the second agent appoints a third agent, and so on indefinitely, even up to one hundred agents. Therefore, according to what is stated in Section 23, where we are stringent and do not combine the agent with the Beit Din, in this case too we should be stringent and establish a Beit Din of three members, as well as having separate witnessing of the delivery apart from the Beit Din, as stated in Section 24. This is the common custom, and it should not be changed.

Even though regarding the statement "in my presence" and "in my presence" one should not change the wording from the decree of the Sages, as stated in section 34, but this wording of "the agent of the court" may be said in any manner he wishes, as long as the subject matter indicates that he was appointed as an agent by the first party in court, or he says "I was appointed as an agent before the court," or something similar. In this case, there was no decree to not change the wording, and it is explicitly proven in the Talmud there that the court does not appoint him as an agent, but the agent appoints him as an agent before the court (Gra, section 31).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 9 that even if the second messenger did not say anything, if he has authorization and it is a situation of potential marital strife, one may be lenient. Thus, each person should say to his fellow: "I, [name], son of [name], appoint you, [name], son of [name], to be my messenger in my place and for my needs, and your hand shall be as my hand, etc., to divorce [name], daughter of [name], the wife of [name], son of [name], in any place where you find her. And I give you permission to appoint a messenger and a messenger of a messenger, etc. And as soon as the get (bill of divorce) reaches the hand of [name], daughter of [name], the wife of [name], son of [name], she will be divorced, etc., as explained below in the order of the get. And a court-appointed messenger does not need authorization like the first messenger, but we customarily use authorization like for the first messenger. And even if only two were signed on the authorization and it was written in the language of testimony and not in the language of judgment, the second messenger is trusted to say that there were three or that he was with them. And the principle that a witness cannot become a judge does not apply here, and we are not concerned about a mistaken court unless we know that those who arranged the get are not knowledgeable, in which case, even if it is written properly, we are concerned about it. End of quote.

Now, regarding what is written that when nothing is said and there is authorization in his possession, it is permissible to be lenient in a case of potential agunah (a woman bound in marriage) as stated in Section 8. There is a significant difference between whether the authorization is validated, in which case it is straightforward to be lenient even not in a case of agunah, and if it is not validated, then certainly it is necessary to be stringent unless it is a case of agunah and a pressing situation, as mentioned in Section 10. And regarding what is written that a court-appointed agent does not need authorization like the first agent, the reason is straightforward: just as the Sages trusted the first agent to say "it was written and signed in my presence" because the get (divorce document) is in his possession, so too the second agent is trusted to say "I am a court-appointed agent" since the get is in his possession. However, in any case, the custom is that this agent also has authorization like the first agent, as they have adopted the custom of having authorization even though it is not required by law.

However, regarding what was written that even if only two were signed and it is written in the language of testimony, the messenger is believed to say that there were three or that he joined them, etc., I do not understand what kind of credibility applies to this. For necessarily there were three: the two signatories and the messenger. And so it is explained in the source of the law in the Rivash (Siman 318, see there). One could say that his intention was that perhaps intentionally they did not join him with them, and there were only two, which is not a court. The text comes to teach us that we do not worry about this, for why should we be concerned about something when we know there were three with the messenger? And if it is because it is written in the language of witnesses, the Talmud already said about such a case that it does not matter if it is written in the language of witnesses and signed by judges or vice versa (Gittin 33a). The main reason is that since the messenger is believed without the document, as it is written because the get (bill of divorce) is in his hand, therefore, as long as we can say that the document does not contradict his words, we say so. And know that from his words we learn that the second messenger also joins with the court, contrary to the opinion of some who are uncertain about this (see Pitchei Teshuvah, section 16).

It has already been explained in Siman 141 that agency does not require being in the presence of the principal. Therefore, the first agent can appoint a second agent in a court of law even not in the presence of the second agent. He states before the court, "I hereby appoint so-and-so to be my agent," and the first agent then departs. When the second agent arrives, the court gives him the get (divorce document) and informs him that the first agent appointed him as an agent. The second agent can then say when delivering it to the woman, "I am an agent of the court." Furthermore, the first agent does not even need to appoint the second agent himself; he can transfer his agency to the court, and they will appoint another agent. The court can appoint a second agent not in the presence of the first agent. This is what is stated in the Gemara (29b): "Hand over your matter to us, etc."—meaning, say before us (the court) "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," and leave the get with us, and we will appoint a second agent in your place who will be an agent of the court. The authority of the court is effective in this matter, as they can appoint an agent in his place when he so instructs.

However, our teacher, the Rema, questions this, arguing that in such a case the second person cannot claim to be a court messenger since he did not hear the first person say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed." This rule was only established when the person himself heard "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" from the first person. His words in section 10 are: "There are those who say that it is not valid for him to say 'I am a court messenger' since he did not hear the messenger say 'in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed.' Rather, he needs authorization, or the document needs to be validated by its signatures." For, in the authorization, it is clarified that he said "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," and when there is validation, "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" is not needed. He follows his reasoning that authorization alone is not considered validation. We have already explained that this applies to authorization that is not validated, as mentioned in sections 8 and 43. Regarding the essence of this stringency, there is room for doubt, as it does not explicitly seem so in the Talmud there, and this has already been questioned (Avnei Miluim).

A blind person in both eyes cannot deliver a get (bill of divorce) because he must say "It was written and signed in my presence," and he cannot do so since he does not see. Even according to the opinion that hearing the sound of the quill is sufficient, how can he say "It was written in my presence" when he did not see the writing? And if he says, "I heard the sound of the quill," this is not in accordance with the enactment of the Sages (Rosh). Therefore, if the get was written and signed in his presence before he became blind, and then he became blind before delivering it to the woman, it is valid, and he can say "It was written and signed in my presence." He must deliver it in the presence of three people because he himself is disqualified from serving as a judge, as mentioned in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 7. One might ask, isn't a blind person also disqualified from testimony, as stated in Siman 35, and even if he became blind in the middle of the testimony, he is disqualified, as mentioned there? How, then, can he be valid for delivering the get and testifying "It was written and signed in my presence"? The answer is that here, even those disqualified from testimony, such as a woman or a relative, are valid, as we have already explained. Therefore, he is also valid, and his disqualification is only regarding the statement "It was written and signed in my presence." Hence, if he saw at the time of the writing, it is valid (Tosafot 23a, s.v. "and he").

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch (section 11) wrote that a blind person must recognize the woman by her voice. If he does not recognize her by her voice, it does not help that others tell him it is she, even though for a sighted person, it does help. The reason is that for a blind person, there is more concern that he might be deceived (Tosafot 23a). Note that according to the Talmudic discussion there, it is not necessary to say this according to the conclusion. Nevertheless, it appears from the early authorities that they adopted this reasoning even according to the conclusion. There are those who are concerned that nowadays we do not rely on voice recognition even for Torah scholars (Sma, end of section 262). Also, regarding a lost get (divorce document), there are those who are cautious not to rely on voice recognition (Beit Shmuel, subsection 18). What is the difference between physical recognition and voice recognition? In truth, there is no connection between the two. It is not that physical recognition does not exist now, but rather that we do not trust it. This lack of trust only applies to situations where there is a suspicion, such as in the case of a lost item where there is a desire for the object, and similarly with a lost get where one might say it is the get because he knows it was lost. But here, what is there to suspect him of? Moreover, besides voice recognition, he gives it to her in front of witnesses, and generally, they know her, as do other local people who recognize her.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in paragraph 11 that for one who is not blind, if he does not recognize her, we require two valid witnesses who are neither relatives nor disqualified individuals. And his words are perplexing, for it is explicitly ruled earlier in Siman 120 that recognition is valid even through relatives, and it is explicitly stated in the Gemara in Yevamot (39b) for the reason that something destined to be revealed is not lied about. Furthermore, if valid witnesses are required, why should the blind person not rely on them? Is there anything for which we do not rely on two witnesses? It is obvious that what the early authorities said, that the blind person should not rely on others, is only when they are not valid witnesses. But with valid witnesses, what reason is there not to believe them? And it is true that the author of the Terumat HaDeshen wrote similarly in Siman 238 and added that for a blind person, even with two valid witnesses, one should not rely on them. This is even more perplexing as I have written, and many of the great authorities have objected to this and wrote that it was only said as a matter of preference (Taz and Beit Shmuel in subsection 19). It does not seem so, and even as a preference, it is perplexing. Therefore, it appears to me that their intention is not that they testify as formal witnesses, for in such a case, even for a blind person, it is effective, and for one who is not blind, even relatives are effective when testifying formally due to the principle that something destined to be revealed is not lied about. Rather, their intention is that they are speaking verbally and not as formal witnesses. This requires further investigation.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 12: If there are witnesses that the husband handed the blind person this get for divorce, it is valid, since there are witnesses, and it is not necessary to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," and he gave it in the presence of those very witnesses. And if it has been validated through its signatures, it is valid in all respects. This is the end of the quotation, and it is from the Tur in the name of the Ramah. He wrote that therefore these very witnesses are needed so that it should not be a case of "half a matter," as explained there. And this is according to the opinion of the Rif and Tosafot (Baba Batra 56b), as we explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 30, that whenever there is no benefit from the testimony, it is called "half a matter." And similarly, in the case of handing the get to the blind person, no matter is completed, and it is not similar to a woman who appoints an agent to receive the get, where she needs two sets of witnesses—one set to say "in our presence she said," and another set to say "in our presence he received." And it is valid when they are not one set, as we wrote in the previous section, that in that case, the witnesses of the statement do not need to be the witnesses of the receipt, since the get is in his hand and she is already divorced by his receipt (Tosafot Gittin 63a). However, in the case of an agent for delivery, there is no benefit in his receipt as long as he has not handed it to her (but according to the explanation of the Nimukei Yosef there, that they testify about the agency, they are equal, as explained there. Examine this carefully). But according to the Rashbam there, that whenever it is not at the same time, it is not called "half a matter," as explained in Choshen Mishpat there and in section 145, it is not called "half a matter" here, since they saw all that could be seen. And it appears that the Ramah does not hold this reasoning (see Beit Shmuel, subsection 21, where there is a typographical error).

And it is puzzling regarding our teacher, the Beit Yosef, that in this section he ruled straightforwardly according to the opinion of the Ramah. And in section 18, regarding when the agents are two or one of them, that they do not need to say "Befanai Nechtav, U'Befanai Nechtam" (It was written in my presence, and it was signed in my presence), the Ramah's opinion there is also that he should deliver it in the presence of those witnesses due to the concept of "half a matter," as explained in the Tur. And he did not rule straightforwardly like him there, but rather wrote it in the name of "there are those who require," etc. (see there and in the Beit Yosef, section 39). But in truth, his words are precise if we scrutinize how he wrote in this law that when there are witnesses that the husband delivered for divorce, there is no need to say "Befanai Nechtav, U'Befanai Nechtam." From where do we know to say this? For there is neither the validation of the get requiring the signatures nor the rabbinic enactment of saying "Befanai Nechtav" here. And it is not similar to the law below where two brought a get, for there it is because they made both or one of them an agent. But when the agent is not one of these two, it is obvious that the agent must say "Befanai Nechtav, U'Befanai Nechtam," as explicitly written by the Rashba at the beginning of chapter 2 and the Maggid Mishneh in chapter 7, law 14 (see there). And it is also clear from the words of the Tur and all the early authorities that at the very least, one of these two must be the agent, and not when the agent is another person. Therefore it seems clear to me that certainly in such a case, he must say "Befanai Nechtav, U'Befanai Nechtam." However, if those two are also witnesses to the delivery, it is also considered a complete matter regarding that the agent does not need to say "Befanai Nechtav, U'Befanai Nechtam," for since they saw the entire context of the get, there is no place left for the husband to contest. And according to this, what our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote, "and he gave it to her in the presence of these witnesses themselves," is not because of the law of "half a matter" regarding testimony, for in this, he does not agree with the Ramah. On the contrary, he disputes him (in the Beit Din, where he wondered about it, for the witnesses of the agency alone, see there, and it is the opinion of the Nimukei Yosef in Bava Batra there). Rather, regarding that the agent does not need to say "Befanai," for this, a complete matter is necessary. Otherwise, he would need to say "Befanai Nechtav, U'Befanai Nechtam." And this blind person cannot say it, and once the signatures are validated, it is obvious that nothing is needed, and a blind person can be an agent as long as he recognizes the husband and the wife by their voices. And if he became blind before the delivery, we do not require him to recognize by voice, only the wife. But when he was blind beforehand, it is obvious that he needs to recognize both the husband and the wife.

The sages taught in the Mishnah (23b): A woman herself can bring her own divorce document, provided that she must say "It was written and signed in my presence." The Gemara questions: How can this be found? For when the divorce document reaches her hand, she is already divorced. The Gemara answers: Such as when the husband gives her the get and says to her, "Be a messenger to deliver it until you reach such-and-such place, and there you will become a messenger to deliver it, or you will hand the get to a court, and the court will appoint another messenger, and you will receive the get from that messenger." Consequently, she also has the status of a delivery messenger, and when she hands it over to the messenger or to the court, she must say "It was written and signed in my presence," just like other messengers. At first glance, there is nothing novel in this ruling. What does it teach us? And if it is because of this very ruling itself, there is not much novelty since the husband has the right to stipulate whatever he wants, and consequently, when he makes her a messenger, she needs to say "It was written and signed in my presence." (It can be said that it teaches us that she is not called a messenger who was not appointed for the purpose of divorce, as Tosafot explain there, and similar cases, but this is a forced explanation.)

And from the words of the Rambam in Chapter 7 and the Raavad in Chapter 12, we learn a resolution to this issue: According to the Rambam, it informs us that only when the husband stipulated this condition upon her does she need to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed." But a regular woman bringing a get (divorce document) before us does not need to say anything. Even if the get is not certified, we permit her immediately, and when the husband comes and challenges it, we will require certification. Accordingly, our Mishnah teaches us another significant point: that this woman, even though if she wanted, she would not need to say anything and could just present her get before us, and we would permit her like any other woman bringing their get. Therefore, even when she says that the husband appointed her as an agent, as it says, why do we require her to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed?" She should be believed due to the principle of "miggo" (since she could have said something more advantageous). It informs us that we do not say so, and she needs to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" (and so wrote the Ran in the second chapter).

The Rambam states: A man who gives a get to his wife, and it is written and signed in her presence, and he says to her, "You are my agent to deliver it to such-and-such a court, and they will appoint an agent to give you this get, and you will be divorced by it," she is believed to say before them "It was written and signed in my presence," and they take it and give it to an agent to give it to her according to the husband's instructions. 

When does this apply? When the husband stipulated this condition to her. But if he did not stipulate this to her, and he simply gave her the get, and the get is in her possession, she does not need to say anything. She is presumed to be divorced, since the get in her possession is written according to the law, and the witnesses are signed on it. Even though we do not recognize the handwriting of those witnesses and it has not been validated, we do not suspect that it might be forged, since she would not harm herself. Moreover, the witnesses signed on the get are as if their testimony has been examined in court unless there is a challenger. Therefore, we maintain the get in its presumed validity, and she can marry, and we do not suspect that it might be found to be forged. Just as we presume the get to be valid when the agent brings it until the husband challenges it or brings evidence that it is forged or nullified, because if we were to be concerned about such things and the like, we would have to be concerned about a get that the husband gives in our presence that he might have nullified it afterward or that invalid witnesses signed it, making it like an internal forgery, or that it was written not for the sake of the proper intent. Just as we are not concerned about these and similar matters but rather presume its validity until it is known to be nullified, so too we are not concerned about the agent or the woman herself when the get is in her possession. The laws of prohibitions are not like the laws of monetary matters.

And so wrote the Rambam at the beginning of Chapter 12, that a woman who is established as a married woman is not believed to say "I am divorced," but if she brings a get (divorce document), she is believed even if it is not validated, see there. And we learn from his words a major principle concerning prohibitions: Even if something is established with a presumption of prohibition, if someone brings a written proof showing that this matter has left the presumption of prohibition, even if the document is not validated and there are several concerns to invalidate it, nevertheless, we do not invalidate it as long as its invalidity has not been clarified, and the matter leaves the presumption of prohibition. And although in monetary matters, if someone brings a promissory note, we do not extract money from another based on it until the document is validated, even if we do not know whether it is forged or not, as is evident from the Rambam's words in Chapter 13 of Laws of Creditor and Debtor, and in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat, Siman 106, see there. And this is what he precisely stated, that the laws of prohibitions are not like the laws of monetary matters, because in monetary matters, the other party holds the presumption, which is not the case with prohibitions. And although with a get (divorce document), money is also extracted since she collects her ketubah, this is due to a condition of the ketubah that states, "When you marry another, you shall take what is written for you," similar to when she says her husband died and she collects her ketubah. But the essence of the matter is a matter of prohibition (and see Yoreh De'ah, Siman 118, Paragraph 9, and in the Shach, Subsection 31, and scrutinize it well).

And even though there is room to question the fundamental matter that we do not need [the husband's] trustworthiness according to what was mentioned at the beginning of this chapter in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud, that the husband is not suspected of causing her to be prohibited by divine decree, and she also would not cause herself to be prohibited, as Maimonides wrote, that due to the stringency we imposed on her at the end, we hold in chapter 17 that she is believed to say her husband died, and similarly here, nevertheless, if not for the trustworthiness of the document, we cannot rely on this, for perhaps she relies on forgery and will deny it based on false witnesses. Rather, certainly the primary matter is the trustworthiness of the document. And know that what was written, that if we were concerned about these things, we would have to worry, etc., perhaps they nullified it, end quote, there is no question about this, for Maimonides himself wrote in chapter 6, law 100, that indeed we are concerned about this, and we do not allow him to leave until the completion of the get (divorce document), see there. Certainly, this is so, that in a place where it is possible to rectify this, we certainly should be concerned and rectify, like if he gives the get to the woman in our presence. And here it means to say that if it would enter your mind that we should be concerned about this by law, we would have to establish that a get should not be given through an agent due to the concern of nullification. Rather, certainly, by law, we are not concerned about this except when he is present, and where we can rectify this concern, it is certainly proper to rectify, as was written in chapter 6.

However, the Ra'avad of blessed memory wrote in Chapter 12 as follows: "I say that it should be validated by its signatures even though no objection has been raised against it." According to this, he holds that the Mishnah which states that a woman herself brings her own get (divorce document) is a leniency, teaching us that although when a woman brings her own get, we do not allow her to remarry until the signatures are validated, nevertheless, if she says "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" it is sufficient, and the husband cannot object, just as with an agent. Thus, the Talmud questions: once the get reaches the woman's hand, she is already divorced. What use is her saying "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," since she is already divorced? Just as an agent's statement is only effective at the time of delivery, if not said at the time of delivery, the get is taken from her and returned with the statement said properly, as explained. Since the regulation of saying "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" is only effective at the time of delivery, and thus this woman, who is already divorced, what benefit is there in her saying "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed?" Therefore, she needs validation. The answer is that she was not yet divorced, as the husband told her to go to a certain place and appoint an agent, as mentioned. Therefore, her statement "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" is effective. (I learned this from the words of the Rivash, section 385, and the Lechem Mishnah's effort on this matter in chapter 7 was unnecessary.) According to this, the husband intended for her benefit that she would not need validation. From the words of the Ra'avad, we learn that according to his view, any document that deals with a matter of prohibition cannot change that status without validation.
