And according to him, Rabban Gamliel's ordinance that witnesses should sign the get was so that validation of the signatures would be readily available, unlike if witnesses were required to appear. According to the Rambam of blessed memory, it is simple that no validation is needed unless the husband objects.

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 13 the opinion of the Rambam, and therefore he wrote that she is presumed to be divorced even without validation, etc. And even if he tells her, "Do not get divorced with it except in such-and-such court," it is merely a condition, and when she comes to that court and the get (divorce document) is in her possession, she is divorced with her initial acceptance, and there is no need to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" unless he instructed her to deliver it to the court and for them to appoint an agent, as he wrote. And in paragraph 14, he wrote the opinion of the Raavad that without validation, it is never permissible even if there are no objections, and he concluded there: "And we have never heard of anyone who acted leniently in this matter." End quote. And perhaps this is also why the custom among us is not to deliver the get into the woman's hand, but rather a release from the court, and this serves as validation because what benefit is the get to her if she needs to validate it.

It is stated in the Gemara (5a) that if a husband himself brings a get (Jewish divorce document) that was written in another place and brings it here to divorce his wife, he does not need to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" (b'fanai nichtav u'b'fanai nichtam). This is because the reason for saying "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" is so that the husband does not come and contest the validity of the get. Here, however, he himself is bringing and giving it, and he does not contest it. And even though it was already written and is dated earlier, there is no disqualification in this like with an agent bringing a get, for this has a public reputation (kol). Nevertheless, our master, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 14 that when the husband gives the get to his wife, his status is like that of an agent, and he must say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" so that we do not come to make a mistake with another agent, since nowadays people are not well-versed in Torah, end of quote. These words are puzzling, and who can innovate such a decree? On the contrary, in several matters our status is like that of people well-versed in Torah, and in the matter of a get, this reasoning is not found in the Gemara except concerning the requirement for the sake of the wife (lishma). And we hold by the reason of certification (kium), and see the Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 27.

Since the agent must declare "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," he needs to be present for the writing and signing of the get (divorce document). However, the Sages leniently ruled that he does not need to be present for the writing of the entire get; because the main aspect is the validation of the signatures, the writing is only important to prevent confusion with other documents, as stated. Therefore, they ruled leniently that even if he was only present at the writing of the first line, he does not need to be present afterward (Gittin 5). Moreover, even if he only heard the sound of the quill or the sound of the scroll (ibid.), and Rashi explains that the first line includes the names of the man and woman and the date. According to this, in our gittin where the first line only contains the date, the agent needs to be present for several lines. However, from Maimonides and all the early authorities, it does not appear so; the main point is the beginning of the first line, indicating that the scribe is writing for the sake of the participants, and this intent covers the entire get, even if it does not contain the essential parts. It is proper to be stringent initially (according to Rashi) (Beit Shmuel, section 28). Regarding the sound of the quill and the scroll, Rashi offers two explanations: one is that he heard when the quill and the parchment were prepared for writing, and the second is that he heard the sound of the quill while writing and the sound of the scroll when being written upon. It seems that Maimonides also interpreted it this way, and this is also implied in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 15. They further stated that one should not be stringent and require the agent to be present for the writing of the entire get to avoid casting doubt on previous gittin that were not done this way. Even though in several matters they did not worry about such doubts, in this case, the Sages were concerned, and one should not change this practice.

Therefore, our Sages (beginning of Chapter 2) stated that the essential part is the first half of the Get (divorce document). When [the messenger] says, "It was written in my presence" regarding the first half or even the first line, it is sufficient. Even if the scribe went to the market after writing part of the Get and then returned and completed it, we are not concerned that someone else might have found it and told him to write it for another woman. However, the second half is of no significance. Yet, the signatures are crucial; the messenger must witness the writing of both signatures from the beginning to the end, as they are the essential part. Therefore, if he says, "It was written in my presence," but not the entire signing, or "It was signed in my presence," but not written at all, it is invalid. Even if he says, "The last half was written in my presence," it is invalid, as the essential part is the first half, and the first line is sufficient, as mentioned.

Therefore, if one witness says "It was all written and signed before me," but the other witness does not, and even if he says, "I am the second witness, and the first one signed before me, and the second signature is mine," it is invalid. Even though the primary validation of a document is when someone says, "This is my signature," why should it be less effective than saying "It was signed before me"? For the Sages have said either the entire validation of the get (divorce document) is based on the get itself or entirely on the rabbinic enactment (Gittin 5a). Therefore, in such a case, the get should be validated by verifying both signatures. The reason is that when he says "I am the second witness," he is testifying about the essence of the get, and when he says "It was signed before me," he is only testifying about the signature. What he testifies about in one instance, he does not testify about in the other. The Sages did not establish that one witness should be trusted for half of the testimony (Ran). However, if two testify about the second signature, it is effective. Even if he and another testify about the second signature, it is valid because there is no issue. If he alone had said "It was signed before me," it would have been effective, and when two testify about his signature, it should not be less effective. Even though the get is validated in three parts by his testimony and the fourth by someone else, in validating documents, when someone says, "This is my handwriting, and this is the handwriting of the second, and another witness testifies with him about the second," it is not considered valid as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 46. Here, it is effective, and we do not worry about this because, without the other, it would be validated based on his testimony, as the Sages trusted him as if he were two (Rashi).

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 17: If there are three witnesses signed on it and two signed in his presence, even though the third did not sign in his presence, it is nothing. The explanation is as follows: For example, if after one signed, he left and did not see when the others signed. Even though all the witnesses of the get (divorce document) do not sign without each other when he said, "All of you sign," because of witnesses, they need to sign all on the same day and in each other’s presence as stated in section 120. Nevertheless, in this case, which is similar to the validation of documents, they were lenient and only two witnesses are required for validation (Gra, note 52; Avnei Shoham, note 34).

The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 7, Law 14: "When two individuals bring a get (bill of divorce) from outside the land [of Israel], even though it was not written and signed in their presence, since the husband gave it to them to deliver to his wife, they should give it to her and she is considered divorced. This is because the husband cannot contest this get even though it is not validated, for his messengers are like his witnesses. If these two individuals say, 'She was divorced in our presence,' she is divorced even if there is no get present." And it seems from his words that it is specifically when both of them are messengers to deliver the get, but if one of them is a messenger, even though there are two individuals present and thus witnesses are available to validate it, it does not help. And so Rashi, of blessed memory, wrote (Gittin 16b) that two who bring a get do not need to say "It was written and signed in our presence" (b'fanei nichtav u'b'fanei nichtam). Why did they require this statement? Because there are no witnesses available to validate it, but here there are witnesses available to validate it, and therefore the get is valid even if they say nothing. And if you ask, since in the end, they are two, what difference does it make if both are messengers or if one of them is? After all, witnesses are available to validate it. The Rabbis did not differentiate between one who comes with a group of people and one who comes alone, since people do not distinguish and check in such cases, as it is not evident. But if you start to validate this, they will validate that. However, when two bring it, it is evident and uncommon, and the Rabbis did not impose a stringency in this case. Thus, it is explicitly stated that it is specifically when both are messengers.

However, Tosafot, the Rosh, the Rashba, the Ran, and the Tur ruled that even the messenger (shaliach) is only one person, but the second one testifies about the agency, that in his presence the husband gave this get (divorce document) to the first to deliver to his wife. This is considered as if both are messengers, and there is no need to say "in my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" (b'fanei nechtav u'b'fanei nechtam), because it is as if both are messengers since he testifies about the agency. They wrote that it is possible that even the Rambam would agree with this, and his intention was only to exclude when the second comes in his company and has no connection to the agency. But whenever he testifies about the agency of the first, the husband cannot dispute anymore (Rashba and Maggid Mishneh there). It is possible that even Rashi would agree with this, and this is implied from the language of Tosafot and the Rosh, who did not come to disagree with Rashi, of blessed memory. And there are those who hold that when both are messengers, or when one is a messenger and the second testifies about the agency, they also need to be combined (i.e., to act together) so that it should not be a partial matter (Tur in the name of the Ramah). Our master, the Beit Yosef, in his book, questioned this, stating that this is not related to a partial matter, since they are testifying about the agency. And there is another reason that it is not a partial matter, because they saw everything they were able to see (as Rashbam wrote in Bava Batra 56a). Nevertheless, our master, the Beit Yosef, was concerned about this opinion and wrote it in section 18, and these are his words: "And there are those who require that it be handed over in the presence of the witnesses of the agency themselves." And what is written in section 12 is stated completely according to this opinion, as we elucidated with the help of Heaven in section 51.

The Rambam wrote that if there are two agents, the husband can no longer contest the get (divorce document). The Tur did not write this. Instead, the Tur wrote: "If there are two agents bringing the get, they do not need to declare 'it was written and signed in my presence;' rather, it is given to her even though it is not validated by its signatures, and she may remarry with it. However, if the husband comes, he can contest it and claim it is forged, and it must be validated by its signatures." The Beit Yosef already questioned this view, asking how the husband can claim it is forged when these two agents contradict him. Therefore, he omitted this opinion in the Shulchan Aruch. However, the Rema wrote: "Some say if the husband comes and contests it, it must be validated by its signatures." This is the opinion of the Tur, and its intention is explained (Beit Shmuel se'if katan 37) that the husband claims he deliberately gave them a forged get to entrap her. Although we wrote in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud that he is not suspected of entrapping her before Heaven, this applies generally when there is no need to suspect this. But if he contests and claims entrapment, his claim is valid. Besides this, the term 'contesting' generally implies all types of contesting, including claiming it is forged. The language of the Jerusalem Talmud that we brought at the beginning of this section also implies that the husband is not believed to say at all that he entrapped her before Heaven. Moreover, if we believe the husband in everything he says, what will we do if he says he nullified the get or that it was written not for its intended purpose, or similar claims? Therefore, without proof, he is not believed to say anything after the get has come into her hands, except to claim it is forged, and it needs validation like all documents. As long as the signatures are not validated, he can claim it is forged. Know that the Tur is not alone in this opinion; Rashi also holds this view. (Rashi wrote at the beginning of Gittin in the commentary starting "That they brought it in the presence of two," and both became agents, etc. For according to Rava, they do not need to declare because they are two. If the husband contests, they are available to validate it.)

It appears to me that they are not in disagreement at all, and the matter is as follows: Certainly, when two people bring a get (divorce document) and say, "We are messengers from your husband who sent you this get," the husband can no longer contest it. This is what Maimonides is referring to, as is evident from his language when he wrote, "If the two said, 'In our presence she was divorced,' etc." It clearly implies that they said something, and even though they did not say, "In our presence it was written and signed," they certainly said that they are the husband's emissaries to deliver the get. However, the Tur did not mention this at all, and Rashi explicitly explained (Gittin 16b) that even though they did not say anything, they handed over this get to her. Therefore, as long as the signatures have not been validated, the husband can contest and say it is forged. What is this similar to? It is like two people who bring a promissory note signed by Reuven, stating that Reuven owes Shimon money, and they did not say anything. Can Reuven not claim it is forged? For we do not find such a distinction anywhere. It is a general rule that as long as the signatures are not validated and two witnesses did not testify that so-and-so borrowed from so-and-so, it is not considered validated. The same applies here. It is obvious that the trustworthiness of the witnesses depends on their testimony, as it is written, "If he does not testify," and not when they are silent, even if it is evident from their actions (and the Atzei Giborim answered that if he contests and it becomes clear that there were two witnesses, his contestation is nullified. See there. But it does not seem so, for if that were the case, the Tur should have said so, and it would not be considered validated by their signatures. And what he wrote that they themselves need to come, I do not understand what difference it makes if they themselves or others testify that there were two witnesses. And what he wrote that they need to come before the court specifically requires further investigation. The correct explanation is what was mentioned).

Two people who brought a get (a bill of divorce), and one says, "It was written in my presence," and the other says, "It was signed in my presence"—if both of them are messengers, or even if one of them is a messenger and the other testifies about the agency, it is valid. This is because we do not actually need their statements at all, as has been explained. But if only one of them is a messenger and the other does not testify about the agency, it is invalid and should not be given to her until it is verified by its signatures. For the Sages trusted the messenger, but not someone else, and he must say both things: "It was written in my presence" and "It was signed in my presence." Furthermore, even if two people who are not related to the agency say, "It was written in our presence," and the messenger says, "It was signed in my presence," it is still nothing and should not be given to her until its signatures are verified. And even though the trustworthiness of the messenger is not greater than that of two people, and here two people testify about the writing, it is still invalid for another reason: since the messenger only testifies about the signatures, it might lead to confusion with the verification of other documents, where they might say that one witness is enough and not realize that here there are two others testifying about the writing. However, if two people say, "It was signed in our presence," and the messenger says, "It was written in my presence," it is valid, because since two people testify about the signatures, the get is considered verified, and there is no need for the messenger’s statement at all (Tosafot 17b, s.v. "echad"). And know that the Tur wrote in this matter as follows: "But if one of those who says 'It was signed in my presence' is the sole messenger, it should not be given until there is another with him." The commentators were puzzled by this, because since two people testify about the signatures, this is a complete verification, and why do we need another person? Some have written that it is a scribal error, and it should say, "But if one says 'It was signed in my presence'..." However, this does not seem correct from the arrangement of his words, and it is superfluous. See there.

The Law of a Conditional Get. It contains 87 sections:
Because Rambam has some perplexing matters in the laws of conditions in divorces that the early authorities found puzzling, and even the commentators on his work, the Maggid Mishneh and the Kesef Mishneh, were puzzled by him. In our humble opinion, he is not alone in this, as the Raavad did not criticize him on this matter, and the Tur copied his words. Therefore, we will explain them with the help of Heaven.

And these are the words of the Rambam in Chapter 8 of Hilchot Gerushin: If a divorce is conditional, if the condition is fulfilled, she is divorced, and if the condition is not fulfilled, she is not divorced. We have already explained the laws of conditions in Chapter 6 of Hilchot Ishut, and it is explained there that if one divorces on a condition, once the condition is fulfilled, she is divorced at the time the condition is fulfilled, not at the time the get (divorce document) is given into her hand. Therefore, the husband can cancel the get or add to his condition or stipulate a different condition as long as the first condition has not been fulfilled, even though the get has already been given into her hand. If the husband dies or the get is lost or burned before the condition is fulfilled, she is not divorced initially. She should not remarry until the condition is fulfilled, but if she did remarry, she does not have to leave her new husband unless she can no longer fulfill the condition, in which case the condition is nullified. It is also explained there that if he said to her, "You are divorced from now or from today on the condition of such and such," or if he said, "You are divorced on the condition of such and such," once the condition is fulfilled, she is divorced from the time the get was given into her hand. Therefore, he cannot cancel the get or add to his condition once the get has been given into her hand. If the get is lost or burned, even if the husband died before the condition was fulfilled, she fulfills the condition after his death and has been divorced since the time the get was given into her hand. She may remarry initially even though the condition has not yet been fulfilled, and we are not concerned that the condition might not be fulfilled since the condition was made "from now" or "on the condition." End of quote.

And they were astonished at him for writing, without qualification, that if she remarried, she does not have to leave [her second husband]. Why should she not have to leave? Since the validity of the get (divorce document) is from the time the condition is fulfilled, if the husband died or the get was lost, she is not divorced, as he himself wrote. Therefore, if she remarried before the condition was fulfilled, she is still a married woman, so how did he rule that she does not have to leave? Therefore, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, ruled in the first section that if she remarried, she must leave and did not mention the opinion of the Rambam at all. And in Chapter 9, Law 5, the Rambam wrote regarding one who divorces on condition and the get is extant at the time the condition is fulfilled, even though it is not in her possession, it is still a valid get. This is also puzzling, since the validity of the get is at the time the condition is fulfilled, it certainly needs to be in her possession (and see the Beit Yosef, Siman 146, Subparagraph 2).

And also what is written in Siman Pe Tet (Chapter 88), and this is the language: "One who was divorced conditionally and was betrothed by another before the condition was fulfilled — if the condition is fulfilled, she is betrothed, etc." And it is explained that his intention is regarding a general condition and not a condition of "from now" or "on the condition" (Beit Shmuel there, Section 5). It is difficult, how could the second betrothal take effect, for she is still considered a married woman? And he explicitly wrote himself in Chapter 6 of Ishut regarding conditions of betrothal that without "from now," she is considered single before the fulfillment of the condition, and similarly, in the condition of a get, she is considered a married woman. Also, what he ruled regarding the condition "from now" that she can marry before the fulfillment of the condition is very difficult — why do we not worry that the condition will not be fulfilled and she will be a married woman? And what is the difference between a general condition where we are concerned that the condition might not be fulfilled and a condition of "from now" where we are not concerned? The Tur indeed ruled that she should not marry, and if she did marry, we separate them until the condition is fulfilled. And some differentiate between a condition of "sit and do not act," where we are not concerned that she will transgress in practice, and a condition of "arise and act," where we are concerned that she will not fulfill it (Ran). And some differentiate between a condition that is in her power to fulfill and one that is not in her power to fulfill (there in Chapter 7). And some are stringent in every case (there).

Aside from this, we find that the Rambam presents matters regarding the conditions of divorce documents in a manner unlike other subjects. He wrote at the beginning of Chapter 9 that if a man divorces his wife effective at a later fixed time, she is divorced when that specified time arrives. This is similar to a condition but is not exactly a condition. It is similar to a condition because she becomes divorced when the specified time arrives, but it is not a condition because when one divorces based on a condition, the divorce takes effect immediately, whereas in this case, the divorce does not take effect until that specified time. Therefore, when one divorces based on a condition, he must double the condition, but in this case, he does not need to double his statement nor comply with the other conditions we explained. For example, if one says to his wife, "This is your divorce document, but you will not be divorced by it until after 30 days," she is not divorced until after 30 days. If the husband dies, or the divorce document is lost or burned within those 30 days, she is not divorced. If she placed the document on the side of a public domain and it was stolen or lost from there after 30 days, she is divorced, since the document existed on the day she would be divorced, and she designated it in a place that is not a public domain, as the sides of a public domain are not considered like the public domain itself. And a similar ruling exists regarding betrothal in Chapter 7 of the Laws of Marriage, but it is not elaborated upon there.

Additionally, he wrote: Similarly, if the divorce is contingent upon an action, its law is like that of a divorce set for a later time. How so? For example, if a man says to his wife, "This is your bill of divorce, but you will not be divorced with it until you give me two hundred zuz," she is divorced after she gives it, and there is no need to double his condition or for the other legal requirements of conditions that we have explained, since he did not divorce her on a condition but rather has not yet divorced her; he merely made the divorce contingent on the performance of such and such action, and afterwards she will be divorced. And behold, in the laws of marriage, it is not explained in the betrothal cases like this, and in this language. See there.

He also wrote: What is the difference between one who divorces conditionally and one who sets a time for the divorce or makes it dependent on an action? The one who divorces conditionally has initiated the divorce but it is not completed until the condition is fulfilled. Therefore, when the condition is fulfilled, she is divorced if the get (bill of divorce) is still valid, even if it is not in her possession. She does not need to take it again or have it in her possession after the condition is fulfilled, since it originally reached her as a divorce. If she marries before the condition is fulfilled, she does not have to leave her new husband, as we have explained. But if the divorce is dependent on a specific time or action, the get does not reach her as a divorce but as a deposit until the specified time or action occurs. Therefore, when the time arrives, the get must be in her possession or she must take it again, or it must be in the place designated for it, even if it is not in her possession, as we have explained. Only then does she become divorced by it. If she marries before the specified time arrives or before the action upon which the divorce is dependent is performed, she must leave her new husband and the child is a mamzer (illegitimate), since she is still fully married and there is no valid divorce. And such things have not been taught to us anywhere, besides the difficulty it poses, as I have written.

Additionally, it is written: If a man gives a get (divorce document) to his wife and says to her, "If you do not give me two hundred zuz, this is not a get," or "You are not divorced," this is not a valid divorce at all. It is neither a conditional get nor dependent on any action. And the same applies to anything similar. And even though it might imply that if she gives the money, she would be divorced, as one might infer a positive from a negative statement, since he did not explicitly mention divorce and did not say to her, "Behold, you are divorced," or "This is your get," she is not considered divorced. This is what the Maggid Mishneh wrote. However, I am puzzled because we hold that when one is engaged in the matter at hand, even if he gives her the get without any specific statement, whether in divorce or betrothal, she is considered divorced or betrothed, even if he did not say anything, as Rambam himself wrote in Hilchot Gerushin (Laws of Divorce) Chapter 1, Halacha 11, regarding divorce, and in Hilchot Ishut (Laws of Marriage) Chapter 3, Halacha 8, regarding betrothal. Therefore, we must say that the reason is because a condition requires a double stipulation, and this was not a double stipulation. Hence, on the contrary, we should say that the condition is nullified and the action is valid (see Gra, Siman 146, Se'if 14, and it requires further investigation. Also, see Tosafot, Gittin 75, s.v. "to exclude"). Furthermore, why did he not explain a similar law in betrothal?

He further wrote: One who wishes to divorce on a condition, and the matter of his condition is that the divorce will not take effect until a certain time, should express this matter in the language of a condition and make the condition dependent on his coming at a fixed time or on his going. How so? For example, if he says to her, "If I do not come from now until thirty days, this is a get (divorce document), but if I come within thirty days, it will not be a get," and he gives her the get. Or he says to her, "This is your get on the condition that I do not come to this city for thirty days," and similarly, for any such case. And I do not know what he meant to teach us, for the laws of conditions have already been explained in the laws of marriage, and also in chapter 8 of the laws of divorce, it is written that all the laws of conditions are required. What difference does it make whether the condition is "if you give me two hundred zuz" or "if I do not come from now until thirty days"? And what he wrote "on the condition," and his intention that in this case, there is no need for the laws of conditions, has also already been explained in the laws of marriage, chapter 6, law 17. See there.

Therefore, it is clear to me that the Rambam of blessed memory holds that the conditions of a get (divorce document) are different from the conditions in betrothal, sale, and gift. The reason is that the concept of a condition applies in matters where both parties have a say, such as in betrothal, where just as the man only betroths with his consent, so too the woman only becomes betrothed with her consent. Similarly, in a sale, the consent of both the buyer and the seller is required, and in a gift, the intent of both the giver and the receiver is necessary, since one cannot force someone to accept a gift. This applies to all matters in the world, and consequently, when there are two parties who need to agree and they only agree on certain conditions, it makes sense. However, in the case of a get, the woman has no say at all, and everything depends on the husband's will; if he wants to divorce her, he divorces her even if she does not consent, as this is the Torah law.

Therefore, we find that our sages of the Mishnah and the Gemara have clarified conditions in betrothal involving money in two ways: "Behold, you are betrothed to me on the condition that I give you two hundred zuz" (Kiddushin 60a), "on the condition that I speak to the ruler on your behalf" (Kiddushin 63a), "on the condition that I work for you as a laborer" (Kiddushin 63a), and there are conditions that depend on her (Kiddushin 50a). However, in a get, we only find conditions that depend on her: "on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz" (Gittin 74a), "on the condition that you serve my father," "on the condition that you nurse my son" (Gittin 75a). We do not find a condition where he gives money, and it is clear that in betrothal, she does not want to be betrothed to him in any other manner. But in the case of a get, why would he need to give her money? She is divorced against her will, and on the contrary, conditions where she gives him money make sense, such as if she requests a get and he says he only agrees on certain conditions.

However, this too is perplexing. Why must he give her a get (divorce document) now and stipulate that the get should not be effective until she gives him the money? Instead, let him not give her the get until she gives him the money, and then he shall divorce her. In the case of betrothal, it is understandable that each party is compelled to act out of concern that the other might later regret it, so they bind themselves in a specific manner from the outset. But in the case of a get, why is a condition necessary? At any time he wishes, he can divorce her, and when she gives him the money, he can divorce her then. Perhaps it is possible that he wishes to divorce her when she gives him the money but is concerned that when she has the money, a scribe and witnesses might not be available. Therefore, he writes the get now. But even in such a case, who compels him to make a condition? He can give her the get and say, "This is your get, but you will not be divorced by it until after you give me such and such amount of money." Who compels him to make a condition?

And certainly the truth is so, and this is what the Rambam clarified in Chapter 8, Law 4, that the divorce is contingent upon an action, as he said, "This is your get (divorce document), but you will not be divorced by it until you give me two hundred zuz," which we brought in Section 6. And there is no need to worry that she might retract, for it is not dependent on her will at all.

And behold, if this man did not do so and gave her a get (divorce document) with a conditional clause, saying "if you give me two hundred zuz," and he did not need to do so, it indicates that his intention was to agree to her desire that the get should begin from the time of giving and not be completed until after the receipt of the money. Therefore, if she marries another before the condition is fulfilled, she is not considered a married woman who married unlawfully, but rather she fulfills the condition and remains with him. However, since he did not say "from now," we say that he reserved for himself the power to annul the condition, or to add to it, or to condition another condition, or to annul the entire get. The get is considered complete only after the condition is fulfilled. Even though it is not in her possession, since it reached her as a divorce document, the reasoning is that since we need to give her some legal standing due to the condition he made, which he did not need to do, we give her only one primary legal standing: that she is not considered a married woman from now, as this is her main desire—that she should give him money or some other condition he stipulates with her, like serving his father or nursing his son and similar conditions. Therefore, if she married, she does not need to leave [the second husband], and it follows that the get does not need to be in her possession. However, other powers, such as not being able to annul the get or change the condition or annul it or add to it, where do we derive that he did not reserve for himself? Certainly, he reserved for himself, and it follows that the get needs to be complete until the condition is fulfilled.

And if this man added to the condition for her benefit something that was not necessary, such as if he said "from now" or "from today" or "on the condition" which has the same status as "from now," it is presumed that he fully intended to divorce her from now as a complete divorce and presumably he is confident that she will fulfill the condition. Otherwise, he would not have said "from now" and given her all the powers. Therefore, he cannot annul the get (divorce document), nor add to the condition, nor annul it, nor exchange it for another condition, as the get is finalized and there is no need for the get to be complete until the condition is fulfilled. And she is able to marry another because there is no doubt that she will fulfill the condition; otherwise, he would not have said "from now." And it refers to a situation where she has the ability to fulfill the condition; otherwise, he would not have said "from now." And behold, in the condition of "from now" or "on the condition," in all conditions, it is as it is written in Siman 38 regarding betrothal, except that with a get, there are those who say that even with "from now," he can annul it. And our teacher, the Rema, brings this opinion at the end of section 2. And the reason is that they hold that since the main party with decision-making power in a get is the husband, even a condition of "from now" does not prevent him from retracting it. And several early authorities hold this view (see the Gra, sub-paragraph 17). And the Ramban, Rashba, and Maggid Mishneh hold in this matter like the Rambam (there) that the condition of a get should not be inferior to the condition of betrothal. And according to what is written in the view of the Rambam, on the contrary, the condition of a get is preferable to other conditions since it was not necessary and he made it, showing that he gave her additional powers, as we have explained.

According to this, if he divorces her after a set time, such as saying, "This is your get (divorce document), but you will not be divorced with it until after 30 days," or if he makes it contingent upon an action, like saying to her, "This is your get, but you will not be divorced with it until you give me 200 zuz," there is no matter of a condition here at all. There is no beginning to this get until the 30 days pass or until she gives the 200 zuz. Therefore, the get needs to be in her possession at the completion of the 30 days or at the time she gives the 200 zuz. This is what is explained in Chapter 9, where the difference between a condition and setting a time or making it contingent upon an action is clarified as we have explained. The ruling regarding the sides of the public domain, which is not like the public domain, will be clarified in Siman 146 with the help of Heaven.

And since a get (bill of divorce) that is contingent on an action has no beginning as a get, therefore Maimonides wrote correctly that if he gave the get and said to her, "If you do not give me two hundred zuz, you are not divorced," this is not a get at all. And this means even if she gives him the two hundred zuz. And although the statement "This is your get" is not an absolute requirement when they are engaged in that matter, that applies when he gives it to her now as a get. But if it is contingent on an action, it is only like a deposit in her hand. Therefore, it never comes into her hand as a get. And even when she gives him the money, he did not say anything at that time, and earlier he did not mention "This is your get," so it turns out he did not divorce her. And even if we say that from a negative you understand a positive, that applies if he gave it to her as a get, which is not the case when he gives it as a deposit. (And this is the intention of the Maggid Mishneh that we brought in paragraph 8).

And this that is written about one who wishes to divorce on a condition, which we brought in section 9, it seems to me that there is a different intention hidden here. For behold, according to what we have explained, the condition of a get (divorce document) is different from other conditions in general. In a get, even with a condition, the get begins from the time of giving it and not from the fulfillment of the condition. For this reason, if she remarries, she does not have to leave, as we have explained. This applies only to a condition that she has to fulfill, such as giving him money or nursing his son, and similar cases, for the reason we have explained, that since her consent is not needed, why would he need to make a condition, as we have explained. Hence, this applies only to a condition that she has to fulfill. However, for a condition that he stipulates upon himself, in truth there is no need for a condition, only his desire to stipulate it as a condition, like his desire to divorce after thirty days, and his desire to make it conditional upon whether he comes or does not come, and similar cases, surely this condition is treated like any other condition. If he stipulated in the language of "if," the get does not take effect at all beforehand, and if she remarries, she must leave. In the condition of "from now" or "on the condition," the get takes effect immediately. We do not say that since this condition is different it should follow the rule of a condition that she must fulfill. Again, there is no difference between "if" and "on the condition," and "on the condition" does not take effect beforehand. This teaches us that it is not so.

And this is what is written: One who wishes to divorce on a condition, and the matter of his condition is that she will not be divorced until a certain time (meaning that in this case, there is no need for a condition at all, but he desires it so), he expresses this matter in the language of a condition, etc. This means that since he expresses this matter in the language of a condition, it necessitates all the laws of conditions: the positive must precede the negative, the condition must precede the action, the condition must be doubled, and "on the condition" does not require all the laws of conditions. This condition is like other conditions in matters of betrothal, purchase and sale, and the like, such as the condition "if I die" or "if I do not die". This distinction we made between conditions of divorce and other conditions only applies to a condition where she must perform an action as stated (as it appears to me). It is also possible to say that his intention is that since this condition is for setting a time, even though it is in the language of a condition and requires the laws of a condition, in this case, even "on the condition" is not like "from now", and this requires further investigation. It appears according to the first interpretation that in all matters it is similar to all conditions.

And there is proof for the Rambam that with a condition of "if you give me two hundred zuz when you marry, you shall not go out" from the Talmudic discussion (74a) where the Amoraim disagree whether a condition is as if it is now or not, both in divorce and in betrothal. In betrothal, it is said that this applies to extending her hand and accepting betrothal from another. And in divorce, it is said that this applies to the tearing of the divorce document there. And from the fact that it does not say also in divorce that it applies if she accepted betrothal from another, it is inferred that in divorce, even if she held betrothal (see Tosafot who say that it could have said this difference, but it is forced, and in betrothal 60, they wrote another answer that also according to Rabbi Yehuda, she needs a divorce out of doubt, and it needs examining, as there is still a difference between definite betrothal and doubtful betrothal as the Maharsha wrote in Gittin there in the intention of Tosafot, and examine it well).

And regarding what was ruled that in the case of "from now" she may marry from the outset, even though it was taught there as a condition that "on the condition that after" she should not marry until she gives, nevertheless, the Rambam rejected this from the halacha. For at the beginning of Chapter "HaMegarash" it is explicitly explained there that in all conditions of "on the condition that" she is permitted to marry immediately (and so wrote the Magid Mishneh in Chapter 8, Law 1, see there). And it is also possible to say that the baraita deals with a case where she does not have money, for certainly we are concerned that perhaps she will not be able to fulfill her condition.

All of this is the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, and the Raavad did not disagree with him. The Tur also brought his words, but most of our rabbis disagree with this and hold that even in the case of a conditional get, if she gets married, she must leave. Similarly, in the case of "from now," she should not marry initially. It is proper to be stringent in practice according to both opinions, and it appears that the Shulchan Aruch has adopted the opinion of those who disagree as fundamental.

The Tur writes that a divorce given on a condition is like any other act done on a condition: the act is not valid unless the condition is fulfilled. If the condition is not fulfilled, there is no divorce at all, and even if he is a Kohen, she is permitted to him. However, this is only if the condition is made in accordance with the proper halachic procedure, which requires that the condition be doubled, the condition precedes the act, the affirmative precedes the negative, the condition and the act concern different matters, the act can be carried out through an agent, and it is something she can do, as explained in the laws of betrothal. If the condition is not made according to these rules, the condition is nullified and the act remains valid. We have already explained the rules of conditions in Siman 38, and it is also explained there in section 46 that some of the early authorities hold that these rules are only required stringently and not leniently. Therefore, one should definitely follow the stringent opinion, as our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote there in section 4 (and the Chavat Yair agreed in section 4, and see there section 6). However, regarding the statement that if the condition is not fulfilled, even if he is a Kohen she is permitted to him, there is no disagreement. This is explicitly stated in the Mishnah (Gittin 81a) that she is not disqualified from marrying a Kohen if the condition is not fulfilled, even if the condition was "from now." This also applies to a Kohen who is on his deathbed and divorces his wife but does not die; she is still permitted to him.

The opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 7 of Ishut is that in a condition of "from now" (me'achshav) and similarly "on the condition that" (al menat) which is like "from now," there is no need for a double condition, nor to precede the condition to the action. However, it must be something that can be fulfilled. This is also the opinion of the Rif (Chapter 7), and this is the opinion of Rav Hai Gaon and the Raavad of blessed memory. But the Rosh of blessed memory wrote (there) that even in "from now," and certainly in "on the condition that," all the laws of conditions are necessary. This is also the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam and the Ri, the author of Tosafot (Avodah Zarah 75a). The Ramban and the Rashba of blessed memory were uncertain about this, and consequently, the ruling is to be stringent. The simple custom is that even in the condition of "from now," all the laws of conditions are practiced, just as in the condition of "a dying man who divorces from today if he dies." It is clear that because it is a dispute among the authorities, one should be stringent in all aspects. Similarly, regarding "on the condition that," some say that its law is not like "from now," as written in Siman 38.

The Tur also wrote that when the condition is fulfilled, the get (divorce document) is retroactively valid from the time of its delivery. Therefore, if the husband dies or the get is burned or lost before the condition is fulfilled, it is still considered a valid get. This applies in a case where he says "from now" or "on condition," which is equivalent to "from now." How so? If he said to her, "This is your get on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz after thirty days," the get is valid immediately, and when she gives it to him, she is retroactively divorced, even if the get is burned. However, she may not marry another person until she gives it. If she marries, the Ramah wrote that he must divorce her until the condition is fulfilled, and if she fulfills the condition, he can remain married. The Rambam wrote that she can marry immediately and we are not concerned that she might not give it, since the condition was "from now" or "on condition." But this does not seem correct, for it is explicitly stated in a Baraita that she may not marry another until she gives it. End of quote.

And behold, what is written that "on condition" (al menat) is like "from now" (me'achshav) is also the opinion of the Rambam and most of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). However, there are those who say that "on condition" is not like "from now," and we have already explained this in Siman 38. Our master, the Beit Yosef, in most places, did not concern himself with this opinion; however, in Siman 144, Section 4, regarding the condition "that the sun shall come out of its sheath" (see the Ba'er Heitev there, subsection 7), it is possible that only in a condition that happens by itself, such as the sun coming out of its sheath, where the condition does not depend on a person's action, he was concerned with this opinion because in such a case, the language of "if" does not apply so much, as it is certain that the sun will come out. Therefore, he uses the language "on condition" (al menat), meaning, "on this condition, I am giving you the get (divorce document) at the time the sun comes out of its sheath." However, our master, the Rema, in this Siman, Section 2, was concerned with this opinion in all cases, and we follow the stringent approach in every matter.

And what is written in the name of the Ra'avad that he should separate from her until the condition is fulfilled, the intention is not to divorce her with a get (bill of divorce) but rather mere separation. And as it is written in the Shulchan Aruch, section 2, and these are his words: "He should separate from her until the condition is fulfilled." And what is written in the name of the Rambam, we have already explained to reconcile his words in section 2. And some say that if the condition is within her power to fulfill and it is a passive condition, she is allowed to marry immediately because we do not worry that she will actively transgress it. But a condition that is not within her power, even if it is passive, or a condition that is active, even if it is within her power, she is forbidden to marry until the condition is fulfilled (Ran, chapter 7). In the Shulchan Aruch, this opinion is agreed upon, and this is the primary ruling. The Tur did not mention here whether he can nullify the condition with "from now," but at the end of the section, he wrote the language of the Rambam in chapter 8 that we brought, and he agreed with all his words, except regarding what permits "from now" to marry, he disputed him. And it seems that he also agrees with the Rambam that with "from now" he cannot nullify the condition. And if he can nullify it as we explained, and so it is concluded in Shulchan Aruch, section 2. And there are those who say that even with "from now" he can nullify, and it is proper to be stringent.

The Tur also wrote that if one did not say "from now" and "on condition," but rather said, "This is your bill of divorce if you give me two hundred zuz after thirty days," it does not take effect until the time of giving. If the bill of divorce was torn or lost before the giving, she is not divorced, end quote. And certainly if he died [before the giving]. Now, the Tur did not mention how he holds regarding if she married before the condition was fulfilled—whether she must leave [the second husband] according to the opinion of most authorities, or if she does not need to leave according to the opinion of the Rambam. At the end of the section, the Tur copied the words of the Rambam and did not disagree with him on this matter, implying that he holds like him. Therefore, we wrote in Section 21 that the Tur agrees with the Rambam. However, our teacher the Beit Yosef omitted the words of the Rambam in Section 2 and, on the contrary, wrote that if she married, she must leave. Likewise, in Section 148, he intentionally omitted the opinion that if she married, she does not need to leave (and the Beit Shmuel in sub-paragraph 2 wrote that the Beit Yosef holds like the Rambam, which is questionable and not so, and the Gra in sub-paragraph 8 also wrote similarly, see there).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote at the end of Section 2 that there is an opinion that even if one does not say "from now" or "from today" or "on the condition," it is considered as if he said "from today" because the date on the get (divorce document) proves it. Therefore, we are stringent in this matter. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that there is an opinion that even with a condition of "from now," it can be nullified, and one should be stringent.

The explanation of these matters is that Rabbi Yose holds (Bava Batra 136a) that a gift document that has a date is considered as if it says "from today," and this is the halacha, as the Rambam wrote at the end of the Laws of Acquisition and Gifts, and the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 258. It is also stated in the Talmud in Gittin (72a) that this applies to a get as well. However, the Rambam did not rule this way regarding gittin, and there were those who wondered about his reasoning (Ran, end of Chapter 7). But his reasoning is because it is said that Rav established to write in the get "from this day" to exclude the opinion of Rabbi Yose (Gittin 85b). And indeed, Rashi wrote that this is merely for enhancement, but for the halacha, we follow Rabbi Yose. Several of the Rishonim wrote similarly, though some are uncertain about this (Arba'ah Turim, end of Chapter 7). The Tur in Siman 144 also has doubts about this. From the words of the Rif in Chapter 8 of Bava Batra, it is clear that due to the stringency of gittin, we do not rule according to Rabbi Yose. It is explicitly stated there that we do not rule leniently like him but not stringently either (Ran there). However, the Rambam holds that due to Rav's enactment, this opinion was dismissed from the law. For the halacha, we certainly follow our teacher, the Beit Yosef, that we are stringent in this matter.

In my humble opinion, it seems to me that we have already explained in Choshen Mishpat, section 158, paragraph 3, that this ruling, which we hold, applies when the giver instructed to write the date. If so, why did he instruct to write, since the giver of the gift is transferring it after death? He should have written that it should be acquired after his death. Rather, it is certain that this means that it is from today and after death, so that the body is acquired from today and the fruits after death. But when the giver did not instruct to write the date and the witnesses themselves wrote it, as is the manner of deed writers, there is no proof from the date that his intention was from today. See there, and the reasoning is logical. Accordingly, also in a bill of divorce, this law only applies if the husband instructed to write the date. It is not customary for the scribe to write on his own beyond the enactment of our sages to write the date. In such a case, we certainly hold like the Rabbis. This is what the Rif wrote in Gittin (chapter 7), and the halacha follows the Rabbis in standard bills of divorce. What is written in Bava Batra, that we hold strictly in this regard, applies when the husband instructed. (And regarding the Rif's question in Bava Batra, about Rav's contradiction, and his answer due to stringency, see there: this implies that Rav enacted this in all cases, and this answers the questions posed to him. Therefore, the Rambam, who deals with standard bills of divorce, omitted this entirely. Delve deeply into this matter.)

Furthermore, the Tur wrote in Choshen Mishpat there in the name of the Ramah that specifically when one gives a gift to take effect after his death, we say that the date on the document proves its validity. For why would he need to write the date? He should write that he is giving it to him after his death. But in the case of a gift set for a certain time, such as after 30 days, we do not say that the date on the document proves its validity, because it is necessary to write the date to know when the 30 days are up. And so our master the Rema ruled there. Consequently, regarding a get (divorce document), since it cannot take effect after death, as a get after death is not valid, we do not say that the date on the document proves its validity. And the Talmud in Gittin there indeed deals with the matter if one divorces from today and after his death, see there (and there is a question on the Shach’s query in Choshen Mishpat there, subparagraph 2, see there). This is also clearly implied from the precise language of the Rambam at the end of the laws of Acquisition, who holds like the Ramah, see there. Therefore, he omitted this. However, in practice, one should be stringent and say that it is a doubtful legal matter, as ruled by the Tur and Shulchan Aruch.

And this is what our master, the Rema, wrote: "There are those who say that even with a condition of 'from now,' it can be nullified, and one should be stringent." From his words, it seems that in all matters of conditions of 'from now,' there are those who say it can be nullified. I have not clarified who these dissenters are. It is true that the Tur wrote at the end of this section in the name of the responsa of the Rosh, regarding someone who gave a get (divorce) with the condition of 'from now' if he does not come within two years, that he can nullify the condition and she can remarry immediately. And the same applies to any condition, even if the condition is for her benefit. And so too wrote the Itur, see there. However, the Rosh clearly explained his words in his responsa (Klal 46) that it is specifically in a condition that was not to her detriment, and on the contrary, for her benefit, like this condition that if he comes within the time, he returns to her, he can nullify it and the get is retroactively valid. But in a condition that is to her detriment, like "on the condition that you give me 200 zuz," if he nullifies it, his words are meaningless, for he gave the get on a condition to cause her distress, and he did not distress her, see there. And so too wrote our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great work, see there. And what the Tur wrote, "even if the condition is for her benefit," he means to say, and how much more so a condition that is neither for her benefit nor to her detriment. And it is possible that the Itur also holds this view, for the Tur aligns his opinion with that of the Rosh, as he wrote.

And behold, the Ra'avad also wrote in Chapter 9, Law 9, that in the case of a condition, as long as the condition has not been fulfilled, it can be nullified. His words end there. And it is clear that he is not referring to a case of "from now," because if that were the case, why did Rambam remain silent in Chapter 8, Law 1, where he wrote that a condition of "from now" cannot be nullified? It is a rule among the decisors that in any place where the Ra'avad did not object to Rambam, he agreed with him. Therefore, it is certain that the Ra'avad only spoke concerning a condition set for a future time, as is explained there. And in this case, too, he is not referring at all to a condition of "from now."

Similarly, the Ramban, of blessed memory, who holds that even in a condition of "on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz," it can be annulled only if she also agrees to its annulment. Then the get (divorce document) is nullified. But he himself cannot annul it, as the Ran, of blessed memory, writes in his name (in the seventh chapter). However, that he would have the ability to annul the condition and validate the get without the condition, we have not heard from his words. The Ran himself holds that even both of them cannot annul it, except in a condition that is for her benefit, as mentioned. On the contrary, the Maggid Mishneh writes that the Ramban and the Rashba ruled like the Rambam, as mentioned. Only the Mordechai writes (there) and states: "This requires further investigation, for it is possible to say that 'on the condition' and 'from now' does not help except after the condition is fulfilled, but before it is fulfilled, he can annul it and retract." And there it discusses also the condition of giving two hundred zuz, as mentioned. And even the Mordechai did not rule explicitly thus but remains uncertain about it. And since most of our rabbis do not hold this way, it seems this is the main ruling in practice. Nevertheless, since it has come from the mouth of our Rabbi, the Rema, to be stringent, one should not be lenient except in a case of a chained woman (agunah) and in pressing circumstances (see the Gra, note 17, where it appears from his words that the Raavad and the Rosh hold this way, and this requires further investigation).

He said to her, "On the condition that you give me two hundred zuz from now until thirty days," and he died within the thirty days before she gave it to him, she cannot fulfill the condition and give it to the heirs, as it implies "to me" specifically and not to the heirs (Gemara 74 and the first opinion). The Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 3, ruled that since it says "to me" and not "to my heirs," the divorce is nullified, and she must perform chalitzah or yibbum. From the language of the Tur, it seems that as soon as he dies, the divorce is nullified, and this reasoning is correct because it is impossible to fulfill the condition. However, from the language of the Shulchan Aruch, which states "since the thirty days have passed and she did not give it to him, the divorce is nullified," it implies that before the thirty days are completed, the divorce is not yet nullified, even though it is impossible to fulfill. This is also clarified from the language of the Rambam in Chapter 8, end of Halacha 21, where he follows his reasoning in Chapter 9, Halacha 11, saying "from now, if I do not come within twelve months," and he died within the twelve months, that even though it is impossible for him to come, nevertheless, as long as the time has not passed, she should not marry, because we require the condition to be nullified in actual reality and not potentially as long as it has not come to fruition (Maggid Mishneh). The Tur follows his reasoning in Section 144 that in the case where we are strict about "from now, if I do not come within twelve months," and he died, that she should wait until the twelve months are completed, this is because of a decree lest he might have died. But fundamentally, since it is impossible to fulfill the condition, the get is nullified immediately, and she can perform yibbum. (This appears to me.)

The Rambam further wrote there: If a man said to his wife, "This is your get (divorce document) on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz," and he did not set a time limit, and he died before she gave it, she cannot give it to his heirs, for he conditioned it only that she give it to him. Nevertheless, the get is not nullified, for he did not set a time limit. Therefore, even if the get was lost or torn before he died, she may not marry another man until she performs chalitzah (the ritual of removing a shoe). This is also written in the Shulchan Aruch there, and this follows his (the Rambam's) reasoning that even though the condition cannot be fulfilled because he died, still, as long as the get is not explicitly nullified, meaning the time set has passed and she has not given it, the get is not completely nullified. Consequently, when no time was set, the condition can never be fulfilled, and therefore she cannot marry without chalitzah. The Tur brought his words and objected as follows: "I do not understand his words. Since she can never fulfill the condition, why should the get not be nullified?" And he (the Tur) did not hold of this distinction between potential nullification and actual nullification, since it can never come into effect.

And regarding the main issue that they ruled "to me specifically and not to my heirs" in the Gemara (74a), there is a dispute about this. For Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel holds "to me and even to my heirs," while the Rambam and the Tur/Shulchan Aruch ruled like the first Tanna. However, there are those who rule like Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel that she can give to the heirs (Hagahot Maimoniot Chapter 8 in the name of the Tosafot). And this is also elucidated from the words of Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) in paragraph 8, that for any delay which is not caused by her, we should be stringent, and it will be explained there with God's help (and so writes the Beit Shmuel in subparagraph 5).

However, in this law, it seems to me that there is no practical difference. What will she gain if she gives to the heirs? In the end, she will not be exempt without chalitzah due to the opinion of the Rambam and the Tur/Shulchan Aruch. But the practical difference is when a time is set; she should not perform Yibbum (levirate marriage) when the time arrives, and she always performs chalitzah and not Yibbum. And this is also when she gives to the heirs. But if she does not give, according to all opinions, the get (divorce) is nullified when the time arrives, and according to all opinions, she either performs chalitzah or Yibbum.

And if so, what will she gain if she gives to the heirs? And one cannot say that she will gain when she does not want to perform Yibbum, because then if she gives to the heirs, the court will not allow the levir to perform Yibbum with her and will compel him to perform chalitzah according to her will. For if they want to compel her to perform Yibbum, they will not accept the money from her, and the get will be nullified because giving against one's will is not considered giving, as will be explained, unless the heir is the father and he accepts the money, and automatically, the brother will not be able to perform Yibbum with her.

And know that what we have written according to the opinion of the Rambam, that as long as the condition has not yet been fulfilled, even though it is impossible for it to be fulfilled, nevertheless until the time comes she is not considered divorced. This is also written by the Maggid Mishneh. If so, how did the Rambam write that in the case of "from now if you do not give me 200 zuz within 30 days" she can marry immediately and we are not concerned that she might not fulfill the condition? Even though she will fulfill it, the condition has still not been fulfilled, and we must distinguish between the negation of the condition and the fulfillment of the condition. In the fulfillment of the condition, even though it has not yet come into effect, it is considered as if it has been fulfilled, unlike in the case of its negation. There is a significant reason for this matter: the fact that the condition negates the act is a decree of the Torah, and therefore we require all the laws of conditions. Therefore, in the fulfillment of the condition to uphold the act, it is considered as if it has been fulfilled from now, since the act has already been accomplished. However, in the negation of the condition to nullify the act, we do not say that the act is nullified until the negation of the condition has come into effect. As long as the negation has not come into effect, the act is not nullified, since it has already been done (in my opinion).

However, the language of the Rambam, who wrote "even though the get was lost, she should not remarry until she performs chalitzah," is very puzzling. This is not an additional stringency at all, as it is obvious that since the condition cannot be fulfilled, the get is nullified, and she requires chalitzah. The additional stringency is that she is forbidden to perform yibbum (levirate marriage). Therefore, it should have said "even though the get was lost, she performs chalitzah and does not perform yibbum" (Magid Mishneh). Moreover, there are other precise points in his language (see there in the Magid Mishneh). It appears to me that this is what it means: even without setting a specific time, we say "to me and not to my heirs." We do not say that since no time was set for its delivery and it is within her power to deliver it whenever she wishes, even after a long time, that surely, even if he dies, she can give it to his heirs. We do not say this. Rather, even in such a case, it is "to me and not to my heirs." Therefore, the get is never nullified, as it is within her power to give it even after a long time. And even if the get was lost during his lifetime, as it has already been explained that in a condition of "from now," we do not worry about the loss of the get, and she can fulfill the condition after his death. I might have said that in such a case, where the get was already lost during his lifetime, it is obvious that his intention was that she should fulfill it even after his death by giving it to his heirs. Since the get was already lost, the bond between them was already dissolved. Therefore, it comes to inform us that even in such a case, the condition cannot be fulfilled, and therefore, she should not remarry until she performs chalitzah.

From the words of the Rambam, it is clarified that if someone says, "on the condition that you give me 200 zuz," and no time frame is set, she is able to give it even after many years. And even though above in Siman 114 it is ruled that if a man marries a woman and agrees to support her daughter for five years, he is obligated to support her immediately for the first five years, as stated there, and this is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, Ketubot (Chapter 12), it can be said that it is not comparable. There, he betrothed her on that condition, and we can testify that her intention was on that condition since her daughter needs to eat. Therefore, the obligation falls immediately. This is not the case here; certainly, she requested the divorce from him. Otherwise, who forces her to give the money? And he gives her the get (divorce document) on the condition that she gives him the money, which depends on her discretion as to when she wants to give it. Nevertheless, even here, if it appears from the context that his intention was for the condition to be fulfilled immediately, like "on the condition that you serve my father for two years" or "on the condition that you nurse my son for two years," it is certainly understood to mean the first two years, as will be explained with God's help. The reason is that since the father needs to be served and the son needs to be nursed, why should they wait for a later time? Therefore, the obligation falls immediately. This is not the case with "on the condition that you give me 200 zuz," as I have written and as explained in Chapter 8, Halacha 22, and what seems correct to me, I have written.

Rambam wrote (there): "This is your get (divorce document) on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz from now until thirty days. If she gave it within thirty days with his consent, she is divorced; after thirty days, she is not divorced. If she gave it to him against his will and he does not want to accept it, it is an invalid get until she gives it with his consent. If he later said to her within the thirty days, 'It is forgiven to you,' she is not divorced because the condition was not fulfilled." And indeed, what he wrote, that if it is given against his will the get is invalid, his intention is that it is invalid rabbinically because he holds that from the essence of the law, giving against his will is considered giving, and therefore, from the Torah, the get is valid. However, rabbinically, it is invalid (Beit Shmuel, section 7). In the Gemara (75a), there is a dispute about this, and the Rosh and the Rashba ruled that she is doubtfully divorced, and it is a doubt from the Torah (and similarly, the Ran wrote in the name of others there). Even according to the Rambam, it seems that specifically when he at least accepted it, and some say that even if he did not accept it, since she wanted to give it, it is considered giving according to the Rambam (Beit Yosef in the name of his teacher). Some have deduced this from his language, where he wrote, "and he does not want to accept" (and so wrote Beit Shmuel, section 7). They also wrote that when he accepted it, even against his will, according to all opinions, it is considered giving (there). It does not seem so from the words of the Rosh and the Rashba there. Therefore, according to the law, in any case, she is doubtfully divorced, and one should not be lenient about this. And not in his presence, it certainly is not considered giving.

And this that is written, that if he retracted and said within the thirty days, "It is forgiven to you," she is not divorced, and it implies that the get is certainly nullified, even if he dies afterward (see there, subparagraph 8), since the condition was not fulfilled at all. And it has already been explained that in a case of "on condition" and "from now," he cannot add to his condition or nullify it. And we do not say that forgiveness is like the fulfillment of the condition, for he says, "It is as if I have received it," since the condition was to cause her distress, and behold, he did not distress her (Gemara 74b).

And the Rashba (of blessed memory) wrote (there) that all this is in the case where he says "You are released from me," but if he said to her, "This is your get without any condition," she is divorced and he does not need to take it back from her. The reason for this is that certainly he cannot nullify the condition based on the first giving, but if he nullifies the first giving and makes another giving without a condition, she is divorced by this giving. And if it is difficult to understand, that if so, he should take it back from her and then return and give it to her, in truth, this is not necessary. And this is similar to what is written in Siman 138, where if he gave her the get while she was sleeping and she awoke and he said to her, "This is your get," it is sufficient, and he does not need to take it back from her. There, even without taking it back from her, it is considered as another giving. And it is not similar to the case of a messenger who did not say "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed" at the time of the giving, where he needs to take it back from her and give it again and say "In my presence it was written and in my presence it was signed," as written in Siman 142, because there the enactment was specifically to say it at the time of giving, as mentioned there. And it is also not similar to what is written in Siman 137, where he said to her, "You are divorced except from so-and-so," where he needs to take it back from her and release her completely with a second giving. There, the reason is because the first giving has the effect of invalidating her for priesthood, as mentioned there. Therefore, it is necessary to make a second giving. But here, without fulfilling the condition, she is not invalidated for priesthood, and the first giving does not help at all. Therefore, the second statement he says to her, "This is your get" or "This is your get without any condition," is considered as a new giving, as if he is giving it to her now. (And what the Beit Shmuel wrote at the end of subparagraph 9 is difficult to understand, and perhaps there is an error in the text, and it should say, "Nevertheless, one can nullify the giving, etc.") See what is written in paragraph 60 there.

And know that it was taught in a Tosefta (Chapter 5): "This is your divorce on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz," and then he retracted and said, "This is your divorce from now," he has said nothing. What should he do? He should take it back from her and give it to her again. Thus is the conclusion. This implies that a new giving is needed. Indeed, if he gave it to her while she was asleep and she woke up, there is a dispute in the Gemara (78a) whether a new giving is required or not. And we hold according to the opinion that a new giving is not required. The Tosefta holds according to the other opinion, and we do not rule this way (Rashba there).

He said to her, "This is your get (divorce document) on the condition that you give me a certain utensil or a certain garment," and that utensil or garment was lost or stolen. Even if she gave him a thousand zuz (a large sum of money) in its place, it is not a valid get until she gives him that specific utensil or garment that he mentioned. And so the Halacha (Jewish law) is decided in the Talmud (Gittin 75a, not according to Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel). The reason is that the condition was not fulfilled, as money is not the same as a garment, and we do not say, "What difference does it make if it is the item itself or its value?" because ultimately the condition was not fulfilled. Additionally, it is generally assumed that anyone who divorces does so out of animosity. Therefore, we say that he certainly intended to cause her distress, and his intention was specifically for the garment or the utensil (Rashi, Gittin 74b). Also here, if he wants to make another stipulation, he does not need to take it from her; he only needs to say to her, "This is your get without any condition," and it will be like a different giving, as stated in section 42 in the name of the Rashba (and this is also the intention of the Rambam as explained by the Maggid Mishneh).

And regarding the aforementioned law, the Rosh wrote as follows: "It seems that from his own intention it is a valid get (bill of divorce), and even though 'they are forgiven for you' it is not a get, because there she did not cause him distress, but here, since she gave the money and caused distress about the garment itself, he can forgive." End of quote. Similarly, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 6, wrote: "There is one who says that if he consents to accept the money, it is a get." End of quote. These matters are perplexing, for if so, it must be said that the dispute in the Talmud is when he does not consent to accept the money, and it is impossible to say this because an involuntary giving is not considered giving according to all opinions. It is possible to differentiate that specifically when he completely retracts from his condition, not wanting to accept according to the condition, we say that an involuntary giving is not considered giving. But if he wants the condition to be fulfilled and the difference is between the vessel and the money, it is considered giving. (This is the intention of the Beit Shmuel, section 10.) And from the Rashba, it is explicitly clear that even if he wants to accept the money, this is not fulfilling the condition, see there. Therefore, this law requires further study, and it is a doubtful case of law, and several of the great authorities have challenged this (Rashi, Dov, Bach, and Maharshal).

He said to her, "On the condition that you give me two hundred zuz from now until thirty days," even if she did not give it to him until the thirtieth day at its end, she is divorced. But if he said to her, "At the beginning of the first day of the month, from now until thirty days," and she gave him the money at the end of the first night of the second month, it is uncertain whether she is divorced.
