For it is uncertain to us if thirty days means an exact thirty-day period, in which case the time has passed, or if thirty days means as people commonly say, and there is no strictness about exceeding one night, and she requires a second divorce. If he dies before giving her a second divorce, she performs chalitzah and does not enter into levirate marriage (Tur).

Rambam wrote in Chapter 8, Law 19: If he stipulates that she should do something without specifying a time, it is as if he specified one day, since he did not specify how long she should do it. How so? He said to her, "This is your get (divorce document) on the condition that you do work with me," or "on the condition that you serve my father," or "on the condition that you nurse my son." If she did work with him or served his father for one day, or nursed his son for one day within the time that the child is nursing, which is within 24 months, it is a valid get. If the son or the father died before she could nurse or serve, it is not a valid get. He said to her, "on the condition that you nurse my son or serve my father for two years," she must fulfill the time specified. If the son or the father died within that time, or if the father said, "I do not want her to serve me," it is not a valid get, because the condition was not fulfilled. Similarly, in all such cases, the same rule applies. (And he ruled according to Rav Ashi (75b) as the Rif mentioned there, and also ruled according to the first tanna of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel in the Mishnah there, that even in cases where the delay is not due to her, it is not a valid get.)

And even though in monetary matters when a person obligates themselves without specifying a time, their intention is for as long as needed, in the case of divorce, the reason is that it is established that anyone who divorces his wife intends to cause her distress and not for his own benefit. For most divorces are due to hatred, and causing her distress for one day is sufficient. This is different from monetary matters where if someone says "on condition that she serves or provides for him," his intention is certainly for as long as needed (Ran in the name of the Rashba). We also explained this in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 60, Se'if 6, with G-d's help, see there. 

And one cannot say, "From where do we know that his intention is only to cause her distress? Perhaps he also intended for his own benefit?" It can be answered that if this were the case, he would have specified that she should nurse or serve for such and such a time to cause her more distress. But certainly, since he did not specify, his intention was only to cause her distress, and one day is sufficient (so it seems to me). Therefore, if the son or father dies before the nursing or serving, it is not a valid divorce since his condition was not fulfilled at all, as his intention was to cause her distress and she was not distressed. 

And even without this, the condition must necessarily be fulfilled. Therefore, if he stipulated two years and they died before the time, or if the father does not want her service, even if she did not provoke him and the delay is not from her, nevertheless, ultimately, the condition was not fulfilled (and the Ran wrote similarly according to the Rambam's view, see there). 

And some say that according to this opinion (of Rav Ashi), in a case of an unspecified time, one day is sufficient. If they died before and she did not nurse or serve at all, it is a valid divorce, since he did not specify the time, his intention was for when she would need to, and when she does not need to, the condition does not delay (Tosafot and Rashba). And certainly, in all cases, one should be stringent (Beit Shmuel, section 15). 

And indeed, in the Jerusalem Talmud (there), there is a dispute about this, see there. And some say that if he stipulated two years and they died before the two years were completed or the father does not want her service and she did not provoke him, it is also a valid divorce, as any delay not from her is considered a valid divorce (Rosh in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, Rabbi Yitzchak, and Rashba Gaon). And it is obvious that in this case too, one should be stringent in every matter since it is a dispute among the authorities.

However, the Rosh of blessed memory and other early authorities ruled that even if he simply said, "on the condition that you nurse my son" or "that you serve my father," she is required to nurse the child for up to two years and serve the father for his entire lifetime (as per Rava there). Since he did not specify a time, his intention is for as long as it is needed. In this case, it is clear that if she began to nurse or serve even for a single moment and they died, it would be considered a valid divorce since the condition was fulfilled. But if he says he does not want her service anymore, even if she did not anger him, this requires further consideration. It seems more reasonable that in such a case, if no time was set and she began to serve and the father no longer wishes her service, and she did not anger him, it is considered that the condition was fulfilled (as the Beit Shmuel wrote at the end of section 16, and this is also evident from the arrangement of the Mishnah that the dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis is only regarding the setting of time, and this is also apparent from the early authorities).

It appears to me that in the case where a man stipulates "on the condition that you work for me," even the Rosh would agree with the Rambam that if he stated it generally, it means for one day. Otherwise, what limit would there be to this condition? For example, with nursing, the limit is as long as the child is not two years old; with serving the father, it would be for the lifetime of the father or for the lifetime of a certain person, which would be considered a severance as will be explained. However, if we say that the requirement to perform labor is indefinite, meaning she would have to work for him all her life, this would not be considered a severance at all, similar to the condition "on the condition that you do not drink wine all your life," as will be explained. Presumably, his intention was not to cancel the divorce because of this condition. However, it is possible to say that since he said "on the condition that you work for me," the condition applies for his entire lifetime, which would be considered a severance as will be explained. Further investigation is needed.

The Tur wrote that during the specified time, she is not allowed to marry, lest the condition not be fulfilled. I do not understand what this adds, as in all conditions, the Tur holds that she is not allowed to marry before the condition is fulfilled, and this has already been explained there. It seems to me that it means to inform us that even according to the Rambam, who in all conditions of "from now" or "on the condition" permits her to marry and we do not worry that the condition will not be fulfilled, as he wrote. Nevertheless, in such a condition that depends on others, like in service where the father might not agree to her service, or in nursing where the child might die within the specified time, or might not want to nurse from her, or her milk might stop, and similar cases, even the Rambam agrees that she should not marry until the condition is fulfilled if a time was set. According to the Rosh, this applies even if no time was set, as explained.

Based on what has been explained, according to the Rosh, even in a general case, she needs to nurse until the child is twenty-four months old. Consequently, if the child is one year old at the time of the divorce, she does not need to nurse for two more years, but only for one more year, and similarly in all such cases. The Tur writes in the name of the Ramah that this applies when the condition was made before the child was two years old; we say that his intention is until the child is two years old. But if the condition was made after the child has completed two years, we say that his intention is for as long as it is appropriate to nurse, up to four or five years. The Rosh disagrees, arguing that, on the contrary, if the condition was made afterwards, even if she only nursed for one hour, she has fulfilled the condition. And logically this is correct, for in such a case, it is clear that his intention is only to cause her distress and not for the benefit of the child, and one hour is sufficient. (See the glosses of Maharlanach who raises an objection from the Talmud but does not resolve it in this manner, and examine this carefully).

Additionally, it is written: "It seems to me that if he said 'on the condition that you nurse my son for six months,' we consider whether the remaining time for nursing the child, that is, until he reaches two years old, is more than six months. If so, then surely he does not intend to cause her distress but rather to ease her burden so that she does not have to nurse the child for the full twenty-four months. Therefore, if the child dies after she has nursed him for a short time, it is a valid get (divorce). However, if less than six months remain for the nursing period, then clearly, since he specified six months, he intends to distress her. If the child dies within those six months, it is not a valid get." Thus ends the quote. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote on this matter that the words are not compelling. He did not explain his reasoning. It seems to me that his reasoning is that since we hold that even if the delay is not caused by her, it is not a valid get if a time was set and the time was not completed, as we have written. So, what difference does this case make? It must be that the Tur holds that since the child needs to nurse for more than six months and he eased her burden by only requiring six months, presumably his intention was also that if there was no need for even six months, it would still be a valid get. However, this is not necessarily the case, for perhaps he did not want the child to nurse for the full two years. Hence, this remains a doubtful ruling. I am puzzled that these laws are not mentioned at all in the Shulchan Aruch.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 9: "Some say that when we state that if she nursed or had intercourse for one day, it counts as a valid divorce, it is not specifically one day, for even one hour suffices. There is also an opinion that it must be one complete day, including the night and the day." These words are puzzling, for when we say "one day," it is not specifically one day; this applies generally, as Tosafot and the Tur have written, and no one would ever dispute this. This is the law he mentioned himself previously in section 8, so why did he write it as "some say"? And that which he wrote, "There is an opinion that it must be one complete day, including the night and the day," is the opinion of the Rema in the Tur when he explicitly stated "one day," and he holds that even a period of a full 24 hours is not sufficient if it does not include a complete night and day, as explained in the Tur. What is the connection between these two concepts? (And this is the intention of the Ba'er Heitev in section 18).

However, his intention is clear, but he abbreviated his words. From the words of the Ran, it is explicitly proven that even if he specifies one day, one hour is sufficient. For in the Gemara, there is an establishment here in a general case and here in a specified case, meaning in a general case two years are needed, and in a specified case, one day is sufficient (the establishment of Rava). And the Ran wrote that according to everyone, "one day" is not literal but even one hour, end quote. And it means that for all establishments, this is the case, and so he wrote earlier regarding the entire subject that specifically when she did not begin to nurse at all, but if she began to nurse, where it is not necessary until two years, it is sufficient. And it is explicitly implied that this also applies to specifying one day, see there. Therefore, he wrote this in the name of those who say, and consequently, this opinion is different from the opinion of the Ramah in the Tur. And from the words of the Rashba, it is explicitly clarified that he does not agree with the Ramah, who wrote in specifying one day, even though he is lenient on her, he specifically meant that if he dies before she nurses him, she is not divorced, end quote. And it is explicitly implied that if she nursed him a little, she is divorced, because since he said one day, his intention was not specifically for a day but rather to nurse him a little. Therefore, in law, it is a doubtful divorce (and because in the Shulchan Aruch, the law of specifying one day is not mentioned at all, the Beit Shmuel had difficulty with his words, thinking it referred to a general case).

If he stipulated with her on the condition that she would pay for the nursing, it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that even according to the opinion that generally considers a single day sufficient, when he specifies payment for nursing, his intention is for the entire two years. Additionally, it is implied there that if the child dies before the two years, she is not required to pay more, since she paid for the entire time the child was alive (see Beit Shmuel, section 12, who is brief in his explanation). However, if she did not begin to pay at all and the child dies, it is not a valid divorce, since the condition was not fulfilled at all. And if he said on the condition that she pays for two years of nursing, even if the child dies before, she must pay him in full, as it is explicitly implied in the Jerusalem Talmud that this is as if he said on the condition that she nurses for two years. And it appears to me that this is what we have learned in the Tosefta (chapter 5): "On the condition that you serve my father for two years, on the condition that you nurse my son for two years," the condition must be fulfilled even after death. There is no other explanation for this except that certainly, it refers to when he said payment for two years of nursing or service. If the father or the child dies before the two years, she must pay the fee up to two years to the husband.

It is stated in the Gemara (76a): The Rabbis taught: If a man said to his wife in the presence of two witnesses, "This is your bill of divorce on the condition that you serve my father for two years," and then he said to her in the presence of two witnesses, "This is your bill of divorce on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz," his last statement does not cancel his first statement. If she wishes, she may serve his father; if she wishes, she may give him two hundred zuz. But if he said to her in the presence of two witnesses, "This is your bill of divorce on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz," and then he said to her in the presence of two witnesses, "on the condition that you give me three hundred zuz," his last statement cancels his first statement. Rashi explained that in the first instance, he did not deliver the bill of divorce to her in their presence, for if he had delivered it, she would have been divorced under that condition, and he would not be able to stipulate another condition. Rather, he said in their presence, "When I deliver it to her, I will deliver it under this condition." And in the second instance, he delivered the bill of divorce (there). We have already written this in the name of the Rambam, of blessed memory, that in the case of a condition "on the condition that," he cannot add to or cancel the condition. Therefore, Rashi, of blessed memory, was forced to explain this way. And so wrote the Tur, see there. It is obvious that according to the opinion we explained, even in the condition of "from now," he can cancel it, and the Baraita can be understood in its simple meaning.

And behold, the Rambam, of blessed memory, copied the language of the Talmud in Chapter 8, Law 18, but did not explain it. It is necessary to say that his intention is also like Rashi's explanation, since he holds that "on condition" (בע"מ) cannot be nullified. This is difficult, and it seems more likely that the Rambam is dealing with a condition of "if" and not "on condition" (according to the Maggid Mishneh). It appears clearly so, as he wrote: "one who gives a get (divorce document) to his wife on a condition, etc." and omitted the Talmud's language of "on condition." He holds that the Baraita means that "on condition" is not considered as "from now," and therefore it can be nullified. But we hold that it is considered as "from now," and it is necessary to explain it this way. In truth, according to Rashi's explanation, it is difficult, because since the first time he did not give it to her, and the second time he gave it to her, we should only consider the second time when he gave it to her. This is indeed the opinion of the Ramban, of blessed memory, as the Maggid Mishneh wrote there. He added that the Talmud is dealing with a case where even the second time he did not give it to her, and afterward, he gave it to her unconditionally in the presence of two sets of witnesses. So wrote the Ran there. This is the opinion of our teacher, the Rema, in Section 10, but he should not have written this regarding the words of the Mechaber, which are like the words of the Rambam, who omitted the language of "on condition." It is possible that he holds like the first explanation, that the Rambam and the Mechaber are dealing with "on condition" and did not give it to her the first time, as Rashi explained. This also seems to be implied in the Tosefta there.

However, in truth, it can be said according to the straightforward understanding of the Rambam that he is referring to a conditional (get) and he handed it to her the first time. It has already been explained in section 42 that although he cannot nullify (the condition), nevertheless when he makes another handing over and says to her, "This should be your get without any condition," he has the ability to do so, and he does not need to take the get back from her, as stated there in the name of the Rashba. According to this, it is well explained, for here it is stated in the language of the Talmud that when he said to her the second time, "This is your get on condition," and she agreed to this, it is considered as another handing over (of the get) (refer to Ran). However, the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch did not write in the language of the Talmud but rather wrote, "and he reverted and stipulated another condition." And the clarification in his words as written earlier is that he is not referring to a conditional (get) but rather to a condition of "if" (refer also to Beit Shmuel section 19).

And know that from Rashi and the Tur it is evident that they do not agree with the opinion of the Rashba, which we wrote about in section 42. According to the Rashba, who holds that with a different giving, one can nullify the previous condition even if it was given on condition (al menat). If so, who forced them to interpret that he did not give it to her in the first giving? Rather, it is certain that they hold that even in such a case, he cannot nullify it, even if she also agrees to this, unless she returns the get to him and makes an entirely new giving, as per the simple understanding of the Tosefta that we brought in section 43. Also, the Ran of blessed memory was astounded by this ruling, and his words are: "And certainly this is a wonder, for since he gave it to her on condition (al menat), which is like saying 'from now,' how is it in their power to nullify it?" And he is referring there to a case where he says to her afterward, "This is your get on condition, etc.," which is like a different giving. Therefore, this ruling of the Rashba is a doubtful matter of law, and one should be stringent in every situation.

And we learn from the words of our Sages that when one stipulates two conditions one after the other, if they pertain to the same matter, the latter condition nullifies the former. This is true whether the second condition adds to the first, such as if the first condition mentioned a hundred and the second two hundred, or vice versa, where it reduces from the first (Tur). If the second condition pertains to a different matter, the latter does not nullify the former, and she can choose whichever condition she prefers. If the first condition was made in the presence of Reuven and Shimon, and the second in the presence of Levi and Yehuda, and the second condition is about a different matter which does not nullify the first, it must then be presented before all of them. Only then can she choose whichever condition she prefers, and not in any other manner (as is evident from the words of the Maimonides and the Rema; be precise). And our Sages said there that a witness from the first group and a witness from the second group do not combine when the second condition is about a different matter. They do not combine to testify that there was a condition in this get. As long as two witnesses from the first group or two from the second group do not come, the get is valid by the signatures of the witnesses, and they do not have the power to establish a condition in the get (Ran there). The reason why a witness from one group and a witness from the other do not combine, even though in all prohibitions and monetary matters they do combine, is because each condition is an entirely different matter (Beit Shmuel, section 2).

He said to her, "This is your get, but the paper is mine," she is not divorced (Gemara 20b). Since the paper is his, he has given her nothing, and it is as if the letters are floating in the air (Rashi). However, if he said, "On the condition that the paper is mine," she is divorced, because a condition is considered as if it is from now, and it is like a gift on the condition of return, which is considered a valid giving, provided she returns it in the end, fulfilling the condition, and then the get is valid from the time it came into her hand (Tosafot). But if "on the condition" is not considered as if it is from now, then the get's effectiveness is at the time of the condition's fulfillment, and by then the get has been returned to him, so with what will she be divorced? It has already been explained in Siman 38 that with a condition, the laws of conditions do not apply, though there are those who disagree. If he said to her, "This is your get, and the paper between the lines is mine, yet the get shall be bound as one book," there is a question unresolved in the Gemara there, and it remains a doubtful get.

It has already been explained in Siman 38 that a condition which cannot be fulfilled is not a valid condition; the condition is void and the act remains valid, as it is considered merely as idle talk and jest, for he knows that it is impossible. Therefore, if he says, "This is your get (divorce document) on the condition that you ascend to the heavens or descend to the depths, or swallow a reed that is four cubits long," and similar such things, it is not a valid condition and the get is valid.

However, if it is possible to fulfill the condition but it involves a prohibition, such as if he says, "on the condition that you eat pork," and similar things, then it is a valid condition. What does it matter to him if she eats something prohibited? On the contrary, it is possible that he wishes to take revenge on her and says, "If you want the get, eat pork and you will be flogged," and his intention is a serious condition.

One should not ask how he can stipulate a condition that involves violating Torah law, given that a condition that contradicts the Torah is void. This is not a question, for he is not forcing her to do this; if she does not wish to fulfill the condition, she will not be divorced. He is not compelling her to get divorced and violate the Torah. If she does not get divorced, she will not violate the Torah. This is not similar to one who betroths a woman on the condition that she has no marital obligations towards him, where the condition is void because he is making a condition upon himself and how can he violate Torah law? Since he desires the betrothal, the condition is void.

But in the case of a get (divorce) and likewise in betrothal, when the condition is placed upon her, the condition rightfully takes effect and the choice is in her hands. Based on this, it seems to me that in a case where there is a Torah commandment to divorce her, he cannot make such a condition. However, I have not found this ruling in the decisors, and the matter requires further investigation regarding the law.

This condition that she can stipulate a prohibition is when the prohibition concerns her alone, for the reason we have written. However, in a prohibition that concerns another, such as a prohibited sexual relation, for example, if he says to her, "On the condition that you have intercourse with my father or your father or other forbidden relations," it is not a valid condition, since he knows that the other person will not agree to this, and his intention is not for a serious condition but rather to exaggerate in words. The get (divorce document) is valid. But if the condition was "on the condition that you have intercourse with a specific person who is not forbidden to her," it is a valid condition, as will be explained before us with God's help.

If the stipulation was the reverse, that she should not have relations with the father, and she did have relations with him, it is obvious that the get (divorce document) is nullified. However, generally, we do not concern ourselves with this possibility that she may have had relations with him even if she was secluded with him, unless witnesses came and testified that she did indeed have relations with him. We do not say in this case "the witnesses of seclusion are the witnesses of relations" because they are certainly not suspected of violating such a severe prohibition. Therefore, she is also permitted to marry another man, and we are not concerned that she might violate the stipulation and have relations with him, thereby nullifying the get. It seems to me that if they were already suspected of such behavior, even though there is no clear testimony but only a persistent rumor, we do indeed have to be concerned that she might violate the stipulation. We would not allow her to marry unless he gives her another get without any stipulation. Why should we cause an increase of mamzerim (illegitimate children) in Israel? Such a promiscuous woman certainly must be divorced, and therefore it is proper to insist that he gives a get without any stipulation (as it appears to me). If he said "on the condition that you do not marry my father" and she married him, it is a get that does not bind her in marriage.

The Tur wrote: If he said to her, "On the condition that you marry so-and-so," it is considered a valid get (divorce document) like any other condition, and when she marries him, the condition is fulfilled. However, the Sages said (Gittin 83a): She should not marry either that specific person or another person. Not that specific person, lest people say they are exchanging their wives with each other as a favor. Nor another person, as long as the condition (of marrying that specific person) has not been fulfilled. If she married that specific person, she need not leave him. If she married another person before marrying that specific person, she must leave him. If she fulfills the condition by marrying that specific person, the get is retroactively valid. If she does not fulfill the condition, her children are considered mamzerim (illegitimate). And the Rambam wrote in Chapter 8, Law 17, in these words: If she married another person before marrying that specific person, the get is nullified, the child is a mamzer, and she needs a get from the second husband. The Raavad objected to this, asking why the child should be a mamzer, since if she later marries that specific person, the condition is fulfilled, as the Tur wrote. However, the Rambam’s opinion seems to be that the condition was that she must marry that specific person first, and since she married another person, the condition is nullified and the get is void. This also seems to be the opinion of the Maggid Mishneh, as it is clear that the Rambam’s view was that she is prohibited from marrying another person as long as that specific person has not married and divorced her, and the second marriage was in violation of the prohibition of a married woman marrying another man. And this is why the Rambam wrote that she needs a get from the second husband, as a rabbinic decree, so that people do not say a married woman can leave without a get. As it is also stated in Siman 17, if she was told her husband died and then married, and later the husband returned, she needs a get from both men, and all the more so in this case, where not everyone knows the conditions.

Even according to the opinion of the Tur, if she marries another man and he divorces her, and then she marries that certain individual and he divorces her, she is forbidden to return to the former, as it would be considered as taking back his divorced wife after she had been married to another. Moreover, even if the first husband dies or gives her a subsequent divorce without any conditions after she married the other, she remains forbidden to the former husband forever and he must divorce her and never take her back, because once she married him in prohibition as a married woman, she becomes permanently forbidden to him, similar to a sotah who is forbidden to her husband and the adulterer even after the husband's death (as mentioned there in the name of the Ramah, though his wording is perplexing, see there). And I have seen someone write that there are some early authorities who hold that if she marries another, she is permitted to that certain individual even initially when the other divorces her, because in such a case it is not applicable to say that they give their wives to each other as a gift, as the other husband ends the marriage (Beit Shmuel, subsection 26, in the name of the Tosafot). But I wonder how this can be permitted, as the permissibility depends on marrying another in the prohibition of adultery, which is a more severe prohibition than saying that they give their wives to each other as a gift. However, it is certain that if she marries another and has children from him, she must be divorced and marry that certain individual to legitimize the children according to the Tur. But if she has no children from the other, it is certainly not proper that she should marry that certain individual (and the Tosafot did not write this according to the final conclusion, as the Beit Shmuel himself wrote, and they wrote it according to Rav Nachman, as it seems that he thought she could do so from Ravah’s objection, see there).

All this applies when she married another man. But if she only became betrothed to him and has not yet had relations, and she is not considered a definite adulteress, she must leave him and requires a rabbinic get (divorce document). And if the condition was fulfilled that the specific man married her, even if he subsequently divorced her, she is forbidden to marry the other man to whom she was betrothed, because it would be considered as if he is remarrying his betrothed wife after she had married another. However, if that specific man did not marry her, and the first husband died or divorced her with another get without conditions, she is permitted to return to the one who betrothed her.

From what our Sages of Blessed Memory said, that she should not marry that particular man so that people will not say that they exchange their wives as gifts, our teacher the Rema wrote in paragraph 15 that even if he did not explicitly stipulate with her that she should marry that man, but it is evident that he divorced her for this reason - for example, if that man gave him money to divorce her and he provides her with sustenance so that he can marry her, and any similar case - these are his words. And certainly, if the court has the power to protest such cases, the obligation falls upon them, for this is one of the actions close to promiscuity and it is not fitting for a Jew to do such things.

And if he said to her, "on the condition that you have relations with so-and-so," it is obvious that this should not be done because people will then say that wives are giving themselves to others as gifts. This is also stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. However, there is an even greater prohibition here: how is it possible for her to have relations with him? Until the completion of the act, she is still considered a married woman because the condition has not yet been fulfilled, so how can she have relations with him at the beginning of the act when she is still considered married? 

In the case of marriage, this issue does not apply because marriage can occur without sexual relations. Once she is married to him through the chuppah (wedding canopy) and kiddushin (betrothal), the condition is fulfilled, and any subsequent relations are permissible. But with the condition that she must have relations, the initial act of relations is prohibited. Nevertheless, if the condition is fulfilled, whether through an act of prostitution or through marriage, it is considered a valid divorce.

It seems to me from the Talmudic discourse (Kiddushin 4b) that he is permitted to maintain her. One should not question how the condition can be valid given that it is prohibited for that specific man to have relations with her. It has already been explained that when the prohibition applies equally to another, such as "on the condition that you have relations with my father," the condition does not take effect. However, in this case, the specific man can make it permissible by marrying her, thus having relations in a permissible manner. This is evident from Rashi's commentary there (s.v. veL’Abayei) that marriage is included in the term "relations," but "relations" are not included in the term "marriage." Therefore, if he said, "on the condition that you marry so-and-so," and she only had relations with him, it is not considered fulfillment of the condition. This is also implied by the poskim (as it appears to me). (Refer to the Tur, what he wrote in the name of the Rashba, and this requires further study).

And if the condition was the opposite, stipulating that she must not marry a certain person, then according to the opinion found in Siman 137 that this is considered a reservation in the get (divorce document), the get is invalid. However, according to most authorities who do not consider this a reservation in the get, as mentioned there, if he said simply that she must not marry a certain person, the get is entirely invalid, as this does not constitute a proper severance since she is perpetually bound by it, as will be explained. But if he said she must not marry a certain person until a specified time, then the get is valid, and the condition will be fulfilled, as will be explained.

The Tur wrote that she is permitted to marry immediately because she can fulfill the condition, as she cannot marry him except with her consent. There is no remedy to permit her to him unless the divorcer betroths her again and then divorces her without any condition. However, it is not a remedy to permit her by taking the get from her and returning it to her without any condition, because it is no longer in his control, as he gave her a complete get, only he imposed a condition. These are the words of the Tur. Similarly, it is stated in the responsa of the Rosh (45:26). 

One must be precise about this, as we have explained several times in this section that as long as the condition has not been fulfilled, he can give another get without a condition, and even without taking the get from her, as we explained in section 42. The Tosefta explicitly states this regarding taking the get from her, as we explained in section 43. The Tur himself at the end of this section wrote in the name of the Rosh that someone who gave a get from now if he does not come within two years can annul the condition, and she can marry immediately.

And we must say that they hold that there is a distinction between different types of conditions. A condition that depends on the fulfillment of an action, such as "on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz," as in the case of the Tosefta, or even if it does not depend on the fulfillment of an action but on the passage of time, such as not coming within two years, certainly the get (divorce document) is not considered completely finalized because it is still lacking an action and time. Therefore, he can nullify it or give it to her again without the condition because she is still bound to him. In contrast, with a condition like "on the condition that you do not marry so-and-so," which is a passive condition and within her ability to fulfill, the get is considered finalized and she is separated from him. This is what the Tur wrote regarding "on the condition that you serve my father," and then he said, "on the condition that you give two hundred zuz." Specifically, if he did not give her the get initially, if he gave it to her, he cannot change the condition. This is a different matter because he did not come to make another giving but another condition, and he does not have the ability to do this, according to the Rambam at the beginning of this section, that in the case of "from now," he cannot nullify it (see Beit Yosef and Beit Shmuel, subsection 30). The matters are not clear to me, and it seems clear to me as I have written, and be precise. And know that if the husband dies before she marries anyone else, she is permitted to marry that specific person immediately (Beit Yosef) (see Gra, subsection 40, and according to what I have written, everything is clear, and be precise).

However, there is an opinion that she should not marry until that specific person dies (Rashba in the name of R' Chananel). Our master, the Beit Yosef, brought these two opinions in section 16, where he agrees with the opinion that in all conditions, even in a passive condition, she is forbidden to marry until the condition is fulfilled. Therefore, if he also said to her, "on the condition that you do not drink wine for a certain period," she is forbidden to marry during that period out of concern that she might transgress (there, 4:82, s.v. "in all"). But the opinion of the Tur and most of the authorities is that in passive conditions, we do not worry that she will transgress, and so it is explicitly stated in the Tosefta (chapter 5): "On the condition that you do not go to your father's house from now until thirty days, on the condition that you do not drink wine from now until thirty days, this is a valid get, and he does not worry that she might go or that she might drink." The Tur holds that only in an active condition, like "on the condition that you give me 200 zuz," she is forbidden to marry until the condition is fulfilled. According to the Rambam, even in such a case, she is permitted to marry, as has been explained.

And also, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, even though he brought the opinion of "there are those who say," it is clear that he does not hold this opinion in practice. Otherwise, what is it that he wrote in Section 21, "If one stipulates that she should not go to her father's house until a certain time," that we should not attempt such a get (divorce document), because it is impossible for her to restrain herself from going to her father's house, and the get would be invalid, and her children would be considered mamzerim (illegitimate). This is his exact language. According to the opinion of "there are those who say," we would not allow her to remarry until the time of the fulfillment of the condition—what concern of mamzerut (illegitimacy) is there in this? Rather, it is certain that he holds the law according to the Tur (see Ba'er Heitev, note 29, who is astonished that the Shulchan Aruch brought this opinion). And know that in a condition that she should not marry a certain person, even if she had illicit relations with that person, the get is valid, and the child born from that intercourse is legitimate, because the condition was only regarding marriage.

On the condition that [the woman] will not marry a specific man until a certain time, even if there was an interruption, such as if after the divorce she married another man and he subsequently divorced her without specifying any conditions or she became widowed, nonetheless, the condition of the first [divorce] remains in effect. She is still not permitted to marry that specific man until the time set by the first [husband]. If she marries him within the time set by the first [husband], the divorce is nullified and her children, even from the second [husband], are considered mamzerim (illegitimate). And even though there is no valid marriage since she is considered a married woman (as the condition was not fulfilled), and there cannot be a valid marriage to a married woman, nonetheless, this was the condition set. This is not similar to the case of a condition forbidding marriage to one's father, where marriage is inherently not applicable, because in that case, even without the condition, marriage to one's father is impossible. But in this case, marriage could apply if not for the condition. Therefore, the condition was set that she should not marry that specific man, meaning she could potentially marry him, but [the first husband] does not wish for that, and thus imposes the condition that she should not marry him. Regarding her marriage to him, she will be considered as if she were a married woman. (See Beit Shmuel, section 31).

And know that what we have written, that even if she married another, the condition is not nullified, this is an explicit Gemara (Yevamot 93a) which says there that if she went and married someone from the marketplace and had children, and then became widowed or divorced and married the one who was forbidden to her, the get (divorce document) is nullified and her children are mamzerim (illegitimate). However, in what we have written, although there is no marriage according to the law since she is a married woman, nevertheless, this was the condition. This is not similar to the case of the father's marriage. So wrote the Rashba in his chiddushim there. But our Rabbis, the Ba'alei Tosafot, there compared these cases and wrote that there is no marriage in this case, like in the case of the father or your father. And they wrote that the Gemara's statement that she married the one forbidden to her means that she married him after the death of the one who divorced her. Their words are puzzling because after his death we do not need his condition or his get, and she is permitted by his death, as we wrote at the end of paragraph 73.

The truth is that regarding this matter there is a dispute among the earlier authorities (Rishonim). There are those who hold that even if the divorcer (the husband) dies, nonetheless his condition stands. And there are those who disagree with this. The Tosafot hold that the condition stands. This dispute is found in the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (BaHaG) at the beginning of the laws of Gittin, and the Rashba (on page 83, in the passage that starts with "Ela") brings it. His words are: "Certainly, he said to her 'All the days of the life of so-and-so,' and she married immediately. And she had children during the life of the first husband, and the first husband died during the life of the second husband, and she had children after his death. And the one on whom the condition depended is still alive. And she drank wine during his lifetime, and after the death of the husband, the get (divorce document) is nullified retroactively, and the first children are considered mamzerim (illegitimate), the latter ones are not mamzerim, and she is forbidden to the second husband." The Rabbis dispute this, saying since during the husband's life she did not violate the condition, and only after his death did she violate it, since the husband died, the condition is void, and the get is not nullified retroactively. These are the words of the BaHaG.

Thus, there is a dispute among the Geonim regarding any condition that he (the husband) sets for a certain period of time. If the husband dies within that time, there are some Geonim who hold that nonetheless she is forbidden to violate the condition for the entire duration, and if she does, the get is nullified retroactively. And there are some Geonim who hold that since he has died, she does not need to fulfill the condition, for now she is permitted by his death, and throughout his life she upheld the condition. The Tosafot hold like those who prohibit, and the Rashba agreed with this, bringing proof from what the sages said: "All the days of your life" is not a valid separation, but "all the days of his life" is a valid separation, for even in the case of "all the days of your life," the condition can be fulfilled when he dies and she is alive, and she is then permitted. Thus, certainly the opinion of those who prohibit is correct. Refer to there (in the Rashba). And what we wrote at the end of section 73 is according to the opinion of those who permit.

And the reasoning of those who prohibit is straightforward: since he stipulated the condition for a certain duration, his intention was that it should be upheld whether he lives or dies. Those who permit hold that any person who divorces does not concern himself at all with what will happen after his death, and any condition he makes is intended to be fulfilled only during his lifetime. After his death, she can do as she wishes. This is what the Sages said, "All the days of your life" is not a severance; although it may become permitted upon his death, nevertheless, according to the wording of the condition, which ties it to all her days, this is not a severance. The Maggid Mishneh also brought this dispute in Chapter 8, Halacha 11, and agreed with the prohibiting view, writing that even the Rambam holds this way, see there (although it is not conclusive) (see Responsa of Rabbi Akiva Eiger, Siman 126). All this is not related to what was written in Section 34 regarding the opinion of the Rambam, who holds that the condition must come into effect, see there. It is not related to this, and furthermore, there it concerns the annulment of the condition, whereas here we are discussing the fulfillment of the condition, as mentioned in Section 37. We have proven this from the words of the Rambam himself, and here we are dealing with the fulfillment of the condition.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 19: "On the condition that you will not marry so-and-so, it is a valid get (divorce document), but she should not marry until that so-and-so dies, because we are concerned that she might be compelled to be with him." The Rosh in Chapter 9, Siman 2, brings from the Tosefta: "On the condition that you will not marry so-and-so, we are concerned that she might be with him." However, in the Tosefta (Chapter 4) that we have before us, it says: "On the condition that you will not marry so-and-so, it is a valid get, and we are not concerned that she might go and be with him." We must say that the version we have is corrupted. And one should not ask: the Tur and Shulchan Aruch hold that we are not concerned that she will violate her condition, as mentioned in Section 74, so why are we concerned here? It can be answered that certainly she will not violate the condition, but we are concerned that this so-and-so might force her, as explained in their words. 

And one should not ask: why are we not concerned about the condition of "on the condition that you will not marry my father or your father" that she might be with them, as the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 13? We explained the reason is because there is no concern that they will violate the prohibition of arayot (forbidden relationships). And if so, why are we concerned that so-and-so might force her, as then the condition would be nullified, and she would be a married woman, and how could he violate the prohibition of arayot? There are those who answered that the concern is that she might be with him after the death of the divorcer (Beit Shmuel, Subsection 32). This is surprising because this is only according to those who hold that the condition extends even after his death, but according to those who disagree, as mentioned in Section 78, this is not a concern at all. And even according to those who prohibit, why should we be concerned that the husband might die first?

It seems to me that the reason for this concern is that certainly, this divorcer, when he made such a condition "on the condition that you will not marry so-and-so," most likely suspected him. Otherwise, why make such a condition? And since she was suspected of him, we are certainly concerned about the overpowering of the evil inclination. But in the case of "my father or your father," it could be that he made such a condition to vex her or them, and also in cases of close relatives, the evil inclination does not dominate as much, as it says in the Talmud (Yoma 69b). Therefore, we are not concerned, unlike the case of a married woman, where we are concerned.

One must not impose a condition on her that binds her for her entire life, such as "on the condition that you do not eat meat" or "that you do not drink wine forever" or "all the days of your life." Thus, our sages have said (Gittin 83b): "This is your divorce on the condition that you do not drink wine all the days of your life" is not a proper severance, as only death separates them, for she remains bound to him until her death (Rashi). What benefit is the divorce if after her death she does not need a divorce? But if he said "all the days of my life" or "all the days of so-and-so's life," it is a proper severance because after his death or the death of so-and-so, she will be permitted to drink wine. Although it might seem that since during all the days of his life she is bound to him, it is not a proper severance like "all the days of your life," nevertheless, the reasoning of the Talmud is not so. Since it is possible for her to fulfill his condition, it is a proper severance. Thus wrote the Rashba of blessed memory there, and the reason must be stated. Indeed, the condition is a separate matter, and we do not concern ourselves with the fact that she is bound to him by the condition for all his life. Only "all the days of your life" because she has no release ever from the matter she was forbidden in, and until her death, she remains bound to him in this matter because of his authority. Therefore, she is not completely severed from him for this matter all the days of her life. The Torah stated "a document of severance" that she is completely severed from him. It is necessary to leave her a time in her life when she is completely severed from him. Therefore, in "all the days of my life," she will be severed from him after his death. Even though without this, his death severs her from him, she is already severed from him in his life from the moment of the divorce, and the condition is a separate matter. Even in this small part, she has a release in her life when he dies.

The poskim (decisors of Jewish law) have written that even if he is a child and she is elderly, or if the condition was stated for fifty years, which certainly she will not live that long, it is still a valid get (divorce document). We are only concerned with the language, in that the language of the condition must allow for a complete separation. Therefore, there is an opinion that even if the time was extended beyond the typical lifespan of a human being, such as if he said one hundred years or more, since it is a definitive matter, it is considered a valid get. This is all for the reason we have explained, that a condition is a separate matter. According to most poskim, she can remarry immediately, and we are not concerned that she will violate the condition. We mentioned a singular opinion in section 74 that prohibits her from remarrying until the condition is fulfilled. According to this opinion, if the time was extended, the get is of no benefit to her, except that if she commits adultery, she would not be judged as a married woman but as a single woman. The primary ruling follows the majority of the poskim, as ruled in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, and this is explicitly stated in the Tosefta as we have written there.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 21: If he said to her, "On the condition that you do not go to your father's house until a certain time," even though the get (divorce document) is valid and the condition is upheld, no one should strive to have a get given with such a condition, because it is impossible for her to refrain from going to her father's house, and it turns out the get is void and her children are mamzerim (illegitimate). If the one divorcing is among those who we compel to divorce, and he did not want to divorce except with this condition, we compel him to divorce without this condition. 

It appears that the same applies if it is a mitzvah to divorce her, such as if she is promiscuous. Even though we cannot compel him, we must strive greatly not to give it on such a condition. It seems that for other conditions, such as "you shall not eat meat or drink wine," we do not fear she will transgress, which is surprising, because certainly there is concern in this case as well. Perhaps he meant this as an example only. In any case, we infer from his words that she is permitted to remarry before the condition is fulfilled, otherwise, what illegitimacy would there be, as stated in section 75. 

However, if he said, "On the condition that you never go to your father's house," this is not a valid severance (Gittin 21b), just like "on the condition that you never drink wine." Even though when her father dies or the house is sold to another, it is no longer considered her father's house, as stated in Nedarim (46a), "Konam (a type of vow) to your house I will not enter," if he dies or sells it to another, it is permitted. Here, he said "your father's house," meaning all his descendants are called his house, even after his death, as written regarding Tamar, "Sit as a widow in your father's house" and her father had already died (Tosafot). Some say it indeed refers to when he said "this house," which is always forbidden, as stated in Nedarim there (Rashba). Even though in such a case, if the house falls or burns and they build another, it is permitted, as written in Yoreh De'ah 216, nevertheless, it is not expected to collapse or burn. According to Rambam, it is understandable without this, as will be explained with God's help (Ran). In the case of sale, according to the first explanation, even if it is sold, perhaps he will buy it back (Magid Mishneh).

The Tur wrote: The Rambam said that if a man tells a woman, "On the condition that you do not marry so-and-so," this is not considered a valid bill of divorce, similar to the conditions "on the condition that you do not drink wine" or "that you do not go to your father's house." However, this is not correct, because it is possible that the specified person might die during her lifetime, thereby annulling the condition, and it would then be a valid bill of divorce. This is different from the condition "that you do not go to your father's house," because even after her father’s death, she would still be prohibited from entering it as it would still be called by her father's name.

The Rambam's reasoning is that she should not be bound by the condition forever. Therefore, in the condition that she does not marry so-and-so, as long as he is alive, she is bound by the condition. After his death, the condition no longer applies, as marriage after death is not possible. Thus, with this condition, she is essentially bound forever as long as the condition is relevant. Even though after the person's death the condition is annulled, the condition of marriage persists as long as marriage is possible, similar to the condition "that you do not go to your father's house," which is possible to permit if the father dies or sells the house to another, but then it would no longer be her father's house. Thus, the condition regarding her father's house applies as long as the term is relevant. The same applies here (according to the Ran and Maimonides). According to what was stated earlier, she is prohibited from the house forever.

It is also possible to say that the Rambam wrote that if he said to her, "On the condition that you do not marry so-and-so for fifty years," it is a valid get (divorce document). Refer to there, even though it is possible and likely that she will not live another fifty years. Rather, he holds that we follow the wording of the condition. When he stipulated that she should not drink wine all the days of so-and-so's life, he set a limit to the matter for all the days of his life, and his wording includes a term of severance, meaning after his lifetime. Similarly, when he stipulated for fifty years. But when he stipulated generally, "On the condition that you do not marry so-and-so," implying forever, his wording does not include a term of severance. The same applies to "On the condition that you do not go to your father's house." And you should know that this is the case, for do we know that in all the days of so-and-so's life, he will die before she does? What would we do if she dies first? She would be prohibited for all her life. Rather, we do not worry about this, since according to the wording of the condition, she is not prohibited forever. All the more so that stringently, when he prohibited her with the wording of the condition forever, it is not considered severance, even though it is possible that the condition would be nullified if he dies first. (This seems to me).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 22, brings these two opinions and writes that we adopt the stringencies of both. It is straightforward. He further writes in section 23: If he said to her, "On the condition that you do not drink this wine forever," or "that you do not ascend this tree or this wall forever," and the wine was spilled, the tree was cut down, or the wall fell, this is not considered a valid bill of divorce, since she was never permitted in what she was prohibited. There are those who say that since the condition persists only as long as the wine, tree, or wall exists, it is a valid bill of divorce. We adopt the stringencies of both opinions. The first opinion is that of the Rambam, and the Tur challenges him because in the Tosefta (Chapter 5), it explicitly says the opposite. It teaches: "On the condition that you do not ascend this tree forever," and the tree was cut down, it is a valid bill of divorce. However, in our version of the Tosefta, it is phrased differently: "On the condition that you do not ascend this tree," and "on the condition that you do not ascend this wall," and if the tree was cut down or the wall was destroyed, it is a valid bill of divorce. "On the condition that you ascend this tree," and "on the condition that you ascend this wall," and if the tree was cut down or the wall was destroyed, it is not a valid bill of divorce. It does not use the term "forever." The Rambam holds that because it did not use the term "forever," and generally, trees and walls are subject to being cut down and destroyed, this language does not imply permanence. However, "on the condition that you do not marry so-and-so" implies permanence, since no time limit was set. But with trees and walls, in general, it is not permanent because they are expected to be cut down or fall. Nevertheless, if he uses the term "forever," she would be forbidden even with respect to the tree and the wall. This aligns with what we wrote about the Rambam's opinion in the previous section, that according to our explanation in section 84, she is ultimately prohibited by this condition regarding ascending the tree and the wall forever, because after they fall, the term "ascend" does not apply to them, as is evident.

However, in truth, in the Rambam, there is no ruling at all regarding a wall and a tree. And these are his words in Chapter 8, Law 11: "Therefore, if one says, 'This is your get on the condition that you do not eat this meat forever, or that you do not drink this wine forever,' this is not a get because this is not a complete severance. If he says 'for 30 days,' it is a get." And it is possible to say that only in a matter where there is pleasure, when he forbids it forever, it is considered that she is not severed from him since she is compelled to restrain her desire because of his condition. And even if the wine spills or the meat is lost, ultimately, with this condition, she is forbidden forever because after they are lost, eating and drinking are no longer relevant, as he wrote. But regarding climbing a wall or a tree, where there is no desire, we are not concerned about this at all.

**The Law of the Claim of Compulsion in the Condition of a Get and Other Laws of Conditions. Comprising 45 Sections:**

In the previous section, two types of conditions in a get (divorce document) were explained. The first is a condition that she must fulfill, such as "on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz," and similar cases. The second type is a condition that depends on him, such as "if I do not come from here until thirty days." Now, in all of the Torah, we hold that "compulsion is excused by the Merciful One," and based on this, we would have said that any condition that was not fulfilled due to compulsion should be considered as if it were fulfilled. However, regarding a condition that she must fulfill, this does not apply, as explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 21, where it states that one person should not be obligated because of another’s compulsion, for "compulsion is excused by the Merciful One," not that the Merciful One obligates. Therefore, when he says to her, "This is your get on the condition that you give me two hundred zuz," even if she was compelled and could not fulfill the condition, nevertheless, the get is nullified. How can we obligate him to fulfill the get because of her compulsion? What does he have to do with her compulsion? In the end, the condition was not fulfilled. However, in a condition that depends on him, such as "if I do not come" and he was compelled and did not come, the get should be effective, and we would have said it should not be a get since he was compelled, and since "compulsion is excused by the Merciful One," it is considered as if he had come. Nevertheless, the Sages said that there is no claim of compulsion in gittin (divorce documents), and it is a get. This is an enactment of the Sages (beginning of Ketubot, according to the first version of Rava that there is no compulsion in gittin, which is the ruling of all the poskim except for the Mordechai in the third chapter of Gittin in the name of the Geonim, who ruled according to both versions stringently, and this is a singular opinion. See Beit Yosef and the Gra, section 1).

The reason for the enactment, the sages said, is for the benefit of modest women and promiscuous women. The benefit for modest women is because sometimes it happens that there is no coercion, and the get (divorce document) is valid, but she might be stringent upon herself and think that he was coerced, even though from a legal standpoint there is no need to be concerned about this since most men are not coerced (Tosafot). As a result, she would remain an agunah (a woman who is chained to her marriage) forever since he has already diverted his mind from her and they are already divorced. With promiscuous women, it is the opposite. Sometimes she might know that he was coerced and the get is invalid, yet she would say that he was not coerced. In this case, she would marry someone else, and when it becomes clear that he was indeed coerced, the get would be nullified, and the children from the second husband would be mamzerim (illegitimate) (Tosafot, Gittin 33). 

Everyone who sanctifies a woman does so with the understanding of the sages, and therefore they say at the time of sanctification "according to the law of Moses and Israel" (Tosafot). Since the sages enacted that in all cases of divorce on condition, the claim of coercion would not help them, from the outset, the divorces are made with this understanding (so wrote the Perisha there, and this is what is meant by "the sages annulled the betrothal," meaning that if he says he did not divorce according to their understanding, the betrothal is annulled. Consequently, he would not say this since it is of no benefit to him. So too, wrote the Rashba in his responsa, section 1063).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Tosafot (there), wrote that there are three types of duress: duress that is very common, duress that is somewhat common but not very common, and duress that is not common at all. According to the law, it is as follows: Very common duress is like the case where a person said, "If I do not come from here within thirty days, it shall be a get (divorce)," and he came within the time, but was stopped by a river that blocked his way, and the ferry was on the city side, and he could not cross. He shouted from across the river, "See that I have come, see that I have come," but Shmuel said, "It is not called coming" (Gemara there), and it is considered a get. In this case, it is clear that according to the law, there is no claim of duress even without a stipulation because since it is very common, he should have stipulated on the condition that no duress occurs. Since he did not stipulate, he caused his own loss.

Duress that is somewhat common but not very common, even though according to the law there is a claim of duress because it is not very common and he did not think he needed to stipulate, but because of the decree regarding modest and immodest women, there is no claim of duress as explained.

Duress that is not common at all, such as a house collapsing on him or being bitten by a snake, there is a claim of duress, and the decree does not apply here because modest women would not think that such a duress occurred to him, and the same with immodest women. Therefore, in this case, we hold that there is a claim of duress in divorces. This is agreed upon by the Rosh there, the Ran (chapter 3 of Gittin), the Maggid Mishneh (chapter 9), and the Mordechai (chapter 7).

If he became ill within the time or died, this is duress that is somewhat common but not very common (as explained from the Gemara). Nevertheless, in the case of death, it can be said that the decree does not apply because death is well-known (Tosafot). Captivity is also duress that is somewhat common but not very common and does not cancel the get because of the decree, and he did not stipulate on the condition that no duress occurs. (What the Rema wrote at the end of section 1 that captivity is common means that it is not like being bitten by a snake, as explained by the Chelkat Mechokek and the Beit Shmuel in subsection 3).

In my humble opinion, it seems that nowadays when the government supervises the country well, captivity is duress that is not common at all, and it requires further study according to the law. (In Shulchan Aruch section 1, illness is compared to being delayed by a river because according to the law, they are equal) (and in the Be'er Heitev subsection 3, it is written in the name of the Beit Yosef that captivity is considered duress that is not common).

In this matter that we have said there is no claim of coercion in a get (bill of divorce), even if he revealed his intention that he does not wish to divorce and it is evident that if he had known that it would come within the time frame, he would not have divorced her, and similarly in other conditions in such a case, nevertheless, since he did not explicitly stipulate that if coercion occurs the get will be nullified, the get is valid, for revealing one's intention in a get is not considered significant.

The Mordechai (in Chapter 3) wrote that the RIBaN ruled that even "by the hands of Heaven" (i.e., natural causes) there is no coercion in matters of divorce. In the Book of Professions, it is ruled that coercion by human hands does not count as coercion, but coercion by the hands of Heaven does count as coercion. This is also the ruling of the two yeshivot. Some bring a proof to this from the statement of our Sages (Avodah Zarah 40b) that if a lion eats [someone], there is a claim of coercion. End of quote. There, it is explained that this is their intention. However, according to the distinctions that were clarified, there is no proof from this, as this is an extremely uncommon form of coercion, and there is indeed a claim of coercion. This is the opinion of the RIBaN, but this view is not brought in the halachic decisors at all. We need to investigate why the opinion of the early Geonim in the two yeshivot was rejected.

And it seems to me that even the Geonim do not disagree with everything that has been explained if we scrutinize, for it is implied from the words of the Mordechai that even the Geonim hold that there is no claim of coercion in divorce, like the first opinion of Rava as explained there. And the distinction they make between human-caused and divinely-caused is to resolve the case where a lion devoured [the husband], and if so, how did they differentiate, for illness is also divinely-caused. And the essence of the discussion that there is no coercion refers to illness, and already our teacher the Beit Yosef wondered in his great work about the words of the Mordechai and leaned towards the words of the Geonim who rule according to the latter opinion that there is coercion in divorce. And his words are puzzling, for if so, why did they need to differentiate between human-caused and divinely-caused; they should have said directly that there is coercion in divorce. And indeed, in the Gemara, they compare the stopping of a ferry to illness, and the stopping of a ferry is human-caused. Rather, certainly, the main opinion is like the Mordechai, that the Geonim also rule that there is no claim of coercion in divorce. And this is also clearly implied from the words of the Hagahot Maimoni in chapter 9. And it could be said that they interpret the illness in the discussion there as an illness caused by cold or heat, and such an illness is called human-caused, as the sages said (Ketubot 30a) "everything is in the hands of Heaven except for cold and heat", implying that cold and heat are called human-caused. But even this is difficult, for in the Gemara they said simply "illness", which implies all types of illness.

Therefore, it seems to me that a different intention is embedded in their words. Indeed, when we say there is a distinction between matters in the hands of humans and those in the hands of Heaven, it should not be understood literally. Surely, all occurrences that befall a person are under Divine Providence, as our Sages said: "A person does not stub his toe below unless it has been decreed upon him from above" (Chullin 7b). This is also explicitly stated in the verse: "A man's steps are directed by the Lord." However, the intention is that matters in the hands of humans are those that are habitual and commonly occur, and it is not apparent that they are from Heaven, such as sickness or a ferry accident and similar occurrences. Matters in the hands of Heaven are those that are clearly recognizable to everyone as being from Heaven, such as being eaten by a lion or bitten by a snake and similar occurrences. This is also the distinction between what is common and uncommon, and between what is not common at all.

There are those who say that nowadays, after the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom which states that a woman cannot be divorced against her will, if she stipulated a condition upon him, whatever it may be, the claim of coercion (ones) does not help (Beit Shmuel, section 1), even if it is a totally uncommon form of coercion. The explanation of the matter is as we wrote in section 1 regarding a condition that he stipulated upon her to fulfill, and she did not fulfill it, he can say, "what do I care about your coercion? I only agreed to give the get under this condition." Similarly, now she can also say this. However, there are those who disagree with this (Bayit Meir and other great authorities as cited by the Pitchei Teshuvah). And this seems to be the main opinion, as it appears that Rabbeinu Gershom did not decree in this matter, and it is not considered a forced divorce. Also, even one who transgresses and divorces against the will, the majority of great authorities hold that it is a valid get, as stated in Siman 119. Nevertheless, for the practical ruling, it requires further study. Perhaps, when she stipulated upon him that she accepts the get on this condition, his intention was also that if the condition is not fulfilled, there will be no get under any circumstances, even if he is entirely coerced and it is an uncommon coercion. This is not comparable to a condition he stipulates, such as "on the condition that I do not come," and the like (and it seems to me that this is why the Beit Shmuel was precise in saying that she stipulated upon him; see there and examine it carefully).

The Tur wrote: Similarly, if he said, "This is your Get (divorce document) on the condition that if I do not appease you so that you consent within thirty days, it will be a Get," and he appeased her but she did not consent, it is a Get, even though he was coerced, because he did appease her with many attempts and she did not consent. It is possible that she would consent if he had a lot of money, and he is coerced because he does not have it. Even so, there is no coercion in Gitin (divorce documents). End quote. This law is in the Gemara (30a). The explanation is that this language—"if I do not appease you, it will be a Get"—does not mean that it depends on her consent, and if she does not consent it is a Get. For if so, there would be no need for all this elaboration, and it could be said briefly: since she did not consent, the condition is fulfilled and it is a Get. Rather, the explanation is that the condition was from his side: if he does not do everything possible to appease her, it will be a Get. But if he does everything in his power to appease her, the Get is nullified even if she does not consent, since he did everything he could (Tosafot there and Ran there). Therefore, if he indeed gave her a lot of money and she was not appeased, the condition is nullified since he did everything. But if he did not give her a lot of money to appease her, it turns out that he did not do everything he could, and the condition is fulfilled and it is a Get. And even though the reason he did not give her a lot of money is not due to lack of will but due to lack of ability, and he is coerced, nevertheless, there is no claim of coercion in Gitin. This is what the Tur wrote: "And it is possible that she would consent"—the explanation is: since it is possible that she would consent with a lot of money and he did not do so, even though he is coerced in this matter, it is a Get. The Rambam did not bring this law at all, and it seems to me that his reason is because this depends on the language of the country, whether "if I do not appease you" means the condition is on him, as stated, or the condition is on her, meaning if she does not consent, it will be a Get. Therefore, he omitted this law entirely.

The Tur wrote: "If he did not say 'from now,' but rather, 'If I do not come within 30 days, it should be a get [divorce], and if I come within 30 days, it should not be a get,' the Rambam wrote that the get does not take effect until the completion of the 30 days if he did not come. Therefore, if he died within this time, it is not a get at all, and she requires yibbum [levirate marriage]." The Raavad wrote that it is a get, and she is permitted to marry anyone. The Ra'ah differentiated and wrote that if the condition was not written in the get, it is not a get at all, and she requires yibbum. If the condition was written in the get, it is doubtful, and she should perform chalitzah [ceremony to release from levirate marriage] and not yibbum. Some say that it is always doubtful, and she should perform chalitzah and not yibbum. This is also the opinion of the Tosafot, that she should perform chalitzah. End of quote.

The explanation of the matter is that we have already clarified in Siman 143, section 28, that regarding documents, we hold according to Rabbi Yossi that the date on the document proves its validity, meaning it is effective from now even if this is not explicitly stated. Otherwise, why would we need the date? This is also said regarding a get (divorce document). Therefore, even without stating "from now," its status is as if it were said "from now." This is the opinion of the Raavad, who ruled that it is a valid get and the woman is permitted to remarry because it is considered as if it were stated "from now." However, the Rambam did not rule this way in matters of gittin (divorce documents) due to the reasons we explained there. Moreover, his reasoning is straightforward: since it is a rabbinic enactment to write the date in a get, the date alone does not serve as proof that his intention was "from now" (Bach). The Rema distinguishes between oral and written conditions; when the condition is written in the get, the date proves it means "from today," but when the condition is oral, it could be said that when he handed it to her with this condition, he retracted the date on the document (Rashi, Gittin 72b). Because the Talmud (there) has someone who doubts this, the Rema ruled that if the condition is oral, it is a doubt. This is according to Rabbi Yossi, but according to the Rabbis who disagree with Rabbi Yossi, orally it is certainly not a get, and in writing, it is a doubt, since they might only dispute oral conditions and not written ones. Therefore, they hold that orally it is not a get, and in writing, it is a doubt. The Yesh Omrim and Tosafot hold that it is always a doubt, and she must perform chalitzah and not yibbum because there is a doubt whether we hold like Rabbi Yossi in gittin and whether Rabbi Yossi also said this regarding oral conditions. Therefore, in Shulchan Aruch, section 2, they summarized it as a doubt and did not differentiate between oral and written conditions, holding like Tosafot (and before the Beit Yosef, there was a different version in the Tur as the Bach wrote there).

However, what we have written in the opinion of the Rema, who ruled not like Rabbi Yossi, seems forced. Therefore, it appears to me that he follows his own reasoning, according to what the Tur wrote in his name in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 158, that the date on a document only proves something when given after death. In a get (bill of divorce), this does not apply, as stated in Siman 143, section 30. Based on this, even according to Rabbi Yossi, we do not say in gittin (divorce documents) that the date on a document proves anything.
