However, in other documents, there is doubt because perhaps, since it is not customary to write conditions in a get, as it is not a financial document that would include details, and indeed we hold that one should not write a condition in a get, as stated in Siman 147. Therefore, since this person wrote a condition in the get, there is a doubt that perhaps in this case we do say that the date on the document proves something according to Rabbi Yossi. (Refer to the Beit Shmuel, Siman 4, and according to what we have written, it is straightforward.)

There is someone who has raised a significant question regarding this law. We write in a get (divorce document) "from today and forever," and it is stated in the Gemara (Gittin 85b) that this was instituted to exclude the opinion of Rabbi Yose, meaning not to rely on the date of the document alone but to write explicitly "from today." If so, why have the decisors been vague about these laws, and how did the Tur and Shulchan Aruch rule that it is doubtful when it is written "from now" (Beit Shmuel there)? In truth, if so, there is reason to be puzzled by the Rambam and all the decisors who wrote many laws regarding such conditions, that the get is not effective until the condition is fulfilled. Why did they write this? According to our version, these laws do not apply at all. It is also puzzling concerning the Talmud: why did it not say that nowadays, when we write "from today and forever," she is divorced from now, as it said similarly in other documents (Bava Batra 171b)?

Therefore, it appears to me that this rule, that the date of a document provides evidence for it, is only when the party himself writes or instructs to write the date, as stated in Choshen Mishpat there, and we brought this up in Siman 143, Se'if 29. I also found this reasoning in the Maharik, Shoresh 94, and it is quoted in the name of the Rashba, see there. According to this, even in the formula "as of today," since it is a general formula and not written by the instruction of the owner, we certainly say that a verbal condition nullifies it. Although in the Gemara the conclusion according to Rabbi Yossi is that even verbally he holds that the date of the document provides evidence (for Rava holds this way), this is only when he wrote it himself or instructed to write, but not in a general case. Nevertheless, in practice, one should be stringent, even though the language of the poskim clearly indicates that they were not concerned with this.

In the Gemara (76b), there is a question about a conditional statement: "From now, if I do not come within twelve months," and he dies within that period. Even though it is certain that he will not come, perhaps she is not permitted to remarry until the completion of the twelve months. The matter remains unresolved (teiku), and we rule stringently. The reason, as written by the Tosafot, is that we make a decree in the case of death due to the concern that it might be confused with a situation where he did not die, as it is not known to everyone that he died, and they would wonder why she is permitted to remarry. However, at the end of the time period, everyone knows that the condition has been fulfilled. This is also the opinion of the Rosh and the Tur. But the Rambam holds that according to the fundamental law, it is possible that as long as the condition's negation has not been actualized, even though it is potentially actualized, it is not considered the negation of the condition. We have already written about this in the previous section 34, and we explained there in section 37 that this applies only to the negation of the condition and not its fulfillment, for the Rambam himself ruled that in a case of "from now, if you do not give me 200 zuz within 30 days," she can remarry immediately. See there for the reasoning behind the difference between these cases. (And in the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter 7, halacha 3, a different reason is given.)

And these are the words of our teacher the Beit Yosef in paragraph 3: "This is your bill of divorce from now if I do not come from here until twelve months, and he died within twelve months, she is divorced. But if she has a yavam (levirate husband), she should not marry without chalitza (ritual of release) until twelve months have passed. And if she married, she does not have to leave her husband." End of quotation. And it appears that, according to all the authorities, if she married, she does not have to leave her husband, even according to the Rambam who considers it a complete prohibition, as he wrote. And there is someone who says that, according to the Rambam, if she married, she must leave (Beit Shmuel, sub-paragraph 5). All the more so for those who hold that there is a doubt as to whether he intended to divorce her only after twelve months, as he did not anticipate his own death (Ran, end of chapter 7). And it seems to me that, according to the Rambam, it is certainly impossible to say so, for he holds at the beginning of chapter 8 that even in a case where the condition is that if she gives him two hundred zuz without "from now," if she married, she does not have to leave, and we explained his reasoning in the previous section, paragraph 10, see there. And all the more so in a case of "from now if I do not come after twelve months," she does not have to leave. And it is true that in paragraph 17 there, we explained that in this condition, if she married, she must leave without "from now," and we differentiated between a condition which she must fulfill and a condition which he must fulfill, see there. Nevertheless, since he is lenient in a condition which she must fulfill also without "from now," all the more so in a condition which he must fulfill with "from now." And also, those who hold the reasoning that he did not intend to divorce her only after twelve months, it is also impossible to say it plainly, for he said "from now." Rather, the explanation is that perhaps his intention was that at the end of twelve months she would be divorced from now, and certainly, this is the case. Therefore, she should not marry initially, even when it is certain that the condition will not be fulfilled, because this was his intention. However, at any rate, why was his intention so? Because he did not anticipate his own death, as we said. And consequently, it is understood that if he had anticipated his own death, he would have divorced her immediately, for his intention was not to provoke or distress her. Ultimately, it was all his intention because of the fulfillment of the condition. And since this is so, consequently, when he died, and it is impossible for the condition to be fulfilled, even though we do not permit her initially, why should she leave if she married? For we know clearly that he will not come, and ultimately, she will be divorced retroactively. Nevertheless, in practice, it is possible to be stringent, and the matter requires investigation in law. Nevertheless, since according to Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur, it is clear that she does not have to leave, we can rely on them so as not to separate a woman from her husband. Moreover, even according to the opinions explained, it also seems so (that his intention was merely an expression of his intent and is of no consequence).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: If he gave her a get (divorce document) at night and said to her, "This is your get on the condition that the sun emerges from its sheath," and he died that night, this is a valid get. But if he said to her, "If the sun emerges from its sheath" or "When the sun emerges from its sheath," and he died that night, this is a doubtful get. And some say that even with the condition we are stringent unless he explicitly said "from now." Thus are the words of the Beit Yosef.

Explanation of the matter: When it is "on condition" (בע"מ) that it is like "from now" (כמעכשיו), she is considered divorced at night. But if it is "if she goes out" or "when she goes out," it is a get (divorce) after death. However, the doubt is perhaps we hold like Rabbi Yosi that the date on the document proves it is like "from now," as it is stated in the Gemara (end of chapter 7). And there are those who say that "on condition" is not like "from now," and we mentioned this view in Siman 38, see there. And they were puzzled why our master the Beit Yosef only took this view into account in this specific case and not in other places (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 7). It seems to me that in this matter, the phrase "on condition" is not understood. For if it were about a condition that a person must do or not do, it is appropriate to say "this is your get on condition that you do such and such for me." But regarding the rising of the sun, what condition is relevant here? Surely, the sun will rise, and this is only like saying that the effect of the get will be then. And therefore, even though it is clearly stated in the Gemara that in this case it is like saying "from now," nevertheless, in this specific case, he was concerned for the dissenting opinion and held that in practice, it is not like "from now" (and do not refute me with the words of the Ran on the Mishnah "this is your get" there, for he did not write his reasoning regarding "on condition" there, see and be precise).

And that which is written, "When the sun emerges from its sheath," is similar to "if it emerges" regarding the dating of a document. Therefore, it is a doubt, as some of our Rabbis hold that with "when it emerges," even according to Rabbi Yossi, we do not say that the date of the document proves [the time], since it explicitly states "when it emerges" (Rashi, end of Chapter 7). The same applies to any condition, such as "this is your get when you give me two hundred zuz," and the like. Certainly, for stringency, we should be concerned about this opinion. This also seems to be the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 9, Halacha 15, where he writes: "This is your get when the sun emerges from its sheath, and he dies at night, it is not a get. If he said 'on condition that the sun emerges,' and he dies at night, she is divorced, and when the sun rises, the condition is fulfilled. The condition was that if the sun rises, it will be a get, and if it does not rise, it will not be a get, and he dies at night, it is not a get," etc. End of quote. And it needs to be understood that since he holds that "when it emerges" is the same status as "if it emerges," why did he separate them into two laws? Rather, surely it is because they are not based on the same reasoning. For "if it emerges," according to Rabbi Yossi, is like "from now," and only the Rambam does not rule like him, as we have explained. But "when it emerges," even according to Rabbi Yossi, is not a get.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah: If a man says, "If I do not come from now until twelve months, write and give a bill of divorce to my wife," and they wrote the bill of divorce within the twelve months and gave it after the twelve months, it is not a valid bill of divorce. This is because the agents deviated from what he commanded, which was to write only after the twelve months. We do not say that he was only particular about the giving and not about the writing, for certainly, he was particular about the writing as well (Ran, end of chapter 7). A person does not wish to predate a bill of divorce when it is not yet necessary. Even if he said, "Write and give a bill of divorce to my wife if I do not come from now until twelve months," and they wrote it before the twelve months, it is not a valid bill of divorce (as stated in the Mishnah). We do not say that since he could have said, "If I do not come, write and give," and he said, "Write and give if I do not come," maybe his intention was to write now. We do not say this, for certainly, his intention was to write later (Gemara, end of chapter 7). All this is for the reason we explained, and it is clear from the language of the Talmud and the poskim that it is not a valid bill of divorce at all according to Torah law. Even though he did not stipulate according to the laws of conditions, there is no hindrance, for the laws of conditions are not required when he speaks to an agent, for he is only his agent in this specific manner and not if he deviates from his words (Bayit Chadash in the name of Ran and Rashba). There is no difference whether they wrote the earlier date in the bill of divorce or whether they wrote the date after the twelve months, for since they deviated from his words, the bill of divorce is nullified according to Torah law (Beit Shmuel, section 8).

We also learned there in the Mishnah (chapter 7): "If he wrote [a bill of divorce] after twelve months and gave it after twelve months and he died, if the divorce preceded the death, it is a valid divorce; but if the death preceded the divorce, it is not a valid divorce. And if it is not known [which occurred first], this is the case of a woman who is 'divorced and not divorced.'" These are the words of the Mishnah. At first glance, there seems to be no novelty in these laws at all. However, it seems to me that it teaches us much, for if only the giving of the divorce precedes the death, it is considered a valid divorce, even if the giving was much later after twelve months, as our master the Rema wrote in section 5: "If he did not give it to her immediately after twelve months but rather much later, even if the delay was because the woman did not want to receive it immediately, it is still a valid divorce, provided that the husband is alive." And we do not say that his intention was specifically immediately after twelve months. And so, the Tanna teaches us that if it is not known, it is considered a doubt. We do not say that we establish him with the presumption of life until the divorce and she is certainly divorced, because now he is dead, we doubt that perhaps he died before the divorce (Ran). Similarly, we do not say the opposite, that since he is dead now, he was also dead from the beginning, as this reasoning appears in section 37: since she is now an adult, she was also an adult in the morning, and she should undergo levirate marriage. It has already been explained there in section 38 that whenever there is a presumption against it, we do not say this reasoning. And here, there is a presumption of life and a presumption of a married woman against this reasoning. And there, regarding an adult woman, there is no presumption of youth against her, for on the day that completes six months, there is neither a presumption of youth nor a presumption of adulthood, as explained there.

We learn in the Gemara (end of chapter 7): The Sages taught: If someone says "This is your get (divorce document) if I do not return after a week," this means the Sabbatical year, therefore they wait for him the entire eighth year, because the entire eighth year is called "after the week." And if he says "after a year," they wait for him a month; and if he says "after a month," they wait for him a week; and if he says "after Shabbat," they wait for him three days, which are Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday, as these are called "after the Shabbat." And if he says "before Shabbat," it is counted from Wednesday. The reasoning is because when he specifies a time that is cumulative from smaller units, such as the Sabbatical year which is composed of years, it is called "after" its cumulative unit that follows it. The Sabbatical year is composed of years, therefore they wait a year; a year is composed of months, therefore they wait a month; a month is composed of weeks, therefore they wait a week. Following this logic, "after Shabbat" should also imply the next day, since the week is composed of days. However, in common speech, when people say "after Shabbat," they mean up to and including Tuesday, and "before Shabbat" means from Wednesday onwards. Presumably, his intention is according to common speech. And there is no difference whether he is at the beginning, middle, or end of the Sabbatical year, for even if he is at the end of the Sabbatical year, it is considered a year since he used the term "Sabbatical year" (Tosafot). The same applies to a year and a month.

The Tur writes: If one said, "Write a get (divorce document) and give it to my wife if I do not come after the week," they should not write and give it until two shemitah (sabbatical) years have passed — the one they are currently in and the first year of the subsequent shemitah cycle. Likewise, for a year, they should wait the entire year and one month afterwards. For a month, they should wait the entire month and one week afterwards. For a week, they should wait the entire week and three days afterwards. This is similar to Rashi's explanation, but Rashi explained it when he gave her the get and said so, whereas the Tur explains it when he commanded to write it. The reasoning is the same for both. The Tur also wrote that in all these cases, one should not act earlier than stated, but if they delayed, it is of no concern. This aligns with what was written in section 21, that his concern was only to not act earlier, but he is not particular about a delay in time.

However, the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 9, Law 23: If he said to them, "Write and give my wife a get after the week," they should not write it except after a year from the week. If he said to them after a year, "Write it," they should not write it until after a month from the second year. If he said to them after the month, "Write it," they should not write it until after the Sabbath from the second month. If he said after the Sabbath, "Write it," they should not write it until after the Sabbath until the end of the third day. If he said to them, "Write and give it to her before the Sabbath," they may write it from Wednesday until the end of Friday and give it to her. Thus, if they delayed beyond the time he specified and then wrote and gave it to her, such as if he said to them after the month and they wrote and gave it to her after two Sabbaths from the second month, it is invalid. End of quote (see what was mentioned in Siman 141, section 123).

The Rosh of blessed memory interprets that their intention is not to write until the end of the year following the Shemitah year, and he argues that it is certainly permissible to write throughout the entire year following the Shemitah year. However, the Tur, the Ran, and the Maggid Mishneh interpret the words of the Rambam similarly, meaning that it is permissible to write throughout the entire year following the Shemitah year. According to the version of the Rambam before us, it is clear that it is like the words of the Rosh, for he explicitly wrote that after the year they do not write until after the second month, and so too after the month and after the week. However, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in his book Kesef Mishneh that this version is mistaken, and the correct version for "after the year" is that they write until the end of the month, and for "after the month" they write until the end of the week, and for "after the week" they write until the end of Tuesday. This is also written in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 6. And what was written "after the week, they only write until the year" means that they write throughout the entire year and no more. And this is what he wrote regarding delaying beyond the specified time, such as after the month, they wrote and gave it to her after two weeks of the second month—not precisely after two weeks, but meaning after the first week has passed and the second week has entered. And this disqualification of delaying beyond the specified time, even though we wrote in Section 21 that delay does not invalidate, is because here the time for writing is limited. But in Section 21, his intention was only to prohibit writing beforehand.

Based on the above, it could be that the Rambam does not disagree with Rashi and the other poskim (legal decisors) except in the interpretation of the baraita, but in this case, he agrees that if he said, "If I do not come until after the week," it is necessary to wait until a year after the Sabbatical year has passed and not to write then, and not before. And if they delayed the time, it is also valid because his main intention was not to write before. This is unlike the Rambam's interpretation, which does not depend on "if he does not come" but rather states simply, "Write and give after the week," meaning they write all year after the Sabbatical year and not beyond that (as the Beit Shmuel wrote). Therefore, all the poskim do not disagree in practice. And what the Rambam ruled regarding a delay, that it is invalid, means invalid by rabbinic law, and if she married, she does not have to leave, as stated in Siman 150. And why is it not a doubt from the Torah? Because indeed, it can be said that all delays, even very extended ones, are included in the term "after," but the Sages were concerned not to write except at a time that can be understood from the language as "immediately after." Therefore, this is only a rabbinic invalidity (Beit Yosef). Nevertheless, the Shulchan Aruch ruled that she is doubtfully divorced (see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 11).

The Tur writes in the name of Rabbeinu Chananel that if one says, "This is your get (divorce document) after the Shemitah year," it is not a get until the end of the first year of the eighth cycle and the first month of the second year. Similarly, with "after a year," "after a month," and "after a week." The Rosh disagrees with this and holds that she is divorced immediately after the week, and similarly for the other cases. It is not comparable to one who says, "This is your get if I do not come after the week," as we cannot say that it will be a get if he does not come within the week. If so, he should have said, "If I do not come within this week." Rather, since he stipulates the time of his coming after the week, it necessarily means if he does not come at the time called "after the week," which is a year from the coming week. "After a year" refers to one month from the months of the coming year. "After a month" refers to one week from the weeks of the second month. "After a week" is a term people use to divide the days of the week: half are called after the previous week, and half are called before the coming week. But one who gives a get to his wife to take effect after the week, why should it not take effect immediately after the Shemitah? The set time was so that she would not be divorced within the week. If his intention was until the eighth year passes, he would have said "after the week." It appears clearly that there is a printing error, and it should say "he would have said a year after the week."

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 6: "Some say that if one says 'after twelve months,' it is as if he said 'after a year.' If one says 'after thirty days,' they write 'one day after thirty days.'" And in this case, saying 'after thirty days' is not similar to saying 'after twelve months.' The reason is simple: when mentioning a month, it means after one from the count he took, and its rule is as after a year. Therefore, when saying 'after thirty days,' it also means one from the count he took, and consequently, it is not similar to after a month, and similarly in all such cases.

The Tur wrote that if one says, "If I do not come until after the festival," they should not write and deliver [the document] until fifteen days have passed after the festival. And so wrote the early authorities in the name of R. Chananel, who stated that they did not know the source of this ruling. Therefore, some say that just as the days of the week are divided between the two Sabbaths, so too are the days between one festival and the next divided between the two festivals. Thus, "after the festival" would be half the time between one festival and the next. The Rif wrote similarly in his responsa (as cited by the Beit Yosef in the name of the Ran and the Rama). However, according to this, the rules would change for each festival period, as the time between Passover and Shavuot is short, between Shavuot and Sukkot is longer, and between Sukkot and Passover is much longer. It appears that according to common parlance, there is no distinction, and the reasoning of R. Chananel and the Tur seems to be from the Mishnah in the first chapter of Ta'anit (10a), which states that when they went up for the pilgrimage, the last person would reach home fifteen days after the festival. It is explained in the Talmud (Bava Metzia 28a) that this was during the time of the Second Temple. Therefore, it was certainly called "after the festival" for fifteen days, and consequently, when we were exiled from our land, this designation did not change, even afterward, because we are in the exile of the Second Temple, may it be speedily rebuilt in our days.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in his great book in the name of the Rashba and the Ran that the period of a year, month, and week is not explicitly defined. At first glance, it seems that before these periods is like after them, as we say regarding Shabbat. However, this is not implied in the Jerusalem Talmud. Thus is his language. The explanation in the Jerusalem Talmud (end of chapter 7) is as follows: Rabbi Bon bar Chiya asked Rabbi Zeira, "Here is your divorce document, valid on the eve of Passover," meaning if I do not arrive before Passover. He responded that even according to the view that all thirty days after the festival are considered as after the festival, the thirty days before Passover are not considered as before Passover. Hence, it is clear that we do not derive the laws of 'before' from 'after.' We cannot interpret the Jerusalem Talmud as referring to the eve of Passover literally because then the thirty days would not be included. However, 'before' is like 'after' in that it is obvious that the eve of Passover is literally the eve of Passover, and what was the question? Therefore, it is certain that his intention was when he said 'before Passover' (what is written there in Shabbat Kodesh as proof for the explanation we wrote in section 27 and not like the Rosh is not a proof because it uses a brief language and its intention is if I do not come further). There it is also stated that if he said on Saturday night, there is a doubt until the following Friday night, and this is difficult because in the Talmud it is explicitly understood in several places that Saturday night is only called the night after Shabbat. In the Jerusalem Talmud, it also says the same regarding vows, and it is clear that in the language of people, it is not so. This requires further study. Also, see Yoreh De'ah, section 240.

And know that there are those who are uncertain about the term “tuch” (within), such as in the phrase "if I do not come within a certain time," perhaps it means the middle of the time, as Rashi explained on the verse "and the tree of life in the midst of the garden," which he interpreted as being in the middle of the Garden of Eden, and so did Onkelos translate. However, there is no doubt in this matter at all, and it is proven from many places that until the end of the designated time is called “tuch.” And from the tree of life there is no proof at all, for there, the verse is entirely superfluous, for it already wrote earlier that the Holy One, blessed be He, planted in Eden all kinds of trees, and it would have sufficed to say that He also planted there the tree of life and the tree of knowledge. Why then say "in the midst of the garden," since it is already speaking about the garden? Rather, certainly, it comes for an exposition that it was in the middle. And behold, regarding the impurity of an earthenware vessel, it is written "everything that is within it shall be impure," and the impurity reaches the walls of the vessel. And in the offering of the Passover lamb, it is taught "and he places its legs and its inner parts within it" (beginning of chapter 7 of Pesachim), and in the Gemara there, Rabbi Yehuda calls it "tuch, tuch." And is there an obligation to place them in its middle? (See there in Rashi's commentary).

And there are those who are uncertain about one who says "from today until a certain day" or "from now until twelve months" or "until thirty days," whether the last day is included or not. The uncertainty is whether "until" includes that day or not (Ba'er Heitev 1, in the name of Maharit). In my humble opinion, it seems that "until" does include the last day. Although there is a dispute among the Tannaim and Amoraim about whether "until" includes the last day or not (Nazir 6b and Niddah 58a), and it is explicitly stated by our sages (there) that some hold it includes the last day and some hold it does not include the last day, and in the vernacular it is understood as "until" and not including the last day (Ran on Nedarim 61a), it nonetheless seems clear to me that this applies to something that is distinct and separate from what precedes it, like "until Passover" or "until the festival," because these days have a different name from what precedes them. However, in matters that are not distinct from what precedes them, "until" includes the last day. Therefore, the sages ruled regarding the times of prayers that "until the fourth hour," "until the sixth hour," means that it includes the last hour, as it is stated in Berachot (27a), because the hours are equal in their names. And in the language of the Torah, it is the same, as it is written concerning chametz, "from the first day until the seventh day," and it includes the seventh day. And concerning a leper, it is written "from his head to his feet," and it does not include the feet (Arachin 18a), because the head is a separate entity, and so are the feet. And from our Mishnah itself, it is proven so, for it teaches: "This is your bill of divorce if I do not come from now until twelve months," and if he dies within twelve months, it is not a bill of divorce, and the bill of divorce is completely void. And we have already clarified that "within" means the entire time, and it implies explicitly that if he even dies on the last day, the bill of divorce is completely void. And if you think that there is uncertainty about this, the Talmud and the poskim would not have omitted to discuss this to prevent stumbling. Therefore, it is certain that there is no doubt about this. (And I do not have the responsa of Maharit to examine it now, but it is necessary to consider this for the halacha, and Kenesset HaGedolah wrote that it is good to make the condition explicit about a certain day, see there).

We learned in a Baraita (76b) that if a man said to his wife, "This is your get (divorce document) as long as I do not appear before you for thirty days," and he was going and coming, going and coming, since he did not seclude himself with her, it is a valid get. And there is no concern for an "old get," since he did not seclude himself with her. This is the conclusion of the Baraita. 

The explanation is that the condition was that the get would be valid when he did not see her for thirty consecutive days. The Tanna teaches us two things: first, that it is not necessary for the condition to be fulfilled immediately. Therefore, even though he was going and coming and saw her occasionally, nevertheless, when the condition is fulfilled—meaning he distanced himself from her for thirty days and did not see her—the get is valid. Additionally, the Tanna teaches us that there is no concern that he might have secluded himself with her, which would render the get invalid due to suspicion that they might have had relations and she might give birth to a son afterward. People might then see that the date of the get is earlier than the conception of the son and might say that the get is prior to the birth of the son. This will be explained in Siman 148. This invalidation is Rabbinic, and here, since we did not see him seclude himself with her, even though he saw her occasionally, we do not worry about an "old get." When the condition is fulfilled, it becomes a valid get.

The Talmud questions: Should we be concerned that maybe he appeased her? And it answers by stating that he says, "You are trusted by me to say that I did not come." Rashi explains that the concern is that perhaps when he came to her, he appeased the quarrel between them and secluded himself with her. Then, later, the husband might come and contest, claiming that he appeased her. The answer is that at the time of the condition, he says, "I am giving the get (divorce document) on the condition that you are trusted by me as if you were a hundred witnesses to say that I did not come and seclude myself with you and appease you." Similarly, the Talmud questions regarding the Mishnah that states, "From now, if I do not come within twelve months and I die within the twelve months, this is a get." The Talmud asks if we should be concerned that he might have appeased her, and it answers again that he says, "You are trusted by me to say that I did not come." Rashi explains (29b) that we should be concerned that he might have appeased her within the twelve months, which is a long time to come. This is not similar to sending a get from overseas and not setting a time for how long it should be in his hand, because in that case, there is no concern that he might have appeased her, as the husband would think that the messenger preceded him and the get already reached her, and he would not remove himself from the doubt. Similarly, the Gemara questions about one who sent a get to his wife and told the messenger not to give it to her until thirty days pass. The Talmud asks if we should be concerned that he might have appeased her, and Rashi explains that perhaps the husband came to her within the thirty days, secluded himself with her, appeased her, and had relations, making the get an "old get." The answer is that it refers to a betrothed woman, who is not yet dear to him, and he does not seek to appease her. This concern only exists with a married woman.

One might ask, according to this, if someone deposits a get (divorce document) with a third party to be given to his wife at a specific time and he is in the same city as her, should we be concerned that he has reconciled with her, since he doesn't need to leave his place? Additionally, since the get was deposited for a set time, it implies that he is also willing to move from his place to reconcile with her, especially when he is in the same city. The answer to this is that the sages have already stated in a similar case that if he had reconciled with her, there would be rumors (Gittin 18b). And since there are no rumors, it is clear that he has not reconciled with her. Why would there be rumors? Because the neighbors hear their quarrels, and when he reconciles with her and the quarrel ceases, everyone notices (Rashi there). It must be said that this reasoning only applies when they are in the same city, where initially the neighbors hear the quarrels, and naturally, they notice when the reconciliation occurs and the quarrels cease. But when he is not in the same city, there is no such awareness, even if he comes secretly and reconciles with her, because the old quarrels have already been forgotten, and the awareness is only when the reconciliation follows immediately after the quarrel. Therefore, in all these cases, the Talmud did not state this reasoning (this must be said according to Rashi's explanation, and what Tosafot wrote there, in the discussion beginning with "we are concerned," that when he leaves, he likely intends for her benefit and there is no quarrel, cannot be said according to Rashi, as he explicitly explained at the end of the chapter that he reconciled the quarrel between them).

And behold, according to Rashi's explanation, the primary concern that he may have appeased her is due to the possibility that he had relations with her, making the get (divorce document) a "get yashan" (old get). The Tur similarly writes, stating: "If he told her, 'This is your get when I pass in front of you for thirty days,' etc., even though he was coming and going, we are not concerned that he may have secluded himself with her in the meantime, making it a get yashan, provided that she had initially believed him," etc. And one should not ask why we need to worry about the minor concern of a get yashan, which is invalid only rabbinically as we have written. For if we are concerned that he may have come and appeased her, then the condition that he did not pass in front of her for thirty days has not been fulfilled, and the get is nullified biblically. The answer is that we do not worry about the time that he passed in front of her for thirty days, fearing that he may have come in the middle, because we do not need to be concerned about this. According to Torah law, we maintain the presumption of the matter, and there is no need to worry about something we have not seen, and a doubt does not remove a certainty (as the Maggid Mishneh also writes in Chapter 9, Law 11). Rather, the concern is about the time he was coming and going. This is also clear from the precise wording of the Tur that we have cited.

And one should not question this resolution, for in a case of "from now if I do not come from here within twelve months," we are concerned that perhaps he came in the middle and it becomes an "old get" (divorce document), which would invalidate the get because the condition was not fulfilled. In this case, too, it can be said, as was written, that certainly if he came, the get is invalidated by Torah law. However, in truth, there is no need to be concerned about this by Torah law since we did not see him, as was written. But regarding the "old get," which is merely a rabbinic concern, the sages decreed on this even though by Torah law it is not a concern. Therefore, we also decree in this case. And you should know that this is so, for if not, what benefit is there in the trust that he gave her? After all, we should still be concerned about this. Rather, it is certainly only a mere concern that he might cast doubt, and consequently, when he trusts her, he will not cast doubt. And even if he does cast doubt, he is not believed (and so wrote the Tosafot there on 18b and the Ran at the end of chapter seven, see there). (And according to what was written, the difficulty raised by the Bach and the Beit Shmuel in subsection 14 is resolved).

However, Tosafot and Rambam have a different approach to this matter, as the concern of "perhaps he appeased her" is not due to the issue of an old get (divorce document) but rather due to the concern of the cancellation of the get. And these are the words of the Rambam in Chapter 9, Law 9: If he stipulated that she would be divorced when he would leave from before her for thirty days, and he was going and coming, going and coming, and did not seclude himself with her, when he goes and stays away for thirty days she will be divorced. And even though he was going and coming within the thirty days, since he did not seclude himself with her, this is a valid get. In what case are these words said? When he stipulated and said that she is trusted to say that he did not appease her. But if he did not trust her, we are concerned that perhaps he appeased her when he was going and coming, and she forgave him and he then canceled the get when he appeased her. Due to this concern, the get would be invalid after thirty days. Similarly, one who says to a woman, "This is your get after twelve months," and he was with her in the city (as explained in the commentary on the Mishnah, beginning of Chapter 4 of Rosh Hashanah), we are concerned that perhaps he appeased her, unless he says she is trusted to say that he did not appease her. End quote.

Moreover, he wrote: Similarly, all conditions which depend on her consent, should she wish to forgive them to her husband, the get (divorce document) is invalid. We are concerned that perhaps he appeased her until he says, "She is trusted by me." In which case are we speaking? In the case of a woman divorcing from marriage, where his heart is familiar with her. But in the case of a woman divorcing from betrothal, we are not concerned that he appeased her. End of quote. He also wrote: This is your get from now if I do not come from here until twelve months. We are not concerned that perhaps he came secretly, for it is not the way of people to come secretly. If the time he set passed and he did not come, she is divorced. End of quote. According to him, on the contrary, the concern that perhaps he appeased her only exists when they are in the same city. In the case of "when I pass from before you," the concern is only during the time he went and returned. But once he left from here, we are not concerned that he came secretly, due to the reason he wrote. And in the case of "from now if I do not come until twelve months," he ruled like the first version in the end of the chapter who taught it in the Baraita. But regarding the Mishnah, this ruling does not apply. See there. And he means that we do not need to be concerned about his secret return. According to him, the sugya (discussion) on page 29b is rejected from the halacha, and the sugya follows the later version. Most of the poskim (decisors) disagree with him, and so it seems from the Rif. See there.

His words need clarification regarding what is relevant about conditions that depend on her will. Is the get (divorce document) or the condition dependent on her will? Whether the condition is something she must do, like giving two hundred zuz, serving his father, or nursing his son, or whether the condition is something he must do, like if he doesn't come or if he doesn't appear before her, everything depends on his will. He can annul the condition and annul the get if it is not made on condition or from now, as stated in Chapter 8 and explained in Siman 143. But with the woman, nothing depends on her. Indeed, the Raavad has already challenged this, saying: "I do not understand what this forgiveness is and what she has the power to forgive regarding the conditions. The appeasement is only that he was appeased with her not to divorce her, and the get in her possession is void." So also explained the Tosafists and Rabbeinu Chananel, as stated by the Rashba.

From the words of the Maggid, it is clarified that the Rambam's intent is that he is referring to a condition where the husband cannot annul it, but if she also agrees, they can annul it. This is the opinion of the Ramban, of blessed memory. According to this, what he said that it depends on her consent means that she also needs to agree to its annulment. This is what he means when he says that he appeased her and she forgave him, and then he annulled the get (bill of divorce), meaning that since she agreed to its annulment, he can annul it (and so writes the Beit Shmuel, section 15). However, it is clearly strained, for the Rambam did not write that he is referring to a conditional agreement. Furthermore, how could he not write this law in chapter 8, where these laws are primarily discussed? Additionally, according to their words, it would seem that the Rambam holds that even for conditions that she has to fulfill, we are concerned that perhaps he appeased her, as mentioned in the name of the Ramban. But he cited the responsa of the Rif that in other conditions, like if she has to give him 200 zuz, we are not concerned that perhaps he appeased her. And generally, the Rambam follows his own method (and it is true that the words of the Rif require examination and clarification, but as his words are interpreted, so should the words of the Rambam be interpreted).

Therefore, it seems to me that another intention is hidden in his words. Behold, when a husband divorces his wife, it is for one of four reasons: the first is when he hates her; the second is when she hates him and requests a divorce from him; the third is when, due to quarrels and conflicts, he comes to anger and divorces her; and the fourth is when he divorces her so that she will not need to undergo levirate marriage, such as if he is ill or if he is traveling to a distant land so that she will not remain an agunah (a woman bound to a missing husband).

It is understood that in the first case, when he divorces her because he hates her, he does not set any conditions and does not delay, but divorces her immediately. In the second case, when she hates him and requests a divorce from him, he sets a condition upon her to give him money or something similar. In the third case, when he divorces her because of quarrels and conflicts, it is customary for the husband to write a get (divorce document) and place it with a third party or give it to her, setting a condition to delay the time up to thirty days or something similar, so that within that time he might reconsider.

And we have already explained that this concern, that perhaps he appeased her, is only a rabbinic concern (d'Rabbanan). According to Torah law, we rely on the presumption (chazakah) as stated by the Maggid Mishneh. It follows that there is no need to worry about this concern even rabbinically if we saw the opposite in practice (Lechem Mishneh). Therefore, under the condition that she must fulfill, if she did not fulfill it, the get (divorce document) is invalid. But if she fulfilled it, why should we be concerned? When she fulfills it, it is presumed that he did not annul the get, for if he had annulled it, what compelled her to fulfill the condition? And to say that she gave it to him as a gift, why should we be concerned about such a strange and distant matter? On the contrary, it is more likely that he had compassion on her and forgave her so that the get would be valid even without fulfilling the condition, and there is no stumbling block in this (this is the intent of the Rif in his responsa). Similarly, in the fourth case, when he divorces her so that she does not need to marry the levir (yavam) or remain an agunah (a chained woman), why would he annul the get? There is no reason to be concerned about this.

However, in the third case, when he divorces her due to quarrels and arguments, and therefore the time is extended, there is certainly a concern that they might have reconciled with each other. And since they have reconciled, the act of giving the get (divorce document) becomes like a foreign matter to them, and there is a concern that he might have nullified the get. This is what is meant when it is said that if he divorces her, he should stay away from her for thirty days, as there is a concern that he might have appeased her and she forgave him, meaning she forgave the quarrels and arguments. Consequently, there is a concern that afterward he nullified the get since the reason for the get has been removed. Similarly, it is written that any conditions dependent on her will, if she wishes and forgives them to her husband, the get is nullified. We are concerned that he might have appeased her.

The explanation is as follows: a condition that she must fulfill is not considered dependent on her will, for her will is to obtain the get, and for this, she gives money, and it is dependent on the husband's will to forgive her the condition and for the get to be valid without the condition, as the Rif wrote. But a get that came about due to quarrels and arguments is considered dependent on her will, for if she wishes to forgive the quarrels and reconcile with him, this nullifies the reason for the get. In this case, we are concerned that he might have appeased her, as stated. And when it is written that the get is nullified, it means that the reason for the get is nullified.

Therefore, if there is a condition of "from now if I do not come within twelve months," we are not concerned that he might have appeased her, for there is no reason for this concern. This is what is meant by saying that people do not generally come secretly, meaning there is no reason to suspect this. Even if there might have been quarrels and arguments between them, there is no concern that he came secretly, as we do not suspect something that is not commonly done. The main concern is only when they are in the same city and he divorces her due to quarrels and arguments. According to this, his words align with the Rif's opinion, and it does not matter how the condition was made, whether "if" or "on the condition" or "from now." It is clear that if the condition was "if," he can nullify it alone, and if it was "on the condition" or "from now," both must agree, as Ramban states. Or it is possible that he holds that even both cannot nullify it, as this seems to be implied by his words in Chapter 8, where he does not mention this law at all, and some of the early authorities hold this way. This is why it was necessary to state "from now if I do not come," that it is not the way of people to come secretly, not because of the nullification of the get, but because the get is automatically nullified since the condition was not fulfilled, as he did not come.

However, in practice, one must consider all opinions, and in all types of conditions, there is this concern of appeasement alone. Therefore, if the condition is such that it is beyond their control, there is no concern for appeasement, and the condition will certainly be fulfilled. This is also what the Rashba wrote. But in other types of conditions, even if it is a condition that she must perform, we are concerned that perhaps she appeased him. Therefore, when making the condition, she must be given credibility. The words of our master, the Beit Yosef, in Section 7 at the end of the section: "And the custom is to stipulate at the outset that she is trusted to say that she did not appease him. And if, when he made the condition, he attached it to his arrival with witnesses, the get (divorce document) will not be nullified upon his arrival unless witnesses testify that he came and the time has passed, and they do not testify that he came, according to everyone, we do not worry that he came even if she was not trusted." However, in our times, we do not practice any conditions in a get. Nevertheless, in a situation where it is necessary to make a condition, it should be explicitly stated that she is trusted to say that she did not appease, and consequently, no blemish will be cast, and even if he protests, we do not concern ourselves with it as explained. And if he does not wish to grant her credibility, he should stipulate that the get will not be nullified unless witnesses testify, as mentioned.

**The Law of a Sick Person Who Divorces So That She Will Not Be Bound to Yibbum, and If He Recovers. It Contains 32 Sections:**

Some of the great scholars have questioned a case of a person on his deathbed who gives a get (divorce document) to his wife with the intention that she will not be bound to yibbum (levirate marriage), and it is found that he is divorcing her out of love. From where do the sages derive that this act constitutes a valid get? For in the Torah, in the section dealing with divorce, it is written, "if she does not find favor in his eyes," etc., and perhaps the Torah only commands the permissibility of a get when he divorces her out of hatred, not when he divorces her out of love (Levush in the response of Maharam of Lublin, Siman 123, and his answer is strained, see there). However, in truth, there is no question about this. Not only according to those who hold that even according to Beit Shammai, who said that one should not divorce except if he finds some unseemly matter in her, it is not a mitzvah or obligation but merely good advice (Mishneh Torah, Chapter 10, Halacha 21), but even according to what is said in Siman 119, Section 5, that it does not appear that way from all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), and from the Talmud and Jerusalem Talmud, nevertheless, it has been explained there in Section 2 that this applies to forced divorce and not when he divorces her willingly (so wrote the Beit Yosef there). And there is clear proof for this, as the Torah also addresses when she desires the divorce, for it is derived from "and she shall be sent away," which teaches that she can appoint an agent (to receive the get), and it is obvious that she would not appoint an agent if she did not desire the divorce (my esteemed brother-in-law, the Baal HaMeor on the Aruch HaShulchan). But from this, there is no clear proof, for one could say that it refers to when he hates her and she also hates him, and therefore she appoints an agent, and the nature of the matter is as "like water reflects the face," and this reasoning is found in the Talmud (Yevamot 117a). However, it has also been clarified from the times of the early prophets that everyone who goes to war in the house of David writes a get for his wife, and it is derived from a verse (Shabbat 56a), and they did so to prevent wives from becoming agunot (chained women). Moreover, it is explained at the end of Gittin that even according to Beit Shammai, who holds that one should not divorce except if he finds some unseemly matter in her, nevertheless, if he transgressed and divorced, what he did is done, indicating that concerning the validity of the get, it makes no difference why he divorces her. If she is divorced, the get is valid, but initially, the Torah warned not to do so. And how can it be understood that the Torah differentiates between initially and after the fact? Certainly, concerning the essence of the get, there is no difference between divorcing due to unseemly matter or any other reason. The Torah's concern is not about the essence of the get but about her humiliation. Indeed, according to Beit Shammai, it is forbidden when he divorces against her will without an unseemly matter, and similarly to Beit Hillel without her burning his food, as stated at the beginning of Siman 119. Consequently, when she desires the divorce and there is no humiliation in the divorce, he can divorce her even initially, even when divorcing out of love, for concerning the essence of the get, there is no difference for what reason he divorces her (and also a proof from Moses our teacher, who divorced Tziporah according to the explanation of Onkelos after sending her away).

It is self-evident that although the seriously ill person (Shechiv Meira) divorces out of fear that he might die, nevertheless, the get (bill of divorce) must take effect during his lifetime, for there is no get after death. Therefore, we learned in our Mishnah (72b): "This is your get if I die," "This is your get from this illness," "This is your get after death"—he said nothing. "From today if I die," "From now if I die"—this is a get. "From today and after death"—it is a get and not a get. If he dies, she performs chalitzah and does not enter into levirate marriage (yibbum). End of the Mishnah’s words. And in the Tosefta (Chapter 5), it is taught: "This is your get from today if I die from this illness," "If I die from this illness, this is your get from today"—his words stand, etc. End of the Tosefta’s words. (And from here it is difficult for those who require the laws of conditions in [the case of] 'from now'; and it will be explained in paragraph 18).

And behold, in the case of "This is your divorce after death," the reason is simple that it is not a divorce at all, and if he dies, she undergoes Yibbum (levirate marriage) because there is no divorce after death. Similarly, in the case of "This is your divorce from this illness," it implies from this illness and onward, and since he died from the illness, it turns out that the divorce only takes effect after death (Rashi). And in the case of "This is your divorce if I die," it also implies that he is divorcing her after death. And even though the phrase "if I die" does not necessarily mean after death – indeed, when he says "from today if I die," it is a valid divorce – if we think that "if I die" means specifically after death, then the ruling should be as "from today and after death." However, "if I die" implies two meanings: it could mean from today, as if he says "this is your divorce from now if I die," and it also implies simply "this is your divorce if I die," and then the divorce takes effect. Therefore, when he explicitly says "from today if I die," it must mean from today. But when he does not say "from today," it is as if he said "after death" (Gemara). For if his intention was from today, he would have said so. Therefore, it seems to me that if he claims after giving the divorce that his intention was from today, his claim is valid, and we proceed stringently. If he dies, she performs Chalitzah (removal of the shoe) and does not undergo Yibbum. If he was a Kohen (priest), she is forbidden from returning to him. And even though in all conditions, this phrase is certainly not like "from now," such as when he says "this is your divorce if you give me two hundred zuz" and the like, as stated in Siman 143, nevertheless, here it is different because this is not a condition but an extension of time (Beit Shmuel, Subsection 1). Moreover, in this case, it is likely he knew that there is no divorce after death. Therefore, it seems to me that we follow his claim stringently, as stated.

Some say that even in the three cases that were explained: "This is your get if I die," "This is your get from this illness," and "This is your get after death," it remains a doubt. The reason is that it has already been explained in Siman 143 that, according to Rabbi Yossi who holds that the date on the document proves that it is from today, every get or document which has a date written on it is considered as if it says "from today." Therefore, according to the authorities who rule according to Rabbi Yossi, the law in all these cases is like "from today if I die" and "from today and after death." Thus, it would be a get and not a get. However, according to the opinion that we explained in the previous Siman, Section 19, in the case of "This is your get after death," even according to Rabbi Yossi, we do not say that the date on the document proves anything. We also explained several details there, and we also explained in Section 13 that since it is written in the get "from this day and forever," it is itself like "from today." See there what we wrote. Nevertheless, it remains a doubt, and in all cases, she performs chalitzah and does not undergo yibbum (as the Beit Yosef also wrote, see there).

And if he says "from today if I die," the reason is simple as we have said, and all the more so if he says "from now if I die," since "from today" can mean the end of the day. This will be further clarified. And if he says "from today and after death," it is a [valid] get and not a get because we are uncertain about his intention. If he intended it as a condition, as in "from today if I die," then once he dies, the condition is fulfilled, making it a get from the time of giving. But if he went back on "from today" and said "after death," he nullified what he said about "from today," and it is not a get. Therefore, she performs chalitza and does not undergo yibum. This is not similar to what is written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 257, regarding a gift when he says "from today and after death," where there is no doubt, because certainly, there it involves two aspects: the body and the produce. He means to say the body is acquired from today and the produce after death, as explained there. But in a get, this is not applicable. Therefore, there is doubt whether it is a condition or a retraction. Some say that only "from today and after death" is in doubt, but not "from now and after death" (Tur in the name of the Ramah). This does not appear to be the case according to all the poskim, and this opinion is not brought in the Shulchan Aruch. It is explicitly implied in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 7, end of Halacha 3) regarding hefker (ownerless property), that if he says "from now after thirty days," it depends on the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis.

Some of our rabbis have written that if a man says, "From today if I die," and he dies on that same day, it is a doubt, because perhaps he intended the effect of the get (divorce document) to apply only at the end of the day (Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot there). And there are those who say that "from today" is like "from now" and his intention is that it should be a get immediately, for presumably he gives it out of fear that he might die. And if he is afraid he might die, he is certainly also afraid he might die on that same day, so definitely he means immediately. Nonetheless, it is proper to be stringent (Tosafot there in the name of Rabbeinu Elchanan). This is what our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 2: it is better that he says "from now" than "from today," for if he says "from today" and dies within that day, there is a doubt that perhaps his intention was for the end of the day, and there is no get after death. Even though if he says "write it after a year," they write it immediately after the year, as we wrote in the previous section, and it is explained there that "after a year" means a month after the year, and why should we not be concerned that his intention is for the end of the month (Beit Shmuel subparagraph 5)? It can be said that anyone who divorces because of fear of death delays his get as much as he can until the moment before his death, as will be explained, and it did not occur to him that he might die today. Before the end of the day, he felt he still had life. And although this is an excessive stringency, nonetheless, Heaven forbid to be lenient in a matter where Rabbeinu Tam was uncertain.

Even if he says "from now" and dies on the same day, where there is no ambiguity in the expression, nevertheless, witnesses must testify that she received the get (divorce document) during his lifetime. And although in every get we do not require witnesses to testify about the timing, and it is sufficient with witnesses to the signing, and this was the decree of Rabban Gamliel that witnesses should sign on the get, as stated in Siman 120 and 133, nevertheless, here it is impossible to rely solely on the signing witnesses, since from the time written in the get her release is not evident until the next day, as hours are not written in the get. It could be that it was written close to evening, and he died in the middle of the day. Therefore, she must bring witnesses before us that she received it before he died (Beit Yosef and Beit Shmuel, subsection 6), and something similar is explained in Choshen Mishpat at the end of Siman 240, see there. This is also written in the Tur.

And know that many of our Rabbis, the Tosafists, Rabbi Chananel, the Rosh, the Ran, the Riaz, the Mordechai, and Maharam of Rothenburg (Teshuvot Maimoni, siman 30) wrote that when one says "from today if I die" or "from now if I die," his intention is not that the get (divorce document) will take effect immediately upon his death, but rather that it will take effect one hour before his death. And they hold that this is what is stated in the Gemara (73b) that the days in between (the declaration and the death) are like a married woman certainly, or like a married woman in doubt, as it is considered as though he said the get will take effect from the time I am in the world, meaning close to his death. According to this, if the get is torn before he dies, the get is invalid (Mordechai and Teshuvot Maimoni there). Also, the get must be in her possession at the moment close to his death, and if it is in someone else's possession, the get is not valid. And if she remarries with this get, the children are rabbinically considered mamzerim (illegitimate) (there). This is not similar to all other conditions, where when one says "from today" or "from now," the get takes effect immediately if the condition is fulfilled. Here it is different because, since the primary reason for the divorce is the concern of death, he delays the get as much as he can until close to his death. Rashi, Rambam, and the Tur do not hold this way and they hold that "from today if I die" is like all other conditions as is evident from their words.

Therefore, it is very surprising that our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, did not mention this opinion at all. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in his work Darkei Moshe, in section 1, as follows: "The Mordechai, in the name of Rabbi Meir, wrote that the get (bill of divorce) should be valid at the time of the husband's death. And if it is not valid, she must leave." And in section 143, it is explained that many authorities disagree, etc., end quote. And I am very perplexed, for this is also the opinion of the Tosafot in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, as well as Rabbeinu Chananel, the Rosh, the Ran, and the Ri'az, necessarily so, because since they explained that it is as if he said, 'from the time I am in the world,' it must be that the get needs to be valid and in her possession close to his death. And on the contrary, more than the opinion of Rashi, the Rambam, and the Tur, we have not seen anyone who disagrees with this. And furthermore, it is even more surprising that the Tur did not mention the opinion of his father, the Rosh, of blessed memory, on this matter. Moreover, in section 148, the Tur wrote regarding 'from today if I die,' that the days in between are considered as a doubtful married state, and this follows this opinion. And if so, why did he not mention that the get needs to be valid until close to death? And in the Shulchan Aruch, even by name, he did not mention this as a separate law, but rather in relation to all conditions, see there (and see Beit Shmuel, subsection 3, who raised this issue, and what he wrote also in the name of the Tur, I do not know from where he derived this).

It seems to me that their reasoning is based on what is taught in the Tosefta (Chapter 5): "This is your get from today if I die. During the interim days, he is entitled to her findings, etc.," according to Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Meir says it is a doubt. Rabbi Yose says her intercourse is pending. The Sages say she is divorced in all respects, provided that he dies." And the law follows the Sages. According to this, it is proper that they did not mention this law because even according to the earlier authorities who explain differently than Rashi in that discussion, in any case, the law follows the Sages, and she is divorced from the first hour if he dies. This is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Darkei Moshe, that most of the poskim dispute this, and only Maharam agrees, but our other teachers do not agree because the law follows the Sages of the Tosefta. And although in the Talmud (74a) the version is that the Sages say "she is divorced and not divorced," nevertheless according to the version of the Tosefta, it is not so, and it is possible that this was their version in the Gemara. And so wrote the Rambam in Chapter 9, Law 19: "In all these conditions, all the days from the giving of the get until he dies and the condition is fulfilled, she is divorced in all respects, provided that she does not seclude herself with him." This is explicitly according to the version of the Tosefta, and so is the version of the Rif according to what the Rosh wrote in Chapter 7, Siman 4 (however, regarding the Tur, it is questionable since the Rosh did not agree with this, as mentioned there, and follows the method of his teacher, Maharam of Rothenburg. And there in the Responsa of the Maimonides, Siman 30, the responsa is addressed to the Rosh, as mentioned there).

Practically speaking, one should certainly be stringent that the get (bill of divorce) should be complete and in her possession until he dies. However, in retrospect, it seems to me that one can be lenient and rely on all these authorities for the reasons we have explained. Some of the great later authorities were stringent about this even in retrospect, while others were lenient. Among the lenient is the Radbaz, and one can rely on them in retrospect. Furthermore, it seems to me that in our times, when it is customary to translate even into foreign languages, and the sick person explicitly says that he is divorcing her from this moment, there is certainly no concern about this. Indeed, we must understand the principal explanation of our sages who interpreted it as if he said "from the time I am in the world," which seems impossible, for he says "from today." Rather, surely the explanation is "from today that I am alive," and not literally "from today." Therefore, when he explicitly says "from now," and especially when he specifies it in a foreign language, one can certainly rely in retrospect on the great authorities who permit it (as it seems to me), all the more so because we do not generally practice conditions at all, as will be explained.

There are those who are even stricter with other conditions in the case of "from now," requiring that the get (bill of divorce) be complete until the fulfillment of the condition and that it be in her possession (Rabbi Yitzchak Minz in the order of the get and Mahari Kolon). Their words have been rejected, as it is written earlier in section 143, where it is clearly explained in the Rambam at the beginning of chapter 8 and in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch there, to the contrary. It is possible that their intention was regarding a condition such as "if I do not come within thirty days" or similar, where the condition extends over time and his intention is to delay as much as possible, and it is like "from today if I die." Nevertheless, their words are not the main opinion, and it is only preferable to be stringent in this from the outset. But after the fact, there is no concern even for those who are stringent regarding "from today if I die," especially since we have explained that even there it is permissible after the fact.

The Rambam wrote that when a person on their deathbed (shechiv me'ra) writes a get (divorce document) for his wife and divorces her, if he then recovers, he cannot retract it. This is because his get is not like his gift. If we were to say that he can retract it, people might say that his get takes effect only after death, similar to his gift which only takes effect after death. Therefore, the get is not invalidated if he recovers.

The reasoning is that in the case of a gift from a deathly ill person, it is established that if he gives away all his possessions and then recovers, he can retract the gift. Even if he gives only a portion of his possessions while on his deathbed, he can retract it if he recovers because he gave it only due to the fear of death. Regarding a get, it would seem as if he is giving it due to the fear of death, as it is evident to all why he is giving her the get. We might have thought that if he recovers, the get would be invalid even if he gave it without specifying the reason.

Nevertheless, to prevent people from saying that the acquisition of the get is like that of a gift, taking effect only after death, if he recovers, he cannot retract it. Anyone who betroths or divorces does so with the understanding that it is according to the rabbis' interpretation (as per the Gemara in Gittin 73a). Since the rabbis have decreed this, he resolves in his heart to divorce in every situation, even if he recovers from his illness, as stated in the beginning of section 144.

From the words of the Rambam, it seems clear that he is discussing a case of a deathly ill person (shekiv me-ra) who divorced without any condition, meaning without stipulating "from today if I die," following Rashi's interpretation in the Gemara there. Similarly, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 4, stating: A deathly ill person who divorced without any condition, meaning without stipulating "from today if I die," we do not interpret his unstated intention as we do in the case of a gift, because a get (divorce document) is different, and if he recovers, the get is not retracted. However, the Tur wrote: And in a case where he said "from now," the get is effective even if he did not die from his illness but recovered, although in the case of a gift it is not so, for as soon as he recovers, the gift is voided. In the case of a get, it remains valid unless he explicitly stated that if he recovers, it should not be a get. Therefore, he must say, "if I do not die, it should not be a get," etc. It is clear that this also refers to the case of "from now if I die," which is the opinion of Tosafot in the Gemara there (as is also evident from the Bach there, and the words of the Beit Yosef in the Beit HaBechirah are questionable and require further study). His words are puzzling because according to Tosafot there, it is only valid if he recovered and then died from that illness, but not if he fully recovered, as explained in their words. The Tur, in any case, states that it does not retract unless it is said that he recovered and then died or that his intention was "from now if I die" rather than "from now" without any stipulation. And even though if that were the case, he should have stated simply "divorced without stipulation," but since until now he only mentioned "if I die" and "from now if I die" and did not mention "divorced without stipulation," he therefore also used the term "from now."

It is a matter of doubt since it has been explained that from a legal standpoint, a person on their deathbed (shechim me'ra) should be able to retract, except for the concern that people might say there is a get (divorce document) after death, as has been stated. Therefore, if he divorced with an "effective immediately" clause (me'achshav), as is customary among us, and divorced without specifying conditions, we should say that if he recovers, the get is retracted. Moreover, every get is considered as if "effective immediately" since it is written "from this day and forever." In the times of the Talmud, this was already the standard formula.

Conversely, one could question how it is possible to say that from a legal standpoint, if he recovers, the get is retracted, when the get states "from this day and forever." Indeed, it seems clear from the fact that the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) did not mention this issue, that if one says "effective immediately," he cannot retract. This is especially true according to the words of the Tur, as we explained in the previous section. The reason is simple: there would still be a concern that people might say that a get "from today and after death" is valid (see Beit Shmuel, section 7).

The Talmud needed to state this reasoning, that people might say there is a get after death, based on the primary law of writing a get, which does not require the phrase "from this day and forever." However, since it has become customary to write "from this day and forever," this reasoning is not needed. This could also be the intention of the Rambam. Alternatively, it could be that writing the phrase "from this day and forever" is not proof, and there would still be room for suspicion. Furthermore, it is possible to say that if he recovers, the get is retracted since this is a general formula and not specifically instructed by the husband, as we mentioned in Siman 144, section 14.

Rambam wrote in chapter 9, law 20: A sick person who wishes to divorce his wife conditionally upon his death so that she does not fall before a levir (brother-in-law), and if he recovers she will not be divorced, and he does not wish to divorce her from now so that his mind does not become disturbed. Thus, he writes in the get (divorce document) after writing the essential part or he says to her when giving the get: "If I do not die, this will not be a get, and if I die, it will be a get, and if I do not die, it will not be a get." This is to make the condition double and to have the positive before the negative, and he should not begin with a statement of calamity. If he dies, she will be divorced upon his death, provided that the get reaches her hand before his death. End of quote, and this is from the Talmud (75b), see there.

The explanation of his words: When a person on their deathbed (שכ"מ) wants to divorce from now, nothing else is needed except to say to her, "from now if I die." And according to the Rambam, in a case of "from now," there is no need for all the conditions of a stipulation, as he wrote in the sixth chapter of Ishut and we explained in Siman 38. However, if he does not wish to divorce from now but rather before his death, the laws of stipulation apply, requiring the condition to be doubled, and the positive condition to precede the negative one. The positive condition is "if I die, it will be a get (bill of divorce)," because even though they certainly do not wish for him to die, nonetheless, regarding the matter at hand, which is the fulfillment of the get, it is when he dies. And we do not follow the intention in this matter (as explained in the Taz's introduction to Yoreh De'ah). According to this, it suffices for him to say, "if I die, if I do not die," but to avoid opening his mouth to the Satan, he should first say, "if I do not die." This is not essential to the condition, because afterward, he says, "if I die, if I do not die," and one should not say, "why assume to throw this 'if I die' after the 'if I do not die' that follows it? Let us throw the 'if I do not die' that precedes it," and it would be the negative before the positive. For it can be said that the main reason we require the positive before the negative is so that he does not conclude with the positive, as a person is held by their final words. Therefore, since he concludes with the negative, we do not worry about what he opened with the negative (Ran chapter 7).

But the essence of his words is perplexing: without "from now," how could it be a valid Get (divorce document)? For we hold that in the case of "this is your Get if I die," it is considered a Get after death, and they resolved this by saying that the doubling of the condition removes it from the category of after death. When one does not double the condition, he holds that it is like saying "after death," and therefore does not double it, because there is no need to double it for after death. But when he doubles it, he reveals his intention that he says so as a condition according to the laws of conditions, and when the condition is fulfilled, it is a Get. For we have already explained in section 3 based on the Talmud that the phrase "if I die" implies two meanings, and it is not necessarily after death. And by doubling the condition, it proves that this is only a condition, and the effectiveness of the Get is before his death. And it is impossible to say "from now," because with "from now," there is no need for the laws of conditions. And with "if I die" alone, it is not a condition but an extension of time, as we explained there. And from the Tosefta that we brought in section 2, it is clearly proven that there is no need for the laws of conditions with "from now," for it is stated there: "This is your Get from today if I die from this illness, if I die from this illness, this is your Get from today." His words stand there, and behold, "this is your Get from today if I die" is an act preceding the condition, and in the laws of conditions, the condition must precede the act. But surely, as we said, from this Tosefta, it is difficult for the Geonim who require the laws of conditions even with "from now," for in the Mishnah, one could say it is not precise, but in the Tosefta, where we have stated the matter and its opposite, it is difficult.
