But the Tur wrote that one must say: "If I do not die, it will not be a get (divorce), and if I die, it will be a get from now." And if he does not die, it will not be a get. Then, it is nullified if he stands (recovers). But if he wants that it should not be nullified immediately when he stands, but rather after a certain time, he should say: "If I die by such-and-such a time, it will be a get from now, and if I do not die by such-and-such a time, it will not be a get."

And so it is written in the Shulchan Aruch, section 5, and so wrote the Ramban, Rashba, and the Maggid Mishneh, of blessed memory. They hold that even in the case of "from now," the laws of conditions apply, and they did not concern themselves with the Tosefta that we brought. Moreover, they already wrote that according to the fundamental law, we hold that a doubled condition is not necessary at all, nor all the laws of conditions (Rashba and Ran), for we do not hold like Rabbi Meir. It is only a stringency that the sages of the Talmud were stringent about in gittin (divorces), and therefore they were also stringent in the case of "from now." 

And the common custom is to say "from now," and if he did not say "from now," it is a doubt, and she does chalitzah and does not perform yibbum (levirate marriage), because most of the poskim (decisors) disagree with the Rambam, of blessed memory. In the order of the get, it will be explained that one should not state any condition before the writing of the get. See there.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that one should not say the language "if I die" or "if I do not die," but rather "if I die" or "if I do not die," for this is the language of the sages. And in retrospect, there is no concern.

The Tur wrote: If he did not recover from his illness, nor did he die as a result of the illness, but was bitten by a snake or the house collapsed on him and he died, it is not considered a valid get (divorce decree), since the condition he set was only regarding a natural death from the illness. Such an unusual accident is not common and was not in his contemplation, so it is not a get, whether he said "from today if I do not recover from this illness" or if he said simply "if I die from this illness." However, Rabbeinu Chananel ruled that if he said "from today if I die from this illness" and the house collapsed on him or he was bitten by a snake, it is not a get; but if he said "if I do not recover from this illness" and the house collapsed on him or he was bitten by a snake, it is a get. The Rambam wrote that in the case of "if I do not recover from this illness," it is a doubtful divorce. However, this does not seem correct to my master, the Rosh, as in both cases it is not considered a get.

In the Tosefta (Chapter 5) and the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 7, Halacha 4), it is explicitly stated like the words of Rabbi Chiya, and in the matter of the reason that if he dies from this illness, when the house falls on him or a snake bites him, the condition has not been fulfilled, for he did not die from this illness. However, when he says, "If I do not recover," he is making the divorce conditional on his recovery and not on any specific cause of death. And since he did not recover, it is a valid divorce. But our Talmud (73a) equates the law of the beginning with the end, as it says there that the end contradicts the beginning and does not differentiate with this reasoning. Because it holds that even if he says, "If I die from this illness," it is not necessarily meant that he will die due to the illness itself, for since his main intent is that she should not need to perform yibbum (levirate marriage), what difference does it make if he dies from the illness or from another cause? And "If I die from this illness" is like saying, "If I do not recover from this illness." And if you say that this is certainly the case, but it did not occur to him that such an accident would happen to him, then even with "If I do not recover," the law would be the same. And this is the opinion of the Rosh, who ruled that in both cases, it is not a valid divorce. And the Rambam ruled that if he says, "If I do not recover," it is a doubt, because he is uncertain about the interpretation of the Talmud, whether it disagrees with the Tosefta and the Jerusalem Talmud or if they can be reconciled. And the law is decided stringently like the Rambam, and this is also ruled in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 6.

There are those who pose a significant question regarding this matter, as it is established in the beginning of Siman 144 that an uncommon coercion (ones delo shachiach) is not considered, and the get (divorce document) is nullified under any condition involving uncommon coercion, as stated there. Why then do we maintain here that it is a doubt (as brought by the Beit Shmuel in Subsection 10)? After all, the fundamental principle of the law there is from this matter, as mentioned there. It is even more problematic according to the opinion of the Rosh, who holds here that it is a definite get, yet this is an uncommon coercion which is not considered.

The answer to this is that he deviated from the language of the Sages and from the language of the world, where the get is contingent on death, and he said "if I do not recover." Presumably, his intention was that any reason whatsoever, as long as he does not recover, it should be a get. This is implied in the Jerusalem Talmud. However, the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch, due to the severity of matters concerning a married woman, were uncertain about the interpretation of the Talmud and therefore were stringent in this matter.

It seems to me that even if he did not say "if I die from this illness" but rather "if I die" in general, and he was eaten by a lion or bitten by a snake, it is not a get, because an uncommon coercion is not considered. The Talmud and the poskim who mentioned "from this illness" did so because without "if I do not recover," it is necessarily understood to mean "from this illness," and therefore they also mentioned "if I die" in this context. However, the same applies to "if I die" in general, and this matter requires further study for a definitive ruling, even though it seems to me as I have written.

You should know that this is indeed the case, as the Ramban, Rashba, and Ran hold that if he said "if I die from this illness" and he died from another cause, even a common cause, it is not a get, even if he died as a result of this illness from which he did not recover. Since his death was not due to the illness itself, it is not a get, even from a common cause (as noted by the Beit Shmuel in Subsection 9). Therefore, why did the Talmud and the poskim mention the collapse of a house and a snake bite, which are uncommon, to teach us that even in common causes, it is not a get? It is certain that they mentioned it in passing concerning "if I do not recover." Nevertheless, in practice, one should be stringent.

Maimonides wrote (there) as follows: "Here is your bill of divorce from now if I die from this illness. If he recovered and went out to the marketplace, but then fell ill again and died, we assess whether he died from the first illness. If he did, it is a valid bill of divorce; if not, it is not a valid bill of divorce. If he transitioned from one illness to another without going out to the marketplace, it is a valid bill of divorce, and no assessment is needed." His words indicate that even if he went out to the marketplace without a crutch, since he fell ill again and it was assessed that he died from the first illness, it becomes evident that the act of going out was of no significance, and certainly he had not fully recovered from that illness since he died from it (Beit Yosef). It seems clear that this applies only if he fell ill immediately, but if some time passed and he fell ill, it is not a valid bill of divorce, for it is considered a different illness similar to the previous one. If he transitioned from one illness to another without going out to the marketplace, even if he walked in his house without a crutch, it holds no significance. Likewise, if he went out to the marketplace with a crutch, it holds no significance. I learned this from Maimonides' words in Chapter 4 of the Laws of Murderers, where he wrote: "The phrase 'on his crutch' mentioned in the Torah does not mean that he walks while leaning on a bed or another person, for even one who is about to die can walk on a crutch. Rather, 'on his crutch' means he walks on the crutch of his vitality and does not need any other support to lean on." This is also how Onkelos translated it, and it is taught in the Mekhilta on this verse. The verse in the Torah states, "If he rises and walks outside on his crutch, the one who struck him shall be cleared." Since the intention is 'on the crutch of his vitality,' it implies that leaning on a bed or another person, even outside, holds no significance. This is Maimonides' view. And even though in the Talmud (72b), it explicitly says that if he walks outside on a crutch, an assessment is needed, and it is clearly explained that if he walked outside without a crutch, no assessment is needed, Maimonides holds that this is not according to the conclusion of the Talmud. (This is only for Rava's initial understanding and not according to the conclusion of Rabbah and Rava, who do not follow Rava's initial understanding). Even though Maimonides himself interprets that it applies universally, as evidenced by his words we cited in section 13, he nonetheless holds that this law applies even to "from today if I die from this illness," as per the opinion of Nachmanides, cited by the Ran in the discussion there. This also seems to be the opinion of the Rif and the Rosh, who did not mention this discussion of the crutch at all. Investigate this thoroughly.

However, the Tur writes as follows: "If he recovered from his illness and went to the marketplace without a support, like healthy people, even if he later fell ill again and died from the first illness, the get (divorce document) is void, because he recovered in the meantime. If he did not go to the marketplace, even if he transitioned from one illness to another and walked in his house without a support, it is a get, and no estimation is needed because he certainly died from this illness. If he recovered and went to the marketplace with a support, if he did not transition from one illness to another, but his illness worsened and he died, even if he had a period of improvement in the meantime, no estimation is needed because it is certain he died from the first illness. However, if he transitioned from one illness to another, since he recovered and went to the marketplace with a support, an estimation is required to determine if he died from the first illness. If he did, it is a get; if not, it is not a get." End quote. I am astonished by our teacher, the Beit Yosef, who in his major work wrote that the Tur's way is the straight path, yet in the Shulchan Aruch, section six, he did not mention this opinion at all, which requires investigation. Some say further that even if he transitioned from one illness to another and did not go to the marketplace, an estimation is needed because since he said "from today if I die from this illness," perhaps the other illness does not stem from the first illness, and it is not a get. Therefore, an estimation by doctors is needed to determine if the second illness derives from the first illness or not (Beit Yosef in the name of the Rashba). However, if the first illness was severe and did not resolve, even if he fell into another illness, no estimation is needed because he was also likely to die from the first illness (ibid.).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 8 that if a person on their deathbed gave a divorce (get) and said "from today if I die" without specifying further, and then recovered, the divorce is nullified. We do not say that he meant "if I die at any time" but rather "if I die from this illness" was implied. However, if a healthy person said "from today if I die," it certainly means if he dies during his lifetime, and whenever he dies, she is divorced, as quoted. And although one might question what kind of condition this is, since it is obvious that at some point he will die, it can be explained that we do find such a condition, like "if the sun emerges from its sheath" in the previous section (Ran).

And that which we have said regarding a deathly ill person (shechiv me'ra), that even if he died without specifying which illness, if he recovered, his get (divorce document) is nullified—this is only if he recovered completely, becoming as strong in body as before. However, if he did not recover completely, even if he walked in the market without a cane, and even if he died from another illness, the get remains valid. This assessment is only relevant if he specified "from this illness," but without specifying "from this illness," as long as he did not recover completely, no assessment is needed, and the get is valid (Ramban and Ri'az, cited in Beit Yosef and Beit Shmuel, paragraph 12). There are those who disagree (mentioned there in the name of the Maggid Mishneh), and this also seems to be the language of the Tur, see there.

Furthermore, it is written in Section 9, a good piece of advice according to the great sages of the world to be cautious of deceitful individuals in the case of a conditional get (bill of divorce) given by a deathly ill person who says, "If I die from now until a certain day, it shall be a get," and he should not say, "If I die from this illness," so that the condition should not depend on the illness. For perhaps an unscrupulous person will come and persuade the doctor to say that he did not die from that illness but from another illness to which he transferred, and thereby cast aspersions on the get. These are the exact words. This only applies to the first opinion mentioned in the previous section, for those who disagree make no distinction, as even if he did not say "from this illness," it is as if he had said it (see Beit Yosef, sub-section 12). However, according to the first opinion, there is a concern even according to Maimonides, for if he transfers from one illness to another, there is no need for an assessment, because we say that surely the first illness remains, and we must be concerned that the doctor might be persuaded to say that the first illness did not remain at all (see there, sub-section 15).

And know that there are some of our rabbis who wrote that in this era, we are not proficient in estimating whether the person died from the first illness or not (Responsa of Maimonides, Siman 30). Therefore, our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 9 that one should not rely on the estimations of doctors in this era. It has also been clarified that there is a dispute among the early authorities whether, in the case of "from now" (me'achshav), a doubled condition and all the laws of conditions are necessary or not, and one should be stringent in all matters related to the prohibition of a married woman.

And because there are several complications and difficulties with a conditional get (bill of divorce) given by someone on their deathbed, the Mordechai (Chapter 7) writes that Rabbi Yehuda from Paris always endeavored that a get given by someone on their deathbed should not be conditional but rather a plain get. And if it is because they desire that if he recovers, they will remarry, they can accept upon themselves a fine according to the community's enactments, similar to the conditional engagements customary among us, or give collateral such that when he recovers, they will remarry. And so too wrote our Rabbi, the Rema, that it is proper to do so and strive for this, unless he is a Kohen, in which case it is necessary to make the get conditional, for otherwise, she would be forbidden to return to him. Likewise, if the ill person only desires a conditional get, one should not overly press him to give an unconditional get because there is a concern that due to the distress, his mind might become disturbed. This matter requires much consideration, as many sages were concerned about the disturbed state of mind of the ill, and the wise man has his eyes in his head to understand the nature and circumstances of the ill person.

This ordinance that we have written about is referred to by the poskim as the decree of Rabbi Yehuda of Paris. According to Tosafot (Shabbat 56a, Gittin 73a), during the wars of the House of David, they would similarly give their wives a complete bill of divorce so that if they died in battle, their wives would not be subjected to levirate marriage. However, they did this discreetly to avoid public knowledge, and upon returning from war, they would remarry their wives. For this reason, Batsheva was permitted to David because Uriah had divorced her (see Maharsha at the end of Gittin in the commentary starting "So that future generations will know").

It is clear that if, after recovering, the woman does not wish to remarry him, she pays the penalty or forfeits the collateral, and he cannot nullify the divorce after she has been generally divorced and the get (bill of divorce) has been torn up. Approximately three hundred years ago, one of the leading scholars challenged this practice, asserting that the subsequent remarriage indicated a condition that if he did not die, it would not be a valid get. The sages of the generation opposed him, nullified his words, and decreed not to cast aspersions on this matter. They were very correct in this, and the main reasoning of that scholar was due to the assumption that had he known she would not want to return to him, he would not have divorced her.

We have already explained in Siman 42 that in matters of divorce and betrothal, we do not follow assumptions. For this reason, we rule that revealing one's intention regarding a get is not considered significant, and therefore there are no laws of asmachta (reliance) in gittin (divorce). The reason is that the validity of gittin and kiddushin (betrothal) depends entirely on the witnesses, and what transpires privately between them has no effect. We follow only the action and spoken words, not the thoughts in the heart, which is the primary reason for assumptions and reliance.

However, in monetary matters, witnesses are created only for lies (and even according to what Tosafot wrote at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Gittin in the commentary starting "So that future generations will know," this does not apply here, as we cannot ascertain his intention ourselves, and it is also not similar to what Beit Shmuel wrote in Siman 42, subparagraph 12, in the name of Mordechai. There, it was like actual evidence, and even regarding this, the Rashba disagreed. See there. I am very astonished at the genius author of Mishkenot Yaakov in Siman 34, who felt confident to support the words of Maharam Lublin against all the great scholars of the generation. All his words, according to what we have written, are completely rejected. This is also written by Beit Shmuel in subsection 16 and Bach in Siman 148, and Heaven forbid to argue on this. Consider this well).

A woman who was divorced conditionally, as was stated, and the husband died, she does not need to mourn for him since she was already separated from him. Nevertheless, there is no prohibition if she wishes to cry for him and follow his bier (Rema). We do not suspect that people will say she is a widow and not a divorcee and permit her to a Kohen (Beit Shmuel, subsection 17), since the matter of the divorce is known publicly. This is not similar to what is written in Siman 17, where we do not allow an agunah to mourn unless we know clearly that her husband died, because there we are concerned that perhaps he did not die, and she is still a married woman. Nevertheless, it seems to me that here we only allow her to cry and follow his bier, but if she wishes to observe the seven days of mourning and the thirty days, we object, lest this causes confusion when they see that she is behaving completely as his wife, and they will say that the divorce was invalid and she is a widow and not a divorcee and permit her to a Kohen.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that if a man who is on his deathbed gave a get (divorce document) to someone and said, "Acquire this get for my wife so that she does not fall before a yavam (levirate marriage),” and he died before it reached her, she is in a state of doubtful divorce and must perform chalitzah (ceremonial release from levirate marriage) and cannot perform yibbum (levirate marriage). This is because the question, which remained unresolved in Yevamot Chapter 15, is whether we say that this is a merit for her and one can act meritoriously on behalf of someone not present, or perhaps she loves the yavam and desires to perform yibbum, and this is not a merit for her. Based on this, the Maharshal wrote in Yam Shel Shlomo, Yevamot Chapter 15, Siman 21, as follows: "It would seem that nowadays, when yibbum is not practiced, it is certainly a merit for her. However, since I have written that if both parties intend to fulfill the mitzvah, we do not protest against them, therefore, even nowadays, we must be concerned. However, in places where the enactment of Rabbeinu Gershom, which prohibits taking two wives and divorcing against the wife’s will, has spread, it is certainly a merit for her, for it is unreasonable to say that she would hope his wife would die so that he would marry her. Nevertheless, my heart does not permit me to be lenient initially to divorce her through another, but after the fact, she is divorced and exempt from chalitzah." All the more so in the case of a minor yavam, as Mordechai wrote there in the name of Avi HaEzri and Rabbeinu Tam, that after the fact, she is exempt from chalitzah. The Taz also wrote plainly that nowadays it is a merit for her, specifically when he grants it conditionally, for otherwise, it is not a merit for her, as he might not die and might not marry her again, and it is certainly a detriment for her (Pitchei Teshuva, Radbaz). Note that what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote, that if he died before it reached her, she is in a state of doubtful divorce, clearly means that if it reached her before he died, she is divorced. Even though he did not appoint him as an agent to deliver it, since his primary intention was for it to reach her, but he was concerned he might die first, therefore he said "acquire it for her." But certainly, his intention was not that he should not be an agent to deliver it, and we testify that this was his intention. See what I wrote in Siman 140, Section 16.

The Law of Divorcing After a Set Time and Other Conditional Laws. It contains twelve sections: The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that if one divorces his wife after a set time, she is divorced when the set time arrives. This is similar to a condition but is not a condition. It is similar to a condition in that she becomes divorced when the set time arrives, but it is not a condition because one who divorces on a condition has already divorced, whereas in this case, the divorce does not take place until the set time arrives. Therefore, one who divorces on a condition must double his condition, but this does not require doubling of words or other legalities of conditions. For instance, if one says to his wife, "This is your get (divorce document), but you will not be divorced with it until after thirty days," she is not divorced until after thirty days. And if the husband dies, or the get is lost or burned within the thirty days, she is not divorced. These are the words of the Rambam at the beginning of Chapter 9, and we have already brought his words in Siman 143, Section 5, and explained it with G-d's help in Section 15. Note that it is not only when he says, "and you will not be divorced with it until after thirty days," but the same applies if he says, "This is your get, and you will be divorced with it after thirty days." Similarly, later on, regarding "you will not be divorced with it until you give me two hundred zuz," it is not specifically this language, but the same applies if he says, "you will be divorced with it after you give me two hundred zuz," for all this depends on time or action (Bava Metzia).

They also wrote a law: If one placed the divorce document (get) on the side of a public domain and it was stolen or lost after thirty days, she is considered divorced, since the get was valid on the day she was divorced, and he designated it in a place that is not a public domain, as the sides of the public domain are not considered a public domain. End of quote. This is also from the language of the Rambam there. The explanation of the matter is that in the Gemara (Ketubot 86b), it is explained that regarding acquisition, the sides of a public domain are like an alleyway and a marsh where one can acquire, and it is not like a public domain, although regarding Shabbat, it is considered as a public domain because sometimes many people push and enter there, but not for acquisition purposes (Rosh there). Therefore, both regarding monetary matters, such as if one said, "Pull this cow and it will not be acquired by you until after thirty days," and when the time is up, it stands on the sides of the public domain, the buyer acquires it. Similarly, regarding a get, as said.

Behold, there are some of our Rabbis who explain that in both cases, it refers to "from now" (Ran there in the name of the Ra'avad) where he says, "This is your get (divorce document), but you will not be divorced with it except from now and after thirty days." And similarly with property, where he says, "Pull this cow and acquire it from now and after thirty days." For without "from now," we say there (Bava Metzia 2a) that he does not acquire it, because since the pulling was done earlier and the acquisition is after thirty days, how can the previous pulling effectuate an acquisition that is after thirty days? Similarly, with a get, without "from now," it would be like "Take your get from the ground" (ibid.). And if one asks, regarding a get, we hold "from today and after death," which is a doubt whether it is a condition or a retraction, as written in the previous section. Consequently, the same applies to "from now and after thirty days." Therefore, either way, if it is a condition, public domain is not required, and even in the public domain, it would be a valid get because the act of the get is already completed. And if it is a retraction, it is like without "from now" (so asks the Ran there). One could answer that either they hold it is a condition and we do not hold like that (they hold like Shmuel in Kiddushin 59a, and we hold like Rav there), or there is a distinction between "from today and after death" and "from now until thirty days." For "from today and after thirty days," it can be said that it begins today and completes after thirty days, for the get is valid after thirty days just as before thirty days. But with "from today and after death," it cannot be said that it completes after death, for there is no get after death. Therefore, it must be either a condition or a retraction (Tosafot there, s.v. kol). And note well.

Some of our rabbis have explained that in both cases, the discussion is about a situation where the condition of "from now" (me'achshav) is not applied (Ran there). This is different from the case of "Here is your get on the condition that it lands on the ground," where as long as it has not left her possession, she is divorced, as there is a giving for the sake of divorce, but he does not want the get to take effect until the thirtieth day and the get must be in her possession at that time. And even though the Rambam, of blessed memory, explains in Chapter 2 of Sales that it is regarding "from now," nevertheless, concerning a get, he also holds that it is not referring to "from now," because with "from now," there is a doubt whether it is a condition or a retraction. And even if it is placed in a public domain, there remains a doubt (Kesef Mishneh there and Beit Shmuel 1). This is not comparable to monetary matters where the acquisition is through pulling (meshicha), and the pulling does not occur after thirty days, unlike a get, which exists and is placed in a location appropriate for acquisition (Hagahot Maimoniyot). This is also the opinion of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, who wrote in Choshen Mishpat at the end of Siman 197 that they are discussing "from now," and here they wrote like the Rambam. Additionally, it appears that the Rambam fundamentally holds that it is a condition, but in matters of divorce and marriage, due to the stringency of issues concerning prohibited relations, they were stringent in this matter (Avnei Shoham).

They further wrote: Similarly, if one makes the divorce conditional on an action, it is considered as if he divorces after a certain time. How so? For example, if he says to his wife, "This is your bill of divorce, but you will not be divorced by it until you give me 200 zuz," she is divorced after she gives [the money]. There is no need to double the condition or to follow the other rules of conditions, for he did not divorce her conditionally, but rather he has not yet divorced her. Instead, he made the divorce dependent on the performance of a particular action, and after that she will be divorced. What is the difference between one who divorces conditionally and this case, where he sets a time for the divorce or makes it dependent on an action? The one who divorces conditionally has already enacted the divorce, but it is not completed until the condition is fulfilled. Therefore, when the condition is fulfilled, she is divorced if the bill of divorce is still valid, even if it is not in her possession, and she does not need to retrieve it or have it in her possession after the condition is fulfilled, for it initially reached her as a bill of divorce. However, if the divorce is dependent on a time or an action, it did not initially reach her as a bill of divorce but rather as a deposit until the set time or the performance of the action. Therefore, when the time arrives, the bill of divorce must be in her possession, or she must retrieve it, or it must be in the place designated for it, even if it is not in her possession, as mentioned. Only after this does she become divorced by it. If she marries before the set time or before performing the action that the divorce is dependent on, she must leave [the second husband], and the child from him is a mamzer (illegitimate), for she is still fully married and there is no divorce here. These are also the words of the Rambam there, which we brought in Siman 143, paragraphs 6 and 7. In paragraph 13, we explained the reasoning behind why, with a condition, the bill of divorce must be complete even if it is not in her possession. There, it is also explained that he holds that even with a condition, if it is not specified as "from now," if she marries before the condition is fulfilled, she does not have to leave [the second husband]. There (in Avnei Miluim, section 2), it also says that the Beit Yosef holds similarly that she does not have to leave, but we explained there that this is not so, and I do not understand his precision in quoting the Rambam's language. Investigate this thoroughly.

There are those who say that what is written, "A virgin, in time or in action," means that the bill of divorce (get) must be in her possession, and if it is not in her possession, it is not a get. This is according to those who rule not like Rabbi Yossi, who states that the date on the document proves it. But according to those who rule like Rabbi Yossi, it is a doubtful get, as it is similar to "from now and after thirty days" (Beit Shmuel, note 3). It seems to me that according to the language explained, "and you will not be divorced by it until after thirty days or until you give me two hundred zuz," this explicitly uproots the date of the document. This ruling only applies when he says, "This is your get, and you will be divorced by it after thirty days or after you give me two hundred zuz," as we wrote at the end of section 1 (and it is different from section 3, see there and understand it well).

They also wrote: If a man gives a get (bill of divorce) to his wife and says to her, "If you do not give me two hundred zuz, this is not a get," or "You are not divorced," this is not a divorce at all. This is neither a conditional get nor dependent on an action. And similarly, any case like this. And this too is from the words of the Rambam, and we explained it there in section 8, see there. And the main reason we explained there in section 16, see there well.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 3 that if a man says to a woman, "You are divorced, but if you do not give me two hundred zuz, you will not be divorced," she is divorced even if she did not give [the money], because he did not double his condition. This is according to the Rambam, who holds that by law, a condition must be doubled in matters of divorce and marriage. However, it has already been clarified that some of our rabbis believe that, fundamentally, there is no need for a doubled condition, as we do not follow Rabbi Meir's opinion, and it is only required as a stringency. Therefore, in practice, one should act stringently, and it becomes a case of a doubtful divorce. He himself mentioned this opinion in Chapter 38, Section 4. How then did he rule definitively here? It is possible that he relied on what he wrote there.

The Rambam writes in Chapter 8 of Hilchot Gerushin: If a woman was divorced on condition and married another man before the condition was fulfilled, if the condition was fulfilled, she is betrothed to the latter. If the condition was not fulfilled and the divorce is nullified, she does not need a get (divorce document) from the second man because the betrothal does not take effect with her. However, if she married and the condition was not fulfilled, and the divorce is nullified, she needs a get from the second man, as we have explained. End of quote. This was also copied by the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in paragraph 4. It is clear that this refers to a condition of "on the condition that the divorce takes effect retroactively." Therefore, if the condition is fulfilled, she is betrothed to the latter. (The Gra, section 16) And all the matters discussed earlier refer to "on the condition," as mentioned there, because without "on the condition," how can it be said that she is betrothed when the condition is fulfilled, and the effect of the divorce is only when the condition is fulfilled, and at the time of accepting the betrothal, she was still a married woman. There are those who want to say that it refers to "if" and not "on the condition," and the Rambam follows his own reasoning that even in the condition of "if," if she marries, she does not have to leave. (The Beit Shmuel, section 5) This does not seem correct because, if so, how could the Tur and Shulchan Aruch leave their words ambiguous, and many disagree with him on this, as mentioned in the beginning of section 143. However, according to the Rambam, it is certainly the case that the betrothal takes effect, and his reasoning we have explained there with God's help.

However, the Raavad of blessed memory primarily disagreed with the Rambam of blessed memory on this matter. The Rambam compared this law to a case where a woman heard that her husband had died and got betrothed to another man, and then her husband returned. In such a case, she does not need a get (divorce document) from the second man and is permitted to return to the first husband because everyone understands that the betrothal was a mistake. This is unlike a case where she married another man, in which she would require a get from both men and must leave both, as stated in Siman 17. The two cases are not similar because in the former case, everyone sees that the betrothal was a mistake since the husband is alive. The rule that if she marries another she must leave both husbands is a penalty imposed by the Sages for not verifying the husband's death, as mentioned there. However, in the case of a conditional get, how can anyone know if the condition was fulfilled or not? People will certainly say that the condition was fulfilled and the second betrothal is valid, requiring a get from the second man. Consequently, she would be prohibited from returning to the first husband so that people do not say he is remarrying his divorced wife after she was betrothed to another, as stated in Siman 46. But according to the Rambam, she is permitted to return to the first husband since she does not need a get from the second man.

The Maggid Mishneh wrote to reconcile the words of the Rambam: that which he wrote, that if the condition was not fulfilled, the get (bill of divorce) is void and she does not require a second get, this is in a case where the condition was not to do a certain thing and she transgressed and did that thing, where she actively nullified it. Or even in a condition to do a certain thing but a time was set for it and the time passed and she did not do it, and similarly in all such ways where the condition was nullified in practice and the get is void. However, in the case of a condition to do something without a set time and it is still within her power to fulfill it whenever she wishes, if the condition is fulfilled she will definitely be divorced and she requires a get from the second one. We are concerned that she might fulfill the condition and the second marriage will take effect, and consequently, she is prohibited from returning to the first husband so that people will not say that one returns his wife after she was married to another. The rule is that whenever she requires a get from the second one, she is prohibited from returning to the first one. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, agreed with his words in his great book, and based on this he wrote these things in Shulchan Aruch, section 5.

However, their words are perplexing because the primary reasoning of the Ra'avad is that people might say that the condition has been fulfilled since the matter is not evident to everyone. Therefore, even if the time has passed or the condition involves a prohibition and she transgressed and acted, they might say the opposite because the matter is not evident to everyone, similar to a woman who is told her husband died and then he comes back alive. This has already been challenged (by the Lechem Mishneh and the Mishneh Lamelech). Some explain his words that the Rambam holds that they will never suspect a prohibition because there is a possibility to say that she returned under a permissible circumstance since the condition was not fulfilled and the second marriage is invalid. In every case where we are concerned about something like this, it is because there is an inherent prohibition in it, and therefore, they will also attribute this to a prohibition. But in the case of a conditional get (divorce), they will not attribute it to a prohibition at all (Beit Shmuel, section 6). It seems to me that the intention of the Maggid Mishneh is also this, and he holds that the Ra'avad would not disagree on this. The primary objection is for a condition that she still has the ability to fulfill, as is evident from his language where he writes, "Therefore, I say in every case where you find that the condition is in her power to fulfill, etc., she needs a get and is forbidden to the first husband," end quote. And to this, the Maggid Mishneh says that even the Rambam, of blessed memory, does not disagree, as stated.

One does not write a condition in a get (divorce document), and if one wrote it, what is its status? This section contains thirteen paragraphs:

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 8, Law 3: How does one divorce on a condition? Not by saying, "Write a get for my wife on this condition" or "Write and give it to her on this condition", and it is needless to say that one should not write within the get, "So-and-so divorces so-and-so on this condition". Rather, how does one proceed? He tells the scribe to write and the witnesses to sign, and they write a valid get without any condition in the world. Afterwards, he gives her the get and says to her, "This is your get" or "You are hereby divorced with this, on the condition of such and such". Or he tells them or the agent, "Give her this get on the condition of such and such". These are the words of the Rambam, and similarly it is written in Shulchan Aruch, Section 1.

The condition written in the get (bill of divorce) after the main part of the get has been completed, this is a valid get whether it was written before the witnesses signed or after they signed. But if the condition was written before the main part of the get, even if it was written with a specific stipulation, it is considered a questionable divorce because he still retains some rights in the body of the get. Likewise, if the condition was made orally before the main part was written, it is considered a questionable divorce. These are the words of the author, and it has been copied in the Shulchan Aruch, section 2.

And afterwards, Rambam writes many laws regarding conditions and writes about the laws of conditions that invalidate the get (divorce document), such as if he left something out of the get by saying "except for so-and-so" or "on the condition that you do not marry so-and-so," and these laws are explained in Siman 137. And afterwards, in law 16, he writes as follows: "Anyone who divorces on a condition that invalidates the get, such as if he made a condition that she should not eat meat or drink wine all her life, or that she would be permitted to everyone except for so-and-so, or if he made other conditions before writing the essential part of the get, if the condition was written in the get and he then erased it and gave it to her, it is a doubtful divorce. And if the condition was verbal, he should take back the get from her and give it to her again without any condition at all or with a valid condition." This was copied in the Shulchan Aruch, section 3, and other opinions were not brought at all. Now, with God's help, we will explain the opinion of the Rambam.

Maimonides, of blessed memory, holds that any condition stated before the essential part of the get invalidates the get, whether the condition is written in the get or spoken orally. He explains the rationale: because this leaves a residual right in the body of the get. The Torah states, "he shall write her a document of severance," implying that at the time of writing, there should be a complete severance between him and her. Since a condition was posed before the essential part, it indicates that the get was written conditionally, and if the condition is not fulfilled, there will not be a complete severance. Hence, at the time of writing, the severance was not absolute. Additionally, there is a concern of retroactive clarification (Breira); when the condition is fulfilled, we would have to say that it has been clarified retroactively that the get was written for a complete severance. In matters of Torah law, we hold that there is no retroactive clarification (Breira) (Hilkhot Ishut). This reasoning is also found in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 3, Halacha 1), and even though there is a dispute there regarding this, it is possible to interpret that the conclusion aligns with this reasoning (Rabbi Hananiah and Rabbi Yochanan hold this view according to Rabbi, while Rabbi Yudan rejects it, and Rabbi Chinana upholds their words. Although this is according to Rabbi and not the Rabbis, nonetheless, the concern regarding conditions before the essential part is also agreed upon by the Rabbis, and as Rava in our Talmud, Tractate Gittin, 85a, follows his view which will be explained later. Since this reasoning is not entirely clear, Maimonides wrote that it is a case of doubtful divorce).

According to his words, that which is found in the Talmud (Gittin 84b) where Rava said to those who write bills of divorce, "Be silent, be silent to the husband (not to mention any condition) until you write the essential part of the get," this is not because of a decree that will be explained according to those who disagree with the Rambam, but rather this is the fundamental law. Before the essential part, any kind of condition invalidates the get, even if stated verbally. This is what Rava said there, "The dispute is after the essential part, etc., but before the essential part, all agree it is invalid." Refer there, for this is due to the fundamental law. And because it is possible to interpret that it is not from the fundamental law but rather due to a decree, therefore he wrote that she is in doubtfully divorced. The invalidation before the essential part applies even when the condition is fulfilled and even verbally, and certainly if it was written, even if it was later erased, it is invalid.

And after the essential part (of the get), certainly, ideally one should be careful not to write any condition in the get, not because it is inherently forbidden, but because not everyone is knowledgeable about the difference between what comes after the essential part and what comes before, and the difference between a condition that invalidates the get—such as "except for so-and-so" or "you shall not drink all the days of your life"—and a regular condition (as explained by the Maggid Mishneh). However, after the fact, it does not matter for any conditions that do not invalidate the get, as written and oral conditions are equal. Even if they wrote the condition before the signatures, even though it appears as if the witnesses signed on a condition, nevertheless, we do not worry about this, as we hold that "on condition" (al menat) constitutes a valid get and this is not considered forged from within. And if it is after the essential part, it is valid in one of two ways: either the condition was fulfilled, or it was not fulfilled and he annulled it and then erased it, and orally if it was not fulfilled, it has been explained in Siman 143 in detail. And if a condition that invalidates the get was written in it, even after the essential part, even if he annulled and erased it, she is doubtfully divorced, and certainly, if he did not erase it, the get is invalid from the Torah (as explained by the Beit Shmuel, section 3). But orally, after the essential part, he takes the get from her and gives it back to her without a condition or with a valid condition, so the get is not invalidated. But if it was written within it, even after the essential part, it is a doubt from the Torah, as perhaps by writing this the entire get is invalidated. There are those who imply from their words that according to the Rambam, in conditions that invalidate the get, if it was written after the essential part and erased before giving, she is not doubtfully divorced, and only if it was not erased at the time of giving does erasing not help (as explained by the Gra, section 3 in the middle of the discussion, "since it was not erased at the time of giving, etc."). But the Maggid Mishneh in Hilchot Gerushin 16:6 explicitly states as follows: "If he wrote a condition in the get, if it is among the conditions that invalidate the get, etc., wherever it is written, even if he annulled and erased it and did not mention it at all at the time of giving, the get is invalid and has no remedy," end quote (and this is also indicated by the Beit Shmuel, section 4). And all this is according to the Rambam's opinion, and it also appears to be the opinion of the Rif and the Rosh.

And the Tur brings from the responsa of the Rif, who is even more stringent, that even if the condition is written after the essential part of the get, and even if it is written behind it, it invalidates the get. These are the words of the Tur after he brings the words of the Rambam: "And even more so, the Rif is stringent, as he wrote in his responsa that one who gives a get on a condition, etc., but to write the condition within the get or behind it is not permissible, because if it is written within it, the husband has a right within it, and it is not considered a severance." End quote. 

These words are puzzling because, even if we explain that he does not mean it is not a severance but rather invalid from a rabbinic standpoint, from where do we derive this? For the most stringent opinion in the Talmud there is Rava, and he says that regarding writing after the essential part, Rabbi and the Sages disagree: Rabbi decrees it invalid due to a concern for writing before the essential part, and the Sages do not decree this. And it is known that the law follows the Sages. And even though initially, it should not be written even after the essential part because Rabbi invalidates it, and in matters of divorce, we strive to satisfy all opinions, which is the reason for the Rambam's ruling that initially one should not write a condition in the get, as he wrote. Nevertheless, to invalidate it post facto, we have not heard, and the Rif himself ruled similarly in the chapter "HaMegareish," see there. Therefore, practically, it is difficult to be lenient since the Rif's responsa was pronounced, and the Tur brought it.

And the opinion of our rabbis, the authors of Tosafot, is that a condition invalidates the Torah (i.e., the Torah requirement for a valid document) only if it nullifies the get (divorce document) and was written before the essential part (the "toref"). But if it was written after the essential part, even if one said it beforehand, it is not invalid according to Torah law and is not considered as having been written not for the sake of severance, because the scribe's intention regarding this condition does not apply at the time of writing the essential part, since it has not yet been written in the get (Tosafot, Gittin 4b, s.v. "aval"). And the reason for this matter is that the scribe and witnesses write only with the intention of what the husband will ultimately want (Rashba, ibid.). And this is according to Torah law.

However, from a rabbinic standpoint, any condition placed before the essential part of the get (bill of divorce) renders it invalid when written in the get, as a decree lest one might write a condition that nullifies the get, such as "except for so-and-so." A condition that nullifies the get invalidates it even if written after the essential part, as a decree lest one might write it before the essential part. This applies to written conditions, but an oral condition does not invalidate the get unless it is a condition that nullifies the get. Likewise, any condition before the essential part that nullifies the get, even if stated orally and later revoked, invalidates the get as a decree lest one might write it before the essential part. When we say that any condition before the essential part invalidates the get when written, it is when the condition was not fulfilled and was erased, even if the condition was nullified, as a decree lest one might write a condition that nullifies the get, which erasure does not correct since it was not written for the sake of severance (Tur in the name of Rabbi Isaac). However, if it was fulfilled, we have no issue with it, even if written before the essential part. Any condition after the essential part is valid when written, even if not fulfilled, as long as it was erased and nullified. Some say that any condition before the essential part is invalid even if stated orally, as a decree lest one might write a condition that nullifies the get (Rashba). Although this is also merely a decree lest one might write it, as stated, this invalidation is fundamentally from the Torah when not nullified. Even at the time of giving, if one says "except for so-and-so" or "you shall not drink all your life," the get is nullified according to Torah law. Therefore, rabbinically, we are stringent with any condition, even orally, if it was made before the essential part. However, many of our rabbis, including Raavad, the Meor, Ramban, and Rashba, hold that other oral conditions do not invalidate the get at all, even before the essential part, as we do not decree to that extent (Gra there).

And what is called "before the essential part"? The Tur wrote that before "and you are permitted to any man" is called before the essential part. But the Rashba wrote in his responsa that this is not considered the essential part (Beit Yosef), for even without this, there are several expressions in a get (divorce document) that are considered important, such as "and you are permitted to any man." In ancient get templates, this phrase was not written at all, and Rabbeinu Tam instituted the practice of writing it (Gittin 26a). And we have already written about this in Siman 125.

And behold, regarding the law, we certainly are stringent like the words of the Rif in his response that no condition should be mentioned in a get (divorce document), and even verbally it is forbidden to mention any condition before the writing of the get, according to the words of the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch. If a condition was mentioned, it would be considered a doubtful divorce. If he is about to embark on a journey and is compelled to leave before the writing of the get and wishes to instruct to write a get and deliver it to an agent on a condition, he should command that it be written and given to the agent without mentioning any condition to the scribe or the witnesses. However, afterward, he should tell the agent in front of other witnesses, "This get that I instructed to be given into your hand, deliver it to my wife on such and such a condition," and the scribe and witnesses should not know about this at all (Beit Shmuel, section 1, in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak ben Lev). Some are hesitant about this because, after all, the condition was mentioned before the writing of the get. Therefore, they wrote that even to the agent it should be given simply and he should say to him, "Do as you wish" or "Deliver it to her without any condition or with a condition," only beforehand he should reveal his intention to the agent that his desire is on such and such a condition, and naturally when he hands it over to the agent, even if he gives him the freedom to do as he wishes, the agent will presumably act according to his intention (Kenesset HaGedolah). And behold, there are other ways in this matter, but indeed one should avoid any condition in a get, and so the custom is among us not to give a get on a condition unless in the case of a seriously ill person if he is a Kohen, as it is written in section 145, because with a condition it is likely to lead to failure. I have never heard of giving a get on a condition, and so one should practice unless in a situation of pressing need and potential agunah (a woman who is chained to her marriage) where it is not possible otherwise.

There are those who say that what the Rambam wrote, that in the case of an oral condition, he must take the get (divorce document) back from her and give it to her again without the condition or with a valid condition, applies to a condition like "except for so-and-so," where the initial giving of the get is effective to disqualify her from marrying a kohen. But in the case of a condition like "all the days of my life," which has no legal effect, there is no need to take the get back from her; rather, he cancels the condition and says to her, "This is your get without the condition I mentioned," and that suffices. This is explained in Siman 137 and 138, that if the initial giving of the get was of no consequence, there is no need to take it back from her (Beit Shmuel, subsection 6). Similarly, in all conditions that do not invalidate the get, if he cancels the condition, there is no need to take the get back from her; rather, he says to her again, "This is your get" (there).

There are those who say that if a condition was stipulated before the essential part of the document, according to the Rambam, the get (divorce document) is invalid, but according to those who disagree with him, it is valid. As it is written, if the condition was not made according to the law, even if there is doubt whether it was made according to the law or not, and this get was delivered to her, the get is valid due to a double doubt: doubt whether the condition was made according to the law, and even if you say it was made according to the law, there is doubt whether the law follows the Rambam or those who disagree with him. And when the condition is fulfilled or the condition is nullified as explained, it is valid (Kenesset HaGedolah in the name of R. Yosef Ibn Lev). This is only according to those who hold that a double doubt permits in place of a presumption, but according to those who hold that a double doubt does not permit in place of a presumption, she is forbidden, as she is presumed to be a married woman. It is possible that even those who hold this would permit, because here there are three doubts, since according to the Rambam it is also only a doubtful divorce, as written (and so writes the Shakh in Yoreh De'ah 110 in the rules of double doubt, section 32, and see there in the Taz, section 15). However, it seems to me that this should not be called three doubts, since the two doubts, the doubt of the Rambam and the opinion of those who disagree, are one doubt regarding whether before the essential part is valid or not.

**The Law of an 'Old Get' and a Conditioned Get; It is Forbidden to Be in Seclusion with Her. This Section Contains 18 Paragraphs:**

A man should not divorce his wife with an 'old get'. And what is considered an 'old get'? Any time he has been in seclusion with her after it was written for her (Mishnah 79b). This is a decree lest people say her get predates her son (Gemara), for he might delay the get in his possession between writing and giving it for two or three years, and she may have children from him within that time. And afterwards, he divorces her with it, and in time when the matter is forgotten, they will see the date of the get as preceding the birth of the child and will think it was given to her from the time of writing and say that the child was born from a single woman, which would be a blemish for the child (Rashi). And although the child is legitimate from a single woman, nevertheless, it is a great disgrace for people.

If she was divorced with an old get, she may marry ab initio (Talmud). It is not comparable to all other rabbinic disqualifications because this is merely a slight concern of rumor. Even if a child were born from a single woman, it would not be disqualified, as it is written. Rashi explains that if she was divorced and her husband went to a distant land, she may marry ab initio. It is clear from his words that we only do not trouble her to obtain a get from afar. However, if he is here, we do not allow her to marry until he gives her another get, and we compel him to do so. But from Maimonides, Chapter 3, Law 5, and from the Tur, it does not seem so. (See Beit Yosef).

There is a question regarding this matter, for in any case, it is an invalid get (divorce document) because it is predated (according to Lechem Mishneh there and Tosafot 27a, s.v. "HaGa"). It must be said that he should send her the get via a messenger, which is valid as stated in Siman 127 there (and so wrote the Rashba). However, the Tur wrote the opposite, and these are his words: "And if she was divorced with it, she may marry ab initio, provided the get was given from his hand to hers as explained above." And his intention is based on what is written in Siman 141, and these are his words: "A husband who wrote a get for his wife and then was secluded with her, we hold that she should not be divorced with it, as explained later in Siman 148. But if she was divorced with it, she may marry ab initio, provided the get was in the husband's hand and he gave it directly to her hand. However, if he sent it to her via a messenger and then secluded with her after handing it to the messenger and the messenger gave it to her, she should not marry with it ab initio, and if she did marry, she need not divorce." These are the words of the Tur there. The reason was explained by the Rosh (Chapter 8, Halacha 8) in the name of the Ramah: Certainly, the Sages were concerned ab initio that he should not give it to her after seclusion, lest people say the get preceded the birth of the child. But if he gave it to her, she may marry ab initio, for if it were true that he had relations with her, he would be concerned about the blemish to his children and would write her another get. However, if he handed it to a messenger before seclusion, and the messenger gave it to her after seclusion, she should not marry with it ab initio, for if he had instructed the messenger, he would indeed give another get as stated there. Thus, it is predated, and one cannot say that he holds the opinion we brought in Siman 127, Paragraph 30, that a predated get is only when it is written at an earlier time or written by day and signed by night. But when it is written and signed on the same day, even if it remained for a long time in the husband's possession, it is not considered predated. This is the opinion of the Rambam as stated there. However, in Paragraph 31 there, we clarified that the Rosh and the Tur hold that this too is considered predated, as stated there.

There are those who wish to say that the intention is not literally from his hand to hers, but rather that now he will send it to her via a messenger, and the main intent is that the get (divorce document) was in his possession after the seclusion (reference). However, the language does not imply this, and in such cases, it should not be left ambiguous but rather clarified. There are those who say that if he has already given her the get, she may remarry because in a case of urgency, the Rosh and the Tur also hold in Siman 127 that it is valid (reference). It is not possible to say this, as the Tur explicitly wrote that this is only when it is impossible to obtain another get. Here they explicitly wrote that she may remarry initially and did not mention at all the opinion of Rashi which we brought when he went to a distant land (reference). Some say that it refers to a case where the get is not predated, and he secluded with her on that day before giving it (references). And even though in such a case the decree that people might say the get was given before the birth does not apply, they still issued a decree lest he stays with her for a long time (reference). These words are strained because if so, it should have been clarified that only in such a case she may remarry initially, and from the fact that they left it ambiguous, it is clear that their intention is in every case. Furthermore, from where do we say that we should issue a decree upon a decree (reference)?

It seems to me in their intention, if we examine the primary law of a "stale" get (divorce document), as the Sages said (Gittin 18a), "A person does not bring calamity upon himself," meaning it is uncommon for a husband to write a get and delay delivering it for many days. Rather, it is certainly dealing with a case where he prepared the get to send it through a messenger and a circumstance occurred that caused it to be delayed with the messenger for many days, and in the meantime, he secluded himself with her. In a get sent through a messenger, there is no concern of it being predated. For this reason, the Rosh and the Tur said that when it arrives to be given to her, he should take it into his own hand and give it to her, and not have the messenger deliver it, due to the reason explained. This is also precise in the language of the Rosh and the Tur in Siman 141, see there. And now, the issue of being predated does not apply, as the invalidity of a predated get is due to concerns of promiscuity and property rights, as explained in Siman 127. When it is sent through a messenger, there is publicity regarding it, as explained there. The publicity is immediate, but over the years, when they see the date on the get and the matter is forgotten, they will say the get predated the birth of her child.

And these are the words of the Rambam (Maimonides) in chapter 3: If someone wrote a get (divorce document) to divorce his wife and then changed his mind and did not divorce her, and afterwards secluded himself with her after writing it, he should not divorce her with that same get if he wishes to divorce her later. However, if he did divorce her with that old get, she is considered divorced and may remarry based on it from the outset, since it was written for her sake and he gave it to her now with witnesses as required by law. So why shouldn't he divorce her with it from the outset? It is a decree lest people say her get preceded the birth of her child, end quote. And similarly, it is written in the Shulchan Aruch, section 1. The Rambam elaborated in his language to answer what we asked, that a person does not bring misfortune upon themselves in advance. Therefore, he states that at the time of writing, his intention was indeed to divorce her, but afterward, he changed his mind and was with her as husband and wife, and later, after some time, he decided to divorce her. There is no defect of being early, as he follows his view that as long as it was written and signed without being predated, even if there was a delay between writing and giving, there is no concern of predated, as stated at the beginning of chapter 2. We brought this in section 127:30. Therefore, he was precise in his language "since it was written," meaning there is no defect in it. According to his opinion, he can deliver the get either by himself or through a messenger. However, the Rashba wrote that it must be delivered specifically through a messenger due to the concern of being predated, as we explained. Thus, there are three differing opinions on the matter: according to the Rosh and the Tur, it is only permissible to deliver it by himself; according to the Rashba, only through a messenger; and according to the Rambam, he can do as he wishes.

However, there is a significant question to ask regarding the Rambam's opinion. After all, he himself wrote in chapter 9 that if the husband meets with his wife between the writing and the giving of the get (divorce document), even if they did not seclude themselves, we are concerned about the nullification of the get. This concern is based on the possibility that he reconciled with her, as mentioned in the Talmud, and as we explained in section 144. All the more so here, when they did seclude themselves, there is a concern about the nullification of the get. And while this is not a difficulty for the Tur, who explains the concern of reconciliation as a possibility of seclusion and thus the get becoming old, following Rashi's explanation as mentioned by the Tur in section 144, it is difficult for the Rambam. The answer to this is that this concern only exists when the get is already in her possession. However, if after their seclusion, he gives it to her himself or through his messenger, there is no concern that he nullified it, for if he had nullified it, he would not have given it to her (Beit Shmuel, section 1).

And know that there is one who says that from the Jerusalem Talmud it is understood that if he divorced her due to a matter of sexual immorality, there is no concern of an "old get" (divorce document) because she is repulsive to him and he will not come upon her (see there, subsection 4). However, this is not so, for the Jerusalem Talmud only states that this is the reasoning of Beit Shammai, who were not concerned about an old get because they held that one does not divorce his wife unless he finds a matter of sexual immorality in her. But according to Beit Hillel, there was a rabbinic decree in every case, because not everyone knows the reason for the divorce (and so writes the Tosefot Yom Tov).

We have already written that from the language of the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, it is understood that when she is divorced with an old get, she may remarry initially even though the husband is present. But Rashi, of blessed memory, wrote that this is specifically when the husband has gone to a distant land. However, if he is in the city or in another nearby city, one should strive to obtain another get (and the Ran also wrote this, see there). In practice, one should be stringent according to Rashi’s opinion (Yam Shel Shlomo, Chapter 8, Siman 11).

The Tur wrote that if someone who is critically ill writes a divorce (get) for his wife, effective from now if he dies, he should not seclude himself with her except in the presence of witnesses. This follows the opinion of Rabbi Yosi, as we hold that the days between the divorce and death are a period of doubtful divorce. We are uncertain whether the divorce takes effect immediately or at the time of death. Therefore, she is considered his wife and he is obligated to support her. However, anyone who has relations with her during this period brings a provisional guilt offering because she is considered possibly divorced. Therefore, he should not seclude himself with her, because if the divorce does not take effect until the time of death, it would be considered an "old divorce." If it takes effect immediately, it is like any person who secludes himself with his divorced wife, who would then need another divorce. Therefore, if he secluded himself with her, she would need a second divorce out of doubt. This applies specifically to those who were married, as they have a familiar relationship, but not to those who were only betrothed. Furthermore, two witnesses must see them seclude themselves together; if one saw them in the morning and another saw them in the evening, they do not combine. If he explicitly stated that the divorce should not take effect until the time of death and he secluded himself with her in the meantime in the presence of witnesses, or if he gave her a conditional divorce that has not yet been fulfilled, there is no concern that he had relations with her for the sake of betrothal. Nonetheless, she should not initially remarry based on this divorce, but if she did remarry, even initially, she may remain married. He may seclude himself with her even with the testimony of one witness, even if that witness is a servant or maid, except for her maidservant, because she is familiar with her. 

(End of text)

Behold, what was written that we hold according to Rabbi Yose (R"Y) that the days between the giving of the get (divorce document) and death are considered a doubtful divorcee has already been explained by us in Siman 145, Section 10, that this is according to the version in the Gemara (74a) that the Sages also hold like R"Y. However, the Rif and the Rambam, whose version is based on the Tosefta, hold that the Sages believe she is fully divorced, and therefore the law is not according to Rabbi Yose. Hence, the Rambam did not mention this law, and it is also not mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch, as we explained there that they hold according to the Rambam's version. The Tur follows the approach of his father, the Rosh, who agrees with our version. And what was written that one who has relations with her brings an asham talui (a provisional guilt offering) is indeed stated in the Gemara because we are uncertain at the moment of intercourse whether she is divorced, as perhaps this is the moment close to death, or perhaps it is not yet this moment, and she is still a married woman. Therefore, if the husband dies, the one who had relations with her is liable for an asham talui, and if he does not die, he brings a sin-offering (Rashi). And there are those who say that they hold that for an asham talui, one does not need an instance of a piece from two pieces (Tosafot there). It is difficult to say this about the Tur, as we certainly hold like the opinion that we need a piece from two pieces, as this is proven by the Gemara in Keritot (18a), and so the Rambam ruled in Chapter 8 of Shgagot. Therefore, it appears to me that the Tur holds like the Rambam there, that the reason we need two pieces is because for an asham talui the prohibition must be established, and a doubtful divorcee is considered an established prohibition, as she was up until now in the status of a married woman. A proof for this is from the words of the Rambam there in Law 3, who wrote similarly regarding anyone who has relations with a married woman when one witness says that her husband died and another says he did not die, that he is liable for an asham talui, and the same applies to a doubtful divorcee, as the prohibition is established. And Tosafot must say that they wrote according to the opinion in Keritot there that the reason is because it is possible to clarify the prohibition, and here at this moment it is impossible to clarify, obviously, or they wrote according to the opinion that the reason is based on the principle of "yesh em la-mikra," and the first opinion is primary, as so holds Rav Zeira and Rava there, and examine this well.

And know that this explanation we have written follows Rashi’s interpretation there. However, from the language of the Tur, it seems that the uncertainty is straightforward, as we are unsure whether this language means immediately or if the get (divorce document) will take effect close to his death. Similarly, the Rashba, the Rosh, and the Ran wrote, and therefore one who has relations with her is obligated to bring a conditional guilt offering. It must be said that the uncertainty is not dependent on his intention, for if it were, we could ask him what his intention was. Rather, the uncertainty is in the language itself according to all opinions, and he is not believed to say that he intended one way or another. (And the Tur follows the approach of Tosafot, who do not interpret ‘from the time I am in the world’ as Rashi does, but rather that it refers to ‘from today if I die’. However, there is an issue with the Tur’s position, for according to this it must be said that Rabbi Yehuda holds of retroactive clarification, as Tosafot and the Rashba wrote there, as is evident in Gittin 25b. But we hold that in matters of Torah law there is no retroactive clarification, and it must be said that in matters dependent on others’ decisions, retroactive clarification is valid, and this requires further study.)

And this is what is said in the reasoning: that he should not be secluded either due to the concern of an old get (divorce document) or due to the concern of betrothal is straightforward. And the distinction made between [seclusion] from betrothal and from marriage is regarding the concern of betrothal, for if it were the concern of an old get, it would also apply to betrothal. And what is required of witnesses is not needed for an old get. The distinction between betrothal and marriage is that in marriage, since he is familiar with her, we say that the witnesses to seclusion are also witnesses to intercourse. But in betrothal, we do not say this. However, when we know that she has had intercourse, even in betrothal, we say that he had intercourse for the sake of betrothal, as will be explained in Siman 149. Therefore, two witnesses together are required, as is the law of witnesses for betrothal. Testimony that one saw first and the other saw afterward is not valid. Additionally, it is necessary that both he and she see the witnesses, because a person knows that betrothal without witnesses is nothing, and certainly, he had intercourse only for the sake of fornication (Beit Yosef). Even if he saw them and she did not, there is no concern of betrothal (ibid.), for in betrothal, the intention of both is required, and since she did not see them, she intended only for fornication. Also, what was said that if he explicitly stated that the get would not take effect until close to death, even if he secluded with her in the presence of witnesses, there is no concern of betrothal, is straightforward, for she is still a married woman. And even though it could be said that they might have thought that perhaps this is the time close to death and the get took effect, and he betrothed her, nevertheless, we do not need to be concerned to such an extent.

However, what is written that even if he gave a get (divorce document) conditionally and the condition has not yet been fulfilled, there is no concern of betrothal, this is puzzling. Why is there no concern of betrothal? Is it not possible that they think the condition will be fulfilled and the get will be valid, and he cohabits with her for the sake of betrothal? Indeed, the Rambam holds this view, as will be explained with God's help. And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote that the Tur is referring to a condition where the get does not take effect until the fulfillment of the condition, and until its fulfillment, she is a fully married woman, and there is no concern of betrothal. But in the case of a condition from now, there is a concern of betrothal, and the Tur does not hold like the Rambam at the beginning of chapter 8, who also considers a condition of "if" (where if she married before the fulfillment of the condition, she does not have to leave her husband). See there, and this requires further study. First, if so, the Tur should not have left things ambiguous. Additionally, it appears clearly that the Tur agrees with the Rambam in this, as he brought his words at the end of section 143 and did not object to him. And we have explained this there in section 21 (and also the Beit Shmuel in subsection 7 wrote that the Tur holds in the condition of "if" like the Rambam; see there).

Therefore, it appears to me that the Tur has a different opinion on this matter and holds that the concern of betrothal only exists either if she is completely divorced, as in the case in Siman 149, or if there is a reason to say that the get (divorce document) has already taken effect, such as when it is stated "from today if I die," where there is a doubt that the get may take effect immediately and he cohabits with her for the sake of betrothal. And even though there is a doubt that he might not die and she would not be divorced, nevertheless the doubt is not dependent on them, and there is a concern that he might die and she would be divorced from now, and therefore he cohabits with her for the sake of betrothal. However, with a get that is dependent on a condition, it is not applicable at all to say that he cohabits with her for the sake of betrothal because, in any case, if they desire betrothal, they would not fulfill the condition, and consequently the get is nothing. And we are discussing a standard condition where the matter is dependent on him or her, and it is obvious that if they do not want to separate, no one forces them to do so. Therefore, certainly, if the condition is fulfilled, it indicates that they desire the divorce, and consequently, his cohabitation is merely licentiousness, and there is only a concern of an old get.

And also that which he wrote, "Nevertheless, she should not initially get divorced with it, but if she did get divorced with it, she may even remarry initially," the reason is that this is its law, as the concern of an old get (divorce document) is as explained.
