However, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, raised an issue with his wording, where he wrote "she should not get divorced with it," etc., since she has already received the get, what is relevant about "she should not get divorced with it"? See there. Additionally, they raised an issue with his ruling that if she did get divorced with it, she may remarry initially, as this contradicts what he wrote at the beginning of this section, that it is only valid if he gives it to her now from his hand to hers (Beit Shmuel, subsection 7). And it appears to me that one difficulty resolves the other, and on the contrary, therefore he precisely wrote "she should not get divorced with it," etc., and "if she did get divorced," etc., meaning that the fact that the get is in her possession does not help at all, as it now needs to be given to her, and regarding this, he says "she should not initially get divorced with it," meaning even if he takes the get from her and gives it to her again, this should not be done initially. But if she did get divorced with it, meaning he performed the act and took the get from her and gave it to her now, she may remarry initially, as is the law of an old get explained at the beginning of the section.

However, the Rambam (may his memory be blessed) wrote in Chapter 8, Law 2, and these are his words: "Anyone who divorces on a condition, whether he says 'from now' or 'if it will be' or 'if it will not be,' he should not seclude himself with his wife as long as the condition has not been fulfilled, except in the presence of a witness, even a servant or a maidservant, except for her maidservant or her young son, because she is not ashamed to be intimate in their presence. It is known that if he secluded himself with her in the presence of two witnesses together, even if the condition is later fulfilled, it is a doubtful divorce, perhaps he had relations with her and annulled the get (divorce document), as will be explained in these laws." End of quote. His intention is what is written in Chapter 10: "If one divorces his wife and then has relations with her or secluded himself with her in the presence of witnesses, we are concerned about the validity of the marriage (according to the Maggid Mishneh)." This will be explained in the next section with God's help. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Paragraph 2 almost in the language of the Rambam, only adding that he and she saw the witnesses. Refer to there. And we have already explained this in the language of the Tur.

Indeed, it is perplexing, and how can we be concerned about the validity of the betrothal? If so, who compels them to fulfill the condition? It is difficult to say that we are dealing with a condition not dependent on them, as it is stated that anyone who divorces on a condition implies any condition. One must say that the reasoning is as follows: Since we saw that the Sages were concerned about the issue of "from today if I die" regarding betrothal, even though they initially intended the get (bill of divorce) to exempt her from levirate marriage, nevertheless, perhaps later they rekindled their love and betrothed her anew, disregarding what would happen afterward. Similarly, we must be concerned with any conditions, that now upon their reunion, they rescinded their previous intent and intended for betrothal, and afterward, upon their separation, remained with their original intention to fulfill the condition. Even though this is not beneficial since she has already been betrothed, they think it would be beneficial. In matters of forbidden marriages, even slight concerns are taken into account.

Moreover, know that in guarding a watchman is sufficient even if he comes and goes, and he does not need to sit there all day. However, at night, it seems that superior guarding is required. For a sick person, guarding is needed even if he is gravely ill, and even when he is in his death throes. A minor boy or girl who understands the reason for intercourse, such as those who are twelve years old, are considered a guard for this matter.

A man who divorces his wife and subsequently has relations with her or secludes himself with her. It contains fifteen sections:
A man who divorces his wife, whether from betrothal or from marriage, and then subsequently has relations with her in the presence of witnesses before she marries another, requires a second get (divorce document) from him, as it is certainly presumed that he had relations with her for the sake of marriage (Tur). A person does not engage in promiscuous relations with his former wife, as she was once his wife. It is presumed that he takes her back and did not have relations for promiscuous purposes. Even if witnesses saw him giving her money, it is not considered payment for illicit relations, because this is a strong presumption that a person does not have promiscuous relations with his wife when he has the option to make it a mitzvah (commanded act of marital intimacy). Therefore, she is considered married with a strong presumption of certain marriage (Rambam, Chapter 10, Halacha 17).

It is clearly explained from the language of the Rambam and the Tur that we only consider her to be married with definite kiddushin (betrothal), not with doubtful kiddushin. The practical difference is that if she received kiddushin from another man, the kiddushin would not be effective (Bach and Beit Shmuel, section 3). It is obvious that this applies only when the witnesses saw them and they saw the witnesses, as mentioned in the previous section, paragraph 10, in the name of the Tur. And our master, the Rema, wrote: "Or if it is known to all that he had relations with her, such as if he married her," end quote. This means that this is also considered as if he had relations with her in the presence of witnesses. The Tosafot wrote a similar reasoning in Yevamot (45b, "Who") regarding immersion, see there. We have already mentioned this in section 26, paragraph 5, see there. There is further support for this reasoning from what our Sages said (ibid. 109b) regarding a minor who did not refuse (her husband) and then matured and got married, that she does not require a get (divorce document) from the second (husband) because the first one certainly had relations with her with the intention of kiddushin, knowing that the kiddushin of a minor orphan is worthless. Even those who disagree there argue that his intention was based on the original kiddushin, see there. However, in the case of a divorce, this does not apply. In that instance, there were no witnesses to the relations, but since she lived with him in the manner of a husband and wife, and he had relations with her, it is considered as if there were witnesses. Similarly, since our Sages said that if he had relations with her in the presence of witnesses, it is certainly for the sake of kiddushin, so too, if it is known to all that he married her, and they lived together in the manner of a husband and wife, it is not inferior to having witnesses. However, one could argue that in that case, it is clear to us that he had relations with her, as the simple reading of the language of the Gemara there implies. But the Rivash wrote at the end of section 193: "And the Ra'ah wrote that a minor who matured does not need witnesses of seclusion because, since she is his wife and lives with him, everyone knows that he secluded with her and had relations with her," end quote. However, the Rivash himself, at the end of section 6, brought this in the name of the Ra'ah and wrote that this is a minority opinion, as all the early authorities wrote that she needs witnesses of seclusion, end quote (and see Maggid Mishneh, chapter 11 of Laws of Divorce, law 6). It seems to me that in section 6, he wrote this only regarding his question there, where she was never his wife according to Jewish law, see there. Nevertheless, there are those who question this ruling (Beit Shmuel, section 1). Therefore, one should be stringent in matters of forbidden relationships.

It is a simple matter that this presumption, that a man does not engage in licentious intercourse with his wife, only applies when there is no sin involved in this intercourse. Therefore, if she is a menstruant (niddah), which involves the sin of kareth, or if he is a Kohen and it is forbidden for him to take back his divorced wife, or if she had relations with him after marrying another man and becoming widowed or divorced, or if he currently has another wife and it is a place where it is forbidden to marry two women, we do not apply this presumption (Mechaber, Chapter 10, Halacha 18 and Ba'er Hetev in the name of several great authorities). Nevertheless, some say that if the betrothal is valid, we must be concerned about the betrothal (ibid. in the name of Knesses HaGedolah), and even though this does not seem to be the case, one should be stringent in this matter and require a get from him. It is obvious that if she accepted betrothal from another man, she would need a get from him. The general principle in the prohibition of a married woman is that if it is impossible to clarify the law directly from the Talmud, one should always take the stringent approach. (There is some evidence for this opinion from the Sugya at the end of Chapter 8, where we establish the Mishnah when they did not see her engage in intercourse. It implies that if they saw her engage in intercourse, even Beit Shammai agrees, and they hold that he should not divorce her unless he found in her a matter of indecency, as stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. Examine this carefully.)

And all this is when we know that he had relations with her. But if we do not know that he had relations with her, and she was only secluded with him in the presence of witnesses, and the two witnesses were together, and he and she saw the witnesses, in this there is a distinction between betrothal and marriage. If she is divorced from the marriage, we say that the witnesses to the seclusion are the same as the witnesses to the intercourse, and it is presumed that he had relations with her because they are familiar with each other. However, if she is divorced from the betrothal, where they are not familiar with each other, we do not say that the witnesses to the seclusion are the same as the witnesses to the intercourse. Nevertheless, if we see that they are familiar with each other, recognizing each other through gestures and winks, and they have great closeness, her status is like that of a married woman, and we are concerned about the sanctity of the marriage.

And even from the marriage, we do not say that he definitely had relations with her to consider it a definite marriage, but rather it is a doubtful marriage in the sense that she needs a divorce (get) from him. However, if another man betrothed her, she would also need a get from the second one. And so wrote the Rambam, that we are concerned that perhaps they had relations, which implies it is merely a concern. And so wrote the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. And even though from the language of Rashi of blessed memory it does not seem so, as he wrote that since they saw them seclude themselves, there is no need for testimony of relations, for it is certain, as we are witnesses that since they are familiar with each other, they did not separate from one another. Nevertheless, the main ruling is as we wrote, especially since this is a stringency.

And know that some of the early authorities wrote that it's only initially (lekhatchila) that she needs a second get from him if she secluded herself with him, but after the fact (b'dieved), if he went overseas, she can remarry lekhatchila as in the case of an old get (the Gemara, Chapter 6). However, this is not the opinion of all the poskim, for certainly it is considered a doubtful kiddushin (Rema in Darkei Moshe). And indeed, this is the approach of the Jerusalem Talmud, which links this dispute to the dispute regarding an old get, as mentioned there. However, this is not the approach of our Talmud. (And it is clear that the author of the Jerusalem Talmud is Rabbi Yochanan, and he also holds in our Talmud that without witnesses seeing intercourse, a second get is not required, and our Talmud disagrees with him. Perhaps this is the reason some rule according to Rabbi Yochanan, as the Ran writes, because the Jerusalem Talmud agrees with him. But according to the law, it is not so, for according to Rashi it is certainly considered kiddushin, as he wrote).

It appears to me that even according to the authorities who are concerned about prohibited intercourse where the man had relations with the intention of marriage, if the marriage can take effect as stated in section 3, nevertheless, if he secluded himself with her, they agree that when there is prohibited intercourse, we do not say that the witnesses to the seclusion are also witnesses to the intercourse. This is also the ruling of the Radbaz, of blessed memory, that in the case of intercourse we are concerned, but in the case of seclusion we are not concerned when their intercourse is prohibited. It seems to me that there is no disagreement on this. Similarly, if both of them say that he did not have relations with her, it appears that even if their intercourse is not prohibited, we are not concerned about the marriage (Shulchan Aruch). There are some who dispute this (Beit Shmuel, section 4), and there are also some who dispute regarding seclusion alone, even when there is prohibited intercourse (Even HaEzer, section 33), and the ruling is unclear. See also section 10.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles writes: "But if one was secluded with his betrothed, even though they are familiar with each other, we are not concerned [about the validity of the marriage] unless it was witnessed that he had relations with her." It is explicitly explained that if it was witnessed that he had relations with her, we are concerned about the marriage. And even though regarding a single woman, in general, we do not say that a man does not make his relations promiscuous, as will be explained, nevertheless with his betrothed, whom he is supposed to marry, we say that he had relations for the sake of marriage. And logic supports this, for if we say this presumption regarding his betrothed whom he divorced, all the more so for this one who is designated to marry him. The source of this law is from the responsa of the Ramban (brought in the Beit Yosef). There are those who say that from this responsa it seems that even if it was certain that he had relations with her, we do not say this presumption, and she is like a regular single woman (Beit Shmuel, section 6). However, this is not so. On the contrary, it is clearly explained there as I wrote. The text there reads: "A betrothed man who would enter his father-in-law's house, etc., if he slept with her and they were secluded at night in front of witnesses, since they are familiar with each other, and nevertheless, as long as they did not see them having relations, we are not concerned about the marriage, etc." But if they saw them having relations, we are concerned. And what is written at the end of the responsa, that even if they saw them having relations, we are not concerned, refers to an ordinary woman and not to his betrothed. Refer there. And this is the main point of the law. However, it is possible that we do not consider it definite marriage but rather doubtful marriage.

It is clear that this presumption [of remarriage] is only stated when the husband knew that she had already been divorced. But if he thought that she had not yet been divorced, as in the case where a man sent a get (divorce document) to his wife and afterwards canceled the get, and then had seclusion with her, and later it was clarified that the get had already reached her hands before it was canceled—she does not need a second get from him. Certainly, in this case, it cannot be said that he had marital relations with her for the sake of a new marriage, because he believed that the get was canceled and did not intend to remarry her, but rather had relations based on the original marriage. Therefore, even if it is certain that he had relations with her, we are not concerned about [the possibility of] a new marriage.

There was an incident involving a man who divorced his wife and later secluded himself with her in the presence of witnesses. He did not divorce her a second time, and she then took another man and he betrothed her as a concubine. She stayed with him for some time as a concubine. The Rosh, of blessed memory, ruled that she is forbidden to both men and requires a get (bill of divorce) from both. This is because the second man certainly had relations with her, and she is forbidden to him since she is possibly still married to the first man due to their seclusion. She also requires a get from the second man since, according to the seclusion, she is not considered definitely married but only possibly married, as we have written. Know that from this ruling there is proof for those who are uncertain, as we have written in Section 7, that even if they say there was no intercourse, they are not believed. It is presumed that in the case of the Rosh, they investigated and said there was no intercourse, as this seems from the flow of the text, and nevertheless, they did not pay attention to their words.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 10, Law 19: "Some of the Geonim ruled that any woman who has relations in the presence of witnesses requires a get (divorce document) due to the presumption that a person does not engage in licentious relations, etc. However, it is not appropriate to rely on them, for the Sages only stated this presumption regarding a man's wife whom he divorced, or when he betrothed on condition and then engaged in relations without specifying, since she is his wife. In the case of his wife, we presume he does not engage in licentious relations unless he specifies that it is a licentious act or clarifies that he is engaging in relations conditionally. But with other women, any promiscuous woman is presumed to engage in relations for the sake of licentiousness unless it is specified that it is for the sake of marriage, etc." So wrote the Rosh at the end of Chapter "Hazorek," stating: "But if witnesses saw a man engaging in relations with a random woman, we do not suspect it is for the sake of marriage, for Rabbi Eliezer said that a single man who has relations with a single woman makes her a harlot, and we do not say he engaged in relations for the sake of marriage, nor do we distinguish whether he engaged in relations in the presence of witnesses or not in the presence of witnesses. Similarly, a man may marry his father's violated or seduced woman, and we do not suspect that perhaps his father engaged in relations for the sake of marriage and she is his father's wife." So wrote Maimonides, and so wrote the Rashba and the Ran there, and so wrote the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. Only the Mordechai (Chapter 3 of Kiddushin) was concerned about this. See there.

Therefore, I am astonished by our Master, the Rema, in Siman 33, who wrote: "There are those who say that if an unmarried man engages in relations with an unmarried woman in the presence of witnesses, we suspect that he intended this for the purpose of marriage, etc., and there are those who are lenient, etc." His words imply that he took into account a singular opinion against all of our Sages. And in the Tosefta at the beginning of Kiddushin, we also learned: "Any intercourse that is for the purpose of marriage establishes marriage, and if it is not for the purpose of marriage, it does not establish marriage." This is the end of its language, and it is obvious that the Tosefta does not mean intercourse for the purpose of promiscuity, for what would it be teaching us? But certainly, it refers to a general case, aligning with the words of our Sages. And the Terumat HaDeshen wrote at the end of Siman 209: "It seems that, with any logical argument, we reject this assumption, etc., for the Rambam wrote correctly that it is far-fetched to think that a man and woman, succumbing to their desires, would engage in intercourse for the purpose of marriage." And nowadays, in our generations, this is not common at all. And there, it is explained further that even if he promised to marry her, see there. And even more so, the Rivash wrote in Siman 6 about a man and woman who, during the persecutions, were coerced and married each other according to the customs of the Gentiles, and afterward, the persecutions ceased. Although they continue to live together every day in the manner of husband and wife, we still do not suspect marriage. And our Master, the Beit Yosef, brought this in Siman 6 and explained that the reason is that since they married according to Gentile customs, it is as if they explicitly stated that their intention was not for marriage, and she is permitted to another man, even though she had a child from him, see there.

Additionally, I am puzzled why the author did not correct here in Section 5 to refer to Section 33 where there are those who disagree, as is his usual practice in all places. Furthermore, why did he establish this law in the laws of Kiddushin and not in this section, which is the primary source of these laws? Therefore, it is possible to say that in the case of general promiscuity, even he agrees that there is no one who considers it significant. And there, it refers to a situation where there were words of betrothal between them, even though they were not yet betrothed. Nevertheless, in such a case, it is possible that there is a reason to be concerned according to those who are stringent when there are witnesses, even though from the arrangement of his words there, it does not seem so. Know that the great scholars of the world have agreed that even in a place where, according to the law, there is a reason to be concerned about betrothal, as explained, if he is known to be promiscuous and licentious, this presumption does not apply to him. But if he is not known to be promiscuous, even if he secluded himself with her on the road, there is concern for betrothal. And it seems to me that therefore the Tanna taught us "and she stayed with him at the inn" (see Ketubot 65 and Orach Chaim, Section 240, Paragraph 13, and examine this carefully).

Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote in chapter 9, law 25: "If he secluded himself with her after ordering the writing, signing, and giving of the get, they should not write it. All the more so, if the get was given into her hand after he secluded himself with her, the get is invalid, lest he have had relations with her. All the more so, if it was not written. And if they wrote and gave it to her after he secluded himself with her, it is not a get." These are his exact words. His intention is not to equate the reasons. In the case where the get was given into her hand, the doubt is whether he had relations for the sake of betrothal, as explained. Here, this reasoning does not apply; rather, he is saying that in a place where the get has already been completed, we are concerned that seclusion might be for the sake of betrothal. Consequently, the get is invalid, meaning that the act of the get is not fulfilled because of the concern that she might have been betrothed. All the more so, when it has not yet been written, he does not need to betroth her, only to nullify his statement. It is obvious that the statement is nullified, and it is not a get.

The sages of the generations, the Ramban, the Rashba, the Ran (end of chapter 8), and the Maggid Mishneh were perplexed by him. From where did he derive the notion that the get (divorce document) is entirely nullified? After all, in the case of seclusion, it is only a doubt, and here too, there is a concern that perhaps he appeased her and nullified the get, making it a doubtful divorce. However, to say that it is certainly nullified has no basis. Therefore, they ruled that if he secluded himself with her and afterward wrote and gave her the get, she is doubtfully divorced. This is also the ruling of our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 7, who did not mention his opinion at all. Indeed, this is the primary ruling in law. However, for this, seclusion is not required, for it has already been clarified in section 144 that if he met with her between the writing and the giving, we are concerned that perhaps he appeased and nullified the get unless he says, "She is trusted to say that I did not come to her." And this cannot be said, for in the case of seclusion, her statement does not help, as it is explicitly proven in the Talmud (76b) that even in the case of seclusion, her statement is valid. Rather, there is a concern of an old get, as mentioned there (that it is stated regarding an old get that we are not concerned since he did not seclude with her, and it is established with "she is trusted" etc., clearly proving that in the case of seclusion, there is only a concern for an old get). However, the truth is that this is the case, and this is what they dispute with him, that even here, it is not a definite nullification of the get but a doubtful nullification. In such a case, seclusion is not required (and from the commentary of Beit Shmuel, section 7, it implies that in this case, her trustworthiness does not help, and this is perplexing, for from the Talmud, it clearly implies that it does help, as I have written). The opinion of Maimonides appears to be that since the Talmud is concerned about the nullification of the get even without seclusion if she was not given trustworthiness, then certainly if he secluded with her, there is no doubt that he nullified it. And all the more so in such a case when it was not yet written, it can be said that an action nullifies a statement. And it seems from his words that he holds that with seclusion alone, his statement is nullified. And the a fortiori argument he brought is only proof that every man seeks after his wife to take her back even after she is divorced, and all the more so when she is not yet divorced and no action has been taken, only a mere statement that he seeks after her, and with his seclusion, his statement is nullified. And the law is established according to those who dispute him.

What is the difference in a get between a Biblical and Rabbinic invalidation? This consists of 12 sections: Know that the Rambam of blessed memory provided a general rule in Chapter 10: Whenever he wrote in his work that the get is void or it is not a get, it is invalid according to the Torah. And whenever he wrote that the get is invalid, it is only Rabbinically invalid. Refer there. This rule is not found in the Talmud and other decisors. Certainly, when they said the get is void or it is not a get or she is not divorced, it is invalid according to the Torah. However, even in a place where they said it is invalid, it can also be according to the Torah (according to the Maggid Mishneh). There are cases where the term invalid means Rabbinic, and there are cases where it means that it is only invalid initially but she should not remarry, and the matter is understood according to its context (ibid.).

Any case where a get (divorce document) is invalid according to Torah law, she remains fully married, and if she marries another man, she must separate from him and the offspring from this union is considered a mamzer (illegitimate). If her original husband was a kohen, she is not prohibited to him because of being a divorcee, except in the case where a man divorces his wife and says to her, "You are hereby divorced from me but not permitted to any other man." Even though this is not a valid get, she is disqualified from marrying into the priesthood (kehuna) by rabbinic decree. This is based on the verse that states, "A divorced woman from her husband shall not be taken" (Leviticus 21:7), and the sages said (Yevamot 94a) that even if she is only divorced from her husband, she is disqualified from the priesthood. This is known as the "scent of a get" which disqualifies her by rabbinic decree. The Rambam wrote similarly, and according to his opinion, it is merely an asmachta (a rabbinic support based on a biblical text). However, from the Talmud in Gittin (8b), it clearly implies that from the Torah she is disqualified from the priesthood. It is possible to reconcile the Talmudic view with the Rambam's by interpreting the Talmudic text as indicating rabbinic law rather than Torah law. Additionally, the Jerusalem Talmud (beginning of chapter 9) implies that from the Torah, the "scent of a get" requires her to be permitted to at least one man. The Kesef Mishneh's difficulty from Yevamot can also be resolved easily, as R. Eliezer ben Mattia's interpretation is an asmachta, for why would we need a verse for something that is obvious?

And there are those who say that even if he says, "You are permitted to everyone except for so-and-so," she is not disqualified from marrying a Kohen according to Torah law, according to Maimonides (Beit Shmuel, subsection 5). However, this does not seem to align with the Talmud there, which states that he must take the get from her and give it back to her and say, "You are permitted to everyone," because the initial giving was effective in disqualifying her from marrying a Kohen. And if you were to think that according to Torah law, it was not effective at all, there would be no need to take it from her, as it is forced to say that it was effective Rabbinically. According to Rabbinic law, it is only a decree and does not have intrinsic validity in the essence of the get (and similarly, it is written in the name of the Shita Mekubetzet that in this case, it is clear that she is disqualified from marrying a Kohen according to Torah law. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it seems there is a dispute about this, see there, Chapter 9, end of Halacha 1. And it must be said that the phrase "they were concerned" means that they were concerned that according to Torah law, it is invalid. Consider this well).

And with this that the Rambam wrote that aside from this, all Torah disqualifications do not disqualify her from the priesthood, the Ra'avad wrote that this is not a rule, for in any case where the invalidity of the divorce document is not explicitly evident, she is disqualified from the priesthood, lest people say that a divorced woman is permitted to a priest. See there. I do not know of any Torah disqualification that is not explicitly evident. And it cannot be said, for instance, in a case where it was given conditionally and the condition was not fulfilled, since this matter is not evident to all. And behold, we have explicitly taught that she is fit for the priesthood (Gittin 81a). Nor can it be said that his intention was in a case where the condition was placed upon her for all her life, for surely she is fit for the priesthood, as there is no greater proof than this, as written in Siman 146. And it is possible to say that his intention was in a case where it was not conditional but contingent, according to those who rule that without a condition, it is nothing. And for us, in any case, it cannot be said thus, for she is doubtfully divorced, since according to the Rif and the Rambam the divorce is valid, as written in Siman 133. This requires further investigation.

When she marries another man with a get that is invalid according to Torah law, she requires a get from the second husband by rabbinic decree so that people do not say that a married woman can leave without a get. She also needs a get from the first husband to permit her to marry anyone else, and she is prohibited to both men forever, even if she married in error, such as not knowing that the get was invalid. This is to prevent people from saying that he took back his divorced wife after she married another (Rambam). She is prohibited to the second man as well because the Rabbis penalized her since they committed a great sin (Meiri). If either of them transgressed and married her, they must divorce her, and we compel them to do so. All the thirteen methods listed in the Mishnah in the chapter "HaZorek" (Gittin 79a) and explained in detail in Siman 17, Sif 257 apply to them. However, regarding inheritance, some say that her first husband inherits her because he did not commit a sin, as written in Siman 17. But if she only became betrothed to another man and did not yet enter the chuppah with him, she is permitted to her first husband and does not need a get from the second because no sin occurred between them. Some say that even if she only became betrothed, she requires a get from the second and is prohibited to both (Raavad there). It seems to me that the reason is that it is not similar to the case where they told her that her husband died and she became betrothed, where she is permitted to the first because everyone sees that the testimony was false. But with a get, not everyone knows that the get is invalid, and they will say that he took back his divorced wife after she became betrothed to another. According to Rambam, it can be said that with betrothal, there is no decree because it could be said that there was a condition in the second betrothal that was not fulfilled. But with marriage, there is no condition. Therefore, some say that the reason she is prohibited to the first is not because of a decree but because of a penalty, similar to the second. Therefore, with betrothal, where there is no sin, the Rabbis did not penalize her (Meiri there, and scrutinize carefully).

When she is forbidden to both of them and needs a get (divorce document) from both of them, there is no difference whether she received a get from both of them or did not receive from one of them, such as if one of them died. According to Rambam's reasoning, when the second one dies, it would be possible to permit her to the first one. It makes sense that when she received a get from the second one, people might say that the first one took back his divorced wife after she had been married to another because they saw that she received a get. But when she did not receive a get from the second one, they would not say this, as it is not so. The Sages did not differentiate, and furthermore, people would still say that she married another man who died, and then the first one took her back (there).

And in any case where the get (divorce document) is invalid only by rabbinic decree, she is disqualified from marrying a kohen by Torah law. She should not marry initially, but if she does marry, she need not divorce, and the child is legitimate. They should write her another valid get, and she may remain with her husband. If it is impossible to write another get and the husband was a pious man and divorced her of his own accord, this is praiseworthy if she does not have children. However, if she has children, he should not divorce her lest it casts aspersions on the get (Rambam). There is no need to question that if so, one should not give another get when she has children due to such aspersions, since it can be said that by giving a get alone, there will be no aspersions on the children, as people will say the get was given to remove any doubts (Beit Shmuel, subsection 2). And proof of this is that she remains with her husband, unlike the case where he divorces her, which would certainly cast aspersions.

From the language of the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, it is understood that in all rabbinic disqualifications, if she marries, she does not have to leave him. However, there are those who say that in the case of a prior disqualification, even if it is rabbinic, if she marries she must leave him if she has no children (Beit Shmuel in the name of the Ran). This has already been explained in Siman 127, see there. It is also clear that in rabbinic disqualifications, if she marries or is betrothed to another and he dies or divorces her, from the perspective of Torah law, she is forbidden to the first one. Since the get (divorce document) was valid according to Torah law, the second one's betrothal is valid, and she is forbidden to the first one as a divorced woman who was betrothed to another.

And the matter in which we are stringent regarding gittin (divorce documents) even though the Sages were stringent on this not from the essence of the law but because of the stringency, like an old get (divorce document) or something attached in the writing of the form which we decree due to the essential parts (of the document) (according to the Gra) and similar cases, since the get is kosher (valid) regardless, but we are stringent to write it initially. If the get was not written, it is kosher, as it is not worse than an old get, concerning which we hold that if she was divorced with it, she may remarry initially. There are those who want to say that in all rabbinic invalidations, in a pressing situation, we validate them after the fact, and if she was divorced with it, she may remarry initially (Mordechai, end of Chapter 7 in the name of Rabeinu Eliezer). However, this is not implied by all the decisors. If the invalidation is from the essence of the law, like an antedated get or similar cases, she should not remarry initially, but if she did, she does not need to leave the marriage. Regarding an antedated get itself, there are several distinctions, as written in Siman 127, and there are antedated gets which are more severe than all rabbinic invalidations. See there.

And it is a simple matter that a stringency which is not from the law of the Talmud but from the stringency of the later authorities, if she was divorced, she may remarry initially. And even if she was not divorced, but it is difficult to obtain another get (divorce document), one may use it initially.

And any woman who has a doubtful divorce, and the doubt is of a biblical nature, she should not remarry. If she does remarry, she must leave, and the child from the second husband is a doubtful mamzer (illegitimate child). All the stringencies that apply to a definite Torah prohibition also apply in cases of doubt. Moreover, sometimes the doubt is more stringent than the certainty, as when she gets betrothed to another man while in doubt, she requires a divorce from the second man and is prohibited to the first, because perhaps the second betrothal was valid.

If a man divorces his wife with a get (divorce document) that is invalid rabbinically, or even with a get that is possibly invalid according to Torah law, and she has not yet remarried, and the first husband wishes to take her back, he must betroth her anew even if the get is possibly invalid according to Torah law, because perhaps the get is valid and she is considered single. However, one should not recite the seven blessings (Sheva Brachot) because in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient, and there is a prohibition against reciting a blessing in doubt. Even if the get is valid according to Torah law and invalid rabbinically, there is no need for the seven blessings because she is not completely single. Additionally, the blessings are rabbinic, and in cases where the get is rabbinically invalid, the sages did not impose the obligation of the blessings. But in cases of doubt regarding rabbinic invalidity, it seems to me that the seven blessings should be recited. There is also no need for a new ketubah (marriage contract) even in cases of rabbinic invalidity. This can be learned from the conditions of the ketubah which state that if she marries another man, she will take what is written for her, and since she cannot marry another man initially, there is no need to write her a new ketubah, and she retains her original ketubah. All the more so in cases of doubt according to Torah law or doubt regarding rabbinic invalidity, it seems to me that a new ketubah should be written, and this requires further study. It is obvious that if the get is valid and only invalidated due to the stringency of the poskim (decisors), she would require the seven blessings and a new ketubah.

The Law of a Mistake Where the Get and the Receipt Were Switched, and This Has Eight Sections:
Our sages taught in the Mishnah (p.): A scribe wrote a get for a man and a receipt for a woman, and he erred and gave the get to the woman and the receipt to the man, and they handed them to each other. The scribe wrote the get to be given by the man to his wife, and the receipt was written for the woman to give to her husband when he pays her the ketubah, as proof (see Tosafot s.v. "katav"). The scribe erred and gave the get to the woman and the receipt to the man. They did not open them to check, and the husband gave the receipt to the woman instead of the get, and the woman gave the get to the husband instead of the receipt. Later, it was found that the get was in the possession of the man and the receipt in the possession of the woman. If she married another man, she must leave both this man and the other, and she requires a get from both. All thirteen consequences that we considered in Siman 17, Section 257, and all that we wrote in the previous Siman, Section 5, apply here. She is close to negligence, as she should have read them (Yevamot 91b).

And specifically, this is only when the husband raised an objection before she married another man. However, if he did not object until after she married, we do not pay attention to it. We say that they conspired together to take her away from her second husband and return her to him, and he now gave her the receipt, and she gave him the get (divorce document) to show that they exchanged them. And even though, according to the truth, he would not benefit from this even according to the conspiracy, since she is also forbidden to him as we have said, nevertheless, sometimes he does not consider that she is forbidden to him and makes a conspiracy. It appears from the Talmud and the decisors that they established this and did not grant them credibility even if they swear that they are telling the truth, unless they bring witnesses. Thus, the Sages said there, "He cannot lose the rights of the second [husband]." Certainly, if it were as they said, he would not have been silent initially before she married and would not have allowed her to marry. He is not believed to say that she did not open [the matter] until after she married, as this is not the way of the world (see there in Tosafot, first chapter).

And there is a question regarding this: How is it possible for there to be a mix-up between a get (bill of divorce) and a shover (receipt of payment), considering that we hold that one is obligated to read the get before giving it, as stated in Siman 135? The answer to this is that they read it, and from the reading until the giving, a little time passed, and in the meantime, they got switched. This is what the early authorities wrote. It seems to me that this is why the Mishnah is precise in attributing the mistake to the scribe, because this is also our custom: after the reading and after the questions asked of the scribe and witnesses, the get is handed over to the scribe to fold it. It is common for the husband and wife to be meticulous about the calculations of the ketubah (marriage contract) before the divorce, and therefore they prepare the shover, and both documents are written by the scribe. It happened that when the scribe folded the get, the shover was also folded with him, and he mistakenly exchanged the papers. The reading after the giving is not essential, as stated there.

It is not specifically when she marries another man, as the same applies if she becomes betrothed (Bach and Beit Shmuel). Even a bill of divorce (get) is not required from her first husband, even though she would be permitted to marry the second, because the Rabbis did not believe him completely (ibid). It also appears to me that if he is a Kohen, he is not believed to take her back, even before she marries another, as there is also a concern of collusion that they are retracting the get. Therefore, we do not allow him to take her back, but she requires another get, because she has made herself forbidden as a married woman by saying that she has not yet been divorced. Furthermore, as long as she has not yet married or become betrothed to another man, they are believed regarding the matter that she should not marry another with this get (and even if he himself disputes it, we force him to give another get).

And know that the reason we wrote that they are not believed when she has remarried due to the concern of collusion is as Rashi and the Ran, of blessed memory, wrote. It is necessary to say this according to the language of the Mishnah, that the bill of divorce is in the husband's hand and the receipt is in the wife's hand, and we do not believe them after she has remarried someone else. We must say that they later handed them to each other based on collusion. According to this, the language of the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch is puzzling. The Rambam writes in Chapter 10, Law 11: "If the scribe wrote and mistakenly gave the bill of divorce to the woman and the receipt to the man, etc., and if she remarried and afterward the husband produced the bill of divorce and claimed she is not yet divorced because the bill of divorce is still in his possession and had not reached her hand, we do not listen to him to prohibit her to her second husband. Rather, she is presumed to be divorced, and the bill of divorce must have fallen from her hand and he found it. Therefore, he aims to prohibit her to her second husband." From his words, it is clear that it is only the husband who says this and not the wife, for if it were the wife, why attribute it to a fall? We should say that she handed it to him, and indeed from the language of the Mishnah it is explicitly clear that both of them are making this claim.

It seems to me that the Rambam does not agree with the reasoning of "kanunya" (collusion), as what would one gain from this since she is now forbidden to him. He also does not agree with the explanation we wrote in section 2, that he would not take it to heart, because if we say so, several laws of "migo" (a principle in Jewish law) and similar matters would change. Additionally, it is difficult for the Rambam to understand how it is possible to interpret the Mishnah as if the exchange was revealed before the marriage; for if so, how did she marry someone else afterward, since it was taught that she must leave both this one and that one? Is there any more promiscuous woman who would do such a thing? Furthermore, in the Talmud Yevamot (91b), it is stated regarding the reason she must leave both that she should have demanded a bill of divorce, as we wrote in section 1. According to what we wrote, she married intentionally, since the exchange was revealed before the marriage, so why do we need the reasoning of a penalty?

Therefore, the Rambam interprets this differently, for this distinction we made between before she was married and afterwards is not universally accepted. Only Rabbi Eliezer holds this in the Mishnah, and the Tanna Kamma disagrees with him. We follow the ruling of Rabbi Eliezer, as stated by the Rif and the Rosh (see there). The Jerusalem Talmud questions: what are we dealing with here? If it is clarified that there was a mistake and an exchange, how can Rabbi Eliezer disagree? And if it is clarified that there was no mistake, how can the Tanna Kamma disagree? It resolves that we are dealing with a case of doubt (see there), meaning we do not know anything for certain, only the husband claims so. Accordingly, we are not dealing at all with a case where she also supports his claim, but rather he claims there was an error and it is impossible to verify, for example, if the receipt is no longer in existence. Therefore, the Tanna Kamma says he is believed because his claim is plausible, and even if she was married beforehand, we penalize her because she should have given the get (divorce document) immediately after receiving it to be read by witnesses, which would have prevented any grounds for dispute. Since she did not do so, we penalize her, as stated in Yevamot. Rabbi Eliezer holds that if he disputed after she was married, we do not pay attention to him. The Rambam explains in his commentary on the Mishnah that if we were to accept everyone's claims, it would lead to people casting aspersions to force a woman to leave her second husband. Even though she did not act correctly by not having the get read immediately after receiving it, we do not force her to leave her husband because of this. This is what is taught in the Mishnah: after some time, the get is found in the husband's possession and the receipt in the wife's possession. The intention is not that this is verified, but that he claims it due to the scribe having both documents, which could lead to a mix-up. This is what the Jerusalem Talmud means by a case of doubt. The Rambam says even if he shows us the get, we say it fell from her hand and he found it. But if she also claims the same and produces the receipt before us, she must leave both husbands, and we do not suspect a conspiracy. (See Bava Batra 172b: regarding falling from an individual, it is not common. This is difficult for the Rambam, and it can be explained according to the explanation brought by the Rashbam there, that the one who lost it would protest. This applies only to monetary documents, but regarding a get, what would she have to protest about? See Tosafot Yevamot 116, s.v. "for what purpose," and study well.)

And know that what we have written, that even if she is betrothed, her status is like being married, in the Jerusalem Talmud there is a dispute about this, and it concludes thus. See there. And the commentators of the Jerusalem Talmud want to say that according to our Talmud and the Rambam, it is not so, but this is not necessarily the case. And so wrote the Rashba, of blessed memory, that the same applies if she is betrothed, and so wrote the later authorities.

Laws concerning when the husband or the wife claims they are divorced or when witnesses contradict each other. This section contains 22 subsections:
A husband who says, "I divorced my wife," is not believed to establish her as a divorced woman even from now on, neither regarding her ability to marry another nor regarding if he dies childless, she would be permitted to the general public. Nevertheless, out of stringency, we are concerned for his words such that if he dies, she performs chalitza and not yibbum. This is the ruling of all the poskim (decisors), and so it is in the Talmud (Bava Batra 135a). It appears that she is also prohibited to marry a kohen, and similarly, if he is a kohen, she is prohibited to him. Even if he is an Israelite, they are prohibited from secluding themselves together because, out of stringency, we believe him that she is divorced, and it is forbidden for him to seclude himself with an unmarried woman. Therefore, we say to him, "Do one of two things: either give her a get (divorce document) now in our presence and she will marry another, or betroth her again and live together." In all of this, there is no difference whether she admits to his words or denies them, due to the reason that will be explained with God's help.

According to the fundamental law as clarified in the Talmud (134b), it should be that if he says he divorced her now, he should be believed even to allow her to marry someone else, since he has a "migo" (a legal presumption) that if he wanted, he could divorce her now. Consequently, for this reason, even if she contradicts him, it means nothing, since her consent is not required for a get (divorce document); she has simply rendered herself forbidden to others by her own admission. Even in our times, with the enactment of Rabbeinu Gershom, if he divorces her, she is indeed divorced. If he says he already divorced her, fundamentally, he does not need to be believed, not only in regard to not remarrying another, but even if witnesses come and testify she committed adultery, she would be executed (in Temple times), since concerning past events, he does not have a "migo," as he cannot make her retroactively divorced. We do not say that in the past he could have divorced her, because we do not apply a "migo" retroactively. Consequently, even if she admits to his words, we do not accept it, because once she is established as a married woman, she cannot be removed from this status except by witnesses or clear proof.

And if he says, "I have already divorced her," whether he is believed for the future depends on the dispute regarding whether we split the statement concerning one entity, such that we believe part of his words and not the other part. This means that if he says about this woman that she has been divorced already, we believe him concerning her status from now on to consider her a divorcee, but not retroactively. Or, whether we do not split the statement concerning one entity, as we rule with two entities, like when someone testifies that a certain person had relations with his wife, he is a valid witness regarding the other person but not regarding his wife (Sanhedrin 10a). However, regarding one entity, there is doubt whether we split the statement or not. This is the case in the Talmud there. And even though we find in the Gemara that we do split the statement regarding one entity, like in the case of a sick person who writes all his possessions to his servant, and the law is that if he recovers, he retracts his gift. If he wrote to his servant and recovered, he retracts the property but not the servant (Gittin 9a). And we split the statement of the gift (as Rashi explains there) regarding the servant to take effect but not the property. Nevertheless, this is not comparable. Firstly, because even there, it is like two entities—the servant and the property. Also, there, it is necessary to say so because he has acquired the status of a free man, and it is impossible to return him to servitude, as explained there. And there is a dispute in the Gemara (Bava Batra there) whether we split the statement concerning one entity or not. This is the fundamental law that needs to be ruled upon.

However, in practice, the Gemara there ruled that one must be stringent and he is not believed to permit her to the general populace, even if he says, "I have just now divorced her." The reason is that even though he has a "migo" (a presumption of truthfulness, as he could have made a different claim), as we have written, nevertheless, there is a refutation to this migo. If it were true that he divorced her, there would be a rumor about it (Rashbam and Tosafot there), and it would be similar to a migo in the presence of witnesses (ibid.). Nevertheless, this is not exactly like a migo in the presence of witnesses because people sometimes divorce discreetly (Ketubot 23a). However, there is still some refutation to this migo because in many instances, the practice is to divorce publicly (ibid.) to publicize that she is divorced. This is what the Sages said (Arakhin 23a): "Does everyone who divorces do so in court?" meaning that often divorces are done in court to publicize the divorce, though there are those who are embarrassed by the publicity and do not divorce in court but discreetly at home. Consequently, in practical halakha, whether he says, "I have just now divorced her," or "I divorced her a long time ago," one must be stringent in every aspect. If he dies, she performs chalitzah and does not enter into levirate marriage. Even if he says, "I divorced her a long time ago," perhaps we split his statement and he is believed for the future but not for the past. There is no difference whether she admits it or not, as has been explained.

It is obvious that if she marries another man during her husband's lifetime before he divorces her with a get, we remove her from the second husband, and she needs a get from both of them and is forbidden to both. All thirteen stringencies apply to her. However, it is possible that we do not impose upon her all thirteen stringencies, as both claim she is divorced, and we have no clear evidence to contradict them. This seems to be the case. But if he is a kohen, she is definitely forbidden to him, as stated in section 1 (and in the Beit Shmuel, section 2, there is a scribal error, as stated in the Turei Zahav and Beit Meir). There is no difference in all this even if they say she was divorced in another city, for in most cases it would have become known. All this applies when she was known to be his wife, but otherwise, they are believed in all matters because the same mouth that prohibited is the one that permitted. It is clear that if she subsequently committed adultery and bore a child, since she was known to be a married woman and we ruled that they are not believed, the child is a doubtful mamzer (Beit Shmuel there).

Know that in the language of the Rambam on this matter, there are things that require explanation. Here are his words in Chapter 12, Law 5: "If the husband says, 'I divorced my wife,' he is not believed, but we are concerned about his words and she becomes a doubtful divorcée. Even if she admits that he divorced her, perhaps he intended to harm her, or he divorced her with an invalid get (divorce document) and she does not know, or perhaps she is brazen because she believes him (as is stated in the Tur). Therefore, we say to him: 'If what you say is true, you are still together, so divorce her now in our presence.'" End quote. 

It seems to me that the question arises: Why did the sages see fit to be stringent in this matter, considering that he has the principle of "miggo" (a Talmudic principle that allows a claim to be believed because the claimant could have made a stronger claim)? What we wrote, that if he had divorced her, there would have been a public announcement, they do not hold by this, as it is clearly stated by the sages that people sometimes divorce in secret. Even though we resolved these matters in Section 4, it seems a forced explanation. 

It appears to me that the reason for the stringency is similar to what we hold in Yoreh De'ah, Chapter 1, that whenever the matter can be clarified, we clarify it and do not rely on presumptions. Here too, since there is a remedy that he can divorce her in our presence, we do not rely on "miggo." Therefore, even if she admits to his words, and we hold that a woman who says to her husband, "You divorced me," is believed even if he denies it, and certainly when he admits it, we say that on the contrary, it is worse because perhaps he divorced her with an invalid get or intended to harm her, or since she is supporting his claim, she is brazen. This means that the reason she is believed is due to the presumption that she would not be brazen, as we wrote at the beginning of Chapter 17, and this is only when he denies it, not when he also says so. In this matter, when she says to him, "You divorced me," and he denies it, the Rambam holds that she is believed in all respects, as he wrote earlier, and we do not say that if she were divorced, there would be a public announcement. This shows that the reason of the public announcement is not valid. 

Regarding the law, it is explained at length in Chapter 17, with the help of Heaven, as referenced there. (And the language "doubtful divorcée" is difficult according to what is written, and it must be said that he holds that by themselves, they are not believed to remove her from the presumption of being a married woman, and this requires further investigation).

In Siman 17, Se'if 86, it is explained that when there is a contradiction regarding his death—two people say he died and two people say he did not die—and she also says he died, she should not remarry. If she does remarry someone else, she must leave him, and he is obligated to bring a suspended guilt offering or a sin offering. However, if she marries one of her witnesses who says he died, she does not have to leave him. There, in Se'if 87 and 88, we explained the reason for this—see there. But regarding a get (divorce document), it is not the same. When two people say she was divorced and two people say she was not divorced, and she also says she was divorced, the sages said (Ketubot 22b) that she must always leave, even if she married one of her witnesses who says she was divorced.

And two reasons are given for this in the Gemara there as to why the law of a get (divorce document) is different from that of death. One reason is that in the case of divorce, she can contradict him even when the husband comes and says, "I did not divorce you," but in the case of death, she cannot contradict it. This means that in the case of death, we consider her certainty when she says, "My husband died," to be absolute and certain. Therefore, its law is like the doubt whether a substance is forbidden fat or permitted fat, when someone says with certainty that it is permitted fat, as stated there. But in the case of divorce, her certainty is not considered at all, and we say that even now she does not know with certainty. And this, that she says, "I was divorced," is because she imagines that it will not be revealed as false, and even if he comes and says, "I did not divorce you," she will contradict him in his presence. And although a woman does not usually brazenly contradict her husband, and for this reason, she is believed to say, "You divorced me," even when it contradicts him, this is only when there are no witnesses supporting her. But when there are witnesses supporting her, she will brazenly contradict him, and therefore her status reverts to being in doubt like the case of forbidden fat and permitted fat, and she is liable to bring a conditional guilt-offering. According to this reasoning, if she marries, she must leave even if they say that she was already divorced.

And the second reason is that certainly when they say that she was divorced a long time ago, if she marries one of her witnesses she does not have to leave him, as in the case of death. But this that we said she must leave, is when they say that she was recently divorced, and we say to her, "If so, show us your get (divorce document)." And from the fact that she did not bring the get before us, we infer that it is a lie. But when they say that she was divorced a long time ago, it can be said that the get was lost, unlike in the case of a recent time, where it is not common for it to be lost, and it is evident that they are lying. And the Rif ruled according to this reasoning, see there. And even though when there is no contradiction from witnesses, we do not worry about it when she says "my get was lost," even when the witnesses say that she was recently divorced, and certainly this is the case. But when two witnesses contradict and say she was not divorced, the ruling is that she does not have to leave if she married one of her witnesses, for this is like the case of a doubt whether it is forbidden fat or permitted fat. When one says "I am certain it is permitted fat," and therefore when there is some evidence that it is not permitted fat, we do not allow him to eat it, unlike when it is certainly permitted fat, we do not worry about it and say that there is some error in the evidence. This case is similar.

In this way, the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 3 will be explained. And this is what he says: If two people say she was divorced and two people say she was not divorced, even if the husband stands and she says to him, "You divorced me," she is considered to have the status of a completely married woman because the witnesses support her, and it is possible that she is being brazen. Therefore, if she marries, she must leave, and the child is a mamzer (illegitimate). This applies when they say she was divorced now, for they say to her, "If it is true, produce your get (divorce document)." But if the witnesses say she was divorced several days ago, it is possible the get was lost. And since she says with certainty, "I am divorced," and two witnesses testify for her, even though the other two contradict her, if she marries one of her witnesses, she does not have to leave, because she and her husband know with certainty that she is permitted, and it is presumed that they would not ruin themselves. But if she marries someone else, since the matter is doubtful to him, and similarly, if she says, "I do not know," she must leave, and the child is a doubtful mamzer. However, in any case where there is no contradiction, but they say she was divorced now, and we say to her, "Show us your get," and she says it was lost or torn, we do not worry about her. This concludes the text.

If there is no absolute contradiction between the witnesses, but rather two say, "We saw that this woman was divorced," and two say, "We did not see," if they were not all in one courtyard, we do not concern ourselves at all with those who say, "We did not see," and they are not considered as contradicting. She may even remarry ab initio, because surely one would not expect everyone in the city to hear about the get (divorce document). However, if they were all residing in one courtyard, it is certainly strange that they did not hear about the get. Nevertheless, they are not completely considered as contradicting, because there are people who customarily divorce in private due to embarrassment. Therefore, ab initio, she should not remarry until she receives another get. But if she has remarried, she does not have to leave the marriage, and the child is legitimate. Even if she has no children, she does not have to leave. And even according to the opinion of Rashi and the Ran, who wrote that a divorce has a public aspect, we are still not concerned about the contradiction of witnesses in this matter, and we say that she was divorced privately (Beit Shmuel sec. 7), for even according to their opinion, it is not a rule that a divorce necessarily has a public aspect, as written in paragraph 4 there.

Some of the early authorities raised an objection: If so, why specify that they did not see her get divorced, that she should not leave, even if they say clearly that she was not divorced, if she married, she should not leave, as it is written. They answered that in that case, it is specifically when she married one of her witnesses, but here, even if she married another, she should not leave. Additionally, in that case, it is specifically when the witnesses who testified that she was divorced say that she was already divorced, not that he divorced her now, as it is written. But here, even if they say that he divorced her now, she should not leave (Ketubot 23a, in the name of Ramban, of blessed memory). And there is one who says further that here, even if she does not say with certainty that she was divorced, she should not leave (there, in the name of Ra'ah). This requires investigation, as it appears from reasoning that since there are doubts before us—that these did not know about the get (divorce document), and she also does not know clearly—why should she not leave? And perhaps this is not a doubt at all, that initially, she should not marry only because of gossip, as Rashi explained. Therefore, if she married, she should not leave. (And according to this, it is possible that even if she did not marry and another get cannot be obtained, she may marry initially, since it is only because of gossip. However, since the early authorities did not explain this way, it shows that they hold that in any case, she should not marry. This requires further deliberation, and analyze this well.)

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles wrote in Section 4 that there are those who say that if it is claimed that they were all present together and two say, "We did not see," this constitutes a contradiction, because such a significant matter would not be done in private. These are his words. And similarly, we rule this way in Choshen Mishpat, the end of Section 29, and from there it is explained that this is specifically when they say, "Our hands did not leave their hands," see there (in Sema, Subsection 12). 

It is possible that in the case of a get (divorce document), even if it is not in such a manner, it constitutes a contradiction. This is because, specifically in cases like loans or similar matters that are completed in a short time, we require such a manner. But in the case of a get, where the writing and arrangement take time, it constitutes a contradiction even if not in such a manner.

Furthermore, it is explained from there and from Section 30, that if the contradiction is in a manner where the two who say they saw the divorce claim that these two were also with them, and these others deny it, it is not considered a contradiction. This is because a witness does not precisely remember who was with him at the moment of testimony, and it might seem to them as such (and it is strained to differentiate between one and two). 

There is a doubt if the two witnesses who testify that the divorce occurred say that not all were present together, and the others say they were present together, whether this is considered a contradiction or not. It seems that it is considered a contradiction and requires further investigation (see Shevuot 41b and Choshen Mishpat, Section 70, Subsection 2).

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote (there) that a woman who is not known to be married, and one witness comes and says she was married and then divorced, and another witness comes and says she was not divorced, both of them are testifying that she is married, and one testifies that she is divorced, and the words of one do not stand against the words of two. Therefore, she should not marry, and if she marries, she must leave, end quote. And even if she says herself that she was divorced (Lechem Mishneh), and although in the case of one witness saying he died and afterward another comes and says he did not die, we do not hold this way as it is written in Siman 17, this is because in the case of an agunah (a woman whose husband is missing) they were lenient that one witness is considered like two, and the words of one do not stand against the words of two as written there. This is not the case with divorce. Similarly, it is not comparable to the case where one witness says she was betrothed and one witness says she was not betrothed, as we hold in Siman 47 that she does not have to leave, because there both are testifying about a single woman, and the words of one do not stand against the words of two. Here, both are testifying about a married woman (Gemara).

The Tur wrote: One witness says she was divorced and another says she was not divorced, she should not marry. If she did marry, if she was presumed to be a married woman, she must leave [the second husband] in any case. If she was not presumed to be a married woman except based on their testimony, if there is a contradiction in their testimony, such as one says she was divorced and the other says she was never divorced, she may marry initially. If there is no contradiction in their testimony, such as one says the bill of divorce was thrown close to him and the other says it was thrown close to her, if she married, she must leave, as the Tur wrote. And similarly, it is written in the Shulchan Aruch, Siman 5. The reason is that since they contradict each other, it is impossible to join their testimonies, and one of them is invalid. Consequently, she remains presumed to be single and therefore may marry initially. However, in the case of the bill of divorce being close to him or her, this is not a contradiction, as people are prone to err in such matters. Consequently, she is presumed to be a married woman based on their testimony, and therefore one witness is not believed to remove her from the presumption of being a married woman (Ran). And what they wrote at the beginning, "she should not marry," is a common expression because this is the language of the Talmud. But in truth, there is no actual ruling here that she should not marry initially, for if she was presumed to be a married woman or based on their testimony when there is no contradiction between them, then even if she married, she must leave. And without a presumption, she may marry initially. And in the language of the Talmud, "she should not marry, and if she married, she must leave," meaning we warn her not to marry, and if she transgressed and married, she must leave.

From the language of the Rambam, as we have brought, it is evident that in every situation she must leave, for he did not differentiate as the Tur did (and see Beit Yosef, section 9). We can say that it refers to a case where she herself said, "I was married and I got divorced," thus establishing herself as a single witness. She is not believed due to the principle of "the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted," since there are witnesses. Consequently, she forbids herself based on her own statement, and a single witness cannot release her from her prohibition (as the Ra'ah writes there). However, this too should have been explained. In truth, there are early authorities who said that there is no issue of conflicting testimonies here, as these are two separate testimonies. One set of witnesses testifies that she was married, which does not contradict the other. Additionally, one witness testifies to the divorce and another contradicts him. The testimony regarding the marriage stands, and the fact that they do not join together applies to the future, not the past. Here, the testimony about the marriage takes precedence over the contradiction concerning the divorce (as explained there in the name of the Rashba and his students).

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Ketubot 22a): A woman who says, "I was married and now I am divorced," is believed, because the mouth that prohibited is the mouth that permitted. However, if there are witnesses that she was married and she says, "I am divorced," she is not believed. And some say that this credibility when there are no witnesses is specifically when she said within twenty-four hours that she is divorced, but after twenty-four hours, she is not believed unless she provides a valid reason for why she did not say it immediately (R' Yitzchak in the Tur). Their reasoning is that this is akin to retracting her statement and requires a valid reason (Hagahot Maimoniot, beginning of chapter 12). And some say that certainly when she says, "I was married and now I am divorced," this needs to be immediate, but if she says it after some time, she needs a valid reason. However, if she says, "I was married," which does not imply at all that she is currently married, she is believed even after some time to say, "I am divorced," even without a valid reason (there). And some say that we do not require it within twenty-four hours, but nevertheless we require her to say, "I am divorced," at the time they are engaged in that matter (R'MaH in the Tur). The opinion of the Tur seems to follow the previous opinion (there). And our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 6, only mentioned the first opinion (there) (and possibly the second opinion that differentiates between "I was" and "I am" holds that it should be explicitly stated, and refer to the Beit Meir and Shach, section 110, and consider carefully).

When there are witnesses, she is not believed, and even if she has married, she must leave her husband. Even if she married before the witnesses came and testified that she is a married woman, she must leave him. One should not question this by saying that it is not the way of pleasantness to initially permit her to marry and then later force her to leave her husband. We can explain that we certainly warned her beforehand, saying, "Be aware that witnesses might come. Do not marry until you bring proof of your divorce." It is upon her to know if there is a concern that witnesses will come or not. If she did not act accordingly, she has caused her own misfortune. This applies specifically to two witnesses, but one witness is of no consequence. Likewise, if there is a rumor that there are witnesses in a certain place who know that she was a married woman, we do not allow her to marry until she brings proof of her divorce. This leniency is only applied to a captive woman, as explained in Siman 7, but not to a married woman.

And even though she is not believed when there are witnesses, nevertheless, as a stringency, we are concerned about her statement, and she is disqualified from marrying into the priesthood forever. If her husband dies, even though we do not allow her to marry freely, we also do not allow her to enter into levirate marriage. She must perform the halitzah ceremony and cannot enter into levirate marriage. Even if witnesses come and say they heard she is divorced, this is not considered valid testimony to remove her from the presumption of being married, as this is akin to testimony from hearsay, unless the witnesses testify that they know she is divorced. Nevertheless, as a stringency, we are concerned about what they heard. All this applies when the witnesses testify that they know she is married, but if they do not testify that they know she is married, and only say they heard she was betrothed or heard she was betrothed and divorced, their testimony is considered as mere rumor. There are various detailed laws about this, which are explained in Siman 46. When there are witnesses who know she is divorced, she is permitted in all respects, even if they testify that she divorced recently and the get (divorce document) is not before us because she says it was lost or torn. She may marry l'chatchila (initially), and this is not a deficiency unless there are contradicting witnesses, as explained in section 9.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 9: If she produced a get (divorce document) from her possession and said, "My husband divorced me with this," she is believed, and she may remarry with it even though it is not validated, as stated in sections 141 and 142. If the husband comes and contests, saying, "It fell from me, and she found it," he is not believed, for he admitted that he wrote it for her, and it came from her possession. But if the husband says, "It was conditional, and the condition has not yet been fulfilled," or "It was a deposit," or "I never wrote it," or "It is forged," it must be validated by its witnesses or by the court, as stated in sections 141 and 142. If it is not validated, she is not considered divorced to the extent that she may marry others, but she disqualifies herself from marrying a kohen. There are many detailed laws on this matter, which are explained at length in their proper places.

Furthermore, it is written that a woman who holds a court document cannot remarry with it until the signatures of the court are recognized. And it has already been clarified there that the recognition of one signature suffices. And know that our teacher, the Rema, wrote at the end of Siman 142 that in a case of potential agunah (a woman bound to her marriage without the possibility of divorce), one can rely on the signatures even without the formal validation by the court, because according to Torah law, witnesses signed on a document are considered as if their testimony was scrutinized in court. Also, one can rely on the authorities who hold that a court document does not require validation. Why did he not correct similarly here?
