It can be said that he relied on what was written there, or it is possible to distinguish that there, where the get (divorce document) itself is present, we rely on it as it is considered as definitive proof that it is not forged. But here, with just a written document, we are concerned about forgery. There are some prominent authorities who disagree on this (as written in the Pitchei Teshuvah, subparagraph 19). It seems to me that if there is a signature on the court document, certainly one can rely on it in a case of potential agunah. However, in our times, it is clear that it should be verified through the postal service and by iron wires (possibly referring to modern communication methods), and she should not remarry until it is verified. All of this applies when she is established as married, but otherwise, there is no need for any of this.

The Tur wrote that they asked the Rosh, of blessed memory, about a certain get (divorce document) where witnesses testified that one of the signatories of the get was a thief, but there were also witnesses who testified that he repented, as they saw him fasting and laying tefillin, and also that an oath came to him, and he refused to swear. The Rosh responded that the get is invalid, even though it was not publicly declared that he was invalid. The repentance he did is not effective until he makes restitution for the money he stole. They also asked about a get where the scribe testified that the husband did not instruct him to sign, and one of the signing witnesses himself also testified similarly. The Rosh responded that the get is invalid. Even if the handwriting of the witness is verified from another source, he is believed to say that the husband did not instruct him to sign. This is not considered as testifying falsely about oneself, as it can be said that since he was instructed to write, it does not appear to people as a false signature. Moreover, since the scribe also testifies this way, the get is invalid (Beit Yosef).

The law regarding finding a get (divorce document) in the marketplace and to whom it should be returned. This section contains 14 paragraphs: In Siman 132, it was explained about a messenger who brought a get and lost it, and it was found. If it was found immediately, it is valid, but if not, we are concerned that it might belong to another man with the same names, and there is no allowance unless caravans are not common, and it has not been established that there are two men named Yosef ben Shimon. Alternatively, if the messenger provides a more distinctive sign, such as a hole next to a specific letter, which is a more distinctive sign than those used for returning lost items, called a medium sign, and regarding lost items, it is considered a distinctive sign according to the Rambam and other authorities. We have explained this in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 267, Paragraph 5. This applies when the messenger lost it. In this Siman, it will be explained about a get found in the marketplace and there is no messenger to claim it was lost. Instead, the husband and wife are in dispute: the husband claims it fell from him as he wrote it but decided not to give it to her, so she is still married, while the wife claims that he already handed her the get and she is divorced, and it fell from her. There are no witnesses to clarify the matter.

And so our Sages said (Baba Metzia 28a): If he gives identifying marks of the get (bill of divorce) and she gives identifying marks of the get, it should be given to her. This is specifically with a distinct mark, such as a hole beside a particular letter, for this proves that the get was in her possession; otherwise, how would she know? But with other signs, it is possible she saw them when the husband held it in his hand. Similarly, if she gives a sign regarding the thread with which the get was tied and specifies exactly the length of the thread, it should be given to her. However, if she says the get is long or short, or the thread is white or black, this is meaningless. The Rif wrote that it is specifically a hole beside a particular letter or the length of the thread, and no other sign. And it seems that even if she specifies the exact length and width of the get, it is not a valid sign. This is explained in the Gemara there, where we learn: If we say it is about its length and width, perhaps she saw it while he was holding it. And this is not similar to the length of the thread, as it is not usual to stretch out the thread while holding the get. It is further explained there that when giving a sign about the container in which the get was placed—if he says it was in a box and she says it was in a box, and it is a leather pouch—it should be given to him. Why? Because she would know that everything he has, he places in the box. The commentators (Ran and Nimukei Yosef) wrote that if she gives a poor sign on the get and it cannot be returned to her, it is not given to him or her, even if he gives a distinct sign. For him, it is not proof, as they wrote. This is regarding the signs of the get itself, but with external signs, such as saying it was placed in a box, it is returned to him, as this proves it was still with him. And it cannot be said that she placed it in her box, as it is not usual for a woman to put it in a box; she guards it more carefully because she wants to remarry with it. Therefore, this is a sign only for him and not for her.

There is a question regarding this matter: why do we not return the bill of divorce to her, since a woman who claims, "My husband divorced me," is believed even when there is no bill of divorce before us? All the more so should she be believed when there is a bill of divorce. The answer to this is that, on the contrary, when there is a bill of divorce, it is worse. The reason she is believed is due to the presumption that a woman would not be so bold as to lie in the face of her husband. But when there is a bill of divorce, she is emboldened and dares to lie (Tosafot there, 18b, s.v. "Ein"; similarly in Gittin 27a). This is like the case in the previous section where, when there are witnesses, she is emboldened and dares to lie, and the same applies to a bill of divorce.

Additionally, there is a question regarding why we do not return the get (divorce document) to him when she does not provide a distinct identifying mark. It makes sense if he also does not provide a distinct identifying mark, as there is a concern that he might use it to divorce her or that it might be another get with the same names, as discussed in Siman 132. However, if he says that there is a hole next to a certain letter, why do we not return it to him and let him do as he wishes with it? The answer is that we are concerned that it may have fallen from her, and she needs the get to collect her ketubah (marriage contract) in places where ketubot are not written. As it is taught in the Mishnah (Ketubot 89b): if she produces a get but not a ketubah, she collects her ketubah. If we return it to him, he will claim that she has already been divorced, and when she demands her ketubah, he will say that he has already paid her, bringing proof by showing that the get is in his possession, as Rashi explains in Gittin 27b. Over time, the matter will be forgotten that the get was found and returned to him, and she will not be able to clarify the situation as it actually was.

There is another question regarding this matter: Why did we say that if one finds it in a pouch, he should return it to him and he can do with it as he wishes, even to divorce with it? After all, there is no distinctive sign here, and we should be concerned that it may belong to someone else, as per Section 132. The answer to this is that indeed we must say that there are no frequent caravans and there is no established presence of two Yosef ben Shimon (as per Tosafot Gittin 28a, see there). And in the previous law, we do not return it to him even in such a case for the reason we wrote, lest he wishes to cause her to forfeit her ketubah. And some say that indeed, giving it to him does not mean that he is permitted to divorce with it, but rather that it is not given to her (Rosh, Chapter 2 of Bava Metzia, Section 14, see there).

And this is what we have learned (Bava Metzia 18a and Gittin 27a): If one finds a woman's get (divorce document) in the marketplace, if the husband admits [that it is the get], it should be returned to the woman. If the husband does not admit, it should not be returned either to this one or to that one. The Rif writes there that this is referring to a case where she did not provide a definitive identifying mark, as he explains. And the Gemara establishes it in a scenario where there is no concern that it might be a different get because caravans are not frequent, nor is it established [that there are other such documents around]. And when the husband admits, it should be returned to the woman, whether he admits that he still needs to give it to her (as it appears from Rashi's commentary) — meaning, it should be given to her now as a divorce by the husband's directive — or whether he admits that he already gave it to her and it fell from her (as Tosafot explain in Gittin 27a, s.v. "when"). Nevertheless, he is not believed when there is a concern of a different get. And even though there are those who hold that a husband who says "I have divorced my wife" is believed, that is for the future and not retroactively. And when he says it retroactively, he is not believed even for the future (as discussed there, and it is a complex issue, as there is also a dispute in Bava Batra 134a. And if their intention is that we hold he is believed, it is more problematic, as there we conclude that he is not believed, as written in Siman 152, and it is a difficult matter). Therefore, in such a scenario, it should also be returned to her as a divorce. And if you ask why all this is necessary, since a woman who says to her husband "you divorced me" is believed, we have already written that when there is a get, she is not believed because she would be brazen and lie. Furthermore, she is only believed when the husband denies it, because she would not be brazen, but not when he supports her, as written there. And this, that when the husband does not admit, it should not be returned either to this one or to that one — the reason is simple: it cannot be returned to her because she did not provide a definitive identifying mark, and due to the reason of credibility, it cannot be returned to her, because when there is a get, she would be brazen, as written. And it cannot be returned to the husband, even though there is no concern here that it might be a different get, nevertheless, due to the concern that he might want to cause her to lose her ketubah, as written in Section 4.

All of this follows the opinion of the Rif, and it also appears to be the opinion of the Rambam in chapter 18 of Hilchot Gezeila, where he writes: "If one finds women's bills of divorce (gittin), if the husband acknowledges them, they should be returned to the wife. If the husband does not acknowledge them, if the woman provides a clear identifying mark, it should be given to her; if not, it should not be given to either party. If the husband says it fell from him and gives its identifying marks, and the woman also says it fell from her and gives its identifying marks, it should be given to her, provided she gives a clear identifying mark, such as saying there is a hole next to a specific letter, which she would not know unless it had come into her possession. If he says the identifying mark is the string tied around the get, and she also says the identifying mark is the string, it should be given to her, provided she gives a clear identifying mark, such as the length measurement of the string. But if she says it is red or black, this is not a clear identifying mark. If he says it was placed in a certain container, and she says it was placed in a certain container, it should be given to him because this is not a clear identifying mark." This is the conclusion of his words. This clarification that if the husband acknowledges it, it should be returned to the wife, applies in a situation where there is no concern for another get, where there are not two men named Yosef ben Shimon, and caravans are not common. These rulings rely on what is written in chapter 3 of Hilchot Gerushin regarding a messenger when a get is lost (as explained by the Maggid Mishneh).

Additionally, it appears to me, based on my humble opinion, that Maimonides holds that in this case, there is no need to be concerned about another get (divorce document). Although he himself ruled in Chapter 12 of the laws of divorce that a husband who says "I divorced my wife" is not believed, even if she admits to his words, he holds that this is when there is no get before us. However, when there is a get before us and the man and woman say that she has already been divorced, we do not need to be concerned about another get. This is specifically when she is also present and says this. Therefore, Maimonides, who discusses the case here where she is before us, as is evident from his words when he writes "if she gave a distinctive sign, etc.," it is clear that she is before us and claims that she has already been divorced. Consequently, the term "admits" means that she admits to her own words. But in the Gemara there, where it was necessary to establish that there is no concern about another get, this is because the language of the Baraita does not indicate that she is before us. And when it says "when he admits," it does not mean that he admits to her words, but rather that he admits regarding this get that it is his. Consequently, we cannot rely on his statement, as I have written. Additionally, it is necessarily understood according to Rashi's interpretation that he admits he needs to give it to her, for she is not here for us to say that he admits to her words, and consequently, there is a concern for another get. (And perhaps because of this, Rashi was compelled to explain it this way. And when it concludes, "the husband does not admit, etc.," it does not mean that she is here, but rather that we do not need to seek her out and deliver it to her, for it is impossible to return it to her). (And the Tosafot explain that she is here, see there).

According to the Rosh of blessed memory, there is a different approach in all this which he wrote (in the second chapter of Bava Metzia, Siman 14) that when he says "it fell from me" and she says "it fell from me," she is believed if she only provides an intermediate sign for which a lost item is returned. The Talmud there does not specifically mean a hole near a certain letter, and this does not exclude only weak signs like whiteness and redness. Similarly, if she provides a sign regarding the length and width of the get (divorce document), we return it to her. What seems to imply there that we do not return it to her is when she does not precisely specify the measurement. His reasoning is that we hold that a woman who tells her husband "you divorced me" is believed, and if it is because when there is a get she would be brazen and assertive, since the signs support her, the get does not contradict her words. Therefore, to return it to the husband so he can divorce with it, we need a clear sign like a hole near a certain letter, as in the case of a messenger in Siman 132. But to return it to her when she says she is already divorced, she is believed even with an intermediate sign, just like with any lost items. And indeed, when he says it is in a bag and she says it is in a bag, if not for the reason that she knows that everything he has, he places in the bag, it would have been returned to her even though this is not a clear sign. The fact that it is returned to him is not for him to divorce with it, because certainly he cannot divorce her with this get since he did not provide a clear sign, but the intention is that it should not be given to her.

And according to his words, that which it states in the baraita, "If one finds a woman's get (divorce document) in the marketplace, if the husband admits, he should return it to the woman," refers to a case where she does not provide even an intermediate sign (and this is his intention in the first chapter there, siman 45, and study it well). And this, which the Gemara (there 18b and Gittin there) establishes with a sign of a hole next to a specific letter, is when he provides the sign because he wants to divorce her now with it. But if she provides the sign and says she has already been divorced and it fell from her, an intermediate sign is sufficient. Additionally, it can be explained that even if he admits she has already been divorced, it is still nothing, because since she did not provide any sign, she is not believed. And he, who says he divorced her, is not believed either, as this is the ruling we follow. Therefore, it specifically requires a hole next to a specific letter or when they have not been established (as husband and wife) and caravans are not frequently found there. See there.

The words of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch are wondrous in this matter, and this is what the Tur says: "If one finds a woman's get (divorce document) in the market, if the woman gives a sign, such as saying there is a hole next to a certain letter, and she says that she has already been divorced with it and that it fell from her, it should be returned to her even if the husband denies it and claims that it fell from him and that he never divorced her but only commanded it to be written and has not given it yet, even if he also gives a sign. But if she does not give a sign and the husband denies it, it should not be given neither to him nor to her." And these are the exact words of the Rif and the Rambam, that we specifically require a clear identifying mark.

And afterwards he wrote as follows: "If the husband admits that he wrote it and says that it should be given to her for the purpose of divorce, if it is found in a place and at a time when it is appropriate to return it, and there is no concern that it fell from someone else, as I explained above (Siman 132, where it is found immediately or there is no presumption of death and it was not established), it should be given to her and she will be divorced from that moment. If not, it should not be given to her." This applies according to all opinions as we have explained, but according to the Rif, it refers to when she does not provide a distinctive sign, and according to the Rosh, it refers to when she does not provide even a medium sign. And just from the wording of the previous statement, it seems that his intention is like the Rif, as is evident (and this is like Rashi's explanation, who admits to giving for the purpose of divorce as mentioned).

And afterwards he wrote, and these are his words: "If he (the husband) admits that she (the wife) was divorced with it (the get) and she asks to collect her ketubah with it, as in the case where it is taught: 'She produced a get but there is no ketubah with it, she collects her ketubah.' And he says that he already paid it and she returned it to him and it fell from him, he returns it to her even if she does not say there is a hole next to a certain letter, only when she says a clear sign (a clear sign is in the case of a lost item) such as saying the number of fingers in the length or width of the get, or she says the measure of the string tied to it. But if she said the get was long or short and does not specify its measure, or the string was white or black, or she said it was placed in a purse or a bag, it is not a sign to return it to her with it." End of quote. And these words are according to the opinion of the Rosh and not the Rif. And some say that what he wrote, "even if she does not say there is a hole, etc.," refers to the beginning of the section and is according to the opinion of the Rosh (Bach and Beit Shmuel, section 5). And these words are puzzling because if so, why did he elaborate so much, and besides the difficulty in the language, why did he need to mention the matter of the ketubah, since it is obvious that when the get is returned to her, she will collect her ketubah. Moreover, according to this, there are many precise details.

Therefore, it seems that according to the law, the Tur agrees with the Rif that to believe her claim of being divorced, a specific marking next to a particular letter is necessary. Since there is a divorce document, she is bold in her assertion. Conversely, it seems to the Tur that the method of the Talmud in Bava Metzia there does not specifically require a marking next to a particular letter, as it only mentions white and red, which are inferior signs, and this aligns with the Rosh. Therefore, the Tur adopted a different method in this matter. Certainly, the Baraita that states "if one finds a woman's divorce document in the market, when the husband admits it" should be interpreted according to the Rif, as it appears to me to be the correct law, and not like the Rosh. The Talmudic discussion in Bava Metzia should be interpreted according to the Rosh, but it is not addressing the permissibility of a married woman, as in this case both agree, and the dispute between the man and woman is only concerning the ketubah. Therefore, this ruling is like other monetary laws, where an intermediate sign is sufficient (see Gra, sections 1 and 4). And if it is difficult regarding the prohibition, how are they trusted, it can be said that it is referring to a situation where there are witnesses that she was divorced, or it was found immediately, or there is no presumption, and the dispute between them is only regarding the ketubah. Our teacher the Beit Yosef only copied the words of the Tur in the Shulchan Aruch and also did not explain it in his great book (and the words of the Gra in section 7 are difficult, as according to the Tur there is no need for this at all, and the Rosh according to his method required this — see there and examine well).

Those who are obligated by law to divorce when the wife demands a get, and additional laws. This section contains sixty-six paragraphs:

The sages taught in the Mishnah (at the end of the chapter "Hamadir"): These are the ones whom we compel to divorce (with the permission of the authorities): someone afflicted with boils, who is a leper (Rambam), and who is extremely repulsive and foul-smelling to the extent that the wife cannot tolerate him (Kenesset HaGedolah). If the doctors are divided on whether he is such a leper or not, if the majority of them agree that he is, we compel him to divorce (ibid.). Similarly, if he has nasal polyps causing bad breath or a foul-smelling nose, or if he has sores in his mouth and emits foul-smelling saliva, we compel him to divorce (ibid.). Additionally, if he has a disease called "French disease" (syphilis) known in our language as "Vienneres," and the doctors agree that marital relations with him will cause his flesh to decay, like the melting of one's flesh (Zechariah 14:12), and if he has a strong foul odor or is extremely repulsive to the extent that the wife cannot tolerate him, we compel him to divorce (see there in Kenesset HaGedolah). All these cases apply when the doctors say that he cannot be healed. If he claims to have been healed and she does not believe him, it seems that we should consult the doctors (and there it is written that there is doubt in this matter, but I do not understand what doubt there can be in a matter that can be clarified by consulting doctors).

And so we have learned there that there are certain professions from which one can compel [a spouse] to separate due to the nature of the work, as she can claim, "I cannot tolerate this." These include: a collector of dog excrement, as there are places where it is used to process leather; and those who soak garments in it before washing them for a day or two. Similarly, a tanner who processes hides, or one whose trade is to cut copper from its source, meaning to extract copper from the earth. All these are professions that emit foul odors, and not everyone can tolerate them. However, for other types of work, even the most degrading, a woman cannot protest against her husband, even if she is of noble lineage. As our sages said, "Skin a carcass in the marketplace and do not say, 'I am a priest or a great man.'" (Pesachim 113a).

There is a doubt whether if his work is to clean latrines, if she can compel him to divorce her. It seems that it is certainly more severe than the case of dog excrement, as human excrement is more foul-smelling, as is evident in Orach Chaim, Siman 79, Se'if 4. However, it is possible that specifically in the case of dog excrement, where he collects it in one place to work with it, they can compel him, but in the case of someone who cleans latrines and removes the excrement and disposes of it, they cannot compel him. The matter requires further investigation to determine the law.

All these cases where they are compelled to divorce, the women are given their basic ketubah amount, but they do not receive the additional amount of the ketubah. This is because the additional amount was granted based on his own volition, and not with the intention that he would be compelled to divorce against his will and give away his money (Beit Shmuel section 1). However, some say that in the case of one afflicted with boils, if this condition existed before he married her, in which case we do not allow her to stay with him for his benefit even if she wishes to, as will be explained, and consequently she is able to compel him to divorce her, he is obligated to also give the additional amount since he knew about it and willingly chose to harm his own property (ibid.). It appears that this is specifically when it is clearly known that the boils make intimacy difficult for him, and we do not allow them to be together without witnesses. But if it is not clearly known, he does not need to give the additional amount.

In all these matters, we do not compel him to divorce her except when she demands a divorce. However, if she wishes to remain with her husband, we do not interfere with her. Even when she demands a divorce, we do not compel him unless the issue arose after they were married, or even if it was prior, but she was unaware of it. However, if it was known from before, whether it was an illness or a profession, and she was aware of it, we do not compel him to divorce her, for she accepted it knowingly. She cannot claim that she thought she could accept it but now finds she cannot, for we would respond: even if your claim is true, how can we compel him to divorce you? This would be a coerced divorce since you knew and accepted it.

Except in the case of one afflicted with boils, even if it was known from before and she accepted it, and even if he stipulated with her that she would stay with him, and even now she says, "Leave me and I will live with him," we do not permit it. All the more so if he became afflicted afterward and she wishes to stay with him, we do not permit it. In all these cases, when we compel him, it is for her benefit. However, in the case of one afflicted with boils, it is more beneficial for him to separate from her than for her, because sexual relations would harm him, cause his flesh to deteriorate, and pieces of flesh may fall off. Therefore, we prevent them from being together unless she says she will live with him with witnesses ensuring he does not have relations with her. In this case, we listen to her. Consequently, since we do not allow them to be together and she requests a divorce, we compel him to divorce her and give her the ketubah, as stated in the previous section.

There are those who say that in all matters, she can say, "I thought I could accept it, but now I cannot," and they compel him to divorce her, unless he made a prior condition with her that she should know that his work is such and such, or that he has bad breath or something similar, and she accepted the condition. In that case, they do not compel him because it is impossible to compel him since there was a condition. But in a general situation, even though she knew about it, she can still say, "I am now unable to accept it" (Ran at the end of the chapter "Hamadir" in the name of some opinions, and this is the opinion of the Rashba). Consequently, since there is a dispute on this matter, it is impossible to compel him. It is a great principle in compelling a get (divorce) that whenever there is a dispute regarding the compulsion, we follow the stringent view to avoid a get being coerced according to those who believe it should not be compelled. Therefore, this opinion was not brought in the Shulchan Aruch. See there and see what I wrote in section 63.

If a woman’s husband had bad breath or a nasal odor or collected dog excrement or similar, and he died, and she fell before his brother for levirate marriage (yibbum), and the brother had the same defect as her husband, the Sages stated in the Mishnah that she can say, "I could tolerate your brother, but I cannot tolerate you," and we compel him to perform chalitzah and give her the ketubah. One might ask, according to the previous opinion, what is the novelty here, since she could have said the same to her husband, as it says there, and certainly to the levir, whom she did not accept at all. The answer is that, on the contrary, there is a greater novelty with the levir than with the husband. With the husband, she could say, "I thought my nature could tolerate this, and now I see I was mistaken." But when she already tolerated it from her husband, and we see that her nature could tolerate it, why should the choice now be against the levir in a matter that the Torah imposed upon her? We are witnesses that her nature could tolerate it. Nevertheless, the Sages said that she can say so because she can claim, "I loved my husband and my nature could tolerate it, but I do not love the levir, and therefore my nature cannot tolerate it." (This seems correct to me).

If someone urinates in bed at night and does not feel it, and she says she cannot tolerate it, we do not compel him to divorce her, nor do we compel her to remain with him (Kenesset HaGedolah in the name of Radbaz). Similarly, in any situation where there is doubt and we do not compel him to divorce, nevertheless, we also do not compel her to remain with him, and she is not considered rebellious (Avnei Shoham, subsection 2). This also seems to me to apply to other defects or shortcomings that, according to the law, we do not compel him [to divorce], but we also do not compel her [to remain with him]. This is no less than a case where she says "he is repulsive to me" as in Siman 77, and we treat her according to all the rules explained there. This is only in a case where indeed several people cannot tolerate it, but if he has a broken hand or leg or loses one eye, she is considered rebellious as will be explained, for this is not something repulsive.

And our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: A man who developed blemishes after he married, even if his hand or foot was amputated or he became blind in one eye, and his wife does not want to stay with him — we do not force him to divorce her and give her a ketubah. Rather, if she wants, she can stay; and if she does not want, her status is like that of a rebellious wife. And it seems to me that this is specifically regarding blemishes of this sort, which the mind can tolerate. But in a matter that some people cannot tolerate because of repulsiveness, her status is not like that of a rebellious wife.

Even in the case of the amputation of a hand and a leg, the opinion of the Rosh and the Tur is that it specifically refers to the amputation of one hand, one leg, and the blinding of one eye. But if both hands or both legs were amputated, or both eyes were blinded, we compel him to divorce her, because such a person is not suitable for anything and is like one who has passed away and is nullified from the world. This also seems to be the opinion of our teacher, the Rema, in Section 4 (and see the Gra, Section 16, who disagrees with this). And this is specifically if this happened afterward, but if he was like this from the beginning, it depends on the dispute in Section 6 (Beit Shmuel, Section 8). It is possible that in this case, everyone agrees that she cannot claim, "I thought I could accept it, but now I cannot," because this is not something repulsive, and this defect would not have been hidden from her. Nevertheless, her status is not like that of a rebellious wife (ibid).

The Rosh wrote in his responsa (Klal 43, Siman 3): "Regarding her claim that her husband is insane and his foolishness increases daily, and she requests that he divorce her, etc., and her father was poor and due to his financial straits married her off to him, and she thought she could tolerate it but now realizes she cannot, etc., and Reuven responds that she recognized it beforehand and accepted it, and that he is not insane, just not knowledgeable in worldly matters, etc. I do not see grounds to compel him to divorce her, as we cannot add to what the Sages enumerated, etc. Therefore, we should not compel him to divorce her, but she should appease him to divorce or accept him and be sustained from his assets." End quote. It is clear that we do not compel her to stay with him either, and consequently, when she is not with him, she is not entitled to receive sustenance, for it is obvious that a woman only receives sustenance when she lives with her husband (and in Shulchan Aruch, this is in Siman 5).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 5: "If someone is epileptic, some say that it is not considered a defect and one cannot be forced to divorce because of it. Nevertheless, one cannot force her to stay with him since she came with a claim. Others say it is considered a defect in a man and he can be forced to divorce." And since there is a dispute among the authorities, one cannot compel. It appears that there is no difference whether the epilepsy occurs from time to time or without a set time. Although regarding a woman, everyone agrees it is considered a defect, as stated in section 115, there is a distinction since a woman is generally willing to accept any condition (Mordechai and Hagahot Ashri). However, there are matters that are the opposite, and this requires further investigation (see there and in Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 9). It is clear that if it is a type of epilepsy where marital relations are dangerous for him or her, he can be forced to divorce (see Beit Shmuel there). Understand that all these coercions are not just through words, since a servant is not corrected through words alone, but through all types of coercion that can be applied. In section 63, this will be further explained.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 8: If it is known that the man wants to go to another country, they shall make him swear that he will not go, or they shall compel him to divorce her before he goes, temporarily. This means that he should divorce her on the condition that if he does not return by a certain time, he does not wish to divorce her completely without conditions. And we do not compel him to give a get (divorce decree), for we only compel for what the Sages explicitly stated, and this is not found in the Gemara. Rather, we compel him not to go to another country, and she is not obligated to follow him, as it is written in Section 75. And if because of this coercion he is forced to give a get, it is not considered a coerced get, for we do not compel him to give a get; rather, he himself gives a get to escape the other coercion (see Gra, commentary 148). We have already explained this in Section 134, Paragraph 25.

Additionally, it is written in Section 9: If it is known that a person is not permitted to remain in a place due to danger to life, we compel him to divorce her, for she is not required to follow him. The intention is not that we force him to issue a get (bill of divorce), Heaven forbid, but rather we compel him not to abandon her. Consequently, in order to save himself, he will agree to divorce her on his own, as it is not considered coercion. All these matters are done only when it has been clarified to the court that this is indeed his situation, and we do not rely solely on her words without verification. Similarly, if he stipulated with her at the time of marriage that she would follow him to a specific country, she is obligated to go, and if not, she will leave without receiving her ketubah (marriage contract).

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in paragraph 1: "And some say that if he has turned away, we force him through secular courts to issue a divorce, provided that he annuls at the time of the get (divorce document)." This means that the secular courts would state and compel him to follow Jewish law regarding the get, as explained in section 134 there, provided that he annuls all the declarations at the time of the get, as mentioned there. And this is the main ruling in law, and so is the simple custom. And what he wrote further, that there are those who disagree and say that we do not force [a divorce], or for other violations of religious conduct, etc., the intention is not if he has completely turned away, obviously. And even here it is written that if he sins against her, such as feeding her forbidden food, or violating what he has obligated himself to her not to irritate her and not to hit her, or he vows and does not fulfill, resulting in the death of his children due to the sin of vows, as our Sages said (Shabbat 32b), and even though this is not explicitly found in the Talmud, one could say it is an a fortiori argument: if for bodily distress, like bad breath, we force [a divorce], all the more so for the danger to life when he feeds her forbidden food. Similarly, when he irritates and hits her, it is worse than bad breath. And when his children die, it is obvious that it is worse than bad breath, for the distress is immeasurable, and this affects everyone. And even though in the Talmud there are other sins for which children die according to some Tannaim, nevertheless, for all of them we do not force [a divorce] because it is a dispute, and this opinion that children die due to the sin of vows is the main one in law, as it appears there (and so it is indicated in Ketubot 73b). Moreover, there is an opinion there that she herself dies due to this sin.

Additionally, it is written: If someone is a frequenter of prostitutes and his wife complains about him, if there is testimony that he was seen with adulterers or he confessed, some say we compel him to divorce. However, the fact that children are brought to him does not raise concern that they might be lying about him. And even though for other transgressions, when it does not directly affect her, we do not compel him to divorce, nevertheless, for a frequenter of prostitutes we do compel him because it certainly affects her marital relations, as a frequenter of prostitutes despises permissible relations and finds stolen waters sweeter. It is certain that she finds him repulsive and there might even be danger involved. Not only according to the Rambam, who says that when a wife claims "he is repugnant to me" we compel him to divorce, but even according to those who disagree, they would agree in this case. As it is clear from the Talmud that in the case of one who withholds marital relations, we compel him to divorce, and certainly in the case of a frequenter of prostitutes, which is worse. All this applies when the matter has been thoroughly clarified.

It is further written in section 3 that a man who is prone to anger and habitually expels his wife from the house, we compel him to divorce her. Because through this behavior, he sometimes does not provide for her and abstains from marital relations more than her due time, and this is considered as rebelling against providing sustenance and marital relations. And so ruled the Rashba. Consequently, we do not hasten to force a divorce, for even in the case of someone who takes a vow, it is explained in sections 70 and 77 how to proceed, and all the more so in this case. Rather, the intent is that initially, we chastise him according to the discretion of the court, and if this does not help, we compel him to divorce. However, in the responsa of the Rashba (no. 493), it seems that since he is accustomed to this behavior, it is impossible to live with him in a legal manner, and we compel him immediately. Nevertheless, as I have written, until he becomes accustomed to this behavior, we generally do not remain silent about it. Consequently, when it does not help and he is habitual in this behavior, legal proceedings are no longer effective.

Additionally, it is written: A man who strikes his wife commits a transgression, just as if he struck his friend. If he is accustomed to doing so, the court has the authority to discipline and punish him with all forms of admonishment and coercion, and to make him swear that he will not do it again. If he does not heed the words of the court, some say that he can be compelled to divorce her, provided that he is warned once or twice beforehand, because it is not the way of the Jews to strike their wives, and this is an Egyptian practice. This is all when he initiates it. But if she curses him without cause or disrespects his parents, and he rebukes her with words and she does not heed him, some say that it is permissible to strike her, while others say that even a bad wife should not be struck. The first opinion is the main one. If it is not known who is at fault, the husband is not believed to say that she initiated it, because all women are presumed to be of good character. Other women are placed between them to observe whose fault it is. If she curses him without cause, she goes out without her ketubah. It seems to me that this applies specifically if she is accustomed to doing so and after she has been warned, as stated above in Siman 115. If she leaves his house and borrows and eats, if she goes out because he struck her constantly, he is obligated to pay, as stated above in Siman 70. The general rule in these matters, even in our times when we do not have the power to enforce religious judgments, is that we still try to make peace between a man and his wife. If we see that peace cannot be made between them, we try to arrange a divorce by mutual consent, and this is our practice.

A man and his wife who are quarreling, and it is understood that the cause of this is a man or woman in their household or neighborhood, such as her mother-in-law or sister-in-law or her enemy, or the like, it is incumbent upon the Beit Din (Jewish court) to expel them from their house and neighborhood. The husband cannot say, "I will not expel them because of my wife," and we do not listen to him, because there is no greater obligation than the husband's duty to honor and love his wife and not to cause her distress. And this is how the early authorities ruled (as stated in the Avodat HaGershuni, letter 10, in the name of the Mahari"v).

The Tur wrote: "One who says, 'I will not support and provide,' or who refuses to engage in marital relations, we compel him to divorce her immediately and give her the ketubah if she desires." But the Rif and Rambam in Chapter 12 of Hilchot Ishut ruled that we compel him to support her, because before compelling him to divorce, it is better to compel him to provide her with sustenance. This is also the ruling in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 3. However, the Rosh and the Tur are of the opinion that a woman is embarrassed to come to the court every time to claim her sustenance, and no person can live with a snake in one basket. This is also the ruling of the Ba'al HaGoleh, and both opinions are found in the Gemara (at the end of the chapter "HaMadir"). The Rosh brought from the Jerusalem Talmud (Gittin, Chapter 9, Halachah 9) which ruled similarly, and it says there: "If they compel him because of a bad odor, then certainly they should compel him because of 'life sustenance.'" And it seems to me that the Rif and Rambam did not consider this, because in our Talmud it is stated in a perplexing language regarding one who says they compel him to divorce, see there. Moreover, it seems that the Jerusalem Talmud also holds this way, because afterwards it is stated there in the Jerusalem Talmud: "Rabbi Yasa in the name of Rabbi Yochanan said: One who says, 'I will not support and provide,' they tell him, 'Either support and provide, or be exempt.'" Hence, they also warn him afterwards to provide support, and they do not compel him to divorce immediately. And it cannot be said that this is only after his statement without any action of not supporting, as this is obvious, for a mere statement is nothing, and a person might declare and not act. However, the truth seems to me that all opinions do not differ in principle, for it is certainly strange to say that immediately the first time he does not provide her sustenance, they would compel him to divorce immediately. It is clear that they observe and admonish him, and speak to him words of rebuke, and if he persists in his rebellion, they compel him to divorce. The Rif and Rambam intended not that they would always compel him to support her, but at the beginning of his rebellion, they would try a few times to compel him to support, and if it does not help, they compel him to divorce. And the Rosh's intention is clear that not the first time they compel him to divorce. Also, the Talmud does not differ, only it wonders about the language that says, "One who says, 'I will not support and provide,' he must divorce and give the ketubah," which implies immediately, but it is not so. Initially, they compel him to support, and if it does not help, they compel him to divorce. This is also the intention of the Jerusalem Talmud, as it seems to me.

The Rambam of blessed memory (ibid) and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that if the court cannot compel him to provide sustenance, such as if he has no means to support and does not wish to work to earn and provide sustenance, if she desires, they compel him to divorce immediately and give the ketubah. The same law applies to someone who does not wish to engage in marital relations. And if he does not have the means to give the ketubah, it remains a debt upon him until he is able to pay (Rambam). Regarding compulsion, marital relations and sustenance are equal. However, regarding the specific laws of a rebellious husband, there are differences concerning adding to her ketubah, as explained in Siman 77 (Beit Shmuel, note 7). There is a question if he provides her sustenance but less than what he himself consumes, whether they compel him to divorce for this or not. It seems that they do not compel him to divorce, but they should rebuke and reprimand him, as this is a wicked and cruel act, until he repents from his ways and understands that she ascends with him and does not descend with him.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Yevamot 64a): If a man married a woman and stayed with her for ten years and she did not bear children, he is not permitted to neglect [the mitzvah of procreation]. And it is stated there in a Baraita: If a man married a woman and stayed with her for ten years and she did not bear children, he must divorce her and give her the ketubah, for perhaps he did not merit to be built up from her. Although there is no explicit proof for this matter, there is a hint to it from the verse, "At the end of ten years of Abram's dwelling in the land of Canaan" (Genesis 16:3), to teach you that the years of dwelling outside the Land do not count towards this calculation. Therefore, if he or she became ill, or both were imprisoned, these years do not count towards the ten-year calculation.

Explanation of the matter: For the fulfillment of the mitzvah of procreation (Pru Urvu), the Sages assessed that a woman who has not given birth within ten years of being with her husband is unlikely to bear children anymore. Therefore, the obligation falls upon him either to divorce her and marry another or to marry another in addition to her (Nimukei Yosef) in places where it is permissible to take two wives. The choice is his, and she cannot say, "Why divorce me? Take another wife," because he can respond that as long as he does not divorce her, no other woman will agree to marry him (ibid.), since most women are not willing to share a husband with another woman due to the enmity it breeds between co-wives. Therefore, the Tanna stated precisely that he is not permitted to neglect the mitzvah, meaning he must do one of these two things. To avoid misunderstanding that the intention is only to take another wife and not to divorce her, the Baraita explicitly clarifies that he has the option to divorce and give her the Ketubah. This applies specifically if she has not given birth at all, but if she has given birth to even one child, even though the mitzvah of Pru Urvu is to have a male and a female, there is no concern in this matter (ibid.). There is an opinion that says that if he does not have both a male and a female, he is obligated to divorce her, but this is not the case (Rashba and Nimukei Yosef).

The Tanna brings proof from Abraham, who waited with Sarah for ten years in the land of Canaan, and afterwards married Hagar. Why did Abraham not take this into consideration while he was in the diaspora, where he stayed with her for much more than ten years and did not marry another? This is because he knew that he was infertile and would only merit children in the Land of Israel, as the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to him: "Go from your land, etc., and I will make you a great nation." Therefore, when he had stayed ten years in the Land of Israel and Sarah had not borne him children, he took this into account and married Hagar. The Tanna means that the time spent in the diaspora does not count toward the ten years. This does not apply universally, for if it did, this law would be nullified in the diaspora, and be fruitful and multiply is an obligation of the body and is obligatory everywhere (as stated there). Additionally, the majority of the world is fruitful and multiplies in the diaspora, and would we attribute this to the punishment of the diaspora due to one in a thousand (Rosh)? Furthermore, it is explicitly proven in the Talmud there that the Amoraim in Babylon observed this law (as stated there). Rather, this only applies to Abraham, who did not take this into consideration in the diaspora because he knew that he had to ascend to the Land of Israel.

Indeed, there are those who say that if a person who is accustomed to residing in the Land of Israel goes out to the Diaspora, the time spent in the Diaspora does not count towards the ten years (Rashba in the name of Raavad). This also appears to be implied in the Jerusalem Talmud. Additionally, there are those who say that if someone lived with his wife in the Diaspora and then came to the Land of Israel, the time spent in the Diaspora does not count, and he counts ten years from the day he starts residing in the Land of Israel, because perhaps the merit of the Land will stand by them (ibid.). In this regard, we do not find any explicit disagreement among the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), and in any case, it is agreed upon by all our Rabbis that this law applies in every place and at all times. In the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (Sma"g), positive commandment 49, there is something puzzling, and this is its wording: it seems that if he stayed ten years even in the Diaspora, he should divorce her, and so ruled Rabbeinu Moshe and Rabbeinu Alfasi. However, I saw in the Jerusalem Talmud, Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says: “After ten years, etc.,” exclude the years spent in the Diaspora. And it is also taught: if he was sick or she was sick, or he went to the Diaspora, they do not count. End of quote. I do not understand his intention, and this is also found in our Talmud as I have written, and it requires further study (see there in the Mahara"sh).

And the explanation of the matter that the Baraita said, "Therefore, if he was ill, etc." means that just as Abraham was not naturally fit to father children, and it was attributed to this, it is evident that we attribute this event to any illness that could have occurred. Thus, even if he or she was ill, even though they had relations during the entire time, nevertheless, we attribute the lack of conception to his or her illness. Similarly, when they were imprisoned, even though they had relations there, we attribute the lack of pregnancy to the anxiety of being imprisoned. However, this does not mean when they did not have relations at all, because if so, there is no novelty in this (Rosh). Therefore, it says that both were imprisoned, because if only one was imprisoned, it is obvious that since they were not together and did not have relations, it would not be considered at all. But from the language of the Jerusalem Talmud that we brought in the previous section, it does not seem so.

And the reason for this matter is that we consider all these concerns to nullify the mitzvah of procreation (Pru Urvu). For truly, it is a great stringency that the sages imposed on him to divorce her, for in all other commandments, a person is not obligated to do more than the commandment of the Holy One, blessed be He. And in this mitzvah, the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded us in His Torah to marry a woman in order to bear children. And since he married a woman who is not known to be barren or an aylonit (a woman who cannot have children due to underdeveloped sexual characteristics), and she is fit to bear children, what more can he do? It is in the hands of the Merciful One that he does not have children. However, because of the greatness of the mitzvah of procreation, the sages imposed on him to try himself with another woman, perhaps he will be built from her. Therefore, they limited the time for this to ten years. And also, if there is any reason we can attribute to the lack of childbirth, we attribute it even to a minor reason.

And this is what our sages said: "He should divorce her and give her the ketubah, lest he was not fortunate to build a family with her." This means that even though we could attribute the issue to him being unfit to procreate—since if he says, "I know myself that I am unfit to procreate," it is obvious that we do not compel him to marry another woman. And this is evident in the Talmud there (where it is said that the progeny were uprooted from the head of the household), for a person is believed about himself when we see that he is not acting out of rebellion (as explained by the Nimukei Yosef there). Therefore, why do we not attribute the issue to him being unfit to procreate? Because due to the greatness of the mitzvah, as long as it has not been clarified that he is incapable of procreation, we do not attribute the issue to him but to her. And if you question, "From whichever perspective, if we attribute the issue to her, why should he give her the ketubah? Even when there is doubt in the matter, how can you extract money out of doubt?" The tanna teaches that we do not attribute the issue to either him or her, but rather say that perhaps he was not fortunate to build a family with her. This means that both are fit to procreate, but together they are not fit, and this is not considered extracting money out of doubt, for most women are fit to bear children, and we do not see signs of her being barren or an aylonit (a woman who does not mature physically), and she is presumed to be entitled to her ketubah. Therefore, he gives her the ketubah. See also in section 30.

If he does not want to listen to us, we compel him to divorce her, as with all commandments for which we compel, even if she claims that the prevention is from him, such as she says he is not capable of ejaculation like an arrow or similar, we do not listen to her and compel him to marry another (Beit Shmuel, section 23). Specifically, if he himself says he is not fit to procreate, then we do not compel, as it is written, even if he says, "I do not cohabit with her, and I dwell with her in the presence of witnesses so as not to be alone with her," meaning he will necessarily have to marry another, we do not listen to him, whether she says so, he says so, or they both say so. Rather, he divorces her and marries another who is fit to bear children (Gemara, end of chapter "Hamedir"). The reason is that generally, as long as he is tied to her, they will not give him another (Rosh and Ran there). And what we wrote in section 23, that the choice is in his hands to marry another and not divorce her, is certainly so. If he marries another, why should we compel him to divorce? Even here, we say we do not rely on his words because of the explained reason, that they might not give him another. And we have already written that all this applies when he has not procreated at all. But if he has viable offspring, even if he does not have both a son and a daughter and has not yet fulfilled the commandment to be fruitful and multiply, we do not compel him to divorce. Even if he only has a daughter. And in section 1, it is explained that in our times, we do not usually compel at all.

And it has already been explained that if there is a reason to attribute the lack of childbirth to, we attribute it to that reason and count ten years from the day the reason ceased. Certainly, if he was not at home for a period of time, it is not included in the count. Similarly, if they had children and they died, we count ten years from the day they died. Likewise, if she miscarried, even within forty days, we count ten years from the day she miscarried. However, if she miscarried three consecutive times, she is presumed to be prone to miscarriages, and he is obligated to divorce her and marry another. He must give her the ketubah (marriage contract payment), and he cannot say, "Why should I give you the ketubah? You are prone to miscarriages," because she can say that it was he who did not merit to build a family with her. Therefore, she is also permitted to marry another. The reason we assume it was he who did not merit to build a family with her, and not the reverse, is because we see this as a matter of divine punishment. It makes sense to say that he was punished by not being able to fulfill the mitzvah (commandment), whereas she is not commanded in the mitzvah of procreation, so it is less likely to say that she was punished in this way (Yevamot 64b). And even though certainly it is also a punishment for her, since every woman desires children, nonetheless, his punishment is greater than hers. Therefore, we attribute the issue to him and not to her. (If she miscarries three times even before ten years, he should divorce her.)

If there is a contradiction between him and her, where according to his words he is not yet obligated to divorce her, and according to her words he is obligated to divorce her, such as if he says she had a miscarriage within ten years and therefore the count is from the time of the miscarriage, and she says she did not have a miscarriage, she is believed. This is what our Sages said: If she had miscarried, she would not maintain herself as barren, and thus it is evident she speaks the truth. Similarly, if he says she only had two miscarriages and she says she had three, she is believed, for if it were not as she said, she would not maintain herself as one who miscarries. And since according to her words he must divorce her and give her the ketubah, and he contradicts her with certainty, this is like any monetary claim, and she needs to take an oath (hesset) that she did not miscarry or that she miscarried three times, for with this claim he would be obligated to give her the ketubah. And even though she is not specifically claiming the ketubah, nonetheless, this is similar to a debtor who says the time for payment has not yet arrived, where the lender must swear regarding the loan with a document, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 73. And even though wherever the lender swears and collects, a stringent oath is required, nonetheless, in the case of contradicting the time alone, a hesset oath suffices (Sema there, section 12). And even though the Sages believed her on the essence of the matter for the reason explained, nonetheless, regarding the ketubah she needs to take an oath because he contradicts her. And although she has a presumption (chazaka) as we wrote, we do not follow the majority (rov) or the presumption (chazaka) in monetary matters.

And this is what we said regarding the reason that she is believed because she did not establish herself as barren, it is not specifically when she explicitly says "I am barren," but rather because she says, "I did not miscarry within ten years," and the world considers the absence of birth within ten years as being barren. Even though we permit her to marry another and attribute the absence of birth to him, saying that he was not fortunate to have children from her, nevertheless, in the eyes of the world, she is considered barren, and who knows if someone will be found to marry her? Therefore, she is believed even when she does not explicitly say "I am barren" (Yam Shel Shlomo, Yevamot, Chapter 6, Section 43). However, from Rashi’s explanation there, it seems that it is specifically when she says "I am barren," as he explains regarding what is said in the Gemara there: she says "I did not miscarry, but I am barren." And this is what was clarified, that specifically after three instances she is considered one who frequently miscarries, even though regarding marrying a third husband after ten years she is considered barren even with two instances, as will be explained. Nevertheless, regarding miscarriage, it is not so, because many women miscarry at the beginning of their pregnancy (Nimukei Yosef). And some say that even regarding miscarriage, she is considered established with two instances, but we do not rule this way, as most of the early authorities concluded, and so it appears from the Talmud there (Avnei Shoham, Section 27).

And this, that we do not worry that she may have set her eyes on another man and thus should not be believed, as in the case when she says, "I am impure to you," or "There are heavens between you and me," where we do worry that she may have set her eyes on another man, as taught at the end of Nedarim, is because here it has been ten years without her having children. And in the case of a woman who miscarries three times, we also do not worry about this, since according to his words, she is also miscarrying. And some say that specifically when the court forces him to divorce her, and he excuses himself by saying she miscarried within ten years, then when she says, "I did not miscarry, I am barren," she is believed (Nimukei Yosef and Yam Shel Shlomo). And similarly, in the case of miscarriages, it is also when the court forces him to divorce, and he excuses himself by saying she miscarried only twice, then when she says, "I miscarried three times," she is believed. But otherwise, she is not believed because we worry that she may have set her eyes on another man. And it appears from their words that even after ten years, we worry she may have set her eyes on another man, and similarly when we know that she is indeed miscarrying. This requires further investigation because it would seem that since there is evidence for this matter, we should not worry about it (as also appears in Tosafot, Nedarim 65b, s.v. "between him and her," and see Beit Shmuel, section 29). This will be further clarified with God's help.

And there is a question regarding this: Why should he not be believed with a miggo (a legal presumption) that if he wanted, he could say, "I know myself that I am not fit to father children," in which case we would not force him to divorce her, as stated in section 29? Some answer that since, according to his own words, she miscarried twice, and we see that he is capable of fathering children, we no longer believe him when he says he subsequently became impaired (Nemukei Yosef). And although if he says so, he is believed, nevertheless, this is not a miggo. However, this is in the case of a woman who miscarried. But if ten years have passed and she has not given birth, if he says she did not miscarry at all, why should he not be believed with this miggo (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 30)? And there are those who say that this also applies when he fathered a child once (ibid), but this is a strained interpretation. If so, the Talmud and the codifiers should have stated explicitly that she is only believed in this context. Therefore, it seems that this is not a miggo at all, for just as she is believed because it is not in her interest to consider herself barren, similarly, he does not have a miggo for the same reason, as it is not in his interest to consider himself sterile. And although if he says so, he is believed, nevertheless, he does not have a miggo (ibid). Furthermore, it seems evident to the Talmud that her presumption is a strong presumption, and a miggo does not apply in the presence of a strong presumption, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 82, in the principles of miggo, letter 2. See there.

If a man is with his wife for ten years and divorces her because she did not bear children, she is permitted to marry a second husband. This is because, as we have written, we attribute the reason to the husband not being blessed to have children with her, and not because she is barren. If she remains with the second husband also for ten years and does not bear children, her status with him is the same as with the first husband. If the second husband divorces her, she should not marry a third husband, because after two instances, it is established that she is not fit to bear children. Although in monetary matters a presumption is not established with less than three instances, in this matter, two instances are sufficient to establish a presumption. However, regarding miscarriage, the law is like monetary matters, as we have explained in section 32. This is also stated by the sages in Yevamot (64b) - see there. The reason, in my opinion, is that for something that deviates from the norm of other people, two instances are enough to establish a presumption. In monetary matters, a presumption cannot be established with less than three instances in any matter (see there and examine it well). There are also other reasons for this (see Rif and Yam Shel Shlomo, and it requires further examination).

And if she married a third (husband), we compel him to divorce her immediately, and she does not have a ketubah unless he was aware of her condition and married her with that understanding, in which case he is obligated to give her the ketubah, and he has brought the loss upon himself. Regarding compelling him to divorce: if he has another wife or has already fulfilled the commandment of procreation, we do not compel him to divorce, for all these laws apply when he has not yet fulfilled the commandment of procreation. Therefore, this third husband, if he has fulfilled the commandment of procreation and married her even without being aware of her condition, she has a ketubah if he wishes to divorce her (Beit Shmuel). And do not ask why she does not have a ketubah from the third (husband) when he divorces her before living with her for ten years, since it is established that regarding monetary matters, a presumption is not formed in less than three times as it is written. Although there is a distinction between extracting money and retaining what is in his possession, it does not appear so, as is evident from the Talmud, which states generally that regarding monetary matters, a presumption is not formed in less than three times. Here, it can be said that the reasoning is different: since we compel him to divorce when he has not fulfilled the commandment of procreation and does not have another wife, and he was not aware of her condition, his purchase is considered a mistaken purchase, and therefore she does not have a ketubah (Tosafot there, s.v. Tetse).

And since it has been clarified that regarding the prohibition, a presumption is established with two times, and for this reason, she does not have a ketubah from the third [husband] as it is written, there is a question about this: why does she have a ketubah from the second [husband] when she lived with him for ten years and did not give birth? After all, now she is presumed to be barren, and the second [husband] could also say, “My marriage was a mistaken transaction, and I will not give you a ketubah.” It can be said that since she married him permissibly and for the first ten years she was his complete wife, it follows that afterward, when we force him to divorce her, he is obligated to give her her ketubah, for she was his complete wife for ten years. This is not the case with the third [husband], where his transaction is completely mistaken since we force him to divorce her immediately (I learned this from the words of the Nimukei Yosef). This also appears from the Jerusalem Talmud and it will be further explained shortly (Tosafot, s.v. "Niset").

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 18: If she stayed with the third husband for ten years and did not give birth, if she has not collected her ketubah (marriage contract payment) from the previous husbands, she does not collect it. If she did collect it, she does not have to return it. The reason is that they can say to her, "It has become clear that you are barren." If she collected it, she does not have to return it because she can say, "Now I have become impaired, and with you, I was correct, and you did not merit having children from me."

However, to extract payment from them with this claim is impossible, because they are in possession of the money, and she cannot prove her claim. And even though, as we said in the previous section, she married them with permission, and why should they not pay her the ketubah? It can be said that the reason we mentioned only applies where the presumption is not yet entirely established, meaning she was not presumed barren three times, but only twice. Although for prohibition we are stringent, nonetheless regarding her ketubah, she extracts payment from them since she married with permission and she can still say, "You did not merit having children from me, and it is not that I am barren." And since she was with them for ten years, she is entitled to the ketubah.

However, if her barrenness is fully established in three instances over ten years each time, it is obvious that they can say to her that it has now been revealed that our purchase was a mistaken purchase, because everyone knows that a person marries a woman only to have children. Therefore, she is not entitled to a ketubah. But if she collected it, she does not have to return it because she can say, "Now I have become impaired," since she collected it lawfully at the time of the act.

And there is no question that if so, the first two husbands will always say, "We will not give you a ketubah until you marry a third husband and stay with him for ten years and it becomes clear whether you are entitled to the ketubah or not." We never find that when the obligation is clear now, the debtor would say, "I will wait many years, and perhaps it will become clear that I am not liable." Moreover, she can say, "I do not wish to marry at all," and it will never become clear.

When she married the third husband and he divorced her without a ketubah, as mentioned, and then she married the fourth husband and bore a child, she cannot claim a ketubah from the third husband by arguing that it has now become apparent that she is not barren and that it was only with him that she did not conceive, because he can claim that she has now been cured and not earlier. The general principle is that if at the time of the event, according to the depth of the law, he is exempt from the ketubah for any reason, even if it later appears that the reason was not as initially thought, we employ all available means to assert that at the time of the ruling, the reason was valid. Conversely, if not so, no ruling would ever stand. Likewise, the third husband cannot claim that had he known she was capable of bearing children, he would not have divorced her, claiming that his divorce was a mistake, because she can also say that she has now been cured (Gemara there). There is no question of how we can rely on this in matters of prohibition, because it is merely a rebuttal to his claim. The main reason is that we are witnesses that the third husband, when he divorced her, did so in any case (Rashi), even if she would later bear children, as he divorced her due to a presumption that she was barren, which is not a definite sign. When he divorced her, even with the possibility that she might bear children, he divorced her, and he cannot contest this. Therefore, the sages did not require to inform them at the time of the get (divorce) that if the divorce is due to this reason, he cannot remarry her ever, as they required in cases of vows, an ailonit (a woman who does not develop signs of puberty), and one who brings a bad name upon her, as mentioned above in Siman 10, because there is a clear presumption regarding the reason for the divorce, and they were concerned about potential complications and required notification. But here, it is a minor presumption and merely a sign, and everyone knows that he divorced her in any case and he cannot contest it (Nimukei Yosef).

It has already been explained in Siman 1 that a woman is not commanded to be fruitful and multiply (procreation), nor is she commanded regarding "settling the world" (having children), but she is included in the general commandment of "settling" and not that the mitzvah is upon her, as mentioned there in paragraph 4. Therefore, if a woman comes to the Beit Din (Jewish court) and says, "My husband is not able to have children because he is sterile," and this is verified by him or by doctors, and she is not lying, nevertheless, we tell her, "Go your way," and she does not have the ability to compel him to give her a get (divorce) and ketubah (marriage contract payment), because she is not commanded on procreation (Yevamot end of chapter 6).

It seems somewhat from Rashi's interpretation there that if she requests a get without the ketubah, we can compel him to give it. Similarly, if she says, "Even though I am not commanded on procreation, I still desire to have children so that I have someone to rely on in my old age," and she does not yet have any son or daughter, neither from him nor from another man, her claim is valid, and we compel him to divorce her and give her the ketubah. Also, even if she does not claim this, but says that he cannot live with her in the normal way because he is impotent and she requests her marital rights and he does not deny it, or she verifies this through doctors, we also compel him to divorce her and give her the ketubah (see Beit Shmuel, paragraph 18). This is no less than a man with boils, whom we compel to divorce her because he is not permitted to engage with a woman. It seems to me that in this claim, even if she already has sons and daughters, she can compel him to divorce her and give her the ketubah because it is difficult for her to be without marital relations, and more than a man desires to marry, a woman desires to be married (and in Ketubot 64b, it is regarding distress as Rashi explains there and not regarding desire, investigate thoroughly). Even within ten years, her claim is valid if he does not deny it.

And if in this matter there is a contradiction between him and her, where he says that the prevention of childbirth is from her and she says that it is from him, and it is impossible to clarify, our Sages said in this language (Yevamot 65b): "He says it is from her, and she says it is from him. Rabbi Ami said: She is believed, for matters that are between him and her, she is believed. What is the reason? She is certain that her womb is open like an arrow and she is not conceiving, but he is not certain." Consequently, her claim is considered definite and his claim is considered doubtful. And thus, it is established by our Sages that a woman senses this more than a man. And one should not say, "Why are we not concerned that she has set her eyes on another?" Some of our Rabbis wrote that this applies after he has been with her for ten years and she has not given birth (Tosafot there). And so wrote the Tur, that in such a case, this concern does not apply because there is evidence for the matter, unlike the opinion mentioned in Section 33 there. And if you ask, "If so, why do we not compel him in any case?" It could be said that it refers to a case where he has children from another woman, for in such a case, we do not compel him as explained. Only when she comes with a claim for support in her old age, then we compel him if he agrees, as mentioned. And even if he does not agree, she is believed for the reason that she is certain.

Some of our rabbis have written that the dispute is only regarding the ketubah (marriage contract), but regarding the divorce itself, the court compels him, for example, if he has delayed for ten years and has no children. He wants to avoid paying her ketubah by claiming that she is not fit to bear children and that the marriage is a mistake, while she denies this and claims that the issue is with him. She is believed, and he is obligated to give her the ketubah. This is the opinion of the Rif (Rabbi Isaac Alfasi) of blessed memory, and the reason she is believed is that since she claims with certainty and by law is entitled to the ketubah, he cannot make her lose it with his uncertain claim (Nimukei Yosef). It seems somewhat that if she married a third husband and by law is not entitled to the ketubah, as stated, she cannot extract the ketubah from him with her certain claim. Some say that even in such a case, she is believed (Ribam in Tosafot there). And although we hold in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 75 that in a case of certainty versus uncertainty, we maintain the money in the possession of the defendant, nevertheless, in the case of a ketubah where she has married, her certain claim is effective. This requires further study, and according to many authorities, this is not the case.

According to what has been explained, the reason she is believed is because she knows (the matter) as if it were shot like an arrow, and he does not know; thus, it is a case of certainty versus uncertainty. Consequently, when the claim is one of certainty versus certainty, such as when she claims that he lacks the strength of men or does not engage with her in the usual manner, and he denies it, she is not believed. Even though at the end of Nedarim it is stated the opposite, that what he knows is like her knowledge, and she is believed because she would not brazenly lie in front of her husband, and in matters that he does not know, like "shot like an arrow," she is not believed. The reason is simple: there, she seeks to separate herself from her husband, and he does not want to divorce her, and the court does not force him since it is within ten years. In such a case, where he cannot refute her claim, she is not believed to release herself against his will, for in such a case she might brazenly lie.
