However, in matters he knows as well as she does, if he denies it, we assume she is telling the truth, as there is a presumption she would not lie about something he knows to be a lie. But here, he seeks to divorce her, or the court forces him since it is after ten years, and she does not want to leave. The dispute is only regarding the Ketubah. Certainly, in matters of monetary claims, certainty versus uncertainty is preferable to certainty versus certainty (Ramban and Ran at the end of Nedarim). However, this applies only to the explanation in the previous section and not according to the explanation in section 41, where it was also stated that she seeks to release herself from him, as mentioned there. But this also makes sense, as just as we are uncertain if she can release herself from him within ten years and suspect she is lying because she has set her eyes on another, the reasoning is that in matters he does not know as well as she does, it is easier for her to brazenly lie than in matters he knows as well as she does. But here, since the release from him is clear to us because it is after ten years, as mentioned there, and the dispute remains only regarding the Ketubah, it is like any monetary claim where certainty versus uncertainty is preferable to certainty versus certainty (and see the responsa of the Rambam on the laws of marriage, section 6, and consider this well).

And know that in all these matters, there are perplexing statements in the words of the Rambam, of blessed memory, in Chapter 15 of "Ishut" (Laws of Marriage), where he writes the following: If a man marries a woman and she remains with him for ten years and does not give birth, he must divorce her and give her the marriage contract (ketubah), or marry another woman who is capable of bearing children, etc. If she remains with him for ten years and does not give birth, and he ejaculates forcefully, it is presumed that the illness is from her, and she leaves without the marriage contract, etc. But if he does not ejaculate forcefully, it is presumed that the illness is from him alone, and he must divorce her and give her the marriage contract, etc. If he claims that the impediment to childbirth is from her, and she claims that it is from him because he does not ejaculate forcefully, she is believed, etc. If she says she does not know whether the impediment is from him or from her, she does not have a principal marriage contract; the money remains in the possession of its owner until she claims with certainty that he does not ejaculate forcefully. And why is she believed? Because she can sense whether he ejaculates forcefully or not, whereas he cannot sense this. End of quote.

Additionally, it is written: A woman who comes to demand from her husband to divorce her after ten years because she has not given birth, and she says that he does not "shoot like an arrow" (i.e., he is impotent), we listen to her. Even though she is not commanded to be fruitful and multiply, she needs children for her old age. We compel him to divorce her, and he gives her the principal amount of the ketubah only, etc. And later in the laws of chapter fifteen, it is written: A woman who comes to the court and says, "My husband cannot perform marital relations in the normal manner that leads to childbirth, or he does not 'shoot like an arrow,'" the judges make a compromise and tell her, "It is proper that you live with your husband until you have waited ten years and have not given birth, and then you may demand [a divorce]." They negotiate with her about this matter and do not compel her to stay, nor do they judge her as a rebellious wife. Instead, they prolong the matter until they make a compromise. This is from the Mishnah at the end of Nedarim.

According to his words, even in the case of the first husband who waited ten years, where we compel him to divorce her and give her the ketubah (marriage contract), this is specifically when the impediment is from him or when she says that the impediment is from him. But if there is merely doubt about the matter, she does not receive the ketubah. According to this, one might ask: how can we find a case where we compel him to divorce and give the ketubah? If it has been clarified or if she says that the impediment is from him, why should we compel him to divorce her? After all, he is not fit to procreate. And if it has not been clarified, she does not have a ketubah (as noted by the Beit HaLevi in the name of Rabbi Yosef Ibn Lev). 

Indeed, the Ra'avad, of blessed memory, objected, stating that in the case of the first and second husbands, she is entitled to the ketubah in any situation. And it must be said that the Rambam holds that although she is believed to say that he does not shoot like an arrow (i.e., he is impotent) regarding the collection of her ketubah, nevertheless, regarding his prohibition, they should not compel him to divorce to fulfill the mitzvah of procreation, she is not believed (as noted there). And it is far-fetched to say this because if so, his ruling applies only when she says so. And from the structure of his words, it seems that even if it is known that he does not shoot like an arrow, he should divorce and give the ketubah, as he explicitly wrote before the ruling where she says so, as mentioned.

And therefore it appears to me that the Rambam holds that even when it is clarified that he does not shoot like an arrow (i.e., he is infertile) and he is obligated to give her a ketubah, we still say that he has not merited to build from her (i.e., have children). And when he marries another woman, the matter will be rectified. Therefore, we compel him to divorce her. And if she marries a third man, even though he also does not shoot like an arrow, she still must leave him without a ketubah, as it is written there later, because her fortune caused it, and she has established through three men that anyone who is with her does not shoot like an arrow (i.e., she is infertile). (And with this, the question of Tosafot at the end of Perek Hamadir and in Yevamot 64 can be resolved. Tosafot asks whether we compel him to divorce her when it is clarified that he does not shoot like an arrow. And those who hold that we do not compel him can establish the Mishnah as referring to a case where it was not clarified. Nevertheless, he is obligated to give her a ketubah according to all the poskim. Note well.)

And this which was written: When she demands a divorce after ten years and says he does not shoot like an arrow, we listen to her and compel him to divorce and give the ketubah. One should not ask why we need to wait for her demand; should we not compel him to divorce on his own account? The answer is simple: for example, if he has another wife or has already fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation. However, in the Gemara it is explained that this is specifically when she says "I need a staff for my hand and a hoe for my burial," but otherwise, we tell her "Go, you are not commanded [to procreate]." From his words, it is clear that in a general case, we compel him, and the court does not tell her "Go, you are not commanded [to procreate]." It seems to me that he holds that certainly, in a general case, her intention is that she wants children to support her in her old age, and we do not assume that she is mistaken and thinks she is commanded to procreate. This is also clearly implied in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of the sixth chapter of Yevamot, where it states that if she comes to marry, we listen to her words. Although it can be said that the Jerusalem Talmud is speaking when she has no husband at all, it does not seem so, and so writes the Ketzot HaChoshen and the Pe'at HaShulchan there. In the Gemara, they asked her to investigate the matter if she knows she is not commanded to procreate because they understood from her words that she did not know, as it implies there from the wife of Rabbi Chiya, who asked him if a woman is commanded to procreate. And certainly, Rambam agrees that if we understand that she is demanding a divorce because of the mitzvah, we inform her that she is not commanded to procreate. But in a general case, why should we assume she does not know? It is well known to everyone that a woman is not commanded to procreate, and presumably, she comes because of her claim for support in her old age. (And this is what is said in the Gemara: perhaps she comes because of a claim. This means, as stated earlier, not because the law follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, but meaning she knows the law and presumably comes because of a claim. And pay close attention to this).

And when do we listen to her words? After ten years. But within ten years, we endure with her and ask her to bear it. Nevertheless, if she is not willing, we do not judge her as a rebellious wife. This is the latter ruling of the Nedarim. It seems to me that this applies only when she says he does not emit like an arrow and the matter is not clarified. But if he admits or it is clarified that he does not emit like an arrow, even within ten years, we compel him when she demands a divorce. It is possible that even if she does not demand it from her side, we compel him to fulfill the mitzvah of procreation, as it is said that perhaps it will be fixed with another woman. And it has been clarified that only after ten years do we compel. Certainly, this is true, for within ten years we do not attend to the matter. But when we know of this, perhaps we also compel within ten years by law. Nevertheless, it is possible to say that in any case we wait until ten years, for perhaps the matter will be resolved. This also seems to be implied from the general language of the poskim. (And in paragraph 59, the opinion of the Rema will be clarified, that we compel, as mentioned there).

This is according to the opinion of the Rif, the Rambam, and the Tosafot. However, in truth, there are some of our Rabbis who hold that even within ten years, when she says "The heavens are between me and you," meaning that he does not shoot like an arrow or that he is unable to come upon her in the natural manner, we compel him to divorce and give her the ketubah. They only differentiate between whether she mentioned the ketubah or not. If she demanded her ketubah, she is not believed, and we do not listen to her words. But if she did not mention the ketubah, we compel him, because when she mentions the ketubah, we suspect her of lying and only wanting to collect the ketubah. They compared this matter to what is stated in Siman 17 regarding a woman who says, "My husband has died," that she is believed, but when she demands the ketubah, she is not believed. (And in this, they differentiate between the case in Yevamot and the end of Nedarim. This is the opinion of the Tosafot at the end of Nedarim and Tosafot in Yevamot 26b, s.v. "ki," and the responsa of the Rosh, Siman 43, and the responsa of Maimonides, Siman 6. There, it is explicitly proven that it refers to immediately after the marriage. See there.)

But after ten years, I have not found any opinion among the early authorities that would hold that she is not believed even when she demands her ketubah. Therefore, I am perplexed by the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 6, which state that if she demands her ketubah, she is not believed even after ten years. See there. I am further perplexed because in the Gemara at the end of chapter 6 of Yevamot, it is explicitly stated otherwise. There, it says: A woman came before Rabbi Ami and said to him, "Give me my ketubah." He said to her, "Go, you are not commanded to do so." She said to him, "Provide for me from my support." What will be with this woman? He said: In such a case, we certainly compel him, etc. See there. And it is explicitly stated that she demanded her ketubah, and nevertheless, when she came with a claim for support in her old age, we compel him. And this was after ten years, as is proven from the Rif and the Rambam, of blessed memory. And it is clear to me from their words that they have a different approach to this, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

The opinion of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch is to distinguish between different claims. Regarding the claim of "射 as an arrow" within ten years, we do not listen to her at all. Even after ten years, when she demands her ketubah, she is not believed. This is their ruling in paragraph 6. However, regarding the claim of "he does not have the strength of men" and he denies it, we do listen to her even within ten years, but if she demands her ketubah, she is not believed. This is their ruling in paragraph 7, as explained there. One can explain that after ten years, even when she demands her ketubah, she is believed. The reason is simple: regarding "射 as an arrow," since he does not know, we say that she has the audacity, which is not the case with the claim of "the strength of men." According to their opinion, one must say that the incident of Rabbi Ami that we mentioned was regarding the claim of "the strength of men" and it was after ten years.

Here is the translation of the passage:

And these are the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in Section 6: A woman who demands a divorce on the grounds that she is not suitable to build a family with him is not listened to. However, if she claims that she desires to have a child so that she will have a son to rely on, and she currently has no son (and the same applies to a daughter), and she says that he is the cause, as he does not emit semen like an arrow, if she has lived with him for ten years and did not conceive, and she is not demanding her ketubah in order to suspect that she is demanding a divorce to collect her ketubah, and she is not tying the demand for divorce to any other matter, then she is listened to, even if he has children from another woman. For perhaps he became defective afterward, and he is compelled to divorce her and give her the basic ketubah amount of one hundred or two hundred zuz, but not the additional amount, and he should return to her the dowry that she brought to him. And he has the right to impose a cherem (ban) on her claim if it is something she is not certainly aware of, and afterward, he should give the ketubah, end of quote. And indeed, the beginning of his words follows the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, that it is specifically when she says he is the cause. But this statement that she is not demanding the ketubah is not according to his opinion, as I have written. And that which he wrote that she does not get the additional amount, the Rambam also wrote and explained the reason that he did not write the additional amount with the intention that she should leave at her will and take it, end of quote. Therefore, the dowry that she brought needs to be given to her, and some say that he should also give her an additional third of the dowry. But gifts and presents that the husband gave her at the time of the engagement, he does not give her. And gifts that others gave her, whether from the husband's side or her side, there is a dispute whether he should give them to her or not (Kenesset HaGedolah and Avodat HaBayit Section 16). And it seems to me that what was given from his side, he does not give to her, and what was given from her side, he gives to her.

And our master, the Beit Yosef, completely omitted what the Rambam wrote there, that when it becomes clear that he ejaculates like an arrow and we force him to divorce her, he does not give her the ketubah but she does receive the additional amount. He explained the reasoning so that she should not be less than an ailonit (a woman who does not develop sexual characteristics) whom he did not recognize as such, who receives the additional amount. And indeed, there are those who disagree with him regarding an ailonit. Nevertheless, he himself ruled in Siman 116 regarding an ailonit like the Rambam. He also omitted what the Rambam wrote that if it becomes clear that he does not ejaculate like an arrow, he gives her the ketubah and the additional amount. It is possible that because it is obvious, he did not need to explain it. Moreover, it seems more likely that he holds that in such a case, we do not force him to divorce her at all. This also seems to be the primary ruling in practice. The previous ruling relied on what was written in Siman 116 regarding an ailonit, and it is a fortiori from there, as is clear.

It is also written: If he says, "I will marry another woman in addition to her and test myself," we listen to him. If the second woman gives birth, the first one goes out without a ketubah. If not, he must divorce both and give a ketubah, or marry a third if he can support them. There is an opinion that if the second woman also says he does not shoot like an arrow, he must divorce both and give a ketubah. In any case, if it is known that he is sterile and she comes with a claim, he must divorce immediately. And behold, the Tur and the Nimukei Yosef wrote according to the first opinion. Although it is not explicitly stated in the Gemara that the first one loses her ketubah in this case, and the Gemara only states that she cannot prevent him from marrying another woman, nevertheless, logic supports this, and it is also proven from the Rambam, since he ruled that if it is clarified that he "shoots like an arrow," she loses her ketubah, all the more so if he had a child with another woman. And one should not ask, as the Gemara explains the reason is perhaps he was not destined to build with her, and if so, what difference does it make whether he "shoots like an arrow" or if the second one gave birth to him? It can be said that this reason only applies when she says so, not when the matter is clarified, for how can she extract money from him with such a flimsy claim when it is clarified that the impediment is from her?

And that which is written, "or he should marry a third [wife] if he can support her" – it is clear that also in the case of the second wife, he must be able to support her as is evident in the Gemara. However, it teaches us that he has the ability to withhold the ketubah from both and test himself with a third wife. The reason for this is that we have already explained that in monetary matters, a presumption is not established with less than three times. In this, the "yesh mi she'omer" (there is one who says) disagrees and holds that when even the second wife says that he does not shoot like an arrow, he cannot withhold until the third because regarding prohibition, a presumption is established with two times, and he is obligated to divorce them and is therefore obligated in their ketubah. And if the second wife also needs to wait ten years, there are two opinions in the Tur, see there. (And see Beit Shmuel, section 15, and the Gra, section 32, and what appears correct to me, I have written in the explanation of the Shulchan Aruch, and examine it well).

And this is what it says: If it is known that he is sterile, he must divorce her immediately when she comes because of a claim, even though from the words of the Rif and the Rambam it seems that before ten years we do not attend to her. This is all when his sterility has not been confirmed. And although it has been clarified that he does not shoot like an arrow, this is not considered sterility. The proof is that the Rambam calls this a sickness, and the way of a sickness is to be healed. Sterility is another matter, where he is entirely unfit to procreate. And even though the Rosh wrote in the sixth chapter of Yevamot, "And we do not worry that maybe she has set her eyes on another man, it speaks when we know that he is sterile and he has stayed with her for ten years." This implies that without ten years, even though he is sterile, we do not attend to her claim. It must be said that his intention is that he does not shoot like an arrow and similar cases, not actual sterility. The proof to this is that the Tur also rules this way, and how could he not mention his father's opinion, the Rosh? Moreover, this goes against straightforward reasoning; how can we rely on a miracle that a sterile man will procreate? Therefore, it is certain that the Rosh was not precise in his language since he was dealing with the matter of not shooting like an arrow. This is also clearly implied in the responsa of the Rosh, general section 43, siman 6, where he did not mention ten years and ruled that we compel him. Look there (and see Beit Shmuel, siman 16, and the Gra, siman 33. It seems to me as I have written, and the Gra also wrote that this is the main ruling as the Shulchan Aruch ruled. Look there and examine well).

And know that after this section, our teacher the Rema wrote as follows: "The same applies if he waited ten years and she did not bear children, and she comes with a claim that we compel him to divorce her and give her the ketubah. In such a case, it does not help for him to say, 'I will check myself with another woman,' because nevertheless, the first woman does not lose her ketubah since she was not established with three men. And the reason she needs to claim that he does not ejaculate like an arrow is when it is known that he already had children, then we attribute the issue to her, unless she claims that he does not ejaculate like an arrow or with the third husband she has already been established. This appears to be the opinion of the Tur and the conclusion of Tosafot and the Rosh." And the commentators have already wondered about him, as this is exactly the opposite of the words of the Mechaber (see Ba'er Heitev section 17 and the Gra section 35).

In my humble opinion, it seems that his words are clear, and he is referring to what the author wrote: "And there are those who say that if the second wife also claims that he does not shoot like an arrow, he should divorce both and give a ketubah." In any case, if it is known that he is sterile and she comes with a claim, he should divorce her immediately. About this, it is said: "And the same applies, etc." This means that the one who says this really disputes the first opinion, which is the opinion of the Rambam. From his words, it seems that before ten years, we do not listen to her in any matter and the Rema does not differentiate between not shooting like an arrow and being completely sterile, contrary to the opinion we wrote in section 57. Even after ten years, she needs to claim that he does not shoot like an arrow. The one who says this holds that if it is known that he is sterile and she comes with a claim, he should divorce her immediately. Therefore, if it is known that he does not shoot like an arrow even within ten years, we compel him to divorce and give a ketubah. The same applies after ten years, when she comes with a claim, even if she does not claim that he does not shoot like an arrow, we compel him to divorce and give a ketubah. It does not help if he says he will test himself with another woman. In the Gemara, this was only said regarding the permission to marry another woman, or the Gemara deals with within ten years. This implies from the Gemara that she claims that the delay is from him, and he claims it is from her. This implies that it refers to the previous discussion of having waited ten years. Thus, even after ten years, she needs to claim that the delay is from him. This is when he already has children, and it is evident that the delay is from her, then she needs to claim that the delay is from him and that he became impaired after having children. As Tosafot and the Rosh wrote there, and this is learned from the words of the Tur, who wrote: "If he comes to divorce within ten years without a ketubah, and he says she is causing it, and she says he is causing it because he does not shoot like an arrow, she is believed, etc." Thus, according to the Tur, the Gemara deals with within ten years, and although the Tur only says this when he comes to divorce her without a ketubah and not when she releases herself from him, as written there, nevertheless, the Tur holds that the Gemara deals with within ten years. Our master, the Rema, holds the law as Tosafot wrote plainly that after ten years, she does not need to claim that he does not shoot like an arrow unless he already has children. Similarly, Tosafot wrote in their third answer that in the case of the first two wives, they have a ketubah in any case, and only the third needs to claim this. The Rosh also brings all the words of Tosafot there, and this is what he wrote, that this is the conclusion of Tosafot and the Rosh, not like the Rambam of blessed memory. This also seems to be the opinion of the Tur at the beginning of this section, although his conclusion is not so. Therefore, he precisely wrote that the Tur's opinion is so, and the conclusion of Tosafot and the Rosh, but the conclusion of the Tur is not so, and the Tur writes at the end only the words of the Ramah. Although he disagrees with him somewhat, mainly he is not as written earlier at the beginning of the section. See there carefully, and with this, all his words are explained.

They further wrote in Section 7 as follows: If she claims that he does not have the strength of men to come upon her and requests a divorce, and he denies it, some say that she is believed, and even if she has not waited ten years, he is compelled to divorce her immediately, but he does not have to give her the ketubah. If he divorces her of his own accord without coercion, he must give her the ketubah. Some say that even if he can have relations with another woman, he must give this one the ketubah because since he cannot come upon her, she can say, "I gave myself to you; what more can I do?" This applies when she is not claiming her ketubah, but if she claims her ketubah, she is not believed, and they do not compel him to divorce her. And we have already written in Section 52 that their opinion is to distinguish between the claim of "shooting like an arrow," since he does not know, she is believed, specifically after ten years. According to the opinion of our teacher, the Rema, after ten years, there is no need for the claim of "not shooting like an arrow," as it is written, and he must give her the ketubah as per the law of certainty and doubt. But in the claim of the strength of men, it is the exact opposite, for regarding the ketubah, she is never believed since he denies it with certainty, and it is certainty against certainty. But regarding compelling him to divorce her without the ketubah, he is compelled immediately after the marriage and does not need to wait ten years, since she denies him to his face in a matter he knows, and there is a presumption that she would not be so bold before her husband (and this is the difference between the discussion in Yevamot and the end of Nedarim, and pay close attention). But to extract money based on a presumption is impossible since the presumption of money is stronger even than a majority, and certainly stronger than a presumption. Therefore, when she claims the ketubah, we suspect that she is lying entirely, only seeking to extract money. The view of the "some say" is not explicitly stated in the early authorities, only our teacher the Beit Yosef brought it in his great book in the name of Orchot Chaim, and his reasoning seems to me to be that since the Gemara says "perhaps he was not worthy to be built from her," its meaning is that even if it is clarified that he can be built from another, he still must give her the ketubah. And know that this opinion to distinguish between the claim of "shooting like an arrow" and the claim of the strength of men is against the words of the Rambam in Chapter 15 of Ishut, Halacha 15, who equates the two claims together (and this depends on the interpretation of "the heavens between me and you" at the end of Nedarim, see there in the Gemara and in the Jerusalem Talmud, and pay close attention).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 7 that some say that in our times, when there are brazen women, she is not believed. Nevertheless, in a place where there are reasons and presumptions that she is telling the truth, she is believed. And if there is reason to believe that he cannot have relations with her because her womb is narrow and she is a virgin, or because of the softness and weakness of his teeth, this is considered, and we do not compel him to divorce her. And some say that even in a place where he is not compelled, nevertheless, we do not compel her to reconcile with him, and we do not judge her as a rebellious wife, but rather, we prolong the matter until they come to an agreement or until ten years pass and she does not bear children. And it is clear that after ten years, even now, he is compelled, both for the nullification of the mitzvah of procreation and when she claims for the support of her old age. This is also the ruling. And it is true that nowadays compulsion is not applicable since we do not have permission, as is known. Nevertheless, it is a great mitzvah to strive that he should divorce her. And indeed, many of the early authorities held that there is no decree of Rabbeinu Gershom in this matter, even if the custom is otherwise, as stated by the Nimukei Yosef and the Ritva in the end of Chapter Six of Yevamot, and as I have written in Section 1.

Furthermore, it is written: the same law applies if a man betroths a woman who is forbidden to marry him or another, we compel him to divorce her. His intention refers to betrothals that cannot lead to consummation, such as if he betrothed one of two sisters, for we hold that this is considered betrothal, as stated in Siman 41. These sisters are forbidden both to him and to others. It is obvious that we compel him to divorce them. Similarly, as mentioned in the responsa of the Rashba, when he says "your two daughters to my two sons" and the like (the Gra in sk 146, and the efforts of the Levush and the Ba'al HaGolah to understand his intention are unnecessary. The citation of the responsa of the Rosh is an error; the second law is indeed found in the responsa of the Rosh). It is further written: if she claims that her husband does not lie with her and does not have relations with her, her law is as one who claims that he does not have the strength of men. It is obvious, as in this case too it is known whether she is lying or not. It is clear that anyone who marries a woman in a forbidden relationship, even if it is a rabbinic prohibition such as secondary forbidden degrees of kinship, we compel him by all means to divorce her. Regarding the ketubah, this is explained in Siman 116, see there.

All matters of coercion discussed in this section involve a dispute among the early authorities regarding whether coercion is only verbal or also involves physical coercion, such as beatings and similar methods. The language of our sages, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 21 is as follows: "All those whom they said should be forced to divorce, we coerce even with whips." And there are those who say that anyone about whom it is not explicitly stated in the Talmud that we force him to divorce, but rather that he should divorce, we do not coerce with whips. Instead, we tell him, "The sages have obligated you to divorce, and if you do not, it is permitted to call you a sinner." And since there is a dispute among the authorities, it is proper to be stringent and not coerce with whips so that the get (divorce document) should not be considered coerced. However, if he has a wife who is involved in transgression, everyone agrees that we coerce with whips. In any place where we do not coerce with whips, we also do not excommunicate him (as was done in ancient times, and nowadays it is forbidden by state law). Nevertheless, we can decree upon all of Israel (with government permission) not to do him any favor, nor to engage in business with him, nor to circumcise his sons, nor to bury him until he gives a get, and with all the severity that the court desires. They can be stringent in such a manner, except they should not excommunicate him (as this is considered complete coercion). But someone who does not fulfill his marital duties, they can excommunicate and ban him (as was done in ancient times, as mentioned above) until he fulfills his marital duties or divorces, for this is not coercion regarding the get but rather to fulfill his marital duties. Similarly, in all similar cases. Also, if someone divorced his wife with a valid get and there arose some suspicion about the get, it is permitted to coerce him to give another get. In any case where there is a dispute whether to coerce or not, although we do not coerce him to divorce, we do coerce him to immediately give her the ketubah (marriage contract) and the dowry she brought to him. However, not the additional amount or the gifts he gave her.

They further wrote in section 22 that it is necessary to impose a prohibition on all those present at the time of the giving of the get (divorce document) not to cast aspersions on the get. They mention that Rabbeinu Tam decreed in a gathering with his students against anyone who casts aspersions on the given get, and this is the established custom in all Jewish communities. The text of the decree is found in Mordechai at the end of Gittin, see there. All of this is only to prevent general aspersions. However, a Torah scholar who has come into possession of the get or has heard about the get and has a serious doubt about it, Heaven forbid that he should remain silent. On the contrary, he is obligated to ask the officiating rabbi for his reasoning and explanation. If after thorough discussion it is agreed that another get is necessary, efforts are made to obtain another get. All the responsa of the great sages of Israel are filled with such matters.

Furthermore, it is written in Section 23: If the husband swears to give a good divorce (get), they should release him first so that it does not appear to be coerced. However, he should provide collateral if he wishes. Refer to Section 134, Paragraph 4. In the case of a reversed divorce, there is no need to inquire if he swore or vowed, since he needs to divorce her by law. However, they should ask him if he is divorcing willingly, and they should also ask his wife. This is the plain custom. Certainly, if he swears not to divorce, they need to release him according to the opinion that if he acts, it is not effective. This is also our practice in arranging the divorce, even though, according to the strict law, this is not included in the principle of "if he acts, it is not effective." Moreover, there is doubt if the main ruling of the law is effective or not. Nonetheless, who would involve themselves in a divorce with uncertainties? And even in the case of swearing to divorce, we say that everything a person does willingly is not considered coercion, as stated in Section 134, and as written by the Rosh in Chapter 3 of Nedarim and the Mordechai in Chapter 3 of Shevuot. Despite this, they release him, and certainly so if he swore not to divorce.

They further wrote in section 24: One who accepted upon himself the Nazirite vow of Samson to divorce his wife is permitted to divorce her, and it is not considered as divorcing under coercion. It is good to divorce with two writs of divorce, giving them to her one after the other. The reason is that this is not considered coercion, since he can fulfill his vow and not divorce her. This is clearly proven from a straightforward Mishnah in Gittin (45a). And they wrote that it is good to divorce with two writs of divorce because the Nazirite vow of Samson has no annulment. Therefore, it appears somewhat compelled, unlike other vows which have annulment. Therefore, it is good to use two writs of divorce: one to fulfill his vow, and the second as a complete divorce (Taz).
By the grace of God, the laws of divorce are concluded.

### Laws of Refusal by a Minor. It contains 49 sections:

It is well known that a minor girl is under the authority of her father, and when he accepts her betrothal, it is considered a Torah-sanctioned betrothal, as it is written, "I have given my daughter to this man." When she has no father, she cannot be betrothed until she reaches the age of majority. However, the Rabbis instituted marriage for a minor girl so that she would not be treated promiscuously; it is better that she have a husband and be protected (Yevamot 112b). Therefore, although the Sages were stringent with a father not to betroth his minor daughter initially until she grows up and says, "I want this man" (Kiddushin 42b), nevertheless, in the case of an orphan who has no father and no one to protect her, it is better to betroth her as stated. Additionally, it is not akin to a Torah-sanctioned betrothal which requires a divorce (get), and perhaps she might despise him, and he might not want to divorce her. This is not the case with Rabbinic betrothal, which does not require a get, and she can leave through refusal (mi'un), as will be explained. The Sages were not concerned in such cases, for if she despises him, she will refuse and leave (according to the law of the kingdom, one should not marry off a minor girl).

And sometimes, there is a case where even if she has a father, she still has the status of an orphan. For example, a minor whose father married her off, and she became widowed or divorced during her father's lifetime while she was still a minor, her father no longer has authority over her, and she is called an orphan during her father's lifetime. Just as reaching maturity removes her from the father's authority, so too does marriage. Thus, we have learned in the Mishnah (Ketubot 43b): "Once he has married her off, the father no longer has authority over her." She is capable of becoming betrothed and married in rabbinic marriages and can exit through refusal (mi'un). One should not ask, according to the first reason in the previous section, why the Rabbis instituted marriage for her if she has a father to guard her. This is because, since she has left his authority, he no longer guards her. Moreover, since it was necessary to institute marriage for orphans, it is necessary to include her as well, since her status is like an orphan. According to the second reason we explained, the matter is straightforward.

And by whom should the minor be married? It appears from the words of the Talmud and the early authorities that it is specifically when the minor is married by her mother or her brothers or by a court that sees to her welfare and protection. But if she marries by herself, it is of no consequence, and she does not even need to perform mi'un (refusal), as it is merely considered seduction and the seduction of a minor is considered coercion (Beit Shmuel, section 5). However, from the language of Maimonides in the Laws of Marriage, chapter 4, law 7, it becomes clear that even if she marries by herself, it is considered a marriage, and she needs to perform mi'un. Further clarification on this matter will be provided with God's help. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, Yevamot (chapter 13, halacha 2), it is explicitly implied like Maimonides, as it states there: "It happened with Rabbi Eliezer who had a minor niece and he said to her, 'Go and marry,' and she replied, 'I am a maid to wash the feet of my master's servants,' and he married her." This shows that she married by herself alone. And even though it is stated in the Mishnah there (107b): "What is a minor who needs to perform mi'un? Any minor whom her mother or brothers married off with her consent. If they married her off without her consent, she does not need to perform mi'un." This does not mean that without her mother and brothers she does not need mi'un, but it teaches us that even if her mother and brothers married her off, she does not need mi'un if it was without her consent. Further details on this will be explained in section 9 with God's help.

And specifically when they married her with her consent, but without her consent it is nothing, as it is written. And it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud there that with her consent is considered when they made for her clothing and jewelry and mentioned to her the husband. But if they did not mention to her the husband, it is nothing and it is considered without her consent. And there is a doubt if they mentioned to her the husband and did not make for her clothing and jewelry whether this is considered with her consent or not. It appears that it is with her consent, and the mention of clothing and jewelry is the usual manner because without this she would presumably not agree. But once she agrees, it does not matter to us. And this is also implied from the general language of the poskim (decisors).

The Talmud explains that both a betrothed and a married woman require refusal (mi'un). Some say that a betrothed woman does not need refusal unless she herself accepted the betrothal, but if her mother and brothers accepted the betrothal, she does not need refusal, for a minor cannot have an agent (Nimukei Yosef, Yevamot, chapter 13, in the name of Ramban). Others disagree with this (Yam Shel Shlomo, ibid). This also seems to be the opinion of Rambam and the Tur. According to this, in the case of an orphan whose father is still alive, if the father accepted the betrothal with her consent, she also requires refusal, for the father is not less significant than her mother and brothers (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 1). And although a minor cannot have an agent, nevertheless, just as the rabbis instituted marriage and betrothal for her, so too did they institute an agent for her.

And until when can she refuse? Until she grows up, as will be explained. And from when can she refuse? The sages taught in the Mishnah (107b): Any minor who does not know how to guard her betrothal does not need to refuse. And so the halacha is decided in the Gemara there. And what is this measure? The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 4 of Ishut, Law 8, that this is from six years old to ten years old. Then we test and discern her understanding: if she recognizes and understands matters of marriage and betrothal, she needs to refuse; if not, she does not need refusal. And if she is older than ten, even if she is very foolish, she needs refusal. And if she is younger than six, even if she is very clever, she does not need refusal. And he holds that the measure in the Mishnah is only from six to ten, no less and no more. And although the simple reading of the Mishnah seems that there is no measure in her years, nevertheless, since in Gittin (65a) it is stated that the measure for a minor to refuse is like the measure for minors whose transactions in movable property are valid, and in the measure of minors it is said there (59a) that this is from six to ten, therefore he explained that the statement of the Mishnah is also in this measure.

There is a question regarding this matter, since the Rambam himself ruled in Chapter 29 of the Laws of Sales that in the case of a minor's transactions with movable property, an examination is needed from the age of six until he grows up, even if he is over ten years old. So why does it state here that over the age of ten in all cases, refusal (mi'un) is needed (Lechem Mishneh)? The answer to this is that certainly the types of knowledge are not comparable to each other. For refusal, she only needs to understand the concept of betrothal, but in the case of buying and selling, the knowledge required is to understand the ways of commerce. And in Gittin, it was not said that after the age of ten examination is not needed, but rather that there are types of minors who have a sense of commerce from the age of six, and there are those who have no sense until the age of ten. From then onward, there are those whose sense is weak and one cannot rely on their transactions, and there are those whose sense is proper and one can rely on them. And since from the age of ten each one has some sense of commerce, it follows that regarding betrothal and marriage, the sense is sufficient for the matter of refusal. Indeed, there are some authorities who hold that even in that case, after the age of ten, examination is not needed, as the Tur wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 235, in the name of the Ramah.

However, the Tur in Siman 43 has a different opinion on this matter, that even a girl less than six years old, if she is given a nut and takes it and throws away a pebble, she requires mi'un (refusal), because when she reaches this level, she knows how to safeguard her betrothal. And this is also the opinion of Rashi and Tosafot and the Rosh in Gittin according to their version there, and they hold that she does not need to safeguard the betrothal more than she safeguards a nut or a date and similar items. But the Rambam holds that the safeguarding is not like the safeguarding of a nut or a date but rather the safeguarding of the betrothal, that she knows they are betrothal. And I am astonished at our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, who only brought the opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, and earlier in Siman 141 they brought the opinion of the Tur. Therefore, it seems that they relied on what is written there. And know that anyone who does not require mi'un goes to her mother's house as if she was never betrothed at all and does not need to say anything. Also, understand that what the Rambam wrote, that from the age of ten, even if she is very foolish, she requires mi'un, does not mean she is like a shoteh (insane person), because for a shoteh, even if she is an adult, they did not institute marriage and betrothal for her. Rather, the intention is that she is not sharp in her intellect (Beit Shmuel, note 4).

And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in section 2 that there are those who say that all this is when she marries with the knowledge of her brother and mother, but if she marries without their knowledge, she does not need to perform refusal (mi'un). And there are those who say that if she has reached the age of understanding (pa'utot), she needs to perform refusal. The explanation of the matter is that we have already written in section 3 that from the language of the Talmud in the Mishnah in Yevamot and from the language of the poskim, it implies that if she betroths herself without the knowledge of her brother or mother, it is nothing, and she does not need to perform refusal. And this is the opinion of the first view. And there we explained that from the language of Maimonides, it explicitly implies that the knowledge of her mother and brother is not required, and this is also explicit in the Jerusalem Talmud. Therefore, the second opinion holds that both are true: in the measurement of the Mishnah in Yevamot, when she knows how to guard her betrothal, which is before the age of understanding when she guards the betrothal like guarding a nut or a date and she is very young, in this case, the knowledge of her mother and brother is required. But in the measurement of the age of understanding, which is the measurement of Maimonides, she needs to perform refusal even without their knowledge (and the measurement in Gittin is not the measurement of the Mishnah in Yevamot).

What is considered a refusal (mi'un)? Any instance where she says, "I do not want this man as my husband" or "I do not want the betrothal that my mother and brothers arranged for me," and she says this in front of two witnesses, this is sufficient, and she goes out without a get (divorce document). Moreover, even if she is sitting in a litter being carried to the wedding canopy to her husband's house and she says, "I do not want him as my husband," this is considered a refusal, even though she does not return to her mother's house (as inferred from Rashi, Ketubot 108a). Furthermore, even if she is in her husband's house after the marriage and guests come to her husband, and she stands and serves them and says in their presence, "I do not want this man as my husband," this is considered a refusal (Gemara), even though the guests are neither a court nor witnesses and will not inform anyone of this (Rashi). And even though she is still in his house, she leaves him without a get. Moreover, even if her husband sent her to fetch something from the shopkeeper and she said there in front of two witnesses, "I do not want my husband," this is considered a refusal, even though one might say that she said this out of anger because he troubled her. Furthermore, even if she did not explicitly say, "I do not want him," but rebelled against her husband, and the husband followed her and people said to her, "See, your husband is following you," and she replied, "May your husband be yours," this is also considered a refusal. Similarly, even if she did not say anything, but left her husband and betrothed herself to another while she was still a minor, this is considered a refusal, even if she was married to him (Gemara). However, if she left her husband without saying, "I do not want him," and without accepting betrothal from another, this is not considered a refusal.

There is a doubt whether, after the refusal (miyun), if she remains in his house and he has relations with her, if the refusal is nullified or not. It appears that it is not nullified, because once she refuses, she is considered only as seduced, and the seduction of a minor is considered coercion. Even according to the Rambam, who does not hold that the seduction of a minor is coercion, nevertheless, there is no valid marriage here but merely promiscuity. Certainly, it is forbidden for him to have relations with her after her refusal, for before the refusal it is not considered promiscuity since he married her according to the enactment of the sages. However, after the refusal, it is considered mere promiscuity.

A minor girl [who was married off by her mother or brothers] can refuse [the marriage] whether from betrothal or from marriage, and in front of how many people can she refuse? Even though it is taught in the beginning of Sanhedrin that refusals require three [judges], we nevertheless hold in Yevamot (107b) that two are sufficient. This means that the essential refusal is valid even with one [judge], but two witnesses are needed to testify about the refusal (Beit Shmuel, section 8). A minor girl can refuse even not in the presence of the husband and not in the presence of a court. There is an opinion that this is only acceptable after the fact, but ideally, three are required as in the Mishna there (Tosafot in the name of Rabbi Chananel). If she marries another or is betrothed while still a minor publicly, three are not required; but if it was done in private, three are required ideally (Beit Shmuel, section 9). The reason for requiring three ideally is not to constitute a court, but to ensure publicity, and publicity is achieved only in the presence of three, as is evident in the Talmud regarding objections (Bava Batra 39b). Note that the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG) in the laws of refusal cites in the name of Halachot Gedolot that it must be specifically with three, but in our version of Halachot Gedolot in the laws of refusal, it does not say so. However, at the end of the laws of divorce in Halachot Gedolot, it appears to follow the version of the SeMaG, where it is written regarding a document of refusal how a certain woman came before us to the court, etc. The later authorities did not mention his opinion at all, which requires further investigation.

She refused her husband and married another man, she can also refuse him and likewise the third and the fourth as long as she is a minor. Similarly, if her husband died and she remains bound to the levirate marriage, she can also refuse, and the levirate bond is removed from her because she refused her first marriage and uproots it. However, in one aspect, it is not similar to a regular refusal, for if she refuses her husband, she is permitted even to his father. But if she refuses the levir, although she uproots her first marriage, she is still forbidden to his father. The reason is that at the time she falls to levirate marriage, she appears as his daughter-in-law because she did not refuse during her husband's lifetime. Similarly, regarding the co-wife of a forbidden relative, she performs the chalitzah and does not undergo levirate marriage, as will be explained in Siman 173, because at the time she falls, the co-wife appears as the co-wife of a forbidden relative as stated there. And precisely to the father of the levir she is forbidden, but to other relatives of the deceased who are forbidden relatives to her, she is permitted, because since it is only due to appearance, it only applies to the father who she appears to be his daughter-in-law and not to other relatives. There are those who prohibit also other relatives, and even according to this opinion, only the relatives of the deceased are forbidden and not the relatives of the levir whom she refused. And even to the other brothers, she is permitted when she refused the levir, for she only refused him and not the other brothers. It seems that this is only when she said, "I do not want this levir," even though she thereby uproots the first marriage. Nevertheless, it can be said that she uproots it concerning him and not concerning the other brothers. But when she said, "I do not want my deceased husband," she is forbidden to all the brothers according to those who prohibit (it seems to me) that even with this language she can refuse (as explained in Rashi, Yevamot 13, s.v. "and she refuses").

Those two [witnesses] before whom a girl performs mi'un (refusal of marriage) need to be certain that she is still a minor. They write a document of mi'un for her, sign it, and give it to her—not because it is obligatory to give it to her, but so that she has proof that she performed mi'un. This document is not like a get (divorce document) where the writing and giving are essential. Therefore, it does not need to be written specifically for her, nor does it need to be handed to her at all, nor does it need to follow any of the laws of a get. The format of a get is not written in it, so it does not appear to be a full-fledged get and cause confusion (Tur). It is merely an act of the court and serves only as a proof document. This is its format:

On Shabbat, on such and such date in the month of such and such, in the year such and such from the creation of the world, so-and-so, the daughter of so-and-so, refused (the marriage) before us and said, "My mother or my brother misled me and betrothed me" (and if she is married, they write, "and they married me"). (And for those authorities who say that even if she betrothed herself, she requires refusal, they write, "I misled myself and betrothed myself or married myself") to so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, and I am a minor. Now I reveal my intention before you that I do not want him, and I do not remain with him. And now so-and-so has been examined, and it has been clarified to us that she is still a minor. We have written, signed, and given it to her as proof and evidence in her hand, said so-and-so, son of so-and-so, and said so-and-so, son of so-and-so. It is good to validate the signatures in a court of law, as perhaps the witnesses' signatures will not be recognized, and when it becomes known that she was married or betrothed to so-and-so, they will not permit her to marry.

And those before whom a girl performs "mi'un" (refusal of a marriage) need to recognize her and her husband so that there is no deceit in the matter. If not, they should not engage in the "mi'un." Therefore, anyone who witnesses the "mi'un" can write a get (divorce document) of "mi'un" for her, even if they do not recognize her, because certainly, those before whom she performed the "mi'un" recognized her. This applies ideally, but after the fact, even if they do not recognize the husband, only the woman, it is sufficient. For even if he is not her husband, she can refuse the marriage not in his presence, as we have said. The main concern is recognizing the woman, for perhaps it is another woman who has been persuaded to say that her name is the same (as the real woman). And even though there is still a concern that perhaps there is indeed a minor girl with the same name as this one, and she will say that her husband's name is the same as the husband of this one because a deceiver has persuaded her to say so, and after she says she refuses and receives the get of "mi'un," the deceiver will take the get from her and give it to the other woman. Nevertheless, this is a slight concern and not very common. (See Beit Yosef and Beit Shmuel, section 10, and examine carefully).

And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, raised a difficulty in his work Bedek HaBayit: How can other people write a document of refusal based on the fact that those before whom she refused recognize her? It has already been clarified that refusal is effective even before strangers who do not recognize her, certainly. Moreover, are all people experts in the law, such that they would only allow refusal before them if they recognize her? Certainly not. And refusal occurs without preparation, as the minor girl comes and refuses. 

And it appears to me that certainly, if the people witnessing the refusal saw that the refusal was done without preparation, then it is obvious that they do not write [the document] unless they recognize her. And what the Sages said, "they write even if they do not recognize her," refers to when the refusal was done with preparation. And it is obvious that this was done by expert people who are knowledgeable in the laws of refusal. And this is explicitly implied in the Gemara there, that it refers to refusal done by a court. Refer to it there (and this also resolves the difficulty raised by the Beit Shmuel at the end of section 211, refer there and examine carefully).

The sages taught in the Mishnah: If a young girl refuses [to continue the marriage], he is permitted to marry her relatives and she is permitted to marry his relatives; and she is not disqualified from marrying a kohen (Yevamot 108a) because it is as if the betrothal never existed. However, if he divorces her with a get (bill of divorce), even though the get is only rabbinic, he is prohibited from marrying her relatives and she is prohibited from marrying his relatives, and she is disqualified from marrying a kohen. If she marries a kohen, there is uncertainty whether the children are rabbinically disqualified or not. Although it seems that rabbinically the children are disqualified, similar to chalitzah (levirate shoe removal) which is also rabbinically prohibited, and it is explained in Siman 7 that she and her children are rabbinically disqualified, nonetheless, one could argue that it is not comparable to chalitzah, which is supported by a scriptural verse, whereas the get of a minor is entirely rabbinic and its law is like secondary forbidden relationships, where it is explained that the children are not disqualified. This matter requires further investigation. Additionally, a girl who refuses does not need to wait three months after refusing, but one who is divorced with a get must wait. Even though a minor cannot become pregnant, the sages did not differentiate as it is written in Siman 13. Similarly, a girl who refuses does not receive a ketubah, but one who is divorced with a get receives a ketubah like all other women.

When she refuses [to stay married] to her husband and marries another, and then refuses [to stay married] to him as well, she is permitted to return to the first one. However, if she left the first one with a get (divorce document), she is forbidden to return to him. The reason is that there is a concern that since he divorced her with a get, perhaps after she marries another, he will persuade her until she refuses the second one. But if she left through refusal, we do not worry about this, because it is assumed that he already tried to persuade her while she was with him, and she was not persuaded (Talmud). Therefore, if she left the first one with a get, even if she left the second one through refusal, she is forbidden to return to the first one. Certainly, if she left the second one with a get or he died, this is explicitly like taking back his divorcee after she married another. But if she left the first one through refusal, even if she left the second one with a get or he died, she is permitted to return to the first one. A general rule is that anyone who is forbidden to return to the first one is also forbidden to his relatives, such as his father or brother. Even though there is no concern of persuasion with them as we mentioned, nevertheless, we decree concerning them because of him, that if not for this, the law would not stand. And wherever she is permitted to return to him, it is obvious that she is permitted to his relatives since the original betrothal is nullified, and it is as if she was never betrothed at all.

And furthermore, the Sages said (there) that even if she went out from him with a get (divorce document) and afterwards he remarried her and she then went out from him with mi'un (refusal), the mi'un nullifies the previous get. And when she marries another and either refuses or is divorced, she is permitted to return to the first husband. Likewise, if the first time she went out with mi'un and the second time with a get, the get nullifies the mi'un. And similarly, if she married several men and left them several times with a get and mi'un, whichever she left with a get at the end, she is forbidden to return to him, and whichever she left with mi'un at the end, she is permitted to return to him. And the same law applies concerning the priesthood, as mentioned above in Siman 6, and there it is stated that according to the Tur, regarding the priesthood, even the mi'un of another nullifies his get.

The one who refuses (a marriage) does not receive a ketubah, but she does receive the additional amount, for the ketubah is a rabbinic enactment, and they did not decree it for when she departs of her own will by refusal. However, the additional amount he gave her out of affection, and he knew that she had the ability to leave by refusal. And while she is under him, he is obligated to sustain her and to redeem her, and he eats her fruits. But if he went overseas and she borrowed and ate or redeemed herself and then stood and refused, he is not obligated to pay, even though he ate her fruits. Not only that, but even if the fruits are still intact, that he collected and brought into his possession and has not yet eaten, he is not obligated to return them, for such was the enactment. And her property of iron sheep (permanent dowry) and of usufruct (temporary dowry), if they are intact, she takes them, and if they are lost, the iron sheep he pays for, but the usufruct he does not need to pay for. Thus ruled our master the Beit Yosef in section 10, and his words are puzzling, for in Ketubot (101a) it is explicitly stated that when they are lost, he does not need to pay, and so ruled the Rambam in chapter 24 of Ishut, and the reason is that perhaps if she had not refused, she would have died first, and he would inherit her. And if they were lost due to his negligence, some say also that he is exempt (Tosafot), and some say that in usufruct, if he used them unlawfully, he is obligated to pay (Ran there). And the great later authorities already disputed him (Beit Shmuel section 13 and the Gra section 28, and in the Tur there is a textual error).

And until what age can a daughter perform mi'un (refusal)? Until she grows up and reaches twelve years and one day, and afterwards brings two pubic hairs. If she brings hairs before this, they are meaningless and are considered merely as warts. Even if she brings hairs within her twelfth year, for the purposes of vows she is considered an adult when she knows for whom she vowed, as stated in Yoreh De'ah section 233. This is referred to in the language of the Talmud (Niddah 45b) as "within the time," meaning within the time when she becomes an adult, i.e., at the end of the year. The halacha is established in the Gemara (there 46a) that regarding two hairs, "within the time" is like before the time, and they are merely warts. She must bring other hairs after twelve years. Additionally, the Gemara (there) states: Rava said, a minor who has reached her years does not need an examination; there is a presumption that she has brought signs of adulthood. The Talmud explains that this presumption applies only to mi'un and not to chalitzah, meaning this presumption is only for stringency and not for leniency. Therefore, she does not perform mi'un once she reaches twelve years and one day, even if we do not know she brought signs. But for chalitzah, which requires adulthood, she should not perform it unless we clearly know she brought signs, and we do not rely on this presumption. This will be explained in section 169.

And this that we have said that the hairs within the [designated] time period are of no consequence is specifically when it is known that they were within the [designated] time period, as Maimonides wrote in Chapter 2 of Ishut, Law 19, and this is his language: When do we say this? When they were examined within the [designated] time period and it became known that they were a mole. But if they were not examined until after the [designated] time period and two hairs were found there, they are presumed to be signs [of maturity], and we do not say that perhaps they grew before the [designated] time period to be a mole. And even leniently, like for the case of halitzah, we follow this and it is not similar to when we have not seen any signs at all, where we do not say there is a presumption that she has brought signs [of maturity], as we said there, since we do not see that she is grown up, for maturity is only through two things: years and signs. And since we do not see signs, we do not remove her from the presumption of her childhood except strictly and not leniently. But when we see signs, she is grown up before us, and why should we be concerned that she had these signs in her childhood?

It is further stated there in the Gemara (48b) that all minors who are examined are examined by women. It is mentioned there that Rabbi Eliezer entrusted the examination to his wife, and Rabbi Yishmael entrusted it to his mother. And these are the words of the Rambam there: "When examining a girl, whether it is during the time (which is the entire twelfth year), before this time, or after this time, they are examined by fitting and trustworthy women. Even one woman can perform the examination, and we listen to her if she says the girl has reached maturity or not." And it is clear from his words that the women are trusted whether to be stringent or lenient. In truth, there is no reliance on them to be lenient, for before the time, even if they say they found hairs, it means nothing, as stated. After the time, if they say they found, we have the presumption of Rava. So also wrote the Rif in Yevamot at the end of chapter 13: "Therefore, all who are examined are examined by women; this is the law, whether for chalitzah or refusal, for we rely on the presumption of Rava." And so also wrote the Rosh in Niddah there. Similarly, it is evident from the language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 15. And even though it is stated in Niddah there that they are trusted to be stringent and not lenient, that is according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon and in regard to during the period. But for us, we hold that during the time is like before the time, and we consider during the time and during the period as one matter.

Even though sometimes a leniency results from their examination, such as when they examined within the time and said they found two hairs, and afterwards they examined after the time and said they also did not find more than these two hairs, and it turns out that we consider her a minor and she would refuse [the marriage], it is still said that there is no Torah-level concern here. Because if he had relations with her after she matured, she does not refuse, as will be explained later, since we suspect that perhaps the signs [of maturity] fell out. And if he did not have relations with her after she matured, there are still no Torah-level betrothals here. Even if we say there is a doubt of Torah-level betrothals without him having relations with her after she matured (see Beit Shmuel, section 32), this is all when she is definitively considered mature. But here, she is not yet considered mature. (The objection of the Ra'avad mentioned by the Kesef Mishneh in chapter 20 is completely unclear, and the Lechem Mishneh also objected to it. However, I do not understand what the Lechem Mishneh was trying to explain regarding the words of the Rambam. The explanation of his words is like that of the Rif, as I wrote. Note this well.)

However, there is an approach among the early authorities that on the last day of the twelfth year for a female and the thirteenth year for a male, there is a dispute in the Gemara whether it is considered as after the time or as before the time. We hold that it is considered as after the time (this is within the period according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot and the Rosh there, and the law follows Rabbi Yehuda). In this case, we hold that a woman is believed to be stringent but not lenient, meaning she is believed to say that she has grown hairs and therefore does not perform mi'un (refusal) or that she has not grown hairs and therefore does not perform chalitza. However, she is not believed to say that she has grown hairs to perform chalitza or that she has not grown hairs to perform mi'un. This is the opinion that our Rabbi, the Ramah, wrote in Section 14, and his intention is if it has been verified by men, and he is not dealing with the matter of the credibility of women. Also, in Section 15, where he deals with the examination by women, he did not mention this because without this we do not have any practical difference in their credibility, for according to the Rif, the Rambam, and several early authorities, the hairs are not effective at all on this day, and without this, it is considered as before the time (for they explain that within the period is within the time). The Ramah only brought these opinions to be stringent according to Rabbeinu Tam, and there is a difficulty in the Beit Shmuel, Section 20, who questioned the Tur and the Ramah, and it is clear as I have written, and pay attention to this matter.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 14 that there are those who say that if hairs were seen before twelve years and they are still present after twelve years, even though she did not grow other hairs after twelve years, she is considered an adult for the purpose of refusal (mi'un), but still considered a minor for the purpose of chalitza. In any case, regarding the examination of women, some of our rabbis hold this view (Rashi and Tosafot, 48b, s.v. b’shlama), contrary to the opinion of the Rambam which we explained in Section 25, that these rabbis believe that any leniency derived from their examination is not credible. However, regarding the examination by men, it does not seem reasonable to say this. So wrote the later authorities (Bach, 21, and the Gra, 156). Also, our master the Beit Yosef held this view and relied on what he wrote later that the examination is done by women and did not need to explain that the examination by men is not the same because it is not the way of men to examine, and it is inappropriate. Moreover, for practical law, there is no difference at all in this matter because he wrote at the end of this section that nowadays, it is proper to be stringent that she should not refuse after twelve years even if no hairs are found at all. Certainly, this is the case if she had hairs beforehand, and it is clear that this is his intention. The great later authorities wondered about him in vain.

Rabbi Moses Isserles (Rema) wrote (there), "If there is doubt whether she has reached twelve years old or not, we go stringently." And it is obvious that this is a case of doubt concerning a Torah law. Even when there is a double doubt (safek sfeika), such as a doubt whether the signs [of maturity] have fallen off or not, which creates a double doubt, namely, whether she has reached the age and even if she has, perhaps the signs were not present, nevertheless, the Rashba is inclined to be stringent in his responsa (Ariv) and did not explain the reason. It appears from him that this is a double doubt from one source, as it is essentially one doubt – whether she is a minor or an adult (Beit Shmuel, section 22). 

Nevertheless, it seems that this is only when there is a concern of Torah law, such as if someone had relations with her from the time of the doubt, or even if he did not have relations but the betrothal occurred at the time of the doubt. But without this, even if she is now an adult, there is no Torah-level marriage unless we say that even when she grows up and he did not have relations, it becomes a Torah-level marriage. This does not seem to be implied from Rabbi Yosef Karo in section 21, and this will be further clarified with God's help in section 32.

And this which has been explained that she can refuse [to marry] after twelve years when examined by men and no two hairs were found, in what case does this apply? When no relations occurred after she grew up. Because then, even if we suspect that the hairs might have fallen out, there is no Torah-level betrothal. But if relations occurred after she grew up, then if she had hairs and they fell out, she is considered a married woman by Torah law. For in the relations that occurred after she grew up, there is intent for betrothal, and they do not rely on the initial betrothal which was only rabbinic. She cannot refuse [the marriage] even if they examined thoroughly and found no signs, because we fear that the signs might have fallen out.

If another man betrothed her after she had relations with her first husband when she was an adult and she had two pubic hairs at that time, she does not need a divorce from the second man. It appears that even if only women examined her and said she had pubic hairs, she does not need a divorce from the second man because she also has the presumption (chazakah) established by Rava. If it is not known whether she had pubic hairs, she certainly requires a divorce from the second man out of doubt. If she refused the second man after she grew up and had relations and was examined and found not to have pubic hairs, and then she was betrothed to another man, she requires a divorce from both men and is forbidden to return to the first man so that people will not say she married another man after she was divorced. If she married the other man, she must leave both men, and the child is a doubtful mamzer (illegitimate) from both. From the second man, the child is a mamzer, since she might have been an adult with the first man. From the first man, the child is also a mamzer, since she might have reached adulthood with the second man. If, at the time she had relations with the first man during her adulthood, he explicitly said that he was having relations with her based on the original betrothal, it is as though he did not have relations with her (Beit Shmuel 31). There are those who question this (Maggid Mishneh and Kesef Mishneh on Chapter 4 of Hilchot Ishut, Halacha 7, and Responsa Radach Bayit 24). Even from the language of the Rambam, it does not seem so, and this is also implied in Yevamot 109. Investigate further.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in paragraph 21: If a girl brings forth two pubic hairs after the age of twelve and then engages in sexual intercourse, it is considered a doubtful betrothal. If he wants to divorce her, she requires a rabbinic divorce (get) due to the doubt. If he does not divorce her and she becomes betrothed to another man, she requires a get from both men. If they wish, the first can divorce her and the second can marry her. However, if the second one divorces her, the first one should not marry her again, lest people say he remarried his divorcee after she was betrothed to another. If the second man has relations with her before the first one divorces her, she must leave both, and the child from the second man is not a mamzer (illegitimate). But if the first man has relations with her before the second one divorces her, the child is a mamzer. Thus is the conclusion of the Shulchan Aruch (the Avnei Shoham questioned the Bach on this, but there is no question here, as this is the opinion of the Rif, and study this well).

It is explained from their words that as long as he did not have relations with her after she reached maturity, there is no concern of Torah-level marriage. This is also implied in Niddah (46a), where it states that only if he had relations with her at a later time is there a Torah-level doubt, but if he did not have relations, there is no Torah-level doubt. However, in Yevamot (109b), the Gemara raises a question about whether the betrothal of a minor girl is pending until she matures, and the betrothal grows with her and becomes complete even if he did not have relations with her. The Rif writes there that this question was not resolved. However, from the Rif's own words, it is clear that the question only concerns rabbinic betrothal. From the Talmud, it is explicitly proven that the doubt pertains to Torah-level betrothal. The Ba'al HaMaor already questioned the Rif's words, and in Sefer HaZechut, Ramban elaborated to uphold the Rif's words. It is explained there from his words that some of the Geonim held that this is a Torah prohibition. This requires further study. (Perhaps because this entire topic follows the opinion of Rabban Gamliel, while we hold like Rabbi Eliezer that we teach the minor to refuse him, as stated in the first chapter of Niddah 8a. See there and examine this well.)

The Tur wrote: "Even if she did not marry another after she grew up and became betrothed, she requires a get (divorce document) from the second one and is forbidden to return to the first one. However, if someone else seized her by force and betrothed her through intercourse, she does not require a get from the second one and is permitted to return to the first one." And indeed, this is how it is in the Gemara there (110a), and it is stated there that the Rabbis imposed a fine on him because he did not act properly. They annulled his betrothal, and it is not only if he betrothed her with money, but even if he betrothed her through intercourse, they considered his intercourse as licentious intercourse. This is what the Tur wrote, "and betrothed her through intercourse" — stating a novelty, even if he betrothed her through intercourse, and all the more so with money. However, the Rif, Rambam, and Rosh omitted this, perhaps because they hold that only the sages of the Talmud had this power (see Beit Yosef, who wrote that they did not hold of this interpretation, and it requires further study. Examine it well).

And in this context, it has been explained that if the first husband had relations with her before the second husband divorced her, the child is a mamzer (illegitimate). The Tur wrote in the name of the Raavad, of blessed memory, that even if the second husband had relations with her before the first husband divorced her, she is permitted [to the first husband] because there is no severe prohibition in this case.
