We do not decree in this instance, as we do in the case of a woman whose husband went overseas, because there is neither a prohibition of ervah (incest or adultery) nor a Torah prohibition involved. The Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote similarly and added that even though the Sages decreed that one must leave both husbands in cases of rabbinically forbidden marriages, this applies to the specific circumstances established by the Sages regarding divorces and their stringencies concerning those who deviate from their regulations. However, in general prohibitions where the Sages did not institute such a decree, we cannot create new decrees on our own.

Our Sages said (Niddah 52a) that the two hairs must have follicles at their roots, as this is a sign that the hairs are drawing nourishment from the body. However, without follicles, they are meaningless. Yet, it is not necessary for each hair to have its own follicle, for even if two hairs draw from one follicle, it is sufficient. And although on the head it is impossible for two hairs to draw from one follicle, on the body it is possible (ibid.). For on the head, the Holy One, Blessed be He, created each follicle to nourish only one hair, because if two hairs drew from one follicle, it would cause blindness. But on the body, we are not concerned about this (ibid.). Additionally, our Sages said that even follicles without hairs are a sign of maturity. So why did the Sages say that two hairs are required everywhere? Because one follicle is sufficient for the signs of maturity, as mentioned (ibid.).

And know that from the words of Rashi, of blessed memory (Beitzah 28b, s.v. Shafud), it is explicitly clarified that this matter of indentations is not a sign because indentations are effective without hairs, but rather because it is impossible to have an indentation without a hair. Certainly, there were hairs there that fell out. Refer there. According to this, if there is a hair in the indentation and it is not long enough according to the measure that will be explained, it is not a sign. Regarding part of it, it seems inappropriate to say that it fell out. And as the words of Rashi, of blessed memory, are clarified, this is also explained in the Rambam and Shulchan Aruch, section 16. Refer there (and see Nodah B'Yehudah, section 93, and I do not know what effort was made in this matter).

The measure of the length of the two hairs, the Sages taught in a Mishnah there: Rabbi Yehuda says, enough to bend their tips to their roots; Rabbi Eliezer says, enough to pluck them with a fingernail, meaning to grasp a little; Rabbi Akiva says, enough to be removed with scissors. And the Gemara ruled that the law follows all of them to be stringent: She does not perform mi'un (refusal) once the hair can be plucked with a fingernail, and she does not perform chalitzah until the hair can be bent to its root (Ran at the end of Chapter 3 of Yevamot). And Maimonides holds that removal with scissors is the smallest measure. In Siman 169 in the explanation of the procedure of chalitzah, it will be explained that the length must be as wide as a finger, and this is not from the law itself but because in all measures it is necessary to know the years. If there is a cavity, the width of a finger does not require anything (Beit Shmuel, Subsection 28).

And in which location the two hairs should be found is also a matter of dispute in the Gemara (Talmud). The Rambam (Maimonides) ruled that they need to be in the place of the pubic area, and the entire pubic area is a place for signs, whether above, below, or on the genital organs themselves, and they need to be in one place. This means that both must be above, or both below, or both on the genital organs. And know that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, was puzzled about where this came from, and therefore omitted it in Section 17. But this is not the case, for the Rambam explained what is stated in the Gemara, that "both in one place" refers to the pubic area, and this is also implied by the Rif (Rabbi Isaac Alfasi), and so wrote the great latter authorities (the Gra in Siman 62).

But some of our rabbis hold that one should be stringent regarding the matter of refusal, as those who hold in the Gemara there that even if one is on her back and one on her stomach, and her back literally and her stomach literally, even at a distance from the place of nakedness, and similarly even one on the joints of her fingers and one on the joints of her toes, as the Tur wrote there. And regarding the matter of chalitzah, she should not perform chalitzah until both are in the same exact place and at the place of nakedness, according to the opinion of the Rambam. And so wrote the Rosh, that one should be stringent in accordance with all opinions. And since this examination is difficult to conduct over the whole body, there may also be dimples.

Therefore, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 22, that in our times, a girl cannot perform mi'un (the act of a minor girl refusing her marriage arranged by her brother or mother) after she reaches 12 years old, even if the husband did not consummate the marriage and even if we see that she does not have hairs or signs of puberty. This is because we are not proficient in distinguishing whether there are signs or not, and who can examine the entire body to confirm the truth of this matter? And even though if the husband did not consummate the marriage it is only a rabbinic doubt, nevertheless, a doubt due to lack of knowledge does not fall under the category of doubt. And even though a lack of knowledge for the whole world is considered a doubt, as it is stated in Yoreh De'ah in the rules of Sefek Sefeka, Siman 110, here it is not a lack of knowledge for the whole world, but it is impossible to entrust this matter to the public, and therefore we must be stringent (see also Beit Shmuel, section 34, and according to what was stated, it is clear).

The Sages said (Yevamot 12b) that children are considered signs [of maturity]. From the words of the Rambam in Hilchot Ishut 2:9 and 19:14, it is evident that they are literally like signs, and if she gives birth after twelve years, it is a sign of adulthood even if she has not brought forth two pubic hairs. If she gives birth before this, it is not a sign of adulthood, and she is still considered a minor, similar to signs that appear before the appropriate time. However, from the words of other decisors, it is clear that children at any time are considered as signs after the appropriate time, and even if she gives birth earlier, she is considered an adult. There are those who hold that children are evidence of signs, and even if the signs are not found, we are concerned that they may have fallen out. Others say that even from the time she became pregnant, she cannot refuse [a marriage arranged by her father], because pregnancy itself is considered like signs or evidence of signs, and we are concerned that they may have fallen out (Tosafot there 13a, Beit Shmuel 17, and the Gra 47). According to this, there remains a doubt in Torah law.

Two hairs are considered the lower sign. There are eight upper signs in a woman, which Rambam lists in Chapter 2, and these are his words: "A girl has signs from above, which are called the upper signs, and they are as follows: when she bends her arms backward and a crease is formed in the area of the breasts; when the tip of the breast darkens; when a person places a hand on the tip of the breast, and it sinks and takes time to return; when the tip of the breast splits and forms a small ball at its end; and my teachers explained that this refers to the splitting of the tip itself; when the breasts sag; when the breasts shake; when the crown, which is the fleshy part above the genital area towards the abdomen, becomes prominent; and when this flesh becomes soft and not hard." End of quote.

And it is further written that all these signs: if one of these signs appears in a girl who is twelve years old or younger, it is not regarded; she is still considered a minor. If she becomes twelve years and one day old and one of these upper signs appears, it is not regarded unless there is also a lower sign. If the lower sign does not appear and one of these upper signs appears, she is in doubt between being a minor and a young woman, and we rule stringently. If all the signs appear but the lower sign does not, she is definitely considered an adult, for it is impossible for all the signs to appear unless the lower sign has already appeared and then disappeared. And know that among these signs we have considered, there are signs of maturity as explained in the Gemara (Niddah 47a). According to Rashi's explanation there, all of them are signs of maturity and not signs of adolescence. From the words of Maimonides, it is explained that all the upper signs cannot appear before the lower sign, but it is possible for one of them to appear first. Other sages explained that even one of them cannot appear before the lower sign. And so it is taught in the beginning of Chapter 6 that it is impossible for the upper sign to appear before the lower sign, implying that this refers to one of them. Maimonides interprets this as referring to all of them.

Maimonides wrote (there): If a girl reaches twelve years and one day and has not brought forth two pubic hairs, even if signs of an "aylonit" (a woman who does not develop secondary sexual characteristics) appear in her, she is still considered a minor until she reaches twenty years. When she brings forth two pubic hairs, even if this occurs in her twentieth year, she will be considered a "na'arah" (a young woman) for six months, and afterwards, she will be called a "bogeret" (a mature woman). If she is twenty years minus thirty days and has not brought forth two pubic hairs, and signs of an "aylonit" appear in her, she is considered an "aylonit." If these signs do not appear, she is still considered a minor until she brings forth two pubic hairs or until she reaches thirty-five years and one day. If she reaches this age and has not brought forth two pubic hairs, she is called an "aylonit," even if none of the signs of an "aylonit" appear in her. Thus, you learn that an "aylonit" does not have a period of "na'arut" (youth) but transitions directly from being a minor to being a "bogeret." These are the signs of an "aylonit": she does not have breasts, experiences pain during intercourse, does not have the body contours of a woman, has a deep voice, and cannot be distinguished between a man and a woman. The "na'arah," the "bogeret," and the "aylonit" are all considered adults. End of text.

And this is what he wrote: "If she is twenty years old minus thirty days and she shows signs of being an aylonit (a woman who does not develop secondary sexual characteristics), she is considered an aylonit." All the early authorities were astonished by this statement, questioning where such a calculation comes from and where we find a similar example. On the contrary, we hold that thirty days in a year is considered a full year. Therefore, if she is nineteen years and thirty days old and shows signs of being an aylonit, she is an aylonit. To the Tur, this was so obvious that he wrote it was a scribal error in the writings of the Rambam. However, we cannot say this because in the commentary on the Mishnah in Niddah, chapter 5, the Rambam explicitly writes this as well, indicating that this is his opinion (Tosafot Yom Tov). Furthermore, they raised another difficulty: in the Mishnah there, it is taught that if a woman is twenty years old and shows signs of being an aylonit, she is considered an aylonit. The Gemara there states that if thirty days have elapsed from her twentieth year, it is considered as if she is twenty for all matters. According to the Rambam, it should have been stated that eleven months have elapsed, but the explanation is that only thirty days have elapsed from the year (Aruch HaShulchan).

And it appears to me, on the contrary, that from this language, the Rambam derives that according to their interpretation, it should have said "the twentieth year that only thirty days have entered into it," meaning that the woman only entered thirty days into this year, as it refers to the woman. Furthermore, do we say in every matter that thirty days in a year are considered a year? For they only said this regarding Orlah (Rosh Hashanah 10a). And on the contrary, regarding the years of women, it is explicitly stated (Niddah 44a, 45a) that we do not say so, and those who hold so, we do not rule according to them, see there. Moreover, regarding Orlah itself, there is a dispute about this, and there is an opinion that even one day in a year is considered a year, but we hold that thirty days are considered a year, and this is not a definitive halachah in all places. Additionally, where do we find such an example that in the Mishnah we learned twenty years, and we would interpret that it only began in the twentieth year for thirty days? It is clear to me that for this reason, the Rambam interpreted it as follows: In all the years of maturity for males and females, we require the years in their entirety, as it is taught: a girl of three years and one day, a boy of nine years and one day, a girl of twelve years and one day, a boy of thirteen years and one day. And here, we did not teach a girl of twenty years and one day. Hence, we do not require the year in its entirety. Therefore, the Talmud explains that even if the year is not yet complete, lacking thirty days of the year, this is the meaning of the phrase "that have passed from it," meaning that thirty days have passed from it that the woman has not yet entered. Therefore, it does not say nineteen years and eleven months, as this is not the way of the Tanna, since it is almost the entire year, and thus they include it in the years. The reason is simple, for the counting of the year is by months as it is mentioned in Rosh Hashanah there. Therefore, since it is proven from the Mishnah that we do not require the year in its entirety, we subtract one of its counts, which is a month.

And know that from the language of the Rambam it appears that the law of bringing signs (of maturity) and the signs of an ailonit (a woman who does not develop secondary sexual characteristics) are the same. Just as with the bringing of signs, one becomes an adult at that time and not earlier, so too with the signs of an ailonit at the age of twenty. (And so too wrote the Yeshuot Yaakov in Yevamot, Chapter 8, Section 31.) However, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in Choshen Mishpat, Section 235, wrote that a twenty-year-old male and a twenty-year-old female, when they bring signs of a saris (a man who does not develop secondary sexual characteristics) and an ailonit, respectively, become retroactively adults from the age of thirteen and one day for a male and from the age of twelve and one day for a female. The signs of a saris and an ailonit are signs of maturity in their time; only these signs are delayed in appearing. This is a dispute in the Gemara (Yevamot 80a), where Rav holds that one becomes a saris retroactively, and Shmuel says that he was a minor at that time. The halacha follows Rav in matters of prohibitions. Moreover, even if they bring hairs after this, it is nothing, since they previously brought the signs of a saris and an ailonit (Yevamot 80a). And so wrote Rabbeinu the Rema in Section 12.

According to this, there is a question: how can she refuse after twelve years and one day if she has not brought forth signs of puberty? We should be concerned that perhaps signs of being an aylonit (a woman who does not develop secondary sexual characteristics) will be found in her, and she will retroactively be considered an adult. And even though we do not generally worry about the minority case of an aylonit, this is so when no flaw is seen. But in this case, where she has not brought forth signs of puberty, and certainly if some signs of an aylonit are seen in her, why should she refuse (Beit Shmuel, Section 19)? However, if no marital relations occurred after she turned twelve years old, there is no concern of Torah-level betrothal. And even if marital relations occurred, we can say that either way, if she is an aylonit, it was a mistaken betrothal and does not require a get (divorce document), and if she is not an aylonit, she is still a minor (there). And even though Maimonides, of blessed memory, holds in Chapter 4 of Hilchot Ishut that an aylonit is fully betrothed by Torah law, as he wrote in Section 44, he also holds that she does not become an adult retroactively, as he wrote. (And I am puzzled by the Beit Shmuel, who struggled with the opinion of Maimonides, of blessed memory).

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in his book Darkei Moshe at the end of this section, quoting Maharam of Rysburg, that it is not appropriate to allow refusal (mi'un) in our times at all, even if the girl is not yet twelve years old. Firstly, this avoids confusion with the status of a regular wife, and secondly, it prevents a situation where she might refuse in front of three unlearned individuals. This is also stated in the responsa of Maharam Padua, section 13, citing Rabbi Yaakov Moelin (Maharil), who elaborated extensively to show reasons for stringency in our times. However, Rabbi Yaakov Pollak allowed a woman to refuse in his days, but all the great rabbis of Ashkenaz disagreed with him. Nonetheless, the matter was permitted, and she remarried another man without a get. Based on this, the Shulchan Aruch writes at the end of this section: "According to all opinions, if she is less than twelve years old, she can refuse even in our times." This aligns with Rabbi Yaakov Pollak's actions, contrary to those who are stringent and say that refusal is not allowed at all in our times.

However, there is a difficulty with this leniency. Rabbi Shlomo Luria (Maharshal) wrote in his work Yam Shel Shlomo, chapter 13 of Yevamot, section 17: "In recent times, it has been customary not to allow refusal, and this practice was established by the sage Rabbi Menachem Me'il Tzedek, with the agreement of all the great sages of the generation before us, especially the righteous and pious Rabbi Yaakov Margolies, Rabbi Pinchas of Prague, and Rabbi Yaakov Moelin. One great sage of the previous generation conducted a case where an orphan refused her husband and remarried based on this refusal, but it was reported that this second marriage did not succeed. Therefore, I agree with the decree of the earlier sages not to allow refusal. Even if she refuses, it should be disregarded and she should be prohibited from remarrying until she is divorced. However, if she has already remarried..." 

Additionally, Rabbi Moshe Isserles himself wrote in section 1 that initially, the court should be careful not to marry off a young orphan if it seems likely that it will lead to refusal. The court should judge based on what they see. That is, if it seems that refusal will not occur, they may marry her off. The sages explicitly stated in Yevamot 109: "A person should always adhere to three things and avoid three things: adhere to chalitzah, making peace between people, and annulling vows; avoid deposits, guarantees, and refusals." The reason given is that she might grow up and regret it. Tosafot there quotes R' Chanoch from the Geonim, stating that an orphan should not be betrothed until it is proven that she is an adult to avoid refusal. According to the Geonim, the rabbinic enactment of marriage was specifically to prevent her from being treated without respect. Thus, even the Tosafists and Geonim were concerned about avoiding refusal. Additionally, in my youth, I heard that in the previous generation there was a case of refusal that caused great commotion among the sages of the generation, but I do not know the outcome. Nowadays, this practice is neither seen nor heard of at all, as we do not marry off young girls, and according to the law of the land, this is also prohibited. 

End of the laws of refusal, with G-d's help.

The Law of Yibbum and Which Offspring Exempts from Yibbum, Containing 48 Sections: It is written, "When brothers dwell together, and one of them dies and has no son, the wife of the deceased shall not marry outside the family to a stranger; her brother-in-law shall go to her" (Deuteronomy 25:5). This is a positive commandment that when a brother dies without offspring, his brother should marry his wife. The Torah permits the wife of his brother who died without offspring from the general prohibition of incestuous relationships. Not only is she permitted, but it is also an obligation upon him. Initially, before his brother married her, she was generally permitted to him—if he wished, he could marry her, and if he wished, he could choose not to. Once his brother married her, she became forbidden to him with the prohibition of incest, which is punishable by karet (excision). When his brother dies without offspring, she becomes permitted to him again. However, this permission is not like the initial one, which was at his discretion, but rather the Torah decrees that he must marry her. Therefore, it is stated, "Her brother-in-law shall go to her," meaning it is an obligation upon him to marry her (Yevamot 39b). There is no difference whether she was his brother's wife from marriage or from betrothal, for even a betrothed woman is called his wife.

It is written in the Torah, "and he has no son," but this does not specifically mean a son, as the same applies to a daughter, a son's son, a son's daughter, a daughter's son, or a daughter's daughter, even to the tenth generation. We learn this from the phrase "he has no" which we expound to mean "he has no offspring" (Rashi on the Chumash). And although the sages derived from this exposition (Yevamot 22b) that even a mamzer son exempts from levirate marriage, these expositions are balanced, and we learn all of this from here (Tosafot Bava Batra 109a, 115a). Furthermore, it is written in the section on levirate marriage, "his name shall not be erased from Israel," and since he has a daughter or the offspring of his offspring, his name is not erased (Rosh, Chapter 2).

Therefore, if he left behind a son or a daughter or descendants from the son or descendants from the daughter until the end of all generations, whether from this wife or from another wife, even if it's a son or daughter from a concubine, or even if it's a mamzer (illegitimate child) or mamzeret (illegitimate daughter), or the descendants of their descendants, even if they converted to another religion, this exempts his wives from chalitza and they are forbidden to undergo yibbum. This is because they fall under the prohibition of "the wife of a brother who has children." And if the descendants were alive at the time of his death, even if they died immediately after his death, or even if they were ill or in a state of near-death or injured to the point that they could not live, as long as they were alive at the time of his death, it exempts them from chalitza and they are forbidden to undergo yibbum.

But if he had a son from a maidservant or from a gentile woman, he does not exempt [from levirate marriage], as it has already been explained in chapter 15 that such a son is not attributed to him but rather to his mother, and he is not considered his son in all matters. There are some of the Geonim who ruled that a son from his maidservant does exempt because it is certain that he freed her, as a man does not engage in sexual relations in a licentious manner. The Rambam objected to them in chapter 10 of Gerushin, stating that we only say this regarding a woman who was divorced or betrothed conditionally, but otherwise, ordinary sexual relations are considered licentious. And the Rosh, of blessed memory, was concerned with the opinion of the Geonim and ruled that she should perform chalitzah and not yibum, and the Tur also wrote that this is the opinion of Rav Natronai Gaon, of blessed memory. (And the Shulchan Aruch did not mention this because it is obvious since he brought two opinions, implying that she should perform chalitzah and not yibum, and see Beit Shmuel, subsection 2). And know that a son from a maidservant or a gentile woman, even if he was later freed or converted, does not exempt because he is not his son. A brother from the father performs yibum even if they are not from the same mother, but a brother from the mother and not from the father does not perform yibum, as will be explained in chapter 157.

Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in the first chapter of Yibum, law 5: If someone dies and leaves a pregnant wife, if she miscarries after his death, she should undergo yibum. If she gives birth and the child is born alive into the world, even if the child dies immediately after birth, his mother is exempt from chalitzah and yibum. However, according to the Sages, it must be definitely known that the months were completed and that he was born after a full nine months. But if it is not known how many months he was born after, if he lives for thirty days, he is considered a viable child and exempts his father's wife from chalitzah and yibum. If he dies within the thirty days, even on the thirtieth day, whether he died from illness or fell from a roof or was eaten by a lion, he is considered a doubtful viable child, and the woman requires chalitzah according to the Sages, but she should not undergo yibum. 

It is understood from his words that, according to Torah law, any child that is born is presumed to be viable even if he dies immediately, as we follow the majority of infants who are viable. However, according to Rabbinic law, any child who has not lived for thirty full days, even if he did not die from illness but from some other cause, is considered a non-viable child in terms of requiring chalitzah. If he lives for thirty full days, he is presumed to be a viable child even if he dies from illness, and no distinction is made whether he was born after nine months or eight months, or whether his hair and nails were fully formed or not.

However, in the first chapter of Milah, law 13, it is written: If someone is born in the eighth month, if he is complete in his hair and nails, he is considered a complete child and is a seven-month baby who was delayed, and it is permissible to move him on Shabbat, and he is not like a stone, and he is circumcised on Shabbat. But if he was born with defective hair and his nails are not complete in their formation, he is considered an eighth-month baby who was not fit to be born except in the ninth month and came out before he was fully developed. Therefore, he is considered like a stone and it is forbidden to move him on Shabbat. Nevertheless, if he survives for thirty days, he is considered a viable child like any other newborn in all respects, because any human who survives for thirty days is not considered a miscarriage. And if someone is born in the seventh month of gestation and is born complete, he is considered a viable child and is circumcised on Shabbat. If it is uncertain whether he is a seven-month or eight-month baby, he is circumcised on Shabbat in any case, etc., because if he is an eight-month baby, it is like cutting flesh, etc. End of citation.

In Chapter 2 of the laws of murder, ruling 6, it is written: "Whether one kills an adult or one kills a newborn child, even if it is just one day old, he is liable to be executed for it, etc., provided that its months were completed. However, if it was born before nine months, it is considered a miscarriage until it survives thirty days, etc." End of quote. And in the first chapter of the laws of inheritance, it is written: "If the mother dies and then the son dies, even if he was just one day old and his months were not completed, since he lived for one hour after his mother, he inherits and bequeaths, etc." End of quote. And in the first chapter of the laws of mourning, it is written: "Any child who does not survive thirty days is considered a miscarriage, and one does not mourn for him, even if he dies on the thirtieth day. But if it is certainly known that he was born after a full nine months, even if he dies on the day he was born, one mourns for him. A nine-month-old who is born dead, and an eight-month-old who dies even after thirty days, is considered a miscarriage, etc." End of quote.

And in the first chapter of the laws of impurity of a corpse, law 14, it is written: "Even a one-day-old infant who touched, carried, or was under the same roof as a corpse becomes impure, and he is considered impure from a corpse, provided he was born after a full nine-month term. But an eight-month-old infant is like a stone and does not contract impurity." So it is written. And at the beginning of the ninth chapter of the laws of impurity of the plague, it is written: "All can become impure through plagues, even a one-day-old infant." So it is written. And he leaves it unresolved. And similarly in the first chapter of the laws of reclining and sitting, see there. And one must understand his opinion in all these matters, for he did not equate the laws with each other.

According to the Magid Mishneh, the Rambam holds that, by Torah law, a baby is presumed to be a viable offspring through one of three signs: First, if its hair and nails have completed growing, even if it is an eight-month baby, we say it is a seven-month baby that lingered in the womb (Yevamot 80, like Rabbi [Yehuda Hanasi]). Similarly, if it survived for thirty days, even though its hair and nails are not fully developed and it is an eight-month baby, we also say it lingered (like Raban Shimon ben Gamliel in that context). The rule is that any baby that survives for thirty days is not considered a stillborn, even if it is an eight-month baby and its signs are not developed. If it is known that its months were completed (i.e., it was a full-term baby), it is considered viable even if it dies immediately. This is the Torah law. However, the Sages were stringent in some matters. Regarding inheritance, they maintained the Torah law because, in matters of money, leniency or stringency does not apply since what is lenient for one person is stringent for another. In the case of a murderer, we require either the completion of its months or survival for thirty days. But for an eight-month baby whose hair and nails are fully developed, although it is viable by Torah law, as the Magid Mishneh wrote, since the Sages were stringent, one cannot be executed for killing it. Therefore, in mourning as well, one only mourns if it completed its months or survived for thirty days. This is why it is written in the context of levirate marriage that, by Torah law, if the baby was born alive, even if it dies immediately, it exempts (the brother's wife from levirate marriage), and that refers to a case where its hair and nails were completed. However, the Sages were stringent until it is known that its months were completed or it survived for thirty days (Magid Mishneh, Chapter 1 of Yibbum).

And his words are puzzling, for according to this, in every place where the Rambam mentions "born" simply, his intention is that the hair and nails have finished, as he wrote regarding Yibbum. If so, why did the Rambam write concerning impurity that a one-day-old child transmits impurity specifically when born after nine months and not when born after eight months? For if his signs are complete, he is considered by Torah law as a whole child, and we say that he lingered (similarly, the Kesef Mishneh raises this difficulty in the first chapter of Nachalot). Additionally, it is difficult with what the Maggid Mishneh wrote, that if he lingered for thirty days, even rabbinically, they mourn for him, even if he is an eight-month child. And this is not what the Rambam wrote regarding mourning, as he stated. And the Maggid Mishneh himself found difficulty with his words in the first chapter of Nachalot. There are many more intricacies and considerations.

Therefore, it seems to me that the words of the Maggid Mishneh are true, but there is something to add: the source of the Rambam for all these matters, in my opinion, is from the Tosefta Shabbat, Chapter 16, where it says: "An eight-month-old [fetus] is like a stone etc. What is an eight-month-old [fetus]? Any fetus whose months have not been completed. Rabbi says: Signs are recognizable in him—his hair and nails that have not finished developing. Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel says: Any [fetus] that survives thirty days is not a miscarriage." Look there. And it seems that Rabbi and Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel do not disagree (as is also evident in Yevamot there), as both agree that either one of two signs is sufficient: either the completion of hair and nails or the survival of thirty days, even if its signs are not complete. And we say that this is a seven-month-old who was delayed (according to Rabbah Tosafah there), but the Rabbis disagree with them and hold that if the months have not been completed, neither the completion of hair and nails nor the survival of thirty days is effective (as it seems in Shabbat 136). And look there in Tosafot and scrutinize. According to this, for the Rabbis, it is entirely the opposite, and they hold that for an eight-month-old nothing is effective. According to their opinion, Rabbi Avahu said in Yevamot there that no action is taken with an eight-month-old until he is twenty years old. Look there (and he interprets like Tosafot and not like Rashi there, and scrutinize). Therefore, this law of Rabbi Avahu is not found anywhere in the Rambam because he does not rule like the Rabbis. Additionally, the Rabbis hold that for ordinary births, nothing is needed. But Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees on two points: he holds that for an eight-month-old, thirty days is effective, and for ordinary births, they are not presumed to be miscarriages until thirty days have passed (and this is the opinion of Tosafot in Shabbat there and in Yevamot there). Rabbi holds the same, and the Rambam rules like them (because of the incident of Rabbah Tosafah and because Shmuel in Shabbat there ruled the law like Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel).

It is known that Rambam's approach is to rely on his own words from place to place, as he warned about this principle at the end of Chapter 2 of Hilchot Ishut, see there. Therefore, in the laws of circumcision, which is the first law according to the order of his books, he explained well that a baby born at eight months who has not completed his physical signs and has not lived for 30 days is considered a full-fledged stillborn. If he completes his signs or lives for 30 days, he exits the status of a stillborn according to Torah law, and we circumcise him on Shabbat, as well as in the case of ordinary newborns. In circumcision, it is not possible to be stringent from a rabbinic perspective and violate the positive commandment of circumcision on the eighth day. In the laws of levirate marriage, he did not write at all about the law of an eight-month baby, relying on what he wrote in circumcision. He only wrote about ordinary newborns that according to Torah law, they are exempt in any case, even if they die immediately, and only rabbinically is it required to wait 30 days, also for ordinary newborns like Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel, or if it is known for certain that they completed their months. There is no need to ask that just as we said about an eight-month baby that if his hair and nails are completed, he is considered as if he lived for 30 days, we should say the same for ordinary newborns. This is not a question because certainly according to Torah law it is so, but rabbinically the main thing is the 30-day waiting period, similar to an animal requiring seven days. Regarding inheritance, where it is necessary to follow Torah law, he only wrote the Torah law and referred to a case where the hair and nails are completed, as is usual for ordinary newborns, even if we do not know for sure that he completed his months. An eight-month baby does not need to be mentioned because he relied on what he wrote in circumcision, as mentioned. In the case of a murderer, due to the severity of taking a life, it is also stringent rabbinically. What he wrote there about being born in less than nine months means that it is possible that we do not know for sure that he completed his months, and he relied on what he wrote in levirate marriage. Only in mourning, because the law follows the lenient opinion in mourning, he ruled according to the Rabbis that even a 30-day waiting period does not help for an eight-month baby, certainly (like Rabbi Abahu in Yevamot, as mentioned, and pay close attention). In impurity, he wrote even a one-day-old infant, provided he was born after nine months. He was precise in writing "born after nine months" and did not write "completed his months," meaning like ordinary newborns who are assumed to be born after nine months. Regarding an eight-month baby, he wrote that he is like a stone, being precise in writing so, as mentioned in circumcision, to mean that his hair and nails were not completed and he did not live for 30 days, relying on what he wrote there. In leprosy and discharge, he generalized and relied on what he wrote regarding corpse impurity, as is his way.

And know that the completion of nine months can only be established when he had relations with her at the time of her immersion and then separated from her, and she gave birth nine months later (Tur). Otherwise, who can know when she became pregnant? And I am puzzled, for even without this, it is possible to know. For the Sages have said (end of Niddah) that a woman does not become pregnant except near her immersion or near her menstrual period. Therefore, in a woman who has a regular period, it is possible to determine if there are nine months from near her menstrual period. And one cannot say that this is not precise, for it clearly implies in the Talmud (Sotah 27a) that it is exact. And it must be said that this is usually the case, but there is a minority for whom it is not so (Tosafot Sotah there). And in all of the Torah, we follow the majority. But in this matter, the Sages were stringent and did not follow the majority. Otherwise, most births result in viable children. But the Sages were stringent in this matter, as well as regarding the eight days with an animal, as the early authorities wrote. Therefore, it is impossible to know in any other way except when he separated from her. Furthermore, since there is a dispute about whether it is near her immersion or near her menstrual period, it is consequently impossible to know. For if there are nine months from her immersion, perhaps the law follows the one who says near her menstrual period, and the months have not been completed. And if there are nine months from near her menstrual period, perhaps the law follows the one who says near her immersion. And necessarily, she delayed two weeks. And if so, who can say that she did not delay a month and a half, and it is from the previous immersion, and he is an eight-month baby?

The Tur writes that if it is not known whether the months were completed (i.e., if the child was born after a full-term pregnancy), if the child lived for 30 days and its hair and nails were fully formed, then it is considered viable. But if the child did not live for 30 days after birth, even if it died on the 30th day or even if it lived for 30 days but its hair and nails were not fully formed, it is a doubt whether it is a miscarriage or a viable child, and the widow performs chalitza and does not do yibum. And our master, the Beit Yosef, was astonished, because since it lived for 30 days, nothing more is needed, even if its hair and nails were not fully formed, and there is no one who holds otherwise. Therefore, he did not bring this opinion in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 4. And our master, the Rema, brought the opinion of the Tur in the name of "some say." And there are those who say that among the poskim, there are those who hold like this because Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel said that surviving is an additional sign on the words of Rabbi, and they hold that the signs must be completed and it must survive. But this is not correct, for certainly the completion of the signs requires survival, as we hold like Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel, but survival does not require signs. And as it is written in Section 12, even though from the Torah they are equal, nevertheless, from the Rabbis the main criterion is surviving for 30 days.

It appears to me that the Tur stated his own reasoning, because although it is not explicitly found, we must necessarily say so, since it is impossible for a viable child not to have completed hair and nails. Proof for this is from the language of Rabbi, who said: "What is an eight-month child? Signs prove him—anyone whose hair and nails have not completed." This clearly implies that this is a definitive sign. In the Tosefta, the version is "his signs testify about him," see there. And necessarily, we must say that what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel stated, "Anyone who survives thirty days is not a stillborn," means: even if his signs are complete, if he has not survived thirty days, he remains in doubt as a stillborn. But if he survives and his signs are not complete, it is obvious that he is nothing (not viable). And it is a fortiori: if Rabbi says that even when his signs are complete and he was born in the eighth month, if he survives, he is considered a seventh-month child, as we have stated; all the more so if he survives thirty days and his signs are not complete, we say he is an eighth-month child. And one cannot say that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the lack of completion of signs is not a proof at all, for firstly, since Rabbi says that this is a definitive sign, it is not reasonable to say they disagree on tangible matters. Moreover, if so, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel should have said, "These signs are not proof, but rather whoever does not survive." And since he did not say this, it is clear that he does not disagree on this point. And in the case of a child who has completed its months, it is impossible for the signs not to be complete. Therefore, the Tur only wrote his ruling in cases where it is not known whether the months are complete, because in a case where the months are complete, this reality is impossible. It is possible that this is also the opinion of the Rambam and other authorities, and because of the great simplicity of the matter, they did not need to mention this explicitly. This is the opinion of our master, the Rema, and this is how one should rule.

However, even according to the Tur, if he lived for thirty days and then died, and it was not checked whether his hair and nails had fully developed, we rely on the presumption that he was viable. This is because, according to Torah law, once he comes into the world alive, he exempts [the mother from levirate marriage] (Taz and Beit Shmuel, subsection 6). And in any case of doubt whether he completed his months, she performs chalitzah and does not undergo yibbum. And anyone who dies within thirty days, and it is not known for certain that he completed his months, is considered a doubtful case. Even if he was born dead and miscarried, if there is only a doubt whether he completed his months, the Tur writes that she does not undergo yibbum but only performs chalitzah (see Beit Shmuel, subsection 7, who remains in doubt; his intention is to what is written in Beit Yosef that his proof comes from Nazir 13, which is puzzling because we do not follow Rabbi Shimon there but Rabbi Yehuda. However, in Beit Dovid HaChaim, this was corrected that there is proof from the beginning of the chapter "HaCholotz" as written in Siman 164, section 2. Refer there and examine closely).

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in paragraph 4: "There are those who say that nowadays, even if the fetus has entered the ninth month by just one day, excluding the day it was conceived, it is considered a viable child. And even though it is said in the Gemara that a woman who gives birth at nine months does not give birth prematurely, many have already wondered about this because sensory experience contradicts this. Instead, we must say that the matter has now changed, and this is true for several things. However, the months of pregnancy are each considered 30 days, and we do not count them according to the calendar years." End quote.

I am astonished by his words for two reasons: First, there is a dispute about this in the Talmud, as is evident in the Gemara (Yevamot 42a), which states in this language: "Even according to the opinion that a woman who gives birth at nine months does not give birth prematurely," etc. And in Niddah (27a), it is stated: "This is understandable according to the opinion that a woman who gives birth at nine months gives birth prematurely," etc. It is explicitly clear that there is a dispute about this. Why do we need to say that nature has changed? Let us say that the law follows the opinion that a woman can give birth prematurely.

Furthermore, we must say so because, in the Gemara (Niddah 38a), there is a dispute about whether a woman who gives birth at seven or nine months is based on her months, each being thirty days, or if it depends on the months of the year, where one day in a month is considered a full month. This is referred to in the language of the Gemara as "Shifura Garam," meaning the shofar that the court blows for the sanctification of the month (Rashi). It is clear that according to those who say a woman does not give birth prematurely, they do not hold by "Shifura Garam" (Rashi Rosh Hashanah 11a, s.v. "Afilu"). And Rabbeinu the Rema himself ruled earlier in Siman 4, paragraph 14, that "Shifura Garam," where he wrote that a woman who conceived at the end of Sivan and gave birth at the beginning of Kislev is not a concern because the months cause it, and it is considered a seven-month child. End quote. We must conclude that he holds a woman can give birth prematurely. It is unreasonable to say that for a seven-month child "Shifura Garam" applies, but not for a nine-month child. What sense does that make? It is clearly proven in the Talmud that there is no difference in this matter.

Thus, it is even more difficult to understand why he wrote here that the months of pregnancy are each considered thirty days, which contradicts what he wrote there. Additionally, it is difficult because from the words of Tosafot in Niddah (27a, s.v. "Ela"), it is implied that according to those who say a woman does not give birth prematurely, they do not hold that a fetus can be delayed in the womb. And yet, in this whole section, it is explained that we say the rationale that it was delayed.

And it must be said according to what we wrote in Siman 4, Section 25, that from several places it is clear that the Rambam does not hold by the principle of "the shape causes." We explained there that even Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote this principle only concerning not allowing a woman to leave her husband, but in all other matters, we do not hold by "the shape causes." Consequently, it is clear that in the laws of yibbum (levirate marriage) and chalitza (ceremonial release from levirate marriage), we should rule stringently in this regard. Therefore, even though there is a dispute in the Gemara whether a woman gives birth in incomplete months of nine or not, we should be stringent like those who hold she does not give birth in incomplete months. However, since this contradicts the empirical evidence, I say that in this matter we should not be stringent, even regarding yibbum and chalitza. Regarding the months of pregnancy, we should consider each month as 30 days and not be lenient to say "the shape causes." His explanation is as follows: since we see empirically that women do give birth in incomplete months, we should establish the law accordingly and also say "the shape causes." Therefore, I say it is not so, for even if the law is not "the shape causes" and a woman does not give birth in incomplete months, nature has changed in this matter, as we find in several things (Tosafot Chullin 47a, Avodah Zarah 24a, and Moed Katan 11a).

If the child dies within 30 days and we do not know if its months were completed, she is not believed to say that its months were completed and exempt herself from chalitzah. She is only believed not to perform yibbum, but to marry in the marketplace, she is not believed. For even to testify about another she is not believed, as we require valid witnesses, and all the more so she is not believed about herself. She is only believed to say "my husband died" due to the reasoning that she is careful and marries, as stated in Siman 17. She is not believed to say "my yavam died" to marry in the marketplace (Yevamot 16:15). Similarly, she is not believed to say that the months were completed. However, if the husband, during his lifetime, said that he knows the months were completed, he is believed, as the Torah grants credibility to the father concerning his children (see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 5).

A yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage) who married an outsider, and witnesses testify that the child she bore after her husband's death lived for 30 days, but other witnesses contradict them and say that the child did not live for 30 days. Nevertheless, she is permitted to her husband and does not need chalitza (ritual release from levirate marriage). For although we hold that when there are two sets of witnesses contradicting each other from the Torah perspective, we maintain the status quo, and when there is a presumption of permissibility, she is permitted. Rabbinically, she would be forbidden. However, in this case, since from the Torah she is permitted according to everyone, and the prohibition is only rabbinic, as I have written, she is even rabbinically permitted when there is a presumption of permissibility. Here, there is also a majority which is stronger than a presumption, as most women give birth after nine months, and the child is presumed to be viable. It appears to me that this applies specifically when the contradicting witnesses do not mention any defect in the child other than that it did not live for 30 days. But if they mention some defect, such as saying that its hair and nails were not fully developed, then even from the Torah she would be forbidden according to their words, and she would need chalitza. (This is also implied in the Beit Shmuel, section 9).

Certainly! Here is the translation of the provided passage from the Aruch Hashulchan:

"And all the more so if there are no witnesses that he did not live for 30 days, but merely a rumor, since she has already married, we do not concern ourselves with it, even when there are no witnesses that he lived for 30 days, for we do not concern ourselves with a rumor that arises after marriage. However, if it is before marriage, we do not allow her to marry until the matter is clarified. Similarly, after marriage, if there are witnesses who testify that he did not live for 30 days, and there are no other witnesses to contradict them, she requires chalitzah if she is the wife of an Israelite and is living with her husband. This will be explained in Siman 164. One should not ask, if so, why in the previous section she does not require chalitzah since she is permitted to live with her husband. However, the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote in his responsa (Klal 52) that nevertheless, we are concerned about the rumor because some say that the child of a yevamah (a widow awaiting levirate marriage) who marries someone from the marketplace is a rabbinic mamzer, and they will spread a rumor about her children from the second husband. Only in a case where, according to the law, she must perform chalitzah, as in Siman 164, do we not consider the rumor. This is not the case when, according to the law, she does not need chalitzah; we are concerned about the rumor regarding her children."

The Tur writes: One who says "This is my son" or "I have children" is believed to exempt his wife from levirate marriage (yibbum), even if he was previously known to have brothers. Even if witnesses later come and testify that he has brothers, she is permitted. However, if there are witnesses that he has brothers, he is not believed to say "I have children" to permit her. If he said at the time of betrothal "I have children" and later, at the time of death, he said "I have no children," he is not believed to prohibit her. The Ramah writes that she performs chalitzah and does not enter into levirate marriage. And in Siman 157, it is written: If he was not known to have brothers and he said "I have brothers," he is not believed. If someone comes and says "I am his brother," he is not believed. Even if one witness testifies that he is his brother, he is not believed to remove her from her presumption (that she is free). If he was known to have brothers and he said "I have no brothers," or if he said about someone who was known to be his brother that he is not his brother, the Razah writes that he is believed to permit her. However, the Rambam writes that he is not believed, and this is also the opinion of Rav Alfas, and this is the conclusion of the Rosh, of blessed memory.

Explaining his words: This, that he says "This is my son" or "I have children," even if he is already established as having brothers, he is believed to exempt her [from yibbum] due to the principle of "migo," for he could divorce her and thereby exempt her from yibbum. Therefore, even though she is presumed to be bound to yibbum, he is believed to exempt her because of the "migo." And although the principle of "migo" in the face of a presumption is a matter of debate and unresolved in the Talmud (Bava Batra 5a), this is only when the "migo" contradicts the presumption. But here, the "migo" does not contradict the presumption, as it is true that he has brothers according to the presumption, but he also has children. Therefore, he is believed because of the "migo" (Nimukei Yosef on Bava Batra, Chapter 8). According to this explanation, if he says "I have no brothers," he is not believed based on this "migo" because we would need to believe him due to the "migo" and it would contradict the presumption, which is a matter of doubt in the law. Therefore, he is not believed to permit her to the general public. Similarly, if he was presumed not to have children, he is also not believed to say "I have children" because it contradicts the presumption.

Furthermore, it can be explained that this is not comparable to any "migo" in the face of a presumption, as when the "migo" is only because he could make another claim, it is not strong enough to overturn the presumption. However, here the "migo" is because of something within his power to do, and it is considerably strong to overturn the presumption (Ran on Kiddushin, Chapter 3). And it is established in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 127, that a single witness is believed in matters within his power to do, even in matters with a presumption of prohibition. Therefore, also in such a "migo," he is believed to overturn the presumption. According to this explanation, he is also believed to say "I have no brothers," and he is also believed to say "I have children" even when he is presumed not to have children.

There is another question regarding this matter: How can he be believed with a "migo" (a legal presumption based on his ability to take another action)? For if he were to divorce her, she would be forbidden to a Kohen. And based on this "migo," we are permitting her to the general public as a widow who is not bound to a yavam, and therefore also permitted to a Kohen. Therefore, some say that she is also forbidden to a Kohen, as with any "migo" that does not grant more power to the claim than the "migo" itself. This is explicitly stated in the Gemara in Bava Batra (70b) and as explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 296. However, the Ramban writes that she is permitted to a Kohen, for he (the husband) does not care if she becomes forbidden to the priesthood or not. This "migo" is not weak in his case because his main desire is only that she should not be bound to the yavam, and he can divorce her and she can marry an Israelite. When they come before us, we are compelled to believe them that she is not bound to the yavam, and consequently, since she is not bound, she is permitted to the priesthood (Ramban, Bava Batra 134b). This also seems to be the opinion of Tosafot and the Nimukei Yosef there (and so writes the Maggid Mishneh in the third chapter of Yibbum). Also, there is no question as to how he is believed with this "migo" of being able to divorce her, given that we hold in Siman 152 that a husband who says he divorced his wife is not believed even if he has this "migo." The difference there is that there is a contradiction to his claim that he divorced her since there is no public knowledge of the divorce, as explained there. But here, this does not apply because if he were to divorce her, there would indeed be public knowledge, and we believe him because he has the power to divorce her.

In this way, the words of the Tur are explained. He ruled that if someone says, "I have children," he is believed even if it is established that he has brothers. There is no dispute about this because, even according to the first explanation, he is believed since he does not contradict the presumption. This is specifically when it is not established that he does not have children, as stated in Siman 157, when someone says, "I have no brothers." The Rif, the Rosh, and the Rambam wrote that he is not believed because he contradicts the presumption, while the Ra’avad ruled that he is believed because he holds like the second explanation we wrote, that this "migo" (legal presumption) is strong enough to overturn the presumption. According to this, if it is established that he has no children and he says, "I have children," he is also believed, as we wrote. It seems to me that the Rashba in his novellae to Kiddushin holds the same, as he wrote similarly to the second explanation. There is a doubt according to those who prohibit: if he says, "I had brothers when I married her, and now they have died," is he believed because he does not contradict the original presumption, or perhaps, since it was established that he had brothers, he is not believed to overturn the presumption even in such a case? From the language of the poskim, it seems that in any case, he is not believed. (And know that it appears from Rashi and Tosafot in Kiddushin there, who explained that the dispute between Rabbi and Rav Nachman is only when he contradicts himself from the time of death to the marriage, but if he does not contradict, even Rav Nachman agrees, therefore even if we rule like Rav Nachman, he is also believed according to the Ra’avad. However, there is no proof, as it can be said that they hold like the Ramban wrote to the Rif, that we do not rule like Abaye's explanation, and if it is established that he has brothers, he is never believed to say he has no brothers. Thus, in practice, he is not believed. Investigate this thoroughly.)

And this is what the Tur wrote: that when there are witnesses that he has brothers, he is not believed to say that he has sons. The reason is that since his main credibility is due to "miggo" as stated, it only works against a presumption and not against witnesses. And even though this is not like "miggo" in the presence of witnesses, where he is not contradicting the words of the witnesses, nevertheless, since through the witnesses she is presumed prohibited, he is not believed with his "miggo" to remove her from the prohibition. And this is also clarified from the words of Rashi and Rashbam there, see there. And this is what he wrote: that if witnesses later come and say that he has brothers, she is permitted. The reason is simple: since at the time of the act she was permitted due to "miggo" and these witnesses are not testifying against his claim, she remains in her presumed permitted status as before, as if it had been established that he has sons and she is permitted to remarry.

And know that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 6, wrote this law in the name of certain authorities, and this is his language: "And some say that if there are witnesses that he has brothers, he is not believed afterwards to say that he has sons." And it appears that there is someone who disagrees with this, but we do not see explicitly who disagrees. He follows his own reasoning in his major work that the Rambam disagrees with this, and it requires further investigation because the Rambam does not speak at all when there are witnesses (Beit Shmuel, section 11). However, his intention is clear from what the Rambam wrote at the beginning of Chapter 3 of Yibbum, where he states generally that one who says "I have sons" is believed, and it is explicitly understood that this applies to everyone. And if it were thought that one who has brothers is not believed, the Rambam should have explained this as it is explained in the Talmud. And most people have brothers, so how could he make such a general statement? Rather, it is certain that he holds that since this does not contradict the fact that he has brothers, even if there are witnesses and even if the brothers are present, he is believed. And in the Talmud (Bava Batra there), which says that although he is established to us as having brothers, he is believed, it does not explain like Rashi and Rashbam that he is only believed when he is established and not with witnesses, but because according to the Talmud there, it must be said so. Refer there, but the same applies when there are witnesses.

And this is what the Tur wrote: If a man said at the time of the betrothal, "I have children," and then later said at the time of his death, "I do not have children," he is not believed to prohibit her (the widow from remarrying without halitzah). And the Ra'avan, etc., concluded his words. This also refers to a case when it is known that he has brothers and it is not known that he has children. He is believed when he said, "I have children," as was explained. Therefore, he is not believed to say, "I do not have children." There is a great novelty in this: Even though one might argue that he should not be believed at the time of the betrothal because he says so intentionally so that she will marry him and not worry about falling to yibbum (levirate marriage), and conversely, one might think he should be believed at the time of his death since one could say he speaks the truth so as not to cause her to transgress the prohibition of yevamah le-shuk (a widow marrying someone other than her brother-in-law), nevertheless he is not believed. The reason is that since the Sages believed him initially because of migo (a legal presumption that one who could have lied more effectively is telling the truth), as it was said, it is as if it was established that she is not bound to yibbum, and he is not believed to change this presumption. All the more so if the first statement was not at the time of betrothal and the last statement was not at the time of his death, he is not believed. However, the Ra'avan was stringent in this matter and ruled that she should perform halitzah and not yibbum, because perhaps since he said it at the time of his death, we should believe him to be stringent. This is a dispute in the Gemara there (and the first opinion is according to Rabbi, and the Ra'avan is concerned that the law might follow Rabbi Natan, see there in Kiddushin 64).

And know that what was explained, that he said at the time of the betrothal, does not mean that he betrothed her on this condition, for if it were so, there would be no doubt in this matter at all. For, if he has no children, the betrothal is nothing, and if he has children, she is not obligated to perform yibbum (levirate marriage). Rather, it means that he said this to her at the time of concluding the matter, that they became engaged, but the betrothal itself was without any condition. And there is doubt according to the first opinion that he is not believed to retract, specifically when he says that he never had children. But if he says that they died after the betrothal, he is believed since he is not contradicting his previous statement. Or it is possible that even in this case, he is not believed, because since she was established in a state of permissibility, he is not believed to prohibit her. And this seems to be the implication from the language of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), and as I wrote in section 25 regarding brothers, and the words of the Tur regarding brothers will be explained in Siman 157, with the help of Heaven.

Maimonides (Chapter 20), the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch in section 8 wrote that a single witness is believed to testify that the husband has a son to permit her to marry others. Our master, the Rema, wrote that there are those who disagree, end quote. And behold, the opinion of Maimonides is that just as a single witness is believed to testify that her husband died and she may perform yibbum (levirate marriage) or that her yavam (levir) died and she may marry others, so too he is believed to say that he has a son and she may marry others. And according to this, for those who hold that a single witness is not believed to say that her yavam died and she may marry others, he is also not believed in this case. Therefore, Maimonides, who rules there that in the case of the yavam's death he is believed, and similarly our master the Beit Yosef in section 158, ruled that he is also believed in this case. Our master the Rema, who ruled there that he is not believed, also ruled here that he is not believed. However, this raises a difficulty on the Tur, who ruled here that he is believed and there that he is not believed, refer to there (as it is an unresolved issue as written there).

It appears to me that the laws are not dependent on one another. Even according to those who hold that when it comes to the death of a yavam (levirate husband), one witness is believed, it is still possible that regarding whether he has a son, one witness is not believed. This is the opinion of the Raavad in the third chapter of Yibum (levirate marriage), who holds that in that case, one witness is believed because it is a matter that will eventually be revealed. When the yavam comes and he is alive, his falsehood will be exposed before everyone. However, regarding whether he has a son, it will never be clarified. If it is clarified that in a certain place he does not have a son, he can say that the son is in another place, and vice versa. Even if we say that regarding the death of a yavam one witness is not believed, it is possible that here he is believed. Specifically, when she remains definitely bound (to the yavam), one witness is not believed to remove her from her presumed status of being bound. However, when she is not definitely bound, only doubtfully bound, and the witness testifies that she is not bound at all, it is possible that he is believed. The witness is not considered less reliable than the husband himself, who is believed by virtue of a "migu" (a legal presumption) to say that he has a son, as it is written. Similarly, the witness, although a "migu" does not apply to him, is still not considered less reliable than the party himself. It seems to me that this is the opinion of the Tur (and this resolves the question of the Beit Shmuel in subparagraph 14 and the "Avnei Miluim" and "Pitchei Teshuva". According to what I wrote, it is clear). There is an opinion that the Tur's intention is when the husband went with one wife to a distant land, and therefore one witness is believed because most women conceive and give birth, and the majority supports him (there). However, it is impossible to say so, because if so, the Tur should have specified that only in such a case one witness is believed. Additionally, the Tur brought this in the name of the Rambam, and according to the Rambam, it is obvious that in all cases one witness is believed, as he included this law with the death of the husband and the death of the yavam. Moreover, in such a case the Raavad would not have disagreed with him. Therefore, it seems to me as I have written.

Maimonides wrote (there): One who has relations with a woman, whether she is single or married, and she becomes pregnant, and he says, "This fetus is from me," and even if she agrees with him, although he is considered his son concerning inheritance, he is doubtful concerning yibbum (levirate marriage). Just as she committed adultery with this man, she could have done so with another. How can it be known for certain that this is his son? He has no presumption of legitimacy, and he is always considered doubtful. Therefore, we rule stringently: she must perform chalitzah (a ceremony that releases her from yibbum) and not yibbum. This is the essence of his words. When it is stated that one who says "This is my son" is believed, it refers to when he says it is the son of his wife. But in the case of adultery, how can it be known that she did not also commit adultery with another man? And certainly, in the case of a married woman, most relations are presumed to be with her husband. Therefore, when he is believed to say, "This is my son," it is based on the principle of miggo (a Talmudic principle that allows someone to be believed if they could have made a more advantageous claim), as he could exempt her with a get (divorce document). However, this principle only works to believe him regarding his claim. Hence, with his wife, when he says, "This is my son," and we believe him, there remains no suspicion. But with a prostitute, although we believe him, how can it be known that she did not also commit adultery with another man?

The Tur, in the name of the Rosh, was astonished at his words, for since, according to his opinion, it is a doubt, why should he inherit? And some say that in matters of inheritance, he is believed because he has the ability to give it to him during his lifetime (Gra, note 29). It seems to me that this is only when the father says that he should inherit; he is believed for this reason. But here, the Rambam ruled that he inherits automatically even without his command. The Rosh rightly questioned that if he is certainly not his son, why should he inherit and take away from the definite brothers? Furthermore, it is puzzling, for in the Talmud, Ketubot (14a), it is explicitly proven that in the case of a betrothed couple, when both admit, she is believed. There are those who wish to say that a betrothed couple is different because she is his wife, unlike a regular unmarried woman (Kesef Mishneh, chapter 56). But this is not so, for in the Talmud, Yevamot (chapter 7), it is explicitly proven that they are equal in this respect (and this is the intention of the Maggid Mishneh). Additionally, it is difficult because the Rambam himself ruled in chapter 8 of Terumot, law 14, that if a priest forced or seduced a daughter of Israel and had relations with her, and she gave birth, if we have not heard that she had relations with another and she is not suspected of having relations with others, the child follows his status, and she eats terumah because of her son. Similarly, he ruled in chapter 15 of Issurei Biah, law 17, that if a betrothed woman became pregnant and she says it is from her betrothed and he does not deny it, she is believed, and all the more so if he explicitly says it is from him. Some wish to say that the Rambam is referring to terumah in the present time, which is rabbinic, and in forbidden relations, where we do not consider him a definite mamzer, it is also rabbinic because, according to Torah law, a doubtful mamzer is permitted to enter the congregation (Bach and Beit Shmuel, note 16). But these words have no basis, for in such a case, he would not have left it ambiguous but would have explained it, and this is not his usual manner. It is explicitly clear from his words that he wrote it according to the fundamental law and not because it is rabbinic. Moreover, the idea that a doubtful mamzer is permitted by Torah law is not in most cases of invalids, and the Rambam permits in all cases, so it is a Torah matter (see Beit Shmuel there).

In truth, the opinion of the Rashba and the Rosh is that whenever he has had relations with her and it is not known that another man has had relations with her, and both admit that the child is his, she is exempt from chalitza and yibum. The Maggid Mishneh also agrees with this if she is not suspected of having relations with others. Nevertheless, our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 9, wrote only the opinion of the Rambam, but they added that if they were imprisoned together, and it is certain that the child is his, she is exempt, which is straightforward. Additionally, they wrote that there are those who say that if she is a prostitute exclusively for him, she is also exempt, and it is possible that in this case, even the Rambam agrees, as the Tur wrote there. However, there are those who disagree with this (see Beit Shmuel, section 16, and the Gra, section 30).

In explaining the reasoning of the Rambam, it seems to me that his words are clear, that we have no basis to exempt her (the woman) because it has already been explained in Siman 4, Se'if 31, that the reason a woman is believed to render her child kosher is due to her presumption of propriety, and also because a woman who engages in illicit relations checks herself beforehand. And there in Se'if 32, it is explained that she is not believed to establish that the child is from a specific man if he does not acknowledge that it is his, and regarding forbidden relations, the Rambam only wrote that she is believed to render the child kosher, but not to establish him as the son of a specific man. And in the context of terumot, it is mentioned that she is believed to allow him to eat terumah because we know that he had relations with her, as explained there, and he is believed to feed him terumah because he has the capacity to feed him. This is explained in the Talmud (Ketubot 25b). Thus, it is clear that due to her credibility, she certainly cannot exempt him from yibbum (levirate marriage), because she is only believed to render the child kosher, not to establish him as the son of a specific man. And because of the father's credibility, there is also no exemption, as it has already been explained in this Siman that the reason we believe the father to say "this is my son" to exempt from yibbum is due to a "migu" (a type of legal argument) that he has the power to divorce her. Similarly in terumah, as it is mentioned, he has the power to feed him terumah and to bequeath to him because he has the power to give it to him, and even if he does not explicitly state that he will bequeath to him, nevertheless, since he says that he is his son, why should he not be believed regarding his own matters? But to exempt from yibbum based on the woman's assertion that she did not have relations with another man is not applicable to a migu, because every migu is only credibility regarding the claim that he asserts, and here, even if we believe him that he had relations with her, it is not applicable to believe him that no one else had relations with her, since he himself does not know this. He only believes her, and she is not believed as we have explained. This is why the Rambam was precise in his words, "and how would he know, etc." meaning that she is not believed for this, and he relies only on her credibility.

And even if we do not scrutinize so closely, it is clear that while it is true that both are believed to maintain the child’s status regarding all matters of validity, nevertheless, it is obvious that in terms of taking away from others, they are not believed. For we do not find in any place that the litigants themselves have the ability to remove someone from their status without witnesses. And here, the Torah has granted his brother the right to marry his wife if he dies without children. How can they annul the brother’s right based on their own words when there are no witnesses and no presumption in the matter? And if it is because of the principle of "miggo" that he could divorce her, we have explained that there is no "miggo" here. And even though there is no right for the brother here, since we do not allow her to perform the levirate marriage due to the doubt that perhaps her words are true and he might violate a prohibition, his right is not annulled. Therefore, she must perform the chalitzah and not the levirate marriage. And do not question how this child can then inherit a portion, for this is due to the "miggo" that he could give it to him. Additionally, regarding his own property, he is certainly believed, but not regarding others. However, when he says, "This is my son from my wife," there is both a "miggo" and a presumption that she did not commit adultery with another man, as all Jewish women are presumed to be of good character. This is not the case with this promiscuous woman, who has lost her presumption of good character and has committed adultery with another man as well (and this is the presumption mentioned by the Rambam).

If a woman’s husband and son went overseas and people came and told her that her husband died, she is permitted to remarry and we do not worry that perhaps the son died first, which would obligate her to perform yibbum (levirate marriage). We assume that the son is still alive, and we do not concern ourselves with the possibility that he may have died. However, if she, her husband, and her son went overseas, and she came and said, "My husband died, and afterwards my son died, and I am permitted to remarry," she is believed, since when she left, she was presumed permitted to remarry (Rashi). Additionally, she has a "migo" (a legal presumption) that if she wished, she could have said "My husband died" and remained silent about the son (Tosafot), and thus we would assume the son is still alive. 

But if she said, "My son died, and afterward my husband died, and I am permitted to perform yibbum," she is not believed to perform yibbum. Instead, she must perform chalitzah (a formal ceremony releasing her from yibbum), not yibbum itself, because she is removing herself from her previous status and without chalitzah, she would not be able to remarry freely (Rashi). However, if two witnesses testify to this sequence of events, she is permitted to perform yibbum. Regarding the testimony of a single witness, there is a dispute, which will be clarified in section 158, with God's help.

Some say that her credibility to declare "my husband died and afterwards my son died" is specifically when there is no rumor of their deaths, but when there is a rumor, she is not believed (Hamaor, Chapter 10 of Yevamot). According to both reasons previously explained, she is not believed. According to the first reason, because she was presumed to be permitted to remarry, now that it is heard that both have died and it is unknown who died first, she is not presumed to be permitted, as perhaps the son died first.
