According to the second reason, due to the principle of "migo," we have explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 82, in the rules of "migo," that "migo" does not apply in the presence of a rumor, especially when the rumor is widespread (and similarly in Beit Shmuel, Subsection 16, which contradicts Nodah BiYehuda, Choshen Mishpat, Siman 30; see there). Also, see what we wrote in Section 42.

And if one witness knows about their deaths, whether she is believed to say "my husband died and afterward my son died" — the great scholars of the generation have disputed this based on an incident that occurred after the decrees of 5408 (1648). Some wanted to prohibit her from remarrying without chalitza (a ritual to release her from the obligation to marry her brother-in-law) on the grounds that there is no reason to believe her because she fears the witness and is compelled to say that the son also died. The Taz (Rabbi David HaLevi Segal), of blessed memory, elaborated in this section to permit her for two reasons: 

First, on the contrary, since she fears the witness, presumably she is not lying so that the witness does not contradict her. And furthermore, one witness is not significant, as one witness is not believed to prohibit and to remove something from its status of being permitted, as explained in Yoreh De'ah section 127. According to this reasoning, one should not question that in a matter that tends to be revealed, even one witness is believed, as explained everywhere. One could say that if so, she is also believed for this reason. 

There are those who challenged this from what will be explained in section 158 regarding if she has a son and one witness testified that the son died and afterward the husband died, that she is permitted to perform yibbum (levirate marriage). Here, the witness removes the prohibition status regarding the yavam (brother-in-law) and allows her. If so, the same should apply in the reverse: that the witness removes her from the status of being permitted to the marketplace and puts her into prohibition (this is the intention of the Beit Shmuel at the end of sub-section 16). 

However, this is not a comparison because there, the entire permission is based on the witness, as she does not know if her husband died, and it is permitted based on the witness who testifies that her husband died. Consequently, he is also believed to permit her to the yavam. This is not the case here, where she herself says "my husband died" and is believed, and she has the presumption of being permitted to the marketplace. The witness cannot remove her from her presumption (the magi'ah in the Taz). 

Nevertheless, it seems to me in practice that she should not remarry in the marketplace until the matter is clarified, for we hold that whenever it is possible to clarify, we clarify. It is obvious that this matter can be clarified about who died first. However, when it is not possible to clarify, the ruling appears to be in accordance with the Taz, of blessed memory.

It is a halachic rule that if her husband went overseas and they had no children, and she came and said, "I had a son overseas and he died, and afterwards my husband died, and I am obligated to perform yibbum (levirate marriage)," she is believed, for she left with this presumption. However, if she said, "My husband died first and then my son, and I am permitted to remarry," she is not believed because she is removing herself from her previous presumption. Nevertheless, we are concerned about her words, so she should not perform yibbum but rather chalitzah (the ceremony to release her from levirate marriage) and not yibbum. (Mishnah, Chapter 16)

And some of our rabbis have written that it is specifically when there are witnesses that both have died, but otherwise, she is believed to say, "My husband died and afterward my son," with the presumption that she could have said, "I had a son and he is alive," as the majority supports her, for most women conceive and give birth (Tosafot Ketubot 119a, s.v. "Amai"). And there are those who question this, saying that if so, why is she believed to say, "My son died and afterward my husband," since there are witnesses and she is not presumed to be bound to the levir (Maharam). Furthermore, it can be questioned that even without witnesses, why is she believed to say, "My son died and afterward my husband," let us assert that most women conceive and give birth, and she stands in the presumption of being permitted to the marketplace, so how is she believed against the majority to undergo yibbum (levirate marriage)? Indeed, the Rashba raised this question in his commentaries there and answered that since she left without children and returned without children, she has not left her initial presumption. In other words, in this case, we do not follow the majority because she is presently before us not among the majority of women, and even while she was here, she was not among the majority of women. Therefore, we follow her previous presumption. According to this, even without witnesses, she is not believed to say, "My husband died and afterward my son," because she does not have the presumption we mentioned, since she is before us in the presumption of not being among the majority, as we have explained.

We must say that our rabbis hold that when there are witnesses that both (the husband and the child) have died, it would be logical to say that she should be believed in whatever she says, because she fears being contradicted by the witnesses, as the Taz posits, which we have written in paragraph 39. Nevertheless, when she contradicts her original presumption that was before us, we do not rely on this reasoning in the place of a presumption. Therefore, when she says, "My son died first, and then my husband," she is believed, as she maintains her original presumption that was before us. Even though when there are witnesses, she is not presumed to be bound for levirate marriage, it is not the same, because the witnesses also say that both have died, and she fears lying, as we have written. But when she says, "My husband died first, and then my son," thereby removing herself from her original presumption, she is not believed, because her fearfulness does not override her previous presumption. 

When there are no witnesses, it is considered a strong majority, because even though the child is not before us, it is still possible that he is elsewhere. Therefore, she is believed even to remove herself from her presumption, such as when she says, "My husband died first, and then my son," because the majority is stronger than the presumption. She has a "migo" (a reason to be believed) since she could have said that her son is still alive. Likewise, she is believed to uphold the presumption and say, "My son died first, and then my husband," even though it is against the majority. Nevertheless, since the sages granted a woman credibility to say "My husband died" so that she can remarry, and "My husband died" so that she can enter levirate marriage, from the reason of "she examines," as we have written in Siman 17, and they did not worry about the presumption of the husband's life, as we wrote there. Therefore, they believed her in all that she says for this reason and did not consider the majority either. 

Certainly, when she has the presumption of levirate marriage, she is believed. However, all this is true if we do not say the reasoning of "combining the minority with the presumption," which would weaken the majority. But if we do say this reasoning, she is not believed to remove herself from her previous presumption and to say, "My husband died first, and then my son," because we say to combine the minority of miscarriages with the previous presumption of being bound for levirate marriage, and this weakens the majority that most women conceive and give birth. This will be explained shortly whether we say this reasoning or not (and the Tosafot might have written this not according to the conclusion of the last chapter of "The Woman" - see there and the Beit Meir in Siman 17 and Siman 40, and according to what we have written, everything is clear and understand it well).

It is stated in the Gemara (there) that the case we mentioned, where a woman says "I was given a son and then my husband died and afterward my son died," we are concerned about her statement, and she performs chalitzah and does not enter into levirate marriage (yibbum). This applies specifically when she is already disqualified from marrying a Kohen, even without this chalitzah, such as if she is a divorcee or similar. But if until now she was fit to marry a Kohen, she does not perform chalitzah unless she says that she and her husband were in a hidden place where there were no witnesses. Otherwise, she should not perform chalitzah until the matter becomes clear. The reason is that we are concerned that witnesses might come and testify that she spoke the truth and that she is permitted to marry anyone and did not need chalitzah. We would then need to announce that she is fit to marry a Kohen. However, there may be people who saw the chalitzah but did not hear the announcement, and when they see her marrying a Kohen, they might say that a woman who performed chalitzah is permitted to a Kohen. Therefore, she should not perform chalitzah and should not enter into levirate marriage but should remain in the presumed status of being bound (to the levir) until witnesses come and clarify the matter. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Section 12 brought this ruling, and Maimonides also wrote this in Chapter 3. This is not found in the Rif and the Rosh, but it seems to me that they do not disagree on this matter and only relied on what is stated later in the last chapter of Yevamot. Consequently, this ruling applies here as well (and unnecessarily, the Beit Shmuel struggled with this in Section 17).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 3, Law 16: Similarly, a woman whose husband and her co-wife went overseas, and two people come and tell her that her husband has died, she should neither perform chalitzah nor yibbum forever until it is known whether her co-wife has given birth or not. Why shouldn't she perform chalitzah after nine months from the husband's death and be permitted to marry a non-priest at least? Because if her co-wife has given birth, she is exempt, and if she has not given birth, she performed chalitzah. There is a decree lest it be discovered after the chalitzah that her co-wife gave birth to a viable child, and this woman would be found not to have needed chalitzah, and she might marry a priest after performing chalitzah. An observer who did not know about the witnesses that came might say that a woman who has performed chalitzah is permitted to marry a priest, and he would testify that he saw her permitted to marry into the priesthood by the court. Therefore, if she was originally forbidden to marry a priest, she should perform chalitzah after nine months and marry a non-priest. But this co-wife who was with her husband when he died should wait ninety days like other yevamot and then perform chalitzah or yibbum, without concern for her co-wife in another country since her husband was not with her in that country. So wrote Maimonides, and in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 13, they abbreviated this and omitted the end completely.

And behold, regarding the fundamental principle of this law, there is a significant question. The Mishnah at the beginning of Chapter 16 of Yevamot states that she should neither perform chalitzah nor yibbum. The Gemara there asks why she should not marry into the general populace, since we follow the majority of women who conceive and give birth, and presumably her co-wife gave birth, thus permitting her to marry into the general populace. The Gemara answers that this follows the opinion of Rabbi Meir, who is concerned about the minority. However, we do not rule according to Rabbi Meir. If so, why do we rule like our Mishnah? Even according to what the Gemara concludes there—that in this case, the majority permits her to marry into the general populace, as mentioned, and against this, there is a presumption (chazakah) for yibbum since here he did not have a son—majority is preferable to presumption. But we say that there is a minority of women who miscarry, and the minority combined with the presumption makes it as if it is an even doubt (safek). Therefore, she should neither marry into the general populace nor perform yibbum. Rashi and Tosafot there explain that this is also only according to Rabbi Meir, who considers the minority significant, but according to the Rabbis, we do not combine the minority with the presumption because the minority is considered as if it does not exist. Still, we should not rule like our Mishnah (Yam Shel Shlomo there, Chapter 2). It must be said that Rambam, Rif, Rosh, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch, who ruled like the Mishnah, hold that the reasoning of combining the minority with the presumption is also according to the Rabbis.

The Rashba similarly writes there that this is the opinion of the Rif and the Rambam, and he wrote that there are texts that explicitly state this, that this is also according to the Rabbis. Similarly, Rav Hai Gaon wrote this there. And there is proof for this, as in Kiddushin, Chullin, and Niddah (18a), the Talmud says that Rabbi Meir holds that a minority combined with a presumption weakens a majority. And here we say that it is a fifty-fifty situation. Our Rabbis, the Tosafists, struggled in all these places to differentiate according to their approach that even here it is according to Rabbi Meir. But according to the Rif and the Rambam, it is straightforward because here it is according to the Rabbis. And in practice, it could be that the Tosafists also agree with this, as they wrote in Bekhorot (20a) that even the Rabbis are concerned about combining a minority with a presumption to be stringent. They wrote there in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, of blessed memory, that therefore milk does not exempt from the firstborn status. The Rif and the Rambam ruled that milk does exempt, and it can be said that their reason is because there is a presumption that supports the majority to establish the offspring in a status of non-sacred as it was in the womb, as the Tosafot wrote there. Additionally, the presumption that an animal has not given birth is not a strong presumption because it is common for animals to give birth.

However, there is a question regarding this matter: if so, how can a single person be trusted concerning slaughter based on the principle that most who are involved in slaughtering are experts? Shouldn't we say to combine the minority with the presumption and thus weaken the majority, or it would be fifty-fifty? And indeed, some of the early authorities said that when it is stated that most who are involved in slaughtering are experts, it does not mean the majority but rather all of them. Similarly, Tosafot in Bechorot there states that this majority is a majority and prevalent. However, even without this, it is understandable based on what the Rashba and Ritva wrote here: when do we say to combine the minority with the presumption? It is when the minority diverges from the majority itself, such as here where most women conceive and give birth, from which there is a minority that conceives and miscarries. But regarding a minority that does not diverge from the majority, such as in slaughtering where the majority are experts and a minority are not experts, from the majority of experts the minority does not diverge. We do not say to combine the minority with the presumption. Therefore, the Talmud does not state here that there is a minority of women who do not conceive, because this minority does not diverge from the majority. (The Rashba and Ritva wrote this concerning a child found next to dough, where most children handle dough. And accordingly, this applies to slaughter as well, as is evident. Similarly, R. Yom Tov Algazi wrote this in Bechorot there. Ramban, of blessed memory, has a different approach on this matter, see there in the Rashba.)

A woman whose husband went overseas and died there, and he has no children, leaving her bound to the levirate marriage (yibbum), and a rumor spread that he took a wife abroad, the Rivash ruled in his responsa (Siman 509) that she is forbidden to undergo yibbum until it is clearly confirmed, even though the rumor was not established in a court, due to the severe prohibition involved. However, she is permitted to perform chalitzah immediately since the rumor was not confirmed in a court. For, although if it were known that he indeed had a wife abroad, she would not be allowed to perform chalitzah, as mentioned, it is a minor prohibition and we do not take it into account. But in the case of a Torah prohibition, we are concerned about the rumor, as will be explained in Siman 157.

Who is considered a brother for the purpose of Yibbum, and it contains 27 sections:
The brother who performs Yibbum (levirate marriage) with the wife of his brother who died without offspring must specifically be his paternal brother, even if they do not share the same mother. However, his maternal brother, who does not share the same father, is forbidden to perform Yibbum, and she remains prohibited to him as a forbidden relative, just as she was during his brother's lifetime. This is derived through a Gezeirah Shavah (a hermeneutical principle) from the sons of Jacob. Regarding Yibbum, it is written: "When brothers dwell together," and concerning the sons of Jacob, it is written: "We, your servants, are twelve brothers, sons of one man, etc." The term "brothers" is superfluous, for since it says "sons of one man," it is evident that they are brothers. Rather, it comes to teach about the brothers mentioned in Yibbum, that this brotherhood is like that of the sons of Jacob, who were from one father even though they were not from one mother, as the sons of Jacob were not from the same mother. All the more so if they share the same mother as well (Yevamot 17b). Even if his brother is a mamzer (a child born from certain forbidden relationships) or a completely wicked person, he is obligated to perform Yibbum, for in this matter, we do not derive from the sons of Jacob that they must be righteous like them; we only learn about the definition of brotherhood and not about their qualities. However, if he has a brother who is the son of a maidservant or a non-Jewish woman, meaning his father had relations with a maidservant or a non-Jewish woman and fathered a son from her, he is not obligated to perform Yibbum, for he is not considered related to him paternally but maternally, as is written regarding a son in Siman 156. Consequently, in the case of a maidservant, there is a doubt, and she performs Chalitzah (a ceremony releasing her from Yibbum) and does not perform Yibbum, as is written there regarding a son due to the concern that maybe she was freed. And this brother from a maidservant does not obligate Yibbum even if she was freed when she conceived and married, for his conception was not in sanctity, even though his birth was in sanctity, he does not obligate Yibbum, for the main lineage after the father is from the time of conception, and so it is with a non-Jewish woman.

It is written, "When brothers dwell together," and the tradition teaches that this specifically applies when they had a common dwelling in the world, meaning that the brother was born while the other brother was still alive. This excludes the case where he was born after the brother's death, as he does not obligate his brother's wife to perform levirate marriage (yibbum). This is referred to in the Gemara as "the wife of a brother who was not in his world," meaning that he was not yet in the world at the time when the deceased brother was in the world. However, if he was born during the brother's lifetime, even if the deceased was sick or dying, and this brother was born—even if only his head and the majority of his body emerged from the womb—he is considered to have been in his world and obligates his brother's wife to perform yibbum. She must wait until he matures. Even if this newborn is sick, injured, or dying and cannot live, she is forbidden to marry until he dies. As long as he is alive, she is considered bound to perform yibbum. Note that if the brother is a mamzer (illegitimate child), he obligates yibbum if the father was with the mother of the mamzer, both being incarcerated, and he did not cohabit with her afterward. Otherwise, there is doubt whether he is his brother, and she must perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from yibbum) and not yibbum (as stated in Beit Shmuel, section 1). Although a mamzer is generally not permitted to perform yibbum with a Jewish woman, there is a practical difference when she is also a mamzeret, as he is permitted to perform yibbum with her. In cases of doubt regarding a mamzer, this does not apply.

The halacha has been established in the Gemara (39b) that to testify regarding a brother being the paternal brother of the deceased, there is no need for kosher witnesses; rather, even a relative or a woman is believed to testify. The reason is that this is merely a revelation of a matter that is destined to be revealed, and people do not lie about something that is destined to be revealed. The Rambam writes in Chapter 4 of Hilchot Yibum that even a slave or a maidservant is believed to testify in this matter because, according to the aforementioned reasoning, there is no difference in this regard. Similarly, even a minor, if he is intelligent and recognizes them, is believed to say that this person is the brother of that person, and this is the wife of the deceased. Therefore, based on his testimony, chalitzah or yibbum is performed. Since there is no need for two witnesses and no need for kosher witnesses, everyone is believed regarding this matter, whether to testify that this is the brother of the deceased or to testify that this woman is the wife of the deceased. Even hearsay testimony is believed in this matter since there is no formal requirement for testimony in this case (Beit Shmuel Section 2). Nonetheless, the court must investigate them thoroughly because they are not better than two kosher witnesses in any testimony. It appears to me that even written testimony is valid since we do not require formal testimony, provided that they recognize whose handwriting it is. There is an opinion that even a Samaritan (Kuti) who testifies not in his own interest is believed in this matter, but this does not seem correct (see Beit Shmuel there and examine carefully). However, all these invalid witnesses are valid to testify even if they are not testifying not in their own interest because the reason is that it is a matter destined to be revealed, so it makes no difference whether they are testifying not in their own interest or not.

It appears to me that a wicked person is disqualified from testifying, because since he has cast off the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, he is not concerned even if his falsehood is revealed. And it is not only those who transgress Torah prohibitions who are disqualified from testifying about a woman's husband's death, as stated in Siman 17, Se'if 29, but even those disqualified by rabbinic decree, who are otherwise valid, perhaps this is due to the decree concerning agunot (deserted wives). However, not in this testimony, as many others can be found who recognize them. All the more so, one who is suspected of forbidden relationships is disqualified there and also here because he is suspected of giving false testimony, as stated there in Se'if 30. And in the case of masiach lefi tumo (one who speaks inadvertently), even a wicked person is believed, as stated there in Se'if 31. And it is possible that only there, regarding a Samaritan, masiach lefi tumo is valid, and they are valid as well, which is not the case here. This requires further investigation. Regarding someone suspected of forbidden relationships, we have also written that even there he is not believed as masiach lefi tumo, because perhaps he is cunningly deceptive, as stated there.

And know that the Mordechai in the chapter on the mitzvah of chalitzah wrote that the fact that the Sages validated even a relative or a woman [as witnesses] is when, even without their testimony, he is presumed to be the brother of the deceased, and the relatives merely revealed the matter. As we hold in this case, we say it is merely a revelation of the matter. But if we were not already certain that he is the brother from the father, and relatives brought testimony to this effect, this is not merely a revelation of the matter. However, it does not appear so from all the poskim, for certainly in a case where we are certain that he is not the brother from the father, it is obvious that relatives are not believed, and even one valid witness is not believed until two valid witnesses testify. But when we did not know them at all, why should they not be believed? And what the Sages said, "it is merely a revelation of the matter," this is like something that is bound to be revealed, as it is written. Furthermore, the Rif explains that "revelation of the matter" means that it is neither a matter of prohibition nor a matter of finance, but merely a revelation of the matter that this man is so-and-so and this woman is so-and-so. From his words, it is also proven not like the Mordechai, and this requires further investigation (and his proof from the end of chapter 2 of Ketubot is not a proof, and it is obvious according to the explanation of the Rif).

Converts who converted (in ancient times) and slaves who were freed have no familial relationship at all, even if one of them was conceived not in sanctity and born in sanctity, and the other was both conceived and born in sanctity. Even if they are twins and were born in sanctity, they have no brotherhood unless both were conceived and born in sanctity. Thus, the Sages taught (Yevamot 97b): "Two twin brothers who are converts and similarly freed slaves neither perform chalitza nor yibbum and are not liable for the prohibition of a brother’s wife." If they were conceived not in sanctity and born in sanctity, they neither perform chalitza nor yibbum, but they are liable for the prohibition of a brother’s wife. If they were both conceived and born in sanctity, they are considered as Israelites in every respect. See Yoreh De'ah, Siman 269. (The wording of the Tur here is not precise as he wrote that they are like strangers if they were born in sanctity, while regarding a brother’s wife they are liable as he himself wrote in Yoreh De'ah there. Rather, because this section discusses yibbum, he used this wording.)

This is the language of the Tur: Rav Sherira Gaon wrote, "If a woman fell before a convert to Islam for levirate marriage (yibbum), since her conception and birth were in sanctity, she is bound to the levir and remains in a state of waiting until he performs the halitza (release ceremony) for her." And Rav Yehudai wrote, "If, at the time that her husband married her, the brother (levir) was a convert to Islam, there is no need for halitza from him. And if the husband converted and she remained with him and he died in his apostasy without children, she does not require yibbum because he is not considered his brother, and there is no need for halitza." This is the end of the Tur's words. 

And I do not understand why the wife of a convert does not require yibbum, and also, what difference does it make whether the levir converted before or after the marriage? The Tur concludes, and indeed, our teacher the Beit Yosef in his great book vehemently disagreed with Rav Yehudai's words and wrote that this was a clear mistake, and others wrote in his name that he commanded something he did not, and these words have no root or branch, nor any support at all. Woe to him who is lenient in this matter. Additionally, Rashi of blessed memory responded in his responsa that one should not rely on this at all, and even though he has sinned, he is still considered a Jew, and if he betrothed, his betrothal is valid.

However, in the Mordechai, Chapter "HaCholetz," we find early authorities who hold this view and provided reasons for it, stating that he is no longer considered his brother. They bring a proof from the laws of interest (ribit), as it is written, "that your brother may live with you," and it is permissible to take interest from him because he is not considered his brother. Similarly, "if brothers dwell together," and this one is not considered his brother. The distinction made between whether this transformation occurred at the time of his brother's marriage or not is based on the view that the initial marriage subjects the wife to levirate marriage (yibbum). Therefore, if at that time he was not considered his brother, she is exempt and there is no bond (zika) upon her. This is different from a situation where he was not transformed at the time, in which case the bond of levirate marriage does apply. Another reason is that it is forbidden for her to come to him, and zealots would strike him, so how can the bond of levirate marriage apply to something that is forbidden to her? According to this, the bond is nullified even if he was transformed afterward. They also bring proof from what the Sages said (at the end of "HaGozel Kama"), that if a widow fell before a leprous man, she should be exempt from chalitza because she would not have sanctified herself with this in mind. They answer that for a woman, it is acceptable in any case (see there). But in the case of transformation, where it is certainly not acceptable to her, it is certain that she would not have sanctified herself with this in mind (see also Beit Yosef and Rema, chapter 9).

In reality, none of these are proofs at all, for "your brother" regarding interest does not mean a literal brother but rather a brother in Torah and commandments, and therefore he is not included in the category of a brother. This is unlike "your brother" in the context of levirate marriage (yibum), which refers to a literal brother. For just because he sinned, does he cease to be his brother? The root of brotherhood is a term of attachment and connection, and it applies to brothers from one father and to members of one religion. Indeed, it is written, "Is Esau not Jacob's brother?" (Malachi 1:2) even though he changed. Furthermore, regarding the claim that the initial marriage determines, it is proven in Yevamot (109b) that death determines levirate marriage. And even though it is forbidden for him to marry her, the offspring is not considered a mamzer (illegitimate child). And as long as the offspring is not a mamzer, even though it is forbidden for him to marry her, the levirate bond applies. An example of this is those who are subject to negative commandments: they perform chalitzah (ceremony to release the bond) and do not undergo yibum. And what was stated at the end of the chapter "HaGozel" (Bava Kamma 112a), Tosafot already wrote there that it refers to betrothal and not to marriage. Therefore, it is forbidden to rely on this and exempt her without chalitzah. So, too, wrote the Maharik in Siman 177 and the Terumat HaDeshen in Siman 223.

Therefore, our master the Beit Yosef wrote in the Shulchan Aruch, section 4: "If [the widow] fell before the yavam (levir) who had converted, there is an opinion that permits [it] if he had converted when his brother married her, but it is not to be relied upon. If the deceased had converted, his wife is bound to his brother." And even if he betrothed her when he had converted, his betrothal is valid. Likewise, the offspring of the convert and his offspring's offspring until the end of all generations, if they are from an Israelite, even if she (the mother) is also a convert, their status is as Israelites in every matter.

Nevertheless, our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "However, if she transgressed and married without chalitzah because she did not know she had a yavam, and afterward it was discovered that she has a yavam, she need not leave him." And some say this is only if he performed chalitzah for her afterward. And indeed, the opinion of those who say this is certainly correct, for although she married a yavam to the marketplace, since she did it unwittingly, she performs chalitzah and remains with her husband (see Siman 159). And if she married a kohen, she would naturally have to divorce him. But the first opinion, which holds that she need not leave even without chalitzah and relies on the words of the Geonim, is very puzzling. Since Rashi and Rav Sherira Gaon rejected this with both hands, as did the Tur and the Beit Yosef, and it is also clear from the words of the Rambam, and the proofs are clear, how can one rely on this in a matter that is a Torah prohibition? And the one who holds this opinion is Rav Yaakov of Minz in his responsa, Siman 12, where he extensively justifies the words of the Geonim and distinguishes between kiddushin done willingly, which are certainly valid, as opposed to a zika (levirate bond) that comes automatically. Furthermore, he wrote another reason: since anyone who betroths does so with the intention of following the Sages, how could the Sages establish something that would lead to a stumbling block, and the Torah’s ways are pleasantness. All these things are very puzzling and have no sound basis. Moreover, he wrote that even those who are stringent do so only out of extra caution. This does not seem correct. Therefore, in practice, it is clear that one should not rely on this opinion, and it requires further study.

Furthermore, it is written: If she has two levirs, one of whom is a convert and an adult, and the other is an Israelite and a minor, she should only perform chalitzah with the Israelite. Even post facto, chalitzah with the convert is not effective. However, if he is from the Anusim, post facto it is effective. This is certainly the case that she should not initially perform chalitzah except with the Israelite. But what he ruled, that even post facto the chalitzah with the convert is not effective, follows his opinion that he is not subject to chalitzah and does not require yibum. However, if he is subject to chalitzah, why shouldn't it be effective post facto? And since most Rishonim and Acharonim hold that he requires yibum, as we mentioned, it follows that post facto his chalitzah is valid (and this seems to be the opinion of the Beit Shmuel, subsection 5). Nonetheless, it is possible that to be stringent, one should consider the opinion of the Geonim that he is not subject to chalitzah (Gra, subsection 10). In any case, it seems to me that this is specifically if it is possible to obtain chalitzah from the Israelite. If it is not possible to obtain it, we do not leave her in a state of being unable to remarry, and she is permitted to marry.

Additionally, it is written that if a man betroths a woman and he has a brother who is a "saris" (a eunuch or someone incapable of having children), he can betroth her on the condition—a double condition—that if she falls to the saris for yibbum (levirate marriage), she will not be considered betrothed. This is surprising, for if someone makes a condition counter to what is written in the Torah, his condition is void and the act remains valid. This is also taught in the Tosefta, Chapter 3 of Kiddushin: "If one says, 'You are betrothed to me on the condition that you will not be subject to yibbum,' the condition is void." This is also found in the Jerusalem Talmud at the end of Chapter 7 of Bava Metzia. Furthermore, there is a difficulty with this because it has been clarified in Siman 38 that there is no condition in marriage, as at the time of consummation he nullifies his condition. Indeed, our master the Beit Yosef in his great work refuted this with both hands and wrote that this should be forgotten, etc.

And the opinion of our teacher, the Rema, is that certainly if one stipulates on the condition that she will not be subject to levirate marriage, this is considered a stipulation on something written in the Torah. But if one stipulates that if she falls into levirate marriage, the betrothal will not take effect, this is not a stipulation on something written in the Torah. There is proof for this from what our Sages of blessed memory said (at the end of Perek HaGozel) about a widow who falls before a man afflicted with boils. If not for the fact that any woman would prefer any husband, we would say that she did not consecrate herself with this in mind. The same applies here. Also, the statement that there is no condition in marriage applies generally, but if at the time of intercourse he explicitly stipulates on this condition, the condition is not inferior to one made at the time of betrothal (as the Beit Shmuel also wrote in subsection 6). Additionally, we can say that only for a condition that is uncertain whether it will be fulfilled or not, we say he waived the condition at the time of intercourse. But here, there is no uncertainty, as the condition is for her benefit and is necessary for her. We do not say that he waived it (there). And what our Sages of blessed memory said (Yevamot 94b) clearly that there is no condition in marriage, they meant that this is a matter that is uncommon (Nodah B'Yehudah, Section 56). Similarly, what is written at the beginning of Beit Shmuel that there is no condition in marriage, and as is found in Tosafot there, that it is not customary, etc.

And know that many Geonim agreed regarding conditional betrothal: the Radach in Siman 9, the Chassid who authored "Me'il Tzedakah," the Gaon Nodah BiYehudah in Siman 56, and the Beit Meir in his responsa at the end of his book in Siman 6. And even if he has a deaf brother who is not fit for chalitzah, he can perform a conditional betrothal (see there). Similarly, if his brother is lost, he can perform a conditional betrothal (Bach). And because it is necessary to fulfill all the laws of a condition — a double condition, the positive before the negative, and the condition before the action — and under the chuppah, when betrothing her, it is difficult to do this publicly because of embarrassment, therefore they instituted in Prague to first perform the betrothal only in front of two witnesses conditionally, as will be explained. And after the betrothal, they call another eight people to bless the blessing of betrothal with a quorum of ten. And under the chuppah, they do not betroth her; rather, they read the ketubah and only recite the seven blessings. This is the order of the condition (it appears to me that here they bless after the betrothal — see what I wrote in Siman 34).

The groom says to two valid witnesses in the presence of the bride: "Listen to me, you are witnesses. Since it is my desire to betroth this woman, Sarah the daughter of Abraham, and to marry her, and because of a reason I have, I wish to betroth her conditionally, and also to enter into the chuppah (wedding canopy) with her on this condition, and to consummate the marriage on this condition, and every act of consummation that I perform with her shall be on this condition. This is my condition: if I have viable offspring at the time of my death, or even if I do not have viable offspring but she, Sarah the daughter of Abraham, dies before I do, or even if I die before her but my brother Ishmael the son of Abraham dies before I do, or even if I die before my brother but I divorce her with a get (bill of divorce) before my death, then the betrothal and marriage shall be fully valid. However, if I die before my wife and before my brother, and I do not divorce her with a get before my death, and I do not have viable offspring, then the betrothal, the chuppah, the consummations, and all matters of the marriage shall be retroactively nullified, and the ring that I give her now shall be considered merely a gift and not for the purpose of betrothal." Immediately, he shall give her the ring in the presence of the witnesses and repeat: "On the condition I spoke of, I am giving her this ring for betrothal." Afterwards, eight more people shall be called, and they shall recite the blessing of betrothal over the cup.

Afterward, they will go to the chuppah (wedding canopy), and the ketubah (marriage contract) will be read, and the seven blessings will be recited. Before going to the chuppah, the groom should say to the witnesses: "Listen to me, you are witnesses that I am going to the chuppah on the condition that I spoke of at the time of the betrothal." When they enter the room for seclusion after the chuppah, the groom should say to the witnesses: "Listen to me, you are witnesses that I am entering this room with her on the condition that I spoke of with the bride at the time of the betrothal." At the time of complete seclusion, when they are together in bed, the witnesses should stand behind the wall, and the groom should say to them: "Listen to me, you are witnesses that on the condition I spoke of with the bride at the time of the betrothal, I am coming to her now, and likewise, every time I come to her, if it is not according to the condition I stipulated, this is not an act of a husband and wife but rather as a woman designated without betrothal and without a ketubah." In the ketubah, the witnesses should write on the other side of the ketubah that all the betrothal, marriage, and ketubah were done on such and such conditions, as per the details of the condition explained, and the witnesses should sign this, and the Beit Din (Jewish court) should affirm the signatures so that it serves as evidence if needed. Nevertheless, the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) have written that this is not considered an act of promiscuity, since she is designated to him alone and not like a harlot (Radach there). After all these steps, care should be taken to avoid the nullification of the betrothal and marriage, and it is appropriate to give her a get (divorce document) before he dies while she is still alive.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote: If he was not known to have brothers and said he has brothers, he is not believed. If someone came and said, "I am his brother," he is not believed. Even if a single witness or relatives testify that he is his brother, they are not believed to remove her from her status. If he was known to have brothers and said at the time of his death, "I have no brothers," he is not believed. Similarly, if he said about someone who was known to be his brother, "This is not my brother," he is not believed. If he was not known to have brothers and a rumor spread that there are witnesses in another country who testify that he has brothers, even if he said at the time of his death, "I have no brother," she should be concerned and wait until the witnesses, who were mentioned, come and inquire. And some say that even if he was known to have brothers, he is believed to say, "I have no brothers" (Tur in the name of the Ra'avad). In practice, the opinion of the Rambam and the Tur is also in accordance with the ruling of the Shulchan Aruch.

The explanation of the matter is that when it is not established that there are brothers, it is as if she is assumed to be permitted to the general public (i.e., she is not bound to her brother-in-law for levirate marriage). Therefore, he (the brother-in-law) is not believed to remove her from her presumed status (of being permitted to marry anyone). Similarly, a single witness is not believed to remove her from her presumed status, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 127. Even many relatives are considered like a single witness, and therefore they cannot remove her from her presumed status of being permitted. Only two valid witnesses can remove her from her presumed status.

A significant question arises from this: it is explained in Yoreh De'ah there that in a case where it is not established whether something is permitted or forbidden, a single witness is believed. Here, where it is not established that there are brothers, it is not established that he has no brothers but rather it is not established that he has brothers. So why is a single witness not believed to say that he has brothers?

Proof of this is from what is stated in Siman 156, Section 23, where if it is established that he has brothers and he says he has sons, he is believed due to the principle of "migo" (since he could divorce her). It is explained there that even though we do not say "migo" in the face of a presumption, this is only when the "migo" contradicts the presumption, such as if he were to say he has no brothers, which would contradict the presumption that he has brothers. But when he says he has sons, it does not contradict the presumption, as it is possible for both to be true—that he has brothers and he has sons.

By necessity, it must be that in that case it was not established that he has sons. If it were established that he has sons, we would not need his statement. Rather, it was not established that he has sons, which implies that the lack of establishment that he has sons is not like an establishment that he has no sons. For if it were established that he has no sons, he would not be believed with a "migo" against the presumption. Rather, the lack of establishment that he has sons is like having no presumption at all—neither that he has sons nor that he does not. Therefore, he is believed to say he has sons.

Hence, similarly here, when it is not established that there are brothers, it is as if there is no presumption regarding brothers. So why should a single witness not be believed to say that there are brothers? (And this is the intention of the Beit Shmuel, S"K 7, and in Siman 156, S"K 10, and examine this carefully.)

However, in truth, this is not a question at all, for indeed it is certain that when one is not established as having brothers, it is not considered as if he is established as not having brothers. Nevertheless, regarding the woman, she is considered to be established with the presumption of being permitted to remarry. Similarly, when it is established that he has brothers but not established that he has no children, she is also considered to be established with the presumption of being permitted to remarry. For she is considered to be in a state of prohibition to remarry only when it is established that he has brothers and it is established that he has no children. But if one of these two elements is missing, she is considered to be in a state of presumption of being permitted to remarry, obviously. Therefore, in this case, when it is not established that he has brothers, a single witness is not believed to say that he has brothers because this would remove her from her presumption of being permitted (to remarry), and not because of the presumption regarding the brothers. Similarly, when it is established that he has brothers but not established that he has no children, she is also considered to be in a state of presumption of being permitted to remarry, since it is not established that he has no children. Therefore, a single witness is believed to say that he has children.

And know that there are those who wish to infer from the language of Rashi and the Ran, of blessed memory, that someone who has not been established as having brothers or sons, and did not say "I have sons," and one came and said, "I am his brother," we should be concerned about his words. Consequently, the same applies when a single witness says he has brothers, we are concerned about his words, and she is forbidden to marry into the general population (Beit Shmuel, section 7, and this is also evident from the Bach). He wanted to extend this to other opinions of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) as well; see there. Their intention is based on what is written in Kiddushin (64a) regarding a case where it has not been established that he has brothers or sons. If he said, "I have sons," he is believed. Rashi explains that if a brother came afterwards and said, "I am the brother of the deceased," his statement does not have the power to establish a presumption. The Ran and Rashbam (Bava Batra 134b) wrote similarly. It is understood from this that if he had not said, "I have sons," and one came and said, "I am his brother," he would be believed. However, in my humble opinion, this does not seem correct. Rashi's intention is that since it has not been established that he has brothers or sons, why do we need his statement, "I have sons"? Without this, she is presumed permitted to marry into the general population. Therefore, he explains that the benefit is that if he had not said, "I have sons," and one came and said, "I am his brother," and clarified his words, he would forbid her. Now that he said, "I have sons," even if it is clarified that he has brothers, she is permitted to marry into the general population. The Rosh also wrote that even if two witnesses later came and said he has brothers, she is still permitted to marry into the general population because, based on his statement, it was established that she is exempt from levirate marriage due to the sons he has. Rashi was brief in his words, as is his way, and it seems explicitly from Rashbam there, and the Maharsha also wrote similarly about Rashi's explanation. This is what he wrote, "not all of his words are effective"; the intention is not that he is not believed to say he is his brother. Certainly, even if he is believed, such as if he clarifies his words with witnesses, not all of his words are effective to forbid her because his statement established a presumption that she is permitted to marry into the general population. (And although the Bach inferred this, he wrote in practice according to our words; see there).

Furthermore, it seems clear to me that although someone who says "He is my brother" is not believed, nevertheless, if he says that he will soon prove the matter with witnesses that he is his brother, certainly we should wait for his clarification. After all, even in monetary matters, we tell him in such a case to prove his words, as is evident in Ketubot (27b). All the more so in matters of prohibition. What is written in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch that he is not believed means that based on his statement alone, he is not believed. According to this, the words of Rashi are straightforward: when he says "I have sons," we no longer worry about his words, even if he says he is ready to immediately prove his words with witnesses, as the Rosh wrote.

And this is what is written: that when he is established to have brothers and he says, "I have no brothers," he is not believed. We have already explained there the reason that even though he has a "migo" (a claim that could have been made to achieve the same result more directly), to divorce her, nevertheless we do not say "migo" in the presence of an established fact. And we have explained there that some say he is believed because such a "migo" that he has the power to act upon is said even in the presence of an established fact, and it is not comparable to every "migo". Additionally, it is possible to say that he is not contradicting the established fact, and his intention is that he had brothers and they died (see Beit Shmuel, Subsection 9). And see what is written there in Section 25 that there is doubt even if he explicitly said so, if he is believed. And it appears that he is not believed as is written there.

And what they wrote that if there is a rumor that there are witnesses who say he has brothers, even if he was not known to have brothers, we are concerned about the rumor until it is clarified. And even if he said at the time of his death that he has no brothers, some say this is only when the rumor has been substantiated in court (Nimukei Yosef in the name of Ramban, Chapter 8 of Bava Batra), and some say that even if the rumor has not been substantiated in court, we are concerned about the rumor (Hagahot Maimoniot, Chapter 3, Halacha 3). And it is possible to say that they do not disagree, for if he did not say that he has no brothers, we are concerned about the rumor even if it has not been substantiated in court, since there is no contradiction to the rumor. But if he said, "I have no brothers," we are not concerned unless the rumor has been substantiated in court. This requires further investigation, and see what I wrote in Siman 159, Section 14.

A woman whose husband died and he has neither a son nor a brother, and she is permitted to marry anyone (i.e., she is not bound by levirate marriage), and her father-in-law and mother-in-law are overseas, we do not worry that perhaps her mother-in-law gave birth to a male child and she would be bound by levirate marriage. This is not similar to what is written in Siman 156, Section 44, where if her husband and his co-wife went overseas, she is forbidden to marry anyone until she knows that the co-wife gave birth. The reason we do not worry about her mother-in-law giving birth is because it is not comparable. In the case mentioned there, she is presumed to be bound by levirate marriage and the minority of women who miscarry also supports this presumption. We say in that case that the minority can be combined with the presumption, as explained there. However, here the presumption is that she is permitted to marry anyone, and the majority also supports this presumption of permission, since she would only be bound by levirate marriage if her mother-in-law gave birth to a male child. And all those who give birth, half give birth to males and half to females, and a minority miscarry. Consequently, the majority also permits her to marry anyone, as it is a majority and a presumption that she is free to marry. Therefore, even Rabbi Meir, who is concerned about a minority, here would consider it a minority of a minority and would not be concerned, and certainly the Rabbis would not be concerned (Gemara 119b).

But if her mother-in-law left here pregnant, we are concerned that she might have given birth to a male child, and she would then be bound to him (for levirate marriage). And although in this case, too, there is a majority and a presumption as we have written, nevertheless, since she left while pregnant, she is not presumed to be permitted to the general public (to remarry), and on the contrary, she is somewhat presumed to be bound to a levir, because since she was pregnant and the days of her pregnancy have passed, we do not worry that she might have miscarried, as we establish her status as it was, just as we do not worry about a person that they might have died (Nimukei Yosef), because we presume them to be alive. And for this reason, a woman whose husband died and he had a son in a distant land is permitted to remarry and we do not worry that the son might have died, but we establish him in his presumed status of being alive. Similarly, here we do not worry that she might have miscarried, and there is only an even chance, half males and half females, and consequently, she is forbidden to remarry until she knows what happened with the fetus.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: A yavam (levirate husband) is forbidden to live with his chalutzah (sister-in-law who underwent chalitzah) if he is familiar with her, similar to a betrothed couple. This applies specifically after chalitzah, but before chalitzah it is permitted. The reason is that a chalutzah who underwent chalitzah is forbidden to the one who performed the chalitzah by a negative commandment. Therefore, if he is familiar with her, they are forbidden to dwell in the same courtyard. If the courtyard belongs to him, she must leave; if it belongs to her, he must leave. If it belongs to both of them or to neither, she must leave, because moving a man is more difficult than moving a woman, as stated in Siman 119 regarding a divorced woman. And it has been explained that if he is a Kohen (priest), she should not dwell with him even in the same alleyway. It is possible that the same rule applies to a chalutzah. Alternatively, it is possible that since the prohibition of a chalutzah to a Kohen is only rabbinic, we are not more stringent than with other chalutzot. Before chalitzah it is permitted, because if he were to cohabit with her, they would perform yibbum (levirate marriage). And although we do not practice yibbum but only chalitzah, we do not need to be so concerned that he might perform yibbum with her.

The Trustworthiness of a Woman to Undergo Yibbum (Levirate Marriage) and Whether One Witness is Believed. There are Sixteen Sections:
Just as a woman is believed when she says "My husband has died" to permit her to remarry, so too she is believed when she says "My husband has died" to permit her to undergo yibbum (levirate marriage). It is the same reasoning, that she investigates and is cautious before remarrying, and it is something that is likely to be revealed. Due to the stringency imposed on her at the end (if she lies), leniency is granted at the beginning (believing her without additional witnesses). For these reasons, the Sages deemed it appropriate to believe her so that she would not remain an agunah (a woman unable to remarry because her husband’s status is uncertain), as stated in Siman 17. Therefore, there is no difference whether she remarries someone from the general population or undergoes yibbum. On the contrary, yibbum is more severe if she is lying, because yibbum involves an additional prohibition of ervah (forbidden relations) on top of the prohibition of a married woman. It is obvious that she investigates thoroughly before marrying. Just as if she remarries someone from the general population she receives her ketubah (marriage contract settlement) from her husband’s estate, based on the wording in the ketubah which states "when you marry another, you shall take what is written for you," similarly, if she undergoes yibbum based on her word, the yavam (brother-in-law) inherits his brother’s estate based on her word. As it is written, "He shall rise in the name of his brother," and indeed he rises. Although regarding monetary matters she is not believed, nevertheless, since we derive from the ketubah that whenever she marries another she receives her ketubah, as stated there, all the more so we should derive from the Torah that whenever she undergoes yibbum, the yavam inherits his deceased brother’s estate (Gemara 117a).

Our Sages said (Yevamot 118b) that a woman is not believed to say that her brother-in-law has died so that she may marry someone from the general populace. Therefore, if she, her husband, and her brother-in-law went overseas, and she returned and said, "My husband and my brother-in-law have died," whether she said first that her husband died and then her brother-in-law, or first her brother-in-law and then her husband, she is not believed. This is because she was previously presumed to be bound to her brother-in-law, and she is not believed to say that the brother-in-law died to release herself from him. Therefore, if she was not previously presumed to be bound to a brother-in-law — for example, if her husband did not have a brother here, and only she and her husband went overseas, and she came back and said, "I was given a brother-in-law overseas because my husband's father married a woman there and she bore a son," and then she said, "My husband and my brother-in-law died," whether she said that her husband died first and then her brother-in-law, or that her brother-in-law died first and then her husband, she is believed. This is because she was previously presumed not to be bound to a brother-in-law (ibid.).

And why did our Sages not believe her regarding the death of the yavam (brother-in-law) so that she may marry another man? The Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 3 that it is because it is only a prohibition of a negative commandment and the prohibition seems light in her eyes, so we suspect that she might lie. And even though it is not mentioned in the Talmud and poskim (decisors of Jewish law) regarding this matter that they believed her to say her husband died, the reason is because there is a prohibition of karet (spiritual excision), but the reason is because she is meticulous and careful to remarry, and it is a matter that is likely to be revealed. And due to the severity that we impose on her if she lies, and we conduct with her all the thirteen ways that were explained there, so why not believe her also that her yavam died, since even with her the thirteen ways are applicable when she marries another man, as will be explained in Siman 159. One can say that the Rambam follows his reasoning in Chapter 2 of Yibum that the child is not a mamzer (illegitimate) from a yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage) to another man, and one of the thirteen ways is missing, and perhaps she fears this detail more than all the other details. And even according to those who hold that the child is a mamzer from a yevama to another man, as mentioned there, it is only rabbinically as mentioned there, and she does not care about it. Unlike if she lies about the death of her husband, the child is a mamzer by Torah law. Additionally, one can say that with the yavam, there is an additional reason why they did not believe her, because perhaps she hates the yavam, as for this reason there is a question in the Gemara if one witness is believed to say the yavam died (93b), see there. And therefore she is not believed by herself, as we say that the hatred overcomes her and she desires to marry another man to make her forbidden to him (see Tosafot 94a s.v. ki and examine well).

And similarly, the yavam (brother-in-law who performs levirate marriage) is not believed to say "my brother has died and I will perform yibbum (levirate marriage) with his wife." Even though if he left offspring, he is believed to say that his brother died so that she can marry someone else, because all relatives are valid to testify regarding a woman, nevertheless, for yibbum he is not believed. The Rambam wrote that the reason is that we are concerned he might have set his eyes upon her. Therefore, even though she would be diligent and ensure that the truth is revealed, and we would follow all thirteen ways, nevertheless, since the yavam is testifying for himself, we are concerned that he might seduce her and she might not be as diligent. There is a doubt if this yavam says "I do not wish to perform yibbum with her, but I will perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage)," or in our country where they do not permit yibbum, whether the yavam is believed, since there is no concern that he set his eyes upon her, or whether even in such a case he is not believed. Some say in such a case he is believed (Rashdam and Keneset HaGedolah), and some are uncertain about this (Chikrei Lev Section 17 Subsection 10 and Avodat HaGershuni there Subsection 14). Refer to what I wrote in Section 17 Subsection 36 that it seems according to the lenient opinion, and it is simple that even according to the lenient opinion, he should not have any monetary interest, such as receiving an inheritance from his brother or receiving money from her for the chalitzah, because if he has a monetary interest, it is clear that he is disqualified. Therefore, if he mentions money in his testimony, he is no longer believed, just as a woman is not believed when she claims her ketubah as explained there. Similarly, a man is not believed to say his wife has died so that he can marry her sister, and even one witness is not believed in this case because it does not permit an agunah (a woman bound in marriage due to her husband's disappearance) (Rambam). Therefore, she is also not believed to say "my sister has died" so that her husband can marry her. Some say that nowadays, when it is forbidden to marry two women, one witness is not believed to testify to a man that his wife has died so that he can marry another (Beit Shmuel Subsection 1), and it does not seem appropriate to be stringent about this (and so wrote Knesset HaGedolah Chapter 10 Subsection 20).

Rabbi Moses ben Maimon (Rambam) wrote (there) that a single witness is believed to testify to a yevamah (a widow awaiting levirate marriage) that her husband has died, and she may perform levirate marriage based on his testimony, or that her yavam (the brother-in-law) has died, or that her husband had a son to permit her to marry someone else. Even a slave, a woman, or a Samaritan who testifies spontaneously (without being asked) is believed regarding the death of the yavam, just as they are believed regarding a married woman to permit her [to remarry], etc. And the law of this testimony is like the law of other testimonies in terms of witnesses contradicting each other regarding the death of the yavam, for all matters. Thus is the conclusion of the Rambam. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch also wrote similarly, and in the name of the Rosh, the Tur wrote that specifically to permit her to the yavam, one witness is believed whether he says "your husband died" or "your son died, and afterwards your husband" but to permit her to the general public, he is not believed whether he says "your yavam died" or "your husband died, and afterwards your son." Thus is the conclusion of our teacher, the Rema.

And behold, regarding the matter that a single witness is trusted to say that the yavam (levirate husband) has died, this is a question in the Gemara. Although she herself is not believed, as we explained the reason is because the prohibition is light in her eyes, this does not apply to a witness. The main doubt in the Gemara is whether the reason they allowed an agunah (a woman chained to her marriage) based on one witness is primarily because it is a matter that is likely to be revealed, and in this case too it is a matter likely to be revealed and therefore the witness is believed, or perhaps the main reason is due to the woman's diligence and here she might not be diligent—maybe she hates him, and furthermore, since a child from the yevama (the widow subject to levirate marriage) to the general public is not considered a mamzer (illegitimate), she may not be so concerned to investigate thoroughly. And behold, the Rambam has already explained at the end of the laws of divorce that the main reason is because it is a matter likely to be revealed, see there. Therefore, he ruled here that the witness is believed. Also, the Rif ruled to permit and wrote that even though there are refutations in the Gemara, they are merely refutations and the main principle is to permit. And it seems to me that his reason is also because the main reason is due to it being a matter likely to be revealed (and this also resolves the question of the Rosh in Chapter 10, Siman 4, and the main reason of the Geonim as written). And the fact that a witness is believed to say that he was given a son is also for the reason that it is a matter likely to be revealed.

And behold, the Rambam did not clarify whether a witness is believed to say "your husband died and afterwards your son." Our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled in paragraph 3 that in this case, the witness is also believed. According to what was said, there is no proof for this, as in this case, the principle of "it is destined to be revealed" does not apply. Even though she is believed in such a case, as stated in Siman 156, paragraph 37, this is due to the principle of "migo" (since) that if she wanted, she could remain silent about the son, as stated there. The Rosh also explicitly wrote there that in such a case, it is obvious that the witness is not believed, as "migo" does not apply to a witness, who might intend to cause harm. However, we have further explained there another reason, because she is presumed to be permitted to the general public (to remarry). Therefore, it is well said that the witness is also believed, as the principle of presumption also applies to the witness. Moreover, it is clearly implied there in the Gemara that wherever she is believed, it is obvious that the witness is believed, as stated there ("this should not be a question for you, for even she is believed").

However, from the Rambam it becomes clear that for a single witness, the reason is not due to a presumption and not because she is believed, for the witness is believed to say that a son was born to him even though she left here with the presumption that she is obligated to perform levirate marriage, and she herself is not believed in such a case as it is said there that she is not believed to remove herself from her established status here; the witness is believed. However, it is possible to say that when there is a reason that it is likely to be revealed, we do not need another reason, for in this case, the witness is believed even though she is being removed from her previous status, and she is not believed even though it is likely to be revealed, as the Rambam explicitly explained at the end of Hilchot Gerushin that the reason that it is likely to be revealed pertains to the credibility of the witness. And we have already explained this in Siman 17 with the help of Heaven. And there is no need to ask that when he says a son was born to him, it is not a matter likely to be revealed, for although this can be verified whether a son was born or not, perhaps the son died and then he died, obligating her to perform levirate marriage. The witness is believed in all cases, even when he says a son was born and the son died and then he died, obligating her to perform levirate marriage, or he died and then the son died, making her permitted to the general public. In this, the verification is difficult to ascertain. It can be stated that since the witness is believed that a son was born to him, we no longer need his statement, for we grant the son the presumption of life, and consequently, she is permitted to the general public. The Rambam does not hold the concern mentioned by the Rosh that we suspect the witness might be lying intentionally to entrap her, for why should we suspect the witness of this? This reasoning is not mentioned in the Talmud. And although in the case of a single witness in a quarrel, the Rambam holds that we suspect that perhaps the witness was hired, we have already explained the Rambam's reasoning in Siman 17, section 242, because it was found she was lying. But to say the witness intends to entrap her, from where do we have the basis to suspect him of this?

And one should not ask how it is possible to say that the Rambam ruled that a single witness is believed in the case of a yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage) because the doubt lies in the reasoning behind the credibility of the witness—whether it is due to the fact that the matter is expected to be revealed or because of the witness's carefulness. And he follows his own reasoning that the primary reason is because the matter is expected to be revealed. However, in the case of a single witness in war or conflict, there is also a problem in the Talmud, and it also presents this doubt: if it is because the matter is expected to be revealed, the witness is believed, but if it is because of carefulness, he is not believed. According to this, the Rambam should have ruled that the witness is believed, and he does not rule so. The answer to this is that, on the contrary, this supports our view. It is true that he ruled in the case of conflict that the witness is not believed because we are concerned that she might have bribed him, as he explained there in the reasoning of the Rambam. He was compelled to explain this because this is not a doubt at all regarding the primary reason for the witness's credibility, which is certainly because the matter is expected to be revealed. And in the case of a single witness in war, he also ruled that if the witness said, "I buried him," he is believed, and we have explained the reasoning there in section 231. The reason is because we are concerned about isolated cases. According to the Rif's opinion, even with two witnesses, we are concerned about isolated cases, as we mentioned there in section 232. But the Rambam always holds that the primary reason is because the matter is expected to be revealed. And we have already explained there in section 23 that although we certainly also need the reason of carefulness, without which the sages would have been strict, the main leniency from the Torah is because the matter is expected to be revealed.

However, the Rosh of blessed memory wrote that since the question is unresolved, we go stringently, and one witness is not trusted to permit a yevama (a widow bound by levirate marriage) to marry out into the general population, just as she herself is not trusted. This is because we are concerned that since she hates her yavam (brother-in-law), she might not be precise in her testimony. And this is an a fortiori argument (kal vachomer): if she herself is not believed because we fear that out of hatred she might lie, how much more so she would not be precise when verifying the testimony of another witness. 

The Rosh follows his reasoning that the primary reason for trusting one witness in the case of an aguna (a woman whose husband is missing and cannot remarry) is due to her precision. Here, she would not be precise. If you ask, if so, how can we trust her to say her husband died to allow her to undergo yibbum (levirate marriage)? We should be concerned the other way around: that perhaps she loves him, and out of love, she might not be precise. One could say that the hatred of enemies is greater than the love of lovers (Tosafot 94). Additionally, in the case of love, she would not be confident because perhaps he would not want to perform yibbum and would choose to perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage). But when she hates him, she fears that he would not release her through chalitzah and would insist on yibbum (Rosh). 

Furthermore, in the case of yibbum, she would fear lying because it could result in her children being mamzerim (illegitimate), which is not the case when it comes to marrying out into the general population, as there is no concern of mamzerut from the Torah at all, as discussed in paragraph 3. The Rosh holds that the reason a woman is not trusted to say her yavam died is that we fear she might lie out of hatred.

The Rosh also wrote that if your husband dies, and afterwards your son, and you marry someone else, it is obvious that one witness is not believed, and there is no doubt about this in the Gemara. And even though she herself is believed with a "migo" (a legal presumption) that she could have said "my husband died" and remained silent, and consequently we would establish that the son is presumed to be alive, as stated in Siman 156, Se'if 37, but the witness is not believed. This is because, for him, there is no "migo," as we are concerned that perhaps her enemies hired him to testify falsely, or the witness himself wants to harm her and thinks that if he only testifies about the husband's death, she might find out about the son's death and investigate who died first, and he will not be able to harm her. But if he testifies about both, she will not investigate much and he will harm her. And many have wondered about his reasoning (Yam Shel Shlomo, Chapter 10, Se'if 28, and it is brought in Ketzot HaChoshen, Se'if 17, and in Turei Zahav, Maharshal, Se'if 1), from where did he derive this, as this reasoning and concern are not found at all in the Talmud. Furthermore, if so, why is there a doubt in the Talmud whether the witness is believed to say the yavam (levirate husband) died? Let's say also that he is certainly not believed for this reason. Rather, it is certain that the doubt in the Gemara applies to both matters. And so it seems from Tosafot there. (Additionally, the Rosh's words there are puzzling, for regarding your son dying and afterwards your husband, he wrote that since she is believed to say "my husband died" to perform yibum (levirate marriage), all the more so the witness is believed, even in a case where she is not believed, as in the case of your son dying and afterwards your husband. And in the case of your husband dying and afterwards your son, it is obvious to him that the witness is not believed, even though she is believed. And this requires further study).

And it appears to me that the reason of the Rosh is as follows: For a single witness, there is no distinction between whether he has a "migu" (an argument that he could have used a more advantageous claim) or not, and whether there is a presumption of permissibility or prohibition. Since, according to Torah law, there is no allowance for a single witness to be trusted to change her status from being a married woman, the main reason he is trusted is because she examines and marries carefully. Therefore, it must be that if we say that the witness is trustworthy in any matter, he is trustworthy in all respects. Consequently, she should perform yibbum (levirate marriage), since we find in the Talmud that a witness is trusted to say "your husband died" to allow her to perform yibbum. Therefore, it follows necessarily that he is also trusted to say "your son died and then your husband died" to allow yibbum, and similarly, the reverse: to testify that her yavam (levir) died so that she may marry another man. Since we find in the Talmud that it remains uncertain if a witness is trusted to say "your yavam died" to allow her to marry another man, it necessarily follows that there is at least a doubt if a witness is trustworthy to say "your husband died and then your son died" to allow her to marry another man. One law depends on another, as stated. The reasoning is truly why a witness is trusted to allow yibbum and we are not concerned that out of love she might not examine properly. In the case of the yavam dying to allow her to marry another, the witness is not trusted because we suspect that out of hatred she might not examine properly, for the hatred of enemies is greater than the love of friends. Additionally, out of love, she would not be certain because he might perform chalitzah (a ceremony releasing her from yibbum), as explained in paragraph 10. Also, in the case of the yavam, the child born could be a mamzer (illegitimate according to Torah law), as stated there. Therefore, it necessarily follows that in the case of "your husband died and then your son died," he is certainly not trusted, since the main uncertainty in the Gemara about the death of the yavam is because it is possible that in a matter destined to be revealed, a person does not lie. How could he say "the yavam died" and then the yavam would appear alive before us? Therefore, in the case of "your husband died and then your son died," he would never be caught in his lie, and this is not a matter destined to be revealed, since even one who contradicts him would say both died, just in a different order. Therefore, it is impossible to reveal this to the whole world. Thus, the Rosh rightly states that in such a case, the witness is certainly not trusted. The Rosh's statement that we are concerned that perhaps her enemies hired the witness, or he himself wants to harm her, is not the main reason for the prohibition. The main reason for the prohibition is as explained. However, the truth is that the essential law of the Torah is that a single witness is not trusted to change her status from being a married woman. Why is she trusted with a "migu"?
