Because the essential law of the Torah is that every person is trusted about themselves with a "migu," but a single witness is not trusted about others when there is a presumption of prohibition, and it is not within his control, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 127. Why is this so? Because the Torah did not grant trustworthiness to a single witness, as we suspect he might lie, especially in such a matter where there is concern for enemies or the witness himself is an enemy. Therefore, we must find some reason why the Torah did not trust a single witness. However, the Sages did not trust him due to "diqa" (thorough examination), because in this case, there is no "diqa," as explained.

Regarding the fundamental dispute between the Rosh and the Rambam, of blessed memory, most of the decisors agreed with the Rambam. Several of the major later decisors agreed that in times of need and when there is a concern of a woman becoming an agunah, one can rely on the Rambam, of blessed memory, that a single witness is believed to say that the yavam (the deceased husband's brother) has died, thus allowing the woman to remarry (Beit Shmuel, subsection 2). Consequently, a single witness is also believed to say that your husband died and then your son died, for it is the same reasoning as stated. It is obvious that in our times, when there is no yibbum (levirate marriage) but only chalitza (the ceremony releasing the woman from the obligation of yibbum), a single witness is believed (ibid.), for there is no concern that she might not be precise because she hates him and fears that he might perform yibbum with her. Some also say that in our times, she herself is believed to say that her yavam has died so that she may remarry, but this is not conclusive (ibid.). If the yavam is present and a single witness testifies that a son was born to her husband abroad, some say she should perform chalitza out of doubt (Bach). Others say that since the Sages were strict about chalitza being performed when it is discovered that there was no need for it, and we would permit her to marry a kohen, people might say that a chalutza (a woman who has performed chalitza) is permitted to marry a kohen, as stated in section 156. Therefore, it is better to rely on the Rambam that chalitza is not necessary (Beit Shmuel, ibid.). It seems to me that specifically in section 156, where the matter needs to be clarified, the Sages were concerned about chalitza. Therefore, here too, if it is possible to clarify, she should not perform chalitza until the matter is clarified. However, when it is impossible to clarify, she should certainly perform chalitza out of doubt, for how can we exempt her from chalitza due to a minor concern when there is a dispute among the decisors regarding the fundamental law (and it seems to me that this is also the intention of the Bach, resolving the Beit Shmuel's difficulty).

The five women who hate each other, as explained in Siman 17, are not trustworthy to say that her husband died. Similarly, they are not trustworthy to say that her yavam (levirate husband) died and she may marry someone else, even according to the Rambam who ruled that one witness is trustworthy, and consequently also relatives and women are trustworthy. However, the women who hate each other are not trustworthy. What the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) said about five women is not specific; it is just the language used there. In this matter, there are only two women, for among the five women, one is her husband's daughter, and in the case of yibbum (levirate marriage), this does not apply, because if he has offspring, she is not subject to yibbum (Beit Shmuel). There is no need to testify that the yavam died. Moreover, one of the five women is her rival wife, and it is obvious that in yibbum this does not apply because she herself is bound to the yavam, so how can she be trustworthy (there)? However, it can be said that although she is not trustworthy about herself, she is trustworthy about her rival wife, and it comes to teach us that she is not trustworthy.

Among the five women who are not trusted, one of them is the wife of her husband's brother, as stated in Siman 17. Therefore, if two brothers went to a distant land with their wives, and the wives came before us, one saying, "My husband died," and the other saying, "My husband died," each woman is trusted regarding the death of her own husband, as stated there. Nevertheless, both women are forbidden to remarry, because each one is not trusted regarding the other, being among the five women who are not trusted. Consequently, each one is forbidden [to remarry] because perhaps her husband's brother is still alive, and she is bound to levirate marriage (yibbum). For she herself is also not trusted to say, "My brother-in-law died," as stated.

From this, it is understood that if one of them had a witness according to the Rambam's opinion, or witnesses according to the Rosh's opinion, that her husband died, the other woman is permitted to remarry, because she is trusted regarding her own husband, and there is a witness or witnesses regarding the brother-in-law. The one with a witness or witnesses remains in her prohibition for the reason we mentioned. The same applies even if neither of them has witnesses, but one of them has children from her husband and the other does not. The one with children is permitted because she is trusted regarding her own husband, and she is not bound to levirate marriage because of the children. The one without children is forbidden for the reason we mentioned until the matter is clarified. (This is the Mishnah at the beginning of the final chapter of Yevamot).

Not only that, but even if these women had a yavam (levir) or two yavams here, and they came and each one said that her husband died and she has no children and they performed levirate marriage and the yavams died, each one remains in her previous prohibition. This means that since one is not believed concerning the other, as we have said, and consequently there is concern for each one that perhaps the brother of her husband who is abroad is still alive. Even though each one has already performed levirate marriage here and they were believed that their husbands had died, nevertheless, now that the yavams here have died, if we permit them to remarry in the general community, it would mean that one is believed concerning the other. Therefore, both are prohibited until the matter is clarified. We do not say that since they were permitted to the yavams, they are permitted to everyone (as it says). However, if they had children from these yavams or if they were divorced with a get in a manner that there is no longer any levirate tie upon them, both are permitted. For even if they have yavams, they are not bound to them.

The Law Regarding a Yevama Who Became Betrothed or Married to an Outsider, and the Law When She Undergoes Yibbum by Mistake, and the Laws Concerning Relations for a Woman Obligated in Yibbum. This Section Contains 28 Paragraphs:
Even though a yevama (a widow awaiting levirate marriage) who goes to an outsider is only subject to a prohibition of a negative commandment, as it is written, "She shall not be the wife of the deceased outside to a stranger," and for prohibitions of negative commandments, betrothal is valid, nevertheless, there is a doubt in the Gemara (Yevamot 92b) whether the betrothal is valid. The reason for the doubt is that perhaps from the fact that the Torah uses the language of "shall not be" (lo ti'hiyeh), it intends that there should be no validity (haviya) of betrothal to an outsider, meaning that the betrothal would not take effect. There is an opinion in the Gemara that holds this view. Therefore, the Gemara ruled that if a yevama becomes betrothed or even married to an outsider, she requires a get (divorce) out of doubt. Because there are several opinions on this matter, we will explain them with the help of Heaven (b'siyata d'shmaya).

And these are the words of the Behag (Ba'al Halachot Gedolot) in the laws of Yibbum and Chalitzah: A widow awaiting Yibbum who became betrothed without Chalitzah requires a get (divorce document) from the one to whom she was betrothed, and she is permitted to the yavam (levirate husband), for thus said the Gaon: A widow awaiting Yibbum who married without Chalitzah, if she has no children, she must leave both her husband (with a get) and the yavam (with Chalitzah), and she is forbidden to both of them forever because she would be confused with a woman whose husband went overseas. If she became betrothed but did not marry, if her yavam is an Israelite, he gives her a get and she is permitted to the yavam, but she is forbidden to the one to whom she was betrothed, so that the sinner does not profit. If she married and had children from the second, if her husband is an Israelite, the yavam performs Chalitzah for her, and she remains with her husband, and we do not remove her from him, because a woman whose husband went overseas and they told her that her husband died and she married, and afterwards her husband came, must leave both (her new husband and her first husband), and the child is a mamzer (illegitimate). But it is not so with a widow awaiting Yibbum, for if you say she must leave, you cast aspersions on her children. If her husband is a Kohen and she has children, she does not even need Chalitzah, for when the yavam performs Chalitzah for her, she becomes forbidden to him, and we do not remove her from him so as not to cast aspersions on her children. And he is forbidden to approach her as long as the yavam is alive, for every time he approaches her he stands in a positive commandment, and we are obliged to separate him from her. But when the yavam dies, he is permitted to approach her. These are the words of the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot.

It is not clarified in his words whether he is referring to a case where she was betrothed inadvertently, such as when witnesses testified that the yavam (levir) had died and then he came, or if he is referring to a case done intentionally. The early authorities agreed that his intention was regarding an intentional act because he wrote that a sinner should not profit, and the term "sinner" is applicable to an intentional act (see Beit Shmuel, section 1). Therefore, he ruled that to the one who betrothed her, she is forbidden forever, even if the yavam performed chalitzah (the levirate release). This is more stringent than the case of a married woman who heard that her husband had died and then was betrothed to another, and the husband came, where she is permitted to her husband and also to the one who betrothed her if her husband divorced her or she was widowed, as written at the end of section 17. For there, it was inadvertent and close to being coerced, therefore we do not penalize her. This is not the case here, where it was intentional, so we do penalize her (Rashba).

However, the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote in Chapter 2, Law 20, that if a man who divorced a woman from betrothal (erusin) marries her after her yavam performed chalitzah with her, we do not force him to divorce her. And this is the conclusion of the Ramban and the Rashba, of blessed memory (according to the Maggid Mishneh), because it cannot be more stringent than a married woman who marries another man, even though in this case it was done intentionally. According to all opinions, the yavam can either perform yibbum or chalitzah with her. (And there is a difficulty with the Nimukei Yosef who wrote that the Rambam's opinion is like that of the Geonim, and it is possible that there is a scribal error in his words and it should say Ramban, or it is possible that the Rambam agrees initially and only in retrospect does he hold that she does not need to be divorced, as is evident from his wording, and in this, it is possible that he does not disagree with the Geonim).

And even when the yavam (levirate husband) is a kohen (priest) and she has already become forbidden to him for yibbum (levirate marriage), even if the one who betrothed her divorces her, we do not say that since she is forbidden to the yavam, we should force the yavam to perform chalitzah (levirate release) and she should stay with the one who betrothed her and he should marry her. There is no reasoning that because he committed a transgression intentionally and made her forbidden to the yavam, he should benefit from this. Rather, we compel him to divorce her, and she becomes forbidden to him. And also, she is forbidden to the yavam due to his priesthood, and he must perform chalitzah, and she can marry another.

But if she was betrothed accidentally, such as if they thought she did not have a yavam (levirate husband) or they heard that he had died and similar cases, the Tur wrote that if the yavam wants to perform yibbum (levirate marriage), we compel the one who betrothed her to divorce her. If he does not want to perform yibbum, he performs chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage) and she is permitted to the one who betrothed her, but he must betroth her again after the chalitzah. The reason is that since there is a doubt in the Gemara if betrothal takes effect with a yevamah (a woman awaiting levirate marriage), as mentioned, and the divorce is due to doubt, there is automatically also a doubt whether the betrothal took effect or not. Therefore, out of doubt, he must betroth her again after the chalitzah. The blessing for the betrothal should not be recited because in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient. If the yavam is a kohen (priest), she is forbidden to him, so there is no benefit in compelling him to divorce, and there is no penalty here since it was done unintentionally. He performs chalitzah and she remains with the one who betrothed her. It appears that we compel the yavam to perform chalitzah since it was done unintentionally, as explained in the response of the Rivash, section 482, regarding a yevamah who underwent chalitzah and it was later revealed that the yavam had issued a declaration of protest, and meanwhile, she was betrothed to another. He ruled that we compel him to perform chalitzah, as mentioned. However, there is no proof from there because he had already performed chalitzah, and she became forbidden to him due to his own action. But in the case of a kohen, who is prohibited to her due to the betrothal, even though it was unintentional, it is still possible that he can say she should wait until she grows old or give me a certain amount of money. This is also implied from the words of the Tosafot and the Rosh there, who wrote that we do not compel him to perform chalitzah, and it seems that this applies even in the case of unintentional action (and so wrote the Bach in sub-section 5).

And know that as we have written, it is explicitly stated in the Tur and the Rosh, and so wrote the Ramban, Rashba, Maggid Mishneh, and Nemukei Yosef, that if it was done unintentionally, she is permitted to the one who betrothed her. And what the Bahag, Rif, and Rambam prohibited her to the one who betrothed her, this is when it was done intentionally. The Tosafot and the Rosh and all the early authorities wrote that Rabbeinu Tam ruled similarly in a case where a woman did not know she had a yavam (levirate husband) and was betrothed, and he permitted her to the one who betrothed her after the yavam performed chalitzah. And our master, the Beit Yosef, in his great book, ruled similarly, and even more so, he disagreed with the Terumat HaDeshen, who wanted to be stringent with a yevamah who was betrothed based on a rumor that the yavam had died. The Terumat HaDeshen ruled that this is not considered unintentional since she should not have betrothed based on a mere rumor, and it is considered intentional. The Beit Yosef disagreed and held that this is also considered unintentional, as is written there. And the Levush also ruled that if it was unintentional, she is permitted to the one who betrothed her.

And according to this, there is much to wonder about his words in the Shulchan Aruch, section 1, where he writes as follows: "A woman who is bound to a levir (yavam) and mistakenly betrothed to another man, the stranger who betrothed her gives her a get (bill of divorce), and the yavam either performs yibbum (levirate marriage) or chalitzah (ceremonial release). If the yavam is a kohen (priest) who cannot marry a divorced woman, she must leave the stranger with a get so that the sinner does not profit, and the yavam performs chalitzah for her. If the stranger who divorced her from the betrothal then marries her after the yavam has performed chalitzah, she is not taken away from him." And his words are against all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law).

Therefore, indeed, our teacher the Rema wrote about this, and these are his words: "And some say that even if he subsequently married her, she is taken away from him, since she was betrothed to him in a forbidden manner, and this applies specifically if he betrothed her intentionally. But if he betrothed her unintentionally, not knowing that she had a brother-in-law, if the brother-in-law wishes to perform levirate marriage, the one who betrothed her must divorce her. And if the brother-in-law wishes to perform chalitza (the ceremony to release her from levirate marriage), he performs chalitza, and she marries the one who betrothed her, and he must betroth her again after the brother-in-law performs chalitza." And this seems to be the main opinion. And some say that this applies only in the case of complete unintentionality where they did not know there was a brother-in-law, but if there was a brother-in-law, and it was believed that he had died because that was the prevalent rumor, she must leave the one who betrothed her." End of quote. And there is someone who wants to say that the unintentionality mentioned by our teacher the Beit Yosef also refers to such a case (Bach, section 81). But it is impossible to say this, as in such a case, he would not have left it ambiguous but would have explained it. Additionally, we have already written that in his larger work, he disagrees with this and holds that this is also considered unintentional.

However, in truth, it seems to me that his words are correct, for it is true that the poskim agreed in principle that in a case of inadvertence, she is permitted. Nevertheless, it is clear that the opinion of Behag (Ba'al Halachot Gedolot), the Rif (Rabbi Isaac Alfasi), and the Rambam (Maimonides) is that even in a case of inadvertence, she is forbidden. The proof for this is that they wrote together the laws of one who became betrothed and one who married another before halitzah, and just as in marriage there is no distinction between inadvertence and intentionality, so too in betrothal. Furthermore, from the words of the Tosafot, it is clear that Rabbeinu Tam disagrees with Behag, and according to the poskim, they do not disagree. It is explicitly stated in the Mordechai and in the Sefer HaYashar by Rabbeinu Tam, section 23, that he disagrees with Behag. This implies that Behag's intention also applies to inadvertence, and this is also the intention of the Rif and the Rambam. Moreover, how could it be that they would be so terse and not differentiate between inadvertence and intentionality unless it implies that they are referring to all cases? Conversely, from Rabbeinu Tam's words, it is clear that in his opinion, even in the case of intentionality, she is permitted to the one who betrothed her, as he wrote the reason that in betrothal we do not impose a penalty. This implies that it refers to all cases, and in the incident where he permitted in a case of inadvertence, it was an actual incident, but the same applies even in the case of intentionality according to his opinion (and so wrote the Bach). 

And one cannot ask, according to those who hold that even in a case of inadvertence she is forbidden, how it is possible to say that this should be more severe than a woman who heard that her husband died and was then betrothed to another, who is permitted to the latter when she becomes widowed or divorced. For certainly, there is a great difference in this matter, for in the case of a married woman, since no divorce is needed, the betrothal is nothing, which is not the case with a yevamah (widow awaiting levirate marriage) who needs a get (divorce document). Therefore, it can rightly be said that she is forbidden to him, as it is somewhat similar to one who remarries his divorcee after she was betrothed to another. The same applies here, since he can perform yibbum (levirate marriage) with her, as she is bound to him, and halitzah stands in place of a get. The poskim who differentiated between inadvertence and intentionality expressed their own reasoning, but Behag, the Rif, and the Rambam hold that even in a case of inadvertence she is forbidden. Therefore, the Shulchan Aruch ruled accordingly. 

However, in practice, the main ruling follows the majority of the poskim and the words of our teacher, the Rema (Rabbi Moses Isserles). Moreover, in what he ruled stringently regarding betrothal based on a rumor, the great later authorities (the Bach and the Beit Shmuel, section 6) disagree with him. Likewise, in what he ruled that in the case of intentionality, if he married her, she must be separated from him immediately, they also disagree with him. For we have already written that it is possible that in retrospect, they agree with the Rambam, and especially since Rabbeinu Tam holds that even initially it is permitted, as we wrote. Therefore, one should not be overly stringent in matters of rabbinic origin (and the term "forever" is not so precise, and only the Terumat HaDeshen infers this, while the Beit Yosef and the Bach disagree with him, and so wrote the Beit Shmuel) (see Maharsha, section 92).

In this regard, it is written that another marriage ceremony is needed; this is indeed correct. There are those who wish to be stringent and say that the yavam (levir) should not perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage) until after he divorces her (the widow) (Levush). This is because we require that at the time of chalitzah she should also be fit for yibbum (levirate marriage), as it is written, "But if the man does not want to take his brother's wife..." (Deuteronomy 25:7). If he performs chalitzah before divorcing her, then he is not able to perform yibbum. He is astounded that the poskim (legal decisors) did not write this. In my humble opinion, the poskim acted correctly because if there are many brothers, it is better for her to be divorced first. Otherwise, since he is unable to perform yibbum, it is considered like an invalid chalitzah which requires going through all the brothers. The poskim agree with this and only address the case where there is one brother who does not wish to perform yibbum. In this case, we are not concerned, as there are many instances of chalitzot (plural of chalitzah) where he is unable to perform yibbum, and still, the chalitzah is not invalidated by this. Also here, we do not worry about it. Refer to what I have written in Siman 170, where it is the main law that an invalid chalitzah needs to go through all the brothers (but there it is only rabbinically mandated; see there).

And with what the Behag wrote that if she marries, she must leave both this one and that one and is forbidden to them forever, all the poskim agreed that even if she married unintentionally, this is so. For he brought proof from a woman whose husband went overseas and she married, and there too, even unintentionally, it is so, as written in Siman 17. And the Behag did not write that all thirteen ways apply to her, because the child is not a mamzer, as explicitly stated. And also, the Rambam did not write that all these ways apply to her. But the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that all the ways apply to her, except regarding mamzer, where there is a dispute. For some say that the child is not a mamzer at all, and some say that rabbinically, he is a mamzer. And the yavam must perform chalitza for her, and she must divorce the one she married and marry another. And although in the reverse case we were lenient in Siman 157:11, that even if she married, she should perform chalitza and stay with her husband, this is because the opinion of the Geonim is that chalitza is not needed at all, as written there. But in a case where chalitza is certainly needed, it is obvious that she must leave both this one and that one, and even if the yavam dies, she must leave (Tur), because she married with the prohibition of a yevama to the marketplace. And it is confused with a woman whose husband went overseas, and there it is obvious that in all cases she must leave, even if the husband dies, for she is forbidden to the husband and to the one she married, and here too it is similar.

And in this respect, what the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (BaHaG) wrote, that if the husband is a Kohen and she has children, she should not perform chalitzah (the ritual of releasing a widow from levirate marriage) and she will be forbidden to him until the yavam (levirate husband) dies, and after he dies, she is permitted to him. And if he is an Israelite and she has children from him, the yavam should perform chalitzah for her and she may remain with him so as not to cast doubt upon the legitimacy of the children. The Rif and the Rambam and all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) disagree with him, and it is also evident from the Jerusalem Talmud that even if she has children, she must leave him. And even though there are some of the early authorities who hold like the BaHaG because they are always concerned about casting doubt on the legitimacy of the children, and the Jerusalem Talmud also does not explicitly state that she has children (Ra'avan and Aviasaf in Teshuvot Maimoniyot, Siman 37), nevertheless, the majority of decisors do not hold this way, and so it is ruled in the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch. (And from what the BaHaG wrote, that for every cohabitation, he transgresses a positive commandment, it is a proof to Rashi's explanation at the end of the chapter "HaCholeitz" that according to Rav, there is no negative commandment for a yevama (levirate widow) to the marketplace, and the Tosafot there in the commentary begin with "if," they disagree with him, and all the early authorities criticize Rashi's explanation there. Or it is possible that even BaHaG holds like the Tosafot, but the negative commandment is only at the time of betrothal and marriage, as it is written, "She shall not be the wife of the dead outside," and afterwards at the time of cohabitation, he transgresses "her yavam shall go into her and not another," and it is a negative commandment derived from a positive commandment.)

A widow (yebamah) who married someone from the general population (shuk) under the assumption that she had no brother-in-law (yavam), and a rumor subsequently emerged that she indeed has a brother-in-law — we do not pay attention to the rumor, as post-marriage rumors are not given credence (Beit Shmuel in the name of Rivash). Even if the rumor was established in a court, and even if there is one witness, he is not believed to negate her status. However, if the rumor emerged before she married, we are concerned about it. We have explained this in Siman 157, Se'if 24, see there. And it seems to me that if she went ahead and married, we do not remove her from him. This is also explained there regarding one witness prior to marriage, and we have explained it there in Se'if 21, see there.

And if two witnesses came and said that he has no brothers, and she got married, and afterwards two others came and said that he does have brothers, there are those who say that she should not leave [her marriage] (Beit Shmuel, sub-section 7 in the name of Beit Yosef and Darkei Moshe). But there are those who disagree because we hold that when there are two against two, it is considered a doubt, even though there is a presumption of permissibility. Only if she married based on the testimony of one of the witnesses, and she also says "I am certain," then she does not have to leave. But without this, she must leave (Beit Shmuel). It must be said that the first opinion holds that since two against two is a rabbinic doubt, and from a Torah perspective, we rely on the presumption, and the two who initially came for permissibility established her status as permissible, therefore, we are lenient regarding the prohibition of a yevama to the marketplace, and the child is not a mamzer, because since she married permissibly, she does not have to leave. Additionally, here there are two presumptions of permissibility: immediately when her husband died, she was presumed permissible to the marketplace (Tosafot, Yevamot 31a, s.v. "Nafal"), and afterwards when the witnesses for permissibility came, she was further strengthened in her presumption of permissibility. Therefore, they were lenient in this case regarding the prohibition of a yevama to the marketplace, and she does not have to leave. Nevertheless, the law requires further investigation.

A woman awaiting levirate marriage (shomeret yavam) who committed adultery, even intentionally, is not prohibited to the yavam (levir). If he wishes to perform yibbum (levirate marriage), he may do so. This is not comparable to a married woman who committed adultery with consent, who is prohibited to her husband, because a woman awaiting levirate marriage is not considered a married woman. Even if she marries another man, she is not prohibited to the yavam except due to the confusion with a married woman, as mentioned, and the Sages only decreed against marriage, not against adultery. In the Jerusalem Talmud, Sotah, it is derived from the verse "and it was hidden from the eyes of her husband" and not from the eyes of her yavam. Note that there are some of our rabbis who hold that a woman awaiting levirate marriage who committed adultery is prohibited to the yavam, but their opinion is not brought at all in the Halachic decisors. Similarly, this opinion is not mentioned in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. (Tosafot in Sotah 18a, s.v. "Amri" rule like Rav Hamnuna there, and in Yevamot 92a, s.v. "Aval" they rule not like him there).

And specifically, this applies when the yavam (the brother-in-law who performs levirate marriage) is an Israelite. However, if he is a Kohen (priest), she is forbidden to him because she is considered a zonah (a woman who has engaged in prohibited sexual relations), having had relations in violation of a negative commandment or a positive commandment. It has already been explained in Siman 7 that a yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage) who had relations with another man becomes a zonah, and the child is not a mamzer (illegitimate) even according to the opinion that in the case of marriage the child would be a mamzer by rabbinic decree, as mentioned. In any case, in the context of promiscuity, they did not decree this, just as they did not decree that she is forbidden to the yavam if he is not a Kohen.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 3 that there are those who say she is forbidden to the adulterer because of a penalty. That is to say, even though we hold that wherever she is not forbidden to her husband, she is not forbidden to the adulterer, as it is written in Siman 11. And here, since she is not forbidden to the yavam (levirate husband), why should she be forbidden to the adulterer? Nevertheless, because of the penalty, they forbade her to him, just like in the case of betrothal where it is explained that if she was betrothed intentionally, even though she is permitted to the yavam, she is still forbidden to the one who betrothed her. The same applies to illicit relations and it is merely a penalty. According to this, according to the words of the Rambam there, that if the one who betrothed her transgressed and married her, she does not have to leave him, it is the same here: if the adulterer transgressed and married her, she is not taken away from him. And here, even those who dispute the Rambam agree that this fundamental law is not agreed upon. (See the Beit Shmuel, paragraph 9, who questioned this fundamental law and the Kenesset HaGedolah in Siman 68, who explained the intention of the Nimukei Yosef that only when the yavam does not want to perform yibum because she is repulsive to him due to the illicit relations, they therefore forbade her to the adulterer. But if otherwise, he does not want yibum or in our times when yibum is not practiced, she is permitted to the adulterer. See there, and his words are strained. And indeed, the Maaseh Rokeach in the second chapter of Sotah wondered about the Nimukei Yosef, from where he derived this, and therefore, after the fact, it is obvious that she is not taken away from the adulterer when he married her. And so wrote the Chatam Sofer in Siman 26).

A yevama (a widow awaiting levirate marriage) who mistakenly underwent levirate marriage (yibbum) because she heard that her husband had died, and then her husband returned, if she was married to her husband, she does not need a get (divorce document) from the yavam (brother-in-law) because she is prohibited to him (as erva), and the kiddushin (marriage) does not take effect with her. She is also permitted to return to her husband. This is not similar to a case where a woman marries another man, where we hold that she must leave both this one and that one as stated in Siman 17, because in that case, we are concerned that people might say that her husband divorced her and the other man married her, and thus she would need a get from both of them and be prohibited to both due to the concern that people might say that she returned to her first husband after marrying another. But in the case of a yevama, she does not need a get from the yavam because there is no concern that people might say that her husband divorced her. For if he had divorced her, his brother would not have married her, as she is an erva to him, and everyone knows that her yibbum was in error, and she does not need a get, and consequently, she is not prohibited to her husband. Therefore, if she was only betrothed (arusa) and not married (nesua), she needs a get from the yavam because we are concerned that people might say there was a condition in the kiddushin that was not fulfilled, and the kiddushin was nullified, and his brother married her permissibly, and consequently, she needs a get from him and is prohibited to both.

And know that what we have written, that in the case of a married woman, she is permitted to her husband, so ruled the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch in section 4. However, there are those who disputed this and hold that she is forbidden to her husband (Beit Yosef in Bedek HaBayit and Beit Shmuel in subsection 10). Their reasoning is that certainly there is no concern here that people might say "this one divorced her and his brother married her," as mentioned. But in truth, there are those who hold that a married woman is not forbidden for this reason, but rather as a penalty because she did not investigate properly into the death of her husband. According to this reasoning, she is also forbidden here, and on the contrary, here the prohibition is more severe, as she is both a married woman and the wife of a brother.

In my humble opinion, it seems clear according to the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, that those who believe it is a matter of penalty, this is the opinion of the Rif (whose version is in the fourth chapter of Pesachim. Rather, as the Rosh writes there), and the Rif himself ruled later that if one consummated a levirate marriage mistakenly from the betrothal, no divorce document (get) is needed (as in Yevamot 94b), and it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (beginning of chapter one) that the reason they required a get from the second is to clarify the prohibition of the first, meaning they validate the second marriage to prohibit her to the first (Nimukei Yosef). Therefore, they required a get from the second, and consequently, since they did not require a get from the brother, she is not prohibited to the first. This is also clearly proven in our Talmud there, that when they did not require a get from the second, she is not prohibited to the first, see there (where it says, "his wife should be forbidden to him," let us say not according to Rabbi Akiva, etc., but in marriage, and analyze carefully). 

And if it is difficult, after all, since because she did something forbidden, they penalized her, why did they not also prohibit her here to the first? The Rosh indeed raised this difficulty on the Rif, see there. However, this is also understandable; for in the Jerusalem Talmud there, it is questioned why the Sages penalized her regarding the first when he desires her, and he did not commit a sin. Why did they prohibit her to him? The Jerusalem Talmud answered that it is due to the scent of immorality touching her, meaning because she appears as the wife of the second (Pnei Moshe), which seems to the world that she married him permissibly (there). According to this, regarding the first, no penalty is applicable since what did he sin? Only in a case where she needs a get, as she appears as the wife of the second, she is consequently prohibited to the first. This all applies when she married another man, where it is possible to err and think the first divorced her. But regarding a brother's wife, it is impossible to err in this, as she is always forbidden to him and never appears as the wife of the second, and no get is needed. How could we penalize the first when he did not sin at all? According to this, what our Sages said that the Rabbis penalized is regarding the second, and consequently, she is also prohibited to the first since she needs a get from the second, unlike the case of a brother's wife, where she is in any case forbidden to him, and no get is applicable, and there is no prohibition on the first. It is clear that this is the opinion of the Rif, and this answers the Rosh's question (and the Kesef Mishneh struggled with this, but according to our explanation, it is clear. And it is puzzling on the Beit Yosef in his commentary on the Tur, who wrote that the Rif did not bring the ruling that a yevama, as a married woman, becomes prohibited to the first with betrothal (Yevamot 95b), whereas the Rif brought the ruling of Rabbi Akiva, which is the same, and analyze carefully).

In the Gemara (17b), there is a dispute regarding whether "zika" (levirate bond) exists or not. This means: if the yevama (widow bound to levirate marriage) who is bound to the yavam (levir) has a strong enough bond to be considered as his betrothed even before he performs yibum (levirate marriage) or chalitza (ritual release). The practical difference would be, for example, if the yevama dies before chalitza or yibum, whether the yavam is forbidden to marry her relatives, such as her mother or daughter, and similar cases. If "zika" exists, he is forbidden to her relatives just as he is forbidden to the relatives of his betrothed. If "zika" does not exist, he is permitted to them. And we hold that "zika" does exist, and he is forbidden to the relatives of the woman bound to him. And this is not only the case when there is only one yavam, where it is certainly incumbent upon him, but even if there are many yevamin, the "zika" applies to all of them, and all of them are forbidden to the relatives of the woman bound to them. This is what the Sages taught in the Mishnah (41a): A "shomeret yavam" (a widow awaiting levirate marriage) whose brother betrothed her sister, we tell him to wait before marrying her because she is the sister of the woman bound to him, and it is as if she were the sister of his betrothed until his brother performs yibum or chalitza, at which point her bond to him is severed and he may marry his betrothed. And here there are two brothers, so why should one wait before marrying her? It is certainly because even with two brothers, "zika" exists, and similarly with three or four or more.

And know that what we said, that there is a "connection" (zika), is not from the Torah but rather from the Rabbis, and the Rabbis only prohibited it when one betrothed in a prohibited manner while she was a yevama awaiting levirate marriage, as is implied by the language of the Mishnah we brought: "A yevama awaiting levirate marriage, whose brother betrothed her sister," which clearly implies that he betrothed her sister while she was a yevama awaiting levirate marriage. But if he betrothed her permissibly while his brother was still alive, and she was not yet bound (to levirate marriage), he does not need to wait at all, and he can consummate the marriage (Tosafot Yevamot 18a, s.v. "Shomeret"). And the reason for this is that since it is rabbinic, they did not prohibit it in such a case when he betrothed her permissibly.

Therefore, some say that specifically if he only betrothed her, we do not allow him to marry her. But if he has married her, he is permitted to be with her, for the marriage completely nullifies the levirate bond (zika) (there). This is also the ruling of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 5. Even if he married her and has not yet had relations with her, since he brought her into the chuppah (wedding canopy), the levirate bond is nullified and he is permitted to have relations with her before his brother performs chalitzah (ceremony releasing the levirate bond) or yibbum (levirate marriage) with the widow (Rosh, Chapter "HaCholeitz," Siman 23). The reasoning is as stated: since the prohibition is only rabbinic, they were not stringent in this case (as is evident from the words of the Rosh there). However, there are those who disagree and hold that since there is a levirate bond, even marriage does not help. For if we say that marriage nullifies the bond, then betrothal should also nullify it, since betrothal is a Torah commandment and the levirate bond is rabbinic (Nimukei Yosef, beginning of Chapter 2). But since the Sages prohibited betrothal, they also prohibited marriage, and the permission depends solely on the action of the brother performing chalitzah or yibbum. The first opinion holds that indeed we should say that betrothal also nullifies the bond (see Tosafot 18a, s.v. "Omerim"), but betrothal is not strong enough to nullify the bond, since the bond is also like betrothal. Just as a person with his betrothal is connected to her, so too the levirate bond that the Torah imposed on him connects him to her. And even though with the bond the matter is not yet completed since it requires yibbum or chalitzah, similarly with betrothal the matter is not yet completed until he brings her into the chuppah. But once he has married her, the bond is properly nullified, for with the bond the matter is not yet completed, and with betrothal and marriage, the matter is completely finished. Therefore, the Sages did not see fit to be stringent in this case.

And it is not only in the case where she is definitely bound (to the levirate marriage, yibum) that it is forbidden to marry her relatives, but even in a doubtful case where she might be bound, such as if Reuven died along with his sons and it is not known whether he died before his sons (in which case his wife is permitted to remarry) or after his sons (in which case his wife is bound to yibum), it is forbidden for Reuven’s brothers to marry the relatives of the woman who might be bound (to yibum), because she is considered Reuven's wife until one of Reuven’s brothers performs halitza (releasing her from yibum) or marries her. (This law is derived from the Mishnah regarding two men who betrothed two sisters and do not know which man betrothed which sister, as stated in Yevamot 23b, as explained by the Gra, note 21. Pay careful attention.)

A yevama (a widow awaiting levirate marriage) whose yavam (brother-in-law) betrothed her sister and then the yevama died, it is clear that he is permitted to marry his betrothed and we do not say that since he betrothed her in prohibition, she would be forbidden to him even after the levirate bond is removed. Not only in the case of two yevams, where it is explained that only if he marries her does the levirate bond dissolve, since there is another yavam who can perform chalitza (levirate divorce) or yibum (levirate marriage), but even if he is the only yavam. By betrothing the relative of the woman bound to him, he has in effect invalidated the mitzvah of yibum by his own hands, since even if he divorces his betrothed, the yevama is forbidden to him due to her being the sister of his divorcee. And while it would have been fitting to penalize him, nevertheless, when the yevama dies, he is permitted to marry his betrothed. However, while she is alive, even according to those who permit marrying in the case of two brothers, as mentioned, in the case of one brother, they agree that she is forbidden to him since he necessarily must divorce her because he needs to perform chalitza with his yevama, making her the sister of his chalutza (the woman with whom he performed chalitza). Moreover, it is taught in the Mishnah (41a) regarding a yevama whose brother betrothed her sister and then the second yavam died, leaving only the yavam who betrothed the sister of the bound woman, he must release his betrothed with a get (divorce document) and his brother’s wife with chalitza, for he is prohibited from performing yibum with her because she is the sister of his divorcee, and he is also forbidden to stay with his betrothed because she is the sister of his chalutza.

A woman awaiting levirate marriage (shomeret yavam) to one brother, where the yavam (brother-in-law) betrothed her sister, and afterward her sister died, it is permissible for the yavam to perform levirate marriage with his yevamah (the widow). Similarly, when there were two brothers and one of them betrothed the sister of the woman bound to yibbum (levirate marriage) and the other brother died, the one who betrothed her sister is permitted to perform levirate marriage with the yevamah. We do not say that since she was forbidden to him in yibbum at the time he betrothed her sister, and I do not call her "his yevamah shall come upon her," that she is like the wife of a brother who has children and is forbidden to him forever. Thus, the sages said (there), a yevamah who was permitted at the time she fell to yibbum and was later forbidden when he betrothed her sister and then permitted again when her sister died, she returns to her original permissibility. If he wishes, he may perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage); if he wishes, he may perform yibbum. This is specifically when she was permitted at the time of falling to yibbum, and he betrothed her sister when she was a shomeret yavam. But if he betrothed her sister during his brother's lifetime, and when his brother died, she was not permitted to him, even though afterward her sister died, it is forbidden to perform yibbum because at the time of falling to yibbum, the prohibition of "sister of his wife" stood before him, and she is forbidden to him forever. He must perform chalitzah for her (Tosafot there, s.v. "Why").

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that nowadays, due to the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom that one may not marry two women, if a man has a yevama (a widow bound to him by the mitzvah of levirate marriage), he is forbidden to marry another woman until he performs chalitza (a ceremony releasing her from the levirate bond) with the yevama. This is specifically when the other woman was not already betrothed to him, but if she was already betrothed to him, he is permitted to marry her.

The explanation of his words is as follows: Since we hold that there is a bond (zika) with the yevama, he should not marry another woman before performing chalitza with the yevama, as otherwise it appears as though he is marrying two women. Even though in our countries the custom is not to perform yibum (levirate marriage), since according to Torah law he is obligated to perform yibum, it appears as if he has two wives. However, if the other woman was already betrothed to him, he is permitted to marry her before performing chalitza with the yevama. 

Indeed, the earlier authorities (as mentioned in the Mordechai on Ketubot with glosses) elaborated on this issue, stating that there is no reason to prohibit, even initially, marrying another woman. Even though the sages were stringent about the bond (zika) regarding Torah-level prohibitions, should we also be stringent regarding a rabbinic decree? All the more so in our times when we do not practice yibum. Nevertheless, if the bond (zika) preceded the betrothal, it is appropriate to be stringent in this matter to avoid delaying the yevama and to perform chalitza for her. But if she was betrothed to him beforehand, and even in the case of a Torah-level prohibition it is clarified that if he betrothed her sister before the yibum obligation arose, he is permitted to marry her, then certainly regarding a decree like this one, how could the yevama prohibit his betrothed to him? Furthermore, this matter is elaborated upon there.

The Laws of Sustenance for the Yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage), Her Property, Inheritance, and Burial. This section contains 28 paragraphs:
Since it is forbidden for any yevama to perform halitzah (the ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage) or to enter into levirate marriage within three months of her husband's death, as stated in Siman 164, therefore, during the first three months, she is sustained from her deceased husband's assets. This is because she is held back from marrying anyone else and is akin to any widow who is sustained from her husband's assets. Just as any widow sustained from her husband's assets has her earnings go to the heirs, as stated in Siman 95, so too, in the case of a yevama, her earnings go to the yavam (the brother-in-law) during this time. Since the yavam is the heir, although a yevama sustained from the yavam's assets does not have her earnings go to the yavam, as will be explained, this is because her sustenance from the yavam's assets is not by strict law but as a penalty, as will be explained. There is no arrangement of her earnings in exchange for sustenance in this case. However, during the first three months, when she is sustained from her deceased husband's assets by strict law, she is like she was during her husband's lifetime, where her earnings are in exchange for her sustenance (the Beit Yosef questioned this, see Shach, subparagraph 1).

After three months, she is not provided sustenance neither from the husband's estate nor from the yavam's estate. Even though every widow is provided sustenance from the husband's estate as long as she has not married another, as this is a condition of the ketubah as stated in Siman 93, this is because she does not marry another out of respect for the husband, therefore they instituted for her sustenance. But the yevama (levirate widow) is bound to the yavam (levirate brother), therefore she is not entitled to sustenance from the husband's estate when she has the ability to undergo yibbum (levirate marriage) or chalitza (levirate release) (Rashi Yevamot 41b). And from the yavam's estate, she also does not receive sustenance as long as she has not undergone yibbum (ibid.), as she is no better than any betrothed woman who does not receive sustenance until she enters the chuppah (wedding canopy). If the yavam does not want to perform yibbum or chalitza, she should bring him to court, and they will instruct him to perform chalitza or yibbum. If he does not comply with the judgment, they will grant her sustenance, but if she demands it privately without bringing him to court, it is of no effect.

And our Sages said (there): If he stood trial and fled, she is sustained from the levir, meaning that she brought him to court to either marry her or release her, and he fled, she is sustained from the levir because we penalize him (Rashi). And even though according to the fundamental law, he should be obligated, as he is no worse than a betrothed woman whose time for marriage has arrived and he did not marry her, that he is obligated to sustain her, as we have written in Siman 56. And indeed, some say so (Ramban and Rashba). Nevertheless, one can say that his obligation is not from the fundamental law and is not comparable to a betrothed woman whom he is obligated to marry, but a yevama (widow waiting for levirate marriage) he can perform chalitza (ceremony to release her from levirate marriage) and he would not be obligated to sustain her. And since it is from the aspect of a penalty, it seems that it is specifically when he fled because of her, that he does not want to release her. But if he fled due to another matter, it is not appropriate to say there is a penalty in this case (so wrote the Hagahot Maimoniot in the name of Rashi, but I did not find this in Rashi). And similarly, if he fell ill and did not flee, the penalty does not apply (so wrote the Tosafot in the name of Rashi, and I also did not find this in Rashi).

However, most of our rabbis have ruled that even if he fled due to another matter or fell ill and did not flee, he is obligated to provide her sustenance (Tosafot, Rosh, and Nimukei Yosef there). And it is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Ketubot 5:4) that if he fell ill or went overseas, it is considered as if he fled, and he is obligated to provide her sustenance. According to this, it seems that they hold that it is a matter of law and not a penalty, as we brought the opinion of the "there are those who say." And although in the case of illness, even by law, there is no obligation to sustain her, as we rule in the case of a betrothed woman whose time has come and fell ill, that she is not entitled to sustenance, as we wrote in Siman 56, this is because he fell ill before the time arrived. But if the time arrived and he did not fall ill, and the obligation of sustenance fell upon him, even if he fell ill afterwards, his obligation is not nullified (Rosh). According to this, also here, if he fell ill a little before the end of the three months, he is not obligated to provide her sustenance.

Nevertheless, our rabbis have written that it is a penalty and not a legal obligation (Tosafot and Rosh), and the proof is that we do not find that they instituted that her earnings belong to him. On the contrary, in the Gemara (Ketubot 107a), it implies that her earnings do not belong to him. And if it were a legal obligation for him to support her, they should have instituted that her earnings be in exchange for her sustenance, just as it is with her husband himself (Rosh). And why did they penalize him? Because he did not perform yibbum (levirate marriage) immediately after the completion of the three months when she demanded that he either perform yibbum or halitzah (the ceremony to release her from the levirate obligation). Therefore, it appears that if at the time she became a niddah (ritually impure due to menstruation) and afterward he fled, she is not entitled to sustenance (150).

They also wrote that it is specifically when he agreed to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) and then fled that he is obligated to provide her sustenance. However, if he only agreed to perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from yibbum) and not yibbum, it does not seem that the sages would require the yavam (the brother-in-law) to provide her sustenance even if he fled, since he will ultimately perform chalitzah and not yibbum. Similarly, even if he agreed to perform yibbum, it is only when he fled or became ill that he is obligated to provide her sustenance. But if he neither fled nor became ill, even if he delays a little in performing yibbum, he is not obligated to provide her sustenance because it is uncommon for someone to delay performing yibbum when he is present and has agreed to it. For a short delay, which is usual, they did not establish sustenance for her. And it is simple that if he stood in judgment and did not promise either to perform yibbum or chalitzah, and he keeps postponing her, we compel him to provide her sustenance and other matters until he resolves it. We have already explained that her earnings belong to her at all times until he performs yibbum, even when she is receiving sustenance, and only before the completion of the three months are her earnings his for reasons we have explained in section 1.

Some say that it is specifically when he stood trial after the three months and then fled that he is obligated to provide her sustenance. But if he stood trial within the three months and fled after the three months, he is not obligated to provide her sustenance (Rivash section 4). This is also the ruling of our teacher, the Rema. However, there is no reason for this distinction. For what difference does it make if he stood trial beforehand? Certainly, if he fled before the three months, even if a lot of time passes subsequently, since he was not present when the obligation fell upon him, he is exempt. But if he fled afterward, why should he be exempt? This appears to be the primary understanding, and perhaps this is also their intention (Avnei Shoham section 3 and Gra section 2, and examine this closely). It has already been explained that all the laws applicable to one who flees also apply to one who falls ill.

The Rambam states in Chapter 18 of Ishut, Law 16: If the yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage) demands that the yavam (levir) either perform yibbum (levirate marriage) or halitza (ceremonial release), and he stands before the court and flees, or if he becomes ill or if the yavam is overseas, she is provided for from the yavam’s assets without any oath at all. It is clear from his words that even if he does not consent to yibbum but only to halitza, he is still obligated to provide her sustenance. It appears to me that even according to the opinion we mentioned in Section 6, nevertheless, in our region where only halitza is customary, they agree with the Rambam that he is obligated to provide her sustenance if he flees or becomes ill after three months, and when he has stood in judgment with her. Otherwise, he could keep her in a state of agunah (a woman chained to her marriage) forever. Since the primary obligation is a penalty, as we said, if we say that in our region he would not be obligated to provide her sustenance, this law would be completely nullified, and she would remain an agunah forever.

And regarding what is written, "or if he was in a distant land," the intention is not that he went there after having stood in judgment, for if so, it would have stated as much. Rather, the intention is that he was previously in a distant land, and the judgment took place there, or he sent his representative immediately. He is obligated to provide for her sustenance because he does not reside with her in the same country, which is treated as if he had fled or fallen ill (as is explained). And regarding what is written that she is not made to swear, the intention is as explained there concerning a widow who is sustained from the property of orphans, who is only sustained by taking an oath, as stated there in Law 19. Here it says that no oath is required.

If she was left pregnant, she is entitled to be sustained from the husband's estate until she gives birth, as she is prevented from performing chalitzah or yibbum while pregnant, as mentioned in Siman 164. If she gives birth to a viable child who does not require chalitzah, she is like any other widow who is sustained from her husband's estate until her ketubah is collected. If she gives birth to a doubtful stillborn, whose status requires only chalitzah and not yibbum, she does not receive sustenance, but she takes her ketubah immediately (see Be'er Hetev 6, which requires further investigation). The same law applies to all women who are eligible for chalitzah but not yibbum. Similarly, in our times and regions where yibbum is not practiced, they take their ketubah immediately like other widows, as will be explained in Siman 165, where the community ordinances on this matter will also be clarified. Even a yevamah eligible for yibbum, in places where yibbum is practiced, if the husband instructed before his death that she be sustained from his estate, she is sustained until the yibbum, even after three months (Kenesset HaGedolah).

If a woman falls before a minor yavam (levirate husband) and must wait until he grows up, she has no entitlement to sustenance at all. This is because she cannot receive sustenance from the minor's assets, as he is unable to fulfill the mitzvah until he matures. Additionally, she cannot receive sustenance from her deceased husband's assets after three months, as she is not considered to be delayed by him, since she could theoretically perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage) and remarry after this time. If the yavam is not yet fit for this, it is a heavenly decree. She only receives her ketubah (marriage contract payment) immediately, as it is assumed that the yavam will not marry her but will perform chalitzah for her (as previously mentioned, and according to the Acharonim). Even in places where levirate marriage is practiced, it is explained in the Gemara that they advise him appropriately — if he is a child and she is older, they tell him to perform chalitzah rather than yibbum (levirate marriage). Therefore, it is unreasonable to withhold her ketubah for such a long time, and she is not entitled to sustenance as stated.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) writes in paragraph 3: There are those who say that the reason she is not supported from the property of a minor yavam (levir) is from his assets, and even from the dowry she brought to her husband and he took possession of it. However, if he did not take possession of the dowry, such as if it is still held by a third party, she is supported from her dowry. All the more so in a case where she says that the assets should be given to her in order to preserve the principal until the boy grows up and to be supported from the profits, the money is given to her. The source of this law is from Rabbeinu Peretz, as brought in the Sha’ar HaGoleh (Shiltei Gibborim) on the Mordechai in the chapter "HaCholaytz." There it is explained that it was in the first year after marriage, and they relied on the enactment that the husband does not inherit in the first year, and also relied on Rabbeinu Tam’s opinion that as long as the assets are held by a third party, the husband does not acquire them. Nevertheless, they required the woman to take a light oath that the principal will remain intact until the yavam grows up. It seems to me that it is obvious that if she has property (nichsei melug) from which she is supported, in the case of nichsei melug, the yavam is not considered to have possession, and even from nichsei tzon barzel, she can consume the fruits or half the fruits as will be explained, that the yavam does not have all the fruits of nichsei tzon barzel according to many authorities. Therefore, I am puzzled why she should not be supported from the dowry she brought to her husband and he took possession of it, since a dowry has the status of nichsei tzon barzel as stated in Siman 85, and at the very least, she has half the fruits as will be explained. This requires further study (and it must be said that Rabbeinu Peretz holds like the authorities who say that all the fruits of nichsei tzon barzel belong to him, and regarding the Rema, this requires further study).

But if assets fell to a yevama while she is awaiting yibbum, all agree that she can sell her assets even initially. And even though regarding a betrothed woman, we hold in Siman 90 that if assets fell to her while she is betrothed, she should not initially sell them, and only if she sold or gave them away, it is valid after the fact. The yavam's power is not as strong as the betrothed man's power because the betrothed man’s relationship is one of complete marriage, and one who has relations with her is liable to stoning, whereas a yevama is only subject to a prohibition and perhaps he will perform chalitza for her. Therefore, his power is not as strong as that of the betrothed man. Even if the yavam performed ma'amar with her, it is of no consequence, as ma'amar with a yevama does not establish ownership. Some of the early authorities hold that assets that fell to her after he performed ma'amar should not be sold initially, similar to a betrothed woman (HaMaor, Perek HaCholitz). However, all the early authorities did not write this (and so it appears in Yevamot 39a that according to Beit Hillel ma'amar has no effect in this matter). There is no difference in this matter whether she fell to yibbum from betrothal or from marriage. But the assets that fell to her while she was still under her husband’s domain, the yavam has rights to them as will be explained, and she cannot sell them. However, if she is a yevama from betrothal and assets fell to her while she was betrothed during the life of the betrothed man, she can also sell them initially. The reason is that it is obvious that the yavam's position is not superior to that of the husband. And since regarding the husband himself, while she is betrothed, even though she should not initially sell, nevertheless, if she sold or gave them away, it is valid as stated in Siman 90. Therefore, the yavam's power is weaker than that of the husband, and she can sell even initially, because the yavam has only a connection (zika) to her, which is weaker than her own hand (Rashi, Yevamot 39a, according to Abaye, and even according to Rava, his position is not superior to hers. See Rashi, Ketubot 3a, s.v. Nikhsei Milog, and examine this thoroughly).

The Tur wrote: If properties fell to a woman while she is awaiting yibbum (levirate marriage), she can sell and give them away, and it is valid, etc. In what case are these words said? In regard to nichsei melug (property she retains ownership of), but concerning nichsei tzon barzel (property that becomes part of the husband's estate), she should not sell because the yavam (levir) has a right to them. And our master, the Beit Yosef, was puzzled, for what relevance does it have to say about properties that fell to her while she is awaiting yibbum that they are nichsei melug or nichsei tzon barzel? It is forced to say that while she is awaiting yibbum, she brought them in as nichsei melug or nichsei tzon barzel. I am very puzzled by his puzzlement, for it is clearly explained in the Gemara there that on the Mishnah which states, "Properties remain in their possession, etc., and properties that come in and go out with her remain in the possession of her heirs when she dies and not in the possession of the husband's heirs (this is nichsei melug and nichsei tzon barzel)," Rava establishes there that they fell to her while she is awaiting yibbum. Hence, it is explicitly in accordance with the words of the Tur. Similarly, the Ran wrote in Ketubot (Chapter 8), "And it turns out now according to Rashi's method that nichsei melug which fell to her while she is awaiting yibbum all go to the woman's heirs." And so too wrote the Rashba in the sugya in Yevamot there. Therefore, it is necessary to say that the intention is that she brought them in while she is awaiting yibbum as nichsei melug or as nichsei tzon barzel. (And so wrote the Bach). Alternatively, it is possible to say simply that when she married the husband, she stipulated with him that any properties that would come to her hand after would have the status of nichsei tzon barzel or nichsei melug, and since the yavam inherits all the husband's rights, it turns out that these properties that fell to her while she is awaiting yibbum follow the initial condition. And so it seems to me to be the principal understanding.

And know that there is a dispute among our early sages regarding the rights of the levir (yavam) over her (the yevama's) property, both concerning what she inherited while she is waiting for levirate marriage (shomeres yavam) and what she inherited while she was under her husband's authority. The dispute concerns three matters: the right to sell her property—whether she has the ability to sell it; the right to consume the produce of her property—whether the levir can consume the produce while she is still waiting for levirate marriage; and inheritance—if she dies, whether the levir inherits her property when he has not yet performed the levirate marriage or released her with chalitzah, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

The opinion of the Rambam, of blessed memory, in chapter 22 of Ishut is that all assets that fell to her while she was a yevama in waiting, whether they are Tzon Barzel (iron sheep) assets or Nichsei Melug (usufruct) assets, the yavam (brother-in-law) has no rights to them. He does not inherit them if she dies, and all the assets return to her heirs. Additionally, he does not consume the fruits (profits) of these assets. Regarding sale, she is able to sell them initially. Assets that fell to her while she was married to her husband—if she dies, her heirs inherit all her Nichsei Melug and half of her Tzon Barzel assets, and the yavam inherits half of the Tzon Barzel assets and her ketubah, which is either 100 or 200 zuz. Regarding the fruits, the Rambam holds that the yavam does not consume them at all while she is a yevama in waiting, not even from the Tzon Barzel assets that she brought to her husband. Concerning sale, it is not explicitly clarified in his words, but from the implication of his language there, it seems that she cannot sell any of the assets she brought to her husband, not even from the Nichsei Melug that fell to her while she was under her husband. This also seems to be the explicit opinion of the Rif in the chapter "HaChalitz" in agreement with the Rambam (who holds that the entire Talmudic discussion there and Rava's establishment is only according to Beit Shammai, but according to Beit Hillel, the Mishnah is interpreted straightforwardly as referring to the assets she had while under her husband, and therefore the Rif omitted the entire discussion).

Rashi's opinion is that property that falls to her while she is in a yibbum (levirate marriage) status all goes to the woman's heirs, even if the yavam (levir) has performed ma'amar (a preliminary act of levirate marriage). She can sell it initially, and certainly, he (the yavam) does not eat the fruits (benefits). Property that falls to her while she is in yibbum status is divided between the husband's heirs and her heirs when she dies, except for the dowry of one hundred and two hundred zuz, which belongs exclusively to the husband's heirs. According to Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot, the property that falls to her while she is in yibbum status also belongs exclusively to the husband's heirs, namely the yavam. However, property that falls to her while she is married to her husband belongs entirely to the yavam, and her heirs have no share in it, even her nikhsei melug (property she brought into the marriage and retains ownership of). Consequently, she cannot sell it at all. From the property that falls to her while she is in yibbum status, since it is divided upon her death, she can sell her half. According to Rabbeinu Tam, since it all belongs to the husband's heirs, she cannot sell any of the property. This applies when she falls from a marriage (as opposed to betrothal), but when she falls from betrothal, everything belongs to her and her heirs, and she can sell as mentioned. The law of eating the fruits is like the law of inheritance.

And know that what we have written, according to Rashi of blessed memory, is that property which falls to her while she is under her husband's authority—even if it is "nichsei melug" (property that remains in her ownership but the husband has usage rights)—all belongs to the husband's heirs, who is the yavam (the brother-in-law designated to perform levirate marriage). This seems apparent to me from the Gemara in Yevamot, since the Mishnah refers to property that falls to her while she is awaiting levirate marriage. It is explicitly stated that property which falls to her under her husband's authority does not belong to her heirs at all. Rashi also states this explicitly in Ketubot (83b), in the commentary on "nichsei melug," as follows: "And Rava disagrees with Abaye and says that if it fell to her while she was under him, everyone agrees that the husband’s hand is stronger than hers, and when he dies, his brother stands in his place for levirate marriage and he is like him. If she dies while she is awaiting levirate marriage, her heirs have no claim to it. And the Mishnah is referring to property that falls to her while she is awaiting levirate marriage." This is explicitly in accordance with our view that the yavam stands in place of the husband and is considered like him, and just as the husband inherits all her property, both "nichsei tzon barzel" (property whose value is fixed in the marriage contract) and "nichsei melug," so too does the yavam.

However, the Rashba, of blessed memory, in Yevamot there, and the Ran, of blessed memory, in Ketubot there, wrote according to the opinion of Rashi, of blessed memory, that properties that fell to her during her husband's lifetime should be divided between her heirs and the yavam (levir) when she dies, see there. And I am very puzzled by this. And it is true that from the wording of Rashi in Yevamot there in the commentary "his hand is stronger than hers" and even Beit Hillel agrees that the husband's heirs take from the properties, it somewhat implies like their words that they take a portion of the properties, and Beit Hillel agrees with Beit Shammai that the husband's heirs share with her heirs in properties that fell to her during her husband's lifetime, see there. But from Ketubot, it clearly implies as I wrote, and the wording of Rashi in Yevamot is according to the context of the discussion there, see there, and this requires further investigation. (And the Gra in his commentary Sk. 14 wrote that properties of tzon barzel and properties that fell to her during her husband's lifetime according to Rashi in both cases should be divided, and according to Tosafot both are for the husband's heirs, etc., end quote. And it is puzzling because in properties of tzon barzel even according to Rashi they go to the husband's heirs, as the Rashba and Ran wrote, and furthermore, Tosafot only disagree regarding tzon barzel, see there carefully. And his words according to Rashi are only if we rule like Abaye according to the opinion of the sage that Tosafot brought there, 39a, s.v. "even though," and this requires further investigation.)

Regarding the sale of property, the Rashba of blessed memory wrote that anything under her heirs' control when she died, she is permitted to sell during her lifetime. Anything under her husband's heirs' control when she died, she is not permitted to sell during her lifetime. Concerning the consumption of fruits, it seems logical that the yavam (levirate husband) does not eat the fruits of nichsei milug (property the wife brings into the marriage) even when he performs yibbum (levirate marriage), as the Rabbis did not institute the consumption of fruits for the yavam at all. For the husband himself, the institution of fruits is in exchange for her redemption, and the yavam is not obligated to redeem her, since there is no ketubah for the yavam, nor does she have the conditions of the ketubah from him. However, from the Talmud in Yevamot, it is explicitly understood that any right the yavam has in the land itself, he also has in consuming the fruits. Therefore, the Ran of blessed memory wrote that certainly the yavam eats half the fruits even when she is a shomeres yavam (awaiting levirate marriage), according to the extent of the right he has in the land itself by inheritance when she dies. When he performs yibbum, he eats all the fruits just like the husband himself. Although he is not obligated in her redemption, he inherits all the rights of his brother.

The opinion of the Tur is that in the case of property that fell to her while she is in the status of "shomeret yavam" (a widow awaiting levirate marriage), the yavam (the brother-in-law) has no rights to it, as it is written. And regarding property categorized as "nichsei tzon barzel" (property brought into the marriage with a fixed value) that fell to her while she is a "shomeret yavam," according to Rashi, if she dies, they (her heirs and the yavam) divide it. But according to Rabbeinu Tam, it all goes to the yavam. Similarly, regarding the consumption of the produce of "nichsei tzon barzel," according to Rashi, they (she and the yavam) divide it, but according to Rabbeinu Tam, the yavam consumes all the produce. Also, she is not permitted to sell it. It appears from his words that she is not allowed to sell even half because since he (the yavam) has rights to half, it is like they are partners, and as long as they have not divided it in a court, neither of them is permitted to sell even a part of it because each has a connection to all the property (according to the Bais Yosef, this resolves the difficulty raised by the Bach). And property that fell to her while she was under her husband, in the case of "nichsei tzon barzel," the yavam consumes all the produce, and if she dies, he inherits her. He also inherits her ketubah and the additional ketubah, and in the case of "nichsei melug" (property that remains in her ownership but he has the right to use the produce), they share the produce. If she dies, her heirs and the yavam share her inheritance, and she is not allowed to sell anything at all for the reasons we mentioned. This is the opinion of the Rosh, and it is also the opinion of the Raavad in Chapter 22 of Ishut (Marriage Laws) (they also hold like the opinion of the Rashba and the Ran that in the case of "nichsei melug," they share even what fell to her under her husband, contrary to what we inferred from Rashi of blessed memory).

The words of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, are somewhat puzzling in this matter. This is what it states in Section 6: A yavam (levirate husband) does not have rights to the produce (profits) of the nichsei melug (property owned by the yevama but maintained by her husband) of a yevama under levirate bond. Regarding nichsei tzon barzel (property brought into the marriage that remains the wife's but is managed by the husband), which she brought to her husband, he only has rights to half of their produce. There is an opinion that he has no rights to the produce at all until he marries her, but the first opinion is primary. Some say that even nichsei melug that she acquired while she was still married to her husband is treated like nichsei tzon barzel, and they share the produce. Similarly, they share her inheritance if she dies. In cases where the produce belongs to her, she can sell the land according to her share in the produce. If she dies while under levirate bond, her heirs inherit her nichsei melug and half of her nichsei tzon barzel. If the yavam gave her a gift, her heirs inherit it, and the heirs of the husband inherit the principal and additional amount of her ketubah, and half of the nichsei tzon barzel. The husband's heirs are responsible for her burial.
