Some say that all her nichsei tzon barzel are in the possession of the husband's heirs like the ketubah, and they are not taken from them if they are in possession. End quote.

And behold, regarding what was stated that the yavam (levir) does not have rights to the produce of nichsei melug (property owned by the wife and managed by the husband), this is the opinion of the Rambam. However, what was mentioned that regarding nichsei tzon barzel (property brought into the marriage that the husband is responsible for), he has half of the produce, requires further examination as to who holds this view. According to the Rambam, he has no rights to the produce at all as long as he has not performed yibbum (levirate marriage), and this is what some have written that he brought. According to Rashi, it is true that he consumes half of the produce, but this applies to nichsei tzon barzel that fell to her while she is a yevama (awaiting yibbum), and not to nichsei tzon barzel that fell to her under her husband, in which case the husband consumes all the produce, as the Tur wrote. According to Rabbeinu Tam, even in the case of nichsei tzon barzel that fell to her while she is a yevama, he consumes all the produce, as the Tur wrote. It must be said that he follows his reasoning that he questioned the Tur, since as long as she is awaiting yibbum, the concept of nichsei tzon barzel and nichsei melug does not apply at all. Therefore, it seems to him that according to Rashi and the Raavad, in all cases of nichsei tzon barzel, he only consumes half the produce. However, this requires further examination as none of the early authorities hold this view. (And if his intention was to refer to the Meor in the chapter "HaCholitz," indeed he also holds regarding the produce like the Rambam, and the Milchamot holds like the Tur, see there.)

And what was written, "And some say that even property that fell to her while she was still under her husband, they should share the produce and inheritance, and she is permitted to sell half," this is according to the opinion of the Tur. Only in the case of selling, they disagree with him, as he himself wondered in his large book regarding the Tur's ruling that she cannot sell at all—see there. And what was written afterward that if she died, her heirs inherit all her property, this is the opinion of the Rambam and not as our teacher the Rema wrote, the opinion we mentioned, and he did not correct it afterward because he relied on what he wrote earlier. And what was written that when the yavam (levirate husband) gave her a gift, her heirs inherit it, it is obvious that this is like property she brought into the marriage, and similarly, if the husband gave her a gift, the yavam does not inherit it, as it is like property she brought into the marriage (in the name of the Rashba). And what was written that the husband's heirs are obligated in her burial, this is in the Gemara, as her burial is in place of her ketubah. Similarly, the yavam is not obligated in her medical expenses or her ransom (Beit Yosef). And what was written that some say that all property brought into the marriage is presumed to belong to the husband's heirs, this is the opinion of all the early authorities except the Rif and the Rambam as written, and certainly, we do not take it out from their possession if they are holding it. And if it is not in their possession, it is a doubtful law, and they share it.

There is a question regarding the opinions of the legal authorities who have explained that there are certain properties from which the yavam (levirate husband) eats the fruits (benefits). What should be done when his brother had several wives and he has the ability to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) with whichever he chooses, and he is not permitted to perform yibbum with two? From whom does he eat the fruits? For if we say that he eats from all of them, this is not reasonable, as he only performs yibbum with one. And if he eats from one of them, each one will say, "Eat from the other." It seems to me that he can eat from whichever one he chooses, for he can say, "I will perform yibbum with you," and if he later performs yibbum with another, he must compensate her, for he should not have eaten from her. And the one with whom he performs yibbum does not need to compensate him for what he ate from the other, for she can say, "You should have eaten from mine, and since you did not, it was not your intention then to perform yibbum with me, so rightfully you did not eat." However, to prevent their sale, it seems to me that he can prevent all of them, for they do not suffer a loss from this. Regarding their inheritance, there is no question, for it is clear that when one of them dies, he has no connection with her, and he must necessarily perform yibbum with another. And this is what our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 8: "Reuven died, leaving two wives, and they remain bound to the yavam. If one of them dies, the yavam has no claim to the property, since the other is before him." And if the second one dies, he inherits her, not the first. And if it is not known which one died first, he takes nothing, for he is certainly their heir, and the yavam is in doubt, and uncertainty cannot displace certainty, as will be explained before us (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 13).

And similarly, in the case of a doubt regarding a woman waiting for levirate marriage (shomeret yavam) who died, such as if her husband had children and it is not known who died first, and she requires chalitzah out of doubt, and the yevama (widow) died—the husband's heirs, who is the yavam (brother-in-law), do not inherit her; rather, her own heirs inherit her. This is because her heirs are definitely inheritors, and the yavam is a doubtful inheritor, and a doubt does not take away from a definite status, as will be explained in Siman 163, see there.

This is what we have said: When the yevama (the widow awaiting levirate marriage) dies, the yavam (the brother-in-law) inherits, as has been explained. There is a dispute among the poskim (legal decisors) concerning if the father of the yavam is alive, who is the heir? Some say that the yavam is the heir, and even though the father precedes all his descendants in inheritance, nevertheless, since the son was destined to perform levirate marriage and would have taken his brother's inheritance, even though she (the yevama) died, he (the yavam) is called the heir (Mahariv). Others say that the father is the heir, for as soon as she (the yevama) dies, the bond of the levirate marriage dissolves, and the inheritance falls to the one who precedes in the husband's inheritance. Rabbi Rema writes that although logic supports the latter opinion, and this is somewhat implied by the term "heirs of the husband" in the Mishnah (38a), nevertheless, the Talmudic and Jerusalem Talmudic discussions in the chapter "The Woman Who Fell" imply that the yavam inherits the shomeres yavam (the widow awaiting levirate marriage). Therefore, the father has no part in her inheritance. If there are multiple yevamim (brothers-in-law), see later in Siman 165. End quote (Ab"sh sk12).

Additionally, it is written that all this applies in a place and time where they do not compel [the brother-in-law] to perform chalitzah. However, in a place and time where they compel him to perform chalitzah, it means that she was not fit for yibbum. Some say that in such a case, the property does not remain in the possession of the yavam, and therefore, if she dies, he does not inherit her. Consequently, in regions where they compel chalitzah, he does not inherit her according to this opinion. But from the words of the Tashbatz, which our Rabbi the Beit Yosef brought, and this is the ruling we cited in paragraph 26, it does not seem so. For if it were otherwise, why would we need the reason of "doubt does not remove certainty"? Furthermore, several great authorities disagree with this (see Beit Shmuel, section 11). Additionally, note that in the glosses to Chapter 8 of Ketubot, it is questioned how the woman's heirs collect, since she would only collect with an oath, and a person does not bequeath an oath to his children. The Tosafot in Yevamot 38 also wrote similarly. See also what the Taz answered on this, although it is a forced explanation.

If multiple women fall to one man for levirate marriage, what is their status? This section contains 13 paragraphs:
For one who had multiple wives and died, the levirate marriage (yibum) or the chalitzah (ritual release) of one of them exempts all of them. This does not mean that he is not required to perform yibum or chalitzah with all of them, but rather, it is forbidden to perform yibum with more than one. As it is written: "who does not build his brother's house" – he builds one house, and he does not build two houses. Consequently, when he performs yibum with one of them, the remaining women are prohibited to him as the wife of a brother. Additionally, regarding chalitzah, the Torah did not require performing chalitzah with all of them, as it is stated: "the house of the removed sandal" – he removes one house, and he does not remove two houses (Talmud 44a). Similarly, it is impossible to say that the intention of the Torah is to perform yibum with one and chalitzah with another, because from the derivations we have brought, it is only proven that one should not perform yibum with two or chalitzah with two. However, perhaps one could perform yibum with one and chalitzah with another. But this too is impossible, for in every chalitzah, it must be feasible for yibum, as it is written: "if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife, then she shall remove his sandal." If he does wish to perform yibum, and this second woman, he cannot perform yibum with her, as we have said, and consequently, she is exempt from chalitzah as well (this is the intention of the Talmud there).

And know that our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in his great book that there is no prohibition to perform chalitzah for both women; rather, it is unnecessary to do so, as he wrote. And some disagreed with him and held that there is a prohibition in this matter (Bach and Ateret HaZahav). And there are those who upheld his words (Beit Shmuel), and this is the main opinion: What prohibition is there in removing the shoe and spitting in his face? All the proofs brought by those who forbid it, from the derivations that one should not perform chalitzah for both, and also from the language of the Tosafot and commentators who wrote this, are not proofs at all. The Gemara needed a derivation to teach us that there is no obligation to perform chalitzah for both. This is the language: "Any woman who does not go up for yibbum does not go up for chalitzah," meaning that there is no need for chalitzah. For yibbum, a prohibition is relevant, but not for chalitzah. And for chalitzah, we only needed to ensure that there would be no obligation, as I wrote in the previous section (and similarly written in Responsa Kenesset Yechezkel, siman 68). However, if one performed chalitzah for the second woman, even though according to the law it is nothing, nevertheless, because of the appearance, since it was seen that chalitzah was performed, she is forbidden to marry a kohen (Bach and Beit Shmuel). And it is obvious that if she married, she should not be divorced.

The Sages of Blessed Memory (there) said that if there are two yevamot (widows awaiting levirate marriage) and one is fit for marriage to a kohen (priest) and the other is unfit for marriage to a kohen, for example, if she is a chalalah (a woman of flawed priestly lineage), a divorcée, or a zonah (a woman with prohibited relationships), when he performs yibbum (levirate marriage), he can choose to marry whichever one he wants. However, when he performs chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage), he should perform it with the one who is already unfit for marriage to a kohen. Why should he disqualify the one who is fit for marriage to a kohen when he is not compelled to do so, as he can perform chalitzah with the other? About this, the Sages of Blessed Memory (there) said: "A person should not pour out the water of his cistern when others need it," meaning that a person should not cause harm to others when it is not necessary. This is nothing but a sign of a bad heart, and we compel him to perform chalitzah with the unfit one if he refuses (Beit Shmuel, sub-section 2), for in such a case, we compel one to avoid the behavior associated with the people of Sodom.

If the deceased had many brothers and many wives, it is nevertheless forbidden for more than one wife to undergo yibbum (levirate marriage), and similarly, it is forbidden for more than one wife to undergo chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the widow from yibbum). After the fact, any one of the brothers who performs yibbum or chalitzah suffices, and all the wives are exempted and may marry others. However, ideally, our Sages said (Yevamot 24a) that the mitzvah is for the eldest brother to perform yibbum. If a younger brother precedes and performs yibbum, he has acquired the right. This does not refer to a minor under thirteen years and one day, as his yibbum or chalitzah does not exempt the others. Rather, it refers to the youngest of the brothers. Thus, ideally, the Torah insists that the eldest brother perform yibbum. If there is a firstborn brother, the mitzvah is specifically his. If there is no firstborn, they follow the order of seniority. The general rule is that the eldest brother takes precedence. This matter is a tradition transmitted from Moses at Sinai, and it is supported by scriptural verses as explained in the Talmud. As the Rambam wrote in Chapter 2 of Hilchot Yibbum, Halacha 6, what is stated, "the firstborn which she bears," is learned from tradition that it refers to the firstborn among the brothers, meaning the eldest of them. The phrase "which she bears" is like "which she bore," the future tense used in place of the past tense, referring to the brothers.

And regarding chalitzah (the ritual of removing a shoe as part of the levirate marriage process), whether there is a greater mitzvah for the older brother compared to the younger brother, there is a dispute in the Talmud (Yevamot 39b). The Rif and the Rosh bring the dispute but do not write a definitive ruling. The Rambam and the Tur rule stringently that even in chalitzah, the older brother is preferable. Similarly, our teacher, the Rema, ruled. It is clear that if the oldest brother is not fit for yibbum (levirate marriage), such as if the yevamah (widow) is forbidden to him, or if he is significantly older and it is not a reasonable match for him to marry her, then the second brother takes his place. If the second brother is also not fit, then the third takes his place, and so on indefinitely. Similarly, in the case of chalitzah, if the oldest brother is not fit for chalitzah, for example, if his leg is crooked or similar issues, then the second brother takes his place, and then the third and fourth, as stated.

If the older brother does not want to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) but only chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage), and the younger brother wants to perform yibbum, the yibbum of the younger brother is better than the chalitzah of the older brother, since chalitzah in the place of yibbum is not a mitzvah. However, if neither of them wants to perform yibbum but only chalitzah, it is preferable for the older brother to perform chalitzah, as it is written. Some say that if the older brother has a wife, it is preferable for the younger brother to perform chalitzah rather than the older brother. The reason might be that the chalitzah of the older brother is not appropriate for yibbum according to the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom, who prohibited marrying two wives, even in the case of a mitzvah. It is possible that even in places where they perform yibbum and marry two wives, it is still better for the younger brother who does not have a wife to perform yibbum rather than the older brother who has a wife, so that he does not bring a rival wife into his home. This is also implied from the words of the Ritva, which are brought in the Beit Yosef, Siman 165.

It has been explained that the levirate marriage of a younger brother takes precedence over the ritual release (chalitzah) by an older brother. This does not align with what is stated later in Siman 165, that in our times the mitzvah of chalitzah takes precedence. Even according to those who hold that even in our times the mitzvah of levirate marriage (yibbum) takes precedence, this is only when she consents to the levirate marriage with the younger brother. However, if she does not consent and prefers the chalitzah, the chalitzah by the older brother is preferable. This is the ruling of our teacher, the Rema (Rabbi Moses Isserles) in paragraph 6, and the reasoning behind this is that although levirate marriage is generally greater than chalitzah, we are nonetheless obligated to consider what is best for the yevamah (the widow). The Sages derived this from a verse in the chapter "HaChalutz" (Yevamot 44). See there.

It has already been explained that the commandment is upon the eldest [brother], and if the eldest does not want to either perform chalitzah or yibbum, we do not force him, since the commandment can be fulfilled by another brother. This is not like other positive commandments where we compel observance; rather, this is an enhancement of the commandment. If the second brother also does not agree, we turn to the third, and so on through all the brothers. If none of them want to perform either chalitzah or yibbum, we must return to the eldest and tell him that the commandment is upon him—either perform chalitzah or yibbum. If he still refuses, we compel him, for this is like any other positive commandment since none of the brothers are willing, and the commandment would be nullified if we did not compel one of them. Therefore, we compel the eldest.

Know that when we compel him if he does not want to perform either chalitzah or yibbum, we compel him to perform chalitzah and not yibbum, even though yibbum is a greater commandment. This is because it would not be for the benefit of the yevama (the widow), as no one can live in harmony with a snake in the same basket. We have already explained that we are obligated to look out for her welfare, and thus we compel him to release her with chalitzah.

Even though it has been explained that the levirate marriage (yibbum) of a younger brother is preferable to the chalitzah (ceremonial release) of an older brother, this is only when the younger brother is currently suitable for yibbum. However, if he is actually a minor, under thirteen years and one day, or if he is of age but is currently deaf, the older brother cannot say, "I only desire chalitzah, therefore wait until my younger brother grows up or until he is cured of his deafness and can perform yibbum." We do not listen to him, and we say to him that delaying the mitzvah is not permissible (Gemara 39b), and he should do as he wishes, either perform chalitzah or yibbum.

Similarly, if the oldest of the brothers is at a distance, and the younger brother who is present is suitable for yibbum or chalitzah, the younger brother cannot say, "Since the mitzvah is with the older brother, wait for him until he comes." We do not listen to him for the reason explained—that we do not delay the mitzvah. However, if the older brother is in a nearby location, we wait for him. If waiting incurs expenses and she (the widow) is poor, it is considered as if he is in a distant location (Bach, Taz, and Beit Shmuel).

Even though it is a mitzvah for the older brother to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) or chalitzah (the ceremony to release the widow from the obligation of yibbum), nevertheless, if the younger brother went ahead and performed yibbum, he has fulfilled the mitzvah. Similarly, if the younger brother performed chalitzah, it is valid after the fact, and he is not punished. However, ideally, one should seek out the older brother and give him his due portion of the inheritance, as will be explained in Siman 165.

Rabbeinu the Rema writes in section 4: "Even if the elder brother swore not to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) or chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the widow from yibbum), we compel him to do so, but we do not compel the younger brother. Nevertheless, we annul the elder brother's oath, even though it is only due to appearances." The explanation of these words is as follows: We hold that if one swears to nullify a commandment, the oath does not take effect, similar to one who swears not to eat matzah on the nights of Passover, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, section 236. Here too, he swore to nullify the mitzvot of yibbum and chalitzah, and the oath does not take effect. And even though there is another brother, why should the oath not take effect? Since it is possible for the second brother to fulfill the mitzvah, indeed, if the second brother is willing, it is fine. However, if he is not willing and he is a minor whom we cannot compel according to the law, then necessarily the obligation of the mitzvah falls only on the elder brother. Therefore, it is considered as if he swore to nullify the mitzvah, and it is not reasonable to say that because of the elder brother's oath we should compel the minor, for what does the minor care about the elder brother's oath?

And there is a question regarding this: Why should the oath not take effect? After all, it is established there that an oath takes effect when it includes other matters, such as if one swears not to eat matzah the entire year, and also on the nights of Passover. Since the oath takes effect for the entire year where there is no mitzvah, it also takes effect on Passover through inclusion. Accordingly, here too, if one swore only regarding yibbum, the oath would take effect, and this would not be considered as swearing to nullify a mitzvah, since it is possible to perform chalitzah. Similarly, if one swore only regarding chalitzah, the oath would take effect, as it is possible to perform yibbum. Therefore, since it takes effect on one, it should also take effect on the other through inclusion.

The answer to this is that it is not comparable. There, the oath included a complete non-mitzvah matter, like matzah throughout the year, where there is no mitzvah at all. But here, both chalitzah and yibbum are mitzvot, as the Torah obligates resolving the yibbum connection through one of them. He swears not to resolve the connection through either of them, which is indeed swearing to nullify a mitzvah. To what is this similar? To one who swears not to sanctify either wine or bread. Would we say that since it could take effect on one, it is not swearing to nullify a mitzvah? (Rivash, Siman 159). Moreover, inclusion does not apply here since the actions are not equivalent: chalitzah distances, while yibbum brings closer. It is like swearing not to eat matzah on Passover nights and not to go up to the roof. We do not say that since it takes effect on going up to the roof, it also takes effect on eating matzah. Similarly, inclusion only applies to equivalent actions, like not eating matzah throughout the year and on Passover nights, and similar cases (there). Additionally, some say that inclusion only takes effect when the mitzvah is not explicitly mentioned, like when one says not to eat matzah the entire year. But if he explicitly mentions the mitzvah alone, like if he says not to eat matzah the entire year and on Passover nights, it does not take effect (Tosafot Shevuot 24a, s.v. Ela). According to this view, it is clear that here it does not take effect.

The sages taught in the Mishnah (Yevamot 43b): Four brothers married to four women and they died, and there are other brothers. If the eldest of them wants to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) with all of them, he is permitted to do so. We do not say that since there are many brothers, each one should fulfill the mitzvah because the primary mitzvah is upon the eldest, he can perform yibbum with all of them. It is stated in the Gemara there that this is specifically if he is wealthy and able to support all of them, but otherwise, we do not allow it because it is not a proper counsel to bring them into his house without the means to support them. The same applies that he can perform yibbum with more than four if there are many brothers and they all died; however, the Tanna teaches us in his language a good counsel that he should not perform yibbum with more than four even if he is very wealthy, so that each woman receives her marital duty once a month, as the usual marital duty is once a week, from Sabbath to Sabbath. According to this, if he is already married, he should not perform yibbum with more than three. In our countries, it is forbidden to marry more than one woman according to the decree of Rabbeinu Gershom, as stated in Siman 1. 

Know that what is stated in this Siman, that the eldest brother takes precedence, is when both are complete Jews. But if a yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage) remains for two brothers, one of whom is a Jew and the other a forced convert (anus) from the forced converts of the time, the Jew takes precedence for chalitza (the ceremony releasing the brother-in-law from levirate marriage) even if he is younger than the anus. If the anus performed chalitza first, she is permitted to marry anyone, for although he sinned, he is still a Jew. This is elaborated upon in Siman 157, see there.

### Laws of the Co-wives of the Yevama and Her Relatives. It Contains Eight Sections:

One who marries his yevama (widow of his brother who died childless) renders the co-wives forbidden to him and to the other brothers by a positive commandment (Yevamot 11a), as it is written, "He shall build the house of his brother"—he builds one house and not two houses. Thus, the prohibition derived from the positive commandment (as explained by Rashi) indicates that we do not say that the co-wives remain under the prohibition of being a brother's wife, which incurs karet (excision). For once one of them has undergone yibbum (levirate marriage) or chalitza (ceremonial release), she acts as a representative for all her co-wives, and the one performing yibbum or chalitza acts as a representative for all the brothers. The prohibition of a brother's wife is removed from all of them when the brother dies childless, and only the positive commandment we mentioned applies to them. The Rambam in Chapter 1 explains that the positive commandment is derived from the verse "The yevama shall come unto her"—not unto her and her co-wife, and this is a prohibition derived from a positive commandment. We will explain his reasoning in Section 4, with God's help. The Tosafot there interpret the Gemara as stating that they transgress the prohibition of "He shall not build"—once he performs yibbum with one, the co-wife is called a "not built" wife because he shall not build again. However, they did not derive a positive commandment from the verse "He builds one house and not two houses," as this verse serves to establish the law itself—that he should not perform yibbum with more than one—and not as a positive commandment. See there. Rashi, of blessed memory, holds that the positive commandment is implicitly understood from it.

And similarly, one who performs the act of chalitzah on his yevamah (widow of his childless brother), the woman upon whom the chalitzah was performed and her co-wives are forbidden to him and to the brothers by a negative commandment of "he shall not build" (Deuteronomy 25:9), because once he did not build (i.e., marry her) but performed chalitzah, he may no longer build. This is what Rashi (Yevamot 10b) and Tosafot wrote, and similarly, the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot wrote in the laws of forbidden relations. And it is explained in the Gemara there that they are subject to a negative commandment. Similarly, later (Yevamot 53a), it says there that the entire household is subject to a prohibition. According to this, it is very surprising that the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that this is also a positive commandment, which is against the Talmud. What positive commandment is there in this? It is possible to say that because it is written "the house of the one whose shoe was removed" (Deuteronomy 25:10), we derive that he performs chalitzah on one house and not on two houses, and it is considered a negative commandment that comes from a positive commandment. And in the case of chalitzah, when he performs it again, it does not apply as a prohibition; rather, the intention is that he should not perform another act with them. Consequently, when he has relations with them, he transgresses a positive commandment. (And the Gra in his annotation 2 wrote that there is a scribal error in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, and it should say a negative commandment.)

The words of the Rambam in the first chapter are even more perplexing in this regard. After he wrote the law concerning one who consummates a marriage with his yevamah, stating that he transgresses a positive commandment with respect to the co-wives, he wrote as follows: "Similarly, one who performs chalitzah with his yevamah, the woman who underwent chalitzah and all her co-wives become forbidden to the one who performed chalitzah and to all the other brothers. They are all forbidden to them by rabbinic decree, like secondary forbidden relationships (shniyot). Since his brother died without offspring, the prohibition of ervah (a forbidden relationship) is removed from all his wives. Therefore, kiddushin (betrothal) is effective with them like with shniyot." End quote. The sages of the generations have already expressed astonishment at this, as he makes this a rabbinic prohibition, while in the Gemara it is clear that it is a prohibition of a negative commandment. The Rambam follows this approach also in chapter 18 of the laws of forbidden relations, law 4, where he states: "One who has relations with one of the shniyot or similar cases, such as with a relative of the woman who underwent chalitzah or with the woman who underwent chalitzah herself, does not render her a zonah (a woman who is disqualified to marry a kohen), since she is not forbidden to marry him by Torah law, as stated in the laws of yibbum." End quote.

It appears to me in the reasoning of the Rambam, of blessed memory, that he holds that in the verse "who does not build his brother's house," there is neither a prohibition nor a positive commandment. As we have written, the Tosafists hold that there is no positive commandment here because the verse is needed for itself. Therefore, the Rambam, of blessed memory, ingeniously found another positive commandment in "when a man marries his brother's wife," as I wrote in Section 1. Similarly, he holds that there is no prohibition either in the verse "who does not build," as this too is needed for itself, so that we do not say when there are two women left, that one should be taken in levirate marriage and the other in halitzah, as explained explicitly in the Gemara (44a; see there in Tosafot s.v. "Venaybem," and some books have the version etc., and this was the version before the Rambam).

Indeed, our Rabbis, the Tosafists, had much difficulty with this and were greatly pressed (Yevamot 10a, s.v. "Ihu," and there is a wonder, etc., see there). Another proof for this is that in this law, Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish argue in the case of one who performed halitzah with his yevama and then betrothed her again. Rabbi Yochanan says that there is no liability of karet (excision), and in the Jerusalem Talmud, the version is simply that there is no liability, suggesting there is no Torah obligation at all. According to our version, it is not explicit in Rabbi Yochanan's words that there is even a prohibition. There is proof that there is no prohibition at all, as later (11a), Rav Acha and Ravina argue about one who marries his yevama and then he or one of the brothers has relations with her co-wife. One says it is karet and the other says it is a positive commandment. The Talmud explains that they are arguing in the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish. The one who says karet follows Resh Lakish, and the one who says a positive commandment follows Rabbi Yochanan.

It is difficult why they didn't argue in the exact dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish regarding one who performed halitzah with his yevama and then one of the brothers had relations with her co-wife. One says karet and the other says a prohibition. Rather, it is certain that there is no Torah prohibition according to Rabbi Yochanan, and the law follows him. Although one could say that in the case of one who performed halitzah, Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish did not argue about the brothers, only about the one who performed halitzah himself, as stated there in the sugya. However, why didn't they argue about the brothers? Moreover, in the Jerusalem Talmud in the first chapter, it says: "What do you think, is halitzah a transaction? No, it is a release, etc. Once he has performed halitzah with her, the bond of the deceased is uprooted retroactively." See there. According to this, it is clear that all connections the women had to the deceased are nullified. If so, why would the one who performed halitzah or another brother be liable when he betroths the one who performed halitzah or her co-wife, since they are disconnected from each other and are like strangers to each other?

Additionally, there is some proof from the fact that it is a clear law throughout the Talmud that the sister of a halutzah is not prohibited by Torah law but by rabbinic decree. If we say that everyone agrees there is a prohibition of a prohibition in the one who performed halitzah, why isn't her sister prohibited by Torah law? Although it is not the sister of a prohibited relative, nevertheless, there is some prohibition. (However, this can be simply dismissed, as Resh Lakish says that the sister of a halutzah is prohibited by rabbinic decree, and according to him, it certainly seems there is a prohibition. Pay close attention to this.)

Therefore, from all these proofs, the Rambam, of blessed memory, concluded that there is no Biblical prohibition regarding a chalutza (a woman who performed the chalitza ceremony) and her co-wives. And this statement in the Talmud that they are subject to a negative commandment is a different matter and is not according to the Halacha, as we will explain with God's help. For Rabbi Akiva holds at the end of the chapter "HaCholitz" that a mamzer (a child born from certain forbidden relationships) can result from negative commandments, but this is not the Halacha as is well-known. And consequently, he holds that there is no valid kiddushin (betrothal) in cases of negative commandments, as is famously known in the Talmud, where kiddushin depends on the issue of mamzerut. And the Talmud in Yevamot, where it states in the Mishnah that nothing follows chalitza, meaning that there is no valid kiddushin, establishes this according to Rabbi Akiva. And all the early authorities held that even the Rabbis hold that she is subject to a negative commandment, but they hold that kiddushin is valid in cases of negative commandments. However, the Rambam holds that only Rabbi Akiva holds that she is subject to a negative commandment, and for a different reason: because it is said in Yevamot that Rabbi Akiva holds that the offspring from the close relative of a chalutza is a mamzer, and his reason is that it is written "the house from which the shoe was removed," indicating that she is still considered his "house." And thus Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis also disagree on whether she is still considered his "house" or not. Rabbi Akiva holds that she is considered his "house," while the Rabbis hold that she is not. Therefore, the Talmud's statement that she is subject to a negative commandment, based on the verse "who does not build his brother's house," applies only according to Rabbi Akiva, who considers her his "house" and thus sees a negative commandment and mamzerut resulting from it, leading to invalid kiddushin. But according to the Rabbis, she is not considered his "house" and they are completely separated from each other, as we brought from the Jerusalem Talmud, and they are like complete strangers, with no prohibition. Therefore, when the Talmud states that it is a case of a negative commandment, it is referring to Rabbi Akiva. Likewise, when the Talmud later refers to this, it is also according to Rabbi Akiva. And therefore, the Rambam ruled that the prohibition to marry is Rabbinic. And this that it says in the Talmud, "Perhaps he should perform chalitza first and then yibum," and it is said, "because once he did not build, he shall not build," means that after chalitza, the Torah does not require yibum, and thus it would be a forbidden act like any other promiscuous relations. According to the Rambam, all promiscuous relations are Biblically forbidden without kiddushin, as stated at the beginning of the laws of marriage. But through kiddushin, it is Biblically permitted, and the Rabbis decreed against it. Additionally, it is possible to say that the Rambam interprets like all the commentators that there is a negative commandment according to everyone, but the negative commandment is specifically when he has relations in the manner of yibum. This is what the Torah said: "because once he did not build, he shall not build," meaning in the manner of building (yibum), it is forbidden, but in the manner of kiddushin and marriage, it is permitted, though Rabbinically forbidden. As our Sages said in Kiddushin that everyone agrees regarding one who remarries his divorced wife that if he had relations without kiddushin, he is not liable, because the Torah forbade it in the manner of taking (kiddushin). Similarly, we can say here, the Torah only forbade it in the manner of building (yibum), but in the manner of kiddushin, it is permitted. (And indeed, there are those who have the version that if he performed kiddushin without relations, he is not liable, because the Torah forbade it in the manner of building the house, as brought in Tosafot on Yevamot. This is evidence for our interpretation, and we should scrutinize it further).

The words of the Tur can be somewhat reconciled in this manner: he certainly agrees that there is a prohibition of "he shall not build," but this applies when he comes upon her in the manner of yibbum (levirate marriage) and not through betrothal and marriage. Therefore, when the Tur wrote that the chalutzah (the woman who underwent chalitzah) and her co-wives are forbidden, he means they are forbidden in all manners, even through betrothal. This is not something we derive from "he shall not build," and he also does not want to interpret like the Rambam that this is only rabbinic. Therefore, he wrote that it is a positive commandment. The positive commandment is as stated in section 2, from which it is clear that it is forbidden for him and his brothers to do any act with her and her co-wives, and consequently, it is forbidden in all manners.

The one who performs chalitzah to his yevamah is rabbinically prohibited from marrying her close relatives, such as her mother, daughter, and sister. This decree is similar to that of a forbidden relationship because, to people, a chalutzah appears like a forbidden relationship. The Sages decreed even on her secondary relatives as on the forbidden relationship itself. This is not considered a decree upon a decree, as they were stringent in this matter due to the case of the sister of one's divorced wife, which is a fully prohibited relationship, as well as all her close relatives. To the general public, a chalutzah appears like a divorced woman. Therefore, she is also prohibited from marrying his close relatives. However, the brothers are permitted to marry all her close relatives because they did not perform any act with her, and thus she does not appear to them like the close relative of their divorcee. Therefore, the one who performed chalitzah is not permitted to marry the sister of his chalutzah unless the chalutzah dies, similar to his wife when she dies, allowing him to marry her sister. But regarding her other close relatives, he is prohibited even after her death. There is no difference between a definite chalutzah and a doubtful chalutzah.

And so the Sages taught in the Mishnah (40b): a man is permitted to marry the close relative of the co-wife of his yevamah (the woman from whom he performed chalitzah), but he is prohibited from marrying the co-wife of the close relative of his yevamah. For example, if Jacob performs chalitzah with Leah, he is forbidden to marry Leah's relatives, as we have explained. However, he is not forbidden to marry the relatives of Leah's co-wives, even though all of them were equally bound to him for yibbum (levirate marriage), and he could have performed chalitzah with any of them. The yevamah who underwent chalitzah acts as a representative for all the co-wives, as explained. Nevertheless, since the prohibition against marrying the close relative of the yevamah is rabbinic, as we have explained, they did not decree a prohibition on her co-wives, and there is no risk of confusing one with the other. 

However, regarding the co-wife of the close relative of the yevamah, like Rachel, Leah's sister, who is forbidden to Jacob because she is the sister of his yevamah, if Rachel marries another man and he dies, leaving Rachel with a co-wife, that co-wife is also forbidden to Jacob just like Rachel herself. The reason for this, according to the Sages, is practical: it is common for a sister to accompany her sister to the court for chalitzah, so it might appear that Rachel was present at the time of Leah's chalitzah. People might mistakenly think Rachel was the one who received chalitzah, and if Jacob marries Rachel's co-wife, they might say that he married the co-wife of his yevamah, which is a Torah prohibition. Even according to the Rambam, who holds that this prohibition is rabbinic, it is still very severe, almost like a Torah prohibition, similar to the secondary prohibitions regarding incestuous relationships. According to what we have explained, even the Rambam agrees that there is a Torah prohibition in this case. However, they did not decree a prohibition regarding the close relatives of the yevamah's sister, such as her daughter and granddaughter, as this level of decree was not established.

There are some of our Rabbis who explain that this applies specifically when Rachel, Leah's sister, was married to the deceased brother, and then he also died. Jacob is then prohibited from performing yibbum with Rachel because she is the sister of his yevamah, and therefore he is also prohibited from performing yibbum with Rachel's co-wives and must perform chalitzah with one of them (as explained by the Nimukei Yosef in the name of the Ritva, and similarly by Tosafot and the Rosh, see there and analyze thoroughly). However, if Rachel was married to another man and he died, Jacob is permitted to marry her co-wife.

The surviving brother inherits the estate of his deceased brother, and there are additional laws regarding this. This section contains eighteen paragraphs:

It is written: "And it shall be that the firstborn that she bears shall succeed in the name of his deceased brother" (Deuteronomy 25:6). Our sages received a tradition from Moses at Sinai that the entire verse is to be expounded and refers to the surviving brother (yavam) and not to the child that would be born. "And it shall be that the firstborn" implies that it is a mitzvah for the eldest brother to perform the levirate marriage, as stated in Siman 161. "That she bears" excludes an ailonit (a woman who cannot bear children), meaning if the widow is an ailonit, she is not subject to levirate marriage since there cannot be an establishment of seed. "Shall succeed in the name of his deceased brother" refers to inheritance, meaning that the yavam inherits all the estate of his deceased brother, and neither the father nor the other brothers take any part of the inheritance. "So his name will not be blotted out from Israel" excludes a eunuch (saris), meaning if the yavam is a eunuch who cannot bear children, he does not perform levirate marriage, similar to the ailonit. One should not say that the verse refers to the child that would be born, that he should be named after the deceased brother, with the Torah commanding that the firstborn son to be born should be named after him, such that if the deceased's name was Yosef, they would call the firstborn Yosef, and if the name was Yochanan, they would call him Yochanan. It is stated here "shall succeed in the name of his deceased brother" and it is stated "in the name of their brothers, they shall be called in their inheritance" (Numbers 27:4). Just as the name mentioned there refers to inheritance, so too the name mentioned here refers to inheritance (Talmud Yevamot 24a). Furthermore, it is not logical to say that the firstborn son should inherit all of his father's estate, as there is no reason the other sons born should not take a share. If it refers to the yavam, it makes sense that he takes all the estate, and his children after him will inherit him, but the idea that the firstborn son should inherit everything is not reasonable. Additionally, if this were the case, the verse should have stated "shall succeed in the name of his uncle" (Tosafot).

And all these matters that came through tradition are explicitly mentioned in the writings in the Book of Ruth, where Boaz married Ruth, which was similar to the matter of yibbum (levirate marriage), as it is explained there that he acquired the field of Machlon and Kilyon and married the wife of Machlon, and it is written, "And also Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Machlon, I have acquired to be my wife, to raise up the name of the deceased upon his inheritance, that the name of the deceased be not cut off..." (Ruth 4:10). And Rashi explains that since his wife goes out and comes in the inheritance, bringing in and taking out, people say, "This was the wife of Machlon," etc. See there. Thus, it is explicitly as the tradition of the sages that the raising of the name is through the inheritance, and that the inheritance goes to the yavam (the brother-in-law) as in the case where the inheritance was Boaz the yavam's. And it is not the actual name, for Boaz and Ruth did not call the firstborn child from them Machlon, but rather Oved, as stated there. And it is also explained there that the main thing is the offspring that they will bear, which will be considered as if the deceased had borne, as it is written there, "A son is born to Naomi" (Ruth 4:17). Therefore, the Torah forbade a eunuch and a barren woman, who are not fit for raising seed, as this is the main aspect of raising the name of the deceased. For if the deceased did not leave an inheritance, his wife is still subject to yibbum, and the main aspect of raising the name is through offspring, and also the inheritance is a form of raising the name, as Rashi explains in Ruth. Therefore, the yavam does not take the inheritance until he has relations with her, and even if he performs ma'amar (a formal betrothal act), it does not suffice, for it is not considered raising the name. But if he has relations with her, even if he dies immediately or divorces her immediately, the properties are his, for he has raised the name of the deceased. (And it is questionable if she was from betrothal and she is a virgin, as she does not conceive from the first intercourse, if there is considered to be raising the name in this case. And it seems there is no difference, similar to what the Beit Shmuel wrote in siman 166, sk 6).

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Bekhorot 51b) that the yavam (levirate husband) does not receive the appreciation (increase in value) that the properties have accrued after the death of the deceased brother, and he does not take what is potentially due as he would with what is already in possession. The explanation is as follows: Certainly, the yavam takes the appreciation that the deceased brother's properties accrued because they belong to him, and thus the appreciation is also his. However, if the deceased brother's father died before the deceased brother, and the deceased brother had a share in the inheritance, and before the brothers divided the properties, the properties appreciated in value, and the appreciation occurred after the death of the deceased brother, the yavam takes the deceased brother's share in the father's properties because the deceased brother was in possession of them when he died. The appreciation, however, he does not take alone because it was before the division. But if the deceased brother died before the father, the yavam does not take the deceased brother's share at all, as this is considered "potential" (something he would have taken when the father died) and the yavam does not take potential as he would with what is already in possession. This is not similar to the grandson inheriting the grandfather's properties, where he takes his share even if his father (the son of the grandfather) died before the grandfather. (And regarding appreciation before the division, he does not take even if he has already performed yibbum.)

And our Sages, of blessed memory, derived this (Yevamot 24b) from the fact that the Torah refers to the yavam (levirate husband) as the firstborn, as it states that his status is like that of a firstborn. Just as a firstborn does not receive a double portion from properties that come into the estate after the father's death, or from the appreciation of assets after the father's death but before the division, as explained in Choshen Mishpat, siman 278, so too the yavam. Therefore, some say that any type of potential inheritance from which a firstborn does not receive a double portion, likewise, the yavam does not inherit alone. According to this, with regard to a loan that the deceased left behind, the yavam does not inherit it alone, because in the case of a firstborn this is considered a potential inheritance since the loaned money is considered to be in the possession of the borrower and not the lender. And some say that the yavam receives the loan and other potential inheritances, but he does not receive the potential inheritances of his father if the father dies after his brother. And Rabbeinu Rema wrote that the first opinion is the primary one.

And some say that there is no disagreement at all, that from the property of the brother himself, from a loan that he left, the yavam (levirate brother) certainly takes, since it is entirely his, just as he takes from the appreciation of his property, as mentioned. But from what is expected from the father, even though he died before the father, nevertheless, from a loan that the father left and other expected inheritances clarified there, the yavam does not take the portion of the deceased, just as the firstborn does not take a double portion in this (Beit Shmuel and the Gra, section 8).

And there are those who say that from the words of the Tur earlier in section 60, it appears that even from the brother's own property, the yavam does not take from what is expected (Beit Shmuel, section 2). His intention is to what the Tur wrote regarding the portion of the wedding gift that was supposed to come to the deceased, the yavam does not inherit it. Similarly, it is in the Gemara. However, it seems to me that there is no proof from this, for one who examines the Gemara (Bava Batra 144b) will see that the obligation of the wedding gift, even though it is designated for this brother, is still considered the power of his father, as the father sends through this son, and therefore it is considered as what is expected from the father.

And some say further that even in the father's property, it is considered as possessed (mukhzak), even if he died before the father, and what is called expected is in the property of the father's father (there in the name of the Rivav). But from all the poskim (decisors) it does not seem so. I saw someone who wrote that this is the opinion of Rashi and the Ri Ba'al Hatosafot (Kenesset HaGedolah), but in my opinion, it is not so. It seems his intention is to what is mentioned in Bechorot 52b, to include the property of the grandfather, and see there in Rashi, and there is no proof that it is necessary to say so because of the firstborn. And what Rashi wrote in Yevamot 24b, "the firstborn etc., even the yavam who takes a double portion in his father's property etc., does not take from what is expected," his intention is regarding the loan of his father, as mentioned. And what was said in the name of the Ri, I do not know to which place he referred. And it is clear, as mentioned, that the Nemukei Yosef wrote in the name of the Ritva in Yevamot there, and he wrote that all the commentators agreed so. See there and scrutinize.

However, the one who performs the rite of chalitzah for his yevamah (sister-in-law) does not have any advantage over the other brothers regarding the estate of the deceased. Nevertheless, he does not lose his share (Rashi 40a), and we do not say that he should be penalized for not performing yibbum (levirate marriage) with her. If there is a father, the estate belongs to the father, for he precedes in inheritance, and when he dies, his sons will inherit from him, and each son will take his portion. Even if he (the brother who performed chalitzah) wanted to perform yibbum but she did not want to, and he performed chalitzah for her, we do not say that since there was no impediment on his part, he should inherit everything. Ultimately, he did not perform yibbum, and the Torah ties the inheritance specifically to yibbum. Therefore, he only has a share in the estate like any other heir. All of this applies to the deceased’s estate that exceeds the value of the chalutzah's ketubah (marriage contract). However, if she waived her ketubah in favor of the one who performed chalitzah, he alone takes it (Kenesset HaGedolah), and this is straightforward.

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: Even before he performs chalitzah, if the father seizes the property and claims "I hold like the opinion that the mitzvah of chalitzah takes precedence," and thus compels the brothers to perform chalitzah, we do not remove the property from his possession. This is the law, but there is already a decree that the one who performs chalitzah receives half of the property. This decree will be explained in Siman 165. The explanation of his words is that the father can hold onto the property, and by doing so, none of the brothers will agree to perform yibbum. However, if despite this, one of them performs yibbum, it is obvious that the property is removed from the father and given to the yavam, since the Torah grants it to him. This is also evident from the source of the law in Maharik, Siman 91. And it is understood that in a place where it is ruled that the mitzvah of yibbum takes precedence, the father cannot act in this manner. In a place where yibbum is not permitted, it does not need to be mentioned. This situation refers to a place where there is no clear ruling on this matter, and some perform chalitzah while others perform yibbum. It is obvious that the father cannot seize what belongs to the widow (see also the gloss of the Shach, subparagraph 4).

Rambam wrote in Chapter 5 of the Laws of Inheritance: This is the rule regarding heirs: Whenever there are two heirs, one of whom is a definite heir and the other is a doubtful heir, the doubtful heir receives nothing. If both are doubtful, such that it is uncertain whether this one or that one is the heir, they divide equally. Therefore, etc. If a widow did not wait three months after her husband's death and remarried within three months and gave birth to a son, it is not known whether he is a nine-month child from the first husband or a seven-month child from the second husband. This doubtful heir claims, "Perhaps I am the son of the deceased, and I should inherit all my father's property, and you are not fit to perform levirate marriage with her, as my mother is not subject to levirate marriage." The levir (the brother-in-law) claims, "Perhaps you are my son, and your mother is subject to levirate marriage, and you have no claim to my brother's property." Since this levir is also a doubtful heir, as it is uncertain whether he is the levir or not, they divide equally. Similarly, this doubtful heir and the levir's children divide the deceased's property equally: the doubtful heir takes half, and the levir's children take half, etc. End quote. This is explicitly stated in the Talmud, Yevamot 37b, and similarly stated by the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in this chapter.

There is a question regarding this matter: We have established in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 139, that any monetary doubt where both parties are in possession, like the case of two people holding a garment, they split it. And in a case where neither party is in possession and neither has the presumption of prior ownership, we say "whoever is stronger prevails." Here too, we should say "whoever is stronger prevails," since neither is in possession, and there is no presumption of prior ownership. The answer is that the principle of "whoever is stronger prevails" applies only when each party claims definitively that the item is theirs. We assume that whoever truly owns it will strive to prevail, and the truth will emerge. However, in this case, where the matter is concealed from everyone, "whoever is stronger prevails" does not apply, and dividing it is preferable. Additionally, since both come by virtue of inheritance, it is as if both are in possession, and by law, they must divide it (as per Nimukei Yosef). This is clearly stated in the Gemara (Bava Batra 158b), where it says that since both parties come to inherit, they divide it.

Furthermore, the Rosh wrote in this law (Yevamot, Chapter 8) that even if one of them is in possession of the property, this possession is not valid since the property is presumed to belong to the deceased, and both come with a doubtful claim. Holding the property in doubt does not help (see there). He follows his opinion in the first chapter of Bava Metzia (Siman 13) that possession does not help unless one claims definitively, but possession in doubt does not help. We maintain the property in the presumption of the deceased as the prior owner, and consequently, they divide it.

Additionally, there is no question why we do not consider the property in the presumption of the yavam (the brother-in-law performing levirate marriage), as immediately upon performing the yibbum, he acquires the property, and the one born later comes to take it from him. How can he take it with a doubtful claim? This is not a question, because since most women give birth at nine months, we should consider the one born later as certainly the son of the first husband and the heir. However, because most women show signs of pregnancy by the end of the first trimester, and it was certainly not evident here, if it had been evident, there would be no doubt. Therefore, the majority is weakened, and it is like money in doubt, and they divide it (as per Rashba). Additionally, we do not consider the property of the deceased in the presumption of the yavam unless he performed the yibbum properly, as he was supposed to. But here, he performed yibbum before three months, possibly transgressing a severe prohibition, and should not have performed yibbum. How can we consider him in possession of the property by virtue of yibbum? At most, we consider it a doubt (in my opinion).

However, the opinion of the Rosh and the Tur is that this law only applies when the father of the yavam is still alive. But if the father has already died, the property is presumed to belong to the yavam for another reason: even without yibbum, he is certainly the heir since he is the brother, and the newborn is a doubtful heir, and a doubt does not override a certainty. But when the father is alive, the brother does not inherit at all in place of the father, and he only inherits through yibbum, and both are equal in this right. The Rambam and other poskim did not differentiate in this matter because, according to the reasoning we wrote, since most women give birth at nine months, it is impossible to consider the yavam as a definite heir. On the contrary, we should consider him as a doubtful heir due to the majority, and it is not applicable to say that we do not follow the majority in monetary matters, as this only applies when the other is in possession of the money, which is not the case here where neither is in possession. Even if one were to take hold of it, it would be a doubtful possession and would not be effective, as we wrote. Nevertheless, we do not consider him a definite heir because the majority is weakened, as we wrote. However, in any case, both are in a state of doubt.

(The Maharshal questions the Rosh, arguing that according to the doubtful son's claim, the yavam is not a definite heir. This is no worse than the case of the grandfather and the doubtful heir regarding the yavam's property, and similarly, the Yam Shel Shlomo questions this in Chapter 7 of Perek HaCholitz. But there is no difficulty at all: the Rosh's intention is that while the yavam was in existence as a definite heir, the doubtful son was not yet in existence, and when he is born, he seeks to take from him, which is not comparable to the case of the grandfather and the doubtful heir regarding the yavam's property. And so wrote the Ketzos Hachoshen, and examine this well.)

(And see the Shach in subparagraph 4, whose words require examination. He differentiates this from the case of the grandfather and the doubtful heir regarding the yavam's property, and certainly, this distinction is simple, and they questioned it from the case of the grandfather and the doubtful heir regarding the yavam's property.)

If the doubtful child (safek) dies before the division, and the elder, the father of the yavam, claims that perhaps the doubtful child was the son of the deceased (benei hameit) and he (the elder) is his heir, and the yavam claims that perhaps he (the doubtful child) was my son and I am his heir, it is considered a doubt within a doubt, and the elder and the yavam divide the estate. But if the yavam dies and the doubtful child is alive, the assets belong to the doubtful child in any case (mimah nafshach), whether he is the son of the first deceased (ben hameit harishon) or the son of the yavam, he precedes the elder and anyone else in inheritance of the assets of the first deceased, for either he is his son or the son of the yavam who inherits and inherits from his father.

And regarding what the Rambam wrote about the case of the doubtful son (safek) and the sons of the yavam regarding the property of the deceased, that the doubtful son takes half and the sons of the yavam take half, it is puzzling. Because, according to the doubtful son, who claims that he is the son of the deceased, all the property belongs to him. And according to the sons of the yavam, who also claim to be the sons of the yavam, at the very least he (the doubtful son) should have a portion like one of them. Therefore, he has a definite claim to part of the property, and they have a doubtful claim, and a doubtful claim cannot take away from a definite claim. However, the early authorities have already written that when one has a definite claim to part of the argument, it is not the same as having a definite claim to the entire argument. For example, in the case of two people holding a garment, where one says it is entirely his and the other says half of it is his, we learned at the beginning of Bava Metzia that both swear, and each takes a portion, and we do not say that the entire garment should go to the one who claims it all because he has a definite claim to half. This is because they are not comparable (Tosafot there). This is not similar to what will be explained regarding the doubtful son and the yavam concerning the property of the grandfather, where the yavam is definite and takes everything. There, the yavam knows for certain that he is the heir of the grandfather, and the doubtful son does not know, so it is like he has a definite claim to all the property. But here, the doubtful son himself does not know from which source he inherits, whether from the deceased or from the yavam. Therefore, he is also in doubt. And although, in any case, he has a definite claim to part of the property, this does not apply to all the property, as we explained with the garment. Therefore, he takes half, and they take half.

However, his words are still perplexing in what he wrote that the one in doubt takes half and they take half, for they admit to him that he has a portion, and he does not admit to them at all. Therefore, he should first take the portion they admit to him, and the remainder they should divide. Indeed, all the early authorities have ruled this way, as is written in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 4: "If the one in doubt and the sons of the deceased come to divide the estate of the deceased, he says, 'I am the son of the deceased and will take everything,' and they say, 'You are our brother and have only a portion like one of us.' The portion they admit to him, he takes, and the rest they divide, with him taking half and them taking half." And it is even more perplexing that the Rambam himself ruled similarly regarding the one in doubt and the sons of the deceased in the estate of the grandfather, that the portion they admit to him he takes, and the remainder they divide. See there. Why should the estate of the deceased be different from the estate of the grandfather? It is the same reasoning and the same doubt. (And the words of the Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 7, are perplexing, and what kind of reasoning is this? And the words of the Maggid Mishneh there are lacking understanding. See there.)

It appears to me that the reasoning of the Rambam is that it is impossible to award him a share from two different sources of doubt, and it is also impossible to award him more than his claim. The explanation is as follows: If we give this doubtful portion that they agree to, he would take it based on the power of the yavam, since according to their words, he is the son of the yavam and should take a portion with them. As for the remainder that he would take half of, he would take it based on the power of the deceased, and how can he take from two different sources of power? This is not the case with the grandfather’s property, where everything is based on the grandfather. Similarly, it is impossible to award him more than his claim, as he claims to be the son of the deceased, so how can we give him a portion and consider him as one of the sons of the yavam, which he does not claim to be? And indeed, according to his claim, he is entitled to all the property, but in this case, we do not take his claim into account because there is doubt, and we divide. This ruling is similar to the law explained in Choshen Mishpat, end of Siman 17, that a judge cannot rule for a litigant more than what he claims, even if the judge sees that he could be entitled to more, see there. This case is analogous, but with the grandfather’s property, he claims it as the grandson of the grandfather, and he takes from the grandfather’s property, and we do not concern ourselves with the intermediate powers (i.e., from whom the inheritance passes) of whom they belong to (and perhaps this is the intention of the Maggid Mishneh, see there).

When there is a doubt, and the children of the yavam (the brother who married the widow) come to divide the property of the yavam, the children of the yavam completely reject the doubtful claimant because they are definite heirs of the yavam, whereas he is doubtful if he is the son of the yavam. And a doubtful claim cannot override a definite claim. Furthermore, even if previously the yavam and the doubtful claimant divided the property of the deceased, as was explained, and the property of the deceased was minimal while the yavam left substantial property, the doubtful claimant cannot say: "If you do not give me a share of the property of your father the yavam and consider me as the son of the deceased, return to me half of the property of the deceased that your father the yavam took, and if not, I will return half of what I took from the property of the deceased to the general estate and take an equal share with you from the property of the yavam." Although his claim is good and comes with the strength of an alternative claim, we hold that the initial ruling stands. This means that since the ruling on the doubtful claimant and the yavam was already decided, and at that time it was the main ruling, it does not pertain to the current ruling. Now, too, we rule according to the present law that a doubtful claim cannot override a definite claim. In the Talmud, there is a dispute (there) whether we say the initial ruling stands or the ruling reverts with the alternative claim. The Rif and the Rambam agreed that we hold the initial ruling stands. And some say it is a doubtful law, but we do not remove from the yavam's heirs due to doubt. According to this, if the doubtful claimant seized, we do not remove it from his possession (Beit Shmuel, section 8).

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 4, end of Halacha 2): If the levir (yavam) dies, and the doubtful one (safek) comes to claim his father's portion, if the father was poor, they say to him, "These are your father's possessions." If he was wealthy, they say, "All these are brothers, sons of brothers. Come and inherit your father's portion and your uncle's portion." And the commentators explained that this refers to a case where the doubtful one and the yavam had already divided the deceased's property, as in our Babylonian Talmud. The Jerusalem Talmud holds that the ruling reverts back. However, it appears to me that the Jerusalem Talmud is not discussing this at all, but rather a case where they did not manage to divide the deceased's property until the yavam died. Now they need to divide two inheritances. In this case, the brothers have a stronger claim than the doubtful one. If the deceased was poor and the yavam was wealthy, they can reject him from the yavam's property because they are certain heirs and he is doubtful, as has been stated. And if the deceased's property was substantial and the yavam's property was minimal, since he is also doubtful regarding the deceased's property, they combine all the assets and divide them equally, as if he were certainly a son of the yavam. Even though when the yavam is alive and dividing with the doubtful one, the Jerusalem Talmud agrees that the doubtful one takes half, as stated earlier, nevertheless, when the yavam dies, he does not take more than one of the yavam's sons. Since the two inheritances have not yet been divided, they combine the two inheritances and divide them equally. It is possible that our Babylonian Talmud and all the decisors do not disagree with this. Specifically, when we only have the inheritance of the deceased before us, both are doubtful and the yavam and the doubtful one divide. But when we have two inheritances, the deceased's and the yavam's, and each comes to inherit their father and their uncle, and they know who their father and uncle are, while the doubtful one does not, but still, he also has a father and uncle, and since they certainly know who their father and uncle are and he is doubtful, therefore their power is stronger. They can choose to say, if the first deceased was poor and the yavam was wealthy, to reject him from the yavam's property saying he is the first one's son. And if the reverse, they say, "You are our brother." Just as in any case of certainty and doubt, the certain one has more power than the doubtful one, so too in these two inheritances, they give the certain heirs more power than the doubtful one (as it appears to me). Therefore, the decisors who ruled that the law reverts did not bring proof from the Jerusalem Talmud.

If there is a doubt regarding the status of the child and the yavam (levirate brother-in-law) who come to dispute the inheritance of the deceased elder, and the doubtful heir claims, "I am the son of the deceased and entitled to his place in the inheritance," he is not listened to and is not entitled to anything. This is because the yavam is the definite heir, while the doubtful heir is uncertain, and an uncertainty cannot override a certainty.

However, if the doubtful heir and the sons of the yavam come to dispute the inheritance of the deceased elder, and the doubtful heir claims half, asserting that he is the son of the deceased, while the sons of the yavam claim, "You are our brother, and you have no more share than one of us," and if there are two sons of the yavam, they suggest dividing the estate into three parts, while the doubtful heir claims half, the ruling is as follows: He takes the third that they concede to him, and the half that he concedes to them, they take. The remaining third is considered money in doubt, and they split it, each taking half.

But if the doubtful heir dies and the elder and the yavam come to divide his estate, they split it because both come from a position of doubt. It is not known if he is the son of the deceased, in which case all the property belongs to the elder, as the father inherits the son, or if he is the son of the yavam, in which case the elder has no share. Similarly, if the yavam dies and the elder and the doubtful heir come to divide his estate, they split it between them because both are doubts.

(Note: The difficulty raised by the Beit Shmuel in section 10 according to the Rosh's opinion regarding the doubtful heir and the yavam in the deceased's estate is the same difficulty raised by the Maharshal and the Yam Shel Shlomo, which we mentioned in section 10, and we will clarify it there, with God's help.)

It states in the Jerusalem Talmud (there): If one of the brothers dies, there is certainly a brother and possibly a nephew. This means that if one of the yavam's brothers dies, the doubt (regarding the nephew) does not take anything because the yavam certainly inherits him as his brother, and the nephew, if he is the son of the yavam, is the son of his brother. And doubt does not override certainty. This is when the brother did not leave any offspring, and also if the elder brother (the yavam) is not alive, for otherwise, his brother would not inherit him. It further says there: If the mother of the doubtful (nephew) dies, there is certainly a son and possibly a husband. This means that the husband, who is the yavam, wants to inherit her as a husband inherits his wife, but he does not take anything because the son is certainly her son, and the husband is in doubt. This is not similar to the case of doubt and the yavam regarding the deceased's property, where they share because there, the yavam is certainly a relative of the deceased, as he is his brother, and in the inheritance, there is doubt who is closer to inherit. But here, there is doubt in the core of the relationship, whether he is the husband or not. For if the doubtful (nephew) is the son of the first husband, she was yevama (married in levirate marriage) in a forbidden act punishable by karet (spiritual excision), and she is not his wife at all. Therefore, it says further that even if the doubtful (nephew) dies, her relatives inherit her and not the husband because they are certainly her relatives, and the husband is in doubt whether he is her husband at all, as we have stated.

The yevamah (widow subject to levirate marriage) should neither undergo yibbum (levirate marriage) nor perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage) within three months. This section contains twenty-one paragraphs:

The yevamah should not undergo yibbum until ninety days have passed from the husband's death, excluding the day of death and the day of yibbum. This is because there is a concern that she might be pregnant, and during this time, if her pregnancy is not noticeable, she is certainly not pregnant, as pregnancy becomes noticeable within three months. Although it might be argued that she should wait one more day since conception sometimes occurs at the end of three days, and thus she might have conceived on the day of her husband’s death, with the embryo becoming noticeable at the end of ninety days, leaving one day short, the Sages were very stringent in this matter, even with regard to general differentiation, and certainly with differentiation involving the prohibition of karet (excision). It can be said that it is uncommon for conception to occur exactly at the end of three days and for the pregnancy to go unnoticed until the last moment, making it a very rare occurrence that the Rabbis did not concern themselves with. Moreover, it is rare for intercourse to occur on the day of death and result in conception, making it three rare occurrences that are highly uncommon altogether (see Tosafot Yevamot 37a, s.v. "Rov," and their explanation is not satisfactory regarding a yevamah, as we should be concerned that the pregnancy might be noticeable the next day, resulting in her having engaged in prohibited relations punishable by karet. One must say as explained, and Tosafot did not resolve this because, in general differentiation, this was not necessary. Refer there and consider this carefully).

Even if Elijah were to come and say that she is not pregnant, she is still forbidden to perform yibbum within three months. This was the decree of the Sages, even in cases of general distinction, that one must wait three months, even if she is a minor who is not capable of bearing children, as stated in Siman 13. Certainly, this also applies to a yevamah. Even those who did not decree in cases of general distinction did decree regarding a yevamah (Tosafot 41a, s.v. ha). Even if it is certain that she is not pregnant, such as if she had been separated from her husband, she is still forbidden to perform yibbum. Not only is she forbidden to perform yibbum before this time, but she is also forbidden to perform chalitzah before she is eligible for yibbum, as it is written: "If the man does not wish to take his brother's wife... then she shall remove his shoe" (Deuteronomy 25:7-9). This implies that if he does wish to perform yibbum, he may. It is thus clear that the Torah is particular that she be eligible for yibbum at the time of chalitzah (Gemara, ibid.). Thus, the Sages expounded: anyone who is eligible for yibbum is eligible for chalitzah, and anyone who is not eligible for yibbum is not eligible for chalitzah.

There is a question here: In several places, the sages said that she performs chalitzah and does not undergo yibbum. Furthermore, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 4, ruled that a menstruant performs chalitzah and does not undergo yibbum. Rashi, of blessed memory, explained that this is because it is impossible, similar to the case of the sister of one who performed chalitzah, the sister of one awaiting yibbum, and the doubtful co-wife of an ervah, because if we were to always prohibit, then she would be forever prohibited.
