Therefore, since by Torah law she is eligible for yibbum, she performs chalitzah. But in the case of three months, where it is possible to wait, we wait. This is also written by the Rashba and Nimukei Yosef (and it is also inferred in Tosafot there, s.v. safekot). 

I am puzzled: If so, why does a menstruant perform chalitzah? After all, it is possible to wait until she becomes pure. We must say that it is specifically concerning a matter that touches upon the essence of the law of yibbum, where she is not eligible for yibbum due to a prohibition related to yibbum, that she also does not perform chalitzah. But in the case of a side prohibition, such as a menstruant or similar cases, she indeed performs chalitzah. What is this similar to? When she is ill and it is difficult for her to engage in intercourse, would we say that she is not eligible for yibbum and does not perform chalitzah? There is proof for this from the Jerusalem Talmud, which expounds this teaching from the verse "Her yavam should come to her" etc., that for one whom we say "perform yibbum," we also say "perform chalitzah." For one whom we do not say "perform yibbum," we do not say "perform chalitzah." Thus, it excludes only one who is not eligible for yibbum due to the essence of yibbum, where it is impossible to tell him to fulfill the mitzvah of yibbum.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: If he performed yibbum (levirate marriage) or chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from yibbum) within this time and she was not found to be pregnant, she is exempt and needs nothing further. However, she should not marry another, even though she performed chalitzah, until ninety days have passed since the husband's death. If the yavam (the brother-in-law obligated to perform yibbum) dies within the ninety days or after them, some say she must wait ninety days after his death. If there were two yevamim (brothers-in-law), and one of them died, she is permitted to perform yibbum with the second one within ninety days of the first one's death. End quote.

Explanation of the matter: Even though the Sages prohibited yibbum (levirate marriage) and chalitzah (a form of release from levirate marriage) within three months in any situation, even when it is clearly known that she is not pregnant, as has been explained, nevertheless, after the fact, they did not uphold their prohibition in both yibbum and chalitzah. If yibbum or chalitzah was performed within three months, and it is known that she is not pregnant—such as in a case where she was separated from her husband and similar situations—the yibbum is valid, and she is not separated from the yavam (levir) until the completion of the three months. However, if there is doubt, it appears that she should be separated. There is an opinion that says even in a doubtful case, this is the ruling (Beit Shmuel, sub-paragraph 2). I am puzzled by this opinion, for how can one say this? If she turns out to be pregnant, it becomes a severe prohibition, punishable by karet (spiritual excision) for each and every intercourse, and how is it possible that they would not separate them? See paragraph 15.

And even if the chalitzah was performed within three months, if it is subsequently discovered that she is not pregnant, the chalitzah is valid, and she does not need another chalitzah. Likewise, it is not considered an invalid chalitzah that would require her to perform chalitzah with all the brothers. Nevertheless, she should not marry another man until ninety days have passed from the death of her husband, even if it is known for certain that she is not pregnant. We do not say that since she has already performed chalitzah, she may marry, for in any case, she is not better off than all the widows and divorcees who are required to wait the period of discernment in all cases, as stated in Siman 13.

If the yavam dies within ninety days or after ninety days, and she has still not been taken in levirate marriage or performed chalitzah, some say that she must wait ninety days from the death of the yavam, because we are concerned that he might have had relations with her, as she is closer to him in terms of relations than a betrothed woman, since it is a mitzvah to have relations with her and perform yibbum. And since every betrothed woman must wait, all the more so a yevamah. However, this is only when there was only one yavam. But if there were two yavams and one of them died, the second does not need to wait at all. She is not similar to a betrothed woman because she is as close to him as to the deceased and is not closer in terms of relations to the deceased than to the living yavam. Also, the living yavam could have had relations with her even if he is younger than the deceased, as it has already been clarified that if the younger one precedes, he acquires her. Therefore, as long as it is not known that the deceased had relations with her, the living yavam may perform yibbum with her immediately after the ninety days from the death of the first (Gra, Sk 4).

Nevertheless, according to the opinion of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, when a yevama (a widow subject to levirate marriage) undergoes chalitza (the ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage) within 90 days and it is found that she is not pregnant, the chalitza is valid. This is also implied in the Gemara (41b), which teaches that if brothers performed chalitza for a yevama within three months, she must wait three months from the day of the husband's death. This implies that the chalitza is valid because otherwise, it would have been necessary to state that the chalitza is invalid. Nevertheless, Rabbeinu the Rema wrote that there are those who say that if chalitza was performed within three months, whether she was found to be pregnant and miscarried or was not found to be pregnant, the chalitza is invalid, and she must undergo chalitza from all the brothers as in the case of invalid chalitza, as will be explained in Siman 170. This opinion is found in the Mordechai at the end of Gittin, and it is also the first explanation of Tosafot in Yevamot (35b), in the context of "and found," as well as explicitly in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Perek HaCholitz, which states that if chalitza was performed within three months, it must be repeated after three months. This implies that even though chalitza was performed, it must be repeated. According to this opinion, the Baraita did not mention that the chalitza is invalid because all the brothers performed chalitza within three months, as implied by the language of the Baraita "a yevama for whom the brothers performed chalitza," implying that all performed it. Therefore, since by Torah law the chalitza is valid and only rabbinically invalid, requiring her to undergo chalitza from all the brothers, and since she already did so, no further chalitza is required. However, it cannot be said that the Baraita is not addressing this law but only the law of waiting three months, since if that were the case, what is it teaching us by stating she must wait three months from the husband's death? It is obvious, as she still needs another chalitza after the three months. Therefore, it must be as we have written. Nor can it be said that this opinion disputes the Baraita in our Talmud and follows the Jerusalem Talmud because we do not rule according to the Jerusalem Talmud when it contradicts our Talmud. Therefore, it must be as we have written.

According to this opinion, if there are other brothers, she requires chalitzah from all of them after three months, except from the one who performed chalitzah within the three months, as she does not need another chalitzah from him (Beit Shmuel, subsection 4, and this serves as proof for what was stated earlier; examine this carefully). Nevertheless, if there are no other brothers, she requires chalitzah from this brother after three months (ibid.), because only when there are other brothers is another chalitzah from him unnecessary, as his chalitzah is considered inferior to all of them, and why should she need another chalitzah from him, or if all the brothers already performed chalitzah within the three months, we should not trouble her further, as stated. But when there is only one brother and he transgressed the decree of the Sages, certainly another chalitzah is required after three months to fulfill the decree of the Sages (this seems correct to me).

The Sages taught in a Mishnah (beginning of chapter 4): If a man performs chalitzah (a form of levirate divorce) with his yevamah (brother's widow) and it is found that she is pregnant and she gives birth, if the child is viable, he is permitted to marry her relatives and she is permitted to marry his relatives, and she is not disqualified from marrying into the priesthood. If the child is not viable, he is forbidden to marry her relatives and she is forbidden to marry his relatives, and she is disqualified from marrying into the priesthood. 

There is no difference whether her pregnancy was noticeable at the time of the chalitzah or not: if the child is viable, even if her pregnancy was not noticeable, they are permitted to marry each other’s relatives and she is fit to marry into the priesthood. If the child is not viable, even if her pregnancy was noticeable, they are forbidden to marry each other’s relatives and she is disqualified from marrying into the priesthood (Tosafot).

Even if the chalitzah was performed within three months (of the husband's death), and even according to the opinion that she requires another chalitzah after three months, as has been explained, nevertheless, according to the Torah, the chalitzah is valid (there). And even according to the opinion that she does not require another chalitzah if she was not pregnant, nevertheless, if she was pregnant, there is agreement that she requires another chalitzah, as will be explained. However, since according to the Torah the chalitzah is valid, it is considered chalitzah regarding relatives and the priesthood (see there in Tosafot s.v. "and it is found," etc., and further, etc., the end of the quotation, and this requires further study, as in such a case, all agree that another chalitzah is needed, and review this well).

The law is established in the Talmud there that the chalitzah (ceremonial release from levirate marriage) of a pregnant woman is not considered a valid chalitzah. Even if she subsequently miscarried a fully-formed fetus, we do not say that it is now revealed retroactively that this was not a child at all and she is eligible for chalitzah. And although in many cases we do say that something is revealed retroactively, here we do not say so because this doubt cannot be clarified at the time of the chalitzah, as it is impossible to know the future (Tosafot) — whether she will miscarry or not. At the time of the act, she is considered ineligible for chalitzah. Furthermore, it is possible that at the time of the chalitzah she was capable of giving birth to a fully-formed child, and later something happened that caused her to miscarry, and it turns out that the chalitzah she performed is invalid (Nimmukei Yosef). Additionally, it is written, "and he has no son," and it is received tradition to look into it. And since at that time it was possible for the pregnancy to be sustained, this is not a valid chalitzah (Tosafot). Nevertheless, she should not be exempted without chalitzah, as with a fully-formed child. On the contrary, in this case too, look into it, and she should neither perform chalitzah nor marry as long as she remains in doubt (there).

From the elucidated matters, it is implied that according to the primary law of the Torah, the act of chalitzah (ceremonial release from levirate marriage) is not considered valid. The fact that it disqualifies her from marrying a kohen (priest) is rabbinic and merely a stringency. Therefore, she is forbidden to marry the yavam (levir) afterward. If she did marry the yavam, she must be separated from him. Similarly, if she married a kohen, she must be separated from him as well. Regarding the prohibition of relatives, even if the yavam died before performing another chalitzah, she is still forbidden to his relatives because of the first chalitzah. Likewise, if she died, the yavam is forbidden to her relatives. Even if she gave birth in the usual manner but the child died within thirty days, the child is considered valid according to Torah law. However, if she married a kohen, she must separate from him. Even though if she had not performed chalitzah at all in such a case, and she married a kohen, she would not need to separate, as stated in section 20, and she would be exempt from chalitzah. Nevertheless, here, since she performed chalitzah and rabbinically requires chalitzah, she is forbidden to the priesthood even after the fact, and if she married a kohen, she must separate from him. Even if the yavam died before performing another chalitzah and there is no other yavam, she is still disqualified from the priesthood due to the first chalitzah.

According to what has been explained, that an invalid chalitzah (ceremony of releasing a widow from levirate marriage) requires going back to all the brothers, similarly here, when she (the widow) performed chalitzah while pregnant and then miscarried, she needs chalitzah from all the brothers. However, the Rambam of blessed memory wrote in Chapter 1 that either he or one of his other brothers performs the chalitzah for her, for he holds that an invalid chalitzah does not require going back to all the brothers, as stated in Siman 170. The Rosh wrote that one of the other brothers should perform the chalitzah and not him, because his chalitzah is weakened since he already performed it while she was pregnant, and although it is not considered a chalitzah, nevertheless his power in the zika (levirate bond) is weakened, and it is as if he gave her a get (divorce document) and he cannot perform a valid chalitzah. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 2, wrote similarly. According to this, it must be said that there is no rule here of an invalid chalitzah requiring going back to all the brothers, because chalitzah of a pregnant woman is not considered chalitzah at all. Otherwise, how could they not write that she needs chalitzah from all the brothers according to the opinion in Siman 170 that an invalid chalitzah requires going back to all the brothers? However, it is possible that they relied on what is written later in Siman 170, and the matter requires further study for the halacha (law). (And see the Be'er Heitev, Subsection 7, where it is clear to him that she needs chalitzah from all the brothers).

And just as the removal of the shoe (chalitza) of a pregnant woman is not considered a valid chalitza, similarly, the sexual relations (yibum) with a pregnant woman is not considered a valid yibum to be regarded as fulfilling the mitzvah of yibum. Therefore, after she miscarries or if the fetus dies within thirty days, she requires chalitza from him. If there is another brother, she should perform chalitza with the second brother, and from him she requires a get (divorce document). This will be further explained with God's help. Consequently, if someone marries his yevama (the widow awaiting yibum) and she is found to be pregnant, and she also has another rival wife (tzara), her rival wife should not marry yet. Whether the child will be viable or not, the rival wife is forbidden to marry. Even if the child is viable, and it turns out that they are not subject to chalitza and yibum, we still hold that the child does not exempt (the mother) until birth (Talmud). Certainly, if the child is not viable, they require chalitza. It has been explained that the chalitza of a pregnant woman is not considered a valid chalitza, and similarly, her biah (sexual relations) is not considered a valid biah. Therefore, she will need to perform chalitza after she miscarries. Consequently, the rival wife cannot marry yet and must wait until she gives birth. If the child is viable, she may marry. If the child is not viable, she may marry after performing chalitza.

A yevama (a widow who is subject to levirate marriage) should not undergo yibum (levirate marriage) during her state of niddah (menstrual impurity), and we do not say that since the prohibition of "brother's wife" has been lifted, the matter of niddah is also permitted, for these are unrelated issues. Nonetheless, she is eligible for chalitza (the ceremony releasing her from yibum), and we do not say in this case that if she is not eligible for yibum, she is not eligible for chalitza, for this is a secondary prohibition, as we explained in Section 3, see there. If he transgressed and performed yibum with her during her state of niddah, he has acquired her, and it is considered yibum even though he violated a prohibition that incurs karet (spiritual excision). This is the ruling of the Rosh at the beginning of Yevamot, and likewise ruled the Tur and Shulchan Aruch in Section 4. The Rosh brought proof from Pesachim (72b) where it says that if one had relations with his yevama during her niddah, he is exempt from a sacrifice because he performed a mitzvah, see there. This implies that he acquires her if he had relations with her during her niddah, see there. However, I am puzzled, for there in the Gemara it discusses an inadvertent case where he did not know she was niddah, for he thought he was performing a mitzvah. On the contrary, it is explained there that if it was close to her menstrual period, it is not considered a mitzvah, and if he knew she was close to her period, he would be liable for a sin-offering. But if he did not know, we say he is exempt because he acted with permission, and he did not ask her due to embarrassment. The Rambam also wrote this in Chapter 2 of Shgagot: "One who has relations with his yevama and she is niddah, and he did not know, is exempt from a sin-offering because he acted with permission, etc., for he is not familiar with her to ask." But in a deliberate case, where he knew she was niddah, how do we know that he acquires her through a sinful act that incurs karet? Is this better than matza, where one does not fulfill the obligation with prohibited matza, as explained in Chapter 2 of Pesachim and in the Rambam, Chapter 6 of Chametz, see there? However, there is no proof from there because we derive this from the verse "You shall not eat chametz with it" (Pesachim 35a), and here, since there is no derivation from a verse, logically we say he fulfills the mitzvah of yibum. The Rosh's proof is from what is said there: when one mistook a skewer of notar (leftover sacrificial meat) for a skewer of valid offerings and ate it, he is liable for a sacrifice. They differentiate this from having relations with a niddah yevama because with notar, no mitzvah is performed at all, implying that with his yevama there is at least the mitzvah of yibum. Also, one cannot ask why a stolen lulav (palm branch) is invalid even on the second day of the festival due to a mitzvah performed through a transgression, as stated in Sukkah 30a, and here too it should be a mitzvah performed through a transgression. Tosafot there already wrote that a mitzvah performed through a transgression only applies when the mitzvah is accomplished through the transgression, and without the transgression, the mitzvah would not have been performed. Here, the mitzvah would have been performed even without the transgression once she becomes purified (and this is like the lulav of an asherah tree that Tosafot wrote does not involve a mitzvah performed through a transgression, see there).

Maimonides wrote in the first chapter of Yibum: "If one marries his brother's widow and it is found that she is pregnant, they are separated and they wait. If she miscarries, he may return and fulfill [the mitzvah of yibum]. If she gives birth, even if the child dies on the day it is born, he must divorce her with a get and perform chalitza, and afterwards, she will be permitted to others. If the child survives for thirty days after birth, it is considered a viable child and no get is needed because she is forbidden to him as an ervah. If she gives birth after six months from the time of yibum, the child is considered viable. The child is in doubt whether he is a nine-month child of the first [husband] or a seven-month child of the latter. Therefore, he must divorce her with a get and the child is legitimate. If he has relations with her after she gives birth, any subsequent children will be in doubt as to whether they are mamzerim."

The explanation of his words is that separation is necessary because perhaps the child will be viable, and she would then be bound to him in a case of karet (severe prohibition). What he said, that if she miscarries, he should consummate the marriage again, means he should come to her for the purpose of yibbum (levirate marriage) and establish her as his wife, because the first consummation is considered nothing, as it is stated that the consummation with a pregnant woman is not considered consummation. And if it is asked that if the first consummation is nothing, he should be liable for a sin offering for cohabiting with his brother's wife not in the context of the mitzvah, it can be said that although it was not a consummation to exempt her, nevertheless, since it has been revealed that this is not a viable child, it is not considered as cohabiting with his brother's wife not in the context of the mitzvah (Rashba). For otherwise, how would a yevamah (widow awaiting levirate marriage) who miscarried be able to undergo yibbum, since at the time of the fall (i.e., the husband's death), I would not say regarding her, "the yavam shall come upon her," but certainly, she is not forbidden to him; rather, she needs to wait (there). And if after she miscarries, he does not wish to come to her, she needs a get (divorce document) and chalitzah (levirate shoe removal ceremony): a get to release her from the first consummation, because although it is not considered consummation for leniency, it was considered consummation for stringency (Beit Shmuel, section 9). And it seems to me that if there is another brother, it is better that that brother performs chalitzah for her, because the chalitzah of this one is not so strong, since he has cohabited with her.

And what he wrote, that if she gave birth, even if the child died on the day it was born, she needs a get (divorce document) and chalitzah (ceremonial release from levirate marriage), the reason is clear: it is forbidden for him to be with her, for according to Torah law, we follow the majority of women who give birth to a viable child, and it is a matter of karet (spiritual excision). Therefore, she needs a get for his cohabitation and chalitzah for his connection, as we explained earlier. And what he wrote, that if the child lived for 30 days, she needs nothing, this is simple, and similarly, if it is known that the months were completed. Conversely, even if she gave birth, if the signs of hair and nails were not completed and he did not live for 30 days, this is a complete miscarriage, and he is permitted to marry her. Only if the signs were completed and he did not live for 30 days, and it is not known if the months were completed, then she needs a get and chalitzah because it is a doubtful miscarriage. In Siman 156, we explained the details of these laws, see there. And what he wrote, that if she gave birth after six months, it is a doubt whether it is a nine-month child for the first or a seven-month child for the latter, this is simple.

From the words of the Rambam, it somewhat implies that even if he had relations with her after her pregnancy became noticeable and they were intentional, nevertheless, if she miscarried, he is permitted to keep her. And so some of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) have written. But there are those who say that this is specifically when he married her before the pregnancy was noticeable, since they were unintentional, but if he married her after the pregnancy was noticeable, he must divorce her with a get (divorce document) and perform chalitzah (a ceremony to release a widow from her brother-in-law's obligation to marry her), even if she miscarried, because we penalize them (Nimukei Yosef). And similarly, our master the Rema wrote in section 5. There is a question in this matter, for it is certainly discussing that he had relations with her within three months, for otherwise the pregnancy would have certainly been noticeable. And if so, we should penalize him, for although he transgressed a rabbinic decree, he did not transgress a Torah prohibition, based on what he thought, that she was not pregnant. Therefore, we do not penalize them when she ultimately miscarried (and there is proof from the wife of a Kohen, which will be explained in section 20).

Any yevama (widow subject to levirate marriage) who, according to Torah law, is exempt from yibbum (levirate marriage) but due to a rabbinic doubt is required to perform chalitza (the ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage), such as a yevama who gave birth to a child whose gestation period is uncertain—whether it was a full-term pregnancy or not—but the child's hair and nails were developed, and the child did not survive 30 days or died on the 30th day itself, which is considered as if within 30 days as stated in Siman 156. If she then went and became betrothed to another man or married before chalitza—believing she was exempt from chalitza and yibbum—if the new husband is Jewish, the yavam (brother-in-law) should perform chalitza with her, and she can remain with her new husband. In this case, it is not necessary for her to be divorced, unlike in Siman 159, where, since the yavam has the ability to perform yibbum, he is compelled to divorce her, and the yavam can then do as he wishes with her. However, here the yavam is forbidden to perform yibbum because, according to Torah law, she is considered the wife of a brother who has children, so why should she be divorced?

And if she was betrothed to a Kohen, who is prohibited from marrying a chalutzah (a woman who has undergone chalitzah), he does not perform chalitzah for her. We rely on the majority, as most offspring are viable, and she is exempt from chalitzah, because we do not prohibit a man from being with his wife due to a rabbinic doubt. And even though she remains with her husband under a rabbinic doubt of being a chalutzah, it is still better that she does not perform chalitzah. For if she does, people will say that it was determined that the child was a definite stillborn, and that is why chalitzah was required, and they will come to permit a chalutzah to a Kohen. However, when chalitzah is not required, people will say that it was known that the child was viable, for example, if we are certain that the months of gestation were completed, and that is why chalitzah was not required. They will not say that a yevamah (a widow waiting for levirate marriage) was married to the marketplace (i.e., to a non-relative) without chalitzah (Rosh, Chapter "HaCholitz" Section 5). Indeed, we could even say with regard to a Kohen that she should perform chalitzah and remain with him, for the prohibition of a chalutzah to a Kohen is rabbinic, and they did not decree on a doubtful chalutzah (Yevamot 24a). However, if she performs chalitzah, people will say that she definitely required chalitzah, and they will say that a chalutzah is permitted to a Kohen, as it is written. Additionally, if she performs chalitzah, there will be a stigma on the children she will bear from the Kohen (Tosafot Shabbat 136b, s.v. "and if").

And it is not only a priest, for even if she was married to an Israelite, if the levir (yavam) is not present, she may remain with her Israelite husband, and she is permitted to him without chalitzah (levirate divorce) since she is already married. When the levir comes, he should perform chalitzah for her. Similarly, if she was married to a priest and we did not require chalitzah, if the priest dies or divorces her, the Rambam rules in the end of chapter 2 that she must now perform chalitzah and afterward she is permitted to others. This is because we did not permit her without chalitzah except due to the priest. Therefore, when the priest dies or divorces her, why should she not perform chalitzah now and be forbidden to a priest? There is an opinion that since we exempted her without chalitzah and established her status according to Torah law, we do not require her to perform chalitzah anymore (Shiltei Giborim, Perek HaCholeitz). His words seem reasonable when she has sons or daughters from the priest, for if we require chalitzah, there will be a stigma on the children. It is possible that in such a case, even the Rambam agrees. This requires further investigation (see Tosafot, Shabbat 136b, s.v. "And if," and analyze it well).

Which mitzvah takes precedence, chalitzah or yibbum? This chapter contains 24 sections:

Whether the mitzvah of yibbum takes precedence in our time or the mitzvah of chalitzah is a matter of dispute among the authorities. The Rif (chapter on the one who performs chalitzah), the Rambam (chapter 1), the Rashbam, and the Ra'avyah, citing the responsa of the Geonim (as noted in Hagahot Maimoniot), ruled that the mitzvah of yibbum takes precedence. However, Rabbeinu Tam, Rabbi Chananel, the Ra'avan, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, and other great scholars of France (in the same source) ruled that in our time, the mitzvah of chalitzah takes precedence. And although the Sages explicitly stated (Yevamot 21a) that chalitzah in place of yibbum is not a mitzvah, they nevertheless hold this view for reasons that will be explained. The Tur also wrote that this is the opinion of Rashi; see there.

And the basis of their disagreement is because the Sages taught in the Mishnah at the end of the first chapter of Bekhorot: "The commandment of levirate marriage (yibbum) takes precedence over the commandment of halitzah initially when they intended it for the sake of the mitzvah. Now that they do not intend it for the sake of the mitzvah, they said the commandment of halitzah takes precedence over the commandment of yibbum." And it is stated in Yevamot (39b) that they returned to say that the commandment of yibbum takes precedence over the commandment of halitzah. And not because the generations have improved and they now intend it for the sake of the mitzvah, but because there is a disagreement regarding the commandment of yibbum when one does not intend it for the sake of the mitzvah—whether it is considered yibbum or not. For it was taught: Abba Shaul says, "One who marries his yevamah for beauty, for marriage, or for any other reason, it is as if he encounters an ervah (a forbidden relation), and it is likely that the child will be a mamzer (illegitimate)." And the Sages say, "He shall consummate the yibbum with her in any case." Therefore, the Mishnah in Bekhorot follows the opinion of Abba Shaul. But in the generations of the Amoraim, they returned to say that the commandment of yibbum takes precedence because we follow the Sages and not Abba Shaul. Therefore, the Rif and the Rambam ruled according to the Sages as in the statement that they returned to say. And Rabbeinu Tam, Rabeinu Chananel, and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol ruled according to Abba Shaul because the anonymous Mishnah in Bekhorot follows his view. And so it is taught in the Tosefta in Yevamot, chapter 6. See there. And we do not follow the statement that they returned to say.

And there is a question regarding this: How can we say according to Abba Shaul that it is specifically with the intention for the sake of a mitzvah? We have learned in the Mishnah (Yevamot 6:6) that one who has relations with his yevamah (levirate wife) whether unintentionally, intentionally, by force, or willingly, he acquires her. And behold, he does not intend for the sake of a mitzvah. According to this, the Talmud should have said that the Mishnah does not follow Abba Shaul. And since it does not say so, we infer from here that in this case, even Abba Shaul agrees. And this requires an explanation as to why (Nemukei Yosef, Yevamot 6).

Therefore, some say that everyone agrees that from the Torah, there is no requirement specifically for the sake of the mitzvah, and in any manner that he comes upon her, he acquires her. Therefore, after the fact, Abba Shaul does not disagree. It is only initially that Abba Shaul holds that it is rabbinically forbidden if he does not intend for the sake of the mitzvah. And if he intends for the sake of beauty, it is initially considered as if he is encountering a forbidden relationship. The Rabbis who disagree with him also hold that initially, one should intend for the sake of the mitzvah. However, they disagree with him in that even initially, if he intends for the sake of beauty, it is not considered as if he is encountering a forbidden relationship (there). According to this, there is not much difference between Abba Shaul and the Rabbis, and between the earlier and later teachings. However, from all the earlier authorities, it does not seem so. Furthermore, if so, how does Abba Shaul say that it is almost certain in his eyes that the child would be a mamzer, since from the Torah it is completely permitted? And if his intention is that rabbinically it is close to being a mamzer, why did the Rabbis make such a decree on something that is completely permitted by the Torah? (And from the Tosefta, there is also evidence that in Chapter 6, it states simply like Abba Shaul, and the law of one who comes upon his yevamah, etc., is not found in the Tosefta, and examine this well).

There is also a need to explain the reasoning of Abba Shaul, for it cannot be said that it is because he holds that mitzvot require intention, for if so, how did the Rif and the Rambam rule against him? They hold that mitzvot require intention, as explained in Orach Chaim, Siman 60. Furthermore, regarding something that involves pleasure, the Rambam holds that intention is not required. Therefore, he ruled that if one eats matzah without intention, he has fulfilled his obligation, as explained in Siman 475, because there is pleasure involved, as clarified there (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, subparagraph 14). All the more so with the pleasure of marital relations. Additionally, there is a need to understand the main words of Abba Shaul, who says that one should have intention for the sake of the mitzvah and not for pleasure. How is this possible? For regarding Yishai, the father of David, who was a completely righteous person, David said about him, "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity," and our Sages said in the Midrash Vayikra (chapter 14), "Could it be that Yishai, my father, had intention...?" For even the most pious of the pious cannot be without some element of pleasure, as explained there. All the more so with a mitzvah that applies to all of Israel.

Therefore, it seems to me that Abba Shaul holds that even if we say regarding all commandments that one does not need intent to fulfill the commandment, in the case of yibbum (levirate marriage), it is necessary to intend to fulfill the commandment of yibbum. And when one intends, even if he also has in mind his own enjoyment, we do not consider it an issue since he intends to fulfill the commandment. The reason is that the sister-in-law is otherwise forbidden to him as a forbidden union, and the Torah only permitted her to him when her husband left no offspring and the Torah obligated him in this. Therefore, if he does not intend for the commandment as commanded by the Holy One, blessed be He, he is engaging in a forbidden union. But when he intends for the commandment, he is doing what he was commanded, and if he also intends for his enjoyment, it is not an issue. What is this similar to? To one who eats an olive's worth of matzah on Passover night for the sake of the commandment and also desires to enjoy his eating; this is similar. This is what Abba Shaul said: one who marries his yevama (sister-in-law) for beauty, meaning only for beauty and not for the sake of the commandment. The Rabbis who disagree with him hold that the prohibition of a brother's wife is completely removed when he dies childless and she is entirely permitted to him. Therefore, even if he marries her only for beauty, it is not an issue. And even if, in all commandments, we hold that one needs intent to fulfill them, here the verse "her yavam shall come upon her" reveals to us that he can come upon her in any manner he wishes. And since the prohibition of the brother's wife is entirely removed, it is like eating matzah without intent and under compulsion, where one fulfills the commandment because there is enjoyment in eating, and ultimately the commandment is fulfilled. Similarly, here too. And in the Mishnah in Bechorot, it is also explained this way: that initially they intended for the commandment as well; later, they did not intend for the commandment at all, only for beauty or another matter. Therefore, according to Abba Shaul, this is close to a forbidden union.

Abba Shaul and the Rabbis only disagree regarding the legal status if he committed a sin in such a case when he came upon her only for beauty or if he did not commit a sin. However, Abba Shaul agrees that the act of yibum and its acquisition are valid, and she is considered his complete wife. What is this comparable to? To one who comes upon his yevamah when she is in a state of niddah. Even though he transgressed a prohibition of karet, nonetheless, he has acquired her, as stated in the previous section. Therefore, that which we learned, "one who comes upon his yevamah intentionally acquires her," applies also according to Abba Shaul. Indeed, he has committed a severe sin if his intention was solely for promiscuity, but nonetheless, he has acquired her.

And according to this, even according to the authorities like Abba Shaul and the later opinion that the mitzvah of Chalitzah takes precedence, the concern is only that perhaps they will not intend it for the sake of the mitzvah at all. But if they do intend it for the sake of the mitzvah, even if they also intend it for their own pleasure, we do not object. And certainly if we say according to the opinion mentioned in section 4 that from the Torah there is no concern at all, as it is written there. And according to this, even in our times, if both desire Yibbum and they are taught to intend it for the sake of the mitzvah, it would seem permissible for them even if we know that his intention is also for beauty. And more will be explained about this with the help of Heaven.

Even according to those who say that the mitzvah of yibbum (levirate marriage) takes precedence, this is only when yibbum is good for her. But if the court sees that it is not good for her, such as if he is old and she is young or vice versa, they are obligated to strive for him to perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from yibbum). Thus the sages expounded (Yevamot 44a): "And the elders of his city shall call him and speak to him" (Deuteronomy 25:8) - this teaches that they give him advice that is proper for him. If he is young and she is old, or he is old and she is young, they tell him to go to someone like himself. Also, if he has set his eyes on her money, they induce him to perform chalitzah. All the more so, if he is among those who are compelled to divorce, as explained in Siman 154, certainly they do not allow him to perform yibbum and compel him to perform chalitzah. Similarly, in places where it is forbidden to marry two wives and he already has a wife, they compel him to perform chalitzah even if both of them want yibbum. And when she presents before us valid reasons that she does not want yibbum, even if none of the above conditions apply, if her words are reasonable, we see to it that he performs chalitzah for her and assist her in this.

If the yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage) vowed to prohibit herself from benefiting from the yavam (brother-in-law) during her husband's lifetime, or if she vowed to prohibit herself from benefiting from all Jews and then her husband died, we compel him to perform chalitza (the ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage). For we cannot say that she intentionally made the vow to avoid levirate marriage since her husband was still alive, thus she is considered coerced in this matter. If she finds a sage who can annul her vow, she is permitted to marry him. We do not say that since she was prohibited to him at the time of her husband's death, she remains prohibited, because the prohibition was not due to the matter of levirate marriage. Additionally, a sage uproots the vow from its inception (as explained by the Beit Yosef and the Bach in note 4). One might ask, if so, why do we compel him to perform chalitza? Let him tell her to go to a sage to annul her vow. The answer is that this applies when there is no opening for her vow. If he tells her to annul it by expressing regret, she might say that initial regret is required, as stated in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 228, and how can she claim to regret it from the beginning when she truly does not regret it from the beginning? Therefore, we compel him to perform chalitza.

However, if she made a vow after her husband's death, we ask him to perform the chalitzah (ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage) but do not compel him. How can we force him in a matter that she did intentionally against him? Even if she made the vow during her husband's lifetime, if it appears that her intention was to exempt herself from the yibbum (levirate marriage), such as if her husband was sick or similar situations, we also do not compel him to perform the chalitzah but request him to do so. Some say further that even if it is not clearly known that her intention during her husband's lifetime was for this, we assume it was so until it is clearly known to us that she did not intend for this (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 5, in the name of the Maggid Mishneh). Some say that when she made a vow prohibiting benefit from Jews in general, the yavam (brother-in-law) is not included. This is the opinion of Rashi, the Meor, and the Rashba (there). Consequently, since there is a dispute in this matter, we cannot compel him to perform the chalitzah when she made a vow prohibiting benefit from all Jews during her husband's lifetime, as perhaps we hold by this opinion that she is permitted to the yavam. Therefore, we do not compel but only request (there).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 2: If the yavam was a priest and she went and betrothed herself to another so that he could not perform yibbum with her, her status is as if she vowed not to benefit from him, and we request from him (see Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 7, who thought this was an abbreviation of Rabbeinu Tam, but in any case, was puzzled by this) and we do not compel him to perform chalitzah, since she caused herself to be forbidden to him. These are his words, and it is clear, and this is according to the authorities who hold that the mitzvah of yibbum takes precedence. He further wrote: And there are those who say that if she spat in front of the brothers or did something similar, causing herself to be forbidden to the yavam, she does not have the status of a rebellious wife, since it is impossible for her to perform yibbum from now on. These are his words.

The explanation of his words is as follows: According to the opinions that the mitzvah of yibbum (levirate marriage) takes precedence, if she does not want to perform yibbum with one of the brothers, whether one of them agrees to perform yibbum with her, or the eldest brother wants to perform yibbum with her, and she does not have a sufficient claim for refusing yibbum, she is considered a rebellious wife, as stated in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 1, and a letter of rebellion is written against her, and she is treated as stated in section 77 regarding the law of a rebellious wife against her husband. The same applies when she rebels against the yavam (levir). However, according to the opinions that the mitzvah of chalitzah (the ceremony of releasing the bond of levirate marriage) takes precedence, she does not have the status of a rebellious wife if she does not want to perform yibbum, even if she does not have a sufficient claim.

Hence, since according to those who hold that the mitzvah of yibbum takes precedence, she has the status of a rebellious wife in any situation where it has been clarified that they request him to perform chalitzah for her, such as if she vows to derive no benefit from the yavam and thereby intends to forbid herself to him, as stated, if they request him to perform chalitzah and he refuses, insisting only on yibbum, her status reverts to that of a rebellious wife since she caused this situation (as stated in Beit Shmuel, section 6). Therefore, when she spat in front of the brothers, which has no remedy, she does not have the status of a rebellious wife even if he did not agree to perform chalitzah. The reason is that the status of a rebellious wife applies only when she has the ability to retract, and they impose the status of a rebellious wife so that she will retract. For a vow, she can retract it through the absolution of a sage. If you say that she has no opening for her vow and also has no initial regret, as stated in section 10, since we write a letter of rebellion against her, the opening is created for her in this very act, for if she knew that a letter of rebellion would be written against her, she would not have vowed. However, with spitting, it is impossible to rectify, so there is no benefit in making her a rebellious wife. The same applies if she has betrothed herself to another, for there is no benefit, just as with spitting.

This is why he did not write the law of her betrothal to another, because in this matter, we judge her more severely than a rebellious wife, for we compel the one who betrothed her to divorce her, even though there is no benefit to the yavam in this, so that the sinner should not profit, as stated in section 159. How then can he write that she does not have the status of a rebellious wife, for we penalize her? But with spitting, we do nothing to her. However, in the main laws of a rebellious wife, they are equal whether she has betrothed herself or spat (as stated above, and it clarifies what Beit Shmuel and Gra elaborated on in sections 8 and 22, respectively).

Furthermore, he wrote: "It has already been clarified above that all these distinctions apply according to the opinion that the mitzvah of yibbum takes precedence. But according to the opinion that the mitzvah of chalitzah takes precedence, she does not have the status of a rebellious wife at all if she does not want to perform yibbum," and this is straightforward.

Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (Rashi) z”l holds (Yevamot 39b, s.v. Amar Rav) that even according to the later opinion that the mitzvah of chalitzah takes precedence, if both parties wish to perform yibbum, we do not force them to perform chalitzah. We are not concerned that they may not intend to fulfill the mitzvah and thus violate the prohibition of a brother’s wife. Rather, we allow them to perform yibbum. The opinion of Rabbeinu Tam z”l (Tosafot, ad loc.) is that we do not allow them to perform yibbum unless it is clarified that their intention is for the sake of the mitzvah, such as if they came initially to perform chalitzah, and we say to him, “If you prefer to perform yibbum, we allow you.” In that case, if he wishes to perform yibbum, and she is also agreeable, there is no concern that they do not intend for the mitzvah, since they originally came for chalitzah. This is the opinion of Rabbeinu the Rema in paragraph 1, who wrote that if both wish to perform yibbum, we do not allow them unless it is evident and known that their intention is for the sake of the mitzvah. This is when they initially came for chalitzah, as stated. Even if they did not come for chalitzah but it is known that he fears God or they were previously matched, we allow them to perform yibbum (Maharshal, Chapter 4, Siman 17). Some say that nowadays, we do not rely on the fact that they came for chalitzah as evidence of their intent for the mitzvah, because now everyone knows that generally, yibbum is not permitted. I do not understand why there is a stringency in this matter when, according to Rashi, it is entirely permitted, and Rabbeinu Tam agreed when they came for chalitzah. What does it matter that they know that nowadays yibbum is not generally performed? On the contrary, this is proof that they desired chalitzah. If the concern is that they may be deceptive, what of it, since according to the Rif, Rambam, and the Geonim, the mitzvah of yibbum takes precedence? According to Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam, who prioritize chalitzah, they permitted in such a case. From where do we derive the stringency in this matter? It is true that we have not seen yibbum performed in our country, but if such a case arises, it seems to me that we should not object to them. Especially as I have written that if one intends for the mitzvah, even if he also intends for beauty, there is no prohibition. Certainly, according to the opinion mentioned in paragraph 4, that this is only Rabbinic, it is clear that we should not prevent them from performing yibbum. (What will be explained in paragraph 17 is also a proof to our words. See there and consider well.)

Moreover, regarding the fundamental ruling on this matter, we do not find an explicit decision from our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch. However, from the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, it appears that he holds that the mitzvah of levirate marriage (yibbum) takes precedence. From the words of our teacher, the Rema, it seems that he holds that chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the levirate bond) takes precedence. This is according to the customs of the regions: in the Eastern countries, even today, they practice yibbum, while in the regions of Ashkenaz, France, Russia, Poland, and Austria, they do not practice yibbum at all and follow the opinion of the poskim (decisors) that chalitzah takes precedence. However, we have not heard of being so stringent to rule consistently with the earlier opinion. Also, the great later authorities who divided this ruling into three categories: Firstly, if it is certain that they intend to fulfill the mitzvah, we allow them to perform yibbum. Secondly, when it is not known if their intention is for the mitzvah, we compel them to perform chalitzah by persuasion. Thirdly, if it is certainly known that their intention is not for the mitzvah, we compel them in all manners to perform chalitzah (as per the Bach and Beit Shmuel, section 1). It also seems that if there is even a slight indication that their intention is for the mitzvah, such as when they come to perform chalitzah and similar cases, we do not compel them to perform chalitzah and we allow them to perform yibbum.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section A that according to the opinion that the mitzvah of chalitza (the ritual of removing a shoe) takes precedence, she does not have the status of a rebellious wife if she does not want to perform yibbum (levirate marriage). Nevertheless, we do not compel him to perform chalitza, but we may deceive him if we can, for example, by saying to him, "Perform chalitza on the condition that she gives you a certain amount of money." This is specifically if he is not one of those whom we compel to divorce concerning a husband, as mentioned above in siman 154, etc. And some say that if he has another wife, we compel him and decree upon him until he performs chalitza. And some say even without another wife, if their intention is not for the sake of the mitzvah and she does not want to perform yibbum, and we cannot deceive him, we compel him to perform chalitza. The custom follows the first opinion that we do not compel chalitza at all, even if we know he has set his eyes on money. Instead, we mediate between them according to the enactment of the communities, as will be explained below. End of quote.

The explanation of his words is that the first opinion holds that compelling to perform chalitza (the ceremony of removing the shoe) is only when she provides a legitimate excuse for not wanting to enter into levirate marriage (yibbum) or if he does not want to either perform yibbum or chalitza, as will be explained. However, if he wishes to perform yibbum, it is needless to say that if she also wants it, we do not compel chalitza. This is contrary to the opinions of some great later authorities that we mentioned in Section 15 in the second division. But even if she does not want yibbum, we do not compel him to perform chalitza, even according to those who hold that the mitzvah of chalitza takes precedence, if she does not provide a legitimate excuse as stated. And what do they do? They completely distance themselves, not allowing him to forcefully perform yibbum with her, and also do not compel him to perform chalitza. Rather, if it is possible to deceive him, they deceive him, and if not, they distance themselves from this matter as stated. The second opinion holds that if he has another wife, he is compelled with all forms of coercion until he performs chalitza. The third opinion holds that even without another wife, if she does not want yibbum and we know that his intention is not for the sake of the mitzvah, and it is not possible to deceive him, we compel him to perform chalitza. The custom follows the first opinion, that we do not compel in any case. (The Beit Shmuel in Section 1 was puzzled by the Rema, but there is no wonder here, for so it is in Tosafot Ketubot 64, s.v. "and the laws" as mentioned there).

Further, it is written as follows: All this applies when he says he wants to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) and it is possible to perform yibbum without concern of any prohibition. However, if he says he does not want to either perform yibbum or chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage), we compel him, and this specifically when she comes with a claim as explained above in Siman 154. Nonetheless, if it is possible to deceive him and tell him he will receive a significant sum of money for performing chalitzah, we deceive him so that we do not need to compel him. They should be careful not to deposit the money with a trustee because then we would not be able to tell him that we were deceiving him.

To explain his words, even though when he does not want to perform either yibbum or chalitzah we certainly compel him, this is when she comes with a claim that she wants to remarry, as it says in Siman 154, so that she has someone to rely on in her old age. However, if there is no necessity for her to remarry, we do not compel him at all, and she remains without chalitzah or yibbum. We learn from this that if she is also elderly and not demanding chalitzah because she has given up on remarrying, the court does not compel him to perform chalitzah for her. And indeed, according to the Zohar, chalitzah is a great rectification for the deceased. Nevertheless, we do not have the power to compel because of this; rather, we inform them and request that they perform the rectification for the soul of the deceased, but we do not compel them (and so writes the Chatam Sofer). 

And even though it is a positive commandment to perform chalitzah or yibbum, we do not compel because the commandment is only when she wants to remarry, as it is written, "she shall not be the wife of the dead outside," etc. But when she wants to remain a widow, we do not compel (and see Tosafot Ketubot 64a, s.v. Teva, who says in the first explanation that we compel even without a claim, according to the Zohar). However, when she demands chalitzah and comes with a claim, we compel him to perform chalitzah, and it is better to deceive him than to compel. This is why it is written not to deposit with a trustee, because the reason that a coerced chalitzah is valid is that she can say, "I was deceiving you" (Yevamot 106a), like in the case of the coin and the ferry crossing explained in Choshen Mishpat Siman 264, where he only gets his wage because he can say, "I was deceiving you," and it is the same here. And there it is explained that if he already received the coin, we do not take it from him. Accordingly, we should not deposit with a trustee so that he does not acquire it by the standing of the three of them (as written in the Mordechai, Perek HaCholatz, and still needs examination because it seems we could deceive him through the trustee himself, and perhaps their intention is only when it is truly deposited before the yavam with the trustee, and she tells him to give this amount to the yavam after he performs chalitzah, for in the law of the standing of the three of them, he cannot say, "I was deceiving you," as explained in Choshen Mishpat Siman 81, Seif 17. See there, and it will further be explained in Seif 169).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 2, Law 16: "If a yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage) demands chalitzah (ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage) from the yavam (brother-in-law), and she says, 'I will neither perform chalitzah nor receive the ketubah (marriage contract payment), but rather I will stay in my husband's house like all other widows,' we do not listen to her. For she has been designated to this man by Heaven, and he has the choice to either perform yibum (levirate marriage) or chalitzah and give her the ketubah. Moreover, even if she says, 'I will support myself and remain an agunah (a chained woman) all my life,' we do not listen to her. For the yavam can say to her, 'As long as you are bound to me, I am not given another wife.' And even if he is already married, it is possible that he might marry another woman, or there might be conflict in his household on account of the yevama." 

This was copied in the Shulchan Aruch, Section 3, in brief. His words require explanation. At first, he stated the reason that she was designated to him by Heaven and he has the ability to compel her either to chalitzah or yibum, and this is indeed the truth as the Torah states so, where the matter depends on him. Then afterward, he says that a justification is needed to either give him another wife or to prevent conflict within his household.

However, the explanation of his words is that it is indeed true that the Torah grants him the right to act according to his will, but this applies entirely if she desires to marry, as it is written, "The wife of the deceased shall not be outside..." (Deuteronomy 25:5), and then the choice is in his hands to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) or chalitzah (ceremonial release). But if she does not wish to marry, the Torah does not impose this upon him, as we wrote in section 18. Therefore, the Rambam needed a valid reason, and initially, he says that since it was granted to him from Heaven, this applies when she wishes to remain in her husband's house like all widows and be sustained from his property. In this case, the yavam (levir) can certainly say to her, "I will not give you lodging or sustenance; I will perform chalitzah and give you your ketubah (marriage contract) payment, and you will leave my house." If he demands to perform chalitzah and she demands yibbum, the law is with him, as the Torah depends on him (Rashi, Ketubot 64a). If she does not listen, they write a letter of rebellion against her, even according to the earlier opinion that the mitzvah of yibbum takes precedence (ibid). (Refer to Beit Shmuel, note 9, and it is difficult to understand from where he derived that this is a valid reason, for her refusal to perform chalitzah out of shame, and there is no shame in fulfilling a Torah commandment).

Any yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage) whose ruling is that she should perform chalitza (the ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage) and not yibum (levirate marriage), she receives her ketubah if she has a ketubah, just like any other widow. Additionally, her clothing is appraised for her like a widow. Similarly, if the yavam (brother-in-law) has boils or other blemishes as detailed in Siman 154, he performs chalitza for her against his will since she does not consent to yibum, and she receives her ketubah. Even if these blemishes were present in her husband, she can say, "I could accept your brother, but I cannot accept you," as stated in Siman 154. This is even according to the opinion that the mitzvah of yibum takes precedence. 

Similarly, if blemishes developed in her while she is awaiting yibum, he cannot say, "I only desire yibum and not chalitza, and now she is repulsive to me, and I cannot perform yibum, and I do not want chalitza." We do not listen to him, for his field has been flooded. If he does not want to perform yibum, he is obligated to perform chalitza and give her the ketubah since she has not done anything wrong, and she should not lose her ketubah. This applies even in places where yibum is customary. 

So too, according to the opinion that the mitzvah of chalitza takes precedence, we do not allow him to perform yibum, and if he does not want chalitza, only yibum, and in a situation where we do not force him to perform chalitza as explained, he must still give her the ketubah immediately since her status is like that of a woman who has performed chalitza because the delay is not her fault. He cannot say, "The ketubah was not given to be collected during the husband's lifetime (Ketubot 1:1), and I am in place of the husband, whom I was expected to marry, and since I did not marry her, I will not give her the ketubah. What has she sinned?" Since we do not allow him to perform yibum, and even though we do not force him to perform chalitza, she should not lose her ketubah.

The early authorities established regulations regarding the distribution of the deceased's inheritance between the one who performs chalitzah and the woman who undergoes chalitzah. And although, according to the strict law, the one who performs chalitzah does not receive anything, nevertheless, since in our countries they do not allow yibbum (levirate marriage), the yavam (brother-in-law) can say, "I wish to perform yibbum and thereby acquire my brother's property. And if I am not allowed to perform yibbum, why should I lose out on the property?" And even though this is not a valid legal argument, nevertheless, the early authorities established certain regulations in this matter, as will be explained, so that he will agree to perform chalitzah and the woman will not remain in a state of agunah (unable to remarry), since he cannot be forced to perform chalitzah.

And these are the words of our master, the Rema, in section 4: "All of this is according to the law. However, the communities have enacted a regulation that if the yavam (levir) and the yevama (levirate widow) agree to perform chalitza (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage), they shall divide all the assets left behind, even if half does not reach the amount of her ketubah (marriage contract). They deduct from her share all that she squandered during her husband's lifetime, and she must swear unless they agree without an oath. What he gave as a gift on his deathbed is not deducted from her share at all. The half that falls to the husband's heirs is taken by the one who performs the chalitza, and neither the father nor the other brothers have a share in it. Even if they seize it, it is taken from them, for the main purpose of this enactment was so that they would agree to perform chalitza. Therefore, the one who performs the chalitza is the main party in this matter. Even if the other brothers wish to divide with the eldest brother and say they wish to perform chalitza, they are not listened to if the eldest brother wishes to perform chalitza. All of this applies when half the assets do not reach the amount of her ketubah, as she certainly does not take more than the amount of her ketubah. There is another opinion regarding the communal enactment; therefore, they customarily come to an agreement among themselves. Even if she has a chalitza document from the brothers, she must come to a monetary agreement with them, unless it was explicitly stated to perform chalitza for her at no cost. End of quote."

Behold, if the deceased’s estate contains only double the amount of her ketubah and the property she brought into the marriage, and certainly if it contains less, it implies from his words that she shares with the one who performs the chalitzah. When there is much more, she does not take more than her ketubah and the property she brought into the marriage. However, regarding the surplus of the estate, it is not clarified whether the one who performs the chalitzah takes all of it or if he shares it with the brothers. From the plain sense of his words, it implies that he takes all the estate since otherwise, he would have clarified it. But several of the prominent authorities wrote that they do not share between them more than the amount of her ketubah and the property she brought into the marriage, but the rest of the estate, if there is a surplus, is divided among all the brothers, and the one who performs the chalitzah has no advantage over the other brothers (see Avnei Beit HaSho'eil, Siman 10). The Maharshal, of blessed memory, in Yam Shel Shlomo, Chapter "HaChalitzah," Siman 18, elaborated greatly on this matter. However, in our regions and in our times, we have never heard of anyone behaving according to these regulations but rather they settle according to their ability. Therefore, I did not see a need to elaborate on this, except for the main point that the court is obligated to ensure that the yavam releases her through chalitzah.

### Laws of Yibbum (Levirate Marriage) and Whether It Requires Kiddushin (Betrothal). It Contains 24 Sections:

It has already been explained that Rambam holds that the mitzvah of yibbum (levirate marriage) takes precedence over chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage) even in our times. When the yavam (the brother-in-law) wants to perform yibbum and she (the yevamah, the widow) does not consent and does not provide a valid reason for her refusal, she is considered a rebellious wife. Rambam's words in Chapter 2, Law 10 state: A yevamah who is fit for yibbum but does not want to perform yibbum is considered like a rebellious wife against her husband. We compel the yavam to perform chalitzah for her, and she leaves without receiving her ketubah (marriage contract). Rambam follows his reasoning in Chapter 14 of Hilchot Ishut, where he also rules that in the case of a rebellious wife, we compel the husband to divorce her and she leaves without a ketubah. However, many disagree with him, and in this case, we do not compel the yavam to perform chalitzah for her. (Maimonides' Commentary).

He also wrote that if his brother left many wives, whichever one the yavam (levir) approached for levirate marriage and she did not want to, she is considered rebellious and he performs halitzah (a ritual releasing her from the levirate bond) for her and she leaves without a ketubah (marriage contract), while the other co-wives who were not approached receive their ketubah like other widows, end quote. The reason is simple: since the Torah gave him permission to perform levirate marriage with any of them he chooses, she is considered rebellious (if she refuses). And it is obvious that if she did not want to and he approached another for levirate marriage, she is obligated to undergo the levirate marriage, and if she does not want to, she is also considered rebellious. However, it is possible to say that for two women, it is impossible to judge them as rebellious since he has permission only for one, and he has the option to switch from one to the other, and then the first is not considered rebellious. This appears to be the main point.

Additionally, it is written: If there are multiple brothers-in-law (yebamim) and the eldest brother-in-law requests to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) with her, but she does not want him and prefers another brother, we do not listen to her, because it is a mitzvah for the eldest to perform yibbum. If the eldest says, "I do not want to either perform yibbum or chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from yibbum)," and presents his brother before her, and one of the brothers requests to perform yibbum but she does not want him and prefers another brother who also wants her, she is not considered rebellious. Since the eldest, who is obligated, has stepped aside, they are all equal, and since she wants one of them and he wants her, she is not rebellious. Furthermore, if one of the brothers is in another country and she says, "I will wait for him to come and perform yibbum with me, but I do not want this one," she is not considered rebellious. We tell the one who is not the eldest and is requesting her that if he wishes to perform chalitzah and give her the ketubah, he should do so. If not, since she is willing to wait for his brother, who is not prioritized over him, if the one she waited for arrives and does not want her, we return to the one who requested to perform yibbum, and she does not want him. We tell her, "There is no one else willing to perform yibbum except this one, and the mitzvah of yibbum precedes, so either be yibbumed by him or leave without a ketubah as is the law for all rebellious women." End of quote, and he follows his reasoning as he has written.

All these laws are not explained in the Gemara, and the Rambam wrote them based on his own reasoning and follows his approach there that once the eldest brother steps aside, there is no longer a mitzvah for the eldest brother to precede, unlike what is written in Siman 161. However, the Rashba and the Ra'avad argued against him, stating that the eldest brother always precedes, and just as we adjudicate the law of a rebellious wife against the eldest brother, so too if the firstborn steps aside, the second brother takes his place, and we adjudicate the law of a rebellious wife against him. If the second brother steps aside, we adjudicate against the third brother, and so on for all of them. The Rambam does not agree with this, and this depends on the different versions in the Gemara (according to the Mechaber's opinion). Similarly, they dispute with him fundamentally about this law of compelling to perform chalitzah, as most decisors dispute with him regarding the law of "ma'is alay" (refusal) as written in Siman 77. All these laws do not apply to those who hold that the mitzvah of chalitzah precedes (and therefore, they are not mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch at all).

The commandment of levirate marriage (yibbum) and release (chalitzah) is as follows: If the brother-in-law (yavam) is in one place and the widow (yevamah) is in another place, the yevamah is obligated to go to the yavam. Even if there is a great court (beit din) in the place of the yevamah and only a small court in the place of the yavam, she is still obligated to go to him, as it is written, "And the elders of his city shall call him" (Deuteronomy 25:8), and not the elders of her city (Sanhedrin 31b). However, this is specifically for a place where he lives permanently; she is obligated to go there. But if he has gone from his place to another place for some business and has not permanently moved his residence, she is not obligated to go after him there, for it is not called "the elders of his city" (Nimukei Yosef there). This is also implied in the Jerusalem Talmud, and he is required to come to her place (Beit Shmuel 1). Similarly, if there is no court in his place, he is obligated to go to her place if there is a court there, for in his place there are no elders of his city, as "elders" means a court. If there is no court in her place either, they both go to a place where there is a court, and she goes to a place that is closer to him, since according to the law she is required to follow him, he has the right to proximity (so it appears to me). Similarly, if he lives among non-Jews, it is considered a place without a court, and he cannot tell her to bring a court to his place, for the court is not required to follow him; rather, he must go to the place of the court and release her from levirate marriage. It seems clear that this is specifically when they did not agree on levirate marriage or in a place where levirate marriage is not practiced, but in a place where levirate marriage is practiced and both wish to proceed with it, a court is not needed; he betroths her with a statement before witnesses and consummates the marriage, as will be explained.

When they come before the Beit Din in a place where the custom is to perform yibbum (levirate marriage), they (the Beit Din) give them advice that is appropriate for both of them, whether to perform yibbum or chalitzah (ceremonial release), such as if he is old and she is young, or vice versa, or if he has another wife, and similar situations. They give them advice that it is better for him to perform chalitzah. Regarding this, it is said, "And the elders of his city shall call him and speak to him," meaning they should speak words that are beneficial to them (Yevamot 46a). However, they do not compel him if he does not want to listen to the advice. If he wishes to perform yibbum, he may do so since the Torah grants him this permission, unless he is among those who are compelled to divorce (Responsa of the Rosh, rule 52, siman 7).

The mitzvah of yibbum (levirate marriage) is only fulfilled when he has intercourse with her, and from the Torah, there is no need to betroth her with kiddushin (betrothal). However, the Sages instituted, for reasons of propriety, that he should not have intercourse with her until he first betroths her in the presence of two witnesses with money or a document, and this is called "ma'amar" in the Gemara. This is similar to the enactment of the Sages that one should not betroth a woman through intercourse, even though from the Torah it is permitted to betroth through intercourse. Similarly, they instituted here that he should not have intercourse with her without the kiddushin of ma'amar yevamah. If he has intercourse without ma'amar, he acquires her, but he has transgressed a rabbinic decree. And what is ma'amar kiddushin? He gives her money or an item of equivalent value in the presence of witnesses and says to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me through ma'amar yevamin" (Rashi, there, s.v. "natan").

Rashi, of blessed memory, wrote (there) that the term "ma'amar" does not refer to complete betrothal like Torah betrothal, for betrothal does not take effect with a brother's wife, and the Torah did not permit her to him to become like a regular wife except in the manner of the commandment, and it is intercourse that the Torah wrote about. And so wrote the Ra'avad at the beginning of the second chapter: "And with a yevamah, betrothal with money is not complete betrothal but rather rabbinically ordained, for the yevamah is not acquired by the yavam to be like a regular wife until he has intercourse with her." And this is what our Sages expounded: "And yevamah—intercourse completes her, and money and document do not complete her." However, from this there is no proof, as it could be said that this pertains to the commandment that yibbum has not been fulfilled, but if he betrothed her, it could be said that even by Torah law her status is like a regular wife for those who hold that betrothal takes effect with a yevamah, as written in Siman 159. Why should the yavam be worse off? One could say so, but from the explanations of Rashi and the Ra'avad, it is clear that it is a Torah decree that with the yavam, the yevamah's status is not like a regular wife except through intercourse. Consequently, even if he says to her simply, "You are betrothed to me with this," and does not say it in the manner of yibbum, she is not like a regular wife by Torah law. And although if he betrothed her after halitzah with complete betrothal, she is a regular wife by Torah law, as explained in the Gemara and will be explained in Siman 170, this is because halitzah has released her from the bond of yibbum. But as long as the bond of yibbum is upon her, betrothal does not take effect by Torah law with the yavam. This is also clarified in the words of Tosafot and the Nimukei Yosef at the beginning of the third chapter.

It is clear that the consummation of a yevama (levirate marriage) requires witnesses to the seclusion, just as in the case of betrothal through intercourse. And even though the Rambam and the other decisors did not mention this, it appears that due to the obviousness of the law, they did not need to mention it. This is explicitly stated by one of the early authorities (Shita Mekubetzet on Bava Batra in the name of Riaz). This is also understood from the words of Tosafot (Kiddushin 12b, s.v. mishum). According to this, since it has been clarified that all forms of betrothal do not acquire a yevama biblically, it follows that even if betrothal was performed, witnesses to the seclusion are still required for the consummation because biblically she has not yet been acquired. This is also stated by later authorities (Beit Shmuel, section 2 and the Gra, section 9). One of the great authorities questioned the basic law of whether witnesses are needed at all for the consummation of a yevama, perhaps because the Torah decreed that a yevama shall come unto her in any case, even if they were unintentional or coerced, or if she was asleep, he acquires her, as will be clarified. Therefore, perhaps witnesses are not needed at all (Magid Mishneh, chapter 2). The Maharshal in Yam Shel Shlomo, chapter 25, ruled clearly that witnesses are not needed. See there.

Indeed, it is perplexing because we have learned in the Mishnah that if one cohabits with his yevamah (the widow bound to her brother-in-law) whether unintentionally, intentionally, by force, etc., he acquires her, as will be explained in this chapter. Unintentional means he did not know she was his yevamah, and intentional means for the sake of promiscuity. If one would think witnesses are required, how would this be possible? For it is necessary to designate witnesses for seclusion as in the case of marital relations, as explained in Chapter 33. And there must be awareness of the witnesses, as mentioned in Chapter 42. If he did not know at all that she was his yevamah, there are no witnesses here. Similarly, in the case of intentional promiscuity, if witnesses were designated, then it is not promiscuity. Furthermore, it will be explained that if he intended merely for intercourse, even for bestiality, and cohabited with her, he acquires her. This does not relate to witnesses since he did not intend to cohabit with her at all. Additionally, in marriage, just as he needs to know about the witnesses, so too does she. If she did not know, the marriage is not valid, as explained in Chapter 42. However, in the case of yibbum (levirate marriage), it is clear that witnesses are not required, because it will be explained that if he cohabits with her even while she is asleep, he acquires her. While she is asleep, she knows nothing. Therefore, we must say that since the Torah granted her to him, witnesses are not required, as he can cohabit with her against her will.
