Thus, we also say that he does not need witnesses because the Torah obligates him to cohabit with her. This is not surprising, for even with a get (bill of divorce), which certainly requires witnesses since a matter of sexual prohibition requires at least two witnesses, nevertheless, the Rashba wrote in Kiddushin (65b) that if it is written in his handwriting, witnesses are not required, for it is written, "and he shall write her a bill of divorce," making his writing like witnesses. Similarly, since it is written, "her yevamah shall come upon her," nothing else is required.

Furthermore, we have already explained in Choshen Mishpat, beginning of Siman 241, based on the words of the Talmud there, that in all cases of forbidden relationships (arayot) where we require witnesses, it is because we derive from monetary law (mammon) that in cases of contradiction, witnesses are needed because the matter involves others. Therefore, also in the case of kiddushin (betrothal), even though both parties agree, nonetheless, since it affects others—because through the kiddushin she becomes prohibited to everyone else—it cannot be done without witnesses. Additionally, we explained there that in one particular aspect, a get (divorce document) is similar to monetary law, in that just as in monetary matters where both parties agree, witnesses are not needed because who can object regarding their own money, similarly in a get, since her consent is not required at all and he is able to act according to his own will, therefore if he writes it in his own handwriting, it is valid from the Torah even without witnesses. Therefore, in the case of yibbum (levirate marriage), there is no obligation to others because even before yibbum, when she is awaiting levirate marriage (zekuka), she is prohibited to everyone. Additionally, her consent is not required at all, so why would we require witnesses? Therefore, it is not mentioned in the Talmud or among the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) that yibbum requires witnesses. On the contrary, it proves the opposite, and this requires further investigation.

And know that from the words of our teacher, the Rema, in paragraph 2, where he wrote, "And if he cohabited with her without a prior statement, he has acquired her, specifically if he cohabited with her in the presence of witnesses," it is clear from his words that if there was no prior statement (ma'amar), witnesses are required for the yibbum (levirate marriage). However, if there was a prior statement, witnesses are not required for the cohabitation. The later authorities were puzzled by this, as certainly even with a prior statement, witnesses are required for the cohabitation since the prior statement is only rabbinic (as the Beit Shmuel and the Gra note there).

It appears to me that his opinion is that for the essential act of yibbum, witnesses are not required, as it is written. However, from the fact that the Torah uses the term "taking" regarding the yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage), similar to the term used for the betrothal of a woman, from which we derive the betrothal with money from the term "taking," and regarding the yevama it is also written, "he shall take her as his wife and perform the levirate marriage," it is possible that the Sages based the concept of the prior statement on this. Therefore, while witnesses are not required for the cohabitation itself, for the primary act of taking her as his wife, it is proper to have witnesses or for it to be done publicly, which serves as witnesses (as the Beit Shmuel notes in section 26, subparagraph 1).

Therefore, when he made a prior statement with witnesses, witnesses are no longer required for the cohabitation. But when no prior statement was made, witnesses are required for the cohabitation—not necessarily for the act of cohabitation itself, but for his intention to perform the yibbum and take her as his wife. Therefore, even if the act of cohabitation was accidental or deliberate, he can still designate witnesses beforehand that his intention is to perform the yibbum, and the cohabitation can occur afterwards in any manner (as it appears to me).

The declaration (ma'amar) can be done either with money or with a document, as it appears from the plain meaning of the Talmudic discussion (Yevamot 52b). This is also written in the Shulchan Aruch. However, Maimonides (Rambam) and the Tur only mentioned money because they held that according to the conclusion of the Talmudic discussion, we only have the declaration (ma'amar) with money (see the Gra, note 5, and the Beit Shmuel's unnecessary amazement). Also, in the Tosefta and the Jerusalem Talmud, only the declaration with money is mentioned, see there. And this is the order: He betroths her with money in the presence of two witnesses and says to her, "Behold, you are betrothed to me with this declaration of the levirate marriage with this perutah, according to the law of Moses and Israel." And after the betrothal, he takes her into the chuppah like any other woman, intending to establish a name for his brother (see the Darkei Moshe). And he can perform the declaration through an agent, just like with other betrothals.

And the Rambam wrote in Chapter 2 that just as one sanctifies his yevamah (a widow of a childless brother) so too he recites the wedding blessing in the presence of ten and writes a ketubah (marriage contract) according to the law of anyone who marries a woman. And he did not mention the betrothal blessing, and similarly, it is not mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch. However, from the Tur it is clear that the betrothal blessing is necessary, and so wrote the Yam Shel Shlomo (Chapter 5, Section 2), and this is logical since the Sages equated it to a regular woman. And the text of the ketubah is not like the text of ordinary ketubot, as will be explained. And if he said to her, "You are sanctified to me through the sanctification of my brother," it is nothing, for she is not sanctified to him through his brother's sanctification. And there was an incident with one yavam who, when he sanctified her with a statement, said to her at the time he gave her the coin, "You are sanctified to me with this and with my brother's sanctification," and the Rivash ruled that she is sanctified, as it is like a loan and a coin, for even though with a loan alone she is not sanctified, nonetheless, with a loan and a coin she is sanctified, and here too it is similar.

Even though he can have relations with her against her will, nevertheless, the "ma'amar" (betrothal declaration) cannot be made except with her consent, as with all betrothals. Thus, the sages taught (Yevamot 19b): if someone performs ma'amar with his yevama (levirate widow) without her consent, it is not valid. Since the sages instituted this practice, they did not want to establish that it could be done against her will. Consequently, it does not create a binding acquisition that would require a get (divorce document) for the ma'amar, and chalitza (levirate divorce) alone suffices (Rashi on Kiddushin 44a, s.v. Rabbi). 

And since it is only valid with her consent, therefore, if a minor who was widowed from betrothal (erusin) and is still under her father's authority, he can perform ma'amar with her with her father's consent. But if she was widowed from marriage (nissuin), he must wait until she grows up because a minor does not have the capacity to understand and accept betrothal. 

There is room for doubt because, as relations can occur with her while she is a minor, as will be explained in Siman 167, perhaps ma'amar can also be performed by her mother and brothers, as is done with other betrothals. This matter requires further investigation, and the halachic decisors have not discussed this issue at all.

If she gives birth to a son from him, it is not necessary to name him after the deceased brother, as the verse "he shall be named after his brother" pertains to inheritance and applies to the levir (the brother-in-law who performs yibbum) and not to the child born, as explained in Siman 163. The ketubah that is written for her is not from the levir's assets, as he is not obligated to give her a ketubah since Heaven granted him this woman and he did not choose her of his own will. Hence, his assets are not liable for her ketubah, even if he performed ma'amar with her. Rather, her ketubah is from the assets of her first husband. These assets are indeed the levir's, as he inherits them, as explained there. However, from these assets, the portion that pertains to her ketubah is not entirely his and remains liable for her ketubah like any other woman's. If she dies during his lifetime, he will inherit her. However, if the levir has no remaining assets, the Rabbis instituted that he must provide her a ketubah from his own assets, as any man must do for his wife, so that she should not be easily dismissed by him (Gemara 52b). One should not question that if so, what is the meaning of saying that she has no ketubah from him if there are assets from the first husband – it is obvious, for would she take two ketubot? The answer is that indeed, it could be said so, like a widow who remarries and has a ketubah from both husbands, but it is not said so due to the reason explained. There are other explanations for this which will be clarified at the beginning of Siman 168 (see Tosafot 39a, s.v. "isha").

The ketubah (marriage contract) of a yevama (a widow who is subject to levirate marriage) must be formatted with lines, due to the verses that are written in it. This is the text of the ketubah: On such and such a day, in such and such a month, in such and such a year from the creation of the world, according to the reckoning that we count here in such and such a city, so and so came before us and said to us: My brother from my father has died, and, for the Sages and all of Israel, he left a son and a daughter inheriting and possessing, but in the name of Israel he did not leave, and he left this woman whose name is so and so who was married to him, and it is fitting for me according to the Torah to perform levirate marriage with her, as it is written in the Torah of Moses: "Her brother-in-law shall go into her." And I will serve, honor, sustain, and support you as Jewish men serve, honor, sustain, and support their wives truthfully. And I will give you 200 silver coins, which are your due as was written in the ketubah that your first husband wrote for you. And I will provide for your sustenance, clothing, and necessities as is the way of the land. And so and so agreed to this and accepted the yevama, so and so, in order to establish the name of his brother in Israel, as it is written: "The firstborn that she bears shall succeed in the name of his dead brother." And the dowry that she brought from her father's house, whether in silver or gold, etc., and he accepted and added from his own another 100 zuz, etc. And so and so accepted the responsibility of this ketubah, this dowry, and this addition, and so and so said, "I accept the responsibility," etc. And everything is valid and established as in all ketubot, and all possessions, both movable and immovable, that she brought in will be established for her with the yavam (levir) as with the husband. And after he marries her, he will consume the fruits and is obligated in her redemption (Beit Shmuel, subsection 4).

The Sages taught in a Mishnah (53b): One who has relations with his yevamah (levirate wife), whether inadvertently or intentionally, whether under duress or willingly, even if he was inadvertent and she was intentional, or he was intentional and she was inadvertent, or he was under duress and she was not, or she was under duress and he was not, whether the act was partial or complete, he has acquired her, and there is no distinction between one form of intercourse and another, end quote. And even according to those who rule like Abba Shaul, that if it was not for the sake of the mitzvah it is like encountering a forbidden relation, this is a rabbinic decree, and by Torah law there is no distinction (Nimukei Yosef). And even if we say that by Torah law it is also forbidden, this does not affect the acquisition; he has committed a transgression but still acquires her, just as if he had relations with his yevamah who was a niddah (menstruant). And we have already written about this in the previous section (and so writes the Beit Shmuel, section 5).

A person is considered to have acted unintentionally (shogeg) if he did not know that she was his yevamah (levirate widow), thinking she was his wife or another woman (Rashi). He is considered to have acted intentionally (mezid) if he intended it for licentious purposes and not for the sake of the mitzvah (Rashi). A person is considered to have acted under duress (ones) if he intended it for his wife, but his yevamah overpowered him and he had relations with her (Gemara). Similarly, if both of them acted unintentionally, or both acted intentionally, or both acted under duress (Gemara), what difference does it make? You find a case where both acted under duress, such as when Gentiles forced him and attached him to his yevamah against their will when he was prepared for his wife. Why did we need to say that in the case of duress, he was prepared for his wife? Because if not, since there is no arousal without intention, it would not be considered duress even though in the act itself he is under duress, as explained in the Talmud there.

The general rule is that if he knows that he had relations with her, he acquires her, even if it happened under duress or unintentionally, such as if he did not intend to have relations at all and it happened due to some circumstance, for example, he intended to have relations with an animal and for some reason ended up having relations with her, he acquires her because he intended to have relations in general. However, if he had no intention of having relations at all, he does not acquire her. Thus, our sages said: If he intended to throw a stone against a wall and mistakenly threw it against his yevamah (sister-in-law), he does not acquire her. If he intended to throw a stone at an animal and mistakenly threw it at his yevamah, he acquires her, because he intended to have relations in general. Therefore, if he had relations with her while he was sleeping or as drunk as Lot, he does not acquire her, because there was no intention for any relations at all. However, her intention is not required at all, so even if he had relations with her while she was sleeping, he acquires her. Similarly, if he fell from a roof while aroused and landed on his yevamah unintentionally, he does not acquire her, because there was no intention for any relations at all. But her lack of intention does not matter, because the Torah is concerned with him, not her. This is because we do not require that he specifically intends for her, as it is written, "her yavam (brother-in-law) shall come upon her," which means in any case, even without intention. However, if there is no intention for any relations at all, we do not call this "her yavam shall come upon her," because "shall come upon her" implies intention. Although we do not require intention for her, we certainly require intention for relations in general. Thus, our sages received and expounded in the Jerusalem Talmud: "her yavam shall come upon her" intentionally, but "and takes her to be his wife" unintentionally. This means that one verse is extra, from which we derive that even without his intention, he acquires her. However, from the phrase "shall come upon her," it implies intentionality. Therefore, intentionality for relations is required, but her intentionality is not required. (So it seems to me).

The Tosafot wrote there that a yevama (a widow awaiting levirate marriage) is not acquired except through intercourse with an erect, living member, but with a non-erect member, it is not considered acquisition. And not only according to the opinion that one who has intercourse with a dead member in forbidden relations is exempt, but even according to the opinion that he is liable (Shevuot 18), nevertheless, regarding yibbum (levirate marriage), we require intercourse in a manner that establishes a name, as mentioned there. And although ejaculation of semen is not required, and completion of intercourse is also not required, as it is taught that even with mere penetration he acquires her, nevertheless, all this is in the manner of establishing a name, just that it was not fully completed. But with a non-erect member, this is not the manner of establishing a name. This is what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 8: "And similarly, if he adhered to his yevama without an erection, but with a non-erect member, he does not acquire her." And their intention is not specifically when others adhered him to her that he does not acquire her, but if he himself came upon her with a non-erect member, he acquires her, as there is no difference in this at all, but they mentioned the usual case (as it seems to me). And know that penetration acquires even with inferior intercourse, such as in error or coercion and similar cases, and also not in the usual manner, as this is the law in all forbidden relations that penetration is considered like completion of intercourse, and not in the usual manner is like in the usual manner. There is no need to elaborate on this.

The Tur wrote: And the matter of accidental intercourse acquiring with his yevama in any manner is specifically when she fell to him from marriage, but if she fell to him from betrothal, accidental intercourse does not acquire except to inherit his brother's property and to release her with a get (divorce document) and to exempt her co-wife. However, it does not acquire to inherit her, to become impure for her (as a kohen), or to annul her vows. But with partial intercourse, it acquires for all purposes even if she fell to him from betrothal. And thus, she does not eat terumah through inferior intercourse from betrothal (Gemara 56a). And the explanation of the matter is as follows: Since in general inferior intercourse, like accidental intercourse and similar cases, does not acquire, and only because the verse increased [the law] regarding a yevama as it says, it is logical that it only increased for what is explicitly stated in the verse, such as to inherit his brother's property, as it is written, "he shall rise in the name of his deceased brother," and to exempt her from levirate marriage, as this is the main point, and she needs a get to release her and to exempt her co-wife, as it is written "his brother's house," and we expound that he does not build two houses. But for terumah, to inherit her, to become impure for her, and to annul her vow, he does not have the capability through inferior intercourse unless the husband also had the capability. Then he stands in place of his brother, meaning from marriage. But from betrothal, where the husband also would not have acquired these things, the yavam (levir) is not better than the husband (Tosafot there).

However, regarding "Ha'ara'ah" (initial stage of intercourse), in all matters of the Torah, "Ha'ara'ah" is considered as complete intercourse except in the case of a "Shifchah Charufah" (a designated maidservant), where it accomplishes acquisition for all matters. But in the Jerusalem Talmud, it implies that there is also a dispute regarding "Ha'ara'ah" (see Avnei Yehoshua, who ruled according to Rav there, in the second version). Therefore, our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 9 that some say the same applies to "Ha'ara'ah" (see there). He wrote this based on the words of the Rosh (Chapter 6, Section 5), who wrote that it implies in the Jerusalem Talmud that they dispute "Ha'ara'ah" (see there). And I am puzzled, for anyone who examines the Jerusalem Talmud will clearly see that on the contrary, it is more lenient than our Talmud, as it refers to inadvertent intercourse, where only "Ha'ara'ah" does not accomplish acquisition for all matters, but complete intercourse does, even in the case of inadvertent intercourse and other weakened forms of intercourse as explained. And it seems to me that this is also the intention of the Rosh (see there). Therefore, the Tur did not mention this (but in Tosafot, Niddah 56a, s.v. Ledvarim, it is explicitly as the Beit Yosef, and this requires further investigation; see also the Gra, Section 16).

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote: "There are those who say that one who consummates the levirate marriage (yibbum) must recite the blessing 'Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us regarding the consummation of the levirate marriage.'" This is the conclusion of the Tur in the name of the Itur. And even though he has already recited the blessings of betrothal and marriage, and for all other marriages these blessings suffice, this is because, in those cases, betrothal is required by Torah law. However, for a levirate marriage, these blessings do not pertain to the consummation, which is the primary mitzvah from the Torah. 

And even though it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Brachot 9:3) that one blesses on all commandments at the time of their performance except for betrothal through intercourse, and the Ran explains in the name of the Ramban in the first chapter of Pesachim that this is because it is impossible to bless while together in bed due to the prohibition of 'there shall not be seen among you any nakedness,' and blessing beforehand is not possible because one does not bless on a commandment unless it is ready to be performed. Nevertheless, we do not concern ourselves with this, since it is not found in our Talmud. Additionally, regarding the consummation of the levirate marriage, which is a significant positive commandment, we do not worry about this, and he can bless before entering the bed with her. However, this ruling is not found in other poskim.

**The Law of Yibbum (Levirate Marriage) for a Minor Boy and Girl, and the Chalitzah (Release from Levirate Marriage) of a Minor Boy and Girl. It contains 13 sections:**

Our sages received the tradition that a boy who is nine years and one day old is fit for intercourse, and a girl who is three years and one day old (Niddah 44b, 45a). Below this age, there is no concept of intercourse at all. It is well known that a minor does not have legal ownership (kinyan). If a minor betroths a woman before he reaches the age of thirteen years and one day, it is not a valid betrothal. Therefore, from a Torah perspective, a minor is not eligible for yibbum because he needs to acquire her as a wife, and a minor cannot acquire. Nevertheless, by rabbinic decree, since he is capable of intercourse, she is rabbinically considered acquired by him (Rashi, ibid.), meaning she is bound to him. Therefore, the sages were stringent in this matter. However, this is not a complete acquisition that would allow him to divorce her with a get (bill of divorce), as a minor is not capable of giving a get until he grows up. As our sages said there, the intercourse of a nine-year-old is considered like the statement (ma'amar) of an adult, so she still requires chalitzah due to the bond, and also a get for the intercourse, similar to ma'amar.

However, when she is a minor, the Mishnah teaches that a girl of three years and one day, who is fit for intercourse, if the yavam (levirate husband) engages in intercourse with her and he is an adult, he acquires her completely according to Torah law. And if another man engages in intercourse with her, he is liable for her as a married woman according to Torah law. We do not say that he acquires her only rabbinically, as is the case with an adult, but rather his acquisition is from the Torah (Tosafot Kiddushin 10a, s.v. "V'chayavin," see there). And in this, she is not similar to him, because her consent is not required at all, for the yavam engages in intercourse with her against her will. And as it was explained in the previous section, if he engages in intercourse with her while she is asleep, he acquires her, but if he comes while he is asleep, he does not acquire her. Similarly, with a minor, this is not yibbum (levirate marriage) according to Torah law. And she, in her minority, is subject to yibbum according to Torah law when she is fit for intercourse, for if she is not fit for intercourse, she is not subject to yibbum even rabbinically, as this does not constitute intercourse at all.

And this is regarding levirate marriage (yibbum), but for the act of chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage), we require that both parties be adults and that they have brought forth two pubic hairs after reaching the age of maturity, as hairs that appear beforehand are not considered a sign of maturity. An examination is needed to confirm the signs of maturity, and we do not rely solely on the presumption of age. The reason for the distinction between a woman in chalitzah and yibbum is because the Torah writes "man" in the context of chalitzah—"if the man does not desire"—indicating a man and not a minor. In contrast, regarding yibbum, it is written "her yavam (brother-in-law) shall come unto her," and since there is no explicit command for her consent, we do not require her to be of sound mind. However, in chalitzah, we derive that the woman is compared to the man (Yevamot 105b), meaning that since the verse states "his brother's widow shall go up to the gate" and she is required to perform the acts of chalitzah, spitting, and recitation, it follows that we compare her to the man, requiring that she also be of sound mind, which implies being an adult. (It seems to me that this is Rashi's intent there, for otherwise, we could say the same about yibbum. Examine this well).

Therefore, a minor does not perform chalitzah until he is thirteen years and one day old, and then he must be examined to verify that he has brought forth two pubic hairs. However, if he had two pubic hairs before reaching this age, he is not considered an adult because of them, unless he brings forth two other pubic hairs after reaching this age. Nevertheless, if he is found to have two pubic hairs after reaching this age, we do not suspect that they might have been there beforehand. Similarly, she does not perform chalitzah until she is twelve years and one day old, and she is examined afterward and found to have brought forth two pubic hairs, just as with the yavam. In the Jerusalem Talmud (Chapter 48), it implies that according to Torah law, chalitzah is valid even if she is a minor, and it is only rabbinically that we require her to be an adult. Refer there (see Tosafot there). In our Talmud, it is not so. Therefore, if they performed chalitzah as minors, it is considered nothing. This is not similar to the cohabitation of a minor, which they treated as a formal act because they are destined for a marital life, thus there is substance to it. This is not the case with chalitzah. Even with cohabitation, it is specifically in yibbum because she is bound to him, thus they treated it as a formal act, and he also inherits his brother's property (Rashi), since the property will come into his possession when he grows up and consummates the marriage, making them his. However, the cohabitation of a minor in general is considered nothing. Therefore, if a minor marries a woman and dies, she is exempt from chalitzah and yibbum, as his actions are considered nothing.

A nine-year-old and one day who cohabits with his yevama (sister-in-law) cannot release her with a get (divorce document), as he does not have the capacity to give a get until he matures and cohabits with her again. Then he can release her with a get. However, if he matures but does not cohabit with her after maturing, she cannot be released with just a get; she requires both a get and chalitza (ceremonial release). The get for his earlier cohabitation and chalitza for the levirate bond, as it has not been removed even though he has matured since he did not perform an act with her post-maturity. Similarly, if he cohabited with her while a minor and died while still a minor, or even if he died after maturing but did not cohabit with her post-maturity, and there are other brothers, she requires chalitza and not yibum (levirate marriage). Chalitza is necessary because the bond has not yet been removed, and yibum is forbidden because the Sages considered his cohabitation as resembling ma'amar (a form of betrothal in levirate marriage). This is akin to having the bond of two deceased brothers upon her, as the first bond has not been removed and the second bond is from the minor's cohabitation, which is considered like ma'amar. In the case of ma'amar, the law is similar as will be explained in Siman 174. Therefore, if this minor married another woman after maturing and did not cohabit with his yevama post-maturity, when he dies, his brother must perform chalitza for both women. He must perform chalitza for the first woman because the initial bond still exists, and consequently, the second woman is not exempted by the chalitza of the first, similar to the law of two women from one man. They are not from one brother, as the bond of the second brother is lighter and rabbinic, considered like ma'amar, while biblically she still belongs to the first brother. Hence, they are like two yevamot (widows awaiting levirate marriage) from two houses. Nevertheless, the second woman is also forbidden from yibum by rabbinic decree. If she undergoes yibum and the second woman performs chalitza, people might say that it is permissible to perform chalitza for one woman and yibum for another from the same house, since in the eyes of the public, the first woman is also considered as the second brother's wife. This will be further explained, God willing, in Siman 174.

This minor yavam (levir) who cohabits with his yevama (brother’s widow) is permitted to remain with her and to have regular marital relations with her until he grows up, whether she is also a minor or whether she is an adult. And so the Sages taught in the Mishnah (Yevamot 111b): a minor yavam who cohabits with a minor yevama—they shall grow up together. If he cohabited with an adult yevama, she will raise him, meaning he is permitted to have regular relations with her and she will raise him until he grows up, and then it will be permissible for him to divorce her with a get (bill of divorce) and not before, as we have explained. The tanna (Mishnaic teacher) informs us that we do not say that since a minor is not fit to beget children, there is no obligation to establish a name for his brother, and thus he is committing a transgression with every cohabitation. Although he is a minor and we are not commanded to separate him, she, being an adult, might be considered to be transgressing. However, in reality, there is no transgression here because the Torah permits him. Otherwise, how could it be permissible for him when he grows up, for we hold that any yevama (widow) about whom we cannot say at the time of falling to yibbum (levirate marriage) “the yavam shall cohabit with her” is like the wife of a brother who has children. 

And if you would say that the Torah only permitted a yevama when the yavam was an adult at the time of his brother's death, it cannot be so, for it is written, “When brothers dwell together” (Deuteronomy 25:5), which implies that as long as they had one dwelling together in the world, even for a moment, such as if he was born one hour before his brother’s death, the Torah commands “the yavam shall cohabit with her” when he grows up. Consequently, by necessity, she is also permitted to him in his minority (Talmud). The matter of establishing a name for his brother is only that he cohabits with her in the manner of yibbum, not necessarily that she becomes pregnant from this cohabitation, for even partial intercourse acquires her, as we wrote in the previous section. Rather, certainly, we do not worry about them not being fit to beget children in their minority. Therefore, even if she is excessively old when her husband dies, should we say that there is no mitzvah of yibbum because she is not fit to conceive? The Torah only excludes an ailonit (a woman who is congenitally infertile).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 2, Law 5: A yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage) who was taken in levirate marriage and said within thirty days, "I was not consummated with," even though he says, "I did consummate," and he divorced her, we compel him to perform chalitza (the ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage), since he already divorced her with a get (bill of divorce). And if he has not yet divorced her, we compel him to consummate or to perform chalitza and then divorce her with a get. If he divorced her after thirty days and she says, "I was not consummated with," we request him to perform chalitza for her. And if he admits that he did not consummate, we compel him to perform chalitza. If she says, "I was consummated with," and he says, "I did not consummate," she does not need chalitza because he is not believed to prohibit her to everyone else once he has taken her in. So it is written.

The explanation of his words is that any yevama (widow bound to marry her brother-in-law) who has undergone yibbum (levirate marriage) and has been brought into his house and secluded with him in the usual manner is presumed to have been cohabited with him, as this is a strong presumption. Therefore, when the matter concerns others, such as when he divorces her and she claims she has been cohabited with, and he tries to prohibit her by claiming he has not yet cohabited with her, we do not pay attention to his words even within thirty days, because as soon as he secluded with her, she is presumed to have been cohabited with. All the more so according to those who hold that witnesses are required for the act of cohabitation in the case of yibbum and he secluded witnesses for his seclusion with her, she is presumed to have been cohabited with. Therefore, if there were two women who fell for yibbum and one underwent yibbum and thereby released her co-wife to marry, and when the co-wife comes to marry she says she has not yet been cohabited with, and he also says so, we do not pay attention to their words. This is also explained in the Gemara (112a) that the presumption is that anyone who marries a woman cohabits with her immediately (Rashi). Therefore, even within thirty days, the co-wife can marry. The Rambam did not need to explain this because in writing that he is not believed to prohibit her, it follows that they are not believed to prohibit the co-wife, and this is obvious.

However, in matters that concern only them, and she asserts with certainty that she has not yet had relations, a person is believed to remove the matter from its presumption, even to permit, if the matter is in his control. For this reason, a person is believed regarding slaughtering and other matters, and certainly, he is believed about himself concerning prohibitions. Therefore, within thirty days, he is compelled to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) or to perform chalitza (release from levirate marriage), and even if he performs chalitza, he will need to give a get (divorce document) since he claimed that he had relations. And even if both admit that he did not have relations, he still needs to give a get because of the presumption (Maimonides). And although a person is believed to remove a matter from its presumption with what is in his control, even leniently, as we have said, nevertheless, in this matter, one cannot rely on leniency in a case where desire overwhelms, in a permitted context, and in a matter of mitzvah. Therefore, she needs a get even if he did not betroth her with the yibbum declaration (see Beit Shmuel, subsection 5).

And this is specifically within 30 days, but after 30 days, we do not force him to perform chalitzah (the ritual of removing the shoe) but rather request it from him, because she has made herself a single witness (regarding her husband's death). In this situation, it is not applicable to say that a person is believed about themselves because this goes against human nature to restrain oneself for more than 30 days. Therefore, he is believed that he has consummated the marriage, and she is not believed. However, even so, she has made herself a single witness, and therefore we request him to perform chalitzah for her if he has given a bill of divorce. If he has not given it, he should either consummate the marriage or perform chalitzah. It is obvious that he needs to give a bill of divorce when performing chalitzah because he certainly has consummated the marriage, and all the more so within 30 days as we have stated. If he also admits that he did not consummate the marriage, we force him to perform chalitzah, and he also needs to give a bill of divorce as we have stated.

If he gave her a get (divorce document) before he married her, she is believed even after 30 days to say that he did not have relations with her, and we force him to perform chalitzah (a ritual releasing her from the bond of marriage). Since he gave her a get for her bond, she is forbidden to him, and it is possible that he did not want to have forbidden relations with her (according to the Maggid Mishneh). Therefore, she is also believed against the co-wife. Even if she says, "I had relations," and he says, "I did not have relations," she is forbidden to remarry because there is no presumption that she was married, since it was forbidden for him to marry her. We say that it is possible he did not have relations with her. Note that what we said, that she needs a get, is obvious, because even if he wrote her a get beforehand, she needs another get if they were secluded after the get, as it is likely he had relations with her. Even if he gave her a get before he married her and she was forbidden to him, as we said, we do not say leniently that he did not have relations with her. It is likely he did have relations with her, and she needs another get for his relations. This is also implied in the Gemara there (according to the explanation of Rav Ashi).

And all of this is according to the Rambam's view, but the view of Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur is that within thirty days, we do not go lenient in any matter due to the presumption of her entry (into the marriage), and even against her co-wife, she is believed to say that he did not have relations with her, and she is forbidden to remarry, even if he says that he did have relations with her. Similarly, if she says she had relations and he says he did not, she is forbidden to remarry, because during the entire thirty days, a person might restrain himself, and it is possible that he did not have relations. And even though certainly every married woman is presumed to have had relations, it can be said that a yevama (levirate wife) is different because they are embarrassed from each other. This reasoning is found in the Gemara there, and the Rambam holds that this reasoning applies only to themselves and not to others. Note that we actually find elsewhere in the Talmud (Pesachim 72b) that we do not say that embarrassment from his yevama would prevent him from having relations, and on the contrary, he would have relations without asking if she is close to her menstruation.

And behold, it seems that even according to this opinion, we only say this stringently, but leniently we do not say that he did not have relations with her, even if both of them say that he did not have relations with her, and she requires a get (divorce document) in addition to the chalitzah (ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage). And this is explicitly evident from the words of Tosafot there, that we only say this stringently, as mentioned there. However, from the language of the Tur, it does not imply this, as he wrote: "A yevamah (widow subject to levirate marriage) who was taken in levirate marriage and he wants to divorce her, and he says that he has not yet had relations with her and she needs chalitzah, and she says that she has had relations and a get is sufficient within thirty days, he is believed, and she needs chalitzah. And since she says that they have had relations, according to her words, she requires a get, and chalitzah alone is not sufficient, and we ask him to give a get but do not force him, etc." And from what he wrote that we do not force him to give a get, it is inferred that he is also believed leniently. And from what he wrote "And since she says they have had relations," it is explicitly proven that if she also said they had not had relations, she would not need a get at all, and chalitzah alone would suffice. And I do not know where he gets this from, as it is explicitly proven otherwise from Tosafot, as mentioned. And also from the Rosh, it does not imply this, and he brought from the Jerusalem Talmud that to forbid the rival wife, they are not believed even when both say they have not had relations, even within thirty days. And although the Rosh concludes that when both admit, the rival wife is forbidden, as mentioned, this is all stringently. And in this, the poskim (halachic decisors) also disagree, as the Magid Mishneh wrote. And so ruled Rabbi Yosef Karo in Shulchan Aruch, section 6, that the rival wife is always permitted, even if both admit, and even within thirty days, as mentioned. And in any case, how is it possible to rule leniently to not require her to need a get? This requires further investigation (the opinion of the Rosh regarding the rival wife is that she is not believed if he says he had relations with her, as mentioned. But Tosafot do not hold this way, as mentioned. Analyze this carefully).

Once she has entered into levirate marriage, she is considered as his wife, and the laws regarding the sale of his brother's property apply. This section contains eighteen paragraphs:

The yevamah (widow awaiting levirate marriage), once she has been taken in levirate marriage, is considered as his wife in all respects. He is permitted to divorce her and take her back. We do not say that since he has already fulfilled the mitzvah of yibbum (levirate marriage), the prohibition of marrying a brother's wife returns. The Torah states, "The yavam (levir) shall come upon her and take her as his wife." Once he has performed yibbum, she is his wife. This must be the case, otherwise every yavam would be prohibited from his yevamah after the first marital act through which the mitzvah of yibbum is fulfilled. Similarly, it is written in the Book of Ruth that Boaz took Ruth as his wife, and that situation was akin to yibbum as explained there.

And it has already been explained in section 166, paragraph 15, that she does not have a ketubah from the yavam (the brother-in-law who performs levirate marriage), and her ketubah is from the assets of her first husband. Only if the first husband has no assets, they instituted that she receives from the second (the yavam) so that it would not be easy in his eyes to divorce her, as mentioned there. Just as someone who divorces his wife and remarries her does so based on her first ketubah, as stated in section 100, so too if someone divorces his yevamah (the widow he married via levirate marriage) after she has been taken in levirate marriage and remarries her, he does so based on her first ketubah. This means it is from the assets of his brother as before, and we do not say that since he remarries her at his own will and not by the commandment of levirate marriage, she should have a ketubah from him, because this is not the case. In this matter, her status is like any other woman who was divorced and remarried (Ketubot 82b), and the reason is that in this case, she is certainly not better than an ordinary woman who would have two ketubot. By what right would she gain more than all other women? Consequently, since she has only one ketubah, it remains her first ketubah (see there in the Tosefot Yom Tov).

The early authorities posed a significant question regarding the statement of our Sages that the ketubah of the yevamah (widow subject to levirate marriage) is upon the estate of her first husband and not upon the estate of the levir (the brother-in-law). Since the levir inherits the property of his deceased brother, what difference does this make? We have explained in Siman 166 that it teaches us she does not have two ketubot; however, this explanation did not satisfy our Rabbis. Their reasoning, it seems to me, is that if this were the case, the Sages should have stated that she only has one ketubah. They questioned what difference it makes whether the ketubah is on her own property or on the property of the deceased, since in either case, it is essentially his (the levir's). When the deceased has no estate, they instituted it from [the levir's] own property.

And there are those who explain that there is a significant practical difference because if we were to say that the ketubah is upon his assets, she would only receive a maneh (100 silver coins) as is the law for a widow. But now that it is upon the first husband, she has the ketubah of a virgin, because the first husband married her as a virgin. And if the first husband did not leave any assets, the sages instituted that she only receives a maneh from the second husband (Rashba in Ketubot there and in Ar'a and Tosefot Yom Tov in the 4th chapter of Yevamot, Mishnah 4). There is a question on this explanation because according to this, what they said that her ketubah is on the assets of the first husband is only for her benefit. But in the Gemara, they gave the reason that she does not have a ketubah from him because it was decreed from Heaven that he should acquire a woman, which proves that it is also for his benefit.

Some explain that this is specifically because for all other women, when the husband sells his land, she can collect her ketubah from the purchasers. However, this woman cannot collect from the purchasers who bought the property from the yavam if the deceased had assets, even if they were later lost. (This is mentioned in Tosafot Yevamot 39 and Ran at the end of Perek 8 of Ketubot.) Similarly, if the deceased's assets were sold, she can collect from the purchasers even if the yavam has free assets, and the purchasers cannot claim that they left her free assets, because his assets are not pledged for her ketubah at all. (This is stated by the Rashba there.) It is also obvious that if during her marriage to the second husband, the first husband's assets were lost, the second husband must write her a ketubah so that it will not be easy in his eyes to divorce her. (This is noted in Beit Shmuel, section 2.) It is also evident that when it is said that if the first husband did not leave assets, she has only the principal amount of the ketubah from the second husband and no additional amount, even if she brought a dowry to the first husband, when nothing remains from him. (This is mentioned by the Ran there, who wrote that even though he took out his brother's property, etc., and it is not understood at all, see there.)

Moreover, there is another practical difference: In the Gemara (Ketubot 53b), it remains uncertain whether the daughter born to the yevama has a right to sustenance from the brothers or not. The doubt arises because her ketubah is from the first husband and not from the second. Consequently, she also does not have the ketubah stipulations from the second husband, and from the first husband she likewise has no claim, for she was not born from him. Although she herself definitely has a right to sustenance—if there is from the first husband, she has from the first husband, for he wrote to her, "You shall reside in my house." And if there is none from the first husband, she has from the second, just as they instituted a ketubah for her from the second when there is none from the first. Nevertheless, the daughter, since it is a doubtful matter of law, does not have [a claim]. And so ruled our teacher, the Rema, at the end of this section. Therefore, there is a significant practical difference here: If her ketubah is from the first husband, his daughters do not have the ketubah stipulations either from the first husband or from the yavam. But if there is nothing from the first husband and they instituted a ketubah for her from the second, then his daughters would also have the ketubah stipulations. (And the Tosafot there hold in the first version the opposite—see there.)

Since her ketubah (marriage contract) is tied to the assets of her first husband, the sages therefore said that the yavam (levirate husband) is not permitted to sell any of his brother's assets. Even if the assets are a thousand times the value of her ketubah, he cannot sell even a portion of them without her permission. And although in the case of all other women, the husband can sell, and when the time comes for collecting the ketubah, if free assets are not found, she collects from purchasers, nevertheless, here they closed the way for him because there is no lien on his own assets. And if he sells a portion of his brother's assets, perhaps the remaining assets will be lost, and she will need to pursue the purchasers, which is not agreeable to her (Tosafot Ketubot 1, s.v. "Harotzeh"). And so the sages said (there), if he wants to sell his brother's assets, if he is a Kohen who cannot divorce her and remarry her, he should appease her so that she permits him to sell. And if he is an Israelite, he divorces her with a get (bill of divorce) and remarries her, writing her a new ketubah, and then she is like all other women. And if one asks, if so, why does he need to divorce her? He should write her a ketubah on his own assets. The answer is that this is not agreeable to her because when it is tied to her first husband's assets, she is always secure, as he cannot sell them (Tosafot). But when he divorces and remarries her, she becomes like all other women, and therefore, if he sold or gave away as a gift or divided the deceased's assets with his brother, whether before or after the yibbum (levirate marriage), he did nothing. This is explained in the Talmud there, that even retroactively, his sale is invalid, and they were stringent in this matter for her benefit, so that she would be secure in her ketubah. And even if at the time of yibbum he wants to write her a ketubah on his own assets, he cannot do so without her consent (Avnei Shoham sec. 3).

And know that in what we have written, that one who wishes to sell the property of his brother, if he is an Israelite, he divorces her and remarries her and then can sell, one might ask about this because in Section 2 it was explained that when he divorces her and remarries her, she is restored under the condition of her original ketubah, and consequently, her status remains as before, so how can he sell? Certainly, it is so that when he divorces her and remarries her before she collects her ketubah, she is under the condition of the original ketubah. However, if she collected it after the divorce and he remarries her, she no longer has any connection to the original ketubah. And so it is explained to me from the words of Rashi, of blessed memory (Ketubot 81, s.v. Migerasha), and furthermore, this is when he remarries her without specifying, she is under her original ketubah. But here it speaks of a case where he stipulated with her that her ketubah would be on his property and the original ketubah would be nullified (Rosh there, Chapter 8, Section 13). Similarly, it is taught in the Tosefta of Ketubot (Chapter 9): He marries and divorces and she writes him a receipt for her ketubah.

And this is what our master, Rabbi Yosef Karo, wrote in section 7, and these are his words: "Even if he divorced her and then subsequently took her back without any specific conditions, he cannot sell the property of his brother unless he conditions at the time of taking her back that her ketubah (marriage contract) is upon all his property. Without divorce, if she consents to him on the condition that he writes for her the responsibility of her ketubah on all his property, he can sell." And one should not ask, "If so, why does he need to divorce her?" It can be said that without divorce, the choice is in her hands, but with divorce, he can compel her to agree, as he will not be willing to take her back unless she does so.

It appears from the words of the Rosh and the Shulchan Aruch that without a stipulation, if he remarries her, it will be on the condition of the first ketubah, even if she has collected her ketubah after the divorce, and not as it is written in section 8. Otherwise, why would they need a stipulation? However, this is not a proof, as one could say that the ruling comes to teach us that even if she has not collected her ketubah, if he stipulates with her, it is acceptable. This is also explicitly implied from the Jerusalem Talmud in Yevamot (Chapter 4, Halacha 4), which states regarding this Tosefta: "It depends on the circumstances, or she will cancel her ketubah for him." This means that if he divorces her, he does not need to cancel the ketubah, and it must be as stated that he divorces her and she collects her ketubah. However, from the language of the Rosh, it does not seem so. See there (regarding what is difficult about Rashi, and see the Gra in subsection 8, and it requires further study).

The Sages closed the way for the yavam (levirate husband) regarding the assets of his deceased brother for the benefit of the yevama (levirate widow). Not only is he unable to sell the estate's assets, as mentioned, but even from all that remains of the deceased's movable property, they consider that the yavam should sell them and purchase land with the proceeds, and he will eat the fruits. This is because the yavam could squander movable property, but with land, she is secure. Thus, the Sages taught in the Mishnah there (80): "If his brother left money, land should be purchased with it, and he will eat the fruits. If he left produce detached from the land, land should be purchased with it, and he will eat the fruits." Similarly, for other movable property and produce attached to the land, our master the Beit Yosef also wrote in section 4, and these are his words: "If his brother left produce attached to the land, they should be sold, and land should be purchased with the proceeds, and he will eat the fruits." And it seems to me that he did not bother to elaborate on this because, according to what is explained in the Mishnah there, it is necessary to appraise the value of the produce as it was at the time of death, for what grew in the yavam's possession is not encumbered to her ketubah (and the Sages do not disagree with this, as the Tosefot Yom Tov noted).

And behold, this is the method of the Rif, the Rosh, and the Tur, and similarly the Ramban and the Rashba of blessed memory wrote (as the Maggid Mishneh writes in chapter 22 of Ishut). But the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote there as follows: "If one marries his yevamah, and his brother left behind produce attached to the ground, they should be sold, and land should be bought with the proceeds, and the yavam eats the produce thereof. If he left behind detached produce from the ground, and similarly if he left behind money and movable property, all of it belongs to the yavam, and he may use them as he wishes, and she cannot object because the ketubah is not collected from movable property except by the enactment of the Geonim. And this enactment does not have the power to prevent him from his brother's property or to prohibit it to him under this responsibility, so that he does not deal with them," end quote. (And in the Gemara there, this Mishnah was rejected from the halacha because it follows the opinion that movable property is liable for the ketubah, and we do not hold this way. Therefore, the Rambam holds that although by the enactment of the Geonim the ketubah is collected from movable property, they do not have the power to prevent him as stated.)

And the opinion of all these authorities is that now, after the enactment of the Geonim, movable property is considered like real estate for all matters, and the enactment of the Geonim is treated as if they are encumbered by the law of the Talmud (Hilchot Ishut). However, if it is written in the ketubah (marriage contract) that movable property is encumbered, even the Rambam agrees to this, for since it is written so, they are encumbered to her by law and not by virtue of the enactment (ibid.).

According to all these authorities, even if the yavam (brother-in-law) himself owed his deceased brother a maneh (a specific amount of money), they take it from him, purchase land with it, and he eats the fruits (i.e., benefits from the produce), but he cannot say, "I am the heir, and I am in possession; I will hold onto what I possess." Rather, they take it from him. He also cannot say to her (the widow), "You are not my litigant," because she certainly is a litigant in this case, since all the deceased's property is mortgaged to her, and he (the yavam) owes it to the deceased. They take it from him based on Rabbi Natan's ruling, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 86. However, the Raavad disagrees, because in the Gemara, they rejected this as halacha for the reason that we do not impose two stringencies for a ketubah: one, that movables are mortgaged for a ketubah, and the other, the stringency of Rabbi Natan. But all these authorities believe that in the time of the Gemara, it was a stringency to collect from movables. However, nowadays, movables and real estate are equal in all matters, and there is only the stringency of Rabbi Natan. The Rif, the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch have explicitly ruled this way. (See Beit Shmuel, Sifkat 4, and his words require examination, as it is clearly indicated from the Talmud and the poskim that they treated the obligation as a full debt.)

And just as all the assets are taken from his possession to purchase land, so too if there are assets in the possession of the yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage), they are taken from her possession and land is purchased with them, and he (the yavam, her brother-in-law) eats the produce. For how can we leave them under her control, since the ketubah is not meant to be collected during life? And the yavam stands in place of the husband, and she only has a lien. Thus, the procedure is that he eats the produce of the lands that remain, and all movable property, money, and produce are not given into his hand as long as he has not married her, but are taken from his and her possession and entrusted to the court or a guardian until he marries her. Then, land is purchased with them, and he eats the produce (see Beit Yosef in the name of the responsa of the Rashba).

A yevama (a widow awaiting levirate marriage) who did not have a ketubah (marriage contract) from her husband, whether because he did not write one for her, or she sold it, or forgave it to him, the brother-in-law (yavam) inherits his brother's property and may sell or give it away as he wishes, for there is nothing that prevents him. However, when he marries her, he must write her a ketubah because it is forbidden to remain with a woman for even one hour without a ketubah. The deceased brother indeed committed a transgression by not having a ketubah. Therefore, he must write her a ketubah of one hundred (zuz) as prescribed for a widow's ketubah. Even if he does not write one, she is entitled to it by the enactment of the sages, like other women, and all his property will be liable for her ketubah like all other women. (Thus wrote the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch.) It must be said that the phrase "did not have a ketubah" refers to a case where, even by the sages' enactment, she does not have one, such as if he married her in a place where they do not collect without a ketubah, or similar situations. Otherwise, she would have one by the enactment of the sages.

A yevamah (widow subject to levirate marriage) who did not have a ketubah (marriage contract) from her husband because she was forbidden to him—for example, if she was a secondary relation to a forbidden relative (shni’ah la’arayot)—but she is permitted to the yavam (levir), as she is not a secondary relation to him, the Rambam writes in Chapter 2 of Yibbum as follows: "If the yavam wishes to perform yibbum (levirate marriage), he may do so, and she does not have a ketubah from him, just as she did not have one from her husband. Her entitlement to additional provisions (tosefet) is the same with the yavam as it was with her husband. However, if her husband did not write her a ketubah, or if she sold it or forgave it, the yavam must write her a ketubah, just like any other widow." This is also written in the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 9. 

From this language, it appears that the yavam does not need to write her a ketubah at all, even though she is permitted to him. Since she did not have a ketubah from her husband—because a wife is granted to him by Heaven, and she only has a right to the deceased husband's property—and here, by law, she does not have a right to the deceased husband's property because she was forbidden to him, therefore she also does not have a right from the yavam. This is not comparable to the case where if she did not have a ketubah from the first husband, the Sages instituted one from the second husband, for that is when by law she should have received from the first, but he had no assets. But when by law she does not have a ketubah, why should the Sages institute one from the second? This also appears from the language of the Talmud (Yevamot 85a), where it says that if she was a secondary relation to the husband, she does not have a ketubah from the yavam either. (And similarly, the Bach writes so).

But there are those who say that certainly if his intention is to be with her, he is obligated to write her a ketubah, for it is forbidden to remain without a ketubah. And what the Sages said, that she does not have a ketubah from the yavam, means when he performed yibbum and then came to divorce her before he wrote her a ketubah (Hagahot Maimoniot in the name of Ramban and Rashba). And from the words of Rabbeinu the Rema, it seems that even Rambam does not disagree with this, and this requires further investigation (and see Beit Shmuel section 7). And it is simple that if she was permitted to the husband but forbidden to the yavam, such as if she was a secondary forbidden relation to the yavam but not to the husband, then she has a ketubah from the husband's estate (Hagahot Maimoniot). However, when there are no assets from the first husband, certainly they did not institute a ketubah from the second, for the reason they instituted it is so that he should not find it easy to divorce her, and here, it would be better if he divorced her.

The laws of yibbum conclude here with the help of Heaven.

### Laws of Halitzah, containing 82 sections:

It is written in the Torah: "And if the man does not wish to take his yevamah (levirate wife), then his yevamah shall go up to the gate to the elders and say, 'My husband's brother refuses to establish a name in Israel for his brother; he does not want to perform the levirate marriage with me.' Then the elders of his city shall call him and speak to him, and he shall stand and say, 'I do not wish to take her.' Then his yevamah will approach him before the eyes of the elders, remove his shoe from his foot, spit in his face, and respond and say, 'Thus shall be done to the man who does not build up his brother's house.' And his name shall be called in Israel, 'the house of the one whose shoe was removed.'"

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Yevamot 101b): The mitzvah of chalitzah requires three judges, even if all three are laypeople. The number three is derived from the word "elders" [זקנים] in the verse. The minimum number implied by "elders" is two, but since a court cannot be evenly balanced, we add one more, making a total of three (Gemara). And since it is written afterward, "the elders of his city shall call him," which is superfluous because we already know it refers to the elders, it comes to include even laypeople, provided they know how to recite the verses to the yavam and yevamah, as will be explained. This is evident from the language of the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch. However, some say that "laypeople" does not mean complete laypeople, but rather that they are not ordained or members of their city's Sanhedrin, but they still need to know all the laws of chalitzah (as implied by Rashi and the Nimukei Yosef there). Indeed, how could laypeople arrange chalitzah if they are not proficient in its laws? The first opinion holds that in other matters they can consult those who are knowledgeable, but in the recitation, it is not feasible to consult whether they recited correctly (Tosafot). The custom follows the second opinion, where the city's rabbi joins two Torah scholars and arranges the chalitzah, and the rabbi can join his students, as in this case, the rabbi and his student count as two (Maggid Mishneh, Chapter 4 of Yibbum). The Rambam and the Tur wrote that after the fact, if chalitzah was performed in the presence of unlearned people, it is valid if the yavam and yevamah know how to recite the verses themselves.

The judges should not be related to each other, nor to the levir (brother-in-law) or the yevamah (widow subject to levirate marriage), because chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage) is like a legal matter and even more stringent. In monetary cases, if they accept a relative or someone disqualified, the ruling stands; but in chalitzah, it is invalid because it's not dependent on their acceptance, but on the law of the Torah. Even relatives through their wives disqualify. This means when two women are related through their husbands, such as when they married two daughters of brothers, we say the husband is like his wife, and even two cases of husband-like-wife render the chalitzah invalid. However, a second-degree relation (e.g., second cousin) is valid, as explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 33. According to those who hold there that we do not say two cases of husband-like-wife, it seems here that after the fact, in pressing circumstances, it is valid (see the Gra's commentary, subparagraph 3, and the commentary on the order of chalitzah, and examine carefully).

Even though it is explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 7, that a convert (in ancient times) can judge his fellow convert, and if his mother was Jewish he can even judge a Jew, nevertheless, in the case of chalitzah, we require that the three judges have both their father and mother as Jews. This is derived from the verse "and his name shall be called in Israel," which implies that from every aspect he must be Jewish, and it does not suffice that he was conceived and born in sanctity. The Torah was strict in this regard. (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 3). Some of our Rabbis hold that the Gemara's intention when it stated "until his father and mother are Jewish" means that his mother without his father does not suffice, but his father without his mother does suffice (Tosafot there, Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, and Rabbeinu Tam in Sefer HaYashar). Their reasoning is that even for lineage of the priesthood, according to the one who is more stringent (Kiddushin 77a), the father being Jewish suffices. Their explanation is based on the verse in Ezekiel (44), which states "they shall not take a widow or a divorced woman to be their wives, but only virgins of the seed of the house of Israel." Some interpret this as meaning part of the seed from Israel, and some are stringent and interpret it as requiring all the seed to be from Israel. Hence, we require the father to be Jewish, and it is clear that if the father is Jewish, it is considered "all the seed of Israel," even if the mother is not Jewish. All the more so in the case of chalitzah, where it is not explicitly written "all the seed of Israel" (and this resolves the question of the Gra, subparagraph 8).

It is obvious that other invalid individuals to serve as judges, as explained in Choshen Mishpat Siman 7 regarding monetary matters, are certainly invalid for chalitzah. Therefore, if one of the judges of chalitzah is found to be a relative, disqualified, or a convert, the chalitzah is invalid and another chalitzah is required. However, she becomes forbidden to the brothers and it is considered an invalid chalitzah. Even if she performed chalitzah privately with him, it is an invalid chalitzah and she becomes forbidden to the brothers, as will be explained in this Siman regarding a yevamah who grew up among the brothers, that if she performed chalitzah with one of their shoes, she becomes forbidden to the brothers and cannot perform yibbum, and this will be further clarified in Siman 67 with the help of Heaven.

Even though three judges are sufficient, ideally five judges are needed, and this is the custom of our sages as it is stated in the Gemara (101b) that Rav Papa, Rav Huna, and Rav Ashi followed this practice. This is not required by law but to publicize the matter of halitzah and to prevent her from marrying a kohen (Rashi). For this reason, if she was already divorced, five judges are not needed. Another reason is so that it will be known that she is permitted to remarry (ibid.), and for this reason, in any case, five are needed. This is the established custom and should not be changed. However, if they performed halitzah with three judges, it is valid after the fact. The additional two judges should not be relatives or disqualified individuals, and this is specifically for the ideal situation, but after the fact, it is valid even if those two are relatives or disqualified. This is the ruling of our teacher, the Rema, in paragraph 3. Indeed, this matter is perplexing since we hold that if one of the judges is a relative or disqualified, the testimony and judgment are void even if there are a hundred judges. However, according to our custom, where the two additional judges sit separately and not with the three, it is acceptable because they are not part of the count (Beit Shmuel and Gra, Sk 17, and this is the Rema's intention). But if they indeed sat together, it is invalid (and according to the Nemukei Yosef, it is valid even in such a case if they were designated only to publicize the matter, see there and in Beit Shmuel, Sk 4, and examine this closely).

Rabbeinu the Rema wrote in section 2: "There are those who say it is forbidden to take a fee for performing Chalitzah, as one who takes a fee to judge, his judgments are nullified." And it appears to me that in matters of Chalitzah, one should be cautious not to sit with three judges who receive payment, for we require a valid Beit Din (rabbinical court) from the Torah. Refer to Choshen Mishpat, Siman 9, regarding what compensation a judge is permitted to receive. Even in this matter, it seems to me that it is stringent if one receives payment for Chalitzah because of the appearance of impropriety, similar to the stringency applied to relatives and other matters regarding a Beit Din for Chalitzah more than other Beit Din (as he intends to explain later in section 8). I have seen and heard that the rabbi takes a significant fee for Chalitzah, relying on the sale of the Chalitzah sandal, and this seems to me a great leniency. A mindful person should distance himself from this. It is not comparable to the case where the witnesses of a get (divorce document) take a fee, as I have explained above in Siman 130, also the rabbi who arranges the get, as I wrote above in the order of the get, section 4. For those reasons do not apply to Chalitzah." However, for the additional two (judges), there is no concern if they take a fee, since they sit independently and are merely to publicize the matter.

And there is a question about this: How is it possible that these two [judges] are only for the purpose of publicizing the matter, when it is proven in several places in the Talmud that publicity is not achieved with fewer than ten [people] (Yevamot 67a, Ketubot 7b, Bava Batra 142a)? The answer is that certainly, for the sake of publicity alone, we would not trouble ourselves to add judges. It is only because in the Talmud, there is a Tanna who holds that, by the strict letter of the law, five judges are required (see there), that they were precise in this manner. Even though the halachah is not according to him, nevertheless, we do so for the sake of publicity, since some degree of publicity exists even with fewer than ten. Additionally, it can be said that in truth, there are ten: the five judges, the two witnesses who are established according to custom (as will be explained), the yavam (the brother-in-law), and the yevamah (the sister-in-law), and it is inevitable that one or two people from the public will respond, "Remove the shoe," as will be explained.

It is written, "And his brother's wife shall go up to the gate, to the elders" (Deuteronomy 25:7). From here the Sages derived (Yevamot 101b) that judges must establish a designated place for the chalitzah (ceremony of removing the shoe) so that there will be a place prepared for this purpose. Establishing the place is done verbally, with the three judges saying to the other two, "Let us go and sit in such-and-such place to conduct the chalitzah." It is also sufficient for the rabbi to say this. 

If the chalitzah was conducted without establishing the place, Rambam wrote that it is valid because this is not an absolute requirement. Some say that establishing the place must be done on the same day, and others say it can be done the day before. The common custom is that after the mincha prayer on the day preceding the chalitzah, the place is established. If the chalitzah is to be performed on the first day of the week, the place is not established on Shabbat, as this would be considered a preparatory act for a weekday. Instead, it is established on Friday. 

The place should be in a prominent location within the city, meaning a well-known place. Our custom is to perform the chalitzah in the synagogue or the largest study hall in the city. After mincha on the preceding day, all the judges stand and say to the three judges or the rabbi says to all of them, "Let us go and establish the place for the chalitzah that will take place tomorrow." They then go to the place where the chalitzah will be arranged, and the three judges sit on one bench with the other two beside them, as will be explained in the order of the chalitzah. Even at night, they can establish the place, as this is not considered the beginning of the judgment but merely a preparatory act.

On the day they appoint the place, the judges send to warn the woman that on the next day, the day of the chalitzah (ceremony of releasing a widow from marrying her brother-in-law), she should not eat or drink anything until after the chalitzah. Even the customary mouth rinsing upon waking in the morning should not be done. This matter is essential because we require the spitting to come from her saliva itself and not due to any other cause. Therefore, the attendant must warn her about this because if she does not observe this, they will have to postpone the chalitzah to another day. They also warn her not to spit at all before the court until the time of the spitting, and if she feels compelled to spit, she should swallow it or use a handkerchief. They also warn her not to talk much while standing before them, only responding as instructed, and not to clean her teeth so that no blood will mix with the saliva. They repeat these warnings again in the morning before the chalitzah. It is also customary for the yavam (the brother-in-law) to wash his right foot the day before the chalitzah so that it will be easier to wash the next day, not relying on the washing from the previous day. It is also good for him to cut the nails of his right foot. They also inspect the day before the chalitzah to see if the nails are long enough for the chalitzah. Any other matters that need investigation are better examined the day before the chalitzah. Additionally, they teach the yavam and the yevamah (the widow) on the day before the chalitzah to recite the verses correctly in one breath. However, this is not essential, and if it was not done the previous day, it can be done on the day of the chalitzah.

One may only perform Chalitzah during the day, and if it was done at night, the Chalitzah is invalid. This is because Chalitzah is considered the beginning of a judicial procedure, and the beginning of a judicial procedure is invalid at night (Talmud Bavli, Sanhedrin 34b), as is stated in Choshen Mishpat, section 5. Even if one argues that in monetary cases it is valid post-factum at night, in the case of Chalitzah it is invalid because it is written "thus" and "thus" indicating an imperative (Yam Shel Shlomo, chapter 12, section 21). Why is Chalitzah considered a judicial procedure? Because the widow collects her Ketubah after the Chalitzah, and furthermore, the Torah made it a judicial procedure, as the elders sit and she comes before them, and they call to the Yavam (the brother-in-law), which is more stringent than a regular judicial procedure. Therefore, there is no distinction between the Chalitzah of a married woman and that of a betrothed woman (Nimukei Yosef writes that it is because of the Ketubah, and therefore some are of the opinion that in the case of a betrothed woman, Chalitzah can be performed at night, but in truth, this is unnecessary).

And know that all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) categorically disqualify a chalitzah (ceremony of removing the shoe) performed at night, as it is written. However, according to the Talmudic discussion (there), it depends on two interpretations, see there. But they ruled stringently, and according to this, if they performed the chalitzah at night, it is a case of uncertain chalitzah, and she is forbidden to marry a kohen (priest) and requires another chalitzah from all the brothers, as is the law with a disqualified chalitzah. It is possible that she does not need another chalitzah from all the brothers because this chalitzah is either entirely valid (according to the first interpretation where we follow the sages) or entirely invalid (according to the second interpretation). The poskim left their words in general terms, and this requires further study (see Tosafot Shabbat 42b s.v. V'hainu and examine carefully).

One does not perform chalitzah on Shabbat and Yom Tov, as this is one of the rabbinic prohibitions enacted by our Sages (Beitzah 36b) due to the concern that one might write a chalitzah document. As it is taught there: one does not perform chalitzah or yibbum on Shabbat and Yom Tov. Even according to the opinion that permits betrothing a woman on Shabbat when he has no children, as explained in Orach Chaim, Siman 339, and consequently, the same applies to yibbum when the eldest brother performs yibbum, as per the primary mitzvah of yibbum, as demonstrated in the Talmud (ibid. 37a, where it asks, "But he is performing a mitzvah," according to the explanation there). Nevertheless, regarding chalitzah, it is definitively prohibited. However, on Chol HaMoed, chalitzah is permitted, as we adjudicate capital cases (dinei nefashot) and financial cases (dinei mamonot) on Chol HaMoed (Moed Katan 14b), and if it is because of writing, one may write legal documents (shtarot) on Chol HaMoed.
