Even according to the opinion that prohibits, as written in Orach Chaim, Siman 545, a chalitzah document is permitted according to all opinions, as stated there. Some say that one should not perform chalitzah on Erev Shabbat and Erev Yom Tov, and this is the custom, as we do not convene courts except in pressing circumstances, as written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 5. In pressing circumstances, chalitzah can also be arranged on Erev Shabbat and Erev Yom Tov.

It is necessary that it is known that he is the brother of the deceased and that they existed in the same world, meaning he was not born after the death of his deceased brother, and that she is the wife of the deceased. Even if there is only one witness who testifies to this, it is sufficient, even if the witness is a relative, or a woman, and she is a relative, or a servant, or a maidservant, or a minor who is knowledgeable and intelligent. They are believed because it is a matter that will eventually be revealed, and people do not lie about such things, and it is merely a revelation of information (Gemara 39b). This is neither a matter of prohibition nor a matter of money (Rif), and it is not among the things that require formal testimony (from the Rif it seems that it does not need the reason of eventual revelation). Even a maidservant is believed (Tur). All these are also believed regarding the fact that they existed in the same world (Explanation of the Sefer HaChinuch).

Some say that in a time of need, such as when the yavam (levirate husband) wants to travel abroad and there is no one who recognizes him as the brother of the deceased, they perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage) even if they do not recognize him. Afterwards, they should seek out witnesses who recognize him (as stated there in the name of the Or Zarua). According to this, the ruling that we maintain later on, that any two people who saw the chalitzah can write a chalitzah document even if they do not recognize them [the participants], is because the judges would not perform the chalitzah unless they recognized them. However, according to this opinion, we do not rule this way, for perhaps it was a time of need and they performed the chalitzah without recognition. It is possible that we are not concerned about the time of need. This requires further investigation (see Talmud, Kiddushin 106a).

The judges need to know that ninety days have passed since the husband's death, excluding the day he died and the day she performs the chalitzah. This is merely a clarification, and it suffices to have the testimony of a relative or a woman, as stated (there). They also need to know that the yavam (levir) is thirteen years and one day old, and the yevamah (widow) is twelve years and one day old, and that they have both brought forth two pubic hairs after reaching these ages. Hairs that appeared before this time and remained afterward are not considered signs but are merely superficial, as written in Siman 155. If the yevamah has fully developed breasts, there is no need to check for hairs. Similarly, if the yavam has a full beard, there is no need to check for hairs. The measure of the hairs is explained there. Some say that the examination of the breasts must be done by men and not by women, but the abundance of hair can be assessed by women. Certainly, if we know that the yevamah has reached the appropriate age, it suffices for women to examine her, as stated there. Therefore, the matter of examining the breasts requires men only when the age is unknown to us. Nonetheless, the abundance of hair can be examined by women since it is something that can be revealed. However, the sign of the breasts is not considered something that is easily revealed, as the recognition is not as evident. Similarly, the presence of only two hairs cannot be relied upon from women when the ages are unknown to us, as stated there (see Beit Shmuel, section 7, and it appears to me as I have written, and examine this carefully).

We do not rely on the counting of years based on the testimony of relatives or women, only on the testimony of qualified witnesses. However, some say that if a person is established among the neighbors as having reached the age, and this establishment is not based on what they heard from relatives but rather from their own estimation or from hearsay from others, we rely on this presumption to consider them as adults. If an investigation was conducted, even based on the testimony of women, and they found two pubic hairs as required by law, we perform chalitza (a ritual to release a widow from levirate marriage) based on this, for we rely on presumptions in cases of stoning and burning (capital punishments).

Similarly, if there is a rumor that they are of age, and upon investigation, even based on the testimony of women, they are found to have two pubic hairs as required by law, we rely on this. In such matters, a rumor holds the same weight as a presumption (as noted in Beit Shmuel, section 9). However, it is not valid if they simply saw him being called up to the Torah, for a minor can also be called up to the Torah. Even in aliyot (Torah readings) where it is customary not to call up a minor, we do not rely on this. Similarly, we do not rely on the fact that he served as a prayer leader. If the rumor stems from such things, it amounts to nothing, for it is not a full presumption.

Even without the presumption of the neighbors, if there is an abundance of hair or if the hair is long, as is customary for an adult man or woman, it is presumed that they have reached the age of majority. We rely on this presumption and perform chalitzah (the ceremony that releases a widow from the obligation to marry her brother-in-law). Based on this presumption, there is no need to check for follicles in the hair, as long as there is an abundance of hair or the hair is long. Even though it was explained in Siman 155 that we are not expert in examining follicles, and therefore, without this, it is impossible to check for follicles, it can be said that this applies to the entire body. It can be said that we are not experts, but to check under the two hairs, we are experts (Shach, Siman 10). However, when there is an abundance or length of hair, there is no need for further checking. Similarly, if they are tall in stature, we can also rely on the presumption that they are of age, even if they have only brought forth two hairs. It has already been explained in Siman 155 that boys are considered as signs of maturity. If only a girl is presumed to be of age, she performs chalitzah. Refer to what is written there (and refer to Siman 11). (The question of the Bach and the Beis Shmuel in Siman 155 requires further analysis, as, on the contrary, it is explained there the opposite: that the lack of expertise is in not having a follicle, based on the entire body. Refer there).

The judges sit in the place they designated yesterday, and they sit as in a court case. They should see that the two (the yavam and yevamah) sit on the side so that it is known that they are not essential to the court proceedings, as the halitzah requires only three judges, as it says, "the yavam and yevamah shall come before the three judges," as it is written, "and his brother's widow shall go up to the gate to the elders," and they shall stand before them. The primary mitzvah of halitzah is ideally performed while standing, like litigants who stand before the judges. However, if the person is weak or elderly, they give him a staff to lean on. But if the halitzah was performed while sitting, it is valid after the fact. Therefore, a sick person who cannot stand may perform halitzah while sitting from the outset, as anything that has no remedy is considered as if it has already been done after the fact. The customs regarding this will be explained later in the order of halitzah, see there.

When the yavam (levirate husband) agrees to perform chalitza (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage), he is instructed to nullify any prior declarations, similar to a get (divorce document). If he had previously made a declaration, the chalitza is invalid. Likewise, if he was coerced into performing the chalitza, it is invalid because chalitza must be done willingly and not under duress. Although some hold that the mitzvah of chalitza takes precedence, and one might argue that coercion is permissible since it aligns with the law, the majority of poskim (halachic decisors) agree that coercion in chalitza is forbidden. Coercion is only permitted in situations specifically sanctioned by the Sages. There is a question if the yavam desires to perform chalitza and she does not, whether she can be coerced. This is because the primary requirement is his willingness, not hers. Alternatively, since she must actively participate in the chalitza ceremony, it is invalid if she is coerced. This latter view is also plausible.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (101a): If she performed chalitzah with a sandal that is not his, her chalitzah is valid, as it is not required that it specifically be his. Even though it is written "his shoe," the Sages accepted (103b) that even if the shoe is not his, it is valid. The reason it is written "his shoe" is to indicate that it should fit his foot (there), just as it cannot be said that his foot belongs to someone else, but rather the intention is that she removes it from his foot. Similarly, the term "his shoe" does not literally mean it must belong to him, but rather that it fits his foot, meaning it matches the size of his foot. Nevertheless, the Sages there noted that ideally, they should give him the sandal to walk in it a bit, so it will be seen that it fits the size of his foot. Therefore, ideally, they should give the yavam the chalitzah shoe as a gift, and some say he should also walk in it a bit so it appears as his, and consequently, it will be evident if it fits the size of his foot. However, after the fact, if they did not give it to him and he also did not walk in it beforehand, it is valid, provided that at the time of chalitzah it fits the size of his foot and he can walk in it well.

Regarding the matter of the shoe used for "Chalitzah" (the ceremony of removing a shoe): You should know that in the times of the Talmud, they had two types of shoes—one called "minal" and one called "sandal." According to the Torah, there is no difference, as the Torah uses the term "na'al," which implies both a "minal" and a "sandal." The term "minal" is a rabbinic term (Rashi 102a). In the verse "iron and copper shall be your shoes," the term used is not "na'al" but rather a term for a lock and bolt (ibid.). In the times of the Talmud, they were meticulous to perform the Chalitzah only with a sandal, for reasons that will be explained. Some prohibited using a "minal" from the outset, while others permitted it even initially. However, in our times, and even in earlier times, we perform Chalitzah with a "minal" because it is not customary for us to wear sandals, and their shape is almost unknown to us. This is similarly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Chapter 48, where Rabbi Yossi said, "Once, I went to Netzivin and saw an elder there. I asked him whether Rabbi Yehoshua ben Beteira performed Chalitzah with a 'minal' or with a 'sandal.' He replied, 'Is there a sandal in our locality?' (etc.)" (See there). In our Talmud (ibid.), this story is recorded differently. The Rambam and all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) do not mention the sandal at all. Nevertheless, we make some modifications to the Chalitzah shoe from the usual design so that it somewhat resembles a sandal, as will be explained further with God's help.

The shoe is made of soft leather like ours, and the sandal is made of hard, processed leather (Rashi). And since it is punctured, it cannot be repaired. But the shoe, even if it is torn, can still be worn, and it is forbidden to perform the chalitzah with a torn shoe. Therefore, the sages chose the sandal for this reason, and thus they said (102a) it is a decree because of a worn-out shoe, meaning torn, or alternatively because of half a shoe, meaning that even if only half of it remains, it can still be worn with difficulty, and in truth, it is not considered a shoe. Therefore, it will be explained that we customarily make the chalitzah shoe from somewhat hard leather so that it resembles a sandal, and additionally, we customarily make other things similar to a sandal, as will be explained with God's help.

The form of the sandal, as explained by Rashi (Shabbat 60a), is such that it has two openings and can be worn from both sides, but it is distinguishable which side is the front and which is the back. When it is worn the other way around, it appears that the person entering is actually exiting (ibid.). The distinction is evident on the sole upon which one steps, obviously. Some have written that the sandal is made from one piece entirely, whereas the shoe is made from two or three pieces, similar to our shoes (Nimukei Yosef, Chapter 48, in the name of the commentators). However, from Rashi’s words there, it does not seem so, as he implies that the sandal is also made from two pieces, with its sole attached to the upper part using nails or other means. Others have written that it is made from two pieces, but the stitching is on the outside and not on the inside; therefore, the same applies to the shoe used in the Chalitzah ceremony, as will be explained with God's help. We learned in Chapter 48 that a sandal without a heel is invalid, meaning that the back part of the foot must enter into the sandal, unlike a type of shoe we have called a "pantofel" or "steckschuh," which do not have a heel. In Chapter 26 of Keilim (Mishnah 4), it is explained that the sandal has a nose that rises in front of the toes and has two ears (straps). And it is explained there that there are several types of sandals (e.g., "sandal amqi ladiki") that have straps and do not require tying; rather, one stretches the straps, and they close by themselves. However, a typical sandal has two ears and loops, similar to what we make for small children.

It is further explained in the Gemara (102a) that there was a type of sandal that was very tightly fastened to the foot, and there was another type that was not fastened as tightly and had "shnatzim," which means two thin and short straps made at the edge of the sandal to tie it around the leg. Some say these are the hooks that we make (Nimukei Yosef). It seems that this refers to the "ears" mentioned in the Mishnah in Keilim. They also said there that it still requires a "mitna," meaning leather straps to double over and fasten it tightly (there). In this case, when she unties the straps and the hooks and removes his shoe, it will be clear that it is a proper chalitzah (Gemara), meaning that she performed the act of chalitzah by untying and removing it from his foot. Simply removing it from the foot alone does not make it as evident. And this is the custom, as will be explained with G-d's help.

It is written, "And she shall remove his shoe from off his foot" and it is not written, "And she shall remove his shoe from his foot." Our Sages have received that even "from off his foot" is valid, but from above the foot, it is invalid (Yevamot 103a). This is what we have learned in the Mishnah there: "From the knee and below, her removal is valid; from the knee and above, her removal is invalid." The explanation of matters is that the term "foot" refers to the sole of the foot where the toes are, and in height, it reaches up to the protruding bones on either side, which in our language is called "kna’khil" and in foreign language "kabil’a," and in the language of the Gemara (there), "istura," and in the language of the Mishnah "korsel" (Oholot 1:8). From there and above begins the leg and extends up to the knee, and in our language "kani’a," and in the language of the scripture "berakhim" (knees), and in singular "berekh." Therefore, a shoe that is above the knee, like our tall boots which are called "stivl"—if they reach above the knee, they are invalid for chalitza. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is stated that even tying the straps above the knee is invalid. The Rosh (Perek 48, Siman 7) elaborated that there is no reason at all to invalidate when the tying is above the knee, for tying is not specified in the Torah, nor is it a law given to Moses at Sinai, and according to the Torah, tying is not required at all. Therefore, he says that the Jerusalem Talmud is referring to a situation where without tying, the shoe would fall off the foot, and since the main support is the tying, the tying is considered as part of the shoe itself and is invalid if the tying is above the knee. But where the shoe remains in place and one can walk in it without tying, it does not matter if the tying is above the knee. However, from other early authorities who did not specify their words, it does not seem so, and likewise, the Rambam wrote in Chapter 4, Halacha 16, that if the shoe is tied above the knee, it is invalid. His words imply that in all cases it is invalid. The Maharshal in Yam Shel Shlomo (there, Siman 15) agreed with the Rosh’s ruling and wrote: "Nevertheless, regarding the straps being tied above the knee, his words seem correct where the shoe is not large and one can walk well without tying; the chalitza is valid ex post facto and it is as if it were not tied at all." However, in this, he disagrees and holds that if without the tying, one could not walk at all, then even with tying, it is invalid, for this is not considered his shoe. But if one could walk in it, but with tying, one can walk better, it is valid. And there in Siman 8, he explained that a shoe without straps and without hooks and loops, even if the shoe fits well on the foot, without tying, the chalitza is invalid. But when there were hooks and loops, even without straps, or there were straps and they were not tied, it is valid ex post facto if one can walk well without tying. And likewise, straps without hooks, when the straps were tied, it is valid, and one of them prevents even ex post facto. And even if Elijah comes and says that we do not need straps and hooks and loops, we do not heed him, for it has already become customary.

The shoe must be entirely made of leather, as supported by the verse in Ezekiel "And I clothed you with leather shoes." Therefore, all its stitching must be with leather. Thus, our sages taught: A sandal sewn with linen cannot be used for Chalitzah, as it is said, "And I clothed you with leather shoes" (Yevamot 102b). Nevertheless, some say that this is only for the ideal situation, but after the fact, it is valid, as this derivation is merely a support. However, most authorities invalidate even after the fact, and this is the common custom, and it is a complete derivation. Otherwise, shoes made of other materials would be valid. The first opinion holds that even if it is a support, the essential nature of a shoe not being made of leather is not considered a shoe at all, as the common practice is only to make shoes from leather, and it is not substantial. For if, in some place, it were customary to wear shoes made of other materials, we would validate also other materials, and this is not reasonable at all. Therefore, the main ruling is that if it is not sewn with leather, it is invalid, contrary to the opinion that nowadays, when shoes are sewn with linen, they should be sewn with linen. Heaven forbid to do so. And so wrote our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 15, and this is the main ruling.

However, the straps do not need to be made of leather. Some say that the straps must also be made of leather, and this is the prevailing custom, as noted in the Shulchan Aruch there. Indeed, in the Talmud there, it is only mentioned that if they are made of hair, it is acceptable. This is because hair from an animal is not inferior to leather. Nevertheless, if the entire shoe is made of hair, it is not valid for chalitza (the ritual of removing a shoe) because it is not called a shoe. They also said there that a shoe made of hair is called "korka," which means it is similar to a shoe and is thick leather attached to another thick leather with glue. Similarly, if one makes a shoe entirely of hair, it is necessarily thick because they are glued together, and this is not called a shoe at all, as it has its own name, which they call "korka" (according to the Nimukei Yosef). According to this, some opinions also permit using hair (there). The first opinion is that of the Tur, who wrote that the straps do not need to be made of leather. There is also someone who says that the Tur's intention is that they do not need to be made of leather and that hair is acceptable, but not from other materials, and they do not disagree at all (according to the Bach and the Beit Shmuel, section 14). However, it does not seem so, because if that were the case, the Tur would not have stated it simply but would have explained it. It is clear that the Tur permits anything, following the opinion of his father, the Rosh, as we wrote in paragraph 26, that the straps are not essential. Indeed, if one can walk well without straps, it is possible that everyone agrees that it is valid with any material (and so wrote the Beit Shmuel there). This is the context in which the Tur is speaking. But if the primary function of walking is through the straps, the Tur agrees that they need to be specifically made of leather or hair, and this is the main ruling. Know also that the hooks and eyelets must also be specifically made of leather or hair, as they are considered like leather.

Ideally, the leather should be somewhat stiff so that it resembles a sandal, as mentioned in Section 22. Nevertheless, it seems to me that it should not be too thick and hard, as it would lose its status as a shoe, as mentioned in Section 28. Similarly, some say that the stitches should be on the outside and not on the inside, also for this reason, so that it resembles a sandal (in Shulchan Aruch, Section 16, there is a textual error). This is the common custom, and it should not be changed. However, it seems to me that if the stitching is done on the inside, it does not invalidate the shoe after the fact, as none of the early authorities mentioned this except for the Sefer Mitzvot Katan (Sma"k). This is also implied by the words of the Yam Shel Shlomo (Yesh"sh) there, that this is only for the sake of enhancement. See there, and further examination is needed.

And some say that the entire shoe should be made from one piece, also for the reason we mentioned that it should resemble a sandal. However, this is not the custom, and none of the decisors wrote this, as we have already explained in section 24 regarding sandals, from Rashi it is clear that it was not from one piece. Furthermore, it is known that the way of the shoe is that the leather of its sole, which they call "padaswa," and the leather of the heel, which they call "fayata," needs to be hard leather, different from the leather of the shoe, as this is the common practice. It is almost impossible to walk well in any other manner, as is known.

Therefore, our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 16 as follows: "But the custom is to ideally remove the shoe with a shoe that is sewn from the outside and also that it is made of two pieces, meaning that its sole, which is called 'shole' and in our language 'padashva,' is a separate piece, and also the straps are a separate piece sewn into it. And they should be careful that the leather of the sandal should not be smeared with oil to soften it." End quote. And it is not specifically two pieces; the same applies if it is made of three pieces. And so wrote one of the great authorities (Chatam Sofer, section 112), and it also appears explicitly from the words of the Yam Shel Shlomo (section 5), who wrote that the heel and the place where one treads should be very hard. See there. And it is necessarily so that it is impossible to make the 'panta,' which is the main part of the shoe, together with the heel from one piece, because the 'panta' is soft and the heel is hard. And making the heel together with the sole is known to be very difficult. Therefore, we make it from three pieces: the 'panta' separately, the heel that surrounds the back of the foot and the thick flesh of the foot in front separately, and the sole separately, and they are sewn together with external stitches using leather or hair threads.

And that which is written that it should not be anointed with oil to soften it, it seems the reason is that it should be similar to a sandal in its hardness, as is stated. However, it needs to be blackened, as will be explained. However, the Shach there wrote that the custom is to polish it and smooth it like the upper part of a shoe, and if it has dried out, it is appropriate to anoint it so that it will be suitable for walking. The side of the hair of the leather should be on the outside, and the side of the flesh (smooth side) on the inside. The body of the shoe should be black and it should be sewn from the outside with a white strap. End of quote. And this is the custom.

The Tur wrote: "And whatever kind of leather the sandal is made from is fine, and not like the words of Rabbeinu Tam who wrote that it needs to be from the hide of a pure animal," end quote. Many of the early authorities were astonished by this, but several of the later authorities were stringent in this matter since it was said by Rabbeinu Tam, and so it is written in the Shulchan Aruch, section 17: "Some say that initially, it should be made from the hide of a pure animal, and also the straps and hooks on it, and also the stitching straps, all should be from a pure animal, and this is the custom," end quote. And it seems to me that there is a significant reason in this matter, and this is the reasoning of Rabbeinu Tam of blessed memory. For certainly, if we say that "from what is permitted in your mouth" is required only for Torah scrolls, tefillin, and mezuzot because sacred writings are written on them, certainly we do not need the hide of a pure animal. But if we say that a shofar made from the hide of an impure animal is invalid, as the Ran writes in the fourth chapter of Rosh Hashanah, and this is the ruling in Orach Chaim, section 586, it follows that for other commandments, we also require "from what is permitted in your mouth," and certainly, we also require this for the chalitzah (ritual of removing a shoe). And even though the walls of a sukkah are valid even from an impure animal, as is evident in Sukkah (23a), and the walls of a sukkah are from the Torah, this is because even inanimate and plant materials are valid, and an impure animal is no worse than them. But with the shofar, where we require it only from a living creature, it must be "from what is permitted in your mouth," and similarly with chalitzah, if a shoe were valid from anything, even from an impure animal, it would be valid. But since the sages said (102b) that a sandal sewn with linen is invalid, it is evident that specifically, we require it from a living creature, and therefore, it must be from a pure animal. (And this resolves all the objections raised against Rabbeinu Tam of blessed memory).

The shoe should have two straps to tie it with, one on each side, and they should be long enough to wrap around the foot two or three times. Some say that these straps should specifically be white, but the entire sandal may be black both on the outside and inside. If the straps have become blackened due to age, one need not be particular. The common custom among us is that the whole shoe is black on the outside except for the straps. There are some of the Geonim who objected to this and hold that since nowadays everyone uses black straps, they should specifically be black (according to the Gra, section 66). We do not have the power to change from the established custom and the ruling of the Shulchan Aruch. Especially in our times, when straps are not worn at all, there is no difference for us between black and white straps. Therefore, the custom in all the rabbinical courts is to use white straps.

They should make something like a knot which is called "chumarta" in the language of the Gemara. These are like large hooks on one side of the shoe, and on the other side, they should make a short strap with a hole to insert the knot into the hole, like loops and hooks. They should make two knots and corresponding holes, and some say they should make three knots in this manner, but not less than two. The custom is to make three, although there is no reason for this, as two are needed to secure it to the foot, as was also the case with the sandal, as is evident from the Mishnah in Keilim (Chapter 26). However, there is no reason for three, but nevertheless, one should not deviate from the custom. Note that the knots should not be from the shoe itself but rather another short strap attached to the head of the shoe, and similarly on the other side with the holes and hooks made of somewhat stiff leather. These stitches that sew the straps and hooks should be from the outside, as mentioned with the shoe itself, and this is the custom.

Some say that there should not be a strap like those commonly used in shoes, so that there should not be an additional layer. This is what is written in Shulchan Aruch, section 20. "Strap" seems to mean an additional piece for the shoe. Certainly, this is merely an added stringency, for even if one wears two actual shoes, if one removes both, it is valid as will be explained. All the more so with a strap. The issue of an additional layer is only relevant in one of two scenarios: either from the knee and above, or removing the upper shoe while the lower one remains on the foot. But not when removing both. This is also agreed upon by the leading later authorities (Bach, Siftei Kohen, and Drisha u’Prisha).

The Mordechai wrote that the custom is to make the shoe large up to half the calf, meaning large in height. However, in the She'iltot (section 16), it is written that the Or Zaru'a wrote that the height of the shoe should be such that it covers the ankle bone (which aligns with the Mordechai). The Ra'avyah wrote that the shoe should be lower than the ankle bone, as it is taught in the Mishnah: "If she removed it from below the knee, the removal is valid," implying that after the fact it is valid, but initially, it should not be made higher, only up to the ankle bone, which is the knuckle, and no higher. Only the heel should be slightly higher, as is customary for a shoe. This is the custom, and nothing about this is mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch. However, from what they wrote in section 20, namely, "They make the shoe's tabs short so that the loops and hooks are on the shoe and not on the foot, to avoid the issue of 'overly ornate,'" it seems this follows the view of the Mordechai and the Or Zaru'a. According to the Ra'avyah, it would not be relevant to mention the tabs of the shoe because there are no tabs; rather, the upper part of the shoe should not be so long that the hooks and loops are on the flesh of the foot and not on the upper part of the shoe, due to the issue of 'overly ornate' (as we have already explained that fundamentally, this is not an issue of 'overly ornate' and is merely a stringency). However, there is no proof from this, as one could say that the Shulchan Aruch's intention is regarding the loops and hooks themselves, as this is the language used in the Mishnah in Keilim, as mentioned in section 24. The intention is to make them short so that the hook and the surrounding hole of the loops rest on the actual foot bone. This seems to be their main intention, even though the language is not entirely clear (and this is also the view of the Levush). They also wrote there that some say to sew a border around the top of the shoe, but this is not customary. One should be careful to sew it with stitches close together, and if they are not close together, it is not a properly made shoe that is suitable for walking. The reason for not making a border is possibly because they were meticulous that nothing extra should be on the shoe due to the issue of 'overly ornate,' and to make a border, it is necessary to sew it with some additional material. It has already been explained that all such matters are merely stringencies.

They further wrote in section 21 that it should be made in the form of the right foot and should be worn on the right foot, and it should match the size of the foot—not so large that it is not suitable for walking in, nor so small that it does not cover the majority of the foot, nor torn to the extent that it cannot be walked in. And behold, regarding torn and small shoes, they are completely invalid. However, regarding a large shoe that is not suitable for walking in, we have already written in the name of the Rosh that even if one cannot walk in it, if with straps it can be tied and made walkable, it is valid. But in the name of the She'iltot we explained that if one cannot walk in it at all without the straps, then even with the straps it is invalid. Only if one can walk in it without the straps, albeit not well, such as if it is not much larger than the size of the foot, then it is valid with the straps making it walkable when tied. This can also be said in the opinion of the Rosh. Therefore, according to the law, if it is only slightly larger than the size of the foot, in such a way that one can wear it and walk in it even if the walking is not good, it is valid. But if it is much larger, it is invalid. And what they wrote that it should be made in the form of the right foot, this is in places where they sew the shoes this way. However, there are many places where they sew them identically for the right and left, as is known. Nevertheless, we are somewhat meticulous that it be sewn with a slight distinction that it is for the right foot. It is difficult to explain this in writing, but every shoemaker knows how to make it with a distinction that it is for the right foot.

He should put on the shoe on his foot when it is bare and not over stockings. It is obvious that if she removed the shoe from the stockings and the stockings remained on his foot, the chalitza is invalid because this is considered "removing over something" (Beit Shmuel, section 25), and the leg needs to be exposed. However, if she removed the shoe together with the stockings, it is valid after the fact (Beit Shmuel, ibid). But if she removed them one after the other, it is certainly invalid, because at the time of removing the shoe, it was "removing over something", and at the time of removing the stockings, it is not considered removing a shoe at all. For this reason, some are meticulous that there should not be mud stuck inside the shoe, and also for this reason, some require washing the right foot thoroughly. Although these are just stringencies (Beit Shmuel, ibid), they are proper stringencies and this is the simple custom, and Heaven forbid to change from this. However, after the fact, we do not invalidate the chalitza because of this. Additionally, there are those who say that the yavam should tie the edge of his pants above his knees so that the judges can clearly see that there is nothing between his foot and the shoe, and this is the simple custom.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 28 as follows: One should wear the shoe and wind the straps around the shoe on his foot, and tie them together with a double knot, one on top of the other. The second knot should not be tightened with great strength so that it can be untied with the right hand. There should be a bow on them. The knot needs to be on the flesh of his calf and not on the ears of the shoe. Therefore, one must cut the shoe both in front and in back, like a notch, so that the returning strap adheres directly to his bare foot. He should wrap the straps twice around the calf until the ends of the straps come to the front of the calf, above the ears of the shoe, that is, on the bare calf. The knots should be on the front of the calf and not on the back. The knots on the ear should be inserted into the holes on the other ear. End of quote.

From their words it is explained that the wrapping of the straps is around the shin, which is below the knee and above the instep, corresponding to the "Shin Bein" (shin bone). So wrote the Levush, and several other great authorities, as cited in the Yesh Sh'vut (Siman 6). The Yesh Sh'vut itself wrote: "Nevertheless, it appears to me that since the primary act of Chalitzah (removal of the shoe) is the untying of the knots, it is therefore better to make the knot of the straps on the foot and not as several great authorities wrote that one should wrap until tying above the shoe, on the shin, which is called 'Shin Bein' in the Ashkenazi language. This seems to me a bad practice, since the primary Chalitzah is at the foot and the untying of the knot should be like the removal of the shoe, and therefore it should be on the back of the foot below." And know that anyone who wishes to follow the Yesh Sh'vut must make four small loops, two on each side, so that during the wrapping of the straps, they can be wrapped through the loops, and then it will be possible to wrap them on the back of the foot. Without this, it is difficult to wrap them there, whereas with wrapping on the shin, these loops are not necessary, obviously. Additionally, according to the Yesh Sh'vut, the straps need to be sewn above the clasps so that they can be wrapped from top to bottom until the knot is on the foot. And so it is written there. But for those who wrap on the shin, it is better that the straps be tied below the clasps to wrap from bottom to top. In terms of the halachic ruling, there is no difference where they are tied and sewn, and therefore it is not clarified in the Shulchan Aruch. There were those who used to tie them between the clasps, which is below the two upper clasps and above the third clasp. This was the practice of Maharil Bruna in the name of his father (there). The Nimukei Yosef explicitly wrote that the two straps should be either below or above the clasps. Therefore, one can do as they wish.

And this is what is written in the Shulchan Aruch: to cut the shoe in front and behind like a notch to wrap around the flesh of the foot. This is the custom. Some make two notches, and some make three. On the sides of the shoe, they make small notches below the notches behind the foot. Some have loudly objected to these notches, as it appears like a torn shoe, as the Shach wrote there. Nevertheless, our custom is to make two notches behind and two small notches on the sides. The order of the wrappings will be explained, with God's help, in the order of chalitzah, section 18. Some do not make notches on the sides of the shoe, only behind. This is our practice.

She performed chalitzah with a wooden sandal, or a sandal made of cork, papyrus, or fiber, and they are not covered with leather on the outside; or she performed chalitzah with his left foot; or the shoe was so large that he could not walk in it at all, such as being excessively large; or the shoe was so small that it did not cover most of his foot; or it was torn so that he could not walk in it; or with a sandal that has no heel, like a slipper; or with a fabric slipper, even if it is made of felt, which is a type of heavy fabric that protects like our felt shoes – the chalitzah is invalid, for this is not a shoe at all. And the invalidity of the left foot is because we derive the foot of chalitzah from the foot of a metzora, about whom it is written, "upon the big toe of his right foot" (Leviticus 14:25). However, if it was made of wood and covered with leather on the outside, or if it was made of leather with linen sewn inside, or if she performed chalitzah with a left shoe on the right foot, the chalitzah is valid post facto. (There are those who, in pressing circumstances, wish to rely on Rabbi Eliezer there who validates with the left foot, but heaven forbid to say so, and there is no need to elaborate on this at all).

A shoe of idolaters, which means they place the shoe on the feet of the worshipped image and walk the image with the shoe, is actual idol worship. One should not perform chalitzah with it, but if she did, her chalitzah is valid. However, with a shoe that is an offering to idols, or from an idolatrous city, or made for the burial of the dead, if she performed chalitzah with it, her chalitzah is invalid. This is stated in the Gemara (103b) where it is also mentioned that a sandal that is quarantined or confirmed as leprous, meaning from garments afflicted with leprosy, is also valid. The reason for these distinctions is as follows: offerings and items from an idolatrous city are meant to be burned and are thus considered crushed to the extent that they are not considered shoes at all. For burial items, they are not made for walking. However, quarantined and confirmed leprous items, although they also need to be burned, are still called garments by the Torah at the time of burning, and he burns the garment, thus retaining the status of a shoe. Additionally, a shoe of idolaters, if it belongs to a Jew and cannot be annulled, makes her chalitzah invalid since it is meant to be burned. What we stated about chalitzah being valid refers to the shoe of a non-Jew, which can be annulled and does not need to be burned. According to Tosafot, it is valid only after annulment, and according to Rashi, even before annulment, provided he did not intend to acquire it. If he intended to acquire it, it becomes the property of the Jew. If you ask, when he does not intend to acquire it, is the shoe not his? The answer is that it has been clarified that with a shoe that is not his, her chalitzah is valid after the fact. What we prohibited regarding offerings does not mean the shoe itself is an offering, as in such a case it would not be prohibited, for offerings must be similar to those in the Temple. Rather, it means that the animal was an offering, and he made a shoe from its hide (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 23 and Beit Meir section 23), and refer to Yoreh De'ah, section 139.

Our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote: If someone is proficient with both feet or if she is proficient with both hands, they should perform the ritual with the right one. And if she is left-handed, she should perform it with her right hand, which is the left for every other person. If someone is left-footed, some say that he should perform the ritual with both feet, using the right shoe on the right foot and the left shoe on the left foot. And there are those who are uncertain and say that he has no remedy. However, the custom follows the first opinion. This concludes the text.

Explanation of the matter: When a person is proficient with both hands, we follow the general rule of using the right hand, as with tefillin. An "iter yad" (left-handed person) uses his right hand, which is the left hand of every person, for tefillin. According to this, it would seem that an "iter" with his foot (left-footed) would perform chalitzah (the ritual of removing the shoe) with his right foot, which is the left foot of every person. However, many poskim (halachic authorities) have written that the matter of chalitzah is not related to tefillin. For tefillin, the Torah decreed the weaker hand, which requires determining which hand is weaker for this person. But for chalitzah, which we learn from the word "foot" in the context of a metzora (leper), it certainly does not make a difference whether one is "iter" or not, as for metzora it also mentions the ear, and just as there is no difference in the ear between an "iter" and a non-"iter," so too with the foot. Additionally, the foot is not comparable to the hand, as there is not much difference between the right and left foot. Some say that for an "iter" there is no right side at all, and it is considered a defect regarding right and left. Concerning the right, it is considered as lacking. This is the opinion of those who think there is no remedy for him. Those who believe he should perform chalitzah with both feet are uncertain whether it is similar to tefillin or not. However, the opinion of the Tur is that it is exactly like tefillin, and he performs chalitzah with his right foot, which is the left foot of every person. The opinion of the Shiltei Giborim (Siman 22) is the opposite, that he should perform chalitzah with the right foot of every person. Therefore, the practical ruling follows the Shulchan Aruch, to perform chalitzah with both feet simultaneously, with two shoes. If he performs chalitzah with one of them, it might not be according to halacha, and it would be a disqualified chalitzah, requiring him to repeat with all the brothers (meaning all the brothers of the deceased). Some say there is no concern about this (Bach), as they intend to fulfill the obligation according to the law (Beit Shmuel, Siman 24). It is obvious that if there is a brother who is not an "iter," it is better that he perform the chalitzah, even if the "iter" is older. The sign of an "iter" is if he lifts his left foot first (Shiltei Giborim). It seems to me that if they did not know about his being an "iter" and he performed chalitzah with his right foot, one can rely post facto on the Shiltei Giborim, which is also the opinion of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol and Sefer Mitzvot Katan (Aruch Hashulchan, beginning of the chapter on the sciatic nerve).

The yavam (levirate brother-in-law) must say, "I do not wish to take her," with the "heh" pronounced clearly. She must say, "My yavam refuses to establish a name for his brother in Israel; he does not want to perform the levirate marriage." The Gemara (106b) states that it is advisable not to pause at all between the words "I do not" and "wish to take her," or between "he does not" and "want to perform the levirate marriage," so it does not appear as if he is saying, "I wish to take her," or "my yavam wants to." However, post facto, if there was a pause after "I do not," there is no concern, as everyone sees that "wish to take her" completes the phrase "I do not." This is not the case with "he does not want to perform the levirate marriage," where we are concerned even post facto that they might say it refers to something else. But with "I do not wish to take her," there is no such issue. This is according to Rashi's explanation. However, Rambam has a different interpretation and holds that there is no difference between the two phrases, as long as they can be read in one breath; even if read with a pause, it does not matter, similar to the principle stated by the Sages: "Anything suitable for mixing, mixing does not prevent it." The Gemara implies that the main concern is with "he does not want to perform the levirate marriage" because, generally, it is harder for a woman to familiarize herself with the text than a man. However, in practice, there is no difference, and the common custom follows Rashi, with a focus on reading it in one breath. (Note: the language of Shulchan Aruch, section 29, is not precise, and see Beit Shmuel, section 157.) The verses should be recited standing and in Hebrew specifically, as it is written, "thus and thus," which is a requirement. Similarly, we derive this from "And the Levites shall answer and say," which must be in Hebrew (Sotah 32b).

It is stated in the Gemara (103a): One who performs chalitzah must press his foot to the ground, meaning he should press his foot firmly on the earth. The apparent reason is that since the Torah commands "and she shall remove his shoe from his foot," the removal must be clearly noticeable. If his foot is suspended in the air and she removes his shoe, the act is not as evident because she is not exerting effort at all. Therefore, he must press his foot to the ground, and when she lifts his foot and removes the shoe, the removal is clearly noticeable. Additionally, when a person normally removes his shoe, he lifts his foot from the ground, so lifting the foot is also part of the removal process. Hence, he must press his foot to the ground so that she lifts his foot from the ground. If he did not press his foot to the ground and she removed his shoe while it was in the air, some disqualify it and some validate it, as the Sages said it is a mitzvah but not an absolute requirement. This is the opinion of the Raavad. However, the Tur writes in the name of the Rif and the Rambam that it is invalid. Our teacher the Beit Yosef in his major work expressed doubt about this and wrote that their opinion is not so. Nevertheless, he wrote in the Shulchan Aruch, section 32, that there is an opinion that if he did not press his foot to the ground, the chalitzah is invalid. However, the Yam Shel Shlomo ruled straightforwardly (Siman 15) that after the fact it does not invalidate. See what was mentioned in section 50.

Therefore, the order is as follows: the yavam (levir) should stand next to a wall or a pillar and lean on it, pressing his foot into the ground. She (the yevamah, or widow) stands bent over and unties the laces of the shoe with her right hand only. Afterwards, she also unties the hooks with her right hand only. She then grabs the back of his foot with her left hand, lifts his foot, and holds it in the air. With her right hand, she removes the shoe from the heel and then takes off the entire shoe with her right hand. All of this is done without the assistance of the left hand, as this is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud. Throughout this, she should not be sitting or on her knees, but rather standing and bending over. Immediately after she has removed the entire shoe from his foot, she should throw the shoe to the ground as someone does in anger, because he did not wish to establish a name for his brother. Our sages have said that if she is one-handed, she may remove it with her teeth, as it is not written "and she shall remove it with her hand." From this, we learn that if she removed it with her left hand, it is also acceptable after the fact. The Jerusalem Talmud only stated the right hand for the mitzvah, but not as an absolute requirement, and thus ruled the early authorities, of blessed memory.

Our sages said (102b): Whether he untied it and she removed it, or she untied it and he removed it, it is invalid until she unties it and she removes it. This means that the untying of the straps is essential and she must untie them, for this is also included in "and she shall remove his shoe." And we have already explained that the opinion of the Rosh is that only if it would be difficult to walk in it without the straps, like the sandals of their time which could not be walked in without tying, but if one can walk in it without tying and she removed it from his foot, even though he untied the straps, her removal is valid. The great later authorities agreed with this (Beit Shmuel 131 and the Gra 117). From this it is implied that the concern is only about the straps that she must untie, but regarding the opening of the hooks, there is no concern after the fact if he opened them. This also provides some support for what was said in section 48, that the lifting of the foot is not essential after the fact, since it is not considered an essential part.

If his leg is crooked backward or turned to the side, or if he walks on his toes, our sages said (Yevamot 103a) that he does not perform the chalitzah. Some of our rabbis explained the reason is because he cannot press his foot on the ground (Rif). If we say that pressing the foot is not essential, this reason is not correct. However, nevertheless, it can be said that even though it is not essential, it is still proper to press the foot on the ground. Some say this is the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 4 (Magid Mishneh). But some of our rabbis explained the reason is because if the leg is crooked or turned to the side, the shoe is removed from the top of the foot and not from the foot itself. Crooked does not mean that it stands as usual but rather that it is bent to the sides or backward, meaning the back of the foot is down and the top of the foot is up. And when he removes his shoe, he removes it from below the foot, and the Torah said "his shoe from his foot" (Raavad and Rosh, Chapter 7). And if he walks on his toes, certainly he is not fit for chalitzah at all, because he does not have a foot (there), as toes are not considered a foot and he does not walk on his foot. We cannot ask the poskim who hold that a left-handed person performs chalitzah with his right foot, which is the left foot for everyone, that this person should be treated like a left-handed person and perform chalitzah with his left foot, which for him is like his right. This is because a left-handed person from birth has the strength in his left foot that everyone has in their right, which is not the case with a damaged foot, and even if the damage is from birth, the essential strength that is supposed to be in the right foot is not present in his left foot.

The Mishnah teaches that if the chalitzah (ceremony of removing the shoe) is performed from the knee and below, the chalitzah is valid, but if from the knee and above, the chalitzah is invalid. We have already written that the Jerusalem Talmud explains this regarding the tying of the shoe. If the tying is above the knee, it invalidates the chalitzah, and the Rosh interprets the Jerusalem Talmud to mean that this is only when it is difficult to walk without tying it. But if one can walk without tying it, we do not worry if the tying is above the knee, as the tying does not invalidate at all. And in any event, according to this interpretation, it does not pertain at all to someone whose leg was amputated. For one who has an amputated leg, even from the knee and below, does not perform chalitzah, because the main part of the leg is the foot, and if there is no foot, there is no "and she removes his shoe from his foot." A proof of this is from the case of a reversed foot, which was explained that he does not perform chalitzah, and how is one whose foot is reversed worse than one whose foot is entirely cut off? This is the opinion of the Rif, Rambam, and other poskim. According to this opinion, it is clear that if the shoe reaches above the knee, it is invalid, and this is an a fortiori argument from tying. We have already explained that the height should only reach up to the instep, which is the ankle.

But the opinion of R. Chananel, the Maor, the Rashba, and the Rosh, of blessed memory, is that the Mishnah refers to one whose leg was amputated. If it was amputated below the knee and there is a place to insert the shoe and tie it even below the knee, and he cannot walk without tying it (see Beit Shmuel, section 35), then the chalitzah is valid. For anything below the knee is called "his foot," meaning the entire length of the lower leg. This is not similar to an inverted foot, where he does not perform chalitzah because he cannot press his foot to the ground. However, the amputee presses his stump to the ground (Tosafot 103a, s.v. "man"). The opinion of Rashi, of blessed memory, also seems to align with this view. But Tosafot holds according to the first opinion, and consequently, since it is a dispute among the authorities, the amputee does not perform chalitzah. And if he did perform it, the chalitzah is invalid. It is possible that she does not need to go through the process with all the brothers, as with all invalid chalitzot, since according to those who deem it valid, it is entirely valid; and according to those who invalidate it, there is no chalitzah at all in this case (see Beit Shmuel, section 33).

If one tore the shoe off his foot or burned it while it was on his foot, the chalitzah is invalid because chalitzah requires removing (the shoe), not tearing or burning. Even if he tore or burned part of it and then removed the rest, it is invalid because the entire shoe needs to be removed (see Bach, Siman 36). The Rambam wrote in Chapter 4, Halacha 21, that if he was wearing two shoes and removed the upper one, even though the lower one was torn until his foot was revealed, the chalitzah is invalid. This is not a novelty because the primary chalitzah is with the lower shoe, and it was not fulfilled. The novelty is that you might say since the foot was revealed, and there was a chalitzah with the upper shoe, it is valid. Therefore, he teaches us that it is invalid. This is according to the Rambam's version of the Gemara (102a). However, according to Rashi's version, even if he tore the upper one and removed the lower one, as long as he did not remove the torn upper one from his foot, the chalitzah is invalid. Even though he removed the lower one, which is the main one, since the torn upper one is still on the foot, the foot is not completely revealed. It is possible that the Torah insists on the complete revelation of the foot. But if he removed both shoes together, the chalitzah is valid. All the more so if he tore the upper one and threw it away and then removed the lower one. If he removed the upper one but not the lower one, obviously there is no chalitzah at all because it is considered as if he has not removed anything (what the Bach wrote in Siman 37, that if it is tied above the knee and similar cases, the chalitzah is invalid, in my opinion, this is only if it was tied above the knee or similar cases because the main chalitzah was not on the foot. But in such a case as this, there is no chalitzah at all and this requires further study. And according to what the Bach wrote about two shoes, she needs to remove both together, because if she removes the upper one first and then the lower one, the removal of the upper one is an invalid chalitzah).

After removing the shoe, she needs to spit in front of the yavam (the brother-in-law) as it is written, "and she shall spit before him." Therefore, she should stand after the removal of the shoe opposite the yavam and spit on the ground in front of the yavam so that he sees the spit. She should be instructed to gather a lot of spit in her mouth so that it is visible to the judges from the moment it leaves her mouth until it reaches the ground, or at least until it is opposite the face of the yavam, as the entire act needs to be done before the elders as the verses prove. However, after the fact, if the judges did not see the spit leave her mouth, it's not a problem, as the main thing is that the yavam sees the spit. Therefore, the sages said (106b) that if she is tall and the yavam is short, the spit needs to reach his face. If it dissipates before reaching his face, she needs to spit again. However, if he is tall and she is short, it is still considered "before him" even though her mouth is much lower than his face, as "before him" means that he sees the spit, and he does see it.

And this is the language of the Shulchan Aruch, section 39: If she spat and the wind carried it away before it reached his face, for example, if she is taller than him, she needs to spit again. But after it has reached his face, even if it did not reach the ground, it is valid. Therefore, if he is tall and she is short, it is still considered "before him." End quote (and see the glosses of the Aruch HaShulchan, subparagraph M).

A yevama who spat blood, according to the Raavad and the Rosh (Siman 12), even without any saliva, it is considered spitting, and she does not need to spit again, as "she will spit" is written in general terms, and spitting blood is included, since it does not specify that she must spit saliva. However, the Rif, the Rambam, and the Rashba ruled that spitting blood is not considered spitting, as general spitting refers to saliva. This is proven from the verse "if the zav spits on the pure individual," and therefore, only when she sucks in her mouth and spits blood is it considered spitting, since it is impossible without some saliva. But in a general spit or if she opens her mouth and blood flows out, there is no saliva, and she needs to spit again. This is also explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud and explained by Rashi (105a, s.v. "Does it write 'saliva'?" etc., "and it is impossible without some saliva," end quote). The same is written by the Yam Shel Shlomo (Siman 24).

There is a question regarding this issue: even though there are traces of saliva in the blood when she sucks, the saliva should be nullified by the blood since, according to Torah law, the majority nullifies the minority. The answer to this is that nullification applies only when the substance being nullified is not recognizable. However, here, the saliva is recognizable on its own and is not nullified (Mordechai, end of Chullin, see there). According to this, we must say that when the Sages said it is impossible without traces of saliva, they meant recognizable saliva. Therefore, the poskim (decisors) should have clarified this since it has practical implications for the law.

Another explanation is that nullification only applies when each substance was initially recognizable on its own and then mixed together. However, here, from the moment of their emergence, they were mixed, and thus nullification does not apply (ibid.). This means that the nullifier did not yet have significance in the world to nullify the minority of it. Therefore, even though we find the opposite reasoning that any prohibition that was not recognizable from the beginning is nullified even in a matter that has a permitted use, as stated in Yoreh De'ah 102 and Orach Chaim 326 (Magen Avraham, subsection 5), this is because the nullifier was recognizable beforehand. Hence, its power is strong to nullify the unrecognizable minority, even in a matter that has a permitted use. But here, since the nullifier was also unrecognizable, their power is equal, and they do not nullify each other (Noda B'Yehuda, Yoreh De'ah, section 54).

Additionally, it seems to me that this reasoning only applies when the prohibition and the permission are not distinctly recognizable in their origin and growth process. However, when they are recognizable in their very creation and growth process, we do not say this reasoning. Therefore, in a limb that the fetus has expelled and becomes forbidden, as stated in Yoreh De'ah 14, that the milk of the fetus becomes forbidden due to the mixture with the milk of this limb, if the entire animal has enough to nullify the milk of this limb, it is nullified, as stated there (Siftei Kohen, subsection 12), even though they were not initially recognizable. Similarly, when moving a perforated pot in a vineyard, if it increases by two hundredfold, it is forbidden even though the nullified item was not recognizable. Likewise, regarding the immersion of rivers with an increase in dripping water over flowing water, as explained in Yoreh De'ah 201, the dripping water was never recognizable since this is its growth and creation process. How can we say that it has no significance? Therefore, the milk is as if both are before us and is nullified when there is enough to nullify it. The dripping water has significance and cannot be nullified when it increases. Similarly, in a vineyard that has a part of two hundred, which is the measure that is not nullified, it cannot be nullified because it was not recognizable. But in the spitting of blood, where the source is not recognizable and it is not usual for a person to spit blood, it therefore has no significance if it was never recognizable (and with this, the difficulty of the Mishneh L'Melech, Chapter 1 of Tumat Midras, Halacha 14, and all the difficulties of the Noda B'Yehuda there are resolved).

Saliva that is not naturally produced but caused by food making the saliva flow is not considered saliva at all and is less significant than blood because it is not considered spitting at all. Therefore, if she ate garlic or cress or similar things that increase saliva and saliva flowed from her mouth, even if it appeared as if she spit forcefully, it is not considered spitting. Therefore, the custom is to prevent her from eating any food or drinking any drink before the chalitzah because we are not knowledgeable about what causes saliva. She should also minimize her speech until after the chalitzah since speaking also generates saliva that is not natural. Additionally, she should be careful not to brush her teeth until after the chalitzah to avoid causing blood in her mouth. This is also the custom. (See Ba'er Heitev, section 142, and according to what I have written, it is clear that their intention is not specifically to the flowing, but rather that these things lead to it. Consider this well.)

After the spitting, she recites the verse: "So shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother's house, and his name shall be called in Israel, 'The house of the one whose shoe was removed.'" She recites it while standing, and it is essential that she is taught the meaning of the words so that she understands what she is saying. Similarly, she should understand what she said earlier, "My brother-in-law refuses..." and also what the brother-in-law said, "I do not wish to take her," and that he understands what he and she are saying. The main point here is that they both understand the entire matter of the chalitza and what the Torah commanded. 

It is incumbent upon all those present that immediately when the yevama (widow) finishes the verse, they all respond three times, "Remove the shoe." This is also explicitly stated in the Gemara (end of chapter 48): "It was taught: Rabbi Yehuda said, 'Once we were sitting before Rabbi Tarfon, and a yevama came to perform chalitza. He told us, 'Everyone should respond, "Remove the shoe, remove the shoe, remove the shoe."'"

Some say that the yevama herself should also say "Remove the shoe" three times when she finishes the verse. There is a reason for this (as written in the Hagahot Maimoniot, chapter 4, in the name of the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot), and it will be explained in section 82.

The procedure for chalitzah (the ceremony of releasing a brother-in-law from the obligation to marry his brother's widow) is as follows: She first says, "My brother-in-law refuses to establish a name for his brother in Israel; he will not perform the duty of my brother-in-law." Then the brother-in-law says, "I do not wish to take her." After this, she removes his shoe from his foot, spits in front of him, and then recites, "This is what shall be done to the man who does not build up his brother's house," and "His name shall be called in Israel, The house of him whose shoe was removed."

The order is not critical. If she spits before removing his shoe, the spitting is still valid, and we do not allow her to spit again after the shoe removal to maintain the proper order, lest people say that the first spitting was ineffective. If she later desires to enter levirate marriage (yibbum) and he consents, they could do so. However, after spitting, she becomes disqualified from yibbum, so we do not allow her to spit again to ensure everyone understands that the spitting before the shoe removal is valid, and she is prohibited from yibbum thereafter (Gemara).

Similarly, if she says, "This is what shall be done," before spitting or if neither of them recites the verses, the chalitzah is still valid. The main part is the removal of the shoe. Therefore, if she only removes the shoe without reciting or spitting, the chalitzah is valid. All the more so, if she removes the shoe and spits without reciting, or removes the shoe and recites without spitting, the chalitzah is valid. However, whatever can be corrected should be corrected: if she did not spit initially, she should do so after the process. But if she recited and spat without removing the shoe, it is invalid, and she becomes disqualified from yibbum as well. However, recitation alone does not disqualify her from yibbum.

The Gemara (105a) explicitly states that "This is what shall be done to the man" refers to the acts of removing the shoe and spitting. The removal of the shoe completes the chalitzah, and the spitting disqualifies her from yibbum. However, the recitation is not critical and does not affect the validity (Rambam). The disqualification by spitting is a rabbinic enactment, lest people think it was the spitting after the shoe removal that was effective, given that this is the normal order. However, the recitation, which can occur before the shoe removal, does not lead to such confusion (105a).

This is what we have said, that the recitation is not essential. To what does this apply? To those who are fit to recite, who can speak. But a mute man or a mute woman who cannot speak may not perform chalitza, and if they did, their chalitza is invalid. This is a general rule throughout the Torah: even though the matter is not essential, we still require the person to be fit for this matter (104b), as with anything that is fit for mixing, the mixing is not essential for it. For if not, why did the Torah command to do this thing, given that it later minimized it, saying it is not essential? It is certainly the intention of the Torah that the person be at least fit for this matter. Therefore, if he is mute or she is mute, the chalitza is invalid. Similarly, if a minor girl performs chalitza, if he is an adult, the chalitza is invalid. But if he is a minor, even if she is an adult, the chalitza is nothing at all. Also, in the case of invalid chalitza, there is no prohibition, and she can later perform yibbum with him or another brother. Similarly, the chalitza of an imbecile, and some say also the chalitza of a deaf-mute man or woman, is nothing at all, as a deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor are considered equal throughout the Torah. Some say that a deaf-mute man or woman is equivalent to a mute man or woman, where the chalitza is at least invalid, and they are not like an imbecile, for they have some understanding. In chalitza, when the court stands over them and instructs them, there is some semblance of proper understanding. The Torah explicitly excluded a minor but not a deaf-mute. Though it is not valid chalitza, it is still not excluded from invalid chalitza. This is the opinion of Tosafot (104b, s.v. Veha) and the first opinion is that of the Rambam (see Beit Yosef, section 144).

This is the language of the Shulchan Aruch, section 49: A minor who performs chalitzah for an adult, her chalitzah is invalid, and she becomes prohibited to all the brothers. When she grows up, she must perform chalitzah with one of them, and she does not need to repeat the chalitzah with all the brothers. The explanation is that even though any invalid chalitzah requires repeating with all the brothers, in the case of a minor's chalitzah, it is not so. This is because, according to the Rif, a minor's chalitzah is valid, as the term "man" is written in the Torah to exclude a minor, but the Torah does not exclude a minor girl at all. Conversely, there are some authorities who hold that the chalitzah is nothing and is not even considered an invalid chalitzah, likening it to the chalitzah of a mentally incompetent person. Only the opinion of the Rambam considers it an invalid chalitzah. Therefore, regarding the issue that she does not need to repeat the chalitzah with all the brothers, we rely on these authorities (Bach, subparagraph 50, in the name of Terumat HaDeshen). The reason for these opinions depends on the variant readings in the Gemara (105b) and in the Mishnah (104b; see there and in Bach, subparagraph 49).

A blind person should not perform the chalitzah ceremony (the ritual of removing a shoe to release a widow from the obligation to marry her brother-in-law) initially because he cannot see the spittle of the yevama (the widow). However, if he did perform the chalitzah, it is valid because seeing the spittle is not an essential requirement. One should not argue that he must be fit for this act as is required for the recitation because the Torah commanded the recitation, but it did not command the seeing of the spittle. This requirement is only from the rabbis, and what we wrote about "she spits in front of him" is just a support, as “in front of him” does not imply that he needs to see the spittle. Therefore, the opinion of the Ra'avad is that if there is no other brother, he can perform chalitzah initially so that she should not remain in a state of being unable to marry. The Nimukei Yosef wrote similarly at the end of chapter 48, and one can rely on them in pressing circumstances. It can be said that Rambam also agrees with this and does not discuss cases where there is no other brother. Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) ruled explicitly in this manner in the end of section 172. Therefore, even though the language of the Shulchan Aruch in this section, paragraph 48, implies that we rely on this only after the fact, in the case where there is no other brother, we can rely on this initially (as also written by the Pri Toar in subparagraph 39 in the name of Responsa Perach Shoshan). If she is blind or he is blind in one eye, there is no concern at all, and they can perform chalitzah initially in any case. (See Beit Yosef, who suggests that perhaps the Ra'avad holds that the mitzvah of chalitzah takes precedence, and the Rambam does not hold this way. According to this, even according to the Rambam, he would agree that a blind person can perform chalitzah initially if there is only one brother. This is the intent of the Rema later in section 172. Otherwise, his words would not make sense. See and understand.)

All matters of chalitzah require intention, meaning that both must intend that through this act, she is released from his bond and can marry another. This is taught in the Gemara (102b): whether he intended and she did not, or she intended and he did not, the chalitzah is invalid until both intend together. And it is explained in Rashi's commentary there that the intention must be for the mitzvah, meaning that through this act, she is released, as stated, for this is the Torah's decree. This is also implied by the language of the Rambam and all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), that the intention must be for the mitzvah, contrary to some who are uncertain about this. Now, if for the entire Torah mitzvot require intention, it is not surprising here. But if we say that for the entire Torah mitzvot do not require intention, why is intention necessary for chalitzah?

And it seems to me that chalitzah (the ceremony of releasing a widow from levirate marriage) is not comparable to other mitzvot. In all other mitzvot, the act of the mitzvah is recognizable, such as blowing the shofar or taking the lulav, as these actions are not typically performed outside of the context of a mitzvah. Similarly, eating matzah is not something commonly done, as people usually eat leavened bread. Therefore, even without specific intention, the mitzvah is evident. However, with the removal of the shoe and the spitting (as part of chalitzah), a person is compelled to do these actions regularly, and if they do not intend the mitzvah, there is no mitzvah act at all. There is proof of this from the Torah itself, as the Torah required the recitation of verses during chalitzah, something not found with most other mitzvot. Presumably, the Torah insisted that this be done with the intention of fulfilling a mitzvah. This is not comparable to yibum (levirate marriage), where even if it is performed inadvertently, intentionally, or under duress, the mitzvah is fulfilled, as the Torah emphasized "and she shall be his wife" in any case, as stated in Siman 166. Furthermore, in yibum, the Torah's intention is to establish a name for his brother, and this establishment occurs even without specific intent, unlike chalitzah, where without intention, the act is not considered a mitzvah at all.

There are those who ask about this: if so, if the one who performs the chalitzah turns around, since he certainly does not intend the mitzvah, what does his chalitzah help (Chacham Tzvi)? From this, it was proven that intention for the mitzvah is not required. And some have answered that according to Torah law, it suffices with the intention of either one of them. Therefore, if he turns around, since she intends the mitzvah, that is enough. And what our Sages said, that both need to intend, that is rabbinic. And in the case of turning around, we rely on the Torah law (Beis Meir). However, this does not seem to be the plain meaning of the Talmud and the poskim. It appears to me that there is no question at all because since he says he intends to release her from his levirate bond and says he does not want to take her, and he allows her to remove his shoe and spit before him in front of the court, he is performing the mitzvah like any proper Jew. What is this comparable to? It is like one who divorces his wife. Should we say he does not intend to release her with this get? Certainly not. Since he gives her the get and says, 'This is your get,' and commands the scribe to write it for her sake, we do not say that in his heart he imagines the opposite. Why should chalitzah be any different from a get? It is not comparable to the case where a scribe writes a get without intention because in that case, since during the entire writing of the get he must intend it for her sake, we do not trust him. But when he is the one divorcing and commands the scribe to write it for her sake, we say that at the time of his command, he resolved in his heart accordingly. The same applies to chalitzah, where the intention is only required at the time of the act. Moreover, do we really require the one performing the chalitzah to intend for the sake of Heaven specifically? The intention of the mitzvah is considered when he intends with this act to release her from his levirate bond, and this even the one who turns around intends. Otherwise, who compels him to do this?

Even though without the intention of both parties the act is not valid, nevertheless, if he had the intention and she did not, or she had the intention and he did not, it is considered an invalid chalitzah, and she is disqualified from yibbum with him and with all the brothers. However, if neither of them had the intention, it appears from the language of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) that it is considered nothing. Therefore, if a yevamah (widow bound to marry her deceased husband's brother) who has matured among the brothers, and we saw that she removed the shoe of one of them, she is forbidden to undergo yibbum because we are concerned that there might have been an intention for chalitzah. Hence, she requires a valid chalitzah to permit her to marry others. But as long as we have not seen her remove the shoe of one of them, she is permitted to undergo yibbum, and we do not worry that she has performed chalitzah. Even if she removed the shoe privately, still, in terms of disqualifying her from yibbum, it is effective even if done privately (Rambam, Chapter 4).

Know that from the discussions in the Talmud (102b), it seems to me that according to one view, even if one of them did not have the proper intention, the act is invalidated. For it is stated there: a yevama who has matured, etc., we do not worry that she might have performed the ritual of chalitza with the sandal of one of them.
