The Talmud questions: the reason is that we did not see [the act], but if we did see it, do we indeed worry? Yet it was taught in a Baraita: whether... until both intend. The Talmud resolves: this means that even if we saw it, we do not worry that they had the proper intention. And there is another opinion that the reason is that we did not see it, but if we did see it, we do worry. And when it is taught that intention is required, this is to permit her to the general public, but regarding the brothers, it is invalid. 

And according to this version, even without any intention, it is invalidated. Therefore, Rambam, Tur, and Shulchan Aruch, who ruled according to this version, that according to the first opinion, even if we saw it, we do not worry, then how did they derive that the intention of one of them is necessary? Furthermore, one could challenge the wording of Rambam and Tur/Shulchan Aruch, who wrote that if we saw her remove the shoe of one of them, she is forbidden to perform yibbum, lest they had the intention for chalitza. This implies that we worry that both had the intention, which is not in accordance with any opinion: not with the first view that we do not worry, and not with the second view that even without intention, it is invalid.

And it is clear to me that they had a different version in the Gemara, as proven by the Maggid Mishneh who copied the Talmud in this language from the Rif. When it asks from the Baraita, it answers: "These words are to permit her to the world, but to the brothers, she is invalidated," and it does not read "and it teaches that intention is required." According to this version, the explanation is that knowing for certain that both intended is required to permit her to the general public, but for invalidating her to the brothers, she is invalid even if we do not know for certain, as we suspect that perhaps they intended. However, according to our version, this can also be explained, although the language is somewhat strained. And this is clarified from Rashi's explanation, who writes: "And some say the reason is because we did not see that she performed chalitza, but if we saw that she did, we suspect that perhaps they intended, and she is invalidated to them." This means that the invalidation is only because we suspect that they might have intended. According to our explanation that to permit her to the general public, we need to know for certain that both intended, there is proof from the words of Tosafot, who write: "From the fact that it states 'until both intend together,' it implies that we need to know that they are intending for chalitza." This is explicitly as we explained. 

It was asked here why she is invalid even without intention, and it was answered that this was stated for the sake of completeness, but in truth, she is invalid even without intention. Alternatively, it can be said that the invalidation is because we suspect that there was intention, but if she also did not intend, she is not invalidated. Maharil Nach expressed surprise about this in his glosses on the Tur, and the Bach also struggled with this. It is clear as we stated, and the Rosh explicitly writes that if it is known that both did not intend, she is not invalidated. This also seems to be the opinion of the Beit Shmuel in subsection 145, and the Nimukei Yosef writes that from a legal standpoint, she is not invalidated without both intending, but only because of the appearance, she is invalidated by her intention alone. This is also written by the Shiltei Giborim, and it is difficult to understand his source. Therefore, what is stated in section 67, that she is invalidated by the intention of one of them, has no foundation except according to the words of the Nimukei Yosef. Therefore, this requires further investigation, as from all the poskim it is clear that if we know for certain that one of them did not intend, it means nothing.

And all this applies to the removal of the shoe by one of the yevamim (brothers-in-law). However, regarding spitting and reciting before them, Rambam does not mention anything about this. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 45, write that if she spat before the yavam (brother-in-law) in front of a court, she is forbidden to undergo levirate marriage. However, this is specifically when she spat saliva, but if she spat blood before him, she is not disqualified by this unless there is saliva mixed with it (even according to those who permit the act of spitting blood alone during the chalitzah). If she only recited the declaration, she is not disqualified from levirate marriage. And they divided this law into three distinctions: regarding the removal of the shoe, she is disqualified even if she removed it in private if there is suspicion of intent. For recitation, she is not disqualified in any situation. For spitting, if she spat before him in front of a court, she is disqualified; if not in front of a court, she is not disqualified. None of this is explained in the Gemara, but the logic is as follows: if we say that she is disqualified by spitting even in private, life would not be manageable since people naturally spit, and this is not an apparent act at all. But in front of a court, it is considered an obvious act. Recitation, even in front of a court, is nothing since it is not an act at all. However, the removal of the shoe is a significant act, and it is not customary to remove someone else's shoe; therefore, there is suspicion in any situation when there is concern for intent. And this is the consensus of all the authorities.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 46: "There are those who say that one should be cautious that the yevama (widow) does not spit before the yavam (brother-in-law) prior to the halitza (ceremonial removal of the shoe), so that the halitza does not become invalid and she would need to repeat the process with all the brothers." End quote. This is an excessive stringency, for what relevance does an invalid halitza have when they are involved in the procedure of halitza? And if it is because she spit before the removal of the shoe, it has already been clarified that the order is not crucial. Furthermore, the Shela (Shnei Luchot HaBrit) already expressed displeasure with this in section 23. Nevertheless, the custom is that she refrains from spitting until the judges instruct her to do so.

The Sages said (Kiddushin 6a) that a conditional chalitza is valid. What is an example of a conditional chalitza? If they said to him, "Perform the chalitza on the condition that she gives you 200 zuz," the chalitza is valid even if she gives him nothing. Even if the condition was repeated, and even if he said to her at the time of the chalitza, "On the condition that you do not marry another man," and repeated his condition, it is still nothing. The reasoning is that, by law, no condition should invalidate the act, but we learn from the sons of Gad and Reuben that a condition, if made in accordance with the law, can invalidate the act if the condition is not fulfilled. However, we only learn from them about conditions that can be fulfilled through an agent, similar to the condition of the sons of Gad and Reuben, where a matter of money can be fulfilled through an agent. Similarly, in the context of divorce and betrothal, one can betroth and divorce through an agent, and betrothal through intercourse, even though it cannot be fulfilled through an agent, is compared to other forms of betrothal (Ketubot 74a). Since a person has complete control over the matter and can do it through an agent, he also has the power to attach a condition to it (Tosafot there). However, chalitza, which cannot be done through an agent, as one cannot tell his agent to take money from her and perform the chalitza for her with witnesses, therefore, there is no power of condition in chalitza, and the condition does not invalidate the act of chalitza, even if the condition is not fulfilled. And although chalitza requires intent to release her, it is certainly the case that he intended to release her completely; he merely thought to prohibit her based on the condition of 200 zuz or that she should not marry another man. But the condition does not apply here, and he did not prohibit her due to the chalitza but due to the condition (Beit David and Beit Shmuel).

And one should not ask why she is ultimately exempt from the money. Granted that the condition does not impede the chalitzah itself, nevertheless, she should be obligated to give him the money because she agreed to it. The true reason she is exempt from the money is because she can claim that she was merely deceiving him, as she is not intrinsically obligated to give him money. She was compelled to promise in order to allow her to remarry. Since this does not obstruct the chalitzah process, she is also not obligated to give him the money according to monetary law. This is similar to a case where someone needs to cross a ferry and the ferry owner refuses to take him unless he promises a hundred coins. He can say that he was deceiving him and is only liable for the usual fare, as stated in Choshen Mishpat 264. The same applies here. In the case of chalitzah, there is no standard fee, as he is religiously obligated to perform the chalitzah. Therefore, she is completely exempt.

And since the reason is because of this, therefore she is exempt only when according to Torah law he was obligated to perform Halitza. But when he could have performed Yibbum according to Torah law, and he agreed to perform Halitza because of monetary considerations, although the Halitza is valid, nevertheless she is obligated to pay him his fee, like any other hired worker, because he lost the opportunity for Yibbum because of her. And this obligation is not from the law of conditions, but like any other hired worker. 

I am uncertain whether we assess what she should pay him or according to his stipulation, for he could say, "To me it is worth this much, as I stipulated." And from the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 50, it implies that we assess, and from the language of the Nimukei Yosef it implies that she gives according to the condition. See there. Therefore, if there is a valid claim that she does not desire him, such as he is not suitable for her, she is exempt from anything, and similarly in other such cases.

According to this, in our countries where Yibbum is not allowed, it would seem that in all cases she is exempt. However, from the language of the poskim it does not imply this, and the reasoning is that since the Torah gave him the option to perform Yibbum, he can say, "I desire Yibbum."

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: "But if she gave him the money or deposited the money with a third party, she cannot retract." This is the end of the quotation from Choshen Mishpat, section 264. The issue of the third party holding the money is not mentioned there; however, we have already explained in section 18, based on the Mordechai in the chapter "HaCholitz," that if she handed over the money to the third party in his presence and told the third party, "When he performs the chalitzah for me, give him the money," the third party is obligated to give it to him because he has already acquired it in the presence of all three. But if they did not explicitly speak about this three-party arrangement, and he simply said, "I will not perform the chalitzah for you until you deposit such-and-such amount with so-and-so," and she deposited it, this is nothing, as he has not acquired it. And even if she gave a promissory note and accepted it through a formal acquisition, it is nothing (as is evident in the responsa of the Rashba, section 1040).

They told him, "Perform chalitzah for her, and thus you will marry her," because he was ignorant of the law, or they told him, "Perform chalitzah for her, for this is a mitzvah, but you won't lose anything, as if you want to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) afterwards, you may do so," and similar statements that misled him—this chalitzah does not permit her to marry others. This is not comparable to the previous case where he intended to permit her to others but mistakenly thought he would receive money; in this case, he did not intend to permit her to others, and a chalitzah without intent, as has been explained, does not permit her to marry others. However, she is disqualified from yibbum through this chalitzah. Therefore, we compel him by all means to release her afterward with a proper chalitzah. The rule is that in any case where she is disqualified from yibbum, we must compel him to release her properly according to Torah law with an appropriate chalitzah.

It is clear that just as a get (divorce document) must be given willingly and a declared protest invalidates it, as stated in Siman 134, so too with chalitzah (the ceremony releasing a widow from levirate marriage). The manner of nullifying a protest in chalitzah will be explained in the order of chalitzah. In a situation where the Sages said that one is compelled in chalitzah, it means to force him until he says "I am willing," just like with a get. If he declared a protest about the chalitzah and did not nullify the protest at the time of the chalitzah, the chalitzah is invalid, and another chalitzah is required. This has all the laws of invalid chalitzot, and the law of a forced chalitzah by Jews or by non-Jewish courts is the same as the law of a forced get, which was explained there that they compel him to comply with the Jewish courts.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef (Rabbi Yosef Karo), wrote in section 52: "If they told him, 'This woman does not want you through yibbum (levirate marriage), but rather perform chalitzah for her and remove her bond, and she will marry you through marriage,' there is an opinion that says that her chalitzah is valid." End quote. This is also explained in the Jerusalem Talmud. The reason is that even though he was mistaken in thinking that he would marry her afterwards, nevertheless, in this chalitzah, he intended to remove her bond and permit her, and what do we care about his mistake in thinking he would marry her afterwards? Nevertheless, there are those who disagree with this, and this appears to be the opinion of the Rambam (Maimonides). There is no proof from the Jerusalem Talmud, as there is a dispute there about this. It could also be said that they indeed compelled him to later give a valid chalitzah, and the Jerusalem Talmud was brief about this. However, the Rashba ruled in accordance with the Shulchan Aruch.

The law of an invalid Chalitzah is as follows: it invalidates her from marrying any of the brothers through Yibbum, it disqualifies her for the priesthood, and prohibits her from marrying his relatives. The reason is that this Chalitzah is still considered a Chalitzah. Therefore, in all these cases, its law is like that of a valid Chalitzah, except that she is not permitted to marry anyone else until a valid Chalitzah is performed for her. And these are the words of the Rambam in Chapter 4, Law 26: "In any case where we said that it is not a Chalitzah, or that he did nothing, or that it is nothing, it is as if she had not received Chalitzah from him, and his relatives are not prohibited to her, and she is not disqualified from marrying a priest, and she is permitted to marry one of the brothers through Yibbum. And in any case where we said her Chalitzah is invalid, his relatives are prohibited to her, etc., and she is not permitted to marry a stranger until a valid Chalitzah is performed for her. If she transgressed and married, he performs a valid Chalitzah for her while she is under her husband, and we do not remove her from him." End quote. Since she has already been prohibited to him, why should we take her away from her husband for no reason? Nevertheless, we separate her from her husband until the Yavam performs Chalitzah for her. And know that this general rule laid out by the Rambam should not be applied to the expressions of other decisors, just as the general rule concerning a get—expressions of "invalid" and "void"—should not be applied as written in Siman 150. See there.

After she has performed the chalitzah, the court writes her a chalitzah document as proof that she is permitted to remarry. If the court did not write it for her, two other individuals can write it, even if they do not recognize the brother-in-law or the sister-in-law, because the court would not have performed the chalitzah if they did not recognize them. We have already explained in section 15 that there is some slight uncertainty about this matter. The document needs to be lined because it includes statements made by the brother-in-law and the sister-in-law. This is the format of the chalitzah document as written by the Rambam and the Tur (we do not follow the practice of writing a chalitzah document as mentioned in the order of chalitzah. Note that we did not write the explanation of the order of chalitzah in the Shulchan Aruch because we have already explained everything in the main text).

On such-and-such day of such-and-such month in such-and-such year from the creation of the world according to our counting here in such-and-such place, we, the judges, some of whom have signed below, were sitting as a court of three together, and before us came such-and-such daughter of such-and-such, widow of such-and-such son of such-and-such. And a man named Ploni Almoni was brought before us, and she said to us: "This Ploni Almoni is the brother of my deceased husband from the same father, whom I was married to, and he has passed away, leaving no children to inherit or continue his name in Israel. This Ploni Almoni, his brother, is obligated to perform levirate marriage (yibbum) with me."

Now the judges said to him: "If you wish to perform levirate marriage with her, do so; if not, remove your right shoe before us and perform the rite of halitzah." And she made known that this Ploni Almoni is indeed the brother from the same father of her deceased husband. We said to him: "If you wish to perform levirate marriage with her, do so; if not, remove your right shoe before us and perform the rite of halitzah."

He answered and said: "I do not wish to perform levirate marriage with her." Immediately, she called out: "My brother-in-law refuses to establish a name for his brother in Israel; he does not want to marry me." And we called him and he said: "I do not wish to take her." And she removed his right shoe, and spat before him, with the spittle visible to us on the ground. Then she recited: "Thus shall be done to the man who does not build up his brother's house, and his name shall be called in Israel 'the house of the removed shoe.'" We, the judges, and all who were present, called him "the removed shoe" three times.

After this act was done before us, we permitted this woman to marry any man she desires, and no one shall protest against her from this day onward forever. She requested from us this document of halitzah, and we wrote it, signed it, and gave it to her for her benefit and as proof according to the law of Moses and Israel.

And the three judges sign, and she does not need to wait three months and is permitted to marry immediately.

The Ba'al Halachot Gedolot wrote: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Moses, "Tell the yavam (levirate husband) that if he does not wish to perform yibbum (levirate marriage), he is rejecting the mitzvah due to the frailty of his body. Therefore, he should remove his shoe like a mourner or an excommunicated person who customarily goes barefoot. With the foul drop that is in his body, he could have established offspring for his brother. Therefore, she spits in front of him a foul drop, and the judges respond three times, 'Remove the shoe like a mourner, remove the shoe like an excommunicated one, remove the shoe like a rebel against the commandments of Sinai.'"

In the name of Rabbeinu Yechiel of Paris, it is found that the woman wails in front of the court, saying that her husband will be like one who is dead without offspring, and the yavam responds, 'I do not wish to take her,' meaning he does not care if he remains without offspring. From then, she removes his shoe to tell him to mourn his brother, for from now on he is like one who is dead, and he will be forgotten since he does not establish offspring for him. She spits in front of him, meaning to say, 'It was not because of your beauty that I desired you,' and she calls him thus to embarrass him for not performing yibbum. Also, those standing there call out three times, 'Remove the shoe,' to publicize his shame.

Law of a Get and Maamar in Yevamah, and a Get after a Get, as well as Maamar. Containing 35 sections:
Even though, according to the Torah, a get (divorce document) does not affect a yevamah (a widow bound to her brother-in-law) since only chalitzah (a formal release ceremony) permits her to marry others, nevertheless, the Sages decreed that any get which disqualifies a wife from marrying a kohen (priest) similarly affects a yevamah. If one of the brothers gives her a get, it disqualifies her and her co-wives from him and all the brothers from performing yibum (levirate marriage), and she is not permitted to marry others until chalitzah is performed for her. The reason for this enactment is that the Sages were concerned that if they allowed yibum after a get, people might come to perform yibum even after chalitzah, reasoning that just as a get releases a woman from her husband, chalitzah releases a yevamah from the yavam (brother-in-law). They might think that just as she is permitted after a get, she is permitted after chalitzah, and then perform yibum after chalitzah (Yevamot 50b), which is prohibited by the commandment "he shall not build" (Deuteronomy 25:9).

And similarly, the betrothal (ma'amar) in the case of a yevama (a widow awaiting levirate marriage) is considered as betrothal through money, even though according to Torah law it does not effectuate anything at all, as it is written, "Her brother-in-law shall come unto her and take her to him as wife" (Deuteronomy 25:5), and thus, cohabitation completes the levirate marriage, and money and a document do not complete it (Kiddushin 14a). Nevertheless, the Sages stated that ma'amar is effective in this regard: if one of the brothers performs ma'amar, she becomes prohibited to all the other brothers, and none of the brothers can consummate the levirate marriage with her except the one who performed the ma'amar. Similarly, if multiple co-wives fall before him (the yavam) and he performs ma'amar with one of them, he disqualifies all the co-wives from himself, as he cannot consummate the levirate marriage with any other except the one with whom he performed ma'amar. The reason for this is that the Sages were concerned that if they permit another brother to perform the levirate marriage or allow him to consummate the marriage with another co-wife, the brothers might come to perform levirate marriages even after the first one divorces her, or to consummate with another co-wife after performing levirate marriage with this one, because they might say that just as betrothal (kiddushin) is a form of acquisition and cohabitation is also a form of acquisition, there might be a permission after betrothal just as there is a permission after cohabitation. However, the Torah states that one brother performs the levirate marriage, not two, and one house is built, not two houses.

And if he wishes to release her after the ma'amar (betrothal), she requires a get (bill of divorce) and chalitzah (ceremonial release), a get for the ma'amar and chalitzah for the bond. He should first give the get and then perform chalitzah (Rambam and Ra'avad in Chapter 3, Mishnah 5). The reason is because the Torah states that after chalitzah she is permitted to marry outside (the family), but here, after chalitzah, she is still forbidden due to the ma'amar. Therefore, the get precedes the chalitzah. However, after the fact, if chalitzah was performed before the get, it is acceptable, because according to Torah law, she is indeed permitted after chalitzah. But ideally, it is not proper for there to be an impediment after chalitzah, and therefore the poskim (decisors) did not mention this ruling. This matter is clarified in Rashi's commentary (27a, s.v. chalatz l’ba’alat ma’amar).

And since the "ma'amar" (the formal declaration of intent to perform levirate marriage) does not establish a complete acquisition, and a "get" (bill of divorce) does not effect a complete rejection, for the acquisition by "ma'amar" and the rejection by "get" are only by rabbinic enactment due to a decree, as stated, therefore, any action performed after the "ma'amar" or after the "get" is effective for some matter, as will be explained. They are not like yibbum (levirate marriage) and chalitzah (ceremonial release from levirate marriage), after which no further actions have any effect. Consequently, a "get" after a "get" and a "ma'amar" after a "ma'amar" are effective, as are a "get" and chalitzah and cohabitation after a "ma'amar," and a "ma'amar" and cohabitation and chalitzah after a "get," whether with one levir and two yevamot, or with one yevamah and two levirim, or with two yevamot and two levirim, as will be explained. We do not say that all the power of the "ma'amar" was established at the first instance, and all the rejection power of the "get" was established at the first instance, and there is no further power in another "get" after a "get" or another "ma'amar" after a "ma'amar." On the contrary, since this is only by rabbinic decree, they instituted that each levir from the brothers of the deceased has power in the act of his "get" and his "ma'amar," and similarly for each yevamah (Talmud, there).

How is a "get after a get" defined? If a yavam (levirate husband) gives a get (divorce document) to his yevama (levirate widow) and then gives a get to her co-wife, he becomes prohibited to the relatives of both women. This is because they become like the relatives of his divorcee, who are forbidden to him as if he had given a get to two of his own wives. Similarly, if two yevamim (levirate husbands) give a get to one yevama, one after the other, both become prohibited to her relatives. This is because she is considered divorced from both of them; even after the first one's divorce, she remains bound to them and is not permitted to marry someone from outside (the family). Therefore, the second get is like the first get. Likewise, if there are two yevamim and two yevamot (levirate widows), and each one gives a get to one of the women, each man becomes prohibited to the relatives of the woman to whom he gave the get. If both men give a get to both women, then both men are forbidden to the relatives of both women. (It is obvious that, according to the opinion which will be explained, that a disqualified chalitza [levirate release] requires chalitza from all the brothers, in any case, all are forbidden to her relatives due to the chalitza.)

And our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 5 as follows: "And when they come to perform the chalitzah, according to the opinion that a disqualified chalitzah requires repetition with all the brothers, in the case of two yevamim (brothers-in-law) and one yevamah (sister-in-law), she needs chalitzah from each one. And there is one who says that the same applies to one yavam (brother-in-law) and two yevamot (sisters-in-law), where he gave a get (divorce document) to both, he must perform chalitzah with both. According to the opinion that a disqualified chalitzah does not require repetition with all the brothers, even in the case of two yevamim and one yevamah, one chalitzah is sufficient. And this is the opinion of the Rosh, of blessed memory. The matter of a disqualified chalitzah requiring repetition refers to when she was fully bound (to the brothers) and became disqualified because her bond was weakened. But a disqualified chalitzah from the outset does not require repetition." End of quote.

Explanation of the matter: There is a discussion regarding an invalid chalitzah and its explanation, and there is a disagreement among the authorities regarding the definition of an invalid chalitzah. According to Rashi, of blessed memory (26b), any chalitzah where the yavam (levir) is unable to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) is considered an invalid chalitzah because its power is diminished. Therefore, she must approach all the brothers, and none of them can release her with such a diminished chalitzah. This applies in the case of two yevamim (levirs). However, in the case of one yavam and two yevamot (levirate widows), he performs chalitzah with one of them, and the other is exempted (this is evident from Rashi's commentary on the Mishnah of Rabbi Gamliel (50a) and in the Gemara there, see there). For what would be added by the chalitzah of the second one, since all his power was given to the first one? However, if the chalitzah of one is better than the other, he should not perform chalitzah with the second one but with the one whose chalitzah is better, such as in a case of two yevamot and the yavam gave a get (bill of divorce) to one of them. Her chalitzah does not exempt her co-wife because her bond was weakened by the get (27a, s.v. "leb'alat ha-get"). But when he performs chalitzah with the co-wife, the one who received the get is exempt, and although she is forbidden to the yavam, even the co-wife, her chalitzah is better than that of the one who received the get. And in a case where they are equally diminished, such as one received a get and one he performed ma'amar (betrothal-like act) with (27a, s.v. "ki hadadei"), he may perform chalitzah with whichever he prefers. And certainly, when both received a get or both received ma'amar (what the Tosafot questioned on Rashi from "machzir gerushato," that the co-wife is exempted by her chalitzah in the first chapter (11a), it can be simply said that in the case of "machzir gerushato," the Torah increased the significance of chalitzah, as the Beit Shmuel wrote in Siman 174, Se'if Katan 4, see there).

And the opinion of our Rabbis, the Ba'alei HaTosafot, is that a deficient chalitzah is only termed as such when it damages or weakens the bond, such as when a get (bill of divorce) is given, or ma'amar (betrothal) is performed, or if she is the sister of his zikkukah (the woman bound to him by levirate bond) or the sister of his chalutzah (a woman who underwent chalitzah with him). But the fact that he cannot perform yibum (levirate marriage) does not classify it as a deficient chalitzah, since the bond remains intact (Tosafot Yevamot 11a s.v. "Or" and Yevamot 20a s.v. "And chalitzah"). Contrary to this, the Tosafot hold that even when there is one yavam (levir) and two yevamot (levirate widows), and the chalitzah is deficient, he must perform chalitzah with both of them (Yevamot 50a s.v. "Need"), as there is not enough strength in one of them to exempt the other through such an inferior chalitzah. There is an established principle in the Gemara that this concept of deficient chalitzah does not exempt concerning the co-wife, but regarding herself, she is exempted by any form of chalitzah (Yevamot 27a and another explanation). This will be explained in this section.

And regarding the main law in this matter, the Rosh wrote (Chapter 3, Section 2) that from the words of Tosafot, it appears that the halacha is that a deficient chalitza does not need to be repeated with all the brothers. This is also the opinion of the Raavad, who holds that this is also the opinion of the Rif (there). However, when there are two yevamot (widowed sisters-in-law) and the chalitza of one of them is more valid than the other, even though hers is also not completely perfect, we still prefer the more valid chalitza. This is specifically the case initially, but after the fact (b'dieved), if the inferior one performed the chalitza, it is valid for herself. It only disqualifies regarding her co-wife, but not for herself (as explained in the "Ibai'it Eima," and so too is written by the Kesef Mishneh there, section 4, in the opinion of the Raavad according to the Rif, see there). This is also the opinion of the Rashba (beginning of Chapter 3), who wrote that this is also the conclusion of the Jerusalem Talmud, see there (and according to our version of the Jerusalem Talmud, at the beginning of Chapter 3, Rav's opinion is that it does not need to be repeated with all the brothers, and Shmuel's opinion is that it does, contrary to our Talmud. The conclusion of the Jerusalem Talmud is the opposite, but the Rashba's version there is like our Talmud, see there and investigate thoroughly).

However, the opinion of the Ramban, the Ra'ah, and other great early authorities, as well as the Rif, is that a defective chalitzah requires repeating with all the brothers. Similarly, if there is one yavam and two yevamot, he must perform chalitzah with both. This applies when both chalitzot are of equal status. However, if one of them is superior to the other, even if it is still defective—for example, if two sisters fall before him from two brothers and each sister has a co-wife—since it is prohibited to perform yibbum with either the sisters or the co-wives due to the prohibition of "sisters of one's wife" in a state of zika, the sisters are more severe than the co-wives because zika is not strong enough to render the co-wife like an erva herself (Talmud). Therefore, if he performs chalitzah with the sisters, the co-wives are not exempt; if he performs chalitzah with the co-wives, the sisters are exempt. Similarly, in all such cases. The Rambam has a different approach in all of this, as will be explained with God's help.

And with this, all the matters of the Shulchan Aruch have been clarified. In the explanation of an invalid chalitzah, they decided according to the opinion of Tosafot. Practically, they wrote two opinions without deciding between them. And in the case of one yavam and two yevamot, if both need chalitzah in the case of an invalid chalitzah, it appears their opinion is that it is not necessary. They brought someone who holds that it is necessary in the name of "there are those who say." Therefore, in all the laws in this chapter, they concluded that the chalitzah of one of them exempts the other. Only in section 7 did they bring this opinion also in the name of "there are those who say," as will be explained to us with the help of Heaven (and this is also what is implied by the Beit Shmuel, subsection 7, see there).

And know that in the Jerusalem Talmud there, they attribute the dispute regarding a disqualified chalitzah (levirate shoe removal ceremony) — whether it requires all the brothers or not — to the reasoning behind chalitzah: whether chalitzah constitutes acquisition or exemption. See there. The explanation of "exemption" is straightforward: through chalitzah, she is released from the bond (zika). In the explanation of "acquisition," the commentators of the Jerusalem Talmud write that it is as if she is acquired through this chalitzah. This does not seem correct to me, for what kind of acquisition is this? On the contrary, she is separated from him. Therefore, it seems to me that it refers to the yevama (widow bound by levirate marriage) who acquires herself from his authority — which he had over her — to her own authority. This is like the language of the early Mishnah in Kiddushin where it states "she acquires herself through chalitzah and the death of the yavam (levir)." According to our version of the Jerusalem Talmud, one who holds that she requires chalitzah from each one believes that chalitzah constitutes exemption, and one who holds that it is not required believes that chalitzah constitutes acquisition. The explanation is as follows: if it is merely exemption, though she is released from him, she is not released from the other yevamim (brothers) with such a deficient chalitzah and requires exemption from them as well. But if chalitzah is acquisition, since she acquires herself to her own authority, she is entirely free and exempt from all of them.

However, the Rashba reverses the version, as he wrote, and it should be explained as follows: if chalitzah is acquisition, since it is a deficient chalitzah, the acquisition is not strong and can only grant her a partial acquisition, requiring chalitzah from all the brothers. This is unlike if chalitzah is merely exemption, meaning he removes himself from her, it is known that removal from property is easier than acquisition, as a weak expression like "no claim or argument" suffices, as explained in the end of the first chapter of Ketubot. Therefore, she does not require chalitzah from all the brothers, as his removal alone exempts her from all of them. According to this, since in our version the reasoning is reversed from that of the Rashba, even though in our Talmud it appears in many places that chalitzah constitutes exemption, we cannot decisively rule based on this reasoning, as it can be reversed in either direction (as mentioned above).

And according to the Rambam, of blessed memory, there is another opinion on this matter, and these are his words in Chapter 5, Law 9: "The intercourse that the yavam (levir) performs with his yevama (levirate widow), whether initially or after having performed ma'amar (a form of betrothal) with her, and nothing else preceded it, is called valid intercourse. But if ma'amar from his brother preceded it, or a get (divorce document) either from him or his brother, whether with her or her co-wife, or if ma'amar with her co-wife from either him or his brother preceded it, it is called invalid intercourse. The chalitza (formal release) that the yavam performs with his yevama initially, if nothing else preceded it, is called an excellent chalitza. But if a get or ma'amar preceded it, whether from this yavam or another yavam, whether with her or her co-wife, it is called a deficient chalitza. Multiple yevamot (levirate widows) coming from one household, once one of them has valid intercourse or performed an excellent chalitza, all are permitted (to marry others), and the bond of yibum (levirate marriage) is removed from them. But if one of them had invalid intercourse or received an invalid ma'amar, they are all forbidden to yibum, and the one who had intercourse or received the ma'amar requires a get, and each requires chalitza to permit them to others, for the bond of yibum is not removed by invalid intercourse. If one of them had a deficient chalitza, she is permitted to marry others, but her co-wife is forbidden until she too performs chalitza, or until all the brothers perform chalitza with the first one who had the deficient chalitza, for a deficient chalitza does not remove the bond of yibum from this household until all the brothers perform chalitza, or each one performs chalitza." And in Chapter 7, Law 9, he wrote: "Three brothers, two of whom are married to two sisters, and each of them has a co-wife, and the brothers married to the sisters died, and the sisters and their co-wives fell before the yavam. If he performs chalitza with the co-wives, the sisters are exempt. But if he performs chalitza with the sisters, their co-wives are not exempt until the co-wives perform chalitza, because the chalitza of the sisters is not an excellent chalitza, and a deficient chalitza does not exempt the co-wife as we have explained. And it seems to me that this is the law with two yevamot coming from one household, and one of them is forbidden to her yavam because of a secondary prohibition or a positive commandment. If he performs chalitza with the forbidden one, her co-wife is not exempt. If he performs chalitza with the co-wife, the forbidden one is permitted." End of quote.

And all the commentators have already wondered about his words, for it seems from his words that he rules that a defective chalitzah must be performed by all the brothers. If so, how does he rule that when he performs chalitzah for the co-wives, the sisters are exempt? After all, the chalitzah for the co-wives is also a defective chalitzah. Moreover, from where does he derive this idea that a defective chalitzah, just as there is an ordinance that all the brothers must perform chalitzah for her, so too there is an ordinance that he must perform chalitzah for all the yevamot, and then there is no need for chalitzah from all the brothers? And from where does he derive that when chalitzah is performed for all the yevamot, the co-wives are also exempt? And furthermore, we find this ruling problematic, as this law that if he performs chalitzah for the sisters, the co-wives are not exempt, but if he performs chalitzah for the co-wives, the sisters are exempt, is a saying of Shmuel in the Gemara (27a). And it also says there that if he performs chalitzah for the one who received the get, the co-wife is not exempt; if he performs chalitzah for the co-wife, the one who received the get is exempt. If he performs chalitzah for the one who received the ma'amar, the co-wife is not exempt; if he performs chalitzah for the co-wife, the one who received the ma'amar is exempt. See there. And why is there a distinction in these laws? (And the Ra'avad remains with a difficulty, and the Lechem Mishneh exerted much effort on this, and see Beit Shmuel, section 14, and the Gra, section 47).

In my humble opinion, it appears that Maimonides holds that the rule that a defective chalitzah (ceremony of removing the shoe) requires repetition by all the brothers applies when the defect is due to an action by one of the yevamim (brothers obligated to perform levirate marriage), such as when one of them gave a get (divorce document) to one of the yevamot (widowed sisters-in-law) or performed a ma'amar (betrothal act). But if the chalitzah was originally a defective chalitzah not due to an action, its status is not like a defective chalitzah except in the sense that the most distinguished one among the brothers should perform the chalitzah, even if this most distinguished one is also performing a defective chalitzah (this is similar to the reasoning of the Tosafot in Section 8). Maimonides also holds that since we follow the ruling that a defective chalitzah releases the woman with regard to herself (as the Rif wrote), it follows that if this yavam (brother) gave a chalitzah to all the yevamot, they are all released, because each one is released by her own chalitzah. Consequently, it is necessary to say that if all the brothers gave a chalitzah to one of the yevamot, they are all released. Otherwise, how would we ever find a situation where a defective chalitzah requires repetition by all the brothers, since a defective chalitzah releases with regard to the woman herself, as mentioned? Therefore, it is certain that this applies with regard to the co-wives; when she received a chalitzah from all of them, each of the brothers performed the chalitzah, and they are all released by this. This is why the Sages did not say that a defective chalitzah requires each yevamah to receive a chalitzah, as this would have no significance since each one received a chalitzah. Maimonides holds that the rule that a defective chalitzah requires repetition by all the brothers is an established law with no disagreement, except regarding the interpretation of this matter.

Let us clarify our discussion. In the Gemara, there is a dispute between Rav and Shmuel. According to Rav, in all cases, she must go back to all the brothers, while Shmuel holds that in all cases she does not need to go back (since he equates sisters and co-wives with the case of a woman with a get and her co-wife, and a woman with ma'amar and her co-wife, as discussed there). According to the general principles of the Talmud, the halacha follows Rav in matters of prohibition. Nevertheless, the Geonim ruled according to Shmuel, as the Rif writes, and their reasoning is as the Rosh explains there, because Rabbi Yochanan holds like him (Yevamot 27: If the second one dies, the first one is permitted).

Therefore, the Rambam holds that we do not rule like Shmuel except in the case of sisters and co-wives, because in this Rabbi Yochanan agrees with him. However, in cases that involve an action, such as a get or ma'amar, we hold like Rav that she must go back to all the brothers. And even though Rav does not explicitly discuss this, it is a fortiori from the case of sisters, as explained. And there is proof for this from the Talmud's general statement (Yevamot 26:), which says that it is a defective chalitza, and a defective chalitza requires her to go back to all the brothers, as explained there. This implies that this is indeed the law. Additionally, in chapter 3 (Yevamot 51:), the Talmud questions this ruling, saying, "Let this be a refutation, etc.," and responds that defective chalitza requires her to go back to all the brothers, as explained there. This implies that this is indeed the law.

Moreover, earlier, the Talmud first establishes the ruling according to Shmuel and then also establishes that defective chalitza requires her to go back to all the brothers, as explained there. This implies that both rulings can be upheld, and they do not contradict each other. Therefore, it seems to the Rambam to rule partly like Shmuel and partly like Rav. There is also proof from the Talmud's effort (Yevamot 27:) to find a distinction between sisters and co-wives according to the opinion that there is a zika bond, and Rav Ashi concludes that the zika bond is not strong enough to render the co-wife like an ervah, as explained there.

This certainly only applies to sisters and co-wives because with sisters there is a Torah prohibition. But in the case of a woman with a get and a woman with ma'amar, what difference is there between them and their co-wives? According to Torah law, a get and a ma'amar are nothing, and according to rabbinic law, since he gave a get to one, the co-wife is also forbidden, and similarly, when he performed ma'amar with one, the co-wife is also forbidden. Therefore, what difference does it make between them and their co-wives?

Therefore, the Rambam correctly ruled that one of them does not exempt her companion, unlike with sisters and co-wives, where the co-wives are preferable to the sisters. (In the Rif, it is impossible to say this because he copied all of Shmuel's words, as explained there. Perhaps, for the halacha, he also intended to rule only regarding sisters according to Shmuel, and this requires further investigation.)

And just as there is a concept of a subsequent divorce (get) after a previous divorce, so too there is a concept of a subsequent levirate betrothal (ma'amar) after a previous levirate betrothal. If he performed a ma'amar with this one and a ma'amar with that one, both require a get and chalitzah, but only one needs chalitzah. According to those who hold that in the case of two yevamot (widows awaiting levirate marriage) and one yavam (levir), both must perform chalitzah, just as in the case of two yevamim (levirs) and one yevamah (widow), he must perform chalitzah with both. Similarly, there is a concept of a subsequent ma'amar in the case of two yevamim and one yevamah. If one performed a ma'amar with her and then the second did so, she requires a get from both and chalitzah from both, unless according to the opinion that a levirate bond (chalitzah) considered invalid (psulah) must be repeated with all the brothers, then one chalitzah from one of them suffices. Also, in the case of two yevamim and two yevamot, if one performed a ma'amar with one and the other with the second, each needs a get from the one who performed the ma'amar with her and both require chalitzah. It is better that each perform chalitzah with the one who did not perform the ma'amar with her.

And similarly, an action can invalidate another engagement, such as if he performed a "ma'amar" (betrothal by levirate marriage) with her and then gave her a bill of divorce (get) or performed the rite of chalitzah (releasing her from levirate marriage), or if the second brother gave her a bill of divorce or performed chalitzah with her, or had relations with her, or if he or the second brother gave a bill of divorce to the co-wife of the woman with the ma'amar or performed chalitzah with her or had relations with her, the action taken after the ma'amar is effective in prohibiting the woman with the ma'amar to all the brothers, and they are prohibited from marrying her close relatives. She needs a bill of divorce from the ma'amar or from the relations that occurred after the ma'amar that the second brother had with her. Similarly, for the co-wife, if they performed a ma'amar after her ma'amar, or if they had relations with the co-wife after the ma'amar of this woman, the co-wife also needs a bill of divorce. And just as this is the process of permitting them to marry outside, so it is.

If she herself had another action performed upon her after the ma'amar (betrothal), she requires chalitzah (a form of divorce in the context of levirate marriage) from all the brothers. Additionally, all the co-wives also require chalitzah according to those who hold this view regarding an invalid chalitzah, as mentioned. Moreover, for the chalitzah, she also needs a get (divorce document) for the ma'amar. It has already been explained that ideally, the get should precede the chalitzah, but after the fact, there is no obstruction if it doesn't, as mentioned in section 3.

If the second brother comes upon her after the ma'amar of the first, she requires a get from both of them. If he comes upon the co-wife after making a ma'amar with this one, both require a get from him. Similarly, if the brother comes upon the co-wife, the co-wife requires a get from the brother. Likewise, if they performed a ma'amar with the co-wife, the co-wife requires a get.

If to one he performed a ma'amar and to another he gave a get, both require chalitzah, or one of them according to the opinions that have been explained. The same law applies if one performed a ma'amar with one and the second gave a get to the other.

And similarly, if the initial act was a get (divorce document), any subsequent act performed after the get is effective. For example, if after the get he had relations with her, or performed ma'amar (a form of betrothal in levirate marriage) with her, or if his brother had relations with her or performed ma'amar with her, or if he or his brother had relations with the co-wife or performed ma'amar with her, whatever is done after the get is effective to prohibit her close relatives and to require a get for the one who received the ma'amar or had relations with her. And what is the remedy to permit them to the general public? This is how: when he performed ma'amar or had relations with her after the get, she requires a get and chalitzah (ceremony releasing a widow from levirate marriage) from one of the brothers or from all the brothers. Similarly, all the co-wives require chalitzah, and this is according to the opinions that have been explained. And if he or his brother performed ma'amar with the co-wife after the get, or had relations with the co-wife, the co-wife requires a get and chalitzah from one of them or from all of them, or from all of them according to the opinions that have been explained. And similarly, if he performed chalitzah with the co-wife after the get, both of them are prohibited to their close relatives. And similarly, his brother who performed chalitzah with the one who received the get or with the co-wife, the one who received the get is prohibited to the one who gave the get and the one who received the chalitzah is prohibited to the one who gave the chalitzah. But if he himself performed chalitzah with the one who received the get, no additional act has been added here, because from the time of the get he is already prohibited to her close relatives, and this has the status of an invalid chalitzah as has been explained.

However, if the initial act was consummation (yibbum) or chalitzah, nothing else is needed afterward. Since this is the commandment of the Torah, and with this act, the bond (zika) with the entire household is removed, what use would any subsequent act be? Any actions performed with the other wives of the deceased are like actions done with a foreign woman. Consequently, it is understood that only the act of a get (divorce) or chalitzah has no benefit, but the act of consummation or ma'amar (a form of betrothal) creates a situation where a get is necessary for the one who received the ma'amar or was consummated with, since even with an ordinary woman this requires a get. Furthermore, if the one who performed yibbum with one wife subsequently consummates with her co-wife, she needs a get. Similarly, if he gave her a ma'amar, since betrothal takes effect with her, and certainly if he performed chalitzah with one and then performed ma'amar or consummated with her, she needs a get, because betrothal takes effect with a chalutzah. However, if he performed yibbum with her and then gave her a ma'amar, it is nothing because she is already his wife. Likewise, if the brother gave a ma'amar to the one he was supposed to perform yibbum with, it is nothing because betrothal does not take effect with a married woman, and even if he consummated with her, it is considered merely an act of fornication. But if he consummated with the co-wife or gave her a ma'amar, she needs a get. Similarly, if the brother gave a ma'amar to the chalutzah or consummated with her, she needs a get.

And even though consummation (bi'ah) and the act of releasing (chalitzah) are equal in terms of the actions that follow them, this is only when no action preceded the consummation or release. For then, no action taken afterward is effective, as we have written. However, if an action precedes the consummation or release, then chalitzah is not equal to bi'ah when an action is performed afterward. This means that in the case of bi'ah, when an action like a divorce document (get) or a declaration of intent (ma'amar) precedes the consummation but is not related to the woman with whom the consummation occurred, it is called an invalid consummation and any action taken after the consummation is effective. But in the case of chalitzah, even if an action like a get or ma'amar precedes the release and it is called an invalid release, nonetheless, no action taken after the release is effective, for the reason that will be explained in section 24 (the action that is effective after consummation is only chalitzah, and pay close attention).

Therefore, if he gives a get (divorce document) to one and has relations with another, or performs ma'amar (a form of betrothal) with one and has relations with another, the subsequent actions are effective. If he or his brother then performs chalitzah (a ceremony to release the widow from levirate marriage) with a third woman, they become prohibited to her relatives, and the one he had relations with does not suffice with just a get like any other yevamah (widow awaiting levirate marriage), but she needs both a get and chalitzah. If the prior action was a ma'amar, the one with the ma'amar also needs a get. Thus, the Sages taught in the Mishnah (Yevamot 50a): "If he gave a get and then had relations, she needs both a get and chalitzah, etc. If he performed ma'amar with one and had relations with another, they need two gittin (plural of get) and chalitzah." And whether they are all exempt with one chalitzah and one yavam (levir) depends on the opinions discussed. However, with chalitzah alone, it is not so. For example, if he gave a get to one and then performed chalitzah for her or another, and afterward he or his brother gave chalitzah to another, he is not prohibited from the relatives of the other. Similarly, if his brother gave chalitzah to the first one, he is not prohibited from her relatives. And if he performed ma'amar and then chalitzah, no subsequent chalitzah is effective, and it is as if it never happened. But if he performed ma'amar or had relations, whether he or his brother, whether with the one who had chalitzah or another, she needs a get, for this is also the case with any other woman, as it is stated.

And the reason for the matter is as follows, and so it is stated in the Gemara (50b): "And why did the Rabbis say that an invalid cohabitation still has an effect?" They said, if cohabitation follows a get (divorce document), it is a decree because of cohabitation after chalitzah (ceremony releasing a widow from levirate marriage). Meaning, if you say that a get alone is sufficient, people will come to cohabit even after chalitzah, because in the eyes of the public, a get and chalitzah are equivalent. Therefore, they made a distinction that the get invalidates the cohabitation and chalitzah is also required. And if cohabitation follows ma'amar (betrothal by the brother-in-law), it is a decree because of cohabitation after ma'amar, meaning that if we say that chalitzah is not needed when ma'amar is done with one and cohabitation with another, people will say that it is permissible to cohabit with one and then cohabit with another, since in the eyes of the public, ma'amar and cohabitation are equivalent. Therefore, they decreed that chalitzah is still required for recognition that the ma'amar invalidates the cohabitation. And since after cohabitation chalitzah is required, any action after cohabitation is effective because it is still before the release, and therefore the action is effective. But with chalitzah in such a case, we are not concerned, because there is no decree that chalitzah after a get requires another chalitzah, as they will not say, just as chalitzah after a get is effective, so too chalitzah after chalitzah is effective, and they will come to perform chalitzah for a second woman after performing chalitzah for the first woman. What does it matter to us? Is there any prohibition in performing chalitzah? Similarly, with chalitzah after ma'amar, there is no decree because of chalitzah after cohabitation, meaning they will not say, just as chalitzah after ma'amar is effective to release, so too chalitzah after cohabitation is effective, that if someone cohabits with his yevamah (levirate widow), he can release her with chalitzah and not with a get. It is obvious that they will not say so, since we require a get for ma'amar, and it is obvious that they will require a get after cohabitation, and we will not come to any error. Therefore, any action is not effective after chalitzah, because with chalitzah the matter is completed.

The statement of "Yebamin" has already been explained as being rabbinic, for according to Torah law, betrothal does not work for a yevama (a widow awaiting levirate marriage) except through intercourse, and the sages instituted that a ma'amar (betrothal declaration) would require a get (divorce document). There is no difference whether he said to her "Be betrothed to me" in a general manner or if he said to her "Be betrothed to me through the levirate bond," she requires a get for the ma'amar. However, regarding a ma'amar after chalitza (ceremonial release from levirate marriage), which we said requires a get, for indeed, even with a regular woman when he betroths her, she requires a get, and even though she is forbidden to him by a negative commandment, the betrothal is still effective for those bound by negative commandments. It would seem logically that only when he betroths her in a general manner does she require a get, but if he said to her "Be betrothed to me through the levirate bond," a get is not required, for the bond has already been nullified through chalitza. Indeed, this is the opinion of the Raavad and Ramban of blessed memory. However, the Rif of blessed memory ruled (in the third chapter) that even if he said to her "Be betrothed to me through the levirate bond," she requires a get, and so ruled the Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch in section 13. This is by rabbinic decree, for just as they instituted that such a ma'amar takes effect with a yevama before chalitza, so too they instituted after chalitza. If he said "Be betrothed to me" in a general manner, the betrothal is effective by Torah law, for betrothal is effective for those bound by negative commandments. If he said "through the levirate bond," it is effective by rabbinic decree (Beit Shmuel section 9). Even if he performed an invalid chalitza, the betrothal is not effective by Torah law (ibid.). Even according to the opinion that an invalid chalitza requires repeating with all the brothers, if he betrothed her through the levirate bond with the brother who has not yet performed chalitza, the betrothal is not effective by Torah law (ibid.), for by Torah law, there is no need to repeat with all the brothers.

Based on what was explained, that a divorce document (get) is effective after a statement of intent (ma'amar), as mentioned in Section 18, if the divorce document is given by the one who performed the ma'amar to the woman involved in the ma'amar, there is a difference between one type of get and another. If he gave her a get for his bond (zika) to her, meaning he did not give her a get for the ma'amar he performed with her but rather for the yibbum bond, under his mistaken belief that the get would dissolve the bond, she becomes invalidated to him and to all the brothers, and she requires a get for the ma'amar and a chalitzah for the bond, according to the laws explained there. Similarly, if he gave her a get without specifying, it is as if he specified it was for the bond. However, if he gave her the get explicitly for the ma'amar, meaning he clearly stated that he is divorcing her with this get for the ma'amar he performed with her, then the ma'amar is nullified by this get, and she remains bound as she was before. Nonetheless, she is only permitted to the other brothers and not to him, and the co-wife is permitted to him as well (as explained in the Nimukei Yosef on Chapter 3, under the entry "Amar Rava"). However, she herself is forbidden to him because he performed an action with her (there). Some say she is also permitted to him, and even according to this opinion, it is only permitted after the fact (b'dieved), but initially (l'chatchila) it is forbidden because we decree a get given for a ma'amar due to a get given for a bond (as explained in Tosafot 32b, under the entry "Get," and the main ruling is in Chapter 3, 52b, where we follow Rava and not Rav Chanania, and in Rashi there under the entry "or perhaps," it is explained that she is forbidden to him, not like some say there).

It has already been explained that the yavam (brother-in-law performing levirate marriage) must be thirteen years and one day old. A minor does not have the power to perform either yibum (levirate marriage) or chalitza (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage). Certainly, he also cannot perform ma'amar (a formal declaration of intent to marry the yevama) or give a get (divorce document), and his actions are considered null. Nevertheless, if he cohabits with the yevama when he is capable of intercourse, meaning when he is nine years and one day old, the sages considered his intercourse as equivalent to the ma'amar of an adult. Therefore, if he cohabits with the yevama, he disqualifies her from all the brothers, and she can only be rectified through chalitza or by waiting until he matures and performs yibum with her. If, after he has cohabited with her, his older brother then cohabits with her or her co-wife, or performs ma'amar, or gives a get, or performs chalitza to either her or her co-wife, she becomes prohibited to the minor. Similarly, if the minor again cohabits with her co-wife, or if his brother, who is nine years and one day old, cohabits with her or her co-wife, she becomes prohibited to him, just as in the case of ma'amar following ma'amar. She can only be released through chalitza with the adult, and her status is like that of a chalitza that was improperly performed. It should be noted that this intercourse by a nine-year-old is effective even after the adult has performed some action with her, unlike the minor's ma'amar, as will be explained.

And even though the statement of a minor is of no consequence, nevertheless, the Sages said (there) that if the statement of this nine-year-old boy precedes the first act of the yevama (the widow who is subject to levirate marriage), his statement is effective in disqualifying her for the brothers. It is not like the statement of an adult, which is effective in all matters even after some act, as explained. The reason is simple: the act of consummation (bi'ah), which is a significant act, was decreed by the Sages to be effective even if it is not the first act. This is not the case with a statement (ma'amar), which even for an adult is only rabbinic. Moreover, the betrothal (kiddushin) of a minor is of no consequence, except that since she is bound to him, they gave some power to his statement from the day he is fit for consummation. This power suffices when it is at the beginning and not after an act.

Therefore, if the older brother performed ma'amar (a formal betrothal) and subsequently this nine-year-old boy performed ma'amar with her or her co-wife, his ma'amar does not invalidate her for the older brother, and the older brother is permitted to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) with her. However, if the nine-year-old boy initially performed ma'amar and then his brother, who is also nine years old and one day, performed ma'amar with her or her co-wife, it could be said that the second brother's ma'amar invalidates her for the first brother. Since both are nine-year-olds, the first does not have more power than the second. A get (divorce document) and chalitzah (a ceremony releasing from yibbum) are entirely ineffective for a minor, whether at the beginning or later, because his actions are meaningless. The Sages only decreed regarding ma'amar because it is akin to cohabitation. Therefore, in some respects, they likened it to cohabitation, and it is effective when it is the initial act, as stated. A child younger than nine years old has no legal cohabitation, and certainly, his ma'amar is meaningless. The cohabitation of a deaf-mute or a mentally impaired person is considered complete cohabitation, as taught in the Tosefta Yevamot (Chapter 11), and it will be further explained in Siman 172. The cohabitation of a saris chamah (a man who is naturally impotent) appears to me to be like the cohabitation of a minor, and this requires further study. It has already been explained in Siman 167 that a minor who cohabits with his yevamah (levirate widow) cannot release her with a get until he grows up and cohabits with her again; then he can release her with a get. If he did not cohabit with her after he grew up, she requires both a get and chalitzah, as explained there. Similarly, it is explained there that a minor yevamah who is three years and one day old, who is suitable for cohabitation, if an adult yavam (levir) cohabits with her, he acquires her. If a minor yavam cohabits with her, they must grow up together, as explained there.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 17: A man who performed Ma'amar (a form of betrothal) with his yevama (sister-in-law) or gave her a get (a bill of divorce), and she has a co-wife, when he comes to perform chalitzah (a ritual to release her from the obligation of levirate marriage) with one of them to permit them, the chalitzah of the one who received the get or the Ma'amar does not release her co-wife. However, the chalitzah of the co-wife releases the one who received the get completely, and for the one who received the Ma'amar, it releases her from the chalitzah, but she still needs a get for the Ma'amar. If he performed Ma'amar with one and gave a get to the other, he may perform chalitzah with whichever one he chooses, and this releases the second one, as has been explained. And there are other opinions among the poskim (decisors), and we have already explained this in the laws from Section 6 to Section 17.

Additionally, it is written in paragraph 18: If two yevamot (levirate widows) from one household fall before him, one of whom is forbidden to him (by law) and the other permitted, when he performs yibbum (levirate marriage), he should marry the permitted one. When he performs chalitzah (the ceremonial release), he should release the forbidden one. There is an opinion that if he performs chalitzah on the forbidden one, the co-wife is not permitted. If he performs chalitzah on the co-wife, the forbidden one becomes permitted. And there are those who believe that both require chalitzah (see the commentary of the Gaon of Vilna, note 144). This has also been clarified in our previous discussions, as stated in the previous paragraph, and will be further elucidated in chapter 174, with God's help.

It is further written in Section 19: "Many widows that come from one household, once one of them has been cohabited with in a valid manner, or if a valid chalitzah has been performed, all are permitted, and the levirate bond is removed from them. But if one of them was cohabited with in an invalid manner, or if an invalid ma'amar was given to her, all are forbidden to perform yibbum, and the one who was cohabited with or given a ma'amar requires a get, and each one of them requires chalitzah to permit her to marry someone else, as the levirate bond is not removed by an invalid cohabitation. If one of them performed an invalid chalitzah, the one who performed the chalitzah is permitted to marry outside, but her co-wife is forbidden until she also performs chalitzah or until all the brothers perform chalitzah for the first one who performed the invalid chalitzah, as an invalid chalitzah does not remove the levirate bond from this household until it is repeated with all the brothers or until each one performs chalitzah. This is the opinion of the Rambam, and it is disputed, as explained in the words of the Tur." End quote. "We have already explained the opinion of the disputants, and we have also clarified the opinion of the Rambam with God's help, and we have resolved the objections raised against him" (see the lengthy discussion in Avnei Shoham, note 14, which brings the version of the Tur regarding the Rambam, but the version of the Maggid is primary).

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 5, Law 17: Two levirs who perform levirate marriage (yibbum) on two women who come from the same household, and it is not known who performed the marriage first—both must give a get (divorce document) and are permitted to others but prohibited to the levirs. Therefore, if Reuben had two wives, one in Akko and one in Tzor, and his brothers Shimon and Levi, one in Akko and one in Tzor, and they heard that Reuben died, neither of them should perform yibbum until it is known what the other brother did. If one of them proceeded and performed yibbum, we do not force him to release her until it is known that his brother performed yibbum first. If one wants to perform chalitzah (the ritual of releasing from levirate marriage) before knowing what his brother did, we do not prevent him. This is the end of the quotation.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, copied this in Shulchan Aruch, section 20, but omitted what was said that one should not prevent him from performing chalitzah. This is because in his book, the Kesef Mishneh raised a difficulty: Why is this different from a woman whose husband went overseas and her co-wife remained abroad, where she is forbidden to perform chalitzah because perhaps her co-wife is pregnant and exempt from chalitzah, and thus she would require a proclamation for the priesthood, as is stated at the end of section 156 (and the Lechem Mishneh raised the same difficulty). One could say that according to the Rambam, there is no need to be concerned about this, for it is forbidden to perform yibbum until it is known what the other did, and therefore there is no need to be concerned about this (Beit Shmuel, section 15). However, still, there is a concern that perhaps the other performed chalitzah first and his chalitzah is invalid, and thus she would require a proclamation for the priesthood (ibid). Therefore, one could say that this concern exists only there because it is possible to ascertain whether the co-wife is pregnant or not, but here, it is never possible to verify because even if the second has not yet performed yibbum or chalitzah, perhaps tomorrow he will perform chalitzah or yibbum, and thus the woman here would remain an agunah (chained woman) all her life. Therefore, they did not worry about this (Maggid Mishneh). Nevertheless, it is not clear because what relevance does agunah have; they can inform each other who will perform chalitzah or yibbum. Therefore, it seems to me that the concern of requiring a proclamation for the priesthood was only considered in a very common matter, as it is customary that every woman conceives from her husband, but for another concern, they did not worry about this (and there is some proof from what Tosafot wrote in Yevamot 119a, s.v. Rabbi Meir, etc., or perhaps it does not depend on an action but comes naturally that a man engages with his wife, end quote).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in his major work in the name of the Gaonic responsa that in the case of two yevamim (levirs) who performed yibbum (levirate marriage) with two yevamot (levirate widows), they must divorce them, and one of them also requires chalitzah (ritual release from levirate marriage). This is because perhaps one of them performed maamar (betrothal in levirate marriage) with one of the widows, and afterward his brother consummated marriage with the other widow, making it a case of intercourse after maamar. And even if the brother who performed maamar subsequently consummated with the first widow, it is still considered invalid intercourse. However, in the Shulchan Aruch, this matter is not mentioned. It can be said that his (the author's) opinion is that since the primary law of maamar is rabbinic, we do not need to be overly concerned with this doubt, as it is a case of doubt in a rabbinic matter, where we are lenient. This is also implied by the Rambam of blessed memory.

The Law of Two Yevamot: a Minor and a Deaf-Mute, or Both Equal. Containing Twelve Sections:
It has already been explained that if there are two yevamot from the same household, one performs yibum (levirate marriage) or chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from yibum) with one of them, and the co-wife is also exempt. If he subsequently performs any act with the co-wife, it is considered nothing, and it is as if he did an act with a foreign woman. The same law applies when a man leaves two wives, both of whom were married to him in rabbinic marriages, such as two minor orphans who were married by their mothers or brothers, or two deaf-mutes. For a minor orphan and a deaf-mute do not have marriages according to Torah law, but only rabbinic law instituted marriages for them so that they would not be treated as ownerless, as stated in Siman 43 and 44. They are not subject to chalitzah, as stated in Siman 169. However, the yavam has the option to perform yibum with one of them. A deaf-mute has no other remedy except yibum, and a minor can wait until she grows up and becomes eligible for chalitzah. When a man leaves two minors or two deaf-mutes and the yavam performs yibum with one of them, the second is also exempt. If he or his brother subsequently performs yibum with the second, it does not invalidate the first yibum, because the status of both is equal. Thus, the sages taught (Yevamot 111a): If a man was married to two minor orphans and died, and the yavam performs yibum with the first and then with the second, or his brother performs yibum with the second, it does not invalidate the first yibum. The same applies to two deaf-mutes. It is forbidden for him to maintain the second wife, and she requires a get (divorce), for even with adult women a get would be required, as stated in the previous Siman, and certainly with minors and deaf-mutes, where the original bond is very weak. The Rambam in Chapter 5, Law 26 wrote regarding a minor that she should be taught to refuse (miyun) so that the first wife can be maintained. The Tur and Shulchan Aruch, Section 5, also wrote this, intending that she would not be disqualified from marrying a Kohen because of the get. The Gra (Commentary 8) raised an objection, stating that this only applies to an adult and a minor, but this is not necessarily conclusive. The Maggid Mishneh agreed with this interpretation.

If a man leaves two wives, one an adult and one a minor orphan, or one competent and one deaf, the consummation of the marriage (yibbum) or the ceremony of release (chalitzah) with the adult or competent wife exempts the younger or deaf wife. However, the consummation of the marriage with the minor does not exempt the adult, nor does the consummation with the deaf wife exempt the competent one (Yevamot 110a). The reason is clear: how can a marriage valid only by rabbinic decree exempt one that is biblically valid? If, after consummating the marriage with the adult wife, he or his brother then consummates with the minor wife, the minor wife requires a get (divorce document). According to Maimonides, we instruct the minor to refuse him. 

In the case of a competent and a deaf wife, if he consummates the marriage with the competent wife and then he or his brother consummates with the deaf wife, according to Maimonides, she also requires a get since a deaf wife cannot refuse. Although the consummation with the adult or competent wife already removes the bond, it has already been explained that there can be a second consummation even with two adult and competent wives, necessitating a get if the second consummation was intended as marriage or yibbum (Yevamot). The marriage or consummation is effective, even more so when the second wife is a minor or deaf whose bond is not fully complete, and the marriage or consummation is effective. If he intended the consummation for licentiousness, it means nothing. It seems to me that the same law applies to two minors or two deaf wives, as explained in the first section.

If the yavam initially cohabits with the deaf-mute woman and then he or his brother subsequently cohabits with the fully competent woman, he invalidates the deaf-mute woman. This is because a bond (zika) from Torah law invalidates a bond from rabbinic law. Therefore, the deaf-mute woman must be released with a get (divorce document). However, the fully competent woman is also forbidden to him because, in any case, the deaf-mute woman preceded her, making it like two women from one household. Therefore, the fully competent woman must also be released with a get. Yet, she is still not fully released from the bond because a previous incomplete cohabitation took place, which is considered a defective cohabitation. Therefore, after the get for the fully competent woman, she also requires chalitza (ceremonial release) to permit her to marry someone else.

However, in the case of a minor and an adult woman, if the man initially engages with the minor and then either he or his brother subsequently engages with the adult woman, we do not need to prohibit the adult woman, because there is a remedy to annul the engagement with the minor through refusal (mi'un), making it as though he had never engaged with her at all.
