Therefore, we instruct the minor to refuse him, and the adult woman can remain with him or his brother. This is not considered as if he had engaged with her in a complete manner because the refusal annuls even complete rabbinic betrothal and marriage, and certainly if she is a yevama (a widow awaiting levirate marriage). However, this remedy cannot be applied to a deaf-mute and a fully competent woman, because a deaf-mute is not subject to refusal, as refusal was only instituted for a minor orphan.

There is a doubt according to the Rambam regarding two minor girls when one had sexual relations with him, and then he or his brother had relations with the second one. Does the second one require refusal (mi'un) as it is written, if there is a way for the first one to refuse and the second one to remain with him or with his brother? From a logical perspective, it would seem permissible because refusal completely nullifies the act. However, from the wording of the Rambam, it does not imply this. Otherwise, he would have said that one of them should refuse. It can be said that the reason is that we do not allow the second one to use the remedy of refusal, as it was done in a forbidden manner, and we only permit the first one because her act was permissible, not the second one. This also seems to be the implication from the wording of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 5. See there and what is written in Section 11.

If the deceased left two wives, one a minor and one a deaf-mute, there is a different ruling in this case. And even though both marriages are rabbinic, they are not comparable to each other. The reason is explained in the Gemara (Yevamot 110b) that the bond (zika) of the deaf-mute is partially acquired and partially reserved, whereas the bond of the minor is uncertain—either it is fully acquired or not acquired at all.

To elaborate: although both marriages are rabbinic, their acquisitions are not identical. The marriage of the minor is conditional until she grows up and does not refuse (miyun). If she does not refuse, it retroactively reveals that she was completely acquired. If she does refuse, her acquisition is entirely nullified. However, the deaf-mute is bound to her husband forever, as she cannot refuse. If her husband does not wish to divorce her, she remains his wife like any other woman. Yet, her acquisition is not complete because she will never reach full mental capacity, and it is likely that she is not fully acceptable to him.

In contrast, the minor will eventually reach full mental capacity. Therefore, their bonds are not equal. The bond of the deaf-mute is somewhat certain but not complete because her acquisition is partially reserved. The bond of the minor, however, could be fully binding if she does not refuse, making her bond stronger than that of the deaf-mute. The intercourse (bi'ah) of the deaf-mute does not release the minor or she might not be bound at all if she refuses, making the bond of the deaf-mute stronger, and the intercourse of the minor does not release her.

If both were eligible for chalitza (the ritual release from levirate marriage), the ruling would be straightforward that both should perform chalitza. However, the deaf-mute is not eligible for chalitza at all, and her rectification is only through yibbum (levirate marriage). Similarly, the minor is not eligible for chalitza while she is still a minor, only when she grows up. It is impossible to marry both of them because it is forbidden to build two houses from one (i.e., to marry two women who were married to the same deceased man). And it is impossible to marry one of them because the other is not released by the intercourse of this one.

And it is stated in the Gemara there that there are two solutions to this issue: one, Rav said that he should marry the deaf woman and divorce her with a get, and the minor should wait until she grows up and then perform chalitzah. He cannot marry her now since he has already married the deaf woman, and he also cannot keep the deaf woman when the minor grows up, as when he performs chalitzah with her, the deaf woman will be invalidated because "he shall not build" applies, since the intercourse with the deaf woman did not exempt her, as we have written. Therefore, for the time being, he should perform yibbum with the deaf woman, and if the minor grows up and performs chalitzah, he should then divorce her. There is also another solution, as we have written regarding an adult and a minor: when he first has relations with the minor, we teach the minor to refuse, and the adult becomes permitted, as we have written in section 4. Similarly, here we can do the same, teach the minor to refuse, and he can perform yibbum with the deaf woman without needing to divorce her.

The Rif and the Rambam indeed ruled that a minor can refuse (mi'un) and a deaf-mute can perform Yibbum. If he wishes to divorce her afterward, he divorces her and she is permitted to marry others. However, the Ra'avad ruled according to the decree of Rav that the deaf-mute should perform Yibbum and then divorce her, and the minor should perform Chalitzah when she grows up. His reasoning is that the decree of mi'un was established only to fulfill the mitzvah of Yibbum, which is a Torah obligation, as in the case of a minor and an adult woman mentioned in Section 4, where Yibbum is a Torah obligation for the adult woman. But regarding the decree for the deaf-mute, which is not from the Torah, it is sufficient to fulfill the rabbinic mitzvah of Yibbum with the first intercourse or until the minor grows up. We do not need to resort to mi'un for her, as it is preferable to avoid mi'un (Yevamot 109). The Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, Section 1, ruled according to the Rif and the Rambam that certainly if he wishes to divorce her, no one will prevent him. But if he does not wish to divorce her, why should we not establish a decree for this unfortunate woman? This is certainly also a mitzvah. Furthermore, the reasoning to avoid mi'un, as the Sages said, is that she might regret it when she grows up. Here, there is no such concern, as she is ultimately forbidden to him and she will separate through Chalitzah (Ramban). Therefore, the decree of mi'un is preferable.

And the Rambam, of blessed memory, wrote (there): If the yavam first had relations with the minor and then he or his brother had relations with the deaf-mute, he did not invalidate the minor, and the deaf-mute requires a get (divorce document) because intercourse with the minor is superior to intercourse with the deaf-mute, since the minor will become fit over time. Therefore, he should maintain the minor who was first engaged in intercourse. End quote. His words are clear because intercourse with the deaf-mute does not invalidate the minor for him, since the minor is either entirely obligated (for yibbum) or not obligated at all, as we have said. Therefore, in whatever way you look at it, if she is entirely obligated, she is preferable to the deaf-mute, and intercourse with the deaf-mute does not prohibit her, as we have said. And if she is not obligated at all, she is like a stranger and does not belong to this household. This is also the version in the Mishnah in Yevamot (111b): If the yavam had relations with the minor and then went and had relations with the deaf-mute, he did not invalidate (the minor). And when he wrote that intercourse with the minor is superior, his intention was to say that it is not only if she is not fully acquired that it is obvious she is like a stranger and permitted, but even if she is acquired, she is preferable to the deaf-mute. For if she is acquired, her acquisition is complete, as we have said. And the reason is that after she grows up, if she does not refuse (the marriage), she will have full mental capacity, which is not the case with the deaf-mute (and this resolves the question of the Lechem Mishneh, see there).

However, the version according to Rashi of blessed memory, as well as the version according to Tosafot and the Raavad of blessed memory, is that if he first had relations with the minor and afterward with the deaf-mute, he invalidates the minor. They explained the reason being that perhaps he first had relations with the deaf-mute and then with the minor, and the minor certainly invalidates the deaf-mute. For if she (the minor) is entirely bound (in levirate marriage), she takes precedence over the deaf-mute who is only somewhat bound. And perhaps she (the minor) is entirely bound and pushes aside the deaf-mute so that there should not be two women from one house (in levirate marriage). Therefore, they decreed as well in the case where he first had relations with the minor and afterward with the deaf-mute, that the deaf-mute also invalidates her. And in the Shulchan Aruch, only the opinion of the Rambam is brought.

If he first had relations with the deaf-mute woman and then he or his brother had relations with the minor, the Rambam wrote that the deaf-mute woman is disqualified, and we instruct the minor to refuse, and the deaf-mute woman leaves with a get (divorce document). And the disqualification of the deaf-mute woman, we have explained the reason. Also, the refusal of the minor follows his opinion as we have written. The refusal is so that she does not need to wait until she grows up to perform chalitzah (a ceremony to release a widow from marrying her deceased husband's brother). However, what he wrote that the deaf-mute woman leaves with a get, his words are puzzling. Why should she leave with a get? After all, the refusal uproots the connection retroactively, as he himself wrote regarding two minors. The Rashba has already questioned him on this (and the Kesef Mishneh mentioned it and left it as a question). It seems to me that the Rambam's opinion is that when he first had relations it was completely permissible, so we dismiss the prohibition of two houses based on the refusal. This is different when his initial relations were not according to the law; he should have made sure the minor refused before he had relations with the deaf-mute woman. Moreover, from the moment he had relations with the minor, the deaf-mute woman became prohibited. Since she was prohibited even for a moment, she cannot return to being permissible. The proof for this is from what he wrote in Section 5 regarding two minors, where the second one does not return to being permissible based on the refusal of the first one. The words of the Tur are very puzzling, as the Yam Shel Shlomo wrote in the second chapter of Bava Kamma, section 23.

It appears to me that in all the laws clarified regarding minors, if they have reached maturity by the time of yibbum (levirate marriage), we follow the status at the time of their falling into yibbum. If the minor has matured in the meantime, then there is no option for refusal (mi'un) because, in her adulthood, she cannot refuse as stated in Siman 155. Therefore, it is necessary to judge according to the status at the time of falling into yibbum, whether for permissibility or prohibition. Similarly, if a deaf-mute becomes capable of hearing and speaking by the time of yibbum, we judge according to the status at the time of falling, and they are then eligible for chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the brother-in-law from yibbum).

The law concerning a eunuch, a deaf-mute, an imbecile, a hermaphrodite, and an ailonit (a woman who does not develop signs of puberty). It contains twenty-nine sections.

A eunuch is not subject to yibbum (levirate marriage) or chalitzah (the ceremony of releasing the widow from levirate marriage), whether the yavam (the brother-in-law) is a eunuch or the deceased was a eunuch. This matter is explicit in the Torah, as it is written "to establish a name for his brother," and a eunuch is not capable of establishing a name. Therefore, when the yavam is a eunuch, he is not subject to yibbum, and since he is not fit for yibbum, he is also not subject to chalitzah. This is the tradition received from the Sages: anyone who is not eligible for yibbum is not eligible for chalitzah, as it is written, "And if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife, then his brother's wife shall go up to the gate, etc." This implies that if he desires, he performs yibbum. Therefore, anyone eligible for yibbum is eligible for chalitzah, and anyone not eligible for yibbum is not eligible for chalitzah (Yevamot 20). Similarly, when the deceased was a eunuch, his wife is not subject to yibbum, as it is written, "And his name shall not be blotted out from Israel," excluding someone whose name is already blotted out (Rashi on Yevamot 79b). Consequently, his wives do not require chalitzah either, as mentioned. Likewise, an ailonit is not subject to yibbum because she is incapable of bearing children and thus cannot establish a name. Therefore, she is also not subject to chalitzah, as mentioned, since chalitzah is dependent on yibbum.

Not only are they exempt from chalitzah and yibbum, but there is even a karet prohibition in yibbum when they are unfit for it, as the prohibition of a brother's wife, which carries karet, remains upon them. Therefore, a eunuch who has relations with his brother's wife does not require a get from her, and if there is another brother, his intercourse and chalitzah do not exempt her. The other brother must perform chalitzah for her, and regarding yibbum, it seems that it is forbidden to perform yibbum with her since the eunuch had a disqualifying intercourse with her, making her unfit for yibbum. Alternatively, it is possible that since he is entirely unfit for yibbum, it is like general promiscuous intercourse and does not disqualify her from yibbum. The same law applies to an aylonit (a woman who is unable to have children). If she has a co-wife, the co-wife should perform yibbum or chalitzah. Similarly, if the deceased was a eunuch, and his brother has relations with his wife, he is liable for karet, as she is a brother's wife not in the context of a mitzvah.

Similarly, their chalitzah (ritual of removing a shoe to release a widow from levirate marriage) is of no consequence. If a eunuch performs chalitzah for his brother's wife, she does not become disqualified from marrying a kohen (priest). Likewise, if chalitzah is performed for the wife of a eunuch, she does not become disqualified from marrying a kohen. Similarly, a definite aylonit (a woman who cannot bear children) who undergoes chalitzah, it is of no consequence, and she may marry a kohen who has fulfilled the commandment of procreation (see Mishnah 61a). This applies to a definite eunuch and a definite aylonit. However, if there is doubt whether he is a eunuch or she is an aylonit, they perform chalitzah and not yibum (levirate marriage), and their chalitzah disqualifies her from marrying a kohen. It is not relevant to say that since they are not subject to yibum, they are not subject to chalitzah, for due to the doubt, they are forbidden in yibum, and perhaps they are subject to yibum by law, and it is like any case of doubt in prohibition of intercourse. Therefore, they are obligated in chalitzah by law.

The Sages said (79b) that there is a eunuch who is subject to chalitzah, and thus the Sages taught in the Mishnah there: A human-made eunuch performs chalitzah and chalitzah is performed for his wife because he had a time of fitness. A natural eunuch does not perform chalitzah nor is chalitzah performed for his wife because he did not have a time of fitness. Therefore, what has been clarified regarding a eunuch is about a natural eunuch and not a human-made eunuch. And what is a natural eunuch? One who was born this way from his mother's womb. A human-made eunuch is one who became a eunuch later, and his testicles were cut by human hands or other organs of the reproductive system that prevent procreation. This is the "wounded in the stones" mentioned in the Torah, who is forbidden to enter the congregation of Israel, and his laws are explained in Siman 5. Therefore, the Sages said he performs chalitzah and chalitzah is performed for his wife, but they did not say he performs yibbum because although from the essence of the law of yibbum he is permitted and obligated to perform yibbum and is considered a yibbum candidate, there is another prohibition on the woman who is not permitted to marry him. Therefore, if this eunuch cohabits with her, he acquires her by the law of yibbum and then divorces her with a get because it is forbidden to keep her. If she is a convert who is permitted to marry a wounded in the stones, he performs yibbum with her from the outset, and she becomes his wife. Similarly, when the deceased was a human-made eunuch, yibbum or chalitzah is performed for his wife because his brother is permitted to her (and what was taught "and chalitzah is performed for his wife" is incidental to "he performs chalitzah," and understand this well).

It turns out that the prohibition of disqualification from the congregation, as explained in Siman 5, is the opposite of the prohibition of levirate marriage. In the case of disqualification from the congregation, only a eunuch made by man (i.e., someone who was castrated) is prohibited, but a naturally born eunuch (i.e., someone born without the ability to procreate) is not prohibited, as stated there. However, in the matter of levirate marriage, it is the opposite: a eunuch made by man is eligible for levirate marriage, whereas a naturally born eunuch is not eligible. The reasoning is that the Torah only prohibits entering the congregation for someone who has undergone an act that prevents procreation, as it is written, "He with crushed testicles or severed member shall not enter the assembly of the Lord" (Deuteronomy 23:2) because it disrupts the settlement of the world. This does not apply to someone born this way or who became so by divine intervention, as stated there, because he did not perform an act on his own body. But regarding levirate marriage, it must be that the Torah’s concern is that the yavam (levir) should be capable of establishing a name [for his deceased brother], meaning from birth he should be fit to establish a name and not someone who was later disqualified. Otherwise, the mitzvah of levirate marriage would never be applicable, for if we were to say that the brother who became disqualified is not fit for levirate marriage, then also the deceased who became disqualified would render his wife unfit for levirate marriage, as it is written, "so that his name is not blotted out of Israel" (Deuteronomy 25:6). There is no person whose procreative power has not diminished before his death due to suffering, so how would you ever find a case of levirate marriage? Rather, it is certain that the Torah only concerns itself with the state at birth. Similarly, with the brother performing the levirate marriage, we do not worry about what happened to him afterwards (as Rava intended when he said, "Otherwise, you would never find a woman [eligible for levirate marriage]," and see Rashi there and examine it closely).

And one might ask, ultimately, a castrated man is prohibited from levirate marriage (yibbum) due to the prohibition of being unfit for the congregation. Therefore, he is not eligible for yibbum, and consequently, he should also not perform chalitzah. The answer to this, it seems to me, is like what the Talmud says (20b) regarding a widow to a High Priest, or a divorced or chalutzah woman to a regular priest: when they fall to levirate marriage, they perform chalitzah and do not perform yibbum. Biblically, he is permitted to have the initial intercourse because the commandment of yibbum overrides the negative commandment. However, we decree against the initial intercourse due to the possibility of a second intercourse. Similarly, in the case of a castrated man, he is certainly eligible for yibbum biblically because the positive commandment of yibbum overrides the negative commandment of "a wounded man shall not enter." However, we decree against the initial intercourse due to the possibility of a second intercourse. Therefore, she is obligated in chalitzah.

A human eunuch is someone whose genitals or testicles have been cut, severed, or crushed by human action; such a person is called a "human eunuch." When he reaches the age of thirteen years and one day, he is considered an adult, but he never develops signs of puberty if the act was done to him in his youth. Similarly, the "aylonit" (a woman who does not develop sexual characteristics) we mentioned refers to someone who was created that way. However, if she later became defective, such as if someone sterilized her reproductive organs or she drank a potion that causes sterility, she is not considered an "aylonit" and can perform chalitzah or yibbum. Just as the Torah does not concern itself with what happens after birth in the case of a male performing yibbum, the same applies to a yevama (a woman awaiting levirate marriage), as it is the same reasoning and the same matter.

And the signs of a "saris chamah" (a man who is naturally impotent) are written by the Rambam in Chapter 2 of Ishut, Law 13, and these are his words: These are the signs of a saris: Anyone who does not have a beard, whose hair is defective (soft), whose flesh is smooth (smooth like a woman's flesh, as it is typical for a man's flesh to be hairy, Rashi, ibid.), whose urine does not produce foam, and when he urinates, it does not form an arc (the stream does not go far when he directs it upwards and it does not form an arc, Nimukei Yosef, ibid.), whose semen is thin (it is not thick but clear like water), whose urine does not ferment (it does not become foul-smelling when left in a vessel), who bathes in the rainy season without his flesh emitting steam, whose voice is defective, and it is not distinguishable whether it is a man's or a woman's voice. This is the one who is called a "saris chamah." End of quote.

And the signs of an aylonit (a woman who does not develop signs of puberty) are written there in Law 6, and these are his words: And these are the signs of an aylonit: anyone who does not have breasts and has difficulty during intercourse (because intercourse is difficult for her), and she does not have the lower abdomen like women (as it is stated in Niddah 47b), and her voice is deep and she is not distinguishable between man and woman. And the Rambam holds that although in the Gemara in Yevamot there it is stated in this language: The Rabbis taught: What is a saris hama (one who is naturally sterile)? And these are his signs: anyone who does not have a beard, and his hair is thin, and his flesh is smooth. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: Anyone whose urine does not foam. And some say: Anyone who urinates and does not form a dome. And some say: Anyone whose semen is watery (or dim). And some say: Anyone whose urine does not ferment. Others say: Anyone who bathes in the winter and his flesh does not steam. Rabbi Shimon ben Azai says: Anyone whose voice is thin and is not distinguishable between man and woman. And what is an aylonit? And these are her signs: anyone who does not have breasts and has difficulty, etc. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: Anyone who does not have the lower abdomen like women. Rabbi Shimon ben Azai says: Anyone whose voice is deep, etc. And the Rambam holds that it is not a dispute, but each one adds to the other, and he ruled that all are required.

And it explains there that these signs do not validate someone as a "saris" (a male eunuch) or "aylonit" (a female who does not develop signs of puberty) unless they are twenty years old minus thirty days, and the reasoning for this is explained in Siman 155. Before this time, even if these signs appear, they are still considered minors until they reach this age with these signs, and then we will consider them adults, but he is a saris and she is an aylonit. If by this time these signs have not appeared and they do not have two pubic hairs, they are still considered minors until the majority of their years have passed, which is thirty-five years and one day. Then we will consider them adults, and he is a saris and she is an aylonit even if none of these signs are present. In all this, they are equal.

However, one distinction is written between a saris (a eunuch) and an aylonit (a woman who does not develop signs of puberty). For a saris, we require all the signs of a saris only if he has two hairs in his beard. Then, even if he does not have two hairs below, we cannot consider him an adult saris until he has all the signs that have been clarified. But if he does not have two hairs in his beard, then even if he only shows one of the signs of a saris that have been clarified for this time, we consider him an adult saris. And for an aylonit, in any case, all the signs are necessary. The reasoning is simple: in a woman, there is no hair in her beard, so it is not a deficiency that she does not have hair in her beard. But in a man, this additional deficiency—lack of two hairs in his beard—exists. Therefore, one sign of a saris is sufficient when he is twenty years old minus thirty days. (And the reason is that in the Gemara Yevamot 80, there is a dispute between Rabbi Hoshaya and Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Hoshaya says all signs are required, and Rabbi Yehuda says even one sign is enough. The Gemara explains that they argue when there are no two hairs in the beard, and the ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda. Likewise, the Rif ruled, and his opinion is that since Rabbi Yehuda agrees that if there are two hairs in the beard, all the signs are required, it is evident that for a woman this deficiency does not apply, and it is as if she had them. Therefore, all signs are required.)

The Tur disagrees with him regarding an aylonit (a woman who does not develop secondary sexual characteristics) and his words are: "And these are the signs of an aylonit: anyone who does not have breasts, or for whom intercourse is difficult, or whose voice is like that of a man, or who does not have elevated and rounded flesh like a spoon above that place. With any one of these, she is considered an aylonit." And his reasoning, it seems to me, is as follows: Tosafot and the Rosh extensively examined these signs, questioning what the beard has to do with it. After all, if they are signs of maturity, then all signs of a saris (eunuch) should not help, just as when secondary sexual characteristics appear on the lower body, he is considered mature and not a saris, even if he has all the signs of a saris. And if they are not signs, why do they matter such that we require all the signs?

From their words, it emerges that the place of the beard is not like the rest of the body, because it is common for hair to grow there. Therefore, secondary sexual characteristics in the beard do not exclude one from being a saris when he has all the signs until his beard is fully grown. And when his beard is fully grown, no signs of a saris will help, and he is considered as having secondary sexual characteristics on the lower body. 

Accordingly, when there are secondary sexual characteristics in his beard, just as there is an advantage to this, there is also a disadvantage if his beard is not fully grown. This also seems evident from the Tur himself later in this section. Therefore, the aylonit must be like a saris who has not developed secondary sexual characteristics in his beard, and one sign of an aylonit is sufficient. Otherwise, she would be judged like a saris who has developed secondary sexual characteristics in his beard, and if so, she would be judged as if her beard is fully grown, and no signs would help her. Rather, she is certainly like a saris who has not developed secondary sexual characteristics in his beard at all, who has neither the advantage of secondary sexual characteristics in the beard nor the disadvantage of an incomplete beard.

According to what has been explained, the main principles of these laws are as follows: A boy of thirteen years and one day, and a girl of twelve years and one day, if they have not shown two pubic hairs, are considered minors until twenty years of age. According to the Rambam, this period is until twenty years minus thirty days. Even if they show signs of a saris (eunuch) or an aylonit (infertile woman), they are not classified as such. A man who reaches this age without showing two pubic hairs in his beard, if he has shown only one sign of a saris, he is considered an adult and a saris. If he has not shown even one sign, he remains a minor until thirty-five years and one day, at which point he is considered an adult and a saris without any signs. If he has two pubic hairs in his beard, he needs all the signs, as mentioned. For an aylonit, at this age, according to the Rambam, she needs all the signs of an aylonit. If she is younger, she is considered a minor until the majority of her years. According to the Tur, one sign suffices. Note that if at this age they have shown signs of a saris or an aylonit, according to the opinions explained, even if they later show two pubic hairs, it is of no consequence (Tur), and they remain a saris and an aylonit forever. This applies specifically before twenty, if they have shown two pubic hairs, they are then adults, and all the signs of a saris or an aylonit will not suffice to classify them as such. Similarly, the law applies to a man if his beard has filled in (what the Beit Shmuel questions in subparagraph 5 about the Beit Yosef, it seems to me there is no difficulty at all, as there is also a distinction between less than twenty and more than twenty, just like with the two pubic hairs themselves, and everything fits well, and be precise).

If, before reaching the majority of their years, they have grown two pubic hairs, they are considered adults. Even if they subsequently exhibit signs of being a saris (a man with signs of impotence) or an ailonit (a woman who does not develop secondary sexual characteristics), these signs are meaningless, and they remain adults from the day they grew the two hairs (Beit Shmuel 67). We do not judge them as a saris or an ailonit because only if the signs of being a saris or an ailonit precede the growth of two hairs after the age of twenty, the subsequent growth of two hairs is ineffective, as mentioned. But not when the two hairs precede. Therefore, from the age of twenty until the majority of their years, whoever shows signs first remains as such. If the two hairs come first, they are considered adults and not a saris or an ailonit. If the signs of being a saris or an ailonit come first, the subsequent growth of two hairs is ineffective, and they remain a saris or an ailonit. (In the Shulchan Aruch, these laws are greatly abbreviated, and the Rema in Section 5 writes: "If there were two hairs on other parts of the body, etc.," meaning either before twenty or afterward, before the signs of being a saris or an ailonit appeared).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 6 that there are those who say that we should not presently judge the case of a definite eunuch, because we are concerned that perhaps he had hairs that fell out or he had follicles, and we are not proficient as it is written in Section 155 regarding refusal. Therefore, we judge him as a doubtful eunuch and he performs chalitzah, and this is the appropriate ruling to instruct. And it appears that this also applies to an aylonit (a woman who does not develop signs of puberty) and all the more so than a eunuch, because certainly people cannot ascertain all the signs of an aylonit according to the Rambam, who requires all the signs as it is written.

In section 1, he writes as follows: "If there is a doubt whether someone is a eunuch, he performs chalitzah (ceremonial shoe-removal) and we do not presume him to be definitely a eunuch unless one of the signs of being a eunuch was seen in him from birth, such as that he urinated without forming an arc. But otherwise, we must be concerned that he became defective after birth and he must perform chalitzah." One should not infer from this that if the sign was seen from birth, we consider him definitely a eunuch, which would contradict what he wrote in section 6 that we cited in the previous section. That is not the case, as what is written here also follows the basic law, and these are the words of the Tosafot (Yevamot 80a, s.v. "Until") that the signs of being a eunuch must be present from his mother's womb. Therefore, if we did not see the signs from birth, we cannot judge him as definitely a eunuch, even without the concern of hair or pits. In section 6, he wrote according to the stricter opinion due to the concern of hair and pits. Therefore, in any case, we do not judge him as definitely a eunuch (and so wrote the Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 8).

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 8: An androgynous person is not subject to chalitza or yibbum, and some say that his status is like a male in all respects. The first opinion is that of the Rambam, and his words are: In chapter 6, those who have no connection at all are a saris chamah (one who is naturally sterile) and an androgynous person, because they are not fit to procreate and never had a moment of fitness. And so it is explained in the Tosefta (chapter 11), and so wrote the Rif at the end of the first chapter of Yevamot. From this, it is clear that even though throughout the entire Torah we hold that an androgynous person is of doubtful status—whether male or female—nevertheless, this is not the reason they are not subject to chalitza and yibbum, for concerning intercourse, they are considered a complete male according to the Rambam, as he ruled in chapter 1 of the Laws of Forbidden Intercourse, law 15, that one who has intercourse with an androgynous person in their male organ is liable, etc., and it is permissible for them to marry a woman. And we have already explained his reasoning in section 24, subsection 2, and in section 44. However, their exemption from chalitza and yibbum is because they are not fit to procreate naturally, and their status is like a saris chamah.

The opinion of the "yeish omrim" (some say) is the opinion of the Tur in this section, who wrote as follows: "An androgynous person, Rambam wrote that his law is like that of a saris chama (a eunuch by natural causes), etc., and this is also the opinion of the Rif. But according to Rabbi Yehudah, his law is like that of a complete male in all respects, and this is also the conclusion of my father, the Rosh, of blessed memory." End quote. His words are puzzling; what is the connection between these matters? Additionally, the Rosh's conclusion is not related at all to this matter but rather to the idea that his law is like that of a complete male, and certainly, that is the case. However, regarding chalitzah and yibbum, his law is like that of a saris chama (Beit Yosef). Indeed, on the contrary, the Rosh also brought in the first chapter of Tosefta, which we mentioned there, and all the poskim (decisors) have already challenged him on this (Beit Yosef, Bach, Maharshal, Gra in section 18, and he challenged the Beit Shmuel). 

It seems to me that he follows his reasoning in section 44, where he wrote that an androgynous person who is betrothed to a man, according to Rambam, it is a doubtful betrothal, and he disagreed there. Hence, according to Rambam, although regarding intercourse on the male side he is like a male, nevertheless there is also a doubt of female, and therefore we are concerned for the betrothal when a man betroths him. Consequently, necessarily, he is not capable of reproduction, either because he has no seed or his seed is not fit for reproduction, and he is similar to a saris chama, for if he were capable of reproduction, how could there be a doubt of female in him? But the Tur, who holds that he is certainly male, even leniently, and we are not concerned at all for his femaleness and say that he is merely a male with an opening, who told us that he is not capable of reproduction? 

And the Tosefta holds that he is a doubtful male, doubtful female; therefore, necessarily, he is not capable of reproduction, as we wrote. But if we say that he is a complete male, from where do we derive that he is not capable of reproduction? In any case, if he has signs of being a eunuch, we would exempt him for this reason and not because of his androgyny. Necessarily, he does not have signs of being a eunuch, and it is possible that he is also capable of reproduction. Therefore, in practice, she performs chalitzah and does not undergo yibbum (and perhaps this is also the intention of the Beit Shmuel, see there and examine it well).

A tumtum (a person whose sexual characteristics are indeterminate or obstructed) performs chalitzah (a ceremony releasing a widow from the obligation of levirate marriage) and does not enter into yibbum (levirate marriage), because there is a doubt whether they are male or female. If the obstruction is removed and the person is found to be male, he may choose to perform chalitzah or yibbum. There are those who say that even if he is found to be male, there is still a concern that he might be a seris chamah (a type of eunuch) even if he does not show signs of being a seris, because the fact that he was obstructed may have damaged his procreative ability, and he is not fit to father children. Therefore, we act stringently, and he performs chalitzah and does not perform yibbum. If he has other brothers and he performed chalitzah, he disqualifies her from them (i.e., the brothers), and she is forbidden to enter into yibbum with any of them. She requires chalitzah from one of them, and perhaps from all of them, because it is considered a deficient chalitzah, and she needs to go around to each of the brothers according to those who hold this opinion. However, it seems more likely that this is not considered a deficient chalitzah, because either he is fully capable of performing chalitzah or he is not capable at all.

Rambam wrote in Chapter 6, Law 4: "These individuals perform chalitzah and do not perform yibbum, etc., and a man with crushed testicles, etc., and an extremely old man whose strength has weakened and faltered. If he has relations, a eunuch acquires, etc." End quote. Indeed, this is also stated in the Tosefta, Chapter 2, that an old man performs chalitzah and does not perform yibbum, see there. This is brought by the Rif and the Rosh in Chapter 2, see there. 

However, these statements are puzzling because in the Tosefta, Chapter 11, it is explicitly stated that an old man performs yibbum, and this is also explicitly stated in the Gemara (20b). How could the Rambam rule according to the Tosefta in Chapter 2, which contradicts the Gemara and another baraita in the Tosefta itself?

It seems clear to me that the Rambam, seeing that the Toseftas contradict each other, divided them based on his own understanding. Certainly, if he is an old man who is still fit for intercourse, it is permitted to perform yibbum initially even if his strength to procreate is gone, since he had a time of fitness. The Gemara and the Tosefta in Chapter 11 refer to this case. The Tosefta in Chapter 2 refers to a situation where he is not fit for intercourse at all due to his weakened strength. Therefore, the Rambam wisely stated that his strength has weakened and faltered, meaning he is not fit for intercourse at all. 

(And although the Toseftas also contradict each other regarding a eunuch, as mentioned there, this is not a difficulty at all. In Chapter 2, it refers to a rabbinic prohibition, as stated in the Gemara there, due to a decree concerning the first intercourse because of the second intercourse. In Chapter 11, it refers to a Torah law, and this does not apply to an old man. Delve into this and understand it well).

According to this, it is surprising regarding our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 10, who wrote: "An elderly person who has lost his strength and faltered in his judgment is like a eunuch in matters of levirate marriage and halitza, except that if he cohabits with his sister-in-law, he may keep her." This is perplexing because if he is capable of cohabitation, why should he not perform levirate marriage even initially? It appears that he interprets the case as referring to someone fit for cohabitation, and what the Gemara permits is only after the fact, while the Tosefta prohibits it initially. This also seems to be the position of the later authorities (see Beit Shmuel, subsection 12, and the Vilna Gaon). However, it is clear that Maimonides' intention is as stated, and there is clear evidence for this from what Maimonides concluded: "If a eunuch cohabits, he acquires [the woman], but he did not write this regarding an elderly person." This implies that in the case of an elderly person who is not fit for cohabitation at all, and this requires further investigation for the halacha. The language of the Tur also seems to support their view (see there), and the Yam Shel Shlomo in the first chapter, section 13, writes that he is not fit for cohabitation, and this is explicitly as we have stated.

In the case of an elderly yevamah (widow subject to levirate marriage) who cannot bear children, we do not find anywhere that she should not ideally enter into levirate marriage (yibbum). On the contrary, the Rambam there, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch (section 16) ruled that an elderly or barren woman should ideally undergo yibbum. If so, why were the sages stricter with an elderly man than with an elderly woman? According to our interpretation that it refers to an elderly man who is not capable of intercourse, it makes sense, because with an elderly woman this issue does not apply, and she is always capable of intercourse being "passive ground" and not active. However, according to the interpretation of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, it is difficult. We must say, according to his view as well, that it is not because he is not capable of fathering children, but because his intercourse is not complete due to his weakened strength. Consequently, if he is capable of complete intercourse, he is permitted to perform yibbum even ideally according to all opinions, and this is the main ruling in the law.

It is taught in the Tosefta (Chapter 2): A deaf-mute woman and an imbecile may undergo yibbum (levirate marriage) but may not perform chalitzah (the ceremony to release from yibbum) because chalitzah requires intention, whereas yibbum does not. Even according to the opinion of Abba Shaul, who holds that there is a primary prohibition when the intention is not for the sake of the mitzvah, it does not invalidate the act when intention is not possible, and here it is considered as if it were after the fact. This is also the ruling of all the poskim (decisors of Jewish law). All the more so, a minor girl may undergo yibbum, as stated in Siman 167. This is also explicitly clarified in the Gemara (61b). If he wishes to divorce her afterwards, the law is as follows: A deaf-mute woman can be divorced with a get (bill of divorce) after he has had relations with her, for just as her entry into marriage is through gestures, so too is her exit through gestures, like one who marries a deaf-mute. An imbecile woman cannot be divorced unless she knows how to guard her get and herself. A minor girl cannot be divorced until she matures, because her yibbum is by Torah law, and in her minority, she cannot receive a get by Torah betrothal laws unless she has a father who can receive her get, as stated in Siman 141 (Beit Shmuel, Section 13). It is possible that in yibbum, the father has no authority to receive her get, and only when he betroths her by his will does the Torah grant him the right to receive her get, but not in yibbum. This matter requires further study. Alternatively, it is possible that she herself can receive her get in her minority if she knows how to guard her get, and some of the early authorities hold this view (Nimukei Yosef on Chapter 13 in the Mishnah of a minor yavam who performs yibbum with a minor yevamah, they should grow up together. He wrote: If he wishes to divorce her, he cannot until he matures because a minor's get is not a valid get, and likewise she until she knows how to guard her get. End quote. This also appears from Rashi there who did not explain otherwise. See there).

The Rambam wrote in Chapter 6, Law 3: "These individuals perform yibbum (levirate marriage) but do not perform chalitzah (ceremonial release): a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor, because they lack the mental capacity to perform chalitzah. When a deaf-mute performs yibbum, he can never divorce her afterward because his intercourse makes her a fully married woman, and his divorce is not a complete divorce. A boy who is nine years and one day old can no longer divorce until he grows up." End of quote. 

For a boy younger than nine, his intercourse is not considered intercourse at all. Even when he grows up, he cannot divorce unless he has intercourse with her after reaching adulthood. Otherwise, his intercourse is like the ma'amar (betrothal) of an adult, as stated in Siman 170. Therefore, if he did not have intercourse with her after reaching adulthood and wishes to divorce her, she requires both a get (divorce document) and chalitzah: a get for his ma'amar (i.e., his intercourse which is like ma'amar) and chalitzah for the levirate bond.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 12 that when a deaf-mute performs yibbum (levirate marriage), he cannot subsequently divorce. This is specifically in the case where his brother who passed away was of sound mind. However, if the deceased brother was also a deaf-mute, he can divorce her with a get (bill of divorce) after consummating the marriage. Just as his brother married through gestures, he can also divorce through gestures. This law is explicitly stated in the Gemara (Gittin 71a). Therefore, we must say that when Rambam wrote that a deaf-mute cannot ever divorce, he was referring to a case where his deceased brother was of sound mind, and he did not need to specify this because it is generally assumed, as most people are not deaf-mutes. This is also what Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in his major work. Some want to say that Rambam's intention was also in the case where his deceased brother was a deaf-mute, but this is not the main interpretation. Although according to the Jerusalem Talmud, this is the case, as it holds that a deaf-mute who married a woman of sound mind can divorce her through gestures just as he married her through gestures (beginning of Chapter 14 of Yevamot), this does not apply when he consummated the marriage. However, this is not the approach of our Talmud (Bavli), and neither Rambam nor other poskim (decisors of Jewish law) adopt the Jerusalem Talmud's stance on this. Therefore, the main ruling is as stated (and see Beit Shmuel, Subsection 14, and the commentary of the Gra, Subsection 26).

Two brothers, one of whom is of sound mind and one who is deaf, are married to two women who are of sound mind. If the deaf brother, who is married to a woman of sound mind, dies, then the brother who is of sound mind has the option to either perform chalitzah (the ceremonial release) or yibbum (levirate marriage). We do not say that since, according to Torah law, his brother's marriage was not fully valid, yibbum is not required. According to Torah law, this is indeed the case, but since, from a rabbinic perspective, she is considered like an unmarried woman, he can either perform yibbum or chalitzah. This is the case when the women are not related to each other. If they are related, their ruling is explained in Siman 175. If the brother who is of sound mind, married to a woman of sound mind, dies, his deaf brother cannot perform chalitzah because he is not capable of doing so. Therefore, he marries her and never divorces her because his brother's marriage was valid according to Torah law, and the deaf brother is not capable of divorcing a marriage valid under Torah law, as explained in Siman 121.

Two intelligent brothers are married to two women, one of whom is intelligent and the other is deaf. If the intelligent brother married to the deaf woman dies, the deaf woman is not subject to chalitza (the ritual of removing the shoe). Instead, the brother marries her, and if he later wishes to divorce her, he may do so with a get (divorce document), because his brother's marriage to her was also through gestures, as mentioned in Section 25. If the intelligent brother married to the intelligent woman dies, the brother may choose whether to perform chalitza or to marry her (Yevamot Chapter 14). This is not surprising at all, but it informs us that we do not decree that if the husband of the intelligent woman dies, chalitza should not be performed because of the case where the husband of the deaf woman dies.

Two brothers, one deaf and one hearing, are married to two women, one deaf and one hearing. The deaf woman is married to the deaf man, and the hearing woman is married to the hearing man. If the deaf man, who is married to the deaf woman, dies, she is not eligible for chalitzah, and his hearing brother performs yibbum (levirate marriage) with her. If he wishes, he can later divorce her with a get (writ of divorce), since his brother's marriage was also established through gestures. If the hearing man, who is married to the hearing woman, dies, his deaf brother marries her and can never divorce her, because his brother's marriage was valid according to Torah law, and his divorce is accomplished through gestures. If both brothers were deaf, or their wives were deaf, and certainly if they were all deaf, when one of them dies, the other performs yibbum. If he later wishes to divorce her, he can do so with a get, due to the reasons explained. They are not eligible for chalitzah.

A blind man can perform yibbum (levirate marriage) even though he cannot see her; he performs yibbum based on witnesses who say that this is his yevamah (sister-in-law). However, for chalitzah (the ceremony releasing a widow from levirate marriage), he is not fit initially because he cannot see the spit, as we explained in Siman 169. And we have already clarified there that if he performed chalitzah, it is valid after the fact because this does not invalidate it. Furthermore, Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 15 that if there is no other brother except him, he performs chalitzah even initially since it cannot be done otherwise. The wife of a minor and the wife of an imbecile are exempt from both chalitzah and yibbum because marriage was not instituted for them, as with the deaf-mute. However, the wife of a deaf-mute, an elderly woman, and a barren woman are like all other women and perform chalitzah or yibbum, even though they are currently not fit to bear children, because they had a period of fitness. Therefore, if she is barren from birth, like an ailonit (a woman who never develops signs of puberty), it seems to me that she is forbidden to perform yibbum and performs chalitzah. (The intention of the Rema is that even according to those who hold that the mitzvah of yibbum takes precedence, as the Beit Yosef ruled in Siman 169 that initially he does not perform chalitzah, nevertheless, according to our practice, they also agree that he performs chalitzah initially).

A yevama (widow bound by levirate marriage) who is forbidden to the yavam (levir) due to a prohibition carrying a penalty of karet (spiritual excision) and her co-wife. And it contains thirty-nine sections:

Even though a brother's wife is generally a forbidden relationship (ervah) and incurs the penalty of karet, the Torah permits it when the brother dies without offspring and obligates him to perform yibbum (levirate marriage). However, when there is an additional prohibition of ervah in this yibbum, the yibbum is nullified, and the prohibition remains, incurring karet. For example, if Reuven marries the daughter of his brother Shimon and then dies without offspring, Shimon is forbidden from performing yibbum with her since she is his daughter. Similarly, if their wives are sisters and one of them dies, the other brother is forbidden from performing yibbum with her since she is his wife's sister. This applies to all cases of ervah. If there is another brother for whom the yevama is not an ervah, he may perform yibbum or chalitza (ceremonial release). If there is no other brother, she leaves without any requirement, and chalitza is not needed, as it has been explained several times that any case not subject to yibbum is also not subject to chalitza.

Not only is the ervah (a woman forbidden to a man due to a severe prohibition) exempt from chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from the obligation to marry her late husband's brother) and yibbum (levirate marriage), but even her co-wife, such as when the deceased had two wives, one of whom is an ervah to the yavam (the brother-in-law) and the other is not an ervah, the law of the co-wife is the same as that of the ervah. It is forbidden for him to perform yibbum with her, and he incurs karet (spiritual excision) if he does so. Moreover, even the co-wife of the co-wife, such as if there was another brother who was permitted to both and performed yibbum with the co-wife and then died, causing his wives to fall before this brother, just as he is forbidden with the one who performed yibbum with the deceased because she is like an ervah to him due to the fall from the first brother, so too he is forbidden to all the wives of this second brother because they are co-wives of the co-wife, and their status is like that of an ervah. Similarly, if there was a third brother who performed yibbum with the co-wife of the co-wife and died, this brother is forbidden to all his wives because the co-wife of the co-wife is like an ervah to him. Therefore, even the co-wife of the co-wife of the co-wife is like an ervah to him, and so on indefinitely. This is what the sages taught at the beginning of Yevamot: fifteen women exempt their co-wives and the co-wives of their co-wives from chalitzah and yibbum forever.

And the reason for this matter is that although we hold that a positive commandment overrides a negative commandment, this is only when there is no "karet" (spiritual excision) associated with the negative commandment. But a negative commandment that has "karet" associated with it, the positive commandment does not override it, because the rule that a positive commandment overrides a negative commandment is derived from the case of mixing wool and linen in tzitzit, and there is no "karet" in this. Therefore, the positive commandment of yibbum (levirate marriage) does not override the prohibition that has "karet" in this case of yibbum. And although yibbum overrides the prohibition of "karet" of a brother's wife, this is because the essence of the mitzvah of yibbum is thus, and it cannot be done in another manner. If not for this, the mitzvah of yibbum would be nullified. But it does not override another prohibition of "karet" when the mitzvah of yibbum can be fulfilled without it (Tosafot Yevamot 3b s.v. "Negative Commandment").

And one might ask, isn’t one of the thirteen principles by which the Torah is expounded the rule of "Binyan Av" (building a principle from one case)? Meaning, learning one matter from another by comparing them. If so, should we not learn all forbidden relationships from the case of "Achos Ishah" (the wife of one’s brother)? Certainly, this would be the case if it was possible to learn the prohibition of another forbidden relationship solely from the prohibition of "Achos Ishah." However, here, when we try to learn the prohibition of another forbidden relationship from "Achos Ishah," the prohibition of "Achos Ishah" would apply to the other forbidden relationship as well, and we do not derive two prohibitions from one prohibition (Gemara Yevamot 7b). Furthermore, even with one prohibition, we do not learn in this manner because the prohibition of "Achos Ishah" that existed was nullified when the brother died childless, for she is no longer the wife of his brother since he has already died. This is not the case with another prohibition you wish to permit, such as the prohibition of one's daughter or the prohibition of one's wife's sister, where this prohibition causes the prohibition and the prohibition still remains in place (Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Yevamot).

And the Torah itself explained this matter regarding the nakedness of one's wife's sister, as it is written, "And you shall not take a woman to her sister, to be a rival to uncover her nakedness while she is alive." The word "while she is alive" is superfluous, as it could have simply stated "to uncover her nakedness," and we would know that it is forbidden during the lifetime of his wife, but permitted after her death. Our sages accepted this interpretation (Yevamot 3a): It is stated here "while she is alive" and it is stated regarding the levirate marriage "her yavam shall have intercourse with her." The Torah commands that even in a situation where levirate marriage applies, if there is a prohibition of one's wife's sister, it remains forbidden. 

I only know about her (the wife's sister); from where do we learn about her co-wife? It is stated "to be a rival" (which is entirely superfluous), and it was received through tradition that this refers to the co-wife of one's wife's sister in the context of levirate marriage. That is, the law of the co-wife is the same as that of the forbidden relationship itself. And I only know about the co-wife; from where do we learn about the co-wife's co-wife? As it is written "to be a rival," and it could have written "to rival," but it wrote "to be a rival" to teach us also about the co-wife's co-wife, and so on forever. And we derive all forbidden relationships from one's wife's sister: just as one's wife's sister is forbidden in the context of levirate marriage, so too all forbidden relationships and their co-wives. 

And one should not ask why we derive all forbidden relationships from one's wife's sister and not from one's brother's wife. This is not a question for two reasons: one, because we derive stringencies; and furthermore, when we derive other forbidden relationships from one's wife's sister, they are similar to each other, as both involve two prohibitions of forbidden relationships. This is not the case with one's brother's wife, where there are not two forbidden relationships, as we have written. Also, the second reason we wrote in the previous section is not similar to one's brother's wife.

And if you ask why we need a scriptural verse, since we have already explained this logically, the Gemara there has clarified that the verse is necessary in a case where the deceased had married his wife and died, and she fell to his brother for levirate marriage. Before the levirate marriage could take place, the brother married her sister or one of the other forbidden relatives to this yevama. I might have thought that since she already fell to him for levirate marriage and the prohibition of his brother's wife was permitted to him, the prohibition of the wife's sister would also be permitted because the commandment of levirate marriage should override this prohibition. Therefore, the verse is necessary to teach us that in all cases, the commandment of levirate marriage does not override another prohibition. Similarly, one could say that we need a verse for the co-wife, as logically we would not know this, but if so, it would have sufficed for the verse to teach "to rival her" to inform us that the co-wife is like the erva (forbidden relative), and similarly, the co-wife's co-wife. But the verse "upon her" is still superfluous, and therefore, it must be said as we have explained. (And the position of Rava is not mentioned here, as Tosafot there wrote that Rava disagrees with Ulla and holds that partial intercourse is not considered intercourse. We hold like Ulla, as Rambam and Raavad wrote in the third chapter of "Entering the Temple Mount"; see there.)

There is another exposition in the Gemara (8b): Rabbi says, "And he shall take her" (ve-lakach) and "and she shall be taken" (ve-lakcha) and "he shall perform yibbum" (yibem) and "she shall be performed yibbum" (ve-yibma) to prohibit co-wives and prohibited relations. It is explained in the words of the Rambam, Chapter 6, Law 9, that the interpretation is as follows: From the fact that it is written "ve-lakcha" and not "ve-lakach," it implies that specifically when he has acquisition in her and marriage is effective with her, she is bound to yibbum. This excludes a prohibited relation (ervah) where marriage is not effective, and from "ve-lakcha" we learn that if he cannot build even part of the house because he has no acquisition in her, he does not build even part of it, and thus the co-wife of the prohibited relation is also prohibited to him because she is the wife of his brother, for he has no bond with her. Thus are the words of the Rambam. 

(He does not interpret like Rashi and Tosafot; see there. According to his explanation, we must say that the text does not read "What does 've-lakcha' mean? In any case where there are two..." but rather "In any case where...," and the exposition is from the word "house" and "ve-lakcha" itself refers to the ervah as written. And what the Maggid Mishneh wrote, that he did not bother to write according to the conclusion that ervah does not need a verse, and there is no practical halachic difference; see there. And his intent is according to Rava; see there, this is not needed. And as I wrote in the previous section, we do not follow Rava. And this is why he took the exposition of Rabbi and not the Baraita on it, because he holds that it needs the ruling of a court, as he wrote in Chapter 12 of Shgagot. And as it is in the Gemara there, and Rabbi needs that verse for another purpose; see there and understand well.)

There is a question here because we said that when the yevama (widow awaiting levirate marriage) is an erva (forbidden relation) to the yavam (brother-in-law), there is no requirement of chalitza (ceremonial release) or yibum (levirate marriage). Therefore, when she was a niddah (menstruant) at the time of the fall (i.e., when she became a widow), should her status be like that of an erva since a niddah is among the forbidden relations? The answer to this is that a niddah is not comparable to other forbidden relations because the fundamental prohibition of all other forbidden relations is specifically on the yavam, not on other people. However, a niddah is prohibited to everyone, and even to her husband she must wait until she becomes pure. Additionally, a niddah is expected to become permissible, unlike other forbidden relations. Even the sister of the wife, if the wife died after the fall, is forbidden to the yavam because we do not say at the time of the fall that "the yevama shall come unto him" since she was not in a state of becoming permissible afterward. We cannot assume that the wife would die. This is not the case with a niddah. Furthermore, if one transgressed and had relations with her while she was a niddah, he acquires her for yibum (Pesachim 72b), although he transgressed a prohibition of karet (severe spiritual excision), which is not the case with other forbidden relations (see Tosafot and Rosh at the beginning of Yevamot).

And know that what we have written, that a co-wife is considered like the ervah (forbidden relation) itself, only applies in the context of the mitzvah of yibbum (levirate marriage) and not in other contexts. For example, if it is his daughter or his wife's sister who married another man and that man died, leaving other wives, he is permitted to the other wives. Similarly, if his mother was married to another man who died and left other wives, he is permitted to them (Mishnah 13). Thus, the Sages have received the tradition that only in the context of yibbum is the co-wife forbidden, but outside the context of yibbum, meaning not in the context of levirate marriage, the co-wife is not forbidden. We also derive from the verse "and she shall perform the levirate marriage" that only in the context of "and she shall perform the levirate marriage" is the co-wife forbidden, but outside this context, she is permitted. It is not surprising that there should be a difference between the context of yibbum and outside of it, for certainly it is so. What relevance does a co-wife have to an ervah? Rather, in the context of yibbum, since she is exempt from yibbum, the co-wife remains in the prohibition of a brother’s wife, which carries the penalty of karet due to this very prohibition.

And behold, regarding all forbidden relationships, there is no distinction between during the lifetime of the forbidden relative and after their death, except for the sister of one's wife and one's mother-in-law after death, where there is a disagreement among the decisors. We have explained this in Siman 15, section 16, see there. Therefore, according to the decisors who hold that after death it is not a matter of karet (excision) but rather a prohibition of a negative commandment or a positive commandment, in such a case she is subject to chalitza (ceremonial release from levirate marriage) as is the law for all who are subject to negative commandments, as will be explained in Siman 174. This is also the opinion of later authorities (Kenesset HaGedolah and Noda BiYehuda).

If the yevamah (widow awaiting levirate marriage) was forbidden to the husband through a forbidden relationship that incurs karet (spiritual excision), she is considered as if she was never his wife at all, since the kiddushin (betrothal) and nisuin (marriage) do not take effect for him with her, and it is merely illicit relations. Therefore, when he dies and leaves behind other valid wives, he performs chalitzah (ritual release from levirate marriage) with one of them or performs yibbum (levirate marriage), and their status is not like that of co-wives of an ervah (forbidden relative). Even if this ervah was also an ervah to the yavam (levir), nevertheless, the co-wives have no relevance in this matter (Bach, section 4). If she was only an ervah to the husband and not to the yavam, the yavam is permitted to her, not through levirate marriage, but as an ordinary woman, for she is not considered the wife of his brother.

The yevama who is a doubtful erva to the yavam, such as if he betrothed a woman with doubtful betrothal, and her sister is married to his paternal brother, and his brother dies leaving another wife. Hence, this woman is a doubtful co-wife of an erva. She should perform chalitza and not yibbum. All the more so, the sister of the woman who is a doubtful sister of his betrothed cannot perform yibbum and requires chalitza, even if there is no other wife, because she might not be the sister of his betrothed since the betrothal is in doubt. Therefore, if he gives her chalitza, both are prohibited to him, because this one whom he betrothed in doubt must be divorced, as she might be the sister of his chalutza, since perhaps the betrothal did not take effect, and the chalitza is a full chalitza. And even though the prohibition of the sister of a chalutza is only rabbinic and they did not decree in cases of doubt, nevertheless, initially it is forbidden (Bach). And some say that even post-factum it is forbidden (Beit Shmuel, section 3), even though it is a rabbinic doubt, nevertheless they decreed due to the sister of his divorcee (Nimukei Yosef, Chapter 2).

The Tur wrote: I saw in the words of the Rambam that if the yevama (the widow) is in doubt whether she is prohibited to the husband, she performs chalitza (the rite of release) and does not undergo yibum (levirate marriage). It seems that this is a scribal error, because logically she should undergo yibum. For if she is not prohibited to him, she is obligated to the yavam (levir); and if she is prohibited to him, the kiddushin (betrothal) does not take effect with her, and she is like a stranger woman to the yavam. End quote. Many things have been said about this (see Beit Yosef, Bach, and Beit Shmuel, section 2). However, the truth is that the Rambam's intent is in a case where someone betrothed one of two sisters and did not know which one he betrothed, so each is in doubt of being prohibited due to being the sister of his wife. When he dies and they fall before the yavam, he cannot perform yibum with either of them due to the doubt of being the sister of the one to whom he is obligated, so he performs chalitza with both of them (Maggid Mishneh, chapter 6, halacha 13). This is explicitly stated in the Gemara (Yevamot 41b). However, in the case of a different doubt of prohibition that is not related to the yavam, either chalitza or yibum is performed (as stated in Shulchan Aruch, section 5, though his words at the beginning of section 3 need examination).

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (30b): Any case where there is doubt regarding the marriage or divorce, these co-wives must perform chalitzah and may not do yibbum. How so? A case of doubtful marriage: if he threw her the marriage contract and it is uncertain whether it landed closer to him or closer to her, this is a case of doubtful marriage. A case of doubtful divorce: if he wrote a bill of divorce in his own handwriting but there are no witnesses, or there are witnesses but no date, or there is a date but only one witness, this is a case of doubtful divorce. Therefore, this woman is certainly forbidden to the yavam (levirate husband), but his deceased brother had a doubtful marriage or doubtful divorce with her. Hence, the co-wives are doubtfully considered the co-wives of a forbidden relation, and therefore they perform chalitzah and do not do yibbum (in Shulchan Aruch, Section 6, the text should read according to the version of the Baal HaGoleh: a yevamah who is forbidden to the yavam, and the version of the Ba'er Heitev is very strained). 

Regarding the doubtful divorce mentioned by the Tanna, it is not precise, for according to the Torah, it is a valid divorce, and only rabbinically is it considered invalid. The Mishnah teaches us that even though according to the Torah she is already divorced and the yavam may perform yibbum with the co-wife, rabbinically she must perform chalitzah and not yibbum (Nimukei Yosef). The doubts mentioned in marriage also apply to divorce, but the doubts mentioned in divorce do not apply to marriage (see the Gemara and Tosafot there), for they did not establish a date for marriage. Similarly, if he wrote in his own handwriting and there are no witnesses, or if there is only one witness, it is valid for marriage (Nimukei Yosef). Some raise doubts about this, arguing that even in marriage it is invalid rabbinically, and therefore this excludes only the date, which is valid in marriage even rabbinically (see Nimukei Yosef and Tosafot). This has already been explained in the laws of marriage by document in Siman 32. See there.

And behold, in the case of doubtful betrothal, even though the co-wife remains in the presumption of being permitted to the levirate marriage, nevertheless, because of the doubt, she does not undergo levirate marriage. Conversely, in the case of doubtful divorce where the husband threw a get (divorce document) and it is uncertain whether it landed closer to him or closer to her, even though the co-wife remains in the presumption of being permitted to the general public (i.e., to remarry), nevertheless, because of the doubt, she requires chalitza (ceremonial release from levirate marriage) and they did not follow the presumption in this case due to the severity of the prohibition, and also because there is a remedy through chalitza. Similarly, if there are two sets of witnesses, one set says the betrothal or the get was closer to him and one set says it was closer to her, even though according to Torah law when there are two sets of witnesses, we establish the matter according to the presumption, nevertheless, the Sages were stringent not to follow the presumption. In both cases of betrothal and divorce, she performs chalitza and does not undergo levirate marriage. Similarly, when there are two witnesses, one says it was closer to him, and one says it was closer to her. (Gemara)

Reuven and Shimon, brothers, who married two sisters, and one of the sisters died during her husband's lifetime, and afterward, the husband died and left another wife. The yavam (brother-in-law) is permitted to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) with her, as she is not considered a co-wife of an erva (forbidden relative), since at the time of the deceased husband's death, the erva was not alive. Similarly, if he divorced her before he died, and even if he married the co-wife before he divorced the erva or before she died, we do not say that at one moment she was the co-wife of an erva. For we hold that the death of the brother determines the obligation of yibbum, and therefore, since at the time of death the erva was not alive or had been divorced, the co-wife is no longer considered a co-wife of an erva. The same applies if the erva was a minor and refused (mi'un) him during his lifetime, the co-wife is permitted to be taken in yibbum when he dies. However, if she did not refuse him during his lifetime and refused him after his death, even though according to the basic law it is permitted to perform yibbum with her co-wife, as the refusal nullifies her marriage from the beginning, nevertheless, the co-wife should perform chalitza (ceremonial release from levirate marriage) and not yibbum, because at the time of falling to yibbum, she appeared as the co-wife of an erva. And even though the primary marriage is only rabbinically binding, they were stringent in this matter due to the severity of the prohibition, and also because chalitza is possible, and certainly if she did not refuse at all.

If there is a doubt whether the ervah (prohibited relation) died during his lifetime or after his death, such as if a house collapsed on him and on the ervah of the yavam (brother-in-law), and it is not known who died first, it is clear that according to Torah law, the co-wife performs chalitzah (the ritual of release) and does not undergo yibbum (levirate marriage) because there is a doubt regarding the fundamental matter. However, it is possible to say that according to Torah law, she remains in a presumed state of being permitted to the general public, and the Sages were stringent in this matter. This is also implied in the Gemara (31a, and see there in Tosafot, s.v. "Nafal").

If the co-wife is an ailonit (a woman who does not develop signs of puberty and is thus considered incapable of bearing children), her co-wife is subject to levirate marriage (yibbum). It is not only the case if the deceased brother did not know that she was an ailonit, which would be considered a mistaken transaction because she would not have been his wife, and therefore not a co-wife of an ervah (a woman forbidden to the yavam). Even if he was aware and the marriage was valid, and similarly the betrothal and marriage were valid, nevertheless, the co-wife is subject to levirate marriage. Since the ailonit is not subject to levirate marriage, the obligation of levirate marriage falls solely upon the co-wife. The Torah only forbids the co-wife of an ervah in the context of the mitzvah of levirate marriage, as it is written. Since this ailonit, even without the presence of an ervah, is not fit for levirate marriage, her co-wife is considered a co-wife of an ervah outside the context of the mitzvah (Rashi 12b, s.v. halakhah in the name of BeHaG).

If he performed Yibbum (levirate marriage) with the co-wife because he thought that the ervah (the prohibited relative) was an aylonit (a woman who cannot bear children), and afterward it was clarified that she was not an aylonit, she must leave her Yavam (levir) without a get (divorce document), and the child is a mamzer (illegitimate), because Kiddushin (marriage) does not take effect with the co-wife of an ervah, as she is the wife of a brother not in the context of a mitzvah, and she is liable for karet (spiritual excision) (see Beit Shmuel, section 9). If it is found that she is possibly an aylonit, it appears to me that she requires a get out of doubt, and the child is a doubtful mamzer. Chalitzah (ceremonial release) is not needed in any case, for if she is not an aylonit, then there is no need for chalitzah, and if she is an aylonit, the Yibbum is valid and she has already been married through Yibbum.

And if the opposite case occurs, where the co-wife married someone from the marketplace because she was considered a co-wife of a forbidden relative (ervah), and afterward it was clarified that the forbidden relative was an aylonit (a woman incapable of bearing children), and thus the co-wife requires chalitzah from the yavam (levirate brother), she must leave her [current] husband with a get (divorce document) as is the law for a yevamah (levirate widow) who married someone from the marketplace, as explained in Siman 159. The yavam must perform chalitzah and not yibbum (levirate marriage), as she is forbidden to him, as stated there. If initially she did not marry someone from the marketplace but was only betrothed, he should give her a get, and the yavam should either perform chalitzah or yibbum, since in the case of betrothal, she is not forbidden to the yavam, as stated there. And it appears to me that even if she is found to be a doubtful aylonit, the law is the same, because she might indeed be an aylonit and marrying someone from the marketplace would be forbidden.

If a man's wife willingly committed adultery and there are witnesses, and he dies without children, and she falls before his brother for levirate marriage, her status is like that of an ervah (a forbidden relative). Not only is she exempt from chalitzah and yibbum (levirate marriage), but even her co-wife is exempt, just like the co-wife of an ervah. Thus, our sages said (Yevamot 11a), "The co-wife of a sotah (a woman suspected of adultery) is forbidden." What is the reason? Because the term 'defilement' is written regarding her, similar to the term used for ervah, as it is written, "And she was secluded and became defiled," and regarding ervah it is also written, "Do not defile yourselves with any of these things." However, if the wife of a Kohen (priest) was raped, there is a doubt whether she and her co-wife are exempt from chalitzah. Although she is forbidden to her husband and is considered defiled to him, as it is stated in the Gemara (Yevamot 56b), "If the wife of a Kohen was raped, her husband is flogged because of her defilement," this is due to the sanctity of the priesthood. But regarding her own status, she is not considered defiled in essence, but only regarding the priesthood. (This resolves the difficulty posed by the Bach and Beit Shmuel in Seif Katan 10).

However, I am greatly puzzled by this doubt, as it is clearly stated in the Gemara in Sotah (6a) that even a yevama (a woman awaiting her brother-in-law's levirate marriage) is required to perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from this obligation) if her brother-in-law has been disqualified from the sanctity of the priesthood. Certainly, she requires chalitzah, and all the more so, her co-wife either needs chalitzah or can enter into levirate marriage.
