This is no less stringent than any other prohibitions of negative commandments, and this requires further examination. (I later found this question in the Mishneh LaMelech, Chapter 6).

However, in the case of a suspected sotah, such as when her husband warned her and she secluded herself, and it is not known whether she became defiled or not, even though she is forbidden to her husband, nevertheless, she performs chalitzah (the ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage) and does not undergo yibbum (levirate marriage). But her co-wife either performs chalitzah or undergoes yibbum. This is because the status of a suspected sotah was only excluded in relation to the prohibition to her husband. And since the yavam (levir) derives his right from his brother's marriage, he is in the place of the husband, and she is forbidden to undergo yibbum with him. However, chalitzah is required (Tosafot Sotah 5b s.v. elu). Therefore, the co-wife undergoes yibbum as well (and see Tosafot Yevamot 11a s.v. tzaratah).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 11 that there are those who say that even if she certainly committed adultery, she requires chalitza, and the same applies to her co-wife, and one should be stringent. Therefore, if someone has a wife who was switched, even though she certainly committed adultery, her co-wife requires chalitza. These are his words. And the same applies to her herself needing chalitza, but her chalitza does not exempt her co-wife (Beit Shmuel, section 12), as her chalitza is considered a disqualified chalitza. Now, this opinion is a solitary one, and the Rif, the Rambam, the Rosh, and the Tosafot ruled according to the first opinion, which is explicitly a Gemara in Yevamot there. However, the Ra'avad, of blessed memory, was stringent in this matter according to the discussion in Sotah (5b), see there. And the Tosafot and the Rosh in Yevamot have already answered that the discussions do not contradict each other, and I do not know why he was concerned about a solitary opinion. It must be said that it is because the straightforward reading of the discussion in Sotah does not indicate this (as the Gra wrote in section 12, see there). And it seems to me that in the case of being switched, even the first opinion agrees that they only said she and her co-wife are exempt when there are witnesses and not when there are no witnesses in the matter, even if it is clear that she committed adultery, and even if she says she committed adultery, for the verses about the Sotah refer to witnesses, as explicitly stated there.

A woman whose husband went overseas and she remarried based on the testimony of witnesses or a single witness, with the court's permission, and afterwards her husband came back and died—her co-wife is permitted to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) and is not considered like the co-wife of a sotah (a woman suspected of adultery). This is because she remarried with the court's permission, and according to the Torah, she is even permitted to her original husband, and only rabbinically is she forbidden to him, as stated in Siman 17. Therefore, she herself also requires chalitzah (a formal release from levirate marriage) and does not perform yibbum due to rabbinic decree, just as her husband was rabbinically forbidden to her, as he derives his status from the husband. However, her co-wife is permitted either through chalitzah or yibbum (Yevamot 11a).

The wife of a brother who was not in the world (i.e., a brother who was born after the deceased brother died) is not subject to levirate marriage (yibbum), as it is written: "When brothers dwell together," meaning they must have had one dwelling in one world. Since she is not subject to levirate marriage, she is like the wife of a brother in a non-commanded context, which is forbidden and incurs karet (spiritual excision), and she exempts her co-wife. How so? Reuven died, and his wife fell before Shimon, his brother, for levirate marriage. Subsequently, another brother named Levi was born to their father. Levi is liable to karet for marrying Reuven's wife. There is no difference whether Levi was born before Shimon performed yibbum with Reuven's wife or after Shimon performed yibbum, for even though by the time Levi was born, she had already been taken in levirate marriage and was not found in the bond of the first brother's marriage, she still has the status of the wife of a brother who was not in the world. Therefore, when Shimon dies and she falls before Levi for levirate marriage, she and her co-wife are exempt from chalitzah (the formal ceremony releasing the widow from yibbum) and yibbum, as per the law of the co-wife of a forbidden relation. If Shimon died before he performed yibbum with her, her co-wife performs chalitzah and does not undergo yibbum, because since we maintain that there is a bond (zika), she is considered the co-wife of a brother's wife who was not in the world in the context of the bond. Nevertheless, she performs chalitzah because she is not a complete co-wife, as she had not yet undergone yibbum. The same applies if Shimon performed ma'amar (a betrothal-like act in the context of yibbum) with her; her co-wife performs chalitzah, as ma'amar does not establish a complete acquisition. (The Tur criticized the Rambam for what he wrote in Chapter 6, Halacha 18 regarding this law of performing ma'amar, etc., for even without ma'amar, the law is the same since there is a bond. However, the Rambam adhered to the language of the Mishnah in Yevamot 18:1: see there).

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch, section 14, wrote: A minor who is not an ervah to him, and he dies and the minor refuses to marry the yavam (levir), she is forbidden to him and permitted to others without chalitzah if there are no other brothers. Specifically, she herself is forbidden, but her co-wife is permitted to him. And even she is permitted to the other brothers, provided she did not refuse them. To explain: We hold that even after the husband's death, she can refuse the yavam and annul the first marriage, as she refuses the levirate bond. If she simply refuses, saying she does not want the levirate bond, she is separated from all of them. But if she says she does not want the levirate bond with this specific yavam, she is only exempt from him and not from the other brothers, since she does not want his levirate bond but is willing with others. If she says she does not want the first marriage either, she is separated from all. Hence, when she refuses this yavam, she is permitted without chalitzah if there are no other brothers, but if there are others, she is not exempt from them. However, she is forbidden to the yavam she refused. Although we hold in Siman 155 that when she refuses her husband, she is permitted to his father because she has completely annulled the marriage and is like a stranger, here too, why should she be forbidden? Because since she did not refuse her husband while he was alive, she appears as his brother's wife and not in the context of the mitzvah, since she refused. Therefore, her co-wife is permitted because there is nothing that would forbid her. Likewise, any of the other brothers can perform yibum with her. If they do not want to perform yibum, one of them must perform chalitzah with her (explained according to the words of the Ramban in Milchamot).

From the words of the Rambam in Chapter 11 of Hilchot Gerushin, Law 17, it becomes clear that even if she refuses one of the yevamim (levirate brothers), she is exempt from all of them due to the bond, but she is permitted to them. See there. And there are those who want to link this dispute to the disagreement explained in Siman 155, Section 13, regarding if she refuses the yavam (levir), whether she is prohibited to his father and also to other relatives of the deceased. See there. However, it is impossible to say this, for our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled there like the Rambam that she is permitted to other relatives, and here he ruled that she is not exempt from the others. Therefore, it is certain that these matters are not related to each other. (Refer to the Beit Shmuel, section 18, and there is no necessity in this. Besides, it is possible to reconcile the words of the Rambam with those of the Ramban by distinguishing between when she explicitly says, "I only wish to be exempt from you." Delve into this thoroughly.)

The Tur further writes: A minor who was married to his maternal brother or his mother’s brother, and he died, and she then married his paternal brother, and he died, and she fell before him for levirate marriage while still a minor, she cannot refuse to annul the first marriage in order to be eligible for levirate marriage. Her co-wife performs chalitzah (the removal of the shoe ceremony) and does not enter into levirate marriage. It appears that she too performs chalitzah if she refuses. The explanation of the matter is that the wife of his maternal brother is a biblical prohibition, and the wife of his mother’s brother is a secondary prohibition to the forbidden relationships, as stated in Siman 15. Therefore, she cannot now refuse the first marriage to allow levirate marriage, because at the time of falling for levirate marriage, she appears as a forbidden relative or a secondary relationship. This is like what is stated in Siman 155, that if she refused the levir, she is forbidden to his father because at the time of falling she appears as his daughter-in-law. The same applies here. Her co-wife performs chalitzah and does not enter into levirate marriage. It is not necessary to say that this is the case when she was the wife of his maternal brother, but even when she was the wife of his mother’s brother, who is a secondary prohibition, and we hold that the co-wife of a secondary prohibition is permitted in levirate marriage, as will be explained in Siman 174, nevertheless here the co-wife is forbidden to enter into levirate marriage. Just as they forbade the co-wife of his daughter to enter into levirate marriage when his daughter refused after death because at the time of falling she appears as the co-wife of his daughter, similarly, if they permit this secondary relationship to refuse after his death to allow her co-wife, they would also come to permit the co-wife of his daughter (Rif, Beit Shmuel). This is what is meant by saying that she too performs chalitzah if she refuses, referring to the wife of his maternal brother, for without refusal she would be exempt. Although she is only a rabbinic prohibition like the marriage of a minor orphan, nevertheless, the marriage of his paternal brother is no better than the marriage of his maternal brother (Gra, Siman 20). However, the wife of his mother’s brother, even without refusal, performs chalitzah, because the marriage of the wife of his mother’s brother is a secondary rabbinic prohibition, while the marriage of his paternal brother is a biblical prohibition with an adult, and therefore this marriage is superior to the first marriage and a rabbinic bond applies to her, and she requires chalitzah.

The language of our master, the Beit Yosef, in section 13 is puzzling in this matter, where he wrote as follows: A minor who was married to his maternal uncle (this is the correct version) who is a secondary prohibition to him, and he died, and she married his paternal brother, and he died, and she fell to levirate marriage while still a minor, we do not say she should perform refusal to annul the first marriage so that she can undergo levirate marriage. Rather, her co-wife performs chalitzah and does not undergo levirate marriage, for she also performs chalitzah if she refuses. And it is difficult, for even if she does not refuse, chalitzah is required (there). And it must be said that this is what he meant: If she does not refuse, her co-wife is not exempted by her chalitzah, but if she refuses, she exempts her co-wife. And the explanation is that her chalitzah alone is sufficient if she refuses. (And regarding what the Gra asked, that a co-wife of a secondary prohibition does undergo levirate marriage, we have already resolved this based on the words of the Rif, that refusal after death is more severe due to the decree concerning the co-wife of one’s daughter, and one should delve into this).

And know that this law is stated in the Gemara (Yevamot 108b) in the following language: "Behold, there was the wife of the brother of his mother, who is a secondary relation to him (and he died), and his paternal brother married her and then died—what is the law regarding her refusal now to uproot the first marriage and let her co-wife undergo levirate marriage?" They asked Rabbi Akiva, and he forbade it. There are some who do not have the reading "her co-wife" because it is obvious to them that her co-wife is permitted even without refusal, as is the law concerning the co-wife of a secondary relation. Instead, the question was about the secondary relation herself (Rashal and in Yam Shel Shlomo, Chapter 13, Section 12, and the Gra there). The Rambam omitted this law entirely, and the Maggid Mishneh already wondered about this in Chapter 11 of Gerushin (Divorce), see there. Additionally, he did not write at all the law of refusal after death, except regarding his daughter-in-law who refused the levir; she is forbidden to his father because she appears at the time of the fall as his daughter-in-law. It is possible that he relied on this in all matters, and regarding her co-wife, it is obvious to him that she is permitted, and this requires further study. Similarly, the law is if she wishes to refuse the marriage to his paternal brother in order to allow her co-wife to undergo levirate marriage—this is forbidden according to the first opinion (Maharam there, who upholds the reading "her co-wife" and explains thus, and the Gra there has many objections to this, and his main objection is from the fact that we hold the co-wife of a secondary relation is permitted. We have already explained this, and according to Rashal and the Gra, also in the Rif, the co-wife [is permitted]).

It has already been explained that the co-wife of a definite sotah (a woman suspected of adultery) is exempt from chalitzah (the ceremony releasing a widow from levirate marriage) and yibbum (levirate marriage), while the co-wife of a doubtful sotah must perform chalitzah but cannot perform yibbum, and her co-wife may perform yibbum. According to this, there is a doubt because we hold that just as she is forbidden to her husband, she is also forbidden to her paramour. If the paramour transgressed and married her and then died, what is her status regarding chalitzah and yibbum, and similarly, what is the status of her co-wife? (Maggid Mishneh, Hilchot Sota, Chapter 6, Halacha 19) From the Yerushalmi Sotah (beginning of Chapter 5), it seems that they have the same law, as it is taught there: just as she is forbidden to the brother of her husband, so too she is forbidden to the brother of her paramour. Look there, and its intention is when the paramour married her and then died (ibid.). And it seems so because regarding the paramour it is also written "and she is defiled" as explained there in the Mishnah.

One who died and did not leave a definite wife at all but rather a doubtful wife, such as if he had a doubtful betrothal or a doubtful divorce, in the case of doubtful betrothal he may perform levirate marriage or chalitzah, for if there was no betrothal, she is a stranger to him and he is permitted to her. However, in the case of doubtful divorce, she performs chalitzah and does not enter into levirate marriage, for perhaps the divorce is valid and she would be the divorced wife of his brother, which is a severe prohibition (karet). And in the Tosefta (Chapter 12) that we learned, all cases of doubt perform chalitzah and do not enter into levirate marriage, it does not refer to doubtful betrothals, and this is explicitly explained in the Gemara (41b). See there.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (108b): If a man divorces his wife and remarries her, she is permitted to the yavam (levirate marriage), and we do not say that at the time she was divorced, she became forbidden to him as his brother's divorced wife, which is a prohibition punishable by karet (spiritual excision). How can she now be permitted? Since at the time of the levirate bond, she was permitted to him, we do not concern ourselves with the previous prohibition, as the primary consideration is the status at the time of the levirate fall. Similarly, if a man divorces an orphan girl and remarries her, meaning he married an orphan girl through rabbinic marriage, divorced her, and remarried her, she is permitted to the yavam. Just as her marriage was rabbinic, so too is her divorce rabbinic (and we need further clarification as mentioned in Siman 141:9, and we must say it is not specific). But if a minor girl who was married by her father—that is a Torah marriage—was divorced as a minor by her father—that divorce is also from the Torah—and he remarried her afterward, those are rabbinic marriages because once she is married, her father has no authority over her, and this is what is called an orphan in her father's lifetime. If she dies while still a minor, or even if she grows up and he did not have relations with her after she grew up, she is prohibited to the yavam because from the Torah she is his brother's divorced wife, and he is liable for karet. According to the Rambam, she is also exempt from chalitzah (ceremonial release from levirate marriage). However, the Tur wrote that she must perform chalitzah, and perhaps his reasoning is that not everyone knows the difference, and they will say that a yevamah (levirate widow) can go out to the marketplace without anything. It is better that her co-wife perform chalitzah and exempt her as well, because if she performs chalitzah, her co-wife will not be exempted by her chalitzah (Beit Shmuel, Siman 22), as her chalitzah is not considered valid as mentioned.

And similarly, the law applies to a hearing woman who became deaf, and when he divorced her, she was a hearing woman who became deaf and then remarried and her husband died, she is forbidden to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) because her divorce is from the Torah and her second marriage is rabbinic. However, if she regained her hearing while married to him and he had relations with her after she regained her hearing, similarly, a minor who matured while married to him and he had relations with her after she matured and then he died, they are permitted to perform yibbum because their marriage then becomes a Torah marriage. For a minor and a deaf-mute have the same law, and all the more so, if he remarried them after they regained their hearing or matured, then even if he did not have relations with them, they are permitted to perform yibbum because the marriage is considered a Torah marriage.

A minor whose divorce is recognized by Torah law but whose return is rabbinic, is forbidden to perform yibbum (levirate marriage). Similarly, a deaf-mute woman in such a situation—her co-wife is permitted to perform yibbum and does not have the same status as a co-wife of an ervah (a woman forbidden to the yavam by Torah law), because by Torah law she is not considered the wife of the deceased, as she is exempt even from chalitzah (the ceremony that releases her from the obligation of yibbum) according to the Rambam, as stated. Therefore, she is not a co-wife at all. This is different from a minor who is an ervah to the yavam, since her co-wife must perform chalitzah and not yibbum, as mentioned at the beginning of Yevamot. There, the ervah status arises due to the inherent relationship to the yavam, such as his daughter or sister-in-law. But here, the ervah status is due to the relationship to the deceased brother. Consequently, if we follow Torah law, she is not an ervah at all since she was already divorced. If we follow the rabbinic ruling, she has returned and is considered his wife, and thus not an ervah to the yavam.

And it appears to me that this reasoning is found in the Jerusalem Talmud (Perek Beis of Shabbos, Halacha Vav), where there is a dispute on this matter, and it states the reasoning of the one who permits in this language: "Regardless of which side you take, her co-wife is permitted." The text concludes: "And it means if you follow the side that the deceased has a property interest in her, which is from the Rabbis that he took her back, then her co-wife is permitted because she is not inherently forbidden to the yavam (levirate husband). And if you follow the side that he has no property interest in her, which is from the Torah, that he has no marital bond with her from the Torah, then her co-wife is also permitted because she is not at all the co-wife of a forbidden relative since she has already been divorced." It is possible that this is the reasoning of the Rif and the Rambam in chapter 6, where they ruled that her co-wife can perform yibbum (levirate marriage). (And in the Gemara there, it is only according to Rabbi Eliezer; see there and examine it well.)

Our early sages (Ramban, Rashba, Rosh, and Nimukei Yosef) provided a different reason for their opinion: because this minor, if she were to grow up under his care, she would herself be subject to yibbum (levirate marriage). Therefore, it is not appropriate to apply the decree of the rival wife due to the arayot (forbidden relationships) as with other minors who are considered arayot, since in her case, there is also a potential for permissibility over time. We do not decree the rival wife due to her, fearing that people might come to perform yibbum with her, because most people are familiar with the fact that the betrothal of a minor orphan is rabbinic in nature.

The opinion of the Ra'avad and the Me'or is that the co-wife (tzarah) is forbidden to undergo levirate marriage (yibbum) just like she herself is, for we decree the co-wife because of her herself. And in the Gemara there, where they permitted the co-wife, it is not according to the halacha, see there. And indeed, in the Jerusalem Talmud, there is a dispute about this, and the conclusion of the Jerusalem Talmud seems to be towards prohibition. However, many Amoraim permit it there. For the halacha, it seems one should be concerned for those who prohibit it. It is puzzling that the Shulchan Aruch in Section 16 did not mention at all the opinion of those who prohibit, whereas the Tur did bring it, see there.

The law regarding a woman who is forbidden to her brother-in-law by a negative commandment, a positive commandment, or as a secondary degree of forbidden relationship. This section contains seventeen paragraphs:

If the yevama (widow) is forbidden to the yavam (brother-in-law) by a negative commandment or a positive commandment, or if she is a secondary degree of forbidden relationship to the yavam, she must perform chalitza (the ceremony of removing the shoe) and not yibbum (levirate marriage). Why does she perform chalitza and not be exempted from chalitza as in the case of a forbidden relationship? Because there is a valid marital bond with her, and the marriage and betrothal are effective with her. Therefore, she is obligated to the yavam. Furthermore, according to Torah law, they are also fit for yibbum because yibbum is a positive commandment, and we hold that a positive commandment overrides a negative commandment. All the more so for secondary prohibitions, which are entirely permissible according to Torah law, but the Sages decreed that they should not perform yibbum, lest he come to have relations with her a second time, which is forbidden. The mitzvah (commandment) is only the first act of intercourse (Rambam, Chapter 6). One might argue, how can we apply the principle of a positive commandment overriding a negative commandment here, given that whenever we can fulfill both, we hold that a positive commandment does not override a negative commandment? However, this matter was questioned in the Talmud, and they answered that chalitza in place of yibbum is not considered a mitzvah at all (Yevamot 21a). The reason is because yibbum is an act of closeness to establish a name for his brother, while chalitza is an act of distancing. Although the Torah allowed him to perform chalitza, the primary mitzvah is closeness. The Torah simply did not want to compel him to do so.

Therefore, if one transgressed and had relations with his yevama (levirate widow) who is prohibited to him due to negative commandments and positive commandments—whether these prohibitions apply to the priesthood or to the congregation of Israel such as a mamzer (illegitimate child) or a nethin (a member of a servile caste) or similar cases, and certainly in the case of a secondary prohibition—she is acquired as a full acquisition and he must divorce her with a get (bill of divorce), and she and all her co-wives are permitted to others since they have been exempted. And if a yevama who is a widow from a marriage was approached by a High Priest, who is commanded against marrying her both by a positive and a negative commandment, her co-wife is not exempted since a positive commandment does not override both a negative commandment and a positive commandment. And since he did not acquire her fully according to Torah law, her co-wife is not exempted until she performs chalitza (a ritual to release her from levirate marriage). However, she herself is exempted since, after all, he had relations with her. This is also implied by the Talmudic language (Yevamot 20a: one says she exempts her co-wife, etc., and see Rashi there, and it requires further study. See what I wrote in paragraph 4, and examine it closely). And we have already explained in Siman 170 that according to the Rambam, she herself is exempted by a deficient chalitza. See there. And certainly by deficient intercourse (see there at the end of Subsection 3).

The co-wives of those who are liable for negative commandments, positive commandments, or secondary forbidden relationships either perform chalitza or yibbum, as the Torah only forbade the co-wife of a forbidden relationship, as it is written "to vex her" regarding the sister of one's wife, which is a case of karet (excision), and from this we derive the laws of co-wives, as explained in Siman 173, but not in these cases. This is also what is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Nimukei Yosef), though I did not find this in the Jerusalem Talmud. In the Tosefta (Chapter 1), we learn the opposite, as it is written there: "In what case are we speaking? In a woman who has no valid betrothal. But in a woman who has valid betrothal, her co-wives perform chalitza and not yibbum." These are the words of the Tosefta. However, in our Talmud (20a), it is clearly permitted, as it says there: "Some say that any prohibition which is a forbidden relationship causes her co-wife to be forbidden, but if it is not a forbidden relationship, her co-wife is not forbidden." See there. It is difficult to understand why the Nimukei Yosef did not bring this Gemara.

And there is a question regarding this matter: according to what was stated, when the mitzvah of yibbum (levirate marriage) involves both a positive commandment and a negative commandment, the positive commandment of yibbum does not override it, even according to Torah law, and she requires chalitzah (the ceremony of release) according to Torah law. And indeed, anyone who is eligible for yibbum is also eligible for chalitzah, and vice versa. And since she is not eligible for yibbum, she should not require chalitzah either. The answer to this is that the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot (B"H"G) wrote (in the laws of forbidden relationships) that the statement of Rav Giddel in the name of Rav is specifically about a widow from marriage (not betrothal). Although, according to Torah law, she is not eligible for yibbum, the Torah still requires chalitzah. The explanation of his words is that in the Gemara (20a), they discussed why those who are forbidden due to negative commandments perform chalitzah and not yibbum, and Rav Giddel explained that the verse states, "And his brother's wife shall ascend to the gate"—the term "his brother's wife" is superfluous. Why does the verse say "his brother's wife"? To teach that there is one yevamah (widow) who is eligible for chalitzah but not for yibbum. The Gemara rejects this and concludes that according to Torah law, yibbum is overridden, but the Rabbis decreed against the first intercourse due to the second intercourse, as stated. And this is what the B"H"G meant: this interpretation applies to those who are subject to both negative and positive commandments together (see the Rashba's commentary there). And according to this, if he has intercourse with her, she is not exempt, which is contrary to Rambam, section 2.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch, in Section 1, write that the chalitzah (ceremony of removing a shoe) of a woman subject to a prohibition (whether a negative commandment, a positive commandment, or a secondary prohibition) does not exempt her co-wife, but the chalitzah of the co-wife exempts her. Their words are based on the Rambam in Chapter 7, who rules that an invalid chalitzah does not exempt the co-wife. And he wrote in Law 10: "It appears to me that this is the law regarding two yevamot (widows awaiting levirate marriage) coming from the same household, and one of them is prohibited to the yavam (levir) due to a secondary prohibition or prohibitions of negative or positive commandments, that if he performs chalitzah with the prohibited one, her co-wife is not released; if he performs chalitzah with the co-wife, the prohibited one is released." This concludes his words. 

They were astonished by this because in the Gemara (20b), it is clearly the opposite. The Gemara brings a Baraita: "A prohibition of mitzvah or sanctity—if he has intercourse with her or performs chalitzah with her, her co-wife is exempted." And it is stated similarly in other places. Some want to say that this is referring to a case where the co-wife is also prohibited like her, and in such a case, even an invalid chalitzah exempts the co-wife, as stated in Siman 170 in a similar context (Beit Shmuel Siman 170, Section 13). However, this does not appear to be the case, and the Rambam should have clarified this. Additionally, the Tosefta (Chapter 6) elucidates the opposite: "It was taught there, if one of them was prohibited, etc., a prohibition of erva (a severe prohibition), and he performed chalitzah with her, he accomplished nothing. If it was a prohibition of mitzvah or sanctity, and he performed chalitzah with her or had intercourse with her, her co-wife is exempted." This concludes his words. It is thus explicitly stated that only she is prohibited, not her co-wife.

Some have explained that the Baraita in the Gemara holds that there is no zika (levirate bond) (Gra, Section 45). According to this opinion, even a deficient chalitzah exempts the co-wife (Tosafot 26b). However, we hold that there is a zika. This too is problematic because if so, the Gemara should have raised this objection to the opinion that holds there is a zika. Nevertheless, without this Baraita, there is a dispute among the Tannaim on this matter (Rabban Gamliel and the Sages, 51a). Furthermore, it is difficult because in the Yerushalmi (Chapter 2, Law 3), it also states that a prohibition of mitzvah or sanctity—if he performs chalitzah with her, her co-wife is exempted. And the Yerushalmi holds (in Chapter 3) that there is a zika.

And there are those who explain that the baraita in the Gemara is dealing with a Torah law (Bach), and this seems to be the primary explanation. Although secondary relationships are primarily rabbinic, it should be understood as follows: the fact that a deficient chalitzah does not exempt her co-wife is a rabbinic stringency. The proof is that the fundamental aspect of this law pertains to the woman who received a get (divorce document) and the woman who received a ma'amar (betrothal declaration), as stated in Siman 170, and this is only rabbinic. This baraita is from the Tosefta we brought, which fundamentally only came to separate this from a forbidden relationship, as we mentioned that in a forbidden relationship, the chalitzah is worthless. In a mitzvah and sanctity, the chalitzah is valid according to the main law, even to exempt her co-wife. It does not deal at all with this stringency that a deficient chalitzah does not exempt her co-wife. This is what Rambam innovated, that it seems to me from reasoning that since they were stringent with a deficient chalitzah that the co-wife is not exempted by it, the chalitzah of a mitzvah prohibition and sanctity is not better than all deficient chalitzot (and this resolves the questions of the Beit Shmuel, subsection 13).

Nevertheless, regarding the law, although in this chapter it follows the opinion of the Rambam, in chapter 170, section 18, it implies that they hold primarily according to those who disagree with him and maintain that an inferior chalitzah (release from levirate marriage) is only considered such when it was subsequently damaged by a get (divorce document) or ma'amar (betrothal) and not when it was originally so, as we explained there in section 8. Additionally, we have explained much about the opinion of the Rambam there with God's help.

And this is the language of the Shulchan Aruch there: "If two yevamot (widows subject to levirate marriage) from one house fell to him, one of whom is forbidden to the yavam (levir) and the other permitted, when he performs yibbum (levirate marriage), he should perform it with the permitted one, and when he performs chalitzah, he should perform it with the forbidden one. And there is an opinion that if he performed chalitzah with the forbidden one, the co-wife is not released," etc. Thus, they wrote the opinion of the Rambam in the name of "there is an opinion," and therefore they were brief here and relied on what was written there, mentioning only the secondary prohibition and not the prohibitions of negative commandments and positive commandments, as they have the same law.

However, when he performs Yibbum (levirate marriage) with the one who is prohibited to him, there is no dispute, as all agree that her co-wife is exempt. And although in the Jerusalem Talmud there is a disagreement about this, nevertheless its conclusion is also that her co-wife is exempt, see there. One should not question, according to the Rambam, why we are more stringent with Chalitza (ceremonial release from levirate marriage) than with Yibbum (and the Gra there raises this difficulty, see there), for it can be simply said that in the case of Chalitza, it is possible to be stringent and also give Chalitza to the permissible one, but in the case of Yibbum it is impossible to say that he should perform Yibbum with the permissible one, and to suggest that he should perform Chalitza with the permissible one would lead to confusion, as people might say that the Yibbum with the prohibited one is invalid and they would come to perform Yibbum with the permissible one, resulting in two sisters-in-law from the same household being married off. And although with intercourse following a divorce or after a declaration of intent to another, they were more stringent than with Chalitza, as explained in the Gemara (50b), there it is a decree for a specific reason as stated there, and we have already explained this in Siman 170, whereas here this decree does not apply, and they did not want to be stringent and require Chalitza after Yibbum. Furthermore, there the confusion was caused by a previous divorce or declaration, as everyone knows that these are rabbinic and will not lead to the confusion of Yibbum with two women from the same household, unlike in the case of a prohibition of a negative commandment or a positive commandment. Also, secondary prohibitions were not changed from the rule of those who are prohibited by negative commandments and positive commandments, and as it is a law of the Torah for the world that secondary prohibitions are derived from the verse "And they shall keep My charge" and they treated it as a Torah law. And since, according to the Torah, she is obligated in Yibbum, therefore if he performs Yibbum, they did not require anything else for her co-wife. And even according to the one who holds that the commandment of Chalitza is preferable, this is because he might not intend it for the sake of the commandment, but after the fact, since he has already performed Yibbum, it is certainly the primary commandment. Therefore, when he performs Yibbum, her co-wife is exempt, and he is obligated to divorce her with a get (bill of divorce). I am very puzzled by the language of the Shulchan Aruch at the end of paragraph 1, which says "If he wants to divorce her, he divorces her with a get," and indeed he is obligated to divorce her. The Tur also writes this, so it seems to me that this is a scribal error. (And according to what I have explained, the difficulties of the Gra in Siman 170 and the difficulties of the Beit Shmuel there are resolved. Study this well.)

A widow who falls to yibbum (levirate marriage), and the deceased husband had held her in a forbidden manner due to her being one of the prohibited relatives (chayavei lavin) or an obligatory mitzvah (aseh) or a secondary prohibition (sheniya), but she is permissible to the yavam (levir), she can perform yibbum. We do not say that since yibbum comes from the brother who died, and he himself held her in a forbidden manner, how can his brother perform yibbum with her? These issues are not connected. Since the marriage (kiddushin) is valid with her, she is eligible for yibbum according to Torah law, and he is required to perform yibbum with her. The prohibition that was on his brother is not on him, except if this yevamah (widow) was from the prohibition of remarrying his divorced wife after she had married someone else, in which case the Sages (Yevamot 11a) said that the yavam is not permitted to perform yibbum with her; rather, she must perform chalitzah (ceremony releasing her from yibbum), and her co-wife either performs chalitzah or yibbum. This is also the ruling of all the poskim (halachic authorities).

The reason it differs from all other prohibitions (lavin) was explained by our Sages in the following manner: "If she became forbidden to him in a permissible state, then when she is in a forbidden state, how much more so?" (Yevamot 3b). The explanation of this is that in all other prohibitions, she was never permitted to the one who would consummate it. Therefore, since the law of yibum (levirate marriage) applies to him, he is permitted to perform yibum. However, in the case of one who remarries his divorced wife, at the time when he married her and even when he divorced her, she was permitted to him. Yet, to the yavam (levir) she was forbidden with a karet prohibition. After she married another, she became forbidden also to her original husband. So how is it possible that by returning to her original husband in a forbidden state where she was previously permitted to him, she should become permitted to the yavam where she was previously forbidden? And indeed, the essence of yibum is through her return, which is in a forbidden state. Therefore, her case is different from all other prohibitions.

The Maggid Mishneh (Chapter 6, Halacha 13) wrote that if [the woman] has a co-wife, the co-wife is exempt through the chalitzah of the one who returns his divorced wife and not through her yibbum. There is a difficulty with this because this only applies to a widow [married] to a High Priest, where there is a positive and negative commandment, but the one who returns his divorced wife is only a negative commandment like all other negative commandments, and from the Torah, she is subject to yibbum. However, his reasoning is simple as the Rashba wrote in his novellae (Yevamot 20b) that one who returns his divorced wife from the Torah is not subject to yibbum but only to chalitzah, based on the verse "and his brother's wife shall go up to the gate," as explained in the name of the Bahag in Section 4 regarding a widow to a High Priest. The reasoning is as explained that it is different from all other negative commandments due to the reasoning in the previous section (and the Taz unnecessarily lengthened on this, and this is the intention of the Bach in Subsection 4, and it is almost explicitly stated in the Maggid Mishneh itself). (And we have already written that it seems that the Rambam does not hold like the Bahag, and regarding one who returns his divorced wife, he did not mention anything.)

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote that the sister of a chalutzah (a woman who underwent the chalitzah ceremony) is rabbinically prohibited. Therefore, if she falls before a yavam (levirate husband), she undergoes chalitzah and not yibbum (levirate marriage). Similarly, her co-wife is rabbinically prohibited and undergoes chalitzah and not yibbum. The reason for this stringency, more than for other rabbinically prohibited marriages where the co-wife is permitted to yibbum, is because the Sages equated a chalutzah to a divorced woman, as in the eyes of the public they are considered equivalent, and the sister of a divorced woman is a complete ervah (forbidden relative). Therefore, they also prohibited the co-wife of the sister of a chalutzah from yibbum, similar to the co-wife of the sister of a divorced woman, who is prohibited from yibbum as the co-wife of an ervah. All the more so, if one of the brothers committed a transgression and married the chalutzah and then died, her co-wife is also prohibited from yibbum.

The sages taught in the Mishnah (Yevamot 31b): Three brothers married to three unrelated women, and one of them died, and the second performed ma'amar (a form of betrothal specific to levirate marriage) with her and then he died. These women should perform chalitzah (a ritual to release a widow from the obligation of levirate marriage) and not yibbum (levirate marriage). As it is stated, "and one of them dies, her yavam (brother-in-law) shall come upon her"—this applies to one who has the bond of one yavam and not to one who has the bond of two yevamim. This is merely a rabbinic support, as the essence of ma’amar is only rabbinic, as explained in Siman 170. Furthermore, if it were Torah-mandated, chalitzah would not be required either (Gemara). Rather, according to Torah law, one would be permitted to perform yibbum with either of them, as each is from a separate household. However, the Rabbis decreed that since the second performed ma'amar with her, she appears as his wife, and it would be like two yevamot from one household, and people might say that one is permitted to perform yibbum with two women from one household.

From a legal standpoint, the stringency should only apply to the woman upon whom the condition of two yibbum bonds (zika) is apparent, and not to her co-wife, meaning the second wife. However, a decree was also made concerning her due to the concern that people might say that with two women from one household, one can perform chalitza with one and then yibbum with the other, just as in this case with the two wives of the second brother—one performs chalitza and one performs yibbum. And after chalitza, it is forbidden by Torah law to perform yibbum. Therefore, they decreed that neither of them should perform yibbum and both should perform chalitza. But if he did not perform ma'amar with her, even though she is bound to the second brother and it appears as though she has the bond of two yibbum obligations, nevertheless, since this is only rabbinically mandated, they did not impose the stringency without performing ma'amar.

And even if he (the second brother) performed ma'amar (a form of betrothal) with her, but then gave her a get (a bill of divorce) and explicitly stated that the get was for his ma'amar, and then died, the third brother is permitted to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) with either of the two (widows), for each one comes from a different household. The ma'amar that the second brother performed is nullified by the get, and it is as if he never performed ma'amar. This is specifically when he stated that the get was for his ma'amar, but if he gave her a get without specifying, she is forbidden to perform yibbum, for the get is considered to cause her harm, but the ma'amar remains in effect. If he were still alive, she would need another get from him for his ma'amar.

It has already been explained in Siman 170 that the intercourse of a minor who is nine years and one day old is akin to the union of an adult. Therefore, if Reuven dies and leaves two brothers, one older and one a minor who is nine years old, and the minor consummates with his yevama (sister-in-law) and then dies, the older brother performs chalitzah (a ceremony releasing her from levirate marriage) and does not perform yibbum (levirate marriage), because she is subject to the bond of two yevamins (brothers), and his intercourse does not establish a full acquisition. However, if the older brother consummates with his yevama and then dies, the third brother performs yibbum, because the bond of the first brother was nullified by the intercourse of the second brother, and she is only subject to the bond of the second brother.

It has already been explained in Siman 44 that a woman who is half-maidservant and half-free and was betrothed to Reuven, and afterward was freed, and then was betrothed to Shimon, requires a get (divorce document) from both of them because there is a doubt whether her betrothal to the first one was completed when she was freed and the second betrothal did not take effect at all, or whether the first betrothal was nullified because she became a different entity and only the second betrothal took effect. Therefore, the Sages said (Gittin 43a): A woman who is half-maidservant and half-free who was betrothed to Reuven, and then was freed and betrothed to Shimon, his brother, and both of them died, and she fell to Levi, their brother, for levirate marriage, she can be married to him. I do not consider her to be a wife of two deceased brothers, which would be akin to having the bond of two yevamim (levirate brothers) upon her, because in any case, she is only the wife of one of them. If Reuven's betrothal was completed upon her being freed, then she is his wife, and Shimon's betrothal did not take effect at all. And if Reuven's betrothal was nullified by her being freed, then she is only Shimon's wife. Therefore, she can be married to Levi in any case. However, if Shimon is not Reuven's brother and is a stranger to him, when they died, Reuven's brothers and Shimon's brothers must perform chalitzah (ceremonial release from levirate marriage) for her because of the doubt, or one of them should first perform chalitzah and then the other can marry her, because if the betrothal of his brother took effect, she is his yevamah (levirate widow), and if Reuven's betrothal took effect, she has already been released by Reuven's brother and is free and permitted to him. But to marry her without chalitzah is forbidden because perhaps she is bound to the other one, and it would be as though a yevamah was married to the public without chalitzah.

A yevama (a widow bound by levirate marriage) who was forbidden to the yavam (levir) at the time of her husband's death and was later permitted. This contains 29 sections:

The Sages said: Any yevama about whom I cannot say at the time of her husband's death that "her yavam shall come upon her" is considered as a brother's wife who has children and is forbidden to him. The explanation is that any yevama who is not suitable for levirate marriage at the time of her husband's death due to a prohibition of ערוה (a forbidden relationship) is forbidden to him forever, even if the prohibition is later removed. For example, if two brothers are married to two sisters, and one of them dies, causing his wife to fall to the other brother, and she is forbidden to him because she is the sister of his wife, even if his wife subsequently dies, making her sister permitted to him after her death, she remains forbidden to him and he is liable to karet (spiritual excision) because at the time of her husband's death she was an ערוה to him. The reason for this is that a brother's wife is an ערוה unless the Torah permitted her to him when her husband dies childless. Since at the time of her husband's death she was an ערוה to him due to another ערוה prohibition, the prohibition of the brother’s wife remains in full force, such that even when the other prohibition is removed, this prohibition of the brother's wife persists.

Not only in a case where at the time of falling to yibbum she was permitted to the general public, but even if she was already bound to this house, such as if they had a third brother to whom she was not prohibited and he performed yibbum, and even if later the wife of the second brother, who was her sister, died, and then the third brother died, which would have been doubly favorable – that she had originally been bound to this house and now, at the time of falling from the third brother to the second, his wife had already died and she fell before him permissibly – nevertheless, since the first time she fell before him it was in prohibition, her status is like a brother's wife who has children and she remains prohibited to him forever. Even if the wife of the second brother died before the third brother married her sister, she is still prohibited to him for the reason explained. Furthermore, even her co-wife is treated as the co-wife of an ervah. For example, if the third brother had another wife who was not prohibited to the second brother, he is also prohibited to the co-wife, just like the co-wife of an ervah, because since she remains prohibited from the first fall as a brother's wife, her status is like an ervah who also prohibits her co-wife and the co-wife of her co-wife, and this remains the law as explained in the laws of ervah in Siman 173.

Not only do we follow the moment of the fall (when the brother dies) to determine a prohibition, but even for permissibility, if at the moment of the fall she was permitted to him, even though she later became prohibited to him, if the prohibition is removed, he is allowed to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) because at the moment of the fall she was permitted to him. How so? If there were three brothers, two of whom were married to two sisters, and one of them died, and his wife became bound (in levirate marriage) to the third brother who was not married to the sister, and before he had a chance to perform yibbum, the second brother who was married to the other sister died, resulting in both women becoming prohibited to the third brother since he now faced two sisters bound by levirate ties. If the wife of the second brother then died, the first woman reverts to being permissible to him, even though she was prohibited in the interim, because she was permitted to him at the moment of the fall. However, if the wife of the first brother died, the second woman is not permitted to him because at the moment of her fall she was prohibited to him, even though the prohibition was only due to the levirate bond, she remains permanently prohibited.

If two sisters fall before him from two brothers, what should he do to permit them to marry others? It is impossible to release them without anything, for she is not exactly the sister of his wife, as each one is only bound to him (zokukato) and not his wife, since he has not married her yet. Consequently, it is understood that he is obligated to perform chalitzah for both of them. However, if they have co-wives, he should perform chalitzah for the co-wives and not for the sisters, because the chalitzah of the sisters is considered a weak chalitzah and does not exempt the co-wives (Yevamot 27a), as stated in Siman 170.

If two sisters fall before him (for levirate marriage) from two (deceased) brothers, if there is another brother, there is an easy solution: the first can undergo yibbum (levirate marriage), meaning that one of the brothers performs chalitzah (ritual release) for the second sister, and the first sister is permitted. For what difference does it make if the second one died or if she underwent chalitzah? After all, even with chalitzah, her bond is removed, and the first one can return to being permitted. However, initially, they prohibited doing this as a decree, lest they first perform chalitzah for the first sister and then do yibbum with the second, since not everyone is aware of the difference between them. This is a complete prohibition, for the second one was forbidden at the time of her fall, just as she would not be permitted by the death of the first one. But after the fact, if they performed chalitzah for the second one, the other brother is permitted to the first one. This is what the sages taught in the Mishna (beginning of Chapter 3): “Four brothers, two of whom are married to two sisters, and the married ones die—these (the sisters) perform chalitzah and do not undergo yibbum.” And we do not say initially to perform chalitzah for the second and yibbum for the first because of the decree, as mentioned (28a). And know that what we said, that the first one is permitted to undergo yibbum with the other brother, this is according to the one who holds that an invalid chalitzah does not need to be repeated with all the brothers to permit herself, as we wrote in Siman 170. For those who hold that she needs chalitzah from all the brothers, this is an invalid chalitzah since she is the sister of his levirate bond. And since she also undergoes chalitzah with the second brother, how can he perform yibbum with her sister, for she would then be the sister of his chalutzah (Beit Shmuel, Subsection 3).

And similarly, if among the brothers there is one for whom the first yevama (widow subject to levirate marriage) is forbidden (as an ervah), and consequently, he is permitted to the second yevama, for she is not the sister of his zekkuka (the woman bound to him by levirate bond), since the ervah is not bound to him, and he performs yibbum (levirate marriage) with the second yevama, the first yevama becomes permitted again, and one of the brothers is allowed to perform yibbum with her. However, if one of the brothers for whom the last yevama is an ervah performs yibbum with the first yevama, the last yevama remains forbidden to all the brothers because she was forbidden at the time of the fall (when the obligation for levirate marriage occurred), and she requires chalitzah (levirate release) from one of the brothers or more, according to the opinions explained in Siman 170 regarding invalid chalitzah. If he does not perform yibbum with the first yevama, he performs chalitzah with her, and all the other brothers perform chalitzah with both of them and do not perform yibbum because of the reason explained.

Two brothers married to two sisters, and both died, and it is not known who died first. They have other brothers, but it is impossible for either of the brothers to perform levirate marriage (yibbum) with either of the sisters because the obligation of levirate marriage (zika) falls upon both sisters, and each one is the sister of his levirate bond. Therefore, they must perform chalitzah (a ceremony releasing them from the levirate bond) and cannot perform yibbum, as explained. Even if one of the sisters was forbidden to one of the brothers by a negative commandment (lav) or a positive commandment (aseh), and certainly in the case of a rabbinic prohibition (issur shniya), they must perform chalitzah and cannot perform yibbum, for a prohibition of a lav or aseh does not override the levirate bond. However, if one of the sisters was an ervah (a woman forbidden due to a severe incest prohibition) to one of the brothers, then the other sister is permitted to him; if he wishes, he can perform chalitzah, and if he wishes, he can perform yibbum, for his levirate bond does not fall upon both sisters, as there is no levirate bond with the ervah. There is a significant point in this law: even though it is not known who died first, we do not say that after one sister has performed chalitzah, the other sister becomes permitted, for perhaps she (the one who performed chalitzah) was the first to fall to levirate marriage, and thus the yevamah (sister-in-law) who was permitted and then forbidden and then permitted again, as explained, is not considered so because there is doubt in the matter. For perhaps she (the one who performed chalitzah) is the latter, and it is a doubt of a Torah prohibition. Even though this is not his wife's sister but rather the sister of his levirate bond, since we hold that there is zika (a levirate bond) (see Tosafot 27b s.v. "aval").

The language of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch is as follows: If there are four brothers, and two of them are married to two sisters, and the ones married to the sisters die simultaneously or one after the other before they had the chance to perform the levirate marriage (yibbum) with the first, both sisters perform chalitzah and do not perform yibbum, as it is impossible for either of them to perform yibbum due to the prohibition of marrying the sister of one’s zika (levirate bond). If they had already married them, they are not removed from them. These are the words of the Tur, and in Shulchan Aruch, Section 3, it is written in this manner: If they had already married each one of the sisters, they are removed from them, and there is one who says they are not removed. These are the words, and in Rambam, Chapter 7, it is written: If they had already married them, they are removed. Indeed, this is proven in the Gemara (28a). The words of the Tur are perplexing, and therefore, there is one who says it is a scribal error (Bach). However, also in Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, he ruled similarly that they are not removed, but in his Code, he retracted. Therefore, it appears that the Tur holds that they are not removed. His reasoning is that even though it is explained in the beginning of Chapter 3 that the Tanna Kamma holds they should be removed, and Rabbi Eliezer holds it is a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, but in Eduyot, Chapter 5, Rabbi Eliezer lists it among the stringencies of Beit Hillel, and Abba Shaul in Yevamot (28a) holds that Beit Hillel is lenient. The Ra'avad wrote there in Eduyot, in the Gemara in Yevamot, it is reversed, etc. Therefore, the law is that if they had already married them, they maintain them. These are the words of the Tur. Refer to Tosefot Yom Tov at the beginning of Chapter 3 of Yevamot and examine it well.

According to the ruling of the Rambam, even in the previous case, when it is not known who died first, if they preceded and married, we take [the woman] away from them (Maggid Mishneh). However, according to the Talmudic discussion there, it is explained that from the second husband, we do not take her away, because there is doubt in the matter; perhaps the first one performed levirate marriage with the second wife, and she is the first one, making her a yevama (levirate widow) who was permitted, then forbidden, and then permitted again (Beit Shmuel, subsection 4).

They further wrote: If one of them is forbidden to one of the brothers-in-law due to the prohibition of erva (a forbidden relationship), he is permitted with the other, for the erva is not bound to him, and it turns out that only one is bound to him. The second brother-in-law is forbidden to both. If one of them is forbidden to this one due to erva and the other is forbidden to the second due to erva, the one forbidden to this one is permitted to that one, and the one forbidden to that one is permitted to this one, for each is only bound to one. However, if they are only forbidden to them due to a prohibition of a negative commandment (lo ta'aseh) or a positive commandment (aseh), and certainly if it is a secondary prohibition, the bond is not annulled from them, and they must perform chalitzah and not yibbum. End of quotation, and it is straightforward.

They further wrote: If there are three brothers, two of whom are married to two sisters, and one of the husbands of the sisters dies, and afterward, the husband of the second sister dies, resulting in both sisters falling before the third brother (for levirate marriage), both are forbidden to him because they are rivals to each other in their levirate bond. Therefore, they must perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing them from levirate marriage) and not yibbum (levirate marriage). (We have already explained this.) If he performed ma'amar (a form of betrothal) with the first sister, and afterward the second sister falls before him, he must release the one with whom he performed ma'amar with a get (divorce document) and chalitzah, and the second one with chalitzah. And the reasons for these matters have already been explained in Siman 170 with the help of Heaven.

Three brothers, two of whom are married to two sisters and one is married to a non-relative. The one married to the non-relative dies, and one of the brothers married to the sisters marries his wife, and then he dies. The wives fall before the second brother married to the sisters for levirate marriage. The first wife, who was previously married, is considered a complete forbidden relative (ervah) to him, and the second wife, who could have been taken in levirate marriage, must go out because she is the co-wife of an ervah and is exempt even from chalitzah. However, if he has not yet taken her in levirate marriage, even if he has performed ma'amar (a preliminary act of levirate marriage) with her, she requires chalitzah because she is not yet considered a co-wife of an ervah and cannot be taken in levirate marriage, even if ma'amar has not yet been performed with her. She is considered the co-wife of a sister-in-law under bond (zika), and likewise, conversely, if one of the brothers married to the sisters dies first, and afterward the brother married to the non-relative dies, she performs chalitzah and not levirate marriage for this reason.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah: Three brothers, two of whom are married to two sisters and one is married to an unrelated woman. If one of the husbands of the sisters divorces his wife and the brother married to the unrelated woman dies, and then the divorcing brother marries the widow, and then he dies, this is the case they spoke of when they said: In all cases where they died or were divorced, their co-wives are permitted. And the Gemara deduces: The reason is that the husband of the sisters divorced his wife first and then the brother married to the unrelated woman died, so that the co-wife never even became bound by levirate bond (Rashi). However, if the brother married to the unrelated woman died first and then one of the husbands of the sisters divorced his wife and then died, she is prohibited to the third brother.

According to the view of Rashi and Tosafot, it is specifically when the divorcee marries the foreign woman and then dies that she is forbidden to the third brother, because she was the rival wife of the forbidden relation prior to the divorce, and her connection derives from the divorcing brother. If he did not marry her, her connection is not from him but from his first brother. And even though she was also bound to the divorcing brother, nevertheless, the power of his bond is not as strong as when he dies, compared to when he is alive, since each one could have married her (see Mishneh Torah, Chapter 6, in the name of the Rashba). And if you ask why she is allowed to marry him, since she is the rival wife of his wife's sister through the bond, it can be said that it is not considered the rival wife of the wife's sister through the bond unless he married her and then died, causing both to fall before the third brother from the second brother. But when he is alive, this is not the case (Tosafot). And the explanation of the matter is: how can we forbid the foreign woman to any of the brothers on account of the closeness of their wives, for she is only fit for one of them? Therefore, the one who marries her indicates that the foreign woman was bound to him from the death of the first brother. Therefore, when he divorces his wife after marrying this one, the foreign woman was, for one moment, the rival wife of his wife—that is, until the divorce. Consequently, when he subsequently dies, this foreign woman is forbidden to the third brother because she was, for one moment, the rival wife of his wife's sister. However, in section 20, we explained a different intention in this matter, see there.

And there is still a question: What does it matter that she (the foreign woman) was the co-wife of his wife's sister until the divorce? After all, when this second man died, she had already been divorced, and at the time of the second man's death, she was not the co-wife of his wife. And we hold that death determines (the obligation of yibbum) and not the initial marriage. For in the case of the forbidden relative herself, if he divorced her and then died, her co-wife is permitted to undergo yibbum, as stated in Siman 173. The bond of the forbidden relative is not stronger than the forbidden relative herself.

Indeed, from the words of Rashi of blessed memory, it is implied there that what we said, that if he married her and then divorced her, she is forbidden, is not according to the final conclusion, for we hold that death determines (the status), but according to the one who maintains that the initial marriage determines. However, according to the law that death determines, even if he married her and then divorced her, she is permitted and not forbidden to the third man unless the second husband died and did not divorce his wife at all. Since we hold that there is a bond (zika), it is as if she also came from the second husband, and even if the second did not marry her, she is forbidden to the third because she is the co-wife of his wife's sister by bond (zika). (So wrote Rashi to explain Rava there in the commentary "This is..." for Rava holds that death determines, etc. End quote. And so it appears from the Gra in section 18, see there, and in the Beit Shmuel in section 8, and the Tosefot Yom Tov there did not write so, see there and examine thoroughly).

But Maimonides, of blessed memory, in Chapter 6, Law 25, did not rule this way. His words are as follows: "Three brothers, two of whom are married to two sisters and one is married to a stranger. If the one married to the stranger dies, and afterwards one of those married to the sisters dies, the stranger performs chalitzah and does not undergo yibbum, because she is the co-wife of the sister of his wife by the bond of his brother who died last. Furthermore, even if one of those married to the sisters divorced his wife after the one married to the stranger died, and then the one who divorced dies, the stranger performs chalitzah and does not undergo yibbum, since she became the co-wife of the sister of his wife by the bond for a moment. For if she were to undergo yibbum, it might lead to permitting her even if the one who died last hadn't divorced his wife. And why didn’t they decree this concerning marriage? Because the prohibition of the co-wife of a forbidden relation in marriage is known to all, and they will not permit the co-wife if the forbidden relation was not divorced. But the prohibition of the co-wife of a forbidden relation by the bond is not known to all, and they might permit the co-wife even if the forbidden relation was not divorced." Thus are his words.

And this distinction is not necessary, because it is simple to distinguish that regarding a forbidden relation (erva), since he divorced her before she fell before the yavam (levirate husband), the divorce is effective for her, since when the co-wife falls before the yavam, she falls in a permissible state. However, here, regarding an outsider (not a relative), since at the time of falling, she falls with the prohibition of levirate bond (zika), the divorce does not take effect for her. And the Rif, of blessed memory, wrote this distinction in Chapter 3, where he wrote that this distinction is more reasonable than the previous distinction.

It appears to me that the Rambam did not accept the distinction made by the Rif, for indeed, one can question both according to their view and according to Rashi's view, what prohibition there is in the warning to the third brother when the second brother has not taken her in warning, even if he has not divorced his wife at all. In what way is the warning considered the co-wife of his wife's sister by virtue of zika (levirate bond)? After all, the second brother could have taken her in marriage, and she would not have been forbidden to him due to the zika of the co-wife of his wife's sister from the third brother. Similarly, the third brother could have taken her in marriage, and she would not have been forbidden to him due to the zika of the co-wife of his wife's sister from the second brother. So why now, when one of them dies, is she forbidden to the remaining brother? As I wrote in paragraph 14, the zika of the second brother does not have greater strength when he dies than his zika had while he was alive, as each one could have taken her in marriage.

And it must be said that the reasoning is certainly so: when both are alive, he is permitted to perform yibbum (levirate marriage) with one of them. But when the yibbum is after the death of one of them, the other woman seems to be as if she is bound to the deceased brother, since the third brother waits with his yibbum until the second one dies, and did not perform yibbum before. It shows that she was bound to the second one, and therefore the third brother did not perform yibbum during his lifetime, and when he died, he performed yibbum. And this is certainly like the co-wife of his wife's sister in [the context of] zika (levirate bond) (and this is the intention of the Tosafot in section 14, and not as it is written there). According to this, it is impossible to say the reasoning of the Rif that at the time of the fall (i.e., the requirement for yibbum) she falls before him in a state of prohibition due to the zika, for there is no prohibition of zika as long as both are alive. Therefore, the Rambam needed the first reasoning, that because it is a light prohibition, they might come to permit it even when he did not divorce her. However, according to Rashi, it is only forbidden if he did not divorce her, and according to the Rambam, even if he did divorce her, it is still forbidden due to the decree lest they permit it even without a divorce.

Some of our Rabbis hold that, in truth, if the second brother did not marry the widow and he died, the third brother is permitted to perform Yibbum (levirate marriage) even if the second brother did not divorce his wife at all. This is based on the principle we explained that his power (to cause prohibition) is not stronger in death than it was in life, as the third brother could have performed Yibbum. The prohibition is only when the second brother married the widow and then died. In such a case, if he did not divorce his wife, she is considered a full-fledged co-wife of a prohibited relative (Tzaras Ervah). However, even if he divorced her, and even if he did so before marrying the widow, the widow is still considered as her co-wife from the moment of the first husband's death. This is because it later became clear that she was bound to him (the second brother) for Yibbum, and therefore, even though in the case of a full-fledged prohibited relative, if he divorced before his death, the co-wife is permitted, in this case, they were stringent because she fell into the prohibition of being bound to the sister of his wife when the first husband died. This is the opinion of the Ra’avad and the Rashba, of blessed memory, and they wrote that this is also the opinion of the Rif, of blessed memory, whose intention is specifically when he married her.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 8 have a different approach to this matter and hold the opposite view. If the second brother marries the stranger, even if he subsequently divorces his wife after marrying her and then dies, the stranger is permitted to the third brother. Their reasoning is straightforward, similar to the established law that in any case of a co-wife of a forbidden relation, if the forbidden relation is divorced and then the brother dies, the co-wife is permitted. Here too, once the second brother marries the stranger, she becomes a bona fide co-wife of a forbidden relation concerning the third brother. This is taught in the Mishnah: "And all of them, if they are divorced, their co-wives are permitted." The prohibition applies when he did not marry her, and the brother of the stranger dies before he divorces his wife. Even if he divorces her afterward and then dies, the stranger is forbidden to the third brother because the second brother's wife, who is the sister of the third brother's wife, was her co-wife in potential. They differentiate between when both are alive and when one has died, as explained in section 20. Thus, all opinions are clarified. (And this is what the Tur and Shulchan Aruch mean by "even if he did not marry the stranger," etc., which implies all the more so if he married her and did not divorce her at all, and the Tosefot Yom Tov unnecessarily wrote that the Tur's statements contradict each other. Their intention is clear as I have written, and what the Rosh wrote also does not provide proof as his words are ambiguous. Investigate this thoroughly.)

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that the same applies if he was married to a non-Jewish woman and had children; she is forbidden to him because of the bond of his brother's wife who has children. In other words, if three brothers were married to three unrelated women, and one of them had children and then the brother without children died, and subsequently the brother with children died, the first woman is forbidden to the third brother. This is similar to the previous law where if two brothers were married to two sisters and one to a non-Jewish woman, and the brother married to the non-Jewish woman died, even though each brother could have married her, if one of the brothers married to the sisters subsequently died, the non-Jewish woman is also forbidden to the third brother because she appears as the co-wife of his wife's sister through the bond, as explained. Similarly, even though initially each brother could have married her, if subsequently the brother with children died, the first woman is forbidden to the third brother because she appears bound to the dead brother, and his wife is forbidden to him because he has children, and thus this woman is also forbidden as her co-wife.

Nevertheless, this ruling is perplexing to me. Besides the fact that it does not align with all the opinions we have explained, it is difficult for me to understand what example it provides for the previous ruling. In that case, the co-wife appears as the co-wife of his wife's sister, for his wife's sister is also bound in the matter of levirate marriage, except that she is prohibited, and the co-wife is like her co-wife, as we have written. But here, where he has children, his wife is not bound in the matter of levirate marriage, for the term 'bound' applies only when he did not leave children, as this is the essence of the levirate marriage passage. However, in the case of someone who has children, what relevance does he have in the matter of levirate marriage? Therefore, how does she appear bound to him? Moreover, the Talmud and the poskim did not omit mentioning such a common ruling, that if one died without children and had brothers, and in the meantime another brother died who had children, the first wife would be forbidden to the remaining brothers. This requires further investigation.

It has already been explained in Siman 172 regarding the laws of yibbum (levirate marriage) for a minor or a deaf-mute, which are rabbinic marriages, how their laws apply. Now we will explain their laws in relation to the prohibitions of incest in yibbum. If two brothers, both of sound mind, are married to two sisters who are minors or deaf-mutes, and one of them dies, the wife must leave because of the prohibition of being the sister of a wife, since the marriages of both are equal. If one is of sound mind and the other is a deaf-mute, and the husband of the deaf-mute dies, the wife must leave because of the prohibition of being the sister of a wife. If the husband of the one of sound mind dies, he must divorce his wife with a get (bill of divorce), since their marriage is rabbinic, and she is forbidden to him because of the prohibition of being the sister of his wife who fell to him for yibbum according to Torah law. He must release his brother's wife through chalitzah (a ceremony releasing her from the obligation of yibbum), and it is forbidden to perform yibbum with her rabbinically because she is, in any case, the sister of his wife rabbinically.

If there is one sister who is an adult and one who is a minor, and the husband of the minor dies, she must go out due to the prohibition of marrying a wife's sister. If the husband of the adult dies, we instruct the minor to refuse her husband, and the adult sister performs yibbum (levirate marriage). However, with a deaf-mute, this remedy is not applicable. But with a minor, since it is possible for her to refuse, even though it is preferable to avoid refusals, nonetheless, in order to fulfill the mitzvah of yibbum, we instruct her to refuse. And if she does not refuse and grows up with him, even if he cohabits with her after she has grown up, we force him to divorce her since she was prohibited to him when she was a minor, since we hold that there is a bond (zika). This is the ruling in the Talmud (Yevamot 110a, the law follows Rabbi Eliezer). Some say that the Talmud only ruled this way initially, but after the fact, if she grows up and he cohabits with her, the bond is nullified and she is permitted to remain with him (Bach). However, their opinion is not accepted, for even after the fact, since the mitzvah of yibbum applied to him, the yevama (sister-in-law) is not released by the fact that her minor sister has grown up with him (Beit Shmuel 10, according to Rabbi Gershom, who holds that if one betroths the sister of his yevama, the yevama is released, but we do not hold this way).

Two brothers, one of whom is competent and the other is deaf-mute, are married to two sisters who are either both competent or one is deaf-mute and one is competent, with the competent one married to the competent brother. If the deaf-mute brother, who is married to the deaf-mute sister, or the deaf-mute brother who is married to the competent sister, dies, she is released because of the prohibition of "a sister of a wife." If the competent brother, who is married to the competent sister, dies, and his connection is biblical with his brother, and the marriage of the deaf-mute is rabbinic, whether his wife is competent or deaf-mute, the deaf-mute divorces his wife with a get (bill of divorce), because just as the marriage was through signaling, so too is the divorce.
