For the wife of the competent brother, there is no solution, and she is forbidden forever, because the deaf-mute is not fit for chalitzah (the ritual of releasing a widow from levirate marriage), and yibbum (levirate marriage) is forbidden by rabbinic law, since rabbinically she is considered an ervah (forbidden relative) to him as "a sister of his wife." The divorce does not help because at the time she fell to him, she was forbidden to him rabbinically.

Two deaf-mute brothers married to two sisters who are hearing or deaf-mute, or one is deaf-mute and one is hearing; similarly, two deaf-mute sisters married to two brothers who are hearing or deaf-mute, or one is deaf-mute and one is hearing, and one of them dies—[the surviving brother's wife] shall leave because she is the sister of his wife, as their marriages are considered equal. Therefore, if they were strangers to each other, they shall perform yibbum (levirate marriage), and if afterwards they wish to divorce, they shall do so with a get (bill of divorce). All this is explained in Siman 172, see there.

Two brothers, one of whom is fully competent and the other is deaf-mute, and the deaf-mute is married to two fully competent women, one of whom is forbidden to the competent brother (e.g., she is his wife's sister or similar), both women are exempt from chalitza and yibbum because the marriage of the deaf-mute is Rabbinic and his bond is Rabbinic. If both brothers are fully competent and one of them is married to two women, one fully competent and one deaf-mute, and the deaf-mute woman is forbidden to his brother, when the husband with the two wives dies, the competent woman falls to his brother for yibbum. She is not considered a co-wife of a forbidden relation since the marriage of the deaf-mute is Rabbinic, and she is only Rabbinically a co-wife of a forbidden relation. Therefore, the competent woman performs chalitza and does not undergo yibbum (Tosefta Chapter 9). The Rambam wrote in Chapter 7: "Wherever we said two sisters, one of two sisters, or a woman and her daughter, or a woman and her daughter's daughter, and similar cases, the matter is that they are two women, one of whom is a forbidden relation to the other, and it is impossible to marry both because of the forbidden relation." And one must know that in one respect, one's wife's sister is different from all other forbidden relations because all other forbidden relations are prohibited forever, even if the forbidden relation dies, but one's wife's sister is only prohibited during her lifetime, even if she was divorced, and not if she died before falling to yibbum.

Laws regarding doubts in Yibbum and laws of mixtures in Yibbum. This section has seventeen paragraphs:

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (23b): One who betrothed one of two sisters and does not know which one he betrothed, must give a get (divorce document) to each one. It has already been clarified in Siman 41 that even if they were never recognized, meaning that even at the time of betrothal he did not know which one he betrothed, and he could not be with either of them since perhaps she is the sister of his wife, and this would be a betrothal that is not fit for consummation, nevertheless it is considered a betrothal. For we hold that betrothal which is not fit for consummation is still considered a betrothal (and the Talmud there which establishes that they were recognized and later became mixed up, this is according to Rava, but we hold according to Abaye, as the Rif explains).

We also learned: If a man dies and he has one brother, he performs chalitzah (a form of releasing a widow from the obligation of yibbum, or levirate marriage) with both of them, because it is not known which one is his yevamah (the widow awaiting yibbum). He cannot perform chalitzah with one and yibbum with the other, because the sister of his chalutzah (the woman he released through chalitzah) is forbidden to him by rabbinic law while she is alive. He also cannot perform yibbum first, because perhaps she is not his yevamah, and he would be engaging with the sister of his zukkah (the widow awaiting yibbum), which is like his wife (Rashi). If he has two brothers, one performs chalitzah and one performs yibbum. This means that one brother first performs chalitzah with one of the widows, and the second brother, if he wishes, performs yibbum with the second widow. If she is his yevamah, it is proper, and if she is her sister, he does not engage with the sister of his zukkah, as the chalitzah has removed the zukkah (there). And there is no need to decree that perhaps he will perform yibbum first before chalitzah is done for her, because for this reason, there is no decree. Even if this happens, perhaps the zukkah will come to him, and although it is forbidden to do so, we do not decree because of this (see Tosafot there 24: d.h. "if"). It is also possible to say that according to the opinion that the mitzvah of yibbum precedes chalitzah, it is proper to do so. First, one brother performs chalitzah for one widow, and afterwards, the second brother performs yibbum with the other widow, because perhaps the yevamah will come to him and he will fulfill the mitzvah of yibbum (as it is said in Yevamot 98b: see there).

We also learned: If they [the brothers] preceded and married [the sisters], we do not remove them from them. This means that if a man has two brothers and each one married one of the sisters before consulting the court, we do not remove [the wives] from them. Each one can claim, "I married the one who was required [to me] or her sister after she was married to the second [brother]." This means that it is possible that both of them married permissibly: the one who married first was the required one, and the second was her sister. Alternatively, it could be the opposite, that the first one married the sister of the required one at that time; this would certainly be forbidden. But once his brother came and performed levirate marriage with the second, who was his yevamah (levirate widow), the bond of the other one retroactively dissolves. (There)

The Tosafot and the Rosh wrote that specifically in this case, they do not remove her from him because one can say that each one did not commit a prohibition as was said. But if one marries the sister of his yevama, he must certainly divorce her since he certainly engaged in a prohibited act. And even according to the opinion explained in Siman 158 that they do not remove her, this is when he betrothed her first and did not yet engage in a prohibited act, as the bond is dissolved through betrothal as explained there. But if he engaged with her without betrothal, since the intercourse was prohibited, she is removed from him (Tosafot).

And behold, the Tur also wrote this, and according to this, it contradicts itself with what it says in Siman 175 about four brothers, where two are married to two sisters and they die, that they perform chalitzah and not yibum, because each one encounters the sister of his zeka. And the Tur wrote there that if they went ahead and married, we do not remove them from their wives. Therefore, the later authorities wrote that it is a textual error in the Tur (Beit Yosef and Bach). And we explained there in Section 8 that there is no textual error and that the Rambam wrote similarly in his commentary on the Mishnah, and this is also the ruling of the Ra'avad in Ediyot. Nevertheless, it can be said that there is no contradiction here and it is not similar to the aforementioned case. Here it discusses encountering the sister of his zeka without the mitzvah of yibum, but in the name of the mitzvah of yibum, it applies to each one. Although initially it is forbidden because of the sister of the zeka, nevertheless, if the prohibition was transgressed and the second one was married through yibum, the mitzvah of yibum is fulfilled, and therefore, we do not remove her from him. This is not the case here; even if the prohibition was transgressed, there is no mitzvah here at all, and therefore, we remove her from him.

Some say that since we learn in the Mishnah this law that if they preceded and married, we do not remove [the wife] from them, whether it is two brothers or one brother. This implies that for one brother, if he performed chalitzah (the ceremony of releasing) with one of them and married the other, he must divorce her even post facto, because perhaps he married the sister of his chalutzah. And although the prohibition of the sister of a chalutzah is rabbinic and is a rabbinic doubt, they still prohibited it even post facto because they decreed the sister of a chalutzah due to the sister of a divorced woman, which is a severe prohibition with karet (spiritual excision). Therefore, they strengthened their decree even in a case of doubt and post facto when there is only a possibility that she is prohibited to him (Nimukei Yosef). And all the more so if he initially married one and then performed chalitzah with the other or did not perform chalitzah at all (see Beit Shmuel, section 1).

The Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch also wrote that what is stated in the Mishnah—if they (the brothers) went ahead and married (the widows), they are not removed from them—this applies when they married before they asked the court, as implied by the term "went ahead," meaning they acted before asking (and this is also apparent from Rashi). However, if they asked the court and the court instructed them that first one brother should perform the chalitzah (ceremony of release) for one widow, and then the second brother should marry the second widow, but they both went ahead and married, they are to be removed from them because they transgressed the court's directive.

We also learned: If two men betrothed two sisters, and each one does not know which one he betrothed, this one gives two bills of divorce, and that one gives two bills of divorce. If one of them dies and he has a brother, and the other one dies and he has a brother, each brother performs chalitzah (a ceremony to release a widow from levirate marriage) with both women, because each one is prohibited from performing yibbum (levirate marriage) lest he marries the sister of his zeka (woman bound by levirate ties) (Rashi). If one has one brother and the other has two brothers, the single brother performs chalitzah with both, and the two brothers, one performs chalitzah and the other performs yibbum. First, the one performs chalitzah with her, and then the other performs yibbum, because in any case, if she is his yevamah (widow awaiting levirate marriage), it is fine, and if not, the levirate bond is removed from her by the preceding chalitzah. If they went ahead and married them, they are not removed from them as explained. And know that it is stated in the Gemara (24a) that in all cases we learned here, if they went ahead and married, they are not removed from them, even if both are priests (kohanim), because the prohibition of a chalutzah (a woman released from levirate marriage) to a priest is rabbinic, and they did not decree in the case of a doubtful chalutzah. This is not similar to what is stated in section 6, where they decreed the sister of a chalutzah because of the sister of a divorcee, even in doubt. And if so, why do we not decree for the priests because of a divorcee? It can be said that it is not the same because the sister of a divorcee is an ervah (forbidden relationship) and punishable by karet, but a divorcee to a priest is only a negative commandment. Therefore, they were not stringent in the case of a doubtful chalutzah because of a doubtful divorcee, since even the definite case is only a negative commandment.

If this one has two brothers and that one has two brothers, the brother of this one performs chalitzah (the ceremony releasing a yevamah from levirate marriage) with one woman, and the brother of that one performs chalitzah with one woman. Then the brother of this one marries the one who underwent chalitzah from the other, and the brother of that one marries the one who underwent chalitzah from the first. In any case: if this woman was his yevamah, he is properly marrying her, for his brother performed chalitzah not with her but with her sister, who was not his yevamah, and it means nothing. And if she is not his yevamah, he is properly marrying her, for she is a stranger, and there is no issue of "sister of his yevamah" because his brother performed chalitzah with her sister who was his yevamah, and the bond is broken. And if there is a concern of "yevamah going to the marketplace," she has already performed chalitzah with her husband's brother (Rashi).

If two brothers of one man came forward and performed chalitzah (a ritual to release a widow from the obligation of levirate marriage) with both women, because they did not know which one was the yevamah (the widow subject to levirate marriage), the other two brothers should not marry one of them and the other marry the other, because the first one may end up marrying the sister of his zekuah (the one he is bound to). Instead, one brother should first perform chalitzah with one of them, and then the second brother should marry the other one. In any case (m'manavshach), if she is his yevamah, it's fine, and if she is not his yevamah, he has not encountered the sister of his zekuah, for his brother has already performed chalitzah with his yevamah. And there is no concern of yevamah to the market (marrying someone else), because she has already undergone chalitzah from her husband's brother, as she has already undergone chalitzah from all of them.

And if these last two (brothers) preceded and married after the Chalitzah of the first two (brothers) and did not come to ask in the Beit Din (rabbinical court), we do not remove (the women) from them. For here, there is only a doubt regarding the prohibition of a sister of a Yevama (levirate bond) in the first marriages of these two (brothers). Because it can be said that it was proper for both of them: the first (brother) married his Yevama, and the second (brother) married an unrelated woman (who was already released from the levirate bond by Chalitzah from the first brothers). And even if it happened the other way around, that the first (brother) married the sister of his Yevama, nonetheless, since the second (brother) came and performed Yibum (levirate marriage), the bond was removed from him, and his wife became permitted to him. And what was done improperly, was done (Rashi).

If a woman's husband went overseas, and they heard that he died, and she remarried based on the testimony of witnesses or the decision of a court, as stated in section 17, and afterwards her first husband, whom the witnesses had falsely testified about or had mistakenly thought was dead, returned and both her first husband and the second husband died, the brothers of each husband must perform chalitzah (a form of levirate dissolution) and not yibbum (levirate marriage). The brother of the first husband performs chalitzah according to Torah law but does not perform yibbum by rabbinic decree (Gemara 91a) because the Sages imposed a penalty for her not being meticulous in verifying the testimony about her husband's death. The brother of the second husband performs chalitzah by rabbinic decree because, according to Torah law, she is not considered his brother's yevamah (levirate widow) at all, since the marriage of his brother was not valid. However, the Sages required chalitzah to prevent people from saying that the first husband divorced her and the second husband married her, and thus neither yibbum is performed by Torah law nor by rabbinic law. But her co-wife may undergo yibbum with the brother of the first husband, as stated in section 173.

A woman had children and her daughter-in-law also had children. Both she and her daughter-in-law each gave birth to two boys in hiding, and the children got mixed up and grew up. They married women, and then the daughter-in-law's sons died. The sons of the daughter-in-law must perform chalitzah (the ritual of removing a shoe) for both of the widows first and not yibbum (levirate marriage), because each widow is in doubt whether she is the wife of his brother, which is permitted to him, or the wife of his father's brother, which is forbidden to him as a close relative. However, the sons of the elder woman have a different rule. After the sons of the daughter-in-law have performed chalitzah, they may perform either chalitzah or yibbum, because in any case, if she is the wife of his brother, he is obligated to perform yibbum, and if she is the wife of the daughter-in-law's son, she is the wife of his nephew and permitted to him after chalitzah has already been performed. This same reasoning applies to each case, of course.

And if the definite sons of the elderly woman and of the bride have died, and the doubtful ones remain, the doubtful ones to the wives of the elderly woman's sons perform chalitzah and do not perform yibbum, since each one is a possible wife of his father's brother. However, for the wives of the bride's sons, initially one of the doubtful ones performs chalitzah, and afterward, the second performs yibbum regardless. For if the one who performed chalitzah is the son of the bride, then he has performed chalitzah for his brother's wife, and therefore the second doubtful one is the son of the elderly woman and is permitted to marry his brother's wife after she has been released from yibbum. And if the one who initially performed chalitzah is the son of the elderly woman and thus performed chalitzah for his brother's wife and did nothing, then the second doubtful one is the son of the bride, and he performs yibbum with his brother's wife.

The woman who did not wait three months after her husband's death or after her divorce and married another man and gave birth, and it is not known whether the child is from the first husband and was born at nine months, or from the second husband and was born at seven months, and she had children from both the first and second husbands, and the doubt increased, and he married a woman and died. The children from the first and second husbands perform chalitzah (the ceremony of release) and do not perform yibbum (levirate marriage) because each one is in doubt whether he is his brother from the mother but not from the father, and there is a penalty of karet (spiritual excision) upon him. Similarly, the doubt applies to their wives; he performs chalitzah and not yibbum for the same reason. If each of the first and second husbands had a son from another woman and they died, this doubtful son performs chalitzah or yibbum for their wives. If he is his brother from his father, he performs chalitzah or yibbum for his yevamah (widow awaiting levirate marriage), and if he is not his brother, she is a stranger to him and is permitted to him since she has no other levirate tie. If the doubtful son died and one of the certain sons of the two brothers performs chalitzah first, then the second can perform yibbum, because in either case, whether she is his brother's widow, she is his yevamah, and if not, she is a stranger to him and has already been released by chalitzah from the brother who is certainly her yavam (levir). Similarly, when they died and each had many sons from another woman, one of the certain sons performs chalitzah first, and then the doubtful son can marry her for the reason explained.

Five women, each of whom had a known son, gave birth in a hidden place, and the babies got mixed up. The children grew up, got married, and died, leaving their wives in a situation of levirate marriage (yibbum) before the five known men, none of whom know which woman is the wife of his brother. This is their solution: Four of the known men perform chalitzah (the ceremony releasing the widow from levirate marriage) with one widow, and the fifth man marries her after she has undergone the four chalitzahs. If she is indeed his brother’s widow, she becomes his levirate wife, and if she is not, she is a stranger who has already been released by one of the four who must necessarily be the levir. The same procedure is followed with the second widow—four perform chalitzah, and the fifth marries her. This continues for all the widows. In theory, one man could marry all the widows after they have each undergone four chalitzahs, but it is better this way, as it allows for the possibility that each woman might end up with her actual levir, fulfilling the mitzvah of yibbum. 

If one of the known men dies, four of the uncertain men perform chalitzah with the widow, and the fifth performs yibbum. If some of the known men are priests (kohanim) and some are not, the kohanim perform chalitzah and do not perform yibbum, lest they end up with a woman who has undergone chalitzah, which is forbidden to them. The non-kohanim perform yibbum. Similarly, if among the known men, some of the uncertain men are maternal brothers (sharing only the same mother) and some are paternal brothers (sharing both the same mother and father), those who are only maternal brothers perform chalitzah and do not perform yibbum, as it would be a severe prohibition (karet). The paternal brothers either perform chalitzah or yibbum. If some of the known men are kohanim and some are maternal brothers, all perform chalitzah and do not perform yibbum.

In cases of mixtures that we have mentioned, sometimes a person performs chalitzah for his mother, his sister, or his daughter. How can this occur for his mother? If his mother and another woman gave birth to two boys in secret, and he is one of them, and they have two certain boys, such as Rachel, the wife of Jacob, who gave birth to Joseph, and Hannah, the wife of Reuben, who gave birth to Hezron, and afterwards Rachel and Hannah gave birth to two boys in secret, and Jacob and Reuben died, and Joseph married Hannah, and Hezron married Rachel, and Joseph and Hezron died, and the mixtures fell to yibum. Rachel fell to the son of Hannah, who is the brother of Hezron, and Hannah fell to the son of Rachel, who is the brother of Joseph. Since it is not known who is her son and who is her yavam, she needs chalitzah from both of them. Thus, he performs chalitzah for his mother out of doubt. How does this occur for his sister? If his mother and another woman gave birth to two girls in secret, and his mother gave birth from another man whom she married after his father's death, and they got mixed, and it is not known which daughter belongs to which mother, and two brothers of this one, who had brothers from his father but not his mother, married the mixtures, and both fell to this one for yibum, and one of them is his sister from his mother, and if he recognized her, she would not need chalitzah. Now that he does not recognize her, she needs chalitzah. How does this occur for his daughter? If his wife and another woman gave birth to two girls in secret, such as the wife of Reuben and the wife of Simon, who gave birth to two girls, and they got mixed, and two brothers of Reuben married them. It turns out that Reuben performs chalitzah for his daughter out of doubt when his two brothers died, and if he knew who his daughter was, he would not perform chalitzah for her. Now that he does not know, he necessarily performs chalitzah for his daughter because of the doubt (Gemara 99a). This concludes the laws of chalitzah.

Laws of a Violator, a Seducer, and a Defamer. It contains 46 sections:

A seducer or a violator of a virgin of Israel pays fifty silver shekels of Tyrian currency, as explicitly stated in the Torah regarding a violator in Parashat Ki Teitzei and a seducer in Parashat Mishpatim, whether she was the daughter of a prominent person in Israel or the daughter of a lesser person in Israel (Arakhin 14b). For all matters of fines, the amount is the same for everyone. There is a difference between a violator and a seducer: a seducer does not pay the fine unless he does not marry her, as it is written, "If her father utterly refuses to give her to him, he shall weigh out money according to the dowry of virgins" (Exodus 22:16). The intention is the same as the fine specified for a violator, where it is written, "The man who lay with her shall give to the girl's father fifty shekels of silver" (Deuteronomy 22:29). But if he marries her, he is exempt from the fine and instead writes her a marriage contract like other virgins. Additionally, he is not forced to marry her. However, in the case of a violator, he pays in all circumstances, and even if she and her father agree for her to marry him, he marries her against his will, even if she is lame or blind or similar, for it is written, "She shall be his wife," which implies against his will, as explicitly stated there in the verse, "He cannot send her away all his days" (Deuteronomy 22:29), except with her consent. Therefore, she does not have a marriage contract, for the marriage contract was instituted so that it should not be easy in his eyes to divorce her, and in this case, he cannot divorce her without her consent (and see what is written in Siman 66 that in our times when it is forbidden to divorce against her will, there is reason to say similarly regarding the marriage contract. See there).

Rambam wrote in Chapter 1 of Naarah: Who is considered a seducer and who is considered a rapist? A seducer acts with her consent, whereas a rapist forces her against her will. Any woman who is violated in the field is presumed to have been raped, and she is judged as a rape victim unless witnesses testify that she was willing. Any woman who is violated in the city is presumed to have been seduced because she did not scream, unless witnesses testify that she was raped, such as if he drew a sword on her and said, "If you scream, I will kill you." And the Raavad wrote that he does not understand what practical difference this presumption makes. If there are witnesses, they should testify whether it was by force or willingly. If there are no witnesses, there is no fine. And regarding shame and degradation, this is a general rule in judgment: the burden of proof falls on the claimant. And he is always believed to say it was with consent unless she brings proof that it was by force.

The Rambam's intention is that the case involves witnesses who stood at a distance and saw the event but could not determine whether it was consensual or coerced. Therefore, in a city, the presumption is that it was consensual, and in a field, the presumption is that it was coerced (as stated in Maimonides and Kesef Mishneh). The principle of "the burden of proof rests upon the claimant" does not apply here because this is considered clear to us. The Rambam learned this from the verse regarding the betrothed maiden, which states that if it happened in the city, both are executed, and if in the field, only he is executed. This clearly indicates so. The Ra'avad holds that the verse speaks of the usual way things happen, and it does not necessarily mean this specifically, since in capital cases, we require a warning, and the witnesses must know clearly how the event transpired. Therefore, there is no distinction between city and field. This is also taught in the Sifrei on the verse “for he found her in the field,” which states: One might think that in the city she is liable and in the field she is exempt, but it says “she cried out, etc.,” and if she has no one to rescue her, whether in the city or in the field, she is exempt, and if she has someone to rescue her, whether in the city or in the field, she is liable. The Rambam would explain that this is not meant literally, since there was a warning, but nonetheless, since the Torah states it this way according to the usual way things happen, in terms of a fine where no warning is needed, only the witnessing of the event from a distance without clear knowledge as stated, we follow the usual way things happen as written in the Torah, and neither party is believed to claim the opposite without evidence. Also, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (Positive Commandments 54) wrote like the Rambam.

From when does a girl have the status of being eligible for a fine? From the age of three years and one day until she matures. If she was violated before the age of three years, the act is not considered a sexual act. If she was violated after she matured, she is not eligible for a fine, as it is stated: "a young virgin woman"—not a mature woman. This is the opinion of the Rambam there (following the Sages in Ketubot 40a), while R. Chananel and the Raavad ruled that it specifically refers to a "young woman" and not a minor (following R. Meir there). The Rosh and the Tur agreed with the Rambam, and similarly wrote the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol there.

And behold, according to the opinion of the Rambam and the Tur, it appears that in the case of a minor, it is never considered consensual, for the seduction of a minor is considered coercion. However, the Rambam does not hold this view, as is evident from his words in Chapter 2 of Sotah and Chapter 3 of Ishut, and we have already explained his reasoning in Siman 68. Therefore, he does not mention this. But regarding the Tur, it is difficult to understand why he did not mention this.

The fifty sela'im are a fine for the evil act that he committed. But aside from this, he must also pay for shame, depreciation, and pain in the case of a rape victim, and for shame and depreciation in the case of a seduced woman, for there is no pain in the case of seduction. These compensations are not the same for everyone, but rather they depend on the specific circumstances, as in the case of shame, which depends on the one who shamed and the one who was shamed. It is not the same to shame an important young woman from a distinguished family as it is to shame a despised woman from a lowly family. Similarly, it is not the same for the one who is shamed by an important person as it is for the one who is shamed by a despised and contemptible person. Therefore, the court assesses the status and value of both the perpetrator and the victim and estimates how much the father and family would have paid to prevent this from happening to her by such a person, and that is what he must pay.

We assess the amount she is worth now compared to what she was worth initially. This means that we evaluate her as a maidservant sold in the market based on her beauty and her family, even though she is not actually being sold and it is disgraceful for her to be sold. Nevertheless, it is necessary to evaluate her this way because her disgrace has already been assessed through the damages for humiliation. And even though a maidservant sold for labor does not differ whether she is blemished or not, there is still a difference. Sometimes a person has a servant whom he cherishes and wishes to marry her to a beautiful and distinguished woman, such as this one, and we assess how much more he would give for her when she is a virgin compared to when she is not. And this is what he would give her (Ketubot 40). The pain is assessed based on her youth and her health, how much she suffered, and this is what is given to her in the case of rape (and see Tosafot there 39, s.v. "pain").

It is written, "and she shall be his wife; he cannot send her away all his days." Therefore, if he transgressed and divorced her without her consent, he is not flogged for this negative commandment, as it is considered a negative commandment that is rectified by a positive commandment. And even though the positive commandment precedes the negative commandment, a negative commandment that is rectified by a positive commandment is only called such when the positive commandment comes after the negative commandment. Nevertheless, since it is written "all his days," which is superfluous, it implies that "all his days" refers to standing and returning her (Makos 14b). Therefore, we consider it a negative commandment rectified by a positive commandment, and we compel him to return her, and he is not flogged unless he was a priest, who is forbidden to a divorced woman. In that case, he is flogged. Or even if he was an Israelite, if she was betrothed to another or died before he could return her, he is flogged because he transgressed the negative commandment and cannot fulfill the positive commandment within it. This is the ruling of the Rambam and the Tur (and the authorities rule like the opinion in Makos that says "fulfilled and not fulfilled," and likewise in the laws of Sanhedrin, chapter 16, and we have written about this in Choshen Mishpat, section 97. But according to the opinion that says "nullified and not nullified," he is not flogged unless he vowed not to return her in front of many people, as stated there in Makos 16. And it is a question regarding a priest why it is not considered nullified by his own actions. See there and delve deeply).

When the raped or seduced woman is forbidden to him, and even if she is not forbidden by a severe prohibition but is only subject to a negative commandment or a positive commandment, or even if she is a secondary relative forbidden by rabbinic decree, he is not allowed to marry her. This is derived from the verse "and she shall be his wife," which implies a woman who is fit for him to maintain as a wife. We do not say that a positive commandment should come and override a negative commandment, nor do we interpret "a woman who is fit for him to maintain" as unnecessary. The explanation is that "she shall be his wife" means with her consent, when she desires him, and not when she is compelled to marry him (see Tosafot Ketubot 40a, s.v. Naiti). Here, the principle that a positive commandment overrides a negative commandment does not apply, because the positive commandment is weak. For if she says, "I do not want him," the positive commandment is completely nullified (Gemara there and as explained by the Ran). Therefore, it is an obligation to teach her to say, "I do not desire him" (Rashi). Furthermore, since there is also a prohibition upon her, how can she transgress something that depends on her will? For this reason, even a secondary relative is forbidden, because since she can say, "I do not want him," this positive commandment does not override even a rabbinic prohibition (Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, Positive Commandments 54, and also the Yeshuot Yaakov, Even HaEzer, Siman 14). I am astonished by the Beit Yosef, the Ba'er Hetev in Siman 3, and the Mishneh LaMelech in Chapter 1 of the laws of a maiden who was violated, who struggled with the reason for the secondary relative there.

And all of this applies to the case where he marries her. However, he is obligated to pay the fine even if she is not fit to marry, and we do not say that since the verse "and she shall be his wife" does not apply, he is also exempt from the fine. For in one verse, the Torah explicitly includes those who are prohibited by negative commandments and those who are subject to karet with regard to the fine, as it is written, "he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins," and it could have written "the dowry of a virgin," like the beginning of the verse where it says "if a man entices a virgin," and it says "virgins." Additionally, the "hey" at the beginning of the word includes both those who are prohibited by negative commandments and those who are subject to karet (Sanhedrin 29b). And so the Sages taught in the Mishnah there: These are the young women who have a fine—one who comes upon a mamzeret, etc., one who comes upon his sister, etc. Even though they are subject to karet, they are not subject to death by the court, for when there is a death penalty by the court, such as one who comes upon his daughter, he is exempt from the fine, for he is subject to a greater punishment, and a person does not die and pay. And even if it was done inadvertently or deliberately without a warning, we hold that those who are subject to death inadvertently are exempt from payments (Sanhedrin 35a), and certainly when it is done deliberately without a warning. Similarly, for those who are prohibited by negative commandments, the obligation is only in the case of inadvertence or deliberation without a warning, for if they were warned, he is flogged, and we hold that one is not flogged and pays. But with regard to inadvertence and deliberation without a warning, it is not similar to those who are subject to death. And this is the opinion of the Rambam in the first chapter of Naarah (see there), where he rules according to Rabbi Yochanan there and not according to Reish Lakish, and the Sha'agat Aryeh there chapter 4 disputes him because Rava holds like Reish Lakish, but also the Tur wrote like the Rambam.

In several places in the Gemara, it is explained that the obligation of a fine applies even if he had relations with her not in the usual manner. In Yevamot (59a), it is said, "And she shall be his wife," referring to a woman who is fit for him, excluding a widow for a High Priest, and it is interpreted as referring to relations not in the usual manner. Hence, it is excluded due to the prohibition of the priesthood alone, but regarding the fine, he is liable. Similarly, in Ketubot (40b), it is said, "If two men had relations with her, one in the usual manner and one not in the usual manner, they would say: a complete man fifty, a blemished man fifty." Hence, he is liable for the fine even for relations not in the usual manner. Also, in Kiddushin (9a), it is said that if ten men had relations with her, and she is still a virgin, all of them pay the fine. This is also the ruling of Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur, and all the early authorities. Similarly, it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, Ketubot Chapter 3 (Halacha 6), that if ten men had relations with her not in the usual manner, all of them pay the fine, and she can choose who will marry her. Once she has chosen one of them, the rest are exempt from the obligation to marry her, as it says, "And she shall be his wife." However, before she marries the one she has chosen, she can choose another one.

Accordingly, the words of the Rambam in the first chapter of "Na'arah" law 8 are very puzzling, and this is what he says: "A rapist or seducer is not liable for the fine unless he had intercourse with her in the usual manner and with witnesses, and no warning is needed." Similarly, he wrote there in the second chapter, law 8: "If two men had intercourse with her, one in the usual manner and one not in the usual manner, the one who had intercourse with her not in the usual manner, if he is first, is liable for embarrassment and devaluation, and if he is last, he is liable only for embarrassment, as she has already been devalued. The one who had intercourse with her in the usual manner, whether first or last, is liable for the fine and for the other matters. However, the embarrassment and devaluation of a girl who has not been defiled at all are not like the embarrassment and devaluation of one who has been defiled not in the usual manner." And indeed, the Raavad, the Rosh, the Ran, and several of the early authorities have already expressed astonishment at his words and rejected them, as the Tur wrote there.

However, he is not alone in this opinion, as the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG) there also rules similarly, and this is the opinion of Rashi (Sanhedrin 73b) who wrote that a fine is only imposed upon the completion of intercourse, as the verse emphasizes the virginity, as it is written "a virgin girl," etc., end quote. Similarly, this is the ruling of the Meiri and one of Rashi's teachers (Shita Mekubetzet Ketubot there). However, in the Gemara of Ketubot, they explain that it does not refer to two virgins, but rather to one who was previously violated by someone in an unnatural manner, and subsequently another had intercourse with her in the natural manner. The second one is liable even though she was already damaged by the first, for her damage is not comparable to one who is penetrated for the first time in the natural manner. And the language of the Talmud also implies this, for if it were not so, it should have said "these are cases where they had intercourse with two virgins," etc. (and indeed the Maharshal raised this difficulty). This is also evident from Rashi's commentary there and in Arakhin (15a), see there thoroughly. And from Yevamot there is no proof, since as it derives from the verse "and she shall be his wife," a woman suitable for him, it is not according to the halakha of the Mishnah that lists those young women, for we do not derive "a woman suitable for him," and it follows the opinion of the Tannaim in the Baraita who interpreted it in this manner, not according to the Mishnah. And we rule according to our Mishnah. Based on this, it can also be said in Kiddushin there that it follows the opinion of those Tannaim and not according to the halakha. And the plain meaning of the sugya in Sanhedrin there implies this, see there (so it seems to me). Another reason will be explained in section 22.

And this is what the Rambam wrote in Chapter 1, Halacha 5: "If she was raped, she is forbidden to him, even if it is only a positive commandment, and even if she is a secondary relation, he should not marry her. Similarly, if something immoral is found in her after he has married her, he should divorce her, as it says, 'and she shall be his wife'—a woman who is appropriate for him." End quote. This is not because he interprets the verse this way, as it is clearly proven in the Gemara that according to our Mishnah, we do not interpret it this way. Rather, he did not want to elaborate on the Gemara’s reasoning, which states that there is no principle of a positive commandment overriding a negative commandment here, as I have written. And this is his method in several places, to adopt the straightforward interpretation even if it is not in accordance with the halacha. This is also the method of the Talmud, as Tosafot writes in several places (see Tosafot Shabbat 132a, s.v. ha'hi).

A High Priest who rapes a virgin or seduces her should not marry her because he is commanded to marry a virgin, and at the time he marries her, she is not a virgin. If he does marry her, he must divorce her with a get (bill of divorce), as the intercourse he had with her is not considered as marriage, since it was for the purpose of fornication. And although for the matter of the ketubah (marriage contract) this intercourse is considered as marriage, as he gives her the ketubah of a virgin in the case of seduction, as mentioned, this is in regard to financial matters so that the sinner does not profit, but not in regard to the prohibition.

If he had relations with a virgin and she and her father did not manage to bring him to court before she died, he is exempt, as it is stated, "and he shall give to the father of the young woman" (Deuteronomy 22:29), and not "to the father of the deceased." The term "the young woman" is superfluous, as it should have written "and he shall give to her father." Rather, it comes for a derivation, and we do not interpret "the young woman" as referring to a previous state, as we interpret elsewhere. Otherwise, it would not have been written at all, and logically, we would know that he pays because his obligation is presumably from the time of the act. Rather, it certainly comes to exempt him when she dies before being brought to court. (Tosafot)

However, the father does not prevent (from receiving the fine), for although it is written, "and he shall give to the father of the young woman," nevertheless, if she is an orphan, the fine is given to her in the case of rape. In the case of seduction, it is not applicable to give to her because she has waived it. Similarly, a young woman who was betrothed and then divorced, the Sages taught that her fine goes to herself, even if she has a father, as it is written, "who was not betrothed," and we derive that if she was betrothed and then divorced, the fine goes to herself (Ketubot 38a). Because without a divorce, the fine does not apply since he would be liable for the death penalty. Therefore, it refers to a case where she was divorced, and it follows that the same applies to an orphan. See also what I have written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 38, Se'if 26 regarding the opinion of the Rambam on this matter.

The Rambam wrote there: These are the ones who do not receive a fine: a mature girl (bogeret), one who refuses (mema’enet), an ailonit (a woman who does not develop secondary sexual characteristics), an insane woman (shotah), a deaf-mute (chereshet), and one who has a bad reputation from her youth, where two witnesses testify that she solicited them for promiscuity. Also, a divorced woman from marriage who is still a young virgin girl, but a divorced woman from betrothal, if she was raped, she receives a fine, and the fine belongs to her. But if she consented, she does not receive a fine. And behold, a bogeret is explicitly excluded by the verse "na'arah" (young girl) and not bogeret. Similarly, a mema’enet, since she was under a husband, is not a virgin. However, regarding an ailonit, shotah, and chereshet, the early authorities were puzzled by the Rambam's ruling and rejected his words. In the Gemara (36a), it is explained that this is dependent on a minor girl. One who obligates a fine for a minor girl also obligates it for an ailonit, because an ailonit does not have the period of youth, transitioning from minor to mature directly at the age of twenty if she shows signs of being an ailonit, as mentioned in sections 155 and 172. One who exempts a minor girl also exempts an ailonit. Similarly, a shotah and chereshet are like minors. Therefore, since we hold that a minor girl receives a fine, as the Rambam himself wrote, how can he rule that these do not receive a fine? Thus, it is ruled that these do receive a fine, and so wrote the Tur.

However, in truth, it appears to me that the Rambam, of blessed memory, had a different approach regarding the conclusion of the Talmud there. He held that there is a distinction between a minor (ketanah) and an aylonit, and a fool (shotah) and a deaf-mute (chereshet). His reasoning is as follows: the one who obligates a fine for a minor is based on the Gemara (40b), which states that because the term "na'arah" (young woman) is written without the letter "hey," it implies even a minor. However, in any case, the term certainly includes a young woman (na'arah). How, then, can we obligate a fine for an aylonit who is never considered a young woman? Similarly, for a deaf-mute and a fool, it makes sense to obligate a fine for a minor who is currently a minor and will become a young woman, but these others will never reach the status of a young woman. This is what the Talmud says there (36a): "This Tanna agrees with him on one point and disagrees on another," meaning, regarding a minor, he agrees with the Rabbis that a fine is obligated, but regarding an aylonit, he agrees with Rabbi Meir (as the Rabbis obligate as explained in the subsequent Baraita that a deaf-mute, fool, and aylonit have a fine, not as Rashi explained, and this is clear. The Beit Yosef also writes this in the name of the Maharik. See there and examine it well).

The convert, the captive, and the freed maidservant, if they converted, were redeemed, or were freed when they were three years old or less, such that they were not fit for intercourse, are presumed to be virgins and are entitled to a fine. If they are three years and one day old, and certainly if they are older, they are not entitled to a fine, as they are presumed to have been deflowered, as it is written in Siman 66 regarding the claim of virginity, see there.

The Tur writes: The Rambam stated that any girl who is entitled to a fine is also entitled to compensation for humiliation and depreciation. If she was raped, she is also entitled to compensation for pain. Any girl who is not entitled to a fine is not entitled to compensation for humiliation or depreciation if she was seduced or raped, except for a mature girl, a rebellious wife, an imbecile, and a deaf-mute. How so? One who rapes a mature girl or a rebellious wife, although they are not entitled to a fine, they are entitled to compensation for humiliation, depreciation, and pain. One who rapes an imbecile or a deaf-mute pays for the pain alone. However, one who seduces any of them is exempt from everything. So wrote the Rambam. And I do not understand his words: what is the connection between pain, humiliation, and depreciation to the fine? Even though they are not entitled to a fine, why should they not be entitled to the other compensations? So wrote the Tur (and the Beit Yosef also remains perplexed). Indeed, these words are astonishing against the Talmud and reason, and it is surprising that the Raavad remained silent on this matter.

Therefore, it appears to me that there is another intention hidden in his words, and he also agrees that there is no issue of a fine for shame, degradation, and pain, and there is a scribal error in his writings. Instead of "refusing woman" it should say "woman who cannot conceive," and it is his opinion that shame, degradation, and pain only apply to a virgin, as is evident from the Talmud which states that the estimation for degradation is between a virgin maidservant and a non-virgin (40a). It is also evident in Sanhedrin (73a) that degradation refers to the loss of virginity. For this reason, Rambam only obligates these fines for regular intercourse, which involves the loss of virginity, but for a non-virgin there is no degradation, and similarly, there is no pain for a non-virgin, as evident from the Gemara (39b). Regarding shame, although it is not explicitly stated, it is certainly similar to degradation, as we do not find in the Gemara any indication that there is shame without degradation. The reasoning also supports this, as the shame is related to the husband who marries her and does not find her to be a virgin. Rambam lists ten women who do not incur a fine: a mature woman, a refusing woman, a divorced woman from marriage, a woman who cannot conceive, an insane woman, a deaf woman, a convert, a captive, a freed maidservant over three years old, and a woman with a bad reputation. These six — the refusing woman, the divorced woman, the convert, the captive, the freed maidservant, and the woman with a bad reputation — are all presumed to be non-virgins. This is why he wrote that any woman who does not incur a fine also does not receive other compensations, whether in cases of rape or consensual relations, because they are non-virgins, except for a mature woman, a woman who cannot conceive, an insane woman, and a deaf woman. However, for the insane woman and the deaf woman, only pain is relevant, not shame or degradation, as is obvious. (And I could say that there is no scribal error here and he holds regarding the refusing woman as per Tosafot 35a s.v. "the refusing woman," and a woman who cannot conceive is not considered a virgin for him as she is not fit to marry, but all this seems forced, and therefore it appears clear as I have written) (see Rashi Me'ilah 19a s.v. "he challenged him").

There are three compensations for a seducer and four for a rapist, all of which go to the father. This is because any benefit derived from a daughter's youth belongs to her father, and furthermore, he has the authority to give her in marriage to someone repulsive or afflicted with boils, which would bring her embarrassment, damage, and suffering. Therefore, although the Torah only specifies that the fine goes to the father, nevertheless, all other compensations also belong to the father. If she has no father, they belong to herself. In any case where it belongs to herself, it does not apply to a seduced woman, as she forgives it. However, when she is a minor, it could be said that a minor's forgiveness is meaningless, and Tosafot write this as well (Bava Metzia 42b). But Maimonides does not seem to imply this, as he writes in Chapter 1, Law 9, that if she is divorced from betrothal, the fine belongs to herself, as a seduced woman has no fine, and he does not differentiate between a minor and a young woman. See there, and this requires further investigation (Maggid Mishneh on Chapter 2, Law 13). Additionally, in the case of a minor, seduction does not apply, as seduction of a minor is considered rape. However, Maimonides follows his own reasoning, as he does not hold this view, as explained in Section 5.

Maimonides writes in Chapter 2, Law 16: A daughter who was betrothed and then divorced, the fine is solely hers. If she was raped or seduced and subsequently betrothed to another, the fine and other compensations belong to her father, since betrothal does not remove her from her father’s authority. His reasoning is that if she was raped or seduced after being betrothed and divorced, only the fine belongs to her, but the shame, degradation, and pain are her father's. This is because, according to the original law, the fine should also belong to the father, as she did not leave his authority; however, the Torah decreed that the fine belongs to her, as mentioned in Section 17. Therefore, the fine alone, which is explicitly stated in the Torah, suffices. Furthermore, the father still has the right to degrade or shame her by giving her in marriage to a repulsive or diseased person. But the Rosh disagrees and holds that everything belongs to her, as mentioned in the Tur.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (Chapter 4): A young woman who was seduced—her shame, her degradation, and her fine belong to her father. And the pain (suffered) in the case of rape, if she had gone to court before her father died, then they belong to her father (even if they have not yet been collected). If the father died, they belong to her brothers (who inherit him). If she did not have the opportunity to go to court before her father died, they belong to her (since the father does not acquire [the rights] before the court case). And the same law applies if she matured before going to court or got married before going to court—they belong to her (because maturity and marriage remove her from the father's authority). Therefore, if the case was not brought to court before she left his authority, he does not acquire the fine or any of these matters.

There is a question regarding this matter: it is understandable concerning a fine, as it can be said that the Torah did not grant it to the father before standing in court. But in the case of shame and depreciation, which are considered complete monetary payments, why does the father not acquire them beforehand and bequeath them to his sons? The answer is that for this purpose, shame and depreciation are compared to a fine, as it is written, "because he has violated her," implying that just as there is shame and depreciation, so too is there a fine (Tosafot 38b, s.v. yesh beger). This is the opinion of the Rambam in Chapter 2, Law 15, see there. However, some of our Rabbis hold that this comparison applies only to the fine (Ran there), and this is the opinion of the Raavad there. The criticism of the Raavad is unwarranted (Kesef Mishneh, and so wrote the Maggid Mishneh). Nevertheless, according to the Rambam, it cannot be said that he holds that the fine is compared to shame and depreciation, for in the case where she was betrothed and divorced, he distinguishes between them as written in Section 24. Therefore, it seems to me that the Rambam holds that as long as the fine has not been acquired, neither has the shame and depreciation, for since they result from the intercourse and the explicit payment in the Torah is the fine, he has not acquired them before standing in court. This is also implied in the Jerusalem Talmud, that the shame and depreciation from intercourse are not similar to the shame and depreciation from injuries, see there in the beginning of Chapter 4.

There is also a question here, since she acquired the right when the father died or when she reached maturity before standing trial, how can she collect in the case of seduction, as she has waived the right? And it is taught that a young woman can waive the right. Some say that the teaching that if she did not have the chance to stand trial before the father died, the right belongs to her, applies only to a case of rape, but in the case of seduction, she has waived it (Ramban). Others say that this also applies to seduction, because at the time of the act, she could not waive it since it belonged to the father, and therefore she acquired it later in the case of seduction, as waiver is not relevant afterwards. Waiver pertains to the time of the act, and at that time she did not have the authority to waive it (Ran and Ritva). Some say that the Raavad's intention in his objection is that in the case of seduction, the obligation does not apply since she waived the right, as explained by the Yesh Shlomoh and Tosefet Yom Tov.

Maimonides wrote (there) that a person does not pay a fine anywhere based on his own admission but only based on witnesses. Therefore, one who says, "I raped or seduced so-and-so's daughter," does not pay a fine, but he does pay for humiliation and damage based on his own admission. Similarly, if a girl sues a man in court and says, "You raped or seduced me," and he denies it, he must take an oath of heset, because if he admitted it, he would pay her for humiliation, damage, and pain based on his own admission. And behold, in the case of rape, it is clear, but in the case of seduction, she has waived it. The commentators wrote that indeed the Ra'avad objected to this (Kesef Mishneh and Maggid Mishneh), and it seems from the intention of Maimonides that the explanation is that she has a father and she is suing that he should pay the father, and she is called his litigant, even though the payments are not hers, because the payments came about due to her.

Additionally, it is written: If she says to him, "You raped me," and he says, "No, but I seduced you," he must take an oath according to the Torah concerning the pain caused, and he pays for the embarrassment and depreciation, for he has admitted to part of the claim. And it must be said as stated, for otherwise, there is no partial admission according to his words (as noted). And know that all this applies to a minor or a young woman, but if an adult woman claims, there is no oath of partial admission since it belongs to her, and if he says, "I seduced you," she receives nothing, and even the oath of heses is not to be administered in our times because there are many promiscuous women, and if we require an oath for every such claim, it would be endless. And we have already explained this in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 87, Se'if 27. And what our teacher, the Rema, wrote in this Siman, that if a prostitute claims that someone vowed something to her for her services and he denies it, he must take an oath like in other claims - this is when he admits to having relations with her but denies the payment, not when he completely denies it. However, if it is clear that the incident is true, the court should ensure she is compensated according to their discretion. And even if he promised to marry her, it means nothing, for she is a prostitute and did it for the sake of promiscuity (Maharik, Shoresh 129). And although some later authorities hesitate in this matter (Avnei Miluim and Pitchei Teshuva, Siman 1), the main opinion is that he is not compelled to marry her. If she claims that she bore his child and demands child support, if he admits the child is his, he is obviously obligated for the child's support. If he does not admit it, he is not to be made to take an oath on this (Beit Shmuel, Siman 4, Se'if 26). And we have already explained this in Siman 22, Se'if 4.

A rapist and a seducer are judged by three ordained judges in the Land of Israel, but nowadays we do not judge this as it is stated in Choshen Mishpat, chapter 1. It is explained there that the Geonim wrote that nevertheless, we pressure him to appease her with monetary compensation, and when the court sees that he gives an amount close to the required sum, it is sufficient. Similarly, if he appeases her with words and she agrees, we do not mind. Note that a rapist is defined when the initial act of intercourse was by force, even if afterward she consented, because the evil inclination overcame her (Ketubot 51b).

The one who is rumored to have had relations with an unmarried woman and wants to marry her, there are those who say he should not marry her because of gossip, which would strengthen the rumor. And there are those who say, on the contrary, it is a mitzvah to marry her, as we find in the Torah regarding a young woman who was raped or seduced. The first opinion is primary because we do not know for certain that he had relations with her. Nevertheless, if there is a concern that she might turn to bad ways, it is permissible to marry her, and it is a mitzvah to involve oneself in this. However, if it is certain that he had relations with her, it is obvious that it is a mitzvah to marry her, but we do not force him to do so, as even in the case of a young woman who was seduced, we do not force him, as explained, and certainly in the case of an adult woman. If she is rumored with two men, the first is merely a rumor, and the second has added to her disgrace, it is a mitzvah for the second to marry her. If she is rumored with both equally, one being married and the other unmarried, it is a mitzvah for the unmarried one to marry her. So ruled our master the Rema in this chapter.

The Torah's requirement for monetary compensation in cases of rape and seduction applies if the act has already occurred by chance. However, a father is prohibited from allowing his daughter to engage in prostitution, as it is stated, "Do not profane your daughter to make her a harlot." Any individual who prepares themselves for prostitution, whether with their own consent or with the consent of their father, is considered a prostitute. There is no distinction in this regard between a virgin and a non-virgin, and the court has the authority to impose fines to create a preventive measure. This is drawn from the Rambam, at the end of Chapter 2 of "Na'arah Betulah" (The Virgin Maiden). This is even more applicable in the case of an adult woman where there is the prohibition of Niddah (menstrual impurity), which incurs the penalty of karet (spiritual excision). The source of impurity is prostitution, as explicitly stated in the Torah.

Defamation (Motzi Shem Ra) as written in the Torah: This occurs when a man betroths a virgin girl, and after some time he marries her and has relations with her. He then comes to the court and claims that he did not find her to be a virgin and that she had been unfaithful after the betrothal. If the matter is true, she is liable to be stoned. If it is found to be false, he is punished with one hundred silver coins and is flogged, and he is not permitted to divorce her ever. All of this is clearly explained in the Torah in the portion of Ki Teitzei, and the fine is given to her father. If she is an orphan, the fine belongs to her (Ketubot 44b). And although in all other areas of Torah law we hold that a person does not receive both lashes and a monetary penalty, defamation is different because it is a fine. The principle that a person does not receive both lashes and a monetary penalty is derived from the verse "according to his wickedness," meaning for one wickedness you punish him and not for two. This applies to monetary payments and not to fines (Makkot 4b and see there in Tosafot). The obligation from the husband applies only in the case of a virgin girl, as it is written in the verse, and not in the case of a minor. Although in the case of fines for rape and seduction we also impose penalties on a minor, as written, nevertheless, since throughout the Torah the term "virgin girl" is written without the letter "hei" at the end, and in the context of defamation it is written with a full spelling including the "hei," we deduce that the Torah speaks of a fully mature virgin girl and not a minor (ibid.).

In the Gemara (46a), there is a dispute among the Tannaim regarding whether the obligation for spreading a false rumor (motzi shem ra) applies specifically when the husband has had the first intercourse and says he did not find virginity, and according to this, the verse that states "and they shall spread the garment" should be taken literally to show that he spread a false rumor, since virginity was found. Or, whether the obligation also applies even if he has not yet had intercourse but brings witnesses that she committed adultery while betrothed to him. According to this, "and they shall spread the garment" is interpreted as clarifying the matter. This is how it is presented in the Gemara there. 

Maimonides, the Raavad, and the Tur ruled according to the opinion that it is specifically when he has had intercourse (like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, whose teachings are few but clear). And this is the conclusion of the discussion: he is not liable until he has intercourse in the usual manner and also spreads a false rumor that she had intercourse in the usual manner while betrothed to him. 

According to this, it is surprising regarding Maimonides in chapter 3 who wrote that the verse "and they shall spread the garment" is a respectful expression, referring to the deliberation in private matters, and similarly, the phrase "and these are the tokens of my daughter's virginity" refers to the witnesses who refute the husband's witnesses. This is difficult because since he ruled that it applies only when he has had intercourse, the verse should be interpreted literally.

And it appears to me that his words are very correct in this matter, and necessarily it is impossible to interpret it literally, for the spreading of the garment neither adds nor subtracts. For if the husband did not bring witnesses to her adultery, it amounts to nothing; and if he did bring witnesses, she is stoned, for by the testimony of two witnesses a matter is established. And if the father brought witnesses and they disproved the husband's witnesses, which is the essence of this matter as will be explained, even if he does not spread the garment, what of it? Therefore, it is truly interpreted that this is merely a matter of honor. And this is what they said in the Gemara according to the opinion that it refers to when he had intercourse with her, as it is written, "And they shall spread the garment," etc., "and these are the tokens of my daughter's virginity," meaning that since the Torah used the expression of spreading a garment for this investigation and inquiry, it cannot be entirely removed from its literal meaning, implying there is a garment and he had intercourse with her. But according to the opinion that it applies even if he did not have intercourse with her, this expression does not apply at all. And many of the early authorities struggled with this. And according to the Rambam, it is straightforward. (And see Tosafot there, s.v. "Bishlama," and the commentary of the Rashba there, who also struggled with this. According to our explanation, it is straightforward with the help of Heaven. And study it well).

And it appears to me that what our Sages said, that one is not liable until he engages in intercourse in the usual manner and emits semen in the usual manner, as stated in paragraph 34, and at first glance it is puzzling, for in all other prohibitions of illicit relations there is no difference between the usual manner and an unusual manner. And where did we learn that for the emission of semen we require everything to be in the usual manner? But it is certainly because the Torah expressed this in the language of "spreading a garment" to indicate that the primary claim is concerning the virginity, and consequently, this applies only in the usual manner.

It is a positive commandment from the Torah that the wife of someone who brings a false accusation (Motzi Shem Ra) should remain his wife forever, and he cannot divorce her against her will, as it is stated: "and she shall be his wife" (Deuteronomy 22:19), even if she is blind or afflicted with boils. If he divorces her without her consent, he violates a negative commandment, as it is written: "he may not send her away all his days" (Deuteronomy 22:29). He is compelled to take her back, and he does not receive lashes, as it is stated regarding a rapist. If another man betroths her first, or if she dies, or if he is a priest who is prohibited from marrying a divorcee, he receives lashes according to the opinion that holds "they upheld but did not uphold" (i.e., the transgression remains even if the commandment cannot be fulfilled). According to the opinion that holds "they nullified but did not nullify" (i.e., the commandment is nullified if it cannot be fulfilled), he does not receive lashes unless he vowed in public, as it is stated regarding a rapist.

If there is found in her a matter of sexual immorality, or she was forbidden to him even by prohibitions punishable by lashes or positive commandments, and even second-degree prohibitions, he should divorce her with a get (Jewish bill of divorce), as it is stated, "and she shall be his wife" - a woman suitable for him. And why does a positive commandment not come and override a negative commandment? Because it depends on her will; if she says "I do not want him," there is no positive commandment here. Therefore, it is possible that she will say this, and both the positive and negative commandments will be fulfilled. And we have explained the reason for this matter in the case of rape, where even a rabbinic prohibition does not override it. See there, and the same applies here.

The Rambam wrote: How is defamation (motzi shem ra) defined? When a man comes to the court and says, "I had relations with this young woman and did not find her to be a virgin. When I investigated the matter, I discovered that she had engaged in promiscuity after I betrothed her. Here are my witnesses who testify that she committed adultery in their presence." The court listens to the witnesses and examines their testimony. If the matter is found to be true, she is stoned. If the father brings witnesses and the husband's witnesses are found to be false, those witnesses are stoned, the husband is flogged, and he must pay one hundred selaim. Regarding this it is said, "These are the tokens of my daughter's virginity" — these are the witnesses who will make the husband's witnesses false. If the husband then brings other witnesses and they make the father's witnesses false, the girl and her father's witnesses are stoned. Regarding this it is said, "If this thing is true." It was learned by tradition that this passage involves witnesses and false witnesses and false witnesses of false witnesses. This means that what is written in the passage, "I did not find your daughter to be a virgin," refers to witnesses, as without witnesses it is nothing. And then it says, "These are the tokens of my daughter's virginity," which refers to witnesses who refute the husband's witnesses. And it says, "If this thing is true," which refers to the false witnesses of false witnesses. This applies specifically to refutation, but in the case of contradiction, no action is taken because in refutation the Torah decrees to believe the latter witnesses, whereas in contradiction it is one set of witnesses against another, and neither she nor he is punished. If he wishes to divorce her, he may do so without giving her the ketubah, as it is one set of witnesses against another, and the money remains in the possession of its owner. The difference between contradiction and refutation is explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 38.

Furthermore, he wrote: If someone slandered her and she is now a bogeret (an adult woman), even if he brought witnesses that she committed adultery while she was a na'arah (a young girl), he is exempt from lashes and the fine. If it is found to be true, she is stoned even though she is now a bogeret because at the time she committed the adultery she was a na'arah. The explanation of his words is that we hold that a na'arah who is betrothed and commits adultery is punished by stoning, while a bogeret who is betrothed and commits adultery is punished by strangulation. And regarding one who slanders, it is written "na'arah" and not "bogeret." Therefore, when he slanders her while she is a bogeret, the law of the passage does not apply. Nonetheless, she is judged by stoning because we hold that all those liable for death are judged by the death penalty that was applicable at the time of the offense, even if the witnesses testified when their status and body had changed. Even if, if they committed the offense now, they would be judged by a different death penalty, we do not say that the death penalty should change because the status or body has changed (Gemara there). But his liability for slander is at the time of the slander, and then she is a bogeret, and therefore he is exempt. And in the Sifrei they expounded "and he shall give to the father of the na'arah," and not to the father of the bogeret.

And know that in the case of a defamation of character (motzi shem ra), she is not liable for stoning unless witnesses testify that she committed adultery while she was betrothed. However, if they testify that she committed adultery after entering the chuppah (bridal canopy) but before she had relations with her husband, she is not judged with stoning, but rather with strangulation like all married women. However, some of our sages hold that the matter of defamation of character, since it is a novelty that the Torah introduced with a penalty and lashes, therefore, even if they testify that she committed adultery after the chuppah, she is liable for stoning (Rashbam in Tosafot there), as this is implied by the verses: "And if this thing be true" implies in all cases, and "then they shall bring out the damsel... and stone her" (Tosafot Ketubot 45a, s.v. "amar"). This is also the opinion of the Rambam as he wrote in Chapter 3 of the Laws of Forbidden Relations, Law 8, and the Ra'avad objected to him there.

Any young woman who does not have a penalty if she was raped or seduced, similarly, one who brings forth a bad name about her is exempt from lashes and from payment. Moreover, the case of one who brings forth a bad name is stricter than these, for even a Gentile woman or a maidservant who converted to Judaism before the age of three has a penalty as stated. Nevertheless, the laws of one who brings forth a bad name do not apply to them. Furthermore, even if she was born in Israel, if her conception was not in sanctity, these laws do not apply to her, as it is stated: "because he has brought forth a bad name upon a virgin of Israel," meaning that her conception and birth must be in Israel.

And the Rambam wrote: If one betrothed a young woman, divorced her, betrothed her again, and then brought a bad name upon her, and brought witnesses that she had committed adultery under the first betrothal, and the witnesses were found to be false, he is exempt. Similarly, if she was his yevamah whom he married, and he brought a bad name upon her, and brought witnesses that she had committed adultery under his brother's betrothal, and the witnesses were found to be false, he is exempt from lashes and from payment. And anyone who is exempt, if he wishes to divorce her, he may divorce her.

The explanation of his words is that in the Gemara (46a), they expounded "I have given my daughter to this man," and not to the yavam, meaning that if he brought a bad name upon his brother’s marriage, he is exempt. And regarding the first marriage, there was a question that was not resolved, and therefore he ruled leniently. According to this, his words are puzzling in what he said: "if he wishes to divorce her, he may divorce her." With a yavam, it is understandable, but regarding the first marriage, even though due to the doubt he does not receive lashes and is not required to pay, nevertheless, concerning the prohibition of "he cannot send her away," it remains a biblical doubt and should be dealt with stringently (Milchamot Hashem).

It is forced to say that his final words only refer to the yavam. Additionally, it is difficult because his words imply that even if he divorced her from the betrothal the first time, he is exempt. And in the Gemara, they said regarding the question of the first marriage, it clearly implies that he married her the first time, and so Rashi explained there. And perhaps he holds that in this case, it is obvious that it is nothing because he did not bring the bad name upon the first marriage, and he read in the text "under the first betrothal."

It seems to me that he holds that since bringing a bad name is a novelty in that he receives lashes, pays, and she is stoned even if she committed adultery after the chuppah, as it says, you only have what is novel about it. And proof of this is that in the Jerusalem Talmud, it also excludes if it was a betrothal of a Hebrew maidservant, and similarly, if he had relations with her during the betrothal and brought a bad name, it excludes her. Therefore, the first betrothal is also excluded. (And the Gemara that said there, it is clear at least one thing, etc., this and not the yavam, it means since it was taught that the yavam's betrothal is excluded, consequently, the first betrothal is also excluded).

Additionally, he wrote that one is not liable until he has intercourse with her in the usual manner and emits semen during intercourse in the usual manner. If he had intercourse with her in an unusual manner and said he did not find her a virgin, he is exempt, but he is given lashes of rebellion. Similarly, if he says he did not find her a virgin and does not claim that she committed adultery under him, or if he claims that she committed adultery under him but did not bring witnesses and they came on their own, he is exempt, even though the witnesses would be executed if they were found to be false witnesses, as it is written. And all of this is because, as we have said, you only have what is explicitly stated, and it is clear that if witnesses come and testify that she committed adultery before the betrothal, she is not liable at all, but his acquisition is considered a mistaken acquisition. And it requires further study regarding what is written, that if he had intercourse with her in an unusual manner and said he did not find her a virgin, how would he know this, since he did not have intercourse with her in the place of virginity? And it seems that because of this, he receives lashes of rebellion, meaning that even according to his words, he is speaking falsely.

It is written in the Torah regarding the defamer that if the matter is true, she is stoned at the entrance of her father's house. This is not an absolute requirement, and the proof is that in the case of a betrothed young woman who committed adultery, it is written in the same passage that the stoning takes place at the gate of the city. Why should the location at the entrance of her father's house be an absolute requirement for the defamer? Rather, it is certainly just for the sake of a mitzvah. Thus, the Sages taught in the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 44a) that "the phrase 'at the entrance of her father's house' is stated for the sake of the mitzvah, but it is not an absolute requirement." The reason for the mitzvah is to shame them, saying, "See the offspring you have reared" (Sanhedrin 45a).
