Therefore, her mother is also mentioned in that passage to shame them both, as is evident from the Sifrei. Why specifically in the case of the defamer and not in the case of a betrothed young woman who committed adultery? Because since she was married, and her father and mother did not know of the evil deed she committed, they presumably did not supervise her (in my opinion). The Rambam, of blessed memory, has puzzling words regarding this matter in Chapter 3 of the Laws of Adultery, see there.

The law of defamation: This is adjudicated only when the Temple was standing and by a court of 23 judges, because it involves capital cases. If the matter is true, the person is stoned, and we do not judge capital cases in our times. However, cases of rape and seduction are judged even in our times when there was a court of ordained judges, even after the destruction [of the Temple]. But now, these cases are also not judged, as stated in Choshen Mishpat, chapter 1. Know that in cases of defamation, although initially they are not judged by fewer than 23 judges, if the matter is found to be false and a fine needs to be imposed, it is judged by three judges according to Maimonides. We have explained this in Choshen Mishpat, chapter 3, section 19, with God's help. The laws of false witnesses in cases of defamation are explained there as well, in chapter 38, section 26. See there.

Here concludes the laws of rape and seduction, with the help of God.

Laws of Sotah in the times of the Temple and in our times. Containing 87 sections:

The warning mentioned in the Torah, "and he warned his wife" — this is when he tells her, "Do not seclude yourself with such-and-such a man." And what is the language of warning? The Gemara at the beginning of Sotah discusses this. One opinion says it is a language of anger, as it is written, "They have provoked Me to anger with a non-god" (Deuteronomy 32:21), and similarly, "For jealousy enrages a man" (Proverbs 6:34). Another opinion says it is a language of warning, as it is written, "And the Lord will be zealous for His land" (Joel 2:18). Similarly, regarding the phrase "a spirit of jealousy," there is a dispute there. One opinion says it refers to a spirit of purity, and the other says it refers to a spirit of impurity. There is also a dispute there — one opinion says it is forbidden to warn, and the other says it is obligatory to warn. The truth is that both are the words of the living God. When a man sees some immodest behavior in his wife, it is obligatory to warn her, and this is considered a spirit of purity when he warns her. However, if he does not see anything in her and only warns her out of anger, this is considered a spirit of impurity, and it is forbidden to warn. In such a case, the warning is a language of anger.

And in the Torah, this matter is explained, as it is written, "And a spirit of jealousy passed over him, and he was jealous of his wife, and she was defiled; or a spirit of jealousy passed over him, and he was jealous of his wife, and she was not defiled." According to the commentators, this is one matter, meaning there is a doubt whether she was defiled or not defiled. It should have said, "And she was defiled or not defiled," but certainly the verse means that sometimes a spirit of purity passes over the man, and he warns his wife not to be secluded with a certain person, such as when she is defiled, meaning he sees signs of impurity in her, which is licentiousness. Or sometimes a spirit of impurity passes over the man, and because of anger, he is jealous of his wife, which means when she is not defiled, meaning he does not see signs of impurity in her, and this teaches us.

For the law, there is no difference whether he warns her because of anger or because of immodesty he saw in her. They have the same law, and his warning is considered valid, and all the laws of the Sotah, which will be explained, apply. The Rambam at the end of Hilchot Sotah, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch, who wrote that it is a mitzvah to be zealous for their wives, refer to when he sees in her some immodesty or improper behavior, as will be explained later in this section, with the help of Heaven.

The primary law of a Sotah is as follows: When a husband warns his wife in the presence of two valid witnesses and says to her, "Do not seclude yourself with so-and-so," and she transgresses this and secludes herself with him and remains for the amount of time it takes for defilement to occur—which the sages estimated as the time it takes to roast an egg on a moderate fire and swallow it—and in the Jerusalem Talmud it states that this measure is after removing the apron, she becomes forbidden to her husband until she drinks the bitter waters and the matter is tested. This was the practice when the Temple was standing. Now, she is forbidden to him and must leave without her marriage contract.

And we hold that the warning and seclusion must be specifically with two valid witnesses: he should warn her in front of witnesses, and two witnesses should testify that she secluded herself with that man for the amount of time specified. And if after the warning and seclusion even one witness comes and testifies that she became defiled, he is believed, and she does not drink the bitter waters and is forbidden to her husband and must be divorced without a ketubah, even if the witness is disqualified from testimony, as will be explained. And why did the Torah believe one witness? Because there are grounds for suspicion, for he warned her and she secluded herself, and it is assumed that he speaks the truth that she became defiled. And even if this witness to the defilement is one of the witnesses of the seclusion or the warning, he is believed.

Even a woman, a slave, a maidservant, and someone disqualified from testimony due to a rabbinic transgression, and even a relative, are believed in the testimony of a sotah (a woman suspected of adultery) after the warning and seclusion to testify that she has committed adultery. She would be forbidden to her husband forever, would not drink the bitter waters (as part of the sotah ritual), and would leave without her ketubah (marriage contract). Since the Torah believed a single witness due to the logical reasoning (regarding the suspicion), everyone is believed in this matter. Even five women who hate each other, as mentioned in Siman 17, are believed to testify about each other that they became impure when the warning and seclusion happened with witnesses. They are believed to forbid her to her husband and to prevent her from drinking the bitter waters, but not to forfeit her ketubah. She would take her ketubah and be divorced with a get (divorce document) (Rambam, Chapter 1, Halacha 15). And this is what the Sages taught in the Mishnah (Chapter 6): Even a slave, even a maidservant are believed, even to disqualify her from her ketubah. Her mother-in-law, her mother-in-law’s daughter, her co-wife, her sister-in-law, and her husband’s daughter are believed, but not to disqualify her from her ketubah, only that she should not drink, as mentioned there.

And the reason appears to me that, by law, a single witness should not be deemed credible concerning her ketubah, as we do not find a single witness credible in matters of money. In truth, in the Jerusalem Talmud (Yevamot 6:2), there is an opinion that states this. However, it is said there that just as in the case of a married woman (adultery), where we do not find that a single witness is credible, yet the Torah decreed in the case of a Sotah (suspected adulteress) that a single witness is credible due to the circumstances, so too in monetary matters. Therefore, regarding these women who hate each other, since their entire hatred is due to monetary reasons, as explained in Yevamot (117a), although in matters of prohibition they are credible due to the circumstances, nevertheless, in monetary matters, where their entire hatred is because of this, the sages did not want to deem them credible.

It also appears to me that the principle that a single witness is believed to say that she became impure applies specifically to the man about whom the husband warned her and with whom she secluded herself. However, regarding another man, the witness is not believed. Since the credibility is based on the rationale of "raglayim ladavar" (reasonable grounds), there are reasonable grounds only concerning this specific man, as we see that her desire overpowered her to seclude herself with him after the warning, but not with another man. Even though the prohibition is the same with another man as with this one, nevertheless, we did not see her desire overpower her for another man. (And what the Beit Shmuel wrote in section 11 regarding that instance has no basis, and Rashi was referring to the common practice.)

Rambam writes in the first chapter of Sotah: If one witness comes and says she defiled herself, she does not drink, as it is stated, "One witness came and said she defiled herself." If another contradicts him and says she did not defile herself, we do not listen to him because one witness regarding the defilement of a Sotah is like two, and the words of the latter do not override the words of the first, who is like two. If both came together, one saying she defiled herself and the other saying she did not defile herself, or if one said she defiled herself and two came and said she did not defile herself, she drinks. If one valid witness and numerous women or many invalid witnesses together, the valid witness says she defiled herself and the women or invalid witnesses say she did not defile herself, she drinks, because one witness and many invalids are considered as half and half. If they were all invalids, follow the majority. How so? If two women say she defiled herself and three say she did not defile herself, she drinks. If three say she did not defile herself and four say she defiled herself, she does not drink. If they were half and half, she drinks. So wrote the Tur, and some say that a valid witness is not considered as two unless they ruled based on his testimony. We have already explained this in Siman 17, Section 93. The general rule is that in a balanced doubt, she drinks, for the main purpose of the drinking is to clarify the doubt.

Kinui (warning) is only when he tells her, "Do not seclude yourself with so-and-so." But if he tells her, "Do not speak with so-and-so," even if his intention was to distance her from him, nevertheless, this is not considered the language of Kinui. And if she secluded herself with him, she is permitted to her husband. Similarly, if he told her, "Do not seclude yourself," and she spoke with him, it amounts to nothing. All the more so if he told her, "Do not speak," and she spoke (Gemara 5b). We do not say that since the Torah forbids her due to seclusion after Kinui because of the husband's insistence—since without Kinui she is not forbidden due to seclusion alone—therefore, what difference does it make if he used the language of seclusion or the language of speaking, since in the end he is insistent? Nevertheless, we require that he explicitly warns her about something that she transgresses, which is the language of seclusion.

And even if he warned her using ambiguous language, this is specifically when he said to her, "Do not seclude yourself" in general terms, and certainly if he said, "Do not seclude yourself so that he does not come upon you in the usual manner or in an unusual manner," as is well known throughout the Talmud where they discussed various forms of intercourse. But if he said to her, "Do not seclude yourself with so-and-so so that he does not hug or kiss you, or become infatuated with you in other parts of the body, and the like," this is not considered a valid warning (kinui) because in these cases she does not become forbidden to her husband (Talmud 26b), and we require that he warns her about something that would render her forbidden. And if you ask why this is different from a general warning of "Do not seclude yourself," since in seclusion itself she is certainly not rendered forbidden, the truth is that it is not comparable, for in a general seclusion warning, his intention is that he should not come upon her as an adulterer and adulteress, where the seclusion is for the purpose of intercourse. But when he specifies those actions that have been clarified, it is certainly his intention that he does not suspect her of intercourse but of other forms of closeness, and therefore she is not rendered forbidden thereby. For this reason, there is an opinion that if he said to her, "Do not seclude yourself so that he does not rape you," this is not a valid warning because in the case of rape she is not rendered forbidden (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Sotah 3:3), and we require that he warns her about something that would render her forbidden.

And know that the previous ruling is explicitly explained in the Gemara there, and this is what it says: "And a man lies with her," which excludes if he secludes her through bodily contact. This ruling is not found at all in the Rambam, and from his words in Chapter 3 it clearly appears that he interprets it regarding the one who has intercourse with her, where the warning was simply "Do not seclude yourself," but the one who has intercourse with her used bodily contact. And these are his words there: "A woman who committed adultery under duress or by mistake, or if the one who warned her had intercourse with her through bodily contact, the water does not test her, etc." End quote. And it is explained in the Gemara, excluding if he warned her and the one who had intercourse with her did so through bodily contact. His reasoning seems to be that since they derived this from the verse "and lies with," it presumably does not refer to the warning but to the intercourse of the one who had intercourse. Additionally, why should it be worse than a simple warning, as we have written. But Rashi and Tosafot wrote as we have written (and it is difficult regarding the Maggid Mishneh there who labored on this, see there. And regarding what he questioned, why he did not write even a kiss, the reason is simple: between a kiss and an initial act of intercourse, it is difficult for witnesses to distinguish, unlike bodily contact, which they see clearly. And scrutinize this well).

Anyone can be a witness for her, even her father, her father-in-law, her brother, her brother-in-law, a non-Jew, a servant, her son, or her daughter. Even though there is no prohibition of seclusion with her father or her son, as a person is allowed to be secluded with his mother or daughter, as mentioned in Siman 22, it is still considered a valid warning. This is also stated in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Sotah. Therefore, it is possible to warn her against being secluded with two men at once, saying to her, "Do not be secluded with Reuven and Shimon together," even though it is permitted for a woman to be secluded with two kosher men, as mentioned there. If she is secluded with both of them and remains for the time it takes to become ritually defiled, she is prohibited until she drinks [the bitter waters], and in our times, she is prohibited forever and must be divorced without receiving her ketubah. However, if she was secluded with only one of them, she does not become prohibited to her husband, as it would be considered seclusion without a warning, which does not prohibit a woman. And even though in the laws of seclusion, one person is worse than two, in the matter of warning, the seclusion must be as he warned her.

It is stated in the Gemara (26b) that a "shachuf" (a man with a certain physical condition) can cause his wife to become forbidden to him. Rashi explains that his flesh is scabbed, wasted away, and dry, lacking strength. Tosafot, citing R. Chananel, explain that he does not engage in intercourse in the usual manner and does not ejaculate. It appears that nevertheless, he does engage in intercourse, and through his intercourse, she becomes forbidden. Otherwise, it would not be worse than intercourse in an atypical manner, which does not cause her to become forbidden, as mentioned. The Rambam, at the beginning of Chapter 1, writes: "A 'shachuf' is a man who does not become erect and does not procreate." It is difficult, because since he does not become erect, his intercourse is with a flaccid organ, and Rambam himself rules in Chapter 1 of Hilchot Ishut that intercourse with a flaccid organ is not considered intercourse at all. And even though he does not hold the opinion that atypical intercourse causes her to become forbidden, it is still difficult why she should become forbidden through seclusion with him, since he is not capable of intercourse. It must be said that he does not become erect to the extent that he can procreate, but regarding intercourse, there is some degree of erection.

The Rambam wrote there: If he said to her, "Do not seclude yourself with such-and-such a man," and he was a minor less than nine years and one day old, or if he said to her, "Do not seclude yourself with this animal," this is not a valid warning, as it is stated, "and a man lies with her," which excludes a minor and an animal, for they do not render her forbidden to him. And even though in every case a minor is defined as under thirteen years and one day, nevertheless, regarding intercourse, a minor is defined as less than nine years old (and the Ra'av, in Chapter 4, Mishnah 4, explained "less than thirteen," see there; and similarly, it appears from Tosafot, 26b, s.v. "but," see there).

We hold that if a husband forgives his warning, the warning is forgiven, and it is as if he never warned her at all. If she secludes herself afterward, she is permitted. The reason is that the warning is only because of his personal objection, and therefore if he forgives, it is forgiven. However, this is specifically before the seclusion; but after the seclusion, he cannot forgive, for she has already been forbidden and will not return to permissibility until she drinks [the bitter waters]. Similarly, if he divorces her, the warning is nullified. If he remarries her, he must issue a new warning if he wishes to warn her, for the first warning was nullified by the divorce since she had already been separated from him.

Rambam wrote (there): If he warned her in the presence of two witnesses, and he saw her seclude herself with the man about whom he warned her, and she stayed there long enough to have become defiled, she is forbidden to him, and he must divorce her and give her the ketubah, for he cannot make her drink [the bitter waters] based on his own testimony. Similarly, if people are heard gossiping about her after the warning and seclusion, to the point that he hears women spinning by moonlight discussing her infidelity with the man he warned her about, she is forbidden to remain with him, and he must divorce her and give her the ketubah. If a single witness comes and testifies to him that she secluded herself with the man after the warning and stayed long enough to have become defiled, if he trusts the witness and relies upon his testimony, he must divorce her and give her the ketubah. If not, his wife remains permitted to him. Thus wrote the Tur.

And behold, what is written, that when he or a single witness saw the seclusion after the warning, she becomes forbidden to him, is not explicitly stated in the Gemara. It is written based on reasoning that since the Torah forbids her with two witnesses to the seclusion after the warning, the same applies to his own sighting or that of a single witness. As it is written in chapter 24 of Ishut and in the Tur above, section 115, if he saw himself that she committed adultery or a single witness saw her committing adultery and he relies on it, she becomes forbidden to him. They equate seclusion after the warning to actual adultery, not to an indecent matter, for which a woman is not forbidden to her husband according to most authorities, as stated above in section 11. And even though, essentially, seclusion after the warning is not comparable to adultery—for adultery has no remedy while seclusion has a remedy through drinking the bitter waters—nevertheless, as long as she has not drunk, she is forbidden to him as if it were actual adultery. And since he cannot make her drink based on his own testimony or that of a single witness, it follows that she becomes forbidden to him, and he must give her the ketubah, for regarding monetary matters, a single witness is not trusted, and certainly not himself. And we have already written in section 115 that the prohibition based on a single witness is not by strict law but to avoid suspicion. And it seems to me that this is why the Rambam here, when he saw the seclusion himself, wrote that she is forbidden to him, but did not write so regarding a single witness, indicating that it is not by strict law but to avoid suspicion, and we explained this at length there. And know that in seclusion after the warning, there is no difference whether she denies the witness or not, for seclusion after the warning is likened to adultery and there are grounds to believe it (and so wrote the Beit Shmuel, subsection 7). Similarly, there is no difference whether her husband is in the city or not, or whether the entrance is open to the public domain or not, since it occurred after the warning.

However, regarding what was written, that after warning and seclusion she becomes forbidden to him and he must divorce her and give her the ketubah, this—that she becomes forbidden to him—is a clear Mishnah (Chapter 6). But they questioned why he should give her the ketubah, since it was already written that after warning and seclusion she loses her ketubah. And they answered that his intention was that there is only one witness regarding the seclusion (as is found in certain sources). But this does not seem to be the case, for if so, it should have been explained, and furthermore, he should have written this after the ruling concerning one witness. Also, from his commentary on the Mishnah, it does not seem to be the case. And it appears to me that his intention is after seclusion according to witnesses, and he is referring to the time when the Temple is standing. And what he wrote earlier, that after warning and seclusion she becomes forbidden and must leave without a ketubah, he clearly explained that in this time period, when there is no water to test her. But during the time of the Temple, he cannot deprive her of her ketubah, for she could say, "I will drink the water and be tested." And this is what he means, that when there is gossip after the warning and seclusion, she becomes forbidden to him, but nonetheless, she does not lose her ketubah, for she can say, "I will drink and test myself," and will we lose her money because of gossip? Therefore, the Tur did not write this ruling, because in our time, this does not apply, as I have written.

This explanation that warning (kinui) and seclusion (setirah) require two witnesses is derived from the Mishnah at the beginning of Sotah, and this is the law. And in the Gemara there, it is stated that Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehudah says in the name of Rabbi Elazar (this is how it should be written, and so it is in the Tosefta, and examine it closely) that warning can be done with one witness or by the husband himself, but seclusion requires two witnesses. And it is stated there: Rabbi Chanina of Sura said that a man should not say to his wife in this time, "Do not seclude yourself with so-and-so," because perhaps we hold according to Rabbi Yosei that warning can be done by the husband himself, and she will be secluded, and now there is no way to test a sotah (suspected adulteress) and she will be forbidden to him forever. And although if so, even in the time of the Temple one should be cautious about this, since by his own warning he cannot make her drink without two witnesses to the seclusion, nevertheless, in the time of the Temple, there is not so much concern, because perhaps there will be witnesses to the seclusion, and also he can warn her in front of two witnesses and make her drink. But in this time, there is no recourse, and one should not ask. Now, in this time, what concern is there when there are no witnesses to the seclusion? This is not a question: firstly, because perhaps there will be witnesses to the seclusion, for without warning she is not forbidden, and with warning she is forbidden. And further, even without witnesses, she would be forbidden according to the Rambam and the Tur, who ruled that seclusion by the husband himself after warning in front of two witnesses forbids her, as was written in section 18. Consequently, according to Rabbi Yosei, she is also forbidden after his own warning.

According to the primary law, we should not be concerned with this statement since we hold according to our Mishnah that warning [to a wife] is specifically in the presence of two witnesses. It is clear that this is the opinion of the Tur, who cites this law in the name of the SeMaG. The SeMaG was concerned with this law, but from the words of the Rambam in the 24th chapter of Hilchot Ishut, it appears that this is a definitive law. His words are: "If he said to her privately, 'Do not seclude yourself with a certain man,' and he saw that she secluded herself with him and stayed the time sufficient for defilement, she is forbidden to her husband in these times when there is no Sotah water." This is very surprising since in the laws of Sotah, he explicitly ruled that the warning must be in the presence of two witnesses and did not mention this at all. How could he rule there like Rabbi Yosi? It seems clear to me that everything revolves around the axis we explained earlier in chapter 115, that most of the words of the Rambam in these matters are not definitive laws but just to fulfill the obligation of being stringent. The Ri"f in the third chapter of Kiddushin holds similarly, as I explained there at length. The Rambam believes that Rabbi Chanina of Sura, who says this law, only intended it to fulfill the obligation of being stringent and not as a definitive law. And you will understand this since otherwise, where do we find that we rule like a Baraita of a single opinion against an explicit Mishnah? Therefore, it is certain that this is just to fulfill the obligation of being stringent, and that is why the Rambam did not write this law in the laws of Sotah but only in the context of fulfilling the obligation of being stringent. Earlier in chapter 115, paragraph 56, we wrote about this matter to differentiate between the drinking of Sotah water and the prohibition to the husband. This is the approach of the commentators and it seems from the words of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in chapter 115 and in this chapter, paragraph 7. However, it seems to me that if one errs in warning his wife, there is a simple solution: he should forgive the warning. It has already been explained that forgiveness is effective for the warning prior to seclusion. If he did not do so and saw that she secluded herself, it seems to me that after the fact, she should not be prohibited. This is also the opinion of the Bach and the Drisha, and their questions on the Rambam’s words are not difficult at all with what I have explained. Pay close attention to this.

It has already been explained that seclusion without prior warning does not prohibit a wife to her husband, even if two witnesses testified about the seclusion and they stayed together long enough to commit a transgression. Thus, our sages said, "We do not prohibit [a wife] based on seclusion" (Kiddushin 81a). The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 6 that we do not prohibit based on seclusion, even if they secluded themselves for the purpose of sin, unless there was a prior warning. Nonetheless, there is a prohibition for a woman to seclude herself, as stated in Section 22, but this does not result in prohibition [to her husband]. Note that what is written, "even if they secluded themselves with the intention of sin," does not result in prohibition, contradicts the words of Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) in Section 7, Paragraph 11. We have already explained there in Paragraph 22, where we wrote the opinions of the commentators and what appears correct to us with the help of Heaven.

If he did not warn her and a single witness comes and tells him that his wife committed adultery and she remains silent, if he trusts this witness and relies on him as if he were two witnesses, he must divorce her and give her the ketubah. If not, she is permitted to him. And some say that if she remains silent, even if the witness is not trusted by him as if he were two witnesses, he must divorce her (Beit Shmuel, subparagraph 8, in the name of Rashal). And we have already explained in Siman 115, paragraph 24, that the primary opinion is the first one, as we wrote there further on this matter.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in Section 9: "And it is the same if she herself says to him that she has committed adultery, that she is forbidden [to him]. And some say that in our times, when there is the decree of Rabbenu Gershom not to divorce a woman against her will, he is not believed to say that he believes her or that he believes the words of the witness, because we are concerned that perhaps his eyes are on another and he says that he believes her even though he does not believe her. And we distance him for saying that he believes her and thereby causing the annulment of the decree of Rabbenu Gershom. And it is the same in any case where one cannot divorce without the wife's consent. And some say that we force him and he must live with her even though he says that he believes the words of the witness, as long as the wife does not admit or even if she herself said 'I am impure to you' and then retracted and gave a valid reason for her original words. But there are those who disagree and hold that even in our times he is believed. And if he had a quarrel with her, he is not believed to say that he believes the words of the witness, because it is certain that he said so out of hatred." End of quote.

And the great later authorities in their many responsa have labored over his words, and with God's help, we have clarified his words in Siman 115 from Section 27 to Section 32, all based on what we have written that the prohibition is not from the letter of the law but to fulfill the obligation of being stringent. Therefore, we can be stringent in this matter in our times. And in Section 43, we clarified there how the law applies when the husband himself says that he saw her commit adultery, see there. And in Section 31, we clarified there that when there are grounds to suspect in our times, she is forbidden, see there.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 10: If someone spreads rumors about his wife claiming she committed adultery and then later says that it is not true, but he made the claim out of anger, if he gives a valid reason for his words, she is permitted to him; but if not, she is forbidden to him. This implies that another reason is required. However, in the responsa of the Rosh, section 32, it is explained that the anger itself is considered a valid reason. Therefore, some say that indeed another reason is required (see Pitchei Teshuvah, subsection 24). This is not clear to me, as certainly, anger is a good reason, and the intent of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch is that the cause of the anger must be clarified. If it appears to the court that the matter justifies bringing him to a state of anger, it is a good reason. If not, we do not believe him regarding the anger he claims. And in our times, the ruling is explained in section 115, clause 43; see there.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 3: A minor girl who was married off by her father and committed adultery willingly—there is an opinion that she is forbidden to her husband. Therefore, her husband is given the opportunity to warn her in order to forfeit her ketubah. However, there is another opinion that she is not prohibited to her husband unless he is a priest. The reasoning is that the seduction of a minor is considered coercion. The first opinion is that of the Rambam in Chapter 2 of Sotah and Chapter 3 of Laws of Forbidden Relations, who does not hold this reasoning. All other authorities have rejected his view. We have clarified his intention with the help of Heaven in Section 68, Paragraph 8, and in Section 6, Paragraph 30. See there.

And Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote that a married woman who committed adultery unintentionally, thinking that the man she was with was her husband when it was actually someone else, is permitted to her Jewish husband. However, if she committed adultery under the belief that it was permissible to do so, this is considered as intentional and she is forbidden to her Jewish husband, as it is written, "and acted unfaithfully against the Lord" (Numbers 5:12), which means she acted unfaithfully against her husband. Thus, even if she thought it was permissible to commit adultery, she still acted unfaithfully toward her husband. Therefore, even if we say that someone who acts under the belief that it is permissible is considered unintentional, she still betrayed her husband (Bayit Chadash, subparagraph 4). Even if she was modest and committed adultery willingly to save many Jewish lives, it is still considered full willingness in terms of adultery, and she would be forbidden to her husband, as proven by the case of Esther, who was forbidden to Mordechai (ibid). But if she thought the man was her husband, she is considered completely unintentional and is believed on this account with the justification that she could have claimed she was forced. Therefore, it seems to me that if there are witnesses that it was done willingly and she has no justification, she is not believed to claim otherwise, and this requires further study. A mentally incompetent woman is obviously worse off than a minor and has no will at all, and it appears that a deaf-mute is considered like a minor. Therefore, according to Maimonides (Rambam) who holds that in Torah marriages a minor has will, if a deaf-mute was married while sound-minded and then became deaf-mute and committed adultery willingly, she would be forbidden according to Maimonides' opinion.

Additionally, it is written: A woman who secluded herself with men on the way and then came and said, "I secluded myself and was raped," some say she is believed with a *migu* (a legal principle allowing a claim based on a stronger potential claim) that she could have said she was not raped. Others say she loses her *migu* since she secluded herself improperly. And it seems that even according to the latter opinion, this only applies when there are witnesses to the seclusion, because otherwise, she does have a *migu* that she was not secluded. Additionally, this is specifically when she secluded herself with one person, because with two people there is no prohibition of seclusion, as stated in Siman 22. And even though it is explained there that with promiscuous individuals, even with ten it is forbidden, she does not need to assume they are promiscuous, and all Jews are presumed to be of good character (in my opinion).

We remove a woman from her husband by means of witnesses to her impurity, even if they did not see an act as explicit as a spindle in a tube, as long as they saw them attached to each other and behaving in the manner of adulterers. Any woman who becomes forbidden to her husband, whether through warning and seclusion or not, once she is forbidden to her husband, she is also forbidden to the adulterer. It is learned from tradition: "and she has been defiled" (Numbers 5:29), meaning she has been defiled both to her husband and to the adulterer. Therefore, if he transgresses and marries her, we remove her from him and he must divorce her, even if she has many children from him. And any woman about whom two witnesses come and testify that she committed adultery with this man while she was still married to her first husband, she must be divorced from him with a get (bill of divorce), even if she has many children. These laws have already been explained in Siman 11, and there are many detailed laws regarding the prohibition of the adulterer, as well as in the case of seclusion without warning where there are witnesses to inappropriate behavior, which are also explained there, so refer to it.

There are those who say that if a woman committed adultery with a Gentile and subsequently converted, it is permissible for him to marry her after divorce or after the husband's death. We do not say that just as she is forbidden to her husband, she is also forbidden to her paramour, except in a case where she would not have been forbidden to him otherwise. But with a Gentile, since in any case, marriage is not valid with him, and furthermore, he is considered like a newborn child. Therefore, if someone committed adultery with his wife's sister and her husband divorced her, she is forbidden to her paramour after his wife's death. Not only does the second reason not apply to him, since he is not like a newborn child, but even the first reason does not apply to him. Although, even without this, she is forbidden to him because of the prohibition of his wife's sister's nakedness, nevertheless, she would have been fit to be permitted to him after his wife's death. But with a Gentile, this does not apply, because what makes her permitted to him afterward is that he is not the same as he was before, as he is considered like a newborn child (see Beit Shmuel, section 13, and the Gra, sections 22 and 23, and scrutinize carefully).

If a woman claims that a certain man is pursuing her but he denies it, she is not believed to the extent that we would punish him. However, we should still be concerned and decree that he should not speak with her at all and that they should not live in the same neighborhood. This means that he is not obligated to move away from his current residence, but he should not move into her neighborhood. If they currently live in the same neighborhood, she should be the one to move away. How can we force him to move away when he denies the accusation? However, if he is known to be suspect in matters of immorality, it is proper to rebuke him sternly, threaten him, and distance him from her neighborhood. They should warn him that if he does not behave properly, he will be ostracized and expelled from the community with a strong hand, as our Sages said at the end of Kiddushin: "We administer lashes for a bad reputation," and as Maimonides wrote in Chapter 24 of Sanhedrin.

The Sages received a tradition that a woman does not drink and repeat (the ritual) with one husband and one paramour. However, with two paramours, even with one husband, or with two husbands, even with one paramour, she drinks and repeats. They derived this from the verses in the section of Sotah, as explained in the first chapter of Sotah. How so? If Reuven was jealous of his wife with Shimon and she secluded herself and was tested by drinking the waters, he cannot make her drink again with regards to Shimon, even if he divorced her and she married another after the divorce. (This is implied by Rambam in Chapter 1, Halacha 13; see there and scrutinize.) If he was jealous of her with Shimon another time and she secluded herself, he cannot make her drink again but she is forbidden to him forever, as it is in our times. But regarding another man, he can make her drink, and so too with a third and fourth, indefinitely. If Reuven divorced her and she married Levi, Levi can also make her drink with regards to Shimon. If Levi divorced her and she married Yehudah, Yehudah can also make her drink with regards to Shimon, and so on indefinitely. All this is a decree of the Torah.

And these are the cases where the court administers a warning to women without the knowledge of their husbands: if her husband became deaf or insane after marrying her while he was of sound mind (since she is still married according to Torah law), or if he married her while he was already deaf, in which case there is no Torah-recognized marriage and therefore no basis for a warning. Similarly, if her husband is overseas or imprisoned, in all these cases, if the court hears that people are gossiping about her having an intimate relationship with a certain man, they call her and tell her not to seclude herself with that man. If witnesses later come and testify that she secluded herself with him and stayed with him for the amount of time it takes to become defiled, she becomes forbidden to her husband forever. Her marriage contract is torn, and she is not entitled to support from her husband's property. When her husband becomes sane, returns from afar, or is released from prison, he must give her a bill of divorce. However, he cannot make her drink the bitter waters (sotah) because the drinking of the waters only applies when the husband himself administers a warning, as explicitly stated in the Torah. The court's warning is solely to prevent her from sinning.

A woman whose husband warned her (against seclusion with another man) and she secluded herself (with him), and he wants to make her drink (the bitter waters), but she does not want to, we do not force her to drink. Whether she says "I have become impure" or she says "I have not become impure," but nonetheless says "I do not wish to drink," we do not force her, and she leaves without her ketubah (Rambam, end of Chapter 2). Even if they brought her up to the Temple and prepared her offering and wrote the scroll, as long as they have not erased the scroll, she can say "I am not drinking" even if she does not say that she has become impure. (Proof is from Mishnah 6, Chapter 3: "And these whose meal offerings are burnt: the one who says 'I am impure to you,' etc., and the one who says 'I am not drinking,' etc." This is even if she says "I am pure," for otherwise it would be the same as the beginning clause).

And similarly, if the husband does not want to make her drink [the bitter waters], even though she wants to, she does not drink and she takes her ketubah and leaves. He cannot say that since you are prohibited to me due to your seclusion, I will not give you the ketubah, for she can say that since the Torah gave you the right to test me with the water because I am pure, make me drink and I will not lose my ketubah. The reason for these two rulings is that the Torah did not compel her to drink the water, but rather gave permission to clarify the doubt if they want to. Therefore, if one of them does not want the drinking, we do not compel them. All the more so when her husband has had relations with her after her seclusion, then the water does not test her, as will be explained, she does not drink and takes her ketubah and leaves. It is not possible to cause her to lose her ketubah because of a prohibition he committed, even though she also did not act properly by allowing herself to be in a situation where he could come upon her. Nevertheless, the main prohibition is upon him, for she can say, "I know I am pure, but he committed a complete prohibition."

And these are the women who are not fit to drink [the bitter waters], even though they and their husbands want her to drink. However, once witnesses to the seclusion after the warning have come forward, they are forbidden to their husbands forever and go out without a ketubah, just as it is nowadays, since according to the Torah, they are not to be given to drink. The Rambam wrote in chapter 2 that there are fifteen such women, and these are they: an engaged woman, a woman awaiting levirate marriage, a minor married to an adult, an adult married to a minor, the wife of a hermaphrodite, the wife of a blind man, the wife of a lame man, the wife of a mute man, the wife of a man who does not hear, or a man who has a severed hand. Similarly, if she is lame, or mute, or does not hear, or has a severed hand, or is blind, all these are not fit for drinking.

And from where do we know that they are not fit? As it is stated, "If a woman goes astray under her husband" – this excludes a betrothed woman and a woman awaiting levirate marriage, as they are not yet fully under their husband's authority. "A woman" – this excludes a minor. "Under her husband" – this excludes the wife of a minor and the wife of an androgynous person, who is not considered a man. "And it was hidden from the eyes of her husband" – this excludes the wife of a blind man. "And the priest shall set the woman" – this excludes a lame woman. "And place it on her hands" – this excludes one who does not have a hand, or if it was bent or dry and she cannot take it, even with one hand, as it says "her hands". "And the woman shall say, 'Amen'" – this excludes a mute woman. "And he shall say to the woman" – this excludes one who does not hear. And it says, "If a woman goes astray under her husband" – until she is complete like him and he is complete like her. Thus, you learn that anything that prevents her from drinking prevents her husband from giving her to drink, and any defect that prevents the husband from giving her to drink, a similar defect in her prevents her from drinking.

There are also women who do not drink [the bitter water] due to a prohibition, as will be explained. However, this section only considers those for whom there is no prohibition at all. It does not consider the wife of an imbecile, for it is obvious that "the man shall bring his wife" does not apply when the husband lacks any understanding. Including the wife of an androgyne follows his opinion in the first chapter of the laws of marriage that an androgyne can marry a woman, whereas other authorities do not consider this a valid marriage at all. Similarly, one who says "I will not make her drink" cannot make her drink anymore (Maggid Mishneh, chapter 2), even if both parties consent to the drinking (as inferred from Tosafot, Yevamot 95, s.v. אילימא). This reasoning is puzzling: why should he not be able to make her drink if she agrees? It is possible to say that the reason is that once he says "I will not make her drink," it implies he knows of some sin that prevents him from making her drink, and similarly when she says "I will not drink" (most of these laws are in chapter 24, see there).

He expressed jealousy over his betrothed or the woman awaiting levirate marriage with him, and then he married her and had relations with her, and afterward she secluded herself [with another man], she drinks like any other woman (Sotah 26a). For the warning is not invalid even though it was given before the marriage, since the seclusion occurred afterward and we apply the verse "under your husband" to her. And this is specifically when the husband had relations with her before the seclusion, for otherwise, even if he warned her when she was already married and she secluded herself, if the husband had not yet had relations with her at all (such as if she entered the bridal canopy but was not consummated), she does not drink, and she leaves without a ketubah and is forbidden to him forever, as it is stated, "and a man lay with you aside from your husband," implying that the husband's intercourse precedes the intercourse of the adulterer (Sotah 24a).

The convert and the freedwoman, and the wife of the convert and the wife of the freed slave, and a mamzeret (a woman born from a forbidden union) and the wife of a mamzer, and the wife of a man impotent from birth or made impotent by human action, who are permitted to their husbands, are like all other women and drink [the bitter waters]. And although it is written in the Sotah section, "Speak to the children of Israel," nonetheless, the convert and the freedwoman also drink, etc., because the Torah included them (see Talmud Sotah 26a). Similarly, the wife of a Kohen drinks, and we do not say that since it is written "and she was not seized," meaning she was not raped and therefore is forbidden, and if raped, she is permitted, and regarding a Kohen she is forbidden even if raped, therefore she should not drink. We do not say this, because this has nothing to do with the drinking of the waters, which is a test to determine if she was unfaithful at all (Sotah 26a). And the Torah, which says that if she was seized she is permitted, is to teach us that if a wife of an Israelite was raped, she is permitted to her husband, but this has nothing to do with the drinking of the waters.

The Rambam wrote (there) that for a pregnant or nursing woman, one administers the Sotah waters to her as she is. This means that we do not wait for her to give birth or to wean her child. Similarly, Rashi explained (26a), and there was astonishment about this, questioning why we do not worry about the danger to the child and wait (Tosafot). From the Rambam's own words in Chapter 12 of Sanhedrin, it is clear that whenever there is no delay in judgment, we wait until she gives birth (Maggid Mishneh). It seems to me that their reasoning is that if we knew for certain that she was impure and would die, we would wait. But here, it is uncertain, and it is more likely that she is pure since she is willing to drink, as it is in her hands not to drink, as explained. Therefore, why should we wait, since she is crying out that the drinking will prove her purity? Nevertheless, some say that while she is pregnant or nursing, we do not make her drink, and the intention of the Talmud is that she drinks afterward. This teaches us that we do not say that since she is currently not fit to drink, she is also not fit for the warning of seclusion, but rather she is fit for the warning (Tosafot there and Maggid Mishneh and it requires further investigation as this is derived from a betrothed woman, and examine carefully).

A woman who was about to drink, and her husband died before she drank, she neither drinks nor takes her ketubah from the heirs. It appears to me that even if he died after the scroll was erased, she does not drink, because the main purpose of the drinking is to clarify if she is permitted to her husband or not, and when he dies, clarification is not relevant. Her law is like that of a woman who says "I am defiled" after the scroll is erased, as will be explained later, with God's help.

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (beginning of Chapter 4) that a yavam (levirate husband) can administer the sotah water to the woman based on his brother's warning. If his brother warned her and then died, and the yavam married her, and afterwards she secluded herself, the yavam administers the sotah water based on his brother's warning. Similarly, if the yavam warned her after he married her and then he died, and his second brother married her, and afterwards she secluded herself, the second brother administers the sotah water. However, if the yavam warned her while she was still awaiting levirate marriage and then he died, and his second brother married her and she secluded herself, he does not administer the sotah water based on the first yavam's warning. Since the first one did not marry her, the levirate marriage of the second brother derives from the first brother and not from the first yavam, and she is not the wife of the first yavam. The Rambam does not mention this at all, and it is not mentioned in our Talmud either. (And one cannot say that from Kiddushin 27b it does not imply this, for if it were like the Jerusalem Talmud, we could establish it in such a manner, as the Jerusalem Talmud also says this in Chapter 2. Therefore, there is no contradiction, and this is the truth for the one who examines there carefully; and pay close attention).

Rambam wrote (there): Any man who has ever committed a forbidden act of intercourse after reaching adulthood, the bitter waters do not test his wife. Even if he had relations with his betrothed in his father-in-law's house, which is forbidden by rabbinic decree, the waters do not test his wife, as it is stated, "And the man shall be free from iniquity, and the woman shall bear her iniquity." Therefore, if his wife is forbidden to him due to a prohibition punishable by a negative commandment or a positive commandment, even if it is a secondary prohibition, and he warned her and she secluded herself, she does not drink but rather leaves without her ketubah and is forbidden to him also because of this. These are his words, and it is a novel matter, for the interpretation of "and the man shall be free from iniquity" is brought in the Talmud in several places, and in all of them it is proven that only if the husband had relations with the suspected adulteress after she secluded herself does it prevent the drinking of the waters. So explained Rashi, Tosafot, the Raavad, and all the commentators. But that another act of intercourse would prevent the test, we have not heard.

However, in the Sifrei at the end of Parashat Sotah, it explains according to the Rambam, and this is its language: "Why does it say, 'And the man shall be free from iniquity'? When the man is free from iniquity, the woman shall bear her iniquity, not like it is said, 'I will not punish your daughters when they commit harlotry, for they themselves go aside with harlots,' etc. It says to them, 'Since you pursue harlotry, even the waters will not test your wives.' Therefore, it says, 'And the man shall be free from iniquity'—that specific iniquity." End quote. This means the iniquity of harlotry, but another iniquity does not prevent the waters from working. Also, in our Talmud at the end of Sotah, it proves this, as it is taught: "When adulterers increased, the bitter waters ceased," etc., and the Gemara brings this teaching that "the man shall be free from iniquity." Rashi himself explains there, and this is his language: "Free from the iniquity of adultery with a prohibited woman, whether this one who secluded herself or another." End quote. Thus, this is clearly according to the words of the Rambam, may his memory be blessed. The Gemara, whenever it brings this teaching regarding when another man had relations with her after her seclusion, certainly includes this as well, that he is not free from iniquity. The Gemara deals with this matter, but in any case, any forbidden relations prevent the waters from working.

(And what Raavad questioned from the matter of 24: and his intention that they said there that he had relations with his betrothed in his father-in-law's house, and the commentary of Kesef Mishneh is strained. One could simply say that the prohibition is because of a bride without a blessing, and one could say that they blessed the seven blessings, and in any case, she is not considered married because she did not enter his domain, but there is no prohibition here. And this that he did not bring that the harlotry of his sons and daughters also prevents, it seems to me that he holds that certainly by law it cannot be said that the father is punished for the sin of his children, only the verse speaks in a moral way that they were very promiscuous, and therefore, he certainly is not free from iniquity. And what the Maggid Mishneh questioned, that if so, there would be a slander on the women that they would say because he had forbidden relations, from the waters, etc., we need not worry, for all of Israel is presumed to be righteous, and indeed, when adulterers increased, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai ceased the practice. Thus, it seems to me in the opinion of the Rambam, may his memory be blessed.)

He also wrote that if one transgressed and married his friend's pregnant or nursing wife, she drinks [the bitter waters] since there is no [actual] transgression here. So it is written in the Gemara (26a) and in the Tosefta (Chapter 5). This means that although it is forbidden for him to marry her, nevertheless, the act of intercourse itself is not inherently forbidden, but only due to the decree concerning the child. Therefore, it is possible for him to separate from her for twenty-four months and then be with her, and it is not similar to other prohibited acts of intercourse where the act itself is inherently forbidden.

If this wife, for whom he was jealous, is old or barren or an ailonit, and he has no other wife who is fit to bear children and he has not yet fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation (Pru Urvu), the sages taught in the Mishnah (Chapter 4) that he does not give her the bitter waters to drink. But if he has fulfilled the mitzvah of procreation or he has another wife fit to bear children, he does give her to drink. The reasoning behind this matter is that the Torah permitted giving the bitter waters to drink to make peace between a man and his wife. Here, our concern is not with peace, because by doing so, he would not fulfill the mitzvah of procreation (Pru Urvu). 

And it should not be asked: on the contrary, let her drink and we will fulfill “and she will be cleared and will conceive seed,” because truly this verse only speaks of one who is fit to bear children. If she was giving birth in pain, she will give birth with ease; if she was giving birth to females, she will give birth to males (Rambam). Therefore, as soon as she secluded herself after the warning, she leaves without a ketubah.

Furthermore, one should not ask how it is possible to give them to drink if he has fulfilled Pru Urvu, as we do not say “and she will conceive seed” regarding them, because the Torah does not insist that she be fit to bear children (Raavad). And thus the Torah said that if she is fit to bear children, she will conceive seed, but this is not a hindrance.

And the Rambam wrote (there) if he had a wife and children and they died between the warning and the seclusion, she is already seen to drink and he gives her to drink. If he had no children or no wife fit to bear children except this barren woman and the like, and a son was born to him from his divorced wife between the warning and the seclusion, she is already disqualified from drinking, end quote. And this is from the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter 4. The reason is that everything follows the time of the warning. And it appears to me that "son" is not specific but rather son and daughter, for otherwise he has still not fulfilled the commandment of being fruitful and multiplying. And there are those who are uncertain if he became a eunuch between the warning and the seclusion if she drinks as when the wife and children died, or perhaps in a Torah prohibition we do not say this, for she has become forbidden to him (Maggid Mishneh). And it appears to me that this law is like when the husband died before the drinking, for what difference does it make if he died or separated from her because of the eunuch prohibition. Moreover, the primary purpose of the water is to make peace between them, which is obviously impossible here. (The laws Rambam wrote in chapter 2 from halacha 12 until the end of the chapter have already been explained in section 11 and some have also been explained in this section).

How is the procedure of giving the Sotah to drink when the Temple was standing? The husband comes to the court in his city and says to them, "This wife of mine, I warned her not to seclude herself with so-and-so, and she secluded herself with him. And these are the witnesses. And she says that she is pure, and I want to give her the water to drink to test the matter." The court investigates the words of the witnesses, and if it is true that he warned her in the presence of two witnesses and there are witnesses to the seclusion, they send him and her to Jerusalem. For the Sotah is only given to drink in the great court of seventy elders in the Temple. We derive this from a verbal analogy (gezera shava). It is written regarding the Sotah, "And the priest shall do to her according to all this law," and it is written there, "According to the law they instruct you." Just as there it is done in the great court, so too here it is done in the great court (Gemara Sotah 7a). One should not ask why we need a verse for this. It is obvious that since there is a sacrifice for the Sotah, and also the dust must be taken from the Temple floor to put into the water as explained in the verse, it is clear that it cannot be done anywhere other than Jerusalem. For without the gezera shava, I would say that the warning, the writing of the passage, and the oath could be done in the court of the city, and afterwards they would go up to the Temple for the sacrifice and drinking of the water. Therefore, the gezera shava teaches us that all this law of the passage is only done in Jerusalem. And furthermore, it is true that Jerusalem is required, but how do we know that the great court is required? Perhaps it suffices with the court of twenty-three that sits at the entrance of the Temple Mount (Rashi). Therefore, the verse teaches us that specifically the great court is required.

When they send her to Jerusalem, they assign two Torah scholars to guard her so that her husband does not come upon her on the way. They inform him that she is forbidden to him until she drinks the bitter waters, as it is written. Her husband is not believed regarding her, even though the Torah believed him in matters of niddah (menstrual impurity) and permitted seclusion. This is because niddah is a severe prohibition, and he takes it seriously. However, in the case of a sotah (a woman suspected of adultery), which is a lighter prohibition, he is not believed. This requires two people because the law states that on the road, there is a prohibition of seclusion with two people, as one might need to relieve himself, leaving the other alone with her, as stated in Siman 22. Additionally, there need to be witnesses in case he comes upon her. The Torah scholars are required so they know how to warn and caution him not to come upon her (Talmud, there).

This is the wording of the Rambam in Chapter 3: "When they arrive in Jerusalem, the Great Court seats her among them and intimidates her, not in the presence of her husband, and frightens her greatly so that she will not drink. They say to her, 'My daughter, wine does much, levity does much, youth does much, bad neighbors do much. Do not cause the great name that is written in holiness to be erased by the water.' They tell her, 'My daughter, many preceded you and were swept away, and great and precious people were overcome by their inclinations and failed.' They recount to her the story of Judah and Tamar his daughter-in-law, and the story of Reuben with his father's concubine in its plain meaning (for according to the interpretation, he did not sin, as in Shabbat 55), and the story of Amnon and his sister, to make it easier for her until she confesses. If she says, 'Yes, I have been defiled,' or 'I will not drink,' she leaves without a marriage contract and goes away." End of quote. And all of this is explained in the Mishnah (7). However, what he wrote, that they intimidate her not in the presence of her husband, he wrote from reasoning, because since our intention is for her to confess, it is easier for her to confess not in the presence of her husband. But what he wrote, that they seat her among them, I do not know from where he derived this, and why they would seat her among them. Perhaps he did not mean it literally.

If she insists on her claim that she is pure, they bring her to the eastern gate of the Temple courtyard, which is opposite the Holy of Holies, and they move her from place to place to tire her out until her spirit is weakened, hoping she might confess. If she still insists on her claim, they bring her in front of the eastern gate from the outside and stand her there, and they remove her fine clothes to disgrace her, hoping she might confess. If she was dressed in white garments, she is dressed in black. If the black garments are becoming to her, she is dressed in garments that are not becoming. They remove her jewelry and all her gold and silver ornaments. They gather a large assembly of women around her, and all the women present there are obligated to see her, as it is stated (Ezekiel 23:48), "All women will be admonished and not commit lewdness as you have done." Any man who wishes to see her may come and see her. She stands among them without a veil and without a scarf, but in her regular clothing and the cap on her head, as she would be in her house and not in public. Her servants and maidservants are not allowed to remain with her because she recognizes them and their presence might comfort her, and we want her to possibly confess. However, her relatives are allowed to stay there because their presence brings her more disgrace.

And know that the order of the Mishnah does not correspond to the order of the Torah portion, and the order of the Rambam in Chapter 3 is different from both of them. The order of the Torah portion is as follows: He became jealous of her, and she secluded herself. He brings the woman and her offering, and the priest brings an earthenware vessel and puts into it half a log of water from the laver, and puts earth from the floor of the Temple into it. He stands the woman at the Nicanor Gate, grasps her clothing, and uncovers her hair. He places the offering on her hands, and in the priest’s hand are the waters. He adjures her and stipulates with her, writes the scroll, erases it, gives her to drink, takes her offering, places it in a sacred vessel, waves it, brings it near (to the altar), takes a handful, and burns it.

According to the order of the Mishnah, it appears as follows: He becomes jealous of her, and she secluded herself. He brings the woman up and threatens her, and stands her at the Nicanor Gate. He holds her clothing and dishevels her hair. He brings the meal offering and places it in her hands. He brings an earthenware vessel and puts into it half a log of water from the laver, and places in it dust from the floor of the Temple. He makes her swear an oath and stipulates with her. He writes the scroll and erases it, and gives her to drink. He takes the meal offering and places it in a service vessel, waves it, brings it near, takes a handful, and burns it.

And the order according to the Rambam is as follows: If a man becomes jealous of his wife and she goes into seclusion, he brings the woman up and they intimidate her. They bring her up to the Nicanor Gate, and the priest makes her swear an oath and writes the scroll. He brings an earthenware vessel and puts water in it, and dust from the floor of the Temple, and erases the scroll into the water. Then he grasps her garments and dishevels her hair. After that, he brings the offering and places it in her hands. He takes the offering and puts it into a service vessel, waves it, brings it near the altar, takes a handful, and burns it. Before bringing the offering, the priest makes her drink, as it says. And aside from the unusual order, the Jerusalem Talmud (Sotah 3:2) states that everyone agrees that the erasure must be close to the drinking, so how can he delay the erasure so much before the drinking? And our Rabbis, the authors of Tosafot, have already written (Sotah 17b s.v. Kodem) that the order of the passage is primary. Therefore, we will explain with the help of Heaven according to the order of the passage. And already they have wondered about the Rambam (Kesef Mishneh, Tosefot Yom Tov, Maggid Mishneh), and the Mishnah does not speak about the order but about the laws. And you should know that the Mishnah precedes the writing of the scroll to the oath, and this is impossible as explained in the Gemara (Sotah 17b).

When she stands opposite the eastern gate and her fine clothes have been removed from her, her husband brings her offering, because he is obligated to bring all her obligatory offerings. What is her offering? Not an animal or a bird, but a meal offering of one-tenth of an ephah. It is different from all other meal offerings, as all other meal offerings are made of wheat, but this one is made of barley. And although the Omer offering is also made of barley, that one was sifted until it became fine flour, whereas this one is coarse flour mixed with bran. Because she acted like an animal, her offering is the food of an animal. Even if she is pure, by her seclusion she acted like an animal. All other meal offerings require oil and frankincense, but concerning this one it is written, "He shall not pour oil on it, nor put frankincense on it." If he adds oil or frankincense, he transgresses a negative commandment. The purpose is that her offering should not be of a fine nature. All other meal offerings are brought in service vessels, but this one is brought by the husband in an Egyptian basket, which is a basket made of palm twigs. Because she acted like an Egyptian woman, her offering vessel is an Egyptian basket. The husband stands with the offering.

And afterwards, the priest brings an earthenware vessel, meaning an earthenware utensil, and puts into it half a log of water from the laver, as it is written, "holy water," and "holy" means that it has been sanctified in a service vessel (Rashi 15b). The vessel should be new, and the water does not need to be spring water (Gemara there). He measures the half log of water with the half log measure of sanctity that was in the Temple. The priest enters the sanctuary, turns to his right, where there was a place one cubit by one cubit with a marble tablet and a ring fixed there. He lifts it and takes dust from underneath it and puts enough so that it is visible on the water, as it is said, "and from the dust that will be on the floor of the Tabernacle, the priest shall take and put it in the water." If there is no dust there, he brings dust from outside and places it there and takes from there (Gemara), because the place sanctifies it (Sifri). And even though the text says "Tabernacle," the Sages have already said that the Temple is called the Tabernacle and the Tabernacle is called the Temple (beginning of Eruvin). Moreover, here the verse refers explicitly to the Temple, as it is stated in the Gemara (16a, and see Tosafot there). He also adds something bitter to the water, like wormwood or something similar (20a), as it says, "bitter waters," meaning they are already bitter before the erasure.

Afterward, the priest comes and stands the woman at the Nikanor Gate, while the priest stands outside and grasps her garments opposite her face and tears them until he uncovers her heart. He uncovers her hair and unbraids her head’s braids to disgrace her. He brings an Egyptian rope and ties it above her breasts so that her clothes do not fall and leave her naked, as all her clothes are torn, even her undergarment. And why an Egyptian rope? To remind her of the Egyptian deeds she committed. However, this is not essential; if an Egyptian rope is not found, another rope may be brought.

And behold, it is understood that this task is not a respectable task for a priest, and who would be willing to do it? Therefore, it is taught in the Tosefta (Chapter 1) that they would cast lots among themselves, and whoever the lot fell upon had to perform this task. Even if the lot fell upon the High Priest, he was obligated to do it. And the priest, when uncovering her hair, would turn his face away.

Afterwards, the priest places the meal offering on her hands to tire her out, perhaps she will admit, and the priest holds the bitter waters in his hand and makes the woman swear the oath of the curse in a language that she understands, for the portion of Sotah can be said in any language (Sotah 32a). The priest informs her that this matter was caused by the warning and the seclusion, and he says to her in a language that she understands the following: "If no man has lain with you, and if you have not gone astray in impurity while under your husband's authority, be cleared by these bitter waters that bring a curse. But if you have gone astray while under your husband's authority, and you have become impure, and a man other than your husband has lain with you, may the Lord make you a curse and an oath among your people by making your thigh fall and your belly swell. May these bitter waters that bring a curse enter your bowels, causing your belly to swell and your thigh to fall." And she says, "Amen, Amen," also in a language she understands. The priest informs her that the belly will be affected first and the thigh afterwards, so as not to discredit the waters.

Afterwards, the priest brings a scroll of pure leather, like a Torah scroll, and writes on it in Hebrew with ink that does not contain kankantum (iron sulfate), because it needs to be written in a way that can be erased. The writing must be done for its specific purpose, just like a get (divorce document). Thus, it is taught in the Tosefta of Gittin (Chapter 2) that a scroll of the sotah (a woman suspected of adultery) that was written not for its specific purpose is invalid, as it is stated "and the priest shall do for her according to all this Torah," implying that all actions must be done for its specific purpose. The wording "for her" is interpreted similarly to a get. It is not written on a tablet, paper, or diphthera (untanned parchment), but only on a scroll of processed leather, as it is stated "in a book." It is not written with komus (sap) or kankantum or any substance that leaves a lasting mark, but only with ink. In the section on the get, we explained what qualifies as ink. He writes all the statements with which he made her swear, letter by letter, word by word, and he writes in Hebrew as it is written in the Torah. He writes the name of God as it is written and not as it is pronounced. He does not write "Amen, Amen" (Sotah 17a), but only up to "and the woman shall say," excluding the phrase "and the woman shall say."

Afterward, he erases the scroll in the water, and the erasure must also be for its intended purpose. He should erase it thoroughly until no trace of the letters remains visible. The hide is then taken out of the water, and immediately the priest gives her to drink, and she drinks all the water without leaving any remainder. Afterward, he takes her meal offering from the Egyptian basket and places it into a sacred vessel. He does not add oil or frankincense, as it is written. He places the sacred vessel in her hands, and the priest places his hand underneath it, and he waves it in the east as with all other wave offerings of meal offerings, moving it forward and backward, raising and lowering it. The waving requires the hand of the owner and the hand of the priest. The owner of the meal offering of the Sotah is the woman. Some say that the priest did not place his hand directly under hers but rather she held the top of the vessel while the priest held the bottom of the vessel (Tosafot Kiddushin 36b). However, from the Jerusalem Talmud, it appears as stated plainly, and this is also explained by the Rambam. Afterward, the priest brings the meal offering to the southwest corner of the altar like other individual meal offerings, takes a handful, and burns it on the altar. The remainder is eaten by the priests. It is obvious that the meal offering is mixed only with water, and with this, all the acts of the Sotah are completed.

And afterwards, if she was pure, she goes out and leaves, and she is permitted to her husband. But if she is impure, her face immediately turns green, her eyes bulge, and she becomes filled with veins. The priests then say, "Take her out, take her out, so that she does not become a menstruant and defile the entire courtyard." They take her out of the Women's Courtyard where she was standing, and from the entire courtyard. Her belly swells first, and then her thigh falls, and she dies. At the moment she dies, the adulterer who caused her to drink also dies, and wherever he is, he dies in the same manner, with his belly swelling and his thigh falling. Thus, the Sages taught in the Mishnah (Sotah 27b): just as the water tests her, so too the water tests him, as it is said, "and they shall come" (Numbers 5:22). It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that the word "the curses" (המאררים) in gematria is 496, corresponding to the 248 limbs in her and the 248 limbs in him (and we do not count the additional limbs in a woman because they do not impart impurity in a tent).

And the Rambam wrote that all this is when the husband has never engaged in forbidden intercourse, for otherwise, the waters do not test his wife, as it is written. And if he transgressed and gave her the waters to drink, he adds to his sin by causing the ineffable name to be erased in the water in vain, and he brings discredit upon the waters of the Sotah, as his wife will say that she committed adultery and the waters did not test her, while she does not know that the husband's evil deeds caused this. Therefore, when adultery became widespread openly in the Second Temple period, the Sanhedrin abolished the bitter waters and relied on what is written in the tradition: "I will not punish your daughters when they commit harlotry..." (Hosea 4:14). End of quote.

The Sages accepted that a woman who has the merit of Torah study, for example, if she sent her children to school to study Torah or assisted her husband in studying Torah, it is possible that the waters will not test her immediately, as Torah protects from misfortune both while one is engaged in it and when one is not engaged in it, whereas a mitzvah only protects while one is engaged in the mitzvah. There is a merit that can delay for a year or more. Nevertheless, it is evident that she is impure and forbidden to her husband, for even though she does not die immediately, she will still waste away and deteriorate, heavy ailments will come upon her, and she will eventually die with the swelling of the belly and the falling of the thigh. Even now, the ailments are from the belly and the thigh.

And so it is explained from the words of the Rambam, who wrote the preceding law and then wrote: A sotah who drank the bitter waters and did not die immediately is permitted to her husband, even if he is a priest. And even if illnesses began to come upon her and other limbs became afflicted, since her belly did not swell and her thigh did not fall, she is permitted. But once her belly begins to swell and her thigh begins to fall, she is forbidden and it is certain. So concludes the text. And seemingly, this contradicts his previous statements, but according to what we have said earlier, it is understandable.

Furthermore, it is written: A sotah who drank [the bitter waters] and was found to be pure will become strengthened, and her face will shine. If she had any illness, it will leave her, and she will conceive and give birth to a male. If it was her nature to give birth with difficulty, she will give birth quickly. If it was her nature to give birth to females, she will give birth to males. These are the words of the text. 

And in this, it should also be said that generally, this is the case. For it cannot be stated as an absolute rule that every pure woman will become strengthened. If so, how could it have been written earlier that she is permitted to her husband even if illnesses come upon her? Rather, it is certain that this is not an absolute rule. The proof of this matter is that even an ailonit (a woman who cannot have children) drinks [the bitter waters] when her husband has children, as it is written, even though it is impossible for her to fulfill the verse "and she will conceive seed" as written.
