Therefore, it is certain that this is only generally the case. (And this is also evident from the critique of the Raavad in chapter 2, halacha 10; see there.)

It is a clear matter that if two witnesses come forward testifying that she is impure, even after she has drunk the water, and even if nothing happened to her from the water, she must leave her husband without a ketubah and is forbidden to him forever, for nothing stands in the face of witnesses. And if you ask, why then did the water not test her? It was received in tradition that when there are witnesses who know of her infidelity, the water does not test her. Additionally, perhaps her husband is not free of sin. But if one witness comes forward and testifies that she was impure, we do not regard him, and she remains with her husband since after drinking the water, one witness is not considered credible. And a woman who committed adultery under coercion, or by mistake, or if the adulterer approached her through limbs, meaning he acted crazily with her and did not have intercourse with her in the usual manner or the unusual manner, the water does not test her. Therefore, she should be informed of all this beforehand. And one should not ask, why then is the wife of a Kohen permitted to him after drinking the water, should we not be concerned that she was coerced? We say that we do not concern ourselves with this on our own, as coercion is uncommon, likewise, mistakes in adultery are uncommon because most acts of intercourse are intentional and not coerced. For coercion has a voice, as Tosafot stated in Ketubot (9a, s.v. ve’iba’it).

"Amen, Amen," which she says, means "Amen" to the curse and "Amen" to the oath. That is to say, she declares "Amen" that she has not become impure, which is the acceptance of the oath, and "Amen" that if she has become impure, the curse should come upon her, which is the acceptance of the curse (Rashi 18b). For "Amen" includes both acceptance and oath, and it is as if she has uttered the oath herself (Shevuot 36b). Additionally, the repetition of "Amen" includes the concept of extending the oath, which means that he can make her swear even about another man with whom he did not express suspicion. Thus, the sages taught in the Mishnah (18b): "Amen from this man, Amen from another man," and that she did not commit adultery while betrothed, before marriage, and after marriage. However, he cannot extend the oath to include that she did not commit adultery before betrothal, because one can only extend an oath concerning something that would make her forbidden to him. Before betrothal, even if she committed adultery, she is not forbidden to him. Similarly, if she was divorced and he took her back, he cannot extend the oath to include adultery after the divorce but only to the adultery of the first marriage before the divorce. Likewise, if she was his yevamah (widow awaiting levirate marriage), he cannot extend the oath to include adultery when she was awaiting yibbum, because we hold that a yevamah who committed adultery is permitted to her yavam (brother-in-law). However, he can extend the oath to include that she did not commit adultery while she was married to his brother, as in that case she would be forbidden to the yavam. The general rule is that in any case where she would not be forbidden to him if she committed adultery, he does not stipulate with her (there in the Mishnah).

Furthermore, included in the "Amen, Amen" are both "Amen" regarding the past and "Amen" regarding the future. This means that she accepts upon herself regarding the future that if she commits adultery while under his authority or after he divorces her and takes her back, the waters will then test her, and all the occurrences will happen to her, including the swelling of the belly and the falling of the thigh. All these matters are explained to her before she drinks.

A sotah (a woman suspected of adultery) who says, "I will not drink," if it is seen that she says this out of fear and fright, having been alarmed by the proceedings and the water, she may retract after she has calmed down and say, "I will drink." However, if it is seen that she is composed and not alarmed or frightened, and she says, "I will not drink," it is considered as an admission that she has been defiled, and she cannot retract and say, "I will drink."

However, there are times when we do not take her into consideration even when she says "I will not drink," and that is before the scroll is erased. If she says "I will not drink," we listen to her, and the scroll is stored under the hinge of the Temple (Jerusalem Talmud), the water is poured out and is not valid to be used for another Sotah, as it must be specifically for her, as it says, and her offering is scattered on the ashes in the courtyard. But if the scroll has already been erased, then if she explicitly says, "I am defiled," the water is poured out, as it has no sanctity even though the name was erased into them; nonetheless, it is not recognizable, and her offering is scattered on the ashes. But if she says, "I will not drink," we do not take her into consideration, and we force her against her will and give her to drink.

And the reason for this matter is that by her saying "I will not drink," it is not a complete admission of impurity, but rather from an estimation we say that presumably she has become impure, and therefore she says "I will not drink." Therefore, when the holy name has been erased, we do not rely on estimation until she explicitly says that she has become impure. And as long as she has not explicitly said so, we maintain that she should drink. Also, we intimidate her, and the priest says to her: "My daughter, if it is clear to you that you are pure, do not be afraid at all and drink the water, stand by your integrity, and do not be afraid at all, because the water is like a dry potion placed on dry flesh, that if there is a wound it penetrates and descends, but if there is no wound, it does nothing."

A sotah (a woman suspected of infidelity) is only given the bitter waters to drink during the day. Similarly, the scroll (used in the sotah ritual) is only written during the day, and the entire day is valid for this purpose. Ideally, this should be done from sunrise, but after the fact, it is valid if done after dawn (Megillah 2:2). If it was written at night, it is invalid, and similarly, if the water was given to her at night, it is also invalid, as it says, "And he shall write... and he shall cause her to drink..." and it also mentions bringing her offering, just as her offering is brought during the day, for all offerings are invalid at night, as it is written, "On the day that He commanded the children of Israel to bring...," so too, the writing and giving to drink at night are invalid. This teaching is written by the Rambam in chapter 4. However, in the Talmud (Megillah 17b), they derive from the verse "The priest shall do for her according to all this law" and it is written "According to the law which they shall teach you and according to the judgment," just as judgment is done during the day, so too the scroll of the sotah and all actions concerning the sotah (Tosafot) are done during the day. 

(It seems to me that this is why the Rambam changed the derivation from the Gemara, as it is Rava who says this in the Gemara, and the Rambam follows his own reasoning in chapter 3 of Sanhedrin, as we explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 5, Se'if 10. The Gemara did not accept the Rambam’s derivation because it wanted to derive all the laws of the sotah, and investigate this thoroughly).

In the beginning of Shekalim, it is taught that on the fifteenth of Adar, the Sanhedrin would see to communal needs, and the Tosefta and Yerushalmi explain various communal needs, including giving the bitter water to the suspected adulteresses (sotah). Thus, the Rambam writes in the beginning of chapter 4 that on the fifteenth of Adar, the court attends to communal needs and examines those who are fit to drink (the bitter water) to give them to drink, and those who are fit for the warning (of the sotah process) to expel them without a ketubah. And at all times, suspected adulteresses are given the water to drink. His intention is that the Yerushalmi does not mean that only on the fifteenth of Adar are the suspected adulteresses given the water to drink, for certainly at all times they are given to drink. Rather, the intention is to examine those who need to drink (as is evident). And that which is written "at all times" means the entire year, but only during the day. And it is also clear that they are not given to drink on Shabbat and Yom Tov, for it requires the erasure of the scroll and the offering of a sacrifice, which cannot be done on Shabbat and Yom Tov.

One does not give two Sotahs to drink at the same time, as it is stated, "And the priest shall set the woman before the LORD," implying her and not her and her companion, but her alone. (Sotah 8a) Even if two priests are involved, each with one of the women, it is also forbidden to do it together (ibid.). Even if they are not drinking at the same time but are both standing in the courtyard together to be given to drink, it is forbidden. The reason given in the Gemara is that one does not perform commandments in bundles (Rashi there implies that with one priest, the reason is because of bundles, and thus with two priests it is due to the verse. This requires further study, for the verse speaks of one priest).

One must write the verses in the Megillah in the order we have mentioned, and if they were written out of sequence, it is invalid (17b). For it is written "these curses" (indicating) that they should be in the order they are written in the text. Similarly, if it was written before the oath was administered, it is invalid, as it is written "and he shall administer the oath and write" (ibid). If it was written as a letter without ruled lines, it is invalid, as it is written "in a book." Likewise, if it was written on two columns, it is invalid, as it is written "in a book" — the Torah states one book, not two or three books (18a). Rashi explains this as referring to the columns of a Sefer Torah which are made in separate columns. Tosafot explains that it specifically refers to when it is cut into two pieces. This also appears to be the opinion of the poskim regarding a get (bill of divorce) that as long as it is one piece, we are not concerned with two columns. Rambam, however, seems to rule stringently. We have already explained that it must specifically be parchment and ink that can be erased, and if not, it is invalid. There should be no trace of writing left at all. Furthermore, it must specifically be written by a priest, and if it was written by an Israelite or a minor priest, it is invalid, as it is written "and the priest shall write," implying that it must be an adult who is eligible for service.

One must write the entire text and then erase the entire text. However, if one wrote one letter or one word and then erased it, and then continued to write and erase until the end, it is invalid. Similarly, if the text was written without the proper intention or erased without the proper intention, it is invalid. If one wrote two scrolls for two different sotahs and erased them into one cup or into two cups and then mixed them into one cup and gave it to both of them to drink, it is invalid because neither one drank her own scroll. But if they were erased into two cups, mixed, and then separated back into two cups, Rambam writes that one should not give it to them to drink, but if it was given, it is valid. I am perplexed because in the Gemara it remains unresolved (teiku), and the uncertainty is due to the concept of selection (bererah). We hold that there is no selection (ein bererah), and perhaps this is because it is not a complete selection, as mentioned in Tosafot. If the water spilled after erasing, one writes another scroll and brings new water. If the water spilled but some remained, one should not give it to drink, but if it was given, it is valid. (In the Gemara, there is a question regarding giving to drink using a sponge or using a tube, and it remains unresolved (teiku). I do not know why Rambam omitted these cases. According to his opinion on the previous laws that in any unresolved case (teiku) it is valid after the fact (b'diavad), it would also be valid in the cases of the sponge and the tube after the fact).

Rambam wrote: "Our water for the Sotah is disqualified by being left overnight." Certainly, this is correct, for it has been sanctified in a sacred vessel, and anything sanctified in a sacred vessel is disqualified by being left overnight, as it is taught at the beginning of the second chapter of Me'ilah. However, in the Jerusalem Talmud, there is a dispute regarding this. There is an opinion that since it is not offered on the altar, it is not disqualified by being left overnight (and examine more there). It seems to me that regarding being taken out [of the Temple precincts], everyone agrees it is not disqualified, for we do not find disqualification by being taken out for something that is not offered on the altar. If the water becomes impure, there is uncertainty whether other water is needed or not.

It has already been explained that the priest needs to place the dust into the water, as it is written in the scripture. If he placed the dust into the vessel first and then the water, it is invalid (Talmud Sotah 16b). It has also been explained that if there was no dust on the ground of the Temple, he should bring dust and place it there, but he should not dig with tools to take the dust. If he did so, it is valid. He should not place ash instead of dust, and even though regarding the covering of the blood, ash is considered as dust (Chullin 88a) as it is written in Yoreh De'ah, Section 28, here, since it is written "from the ground of the Tabernacle," we require specifically dust (Sotah 16b). The decayed matter of vegetation is considered like dust because it comes from the dust (ibid.).

Even though it was explained that the drinking of the water comes before the offering of the sacrifice, nevertheless, if he offered [the sacrifice] and then gave her to drink, it is valid. Thus ruled the Rambam, and so it is in the Yerushalmi at the beginning of the third chapter. In our Talmud, this matter is not explicitly stated. From Rashi's commentary (19b, s.v. h.g.) it appears that it is not valid. However, the Tosafot there also wrote like the Rambam, and the reason is that in the verse it is written "and he shall make her drink" even after the offering. Therefore, although the primary [interpretation] follows the previous verses that indicate drinking before the offering, nevertheless, after the fact, it is valid. This is the intent of the verse.

Rambam wrote: If her meal-offering became impure before it was placed in a service vessel, it is to be redeemed like all meal-offerings that became impure before being sanctified in a service vessel, and she should bring another meal-offering. If the meal-offering became impure after it was placed in a service vessel, it is to be burned. Similarly, if she declared "I am impure" before the meal-offering was scooped, or she said "I will not drink" or her husband does not want to make her drink, or witnesses of her impurity came, or he died, or she died, the entire meal-offering is burned. If any of these happened after the scooping, the remnants are not eaten. This is the end of his words.

In the Tosefta, Chapter 2, it is taught that the remnants are eaten, and a reason is given that since it was brought on a doubt, it atoned for the doubt and it is now resolved. Refer there. Similarly, it is taught in Chapter 6 of Karetot regarding a dependent guilt-offering, that if it became known after the blood was sprinkled, the meat is eaten, and Rambam himself ruled this way in Chapter 4 of the Laws of Misappropriations. Refer there. Nevertheless, he did not rule this way here because there is a dispute in the Jerusalem Talmud in Chapter 2, and he ruled stringently. One can differentiate between this and the dependent guilt-offering because the sprinkling completely finalizes the sacrificial act, but in the case of a Sotah, the main purpose is to make peace between them and clarify whether she is impure or pure. Therefore, if one of them dies or witnesses come, the main purpose is completely nullified, and it is like a dependent guilt-offering when it becomes known before the sprinkling, in which case the meat is burned, as stated there. Nevertheless, further examination is needed, as this Tosefta is also brought in the Gemara in the first chapter (4b).

It is well-known that the meal offering of a Kohen is entirely burnt as it is written, "Every meal offering of a Kohen shall be wholly burnt; it shall not be eaten" (Leviticus 6:16). There is neither a handful taken nor any remnants. The meal offering of the wife of a Kohen is not like that of an ordinary Israelite, where a handful is taken and the rest is eaten (Mishnah Sotah 23a). Therefore, if the sotah (suspected adulteress) is the wife of a Kohen and her offering is considered as his offering as well, since he brings it as stated, the Sages said (ibid.) that it cannot be offered entirely because she has a share in it, nor can a handful be burnt and the remainder eaten because he has a share in it. Thus, the Sages commanded to take a handful from the meal offering and burn only the handful, while the remainder is neither eaten nor burnt but scattered on the ash heap in the Temple courtyard. The remnants are treated as invalid offerings, and although invalid offerings are usually burnt, this is only when they were initially fit and then became invalid. However, these remnants were never fit from the beginning, so they are scattered and lost as they were destined for loss from the start.

If a man warns his wife in the presence of many people and she secludes herself with each of them, he brings one offering for all of them when he makes her drink, as it is stated, "It is a meal offering of jealousy" (Numbers 5:15)—one offering for many acts of jealousy (Keritot 9a). All the more so, one drinking is sufficient for all of them, since even in one drinking he can stipulate for others, as it is written. The Rambam wrote, "If witnesses are found to be false, her offering is taken out to be non-sacred," end quote. This means that witnesses came and refuted the witnesses of the seclusion, so there is neither sanctity of the mouth nor sanctity of the vessel, and there is no misuse of it, for it was an error (Rashi 6a, s.v. "her offering"). We do not worry that people will say it is being taken out from a sacred vessel to non-sacred, because false witnesses have a public voice, and everyone knows it was an error (Gemara ibid). This is only before the handful is taken, but after the handful is taken, it is burned (Tosafot ibid), because once a complete service has been performed with it, it is a disgrace to holy things to take it out to non-sacred, and therefore it is burned by rabbinic decree. The Rambam was silent on this. Know that it is a simple matter that the scroll of the Sotah must be written on parchment from a pure animal, and so it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (Sotah 2:4).

The Rambam writes in Chapter 4 of the Laws of Sotah that it is a commandment of the sages upon the Jewish people for a man to be zealous on behalf of his wife, as it says, "And he was zealous on behalf of his wife." Anyone who is zealous on behalf of his wife is imbued with a spirit of purity. However, he should not be zealous out of frivolity, nor out of jest, nor out of levity, nor out of quarrel, nor to instill fear in her. If he did become zealous before witnesses out of any of these reasons, it is considered a valid act of zeal. This is the end of his words.

And we have already written at the beginning of this chapter that his intention is when he sees in her some inappropriate behavior. And what he wrote, that if he became zealous out of any of these reasons, it is still considered valid, has been questioned because the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of Sotah implies that his act of zeal is not valid. However, his words are clear because the Jerusalem Talmud holds that it is a mitzvah to be zealous and does not bring a dispute on this matter. But in our Talmud, there is a dispute on this matter, as we wrote at the beginning of the chapter, and we have explained that there is no contradiction at all. If she is innocent, it is certainly forbidden to be zealous, but if she is licentious, it is a mitzvah to be zealous. Both approaches are explained in the Torah, as we wrote there, and the Torah explains that the zealous act is effective. According to our Talmud, even the simple reading of the first Mishnah implies that it is forbidden to be zealous, as explained in the Gemara at the beginning of our tractate. This is obvious when she is innocent, as we wrote. Nevertheless, his act of zeal is valid, and therefore the Rambam ruled accordingly. (The Kesef Mishneh and many commentators of the Jerusalem Talmud have struggled with this, but according to what we have written, it is straightforward and simple.)

Another proof that the Rambam is discussing a case where she is somewhat immodest is from what he writes afterwards: "It is not proper to immediately jump and be jealous in front of witnesses, but rather [he should speak] with her privately, gently, and in a manner of purity and caution in order to guide her on the correct path and remove the stumbling block." This clearly shows that he is discussing a case where she is not following the correct path. Similarly, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch write at the end of this section, concluding with their words: "Anyone who is not particular about his wife, children, and household members, and does not admonish them and constantly supervise their ways to ensure they are free from any sin or transgression, is considered a sinner, as it is stated: 'And you shall know that your tent is at peace, and you shall inspect your habitation and not sin.'" 

With the help of Heaven, we have completed the section on Sotah and the entire Even HaEzer.
